Advancing full and rigorous self-governance of the Party in depth with the spirit of self-reform 以自我革命精神把全面从严治党向纵深推进 Yang Jinwei Writing in Guangming Daily in July 2022, Yang Jinwei takes up how the Communist Party of China should sustain its vitality as it pursues the second centenary goal. The commentary argues that full and rigorous self-governance of the Party is the Party's great practice of self-reform in the new era. In Yang's account, it must be pushed further in depth through a firm spirit of self-reform. The piece is organised in three parts. The first presents self-governance as the practice of self-reform since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The second claims it has opened a new realm of self-reform for a century-old Party. The third sets out how to advance it in depth. Yang draws throughout on statements by Xi Jinping and on the 2021 Party resolution on its century of struggle. Yang treats the willingness to carry out self-reform as the Party's most distinctive trait and greatest strength. The article cites a historical sequence from the 1927 Emergency Meeting, the Gutian and Zunyi meetings and the Yan'an rectification to the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978). In this reading, repeated corrections let the Party turn crises around. Since 2012, Yang says, the Central Committee has confronted the "four tests", the "four dangers" and the "four impurities", starting with the eight-point regulations. Yang credits it with a decisive victory in the anti-corruption struggle and a stronger oversight system, and reads this as the "second answer" to the historical cycle of rise and fall. Yang also stresses that the Party has no special interests of its own and represents the fundamental interests of the people. Yang calls for upholding the Party's overall leadership and for treating loyalty to the Central Committee as the first task of political building. Party members are to grasp the Two Establishes, strengthen the four consciousnesses and carry out the Two Upholds. Yang further proposes keeping strictness as the long-term keynote, with thought, oversight, discipline, cadre management, conduct and anti-corruption work all kept strict, and pursuing the aim that officials dare not, cannot and do not want to be corrupt. Read the original if you want a compact example of how the Party's official press framed self-reform and Party discipline in mid-2022.

The people are the Party's greatest source of confidence in governing and building the country 人民是党执政兴国的最大底气 Yang Limin This short commentary, published in the People's Daily in July 2022, takes up the principle of 'putting the people first', one of the ten historical lessons in the Resolution on the Party's major achievements and historical experience adopted by the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021). Yang argues that the people are the Party's root, lifeblood and strength, and hence its greatest source of confidence in governing and building the country. The piece moves from the Party's founding mission to its history and then to the role of the people in making history. It draws on Xi Jinping's statements and on the Communist Manifesto, and it surveys the Party's record from its founding through the founding of the People's Republic and reform and opening up to the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Yang contends that the people's standpoint is the Party's fundamental political position and what distinguishes a Marxist party from others. Quoting the Manifesto's contrast between minority movements and the proletarian movement of the immense majority, Yang says the Party has escaped the pursuit of narrow interests and set itself the original aspiration and mission of securing the people's wellbeing and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Yang names close ties with the masses as the Party's greatest political strength and estrangement from them as its greatest danger once in power. The mass line is described as the Party's lifeline. Yang cites the achievement of a moderately prosperous society for over 1.4 billion people and the development of whole-process people's democracy as evidence. Yang concludes that on the new journey the Party will keep to the people's standpoint, respect their initiative and draw on their creativity to achieve new accomplishments. Yang presents this as following from the historical-materialist view that the people drive history. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Party commentary presents the people-centred principle in the 2021 historical resolution.

The theoretical positioning of Engels's critique of religion 恩格斯宗教批判思想的理论定位 Wang Beite Chen Tianjia How should Engels's critique of religion be located within the history of Marxism? Wang Beite and Chen Tianjia, writing in Science and Atheism (2022), argue that it should be read as a single organic whole grounded in historical materialism, running from his first critique of religion in 1839 to his work on early Christianity in 1894. The authors begin by noting two research routes: studying Engels together with Marx as part of Marxist atheism, which they say obscures each thinker's own development, or studying Engels separately, which rarely treats his view of religion as a system. They also review two disputes: whether the late Engels softened towards early Christianity, and how his thinking should be divided into periods, with proposals ranging from two to four stages. The article answers on three points: the starting date, the logical continuity of his thought, and the function of atheism. On the starting point, the authors reject 1845, the date usually given for historical materialism, and choose 1839, when the still-religious Engels published Letters from the Wuppertal. They read it as exposing the social harm of Pietism and linking religion to capitalist exploitation of workers, and so as already containing two elements of the communist movement: the aim of material and spiritual emancipation and the working class as its agent. On continuity, they argue that fine periodisation would split Engels's thought and set 'young' against 'old'. They hold that he was always a firm critic of religion, that his critique developed in step with historical materialism, and that it was always tied to the workers' movement. In this account his late, milder remarks on Christianity were a tactical stance, not a defence of it, and his opposition to Dühring's call to ban religion followed from the view that religion will persist while the producers remain enslaved to the means of production. On atheism, the authors read Engels's remark that atheism is itself 'a religion' as a statement that it is the negation of theism and shares its category as a worldview, not as a concession to religion. They argue that atheism is a long-term practical struggle and a bridge to communism, to be advanced through a secular state, not coercion, and that it also guards against idealism, pseudo-science and mysticism. They add that this has value for ideological work in China in the primary stage of socialism. Read the original if you want a Chinese-language argument for treating Engels's religious critique as continuous from 1839 to 1894, or want to follow the debates on his periodisation and his view of Christianity.

The Communist Party of China's persistent self-reform: historical course and lessons 中国共产党坚持自我革命的历史进程及经验启示 Duan Yan Taking its cue from the 2021 Party resolution on the Party's major achievements and historical experience over the past century, which lists "adhering to self-reform" among the Party's valuable experiences, Duan Yan examines how the Communist Party of China has practised the Party's self-reform since its founding. The article argues that courage to uphold truth and correct errors, self-criticism, purging its own ranks and building institutions have together made self-reform the Party's most distinctive political quality and advantage. The article is a chronological survey in four periods: the New Democratic Revolution, socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the new era of socialism with Chinese characteristics. A final section draws four lessons for the present. Duan cites Party resolutions, campaigns and meetings as evidence, from the August 7 Meeting and the Zunyi Meeting to the 1981 historical resolution and the Party's regulations since the 18th Party Congress (2012). For the revolutionary years, Duan stresses struggle against Right and "Left" deviations, the Gutian Conference, the Yan'an rectification movement and the establishment of Party schools. After 1949 the focus is on rectification campaigns, the "Three-Antis" movement and criticism and self-criticism, including Mao Zedong's self-criticism at the 1962 enlarged work conference. In the reform era Duan highlights the restoration of discipline inspection bodies, anti-corruption work under Jiang Zemin and Hu Jintao, and the 1978 truth-criterion debate. Since 2012, Duan points to new forms of Party-wide education campaigns and a growing body of Party regulations, together with a "zero tolerance" approach to enforcement. Duan draws four lessons: put the people first and accept their supervision; strengthen ideals and convictions through Marxist theoretical education, including Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era; push anti-corruption work deeper, building mechanisms so that officials do not dare, are unable and do not want to be corrupt; and rely on institutions and Party regulations to make self-reform lasting. In Duan's view, this path of using self-reform to drive social revolution will sustain full and rigorous self-governance of the Party on the road to the second centenary goal. Read the original if you want a chronological, officially aligned account of how Party historiography presents self-reform from the 1920s to the 2020s.

The three dimensions of contemporary Western left-wing scholars' critique of capitalist modernity 当代西方左翼学者资本主义现代性批判的三重维度 Han Qiuhong Han Qiuhong asks how contemporary Western left-wing scholars have carried the critique of capitalist modernity into the digital age and the Covid-19 pandemic, and whether their answers are scientifically sound. The article argues that these scholars offer new accounts of alienation, of the revolutionary subject and of the path to emancipation. In Han's assessment, however, they compromise on the proletariat's historical identity and on the road beyond capitalism, and they do not hold to Marxism's basic standpoint, principles and method. A theory that is not thoroughgoing, the article concludes, cannot become a material force that grips the masses. The article is organised in three parts: "new alienation", the "new subject" and the "new path". It draws on Hartmut Rosa, Slavoj Žižek, Jacques Rancière, Antonio Negri, Alain Badiou, David Harvey, Noam Chomsky, Giorgio Agamben, Judith Butler and others, with Marx's theory of alienated labour and fetishism as the stated starting point. Han uses the pandemic and the ecological crisis as the main test case throughout. On alienation, Han reports that these scholars see acceleration, digital technology and surveillance-based control making alienation universal, hidden and legitimated, so that it is no longer confined to one class. Han's criticism is that their critique targets cultural values rather than analysing the contradictions of capitalist relations of production. On the subject, the scholars define a "new proletariat" as radical, made up of the politically excluded (the poor, refugees, migrants), and bound by a shared community consciousness. Han argues that this rests on political and cultural difference and drifts into metaphysics, antinomy or utopianism, with little practical effect. On the path, they attack neoliberalism and call for a "new communism", but Han finds that they cannot say how value differences are reconciled, how solidarity endures or how a new order gains legitimacy. Han concludes that "new communism" differs fundamentally from scientific socialism. Its community is, in Han's reading, an interest-based grouping rather than the "association of free individuals" and only a reactive utopia in the face of crisis. The article attributes this to the scholars' wavering commitment to communism and to their treatment of Marxism as an object of study rather than as a guide to social change. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist assessment of Rosa, Žižek, Negri and other Western left thinkers on alienation, the subject and communism in the pandemic.

Correctly distinguishing socialism with Chinese characteristics in the CPC's century of history A rebuttal of several "equation theories" about socialism with Chinese characteristics 正确辨析中国共产党百年史上的中国特色社会主义 Wang Gang Wang Gang takes up a set of claims, at home and abroad, that socialism with Chinese characteristics has fundamentally 'changed colour' and is really something else. The article calls these 'equation theories' and argues that they stem from ideological bias, neoliberalism and historical nihilism. Its thesis is that socialism with Chinese characteristics equals none of the four things it is said to be, and that it is, first of all, socialism. The article is organised in four sections, each rebutting one alleged equation: with capitalism with Chinese characteristics, with state capitalism, with democratic socialism, and with Confucian socialism. It draws on Marx, Engels, Lenin, Stalin, Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping. It also traces the history of the concepts involved, including state capitalism in Soviet Russia and early People's Republic China, and the shift in names from social democracy to democratic socialism and back. On capitalism, Wang argues that equating planned economy with socialism and market economy with capitalism originated with Stalin and was later absorbed in China. After the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978), Deng treated plan and market as instruments rather than system categories. Wang adds that public ownership remains dominant and the state economy holds key sectors. On state capitalism, Wang follows Lenin's distinction: under proletarian power it is a restricted, instrumental form serving the transition to socialism, so Western use of the label confuses appearance with essence. On democratic socialism, Wang finds three basic differences from socialism with Chinese characteristics: guiding ideology (pluralism versus Marxism), the view of democracy (rejecting versus upholding the people's democratic dictatorship), and ownership (private ownership tolerated versus public ownership). On Confucian socialism, Wang holds that Marxism spread in China because it was scientific truth and met practical need, not because of Confucianism. Traditional terms such as 'moderately prosperous society' have been given new meanings, and the Party's promotion of traditional culture is selective, not a restoration of Confucianism. Wang concludes that socialism with Chinese characteristics upholds the basic principles of scientific socialism while giving them Chinese features. In this reading, the 'Chinese characteristics' must not erase the socialist character, and the 'equation theories' ultimately aim to remove the leadership of the Communist Party. Wang also warns against overstating its universality, since it is neither a template from the classics nor a copy of other countries' practice. Read the original if you want a detailed Party-theory rebuttal of the claims that China is state-capitalist, social-democratic or Confucian-socialist, with its use of Lenin and Deng.

The social-critique stage as the fifth stage of Marx and Engels's view of religion 社会批判阶段是马克思恩格斯宗教观的第五个阶段 Zhu Fengkai Peng Wuqing Zhu Fengkai and Peng Wuqing take up the periodisation of Marx and Engels's view of religion. Chinese scholarship commonly divides it into four stages: religious critique, political critique, economic critique and cultural critique. The authors argue that the literature stops too early and that a fifth stage, "social critique", follows in the late works of both thinkers. The article was published in Science and Atheism in 2022. The article first reviews the four-stage scheme, which it traces to Chen Rongfu's 2009 article. It notes that other scholars (Lü Daji, Niu Sulin, Zeng Chuanhui) use different labels for essentially the same early stages. Second, it defines the fifth stage and argues that it was bound to arise. Third, it compares research methods across the stages. Finally, it assesses the significance of the new stage. The main sources are Engels's late letters to Conrad Schmidt, Franz Mehring and Joseph Bloch, and Marx's Capital, Volumes I and III. The authors define the social-critique view of religion as one based on historical materialism. It examines real historical social formations as a whole and explains religion from them, while recognising religion's reaction on those formations. They draw three points from Engels's letters: the "resultant" of many social forces, the need to study the conditions of existence of each social formation, and the reciprocal action of ideology. They read Engels's 1890 letter to Schmidt as reversing the earlier direction of analysis, from social existence to religion. In Capital, Volume III, they find Marx deriving the fetish form of capital from real-life relations, which they take to show a conscious shift beyond the economic approach of Volume I. On method, the authors describe a progression from the conceptual induction of the first two stages, through economic analysis, to a comprehensive social analysis. They call this a spiral ascent and a "second leap" from cognition to practice. They argue that this stage gives a theoretical basis for questions such as freedom of religious belief, the Party's stance on scientific atheist education, and the relation between religious work and united front work. It also reflects the open, non-dogmatic character of Marxism, with the aim of overcoming religious self-alienation and achieving human emancipation. Read the original if you work on Chinese debates about Marxist theories of religion and want to see how a fifth stage is argued from Engels's late letters and Capital, Volume III.

On education in patriotism, collectivism and socialism and in the "four histories" among religious circles A commentary on Xi Jinping's instruction at the 2021 National Religious Work Conference 浅谈“在宗教界开展爱国主义、集体主义、社会主义教育，有针对性地加强党史、新中国史、改革开放史、社会主义发展史教育” Zhang Xinying This commentary, published in the journal Science and Atheism in 2022, interprets a directive Xi Jinping gave at the National Religious Work Conference on 3 December 2021. The directive called for education in patriotism, collectivism and socialism among religious circles, and for stronger and better-targeted education in the history of the Party, of New China, of reform and opening up, and of socialist development (the "four histories"). Zhang argues that this is a top-level strategic design for guiding religion to adapt to socialist society, and that religious figures are duty-bound to carry it out. The article has six numbered sections. They cover the significance of the directive and the standards the Party sets for religious representatives; the relationship between the "two educations"; the historical resources religious circles can draw on; the need to stress the "two establishes" and the achievements since the 18th Party Congress (2012); the use of the 2021 Party history resolution as a core text; and ways of making the education targeted. Zhang also lists the six points in a summary near the end. Zhang's central distinction is that the patriotism, collectivism and socialism education supplies a value compass for the Sinicization of religion, built on the core socialist values. The "four histories" education is its source of internal momentum, because it offers concrete evidence from the Party's record. Zhang holds that, in contemporary China, patriotism means unity of love for the country, the Party and socialism, and so Party history should be the focus. The article draws on a record of patriotic religious figures from the late Qing through the revolutionary, socialist and reform periods, and it says the Party's 2021 resolution should be studied together with the two educations. Zhang adds that the education should be tailored by religion, region and audience, and aimed at problems in the five religions' Sinicization plans and in religious conduct. Zhang concludes that the two educations should not be a short-term campaign. They should become a long-term, routine course in political and ideological education for religious circles. Zhang expects religious circles to use the opportunity to improve themselves and to answer the Party's expectations with new results in the Sinicization of religion and in religious affairs governance. Read the original if you want an official-line account of how Party theorists justify and plan political education for religious circles in China after 2021.

Unswervingly following the path of Chinese modernization 坚定不移走中国式现代化道路 Qin Qiang This commentary, first published in China Social Sciences Today on 26 May 2022, asks what it takes to keep to the path of Chinese modernization. Qin Qiang argues that the path must be pursued by linking the overall strategy for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation with the "great changes unseen in a century". It rests on four elements: the new development stage, the new development philosophy, the new development pattern and high-quality development. The piece follows the sections headed historical position, source of momentum, key link and essential requirement. It draws on the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021), which stated that the Party has opened a Chinese modernization path and created a new form of human civilisation. Qin reads the new development stage as the move from \"standing up\" and \"becoming prosperous\" to \"becoming strong\". The stage is also one in which the principal contradiction is between people's growing needs for a better life and unbalanced, inadequate development. The new development philosophy of innovation, coordination, green development, openness and sharing is presented as the source of momentum. Qin says it has shifted the economy from asking whether something exists to asking whether it is good. The new development pattern is called the key link. It is described as a proactive move, not a stopgap: open dual circulation, built on a unified national market, with domestic demand as the basic driver. Qin concludes that the four elements form one logical whole. The stage defines the historical position, the philosophy gives direction, the pattern sets strategic priorities, and high-quality development is the fundamental purpose. Together they are said to guide the building of a modern socialist country and a new form of human civilisation. Read the original if you want a short, official-style account of how Party discourse in 2022 linked these four concepts.

Paths for advancing the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times 推进马克思主义中国化时代化的路径选择 Jiang Zhengjun This short commentary, first published in the China Social Sciences Today in April 2022, asks how the Party should continue adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Jiang takes as a starting point Xi Jinping's remark that Marxism is why the Party and socialism with Chinese characteristics succeed. Jiang presents theoretical innovation as one of the key lessons of the Party's century of struggle, drawn up at the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021). The piece briefly traces the sequence from Mao Zedong Thought through Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents and the Scientific Outlook on Development to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. It then sets out six requirements, each framed as a four-character maxim. Jiang argues that adaptation must not abandon the Marxist "forefathers", meaning its stance, viewpoint and method. It must also draw on foreign achievements without wholesale Westernization, and read the major trends of the age. In addition, it must address China's actual conditions and practice, and draw on fine traditional Chinese culture through creative transformation. Jiang cites concepts such as a moderately prosperous society, a harmonious society and a community with a shared future for mankind as rooted in Chinese civilization. The last requirement is to distil the practical wisdom of the people, citing Deng Xiaoping on reform ideas originating with the masses. Jiang concludes that the Party should keep to emancipating the mind, seeking truth from facts and keeping pace with the times, and should answer the questions of the era and the people. The aim is to open new horizons for contemporary Marxism in China and twenty-first-century Marxism. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official 2022 account of how Marxism is to be "sinicized" and kept current.

The Chinese Communist Party's exploration of governing the Party through institutions 中国共产党制度治党的探索历程 Chi Buyun This newspaper commentary, first published in the China Social Sciences Today in May 2022, traces how the Chinese Communist Party has developed "governing the Party through institutions". Chi defines this as a system of intra-Party regulations that adjusts relations within the Party and between the Party, the state and society. The author argues that understanding of this approach deepened over more than a century of struggle, and that it has become an important support for preserving the Party's vanguard character. The article follows four periods. It begins with the New Democratic Revolution, then moves to socialist revolution and construction, the era of reform and opening up, and finally the new era since the 18th Party Congress (2012). For each period Chi cites key documents, Party congresses and statements by leaders from Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping to Jiang Zemin, Hu Jintao and Xi Jinping. In Chi's account, the early Party built rules to unite revolutionary forces: the concept of intra-Party regulations was articulated, the Party constitution was refined, and the 7th Congress (1945) systematised democratic centralism. After 1949 the Party tried to combine ideological education with discipline, and the 8th Congress (1956) advanced institutional rules, though the author concedes that broad consensus and lasting mechanisms did not form. Reform-era leaders, Chi says, raised institution-building to a central place. Since 2012 the Party has set the goal of a fairly complete system of intra-Party regulations, and the author reports more than 3,600 such regulations in force by July 2021. Chi also lists the "seven focuses" guiding further improvement, including full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. Chi concludes that ideological and organisational Party-building must be combined with institutional governance, and that political discipline should be strengthened as the foundation. The author calls institutional governance the Party's "unique code", an expression of why Marxism and socialism with Chinese characteristics work, and claims it offers a useful reference for party governance worldwide. Read the original if you want a concise official-style historical outline of how Party regulations are framed in Chinese Party-building discourse as of 2022.

The era of the classics and the classics of the era 经典的时代与时代的经典 Zhou Jiaxin Zhou Jiaxin asks how the classic works of Marx and Engels should be read today, and answers that the Two Integrations offer the method. In this commentary, published in the China Social Sciences Today in May 2022, Zhou argues that returning to the classics means returning to the era in which they were written. This shows both their power of truth and their value for the present. Zhou frames the piece with Xi Jinping's call to uphold Marxism as the guiding principle of Chinese philosophy and social science. The article is organised in three sections, each tied to a stage in the relation between the classics and their time: observing the era and discovering excellent culture; grasping the era and transforming traditional culture; leading the era and shaping cultural tradition. The material covers German classical philosophy, classical political economy and the socialist and communist currents of the nineteenth century. It also covers Marx's and Engels's turn to materialism, their relation to Hegel's dialectic, and Engels's later writings addressed to German, French and British workers. Zhou's central claim is that Marx and Engels never simply accepted an existing school. In Zhou's account, they critically absorbed the best intellectual achievements of their time and gave them new content. Materialism became dialectical and historical materialism, Hegel's dialectic was changed from a mystical to a rational form in the course of working out the theory of surplus value, and scientific communism joined a new worldview with workers' movements and advanced cultural traditions. Zhou then argues that the two thinkers also shaped cultural tradition. Engels's later works, including Ludwig Feuerbach, Anti-Dühring and his texts on the history of the German and British movements, countered vulgar materialism and petty-bourgeois socialism. They helped workers see their own intellectual lineage. Zhou concludes that the creation of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era is likewise an innovation that combines Marxism's basic principles with China's realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture. In Zhou's view it also leads the era and preserves and brings out the Chinese nation's excellent cultural achievements. The closing call is to return to the era of the classics, find their value for today and move toward the classics of the era. Read the original if you want a short, Party-theory-oriented example of how Chinese scholars use the Two Integrations to frame the reading of Marx and Engels.

Marx on the relations of private property A reading of Notebook II of Marx's Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 马克思关于私有财产关系的论述 Zhang Na Zhang Na reads Notebook II of Marx's Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 to ask how Marx understood private property and what lies at the heart of the opposition between capital and labour. The article argues that, although Notebook II survives only as a fragment, it conveys Marx's central views on private property and is valuable for understanding the critique of political economy and capitalist relations of production. Its thesis is that the opposition of capital and labour is at root an opposition between abstract and concrete labour, which produces alienated labour. The piece first sets out three aspects of private property in the notebook: the normal relation, in which capital controls the worker's existence; the fixed moment, the struggle between landowner and capitalist; and the necessary process, the three stages of the relation between capital and labour. It then asks what the opposition of capital and labour consists in. Finally it considers how that opposition might be sublated, and where this attempt stops. Zhang's reading of the third aspect is that capital and labour move from identity, through simple opposition, to an inner opposition. The author links these stages to the emergence, early period and maturity of capitalism, and sees in them Marx's inheritance of Hegelian dialectic. In the mature stage the opposition is hidden inside each side, so that a worker becoming a capitalist is presented as personal fulfilment. Zhang then reasons that capital, as accumulated labour, takes the general form of abstract labour because it can buy any concrete labour at any time. Capital thus confronts concrete labour and gains command over the worker, the product and labour itself. Zhang runs this through the four determinations of alienated labour. For sublation, Zhang proposes that abstract labour be reunited with concrete labour, with workers taking part in creating and sharing the value of capital. The author describes this as easing the four alienations: products no longer simply confront the worker, labour is partly voluntary, it partly regains its character as an essential human need, and relations with others become less purely those of domination. Zhang adds that this is only a historically specific attempt, comparable to Marx's account of distribution according to labour. Sublating private property is completed only in a communist social form, where people fully appropriate their labour and its relations of production. Read the original if you want a short Chinese commentary that reads Notebook II through the abstract and concrete labour distinction and draws a contemporary conclusion about worker participation in value sharing.)

Correctly understanding and grasping the characteristics and behavioural laws of capital 正确认识并把握资本特性和行为规律 Zhang Kai Wang Shengxiao Published in China Social Sciences Today in May 2022, this short commentary responds to Xi Jinping's April 2022 call, at a Politburo study session, to strengthen research on capital theory under new conditions. It also responds to the December 2021 Central Economic Work Conference's call to grasp capital's characteristics and behavioural laws. Zhang and Wang argue that the dual nature of capital is the theoretical basis for doing so, and that practice now requires a theory of capital governance. The authors start from Marx's dual character of labour and carry it over to capital. They then describe the structure of capital in the primary stage of socialism and set out three practical requirements of governance. The text ends with a short address to leading cadres. Zhang and Wang hold that capital is both a process of producing use-values, which reflects the productive forces, and a process of producing surplus value, which reflects the relations of production. They argue that this duality yields both capital's positive role as a factor of production and its negative effects. In their account, state-owned, collective and non-public capital are transformed forms of this contradiction, and the public forms decide the direction of the capital structure. On governance, they name three requirements: Party leadership over economic work, the Two Unwaverings, and a new type of government–business relationship. They say the last is needed to curb the pull of non-public capital away from the real economy and its tendency towards monopoly, including data monopoly by internet platforms. The authors conclude that cadres must master the dual nature of capital and use the "invisible hand" and the "visible hand" correctly. They present this as part of the political economy of Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how Chinese economists in 2022 framed capital governance in Marxist terms.

Foreign scholars on the metaverse 国外学者论元宇宙 Wu Jing Deng Yulong This literature review, published in Foreign Theoretical Trends in 2022, surveys how scholars outside China have treated the metaverse. The authors define it as an artificial space running parallel to the real world and built on augmented reality, virtual reality and 3D technologies. They organise the foreign work into four clusters: the role of digital technology in building metaverse scenes, communication within it, the relation between virtual and physical worlds, and the social effects of the technologies involved. The review summarises about two dozen English-language studies from roughly 2011 to 2022, each presented in a short abstract. They are drawn from computer science, information management, communication studies, urban studies, philosophy and media studies. Examples include Dionisio, Burns and Gilbert on 3D virtual worlds, studies of Second Life communication, David Chalmers's Reality+, and critical work on Facebook's virtual reality and on the television series Black Mirror. The authors present the third cluster as the central philosophical divide. One camp, including Aas, Madary and Metzinger, and David van der Merwe (who reads the metaverse through Foucault's heterotopia), holds that virtual and physical worlds differ in kind. Janet Murray argues that virtual reality, like earlier media, does not erase the boundary between them. The other camp, represented by Chalmers, treats virtual reality as real in the ontological sense and calls it 'Reality+'. The fourth cluster, in the authors' account, argues that these technologies are not neutral. Egliston and Carter point to data appropriation, workplace evaluation and exclusion of disabled bodies. Jin Kim's reading of Black Mirror stresses algorithmic discipline and the neoliberal subject. Other studies stress benefits such as cheaper corporate communication and better team collaboration. The review does not advance a thesis of its own. It reports that foreign scholars see the metaverse as depending on technical breakthroughs, common standards and collective effort, and that they give growing attention to its hidden risks. Read the original if you want a compact guide, with full bibliographic details, to English-language scholarship on the metaverse, or if you want to see how Chinese Foreign Marxism studies present this literature.

A century of grassroots Party building by the Communist Party of China and its lessons 中国共产党基层党建的百年实践与启示 Jia Gangtao Gao Hongbo Jia Gangtao and Gao Hongbo, writing in Guangming Daily in July 2022, ask what a century of work at the grassroots of the Communist Party of China offers for Party building today. Their thesis is that attention to the grassroots has been a 'glorious tradition' of the Party and a precondition of its growth. In their account, it ensures that central decisions reach 'the last mile' and strengthens the Party's base for governing. The newspaper commentary draws on Xi Jinping's statements on grassroots organisations. The article has two parts. The first surveys grassroots Party building by period: the New Democratic Revolution under Mao Zedong, the early People's Republic and the Eighth Party Congress, the reform era under Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin and Hu Jintao, and the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The second turns to the present and sets out requirements for Party building in the new era, with examples of organisational and institutional innovation. For each period the authors link grassroots work to the Party's guiding ideas of the time. Examples are Bolshevisation and the 'great new project' of Party building, the Three Represents, the Scientific Outlook on Development, and, after 2012, the mass line campaign, the 'Three Stricts and Three Honests' and the 'Two Studies, One Doing' education drives. For today they name four requirements: arming Party members with theory, including the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds; full and rigorous self-governance of the Party; raising 'organisational strength' (zuzhili); and institution-building. They cite Party regulations for rural areas, state-owned enterprises and universities. They also cite innovations such as branches 'built on the industrial chain' or 'on the front line of epidemic prevention', 'Internet Plus Party building' and 'Party building plus grids'. The authors conclude that grassroots organisations are the Party's 'nerve endings' and the 'foundation' of its governing edifice. They hold that the Party should draw on its historical experience, innovate in methods, let Party building lead social governance, and never relax its grassroots work. They present this as a basis for building a modern socialist country. Read the original if you want a concise official-style periodisation of grassroots Party building and the main lines of its current policy priorities.

Cults and the predicament of defining new religions Two approaches: secular anti-cult organisations and the sociology of religion 膜拜团体与新宗教界定的困境 Shao Peng Shao Peng takes up the long-disputed question of how to define "cults" and "new religions", a field in which, the author says, ideology and subjective feeling readily intrude. Negative views treat such groups as the most dangerous and abnormal forms of religion, while positive views see them as building distinctive religious meaning and experience. Shao argues that these attitudes correspond to two main routes of definition, the secular anti-cult organisations and the sociology of religion. Neither is fully satisfactory, but each succeeds within its own field. The article opens with the terminological problem: alternatives such as "new religious movements", "alternative" or "marginal" religions are all judged imperfect, and every religious tradition was once "new". It then examines the International Cultic Studies Association (ICSA), formerly the American Family Foundation, founded in 1979, and the criteria for cults put forward by Margaret Singer and Michael Langone. The third section turns to William James's notion of an "unseen order" as the sociology of religion's alternative, with examples including the Unification Church, the Raelians, Scientology and Aum Shinrikyo. A short conclusion draws practical implications for China. Shao reports the main objections to ICSA's fifteen-point list of cult traits: it does not say how many traits make a cult, it does not define what is "excessive", and it cannot separate the few dangerous groups from many harmless ones. Practices such as long meditation, proselytising, fundraising and heavy time commitment also appear in mainstream traditions, and ICSA's "brainwashing" claims lack empirical support. The "unseen order" approach, by contrast, treats new religious movements as social experiments in harmonising with a different order. Shao credits it with explaining myths and rituals but finds it too broad: it neglects real dangers, blurs the line between ordinary religions and cults, and may itself be subjective in its leniency. Shao concludes that a definition satisfying all sides is unlikely, but research can proceed, and the debate itself advances it. The article notes that ICSA's methods have helped many people harmed by cults, and that the "unseen order" is an accepted tool in religious studies. For China, which Shao describes as governing cults amid complex domestic and international conditions, ICSA's operational criteria are said to help detect groups early. The "unseen order" is said to be less useful for judging a group but helpful for understanding it and for building the discourse of cult governance. Read the original if you want a critical overview of how Chinese scholarship engages Western anti-cult and sociological debates on defining cults and new religions.

The world-historical contribution of the "new form of human civilization" “人类文明新形态”的世界历史贡献 Wu Hongzheng Wu Hongzheng takes up the Party's claim, made in Xi Jinping's speech at the centenary of the Communist Party (2021) and in the Party's 2021 historical resolution, that socialism with Chinese characteristics has created a "new form of human civilization". The article asks what world-historical contribution this form makes. Its thesis is that it makes four: it develops Marx and Engels's theory of world history, it holds the commanding height in the "great changes unseen in a century", it leads the trend toward a community with a shared future for mankind, and it advances the world-historical course of scientific socialism. The article opens with a conceptual account of the new civilization form, built from five spheres (material, political, spiritual, social and ecological) and five defining attributes. It then devotes one section to each of the four contributions, drawing on Marx and Engels's writings on world history, on Hegel's philosophy of history, on Huntington's "clash of civilizations" and on Wolfgang Streeck's diagnosis of capitalism. The closing section places the concept within a periodisation of scientific socialism as "three 70-year periods" and ties it to the essential features of Chinese modernization. Wu argues that the new form is socialist and therefore different from the capitalist civilization Marx called the most "barbarous". The author holds that it rests on the creative transformation of traditional Chinese culture and is a transitional form, since it arose while two systems coexist and has not reached communist civilization. Its outlook of "exchange and mutual learning" is set against Western-centrism, "universal values" and the clash-of-civilizations thesis. Wu reads this as extending Marx and Engels, who offered no concrete theory of how to build a new civilization, by showing that socialism can create one within a single country and before capitalism disappears. In the author's account, the capitalist order is in historical difficulty and an "East rising, West declining" trend is under way, so that this form gives a basis for a community with a shared future for mankind that capitalism's zero-sum logic cannot supply. Wu concludes that the new form is not only "Chinese" but "human", adding new elements to the family of civilizations and carrying forward scientific socialism's aim of human freedom and liberation in the "third 70 years", when the author says the centre of world socialism lies in China. The article is a Party-theoretical interpretation that follows official documents closely. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist scholar links the official concept of a new form of human civilization to the Marxist theory of world history, the community with a shared future for mankind and the history of world socialism.

Understanding the great founding spirit of the Party as the "wellspring" of the Party's spirit 深入理解伟大建党精神是党的“精神之源” Qi Biao Published in Guangming Daily on the eve of the Party's 101st anniversary, this commentary takes up Xi Jinping's description of the great founding spirit of the Party as the "wellspring" of the Party's spirit. Qi Biao argues that the formulation explains both the Party's century of achievement and the source from which its other great spirits flow. The author holds that studying this source in the light of how the Party's spirit formed and developed helps to carry on the "red bloodline" and supplies spiritual momentum for building a modern socialist country and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The article has three sections. The first examines how the founding spirit took shape, the second its relation to the Party's spiritual lineage, and the third what the Party should do to preserve its roots. Qi draws on Xi's remarks at sites such as the Peking University Red Building, Fengze Garden, the venue of the First Party Congress and the South Lake in Jiaxing. The text ends with a quotation from Li Dazhao on the revival of "Young China". Qi's core argument is that the founding spirit gathers several tributaries: Marxism and its revolutionary spirit, the great national spirit built up over millennia, and the experience of modern revolutionary pioneers. It was present when the Party was founded, even though it was systematically summarised only in 2021. The author then identifies five features in how the Party's spiritual lineage is passed on: multiple bearers, from early pioneers to Party organisations and the masses; varied forms, from the Jinggangshan spirit to the anti-epidemic spirit; richer and more innovative content, as in the Soviet Area spirit or the poverty-alleviation spirit; era-specific themes in each historical period; and a highly stable "gene" of original aspiration and mission. In this account the founding spirit is the red thread running through all of them. Qi concludes that confidence in the Party's future rests on its character as a vanguard with no interests of its own, on its historical mission, and on its attention to history and tradition. The author calls for keeping up the spirit of "revolution plus desperate effort" and for not abandoning frugality, struggle and caution, and presents Party history study and the "four histories" education as means to this end. Qi presents carrying on the Party's spirit as essential both to the Party's vitality and to national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want an official-academic account of how the Party's spiritual lineage is framed in the run-up to the 20th Party Congress year.

"Opening, continuation, turn, conclusion": one way to understand the great founding spirit of the Party “起承转合”：理解伟大建党精神的一个视角 Jiang Youfu This newspaper commentary, published on the Party's anniversary in 2022, asks how the official formulation of the great founding spirit of the Party can be read as a coherent whole. Jiang Youfu argues that its eight phrases and 32 characters form four tiers that follow the classical Chinese compositional pattern of qi-cheng-zhuan-he (opening, continuation, turn, conclusion). The article takes the four tiers in turn. Each is paired with one couplet of the formulation: upholding truth and ideals; putting the original aspiration into practice and shouldering the mission; fearing no sacrifice and fighting bravely; and being loyal to the Party and true to the people. Jiang reads the first couplet as the historical and logical starting point: Marxist truth and the communist ideal are the ideological precondition of the Party, and truth and ideal are two sides of one thing. The second couplet makes them concrete as the original aspiration and mission, which the author describes as seeking happiness for the Chinese people and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, realised through successive historical paths. The third extends this into courage in struggle, which Jiang says matters in the new era because upholding socialism with Chinese characteristics is a hard social revolution. The fourth gathers the rest: loyalty to the Party, which the author ties to upholding the Central Committee's centralised leadership, is presented as consistent with the Party's people-centred stance. Jiang concludes that this structure shows the founding spirit to be the source of the Party's spirit and foundational to its century of struggle. The author adds that it also serves as a practical guide for building a modern socialist country and achieving national rejuvenation, and calls for full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. Read the original if you want a short example of how official Party-history discourse explains the logic of the founding spirit.

On the contemporary construction of the correct view of Party history 论正确党史观的当代建构 Xu Chengfang Writing in 2022, on the eve of the 20th Party Congress, Xu Chengfang asks why and how a "correct view of Party history" should be built. The term was first put forward by Xi Jinping in February 2021 and repeated in the explanation of the third historical resolution that November. Xu argues that building this view is a continuing process with three linked parts: a theoretical core, a political subject and a social foundation. It is needed to counter historical nihilism and to anchor socialist ideology. The article opens with the necessity and significance of the project. It cites four reasons: opposing historical nihilism, giving the ideology a base, strengthening historical consciousness and confidence, and the project's domestic and international significance. Three sections then follow. The first sets out the content of the view, the second the groups who must hold it (leading cadres, all Party members and the people), and the third the social supports: the internet, exhibition venues and theme parks, organisational systems and the economic base. Xu's central claim is that the view's theoretical core rests on Marxist philosophy, above all historical materialism, and takes its authoritative form in the three historical resolutions (1945, 1981, 2021). The third resolution is described as having five components. These are an affirmative overall judgement, the theoretical leaps of Marxism's adaptation to Chinese conditions, a summary of the four great achievements, and ten lessons. It also includes the evaluation of past errors, such as the Cultural Revolution, and a forward-looking section, with the Two Establishes as a highlight. Xu draws on Mao's critique of Dean Acheson's idealist history and on the Soviet case. In Xu's reading, the Soviet Party's split over its history, after the distortions of the Short Course, contributed to its collapse. Xu concludes that the correct view of Party history assesses the past, confirms the present and opens the future. It lays a political and ideological basis for the 20th Party Congress and reflects the Party's maturity. The author calls for lasting study of Party history among senior cadres, "cultivation" of the view in all members, and its popularisation through new media and the economy. Read the original if you want a detailed account of how Party theorists in 2022 framed the third historical resolution and the fight against historical nihilism as a programme of ideological construction.

On the new journey we must uphold the Party's overall leadership 新征程上必须坚持党的全面领导 Wang Konglong This newspaper commentary, published in Economic Daily on 30 June 2022 shortly before the 20th Party Congress, argues that the Party's overall leadership must be upheld on the new journey towards national rejuvenation. Wang's thesis is that this leadership is the decisive factor behind China's historical achievements and institutional strengths. The piece has four sections. It reviews a century of Party struggle, presents Party leadership as the key to the advantages of China's system, explains why the authority of the Party Central Committee and its centralized, unified leadership must be defended, and ends on the Two Upholds. Wang contends that since the Opium War the goal of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation has organised all Party struggle, and that without the Party there would be no new China. Party leadership is called the greatest advantage of socialism with Chinese characteristics, and the condition for the other advantages, including the basic economic system, the Two Unwaverings and common prosperity. The Central Committee is likened to the commanding piece in a game of chess, and obedience to it is to be unconditional. Wang adds that this authority is concrete, and starts with upholding Xi Jinping's core position. Wang concludes that the Two Establishes were the choice of history, the times and the people. Cadres should strengthen the Four Consciousnesses, hold to the Four-sphere Confidence and practise the Two Upholds. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated scholars framed the case for centralized leadership just before the 20th Party Congress.

Research on the Party's governing discourse and the construction of philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics 党的执政话语研究与中国特色哲学社会科学建构 Qi Weiping Writing in Guangming Daily in June 2022, Qi Weiping argues that studying the Communist Party of China's governing discourse (zhizheng huayu) is an important task in building philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics. Qi presents it as a duty of Chinese scholars to condense the Party's governing narrative into Chinese concepts and to "tell the story" of the Party's rule well. The piece takes its cue from Xi Jinping's speech at the centenary of the Party's founding and his call to build Chinese discourse and narrative systems. The article is organised in four parts. It first calls for greater theoretical rigour in research on governing discourse, then examines how that discourse was formed, from the revolutionary period to the present. It then lists a series of innovations in governing discourse since the 18th Party Congress (2012), and ends with the need to strengthen the discourse's communication at home and abroad. Qi's central claim is that governing discourse is both a political and a cultural phenomenon, resting on identifiable concepts, categories and logic, and should be studied with linguistics, political science, communication studies and organisational behaviour. In Qi's account, it took shape from the local governing experience of the Jiangxi-based Soviet regime and the Shaan-Gan-Ning Border Region, through the People's Republic's "serve the people" formulations, to new expressions under Xi. Qi identifies six areas of new-era innovation: upholding Party leadership, the original aspiration and mission, preserving the Party's vanguard character and purity, modernization of the system and capacity of national governance, goals of national development such as the Chinese Dream and Chinese modernization, and full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. Qi concludes that scholars must also raise the communicative power of this discourse, since discourse gains vitality only through effective dissemination. Qi calls for research on communication mechanisms, media platforms, responsible actors, innovation in methods and platforms for international communication, linking this to the claim that China's economic growth and long-term stability demonstrate the effectiveness of Party rule. Read the original if you want an example of how a Party-affiliated scholar frames governing discourse as a research field and a task for Chinese social science.

Eroding capitalism Erik Olin Wright on a new twenty-first-century strategy against capitalism 侵蚀资本主义 Duan Zhongqiao Duan Zhongqiao presents the late Erik Olin Wright, American sociologist and leading figure of Analytical Marxism, and the strategy he set out shortly before his death in 2019 in How to Be an Anti-Capitalist in the 21st Century. The article explains why Wright thinks capitalism should be opposed and what he proposes: "eroding capitalism", a strategy that combines elements of earlier approaches. Duan treats it as theoretically and practically significant, though not yet shown to be feasible. The article has three parts. It first sets out Wright's moral and class-interest grounds for opposing capitalism. It then reviews the five twentieth-century strategies Wright identifies: smashing, dismantling, taming, resisting and escaping capitalism. Finally it describes how these were embodied in four political currents and how eroding capitalism emerged from them, with Wright's own assessment of its appeal and weakness. In Duan's account, Wright argues that opposition cannot rest on class interest alone, because the middle strata have ambiguous interests and many people act on moral values. Capitalism, Wright holds, obstructs equality/fairness, democracy/freedom and community/solidarity. Wright sees the five older strategies as having failed or faded: revolution produced no assured democratic alternative, state-led dismantling was halted, and neoliberal globalisation reversed the taming of capitalism. Eroding capitalism instead treats any economy as a mix of capitalist and non-capitalist forms. It proposes building democratic, egalitarian and cooperative relations in the gaps of the system, from below and through the state, until they displace capitalist dominance, much as proto-capitalist relations eroded feudalism. Wright calls the strategy "both attractive and far-fetched": attractive because it can proceed without state sympathy, far-fetched because capitalist power would destroy any serious threat. He answers by stressing economically democratic socialism as the goal, deepening democracy, and forming politically organised collective actors. Duan credits Wright with rebutting claims that capitalism has no alternative, analysing earlier strategies even-handedly and giving fresh grounds for opposition. Duan also concedes that the strategy lacks a feasibility argument and remains largely utopian. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese-language guide to Wright's late work and a Chinese philosopher's assessment of it.

An analysis of Mariátegui's thought on adapting Marxism to Latin America 马里亚特吉马克思主义拉美化思想探析 Ling Zhehong After the October Revolution and the founding of the Soviet Union, Marxism in Latin America split between dogmatic imitation of the Soviet model and reformism. Ling asks how the Peruvian thinker José Carlos Mariátegui (1894–1930) answered the question of where Latin American Marxism should go. The article argues that he insisted on the dialectical method of Marxism and, by 'Latin Americanising' it, opened a socialist road suited to the region, which makes him the 'father of Latin American Marxism'. The article has three parts. The first places Mariátegui in the spread of Marxism in Latin America from the 1850s, the weakness of petty-bourgeois-led socialist groups, the rise of Eurocentrism and 'Latin American exceptionalism', and the reformism of Haya de la Torre's APRA. The second sets out his original contributions, drawing mainly on Seven Interpretive Essays on Peruvian Reality (1928), the journal Amauta and the founding of the Peruvian Socialist Party. The third turns to his influence, including on Cuba, and to lessons for today. Ling's central claim is that Mariátegui treated Marxism as a method rather than a set of conclusions. He analysed Peruvian history in three periods (Inca, Spanish colonial, republican) and located the roots of oppression in landholding and imperialism. On this basis he called for a socialist revolution relying on the proletariat and the Indigenous majority. Ling adds that he built consensus through cultural leadership: proletarian periodicals, education for workers, a vanguard party, and the use of Indigenous communal traditions and myth to win support for communism. Ling reads this as a dialectical unity of universality and particularity. Ling notes that Latin American communists later turned from dogmatism to nationalised Marxism, and that Mariátegui influenced Cuban revolutionaries. The author then asks why the region's left has not reached socialism, and answers with incomplete localisation, Western pressure and deviations such as Shining Path. The lessons Ling draws are that Marxism must be combined with national conditions, that localisation must keep Marxism's basic principles and the leadership of a proletarian vanguard party, that socialism must be studied in practice, and that it must struggle against capitalism. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist assessment of Mariátegui, which also uses his case to argue about democracy, Party leadership and the Western pressure on socialist countries.

China studies in Spanish-speaking countries in 2021: a review 2021年西班牙语国家的中国研究评述 Chen Lan Jin Chengwei This review, published in Foreign Theoretical Trends in 2022, surveys how scholars and commentators in Spain and Latin America wrote about China in 2021, the year of the Communist Party's centenary. Chen and Jin report that research has moved beyond traditional sinology and bilateral trade towards China's domestic and foreign policy, and towards the institutional, ideological and strategic sources of its economic success. They conclude that Spanish-language scholars are generally positive towards China's governance and path, with some exceptions. The authors draw on primary Spanish-language sources: commentaries in mainstream media, reports from Latin American and Spanish think tanks, and papers and books indexed in the Ibero-American journal network REDIB. Part one covers four hot topics: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, the Party's centenary achievements and lessons, China's pandemic response, and Sino-US relations and the international order. Part two analyses the features of this research and their causes, and a short conclusion follows. On the centenary, the review reports that scholars such as Xulio Ríos, Patricio Giusto and Raúl Ramírez attribute the Party's success to five factors: continuity combined with theoretical innovation in adapting Marxism to Chinese conditions; adaptability; a demanding system of selecting officials; high governance efficiency, for example in regulating digital monopolies; and development-oriented social cohesion. Chen and Jin note that views differ on whether China will reshape the international order, citing Eugenio Anguiano Roch's expectation of a new bipolarity against Pablo Pareja Alcaraz's caution. They explain the generally favourable tone by four factors: a crisis of democratic politics in Latin America (the authors cite a 2021 Latinobarómetro finding that only 25% of Latin Americans are satisfied with democracy), the left's long search for alternatives to the international order, resonance with Chinese policies on poverty and party–mass relations, and a core of researchers who have studied or worked in China. The authors conclude that many scholars link China's success to the Party's leadership and socialism with Chinese characteristics. They also hold that some scholars, especially Spanish researchers, remain bound by Western theories and democratic values, and so misread China. Chen and Jin call for deeper academic and people-to-people exchange and frank dialogue to correct these misunderstandings. Read the original if you want a detailed, name-by-name map of Spanish-language writing on China in 2021, as seen from a Chinese academic perspective.

The practical path for the Communist Party of China to meet risks and tests through self-reform in the new era 新时代中国共产党以自我革命应对风险考验的现实路径 Duan Yan How should the Communist Party of China deal with the risks and tests it faces in the new era? Writing in 2022, Duan Yan answers that the Party must rely on self-reform, which the article calls its most distinctive quality and greatest strength. Following Xi Jinping, Duan presents self-reform as the Party's second answer to the question of how to escape the historical cycle of rise and fall, and as the key to moving from victory to victory. The article is organised around the four long-term tests named in Xi Jinping's formulation: the test of holding power, the test of reform and opening up, the test of the market economy, and the test of the external environment. Each test is matched to a field of Party building: ideological and organisational purity, institutions and the constraint of power, leadership of the socialist market economy, and theoretical armament and innovation. Each section first describes the problems Duan sees and then sets out measures. Duan's argument has three main strands. On long-term rule, the author lists weak ideals, lax organisational life and formalism, and calls for stricter admission and exit of members, stricter organisational routines and cadres selected by political standards. On reform and opening up, Duan stresses Party regulations built around the Party Constitution, democratic centralism, criticism and self-criticism, combined internal and mass supervision, and continued anti-corruption work. On the market, the author argues that Party leadership should use, regulate and steer capital, set "traffic lights" for it, uphold the basic economic system, extend supervision to all public officials, and build a "close and clean" relationship between government and business. On the fourth test, Duan holds that the basic path is to study Marxism and its Sinicised theoretical achievements, including Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, through regular education campaigns. The author also calls for the Two Integrations, joining Marxism with China's concrete realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture. The article concludes that this self-reform keeps the Party advanced and capable amid great changes at home and abroad. Read the original if you want a systematic statement of how official Party-building discourse links self-reform to specific institutional and ideological measures.

The "Two Betters" as the Communist Party of China's solemn commitment and historical mission “两个更好”是中国共产党的庄严承诺和历史使命 Mao Zhecheng This commentary, first published in Guangming Daily in June 2022, interprets Xi Jinping's instruction, given during an inspection tour in Henan, to build the revolutionary old areas better and let their people live better lives, known as the "Two Betters". Mao argues that the instruction expresses Xi's concern for old-area residents, reflects the Party's political responsibility to carry out its founding mission, and gives a basic guide for revitalising these areas. The piece has three parts. The first recalls the old areas' role in the revolution and the Party's later poverty-relief record there. The second sets out how development should proceed in the new stage and cites local examples from Jiangxi, Xinyang and Yan'an. The third links the instruction to common prosperity. In Mao's account, the old areas were the root of the Party, the army and the People's Republic, and their people made great sacrifices. The Party has repaid this through successive poverty-alleviation models and the victory over poverty. Today, the author says, the areas must follow the new development philosophy, build on local resources, use Party building to serve the masses, and pursue high-quality development. Mao cites the end of 2020 figures of 98.99 million rural people lifted out of poverty, 832 counties removed from the poverty list and 128,000 villages. The author adds that Xi has visited old areas more than thirty times and that central policy support has been refined from "1258" to "1+N+X". Mao concludes that, with people-centred development and consolidated poverty-alleviation gains, the old areas will be built better and common prosperity will be realised. The article presents the old areas as a "special revitalisation zone" for that goal. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary ties the Party's revolutionary history, rural revitalisation and common prosperity together.

"Telling the story of the Communist Party of China well to the world" The multiple narratives of the CPC's external discourse system in the Yan'an period “向世界讲好中国共产党的故事” Wang Haijun How did the Communist Party of China (CPC) make its voice heard abroad during the Yan'an period, when the Kuomintang (KMT) imposed a tight news blockade? Wang argues that the Party built an external discourse system that conveyed a core revolutionary message of political democracy, economic self-reliance, press freedom and active resistance to Japan. In Wang's account, this let the international community form an accurate picture of the Party and its place in the War of Resistance. The author notes that existing domestic scholarship on the contest over discourse power between the two parties is thin. Drawing on archival material and combining Party history with communication studies, the article is organised in four parts: why the system was built, how, what it said, and with what effect. The causes include KMT smear propaganda, the search for foreign aid, KMT cultural controls (over 200 decrees in 1938–1945, as cited), and the Party's own emphasis on external publicity. The article ends with lessons for present-day international communication. The core of the argument is the set of narrative strategies. The Party created dedicated bodies such as the Yan'an reception office and the Southern Bureau's publicity group, and published foreign-language periodicals at home and abroad. It also invited foreign journalists, including Edgar Snow, Agnes Smedley and Israel Epstein, to speak on its behalf, and it used film, photography and radio, notably Xinhua's English-language broadcasts from 1944. It also drew on united-front allies and overseas Chinese. Wang says these channels presented the CPC as firmly Marxist, the mainstay of resistance, led by approachable and honest leaders, backed by a disciplined army, serving the people's welfare and practising democracy. Wang contends that this contrasted with the KMT's image of corruption. Wang concludes that the effort broke the KMT blockade, disillusioned Western observers about the KMT government, and raised foreign recognition of the CPC. Over a hundred foreign visitors came to Yan'an, and 25 Chinese translations of their works appeared in 1938–1946, according to the article. For today, Wang calls for an open and proactive stance, for inviting foreign media to report, and for telling China's story in a rounded way that also admits shortcomings. Read the original if you study CPC history, wartime propaganda or the roots of present-day debates on international communication, and want a source-based account of foreign journalists' role.

On the views of war and peace held by the US ruling group after the Cold War 论冷战后美国统治集团的战争与和平观 Li Shenming Yin Bin Li and Yin ask how the US ruling group has understood war and peace since 1945, and how those views have supplied a theoretical basis for successive administrations' foreign policy. Their thesis is that Washington has used war and peace as two complementary instruments for building a global order under its own leadership, aimed mainly at socialist states and the Third World. They treat Richard Nixon, the president who wrote most on the subject, as the fullest and most systematic voice of that ruling class, whose views the authors say became mainstream in the West. The article is built as a thematic survey of statements by Nixon, Truman, Eisenhower, Kennedy, Johnson, Kissinger, Dulles, McNamara, Taylor, Kennan and others. It has six sections: war as a tool of power and influence; peace as a way of tolerating conflict; nuclear weapons; combining peaceful means with firm action; "peaceful evolution" of communist states; and arms control. It follows these views from the start of the Cold War through the Soviet collapse and into the twenty-first century. The authors report that US leaders treat the Cold War as a total contest of political ideas and economic systems, and the developing world as its main battlefield, with the aim of a "world family" resembling the American system. In their account, Nixon's "genuine peace" is not the end of conflict but a means of tolerating it, inseparable from strength and deterrence. Trade and friendship are said to be dismissed as myths, and disarmament as a logical fallacy. The authors then trace shifting nuclear strategy: limited nuclear war while the US held superiority, and a view that war between superpowers was obsolete once strategic parity arrived. They give particular weight to the line, from Eisenhower onward, of using all peaceful means to induce change inside communist states. They cite Nixon's remarks that US–China relations have a limit that cannot be crossed, and that the Soviet defeat is only a first step toward freedom's worldwide victory. The article has no separate conclusion. It ends with the US view that comprehensive nuclear disarmament is an impossible dream and that nuclear weapons must stay part of American strategy under American leadership. The authors' purpose is to expose the ruling group's own stated outlook, which they describe as combining deterrence, economic and ideological means, and gradual subversion. Read the original if you want a dense compilation of US Cold War and post-Cold War strategic statements, organised by a Chinese Marxist research centre in 2022 to show how it reads American thinking on war, peace and "peaceful evolution".

The sources of strength behind the Communist Party of China's century of achievement 中国共产党铸就百年辉煌的力量源泉 Zhao Xiaohu Mao Junji Zhao Xiaohu and Mao Junji ask why the Communist Party of China was able to achieve what it did over its first hundred years. In this newspaper commentary, they answer that four forces acted together: the power of faith, of theoretical innovation, of bold practice and of self-reform. In their account, these forces kept the Party at the forefront of its age and let it advance through setbacks. The piece takes each force in turn under its own heading. It draws on Xi Jinping's 2021 speech marking the Party's centenary, on the 2021 Party resolution on its history, and on statements by Mao Zedong. It ends with a short look ahead to the Party's second centenary goal. On faith, the authors say the Party's ideals rest on Marxism, on the family-and-country sentiment of traditional Chinese culture and on the aim of national independence. They tie these to the founding spirit. On theoretical innovation, they stress a practical, seek-truth-from-facts style of thought. They also stress that each theoretical advance has been followed by Party-wide study, so that theory becomes material force. On practice, they trace a line from the revolution through construction and reform and opening up to national rejuvenation. On self-reform, they argue that the Party has no special interests of its own. They present Mao's call for popular supervision and Xi's idea of self-reform as two answers to the problem of keeping the Party from degenerating. The authors conclude that if the Party keeps and develops these four forces, it will find a successful path for building and strengthening itself under long-term rule. They write as the Party begins its "new journey" towards the second centenary goal, amid what they call changes unseen in a century. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-school scholars present the sources of the Party's success in official discourse.

The logic behind the formation of Party-building discourse 党建话语的生成逻辑 Sun Zhaohong Writing in Guangming Daily in June 2022, Sun Zhaohong takes up Xi Jinping's instruction to improve the discipline, academic and discourse systems of Party building. The commentary asks how the Communist Party of China's distinctive Party-building discourse came into being. Sun argues that it rests on three logics: historical, theoretical and practical. The piece is short and organised under three headings. It moves from the discourse's origins in the early Party and the Comintern's influence, through the Mao Zedong era, to the vocabulary of the new era since the 18th Party Congress (2012). On the historical logic, Sun argues that the discourse grows out of the Party's experience and changes with it. The slogan "branches built on companies" emerged from the lessons of the failed Autumn Harvest Uprising and is now applied online, in villages and along industrial chains. Mao's and Xi Jinping's answers to the "cave dialogue" question, popular supervision and the Party's self-reform, are said to show continuity and development together. On the theoretical logic, Sun presents the discourse as a product of the Two Integrations: Marxism combined with China's realities and with fine traditional culture. Sun cites Mao's "seeking truth from facts" and Xi's use of classical sayings to educate officials. On the practical logic, discourse arises from practice and answers the questions of the times and of the people. Sun concludes that the Party's capacity to respond to changing conditions explains its growth from a handful of members to over 95 million, and that its evolving discourse carries this capacity. Sun calls for new concepts, categories and formulations in Party building to strengthen Marxism's explanatory power. Read the original if you want a concise official-academic account of how Party-building terminology is framed and justified.

An advanced organisation that keeps close to the Party and stays at the forefront of the times Self-reform and the Communist Youth League 紧跟党走在时代前列的先进组织 Dong Yuyi Writing in 2022, Dong Yuyi, secretary of the Qinghai Provincial Committee of the Communist Youth League, takes up Xi Jinping's speech at the League's centenary.
