In it Xi said the League can keep pace with the times, youth development and practical innovation only if it dares to undertake self-reform. Dong argues that the League, as the Party's assistant and reserve force, should follow the Party's own practice of self-reform. The aim is a League that reassures the Party, satisfies young people, meets the needs of social development and stays at the forefront of the times. The commentary is organised under three headings: keeping to the correct political direction, deepening reform of the League's own work, and advancing full and rigorous self-governance of the League. It draws on the Party's hundred-year experience and on Xi's remarks on youth work. It is a programmatic essay for League cadres rather than a study of historical cases. On direction, Dong holds that the League's political positioning, original aspiration, functions and line must not change. This requires absolute Party leadership, the Two Upholds and the Two Establishes, and the path of mass organisations with Chinese characteristics. It also requires the League to keep its political character, advanced nature and mass character. On reform, Dong proposes extending services to emerging, disadvantaged and marginal youth groups, and restructuring work so that objects, content, forces and platforms become more social. Further proposals are to strengthen county-level and branch organisations, recruit talent beyond formal League and institutional boundaries, build internet-based work, and widen coverage into non-public enterprises and new social organisations. On self-governance, Dong calls for raising political standing, grasping the laws of youth growth, creating a supportive atmosphere and promoting overall planning under the Implementation Outline for Full and Rigorous Self-Governance of the League in the New Era. This would be done while learning from, but not mechanically copying, full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. League cadres are urged to be friends of youth rather than 'youth officials', to stay close to the grassroots and to be ready for great struggle. Read the original if you want a practitioner's account of how Party discourse on self-reform is translated into working guidance for the Communist Youth League.

Nine theses on twenty-first-century socialism 21世纪社会主义的九大论题 Fred Block This text is a Chinese translation, with cuts, of an article by the American sociologist Fred Block from Politics & Society (2020). Block takes up the question that Erik Olin Wright's How to Be an Anti-capitalist in the 21st Century left implicit: what a socialist society might look like. Block's answer is nine theses that he says follow Wright's theory of 'eroding capitalism'. He presents them as procedures and institutional arrangements for a more democratic, just and sustainable society, not as an ideal end of history. Block frames the theses as an attempt to reconcile pragmatic reformers with heirs of the revolutionary tradition, and as a reply to Ira Katznelson's question whether liberal socialism is possible. He calls them a designer's preliminary sketch, not a builder's blueprint. The first four set design principles that distinguish this vision from earlier Marxist conceptions. The next four describe how a more socialist economy would work, and the last takes up the global green new deal. Block says the discussion is rooted in US and Western European politics, but he hopes it can connect with transformation projects elsewhere. Block argues first that socialism would be a 'real utopia' that does not end domination, so it would need strong democratic institutions and constant vigilance. Socialism would also have plural forms of ownership (state, worker-owned, non-profit, small private, and stakeholder corporations), because a single dominant form concentrates power. Politics would combine liberal-democratic safeguards, including strict limits on money in elections, with empowered participatory governance in workplaces and communities. Equality would be Michael Walzer's 'complex equality', backed by basic income, wealth and inheritance taxes, and caps on incomes and on the ownership stakes of founders. Block describes an economy that pursues qualitative improvement and technological innovation while cutting inputs of labour, capital and raw materials. He also describes a 'habitation society' in which residents democratically decide how communities develop. Innovation would rest on public and non-profit research and shared knowledge, and finance would be tiered, competitive within each tier, and non-profit. He concludes that a global green new deal, with an inclusive and democratic broad front, is a logical and feasible route towards twenty-first-century socialism. Read the original if you want a Western left-liberal attempt to turn Wright's 'real utopias' into concrete institutional proposals, or if you want the full English text, which is available in Politics & Society.

The Communist Party of China's valuable experience in seizing the historical initiative 中国共产党把握历史主动的宝贵经验 Hou Yanshe Lü Mingyang Hou Yanshe and Lü Mingyang ask how the Communist Party of China (CPC) has managed to "seize the historical initiative" (bawo lishi zhudong), a phrase Xi Jinping used repeatedly in speeches around the Party's centenary in 2021. Writing in 2022, they treat it as an epistemological, practical and methodological question tied to the fate of the Chinese nation. Their thesis is that the Party's century of achievement rests on six interlocking sources of experience, which they present as an organic system. The article is organised in six sections, each naming one element of seizing the initiative and its role. These are following historical laws (the precondition), firm historical confidence (the foundation), respecting the historical subject, meaning the people (the driving force), strengthening historical responsibility (the focal point), grasping historical opportunities (the key), and daring to carry out self-reform (the essence). The authors draw on Marx and Engels, Xi Jinping's speeches, Deng Xiaoping, and the 2021 Party resolution on the Party's major achievements and historical experience. They illustrate the points with episodes from Party history, from the Zunyi Meeting to the post-2012 anti-corruption campaign. In the authors' account, historical materialism allows the Party to treat history as law-governed while still stressing the active choices of historical agents. Historical confidence comes from summing up successes and failures and from Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, and it is bound up with the Four-sphere Confidence. They argue that the Party seizes the initiative by relying on the masses, in line with the mass line, and by carrying the responsibilities of national rejuvenation and of a community with a shared future for mankind. Past opportunities, from the Soviet October Revolution through reform and opening up to the \"two overall situations\", were exploited by correctly reading the era. The authors present self-reform as the decisive element, an answer to the \"historical cycle\" of rise and decline, and contrast it with other parties that, they say, lacked scientific theory and represented narrow interests. Hou and Lü conclude that the six aspects form one system, grounded in the fact that the Party has no special interests of its own. They call for updating the Party's leadership methods and mass line, organising and educating the people, widening channels for popular views, and strengthening the Party's institutions of self-reform so that it does not change in character. They also stress political initiative as part of historical initiative. Read the original if you want a systematic, officially aligned account of how Party theorists frame \"historical initiative\" in terms of laws, confidence, the people, responsibility, opportunity and self-reform.

Historical lessons from a century of building the intra-Party political ecology of the Communist Party of China 中国共产党百年党内政治生态建设的历史经验 Lin Ting Writing in 2022, Lin Ting asks what the Communist Party of China's hundred years of efforts to build a healthy intra-Party political ecology can teach the Party today. Starting from Xi Jinping's statements since the 18th Party Congress (2012) that a clean political ecology is the soil of good Party conduct, Lin argues that the Party's experience yields four lasting principles and four tasks for the future. The article has three parts. The first applies historical materialism to define the political ecology as the overall environment, atmosphere and habits of Party organisations and members. It traces its changing emphasis through the new-democratic revolution, socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the new era. The second part draws out four basic lessons. The third identifies remaining problems and four directions for further work. Lin's four lessons are these. First, political development must take the lead, uniting Party spirit and the people's character, securing unity of thought, politics and action, and upholding the authority of the Central Committee. Second, ideological, theoretical, institutional and spiritual work must be combined: ideological work as the foundation, theory as the core, rule-based governance as the safeguard and the Party's spiritual lineage as the driving force. Third, organisational structure must be matched by political culture. Fourth, internal construction must be matched by outward influence, which Lin links to combining the Party's self-reform with social revolution. Lin holds that a good political ecology depends on the Party's leadership, and that the leadership role rests on these combined efforts. Looking ahead, Lin notes continuing problems: a political base that needs consolidating, uneven initiative in self-reform, a gap between current anti-corruption work and a systematic institutional framework, and limited influence on wider social norms. Lin calls for upholding Party leadership against internal and external risks, sustaining the spirit of great struggle and self-reform, building long-term mechanisms to remove the conditions for corruption, and using "Party governance" to advance "state governance". Read the original if you want a detailed account of how Party-theoretical writing frames the Party's century of internal discipline and organisation, and its justification for continued strengthening of Party leadership.

A critique of George Brenkert's ethical interpretation of Marx's thought on freedom 评乔治·布伦克特对马克思自由思想的伦理学阐释 Qu Xuan Lin Jinping Qu Xuan and Lin Jinping examine the American ethicist George G. Brenkert's attempt, in Marx's Ethics of Freedom, to build an ethics out of Marx's thought on freedom. The authors ask whether Marx has an ethics at all, how historical materialism relates to ethics, and what kind of ethics Brenkert finds in Marx. Their verdict is that the interpretation is of mixed success: it makes real contributions, but its ethical lens over-extends ethics and narrows Marx. The article has three parts. The first reconstructs Brenkert's reading of historical materialism as Marx's "meta-ethical" methodology. The second sets out his claim that freedom is the "cardinal virtue" of Marx's virtue ethics, and his replies to Allen Wood, Bertell Ollman, Eugene Kamenka and Isaiah Berlin. The third, which is the authors' own assessment, lists four weaknesses and several merits. In the authors' account, Brenkert rejects technological determinism by widening "productive forces" to include workers' moral and value structures, so that the mode of production becomes the explanatory basis and values find a place in it. Marx rejects deontological ethics but retains a meta-ethics and a virtue ethics, in which freedom is a form of self-determination involving self-objectification and harmonious community with others. Brenkert also argues that Marx's freedom is neither Berlin's "positive" liberty nor a rival value among others. Qu and Lin criticise his "pan-ethical" tendency. In their view Brenkert treats Marx as an ethicist, although Marx asked which social system favours free human development. They add that Brenkert weakens Marx's break with moralists such as Kant and Proudhon, and leans too heavily on the early texts. Qu and Lin still credit Brenkert with a constructive account of historical materialism that reconciles historical necessity with human agency. They also credit him with identifying freedom as Marx's central value, with a non-dogmatic reading of Marx, and with effective rebuttals of misreadings. They conclude that the shortcomings Brenkert finds in Marx stem from his ethical viewpoint rather than from Marx's thought, but that he remains a bold and insightful scholar. Read the original if you want a critical Chinese assessment of an Anglophone ethical reading of Marx and of the debates over Marx, justice and freedom.

Historical lessons from a century of building the Communist Party of China's intra-Party political ecology 中国共产党百年党内政治生态建设的历史经验 Lin Ting Written in the year after the Party's centenary, this article asks what a hundred years of effort to build a healthy "intra-Party political ecology" can teach the Communist Party of China. Lin Ting defines the concept as the overall environment, atmosphere and habits in which Party organisations and members live and work. The author argues that this ecology has existed since the Party's founding, that it has developed in step with the Party's historical missions, and that sustaining it is essential to the Party's vanguard character and purity. The article has three parts. The first applies historical materialism to the topic, treating the political ecology as an objective, composite product of many forces and as the result of the Party actively taking up its mission in four periods: the New Democratic Revolution, socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the new era. The second part draws four basic lessons from the century. The third turns to current problems and to how the work should continue. In the core of the argument, Lin holds that political development must lead the whole effort, because it secures the unity of Party spirit and the people's character, a unified will across the Party, and the authority of the Party Central Committee. Lin then names four mutually reinforcing means: ideological, theoretical, institutional and spiritual Party-building. Organisational structure and political culture are said to need parallel development. Building inside the Party is said to be inseparable from its outward influence on government conduct and social norms, which the author links to the Party's "self-reform" and to social revolution. Lin finds that, despite results since the 18th Party Congress (2012), problems remain: the political base of governance needs consolidating, the Party's drive for self-reform is not yet sufficiently self-motivated, the anti-corruption institutional system is incomplete, and the Party's role in shaping social attitudes needs strengthening. The author calls for upholding Party leadership, keeping up the spirit of struggle and self-reform, establishing long-term mechanisms against corruption, and using "Party governance" to advance "state governance". Read the original if you want a detailed example of how Party-building scholarship in China frames the Party's history, institutions and tasks through the idea of a political ecology.

The formation, characteristics and practical value of the spiritual lineage of Chinese Communists 中国共产党人的精神谱系的形成原因、特征表现及现实价值 Liu Haifei Writing in 2022, Liu Haifei takes up the concept of the "spiritual lineage of Chinese Communists", which Xi Jinping used in 2021 and which the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021) described as having the great founding spirit of the Party as its source. Liu notes that scholarly work on the concept is still thin on its causes, features and value, and sets out to address all three. The article argues that the lineage arose from several converging historical, ideological and organisational conditions, that it has identifiable external and internal characteristics, and that it retains concrete value for Party building today. The article is organised in three parts. The first gives six reasons for the lineage's formation. The second describes its features at three levels: outward form, inner substance and value choices. The third sets out six areas of practical value. Examples are drawn from the Party's revolutionary, socialist construction, reform and new-era periods, including the Jinggangshan, Long March, Yan'an, Daqing, Lei Feng, Special Economic Zone and anti-epidemic spirits. On causes, Liu points to traditional Chinese spirit and cultural "genes"; Marxist belief as a "catalyst"; the national longing for rejuvenation after modern humiliation; the Party's tradition of ideological and political education and cadre training; the exemplary role of martyrs, heroes and models as carriers of each spirit; and the Party leadership's formal articulation of the concept since the 18th Party Congress (2012). On characteristics, Liu describes the lineage as systematic, successive across four historical periods, and broad in field, trade, region and naming. Its inner substance is summarised as loyalty, firm conviction, hard struggle, dedication, seeking truth from facts, service to the people and innovation. Its value choices are said to be sacrificing life, favouring righteousness over profit, and putting the collective before the family. Liu argues that the lineage has six practical functions: unifying thought and rallying strength in a Party of over 95 million members; maintaining the Party's vanguard character; purifying the political ecosystem, with Yan'an spirit as an example; training revolutionary successors; fostering a healthy social ethos; and stimulating economic production, since spiritual force can become material force. Liu calls for continued propagation of these spirits through education, media and the example of Party members. Read the original if you want a systematic Chinese-language account of how the Party's "spiritual lineage" is classified and justified, with many named examples of individual spirits.

Grasping the historical significance of the Party's centenary struggle as a whole 从整体上把握党百年奋斗的历史意义 Wang Binglin Shi Zhuoqun The 2021 Party resolution on the major achievements and historical experience of the Party's century of struggle sums up the significance of that struggle in five dimensions: the people's fate, the choice of path, theoretical innovation, world influence and the Party's self-reform. Wang and Shi, writing from the perspective of teaching the course Outline of Modern and Contemporary Chinese History, argue that the five should not only be explained one by one but grasped as a whole. They hold that this requires joining the historical, theoretical and practical logics, a grand view of history and systems thinking, so as to strengthen students' historical confidence and emotional identification with the Party. The article is organised in three parts, each tied to one methodological requirement. The first sets the Party's struggle in a long vertical sweep of Chinese civilisation and modern history and in comparison with the West. The second applies systems thinking to the link between theory and practice across the five significances. The third asks for historical confidence that connects past, present and future, drawing on the resolution's "ten upholds" of historical experience. In the first part, the authors recount the capture of Beijing and Nanjing by foreign invaders and the failure of earlier national salvation schemes. They present the Party's centenary as a unified pursuit of national rejuvenation through liberating productive forces while standing with the people, and as the exploration of Chinese modernization. In their account, this has broken the Western monopoly on development models, civilisational forms and democratic forms, and has refuted the "end of history" and "China collapse" theses. The second part argues that Party leadership is the most essential feature of socialism with Chinese characteristics and that each stage of Marxism's adaptation produced a leap in theory and practice. It also claims that the Party's work has shaped world history, from the anti-fascist war to the survival of socialism after the Soviet collapse. The third part calls for a correct view of Party history that opposes historical nihilism, and for linking the significances with the three great relationships of Party and people, theory and practice, and China and the world. It also attributes the Soviet failure partly to a clash between Marxism and Russian Orthodox culture, in contrast with the affinity the authors see between Marxism and Chinese traditional culture. The authors conclude that historical confidence rests on the Two Integrations, on honestly facing the Party's past errors, and on full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. They present self-reform as the second answer to the historical cycle of rise and decline, after the people's supervision. Read the original if you want to see how a Party-school-style teaching approach frames the 2021 resolution as a unified whole for classroom use.

On the unity of theory facing reality and reality tending towards theory With a note on an important proposition in Marx's "Contribution to the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Law: Introduction" 论理论面向现实与现实趋向理论的统一 Guo Dajun Chinese scholars broadly agree that theory should face reality, but Guo Dajun notes that whether reality should also tend towards theory remains disputed. Guo takes Marx's line in the 1844 Introduction to the critique of Hegel's philosophy of law, that it is not enough for thought to strive towards realisation and reality itself must strive towards thought, as the starting point. The article's thesis is that the two directions are inseparable aspects of the theory–reality relation and that only their mutual interaction and conversion can resolve it. The article has three parts. The first rereads Marx's discussion of 'abolishing philosophy' and 'realising philosophy' through his critique of the German 'theoretical political party' (the Young Hegelians) and the 'practical political party'. The second asks how theory should face reality, and the third why reality should tend towards theory. Guo draws on Marx, Engels and Lenin, and on examples including skyscraper construction, the 2008 Sanlu milk-powder scandal, non-Euclidean geometry, semiconductors and the post-1978 reform experience. In Guo's reading, Marx's phrase means neither rejecting all philosophy nor rejecting theory. It means clearing out the idealism of Hegelian philosophy and turning theory into practical transformation. Guo then argues that theory serves reality through four functions: explanation, criticism, regulation and guidance. Theory must do so as theory, which Guo says means avoiding both withdrawal from reality and pragmatic trend-chasing, and recognising the intermediate link of practical concepts between theory and action. For the converse thesis, Guo holds that practice is limited by historical conditions and by the non-rational factors of its agents. Theory's relative independence and forward-looking character lets it predict trends, set goals and correct these limits. Guo concludes that theory alone facing reality is insufficient and that reality must also tend towards theory. Guo warns against 'practice-ism' (a term attributed to Zhao Jiaxiang), which downplays theory, and against short-term, countermeasure-style research. Guo urges long-term theoretical study and cites the Party's experience of theoretical leadership, Deng Xiaoping's theory of socialism with Chinese characteristics, and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's close reading of Marx's 1844 Introduction applied to current debates on theory, practice and research culture in China.

The Communist Party of China's century of struggle has fundamentally changed the future and fate of the Chinese people 中国共产党百年奋斗从根本上改变了中国人民的前途命运 Han Xiping Han Xiping elaborates a key judgement of the Party's 2021 Resolution on the major achievements and historical experience of the Party's century of struggle: that the Communist Party of China's century of struggle has fundamentally changed the future and fate of the Chinese people. The article argues that the Party has consistently taken the people's standpoint as its basic political stance, and that this has produced an irreversible change in the people's condition, from a survival crisis to the pursuit of a better life. The article has three parts. The first examines how the Party worked to change the people's fate, through its goals, its assessment of the principal contradiction in society, and its lines, principles and policies. The second sets out the results: better living standards, a changed political status for the people, and a growing sense of happiness. The third looks ahead to the strength accumulated in the century of struggle and to the tasks of the new era. Han's central move is to treat the people's happiness, needs and interests as the basis of Party practice. On this reading, the Party defines itself as the one answering the exam paper and the people as the examiners. It also judges shifts in the principal contradiction by the changing needs of the people, from survival in the New Democratic revolution, to material and cultural needs after 1949, to the present contradiction between the people's growing need for a better life and unbalanced and inadequate development. For the results, Han contrasts pre-1949 China (80 per cent of people said to be hungry or half-starved, life expectancy of 35) with a moderately prosperous society for over 1.4 billion people and a life expectancy of 77.3. Han credits whole-process people's democracy with making the people masters of their own fate. The article also compares China with a world marked, in its account, by inequality and extreme poverty. Han concludes that moderate prosperity is a new starting point. China's material strength (GDP above 100 trillion yuan, per capita GDP above US$10,000), institutional strength and spiritual strength, in Han's account, now underpin further progress. Han describes four directions for the new era: resolving the principal contradiction through the new development philosophy and high-quality development, advancing common prosperity in stages towards 2035 and mid-century, and promoting the all-round development of the person, which Han presents as the highest Marxist goal. Read the original if you want to see how a Party-school style commentary on the 2021 Resolution presents the people-centred logic of the Party's history and its stated goals for the new era.

The great founding spirit of the Party: generative logic, connotations and ways of promoting it 伟大建党精神：生成逻辑、内涵意蕴与弘扬路径 Zhang Shihai Writing in Studies on Marxism (2022, no. 2), Zhang Shihai takes up the "great founding spirit" of the Communist Party of China, which Xi Jinping first formulated in his speech at the Party's centenary on 1 July 2021 and called the "source of the Party's spirit". The article asks how this spirit came into being, what it contains and how it should be carried forward. Zhang argues that it arose from the national project of rejuvenation, Marxism and traditional Chinese culture, and that it must now be turned into practice through four paths. The article has three parts. The first reconstructs the spirit's generative logic in four strands: the goal of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, the scientific and truth-bearing character of Marxism, the nourishment of fine traditional Chinese culture, and the early Party-founding activities from 1920 to the Second Party Congress in 1922. The second part analyses the four phrases of Xi's formulation. The third sets out how to promote the spirit in the new era. In Zhang's core argument, each pair of phrases expresses a dialectical unity. Upholding truth and ideals joins truth and value; putting the original aspiration into practice and shouldering the mission joins theory and practice; fearing no sacrifice and fighting bravely joins the revolutionary and the political; and loyalty to the Party and not failing the people joins Party spirit and the people's character. The Party's mission is said to have taken concrete form in the stages of \"standing up\", \"becoming prosperous\" and \"becoming strong\". For promotion, Zhang proposes deeper theoretical elaboration, institutional mechanisms for publicity, supervision and feedback, a objective and respectful treatment of traditional culture, and the integration of the spirit into the \"four greats\": great struggle, great project of Party building, great cause and great dream. Zhang concludes that promoting the spirit is a major historical task of the new era and that it must move from theory to practice. The author notes that existing research has said little about its practical functions and paths, and calls for work on the relation between the founding spirit and the Party's broader spiritual lineage. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially aligned account of how Chinese Party scholars interpret the founding spirit and propose to institutionalise it.

A history of the Chinese translation of key concepts in Lenin's economic writings The cases of "market", "commodity economy" and "state capitalism" 列宁经济学著作中若干概念的汉译史 Zhou Qiang How did concepts that Lenin first treated as capitalist categories come to be part of socialist political economy in China? Zhou Qiang takes up this question by tracing the Chinese translation and reception of three terms from Lenin's economic writings: "market", "commodity economy" and "state capitalism". The article argues that the shifts in their meaning are a miniature of the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, and that they show the process to be one of repeated movement between text and practice rather than straight importation. The article begins with a survey of Lenin's scattered economic writings, from his polemics with the Narodniks to the New Economic Policy (NEP) texts, such as "On the Tax in Kind" and "On Cooperation". It then follows their Chinese translation from the May Fourth period through the Yan'an years to the post-1978 reform era. Three sections take each concept in turn, giving its Chinese etymology or Japanese and Russian origins, Lenin's own shifting usage, the early Chinese translators and journalists (including Qu Qiubai, Wei Zhi and Li Chunfan), and later Party reinterpretation. Zhou's core claim is that each concept underwent a double shift. Lenin first placed market, commodity economy and state capitalism in the capitalist sphere. After the setbacks of War Communism he moved them into socialism: the market became a channel of exchange, and state capitalism a form controlled by the proletarian state. Zhou then shows Chinese Communists doing something similar. Deng Xiaoping separated the market from the question of social system, calling planning and market "economic means". The 1984 Party decision on economic reform spoke of a "planned commodity economy", and state capitalism was used in the socialist transformation of private industry and commerce. Zhou reads the state-capitalist elements of today's mixed ownership system, such as joint ventures and contract processing, as useful supplements to the socialist economy. Zhou concludes that changes in meaning arising from translation, cultural context and practice are not distortions but creative developments within Marxist standpoint and method, and that they avoid dogmatism. Citing Xi Jinping's 2016 remarks on discourse systems, Zhou calls for Chinese political economy to coin new concepts and terms that carry Chinese features yet can be understood internationally. Read the original if you study the history of Marxist terminology in China, the reception of Lenin's NEP, or the conceptual lineage of the socialist market economy.

The Communist Party of China's century of struggle has fundamentally changed the future and destiny of the Chinese people 中国共产党百年奋斗从根本上改变了中国人民的前途命运 Han Xiping This article expounds a sentence from the 2021 Party resolution on the Party's major achievements and historical experience of the past century: that the CPC's century of struggle fundamentally changed the future and destiny of the Chinese people. Han Xiping argues that the Party's founding mission of seeking happiness for the people and rejuvenation for the nation has produced an irreversible change, from a crisis of survival to the pursuit of a better life. The text is organised in three parts. The first examines how the Party has worked to change the people's fate, through its goals, its judgements about the principal contradiction in society, and its lines and policies. The second sets out the results in three dimensions: quality of life, the people's status, and their sense of happiness. The third looks to the future, with four themes: accumulated strength, resolving the principal contradiction of the new era, common prosperity, and all-round human development. Han's central move is to treat the people's standpoint as the thread running through all Party activity. The author holds that the Party defines its goal by the people's wish for a better life, and that at each stage it has used the people's changing needs to identify the principal contradiction and set its direction. The article traces this from the New Democratic Revolution, through the post-1956 and reform-era formulations, to the contradiction between growing needs for a better life and unbalanced and inadequate development. The second move is a double comparison. Han contrasts old China, citing figures of 80 per cent of people hungry and average life expectancy of 35, with present life expectancy of 77.3 and a moderately prosperous society for over 1.4 billion people. The author also contrasts China with a world described as marked by inequality and extreme poverty, and presents whole-process people's democracy as the institutional form of the people's mastery of their own destiny. Han concludes that a moderately prosperous society is a new starting point. The author points to material strength (GDP above 100 trillion yuan, per capita GDP above US$10,000), institutional strength and spiritual awakening as the basis for further progress. Han expects the new development philosophy, high-quality development and staged steps towards common prosperity by 2035 and mid-century to lead to more equal and freer lives, in line with Marx's goal of free and all-round individual development. Read the original if you want a representative example of how Party-affiliated scholars in 2022 interpreted the century-of-struggle resolution through the idea of the people's standpoint.

Tracing the historical formation of the moral dimension of "British Marxism" 追寻“英国马克思主义”道德之维的历史生成 Zhang Liang Zhang Liang asks where the moral and ethical turn in British and Anglo-American Marxist thought came from. The author argues that debates on Marxism and justice, now lively in China, cannot be understood apart from the moral dimension of "British Marxism". In Zhang's account, that dimension arose directly from the "socialist humanism" controversy in the early British New Left, roughly 1956 to 1960. The article first examines why Edward Thompson revived a nineteenth-century British ethical socialist tradition. It then follows the debate through three participants: Thompson's essay "Socialist Humanism: An Epistle to the Philistines" (1957), Charles Taylor's reply "Marxism and Humanism" in The New Reasoner, and Alasdair MacIntyre's "Notes from the Moral Wasteland" (1958–59). A short closing assessment lists the debate's intellectual effects. Zhang says Thompson "invented" the ethical socialist tradition, running from Carlyle and Ruskin to William Morris, in his 1955 book on Morris. The author gives three reasons: the Communist Party's suppressed Romantic tendency was reviving, the Party wanted to reclaim Morris from bourgeois scholars, and post-Stalin humanist Marxism was spreading. Thompson then read Stalinism as a locally successful Marxism marked by anti-intellectualism, moral nihilism and denial of workers' creative agency, and set "socialist humanism" against it. Taylor agreed with the critique but argued that it did not settle the matter. Questions about means and ends, justice and rights, liberation and freedom, and goals and process remained, so he called communism "an unfinished humanism" needing reconstruction. MacIntyre held that Stalinists and their moral critics were two sides of one means–end model. He proposed a "third position" in which morality must be rooted in a historically conceived theory of human nature and realised in the real struggles of the oppressed. Zhang concludes that the debate toppled Soviet Marxism's orthodoxy on the British left and encouraged a native Marxist tradition. It also filled a perceived moral gap in Marxism, opened the left to continental currents and stimulated close study of Marx and Engels. These effects, the author adds, could only fully mature after the New Left ended in the early 1980s. Read the original if you want an intellectual-history account, from a Chinese scholar, of how the New Left's humanism debate underlies later Anglo-American Marxist work on morality and justice.

Upholding a correct view of Party history 坚持正确党史观 Han Xiping This short commentary, published in the People's Daily in June 2022, asks how the Communist Party's history should be viewed. Han argues that a correct view of Party history rests on the methods of dialectical and historical materialism. In Han's account, this view consolidates the results of Party history study and education and helps the Party grasp the theme, main thread and mainstream essence of its history. Han builds the piece around Xi Jinping's explanation of the 2021 Resolution on the Party's major achievements and historical experience, adopted at the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee. Three requirements structure the text: Party history should be viewed in concrete historical terms, objectively and comprehensively, and in terms of connection and development. Each is illustrated with passages from the Resolution. On the first point, Han cites Lenin on considering the objective content of historical processes in specific conditions, and notes that the Resolution divides the century into four periods with distinct tasks and achievements. On the second, Han points to the Resolution's treatment of the periods before and after reform and opening up as connected, so that the achievements of the earlier period prepared the later one despite serious setbacks. On the third, Han presents the three historical resolutions as consistent with one another, with the latest focusing on the achievements of the new era. Han concludes that this method brings out the Party's founding mission of seeking happiness for the Chinese people and rejuvenation for the nation. In Han's reading, it shows why the Party, Marxism and socialism with Chinese characteristics succeed, builds consensus and strengthens historical confidence. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary frames the methodology of Party history writing after the 2021 Resolution.

Interpreting the Chinese path, stimulating discursive innovation 阐释中国道路 激发话语创新 Wang Aiping Writing in the China Social Sciences Today in April 2022, Wang argues that China's growing place on the world stage requires close study of the relationship between the "Chinese path", "Chinese theory" and "Chinese discourse". Building theory and discourse on the basis of the path is described as an epoch-making, comprehensive theoretical undertaking, with significance for the Chinese nation and for world history. The commentary has three sections. The first presents the Chinese path as a contribution to world civilization and cites growth figures from reform and opening up. The second takes up Chinese theory and its link to Marxism. The third addresses Chinese discourse and its place in international communication. Wang contends that the path is the premise of theory: practice drives theoretical innovation, and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation needs its own theory. Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era is presented as a theory of national strength and as an original contribution to discourse. Chinese discourse is defined as the theoretical expression of the path. It should combine Chinese and foreign elements, drawing on Chinese tradition while learning from the West. The author says Chinese modernization has broken the West's monopoly over the terms "modernization" and "civilization". Wang calls on Marxist scholars to build disciplinary, academic and discourse systems with Chinese characteristics, and to offer solutions for a community with a shared future for mankind. Wang expects Chinese theory and discourse to reshape international communication and to support countries that want development while keeping their independence. Read the original if you want a short example of how official scholarship links Chinese modernization to the project of building Chinese discourse.

The ideological foundations of the spirit of self-reform 自我革命精神的思想底蕴 Wen Panya This short commentary asks what intellectual resources lie behind the Chinese Communist Party's insistence on self-reform, which the 2021 resolution on the Party's century of struggle lists as one of ten historical experiences. Wen argues that the Party's persistence in self-reform draws on the deep substance of Marxism, and that this can be seen in three of Marxism's features: its scientific and truthful character, its popular and practical character, and its openness and timeliness. The article opens with the claim that courage in self-reform is the Party's most distinctive trait and greatest strength. It credits the Party since the 18th Party Congress (2012) with strengthened capacities for self-purification, self-improvement, self-renewal and self-elevation, a reversal of laxity in Party governance, and an overwhelming victory in the anti-corruption struggle. Three sections then take each of the Marxist features in turn, ending with a look at the present international setting. On the first feature, Wen cites Marx and Engels's 1850 Address of the Central Authority to the League and Lenin's endorsement of self-criticism as foundations for a proletarian party's self-reform, and presents Xi Jinping's systematic remarks on its meaning and methods as continuing them. On the second, Wen argues that self-reform must target the problems the masses complain of most, and that the people's interests are its standard. The author links this to Marxism's practical orientation towards changing the world, and describes the post-1949 move from campaign-style governance to institutional thinking, together with the successive Party education campaigns since 2012. On the third, Wen holds that self-reform is an open, developing system, and that it has enabled the Party to escape the historical cycle of rise and fall. Wen concludes that on the new "road to the examination" of building a modern socialist country, the Party must treat itself as a special object of revolution, which the author calls the hardest and highest-level kind. Doing so, the article says, is the key to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and to meeting the risks of the pandemic, international conflict and the "great changes unseen in a century". Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary in 2022 grounded the Party's self-reform in Marxist classics and the discourse of Xi Jinping.

Deepening the "Two Integrations" on the new road of the examination 深化“两个结合” 走好赶考之路 Dong Yanfang Writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in March 2022, Dong Yanfang takes up the resolution on the Party's century of struggle adopted at the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021). The resolution calls for combining the basic tenets of Marxism with China's concrete realities and with its fine traditional culture. Dong argues that these Two Integrations must be deepened as the Party leads the people towards the second centenary goal, which the article calls a new "road of the examination". This short commentary is organised around four areas in which the Two Integrations are to continue: putting the people first, upholding fundamental principles while innovating, achieving common prosperity, and promoting human progress. Each section pairs a Marxist source, such as the Communist Manifesto, Marx's 1857–58 manuscripts or Engels, with classical Chinese texts including the Book of Documents, the Book of Songs and the Book of Rites. Dong's central move is to present Marxist principles and Chinese tradition as pointing the same way in each area. Min-ben (people-as-foundation) thought is set beside the Manifesto's "movement of the immense majority". The Chinese ideals of renewal, shared wealth and "all under heaven belongs to all" are set beside Marx on production aimed at the wealth of all. Dong credits this approach for the Party's success and for Chinese modernization. The article also holds that absolute poverty has been resolved, which it says lays the base for common prosperity. Dong calls for policy to rest on the people's approval, for continued innovation alongside established achievements, for narrowing regional, urban–rural and income gaps, and for peaceful, mutually beneficial development that builds a community with a shared future for mankind. The aim is to write a new chapter of twenty-first-century Marxist theory of international relations. Read the original if you want a compact example of how the Two Integrations are presented in official-academic commentary on the Party's historical resolution.

Re-examining the Frankfurt School's paradigm of Enlightenment critique 审视法兰克福学派启蒙批判范式 Wang Xiaodong Li Jingzi Wang Xiaodong and Li Jingzi ask what Horkheimer and Adorno's critique of the Enlightenment contributes, and where it falls short. Writing in a newspaper piece of April 2022, they argue that the critique offers a valuable view of technological rationality and of domination in advanced industrial capitalism, but that it needs critical scrutiny because it is not consistently historical-materialist. The article first reconstructs the "cultural critique paradigm" set out in Dialectic of Enlightenment. It then assesses the paradigm's value and sets out three limits. The authors place the paradigm among its influences: the young Marx, Lebensphilosophie, existentialism, Freudianism and early Western Marxism. In the authors' account, Horkheimer and Adorno reduce the Enlightenment to rationalism, anthropocentrism and progressivism. They analyse it as a threefold alienation: of humans from nature, from one another and from themselves. On this view rationality has turned into instrumental and technical rationality and become a new myth. Wang and Li answer that this picture is partial, because the Enlightenment was plural (French, Scottish, German) and the critique mainly targets the French variety. They also hold that it neglects the Enlightenment's historical progressiveness against feudal absolutism. Above all, they say it wrongly blames reason itself for modernity's crises. Irrational interests and desires, capital and institutional arrangements stand behind instrumental reason, and the authors see Nietzsche, Foucault and the Frankfurt thinkers as rejecting reason instead of criticising these. The authors conclude that Horkheimer and Adorno accepted Marxism's humanism and its critique of capitalism but did not fundamentally hold to historical materialism. They call for a total historical and practical analysis of the roots of rationality. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese Marxist assessment of the Frankfurt School's critique of the Enlightenment.

The illusion of the technological promise and accelerated capitalism 科技承诺幻象与加速资本主义 Yu Tianyu This short commentary, published in China Social Sciences Today in April 2022, asks why technological progress in modern Western capitalism has not freed people from toil. Drawing on Hartmut Rosa's Social Acceleration: A New Theory of Modernity (rendered in Chinese as a critique of the theory of social acceleration), Yu argues that the 'technological promise' is an illusion: technology has been turned from a tool of human liberation into a tool by which capital rules people. The piece has three main sections: capital logic and technological domination; the 'mission' of technology in accelerated capitalism; and the supposed remedies of 'slow living' and 'resonance'. It begins from Rosa's closed loop of acceleration, in which faster technology speeds social change, social change speeds the pace of life, and the pace of life demands still faster technology. Yu contends that the loop serves capital's valorisation. Capital stimulates unlimited desires, and satisfying them requires faster production and thus faster technology, so the more technology develops, the busier people become. Technology also lets capital try to push past natural limits, Yu argues, by squeezing more from existing resources and by ecological exploitation of latecomer countries, including through offshore factories and war. The author describes 'slow living' as essentially 'fast', since any pause is repaid with interest, and calls 'resonance' a reformist submission to capital. Yu concludes that acceleration cannot be undone within capitalism, because it springs from capital's drive to expand without limit. The real task is to dissolve the power of capital and tame capital logic, abolishing its dominance while keeping and transforming its positive elements, in order to move beyond capitalist civilisation. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese Marxist reading of Rosa's acceleration theory and its critique of 'slow life' and 'resonance'.

The "first turn" in Marx's philosophical thought 马克思哲学思想的“第一次转向” Yu Zaihai Why did the young Marx move from Kant to Hegel? Yu Zaihai argues that Marx's move to the University of Berlin in October 1836 marked the first node in the development of his philosophy, and that the shift was driven by the need to overcome the opposition between the "ought" and the "is". In Yu's reading, Marx turned to Hegel for the same reason Hegel had criticised Kant: to find a way into concrete ethical life. The piece is a short newspaper essay. It begins with Marx's letter to his father of 10 November 1837, then sets out external and internal causes of the turn. It then reconstructs the difference between Kant's and Hegel's philosophy, covering Kant's theoretical and practical reason, the moral philosophy built on freedom, its dualist flaw, and Hegel's critique. It ends with three inferences about what the turn meant for Marx. Yu names two external causes. Bonn was dominated by Romanticism, while Berlin was a stronghold of Hegelianism, and Marx absorbed Hegel through Eduard Gans's teaching and the "Doctor Club", where Bruno Bauer and Friedrich Köppen influenced him most. The internal cause is that Marx met an obstacle when he built a philosophy of law on Kant–Fichte lines, namely the opposition between what exists and what ought to be. Yu reconstructs Kant's moral philosophy (duty over happiness, the categorical imperative, the deposit example). Yu then presents Hegel's objection that the universalisation test is purely formal and cannot exclude even the absence of property, so that Kantian morality turns freedom into an "ought" that is never realised. For Hegel, ethical life belongs to objective spirit. Yu draws three conclusions. The turn was an inner necessity, not a chance interest. It was the key step by which Marx moved from Kant–Fichte idealism toward Hegel. Marx's approach to Hegel was already distinctive: neither the Old Hegelians' fascination with the system nor the Young Hegelians' selective use of it drew him, but Hegel's ending of Kantian dualism, which suggested to Marx a way to "realise" philosophy. Yu holds that this insight separated Marx from the Hegelian schools and set the course of his later work. Read the original if you want a compact account of the intellectual reasons behind Marx's Berlin-period turn from Kant to Hegel, as presented in Chinese scholarship.

Unwaveringly upholding and strengthening the Party's overall leadership 毫不动摇坚持和加强党的全面领导 Sang Xuecheng This newspaper commentary, published in 2022, argues that the Party's overall leadership must be upheld and strengthened without wavering in the new era. Sang begins from the first of the "Ten Clarifications" that summarise Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. That clarification names Communist Party leadership as the most essential feature and greatest strength of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Sang holds that only such leadership can let the country manage both the strategic overall situation of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and the world's "changes unseen in a century". The piece is organised under four headings. It first sets out what upholding the Party's overall leadership means. It then turns to the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds, to arming the whole Party with Xi Jinping Thought, and to full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. Sang draws on Xi's statements and on the 2021 Party resolution on the Party's history. On the first point, Sang says the Party's leadership should be understood through historical, theoretical and practical logic. In this account it is the choice of history and the people, and it rests on the Marxist theory of the party. Sang adds that since the 18th Party Congress (2012) Xi's statements have enriched Marxist ruling-party theory. Because the Party is "the leading force in everything", its leadership must be comprehensive and systematic, covering economic, political, cultural, social and ecological work. On the second point, Sang attributes the historic achievements of the new era to Xi's position as the core of the Central Committee and the Party, and to the guidance of his thought. Sang calls for stronger political, ideological, theoretical and emotional identification with the Two Establishes, to be turned into action. Sang also presents the Party's "self-reform" as the way to overcome the Party's own problems. The piece warns that corruption is still a serious challenge despite the "overwhelming victory" of the anti-corruption campaign. Sang concludes that, on this "road of the exam", the Party must treat studying Xi Jinping Thought as its first political task. It must keep adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, and must keep up strict Party discipline. The aim is to keep the Party from losing its character and to ensure it remains the strong leadership core of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Party commentary in 2022 tied the Party's overall leadership to the Two Establishes, theoretical study and the Party's self-reform.

The essentials and advantages of the new path of Chinese modernization 中国式现代化新道路的要义与优势 Wang Heng Writing in the China Social Sciences Today in December 2021, Wang Heng asks what is "new" and what is "good" about the path of Chinese modernization, a path Xi Jinping presented at the Party's centenary celebration. Wang argues that it can be grasped by comparing it with Western modernization, and that it differs from that model in four ways. The short commentary is organised as four numbered claims, each pairing a defining feature of Chinese modernization with a shortcoming Wang attributes to the Western path. It closes with a brief statement of the path's significance for China and for developing countries. First, Wang calls it socialist modernization. Capitalist modernization, driven by surplus-value extraction, is said to produce alienation, polarisation and social atomisation, while the socialist path is people-centred, aims at common prosperity and can concentrate resources on major undertakings. Second, it is scientific development: comprehensive, coordinated and sustainable, in contrast with Western materialism, consumerism and the "pollute first, clean up later" route. Third, it is peaceful development. Wang contends that Western powers built modernity on colonial plunder, whereas China pursues win-win openness and a community with a shared future for mankind, rejecting the logic that a strong state must seek hegemony. Fourth, it is independent: no single universal model exists, so each country must find a path suited to its own conditions. Wang concludes that the path belongs to China and to the world. It is described as the necessary road to national rejuvenation and as offering developing countries a wider range of routes, a "Chinese approach" to modernization. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned statement of how Chinese modernization was contrasted with Western models in late 2021.

Establishing a correct view of Party history through systems thinking 以系统思维树立正确党史观 Shi Shiyue Writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in March 2021, ahead of the Party's centenary, Shi Shiyue takes up Xi Jinping's call, made at the mobilisation meeting for Party history study and education, to "establish a correct view of Party history". Shi argues that this requires systems thinking, and that Party history is a systematic, innovative and practical history. The article treats such thinking as a way to raise Party members' ability to understand what that history means. The short commentary is organised around four attributes of systems thinking: wholeness, dynamism, hierarchy and openness. Each gets its own section, covering the value of Party history as a whole, its four periods, its record of governance across several fields, and its orientation towards the future. On wholeness, Shi presents the century as a history of struggle and sacrifice, citing revolutionary martyrs such as Li Dazhao and later figures such as Wang Jinxi and Jiao Yulu. In the author's account, this history carries traditional virtues and also the values of the Party's self-reform, innovation and putting the people first. On dynamism, Shi divides the century into four periods: New Democratic Revolution, socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the new era under Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The article describes these as moves from standing up, to growing rich, to growing strong. On hierarchy, it surveys achievements in politics, the economy, culture and ecological civilization. On openness, Shi points to the elimination of absolute poverty as the first centenary goal. The article says the Party will now pursue the second centenary goal of building a modern socialist country, guided by the experience and spirit contained in Party history. Shi concludes that learning from history should shape the daily practice of every member and citizen. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Party-school commentary frames the 2021 Party history study campaign through a four-part systems schema.

Tracing and reflecting on Chinese modernization from a century-long perspective A scientific understanding of the Sixth Plenum's judgement on the historical significance of the Party's century of struggle 百年视野下中国式现代化的溯源与思考 Hou Weimin Writing in 2022, Hou Weimin asks how the Communist Party's century of struggle should be understood through the lens of Chinese modernization, taking as its guide the resolution on the Party's major achievements and historical experience adopted at the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021). Hou argues from historical materialism that Chinese modernization is the outcome of accumulated historical energy, confirms the objective laws of social development, and demonstrates the necessity and practical truth of the socialist road. The article has five sections. It begins with the accumulated conditions behind Chinese modernization's starting point, then turns to its convergence with national rejuvenation, to its unity with the Marxist theory of practice, to its fit with a new form of human civilization, and finally to its link with Party leadership. Hou draws on the Resolution, Marx, Engels, Mao Zedong and Xi Jinping, and on Western figures such as Huntington, Weber, Marcuse and Macron. Hou also cites GDP, poverty-reduction and trade figures. Hou's central claim is that Chinese modernization departs from the Western model, which the author characterises as marked by war, plunder and instability. Four features are said to follow: peaceful rise, long-term stability alongside rapid growth (which Hou presents as refuting Huntington), active opening up, and a changed international position. Hou holds that public ownership as the main body of the economy and the socialist market economy explain this success, and that earlier non-Marxist modernization schemes in China failed. Chinese modernization is described as the third landmark shift in world history favourable to socialism, after the October Revolution and the 1949 revolution. Hou says it also creates a new form of human civilization that rebuts Weber's claim that modern capitalism belongs to the West. Hou concludes that Party leadership is the decisive condition of this path. The argument is that socialism, unlike earlier social formations, begins with scientific theory and so needs a vanguard party with no interests separate from the people's. Hou contrasts India's slower modernization as the result of lacking such a party. Hou also credits Party leadership with keeping the socialist market economy under public ownership, supporting common prosperity and reducing poverty. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese economist reads the 2021 Resolution to present Chinese modernization as an alternative to capitalist modernization and as a stage in world socialism's history.

The "non-identity" dimension of Marx's empirical research method 马克思经验研究方法的“非同一性”维度 Yang Lei This short commentary, first published in China Social Sciences Today in January 2022, asks what distinguishes Marx's empirical method from both the speculation of the Young Hegelians and the empiricism of English and French philosophy. Yang argues that Marx combined empirical material with theoretical processing, and that methodologically he rejected metaphysical thinking based on "identity" while stressing the positive significance of "non-identity". The article is organised under three headings that Yang takes to express this stress: matter (质料, zhiliao), the particular or individual, and difference. It draws mainly on The German Ideology, on Marx's late writings about Russia, and on Hegel's Phenomenology of Spirit. Yang first argues that Marx grounded theory in material life, so that thought and institutions are historical products of material needs rather than eternal essences. Under capitalism, identity appears as the absolute rule of capital logic, which Marx countered by showing that capitalist production relations are transitory. Second, Yang reads Marx's starting point in living individuals as a critique of capital and metaphysics, which together reduce people to abstract forces. Third, Marx's study of Russia is presented as a case of concrete analysis: Marx rejected turning his account of Western European capitalism into a universal philosophy of history, and held that Russia's path depended on its historical setting. Yang concludes that, for Marx, experience is not static but expands with time, place and conditions, so it cannot be grasped through fixed concepts. Marx's empirical method is thus aimed at the self-emancipation of concrete, varied individuals and at paths of development that differ by country. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese-language account of how Marx's method is connected to the theme of non-identity.

Abstraction becomes domination: Marx and Lefebvre 抽象成为统治：马克思与列斐伏尔 Yan Jinggao This short commentary, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in March 2022, asks how Henri Lefebvre carries forward Marx's diagnosis of modern abstraction. Yan argues that Marx criticised the paradox that individuals are now ruled by abstractions, and that Lefebvre took up the formula of abstraction (capital) becoming dominant to conclude that abstract space has become dominant. Yan adds that neither thinker falls into despair, since both rely on the liberating force of the dialectic of history. The article has three parts: abstract capital as ruler, abstract space as ruler, and the path to breaking abstract domination. It moves from Marx's account of money, exchange value and capital to Lefebvre's theory of the production of space, and ends with their shared view of resistance. In Yan's reading, Marx shows that money fetishism and the capital relation make people dependent on things, and that economic globalisation spreads this rule worldwide. Lefebvre, in Yan's account, shifts the focus from the production of things in space to the production of space itself. Abstract space becomes the 'subject' of social relations and daily life, erasing lived experience and admitting only objects with exchange value. Yan presents it as an objective abstraction, whose closest concrete form is state monopoly capitalism, and whose urbanisation, statisation and globalisation form a spatial trinity. Yan concludes that domination by abstraction is not inescapable. Capital's self-negating nature, as Marx describes it, matches abstract space's need to produce spaces of difference, which signals the dissolution of that domination. Yan adds that Marx places the agent of change in the proletariat, while Lefebvre places the possibility of spatial liberation in city margins, slums and forbidden spaces of resistance. Read the original if you want a compact introduction to how Lefebvre's theory of space is linked to Marx's critique of capital.

The contemporary value of the Marxist idea of integrated urban–rural development 马克思主义城乡融合发展思想的当代价值 Yan Yuanfeng This short commentary, first published in the China Social Sciences Today in January 2022, asks how the Marxist idea of integrated urban–rural development can address the urban–rural divide. Yan argues that Western development economics entrenches that divide, while Marxism shows its overcoming to be historically necessary. China's rural revitalization strategy is presented as a new practice that puts this idea to work. The piece begins with Marx's account in Capital of how capital expropriated rural populations, then turns to Western theories, to Russia after the Soviet collapse, and to Marx and Engels on town and country. It ends with three advantages that Yan attributes to China. Yan contends that the theories of Lewis, Perroux and Friedmann share a city-centred stance that treats rural sacrifice as inevitable. As the typical case, the author cites Russia's post-1991 "shock therapy", citing figures from Medvedev in 2019 on rural infrastructure. Yan reads Marx and Engels as holding that the town–country opposition can and must be abolished, partly for ecological reasons, and that small peasants should be led towards cooperation rather than expropriated. Yan then names three Chinese advantages: the resolution of private land ownership, long-standing priority for agriculture and rural areas, and the leadership of the Communist Party of China. Yan concludes that rural revitalization is the opening move towards common prosperity. Success in agricultural modernization and peasant prosperity, the author argues, would resolve the urban–rural opposition and lay the material basis for a higher social form. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Chinese commentary links Marx and Engels on town and country to current rural policy.

A reader's guide to Marxist historical studies of merchant capital 马克思主义的商业资本主义史研究阅读指南 Jairus Banaji This text is a Chinese translation of a bibliographic reading guide by the historian Jairus Banaji on Marxist work about merchant (trading) capital. Banaji argues that Marxists should not build histories of capitalism on the rigid definition in Chapter 16 of Capital, Volume III, where commercial capital is a mere function of industrial capital. In Banaji's view, the more productive material lies in Chapter 20's remarks on possible 'transitions' within capitalism, though even that chapter is judged inadequate. The guide opens with Marx's own scattered writings on merchant capital and the unresolved problem of 'commercial workers', whose labour creates no value yet is waged. It then surveys works in thematic and chronological groups: general studies of 'commercial capitalism' (Pokrovsky, Tawney, Banaji's own work); ancient Rome; late medieval and early modern cases (Venice, the Mediterranean sugar trade, Florentine silk, Braudel, Portugal, Brenner, Kriedte, Chinese 'sprouts of capitalism'); the slave trade and cotton; debates on British capitalism; peasant household production; and the twentieth century. Banaji's central moves are to present merchant capital as an essentially modern form rather than an 'antediluvian' one, and to show it organising production, controlling labour and shaping states. Examples include Venetian merchants' hold on their republic, merchant investment in early mechanised Italian silk mills, and putting-out systems. The guide also highlights the subordination of commerce to industry, which Porter and Livesay place mainly in the nineteenth century, and merchant integration into supply chains, as in Chen Hansheng's study of British American Tobacco and Chinese tobacco growers. Banaji cautions against reading terms such as Beckert's 'war capitalism' as theoretical rather than historical categories, and notes Brenner's refusal to call London merchants capitalists. Banaji's overall implication is that the history of capitalism cannot be written from industry alone, and that works from Pokrovsky to Harriss-White's study of West Bengal supply evidence for a richer typology of capital's forms. The guide gives no single programme, but flags Marx's unresolved treatment of commercial labour and the neglect of merchant capital under Stalinism. Read the original if you want an annotated bibliography of Marxist and adjacent scholarship on merchant capital, covering Europe, Africa, India, Russia and China, from a leading historian of the field.

The new era as a new field for research on Party history and the history of New China 新时代是党史新中国史研究的新领域 Qu Qingshan Writing in 2019, on the 70th anniversary of the People's Republic, Qu Qingshan asks what the "new era" that began with the 18th Party Congress (2012) means for the history of the Communist Party and the history of New China, and what it demands of historians. Qu holds that the two histories largely overlap, with Party history as the core of New China's history. The article's answer is that the new era is an integral part of both, a new epochal coordinate and a new milestone, and therefore a new and important field of research. The article is organised in four parts, each taking a different vantage point on the new era: the two historical tasks the Party has carried since 1921, the Party's "historical position", the realisation of the great national dream, and finally the implications for historical scholarship. It divides the record into four periods, each tied to a keyword: revolution (1921–1949), construction (1949–1978), reform (1978–2012) and rejuvenation (2012 to mid-century). It draws on Xi Jinping's statements and on official figures, such as GDP rising from 51.94 trillion to 90.03 trillion yuan between 2012 and 2018. Qu's central move is to present the four periods as one continuous struggle: saving the nation, building it, enriching it and, in the new era, making it strong. The new era is both a continuation of the reform period and a qualitative leap, justified by three factors: a world undergoing "changes unseen in a century", China's strongest development conditions in modern times, and a shift in the principal contradiction in Chinese society. Qu also stresses that the new era links the "two centenary goals" and the two-step plan to 2035 and mid-century. Counting to 2049, the new era would take up 38 per cent of New China's history and 29.7 per cent of the Party's, which Qu takes as reason enough to study it. Qu rejects the saying that contemporaries should not write contemporary history, arguing that history and reality have no sharp boundary. The article names the field's difficulties: events still unfolding, the need for specialist knowledge across many sectors, and the task of sifting abundant public information. Qu calls the field under-studied, since existing work is mostly about current problems and not about history, experience or laws of development. Qu calls on historians to follow Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, combine Party spirit with scientific method and serve the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want an authoritative statement of how Party historiography is told to periodise the PRC era and fold the Xi period into Party history.

Upholding the Party's overall leadership is the choice of history and the people 坚持党的全面领导是历史和人民的选择 Wang Junwei This commentary, first published in the People's Daily, takes up the sixth plenary session of the 19th Central Committee's 2021 Resolution on the Party's major achievements and historical experience. Wang notes that the Resolution puts Party leadership first among the "ten affirmations" of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The article's thesis is that upholding the Party's overall leadership is the choice of history and of the people, and the only route for upholding and developing socialism with Chinese characteristics. The piece has three parts. The first reviews the Party's history from its founding through the revolution, socialist construction, reform and opening up, and the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The second turns to the Two Establishes and the role of a leadership core. The third deals with maintaining and improving the institutional system of Party leadership. Wang argues from historical experience that when overall leadership is upheld thoroughly, the cause of the Party and the people advances smoothly, and when it is weakened, the cause takes detours or suffers setbacks. Examples include the lessons of the failed Great Revolution, the leading role in the anti-Japanese united front, and the Party's answers at each turning point after the Cultural Revolution. The author holds that a strong leadership core has always been decisive in critical moments, citing the Zunyi Meeting and the 1945 Resolution on historical questions. On that basis Wang presents the Two Establishes as the most important political outcome since 2012, and describes Xi Jinping as a core tested by history and practice and as the principal founder of the thought that bears his name. Wang concludes that, amid what the article calls a century of change in the world and a once-in-a-century pandemic, the Party must grasp the decisive significance of the Two Establishes and carry out the Two Upholds. The author calls for the leadership system to be improved: mechanisms for keeping the founding mission in mind, institutions defending the authority of the Central Committee, systems for governing for and by the people, and full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the official Party narrative justifies overall leadership and the leadership core on historical grounds.

The Party's system of leadership institutions continues to improve 党的领导制度体系不断完善 Li Zhenghua This short commentary, first published in the People's Daily, takes up the statement in the Resolution adopted at the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021) that the system of Party leadership institutions has been continuously improved. Li Zhenghua argues that since the 18th Party Congress (2012) the Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core has made perfecting this system a priority, with notable results. The article describes three strands of work: top-level design around the principle that Party leadership is China's fundamental leadership system; institutions that safeguard the authority and centralised, unified leadership of the Central Committee; and measures to extend Party leadership to every type of organisation. Li reports that the 19th Party Congress (2017) wrote into the Party Constitution the principle that the Party leads everything, and that the Fourth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2019) defined Party leadership as the fundamental leadership system. The author lists intra-Party regulations on Central Committee work, local committees, Party groups and reporting of major matters, and describes stronger decision-making and coordinating bodies, democratic centralism and political supervision tied to the Two Upholds. Li adds that Politburo members now submit annual written reports, and that the Party's leadership of the legislature, government, judiciary, armed forces, enterprises and grassroots bodies has been regularised. Li concludes that these arrangements have built a system of Party leadership running from the centre to the grassroots, making Party leadership more mature and settled. In Li's account, this has strengthened the Party's consistency with the Central Committee and its role in coordinating all sides. Read the original if you want a concise official-line summary of the institutional measures taken to consolidate Party leadership after 2012.

The history of the Communist Party of China is a history of self-reform 一部中国共产党史就是一部自我革命史 Zhang Taiyuan This commentary, published in Guangming Daily in May 2022, takes up the claim in the Party's 2021 historical resolution that courage in self-reform is what distinguishes the Communist Party of China from other parties. Zhang argues that the Party's hundred-year history is itself a history of self-reform, and that this capacity explains how it has survived and grown while many other communist parties collapsed. The piece is organised in three parts. The first traces the sources and record of the Party's self-reform; the second identifies criticism and self-criticism as the means by which it is achieved; the third turns to full and rigorous self-governance of the Party since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Zhang draws heavily on Xi Jinping, Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping, along with the 2021 resolution. Zhang holds that self-reform as the Party's most distinctive trait comes from two sources: the nature of a Marxist party, which must keep adapting to new struggles, and Chinese traditional culture, whose self-renewing spirit the Party inherits. In this account, every major turning point, from the first United Front to the shift from a planned to a market economy, was achieved through self-reform, and the Party repeatedly recognised and corrected its own errors. Criticism and self-criticism is described as the indispensable weapon: without it, self-reform is impossible.
