Zhang adds that the Party must accept supervision by the people and not carry out self-reform behind closed doors. Zhang concludes that self-reform is bound up with the Party's leadership of social revolution, and that its strength comes from the objective needs of that revolution. Since 2012, the author says, the Party has acted decisively against entrenched ills. Zhang calls on the whole Party to keep up the political awareness that full and rigorous self-governance of the Party is always a work in progress, even after the anti-corruption campaign's overwhelming victory. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-school scholars present self-reform as the key to the Party's historical continuity and its Marxist character.

The Communist Party of China's contributions to world socialism over the past century 百年来中国共产党对世界社会主义的贡献 Yan Rong Taking its cue from the Resolution on the Party's century of struggle adopted at the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021), this article asks how the Communist Party of China (CPC) has contributed to world socialism. Yan argues that over its first hundred years the Party made major contributions in four areas: practical paths, theory, institutions and culture. The article presents these as part of the Resolution's claim that the Party's struggle displayed the vitality of Marxism and shaped world history. The article is organised into four sections. The first traces three paths: the New Democratic revolution, socialist transformation and construction, and socialism with Chinese characteristics. The second covers the three theoretical achievements of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times: Mao Zedong Thought, the theoretical system of socialism with Chinese characteristics, and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The third sets out the institutional system of fundamental, basic and important institutions, and the fourth the Party's socialist culture. Yan contends that each stage extended Marxism and the international communist movement. The Chinese revolution is described as the first case of proletarian dictatorship achieved by encircling the cities from the countryside. Reform and opening up is said to have carried China through the low ebb after the Soviet collapse and to have given developing countries a new option, which the article links to Chinese modernization. On institutions, Yan treats Party leadership as the most essential feature and attributes the Soviet collapse to weakened Party leadership and the abandonment of Marxism's guiding role in ideology. The article says the institutional system underpins what it calls "Chinese governance" against "Western chaos" amid rivalry with the United States and the West. On culture, Yan combines excellent traditional Chinese culture, revolutionary culture (the spirit of more than 90 revolutionary spirits) and advanced socialist culture. Yan concludes that the Party has answered the historic question of what socialism is and how to build it, and that it has made the Marxist theory it developed available to other countries. The article states that the Party has grown from about fifty members to over 95 million and is the world's largest governing party. It expects the Party to contribute more to world socialism as it builds a modern socialist country in all respects. Read the original if you want a representative, official-line account of how Party scholars frame the CPC's centenary role in the history of world socialism.

Party leadership as the fundamental guarantee for running socialist universities with Chinese characteristics well 党的领导是办好中国特色社会主义大学的根本保证 Sun Liang Taking its cue from Xi Jinping's remarks during a visit to Renmin University of China, this commentary in Guangming Daily argues that Party leadership is the fundamental guarantee for running socialist universities with Chinese characteristics well. Sun treats Xi's call to uphold Party leadership and Marxism's guiding position, and to forge a new path to world-class universities with Chinese characteristics, as the framework for the discussion. The piece first traces Party leadership of higher education through four periods: the new-democratic revolution, socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the years since the 18th Party Congress (2012). It then sets out four ways in which, in the author's view, Party leadership shapes universities. Sun describes leadership as giving universities their soul of conviction, their institutional foundation, their driving force and their path of development. Conviction means passing on Marxist belief, including Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The institutional foundation is the president responsibility system under the leadership of the Party committee, together with democratic centralism and Party control over direction, cadres, talent and ideology. Leadership is also said to keep universities united and to rule out simply copying foreign models. Sun concludes that the president responsibility system under Party committee leadership must be upheld and improved. The author also calls for stronger grassroots Party organisations and for ideological and political work to run through all teaching, so that universities remain a front line for training socialist builders and successors. Read the original if you want a short example of how official commentary justifies Party leadership in higher education.

Three dimensions of upholding the authority of the Party Central Committee 维护党中央权威的三个维度 Yuan Yinchuan Zhang Xiaohui Yuan Yinchuan and Zhang Xiaohui ask why the authority of the Party Central Committee must be upheld, and answer from three angles: theoretical, historical and contemporary. They open by rejecting what they call a Western-centric discourse that presents capitalist liberal democracy as a universal model and denies the diversity of political civilisations. Deconstructing that discourse, they argue, helps explain the Communist Party of China's century of struggle and strengthens practical commitment to the Two Upholds. The article has three main sections. The theoretical section traces the Marxist theory of authority from Marx and Engels through Lenin. The historical section reviews the Party's revolutionary, construction and reform periods. The contemporary section links the issue to national rejuvenation, to what the authors call great changes unseen in a century, and to the Party's self-governance. The authors argue that, for Marx and Engels, authority arises from cooperative production and takes on a class character in class society. In their account, the proletarian party needs authority to unify will against anarchists such as Bakunin, and Lenin defended the necessity of party and leader authority. The historical section treats the Zunyi Conference, the struggles against Zhang Guotao and Wang Ming, the Yan'an rectification, and Deng Xiaoping's call that the centre must have authority as lessons that the Party succeeded because its Central Committee had a core. The authors present democratic centralism as the organisational principle that joins authority with intra-Party democracy. They also hold that leaders arise from the masses and should not be exaggerated into something separate from them. For the present, the authors contend that the Party's leading core is indispensable to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. They describe Western politics as in disorder and Chinese governance as ordered, and maintain that upholding the Centre's authority represents the people's fundamental interests rather than personal power. They stress full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, citing intra-Party regulations issued since 2012, as the means of institutionalising the Two Upholds, and call for ideological, political and practical self-awareness among Party members. Read the original if you want a representative example of how Party-school scholars ground the Two Upholds in Marxist authority theory and Party history.

Ensuring that the Party always exercises overall leadership and coordinates all sides 确保党始终总揽全局协调各方 Qin Long Ji Ruixia This short commentary, first published in the People's Daily and posted in May 2022, takes up the Party's principle of "taking overall responsibility and coordinating the efforts of all sides". Qin and Ji argue that the Party's leadership is the fundamental guarantee for managing China's affairs and for national rejuvenation. Ensuring that the Party always plays this role is, in their view, both the key experience behind past success and the basic guarantee of future success. The piece is written as an interpretation of the Resolution adopted at the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021) and quotes it repeatedly. It first reviews the record since the 18th Party Congress (2012), then explains why the principle remains essential in the new journey, and finally names two ways to uphold it. The authors contend that, under the Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core, the Party's leadership has been applied to all fields, and that this explains the historic achievements and changes of the new era. They present these as proof that the Party's overall leadership is the only path for sustaining and developing socialism with Chinese characteristics. Although conditions for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation are now stronger, they warn of foreseeable and unforeseeable risks. The first measure is to grasp the decisive significance of the Two Establishes and strengthen the Two Upholds. The second is to improve the institutional system of Party leadership, described as the "four beams and eight pillars", so that the Party's leadership is comprehensive, systematic and holistic. Qin and Ji conclude that without the Communist Party there would be no national rejuvenation, and that there must be no wavering or ambiguity on this principle. They call for stronger institution-building at every level and in every area, together with more scientific, democratic and law-based governance. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary in 2022 framed the Party's overall leadership after the Sixth Plenum Resolution.

The Communist Party of China is the most reliable backbone of united struggle 中国共产党是团结奋斗最可靠的主心骨 Xu Jingong Taking its cue from Xi Jinping's statement that united struggle is the only way for the Chinese people to create great historic achievements, this newspaper commentary argues that the Communist Party of China is the Chinese people's backbone and the most reliable backbone of united struggle. Xu presents the Party's leadership as the key to both past successes and future ones. The piece is organised under three headings: the unity of Party spirit and the people's character, a mission and goals that unite popular consensus, and institutions and mechanisms for great unity and solidarity. It runs through the Party's history from the New Democratic Revolution to the new era. Xu first contends that the Party has no interests of its own, which makes it, in the author's account, the one force able to unify the people. Late Qing and republican-era reformers, by contrast, lacked the political vision and selflessness for lasting unity. Second, Xu reviews how the united front changed with each period's tasks, from the anti-Japanese national united front to the current drive for common prosperity. Third, Xu lists six institutional arrangements under Xi Jinping: the new type of party system, work with non-Party intellectuals, forging a strong sense of community among the Chinese nation, the sinicization of religion, guiding non-public-sector entrepreneurs, and mobilising compatriots in Hong Kong, Macao, Taiwan and overseas. Xu concludes that Party leadership, shared goals and institutional guarantees together turn unity into a lasting capacity for struggle. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary in 2022 framed the united front and the Party's leading role in national unity.

Raising philosophical thinking and grasping the direction of development A study of General Secretary Xi Jinping's philosophical wisdom and major practice 提高哲学思维 把握发展方向 Zhou Dan Huang Weiming This commentary, first published in the China Social Sciences Today in March 2022, starts from the Party's tradition of studying and applying philosophy. Zhou and Huang note that General Secretary Xi Jinping has repeatedly urged leading cadres to study Marxist philosophy, so as to improve their strategic thinking, ability to make comprehensive decisions and ability to manage the overall situation. The authors argue that Xi's work in Fujian Province offers concrete examples of a series of philosophical modes of thinking applied to practice. The piece is organised under nine headings, each naming a mode of thinking: strategic, historical, dialectical, innovative, rule-of-law, bottom-line, systems and precision thinking. Each section opens with a definition and a quotation from Xi, and then lists, usually in three or four numbered points, examples from his years in Fujian. These cover posts in Xiamen, Fuzhou, Ningde and at provincial level, with cases such as the Digital Fujian and Ecological Fujian initiatives, the Jinjiang experience, collective forest tenure reform and poverty reduction in eastern Fujian. The authors' central move is to read each local initiative as the application of a specific philosophical method. Under dialectical thinking, they cite Xi's use of the image of water dripping through stone to explain the law of the transformation of quantity into quality, and his use of the 'two-sided' and 'key-point' approaches in planning eastern Fujian's development. Under systems thinking, they describe the 'six constant principles' of the Jinjiang experience as six subsystems forming a whole, and the 'one-building office' as an example of the whole being greater than the sum of its parts. Under rule-of-law thinking, they point to integrity regulations for officials in Ningde and the innovation of forest-rights mortgage loans. Under precision thinking, they describe fieldwork in Junying village and the 'Three Heroic Islands', where Xi is said to have prescribed measures matched to local conditions. The authors conclude that Xi's reform exploration and practice in Fujian left a deep impression on local cadres and the public in thought, courage and sentiment. In their account, this has become a valuable spiritual resource and a driving force for continuing reform and development. The text is a short, example-driven account in the official idiom, and it presents Xi's practice as a model of applied philosophy for cadres. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese official commentary links Xi Jinping's early local work to a catalogue of philosophical thinking methods promoted for cadre study.

Leading social revolution with the Party's self-reform 以党的自我革命引领社会革命 Lü Hong Shi Yufan This commentary, published in the China Social Sciences Today in March 2022, takes up the strategic idea in the Resolution on the Party's centenary achievements and historical experience, adopted at the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021). That idea is that a great self-revolution should lead a great social revolution. Lü and Shi argue that the Party's self-reform is the precondition and the key for carrying forward the social revolution of socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era. The piece has three parts. It first sets out the close link between the two "revolutions" in the history of Chinese revolution and construction, and in the present. It then explains how self-reform guides the social revolution. Finally it proposes ways to advance and deepen self-reform, drawing throughout on quotations from Xi Jinping and Party documents. The central argument is that the two revolutions are mutually reinforcing. In the authors' account, the Party's achievements come from advancing both its own construction and social change in the economy, politics, law, ecology and culture. In the new era, the authors say, the complex and sharp struggles of socialist construction demand a stronger Party, able to meet what they call the "four tests" and "four dangers". Self-reform is said to guide the social revolution in three ways. It secures the leadership foundation, by keeping the Party's purpose of serving the people. It supplies ideological guidance, through campaigns of concentrated education from the Yan'an rectification movement to the recent Party history study. And it forges a leading force in the "critical minority" of leading cadres, through anti-corruption work and the "five qualities" and "eight abilities" required of them. The authors conclude that self-reform must be pursued comprehensively. They call for guidance from Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, and for full implementation of the general requirements for Party building set out at the 19th Party Congress (2017). They also propose concrete measures: strengthening political discipline through the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds, building a culture of integrity, encouraging cadres to take responsibility, and improving supervision mechanisms. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary in early 2022 presented the link between Party building and social transformation.

Upholding the practical logic of theoretical innovation 坚持理论创新的实践逻辑 Hui Zhaoyang This short commentary, originally published in the China Social Sciences Today newspaper on 31 March 2022, takes up one of the "ten upholds" in the Resolution on the Party's major achievements and historical experience over the past century, adopted at the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021). Hui Zhaoyang argues that upholding theoretical innovation is a key reason for the Party's success, because a nation at the forefront of its age cannot do without theoretical thinking and correct guidance. In Hui's account, theory must develop with practice rather than harden into dogma. The article is organised in three sections. The first sets out the vitality of Marxist theory and the innovation that each era requires, citing Engels, Lenin and Xi Jinping. The second traces the Party's century of practice-driven theoretical exploration through revolution, construction and reform. The third discusses how innovative theory guides practice and what is required for the future. Hui's central move is to present Chinese Marxism as a sequence of theoretical achievements, each answering the major questions of its period. These are Mao Zedong Thought, Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents, the Scientific Outlook on Development and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The article describes each as the product of combining Marxism's basic principles with China's concrete conditions, and, under Xi, with fine traditional Chinese culture. It credits them with successive leaps in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Hui further holds that Xi Jinping Thought is open in character, will keep being enriched in the Party's governing practice, and is distinguished by its popular character, practicality, timeliness, creativity and scientific rigour. Hui concludes that, on the path to a modern socialist country and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, the Party must keep using Marxism to observe, grasp and lead the times. The first task, Hui says, is to study and master the Party's innovative theory so that it can be applied flexibly in new practice. Research on Xi Jinping Thought should rest on solid scholarship, be practice-oriented and take an international view, uniting learning with application. Practice and theoretical innovation, the article says, have no end. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated commentary in 2022 presented the lineage of theoretical innovation after the Resolution.

The threefold meaning of "walking our own path" “走自己的路”的三重意涵 Gao Xing This short commentary, published in China Social Sciences Today in March 2022, takes up Xi Jinping's statement at the Party's centenary celebration (2021) that "walking our own path" is the historical conclusion of a century of struggle. Gao argues that the phrase has three layers of meaning: socialism with Chinese characteristics is the correct path, independence and self-confidence must guide its advance, and comprehensive deepening of reform is the way to sustained development. The article proceeds in three sections that match these meanings. It first looks back at failed late-Qing and early Republican attempts at national salvation, then at the Party's revolutionary and socialist history. It then turns to the spirit of independence and the Four-sphere Confidence, and finally to reform and opening up since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Gao contends that earlier reformers such as those of the 1898 Reform Movement and the 1911 Revolution failed because they copied foreign models rather than adapting world experience to Chinese conditions. In the new era, the author says, Chinese modernization rests on the coordinated development of the economy, politics, culture, society and ecology, which avoids treating modernization as merely industrial and instrumental. Gao presents independence and the Four-sphere Confidence as the means of keeping China's destiny in its own hands, and lists four principles for deepening reform: Party leadership, a people-centred approach, development as the first priority, and opening up. Gao concludes that a country should judge its path by whether it resolves the historic tasks it faces, and that China's development achievements show socialism with Chinese characteristics to be a successful path. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the official 2022 narrative links the centenary "historical conclusion" to reform and the Four-sphere Confidence.

The theoretical content and practical orientation of Marxist epistemology 马克思主义认识论的理论内涵与实践旨向 Huang Weijie Writing in a newspaper commentary, Huang Weijie asks how Marxist epistemology can respond to challenges from twentieth-century Western cognitive science. Huang argues that research should consolidate the basic principles of Marxist philosophy and hold to "proceeding from reality in everything" as the fundamental requirement, attending to the concrete historical relation between knowing subject and object of knowledge. The article develops three aspects: the content of the "active theory of reflection", the theoretical value of the claim that practice is the source of knowledge, and the practical orientation of the "second leap" in the movement of cognition. It draws on Marx's 1844 and 1857–58 writings, The German Ideology and Engels, and contrasts Marxism with Anglo-American cognitive science and French structuralist epistemology. Huang contends that Western approaches centre on the individual subject's cognitive structures and drift towards subjective constructivism. Marxism affirms the subject's activity but stresses that the mediating systems, including sense organs, abstract categories and language, are products of social history and practice. Both object and subject are shaped by practice: the sensuous world is a product of industry, and production also produces the subject. The "second leap", from knowledge back to practice, is described as a gap in Western epistemology, which Huang says is therefore confined to speculative debate. Huang concludes that Marxist epistemology should move beyond purely speculative treatments of the subject–object relation and describe their historical relation under concrete conditions. Huang calls for work based on China's concrete practice, so that narrating Chinese experience and telling China's story become an extension of a practice-oriented epistemology. Read the original if you want a brief statement of how a Chinese scholar uses Marx's texts to answer Western cognitive science and to link epistemology with the aim of telling China's story.

A short philological study of the Paris Manuscripts 《巴黎手稿》文献学研究小探 Sheng Fugang This short article, first published in a Chinese newspaper in March 2022, takes up three philological questions in research on Marx's Paris Manuscripts (the 1843–45 economic studies). Its aim is to clarify how the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 relate to the notebook of excerpts known as the Comments on Mill. Sheng argues, drawing on the debate among Soviet, Japanese and MEGA editors, that the interleaved order of writing proposed by Nakagawa Hiroshi and Rabin is the more coherent one. Sheng first describes the structure of the three 1844 manuscripts, most of the second of which is lost. The article then lists the nine excerpt notebooks as published in MEGA1 I/3 (1932) and notes that MEGA2 redistributed them. In MEGA2 IV/2 (1981) seven notebooks stay under the Paris period, while the Lauderdale and Boisguilbert excerpts move to the Brussels notebooks and the Xenophon excerpts are added. The second section reviews the dispute over the order of composition. A closing section turns to alienation, and breaks off after two questions. Rabin (1969) proposed the sequence Manuscript I, then notebooks IV and V (Ricardo, Mill), then Manuscripts II and III. Nakagawa had suggested something similar in 1968. Their reasons include that Manuscript I cites neither notebook and that Manuscripts II and III cite the Comments on Mill. Taubert, editor of MEGA2 I/2, holds that the Ricardo and Mill excerpts came after the 1844 manuscripts. Sheng finds this unpersuasive, because Marx names Ricardo and Mill in the later manuscripts when denouncing the cynicism of bourgeois political economy. Some scholars use this order to argue that the Comments on Mill, with its 'alienation of exchange', surpasses the 'alienated labour' of Manuscript I. In their view Manuscript I remains in Feuerbach's anthropology and has no social-relational concept of species-essence. Sheng questions this by arguing that Feuerbach's alienation was not one-directional or merely negative, since recognising God as human essence reconciles the believer with the species-essence. Sheng adds that Marx's On the Jewish Question had already identified money as the alienated essence of human labour and existence. Sheng concludes that the Nakagawa–Rabin sequence is the internationally accepted account and that the question of whether alienated labour or alienated exchange is the higher form needs reassessing. The text ends abruptly after raising this second question, so the full answer is not developed. Read the original if you work on the textual history of the Paris Manuscripts or MEGA and want a compact, citation-rich guide to the editorial and compositional debates.

Keeping the destiny of China's development and progress firmly in our own hands 把中国发展进步的命运牢牢掌握在自己手中 Sun Laibin This commentary, published in the People's Daily in May 2022, argues that China must keep the destiny of its development and progress firmly in its own hands. Sun Laibin presents "walking our own path" as a historical conclusion drawn from a century of Party struggle and as a requirement for the new journey towards the second centenary goal. The author holds that, whatever risks arise, the Party will lead the people along the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics, upholding independence and self-reliance. The article has three parts. The first reviews the Party's century through four stages: the new-democratic revolution, socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era. It relies on the resolution adopted at the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021). The second part explains why control over China's fate is necessary, and the third sets out what steady progress towards the second centenary goal requires. Sun's central claim is that every achievement of the Party and people came through struggle, not as a gift from others. The author gives three reasons for self-reliance now. Chinese modernization has no ready-made model, since modernization takes more than one form and China's culture, history and national conditions require its own path. Rising risks near the goal of national rejuvenation, in a world undergoing great changes unseen in a century, call for strategic composure. Finally, Sun contends that no nation has become strong by depending on outside forces or copying foreign models, and that the new development pattern, whose essence is high-level self-reliance, secures the initiative in development. The article says China welcomes useful suggestions and learning from others but rejects lecturing from self-appointed "schoolmasters". Sun calls for three commitments: unwavering adherence to Party leadership, described as the defining feature and greatest strength of the system; firm adherence to socialism with Chinese characteristics, avoiding both the "old closed and rigid path" and the "evil path of changing banners"; and strategic composure, including pursuing reform and opening up at a higher level. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the official line on independence, self-reliance and the Party's historical experience was presented to a general readership in 2022.

The basic pattern and development trends of research on "cults" in graduate training A bibliometric analysis of doctoral and master's theses, 1990–2020 研究生培养中对邪教问题研究的基本格局和发展趋势 Cheng Xuejun Li Xuqing Cheng and Li ask how research on xiejiao (rendered "cults" in official English usage) has been distributed within China's graduate education between 1990 and 2020, and where it is heading. Using bibliometric and text analysis, they argue that the field is geographically concentrated, institutionally scattered, thinly staffed and shaped by political events. They frame the study as a response to Xi Jinping's call at the 2021 national religious work conference to build a research force in Marxist religious studies. The sample is 205 doctoral and master's theses (32 doctoral, 121 academic master's, 52 professional master's) drawn from the CNKI and Wanfang databases. The authors analyse them by region, institution, discipline, supervisors and teacher–student lineages, and by five research perspectives: the history of secret sects and "hui dao men"; specific groups; law and policy on prevention and punishment; theoretical study of cults; and the relation to overseas new religions. They also trace changes by decade and degree type. The authors report that Beijing produced 28% of theses, nearly three times Shanghai's share. Output surged after the 1999 Falun Gong incident and the founding of the China Anti-Cult Association (2000), then declined, which they read as academic research responding quickly to current events and public opinion. Only about 3.5% of institutions sustained a research team, and 92% of supervisors guided just one thesis. Lineages rarely go beyond two generations, mainly because graduates move into other work. The authors also find that the leading institution has shifted from Renmin University and Shandong University to the People's Public Security University of China, and that law is becoming the dominant discipline, partly because of the expansion of professional degrees. Cheng and Li conclude that the field lacks a stable team and a developed academic lineage, which they say hinders its institutionalisation. They propose treating the topic as a priority, with special state-funded graduate quotas and international exchange. They also call for stronger supervisor training, policy and funding support for universities and institutes, and a multidisciplinary collaboration network with common core courses. Read the original if you want detailed data on how Chinese universities have trained researchers on this topic, or on how state priorities shape that research.

Firmly establishing a correct view of Party history 牢固树立正确党史观 Wang Guang Writing in 2022, after the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021) adopted its resolution on the Party's history, Wang Guang takes up the question of what outlook should guide the study of the Communist Party's past. The author argues that one's view of history largely determines one's attitude and method towards it. On this basis Wang contends that the Party must firmly establish a "correct view of Party history" grounded in historical materialism, as Xi Jinping has repeatedly stressed. The commentary rests on three arguments for why this matters: a correct view is needed to understand the Party's hundred-year struggle, to reveal historical laws that guide the Party and the country, and to oppose historical nihilism. It draws throughout on Xi Jinping's statements and the plenum communiqué. It places the Party's centenary at the meeting point of the "two centenary goals", linking modern China's suffering with the goal of national rejuvenation. Wang's first claim is that earlier struggles, from the Taiping movement to the 1911 Revolution, failed for lack of scientific theory and an advanced class force, whereas the Party succeeded by integrating Marxism with Chinese realities and traditional culture. The second is that recognising historical law is, in Marxist terms, the dividing line between materialist and idealist history. The author presents the Party's century as a history of exploring and applying such laws, and says Xi's innovations deepened understanding of the laws of Communist Party governance, socialist construction and human social development. Third, Wang describes historical nihilism as exaggerating errors, sensationalising Party history or reading it as gossip, and cites Xi's view that Soviet collapse followed the wholesale negation of Soviet history. Wang reports that since the 18th Party Congress (2012) the Party has set the record straight, neither hiding mistakes because of achievements nor denying achievements because of mistakes, and that nihilism has been firmly curbed. The author adds that more research and more popular forms of communication are needed so that the orthodox history becomes a shared consensus. The piece closes by calling on the Party to follow Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and draw spiritual strength for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated scholars in 2022 framed the official view of Party history and the campaign against historical nihilism.

From national legislation to social cooperation The shift in early modern English utopian thought 从国家立法到社会合作 Wang Chuangchuang Engels, in Socialism: Utopian and Scientific, said that utopian socialists sought to impose an ideal society on society from outside through propaganda and model examples, but he did not examine the history of these two means or how they relate. Wang takes up that gap for early modern England and asks how utopian authors imagined turning an ideal social order into political practice. The article argues that English utopian thought shifted in the late seventeenth century from seeking change through state legislation to building small cooperative model communities. The article proceeds in three parts. The first examines the earlier mode, from Thomas More's Utopia (1515) through Bacon, Burton, Harrington and Gerrard Winstanley. The second traces the rise of the 'little commonwealth' after the Restoration, in Peter Cornelis Plockhoy's 1659 work on the happiness of the poor, John Bellers's proposal for an industrial college, and the 1698 community scheme by 'Philadelphus'. The third explains the change by religious and socio-economic factors. Wang argues that the earlier utopias imagined a legendary lawgiver and addressed kings or parliaments, either as mirrors for princes or as petitions. Their authors did not intend to mobilise the masses. The later schemes were embedded in existing society, funded by wealthy investors and run on joint-stock lines, and they relied on cooperation across classes. Bellers, for example, told the rich that investing was a moral duty, would bring returns and was unavoidable because they depended on the labour of the poor. Wang attributes the turn to the authors' dissenting or Hermetic leanings, the growth of poverty and the defence of private property, which made redistribution by law seem unrealistic. He also points to the rise of joint-stock companies as a model of organisation and fundraising, and to the political instability since the civil war. Wang concludes that, in the context of its time, the small-commonwealth model was progressive in proposing social cooperation as a remedy for poverty. As capitalism developed and class conflict sharpened, appeals to the bourgeoisie to give generously increasingly became utopian in the pejorative sense. Wang notes that small utopian communities became the main form of utopian activity after the eighteenth century. Read the original if you are interested in the pre-history of utopian socialism, early English utopian writers, or the link between joint-stock companies and ideas of cooperative community.

Problems in the study of American atheism and proposed remedies 陈发扬：美国无神论研究存在的问题及对策 Chen Fayang Chen Fayang asks why China needs to study atheism in the United States and what is wrong with the existing research. The article argues that sharpening ideological struggle between China and the United States makes systematic study of American atheism necessary, and that current work is too thin in researchers, content, methods and output. Chen presents the study of American atheism as a way to "know oneself and know the enemy" in that struggle. The article has four parts. It first sets out the rationale, citing recent US legislation on Uyghurs, Tibet and Hong Kong, which Chen describes as ideological interference in China's internal affairs. It then surveys Chinese and foreign scholarship on the origins, definitions and classifications of atheism, on modern figures such as Einstein, and on contemporary American atheists' experiences. It then lists four weaknesses and ends with four matching recommendations. Chen reads American atheists' position as evidence about US ideology. The article cites estimates that atheists are 2% to 14% of the population, and a 2007 Gallup poll in which 53% of respondents would not vote for an atheist president. From this Chen concludes that American claims about freedom and democracy do not hold for atheists. The surveyed studies include work on stigma, marginalisation and the psychological strain of atheists, including atheists of colour. Chen finds few Chinese specialists, many of whom only translate. Chen also doubts that foreign researchers are objective and notes that the research gives little attention to atheism's history since the founding of the US or to the influence of American Marxists. It relies on texts rather than surveys or interviews, and it has produced no monographs. Chen calls for specialised conferences and graduate and postdoctoral research directions to draw in more scholars. The article also asks for work on the historical development of American atheism and its schools, and on its relations with American Marxists. It proposes field interviews and questionnaires among workers, farmers, business owners and students, plus theories borrowed from American researchers, such as minority stress theory. Chen also wants analysis of atheists' difficulties, forecasts of trends, and monographs and reports. Read the original if you want a Chinese view of how American atheism is studied, with many cited authors, and of why it is tied to ideological security.

The core meaning, formation logic and contemporary call of the great founding spirit of the Party 伟大建党精神的核心要义、生成逻辑及时代呼唤 Zhang Guozuo Liu Xinwei Writing in 2022, shortly after Xi Jinping's speech at the centenary of the Communist Party of China (2021), Zhang Guozuo and Liu Xinwei take up the "great founding spirit" of the Party that Xi summarised in four pairs of phrases. The article asks what this spirit means, why it arose and why the new era needs it. Its thesis is that the spirit has four inseparable dimensions, arises necessarily from theory, history and practice, and must be upheld today. The article has three parts. The first sets out the core meaning of the four dimensions: adhering to truth and ideals, putting the original aspiration into practice and shouldering the mission, fearing no sacrifice and fighting bravely, and being loyal to the Party and not failing the people. The second explains how the spirit was formed. The third turns to the present and shows what each dimension requires in the new era. Examples include revolutionary, Korean War, construction-era and new-era heroes, and model Communists such as Wang Jinxi, Jiao Yulu and Lei Feng. Zhang and Liu identify "truth" with Marxism and "ideals" with communism and, for China, socialism with Chinese characteristics. They read the Party's original aspiration and mission as seeking happiness for the Chinese people and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Loyalty to the Party and the people expresses the unity of Party spirit and the people's character. The authors stress that the four dimensions form one whole: without practice, loyalty and sacrifice, "adhering to truth" becomes empty talk. The spirit's formation is explained in three logics. Theoretically, Marxism is scientific, practical, revolutionary and people-centred. Historically, earlier attempts at national salvation failed for lack of scientific theory, firm ideals, devotion and roots among the people. Practically, great revolutionary, construction and reform practice necessarily produces a great spirit, and the later spirits in the Party's "spiritual lineage", such as the Jinggangshan, Long March and Yan'an spirits, derive from it. For the present, the authors argue that adhering to truth and ideals lets the Party resist erroneous trends they name, including historical nihilism, "universal values", neoliberalism and Western constitutional democracy. Putting the original aspiration into practice is needed for the long relay toward national rejuvenation. The fighting spirit is needed for the long, complex struggles that Xi has warned of. Loyalty to the Party and the people is presented as what preserves the Party's advanced nature and purity. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned exposition of how Chinese Party theorists structure and justify the founding spirit, in the framework Xi set out in 2021.

Causes, results, value: a three-dimensional reading of Engels's late study of Christianity 起因·成果·价值：恩格斯晚年基督教研究的三维解读 Yan Yu Why did Engels, in his last years, turn to early Christianity, and what did the turn yield? Writing in Science and Atheism in 2022, Yan Yu argues that the decisive cause was the practical needs of the socialist movement, which runs as a single thread through the whole enterprise. The article places this argument within the National Conference on Religious Work of December 2021 and the call for the sinicization of religion. The article is organised in three parts: causes, results and value. On causes, it discusses Engels's earlier critique of religion, the death of Bruno Bauer in 1882, and the struggles of the 1890s within the labour movement. On results, it examines three works, Bruno Bauer and Early Christianity, The Book of Revelation and On the History of Early Christianity, under three headings: early Christianity compared with socialism, the nature and conditions of religious prophecy, and the formation of a world religion. The value of this work is then assessed for content, method and practice. Yan holds that Engels's comparison of early Christianity with socialism served to defend scientific socialism against Fabianism, reformism, the abuse of 'materialism' as a slogan by the Social Democratic 'Young' faction, and religious-style deception inside socialist currents. Both movements, in Yan's account, arose among the oppressed, but Christian deliverance lies in a beyond, while socialism changes the material world through practice. Engels is also read as tracing prophecy to pseudonymous authorship and the authority of its real authors, and as explaining Christianity's rise through the Roman Empire's dissolution of national religions, the doctrine of redemption through Christ's sacrifice and simplified ritual. Methodologically, Yan credits Engels with moving from religion in general to specific religions and stages, grounded in historical sources. Yan concludes that Engels's late work completed Marxist theory of religion in both thought and practice. The article connects this to present policy: it calls for using Marxist theory of religion to guide religious work, to keep the sinicization of religion and the adaptation of religion to socialist society, and to guard against Western use of religion to divide China. Read the original if you study Marxist theory of religion, Engels's late writings, or how Chinese scholars link classical texts to current religious policy.

A struggle of nation and class hidden beneath religious appearances Marx's critique of Bauer on the Jewish question 隐藏在宗教表象下的民族与阶级之争 Wang Chen This article, published in the journal Science and Atheism (2022, no. 2), re-reads Marx's "On the Jewish Question" (1844) as a reply to Bruno Bauer's 1842 essays. Wang argues that the dispute only appears to be about Judaism versus Christianity. In Wang's reading it is really a dispute over whether nation or class offers the "way out" for human beings, and Marx's critique "substitutes" a class perspective for nationalism. The author sets the debate in 1840s Germany, where nationalism and anti-Semitism were growing. The article has three parts: Bauer's view that "privilege" is the key to the Jewish question; Marx's view that the "Jewish spirit" is the key; and a comparison of the national and class solutions. Wang also draws on theories of the origins of the modern nation, including Benedict Anderson's Imagined Communities, and notes that some foreign scholars cite the text to portray the young Marx as anti-Semitic. According to Wang, Bauer treats Jewish exclusiveness, rooted in religious law, as a "religious privilege" and a "civil privilege" (above all moneylending). Bauer concludes that Jews must give up their religion and national particularity and merge into the new nation-state. Marx replies that after political emancipation religion is a private matter in civil society, so Jews need not abandon their faith to become citizens. The real source of oppression is the worldly "Jewish spirit", meaning practical need, egoism and the worship of money, which Marx finds to be the principle of civil society as a whole. Wang argues that Jews were therefore not opposed to the nation-state but helped drive its formation, and that political emancipation, resting on bourgeois egoism, cannot emancipate them. Wang concludes that, for Marx, the Jewish question can be resolved only by abolishing private property through the proletariat's class struggle, with philosophy and the proletariat joined together. The article then turns to the present. Wang says that because China remains in the primary stage of socialism, the Party must take religious questions seriously. Wang calls for vigilance against foreign forces that invoke religious freedom and narrow nationalism, and for linking the proletariat's historical mission to the Chinese Dream and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, on the basis of the Four-sphere Confidence. Read the original if you are interested in how a Chinese journal on religion and atheism interprets Marx's early writings on nationalism, religion and class, and applies them to contemporary policy.

Continuing to carry forward the spirit of historical initiative through fearless responsibility and great struggle 在无畏担当和伟大斗争中继续发扬历史主动精神 Xu Xiaoming This short commentary, first published in Guangming Daily in March 2022, takes up Xi Jinping's speech at the opening of the spring 2022 training course for young and middle-aged cadres at the Central Party School. Xu argues that Party members, especially leaders, must carry forward a "spirit of historical initiative" by taking responsibility and being willing to struggle. In Xu's account, only this can realise the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The piece first defines historical initiative as the Party's conscious, Marxist-guided effort to transform society on the basis of historical laws. It then surveys the Party's century of history, then turns to present-day shortcomings and the international setting of the early 2020s. Xu's central claim is that responsibility and struggle reinforce each other: taking responsibility tempers the courage to struggle, and struggle shows the capacity to bear responsibility. The article says this pairing runs through the Party's history and its "spiritual lineage", from the Jinggangshan spirit to the anti-epidemic spirit. Xu criticises a minority of cadres who lack both qualities, who avoid major tasks or shy from taking a stand on questions of principle, and says this weakens the Party's fighting capacity. Xu concludes that the Party faces growing risks amid what it calls great changes unseen in a century, protectionism and the pandemic. Cadres are urged to keep "the nation's most important interests" in mind, take the initiative in struggle and pass the spirit on. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Party media framed cadre conduct and struggle after Xi's 2022 Central Party School speech.

Daring to advance theoretical innovation on the basis of practice 勇于推进实践基础上的理论创新 Xin Ming This newspaper commentary, published in Guangming Daily in March 2022, takes \"adhering to theoretical innovation\" as one of the main lessons of the Communist Party of China's hundred-year struggle. Xin Ming argues that it explains both how the Party led the nation from \"standing up\" to \"becoming prosperous\" and then \"becoming strong\", and why Marxism keeps its vitality. Xin's thesis is that theory must be tied to Chinese realities, answer the questions of the age and grow out of practice, so that Marxism is continually adapted to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The article has three sections. The first traces the leaps in the adaptation of Marxism to China, from Mao Zedong Thought through Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents and the Scientific Outlook on Development, to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The second sets these theories against the changing character of each era: war and revolution, then peace and development, then the present period of \"changes unseen in a century\". The third gives examples of how practice since the 18th Party Congress (2012) has produced new theory. Xin's central claim is that Marxism has been applied in China through the Two Integrations: combining its basic tenets with China's concrete realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture. Each stage of theory, in this account, answered the main questions of its time, and the \"Ten Clarifications\" of the new-era thought are presented as a further deepening. Xin then stresses that practice is the source of theory, with examples ranging from the Jinggangshan base area to reform and opening up. For the current era, Xin links the thought's claims on Party leadership, the principal contradiction, whole-process people's democracy, common prosperity and ecological civilization to specific achievements of the past decade. The article also describes Chinese modernization as having created a new form of human civilization and offering other countries a new option. Xin concludes that over a century the Party has kept theoretical guidance and practical exploration in dialectical unity. In this account, the interaction tests Marxism's scientific character and truth, and shows its popular, practical, open and time-bound qualities. The piece is an official-line statement of how theoretical innovation is understood in Party discourse in 2022. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the Party's narrative links the stages of Marxism's adaptation to China with the era-specific questions each is said to have answered.

Walking the new "examination road" well requires always preserving the unity and solidarity of the Party 走好新的赶考之路必须始终保持党的团结统一 Sun Cunliang Writing in Guangming Daily in March 2022, Sun Cunliang takes up the 2021 Resolution on the Party's major achievements and historical experience, adopted at the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee. Sun builds on its statement that "ensuring the unity and solidarity of the Party is the Party's lifeblood". The article argues that, as the Party starts a new "examination road" towards the second centenary goal, keeping its unity is both the key to past success and the basic guarantee of future success. The piece has three parts. The first reviews the Party's history, from the first Party constitution at the Second Congress, through the Zunyi Conference (1935) and the Yan'an rectification campaign, to the Eighth Congress, the reform era and the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The second sets out why unity remains fundamental on the new road. The third lists concrete means of keeping it. In Sun's account, unity guaranteed each stage of achievement: new-democratic revolution, socialist construction, reform and opening up, and the new era. Looking ahead, Sun gives three reasons why unity is the "fundamental guarantee". It rallies all ethnic groups, citing Deng Xiaoping that national unity begins with the unity of the Party and especially its leadership core. It enables the Party to withstand growing external and domestic risks, including what Sun calls ideological bias abroad and economic downward pressure at home. It also allows strategic decisions in the interest of the whole Chinese nation, because in Sun's view the Party has no interests of its own. Sun then names four means: shared ideals and convictions, a tight organisational system, a strong body of members, and iron discipline. Sun calls for study of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, for democratic centralism, and for upholding the Party centre's authority and Xi Jinping's core position through the Two Upholds. Sun also calls for grassroots organisation, strict political vetting of new members, opposition to factions and double-dealing, and strict enforcement of political discipline. Read the original if you want a concise statement, in the official Party-building idiom of 2022, of how unity and centralised leadership were framed as the condition for the Party's next stage of work.

Understanding the deep meaning of "drawing on history to open up the future" 深刻认识和把握“以史为鉴、开创未来”的深厚意蕴 Sang Jianquan This commentary, first published in Guangming Daily on 22 March 2022, explains what Xi Jinping's call to "draw on history and open up the future" involves. Sang Jianquan writes in the wake of the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021), which summed up the Party's major achievements and historical experience over its first century. The author argues that the call can be grasped through three tasks: understanding historical laws, strengthening historical confidence, and taking the historical initiative. The piece is organised under three headings that follow these tasks. The first covers the Party's understanding of the laws governing Communist Party rule, socialist construction and human social development. The second goes through confidence in the path, theory, system and culture. The third turns to the present context of global change and the Covid-19 pandemic. On historical laws, Sang holds that since the 18th Party Congress (2012) the Central Committee has deepened understanding in each of the three areas. It has done so through full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, a revised assessment of the principal contradiction in society, the Belt and Road Initiative, a community with a shared future for mankind and Chinese modernization. On historical confidence, the author asserts that socialism with Chinese characteristics is the only correct path, that Marxism adapted to the Chinese context and the needs of our times has produced the guiding theories, and that the institutional system has proved effective. Culture is described as the basis of the other three forms of confidence. On historical initiative, Sang calls for grasping the main trends of history, locating China's position in the new era and the primary stage of socialism, and seizing opportunities. The author describes the period as one of strategic opportunity in which crisis and opportunity coexist. Sang concludes that studying the Plenum's spirit and Xi's speeches will help the Party and people build a modern socialist country and achieve the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The piece is an authoritative-style interpretation of the Plenum rather than a historical study. Read the original if you want a compact example of how the 2021 history resolution was presented to a general readership in Party media.

Showing the truth-power of Marxism in the unity of theory and practice 在理论和实践的统一中展现马克思主义真理力量 Xue Qing This short commentary, first published in Guangming Daily on 17 March 2022, takes as its starting point a passage in the Party's 2021 historical resolution. The passage says that Marxism will show greater truth-power in China if the Party advances theoretical innovation through new practice and guides that practice with new theory. Xue argues that this expresses the dialectical unity of theory and practice, and that Marxism's truth-power depends on grasping the essence, source and destination of theoretical innovation. The article is organised around three questions: what theoretical innovation is in essence, where it comes from, and where it should go. Each is answered from the standpoint of Marxist epistemology and illustrated with quotations from Marx, Lenin, Mao Zedong and Xi Jinping. On essence, Xue holds that cognition is the active reflection of practice, so innovation must uphold the primacy of practice and also the basic principles of Marxism. These two commitments, in Xue's account, are not in conflict. On source, innovation comes from practice in three dimensions: China's concrete conditions, the world situation, and the future. Xue presents Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era as the product of such practice. On destination, theory must return to practice through the unity of knowing and doing: a true grasp of what is changing and unchanging, and real problem-solving in reform and development. Xue concludes that if the Party keeps Marxism as its guide and continues adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, Marxism will shine more brightly in China. Read the original if you want a compact example of how official commentary frames theoretical innovation in epistemological terms.

The "difference analysis" method of Western "Marxology" and its contemporary reassessment With a discussion of the Marx–Engels relationship question 西方“马克思学”的差异分析方法及其当代反思 Zhao Li Zhang Liang Writing after the bicentenary commemorations of Marx and Engels, Zhao and Zhang argue that the method Western "Marxology" used in the twentieth century, "difference analysis", is still alive. They cite recent work by Norman Levine, Terrell Carver and Gareth Stedman Jones as examples. The authors hold that the method is a legitimate, "neutral" tool of the history of ideas, but that some Western scholars have pushed it past its proper limits. In their view this has a covert negative effect on Marxist research in China and calls for vigilance. The article first traces three stages in the Western use of the method: Sidney Hook's partial analysis of dialectics from the 1930s; the systematic analysis of Maximilien Rubel and Levine from the 1960s; and Carver's hermeneutic version from the 1980s. It then sets out four limits on the method: its premise, its historical limit, its role limit and its human limit. A closing section on each limit ends with the authors' own response to the Marx–Engels relationship question. Zhao and Zhang contend that Western Marxology starts from a "presumption of guilt" against Engels. They accept that two individuals with different backgrounds and styles will differ, and that these differences helped their collaboration. But they say "opposition" theorists inflate such differences into essential ones. The authors also argue that Marx's and Engels's thought developed through three historical periods, so the late Engels, writing after 1883, cannot be set against the earlier Marx. They describe the Marxology of the 1844 Manuscripts as an anachronistic comparison. The two men divided theoretical labour, with Marx on political economy and Engels on science, military affairs and the workers' movement. The authors argue that this division still left them in agreement in spirit and essence. They call the idea that Engels "invented" Marxism a politically motivated conspiracy theory, and insist the question is political as well as academic. On the human limit, the authors defend the Marx–Engels friendship and Engels's editing of volumes II and III of Capital against the doubts raised by Rubel and Carver. They also reject the claim that the friendship rested on financial dependence. They conclude that comparing differences between Marx and Engels is academically legitimate. Such work must, however, begin from a scientific understanding of their relationship, respect historical context, and refuse sensational exaggeration. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist critique of Levine, Rubel, Carver and Hook on the Marx–Engels question, and a view of how Chinese scholars frame its political dimension.

Contemporary Western left research on the middle class: current state and problems 当代西方左翼的中产阶级研究：现状和问题 Zhang Jin This review, published in Foreign Theoretical Trends in 2022, surveys how Western left scholars have studied the middle class and the class structure of contemporary capitalist countries. It starts from the apparent gap between Marx and Engels's claim that class structure tends towards simplification and the multi-layered class picture seen after the Second World War. Zhang's overall verdict is that the work has real theoretical and practical value, but that it is not thorough enough in its class analysis and pays too little attention to the revolutionary side of Marxist class theory. The article has four parts. It first discusses how the rise of the middle class challenged Marxist class theory, including Bernstein, Gorz, Bell, Gouldner, Dahrendorf, and Clark and Lipset. It then reviews classic left theories of the middle class by Poulantzas, Wolff and Resnick, Braverman, Erik Olin Wright, and Barbara and John Ehrenreich. Next it covers recent work on the shrinking middle class, its effects, its political positioning and the growth of precarious employment. It ends with an assessment of the field. Zhang argues that objections based on the middle class's rise misread Marx. In this account Marx did not overlook intermediate classes, and his class analysis is a historical-materialist analysis of exploitation grounded in unequal ownership of the means of production, not an empirical description of class composition. Recent left scholars, in Zhang's summary, document the middle class's squeeze since the 1980s, including the claim that white working- and middle-class anger is redirected towards immigrants and globalization, so that class, race and gender conflicts overlap. They also debate whether the 'precariat' is a new class, as Guy Standing holds, or an expression of heterogeneity within the proletariat, as Antunes and Jonna and Foster argue. Zhang credits these scholars with defending Marxism and with intersectional analysis that helps explain Western collective action. The article nonetheless faults Wright, Zweig, Wolff and Resnick for dividing classes by power, skill or role in surplus-value production rather than by ownership of the means of production. Zhang contends that this leaves them unable to see the middle class's proletarian character and hides the deepest class relations. The article also finds their treatment of the middle class's political and revolutionary role in new social movements shallow. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist overview of Western left class theory, with many names and sources, and an example of how it is assessed against orthodox Marxist class analysis.

The resolute leadership of the Communist Party of China 中国共产党的坚强领导 Song Yuehong Song Yuehong takes up the question of why the Communist Party of China's leadership is, in Xi Jinping's words, the fundamental political guarantee for calmly meeting major risks and challenges. The article argues that Party leadership is a historical necessity and the choice of the people. In Song's account it is the foundation and lifeblood of the Party and state, and it is tied to the interests and fate of all ethnic groups in China. This is a short commentary published in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2022, after the Party's centenary and the 19th Party Congress period. It is organised as five "always" principles: putting the people first, remembering the original aspiration and mission, playing the role of leadership core that oversees the overall situation and coordinates all parties, daring to struggle and being good at winning, and carrying out self-reform. Each section links the Party's historical record, especially since the 18th Party Congress (2012), to its present role. Song contends that the Party's roots, strength and legitimacy lie in the people. In this reading, the people were liberated from oppression through the founding of the new China, and the Party's "people-centred" approach has since produced a moderately prosperous society and a rise in the people's sense of fulfilment and security. The article holds that Party leadership is comprehensive and systematic, covers economic, political, cultural, social, ecological, military, diplomatic and Party-building work, and has been strengthened by improving the institutions of socialism with Chinese characteristics and the system of national governance. Song cites the poverty-alleviation campaign and the response to COVID-19 as proof of the Party's organising capacity. The author presents full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, including the anti-corruption campaign, as the means by which the Party escapes the "historical cycle" and keeps its vanguard character. Song concludes that only by upholding Party leadership can the people be given a better life and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation be achieved. The author maintains that the Party's leadership, its institutions and its self-reform must be sustained over the long term, and that these have enabled the nation's leap from "standing up" to "becoming prosperous" to "becoming strong". Read the original if you want a compact example of how the official case for Party leadership was framed in 2022, in the vocabulary of the new era.

The six shifts in the Communist Party of China's theory of inter-party relations in the new era 论新时代中国共产党党际关系理论的六大转换 Yang Xiaojun Yu Haiqing How has the Communist Party of China's thinking on its relations with foreign parties changed since the 18th Party Congress (2012)? Yang and Yu argue that the four principles of inter-party relations (independence, complete equality, mutual respect, non-interference in internal affairs), set out at the 12th Party Congress in 1982, have entered a stage of "sublimation". They hold that Xi Jinping's call for a "new type of party relations" inherits and develops those principles, and they identify six shifts in the theory. The article first reviews existing research, which stresses four "new" features of the new-era guiding thinking: its theoretical basis, the way it defines party functions, its focus and its value goal. The authors say this work is mostly single-angle and propose a comprehensive reading. They then examine six dimensions: strategic guideline, strategic thinking, premise and foundation, strategic focus, partners and scope, and external communication. A further section analyses the forces driving the changes, and a closing section looks ahead. In the authors' account, each shift moves from a reform-era position to a new-era one. The guideline moves from stressing economic development to stressing political support; thinking moves from integrating into the world to shaping it; the foundation moves from the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence to a "new type of international relations"; the focus moves from non-interference to mutual learning; and the scope moves from bilateral to multilateral ties. External communication moves from "connecting China and the world" to "bridging" them. Three drivers are named: the global governance deficit, the changing world party landscape (the decline of established parties and the rise of populist ones after the 2008 crisis), and the need to turn China's strength into international discourse power. The authors add that the shift in premise is "not absolute", since the Five Principles still matter. Yang and Yu propose three directions. Parties should promote global governance through international party cooperation, rejecting unilateral dominance and building institutional platforms. They should advance the new type of party relations through exchange of governance experience, especially on Party building. And they should use home-hosted platforms organised by the Party to convert national strength into international discourse power. Read the original if you want a detailed Chinese-language account of how Party scholars frame the continuity and change in the Party's foreign-party work since 2012, with the main speeches and summits cited.

Marxist research should treat the study of religion as a discipline equal in importance to philosophy 马克思主义研究应把宗教学作为和哲学 同等重要的学科 Li Shen Li Shen asks why Marxist research should give the Marxist study of religion (Marxist religious studies) the same standing as Marxist philosophy. The article, published in the journal Science and Atheism in 2022, argues that the two are not separate fields. Marxist philosophy grew directly out of German classical philosophy, which Li describes as in effect Germany's religious studies of the day, so that Marxist philosophy is also Marxist religious studies. The article proceeds in four parts. It first examines German classical philosophy as a critique of religion, taking in Kant, Hegel, Strauss, Bauer and Feuerbach. It then turns to Marx's critique of Hegel and the Young Hegelians, and to Marx and Engels's critique of Feuerbach, drawing on texts such as the Contribution to the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right: Introduction, The German Ideology, the Theses on Feuerbach and Ludwig Feuerbach and the End of Classical German Philosophy. A final part draws out the relation between Marxist philosophy and Marxist religious studies. Li contends that many of the best-known philosophical statements by Marx and Engels were first statements about religion. Examples are "man makes religion", religion as "the opium of the people", and Engels's basic question of the relation of thinking to being, which Li reads as first of all a question about religion, since it arises from ideas of soul and the creation of the world. In Li's account, German classical philosophy still kept "a religious tail", with Kant's moral God, Hegel's absolute idea and Feuerbach's religion of love. Marx and Engels therefore had to criticise it, moving from criticising heaven to criticising earth. They also criticised Feuerbach for neglecting revolutionary practice and for treating the human essence as an abstraction rather than the ensemble of social relations. Li holds that historical and dialectical materialism were thus achievements in religious studies as well as in philosophy. Li concludes that Marxist philosophy and Marxist religious studies share one root and one theoretical foundation, and that understanding the former requires studying religion in depth. He cites Ren Jiyu's view that Marx's founders made religious studies a science. Li says Marxist religious studies has long been absorbed into philosophy or not recognised, and so has been underdeveloped in China. He notes that the national religious work conference of December 2021 called for strengthening the discipline, and calls on Marxist research to give it equal weight with philosophy. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese specialist in Marxist religious studies makes the case for the discipline's standing, through a reading of Marx and Engels's texts on religion.

Party leadership as the fundamental guarantee for running universities with socialist characteristics well 党的领导是办好中国特色社会主义大学的根本保证 Sun Liang This short commentary in Guangming Daily (May 2022) responds to Xi Jinping's inspection visit to Renmin University of China. Sun Liang argues that Party leadership is the fundamental guarantee for building universities with Chinese characteristics and a world-class standing. Sun treats it as the most essential feature and most distinctive strength of such universities. The piece first sketches the Party's leadership of higher education across four periods: the new-democratic revolution, socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the years since the 18th Party Congress (2012). It then sets out four ways in which Party leadership supports universities, and closes with practical requirements. In Sun's account, Party leadership provides a soul of conviction, since it secures the transmission of Marxist belief and the study of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. It also provides an institutional foundation, chiefly the presidential responsibility system under the leadership of the Party committee, together with democratic centralism and Party control over direction, cadres, talent and ideology. It supplies a driving force, keeping thought, action and strength unified. And it charts a development path, because Sun, citing Xi, holds that Chinese universities should not copy foreign models. Sun concludes that the Party committee-led presidential responsibility system must be upheld and improved. Sun also calls for stronger grassroots Party organisations, fostering virtue through education as the central task, and ideological and political work throughout teaching. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary frames Party leadership in higher education after Xi's 2022 visit to Renmin University.

The history of the Communist Party of China is a history of self-reform 一部中国共产党史就是一部自我革命史 Zhang Taiyuan This newspaper commentary, written after the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021), asks why the Communist Party of China has endured and grown over a century. Zhang Taiyuan answers that the Party's willingness to carry out self-reform is its most distinctive trait and its greatest strength. On this reading, the history of the Party's cause and the history of its own growth are one and the same: a history of self-reform. The piece opens with Xi Jinping's remarks and the Party's 2021 historical resolution, then proceeds in three steps. It first shows how the Party has demonstrated self-reform in practice. It then turns to criticism and self-criticism as the means by which self-reform is achieved. Finally it takes up the Party's present drive for full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, drawing throughout on Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi. Zhang argues that the trait comes from two sources: the nature of a Marxist party, which must keep adapting to new struggles in pursuit of communism, and Chinese traditional culture, which the author says gives the Party something no other party or political force possesses. The Party's strength is said to have formed in revolutionary history, since every major turning point, from the First United Front to the shift from a planned to a market economy, was achieved through self-reform. A typical form is correcting its own mistakes, and reform and opening up is presented as having drawn its impetus from reflection on earlier errors. Criticism and self-criticism are called both the typical expression of self-reform and the only route to it, and Zhang stresses that the Party must accept supervision by the people rather than reform behind closed doors. Zhang concludes that the Party's self-reform is bound up with its social revolution and decides its rise or fall. The author points to the campaign since the 18th Party Congress (2012) against entrenched ills and corruption, and quotes Xi that the work remains "always on the road" and that weariness must not set in. If the Party keeps up self-reform and preserves its advanced and pure character, the author holds, it will keep its Marxist character and remain invincible. Read the original if you want a concise, official-line account of how Party scholars present self-reform as the key to the CPC's historical success.

"To achieve the complete liberation and independence of the Chinese nation" The Party's accounts of and responses to the September 18 Incident, and their historical significance for national rejuvenation “以求中华民族彻底的解放和独立” Zhang Hao Writing in Guangming Daily in May 2022, Zhang Hao asks how the Chinese Communist Party understood and answered the September 18 Incident of 1931, the Japanese seizure of north-east China, and what that meant for national rejuvenation. Starting from Xi Jinping's description of the incident as the starting point of China's War of Resistance and the prologue to the world anti-fascist war, Zhang argues that the Party saw early on that the incident was historically inevitable. Zhang holds that its statements and policies pointed the way from national crisis towards the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The article draws on Party declarations, resolutions, newspaper editorials and writings by leaders including Mao Zedong, Zhou Enlai, Zhang Wentian, Wang Jiaxiang, Dong Biwu and Qin Bangxian, from 1931 to 1946. It is divided into two parts. The first covers the Party's analysis of why the incident occurred and what it signified. The second covers how Party policy shifted in response. In the first part, Zhang reports the Party's argument that the incident followed from Japan's long-planned continental policy. The sources Zhang cites name several causes: economic crisis in Japan, hostility towards the Soviet Union, the Guomindang's non-resistance, and support from other imperialist powers. Zhang also reports that Party statements, from the 1931 declaration through Zhou Enlai's later essays, treated the incident as the beginning of a second world war and of fascist aggression in Asia. In the second part, Zhang traces a turn from domestic revolutionary war to a national war of liberation. The Party criticised non-resistance and reliance on the League of Nations, moved towards the anti-Japanese national united front, and began a new stage of armed struggle. It also developed the view that patriotism is internationalism applied in a national revolutionary war, and tied this to a world anti-fascist united front. Zhang presents this as the Party's renewed exploration of the path of new-democratic revolution.
