Zhang concludes that the incident, though the first step of a war that brought great suffering, also gave the Chinese nation the chance to stand up. After fourteen years of resistance, which Zhang calls the first complete victory over foreign invasion in modern times, the Party's persistence in fighting to the end is said to have ended a century of humiliation and nurtured new hope of rejuvenation. Read the original if you want a source-based Chinese Communist Party account of how its wartime leaders interpreted 1931 and linked it to national independence and rejuvenation.

The Party's system of leadership institutions continues to be improved 党的领导制度体系不断完善 Li Zhenghua This short commentary, published in the People's Daily in May 2022, takes up a line from the Resolution adopted by the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021): that the system of Party leadership institutions has been continuously improved. Li Zhenghua argues that since the 18th Party Congress (2012) the Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core has given priority to building this system, with many new rules and notable results. The piece is organised in three parts: top-level design around the idea that the Party's leadership system is the country's fundamental leadership system; institutions for upholding the authority and centralised, unified leadership of the Central Committee; and measures to consolidate foundations, build on strengths and address weaknesses. Li reports that the 19th Party Congress (2017) wrote into the Party constitution the principle that the Party leads everything, and that the Fourth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2019) defined the Party's leadership system as the fundamental one. The author lists Party regulations on Central Committee work, local committees, Party groups and reporting of major matters, together with stronger decision-making and coordinating bodies, democratic centralism, Party political building and political oversight centred on the Two Upholds. Li also cites the Party's leadership over the legislature, government, courts, armed forces, enterprises and grassroots organisations, and annual work reports to the Central Committee. Li concludes that these arrangements form a leadership system running from the centre to the grassroots, ensuring the Party's leading role in all kinds of organisations. In Li's account, this has strengthened consistency with the Central Committee and the Party's capacity to govern. Read the original if you want a compact, official-line overview of the Party regulations and institutional measures presented as consolidating Party leadership after 2012.

Providing a fundamental political guarantee for the development of the Party and the state 为党和国家事业发展提供根本政治保证 Xu Weixin Writing in the People's Daily in May 2022, Xu Weixin takes up the first of the 13 areas in which the Party's 2021 historical resolution (adopted at the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee) records achievements of the new era: upholding the Party's overall leadership. Xu argues that this has been one of the most important achievements since the 18th Party Congress (2012) and is the fundamental political guarantee for the continued opening of new prospects for socialism with Chinese characteristics. The commentary has three parts. It first presents theoretical innovations in Xi Jinping's thinking on Party leadership. It then reviews practical results under three headings: a more complete system of institutions, a tighter organisational system, and more sound mechanisms and methods. It ends with three requirements for ensuring that the Party remains a strong leadership core. On theory, Xu presents Xi's claims that Party leadership is the defining feature of socialism with Chinese characteristics and that it must be comprehensive, systematic and holistic, covering every sphere from the economy and culture to national defence, foreign affairs and Party building. Xu singles out the authority and centralised, unified leadership of the Central Committee as the highest principle of that leadership. On practice, the author cites writing the Party's leadership into the Constitution, new Party regulations on propaganda, united front, political-legal and national security work, and reforms creating or upgrading central commissions and leading groups. Xu also lists the strengthening of grassroots organisations, a cadre selection and management system, and requirements for reporting to the centre, political supervision and inspection. Looking ahead, Xu calls for a firm grasp of the decisive significance of the Two Establishes and for the Two Upholds to be put into practice. Xu also calls for keeping a people-centred position, with the Party representing no special interests and working towards common prosperity, and for the Party to play its role of overseeing the whole situation and coordinating all parties. The aim is to mobilise society for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a concise, official-line account of how Party leadership is presented in Party media after the 2021 resolution, including the institutional measures it cites.

The causes of the Soviet collapse, analysed thirty years on 30年后深析苏联解体原因 Vladimir Nikolaevich Shevchenko This text is a Chinese translation of an article by the Russian philosopher Vladimir Nikolaevich Shevchenko, written on the thirtieth anniversary of the Soviet Union's dissolution in December 1991. Shevchenko asks why the USSR collapsed so quickly and argues that the main cause was the degeneration of part of the Party and state elite. External pressure, in the author's account, was an important secondary factor, and the collapse was not historically inevitable. The article opens with Putin's December 2021 remark that the collapse was a tragedy for most Russians, and with his claim that the country lost about 40 per cent of its territory, productive capacity and population. It is organised in three sections: the elite's degeneration as the principal cause; external factors, above all Cold War psychological and informational pressure; and the need to build socialism in line with a country's own conditions and civilisational character. It closes with remarks on nationality policy and on Russia–China relations. Shevchenko holds that the elite judged socialism inefficient, chose Western-style capitalism and used Gorbachev's reforms as cover for a plan to dismantle the system and privatise state property. As evidence, the author cites Aleksandr Yakovlev's own later writings, in which he describes a tactic of using Lenin against Stalin, then social democracy against Lenin, then liberalism against revolutionary spirit. Shevchenko adds that Western Cold War strategy worked on Soviet values and historical memory, and that Soviet ideology had no answer to spiritual needs once consumerism spread from the late 1960s. The author also says reformers ignored the particularities of Soviet socialism and of Russian civilisation, which in this account prizes social justice and spiritual over material needs. Shevchenko contrasts this with the path of reform and opening up and socialism with Chinese characteristics, which the author says Russian Marxists admire as a way of keeping socialist ideals while adapting to national conditions. The article claims that a renewed socialism could have emerged in the USSR had civilisational specifics been respected. It says the Soviet nationalities policy had been a real achievement and that reformers deliberately stirred nationalism. The author notes growing nostalgia, the role of the Eurasian Economic Union in restoring ties, and Russia's close relationship with China. Read the original if you want a Russian Marxist philosopher's view of the Soviet collapse as published in a Chinese journal, or an example of how Russian–Chinese ideological affinity is framed.

China is the protagonist of the world in the twenty-first century 中国是21世纪的世界主角 Egon Krenz This text is a Chinese translation of a commentary by Egon Krenz, the last General Secretary of the Socialist Unity Party of the German Democratic Republic. Krenz argues that China is the leading actor of the twenty-first century, just as revolutionary France was in the eighteenth and the October Revolution in the twentieth. He presents the Communist Party of China's survival and success as a vindication of Marxism after the collapse of the Soviet Union and of his own party. The piece begins as a reaction to the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021), held thirty years after the Soviet collapse. It then moves between three themes: China's achievements and long-term goals, Krenz's own East German experience and the state of present-day Germany, and the foreign policy of the new German coalition government formed in December 2021. It closes with the Western reaction to China and the choice between socialism and barbarism. Krenz holds that socialism with Chinese characteristics results from combining Marxism with Chinese conditions under Party leadership. He describes it as part of the international communist and workers' movement. He credits the Party with defeating poverty and building the world's second-largest economy. He also says no other world leader offers a comparable long-term vision. Turning to Germany, he criticises Foreign Minister Annalena Baerbock's 'values-based' policy and the NATO line towards China. He calls the German frigate's deployment to the South China Sea a provocation. He sets this against Xi Jinping's pledge, at the 19th Party Congress (2017), of a community with a shared future for mankind and of peaceful development. Krenz also says that Western hostility to the Belt and Road Initiative stems from opposition to Communist leadership. Krenz concludes that the harder Western politicians and media vilify China, the more clearly China is on the right path, and he points to its handling of Covid-19 as evidence. Citing Rosa Luxemburg's quotation of Engels, he says China has chosen socialism over barbarism and that other countries will follow. He also argues that China needs military strength to deter imperialist aggression. Read the original if you want to see how a former East German leader interprets China's rise and German policy towards it, or how the Chinese side presents foreign support for the Party's account of its history.

The Sixth Plenum of the 19th CPC Central Committee advances the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation 中共十九届六中全会推动中华民族实现伟大复兴 Yuri Tavrovsky This is a Chinese translation of a commentary by the Russian scholar Yuri Tavrovsky on the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (November 2021). Tavrovsky argues that the plenum matters beyond the problems of the day: its Resolution on the Party's major achievements and historical experience over the past century both reviews the past and sets out a clear course for the future. He presents it as a guarantee that China will reach national rejuvenation by 2049. The article places the 2021 Resolution beside the two earlier Party history resolutions, of 1945 and 1981, each issued before a new breakthrough. It then reviews the stages of the Chinese Dream plan and the Party's renewed stress on "socialism" after the 19th Party Congress (2017). Much of the text turns to the international setting: the Biden administration's policy towards China, the December 2021 "Summit for Democracy", and Russia's position, including a round table at the Izborsk Club. Tavrovsky contends that China met the first-stage targets of its plan on schedule despite the pandemic and what he calls US containment. He cites GDP of 100 trillion yuan, per capita income of 10,000 dollars and the elimination of absolute poverty. He argues that Washington, under neo-conservative influence, sees China's socialist ideology, not its trade surplus, as the main challenge to liberal capitalist hegemony. In his account, a global "anti-China international" is unlikely to succeed: US "democracy" is in crisis, many states tie their prosperity to China, and Russia will not join. Tavrovsky concludes that socialism with Chinese characteristics is becoming the mainstream of world socialism and offers Russia a useful reference as it looks for its own path. He presents China's system as a distinct "people-centred" model, not imposed on others, and supports the plenum's emphasis on defending the Party's overall leadership and Xi Jinping's core position. Read the original if you want to see how a Russian pro-socialist analyst reads the 2021 Resolution against US–China rivalry and Russia's own search for a development model.

Western left-wing scholars' reexamination of media imperialism theory in the digital age 数字时代西方左翼对媒介帝国主义理论的重新审视 Song Xin This literature review surveys work from the 2010s onwards in which Western left-wing scholars revisit media imperialism theory, the body of thought that dominated international communication studies in the 1970s and early 1980s. Song argues that these scholars defend the theory against claims that it is obsolete, extend it through the critique of digital labour, and sketch new proposals for reforming the media sphere. Song's own verdict is that the work is valuable but remains shallow in places. The article has three main parts. The first covers the defence and revision of the theory: replies to critics, debates over its scope, and the question of whether media play a leading role in present-day imperialism. The second turns to labour, covering the international division of digital labour and the dispute over whether the labour theory of value can explain unpaid user activity on platforms. The third examines reform proposals, from public values on internet platforms to socialist public-service media. The scholars discussed include Colin Sparks, Christian Fuchs, Kaarle Nordenstreng, Antonio Casilli, Adam Arvidsson, José van Dijck and Graham Murdock. Song reports that the scholars reject the view, associated with Munawar Sabir, that social media have neutralised media imperialism, and argue that platform monopolies and infrastructure still serve capital. On scope, Nordenstreng, Ampuja and Callinicos contend against Sparks that imperialism combines economic competition between capitals with geopolitical competition between states. Fuchs tests Lenin's five features of imperialism and concludes that information is important but not dominant, so one can speak of the imperialist character of media without calling the new imperialism media imperialism. Fuchs also answers Arvidsson by arguing that unpaid work, from slave labour to platform use, is still exploited, and that digital production forms a global web of interdependent exploitation, which in his view extends exploitation to platforms rather than ending the labour theory of value. On reform, Song sets van Dijck's multi-level, EU-centred proposals for public values against Fuchs's argument that genuine public-service media require overthrowing capitalism through the united class struggle of communication workers. Song concludes that the scholars expose exploitation in transnational media value chains but do not penetrate to the depth of imperialist practice, and that their alternatives are somewhat utopian yet reasonable in part. In Song's assessment, their work effectively defends imperialism theory, enriches Marxism and offers a framework for understanding contemporary media imperialism. Read the original if you want a map of Western left debates on media imperialism, digital labour and platform power, as seen from a Chinese Marxist perspective.

The forms, course and lessons of the evolution of the Communist Party of China's discourse on long-term governance 中国共产党长期执政话语演进的形态、历程与启示 Yang Binbin Yang Binbin asks how the Communist Party of China (CPC) has talked about its own long-term governance (长期执政) over the past century, and what that vocabulary reveals. The article argues that the discourse is a key part of Party political language and records a historical change in the Party's view of governance: its grasp of the laws of ruling, its summing-up of experience and its growing capacity. Yang notes that the 6th Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021) listed how to build a Marxist party in long-term power as one of the major questions answered by Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The article has three parts. The first sets out the discourse's basic forms: long-term governance as a concept, as a body of propositions and judgements, and as a mission. The second traces its history through three periods: socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the new era. The third draws lessons for how Party discourse should be used and built. Yang draws on speeches and Party documents from Jiang Zemin to Xi Jinping. Yang argues that the concept moved from a descriptive account of a Party already long in office to a normative demand that it stay in power. It first appeared in a Jiang Zemin speech on corruption and bureaucratism and was later developed into terms such as the 'long-term governing party'. Propositions such as long-term governance as a 'test', rule by law and the 'historical cycle' problem are said to show deepening understanding, as are judgements such as 'corruption is the greatest threat' and 'divorce from the masses is the greatest danger'. Yang then presents long-term governance as a political mission with three aspects: awareness, resolve and capacity. The article contrasts the CPC with Western bourgeois parties, for which office is said to serve particular interests. Across the periods, Yang describes a shift from theoretical proposition to practical task, then to system-building, and finally to the Party's self-reform and full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. Yang draws three lessons. Long-term governance discourse should guide the Party's political leadership, ideological influence and organisational strength, in part by raising the political ability of the 'key minority' of officials. It should also be built into a coherent system of concepts, discourse and theory that explains the strengths of China's institutions, and Yang recommends standardising the phrase 'long-term governing Marxist party'. Finally, it should win popular recognition through education in Party history and by presenting the Party's rule as people-centred, scientific and modern. Read the original if you want a close, Party-internal account of how the vocabulary of long-term rule was formed and how Chinese scholars propose to use it.

New means of current US ideological infiltration of China and how to respond 当前美国对华意识形态渗透的新手段及其应对 Liu Jianhua Writing in 2022 in the Journal of Huaqiao University (Philosophy and Social Sciences), Liu Jianhua argues that ideological infiltration is a habitual US instrument for maintaining hegemony and that, as China's strength has grown, Washington has added new and more concealed forms of it. The article's thesis is that these new means threaten China's ideological security and must be recognised and countered actively. Liu treats this as a quiet war alongside the trade, technology, opinion and military contests the author attributes to the United States. The article has four parts. It first presents infiltration as a long-standing US method, citing the Soviet collapse, Japan and South Korea, the Middle East and 'peaceful evolution' directed at China. It then identifies four new means: figurative (具象化), hyped-up (炒作性), inducement-based (诱导性) and academic infiltration. It goes on to describe the harm each does, and ends with countermeasures for each. Liu defines figurative infiltration as the spread of US values through films, consumer brands and symbols, aimed at young people along a path of inducement, identification and isomorphism. Hyped-up infiltration, in this account, uses media dominance to amplify China-related incidents and narratives such as the 'China threat' or 'forced labour in Xinjiang' as 'discourse traps'. Inducement-based infiltration is said to use money and other benefits to corrupt officials and opinion-formers, with Xinjiang textbooks and the 2019 Hong Kong unrest given as examples. Academic infiltration, which Liu calls the deepest, works through exchanges, textbooks and 'index traps' that present the West as superior. Liu claims these erode the education in core socialist values, weaken citizens' political discernment, endanger political security and risk repeating the Soviet experience. For countermeasures, Liu proposes giving mainstream ideology a more tangible, sensory form and telling China's story well, and standing firm in the contest over international discourse, following Mao Zedong's call to 'cast away illusions and prepare for struggle'. Liu also calls for stronger rule-of-law measures, including new 'anti-infiltration' and 'ideological security' laws. Liu further proposes building a philosophy and social science system with Chinese characteristics, guided by Marxism, that learns from foreign work without copying it. The author concludes that the struggle will be long and complex. Read the original if you want a Chinese official-academic view of how US ideological influence is perceived and what policy responses are proposed.

The significance for our times of upholding the Party's overall leadership 坚持党的全面领导的时代意蕴 Guo Qingsong Writing in Guangming Daily in May 2022, Guo Qingsong takes up Xi Jinping's formulation at that year's Two Sessions of "five musts" (five paths that must be followed) and "five favourable conditions" for China's development. Guo notes that upholding Party leadership comes first in both lists. The article's thesis is that in the new era, sustaining socialism with Chinese characteristics and the cause of the Party and state requires upholding the Party's overall leadership. The commentary is organised in six numbered sections. Each presents Party leadership as the necessary basis for one goal: building a Marxist party in long-term power; upholding and developing socialism with Chinese characteristics; building a modern socialist country in all respects; achieving common prosperity; realising the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation; and promoting a community with a shared future for mankind. Guo draws mainly on Xi Jinping's statements, the 19th Party Congress (2017) and the 2021 Party resolution on history. Guo argues that the Party has written "the Party leads everything" into its constitution and Party leadership into the state constitution, giving overall leadership an institutional form. In Guo's account, the Party has given two answers to the historical cycle of rise and decline: popular supervision, as Mao Zedong said at Yan'an, and now the Party's self-reform. Guo holds that institutions are fundamental and long-term, so strengthening the system of Party leadership lets the country meet risks by keeping direction, balancing interests and pursuing reform. On common prosperity, Guo says it is a political as well as an economic matter. It requires Party-led work on regional, urban–rural and income gaps, stronger redistribution, "traffic lights" for capital, and regulation that harnesses its positive role while curbing its negative effects. For the Chinese Dream, Guo says the Party secures the Chinese path, spirit and strength. Guo concludes that, amid what the Party calls great changes unseen in a century, Party leadership ensures that China pursues its own rejuvenation within humanity's shared development. In Guo's account, the Party advances a globally shared approach to governance and a more just world order. The piece is a representative statement of the official case for Party leadership as a precondition for each national goal. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Party-school commentary in 2022 linked Party leadership to modernization, common prosperity and foreign policy.

Leading the great social revolution through the great self-reform 以伟大自我革命引领伟大社会革命 Liu Jingbei This short commentary in the People's Daily takes up the tenth of the "ten clarifications" in the resolution on the Party's century of struggle adopted at the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021): leading the great social revolution through the Party's great self-reform. Liu argues that the formula has a Marxist theoretical basis, rests on the Party's historical experience and marks a defining feature of governance in the new era, and calls for study and implementation of Xi Jinping's strategic thinking on the Party's self-reform. The article is organised in three parts, each beginning with the same phrase: the theoretical logic in Marx and Engels, the lessons of the Party's hundred years, and the practice since the 18th Party Congress (2012). It closes with a short call to action for the road to the second centenary goal. Liu reasons that Marx and Engels described the abolition of class exploitation as the deepest social revolution, one that does not occur spontaneously and needs a real social force. An advanced party can play that role only if it arms itself with theory, stays close to the people, clears away negative phenomena and keeps discipline, so a Marxist party must carry out self-reform as well as social revolution. In Liu's account, the Party's history shows the two reinforcing each other. Since 2012, full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, covering political, ideological, organisational, conduct, discipline and institutional building, is said to have removed serious hidden dangers and found a way to escape the historical cycle of rise and fall. Liu concludes that on the "new road to the test" towards the second centenary goal, the Party must keep up its self-reform and improve its capacity for self-purification, self-improvement, self-renewal and self-advancement, so that it does not change in character. Read the original if you want a concise, officially framed statement of how Party-building discourse links self-reform to the wider revolutionary project.

Full and rigorous self-governance of the Party as a great practice of the Party's self-reform in the new era 全面从严治党是新时代党的自我革命伟大实践 Li Zhiyong Writing in the People's Daily in May 2022, Li Zhiyong takes up the question of how the Communist Party of China can stay vital as a long-ruling Marxist party. Li's answer is that full and rigorous self-governance of the Party is the necessary path. In the article's account, it is the Party's self-reform in practice, and it allows the "great self-reform" to lead the "great social revolution". The commentary opens with Xi Jinping's formulations and has three sections. The first assesses what the policy has done since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The second sets out the lessons Li draws from the experience. The third lists tasks for the new journey towards the second centenary goal. It is a Party-building piece, not a scholarly study, and it relies on official wording throughout. Li makes three main moves. First, Xi's statements on the subject are said to have enriched Marxist Party-building doctrine by answering what kind of long-ruling party to build and how. Li says the results include a reversal of earlier laxity, an "overwhelming victory" in the anti-corruption struggle, a stronger Party organisation and a fuller system of Party regulations. Second, Li calls this the "second answer" to the "cave question" of escaping the historical cycle of rise and fall. Mao Zedong's first answer was to let the people supervise the government. Third, Li draws lessons: uphold the Party's overall leadership; let political development lead; treat ideological work as foundational; implement the Party's organisational line; keep up work on conduct, discipline and anti-corruption; and govern the Party through institutions and regulations. Looking ahead, Li calls for planning self-governance within the overall cause of the Party and the state, with political development in the lead. Li also urges resolving problems that people complain about most, such as those in education, healthcare, pensions, the environment and food and drug safety, and keeping a strict tone for the long term with responsibility firmly placed. Read the original if you want a compact example of the official line on Party self-governance, as stated by a senior Party-building official shortly before the 20th Party Congress.

Overseas studies of the Chinese Communist Party's revolutionary history in Chinese translation since reform and opening up: a review 改革开放以来海外中国共产党革命史研究译著评介 Zhang Deming This is a review of foreign scholarship on the Chinese Communist Party's revolutionary history before 1949, as it has reached Chinese readers in translation since reform and opening up. Zhang notes that domestic scholars have paid some attention to overseas studies of Party history but have not systematically surveyed the translated works on the revolutionary period. The article sets out to map these translations, identify their research hotspots and discuss how to deepen engagement with them. The first part surveys translated works by period and theme: the Party's founding (1921–27), the Jiangxi Soviet period and the Long March, the War of Resistance against Japan, and the civil war. It then covers the Party's foreign contacts, the role of the Comintern and Soviet advisers, and general studies of the revolution and of Marxist historiography. A long section treats biographies of Mao Zedong, including two series of translated overseas Mao studies, and studies of Li Dazhao, Qu Qiubai, Zhou Enlai, Deng Xiaoping and others. The second part draws out characteristics of this scholarship, and the third offers reflections and recommendations. Zhang argues that overseas work offers models worth learning from. It draws on interdisciplinary methods, pays close attention to detail and comparison, and uses archives held abroad in Russia, Japan and elsewhere. Authors such as Schwartz, Meisner, Schram, Goodman, Selden and Pepper combine micro and macro perspectives, place events in wider contexts and study local cases. Zhang also reports their new arguments, such as Pepper's view that land reform mainly overthrew the rural elite. Zhang cautions that some works lack primary Chinese sources and are shaped by ideology, Western-centrism and Cold War thinking. Some, in Zhang's judgement, contain serious misreadings or deliberate vilification, and Zhang cites Wang Rongzu's typology of such errors. Zhang identifies gaps in the translation effort: too many English-language titles, too few from other languages and regions, dated selections, uneven translation quality, and many representative works still untranslated. Zhang calls for specialised institutions and multilingual researchers, and for timely rebuttals of errors and of historical nihilism in foreign journals and conferences. Further proposals are to translate Chinese scholarship abroad, to buy more foreign books and journals, to revive a Party-history digest of overseas research and to create dedicated funding and a database. Read the original if you want a bibliographic guide to Chinese translations of foreign works on the CCP's pre-1949 history, or an example of how Party-history scholars assess overseas research and propose to respond to it.

Gaining a deep grasp of the intrinsic laws of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party 深入把握全面从严治党的自身规律 Zhou Jingqing This commentary, published in Guangming Daily in May 2022, asks how the Communist Party of China should understand and follow the laws that govern its own strict self-governance. Zhou Jingqing starts from Xi Jinping's statement that strict governance has its own laws, and that this holds all the more for a large, long-established party. The author's thesis is that, since the 18th Party Congress (2012), the Party has advanced full and rigorous self-governance of the Party by following these laws, and that it must keep doing so in the new great project of Party building. The article is organised around six paired principles, each presented as one dimension of the governing law. They are: preserving tradition together with innovation; problem orientation together with value orientation; treating symptoms together with root causes; comprehensive advance together with breakthroughs at key points; popular supervision together with the Party's self-reform; and ideological Party building together with institutional governance. Each section pairs a statement of principle with Xi Jinping's formulations and examples of Party practice since 2012. Zhou makes three main moves. First, the author traces strict governance from the early call for an "iron discipline" Party through the Gutian Conference and the Yan'an rectification to its entry into the Party constitution, to show continuity of thought and line. Second, Zhou ties the problem-oriented method to the aim of winning popular support, and describes anti-corruption work as combining "not daring, not being able and not wanting to be corrupt", with pursuit of "tigers", "flies" and "foxes" alongside institutional reform and ideals. Third, Zhou frames the Party's self-reform and popular supervision as the first and second answers to the "historical cycle" question Huang Yanpei put to Mao Zedong in 1945. Zhou also stresses that ideological education and rule-making need each other, citing 3,615 Party regulations in force as of 1 July 2021. Zhou concludes that these paired principles together make up the laws of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, and that following them gives strong political guidance and a guarantee for the new journey. The text presents ideological Party building and institutional governance as complementary, with neither effective alone. Read the original if you want a concise, official-line account of how Chinese Party scholars set out the principles behind the post-2012 Party-building and anti-corruption campaign.

Showing the logic of China through the story of the Communist Party of China 通过中国共产党的故事彰显中国之理 Zhang Xiaomeng This short commentary in Guangming Daily (9 May 2022) responds to Xi Jinping's inspection visit to Renmin University of China. Zhang Xiaomeng argues that telling the story of the Communist Party of China well is a key way to show the logic behind China's path, and that philosophers and social scientists should take this up. The piece offers three reasons, each in its own section. Telling the Party's story supplies China's wisdom and proposals for the questions of the age; it is integral to building a world-class university with Chinese characteristics; and it helps the world decode China. On the first point, Zhang says the Party's century of experience is a shared spiritual asset of humanity. In the author's account, Chinese modernization is not a copy of earlier paths and has created a new form of human civilization, which can help the international community build consensus at a historic crossroads. On the second, Zhang holds that a university's world-class standing depends on whether it can merge answers to the questions of China, the world, the people and the times, and balance national character with global outlook. On the third, Zhang argues that understanding China requires understanding the Party, and that international communication should draw on Chinese culture as the basis of a new external discourse, seeking consensus through equal dialogue. Zhang concludes that scholars should use the strengths of philosophy and the social sciences to tell the Party's story in depth and with innovation, and so raise the global influence of the Party. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Party-affiliated academics link international communication, university building and Chinese modernization.

The century-long evolution of the Communist Party of China's slogans guiding the direction of the youth movement A historical study based on May Fourth commemorative texts 中国共产党引领青年运动方向口号的百年演变 Guo Xiang Guo Xiang asks how the slogan that the Communist Party of China (CPC) uses to steer the youth movement has changed over a century, and what those changes show. The author treats the slogan as a compressed "signature symbol" of the Party's discourse and argues that each change reflects the Party's mission and discursive system of the time. The thesis is that the slogan has moved through three discourses, revolutionary, reform and strong-country, while keeping a constant structure of political, social and mission-oriented guidance. The study draws on speeches by Party leaders at May Fourth anniversaries and on May Fourth editorials in the People's Daily, beginning with Mao Zedong's 1939 speech "The Orientation of the Youth Movement". It is organised by period. The first part covers the new-democratic revolution and the era of socialist revolution and construction. The second covers reform and opening up, and the third covers the new era. The author notes that earlier research on May Fourth commemoration has paid little attention to these slogans. Guo argues that "integration with the workers and peasants" had a dual meaning before 1949. It mobilised student and intellectual youth, whom Mao classed as petty-bourgeois, to organise the masses. It also required them to learn from workers and peasants and to overcome their own vacillation. After 1949 the signified shifted towards training youth to be both "red and expert", and during the Cultural Revolution the slogan was reduced to ideological remoulding. In the reform era it became "integration with practice and with the people", and from 1999 "two upholds": upholding Party leadership and advancing with the people's great practice. In the new era, Guo says, the slogan centres on struggle for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and a community with a shared future for mankind. "Struggle" replaces "practice" as the key word, which the author reads as expressing the Four-sphere Confidence in plainer, more popular language. Guo concludes that the slogans always centre on the Party's mission, record the development of its ideological discourse, and express constant commitments to Party leadership and putting the people first. The referents of "youth" and "the masses" have widened, and a world-oriented guidance has been added in the new era. The author argues that identifying these patterns builds historical consciousness and helps Party youth work today. Read the original if you study CPC discourse, youth policy or May Fourth commemoration and want the textual evidence, including word-frequency tables, behind the slogan's changes.

On Mao Zedong's original contributions to Marxist philosophy 论毛泽东对马克思主义哲学的原创性贡献 Zhao Shifa Zhang Hao Zhao Shifa and Zhang Hao ask in what sense Mao Zedong's philosophical thought is an original contribution to Marxist philosophy. They write against dogmatist and empiricist denials of this originality, and against Western-centric views that reject a distinctively Chinese path to modernity. Their thesis is that Mao's contribution was not ordinary theoretical innovation but originality in the strict sense. In their account it achieved the first historic leap in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, in its philosophical dimension. The article has three parts. The first defines originality and sets out the substance of Mao's contribution. The second surveys its content: Mao's theory of modernization and his critique and remaking of the core ideas of Western capitalist modernity, namely science, democracy, freedom, equality and fraternity. The third discusses its theoretical and practical significance, including for Party-building and the international spread of Chinese discourse today. The authors define originality as building on predecessors, not copying them, and as speaking one's own words through "continuing" or "countering" earlier theory. They also count an originality of theoretical thinking, in which new experience from practice is abstracted into theory. Mao's work shows this in content (the universality and particularity of contradiction, practice and cognition, seeking truth from facts, new-democratic theory) and in form (making Marxist philosophy "speak Chinese" through everyday formulations). It also shows it in transcending dogmatism and empiricism. The central claim is that Mao reworked each Western modern ideal. He treated science as seeking truth from facts, democracy as people's democratic dictatorship and self-criticism, and freedom as knowledge of necessity and transformation of the world. He tied equality to labour and the fight against bureaucracy, and replaced "fraternity" with serving the people wholeheartedly. The authors reject Western readings of Mao as a voluntarist or as a nationalist who was not truly Marxist. The authors conclude that Mao's contribution enabled the modern enlightenment of the Chinese people, laid the theoretical basis for a path of modernization different from the West's, and supports the Party's theoretical innovation today. They also argue it offers a method for countering Western ideological pressure and for communicating Chinese discourse, including in building a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic case for Mao's philosophical originality, including his treatment of the Western ideals of science, democracy, freedom, equality and fraternity.

Views of patriotism in British society 英国社会的爱国主义观 Chen Dan This article asks how patriotism is understood in Britain, where, the author notes, it is a sensitive topic and attitudes differ between groups. Chen Dan argues that three groups hold distinct positions. The government and mainstream politicians value national identity and, at times, openly promote patriotism. Scholars, teachers and some media commentators are cautious or sceptical. Ordinary people rarely voice patriotic feeling in public, though it surfaces on particular occasions. The article is organised in three parts: politicians, then scholars, schoolteachers and media, then the general public. It draws on British legislation and policy such as the 2002 Nationality, Immigration and Asylum Act, citizenship ceremonies from 2004 and a 2008 education proposal. It also cites statements by Gordon Brown and Labour MPs, debates in the philosophy of education, studies of teachers' practice, and opinion surveys from 2002 to 2020. On politicians, Chen holds that government policy aims to build national belonging and loyalty to the Crown, and that the terrorist attacks of the early 2000s, including the London bombings of July 2005, strengthened this concern. Some Labour MPs, facing falling support, now urge a 'progressive patriotism', while parts of the Labour left once avoided the subject. Among scholars, Chen reports little consensus on the legitimacy of patriotic education. Michael Hand and others fear it may foster exaggerated claims or exclude non-British pupils, and they recommend teaching patriotism as a controversial issue. Teachers, in Chen's account, mostly avoid or doubt the subject. Surveys show that people are increasingly reluctant to express patriotism in public, that older people are more patriotic than the young, and that identity varies across the four nations. Pride in the British Empire is also reported. Chen adds that feeling surfaces at events such as the 2012 Olympics and in worry about Brexit, the pandemic and political leadership. Chen concludes that patriotism is a contested subject in Britain: officials stress national identity, scholars and commentators are wary, and the public is reserved but can be stirred. The author presents British patriotism as tied to national unity, to disputes over Britishness and to public anxiety about the country's future. Read the original if you want a descriptive, survey-based overview of British attitudes to patriotism, with many references to British sources, written from a Chinese Marxist-studies perspective.

The logical progression of Lenin's understanding of socialism 列宁认识社会主义的逻辑进程 Zhao Pei Lenin's views on socialism shifted sharply between 1917 and the early 1920s, and some of them appear to contradict one another. Zhao Pei asks whether a consistent logic runs through these changes. The article argues that it does: in each phase Lenin started from the concrete reality of economically and culturally backward Russia, and his conclusions changed as the tasks changed. Zhao holds that clarifying this logic is necessary for understanding Lenin's thought as a whole and for reflecting on socialist practice. The article follows three stages. The first covers the period after the February Revolution, when Lenin pressed for a socialist revolution against opposition from other parties and from within the Bolsheviks. The second covers the years after October 1917, with the Brest-Litovsk peace, foreign intervention, civil war and "war communism". The third covers the New Economic Policy adopted in 1921 after the Tenth Congress of the Russian Communist Party (Bolsheviks). A closing section draws out three general features of Lenin's cognitive path. Zhao reads Lenin's call to continue the revolution as resting on the crisis of dual power, hunger and war, not on any claim that Russia was ready for socialism. Seizing power was a precondition for moving towards socialism, not socialism itself. After the revolution Lenin stressed that building a new economic base was harder than defending power. Zhao presents war communism as a measure forced by war, and the turn to a food tax and the New Economic Policy as a response to the crisis of 1920–21. Lenin then accepted that direct transition had failed and that markets and "state capitalism" could serve as intermediate links, with the proletarian state supervising and regulating private trade. Zhao argues that because Lenin's premise was backwardness, whereas Marx and Engels assumed fully developed capitalism, his conclusions differed from theirs. Zhao counts as his innovations the possibility of a socialist revolution winning first in a backward country and the idea that a ruling Communist Party must learn to use the market. Zhao concludes that Lenin's thought is consistent in its logic although its conclusions changed. Zhao also names a limit: Lenin continued to treat the market economy as capitalist and outside socialism, which Zhao says produced an incompatibility between market and socialism and lies behind the eventual ending of the New Economic Policy. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly account of how Lenin's views developed from the 1917 revolution to the New Economic Policy, and how Chinese writers frame his treatment of markets and socialism.

Making Party history study and education regular and long-term by following the mass line well 在走好群众路线中推动党史学习教育常态化长效化 Liu Tongfang Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2022, Liu Tongfang takes up the Central Committee General Office's opinion on making Party history study and education regular and long-term. The article argues that this can be achieved only by following the Party's mass line well in the new era. Liu presents the mass line as both the lesson of the Party's history and the practical route by which study of that history is turned into results. The piece has three parts. The first sets out why the people are the foundation of the Party's founding, flourishing and strengthening. The second argues that following the mass line is a necessary requirement of regular, long-term history education. The third identifies three areas in which effort should be concentrated in the new era. In the first part, Liu says the Party's roots, lifeblood and strength all lie in the people. The author points to the growth from a small party of a few dozen members to one of more than 95 million, and treats this as evidence that popular support explains its successes. The second part gives three reasons for the requirement: it expresses the Party's nature and purpose and the character of a Marxist party; it serves the Party's original aspiration and mission and its governing capacity; and it preserves the Party's vanguard character and purity and secures its governing position. Liu warns that advanced status and ruling status are not permanent, and that losing touch with the masses endangers them. The third part calls for work in three areas: firm awareness of the Party's purpose and better work style, including the eight-point regulations; putting the people-centred philosophy of development into practice and consolidating the "Doing practical things for the people" campaign; and strengthening grassroots governance and institutions. Liu concludes that the unity of knowing and doing is what matters most for regular, long-term history education. Study results must become real action in the service of the people. By taking root among the people and relying on them, the Party can consolidate its governing base and advance towards the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a representative example of how Party-history education is linked to the mass line and to grassroots work-style and governance requirements in 2022.

The theoretical evolution and practical explorations of the Spanish Socialist Workers' Party 西班牙工人社会党的理论演进与实践探索 Zhang Min How has the Spanish Socialist Workers' Party (PSOE) adjusted its guiding ideas as conditions changed over its 142 years? Zhang argues that the party, the first in Spain founded by the working class and the first to spread Marxism on the Iberian Peninsula, has creatively applied Marxist theory to Spanish conditions. In the author's account, it has repeatedly renewed itself in theory, opposed American-style neoliberalism and upheld fairness and equality. The article is organised around the three eras in which the party has governed since winning the 1982 election: the González era (1982–1996), the Zapatero era (2004–2011) and the Sánchez era (2018 to the present). For each, Zhang describes the guiding ideology, the main policies in economic, social and foreign affairs, and the reasons the government later lost support or faced difficulty. Zhang's central move is to present each leader's ideology as a response to the previous period's failure. González's pragmatic "Gonzalism" moved the party from radicalism to moderation, treated Marxism as a non-dogmatic tool, and pursued Europeanization, accession to the European Community, a welfare system and a global diplomatic outlook. Corruption scandals and recession ended it. Zapatero turned to republicanism and "civic socialism", drawing on Rawls, Barber and Pettit, and expanded gender equality, immigrant rights and historical memory of the Franco period. The author says his continued neoliberal economic policy and the 2008 crisis undermined this, and that leniency toward regional autonomy fed nationalist demands. Sánchez, facing a fragmented party system, advanced "social patriotism", formed the first left-wing coalition government with Podemos in 2020, and introduced a pandemic relief package, the "four Spains" green and inclusive agenda, and a government accountability report. Zhang concludes that across these periods the party has sought a fair socio-economic system and a development path suited to national conditions, which in the author's view supplied a practical basis for building a modern state and a globally oriented foreign policy. The article ends cautiously, noting that the pandemic and the Russia–Ukraine conflict leave the party facing serious challenges in consolidating power. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic overview of how PSOE ideology has been characterised across its governing periods, or an example of how Chinese scholars present European social democracy.

A full grasp of the theoretical content and epochal significance of advancing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation through Chinese modernization 全面把握以中国式现代化推进中华民族伟大复兴的理论内涵和时代意义 Yan Xiaofeng Writing in 2022, Yan Xiaofeng takes up the second of the "ten clarifications" in the Resolution on the Party's century of struggle, adopted at the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021). That clarification names the general task of upholding and developing socialism with Chinese characteristics as socialist modernization and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, to be pursued through Chinese modernization. Yan argues that the formula is a concise statement of that task and a guide for the new journey towards the second centenary goal. The article has three parts. The first examines the organic unity of socialist modernization and national rejuvenation, tracing it through the Party's four historical periods. The second presents the Chinese modernization path as the necessary road to rejuvenation. The third sets out the significance of the formula for the adaptation of Marxism to China, for the leap from "standing up" and "becoming prosperous" to "becoming strong", for developing countries, and for socialism worldwide. Yan's central claim is that modernization and rejuvenation are two descriptions of one process, not two tasks. Modernization is the core content and necessary stage of rejuvenation, while rejuvenation is modernization's fundamental purpose. Chinese modernization is thus the route, driving force and support of rejuvenation, and rejuvenation is its theme and vehicle. Yan holds that the Chinese path is a socialist path, essentially socialism with Chinese characteristics. Following the Resolution and Xi Jinping, the article says this path resolves problems of Western modernization: capital-centred development, polarization, materialism and external expansion. Yan says it creates a "new form of human civilization" with material, political, spiritual, social, ecological and human dimensions, and a community with a shared future for mankind. Yan concludes that the formula is an important component of the new leap in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, and the basic guide to becoming strong. It also offers developing countries an option other than Westernization or surrendering sovereignty. Yan adds that success in modernization would strengthen the appeal of socialist ideology and the credibility of the socialist system against capitalism, contributing to the "two rejuvenations" of nation and socialism. Read the original if you want a detailed Party-theory account of how Chinese modernization was tied to national rejuvenation in the period just after the 2021 Resolution.

Fully implementing the Party's theory of religious work in the new era 全面贯彻新时代党的宗教工作理论 Zhu Xiaoming This article, published in Studies on Marxism in late 2021, responds to the National Conference on Religious Work of December 2021, which formally put forward the "Party's theory of religious work in the new era". Zhu Xiaoming argues that scholars must study and apply this theory in full, grasping its core meaning, its spirit and its practical demands, and use it to strengthen the discipline of Marxist religious studies. The article has three parts. The first places the theory in relation to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, to the Party's earlier theory of religion, and to the Marxist view of religion. The second sets out the "nine musts" and eight issues that Zhu says need correct handling. The third reviews the history and present state of Marxist religious studies in China, from Ren Jiyu's work in the 1980s to recent textbooks and seminars. Zhu's central claim is that the theory combines individual freedom of religious belief with the Party and government's social-level education, management and guidance. "Fully" means guarding against loosening the latter or neglecting the former. Zhu distinguishes the essence of religion (illusory) from the essence of religious work (mass work), and holds that neither claim cancels the other. Zhu also separates religion's individual character, a private choice, from its social character as organised groups subject to law. Calls to "let go" of religion are said to rest on ignoring the second. Zhu presents sinicisation of religion and rule-of-law management as paired levers, and describes foreign religious infiltration and Western use of the "religion card" as risks. The article also treats atheism and theism as a contest in the ideological sphere. It asks Party members to uphold and actively propagate Marxist atheism, answers three objections to such propaganda, and says it should not target religious believers or take place in religious venues. Zhu concludes that Marxist religious studies must be built on theory, drawing on Ren Jiyu's tradition. The author notes a drift towards theologisation and Westernisation in the 1990s and says recent conferences, textbooks and courses show renewal. Read the original if you want a detailed account of how a Party-affiliated scholar of atheism interprets the 2021 religious work line, including its treatment of atheist propaganda and Marxist religious studies.

Total subsumption: a new feature of exploitation under platform capitalism 总体吸纳：平台资本主义剥削的新特征 Wu Jing Marx distinguished formal and real subsumption of labour under capital. Wu Jing asks how this pair of concepts can be extended to platform capitalism, where digital technology has altered labour, value creation and the relation between capital and society. The article argues that platform capital achieves a new stage, "total subsumption", in which it absorbs not only production-sphere labour but also social risk and the public sphere. The article has three parts. It first analyses the platform as a form that is formally decentralised but strongly centralised in practice, drawing on Schumpeter, Harvey, Deleuze and Negri, and Srnicek. It then examines the gig economy as a deepening real subsumption of labour, citing the 2020 UK Supreme Court Uber ruling and Deleuze and Guattari on machinic servitude. The last part sets out two expressions of total subsumption: financial capital's control over industrial capital, and capital's absorption of publicness, discussed with Zuboff and Stiegler. Wu contends that Deleuze's and Negri's optimism about the internet's decentralisation belongs to a pre-platform age. In Wu's account, platforms monopolise data and algorithms, and users who generate the data have no knowledge or ownership of it. Gig workers face ambiguous employment status, lack contracts and unions, and become subordinate to algorithms, so that absolute and relative surplus-value exploitation occur together. Wu finds Hardt and Negri's call to extend real subsumption to society too broad to capture platform capital's hierarchy of capital forms, and proposes total subsumption as the more precise concept. Venture capital funds loss-making platforms in order to profit in financial markets, and algorithmic prediction shapes user behaviour and social relations, which Wu links to Zuboff's "instrumentarianism". Wu concludes that platformisation has become the key principle of economic control, creating a seamless space of power. The author says it brings weaker privacy, diluted individual expression and loss of workers' freedom of choice, which accelerate platform expansion but also add uncertainty to it. Read the original if you work on platform capitalism, the gig economy or Marx's subsumption concepts and want to see how Deleuzian and Western Marxist sources are combined in a critique of digital exploitation.

Mao Zedong's six assertions on what the Communist Party of China "lives on" 毛泽东关于中国共产党“靠什么吃饭”的六个论断 Wang Jin Wang Jin takes up a set of colloquial formulas in which Mao Zedong explained what the Communist Party of China "eats by", that is, the basis of its success. The article identifies six assertions: the Party lives on the truth of Marxism-Leninism, on seeking truth from facts, on science, on solving problems correctly, on honesty, and on summing up experience. Wang argues that, read together, they point to a single theme: the Party advances by continuing its self-reform and strengthening its own building. The article is written for the centenary of the Party's founding (2021) and is organised as six sections, one for each assertion. Each section ties the phrase to the occasion on which Mao used it, such as the 1942 talk "Oppose Stereotyped Party Writing", the 1954 remarks on the 1911 Revolution, and a 1965 conversation with Cheng Siyuan. Wang then illustrates it with episodes from the revolutionary, socialist-construction and reform periods, including the Xunwu investigation, the 1962 Seven Thousand Cadres Conference and "On the Ten Major Relationships". Wang's main move is to give each phrase a concrete meaning. "Truth of Marxism-Leninism" means making Marxism the guiding ideology of the Party and the state. "Seeking truth from facts" is presented as the living soul of Mao Zedong Thought, and Wang says the Party's setbacks came from departing from it. "Science" is read as acting on objective laws through investigation and research. "Solving problems correctly" is linked to relying on the masses and the principle "from the masses, to the masses". "Honesty" covers modest conduct, truthful reporting, and admitting and correcting errors, with Mao's self-criticism in 1962 as the example. "Summing up experience" covers learning from Chinese history, the Soviet Union and the Party's own record. Wang concludes that the six assertions share one essence: the Party relies on self-reform and on strengthening itself. This spirit of turning the blade inward is said to have driven the great social revolution and the Party's achievements in revolution, construction and reform. Revisiting them is meant to help build a Marxist party that is resolute, has the people's support and is ready for self-reform. Wang also ties this to carrying forward socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era. Read the original if you want to see how Party scholars turn Mao's colloquial sayings into a framework for Party building, with the historical episodes each saying is attached to.

The inherent value of the "ten upholds" historical experience “十个坚持”历史经验的内蕴价值 Huang Rongsheng This commentary, published in Guangming Daily in April 2022, takes up the "ten upholds" (ten adherences) of historical experience summarised in the Resolution on the Party's major achievements and historical experience adopted by the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021). Huang Rongsheng asks what values are embedded in these ten lessons. The author argues that they form a unified, mutually connected system that helps answer what the Communist Party is, what it is to do, why it has succeeded and how it can keep succeeding. The piece is a short essay organised under four numbered headings. Each heading names one value or function of the ten lessons: the fundamental guarantee of the success of the cause of the Party and the people; the root of the Party's seizing the historical initiative; the fundamental path by which the Party stays at the forefront of the times; and the source of strength that keeps the Party invincible. Each section draws on episodes from the Party's history, from the revolutionary period to the years after the 18th Party Congress (2012). In the first section, Huang holds that the Party's leadership is what ultimately explains success at every stage, from overthrowing the "three mountains" to socialist construction, reform and the period since 2012. The second section presents struggle, including the Korean War decision and the response to COVID-19, as the way the Party keeps the initiative. The third treats self-reform as the Party's second answer to the "historical cycle" question, after the "cave dialogue" answer of people's supervision. Huang lists measures since 2012: theoretical education, correcting work styles, discipline, and anti-corruption work. The fourth section holds that independence and self-reliance, grounded in Marxism and traditional culture, produced the path of Chinese modernization. Huang concludes that history repeatedly shows these lessons to be decisive: only by upholding Party leadership, struggle, self-reform and an independent path can the Party remain the strong leadership core of national rejuvenation. The text is an official-style interpretive commentary, not an analytical study. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Party-affiliated scholars in 2022 explained the ten historical lessons and linked them to episodes of Party history.

A study of the Anti-Christian Movement of the 1920s 1920年代非基督教运动研究 Sun Qian Sun Qian examines the Anti-Christian Movement that broke out in 1922 and argues that it was, in essence, a patriotic anti-imperialist mass movement launched and led by the early Chinese Communist Party. In the author's account, Chen Duxiu, Li Dazhao, Yun Daiying and other early Communists led the anti-Christian, anti-religion and education-rights movements. The article holds that this leadership prepared the Party, in theory and in practice, for handling religious questions later. The article has two parts. The first sets out why the movement should be read as Party-led: how the Party organised young people through the Socialist Youth League, how the movement served the Party's anti-imperialist and anti-feudal aims, and how Marxism served as its intellectual weapon. The second part draws lessons for the present, on Party leadership of youth, on religious work in relation to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, and on developing a religious theory with Chinese characteristics. Sun draws on Party congress resolutions, League documents and writings by early Communist leaders. Sun argues that the target was never Christianity alone. Citing the Party's second and third congresses (1922, 1923), Sun shows that the Party treated the churches as a pioneer of imperialist economic, political and spiritual aggression, and used the campaign to mobilise patriotic youth. Early Communists also applied a historical-materialist view of religion, tracing its social roots and its dependence on the economic base. They judged its social role dialectically and rejected its promotion. They also developed ideas of freedom of belief, which includes freedom not to believe, separation of religion and education, and self-run Chinese churches. Sun concedes that excessive sharpness and a failure to distinguish ordinary believers from reactionary clergy initially narrowed the movement, but says the Party soon corrected this and sought a united front that would seek common ground on anti-imperialism while setting aside differences of belief. Sun concludes that the movement still offers guidance under Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The author calls for strengthening Party leadership over youth and for arming students with Marxist religious theory in university courses. Religious work, Sun says, should serve the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, national security and ideological security. The author also proposes upholding and developing socialist religious theory with Chinese characteristics, including the "five characteristics" of religious questions. Read the original if you want to see how a Party-affiliated journal in 2022 presents the 1920s anti-Christian campaign as a precedent for current religious policy.

In defence of atheism From the perspective of Kai Nielsen 为无神论辩护 Yang Lei Yang Lei presents the case for atheism made by Kai Nielsen (1926–2021), a Canadian Marxist philosopher and contemporary advocate of atheism. The article asks how Nielsen defends atheism in a secularising but still religiously confused culture. Yang's answer is that Nielsen offers a coherent philosophical case: the concept of God is incoherent, morality does not rest on belief in God, and religion works as an ideology that should be shaken off. The article opens with Nielsen's biography (a vague Protestant upbringing, conversion to Catholicism, later study of anthropology and philosophy) and his main works on religion. These include Contemporary Critiques of Religion, An Introduction to the Philosophy of Religion, Atheism & Philosophy and God and the Grounding of Morality. It then draws mainly on the essay collection Atheism & Philosophy and is organised in three sections, followed by a short closing discussion. The sections cover the falsity of the concept of God, the claim that morality cannot be built on faith in God, and escape from the spell of religious ideology. In the first section Yang reports Nielsen's argument that statements such as 'the world has an infinite, eternal creator' can be neither verified nor falsified, so they are not factual statements and the core of theistic religion is incoherent. Yang adds that, for Nielsen, revelation and religious experience are unreliable. Nielsen also asks why one authority should be accepted rather than another, and he rejects agnosticism as well as theism. In the second section, the good must be understood independently of God. Power and creative ability do not show goodness, and cruelty remains wrong even if God commands it. Morality exists to adjudicate fairly between human interests and needs. The third section treats religion as an ideology that, in Nielsen's view, fosters submission and defers hope to heaven. Yang links this to Marx's critique of religion and to d'Holbach, and cites Nielsen's remark that the richer our concept of God, the poorer our concept of man. Yang concludes that, for Nielsen, morality is independent of religion and people can find meaning in love, friendship, knowledge and self-respect without God. Yang concedes that parts of the collection sound somewhat positivist and empiricist. Even so, Yang holds that Nielsen's philosophical scrutiny of religious belief deepens understanding of atheism and of the nature of faith. Yang ends by arguing that only the scientific atheism of Marxism can dispel religious superstition and reveal the world's materiality and objective laws. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist-academic introduction to Nielsen's philosophy of religion and to how his arguments are used to support scientific atheism.

"Explaining religion through history": Ren Jiyu's understanding of historical materialism and its use in the study of religion “用历史说明宗教” Kong Fanxi Kong Fanxi examines how the philosopher and religion scholar Ren Jiyu (1916–2009) understood historical materialism and applied it to religion. The article argues that Ren's guiding principle, "explaining religion through history" rather than history through religion, grew out of his turn to Marxism after 1949. Kong holds that this principle laid the foundation for a Marxist study of religion in China. The article begins with Ren's intellectual path: his study of the classics, his part in thought reform and land reform, and his 1956 break with Confucianism. It then looks at three fields of Ren's work: Buddhism (the Collected Essays on Han–Tang Buddhist Thought and the three-volume History of Chinese Buddhism), Daoism, with Ren's changing readings of Laozi, and Confucianism, which Ren treated as a religion. A short conclusion pulls these together. On Buddhism, Kong reports that Ren set three principles: religious questions must be placed on a real social footing, ideas must not be treated in isolation, and individual figures must not be overstated against the whole historical process. Applying the base–superstructure relationship, Ren read Buddhism's fortunes as tracking Chinese feudal society. Doctrines that suited the economic base, such as Chan and Tiantai, thrived, while the Faxiang school, transplanted unaltered from India, withered. His Laozi research shows the difficulty of applying the theory. Ren moved from calling Laozi materialist to calling him idealist, and then rejected both labels as imposed later. He drew the lesson that historical materialism means concrete analysis, faithful to what ancients left unclear, and attentive to regional culture such as that of Chu. On Confucianism, Ren derived its religious character from the features of Chinese feudal society. He held that Confucian thought was reworked twice, under the Han and the Song–Ming. He also held that Neo-Confucianism matched the "essence" of religion, the relation between humans and the divine, as well as its outward forms, which he said included Confucius as founder and the doctrine of "heaven, earth, ruler, parents, teacher". Kong concludes that Ren's understanding deepened through concrete research. Kong presents it as a model for combining Marxism's basic principles with fine traditional Chinese culture and for advancing the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context. It also points the way, Kong says, toward a Marxist discipline of religious studies with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a detailed account of Ren Jiyu's Marxist methods in Buddhist, Daoist and Confucian studies, or of how Chinese scholars assess the origins of Marxist religious studies.

Engels's critique and transcendence of Feuerbach's view of religion 恩格斯对费尔巴哈宗教观的批判与超越 Zhao Gaiping Wang Fan Zhao Gaiping and Wang Fan ask how Engels, in criticising Feuerbach, developed a historical-materialist view of religion. They argue that Engels's critique set out the nature, origin, development and eventual disappearance of religion from the standpoint of historical materialism. In their account, this sublated and went beyond Feuerbach and marked the maturity of Marxist religious theory. The article follows Engels's moves in four sections, drawing mainly on Ludwig Feuerbach and the End of Classical German Philosophy, Anti-Dühring and The German Ideology. It first credits Feuerbach with turning religion's "inverted world outlook" from God-centred to human-centred. It then treats Engels's critique of Feuerbach's "new religion of love", of the claim that religious change determines history, and of Feuerbach's inability to find a way to remove religion. A short conclusion draws implications for religious work in China today. The authors argue that Engels praised Feuerbach for showing that God is a projection of alienated human essence, but called him a materialist "below" and an idealist "above". Feuerbach's "abstract man" and religion of love, they say, ignore class society and the social relations of production. Engels replaced this with real individuals acting in history. He also reversed Feuerbach's claim that religious change drives history: using the histories of religion in general and of Christianity in particular, the authors show religion shifting with social conditions and class struggle. Criticism of heaven must therefore become criticism of earth, and theology must give way to politics. On the disappearance of religion, the authors hold that it will fade only when real social relations stop confronting people as alien forces. They list three conditions drawn from Engels: public ownership of the means of production, a great development of productive forces, and a higher ideological and cultural level among the masses. It cannot be abolished by administrative order. They add that China is in the primary stage of socialism, so religion will long persist. They call for developing the economy, raising cultural levels, managing religion by law, guarding against illegal religious activity and pursuing the sinicization of religion. Read the original if you want a close Chinese reading of Engels's texts on Feuerbach and religion, and the policy conclusions drawn from them.

Several issues in building Marxist religious studies 马克思主义宗教学建设若干问题 Jia Runguo This text is a speech by Jia Runguo, published in Science and Atheism (2022, no. 1), given at a seminar co-hosted by the Institute of World Religions, Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, and the Chinese Society for the Study of Religion. Jia presents the seminar as a sign of a high degree of theoretical awareness about advancing Marxist religious studies in the new era, and offers five basic reflections on how the field should be built. The speech moves through five headings: the essence of Marxist religious studies, its distinctive character, its foundations, the key to building it, and the way to complete it. Jia draws on Marx's 1844 introduction to the critique of Hegel's philosophy of right, on the history of religious studies in the People's Republic, and on Xi Jinping's 2016 symposium on philosophy and social sciences. Jia argues that Marxist religious studies is the disciplinary form of the Marxist view of religion, which Jia summarises as five components (religion's essence, origins, forms, functions and policy) and characterises as scientific atheism. Its distinctive character, in Jia's account, is that of a socialist political science of religion, since Marx and Engels' critique of religion led into their critique of politics and economics. Religious studies should therefore observe religion politically and correct what Jia calls tendencies towards theologisation and Westernisation. Jia holds that its basis is the principles of religious studies together with histories of the major religions, and that the two representative current textbooks on the principles of religious studies have diluted the Marxist view of religion, while the Buddhism, Christianity and Islam histories from the early reform era are outdated. Jia concludes that textbooks are the key lever for building the discipline, academic and discourse systems, because nearly three decades of research progress have not been matched in teaching materials. Jia proposes a nationally organised, centrally funded five-tier textbook system: Marxist views of religion, Marxist atheism and principles; histories of the major religions and of atheism; critiques of Chinese and foreign theology and Western religious theory; general histories of Chinese and world religion; and religious anthropology, sociology, psychology and politics. Read the original if you want to see how a senior Chinese scholar sets out the political and pedagogical agenda for Marxist religious studies in the new era.

Carry forward the spirit of historical initiative and travel well the new-era road of "taking the exam" 发扬历史主动精神 走好新时代赶考路 Li Hongwei This short commentary in Guangming Daily takes up the call by General Secretary Xi Jinping, at the opening of a spring 2022 training course for young and middle-aged cadres at the Central Party School, that Party members and leaders should carry forward the "spirit of historical initiative". Li Hongwei argues that this spirit is a valuable asset formed over a century of Party struggle. In Li's account, it shows historical consciousness, confidence, responsibility and creativity, and it requires acting proactively in the face of opportunities, difficulties and risks. The piece is organised in three sections that follow Xi's formula: seizing opportunities without hesitating or waiting; confronting difficulties without shifting responsibility or evading them; and responding actively to risks without shrinking back or dodging. Li draws on classical Chinese sayings, the Book of Changes, the Party's history, and the Fourteenth Five-Year Plan proposals. A short closing passage calls on cadres to throw themselves into the new journey. On opportunity, Li argues that opportunities and crises are dialectically united and can turn into each other. Seizing them requires strategic and systems thinking and the ability to recognise, respond to and initiate change. The author describes the present as a period of important strategic opportunity amid "changes unseen in a century" and the pandemic, and links it to Chinese modernization and a community with a shared future for mankind.
