On difficulty, Li invokes the Marxist view that contradictions are universal and recounts the Party's achievements across revolution, construction, reform and the new era, naming model figures such as Wang Jinxi, Jiao Yulu and Zhang Guimei. On risk, Li calls for vigilance against "black swan" and "grey rhino" events, bottom-line thinking, balancing development and security, stronger risk-prevention mechanisms and readiness for struggle. Li concludes that history favours the resolute and does not wait for the hesitant, and that the Party must therefore vigorously uphold the spirit of historical initiative to win greater victories on the new journey. The text is a hortatory piece aimed at cadres, and it shows how the Party's leadership frames historical agency and risk management in 2022. Read the original if you want a compact example of how official commentary translates Xi's call for "historical initiative" into guidance for officials.

Drawing wisdom and strength from the Party's century of struggle 从党的百年奋斗历程中汲取智慧和力量 Hu Jinyan This commentary, published in the People's Daily in April 2022, asks how the Communist Party of China should draw on its century of struggle as it begins a new journey. Hu Jinyan argues that this requires grasping three interlinked logics of the Party's hundred years, historical, theoretical and practical, in order to understand why the Party has succeeded in the past and how it can keep succeeding. The stated aim is to work towards the second centenary goal and the Chinese Dream of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The piece takes as its basis the Resolution on the Party's major achievements and historical experience adopted at the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021), and quotes Xi Jinping throughout. After a short introduction, it has three sections, one for each logic. The historical section runs from the Opium War through the 1911 Revolution to the Party's founding; the theoretical section covers the successive stages of adapting Marxism to China; the practical section reviews achievements from the Party's founding to the present, including 2021 economic figures. On the historical logic, Hu holds that after the Opium War China became semi-colonial and semi-feudal, earlier struggles failed, and the Party gave the nation new leadership. The conclusion drawn is that without the Party there would be no new China and no national rejuvenation, and that Party leadership is the fundamental guarantee of that goal. On the theoretical logic, Hu stresses the Party's success in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, tracing it from Mao Zedong Thought through Deng Xiaoping Theory to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The article presents the latter as a product of the Two Integrations. On the practical logic, Hu describes the Party's self-reform as leading social revolution, and cites GDP of 114 trillion yuan and per capita GDP above 12,000 US dollars in 2021. Hu concludes that the Party must pass on and develop its successful experience on the "new road to the examination". For this the article calls for understanding the significance of the Two Establishes, strengthening the Four Consciousnesses, and carrying out the Two Upholds. It also calls for upholding Xi Jinping Thought as guidance. Read the original if you want a compact example of how the official narrative of the Party's centenary was presented to a mass readership in 2022.

Grasping the three-fold meaning of the decisive significance of the "Two Establishes" 准确把握“两个确立”决定性意义的三重意蕴 Niu Jun This commentary, published in Guangming Daily in April 2022, takes up the 2021 Party resolution on the Party's century of struggle, which says that establishing Xi Jinping as the core of the Central Committee and of the whole Party, and establishing the guiding role of Xi Jinping Thought, are of decisive significance. Niu Jun argues that this judgement has three layers of meaning and should serve as the fundamental political guide for upholding and developing socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era. The article is organised under three headings. It presents the "Two Establishes" as a requirement of Marxist party-building, as a conclusion drawn from the Party's hundred-year history, and as a necessary guide for the practice of socialism with Chinese characteristics. On the first point, Niu cites Marx, Engels and Lenin on the need for leaders and authority, and on the role of theory in guiding action, to argue that a mature, stable leadership core and a guiding theory mark a mature Marxist party. On the second, Niu traces the Zunyi Meeting, the Seventh Party Congress and Mao Zedong Thought, the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978) and Deng Xiaoping's stress on a core, and then the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). In Niu's account, upholding the Party's core and the authority of the Central Committee, while advancing the adaptation of Marxism, is a principal reason for the Party's successes. Niu concludes that, as the world's largest governing party, the Party needs a core with high prestige and a Central Committee with high authority to meet major risks and challenges. Party members and cadres are called on to strengthen the "four consciousnesses", practise the Two Upholds, and strengthen political development, theoretical study and the Party's self-reform. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Party commentary justifies the Two Establishes historically and doctrinally.

Writing a new chapter of Marxist political economy 书写马克思主义政治经济学新篇章 Liu Yuanchun Liu Yuanchun, writing in the People's Daily in April 2022, takes up one passage of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era: its "clarification" of the basic economic system, the market–government relationship, the new development stage, philosophy and pattern, high-quality development, and coordination of development and security. Liu argues that this passage reflects a deep understanding of the laws of China's economic development. In Liu's account it makes an original contribution to the political economy of socialism with Chinese characteristics and writes a new chapter of Marxist political economy. The commentary is a short theoretical exposition that takes the components of the passage in turn. It covers the basic socialist economic system, the "decisive role" of the market, the triad of the new development stage, the new development philosophy and the new development pattern, then high-quality development, and finally development and security. It closes with economic results since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Liu's central claim is that each component answers a specific theoretical or practical problem. The basic economic system (public ownership as the mainstay, distribution according to work as the mainstay, the socialist market economy) is said to go beyond capitalist logic by guarding against polarisation, class opposition, monopoly and recurrent crisis, while avoiding the defects of the traditional planned economy. Letting the market play the decisive role in allocating resources while the government plays its role better is presented as China's answer to a worldwide economic puzzle, with the Party's formulation shifting from a "basic" to a "decisive" role. Liu also argues that high-quality development is a general requirement for all regions and for the long term, and that security and development are "two wings of one body", each the precondition of the other. Liu concludes that the thought has been proved scientific, truthful, people-centred and practical, citing GDP of 114 trillion yuan in 2021 and per capita GDP above 12,000 US dollars. Liu urges unity around the Party Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core and guidance by this thought. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary frames Xi's economic thought as an advance in Marxist political economy.

Pathways for converting the institutional strengths of Party leadership into high-quality development effectiveness 党的领导制度优势转化为高质量发展效能的实现路径 Huang Qisong This newspaper commentary, published in 2022, asks how the institutional advantage of leadership by the Communist Party of China can be turned into effective governance that delivers high-quality development. Huang Qisong argues that, in the face of what the article calls changes unseen in a century, the key lies with the Party. Only by converting this institutional advantage into national governance capacity, Huang contends, can high-quality development be achieved at root. The piece is organised around five lines of action, each with its own sub-heading: Party building as guidance, self-reform, comprehensive deepening of reform, the new development philosophy, and a people-centred approach. It draws throughout on Xi Jinping's statements, the Fifth and Sixth Plenums of the 19th Central Committee (2020 and 2021) and the Party's centenary speech. Huang's first move is to treat high-quality development as a requirement covering the economy, politics, culture, society and ecology, which in the author's view only the Party's overall leadership can coordinate and unite into a joint force. Second, Huang presents the Party's self-reform as both an essential attribute of a Marxist party and a driving force of development, requiring the removal of conservative attitudes and of institutional obstacles. Third, the article links reform and opening up to the new development philosophy, citing GDP growth from 367.9 billion yuan in 1978 to 114.4 trillion yuan in 2021 as evidence of reform's results. It states that high-quality development is development that applies the philosophy of innovation, coordination, green development, openness and sharing, and that it requires a new development pattern. Huang closes by stressing that high-quality development must benefit the people. The author calls for attention to the changing principal contradiction, to improving livelihoods, to coordinated regional development, and to linking poverty-alleviation achievements with rural revitalisation and common prosperity. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated scholars in 2022 framed Party leadership as the institutional basis of the high-quality development agenda.

Review of recent overseas theoretical debates on common prosperity 近期海外关于共同富裕的理论热点述评 Zhang Xiaoshuang This review, published in Foreign Theoretical Trends in early 2022, surveys English-language discussion of common prosperity after Xi Jinping's August 2021 speech to the Central Financial and Economic Affairs Commission. Zhang finds three main features: researchers treat a historically rooted idea as a new Chinese concept; neoliberal objections reveal a cognitive bias about China; and the world's left sees the pursuit of common prosperity as a response to worsening global inequality and as a practical advance for the socialist movement. The article has three parts. The first covers how overseas scholars and think tanks define the concept's historical meaning, its significance for the present and its possible paths. The second examines neoliberal readings, notably George Soros and others the author describes as market fundamentalists. The third turns to left-leaning and critical voices, including Michael Hudson, John Ross, Martin Jacques, Thomas Piketty and Stephanie Kelton, who present common prosperity as a Chinese proposal on global inequality. On the concept, Zhang reports David Bandurski tracing it to 1953 and arguing that the post-1978 stress on letting some get rich first redefined it, while Bert Hofman reads it as a response to rising inequality since the 2013 Third Plenum. Observers see it as answering three tasks: curbing the disorderly expansion of capital, enlarging the middle-income group, and reinforcing Party leadership. On paths, Hofman contrasts European-style redistribution with policies that make market outcomes more equal, while Nicolas Berggruen and Nathan Gardens propose pre-distribution through universal basic capital. Zhang calls Soros's opposition ideological and the neoliberal critique a display of cleverness, and argues that neoliberalism has produced widening inequality. Left scholars, in the article's account, deconstruct the American narrative and place common prosperity in a continuous history from Mao Zedong through Deng Xiaoping to Xi Jinping. Zhang concludes that, in serious overseas scholarship, common prosperity is increasingly seen as a responsible Chinese solution to inequality, and that the neoliberal reaction shows the contest over discourse rather than any settled analysis. The author also reports that overseas observers remain divided on how it will be implemented and that the answer must be sought in actual policy action. Read the original if you want a guide to who in the English-speaking world has written on common prosperity, and how a Chinese scholar sorts and evaluates these views.

The Communist Party of China's contributions to world socialism over the past century 百年来中国共产党对世界社会主义的贡献 Yan Rong Writing in 2022, after the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021) adopted its resolution on the Party's major achievements and historical experience, Yan Rong asks what the Communist Party of China's century of struggle has meant for world socialism. The article takes up one of the resolution's five historical significances, that the Party's struggle has deeply influenced the course of world history. Yan argues that the Party has contributed to world socialism in four areas: practice, theory, institutions and culture. The article is organised around these four contributions. The first section traces three paths the Party explored: the road of new-democratic revolution, the road of socialist transformation and construction, and the road of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The second covers the theoretical results of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, from Mao Zedong Thought through the theoretical system of socialism with Chinese characteristics to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The third examines the institutional system, and the fourth the culture the Party has built. Yan argues that each contribution rests on independent exploration suited to China's conditions. In practice, the Party's encirclement of the cities from the countryside is presented as a development of Marxism-Leninism. The Party is also said to have survived the collapse of the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe and to have refuted the "end of history" thesis. Institutionally, Yan holds that leadership by the Communist Party, the people's congress system and the guiding position of Marxism in the ideological sphere are fundamental institutions. Citing the Soviet case, Yan contends that weakening Party leadership and Marxist guidance leads to failure. Culturally, Yan describes a fusion of fine traditional Chinese culture, revolutionary culture and advanced socialist culture, which gives the Party a distinct spiritual lineage. Yan concludes that the Party has answered the question of what socialism is and how to build it, and has offered developing countries a new option for modernising while keeping their independence. In this reading, the Party has changed the historical contest between socialism and capitalism in socialism's favour, and will contribute still more as it builds a modern socialist country. Read the original if you want an official-line account of how Chinese scholars frame the Party's centenary significance for the international socialist movement.

Carry forward the spirit of historical initiative and walk well the new road of the "examination" 发扬历史主动精神 走好新的赶考之路 Wang Yibiao Writing in Economic Daily on 24 February 2022, Wang Yibiao takes up a phrase from the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021) and from Xi Jinping's speech to the CPPCC: the Party should "carry forward the spirit of historical initiative" on the "new road of the examination" towards the second centenary goal. The article asks why this spirit is stressed, what it contains and how it can be strengthened. Wang's answer is that historical initiative is the "secret code" of the Party's century of achievements and the spiritual driver of national rejuvenation. The piece has three parts. The first gives three reasons why the spirit matters: it is a conclusion drawn from a hundred years of history, it is part of grasping historical laws, and it is needed to meet risks and challenges. The second sets out its content through the Party's record from the revolutionary period to the new era. The third lists five sources from which the Party should draw strength on the new road. It ends with a call to unite around the Party Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core ahead of the 20th Party Congress, due in the second half of 2022. In the article's account, historical initiative has six elements: scientific planning that respects historical laws; a sense of mission that follows the course of history; innovation that draws on historical wisdom; great struggle informed by historical experience; self-reform grounded in historical self-confidence; and the Party's founding mission. Wang cites Marx's remark that people make their own history under inherited conditions, and Xi's statement that people are not wholly passive in history. Wang also cites episodes such as the Long March, the War to Resist U.S. Aggression and Aid Korea and reform and opening up. For the new era, the article lists regional strategies, poverty alleviation, anti-corruption work and the response to Covid-19. It presents the Party's self-reform as the second answer, after popular supervision, to Mao Zedong's "cave dialogue" question about escaping the historical cycle of rise and fall. Wang concludes that the new road requires drawing initiative from five sources: the latest results of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times; a people-first stance aimed at common prosperity; the spirit of the Party's founding and its ideological lineage; confidence in traditional Chinese culture; and a global outlook oriented to a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a compact example of how the official 2022 narrative linked the Party's history, the third historical resolution and the run-up to the 20th Party Congress.

Era characteristics of the Party's leadership in building a modern economic system 党领导建设现代化经济体系的时代特征 Fu Chunyu Zhao Xinpeng Fu Chunyu and Zhao Xinpeng, writing in the China Social Sciences Today in January 2022, ask how the Communist Party of China has led the construction of a modern economic system and what is distinctive about that leadership in the present era. They argue that the Party made top-level design for this task around high-quality development and supply-side structural reform, and then gave it new content and a new yardstick by linking it to the new development pattern. This short commentary has two main parts. The first covers the top-level design set out at the 19th Party Congress (2017), including the theoretical basis in the new development philosophy and five practical characteristics of the Party's leadership. The second turns to the new stage of development, in which the first centenary goal has been met, and examines how the "dual circulation" strategy of the 14th Five-Year Plan reshapes the task. It draws throughout on Party documents, the Historical Resolution and Xi Jinping's statements. In the first part, the authors present supply-side structural reform as the response to problems such as a manufacturing sector they describe as "large but not strong", and the new development philosophy as the directional guide. They list five features of Party leadership: long-term planning combined with short-term breakthroughs, theoretical innovation leading practice, comprehensive and coordinated advance, effective concrete policies, and learning from others while keeping Chinese characteristics. In the second part, they argue that the new development pattern serves as both macro-level guidance and an objective test of the modern economic system. They identify two criteria, expanding domestic demand and keeping circulation unobstructed, and four new requirements: demand as the strategic base, smooth internal circulation, better investment structure, and coordination of development with security. The authors conclude that the new development pattern and the modern economic system are two sides of one task, and that this combination shows the Party "upholding fundamental principles while innovating". In their view, standards have become clearer, the layout more flexible and the paths more concrete. They hold that only continued, centralised Party leadership over economic work, part of Xi Jinping Thought on the economy, can carry the project forward toward a strong modern socialist country and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a compact statement of how Party commentators in early 2022 linked the modern economic system to dual circulation.

The roots, essence and way out of de-globalization: a historical-materialist perspective 逆全球化的根源、本质与出路：基于唯物史观的视角 Song Dexiao Song Dexiao asks why de-globalization (逆全球化) has emerged and spread, and what could resolve it. Writing in 2022, the author notes that most scholars approach the phenomenon through economics or diplomacy. Song proposes instead a historical-materialist reading tied to the history of capitalism and its globalization. The thesis is that de-globalization is a conflict-laden form of capitalism's own development, essentially a development problem, whose way out is a community with a shared future for mankind. The short article, first published in the China Social Sciences Journal, traces de-globalization from anti-globalization thought to state policy. It names the 2008 financial crisis, the 2016 Brexit vote and Trump's election, and the Covid-19 pandemic from 2020 as turning points. It then moves through three sections: the roots of de-globalization, its essence, and its trend and way out. Along the way Song draws on Giddens, Arif Dirlik and Fukuyama. Song first criticises the 'losers of globalization' or 'losers of modernization' theory. In the author's view, it reduces the issue to the distribution of gains and ignores underlying social relations, and the United States, a major beneficiary despite its trade deficits, shows the problem. Song instead locates the roots in the global expansion of the capitalist mode of production: uneven distribution of gains, the internationalization of capitalism's inherent contradiction between socialized production and private appropriation, and clashes between nations over Western-set rules. The article argues that, with war and colonial plunder no longer available, developed countries shift their crises abroad through trade wars and barriers, as the US did after the 2008 crisis. Song reads this as an extension of capitalism's contradictions to the global scale and as a crisis of its governance, politics and values. Song concludes that de-globalization is a temporary strategic adjustment by developed capitalist states, aimed at a global trading system more favourable to capital, and so it cannot solve capitalism's inherent contradictions or alter the course of world history. The author calls for openly opposing de-globalization, giving up illusions about developed capitalist countries, and pursuing balanced, mutually respectful development that respects each nation's chosen path. Song presents Xi Jinping's idea of a community with a shared future for mankind and the Belt and Road Initiative as the practical answer. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a Chinese scholar applies historical materialism to de-globalization and links it to official foreign-policy concepts.

On the logical starting point of Leninism 论列宁主义的逻辑起点 Shu Xin Liu Kangkang Where does Leninism begin? Shu Xin and Liu Kangkang argue that its logical starting point is Lenin's idea of proletarian hegemony (leadership) in Russia's bourgeois-democratic revolution. They present it as the first theoretical result of combining Marxism with Russian conditions and the earliest link in Leninist theory. In their view, studying it clarifies long-running disputes in Leninism research and the origins of Marxist theories of Eastern societies. The article has three parts. The first reconstructs Lenin's analysis of Russian capitalism through his polemics with the Narodniks and the "legal Marxists". The second sets out the hegemony idea as it emerged in the 1905 debate with the Mensheviks. The third explains why this idea is the logical starting point of Leninism, drawing on Engels's remark that the course of thought should begin where history begins. The authors' central move is that Lenin's reading of Russia's situation lets him reject two errors. Against the Narodniks, he held that Russia was already capitalist. Against the legal Marxists, he held that Russian capitalism was progressive but feudal-tinged and exploitative, so the proletariat faced multiple tasks. From this the authors derive Lenin's four reasons why Russia's revolution differed from European ones. It came in a new epoch. The Russian bourgeoisie was tied to autocracy and would compromise. The proletariat was the most thoroughgoing class. Proletarian leadership would not change the revolution's bourgeois character. Its core is separating the bourgeoisie from the revolution and uniting the proletariat with the urban and rural small proprietors ("the peasantry") in a workers' and peasants' democratic dictatorship. The authors contrast this with China's New Democratic revolution, where the national bourgeoisie kept a place. They also read it as continuing Marx and Engels's 1848 thinking, citing the "three whales" slogan, and as the first clash between Marxism and revisionism in the East. They credit Lenin with holding together the initiative of historical agents and the determining role of the productive forces. The authors conclude that combining Marxism with national conditions while fighting revisionism is the methodological principle of Leninism. They suggest the 1905 formulation contained a tension between proletarian political power and a capitalist republic, which Lenin later resolved. They also find an implicit route to socialism in his thinking, in three steps: a Russian democratic revolution, then world revolution, then socialism with Western proletarian aid. Read the original if you want a detailed account of how Lenin's early debates with the Narodniks, legal Marxists and Mensheviks are said to ground Leninist theory.

A programmatic Marxist document that upholds the methodology of dialectical and historical materialism On the Resolution on the Party's major achievements and historical experience over the past century 坚持辩证唯物主义和历史唯物主义方法论的马克思主义纲领性文献 Wang Qiang Writing in the People's Daily in April 2022, Wang Qiang offers a study-guide commentary on the Resolution on the Party's major achievements and historical experience over the past century, adopted at the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021). Wang argues that the Resolution, by upholding the methodology of dialectical and historical materialism, is a brilliant programmatic Marxist document. In Wang's account it is also a political declaration for Communists in the new era and a guide to action for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The article is organised around four pairs of principles that Wang says run through the Resolution: the materialist conception of history together with a correct view of Party history; grasping the laws of historical development together with seizing the historical initiative; the continuity together with the stages of history; and the historical process together with the process of thought. Each section sets out how the Resolution applies the principle, then draws a lesson for readers. The commentary draws on Xi Jinping's remarks and a quotation from Engels. Wang contends that the Resolution treats Party history in a concrete, comprehensive and developmental way, and that its judgements fit with earlier historical documents. Wang reads the Resolution's "ten upholds" as answering why the Party succeeded in the past and how it can keep succeeding, and as evidence that the Party holds the historical initiative. Wang insists that the Party's different periods are not to be set against one another: continuity must not be denied by stages, nor progress by setbacks. Wang presents the successive "great leaps" from the end of feudal autocracy to the stage of becoming strong as one connected process. On the intellectual side, Wang traces the sinicization of Marxism from Mao Zedong Thought through the theoretical system of socialism with Chinese characteristics to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Wang calls the last the latest result of adapting Marxism to China and says it is twenty-first-century Marxism. Wang concludes that the Party succeeds, and socialism with Chinese characteristics is good, ultimately because Marxism works. Wang calls on readers to study the Resolution's methodology, to see history as a whole that cannot be fragmented, and to avoid subversive errors on fundamental questions. Wang also urges them to strengthen the Four Consciousnesses, the Four-sphere Confidence and the Two Upholds, and to look to the Central Committee. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary in 2022 presented the Resolution's method and its link between Party history and Xi Jinping Thought.

The Communist Party of China's century of philosophical exploration 中国共产党百年哲学探索 Wang Qingfeng Wang Qingfeng takes up the question of what the Communist Party of China's hundred-year struggle has contributed to Marxist philosophy. Writing after the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021), Wang argues that the Party's history is a process of philosophical exploration, combining Marxism's basic principles with China's concrete conditions and with fine traditional Chinese culture. The result, in the article's account, is a subjective and original Sinicized Marxist philosophy. The short article is organised around the three main components of Marxist philosophy. Each section sets out how the Party is said to have transformed one component: the practical viewpoint became the line of seeking truth from facts; dialectical materialism became a dialectical thinking of practical wisdom; and historical materialism became the creation of Chinese modernization and a new form of human civilization. Wang draws on Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping throughout. On practice, Wang presents seeking truth from facts as the most distinctive and original contribution of Sinicized Marxism. In Wang's reading it unites the "measure of man" with the "measure of things", and so turns a "philosophy of practice" into a genuine "practice of philosophy". On dialectics, Wang traces a line from Mao's dialectics of practical wisdom, aimed at solving concrete problems of the revolution, to the "systems thinking" and "strategic thinking" dialectics of the era after the 18th Party Congress (2012). On historical materialism, Wang contends that Marx's path "dismantles the logic of capital", whereas socialism with Chinese characteristics "harnesses" it. This is done by criticising private capital, building a public-ownership capital logic with common prosperity as its aim, and shaping "public-oriented capital", which is said to reflect the people's interests and to move beyond capitalist civilization. Wang concludes that the Party's century of philosophical exploration is a continuing process of Sinicizing Marxist philosophy, and that its final theoretical result is a Marxist philosophy with Chinese subjectivity and originality. Wang says that reviewing this history matters for upholding the socialist path with Chinese characteristics at the meeting point of the "Two Centenary Goals". Read the original if you want a concise statement of how Party-aligned scholarship frames the Party's own philosophical contributions to Marxism.

Making scientific and technological innovation a key support for promoting common prosperity 把科技创新作为促进共同富裕关键支撑 Research group of the Macroeconomic Research Think Tank, Chinese Academy of Social Sciences This newspaper commentary, written by a research group of the CASS Macroeconomic Research Think Tank, asks how scientific and technological innovation can better serve high-quality development and common prosperity. The authors argue that innovation's current driving force is not yet strong enough. They name three problems: R&D that does not focus enough on industrial bottlenecks and demand, weak coordination between science and technology policy and economic and industrial policy, and a limited capacity to turn research results into products. The article proposes concentrating innovation on three areas: the digital economy, green and low-carbon development, and industrial upgrading together with coordinated urban–rural and regional development. Each is treated in a separate section with specific measures. On the digital economy, the authors call for breakthroughs in "choke-point" core technologies and more basic research. They also want small firms and individual businesses to share in digital opportunities, a fair mechanism for distributing the returns on data as a production factor, curbs on platform monopolies, and a larger skilled workforce to expand the middle-income group. On green development, they describe a good ecological environment as the most inclusive form of well-being and urge a market-oriented green technology system, green manufacturing and stronger pollution-control technology. On industry and regions, they propose innovation consortia, upgrading of traditional manufacturing, smart agriculture, and a strategy of science and technology for counties. The authors conclude that the heaviest task of common prosperity still lies in the countryside. They call for consolidating the gains of poverty alleviation, advancing rural revitalization, training new professional farmers, and deepening the science and technology commissioner system so that rural residents can become prosperous through technology. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a Chinese think tank linked innovation policy to the common prosperity agenda in early 2022.

From the complete Capital to an open "critique of political economy" MEGA² Section II and Marx research in Germany 从完整的《资本论》到开放的“政治经济学批判” Zhang Yixiu Zhang Yixiu asks what the completed publication of Section II of the historical-critical edition of the Marx-Engels works (MEGA²) has changed in German scholarship on Marx's critique of political economy. The article, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in January 2022, argues that the edition moves readers away from the image of a single finished Capital and towards an open, unfinished process of research. It adds that recent German scholars use the new material for contemporary critical purposes, unlike the "Marxology" of the twentieth-century West. Section II ran to 15 volumes (23 books) from 1976 to 2012. Zhang notes that it first published many manuscripts, including parts of the 1861–1863 manuscripts and dozens of manuscripts for Volumes 2 and 3 of Capital. It also publishes the main versions of Capital separately, along with Engels's editorial drafts. The article surveys German research under five headings: periodisation, the status of key texts, method, theoretical content (value theory and crisis theory), and the Marx–Engels relationship. On periodisation, Zhang reports that Carl-Erich Vollgraf and Hubmann read the manuscripts as belonging to two projects divided around 1863, the critique of political economy and Capital. On this reading, the six-book plan was largely a publishing strategy. Michael Heinrich, Ingo Stützle and others treat the Grundrisse and other texts as having independent themes. Zhang also presents debates on method and content: Haug, Reichelt, Wolf and Backhaus on value as a relational form, and Schefold on value-form theory as a Weberian "ideal type". Kurz and Henning disagree over whether the falling rate of profit was ever settled. The Marx–Engels question is then shown to depend on wider methodological positions. Heinrich stresses Engels's active shaping of Volume 3, Roth defends Engels's caution, and Krätke and Elbe differ over whether his historical reading distorts Marx. Zhang concludes that German scholars mostly want to free the philosophical wisdom of historical materialism and the method of the critique of political economy from a fixed, dogmatic image of Capital, so as to address present-day capitalism. Zhang says this work is beginning to influence research in China. The article proposes that Chinese researchers, keeping a Marxist standpoint and an open attitude, use the MEGA² materials to move beyond teleological readings and rebuild the path of Marx's critique. Read the original if you want a compact guide to the German scholars and debates around MEGA² Section II, as seen from Chinese Marxist scholarship.

The "non-identity" dimension of Marx's empirical research method 马克思经验研究方法的“非同一性”维度 Yang Lei This short piece, first published in the China Social Sciences Today in January 2022, asks what distinguishes Marx's empirical method from both the speculation of the Young Hegelians and the empiricism of English and French philosophy. Yang argues that Marx rejected metaphysical thinking built on "identity" and affirmed the positive significance of "non-identity". On this reading, it is the interaction of subjective and objective, abstract and concrete, experience and theory that gives historical materialism its scientific character. Yang organises the discussion under three headings: matter (zhìliào), the individual, and difference. Each is tied to a passage or episode in Marx's work, including The German Ideology and Marx's late writings on Russia. Hegel's Phenomenology of Spirit and Dewey's The Quest for Certainty are cited as background. On matter, Yang contends that Marx started from real individuals and their material conditions of life, which can be confirmed by purely empirical means, and so countered the "old philosophy" of ultimate causes. Under capitalism, Yang says, identity appears as the logic of capital, presented as the only rational reality. On the individual, Yang reads Marx as showing how capital and metaphysics together reduce living persons to servants of abstract powers, and as seeking a path to self-liberation for concrete individuals. On difference, Yang points to Marx's letters on Russia, which reject turning his account of Western European capitalism into a universal philosophy of history. Yang concludes that paths of development are plural rather than uniform. Yang concludes that Marx valued experience without being confined to it or worshipping it, and that he insisted on concrete analysis of concrete problems. Experience is treated as changing with time, place and conditions, so research cannot rest on fixed concepts. Read the original if you want a compact account of how Marx's anti-metaphysical and anti-universalist stance is framed in Chinese Marxist scholarship.

Historical specificity and the concretisation of historical materialism Starting from Moishe Postone's reinterpretation of Marx's critical theory 历史特殊性与唯物史观的具体化路径 Tang Zhengdong Tang Zhengdong asks what it means to "concretise" historical materialism, and takes the Canadian scholar Moishe Postone as a test case. If "concrete" means only empirical particulars, concretisation is merely the application of a general theory to an object. Tang argues instead that it should also enrich the general by showing a concrete object's significance in the historical process. Postone's notion of "historical specificity" is judged more profound than post-structuralist localism, yet limited because it cuts the present off from the genetic development of history. The article has four sections. The first explains Postone's historical specificity as a "qualitative specificity", drawing on his work on the Holocaust and on capitalism. The second covers capitalist labour and the commodity, and contrasts Postone with Sohn-Rethel and Christopher John Arthur on exchange abstraction. The third turns to the historical specificity of capitalism's internal contradiction and Postone's "retrospective" reading of the order of Capital, Volume 1. The fourth sets out Tang's own view of how historical materialism is concretised. On Tang's account, Postone's book Time, Labor, and Social Domination reads Marx's mature work as analysing capitalist labour, which constructs an abstract structure of domination, rather than trans-historical labour or property relations. Tang credits Postone with grasping the importance of reproducing production relations and with going deeper than exchange-based theories. But Tang objects that Postone treats capitalism as a contingent form that interrupts history, so he reaches only a surface duality of concrete and abstract labour. He misses the contradiction between productive forces and relations of production, and the division of labour that forces each labour to be exchanged. Citing Marx's 1857 Introduction, Tang holds that in historical materialism the particular rests on what is common, so specificity must be understood genetically. Tang places Postone in a Western left lineage, running from the 1950s through Ernest Mandel and Althusser, that moved wholesale from the "abstract" to the "concrete". In Tang's view, this lineage neither reaches the essential contradiction of the concrete nor grasps Marx's scientific abstraction. Genuine concretisation, he says, places an object within the movement of internal contradictions and studies the laws of its development, which in turn enriches scientific abstraction. He links this to the practice of socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era, which he describes as deepening understanding of both socialist construction and general laws of history. Read the original if you want a Chinese critique of Postone's value-form reading and a view of how Chinese Marxists approach the abstract–concrete dialectic.

Was the Soviet collapse mainly due to an "inability to keep pace with the times"? A rejoinder to Zheng Yongnian 苏联解体主要原因是“不能与时俱进”吗？ Wu Enyuan In November 2021 Zheng Yongnian, head of an advanced research institute at the Chinese University of Hong Kong, said in a press interview that the main cause of the Soviet collapse was the Soviet Union's inability to keep pace with the times. Wu disputes this, and the article, published in World Socialism Studies in 2022, argues that the claim is inaccurate. In Wu's reading, the real cause was the reform line of Gorbachev, not stagnation, self-isolation or "decoupling" from the West. The article answers three of Zheng's propositions in turn. It asks whether the Soviet model after the October Revolution failed to modernise, whether Soviet construction was "innovation behind closed doors", and whether the collapse came from decoupling from the West. Wu draws on Soviet constitutions, reform programmes from Malenkov to Kosygin, trade and technology-transfer figures, and Russian sources, and ends with three conclusions for China. Wu first holds that Zheng's view is internally contradictory. It credits Soviet strength yet denies that the system changed. Wu says the Soviet system was a contradictory unity of progress and defects, and that the 1918 and 1936 constitutions and the abolition of private ownership made it fundamentally different from tsarist Russia. Wu also lists reform efforts under Malenkov, Khrushchev and Kosygin, and argues that these show the system was not simply static. Second, citing Lenin, Stalin and trade statistics, Wu argues that Soviet leaders sought trade and technology from capitalist countries. Examples include concession contracts and Western-built steelworks, tractor plants and a hydropower station. Wu holds that the later restrictions came from Western blockade, the Cold War and the Paris-based export-control committee known as COCOM. Stalin's "two parallel markets" theory was, in Wu's account, partly a forced response and partly a doctrinal limit. Wu concludes that the fatal flaw was Gorbachev's reform and his "humane and democratic socialism", citing Gorbachev's own remarks, Russian polls, Nazarbayev and Xi Jinping's remarks on historical nihilism. Wu draws three lessons. Imperialist containment is constant, and the Trump and Biden administrations' "decoupling" is part of it. Blockade has historically failed to stop Soviet or Chinese development. China should still expand reform and opening up and widen its circle of friends. Read the original if you want a Chinese-Academy-of-Social-Sciences rebuttal of the "closed-door" explanation of the Soviet collapse, with its Soviet trade and technology data.

The Communist Party of China's experience in guiding religion to adapt to socialist society 中国共产党引导宗教与社会主义社会相适应的经验研究 Tian Wei Yang Ping Tian Wei and Yang Ping ask how the Communist Party of China has approached its policy of guiding religion to adapt to socialist society, and what lessons can be drawn for religious work in the new era. They argue that this policy reflects a creative application of the Marxist view of religion and a distinctly Chinese method of religious work. The experience, in their account, answers four questions: why religion should be guided, on what requirements, under whose leadership, and by what means. The article is organised in four parts, each matching one of these questions. It first treats the ideological basis, then the requirements that govern guidance, then Party leadership as the fundamental guarantee, and finally the methods used. The authors support their points with statements by Marx, Engels, Lenin, Mao Zedong, Zhou Enlai, Deng Xiaoping and Jiang Zemin, and with Party documents. These include Central Document No. 19 of 1982 and the 1992 United Front Work Department outline that first stated the formula in full. The authors argue that the Party's scientific understanding of religion has three elements: its illusory nature and social roots, its eventual withering away as a long process, and its dual social role. From this they conclude that guidance is necessary, that administrative coercion is ruled out, and that guidance is feasible because religion can play a positive role. They say the requirements have been enriched over time. The target of adaptation stresses social progress, the means of guidance ("dao") has gained weight in the new era, and the direction is the sinicisation of religion. Leadership, they write, is secured by attention to religious work, coordinated mechanisms (Party committee leadership, United Front coordination, legal administration by religious affairs departments) and cadre training. Guidance is carried out through political, legal and cultural means. Political means centre on uniting religious figures and believers. Legal means centre on administering religious affairs according to law, which the authors illustrate with a count of regulations and with cases such as extremism, the over-extension of the "halal" concept and the commercialisation of Buddhism and Daoism. Cultural means centre on integrating religious doctrine with Chinese culture and core socialist values. The authors conclude that guiding religion is a long process of exploration and that the resulting experience is a valuable asset of the Party. They call for continued summing-up of this experience, linked to practice, in order to enrich socialist religious theory with Chinese characteristics and promote high-quality development of religious work. Read the original if you want a concise, Party-line account of how Chinese scholars present the history, rationale and instruments of official religious policy, with dated sources from 1938 to the new era.

Theory and practice of the Communist Party of Britain in pushing Britain towards socialism in the 21st century 21世纪英国共产党推动英国走向社会主义的理论与实践探索 Lü Jin Feng Fan Lü Jin and Feng Fan ask how the Communist Party of Britain (CPB), a small party re-founded in 1988 by the "Morning Star" faction after the split of the old CPGB, has tried since 2001 to move Britain towards socialism. They argue that the CPB has developed a coherent strategy in theory and practice, but that internal weaknesses and external pressure confine it to slow, difficult progress. The article first traces the party's history: the CPGB's founding in 1920, its four splits, its dissolution in 1991 and the CPB's gradual acceptance as the successor. It then covers the CPB's theoretical exploration through three revisions of its programme, "Britain's Road to Socialism" (2001, 2011, 2020). Next it examines practice in three areas: elections, labour and social movements, and international communist solidarity. A final section assesses the party's difficulties and prospects. The authors report that the CPB's "alternative economic and political strategy" rests on a "Left Programme" and a "broad popular democratic anti-monopoly alliance". The party envisages three steps: building electoral strength; electing a left government that implements the programme; and a decisive confrontation with monopoly capital, ending in what the party calls the dictatorship of the proletariat, defined as rule by the great majority. In practice the CPB stands in elections, with very low national vote shares and somewhat better local results. It also works in trade unions and in women's, anti-racist, environmental and anti-Brexit campaigns, and it supports other communist parties, criticises imperialism and praises China's pandemic response. The authors identify three internal difficulties: small membership (about 1,200 by 2021, by the party's own claim), chronic shortage of funds and debt, and weak intra-party democracy under democratic centralism. External obstacles include the party's 2019 listing on a counter-terrorism extremism watch list, Conservative hostility to unions, and Labour's factional divisions. The authors nonetheless conclude that the CPB, through publications, the Morning Star, educational events and its youth league, is making slow progress and accumulating conditions for socialism. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic overview of a small European communist party's strategy, its organisational limits and its stance towards China.

Contemporary explorations of programmes for achieving socialism by communist parties in developed capitalist countries 发达资本主义国家共产党对实现社会主义方案的当代探索 Wang Yuan Wang Yuan examines how communist parties in developed capitalist countries have recast their roads to socialism. The article's starting point is that neoliberalism has waned since the 2008 financial crisis, while capitalism has found no new development model. Wang notes that the parties of the United States, Britain, France, Japan, Canada and Australia all revised their programmes between 2017 and 2020. The article argues that these revisions share common features but leave the parties facing structural dilemmas. The article is a comparative survey of seven parties. It treats the American 'Bill of Rights socialism', the British 'British Road to Socialism', the French 'historic communist struggle for our time', the Japanese 'democratic revolution–socialist transformation', the Canadian 'people's government–building socialism', the Australian 'democratic stage–revolutionary transformation stage' and the German 'transition to socialism through anti-monopoly struggle'. For each party Wang traces the post-1991 history and then the latest programme, usually its analysis of present-day capitalism and its staged plan. Wang's central observation is that the programmes move away from dogmatism and from insurrectionary language. Several parties soften wording, for example the Japanese change from 'socialist revolution stage' to 'socialist transformation stage'. Wang identifies five shared features: anti-monopoly struggle as the precondition of socialism; a search for peaceful, democratic routes to power; a long, staged process; alliances with new social movements such as environmentalism, feminism and LGBT rights; and Marxist critiques of automation, big data and artificial intelligence as new tools of exploitation. Wang presents this as adapting Marxism to local conditions and the needs of the times. Wang concludes that the parties face two difficulties. No example exists of a peaceful, democratic transition to socialism within a capitalist framework, so the parties are caught between radical extra-systemic struggle, which risks marginalisation or repression, and in-system struggle, which risks absorption. In addition, the shrinking blue-collar workforce and the parties' inability to integrate new social movements theoretically have diluted the appeal of class struggle. Wang expects these parties to remain in the doldrums for a long time and treats the testing of their programmes in practice as their long-term historical task. Read the original if you want a compact, party-by-party overview of recent programme changes among Western and Japanese communist parties, as seen from a Chinese academic perspective.

The Communist Party of China's century-long exploration of, and contribution to, the Marxist theory of science, technology and the economy 中国共产党百年对马克思主义科技经济理论的探索及贡献 Zhang Xinning Zhang Xinning asks how the Communist Party of China, over its first hundred years, developed the Marxist theory linking science, technology and the economy, and what it added to Marxist political economy. The article argues that the Party advanced this theory systematically in three stages and made four contributions: moving from a mainly philosophical view of technology to a political-economic one; from 'explaining the world' to 'changing the world'; from an auxiliary to a leading role for innovation; and from product-based to innovation-based international competition. The article follows the Party's history chronologically. It begins with Marx, Engels, Lenin and Stalin on technology, then turns to the revolution and construction period under Mao Zedong. It next covers the reform and opening up period, from Deng Xiaoping to Hu Jintao, and finally the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012) under Xi Jinping. A closing section sets out the significance of the whole development and the functions of innovation. In Zhang's account, Mao treated natural science as 'a weapon for people's pursuit of freedom' and scientific experiment as a basic form of social practice alongside production struggle and class struggle. He also set a strategy centred on technological revolution, which produced the 'two bombs and one satellite'. Deng's 'primary productive force' thesis made technology the 'gene' of productive forces. This was put into practice through the 863 Programme, the strategy of invigorating China through science and education, and the building of an innovation-oriented country, and Zhang describes a 2003 dispute between self-reliant innovation and technology import that was settled in favour of the former. Under Xi, innovation became the 'primary driving force' of development. Zhang says this extends technology's role beyond the economy into politics, culture, ecology, diplomacy and defence, and ties it to high-quality development and the new development philosophy. Zhang concludes that this body of theory settled doubts in political economy by bringing productive forces back into the discipline, and that it opened a new realm for political economy with Chinese characteristics. The article lists six functions of innovation: industrial change, economic growth, social stability, people's livelihood, ecological protection and national defence. It calls on economists to keep pace with the new technological revolution and to treat innovation as a core subject of research. Read the original if you want a Party-historical account of how Chinese theorists present continuity from Mao to Xi on technology and political economy.

The assertion that "the Party is the highest political leadership force": historical survey, internal logic and practical orientation “党是最高政治领导力量”论断的历史考察、内在逻辑与现实指向 Yang Binbin Yang Binbin examines how the formula "the Party is the highest political leadership force" came into being and what it means for the Chinese political system. The article, published in Party and Government Studies in 2022, argues that the formula is a product of the endogenous evolution of the Party's leadership system. In Yang's account, it carries forward Marxist teaching on the proletarian party and gives it a Chinese discursive form, characterised by principle, timeliness and national character. The article has three parts. The first traces the formula's roots in Marx, Engels and Lenin, then follows the vocabulary around it in Chinese Communist Party documents: "leadership core", "core force" and "leadership force". It dates these usages from the 1920s and 1940s through Mao Zedong's speeches of 1954 and 1956 and the 14th Party Congress (1992) to the 19th Party Congress (2017), Xi Jinping's 2018 speech and the constitutional revision of that year. The second part sets out the formula's internal logic, and the third turns to practical implications for the present. Yang's central claim is that the successive wordings differ in expression but share one principle, the authority of Party leadership, while "highest" stresses its supremacy, with political leadership as the most basic form. The formula is tied to four relationships: the people's democratic dictatorship, the new type of state system (including Party–government relations), the new type of party system (relations between the Communist Party and other parties) and full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. Yang holds that Chinese multi-party cooperation cannot be sorted by Western-centric party theory, and that the Party's self-positioning as a leading, revolutionary and governing party underpins the Party's self-reform. For the present, Yang calls for three things: firm direction, by upholding Party leadership; a more complete institutional system, to strengthen that leadership; and better governance, to optimise it. In practice this means continuing self-reform, raising the Party's leadership and governing capacity, and building a stronger body of concepts and discourse to "tell the institutional story" of Party leadership, in service of modernising national governance. Read the original if you want a detailed genealogy of the Party's own terms for its leadership role and an official-academic view of how that role links to the state, the party system and Party discipline.

Basic experience of upholding and strengthening the Party's overall leadership in the new era 新时代坚持和加强党的全面领导的基本经验 Zhu Jiamei This commentary, published in Guangming Daily in April 2022, takes up the first of the 13 areas in which the Party's 2021 resolution on its century of struggle summarises historic achievements of the new era: upholding the Party's overall leadership. Zhu Jiamei argues that distilling the basic experience of this work matters theoretically and practically for consolidating the Party's governing position and for the new journey of building a modern socialist country in all respects. The piece sets out five lessons, each given its own numbered section. They are: clarifying the issue at the level of theory, proceeding from the Party's political line, perfecting the institutional system of overall leadership, providing strong organisational guarantees, and strengthening and improving ideological leadership. The treatment is a summary of policy and leadership practice rather than a historical or comparative study. Zhu begins from a diagnosis: for a period, some Party members were vague about Party leadership, and its implementation was weakened, hollowed out, diluted and marginalised, with some localities pursuing countermeasures to central policy. In response, the Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core restated that the Party leads everything and placed "upholding the Party's leadership over all work" first among the 14 basic principles of the new era. Zhu then describes the mechanisms that make this operational: political discipline and training for cadres, systems of reporting requests and annual work reports to the central leadership, reformed Party and state institutions, and an organisational chain running from the central Party organisation to grassroots branches, extended into new economic and social organisations. Ideological work, in Zhu's account, rests on ideals-and-convictions education, study of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, and firm Party control of the ideological sphere through responsibility systems. Zhu concludes that this system of leadership, extending horizontally to every sector and vertically to the grassroots, has allowed the country to keep developing through risks and challenges while maintaining political stability and balancing vitality with order. Upholding Party leadership is presented as the foundation of the Party and state and of the people's interests. Read the original if you want a concise, official-register statement of how Party leadership is justified and institutionalised in the Xi Jinping era.

On the atheist character of the spiritual genealogy of Chinese Communists 论中国共产党人精神谱系的无神论特色 Ding Yu Written in the year of the Communist Party of China's centenary (2021), this article asks how Marxist atheism shapes what official discourse calls the spiritual genealogy of Chinese Communists, the series of revolutionary "spirits" that trace back to the founding spirit of the Party. Ding Yu argues that Marxist atheism is the indispensable moral and intellectual ground of this genealogy and the foundation of the Party's mainstream ideology. Understanding this, the author holds, helps keep atheism dominant in the people's thinking. The article opens with Xi Jinping's centenary speech and the Party's century-long struggle for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. It then proceeds through four sections, each linking one feature of the genealogy to atheism: ideals and convictions, the people-centred standpoint, the seeking of truth from facts, and the spirit of struggle. Evidence comes from Xi Jinping's speeches, Mao Zedong's writings and the early revolutionary and Yan'an periods. Ding contends that firm ideals rest on a thoroughly materialist worldview. In this account, belief in the inevitable victory of socialism is scientific, and a Party member who does not hold to atheism cannot be a consistent materialist and will waver in conviction. Devotion to the people is distinguished from religious devotion: believers dedicate themselves to God, while Communists dedicate themselves to the people. Ding also presents seeking truth from facts as an atheist way of thinking, citing the Party's campaigns against fatalism and superstition and Mao's break with dogmatic deference to superiors, the Comintern and books. On struggle, Ding reads atheism broadly as a refusal to fear "ghosts", citing Mao's 1960s Stories of Not Fearing Ghosts. The article proposes three tasks: keep the ban on Party members holding religious belief, directing struggle at separatist, religious-extremist and terrorist forces while uniting believers around the Party, and renew methods of struggle. The last includes resisting Western ideological infiltration, strengthening the Party's voice abroad and reforming atheist education so it wins over the next generation. Read the original if you want an example of how Party-affiliated scholarship ties atheism to the Party's founding spirit, its mass line and its policy on religion.

Using the experience of a century of struggle to increase the Party's wisdom, unity, confidence and fighting spirit 以百年奋斗成就经验推动全党增长智慧、增进团结、增加信心、增强斗志 Liu Jie This commentary, published in Party Building (Dangjian) in 2022, takes up the Resolution on the Party's major achievements and historical experience over the past century, adopted at the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021). Liu Jie argues, following Xi Jinping's explanation of the draft, that studying this record should strengthen four things across the Party: wisdom, unity, confidence and fighting spirit. The article is organised in four parts, one for each of these aims. Each part links the Resolution's summary of the four historical periods and its ten items of historical experience to a task for the Party as it begins a new journey towards the second centenary goal. On wisdom, Liu says the Party's wisdom grew out of a century of practice and the integration of Marxism with China's concrete realities and fine traditional culture, producing successive theoretical innovations from Mao Zedong Thought to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. On unity, Liu presents ideological unity, the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds as the means of binding the Party together. On confidence and fighting spirit, Liu cites the achievements of the past century as grounds for belief in the Party's path, and holds that the Party's self-reform is the key to keeping its resolve and escaping the historical cycle of rise and fall. Liu concludes that a century is only a prologue and calls on Party members to rally around the Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core, study the Resolution and work towards the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a Party official presents the 2021 Resolution to cadres as a tool for study and mobilisation.

Upholding the supremacy of the people is the distinguishing mark separating the Communist Party of China from Western parties 坚持人民至上是中国共产党区别于西方政党的显著标志 Li Dongming Liu Jiazhu This commentary in Guangming Daily argues that putting the people first (人民至上) is the key lesson of the Communist Party of China's hundred years of struggle and the clearest mark distinguishing a Marxist party from Western parties. Li and Liu present this principle as running through the whole of the Party's governance and expressing its fundamental purpose of serving the people wholeheartedly. The article is organised in three sections. The first treats the Party's founding mission, tracing it from the Opium War and the October Revolution through the first two Party Congresses to the founding of the People's Republic. The second discusses the Party's goal of meeting the people's aspirations for a better life, including poverty alleviation and common prosperity. The third takes up governance, using the response to Covid-19 as its main example. In the authors' account, Western parties exist to realise and protect bourgeois interests; two-party and multi-party systems are described as rule by a minority over the majority, with decisions captured by interest groups. The Communist Party, by contrast, is said to have no special interests of its own and to represent the fundamental interests of the broadest masses. Li and Liu cite the elimination of absolute poverty under current standards (98.99 million rural people, 832 counties) as evidence, and contrast Western private ownership and distribution by capital, which they say produce wealth gaps. They also claim that in the pandemic the Party put life first at any cost, which parties that put capital and votes first cannot do. The authors conclude that the people are the source of the Party's strength and the basis of its victories. They call for policy to rest on the principal contradiction in society and national conditions, and to respond promptly to popular demands. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Party commentary in 2022 contrasted the Communist Party with Western parties around the theme of people-centredness.

Full and rigorous self-governance of the Party is the only way for the Party to keep its vitality and walk the new road of the "examination" 全面从严治党是党永葆生机活力 走好新的赶考之路的必由之路 Li Guojuan This short commentary, published in Guangming Daily in April 2022, takes up one of the "five musts" (五个必由之路) that Xi Jinping set out at that year's National People's Congress session, when he joined the Inner Mongolia delegation. Li Guojuan explains the claim that full and rigorous self-governance of the Party is the only path by which the Party can keep its vitality and succeed on its new "examination" road. Li treats the claim as having overall and strategic significance for reaching the Second Centenary Goal. The piece first reviews what has been done since the 18th Party Congress (2012), when full and rigorous self-governance of the Party was placed within the "Four-pronged Comprehensive Strategy" and anti-corruption work was stepped up. It then gives three reasons why this path is necessary, before a brief closing call to action. Li argues, first, that rigorous governance is needed to preserve the Party's advanced nature and purity, which the author calls the essential attributes of a Marxist party. Second, it strengthens cohesion and fighting capacity: Li says the Party's history shows setbacks whenever belief, organisation and discipline weakened, and lists individualism, factionalism, cliques and double-dealing as risks to be removed. Third, it is the political guarantee that the Party's self-reform can lead a great social revolution. In Li's account, the success of the Chinese nation's move from standing up to becoming prosperous and then strong depended on the Party's willingness to reform itself. Li also warns against complacency, including the view that anti-corruption can pause or that rigour has already been fully achieved. Li concludes that the Party should keep its founding mission, deepen full and rigorous self-governance and advance its self-reform. In this way it would provide political security, ideological guidance and leadership for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary in 2022 justified the Party's self-governance campaign and linked it to the Second Centenary Goal.

The Party's third historical resolution and the CPC's methods of summing up its own historical experience 从党的第三个历史决议看中国共产党总结自身历史经验的方法 Zhu Jiamu Zhu Jiamu asks how the Communist Party of China goes about summing up its own historical experience, taking the Resolution on the Major Achievements and Historical Experience of the Party's Century-long Struggle, adopted at the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021), as his case. This short commentary, published in 2022, argues that the Resolution reflects the basic method set out by Mao Zedong and Xi Jinping, namely historical materialism and seeking truth from facts. It also uses three more specific methods that Zhu says are worth studying and applying. The article opens by recalling Mao's remarks on experience and Xi's calls since the 18th Party Congress (2012) to link Party history study with summing up experience and to form a correct view of Party history. It then takes the three methods in turn, drawing on the Resolution's treatment of the four historical periods: the new-democratic revolution, socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the new era. Zhu closes by noting that other methods exist and that the Resolution does not limit itself to these three. The first method is to sum up each period separately while also linking all periods together. Zhu lists the lessons the Resolution draws for each period, then points to problems common to all of them, such as keeping the Party's vanguard character. For this reason the Resolution adds a section on ten lessons from the century, from upholding Party leadership to the Party's self-reform. The second method is to assess experience from today's level of understanding while placing it in its specific historical conditions. Citing Lenin, Zhu says the early move to a public-ownership, highly centralised planned economy must be understood against imperialist threat and scarce capital and talent. The third method is to concentrate on successes without ignoring failures. Zhu says the Resolution treats achievements as the mainstream but openly names problems, such as a period of lax Party governance that allowed corruption to spread. Zhu concludes that the Party values correct methods of summing up experience as well as the experience itself. Studying the Resolution should therefore include absorbing its methods, so as to distil effective approaches, improve the Party's capacity for struggle and governance, strengthen resistance to corruption and risk, and carry forward socialism with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a brief, officially aligned account of the methodological logic behind the 2021 resolution, as presented by a leading Party-history scholar.

Understanding the scientific connotation of the Party's self-reform 深入理解把握党的自我革命的科学内涵 Dai Yanjun This commentary, published in Guangming Daily in April 2022, asks what the Communist Party of China's "self-reform" means and why it distinguishes the Party from other parties. Dai Yanjun argues that self-reform is the Party's most distinctive trait and an essential route to keeping it advanced and pure. In his account, full and rigorous self-governance of the Party since the 18th Party Congress (2012) is the great practice of self-reform in the new era. The article has three parts. The first explains where the Party's capacity for self-reform comes from. The second sets out the tasks self-reform has performed historically. The third examines how the campaign for full and rigorous self-governance of the Party under Xi Jinping has enriched the concept, drawing on episodes from the Zunyi Conference to the Yan'an rectification movement. Dai locates the sources of self-reform in two features: the Party is a Marxist party, and Marxism is an open, developing doctrine; and the Party serves the people wholeheartedly, so whatever harms popular interests is wrong and must be corrected. On this basis he lists four historical functions: correcting errors in decision-making through inner-Party political life (the Zunyi Conference, the Seven Thousand Cadres Conference, the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee); purging politically two-faced people; punishing corrupt elements; and using criticism and self-criticism to achieve unity, with the Yan'an rectification as the model. For the new era he identifies four features: political development as the essential requirement, discipline and conduct as the routinised element, the anti-corruption struggle as the key focus, and the improvement of inner-Party regulations as the move towards rule by law. Dai concludes that self-reform must adapt its priorities and methods to the problems of each period, and that the policies of the Party leadership centred on Xi Jinping have opened a new stage of it. He credits them with an overwhelming victory in the anti-corruption struggle, now being consolidated. Read the original if you want a concise official-academic statement of how Party theorists justify self-reform and tie it to full and rigorous self-governance of the Party.

Mao Zedong's thinking and practice on "we must pay attention to economic work" in the Central Soviet Area 中央苏区时期毛泽东关于“必须注意经济工作”的思考与实践 Yu Shouping Yu Shouping examines the call Mao Zedong made in August 1933, at the economic construction conference of seventeen counties in the south of the Central Revolutionary Base Area, that 'we must pay attention to economic work'. Yu notes that scholarship on this directive is thin and proposes to interpret it through Mao's texts of the period, including 'We Must Pay Attention to Economic Work', 'Our Economic Policy' and 'Show Concern for the Well-being of the Masses and Pay Attention to Methods of Work', set against their historical background. The article argues that the directive guided economic work in the Central Soviet Area, helped break the Kuomintang blockade, improved living conditions and consolidated the base. The article is organised in five sections: the positioning of economic construction relative to revolutionary war; its key tasks (agriculture, industry, foreign trade, cooperatives); mobilising the masses; training cadres; and leadership style and work methods. Yu draws on Mao's speeches and reports, Soviet government decrees and resolutions, and local examples such as Changgang and Caixi townships and Tingzhou city. Yu's central claim is that economic construction had to 'revolve around the central task of revolutionary war'. Mao rejected two mistaken views: that economic work was impossible in wartime, and that it had become the centre of all tasks. In Yu's account, Mao placed agriculture first, with land distribution, organised exchange of labour and women's participation. He also sought the planned recovery of handicrafts and some industry, state-directed foreign trade to evade the blockade, and consumer, producer and credit cooperatives. Yu stresses that mobilisation depended on meeting the masses' daily needs and on strengthening the worker–peasant alliance, through measures such as economic construction bonds. Cadres were to be trained as 'commanders on the economic front'. Yu reports that Mao favoured state, cooperative and private enterprise advancing together, held that private economy was needed in the interests of state and people, and criticised bureaucratic leadership. Yu concludes that Mao's thinking supplied practical guidance and left the Party experience in leading economic work. Rereading it, especially its methods of thought, is said to help in understanding the Party's history and in handling today's economic construction. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-based account of Soviet-period economic policy under Mao, with concrete cases and figures, as presented in Party-history scholarship.

The Party's centenary: historical theme and spatio-temporal fields of the Communist Party of China 中国共产党百年的历史主题与时空场域 Liu Lyuhong Marking the Party's centenary in 2021, Liu asks how the usual account of the Communist Party of China's hundred years can be placed within a wider time frame. The article argues that three overlapping "centuries" must be studied together: modern China from 1840 to 1949, the Party's own century from 1921, and the century of New China from 1949 to 2049. In Liu's reading, one historical theme runs through all three, namely the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The article has three main sections. The first treats the century of modern national disaster as the setting in which the theme of national rejuvenation arose. The second follows the Party's record from early reformers and the founding congresses to the achievements of each period. The third covers the New China century, looking at the goal of a modern, powerful socialist country, the continuing development of socialism with Chinese characteristics, the Party and the people as the "narrative subject", and the external extension of this field. Liu's central move is to derive the theme from the principal contradictions of modern society. Citing the formula of imperialism versus the nation and feudalism versus the masses, the author says these produced two linked tasks, "revolution" and "modernization".
