Peasant movements, self-strengthening, reform and the 1911 Revolution all failed, in the author's account, because they imitated the West. Marxism then supplied the ideological weapon, and the Party took up the task from its first congresses in 1921 and 1922. Liu then traces the Party's step-by-step formulation of the goal: Deng Xiaoping's xiaokang, the three-step strategy, the "two centenary goals" and the modernization of national governance. The author presents foreign policy from Mao Zedong to Xi Jinping as the theme's external side, ending with a community with a shared future for mankind and the Belt and Road Initiative. Liu concludes that studying the three centuries together lets one grasp the Party's past, present and future, as well as the internal logic of national rejuvenation. The author holds that the Party, united with the people, will lead Chinese modernization through the "great changes unseen in a century" and contribute to human well-being. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Party-history scholar fits the Party's hundred years into a longer sequence from 1840 to 2049 around the theme of national rejuvenation.

Upholding the Party's overall leadership is the only way to uphold and develop socialism with Chinese characteristics 坚持党的全面领导是坚持和发展中国特色社会主义的必由之路 Feng Jun Feng Jun's commentary, published in 2022, explains one of the "five musts" that Xi Jinping set out when joining the Inner Mongolia delegation to the Fifth Session of the 13th National People's Congress. The first of these holds that upholding the Party's overall leadership is the only way to uphold and develop socialism with Chinese characteristics. Feng reads this as a summing-up of why the Party has succeeded in the past and how it can keep succeeding. In Feng's account, it also reflects an understanding of the laws governing Party rule, socialist construction and social development. The article follows the Party's record in four stages. It begins with the founding programmes and Mao Zedong's writings on New Democracy. It then covers the establishment of the socialist system in the 1950s and the search for a path of socialist construction suited to China. Its last section turns to the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012), with figures on growth, poverty alleviation and the building of a moderately prosperous society. Feng's central claim is that socialism has been the Party's goal since its founding, and that Party leadership has been the means of reaching it at every stage. Quoting Mao, Feng argues that no revolution could succeed without the Party and that only the Party could lead China to socialism. Feng credits it with the transition of the 1950s, which did not copy the Soviet Union, and with finding a path fitted to Chinese conditions after setbacks, including the Cultural Revolution. Feng also holds that the Party's leadership steered China through the collapse of the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe and so kept world socialism alive. Feng concludes that history and present reality show there would be no new China and no socialism with Chinese characteristics without the Party, and that national rejuvenation depends on its overall leadership. Feng calls for upholding the authority of the Party Central Committee and its centralized, unified leadership, and for the Party's organization to cover all work. Risks and challenges are said to make this more urgent. Read the original if you want an official-line account of how Party history is used to justify the principle of overall Party leadership in the Xi Jinping era.

The profound meaning of historical self-confidence and what the new era requires 历史自信的深刻内涵与时代要求 Jin Minqing Writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in April 2022, Jin Minqing takes up the notion of "historical self-confidence" (lishi zixin), which the Party put forward when summarising its hundred years of struggle. The commentary argues that this confidence rests on the Party's political advancedness, its achievements and its experience, and that it also carries concrete requirements for the new era. Jin first recalls Xi Jinping's statements on the subject since the 18th Party Congress (2012), including his remarks on the Party's 95th and 100th anniversaries and at the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021). The article then has two parts: the content of the Party's historical self-confidence, and four tasks through which it is to be strengthened. Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi are cited throughout, together with the 2021 Party resolution on the Party's major achievements and historical experience. In the first part Jin defines historical self-confidence as the Party's firm confidence in its own history, extended to the history of the Chinese nation, and divides it into five aspects: confidence in the course of history, in historical achievements, in historical influence, in historical experience, and in the spirit of struggle. On this account, the Party's cause conforms to historical laws and the people's wishes, its achievements span four historical periods, and its experience is summed up in the "ten adherences". The fifth aspect, the spirit of struggle, is tied to the founding spirit of the Party and to the Party's self-reform. In the second part, Jin names four requirements: upholding the Party's overall leadership and full and rigorous self-governance of the Party; pursuing Chinese modernization and common prosperity; holding to historical materialism and a correct view of Party history; and the creative transformation of fine traditional Chinese culture. Jin concludes that historical self-confidence is both an affirmation of past achievements and a firm confidence in future development. The four tasks are presented as laying the subjective, practical, cognitive and cultural foundations of that confidence. Read the original if you want a concise statement, from a senior CASS historian in 2022, of how official discourse defines historical self-confidence and links it to Party building and the study of Party history.

Grasping and making good use of the Party's valuable experience of persisting in theoretical innovation 深刻把握并运用好我们党坚持理论创新的宝贵经验 Yang Yanqiu Writing in Guangming Daily in February 2022, Yang Yanqiu takes up one of the lessons set out in the Resolution on the Party's major achievements and historical experience over the past century, adopted at the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021). That lesson is "persisting in theoretical innovation". Yang argues that the Party's history is also a history of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, and that continuing to develop contemporary Chinese Marxism and twenty-first-century Marxism is necessary if the Party is to keep pace with its era. This short commentary has three sections. The first traces how each stage of Party theory arose in response to the demands and themes of its time. The second discusses continuity and innovation across these stages. The third identifies the method of theoretical innovation as the Two Integrations. In the first section Yang surveys the sequence from Mao Zedong Thought, described as the first historic leap in adapting Marxism to China, through Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents and the Scientific Outlook on Development, which together form the theoretical system of socialism with Chinese characteristics and a new leap. The sequence ends with Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, presented as a further leap. Yang holds that each body of theory is grounded in new practice, builds on its predecessors and answers the questions of its period. The article describes the Two Establishes as reflecting the shared wishes of the Party, the military and the people. On method, Yang says that combining Marxism's basic tenets with China's specific realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture is the fundamental way to innovate. Marxism is not dogma, Yang writes, and it can revitalise traditional culture while that culture serves as a source of ideas for the Party's theory. Yang concludes that developing twenty-first-century Marxism and contemporary Chinese Marxism is a historical responsibility of today's Communists, citing Xi Jinping. This means using Marxism to observe and lead the times, drawing on present-day practice and traditional culture, taking a historical and international view, and absorbing the achievements of other civilisations. Read the original if you want a concise, official-line account of how Party theorists present the lineage of Party theory and the role of the Two Integrations.

The people's principal role and the path of Chinese modernization 人民主体性与中国式现代化道路 Yang Xuedong Huang Xiaofang Writing in Guangming Daily in February 2022, Yang Xuedong and Huang Xiaofang ask what distinguishes successful paths to modernization from failed ones. Their answer is that the decisive yardstick is whether a path is people-centred: whether broad popular participation drives modernization and whether its fruits are widely shared. They present the people as the real agent of modernization and the source of the distinctive character of Chinese modernization. The short commentary has three parts. It first sets out the people-centred criterion and contrasts China's path with Western and dependent models. It then lists five features that give Chinese modernization its "people-oriented" character. Finally it draws out four practical requirements for keeping the people at the centre. Historical examples include the post-1949 elections, literacy and public-health campaigns, and Deng Xiaoping's three-step strategy. The authors also cite figures on education, life expectancy and poverty reduction. The authors argue that classifications of modernization by period, region, culture or institutions describe only surface phenomena. In their view the real cause of divergence is whether the people become the principal actors. Late-Qing and Republican-era attempts failed, they say, because the people were not organized. The Communist Party, described as coming from and representing the people, mobilized and empowered them and so avoided exclusion of the masses. The five features are: organizing the people, empowering them to be masters of the country, raising their capacities, meeting their aspirations for a better life, and sharing results. The authors contend that this produced a path of internally driven development. They say it avoids the ills of capital-centred Western modernization and of "growth without development" elsewhere, and that it reached in about seven decades what the West took centuries to build. The authors call for adherence to a people-centred philosophy of development. They also call for judging success by whether people are happy, satisfied and approving rather than by statistics or buildings. They urge widening the reach of the results by narrowing urban–rural, regional and sectoral income gaps and regulating high incomes, and developing whole-process people's democracy so that more people take part. They link this to common prosperity. Read the original if you want a concise official-academic statement of how Party theorists framed the people's role in Chinese modernization on the eve of the 20th Party Congress.

The digital economy and common prosperity 数字经济与共同富裕 Tan Hongbo This commentary, first published in Guangming Daily on 15 February 2022, asks whether the digital economy can advance common prosperity. Tan Hongbo notes that China has eliminated absolute poverty, that the Fifth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2020) set substantial progress toward common prosperity as a long-range goal, and that the digital economy is growing fast alongside it. The article argues that, left unregulated, the digital economy tends to widen income and wealth gaps. Tan therefore calls for regulating its development and building a matching income distribution system. The article has two parts. The first, on whether the digital economy can promote common prosperity, examines the general relationship between technological progress and inequality and then the specific features of digital technology. The second sets out two lines of effort: reasonable regulation of the digital economy, and a distribution system suited to it. Tan cites figures that the digital economy reached 39.2 trillion yuan in 2020, or 38.6% of GDP, growing at 9.7%. Tan makes two main moves. In general terms, technological revolutions have historically coincided with widening gaps, which Tan supports with Thomas Piketty's Capital in the Twenty-First Century and a study of housing-size Gini coefficients by Timothy Kohler and colleagues. Tan adds that innovation tends to produce monopoly power, reinforced by patents. Digital technology adds four features: unequal possession of data as a production factor, increasing returns to scale, network externalities and two-sided platform markets. In Tan's reading these make monopoly easier to form. Dominant platforms can then extract extra profit from merchants through ranking and advertising fees, practise near-perfect price discrimination against consumers using profiling, and stifle rivals. Tan proposes that regulation include price controls such as average-cost pricing, supervision of data collection and the transparency of algorithms, lower entry and exit costs, and compensated interoperability between platforms. On distribution, Tan calls for clarifying data property rights that reflect the contributions of consumers, merchants and platforms while protecting security and privacy. Tan also calls for a tax system adapted to digital trade, including a digital regulatory tax, and for digital technology to be used to improve tax administration and equalise public services. Read the original if you want a concise, policy-oriented economic argument from 2022 on monopoly, data rights and taxation in the context of common prosperity.

From a complete Capital to an open "critique of political economy" MEGA2 Section II and Marx research in Germany 从完整的《资本论》到开放的“政治经济学批判” Zhang Yixiu Zhang Yixiu asks what German scholars have made of the second section of the Marx-Engels-Gesamtausgabe (MEGA2), which covers Marx's economic manuscripts and the editions of Capital, and what Chinese research can learn from them. Published from 1976 and completed in 2012 (15 volumes, 23 books), the section presents all of Marx's surviving manuscripts on the critique of political economy from the late 1850s, together with several editions of Capital and Engels's editorial drafts. Zhang argues that German work based on this material has moved from the image of a finished Capital to that of an open, unfinished process of research. The article first names the section's two contributions to the sources: first publication of many manuscripts, and separate publication of the main versions of Capital, which allows comparison of Marx's drafts with Engels's edited text. It then surveys German scholarship under five headings: periodisation of Marx's thought, the status of key texts, theory and method, theoretical content (value theory and crisis theory), and the relationship between Marx and Engels. Thinkers discussed include Carl-Erich Vollgraf, Michael Heinrich, Ingo Stützle, Wolfgang Fritz Haug, Helmut Reichelt, Dieter Wolf, Hans-Georg Backhaus, Bertram Schefold, Heinz Kurz, Christoph Henning, Regina Roth and Ingo Elbe. Zhang's central claim is that the section's original title, "Capital and its preparatory texts", no longer holds. Vollgraf divides the texts at 1863 into two projects, and the editor Gerald Hubmann is reported as saying there is neither a completed Capital nor a body of manuscripts that merely prepares it. Stützle reads the 1857–58 Grundrisse as a self-clarifying text rather than a key to Capital, and Heinrich distinguishes three stages of work on Capital. Scholars also divide over whether Marx's value categories are logical rather than historical (Backhaus, Reichelt, Wolf), over the falling rate of profit (Kurz against Henning), and over whether Engels distorted Marx (Heinrich and Elbe against Roth and Michael Krätke). Zhang notes that the Neue Marx-Lektüre is not treated in detail here. Zhang concludes that, since the 21st century and especially since the financial crisis, German scholarship differs from twentieth-century Western "Marxology". In Zhang's account, most scholars seek to free the philosophy and method of the critique of political economy from a fixed, dogmatic picture of Capital, not to discredit Marx or Engels. Zhang proposes that Chinese researchers, holding to a Marxist standpoint and an open attitude, use the MEGA2 materials to avoid teleological readings and rebuild the path of Marx's critique. Read the original if you want a concise guide to the main German debates on MEGA2 Section II and on Marx's economic manuscripts.

What the Chinese Communist Party's third historical resolution means for Swiss communists 中国共产党第三个历史决议对瑞士共产党人的时代启思 Massimiliano Ay This is a Chinese translation of a commentary by Massimiliano Ay, General Secretary of the Communist Party of Switzerland, on the resolution on the Party's major achievements and historical experience adopted at the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021). Ay asks what a foreign communist party can learn from this third historical resolution. He argues that it shows how a vanguard party can review its past, close old disputes and plan ahead, and that Swiss communists should study it while developing their own path. The article opens by placing the resolution after those of 1945 and 1981, then moves through sections on the Party's method of correcting errors, the continuity of revolutionary history, the achievements it celebrates, the Party's independence, and what Ay calls an ideological war. It combines a reading of the resolution with remarks on the international situation and on the Western left. Ay contends that, unlike the earlier resolutions, the third is strategic and forward-looking. He holds that the Party's strength comes from never denying its past, which he contrasts with the Soviet party's failure to do so. In his account China's success rests on three pillars: popular trust in Marxism and the Party, a stable political system in which the state outweighs market anarchy and individualism, and the pursuit of the people's welfare against inequality. The Party's central role binds them together. Ay also argues that independence matters: the resolution's insistence on adapting Marxism to China's conditions parallels the Swiss party's 24th Congress slogan, "learn our own history, become our own model". He says Western imperialism is promoting a new cold war and that Western media and some self-styled communists distort the Party, partly to steer young leftists towards a romanticised "Maoism". Ay concludes that the resolution strengthens communists' class consciousness and that ruling and non-ruling parties should keep up internationalist solidarity despite their differences. He urges vigilance against money worship, hedonism, individualism and historical nihilism, which he says the resolution names and imperialism promotes, and suggests that the Chinese Party adopt a prudent "soft power" policy toward Western communist parties. Read the original if you want to see how a European communist leader reads the 2021 resolution and ties it to debates on independence, anti-imperialism and the Western left.

Western new social movements and their influence on left-wing parties 西方新社会运动及其对左翼政党的影响 Zang Xiuling Zang Xiuling asks how the Western "new social movements" that have grown since the late 1960s have affected Western left-wing parties, and what the two might do together. The author defines these movements as loose protests by middle strata and marginal groups, pursuing non-material interests and values. They arose while the world socialist movement was at a low ebb. Zang argues that the movements contain socialist elements but have fatal weaknesses, and that only a merger with left parties can produce lasting resistance to capitalism. The article first traces the movements' history in four stages. They began with the May 1968 events in France, developed in the 1970s–80s through anti-nuclear, green and feminist movements, and turned in the 1990s towards anti-globalisation protest (Seattle, 1999). A new phase followed the 2008 financial crisis and the Covid-19 pandemic, with Occupy Wall Street, Black Lives Matter, the Yellow Vests and Spain's "Indignados". It then sorts left parties into moderate, radical and extreme types and assesses each. It ends with the movements' and parties' predicaments and with proposals. Zang's central claim is that the movements' individualism, identity-based politics, pluralism and lack of leadership or programme weaken them, drawing on postmodern fragmentation. In the author's account, the moderate parties' drift to the centre (the "Third Way", Britain's Labour Party) cost them their working-class base and left them without answers after 2008. The radical parties (Syriza, Germany's Die Linke) have grown livelier but remain unstable and divided. The extreme parties, meaning the communist parties, are marginal and drift towards populism, which Zang calls a temporary, pathological phenomenon. Western Marxist scholars, in Zang's view, stay in an academic "ivory tower" and give the movements no theoretical guidance. Zang calls for left theory to be developed from the practice of the movements and for Western Marxist scholars to engage with society. The author also urges stronger left parties: theoretical innovation, unity among the three party types, a role for trade unions and new organisations, and a clear socialist programme from moderate parties. The aim is to win elections and transform capitalism peacefully. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic view of how Western social movements, left parties and Western Marxism relate, and of the strategy Zang proposes for the Western left.

Upholding Party leadership as the primary experience of the Party's century of struggle 坚持党的领导是百年奋斗首要经验 Liu Hanfeng Why does the Resolution on the Party's major achievements and historical experience, adopted by the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021), list upholding Party leadership as the first lesson of the Party's hundred years? Liu Hanfeng argues that this is the most fundamental reason the Chinese people and nation changed their modern fate. The article sets out to explain how Party leadership should be understood and upheld in the new era, taking the Eighth Party Congress (1956) report's account of the Party's leadership as a basic reference point. The article is organised in three dimensions: historical, theoretical and practical. The historical section traces China's modern revolution from the Opium War, and compares the bourgeois reformers and revolutionaries with the Communist Party. The theoretical section moves through Marx, Engels and Lenin on the proletarian party, then the Chinese Party's own development of leadership theory and the question of proletarian leadership. The practical section reviews institutional arrangements from the Zunyi Meeting through the reform era to the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Liu's core argument is that China's bourgeoisie, tied to imperialism and feudal forces, could not complete the twin tasks of anti-imperialist and anti-feudal revolution, so only a revolution led by the working class could succeed. Theoretically, the author holds that Party leadership rests on the advanced character of Marxist theory and on Lenin's principles of organisation and democratic centralism, which the Chinese Party extended through its doctrine of unified leadership in the base areas. Liu adds that holding proletarian leadership is a long-term task under long-term governance, and that the Party's leadership has been consolidated by institutions. These include collective leadership, reforms to cadre tenure, and, since 2012, a system of leadership institutions covering the Two Upholds, comprehensive Party leadership and full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. Liu concludes that Party leadership is the primary experience because the Party represents the advanced force and the highest political leading force. Upholding it, in the author's account, means continually improving leadership and long-term governing capacity, strengthening the Party's self-reform and its ability to guide social revolution, and improving strategy and tactics. It also means serving the people, pursuing common prosperity, and applying the Two Upholds and democratic centralism. Read the original if you want an official-line account of how Party scholars link history, Leninist theory and institution-building in justifying Party leadership.

The historical course of scientific socialism's development in China over the Party's first century, and its lessons 建党百年科学社会主义在中国发展的历史进程及经验启示 Li Zhengxing Taking up the call of the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021) to understand why the Party succeeded in the past and how it can keep succeeding, Li Zhengxing asks how scientific socialism has developed in China across the Party's hundred years and what lessons follow. The article argues that the Party answered the defining questions of each period by combining Marxism with Chinese conditions, and that this advanced both Chinese practice and scientific socialism itself. The article has two parts. The first sets out three guiding threads and then traces four periods: the New Democratic Revolution (1921–1949), socialist revolution and construction (1949–1978), reform and opening up (1978–2012), and the new era since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The second part draws five lessons, each tied to a basic task, driving force, value or guarantee of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Li identifies three threads: the unity of theory and practice, of logic and history, and of truth and value. In this reading, the Party kept scientific socialism's basic principles while drawing on historical experience. Each period yielded original contributions: New Democratic revolutionary theory and the rural-centred revolutionary road; a peaceful transition to socialism and early theories of construction, despite the errors of "class struggle as the key link" and the Cultural Revolution; the path and theory of socialism with Chinese characteristics; and, in the new era, Xi Jinping's ideas on development, governance, ecology, Party building and a community with a shared future for mankind. The five lessons are to integrate scientific socialism with China's actual conditions, including the primary stage of socialism; to centre work on economic development and the productive forces; to deepen reform and opening up; to put the people first and promote people's all-round development; and to uphold Party leadership and Party building. Li concludes that the Party's century of experience shows these principles must be upheld in order to keep socialism with Chinese characteristics on the right course. The author calls for keeping the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds, strengthening the Party's long-term governing capacity and advancing full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. Read the original if you want a compact, officially aligned periodisation of how Chinese Party theory presents its own relationship to scientific socialism.

The essence of the times of Chinese culture and the Chinese spirit 中华文化和中国精神的时代精华 Sun Jianchang This commentary, published in Guangming Daily on 1 March 2022, takes up one phrase from the resolution on the Party's century of struggle adopted by the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021): that Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era is "the essence of the times of Chinese culture and the Chinese spirit". Sun argues that this formulation offers a new theoretical angle for understanding the Thought, which the resolution also describes as twenty-first-century Marxism and a new leap in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The piece is organised under three headings. The first treats the Thought's roots in the Chinese cultural tradition and its role in guiding cultural development. The second treats the Chinese spiritual temperament, values and strength it is said to embody. The third treats its grasp of the features of the era, its answers to the questions of the times and the direction it indicates. Sun's central claim is that the Thought fuses Marxism with fine traditional Chinese culture. Drawing on Xi's formula of making the past serve the present, Sun says Xi reactivates elements of tradition through a Marxist standpoint and method, and cites ideas such as putting the people first, a community with a shared future for mankind and harmony between humanity and nature. On the Chinese spirit, the author traces a line from ancient ideals such as "all under heaven as one" through the Party's founding spirit to the core socialist values, and argues that the Thought gathers spiritual strength for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. On the era, Sun maintains that the Thought answers questions about the nature and path of socialism, modernization and Party building, and about where the world is heading. Sun concludes that the Thought gives Chinese culture a guiding direction under firm cultural confidence and a Marxist leadership in ideology. It is also presented as offering "Chinese wisdom" and "Chinese solutions" for humanity. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary in 2022 linked Xi Jinping Thought to traditional Chinese culture and national spirit.

Unwaveringly keeping economic development as the central task 坚持以经济建设为中心不动摇 Shi Jianxun Writing in Guangming Daily in February 2022, after the Central Economic Work Conference of late 2021, Shi Jianxun asks why the Party must keep economic development as its central task in the new development stage. Shi argues that the line is a basic experience of the People's Republic and is essential for achieving high-quality development. The commentary is organised around three "logics": historical, theoretical and practical. The historical section traces the line from the Eighth Party Congress to the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978) and the 13th Party Congress (1987), which set out the basic line of "one centre, two basic points". In the theoretical section, Shi holds that the changed principal contradiction of the new era does not alter China's position in the primary stage of socialism. Shi reasons that a better life for the people needs a material base and higher productive forces. Shi also presents economic development as the "key point" within the "five-sphere integrated plan", which does not conflict with coordinating the other four spheres. In the practical section, Shi calls for the new development philosophy, supply-side structural reform and attention to demand management, and treats economic growth as the precondition for common prosperity. Making the "cake" bigger requires the basic socialist economic system, distribution according to work combined with distribution according to factors of production, and the Two Unwaverings. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official rationale for the economy-centred line in early 2022.

The "non-identity" dimension of Marx's empirical research method 马克思经验研究方法的“非同一性”维度 Yang Lei This short commentary, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in January 2022, asks what distinguishes Marx's empirical method from both the speculation of the Young Hegelians and British and French empiricism. Yang argues that Marx rejected metaphysical thinking based on "identity" and affirmed the positive significance of "non-identity". In Yang's account, this is what gives historical materialism its scientific footing. The article is organised around three emphases in Marx's method: matter (质料, the material substrate), the individual, and difference. Yang draws mainly on The German Ideology, Marx's 1877 letter to the editors of Otechestvennye Zapiski, and his reply to Vera Zasulich. Dewey and Hegel are cited as background. On matter, Yang holds that Marx countered the long Western pursuit of an unchanging "One" by starting from real individuals and their material living conditions, which can be verified empirically. In capitalist society, Yang says, "identity" appears as capital's logic posing as the only rational reality. On the individual, Yang reads Marx as showing that capital and metaphysics together reduce living persons to abstract functions, and that the remedy lies in changing the worldly basis of life. On difference, Yang cites Marx's late study of Russia and his refusal to turn his account of Western European capitalism into a universal philosophy of history. Paths of development, Yang argues, differ with historical setting. Yang concludes that Marx valued experience without being confined by it or deferring to it. He treated experience as changing, and analysed concrete problems concretely. Marx's aim, Yang says, is the self-emancipation of free, concrete individuals. Read the original if you want a compact reading of Marx's methodology that links empirical research to a critique of conceptual uniformity and to the question of differing national paths.

The Chinese Communist Party's exploration of agricultural labour mutual aid in the Soviet areas period 苏区时期中国共产党关于农业劳动互助的探索 Geng Lei Geng Lei examines how the Chinese Communist Party experimented with agricultural labour mutual aid in the Soviet areas (the rural revolutionary base areas of the late 1920s and early 1930s). The article argues that, alongside land distribution, the Party used mutual aid to pool scarce labour, sustain farming and support the war effort. Geng notes that scholarship on the topic is thin and offers a preliminary survey. The study draws mainly on the newspaper Red China (Hongse Zhonghua), Soviet government work reports and memoirs. It is organised chronologically and by form: 'Saturday voluntary labour', 'joint cultivation', the 'spring ploughing campaign' with 'ploughing mutual aid', and finally the labour mutual aid societies. Each is set against Soviet Russian precedents, namely Lenin's communist subbotniks and the early collective 'joint cultivation societies'. Geng's central claim is that the Party adapted Soviet models to local conditions. Saturday labour, carried out by Party members, Youth League members and cadres, helped families of Red Army soldiers with farming, so that soldiers need not be recalled home; it also cultivated public-minded habits. Joint cultivation appeared in two variants, one with shared labour but unequal product shares and one with equal division. From 1931–32 the spring ploughing campaign made mutual aid official policy, but enforcement was uneven because mass mobilisation was weak. The labour mutual aid societies, regularised by the 1933 Outline for Organising Labour Mutual Aid Societies, are presented as the mature form. They widened mutual aid from cadre-to-peasant to peasant-to-peasant, and Geng cites 1934 membership figures such as 18,220 members in 329 societies in Xingguo. Geng concludes that, though still at an early stage, these practices raised farm output, advanced revolutionary mobilisation and strengthened peasants' identification with the Party and the Soviet regime. They also supplied experience for later production mutual aid movements. The article offers a way to understand mass mobilisation, army–people relations and rural governance in this period. Read the original if you study the early rural economy of the Chinese revolution, Soviet influence on Communist policy, or need the primary-source citations from Red China.

Recent developments in radical left social movements in Europe and the United States 当前欧美激进左翼社会运动的发展动态 Li Xiaoling Why have radical left social movements become so active in Europe and the United States, and can they change the existing order? Writing in 2021, Li Xiaoling argues that explosive inequality under neoliberal, finance-monopoly capitalism has driven a wave of protest. In Li's view, these movements are constrained by right-wing pressure, internal division and weak organisation, and can succeed only through a broad left united front led by the working class. The article has four parts. It first sets out the background of inequality, using US and European data on income and wealth, the effects of the Covid-19 pandemic, and austerity after the financial and eurozone crises. It then surveys the current movements and their features, from Occupy Wall Street and the Black Lives Matter protests of 2020 to the Spanish indignados, the French "Yellow Vest" movement and Greek anti-austerity protests. A third part examines the movements' internal and external limits, and a final part discusses their likely direction. Li identifies three features of the movements: frequent, large and widespread protest; diverse participants and demands, in which class discourse and identity discourse now coexist; and networked mobilisation with flat organisation, as in the Yellow Vests and the George Floyd protests. Li then argues that the movements stall for three reasons. Right-wing populism is rising and left parties have drifted away from the working class, as the electoral setbacks of Corbyn, Tsipras, Podemos and Sanders show in the article's account. The movements also lack ideological unity beyond Marxism, and their loose, non-violent, online-based organisation offers no constructive alternative to neoliberalism. Li concludes that movements confined to narrow issues or to street protest cannot change the system. The only effective strategy, in Li's reading, is a pan-left united front opposed to the capitalist system and led by the working class. This requires a unified class identity and socialist consciousness, formed above all through workers' struggles, and alliances with groups that capitalism specially oppresses, such as women, ethnic minorities and LGBTQ people. Li holds that the historical trend of socialism replacing capitalism will not change. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic account of Western left protest movements, with figures and examples from 2011 to 2020.

Lenin's early critique of non-Marxist currents of thought in Russia 列宁早期对俄国非马克思主义思潮的批判 Chen Hong Jiang Bo Chen Hong and Jiang Bo ask what Lenin's polemics of the 1890s and early 1900s achieved and what they still offer today. They argue that, in disputes over "the fate of capitalism in Russia", Lenin defended and developed Marxism against three currents: liberal Narodism (populism), "legal Marxism" and the "Economists" inside the Social-Democratic Labour Party. Through these debates, in their account, he set out the laws and special features of Russian capitalist development and pointed the Russian revolution toward its path. The article has four parts. The first three each take one current in turn: Narodnik claims of a "non-capitalist road", legal Marxism's glorification of capitalism, and the Economists' attachment to Bernstein-style reformism. Each is broken into its component theories and the works in which Lenin answered them, including The Development of Capitalism in Russia and What Is to Be Done? The fourth part turns to the contemporary value of this critique for confronting erroneous currents of thought in China. On the Narodniks, the authors report Lenin's rebuttals of their "environmental determinism", their thesis of a narrow domestic market and their "subjective sociology". Lenin argued that the peasantry was already being split by the division of labour and that the ruin of small producers expanded the market rather than shrinking it. Against legal Marxism (Struve, Bulgakov, Tugan-Baranovsky) he rejected theories of agrarian overpopulation, the "law of diminishing soil fertility" and the stability of peasant farming, charging that they treated bourgeois categories as eternal. Against the Economists he rejected worship of workers' spontaneity, "trade-unionist politics" and "amateurishness". He held that socialist consciousness must be brought to workers from outside and that a centralised party of professional revolutionaries must lead. The authors conclude that Lenin's critique drew the line between Marxist and non-Marxist thought and Russianised Marxism. They argue that it supplies theoretical weapons against present-day currents such as extreme democratism and online populism, which they link to Western ideological infiltration. Citing Xi Jinping's "red, black and grey zones" of public opinion, they call for holding the ideological front, upholding Party leadership and adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Read the original if you want a systematic Chinese account of Lenin's early polemics, and of how they are used in current ideological work.

A century of upholding and improving the Party's system of leadership: course and basic experience 坚持和完善党的领导制度的百年历程和基本经验 Wang Chunxi Published in a series of written reflections on the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021), this article asks how the Communist Party of China has built and refined its system of leadership over a century. Wang argues that upholding and improving this system is the basic experience behind the Party's long-term rule and the guarantee of its successes. The article treats the system in a narrow sense (intra-Party leadership institutions) and a broad sense (the full set of institutions through which the Party leads state, society and people). The article has two parts. The first divides the century into four stages: the New Democratic Revolution, socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the new era of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The second draws four lessons from that record. Wang's institutional focus is collective leadership, centralised leadership and the Party's methods of leadership. In the historical account, Wang traces how democratic centralism, collective leadership, the Party committee system and unified leadership centred on the Party took shape before 1949. After 1949 the Party extended unified leadership over state affairs, with Party groups and central leading small groups. Wang says that after 1957 this drifted into Party–government fusion and personal rule. Reform after 1978 restored collective leadership, replaced the chairman system with a general secretary, formalised the leadership core, and set the principle of scientific, democratic and law-based governance. For the new era, Wang describes a Party leadership system with six institutional dimensions, tied to the Two Upholds, the Two Establishes and democratic centralism. The four lessons are: uphold Party leadership over all work, and cite the Soviet collapse as a warning; keep innovating institutions; safeguard the authority of the Central Committee; and use strategic thinking so that Party leadership institutions guide national governance, through Party groups, institutional reform and organisation down to the grassroots. Wang concludes that improving the Party's leadership system means combining "upholding fundamental principles" with innovation, using the spirit of self-reform to strengthen what is described as the greatest advantage of the system. Only by bringing the advantages of the "Chinese system" into full play, the author holds, can "Chinese governance" succeed. Read the original if you want an official-line account of how the Party periodises the development of its own leadership institutions, and how it ties them to the modernisation of national governance.

Full and rigorous self-governance of the Party opens a new realm in the self-reform of a century-old Party 全面从严治党 开辟百年大党自我革命新境界 Zuo Tengfei Zuo Tengfei's commentary in Guangming Daily takes up Xi Jinping's statement at the sixth plenary session of the 19th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection that full and rigorous self-governance of the Party is a great practice of the Party's self-reform in the new era. Zuo argues that this practice opens a new realm of self-reform for a Party now a century old. The article presents the link between self-reform and rigorous Party governance as an answer to how the Party was able to succeed in the past and how it can achieve more in future. The piece has three parts. The first explains why persistent self-reform and strict Party governance keep the century-old Party vigorous. The second reviews what full and rigorous self-governance of the Party has achieved since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The third sets out four pairings of principles for taking it further. In the first part Zuo argues that self-reform preserves the Party's advanced nature and purity, strengthens its creativity, cohesion and combat effectiveness, and keeps it the backbone of the Chinese people. Zuo cites the collapse of the Soviet Union and the upheavals in Eastern Europe, which the article attributes partly to ruling communist parties losing these qualities. In the second part Zuo says the campaign has carried forward earlier Party-building experience and supplied what Xi calls the "second answer" to the historical cycle of rise and decline, after Mao Zedong's first answer of letting the people supervise the government. Zuo adds that it has deepened understanding of how to build a long-governing Marxist party and has underpinned what the article calls the great social revolution, including reform. Zuo calls for pressing ahead by combining mission with problem-orientation, spiritual with capacity building, organisational drive with individual initiative, and upholding fundamentals with innovation. Concrete measures include putting Party political building first, strictly applying the Central Committee's eight-point regulations, sustaining the anti-corruption struggle and building a system of institutional rules for self-purification, self-improvement, self-renewal and self-advancement. Zuo holds that the Party's future success depends chiefly on the Party itself. Read the original if you want a compact example of how the official line on Party discipline and self-reform was presented to a general readership in 2022.

Strengthening the historical confidence of Chinese Communists 坚定中国共产党人的历史自信 Yao Hongzhi Nie Shengping Yao Hongzhi and Nie Shengping take up the call in Xi Jinping's remarks to "firm up historical confidence" and ask where Chinese Communists' confidence in their own history comes from and how it is formed. The commentary, first published in China Social Sciences Today in January 2022, defines historical confidence as a firm conviction in the spiritual value and vitality shown by the Party's own history. The authors argue that no party in the world has more reason to be confident, and that every Party member should take pride in the Party's century of struggle and draw strength from it for the "new road to the exam". The piece has two parts. The first identifies four sources of historical confidence: the Party's major achievements, its contributions to the world, its fighting spirit, and its distinctive strengths. The second sets out a "logical path" linking study of Party history, historical understanding, historical consciousness and historical initiative. In the first part, the authors list the achievements of the new-democratic revolution, socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era. They hold that these changed the fate of the nation. They present Chinese modernization as a new form of human civilization that rejects capital-centred, polarising and expansionist Western modernization. They cite setbacks such as the failure of the Great Revolution and the "Left" errors of Wang Ming as proof of resilience, from which the Party's spiritual lineage grew. In the second part, they describe an ascending spiral. Study campaigns, from the Yan'an rectification to the 2021 Party history study and education drive, deepen understanding. Historical materialism and a "correct view of Party history" turn understanding into historical consciousness. That consciousness in turn produces historical initiative. The authors conclude that Party history study is meant not to console but to raise awareness of historical experience and laws, so that the Party can take the initiative. Having met the first centenary goal, they say, the Party must keep drawing wisdom from its history to answer the "exam" of the second centenary goal and write a new chapter of national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated scholars in early 2022 framed historical confidence and the purpose of Party history education.

A new leap in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context 马克思主义中国化新的飞跃 Yang Xin Yang Xin takes up a formulation from the Party's 2021 historical resolution (adopted at the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee): that Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era is "twenty-first-century Marxism" and has achieved a new leap in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context. Writing in a Party-newspaper commentary, Yang argues that this leap shows itself in five "organic unities" that define the thought's theoretical innovation. The article takes these five pairings in turn: theoretical consciousness and political confidence; theoretical logic and historical logic; the value of the times and practical value; inheriting and promoting tradition and drawing on other civilisations; and the Chinese path and its contribution to the world. Each section is a short exposition that places the thought within the longer history of Marxism's adaptation in China, from Mao Zedong Thought to the theoretical system of socialism with Chinese characteristics and then to the present. Yang's central reasoning is that the Party has advanced Marxism by always joining theory to history. The theoretical logic is the combination of Marxism's basic tenets with China's concrete conditions and its fine traditional culture. The historical logic is the Party's founding mission of seeking happiness for the people and renewal for the nation. Yang presents the three theoretical stages as answers to successive demands: Mao Thought to make the nation "stand up", the Deng-era system to make it "prosper", and Xi's thought to make it "become strong". The thought is also said to answer the era's major questions through the "Ten Clarifications" and to rebut anti-Marxist and non-Marxist currents. Yang concludes that the thought opens a new realm of Marxist development and enriches the path of Chinese modernization in both theory and practice. In the author's account, China's road, as a country of about 18 per cent of the world's population, offers developing countries experience and a new option for those seeking faster development while keeping their independence, and so contributes "Chinese wisdom and a Chinese approach" to human problems. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the official 2022 narrative frames Xi Jinping Thought as a third historic leap of Sinicised Marxism.

Telling China's story well: focusing on the logic of modern narrative 讲好中国故事聚焦现代叙事逻辑 Ling Haiqing This newspaper commentary, published in 2022, asks how China's story can be told effectively in a period when, in the author's account, Western actors control much of the world's political, academic and news discourse. Ling argues that the task is both strategically urgent and theoretically unresolved, and that it can be met only by drawing on the historical and cultural roots of Chinese civilization. The proposed answer is a modern narrative paradigm built on the subjectivity, regularity and purposiveness of the China story. The article opens by presenting storytelling as a source of cultural confidence, a way of rallying support for modernization and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, and a contribution to exchange among civilizations. It then proceeds under three headings: upholding China's standpoint, spreading Chinese wisdom and highlighting Chinese values. Ling draws on Xi Jinping's speeches and on the report to the 19th Party Congress (2017) as models and guidance. Ling first contends that China must be the subject of its own narrative, and that Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era supplies the guiding principle. Storytelling should explain Chinese practice with Chinese theory. Second, the author holds that a discourse system with Chinese cultural features is the practical entry point, and credits Xi with three methods: using distinctively Chinese cultural content (such as the Silk Road idea behind the Belt and Road Initiative), using classical Chinese phrasing, and carrying on the people-centred tradition of minben thought through the notion of putting the people first. Third, Ling argues that emotional narrative links past and present and young and old, and that the Party leadership has derived values from tradition, for example ecological civilization from the idea of harmony between heaven and humanity and a community with a shared future for mankind from the idea of benevolence. Ling concludes that China has the confidence and strength to present its civilization's achievements and its contribution to humanity, so that the world better understands China, its history and its national spirit. Cultural identity, in this reading, is a basic source of national self-confidence and a spiritual force for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Chinese commentary frames international communication, cultural confidence and traditional culture in the Xi Jinping era.

The Communist Party of China's century-long exploration and development of building a modern socialist great power 中国共产党百年来对建设社会主义现代化强国的探求和发展 Song Yuehong Written as part of a series of study essays on the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021) and its resolution on the Party's major achievements and historical experience, this article asks how the Communist Party of China has pursued the goal of a modern socialist great power over its first hundred years. Song argues that the goal has deep historical roots, a broad practical basis and a clear logic of development. In the author's account, it runs from the revolutionary struggle for national independence to the present drive towards the second centenary goal. The article is organised chronologically in three parts. The first covers the New Democratic Revolution and the period of socialist revolution and construction, treated as the fundamental political premise and historical foundation. The second covers reform and opening up from 1978, including the theory of socialism with Chinese characteristics, the primary stage of socialism, the "three-step" strategy and the building of a moderately prosperous society. The third turns to the new era under Xi Jinping and the new stage of development. Song's central move is to read each period as supplying a precondition for the next. Before 1949, Mao Zedong and the Party linked national independence to a plan for industrialisation and a new state. After 1949, socialist transformation and the construction of an independent industrial system laid the institutional and material base, despite what Song calls serious setbacks. Reform and opening up then solved the question of path and stage. For the new era, Song sets out the sequence from a moderately prosperous society to basic modernization by 2035 and a great power by the mid-century. This is tied to the new development philosophy, high-quality development, the modernization of the system and capacity of national governance, and the "five-sphere" and "four-pronged" strategic layouts. Song concludes that the Chinese nation has moved from "standing up" and "becoming rich" to "becoming strong", and that this has created a new path of Chinese modernization and a new form of human civilisation. The author adds that building a modern socialist great power will fully test and display the scientific character, people-centred orientation, practicality, openness and timeliness of Marxism in China. Read the original if you want an official-line, resolution-based periodisation of how Party documents link the revolutionary, Maoist, reform-era and Xi-era goals of national strength.

The Party's century of struggle demonstrates the great vitality of Marxism 党的百年奋斗展示了马克思主义的强大生命力 Liu Jianjun Fan Jiaoyang Taking its cue from the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021) and its Resolution on the Party's major achievements and historical experience, which states that the century of struggle "demonstrated the great vitality of Marxism", the article asks why Marxism has flourished in China. Liu and Fan argue that this vitality comes from Marxism's own theoretical features: scientific character and truth, people-centredness and practicality, openness and development. They hold that it also depends on the Party's century of struggle, which tested, implemented and displayed those features. The article is organised in five parts. It first presents Marxism as the Party's fundamental guiding ideology, tracing the turn to Marxism after the Opium War and the Russian Revolution. The next three parts take each pair of features in turn and walk through four periods: the New Democratic Revolution, socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the new era. A final part considers the international effect of China's experience. The central move is to treat each period as a test case. In the authors' account, Mao Zedong's analysis of a semi-colonial, semi-feudal society, the transition to socialism, the shift to economic construction under Deng Xiaoping, and the policies of the Xi Jinping era each applied Marxist principles to Chinese conditions and were confirmed by results. The authors then show people-centredness being put into practice through the mass line, the concept of "the people", and later formulations such as the Three Represents, putting people first, and a people-centred approach to development. Openness is shown through Marx and Engels revising their own formulations, and through successive theoretical innovations from Mao Zedong Thought to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Together these are said to have produced the Two Integrations' predecessors, the adaptation of Marxism to Chinese conditions, in successive leaps. Liu and Fan conclude that China's success has shifted the global balance between socialism and capitalism in socialism's favour. They claim it strengthens confidence in socialism, countered talk of socialism's end in the 1990s, and offers other developing countries a model of modernization that preserves independence. They say the Party will keep adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Read the original if you want a detailed example of the official Party-history narrative of Marxism's "vitality", organised by period and theoretical feature.

The theoretical logic and practical path of whole-process people's democracy 全过程人民民主的理论逻辑与实践路径 Sun Yingshuai Writing in People's Forum in 2021, Sun Yingshuai asks what whole-process people's democracy contributes to socialist democratic theory and to China's political development. The article argues that it is a major theoretical innovation, a new practice within the political path of socialism with Chinese characteristics, and a form of democracy that, in the author's account, shows the superiority of Chinese-style democracy over Western bourgeois democracy. The piece opens with the concept's recent history: Xi Jinping's first use of "whole-process democracy" in November 2019 at a grassroots legislative contact point in Shanghai, his October 2021 speech to the Central Conference on NPC work, and the March 2021 amendment to the NPC Organic Law that wrote the term into national law. Three sections follow, covering theory, practice and comparative advantage. They move from Marx and Engels, through Mao Zedong's 1949 writing on the people's democratic dictatorship, to the present. Sun first places the concept in a line from the Communist Manifesto's call to "win the battle of democracy" and the Communist League's democratic statutes, through the Chinese Communist Party's people's democracy, to Xi's stress on the people-centred stance. Second, the article describes practice: the people's congress system, multiparty cooperation and political consultation, grassroots self-governance and regional ethnic autonomy, plus consultation mechanisms such as legislative contact points and hearings. It cites 187 draft laws opened to public comment since the 18th Party Congress (2012), and 10 rounds of consultation on the Civil Code that drew over 1.02 million suggestions. Third, Sun names three distinguishing features: Party leadership as the fundamental political guarantee, the people's congress system as the main institutional channel, and a full-chain, all-round, full-coverage design linking election, consultation, decision-making, management and oversight in a closed loop. Sun contrasts this with the "one-off democracy" of the West. Sun concludes that whole-process people's democracy enriches socialist democratic theory, supports the modernization of national governance, and contributes to a new form of human civilization. The author calls for pursuing high-quality development of Chinese-style democracy with greater confidence in the new development stage. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned account of how the concept was introduced, institutionalised and justified in 2021, with the legislative-consultation figures it cites.

The Chinese Communist Party's courage in self-reform: its historical record and underlying logic 中国共产党勇于自我革命的历史呈现与生成逻辑 Wang Feng Guo Yaxin Published in China Social Sciences Today in November 2021, shortly after the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee adopted the Resolution on the Party's major achievements and historical experience over the past century, this article asks why the Communist Party of China can claim that it has the courage for self-reform. Wang and Guo argue that this courage is a defining mark separating the Party from other parties. They present it as one of the main lessons of the Party's centenary and as a guide to future success. The article has two main parts. The first surveys the Party's history in four periods: the New Democratic Revolution, socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the new era of socialism with Chinese characteristics. For each it identifies the specific campaigns and rules through which the Party reformed itself. The second part explains the sources of this drive and then sets out its wider significance. The authors trace the drive to three logics. In theory, self-reform follows from the nature of a Marxist proletarian party that, in their account, has no interests of its own and serves the people wholeheartedly. In history, it is required by the Party's founding mission of seeking the happiness of the Chinese people and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. In practice, it is needed to meet present risks, including a world undergoing great changes unseen in a century and factors that weaken the Party's vanguard character and purity. They then argue that self-reform enriches the theory of Marxist party building, keeps the Party advanced and pure, and gives momentum to what they call the great social revolution. They also hold that it offers a reference for other governing parties. Wang and Guo conclude that full and rigorous self-governance of the Party is never finished and that self-reform has no final note. They call for a scientific summing-up of the century's experience, so that the Party can carry on its new great project of Party building and lead the people through a new "examination". The article is a concise, officially aligned statement of the Party's own account of its history. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Chinese Party scholarship presents self-reform as the thread of the Party's century and as an export-ready governance model.

The Communist Party of China's historic contribution to the progress of human civilization 中国共产党对人类文明进步的历史性贡献 Li Baogeng Marking the Party's centenary, this commentary (originally in the Chinese Social Sciences Today, November 2021) asks how the Communist Party of China has contributed to the progress of human civilization. Li Baogeng argues that, over a hundred years, the Party has made three historic contributions: it liberated the Chinese people and pointed the way to the liberation of the world's peoples, it opened a path of modernization that goes beyond the logic of capital, and it shaped a new form of human civilization through the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind. The piece follows these three headings in turn. It opens by tracing the Party's aspiration to contribute more to humanity from the First Congress's goal of communism, through Mao Zedong's 1956 remark, to Xi Jinping's formulation about seeking happiness for the people, rejuvenation for the nation and "great harmony" for the world. It then reviews the stages of Party history and of modernization, before turning to the contemporary international situation. On liberation, Li contrasts failed utopian thinkers from Plato to Owen with Marxism as a theory of human emancipation, and presents the four "great leaps" (standing up, becoming prosperous, becoming strong) as proof of its truth. On modernization, Li runs from the first generation's revolution and industrial base through reform and opening up to the post-2012 campaigns for poverty alleviation and common prosperity, claiming that this confirms Marx's idea of bypassing the "Caudine Forks" of capitalism. On civilization, Li reads Marx's "two inevitables" and "two never wills" as implying a long coexistence of socialism and capitalism, and argues that the community with a shared future for mankind answers how the two can coexist: through "strong but not hegemonic" states, plural civilizations, just exchange and a human-centred rather than capital-centred logic. In Li's account this idea develops Marx's theory of world history and refutes the "Thucydides trap", the "clash of civilizations" and the "end of history". Li concludes that the Party saved the Chinese nation and, through Chinese modernization, created a new form of human civilization. China, the author says, will remain a builder of world peace and will become a leader and builder of civilizational progress as it grows stronger. Read the original if you want a compact example of how the centenary-era Party narrative links Marxist theory, modernization and the community with a shared future for mankind.

Reform and opening up as a great awakening of the Party 改革开放是党的一次伟大觉醒 Qu Qingshan Qu Qingshan takes up the judgement in the Resolution on the Party's major achievements and historical experience over the past century, adopted at the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021), that "reform and opening up was a great awakening of the Party". The article, a commentary first published in the People's Daily, asks how this awakening came about and why the decision for reform and opening up was taken. Qu's answer is that it rested on several mutually reinforcing foundations: an understanding of the nation's fate, a summing-up of socialist practice, insight into the trend of the times, attention to the people's needs, the Party's nature and Marxist guidance. The text is organised as a sequence of short sections, each naming one basis or feature of the awakening. It begins with the Cultural Revolution and the choices facing the Party in the late 1970s, then reviews the theoretical and strategic achievements of successive leaderships from Deng Xiaoping to Hu Jintao. It goes on to the international context, popular aspirations, the Party's purpose and ideals, the 1978 debate on truth, and the role of the masses. It closes with the results of reform and opening up. Qu argues that the Cultural Revolution exposed serious defects in the system and policies of the time, and quotes Deng Xiaoping to the effect that without reform the cause of modernization and socialism would be lost. The Party, in this account, faced three roads: a closed and rigid old path, a "wrong path" of changing the Party's banner, and a new path of development. It chose the third. Qu holds that the Party could correct its own errors because it has no interests apart from those of the working class and the people. He presents the 1978 debate on "practice as the sole criterion of truth" as the start of the awakening, restoring the line of seeking truth from facts, and treats the masses as the real creators of reform. Qu concludes that the awakening produced reform and opening up as a "new great revolution" that liberated productive forces and raised living standards. He cites China's rise to the world's second-largest economy and largest exporter, and the move from the nation having "stood up" to having "become prosperous". Reform and opening up is described as the key to the fate of contemporary China and to realising the Two Centenary Goals and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a concise example of the official People's Daily framing of the 1978 turning point and the Party's own account of why it chose reform.

Firmly establishing a correct view of development and of modernization 牢固树立正确的发展观现代化观 Lou Qinjian Published in the People's Daily on 18 March 2022, this commentary takes up Xi Jinping's statement that only a people-centred approach to development yields a correct view of development and of modernization. Lou Qinjian argues that this approach answers basic questions about the concept, purpose and driving force of high-quality development and socialist modernization. The author calls for establishing these views firmly so as to create a higher quality of life for the people on the new journey. The article has three parts. It first presents the people-centred approach as the expression of the Marxist people's standpoint and of the Party's founding mission. It then sets out the content of the approach: development for the people, development relying on the people, and development whose fruits are shared by the people. The last part applies the approach to five features of Chinese modernization: high-quality development, common prosperity, the all-round development of the person, green development and a community with a shared future for mankind. Lou's central move is to read the Party's history as proof that the people-centred approach is the source of its victories. The author runs through the New Democratic Revolution, socialist construction, reform and opening up, and the new era, and distinguishes the Party's stance from the traditional Chinese idea of the people as the foundation of the state. In Lou's account, the Party has no interests apart from those of the working class and the broad masses. The author ties sharing to national conditions, holding that it must be universal, comprehensive and gradual, neither standing still nor aiming too high. Common prosperity, in this reading, is not simultaneous or equal enrichment, and requires making the cake bigger while also dividing it better by narrowing regional, urban–rural and income gaps. Lou concludes that every area of modernization should follow the people-centred approach. The proposals include innovation-driven growth, a better market environment alongside a stronger role for government, coordination of development and security, cultural and ethical progress, the "dual carbon" goals, and high-standard opening up with high-quality Belt and Road cooperation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-state officials presented the link between the people-centred approach and Chinese modernization in early 2022.

Adhering to the "Two Integrations" 坚持“两个结合” Tang Zhouyan Wang Xueyuan Tang Zhouyan and Wang Xueyuan take up the formula of the Two Integrations, which Xi Jinping set out at the Party's centenary celebration (2021): combining the basic tenets of Marxism with China's specific realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture. The authors argue that adding the second integration, with traditional culture, greatly enriches the content of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. They present it as a new height and an original contribution to Sinicised Marxism, and say that adhering to it is an urgent need. This short commentary in a Party theoretical journal is organised in four parts. The first three each name a source of urgency: launching the new journey of building a modern socialist country in all respects, passing on and renewing fine traditional culture, and advancing contemporary Chinese Marxism. The fourth reads the integration as an expression of theoretical and cultural confidence. The authors draw mainly on speeches by Xi, Mao Zedong's 1938 report to the Sixth Plenum of the Sixth Central Committee, and the 2021 Party resolution on history. Tang and Wang argue first that Chinese modernization differs from Western modernization, which they describe as built on capital export, colonial expansion and imposed values. In their account, Chinese modernization draws on traditional culture, and further integration is needed so that China can promote exchange and mutual learning among civilizations. They then argue that Marxism develops only by joining national practice. They read Mao's On Practice and the principles of seeking truth from facts, the mass line and independence as products of this integration with traditional culture. They also read the Belt and Road Initiative and a community with a shared future for mankind as bearing the imprint of that culture. Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era is called a model of the Two Integrations. The authors conclude that the Party's integration of Marxism with China's realities and culture has moved from spontaneity to self-awareness and then to confidence. They cite Mao's New Democracy of 1940 as the start of conscious effort, and Xi's advocacy of civilizational exchange as a leap to theoretical and cultural confidence. They hold that Marxism can show its contemporary and global value only by engaging Chinese culture, and that traditional culture must be modernised through Marxist critical inheritance. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party theorists in 2022 justified adding the cultural dimension to the Two Integrations.

Strengthening the economic foundation to ensure progress while maintaining stability 做强经济基础 确保稳中求进 Quan Heng Writing in Economic Daily in March 2022, Quan Heng takes up the "triple pressure" that the Central Economic Work Conference and the Government Work Report said China's economy faces: demand contraction, supply shocks and weakening expectations. The author argues that grasping the nature of these pressures and answering them precisely is essential for assessing the economic situation and for strengthening the economic foundation, in line with the guideline of putting stability first and seeking progress within stability. The commentary has three parts. The first analyses the new features of the triple pressure. The second lists risks that must be guarded against in the coming period. The third sets out the strategic advantages the author sees for China and four directions for dealing with the pressures over the short and long term. Quan notes that demand, supply and expectations rarely all come under strain at once, and that a change in expectations can reshape supply and demand over time. The author finds three features: a complex international background (global supply chain disruption, trade protectionism, rising global PPI); deep domestic causes (low final consumption as a share of GDP, new growth drivers not yet clearly formed); and overlap with older problems, namely the "three-phase superposition" and structural, institutional and cyclical problems. The three pressures can also feed one another through price, cost and inflation expectations. On this basis Quan calls for vigilance against weakening of both external and domestic demand, falling household consumption, a split between upstream and downstream firms and between large and small firms, transmission of PPI to CPI, rising debt and financial risks, and rushed or one-size-fits-all pursuit of the "dual carbon" goals. Quan points to five strategic advantages named by Xi Jinping, including Party leadership and the institutional strengths of socialism with Chinese characteristics, and concludes that the long-term fundamentals are unchanged. The proposed response is to coordinate macro, micro, structural, technology and other policies in the short term. In the longer term, it rests on four tasks: building on the new development stage and high-quality development, deepening institutional reform, advancing technological innovation, and pursuing high-level opening up, including a shift to institutional opening. Read the original if you want an example of how official economic commentary in early 2022 framed the triple pressure and its policy responses.

Common prosperity is an important feature of Chinese modernization 共同富裕是中国式现代化的重要特征 Liu Wei This short commentary, first published in Economic Daily and written in 2022, takes up Xi Jinping's statement that common prosperity is an essential requirement of socialism and an important feature of Chinese modernization. Liu Wei argues that understanding this feature properly matters for upholding and developing socialism with Chinese characteristics and for achieving more visible, substantive progress toward common prosperity for all people. The piece moves from the classical Marxist vision of production aimed at the prosperity of all, through the Communist Party's founding mission, to the present stage. It then contrasts Chinese modernization with the paths of earlier and later modernizing countries, and closes with principles and concrete measures for the new era. Liu contends that common prosperity, like communism, is a long historical process and must fit the primary stage of socialism, rest on economic and social development and follow objective laws. In the author's account, modernization led by elites and capital in early-developing countries left unresolved polarisation between rich and poor, while some late developers that imitated them produced wider gaps, instability or interrupted modernization. Chinese modernization, by contrast, is described as one of common prosperity for all, whose fundamental task is resolving unbalanced and inadequate development. Liu sets out three principles: encourage prosperity through hard work and innovation, first enlarging the "cake" and then dividing it well; act within means; and proceed step by step. Measures include enlarging the middle-income group toward an olive-shaped social structure, equalising basic public services, regulating high incomes while protecting lawful ones, promoting people's all-round development and cultural life, and rural revitalisation. Read the original if you want a concise, official-line academic statement of how common prosperity is framed within Chinese modernization.
