The strategic blueprint for building a modern socialist great power 建设社会主义现代化强国的战略擘画 Gu Hailiang This short commentary, published in the People's Daily in March 2022, explains the "general task" of upholding and developing socialism with Chinese characteristics as set out in Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Gu argues that the task, which combines socialist modernization with the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, condenses the Party's answer to the major questions of the era. The article is organised around three claims about the general task. It clarifies the direction of development in the new era, it sketches a blueprint for a modern socialist great power, and it expresses the Party's resolve to remain true to its founding mission. Gu places the task in a historical line. After the Opium War, China faced two historical tasks: national independence and people's liberation, then national prosperity and the people's happiness. The author traces the Party's pursuit of modernization from industrialization and the "four modernizations" to the start of "Chinese-style modernization" under reform and opening up, and then to the path of Chinese modernization in the new era. In Gu's reading, socialist modernization and national rejuvenation are essentially one. The blueprint envisages basically realizing modernization by 2035 and building a prosperous, strong, democratic, culturally advanced, harmonious and beautiful country by mid-century. Gu lists the features Xi Jinping attributes to Chinese modernization, including its huge population, common prosperity and peaceful development. Gu concludes that the Party's achievements show that the Party is capable, Marxism works and socialism with Chinese characteristics is good. The author holds that national rejuvenation has entered an irreversible historical process and that Chinese modernization will further display the strengths of the system. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned exposition of how Party theorists frame the general task and its historical lineage.

On how historical materialism goes beyond traditional moral philosophy 论历史唯物主义对传统道德哲学的超越 Zhang Guangquan Zhang Guangquan, in a short commentary first published in China Social Sciences Today in February 2022, asks how historical materialism relates to the split between "is" and "ought" that has troubled traditional moral philosophy. The author argues that Marx and Engels turned this apparently epistemological problem into a practical one, and in doing so went beyond traditional moral philosophy. The piece begins with Hume's problem, the claimed impossibility of deriving value judgements from factual ones. Zhang traces its consequences in epistemology, in the long dispute over truth and value, and in philosophy of history, where it has fed doubts about the scientific character of historical materialism. The article then sets out three successive transformations of the problem within Marx and Engels's thought. Zhang holds that traditional approaches treated morality as consciousness detached from the real world, whereas historical materialism derives it from the mode of material production. In the foundational period the problem becomes the unity of the "real human being" (as factual basis) and the "true human being" (as value orientation). In the period of initial establishment it becomes the relation between historical laws and the choice of path. In the period of deepening it becomes the relation between capitalism and communism, where, in Zhang's account, the self-negation of capital's logic drives the transition. Zhang concludes that historical materialism resolves the dilemma by returning the "is" and "ought" relation to real individuals' practice and to the laws of historical development. The author calls on scholars to discuss this question widely, so as to answer doubts about historical materialism's scientific status and to clarify the relation between the communist movement and communist ideal. Read the original if you want a brief statement of how a Chinese Marxist scholar frames Marx's answer to Hume's problem.

The utopian reconstruction in twentieth-century Western Marxism 20世纪西方马克思主义的乌托邦重构 Xie Yuntian Why did some twentieth-century Western Marxists try to rehabilitate utopia, and did the effort work? Xie argues that Ernst Bloch, Herbert Marcuse and others tried to equate utopia with socialism, and that this was both absurd and futile. In Xie's account, any attempt to revive utopia remains a form of feverish fantasy. The newspaper commentary first sets out the background: early twentieth-century liberal anti-utopianism, which treated utopia and socialism as one and so cast doubt on socialism's legitimacy. It then identifies three ways in which Western Marxists reconstructed utopia, and ends with a critique of all three. Xie describes the three methods as follows. Bloch's 'ontological' version grounds utopian spirit in hope and drive. Marcuse's 'aesthetic' version calls for a cultural and instinctual revolution to replace proletarian revolution. Russell Jacoby's 'conceptual' version favours an iconoclastic, purely negative utopianism. Xie holds that these versions are idealist, invert the relation between economic base and superstructure, and lead to political apathy. Rather than defending socialism's legitimacy, the author says, they substituted the false question of utopia's legitimacy for the real one. Citing Engels, Xie adds that their utopias lack any means of realisation, which leaves them even less attainable than the classical utopias. Xie concludes that refuting the liberal charge does not require a road to utopia, and that utopia can be affirmed only if its illusory character is recognised. The author treats these thinkers as well-meaning dreamers whose work is at most a small cultural niche. Read the original if you want a short, polemical Marxist-Leninist critique of Bloch, Marcuse and Jacoby's utopianism, written for a Chinese academic newspaper.

The Party stays at the forefront of the times through self-reform 党在自我革命中坚定走在时代前列 Zhou Suya Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts (2022, no. 5), after the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021), Zhou Suya asks how the Communist Party of China can keep itself at the forefront of the times under long-term rule. The article's answer is the Party's self-reform: Zhou presents it as the route the Party has found to solve its own problems and escape the historical cycle of rise and decline. It is described as a necessary result of the Party's adherence to historical materialism and a correct view of Party history. The article draws on the Resolution on the Party's major achievements and historical experience over the past century and on Xi Jinping's speeches at the plenum and the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection session. It is organised in three parts. The first presents self-reform as the political character of a Marxist party. The second looks at how self-reform has been pushed deeper in the new era. The third addresses the need to advance "two great revolutions" together. In the first part, Zhou ties self-reform to the revolutionary nature, self-critical spirit, vanguard character and purity of a Marxist party. The Party, Zhou says, has no special interests of its own, and this is the source of its courage to reform itself. In the second part, Zhou says self-reform since the 18th Party Congress (2012) rests on firm ideals, steadfast adherence to the Party's original aspiration and mission, and a campaign against corruption with "no forbidden zones", full coverage and zero tolerance. Zhou calls corruption the greatest threat to long-term rule and says the struggle remains grave and complex. In the third part, Zhou argues that the Party's self-reform guides the great social revolution, while that revolution in turn drives self-reform. The degree and effect of self-reform, Zhou says, determine the historical height and practical depth of the social revolution. Zhou concludes that, on the new journey, the Party must keep self-reform going and strengthen the Party's political, ideological, organisational, conduct, discipline and institutional building, together with the fight against corruption. It must also uphold Party leadership over both revolutions under Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Zhou holds that only the Party itself can defeat it, and that the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation will follow if the Party keeps its original mission. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Party-building scholarship in 2022 framed self-reform as both a Marxist principle and a governing method.

The Communist Party of China and a new form of human political civilization 中国共产党与人类政治文明新形态 Xu Junzhong Taking its cue from Xi Jinping's speech at the centenary of the Communist Party of China (2021), which spoke of a new form of human civilization and Chinese modernization, Xu Junzhong asks what kind of political civilization the People's Republic has created. The article's thesis is that the republic's politics is "people's politics" (renmin zhengzhi), which Xu presents as essentially different from Western party politics and as a new political civilization. The article has three parts. The first sets out the logic of people's politics, rooted in Mao Zedong's idea of a "great union of the popular masses", and contrasts it with Western liberal democracy. The second identifies four defining features. The third traces the lineage of people's politics, argues that it belongs to the Marxist political tradition, and lists open problems for its further development. Xu argues that Western party politics is a competition among elites, sustained by money, in which formally equal citizens merely choose periodically between rival groups. People's politics instead rests on "the people", defined historically as everyone except the enemy and therefore internally heterogeneous. Its four features, in Xu's account, are: seeking cooperation among classes rather than contest; balanced planning and proper handling of contradictions among the people; participation by the people themselves, now expressed as whole-process people's democracy; and leadership by the Communist Party. Xu says the Party can play this role because Marxism gives it a people-centred view of history, and because its self-reform keeps it committed to the people. Xu concludes that people's politics is a self-conscious creation of the Party, distinct from both Euro-American democracy and the Soviet model, and warns against judging it by liberal standards. The article also states that it is not perfect. It asks how deputies can avoid becoming representatives of particular strata or interest groups, how popular participation and oversight can be institutionalised, and how the Party can avoid degeneration. Xu calls on Chinese scholars to close the gap between practice and theory using Marxism. Read the original if you want a Party-theory account of how Chinese scholars contrast people's politics with Western electoral democracy, including the problems the author concedes remain.

The Communist Party of China's historical pursuit of fairness and justice and its responsibilities in the new era 中国共产党对公平正义的历史追求和时代担当 Xia Wenbin Published in Marxism and Reality in 2021, the year of the Party's centenary, this article asks how the Communist Party of China (CPC) has pursued fairness and justice (gongping zhengyi) over its hundred years, and what that pursuit requires now. Xia argues that commitment to fairness and justice is a fundamental reason for the Party's leading position, and that a party which keeps the people at heart and upholds fairness and justice will win popular support and move history forward. The article has three parts. The first traces the Party's exploration of the theme through four periods: the New Democratic Revolution, socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the new era. It cites Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin, Hu Jintao and Xi Jinping, and mentions the setbacks of the Cultural Revolution. The second part sets out four core elements of the Party's view. The third looks at how it is being developed under Xi Jinping. In the core section, Xia holds that the Party's view combines Marxist theory of justice with Chinese realities, treats justice as historically and class-conditioned, and is secured by institutions. Drawing on Marx and Engels, Xia contends that justice in capitalist societies is formal and procedural, hiding substantive injustice, whereas China's socialist system aims to unite content and form of justice through public ownership, distribution according to labour, and the people's congress system. Xia also says justice should guide both rule by law and rule by virtue, and that efficiency and fairness must be combined, moving beyond the early reform formula of 'efficiency first, with due consideration to fairness'. For the new era, Xia proposes four routes: institution-building, a people-centred value orientation, deepening reform, and high-level opening up. The article presents the poverty-alleviation campaign and the response to COVID-19 as illustrations, and contrasts them with Western governments, which it accuses of politicising the pandemic and putting capital first. It calls for promoting fairness and justice as shared human values within a community with a shared future for mankind, and for firmly resisting hostile forces that use 'universal values' against China. Read the original if you want an official Party-affiliated account of how fairness and justice are framed in Chinese Party historiography and in the contrast drawn with Western systems.

Deepening understanding of advancing the Party's self-reform in the new era 深化对推进新时代党的自我革命的认识 Wang Weiguo Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts (2022, no. 5), Wang Weiguo, a professor at the School of Marxism, Xi'an Jiaotong University, explains how to understand the Party's self-reform in the new era. The article takes as its starting point Xi Jinping's speech at the sixth plenary session of the 19th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection, which says that the Party has found, in self-reform, a path to escape the historical cycle of rise and fall. Wang argues that the "six musts" Xi set out on self-reform form a unified whole that explains past success and shows how it can continue. The commentary is organised as a series of six sections, each taking one of the "six musts" and arguing for a deeper grasp of it. They cover political development as the guiding principle, ideological development as the foundation, the Central Committee's eight-point regulation on conduct and discipline, the campaign against corruption, the political function and organisational strength of Party organisations, and a system of institutional rules for the Party. Each section opens with a quotation from Xi and ends with practical requirements. In Wang's account, political development is the Party's fundamental development, and its first task is to ensure the whole Party obeys the Central Committee. Wang attributes the achievements since the 18th Party Congress (2012) chiefly to Xi as the core of the Party and to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, and calls for understanding the Two Establishes and practising the Two Upholds. On conduct, Wang says that the eight-point regulation, adopted in December 2012, together with supporting rules, has brought a fundamental turn for the better in Party and government style. On corruption, Wang argues that it takes ever-changing forms and that the struggle will never end while its conditions persist. Wang therefore calls for attacking both "tigers" and "flies", and for pursuing the aim that officials dare not, cannot and do not want to be corrupt. Institutionally, Wang calls for governing the Party by rules and law together, and for stronger oversight of the "key minority", especially top leaders. Wang concludes that deepening understanding of these six requirements is necessary for the Party to keep its advanced and pure character over time, since this does not persist automatically. Practical proposals include firm ideals and convictions, correct views of performance for officials, and stronger grassroots Party organisations. The text also urges overcoming factionalism, individualism and "circle culture" in the Party, and supervision of leadership transitions. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned account of how the Party's self-reform was framed in early 2022 and of the six requirements Xi laid out.

Governing for the people and relying on the people 坚持为人民执政、靠人民执政 Liu Xiaoling This commentary, published in Guangming Daily in April 2022, takes up one of the historical lessons set out in the resolution on the Party's century of struggle adopted at the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021): "governing for the people and relying on the people". Liu Xiaoling argues that the principle sums up the Party's experience of putting the people first, deepens understanding of how communist parties govern, and is the basic guide for the "road to the exam" in the new era. The article has three parts. The first presents the principle as a defining trait of a Marxist party. The second treats it as the source of the Party's strength in governing and building the country. The third turns to the present and sets out what the Party must do to pass the new "exam" on the way to the second centenary goal. In the first part, Liu separates two sides of the principle. Governing for the people is described as the essential feature of a Marxist party, citing the Communist Manifesto and Xi Jinping's 2021 centenary speech on the Party having no interests of its own. Relying on the people is described as a requirement of historical materialism, expressed in the mass line. In the second part, Liu says that winning popular support rests on a party's stance and on its record, and that the leap from "standing up" to "becoming prosperous" to "becoming strong" gave the Party moral standing. The author also says the people's practice and spirit drive the Party's achievements, and that a "two-way commitment" between Party and people explains its ability to overcome hardship. For the new era, Liu proposes three measures. The first is to put the people first and keep the Party's fundamental purpose of serving the people wholeheartedly. The second is to uphold the mass line, fight ideas that sow discord between Party and people, and take the people's well-being as the key measure of political performance. The third is to improve institutions for governing for and relying on the people, by perfecting systems for Party members and cadres to keep in touch with the public, creating online mass-work mechanisms, and strengthening mass organisations. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the 2021 historical resolution's principle of people-centred governance is explained in Party-theory commentary for a general readership.

What determines the rise and fall of a political party: historical warnings from the Soviet Communist Party's failure to reach its centenary 什么决定了一个政党的兴衰——苏联共产党没能走过百年的历史警示 Li Ruiqin Why did a Marxist party that was once among the most powerful in history collapse after only 88 years? Writing in the year the Communist Party of China marked its centenary (2021), Li Ruiqin asks what governs the rise and decline of a ruling party. The article argues that the Soviet party fell because it drifted away from the people, lost its capacity for theoretical innovation, and was finally led by a general secretary who had abandoned Marxism. The article opens with the Bolshevik and Soviet party's achievements: the October Revolution, the Red Army, industrialisation under the five-year plans, the war against fascism, and support for socialist states in Eastern Europe. It then works through three lessons in turn: institutional safeguards against bureaucratism, theoretical innovation and the party's vanguard character, and the quality of party leadership. Li draws on Lenin, Marx, Plekhanov, the Russian communist leader Gennady Zyuganov and the former East German official Schirmer. The piece ends with Xi Jinping's remarks and the Chinese party's institutional arrangements since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Li first contends that Lenin foresaw the revival of bureaucracy and set up supervisory bodies, but that relying on officials' personal consciousness without secure institutions left a latent risk of separation from the masses. Second, Li argues that from the Khrushchev era and especially from the 1970s, ideological rigidity, lifelong tenure and patronage allowed entrenched interest groups to form. In the article's account, these groups shelved critical social-science research, bred a crisis of belief, and eroded the party's legitimacy. Third, the author holds that Gorbachev exploited these problems under the banner of "humane and democratic socialism", used his office to turn personal will into state will, and ended by dissolving both the party (August 1991) and the Soviet Union (December 1991). Who becomes leader may be accidental, Li says, but a Marxist party's leader must stand on the right side of world history. Li concludes that the Soviet party's decline had no hidden cause: it moved away from the people and from Marxism, and its leadership betrayed the trust placed in it. In the author's view, the Communist Party of China has answered the questions the Soviet party left unsolved by combining the right path, scientific theory and effective institutions, and by strengthening supervision and people's status as masters of the country. Li expresses confidence that the Party Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core will lead the cause forward in the new era. Read the original if you want to see how a CASS scholar draws lessons from the Soviet collapse for Chinese Party-building at the centenary.

Taking the correct path that suits China's national conditions 走符合中国国情的正确道路 Leng Rong Writing in the People's Daily in December 2021, Leng Rong takes up one of the ten lessons of the Party's century of struggle listed in the Resolution on the Party's major achievements and historical experience, adopted at the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021): "upholding the Chinese path". Leng argues that the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics has been proven in practice to suit China's national conditions. In this account it is the only route to a better life for the people and to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, and Leng calls for stronger confidence in the path. The commentary is a study-and-interpretation piece in three parts. The first traces how the Party explored and formed a path suited to China across the revolutionary period, the socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the era since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The second places the path within Chinese civilisation and history. The third sets out how the path is to be followed in future. Leng's central claim is that a correct path is hard to find and must be cherished. In the early years, the Party's failure to recognise the importance of its own path, including the leftist errors, is said to have brought heavy losses. Mao Zedong's strategy of encircling the cities from the countryside, and later Deng Xiaoping's call to "take our own path", are presented as the turning points. Leng then argues that the path did not "fall from the sky": it is rooted in over 5,000 years of continuous civilisation, so that confidence in the path, theory and system rests finally on cultural confidence. Leng points to China's rapid industrialisation, rapid economic growth and long-term social stability as evidence that the path is correct, workable and effective. Leng concludes that China should neither return to the "closed and rigid old path" nor take the "evil path" of changing the Party's banner, and should hold unwaveringly to the Chinese path. Leng says this does not mean standing still: China should learn from the beneficial achievements of other civilisations and welcome well-meant criticism. It rejects lecturing from outsiders, insisting that socialism with Chinese characteristics is socialism and not some other "ism". Read the original if you want a concise example of how the official People's Daily framed the "Chinese path" and its link to civilisational continuity after the 2021 Resolution.

Socialism with Chinese characteristics and its multidimensional innovation of the form of human civilization 中国特色社会主义对人类文明形态的多维创新 Jin Fenglin Responding to Xi Jinping's claim at the centenary of the Communist Party (2021) that socialism with Chinese characteristics has created "a new form of human civilization", Jin Fenglin asks in what sense it is "new". The article argues that the answer emerges only when the Party's achievement is set within the long history of traditional Chinese civilization and within a global comparison with Western capitalist civilization. The article has three sections. The first takes the long historical view, sketching the traditional Chinese civilizational form, its Qin-Han and Sui-Tang peaks, and its dynastic cycles. The second compares socialism with Chinese characteristics with capitalist civilization, drawing on Marx, the Keynesian and neoliberal phases, Piketty and US wealth data. The third traces the line from utopian and scientific socialism through Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin, Hu Jintao and Xi Jinping to the present. Jin's first move is that traditional China's agrarian economy, with stagnant productive forces, produced a recurring cycle of dynastic rise and collapse. In Jin's account the Party, through the people-centred stance and the democratic supervision Mao Zedong described to Huang Yanpei in 1945, has taken China out of that cycle and raised the old civilization to a new level. The second move holds that capitalism, whatever its policy adjustments over five centuries, remains defined by the supremacy of capital, the alienation of public power and the exploitation of labour. Jin cites shareholder primacy, the 2008 crisis, "one dollar, one vote" politics, and widening inequality as evidence of a crisis in Western civilization. Against this, Jin credits Chinese socialism with poverty reduction, social security coverage, institutional reform and a market economy that combines state and private capital. The third move is that the five-fold advance of material, political, spiritual, social and ecological civilization has created Chinese modernization. Jin concludes that socialism with Chinese characteristics has renewed traditional Chinese civilization and broken the monopoly of the Western capitalist form. In Jin's reading it also refutes the "end of history" thesis and shows that each country must build socialism from its own conditions, so that different forms of civilization can coexist. A civilization's worth, Jin argues, should be judged by its contribution to resolving international disputes and shared human problems, not by victories over rivals. Read the original if you want an example of how a Central Party School scholar frames the "new form of human civilization" claim through history and comparison with capitalism.

Party-organisation-led cooperatives as an effective path for developing the new-type rural collective economy Lessons from the "Yantai practice" 党组织领办合作社是发展新型农村集体经济的有效路径 Jiang Yu Writing in 2022, Jiang Yu takes up several questions on which, the author says, consensus is still lacking: what the new-type rural collective economy is, why it should be developed, whether it is a "return to the old road", and how it differs from the pre-reform collective economy and from farmer-initiated specialised cooperatives. The article argues that Party-branch-led cooperatives, pioneered in Yantai, Shandong, are an effective and feasible path for gradually strengthening the collective economy under market conditions. The article first reviews the history of rural collectives, from agricultural cooperativisation and the people's communes through the household contract responsibility system to developments since the 18th Party Congress (2012). It then proposes a definition of the new-type rural collective economy and distinguishes it from share-based cooperatives, companies and spontaneous specialised cooperatives. The final section describes the Yantai experience and draws general lessons from it. Jiang concludes from the history that the collective economy is a product of revolution and socialist transformation, not a voluntary association of small private owners, and that household contracting changed only the mode of operation, not the collective ownership of land. The author defines the new-type economy as public ownership in which a group of labourers jointly hold the means of production, and rejects equating it with the unallocated assets of reformed "share-economy cooperatives". Quantifying shares to individuals, Jiang warns, is only a first step. If assets became divisible and transferable they would amount to private ownership. In the Yantai model, the Party branch registers a cooperative in which the village collective and villagers pool land, funds and labour. In Jiang's account, only Party leadership can organise dispersed farmers, keep the cooperatives "public rather than private", and negotiate with capital, as in the Beiluotang village orchard deal. Jiang concludes that the new road of agricultural cooperation must put Party leadership at its core: ideological, political and organisational. The author presents this as a spiral upward from the people's communes rather than a retreat, and calls for institutionalising the Yantai approach and for higher-level governments to give cooperatives financial and policy support. Jiang also says the cooperative form is a workaround, given the absence of a full legal framework for collective economic organisations. Read the original if you want a Party-affiliated policy researcher's detailed case for rural collective ownership and for the Yantai model, including its legal and ownership arguments.

Keeping national strategic priorities in view while continuing to advance rural revitalization across the board 着眼国家重大战略接续全面推进乡村振兴 Han Yang Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in early 2022, Han Yang interprets the Central Committee and State Council's No. 1 Document for 2022 on key tasks in comprehensively advancing rural revitalization. The article argues that, in a period of global upheaval and the pandemic, agriculture, rural areas and farmers must serve as the "ballast stone" and stabiliser of the economy, so that work on them should be governed by the keynote of "stability". The piece is organised around three questions drawn from the document: what to hold on to and how, what to push forward and how, and what to guarantee and how. It opens by placing 2022 within the Party's two centenary goals, the 14th Five-Year Plan and the 2035 targets, and stresses that rural revitalization, unlike poverty alleviation, is a protracted campaign rather than a decisive battle. Han sets out two bottom lines: national grain security and no large-scale return to poverty. On grain, the author cites output above 650 million tonnes for seven consecutive years and calls for "storing grain in the land and in technology", covering farmland protection, seed-source research, machinery and soybean expansion. On poverty, the article calls for continued monitoring, support for industries and employment in lifted-out areas, and stable transition-period policies. Three tasks follow: industrial revitalization through integrating primary, secondary and tertiary sectors and county-level development; steady rural construction that respects farmers' wishes; and better rural governance, given population outflow and ageing. The article cites 292.51 million migrant workers in 2021. For guarantees, Han lists people (talent, training of high-quality farmers), money (public budget priority, rural financial services, agricultural insurance) and land (extending second-round land contracts by 30 years, pilot reforms of homestead land, and cautious entry of collectively owned commercial construction land into the market). The article ends by insisting on full Party leadership over rural work, including the "five levels of secretaries" responsibility system, performance assessments of officials and a coordinating mechanism at central level. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned reading of the 2022 No. 1 Document and its priorities in grain security, poverty-return prevention and rural governance.

Building a new pattern of economic work rooted in market entities 构筑扎根于市场主体的经济工作新格局 Gao Peiyong In this short commentary, first published in Economic Daily and posted in March 2022, Gao Peiyong asks how economic work should be done amid unprecedented risks and challenges in the new development stage. His answer is that it should be rooted in market entities. He presents the Party Central Committee's new judgements, measures and formulations on this point as an innovation in adapting Marxist political economy to China and as part of Xi Jinping's economic thought. The piece first explains the shift from the concept of the enterprise to that of the market entity. It then sets out the status that Xi Jinping assigns to market entities and closes with the tasks ahead under the Central Economic Work Conference's deployment. Gao notes that, under the newly issued Regulations on the Registration and Administration of Market Entities, market entities cover enterprises, individual businesses and farmers' professional cooperatives, that is, every economic unit that creates GDP. In Gao's metaphor, large and medium-sized enterprises are the aorta of economic activity and small and micro units are its capillaries. Moving analysis from one to the other means that economic work and macro policy can reach all sources of GDP. Gao also cites Xi's description of market entities as the main participants in economic activity, the main providers of jobs and the main drivers of technological progress. On this basis Gao argues that, in extreme situations, keeping the economy running depends on preserving market entities, so risk prevention must begin with their risks. Gao concludes that a pattern of economic work rooted in and organised around market entities is taking shape. Under the keynote of "seeking progress while maintaining stability", Gao calls for continued focus on market entities and for efforts to stimulate their vitality. Read the original if you want a brief, authoritative statement of why policy discourse in 2022 shifted from enterprises to market entities.

The evolution of value-form theory: the historical thread of the "New Reading of Marx" 价值形式理论演进——“新马克思阅读”的历史脉络 Li Qiankun This short piece, first published in the China Social Sciences Today (Zhongguo shehui kexue bao) in February 2022, asks how the "New Reading of Marx" (Neue Marx-Lektüre), with its focus on the value form, fits into the longer development of Western Marxism. Li Qiankun argues that value-form theory has advanced along a traceable line in four historical stages, and that tracing it helps clarify the theory's content and significance. The article moves chronologically. It begins with Marx's own foundation of the theory, then covers the rediscovery of the value form in the 1920s, the wave of research from the 1960s to the 1980s, and the period from the 1990s to the present. Along the way it names neo-Kantian, Soviet and Western Marxist currents, the Frankfurt School, the Uno school, the regulation school and the English-language \"new dialectics\" school. Li holds that Marx developed the value form in order to find a scientific starting point for presenting the critique of political economy. The author traces this from the 1857–58 and 1861–63 manuscripts to the successive treatments of the value-form text in Capital. Li then argues that the 1920s were a pivotal stage, because Franz Petry, Isaak Rubin, Pashukanis, Lukács, Sohn-Rethel and Pollock each raised basic questions about the theory. The third stage, in Li's account, was driven by criticism of the welfare state as a new form of state monopoly capitalism. In this stage Backhaus and Reichelt defended Marx's philosophical method against marginalist, neo-Ricardian and Habermasian approaches, while Uno, the regulation school and Christopher Arthur pursued parallel lines. For the present stage, Li links the theory to neoliberal monetisation and financial capitalism, and describes it as grasping the most abstract social reality that the theory can reach. Li draws three conclusions. Value-form theory has always been discussed under concrete historical conditions and for varying theoretical purposes. The foreign Marxist tradition of value-form analysis helps explain the structure of foreign Marxism and its interdisciplinary links with philosophy and sociology. Finally, scholars who debate the theory in speculative, abstract terms risk an ahistorical dead end if they ignore its social and historical grounding. Read the original if you want a compact orientation to the lineage of the New Reading of Marx and value-form theory, as presented by a Chinese scholar of foreign Marxism.

Misreadings of Capital in contemporary French critical theory 当代法国批判理论对《资本论》的误读 Wang Yicheng Writing in a newspaper commentary (China Social Sciences Today, February 2022), Wang asks how contemporary French critical theory reads Marx's Capital. Wang argues that, although these thinkers treat Marx as a forerunner of the critique of modernity and Capital as a resource that cannot be avoided, their anti-essentialist, anti-reductionist and anti-historicist stance leads them to misread it. The article covers the French currents that emerged after the May 1968 events and in response to Western Marxism. It sorts their readings of Capital into four paths: a generalised political economy, a scientific epistemology, an expansion of time and space, and a critique of power. Bataille, Lyotard, Baudrillard, Althusser, Badiou, Lefebvre, Bidet and Foucault serve as examples. Wang's central claim is that these readings detach Capital from its historical-materialist base. Baudrillard's The Mirror of Production, in Wang's account, swaps material production for a sign-based political economy and turns the critique into romanticism. The Althusserian line is credited with restoring Marxism's wholeness but is said to stop at registering complexity without examining Capital's method. Lefebvre's production of space and Foucault's micro-power capture new features of capitalism, Wang says, but explain them through the construction of power, not their social-historical essence. Wang grants the work some scholarly value and notes shared traits: stress on Capital's contemporary relevance, sensitivity to capitalism's structural contradictions, and interdisciplinary borrowing. Yet Wang concludes that the theory falls back into the "phrase-mongering revolution" Marx criticised. By abandoning class analysis and Marx's internal critique, it ends, Wang says, in fragmentation and utopian revolution. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese Marxist assessment of how French post-structuralist and post-modern thinkers treat Capital.

The awareness of real-world problems in the study of Marxist texts 马克思主义文本研究中的现实问题意识 Yang Hongyuan Yang Hongyuan asks what textual study of Marxist works should aim at, and argues that it is more than philology. In Yang's view, proper study unites textual-edition verification, interpretation of the text and elucidation of its ideas. Its final purpose, the article contends, is intellectual elucidation, one level of which is solving real problems or revealing a text's real significance. Awareness of real-world problems is therefore integral to such study. The piece, a newspaper commentary, takes Capital as its test case. The article first redefines what a 'real problem' is and how Capital should be classed. It then examines how changes in real problems shaped the structure of Capital, before drawing out the methodology that emerges from Marx's analysis of such problems. It ends by considering the contemporary value of Capital for present-day problems, including globalization and the significance of the Chinese path. Yang holds that 'reality' in the philosophical sense is fact plus essence, and that only phenomena expressing the features and trends of an era count as real problems. On this basis Capital is Marx's distillation and analysis of the real problems of his time and an enquiry into the laws of social-historical development, as well as the theoretical expression of Marxism as a current of thought. Yang reads the shifting chapter structures of Capital's editions, and Marx's failure to finish Volumes 2 and 3, as responses to changing realities: the 1873 crisis, the defeat of the Paris Commune, and Marx's turn to capitalism's 'prehistory' and to Russia's village commune. Yang notes Marx's warning against turning his sketch of Western European capitalism into a universal philosophy of history. Methodological lessons are drawn from the analysis of money, commodity and capital as social relations, and from comparison with Hegel, Smith and Ricardo. Yang concludes that Capital offers no ready-made answers today but remains a methodological resource, since the present era is still within the transition from history to world history. Questions Yang lists as open to its guidance include the nature of capital, how to govern the logic of capital, artificial intelligence, ecological civilization and human free individuality. Yang also calls for placing Capital within the later history of capital critique and for reassessing it in the light of globalization since the 1980s. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how a Chinese scholar links Marxist textual studies to contemporary problem-solving.

The logical levels of Marx's category of world history 马克思世界历史范畴的逻辑层次 Zhou Kanglin Marx and Engels use the term "world history" (shijie lishi) in several senses, and Zhou Kanglin asks how these senses relate. Writing in a newspaper commentary, Zhou argues that the contexts must be separated and their internal connections clarified before the theoretical essence and practical meaning of Marx's category can be grasped. The starting point is the claim that a world of "integrated" universal exchange has confirmed Marx's prediction that history becomes world history. The article distinguishes three levels in the texts of Marx and Engels. The first is "world-historical significance" as opposed to local, regional or national significance, illustrated by Engels's essay on the condition of England and by The German Ideology. The second is "world history" in the sense of universal history, meaning the whole of human history, which Marx derives from human labour. The third is world history as a form of thought: the transition from closed national history to open, universal intercourse. On the first level, Zhou reads Engels's remark that English workers' poverty had world-historical significance as tied to modern large-scale industry. Zhou reads the German Ideology passage as a mockery of German philosophers' inflated claims for the dissolution of Hegel's system, which had only local significance. On the second level, Zhou cites Marx's 1844 Manuscripts, in which world history is the process of humanity's birth through labour. Zhou says this goes beyond Feuerbach's "sensuous intuition" and treats labour itself as historically developing: regional handicraft produced a "discrete" world history, capitalist machine production an "alienated" one, and communist "self-activity" would produce a truly free and universal one. On the third level, Zhou holds that large-scale industry "first created world history", so that "history becoming world history" and "intercourse becoming world intercourse" are the same thing. Zhou concludes that Marx's category differs from both compiled "world history" and the philosophy of universal history, though both fed into it. Marx and Engels needed the empirical material of national histories, especially English social history, to move the idea to the level of historical science. The bourgeoisie, in Zhou's account, is an unconscious instrument of a revolution that remains unfinished, and only the modern proletariat can rebuild the order of world intercourse. Zhou adds that the levels do not form a straight line of development and are often mixed within one text. Read the original if you want a compact guide to the different meanings of "world history" in Marx and Engels and how Chinese scholars separate them.

Drawing on intellectual resources, innovating theoretical discourse The internal connection between Marx's theory of world history and a community with a shared future for mankind 汲取思想养分 创新理论话语 Meng Yueming This short commentary, published in January 2022, asks how Marx's theory of world history relates to the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind. Meng argues that Chinese Communists took the theory as their intellectual basis in offering "Chinese wisdom" and a "Chinese approach" to global problems. In Meng's view, building such a community will move world history towards a peaceful, orderly and equal stage. The piece has three parts. It first sets out the predictions in Marx's theory, then examines contemporary coordinates of world history, and finally discusses how the community idea is moving from concept to reality, with the Belt and Road Initiative as its main vehicle. Meng reads Marx's global perspective, including his remarks on a "world literature" and on interdependence among nations, as anticipating today's reality, in which no country can stand apart from global risks. Marx's criticism of Eurocentrism and his view that Eastern societies might take a path different from Western capitalism are linked to socialism with Chinese characteristics, presented as an alternative for developing countries. Meng describes the post-2008 "anti-globalization" current as a Western attempt to rebuild a "selective globalization" that benefits only developed countries, and says leadership now depends on the ability to supply public goods. Meng concludes that the community with a shared future for mankind makes Marx's distant goal concrete and practicable. It requires recognising that capitalist-led globalization has not ended, while seeking to transcend its constraints through struggle for development and cooperation amid divergent interests. Meng calls it a path from an "illusory community" to a "real community". Read the original if you want a brief, official-style account of how Chinese commentators ground this foreign-policy concept in Marxist theory.

Understanding the world-historical significance of the Communist Party of China's century of struggle 深刻理解中国共产党百年奋斗的世界历史意义 Li Zhen This article, published in early 2022, sets out to explain what the Communist Party of China's hundred years of struggle mean for world history. It takes as its guide the Party's 2021 historical resolution, adopted at the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee, which places Party history within the history of socialism and of human society. Li argues that the Party's struggle has demonstrated the vitality of Marxism, altered global trends and structures, opened a new path to modernization and offered solutions to problems shared by humanity. The article is organised in four parts. The first treats Marxism's vitality, tracing the adapting of Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times through Mao Zedong Thought, the theoretical system of socialism with Chinese characteristics, and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The second examines changes in the world economic, political and cultural order. The third sets out five features of Chinese modernization, and the fourth reviews the Party's contributions to world peace, common development and global governance. Li's central claim is that the Party's achievements have shifted the balance between socialism and capitalism. In the author's account, Western-dominated dependency relations are being loosened. Li cites China's share of world output, rising from 2 per cent in 1978 to over 17 per cent, and its contribution to global growth. The article presents the post-1991 period as showing that the 'end of history' thesis was wrong. Chinese modernization is described as a non-capitalist route to modernity, defined by its socialist character, common prosperity, self-reliance, the coordinated advance of five civilizations (material, political, spiritual, social and ecological) and peaceful development. Li contends that this breaks the 'path dependence' of developing countries on Western models. The article concludes that the Party has handed history an outstanding answer and that the road ahead is harder still. Li calls for closer unity around the Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core, and for building a community with a shared future for mankind. The text is a Party-historical interpretation rather than an empirical study, and it draws heavily on official documents and leaders' statements. Read the original if you want a systematic account of how Party-history scholarship presents the world-historical meaning of the Party's centenary and its resolution.

The origins and development of the Communist Party of China's commitment to keeping the world in mind 中国共产党坚持胸怀天下的由来及发展 Chen Li Chen Li takes up one of the ten historical lessons set out in the Resolution on the Major Achievements and Historical Experience of the Party over the Past Century, adopted at the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021): keeping the whole world in mind. The article argues that this has been a defining trait of the Communist Party of China since its founding. In Chen's account, the Party has always judged Chinese revolution, construction and reform against the trends of human development and the changing world order. The article has three parts. The first sets out the theoretical and historical grounds for the commitment: Marxism, the world situation at the Party's birth, and traditional Chinese culture. The second follows its practice through the New Democratic Revolution, the early People's Republic and the reform era. The third turns to the new era, covering the Party's guiding statements, the community with a shared future for mankind, the Belt and Road Initiative, global governance, and cooperation on climate, poverty and the pandemic. Chen's central claim is that the commitment follows from Marxism's call to emancipate all humanity, from the Party's reading of events such as the October Revolution, the Paris Peace Conference and the Washington Conference, and from the traditional ideals of 'all under heaven as one family' and 'harmony among all nations'. The Party's early links with the Comintern are cited as evidence. Chen then traces a line from Mao Zedong's internationalist duty and the decision to enter the Korean War, through Deng Xiaoping's repeated statements that China should make a greater contribution to humanity, to the new era. The author cites GDP figures to argue that China's growth has changed its position and responsibilities, and presents Chinese modernization as an option for developing countries that want to grow while keeping their independence. Chen concludes that the Party works both for the Chinese people and for human progress, and calls this the meaning of its 'four for, four seek' formula. The article presents the community with a shared future for mankind, 'genuine multilateralism' and the Belt and Road Initiative as the current form of this commitment, and says China must balance domestic and international priorities. Read the original if you want an official-line account of how Party scholarship ties China's foreign policy and international role to the Party's theory and history.}

Adhering to the strategic policy of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party 坚持全面从严治党的战略方针 Guo Yong Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts (2022, no. 1), Guo Yong takes up the question of how the Communist Party of China should continue its strategy of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party in the new era. Guo argues that this strategy is a distinctive theme of Party building since the 18th Party Congress (2012), and that it rests on the Party's willingness to carry out self-reform. The article is framed by the 2021 Party resolution on the Party's major achievements and historical experience, which Guo cites as setting the direction. The article has three parts. The first sets out the political leadership and guarantee that full and rigorous self-governance provides. The second describes how it runs through every area of Party building: ideals and convictions, work style, the oversight system, anti-corruption and institution-building. The third lists what is needed to achieve "greater strategic results": political conduct, the eight-point rules, coordinated oversight, and an integrated approach to corruption. Guo's central claim is that the Party's vanguard character is forged through continual self-reform rather than given at birth. On this reading, the strategy secures the Party's overall leadership and the authority of the Central Committee against weakened or hollow implementation of its decisions. Guo credits it with underpinning poverty alleviation and the response to COVID-19. In the account of practice, Guo points to ideological education campaigns, the campaign against formalism, bureaucratism, hedonism and extravagance, reform of the Party and state oversight system including the National Supervisory Commission, and "zero tolerance" anti-corruption work. Guo describes the result as an overwhelming victory in the anti-corruption struggle that has now been consolidated. Looking ahead, Guo calls for putting political building first, which means upholding the authority and centralized, unified leadership of the Central Committee. Guo also calls for persistent enforcement of the eight-point rules, since the "four undesirable work styles" persist in disguised forms. Guo further urges better coordination among Party, state, democratic-party, public and media oversight, and an integrated approach in which officials dare not, cannot and do not want to be corrupt. Guo presents this last approach as a theoretical and practical innovation that also supports the modernization of national governance. Read the original if you want a concise official-line account of how Chinese Party scholarship framed Party discipline and anti-corruption policy at the start of 2022.

Theoretical innovation on Party leadership in the new era 新时代关于党的领导的理论创新 Shen Chuanliang Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts (2022, no. 2), Shen Chuanliang takes up the first of the "Ten Clarifications" in the 2021 Party resolution on the Party's major achievements and historical experience. That clarification holds that Communist Party leadership is the defining feature and greatest strength of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Shen argues that it marks a new high point in theoretical innovation on Party leadership since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The article has three parts. The first treats the innovation as problem-driven and assesses its place within the Party's body of innovative theory. The second explains three claims in the resolution: that Party leadership is the most essential feature of socialism with Chinese characteristics, that it is the system's greatest strength, and that the Party is the highest political leadership force. The third turns to practice, covering the requirements to strengthen the "four consciousnesses", stay firm in the Four-sphere Confidence and achieve the Two Upholds. Shen contends that the theory answers real problems. These include vague understanding of, and weak action on, Party leadership, the weakening or hollowing out of its implementation, and poor execution of central decisions. Shen argues that Party leadership determines the nature, direction and fate of socialism with Chinese characteristics. In this account, world socialist history shows that without communist party leadership a socialist cause loses its political, organisational and ideological safeguards, and international competition is largely competition between systems. Shen cites the Party's record, from the new-democratic revolution to the elimination of absolute poverty, as evidence that the Party is the "mainstay" of national rejuvenation. Shen also places this theory first among the core contents of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, and calls it original, enriching the Marxist doctrine of the Party. Shen concludes that theory must become practical force, and that the Four Consciousnesses, the Four-sphere Confidence and the Two Upholds are the path for upholding and strengthening the Party's overall leadership. The Two Upholds, in Shen's reading, are essentially one: upholding General Secretary Xi Jinping's core status means upholding the authority of the Central Committee. Shen also calls for opposing formalism and "two-faced" people. Read the original if you want a concise official-line account of how Party leadership is framed in the 2021 resolution and how it is linked to Party discipline and loyalty.

A historical examination of the Communist Party of China's strategic thinking and its present-day lessons 中国共产党战略思维的历史考察与现实启示 Du Min Du Min asks how the Communist Party of China (CPC) has treated and used strategic thinking over its first hundred years, and what lessons this holds for the present. The article, published in 2021, argues that the Party has consistently prized strategic thinking and applied it well in revolution, construction and reform. In Du's account this is what carried the country "from standing up to becoming prosperous and then strong". The article has four parts. The first traces how successive leadership generations stressed strategy: Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping, the Jiang Zemin and Hu Jintao period, and Xi Jinping. The second surveys how the Party applied strategic thinking in three dimensions: the whole (accurate strategic judgements), the long term (goals and development strategies) and the fundamental (priorities and initiative). The third distils lessons, and the fourth sets out how leading cadres should raise their strategic capacity. Du's central move is to treat strategic thinking as the practical application of Marxist materialist dialectics. It handles relations such as essence and appearance, whole and part, long-term and immediate, principal and secondary. Du holds that the Party's strategic thinking, as expressed in Mao Zedong Thought, Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents, the Scientific Outlook on Development and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, has also enriched dialectics. The second lesson is a people-centred strategic standpoint: the people are the starting point and goal of strategic decisions and the source of their strength and wisdom, which Du illustrates with Mao's, Deng's and Xi's remarks on learning from the masses. Du also records that the 16th Party Congress (2002) was the first to write "strategic thinking" into a congress report. The article further notes that Xi introduced "strategic resolve" in 2012, and the 19th Party Congress (2017) listed strategic thinking first among the leaders' thinking capacities. Du concludes that strategic thinking is "always the way of thinking Communists should establish" and proposes four pairs of balances for cadres. These are coordinating all aspects while stressing priorities, holding to principle while staying flexible, seizing opportunities while meeting challenges, and strengthening resolve while pursuing innovation. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially aligned account of how Party discourse presents strategic thinking across successive leaderships, with many quotations from Mao, Deng, Jiang, Hu and Xi.

The historical-materialist narrative of the Great Founding Spirit of the Party and its dimensions for the new journey 伟大建党精神的唯物史观叙事及新征程向度 Liu Shun Liu Shun asks how the Great Founding Spirit of the Party, as formally put forward in 2021, should be understood. The article contends that its formation and formulation are not a formulaic ideological construction but follow a historical-materialist logic that explains ideas from material practice rather than the reverse. Liu argues that the Spirit arose from the Party's leadership of revolution, construction and reform, and that it should now guide the Party's second-centenary journey. The article is organised into five parts. Four "narratives" – of value, of formation, of problems and of the subject – read the Spirit through historical materialism. A fifth part sets out its dimensions for the new journey. The formation narrative runs through four periods: the New Democratic revolution, the establishment of basic socialist institutions, reform and opening up, and the era since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Liu's core move is to link each element of the Spirit to a Marxist category. On value, the Spirit is said to match historical materialism's stress on actuality: it serves "real people" rather than abstract ones, rests on the practically confirmed path of socialism with Chinese characteristics, and charts the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The author contrasts the Party with Western parties, which are described as driven by interest groups and electoral competition. On problems, the Spirit is read as reflecting the Party's grasp of the basic contradiction between productive forces and relations of production, and of the principal contradiction of each stage, including its redefinition in the new era. On the subject, Liu holds that the people are the fundamental force creating history, and treats the Party's stress on the unity of the people and the "country" as its expression. For the new journey Liu proposes four conversions of the Spirit: into a new upsurge of struggle for a better life, including common prosperity; into new momentum for modernization, through the new development stage, the new development philosophy and a new development pattern; into practice towards the lofty ideal of communism; and into conscious action to build a community with a shared future for mankind. Liu presents these as the Spirit's active role as part of the superstructure. Read the original if you want to see how a 2021 academic article ties the official Party-spirit discourse to historical-materialist categories and to the policy agenda of the second centenary goal.

The evolution of historical nihilist discourse within the CPSU and its lessons for today 苏共党内历史虚无主义话语的演进及当代启示 Ren Chengjin Ren Chengjin treats historical nihilism as a political current rather than merely a cultural or academic phenomenon, and asks how it developed inside the Communist Party of the Soviet Union (CPSU) and what that implies for China. The article, published in Marxist Studies in 2021, argues that the CPSU's loss of ideological leadership was tied to a body of nihilist discourse that negated Soviet and Party history, and that this offers a warning against hostile forces seeking to undermine the legitimacy of the Communist Party of China. The article has three parts. The first traces the discourse through the Khrushchev, Brezhnev and Gorbachev periods. The second examines four causes: weak ideological autonomy in the CPSU, Western ideological infiltration, Russia's own nihilist cultural tradition, and the support of intellectuals, writers and media. The third draws four lessons for China. Ren's account runs as follows. Khrushchev's de-Stalinization and humanist turn opened the way; under Brezhnev, Stalin and Lenin were alternately vilified and sanctified, and dissident subculture grew; under Gorbachev's glasnost and democratization, Party media and a liberal elite made nihilism dominant, culminating in the 28th Party Congress (1990) programme of 'humane, democratic socialism'. Ren holds that these leaders did not intend to negate Soviet socialism but did so objectively. The root cause is internal, namely dogmatism and the uncritical import of Western humanism. Ren treats Western radio broadcasting, support for dissidents and the Nobel Prize in literature as an external 'peaceful evolution' strategy. Ren draws four lessons: build historical identification; hold Marxist ideological discourse power by answering real problems, renewing theory and telling Chinese stories; strengthen the Party's governing base, above all popular support; and keep love of country, love of the Party and love of socialism united. Citing Xi Jinping throughout, Ren stresses that the CPC must avoid Western discursive traps and treat nihilism as an error to be guarded against constantly. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly account of how the Soviet collapse is used in current ideological argument about historical nihilism, with extensive Russian and Western sources cited.

The formation of Mao Zedong's materialist conception of history 毛泽东唯物史观的形成 Tao Jialing How did Mao Zedong come to hold the materialist conception of history? Tao Jialing, in a short piece first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in July 2021, argues that tracing this process helps explain the origins of the historical outlook of Chinese communists. The article holds that Mao's early materialist conception of history formed in three stages between 1918 and 1921. The article follows Mao's writings, letters and activities month by month. It covers the "germination" stage (April 1918 to August 1919), the "formation" stage (September 1919 to December 1920) and the "establishment" stage (January to July 1921). Its sources include Mao's articles in the Xiang River Review, his letters to friends such as Cai Hesen, and the debates of the New People's Study Society. In the first stage, Tao reads Mao's remark that the problem of food is the biggest problem, and his long essay "The Great Union of the Popular Masses", as early signs that social being determines social consciousness and that the people make history. For the second stage Tao lists seven developments: an "economic analysis" of social questions, attention to material production, Mao's sorting-out of competing doctrines through reading the Marxist classics, the spread of Marxist publications through the Cultural Book Society, the decision to found a party, the abandonment of reformism after the failure of the Hunan self-government movement, and a turn to violent revolution. Tao treats his December 1920 rejection of Russell's reformism and of anarchism as the decisive break. In the third stage, Mao's January 1921 letter calling the materialist conception of history the philosophical basis of "our party", and his attendance at the First Party Congress in July 1921, mark its establishment in thought and in practice. Tao concludes that Mao's outlook arose from a dynamic process of "challenging yesterday's self" and mirrors the wider change in Chinese thought. In this account, Mao moved from revolutionary democracy to communism, driven by patriotism, and became a Marxist in belief and in revolutionary practice. Read the original if you want a compact, dated chronology of Mao's intellectual turn to Marxism in 1918–1921, with the key letters and essays identified.

An analysis of the success code of a century-old Party 百年大党成功密码探析 Zhao Zhiyong Teng Cuihua Marking the Communist Party of China's centenary in 2021, the article asks what explains its success. The authors point to the Party's status as the world's largest party by membership, its more than seventy years in power, and what they call the twin miracles of rapid economic growth and long-term social stability, along with lifting nearly 800 million people out of poverty. Their answer is that the Party has "a wise mind, a firm character and rich nourishment". The article is organised around these three "codes". The first is a wise mind, drawn from arming the Party with scientific theory. The second is a firm character, forged through the Party's self-reform. The third is rich nourishment, supplied by the support of the people. Each section is illustrated with episodes from Party history, from the revolutionary period to the post-2012 era, and with passages from Xi Jinping and Mao Zedong. On theory, Zhao and Teng argue that Marxism let the Party resolve the basic questions of the Chinese revolution, and that its success also lay in refusing to treat Marxism, Soviet experience or Comintern instructions as dogma. Theoretical innovation, from Mao Zedong Thought to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, is presented as the result of adapting Marxism to Chinese conditions. On character, they present the Party as one that can face and correct its own mistakes. They argue that its founding mission sustains cohesion, and that anti-corruption since the 18th Party Congress (2012) is vital because corruption could cost the Party its legitimacy, as they say happened to the Soviet Communist Party and the Kuomintang. On the people, they hold that the masses supplied soldiers, grain and practical inventions, such as the household contract responsibility system. They add that popular supervision helps the Party escape the "historical cycle" of dynastic rise and fall. The authors conclude that the Party's history is one of arming the mind with Marxism, strengthening itself through self-reform, and relying on the people. They call for these codes to be kept as the Party leads the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and works toward a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Chinese Party-affiliated scholarship explains the Party's longevity in the centenary year.

The "Ten Upholds" as the key to success running through a century of Party history “十个坚持”是贯通百年党史的成功密码 Xiao Guiqing Xiao Guiqing takes up the ten historical lessons set out in the Resolution on the Party's major achievements and historical experience over the past century, adopted at the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021). These are: upholding the Party's leadership, putting the people first, theoretical innovation, independence, the Chinese path, a worldview of openness to the world, pioneering spirit, dauntless struggle, the united front, and self-reform. Xiao argues that together these "Ten Upholds" are the code explaining why the Party succeeded in the past and how it can keep succeeding. The article, published in Ideological and Political Education Research in 2022, has three parts. The first treats the Ten Upholds as a systematic summary of the Party's history and compares the 2021 Resolution with the earlier historical resolutions of 1945 and 1981. The second sets out why the Ten Upholds secure the Party's lasting strength. The third presents them as a guide for future struggle. Xiao's central claim is that the Ten Upholds are not a stage-specific tally of past policies but an integrated whole. They express the Party's consistent stance, viewpoint and method, and none can be properly understood in isolation: Party leadership, for example, contains the commitments to the people and to theoretical innovation. Following Xi Jinping's four-fold formulation, Xiao says they reveal the fundamental guarantee of success (Party leadership), the source of strength (reliance on the people), the reason the Party holds the historical initiative (theory, independence, innovation), and the way it stays advanced and pure (self-reform). On the last point Xiao presents self-reform as the Party's second answer to the "historical cycle" of rise and decline, after supervision by the people. Looking ahead, Xiao says the Ten Upholds should serve as an ideological weapon for reading a world of "changes unseen in a century", a practical guide for waging "great struggle", a yardstick for judging political right and wrong, and a guide to Party-spirit cultivation. Xiao calls on the Party to cherish, adhere to and develop them as it pursues the second centenary goal and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a representative Chinese Party-theory reading of the 2021 historical resolution and the logic that links its ten lessons.

End or mutation? An analysis of the current state and prospects of neoliberalism Distinguishing the present condition and outlook of neoliberalism 终结还是异变 Lai Qingli Since the 2008 financial crisis, and more sharply during the pandemic, many Western commentators have declared neoliberalism finished. Lai Qingli asks whether this is so and where neoliberalism is heading. Drawing on recent foreign scholarship, the article argues that neoliberalism has ended only in form. In substance it has mutated, and Lai describes it as a return to its own earlier, more polarised stage. The article first sets out the "end thesis" in social, economic and political terms, citing figures such as Joseph Stiglitz and John Bellamy Foster. It then rebuts the thesis on three fronts: inequality, market failure and democratic decline. Finally it divides neoliberalism's history since the 1970s into three periods: Reagan and Thatcher up to 1985, the "humanised" Third Way era of 1986–2006, and the period since the 2007 subprime crisis. Lai's central move is to distinguish "new liberalism" (the welfare-minded, progressive tradition) from neo-classical liberalism (the Hayekian tradition). The two have fused. The first has retreated into cultural matters and has lost its economic voice, while the second dominates economic policy. So critiques of inequality do not show that neoliberalism is ending. Nor does market failure, since in Lai's genealogy neo-classical liberalism has always used state power and legal intervention, such as US "long-arm jurisdiction", to rebuild markets. Democratic decline does not end it either, because it can combine with illiberal, populist or nationalist politics, as with Trump and the Tea Party. Lai describes the resulting form as a "chameleon" and links it to the cyclical movement of capitalism: in crisis and depression, conservative and polarising sentiment grows. Lai concludes that the phenomena contradicting "liberal democratic" common sense mark a new stage of neoliberalism, not its decline. It cannot end unless capitalism and liberalism are replaced, since it cannot resolve capitalism's basic contradiction and only displaces it. Lai calls for continued criticism of its polarising and conservative turn and for articulating a socialist alternative. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist account of neoliberalism's genealogy and why its "end" is judged premature.

Marxism's people-centred and practical character fully carried out in China 马克思主义人民性和实践性在中国得到充分贯彻 Liu Lyuhong This newspaper commentary, published in Guangming Daily in March 2022, takes up a formulation from the Party's third historical resolution, adopted at the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021): that the people-centred character (renmin xing) and the practical character (shijian xing) of Marxism have been fully carried out in China. Liu argues that both qualities have been demonstrated across a century of revolution, construction and reform, and that they will continue to drive the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The piece has three parts. The first treats the people-centred character of Marxism as it appears in the passage from oppression to a moderately prosperous society in all respects. The second treats its practical character, from semi-colonial, semi-feudal China to building a modern socialist country. The third turns to what must be done to uphold both qualities in future. On the first quality, Liu holds that Marxism sees the people as the subject of history and that the Party has kept to this position since its founding. The article runs through the new-democratic revolution, socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the new era, and presents each as a stage in which the Party led the people from national independence to the leap from "standing up" to "becoming prosperous" and then "becoming strong". On the second, Liu argues that practice is what distinguishes Marxism from other theories. The article presents successive Party leaders from Mao Zedong to Xi Jinping as having adapted Marxism's basic principles to Chinese conditions and traditional culture and tested them in practice, guided by seeking truth from facts. Liu concludes that the Party has joined the two qualities in the whole process of revolution, construction and reform, opening up socialism with Chinese characteristics, Chinese modernization and a new form of human civilization. Looking ahead, the article calls for a people-centred approach to development, aimed at common prosperity and at the free and all-round development of the person. It also calls for theoretical innovation grounded in practice, and for continuing to adapt Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the 2021 historical resolution's language on Marxism was explained to a general readership in the official press.

The philosophization of the world and the worldliness of philosophy An inquiry into the conception of justice in Marx's doctoral dissertation 世界哲学化与哲学世界化 Liu Shuyi Since the 1970s, Anglo-American philosophers have debated whether Marx had a theory of justice and whether he supported or opposed it. Liu takes up this question by returning to Marx's first systematic theoretical work, the doctoral dissertation on the difference between the natural philosophies of Democritus and Epicurus. The article argues that the dissertation's formula that "the philosophization of the world is at the same time the worldliness of philosophy" contains the starting point of Marx's view of justice. On this reading, the young Marx treats justice as a value norm centred on real human beings. The article has three parts. The first reconstructs the intellectual context: Marx's early Romanticism and Kant–Fichte idealism, his turn to Hegel, and his closeness to Bruno Bauer's standpoint of self-consciousness, which Liu distinguishes from Marx's own use of the concept. The second part reads Epicurus's doctrine of the atom's swerve as an account of the freedom of self-consciousness. The third part draws out the implications for justice: its subject, its legislator, the role of self-consciousness, and the rights of freedom and equality. A short conclusion places this early view in Marx's later development. Liu's central move is to read the swerve of the atom against Democritus's rectilinear fall. Democritus, in Marx's reading, subjects atoms to blind necessity, whereas Epicurus's swerve introduces contingency and thus freedom of choice, which Liu extends to human beings as self-conscious social beings. From this Liu derives the two-sided formula. The philosophization of the world means philosophy guides and acts upon reality. The worldliness of philosophy means philosophy criticises injustice in practice and overcomes its own abstraction. Justice, Liu holds, is powerless if confined to theory and must be made real. Liu concludes that the young Marx makes the real human being, not gods or God, the subject and legislator of justice.
