Self-consciousness serves as the critic of injustice, such as religious and feudal oppression, and freedom and equality are the rights of that subject. Liu contrasts this with Epicurus, whose freedom is detached from determinate existence, while Marx wants freedom to "shine in" that existence through practice. Liu also notes the view remains idealist and Romantic, and that Marx sublated it later, when he edited the Rheinische Zeitung. Read the original if you are interested in the early Marx, the philosophical roots of the Marxian justice debate, or how Chinese scholars read the doctoral dissertation.

The basic orientation of the new form of human civilization in the course of world history 人类文明新形态在世界历史进程中的基本定向 Wu Hongzheng Wu Hongzheng asks how the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind can move from a concept to something with a real foundation. The article's thesis is that Chinese modernization created a "new form of human civilization", and that this civilization supplies the community's "existent basis" (shicun jichu). Together they make up a world-historical sequence: the new path of Chinese modernization, the new form of human civilization, and the community with a shared future for mankind. Writing in 2022 within Marx's theory of world history, Wu works in three steps. The first sets out what the new civilizational form is and why it is world-historical. The second places the three concepts on a "logical map" of world-historical development. The third explains why the new form of civilization can serve as the community's foundation. Wu draws on Hegel's logic of ground and existence, and cites Piketty, Streeck and Heller to support points about capitalism and political order. Wu argues that the new civilizational form is not a spontaneous "natural-historical process". In Wu's account it arose under the uncertainty of the "great changes unseen in a century" and aims to sublate the logic of capital and the "clash of civilizations" it produces. Wu holds that Chinese modernization was carrying Marx's world-historical purpose from the start, so it did not "enter" world history only after it began to influence the world. Wu calls the contrary view the "greatest metaphysical way of thinking". Under the coexistence of two social systems, Wu contends, only a socialist-led civilization that matches the direction of world history can ground the community. This civilization works through the principles "seeking common ground while reserving differences" and win-win cooperation, and through "common values of all mankind". Wu distinguishes these values from "universal values", which Wu says impose one country's particular values. Wu also proposes "world relations of production" as an extension of historical materialism. Wu concludes that the community with a shared future for mankind gains objective necessity from two sources. It is the basic orientation of twenty-first-century Marxist world-history theory, and Chinese modernization and the new civilizational form provide its existent basis. Wu compares this to the way Marx's "two inevitables" established the necessity of communism. Wu also treats the new civilizational form as a transitional stage that will itself eventually be sublated. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist philosopher grounds the official concepts of Chinese modernization and the community with a shared future in Hegelian and Marxian world-history theory.

Exploring the way forward through hard struggle: new developments among foreign communist parties in 2021 New developments among foreign communist parties in 2021 在砥砺奋进中探索前行 Yu Haiqing This annual survey, first published in Contemporary World in early 2022, reviews how communist parties outside China fared in 2021. Yu Haiqing argues that the parties pressed ahead in an uncertain world, marking anniversaries, holding congresses and contesting elections, while facing multiple difficulties. In the author's summary formula, the parties continued to seek progress amid an ebb tide, survival in the interstices and development in adversity. The article is organised around five themes. It covers centenary and other anniversary celebrations (Portugal, Spain, South Africa, and others); the congresses held by parties in socialist-ruled states, developed capitalist countries, the former Soviet and East European region, and Asia, Africa and Latin America; parliamentary and local election results; reflection on socialist history and efforts at international coordination; and campaigns against imperialism, state power and anti-communism. Yu's central claim is that election results in 2021 showed a sharper split between advance and decline. Gains are cited for the Communist Party of the Russian Federation (18 per cent, 57 seats), the Left Democratic Front in Kerala, the Communist Party of Chile, the Communist Party of Austria in Graz, and the Moldovan communists' return to parliament. Setbacks are cited for the Communist Party of Bohemia and Moravia, which lost all its seats for the first time since 1989, for Italian parties polling under two per cent, and for the Japanese Communist Party. The author also notes that the Kazakh party dropped communist and class-struggle language. Yu adds that the parties used the 30th anniversary of the Soviet collapse and the 150th of the Paris Commune to reflect on history. They also held online forums, including a December 2021 teleconference of 73 communist and workers' parties from 57 countries, and made joint statements against AUKUS, the US blockade of Cuba and anti-communism. The year-long Indian farmers' protest is presented as a historic victory. Yu concludes that the pandemic reduced street action but opened virtual spaces for organising. Looking to 2022, the author sees the parties continuing to explore twenty-first-century socialist paths, with an urgent practical task of devising workable action plans from real conditions. Read the original if you want a compact, country-by-country survey of communist party congresses, elections and joint initiatives in 2021, as seen from a Chinese academic perspective.

The leftward turn of party politics in the Nordic countries and its prospects 北欧政党政治左翼化态势及其前景 Li Hong Writing after the Norwegian Labour Party's victory in the September 2021 general election, Li Hong asks why centre-left parties have returned to government in all four major Nordic countries while populism has grown elsewhere in Europe. The article argues that the return rests on changes in the international environment and in domestic conditions. It also contends that the resulting 'leftward turn' carries a populist imprint and faces serious tests. The article first recalls the Nordic region as a stronghold of European social democracy, then describes how globalisation, the financial crisis, terrorism and refugee flows pushed these parties into opposition as right-wing populist parties rose. It then traces the comeback in Sweden (2014, 2018), Finland (2019), Denmark (2019) and Norway (2021), citing vote shares and seats. The remainder explains the victories, analyses the character of the new left turn and assesses the parties' prospects. Li identifies three causes of the victories. First, the negative effects of neoliberal globalisation produced a 'political pendulum' effect. Second, the parties changed their policies: they restored the welfare state, took over the centre-right's strict control of refugees, and stressed climate change, favouring gradual measures over the Greens' radicalism. Third, fragmented party systems and the centre-right's weaknesses, such as austerity in Finland and the Danish People's Party's slump, worked in their favour. Li argues the turn is populist-tinged because the centre-left kept strict refugee policy, replaced multiculturalism with integration around a 'dominant culture', and attached responsibilities to welfare recipients, particularly migrants. Li lists four challenges: the leading parties' low vote shares (below 30 per cent, below 20 per cent in Finland), unstable multiparty coalitions (the Finnish government fell after six months), strong right-wing populist rivals, and the need to deliver results. Voters, Li notes, chose the centre-left largely out of dissatisfaction with the centre-right. Long-term tenure therefore depends on balancing principle against voters' needs, welfare against growth, and climate action against sustainable development. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly account of Nordic social democracy's recent electoral revival, with election figures for each country.

How the Communist Party of China led young people to Yan'an 中国共产党引领青年奔赴延安 Luo Siliang Zhou Keshu This short commentary, first published in China Social Sciences Today on 5 July 2021 during the Party History study and education campaign, asks why the Communist Party of China could draw so many young people to Yan'an during the War of Resistance against Japan. The authors note that by the end of 1938 more than 100,000 intellectuals, many of them young, had gone there despite hardship and danger. They argue that three factors explain this appeal. The article first covers the Party's patriotic leadership of the anti-Japanese national united front. It then turns to its spread of Marxist theory, and finally to its governance of Yan'an as a revolutionary base. It closes with remarks on youth work today. Luo and Zhou contend that the Party raised the banner of patriotism after the 1931 Mukden Incident, in contrast to the Nationalist government's concessions, and trained cadres at the Anti-Japanese Military and Political University. Second, by adapting Marxism to the Chinese context, works such as Mao Zedong's On Protracted War gave young people a convincing account of the nation's future. Popular works such as Mass Philosophy made theory accessible, and Yan'an grew into a city of study with many schools. Third, the authors describe Yan'an as youthful, song-filled and free of corruption, citing Ding Ling, He Qifang, Mao's 1940 list of Yan'an's virtues and Tan Kah Kee's remark that China's hope lay in Yan'an. The authors conclude that winning over youth was an important reason for the Party's revolutionary victory. They call for equipping today's young people with Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, explained in language they can accept. They also want stronger youth policy and a deeper sense of national feeling. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Party history presents Yan'an's attraction for young people and links it to current youth work.

Methodological features of Engels's critique of erroneous currents of thought 恩格斯批判错误思潮的方法论特征 Jin Siyuan Jin Siyuan asks what methodological features characterise Engels's polemics against erroneous currents of thought, and argues that they show a high degree of methodological self-awareness. The article takes three cases: "true socialism", "socialism of the lectern" (Kathedersozialismus) and the opportunism of the "Young Ones" (Jungen). Jin contends that the critique is marked by scientific rigour, a strongly critical stance and a comprehensive perspective, and that revisiting it has theoretical and practical value for safeguarding mainstream ideological security and improving the governance of social trends of thought. The article is organised in three parts, one for each feature, and each part works through the three cases. It draws on Engels's writings from 1845 to 1848 on true socialism (including the Communist Manifesto and The German Ideology, co-written with Marx), his 1880s–90s defence of Marx against the charge of plagiarising Rodbertus, and his 1890 reply to Paul Ernst and letters to Bloch, Schmidt, Lafargue and Sombart. On scientific rigour, Jin shows Engels collecting and analysing sources on a large scale. In the Rodbertus affair he reportedly consulted at least six texts and established that Marx learned of Rodbertus only around 1859, indirectly through Lassalle, when his critique of political economy was already essentially complete. Jin also credits Engels with combining tight logic with vivid, popular language. On critical stance, Engels is said to expose the reactionary class position of true socialism, whose appeal to "love" replaced revolution, and the apologetic reformism of the lectern socialists, who served Bismarck's state socialism. He is also said to refute the Young Ones' economic determinism and adventurism, noting that treating the materialist method as a ready-made formula turns it into its opposite. On comprehensiveness, Engels combines a focus on key arguments with a view of the whole, and uses Ricardian, comparative and historical angles against Rodbertus. He pairs demolition with construction: after criticising the Young Ones he sets out the proper approach to Marxism, namely studying the original works, and treating Marx's worldview as a method rather than a dogma. Jin concludes that the scientific, critical and comprehensive features of Engels's polemics, together with the methodological self-awareness they reflect, offer practical guidance for studying and researching Marxism today. Read the original if you are interested in Engels's polemical method, in how Chinese scholarship draws on it for contemporary ideological work, or in a compact survey of his critiques of true socialism, lectern socialism and the Young Ones.

2022: Can the Latin American left sustain its strong showing? 2022，拉美左翼能否延续强势表现 Zhang Junrong This newspaper commentary, written at the start of 2022, asks whether the leftward turn seen in Latin American elections in 2021 will last. Zhang describes the region's mood as a "look to the left" (xiang zuo kan) rather than a firm "turn to the left", and argues that left-wing rule is not a settled outcome. The piece reviews left-wing election victories from Bolivia (October 2020) through Peru, Nicaragua and Chile in 2021, noting earlier returns in Mexico and Argentina. It then turns to the region's attitude towards the United States, the limits on left governments' room for manoeuvre, and the two elections of 2022 that Zhang sees as decisive: Colombia and Brazil. Zhang presents the left's return as partly a reaction against the United States. The author cites US interference in Nicaragua's vote, Nicaragua's exit from the Organization of American States, and Peru's withdrawal from the right-led Lima Group. Zhang distinguishes this wave from the earlier "pink tide": voters chose the left mainly out of discontent with right-wing governments, and the left inherits crises such as Argentina's debt and the aftermath of unrest in Chile. In the author's account, structural weaknesses (commodity-dependent economies, unequal distribution under neoliberalism, populist shocks and routine political crisis) add to the pressure. Zhang calls on left governments to avoid party infighting and the old practice of trading high welfare spending for votes, and to find workable reforms. The author expects a left victory in Colombia's March election to weaken US strategy in South America, and the Brazilian contest between Lula and Bolsonaro to settle the region's political direction. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese press view of Latin America's left and US influence at the start of 2022.

The resurgence of the Latin American left: features, causes and impact 拉美左翼回潮的特征、成因及影响 Wang Youming Writing after the 2021 round of Latin American elections, Wang Youming asks why left-wing parties have returned to power across the region and what follows from it. The article argues that the return is the latest swing of a regional "political pendulum" between left and right. In Wang's account it results from both structural features of Latin American politics and external shocks, above all the pandemic, and it carries geopolitical consequences. The article has three parts. The first sets out three features of the left's resurgence, starting from the 1998 election of Chávez in Venezuela, the "right turn" from 2015, and the left's comeback from Mexico in 2018 to Peru, Honduras and Chile in 2021, with Brazil's Lula seen as the likely 2022 winner. The second part examines causes. The third looks at effects within the region and on relations with the United States. Wang identifies three features. The pendulum is swinging faster. All left factions, from radical to moderate, performed well and formed electoral alliances. Yet the left's foundations are shaky, as shown by splits in Argentina's ruling coalition and the impeachment push against Peru's Castillo. On causes, Wang says imported presidential-parliamentary institutions and a polarised party system produce a cycle: leftist welfare policies lead to economic strain, then the right's neoliberalism deepens inequality, and protest returns the left. The pandemic deepened this by hitting the middle and lower classes hardest, and the left also adapted its platforms, for example by adding green-transition pledges and reassuring business owners. On effects, Wang expects regional integration to speed up, citing the 2021 CELAC summit in Mexico City. The author also expects the Biden administration to pursue a "pull the right, strike the left" strategy through investment, support for dissidents, outreach to moderate leftists and "values diplomacy". Wang concludes that the left's return reflects regional political, economic and social factors acting amid systemic turbulence in global governance. Left-wing government has not removed the region's structural contradictions. Divisions within ruling coalitions, policy imbalances and shifting public opinion mean opponents will prepare a new challenge, so the pendulum will keep swinging as it has before. Read the original if you want a Chinese international-studies reading of Latin America's 2021 "election year", including how it treats the left's internal diversity and US policy toward the region.

Reform and opening up and the new path of Chinese modernization 改革开放与中国式现代化新道路 Zhang Shengen Huang Xiaowu Zhang Shengen and Huang Xiaowu ask how the Communist Party's four decades of reform and opening up produced what they call a new path of Chinese modernization and a new form of human civilization. Writing in early 2022, they argue that Deng Xiaoping's concept of 'Chinese-style modernization', introduced at the start of reform, set the direction. In their account, the Party then enriched the concept in stages, from the 1980s to the 19th Party Congress (2017) and the 19th Central Committee's Fifth Plenum (2020). The article is a chronological survey in three parts. The first covers the launch of reform after the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978) and Deng's 1979 formulations. The second follows the stated goals from a 'highly civilized, highly democratic' socialist country with a moderately prosperous society, through the three-step strategy of the 13th Party Congress (1987) and the 15th Party Congress (1997), to the comprehensive building of a moderately prosperous society under the Scientific Outlook on Development. The third turns to the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The authors give four reasons why Deng put forward Chinese-style modernization: the need for realistic goals, lessons from history, knowledge of other countries' modernization, and an assessment of China's conditions. On their reading, the target of the end of the century was lowered from the four modernizations to a 'moderately prosperous' household. They trace how the content widened beyond industry, agriculture, defence and science to democracy, spiritual civilization, social harmony and ecology, which gave the 'five-in-one' overall plan. They report that the 19th Congress brought forward the date for basically realizing modernization to 2035. They also set out Xi Jinping's five features: a huge population, common prosperity, coordination of material and cultural-ethical progress, harmony between humanity and nature, and peaceful development. The authors conclude that the Party's understanding of modernization has deepened continuously, and that the new path and new form of civilization were created within socialism with Chinese characteristics. In their view, the path draws on China's long history, widens the options for developing countries that want independence, and shows the world-historical significance of the Chinese revolution. They urge strengthened confidence in the path, theory, system and culture. Read the original if you want a detailed, official-line chronology of how Party congress documents and Deng-era statements built up the concept of Chinese modernization.

Saving the ecological environment or saving capitalism? A critique of neoliberal "environmental governmentality" 拯救生态环境还是拯救资本主义？ Cai Huajie Wang Yue Cai Huajie and Wang Yue take up a claim they say is often underestimated, including by Anthony Giddens: that neoliberalism is simply hostile to ecological concerns. They argue instead that since the 1970s the rise of neoliberalism and of ecologism has produced a "neoliberalisation" of global environmental governance. Their thesis is that this governance, which they call neoliberalism's "art of ecological governance", lacks political legitimacy and is in essence a device for rescuing capitalism rather than the environment. The article, published in 2021, has three parts. The first describes "ecological capitalisation" as four linked moves: privatisation, commodification, marketisation and financialisation of natural resources. It illustrates these with examples such as English and Welsh water privatisation, payment for ecosystem services, the EU emissions trading system, carbon pricing, green bonds and catastrophe bonds. The second part questions the legitimacy of this governance. The third turns to its underlying nature through Marxist accounts of the human–nature relation. For the legitimacy critique, the authors use three tests. On effectiveness, they cite UN and atmospheric data to argue that market-based governance has brought no marked global improvement, and that gains in the United States and Japan came from command-and-control regulation introduced before neoliberalism. On moral legitimacy, they point to environmental injustice, such as the heavier water-bill burden on low-income households. On cognitive legitimacy, they argue that treating markets as a "natural" tool hides alternatives and local ecological knowledge. For the essence of the matter, they draw on Neil Smith's reading of Marx. Smith describes nature's shift from "formal" to "real" subsumption under capital, and the authors read neoliberal ecological governance as capital seeking a new field of accumulation after steam and railways and after Fordism's fossil fuels. The authors conclude that neoliberal ecological governance is better understood as a saviour of the capitalist crisis than of the ecological one. In their view it cannot succeed, because capital's drive to maximise surplus value cannot get past the finite limits of natural resources. They also warn that presenting markets as the only solution obscures alternative modes of production, including those guided by socialist institutional design. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist critique of carbon markets and green finance, built on Neil Smith's real-subsumption thesis and on the case studies the authors cite.

Continuing to promote the spirit of historical initiative through fearless responsibility and great struggle 在无畏担当和伟大斗争中继续发扬历史主动精神 Xu Xiaoming This short commentary in Guangming Daily (March 2022) takes up Xi Jinping's speech at the opening of a training course for young and middle-aged cadres at the Central Party School. Xu Xiaoming argues that Party members, and leading cadres in particular, must keep up the spirit of historical initiative by combining a willingness to take responsibility with a readiness to struggle, if the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation is to be achieved. The piece defines historical initiative as the Party's conscious, Marxist-guided effort to transform history on the basis of grasping its laws. It then looks back over the Party's century, lists the spirit lineage it has produced, and turns to the present international environment and to shortcomings among some cadres. Xu's central move is to treat responsibility and struggle as mutually reinforcing: responsibility tempers the courage to struggle, and struggle shows the ability to bear responsibility. In the author's account, the Party's history is both a history of responsibility and of struggle, from the Jinggangshan and Long March spirits to the anti-epidemic spirit. Xu says that since the 18th Party Congress (2012) the Central Committee has led major struggles, which demand more of cadres. The article also criticises a minority of cadres who avoid major tasks or decline to take a position on questions of principle, saying this weakens the Party's fighting capacity. Xu concludes that, amid what is described as great changes unseen in a century and the pandemic, risks will grow more complex. Cadres are urged to keep "the nation's greatest interests" in mind, root fearless responsibility in practice, and pass the spirit on. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party Schools framed the call for responsibility and struggle among cadres in early 2022.

Zhou Enlai's 1941 forecast of the Pacific War and his response to it 1941年周恩来对太平洋战争爆发的预判与应对 Li Tian Li Tian asks how Zhou Enlai, then head of the Southern Bureau of the CCP Central Committee in Chongqing, read the international situation in 1941 and how he acted on it. The article argues that Zhou weighed the shifting balance between the fascist and anti-fascist camps and correctly predicted the outbreak of the Pacific War. It also argues that his measures after December 1941 helped China's resistance. Drawing on documents, telegrams and Zhou's commentaries in Xinhua Daily, the article proceeds in four parts. The first follows Zhou's analysis of Japanese–American diplomacy. The second covers his exposure of the 'Eastern Munich plot'. The third examines his assessment of Japanese cabinet changes. The fourth treats the Party's and Zhou's response once the war began, including the evacuation of people from Hong Kong. In Li's account, Zhou saw the Japan–US talks as a bargaining effort that could sacrifice China and weaken the Kuomintang's will to resist. His June 1941 essays distinguished the 'mainstream' of the war from an 'undercurrent' of compromise, and described Japan's 'two-sided policy' of military pressure and diplomacy. Zhou urged independent resistance, while using contradictions among the imperialist powers and not waiting passively for a clash in the Pacific. After the Tojo cabinet took office in October, he wrote that Japan would pursue a 'Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere' by force whichever direction it moved first. He also warned Hong Kong-based comrades that war with the United States was possible. On 14 December he described the Pacific War as protracted, expected early setbacks, and put naval power first. Li concludes that Zhou's analysis and decisions rested on China's national resistance and the global anti-fascist struggle. The article says his commentaries conveyed the Party's position to the public in Kuomintang-ruled areas and gave a strategic basis for the Central Committee's 1942 central task of building strength and consolidating the Party, government, army and people. For Li, the episode confirms that the Party grasps historical trends and was the mainstay of the War of Resistance. Read the original if you want a documented account of Zhou Enlai's wartime assessments of Japan, the United States and the Pacific War, as the CCP presents them today.

The logic behind posing basic theories of the history of the development of Marxism 马克思主义发展史基础理论提出的逻辑 Liang Shufa Liang Shufa asks why "basic theory" (jichu lilun) should be posed as a distinct question for the history of the development of Marxism, a sub-discipline of the first-level discipline of Marxist theory. The author, who has published on the topic since 2012, argues that the question is legitimate. In Liang's account, basic theory is already recognised for Marxism as a whole and for its traditional sub-disciplines, and the same step is now due for the newer sub-disciplines. The article has three parts. The first reviews how basic theory came to be studied for Marxism overall: the 2004 national key research project led by Sun Zhengyu, its 2011 volume, and Yang Geng's later book series. It also sets out the discipline structure, including the 2005 State Council Academic Degrees Committee and Ministry of Education notice that created the first-level discipline of Marxist theory. The second part defines the concept, and the third derives it from the significance of the history of Marxism's development, in theory and in method. Drawing on Mao Zedong's On Contradiction, Liang argues that a discipline is distinguished by its particular contradictions, and that these may be several rather than one. For the history of Marxism's development the author proposes a system of four: history and theory, theory and practice, the universal and the particular, and upholding versus developing Marxism. Liang adds that basic theory is also set apart from general theory by the universality of contradiction. On significance, the author holds that this history answers \"what is Marxism\" and \"how to treat Marxism\" indirectly, by tracing recurring disputes from Bernstein through Lukács and the Sino-Soviet polemics to Deng Xiaoping's rejection of the \"two whatevers\". Its method is historical, resting on two principles: unity of logic and history, and unity of theory and practice. Liang illustrates the first with the expanded concept of productive forces and with new theoretical content in socialism with Chinese characteristics. Liang concludes that the link between the history of Marxism's development and wider Marxist research, above all at the level of method, is also a link between their basic theories. Moving the discussion to the level of basic theory is therefore described as natural and possible. The article is a conceptual and methodological argument for founding a sub-field, not a historical study. Read the original if you are interested in how Chinese scholars define the sub-disciplines of Marxist theory, or in the methodological reasoning behind the study of the history of Marxism's development.

Western new social movements and their impact on left-wing parties 西方新社会运动及其对左翼政党的影响 Zang Xiuling Zang Xiuling asks how Western "new social movements", set against the traditional workers' movement, have reshaped Western left-wing parties and what this means for the future of world socialism. The article argues that the movements have pushed moderate left parties towards the political centre, made radical left parties more active, and driven extreme left parties towards populism. In Zang's view, world socialism can emerge from its trough only if left-party theory is renewed in light of these movements and left parties take the lead in guiding them. The article has four parts. It first traces four stages of the movements: the origin in the May 1968 events in France; development in the 1970s and 1980s (anti-nuclear, green and new feminist movements, and the founding of green parties); transformation in the 1990s after the Soviet and East European upheavals (anti-globalisation, from Seattle in 1999); and a new phase since the 2008 financial crisis (Occupy Wall Street, Black Lives Matter, the Yellow Vests, Spain's Indignados). It then examines the effect on moderate, radical and extreme left parties, discusses the movements' weaknesses, and sets out proposals. Zang characterises the movements as loose, individualist and organised around identity rather than class, with diverse participants, values and demands. This, the author says, weakened trade unions and traditional left parties and ended the parties' monopoly on interest representation. On the parties, Zang takes the British Labour Party's "Third Way" centrism as a case of short-term electoral gain followed by estrangement from its working-class base and failure after 2008. Radical left parties such as Syriza and Germany's Die Linke are described as active only under special conditions and internally divided. Extreme left parties, including communist parties, are said to remain marginal, and their populist turn is judged a temporary symptom of post-crisis political pathology. Zang concludes that both the movements and the left parties have fatal weaknesses and should be fused. The movements lack organisation, goals and theory, while the parties are fragmented and centrist. Zang calls on Western Marxist scholars to leave the "ivory tower" and learn from the movements. The author also urges left parties to build unity across moderate, radical and extreme wings, to engage trade unions and new organisations, and to adopt clear socialist programmes. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic assessment of Western social movements and the left-party spectrum, and of how they bear on world socialism.

Lenin and Bukharin on the theory of imperialism: a comparison Reaffirming the distinctive contribution and multiple purposes of Lenin's theory of imperialism 列宁和布哈林关于帝国主义理论之比较 Zhu Yakun Zhu Yakun takes up the intellectual relationship between Lenin and Bukharin on imperialism. The article is a response to some foreign scholars who, in Zhu's account, stress Bukharin's influence on Lenin, or even call Bukharin the founder of the Marxist theory of imperialism, and so fall into a nihilistic denial of Lenin's contribution. Zhu argues that Lenin's work marks the maturity of Marxist imperialism theory and that Lenin is an important founder of it. The article has four parts. It first sets out five points the two thinkers share, then four points of difference. It then examines their relationship under four headings: the order of their texts, borrowing of ideas, criticism of method, and theoretical surpassing. A final section reaffirms the multiple purposes of Lenin's theory. Zhu engages Western commentators such as Sidney Heitman, David McLellan and Stephen Cohen. On commonalities, Zhu says both men began from the roots of the First World War, saw imperialism as a historical product of capitalism's basic contradictions, centred monopoly and finance capital, treated imperialism as a world system, and opposed Kautsky's ultra-imperialism. The differences are the core. Lenin defined imperialism as a particular historical stage of capitalism, while Bukharin defined it as a policy of finance capital. Lenin held that monopoly coexists with competition, whereas Bukharin held that competition disappears inside the state-capitalist trust. Lenin also analysed transitional forms of dependent states and the national and colonial questions more fully. Against the Western claims, Zhu cites Lenin's earlier scattered writings and 1914–15 texts, and the 148 books and 232 articles behind Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism. Zhu adds that Lenin criticised Bukharin's grasp of dialectics and that Bukharin later absorbed Lenin's definition. Zhu concludes that Lenin answered the questions of the imperialist era earlier, more comprehensively and more systematically, and that Bukharin also enriched the theory. Zhu lists four continuing purposes of Lenin's theory. It advanced Marxist political economy, with monopoly and the law of uneven development. It guided revolution and national liberation, including the founding of the People's Republic of China. It offers a reference for financialization and financial crises today, which Zhu calls an era of financial monopoly capitalism. It also points to criticising and ultimately surpassing imperialism. Read the original if you want a detailed Chinese-language defence of Lenin's priority over Bukharin, with references to the Western debate over their relationship.

Engels's preliminary exposition of the distinctiveness of Russia's path of social development 恩格斯关于俄国社会发展道路特殊性的初步阐述 Yang Zhichen Yang Zhichen asks why the Russian populist Peter Tkachev argued in the 1870s that Russia, with capitalism only beginning and bourgeoisie and proletariat barely formed, could reach socialism earlier than Western Europe. The article reads Engels's polemic with Tkachev, 'On Social Relations in Russia' and its 1875 introduction, as doing two things. It refutes Tkachev's conception of socialism and, in the process, offers a first positive account of what is particular about Russia's path of development. The article is organised in six parts. It begins with Engels's critique of Tkachev's view of socialism, then turns to his reading of the revolutionary trend in Russia and the reasons for it. It next treats the economic dimension of the coming revolution, through the artel (labour association) and the village commune, and its political dimension. The last part covers the revolution's expected effects on Western Europe, Germany and Poland. Yang argues that Engels defined social revolution as the victory of the proletariat over the bourgeoisie and the abolition of class differences. On this definition, both classes must really exist and be developing, and productive forces must be advanced enough to sustain a classless society. Russia's post-1861 reform was producing both classes, the author says, so Tkachev's claim that Russia had neither contradicted the facts. Engels treated the artel and the commune as neither uniquely Russian nor mysterious. The artel needed to develop or it would be swallowed by large-scale industry. The commune could either dissolve through internal differentiation and the pressures of the reform, or develop into a higher social form. The second outcome, in Engels's view as Yang reports it, depended on a proletarian revolution in Western Europe. Yang describes the coming political revolution as complex, layered and staged. It would be driven chiefly by conflict between tsarism and the peasantry, and it might begin as a reform from above. Engels also held that it would matter internationally, because tsarist Russia was the last support of reaction in Europe, and that Poland's true ally was the Western proletariat rather than the bourgeoisie. Yang concludes that for Engels the Russian revolution would be a multidimensional social revolution, not only an economic or a political one. Read the original if you study the history of Marxist debates on Russia, the populists and the Russian commune, or Engels's writings of the 1870s.

Hobsbawm on the threefold logic of the October Revolution 霍布斯鲍姆论十月革命的三重逻辑 Lan Yang Lan Yang reads the work of the British Marxist historian Eric Hobsbawm (1917–2012) as a sustained rebuttal of Western attempts to deny the October Revolution's necessity or legitimacy. The article argues that Hobsbawm's critics confuse judgements of fact with judgements of value. In Lan's account, Hobsbawm separates the revolution as a sequence of historical events from the revolution as a chosen political path, and this yields three connected logics: historical, theoretical and practical. The article first sets out the Western debate. It cites Leopold Haimson, Theda Skocpol, Walter Goldfrank and Jack Goldstone, who give different weight to structural contradictions, war, peasants and state collapse. It then follows Hobsbawm in three sections: the historical logic of 1917, the theoretical logic running from Marx and Engels to Lenin, and the logic of present-day relevance. Lan draws mainly on Hobsbawm's The Age of Empire and The Age of Extremes. On the historical side, Lan reports Hobsbawm's view that two causal chains met in 1917. One was the class conflict of a tsarist autocracy: a peasantry denied agrarian modernization, a concentrated working class, a weak and discontented bourgeoisie, and an inflexible regime. The other was the military catastrophe of the First World War, which weakened the state's control over the army and the countryside. The Bolsheviks, with a disciplined party and the slogan 'bread, peace, land', were the only force able to hold Russia together, so the revolution was neither a coup nor an accident. On the theoretical side, Lan shows Hobsbawm tracing three stages: Marx and Engels's idea of Russian and Western revolutions 'complementing' each other, Lenin's strengthening of it, and the later doctrines of socialism in one country. Hobsbawm sees Lenin as resolving tensions in Marx's thought by making a political organisation, not the level of the productive forces, the decisive factor. Lan concludes that Hobsbawm offers two yardsticks for judging the socialist path the revolution opened: a 'productive-forces yardstick' and a 'value yardstick'. The first holds that new relations of production cannot leap beyond what the productive forces allow. The second holds that socialism must be measured by fairness and the all-round development of the individual. Socialist practice stays vital only when developing the productive forces is joined to these values. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly reading of Hobsbawm on 1917 and on the dialectic between historical constraints and political agency in socialist construction.

Mao Zedong's theory of contradiction and its contribution to Marxist-Leninist dialectics 毛泽东矛盾论对马克思列宁辩证法的贡献 Cheng Guangyun Cheng Guangyun, in a short piece first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in October 2021, asks what readers should focus on when they revisit Mao Zedong's "On Contradiction". Cheng treats the theory of contradiction as Mao's main contribution to Marxist-Leninist dialectics and, with the theory of practice, one half of the "Two Essays". Cheng's thesis is that it works both as a worldview and as a methodology. The article takes Alain Badiou's five propositions on the law of the unity of opposites as its starting point. Cheng groups the first two (all reality is process; every process reduces to a set of contradictions) as a "set theory of contradiction". The remaining three (the principal contradiction, the principal aspect, and antagonistic versus non-antagonistic contradictions) become an "algebra of contradiction". The piece then considers readings by Louis Althusser and Norman Levine, and ends with lessons for the present. On the worldview side, Cheng notes that Mao revised the essay after 1949, replacing the heading "two views of development" with "two views of the universe". In Cheng's reading, this raised the theory from a view of development to a cosmology. Extending Engels's account of Hegel, who moved from a collection of things to a collection of processes, Mao treats the world as a collection of contradictions. Cheng presents this as a unity of ontology and epistemology. On the methodological side, Cheng traces the theory to Mao's military and political dialectics of whole and part, and reads it as a development of Lenin's definition of dialectics as the "algebra of revolution". Cheng also takes up Althusser's "overdetermination" and Badiou's elaboration of it, calling the latter possibly an over-interpretation. Cheng argues that the idea of a "cluster of contradictions" moves dialectics from linear to non-linear, complexity-oriented thinking, and describes the essay as a model work of complexity science. Cheng places Mao closer to Lenin than to Marx, since Mao applied dialectical materialism to the political world, and notes Levine's description of the essay as "Hegelianized Leninism". Cheng attributes this to the era and to China's conditions, and says it should be viewed historically. Three lessons follow. Facing domestic and international contradictions requires strategic resolve, analysing problems with the set theory and resolving them with the algebra. Analysis of the roots of contradictions should add the historical-materialist perspective and treat each case concretely. Methods must respect complexity and avoid simplification. Read the original if you want a brief, Badiou- and Althusser-inflected reading of Mao's "On Contradiction" and its stated relevance today.

Learning from history to open up the future: studying Xi Jinping's speech at the commemoration of the 110th anniversary of the Xinhai Revolution 以史为鉴、开创未来——学习贯彻习近平总书记在纪念辛亥革命110周年大会上重要讲话 Bao Dawei Writing in October 2021 for the Chinese Social Sciences Today, Bao Dawei offers a study commentary on General Secretary Xi Jinping's speech marking the 110th anniversary of the Xinhai Revolution. The article asks what the revolution's failure and its legacy teach about achieving the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Bao's answer is that the revolution's patriotic aims were realised only under the leadership of the Communist Party, and that five lessons from the past 110 years apply to the present. The piece moves in two stages. It first assesses the 1911 Revolution and its limits, drawing on Sun Yat-sen's own writings and speeches from 1894 to 1924, together with remarks by Chen Duxiu. It then turns to five lessons, each introduced with a sentence from Xi's speech: Party leadership, the Chinese path, struggle, the consciousness of the Chinese nation as a community, and a community with a shared future for mankind. In Bao's analysis, the revolution failed for three reasons: its guiding ideas were abstract, its values reflected a class standpoint, and its attitude was not thoroughgoing. It borrowed from Western bourgeois thought, including Rousseau and Montesquieu, in a semi-colonial, semi-feudal country that lacked the conditions for such ideas to work. Bao reads the ensuing warlord period as showing that the real contradiction lay between the productive forces and the relations of production. Bao also stresses Sun's self-reflection after 1912. Sun turned towards socialism, praised the October Revolution, and in the new Three Principles of the People equated the principle of people's livelihood with socialism. On this account, Communists were Sun's most loyal heirs, and the Kuomintang's reorganisation took place with Communist help and Soviet assistance. Bao then ties each of the five lessons to Sun's statements, so that the history appears to support current Party positions. Bao concludes that the dream of the revolution's pioneers is being realised under the Party. In the new journey towards a modern socialist country, amid what the article calls great changes unseen in a century and an 'East rising, West declining' trend, the five lessons are presented as guidance. Bao calls for gathering more closely around the Party Central Committee with Xi at its core. Read the original if you want to see how a Party-line commentary of 2021 draws on Sun Yat-sen's statements to link the 1911 Revolution to current Party themes.

The 1911 Revolution: a milestone on the road to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation 辛亥革命：中华民族伟大复兴征程上的里程碑 Kang Peizhu Shang Nana Kang Peizhu and Shang Nana, writing in a newspaper commentary after Xi Jinping's speech marking the 110th anniversary of the 1911 Revolution, ask what the revolution contributed to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. They argue that, although the bourgeois republic it created ultimately failed, the revolution was a milestone on that road. In their account it supplied the historical conditions on which the Communist Party later built. The article is organised around five contributions, each introduced by a statement from Xi Jinping. They are: conditions for the founding of the Chinese Communist Party; a push to early modernization; a foundation for the consciousness of the Chinese nation as a community; a spur to the nation's intellectual awakening; and an impetus to national liberation movements elsewhere in Asia. A short closing section sets the revolution's limits and the Party's role as its heir. The authors argue that the revolution ended the monarchy, and that the Provisional Constitution of the Republic of China gave citizens rights of assembly and association. They say this allowed hundreds of parties to form and opened the way for new currents of thought, including Marxism. They cite an incomplete count that about a third of the earliest Party members had direct or indirect experience of the revolution. They also credit it with early economic, political and social modernization, citing a 1933 industrial survey and the abolition of customs such as kneeling and foot-binding. On national identity, they argue that the modern concept of the Chinese nation took shape in this period, from the 'five-race republic' idea to Sun Yat-sen's 1919 call to fuse all peoples into one Chinese nation. They also argue that the shift from 'subject' to 'citizen' awakened popular political participation, citing the mass meetings against the Twenty-One Demands in 1915. The authors conclude that the weakness and compromising nature of the national bourgeoisie made a bourgeois republic unworkable in semi-colonial, semi-feudal China. In their reading, this failure showed that the revolution needed new leadership. The Party, founded ten years later, completed the democratic tasks Sun Yat-sen left unfinished, won the New Democratic Revolution and founded the People's Republic. They present the Party as the revolution's most steadfast supporter and the leader of national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the 1911 Revolution is framed in Party historiography of 2021 as a precursor to the Communist Party's role.

Marx's critique and inheritance of the concept of labour in Hegel's master–slave relation 马克思对黑格尔主奴关系思想中劳动概念的批判与继承 Yuan Yiming Yuan Yiming asks how far Marx's concept of labour in the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 was actually shaped by the master–slave section of Hegel's Phenomenology of Spirit, and what Marx criticised and kept from it. The author argues against the habit of reading Hegel through Marx, which flattens Hegel's own terms and context. The thesis is that Marx's reading was a productive 'misreading': it turned Hegel's speculative labour into labour as real human activity, and it dropped elements, such as fear, that did not serve his purposes. The article has three parts. The first sets out Hegel's account of the struggle to the death, of fear and labour, and of the slave's path to self-consciousness, and then lists puzzles about Marx's reception. Marx only noted the heading 'master and slave', yet Kojève, Sartre and Hyppolite treat the passage as decisive for him. The second part reconstructs Marx's critique of labour's abstractness and of its negative side, drawing on Christopher Arthur, Sean Sayers, Löwith, Heidegger and Lukács. The third part assesses the disputes and the disappearance of fear. Yuan makes three main moves. First, following Arthur, Marx's charge that Hegel knows only abstract, spiritual labour is aimed at the 'absolute knowledge' chapter rather than at the slave's material work. Yuan notes that Hegel's slave labour is still bound up with consciousness, so identifying consciousness with the human being is partly a misunderstanding. Second, Marx's critique of Hegel's neglect of labour's negative side leads to alienated labour. At first this has a humanist cast, from Feuerbach. It then moves to social relations, where master and slave become capitalist and worker, mediated by commodity fetishism, and onward to the critique of political economy and the concept of practice. Third, fear drops out because Yuan sees it as a purely conscious factor with no historical weight, while alienation, implicit in Hegel's slave labour, carries more critical force. Yuan concludes that Marx read the Phenomenology anthropologically. He treated self-consciousness as the human being and objectification as the essence of labour, and so converted Hegel's idealism into materialism. The anthropological reading misreads Hegel's intent, since Hegel never meant to discuss real human activity, but it opened the way to a new theory. Read the original if you study the Hegel–Marx relation, the debates around Kojève, Arthur and Heidegger, or the sources of Marx's theory of alienated labour.

Exploring the Frankfurt School's theory of social change 探究法兰克福学派社会变迁理论 Huang Xuan This short commentary examines the theory of social change developed by Franz Neumann and Herbert Marcuse, starting from their joint lecture course at Columbia University in the early 1940s. Huang argues that the two combined philosophy, social theory and Marxist critique of political economy to extend Marx's thinking on social change. The commentary holds that this work shows a more practical and political strand of Frankfurt School critical theory than is usually recognised. The article defines the theory as the study of major transformations in social institutions, centred on freedom and necessity and on the subjective and objective factors behind change. It then outlines the four stages into which Neumann and Marcuse divide the theory: ancient philosophy, medieval theology, the transition from Machiavelli to early capitalism, and Marxist revolutionary theory. It closes with their treatment of value and of the agents of change. Huang reports that, in Neumann and Marcuse's account, the first three stages treat change as adjustment within a given order, even Hegel's dialectic, which could not resolve the conflict between private and public interest. Only the fourth stage turns quantitative change into qualitative change and calls for a radical critique of existing society. On value, Huang says the two held that new values precede new institutions and can become a material force. They kept the proletariat as the subject of change but argued it must be redefined, with intellectuals, students and women also appearing as agents. Huang concludes that Neumann and Marcuse, unlike Pollock and Horkheimer, kept to the decisive role of productive forces and economic relations and advocated revolutionary action. Studying this strand, the article suggests, challenges the accepted view that the Frankfurt School withdrew from practice and politics after the 1940s. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese-language overview of Neumann and Marcuse's four-stage periodisation and of how it positions them within Frankfurt School history.

"Substance" and "subject" in the perspective of the materialist conception of history 唯物史观视域中的“实体”与“主体”之辨 Sun Lin Sun Lin asks how the relation between "substance" and "subject" changes across the history of Western philosophy, and where Marx's materialist conception of history stands within that change. The article argues that the relation is one of the subject's steady surpassing of substance: the status of substance falls while that of the subject rises. In Sun's account this runs from substance as ontology, through "substantial subject" and the "real subject", to the "present subject" (出场主体) of historical materialism. The article is built in four parts. The first traces the concept of substance through Aristotle, Descartes, Spinoza and Leibniz. The second turns to Kant and Hegel, treating substance as a category and then as essence. The third follows Marx, first in his pre-historical-materialist period (doctoral thesis, Rheinische Zeitung, the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844) and then in the works of 1845 and the later critique of political economy. A short conclusion links the argument to contemporary China. Sun's central claim is that Hegel's formula "substance is subject" raised the subject but left it governed by the Absolute, so that it remained an "abstract" substantial subject within what Sun calls the metaphysics of presence. Marx's early critique moved in three steps: "people's reason", civil society, and species-essence. Even the last of these, Sun says, remained an abstract species-subject. From 1845, Sun argues, Marx's "real subject" became concrete as the "present subject": the proletariat in a specific historical setting, marked by agency and class character. Sun distinguishes a broad historical materialism, found in the Theses on Feuerbach and The German Ideology, from a concrete one, found in the critique of political economy. In the latter the subject is the labourer, whose labour has two aspects: reified, substantial labour and emancipatory labour that breaks through reification. Sun concludes that Marx's present subject is both a character in history and its author, a unity that no modern metaphysical system of substance or subject can match. For Sun, the proletariat and labourers remain the reason China still needs historical materialism. Sun ties this to a people-centred stance in contemporary China. Read the original if you want a detailed, text-based account of how Hegel's "substance is subject" is read as the target of Marx's critique, and of how this reading is linked to a people-centred position in China today.

A milestone step: building a moderately prosperous society in all respects 具有里程碑意义的关键一步 Li Bin Wei Anxiong Published in the People's Daily on 10 September 2021, this commentary follows Xi Jinping's announcement at the Party's centenary celebration that the first centenary goal had been achieved. Li and Wei argue that building a moderately prosperous society in all respects is a milestone in the history of the Communist Party, of the People's Republic and of Chinese civilization. In their account it is also a key step towards the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The article has three sections. The first traces how the goal of a "moderately prosperous society" developed from the start of reform and opening up through the 12th, 13th, 14th, 16th, 18th and 19th Party Congresses. The second places the achievement within national rejuvenation, citing economic, poverty-reduction and social-security figures. The third turns to its significance for developing countries and for Chinese modernization. Li and Wei first read the goal as a promise kept to the people and to history, one that successive Party generations carried forward. They present it as the Party acting on its original aspiration and founding mission, with a people-centred standard: the result must be recognised by the people and withstand the test of history. Second, they treat it as material and political groundwork for rejuvenation. They cite 2020 GDP above 100 trillion yuan, per capita GDP above US$10,000, a middle-income group of over 400 million, and the end of absolute poverty for 98.99 million rural people. They credit Party leadership and the socialist system's capacity to concentrate resources, citing the central-provincial-local work mechanism and targeted poverty alleviation. Third, they argue that success in a country of over 1.4 billion shows the "new path" of Chinese modernization is viable. They describe it as distinct from the Western model and as an option for countries that want faster development while keeping their independence. The authors conclude that developing countries are not confined to a single Western path, that each country's own exploration should be respected, and that China's experience offers a "Chinese approach" and "Chinese wisdom". They stress that the achievement is a starting point rather than an end, and they call for keeping to the original aspiration while working towards the second centenary goal. Read the original if you want a compact example of the official People's Daily framing of the 2021 poverty-eradication and moderate-prosperity milestone, including its list of statistics and its claims about international significance.

Understanding and grasping "applying history study in practice" accurately 准确认识和把握“学史力行” Huang Yibing This commentary, first published in the People's Daily on 2 September 2021, takes up the slogan "applying history study in practice" (xue shi li xing) from the Party history study and education campaign of that year. Huang opens with Xi Jinping's statement that this is the campaign's "end point": the results of studying history to understand principle, strengthen belief and uphold virtue must become action that changes both the subjective and the objective world. The article argues that Party members should aim to make their practice forceful, effective and productive. The piece is organised under three headings, each beginning "apply in practice": honing Party spirit, serving the people, and promoting development. Each heading is subdivided into several short exhortations. Huang draws throughout on Xi Jinping's formulations and on the Party's hundred-year history as the source of lessons, and does not discuss particular historical episodes in detail. On Party spirit, Huang holds that it is not innate and must be built through continuous education. The author calls for upholding the Party's overall leadership, strengthening the Four Consciousnesses and the Two Upholds, drawing on the great founding spirit of the Party, and practising strict self-discipline. On serving the people, the commentary treats the Party's history as a record of putting the people first. It links the mass line to the Marxist view of the masses as makers of history, and to whole-process people's democracy and common prosperity. On development, Huang asks cadres to connect history study with their work, by grasping the new development stage, applying the new development philosophy fully, speeding up the new development pattern of dual circulation, and balancing development with security. Huang concludes that Party members should turn history study into concrete results, so as to open up new prospects for the cause of the Party and the state on what the text calls a new "road to the examination", the path towards the second centenary goal. The article is a programmatic statement of how the Party presents the practical purpose of history education. Read the original if you want a compact example of official 2021 language on Party-building, people-centred governance and economic strategy as joined in one campaign slogan.

A Chinese standpoint for research on Western Marxism 西方马克思主义研究的中国立场 Wang Zhiqiang Writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in April 2021, Wang Zhiqiang asks how Chinese scholars should position their study of Western Marxism. The commentary argues that this research must start from Chinese reality and the themes of the age, and serve the development of socialism with Chinese characteristics. It should neither reject Western Marxism wholesale nor copy it uncritically. Wang first notes that Western Marxism became a prominent field in China from the 1990s and peaked in the early 2000s. The author then gives a historical account of the tradition: the shift of the communist movement's centre eastward after 1914–1917, the early Western Marxists (Lukács, Korsch, Gramsci), the Frankfurt School, the student protests of the 1960s, and the left's decline after the 1970s and again after the Soviet collapse. The final sections turn to China's own reception of the tradition and to what research should now do. Wang's central claim is that Western Marxism changed in character once the era of revolution in the West ended. In this reading, early figures still had a political base in European revolutionary practice, while the Frankfurt School's "revolution" became cultural and confined to the realm of ideas, carried by professors and students. The author holds that after the Kent State shootings in 1970 and the rise of neoliberalism, such criticism posed no threat to the capitalist order. After the Cold War ended, Wang says, much of it lost seriousness and became "word bubbles". Wang also rejects the view that Western Marxism liberated Chinese thought from dogmatism, calling this a reversal of logic: reform and opening up came first, and interest in Western Marxism was its result. Some Chinese scholars, the author says, follow each new Western left theory and study it exhaustively without a theoretical judgement of their own. Wang adds that its object, highly modernised capitalism, differs historically from China's task of socialist modernisation. Wang concedes that Western Marxists can help Chinese readers understand contemporary capitalism, its crises and structural contradictions, as Xi Jinping has urged. The author calls for research that shows the "spirit of the times" and a world-historical outlook, at a moment of "great changes unseen in a century" and the Covid-19 pandemic. Chinese Marxist scholars should respond with their own judgements, drawing on contemporary Chinese Marxism and twenty-first-century Marxism. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how a Chinese Marxist scholar frames the proper purpose and limits of studying Western Marxism.

The dual logic of Marx's theory of social progress 马克思社会进步理论的双重逻辑 Zhang Wen Zhang Wen asks how Marx's theory of social progress, which grew out of Enlightenment philosophy of history, came to differ from it, and what logic holds the theory together. The article, a short commentary first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today (2021), argues that the theory contains a dual logic. The first strand grounds progress in "material life relations". The second understands progress as a "natural history". The piece begins with Kant's moral history guided by nature's "hidden plan" and Hegel's self-realising "absolute spirit". It then notes what Marx shares with the Enlightenment: the idea of progress, the belief that humans can advance society by perfecting themselves, and a humanist defence of human subjectivity. The two main sections follow: one on how Marx reads history through material life relations, the other on the meaning of "natural history" in Capital. In Zhang's account, Marx replaces "reason" with "practice", meaning material production by real, empirical people, as the measure of history. Enlightenment thinkers, on this reading, made history an object that served to prove reason, which Zhang calls a fundamental inversion. Marx instead seeks a science of history built on a constant element: the relations of production form the economic structure, and the contradictory movement of productive forces and relations of production is the "power source" of progress. The second logic reads progress as natural history. Humans are natural, sensuous, conditioned beings, so progress follows laws independent of human will. Humans nevertheless transform nature into a "humanised nature", and the unity of lawfulness and purposiveness gives progress its subjective dimension. Human initiative can speed progress, even allowing a "Caudine Forks"-style leap, without cancelling natural history. Zhang reads any such leap as showing the transcendence of material production itself. Zhang concludes that the two logics are not split apart but are united in material production and the core theme of practice, so that Marx's theory forms a rigorous system. The author holds that this system moves the study of history away from idealist approaches, from philosophy of history to a science of history, and gives the best account of progress as the unfolding in empirical time of the contradiction between productive forces and relations of production. Read the original if you want a brief, compact exposition of how a Chinese scholar distinguishes Marx's historical materialism from Kantian and Hegelian philosophy of history.

The "world market" category in the critique of political economy and the globalization of capital 政治经济学批判的“世界市场”范畴与资本全球化 Hu Xiaokun Hu Xiaokun asks how globalization, and the backlash against it, should be understood, and answers that Marx's category of the "world market" is the necessary theoretical mediation. In Hu's reading, the world market is both the historical precondition and the real bearer of capitalist economic relations as a whole. The piece is a short newspaper essay first published in 2021. The article first describes globalization as a centuries-long process driven by the logic of capital, from early colonial trade to finance-dominated imperialism. It then contrasts the ideological image of free trade, international law and Kant's "perpetual peace" with the power struggles beneath it. Finally it turns to Marx's unfinished six-book plan, in which the world market and crises were to come last. Hu argues that international trade is not merely a sphere of circulation but the capitalization of the world in depth and breadth, penetrated by the pursuit of surplus value and a higher profit rate. Because it contains capitalism's property and class relations, the contradiction between socialized production and private appropriation must unfold beyond national borders. The world market can temporarily relieve crises by exporting them, but, Hu says, it pushes contradictions into a wider arena. Hu concludes that debates on globalization and anti-globalization must place globalization within the totality of the capitalist mode of production and treat the international order as capitalism's premise and result. Marx and Engels, the author holds, saw this earlier and more deeply than bourgeois social science, and proletarian revolution must therefore become internationalist. Read the original if you want a compact statement of how a Chinese Marxist scholar draws on Marx's world-market category to critique globalization ideology.

A reassessment of the contemporary value of Rosa Luxemburg's thought on Party organisational building 罗莎·卢森堡政党组织建设思想的当代价值审思 Yang Pingping This short commentary, first published in the China Social Sciences Today on 27 May 2021, asks what Rosa Luxemburg's ideas on building a proletarian party still offer today. Yang Pingping argues that Luxemburg's principle of "self-centralism" enriched the understanding of democratic centralism, and that her thinking, though limited by its historical setting, remains relevant to parties that want to keep their vitality. The article first traces the theoretical and practical sources of Luxemburg's views: the 1903 split in the Russian Social-Democratic Labour Party, Lenin's "One Step Forward, Two Steps Back", the revisionist challenge of Bernstein in the German Social Democratic Party, and her own work in the Polish and German parties and in founding the German Communist Party in 1918. It then examines her stress on organisational principles, covering democracy and centralism, the relation between centre and local organisations, and the parliamentary group. Finally it sets out three ways in which she is said to have ensured the correctness of organisational principles, and notes her limitations. Yang reads Luxemburg's 1904 critique of Lenin as a disagreement over the degree and content of centralism rather than a fundamental split. In Yang's account she wanted centralism combined with majority democracy, close ties between the Party and the masses, and room for local organisations to act, which she saw as a source of revolutionary initiative rather than a retreat into decentralisation. She also held that the parliamentary group shapes the Party's fate and should act as the spokesperson of the masses. Yang argues that Luxemburg recognised the need to balance democracy and centralism earlier than Lenin did, and links her people-centred approach and commitment to Marxism to the Chinese Communist Party's practice of democratic centralism, its mass line, and the regulation on reporting major matters to the Party. Yang concludes that Luxemburg overlooked differences between Russian and Western European conditions, the historical constraints on the masses, and the practicability of Party work. Even so, the author holds that any Party with ideals and convictions must treat its own organisational building as a long-term task and keep improving it with the times. Read the original if you want a brief, Party-oriented Chinese reading of Luxemburg's dispute with Lenin and of how it is tied to democratic centralism in the Chinese Communist Party.

An epoch-making event: the founding of the Communist Party of China 开天辟地的大事变 Ni Bangwen This commentary, published in the People's Daily in September 2021, takes as its starting point Xi Jinping's statement at the ceremony marking the Party's centenary that the emergence of the Communist Party in China was an "epoch-making event". Ni Bangwen argues that the founding of the Party changed the direction and course of the Chinese nation's modern development, the fate of the Chinese people, and the trends and configuration of world development. The author calls for understanding this significance from a broad spatial and temporal perspective. The piece is organised in three parts that follow the three clauses of Xi's formulation. The first treats the nation's direction and course after the Opium War; the second, the future and destiny of the Chinese people and nation, running from the founding of the People's Republic to the reform era and the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012); the third, the Party's effect on the world. Each part opens with a quotation from Xi and then offers a historical account. In Ni's account, the failure of earlier salvation schemes after the Opium War arose above all from the lack of an advanced party as a leading core. The Party, by adopting Marxism and integrating it with Chinese realities and fine traditional culture, is said to have shifted the Chinese people from a passive to an active spiritual state and, through its wars, to have won national independence. Ni then cites achievements: the First Five-Year Plan, the world's second-largest economy, GDP above 100 trillion yuan, per capita GDP above 10,000 US dollars, and the elimination of absolute poverty. Internationally, Ni argues, the founding of the People's Republic broke the colonial system, and Chinese modernization offers developing countries a path that preserves independence. The article describes the community with a shared future for mankind and the common values of humanity as Chinese contributions to global governance. Ni concludes that under Party leadership the nation has moved from standing up, to becoming prosperous, to becoming strong, and that national rejuvenation is now an irreversible process. The author urges keeping the country's fate in its own hands and advancing towards the second centenary goal. Read the original if you want a compact example of the official People's Daily narrative on the Party's centenary and its claimed national and global significance.

Understanding the great historical significance of building a moderately prosperous society in all respects 深刻理解全面建成小康社会的伟大历史意义 Chen Jin Published in the People's Daily on 9 September 2021, this commentary by Chen Jin follows Xi Jinping's announcement at the Party's centenary celebration (2021) that the first centenary goal had been met and a moderately prosperous society had been built in all respects. Chen asks what this achievement means historically and argues that it has three kinds of significance: for the path of modernization, for the strengths of China's institutions, and for the next stage of national rejuvenation. The article is organised in three sections after a brief opening. The first traces how the goal of modernization was defined from Mao Zedong's 1945 slogan on industrialization, through the 1978 target of the four modernizations, to Deng Xiaoping's idea of a 'xiaokang' household. The second concerns poverty alleviation and what it shows about the national system and governance. The third looks ahead to the second centenary goal of a modern socialist country. Chen's central claim is that the goal changed in content as understanding deepened. Deng's xiaokang was first measured by per capita output, with a target of 800 US dollars by the end of the twentieth century. The 18th Party Congress (2012) then set five dimensions, and Xi's 2015 formula treated moderate prosperity as all-round progress across five domains. Chen also treats the elimination of poverty as an essential requirement of socialism. He cites 98.99 million rural poor lifted out of poverty, 832 counties removed from the poverty list and 128,000 villages, and reads this as showing three institutional strengths: centralised, unified Party leadership; a people-centred approach aimed at common prosperity; and the ability to concentrate resources on major undertakings. Chen concludes that the achievement lays a solid base for the second centenary goal and is a key step in the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, one that he calls irreversible. He cites figures including GDP above 100 trillion yuan, per capita GDP above 10,000 US dollars and more than 400 million people in the middle-income group. He also holds that it strengthens the Four-sphere Confidence and offers other countries a Chinese option for developing while keeping their independence. Read the original if you want a concise, official-line account of how Party media framed the meaning of the moderately prosperous society in 2021.

The rejuvenation of the Chinese nation is irreversible 中华民族伟大复兴不可逆转 Shuang Chuanxue This commentary, first published in the People's Daily on 8 September 2021, interprets a central claim in Xi Jinping's speech marking the centenary of the Communist Party of China (CPC): that the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation has entered an irreversible historical process. Shuang argues that the claim rests on historical necessity. It also rests on the Party's leadership and on continued struggle. The piece has three parts. The first sets out the historical foundations of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The second explains why the CPC is the "core of leadership". The third lists what the Party and the people must do in what the author calls the critical period of the rejuvenation. Throughout, Shuang quotes Xi Jinping's speech and presents the Party's hundred-year history as a single narrative. On history, Shuang points to three sources of confidence. One is the long continuity of Chinese civilisation, which Marxism is said to have reactivated in a time of crisis. Another is successive generations' struggle for national revival. The author says each stage created a condition for the rejuvenation: new-democratic revolution, socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era. The third is Xi's formula that "time and momentum are on our side". On leadership, Shuang attributes the Party's capacity to its guidance by Marxism, which was adapted through Mao Zedong Thought, Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents, the Scientific Outlook on Development and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The author also credits the Party's qualities and its focus on a single theme of national rejuvenation over a century. Shuang concludes that the rejuvenation requires three things. These are an enduring spirit of struggle against risks to Party leadership, sovereignty, security, development and core interests; sober awareness of the "examination" the era sets, through the Party's self-reform and a great new project of Party building; and strategic resolve to stay on the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The author rejects both a "closed and rigid old path" and an "evil path of changing banners". Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Party commentary in 2021 connected the centenary narrative to the claim of irreversibility.

Derrida's argument for the politics of Marx's "spectres" 德里达对马克思“幽灵”政治学的论证 Xie Hongyu Why did Jacques Derrida, founder of deconstruction, turn to the figure of the "spectre" when defending Marx after the upheavals in the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe?
