This commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in 2021, reads Derrida's Specters of Marx as an attempt to revive Marx's \"true spirit\" at a time when claims that Marxism is useless or obsolete were widespread. Xie concludes that Derrida's defence rests on turning Marxism into a spectre, which the author judges incompatible with Marxism's own logic of effectiveness. The piece is organised in two parts followed by a critical assessment. The first part sets out Derrida's notion of the spectre, drawing on his reading of Marx's The German Ideology and on Hamlet. The second part follows Derrida's reading of the opening of the Communist Manifesto and the plural \"spectres of Marx\". Xie then draws on Julian Thomson's essay on Derrida's deconstruction of Marxism to explain Derrida's motives. Xie reports that for Derrida the spectre is the phenomenal body of spirit: neither wholly present nor absent, neither living nor dead, and not a mere illusion. Derrida coined \"hauntology\" for this mode of being. Xie reports that Derrida reads Marx's image as a hidden force that frightens old powers and empowers the proletariat, and that those who declare Marxism dead reveal their fear of it. Using the plural, Derrida lists the spectres in the book: Hamlet's father, the theorists Marx expelled, later readings of Marx, the spectres of money and capital, and communism. Derrida argues that this plurality shows the collapse of the Soviet model does not end Marx's spirit, and that its heterogeneity allows constant reinterpretation. Among these spirits he singles out a critical spirit, directed at capitalism and ready for self-critique, citing Engels's 1888 preface to the Manifesto. Xie then argues that the spectre suits deconstruction's critique of the metaphysics of presence and logocentrism, since pure presence cannot be grasped. Derrida used it to join deconstruction to Marxism against the thesis of the end of history. Xie holds that Derrida's openness to endless interpretation conflicts with dialectical materialism. Making Marxism spectral is, in Xie's judgement, the price of Derrida's defence, and it goes against the logic of effectiveness, so the result \"cannot count as genuine Marxism\". Read the original if you want a short, critical Chinese-language summary of Derrida's Specters of Marx and of how Chinese Marxist commentary assesses postmodern Western Marxism.

The obscured horizon: the moral dimension of the materialist conception of history 被遮蔽的视野：唯物史观的道德维度 Zhou Song This short commentary argues that the moral dimension runs through the whole formation and development of the materialist conception of history, but has long been obscured or dissolved. Zhou holds that returning to the actual context of the classic texts helps answer whether Marxism and morality are coherent with one another. The article first traces the denial of this dimension to the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. It then follows it through Western scholarship's opposition of the materialist conception of history to humanism, and through Soviet-influenced Chinese readings that stress only its scientific truth. Zhou names Barth, Kautsky and Kamenka as examples, and cites Chen Xianda in rebuttal. Zhou's central move is to distinguish a complete 'ethical system' from a 'moral dimension', which concerns moral values and standpoints. The materialist conception of history lacks the former but, Zhou argues, has the latter, so that it is not value-neutral 'pure scientism'. Humanism, in Zhou's account, has two senses, as a view of history and as a moral principle. Marx rejected the first and kept the second, giving it a scientific basis. The moral dimension appears in three forms: a scientifically grounded moral critique of capitalism, a strong orientation to moral practice, and a concern for human emancipation and free, all-round development. Zhou concludes that Marx used the materialist conception of history to explain the origin, nature and development of morality, and that the theory never abandoned moral inquiry. Scientific disclosure of historical laws and moral concern are, in this view, two sides of one theory. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese-language statement of the case against reading historical materialism as morally neutral.

The rich implications of Marx's conception of time 马克思时间观的丰富意蕴 Yao Manlin Wu Qiong Yao Manlin and Wu Qiong take up a gap in how Marxist philosophy treats time. Textbooks usually pair it with space as a mode of existence of moving matter. The authors argue that Marx's own texts give time a richer, more concrete content, with at least three layers of meaning: a measure of commodity value, a measure of human emancipation, and a measure that grounds social history. This short commentary in China Social Sciences Today takes each layer in turn. It draws on Capital's analysis of value, the Grundrisse (the 1857–58 manuscripts), the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, and Yu Wujin's reading of Marx's time as "social time". On the first layer, labour time, the authors say Marx grounds exchange relations between commodities in labour time and defines value by socially necessary labour time. They add that Marx treats appropriation of surplus labour time as the capitalist's basic means of exploitation. On the second, leisure time, they report Marx's three stages of human development and argue that disposable free time signals emancipation, while labour in a future communist society keeps a positive, regulating role. On the third, social time, they argue that Marx starts from productive practice, unites natural history and human history through industry, and treats labour as the source of time. The authors conclude that Marx always discusses time within the specific conditions of capitalist society and never in a metaphysical way, unlike traditional philosophy. They call for more scholarly work on this question. Read the original if you want a brief overview of how Chinese scholars link Marx's value theory, his idea of free time and his view of history in a single account of time.

A critical study of the green capitalism current of thought: a literature review 绿色资本主义思潮的批判性研究:一个文献综述 Li Quanxi This literature review, published in 2019, surveys scholarship on green capitalism, the idea that global ecological problems can be solved within the capitalist system. Li Quanxi follows a scholar's three-way typology of Western responses: neoliberal market self-regulation, eco-Marxism or eco-socialism, and intermediate positions that amount to green capitalism. The review's own judgement is that green capitalism cannot resolve the contradiction between capitalism and the ecological environment. The review is organised in five stages of critical analysis: the origins of the current, its essential content, the assumptions behind it, the practical difficulties it faces, and the possibility of going beyond it. For origins, Li points to the failure of sustainable development, the World Bank's Global Environment Facility (1991), and the work of Paul Hawken, Lester Brown and Francis Cairncross. Hawken's Natural Capitalism (1999) is treated as a representative text. Li reports that scholars define green capitalism by three beliefs: economic growth helps solve environmental problems, market principles can protect natural resources, and technological progress can fix ecological damage. Five assumptions are said to underlie this: the iron rule of profit maximisation, underestimation of the environmental crisis, market-centrism, faith in technology (the Jevons paradox is cited against it), and trust in strong government support, with Trump's 2017 withdrawal from the Paris Agreement offered as a counter-example. The reviewed literature then identifies four practical impasses: the unresolved contradiction between unlimited accumulation and scarce resources, the failure of carbon taxes and cap-and-trade, uncontrolled technology, and the interference of what is called ecological imperialism in government governance. On going beyond green capitalism, Li lists proposals from Europe (socialist ecological transition), Latin America (good living, degrowth), India (radical eco-autonomy) and China. Li presents Xi Jinping's socialist ecological civilization thinking as a practical transcendence of a capitalism that is "neither just nor ecological". The review adds that market mechanisms, technological innovation and government governance have positive roles, and that rational elements of green capitalism may be critically borrowed. Read the original if you want a compact guide to Chinese-language critiques of green capitalism and their citations, or an example of how this literature is linked to socialist ecological civilization.

Hypocrisy, exploitation and new imperialism: on consequentialist theories of climate justice 伪善、剥削与新帝国主义——论后果主义气候正义理论 Chen Xiao Huang Ding Writing in 2021, after President Biden's return to the Paris Agreement, Chen and Huang ask what lies behind the ambivalent stance of the United States and other developed capitalist countries on emissions reduction. They argue that consequentialist theories of climate justice, now treated as a basic principle for allocating reduction duties, are in practice a hypocritical doctrine. In the authors' reading it cloaks a claim to global hegemony and a fresh round of exploitation of developing countries behind an appeal to the good of humanity. The article first presents two consequentialist approaches: Nicholas Stern's cost-benefit economics in the Stern Review, which measures welfare by real income, and Eric Posner's "international Paretianism", under which a climate treaty need only be feasible and leave no party worse off. It then examines how these theories let developed countries evade and shift reduction responsibility. Next it analyses "climate exploitation" as new imperialism. A final section reviews existing criticisms and sets out how developing countries should respond. The authors argue that consequentialism judges only outcomes, not motives or process, so it sets aside historical emissions and the fairness of allocation. Stern's tradable emission rights, they contend, legitimise past emissions through the "grandfathering" principle and erase the responsibility attached to them. Developing countries, which industrialised later, inherit polluting industries relocated from the developed world and so bear extra costs. Posner's "feasibility" is said to reflect the balance of political power, so the developing countries' consent is coerced. Drawing on Lenin's account of imperialism, the authors hold that urgency propaganda leaves these countries without time to upgrade technology independently. They then depend on monopolised Western technology, paying patent and service fees and adopting its standards, which locks in technological dependence. The authors note that deontological critics such as Henry Shue, Simon Caney and Steve Vanderheiden, and policy proposals from Brazil and China, stay within distributive justice and do not analyse the capitalist structure behind mitigation. They call on developing countries to recognise the class nature of this theory, to unite as a bloc, to cooperate globally while resisting climate exploitation and reducing technological dependence, and to understand humanity's shared destiny as more than economic growth. Read the original if you want a Marxist-imperialism critique of climate-justice theory, and of Stern and Posner in particular, from a Chinese academic perspective.

Capitalism and democracy in the age of the climate crisis 气候危机时代的资本主义与民主主义 Saito Kohei This is a Chinese translation of an essay by the Japanese scholar Saito Kohei. It asks whether the climate crisis can be handled within capitalism. Saito argues that it cannot: the contest ahead is between capitalism and democracy, and only a deep structural change in the economic system, driven by popular movements, can avert catastrophe. The essay has four parts. It begins with the 2018 IPCC Special Report on 1.5°C and its limits. It then sets out the structural inequalities behind the crisis, together with the ideas of climate justice and a just transition. A third part examines the Green New Deal (GND), Bernie Sanders's programme and left populism. A short conclusion draws on Rosa Luxemburg and Naomi Klein. Saito reads the IPCC report as a call for system transformation that nonetheless rests on the assumption that market-led growth can solve the problem. He points to speculative carbon-removal technology such as BECCS, which would need land several times the size of India and large volumes of water. He says that 30 years of neoliberal delay have ended any chance of gradual solutions. He cites figures showing that the richest 10% emit about half of global CO2 and that 100 firms account for 71% of emissions. From this he argues that climate justice requires planned production guided by a carbon budget, regulated markets, localised production and consumption, and taxes on monopoly capital. He treats the GND as workable only as what Joachim Hirsch calls "radical reformism", backed by unions, NGOs, community groups and indigenous peoples. Without that radical edge it would become "climate Keynesianism", which Saito says would keep extracting the world's resources. Saito concludes that capitalism's pursuit of unlimited growth on a finite planet has reached a crossroads. Technological fixes under existing relations of production will, he says, fail. Left unchecked, the logic of capital would erode democracy and produce "eco-fascism", in which a few monopolise wealth and energy and exclude climate migrants, as Saito says Trump's border wall symbolises. The alternative he offers is to defend democracy and build a freer, more equal society. Read the original if you want a Japanese Marxist's case that climate politics must target capitalism itself, set out through the IPCC, climate justice and the Green New Deal debate.

The great achievements and profound lessons of economic and social construction in new China 新中国经济社会建设的伟大成就与深刻启示 Policy Research Office of the National Development and Reform Commission This commentary, written by the Policy Research Office of the National Development and Reform Commission and published in the People's Daily in September 2021, reviews 72 years of economic and social construction in the People's Republic. It argues that under the Party's leadership the country has created the "two miracles" of rapid economic growth and long-term social stability, built a moderately prosperous society in all respects, and entered an irreversible historical process towards the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The text has two parts. The first lists achievements in seven areas: economic strength and structural change, poverty elimination and living standards, scientific and technological self-reliance, ecological protection, reform and opening up, and national security. The second draws six lessons from this record. Most of the evidence is statistical, and the figures are the author's own. On the record, the article reports that GDP rose from 67.91 billion yuan in 1952 to 101.6 trillion yuan in 2020, and that China moved from a backward agricultural country to the world's largest industrial one. It cites the removal of 98.99 million rural people from poverty under the current standard over eight years, forest cover rising from 8.6% to 23.04%, and a pledge of carbon peaking before 2030 and carbon neutrality before 2060. It credits the Party Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core, since the 18th Party Congress (2012), with historic change in each area. The six lessons are: uphold the Party's overall leadership; keep to a people-centred development philosophy; arm the mind with the Party's innovative theory, namely Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era; keep to the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics, described as the only correct one; improve and develop its institutions; and apply correct methods, including seeking truth from facts and systems thinking. For the "new journey" the author calls for the Two Upholds and for implementing the new development philosophy, building a new development pattern and pursuing high-quality development. Read the original if you want a compact example of the official narrative of seven decades of development, with its headline statistics and standard formulations, as presented for the Party's centenary year.

The world-historical significance of the Communist Party of China's century of struggle 中国共产党百年奋斗的世界历史意义 Tang Junfeng Written for the centenary of the Communist Party of China (2021), this commentary asks what the Party's hundred years of struggle have contributed beyond China. Taking its cue from Xi Jinping's statement that the Party's path, cause and achievements will enter the annals of both the Chinese nation and human civilization, Tang argues that the century has world-historical significance in four respects: modernization, Marxist party-building, world socialism and global peace and development. The article is organised as four numbered sections, each opening with a statement by Xi Jinping and then setting out the author's reading. They deal in turn with a new path to modernization, a new stage in the development of Marxist parties, a new phase of world socialism and a new contribution to peaceful development. Tang draws on the Party's record from the revolutions before 1949 through reform and opening up to the new era, and on the figures reported for poverty reduction. Tang's central claim is that Chinese modernization differs from the Western model, which the author characterises as based on colonial plunder, benefiting few, pursuing growth one-sidedly and tending to hegemony. In Tang's account it relies on self-reliant development, is people-centred, seeks harmony between humans and nature and aims at peace. The author cites 770 million rural people lifted out of poverty since reform and opening up, over 70 per cent of global poverty reduction, as evidence. On party-building, Tang holds that some older socialist ruling parties collapsed because they failed to pair social revolution with the Party's self-reform, whereas the Communist Party of China has used full and rigorous self-governance of the Party to keep its vanguard character. Tang also contrasts it with Western electoral parties, which the author describes as marked by factional strife and money politics. Tang concludes that Chinese socialism has been the mainstay of world socialism since the Soviet and East European upheavals, refuting what the author calls the theories of socialism's failure, China's collapse and the end of history. The Party is said to offer China's wisdom and proposals on global governance through a community with a shared future for mankind and the Belt and Road Initiative, and to promise continued contributions in a turbulent international environment. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the official Party narrative presented the centenary's international significance in 2021.

A towering milestone on the journey to great rejuvenation 伟大复兴征程上一座巍然屹立的里程碑 Wang Jianlang Marking the 110th anniversary of the 1911 Revolution, this commentary, first published in the People's Daily on 21 October 2021, takes up Xi Jinping's speech at the commemoration meeting. Wang Jianlang argues that the revolution, in Xi's words, 'will forever be a towering milestone on the journey toward the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation', because it opened the way for later struggles even though it did not achieve national independence. The article has three parts. The first traces the Chinese people's search for national salvation after 1840, from Lin Zexu and Wei Yuan through the Taiping movement, the Self-Strengthening Movement, the Hundred Days' Reform and the late-Qing New Policies, to Sun Yat-sen's revolutionaries. The second assesses what the revolution achieved and failed to achieve. The third draws five historical lessons from Xi's speech. In Wang's account, the revolution was the inevitable result of sharpening social contradictions in a semi-colonial, semi-feudal China. It ended millennia of monarchical autocracy rather than merely changing a dynasty, and two attempted restorations of the monarchy failed. Wang says the idea of democratic republicanism took hold and freed thought. Yet the revolution lacked a correct path and leading force, so it did not change China's semi-colonial, semi-feudal character. Wang links the October Revolution, the spread of Marxism-Leninism and the founding of the Communist Party, ten years after 1911, to this opening. The Party then became Sun Yat-sen's most loyal successor and carried the task forward. Wang lists five lessons: rejuvenation must be achieved under the leadership of the Communist Party; through upholding and developing socialism with Chinese characteristics, described as the only correct path; through the Chinese people's own heroic struggle; through solidarity and the broadest patriotic united front; and through building a community with a shared future for mankind. Wang concludes that commemoration should mean carrying forward the pioneers' spirit towards the goal of rejuvenation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the official narrative links the 1911 Revolution to the Communist Party's mission and to current slogans.

Interpretive perspectives on Marx and Engels's concept of ideology 马克思恩格斯意识形态概念的阐释视角 Xu Doudou Yi Zhengxuan Marxist theory has three ways of characterising the concept of ideology: negative, descriptive (neutral) and positive. Xu Doudou and Yi Zhengxuan ask which of these fits the texts of Marx and Engels. They argue that the positive and descriptive readings lack textual support and create difficulties of interpretation, so Marx and Engels's stance is, in the end, negative. In their view this negativity stresses the critical element in ideology and supplies a standard for rationalising thought. The article, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in July 2021, has three sections. The first explains the logical difficulties of a "positive" concept of ideology. The second shows the absence of textual grounds for a "descriptive" concept, mainly through a reading of the 1859 Preface's base–superstructure passage. The third defends the negative reading by distinguishing epistemological and sociological dimensions, which it ties to Lenin and the early Althusser. The authors make three main moves. First, they argue that ideology, as an inverted and illusory form of consciousness, lies outside science, which Marx and Engels treat as a positive force. They concede that Marx and Engels point to a way beyond illusion: the proletariat's interests coincide with those of the great majority, and ideology disappears in communism. Lenin's construction of proletarian ideology shows the first real shift from illusory to scientific ideology. Second, they argue that the neutral reading rests on a misreading. In the Preface Marx uses a different German term for "forms of social consciousness", which he describes neutrally, and he treats "ideological forms" negatively. Third, they argue that the negativity is dialectical: an "internal critique" that exposes ideology's distortions and also recognises its transcendent force. It operates as sublation, seen in Marxism's critique of German classical philosophy, the move from utopian to scientific socialism, and the late Engels's stress on the relative independence of the superstructure. The authors conclude that the three interpretive modes each have some validity in particular contexts. Only the negative reading, they argue, matches the "internal critical" meaning of the concept in Marx and Engels. They warn that the descriptive reading can slide into treating ideology as culture or social consciousness in general, which dissolves its critical sense. Read the original if you want a compact, textually grounded argument for a negative reading of Marx and Engels on ideology, set against neutral and positive readings.

From "alienated labour" to "world alienation": Arendt's inheritance and misreading of Marx 从“劳动异化”到“世界异化”——阿伦特对马克思思想的继承与误读 Li Jiaxing Li Jiaxing's short commentary, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in April 2021, asks how Hannah Arendt's concept of "world alienation", set out in The Human Condition, relates to Marx's theory of alienated labour. Li argues that Marx's influence on Arendt is beyond doubt, but that she both inherited his approach and misread his concept of labour. The piece first identifies three points of inheritance: the general way of posing the problem of alienation, the theoretical premise for understanding it, and the critical target of the theory. It then sets out how the two thinkers diverge, tying each to the main contradictions of their eras, and closes with Arendt's limitations. On inheritance, Li says Arendt, like Marx, treats alienation as a historical loss of human subjectivity rather than an eternal fate, and grounds human beings in concrete activity. Her "world alienation" also continues Marx's critique of capitalism, since industrial exploitation leaves people atomised and cut off from the public world. On divergence, Li contends that Marx rooted alienation in the economic sphere, while Arendt, shaped by the Second World War and Nazi persecution, saw it as political and sought a remedy in rebuilding public space. Li concludes that Arendt used Marx to build her own theory rather than developing alienation from a Marxist standpoint. In Li's view she belittles labour as metabolic necessity, confines subjectivity to political action, and lacks Marx's historical analysis of how alienation may take new forms. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese Marxist assessment of Arendt's debt to Marx.

Rethinking the spatial dimension of social critical theory 反思社会批判理论之空间向度 Du Dan Du Dan asks what the "spatial turn" contributes to social critical theory, the foundational theory of the Frankfurt School. The author argues that this turn is neither a simple paradigm reconstruction nor a misreading, but an immanent philosophical critique. It draws on the concept of spatiality, which some Western Marxists used to recover a dimension the older theory neglected. The piece appeared in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in 2021. The article first traces the concept of space and spatiality through Edward Soja, Henri Lefebvre, Manuel Castells, David Harvey and Gramsci. It then turns to Soja's "Thirdspace" and his critical geographical imagination, using Baudrillard's account of the city as a field of signs and codes. It ends with the digital city of the fourth industrial revolution and a return to Marx. Du holds that the philosophical core of the spatial dimension comes from Heidegger, for whom spatiality determines space and is itself determined by temporality. On this basis space becomes a lived world and a dwelling place, not a mere surrounding. Du then argues that platform and algorithmic space is a topological space made of data that nonetheless shapes physical geography, and that the alienation it produces is driven by capital. For this the author turns to Marx's claim that capital seeks to annihilate space with time. Du concludes that spatiality cannot be bypassed in either traditional or digital space research, and that Soja's theory does not yet engage digital space adequately. Some Western Marxists' preoccupation with space and an ideal city, the author says, leaves open whether they can resolve urban injustice. Marx supplies the basic standpoint, so Du calls for a return to him as the starting point. Read the original if you want a short Chinese-language overview of how Soja, Lefebvre and Harvey's spatial thinking is linked to Heidegger, digital capitalism and Marx.

Western new social movements and their impact on left-wing parties 西方新社会运动及其对左翼政党的影响 Zang Xiuling Zang asks how the Western "new social movements" that have risen since the late 1960s are reshaping Western left-wing parties and where both are heading. The author defines these movements as loose, spontaneous protests by middle strata and marginal groups during a low tide of world socialism, pursuing non-material values rather than the material interests of the traditional workers' movement. The thesis is that both the movements and the left parties suffer fatal weaknesses, and that only by combining can they mount a lasting challenge to capitalism. The article first traces four phases of the movements. These run from the French May 1968 events, through the anti-nuclear, green and new feminist movements of the 1970s and 1980s, to the anti-globalisation wave after Seattle in 1999. The last phase covers the period after the 2008 financial crisis and the Covid-19 pandemic, with Occupy Wall Street, Black Lives Matter, the Yellow Vests and Spain's Indignados as examples. It then sorts left parties into moderate, radical and extreme types and examines how each has been affected. The closing section sets out remedies. Zang argues that the movements weakened traditional trade unions and communist and social-democratic parties, and that parties are no longer the only channel for expressing interests. Moderate left parties, such as Labour and the German Social Democrats with their "Third Way", have drifted to the centre. The author says this cost Labour its working-class base and left it without answers after 2008. Radical left parties, such as Syriza, have become more active by opposing austerity. Zang judges this activity relative and temporary because of uneven performance, dependence on mainstream policy failures, and internal splits. Extreme left parties remain marginal and are becoming populist, which the author reads as a passing symptom of post-crisis political pathology. The movements, for their part, are described as fragmented, anti-class, lacking leadership and Marxist theory, and prone to populism. Zang concludes that Western left parties should end internal divisions, build alliances, and win elections to transform capitalism peacefully. They should also lead the movements towards socialism and involve trade unions. The author calls on moderate parties to drop centrism and adopt a clear socialist programme. Zang also urges Western Marxist scholars to leave the "ivory tower", learn from the movements, and develop left-party theory that reaches ordinary people. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic assessment of Western left parties and social movements, including its prescriptions for their future.

A survey of the British left after the Second World War: comparing the ideas of the New Left, the Communist Party and the Labour Party 二战后英国左翼谱系考察——英国新左翼、共产党和工党思想比较 Huang Fei Writing amid what the author describes as a structural shift in the global order, with the Western traditional left in difficulty and the radical right on the rise, Huang asks what the post-war history of three British left currents reveals about the development of the Western left as a whole. The three are the Labour Party, the Communist Party of Great Britain and the New Left. The article argues that the New Left formed largely as a critique of the other two, occupied a middle position between them, and was limited by its own theoretical and organisational weaknesses. The article first sketches the history of each current: the New Left, which emerged after 1956 and declined from the late 1970s; the Communist Party, founded in 1920, which split repeatedly and renamed itself in 1991; and Labour, founded in 1900, which turned toward the centre under Tony Blair. It then compares them along four dimensions: attitude to Marxism, the kind of socialism pursued, strategy for achieving it, and position within the left spectrum. Huang holds that each dimension shapes the next. On theory and values, Huang presents the Communist Party as resting on scientific socialism and aiming at public ownership and a classless society. Labour is portrayed as grounded in democratic socialism and Fabianism, with nationalisation and welfare policies that left capitalist ownership intact. The New Left, by contrast, combined Marxism with ethical socialism and radical traditions in pursuit of a 'humanist socialism'. Huang judges this approach utopian because it was detached from economic structure. In strategy, the Communist Party's 'peaceful transition' mixed parliamentary and mass struggle, Labour relied on gradual parliamentary reform, and the New Left proposed 'peace plus revolution'. From left to right, the author places the Communist Party, the New Left, Labour's left and Labour's right. The author argues that New Left criticism pushed both Labour and the Communist Party toward renewal. Huang credits the New Left with diversifying socialist movements and renewing history, sociology and cultural studies. The author also lists its flaws: no systematic theory, almost no use of Marx's analysis of capitalist economic laws, elitism and weak organisation. Four problems are identified across the Western left: blurred identity, factionalism, unsystematic theory, and criticism outrunning constructive proposals. The article concludes that after the 2008 financial crisis, socialists should use Marx's tools of analysis and critique to go beyond capitalism. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly comparison of the post-war British left, framed by what it implies for socialism today.)

Western left-wing scholars' research on world-systems theory since the twenty-first century 21世纪以来西方左翼学者关于世界体系理论的研究 Zheng Jiwei Song Xin Published in New Horizons (Xin shiye), 2021 no. 4, shortly after Immanuel Wallerstein's death in August 2019, this review surveys how Western left-wing scholars have treated his world-systems theory since 2000. The authors note that before 2000 the literature mainly praised the theory as a comprehensive research paradigm and as a global approach to underdevelopment. They argue that the new-century literature has turned to three questions: the theory's critique of modernization theory, its account of modern world-system and capitalism, and its relation to the Marxist theory of class. The review is organised in three sections matching these themes. The first draws on Cosma Sorinel, Agussalim Burhanuddin, Daniel Chirot, John Bies and Walter Goldfrank. The second covers debates among Andre Gunder Frank, Wallerstein, Samir Amin, William Robinson, Giovanni Arrighi and others on origins, the core–periphery concepts and globalization. The third covers Robert Brenner, William Martin, Chamsy el-Ojeili, Amin and Chirot on class. On modernization theory, the authors report that these scholars see world-systems theory as a deliberate critique, which locates obstacles to development in the international core–semi-periphery–periphery structure rather than in national internal factors. They add that it rejects a single path of development and takes a long historical view. On capitalism, the review sets Frank, who traced a single world system back some 5,000 years, against Wallerstein and Amin, who hold that the modern capitalist system began in the sixteenth century. It also reports Robinson's view that core and periphery are becoming transnational social rather than territorial categories, and that Wallerstein's theory is in effect a theory of globalization. On class, Brenner and Martin accuse Wallerstein of neglecting class and exploitation in favour of exchange relations. El-Ojeili, Amin, Burhanuddin and Chirot reply that he extends Marxist class analysis to the global scale, with core, semi-periphery and periphery resembling bourgeoisie, middle class and proletariat. The authors conclude that world-systems theory grew out of changes in global capitalism, absorbed Marxist class theory and criticised Western modernization theory. They hold that the disputes, even over basic concepts, have enlarged its influence and sharpened scholarly attention to Marxism and the nature of capitalism. They expect foreign academia to keep engaging with it. Read the original if you want a map of post-2000 Anglophone debates about Wallerstein, with names and positions, for research on foreign Marxism or world-systems theory.

The current state and prospects of the Latin American left 当前拉美左翼的发展现状与前景 Yang Jianmin Writing in 2021, Yang Jianmin asks where the Latin American left stands after the "pink tide" that began with Hugo Chávez's election in Venezuela in 1999, and whether it can open a new period in government. The article argues that the region has moved from "the left retreats, the right advances" (2015–2018) to a mixed phase of alternating gains and shared power. In Yang's view the left remains divided at home but has durable political, economic and social foundations, so it will continue to exist in the long term. The article has four parts. It first traces the shift in the regional balance, from the right-wing offensives of the pink-tide years (the 2002 Venezuelan coup, Honduras 2009, Paraguay 2012) through the setbacks of 2015–2018 to the left's return in Mexico, Argentina, Bolivia and elsewhere. It then examines how the Covid-19 pandemic and the 2020 US election favour the left, with case studies of Ecuador, Brazil, Peru, Chile and Mexico. The third part contrasts the left's growing regional coordination with its internal fragmentation. The last part sets out conditions for a new left-wing cycle and the grounds for the left's persistence. Yang argues that the pandemic deepened poverty, public debt and inequality and led many Latin Americans to question neoliberal, right-wing policies. This benefits the left, as do Lula's restored political rights and Biden's replacement of Trump. Abroad, left-wing parties coordinate through the Puebla Group, and the Lima Group's pressure on Venezuela is described as collapsing. At home, Yang identifies three problems: new left forces competing with traditional ones (Chile, Ecuador), policy disagreements once in office (Ecuador under Lenín Moreno), and political fragmentation with ideological polarisation. Yang concludes that whether a new left cycle opens depends on restoring living conditions and building social consensus, showing administrative competence while keeping ties to social movements, and redefining the role of the state. In the author's account, the earlier cycle failed to reform the armed forces, police and judiciary and therefore lost power. The left's resilience, Yang argues, rests on democratic consolidation, wider political inclusion and persistent poverty and inequality, with poverty still above 30 per cent. Read the original if you want a China-based specialist's survey of Latin American left politics from 1999 to mid-2021, with country-by-country electoral detail.

The theoretical dimensions and value of research on the academic history of Western Marxism 西方马克思主义学术史研究的理论维度及其价值 Wang Yuchen Wang Yuchen asks how Chinese scholarship should study the academic history of Western Marxism, and argues that the study has three theoretical dimensions: the "general problematic" (理论总问题) of Western Marxist thinkers, the theoretical logic that follows from it, and its theoretical effects. In Wang's view, grasping these dimensions is an important route for advancing Chinese research on Western Marxism. It also helps in judging the school's theoretical value and in building Marxist theory in China. This short piece appeared in the Guangming Daily in December 2021. The article has three sections. The first explains the concept of the general problematic, which Wang attributes to Louis Althusser, and why it matters for research. The second sets out the problems Western Marxism raised and the logic connecting them. The third assesses the school's effects, first on the later development of Marxism outside China and then on Marxist theory in China. Wang defines the general problematic as the thinking framework and mode of theoretical production that governs a thinker's work. Uncovering it, Wang argues, lets researchers avoid treating a thinker's different phases as homogeneous. It also takes them beyond descriptive introductions to the underlying questions. Wang then reconstructs the school's shared logic. Its thinkers rejected a modern epistemological reading of Marxist philosophy and stressed practice, dialectics and critique aimed at human freedom and emancipation. From this followed theories of contemporary capitalism, visions of socialism, cultural and ideological critique (Lukács, Gramsci, the Frankfurt School, Althusser), critiques of alienation and everyday life, ecological critique and an analytical political philosophy of justice. On effects, Wang sees both positive and negative. The "cultural turn" was exploited by post-Marxists such as Laclau and Mouffe to deconstruct historical necessity and the determining role of the economic base. Eagleton, Jameson, Harvey and Negri instead moved back to political economy. Wang notes that systematic study in China began in the early 1980s and moved from rejection as non-Marxist trends to acceptance. Wang calls for such research to serve Chinese Marxist theory. In this account, Western Marxism has helped deepen understanding of the nature of Marxist philosophy and linked theory to the practice of modernization. It has also produced new sub-fields: cultural philosophy, development philosophy, ecological philosophy and political philosophy. Read the original if you want a concise, officially placed statement of how Chinese scholars justify and frame the study of Western Marxism.

Upholding seeking truth from facts and continuing to advance the great social revolution 坚持实事求是 不断推进伟大社会革命 Li Zhuoqi This short commentary, first published in Guangming Daily on 14 October 2021, takes its cue from Xi Jinping's speech at the Party's centenary celebration. Li argues that seeking truth from facts is the fundamental viewpoint of Marxism and the Party's basic way of thinking, working and leading. In Li's account, practice has repeatedly shown that adhering to it strengthens the Party and the country, while departing from it harms both. The article is organised around four requirements for continuing the great social revolution: starting from China's actual conditions, discerning the general trend of the times, seizing historical initiative, and relying on the people in arduous exploration. Each section pairs seeking truth from facts with a distinct unity, such as scientific and value dimensions, or generality and specificity. Li first stresses that one must proceed both from objective reality and from the needs of the people. Without the scientific dimension, seeking truth from facts loses its objective basis; without the value dimension, it loses popular support. Li then presents the Party's century of experience as a record of reading trends and acting on them, and argues that people are not passive in history. Seeking truth from facts, Li says, offers a methodological guide to finding truth rather than an absolute truth. The author ties the principle to the restoration of the ideological line more than forty years ago, which began a new revolution. Li concludes that today this means recognising that China remains in the primary stage of socialism and addressing the principal contradiction through deepened reform. It also means preparing for a complex international environment, adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, and upholding a people-centred stance. Party members are urged to speak, act and be honest. Read the original if you want a brief example of how the 2021 centenary discourse presented seeking truth from facts as a method for the Party's future tasks.

We must uphold the strong leadership of the Communist Party of China 必须坚持中国共产党坚强领导 Liu Jingbei Writing in Guangming Daily in October 2021, Liu Jingbei takes up Xi Jinping's statement at the Party's centenary celebration that drawing on history to open up the future requires upholding the strong leadership of the Communist Party of China. Liu presents this as the most valuable historical lesson of the Party's century of struggle and as the foundation of the Party and the state. The commentary is built around four requirements. They are to establish and defend a strong leadership core, to arm the whole Party with the latest results of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context, to improve the institutions that secure the Central Committee's centralised and unified leadership, and to hold to Party leadership at critical historical moments. Each is illustrated with episodes from Party history, from the Zunyi Meeting to the period after the 18th Party Congress (2012). Liu argues that the Party's early setbacks came from lacking a mature, stable leadership core, and that victory in the new-democratic revolution followed from Mao Zedong's leadership after Zunyi. Since 2012, Liu says, the core status of Xi Jinping has been the most fundamental reason for historic achievements. Ideological unity, citing Lenin, is the basis of organisational unity, and Liu traces a line from Mao Zedong Thought through Deng Xiaoping Theory to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Liu also lists institutional steps, including democratic centralism, reporting requirements, Party groups in government bodies and inner-Party regulations issued since 2012. Liu concludes that, amid great changes unseen in a century and at a critical stage of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, the country needs unified Central Committee leadership more than ever. Party organisations and cadres are called on to treat the Two Upholds as a political requirement and to keep in step with the Central Committee. Read the original if you want a concise, official-style statement of how Party-press commentary linked the leadership core, ideology and institutions in the centenary year.

The 1911 Revolution and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation 辛亥革命与中华民族伟大复兴 Jin Yilin Marking the 110th anniversary of the 1911 Revolution and the 100th anniversary of the Communist Party's founding, Jin Yilin asks how the revolution should be assessed and what it means for the present. Writing in Guangming Daily in October 2021, Jin argues that the revolution was both a success and a failure, and that it was an essential preparation for the Party's founding and for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The article is organised in four parts: the historical background, from the Opium War and especially the 1894–95 Sino-Japanese War; the revolution's contributions and limitations; its link to the birth of the Communist Party; and the lessons Jin draws for today. It draws on Mao Zedong's 1942 remarks on studying Party history, on Xi Jinping's speech at the 110th anniversary commemoration, and on Sun Yat-sen's own statements. Jin holds that defeat in 1894–95 turned "national salvation" into the central question for patriots, while the Qing court refused reform. In Jin's account the revolution's main achievement was ending millennia of monarchy and founding Asia's first republic, which liberated thought and spread ideas of democracy and republicanism. Its failure lay in leaving the semi-colonial, semi-feudal structure intact, with Yuan Shikai seizing the fruits of victory. Jin attributes this to the lack of a scientific theory, of mass mobilisation and of correct leadership. Drawing on Mao, Jin presents these limits as historical and not the result of individual failings. Many early Communists, including Wu Yuzhang, Lin Boqu, Dong Biwu and Zhu De, took part in the revolution before moving beyond it. Jin links the revolution to the formation of the Chinese nation as a self-conscious community ("Zhonghua minzu"), citing Liang Qichao's 1902 usage and the "five-nation republic" slogan. Jin also presents Sun's support for unification, including on Taiwan, as part of the same tradition. Jin concludes that rejuvenation requires Party leadership and socialism with Chinese characteristics. Citing Sun's formula of the capable person, place and time, Jin calls for readers to carry the effort forward, take part in the Belt and Road Initiative and work towards a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want an example of how the official Party-history narrative of 2021 places the 1911 Revolution within the story of national rejuvenation.

Chinese modernization and a new form of human civilization 中国式现代化与人类文明新形态 Tang Aijun Taking its cue from Xi Jinping's speech of 1 July 2021, which said that Chinese modernization has created "a new form of human civilization", this commentary asks what that claim means from the standpoint of historical materialism. Tang argues that Chinese modernization is a socialist modernization that differs in kind from capitalist modernization, which follows the logic of capital. It also differs from the traditional socialist model that rejected capital altogether. The article first appeared in China Social Sciences Today in August 2021. The piece has two main parts. The first presents Chinese modernization as a mode of modernization that "harnesses capital", and breaks this into three paths. The second sets out four "civilizational logics" that the author says make Chinese modernization a new form of civilization. Throughout, Tang draws on Marx's Grundrisse and Capital, on Deng Xiaoping, and on Xi Jinping's formulations. On capital, Tang holds that the primary stage of socialism still belongs to what Marx called the second social form, whose basic feature is the market economy. China therefore uses and guides global and private capital through the socialist market economy, and also regulates it. Capital's operation is bounded by an "effect boundary" (the "three favourables") and a "scope boundary" that keeps it out of politics, society and culture. State power is to do the harnessing at the macro level, under the rule of law, while keeping its own "people-oriented" character. The four civilizational logics are as follows. First, a people-centred logic, in contrast to capital's compulsion to produce and to consume. Second, a "holistic" logic of comprehensive modernization, summarized as "1+6+1": the modernization of people, six fields, and governance. Third, a "community" logic, drawn from Marx's "association of free individuals", which Tang says goes beyond the atomized individual of civil society. Fourth, a "pacifist" logic that rejects the idea that a strong country must seek hegemony. Tang concludes that this new form of civilization is still being explored and that its ideal principles will not be fully realized in practice. Even so, Tang says they are already visible in common prosperity, public ownership, collectivist values and the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a short, official-line account of how Chinese scholars use Marx's theory of capital and social forms to justify the claim of a new form of human civilization.

Historical experience of innovative development in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context 马克思主义中国化创新发展的历史经验 Xia Guojun Kong Demin Marking the Party's centenary in 2021, Xia Guojun and Kong Demin ask what the history of the Sinicization of Marxism shows. They argue that the Communist Party's founding began a continuous process in which Marxism was creatively developed, and that each stage's theoretical innovation advanced together with practical innovation. The short commentary proceeds chronologically. It covers the New Democratic Revolution, socialist revolution and construction, the period of reform and opening up, the Three Represents and the Scientific Outlook on Development, and the new era of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The authors present Chinese Communists as extending Marx's and Lenin's theory of proletarian revolution. In their account, Marx expected revolution in several advanced countries and Lenin found it possible in Russia, while the Chinese Party won in a semi-colonial, semi-feudal society through the strategy of encircling cities from the countryside and the mass line. They say that Second International opportunists, by contrast, held a vulgar productive-forces determinism that denied the dialectic of the universal and the particular. After 1949 the basic socialist system was established. Later innovations they list include a redefinition of the essence of socialism, the socialist market economy and "one country, two systems". Xia and Kong conclude that this layered record of innovation explains the national leap from suffering to standing up, becoming prosperous and growing strong. They say a historical review reveals why the Party, socialism with Chinese characteristics and Marxism succeed. Read the original if you want a compact, officially aligned periodisation of Marxist adaptation in China from 1921 to the Xi Jinping era.

Historical materialism and the transcendence of historical metaphysics 唯物史观与对历史形而上学的超越 Sun Lin Sun Lin asks how Marx's historical materialism emerged from, and surpassed, the "historical metaphysics" that Hegel built by bringing history into philosophy. The article argues that Hegel, in seeking pure concepts within historical forms, produced only a new myth of metaphysics. Marx's response, in Sun's account, was an internal transcendence that reached a new paradigm in spring 1845. Originally published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in August 2021, the piece is a short overview of that development. The article traces the intellectual history through four steps that Sun labels "questioning", "critique", "restoration" and "reconstruction". It begins with the Kant–Hegel dispute over history and reason. It then follows five stages of Marx's thought, from "self-consciousness" to the "real human being" and "species-essence", then to "sensuous human activity" and "labour". Finally, it contrasts self-consciousness-centred and substance-centred forms of objectification, and the different forms of dialectic. Sun's central claim is that Hegel's objectifying movement ended in a realm of spirit and free will, which gave Marx his point of departure. Marx's early critiques, including those influenced by Feuerbach, stayed within Hegelian concepts, since Feuerbach's "species" derives from the third moment of Hegel's self-consciousness. Only in the fourth and fifth stages is the true agent of history restored. The fourth stage is general historical materialism, found in the Theses on Feuerbach and The German Ideology. The fifth is a concrete version built on "labour", whose socialisation both produces classes and the reified world and supplies the force to overcome it. For Sun, the historical dialectic is the "living soul" of historical materialism and unites philosophy with the critique of political economy, as in Capital. Sun concludes that reconstruction has a theoretical and a practical side. Theoretically, it renews ontology, logic and methodology, with objectifying activity as the thread. Practically, it means applying historical materialism concretely in contemporary China, comparing Chinese and capitalist development concepts, and studying how socialism with Chinese characteristics goes beyond the economic base and superstructure of capitalist globalisation. Read the original if you want a compact outline of one Chinese scholar's periodisation of Marx's break with Hegel and Feuerbach.

Political degeneration, institutional collapse and national disintegration: the 30th anniversary of the CPSU's demise 政治蜕变、制度崩溃与国家分裂——苏共败亡30周年 Zhang Shuhua Writing in 2021, the year of the Chinese Communist Party's centenary and the 30th anniversary of the Soviet collapse, Zhang asks why the Communist Party of the Soviet Union (CPSU) lost power and the USSR broke apart. The article's answer is that the decisive cause lay inside the CPSU: its leadership abandoned scientific socialism, weakened and finally gave up the Party's leading role, and so brought down the state. Zhang presents the comparison as a warning for the Chinese Party in a period of great global change. The article is a historical-political analysis of the Gorbachev years (1985–1991). It first discusses Western ideological pressure and the leadership's loss of belief. It then takes in turn the absolutisation of democracy and glasnost, the takeover of media, the rise of ethnic conflict, informal organisations and radical forces. Further sections deal with constitutional changes (Article 6, multiparty politics, the presidency) and the CPSU's organisational split. A final section draws lessons for China. Zhang argues that Western 'peaceful evolution' and psychological warfare found a receptive audience among Soviet leaders such as Gorbachev and Yakovlev, who turned to social democracy. Their absolute treatment of democracy and openness, in Zhang's account, destroyed ideological consensus, dismantled the Party's authority and encouraged separatism. Zhang holds that the Party's own steps (removing its constitutional leading role, creating a presidency that bypassed the Politburo, letting republican parties act independently, and abandoning democratic centralism) turned it from a leading party into a parliamentary party and then dissolved it. Citing figures on economic decline and over 170 ethnic conflicts, Zhang concludes that without correct Party leadership there would have been no Soviet Union. Among the many explanations of the collapse, Zhang follows Mao Zedong in seeking the principal contradiction, which the article locates in the Party itself. Zhang concludes that the Party's leadership is the key to the success of socialist construction and reform. Zhang calls on the Chinese Communist Party to hold firmly to the Four Cardinal Principles, strengthen the Four-sphere Confidence and the Two Upholds, keep the leading position of Marxism in ideology, and resist Western value diplomacy. The article also stresses reliance on the people and the expansion of whole-process people's democracy. Read the original if you want a representative Chinese official-academic account of the Soviet collapse and the lessons the Chinese Party draws from it, with extensive citation of Soviet and Russian sources.

The logical levels of Marx's category of "world history" 马克思世界历史范畴的逻辑层次 Zhou Kanglin Zhou Kanglin takes up a problem of textual interpretation: the category of "world history" carries several meanings in the writings of Marx and Engels, and these need to be sorted out. The article, a short newspaper piece, argues that the meanings sit at distinct logical levels. Only by separating them and tracing their links can readers grasp the theoretical essence and practical significance of Marx's "world history" as a form of thought. Zhou begins from the present "integrated world", which the author sees as confirming Marx's prediction that history becomes world history. The piece identifies three usages. The first is "world-historical significance" as opposed to merely local, regional or national significance. The second is "world history" as universal history, meaning the whole of human history. The third, which Zhou treats as the central one, is "world history" as the process by which closed national histories give way to universal intercourse. Zhou draws on the English Condition, The German Ideology and the 1844 Manuscripts, among other texts. On the first level, Zhou notes Engels's claim that the misery of the English working class has world-historical significance, because it stems from the modern large-scale industry through which the bourgeoisie rules the world. Zhou contrasts this with the German philosophers' inflated claims for the dissolution of the Hegelian system, which Marx and Engels judged to be of merely local significance. On the second level, Zhou reads Marx's statement that world history is the process of humanity's birth through labour as a break with Feuerbach's "sensuous intuition". In Zhou's account, labour itself has a history: handicraft produced a "discrete" world history, machine industry an "alienated" one, and communist "self-directed activity" would produce a truly free and universal one. On the third level, large-scale industry "first created world history", so that "history becoming world history" and "intercourse becoming world intercourse" are in effect synonyms. Zhou adds that Marx and Engels needed national histories and English social-history material to raise this idea to the level of historical science. Zhou concludes that Marx's world-history thought concerns the historical fact and process by which capital's mode of production binds scattered peoples into one organic whole under the order of the capitalist world market. The author presents the bourgeoisie as the "unconscious tool of history" in a revolution that remains unfinished, and only the modern proletariat can rebuild world intercourse. Zhou also cautions that the meanings do not develop in a straight line and are often mixed together in the same works, so they must be read closely in context. Read the original if you want a compact guide to the different senses of "world history" in Marx and Engels, as understood in Chinese scholarship in 2022.

On the agents of Marxism's development and their types 关于马克思主义发展主体及其类型 Liang Shufa Zhao Danlei Who actually develops Marxism? Liang Shufa and Zhao Danlei take up this question in an article published in Teaching and Research (2021, no. 12). They define the agents (subjects) of Marxism's development as Marxists who take part in the Marxist cause and the "Marxist movement" and who advance Marxism in theoretical form. They argue that these agents share common features but fall into types that differ in their mode of existence and way of acting, not in the size of their contribution. The article restricts "development of Marxism" to the development of Marxist theory. It first explains why classification matters, then separates individual from collective agents. It then distinguishes three senses of development (general, theoretical, innovative) and surveys collective agents (the masses, the proletariat, the proletarian party). It ends with three types of individual theorist. The authors hold that individual agents exist only within collective ones, and that the collective agent is the proletariat, its Marxist party and the community of Marxist theorists. They draw on Marx, Lukács and Rosa Luxemburg to treat the proletariat as the "total subject", while stressing that this status is conditional. Using the German Social Democratic Party and the Soviet Communist Party, they argue that a proletarian party is not naturally Marxist. Only a party that upholds and develops Marxism acts as the "core agent". At the individual level they distinguish professional Marxist theorists, political (practical) theorists and theoretical politicians. The authors judge that political-practical theorists, such as Marx, Engels, Lenin, Mao Zedong and Xi Jinping, are best placed to produce innovation because they combine practical experience with theoretical training. The authors conclude that the "ideal" agent is the innovative agent, and that the real issue is how to find and train more innovative Marxist theorists. They criticise the impression that Marxism's history is only a history of leaders' thought. Leaders' contributions should not be separated from the leadership collective, or from the masses and professional theorists whose work leaders distil. They also criticise professional theorists who detach themselves from practice. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic account of how Marxist theoretical innovation is attributed to individuals, parties and classes.

Gathering cultural strength for the realisation of common prosperity 为实现共同富裕凝聚文化力量 Niu Jiaru Zhang Youjia This short commentary, first published in Economic Daily on 30 September 2021, asks how culture can contribute to common prosperity. Niu and Zhang argue that common prosperity covers both material and spiritual life, and that culture is an important fulcrum for pursuing it within high-quality development. The authors set out five mission tasks: raising the banner, rallying the people's hearts, nurturing new people, reviving culture and presenting the national image. They then work through five areas of practice: ideology, core socialist values, literature and art, public cultural services, and the cultural industry. The authors hold that Marxism is the banner and soul of socialist ideology, so that Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era must guide practice. They also call for strengthening the core socialist values through education, practice and institutional safeguards, and for civic-morality and civilisation-building campaigns. For the arts and culture, they call for a people-centred orientation and works that reflect the people's aspirations. On the cultural industry, they argue that the key measure of quality is whether it supplies products that both meet cultural needs and strengthen the people's spiritual strength, so social benefits come before economic ones. Niu and Zhang conclude that satisfying cultural needs and strengthening spiritual strength must go together. They propose building a cultural atmosphere for common prosperity as part of becoming a strong socialist cultural country, with better public cultural services, digital cultural industries and integrated culture and tourism. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Party-media writing in 2021 linked culture, ideology and common prosperity.

The epochal significance of the new road to the exam 新的赶考之路的时代意蕴 Shang Zhixiao Published in Economic Daily in October 2021, this commentary takes up Xi Jinping's remark at the Party's centenary celebration that the Communist Party has set out on a "new road to the exam" towards the second centenary goal. Shang explains that "sitting the exam" goes back to Mao Zedong's 1949 phrase for the move to Beijing. The author argues that the new exam has new content and new goals, and that studying it helps the Party meet fresh tests. The article is organised as six statements about what the new road rests on: the achievements of the Party's first hundred years, the building of a moderately prosperous society as its starting point, the goal of a modern socialist great power, the "nine musts", the Party's founding spirit, and reliance on the whole people. Shang's central claim is that the new exam continues an unbroken history of passing tests, from the new-democratic revolution through socialist construction and reform and opening up to the new era. The author describes the elimination of absolute poverty as the starting point. The 19th Party Congress (2017) split the thirty years to mid-century into two stages, with modernization basically achieved by 2035. The "nine musts", drawn from Xi's summary of Party history, are presented as the basic guide. Shang also stresses the founding spirit and the Party's self-reform alongside social revolution, and the Party's ties to the people. Shang concludes that the road is hopeful but demanding. The author calls for confidence together with vigilance and readiness for a great struggle with many new historical features. Under Party leadership and with national unity, the author holds, the new exam can be passed with an excellent answer. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned reading of the "new exam" metaphor in the 2021 centenary discourse.

The correct path to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation 实现中华民族伟大复兴的正确道路 Chen Shuguang Published in Economic Daily on 27 September 2021, this commentary follows Xi Jinping's speech at the celebration of the Party's centenary, which said that learning from history and creating the future requires upholding and developing socialism with Chinese characteristics. Chen argues that this path is the correct road to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. In Chen's account, it is an inevitable choice of modern Chinese history and the fundamental direction of China's progress, and the Party and people should follow it with confidence. The article is organised in four sections. The first presents following one's own path as the historical conclusion of the Party's hundred years of struggle. The second asserts that socialism with Chinese characteristics is socialism and not some other "ism". The third turns to results since reform and opening up. The fourth looks ahead to the path's future. Chen first traces the line from Mao Zedong's integration of Marxism-Leninism with Chinese revolutionary practice, through the founding of the socialist system, to Deng Xiaoping's 1982 call to build socialism with Chinese characteristics, and on to the period after the 18th Party Congress (2012). The article then argues that the path keeps the basic principles of scientific socialism while carrying practical, national and contemporary characteristics. It holds that there is no universal development model and that the primary stage of socialism leaves many problems unresolved, so theory, practice and institutions must keep innovating. Chen presents China's industrialisation, its poverty reduction (over 70% of the world's total, by the article's figure) and its roughly 30% contribution to world growth as proof of success. These achievements, Chen contends, break the myths that "there is no alternative to capitalism" and that "modernization equals Westernization", and they open new options for developing countries. Chen concludes that China must avoid both the "closed and rigid old path" and the "wrong path of changing banners", citing the lessons of the planned economy and of the Soviet and East European collapse. In this reading, the Party's theme in the new era remains upholding and developing socialism with Chinese characteristics, and this is also what will secure the goals for 2035 and the middle of the century. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the official narrative links Party history, the Four-sphere Confidence and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation around the 2021 centenary.

The idea of technological alienation in Engels's Dialectics of Nature 《自然辩证法》中的技术异化思想 Wang Guangming Dialectics of Nature discusses many natural-science theories yet never uses the word "technology", and some readers conclude that Engels had no interest in technology or philosophy of technology. Wang Guangming calls this a misunderstanding. In this short newspaper commentary, Wang argues that Engels held rich ideas on technology, and that their foresight shows most clearly in his treatment of technological alienation. Wang first defines technological alienation as the process by which objects created through technical practice become forces opposed and alien to human beings. The piece then notes that, unlike Marx, Engels concentrates on the natural dimension of alienation. It goes on to Engels's account of capitalist agriculture and its effects, the causes of alienation, and a brief closing note on present-day China. Wang reads Engels as recognising technology's contribution to productivity while warning that capitalist technical practice upsets the balance between humans and nature. Engels's example is the soil damage and poisoning caused by fertilisers and pesticides, and his warning is that nature "takes revenge" for each human victory. Wang identifies a subjective cause of alienation in the limits of human knowledge, which cannot foresee all consequences, and two objective causes. One is technology's natural attributes, since its use cannot escape natural law and some losses are unavoidable. The other is the contradictions of the capitalist system, where competition forces constant machine improvement and produces overproduction, disorderly competition and poverty. Wang adds that Engels stayed optimistic that such effects could be regulated. Wang concludes that Engels set out technology's place from the standpoint of historical materialism and analysed the paradoxes of technological development under capitalism. Wang urges that technological innovation, now an important driver of China's development, be guided accordingly, with attention to technology's place in production and to the relation between technical and social progress, in support of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a concise introduction to the environmental and technological themes that Wang finds in Engels.

The good life in the perspective of historical materialism 唯物史观视域中的美好生活 Gao Xue Wang Miao Gao Xue and Wang Miao take up the question of how to understand and realise the "good life" (meihao shenghuo) from the standpoint of historical materialism. They start from the 19th Party Congress (2017) judgement that the principal contradiction in Chinese society is now between the people's ever-growing needs for a better life and unbalanced and inadequate development. The authors argue that Marx and Engels built historical materialism by criticising capitalist alienation and proposing communism as the good life, and that without historical materialism the ideal becomes utopian. This short commentary, first published in China Social Sciences Today in 2021, has two parts. The first traces a shift from ancient to modern conceptions of the good life, running from Socrates, Plato and Aristotle through Machiavelli, Hobbes, Locke and Kant, with reference to Leo Strauss. The second follows Marx's own path, from the Rheinische Zeitung and the critique of Hegel's philosophy of right to the 1844 Manuscripts, The German Ideology and the critique of political economy. In the authors' account, classical political philosophy tied the good life to a moral end and the best regime, whereas modern thought lowered its aim to security, comfort and property. Yet the universal prosperity, freedom and equality promised by modernity were not achieved. Marx and Engels, the authors say, sought to rescue modernity. They located its objective basis in the productive forces created by large-scale industry, and they identified alienation or reification as the product of capital's abstract rule. Capital is therefore both a dominating force and a driver of "civilisation". The authors conclude that because capital logic is the ontological basis of modernity, rebuilding modernity requires appropriating and mastering that logic. They argue this depends on a revolutionary class restructuring social ownership so that capitalist productive forces become social forces. This, they say, is the real road to the good life. Read the original if you want a compact statement of how Chinese scholars link the "good life" of the Party's new principal contradiction to Marx's critique of capital and alienation.

The enrichment and development of the materialist conception of history in the new era 唯物史观在新时代的丰富和发展 Cheng Shiping Jiao Guocheng Cheng Shiping and Jiao Guocheng, in a newspaper commentary first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in August 2021, argue that since the 18th Party Congress (2012) the Party Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core has enriched and developed the materialist conception of history through the practice of socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era. The piece takes four policy ideas and links each to a component of historical materialism. These are the people-centred approach, comprehensively deepening reform, the fighting spirit, and innovation as the primary driving force of development. The authors argue that the people-centred approach deepens the doctrine that the masses are the subject of history. They find three layers in it: relying on the people to achieve the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, treating the people's aspiration for a better life as the Party's goal, and pursuing the free and all-round development of the human being. They present a community with a shared future for mankind as a creative development of the idea of world history. Deepening reform is read as a new development of the principle that relations of production must fit the productive forces, and the superstructure the economic base. Promoting the fighting spirit is said to put into practice the dialectic of social being and social consciousness, by combining respect for objective laws with subjective initiative. The authors say that innovation as the primary driving force extends the theory of historical motive forces. They identify three points: talent as the foundation, self-reliant innovation capacity, and removing institutional obstacles in science and technology. The authors conclude that these developments are a product of the Party's theoretical innovation. They hold that these developments are the guiding thought that must be upheld in the new stage of development and the new journey of building a modern socialist country. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese commentary maps current Party slogans onto the categories of historical materialism.

Kai Nielsen's reconstruction of Marx's moralism: the contextualist perspective and the missing dialectical dimension 尼尔森对马克思道德主义的重构：语境主义的视角与辩证之维的缺失 Shu Guifeng Zheng Dongdong Kai Nielsen is a leading Anglophone Marxist philosopher who rejects the reading of Marx's moral views as moral relativism. This article asks whether his defence of Marx's moralism, built on "contextualism", is theoretically sound. Shu and Zheng argue that, although the defence is well intended, it rests on an understanding rather than a dialectical grasp of historical materialism. In their view dialectics is absent from Nielsen's reconstruction. They note that Chinese scholarship has so far tended to endorse and borrow from Nielsen more than to scrutinise him. The article has three parts. The first sets out Nielsen's contextualism and his "reduction" of historical materialism to it, in answer to critics who see a clash between relative moral ideas and absolute moral standards in Marx. The second reconstructs the philosophical lineage from Kant through Hegel to Marx, to show what unity of fact and value means in historical materialism. The third tests Nielsen's reduction against that structure. According to the authors, Nielsen makes three moves. He recasts modes of production as the concrete situation of a given society, material needs as situational needs, and eternal moral principles as context-bound "moral axioms" or common sense, which he holds are compatible with an objectivist ethics. The authors reply that the relativists' fact–value dualism is Kantian, and that Hegel's dialectic overcame it by uniting potential and actual. Marx, they say, replaced Hegel's absolute Idea with practice, so that the mode of production and ideology stand to each other as content and appearance. Historical materialism therefore contains no dualism for contextualism to repair. Nielsen, they argue, flattens society into a system of empirical appearances, suspends practice as the determining ground, and removes the progressive sequence of historical stages. This, they say, creates the very contradiction he claims to resolve. The authors conclude that Nielsen's contextualism is a product of understanding-based thinking, not of rational dialectical thinking. In their account it lowers historical materialism to the level of understanding and cannot convey its dialectical content. They hold that Nielsen shares the relativists' prejudice against dialectics, which he treats as a subjective conceptual framework. They call for a more critical reassessment of his theory in Chinese scholarship.
