Read the original if you study Anglophone analytical Marxism and the ethics of Marx, or want a Chinese Hegelian-Marxist critique of Nielsen's contextualism.

British Marxist debates on the contemporary working class and their theoretical implications 英国马克思主义关于当代工人阶级的争论及其理论反思 Zhang Liang Zhang Liang revisits a debate among British Marxists in the late 1970s and 1980s about what had happened to the working class and its movement. The article asks what this largely forgotten argument, which began as Western working-class movements entered a long decline, can still teach Chinese Marxist theory. Zhang's answer is that the exchange, though it ended without resolution, yields four lessons on Party leadership, ideological struggle, class alliances and the study of Western class theory. The article proceeds through four camps. It begins with Eric Hobsbawm's 1978 Marx Memorial Lecture, which warned that the labour movement was in crisis. It then examines Ernesto Laclau and Chantal Mouffe, the founders of "post-Marxism", and Stuart Hall's call to "learn from Thatcherism". Finally it turns to Ralph Miliband and Ellen Meiksins Wood, who attacked the first three as a "new revisionism" and a "new 'true' socialism". A closing section draws the lessons. Zhang reads Hobsbawm as tracing the decline to changes in British capitalism: a shrinking manual workforce, more women and migrant workers, sectional divisions and a revival of narrow trade unionism. Laclau and Mouffe, in Zhang's account, turn this into a crisis of Marxist class theory itself. They reject its "essentialism" and hold that class consciousness arises from contingent articulation, so that new social movements may supply new revolutionary subjects. Hall shares the diagnosis but keeps a materialist base. He treats articulation as a process rooted in the interaction of economic base and superstructure, sees ideological hegemony as the central terrain of modern class struggle, and doubts that new movements can by themselves produce a revolutionary subject. Miliband and Wood insist that class struggle remains central and that organised workers cannot be replaced, and Miliband describes a "class struggle from above". Zhang concludes that the dispute was forgotten after the Soviet collapse of 1991, and draws four lessons. First, the working class needs leadership by a Marxist-Leninist party. Second, the Party must hold leadership of the ideological sphere, as Xi Jinping stresses. Third, neither Laclau and Mouffe's abandonment of the working class nor Miliband and Wood's rigid insistence on its leadership is acceptable. Zhang instead points to the united front principle of unity of consistency and diversity. Fourth, Chinese scholars should resume tracking Western class issues and class theory. Read the original if you want a detailed account of how Hobsbawm, Laclau and Mouffe, Hall, Miliband and Wood disagreed about the working class, and how a Chinese Marxist scholar draws political lessons from it.

Research on British Marxist class theory 英国马克思主义阶级理论研究 Fang Jue This short piece, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in 2020, asks how British Marxist class theory has developed since the 1950s. The author argues that it has passed through three research paradigms: a historical one, a political-science one, and a return to, and rebuilding of, a political-economy one. Fang presents these shifts as showing British Marxists' distinctive understanding of historical materialism. The article first places British Marxism within the two dimensions of Western Marxism, critical theory of capitalism and theories of revolution, while noting its differences from continental traditions. It then takes each paradigm in turn. It treats the historians E. P. Thompson and Eric Hobsbawm, then Ralph Miliband and the Miliband–Poulantzas debate, and finally Alex Callinicos. Fang notes that the 2008 financial crisis revived a research field that had gone quiet. On the historical paradigm, Fang reports that Thompson and Hobsbawm treated class as a relation and a historical process, in which experience, customs and national cultural traditions shape class consciousness alongside the capitalist mode of production. The political paradigm, in Fang's account, used class analysis to explain advanced capitalism. It held that the organised working class remains the subject of revolution, rejecting the 'farewell to the working class' thesis. Miliband described the state as an instrument of the ruling class that nonetheless has relative autonomy. After the neoliberal turn and talk of the 'end of class', Fang says that twenty-first-century British Marxists, notably Callinicos in Deciphering Capital, returned to the labour theory of value and the exploitation of surplus value. Fang concludes that the return to political economy is the main trend in twenty-first-century class theory, because capital's drive to valorise itself is unchanged and class struggle remains a valid way to understand modern capitalism. British Marxists, in this reading, treat historical materialism not as an abstract formula but as grounded in modern socialist movements. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese-language overview of how British Marxist class theory is periodised.

Althusser's interpretation of materialist dialectics and its implications 阿尔都塞对唯物辩证法的阐释及其意蕴 Song Kaixuan This short commentary asks what Louis Althusser meant by Marx's "inversion" of Hegel's dialectic and what his reading contributes to the study of Marxist philosophy. Song argues that Althusser's scientistic, structuralist interpretation of materialist dialectics corrected the over-Hegelianised "philosophy of practice" that came to dominate Western "Marxology", but that it goes wrong in treating science as the only proper way of grasping the world. The article proceeds in three steps. It first revisits the "inversion" formula from the Afterword to the second edition of Capital and Engels's later distinction between system and method. It then identifies the relation between subjective activity and objective structure as what Althusser took to be the dialectic's basic structure. Finally it examines Althusser's treatment of materialist dialectics as a scientific form, drawing on The German Ideology and the 1857 Introduction to the Critique of Political Economy. Song reports Althusser's view that Hegel's "shell" cannot be peeled from the "kernel", so that the inversion must be a fundamental reworking of the dialectic's structure rather than a change of position. Althusser's terms "overdetermination" and "structural causality" mark Marx's dialectic as a complex, unevenly developed structured whole, as against Hegel's "expressive causality", in which all differences return to the Absolute Idea. Song adds that this framing, against the background of structuralism's displacement of the subject, recasts Marx's relation to Hegel as one between agency and structural determinism, which Song links to two logics in Marx's own work. Song credits Althusser with an important advance in research on Marxist dialectics. The shortcoming, in Song's account, is forgetting that Marx's critique of political economy aimed at changing the real world. Song concludes that only a proper linking of the determinist and the agency-centred logics found in Marx's texts gives a complete and reasonable account of Marxist theory. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese-language assessment of Althusser's dialectics and its place in debates over structure and subject.

Paths of the Frankfurt School's critique of "civilisation" 法兰克福学派“文明”批判路径 Li Huijuan This short commentary, first published in the China Social Sciences Today in February 2021, asks how the Frankfurt School criticised "civilisation" and why that critique fell short. Li Huijuan argues that civilisation critique runs through the School's "constellation" of critical modes along three paths: dialectics, psychoanalysis and intersubjectivity. The author holds that studying these paths and their gaps has academic value for foreign Marxism studies in China. The article takes each path in turn and ties it to a thinker or pair of thinkers. Horkheimer and Adorno represent the dialectical path through Dialectic of Enlightenment. Marcuse represents the psychoanalytic path through Eros and Civilization. Habermas represents the intersubjective path, which Li presents as a critique from inside European civilisation and its modernity. Li reads Horkheimer and Adorno as tracing enlightenment's reversal into myth and domination, with commodity fetishism as the secularised myth and instrumental reason ending in Auschwitz. In Marcuse's account, as Li presents it, the problem is not "basic repression" but "surplus repression" under the performance principle, so that progress and unfreedom advance together. Marcuse therefore turns to psychological factors in search of a non-repressive civilisation. Habermas, by contrast, tries to rebuild the enlightenment that Horkheimer and Adorno saw as collapsed. He grounds emancipation in dialogue, communication and an "ideal speech situation" that could bridge the transcendental subject's freedom and the empirical subject's unfreedom. Li concludes that the three paths expose the costs of modern civilisation and look for ways to reverse it. Yet in Li's assessment the critique stays within absolute negation and opposition, and its constructive proposals are too idealistic and detached from reality. Li calls for a return to Marx's critique of political economy and sees the School's gradual drift away from it as the root cause of these gaps. Read the original if you want a compact Chinese-language overview of how a Chinese scholar classifies and assesses the Frankfurt School's civilisation critique.

A new departure after a century: the South African Communist Party's fresh explorations of socialism 百年再启程：南非共产党对社会主义的新探索 Li Yujie Marking the centenary of the South African Communist Party (SACP), founded in July 1921, Li Yujie asks how Africa's oldest and most influential Marxist-Leninist party is renewing its search for socialism under new internal and external pressures. The article argues that the SACP, having never abandoned its communist goal, is again setting out on a South African path to socialism by adapting Marxism-Leninism to national conditions, even though its road is far from smooth. The article has three parts. It first surveys the party's hundred-year course, from its early focus on white workers, through its 'Africanisation' in 1924, illegality after 1950, armed struggle and exile from 1961 and 1963, to legalisation in 1990 and entry into the 1994 'Tripartite Alliance' with the African National Congress (ANC) and the trade-union federation COSATU. It then sets out four challenges, and finally the party's responses. Li draws lessons from the century: theoretical creativity, notably the thesis of 'colonialism of a special type'; combining cooperation and struggle within the left alliance; and proletarian internationalism, including close ties with the Communist Party of China. The four challenges are the alliance's dysfunction, the fragmentation of the working class (informal work, falling union density, 32.6 per cent unemployment in early 2021), factional strife and corruption inside the ANC, and doubts about the SACP's own independence and class character, including charges of 'tailism'. The party's responses, in Li's account, are a critique of capitalism as a fourfold crisis, cautious handling of the question of standing independently in elections while pushing to reconfigure the alliance, influence on government through ministerial posts, and party-building. Li concludes that the party's strength lies in interpreting Marxism-Leninism through South African conditions, and that its future depends on rooting itself in workplaces and communities and building a mass vanguard party amid capitalist encirclement. The article notes limits: the SACP's influence has not fundamentally altered the government's neoliberal policies. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly account of the SACP's history, its dilemmas within the Tripartite Alliance and its 2021 action programme, with detailed figures.

A critique of nature-centred ecological views and the construction of a new ecological philosophy Slavoj Žižek's psychoanalytic critique of naturecentrism 自然中心主义生态观的批判与新生态哲学的建构 Shi Fengge Why has the ecological crisis not eased despite decades of Western reflection on it? Shi Fengge takes up this question through the work of the Slovenian thinker Slavoj Žižek. The article argues that nature-centred ecology (environmental ethics, wilderness philosophy, deep ecology) rests on a utopian ontological premise, a perfectly balanced primordial nature. In Shi's account, Žižek's psychoanalytic critique exposes this premise and points to a new ecological philosophy. The article has four parts. It first reconstructs the naturecentric position and its three currents: Schweitzer, Leopold and Rolston's ecological ethics, wilderness philosophy, and Arne Naess's deep ecology. It then sets out Žižek's claim that "nature does not exist", argued from nature's inherent properties and from "second nature". The third part presents his new ecological philosophy, and the conclusion compares it with Marx and Engels. Shi argues that the idea of an intact original nature is a retroactive construction of thought. People need to imagine nature as an ordered whole in order to live in it. Following Žižek, Shi says that evolution is full of catastrophe and contingency, and that humans are "nature's wound". Industry and biogenetic technology have already made nature a humanized second nature. The proposed alternative has two linked parts. The first is a future-anterior temporal outlook, which treats ecological catastrophe as inevitable and so retroactively opens up possibilities for action. The second is collective action, built on strict egalitarian justice, discipline, voluntarism and trust in the people. Žižek takes this to require harsh enforcement, even informers. Shi concludes that the new philosophy shifts ecological thinking from a utopian beyond to workable strategy centred on human value. Shi sees an inner affinity with Marx's view of nature as humanized and with Engels's warning that nature takes revenge on human conquest. Collective action is also linked to Marx's concept of practice. Shi admits the theory is imperfect but holds that it offers a new path for global ecological problems. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist reading of Žižek's ecology and its comparison with Marx and Engels.

Commemoration and reflection by the foreign left on the 200th anniversary of Engels's birth 国外左翼对恩格斯诞辰200周年的纪念与省思 Yuan Qun Wang Enming Yuan Qun and Wang Enming survey how left-wing parties, organisations and scholars outside China marked the 200th anniversary of Friedrich Engels's birth in 2020, and what they said about him. The authors argue that these commemorations reaffirmed Engels's place as co-founder of Marxism and scientific socialism. In their account, the foreign left also defended the contemporary relevance of his thought against long-standing claims that he diverged from Marx. They present the events as part of a turn from the low tide of world socialism towards revival. The article opens with an inventory of the commemorations: conferences in Portugal, Laos, Vietnam, Germany and Japan; joint statements by Marxist-Leninist-Maoist parties; commemorative essays by figures such as Gennady Zyuganov, Brinda Karat and Marcello Musto; and events in Engels's home city of Wuppertal. It then turns to the foreign left's assessments of Engels's historical standing and of the global significance of his work in philosophy, political economy, scientific socialism and military science. Later sections cover the present-day value ascribed to his ideas and the strategies the commemorations proposed. The authors report that foreign commentators describe Engels as an irreplaceable "second violin" who was an original thinker in his own right, not merely Marx's assistant. These commentators credit him with preserving and publishing Marx's legacy and with leading the workers' movement. Against what the authors call the "opposition" theses, which pit Engels against Marx or claim the late Engels abandoned revolution, the cited voices defend the unity of the two men's thought. They also cite figures on billionaire wealth during the Covid-19 pandemic, and other crisis indicators, as evidence that Engels's analysis of capitalism still holds. Karat's reading of The Origin of the Family, Private Property and the State is offered as proof of its continuing value for women's liberation. The authors conclude that the 2020 commemoration continued and deepened the 2018 Marx bicentenary. They report the foreign left's practical proposals: building revolutionary parties, studying and publishing Marxist theory (including a planned joint new edition of Marx and Engels's selected works), and forming broad anti-war united fronts. They add that the left in the imperialist heartlands combined revolutionary optimism with a sober stance, and they call the commemoration a vivid exercise in Marxist-Leninist education. Read the original if you want a detailed catalogue of the parties, scholars and publications that took part in the 2020 Engels commemorations, and of what each said.

The Chinese path in the eyes of foreign left-wing scholars 国外左翼学者眼中的中国道路 Liu Mingming Liu Qi This commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in December 2020, surveys how foreign left-wing scholars assess the Chinese path. The authors note that criticism of China abounds abroad, but argue that a growing number of left-wing scholars are shedding earlier ideological constraints. In their account, these scholars judge the achievements of socialism with Chinese characteristics more objectively, recognise the contemporary value of the Chinese path and place hope in it. The piece is organised in four parts: the reasons foreign scholars give for the path's success; debates over its nature; its significance and value for the world; and the claim that it represents hope for socialism. It draws on Russian specialists, the German China expert Sebastian Heilmann, the Egyptian Marxist Samir Amin, the British writer Martin Jacques, and Schweickart, as well as several unnamed scholars. On success, the authors report foreign views that Communist Party leadership is the key, that gradual reform with pilot-then-extend experimentation beats "shock therapy", and that China's peaceful development avoids the pattern of rising powers becoming hegemons and declining. On the path's nature, they cite Amin's point that land remains state property, and Schweickart's argument that China is not capitalist because wage labour is not dominant and state firms control core sectors. On world significance, they cite Jacques's prediction of an alternative to the Western model and claims that China drives global growth and answered Fukuyama's "end of history" thesis, including in the response to Covid-19. The authors conclude that, for these scholars, China offers hope: public ownership of key sectors and state intervention are seen as checks on capitalist excess, and Vietnam and Laos are said to have followed the model. They close by asserting that the Chinese path is a vivid contemporary expression of scientific socialism and a new direction for socialism. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned digest of foreign leftist opinions of China as presented in the Chinese press, and a list of the foreign authors that Chinese commentators cite.”

Lenin's late thought on the specificity of Soviet Russia's path of social development 列宁晚年关于苏俄社会发展途径特殊性的思想 Yu Min How did Lenin, in his last years, justify and define a distinctive route to socialism for a backward Soviet Russia? Yu Min reads works from after the Tenth Congress of the Russian Communist Party (Bolsheviks) in 1921, notably 'On the Food Tax', 'On the Significance of Gold' and 'On Our Revolution'. The article argues that Lenin developed a coherent theory of a 'special path' that was compatible with Marx's general laws of history and aimed throughout at building a socialist society. The article has four parts. It first traces the roots of the special path in the peculiarity of the October Revolution. It then sets out what the specificity means, examines the goal of the path, and ends with the thought's historical position and its relevance to China. Yu draws on Lenin's texts, on Marx's and Engels's remarks about Russia and Germany, and on speeches by Xi Jinping and Deng Xiaoping. Yu argues that the revolution was special because it was tied to the First World War, which produced a union of peasant war and workers' movement, and because it applied Marxism's 'revolutionary dialectic' instead of copying the German model. From this follow two features of the path. The proletariat seizes power first, while conditions are insufficient, and then uses worker-peasant power to develop the productive forces. It also adopts special measures, such as the food tax, free trade, leasing enterprises to foreign and domestic capitalists, and state capitalism, as 'intermediate links' between small-scale production and socialism. In Yu's reading, Lenin treated these measures as steps toward socialism, not as a retreat from it. He defended them as strengthening the worker-peasant alliance and the dictatorship of the proletariat, and he expected state capitalism to become socialism in the near future. Yu concludes that Lenin was the first to set out systematically how a relatively backward country could build socialism, going beyond Marx's cautious comments and Engels's 'four steps' scenario. The author holds that this thought fits the Chinese Communist Party's seizure of power and its long-term work of creating conditions for socialism. Yu also holds that reform and opening up shares the spirit of the New Economic Policy but goes much further, and that socialism with Chinese characteristics develops Lenin's ideas. Read the original if you want a detailed Chinese reading of Lenin's late texts and of how they are linked to the Party's own account of its path.

Guiding the new "exam road" with the great founding spirit of the Party 以伟大建党精神引领新的赶考之路 Gong Jianfei Fu Gaosheng Published in Guangming Daily on 28 September 2021, this commentary takes up the "great founding spirit of the Party", which Xi Jinping first set out at the ceremony marking the Party's 100th anniversary (2021). Gong and Fu argue that this spirit must be inherited and promoted as the Party and the people set out on a "new road to the exam" towards the second centenary goal, so that the Party can again hand in an excellent answer sheet. The piece takes the four components of the spirit in Xi's formulation in turn: upholding truth and ideals; staying true to the founding mission; being ready to sacrifice and fight bravely; and being loyal to the Party and never failing the people. Each is presented as a distinct "strength" (intellectual, political, spiritual and moral) and paired with a task for the new journey. The authors draw on Party history, from the Soviet areas and the Jinggangshan period to poverty alleviation, and on quotations from Xi. The core argument is that the Party's past achievements flowed from these four strengths and that the same strengths are needed now. On the intellectual side, the authors hold that Marxism, adapted to Chinese conditions and traditional culture, underpinned the leap from "standing up" to "becoming rich" to "becoming strong". They say it must continue to guide Chinese modernization under the new development philosophy. On the political side, they stress the people-centred approach, citing the image of the times as examiner and the people as marker. They cite more than 3.7 million named revolutionary martyrs between 1921 and 1949 and over 1,800 deaths in the poverty campaign as evidence of the spirit of sacrifice. The authors conclude that the second centenary goal is a harder test. It requires Party members and officials to keep up vigilance against risks and long-term struggle, and to guard against factors that weaken the Party's vanguard character or alienate it from the masses. They call for cultivating loyalty to the Party, public virtue in serving the people, and personal integrity. They argue that the Party's nature and the people's interests are identical, so loyalty to the Party means responsibility to the people. Read the original if you want a compact example of how official commentary in 2021 turned the founding spirit into practical tasks for Party cadres.

The historical perspective and contemporary significance of the "three profound changes" “三个深刻改变”的历史观照与现实意蕴 Deng Lingyue This commentary, first published in Guangming Daily on 29 September 2021, takes up a passage from Xi Jinping's speech at the ceremony marking the Party's centenary. In it Xi says the founding of the Communist Party of China was an earth-shaking event that profoundly changed the direction of the Chinese nation, the fate of the Chinese people, and the trends and patterns of world development. Deng argues that these "three profound changes" express the Party's consistent views of history, of the people and of its own role, and give the idea of an "earth-shaking event" its historical and present meaning. The article has three numbered sections, one for each change. The first looks at the Party's origins after the Opium War, the failure of earlier salvation schemes and the arrival of Marxism-Leninism. The second goes through the four historical periods of the Party's leadership, from the New Democratic Revolution to the new era. The third turns to the international effects of the Party's rule, from the founding of the People's Republic to the Belt and Road Initiative and the Party's role in the Covid-19 pandemic. Deng's central claim is that the Party has distinctive sources of strength that earlier Chinese political forces lacked. These are the guidance of scientific Marxist theory, the support of the people, and firm goals backed by a disciplined vanguard organisation. Deng says the Party's class character depends on whose fundamental interests it represents, not on the social origins of its members. In each period the Party is said to have laid the political, institutional and material conditions for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, taking the people from "standing up" to "becoming prosperous" to "becoming strong". Deng adds that socialism with Chinese characteristics has broken the assumption that modernization means Westernization, and so offers other countries a different path and "Chinese wisdom" and "Chinese solutions". Deng concludes that the Party, which holds to Marxist truth and to communist ideals, has created achievements worthy of history and of the people. On the eve of the second centenary goal, Deng says, history has proved and will go on proving the "three profound changes". The piece restates the official reading of the Party's centenary and links the Party's mission to a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a compact example of how the centenary speech's historical judgements were presented to a general readership in 2021.

Common prosperity: an important feature of Chinese modernization 共同富裕：中国式现代化的重要特征 Lu Mingchuan This commentary, first published in Guangming Daily on 27 September 2021, takes up Xi Jinping's statement at the tenth meeting of the Central Financial and Economic Affairs Commission (17 August 2021) that common prosperity is an essential requirement of socialism and an important feature of Chinese modernization. Lu Mingchuan argues that, over the Party's first hundred years, common prosperity and socialist modernization have been united in the practice of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, opening a new path that shows the advantages of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The piece is organised in five numbered sections. Each presents common prosperity as embodying a different aspect of Chinese modernization: its essential requirement, its fundamental standpoint, its main content, its strategic method, and its place in a "new form of human civilization". It draws on Xi Jinping's speeches, Deng Xiaoping's remark on modernization and socialism, and official poverty-reduction figures. Lu contends that capitalist modernization cannot deliver common prosperity because private ownership and exploitation prevent capitalists from sharing wealth with workers. Under the primary stage of socialism, by contrast, public ownership as the mainstay, together with the Two Unwaverings, provides the institutional guarantee, and continued development of the productive forces remains necessary. Common prosperity is described as covering both material and cultural-ethical life, and as neither egalitarianism nor simultaneous wealth: some may get rich first and then help others, by making the "cake" bigger and dividing it well through primary, secondary and tertiary distribution. Lu stresses that this is a long, gradual process, pursued through staged goals from the "two-step" plan to the new two-step plan (basic modernization by 2035, a modern socialist power by 2050). The article also credits the Party since the 18th Party Congress (2012) with lifting 98.99 million rural people out of poverty and eliminating absolute poverty. Lu concludes that common prosperity separates socialist civilization from Western capitalist civilization, which the author describes as centred on capital and producing an accumulation of poverty alongside wealth, even where welfare states have been built. Chinese modernization is thus presented as a new form of human civilization and a contribution to world socialism. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the 2021 official line on common prosperity was explained to a general Chinese readership.

The classical Marxist writers on the authority of the proletarian party 经典作家关于无产阶级政党权威的思想 Lü Yao Published in Chinese Social Sciences Today on 30 June 2021, the centenary year of the Communist Party of China, this short commentary asks what Marx, Engels and Lenin said about the authority of the proletarian party. Lü Yao argues that authority has been a constant issue in party-building and state-building across the history of the international communist movement. Returning to these classical statements, the author says, has theoretical and practical value for strengthening and upholding the Party Central Committee's centralised and unified leadership in the new era. The article is organised in two parts, one on Marx and Engels and one on Lenin, and closes with a short paragraph on the present. The first part turns on Engels's phrase that without authority no concerted action is possible. The second part follows Lenin's work in building a Russian workers' party from the late 1890s, citing What Is to Be Done?, One Step Forward, Two Steps Back and his later campaign against factions. For Marx and Engels, Lü identifies three claims. Proletarian revolution needs authority, because the class must unite its forces against capital's rule, and Engels is quoted as calling revolution an act in which one part of the population imposes its will on another by authoritarian means. The proletarian dictatorship needs authority too: after the Paris Commune, they drew the lesson that a new state must be consolidated, organised and built through centralised authority. Authority and autonomy are relative and dialectically united, so the anarchist Bakunin's rejection of all authority is, in Lü's account, untenable until communism arrives. For Lenin, Lü stresses democratic centralism, with its rules that the individual obeys the organisation, the minority the majority and the whole Party the centre. Lenin also insisted on the authority of the Central Committee and its leaders, on observing Party discipline and statutes, and on banning factional activity, as with the 'Workers' Opposition' after the civil war. Lü concludes that this body of thought informed the CPC's system of organisational discipline, and that the Party has applied it by putting forward the Two Upholds and raising them to an institutional level. Facing what the article calls changes unseen in a century, the author calls for putting Party leadership first, firmly upholding the Central Committee's authority and unified leadership, adhering to a people-centred approach and advancing full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. Read the original if you want a concise, official-line account of how Party scholars link Marx, Engels and Lenin on authority to the current doctrine of upholding the Central Committee's authority.

The obscured horizon: the moral dimension of the materialist conception of history 被遮蔽的视野：唯物史观的道德维度 Zhou Song Zhou Song asks whether Marxism and morality are compatible. The commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in September 2021, argues that the moral dimension runs through the whole creation and development of the materialist conception of history. Zhou holds that it has long been obscured or dissolved, and that returning to the original texts shows the two to be coherent. The article traces the denial of this dimension from the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. It covers bourgeois critics such as Barth, Second International 'orthodox' theorists such as Kautsky, and later Western readers such as Kamenka, who set the historical materialism against humanism. It then turns to Chinese scholarship, which Zhou says was influenced by Soviet interpretive models. Zhou's central move is to separate a complete 'ethical system' from a 'moral dimension': the texts are not a moral treatise, but they carry moral values and standpoints. Humanism, in this reading, has two senses, a view of history and a moral principle. The materialist conception rejects the first and keeps the second, which gives it a scientific foundation. Zhou identifies three layers of the moral dimension: a moral critique of capitalism grounded in scientific analysis, a strong practical orientation, and a concern for human liberation and free, all-round development. Emphasising only scientific truth is, for Zhou, another misreading. Zhou concludes that scientific discovery of historical laws and moral concern for humanity are two sides of one theory. The more scientific the theory, the more it can become moral force for the oppressed to struggle for liberation. Read the original if you want a short Chinese statement of how the moral reading of historical materialism is defended against both Western and Soviet-influenced interpretations.

Theories of Surplus-Value and the research methods of the history of Marxist economic thought 《剩余价值理论》与马克思主义经济思想史的研究方法 Hu Ying Lu Siyuan Hu Ying and Lu Siyuan ask what Marx's Theories of Surplus-Value (1861–63 manuscripts) can teach about how to study the history of economic thought, and in particular the history of Marxist economic thought. They argue that the work, which began as a history of the theory of surplus-value, grew into a first draft of a history of bourgeois political economy. In their view it supplies a model that can be applied to Marxism's own intellectual history. The article has three parts. The first reconstructs how Marx narrated the history: from James Steuart through the Physiocrats, Adam Smith and Ricardo, to Malthus, the Ricardian socialists and the decline into vulgar economics. The second analyses the methods behind this narrative, drawing on Marx's distinction between method of inquiry and method of presentation. The third turns these methods to the history of Marxist economics from Bernstein, Luxemburg and Lenin to the post-1970s debates on plan and market. The authors distil three methods from Marx's practice. First, thinkers are classified by their research methods, shaped by philosophical currents, views of history and the definition of the object of study, so that Marx's materialist dialectic stands against Cartesian, empiricist and utilitarian influences. Second, economic thought is tied to economic reality: Physiocracy reflects a bourgeois society just emerging from feudalism, and Ricardo's rent theory reflects British conditions, treating bourgeois relations as eternal categories. Third, representative figures are chosen by the author's own method; Marx picked Smith, Ricardo and Malthus because they stand for the forms taken by surplus-value and for classical versus vulgar economics. The authors criticise Western histories of economic thought for treating Marx without analysing his social-historical setting. The authors propose that Marxist economic thought be studied on the basis of historical materialism, using the economic histories of capitalism and socialism as the guiding thread. They sketch phases from the monopoly-stage debates of the 1870s–90s through 1917–56 and the postwar boom to the market-oriented reforms of socialist economies. They also set three criteria for choosing representative thinkers: adherence to Marx's basic views, development of his object and method, and influence on later Marxist economics. Rosa Luxemburg serves as the example, with her contribution and her drift towards a mechanical theory of crisis. Read the original if you want a Chinese methodological account of how Theories of Surplus-Value can guide research on the history of Marxist economics.

Mao Zedong's approach to correcting and improving the style of meetings 毛泽东关于纠正和改进会风的思想方法 Deng Yilin Yan Shanhong Meetings are the Party's main means of making decisions and setting policy, and Deng and Yan argue that the style of meetings (huifeng) reflects the work style, morale and cohesion of Party members and cadres. The article contends that Mao Zedong, in both the New Democratic revolution and the period of socialist revolution and construction, treated bad meeting styles as a serious problem and developed a coherent set of methods for correcting them. These methods, the authors say, remain instructive today. The article has three parts. The first sets out Mao's criticism of three kinds of poor meeting style: formalism, bureaucracy and liberalism. The second covers his methods for correcting them: institutional rules, investigation and research, democracy combined with centralism, and the summing up of experience. The third assesses the results. Evidence comes from Mao's speeches and drafts from the Gutian Resolution (1929) through the Yan'an period to the 1950s and early 1960s, plus anecdotes about his own conduct at meetings. The authors argue that Mao read each bad style as a distortion of Party work. Formalism meant stereotyped agendas, reports read from scripts and a 'Party eight-legged essay' format. Bureaucratic style meant a commanding manner and distance from the masses, and liberalism meant aimless debate, extreme democracy and a lack of discipline. On remedies, Mao required meetings to be prepared in advance, short and infrequent, and focused on real problems. He held that 'no investigation, no right to speak', and that investigation should be done in person. He also tied meetings to democratic centralism and the mass line, for example by circulating draft reports for comment before the Seven Thousand Cadres Conference (1962). The authors credit these efforts with three results: a democratic and efficient meeting style, a Marxist study style that links theory with practice (notably in the Yan'an rectification), and a practical, truth-seeking work style. They cite examples including the 7th Party Congress and the 8th Party Congress. They conclude that Mao's experience should guide efforts to improve meeting and work styles on the path towards the second centenary goal. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-based account of how Mao is presented in Party historiography as a model for reforming meeting practice and work style.

Lenin's exploration of Russia's path of social development before the October Revolution, and its significance 十月革命前列宁对俄国社会发展道路的探索及其意义 Xu Qin Research on Lenin in China has concentrated on the October Revolution and the years after it. Xu Qin argues that Russia's turn to socialism also depended on Lenin's work between 1893 and 1917, when he sought a path of development that would speed up the productive forces while serving workers and peasants as far as possible. The article holds that this work pointed Russian workers and peasants towards the correct line of struggle and supplied the scientific premises for the later New Economic Policy. The article takes four questions in turn. These are whether Russia could follow the Narodniks' 'non-capitalist' road; whether the proletariat should lead or merely push forward the democratic revolution of 1905; whether the revolution should take the 'direct' or the 'zigzag' road, which in practice meant boycotting or joining the State Duma; and whether the land question should be solved by the 'American' or the 'Prussian' road. A final section sets out the historical significance of this exploration and what it suggests for the Chinese Communist Party today. Xu reads Lenin as rejecting both the Narodniks' appeal to Russian peculiarity and the Mensheviks' reliance on general laws, while acknowledging the progressive role of capitalism without defending it. On leadership, Lenin is said to have argued that the proletariat must lead the revolution, and to have listed practical conditions: socialist consciousness, correct slogans, suitable forms of struggle and Party cells in non-Party organisations. On the Duma, he preferred the direct road but accepted a compromise when the revolution ebbed, while denying that the Duma could be a revolutionary tool. On land, Lenin backed nationalisation, the core of the 'American' road, because it promised the fastest growth of the productive forces and the best conditions for the peasantry. The 'Prussian' road, carried out by landlords from above, was in his view slow and burdened with serfdom's remnants. Xu concludes that these debates prepared the ground for the October Revolution, which Lenin called the sequel to the 1905 'dress rehearsal', and for the New Economic Policy. The author then draws three lessons for the new era: arm the whole Party with innovative theory and the adapting of Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, grasp the laws and general trends of history, and hold fast to the Party's original aspiration of seeking happiness for the people. Read the original if you want a systematic account of Lenin's pre-1917 positions on the Narodniks, the Mensheviks, the Duma and the agrarian question, and of how a Chinese scholar draws contemporary Party lessons from them.

An analysis of the new historiography of American communism 美国共产主义新史学探析 Yang Ningcong Yang Ningcong examines the "new historiography" of American communism, which the author says has gradually displaced the "traditional" school since the 1980s. The article argues that, unlike in Britain, the two American schools stand in opposition on political stance and discourse. The new school therefore corrects and replaces the old one rather than developing it. Yang contends that it has become the mainstream of the field and matters for the US communist movement. The article has four parts. It first defines the new historiography through four features: its historical stage, its stance, its handling of sources and its view of causal factors. It then explains why the school arose and how that rise shows itself. Next it describes the school's two main tasks. It closes with the school's significance and prospects. Yang draws on Russian historian Maxim Kirchanov, on Theodore Draper and on former traditionalists such as Harvey Klehr and John Earl Haynes. Yang presents the old school as shaped by McCarthyism, using unreliable sources and treating American communism as a Soviet import. The new school is credited with a historical-materialist stance, closer archival work and attention to domestic roots. The causes of its rise include generational turnover among historians, New Left scholars entering universities and neoliberal pressure on students. Others are the post-2008 widening of inequality, internet circulation and digitised Russian archives. Its institutions are the society Historians of American Communism (founded 1982) and the journal American Communist History (2002). Its two main tasks are criticising anti-communism and reassessing the Communist Party USA. The reassessment stresses the party's role as a Americanised, domestic party in the Depression and anti-fascist struggles and in labour, farmer, Black and women's movements. It also stresses the \"irreplaceable\" role of Stalin. Yang concludes that the new school helps Americans, especially the young, judge communism more objectively. In the author's view it also supports the communist movement and gives US communist history a scientific footing. The author warns that the school's work is still fragmented and that traditional historiography may revive under Trump. Yang remains optimistic because archive collections covering 1892–2019 have been assembled at New York University. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic account of how US historians have revised the history of American communism, including the author's own assessment of it.

The role of the Comintern in the founding of the Communist Party of China 共产国际在中国共产党成立过程中的角色作用 Gong Yutao Marking the centenary of the Communist Party of China (CPC), Gong Yutao asks what part the Communist International (Comintern) played in the Party's founding in July 1921. The article argues that the Comintern played a special and important role that should not be forgotten and should be assessed objectively. In Gong's account, its contribution to the founding itself was positive, though it should not be exaggerated. The article has four parts. It first sets out the background: the Comintern's founding in 1919, its drive to create communist parties worldwide, and its Eastern strategy, including the 1920 Baku congress of the peoples of the East. It then follows the Comintern's direct involvement through its envoys Voitinsky, Maring (Henk Sneevliet) and Nikolsky, up to the First National Congress. A third part examines how Comintern requirements shaped the Party's name, programme and resolutions, and a short conclusion weighs the Comintern's overall record. Gong's core argument is twofold. First, the Comintern helped materially: Voitinsky reached agreement with Li Dazhao and Chen Duxiu, helped set up early Party organisations in Shanghai, Beijing, Wuhan, Changsha, Guangzhou, Jinan and among Chinese abroad, and gave funding. Maring and Nikolsky helped prepare the First Congress and, according to Gong, Maring's warning after an intruder appeared saved the delegates from arrest. Second, the Comintern shaped the Party's form. Gong argues that the CPC was built on Lenin's theory of the Party and the Russian model, and that the name, the recognition of the dictatorship of the proletariat, the organisational principles later called democratic centralism, and the break with reformist parties all reflect Comintern requirements, especially the Conditions of Admission of the Second Comintern Congress. Gong concludes that over its 24 years the Comintern's role in the CPC's development was two-sided, and that its negative effects later caused heavy losses and drew wide criticism. Gong says that at the founding stage its work was, in the words of an earlier verdict the article quotes, 'more beneficial than not'. He adds that the First Congress documents often paid too little attention to Chinese conditions, a gap the Second Congress partly addressed with Comintern help. Citing a line the article quotes, he adds that the Party would have emerged without the Comintern, because its founding answered China's own historical needs. Read the original if you want a Chinese official-history account of Comintern envoys, the First Congress and the Party's Leninist and Russian organisational model.

Is negative dialectics a radical dialectics? Adorno's critique of the dialectics of the idea as a case study 否定辩证法是一种激进的辩证法吗？ Li Chunmin Adorno's negative dialectics is often treated as a radical discourse and a new form of dialectics because of its anti-ontological stance and thoroughgoing negation. This article, published in 2021 in a Chinese Marxist-theory teaching journal, asks whether that reputation is deserved. Li Chunmin concludes that radicalism is only the appearance of negative dialectics, which the author reads as a contemporary echo of the dialectical tradition rather than a new departure. The study takes Adorno's critique of Hegelian dialectics of the idea as its single case. It proceeds in five parts: the non-conceptual in the concept and the objectivity of thought; materialist dialectics and a 'non-reflecting' materialism; non-identity and the mediated 'particular'; the linguistic dimension of dialectics; and finally the place of negative dialectics in the dialectical tradition. Li draws on Adorno's Negative Dialectics and engages Kant, Hegel, Heidegger, Husserl and Lenin. Li first reconstructs Adorno's line of thought. Concepts are said to enforce identity and so to suppress the non-identical, yet Adorno does not dissolve conceptual objectivity. He replaces reflection theory with 'constellations' of concepts orbiting the object, and makes negation the measure of dialectics, so that the negation of the negation does not return to affirmation. Li adds that Adorno's particular is itself mediated and not an absolute difference, and that identity can only be resisted by passing through it, as in his example of the exchange principle. On this basis Li distinguishes negative dialectics from postmodernism, since it keeps a trace of reconciliation. Li's central assessment is that Adorno misreads Hegel. Hegel's concept, in Li's account, is reality grasped conceptually, each determination is dissolved in turn, and reconciliations are provisional. Li argues that Adorno therefore remains inside the field of idealist dialectics and never finds a route from concept to thing, whereas Marx opened a different path by introducing historicity. Li still credits Adorno with resisting dogmatism, stressing individuality and difference, and criticising the abstract totalities produced by capital. Li sees this as a point of convergence with Marx and as the rational core of negative dialectics. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist assessment of Adorno that sets his critique of Hegel against Hegel's own texts and against Marx.

A critique of digital labour from the perspective of historical materialism 历史唯物主义视野下的数字劳动批判 Lan Jiang Writing in 2021, Lan Jiang asks how Marxists should understand the new capital–labour relation emerging under digital and platform capitalism, and in particular whether digital labour is real productive labour or merely 'immaterial' or 'cultural' labour. The article argues that digital labour is neither. Drawing on historical materialism, Lan holds that labour is a historical category, and that digital capitalism draws a new line between activities that count as labour and those that do not. The article has three sections. The first contrasts Marx's 'unproductive labour' (services such as the singer's, in the 1857–58 and 1861–63 manuscripts) with the 'immaterial labour' that Michael Hardt and Antonio Negri build on Marx's 'general intellect'. The second reads the passage on hunting, fishing and criticism in The German Ideology to show that labour arises with the division of labour and is not a natural given. The third applies this to digital platforms, drawing on Christian Fuchs, Nick Srnicek, David W. Hill and Moishe Postone. Lan argues that Hardt and Negri, by giving immaterial production a dominant place, overlook the factories, ports and logistics networks that make digital convenience possible. Marx's distinction between activity (Tätigkeit) and labour (Arbeit) shows that the division of labour fixes some activities as labour, which then stand over people as an alien material force; under capitalism, money measures this labour. In the digital age, the article contends, the dividing criterion changes from general value to 'general data'. Activities that can be turned into extractable, exchangeable data, such as ordering vegetables online, become digital labour, whatever the old line between work and leisure or material and immaterial. A data apparatus then becomes the new alien power, turning people into 'data persons'. Lan concludes that the labour behind a click extends to production, warehousing and logistics, which are themselves datafied and hidden behind the screen. The article compares 'vulgar digital political economists' who reduce this to clicks and views with the vulgar economists Marx criticised for turning people into hats. A genuine critique of digital labour, Lan says, must expose the new unequal relations of production beneath the data. Read the original if you are interested in Marxist responses to Hardt and Negri's immaterial labour thesis, or in a philosophical account of how data restructures the boundary between labour and leisure.

A critique of the Frankfurt School from a structuralist perspective Lacan's rebuttal of Adorno's critical theory as a case 结构主义视域下的法兰克福学派批判 Wang Fusheng Pan Xinpei Frankfurt School critical theory and structuralist Marxism are two major currents of Western Marxism, yet the authors observe that they have never engaged each other in any real dialogue. This article, published in Marxism and Reality in 2021, takes Lacan and Adorno as representatives and asks what a confrontation between them would show. Wang and Pan argue that Lacan's account of the 'pseudo-subject' undermines the logic of distinction on which Adorno's critical theory rests. The article has four parts. It first reconstructs the distinctions underlying Adorno's critique, then sets out Lacan's 'post-subject' philosophy through his developmental sequence of mirror stage, language and symbolic order. It then applies Lacan to Adorno, and closes with four reflections on present-day relevance. Along the way it draws on Martin Jay, Raymond Williams, Stuart Hall, Žižek, Althusser and Perry Anderson. According to the authors, Adorno's critique depends on three distinctions: a harmonious pre-modern society versus the one-dimensional, rationalised modern one; autonomous 'true' art versus heteronomous culture-industry products; and negative, non-identical dialectics versus Hegelian coercive identity. Earlier criticisms of Adorno's elitism, whether from Jay, from British cultural materialism or from Chinese scholars of the 1990s, are said to remain at the level of values and so leave this foundation intact. In Lacan's terms, the authors argue, all such distinctions occur inside the symbolic order and differ only in position. High and mass culture alike are signifiers through which the 'little other' governs the subject, so neither expresses autonomy and neither is alienation. They present late Althusser's theory of interpellation as functionally the same insight. The authors add that the critique runs both ways. In their view structuralism's dissolution of subjectivity left it conservative and led to its misjudgement of May 1968, and Lacan's account of the 'real' raises doubts of its own. They conclude that critical theory remains practically useful, since China and other developing countries now show the cultural symptoms it described. They hold that structuralism can temper its elitist tone, that both schools stand far from Marx's political economy and revolutionary practice, and that theory must be rethought for changed conditions such as online culture. Read the original if you want a Chinese attempt to bring Lacanian structuralism into direct argument with Adorno and the Frankfurt School.

Innovative paths for building New Era Civilisation Practice Centres 新时代文明实践中心建设的创新路径研究 Song Huifang Song Huifang examines the New Era Civilisation Practice Centres, grassroots institutions whose construction Xi Jinping announced in August 2018. The article asks what these centres are for, what path the pilot programme has found, and how the model can be extended nationwide. Song argues that the centres are an effective vehicle for spiritual-cultural construction, and that three obstacles must be removed before they can be scaled up. Writing after three years of piloting, Song notes that the pilot units grew from 50 to 500. The article has four parts. It first sets out the significance of the centres: rooting the Party's theory and policy among the people, passing on fine traditional Chinese culture, and raising the level of social civilisation, a target of the 14th Five-Year Plan. It then describes the practical path found in the pilots and reports results in three areas. Finally it identifies problems and offers remedies. Evidence comes from pilot sites such as Rongcheng in Shandong, Longchang in Sichuan, Sixian-type county cases in Jiangsu and Hebei, and Haidian in Beijing. On the path, Song identifies three supports: volunteer service as the main form of activity, a social credit system that converts volunteer points into material rewards and honours so that participation becomes self-motivated, and integration with county-level converged media centres, which supply data platforms and carry the centres' content. On results, the article cites reduced spending on wedding and funeral customs, income growth in a village in Rongcheng, and falling disputes and criminal cases there, as evidence of improved civility, rural revitalisation and grassroots governance. On problems, Song finds formalism and superficial understanding, an imbalance between pilot and non-pilot areas where centres exist only as signboards, and weak progress in urban communities because of a mobile population, ageing residents and scarce funds. Song proposes raising political understanding and training, tightening supervision and assessment, and adapting pilot experience to local needs instead of copying it. Song also calls for paired mutual-aid arrangements, in which universities, troupes, enterprises and social organisations are linked with older urban communities, and for funding that combines government money with social donations, for example community civilisation-practice funds. The article closes by calling for the centres to stay rooted among the people and to build civilisational strength toward the second centenary goal and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a Party-affiliated scholar's account of how these centres operate, with local case data and the official diagnosis of their weaknesses.

Value-form and Marx's theory of the critique of capital Christopher Arthur's "New Dialectic" and an assessment of it 价值形式与马克思的资本批判理论 Tang Zhengdong Tang Zhengdong examines how the British Marxist Christopher J. Arthur, a leading figure of the "New Dialectic" movement, reads Marx's Capital through the value-form. The article treats this as a typical Western attempt to develop historical materialism from the standpoint of capitalism's historical specificity. Tang's thesis is that Arthur's work illuminates the abstractness of capital, but relies too heavily on exchange-value and on the conceptual self-deduction of form. In Tang's assessment, it neglects the objective content of value and the social-historical basis of value relations, and so misreads historical materialism. The article has three main sections. The first criticises Arthur's "systematic dialectic", which he opposes to Hegel's historical dialectic, and tests it against Marx's texts, including the 1857–58 manuscripts and Volume I of Capital. The second addresses Arthur's account of Capital's starting point and of conceptual deduction. The third turns to his two notions of abstract labour, his reading of the labour process and the valorisation process, his revised concept of exploitation, and his view of workers' resistance. Tang argues that Arthur separates system from history and reduces Marx's method of ascending from the abstract to the concrete to a self-moving logic of concepts. For Tang, this is a Hegelian idealism that cannot explain why Marx begins with the commodity or where contradictions come from. Tang also argues that Arthur separates the value-form from the content of value, as Chapter 1 of Capital does not, since the sections on use-value, value and the dual character of labour precede the form and fetishism sections. On abstract labour, Tang holds that Arthur quotes only the first aspect of the exchange between capital and labour. This aspect is ordinary exchange, in which labour appears abstract. Arthur omits the second aspect, capital's appropriation of labour's specific use-value, which creates surplus value. Tang concludes that Arthur treats valorisation as a second labour process alongside the real one, a dualism that falls into the fetishism Marx criticised. His account of workers' subjectivity and class struggle, Tang says, is political rather than grounded in historical necessity. Tang sees the "New Dialectic" as an humanist critique applied to economic categories, which does not use Marx's scientific method on the latest forms of capital. Read the original if you want a detailed Chinese critique of value-form theory and Arthur's reading of Marx's texts.

A review of foreign Marxist critiques of neoliberalism 国外马克思主义的新自由主义批判研究述评 Liu Hui Writing in 2021, Liu Hui reviews how Marxist and left-wing scholars outside China have analysed the rise and crisis of neoliberalism after the 2008 global financial crisis. The review is a systematic survey, and it also assesses the work critically through the Marxist theory of finance capital. Liu's overall view is that these critiques offer useful perspectives, but that several of them depart from that theory. Liu sorts the literature into four perspectives: production, institutions, class and race, and geopolitics. The production perspective covers Baran, Sweezy, Magdoff and John Bellamy Foster of the Monthly Review school, together with David Harvey and Giovanni Arrighi. The institutional perspective covers the French regulation school, the American Social Structure of Accumulation school and Peter Gowan. The class perspective covers Gérard Duménil and Dominique Lévy, and the race perspective covers Daniel Faber and Neil Davidson. The geopolitical section sets Hardt, Negri, Robinson, Panitch and Gindin against Harvey, Callinicos and Davidson. Liu argues that the production perspective is the most faithful to historical materialism. It starts from the shift to monopoly-finance capital and treats neoliberalism as the ideology of that capital. The institutional perspective, in Liu's reading, reverses cause and effect by saying neoliberal policy produced financial power. It therefore places its hopes in state regulation, although the state is already captured by finance capital. Duménil and Lévy's class analysis is praised, but Liu calls their hope in a progressive 'managerial class' unrealistic, since capitalist fractions unite against workers. Liu accepts that the race perspective is right to call right-wing populism a variant of neoliberalism. Liu adds that finance capital has only changed its method of rule, shifting its crisis onto other countries. The geopolitical perspective is credited with bringing inter-state power struggle into Marxist theory. Liu concludes that contemporary capitalism is essentially capitalism dominated by monopoly-finance capital, and that neoliberalism is its system of rule. Financial, social, ideological and geopolitical crises are piling up, and Liu expects right-wing populist neoliberalism to continue and to add uncertainty to world affairs. Liu holds that these critiques continue Lenin's finance-capital tradition and have reference value for developing Marxism in the new era. Read the original if you want a map of Western left debates on neoliberalism, together with a Chinese Marxist assessment that favours the monopoly-finance-capital reading.

The current state, goals and tasks of the communist parties of Central and Eastern Europe 当前中东欧地区共产党的基本状况与目标任务 Li Ruiqin Writing in 2021, Li Ruiqin surveys the communist and workers' parties that were rebuilt or restored in the 16 states of Central and Eastern Europe after the Soviet collapse and the upheavals of 1989. Li argues that most of these parties still uphold Marxism-Leninism and defend the history of socialism, but that they are overwhelmingly weak, are still seeking a way out of the trough, and face heavy pressure both to defend that history and to open new ground. The article moves through six sections. It covers the parties' rebuilding and struggle for legality, including bans on communist symbols and European Parliament resolutions equating communism with Nazism. It then turns to their centenary reflections, their online and international activity, their campaigns against historical nihilism and NATO, and their attention to socialism in China. A final section lists six challenges. Examples come from the parties of Poland, the Czech lands and Moravia, Hungary, Romania, Bulgaria, Slovakia, Albania and Serbia. Li's central claim is that these parties have abandoned armed struggle and work through legal and parliamentary channels. Their main means are party websites, joint statements at international communist meetings, and public statements on contested history. Li presents the Slovak party's rebuttal of a television portrayal of Gustav Husák and the Yugoslav New Communist Party's condemnation of NATO as examples of defending 20th-century socialist history against Western ideological offensives. Li also reports that the parties' media and statements praise China's pandemic response and economic recovery, and cites Bulgarian and Serbian leaders' praise for China and Xi Jinping's idea of a community with a shared future for mankind. Li reads this as a sign of growing socialist strength in the 21st century. Li lists six challenges: weak political influence outside government; limited and mostly extra-parliamentary forms of activity; a hostile geopolitical and ideological environment; frequent party renaming, splits and disunity; the need to respond to popular demands; and the need to cultivate younger members. Li concludes that the road to reviving socialism is long and hard, and that the immediate tasks are to gain legality, enter parliaments and widen mass support. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's overview of how these small parties are portrayed, with many named parties, dates and statements from their own websites.

Historical nihilism in the course of the Soviet Union's transformation 苏联演变进程中的历史虚无主义 Su Yang Thirty years after the Soviet collapse, Su Yang argues that historical nihilism, the wholesale negation of a country's and a party's past, was a factor that cannot be ignored in the Soviet Union's disintegration. Su opens with Xi Jinping's remark that the collapse of the Soviet Union and the Communist Party of the Soviet Union (CPSU) was due in large part to fierce ideological struggle and the negation of Soviet and Party history, of Lenin and of Stalin. The piece, published in Red Flag Manuscripts in December 2021, presents the Soviet case as a cautionary example. The article has three parts. The first traces how historical nihilism spread under Khrushchev, Brezhnev and Gorbachev. The second sets out its main harms: a mistaken view of history, distorted social values and the destruction of political belief. The third draws lessons for contemporary China. On the Soviet record, Su points to Khrushchev's 1956 secret speech on the cult of personality and the literary 'thaw' as the start of the process. Su holds that it accelerated under Gorbachev, who declared that there should be no 'blank spots' in history. Su cites the destruction of school history textbooks in 1988, the abolition of courses such as the history of the CPSU and scientific communism, and the 1990 press law. According to the article, the Party controlled only 27 of 1,800 national periodicals (1.5%). Su also cites figures on Party resignations, including 4.2 million in the year before July 1991. In Su's account, 'glasnost', democratisation and 'pluralism' opened the way for anti-communist and anti-Marxist currents, and 'humane, democratic socialism' displaced Marxism as the dominant ideology. For China, Su calls for upholding historical materialism and a correct view of Party history, strengthening education in Party history and Marxist theory, and holding the right to interpret Party history. Su also calls for firm cultural confidence, since historical nihilism leads to cultural nihilism. A third task is to strengthen governance of the internet, which Su describes as the main battlefield of ideological struggle, and to extend the reach of mainstream discourse online. Read the original if you want an example of how Party-aligned scholarship in 2021 used the Soviet collapse to justify ideological work against historical nihilism in China.

Unswervingly advancing whole-process people's democracy 矢志不渝推进全过程人民民主 Zhu Lingjun This Guangming Daily commentary opens a series on "China's democracy", launched after the State Council Information Office issued its white paper "China: Democracy That Works" on 4 December 2021. Zhu Lingjun argues that the Communist Party has pursued people's democracy since its founding and, over a century, has developed it into whole-process people's democracy. The article follows the Party's history in stages: the New Democratic revolution, the founding of the People's Republic and socialist construction, reform and opening up, and the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). It also refers to the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021), which treated the advance of people's democracy as part of the Party's historical significance. Zhu holds that each stage supplied conditions for the next. Examples include the Soviet governments and the \"three-thirds\" system in the base areas, the People's Political Consultative Conference and the people's congress system after 1949, and regional ethnic autonomy. Later come grassroots self-governance, consultative democracy and democratic centralism. Zhu says the Party combines Marxist people's democracy theory with Chinese practice and traditional culture. Since 2012, in Zhu's account, whole-process people's democracy has covered electoral, consultative, social and grassroots democracy, and every stage from election to supervision. Zhu concludes that the Party's century of struggle made the people masters of the country and gave democracy \"real meaning\". The article predicts that the Party will write a more splendid chapter in the history of human political civilization. Read the original if you want a concise official-aligned periodisation of how Party scholars present the history of people's democracy.

French social inequality as refracted through immigration 移民折射下的法国社会不平等 Peng Shuyi Writing in 2021, Peng Shuyi asks why social inequality has grown in France, a Western country once relatively attentive to fairness, and argues that immigrants, close to 10% of the population, show this inequality most clearly. The article holds that the Covid-19 epidemic exposed and deepened these divisions, and that the root cause is the rise of neoliberalism. Peng adds that the French left, above all the Socialist Party, objectively tolerated the worsening by shifting rightwards. The article has five parts. It first describes immigrants' position in employment, schooling and health, using INSEE figures and the example of Seine-Saint-Denis. It then examines how the epidemic hit immigrants in health, income and children's education. The third and fourth parts turn to neoliberal policy and the changing Socialist Party, and a short conclusion follows. Peng draws on French bodies and commentators (the Observatoire des inégalités, Denis Lafay), on Thomas Piketty, and on André Gorz. Peng's central claim is that immigrants act as a prism for structural inequality. Post-war labour migrants were concentrated in industries that deindustrialisation destroyed, were pushed into insecure service work, and were housed in suburban districts with weak schools and discrimination in hiring. In the epidemic, the article says, cramped housing, jobs that could not be done from home, poorer health and scarce hospitals produced higher infection and death rates. Peng traces the underlying causes to austerity in health and social spending and to state encouragement of informal, flexible employment, drawing on Gorz's argument that cheap personal services grow by impoverishing others. The Socialist Party, in Peng's account, lost its working-class base: workers and employees fell from 22% to 12% of members between 1985 and 2011, while the far-right National Rally absorbed abandoned voters and made immigrants scapegoats. Peng concludes that as long as neoliberal policy orientation remains, the gap between rich and poor in France will not change and will only sharpen social conflict. As evidence of the pro-capital tilt, the article points to Macron's abolition of the wealth tax. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist-leaning analysis of French inequality, immigration and the pandemic, with detailed statistics and a critique of the French left.

The current state and prospects of the Latin American left 当前拉美左翼的发展现状与前景 Yang Jianmin Writing in 2021, Yang Jianmin asks where the Latin American left stands after the "pink tide" that began with Hugo Chávez's election in Venezuela in 1999, and whether a new cycle of left government is opening. The article's answer is that the left has recovered since 2018 and may gain further ground, but is badly divided at home. Yang concludes that, whatever the outcome of a new cycle, the left will remain a lasting force in the region. The article moves through four stages. It first traces the regional balance from the pink tide through the "left retreat, right advance" of 2015–2018 to the present situation of "left and right sharing power". It then examines how the Covid-19 pandemic, forthcoming elections and the 2020 US election affect the left, with country cases: Ecuador, Brazil, Peru, Chile and Mexico. A third section contrasts the left's growing international coordination with its domestic fragmentation. A final section sets out conditions for a new cycle and the structural bases of the left's persistence. Yang argues that the pandemic has exposed the costs of right-wing neoliberal policy, citing rising public debt, higher poverty and scarce vaccines, and so favours the left; the author also treats Joe Biden's replacement of Donald Trump as easing external pressure. Internationally, the left has built coordination through the Puebla Group, and Yang reads Mexico's and Argentina's shifts and Peru's 2021 result as undermining the Lima Group's pressure on Venezuela. At home, however, Yang identifies three problems: new left forces competing with traditional ones (Chile, Ecuador), policy splits among governing leftists (Ecuador under Lenín Moreno), and political fragmentation and ideological polarisation. Yang names three tests for a new left cycle: renewing social consensus and improving living conditions, demonstrating governing competence while keeping ties to social movements, and redefining the role of the state. In the author's assessment, the previous cycle failed to reform the armed forces, police and judiciary, and so did not replace neoliberalism. The left's staying power rests, Yang says, on political reform, party-system change, broader political inclusion and persistent inequality, with poverty still above 30 per cent. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic assessment of the Latin American left in 2021, with country-by-country electoral detail.

A reader's guide to Latin American Marxism 拉美马克思主义阅读指南 Jeffrey R. Webber This text is a Chinese translation of a bibliographic guide by the British-based scholar Jeffrey R. Webber. It sets out a periodised reading list for anyone approaching Latin American Marxism. Webber says that any periodisation simplifies and screens out counter-currents, but argues that a guide of this kind has no alternative. The list is admittedly incomplete and openly selective. It mixes recognised introductions with lesser-known works, and it leans towards history rather than theory. Webber builds on the periodisation in Michael Löwy's anthology Marxism in Latin America from 1909 to the Present. He divides the story into six stages: emergence (1870–1910), revolution (1910–1932), stagnation (1932–1959), revolutionary experiment (1959–1980), abandonment of revolutionary strategy (1980–2000), and transformation and renewal (2000 to the present). Under each stage he recommends mostly English-language, but also Spanish and French, works. They cover Mexico, Peru, El Salvador, Argentina, Brazil, Bolivia, Guatemala, Cuba, Chile, Nicaragua and Venezuela. Webber characterises each stage and then matches it with key books. The stage of revolution, for instance, centres on José Carlos Mariátegui, the Mexican Revolution and the 1932 Salvadoran uprising. In Webber's account, party documents show that the Salvadoran Communist Party took the decision to rise on its own, not on instruction from Moscow. The third stage is one of rigidity under Stalinism and its stagist doctrine, which confined revolutions to a national-democratic framework, and it ran alongside Peronism and Cold War terror. The fourth stage brings in Cuba, Allende's Chile, Sandinista Nicaragua and the dependency-theory debates on modes of production and the world system. Webber also notes that the history after 1959 is often reduced to guerrilla warfare, and he cites a study of the 1969 Córdoba uprising as a corrective. For the neoliberal period, Webber points to retreat, defeat and self-criticism, with many intellectuals turning to post-Marxism or liberalism. He highlights counter-currents such as the Brazilian Landless Workers' Movement (MST) and the Zapatistas. He treats the current stage cautiously. Writing in 2021, he calls it too early to say the left cycle is over, and he sees both the originality of the fourth stage and signs of the dogmatism of the third. Read the original if you want an annotated, period-by-period bibliography of Latin American Marxism and its histories, with brief critical notes on each work.

A critique of nature-centred ecological views and the construction of a new ecological philosophy Slavoj Žižek's psychoanalytic reading of ecology 自然中心主义生态观的批判与新生态哲学的建构 Shi Fengge Why has ecological crisis not eased despite decades of Western ecological thought? Shi examines this through the work of the Slovenian left thinker Slavoj Žižek. The article argues that nature-centrism (environmental ethics, wilderness philosophy, deep ecology) rests on a utopian ontological assumption of a perfectly balanced, original nature. Žižek, in Shi's account, rejects this assumption from a psychoanalytic standpoint and offers a new ecological philosophy built on the future perfect tense and collective action. The article has three main parts. The first reconstructs nature-centrism: Schweitzer, Leopold and Rolston's ecological ethics, which extends ethical concern to non-human beings; wilderness philosophy; and Arne Naess's deep ecology with its principles of biocentric equality and self-realisation.
