The second sets out Žižek's claim that "nature does not exist". The third presents his new ecological philosophy, and a conclusion compares it with Marx and Engels. Shi's core argument is that the "original nature" is a retroactive construction of thought. Humans need to imagine nature as an ordered whole in order to live, and the past cannot be verified. Žižek, Shi reports, calls humanity "nature's wound" (a psychoanalytic trauma). He argues that nature is inherently disastrous and unbalanced, citing a dialectical reading of Darwin and the claim that most human DNA is "junk". Since the emergence of humans, nature has also been a "second nature", and genetic engineering threatens to end it altogether. From this follows an ecology of the "future perfect": disaster is to be accepted as fate, so that action retroactively changes what was possible. Collective action is its counterpart, drawing on Badiou's four moments of egalitarian justice. It calls for strict equality in resource burdens, terror against violators, voluntarism and trust in the people, including the figure of the informer. Shi concludes that nature-centrism has raised environmental awareness but drifts towards ecological utopia. Žižek's philosophy, though imperfect, shifts attention to practical solutions centred on human value. Shi sees links with Marx's view of nature as humanised and socio-historical, with Engels's warning that nature takes revenge for human victories, and with Marx's concept of practice. Shi presents it as a new path for global ecological problems. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist reading of Žižek's ecology and its comparison with Marx and Engels.

Foreign left commemorations and reflections on the 200th anniversary of Engels's birth 国外左翼对恩格斯诞辰200周年的纪念与省思 Yuan Qun Wang Enming Writing in a 2021 issue of Socialist Studies, Yuan and Wang survey how left-wing parties, organisations and scholars outside China marked the 200th anniversary of Friedrich Engels's birth in 2020. They note that disputes over Engels, especially his late thought, have persisted since Marx's death in 1883. The article argues that the foreign left's commemorations affirmed Engels's historical standing and the continuing guiding value of his ideas, at a time the authors describe as a turn from the low tide of world socialism towards revival. The article opens with an inventory of events: seminars in Lisbon, Hanoi, Vientiane and Japan; joint declarations by Marxist-Leninist-Maoist parties; commemorative essays by figures such as Gennady Zyuganov, Brinda Karat and Marcello Musto; and the 'Engels Year' in Wuppertal, with film premieres, demonstrations and wreath-laying. It then turns to four themes: Engels's status as co-founder of Marxism, the world significance of his works, the contemporary value of his thought, and the strategies the foreign left proposed. A short conclusion links the event to the 2018 Marx bicentenary. In the authors' account, commentators from the Communist Party of Vietnam, the Communist Party of India (Marxist) and others rejected claims of a 'Marx–Engels opposition' and of Engels's late abandonment of revolution, and defended him as the indispensable 'second violin'. They credit him with contributions to dialectical materialism, political economy (his 1844 Outlines of a Critique of Political Economy), scientific socialism, women's liberation and military science. Speakers cited the global financial crisis and the Covid-19 pandemic, including the rise in billionaires' wealth, as confirming Engels's and Marx's analyses of capitalism. The authors report that the foreign left drew practical conclusions: building revolutionary working-class parties, strengthening the study, publication and teaching of Marxist theory, and forming broad anti-war and united fronts under the slogan 'Workers of all countries, unite!' They conclude that Engels's doctrines on scientific socialism, party building and the state still guide the socialist movement, and that these left forces, working in the heartlands of imperialism, combine revolutionary optimism with sober judgement. Read the original if you want a detailed catalogue of the parties, scholars and publications involved in the 2020 Engels commemorations, as presented from a Chinese Marxist viewpoint.

The Chinese path as seen by foreign left-wing scholars 国外左翼学者眼中的中国道路 Liu Mingming Liu Qi Writing in China Social Sciences Today at the end of 2020, Liu Mingming and Liu Qi take up how foreign scholars assess the Chinese path. They note that criticism and praise coexist abroad. Their thesis is that a growing number of left-wing scholars outside China are shedding earlier ideological constraints, judging the achievements of socialism with Chinese characteristics more objectively, and placing hope in the contemporary value of the Chinese path. The short commentary is organised in four parts. It first reports the reasons foreign scholars give for the path's success, then the debate over its nature, then its significance for the world, and finally the claim that it represents hope for socialism. It draws on Russian specialists, the German China expert Sebastian Heilmann, Samir Amin, the British scholar Martin Jacques, and the American economist David Schweickart (named in the text as Schweickart), among others. On success, the authors report foreign views that Communist Party leadership is the key factor, together with a gradual reform path that avoided copying other countries, preserved state-owned enterprises and macroeconomic regulation, and was preferable to "shock therapy". They add a view that China's commitment to peaceful development lets it avoid the fate of rising powers that sought hegemony. On the question of nature, they cite Amin, who holds that state ownership of land shows China is not capitalist, and Schweickart, who argues that China fails the test of a market economy with dominant private ownership and wage labour because state firms still dominate core sectors. On global significance, the authors present scholars who see the Chinese path as an alternative to Western models, a challenge to Fukuyama's "end of history" and a driver of global growth. They also cite views that public ownership of key sectors and state intervention guard against financial excess, and that Chinese success makes socialism the best practical hope of the twenty-first century, with Vietnam and Laos named as followers. They conclude that the Chinese path is a vivid contemporary expression of scientific socialism and points to a new direction for socialist development. Read the original if you want a brief, selective overview of favourable foreign left-wing opinion of China, as presented in Chinese official-academic media.

Theoretical basis, historical experience and practical drivers for building a China–Vietnam community with a shared future 构建中越命运共同体的理论基础、历史经验与实践动力 Pan Jin'e Since 2015, Xi Jinping has repeatedly described China and Vietnam as a "community with a shared future of strategic significance". Writing in 2021, Pan Jin'e asks what lies behind this positioning and argues that it rests on three foundations: a shared ideological basis, a store of historical experience, and the practical results and potential of bilateral cooperation. The author presents it as significant for both countries and for world socialism. The article has four parts. It first examines the common Marxist-Leninist grounding of the two parties and the foreign-policy thought of each side. It then reviews the revolutionary friendship from the early twentieth century and the course of relations since diplomatic ties in 1950. Next it surveys political, economic, cultural and pandemic-era cooperation, including trade and investment figures from Chinese customs and Vietnamese sources. A conclusion looks ahead, drawing a comparison with the China–Laos community. Pan's central move is theoretical. Marx's three social forms, ending in the "true community", and Lenin's views on long coexistence of socialism and capitalism are said to justify cooperation in a transitional period. Pan reads the community with a shared future for mankind as a development of this, and the China–Vietnam version as its application to two Party-led socialist states. Pan traces Chinese diplomatic thought from Mao Zedong to Xi, and Ho Chi Minh's thought on joining national independence with socialism. Pan holds that relations returned to course after setbacks because the two parties set clear guidance at each stage, such as "comrades plus brothers" and the "sixteen-character" guideline. Practical drivers include trade rising from US$32 million in 1991 to US$192.28 billion in 2020, border economic zones, and mutual pandemic help. The author also acknowledges that unresolved maritime disputes and negative perceptions among Vietnamese citizens are obstacles. Pan concludes that the community has solid theoretical, historical and practical foundations and is the right approach for the new period. Both countries' development goals are described as aligned, and the author calls for stronger strategic trust, careful handling of maritime issues and an upgrade of the comprehensive strategic cooperative partnership. Read the original if you study Party-to-Party relations in China and Vietnam, or want to see how Chinese scholars link the community with a shared future for mankind to Marxist theory and bilateral history.

Policy adjustment and practical exploration of the South African Communist Party across a century of political change 百年政治变迁下南非共产党的政策调适与实践探索 Zhang Kai Marking the centenary of the South African Communist Party (SACP, founded 1921), this article asks why the oldest and largest socialist party in Africa has survived apartheid repression, the democratic transition and the collapse of the Soviet bloc. Zhang argues that the fundamental reason is the party's consistent use of Marxism to analyse South Africa's concrete conditions, together with timely strategic and tactical adjustments to changing circumstances. The article follows the party chronologically. Part one covers the apartheid era in three phases: 1921–1950, the underground period after the 1950 Suppression of Communism Act (with refounding in 1953), and 1960–1990, when it turned to armed struggle. Part two treats the 1990s transition and the post-Soviet crisis. Part three examines the party's search for socialism after the 1994 election, and a short conclusion assesses its present difficulties. Zhang's central claim is that the SACP's durability rests on a theoretical line and an organisational form. The theory is "colonialism of a special type" and the "two-stage revolution": a national democratic revolution first, then socialism. The form is the Tripartite Alliance with the African National Congress (ANC) and the Congress of South African Trade Unions (COSATU). After 1990 the party reassessed socialism, following Joe Slovo's argument that the Soviet model, not socialism, had failed. It kept Marxism-Leninism while accepting multiparty politics, and it defined itself as a "mass vanguard party" focused on organised industrial workers. After 1994 it pursued socialism by three routes: taking part in government through ANC lists, reshaping the Alliance (notably the Alliance Political Council from 2008 and the 2019 reconfiguration document), and mass campaigns such as the Red October Campaign, which Zhang links to the National Health Insurance plan. Zhang concludes that the SACP, now said to have over 300,000 members and to be the second-largest party, still depends on the Alliance. Its two pillars are weakened: the ANC by factionalism and corruption, and COSATU by fragmentation. The party therefore pushes for ANC renewal and Alliance reconfiguration while exploring contesting elections independently. Zhang notes that whether it eventually leaves the Alliance depends on the Alliance's development and the ANC's direction. Read the original if you want a detailed, Chinese-perspective history of the SACP and its strategy within the ANC-led Alliance.

Historical nihilism in the Soviet Union under Gorbachev: its manifestations, essence and harm 戈尔巴乔夫时期苏联历史虚无主义的表现、实质及危害 Wang Tingyou Writing in 2021, thirty years after the Soviet collapse, Wang Tingyou asks how historical nihilism, as it spread under Gorbachev, helped destroy the Soviet Communist Party and state. The article defines historical nihilism, in the sense used by socialist states, as a current of thought that disparages Communist leaders and heroes and distorts the party's history. In the author's account, its aim is to dissolve socialist ideology, shake the party's ruling position and restore capitalism. Wang's thesis is that it was an important, unavoidable factor in the collapse, driven by Soviet leaders and Western ideological penetration. The article has five sections. It first examines Gorbachev's unrestricted "openness" (glasnost) and the press freedom it brought. It then surveys the nihilist tide in literature, journalism and historiography, including the "blank spots" campaign, the "Great Purge" death tolls, and attacks on Lenin, Marxism and the army. A third section deals with the role of Gorbachev and Yakovlev. A fourth covers Western broadcasting, exchanges, Nobel prizes and foundations, and a fifth draws lessons. Wang argues that Lenin's idea of openness was limited and bounded by discipline and secrecy, whereas Gorbachev's became a one-way street for anti-communist views. The Nina Andreyeva affair is the author's example. Wang concedes that deep-seated Soviet problems gave nihilism its soil, but holds that Gorbachev and Yakovlev played the decisive part. They attacked Marxism-Leninism as an "ideological monopoly", used the language of humanism and "alienation" to call for abolishing the party's leading role, and replaced editors with sympathisers. The author adds that the West used media, student exchanges, prizes and foundations to cultivate pro-Western figures. The harms Wang lists are the loss of the party's ideology and legitimacy, the dismantling of socialist institutions and the stoking of ethnic separatism. Wang draws four lessons, citing Xi Jinping's 2013 remarks on the Soviet collapse. History and leaders such as Stalin must be assessed scientifically, which the author says the Soviet party never did. Marxism's guiding position and communist ideals must be maintained. Ideological work and its leadership must be taken seriously. Defences against Western ideological penetration must be strengthened, along with core socialist values and national unity education. Read the original if you want a Chinese official-academic account of the Soviet collapse that is rich in Soviet-era citations and explains how historical nihilism is understood in China's current ideological debates.

The historical evolution and present predicament of the German Social Democratic Party 德国社会民主党的历史变迁与现实困境 Wu Huiping Wu Huiping asks why the German Social Democratic Party (SPD), the country's oldest party and once the political voice of the working class, has fallen into a lasting crisis in the twenty-first century. The article presents the SPD as a microcosm of the condition of Western left parties, especially centre-left parties in Europe. Wu argues that the crisis stems from a mix of structural change in Western democracy, shifts in the electorate and the party's own strategic choices, and that the party's reforms have so far had only partial success. The article opens with the SPD's history from Lassalle's General German Workers' Association (1863) to the present, covering its periods in opposition, persecution and government. It then traces the eight party programmes from Eisenach (1869) to Hamburg (2007), and describes the party's social base and organisation. A section on current symptoms uses figures on vote share, polling, membership and age structure. The analysis of causes draws on Oskar Niedermayer's framework of party competition, and the article ends by reviewing the SPD's reform measures up to the 2021 federal election. Wu's core explanation works on three levels. First, the framework conditions have changed. Parties have lost standing to social movements, and the Greens, German unification and the refugee crisis have intensified competition from both left and right. Second, the electorate has fragmented. Industrial workers fell from 42.9% to 24% of employment between 1950 and 2020, and loyal voters have given way to swing voters. Third, the party itself has weakened its profile. The 1959 Godesberg Programme moved it to a centre-left catch-all stance, and Schröder's market-oriented labour reforms alienated its working-class base. Wu also points to the dilemma of junior partnership in grand coalitions, factional struggles and unstable leadership. Wu reviews the SPD's response: renewing the social justice agenda (minimum wage, a citizens' income), taking up digitalisation and climate protection alongside a critique of capitalism, and widening intra-party and public participation through primaries and member ballots. The article notes that the SPD narrowly came first in the September 2021 federal election, which Wu attributes largely to mistakes by rival candidates and the steadiness of Olaf Scholz. Wu holds that two structural problems remain: a split over whether to return to a social justice profile or keep the politics of consensus, and low participation in the new democratic procedures. Read the original if you want a data-rich account of the SPD's programmes, decline and reforms, written from a Chinese academic standpoint just before the 2021 election.

The people's democracy of the Paris Commune and its lessons for today 巴黎公社的人民民主及当今镜鉴 Chai Shangjin Marking the 150th anniversary of the Paris Commune, Chai Shangjin asks what its short life (72 days) reveals about the essential features of a socialist state system. The article argues that the Commune was the first great attempt at proletarian dictatorship and a "new, truly democratic state power", and that its principles point the way for building socialist institutions and improving governance today. The article has three main sections. The first reconstructs the Commune's character from Marx, Engels and Lenin: its fusion of legislative and executive functions, universal election and recall of officials, and a "cheap government" with low salaries. The second traces the line from the Commune through Lenin's soviets to Mao Zedong's people's democratic dictatorship and today's Chinese institutions, covering popular sovereignty, proletarian dictatorship and Party leadership. The third uses the Commune as a mirror for criticising Western representative democracy. Chai's central claim is that "the people as masters of the country" is the essence of socialism, and that it rests on proletarian dictatorship and on leadership by a communist party, whose absence the author names as a main reason for the Commune's defeat. On this basis the author describes China's system as one of fused legislative and executive power, in which multi-party cooperation and consultation replace Western party competition. Western representative democracy is characterised as electoral democracy, elite rule on behalf of monopoly capital, and a separation of powers degraded into partisan conflict; the article cites US election disputes and the Capitol events as evidence. Following Engels, Chai holds that the form of government (zhengti) is determined by the class nature of the state (guoti). Chai concludes that the superiority of a system is not a matter of design but is shown through comparison with capitalism and through concrete history. The article endorses Xi Jinping's "eight criteria" for judging whether a political system is democratic and effective, and calls for continuing to improve the system of people's mastery of the country. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Party-affiliated scholar draws on the Paris Commune to defend socialist democracy and criticise Western democratic models.

Main challenges, lessons and implications for centenarian political parties abroad 国外百年政党面临的主要挑战、经验教训及启示 Qian Yingchao Zhong Lianfa Written for the centenary of the Communist Party of China (2021), this article looks at what the history of other long-lived parties can teach. The authors note that more than 70 well-known parties abroad are at least a century old and still active. They include the British Conservative and Labour parties, the US Democratic and Republican parties, the German and Swedish social democrats, the African National Congress and the Indian National Congress. Qian and Zhong argue that these parties face growing, largely unprecedented difficulties, but that their record also holds experience and warnings useful as a mirror for the CPC. The article has three parts. The first sets out four shared challenges since the Cold War, especially since 2000. The second draws five historical lessons of success and five of failure from cases across Europe, Latin America, South Asia, Africa and Mongolia. The third offers five reflections on what drives the rise and fall of such parties. Much of the evidence is electoral and membership data, for example the fall in Labour's vote share and the Indian National Congress's 2014 defeat. On the challenges, the authors point to globalization, informatization and new media weakening old parties' mobilising power. They also cite depoliticization, falling public trust and membership, the rise of new and populist parties, and the decline of some major parties, especially centre-left socialist parties. Among the successes they list a relatively clear guiding ideology that is adjusted flexibly, a broader social base, relatively democratic and tolerant inner-party life, historical contributions to nation-building or welfare states, and electoral systems favourable to the established parties. The failures they list are weak and frequently replaced leaders, factionalism and splits, corruption, sharp policy swings, and dynastic or family rule. From this the authors derive five points. Steadfast ideals sustain parties, including non-governing communist parties that survived hostile conditions. Leaders matter directly. Unity is a party's lifeline. Reform and self-renewal are essential but must be kept in proportion, as the German social democrats' case shows. Strong delivery on promises is needed to hold public trust. Qian and Zhong conclude that the comparison helps clarify the laws of party development and supports the CPC's confidence as the world's largest Marxist governing party in pursuing its second centenary goal. They say some declining parties still retain a capacity for self-repair. The article is written from within the Party's own framework and uses Xi Jinping's July 2021 speech as its closing frame. Read the original if you want a Chinese Party-affiliated scholars' overview of foreign centenarian parties, with the country-by-country data and cases behind the authors' lessons for the CPC.

The major influence of "On Practice" and "On Contradiction" on China's scientific and technological development 《实践论》《矛盾论》推动我国科技发展的重大影响 Cui Haiying Cui Haiying asks how Mao Zedong's philosophical essays "On Practice" and "On Contradiction" (the "two essays") have shaped science and technology in China, and what they offer to the present drive for high-level scientific and technological self-reliance. The article argues that the essays have guided science policy, scientists' thinking and shop-floor production since the 1950s, and that they remain a worldview and a method for the Party's technology work in the new era. The article has three parts. The first surveys how the essays were studied and applied: in science planning and management, in the thinking of leading scientists, among grassroots technicians and workers, and among foreign physicists. The second analyses the internal link between the essays and technological development at three levels: textual, theoretical and practical. The third draws three lessons for self-reliance in science and technology. In the historical survey, Cui cites the 1956–1967 and 1963–1972 science plans, the Daqing oilfield campaign's 1960 decision to study the essays, and testimony from Qian Xuesen, Li Siguang, Zhu Kezhen and Yuan Longping on how the essays informed their work. Cui also cites Japanese physicists such as Sakata Shoichi, and Sheldon Glashow's proposal to name possible deeper constituents of quarks "Mao particles". The author then shows that Mao drew on natural science to build his arguments, and claims that the essays underpin the Party's technology worldview through three habits of thought: seeking truth from facts, dialectical development and a people-centred orientation. The author contrasts the last with Western technology driven by capital and the pursuit of surplus value. In method, the essays are said to yield a hard-working practical spirit and a strong problem-orientation. Cui proposes three lessons. The first is to keep Party leadership unchanged while speeding up institutional adjustment, including a new type of whole-nation system. The second is to rely on internal factors, meaning self-reliance, while using external factors through open cooperation. The third is to unify the subjective and objective worlds by advancing technical innovation, from basic research to core technologies, while holding to a people's standpoint. Read the original if you want a detailed, Party-theoretical account of how Mao's philosophy has been applied to science policy and scientific practice, with many cited cases.

An assessment of the Polish Communist Party's understanding of new trends in contemporary capitalism 波兰共产党对当代资本主义发展新态势的认识评析 Yang Yousun Yang Yousun examines how the Polish Communist Party, a small non-governing party founded in 2002, understands contemporary capitalism. The author treats the party as representative of communist parties in Central and Eastern Europe that are out of power. The article's thesis is that the party's views are both scientific and progressive in many respects and clearly dogmatic and limited in others. The article first traces three successive parties called the Polish Communist Party, from the Luxemburg-led party of 1918 to the present one, which Yang describes as relatively moderate and stable. It then sets out the party's positions under six headings: the collapse of socialism and Poland's capitalist transition; domestic problems under capitalism; the stage of world capitalism; opposition to hegemonism and to NATO and the EU; labour rights; and plans to rebuild socialism. Yang then assesses these positions using Luke March's typologies of the far left, and ends with the party's prospects. The party calls the transition after 1989 a restoration of capitalist relations of production, and describes the current stage as 'globalized imperialism'. It blames capitalism for corruption, bloated administration, a Catholic Church that has become capitalism's appendage, and worsening conditions for workers. It also demands nationalization, central planning, a shorter working week and Poland's exit from the EU and NATO. Yang classes the party as a conservative member of the radical left and a mainly reformist communist party that keeps some conservative traces. Yang praises its support for labour rights, secularism, gender equality and free education, and its pragmatic choice to take part in elections. Yang criticizes its blanket opposition to free-trade bodies, globalization, the Church and the market economy. Yang cites 2018 Eurobarometer data showing 71 per cent of Poles feel close to the EU, and notes that over 90 per cent of Poles are Catholic. Yang concludes that membership remains small (300 registered members in 2017) and that revival will take time, but that the party has long-term vitality. Three reasons are given: capitalism's basic contradictions persist and have been sharpened by the 2008 crisis and the pandemic; the working-class base survives in the employer–worker cleavage; and communist parties are increasingly cooperating internationally. The right-wing Law and Justice government's repression is expected to bring only short-term pressure. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic assessment of a small European communist party, with detail on its programme, its typology and the evidence behind the author's verdict.

Drawing boundless strength from the Yan'an Spirit 从延安精神中汲取无穷力量 Zhao Yaohong Marking the Party's centenary in 2021, Zhao Yaohong asks what the Yan'an Spirit consists of and why it still matters. The author argues that this spirit, formed during the Yan'an period, is a treasure of the Party's spiritual lineage. Zhao holds that studying its scientific content and present-day value helps Party members pass on the "red gene", take on new missions and open new prospects. The article, first published in Red Flag Manuscripts, has three parts. The first describes how the Yan'an Spirit took shape, citing the period's achievements: the sinicization of Marxism, the writing of Mao Zedong Thought into the Party constitution, a mature central leadership and the experience of governing the Shaan-Gan-Ning Border Region. The second sets out its content. The third draws out its contemporary value, quoting Xi Jinping throughout. Zhao characterises the Yan'an Spirit as thoroughly revolutionary, as a sublimated national spirit, as the spirit of an era devoted to national independence and people's liberation, and as a collective spirit with broad popular roots. Its content has four elements: a firm and correct political direction, the ideological line of emancipating the mind and seeking truth from facts, the fundamental purpose of serving the people wholeheartedly, and the pioneering spirit of self-reliance and hard struggle. The author treats these as the spirit's soul, essence, nature and distinguishing feature. In Zhao's account, self-reliance showed in rejecting the dogmatising of Marxism and the sanctifying of Comintern instructions, in keeping independence within the united front, and in surviving blockade and the Japanese "three alls" policy. Zhao concludes that each element should guide Party members and officials today. They should strengthen ideals and convictions, including by studying Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. They should practise seeking truth from facts, which includes Party self-reform and criticism and self-criticism. They should keep the people at the highest place in their hearts, oppose formalism and bureaucratism, and improve mass work. They should also keep up hard struggle in peacetime and oppose hedonism and listlessness. Read the original if you want to see how a Party-school scholar presents the Yan'an Spirit as a framework for Party-building education at the centenary.

The Long March: red flags fluttering in the west wind 长征，红旗漫卷西风 Shi Zhongquan Marking the 85th anniversary of the Red Army's Long March and the centenary of the Communist Party (2021), Shi Zhongquan sets out what the Long March was, how the Zunyi Meeting turned the Party's fortunes, and what the "Long March spirit" means for today. The article, first published in Red Flag Manuscripts (Hongqi Wengao), takes Xi Jinping's 2016 speech on the 80th anniversary as its guide. Shi argues that studying the Long March and its spirit is the best way to commemorate the Party's centenary and to "walk well the Long March of the new era". The article has three parts. The first describes the march of 1934–1936: its scale, its changing routes and destinations, and the final meeting of the three main Red Army forces in October 1936. The second traces the Zunyi Meeting and the meetings before and after it. The third lists the components of the Long March spirit and draws lessons for the present, quoting Mao Zedong's poems and veterans' recollections as illustration. On Zunyi, Shi contends that Mao Zedong's leadership was established gradually. The heavy losses at the Xiang River, which Shi attributes to mistaken leadership decisions, discredited the "Left" line. Meetings at Tongdao, Liping and Houchang then curbed the military authority of Bo Gu and Otto Braun (Li De). Zunyi ended "Left" dogmatism in practice, and later meetings at Goukan, Gougba and Huili consolidated Mao's position. Shi then presents the Long March spirit as five elements: revolutionary ideals, fearlessness of hardship and sacrifice, seeking truth from facts, putting the overall situation and discipline first, and reliance on the people. Shi holds that courage alone is not enough, and that only a correct line turns it into victory. For the new era, Shi calls for upholding firm ideals and convictions, seeking truth from facts and opening new horizons for adapting Marxism to China, strengthening unity and discipline, and following the Party's mass line. The article ties these to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, to common prosperity and to the risks of a world undergoing changes "unseen in a century". It closes by describing the Long March spirit as an inexhaustible source of strength for the "two centenary goals". Read the original if you want an official Party-historian account of the Long March, the Zunyi Meeting and the Long March spirit as used in the 2021 centenary commemorations.

The Autumn Harvest Uprising: the great beginning of a new path for the Chinese revolution 秋收起义：中国革命新道路的伟大开端 Tang Zhengmang Marking the Party's centenary period, Tang Zhengmang revisits the Autumn Harvest Uprising of 9 September 1927, led by Mao Zedong on the Hunan–Jiangxi border. The article, published in Red Flag Manuscripts (Hongqi Wengao), argues that the uprising was the great beginning of the new revolutionary path of "encircling the cities from the countryside and seizing power by armed force". Tang follows Deng Xiaoping in treating the discovery of this path as Mao's greatest achievement. The piece is organised around six themes, each with its own heading: raising the Party's red flag; correcting the direction of advance and opening a rural base; placing the Party branch at company level; introducing democracy in the army; creating the first army discipline; and persevering through setbacks. Tang draws on Mao's letter to the Central Committee, the Sanwan reorganisation of late September 1927, and accounts of the later reactions of Liu Bocheng, Zhu De and Peng Dehuai. Tang contrasts the uprising with the Nanchang Uprising, which still flew the banner of the left Kuomintang. By abandoning that banner and adopting the hammer-and-sickle flag, the article says, the uprising began armed struggle independently led by the Communist Party. On strategy, Tang notes that the plan to take Changsha, in line with the "city-centred" model, failed, and that Mao's decision at Wenjiashi to turn toward the weakly defended countryside took the first step on the new path. Tang credits the Sanwan measures with building a new type of people's army: Party branches at company level, soldiers' committees and the abolition of officer abuse, and early rules that later became the "Three Main Rules of Discipline and Eight Points for Attention". Tang stresses that the uprising was not a string of victories. The forces fell from over 5,000 to about 1,500 men, commander Lu Deming was killed, and Mao himself was briefly captured. Tang presents Mao's steadfastness, including the remark about a small stone breaking Chiang Kai-shek's great water jar, as the spirit that carried the red flag to the Jinggang Mountains. The article concludes that the uprising made important explorations on major questions of the revolution and of building the people's army, and that this path led to final victory in the New Democratic revolution. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-history writing in 2021 presents the Autumn Harvest Uprising and its legacy for army-building.

Letting the Jinggangshan spirit shine with new light for our times 让井冈山精神放射出新的时代光芒 Kuang Sheng Writing in the centenary year of the Communist Party of China (2021), Kuang Sheng asks how the Jinggangshan spirit, formed in the revolutionary base of 1927–1930, should be carried forward under present conditions. Starting from Xi Jinping's 2016 remarks that Jinggangshan was the cradle of the Chinese revolution, Kuang argues that its core is firm conviction and hard struggle, seeking truth from facts and daring to open new paths, and relying on the masses to win victory. Each element, the article holds, must be given a contemporary form. The commentary is organised around four injunctions: to be steadfast believers in the lofty communist ideal and the common ideal of socialism with Chinese characteristics; to place innovation at the centre of national development; to keep up a tireless spirit and an unflinching fighting posture; and to remain the people's servants while meeting their new expectations of a better life. Each section opens with a Jinggangshan episode and then turns to present-day tasks. Kuang draws on Mao Zedong's Jinggangshan-era ideas and on Xi Jinping's formulations. Kuang argues that belief in Marxism is the soul of the Jinggangshan spirit, since genuine communists did not waver after the 1927 defeat. The article says that some cadres' ideals wavered after reform and opening up, and it links firm conviction to confidence in the path, theory, system and culture of socialism with Chinese characteristics. On innovation, Kuang notes that Mao combined Marxist universal truth with Chinese realities and found a rural-centred revolutionary path that "Marx and Lenin never mentioned". In the same way, the new development philosophy and reform are presented as answers to unprecedented problems. On hard struggle, Kuang stresses that China remains in the primary stage of socialism, and calls for strategic resolve and stronger governing capacity. Kuang says the victory in the campaign against poverty is a new starting point and not an endpoint. Uneven development, urban–rural gaps and common prosperity remain demanding tasks. The article calls for a people-centred approach, for the people to be treated as the makers of history, and for consolidating the broadest united front, including harmony among parties, ethnic groups, religions and social strata, and mutual respect among civilisations. Read the original if you want an example of how Party-school commentary turns a revolutionary-era "spirit" into guidance for cadres at the start of the Fourteenth Five-Year Plan period.

Mao Zedong's struggle at Anyuan in keeping to the Party's original aspiration, and its lessons for today 毛泽东在安源的初心奋斗与现实启示 Huang Le Published in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2021, during the Party History Study and Education campaign, this commentary asks how Mao Zedong's work at Anyuan embodied the Communist Party's original aspiration and mission (chuxin shiming). Huang argues that Anyuan, where Mao and others led a ten-year workers' movement from 1921 to 1930, was a key place where Communists first put that mission into practice. The author draws practical lessons for Party members today. The article has three parts. The first presents Anyuan as a model of building the Party among industrial workers and recounts its pioneering steps. The second follows Mao's visits to Anyuan from 1920 to 1930. The third turns to three lessons for the present, introduced with a quotation from Xi Jinping on political awareness and the Party's original aspiration. Huang's central claim is that Anyuan answered basic questions of the Party's early years: how to rely on the working class, how to join Marxism to the workers' movement, how to organise the Party among industrial workers, and how to form a people's army of workers and peasants. The author lists early initiatives such as a Party organisation among workers (1922), a Party-led economic organisation (1922), anti-corruption work (1923) and a Party school (1924). In Huang's account, Mao went down the mines, lived among workers and learned that Communists must change their own attitudes before they could be accepted. Mao also set strategy at critical moments, including the "army of the aggrieved is bound to win" line before the strike and the 1927 Autumn Harvest Uprising planning at Anyuan. Huang draws three lessons. Party members should treat the people as teachers and learn from them with sincerity and humility. They should earn the people's trust, admiration and respect through sacrifice, ability and integrity. Whether they keep the original aspiration is proved by real achievements in practice, not by words. The author ties these lessons to the 14th Five-Year Plan and the new journey of building a modern socialist country. Read the original if you want a Party-history commentary that uses Anyuan to support present-day arguments about Party conduct and mass work, written by a local specialist in Red culture.

The Soviet revolution: an important historical stage in laying the Party's foundations 苏维埃革命：建基立业的重要历史阶段 He Youliang Written for the centenary of the Communist Party of China in 2021, this article asks what place the Chinese Soviet revolution (1927–1937), also called the Agrarian Revolution, holds in the Party's hundred-year history. He Youliang argues that it was a short but pivotal stage in which the Party, facing a threat to its survival, drew on the Soviet Russian model and Comintern support and then independently led the Chinese revolution. In the author's account, it laid the Party's foundations and solved the problems of survival, finding a way forward and building a base. The article is a short commentary in Hongqi Wengao. It first defines the Soviet revolution as armed struggle, land revolution and the building of people's political power. It then sets out six contributions: institutional foundations, a path or model, ways of governing, theoretical results, spiritual character, and lessons from experience. Each is linked to later developments in the Party's history. On institutions, He argues that the Soviet (workers', peasants' and soldiers') congress system, the principle that the Party commands the gun, and people's war set the basis for the Party's leading position. The author treats the people's congress system of the new China as an inheritance and development of the Soviet congresses. On the path, He says the Party found that the Soviet Russian city-centred model did not fit China and switched to encircling the cities from the countryside, with the peasantry as the main force. He cites a Nationalist official who compared the Party's relation to the peasants to fish in water and the Nationalists' to fish on sand. The base areas gave the Party its first experience of partial rule, and Mao Zedong's writings of the period set out the core of what later became Mao Zedong Thought: seeking truth from facts, the mass line and independence. He adds that the Jinggangshan, Soviet Area and Long March spirits became part of the Party's "red genes". The Party later treated the period's errors as lessons, sublating the Soviet model and developing the theory of New Democracy that led to the 1949 victory. The author concludes that the period's practice and legacy merit continued study. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned Chinese account of how Party historians present the 1927–1937 Soviet period as a foundation for later Party rule.

The emotional meaning of the Communist Party of China's hundred-year history 中国共产党百年历史的情感意蕴 Chen Jinlong Writing in Guangming Daily in August 2021, in the run-up to the Party's centenary commentary season, Chen Jinlong asks what emotional values have been built up over the Communist Party of China's hundred years and what they show about the Party. Chen holds that emotion shapes not only individuals but also the value orientation and goals of states, nations and parties. The article argues that the Party's emotional character has five elements, and that it offers one way of explaining "why the Party is able" to succeed. The short piece is organised under five headings: cherishing history, respect for the people, deep love for the country, pride in the nation, and dedication to the world. Under each, Chen draws on statements by Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping, along with commemorative practices and policy initiatives, as evidence of the sentiment in question. On history, Chen argues that the Party judges the past by historical materialism and dialectical thinking, and shows its attachment through memorials, anniversaries and national commemoration days. On the people, the article holds that the Party's original aspiration and mission, its principle of serving the people wholeheartedly and its mass line express respect for the people's strength and interests, including the pursuit of common prosperity. Love of country is traced from Mao's hopes for a free, prosperous and civilised China through the Four Modernizations, the "three-step" strategy and the Two Centenary Goals. Chen reads pride in the nation in remarks on Chinese civilisation, national character and the Chinese Dream, and dedication to the world in internationalist commitments from the anti-fascist war to a community with a shared future for mankind and the Belt and Road Initiative. Chen concludes that these five sentiments give the Party an emotional image and personal appeal. The Party's success, in this account, results from many factors working together, among which emotion is an important one. Read the original if you want a brief example of how official commentary in 2021 framed the Party's centenary through affect and sentiment rather than institutions or policy.

The Communist Party of China's historical experience in building a socialist state 中国共产党建设社会主义国家的历史经验 Liu Fangliang Liu Fangliang asks what historical experience the Communist Party of China has accumulated in building and perfecting a socialist state system. Writing in a newspaper commentary in 2021, Liu argues that the Party has followed a path of "theory as guide, mechanisms in operation, governance as advance" in constructing and developing national institutions. The piece moves through three stages. It first treats the adaptation of Marxist political theory to China, from the revolutionary period through the founding of the People's Republic to the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978). It then turns to institutional mechanisms, and finally to the modernization of the national governance system and governance capacity. Liu argues that the classics left open how a backward Eastern country should build its institutions after crossing the "Caudine Forks", so the Party had to answer this through Chinese conditions. Liu holds that the core institutions stay fixed, namely Party leadership, a predominantly public-ownership economy and the people's democratic dictatorship. Mechanisms such as consultation, supervision and market regulation are adjusted flexibly, and foreign practice is borrowed only at the mechanism level. Since the Third Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2013), Liu says, comprehensive deepening of reform has aimed at modernizing the national governance system and governance capacity, which Liu presents as the next stage of institutional development. Liu concludes that treating governance as the concentrated expression of institutions and their execution criticises and goes beyond Western "society-centred" governance theories, which Liu says dissolve government and neglect authority. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official narrative on how the Party links theory, institutions and governance.

The ethical functions of China's new type of party system 中国新型政党制度的伦理功能 Zhan Shiyou Writing in Guangming Daily (16 August 2021), Zhan Shiyou asks what political-ethical work China's new type of party system does. Zhan argues that the system, built on Communist Party leadership and multi-party cooperation, serves the public good of Chinese society. It does so through five functions: political participation, interest expression, social integration, democratic oversight and the maintenance of stability. The short commentary takes each function in turn under its own heading. It describes the system as rooted in the pre-1949 cooperation between the Communist Party and the democratic parties, and it sets this against party systems of rotation in office and adversarial competition. Zhan's central claim is that the democratic parties are participating parties, not opposition parties, and that consultation channels bring their views into major policy. In interest expression, Zhan holds that the parties should integrate the demands of particular strata into the fundamental interests of the people, turning "interest disputes" into "interest integration". Zhan presents integration as working through Party organisation at every level, grassroots Party building and shared ideals. Democratic oversight is said to help the Party govern scientifically, democratically and in accordance with law, and Zhan cites the 13th Five-Year Plan period as an example. Zhan also contends that the system avoids the social division produced by decisions made from party, class or regional standpoints. Zhan concludes that the system puts into practice a political ethic of "using good to achieve good". Zhan sees it as producing considerable governance effectiveness and as a major contribution to human political civilisation. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how Chinese commentators frame the multi-party cooperation system in ethical terms.

Promoting a community with a shared future for mankind: the mission and responsibility of the Communist Party of China in the new era 推动构建人类命运共同体：新时代中国共产党的使命担当 Liu Guizhen Writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in July 2021, shortly after Xi Jinping's speech marking the Party's centenary, Liu Guizhen takes up one of the "nine musts" set out there: the need to keep promoting a community with a shared future for mankind. The article argues that this task expresses the Communist Party of China's concern for humanity's future and its responsibility to seek peace and development for all. Liu holds that the Party has the capacity and the duty to play a larger role in global affairs. The commentary is organised in three parts. The first sets out the Party's historical and cultural foundations, the second its practical basis, and the third its value orientation. It moves from classical Chinese texts and the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence to poverty reduction, the pandemic response, Chinese modernization and the Belt and Road Initiative, and finally to the notion of common values of humanity. Liu first traces the idea to traditional Chinese thought on harmony, citing the Book of Documents and the Book of Rites. The author then follows a line of continuity from Zhou Enlai's Five Principles in 1953 and Deng Xiaoping's judgement that peace and development are the two major themes of the age, through to the 18th Party Congress (2012) and Xi's 2015 United Nations speech. In the practical section Liu cites figures: 98.99 million rural people lifted out of poverty, agreements with 140 countries and 32 international organisations under the Belt and Road Initiative, and over 350 million vaccine doses supplied abroad by 1 June 2021. Liu contrasts Chinese modernization, described as peaceful, with Western modernization achieved through plunder and war. The third part presents the Party's people-centred stance as the source of the idea. Liu says the common values of humanity (peace, development, equity, justice, democracy and freedom) are the international reflection of that stance, and differ from "universal values" drawn along ideological lines. Liu concludes that the pandemic shows humanity to be a community of shared destiny. In this view, abandoning Cold War thinking, upholding multilateralism and pursuing global governance through consultation, joint contribution and shared benefits is the right path. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the Party's official narrative links the shared-future idea to tradition, foreign policy history, pandemic diplomacy and Belt and Road.

The classical Marxist writers on the authority of the proletarian party 经典作家关于无产阶级政党权威的思想 Lü Yao Published in the centenary year of the Chinese Communist Party, this short commentary asks what Marx, Engels and Lenin said about authority in the proletarian party and why it still matters. Lü Yao argues that authority has been a constant issue in the history of the international communist movement, and that the classical writers' arguments give theoretical support for strengthening and upholding the centralised and unified leadership of the Party Central Committee in the new era. The article is organised around two figures. The first part covers Marx and Engels: the 1847 reorganisation of the League of the Just into the Communist League, their dispute with Bakunin's anti-authoritarianism, and Engels's reflections after the Paris Commune. The second part turns to Lenin's work building a new-type party in Russia, drawing on What Is to Be Done?, One Step Forward, Two Steps Back and his later remarks on factionalism. A brief closing section links these ideas to current Party building. Lü presents Marx and Engels as defending authority on three grounds. Revolution needs it, because united action against the bourgeoisie is impossible without it. The dictatorship of the proletariat needs it to consolidate, organise and build the new state power, as the Commune's lessons showed. And authority and autonomy are dialectically united and relative, so absolutising either is, in Engels's words, absurd. For Lenin, the author reports, a centralised party rests on democratic centralism, on upholding the authority of the Central Committee and of leaders, on discipline and statutes, and on banning factional activity, which Lenin held to be harmful and impermissible, as with the 'Workers' Opposition' after the civil war. Lü concludes that this body of thought has informed the Party's organisational discipline and its institutional system, and that the Party in the new era has put forward the Two Upholds and raised them to the institutional level. Facing great changes unseen in a century, the author calls for placing Party leadership first, firmly upholding the authority and centralised, unified leadership of the Central Committee, and advancing full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned overview of how Chinese commentators draw on Marx, Engels and Lenin to justify central authority in the Party.

Implications of Marx's humanist theory for rural health-based poverty alleviation in China 马克思人本理论对我国农村健康扶贫的启示 Li Xiaoqin Writing in 2021, Li Xiaoqin asks what Marx's theory of the human being (renben lilun) can contribute to China's rural health-based poverty alleviation. The article opens by noting that the number of people lifted out of poverty in China since 1949 exceeds the combined populations of the United States, Russia, Japan and Germany, which it calls a "Chinese miracle". Li argues that Marx's humanist theory, read together with the Communist Party's poverty-relief experience, helps identify the internal laws of anti-poverty work and has both theoretical and practical significance for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The article has three parts. The first summarises Marx's view of the human being under three headings: the essence of the human being, human subjectivity, and the free and all-round development of the person. The second identifies three problems in current rural health-based poverty alleviation. The third draws three lessons from Marx's theory and ends with a short conclusion that links Xi Jinping's statements on rural health poverty relief to this theoretical basis. Li presents Marx's account as follows: human generic essence is free, conscious activity, that is, labour, while the real essence of a person is the ensemble of social relations. People are the subjects of history, with initiative, autonomy and purposiveness. Against this background Li names three problems: poor coordination among policy actors, with fragmented measures and no long-term mechanism beyond the 2020 deadline; weak classified and tiered assistance, leaving heavy costs for serious illness and formalistic chronic-disease management; and weak primary-care capacity, which forces poor patients to seek treatment elsewhere. The lessons follow Marx's formulations. Because poverty stems from alienation under capitalist private property, the author holds that socialism gives anti-poverty work a firm basis. Because people are concrete and historical, policy must meet real needs through targeted measures, big-data registration and dynamic monitoring. Because people exist in social relations, Li calls for mobilising all forces, strengthening primary-care professionals and expanding health education so that rural residents have easier access to treatment and fall ill less often. Li concludes that great practice needs correct understanding to guide it, and that Xi Jinping's statements on rural health poverty relief grow out of his fieldwork in poor areas and are guided by Marx's humanist theory. In Li's view, they inherit earlier thought and open new paths for China's poverty alleviation. Read the original if you want a short example of how Chinese scholars apply Marx's anthropology to a concrete welfare policy field, rural health poverty relief.

The ethical essence of China's new-type party system 中国新型政党制度的伦理本质 Li Yitian This newspaper commentary (Guangming Daily, 16 August 2021) asks why the system of multi-party cooperation and political consultation led by the Communist Party of China has lasted and grown more resilient. Li Yitian argues that, beyond its historical circumstances, the answer lies in the ethical principles the system has consistently upheld. Solidarity, democracy and harmony are said to constrain its development and to form its ethical essence, which distinguishes it from other party systems. The piece opens by presenting the system as a new type of party system rooted in Chinese conditions and in traditional culture. It then takes the three values in turn, in three numbered sections: solidarity, democracy and harmony. On solidarity, Li holds that the system reflects the diversity of interests among Chinese parties and social groups and confirms it institutionally. Recognising differing interests is only a basis, however. Real unity, in Li's account, comes from a shared aim of national independence, people's liberation, national prosperity and the people's wellbeing, which led the democratic parties to choose to work with the Communist Party. On democracy, Li, citing Xi Jinping, says the system seeks the "greatest common denominator" through broad participation and consultation. This, the author argues, gives it ethical legitimacy and makes decisions more scientific. On harmony, Li points to the constitutional leadership of the Communist Party, the participation of democratic parties in state affairs and mutual supervision. Li adds that consultation takes place before, during and after decisions, through meetings, interviews and written exchanges. Li concludes that solidarity, democracy and harmony are built into the system's nature and let it solve Chinese problems as a distinctively Chinese approach. Li presents it as a contribution to modern political civilisation. Read the original if you want a concise official-line account of how Chinese scholars frame the ethical justification of the multi-party cooperation system.

Reflections on the historical limitations of contemporary Western identity politics 当代西方身份政治历史局限性反思 Fang Min Zhu Yun Writing in 2021, against what they call a world undergoing changes unseen in a century, Fang Min and Zhu Yun ask why Western developed countries have struggled since the 2008 financial crisis and the Covid-19 pandemic. They note that thinkers such as Mark Lilla and Francis Fukuyama point to identity politics. The authors argue that contemporary Western identity politics is a historical product of capitalism at a certain stage. In their view it expresses economic and political inequality within capitalism in cultural form, and only the sublation of capitalism can fundamentally resolve it. The article defines identity politics as the politics, arising from the new social movements of the 1960s, of recognising the difference of groups and protecting their rights. It has three parts. The first surveys four forms: the New Left, minority rights movements, the new feminism, and white conservative identity politics. The second examines economic, political and cultural causes. The third sets out three historical limitations. On causes, the authors point to neoliberal globalisation, which they say widened inequality (citing US Census Bureau income shares and Piketty). They also point to a crisis of capitalist democracy, marked by "veto democracy", interest-group capture and declining trust in parties, and to the internal contradictions of multiculturalism. The core argument is that identity politics, as cultural contestation, does not touch private ownership of the means of production. They cite Marx's remark that a Black person becomes a slave only under certain relations. On this reading, the left abandoned class analysis, shifted from emancipatory to performative politics, and became an unwitting ally of neoliberalism. The authors link this to the 2016 Trump vote. The authors further argue that identity politics makes populism a normal feature of Western politics, with left and right populisms each claiming to speak for "the people". They also hold that it threatens world peace through separatism, anti-globalisation and Huntington-style "clash of civilizations" thinking. As an example of the last, they cite a 2019 remark by a US State Department official about China. They conclude that the world's peoples should face the challenge together, and that only by sublating capitalism and building a community with a shared future for mankind can the problem be resolved. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist critique of Western identity politics that draws on Lilla, Fukuyama and Huntington.

Advancing the discipline, academic and discourse systems of contemporary Chinese atheism Studying Xi Jinping's speech at the Symposium on Philosophy and Social Sciences 推进当代中国无神论学科体系、学术体系、话语体系建设 Tian Xinming How should atheism be built as a scholarly discipline in China today? Tian Xinming answers by reading Xi Jinping's speech of 17 May 2016 to the Symposium on Philosophy and Social Sciences, which the article treats as the guiding document for the field. Tian argues that contemporary Chinese atheism must be Marxist atheism, and that its discipline system, academic system and discourse system must be built together under Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The piece appeared in the journal Science and Atheism. The article has three parts. The first defines the fundamental mark of the discipline, namely adherence to Marxism as guiding thought. The second sets out what the construction task involves: a discipline system, an academic system and a discourse system. The third gives the routes to follow, which are integrating three kinds of resources and pursuing problem-oriented theoretical innovation. Tian draws throughout on Engels, Lenin, Mao Zedong's On Practice and Xi's speech. Tian first distinguishes stages of atheism: ancient naive atheism, modern atheism based on natural science, and Marxist atheism. Marxist atheism is called scientific in a stricter sense because it rests on a scientific worldview and view of history. Second, Tian proposes that the discipline system cover historical, theoretical and practical research, plus study of Marxist atheist thought itself. The last is a guide to the discipline but must not replace research on its real object, an argument backed by Engels's warning against using historical materialism as a pretext for not studying history. The academic system is the theory, and the discourse system is the concepts that express it. Tian suggests compiling a general introduction (Gailun) that gathers and assembles existing terms and results. Third, Tian says Marxism is both guiding thought and the primary resource, alongside traditional Chinese culture and foreign scholarship. Tian also takes up questions such as whether Party members may hold religious belief, whether atheist propaganda may reach the general public, and how to counter religious influence. Tian concludes that atheism is a weak discipline that needs to be strengthened. The author proposes that existing results, including the Chinese Atheism Society's recent publications, be integrated into a unified system, and counts this integration as a form of innovation in itself. Tian links the work to full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, religious work and the modernization of national governance. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese scholar of Marxist atheism applies Xi Jinping's guidance on the three systems to the building of an academic discipline.

The mission and tasks of building the disciplinary, academic and discourse systems 学科体系学术体系话语体系建设的使命任务 Qu Lindong Writing in the People's Daily on 2 August 2021, historian Qu Lindong takes up the call to build a disciplinary system, an academic system and a discourse system with Chinese characteristics, Chinese style and Chinese manner (the "three systems"). Qu argues that this is a major task for philosophy and social sciences workers in the new era, and that the three systems form an inseparable whole. The commentary opens with the historical roots of the idea, tracing it to Mao Zedong's 1938 call to give Marxism a Chinese form, and to Xi Jinping's formulation of the task. It then takes each system in turn, using history as the main illustration and drawing on works by Li Dazhao and Bai Shouyi. Qu presents the disciplinary system as the strategic, overall framework, which should be assessed and coordinated to encourage a "large-discipline" awareness and cross-disciplinary work. The academic system is the middle link: it defines each discipline's object, aims, guiding thought, methods and place in society. In Qu's view, combining historical materialism with China's historical reality is the correct path for historiography, and Bai Shouyi's General History of China shows how such a system can be built. The discourse system is the most concrete and complex link. Qu holds that it carries research results to society, and that traditional concepts such as "min ben" (people as the root) and "cai, xue, shi" (talent, learning, insight) can be creatively transformed and joined with Marxist historiography. Qu concludes that discourse-building requires stronger awareness and confidence in national character and continuity, and that the whole undertaking calls for both grand vision and painstaking work. Read the original if you want a short example of how a Chinese historian links the "three systems" agenda to Marxist historiography and to China's traditional historical concepts.

The early critical turn in Marx's critical research An understanding based on Marx's thought in the Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher period 马克思批判性研究中的早期批判转向分析 He Zhendong He Zhendong asks how Marx's mode of critical research changed in the period of the Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher (German-French Annals, 1844), and what that change shows. The article argues that the Introduction to the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right and On the Jewish Question mark an early "critical turn". In this turn Marx moved to a materialist, Feuerbachian standpoint, raised the level of his critique and went beyond his predecessors. The article has four parts. It first examines the theoretical precondition of Marx's critical research, then its practical basis, then the standpoint and form of the early turn. It ends with lessons for present-day Marxist theoretical research. It draws on Marx's doctoral dissertation, his ties to the Berlin Doctors' Club and the Young Hegelians, his Rheinische Zeitung experience, and the 1859 Preface to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy. He first rejects the view that the critique of religion was the starting point of Marx's critical research. In He's account, criticality is an inner way of thinking that Marx already had before he applied it to religion. The German critique of religion was a collective effort by Strauss, Bauer and Feuerbach, and Marx affirmed it only as a stage to be passed through. His own move was from criticising heaven to criticising earth, law and politics. He did this by taking German state philosophy and legal philosophy, as the "copy", as his target, in place of German reality, the "original". On the practical side, He traces the turn to Marx's early intellectual formation and to a four-stage relation with the Young Hegelians: agreement, participation, rupture, transcendence. He also points to the gap between Hegelian philosophy and the material-interest questions Marx met in practice. He concludes that the turn amounted to a shift from idealism to materialism and from revolutionary democracy to communism. He draws three lessons for current research. Scholars should uncover the criticality implicit in the classic texts, since critical theories are plentiful but studies of criticality itself are few. They should absorb "source" theories before examining their own knowledge critically. They should also ask why a given "leaf" comes to block the view of the mountain. Read the original if you want a Chinese-language reading of the early Marx's break with Hegel and the Young Hegelians that centres on method and "criticality" rather than on religion.

Marx's political philosophy and the essence of communist party organisation 马克思政治哲学与共产党组织的本质 Zhang Wenxi Zhang Wenxi asks what Marx meant by the "communist party" and why the question of party organisation has so often been read as a gap in his work. The article argues that Marx's concept cannot be grasped through ideology, class consciousness, special interests or sectarian programmes. In Zhang's reading, it has to be understood ontologically, as a "community of revolutionary proletarians" rooted in material conditions and historical law. The article has two main parts and a short conclusion. The first part, on Marx's supposed "blank space" (liubai), criticises Blanchot, Althusser, Gramsci, Lukács, Badiou and other Western left thinkers who try to fill that gap. It then turns to Lenin as the thinker who revived Marx's concept. The second part offers an "ontological critique" of the concept of the communist party. It draws on the Communist Manifesto, the Marx–Proudhon dispute, the translation of "communisme" and the Paris Commune. Zhang contends that Western Marxists misread Marx by treating the party through transparency of human nature, mystical "community" or the maturity of class consciousness. Lukács, in this account, falls back into a Platonist and subjectivist position. Against this, Zhang says the party's difference from other parties is ontological, not formal. It lies in the relation of domination and being dominated, which the proletarian community aims to abolish. Zhang adds that "communisme" is better rendered as "commonism" (gongtongzhuyi), since the Chinese character for "property" is absent from the French word. The article says this points to a "common" prior to any shared property, interest or value, and that Marx's own definition of the revolutionary party remains open. In the conclusion, Zhang holds that party organisation is not a technical matter and cannot be settled by a rigid, unified theory. Traditional ideas of organisation, in Zhang's account, wrongly set the "backward masses" against the vanguard and ignore Marx's point that changing circumstances and self-change coincide in revolutionary practice. Zhang promises a follow-up article on how the Communist Party of China developed its political form. Read the original if you want a Chinese philosophical engagement with Western Marxist theories of the party, and with the idea of communism as \"commonism\".

The mission and tasks of building the disciplinary, academic and discourse systems 学科体系学术体系话语体系建设的使命任务 Qu Lindong Qu Lindong, a historian, takes up the goal of building disciplinary, academic and discourse systems with Chinese characteristics, Chinese style and Chinese manner (the "three systems"). The piece appeared in the People's Daily on 2 August 2021. Qu argues that the three systems are distinct in emphasis but form one inseparable whole, and that building them is now a major task for Chinese philosophy and social science. Writing mainly from the standpoint of history, Qu first traces the idea to Mao Zedong's 1938 call to give Marxism a Chinese form, and to Xi Jinping's later instruction on building philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics. The article then takes the three systems in turn, using examples from historiography such as Li Dazhao, and Bai Shouyi's General Introduction to Historiography and his multi-volume General History of China. Qu holds that the disciplinary system is strategic and holistic. It should be assessed and coordinated to suit social and scientific change, and it should foster a \"big discipline\" awareness and interdisciplinary work. The academic system is the middle link, in which theory matters most. Qu says that combining historical materialism with Chinese historical reality is the correct path for historical theory. The discourse system carries research results to society and underpins \"discourse power\". Qu proposes that traditional historiographical concepts, such as \"the relation between Heaven and humanity\" and \"talent, learning and insight\", can be creatively transformed and combined with Marxist historiography. Qu concludes that the three systems are a grand undertaking that needs both ambition and painstaking work, and that scholars should advance it steadily. Qu calls for stronger cultural consciousness and confidence, especially regarding national character and continuity in discourse. Read the original if you want a short, official-media statement of how a historian links the three systems to Marxist historiography and Chinese tradition.

The mission and tasks of building the disciplinary, academic and discourse systems 学科体系学术体系话语体系建设的使命任务 Qu Lindong Writing in the People's Daily in August 2021, historian Qu Lindong considers how to build a disciplinary system, an academic system and a discourse system with Chinese characteristics, Chinese style and Chinese manner (the "three systems"). It then takes the three systems in turn, drawing examples mainly from Chinese historiography. On the disciplinary system, Qu stresses overall assessment and coordination, so that disciplines can learn from one another and work across boundaries, citing Li Dazhao's and Bai Shouyi's accounts of history's links to other fields. The academic system, the middle link, is defined by each discipline's nature, and Qu holds that combining historical materialism with Chinese historical reality is the correct path for historical theory, as in Bai Shouyi's General History of China. The discourse system is the most concrete and complex link, because it concerns concepts and terms through which research reaches society. Qu proposes that traditional historiographical concepts, such as "the relation between Heaven and man" and "talent, learning and insight", be transformed creatively and combined with Marxist historiography. Qu concludes that building the three systems is a grand undertaking that needs both ambition and meticulous work. Qu calls for stronger consciousness and confidence about national character and continuity in discourse, and urges scholars to carry the task forward. Read the original if you want a short, officially published statement of how a historian links the "three systems" agenda to Marxist historiography and classical Chinese conceptual resources.

A new look at Spivak's postcolonial feminist critique From the perspective of the theory of imperialist crisis control 斯皮瓦克的后殖民女性主义批判新探 He Najuan Dai Xuehong Does Marxism still explain exploitation in an age of post-industrial prosperity and cultural critique? He and Dai take up this question through Gayatri C. Spivak, whom they present as the first feminist scholar in postcolonial criticism to explain imperialist "crisis control". Their thesis is that Spivak uses a deconstructive reading of Marx's labour theory of value to show how contemporary capitalism shifts its crises onto the Third World and, above all, onto poor women there. For Spivak, they report, cultural and ideological critique alone conceals the material suffering involved. The article has three main sections. The first sets out the contemporary turn in crisis control: its spatial transfer from the imperialist core to the Third World, its transfer from class conflict to gender, and its mixing of pre-modern and modern features. The second gives the political-economy reading, covering use-value, global exploitation and what Spivak calls "epistemic violence". The third turns to her postcolonial feminist critique, which the authors group under three headings, and a short conclusion follows. The authors' central move is Spivak's reading of Marx on use-value. In their account, commodity exchange abstracts away the human labour embedded in goods, as in her example of Nike shoes and Indonesian women workers. This residual labour is a "ghostly" presence, and Spivak treats use-value as a "lever of deconstruction" that could interrupt capitalist circulation. Building on this, she argues that the old worker–capitalist contradiction has become a North–South one. Gender ideology and patriarchal relations obscure the labour–capital contradiction, and women in the global South become a new super-exploited labour force. Spivak's critique of Western feminism has three parts, according to the authors. She deconstructs its claim to universal "sisterhood", which she sees as complicit with imperialism. She traces how the voices of subaltern women are "foreclosed". She also insists on speaking for women within wider institutions and organisations of production, citing the SEWA and Women's World Bank case. The authors conclude that Spivak keeps labour as the sole source of value and sees North–South relations as a continuation of the nineteenth-century capitalist–worker relation. They also note Arif Dirlik's criticism of her. Read the original if you study postcolonial theory, Marxist feminism or the Chinese reception of Spivak as a Marxist thinker.

Anti-corruption governance of the Communist Party of Vietnam in the Đổi Mới period: stages, results and basic lessons 革新时期越南共产党的腐败治理：阶段历程、主要成效与基本经验 Wang Xian Fan Wende Since the launch of Đổi Mới (renovation) in 1986, Vietnam has grown quickly, but the authors note that corruption, which Vietnamese citizens call a 'national calamity', has been one of its 'four major crises'. This article asks how the Communist Party of Vietnam has governed corruption over the period and what China might learn. The authors argue that the Party's approach has moved through three stages, produced real results, and yielded experience that offers 'some reference' for China's own anti-corruption drive. The article has three parts. The first periodises Vietnamese anti-corruption into a campaign stage (1986–2005), a rule-of-law stage (2006–2015) and a comprehensive stage (2016 to the present).
