The second sets out three results: better institutions and specialised bodies, a cleaner political ecology that strengthens the Party's hold on power, and a better climate for economic growth and foreign investment. The third distils four groups of lessons, supported by figures on Party purges, prosecutions, asset declarations and whistle-blower reports. In the authors' account, the early Party rectification campaigns expelled large numbers of members but fell short: a 2000 survey cited in the article found that about 43 per cent of members were suspected of or involved in corruption. The shift began with the 2005 Law on Anti-Corruption, the creation of a central steering committee and an anti-corruption police bureau, and, after the 12th Party Congress (2016), a 'no forbidden zones' policy reaching the military, energy and finance. The authors present the lessons as multi-layered. They list strengthened Party leadership and an anti-'peaceful evolution' struggle, cadre rotation, salary reform and asset declaration, and intra-Party democracy with checks such as the 'four pillars' division of top posts. They add National Assembly questioning, repeatedly amended legislation and Party discipline rules, and combined supervision by the Party, public reporting with rewards, and media exposure. The authors conclude that Vietnam's anti-corruption has curbed corrupt practices to a degree, eased relations between Party and people and consolidated the Party's governing base, though they acknowledge earlier phases did not fundamentally change the situation. They suggest these lessons can inform China's governance of corruption. Read the original if you want a Chinese-published, Party-friendly overview of Vietnamese anti-corruption institutions, with dates, laws and figures, and an indication of what Chinese scholars take from a fellow socialist state.

New trends in the unification of the world's communist parties in recent years and how China should respond 近年来世界共产党联合化新趋势与我们的应对 Yu Weihai Writing in 2021, the centenary year of the Communist Party of China, Yu Weihai asks what the state and trajectory of the international communist movement are amid what the article calls changes unseen in a century. Yu's thesis is that the world's many communist and workers' parties are showing a clear tendency to unite. In Yu's account this differs from the Internationals of the 19th and 20th centuries and amounts to a "new historical feature" that China must study and respond to. The article has four parts. It first describes four manifestations of unification: standing organisational platforms, joint statements, coordinated international struggles and a shared spirit. It then identifies four new features: equal and diverse participants, networked and resonant spatial patterns, continuous and dense activity, and issue-based rather than organisation-based forms. The third part evaluates the trend, and the last sets out policy responses. Evidence includes a list of platforms founded since 1993, the 93-party statement for Lenin's 150th anniversary in 2020, and Yu's own 2019 fieldwork in the United States. Yu argues that unification strengthens the forces opposing capitalism, enlarges the voice of world socialism and renews the content and forms of the movement, which no longer follows "one centre, one line, one model". Yu also stresses limits: some 400 parties, sectarian rivalry, exclusionary platforms, dogmatism and a tension between short-term issues and long-term goals still weaken unity. Many of these parties, Yu notes, criticise socialism with Chinese characteristics, and some call for a new Comintern-style body. Yu proposes that China strengthen research on the international communist movement and on Xi Jinping's theory of a "new type of party relations". Yu rejects calls for the CPC to take up the banner of uniting world socialism and advises a policy of not leading, not carrying the banner, not participating and not opposing. China should instead "develop socialism with Chinese characteristics well", while using the parties' goodwill, as in their praise for China's pandemic response in 2020. This would operate through united-front work, International Department dialogue mechanisms and think tanks. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic and policy view of how the CPC regards the foreign communist parties, with data on their platforms and joint statements.

Marxist political science in Monthly Review in the twenty-first century 21世纪美国《每月评论》的马克思主义政治学研究 Fu Hao Cheng Enfu Fu Hao and Cheng Enfu examine how the American journal Monthly Review, founded by Leo Huberman and Paul Sweezy, has treated Marxist political science since 2000. They argue that the journal has become a representative new force in American left-wing political critique, marked by a radical style, serious scholarship, pluralism and innovative thinking. They also hold that its discussion of some political questions is limited and that its influence on world socialism remains underdeveloped. The article has four parts. It first covers the journal's work on the Marxist theory of the state, then its theory of twenty-first-century imperialism, which the authors divide into three stages. It next turns to its proposals for socialist and eco-socialist revolution. A final section assesses the journal's innovations and limitations. The authors draw mainly on István Mészáros, Michael Lebowitz, Jean-Claude Paye, Noam Chomsky, Samir Amin, William Tabb and John Bellamy Foster. In the authors' account, Mészáros calls for going beyond capital's "Leviathan" state and pursuing substantive equality and democracy. Paye and others criticise the fusion of war law and criminal law, the constitutionalisation of emergency powers, and the prison system. On imperialism, the journal is said to describe a "barbaric empire" (2000–2007), then a period of "cracks in the empire" after the 2008 financial crisis, and from 2016 a "late empire". Foster and Amin reject theories of a "new imperialism" and hold that the present is a stage of global monopoly-finance capital. The journal also characterises Trump's presidency as neo-fascist. For the future, Lebowitz's twenty-first-century socialism rests on a "basic triangle" of social property, social production and social needs, and on producing a "new socialist human being". Foster's eco-socialism relies on an "environmental proletariat" and a two-stage programme, with a minimum programme now and a maximum programme later. The authors credit the journal with three innovations: new theory suited to its time, bold new propositions that go beyond classical Marxism, and an international, pluralist scholarly community. They name three limitations. The journal faces suppression by right-wing forces and financial constraints. It mixes Marxism with Western Marxism and is sometimes metaphysical rather than practical. Its understanding of existing socialist countries, above all socialism with Chinese characteristics, is in their view prejudiced and mistaken. They hope Western left scholars will come to understand it better. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly assessment of Monthly Review's political theory, including how Chinese authors judge its treatment of China.

Knowledge monopoly as an important feature of contemporary capitalism The case of US technological hegemony 知识垄断是当代资本主义的重要特征 Li Yan Writing in 2021, Li Yan asks how knowledge and capital combine in contemporary capitalism and argues that international monopoly capital now practises a "knowledge monopoly" as a defining feature of the system. In the author's account, transnational firms and strategic alliances monopolise the conditions of knowledge production, namely intellectual property and specialised personnel. This gives them control over core technology and, through it, command over non-core production stages, from which they extract surplus value worldwide. The article has three parts. The first reconstructs how Marx and Harry Braverman analysed the union of science and capital. The second sets out five features of present-day knowledge monopoly. The third takes US technological hegemony as a case: domestic promotion of science, the containment of the Soviet Union, Japan and China, and the harms of monopoly. Li draws on Marx's account of science becoming an independent power opposed to labour, and on Braverman's analysis of Taylorism and the separation of "head" from "hand". The author applies this logic to the world economy. Lead firms keep research and design and outsource manufacturing, which sets workers against one another across countries. Intellectual property regimes, patent pools, standards alliances and state power then entrench the monopoly, producing a "centre–periphery" division of labour between "brain" and "limbs". For the US, Li describes federal research funding, talent recruitment, the Bayh-Dole Act (1980) and the TRIPS Agreement (1994). Li contrasts these with export controls on the USSR, trade and technology war on Japan, and entity-list sanctions, visa limits and investigations targeting Huawei and Chinese researchers. In Li's reading, these measures aim to protect monopoly capital's dominance and to keep China "locked in" at the middle and low end of global value chains. Li concludes that knowledge monopoly runs against the socialisation of production and the internationalisation of innovation. It obstructs international cooperation and widens uneven development between countries and between knowledge workers and ordinary workers. Drawing on Lenin on the parasitic character of monopoly capitalism, the author holds that private appropriation turns knowledge, which is shareable and non-rival, into a fetter on scientific progress. Read the original if you want a Marxist political-economy framing of US–China technology conflict, built on Marx, Braverman and Lenin, and a view of how Chinese scholars described it in 2021.

Advancing steadily towards building a community with a shared future for mankind 朝着构建人类命运共同体方向不断迈进 Qin Long Liu Yushan Writing in Guangming Daily in November 2021, Qin Long and Liu Yushan take up Xi Jinping's statement at the centenary of the Communist Party (2021) that 'drawing on history to create the future' requires continuing to build a community with a shared future for mankind. The authors present the concept as part of Xi Jinping's diplomatic thought and as China's answer to the question of where human society should go. They argue that grasping its basic meaning and policy proposals is important for carrying the practice forward. The short commentary has three parts. The first sets out the theoretical, cultural and practical roots of the concept. The second presents it as the Party's responsibility to seek happiness for the people and progress for humanity. The third turns to its policy content in the world economy, international relations and global governance. On roots, the authors claim the concept inherits Marx's idea of the community. In their reading, Marx distinguished 'illusory' communities from the 'real community' in which individuals can be free, and the authors describe the community with a shared future as a transitional form towards the latter. They also trace it to traditional Chinese values of peace and harmony, and to the foreign policy experience from the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence through Deng Xiaoping's judgement that peace and development are the theme of the era. On responsibility, they say it reflects the Party's guidance on humanity's direction, its response to peoples' expectations, and its upholding of the common values of all humanity. On policy, they hold that it favours openness, with the Belt and Road Initiative as a practical platform. They also stress equality among states, rejection of power politics and non-interference, and global governance based on consultation, joint contribution and shared benefits. The authors conclude that, facing great changes unseen in a century and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, the Party will keep to an independent foreign policy of peace. It will also promote the common values of humanity and work with progressive forces towards the community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a concise statement, from the 2021 official-theory perspective, of how the concept is justified through Marxism, Chinese tradition and diplomatic history.

The current state and prospects of the Latin American left 当前拉美左翼的发展现状与前景 Yang Jianmin Writing in 2021, Yang Jianmin asks where the Latin American left stands after the "pink tide" that began with Hugo Chávez's election in Venezuela in 1999, and whether a new cycle of left government is opening. The article argues that the region has moved from "the left retreats, the right advances" (2015–2018) to a phase of mixed gains and losses and power-sharing. The right retains an overall advantage, but Yang holds that the left is recovering, remains seriously divided, and will persist in the region over the long term. The article has four parts. It first traces the shifting political map, from right-wing offensives during the pink tide (the 2002 Venezuelan coup, Honduras 2009, Paraguay 2012) through the rightward swing after 2015 to left victories in Mexico, Argentina, Bolivia and elsewhere. It then examines the effects of the Covid-19 pandemic, elections in Ecuador, Brazil, Peru, Chile and Mexico, and the 2020 US election. A third part contrasts left coordination abroad with fragmentation at home, and a fourth assesses prospects. Yang argues that the pandemic, with its rising poverty, public debt and vaccine scarcity, has led many Latin Americans to question neoliberal policies, which favours the left. Abroad, left parties have cooperated through bodies such as the Puebla Group, while the right-wing Lima Group has weakened after Argentina's withdrawal and Peru's change of stance. At home, Yang identifies three problems: new left forces competing with the traditional left (Chile, Ecuador), policy disagreements once in office (Ecuador under Lenín Moreno), and political fragmentation and ideological polarisation, including the rise of far-left figures. Yang concludes that a new left cycle depends on restoring living conditions and building consensus, proving administrative competence while keeping ties to social movements, and redefining the role of the state. In Yang's view, the previous cycle failed to reform the armed forces, police and judiciary and so lost power. Persistent inequality, poverty of over 30 per cent, expanding political inclusion and party-system change give the left a lasting base. Read the original if you want a Chinese specialist's 2021 assessment of Latin American left politics, country by country, including the electoral data it cites.

Lenin's historical contribution to the ideological doctrine of the new-type Bolshevik party 列宁创建布尔什维克新型政党意识形态学说的历史贡献 Chen Xingliang Chen Xingliang asks how Lenin's treatment of ideology equipped the Bolsheviks to become a new type of proletarian party able to carry the proletarian political revolution over into a socialist social revolution. The article argues that Lenin, working under Marxist guidance and attentive to the changing epoch, established a scientific socialist ideology and interpreted it creatively. In Chen's account this enriched Marxist ideology theory and tied it to Bolshevik practice. The article has three main parts plus a short closing section. It first examines the preconditions: the Russian context at the turn of the twentieth century and Lenin's philosophical and political struggles, including his polemic against empirio-criticism and Bogdanov. It then sets out the distinctive features of Bolshevik party ideology, and finally considers their effect on the fate of the Soviet Union after the October Revolution, through moral education, the Proletkult controversy and the idea of a cultural revolution. Chen's central claim is that, in Lenin's view, the spontaneous workers' movement produces only trade-unionism, which means intellectual subordination to the bourgeoisie. Since no third ideology exists, any weakening of socialist ideology strengthens bourgeois ideology, so socialist consciousness has to be brought to workers by the vanguard through what the article calls inculcation. The Bolsheviks therefore had to act as producers of a scientific, class-based ideology, uniting criticism with revolutionary purpose and treating Marxism as a method rather than a dogma. After 1917, Chen says, Lenin applied this to communist morality for the young and to culture. He rejected the Proletkult school's nihilism toward past culture and held that proletarian culture must absorb the valuable achievements of human thought, while warning against haste in cultural work. Chen concludes that Lenin's ideological principles remained 'living principles' and that the Soviet Union's fate became closely bound up with the Russian Communist Party's reliance on ideology and the way its functions were exercised. In a brief closing section addressed to the present day, Chen calls for safeguarding socialist ideological positions, strengthening cultural confidence and cultural leadership, and for Chinese Communists to build a socialist ideology with strong cohesion and guiding force. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic account of Lenin's theory of ideology, the Proletkult dispute and the link between party ideology and Soviet history.

Trends in the socialist movements of South Asia since the 21st century 21世纪以来南亚社会主义运动的态势分析 Zhang Shulan Zhang Shulan asks how the socialist and communist movements of the eight South Asian states (India, Pakistan, Nepal, Bhutan, Sri Lanka, the Maldives, Bangladesh and Afghanistan) have developed since 2000. Zhang notes that earlier Chinese studies covered only four of these countries and paid little attention to the 21st century. The article's thesis is that the movements share a fragmented structure but show common new trends in domestic alliances, regional geography and international networks. Overall, Zhang judges the movement still weak, with little prospect of near-term revival, yet its trajectory worthy of approval and expectation. The article is organised in four parts. The first sorts the movements into three types: moderate left parties committed to parliamentary struggle, radical left parties within the system, and extreme left parties outside it that pursue armed struggle. Zhang surveys party histories and election results country by country. The remaining parts examine alliances and mergers inside each country, the shifting regional spatial pattern, and the growing international links of South Asian parties. Zhang argues that moderate left parties have declined since the Cold War and are now at a low point, strongest in the mountain states and weakest in the island states. Radical left parties survived the first two decades after the Cold War, but diverge by country: India, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Afghanistan are near their lowest point, while Pakistan shows signs of recovery and Nepal's communists have grown. Extreme left groups, mostly Maoist, have multiplied but face harsher armed struggle because of right-wing repression and because many groups lay down arms and enter parliament. Zhang says left parties increasingly merge or form electoral fronts that last longer than before, driven by a rightward shift in politics, the 2008 financial crisis and the COVID-19 pandemic, and wider cultural and media support. Fragmentation persists, Zhang argues, because of ideological diversity, personality cults and family dominance, and localised bases. Zhang also finds the movement's centre of gravity moving from coastal and island states inland to the mountain states, citing Nepal's 2015 constitution, and legal space expanding, with Afghanistan, Bhutan and the Maldives only recently permitting party politics. On the international side, Zhang reports that moderate and radical parties have joined more international bodies, such as Socialist International and the International Conference of Communist and Workers' Parties. Extreme left groups have built a regional Maoist coordination body, revived a global Maoist platform and joined newer coordination bodies. Zhang concludes that Maoism is a bright spot of the world movement, but that the traditional left remains weak. Read the original if you want a country-by-country survey of South Asian left parties, their alliances and international affiliations, written from a Chinese academic perspective.

Solidly advancing common prosperity through high-quality development 在高质量发展中扎实推进共同富裕 Shi Hong Cheng Jing This commentary in Guangming Daily argues that, in the new stage of development, common prosperity must be advanced through high-quality development. Shi and Cheng hold that the two are highly consistent: each serves as a condition and requirement of the other. The piece begins with the Party's record since the 18th Party Congress (2012), including poverty alleviation and a moderately prosperous society. It then has three parts: why common prosperity is inherent in high-quality development, why high-quality development is the base of common prosperity, and what policies should follow. The authors say high-quality development shifts attention from total output to structural problems, and from "having" to "having well". On this reading, common prosperity is its fundamental purpose and part of its content, through the new development philosophy's principle of sharing. In reverse, high-quality development both "makes the cake bigger", by raising productivity and building a modern economic system, and "divides the cake better", by improving income distribution and narrowing urban–rural and regional gaps. The authors reject both wealth for a few and egalitarianism. The authors propose improving the quality and efficiency of development, with supply-side structural reform and innovation. They also call for upholding the basic economic system and the Two Unwaverings, and for combining distribution according to work with distribution by factors of production. Further proposals include equalising basic public services, advancing ecological civilisation, and enriching cultural life. They tie these to the 2035 and 2050 targets. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned statement of how Party theorists linked common prosperity to high-quality development in 2021.

The correct choice of history and the people 历史和人民的正确选择 Shanghai Research Center for Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era Published in the People's Daily in 2021, the centenary year of the Communist Party of China, this commentary takes up Xi Jinping's statement that history and the people chose the Party to lead the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The Shanghai research centre argues that this choice was correct and must be upheld long-term and without wavering. In its view, retracing how and why the choice was made strengthens the Party's overall leadership, the Party's self-reform and its vitality. The text is organised in three parts: a conscious and rational choice, a continuing and resolute choice, and a correct and inevitable choice. The first covers the period from the Party's founding with about 50 members to the founding of the People's Republic after 28 years. The second moves through socialist transformation, the First Five-Year Plan, reform and opening up, and the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The third explains why the choice is held to be right. The authors present the choice as a process that moved from spontaneous to conscious. Before 1921, they say, other currents and political forces tried to change China and met repeated failure. The Party, armed with scientific theory, won support through land reform, a disciplined army, and its role in the War of Resistance against Japan. They cite Chen Jiageng's 1940 prediction after visiting Chongqing and Yan'an, and Soong Ching-ling's remark at the first session of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference. The people's verdict is then described as renewed in each era through reconstruction and reform, poverty alleviation and the building of a moderately prosperous society, with Xi's line that the era sets the exam, the Party answers and the people grade it. The article concludes that the choice is correct and inevitable for four reasons: the Party keeps to its original aspiration and founding mission, endures hardship and sacrifice through lofty ideals and scientific theory, and maintains strict organisation and discipline under democratic centralism. It describes today's Party as the world's largest Marxist governing party, with over 91 million members and the support of 1.4 billion people. It says the Party will remain invincible if it stays at the forefront of the times and among the people. Read the original if you want an example of the official People's Daily account of the Party's historical legitimacy, as presented in 2021 for the centenary.

Learning Party history to strengthen confidence and gather mighty strength for scientific and technological self-reliance 学史增信 汇聚科技自立自强的磅礴力量 Qu Dacheng Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2021, during the Party History Learning and Education campaign, Qu Dacheng asks what China's scientists and engineers should take from the study of Party history. The article's answer is that the Party's record of leading science and technology, from the revolutionary years to the present, should strengthen the Four-sphere Confidence. It should also build the determination to achieve scientific and technological self-reliance. The piece is a short commentary organised chronologically. It begins with the late Qing and Republican periods, when intellectuals sought national salvation in Western science and founded learned societies. It then covers the Yan'an years, the early People's Republic, the period after the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978), and the era since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Each stage is illustrated with institutions, policies and named scientists. Qu argues that the Party has always valued intellectuals and science. Evidence includes the 1939 decision to recruit intellectuals in large numbers, the Yan'an natural science association, the 1956 call to "march on science", the "Two Bombs, One Satellite" programme, the reform-era slogan that science and technology are the primary productive force, and recent achievements in quantum science, space exploration and vaccines. The author draws a lesson from this history: key core technologies cannot be bought, requested or begged for. Qu holds that the scientists' spirit, which the article lists as patriotic, innovative, rigorous, devoted, collaborative and mentoring, is the moral foundation of this self-reliance. The article also says that China has caught up in some seventy years, and in more than forty years of reform and opening up, with what Western capitalist countries took two or three centuries to build. Qu concludes that scientists should unite around the Party Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core and carry on the self-reliant spirit of earlier generations. The author calls for stronger national strategic science and technology capacity, a larger basic research system, more original "zero to one" results, and the "unveil the list and take command" mechanism for key research projects. The goal is major breakthroughs in key core technologies by 2035 and a place among the leading innovative countries. Read the original if you want a compact example of how official Party-history education is linked to science and technology policy and to the narrative of scientists as patriotic exemplars.

A great revolution in the history of the Chinese people and the Chinese nation 中国人民和中华民族发展史上一次伟大革命 Huang Yibing This commentary, first published in the People's Daily and reposted in October 2021, takes up Xi Jinping's description of reform and opening up as a great awakening of the Party and a great revolution in the history of the Chinese people and nation. Huang Yibing, a deputy director of the Academy of Party History and Literature, argues that the policy was possible because the Party grasped four things: the fate of the Party and country, the lessons of socialist revolution and construction, the trend of the times, and the people's hopes and needs. The piece is organised under four headings that correspond to these four "profound" understandings. It begins with the post-Cultural Revolution question of where China was heading and the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978). It then reviews successive generations of Party leadership from Deng Xiaoping to Xi Jinping, turns to the new technological revolution after the Second World War, and ends with the role of the masses in policy-making. Huang argues that reform and opening up was a decision to shift the Party's work to economic development, liberate and develop the productive forces, and perfect and develop the socialist system rather than abandon it. In the author's account, each leadership generation answered the question of what socialism is and how to build it: Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents, the Scientific Outlook on Development, and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Huang adds that the Party read the era as one of peace and development and, following Deng's thesis that science and technology are a productive force, tied the advantages of the socialist system to advanced technology. The final section holds that every breakthrough in reform came from the practice and wisdom of the people, so the Party must consult the masses and respect their initiative. Huang concludes that over forty years reform and opening up transformed China, the nation, the people and the Party, producing leaps from standing up to growing rich to becoming strong, and from basic subsistence to moderate prosperity. Socialism with Chinese characteristics, in this telling, moved from creation to development to improvement. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the official Party-history narrative presents reform and opening up as continuous with earlier socialist exploration and as a basis for the new era.

The Marxist view of religion and the study of religion in the new era 马克思主义宗教观和新时代宗教学 Jia Runguo Marking the tenth anniversary in 2019 of the Research Office on the Marxist View of Religion at the CASS Institute of World Religions, Jia Runguo argues that religious studies in China has entered a new era in which a Marxist study of religion can be upheld and developed with Chinese characteristics. The author holds that Marxism must remain the guiding ideology of the field, and that the main problems in Chinese religious studies stem from departures from Marxist fundamentals. The piece, published in Science and Atheism, is part retrospective and part programme for the coming decade. The article has four sections. The first restates the founding mission of the field. The second reviews the history of Marxist work on religion from Marx and Engels onwards. The third considers how to study foreign, especially Western liberal, religious studies. The fourth sets out how Marxist religious studies should relate to practice and governance. Jia's central move is to reject the claim that Marxism has a view of religion but no religious studies. The author notes that Marx and Engels were born before Max Müller, began studying religion earlier, and wrote specialised works on it, such as Engels's essays on early Christianity. Jia traces a continuous Marxist tradition through Lenin, early Chinese communists and scholars such as Ren Jiyu. Jia therefore says that only research using scientific theory and methods counts as religious studies, and that research guided by theology should be excluded. The second move concerns the West. Jia says its religious anthropology, sociology and psychology are relatively scientific and worth critical absorption, while Western-centrism, cultural relativism, idealism and the bourgeois standpoint are to be rejected. Jia names Max Weber's The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism as an example of embellishing Christianity and capitalism. Jia calls for Marxist religious studies to be built up in two parts. Theoretical work covers the nature, origins and history of religion and the laws of its emergence, development and disappearance. Empirical work covers the current religious situation at home and abroad, so as to support policy and religious governance. Jia criticises the theologisation and Westernisation of research, and the claimed suspension of belief and academic neutrality, and says these must be firmly abandoned. Jia also complains that the Marxist textbook Religious Studies, part of the Marxist Theory Research and Construction Project, has not been completed in ten years. Read the original if you want a clear statement of the hardline Marxist-atheist position on how religious studies should be organised in China, and of its view of Western scholarship.

Keeping the combative edge of Marxist atheism 保持马克思主义无神论的斗争锋芒 Zhu Weiqun Zhu Weiqun, a former senior United Front official, argues that Marxist atheism in China must not be reduced to a purely philosophical doctrine. In a short piece first published in the journal Science and Atheism and posted in October 2021, Zhu contends that atheism has a political level as well as a philosophical one. Once religious questions are tied to the proletariat's own emancipation, Zhu holds, Marxist atheism necessarily carries a combative edge. The article first sets out the two levels of atheism research and recalls how the Communist Party combined atheism with China's revolutionary and religious realities. It then takes up five disputed questions in turn: whether theism or Marxist atheism brings happiness to the Chinese people; whether Party members may hold religious beliefs; which of the two secures genuine freedom of religious belief; whether atheism should be actively propagated; and whether the freedom not to believe and to propagate atheism is protected by the constitution. Zhu's central claim is that the Party's religious policy works because it rests on a scientific, materialist account of religion, not because it compromises with religion. Zhu maintains that the Party's unity of political programme and worldview distinguishes it from Western parties and underpins its discipline and its rule, so that allowing believers or believing members would bring down the "edifice" of the Party. Zhu warns that weakening atheist propaganda, a change in the balance of believers and non-believers, or a "de-Sinicised" and "extremist" religion linked to foreign forces would harm the Party's position. On the constitution, Zhu endorses Tian Xinming's reading that freedom of belief includes freedom not to believe, and adds a warning that propagating atheism could one day be made illegal. Zhu calls on Marxist atheists to take up atheist work as a responsibility, to propagate it openly and not to set it against united front work, citing Zhou Enlai's 1950 remark that idealism and materialism differ and need not be concealed. Zhu insists that this goes together with the long-term policy of religious freedom and with uniting religious believers around the Party. Read the original if you want a concise statement, from a former senior official in religious and ethnic affairs, of how atheism is defended within the Party's religious policy debates.

Atheist education and the transformation of ideas about medicine and health in the base areas during the War of Resistance 抗战时期根据地无神论教育与医疗卫生观念的变革 Li Ruifang Li asks how the Chinese Communist Party carried out atheist education in the anti-Japanese base areas, how villagers came to abandon superstition for scientific medicine, and how ideas about health changed as a result. The article argues that the Party used Marxist theory to start what Li calls a silent revolution in border-region medicine. In Li's account, this produced a modern transformation of health concepts that served both the war effort and popular welfare. The article opens with a survey of conditions in the base areas, mainly the Shaan-Gan-Ning and Jin-Cha-Ji border regions. Li cites very high illiteracy, epidemic disease, high infant mortality, and a severe shortage of doctors, with shamans (wushen) filling the gap. Li then covers three themes: the contest between doctors and shamans, the Party's prevention-first approach and mass hygiene campaigns, and four areas of changed thinking: regulation of medical qualifications, medical service, disease prevention and treatment, and maternal and child care. Li first argues that shamans could not simply be suppressed, so the Party followed Engels's advice to educate patiently. It publicised cases of harm done by shamans, had shamans publicly confess and sign anti-shaman pledges, and put them under popular supervision. Li presents Mao Zedong's policy of combining Chinese and Western medicine as the way to rebuild medical forces. Second, hygiene campaigns followed the principle of "adapting to circumstances and guiding" (shitai shudao), with the theme of promoting medicine and opposing ignorance. They relied on hygiene competitions, songs, newspapers and free treatment, and Li treats testimony from cured villagers as especially persuasive. Li reports figures for outpatient treatment, midwife training and new-style childbirth to show change. Li concludes that the Party, through dialectical and materialist thinking and a people-centred stance, achieved a modern transformation in the base areas' medical ideas. Li adds that "enemies in the masses' minds" persist, and that weak health provision and insufficient health education still allow new and old superstitions to arise. Li calls for better infrastructure, a more balanced supply of medical resources, better services, and regular health-knowledge education guided by the same principle of adapting to circumstances and guiding. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-based account of how anti-superstition and public-health work were linked in Yan'an-era base areas, as presented from within the Chinese Marxist tradition.

Basic lessons from the Chinese Communist Party's century of philosophical exploration 中国共产党百年哲学探索的基本经验 Ren Ping Marking the Party's centenary in 2021, Ren Ping asks what basic lessons can be drawn from the Chinese Communist Party's century of philosophical exploration. The article, first published in the China Social Sciences Today newspaper, answers that the Party has consistently treated Marxist philosophy as its fundamental worldview and methodology. Ren argues that this is why, in the Party's own phrase, Marxism "works" (xing) and why the Party could lead the Chinese people from standing up to becoming prosperous and then strong. The article is organised around five lessons: raising the banner of Marxism to open up a new path of Chinese modernization; promoting the scientific, practical, people-centred and open character of Marxist philosophy; following the path of adapting Marxism to Chinese conditions by proceeding from reality; developing Marxism in step with the times; and maintaining methodological self-awareness in exploration. It moves from the period after the Opium War through the Mao Zedong era and reform and opening up to the present. Ren's central historical claim is that before Marxism arrived, plans for modernization either clung to tradition or copied the West, and all repeatedly failed. Marxism, Ren says, brought a path different from Western capitalist modernization. Dogmatists such as Chen Duxiu and Wang Ming copied foreign texts and caused two major setbacks. Mao Zedong and the first generation instead shifted from a "foreign logic" to a "Chinese logic" of historical materialism, which Ren links to the Chinese Revolution and later to development. Ren presents the three "theoretical leaps" of Sinicized Marxism (Mao Zedong Thought, the theoretical system of socialism with Chinese characteristics, and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era) as the philosophical expression of this path. The final section lists five kinds of methodological self-awareness: of problems, standpoint, bottom line, path and system. Ren concludes that the Party's new mission calls for building a Chinese Marxism of the twenty-first century. Ren expects Xi Jinping Thought to become the intellectual mark of China "going out to the world". Ren also expects a shift in research from "Sinicization of Marxist philosophy" to "Chinese Marxist philosophy", from foreign Marxism to Chinese Marxism, and from "apprentice" to "contemporary author". Read the original if you want a concise statement of how Party-aligned philosophers in 2021 framed the centenary history as a philosophical lesson and set the agenda for "twenty-first century Chinese Marxist philosophy".

Upholding the materialist conception of history and advancing from victory to victory 坚持唯物史观 不断走向胜利 Zhang Yanguo Published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today on 12 July 2021, just after the Party's centenary, this commentary asks why the materialist conception of history has been the Communist Party of China's guiding banner for a century. Zhang Yanguo argues that it was less a choice by Party members than a choice made by history: the desperate conditions of modern China selected it. The author presents it as the Party's 'immortal' banner, one that leads to victory and opens up the future. The piece has three parts. The first sets out the historical, objective and subjective conditions under which Chinese Communists took up the theory. The second reviews the Party's achievements over a hundred years and the purpose of drawing historical lessons. The third, headed 'Hold high the banner', offers five directions for applying the theory to the building of a modern socialist country. On the historical condition, Zhang describes how the 1911 Revolution ended imperial rule but failed, leaving the nation at a 'valley floor' by the May Fourth period. Marxism arrived via Japan and Russia, and the success of the October Revolution showed its power against rival currents such as Bakunin's anarchism, Proudhon's mutualism, syndicalism and Tolstoyan ideas. Zhang treats the theory's own superiority as the objective condition, citing Engels on practice and theory. As the subjective condition, Zhang points to early revolutionaries such as Li Dazhao, who wrote on the value of the materialist conception of history. The Party, in this account, wrote the theory into its founding documents, using it in the First Congress resolution and the Second Congress manifesto. Zhang concludes that the Party must keep applying the theory in the new era, and lists five tasks. These are to hold firm to the primary stage of socialism and to common prosperity; to coordinate material and cultural-ethical progress; to put innovation at the centre of modernization; to pursue harmony between humanity and nature rather than the Western path of 'develop first, clean up later'; and to follow a path of peaceful development, which the author contrasts with Western modernization marked by colonialism and the 'Thucydides trap'. Zhang presents this as a new model of modernization and a contribution to a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want an example of how a Party-affiliated scholar framed the centenary link between historical materialism and the Party's legitimacy and future agenda.

The formation of Mao Zedong's materialist conception of history 毛泽东唯物史观的形成 Tao Jialing How did Mao Zedong come to adopt the materialist conception of history in his early years? In this short article, first published in the China Social Sciences Today on 19 July 2021, Tao Jialing argues that tracing this process helps explain the origins of the historical outlook of Chinese communists. The author holds that the formation ran through three stages between 1918 and 1921 and ended in Mao's full acceptance of historical materialism. The article is organised chronologically. The first stage, the budding stage, runs from April 1918 to August 1919, from the founding of the New People's Study Society to Mao's writings in the Xiang River Review. The second, formative stage covers September 1919 to December 1920. The third, the establishing stage, runs from January to July 1921 and ends with Mao's attendance at the First Party Congress in Shanghai. Tao draws on Mao's articles and letters to friends such as Cai Hesen, Xiang Jingyu and Luo Aojie. Tao's central argument is that Mao moved step by step from a general concern for the people to a class-based, economic analysis of society. In 1919 his remark that the problem of food is the greatest, and his essay 'The Great Union of the Popular Masses', show early notions that social being determines consciousness and that the masses drive history. The author then lists seven shifts in the formative stage. These include his 'economic analysis' of the 1919 Zhao Wuzhen suicide, his stress on material production, and his reading of the Communist Manifesto and other works. They also include founding the Cultural Book Society, preparing a party after Cai Hesen's advice, abandoning reformism, and embracing violent revolution and the question of state power. In January 1921 Mao rejected moderate reformism, social democracy and anarchism and called historical materialism the philosophical basis of 'our Party'. Tao concludes that Mao's historical materialism resulted from the 'self of today challenging the self of yesterday', a dynamic and continuously constructed process. In the author's view it mirrors the wider transformation of Chinese thought and marks Mao's move from revolutionary democracy to communism. Read the original if you want a compact, chronological account of how Mao's early letters and essays are used in Chinese scholarship to date his turn to Marxism.

Seizing the historical initiative by grasping the laws of historical development 在把握历史发展规律中掌握历史主动 Wu Degang Published in Economic Daily on 26 July 2021, shortly after the Party's centenary, this commentary asks how the Communist Party of China has moved from victory to victory over its first hundred years. Wu Degang's answer is that the Party has repeatedly drawn lessons from its own history, used them to grasp the laws of historical development, and so taken hold of the historical initiative. Wu presents this as the fundamental guarantee of the Party's success. The piece is a short, chronologically ordered reflection built around four sections. Each describes a setting in which the Party, in Wu's account, learned to grasp historical laws: summing up historical lessons, meeting risks and challenges, carrying out reform and innovation, and exploring theory. It runs from the New Democratic Revolution through the founding of the People's Republic and the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978) to the new era, and it quotes Xi Jinping's speech at the centenary celebration repeatedly. Wu argues that the Party is "great, glorious and correct" not because it never errs but because it corrects its errors with its own strength and the strength of the people. Setbacks such as the Great Leap Forward and the Cultural Revolution are presented as sources of experience that led to the 1978 turning point and to reform and opening up. Wu lists the trials the Party overcame, from the failure of the Great Revolution to the Zunyi Meeting, the anti-Japanese united front, and the "four tests" and "four dangers" of the new century. Wu also claims that major judgements, including the decision on reform and opening up and the redefinition of the principal social contradiction, rested on a deep reading of the times. The commentary ties all of this to the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, which it says produced the theoretical system of socialism with Chinese characteristics and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Wu concludes that each systematic review of experience has deepened the Party's grasp of historical laws, unified its thinking and matured its self-building. The Party now sets out on a new "road to the examination" toward the second centenary goal, and Wu says it will advance irresistibly toward national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want a compact example of how the Party's official narrative of its centenary links historical lessons, crisis management and theoretical innovation to the idea of historical initiative.

Opening up a poverty-reduction path with Chinese characteristics 开创中国特色减贫道路 Yuan Hongying Writing in the Party-state newspaper Economic Daily shortly after the centenary of the Communist Party (July 2021), Yuan Hongying takes up Xi Jinping's announcement that China has built a moderately prosperous society and "historically resolved" absolute poverty. Yuan argues that this outcome reflects a poverty-reduction path with Chinese characteristics, led by the Party, and that it has also yielded an anti-poverty theory and experience of wider significance. The commentary is built in three parts. It first traces the Party's anti-poverty record across a century: the revolution against the "three mountains", land reform and the basic socialist system after 1949, large-scale development-oriented poverty alleviation after reform and opening up, and the targeted campaign launched after 2013. It then reports the results and their global contribution. Finally it distils four lessons. Yuan cites figures to show scale and speed: rural poor falling from 770 million in 1978 to 5.51 million at the end of 2019 under the current standard, and the poverty rate from 97.5% to 0.6%. By the international extreme-poverty line of 1.90 dollars a day, the article says, China accounts for over 70% of global poverty reduction in the same period. It adds that China cut poverty faster than the world average and met the UN 2030 Agenda poverty target ten years early. The four lessons are upholding Party leadership; a people-centred approach; using the political advantage of the socialist system in concentrating resources on major tasks; and the strategy of targeted poverty alleviation. Yuan stresses development-oriented alleviation, which shifts from "blood transfusion" to "blood generation", and describes the "six targets" of precision. Yuan concludes that the campaign was a firm step towards common prosperity. The author calls for tackling unbalanced and inadequate development and narrowing urban–rural and regional gaps in order to pursue the all-round development of the people and common prosperity. Read the original if you want a concise, official-register account of how Party-state media presented the achievements and lessons of the poverty campaign at the 2021 centenary.

China's practice of building an ecological civilization 生态文明建设的中国实践 Xia Yizi This short commentary, published in China Social Sciences Today in June 2021, asks how ecological civilization construction should be understood and carried out in China. Xia argues that it is both an important part of China's socialist modernization and a fundamental plan for the lasting development of the Chinese nation, and that it rests on a harmonious coexistence between humanity and nature. The piece has three sections. The first deals with the human–nature relationship and the practical steps needed in the new era. The second places ecological civilization within Marx's theory of world history. The third discusses how China's ecological work bears on building a community with a shared future for mankind, including international cooperation. Drawing on Marx and Engels, Xia holds that humans are part of nature and must respect it. Under the logic of capital, the author says, anthropocentric exploitation alienates humans from nature, so the social form shaped by capital must itself be criticised. Xia presents ecological civilization as a requirement of the laws of world history: modernization needs a new civilizational meaning that includes human–nature harmony, and the Communist Party's century of leadership is said to have produced an alternative to Western capitalist development. Domestically, the author lists three measures: giving priority to conservation, protection and natural restoration; developing green technology and ecologically transforming traditional industry; and strengthening institutions such as environmental inspections. Xia contends that ecological governance cannot be achieved by one or several states alone. China should take part deeply in global ecological governance, strengthen South–South cooperation and build a green Belt and Road Initiative. In the author's view, China's experience offers developing countries a model, and its governance reforms provide a platform for exchange. Xia concludes that China has become a participant, contributor and leader in global ecological civilization, and that advancing it is necessary for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese commentary links ecological policy to Marxist world-history theory and to the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind.

The formation of Mao Zedong's historical materialism 毛泽东唯物史观的形成 Tao Jialing How did Mao Zedong come to adopt the materialist conception of history? Tao Jialing, in a short piece for China Social Sciences Today, holds that studying the formation of Mao's early historical materialism helps trace how Chinese communists' view of history took shape. The article argues that it developed through three stages between 1918 and 1921 and ended in a break with reformism. The article follows Mao's writings, letters and activities in chronological order. It treats a germination stage (April 1918 to August 1919), a formation stage (September 1919 to December 1920) and an establishment stage (January to July 1921). Its sources include Mao's essays in Xiangjiang Review, his commentary on the Zhao Wuzhen suicide, letters to Cai Hesen and other friends, and the New People's Study Society meetings. In Tao's account, the first stage began with Mao's remark that the "food problem" is the greatest, and with his essay "The Great Union of the Popular Masses". Tao reads these as early signs of the idea that social being determines consciousness, of class analysis, and of the masses as makers of history. The second stage is the core of the argument. Tao lists seven developments: an economic-analysis logic, attention to material production, sorting out a jumble of doctrines through reading Marxist works, spreading Marxism through the Cultural Book Society, a plan to found a party after Cai Hesen's letters, abandonment of reform after the failure of the Hunan self-rule movement, and a turn to violent revolution. In this last turn Mao rejected Russell's reformism, Kropotkin's anarchism and education-based change. In the third stage Mao told the New People's Study Society that it should adopt Russian-style communism. He then called historical materialism the "philosophical basis of our party" and attended the First Party Congress in July 1921. Tao concludes that Mao's historical materialism resulted from his "challenging yesterday's self", and that it was a dynamic, constructed process. In this reading it mirrors China's wider intellectual change and marks Mao's move from revolutionary democracy to communism, driven by patriotism. Read the original if you want a concise, chronological Chinese account of how Mao's early thought is periodised and tied to specific texts from 1918–1921.

Re-examining the young Marx's method of critiquing capitalism 青年马克思资本主义批判方法的再检视 Li Meng Li Meng asks how the young Marx criticised capitalism while pursuing human emancipation, and what method that criticism used. The article, published in the Journal of Xiamen University (Philosophy and Social Sciences) in 2021, argues that the standard reading is incomplete. That reading places the young Marx within Feuerbach's humanist materialism and so sees only an external, a priori critique. Li contends that an internal socio-historical critique also emerged and supplemented the external one, and that the two intertwined. The article covers the period from the Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher (1843–44) to the 1844 Paris Manuscripts, with a glance ahead to The Holy Family. It opens with the external critique in Marx's letter to Ruge, the Introduction to the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right, On the Jewish Question and Notebook I. It then takes Moses Hess's On the Essence of Money as a case for the political-economic basis of internal critique, using the "Comments on James Mill". The third section turns to Notebook III and Marx's critique of Hegel's dialectic and of Feuerbach. Li's central claim is that external critique measures capitalism against a normative standard, the return of the human essence, and so cannot grasp capitalism's historicity. Marx's departure from Hess is the first key move. Hess condemned bourgeois society morally and almost wholly negatively. Marx, drawing on Smith, Say, Ricardo and Mill, and on Engels's Outlines of a Critique of Political Economy, recognised the positive side of exchange and civil society and treated capitalism as containing the factors of its own negation. The second move is Marx's shift from Feuerbach's problematic to Hegel's. Marx found in Hegel's Phenomenology the idea of negativity as a moving and creating principle, and with it the rational core of the dialectic. Li says this let Marx push Feuerbach's humanism into the social sphere of real human activity. Li describes the Paris Manuscripts as a polyphony: the external critique stays dominant in form, while internal critique takes over in more and more specific analyses. Li concludes that the two methods are unified under historical materialism. Internal critique allows the external standard to be historically "reconstructed" rather than procedurally "constructed", and it supports a more dialectical view of private property and capitalism. The author adds that in the Paris Manuscripts Marx had not yet reached historical materialism proper, because his attention to reality did not yet cover the production and reproduction of social relations. Read the original if you study the young Marx, the debates over a break between early and mature Marx, or the roles of Hess, Hegel and Feuerbach in the formation of Marx's critical method.

Marx's Brussels Notebooks in China 马克思《布鲁塞尔笔记》在中国 Kong Weiyu This short commentary was prompted by the June 2021 exhibition of the original manuscript of the fourth Brussels Notebook of Marx at the Museum of the History of the Communist Party of China. According to Kong, it is the only relatively complete Marx notebook preserved in China, bought in Europe by a Chinese entrepreneur and donated to the state. Kong notes that the notebooks were published in Germany in 1998 and first shown in China in 2018, yet Chinese scholarship has paid them little attention. The article asks what the notebooks are, why they matter and why they have been neglected. Kong first describes the notebooks, citing the editors of MEGA2: they are Marx's 1845 economic notes from Brussels, his second systematic study of economics, written in French, German and English. The exhibited manuscript has 27 sheets (54 pages, 49 written on) and excerpts Storch, Saint-Maur, Pinto, Child and Bell, with other notes covering Say, Sismondi, Rossi, MacCulloch, Gasparin, Babbage and Ure. The article then turns to their scholarly value, the reasons for domestic neglect, and what the manuscripts mean for Marxist textual research. Kong's central claim is that the notebooks show how the productive discourse of historical materialism took shape in an economic context, just before The German Ideology. Storch, Kong argues, supplied a view of material production as primary and moved Marx's interest from individual labour to material production. Rossi supplied a relational way of seeing production as creating relations of use and of supply and demand, which Kong links to the critique of older 'intuitive' materialism. The technologists Babbage and Ure offered a view of machine production as possibly easing labour and a micro-level analysis of how production works. Kong attributes the neglect to three difficulties: the multilingual text, which requires going back beyond the Chinese Complete Works; the fusion of philosophy and economics in Marx's study; and a research habit of explaining what a theory is rather than how it arose. Kong concludes that research on Marxist texts needs to move from asking what a theory is to asking how it came about, and that scholars should engage more deeply with manuscripts, notes and the MEGA2 materials. Comparing Marx's excerpts and comments with the original works, Kong holds, gives a new perspective on the historical logic of Marxism's formation. Read the original if you want a brief account of the Brussels Notebooks, their contents and their place in Chinese Marx-text scholarship.

The emergence and development of Marx's concept of ideology 马克思意识形态概念的出场及其展开 Duan Guangpeng Duan Guangpeng, in a short piece first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today (2021), asks where Marx's concept of ideology came from and how it developed. The author argues that the concept emerged under the influence of French Enlightenment thinkers and the French Revolution, and also of the German Enlightenment and German classical philosophy. Its unfolding, Duan holds, was tied both to Marx's shifts in philosophical and political standpoint and to his work on historical materialism and on proletarian emancipation. The article has three sections. The first traces the French and German sources, from Napoleon's treatment of the "ideologists" to Marx's reading of Destutt de Tracy's Elements of Ideology in Paris in 1844, and to Kant and Hegel. The second follows Marx's early uses of the term, from the doctoral-dissertation notebooks through the Rheinische Zeitung years to the critique of Hegel's philosophy of right. The third turns to The German Ideology and Capital. Duan's central claim is that Marx moved from a loose, general use of "ideology" to a critical theory of it. In 1842, in the debate on thefts of wood, Marx first applied the term to a concrete political problem. In the critique of Hegel's philosophy of right, the idea that civil society determines the state led him to trace the falsity of ideology to real social life. In The German Ideology, Duan reads ideology first as "false ideas": the ruling class's ideas present its particular interests in a universal form and conceal the true nature of society. Duan adds that Marx did not treat ideology as simply false. It is inherent in a complete social structure, as the "ideological superstructure", and it reflects real common interests. In Capital, Marx criticised commodity fetishism as the core of bourgeois ideology. Duan concludes that Marx turned ideology research into something more than a question of logical or epistemic truth and falsity. Its central task became exposing the real nature of society behind ideological illusion, and Marx's analysis of the concealed discursive strategies of ideology became the core of ideology critique. Read the original if you want a brief overview of the intellectual sources and stages of Marx's concept of ideology, as presented in Chinese scholarship.

Interpretive perspectives on the concept of ideology in Marx and Engels 马克思恩格斯意识形态概念的阐释视角 Xu Douedou Yi Zhengxuan Xu Douedou and Yi Zhengxuan ask how Marx and Engels' concept of ideology should be characterised. They distinguish three ways of defining it in the Marxist tradition: negative, descriptive (neutral) and positive. The authors argue that the positive and descriptive readings lack textual basis in Marx and Engels and create interpretive difficulties, so that their stance is, in the end, negative. In their account this negativity stresses the critical element in ideology and supplies a standard for rationalising thought. The article has three sections. The first explains the logical difficulty of a positive concept of ideology. The second examines the textual grounds claimed for a descriptive concept, mainly the base–superstructure passage in the 1859 Preface. The third defends the negative reading by setting Lenin's epistemological emphasis beside the early Althusser's sociological one. On the positive reading, the authors argue that Marx and Engels treat science as an affirmative force, while ideology is an inverted, illusory form of thought outside science. Ideology could become scientific only under historical conditions, namely the proletariat, whose class interest coincides with the broadest human interest and which needs no illusory principles. Ideology would then disappear in communism. On the descriptive reading, they note that scholars have found different German terms for "forms of social consciousness" and "ideological forms". The former is described neutrally; the latter is presented as distorted reflection of real conflicts. A neutral reading, they warn, risks stretching ideology to mean culture or consciousness in general and dissolving its critical force. The authors then claim that the negativity is dialectical: an internal critique in the epistemological sense, which also sees a transcendent, future-pointing force in bourgeois ideals, and a principle of sublation in the sociological sense. Examples of the latter are Marxism's sublation of German classical philosophy, of utopian socialism, and the late Engels' self-correction on the relative independence of the ideological superstructure. The authors conclude that, whatever partial validity the three modes have in different textual settings, only the negative reading fits the "internal critical" meaning of ideology in Marx and Engels. They also note that Lenin's construction of proletarian ideology showed an initial real transition from illusory to scientific ideology. Read the original if you want a compact argument about the textual basis of Marxist theories of ideology and the debate over neutral versus critical concepts.

Assessing the contextual differences in Western Marxist spatial critique 研判西方马克思主义空间批判的语境差异 Zhang Xinran Spatial critique grounded in capitalist urbanization has become an important part of Marxism outside China, but its relation to historical materialism remains unsettled. Zhang opens with a dispute: Manuel Castells accused Henri Lefebvre's theory of the production of space of drifting from Marxism towards humanism, while Edward W. Soja credited Lefebvre's "provocative inversion" with the shift from Marxist analysis of space to the spatialization of Marxism. The article argues that urban Marxism and historical materialism form two different contexts of spatial critique, differing in concepts, critical paradigms and practical paths. This is a short newspaper commentary, first published in the China Social Sciences Today in June 2021. It is organised in three sections: the definition of the city, the paradigm of spatial critique, and the path of spatial practice. It draws on Marx's Grundrisse and Capital and on Lefebvre, Castells, David Harvey and Soja. On concepts, Zhang says Lefebvre's city is the modern urban form of a third, "urban" age and a commercialised, fragmented space tied to power. Marx's city rests on large European industry, with concentrated production and capital and a proletariat gathered in one place. On paradigm, historical materialism ties space to the mode of production and forms of ownership, whereas urban Marxism presumes historical materialism to be "absent" on space. Lefebvre and Castells took a urban-sociology route, Harvey and Soja a human-geography route, and each expanded dialectics: Lefebvre with a conceptual triad, Harvey with geographical unevenness, Soja with a socio-temporal-spatial trialectic. On practice, Zhang argues that Marx saw spatial alienation as ending only through transforming the mode of production, with the proletariat as the subject. Urban Marxism, in this account, no longer treats the proletariat as that subject or class revolution as the way to sublate alienation. Harvey's "dialectical utopia" and "rebel architects" replace communism and the proletariat. Zhang concludes that urban Marxism offers no workable strategy and never reaches the level of ownership, but that the differences make Marxist spatial research interactive, open and plural. Read the original if you want a compact Chinese account of how Lefebvre, Harvey and Soja are positioned against Marx's historical materialism.

Rethinking the Marxist view of progress 重新认识马克思主义进步观 Zhao Song This short commentary, first published in China Social Sciences Today in May 2021, takes up the claim by some Western scholars that Marx was a "progressivist" whose view of history rests on a metaphysical belief in progress. Zhao argues that this reading distorts Marxism and that the Marxist view of progress must be understood from the standpoint of real human beings. The piece first sets out two Western charges. One, associated with Francis Fukuyama, treats Marx like Hegel as holding an end-of-history eschatology. The other, represented by Sean Sayers, treats Marx's theory as a linear conception of progress. Zhao then answers each in turn. On the first, Zhao concedes that Marx's accounts of a "community of free individuals" and the "true realm of freedom" suggest a goal, but denies that this amounts to historical teleology. In Zhao's reading, history has no preset purpose; it is made by the activity of real people, so history cannot end while people exist. Communism is presented as the start of a new history, and Zhao cites Fredric Jameson's remark that it ends prehistory, not history. On the second, Zhao argues that Marx's late study of "Eastern society" and his reply to Mikhailovsky rejected a single path for all nations. Linear progress, Zhao adds, needs a superhistorical subject such as Hegel's spirit, whereas Marx made human practice the subject. Zhao describes history as spiral, uniting diversity with general laws through the contradiction between productive forces and relations of production. Zhao concludes that equating Marxism with end-of-history or linear progressivism contradicts its humanistic starting point. A correct understanding, Zhao says, must proceed from real human beings and their irreplaceable place in historical progress. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese-language rebuttal of Fukuyama-style and linear readings of Marx.

Leading the innovation of Chinese Marxist philosophy with the problems of the age 以时代问题引领中国马克思主义哲学创新 Wang Zhiqiang Wang Zhiqiang, in a commentary for the Chinese Social Sciences Today (July 2021), asks where innovation in Chinese Marxist philosophy should come from. The answer is that real philosophy distils the spirit of its own age, so innovation must be rooted in the problems of the age. For contemporary China, the author names the country's social reality and the historical practice of modernization as the starting point and driving force. The piece begins with a critique of current research habits. It then looks back at how Marx made his philosophical revolution out of the problems of 1830s–40s Germany. Finally, it traces the sinicization of Marxist philosophy from the late Qing crisis through the Chinese Communist Party's revolutionary period to the post-1978 debates, before returning to the present. Wang describes a widespread routine. A scholar introduces a concept from a modern Western thinker, searches Marx's texts for similar statements and rebuilds a new Marxist narrative. The ending then declares that Marx had already surpassed the Western thinker. Wang sees two basic defects: it shows an inability to grasp the problems of the age or to produce original concepts, and it dissolves the determinate content and philosophical character of Marxism. Against this, Wang reads Marx's critique of German classical philosophy as a way of grasping modernity from within a backward country. The same pattern is traced in China, where Mao Zedong's On Practice, On Contradiction and On New Democracy, and later the debate on practice as the criterion of truth, are presented as answers to the pressing questions of their moments. Wang concludes that grafting Western concepts onto Marxism is appropriate at most in the early stage of modernization, and that China's modernization is not a repeat of the Western philosophical process. Contemporary China is undergoing the largest modernization in human history, and Wang calls it a pioneering practice, the unfolding of the new path of Chinese modernization. Wang poses questions that philosophy must answer, including the standard of Chinese modernization, the new "principled height" of the new path and era, and how to supply universal norms of world-historical significance. Read the original if you want a short statement of the argument, in the official Chinese discourse, against derivative Western-concept scholarship in Marxist philosophy.

A brief analysis of the theoretical limits of Western Marxism through the problem of "discourse" 以“话语”问题浅析西方马克思主义的理论局限 Zhang Dan Zhang Dan asks what the Western Marxist treatment of "discourse" reveals about the limits of that tradition. The short commentary, first published in the China Social Sciences Today in 2021, grants that Western Marxism placed discourse in real social history and responded critically to doubts about classical Marxism. Zhang's thesis is that its accounts of discourse depart from Marxism's basic tenets and carry an idealist, quasi-utopian colouring. The piece looks at three thinkers: Louis Althusser's theory of ideology, Jürgen Habermas's theory of communicative action and "discourse democracy", and Ernesto Laclau and Chantal Mouffe's theory of hegemony. It then widens the point to Western Marxism as a whole, comparing it with traditional Marxism on basic theory, revolutionary subject, method of revolution and choice of path. Zhang argues that all three exaggerate the status of discourse. Althusser stresses ideology so heavily that he neglects the subject's initiative. Habermas treats communication, not productive labour, as decisive. Laclau and Mouffe let discourse generate subjects and reject the determining role of the economic base. For Zhang, this reverses Marx's view that social being determines social consciousness, and it leads to misjudging class contradictions and revolutionary forces. Zhang also finds these schemes unworkable. Habermas's procedures demand much of citizens' culture, willingness and institutions, and Laclau and Mouffe lack concrete analysis of the state. More broadly, Western Marxism is said to weaken the proletariat's role and to favour cultural critique without overthrowing the capitalist mode of production. Zhang concludes that theoretical innovation must keep to Marxism's basic stance and views, since abandoning Marxism solves nothing. The author holds that the tests of the present era should deepen understanding of Marxism's scientific character, in a context of changing domestic and international conditions and competition over ideological discourse. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese academic commentary criticises Western Marxism from an orthodox historical-materialist standpoint.

The ethical dimension of East European neo-Marxism 东欧新马克思主义的伦理之维 Xia Bailing Why did so many East European neo-Marxist schools turn to ethics after the Second World War? Xia argues that the moral problems of the region's socialist states, together with the suppression of individuality and freedom, pushed thinkers to build their own moral theories. In Xia's account, these theories inherited Marx's ethical thought and helped develop Marxist ethics in the contemporary period. The short piece, a newspaper commentary, surveys several currents: Kangrga's metaethics and Stojanović's 'ethics of the revolutionary movement' in the Yugoslav Praxis school, Zygmunt Bauman's morality of the 'Other' in Poland, and Ágnes Heller's 'ethics of personality' in the Hungarian Budapest School. It gives most attention to Heller. Xia's central claim is that East European neo-Marxist ethics was practical and rooted in lived socialist experience. It was also concerned with the rationality of morality, unlike Western Marxist ethics. Heller, in this reading, joins a dimension of personality (individuality, freedom) with a dimension of virtue, so that the good person can both follow social norms and act as an autonomous moral subject. Xia contrasts this with MacIntyre, whose communitarianism is said to neglect individuality, and with Bauman, who is said to stress responsibility to the Other but pay little attention to virtue. Xia concludes that these thinkers extended Marxist ethics creatively, but notes a split. Heller, Fehér and Kołakowski are described as favouring moral individualism over collective requirements, while Kosík, Schaff and Svitak hold that individuals bear moral responsibility to society as a whole. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese overview of how Heller, Bauman and the Praxis school have been situated in debates on Marxist ethics.

The dialectic of objects: the essence of machines and of humans 对象辩证法：机器与人的本质 Liu Zichen This short commentary, first published in China Social Sciences Today in June 2021, asks how technology changes the definition of the human being. Liu sets two materialist claims against each other: Marx's view that free, conscious activity is the species-characteristic of humans, and La Mettrie's "man is a machine". Liu argues that under capital and advancing technology, humans are alienated into machines, and that "the machine is human" may also become possible. The article is organised in three stages: technology as a tool, the human as a machine, and the machine as a human. It draws mainly on Marx's Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 and the Communist Manifesto, and also refers to Heidegger, Marcuse, Descartes, Baudrillard-style notions of hyperreality and the Chinese philosopher Zhao Tingyang. Liu holds that technology begins as an externalisation of human essential powers, with humans as subjects and machines as objects. With large-scale industry, technology becomes bound up with capital and turns into an autonomous force that dominates producers. In Liu's account this produces one-dimensional people, a blurring of the virtual and the real, and dependence on smartphones, networks and algorithms. Liu contrasts Marx, who starts from practice, with Marcuse, who criticises technology from an abstract human essence. Drawing on Zhao Tingyang's "I act, therefore I am", Liu argues that if machines or cyborgs take over all material production, human action shrinks and human existence loses meaning. Liu concludes that one-sided technological development may lead to the "dissolution of the human" rather than human liberation, and cannot by itself reach Marx's association of free individuals. The nature of technology depends on the social system and its application, so social adaptability is the key question. Read the original if you want a brief Marxist-humanist argument about alienation, artificial intelligence and the essence of the human.
