Marxism in the course of the African socialist movement 非洲社会主义运动历程中的马克思主义 Zheng Xiangfu Shu Wenhao Zheng and Shu ask how Marxism has travelled with, and shaped, socialist movements in Africa, and whether it can return to the continent after their collapse. They argue that Marxism in Africa went through three phases: introduction and emergence, flourishing, and decline with reflection. In their view the Marxist-Leninist experiments failed mainly through dogmatism and dependence on the Soviet Union, but Marxism remains a potential alternative to neoliberalism, and its return will be long and tortuous. The article follows African socialism from the 1920s to the present. It covers the founding of the South African and Algerian communist parties, the role of colonial-era intellectuals, Pan-Africanism, the first wave of 'village-community' and democratic socialism, and the second wave of 'African scientific socialism' in states such as Congo, Ethiopia, Angola and Mozambique. It then turns to the post-1990 retreat and closes with three proposals for Africa's future. In the early phase, the authors say, Comintern guidance, Marxist-influenced colonial intellectuals and Pan-Africanism spread Marxism, which for a time served only as one element of Pan-Africanism. After independence, neocolonialism exposed Pan-Africanism's limits, and leaders such as Nkrumah turned towards scientific socialism. The authors list the features of the Marxist-Leninist regimes: vanguard parties, acceptance of class struggle, planned economies and nationalisation. They judge these experiments failures. The causes they identify are reliance on the Soviet model and its patrons, and a failure to resolve the tension between Marxism's universality and Africa's particularity, which left mechanical, dogmatic application in place of real adaptation. The authors offer three conclusions. Neoliberalism's thirty-year record in Africa is a reason for Marxism's revival, and Marx's analysis of capital's expansion explains Africa's poverty. Africa should learn from socialism with Chinese characteristics, a community with a shared future for mankind and the Belt and Road Initiative, and should combine Marxism with national conditions. It should also develop its productive forces first, using the market and accepting aid with care, citing Lenin on state monopoly capitalism as preparation for socialism. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic account of Marxism's history in Africa and of how Chinese scholars see China's role there.

The theoretical foundations of the common values of all humanity 全人类共同价值的理论底蕴 Wen Linbo This short commentary, published in Guangming Daily in October 2021, takes up Xi Jinping's pledge at the Party's centenary celebration to promote the "common values of all humanity": peace, development, equity, justice, democracy and freedom. Wen argues that the concept rests on three theoretical sources: Marxism, traditional Chinese culture and long-standing value consensus in the international community. The article is organised in three sections, one for each source. It draws on Marx, Engels and Lenin, on classical Chinese texts such as the Book of Rites and the Book of Documents, and on international instruments from the Peace of Westphalia to the UN Charter and the Bandung principles. On the Marxist side, Wen reads the concept as confirming world-history theory: deeper global interconnection raises the need for shared values. It also expresses Marx's concern for humanity and his opposition to exploitation and oppression, which Wen contrasts with unilateralism and hegemonism in some Western states. Wen then links it to the ideal of "great harmony under heaven" and the principle of harmony without uniformity, which allow both particularity and commonality. In the international section, Wen presents peace and development as the themes of the age, and fairness and justice as a rejection of power politics. Democracy, in Wen's account, takes different forms according to national conditions and economic base. Wen concludes that the concept has deep theoretical roots and practical relevance, and offers a value basis for peaceful development and for reform of global governance. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the Party press grounded this concept in Marxism, Chinese tradition and international norms in 2021.

Chinese democratic discourse as a critique and transcendence of Western democratic discourse 论中国民主话语对西方民主话语的批判与超越 Li Haiqing Li Haiqing takes up the building of a Chinese discourse system, arguing that democracy is one of its priority areas because Western democratic discourse has long been exported to China and, in the author's account, has shaped Chinese thinking and even produced a partial 'colonisation of the mind'. The article contends that Chinese democratic discourse has been constructed through a critique of Western liberal democracy and that it now goes beyond it. Li links the task to Xi Jinping's concern with China's 'spiritual independence'. The article has five parts. It first dissects Western democratic discourse in terms of content, mode of thinking and interests. It then sets out a five-part framework for Chinese democratic discourse, identifies five of its features, and discusses its value. It closes with a note on remaining challenges. Li draws on Marx's early writings, Schumpeter, Thomas Dye, Huntington, Wang Shaoguang and speeches by Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping. In Li's reading, Western 'liberal democracy' (natural rights, competitive elections, civil society, separation of powers) serves capital and elites. It rests on a hierarchy of civilisations, universalism and an 'end of history' outlook, and it hides the interests of powerful capital. Against this, Li sets a 'five-in-one' Chinese framework: democracy must fit specific national conditions; it operates under the Party's leadership; it depends on state capacity; it spans many fields and the whole process rather than elections alone; and it is judged by its practical function in development and governance. Li presents these features as endogenous, people-centred, complete, absorptive and attuned to the times. Li also stresses that criticising Western discourse does not mean rejecting it wholesale, citing the borrowing and adaptation of 'governance'. Li concludes that Chinese democratic discourse solves China's own problems, deconstructs Western claims to universality, and offers developing countries an alternative path, which Li calls a higher form of human democratic discourse. Li cautions that Western discourse remains strong and that China's own democratic practice, conceptual refinement and international discursive power still need work. Li expects Chinese discourse to gain greater influence over time. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how a Party School scholar frames the contrast between Chinese and Western democracy in the discourse-building campaign.

The pandemic and the crisis of the capitalist system in the view of the foreign Left 国外左翼视域下的疫情与资本主义制度危机 Xing Wenzeng Writing in 2021, Xing surveys how left-wing scholars, commentators and communist parties outside China interpreted the COVID-19 pandemic. The article's starting point is that the contrasting records of capitalist and socialist countries exposed the defects of the capitalist system, which Xing describes as a consensus among the foreign Left. Its thesis is that the pandemic revealed the nature of capitalism and that socialism is the fundamental solution. The article is organised in four sections: the profit-driven capitalist mode of production as the root of the virus's spread; the sharpening of inequality by class and race; the deepening of institutional crisis under neoliberal policy; and the hegemonic features of Western blame-shifting towards China. It draws on figures such as David Harvey, Noam Chomsky, John Bellamy Foster, Christian Fuchs and Michael Roberts. It also draws on statements by the Communist Parties of Britain, the USA, Canada, Australia and Israel, and on pandemic and economic statistics. In Xing's account, citing these sources, capitalism puts profit before life. This is shown in 'herd immunity' strategies, premature reopening and a pharmaceutical and health system that treats care as a commodity. Inequality is then traced to class: the article cites higher death rates among Black and poor populations, mass job losses concentrated among women and minorities, rising billionaire wealth, and state relief aimed at large firms. Decades of neoliberal austerity, privatisation and financialisation are said to have left Western states unable to prepare for the crisis or to cooperate, as in the reported lack of EU aid to Italy. Western accusations against China are read by the quoted leftists as deflecting blame and containing a possible alternative to capitalism. Xing concludes that capitalism is a system that enriches a few rather than protecting the many. In contrast, the article presents China, Vietnam, Cuba and other socialist countries as having controlled the epidemic and restored growth, citing China's 2020 GDP growth of 2.3% and Cuba's low death rate. It argues that this demonstrates the superiority of the socialist system and that longing for socialism will resonate more widely in capitalist countries. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese scholarship at the Academy of Marxism collects and presents foreign leftist criticism of capitalism during the pandemic.

Socialist countries' successful control of COVID-19 shows the superiority of the socialist system 社会主义国家成功管控新冠肺炎疫情彰显社会主义制度优越性 Pan Xihua Writing in 2021, Pan Xihua asks why China, Vietnam, Cuba, Laos and North Korea contained COVID-19 far better, in the author's account, than the developed capitalist countries. The article's answer is that the outcome reflects the superiority of the socialist system. Pan sets the pandemic as a contrast between "disorder in the West" and "order in China". The article reviews the anti-epidemic measures of the five ruling communist or workers' parties under five headings: centralised and unified Party leadership, the ability to concentrate resources on major tasks, a people-centred value orientation, respect for science, and internationalism. Each section describes the five countries in turn, then links the practice to passages from Marx, Engels and Lenin. A closing section discusses lessons for the international response. Pan's central move is to treat each practice as an expression of classical Marxist requirements. Party leadership is presented as the greatest socialist advantage and as the "one source of orders" behind efficient decisions. Public ownership of the means of production is said to give a basis of common interest that lets the state direct scarce resources, as in the Wuhan hospital construction, nationwide medical support and Cuba's free three-tier health system. Pan reads the people-centred principle, the stress on science and the aid China and Cuba sent abroad as practical confirmation of Marxist teaching on the masses, on science as a historical force, and on proletarian internationalism. Pan concludes that the pandemic tested systems of national governance and that, in the article's view, socialism passed while the capitalist states, with delayed responses, "herd immunity" policies and politicised blame, failed. The author does not claim that socialist countries handled every problem perfectly. Pan calls for international solidarity, opposition to politicising public health, and scientific rather than superstitious responses. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Party-affiliated scholar ties comparative pandemic experience to the doctrine of socialist superiority and to classical Marxist texts.

The Party's great practice of leading the people demonstrates the truth of Marxist theory 党领导人民的伟大实践彰显马克思主义理论真理性 Zhang Lixia Writing in the China Social Sciences Today in September 2021, Zhang Lixia takes up Xi Jinping's speech at the centenary of the Communist Party's founding and its answer to why the Party and socialism with Chinese characteristics succeed: "ultimately because Marxism works." The commentary argues that the Party's leadership of the people in practice proves three things: the correctness of the Marxist banner in the Party's line, the loftiness of the Marxist values the Party chose, and the truth of Marxist theory as tested in practice. The short piece has three sections. The first treats socialism with Chinese characteristics as a creative development of Marxism. The second treats it as verifying Marxism's value orientation. The third presents Marxism's basic principles as the theoretical guidance for that socialism. Zhang describes socialism with Chinese characteristics as the product of combining Marxism's basic tenets with China's conditions, and as Marxism's concrete unfolding in China. In this account the theory answers major questions about what socialism is, how to build the Party and what development to pursue, drawing on both Chinese civilisation and practice since reform and opening up. Zhang says that, guided by historical materialism, it has confirmed Marxism's value of serving the people, and that the completion of poverty alleviation and a moderately prosperous society marks a stage towards communism. Marxism and this socialism share the same starting point and goal, the interests of working people. Zhang reads Marx's remarks in Capital and the 1857–58 manuscripts on public ownership and the aim of universal wealth as anticipating common prosperity. Zhang concludes that Chinese practice shows the truth of Marxism, and that the task now is to build a modern socialist great power and keep developing twenty-first-century Marxism. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the Party's centenary discourse in 2021 presents Chinese practice as proof of Marxist theory.

The great changes unseen in a century in the world, seen from the perspective of Marxist philosophy 马克思主义哲学视野中的世界百年未有之大变局 Liu Rui Writing in 2021, Liu Rui takes up the widely used claim that the world is undergoing great changes unseen in a century, whose core the author describes as a shift in the balance of forces from 'the West strong, the East weak' to 'the East rising, the West declining'. Liu argues that many ordinary Chinese hold superficial or one-sided views of this change, and that Marxist dialectical and historical materialism offers a fuller reading. The thesis is that the change is dialectical in nature: its origins combine chance with necessity, its present form combines change with the unchanged, and its future course combines certainty with uncertainty. The article follows a past–present–future sequence in three parts: origins, present condition, and development trend. Each part reviews Chinese scholarly views (for example Guo Shuyong and Ding Weihang, and Quan Heng, on event-driven accounts of origins; Wang Shaoquan, Jin Canrong, Teng Wensheng on manifestations of change) and then draws practical lessons. Each part is tied to a named error that Liu sees in popular thinking: accidental-cause determinism, subjective fantasy of change, and linear historicism. In the first part Liu contends that Western relative decline is the necessary outcome of universal connection and eternal development, and of the basic contradiction of capitalist society. Liu also lists crises in Western economies, politics, society, culture and diplomacy. The rise of emerging-market and developing countries is presented as the rise of a new phenomenon, helped by technology diffusion, 'parallel' modernization and the new technological revolution. The second part stresses what has not changed: using the author's figures, the West keeps its economic, technological and military lead, and China remains the largest developing country, with gaps in manufacturing, services and overall strength relative to the United States. The third part holds that the long-run direction is certain, while the timing, form and outcome of great-power rivalry are not, so both complacent and pessimistic forecasts of China overtaking the United States are rejected. Liu concludes that accurate understanding of the change is the epistemological basis for responding to it and shaping it. The practical proposals include focusing on development and technological self-reliance, strengthening Party leadership, opening up further, avoiding a new Cold War and over-extension abroad, and guarding against 'strategic rashness'. Liu calls for further research on the laws governing great-power rise and decline in periods of world transition. Read the original if you want a systematic example of how a Chinese Marxist philosopher turns official judgements about the global situation into a dialectical framework and policy advice.

The ever-growing South African Communist Party 不断发展壮大的南非共产党 Liu Xiangyang This chapter, from the Report on the Development of the International Communist Movement (2020–2021), asks how the South African Communist Party (SACP) has managed to grow in a hostile, unequal capitalist society, when most communist parties in capitalist countries declined after the upheavals in the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe. Liu argues that the SACP has become a relatively mature Marxist party by combining Marxism-Leninism with South African conditions, preserving unity and adapting its tactics, while still facing serious financial and structural limits. The article has three parts. It first maps South Africa's political landscape: economic inequality, the 2019 election, the African National Congress (ANC) and its alliance with the SACP, and the opposition parties (Democratic Alliance, Economic Freedom Fighters, Inkatha Freedom Party). It then reviews the SACP's hundred-year history from its founding in 1921 through the 1950 ban, underground work, armed struggle and the constitutional negotiations that led to the 1994 election. A third part assesses the party's recent achievements and difficulties, followed by a short conclusion. Liu's core argument is that the SACP pursues a class-based national democratic revolution, as opposed to the race-based politics Liu attributes to the Economic Freedom Fighters. Its tactics have included petitions, non-violent non-cooperation, armed struggle through Umkhonto we Sizwe, negotiation and participation in government. Liu credits it with four achievements since 1994: participation in state administration through the alliance with the ANC and the trade union federation COSATU; leadership of mass movements such as strikes and the annual 'Red October' campaign; support for the poor during the Covid-19 pandemic; and the pursuit of a socialist future. Against these, Liu lists the party's poverty (no office building of its own, 66 per cent of members unemployed), its thin base among workers and professionals, and the difficulty of keeping independence within the alliance. Liu presents the party's decision not to contest elections alone as dictated by its weak social base and by anti-communist and narrow nationalist currents. Liu concludes that the SACP shows that a communist party in a capitalist country is not 'an academic salon for a few advanced intellectuals' and can achieve things if it remains firm in conviction, united and grounded. The author expects it to keep strengthening the ANC-led alliance, enlarge its membership and build conditions for socialism while removing the legacy of apartheid. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly account of the SACP's history, membership data and alliance strategy, and of how Chinese researchers present it as a model for non-ruling communist parties.

The theoretical implications and intellectual wisdom of the "new form of human civilization" “人类文明新形态”的理论意蕴和思想智慧 Gu Hailiang Writing in October 2021, Gu Hailiang takes up the concept of the "new form of human civilization", which Xi Jinping advanced in his speech at the centenary of the Communist Party of China. Gu asks what theoretical basis and intellectual content the concept carries. The article argues that it rests on the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics, takes the coordinated progress of five civilizations (material, political, spiritual, social and ecological) as its substance, and is realised through Chinese modernization. In Gu's view it enriches Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and expresses the wisdom of Marxism adapted to China in the new era. The article is organised in four sections. It first links the concept to the change in the principal contradiction of society since the 18th Party Congress (2012). It then places it in the history of the Party's modernization goals, from the Four Modernizations to Deng Xiaoping's "Chinese-style modernization" and the completion of a moderately prosperous society. The third section treats it as part of the movement from quantitative change to partial qualitative change in the new stage of development. The last section connects it to a community with a shared future for mankind. Gu's central moves are historical and dialectical. He compares the principal contradictions set out at the Eighth Party Congress, the Sixth Plenum of the 11th Central Committee and the 19th Party Congress. He reads the current one, between the people's growing need for a better life and unbalanced and inadequate development, as defining the new form: the "needs" now span eight areas, and the five-sphere construction is the system that supplies them. Drawing on Mao Zedong's 1959 remarks on underdeveloped and more developed socialism, and on Deng Xiaoping and Xi, Gu presents the primary stage of socialism as a dynamic process of accumulation approaching qualitative leaps. The new development stage, he says, is the setting for understanding the concept's direction. Gu concludes that the concept is not specific to China. He argues that it has universal significance through the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind, which he presents as the contemporary continuation of Marx and Engels's theory of world history. The concept embodies scientific socialism's theory of civilizational forms, draws on fine traditional Chinese culture and absorbs the achievements of other civilizations. Gu calls it an important result of twenty-first-century Marxism. Read the original if you want a Party-theorist's systematic account of how the concept is derived from the principal contradiction, the primary stage of socialism and the idea of a shared future for mankind.

The "new material scarcity" crisis of Italian welfare capitalism 意大利福利资本主义的“新物质匮乏”危机 Li Kaixuan Italy was among the first European countries to build a welfare state, yet Li Kaixuan argues that it now faces a worsening "new material scarcity" crisis. The article holds that this crisis, visible well before the 2020 pandemic and sharpened by it, stems from an unjust system of wealth distribution and from the "democratic deficit" of representative democracy. The article has four parts. It first documents the crisis through figures on relative and absolute poverty, inequality, youth unemployment, child poverty, migrants and the North–South gap, drawing mainly on OECD, World Bank and Italian national statistics. It then analyses distribution (financialization, taxation, welfare design), then politics (party representation, EU influence, technocratic governments), and ends with a short conclusion. On distribution, Li draws on Piketty and Anwar Shaikh to argue that financialization lets property-income earners accumulate faster than wage earners. In Italy, firms turned towards financial assets, labour costs fell as a share of turnover, and taxes on property income are lower than those on labour income. Li adds that public-debt interest crowds out social spending. The welfare system is described as doubly unbalanced: pensions dominate spending while unemployment, family and social assistance are thin, and local services differ sharply by region. Neoliberal "recalibration" cut pensions and health spending instead, and the 2019 basic income scheme is judged too restrictive to reduce poverty. On politics, Li contends that the mainstream centre-left Democratic Party has converged with the centre-right, while left parties such as Communist Refoundation have been excluded from parliament. EU rules and technocratic cabinets are said to move reforms beyond voters' scrutiny, and the populist Five Star Movement is judged not to have repaired this lack of representation. Li concludes that the crisis has deep institutional roots: financialization, a regressive tax regime, a welfare system that mainly redistributes within the employed workforce, and a de-politicized reform process. As long as left forces advocating an alternative to capitalism remain marginal and the socialist movement does not revive, Li argues, populist mobilization alone cannot relieve the hardship of lower- and middle-income Italians. Read the original if you want a statistics-heavy, Marxist-inflected account of Italian welfare capitalism and its politics, written from within the Chinese debate on foreign Marxism.

The historical position of the new development stage from the perspective of materialist dialectics 唯物辩证法视域下新发展阶段的历史方位探析 Shuang Chuanxue After the completion of a moderately prosperous society in all respects, China has entered what official discourse calls a new development stage. Shuang asks what historical position this stage occupies and argues that it can only be fixed philosophically, using the worldview and method of materialist dialectics. The thesis is that the new stage is the sprint phase of national rejuvenation and a specific, higher-starting phase within the primary stage of socialism, not a break from it. The article is organised around three lenses. The first, a "grand historical outlook", places the stage within 180-plus years of modern Chinese history, more than 70 years of the People's Republic and more than 40 years of reform and opening up. The second, "dialectical thinking on change", applies the law of the mutual transformation of quantity and quality. The third, "holistic thinking", assesses the stage's future prospects. In the central section Shuang divides the primary stage into three phases: 1956–1978, 1978–2020, and 2020 to the middle of the century. The new stage belongs to the third and is marked by five features: the "two overall situations", high-quality development as its theme, building a modern socialist country as its goal, the new development philosophy, and a new development pattern centred on domestic circulation. Shuang argues that no fundamental qualitative change has occurred. The reasons given are that per capita GDP only just passed US$10,000 in 2019 and that key technologies remain dependent on others. Shuang adds that China remains the world's largest developing country and that the tasks of Chinese modernization are continuous with earlier ones. Looking ahead, Shuang calls for a systemic approach that combines structural, dynamic-open and strategic thinking. The new stage and a later, higher stage are presented as successive and continuous, both within the primary stage. Shuang maintains that the people-centred orientation and the development theme persist, while the content of development grows richer. The article further claims that Chinese modernization, by absorbing the achievements of capitalist civilization while going beyond its limits, opens the possibility of a new type of civilization oriented towards communism. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how a Chinese Marxist scholar uses dialectical categories to justify the periodisation of the primary stage of socialism and the logic of the 14th Five-Year Plan period.

The international communist movement presses forward in a period of turbulence and change Report on the development of the international communist movement, 2020–2021 动荡变革期的国际共产主义运动砥砺前行 Pan Jin'e This annual report, published in World Socialism Studies in August 2021, surveys the international communist movement in 2020 and the first half of 2021. Pan argues that the Covid-19 pandemic and 'changes unseen in a century' have made the trend of the East rising and the West declining more evident. In Pan's account, socialist countries showed institutional strengths while capitalist ones showed weaknesses, yet the world remains one of 'strong capitalism, weak socialism', so the movement must keep pressing forward. The report has four parts. It first covers commemorations of Engels's 200th birthday and Lenin's 150th, and the centenary reviews and tactical adjustments of communist parties. It then compares pandemic responses in socialist and capitalist states, followed by the development plans and party congresses of Vietnam, Laos, North Korea and Cuba. It closes with the external pressures and events of mid-2021, including the Communist Party of China's centenary. Pan's central comparison treats the pandemic as an 'X-ray' of social systems. Using figures for infections and growth, the author credits China, Vietnam, Laos, North Korea and Cuba with unified Party leadership, a people-first outlook and the capacity to concentrate resources. Pan reports that China, Vietnam and Laos had positive growth in 2020. By contrast, Pan reports that in the West the pandemic spread through profit-driven production and neoliberal cuts to public health, with inequality, unemployment and unrest including the Black Lives Matter protests. Pan also reports that some Western communist parties, such as those in the United States and France, built left alliances and gained influence. Pan concludes that socialist parties are reinforcing ideological work against Western 'peaceful evolution' and seeking closer solidarity. Pan reads the Biden administration's 'alliance of democracies' as an attempt to launch a 'new Cold War'. The report describes the July 2021 protests in Cuba as a US-engineered 'colour revolution' and notes the proposed ban on the German Communist Party's election participation. Read the original if you want a Chinese official-academic overview of how the world's communist parties and socialist states were assessed in 2020–2021, with data on the party congresses in Vietnam, Laos, North Korea and Cuba.

A historic debate over the concept of "revolution" and its present-day lessons An examination of the German "November Revolution" “革命”概念的一次历史大争论及其现实启示 Lai Qingli Lai Qingli asks how the different currents of German socialism understood "revolution" during the November Revolution of 1918–1919, and what that history teaches today. Earlier scholarship, Lai says, mostly lamented the defeat and denounced the Social Democratic right for betraying the revolution, and rarely studied the conceptual dispute. The article argues that each current grasped only part of the concept, and that this one-sided, structurally unbalanced understanding helped doom the revolution. The article first outlines the revolution's three phases, from the October 1918 sailors' mutiny to the fall of the Bavarian Soviet Republic in May 1919. It then compares right (Ebert, Scheidemann, Bernstein), centre (Kautsky) and left (Luxemburg, Liebknecht, and council advocates such as Richard Müller) on three questions. These are the means of revolution, its goals, and its essence, meaning why revolt at all and what kind of "civilisation" it should build. A concluding part draws lessons for socialist development. On means, Lai says the right used democracy passively and treated the republic as the revolution's endpoint. The centre promised to remake democracy but stayed rhetorical, and the left sought to break bourgeois democracy through violence and workers' and soldiers' councils. On essence, the right and centre held a linear, Europe-centred view of civilisation, and Lai says this reduced "revolution" to a synonym for "democracy" and made socialists fellow travellers of capitalism. The left aimed at a new civilisation but fragmented, because spontaneity produced competing means and goals, each claiming to embody the essence. Lai concludes that "revolution" must be grasped as a whole, drawing on Marx and Engels, with means, goals and essence corresponding to the subject, object and motive of revolution. Means must not be abstracted into "democracy", and essence must not be abstracted into slogans. Lai calls for a unified, advanced new-type proletarian party, and says socialism and capitalism stand in a relation of negation of the negation, not of earlier and later stages of civilisation. In this light the Party's self-reform and social revolution are presented as permanent themes. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly reading of Bernstein, Kautsky and Luxemburg on revolution, and its argument about revolution's internal balance.

New trends in the unification of communist parties worldwide in recent years and how China should respond 近年来世界共产党联合化新趋势与我们的应对 Yu Weihai Writing around the centenary of the Communist Party of China (2021), Yu Weihai asks what state the international communist movement is in amid what the article calls changes unseen in a century. Yu argues that the world's many communist and workers' parties show a clear tendency towards coordination. In Yu's account, this is a new historical pattern, different from the 19th- and 20th-century Internationals. The article has four parts. It first describes how party unification shows itself: standing platforms, joint statements, coordinated protests and a shared ethos. It then identifies four new features, assesses the trend's effects, and ends with policy proposals for China. Yu draws on lists of international party forums, counts of joint statements, and the author's own 2019 field research in the United States. Yu holds that the new unity rests on equal, voluntary association rather than a single centre, programme or line. It is plural, networked and organised around issues rather than organisations, and parties often belong to several platforms at once. Yu credits it with strengthening resistance to capitalism and showing that the international movement has not left the stage. Yu also stresses that sectarianism persists: the article cites some 400 communist parties worldwide, exclusionary forums and many factions, which Yu says leave unification inefficient. Diversity, in this view, adds cohesion but also breeds dogmatism and sharpens the tension between immediate and long-term goals. For China, Yu proposes more research on the international movement and on Xi Jinping's idea of a "new type of party relations". Yu also urges strategic composure: China should not lead, carry the banner, join or oppose, since developing socialism with characteristics of Chinese characteristics is its greatest contribution. Yu warns that some foreign parties criticise China within joint statements, and adds that other parties' support, such as praise for China's pandemic response, can be used. Yu suggests united-front work, party-to-party dialogue led by the International Department and a national think tank. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic view of how communist party networks are assessed and how China's party diplomacy toward them is framed.

The idea of totality From Hegel and Marx to the founders of Marxism outside China 总体性思想 Yang Haifeng Yang Haifeng asks how the concept of totality passed from Hegel to Marx and then became the entry point through which Lukács, Korsch and Gramsci rethought Marxist philosophy. The article's thesis is that these three first-generation thinkers of foreign Marxism broke with the Second International tradition by recovering totality as the core of Marx's philosophy. Yang opens by noting that modern specialisation and the division of labour have blurred any picture of society as a whole, and that philosophy has repeatedly tried to restore one. The text has three parts. The first traces totality in Hegel's account of the beginning of science as a circle, his critique of Kant's thing-in-itself and the dialectic of self-consciousness, and then in Marx's method in the 1857 Introduction. The second follows Lukács from Soul and Form and The Theory of the Novel through History and Class Consciousness to the late Ontology of Social Being. The third turns to Korsch (Marxism and Philosophy, Karl Marx) and Gramsci, and closes by comparing the three. Yang argues that Marx kept Hegel's totality but changed its ground: totality is rooted in social being and its production and reproduction, not in spirit. In Yang's reading it is a mediated whole organised by a dominant relation, which under capitalism is capital. Marx also saw unbridgeable fractures in this whole, and Yang says Marx did not think reason could reconcile them. For Lukács, totality is both a dialectical method and an ideal state of social being. Reification, rationalisation and the antinomies of classical German philosophy express its absence, and the late work grounds it in labour. Korsch insists that philosophy, political economy and scientific socialism form one revolutionary theory, and that splitting them vulgarises Marxism. Gramsci treats Marxism as self-sufficient and 'organic', and reads hegemony as political, economic and cultural together, not as a purely cultural doctrine. Yang concludes that the three thinkers revived Marxist philosophy against the mechanical Marxism of the Second International and brought the question of subjectivity into the discussion of totality. Their emphases differ. Lukács is the philosopher whose reification critique has strong purchase on reality. Korsch stresses the links between Marx's philosophy, political economy and socialism. Gramsci stresses the unity of politics, economy and culture. Yang adds that their work shaped the Frankfurt School and foreign Marxism from the 1930s to the 1960s. Read the original if you want a close account of how totality links Hegel, Marx and early Western Marxism, from a leading Chinese scholar of foreign Marxism.

Commemoration and reflection by the foreign left on the 200th anniversary of Engels's birth 国外左翼对恩格斯诞辰200周年的纪念与省思 Yuan Qun Wang Enming Yuan Qun and Wang Enming survey how left-wing parties, organisations and scholars outside China marked the 200th anniversary of Engels's birth in 2020, and what they said about him. Their thesis is that these tributes defended Engels's standing against long-running attempts to set him against Marx, and showed his ideas still guide the world socialist movement as it moves, in the authors' words, from a low ebb towards revival. The article first catalogues the commemorations: conferences in Portugal, Laos, Vietnam, Germany and Japan, joint declarations by Marxist-Leninist-Maoist parties, memorial essays by party leaders and academics, and events in Wuppertal and Moscow. It then groups the foreign left's assessments under four headings: Engels's historical position as Marx's indispensable 'second violin', the global significance of his works, their contemporary value, and the practical tasks the left drew from the anniversary. In the authors' account, foreign left voices affirmed Engels as co-founder of Marxism and scientific socialism and as a leader of the international workers' movement. They credited him with contributions to philosophy, political economy, the theory of the family and state, and proletarian military science. The authors report that these voices rejected the 'Marx–Engels opposition' thesis and the claim that the late Engels abandoned revolution for parliamentarism. They also report that speakers read the Covid-19 pandemic, financial crises and growing wealth concentration as confirming his analysis of capitalism. Cited figures include Gennady Zyuganov, Sitaram Yechury and Brinda Karat, along with Vietnamese Party sources. The authors conclude that the 2020 commemoration continued the 2018 Marx bicentenary and that Engels's theory of scientific socialism, workers' struggle and party-building remains relevant. They note the practical proposals the foreign left drew from it: building revolutionary parties, strengthening the study and publication of Marxist theory, and forming anti-war united fronts. They describe the commemorations, held amid what they call an intensifying imperialist anti-communist offensive, as a form of Marxist-Leninist education. Read the original if you want a detailed inventory of foreign left events, statements and sources on Engels in 2020, as reported from a Chinese academic perspective.

The historical significance of China's building a moderately prosperous society in all respects 中国全面建成小康社会的历史意义 Chen Jiangsheng Writing after Xi Jinping's announcement on 1 July 2021 that China had built a moderately prosperous society in all respects and eliminated absolute poverty, Chen Jiangsheng asks what this achievement means for human progress and the prospects of world socialism. The article argues that it is a milestone of Chinese modernization and an unprecedented feat in a developing country of over 1.4 billion people. In Chen's account it marks a shift in the global balance of forces, demonstrates the vitality of scientific socialism, and widens the routes available to developing countries seeking to escape poverty. The article has three main sections. The first sets out changes in the balance between developed capitalist and developing countries, between socialism and capitalism, and in people's capacity for all-round development, using IMF and UNDP figures. The second argues that scientific socialism alone can liberate and develop the productive forces, achieve common prosperity, and give China a bright future. The third reviews China's poverty reduction record and presents it as a new path, a new development idea and a set of experiences for other developing countries. Chen's first move is quantitative. Citing IMF data, the article says emerging and developing economies rose from about a quarter of developed-economy GDP in 2000 to nearly 70% in 2020, with China's output about twelve times larger. It adds figures on research spending, patents and the Human Development Index, noting that China is the only country to have moved from low to high human development since 1990. Second, Chen periodises world socialism: rise after 1917, decline after 1991, and a shift in the balance of forces toward socialism as China reaches this goal. Third, the article treats poverty alleviation as the core of socialism. It credits Party leadership, the people-centred development philosophy and a mix of government-led and multi-actor effort, development-oriented aid backed by social security, and a move from county-level to household-level targeting. Chen asserts that previous liberal, statist and Soviet-style approaches elsewhere yielded little. Chen concludes that only socialism, and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, can carry China from standing up and growing rich to becoming strong. The author accepts that the Chinese path cannot simply be copied but holds that it can serve as a reference for countries with similar needs. Read the original if you want to see how a Central Party School scholar links poverty alleviation statistics to claims about shifting global power and the future of world socialism.

Re-examining Marx's labour theory of value in the context of artificial intelligence 人工智能背景下马克思劳动价值论的再审视 Jia Shupin Jia Shupin asks whether the rise of artificial intelligence (AI) has changed Marx's labour theory of value, and how labour creates happiness under AI. The article answers that AI creates no value itself and that human labour remains the sole source of value. It also argues that AI's effects depend on the social system, and that labour and happiness are only reunited under socialism. The article opens by noting that bourgeois economists are reviving a 'factor theory of value', which Jia reads as an attempt to undermine Marx's theory of surplus value. It then proceeds in three parts: whether labour still creates value under AI; the contrasting outcomes under capitalism and socialism; and how labour produces happiness, with a closing turn to labour education for young people. Jia's central move is to place AI within the productive forces. Drawing on Marx's three elements of the labour process, the author treats AI as a science-and-technology factor that permeates the means of labour, the objects of labour and labourers themselves. Engineers still programme and debug the systems behind 'unmanned factories', so AI is an extension of human labour rather than a replacement. The second move is institutional. Under capitalism, Jia argues, AI raises the organic composition of capital, displaces workers, deepens polarisation and hastens capitalism's crisis, without ending alienated labour. Under socialism, with public ownership and equal labour relations, AI can be steered towards liberating labour, although Jia concedes that wage labour and some alienation persist in the non-public sector. Jia concludes that AI confirms rather than refutes the claims that labour creates value and that labour creates happiness. Short-term job displacement is acknowledged, but the author expects people to adapt and AI to relieve them of heavy toil. Citing Xi Jinping's remark that happiness comes from striving, Jia warns that some young people are over-reliant on AI and averse to labour, and calls for stronger labour education and a social atmosphere that respects labour. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist scholar defends the labour theory of value against AI-related challenges and links the debate to labour education policy.

The Communist Party of China's continuing contribution to the international communist movement 中国共产党为国际共产主义运动持续贡献力量 Ji Zhengju Marking the centenary of the Communist Party of China in 2021, Ji Zhengju asks how the Party's hundred years of revolution, construction and reform have contributed to the international communist movement and the cause of world socialism. The article argues that the Party has made a continuous contribution in four areas: the practical path, theory, institutions and culture. The piece is a commemorative commentary organised in four numbered sections, each opening with a statement of the contribution made "from" one dimension: practice, theory, institutions and culture. It moves from the revolutionary path and the socialist transformation to the reform era, from the sinicisation of Marxism to the institutional system set out at the Fourth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2019), and then to cultural resources. On practice, Ji lists the rural-encirclement revolutionary road, the rapid socialist transformation of the world's most populous country, and the survival and success of socialism with Chinese characteristics after the Soviet collapse. Ji also lists Chinese modernization as an experience for developing countries. On theory, Ji argues that adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times produced a line of theoretical achievements from Mao Zedong Thought to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, which is said to make an original contribution to the movement. On institutions, Ji describes a tiered system of fundamental, basic and important institutions, with Party leadership as the most essential feature. Ji cites the Soviet Union's fate, thirty years after its dissolution, as a warning against weakening that leadership, and presents China's handling of Covid-19 as proof of institutional advantage. On culture, Ji credits the combination of traditional Chinese culture, revolutionary culture and advanced socialist culture, including the spirits of Jinggangshan, Yan'an and the Long March. Ji concludes that a Party that grew from some fifty members to over 95 million is now the world's largest governing party. Standing at the junction of the "Two Centenary Goals", Ji expects socialism with Chinese characteristics to widen and to contribute more to human progress and the international communist movement. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the Party's 2021 centenary discourse frames China's role in the international communist movement.

An analysis of the reform of Vietnam's National Assembly oversight system since Đổi Mới 革新开放以来越南国会监督制度改革探析 Liu Yudi Since the launch of renovation and opening up (Đổi Mới) in 1986, how has Vietnam's National Assembly strengthened its supervision of state organs and officials, and what can China learn from it? Liu Yudi argues that Vietnam has steadily widened and refined National Assembly oversight in response to four concrete problems: the spread of bourgeois liberalization, corruption, uneven implementation of Party Central Committee decisions, and weak supervisory results. In Liu's account, over thirty years of reform have made oversight an indispensable part of the Party and state power-supervision system, although the problems have not been fully resolved. The article is organised around those four problems, followed by a section of lessons for China. It traces changes in who may be questioned, reviewed or subjected to confidence votes, from 1986 through 2013 and beyond. It draws on cases such as the 2006 questioning of Prime Minister Phan Van Khai, the 2010 rejection of the north–south high-speed rail proposal, the Vinashin losses, and thematic supervision of education, higher education, land management and food safety. Liu also lists procedural innovations in questioning and report review from 2009 to 2019. Liu presents the reforms as a response to the shock of the Soviet collapse and to liberal figures within the Party, who the author says promoted multi-party politics and the separation of powers. The Assembly removed such figures and then extended supervision to every body it elects or approves. Against corruption, it concentrated on senior leaders, using confidence votes and evaluations governed by a 2012 resolution, with the posts covered later narrowed to about fifty. To enforce Party decisions, it used thematic supervision teams that review reports, conduct field investigations, hold seminars and cooperate with ministries. To improve effectiveness, it introduced interactive formats such as grouped questions, live debate, one-minute questions and three-minute answers, and added procedural steps. Liu concludes that socialist states should reform the supervision systems of their organs of state power while upholding the Marxist theory of the state and the laws of socialist democracy. Three lessons are drawn for China's National People's Congress: make fuller use of deputies' initiative, coordinate supervisory bodies and mechanisms into a joint force, and perfect mechanisms so that oversight becomes a sharp weapon against corruption. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's account of Vietnam's parliamentary oversight, with dated procedural details and the reform lessons it proposes for China.

Transcending the logic of capital: innovation and development of the basic socialist economic system 超越资本逻辑：社会主义基本经济制度的创新与发展 Dai Jinping Writing in 2021, Dai Jinping asks how the basic socialist economic system, as expanded by the Fourth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2019), can sublate and transcend the logic of capital. The article argues that the shift from a single ownership-based system to a three-part system of ownership, distribution and economic institutions marks a major theoretical innovation. In Dai's reading, it also marks the point at which socialism with Chinese characteristics has largely taken definitive shape after more than forty years of reform. The article has three sections. The first presents Marx's critique of the logic of capital as the key to analysing capitalist society, and notes that Marx himself spoke of capital's "laws" and "tendencies" rather than a "logic of capital". The second traces how contemporary capital has changed, using the three dimensions of valorisation, expansion and reification. The third examines in turn the ownership structure, the distribution system and the socialist market economy. Dai argues that monopolisation, financialisation and globalisation have strengthened capital's logic of valorisation. Financial capital, in this account, is largely fictitious and speculative. Dai cites US data on financial firms' share of corporate profits and the 2008 crisis as evidence that Marx's laws still apply. Rising wealth polarisation, in Dai's view, shows that welfare-state measures cannot touch private ownership of the means of production. Against this, the article holds that public ownership as the mainstay, together with the Two Unwaverings, advances a public "logic of capital" and curbs the excesses of the private one while still using capital to develop the productive forces. Distribution according to labour as the mainstay, with other modes alongside it, is presented as protecting labour income and supporting common prosperity. The socialist market economy is said to reject the opposition between market and state and to combine the "invisible hand" with the "visible hand". Dai concludes that these three institutions together sublate and transcend the logic of capital, and that they supply an institutional base for sustained economic growth, common prosperity and high-quality development. The article also points to the Fifth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee, which restated the Two Unwaverings, distribution according to labour and the aim of a high-level socialist market economy. Dai presents this as strengthening institutional confidence. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist scholar applies Marx's critique of capital to justify the current Chinese ownership, distribution and market arrangements.

The dissemination of Marx's Capital in Germany 马克思《资本论》在德国的传播历程研究 Wang Zhan Wang Zhan asks how Marx's Capital and its large body of manuscripts were spread and received in Germany, the country of Marx's birth and the language of his text. The article argues that this history, which forms part of the wider history of Marxism, shows two things. German scholars developed a double narrative, one revolutionary and one academic. German scholarship is also marked by rigorous philological work and philosophical speculation. The study is chronological and has four parts. It covers the early dissemination under Marx and Engels from the 1860s to the 1890s, then popularisation from the 1890s to the 1930s. It then treats the publication of the manuscripts and the rise of the "New Reading of Marx" from 1930 to the 1990s, and finally developments since 2000. It draws on figures such as Engels, Karl Kautsky, David Riazanov, Henryk Grossmann, Friedrich Pollock, Hans-Georg Backhaus and Helmut Reichelt. Wang first describes how Engels fought the bourgeois economists' "conspiracy of silence" after 1867 by writing reviews and a study outline. Engels also edited later German editions and Volumes II and III. Wang then follows the popular and abridged editions by Johann Most, Kautsky, Julian Borchardt and Kautsky's sons. The article notes criticisms of these editions, for example that Borchardt rearranged Marx's order and that the Kautskys' editions removed the description of workers' conditions and carried a reformist preface. It also covers Kautsky's edition of Theories of Surplus Value. In the middle sections Wang traces the MEGA1 and MEGA2 projects, the early Frankfurt School's readings of Capital, and the "New Reading of Marx". Grossmann read the three volumes as a methodological unfolding of accumulation and breakdown, Pollock stressed money theory, and Backhaus and Reichelt centred value-form theory and the dialectic. Wang notes that MEGA2 Part II, completed in 2012, allows Marx's manuscripts and Engels's edited text to be compared line by line for the first time. Michael Heinrich is cited as saying that debate over Capital now has a sufficient textual basis. Since 2007 student reading campaigns, the Marx Autumn School and the Rosa Luxemburg Foundation's courses have brought Capital to wider German audiences, according to the article. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-based survey of the German publication history and editions of Capital and of the scholarly traditions around it.

The young Engels's critique of classical liberalism 青年恩格斯对古典自由主义的批判 Kou Dongliang Kou Dongliang asks how the young Engels came to criticise and move beyond classical liberalism, and why this matters for the formation of Marxism's new worldview. The article argues that Engels's critique of economic, political and cultural liberalism was an important link in that process. It holds that Engels moved from a vague longing for liberation to a working-class standpoint and a communist vision of freedom. The article follows Engels's development in three stages. It begins with his break with Pietism, his attachment to Young Germany and then to the Young Hegelians, and his assessment of "German liberalism" through to the 1848 revolution. It then turns to his Manchester years (1842–44) and his critique of free competition and "legal freedom" in works such as Outlines of a Critique of Political Economy. It ends with his working-class standpoint, his idea of free labour and his account of communist freedom. Kou's central argument is that Engels saw liberal freedom as formal and bound to private property. On economic liberalism, Engels is said to identify three flaws in competition: the inversion of the human–thing relation, since people become slaves to things; the hostility among individuals pursuing the same interests; and the blindness of production, which produces commercial crises. On political liberalism, Engels acknowledges the historical gains of rights such as the 1824 freedom of association in Britain. Even so, he treats constitutional monarchy and bourgeois democracy as the rule of property and as "illusory" freedom. Kou also notes Engels's judgment that political liberalism could never be realised in Germany, because of a national preference for abstract principle and a weak bourgeoisie that compromised with feudal absolutism. Kou concludes that, from the standpoint of the working class, Engels grounded socialism in the facts of industrial Britain, especially in The Condition of the Working Class in England. He then helped found scientific socialism with Marx. Engels's Principles of Communism defines communism as the doctrine of the conditions of proletarian emancipation and pictures a planned, associated society in which all members develop fully. Kou argues that the Marxist view of freedom thereby surpasses classical liberalism both in its class narrowness and in its illusory content. Read the original if you want a detailed, text-based account of Engels's early intellectual path from German liberalism to communism, drawing on his 1839–45 writings.

Three dimensions of academic-history research on Western Marxism and their contemporary value 论西方马克思主义学术史研究的三个面向及其当代价值 Wang Yuchen Wang Yuchen distinguishes the intellectual history of Western Marxism, which traces how the tradition developed, from its academic history, which builds on that record to examine the tradition's inner theoretical logic, its theoretical effects and its practical effects. The article argues that these three dimensions together structure academic-history research and that each carries value for the present. The article has three sections. The first reconstructs the starting point and unfolding of Western Marxism's theoretical logic. The second assesses its theoretical effects on Marxism outside China, on later schools and on Chinese Marxist philosophy. The third turns to practical effects on Western socialist movements and new social movements. Figures discussed include Lukács, Korsch, Gramsci, Althusser, the Frankfurt School, Sartre, Lefebvre, Jameson, ecological Marxists and analytical Marxists. For Wang, the tradition arose from reflection on failed Western revolutions and began with the question of what Marxist philosophy essentially is. Its thinkers rejected readings of Marxism as an early-modern, knowledge-theoretical philosophy. They stressed its critical and practical side and developed five lines of theory: alienation, cultural-ideological critique, critique of technological rationality, ecological critique and political philosophy. Wang then traces their effects. Post-Marxism borrowed from Gramsci and Althusser while, in Wang's account, distorting them. The late Marxism of Jameson and Eagleton and British cultural studies drew on the tradition more fruitfully. Wang describes foreign Marxism as making two turns, first to culture and then back to political economy. In practice, one strand sought the emancipation of the proletariat as a whole and the other that of the individual. Wang links the second strand to the 1968 student revolts and to ecological movements, and notes the limits of these theories, including subjectivising alienation and mixing up alienation with objectification. Wang concludes that Western Marxism helped Chinese scholars understand the nature of Marxist philosophy. Since reform and opening up it has fed Chinese debates on practice, subjectivity and philosophical form, and has opened new fields such as cultural, technology-critical and ecological philosophy. Wang holds that these fields help address negative phenomena in China's modernization. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's systematic account of how Western Marxism is assessed and used in Chinese Marxist philosophy.

Reflections on the world's entry into a period of turbulence and change amid changes unseen in a century 百年大变局下世界进入动荡变革期的思考与启示 Zhou Miao Writing in 2021, Zhou Miao takes up Xi Jinping's judgement that the world has entered a "period of turbulence and change" (2020), which deepens the earlier assessment of "changes unseen in a century". The article asks how this judgement relates to the established view that peace and development are the themes of the era, and how China should pursue development in a more unstable world. Zhou argues that the turbulence results from capitalist crisis, a shift in the balance between the two systems, and US-led efforts to preserve the old international order. Zhou concludes that China remains in a period of important strategic opportunity. The article has four parts. It first sets out the Marxist concept of an era and the "theme of the era", tracing it from Engels and Lenin through Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and later Party congress reports. It then explains the background to the new judgement under three headings. A third part assesses China's prospects and responses, and a short conclusion ties these to the 14th Five-Year Plan period beginning in 2021. Zhou first distinguishes the world's themes from the nature of the era. Peace and development are the two major strategic questions facing the world, Zhou says, but the era itself is still shaped by capitalism's basic contradictions, hegemonism and an unjust old international order. On the causes of turbulence, Zhou draws on Kondratiev's long-wave theory to place the world economy in a downswing since the 2008 financial crisis. Zhou also describes an "East rising, West declining" trend in the relation between the two systems, driven by the success of socialism with Chinese characteristics. A third cause is the US response to its relative economic decline: Zhou calls neoliberal financialisation a parasitic and unsustainable accumulation model, and argues that US strategy aims to suppress China and shift the costs of crisis onto others. Zhou contends that turbulence does not cancel China's strategic opportunity, which is "great potential" and depends on both objective conditions and subjective effort. The article proposes applying the new development philosophy to achieve high-quality development, coordinating development with security (including financial security), and building a new development pattern centred on domestic circulation. It also calls for reform of global governance and for building a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want to see how a CASS Marxist scholar links Leninist theories of the era and long-wave crisis theory to official judgements about the international environment in 2021.

Adhering to the integration of the basic tenets of Marxism with China's fine traditional culture 坚持马克思主义基本原理同中华优秀传统文化相结合 Wang Yi Writing in a newspaper commentary shortly after the Party's centenary in 2021, Wang Yi takes up Xi Jinping's call to combine the basic tenets of Marxism with China's concrete realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture. Wang argues that this combination has been a major theoretical and practical concern throughout the Party's hundred years. The author presents Marxism and traditional culture as two things neither of which can be dropped without harming China's development. The article has three parts. The first sets out the contemporary value of fine traditional culture, summarised by Xi in six phrases: benevolence, putting the people first, honesty and trustworthiness, justice, harmony and cooperation, and the ideal of great unity. The second traces how the Party has carried forward that culture, from the new-democratic revolution through the Mao era, reform and opening up, and the new era under Xi. The third explains why the two fit together and how traditional culture should be developed under Marxist guidance. Wang's central claim is that Marxism can take root in Chinese culture because the two overlap in content. The examples given are the traditional idea of responsibility for the world and the Communist Manifesto's description of the proletarian movement; the saying that the boat can be capsized by the water and Marxism's view of the masses as makers of history; and the Datong ideal of a world held in common and communism. In the author's account, Marxism is the guiding or dominant consciousness and traditional culture a supporting one, so that valuable historical resources are turned to present use. Wang lists five requirements for the creative transformation and innovative development of traditional culture: Marxist guidance, links to the modern, closeness to the masses, engagement with the world while keeping national distinctiveness, and dialogue with the future. Wang concludes that integrating Marxism with traditional culture is a necessary task in continuing this theme in the new era. The author also credits the approach with strengthening cultural confidence, supporting the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and answering why Marxism works and why socialism with Chinese characteristics is good. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned outline of how Party theory in 2021 framed the relation between Marxism and traditional culture, with historical examples from Mao to Xi.

The Communist Party of China and socialism with Chinese characteristics 中国共产党与中国特色社会主义 Wang Huaichao Zhang Rui Written for the centenary of the Communist Party of China in 2021 and first published in the China Social Sciences Today newspaper, this commentary by Wang Huaichao and Zhang Rui asks how the Party and socialism with Chinese characteristics relate to each other. The authors argue that the two form a single, inseparable whole. In their account, the Party is both the pioneer and the leading core of the cause, and the cause's growth in turn strengthens the Party. The piece has four parts. An opening overview sets out the Party's hundred-year record. Three sections follow: the Party as pioneer of socialism with Chinese characteristics, the Party as its leading core, and the Party's own development in the course of building it. The authors move through the stages of new-democratic revolution, socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). They quote Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping throughout. On the first point, Wang and Zhang trace the idea from Mao Zedong's mid-1950s call to take the Soviet experience as a warning. They then move to Deng Xiaoping's 1982 formulation of building socialism with Chinese characteristics. On the second, they hold that the Party can lead because it stands at the forefront of its time and draws up correct strategic lines. They cite the two-step revolutionary strategy, the general line of the early People's Republic, the judgement that China is in the primary stage of socialism, and the achievements claimed since 2012. They present Party membership growth, from about fifty members in 1921 to more than 91 million by the end of 2019, as evidence of popular trust. The authors then list four areas of Party building. The first is political building, which they break into seven elements, from political direction to political capability. The second is combining ideological education with institutional governance. The third is work style and ties to the masses. The fourth is staying at the forefront of the times amid what they call great changes unseen in a century. They conclude that when the Party flourishes the cause flourishes, and that the two advance together. Read the original if you want a concise example of the official centenary narrative on the Party's leadership and its self-building, with extended quotations from Deng and Xi.

The new-type party system: the global significance of a Chinese story 新型政党制度：一个中国故事的世界意义 Wang Cailing Wang Cailing's commentary, published after the State Council Information Office issued its white paper on China's new-type party system, asks why official discourse moved from "China's party system" (the title of the 2007 white paper) to "the new-type party system". The author argues that the shift answers a practical need to build a Chinese discourse that can break out of Western-centred party theory. The system, Wang holds, is a new paradigm in world party politics and carries significance beyond China. The article has three sections. The first presents the system as a new model that overturns Western classifications of party systems. The second sets out its Chinese characteristics: its historical logic, its roots in traditional culture and its fit with socialist governance. The third discusses its "worldliness" and what it offers other countries, especially developing ones. Wang first rejects the view of some scholars that the system is a later stage of multiparty cooperation, arguing that it was a new-type system from its founding in 1949. Its importance, in this reading, is that it replaces the one-party, two-party and multiparty typology with a distinction between new and old, and rejects judging systems by the number or rotation of ruling parties. Wang adds that in Western theory a party is a "part" in competition with others. The Communist Party and the democratic parties are instead described as forces that jointly pursue the interests of the "whole". Wang traces the system to the united front, to Marxism and to traditions such as "all under heaven for the common good" and great unification. It is said to favour "pluralistic unity" over competition, and to move from "the will of all" to "the general will". Wang concludes that the system is both Chinese and universal. It drew on Western tools and on Soviet lessons while keeping its independence, and it embodies the "common values of all mankind". The author argues that it offers developing countries a "new choice" at a time when Western party politics is in crisis. Wang calls for including this experience in the global body of knowledge, and presents the white paper as a step in that direction. Read the original if you want an example of how official Chinese scholarship presents its party system as a challenge to Western political theory.

The world-historical significance of the Chinese Communist Party's century of practice 中国共产党百年实践的世界历史意义 Dai Yuqi Published in the China Social Sciences Today in June 2021, on the eve of the Party's centenary, this commentary asks what the Chinese Communist Party's hundred years of practice mean for world history. Dai Yuqi argues that under the Party's leadership China has opened a new realm for the socialist road, a new pattern of party development aimed at the people's well-being, and a new direction for human civilization. The piece is organised under three headings that correspond to these claims. The first retraces the history of socialism from Marx and Engels through Lenin's Russia to China, setting out the failed late-Qing and republican attempts at national salvation and the Party's successive roads. The second discusses the Party's people-centred character, its long-term strategic goals and its efforts at Party discipline. The third turns to the problems of capitalist modernity and the Party's concept of civilization. Dai contends that the Party integrated the basic tenets of Marxism with Chinese realities, creating socialism with Chinese characteristics. In this reading, the Reform-era economic system (public ownership as the mainstay alongside several forms of ownership, and distribution according to work) and the success of this path lifted world socialism out of the trough that followed the upheavals in Eastern Europe and the Soviet collapse. On party-building, the author traces a line of strategic goals from the four modernizations to the 'two centenary goals', and presents the Party's self-purification as a model for parties elsewhere. On civilization, Dai sees private ownership as the root of alienation under capitalism and outlines a succession of Party concepts (the Three Represents, the Scientific Outlook on Development, and Xi Jinping's ecological civilization thought) building up a system of material, political, spiritual, social and ecological civilization. Dai concludes that the path opened by the Party's century of practice goes beyond the Western capitalist road and, guided by Marxism, will advance towards a new stage of human civilization. Developing China well is itself presented as a contribution to a community with a shared future for mankind, alongside dialogue with other parties and peoples. Read the original if you want a compact example of how the Party's centenary narrative framed its international and civilizational significance.

An analysis of Marx's thought on economic justice: a study of Capital 马克思经济正义思想探析——以《资本论》为研究对象 Zhu Xinyuan Marx never treated economic justice systematically, and the long-running dispute over Marx and justice has produced divergent and one-sided readings. Zhu Xinyuan takes up the question by reading Capital, and argues that Marx's economic justice thought can be understood in a broad sense, covering economic institutions, activities and ideas, and in a narrow sense, covering justice in production, exchange, distribution and consumption. The article was published in a university journal in 2021. The article has three parts. The first sets out three layers of meaning: justice in economic theory, based on equal rights; justice in economic activity; and justice in economic institutions, meaning communist society. The second identifies two features of the thought: the theoretical character of historical materialism and an ethical character of humanistic concern. The third turns to its contemporary value for China's socialist market economy, at the levels of theory and practice. Zhu argues that, for Marx, the equal rights of the market are formal. Labour-power is sold in the sphere of circulation, which Marx calls the true Eden of the innate rights of man. Beyond that sphere the apparent fair exchange between worker and capitalist is, in Zhu's reading, unfair, because the capitalist appropriates unpaid labour. Zhu holds that Marx affirmed the justice of exchange under capitalism while sharply criticising its production and distribution. Justice is judged by whether a mode of production fits its historical stage, citing Marx's remark that a transaction is just if it corresponds to the mode of production. Zhu also stresses that Marx sought a real path to a just order, rather than an ideal blueprint. That path runs through public ownership, distribution according to labour, and a higher stage in which free time replaces labour time as the measure of wealth. Zhu concludes that this thought offers guidance for China's development, and calls for applying historical materialism to current economic relations. The article points to unequal urban–rural public services and collusion between power and capital as problems. It endorses the shared development philosophy and common prosperity, and calls for legal and credit systems, moral self-discipline among economic actors, attention to vulnerable groups, and tax and social security reform to narrow the wealth gap. Zhu presents the aim as social fairness and justice in general, beyond economic justice alone. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic reading of Capital on justice and its application to China's market economy.

Re-understanding Mao Zedong's dialectics 毛泽东辩证法的再认识 Wang Nanshi Wang Nanshi argues that the originality of Mao Zedong's dialectics has long been overlooked. In Wang's account, the cause lies in two dominant readings of Marxist dialectics, the French-materialist and the Hegelian, which cannot accommodate Mao's distinctive concepts and so trim them to fit. The article's thesis is that Mao's dialectics is a dialectics of practical wisdom, a major innovation in Marxism and a resource for building a Chinese-style system of Marxist dialectics. The article, a short newspaper piece, has three parts. The first defines in what sense Mao's dialectics is one of practical wisdom, drawing on Aristotle's distinction between theoretical and practical activity and on Mao's essay On Contradiction. The second asks why such a dialectics emerged within a Marxism of Western origin, and turns to Chinese modes of thinking. The third examines Marx's Capital and the contribution Mao's dialectics makes to Marxist philosophy. Wang reasons that theory deals with eternal objects and therefore uses fixed categories, while practice deals with changeable objects. On Contradiction presupposes a changeable, heterogeneous world, as shown by the distinctions between principal and secondary contradictions, between principal and secondary aspects, and by the theory of uneven development of contradiction. Drawing on Zhang Dongsun, Wang contrasts Western thought, which probes 'behind' things for a single origin, with Chinese thought, which attends to relations among phenomena and to becoming. Mao's categories, Wang holds, grow from the latter. Capital, by contrast, is read as a materialistically reworked Hegelian dialectics of theoretical wisdom, which builds abstract models and ascends slowly to the concrete. Practice cannot wait for that, so practical-wisdom dialectics supplements it by grasping the principal contradiction directly. Wang concludes that Marxism now contains two dialectics, one for scientific theory and one for forming action plans. They are complementary and mutually determining: theory sets limits on practical wisdom, while practical wisdom supplies the ground for further abstraction. Because practical wisdom has the foundational place and rests on Chinese thinking, Wang holds that a system combining both would be a Chinese-style Marxist dialectics. Read the original if you want a compact philosophical argument for treating Mao's dialectics as a distinct, culturally rooted contribution to Marxism.
