Cuba's model update under the test of COVID-19 and the Eighth Congress of the Cuban Communist Party 新冠肺炎疫情考验下的古巴模式更新与古共八大 He Qin He Qin examines how Cuba, hit in 2020 by COVID-19 and a tightened US blockade, handled the pandemic while pushing ahead with the "updating" of its socialist model, and what the Eighth Party Congress (April 2021) meant for that process. The article, a chapter in a 2021 yearbook on the international communist movement, argues that Party leadership and people-centred institutions produced notable pandemic results, while the update remains behind schedule and now faces a generational handover. The text has three parts. The first covers Cuba's anti-epidemic experience and its overseas medical aid. The second reviews the update process since the Seventh Party Congress (2016), its achievements and problems, and the pandemic-era adjustments, above all the reform of the dual-currency system. The third describes preparations for the Eighth Congress, the leadership succession, Party-building and the congress's economic agenda. On the pandemic, He credits unified Party and government direction, mass organisations and family-doctor clinics, and a long-standing welfare system. The author cites figures such as a cure rate above 93% against a 69% global average, four candidate vaccines in clinical trials, and 53 medical brigades sent to over 40 countries. He presents this internationalism as a contrast with US hostility. On the economy, He lists persistent problems: egalitarian pay with weak incentives, low agricultural output, narrow exports, ageing and pension pressure, and the blockade. The 2020 strategy and the currency reform, which will end the convertible peso, unify exchange rates and shift subsidies from goods to persons, are described as the key step, with official forecasts of an economic fall of 11% in 2020 and inflationary risk of 3,200%. He reports that the Eighth Congress made Miguel Díaz-Canel First Secretary after Raúl Castro stepped down, completing the transfer from the revolutionary generation. It focused on Party functions, ideological work and cadre policy, and committed to deepening the update while keeping the state sector dominant. He concludes that the new leaders face the dual test of holding to the socialist road and renewing the model, and that Cuban socialism can move forward only by balancing reform, development and stability. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly account of Cuba's pandemic response, currency reform and 2021 Party congress, including the official data and documents it draws on.

The theoretical essence of Lenin's New Economic Policy and its contemporary value 列宁新经济政策的理论精髓及其当代价值 Wang Jinfen Yang Xiuqin Writing on the centenary of the New Economic Policy (NEP), Wang Jinfen and Yang Xiuqin ask what is essential in Lenin's turn of March 1921 from War Communism and why it still matters. They recall that Deng Xiaoping, thinking about what socialism is and how to build it, judged that Lenin's approach with the NEP was the better one, and that Xi Jinping praised the NEP in 2013 as the fruit of Lenin's arduous exploration without precedent. The authors argue that four elements of its theoretical essence offer lessons for socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era. The article is organised around these four elements, each treated through Lenin's speeches and writings of 1920–22. They are: popular satisfaction as the basis of Party policy and the measure of its success; starting from practice rather than books; looking at problems politically and avoiding political dangers and errors; and using capitalism to build socialism. Each section ends by linking Lenin's position to statements by Xi Jinping and to present-day Party tasks. In the authors' account, the Kronstadt sailors' revolt and the peasant uprisings and strikes of 1920–21 showed that War Communism, with grain requisitioning and the abolition of trade, had cut the Party's policy off from the people. Lenin therefore treated the people's will as decisive and demanded real economic work over empty talk. The authors say he broke with the conceptions of Marx and Engels, admitting that no book had dealt with state capitalism under communism. They present the NEP as above all a political question, namely the relationship between workers and peasants, resting on an economic union of the two. For this reason Lenin rejected Trotsky's separation of politics from economics and banned factions at the 10th Party Congress. On capitalism, the authors read Lenin as treating it as a necessary intermediate link between small-scale production and socialism, to be channelled into state capitalism. He also warned that Communists lacked the skill to steer it, likening the policy to a car that does not obey its driver, and urged them to out-compete the capitalists. The authors conclude that Lenin's lessons apply today. In their view the Party should put the people's satisfaction first and treat Marxism as developing with practice. They also call for political awareness, sensitivity and judgement among cadres in a period of great global change, noting that some Party members still lack it. And they hold that China must learn from the achievements of capitalism while staying alert to capital's profit-seeking nature and to Western attempts at containment. They say China should neither return to a rigid, closed path nor change its banner. Read the original if you want a Chinese Party-scholarly reading of the NEP, with extensive Lenin quotations, as a guide to current policy on markets, capital and Party leadership.

Real-world challenges in building a community with a shared future for mankind and strategies for meeting them 构建人类命运共同体面临的现实挑战和应对策略 Ren Jie Writing in 2021, Ren Jie asks what obstacles stand in the way of building a community with a shared future for mankind, a concept presented as part of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Ren acknowledges the concept's growing international recognition but argues that its realisation is a long and arduous process facing three real-world challenges. The article also proposes four strategies for dealing with them. The article is organised in four parts. Three sections take up the challenges in turn: differences in strategic thinking and cultural values, gaps in comprehensive national strength, and conflicts over core national interests. A final section sets out responses. Ren draws on Xi Jinping's speeches, Marx on interests, Hedley Bull's idea of international society, UN Secretary-General António Guterres's 2021 debt proposals, and examples from US foreign policy and the Belt and Road Initiative. On the first challenge, Ren contends that states understand freedom and democracy differently, and that US zero-sum and binary thinking, which Ren says is rooted in a sense of mission, leads Washington to misread China's intentions. Ren cites US think-tank reports and the Biden-era Build Back Better World initiative as attempts to contain or replace the Belt and Road Initiative. On the second, Ren notes that developing countries' collective economic weight is rising, yet argues that China's per capita income, military power and cultural influence still lag behind those of the United States, so claims of a 'Chinese century' are unrealistic and unequal strength undermines extensive consultation, joint contribution and shared benefits. On the third, Ren holds that core interests differ across regions, but that common human interests make a higher-level union of nation-states possible. Ren proposes four responses: telling the story of the community well, including through accurate translation of the term and stronger discourse power; delivering on commitments to developing countries' development rights and easing their debt burdens; upholding multilateralism and regional cooperation, with RCEP as an example; and promoting a new international political and economic order, with greater solidarity among developing countries. Ren concludes that when humanity's survival is at stake, national interests must yield to common human interests. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly account of how the concept is defended against perceived US opposition and of what practical communication and diplomatic measures are recommended.

A century of Chinese Marxist political economy: retrospect and prospect 中国马克思主义政治经济学百年回顾与展望 Tian Pengying Marking the centenary of the Communist Party of China in 2021, Tian Pengying reviews how the Party has continuously explored and developed Marxist political economy. The author argues that this history explains how the Party raised its capacity to lead economic development and produced the "two miracles" of rapid growth and long-term social stability. It also, in Tian's view, indicates how new economic achievements can be created and how a 21st-century Marxist political economy can be opened up. The short newspaper essay has three parts. The first traces the adaptation of Marxist political economy to Chinese conditions from the New Democratic revolution through the Mao Zedong era to reform and opening up. The second sets out seven contributions of the political economy of socialism with Chinese characteristics since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The third looks ahead to the field's prospects. Tian presents the process as a sequence of theoretical innovations tied to practice. Mao's New Democratic economic programme, his repeated study of Capital and his theory of the basic contradictions of socialist society are followed by Deng Xiaoping's theory of the socialist market economy and of the primary stage of socialism. For the Xi Jinping era, the seven contributions include the Party's overall leadership of economic work, the people-centred development philosophy, the Two Unwaverings, adapting to the "new normal", letting the market play the decisive role in resource allocation, supply-side structural reform, and the new development stage, philosophy and pattern. Tian describes these as turning the regular patterns of China's practice into a systematic theory. Looking forward, Tian calls for three tasks: summing up great practical experience so that theory and economic practice interact well; grasping major questions of the era, including Chinese modernization and a new form of human civilisation; and engaging with the world governance system amid what the author calls changes unseen in a century. Tian holds that Chinese Marxist political economy offers a "Chinese approach" for other countries' high-quality development and can help guide reform of global governance. Read the original if you want a compact example of how a Party-school-style survey periodises the Sinification of Marxist political economy and lists its official contributions.

The New Economic Policy in Lenin's political perspective A close reading of "Notes of a Publicist" and related works 列宁政治视野下的新经济政策 Yu Liangzao After the shift from War Communism to the New Economic Policy (NEP) in March 1921, capitalist economic elements revived in Soviet Russia and drew doubt and hostility inside and outside the Russian Communist Party (Bolsheviks). Yu Liangzao asks how Lenin answered these voices in two works, "Notes of a Publicist" and "The New Era and the New Forms of the Old Mistakes". The article argues that Lenin placed the NEP in a political perspective, set within international and domestic politics, and that this method guided correct understanding of the policy and still offers lessons today. Yu works through the two texts in four sections. The first covers Lenin's periodisation of the revolution into four stages and his claim that the Party had reached the "highest and most difficult stage". The second sets out what Lenin said relying on the proletariat's revolutionary spirit required. The third examines his critique of erroneous currents. The fourth is Yu's own assessment, which links Lenin's ideas to present-day Party tasks. Yu's central claim is that Lenin read the NEP against the whole course since October 1917 and against the French Revolution and the Paris Commune, rather than as an isolated set of economic measures. In this reading, the revolution had completed the bourgeois-democratic tasks, left the imperialist war and built Soviet power, so a limited growth of capitalist elements under proletarian state power was no cause for alarm. Lenin called it a "concession" and a "strategic retreat" with limits, and Yu reports that he also named dangers: isolation and the risk of restoration. Lenin's tasks were mainly political: set cautious aims, lay the foundations of a socialist economy, regroup a weakened working class and consolidate the worker–peasant alliance. Yu says Lenin classed the Mensheviks, Socialist-Revolutionaries and Second International right as petty-bourgeois reformism making "old mistakes in new forms". He placed the "Workers' Opposition" on the "left", charging it with semi-anarchism and with denying Party leadership. Yu credits Lenin with political discernment and judgement. Yu concludes that Lenin's approach is instructive for the Communist Party of China in a period of "great changes unseen in a century". The author links it to Xi Jinping's calls to strengthen political judgement, political understanding and political execution, and calls Xi's statements a continuation and enrichment of Lenin's thought. Lenin's critique of erroneous currents is also said to bear on resisting historical nihilism, "wholesale Westernisation" and democratic socialism, as the author names them. Read the original if you want a Chinese Party-theory reading of Lenin's NEP texts and of how they are tied to current ideological work.)

The Communist Party of Vietnam: setting out on a new journey through inheritance and upholding fundamentals 越南共产党：在传承与守正中踏上新征程 Pan Jin'e Wei Lichun This chapter, from the Report on the Development of the International Communist Movement (2020–2021), reviews what the Communist Party of Vietnam did in 2020, the year before its 13th Congress. Pan and Wei argue that the Party combined two tasks: upholding Marxism-Leninism and Ho Chi Minh Thought through commemorations, and preparing leadership, documents and strategy for the Congress. In their account, this strengthened the Party's ruling position and public confidence amid ideological pressure and the Covid-19 pandemic. The text has four parts. The first covers the 2020 anniversaries: the Party's 90th, Ho Chi Minh's 130th, Lenin's 150th and Engels's 200th, together with the campaign against hostile forces and what the authors call 'peaceful evolution'. The second examines the turnover of leadership at all levels and the selection of the 13th Central Committee. The third covers the drafting of the Congress documents, the assessment of 35 years of renovation (Đổi Mới) and the targets to 2045. The fourth offers an overall assessment and outlook for 2021. The authors present the commemorations as a deliberate ideological strategy. Central Party directives classified and organised the events, and general secretary Nguyen Phu Trong described the Party's leadership as the decisive factor in all Vietnamese revolutionary victories. In the authors' reading, 'upholding fundamentals' is the root of inheritance and inheritance serves upholding fundamentals. On personnel, they describe detailed cadre standards, such as Regulation 214, and a staged selection process. Yet Trong's third term as general secretary came through a special procedure that bypassed the Party Charter's two-term limit. The authors explain this as a vote by the Congress, as the Charter's highest authority, after no other candidate won a majority of support, and they judge it favourable to continuity. The authors credit the Party's centralised leadership with Vietnam's pandemic record and 2.91 per cent growth in 2020. They summarise the Congress targets: high-income developed status by 2045, with growth of 6.5–7 per cent a year in 2021–2025. They nonetheless judge the goals of escaping the middle-income trap and reaching high-income status hard to square with 2020 per-capita GDP of US$2,750 and the projected growth rates. They also note that a third Covid-19 wave in early 2021 may make the 6.5 per cent growth target difficult. Read the original if you want a detailed Chinese-scholarly account of Vietnamese Party documents, personnel procedures and ideological work around the 13th Congress.

The Communist Party of China has no special interests of its own: the nature of a Marxist party 中国共产党没有自己特殊利益 这是马克思主义政党的性质决定的 Xin Xiangyang This newspaper commentary, published in Changjiang Daily in August 2021, takes up Xi Jinping's statement in his speech at the centenary of the Party's founding that the Communist Party of China has no special interests of its own and never represents any interest group, power group or privileged stratum. Xin argues that this claim follows from the nature of a Marxist party and enriches Marxist party theory. In Xin's reading it also sums up the Party's hundred-year history and the rise and fall of parties elsewhere. The piece is organised around the three negations in Xi's formulation. It first treats interest groups, then power groups, then privileged strata. Xin relies mainly on Xi's speeches since the 18th Party Congress (2012), on the Party Constitution, and on a 2019 Central Committee document on strengthening the Party's political development. Xin contends that a Marxist party has one interest, that of the people. If it acquired special interests, Xin says, it would breed feudal-style dependence and small cliques, and interest groups inside the Party could change its proletarian character. Xin claims that many parties, especially in Western countries and notably in the United States, serve power groups. On privilege, Xin cites Xi's view that the Soviet Communist Party collapsed partly because it became a privileged bureaucratic group cut off from the people. Xin calls for open opposition to privileged thinking, conduct and practices, citing Xi's 2013 and 2018 speeches to the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection. Xin also calls for implementing the Party's 2016 norms on intra-Party political life, which require tighter supervision of leaders and rule out unchecked power and unsupervised "special" members. Read the original if you want a short, official-line account of how Party leaders justify the claim that the Party has no interests of its own and frame the Soviet collapse as a warning.

Courage for self-reform is the distinctive mark of the Communist Party of China 勇于自我革命是中国共产党的显著标志 Zhang Feng Published in Guangming Daily in August 2021, shortly after the Party's centenary, this commentary takes up Xi Jinping's statement that courage for self-reform distinguishes the Communist Party of China from other parties. Zhang asks why the Party emerged from repeated contests among political forces in modern China and became the "backbone" of the Chinese people. The answer offered is that the Party has consistently kept up a spirit of self-reform, which Zhang calls the secret of its longevity and a vivid expression of the great founding spirit of the Party. Zhang breaks the Party's self-reform into four capacities: self-purification, self-improvement in the sense of correcting errors, self-renewal through institution-building, and self-elevation through learning. Each section draws on Marx and Engels, Lenin, Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping, then runs through the Party's history from the anti-Japanese war and the early People's Republic to reform and opening up and the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). On purification, Zhang says the Party must remove whatever harms its vanguard character and purity, and presents the anti-corruption campaign since 2012 as its fullest expression, with its aim of making officials unwilling, unable and afraid to be corrupt. On self-improvement, the argument is that the Party has no interests of its own apart from the people's, so it must correct mistakes and prevent interest groups from forming within it. On renewal, Zhang cites the build-up of intra-Party regulations and a supervision system that "locks power in the cage of institutions". The final section calls the Party a Marxist learning party and says study, ideals and conviction must be strengthened and governing capacity raised. Zhang concludes that self-reform keeps the Party advanced and pure, tied to the people, institutionally robust and theoretically armed. The text frames this as the explanation of the Party's vitality after a hundred years and as the basis for leading a country of 1.4 billion people. The piece calls for study of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and for the Two Upholds. Read the original if you want a compact, officially aligned account of how the Party's own commentators present self-reform and anti-corruption as the Party's defining trait.

On the developmental position of the new era 论新时代的发展方位 Wei Zhiqi Wei Zhiqi takes up a question he says the literature has neglected: where the "new era" declared at the 19th Party Congress (2017) stands in terms of development, as distinct from its historical position. Most existing studies, Wei argues, treat the two as the same and read the new era only through the history of socialism with Chinese characteristics. His thesis is that the new era is a new stage within the primary stage of socialism and sits in a new developmental position of "after having developed". The article has three parts. The first argues that the new era remains inside the primary stage of socialism while forming a new stage of it. The second divides the primary stage into two developmental positions, one of "underdevelopment" and one of "after development", and examines what changes and what stays constant in the productive forces and relations of production. The third sets out three features of the new position. Wei draws on Deng Xiaoping, the 13th and 15th Party Congresses, the Fourth and Fifth Plenums of the 19th Central Committee, and statistics on GDP, income, urbanisation and the Engel coefficient. Wei contends that the primary stage proceeds from quantitative accumulation to "partial qualitative change" and eventually to "comprehensive qualitative change". Four decades of growth have produced a partial qualitative change, a leap in the indicators of the stage's "five" and "nine" characteristics. However, per capita output, regional and urban–rural imbalances, industrial quality and the maturity of institutions show, in Wei's account, that underdevelopment has not fundamentally changed. Its form has shifted from underdeveloped productive forces to unbalanced and inadequate development. The new era is therefore the "second half" of the primary stage, one that partially overcomes, sublates and transcends underdevelopment. Wei identifies three features of the "after developed" position. The essence of socialism now stresses eliminating poverty and moving toward common prosperity. The principal contradiction has become one between people's growing need for a better life and unbalanced, inadequate development. The central mission has moved from becoming prosperous to becoming strong, through the two-step path to a modern socialist country by around 2050. Wei concludes that becoming strong is the main mission and defining mark of the new position. Read the original if you want a Party-theory account of how the "primary stage of socialism" is periodised into stages and how this underpins the new era's tasks.

The problem logic of Western Marxism and its contemporary value 论西方马克思主义的问题逻辑及当代价值 Wang Yuchen Wang Yuchen asks how Chinese scholarship on Western Marxism can move beyond summarising individual thinkers' views to grasping the "problem logic" that organises the tradition. The article argues that this logic starts from a single question, whether the essence of Marxist philosophy lies in its specific conclusions or in a dialectic that unites theory and practice. Wang holds that grasping it helps clarify the tradition's substance and lets it serve as a resource for adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The article has four parts. It first traces the theoretical starting point, from Lukács, Korsch and Gramsci to the humanist and scientistic readings of Marx. It then examines Western Marxism's cultural and ideological critique of contemporary capitalism. A third part treats its theoretical innovations: alienation and everyday-life critique, critique of technical rationality, ecological critique and political philosophy. A final part assesses their contemporary effects and value for China. Wang argues that the early Western Marxists rejected economic-determinist and natural-science readings of Marx, which they blamed for the failure of Western revolutions. They presented Marxism as a modern philosophy of practice centred on a critical, value-laden dialectic. Wang then divides the tradition into theories of the liberation of the proletariat as a whole (Lukács, Gramsci, Althusser, ecological and analytical Marxists) and theories of individual liberation (the Frankfurt School, Sartre). Both turned to culture and ideology, but the first aimed at class consciousness and political revolution, the second at autonomous personality through aesthetics and love. Wang credits the alienation theory with showing that material wealth brought control rather than freedom. Wang also criticises it for tracing alienation to technical rationality rather than private ownership and the division of labour, for treating it as a subjective experience, and for conflating objectification with alienation. Wang concludes that the Western Marxist problem logic has broad value. It set Marx's philosophy apart from modern epistemology, and it opposed the Soviet "dialectical and historical materialism" textbook model. It also shaped urban, ecological and feminist movements, post-Marxism (which Wang says fell into subjective idealism) and the "late Marxism" of Eagleton, Jameson and Harvey, which Wang says returned to political economy. In China, Wang says, it prompted rethinking of the textbook system and of the relation between scholarship and practical relevance. It also opened work on cultural, everyday-life, technology, ecological and political philosophy relevant to the problems of modernity in China's modernization. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's systematic account and critique of Western Marxism's internal logic and of its reception in China.

New circumstances and features of world socialism today 当今世界社会主义发展的新形势新特点 Chai Shangjin Writing in 2021, Chai Shangjin asks how world socialism is developing amid what Chinese official discourse calls changes unseen in a century and the global COVID-19 pandemic. The article argues that socialism faces a major test but also an exceptional opportunity: the trend is favourable, with several bright spots, while the Western capitalist model is in decline. The article is organised in four parts. It first surveys the ruling communist parties of Vietnam, Laos, North Korea and Cuba, covering party-building, economic reform and pandemic response. It then turns to non-ruling communist parties in developed and developing countries, followed by anti-capitalist movements and currents of thought. The final part examines the changing relationship between the socialist and capitalist systems. Chai's central claims run along three lines. The existing socialist states, in the author's account, have kept Party leadership, pursued renewal and opening, and shown institutional strengths in the pandemic, while seeking a strategic community among themselves and backing China's idea of a community with a shared future for mankind. Non-ruling communist parties, the author says, are strengthening organisation, forming left-wing alliances to seek an alternative to capitalism, and benefiting from protest movements such as Occupy Wall Street and Black Lives Matter and from rising interest in a "new socialism". Finally, Chai contends that the pandemic exposed Western governance failures, intensified ideological competition, especially between the United States and China, and accelerated an "East rising, West declining" trend. Chai concludes, citing Deng Xiaoping, that socialism's eventual replacement of capitalism is an irreversible but winding historical course, and that its fate depends on proving its superiority in developing the productive forces. In the author's view, reform and opening up has borne out Deng's judgement, and the success of socialism with Chinese characteristics will increasingly influence the future of world socialism. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially aligned Chinese account of the state of ruling and non-ruling communist parties around 2020–21, with country-by-country data and examples.

The correct path to realizing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation 实现中华民族伟大复兴的正确道路 Li Jie Writing in the People's Daily in August 2021, shortly after the Party's centenary celebrations, Li Jie takes up Xi Jinping's statement that learning from history and creating the future requires upholding and developing socialism with Chinese characteristics. The article is a commentary on that speech. Li argues that this path connects the past, present and future of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, and explains both why the Party has succeeded and how it can keep succeeding. The piece has three sections. The first presents socialism with Chinese characteristics as the necessary choice of China's modern development. The second treats it as the historical conclusion of the Party's hundred years of struggle. The third presents Chinese modernization and a "new form of human civilization" as contributions to the history of the Chinese nation and of human civilization. Li's central claim is that socialism with Chinese characteristics is the dialectical unity of the theoretical logic of scientific socialism and the historical logic of China's development. He reasons that over more than 180 years of national decline and revival, and a century of Party-led revolution, only Marxism, the Party and socialism could save and develop China. In his account the Party opened the paths of new-democratic revolution, socialist revolution and construction, and socialism with Chinese characteristics. These yielded the leap from standing up to becoming prosperous and then becoming strong. Li holds that the path, theoretical system, institutions and culture form one whole, and that this requires the Four-sphere Confidence. He then ties Chinese modernization to the new development philosophy (innovation, coordination, green, open and shared development), each of which he says solves a specific problem. He also traces the widening of the Party's overall layout from two civilizations to the "five-sphere" formula as evidence of deepening understanding of historical laws. Li concludes that Chinese modernization is shaped by China's conditions: a huge population, common prosperity, coordinated material and cultural-ethical progress, harmony between humans and nature, and peaceful development. He says it offers Chinese wisdom, experience and solutions for human problems, and calls for self-confidence, self-reliance, integrity and innovation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the official narrative of the Party's centenary links the historical path, the four spheres of confidence and Chinese modernization.

Unwaveringly following the new path of Chinese modernization 坚定不移走中国式现代化新道路 Zhang Hao Published in Economic Daily on 14 July 2021, shortly after the centenary of the Communist Party of China, this commentary takes up Xi Jinping's claim that the Party has created a new path of Chinese modernization and a new form of human civilization. Zhang argues that this path, opened under Party leadership since the founding of the People's Republic and especially since reform and opening up, is the necessary road to a modern socialist power and to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The author's thesis is that it reflects both the laws of socialist construction and the laws of human social development. The piece is organised in four sections, each naming one feature of the path: it embodies the laws of socialist construction and of social development; it pursues comprehensive and coordinated development; it promotes the all-round development of the person while achieving common prosperity for all; and it develops China while benefiting the world. It ends with a short call to continue on this path. In the first section Zhang describes Chinese modernization as socialist modernization, guided by an evolving Chinese Marxism, led by the Party and centred on the people, and as overcoming what the author calls the inherent defects of capitalist modernization. As a latecomer, China is said to have avoided the Western 'serial' sequence of industrialization, urbanization, agricultural modernization and informatization, and instead pursued them in 'parallel'. The second section traces how the Party's understanding of modernization widened from economic indicators to the 'five-sphere integrated plan' adopted at the 18th Party Congress (2012), matching the goals of a prosperous, democratic, civilized, harmonious and beautiful country. Zhang adds that coordination is an inherent requirement of the social organism, so weak points must be remedied. The third section holds that modernization of the person is the essence of modernization, and that common prosperity requires both enlarging and fairly dividing 'the cake', narrowing regional, urban–rural and income gaps and preventing polarization. Zhang concludes that history and practice show the path to be correct and workable, and that it will be steady and successful. In the final section the author presents China as pursuing peaceful development, contributing to world peace and development, and as a builder of peace and defender of the international order. The author calls on readers to follow the path unwaveringly in order to advance national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the official narrative of Chinese modernization was framed for a newspaper audience around the Party's centenary in 2021.

Innovation and development in the study of modern Chinese history over the past century 百年近代史研究的创新与发展 Wang Xianming Wang Xianming asks how the materialist conception of history (唯物史观) reshaped Chinese historiography and the study of modern Chinese history, and what this means for the field's fresh start in the new era. The author argues that, once Marxism took root in China, historiography underwent a historic turn, and that the materialist conception of history remains an open, developing framework. The short commentary follows three stages. It begins with the replacement of Liang Qichao's evolutionary view of history by materialist history in the 1920s and 1930s. It then turns to the debates on Chinese social history, and finally to research trends since the reform period. Wang contends that, after Li Dazhao's 1920 essay, materialist history became the shared reference of the 'new historiography', even for scholars such as Gu Jiegang and Fu Sinian, who were identified with source-based positivism. In the social-history debates, participants of opposing politics mostly relied on it, and the debates produced a broad consensus on China's 'semi-colonial and semi-feudal' character. In Wang's account, this consensus laid the theoretical foundation of modern Chinese history. Wang adds that the later turn toward ordinary people, daily life and social history, and the interaction of 'revolutionary history' with 'holistic' or social history, corrects dogmatism and confirms the materialist conception of history's basic standpoint. Wang concludes that the materialist conception of history has endured the challenge of various 'deconstructive' currents and continues to develop through inheritance and innovation. Read the original if you want a brief statement of how a Chinese historian presents Marxism's role in the formation of modern Chinese historiography.

An analysis of the main thread of the Chinese Communist Party's century of theoretical innovation 中国共产党百年理论创新主线探析 Shen Jianguo Writing in 2021, the centenary year of the Party, Shen Jianguo asks what runs through the Chinese Communist Party's hundred years of theoretical innovation. The article argues that the main thread is the Party's conscious use of Marxism's theory of the basic contradictions of society to identify and resolve the principal contradiction of each period, so as to meet the needs of the people and raise their "subjectivity". Shen presents this as the core of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The article has three parts. The first sets out what Shen calls the "inner core" of Marxist fundamental principles. The second follows the Party's theoretical innovation through leadership generations: Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin and Hu Jintao. The third lists seven new results of the Xi Jinping era, ranging from a new judgement on the principal contradiction to the new development philosophy, the framework of the basic economic system, and the Party's leadership. Shen's central move is to read the contradictions between productive forces and relations of production, and between economic base and superstructure, as a theory of the people as creators of history. Relations of production and the superstructure must therefore meet people's needs and raise their subjectivity, meaning their autonomy, initiative and creativity. In class society this appears as class struggle, and the theory combines scientific, value-based and revolutionary character. The Party's own principal-contradiction theory is said to share these traits. Shen credits Mao's New Democratic Revolution theory to a correct analysis of China's principal contradiction, and the Eighth Party Congress (1956) with a correct formulation of it. Shen holds that Mao later erred by taking class contradiction as principal, which led to "taking class struggle as the key link". Deng's reformulation, "Three Represents", the Scientific Outlook on Development and the Nineteenth Party Congress (2017) judgement are presented as successive corrections and refinements. Shen concludes that the Party's success rests on correctly judging and resolving the principal contradiction in the revolutionary, construction and reform periods, and on releasing popular initiative. The article describes this as a mutually reinforcing development "for the people, relying on the people, shared by the people", and as increasing people's sense of gain. It also presents the Party's self-reform and anti-corruption work as part of this record. Read the original if you want a Party-theoretical account of a single continuous line, from Mao to Xi Jinping, in the Chinese reading of the theory of the principal contradiction.

Mao Zedong and the establishment of historical research methods in twentieth-century China 毛泽东与二十世纪中国史学方法的确立 Chen Jinlong This short commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in July 2021, asks what Mao Zedong contributed to the methods of historical study in twentieth-century China. Chen argues that Mao, a lifelong reader, researcher and user of history, fixed the basic methods of historical research and so shaped the development of Chinese historiography. The author adds that these methods still guide historical research in the new era. The article is organised around four methods that Chen attributes to Mao: the elaboration and establishment of the materialist conception of history, the advocacy and use of historical dialectics, the practice of historical investigation, and the "letting a hundred schools of thought contend" policy. Each section draws on Mao's own statements, speeches and works, and on examples of how he judged historical figures and events. On the first point, Chen says Mao installed historical materialism against the long dominance of historical idealism in Chinese historiography. Mao treated the people as the subject of history, insisted that events be explained by objective social conditions, and held that the present grows out of the past, so that history must not be severed. On the second, Chen cites Mao's two-sided assessments of Confucius, Chen Duxiu, the 1911 Revolution and the Party's own earlier periods, together with his view that failures, as much as victories, are needed to grasp objective laws. Chen reads these as models of critical inheritance and as a rejection of blanket negation. Chen presents Mao's investigative method as history grounded in fieldwork and documents. Examples include the Hunan peasant report, the Xunwu and Xingguo surveys, the 1941 decision on investigation and research, and the principle of analysing first and synthesising afterwards. On the hundred-schools policy, Chen notes that it was first raised for historical studies, when the journal Historical Research was founded in 1953. Chen links it to the lively debates of the 1950s and 1960s on periodisation, peasant wars and landownership. Chen concludes that these four methods advanced twentieth-century historiography and remain instructive today. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned account of how Mao's methodological views are presented in Chinese scholarship.

Always uphold and raise high the banner of historical materialism 始终坚持和高扬唯物史观理论旗帜 Zhang Yanguo Published in China Social Sciences Today on 1 July 2021, the centenary of the Communist Party of China, this commentary asks what theoretical foundation underlies the Party's century of experience. Zhang argues that historical materialism is the Party's "core skill" (kanjia benshi), and that a party's choice between historical materialism, idealist conceptions of history or others is a dividing line for whether its view of history and method is scientific. The Party must therefore keep this banner raised. The piece opens with the premise that the path a nation takes depends on the theoretical banner its parties raise. It then reviews the Party's own summaries of experience, namely Mao Zedong's "three magic weapons" and Deng Xiaoping's insistence on combining universal Marxist truth with China's concrete conditions. In its second half it sets out three dimensions in which, according to Zhang, historical materialism has guided revolution, construction and reform and opening up. Zhang's central move is to read the Party's famous experiences as the fruit of applying historical materialism successfully. In this reading, the line of "emancipating the mind and seeking truth from facts" embodies dialectical and historical materialism and has let the Party avoid both wholesale Westernization and ossified closure. The three dimensions are as follows. First, the Party located its historical position and stage, which produced successive general lines from New Democratic Revolution to socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era. Second, it applied the law that relations of production must suit productive forces and the superstructure the economic base, analysing the nature of Chinese society and the principal contradiction, and describing reform as also emancipating the productive forces. Third, it treated the people as the fundamental social subject, which Zhang links to the mass line, the aim of serving the people wholeheartedly and a people-centred approach to development. Zhang adds that the Party has also used historical materialism on class struggle, social contradictions, ideology, cultural inheritance and cultural-ethical progress. The author calls on Communists to combine the theory and method with the development of the times, world trends and the people's wisdom, so that it stays a "hard skill" in constant renewal. Doing so, Zhang says, will help the Party grasp the laws and general trend of history and keep the historical initiative. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated scholars framed historical materialism as the theoretical core of the Party's centenary narrative.

The glorious course of the century-old Party in advancing the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context 百年大党推进马克思主义中国化的光辉历程 Wang Huxue He Xiaoxiao Marking the centenary of the Communist Party of China in 2021, Wang Huxue and He Xiaoxiao take up Xi Jinping's statement that the Party's history is one of continuously advancing the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context and of theoretical innovation. The authors argue that every theoretical creation of the Party has depended on the guidance of Marxist theory and on the leadership of successive central collectives. They present the Party's hundred years as an unbroken process of adaptation, with each stage producing a new theoretical form. The article follows four periods in order: the New Democratic Revolution, socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up with socialist modernization, and the new era of socialism with Chinese characteristics. For each period it identifies the leading figures, the key meetings and the theoretical results. These run from Mao Zedong Thought through Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents and the Scientific Outlook on Development to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. A short conclusion draws the strands together. The authors' central move is to read each stage as an answer to a defining question. Early dogmatism, which they link to uncritical reliance on Soviet experience and Comintern resolutions, brought the failure of the Fifth Encirclement Campaign. They credit Mao with the rural-base strategy and with the 1938 formulation of the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context, and they describe the 1945 Seventh Congress as the first historic leap. After 1978, they say, Deng's reforms answered what socialism is, Jiang Zemin's Three Represents answered what kind of Party to build, and Hu Jintao's Scientific Outlook on Development answered what kind of development to pursue. For the period after the 18th Party Congress (2012) they list the people-centred approach, the new development philosophy and the "two mountains" ecological idea as new Marxist advances. The authors conclude that the Party's achievements stem from taking Marxism as its guide while innovating in theory through revolution, construction and reform. They add Xi's 2021 call to combine the best of traditional Chinese culture with the Marxist stance, viewpoint and method. In their view, Marxism adapted to China forms a systematic new theoretical form that serves as a guide to action for the whole Party and people. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned periodisation of the Party's theoretical achievements, as presented in the centenary year.

On the logical path of Marx's critique of commodity fetishism 论马克思商品拜物教批判的逻辑理路 Sun Xiguo Mao Fei Sun Xiguo and Mao Fei take up a gap in existing readings of Marx's theory of commodity fetishism. Some scholars reduce it to the 'reification of social relations', but in the authors' view this does not explain why relations between people must appear inverted as relations between things. They argue that the critique operates on two dimensions: a critique of the economic base from which fetishism arises, and a critique of fetishism as an ideological superstructure. The article, published in Theoretical Journal in 2021, reconstructs the critique as three logical links. It then draws out three implications: against the view that fetishism is merely subjective misrecognition, against the claim that it is obsolete, and for a dialectical view of the commodity. The discussion draws on Capital, Lenin, Lukács, Rubin, Baudrillard, Bailey, Ricardo and Japanese and Chinese commentators. The first link analyses commodity-producing labour. The authors distinguish household labour (private labour organised privately), enterprise-combined labour (private labour awaiting conversion into social labour) and future socially associated labour (directly social). Because labour in the middle form is private yet social, it must be mediated by value; the authors show this by rejecting the labour-money schemes of Owen and Darimon. The second link follows the movement of the value form, from simple to expanded to general form, through which relations between people come to appear as relations between commodities, producing the illusion of reification. The third link is the belief that commodities are all-powerful, found in Ricardo's classical economics and Bailey's vulgar economics. In the authors' account, Marx gives little space to this ideological layer because his real target is the relations of production behind it. Sun and Mao conclude that fetishism rests on objective relations of production, so it will not become obsolete while commodity production relations exist. They hold that Baudrillard's 'sign fetishism' stays at the surface of capitalism. They call for a dialectical view of the commodity: recognise that it arose by historical necessity and promotes the productive forces, and also that it is historically transient. Using commodities to develop production would, they say, eventually dissolve commodities and fetishism from within. Read the original if you want a systematic, Chinese-language reconstruction of the value-form argument and a defence of the economic-base reading of fetishism against Baudrillard and 'subjective misrecognition' interpretations.

Infinite form and the spark of truth: the materialist dialectic in Badiou's The Immanence of Truths 无限形式与真理的星星之火——论巴迪欧《真理的内在性》中的唯物辩证法 Lan Jiang Lan Jiang reads Alain Badiou's 2018 book L'Immanence des vérités, which Badiou presents as the third volume of the Being and Event series, as the possible capstone of his philosophy. The article asks what happens to the finite world once a subject has touched the infinite through a truth procedure. Its thesis is that the book "turns the project around" and builds a new materialist dialectic. In it, finite objects are held to be immanent to truth rather than prior to it. The article opens with Badiou's repeated use of Mao Zedong's phrase "a single spark can start a prairie fire" and his rewording of it in the new book. It then uses Plato's cave to frame the book's question, and sets Badiou's two philosophical manifestos (1989 and 2009) against postmodern and post-structuralist currents. The later sections cover Badiou's two opponents, transcendence and "democratic materialism", his appeal to set theory, and his treatment of the finite. Lan draws on Being and Event, Logics of Worlds, Wittgenstein, Deleuze and Meillassoux. Lan argues that Badiou rewrites Mao's phrase so that the spark is no longer the cause of the prairie fire. It becomes a concrete flash thrown up by an omnipresent infinity. Fidelity to the spark therefore means fidelity to an event, not the manufacture of sparks. The new dialectic fights on two fronts. Against a transcendent One (God, Substance, Nature, Hegel's Absolute), Badiou follows Cantor in separating the infinite from the One, so that the infinite becomes a "multiple without one". Against democratic materialism, whose axiom is that "there are only bodies and languages", he holds that the finite is not given but is the result of an infinite operation of counting-as-one. Lan calls this finitude the central fetishistic ideology of our age. Lan concludes that, for Badiou, liberation is a formal revolution. A new form, even one without objects, is created, subjects incorporate themselves into the generic set it opens, and objects take shape within it. This explains why Badiou privileges mathematics over physics and chemistry. Lan presents this as Badiou's new materialist dialectic and his way of picturing a future society, one that does not return to a primal One. Read the original if you work on Badiou, Marxist ontology or the French reception of Mao, and want a close account of how The Immanence of Truths connects set theory, the critique of finitude and the image of the spark.

Four paths in contemporary French Marxist research and their assessment 当代法国马克思主义研究的四条路径及其评析 Cheng Enhui Chinese scholarship on French Marxism has traditionally concentrated on Althusser, Sartre and Lefebvre, all now dead. Cheng asks what research paradigms exist in French Marxism today, how they develop and how they relate to one another. The article argues that contemporary French Marxism is best understood as Marxism in the post-Althusser era, whose four main paths share a common logic of emancipatory politics while each carrying theoretical weaknesses. The article examines four representatives in turn: Jacques Bidet, Alain Badiou, Jacques Rancière and Étienne Balibar. Each section introduces the thinker's career and then reconstructs one paradigm: Bidet's meta-structure theory built on a reading of Capital, Badiou's philosophy of the event aimed at communism, Rancière's politics of literature and aesthetics organised around equality, and Balibar's work on race and nation, which Cheng labels post-Marxist. A concluding section compares the four with Althusser's legacy and with one another. In Cheng's account, Bidet finds in Marx a double logic of market and organisation, with law logically prior to production. From it he derives a ruling class composed of owners of capital and holders of organisational and knowledge-based competence, opposed to the popular classes. Badiou distinguishes two kinds of politics and holds that an unpredictable event ruptures the existing order and calls a subject into being, so that truth takes the form of the idea of communism. Rancière separates "police" from "politics" and treats politics as the appearance of those with no part, then turns to literature as a way of making the unseen visible. Balibar moves from structuralist Marxism to ambiguous race–nation–class identities and then to "equaliberty", the mutual implication of equality and freedom. Cheng concludes that all four thinkers are tied to Althusser, whether by inheritance (Balibar, Bidet), rebellion (Rancière) or the notion of rupture (Badiou), and that Balibar, Rancière and Badiou share an emancipatory politics for the masses, while Bidet seeks socialism through an alliance of the masses with organisational competence. The weaknesses Cheng names are the risk of wordplay and tautology in equaliberty, the unresolved realities of transnational politics, and, for Rancière and Badiou, a utopian quality and the loss of a historical-materialist foundation. Cheng sees Bidet and Balibar as more grounded in social reality, and Rancière and Badiou as preachers of ideas. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's map of post-Althusser French Marxism and a critical assessment of these four thinkers from a historical-materialist standpoint.

Ultimately, it is because Marxism works 归根到底是因为马克思主义行 Wang Chuanli Published in Qianxian (Frontline) in 2021, the year of the Communist Party's centenary, this commentary expands on a formula in Xi Jinping's speech marking the centenary. The formula holds that the Party's success and the merits of socialism with Chinese characteristics are, "ultimately", due to the fact that Marxism works. Wang Chuanli argues that 170-plus years of history and more than four decades of reform and opening up bear this out. The article has three parts. The first surveys the world history of Marxism from the 1840s: its contest with rival socialist currents, and its adoption in Russia and China. The second considers the Party's century of achievements and credits them to Marxist theory, ideals, method and strategy. The third deals with socialism with Chinese characteristics: its theoretical foundations, the shocks of the early 1990s and the Covid-19 pandemic, and the challenges still ahead. Wang argues that Marxism proved itself against Proudhonism, Dühringism and Lassalleanism, and that Russia and China each reached it only after long searches through other doctrines. In the author's account, the Party's strength rests on rational conviction in Marxist science and on Marxism as a worldview and method. As evidence, the author cites Mao Zedong's foresight in On Protracted War and the Party's united front, mass line and flexible strategy. The author also traces specific policies to Marxist sources. Marx's Critique of the Gotha Programme is said to underlie the theory of the primary stage of socialism, and the Marxist view of the people as makers of history is said to underlie the commitment to common prosperity. Wang reads the Soviet and East European collapse and the pandemic as tests. The author contrasts Deng Xiaoping's confidence in Marxism after 1991 with what is described as division and failure in Western countries, set against China's pandemic response and its 2020 economic growth. Wang concludes that history has shown, and will go on showing, that the strength of socialism with Chinese characteristics ultimately rests on Marxism. The author cautions that China still lags well behind developed countries and that national rejuvenation will demand hard struggle. Read the original if you want an example of how Party-affiliated scholars in 2021 framed the case for Marxism's efficacy around the centenary.

Continuing to advance the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context 继续推进马克思主义中国化 Liu Guangming Writing in the People's Daily on 7 July 2021, days after the centenary of the Communist Party of China, Liu Guangming takes up Xi Jinping's statement that, in drawing on history to open up the future, the Party "must continue to adapt Marxism to the Chinese context". Liu presents this as both a summary of a century of theoretical innovation and a pledge to keep enriching the latest results of that process. The commentary argues that the Party's history is one of continuous theoretical innovation and creation, and that Xi's 1 July speech is a programmatic document for the next stage. The piece is a short commentary in four parts, each framed around remarks by Xi Jinping. The parts deal with upholding the principles of emancipating the mind, seeking truth from facts, keeping pace with the times and being realistic and pragmatic; respecting the new creations of the people in practice; answering the new questions posed by the age; and drawing on new achievements of human civilisation. Liu moves between historical examples, from Mao Zedong to the Party's recent theoretical formulations, and forward-looking exhortations. Liu's central claim is that Marxism stays vital because it is rooted in practice. Liu lists the sequence of theoretical results: Mao Zedong Thought, Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents, the Scientific Outlook on Development and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Each, in this account, arose from answering a major problem of its period and from the people's own practice. Liu cites the household contract responsibility system, which Deng Xiaoping credited to the peasants, as an example of popular innovation later turned into theory. Liu also says that after the late 1970s the Party shifted its theoretical theme to building socialism with Chinese characteristics, reaching conclusions such as that socialism does not equal a planned economy. At the same time Liu stresses holding the ideological line and Marxism's guiding position. Liu calls for freeing thinking from outdated ideas, from dogmatic readings of Marxism, and from subjectivism and metaphysics, so that the Party can deepen its understanding of the laws of Party rule, socialist construction and human social development. Theory should be problem-oriented and should absorb the best of human civilisation, including in the digital and intelligent fields, while starting from China's own conditions. The aim is to make contemporary Chinese Marxism, the Marxism of the twenty-first century, more powerful. Read the original if you want a compact example of how the official press framed the continuing adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context at the centenary of the Party in 2021.

Studying and understanding the Party's innovative theory of the new era 深刻学习领会新时代党的创新理论 Wang Dan Qiu Gengtian This short commentary, published in Chengdu Daily in June 2021, asks how Party members should study Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Wang and Qiu present it as the Marxism of contemporary China and of the twenty-first century, and as the latest result of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context. They argue that study should grasp its theoretical character and also its philosophical method, scientific spirit and political wisdom. The article is organised in three sections: theory lives through innovation; innovative theory arises from innovative practice; and innovative theory guides innovative practice. It opens with a survey of the Party's century of theoretical innovation, running from Mao Zedong Thought through Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents and the Scientific Outlook on Development to Xi Jinping's thought. The core argument is a two-way relation between theory and practice. The authors hold that the Party's theory has always begun where its practice begins, citing the new development philosophy, the green-mountains idea and targeted poverty alleviation as responses to problems after the 18th Party Congress (2012). They then claim that the thought guides practice, pointing to the victory over absolute poverty, the nearly completed moderately prosperous society, epidemic control and GDP above 100 trillion yuan as evidence of its power. The authors conclude that theory stays vital only when it is tied to its era, to Chinese realities and to the people's needs. They call for studying the new theory thoroughly, using it to unify thinking and draw the widest "concentric circle" around the Party, and continuing theoretical innovation on the basis of practice. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Party press presents the lineage of Sinicized Marxism and the theory–practice relationship in 2021.

The great leap from standing up and growing rich to becoming strong 从站起来、富起来到强起来的伟大飞跃 Chen Li Published in the People's Daily on 24 June 2021, in the run-up to the Communist Party's centenary, this commentary presents a Party-history narrative. Chen Li argues that under the Party's leadership the Chinese nation has passed through a "great leap" from "standing up" to "growing rich" to "becoming strong". In the author's account, the dawn of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation now lies ahead. The article is organised in four numbered sections following the Party's history. The first covers the semi-colonial, semi-feudal China after the Opium War, the founding of the Party and the revolution under Mao Zedong. The second covers reform and opening up under Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin and Hu Jintao. The third deals with the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012) under Xi Jinping, including the response to Covid-19 and poverty alleviation. The fourth looks ahead to the goals for 2035 and the middle of the century. Chen's central move is to assign each stage a distinct historical achievement, each tied to a theoretical innovation by successive Party leaderships. The founding of the People's Republic is said to have ended the old semi-colonial order and laid the political and institutional foundation, together with an independent industrial system, for national wealth. Reform and opening up, the author says, released productive forces: the article cites average annual real GDP growth of 9.8% in 1979–2012 against roughly 2.8% worldwide, and a rise in China's share of the world economy from 1.8% to 11.5%. For the Xi era, the article credits Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era with historic achievements, citing the pandemic response, GDP above 100 trillion yuan in 2020 and the end of absolute poverty. Chen concludes that the first centenary goal, a moderately prosperous society, has been achieved, and that the 19th Party Congress (2017) set out goals of basic modernization by 2035 and a strong modern socialist country by mid-century. The author calls the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation a relay race and warns that it will not be easy. Chen urges the whole Party to unite around the Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core, maintain the Four-sphere Confidence and carry out the Two Upholds. Read the original if you want a compact example of the official periodisation of Party history published at the 2021 centenary.

Laying a solid foundation for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation 为实现中华民族伟大复兴奠定坚实基础 Li Jie Published in the People's Daily in June 2021, in the centenary year of the Communist Party of China, this commentary by Li Jie reviews the Party's hundred years. Li argues that since its founding the Party has made the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation its mission, and that through revolution, construction and reform it has carried the nation from "standing up" through "becoming prosperous" to "becoming strong". The piece has three parts. The first surveys the century in three stages: the revolution, the building of socialism after 1949, and reform and opening up. The second describes the situation after the 18th Party Congress (2012) and the prospects for national rejuvenation. The third draws four lessons from the hundred years, and quotes Xi Jinping on each. Li frames modern Chinese history as the pursuit of two tasks: national independence and the people's liberation, and national prosperity and the people's wellbeing. In Li's account the Party achieved the first through 28 years of armed struggle and the founding of the People's Republic. It then laid the basic socialist system and an independent industrial system, and, after the Cultural Revolution, opened the way to socialism with Chinese characteristics through reform and opening up. For the recent period Li cites figures: the world's second-largest economy, GDP above 100 trillion yuan, urbanisation above 60%, a middle-income group above 400 million, and the elimination of absolute poverty. Li presents the new development stage, set out by the Fifth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2020), as the start of a new journey to build a modern socialist country. The four lessons are firm ideals and convictions, standing with the people, seeking truth from facts, and a problem-oriented approach. Li calls on Party members to hold to these on the new journey and to keep a sense of "matters of national importance". Li concludes that no force can stop the Chinese people's advance and that the Party will lead the people to new achievements. Read the original if you want a concise example of the official People's Daily account of the Party's centenary, with its periodisation and its four lessons.

A century of tempering forged the bearing of a great Party 百年淬炼铸就大党风范 Zhao Zhongyuan Published in Economic Daily on 21 June 2021, shortly before the centenary of the Communist Party of China, this commentary asks what the "bearing of a great Party" (dadang fengfan) consists of and how a hundred years of history produced it. Zhao Zhongyuan argues that this bearing is the spiritual distillation of the Party's size and stature, and that it was formed through a century of struggle and trial. Zhao starts from Xi Jinping's 2017 remark that the world's largest party must have the appearance of a large one, and defines "bearing" as an inner quality made visible in conduct. It is built from four elements: conviction, sentiment, character and capability. The commentary devotes one section to each, describing them as tempered by the Party's history. It recommends studying Party history together with the history of the People's Republic, of reform and opening up, and of socialist development. On conviction, Zhao holds that the Party has preserved its "advanced nature and purity" by keeping faith in Marxism, by developing Marxism in step with the times through its integration with Chinese conditions, and by tempering Party spirit in practice. On sentiment, the author says the Party puts the people first and follows the mass line, and that since the 18th Party Congress (2012) it has pursued a people-centred approach. Zhao adds that the Party takes responsibility internationally by promoting party exchanges, advancing a community with a shared future for mankind and opposing unilateralism. On character, Zhao presents the Party's record of struggle, from the revolutionary period to the new era, and names self-reform as its most distinctive trait and greatest strength. On capability, the author cites the Party's achievements: broad people's democracy, rapid economic growth, the end of absolute poverty and the opening of a new drive to build a modern socialist country. Zhao traces these to the Party's roots in Marxism, traditional culture, the people and practice, and to its emphasis on learning. The commentary concludes that further drawing on historical experience will let the Party meet future risks and open new horizons for socialism with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated scholars framed the centenary and the Party's self-image in 2021.

The Communist Party of China and China's modernization 中国共产党与中国现代化 Chen Li Written for the Party's centenary in 2021, the article asks how the Communist Party of China (CPC) relates to China's modernization and what lies behind its success. Chen argues that building a modern country has been the most distinctive theme of the Party's hundred years of struggle. In Chen's account, success came mainly because the Party found a modernization path suited to China's own conditions. The article first divides the century into two stages. Before 1949, the new-democratic revolution removed imperialism and feudalism and created the basic political conditions for modernization. The author recalls the failure of the Self-Strengthening Movement and of Sun Yat-sen's plans, and quotes Mao Zedong on industrialization. After 1949, Chen traces the path from the "four modernizations" through the "three-step" strategy and the "two centenary goals" to the post-2012 period under Xi Jinping. The core of the article lists five features of Chinese modernization. It is led by the Party, which Chen calls the decisive factor, citing five-year plans and long-term blueprints pursued as "one blueprint to the end". It is based on China's actual conditions, above all the primary stage of socialism, a huge population and a poor starting point. It is people-centred, with development for, by and shared with the people. It is comprehensive, covering prosperity, democracy, culture, harmony and ecology, and common prosperity. Finally, it is independent: Chen insists that modernization is socialist, rejecting both the "closed and rigid old path" and the "wrong path of changing banners", and not a single Western model. Chen concludes that the Party's institutional strengths, illustrated by the author's account of the response to the Covid-19 epidemic, justify confidence in the path, theory, system and culture of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The article claims this path widens the options for developing countries that want faster growth while keeping their independence, and offers "Chinese wisdom" and a "Chinese approach" to global problems. Read the original if you want a concise, officially framed account of how Party theorists in 2021 narrated the link between the Party's history and modernization.

Making efforts in studying Party history, grasping the Thought, doing practical things and opening new prospects 在学党史悟思想办实事开新局上下功夫 Tang Weiyao This commentary, first published in Economic Daily on 21 June 2021, takes up the Party History Study and Education campaign launched in the centenary year of the Communist Party. Tang argues that Party members and cadres should keep working along four lines: studying Party history, grasping the Thought, doing practical things for the people and opening new prospects. The aim is to deliver results in the new stage of development. The piece is organised under four headings, each with its own required outcome: a new level in the compulsory course of Party history, a new consciousness of the power of ideas, new results in practical work for the people, and new breakthroughs in nurturing opportunities and opening new prospects. It draws repeatedly on remarks by Xi Jinping. In Tang's account, a century of Party history offers experience that cadres can turn into ideological enlightenment and working skills. Cadres are urged to master the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, to study Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, to evaluate major events and figures correctly and to oppose historical nihilism. Tang says the purpose of study is application: employment, healthcare, education and housing projects, balanced regional development and substantive progress towards common prosperity, while avoiding vanity projects. Tang concludes that, in a world undergoing great changes unseen in a century, history should help cadres respond to risks. Cadres are called on to implement the new development philosophy and the 14th Five-Year Plan, build the new development pattern of dual circulation, pursue high-quality development and strengthen bottom-line thinking. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Party media framed the practical aims of the 2021 history-study campaign.

Heaven and earth overturned, with passion and resolve: a hundred years of the Communist Party of China 天翻地覆慨而慷：中国共产党的100年 Shi Zhongquan Written for the Party's centenary in 2021, this article by Shi Zhongquan offers a narrative overview of the Communist Party of China's first hundred years. Shi argues that the Party's history can be read as four successive struggles: saving the nation, founding the state, enriching the country and strengthening it. Each is tied to a slogan: the Chinese people have stood up, the basic socialist system has been set up, the people have begun to grow rich, and China has begun to grow strong. The article follows the four periods that the Party itself uses: the new-democratic revolution, socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the new era of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Part one treats the founding, with Chen Duxiu as principal founder, and Mao Zedong's leadership to victory in 1949. Part two covers 1949–1978, including the Korean War, land reform, socialist transformation, the First Five-Year Plan, the Great Leap Forward and its correction, the Cultural Revolution and the 1976 arrest of the Gang of Four. Parts three and four review the leadership of Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin, Hu Jintao and Xi Jinping. Shi supports the account with economic, poverty-reduction, military and diplomatic statistics. Shi attributes the revolutionary victory to a new path (encircling the cities from the countryside) and three "magic weapons": Party building, armed struggle and the united front. Chen Duxiu is credited with founding the Party but is described as an immature leader who made right-opportunist errors in 1927, partly because of Comintern instructions. For the reform era, Shi stresses Deng's redefinition of socialism, the primary stage of socialism, and the socialist market economy. Jiang's Three Represents and Hu's Scientific Outlook on Development follow. For the Xi era, Shi lists achievements in the economy, innovation, poverty alleviation, military reform, diplomacy, the Belt and Road Initiative and a community with a shared future for mankind. He also credits full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, including the anti-corruption campaign, which he calls a decisive victory. Shi treats the Cultural Revolution as a disaster while describing Mao's original aims as defending the Party's purity and finding a Chinese road to socialism. Shi concludes that the Party is both a century-old and a strong party, and that after meeting the first centenary goal of a moderately prosperous society in all respects it has begun building a modern socialist country towards the second centenary goal. The text is an official-style historical narrative, mainly of use for seeing how the Party's own periodisation and verdicts were presented in 2021. Read the original if you want a detailed example of the centenary account of Party history, with its statistics and its assessments of Chen Duxiu, Mao, Deng and later leaders.

A historical examination of the early spread of Marxism in Shanghai and its present-day implications 马克思主义在上海早期传播的历史考察及现实启示 Sun Shan Why did Shanghai become one of the main centres where Marxism first spread in China? Sun Shan argues that the early dissemination of Marxism there supplied advanced Chinese intellectuals with an ideological weapon for national salvation, helped bring about the founding of the Chinese Communist Party in Shanghai, and holds an important place in the course of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The article, published in 2021, aims to enrich the history of Marxist dissemination and of the Party's founding. The article has three parts. The first analyses the conditions that made Shanghai a hub: its economic development and tradition of political struggle, its divided jurisdictions and migrant culture, and the concentration of intellectuals and workers. The second examines three channels of dissemination: newspapers and journals, classic books, and organised practical activity through schools, trade unions and commemorations. The third draws lessons for the present. Sun's core argument is that the spread of Marxism in Shanghai resulted from the combined effect of several factors rather than chance. In the author's account, the concession areas offered political 'gaps' and publishing space, while migration produced an open 'Shanghai-style culture'. Sun notes that the city had about 500,000 workers around 1919 and that many students left for study abroad from its port. Dissemination, the article says, moved from the 'clustered' effect of periodicals such as New Youth, Labour World and The Communist, through the 'systematic' publication of classics by firms such as the Commercial Press, to the 'organised' work of workers' schools, unions and commemorations. Sun draws three lessons for the present. First, Marxism must hold to its principles and engage openly with non-Marxist currents, as it did against pragmatism, reformism and anarchism; the author names liberalism and historical nihilism as present-day counterparts. Second, theory must meet social needs and be supported by practice. Third, discourse must be built and popularised, with theory expressed in everyday language for different groups. Read the original if you want a detailed account of Shanghai's material, social and organisational conditions in early Marxist dissemination, and of how a Chinese scholar draws contemporary ideological lessons from it.

The critical dimensions of the young Marx's concept of sensuous consciousness 青年马克思感性意识概念的批判向度 Liu Jianjiang Liu Jianjiang examines the concept of sensuous consciousness (感性意识) that the young Marx developed in the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844. The article, a short piece from a Chinese newspaper, argues that the concept carries a double critique and reveals the original, material ground of consciousness.
