Liu places the concept within Marx's notion of objective activity, which Marx formed by critically absorbing Feuerbach's principle of sensuous objectivity and Hegel's principle of rational activity. The text is organised around two targets: "pure consciousness" in the tradition of rationalist metaphysics, and Feuerbach's "abstract species-consciousness". On the first target, Liu reads Marx as holding that pure consciousness has knowledge as its only act and no genuine object outside itself, so that its objects are mere semblance. Consciousness, in Marx's account, is never pure but is "conscious being", rooted in the sensuous life-process of real people. Liu adds that Marx's critique of political economy applies the same logic: categories such as wages, capital and money construct an "economic fact" that hides the real sensuous conflict of interest between capitalists and workers. On the second target, Liu argues that Marx accepts Feuerbach's sensuous grounding of species-consciousness but rejects its abstraction. For Marx the species is not a natural, silent universality but "the sum of all social relations", produced through objective activity. Liu concludes that sensuous consciousness, as Marx understands it, is pre-conceptual and tied to the language of real life and to human social interaction. It is the consciousness of social being and a confirmation of people's actual social life. Read the original if you want a concise exegesis of how the 1844 Manuscripts link consciousness, sensuousness and social relations against both Hegelian and Feuerbachian positions.

The dialectical moment in Marx's conception of matter 马克思物质观的辩证环节 Xie Yongkang Li Jiaqi Xie Yongkang and Li Jiaqi ask where Marx's materialism comes from and how it fits together with dialectics. Their thesis is that Marx's materialist stance was extracted from Hegel's idealism through a critique of its mystical shell, rather than adopted directly from French materialism or Feuerbach. On this reading, 'materialist' and 'idealist' are two basic moments of dialectics, so the awkward external combination of materialism and dialectics does not arise. The short piece, originally published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in 2021, traces a line from Kant's thing-in-itself through Fichte and Hegel to Marx. It then turns to Marx's account of labour-power, the human being as a natural being, the division of labour, and the conditions and structure of freedom, with references to the 1844 Manuscripts, The German Ideology and Capital. The authors argue that German idealism's core logic is to dissolve the thing-in-itself into the productive activity of mediation, and Marx keeps this logic while defining matter through socially productive labour. Hegel's philosophy has two opposed motives: a demand for the absolute and a longing for substantiality tied to experience. Marx, they say, makes the second motive real, treating the unity of subject and object as a fact of modern productive forces. Labour-power is then a natural force, tools and the division of labour extend the human body and group into nature, and labour always presupposes nature. The authors conclude that human activity is conditioned and human freedom limited. Freedom has two aspects, appropriating external nature and appropriating one's own generic essence, which promote and restrict each other. Alienated labour, the division of labour and value-producing labour are, in their reading, Marx's forms of mediation, to be overcome in realising freedom. Read the original if you want a concise account of Marx's materialism as continuous with German classical philosophy.

The community with a shared future for mankind in light of Marx's theory of intercourse 论马克思交往理论视域下的人类命运共同体 Qian Zhen Qian Zhen asks how Marx's theory of intercourse (jiaowang, also rendered "communication" or "interaction") can illuminate the proposal to build a community with a shared future for mankind. Writing in 2021, the author argues that the community is the latest outcome of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. In this reading it is a new concept of global intercourse aimed at protecting the common interests of all humanity, and it both inherits and develops Marx's theory. The article has three parts. The first reconstructs the basic structure of Marx's theory of intercourse, mainly from The German Ideology, through its links to real human beings, to production and to needs. The second sets out the global problems the author sees today: hegemonism, terrorism, ideological struggle and environmental degradation. It then presents the community through five dimensions drawn from Xi Jinping's speeches: partnership, security, economy, culture and ecology. The third part argues for continuity and development in four respects. In the first part, Qian holds that for Marx people are products of intercourse with nature and with each other, that production is the material basis of intercourse and also depends on it, and that needs drive and shape intercourse. The central claim of the third part is that Marx expected capitalist world history to bring universal and equal intercourse. In the author's account it instead produced unequal subjects and alienated intercourse, with a union of bourgeois interests replacing the "association of free individuals". The community, built on cooperation and win-win outcomes, is said to reshape that pattern and to complete a "second leap" in cognition. Qian adds further claims. The community expresses harmony among nature, humanity and society, drawing on the Chinese ideas of "unity of heaven and humanity" and "all under heaven belongs to all". It unites truth, goodness and beauty, and it supplies a practical route to Marx's association of free individuals, turning a transcendent ideal into an empirical reality. The author concedes that the idea has attracted doubt and that realising it will take generations. The author nonetheless concludes that it is the necessary path towards the free and all-round development of the human being. Read the original if you want an example of how Chinese Marxist scholarship links Marx's theory of intercourse to Xi Jinping's foreign-policy concept.

Lenin's The State and Revolution: a systematic exposition of the Marxist theory of the state 列宁《国家与革命》：马克思主义国家观的系统阐释 Liu Zhiming This article introduces Lenin's The State and Revolution (written in August–September 1917, published 1918) as a systematic statement of the Marxist view of the state. Liu argues that the book answered the major questions of proletarian revolution, guided the Bolsheviks to victory in the October Revolution, and went on to shape the international communist movement and China's revolution, construction and reform. The article also holds that rereading the work still has practical value today. The piece has three parts. The first sets out the historical background: imperialism and the First World War, the Second International's opportunism (Bernstein, Kautsky), the February Revolution and the reversal of July 1917, and Lenin's preparatory notes (the 'blue notebook' Marxism on the State). The second, the longest, summarises six themes: the origin and essence of the state; smashing the bourgeois state machine by violent revolution; proletarian dictatorship and socialist democracy; the political form of that dictatorship, drawn from the Paris Commune; 'bourgeois right' under socialism; and the withering away of the state. The third part draws three lessons for contemporary China. In Liu's reading, Lenin shows that the state is an instrument of class rule determined by the economic base, so that even the democratic republic is the best political shell for capitalism and bourgeois democracy is in essence democracy for the propertied few. Liu follows Lenin in holding that, because proletarian revolution replaces private with public ownership, the old military-bureaucratic machine must be smashed rather than taken over. The Commune's measures (an armed people, recallable officials on workers' wages, a working body in place of parliament, democratic centralism) are presented as the model. The article also reports Lenin's view that socialism still carries 'bourgeois right' in distribution by labour, and that the state withers away only as democracy deepens and communism matures. Lenin's criticism of Bukharin is cited as a case of undialectical thinking about using the state. Liu concludes that the book helps readers reject what the article calls the superstition of Western democracy, citing US figures on money in elections, and affirms socialist democracy with Chinese characteristics and the people's democratic dictatorship. It also underlines the long and arduous course of modernization and communism under the primary stage of socialism, and answers claims that communism is utopian. The article ends by urging readers to strengthen the Four-sphere Confidence and hold to communist ideals. Read the original if you want a compact Chinese-language digest of The State and Revolution and an example of how it is used to defend present-day Chinese political institutions.

"Interdependent social relations" and "concrete justice" A further reflection on the essence of Marx's conception of justice “互依性社会关系”与“具体的正义” Zeng Dong Wang Tiancheng Does Marx have a conception of justice, and what is its substance? Zeng Dong and Wang Tiancheng take up this question against the "Tucker-Wood thesis", which holds that Marx rejected a moralistic critique of capitalism from the standpoint of justice and denied justice a normative place in his philosophy. The authors argue that this reading isolates individual passages. In their view Marx criticised the abstractness and formality of the juridical values of freedom, equality and justice under capitalism, not those values as such, and aimed to give justice new content. The article has three parts. It first distinguishes "dominating" from "interdependent" social relations as the real basis of Marx's thinking on justice, drawing on Marx's three forms of society (personal dependence, objective dependence, free individuality). It then shows how dominating relations underlie Marx's critique of capitalist "abstract justice". Finally it sets out how interdependent relations ground "concrete justice" and summarises three features of Marx's approach. The core argument runs as follows. Both traditional and capitalist societies, the authors say, are dominating: one person or group controls the conditions of existence of another, and relations between people remain instrumental. Capitalist exchange appears free and equal, but the authors argue that once labour-power enters production, surplus value is appropriated without payment and equality gives way to exploitation, with all individuals subject to capital. Justice under capitalism is therefore, in their words, the "justice" of capital's power. Interdependent relations, which the authors tie to communism, are those in which each recognises and promotes the freedom of others, the community is nothing apart from its concrete members, and the means of production belong to associated producers. Concrete justice then means that everyone controls the conditions of their own survival and development. The authors conclude that Marx never defined justice systematically but expressed his view through the historical analysis of social relations. His conception is historical, starts from the character of social relations rather than from atomistic individuals (setting it apart from Lockean liberalism), and measures justice by the degree to which domination is eliminated. They hold that the shift from dominating to interdependent relations is its essence, and that this lets one move beyond superficial debates. Read the original if you want a Chinese-language reconstruction of Marx's theory of justice that answers the Tucker-Wood thesis through his theory of social relations.

Ultimately it is because Marxism works 归根到底是因为马克思主义行 Xin Xiangyang This commentary, published in Guangming Daily in August 2021, takes up Xi Jinping's statement at the Party's centenary celebration (July 2021) that the Communist Party succeeds and socialism with Chinese characteristics is good "ultimately because Marxism works". Xin Xiangyang reads the line as identifying the fundamental reason for the Party's growth and for China's achievements. The author argues that the Party can keep producing new achievements only by continuing to draw on Marxism and developing contemporary Chinese Marxism and twenty-first-century Marxism. The piece is organised under four headings. It treats Marxism's role in the national rejuvenation, Marxism as the guiding ideology of the Party and state, socialism with Chinese characteristics as a product of Marxist principles combined with Chinese realities, and the use of Marxism to observe, grasp and lead the times. It draws on quotations from Xi, Mao Zedong, Qu Qiubai and Ai Siqi, and from Marx on avoiding dogmatism. Xin's central claim is that, after the failures of the Taiping movement, the 1898 reforms, the Boxer movement and the 1911 revolution, Marxism-Leninism gave the Chinese nation a clear direction and moved it "from passivity to initiative" in spirit. Marxism, in this account, changed China, and China in turn enriched Marxism; Xin cites Ai Siqi to say that the seeds of Marxism already lay in Chinese tradition. The author then traces Marxist guidance in four areas: the path, the theoretical system (including Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era), the institutions, and socialist culture with Chinese characteristics. Xin presents these as outcomes of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Xin concludes that Marxism's truth is open to the future and must not become dogma, so the Party must keep adapting it to Chinese practice. Since the 18th Party Congress (2012), the author says, Party members led by Xi have answered the questions of the times, the people, the Party and the world, and are guiding China towards the centre of the world stage and the building of a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a short example of how the official 2021 centenary narrative credits Marxism for the Party's record.

Commemoration and reflection by the foreign left on the 200th anniversary of Engels's birth 国外左翼对恩格斯诞辰200周年的纪念与省思 Yuan Qun Wang Enming Yuan Qun and Wang Enming survey how left-wing parties, organisations and scholars outside China marked the bicentenary of Friedrich Engels's birth in 2020. They argue that these commemorations defended Engels's standing against long-running disparagement and showed that his thought still guides the world socialist movement as it moves, in the authors' words, from a low ebb towards revival. The article opens with a catalogue of events: conferences in Lisbon, Hanoi, Vientiane and Japan, joint declarations by Marxist-Leninist-Maoist parties, commemorative articles by figures such as Gennady Zyuganov, Brinda Karat, Marcello Musto and Michael Roberts, and a 'Engels Year' in Wuppertal. It then reviews what these sources say about Engels's historical position, his contributions to philosophy, political economy, scientific socialism and military science, and the present-day value of his ideas. It closes with the strategies the left drew from the anniversary. The authors argue first that foreign leftists reject historical nihilism and affirm Engels as co-founder of Marxism and a leader of the workers' movement, the irreplaceable 'second violin' beside Marx. Second, they report that these writers answer the claims that Marx and Engels were opposed, or that the late Engels abandoned revolution for parliamentarism, by treating his work as a living weapon. Cited examples include his analysis of capital concentration, said to be borne out by the global financial crisis and the Covid-19 pandemic, and his account of women's oppression in The Origin of the Family, Private Property and the State. The authors conclude that the commemorations continued the 2018 Marx bicentenary and showed Engels's theory to be still relevant to class liberation. They report three practical lessons drawn abroad: building revolutionary proletarian parties, strengthening the study and publication of Marxist theory, and forming broad anti-war and workers' fronts. They add that the left's position in the heartland of imperialism gave its reading of Engels, in their view, both revolutionary optimism and sober realism. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-referenced map of foreign communist and left commemorations of Engels in 2020, including Vietnamese, Indian, Russian and European material, as seen from a Chinese academic viewpoint.

A critique of nature-centred ecological views and the construction of a new ecological philosophy Reading Slavoj Žižek on ecology 自然中心主义生态观的批判与新生态哲学的建构 Shi Fengge Why has the ecological crisis not eased despite decades of Western reflection on it? Shi Fengge argues that the weakness of "nature-centrism" (ziran zhongxinzhuyi) lies in its ontological premise: a perfectly balanced, pristine original nature that humans later damaged. Drawing on Slavoj Žižek, the article calls this premise a utopia and presents Žižek's alternative, a "new ecological philosophy" built on psychoanalysis. The article has four parts. It first reconstructs the nature-centred outlook through three currents: ecological ethics (Schweitzer, Leopold, Rolston, with Barry Commoner's ecological law that nature knows best), wilderness philosophy, and Arne Naess's deep ecology. It then sets out Žižek's critique, mainly from In Defense of Lost Causes. Next it explains the new ecological philosophy's two components, the "future perfect" and collective action. A conclusion compares Žižek with Marx and Engels. Shi's core argument is that, for Žižek, "nature does not exist". Nature is inherently catastrophic and unbalanced, as shown by a reading of Darwin in which evolution is clumsy improvisation, and by the claim that 90 per cent of the human genome is "junk" DNA. Since humans appeared it has also been a "second nature", and genetic technology deepens this. Žižek's response is a time-view in which disaster is treated as inevitable so that action can retroactively change what was possible, together with collective action. The latter is spelled out by reworking Badiou's four moments of the eternal Idea of justice: strict egalitarian justice, terror against violators of environmental rules, voluntarism, and trust in the people, including the figure of the informer. Shi presents this as a response to the "choice deadlock" of unknown unknowns. Shi concludes that Žižek moves the ecological question from a utopian beyond to the practical problem of solving it, while grounding action in human value. The article finds links to Marx's view of nature as humanised and socially historical, to Engels's warning that nature takes revenge on human victories, and to Marx's concept of practice. It admits the new philosophy is imperfect but calls it a new perspective and path for global ecological problems. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist reading of Žižek's ecological thought, and of how it is set against deep ecology and Marx and Engels.

The idea of totality: from Hegel and Marx to the founders of Marxism outside China 总体性思想：从黑格尔、马克思到国外马克思主义的奠基者 Yang Haifeng Modern specialisation and the division of labour have blurred the picture of society and the world as a whole. Yang Haifeng asks how the idea of totality, traced from Hegel through Marx, became the entry point by which Lukács, Korsch and Gramsci reread Marx's philosophy. Yang argues that this move broke with the research tradition of the Second International and founded the tradition of foreign Marxism. The article has three parts. The first compares Hegel's and Marx's conceptions of totality. The second follows Lukács from his early works, Soul and Form and The Theory of the Novel, through History and Class Consciousness to his late Ontology of Social Being. The third turns to Korsch (Marxism and Philosophy, Karl Marx) and Gramsci (the Prison Notebooks), and closes by comparing the three. Yang first shows how Hegel's totality is a mediated circle in which beginning and end coincide, and how Marx keeps this idea in his Grundrisse method. For Marx, a concrete thing is a unity of many determinations, and capital is the dominant relation that organises capitalist society. Yang then lists four differences: Marx grounds totality in social existence rather than spirit; he treats concepts as reflecting real development; he identifies capital as the true starting point and end point; and he sees irreparable fissures in capitalism that reason cannot reconcile. Lukács then uses totality both as a method (isolated facts only count as knowledge when grasped within a whole) and as an ideal state. From that ideal he criticises reification and the antinomies of bourgeois thought. Korsch and Gramsci stress the unity of Marxism's parts: philosophy, political economy and socialism for Korsch; philosophy, economics and politics for Gramsci, whose theory of hegemony Yang reads as political, economic and cultural together rather than merely cultural. Yang concludes that the three thinkers seized the most important content of Marxist philosophy, the totalising study of social life. In doing so they helped remove the mechanical Marxism of the Second International and restored its vitality. Yang notes their differences: Lukács is the radical philosopher, Korsch the theorist of the links among Marxism's components, and Gramsci the revolutionary rooted in Italian reality. Their work, Yang says, directly shaped the Frankfurt School in the 1930s–60s. Read the original if you want a close account of how the concept of totality links Hegel, Marx and the first generation of Western Marxist thinkers, as seen by a leading Chinese scholar of foreign Marxism.

The successful experience of the Communist Party of China is a precious asset for the world 中国共产党的成功经验是世界宝贵财富 Ivan Melnikov This is a Chinese translation of a commentary by Ivan Melnikov, a Russian Communist Party leader and First Deputy Chairman of the State Duma, written for the centenary of the Communist Party of China in 2021. Melnikov argues that the Party's hundred years of leading revolution, construction and reform have produced experience that is a valuable asset for the whole world. He presents the Party as the force that restarted the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The piece follows the Party's history in broad stages. It begins with China's decline into a semi-colonial, semi-feudal society after 1840 and the spread of Marxism after the October Revolution. It then covers the founding of the Party in 1921 and the victory in the wars of liberation. Next come the building of the People's Republic after 1949, reform and opening up from 1978, and the period since Xi Jinping became General Secretary in 2012. The last part turns to Russian–Chinese relations. Melnikov's core claim is that the Party's record in solving national problems explains its authority. He cites the creation of a complete national economic system by 1978 and rising literacy and life expectancy. He also cites China's share of world GDP, which he gives as 1.8 per cent in 1978 and close to 10 per cent by 2010, when China became the second-largest economy. For the period since 2012, he points to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and the Belt and Road Initiative. In his account, the Party now helps address global challenges and promotes progress, cooperation and humanitarianism. Melnikov describes Russian–Chinese relations as the best in history. He bases this on the 2001 Treaty of Good-Neighbourliness and Friendly Cooperation, on cooperation between parties and legislatures, and on friendship societies and cultural exchange. He expresses confidence that firm adherence to the Party's line will bring new achievements. He adds that China's success gives the international communist movement more arguments for the promise of its aims, and that peoples on every continent will draw on the Party's experience. Read the original if you want an example of how a Russian communist politician framed the Party's centenary for a Chinese readership, including its emphasis on Sino-Russian ties.

Why socialist democracy with Chinese characteristics works 中国特色社会主义民主为什么行 Fan Peng Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in mid-2021, Fan Peng asks why socialist democracy with Chinese characteristics succeeds. The author sets the question against what the article describes as disorder in the West: political polarisation, social division, governance failures during the Covid-19 pandemic, and signs of 'democratic deficit' and 'democratic backsliding'. Fan contends that this contrast with 'China's governance' shows that Chinese democracy is a high-quality democracy, sound in concept and workable in practice. The piece is a commentary organised under five headings. It begins with a short account of China's path to democracy from the semi-colonial period through the founding of the People's Republic, reform and opening up, and the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). It then discusses people-centred democracy, whole-process people's democracy, the unity of form and substance, democracy that spurs development and builds consensus, and democracy that combines harmony and stability with vitality. Fan's central claim is that democracy should be judged by substance, practical results and the people's own experience, not by electoral form. The author says Western systems reduce democracy to voting, which leaves citizens passive between elections, and cites George Tsebelis and Mancur Olson to argue that this produces empty procedure and decline. Whole-process people's democracy, by contrast, is said to cover election, consultation, decision-making, management and supervision, with a full chain of mechanisms. Fan's examples are public consultation on draft laws, including the Civil Code, which drew 1.02 million comments from 425,000 people, and grassroots consultation. Fan also argues that the Communist Party, as the highest political leadership force with no special interests, and democratic centralism allow consensus and avoid gridlock. Fan concludes that Chinese democracy fits China's conditions, answers the people's actual concerns and keeps order and vitality together in a country of more than 1.4 billion people. The author presents the Party's century of struggle as a history of extending democratic rights. Read the original if you want an example of how official-affiliated Chinese scholarship in 2021 framed the case for Chinese democracy against Western models.

The grounds for confidence in China's ideological system 我国意识形态制度自信的底气 Hou Huiqin Hou Huiqin takes up the question of why China can be confident in the fundamental system of upholding Marxism's guiding position in the ideological sphere. The 4th Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2019) established this principle as a basic system of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Hou argues that it follows from the laws governing any ruling party, from the logic of human civilisational progress and from the laws of development of philosophy and the social sciences. The article was published in the Journal of Yanshan University (Philosophy and Social Sciences) in 2021. The article has three numbered sections. The first treats ideological leadership as a general law of rule and draws lessons from the collapse of the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe. The second places Marxist guidance within a philosophy of history that moves from class society to the free and all-round development of the individual. The third turns to the social sciences and asks what a Marxist-led discipline system should look like in practice. Hou's core claim is that every ruling class must control the production of ideas as well as material production, so Western charges of 'brainwashing' are, in the author's view, hypocritical. Hou reads the Soviet collapse as beginning with the discarding of Marxist philosophy as 'outdated', which opened the way to historical nihilism, individualism and the removal of Party leadership. In the second section, Hou argues that capitalism's 'abstract individual' is an animal-like, self-interested figure. Genuine individuality, Hou holds, is possible only through the proletariat's conscious liberation and a 'real collective', and so requires cultivating socialist new people. In the third, Hou criticises Western social science for positivism and abstract assumptions about human nature, such as 'economic man', which Hou says serve the existing order. Hou calls for research on objective laws and the whole of society, for Marxist foundations in each discipline's core concepts, and for 'the people' rather than the isolated individual as the subject of knowledge. Hou concludes that the system of Marxist guidance ensures the healthy development of socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era and links Chinese experience with world progress. In practice, Hou calls for Marxist worldview training in all disciplines, theory tied to practice, and criticism and debate that unify understanding, rather than debates over how much space to give individual freedom. Read the original if you want to see how a leading Chinese Marxist philosopher grounds ideological leadership in historical materialism and applies it to the social sciences.

A centenary retrospective and its lessons: the Communist International and its relationship with the Chinese revolution 百年回眸与启示：共产国际及其与中国革命的关系 Wang Zifeng Pan Jin'e Marking the centenary of the Communist Party of China in 2021, Wang Zifeng and Pan Jin'e revisit the Communist International (Comintern, 1919–1943) and its ties to the Chinese revolution. They draw on how communist parties around the world reassessed the Comintern in 2019, its hundredth anniversary. The authors argue that the Comintern was a historical necessity that made major contributions but also committed serious errors, and that this record offers lessons for today's international communist movement. The article has three parts. The first places the Comintern in the world proletarian movement: whether its founding was necessary, what it contributed, and what its faults were. The second follows Zhou Enlai's 1960 remark, attributed to Mao Zedong, that the Comintern was "good at both ends, poor in the middle", and divides its relations with China into three eight-year phases (1919–1927, 1927–1935, 1935–1943). The third draws four lessons for the present. On the first part, the authors reject views that the Comintern was a "premature birth" or the product of subjective will. They cite the Second International's wartime betrayal, Lenin's theory of imperialism, and the growth of left-wing parties after the October Revolution. They list faults that communist parties acknowledged in 2019: over-centralised organisation that subordinated parties to Soviet interests, shifting and mistaken policy towards social democracy, and dogmatic export of the Soviet experience. On China, they credit the Comintern in the first phase with spreading Marxism, helping found the Party, shaping the first Kuomintang–Communist cooperation, training cadres and providing funds, while faulting its concessions to the Kuomintang right. In the second phase, they hold that its "Third Period" theory and its representatives' directives produced three "Left" errors and heavy losses until the Zunyi Meeting of 1935. In the third phase they credit its united-front line, but criticise Soviet pressure and Wang Ming's "everything through the united front" line. The four lessons are: to recognise internationalism as a condition of proletarian liberation, and rebuild international unity among socialist forces; to unite around Marxism and the communist ideal, treating ideological agreement as more important than organisational form; to observe the principles of independence, equality, mutual respect and non-interference in inter-party relations, and to accept diverse paths to socialism; and to use the building of a community with a shared future for mankind as a banner for cooperation among communist parties. The authors present socialism with Chinese characteristics as a mainstay of world socialism. Read the original if you want a Chinese Academy of Social Sciences account of the Comintern's record in China, or the official Chinese reading of how foreign communist parties reassessed it in 2019.

European communists on the successful experience of the Communist Party of China 欧洲共产党人对中国共产党成功经验的探讨 Zhang Jie Published in July 2021, around the centenary of the Communist Party of China (CPC), this short commentary asks how communists from European parties explain the CPC's achievements. Zhang argues that these figures widely praise the Party's record and consider its experience worth learning from elsewhere. The piece collects statements from leaders and members of communist and left parties in Russia, Belarus, Britain, the Czech lands, Germany, Italy, Spain, Switzerland and Portugal. It also cites the European Left. Their remarks are grouped under five headings: theory, history, the people, practice and the world. Zhang reports that these figures credit the CPC's adherence to Marxism and its adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. They also credit its founding mission, its commitment to putting the people first, and its principle of seeking truth from facts. Speakers such as Aleksei Sokol, Robert Griffiths and Maria Teresa Mora are quoted on the Party's ties to the people, the fight against Covid-19 and the elimination of absolute poverty. Alberto Lombardo is quoted comparing China's epidemic response with that of some Western countries. Hans Modrow is quoted saying that human rights and democracy should not be reduced to periodic voting. On the global dimension, the Spanish and Italian party leaders are quoted endorsing the Belt and Road Initiative and a community with a shared future for mankind. Zhang concludes that many European communists admire the CPC's achievements, regard its experience as a model for others, and expect further successes. The text is mainly a thematic compilation of foreign views, which the author presents as support for the Party's approach. Read the original if you want a quick sample of how Chinese commentary presents European communist views of the CPC at its centenary.

Steadily strengthening the political consciousness to achieve the "Two Upholds" 不断坚定做到“两个维护”的政治自觉 Zhang Cong Published in Red Flag Manuscript in 2021, this short commentary asks why the "Two Upholds" are the first task of strengthening the Party's political development. Zhang argues that upholding Xi Jinping's position as the core of the Central Committee and the whole Party, and upholding the authority and centralized, unified leadership of the Central Committee, bear on the success of the Party's cause and its future. Party members, especially leading cadres, are urged to stay in step with the Central Committee politically. The article first looks back over the Party's century, tracing leadership collectives and cores from Mao Zedong through Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin and Hu Jintao. It then turns to the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012), citing the January 2019 Central Committee opinion on strengthening the Party's political development, and ends with practical requirements for the present. Zhang's central claim is that establishing and consolidating a leadership collective and core is a mark of political maturity and a long-standing Party tradition and political strength. In this reading, the Party's achievements in revolution, construction and reform owe most to that tradition. The "Two Upholds" are presented as the new era's form of it, resting on a historical choice by the Party and people. Zhang calls for ideological education so that members grasp why central authority matters, and for strict institutional rules governing internal Party political life. Zhang concludes that making the "Two Upholds" the first task of political development continues the Party's tradition and provides a fundamental political guarantee for building a modern socialist country. Facing a complex international environment and a changed principal contradiction in society, the article calls for a unified Party will. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party media present the Two Upholds in historical and institutional terms.

Carrying forward the great spirit of seeking truth from facts 弘扬伟大的实事求是精神 Jia Lizheng Published in Hubei Daily in July 2021, in the run-up to the Party's centenary, this commentary argues that seeking truth from facts (shishi qiushi) is the living soul of Marxism and the thread running through the Communist Party of China's hundred years. Jia Lizheng contends that the Party's history is a history of struggle to uphold this ideological line, and that it remains the basic guarantee for national rejuvenation. The piece is organised in three parts. The first traces the principle through successive stages: Mao Zedong's 1941 Yan'an report 'Reform Our Study', the restoration of the line after the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee under Deng Xiaoping, and the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012) under Xi Jinping. The second presents it as the key to why the Party 'can', Marxism 'works' and socialism with Chinese characteristics is 'good'. The third ties it to the 'two centenary goals' and the 'two overall situations'. Jia argues that the Party has won support and led the move from 'standing up' to 'becoming rich' to 'becoming strong' because it has consistently followed a line of seeking truth from facts, the mass line and a practical work style. Drawing on Marx's remark that theory becomes a material force when it grips the masses by grasping the root of things, Jia answers that the root is seeking truth from facts. In practice this means identifying real rather than false problems, following objective laws and standing with the people. Jia also calls the principle the spiritual core of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, which is said to have developed by answering the questions of the times. Jia concludes that, as the country begins building a modern socialist country in all respects, the Party must strengthen its stance on seeking truth from facts, implement the line more fully and carry the spirit forward. Doing so is said to help it handle domestic and international situations, manage risks, and advance the Party's self-reform alongside social revolution. Jia calls for cadres to study Xi's remarks, including those at the 120th anniversary of Mao's birth, and apply them in practice. Read the original if you want a representative example of how the Party's official press in 2021 framed seeking truth from facts as a unifying thread of Party history and of Xi Jinping Thought.

The Communist Party of Vietnam's theoretical exploration of socialist construction since Doi Moi 革新以来越南共产党对社会主义建设的理论探索 Yan Jiehua Writing after the 13th Congress of the Communist Party of Vietnam (CPV) in 2021, Yan Jiehua asks how the party has developed its theory of socialist construction during 35 years of renovation (Doi Moi, begun in 1986). The article argues that this exploration has advanced along three lines: the theory of developmental stages in the socialist transition period, the theory of socialist democracy, and the theory of party building. Yan treats these as the CPV's attempt to combine Marxist principles with Vietnamese conditions, and aims to draw lessons for other socialist countries. The article has three main sections, one for each line of theory. The first traces how the CPV's understanding of the transition period developed from the Sixth Congress (1986) through the Twelfth (2016) to the Thirteenth. The second follows the democracy formula, the relationships the party must handle, and the institutions built around it. The third covers party building, including the status of the political system and of cadre work. Yan draws heavily on congress documents and on statements by Nguyen Phu Trong and CPV theorists. On the transition period, Yan argues that the Sixth Congress formed the theory, later congresses tied its stages to industrialization and modernization, and the Thirteenth Congress set new benchmarks. These benchmarks combine overall development level, industrial level and income level, with goals for 2025, 2030 and 2045. On democracy, Yan reads the move from a four-part formula to a six-part one as a step towards a state of law that belongs to, comes from and serves the people. The six parts are people know, discuss, do, inspect, supervise and enjoy, and the Thirteenth Congress added supervision and enjoyment. Yan notes that the formula was institutionalised through party directives, government decrees and National Assembly ordinances on grassroots democracy. On party building, the Thirteenth Congress made building a clean, strong political system a theme alongside party building. It also called cadre work the 'key of keys' and described a five-part pattern: politics, ideology, ethics, organisation and cadres. Yan concludes that significant theoretical problems remain open. CPV theorists admit that the length of the transition period and the number of its stages are unresolved, and that it is unclear whether reaching high-income status in 2045 would end it. Some Vietnamese scholars doubt the new targets, since the goal of becoming a basically industrialised country by 2020 was not met. Yan also notes unresolved questions about the relation between democracy and discipline within democratic centralism, and acknowledges weaknesses in ideological work and in theoretical summing-up. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's overview of how Vietnam's ruling party has framed its post-1986 theory, with detailed references to CPV congress documents and official regulations.

On the scientific meaning and paths to realisation of socialist modernization 论社会主义现代化的科学内涵与实现路径 Zhang Jiangang Writing in 2021, the year China began a new journey of building a modern socialist country in all respects, Zhang Jiangang asks what socialist modernization properly means, what experience China has gained in pursuing it, and by what paths it can be achieved. The article argues that socialist modernization is defined by its aim of serving the people's fundamental interests, by the all-round development of the person, and by the advantages of the socialist system. It holds that the Party's leadership and the socialist basic economic system are the decisive conditions for success. The article has three parts. The first traces the idea of modernization from the late-Qing reformers and the 1911 Revolution, through the Four Modernizations announced by Zhou Enlai in 1964 and 1975, to the contributions of Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin, Hu Jintao and Xi Jinping. The second draws lessons from the historical record. The third sets out four implementation paths. In Zhang's account, three lessons stand out: a correct development strategy is the precondition, scientific and technological innovation is the internal driving force, and state macroeconomic governance is the fundamental guarantee. Zhang describes modernization in China as a process led by the state, with the market playing a full role, not a spontaneous market-driven one. The paths proposed are: upholding Party leadership, which Zhang says gives the Party the capacity to set strategy, push through reforms, lead the times and set an example through Party building. They also include a people-centred development philosophy, covering education, income distribution and social security. Zhang further stresses the basic economic system, with public ownership as the main body and a socialist market economy. Finally, the article presents the new development pattern of "dual circulation", with the domestic cycle as the mainstay, as the route to basic modernization by 2035. Zhang concludes that socialist modernization can succeed only if socialism is combined with modernization, under Party leadership and with the people at the centre. The new development stage, the new development philosophy and the dual-circulation pattern together frame the next phase. The article is largely an exposition of official positions, citing Xi Jinping and Party documents. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned overview of how Chinese scholars in 2021 defined socialist modernization and linked it to the new development pattern.

The Party's external exchanges: an inseparable part of China's revolution and construction 党的对外交往：中国革命与建设事业不可分割的一部分 Yu Hongjun Writing in the centenary year of the Communist Party of China (2021), Yu Hongjun, a former deputy minister of the Party's International Department, argues that the Party's external exchanges have been an integral part of China's revolution and construction since 1921. The article contends that these exchanges have evolved with each period, coordinating with state diplomacy, and that they are now an indispensable component of major-country diplomacy with Chinese characteristics. The article is a historical survey in four periods: the revolutionary war years, the early People's Republic, the era of reform and opening up, and the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012) under Xi Jinping. It draws on episodes such as ties with the Comintern and the Soviet Union, with Ho Chi Minh, and with foreign sympathisers like Edgar Snow, Agnes Smedley and Rewi Alley. It then moves to the founding of the International Liaison Department, the restoration of relations with communist, socialist and centre-right parties, and institutionalised dialogues with US, European, Russian, Japanese and Indian parties. Yu's central claim is that the Party gradually moved from dependence on, and struggle against, Soviet guidance towards independence. From 1955 it abandoned judging other parties by Soviet standards and drafting their programmes. After 1978, the author says, Deng Xiaoping's principle that no party may act as a 'father party' became the four principles of independence, complete equality, mutual respect and non-interference, written into the Party constitution in 1982. Yu argues that this framework let the Party rebuild ties after the 1989–91 upheavals, and that under Xi, exchanges serve the Belt and Road Initiative and the building of a community with a shared future for mankind. The author reports that the Party will neither import nor export models. Yu concludes that Party diplomacy, extended even through the 2020 pandemic by video meetings, has not stagnated but is expanding. In the article's account, understanding China requires understanding the Party, and the Party will keep strengthening exchanges for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want an insider's periodised account of the Party's inter-party relations, with details on institutions, dialogue mechanisms and policy turning points.

The Chinese Communist Party's historical experience of building a socialist state 中国共产党建设社会主义国家的历史经验 Liu Fangliang This newspaper commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in June 2021, asks what experience the Chinese Communist Party has accumulated in building and improving the socialist state system. Liu Fangliang argues that the Party has developed a path of state-system construction that runs from theoretical guidance, through operating mechanisms, to governance. The piece is organised in three parts that follow this sequence. It first treats the adaptation of Marxist political theory to Chinese conditions across the revolutionary period, the founding of the People's Republic and the post-1978 era. It then turns to mechanism innovation, and finally to the modernization of the state governance system and governance capacity. On theory, Liu holds that the classic writers left no detailed plan for building socialism in a backward Eastern country, so the Party had to combine Marxist doctrine with national conditions. Examples include New Democracy, the people's democratic dictatorship, the people's congress system, multi-party cooperation and political consultation under Party leadership, regional ethnic autonomy, and the theory of the primary stage of socialism. On mechanisms, Liu distinguishes a stable state system from dynamic operating mechanisms: the leadership, public ownership and people's democratic dictatorship stay fixed, while institutions, regulations and policies are renewed. Grassroots practices such as the household contract responsibility system were written into the constitution, and foreign borrowing is confined to the mechanism level. Liu concludes that, since the Third Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2013), making governance capacity the concrete expression of the state system has refined it across political, economic, social, cultural and ecological fields. In Liu's view this also criticises and goes beyond Western "society-centred" governance theories that dissolve government and neglect authority. Read the original if you want a concise, official-line statement of how Chinese scholars frame the Party's institutional experience.

Telling the Party's stories well and passing on the red gene 讲好党的故事 传承红色基因 Long Xinmin Published in People's Daily in June 2021, in the centenary year of the Communist Party, this commentary asks how the Party's history can be conveyed so that the 'red gene' is handed down. Long Xinmin argues that the Party's stories are a vivid interpretation of its history and a living teaching resource. The author builds on Xi Jinping's call to tell stories of the Party, the revolution, the base areas, heroes and martyrs, so that the 'red country' never changes colour. The article has three parts. The first treats the Party's stories as carriers of its original aspiration and founding mission, its fine work style and its spirit of struggle. The second explains why these stories matter for Party members and officials, for young people and for society as a whole. The third sets out practical measures for telling the stories of the new era that began with the 18th Party Congress (2012). Examples range from the textbook tales of the 'half a quilt' and Zhu De's carrying pole to Xia Minghan, Jiang Jie, Wang Jinxi, Jiao Yulu and Lei Feng. In Long's account, the stories show communists serving the people and sharing hardships with ordinary soldiers. They also show successive generations making sacrifices in revolution, construction and reform. For officials, the stories nourish the original aspiration and the faith in Marxism, as in the account of Chen Wangdao finding the taste of truth 'very sweet'. For young people, the stories explain where the red state and today's life came from. They are meant to lead young people to follow the Party. For society, models such as Lei Feng are said to raise moral standards and strengthen shared ideals as China pursues the second centenary goal. Long concludes that stories of the new era are still under-represented in textbooks and in literary and artistic work. The author proposes campaigns to collect and create new stories, drawing on poverty alleviation and the fight against Covid-19. The author also wants such stories placed in textbooks, classrooms and students' minds, and calls for a large corps of storytellers made up of teachers, officials, veterans, volunteers and journalists. Read the original if you want a clear example of how official commentary frames Party history education and storytelling as tools for ideological transmission.

Party self-knowledge: the secret of how a century-old Party keeps its advanced nature 政党自知：百年大党长期保持先进性的奥秘 Yu Chongsheng Writing around the centenary of the Communist Party of China in 2021, Yu Chongsheng asks why this Party has kept its advanced nature through a century of history and more than 70 years in power. Yu's answer is "Party self-knowledge": a Party's clear grasp of its own mission, strengths, shortcomings and historical moment. The article presents this as the main secret of the Party's long-term vitality. The article has three parts. The first defines Party self-knowledge, drawing on the Daodejing's idea that knowing oneself is true insight and on Fei Xiaotong's notion of cultural self-awareness. The second explains why it matters, using Mao Zedong's remarks on self-knowledge and the Soviet collapse as a negative case. The third sets out ways to advance it. It opens by noting how few parties worldwide have lasted over a century or governed continuously. Yu argues that Party self-knowledge goes beyond Party confidence because it unites four "selfs": confidence, awareness, introspection and discipline. Awareness comes first logically, since only rational awareness can ground firm confidence. Advanced nature is neither innate nor permanent, so a ruling party must keep checking itself. Yu reads the Soviet Communist Party's fall, citing Ryzhkov and a study of the Soviet system's end, as the result of distorted ideas about socialism and complacency. Yu calls Huntington's explanation of the Party's durability superficial because it ignores advanced nature. Four paths follow: use the Party's theoretical, political, organisational, institutional and mass-line strengths; face its limits and learn from mistakes; meet risks calmly, including by bottom-line thinking and a spirit of struggle; and keep the four "selfs" in proper relation. Yu concludes that the Party's history is a history of the Party's self-reform, expressed as self-purification, self-improvement, self-renewal and self-elevation, each answering a specific weakness of long single-party rule. Yu holds that self-knowledge must be advanced continually, given the "four tests" and "four dangers" the Party faces, and that it is needed for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a Chinese Party-theory account that links Daoist and Confucian-era ideas of self-knowledge to arguments about Party building and the Soviet experience.

The Communist Party of China's century of history and historical initiative 中国共产党百年历史与历史主动 Qu Qingshan Published in Guangming Daily in June 2021, in the run-up to the Party's centenary, this article by Qu Qingshan asks how the Communist Party of China (CPC) has combined respect for objective historical laws with active, purposeful agency. Qu's answer is the concept of "historical initiative". The CPC, he argues, has followed the laws of historical development, conformed to the main historical trend and so seized the initiative at each stage. He frames this as an application of historical materialism, drawing on Xi Jinping's speech of 20 February 2021 launching Party history study and education. The article opens with a theoretical premise. In Qu's account, history has objective laws, but humans have "conscious dynamism", and a Marxist party should unite conformity to law with conformity to purpose. It then moves through five periods, each introduced with the same formula: the founding of the Party, the founding of the People's Republic, socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the entry of socialism with Chinese characteristics into a new era. A final section draws nine lessons from the century. Qu argues that each turning point was an inevitable product or outcome of historical trends. The Party emerged from the failure of earlier attempts at national rejuvenation, the example of the October Revolution, the spread of Marxism-Leninism and the rise of the Chinese working class. The later stages are presented as correct readings of the era: the united front against Japan, victory in the civil war, socialist transformation, and the post-1978 turn to reform and opening up. Qu also reviews the theoretical achievements of successive leadership generations, from Mao Zedong Thought to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Each lesson, such as keeping to the original aspiration, grasping the principal contradiction, struggle, reform and innovation, unity and advancing human progress, is tied to a task for the "new journey". Qu concludes that this grasp of trends carried China from "standing up" through "becoming prosperous" to "becoming strong". He treats the nine lessons as guidance for building a modern socialist country and meeting the "second centenary" goals, including the 2035 and 2050 strategic arrangements. The article is an authoritative statement of the official narrative of Party history in its centenary year. Read the original if you want to see how the Party's official historiography links historical materialism to the claim of a consistent historical initiative across the whole century.

The Communist Party of China's century-long exploration and practice of people's democracy 中国共产党对人民民主的百年探索与实践 Wang Zongli Written in the centenary year of the Party's founding (2021), this article asks how the Communist Party of China has pursued people's democracy since 1921. Wang Zongli argues that the Party's history is a history of struggle for people's democracy: a continuous effort to combine Marxist democratic theory with Chinese conditions, to build institutions of popular rule, to diversify democratic forms and to refine a distinctive path and theory. In Wang's account, this has produced a new road of democracy with Chinese characteristics. The article has four parts. It first traces people's democracy as the Party's goal through the revolutionary periods, the Soviet Republic, the anti-Japanese base areas, the founding of the People's Republic, and the leadership eras from Deng Xiaoping to Xi Jinping. It then examines the meaning of 'the people as masters of the country' and how the scope of 'the people' has changed. The last two parts cover the institutional system of people's democracy and its forms: electoral, consultative and participatory democracy. Wang's central claim is that most Western theorists treat democracy only as a question of political system, whereas Marxism treats it first as the relation between state power and the people, and so as a question of who owns power. Democracy therefore involves the state's class nature, the way organs of power are formed under democratic centralism, and the state's responsiveness to popular interests. Wang stresses that 'the people' is a historical category that has widened, from workers and peasants to include intellectuals, private entrepreneurs and patriots working for national rejuvenation. Since the 18th Party Congress (2012), Wang holds, the institutional system has been strengthened through Party leadership, the people's congress system, a new type of party system, regional ethnic autonomy and grassroots self-governance. Wang describes consultative democracy as a distinctively Chinese form and argues that Western participatory democracy cannot achieve direct popular management because of the limits of capitalist private ownership. Wang concludes that people's democracy is the broadest, most genuine and most effective form of democracy, and a higher type than bourgeois democracy. Wang calls for upholding Party leadership while making democracy more institutionalised, law-based and procedural, perfecting the people's congress system, widening orderly political participation, and combining electoral and consultative democracy. Read the original if you want a Party-historical account of how Chinese scholarship in 2021 framed a century of democratic practice, with a detailed chronology of institutions and electoral laws.

Ten essential points of the political economy of socialism with Chinese characteristics 中国特色社会主义政治经济学十大要义 Cheng Enfu Cheng Enfu asks what the core tenets of the political economy of socialism with Chinese characteristics should be, and how it can develop as a logically self-consistent discipline. Taking Marx's Capital as the model of theoretical logic, the article sets out ten "essential points" covering guiding thought, object, method, tasks, starting point, central concept, axis, standpoint, purpose and policy orientation. Cheng's thesis is that this political economy must remain anchored in Marxism-Leninism and in public ownership as the dominant element of the economy. The article is a programmatic essay published in Theory Monthly in 2021. Each of the ten sections states a positive proposition, usually tied to passages from Marx, Engels, Lenin, Stalin or Mao Zedong. Each section then ends with a list of opposing views that, in Cheng's words, do not help the discipline's logical self-consistency. These include dogmatism towards Marx, foreign or ancient authorities, "ownership neutrality", and the substitution of Western economics for socialist market-economy theory. Cheng's central moves concern object, concept and class relations. The object of study is production relations or economic institutions in the primary stage of socialism, examined together with the productive forces and the superstructure. Cheng proposes beginning, as Capital does, with the commodity, but distinguishes commodities from public and private enterprises. These carry different basic contradictions. Labour is the "meta-concept" and a theory of public surplus value the main thread, with state, collective and cooperative surplus value distinguished from private surplus value. The axis is the relation between public capital and freely associated labour. The article describes methodological pluralism as Marxism as the essence, Western learning as a tool, and Chinese traditional learning as the root. Cheng concludes that the discipline must take the standpoint of the working class and working people, and must oppose private monopoly and expansion. Its aim is to meet the people's growing needs for a better life, and its policy orientation is to perfect socialist economic relations so as to modernise the productive forces and the superstructure. Cheng warns that if private ownership became dominant, the socialist superstructure would sooner or later change in nature. Read the original if you want a concise statement of one influential Marxist-orthodox position on how Chinese political economy should be built, and on its objections to rival positions.

On the intellectual sources of Marx's labour theory of value 论马克思劳动价值论的思想来源 Mei Wentao Where did Marx's labour theory of value come from? Mei Wentao, in an article published in Social Sciences Trends in 2021, follows Lenin's account of classical political economy as one source of Marxism and argues that three strands formed the starting point of Marx's value theory and his economic research. These are the development of classical political economy, the work of Marx's contemporaries, and the shift in Marx's own standpoint, above all his break with Hegel's theory of civil society. The article is organised in three parts. The first traces the early form of the labour theory of value in British classical political economy through William Petty, Adam Smith and David Ricardo, after setting out the economic and philosophical background (Bacon and Hobbes) and the school's three features. The second looks at contemporaries who shaped Marx before his formal turn to economics: Engels, Moses Hess and Pierre-Joseph Proudhon. The third follows Marx's own path from his journalism on the Rheinische Zeitung to his critique of Hegel. Mei's central argument is that Marx built his theory by critically absorbing and then overcoming predecessors' limits. Petty located value in labour time but treated gold and silver as the only value form. Smith distinguished use-value from exchange-value yet wavered, confusing labour expended with labour commanded and splitting value into wages, profit and rent. Ricardo held firmly that expended labour determines value but left open problems such as wages and rent. Among contemporaries, Engels's Outlines of a Critique of Political Economy contributed a proletarian standpoint that questioned private property. Hess criticised alienation from a humanist ethical position, and Proudhon challenged private property and unequal exchange. Mei further argues that the "difficulty" of material interests Marx met in the wood-theft debates, together with Feuerbach's influence, led him from moral criticism of legislators to a materialist view of civil society and the proletariat's historical role. Mei concludes that the labour theory of value is a scientific theory founded on wide absorption of the achievements of human civilisation. Retracing its formation, the author says, has theoretical significance for studying new features of labour under socialism and for grasping the sources of value formation in a socialist market economy. Read the original if you want a compact survey of the classical, contemporary and philosophical antecedents of Marx's value theory, or a Chinese-language treatment of how these sources are linked to current debates on value under socialism.

The materialist conception of history running through Capital 《资本论》中贯穿的唯物主义历史观 Zhang Qiliang Zhang Qiliang asks how the materialist conception of history, which Marx developed from the 1840s onward, reached maturity in Capital. Zhang argues that earlier statements (the 1844 Manuscripts, the Theses on Feuerbach, The German Ideology and the 1859 Preface) remained at the level of a grand macro-narrative or, in Lenin's term, a theoretical "hypothesis". On this reading, only in Capital did it become a concrete, empirically grounded "science", and the article traces six principles of historical materialism that run through the work. The article first sketches the stages in the formation of Marx's historical outlook, then devotes six sections to paired principles. These are the objective and subjective dimensions of historical dialectics; truth and value; the people as makers of history; material productive forces as the driving force of society; means and ends; and conformity to law and conformity to value. Zhang draws on Capital throughout, and also on Hume, Kant and the Western philosophical split between scientism and humanism. Zhang contends that Capital unites an objective logic (the production and reproduction of material life, and the laws of surplus-value production, realisation and distribution) with a subjective logic aimed at the emancipation of the proletariat. Neglecting either side, Zhang says, leads to mechanical materialism or to idealism. Zhang holds that Marx resolved the truth–value opposition by treating them as two mutually conditioning yardsticks of practice. The people's subjectivity is said to be lost under class society, because the makers of history are not its masters, and to return as productive forces and workers' practical capacity develop. Productive forces are analysed through the labour process, the factors determining labour productivity and a three-stage periodisation of tools (hand tools, machines, automation). Zhang concludes that capitalism should be viewed dialectically. Its "civilising" side is an unprecedented growth of productive forces, but factory production sharpens its basic contradiction, and capitalism is not the end of history but a transient stage and the "prehistory" of humanity. Its replacement, however, is conditional and cannot happen at a stroke. Zhang adds that the unity of ends and means will be realised in a future association of free individuals, and that historical law operates within, not outside, human practice. Read the original if you want a systematic, textbook-style account of how Chinese Marxist philosophy reads the historical materialism of Capital through paired categories such as truth and value or means and ends.

C. J. Arthur's "new reading" of Capital and its theoretical flaws C.J.阿瑟对《资本论》的“新解读”及其理论症结 Zhou Luping Zhou Luping examines the "new dialectic" of Christopher J. Arthur, a leading figure of the European "New Dialectic" movement, as set out in Arthur's essay collection The New Dialectic and Marx's Capital (essays of 1993–2002). Zhou argues that Arthur uses Hegel's Logic to criticise rather than defend Capital, and that this feeds a Western current of "anti-Capital" thought which Chinese Marxists must answer. The article has three parts. The first reconstructs Arthur's "critical reading" on three fronts: the labour theory of value and the theory of surplus value, Marx's method, and the theory of proletarian revolution. The second contrasts Marx's route from abstract to concrete with Arthur's and identifies the "theoretical crux" of the new dialectic. The third assesses its content and limits, treating it as a variant of Hegelian dialectics. Zhou's central claim is that Arthur makes the value form the starting point and turns Capital into a "systematic dialectic" of concepts. In Zhou's account, Arthur inserts a "relation of concept to concept" into Marx's sequence, so that dialectics becomes a formal self-development of value cut off from history. Zhou says this replaces the labour theory of value with a theory of "socially necessary exploitation time", treats the Soviet experience as proof that revolution is impossible, and separates Marx's method of inquiry from his method of presentation. Zhou compares Arthur with Proudhon and judges Arthur's level lower, since he stays within exchange, commodities and money and never reaches the capital–wage-labour contradiction. Zhou concludes that Arthur over-philosophises Capital and weakens its critique of political economy, remaining a speculative, idealist reading. Against it Zhou sets Marx's historical dialectic and process dialectic, which aim to show the historical limits of capital and the way to supersede it. Zhou also criticises David Harvey for excluding the first three chapters. The article still recommends taking Arthur seriously, as a "negative example" for correcting the record. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist rebuttal of the New Dialectic and systematic-dialectic readings of Capital, or an example of how such Western work is received in China.

Engels's theoretical contributions to Marx's Capital 恩格斯对马克思《资本论》的理论贡献 Zhang Leisheng Marx's Capital is usually credited to Marx alone, but this article argues that Engels, as his close comrade and collaborator, made lasting contributions to its creation, development and publication. Zhang Leisheng sets aside Engels's editorial, financial and moral support to concentrate on his theoretical contributions, which the author says help readers grasp the essence of Capital and how it was written and developed. The article appeared in the Journal of Peking University (Philosophy and Social Sciences) in 2020. The article has three parts. The first treats Engels and the methodology of Capital, namely materialist dialectics. The second covers Engels's part in developing and completing Capital's theory: three rounds of correspondence with Marx from the 1850s to the 1860s, the revised editions of Volume I, and the editing of Volumes II and III. The third examines how Engels popularised and defended Capital, through reviews, plans for a popular outline and the rebuttal of attacks after Marx's death. On method, Zhang contends that Engels contributed in two ways. In the 1840s he and Marx reached historical materialism by different routes and applied dialectics to economics together. From the 1870s he then systematised materialist dialectics in Anti-Dühring, Dialectics of Nature and Ludwig Feuerbach and the End of Classical German Philosophy, after Marx had left no systematic account. On theory, Zhang shows Engels supplying Marx with factual material and views on rent, money circulation, crises and the turnover of fixed capital. He also criticised the structure of Volume I, and added notes, 37 passages to Volume II and over 80 passages to Volume III, plus appendices on the law of value and the stock exchange. On defence, the author describes nine reviews written to break the bourgeois 'conspiracy of silence', and Engels's refutation of the charge that Marx plagiarised Rodbertus on surplus value. Zhang concludes that Engels's work, in Lenin's words, makes the second and third volumes of Capital the work of both men. He holds that it also protected Marx's reputation and helped spread Marx's theory among the working class. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-based account of Engels's role in the writing, editing and defence of Capital, including the letters and reviews he wrote.

Some basic questions about the "sinicization of Marxism": reflections based on the Chinese Communist Party's centenary course “马克思主义中国化”若干基本问题——基于中国共产党百年历程的思考 Chen Peiyong Writing in the centenary year of the Chinese Communist Party (2021), Chen argues that the proposition of the "sinicization of Marxism" has been repeated so often that its background, substance and present value risk being forgotten. The article sets out to re-examine its meaning by answering five questions: why Marxism was a necessary choice for China, why it had to be sinicized, what sinicization actually is, how its theoretical results relate to one another, and how research on it can be deepened. The article moves through these five questions in turn. It begins with the claim that Marxism's arrival in China was a "choice of history", then turns to the origins of the proposition in Mao Zedong's 1938 report and the two errors it targeted. It then offers definitions and terminology, discusses three relationships among the theoretical achievements from Mao Zedong Thought to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, and ends with proposals for scholars. Chen contends that reading the "choice of history" as merely a correct choice for revolution wrongly implies that Marxism had only nominal guiding force after 1949. In the author's account, the choice was necessary because China had to escape the logic of capital and of hereditary privilege and find an independent path to modernization. Sinicization, in Chen's formulation, targets both dogmatism and empiricism, which still persist, for example in judging reform-era practice by isolated sentences from the classics. It has two sides: "transforming China" with Marxist methods, and "transforming Marxism" by developing theory and speaking in Chinese idiom. Chen distinguishes the process from its result, and a narrow sense of Marxism (Marx, Engels, Lenin) from a broad one that includes its Chinese forms. On this basis Chen holds that the question of whether Marxism is outdated reflects only the narrow sense. The article treats Mao Zedong Thought and the system of theory of socialism with Chinese characteristics as continuous rather than opposed. It notes the scholarly view that Xi's thought is a "third leap", and says whether to call it that depends on how China's historical position develops. Chen concludes that research on sinicization should aim to appreciate the governing wisdom of Communist Party members and the force of sinicized Marxist thought. Researchers should keep their academic independence, seek analytical depth rather than treating the material as merely political documents, and prefer constructive over critical or deconstructive logic. Scholarship should respond to China's real and theoretical problems rather than remain footnotes to the classics. Read the original if you want a Party-affiliated scholar's systematic account of how the sinicization of Marxism is defined and periodised, and of how its theoretical achievements are meant to relate to one another.

Capital and the theoretical themes of Marx's political philosophy 《资本论》与马克思政治哲学的理论主题 Fu Wenjun Fu Wenjun asks how Marx's critique of political economy relates to political philosophy. The article, a short commentary first printed in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in March 2021, argues that the two are not parallel lines but mutually connected sciences that support each other. Fu concludes that Marx's political philosophy has to be read out of the critique of political economy itself, and that doing so matters for research both on Capital and on Marx's political thought. The piece is organised in three parts. The first examines the political picture of the capitalist world that Capital draws. The second considers the political programme that Marx's critique offers. The third presents both the critique and the political philosophy as answers to the questions of the age and as sciences aimed at changing the world. Fu draws on Capital, the early writings and Leo Strauss's definition of political philosophy. Fu's central move is to read Capital as an account of capital's politics. Following the formula that political economy handles political affairs in an economic way, Fu holds that Marx identified economic power as the centre of oppression and, in the article's words, first raised the question of the political nature of the economy. Economic power replaced natural, divine and royal authority and rules through the "silent compulsion" of economic relations. Fu argues that the ideals of freedom, equality and justice serve capital's appropriation of surplus value. The root lies in the separation of labourers from the conditions of labour, so that capital is in essence command over unpaid labour. Fu then argues that Marx's political programme is the abolition of the state and civil society. It rests on the proletariat's association and on using capital itself to abolish capital, since capital is a historically transitory product whose self-negation the critique traces. Fu concludes that, in Marx, both the critique and political philosophy start from human society and real individuals and speak for the proletariat. Both draw on philosophy, politics, economics, history and sociology, and both aim at changing the world and building a new one. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese statement of the view that Capital contains a political philosophy centred on economic power and its abolition.

The social-historical dimension of Engels's view of nature 恩格斯自然观的社会历史向度 Zhu Chunyan Western Marxists such as Lukács, Alfred Schmidt and Norman Levine, Zhu Chunyan notes, read Marx's philosophy as a dialectic of history and Engels's as a dialectic of nature, and so produced the thesis of an opposition between Marx and Engels. This short article in a Chinese newspaper argues the opposite. Zhu contends that Engels, like Marx, always examined nature inside the course of human history, so that his view of nature has a marked social-historical dimension. The article follows Engels's work in three stages. It begins with his early observation of the industrial revolution in the Wupper valley and England, then turns to the decade from 1873 to 1883, when he studied natural science while writing Anti-Dühring and the materials of Dialectics of Nature. It ends with the later formulations in the introduction to Dialectics of Nature and in "The Part Played by Labour in the Transition from Ape to Man". Zhu's central claim is that three paired ideas run through Engels's thought: two "reconciliations", two "elevations" and two "influences". The first is the reconciliation of humanity with nature and of humanity with itself, which Engels linked to abolishing private property. The two elevations are the biological one from ape to human through labour, and a future social one in which people master their social relations. The two influences are the more remote effects of production on nature and on society.
