According to Zhu, Engels's study of natural science had a critical aim, against Dühring's distortion of Hegelian dialectics and Büchner's vulgar materialism and social Darwinism. It also had a constructive aim, which was to unify natural history and human history. Zhu argues that Engels held that foreseeing the social consequences of production is harder than foreseeing the natural ones. On this reading, it requires a complete transformation of the mode of production and the whole social system. Zhu concludes that the Marx–Engels opposition thesis can be answered only by placing Engels's dialectics of nature in the historical development of Marxism and examining the Marx–Engels relationship as a whole. The article adds that since the 1960s, with the environmental crisis, Engels's contribution has won growing recognition in the West. It also says that ecological civilization construction under socialism with Chinese characteristics is putting his ideas into practice. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese-language account of how Engels's early writings on industrial society connect to his later philosophy of nature, and of the case against Western Marxist readings.

Solidly promoting common prosperity for all the people 扎实推动全体人民共同富裕 Xiao Hongchun Wang Ningning This commentary in the Economic Daily (January 2021) interprets the Fifth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2020). The plenum made "more notable substantive progress toward common prosperity for all the people" part of the 2035 goal of basically achieving socialist modernization. The authors argue that this wording is a first for a plenum document. In their view it sets a direction while balancing what is needed with what is possible. The piece has three numbered sections. The first presents common prosperity as an essential requirement of socialism and cites the victory in poverty alleviation as its foundation. It also names remaining problems: uneven development, urban–rural and regional gaps, and weaknesses in people's livelihood. The second sets out principles. The third lists areas for action. The authors stress that common prosperity is a long-term, gradual historical process. They link this to the primary stage of socialism and say it does not mean simultaneous or equal wealth, so some people will get rich first and then help others. They name high-quality development, guided by the new development philosophy, as the key. They also say the cake must be made bigger and then divided well. For future work the authors propose three measures. The first is a long-term mechanism against relative poverty, including monitoring to prevent a return to poverty and links to rural revitalization. The second is stronger scientific and technological innovation. The third is improving the socialist distribution system: distribution according to work as the main form, a higher labour share in primary distribution, and a larger role for tertiary distribution. Read the original if you want a concise early statement of the official policy reasoning behind common prosperity as it entered Party planning.

Solidly promoting common prosperity for all the people 扎实推动全体人民共同富裕 Xiao Hongchun Wang Ningning Writing in the Economic Daily in January 2021, Xiao and Wang comment on the Fifth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2020), which listed 'more notable substantive progress toward common prosperity for all the people' among the goals for basically realising socialist modernization by 2035. The authors argue that the wording gives a clear direction while remaining realistic, balancing what is needed with what is possible. The piece has three numbered parts. The first presents common prosperity as an essential requirement of socialism and cites the poverty-alleviation campaign since the 18th Party Congress (2012) as its foundation. It also lists remaining problems. The second explains the principles and path. The third sets out three areas for action. In the authors' account, common prosperity is a long-term historical process, not simultaneous or equal enrichment, because China is in the primary stage of socialism. Some people must get rich first and help others later. The key, they argue, is high-quality development under the new development philosophy and supply-side structural reform. They also stress that the cake must be made bigger and divided well, with more income for low earners and a larger middle-income group. The authors call for a long-term mechanism against relative poverty, linked to rural revitalisation. They also call for stronger scientific and technological innovation, and for a distribution system in which distribution according to labour is primary, labour's share of primary distribution rises and the 'third distribution' counts for more. Read the original if you want a short, officially aligned reading of how the 2020 plenum framed common prosperity before the topic's later prominence.

The collapse of neoliberal myths and the direction of Western capitalism's evolution 新自由主义迷思的破灭与西方资本主义的演变方向 Wang Pengquan Writing in 2020, Wang Pengquan asks what the Western response to COVID-19 reveals about neoliberalism and where Western capitalism is heading. The article argues that neoliberalism survived the 2008 financial crisis and even intensified, but that the pandemic has now exposed its inner flaws and broken its main myths. In Wang's view this makes a transformation of Western capitalism urgent. The article first sketches neoliberalism's rise after the Keynesian order broke down in the 1960s and 1970s. It then takes three myths in turn: market fundamentalism, extreme individualism and the illusion of "common prosperity" under capitalism. The evidence comes mainly from the United States and Europe, and Wang draws on Henry Giroux, Noam Chomsky, Jeremy Gilbert and others. A final section sets out three expected features of capitalism's evolution. Wang argues that decades of privatisation, austerity and deregulation hollowed out public health systems and medical supply capacity, so that the claim that markets outperform the state failed in the pandemic. Extreme individualism, in this account, serves to blame individuals for failures of the system and to dissolve the collective solidarity that could resist capital. Citing wage, household-finance, unemployment and racial-disparity figures, the article contends that the 2008 bailouts deepened inequality and that the pandemic fell hardest on workers and ethnic minorities. Wang then predicts that capitalism will change faster, rebalancing government, capital and society. Left-wing thought and movements will gain influence, and non-Western experience, above all China's, will become a reference point. Wang concludes that the pandemic confirms the "two inevitables" of Marxism, namely that capitalism will perish and socialism will triumph, and calls for stronger the Four-sphere Confidence. The author also urges close attention to how Western capitalism changes, so that positive elements can be used to build a community with a shared future for mankind and risks to China's external environment can be averted. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist scholar read the pandemic as the end of neoliberal legitimacy and drew conclusions about Western capitalism's course.

Europe's reshaping in the post-pandemic era and the strategy of the Left 后疫情时代的欧洲重塑与左翼战略 Walter Baier This text is a Chinese translation of an article by the Austrian economist Walter Baier, a former chair of the Austrian Communist Party and coordinator of the European left network Transform! Europe. Written in 2020, it asks what the Covid-19 crisis means for European integration and what strategy the European Left should adopt. Baier argues that the pandemic did not cause but accelerated the factors that will shape global development, including the end of unilateral US hegemony. He holds that it exposed structural flaws in the EU and that the Left must use the crisis to contest social hegemony. The article has five parts. It begins with the EU's failed pandemic response, then turns to the coming recession, debt and the left's economic options. It next traces the conflict between market integration and democratic, politically planned integration from the 1951 Coal and Steel Community to Greece in 2015. Later sections cover Brexit and the limits of EU-centred pan-Europeanism, and Europe's place in the world, including relations with the United States, Russia and China. Baier contends that EU treaties require member states to maintain social and health systems while the Stability and Growth Pact limits their finances. In his account, integration has advanced mainly through the market, from the Single European Act to the Maastricht and Lisbon treaties, and has repeatedly overridden democratic and social aims. He argues that the debt burden will deepen inequality between strong and weak states. He proposes abolishing the Pact, using the ECB, the European Investment Bank and the European Stability Mechanism to fund national social and ecological programmes, and imposing capital controls and taxes on wealth and capital gains. He also calls for putting banking and finance under social ownership, rather than relying on austerity and privatisation. He treats the nation state as the Left's basic source of strength and calls for a sovereign, freely elected European Parliament to replace the European Council as the EU's decision-making centre. Baier concludes that Europe should reject a hostile, US-aligned stance towards China, which he notes is the EU's largest trading partner, and should treat cooperation with China as an opportunity. He adds that the European Left, which he says cannot fully endorse China's ideological model, should still work to rebuild international cooperation structures and reduce the risk of nuclear arms races. He presents the opening created by the crisis as temporary, lasting only until Europe's ruling classes reach a consensus. Read the original if you want a democratic-socialist European perspective on EU integration, debt and the post-pandemic order, published in a Chinese foreign-Marxism outlet.

Characteristics and development trends of the American left in the post-crisis era 论后危机时代美国左翼思潮的特征及发展趋势 Pei Shaohua Pei Shaohua asks what marks left-wing thought in the United States after the 2008 financial crisis and where it is heading. Writing in 2020, Pei treats the crisis as an outbreak of capitalism's inherent contradictions and in essence a crisis of the capitalist system. The article argues that the American left is becoming more varied, more oriented towards practice and more favourable to socialism. Pei also holds that its pragmatist cultural roots limit it, and that it needs Marxist theory, a strong party and thorough revolution. The article has three parts. The first identifies three features of the post-crisis American left, drawing mainly on the annual New York left forum. The second traces the cultural roots of this thought to American pragmatism, citing James, Peirce and Dewey and the forum's yearly themes from 2013 to 2019. The third sets out development trends, using the history of American socialism and passages from Marx, Engels and Lenin. On the three features, Pei says eco-socialism, democratic socialism, feminist socialism and Marxism overlap and converge, because each answers the crisis and most point towards socialism. Pei calls democratic socialism a form of the 'petty-bourgeois socialism' that Marx and Engels criticised. Groups at the forum are also trying to turn ideas into action by forming an independent left party, and Bernie Sanders's 2016 campaign is cited as reviving interest in socialism. Pei argues that pragmatism's 'what is useful is true' outlook shapes these demands. It treats ideas as instruments and practice as isolated individual acts, so the left's aims are unlikely to be met given its unclear aims, disunited theory and uncoordinated action. Pei concludes that the American left must be guided by Marxist theory, build a 'strong party' that truly represents the proletariat, and carry out thorough revolution. Pei rejects the hope of change through peaceful movements and elections, citing the suppression of Occupy Wall Street. The article cites a survey in which 40 per cent of Americans would prefer to live in a socialist country, and reads this as a favourable sign. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist scholar assesses the US left, using the New York left forum as evidence, and where Pei thinks it falls short.

Setbacks and reorganisation: a study of South Korean left-wing currents in the twenty-first century 挫折与重组:21世纪韩国左翼思潮研究 Jiao Pei Jiao Pei asks how left-wing thought in South Korea has been reorganised since 2000, after the setbacks that followed the collapse of the Soviet bloc and the Asian financial crisis. The article, published in 2020, treats South Korea as a representative case of a medium-sized, late-developing, export-oriented capitalist country with a Confucian cultural background. Jiao argues that neoliberal reform produced new contradictions, and that left currents regrouped around them, with radical currents likely to fade and Marxist theory likely to regain attention. The article has three parts. The first describes two features of Korean capitalism after 1997: 'monopoly under freedom' and 'extreme poverty amid prosperity'. The second surveys four currents: Trotskyism, 'liquidationism', the New Left and basic income theory, each tied to a representative scholar and to protest movements. The third forecasts the left's future under artificial intelligence and trade protectionism. Jiao relies on Korean statistics on employment, concentration, household debt and welfare spending. On the economy, Jiao argues that deregulation after 1998 strengthened the chaebol rather than weakening them. Easier dismissal and agency labour fragmented workers, and the article cites figures on youth employment, temporary work and the 40 per cent share of irregular workers in 57 large firms in 2017. Jiao presents the four currents as responses to these conditions. Trotskyism, represented by Jung Seong-jin, holds that crisis is unavoidable and calls for a break with the bourgeoisie. Liquidationism, represented by Lee Jin-kyung, rejects Soviet socialism and proposes 'communalism'; Jiao calls it utopian and destructive without construction. The New Left, represented by Cho Dae-yeop and Jung Chul-hee, replaces class analysis with civil-society movements; Jiao says it is broad but struggles to move beyond joint demonstrations. Basic income theory, represented by Kang Nam-hoon, is presented as the most concrete programme, with the 2018 Child Allowance Act as a first step. Jiao concludes that Trotskyism and liquidationism will fade as AI marginalises simple labour and protectionism weakens international labour cooperation. The New Left will deepen its work in feminist, environmental, disability and sexual-minority fields. Jiao expects the theory and method of scientific socialism to regain importance, pointing to the Korean translation of the Marx–Engels collected works from 2012. Jiao ends with the image of the traditional labour movement as the tide, the new movements as waves and the AI-driven technological revolution as a whirlpool. Read the original if you want a detailed Chinese-language survey of Korean left currents, with Korean data and names, written from within Chinese Marxist scholarship.

Recent developments in radical left social movements in Europe and the United States 当前欧美激进左翼社会运动的发展动态 Li Xiaoling Writing in 2021, Li Xiaoling asks why radical left social movements in Europe and the United States have surged since the 2008 financial crisis, what marks them, and why they achieve so little. The article argues that explosive inequality under neoliberal finance-monopoly capitalism fuels the protests. In Li's view, the movements are held back by right-wing pressure, internal division and loose organisation, and their most viable path is a pan-left united front led by the working class. The article has four parts. It begins with the background of inequality, using US data on income shares, the pandemic-era growth of billionaire wealth, and European figures on income growth, poverty and exclusion. It then surveys the movements themselves: Occupy Wall Street, the 2017 women's marches, the George Floyd protests, European anti-austerity strikes, and the "yellow vests" in France. A third part sets out the obstacles, and a fourth the likely direction of development. Li identifies three features of the movements: frequent, large and widely spreading protests; a plural range of participants and demands; and networked mobilisation through social media. The author argues that class discourse (Greek strikes, US teachers' strikes) now coexists with identity discourse (Black Lives Matter, #MeToo), after the earlier "new social movements" had moved away from class struggle. Li then explains the constraints. Right-wing populism is in the ascendant, citing the defeats of Corbyn, Tsipras and Sanders, and left parties have drifted from the working class since the "Third Way". The movements also lack a unifying Marxist ideology, are non-violent and organised only loosely online, and offer no constructive alternative to neoliberalism. Li concludes that movements confined to narrow issues or street protest cannot change the existing order. The author calls for a pan-left united front led by the working class, which is described as a large, internally stratified group of wage earners swelled by the "re-proletarianisation" of the middle class. It would ally with groups subject to special oppression, such as women, ethnic minorities, LGBTQ people and the disabled, and would need class consciousness built through workers' struggles. Li holds that the historical trend towards socialism replacing capitalism will not change. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist academic reading of Western left protest, with data, case examples and a view on the left's strategic prospects.

Mao Zedong and the opening of a new path for the Chinese revolution A dialogue with Professor Sha Jiansun 毛泽东与中国革命新道路的开辟 Li Yuanpeng This is a dialogue, published for the centenary of the Communist Party of China in 2021, between Li Yuanpeng, an associate professor at Guizhou Normal University, and Sha Jiansun, a professor at Peking University's School of Marxism. It builds on Sha's 1983 essay and his 2016 book on Mao Zedong and the opening of the new revolutionary path in the Agrarian Revolutionary War period. Sha's central claim is that Mao was the chief representative of a collective effort that opened the road of encircling the cities from the countryside and seizing power by armed force, and that this road was the only correct one after 1927. Li, who raised the questions while teaching the course Outline of Modern Chinese History, organises the exchange into six topics. They are the definition of the new path; the Party's exploration after the failure of the Great Revolution in 1927; Mao's role; his creative solutions to problems of sustaining rural base areas; the path's significance for the formation of Mao Zedong Thought; and its link to the revival and victory of the revolution through to 1949. On definition, Sha holds that the path has two defining features: protracted revolutionary war as the main form of struggle, and the countryside first, cities later, as the main direction of attack. He therefore judges formulas such as "the road of red political power" or "armed independent regime of workers and peasants" imprecise. On Mao's role, Sha stresses that the path came from the collective wisdom of Party and people, not from one genius. He still credits Mao with early commitment to armed struggle and to the countryside, and with solving problems the classics could not answer. These included building a proletarian party with a peasant membership through ideological work (the Gutian Resolution), shaping a people's army, devising guerrilla strategy and tactics, and framing a land policy of relying on poor peasants and redistributing land by population. Sha argues that this path, much of it contrary to Comintern instructions, shows Chinese communists learning to think independently and combine Marxism with Chinese practice, which makes it a marker of Mao Zedong Thought's formation. He ties this to Mao's essay Oppose Book Worship, which he reads as an early statement of seeking truth from facts, the mass line and independence. The dialogue closes by tracing the path through the War of Resistance and the civil war to the 1949 shift of emphasis to the cities. Read the original if you want a Party-historian's detailed account of how the "countryside encircling the cities" strategy is defined, periodised and credited to Mao within official historiography.

Lenin's theory of strategy and tactics in the socialist movement and its lessons 列宁关于社会主义运动战略与策略的理论与启示 Zhou Miao Writing in 2021, Zhou Miao asks what Lenin's theory of strategy and tactics in the socialist movement can offer at a time of what Chinese official discourse calls great changes unseen in a century, a period the author says the Covid-19 pandemic has accelerated. The article argues that Lenin greatly developed the Marxist theory of strategy and tactics, and that studying it helps China and the world socialist movement keep strategic focus, think strategically and plan accordingly. The article begins with the background: sharpening contradictions in monopoly capitalism, the growth of bourgeois strategic theory, and the earlier work of Marx and Engels, who Zhou says treated strategy as the overall line of the proletarian party and tactics as the concrete means of carrying it out. It then sets out five areas of Lenin's thought: his distinction between strategy and tactics, the analysis of the epoch as the premise of policy, firmness of principle combined with tactical flexibility, internationalism, and the consolidation of Soviet power. A final section draws lessons for present-day China. Zhou's central claims are that Lenin made accurate judgement of the era and of the balance of class forces the basis of strategy, rather than revolutionary sentiment alone. On this basis Lenin proposed that socialism could win first in one country, and later that the fate of world revolution depended on Russia, India, China and other eastern countries. After 1917, the author says, Lenin urged shifting the focus to construction, learning from advanced capitalist civilisation, using divisions among enemies, and winning even temporary and unreliable allies, while rejecting opportunist compromise. Zhou draws three lessons for the present. First, Marxism should guide a clear reading of the era, and Xi Jinping's judgement on great changes unseen in a century is presented as continuing this tradition. Second, the Party should keep the whole picture in view, through the two overall situations, strategic thinking and the bottom-line approach. Third, it should unite all forces that can be united, including through the Belt and Road Initiative and a community with a shared future for mankind, with communist and left parties supporting China's modernization. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist scholar links Lenin's strategic writings to current Party discourse on strategy and the international situation.

How the US Party for Socialism and Liberation understands the Communist Party of China's century of struggle 美国“争取社会主义和解放党”对中国共产党百年奋斗史的认识 Zhong Daobang Writing in 2021, the centenary year of the Communist Party of China (CPC), Zhong examines how the Party for Socialism and Liberation (PSL), a US left-wing party founded in 2004, reads the CPC's hundred years of struggle. The article argues that the PSL is friendly towards the CPC and that its views, though containing some correct judgements, also show shortcomings. Zhong holds that the views deserve attention from Chinese scholars as the voice of a foreign communist party. The article draws on the PSL's newspaper Liberation, which Zhong says carries more than thirty articles on China, and on its 2012 book China: Revolution and Counterrevolution. Zhong arranges the material in four themes: the democratic revolution; development achievements in the Mao Zedong era and the period of reform and opening up; the CPC's role in national security, including disasters and the Covid-19 response; and China's place in the world. A fifth section assesses the PSL's outlook. In Zhong's account, the PSL holds that only the working-class party could lead China's revolution, and that the 1949 victory was among the greatest events of the international communist movement. It credits the CPC's leadership with socialist transformation, growth, scientific progress and effective disaster response, and contrasts these with US performance. It also argues that US imperialism seeks to undermine the CPC, and that China, having risen from a plundered world, is not a member of an "imperialist club" but a source of help for Third World countries. Zhong's assessment praises the PSL's aim of demonstrating socialism's superiority, its holistic and historical method, and its international comparisons. Zhong faults it for suggesting that reforms have a capitalist character, for overlooking the CPC's role in institution-building, national governance and rule of law, and for superficial explanations that credit the socialist system without examining how the Party builds its capacity. Zhong attributes these gaps to limited knowledge of post-reform China and to mechanical reliance on classical texts. Zhong concludes that the PSL's endorsement shows recognition of the CPC among communist and workers' parties in capitalist countries. Zhong therefore calls for firmly upholding CPC leadership and the socialist road, and for rebutting attacks on them. Zhong adds that telling China's story abroad remains a long task, because misreadings of socialism with Chinese characteristics persist, and calls for more communication with foreign workers' parties. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic view of how a small US Marxist party portrays China, or a sample of how Chinese scholars now treat overseas leftist commentary on the CPC.

The Communist Party of China's source of strength and guarantee of victory 中国共产党的力量源泉与胜利保障 Xue Guangzhou Published in Red Flag Manuscripts and posted in June 2021, shortly before the Party's centenary, this commentary asks why the Communist Party of China won the whole country within 28 years and has since achieved what the author calls world-renowned successes over more than seven decades. Xue Guangzhou answers that the Party's strength and guarantee of victory rest on three things: holding to a lofty faith, forming a correct ideological line, and forging a strong ranks of members through strict Party discipline. The article is organised in three sections matching these answers. It moves through the Party's history, from the 1921 first programme, the Long March and the Korean War to reform and opening up and the period after the 18th Party Congress (2012). It draws on statements by Mao Zedong, Li Dazhao and Xi Jinping, and on Marxist classics concerning the proletarian party. On faith, Xue argues that the Party's fate is tied to that of the broad masses, and that, unlike bourgeois parties serving a minority, it serves the great majority. Conviction carried Party members through the defeat of the Great Revolution, the losses on the Long March and the Korean War, and Xue attributes the fall of some officials in the reform era to a failure of faith. On the ideological line, the author holds that integrating Marxism's universal principles with Chinese practice produced the line of seeking truth from facts, which Xue credits with the revolution, socialist transformation and reform, and sees continued in Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. On Party building, Xue traces a tradition of strictness from the first programme through democratic centralism, rectification campaigns and the "two musts", to the eight-point regulations, anti-corruption drive and Party regulations of the Xi era. Xue concludes that full and rigorous self-governance of the Party must continue, because the "four tests" and "four dangers" remain serious and impurities in thought, politics, organisation and style are not yet fundamentally solved. The author calls for strengthening the Four Consciousnesses, the Four-sphere Confidence and the Two Upholds, and for making officials neither dare, nor be able, nor want to be corrupt. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Party commentary around the 2021 centenary framed the sources of the Party's success.

The Communist Party of China and Chinese modernization 中国共产党与中国式现代化 Qin Xuan Published in the People's Daily around the Party's centenary in 2021, this commentary asks how the Communist Party of China relates to the country's modernization. Qin Xuan argues that the Party opened China's modernization drive at a moment of national crisis, shaped Chinese modernization through generations of exploration, and must be upheld and strengthened in its overall leadership if the project of building a modern socialist country is to succeed. The piece has three parts. It first reviews the failed attempts at national salvation before 1921, then traces the Party's exploration of a modernization path from Mao Zedong through Deng Xiaoping to the present, and finally turns to the tasks of the new journey set out at the 19th Party Congress (2017) and the Fifth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2020). Qin's central move is a historical argument by elimination. The Taiping movement, the Self-Strengthening Movement, the 1898 reforms, the 1911 Revolution and various copies of Western political models all failed, in the author's account, to complete the tasks of national salvation and anti-imperialism. Marxism-Leninism, brought by the October Revolution, supplied the direction, and the Party then founded the People's Republic. Qin presents Chinese modernization as a path rooted in China yet open to the world, which has moved China from lagging behind the times to catching up with and leading them. The author cites its status as the second-largest economy and the largest manufacturing country, and holds that it shows the Western route is not the only road to modernization. Qin concludes that a modernization of enormous population, common prosperity, balanced material and cultural progress, harmony with nature and peaceful development needs a leading core, which in contemporary China can only be the Party. The author calls for strengthening the Party through the Party's self-reform and full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, for deriving theory from this experience to enrich Marxist modernization theory, and for realising the 2035 and mid-century goals. Read the original if you want a concise example of the official People's Daily narrative that links the Party's history, Chinese modernization and Party leadership.

Summing up historical experience and strengthening historical resolve 总结历史经验 增强历史定力 He Xinyuan Published in Red Flag Manuscript around the centenary of the Communist Party of China in 2021, this commentary asks what lessons the Party's hundred years of revolution, construction and reform offer for the present. He Xinyuan argues that the Party's history is a "textbook" and "nutrient", and that studying it strengthens the resolve needed to build a modern socialist country and achieve the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The piece is organised around five lessons, each introduced by a short heading: having faith and turning it into a spirit of struggle; being guided by scientific theory and innovating in theory; doing everything for the people and relying on them; correcting mistakes through self-reform; and being responsible as a major country. Each lesson is illustrated with episodes from the revolutionary, socialist-construction and reform periods, and tied to remarks by Xi Jinping at the Party history study and education mobilisation meeting. He contends that faith in Marxism and communism has sustained the Party through defeats, the Long March, the "two bombs and one satellite" programme and reform, and has produced a "spiritual lineage" of revolutionary spirit. The author reads the Party's theory as a continuous process of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, from Mao Zedong Thought to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. On the people, He holds that popular support decides the Party's survival, and that its errors were errors of exploration, corrected in time because of a healthy force within the Party. On international responsibility, He lists the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence, Deng Xiaoping's judgement on peace and development, a community with a shared future for mankind, and the Belt and Road Initiative. He concludes that the Party should keep Marxism as its guide, innovate in practice and theory, stay close to the people and pursue common prosperity. He also calls on Party members, including senior cadres, to keep a revolutionary drive and the Party's self-reform so that praise and success do not breed complacency. Read the original if you want a compact example of how the official narrative of the Party's centenary summarised its "historical experience" for a general Party readership.

A century of the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context 马克思主义中国化的百年发展 Shang Zhixiao Written for the centenary of the Communist Party in 2021, this article asks how the Sinification of Marxism ran through the Party's hundred years and what lessons it offers for the future. Shang Zhixiao opens with Xi Jinping's March 2021 remarks in Fujian on why the Party, Marxism and socialism with Chinese characteristics "work". The author argues that the Party's history is a history of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, and that this process runs through every stage of that history. The piece has three parts. The first traces Marxism's adaptation across four periods: the new-democratic revolution, socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The second surveys the theoretical results: Mao Zedong Thought, Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents, the Scientific Outlook on Development, and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The third sets out lessons for the next stage. Shang presents the adaptation of Marxism as a response to the problem of applying a theory born in Western Europe to a semi-colonial, semi-feudal China. Earlier eighty-odd years of struggle had failed, in the author's account, for lack of both a lasting organisation and sound theory. The article quotes Mao's 1930 "Oppose Book Worship" and his 1938 formulation of "the Sinification of Marxism", and describes the "second integration" of Marxism-Leninism with Chinese reality after 1949. Each leadership generation, Shang says, summarised practice into a systematic theory, so that Marxism changed China and China enriched Marxism. For the next stage, Shang calls for three things: a full and accurate grasp of Marxist standpoint and method, especially dialectical and historical materialism; an understanding of China's basic national conditions in light of the times; and firm struggle against dogmatism and empiricism, described as the great enemies of the process. The article closes by saying theory's vitality lies in continual innovation, and calls for developing contemporary Chinese Marxism and twenty-first-century Marxism. Read the original if you want a concise, Party-line periodisation of the Sinification of Marxism, written for the 2021 centenary.

The Communist Party of China's century of experience in advancing national modernization 中国共产党推进国家现代化建设的百年历史经验 Zhang Shihai Writing in the year of the Party's centenary (2021), Zhang Shihai asks what lessons can be drawn from the Communist Party of China's hundred years of work on national modernization. The author argues that the Party's history is, in a sense, a history of exploring and building modernization, and that this record has produced five basic lessons. These lessons are presented as the basis for continuing to build a modern socialist country. The article is a short Red Flag Manuscripts essay organised around five headings. It first traces how the Party's modernization goals evolved across four periods: revolutionary war, the early People's Republic, reform and opening up, and the era since the 18th Party Congress (2012). It then takes up the people-centred standpoint, the political line, phased goal-setting and the Party's own modernization. A brief closing passage addresses the international significance of the Chinese path. Zhang's central claim is that the Party's success rests on a few consistent practices. One is that it has treated modernization as a strategic task throughout, moving from industrialization to the "four modernizations", then to "Chinese modernization" in the reform era, and to a "modern socialist country" since 2012. Another is that it has held to a people-centred position, with the people as the "supreme judge" of results, and to a correct basic line described as the "lifeline" of Party and state. The author also stresses stepwise planning, from the two-step revolution and two-step construction plans to the three-step strategy and the 19th Party Congress (2017) timetable of basic modernization by 2035 and a fully built modern socialist country by mid-century. Finally, Zhang argues that the Party must modernize itself through self-reform, because a ruling party's capacity largely determines whether a country modernizes. Zhang concludes that the Chinese path offers developing countries a new model, gives practical vitality to scientific socialism and contributes a Chinese approach to global governance. Facing complex domestic and international challenges, the author calls for adherence to these lessons and unwavering effort to build a modern socialist country. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official Party-history narrative on modernization, as it was framed around the 2021 centenary.

The leadership of the Communist Party of China is the choice of history and the people 中国共产党的领导是历史和人民的选择 Yin Hanning Published on the eve of the Party's centenary in 2021, this commentary argues that the leadership of the Communist Party of China is the choice of Chinese history and the Chinese people, not an accident. Yin Hanning holds that practice has already proved this and will continue to do so. The author presents deepening this understanding as a way to strengthen popular confidence in following the Party as the country begins a new journey toward building a modern socialist country and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The article has three parts. The first reviews the political models China tried after the Opium War of 1840 and the 1911 Revolution. The second rebuts the view that the Nationalist government's 1927–1937 decade was a 'golden decade' that could have led to capitalist modernization. The third traces the Party's role from its founding in 1921 through the Northern Expedition, the land revolution, the War of Resistance against Japan and the civil war, drawing on Xi Jinping and Mao Zedong. Yin argues that constitutional monarchy, imperial restorations, parliamentary government, a multiparty system and a presidential system each failed, citing the Qing constitutional documents, the assassination of Song Jiaoren and the 682 groups formed by the end of 1913. Against the 'golden decade' thesis, the author offers five points: history cannot be hypothesised, China remained semi-colonial and semi-feudal, the Nationalist regime faced warlord fragmentation and civil war, the national bourgeoisie was too weak to complete the old-democratic revolution, and Western political models had lost credibility. As evidence, Yin notes that 15 of 16 essays in a 1933 Shen Bao discussion favoured socialist or non-capitalist paths. The author concludes that after these failures, history and the people chose the Party, which gave the struggle for national independence and liberation its 'backbone'. Yin credits it with leading the anti-Japanese united front and, after Chiang Kai-shek's regime lost popular support, founding the People's Republic. The article states that this choice was correct and must be upheld long-term and without wavering. Read the original if you want an example of how a senior Party theorist uses the history of the Republican period to justify the Party's leadership.

The Communist Party of China and China's fine traditional culture 中国共产党与中华优秀传统文化 Jiang Yihua Writing in 2021, the centenary year of the Communist Party of China (CPC), Jiang Yihua asks how the Party has related to China's fine traditional culture over its hundred years. Jiang argues that the Party has combined the basic tenets of Marxism with China's concrete realities, with the development of the times and with that culture. By excavating, inheriting and promoting its essence, the Party is said to have unlocked the culture's inner dynamism and raised it to a new historical level. The article is a Red Flag Manuscripts essay opening with Xi Jinping's call for 'creative transformation and innovative development' of traditional culture. It is organised around four features of the Party's century: putting the people first, seeking truth from facts, staying true to the original aspiration, and applying materialist dialectics. Each section pairs a traditional idea, often quoted from the Xunzi, the Book of Documents, the Laozi or Mencius, with episodes from Party history. On the first point, Jiang argues that the classical ideas of benevolence and the people as the foundation of the state were carried through fully only by the CPC. The author contrasts the Party with the late Qing and Republican societies and parties, which are said to have failed to trust, mobilise and serve the people, and credits the liberation of hundreds of millions of peasants as the source of Party strength. On seeking truth from facts, Jiang points to two turning points, the shift to the countryside after 1927 and the post-Cultural Revolution reform and opening up. On staying true to the original aspiration, Jiang cites traditional awareness of hardship and danger, and describes Party membership screening, democratic centralism, cadre selection by 'virtue first' and anti-corruption mechanisms as an institutional system of self-correction. Materialist dialectics is presented as the method that gave traditional ideas such as the golden mean a scientific character. Jiang concludes that the Party's successes rest on these four commitments, which let it lead the nation from standing up to becoming prosperous and then strong. The essay presents the Party as continuing to open a new era for traditional culture and describes its record as a victory for Marxism and materialist dialectics. Read the original if you want an example of how a Party-affiliated historian frames the centenary narrative through traditional Chinese culture.

The people are the country 人民就是江山 Chen Xiangjian Writing in the centenary year of the Communist Party of China (2021), Chen Xiangjian takes up Xi Jinping's formulation "the people are the country" (人民就是江山), which Xi stressed in speeches that year, including during a May 2021 inspection in Henan. Chen argues that the phrase is significant in two ways. It is a deep summation of the Marxist view of the masses, and it is a solemn declaration of the Party's mass line. The article is a short commentary in two parts. The first part collects a long series of Xi's statements, from the Party's mass-line education campaign through the Long March anniversary, the 40th anniversary of reform and opening up, the fight against COVID-19 and poverty alleviation. Chen presents them as the new-era expression of the Marxist view of the masses and as the point of Xi's "people-centred" development thinking. The second part organises the argument around the three questions of the mass line: for whom, on whom to rely, and who we are. On "for whom", Chen reads the Party's century of struggle as the pursuit of the people's happiness, from the Party's founding through the founding of New China to reform and opening up and the new era. On "on whom to rely", Chen sets the historical-materialist view that the people create history against the idealist view of heroes. The author lists the people's role in the Great Revolution, the Red Army years, the War of Resistance, the Huai-Hai and Yangtze crossing campaigns, and socialist construction. The conclusion is that the Party does not claim credit for itself but attributes every achievement to the people. On "who we are", Chen cites the Party constitution describing the Party as the vanguard of the working class, the Chinese people and the Chinese nation. Chen adds that China's socialist state, in which all power belongs to the people, is a "people's country" in essence and differs fundamentally from one founded on private ownership. Chen concludes that the Party must never separate itself from the masses and must keep the people at the highest place in its heart. Quoting Xi, the article says this means making the fruits of development reach all more fairly, advancing common prosperity, and uniting 1.4 billion people for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Party commentary in 2021 tied Xi's "people" language to the mass line and to Marxist historical materialism.

A century of the Communist Party of China inheriting and promoting China's fine traditional culture 中国共产党继承与弘扬中华优秀传统文化的百年历史考察 Deng Haiying Deng Haiying asks how the Communist Party of China has treated the nation's traditional culture over roughly a hundred years of revolution, construction and reform. The article, published in 2020, argues that Party members are Marxists rather than historical or cultural nihilists, and that the Party has consistently been a faithful inheritor and firm promoter of China's fine traditional culture. The article is a chronological survey in four stages: the revolutionary war years; the early People's Republic; the period of reform and opening up; and the years since the 18th Party Congress (2012). For each stage Deng draws on leaders' statements, policy documents and regulations, institutional measures and concrete cases of protecting cultural relics, theatre, medicine, script and ethnic minority cultures. For the revolutionary period, Deng stresses Mao Zedong's insistence that history must not be severed, and his principle of "taking the essence and discarding the dross", which Liu Shaoqi echoed at the Seventh Party Congress. Deng also cites wartime relic-protection rules and episodes such as the rescue of the Zhaocheng Jin Canon and the peaceful liberation of Beiping. After 1949 the Party kept the line of critical inheritance, expressed in the "Hundred Flowers, Hundred Schools" policy and the maxim "making the past serve the present". Deng describes reform of opera, support for traditional medicine and the simplification of Chinese characters, while acknowledging that the Anti-Rightist campaign, the Great Leap Forward and above all the Cultural Revolution's attack on the "Four Olds" broke this continuity. Deng presents the reform era as a re-evaluation: the Party corrected "Leftist" errors, then linked traditional culture to socialist modernization, the primary stage of socialism and soft power. Since 2012, in Deng's account, the Party under Xi Jinping has taken unprecedented steps. These include Politburo study sessions, Xi's 2014 speech at the Confucius anniversary conference, large-scale cataloguing and heritage protection, wider public access to museums, new media formats and international dissemination. Deng also summarises Xi's ideas on the subject: traditional culture as the nation's "roots" and "soul", creative transformation and innovative development, and a call to study and implement them fully. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially aligned account of how Party narratives portray continuity in cultural policy from the 1930s to 2020.

Building the "three major systems" of CPC history studies, seen through a century of Party history 从百年党史看中共党史学“三大体系”建设 Song Xueqin Writing in Guangming Daily in May 2021, in the centenary year of the Communist Party of China (CPC), Song Xueqin asks how the discipline of CPC history studies should build its disciplinary system, academic system and discourse system (the "three major systems"). The author argues that the experience accumulated across each stage of the discipline's hundred-year development is an essential foundation and resource for this task in the new era. This short commentary proceeds chronologically through four stages. It covers the period from the Party's founding in 1921 to 1949, the early People's Republic, the period of reform and opening up, and the era since the 18th Party Congress (2012). For each stage Song identifies the main researchers, texts and characteristic features of Party history research. Song's central claim is that the discipline has repeatedly developed by combining Marxist guidance with the Party's practical needs. Early Party leaders such as Cai Hesen, Qu Qiubai and Li Lisan wrote Party history to serve political struggle, and the Yan'an rectification movement, Mao Zedong's "How to Study the History of the CPC" and the 1945 resolution on historical questions gave the field its theoretical methods. After 1949 the Selected Works of Mao Zedong formed the core of the academic system, and after the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978) the field corrected the damage of the Cultural Revolution and merged political and academic attributes. For the new era, Song names two requirements: adherence to Marxist guidance, which the author says has repeatedly been shown to determine whether the field prospers or goes astray, and a problem-oriented approach. Song concludes that Party history scholars should start from the practical problems facing contemporary China, respect the "Chinese case" and "Chinese experience", and put forward original theoretical views with distinctive concepts. The aim is a systematic discipline with Chinese characteristics, style and manner that distils regularities of the Party's long-term governance and guides new practice. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned periodisation of how Party history studies developed in China and what a leading scholar expects of the discipline in 2021.

The Party's political building since the founding of the PRC: development, features and lessons 新中国成立以来党的政治建设：发展历程、特点及其启示 Wang Shiyi Zhou Nan Writing in the wake of the 2019 CPC Central Committee Opinions on Strengthening the Party's Political Building, Wang Shiyi and Zhou Nan ask how the Party's political building has developed since 1949, what marks it, and what it teaches. They argue that it has advanced with the times, moving from a tortuous course under socialist revolution and construction to a systematic, leading component of Party building in the new era. Taking a stand on politics, they say, is a basic requirement of a Marxist party. The article is organised in three parts. The first gives a periodised history: 1949–1978; 1978–2012, divided into three stages (1978–1989, 1989–2002, 2002–2012); and the new era from 2012. It follows Party congresses, plenums, intra-Party regulations and the changing layout of Party building, from the four-part to the five-part arrangement. The second part identifies three features, and the third draws six lessons. The authors read the early period as a good start (the 1951 rectification, the 1954 resolution on Party unity, the Eighth Congress) followed, from 1957, by a drift under "Leftist" thinking that reached its worst in the Cultural Revolution. After the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978), they trace recovery through the 1980 guidelines on intra-Party political life, the creation of discipline inspection bodies and Deng Xiaoping's institution-based approach. Under Jiang Zemin and Hu Jintao they describe the "talk politics" campaigns and the Scientific Outlook on Development. Since the 18th Party Congress (2012) they credit Xi Jinping with the most systematic exposition, and with putting political building first and adding discipline building at the 19th Congress (2017). The three features are: upholding the Party's overall leadership; a problem-oriented mix of regular and concentrated education; and strict discipline, moving to full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. The six lessons are: put political building first; hold high the banner of socialism with Chinese characteristics; innovate by freeing minds and seeking truth from facts; serve the Party's political line and long-term governing capacity; strengthen Marxist ideological and political education; and coordinate political building with ideological, organisational, conduct and discipline building. The authors hold that political building is the Party's "backbone" and that its theory and practice have made a historic leap. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially aligned chronology of how Party political building and its regulations developed from 1949 to 2019.

The great historical significance of our Party's creation of Chinese revolutionary theory 我们党开创中国革命理论的伟大历史意义 Zhang Haipeng Published in Guangming Daily on 26 May 2021, in the run-up to the Party's centenary, this commentary asks how a party founded in 1921 has lasted a hundred years, governed for more than seventy, and become the world's largest governing party. Zhang Haipeng answers by pointing to one feature of the Party's history. In Zhang's account, the Communist Party created a revolutionary theory suited to a semi-colonial, semi-feudal country, and this developed Marxism-Leninism. The article follows the Party's theoretical path chronologically. It begins with the Marxist model of urban proletarian insurrection and with Lenin's 1920 ideas on colonial revolution. It then covers the first and second Party congresses, the uprisings after 1927, the Jinggangshan base area, the Zunyi Conference of 1935, the 1938 proposal to adapt Marxism to Chinese conditions, and Mao Zedong's 1949 shift of the Party's focus to the cities. Zhang's central argument is that urban insurrection was one successful form of the general principle of seizing power by force, not the only one. Treating it as universal, as the "urban-centred" line did under Comintern influence and the Party's leftist leadership, confused a specific form with the theory itself. Zhang argues that Mao, drawing on peasant-movement experience, developed the strategy of encircling the cities from the countryside and set it out in his writings, including the 1930 essay against book worship. The leftist line, the author says, caused heavy losses until Zunyi confirmed the new path. Zhang reads this as the first leap in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, which produced Mao Zedong Thought. Zhang also stresses that the countryside was only a means. Citing Mao's 1944 letter to Bo Gu and his 1949 speech, Zhang says the aim was industrialisation and a socialist economic base, and that looking only at the villages and small-peasant economy would be populism. Zhang concludes that this revolutionary theory was a major contribution to the treasury of Marxism-Leninism and laid the foundation for the victory of the democratic revolution and the founding of the People's Republic. Zhang adds that the same method must guide socialist construction after taking power, producing socialism with Chinese characteristics that differs from the Soviet model while keeping Marxism's general principles. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned account of how Party historiography presents the rural-revolution strategy as Marxism adapted to China, and how that account is tied to the centenary.

The path of belief of a century-old Party 百年大党的信仰之路 Xiang Jingyao Marking the Communist Party of China's centenary in 2021, this newspaper commentary asks where the Party's "power of belief" comes from and how it has been built up. Xiang argues that this power is the Party's distinguishing mark and unique strength, and that over a hundred years it has grown together with material force. In Xiang's account it has been consolidated through the most thoroughgoing theory, the loftiest ideals and the most vivid practice of serving the people, and it forms a distinctive driving mechanism of national governance. The piece is organised in three parts: theory as the seed of belief, ideals as the banner that gathers belief, and service to the people as the practical theme of belief. A short closing passage sums up the internal logic of the Party's century of belief-building. The text draws on the history of the new-democratic revolution, socialist construction, reform and opening up, and the new era. Xiang's first move reads Marxism through four lenses: epistemology (a scientific theory), value theory (a theory of the people), practice (a theory that turns belief into action) and intellectual history (an open, developing theory, from Mao Zedong Thought to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era). The second move holds that belief rests on two ideals. The lofty communist ideal gives long-term direction, while the common ideal of socialism with Chinese characteristics gives a present-day footing. Xiang adds that Party members unify personal and social ideals. The third move links belief to three practical themes: \"standing up\" in the revolutionary period, \"becoming prosperous\" in socialist construction and reform and opening up, and \"becoming strong\" in the new era. For the last of these, Xiang cites full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, theoretical innovation, and the new \"two-step\" strategy with the 14th Five-Year Plan and 2035 goals. Xiang concludes that the Party's belief-building lies in studying and applying Marxism, in uniting members around the two ideals, and in leading the people from standing up to becoming prosperous and strong. Looking ahead, the author expects the Party to gather an even stronger power of belief in service of economic and social development and the people's well-being. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated scholarship framed belief and ideals during the 2021 centenary.

Research on modern Chinese history in 2020 An annual survey of scholarship from the Opium War to 1949 2020年的中国近代史研究 Wu Xuebin This is an annual literature review, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in March 2021, of research on modern Chinese history in 2020. Wu defines the field as the 109 years from the Opium War (1840) to the founding of the People's Republic (1949). Citing Xi Jinping's January 2020 addition of the history of socialist development to the Party's three histories, Wu holds that the theme of this period is the Communist Party leading the people towards socialism. The review reports strong results in historiography, theory, institutional and economic history, wartime source collections and Party history. The survey is organised by theme. It covers historiography and the building of the "three major systems" (disciplinary, academic and discourse systems), new angles in historical theory, the War of Resistance against Japan and Party history, institutional history and state governance, and source compilations and databases. Each section lists journal articles and books with a one-line summary of each author's finding. It names economic, foreign-relations, intellectual, conceptual and environmental history only briefly, citing limited space. Wu stresses several clusters. In historiography, scholars on treaty relations, border studies and urban history link their work to building a Chinese discourse system. In theory, debates continue over whether the phrase "sinicisation of Marxist historiography" is valid, how to evaluate historical figures under historical materialism, and how hermeneutics and the "long durée" can correct fragmented cultural and social history. For the 75th anniversary of victory in 2020, wartime work stresses the Party's role as the "mainstay", along with Japanese war responsibility, Nanjing, the north-west rear area and global perspectives. Party-history work covers the First Congress delegates, rebuttals of claims about Yan'an, and revolutionary discourse and base-area finance. Governance studies address official selection, border governance, supervision systems and the Taiping aftermath. Wu notes major source publications, including the eight-volume History of China's War of Resistance against Japan and a 100-volume military source collection. It also lists new databases, among them a platform on the war and modern Sino-Japanese relations and a fourth batch of modern newspapers. The review closes by hoping historians will study Xi Jinping's statements on modern history and Party history, strengthen basic theory and produce works that join history and theory. Read the original if you want a detailed map of 2020 Chinese-language publications, with journal citations, on modern Chinese history, wartime history and Party history.

Establishing a correct view of Party history through systems thinking 以系统思维树立正确党史观 Shi Shiyue Writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in March 2021, ahead of the Party's centenary, Shi Shiyue takes up Xi Jinping's call, made at the mobilisation meeting for Party history study and education, to establish a correct view of Party history. Shi argues that Party members should study the history of the Communist Party of China with a systems mode of thinking that is holistic, dynamic, hierarchical and open. The short commentary is organised around those four features. Each section links one feature to an aspect of Party history: its overall value, its phases of development, its record of governance, and its forward-looking character. On wholeness, Shi presents the century as a history of struggle and sacrifice, citing revolutionary martyrs such as Li Dazhao and Cai Hesen and builders such as Wang Jinxi and Jiao Yulu, and says it educates members by example. On dynamism, Shi divides the century into four periods: New Democratic revolution, socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the new era under Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Shi describes these as the shift from standing up to becoming prosperous to becoming strong. On hierarchy, Shi surveys governance in politics, the economy, culture and ecological civilisation. On openness, Shi cites the elimination of absolute poverty as an achievement that prepares the next goal of building a modern socialist country. Shi concludes that Party history offers practical experience and spiritual resources to guide every member and citizen. The author expects the Party to keep to a people-centred approach and to pursue modernization goals through systematic and creative work. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Party-affiliated commentary in 2021 presented the official framework for studying Party history.

Marx and Engels on the leadership of the proletarian party 马克思恩格斯论无产阶级政党的领导 Duan Guangpeng Published in the China Social Sciences Today in April 2021, the centenary year of the Communist Party of China, this short piece asks what Marx and Engels said about how a proletarian party should lead. Duan argues that their scattered statements form a coherent account of the purpose, the components and the tactics of such leadership. The author presents this account as holding lessons for upholding and strengthening the Party's overall leadership in the new era. The article is organised in three parts. The first takes up the aim of proletarian party leadership, drawing mainly on Marx's introduction to the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right and on the Communist Manifesto. The second breaks leadership into political, ideological and organisational elements. The third sets out three pairs of tactics: the immediate and the long term, alliance and struggle, and principle and flexibility. Duan supports each point with short quotations from Marx and Engels, including their remarks on the Paris Commune and the International Working Men's Association. Duan's central claim is that the party leads because it is independent and has no interests separate from those of the whole proletariat. Its aim is to lead the great majority in seeking the interests of the great majority, up to the free development of each individual. On Duan's reading, political leadership fixes the direction, through independence from bourgeois parties and through authority and centralisation. Ideological leadership supplies the soul, in the form of a scientific worldview whose core is the abolition of private property. Organisational leadership secures effectiveness through democratic principles, discipline, unity, and criticism and self-criticism. In tactics, Duan stresses that a party must work with allies and build a broad united front while keeping its independence and its right to criticise them. It must also adapt to circumstances without abandoning principle, as Marx and Engels did when drafting the International's statutes. Duan concludes that Marx and Engels treated leadership as a systematic process combining goals, elements and tactics, and that this offers a point of reference for Party-building today. The piece is brief and mostly arranges classic quotations under thematic headings, with little discussion of historical debate. Read the original if you want a compact, officially oriented digest of the passages in Marx and Engels that Chinese Party theorists cite on proletarian party leadership.

The twofold logic of Marx's theory of social progress 马克思社会进步理论的双重逻辑 Zhang Wen This short commentary, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in May 2021, asks how Marx's theory of social progress should be understood in relation to the Enlightenment philosophy of history from which it emerged. Zhang argues that the theory contains a twofold logic: history is grounded in "material relations of life", and social progress is at the same time a "natural history" with a subjective dimension. The two are said to be unified in human material production, that is, in practice. The article opens by describing the Enlightenment paradigm, which takes reason as its yardstick and treats history as the movement of a transcendental consciousness, as in Kant's "hidden plan of nature" and Hegel's "absolute spirit". It then proceeds in two main sections. The first examines Marx's move from reason to practice and to the material relations of life. The second takes up his remark in Capital about the development of the economic formation of society as a process of natural history. In Zhang's reading, Marx shares with the Enlightenment the idea of progress, the belief that people can advance society by perfecting themselves, and a humanist defence of human subjectivity. Yet Marx regards Enlightenment thought as inverting its object: history becomes a footnote to reason, split between empirical reality and transcendental rationality. Marx instead seeks a science of history, and finds its constant element in the relations of production and the contradictory movement of productive forces and relations of production, which Zhang calls the "driving source" of progress. The second logic, natural history, stresses that humans are natural beings and that social development obeys laws independent of human will. Zhang adds that humans transform nature into "humanised nature", so that rule-governed necessity and purposiveness coincide. Human initiative can thus help society grasp these laws and even accelerate progress, as in the "Caudine Forks" leap, without negating natural history, because humans do not create matter itself. Zhang concludes that Marx's theory is a rigorous system that breaks with earlier idealist approaches and moves from philosophy of history to science of history. Social progress is presented as the unfolding, in empirical time and space, of the contradictory movement between productive forces and relations of production. Read the original if you want a compact, Chinese-language account of how a contemporary Chinese scholar links historical materialism's driving force with its subjective dimension and with Marx's critique of Enlightenment philosophy of history.

Marx as a social pathologist 作为社会病理学家的马克思 Yang Lei This short commentary, published in a newspaper in 2021, reads Marx as a "social pathologist": a thinker who critically examines, diagnoses and prescribes for the sicknesses of society. Drawing on Axel Honneth's definition of social philosophy as the diagnosis of social developments that obstruct a "good life", Yang Lei argues that Marx dissected capitalism with historical materialism and the theory of surplus value. In Yang's account, Marx issued capitalism a "critical condition notice", a diagnosis and a prescription, and offered a scientific cure. The piece is organised around the medical metaphor in three steps: the illness, the root cause and the remedy. It draws on the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, The Holy Family, the 1863–65 manuscripts, the Communist Manifesto and Capital, volume I. It also cites Honneth, Anthony Giddens, Georg Lukács and Jacques Derrida. Yang follows Honneth's view that Marx's critique moved from an early model of alienation to a mature model of reification. On the illness, Yang argues that capitalism dehumanises people. Alienated labour reduces workers to appendages of capital's self-expansion, and the domination of dead labour over living labour produces fetishism, in which human logic submits to the logic of things. Consumerism and instrumental rationality erode human dignity and critical thought. On the root cause, Yang holds that private ownership of the means of production, resting on class antagonism and exploitation, produces mass impoverishment and a stunted existence for wage-workers. Because of the contradiction between productive forces and relations of production, capitalism is historically transient and, in Yang's reading, cannot be cured from within. As the remedy, Yang presents Marx's communist society, an association of free individuals, in which private property is positively sublated and the logic of humanity overcomes the logic of capital. There, "the free development of each is the condition for the free development of all". Yang concludes, citing Derrida, that Marx remains a contemporary "Prometheus" who lights the way for the proletariat toward a society of "genuine human beings". Read the original if you want a brief, accessible restatement of Marx's critique of alienation, reification and private property in medical terms.

An essay on Marx's philosophy as a philosophy of sensuousness 试论作为一种感性哲学的马克思哲学 Li Chunmin Li Chunmin asks what it means to read Marx's philosophy through the category of sensuousness (ganxing). The article argues that sensuousness is a basic dimension of Marx's picture of the world: for Marx, humans are sensuous beings, the world is a sensuous world, and knowing and changing it is a process of sensuous production. On this reading Marx's philosophy is a philosophy of sensuousness, in which the obscuring of sensuousness marks the loss of human subjectivity and its rebuilding leads to real emancipation. The article was published in Social Science Journal (Shehui kexue jikan) in 2021. The article has four parts. The first treats how the sensuous world and the 'sensuous human being' appear as social and historical products, contrasting Marx with Feuerbach's intuitionism. The second examines four 'abstract totalities' that Marx criticised for floating above sensuous reality: religion, philosophy, the state and morality. The third turns to the capitalist form of sensuousness, taking commodity, money and capital as the empirical system of capital. The fourth sets out four discourses of contemporary sensuous production. Li's central claim is that capital creates two 'supersensuous' worlds, a 'false world' and a 'void world', and that both must be broken. The false world consists of commodity, money and capital, whose fetish character hides the social relations of labour and production behind relations between things. The void world has an existential side, shown in labour-power becoming a commodity, machinery and 'surplus' workers. It also has a value side, shown in the hollowing of moral meaning, culture-industry conformity and the isolated individual. Li stresses that Marx did not criticise the commodification of labour-power on moral grounds, and treated it as a historically progressive event. Following Marx's account of communism as the true return of sensuousness, Li proposes four dimensions of sensuousness today. It is a discourse against capital, a form of social action in economic, political and cultural fields, an ethic of life, and an institutional culture that respects individual difference and creativity. Rebuilding sensuousness is presented as the way to sublate the logic of capital and achieve human emancipation. Read the original if you want a systematic, text-based case for a sensuousness-centred reading of Marx, running from the early critiques of Feuerbach and Hegel to Capital and to contemporary issues such as technology and the body.

On Heidegger's humanist reading of Marx: an analysis based on historical materialism 论海德格尔对马克思的人道主义解读——基于历史唯物主义的分析 Hao Jisong Hao Jisong takes up Heidegger's charge that Marx's historical materialism, although it reaches 'an essential dimension of history', remains the final form of metaphysical humanism and carries a danger of self-destruction. The article asks whether this reading is correct, how the humanist element in historical materialism should be understood, and whether it is still necessary to follow Marx in addressing the historical existence of real human beings. Hao argues that Heidegger misreads Marx, and that Marx's theory of the human being goes beyond traditional humanism. The article has four parts. It first reconstructs Heidegger's critique, drawing on the 'Letter on Humanism' and related texts: production, the Gestell (enframing) of modern technology, and the priority of Being over humans. It then offers two critical comments on this critique. The third part sets out how Marx surpasses traditional humanism, and the fourth contrasts Marx with Feuerbach and with idealism, before turning to capital, technology and communism. Hao's central move is to deny that Marx's 'human being' is the abstract subject Heidegger describes. For Marx, in Hao's account, humans are real, historically determined individuals whose essence is the 'ensemble of social relations', both authors of history and characters in it. Hao adds that Heidegger's own analysis of Dasein is narrow and, in Hao's view, ends up abstract. Hao's second move is that Gestell is not a destiny of Being. Citing Marx on the Luddites, Hao treats it as the concretisation and technicisation of the logic of capital, that is, the capitalist application of technology. The problem of modernity lies in absolutising subjectivity, not in subjectivity as such. Hao also argues that Heidegger's stance of calm waiting for salvation amounts to giving up human agency. Hao concludes that Marx's analysis of capital, overproduction, crisis and the growth of the proletariat shows capitalism to be historically transitory. In this reading, communism is an actual movement through which real people regain mastery over the 'dead matter' of capital. Hao holds that Marx brings the freedom Heidegger sought 'down from heaven to earth', and that his work remains the sharpest weapon for criticising existing society. Read the original if you want a Marxist rebuttal of Heidegger's humanism critique that links ontology to the critique of capital and technology.

Building a contemporary Chinese Marxist discourse system for the twenty-first century 构建面向21世纪的当代中国马克思主义话语体系 Zhang Yantao Gao Chen Writing in 2021, Zhang Yantao and Gao Chen take up the problem that China's development and institutional strengths have not yet been converted into discursive strength. In their account China still suffers from "aphasia" in international discourse, while the West holds discursive hegemony. They argue that building a contemporary Chinese Marxism discourse system for the twenty-first century is a strategic task tied to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and a community with a shared future for mankind. The article is organised around three tasks, each a section: interpreting new concepts, applying new categories, and producing new formulations. It draws on Xi Jinping's 2016 speech on philosophy and social sciences, on Marx, Engels and Foucault, and on Chinese scholars. It cites German classical philosophy as an example of an age producing original thought, and it lists the concepts of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era as the "keywords" of the new discourse. On concepts, the authors say they should be read through practice, theory and innovation. They contend that Chinese practice has succeeded but Chinese theory has summarised, reflected on and prepared for it too little. Some scholars, they say, merely carry Western concepts. On categories, they criticise Chinese academia for repeating Western ideas, issuing political statements in place of research and showing "innovation anxiety". They call for agenda-setting and for a move from an "apprentice mentality" to self-assertion. They add that the discourse must be people-centred, and they cite Foucault's "discourse is power" to argue that contests over discourse are contests over interests, systems and paths. On formulations, they say the discourse must combine "Chinese characteristics" with "universal significance". They hold that the West has monopolised the definitions of freedom, equality and human rights and that its democratic model rests on flawed assumptions. They present the community with a shared future for mankind as a major innovation. The authors conclude that China's scholars must move from interpretation to construction and from commentary to innovation. They propose five goals for the discourse: greater explanatory power, innovative power, communicative power, cohesive power and contributive power. They present "Chinese discourse" as the theoretical expression of the Chinese path and as a sign of national maturity and confidence. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese scholars in 2021 framed discourse power, agenda-setting and the building of a distinctive Marxist vocabulary.

From Marx to Lenin: an intellectual-history study of the classical theory of imperialism 从马克思到列宁：经典帝国主义理论的思想史考察 Meng Fei This article, published in 2020, traces how the Marxist theory of imperialism took shape from Marx to Lenin and asks what it still offers today. Meng argues that Marx laid the analytical foundations without using the term, that Second International theorists produced divergent and ultimately inadequate accounts, and that Lenin's Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism completed the classical theory in a scientific form.
