Meng holds that this theory retains explanatory and critical power for contemporary capitalism. The article has four parts. It begins with Marx's groundwork, then turns to the Second International debates involving Hilferding, Bernstein, Kautsky, Otto Bauer, Rosa Luxemburg and Max Adler. The third part examines Lenin's theory and his comrade Bukharin. The last part discusses the methodological significance of the classical theory and its echoes in later "new imperialism" thinkers such as Samir Amin, Ellen Meiksins Wood, Michael Hardt and Antonio Negri, and David Harvey. Meng contends that Marx's analysis of capitalist expansion, the credit system, internal contradictions and the general analysis of capital supplied the raw material for later theory. In Meng's reading, Second International thinkers split into right, centre and left camps, yet nearly all accepted imperialism's "necessity" and never reached the roots of capitalist operation. Kautsky's "ultra-imperialism" and Bauer's mild view are described as illusions of a benign imperialism, while Luxemburg's account is faulted for making imperialism capitalism's only path. Lenin, by contrast, treats imperialism as a system rather than a policy, as Bukharin does not, and unites logic with reality and theory with practice. His account combines a critique of advanced capitalism with attention to the non-capitalist development of backward countries. Meng concludes that the contemporary world confirms rather than overturns the classical trends: finance capital dominates, multinational monopolies export capital, and exploitation of developing countries and regional conflicts persist, now through funds, technology and culture rather than force alone. The new imperialist system is described as wider, more flexible and cheaper, with oppression more concealed and proletarian revolutionary enthusiasm weakened. Meng presents this as the practical basis for rediscovering the theory and for planning contemporary socialist development. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly overview of how Marx, the Second International and Lenin are positioned in the history of imperialism theory.

Advancing the construction of the disciplinary system of the history of Marxism's development 推进马克思主义发展史学科体系建设 Liang Haifeng This commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today on 25 May 2021, asks how to build up the discipline that studies the history of Marxism's development. Taking Xi Jinping's "5.17" speech on philosophy and social sciences as its starting point, Liang argues that the discipline, which studies the historical process and laws of Marxism's emergence and growth, is a top priority within the wider disciplinary system of the social sciences. Liang says that strengthening the discipline helps trace Marxism to its sources, link theory to practice and to specific national conditions, and advance theoretical innovation in socialism with Chinese characteristics. The article sets out four tasks: a problem-oriented approach, high-quality research output, the training of successor scholars, and the selective absorption of domestic and foreign research. On the first task, Liang reviews how Marx, Engels, Lenin, Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin, Hu Jintao and Xi Jinping each answered the questions of their era. From this the author concludes that research must join the history of ideas to the history of practice. On the second, Liang criticises a restless academic climate that favours quantity, publication and short-term gain over quality, and calls for scholars to immerse themselves in the classic texts. On the third, Liang names the shortage of talent as the biggest bottleneck, citing late establishment of the discipline, thin reserves and young scholars leaving for faster-yielding fields. Liang proposes tiered talent programmes, improved assessment, promotion and reward systems, and implementation of the Party's policy towards intellectuals. Foreign scholarship should be neither rejected wholesale nor followed uncritically, but assessed so that Chinese traditional culture and useful foreign findings serve original Chinese concepts and theories. Read the original if you want a brief, official-register statement of the priorities and perceived weaknesses of Marxism-history research as a discipline in China around 2021.

The contemporary reconstruction of Marx's category of "general intellect" and an assessment of its effects 马克思“一般智力”范畴的当代重构及其效应评估 Sun Leqiang Sun Leqiang asks how contemporary Western left thinkers have redefined Marx's category of "general intellect", what theoretical system they built on it, and how that system should be judged. The article, published in 2021, argues that Italian autonomism and the cognitive capitalism school turned a category tied to fixed capital into a generalised property of living subjects. In Sun's assessment, this move narrows and at the same time inflates Marx's concept, and ends in a "fetishism" of general intellect. The article has three parts. The first follows Paolo Virno's shift from "general intellect" to "intellect in general", together with its consequences for the labour theory of value, "real abstraction" and fixed capital (via Antonio Negri). The second places this reading in a line of social-critical paradigms running from Guy Debord's spectacle through Jean Baudrillard's simulation to Mark Poster's mode of information, and then to Hardt and Negri's and Carlo Vercellone's cognitive capitalism. The third part is Sun's critical evaluation, organised under three headings. In Sun's account, Virno treats immaterial labour as the leading measure of general intellect and says it now creates value directly. Negri holds that "fixed capital is man himself", so that the line between dead and living labour dissolves. Cognitive capitalists periodise capitalism into mercantile, industrial and cognitive stages. Sun replies that Marx meant a society's total "general social knowledge", not individual faculties. Sun also says the autonomists confuse general intellect with the historically changing forms through which it becomes a direct productive force, and ignore that immaterial labour still depends on means of labour. Sun adds that value still rests on abstract labour, so capital absorbs general intellect even in its new form. Sun concludes that the autonomists overstate how far mass intellect has spread. Any such intellect remains capital-dominated, and Marx's full unity of individual, mass and universal intellect belongs to communism. Sun also argues that Marx distinguished immaterial labour that produces surplus value from labour that does not. On Sun's reading, the rise of such labour changes the composition of the working class, as in Engels's "mental-labour proletariat", but leaves Marx's class logic intact. Sun finds the "multitude" a supra-class category and sees the cognitive-class theory as more consistent with Marx, though still tending towards anarchism and reformism. Read the original if you want a Marxist critique of Virno, Negri and Vercellone, built on a close reading of the Grundrisse "fragment on machines".

The exception without exception in the logic of capital, and non-labour as labour A critical reflection on contemporary Western left-wing thought 资本逻辑中无例外的“例外”与非劳动的劳动 Xia Ying Huang Jing'ou Writing against the background of the 2020 Covid-19 pandemic, Xia Ying and Huang Jing'ou ask why contemporary Western left-wing thinkers, for all their radical posture, offer so little purchase on capitalism. The authors argue that these thinkers' "eventalised" method, which rests on a view of history as ruptures, builds an "external" critique of capitalism out of exceptional events. In their reading, this departs from Marx, who sought capital's contradictions inside the logic of capital itself. The article has three sections. The first examines Giorgio Agamben's theory of the "state of exception" and the anti-intellectualism of his pandemic commentary, with references to Žižek, Byung-Chul Han and Rancière, and places it within radical versus conservative political philosophy (Schmitt against Strauss). The second turns to Antonio Negri and Michael Hardt, who locate power in everyday property relations. The third criticises their account of immaterial labour, tracing the ideology of labour from Locke to Marx's critique of alienated labour. The authors argue that Agamben, Han and others, by denying or minimising the epidemic and treating anti-epidemic measures as new control, miss what Western states actually feared: recession. In their account, capital's compulsion to self-valorise is the true everyday micro-power, and each "exception" only produces new forms of capital, as in the rise in tech billionaires' assets. Negri and Hardt see this immanent power correctly, the authors say, but they accept an "ideology of labour" that ties personhood to property through labour. Drawing on Marx's critique of Locke and of alienated labour, Xia and Huang contend that immaterial labour, with its supposed autonomy and "common" character, only generalises labour into all of life, as in the "prosumer" and influencer economy. It therefore cannot produce a revolutionary subject such as the multitude. The authors conclude that both Western left paths, the external critique of exceptions and the internal critique through property and immaterial labour, fail to show a real way out of capitalism. They call for Marx's critique of political economy to be used to analyse the new contradictions within emerging forms of capital and to dismantle the ideology of labour, in order to find a path of emancipation from the power of capital. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist critique of Agamben, Žižek, Han, Negri and Hardt, set against the pandemic debates of 2020.

The centenary Communist Party of China and Africa's revolution and construction 百年中国共产党与非洲革命和建设 Li Xinfeng Written for the Party's centenary in 2021, this article reviews the Communist Party of China's relations with Africa over a hundred years. Li Xinfeng argues that, grounded in shared historical experience, shared development tasks and shared strategic interests, the Party built a new kind of comprehensive strategic partnership with African states. In Li's account this partnership shaped Africa's struggles for independence and its economic construction, and it rests on a consistent Party outlook on Africa, the world and Sino-African friendship. The article has three parts. The first treats the Party's "world revolution" outlook and its support for African anti-imperialist, anti-colonial and anti-hegemonic struggles, including material aid, ideological guidance and African backing for China. The second follows the "common development" outlook through three periods: aid under proletarian internationalism up to around 1978, economic cooperation from the 1980s to the 1990s, and comprehensive cooperation since 2000 under the Forum on China-Africa Cooperation. The third draws five lessons from the record. Li contends that the Party treated African liberation as its own cause. It relied on Lenin's theory of nationalities and colonies and on Mao Zedong's "three worlds" theory, and it later adopted the principle that Africa's affairs should be decided by Africans. Li cites figures on aid, trade and infrastructure, including the 1971 UN vote restoring the People's Republic's seat, where Li says 26 of 76 votes in favour came from African states. Li presents the Tanzania–Zambia railway, the first medical team to Algeria and the Eight Principles of foreign aid as evidence of aid without political conditions. Li holds that policy adjusted to circumstances while the basic stance did not change, and that Xi Jinping's concept of a China-Africa community with a shared future is a further theoretical innovation. Li's five lessons are an unchanged purpose of independence and equal, mutually beneficial development; a consistent people-centred value orientation expressed in the "correct approach to justice and interests"; theory-led yet flexible policy; emphasis on inter-party exchange and sharing governance experience; and an internationalist, mission-driven character guided by a community with a shared future for mankind. Li concludes that these principles will guide China-Africa relations and the Belt and Road Initiative in Africa. Read the original if you want an official Chinese scholarly account of how the Party frames its century of relations with Africa, with period-by-period data and policy milestones.

"Western chaos": populism or a crisis of capitalism? “西方之乱”：民粹主义还是资本主义危机 Xing Caili Why have Western societies since the 2008 financial crisis seen Occupy Wall Street, the Tea Party, the Trump phenomenon, Brexit and France's Yellow Vests? Xing Caili takes issue with the dominant Western explanation, which blames a flood of "populism". The article argues that the concept is too incoherent to explain anything and works as an ideological tool that hides the real cause, a crisis of capitalism, and blames the poor for it. The article has three parts. The first examines the concept of populism, its three main referents in the literature and how its meaning turned pejorative. The second sets out a Marxist crisis theory and asks whether crisis necessarily produces proletarian revolution. The third considers the danger of fascism and the need to revive the world socialist movement. Xing draws on Spanish scholar Marco de la Mora, James Petras, Samir Amin, William Robinson, Marx, Engels and Lenin. Xing argues that "populism" is applied to disorderly popular revolt, to the socialist left and to the conservative right alike, and that the label is applied by double standards. Street unrest abroad is called "democracy", while protest at home is dismissed as mob rule. Tracing the term's history, Xing holds that it was once positive and was turned pejorative after the Second World War by Cold War liberal scholars such as Richard Hofstadter, who equated it with fascism. In Xing's account, the 2008 crisis stems from the basic contradiction of capitalism, now under international financial monopoly capital, which can profit from crises and shift blame onto ordinary people. Crisis is a condition for revolution, but not a guarantee of it. Xing reads the "disorderly resistance" as a sign that the masses lack class consciousness, organisation and revolutionary theory, so they may be led by the left or exploited by the right. Xing concludes that capitalism faces three paths: Roosevelt-style reform, communist revolution or fascism. The first is judged no longer viable and the second is held back by the low ebb of world socialism, so Xing sees a real risk of slipping into fascism. Xing cites Amin, Žižek, Badiou and Robinson as warning of this. The only fundamental way out, Xing argues, is to revive the socialist movement and strengthen communist and other progressive forces. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist critique reads Western populism as a symptom of capitalist crisis and as a contested political label.

Marx and Engels on international trade policy and its contemporary implications 马克思恩格斯的国际贸易政策思想及其当代启示 Zhao Qian Zhao Qian asks what Marx and Engels's writings on free trade and protection can explain about trade policy today, when emerging and long-established economies are both revising their positions. The article argues that, in Marx and Engels, the choice between the two policies depends on who holds an international monopoly in production. Free trade and protection convert into each other under the logic of capital expansion. The author concludes that this reasoning still bears on present-day disputes. The article has four parts and a short conclusion. It first treats late-industrialising countries, which Marx and Engels thought should move from protection to free trade. It then takes advanced countries that slide back from free trade to protection. The third part asks whether protection can restore a lost monopoly. Zhao draws on Marx and Engels's comments on Britain, Germany, the United States, France and Venice, and compares their views with Friedrich List, Raúl Prebisch, Immanuel Wallerstein and modern comparative-advantage theory. Zhao reads Marx and Engels as holding that protection suits backward economies and should end once a sector saturates the home market; the author notes that cartels in protected industries signal this point. Free trade, in turn, rests on a monopoly in production, but it lets capital flow to latecomers, who rise and erode that monopoly, so free trade 'trains its own gravediggers'. Advanced countries then return to protection. Zhao argues that protection cannot reliably restore their position. It weakens the monopolies' incentive to innovate, spreads through retaliation into a spiral of ever wider protection, and shifts costs to consumers and workers. In the author's account, it mainly serves capitalists' interests, as populist protectionism today illustrates. In the conclusion, Zhao says that national value and the international division of labour follow from monopoly in production. Because capital's drive to expand makes free trade the long-run tendency, the author describes current Western protectionism as a reaction against history that cannot last. Even so, Zhao says it hampers emerging countries in the short term. The author calls on them to build real advantages in production, not only in trade. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist reading of protectionism and free trade, with extensive citation of Marx and Engels, applied to today's world economy.

On the links through which the development of Marxism is realised 试论马克思主义发展的实现环节 Liang Shufa Liang Shufa takes up a question that, in his view, studies of the development of Marxism often leave unanswered: how do the general conditions for development actually bring it about? He argues that research must move from identifying general conditions to examining their realisation, and that without this step development research is incomplete or even pointless. His answer is that the three basic conditions (material, political and ideological) take effect through four links: contradiction, situation, problem and mechanism. The article is organised in four sections, one for each link. It begins with contradictions and the situations they generate, turns to problems and the question of what counts as a problem of the age, and ends with a longer section on mechanisms, which it divides into practice, innovative thinking, evaluation and acceptance. Liang draws on Marx's Preface to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy and his remarks on the 'problem' as the slogan of an age, and he closes his account of problems with a quotation from Xi Jinping. Liang holds that the three basic conditions act together as a contradictory whole. He identifies three types of social contradiction: the basic contradictions of society (productive forces and relations of production, economic base and superstructure), class contradictions, and contradictions between systems of ideas. Each, he says, can drive the development of Marxism, differing only in the nature of the driving force. Contradiction leads to struggle, movement and then a situation, which is objective but requires subjective agency to turn into results. As a practical philosophy, Marxism must address practical problems and above all the 'problems of the age'. Liang says the overall problem remains socialist construction and, for China, the question of what kind of socialism with Chinese characteristics to uphold and develop in the new era. Liang concludes that the mechanisms are the active, human element in realising development. Practice shifts the themes, content and pace of theory, and major practical events can lift theory as a whole. Innovative thinking is needed to find themes and to move from experience to theory. Evaluation matters because affirmation, especially from society, strengthens confidence in Marxism. Acceptance, dissemination and absorption count as part of later development of Marxism as a whole. Read the original if you study the methodology of the history of Marxism or want to see how a Chinese theorist builds a general framework for explaining theoretical development.

Ideology and political values of Europe's radical left parties 欧洲激进左翼政党的意识形态与政治价值观 Wang Congcong Wang Congcong asks what ideology and political values Europe's radical left parties share, treating them as a single "party family" rather than as separate national cases. Writing in 2021, when radical right parties were rising in Europe, the author argues that the radical left, despite its internal diversity, is united by a comprehensive critique of capitalism and by a common set of values. Wang says case studies are plentiful but systematic macro-level analysis is lacking, and suggests the findings could inform Chinese Communist Party experience of governance. The article opens with theory: party ideology as the "soul" of a party, the left–right divide, and typologies of party families (Beyme, Mair and Mudde, Lipset and Rokkan). It then defines the radical left through Luke March's "radical" and "left" criteria and surveys classifications by Bache and Moreau, March, and Gomez and others. The author takes as the object of study parties that belong to the Party of the European Left or sit in the GUE/NGL group in the European Parliament. The main section sets out five value clusters: equality and social justice; democracy; freedom and solidarity; sustainable development; peace and internationalism. Wang's central move is to show ideological pluralism beneath shared values. Traditional communist parties such as the Greek and Portuguese ones retain Marxism-Leninism. Successor parties and "new left" parties, such as Die Linke, have moved towards democratic socialism and renounced violent revolution. The Nordic and Portuguese "red-green" parties lean towards eco-socialism. Across these, the author finds common positions: equal rights to work, welfare and gender equality; democratisation of economy, politics and society, so that "democratic power must be stronger than capital"; freedom grounded in solidarity; ecological crisis as a product of capitalist profit-seeking; and opposition to imperialism, militarism and NATO. In Wang's account, these parties criticise capitalism more sharply than social democrats do. Wang concludes that the radical left shows family traits but is marked by tensions between unity and heterogeneity, stability and innovation, and ideal and reality. The last tension is how to transcend the capitalist constitutional order from within it. Parties such as the Greek and Portuguese communists keep a pure ideological stance, while others adopt more flexible, pragmatist "new left" images. Wang adds that ideology shapes alliances: some communist parties refuse cooperation with new-left parties or the Party of the European Left, and "democratic-socialist" parties risk being tamed by power. Read the original if you want a systematic overview of the common values and ideological variants of the European radical left, as presented by a Chinese Marxist scholar.

Historical stages in the development of Marxism and the evolution of its themes 马克思主义发展的历史阶段及其主题演进 Sun Laibin How should the history of Marxism be divided into periods? Sun Laibin argues that existing schemes, such as Fran Franjević's five stages and David McLellan's five-part regional arrangement, reflect Eastern European or Anglo-American viewpoints. In Sun's reading, they say too little about China and do not explain what links the stages. The article proposes dividing Marxism's development from the mid-1840s to the mid-twenty-first century into "four 50-year periods", with human emancipation as the constant theme. Sun justifies the 50-year span in three ways: the Kondratiev long waves of capitalism, the need for a coarse-grained survey of intellectual themes, and Lenin's "two fifty years" of 1908. The article then takes each period in turn. It covers the founding by Marx and Engels, the revisionist dispute and Lenin's work, the Sino-Soviet polemic, reform and opening up, and the present as a period still unfolding. Along the way it notes Western Marxism, dependency theory and a later pluralisation of Western Marxist schools. The core claim is that the theme stays fixed while its concrete form changes with the epoch. Sun labels the four periods as: Marxism established through the scientific demonstration of emancipation; Marxism advancing through social revolution; Marxism advancing unevenly through socialist construction and reform; and Marxism breaking new ground under Chinese modernization. Sun also argues that Marxism's centre of gravity has shifted from Western Europe to Russia to China. For the current period, Sun lists tasks for twenty-first-century Marxism. These include confronting the entanglement of capital logic with global challenges, managing institutional and structural friction between East and West, helping developing countries resolve the dilemma of autonomy and development, and respecting both the international and national character of socialist movements. Sun draws three lessons. The first is the dialectical unity of continuity and change in Marxism's theme. The second is that Marxism advances in a spiral through setbacks, as with Bernstein's revisionism before the October Revolution and the Soviet collapse before the rise of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The third is that Marxists, and Chinese Communists in particular, must take conscious responsibility for advancing Marxism. Read the original if you want a periodisation of Marxism that places China at its centre, together with the official Chinese reading of the twenty-first-century tasks.

Engels on the proletarian party's self-reform and social revolution: basic provisions and their internal relationship 恩格斯关于无产阶级政党自我革命与社会革命的基本规定及其内在关系探究 Yu Yifan Yu Yifan takes up Xi Jinping's formula that the Party must use its self-reform to advance the great social revolution it leads, and asks what Engels contributed to the underlying idea of 'two revolutions'. The article argues that Engels, working alongside Marx and independently in later years, set out a coherent position. In it the proletariat's final goal is a thoroughgoing social revolution, and a proletarian party can accomplish that revolution only by tempering itself through self-reform. The article has three main sections. The first reconstructs Engels's view of social revolution from his political-economic analysis, drawing on his study of English industrialisation, The German Ideology and the Communist Manifesto. The second derives the necessity of self-reform from the class character of the proletarian party. The third examines revolutionary strategy, treating how the party should strengthen itself in order to bring about social revolution. Yu links Engels's points to present-day Party requirements at several places. Yu argues that for Engels social revolution is not merely seizing power. It transforms the economic base and the superstructure, and it abolishes classes and the conditions that produce them, aiming at an 'association' of free people. Political revolution is a necessary step within it. The proletarian party differs from earlier parties, which served minorities seeking power and property. It represents the independent movement of the great majority, and so must keep its scientific worldview and its proletarian character. Yu then sets out four requirements Engels drew from this. The party needs a public programme that states its final goals. It needs a strong capacity for learning and for correcting errors. It must handle internal struggle and unity dialectically through criticism and self-criticism. It also needs strict discipline and democratic centralism, with respect for leaders' authority. Yu concludes that Engels's basic provisions remain a source of principle and practical ideas for the present. In this reading, they bear on the new era's call to use the Party's self-reform to drive a new great social revolution in reform and opening up. Yu connects them to the injunction not to forget the original aspiration, to the building of a learning party, and to the Four Consciousnesses and the Two Upholds. Read the original if you want a Party-school reading that traces the current 'two revolutions' formula back to Engels's texts and shows how Chinese scholars link classical Marxist party theory to Xi Jinping's statements.

New trends in the unification of communist parties worldwide in recent years and how China should respond 近年来世界共产党联合化新趋势与我们的应对 Yu Weihai Writing in 2021, on the eve of the centenary of the Communist Party of China, Yu Weihai asks what state the international communist movement is in amid what the article calls the greatest changes in the world in a century, and what this means for the CPC. Yu's answer is that the world's communist and workers' parties, though numerous and divided, show a clear and historically new tendency towards unification, which the article presents as one of the "new historical features" the Party must study. The article has four parts. It first sets out four manifestations of this unification: organisational platforms, joint statements, coordinated international actions, and a shared spirit. It then identifies four new features, assesses the trend's significance and limits, and closes with recommendations for the CPC. Evidence includes lists of international forums founded since 1993, counts of signatories to joint statements, and the author's own fieldwork in the United States in 2019. Yu argues that today's unification differs from the Communist League, the Internationals and the Cominform. It rests on equal, voluntary association among independent parties, with no common organisation or programme. Its features are plurality of participants, networked and resonant spatial patterns, continuous and dense activity, and a form organised around issues rather than organisations. In Yu's assessment it strengthens resistance to capitalism and renews the movement's content and form, replacing "one centre, one line, one model" with a looser network. Yu also stresses that sectarianism, infighting and exclusivity persist, and that issue-based alliances sharpen the tension between immediate and long-term goals. For the CPC, Yu calls for more research on the international communist movement and on Xi Jinping's theory of a "new type of party relations". Yu urges strategic composure, summed up as not taking the lead, not raising the banner, not participating and not opposing, since some foreign parties criticise socialism with Chinese characteristics and call for a new Comintern-style body. Yu also proposes using friendly parties' support, for example their endorsement of China's pandemic response, through united-front work, International Department-led dialogue and national think tanks. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's account of the networks of foreign communist parties, with data on platforms and statements, and of how this is turned into policy advice for the Party.

Lenin's important contribution to the Marxist theory of ideology and its contemporary value 列宁对马克思主义意识形态理论的重要贡献及其当代价值 Gu Yulan Gu Yulan asks what Lenin added to Marx's theory of ideology and why it matters today. The article argues that Marx unified the critique and the construction of ideology: while criticising German, bourgeois and commodity-fetishist ideology, he built a dialectical-materialist monist view of history. Gu contends that Lenin grasped this unity, defended that view of history against rival currents, and used it to explain how socialist ideology is built. In Gu's reading, this refutes the claim that Marx's theory was purely critical. The article has three parts. The first examines Lenin's polemics against four targets: the liberal Narodniks, Bernstein's reformism, Kautsky's rejection of the dictatorship of the proletariat, and Sukhanov's dogmatism about the path of history. The second sets out how Lenin explained the building of socialist ideology. The third draws lessons for the present, running through Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping. Gu argues that each polemic defended a core Marxist idea: the materialist conception of history against Mikhailovsky, the unity of revolution and reform against Bernstein, and the unity of democracy and dictatorship against Kautsky. Against Sukhanov and Kautsky, Gu says Lenin upheld the unity of the universal and the particular, so Russia could make its revolution first and develop its productive forces afterwards. On this basis, Gu says, Lenin built socialist ideology on three Marxist tenets. Ideology has a class character, so no third kind of consciousness exists between bourgeois and socialist ideology. Theory and practice are united. The working masses are the object of ideological education, and socialist consciousness must be instilled from outside the labour movement, later through a "cultural revolution". Gu concludes that the unity of critique and construction drove theoretical innovation from Leninism to Mao Zedong Thought, Deng Xiaoping Theory and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. For the present, the article calls for upholding Marxism's guiding position in the ideological sphere. That means resisting neoliberalism, historical nihilism, Western constitutional democracy and "universal values", and tying ideological work to socialist practice in order to build an ideology with strong cohesion and guiding power. Read the original if you want a Chinese Party-theory account of how Lenin's ideological writings are used to support current ideological policy.

The significance of the Chinese road in the history of the international communist movement, seen from the "new stage of development" 从“新发展阶段”看中国道路在国际共运史上的意义 Ma Yongjun Tao Enqian Writing in early 2021, Ma Yongjun and Tao Enqian ask what the "higher stage" is to which Xi Jinping says China's socialism must advance from the primary stage of socialism, and why the new development stage demands this. They argue that the primary stage is not the "first phase of communist society" described by Marx, but a road leading towards it. The new stage, in their reading, shows the communist and internationalist character of the Chinese road and gives it significance for the international communist movement. The article has three parts. The first returns to the 13th Party Congress report (1987) to fix the meaning of the primary stage of socialism in space, time, principal contradiction and criteria for ending it. The second reads the "new development stage" (Fifth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee, 2020) as the successor of the "new era" announced at the 19th Party Congress (2017), and traces the path from Deng Xiaoping's "three-step" strategy to common prosperity. The third asks what the "higher stage" will be and what economics it needs. The authors argue that developed countries reach the first phase of communism through capitalism, whereas China, emerging from a semi-colonial and semi-feudal society, takes a socialist road that must absorb capitalist means of developing the productive forces without becoming capitalist. Hence socialism cannot be judged by textbook features but by Deng's dynamic criteria, and the road advances in a spiral, so that apparent retreats, such as the non-public sector, can be progress. They hold that non-public elements are heterogeneous parts of the socialist market economy that must serve the whole, and they criticise scholars who stretch the primary stage over generations. On this basis they argue that in conditions of relative surplus, a "needs–production" economics of common prosperity must replace the capitalist "supply–demand" economics, since capital's profit depends on relative poverty. They conclude that between 2035 and 2050 the primary stage will end and China will move towards a socialist "higher stage", possibly facing the tasks of Marx's Critique of the Gotha Programme. They contend that China would then offer developing countries a socialist road to modernization and show developed capitalist countries a communist future, while also tackling the polarisation those countries have faced since the 1960s and 1970s. Read the original if you want a detailed Chinese theoretical argument on stages of socialism, the non-public sector and common prosperity as the next phase of the Chinese road.

The contemporary predicament of capitalist globalization and its effects 论资本主义全球化的当代困境及其影响 Xie Chang'an Why has capitalist globalization, after its rapid expansion since the 1990s, fallen into serious difficulty? Writing in 2021, Xie argues that the backlash against globalization in the West, and the wider disorder there, are signs that this phase of globalization is in crisis. The article contends that the crisis is the product of Western capitalism evolving into a new stage, and that it will affect world stability. The article first sets out two main forms of contemporary capitalist globalization, using the 'production logic' and the 'capital logic'. These forms are the global production system run by transnational corporations and financial globalization led by finance capital. It then describes the predicament in three aspects and explains its causes under three headings. It ends by considering the consequences for the West and for the international order, with figures on resource use, wealth concentration and the rise of emerging economies. Xie holds that capital logic is decisive and that globalization is the global spread of the capitalist mode of production. The author identifies four relations that shape its course: labour and capital, different forms of capital, capital and the state, and state and state. The predicament is shown through weak growth and unequal wealth, a split between international monopoly capital and Western industrial oligarchs, and populist, protectionist movements such as Trump's policies. Its causes are the basic contradiction of capitalism in a new, globalized form, the resource-intensive global production system with its tendency to push labour out, and the alienation of finance capital, which is tied to US dollar hegemony. Xie concludes that the predicament and the crisis in Western states are two sides of one process, and predicts that Western states may shift the crisis outward, possibly through war. At the same time, emerging and developing countries are rising, China among them. They are reshaping global governance through bodies such as the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank, the Belt and Road Initiative and a community with a shared future for mankind. The author expects this to reduce the surplus value that Western capital draws from the world and to prompt Western containment of rivals. Read the original if you want a Marxist account of globalization, centred on finance capital and monopoly capital, that links the Western backlash and the shift in global power to capitalism's basic contradiction.

The Chinese path in the light of Marx's theory of social formations 马克思社会形态理论视域中的中国道路 Tang Aijun Tang Aijun asks how the Chinese path can be explained from the standpoint of historical materialism, and argues that this requires an accurate reading of Marx's theory of social formations. The article's thesis is that Marx's theory is neither the "five-formation" nor the "three-formation" scheme, nor their sum, but a theory centred on the mode of production that encompasses both. Read this way, it can answer two discursive traps in how the Chinese path is interpreted. The article first reviews the two main positions in Chinese scholarship: the five-formation view (primitive, slave, feudal, capitalist, socialist), defended through texts and the primacy of relations of production, and the three-formation view (dependence on persons, on things, free individuality), defended as more fundamental and more universal. It then reconstructs Marx's mode of production on three levels and uses capitalism as the worked example. Finally it applies the framework to the Chinese path, defined as the socialist modernization pursued since reform and opening up, which the author equates with socialism with Chinese characteristics. Tang distinguishes the technical form of production, the social form of production (exchange and resource allocation) and the social form of production in the sense of ownership. The five formations track ownership, the three track exchange forms, and a further "technological social formation" tracks tools and leading industries. On this basis the Chinese path is placed at three positions at once: a transition from agrarian to industrial and information society, the commodity-market stage of the second formation, and a socialist formation because public ownership remains dominant. From this Tang concludes that it is socialist, not capitalist; that skipping the capitalist "Caudine Forks" is consistent with Marx's laws because the five-stage sequence holds globally rather than for every country; and that its orientation is modernization. Tang also draws out three relationships: underdeveloped primary-stage socialism versus "developed socialism", socialism versus capitalism, and socialism versus the market economy. The author argues that socialism and capitalism now coexist in space, that the market economy is a means and socialism the goal, and that neither traditional-socialist nor Western capitalist discourse can properly judge the Chinese path. The author presents the framework as giving Marxism the interpretive authority over that path. Read the original if you want a systematic account of how a Party School theorist grounds the primary stage of socialism and the socialist market economy in Marx's mode-of-production concept.

On the wholeness of Marxism 论马克思主义的整体性 Hou Huiqin Existing discussions of the wholeness (zhengtixing) of Marxism agree that it matters, but they disagree on how to define it. Many scholars try to ground it in philosophy, political economy or scientific socialism, the "three component parts" named by Engels and Lenin. Hou Huiqin argues that each choice has an unresolved weakness and that the discussion should change course. In Hou's view, the philosophical world outlook (dialectical and historical materialism) is the key to Marxism's wholeness, and the theme of human emancipation through working-class liberation is its core. The article has three parts. The first holds that Engels's and Lenin's three-part scheme served popularisation. It traces the "new world outlook" reading through Marx's planned work on dialectics, Lenin's "single block of steel", Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping. It also criticises the "post-metaphysical turn" of Western philosophy and of Western Marxism. The second part sets out why the world's material unity makes a whole worldview possible. The third part turns to the ideas that follow from this: the proletariat, the people and the real individual, and the theme of emancipation. Hou argues that a whole worldview must solve three problems: the unity of nature, society and mind; the unity of past, present and future; and the unity of appearance, essence and being. Idealism, including Hegel's, and traditional materialism fail on these, whereas dialectical materialism, with contradiction as the source of self-movement, succeeds. From this Hou derives several claims. Political economy and scientific socialism are studies of the laws of history. Marxist categories are "contradictory concepts" that rest on experience but go beyond it. The proletariat is a scientific concept, not an empirical occupational group. Hou says Western social science rests on dogmatic assumptions about human nature. The unifying theme is that capital's polarisation and reification of people can be overcome only through the proletariat's world-historical role. Hou concludes that this theme joins Marx and Engels to their successors and explains why basic Marxist principles have not become obsolete. It also marks the main thread of contemporary Chinese Marxism and twenty-first-century Marxism. Hou ties this to the claim that upholding the Communist Party's leadership means upholding the leadership of the Chinese working class, and warns against "de-classed" talk of the people. Read the original if you want a worldview-centred account of Marxism's unity, with close use of Lenin, Mao and Deng and a sharp critique of Western Marxism and liberal social science.

The centenary course of the Communist Party of Spain and its lessons for our times 西班牙共产党的百年历程与时代启思 He Qin Marking the Communist Party of Spain's (PCE) centenary in 2021, He Qin asks what its hundred years of struggle show about the condition of communist parties in developed capitalist countries. The article presents the PCE as Spain's oldest and most influential communist party, one that has pursued an alternative to capitalism through both struggle and alliance. It concludes that the party's history carries lessons for proletarian parties more widely. The article has two parts. The first divides the twentieth century into four periods: anti-fascist struggle (1921–1939), underground struggle under Franco (1939–1977), the fight for legalisation during the democratic transition (1977–1986), and the "United Left" period from 1986. The second covers the twenty-first century. It looks at the party's congresses from the 16th (2002) to the 20th (2016–2017), its work with left alliances such as United Left and Unidas Podemos, and its positions after the Covid-19 pandemic on the EU recovery plan, Spain's institutional crisis and the crisis of capitalism. He treats the PCE's earlier compromises as the source of its decline. These include the Eurocommunist line of the late 1970s, the abandonment of Leninism in 1978 and the abolition of democratic centralism in 1991. In the author's account, blurred political identity and ideological convergence did not bring strength but deepened splits. The 20th Congress's restoration of Leninism and democratic centralism is read as the result of theoretical self-reflection. He draws three lessons. Marxism is the foundation of a proletarian party. A people's standpoint requires concrete achievements rather than slogans or reliance on anti-establishment consensus. The party must be willing to carry out self-reform (勇于自我革命). He concludes that the PCE still faces internal disunity, strategic adjustment and alliance rebuilding. He also sees its difficulties as exposing the inefficiency and disorder of capitalist parliamentary politics. Given that, in the author's words, the balance between capitalism and socialism still favours capitalism, he argues that the party can realise its "new state" proposals only by strengthening itself and addressing the people's concerns. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic assessment of a European communist party's history, with details on its congresses, alliances and post-pandemic platform.

A century of the Communist Party of China and its historical significance An interview with Cuban historian María Elena Álvarez Acosta 中国共产党百年历程及其历史意义 He Qin This is an interview, published in the centenary year of the Communist Party of China (CPC) in 2021, with María Elena Álvarez Acosta. She is a Cuban historian and professor at the Raúl Roa García Higher Institute of International Relations in Havana, and has studied Chinese history since the 1970s. The interviewer for China Social Sciences Today is He Qin of the Institute of Marxism, CASS. Álvarez argues that the Party's century of leadership has changed China's history and holds lessons for socialism worldwide. The interview runs through eight questions. They cover her research experience, the Party's role in revolution, construction and reform, the Sinicization of Marxism, the opportunities and challenges of the new era, comparisons with other communist parties, the sources of a Marxist party's vitality, the world-historical significance of the centenary, and her good wishes to the Party and the Chinese people. Álvarez says Western scholarship on Asia, Africa and the Middle East is dominated by stereotyping, which she attributes to imposed Western paradigms and Eurocentrism. She describes much Western work on China as distorted and ignorant of its traditions. She holds that China's choice of socialism and, later, of reform and opening up has to be understood through its own historical and cultural specificity. She credits the Party with combining Chinese tradition and reality, adjusting policy as conditions changed, and winning popular support. She cites the theory of the primary stage of socialism, Deng Xiaoping's "crossing the river by feeling the stones" and the three-step modernization strategy. She also praises Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, especially full and rigorous self-governance of the Party and the "Stay true to our original aspiration" campaign, as relevant to other communist parties. Álvarez concludes that a Marxist party stays vital by holding to its mission of working for the people's happiness and by acting on its word. She sees the Party's announced elimination of absolute poverty and the Belt and Road Initiative as giving hope to developing countries. She also points to shared "people-centred" values between the Chinese and Cuban parties. Read the original if you want to see how a Cuban specialist on China presents the CPC's centenary, and how Chinese media frame such foreign views.

The great leap from keeping up with the times to leading the times 从赶上时代到引领时代的伟大跨越 Yan Xiaofeng Writing in the People's Daily in 2021, in the run-up to the Party's centenary, Yan Xiaofeng takes up a formulation from Xi Jinping: that under the Party's leadership China has moved from "keeping up with the times" to "leading the times". Yan presents this as the central achievement of the Party's first hundred years. In the author's account, it shows the Party's aims of securing happiness for the people, rejuvenation for the nation and world harmony. The commentary is organised in three parts. The first traces how the Party found the correct road to national rejuvenation, from the New Democratic Revolution through socialist revolution and construction to reform and opening up. The second discusses the new era of socialism with Chinese characteristics as the marker of the leap to leading the times. The third sets out what it takes to remain at the forefront of the times. Yan's core argument is that keeping up with the times meant bringing China's development into line with the growth of productive forces, the direction of historical progress and the interests of the people. In this reading, it required establishing the socialist system and then launching reform and opening up. Leading the times, by contrast, means coordinating the strategic overall situation of national rejuvenation with the "great changes unseen in a century" in the world, so that each shapes the other. Yan adds that the leap depends on the Party's self-reform, because long-term rule brings constant risks to the Party's advanced nature and purity, and the task of leading is harder than that of catching up. Yan concludes that leadership of the times must be sustained. The author calls for unifying thought and action through Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese characteristics for a New Era, and for advancing towards the second centenary goal. This goal means building a modern socialist country by the middle of the century, with basic modernization by 2035. Yan describes Chinese modernization as socialist, as a developing country's path and as one of unprecedented scale. The author also stresses continually meeting the people's growing need for a better life. Read the original if you want a compact, official-style statement of how Party theorists framed China's historical trajectory on the eve of the centenary.

Studying Party history and grasping the political big picture 学党史和把握政治大局 Jin Chongji Writing in the People's Daily in May 2021, during the Party-wide study campaign on Party history ahead of the Party's centenary, Jin Chongji asks how Party history can help officials meet Xi Jinping's call to "grasp the political big picture". Jin takes Xi's formulation of three capacities as the framework: political judgement, political comprehension and political execution. The main claim is that, at a new historical starting point and amid what the article calls great changes unseen in a century, the key to solving concrete problems is grasping the overall political situation, and that the Party's own history is the best textbook for learning how. The article is a short commentary organised into an introduction and three sections, one for each capacity. Jin draws on episodes from the Party's history: Mao Zedong's wartime and civil-war analyses, the founding of the basic socialist system in the 1950s, Deng Xiaoping's reform-era decisions, Zhou Enlai at the 1955 Asian-African Conference, and the Party leadership under Xi Jinping. Jin cites Mao's essay "On Practice" to justify learning from indirect experience, meaning the experience of earlier generations. On political judgement, Jin argues that a sound judgement must match reality and avoid partial views. Examples are Mao's "On Protracted War" against both defeatism and quick-victory theories, his 1947 assessment of a turning point in the civil war, and Deng's judgement that China is in the primary stage of socialism. On political comprehension, Jin stresses grasping the principal contradiction and what the article calls "matters of national importance": the peasant question in the revolution, the Shenzhen special zones, and common prosperity, which Jin presents as a political issue touching the Party's basis of rule. On political execution, Jin quotes Mao on "grasping firmly", describes Zhou Enlai as combining strategic vision with diligent implementation, and names formalism and bureaucracy as the main obstacles. The remedy Jin offers is investigation among the masses and doing practical work. Jin concludes that studying Party history serves more than commemoration, because it supplies lessons that strengthen the three capacities. Officials can then open the new journey of building a modern socialist country in an all-round way and work towards the second centenary goal. Read the original if you want to see how a senior Party historian linked the 2021 history-study campaign to Xi Jinping's political requirements for cadres, using standard episodes from the Party's past.

Cultivating "civic morality" in the new era, as seen through the epidemic 透过疫情看新时代“公民道德”的培育 Sun Yingshuai Writing in early 2020 in People's Forum (Renmin Luntan, no. 4), Sun Yingshuai treats the COVID-19 epidemic as a test not only of national governance but also of civic morality and civic consciousness. The article argues that the behaviour the epidemic exposed, good and bad, shows why a healthy, modern cultivation of "civic morality" matters. Sun's answer is that this cultivation needs three foundations: an economic base, a sense of community, and a sound public space. The piece begins with the Party's guiding documents on civic morality, including the 2001 Implementation Outline and the Outline for the New Era issued after the 18th Party Congress (2012). It then moves through three headed sections: the economic basis of civic morality; the three "spirits" (scientific, rule-based and equality) that sustain community consciousness; and the interaction of Party leadership, the rule of law and social organisations. Examples come from the epidemic's "social panorama". In the first section, Sun applies the Marxist view that moral imbalance must be explained through economic relations, not ideas alone. Hoarding masks, profiteering and selling fake supplies are read as confirming Marx's remarks on capital and profit. Sun contends that China's public-ownership-based economy, in which state enterprises and public hospitals played a pillar role, allows collectivist values and the idea of the "public" to become mainstream. In the second section, Sun links panic-buying of herbal remedies and belief in conspiracy theories to a lack of scientific spirit. Defiance of quarantine rules is tied to a weak rule-based spirit, and spitting at medical staff, privilege-seeking and heavy-handed local enforcement are tied to a weak spirit of equality. Sun concludes that cultivating civic morality requires strengthening the economic base, fostering community consciousness through the three spirits, and building a public space through Party leadership, the combination of rule by law and rule by virtue, and healthy social organisations. The goal is a spiritual civilisation grounded in legal rules and public order and good customs. Read the original if you want an example of how Chinese Party-affiliated scholarship in early 2020 tied pandemic behaviour to Marxist moral theory and to governance policy.

Carrying forward the Xibaipo spirit and taking the new era's "examination" road well 弘扬西柏坡精神 走好新时代“赶考”路 Yang Jing Sun Yingshuai This commentary, first published in Guangming Daily on 19 August 2020, asks how the Communist Party of China should draw on the "Xibaipo spirit" in the new era. Xibaipo was the Party Central Committee's base before it moved to Beijing in 1949, when Mao Zedong spoke of going to the capital to "sit an examination". Yang and Sun argue that, as Xi Jinping said in 2013, the Party's "examination" is far from over. They hold that the Xibaipo spirit has gained new vitality in keeping the Party's style, its ties with the people and its purity. The article is organised into four sections, each linking a Xibaipo-era principle to present tasks. These are modesty and hard struggle (the "Two Musts"), daring and being skilled at struggle, strict discipline and rigorous Party governance, and vigilance in times of peace together with continuous effort. Each section briefly recalls the Xibaipo period and the Party's record since 1949 before turning to the new era. Yang and Sun argue that the Two Musts remain relevant against formalism and bureaucracy, and call for strict implementation of the Central Committee's eight-point regulation. On struggle, they cite a world undergoing "changes unseen in a century" and Xi's call for struggle across fields from Party governance to national security. On discipline, they credit the 18th Party Congress (2012) and later measures with building a supervision and discipline system that has found a way to escape the "historical cycle" of rise and decline. They connect these measures to the Party's political leadership. The authors conclude that the Party must keep the spirit of "going to the capital for the examination", staying vigilant and working continuously. They call on it to face the "four tests" and overcome the "four dangers", and to pursue full and rigorous self-governance of the Party in order to achieve the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party commentary in 2020 used Xibaipo history to frame the Party's current tasks of discipline, struggle and self-building.

What kind of internet innovation thinking does the new era need? 新时代需要何种互联网创新思维 Zhang Jianyun Writing in People's Forum (2020, no. 17), Zhang Jianyun asks why Xi Jinping stresses "innovation thinking" and what form it should take in the internet age. The article argues that big data, the internet, cloud computing, blockchain and intelligent machines mark a qualitative leap in the productive forces, so that thinking, production and social management must all be transformed accordingly. The piece has three sections. The first explains, from a historical-materialist standpoint, why Xi emphasises innovation thinking, citing his speeches from 2015 onward. The second sets out what the new productive forces demand, centred on innovation in applied technology. The third identifies two defining features of internet-era innovation, which Zhang calls "subversive" and "popular", and draws out their significance. Zhang begins from Marx's point that tools of production distinguish social epochs, and treats the internet toolset as comparable to the steam engine and electricity. Applied-technology innovation, meaning putting everything "online" as electrification once put everything on the grid, is described as the core, hardest and most practically meaningful kind. Examples include smart agriculture, automated manufacturing, online government and services, and the "Internet Plus" strategy launched in 2015. The article then argues that internet innovation is disruptive: it is said to merge production and consumption under consumer-led demand, make planned production achievable on the basis of big data, and replace pyramid-style command structures with flat, self-organising networks. It is also popular: cheap information, cloud services and maker spaces allow ordinary people, not only experts, to innovate. Zhang concludes that big data and the internet will bring humanity into an "informatised socialist era", just as machinery and electricity ushered in industrial capitalism. Innovation must therefore be systemic, and the creativity of the masses should be encouraged, in line with Xi's call to respect the masses' pioneering spirit as a key to socialism's prosperity. Read the original if you want to see how a 2020 Party-theory commentary links Xi Jinping's statements on innovation to historical materialism and to optimistic claims about the internet economy.

The significance and lessons of the Chinese path for modernization in developing countries 中国道路对发展中国家现代化建设的意义和启示 Sun Yingshuai Writing in 2020 after seventy years of the People's Republic, Sun Yingshuai asks what other developing countries can learn from the Chinese path to modernization. The article starts from the Fourth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2019) and Xi Jinping's report to the 19th Party Congress (2017). Both present socialism with Chinese characteristics as offering a new option to countries that want faster development while keeping their independence. Sun's thesis is that these countries can draw on China's development paths, but must also recognise how their own economic, strategic and leadership conditions differ from China's. The article has two main parts. The first identifies three paths worth borrowing: independent development, leapfrog development and common development. The second asks latecomer countries to face three differences from China: the structure of the economy, the strategic position of the state, and the quality of political leadership. Sun draws on Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping, Xi Jinping and Marx, and on Alexander Gerschenkron's theory of latecomer advantage. Comparisons are made with the Soviet Union, post-Soviet Russia, India, South Africa, the Philippines and Indonesia. On the first part, Sun argues that China moved from imitating the Soviet model to seeking a path suited to its own conditions, and that other countries should likewise avoid dogmatism and copying. China's experience of using latecomer advantages, such as opening up, market-oriented reform and the new wave of information technology, is described as a way to avoid the pain of the "Caudine Forks" of capitalist development. Sun adds that in an age when peace and development are the main themes of the era, modernization can no longer rely on colonial plunder. In the second part, Sun contends that China's public-ownership-based economic system, its complete industrial system (39 major, 191 medium and 525 minor categories in the UN classification, according to the article) and its size as a large power give it advantages that few latecomers share. Sun also stresses the Communist Party's leadership core, arguing that China's success owes much to Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping, and contrasts Gorbachev and the leaders of other communist parties. Sun concludes that other developing countries should not copy China. They should instead locate their own advantages in global industrial chains, ideally through close links with China's economy and market. They should also widen their strategic horizons and develop capable teams and leaders from their own social practice. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese scholar presents the "Chinese path" as a reference point for latecomer states, and how the argument ties development strategy to leadership and the Party.

The world significance of institution-building on China's road to modernization 中国现代化道路上制度建设的世界意义 Sun Yingshuai Sun Yingshuai asks what China's institution-building on its road to modernization offers to other countries. Writing in 2020, after the Fourth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2019) adopted its decision on upholding and improving the socialist system, Sun argues that the system, state governance and governance capacity built up under Communist Party leadership give developing countries a new path to modernization. The article presents this as relevant above all to countries that want faster development while keeping their independence. The article begins with the search for a modernization path since the Opium War of 1840, and with what Sun calls the "two miracles" of rapid growth and long-term stability. It then criticises Western modernization theory for equating modernization with "Westernization" or "capitalization". The main body has three parts, which treat the economic foundation, the framework of institutions across all fields, and the political leadership of the Party. A short conclusion places the argument within Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Sun's central contrast is with developing countries that adopted Western models wholesale: private ownership, free markets, separation of powers and a break with their own traditions. In Sun's account these countries met political disorder, economic decline and a loss of governing capacity. China is said to have avoided this by combining socialism with a market economy in its basic economic system, with public ownership as the mainstay, and by building coordinated political, cultural, social and ecological institutions rather than copying Western ones. These include the people's congress system, multiparty cooperation under Party leadership, and an ecological civilization system. Sun treats Party leadership as the decisive advantage. In this reading, the Party supplies the "political guidance" that keeps a country from the economic divisions and political polarization Sun attributes to some other states and to multiparty, decentralised systems in developed countries. Sun concludes that China's institutional experience is a set of innovations that can serve as a reference system for developing countries, and that deeper reform will require more institution-building. The article closes by calling for China and other developing countries to exchange experience and learn from one another's institutions, so as to turn institutional strengths into effective governance. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese scholarship in 2020 framed the international relevance of China's governance model as an alternative to Western modernization.

Three issues in the study of Marx's On the Jewish Question 马克思《论犹太人问题》研究中的三个论题 Liu Xiongwei Liu Xiongwei takes up three questions that have dominated debate over Marx's On the Jewish Question, written in 1843 during the Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher period. Was Marx an anti-Semite? Did his critique of Bruno Bauer's theological framing mean he no longer treated the Jewish question as a religious one? And does his Jewish origin keep his philosophy bound to Jewish civilisation? Liu argues that recent Chinese responses are fragmentary and sets out to clarify the core of each problem. The article reviews positions from Edmund Silberner, Walter Laqueur, Isaac Deutscher, Michael Polanyi, Mehring, Liebknecht, Löwith and others. It has three main sections, one per question, and a short closing section. Liu places the text in the German context of the 1830s and 1840s and in the longer course of Marx's thought, up to The German Ideology and Capital. On the first question, Liu holds that neither the historical setting nor the text supports the anti-Semitism charge. Marx's sharp remarks target Judaism as a religion and the self-interest of some West European Jewish merchants, whom Liu reads as a vehicle for criticising capitalism. Marx's other writings, including his 1842 letter on anti-Jewish articles and his 1843 petition for the Cologne Jewish community, show sympathy. On the second, Liu says Marx shared Bauer's view that religion must be abolished, but Bauer treated the issue as purely theological and abstract. For Marx, political emancipation in France and North America left religion intact in private life and civil society, so emancipation needs the social conditions that sustain religion to be overcome. On the third, Liu accepts that Messianic ideas and Hebrew Bible notions of labour left traces in Marx. Liu nonetheless concludes that Marx, a firm atheist and Young Hegelian, went beyond Jewish civilisation. His limited knowledge of political economy at that stage explains why he used 'Jewish spirit' to depict capitalism. Liu concludes that the influence of Judaism on Marx should not be exaggerated. In the closing section Liu holds that the human emancipation raised in this text became Marx's lifelong task. The principle that social being determines consciousness grew out of the idea that civil society determines the political state and religion. The communism of Capital is described as a scientific deepening of the same ideal. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly rebuttal of the anti-Semitism reading of Marx, with a survey of Western and Chinese literature on the early Marx.

A brief analysis of the ideas on the city in Engels's The Origin of the Family, Private Property and the State 浅析《家庭、私有制和国家的起源》中的城市思想 Meng Ruixia Engels's The Origin of the Family, Private Property and the State (1884) is usually read as a work on the family and the state. Meng Ruixia argues that Engels's account of how the state arose is also an account of how the city arose, and that the book therefore carries ideas about urban development that remain relevant today. The article appeared in the journal Development in 2020. The article is built as a guided reading of the book, following Engels's own order. It begins with his debt to Lewis Henry Morgan's Ancient Society and with the prefaces of 1884 and 1891, including his discussion of Bachofen, McLennan and Morgan on early family history. It then takes in the stages of savagery and barbarism, the forms of family and marriage, the clan among the Iroquois, and the emergence of the state, with Athens as the main case. Meng's central move is to link the book's sequence of private property, class division and state formation to the rise of the city. In this reading, social division of labour, commodity production, the appearance of merchants and metal money, and the concentration of wealth dissolved the clan order. Engels's definition of the state as a public power separate from the mass of the people, with territorial division of subjects and walled towns, is taken as a description of the city as well. Meng cites the French writer Fustel de Coulanges, for whom families, phratries and tribes combined into the city, and concludes that without cities there would be no state. The article adds that the separation of town and country, the greatest division between material and mental labour, is a product of a particular mode of production, and that Marx did not expect it to last for ever. Meng concludes that the twenty-first century is an age of cities, that urban research and urban cultural development cannot do without Marx, and that Marx and Engels, though they wrote no separate work on cities, left basic positions that offer guidance for Chinese urban development. Meng points in particular to resolving the opposition between town and country through their integration, and to urban policy centred on people's harmonious development and on the living conditions of the urban poor. Read the original if you want a short Chinese-language reading of Engels's Origin as a source for Marxist urban thought, or want to see how this classic text is linked to contemporary Chinese urban policy.

Moses Hess and the formation of Marx's thought revisited: the limits of Hess's influence and Marx's conscious critique of Hess 赫斯与马克思思想形成关系再探——赫斯影响马克思的限度与马克思对赫斯的自觉批判 Zou Shipeng Since the 1960s, international scholarship has sharply raised Moses Hess's standing in the making of Marxism, with some researchers treating him as a founder of Marxism and a few suggesting that Marx borrowed from him. Zou asks how far Hess actually shaped Marx's thought and where Marx consciously criticised and surpassed him. The article, published in Fudan Journal in 2020, argues that Hess influenced Marx mainly in radicalism, that this influence was limited, and that treating Hess as a founder of Marxism is an overreach. Zou first reviews the literature. The mainstream Marxist tradition, from Marx and Engels to Lenin, Mehring and Annenkov, limited Hess's role. Lukács called him a failed forerunner of Marxism. The revaluation since the 1960s is linked to the Spinoza revival around Althusser and his successors, to the historical-critical edition of Marx and Engels, and to the rise of Marx studies. The article then has three parts: Hess's place in Marx's formation; Marx's critique and transcendence of Hess; and the political and practical consequences of that break. Zou makes three main moves. First, ontology and philosophy of history: Hess leaned towards spirit over nature, in a Spinozist and Bauerian vein, and ended in a cyclical "sacred history of mankind", whereas Marx from his doctoral dissertation put nature first and moved to a materialist analysis of human history. Second, practice: Hess's philosophy of action, resting on Fichte and Cieszkowski, remained idealist, abstract and moralistic, while Marx's concept of practice joins transforming the world with understanding it. Marx also made the proletariat the historical subject, whereas Hess's nationalism, later Zionism, and his petty-bourgeois intellectual radicalism are said to link him to anarchism and Blanquism. Third, Zou argues that Marx deliberately stopped at radical democracy to avoid being confused with such left radicalism, and that the German Ideology's critique of Stirner and of "true" socialism was aimed at obstacles to historical materialism. Zou concludes that Hess was an intermediate link from the Young Hegelians through Feuerbach to Marx and an important figure in the pre-history of Marxism. Marx's critique of Hess's philosophy of action and "true" socialism was completed before his thought matured, and Hess cannot be counted among its founders. Zou adds that the Althusserian Spinoza revival seems intended to raise Hess and lower Marx, and leaves its assessment to a later article. Read the original if you study the Marx–Hess relationship, the Young Hegelian dissolution, or Chinese scholarly responses to Western debates on Marx's origins.

Ellen Meiksins Wood's "Political Marxism" and its general critique of capitalism: a textual reading based on the Communist Manifesto 艾伦·伍德“政治马克思主义”的资本主义总体批判探析——基于《共产党宣言》的文本学解读 Feng Wangzhou Feng Wangzhou examines how Ellen Meiksins Wood, together with Robert Brenner a leading figure of "Political Marxism", reads the Communist Manifesto as a general critique of capitalism. The article argues that Wood develops this critique along four lines: the bourgeoisie, historical materialism, the nation-state and socialism. Feng contends that her reading helps readers grasp the nature of contemporary capitalism and the prospects for a revival of socialism. The article first introduces Political Marxism, which emerged in the 1970s and has three generations of scholars. Feng describes its method as clarifying the basic concepts of historical materialism and giving prominence to social property relations. It also stresses the historical specificity of capitalism and the separation of the "economic" from the "political". The main section then sets out Wood's four dimensions in turn. A closing section assesses her work, names theoretical gaps, and draws lessons for China and for socialism in the twenty-first century. On the bourgeoisie, Feng reports Wood's claim that capitalism and the bourgeoisie must not be equated. In her view the bourgeoisie is both revolutionary and destructive. Feng adds that, on Wood's account, English capitalism arose from competitive pressures on agrarian producers, not from a rising bourgeois class, and that the French Revolution was led largely by officials and professionals. On historical materialism, capitalism's compulsion to accumulate and maximise profit yields enormous productive capacity alongside a persistent gap with quality of life. Its separation of politics from economics allows it to tolerate formal democracy while leaving economic inequality untouched. On the nation-state, Wood rejects the thesis that globalisation dissolves it, arguing that global capital increasingly depends on territorial states. On socialism, she holds that the working class remains the only force able to transform capitalism, and that socialism requires real democracy. Feng judges Wood's critique comprehensive and profound, and credits her with exposing the fallacy of the "bourgeois paradigm". Feng also identifies three gaps: the shift to post-Fordist and automated production, the contradictory tide of globalisation and "anti-globalisation", and the position of the nation-state, especially in developing countries. Feng draws two lessons: the working class retains its revolutionary role against post-Marxist claims, and capitalism's contradictions are intensifying in an era of neoliberalism and new imperialism. The article presents socialism with Chinese characteristics as evidence of socialism's renewed vitality. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's systematic account of Political Marxism and how it is received and evaluated in Chinese academic debate.

The Marxist basic principles discipline after fifteen years: a review of theoretical research and outlook 马克思主义基本原理学科15年来理论研究的回顾与展望 Zhang Jianyun Zhang Jianyun takes stock of theoretical research in the discipline of the basic principles of Marxism, which was established in 2005 as a second-level discipline within the first-level discipline of Marxist theory. Zhang argues that fifteen years of work produced solid results on foundational questions, but that since about 2016 research has hit a bottleneck. In Zhang's view the discipline still lacks a distinctive problem domain and research paradigm, and the way out lies in genuinely holistic research tied to new productive forces. The article has three parts. The first surveys 2005–2015, when scholars worked on the discipline's nature and status, the definition and content of basic principles, the wholeness of Marxism, the structure of the principles system, practical application, study of the classics, and staffing and teaching. The second diagnoses the current bottleneck, citing a sharp fall in China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI) results for topics such as basic principles and the wholeness of Marxism.
