It argues that the New Left sat between the Communist Party and Labour's left wing, pushed both to renew themselves, and left a diversifying legacy, but was weakened by its own theoretical and organisational flaws. The article first sketches the development of each current: the New Left, which emerged after Khrushchev's 1956 secret speech and faded under neoliberalism from the late 1970s; the Communist Party, founded in 1920 and split several times before its 1991 transformation; and Labour, founded in 1900 and repositioned as a centrist party under Tony Blair. It then compares them along four linked dimensions: attitude to Marxism (theoretical basis), the kind of socialism sought (value orientation), strategy for achieving it (economic, political and tactical), and place in the left spectrum (historical position). Huang treats each dimension as shaping the next. On theory, the Communist Party rested on scientific socialism, Labour on democratic socialism and Fabianism, and the New Left combined Marxist humanism with ethical socialism and native radicalism. Huang argues that Labour's nationalisation and universal welfare amounted to a "welfare capitalism" that left private ownership intact, a view the author attributes to the Communists and the New Left. The Communist Party's 1951 programme proposed a peaceful transition to socialism, which Huang says overestimated socialist elements in Labour governments. The New Left proposed "peaceful plus revolutionary" change, but its humanist socialism, in Huang's judgement, lacked an economic analysis and fell into utopianism. Huang places the currents from left to right as Communist Party, New Left, Labour left, Labour right. Huang credits the New Left with a bridging role: it carried over traditional left features, encouraged diverse social movements and influenced history, sociology, politics and cultural studies. The author also lists its limits: no systematic theory, elitism, loose organisation and little attention to Marx's analysis of capitalist economic laws. The article closes by noting four general weaknesses of the Western left (blurred identity, fragmentation, weak theory, more critique than construction). It argues that, after the 2008 financial crisis, twenty-first-century socialists should use Marx's analytical and critical tools. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly comparison of the postwar British left and its lessons for the Western left.

Western left-wing scholars' critique of contemporary capitalism: the COVID-19 pandemic as an occasion 西方左翼学者的当代资本主义批判：以新冠肺炎疫情为契机 Xie Changfei This article, published in 2020 in Mao Zedong Deng Xiaoping Theory Studies, reviews how Western left-wing scholars responded to the COVID-19 pandemic. Xie Changfei treats the pandemic, following Alain Badiou's notion of an event as a 'site', as an occasion of world-historical significance that exposes the contradictions of capitalism. The review aims to show how these discussions deepen understanding of capitalist contradictions and invite a fresh reading of Marx on capitalist crisis. Xie groups the debates into five themes: the logic of capital revealed in the origin of and response to the pandemic; the poor efficiency of 'cost-benefit' reasoning; the shortages of public goods caused by neoliberalism's hostility to government and praise of the free market; questions of natural life, the legitimacy of wealth production and social justice; and the historical opportunity for a 'new form of communism'. The text proceeds in three parts: the institutional and cultural predicament the pandemic exposes, the new agenda of re-appropriating reproduction, and new trends of solidarity, justice and internationalism. Thinkers cited include Chomsky, Žižek, Negri, Badiou, Agamben, Buzgalin and the epidemiologist Rob Wallace. In Xie's account, these scholars argue that capital's logic severs humans from nature and from their own natural life, and that profit-driven health systems, shaped by neoliberalism and Reagan's dictum that government is the problem, left the poor unprotected. In response, many call for changing the mode of production and for workers to re-appropriate reproduction, meaning the whole socialised process of production, through organised struggle. They also call for non-market ways of producing and distributing resources, for example requisitioning hoarded masks, and for a community that overcomes the isolation the pandemic produces. Because disease does not discriminate, they say, social justice must be equally indiscriminate, resting on socialised production under workers' control; and closed nationalism must give way to internationalist cooperation. Xie judges that this work offers theoretical guidance and a basis for struggle by the world's proletariat and left parties, and that it has a positive role in advancing struggle and unity. Xie also notes a shortcoming: most of these thinkers lack effective practical strategies for escaping capitalism, for organising the proletariat and left organisations, and for leading global cooperation against the pandemic. Even so, Xie sees their continued summoning of the 'spectre of Marxism' as progressive. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist scholar's overview of how Western left thinkers read the pandemic, and how that reading is assessed.

Foreign left-wing thought and movements under the COVID-19 pandemic An overview of research on the foreign left in 2020 新冠肺炎疫情下国外左翼思潮与运动研究——2020年国外左翼思想研究概览 Lei Xiaohuan This review, published in Scientific Socialism (issue 1, 2021), surveys foreign left-wing thought and movements in 2020 and Chinese scholarship on them. Lei starts from the claim that the pandemic exposed the basic contradiction of capitalism more openly. According to the review, foreign left scholars saw a favourable moment for revolution and called for a worldwide resistance movement and for socialism. The review has four parts. It first lists the year's main events: the Marxism Festival in London, the 30th anniversary of the São Paulo Forum, and two Beijing events, a conference on China's anti-epidemic effort and the 11th World Socialism Forum. It then covers the main theoretical themes: commemoration of Engels (200th birth anniversary) and Lenin (150th), critiques of contemporary capitalism and of racial capitalism, debates on socialism, and assessments of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Finally it surveys Chinese studies of the left in North America, Europe, Russia, the Middle East, Africa, Asia and Latin America. Lei reports that Engels's dialectics of nature drew attention during the pandemic, citing John Bellamy Foster and Paul Blackledge on ecology. Pandemic critiques, by Foster, David Matthews, Meredeth Turshen and Annie Thébaud-Mony, trace the crisis to neoliberal health systems and to profit-driven finance capital. Nancy Fraser describes capitalism as an institutionalised social order with three crisis tendencies, and Monthly Review authors treat the George Floyd protests through racial capitalism. Foreign figures such as Gyula Thürmer, Radivoje Dizdarevic and Andrea Catone are cited as praising the institutional strengths of socialism with Chinese characteristics, including its pandemic response. Lei concludes that foreign leftists identify a triple crisis: the pandemic, recession and ecological crisis. In the closing reflections Lei judges that the foreign left is starting to leave the "crisis of critique" it has been in since the 1990s and is returning to real social movements, citing the Yellow Vests and Black Lives Matter. Lei adds that it must adjust its theory and strategy and turn social and workers' movements into socialist ones, noting that some authors say the working class still lacks revolutionary consciousness. On Chinese research, Lei finds coverage uneven and mostly descriptive, giving African anti-capitalist movements as a neglected case. Lei calls for deeper analysis and for judgements about where these movements are heading. Read the original if you want a map of Chinese-language scholarship on the foreign left in 2020 and a bibliography of related journal articles.

Western left responses to the COVID-19 epidemic and the development of socialism 新冠肺炎疫情下西方左翼的应对与社会主义发展态势 Zhao Ting Yang Jingxuan Writing in 2020, Zhao Ting and Yang Jingxuan ask how Western left forces, chiefly communist and workers' parties and left-wing scholars, responded to COVID-19, and what this implies for the world socialist movement after the epidemic. They argue that the epidemic, which they present as a systemic crisis of capitalism rather than a technical or public-health failure, has opened favourable conditions for socialism. They also say that serious obstacles remain. The article has three main parts plus a conclusion. The first surveys five types of left response: analysing the epidemic's roots, criticising bourgeois governments' policies, organising self-help and mutual aid, building united fronts and strikes, and coordinating internationally. The second looks at the post-epidemic period, and the third at the difficulties the movement still faces. Evidence comes mainly from statements and actions of parties in Europe, the Americas, Turkey and Bangladesh, and from thinkers such as Noam Chomsky, Stephen Walt, Max Elbaum and Aleksandr Buzgalin. In the authors' account, left analysts trace the epidemic to capitalist ecological destruction and neoliberal privatisation of health care, and they accuse governments of shifting the burden of crisis onto workers. The authors then identify three conditions favouring socialism after the epidemic. These are a shift of international power towards the East, a globalisation at a crossroads, and a renewed contest between the two systems, in which China, Cuba and Vietnam serve as points of comparison. They add that neoliberalism is declining, that young people are moving left, and that party memberships are growing. Against this, they note that the 'strong capitalism, weak socialism' pattern has not changed. They also point to a divided left, for example over supporting Joe Biden, and to weak radical left parties. The authors conclude that the epidemic again shows capitalist crisis never goes away and that a socialist alternative is needed. They say the Western left and socialist states form a community of shared fortunes, and that socialism's identity rests on putting people first, public medicine and internationalism. They expect the post-epidemic movement to seek development paths suited to each country's conditions under the banner of internationalism. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic view of how Western left parties acted during the 2020 epidemic and how they assessed the prospects of socialism.

The inner logic of the epic struggle of New China over more than 70 years 新中国70多年感天动地奋斗史诗的内在逻辑 Gong Yun Writing in 2021, the centenary year of the Communist Party, Gong Yun asks how the history of New China should be understood as a whole, given its division into the periods before and after the reform and opening up that began in 1978. The article answers that the two periods are an inseparable, unified whole that is consistent in essence. It follows Xi Jinping's formula that neither period may be used to negate the other, and it presents this as a guard against historical nihilism. The article has three parts. The first sets out four forms of consistency between the periods: the nature of society, the social system, Party leadership, and the Party's founding mission. The second argues that the periods are continuous and that the earlier one supplied the later one with its foundations. The third explains why handling the relationship correctly matters for upholding and developing socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era. Gong draws throughout on statements by Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping and on the 1981 Party resolution on history. Gong holds that the pre-1978 period gave the later one its political premise and institutional base, its material and technological base, its theoretical preparation, positive and negative experience, and a favourable international environment. As evidence the article cites industrial and output growth figures for 1949–1978 and the policy ideas of the Mao era, including the "second integration" of Marxism with Chinese conditions. Reform and opening up, in this reading, continued, reformed and developed earlier socialist exploration. Gong also states that the two periods differ markedly in guiding thought, policy and conditions. He describes the relationship as a spiral ascent and as a sublation that keeps the basic socialist system while overturning ideas and institutions unsuited to the productive forces. Gong concludes that the relationship between the two periods is above all a political question. Handling it properly, he argues, helps people grasp the theme, main line and mainstream of New China's history, and it does not require ignoring past errors. It also deepens understanding of the laws of Party governance and of socialist construction, strengthens the Four-sphere Confidence, and builds consensus around the second centenary goal. He warns that hostile forces attack the history of the revolution and of New China in order to confuse people. Read the original if you want a representative statement of the official Party-history line on the "two periods" question, with the main supporting quotations from Mao, Deng and Xi.

The São Paulo Forum at thirty: adjustment and unity of the Latin American left 从圣保罗论坛30周年看拉美左翼的调整与联合 He Qin Marking the thirtieth anniversary of the São Paulo Forum in July 2020, He Qin asks what the Forum's history shows about the trajectory of the Latin American left since the collapse of the Soviet Union. The article argues that the Forum has been the region's main platform for reflection, for the search for alternatives to neoliberalism and for regional unity, but that it now faces hard choices between unity and division and between struggle and compromise. The article first describes the Forum's founding in 1990, at the initiative of Brazil's Workers' Party and with the involvement of Lula and Fidel Castro. It then divides its development into three phases: a founding period (1990–97), a flourishing period (1998–2009) coinciding with the 'pink tide', and a period of stagnation from 2010. It reviews the organisational structure, membership of 123 parties and organisations, host countries, and the main documents of 2017–19. A section covers the Forum's declaration on the Covid-19 pandemic of May 2020. He credits the Forum with pluralism, solidarity and the pursuit of alternatives as its core principles, and with giving the left a platform during the 1990s low tide. The author also identifies historical limitations. In He's account, the loose organisation, shifting membership and persistent disagreement over socialism mean the Forum's documents lack a Marxist analysis of history and reality and give weak guidance to member parties. He sorts the left into armed-revolutionary currents, radical governments that did not change the peripheral capitalist base, and moderate reformists, and cites Atilio Borón's view that there is no socialism without an anti-capitalist revolution. He concludes that neither armed revolution nor parliamentary struggle currently offers a mature path, and calls on the Latin American left to rely on working people, raise its theoretical level, strengthen organisation and adjust its tactics. Its common mission, in He's phrasing, is to seek alternatives through development and development through alternatives, and the move from regional capital integration to integration of the peoples will be long. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic account of the São Paulo Forum's history, documents and internal divisions, or an example of how Chinese Marxist scholars assess the Latin American left.

The Paris Commune revolution and the Paris Commune in the broad perspective of the international communist movement 国际共产主义运动大视野下的巴黎公社革命和巴黎公社 Lin Jianhua Written for the 150th anniversary of the Paris Commune, this article asks what the Commune of 1871 means when viewed across the whole history of the international communist movement. Lin Jianhua argues that the Commune was a rehearsal for Soviet Russia, that the short-lived proletarian regimes after the October Revolution re-enacted the Commune, and that Party building, state-power building and socialist construction form the permanent themes of the movement. The article is organised in three sections. The first places the Commune after the 1848 revolutions and recounts its 72 days, from the National Guard's takeover on 18 March to the 'Bloody Week' of May, together with the local communes in other French cities. The second surveys later short-lived workers' regimes: Finland, Bremen, Bavaria, Hungary, Slovakia and the Chinese Soviet Republic, followed by the socialist states founded around the Second World War. The third turns to the 'three-part movement' of founding a party, seizing power and building socialism. Lin's core move is to treat the Commune as the first genuine working-class regime of a socialist character, and so as the true marker of socialism's passage from theory to system, which Lin says is usually credited to 1917. Citing Marx and Lenin, Lin stresses its two measures against officials becoming masters of society: universal election with recall, and worker-level pay. Lin presents Soviet power as the Commune's heir and the Commune as 'the blossom' to Russia's 'fruit', in Mao Zedong's 1926 words. Lin also holds that the Commune's lack of a proletarian party limited its achievements, and that the brief regimes of 1918–19 repeat its short life. Lin concludes that communist parties must apply Marxism to national conditions, keep democratic centralism and strengthen full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, since gaining power is hard and keeping it harder. Lin points to the loss of power in the Commune, in the 1918–19 regimes and in the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe around 1991. Lin presents socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era, with deepening reform and opening up, as the latest stage of this history. Read the original if you want a Chinese Party-scholar's long-view periodisation of the communist movement that links the Commune, the Soviets and the Chinese Soviet Republic to the present.

An action guide for jointly building a better world 共建更加美好世界的行动指南 Jin Xin Prompted by the publication of Xi Jinping's article "Jointly Building a Community with a Shared Future for Mankind" in the first 2021 issue of Qiushi, Jin Xin presents the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind as both a concept and a practical guide. The author argues that the idea answers the question of what kind of world should be built and how, and that it has won broad international support. The piece, published in Red Flag Manuscripts (Hongqi Wengao) in 2021, has four sections. It traces how Xi developed the idea from 2012 onwards, sets out the concrete proposals China has put forward, reviews China's practical contributions, and ends with directions for the future. Jin draws on Xi's speeches at Moscow, the UN General Assembly, Geneva, the World Health Assembly and the UN's 75th anniversary summit, and on remarks by UN officials. Jin argues that the idea is a Chinese answer to the "question of our times" posed by a world of unilateralism, protectionism, hegemonism and a headwind against economic globalization. In the article's account, the "five persistences" and "five worlds" outlined in Geneva in 2017 form the framework of the idea, which also draws on traditional Chinese values such as harmony among all nations. The proposals are grouped under security, globalization, civilizations, ecology and China's path of peaceful development. Jin credits China with action as well as words, citing poverty alleviation for nearly 100 million people, high-quality Belt and Road cooperation, support for multilateral trade, and anti-epidemic aid to more than 150 countries. The author also lists the bilateral and regional communities China has agreed with partners. Jin concludes that the idea has become a widely welcomed public good and a shared aspiration, with a deepening basis in international public opinion. The author calls for making fuller use of multilateral bodies such as the UN, G20 and WHO. Jin also calls for upholding common values of all humanity, and for China to keep leading by example, including by treating its COVID-19 vaccine as a global public good and deepening Belt and Road cooperation. Read the original if you want to see how a Party journal in 2021 summarised the development, content and practical record of the community-with-a-shared-future concept.

Pushing global governance towards greater fairness and rationality 推动全球治理体制更加公正合理 Luo Laijun Writing in early 2021, Luo Laijun takes up the question of how the global governance system, which the author describes as undergoing great adjustment, change and transformation, can be made fairer and more rational. Emerging economies have become a major new force, new global challenges keep appearing, and existing arrangements show fatigue and retreat. Luo argues that China, as a responsible major country, is willing and able to offer a Chinese approach and Chinese wisdom for reform. The article takes as its guide Xi Jinping's January 2021 address to the World Economic Forum's "Davos Agenda" dialogue, which calls for multilateralism and a community with a shared future for mankind. The short commentary is organised around three principles. The first is a governance mechanism that is plural, equal, inclusive and win-win. The second is a world cooperation pattern of coexistence, joint governance and sharing. The third is building a community with a shared future for mankind. Each section combines extended quotations from Xi with the author's account of Chinese practice in institutions such as the IMF, the World Bank, the UN, the G20, the BRICS bloc and the Belt and Road Initiative. Luo contends that the existing system is in difficulty because it has not adapted to the new global pattern, in which one dominant state or a few hegemonic powers can no longer run world affairs. Reform, in this reading, means improving the system rather than tearing it down, so that it better reflects the interests of emerging markets and developing countries. Luo credits China with pushing for greater voting and decision-making power for these countries, helping to found the BRICS New Development Bank and proposing a "BRICS+" model. The author also names obstacles: some emerging economies have weakened, developing countries are unevenly developed, and their own cooperation mechanisms need strengthening. Against Cold War thinking, zero-sum games and beggar-thy-neighbour policies, Luo sets common consultation, equal rights, opportunities and rules for all states, and shared development gains. Luo concludes that the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind gives global governance its basic direction. The author says the idea has been written into United Nations resolutions and is widely endorsed by member states. China, Luo adds, backs it with action: helping to draft international rules, for example in global internet governance, and supplying platforms such as the Belt and Road Initiative. Read the original if you want a compact example of how a Red Flag commentary in 2021 presented China's role in reforming global governance, built around Xi Jinping's Davos speech.

Developments among foreign communist parties under the COVID-19 pandemic 新冠肺炎疫情下外国共产党的发展变化 Yu Haiqing Chen Airu This survey reviews how foreign communist parties developed in 2020, when the global spread of COVID-19 acted as a major external variable. Yu and Chen argue that the pandemic changed how these parties operate, pushing activity online and bringing pandemic issues onto their agendas. They also contend that the parties kept their traditional concerns, priorities and struggle goals. The authors identify the year's main feature as continuity and change together: passing on revolutionary spirit, widening room to operate, planning ahead and defending what they call just causes. The article is organised in five thematic sections, each built on cases from many countries. It first covers commemorations of Lenin's 150th birthday, Engels's 200th and the 75th anniversaries of events of the Second World War. It then turns to parties marking their centenaries, including those of Turkey, Iran, Britain, India, France and Australia. Further sections cover elections and left cooperation, ruling parties in Vietnam, Laos, North Korea and Cuba together with party congresses elsewhere, and finally campaigning on pandemic, anti-hegemony and solidarity issues. On elections and unity, Yu and Chen report mixed results. They cite gains for the Austrian communists, a slight rise for the Russian Federation party and a large win for the Communist Party of India (Marxist)-led front in Kerala. They contrast these with the Czech Bohemia-Moravia party's sharp fall and with French communist gains that came alongside the loss of traditional strongholds. They describe growing flexibility in left alliances, such as in Bihar, alongside new splits, such as in Nepal. Among ruling parties, they credit Vietnam's pandemic-era growth to balancing epidemic control with economic development. They also report Laos's first recession since the Asian financial crisis and Cuba's losses attributed to US sanctions. On the struggle front, the authors say foreign communist parties backed China's pandemic response, criticised Western governments and argued that capitalism itself drives the spread of the virus. They also opposed outside interference in Belarus and blockades of Cuba and Venezuela, backed anti-racist protests, and led strikes in India. Yu and Chen conclude that the parties remain weak in domestic politics and are still building strength. They suggest that the contrasting performance of two systems during the pandemic gives them a new opening, and that how to turn the crisis into growth needs further thought. Read the original if you want a dense, country-by-country record of foreign communist party activity in 2020 as seen from a Chinese state research institute.

Guiding high-quality development in the new stage with the new development philosophy 以新发展理念引领新阶段高质量发展 Li Chunhua This commentary, published in Economic Daily in February 2021, studies Xi Jinping's call that the whole Party must implement the new development philosophy fully, accurately and comprehensively. Li argues that the philosophy answers basic questions about the purpose, driving force, method and path of development, and that it must guide high-quality development in the new stage. Written as a study of a speech Xi gave to provincial and ministerial leaders on the Fifth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2020), the piece is organised around four ways of grasping the philosophy. These are its fundamental purpose, its problem orientation, a sense of danger and its role as a guiding principle. First, Li holds that a people-centred approach settles for whom development is carried out, and calls for narrowing regional, urban–rural and income gaps. Second, the author says unbalanced and inadequate development remains prominent, citing weak innovation capacity, an unstable agricultural base, large distribution gaps and environmental burdens, and concludes that quality must be given greater prominence. Third, Li urges vigilance and bottom-line thinking so that risks are prevented in time. Fourth, the philosophy should run through every field and the whole process of development, in the spirit of innovation, coordination, green development, openness and sharing. Li concludes that success depends on officials at all levels, who should treat the philosophy as a baton and traffic light, correct contrary views and practices, and be assessed by a performance system that curbs formalism and bureaucratism. The author expects this to secure a good start on the new journey of building a modern socialist country. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary in early 2021 presented the new development philosophy as the framework for the 14th Five-Year Plan period.

Implementing the new development philosophy and building a new development paradigm: starting the 14th Five-Year Plan period well through high-quality development 贯彻新发展理念 构建新发展格局 以高质量发展为“十四五”开好局 Han Wenxiu Writing in early 2021, Han Wenxiu presents an interpretation of the Central Economic Work Conference held after the Fifth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2020). The article takes up how China should assess its 2020 economic record and organise economic work in 2021, the first year of the 14th Five-Year Plan. Han's answer is that policy should remain continuous and stable while the country builds a new development paradigm and pursues high-quality development. The text is a policy explainer in three parts. The first reviews 2020, when China faced the pandemic, a deep world recession and rising external pressure. The second addresses macroeconomic policy for 2021. The third sets out the work needed to take a first step towards the new development paradigm, through eight key measures, and closes with a brief note on balancing development and security. Han reports that China was the only major economy to record positive growth in 2020, with GDP of 101.6 trillion yuan, up 2.3%, and per capita GDP above 10,000 US dollars. Han condenses the lessons of the year into the "five fundamentals", from the authority of the Party Central Committee to scientific and technological self-reliance. For 2021 the author argues that the high headline growth forecasts largely reflect a low base, and that the two-year average is about 5%. Many small firms are still recovering, and social insurance funds and leverage have come under strain. Policy should therefore keep a proactive fiscal policy and a prudent monetary policy, avoid a "policy cliff", and withdraw temporary measures in a calibrated way. Han presents the relatively lower growth pressure as a window for deepening supply-side structural reform. The eight key moves are strengthening national strategic science and technology capacity; making industrial and supply chains self-controllable; expanding domestic demand; advancing reform and opening up, including possible CPTPP accession; securing seeds and farmland; strengthening anti-monopoly work and curbing disorderly capital expansion; tackling housing problems in big cities; and achieving the carbon peak and carbon neutrality goals. Han stresses that the Party's leadership will secure the 2021 targets and a good start to the 14th Five-Year Plan. Read the original if you want an official-line reading of the 2020 economic conference and its 2021 priorities, including platform regulation, housing and climate targets, as presented by a senior policy official.

Three elements of development in China's new journey of modernization: the new stage, the new philosophy and the new pattern 中国现代化新征程发展三要素：新阶段、新理念、新格局 Yu Hongjun Writing in 2021, Yu Hongjun takes up three concepts that the Party leadership has placed at the centre of China's next phase of socialist modernization: the new development stage, the new development philosophy and the new development pattern. The article argues that, set against what it calls a once-in-a-century change in the world, the three concepts form a connected framework. In Yu's account, this framework is a major strategic decision to open a new situation amid that change. It also claims the framework enriches the Marxist view of development. The commentary is built in four parts. The first defines the new stage as the 30 years from the 14th Five-Year Plan (2021) to the second centenary goal in 2050, within the primary stage of socialism. The second goes through the five elements of the new development philosophy and its link to high-quality development. The third explains the dual circulation pattern. The fourth defends the historical meaning of the three concepts against foreign criticism. Throughout, Yu relies heavily on statements by Xi Jinping. Yu argues that the new stage rests on a stronger material base, which the article puts at an economy above 100 trillion yuan, 17 per cent of the world economy and the elimination of poverty. It also rests on a strategic opportunity that the article says outweighs the challenges. The philosophy of innovation, coordination, green development, openness and sharing is presented as the guide to higher-quality growth, and the article lists China's shortfalls under each heading. The new pattern is described as one with the domestic circulation as the mainstay and domestic and international circulations reinforcing each other. It would expand domestic demand and pursue supply-side structural reform, and Yu says this will lessen reliance on export orientation and the 'world factory' model. Yu ties it to US tariffs and technology restrictions. Yu rejects the claims, made by some in the West, that China is turning backward or closing itself off. Yu cites the Belt and Road Initiative, the import expo, free trade zones and the Hainan free trade port as evidence that opening up will widen. The article concludes that the three concepts reflect the laws of development of socialism with Chinese characteristics and will speed the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want an official-line account of how the 'new stage, new philosophy, new pattern' formula was explained to a domestic audience in 2021, including its response to foreign critics.

Fully, accurately and comprehensively implementing the new development philosophy 王舒傲、古梁;完整准确全面贯彻新发展理念 Wang Shu'ao Gu Liang Writing in the PLA Daily in March 2021, Wang Shu'ao and Gu Liang take up Xi Jinping's repeated instruction to implement the new development philosophy fully, accurately and comprehensively, so that the 14th Five-Year Plan period gets off to a good start. The commentary argues that this requires three points of emphasis: the fundamental purpose, a problem-oriented approach and a sense of potential danger. Together they are meant to turn the Party's institutional advantages in leading economic work into governance effectiveness. The piece is organised in three sections, one for each point of emphasis. Each section sets out how the five elements of the philosophy (innovation, coordination, green development, openness and sharing) should be read from that angle. It draws on Xi's speeches, a 1950s remark by Mao Zedong on common wealth and the Fifth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2020). The authors first present service to the people as the "root and soul" of the philosophy. They link it to meeting the people's needs for a better life and to a stronger emphasis on common prosperity, which they describe as a major political question bearing on the Party's basis for governing. They then argue that the principal contradiction of the new era, between growing needs for a better life and unbalanced, inadequate development, should guide targeted measures, such as work on core technologies and supply-chain security. Finally, they call for balancing development with security, with each of the five elements tied to a security task, and for self-reliance whatever the external environment. The authors conclude that the philosophy should run through all development and fields, with innovation as the primary driving force and sharing as the fundamental goal. This, they say, will guide the building of a new development paradigm. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Party-army press commentary presents the new development philosophy at the start of the 14th Five-Year Plan.

Strategic guidance for building a modern socialist country in all respects 全面建设社会主义现代化国家的战略引领 Hao Xianyin Writing in Dongyue Tribune in 2021, Hao Xianyin interprets the Proposal on the 14th Five-Year Plan and the Long-Range Objectives for 2035, adopted at the Fifth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2020). Hao argues that the Proposal is the programmatic document for building a modern socialist country in all respects, and that it rests on a long Party tradition of medium- and long-term planning. The article has four parts. The first reviews planning since 1951, from the "step-by-step" modernization goals (the Four Modernizations, the "three-step" and "new three-step" strategies, and the two-stage plan to 2035 and mid-century) through the thirteen Five-Year Plans. The second sets out the Proposal's blueprint, its guiding principles and its key themes. The third and fourth treat the principles to be followed and the major relationships to be handled in implementation. In Hao's account, the planning record yields five lessons: planning must start from the primary stage of socialism, put the people at the centre, follow a sound development philosophy, reflect the shift from a planned to a market economy, and uphold the Party's overall leadership. Hao presents high-quality development, supply-side structural reform, the "dual circulation" development pattern and common prosperity as the main lines of the new stage. The Proposal's lack of quantified targets is explained as a matter of setting direction, with figures to follow in the outline plan, and as a choice to stress quality over doubling of output. Hao concludes that implementation requires the Party's overall leadership, a people-centred approach, the new development philosophy, deeper reform and opening up, and systems thinking. Five relationships must also be handled: inheritance and innovation, government and market, openness and self-reliance, development and security, and strategy and tactics. The article closely follows official texts and cites Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping throughout. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially aligned reading of the 14th Five-Year Plan Proposal and a historical account of Chinese national planning from 1953 to 2020.

Three paradigms in the study of contemporary imperialism 当代帝国主义研究的三种范式 Xie Fusheng Xie Fusheng's review, published in Marxist Studies in 2020, takes up Xi Jinping's question of what is happening to the world and what China should do amid "changes unseen in a century". Xie argues that theories of imperialism are the Marxist tool for analysing shifts in the world political economy. The article sorts foreign Marxist work since the Cold War into three paradigms, using two questions: has imperialism changed qualitatively since Lenin's day, and is it internally stable? The article surveys "super-imperialism" (qualitative change, stability), "hegemonic imperialism" (qualitative change, instability) and "late imperialism" (quantitative change, instability). The first is represented by Michael Hardt and Antonio Negri's Empire and William Robinson's transnational capitalist class and transnational state. The second covers David Harvey, Ellen Meiksins Wood, Alex Callinicos, and Leo Panitch and Sam Gindin. The third is John Bellamy Foster's account, built on Baran, Sweezy, Magdoff and John Smith. A final section assesses each paradigm and offers Xie's own synthesis. In the critique, Xie holds that Hardt and Negri rely on metaphor and wrongly declare the North–South divide dissolving, and that Robinson overlooks how nation-states still back transnational capital. Harvey, Wood, Callinicos, and Panitch and Gindin are faulted for exaggerating dispossession, ignoring monopoly, or downplaying economic motives. Xie treats Foster's late imperialism as closest to Lenin's insistence that monopoly is central, though it needs fuller work on global production networks. Xie's own account describes contemporary imperialism as the latest stage of capitalism, in which the United States takes surplus value from other countries through global production networks and financialization, backed by international institutions and political and military pressure. Xie describes this order as facing domestic contradictions in the United States, including deindustrialization, financial stagnation and inequality. It also faces international tensions, such as US conflicts with allies and rivals and the trade wars of the Trump administration. For China, Xie calls for coordinating domestic and international priorities, pursuing the Belt and Road Initiative and a new dual-circulation pattern, and reshaping global governance towards a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a structured map of Western Marxist theories of imperialism since 2000, judged from a Chinese Marxist standpoint.

Engels's economic thought on communism and its contemporary value Written to mark the 200th anniversary of Engels's birth 恩格斯关于共产主义的经济思想及其当代价值 Gao Jiankun Cheng Enfu Written for the 200th anniversary of Engels's birth in 2020, this article asks what Engels said about the economic form of communism and what it offers to economic theory and practice in China today. Gao and Cheng argue that Engels's account was not speculative but a necessary conclusion drawn from a dialectical analysis of capitalism. They contend that socialism with Chinese characteristics is internally linked to the higher stage of communism, differing mainly in maturity. The article has three parts. The first reviews Engels on communist productive forces: changes in the mode of labour (working time, the nature of labour, the division of labour) and the integration of sectors, especially town and country. The second covers production relations: public ownership of the means of production, distribution according to need, and conscious planning of the economy. The third draws out the present-day significance, taking Xi Jinping's call to grasp the relationship between the ultimate communist ideal and the common ideal of socialism with Chinese characteristics as its starting point. In the authors' reading, Engels held that abolishing capitalist private ownership would shorten working hours, make labour a form of enjoyment and, through industrial education, end the old division of labour. It would also remove the waste of labour and goods caused by luxury consumption, unemployment and crises. Public ownership would come step by step through state ownership, with cooperatives as an intermediate link under state ownership. Means of production would belong to society and consumer goods to individuals. Distribution would shift as output grows, and some inequality in living conditions would shrink but never vanish entirely. Gao and Cheng then map these points onto China: public ownership as the mainstay with the state sector in the leading role, distribution according to labour as the mainstay, and state regulation combined with the market. They describe these as the same in quality as Engels's communism but different in degree of maturity. The authors conclude that the primary stage of socialism is the initial phase of communist society in a broad sense, and they reject the view that it is not. They call for upholding the basic economic system, strengthening state and collective enterprises, narrowing wealth and income gaps, building a new-type whole-nation system in key technologies and improving the socialist market economy. Read the original if you want a systematic, text-by-text survey of Engels's passages on communist economics and a view of how Chinese economists link them to current policy.

Critique of and reflections on spatial justice theory 空间正义论的批判与反思 Yu Bin Yu Bin takes aim at the growing body of research on "spatial justice", which the author says was started by Western scholars, sometimes under a Marxist banner, and has been taken up by many Chinese academics. The article, published in 2020, argues that spatial justice theory is absurd as theory and is not Marxist. In Yu's view it mistakes symptoms for causes and diverts attention from the capitalist mode of production. The article has four parts. It begins by criticising specific claims by Edward Soja, Henri Lefebvre, David Harvey and Chinese followers. It then argues that appeals to justice are not the method of Marx and Engels. Next it collects the classical writers' remarks on space and compares them with spatial justice theorists. A short conclusion follows. Yu draws mainly on Capital, Engels's The Housing Question and Anti-Dühring-era writings, Marx's letters and Lenin on town and country. Yu's central move is a reversal of causation. Inequalities that appear in space, such as the marginal position of developing countries or the weakness of disadvantaged groups, are in Yu's reading results of exploitation under capitalism, not products of spatial arrangement. Demanding spatial justice therefore tries to remove effects while leaving causes in place. Yu holds that Engels treated talk of justice as a mere symptom of contradictions between relations and forces of production, and that Marx included such words in the International's statutes only after making them harmless. Yu also charges Chinese scholars with misreading Marx's lines on justice and on the "annihilation of space by time". On Yu's reading Marx meant shorter travel times, which the classics welcomed as a progressive effect of capital. Yu adds that the unequal distribution of population and production is compatible with developed productive forces and should be addressed by abolishing the town–country divide. Yu also says Marx put workers' hunger ahead of their housing, and Engels answered low pay by urging organisation, not spatial justice. Yu concludes that spatial justice is reformist, tolerates capitalism and echoes Proudhonist petty-bourgeois demands. Words like "justice" may be used by Marxists only if they do not distract from the main problems. Citing Marx's remark that time is the space of human development, Yu says working-time struggles matter more than spatial ones, and gives the "996" working schedule as a present-day example. Yu urges scholars to leave the noisy field of spatial justice research. Read the original if you want a polemical Chinese Marxist reading of Soja, Lefebvre and Harvey, built on close reading of the classical texts.

Let the torch of multilateralism light humanity's way forward 让多边主义的火炬照亮人类前行之路 Liu Naiya Writing in early 2021, with the COVID-19 pandemic still spreading and the world economy unstable, Liu Naiya asks whether the international community should keep acting alone through unilateralism or choose solidarity and multilateralism. The article answers by interpreting Xi Jinping's 25 January 2021 special address to the World Economic Forum's "Davos Agenda" dialogue. Liu argues that upholding and practising multilateralism, and building a community with a shared future for mankind, is the fundamental way out of current difficulties and the basis for reforming global governance. The commentary has two parts. The first sets out the content of Xi's "four adherences" and explains how multilateralism and the community with a shared future for mankind relate to each other. The second describes China as a defender of multilateralism and a leader in global governance, citing its pandemic cooperation, new international bodies, summits, trade and climate commitments. Liu draws on Xi's speeches and on remarks by UN Secretary-General António Guterres and the 71st UN General Assembly president as evidence of international endorsement. Liu reads Xi's four adherences as openness and inclusiveness, rule by international law rather than the will of one or a few states, consultation rather than confrontation, and keeping pace with the times. The article holds that multilateralism must serve all humanity rather than "small circles", and that the community with a shared future for mankind supplies its values and guiding concept. It treats differences in history, culture and social system as grounds for cooperation. It argues that the 21st-century version should keep core principles while reforming global governance through broad consultation. As evidence of Chinese practice, Liu lists support for the World Health Organization and for developing countries, including African states, in the pandemic. The list also covers the founding of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, BRICS and the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank, the Belt and Road Initiative, a stance in defence of the multilateral trading system, a suspension of debt repayments by the poorest countries, and carbon-peak and carbon-neutrality pledges. The author concludes that more countries will gather under the torch of multilateralism and that China's development benefits world peace. Read the original if you want a representative example of how official Chinese commentary in 2021 framed multilateralism and China's global governance role around Xi's Davos speech.

Upholding and practising multilateralism for the twenty-first century 维护和践行21世纪的多边主义 Feng Weijiang This commentary, published in 2021, interprets Xi Jinping's special address to the World Economic Forum's Davos Agenda dialogue on 25 January 2021. Feng Weijiang takes up the question of how global governance can escape its current difficulties. The author argues that Xi's idea of a twenty-first-century multilateralism, which keeps the core values of traditional multilateralism while adapting to a changed world, summarises the major theoretical and practical problems of global governance and guides the building of a community with a shared future for mankind. The article has two parts. The first diagnoses three predicaments of global governance: the fading of peace and development as governance goals, insufficient macroeconomic policy coordination, and delayed reform of the global economic governance system. The second sets out what twenty-first-century multilateralism offers in terms of goals, policy and institutional space, and a cultural and civilizational outlook. Feng draws on Xi's address, the post-war international order, the Doha Round, the G20 and the Covid-19 recession. In Feng's account, the post-war order was built to prevent another world war and to support recovery, and development later became a further goal. The author contends that collective memory of war has faded, that the Doha Round has stalled, and that trade, financial and technology wars by certain countries could escalate into traditional security conflict. Feng argues that crisis-driven cooperation, which worked after 2007, failed during the pandemic, and that developing countries' voting power in the World Bank and the IMF has not kept pace with their economic weight. Against this, Feng presents Xi's Four Insistences (openness and inclusiveness, international rules, consultation and cooperation, keeping pace with the times), a wider range of institutions including the Belt and Road Initiative, and new agenda items such as climate, energy and digital governance. Feng says this multilateralism rejects zero-sum thinking, the clash of civilizations and civilizational superiority. Feng concludes that twenty-first-century multilateralism reflects Marxist worldview and methodology, socialist advanced culture and traditional Chinese wisdom. The author calls for the common values of all humanity to become the consensus behind it, and for states to practise win-win cooperation, equal development rights and peaceful coexistence. Read the original if you want an example of how a Chinese commentator, writing in a Party journal, frames Xi Jinping's multilateralism and its critique of current global governance.

Engels's important contributions to the international communist movement A perspective from the First International 恩格斯对国际共产主义运动的重要贡献 Liang Haifeng Marking the 200th anniversary of Friedrich Engels's birth in 2020, this short commentary asks what Engels contributed to the international communist movement through the First International. Liang argues that Engels, alongside Marx, gave the International its political programme, defended Marxism's guiding position against rival currents, and drew the lessons that pointed the movement towards a new form of organisation. Engels is presented as an outstanding leader of the movement as well as a theorist. The article is organised around four contributions, followed by a brief note that Engels's work did not end with the International. It moves through the founding programme, the struggle against Proudhonism, the fight against Bakunin's followers, and Engels's assessment of the International's experience after the Paris Commune. Liang draws chiefly on Engels's letters to Marx and on works such as The Housing Question and "On Authority", and adds citations from Xi Jinping on conviction and on theoretical innovation. Liang's central claim is that Engels defended both the doctrine and the organisational unity of the International. On the programme, Marx wrote a document "firm in substance, moderate in form" so as to unite British trade unionists, Proudhonists and Lassalleans, and Engels supported this, expecting workers to move towards scientific socialism through struggle. Against Proudhonism, Engels is said to have exposed a petty-bourgeois reformism that rejected industrial revolution; Liang notes that its influence largely vanished after the Commune. Against Bakunin's Alliance, Engels argued that authority and autonomy are relative and that abandoning political struggle surrenders the means of taking power. The Hague Congress of 1872 expelled the Alliance's members. Liang concludes that after the Commune Engels judged the old forms of international association to have become a fetter, and that the new task was to build independent socialist workers' parties in each country. In this reading, the International had fulfilled its historic mission, and international solidarity had become far stronger than before. Liang presents this as theoretical innovation grounded in practice. Read the original if you want a concise, officially framed Chinese overview of Engels's role in the First International and the debates with Proudhonists and Bakuninists.

The capitalist economic cycle and the hundred-year cycle of world politics 资本主义经济周期与世界政治的百年轮回 Wang Lixin Wang Lixin asks how the recurring crises of capitalism shape world politics, and argues that the world has in effect returned to the 1930s after roughly a century. In the article's account, the deepest root of this "hundred-year cycle" is the capitalist business cycle: each worldwide economic crisis brings profound political change, after which humanity gradually leaves the crisis and returns to the "normal track". Wang names four types of political consequence: domestic social and political crisis with policy shifts, damage to the prestige of liberal democratic capitalism, a changed balance among great powers, and shocks to international norms and order. The article compares the three worldwide crises of the past century: the Great Depression of the 1930s, the stagflation of the 1970s and the financial crisis of 2008. It treats the first and third as having by far the greatest political impact. Its sections follow these cases in turn, drawing on GDP comparisons for Britain, France, the United States, Germany, Japan and the Soviet Union, and on scholarship by Huntington, Przeworski and Larry Diamond. For the 1930s, Wang describes the fall of the Weimar Republic, Japanese militarism and Roosevelt's turn to state intervention and isolationism. The author also notes the rise of fascism as an alternative to liberal democracy, the Soviet Union's growth outside the capitalist system, the weakening of Britain, France and the United States, and the collapse of the internationalist basis of the post-1918 order. The 1970s are presented as a milder case, marked by American retrenchment, a narrowing gap with the Soviet Union and the end of dollar convertibility into gold. For 2008, Wang identifies populism, inequality and social polarisation, a "democratic recession", the relative rise of China, India and other non-Western states, the return of great-power competition, and a crisis of the liberal international order that Trump's protectionism and unilateralism made worse. Wang concludes that populism, extreme nationalism, weakening democracy, power politics and the breakdown of international norms make today's world resemble the 1930s. Seen through this cyclical lens, the "great changes unseen in a century" may be understood more fully, and, the author adds, with more calm and composure. Read the original if you want a historical-comparative account, from a Chinese scholar, of how the Great Depression and the 2008 crisis reshaped domestic politics and the international order.

Learning from Party history to understand why Marxism works Grasping the historical, theoretical and practical logic of "why Marxism is effective" 学史明理深刻领悟马克思主义为什么行 Jing Xing Writing in Chengdu Daily on 31 March 2021, during the Party History Study and Education campaign, Jing takes up Xi Jinping's call to "learn from history to understand principle" (xue shi ming li). The commentary asks why Marxism "works" (xing) in China and answers that this can be grasped through three logics Xi names: historical, theoretical and practical. Jing presents the campaign as a way to reinforce the faith, ideals and original mission of Party members through study of the Party's hundred-year history. The piece is organised under three headings, one for each logic. It begins with Xi's remarks in Fujian, then traces the introduction of Marxism to China after the October Revolution and the founding of the Communist Party. It goes on to compare Marxism with other responses to national crisis since the Opium War, and ends by linking Marxism to the needs of successive historical periods. Jing relies heavily on quotations from Engels, Marx, Mao Zedong and Xi. On the historical logic, Jing argues that the red thread through the Party's history, from its founding through the establishment of the People's Republic and reform and opening up to the new era, is the effort to combine Marxism's universal principles with China's concrete conditions. On the theoretical logic, Jing says that other options, from "Chinese learning as the essence" to bourgeois democracy and wholesale Westernisation, all failed, while Marxism succeeded because of four traits: a thoroughly materialist philosophy, a people-first political stance, a method of seeking truth from facts rather than a creed, and openness to development. On the practical logic, Jing holds that theory is realised in a country in proportion to how far it meets that country's needs, so Marxism has taken root by answering the problems of each era. Jing concludes that Marxism has developed in stages: Leninism, Mao Zedong Thought, Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents, the Scientific Outlook on Development and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. In contemporary China, the author says, upholding Marxism means upholding that last body of thought. Jing calls on every Party member to become a firm believer in and faithful practitioner of this thought, using the campaign's slogan to study history, grasp the thought, do practical work and open new horizons. Read the original if you want a compact example of how the 2021 Party history campaign framed the claim that Marxism "works" in China.

On the historical evolution of Marx's concept of alienation 论马克思异化概念的历史演进 Wang Guangye Wang Guangye asks how Marx's concept of alienation took shape, and why it differs from the versions held by Hegel and Feuerbach. The article argues that alienation, a central concept running through Marx's whole career, was not conceived suddenly. In Wang's account it developed historically, from Hegel's absolute idealism through Feuerbach's intuitive materialism to the analysis of social reality, ending in an economic critique of capital's enslavement of modern people. The article is a work of intellectual history in three stages. It first treats speculative and religious alienation, covering Marx's doctoral dissertation, Bruno Bauer and Feuerbach. It then turns to political alienation, drawing on Marx's writings on the Jewish question and his critique of Hegel's philosophy of right. Finally it takes up alienation in civil society, looking at The German Ideology, Marx's 1844 study of classical political economy and the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844. Wang's central claim is a sequence of reversals. Marx first used Hegel's idea that appearance is the alienation of essence. He then moved towards the religious critique of Feuerbach and the Young Hegelians, but rejected Bauer's view that religious alienation underlies political alienation. For Marx, Wang says, religious alienation arises from the split between the political state and civil society, in which people live a double life, as citizens in a heavenly state and as egoistic private individuals. Against Hegel, Marx then held that civil society determines the state. Political alienation is therefore only a 'copy', and the 'original' is the division within civil society, which must be examined through political economy. Wang reads Marx's analysis of money, the Jewish spirit and the worker's loss of his product to capital as marking this shift. Wang concludes that Marx took over Hegel's and Feuerbach's concept but found it unable to analyse modern capitalist society concretely. Marx therefore turned to the economic level of civil society, where alienation acquires material content and a meaning distinct from earlier abstract notions such as externalisation, objectification and transfer. The article supports its case by citing Hyppolite, who calls alienation the basic concept and source of all Marxist thought. Read the original if you want a compact, text-based outline of how Marx moved from the Young Hegelian critique of religion to the economic theory of alienation.

Critique of digital capitalism and the rebuilding of proletarian collectivity New trends in foreign Marxism in the twenty-first century 数字资本主义批判和重建无产阶级集体性——21世纪国外马克思主义新趋势探析 Lan Jiang Writing in 2021, Lan asks what new directions foreign Marxism has taken in the first two decades of the twenty-first century. The article argues that the post-Cold War claim of an "end of history" has collapsed, that digital capitalism has produced a new, precarious proletariat, and that leading Marxist thinkers abroad now seek to reinvent collectivity, increasingly through a revived party form. The article has three parts. The first treats Francis Fukuyama's end-of-history thesis, with Daniel Bell and Anthony Giddens in the background, and sets against it Occupy Wall Street (2011), the French "yellow vests" (from 2018) and Thomas Piketty's data on the "1%" versus the "99%". The second analyses platform capitalism through Judith Butler, Guy Standing, Nick Srnicek, Slavoj Žižek and Jodi Dean. The third examines disputes over collective subjectivity among Antonio Negri and Michael Hardt, Alain Badiou, Dean, Nancy Fraser and others. Lan's central claim is that digital capitalism changes both the mode and the relations of production. Platforms monopolise data and social interaction, extract rent from what Žižek calls privatised "general intellect", and replace the wage relation with a "bonus model". In this model, as Lan reads Dean, most users on YouTube or Twitter work unpaid while a tiny top tier wins rewards, so that the precariat becomes disposable and cannot organise as industrial workers once did. Platform algorithms, on this account, also deepen individuation: Dean treats the individual form itself as a symptom of capitalism, and Lan says people now lock themselves into isolation. Negri and Hardt still hope for leaderless multitude networks, though in Assembly they concede a need for tactical leadership. Badiou and Dean insist on a vanguard and, in Dean's case, a communist party. Lan concludes that reinventing a collective "we" and returning to party organisation has become a distinguishing feature of twenty-first-century foreign Marxism. In this reading, only a communist party can unite a precariat that has been thoroughly individualised. Lan presents this as evidence of Marxism's renewed vitality in the developed West. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's overview of Western left debates on platform capitalism, precarity and the party, with Dean's work at the centre.

An analysis of Heidegger's thought on authentic human existence from a Marxist perspective 海德格尔人的本真生存思想探析——以马克思主义为分析视角 Wang Shijin Wang Shijin asks how people should understand the tension between falling into inauthentic existence and pursuing an authentic self, at a time when globalisation multiplies outside temptations while individuals increasingly seek personality and self-realisation. The article turns to Heidegger's account of how human existence moves from "fallenness" to authenticity and reads it through Marx's thesis that the human essence is the ensemble of social relations. Wang's thesis is that Heidegger's analysis offers useful insights into individuality, but that real existence is a dialectical unity of individuality and sociality, which Marxism explains more adequately. The article has three parts. The first presents authentic existence and fallenness as the two basic modes of Dasein's being-in-the-world, covering Heidegger's distinction between being-in and being-inside, and the role of understanding in the passage from the "they" to the authentic self. The second sets out the distinctive features of authentic existence: projection (Entwurf), anxiety (Angst), distinguished from fear, and being-towards-death. The third, from the Marxist side, discusses individual responsibility, Mitsein (being-with) and Mitdasein, and the integration of the "small self" into the "large self". Wang reports that for Heidegger fallenness belongs essentially to Dasein and can ease psychological pressure, but leaves people unreflective and evasive of responsibility. Authentic existence requires resoluteness, in which Dasein unfolds its own possibilities, feels anxiety without any external object, and confronts its non-substitutable death. Wang holds that Heidegger gives priority to the individual even while stressing being-with, and defends him against the charge of egocentrism. From Marx and Engels, Wang then argues that material production is the first premise of human existence, that mode of production shapes individuals' ways of living, and that individual freedom is possible only in a genuine community. Wang therefore opposes egocentrism and extreme individualism and favours collectivism. Wang concludes that understanding one's own life's meaning and mission is an irreplaceable individual task, but one carried out within society. Citing Xi Jinping's speech at the 100th anniversary of the May Fourth Movement (2019), Wang says that handling the relation between the "small self" and the "large self" of country and people shows how to combine individuality and sociality. Read the original if you want a Marxist-oriented Chinese reading of Heidegger's Being and Time themes, especially how Chinese scholars connect existential authenticity to collectivist ethics.

New communist horizons in communicative capitalism An interview with Jodi Dean 交往资本主义中新的共产主义视野 Jodi Dean Tomislav Medak Petar Jandrić This is a Chinese translation of a 2018 interview with the American political theorist Jodi Dean, conducted by Tomislav Medak (Coventry University) and Petar Jandrić (Zagreb University of Applied Sciences). It was prompted by Dean's work on media technology and left politics, and it asks what communicative capitalism is and why, in her view, the left needs a communist horizon rather than more democracy. The conversation is organised in five parts: communicative capitalism and the crisis of democracy; Marx's relevance in the digital age; the communist horizon, including religion, the space race, internationalism and liberation theology; the many faces of anti-capitalist struggle, such as platform cooperativism, degrowth and universal basic income; and the relation between crowds and the party. Dean defines communicative capitalism as a form in which communication itself becomes the core of accumulation. Participation and inclusion then feed capital, and a message's circulation value displaces its use value, so that critique is just more shareable content. She argues that Habermasian communicative reason cannot work where people hold opposing conceptions of reality, and that radical democracy only offers more of what already exists. She holds that Marx matters more than ever because of intensified proletarianisation, dispossession through enclosure of communicative commons, and his political writings. Communicative capitalism, she says, extracts value from social material without the commodity form. For Dean the left must name antagonism. She rejects anarchist horizontalism, citing power-law network structures, and she also rejects platform cooperativism, degrowth and universal basic income. She favours rebuilding trade unions and collectivising industry. Dean concludes that the technical conditions for cybernetic communism exist but the political conditions do not, so the task is to build collective will. She defends the party as the effective form of struggle today. In her account it is a voluntary collective of comrades, held together by affective ties, that politicises crowds, which produce only intensity. She traces the left's fragmentation to the collapse of the Soviet and East European bloc and calls for making the communist vision visible again. Read the original if you want a wide-ranging statement of Dean's views on digital capitalism, party and crowd, and on contemporary left strategies, in her own words.

Capitalism, racism and Trumpism 资本主义、种族主义与特朗普主义 David G. Embrick J. Scott Carter Cameron D. Lippard Bhoomi K. Thakore This is a Chinese translation, by Liu Shuhui, of an article by four American sociologists (Embrick, Carter, Lippard and Thakore). It asks what lies behind the racism of Trumpism and whether it is something new. The authors argue that Trumpism rests on "Whitelash", a recurring reaction by white Americans to threats to white supremacy. In their view this racism is systemic and institutional, and Trump's rhetoric is abnormal only in its hostility. The article first sets out a theoretical framework drawing on Omi and Winant, Bonilla-Silva, Joe Feagin, Kimberlé Crenshaw, Patricia Hill Collins and Herbert Blumer. It then defines Whitelash at three levels: structural, institutional and individual. Its main case is immigration, traced from nativist ideology through the Chinese Exclusion Act (1882), the 1920s quota laws, the Bracero programme and 1954 deportations, to Proposition 187, post-9/11 policy and the Obama and Trump administrations. A discussion and a two-part conclusion follow. The authors treat white supremacy, capitalism and patriarchy as built into the structure of American society, so that racism, class domination and sexism reinforce one another. On immigration, they argue that "racial nativism" has worked together with economic interest. Non-white migrants were admitted when they supplied cheap labour and excluded or expelled when they appeared to threaten white economic or political position, and employers often lobbied against enforcement that would cut their profits. They describe Whitelash as peaking in periods of crisis, citing the 2008 recession and the rise of movements for equality. In this account Trump's border wall, Muslim ban and family separations continue a long tradition. They read his fixation on Obama's legacy and his neglect of non-white victims of the coronavirus as signs of a more extreme and abnormal racial politics. The authors answer both "old wine in new bottles?" and "this is not normal!" in the affirmative. Trump's strategies are established white-supremacist ones, but his obstinacy, his reversal of Obama-era liberal policies and his rhetoric risk institutionalising white supremacy and reviving Jim Crow-style practices. They call for research into the ideologies and structural obstacles that block equality, and into how Whitelash relates to minority demands for rights. Read the original if you want a sociological account of Trumpism that places it within long-run American racial and immigration politics, as translated for Chinese readers of foreign theory.

The evolution of the value orientations of contemporary European left-wing parties 当代欧洲左翼政党的价值观念流变 Sun Xixiang Xue Junqiang This short commentary, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in December 2020, asks how the values of contemporary European left-wing parties have changed and why. Sun and Xue argue that these values grew out of the European social-democratic tradition and a critique of liberalism, and that their shifts since 1945 follow changes in capitalism's economic and class structure. The authors treat the parties' ideological blurring and plurality as a product of that changing social base. The article opens with the parties' core values and then moves through three stages: the post-1945 search for social change between state and capital, the exploration of alternatives to capitalism after the Cold War and especially after the 2008 financial crisis, and the present question of who the subject of anti-capitalist struggle is. Examples include Jeremy Corbyn and Ed Miliband in the British Labour Party and figures in the German Social Democratic Party. Sun and Xue say these parties treat freedom, equality and solidarity as one organic whole, in contrast to classical and neoliberal liberalism. They also hold that socialism is not a fixed historical blueprint but a process of pursuing these ideals. After 1945, the authors argue, the parties built a "state–capital–labour" framework, a kind of social or state capitalism. It combined market competition with state regulation and ethical pragmatism, and it led some parties to keep Marxism only as a nominal ideal. The authors then argue that the working class has split and that new social movements and identity politics challenge the working class as sole revolutionary subject. The parties therefore accept the market as the best generator of wealth and ground democracy in individual rights. Their programmes still keep the aim of ultimately abolishing capitalism. The authors conclude that, after 2008, the decline of the Third Way and the rise of populism, Labour and the SPD figures call for a return to social-democratic left traditions through public ownership, collective control and more public investment. They also say the parties have lost some traditional working-class support by tacitly accepting neoliberalism, and must bridge the gap between the old working class and the new working class created by industrial restructuring since the 1990s. For Sun and Xue, changes in capitalism's class structure and in the relations between labour and capital are the root of these ideological shifts. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese academic overview of how European social-democratic and left parties' values are interpreted in China.

A review of recent scholarship on the European radical left 近年来学界关于欧洲激进左翼的研究述评 Shang Yu This literature review, published in Social Sciences Trends in 2020, surveys how scholars have studied the European radical left since it re-emerged after the 2008 financial crisis. Shang notes that after the setbacks to socialism in the twentieth century, researchers mostly looked to the right. The success of Syriza in Greece and Podemos in Spain then drew attention back to the left. The review finds a growing body of work, but one with unsettled concepts and a narrow disciplinary base. The article is organised in six parts. It covers definitions of the radical left, typologies (two-, three- and four-fold), the movement's ideological and policy positions, and comparisons with the European radical right. It then turns to factors shaping the radical left's prospects, divided into party-level and voter-level explanations. It ends with an assessment of the field's achievements and shortcomings and suggestions for further research. Sources include Chinese scholars (Li Qiqing, Lin Deshan, Tian Dewen, Zeng Zhisheng) and Western ones (Luke March, Paolo Chiocchetti, Babak Amini, March and others). On definition, Shang reports three approaches. These stress the 'radical' character (opposition to capitalism, but not to democracy as such), ideology (a position to the left of social democracy) and relations with other left parties. Typologies mostly rest on party origin, ideology or policy, and Shang argues that each criterion has weaknesses. Origin underestimates change after 1991 and 2008, and ideology can diverge from actual policy. Shang then sets out the shared traits of the radical left and right (Euroscepticism, anti-globalisation, populism, anti-establishment stance) and the differences, citing civic versus ethnic nationalism and the left's concern with equality against the right's concern with immigration. Explanations for success are split between external factors (political culture, economic conditions, party competition) and internal ones (past governing experience, electoral thresholds, leadership). Scholars also disagree about the effect of economic conditions, education and manual employment on voting. Shang credits the literature with shifting from case studies to the party family as a whole, with attention to relations with other parties, with predicting a difficult future (citing the fall in the left group's seats in the 2019 European Parliament election), and with mixing qualitative and quantitative methods. The shortcomings listed are unclear core concepts, little historical analysis, neglect of Eastern Europe and of relations with the Greens and traditional communist parties, and an almost purely political-science perspective. Shang calls for agreed definitions, systematic historical study, East–West comparison and interdisciplinary work drawing on history, sociology, psychology and communication studies. Read the original if you want a map of the Chinese and Western literature on the European radical left, including its typologies and its debates about voters, to guide further research.

The French Communist Party's development predicament since the 2008 economic crisis 2008年经济危机以来法国共产党的发展困境 Lin Yingfeng Why has the French Communist Party (PCF) achieved so little since the 2008 crisis, when the crisis was expected to open space for the left? Lin Yingfeng argues that the party's electoral decline reflects three linked difficulties: an unfavourable environment for the European left, an unstable position on the political spectrum, and a weak theoretical project, the "new communism". The article was published in 2020. Lin first documents the decline using results from National Assembly, presidential and European Parliament elections between 2004 and 2019. Seats in the National Assembly fell from 15 in 2007 to 10 in 2012 and 2017, and the party won no European Parliament seats in 2019. The article then examines each difficulty in turn: the wider decline of European left parties, the PCF's factional and strategic oscillation, and the content of its theory. On the external side, Lin argues that since the 1990s the collapse of the Soviet bloc and the spread of neoliberal ideas have pushed many left parties to adapt to capitalism rather than oppose it.
