In the PCF's case, "new communism" and its aim of "going beyond capitalism" are read as reformist, which disappointed lower and middle-class voters. On identity, the party has pursued a "centrist" path modelled on the Socialist Party while its six internal factions disagree, and it has shifted between electoral alliances such as the Left Front and La France insoumise. Lin treats chasing alliances without a stable orientation as the key cause, and cites a fall in membership from over 130,000 (2002–2008) to 47,000 by the end of 2019. On theory, Lin finds that "new communism" no longer confronts the capitalist system itself, blaming neoliberal policy instead, and that it has become so all-encompassing, borrowing from Socialist and Green agendas, that it lacks a core idea. Lin proposes three remedies. The PCF should seek cooperation with other European communist and workers' parties and rebuild international worker organisations. It should clarify its position and take up the banner of opposing capitalism again. It should also complete the theory of "new communism" around a critique of the exploitation behind capitalism's self-improvement, borrowing selectively from other parties. Lin concludes that progress on these fronts would reverse the party's predicament. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's assessment of the French left after 2008, with election figures, factional detail and an account of how Chinese commentators judge the PCF's turn away from anti-capitalism.

Who is the proletariat of the information age? A rebuttal and reconstruction of the radical left's "new proletariat" 谁是信息时代的无产阶级？ Gong Yongdan Gong asks who can serve as the political subject of social transformation in the information age. Western radical left thinkers have answered with a "new proletariat" to fill a perceived "absence of the subject". The article argues that these figures depart from Marx's concept and lose its revolutionary content, and that the proletariat remains the subject of change in a digital form. The article has three parts. The first surveys four proposed subjects: the "multitude" in Hardt and Negri and in Paolo Virno; Slavoj Žižek's "the excluded"; Jacques Rancière's "the part of those who have no part"; and Giorgio Agamben's "homo sacer", together with Jodi Dean's "the rest of us". The second reconstructs Marx's account of the proletariat's origin and essence and measures the new concepts against it. The third rebuilds the proletariat for the era of digital capitalism. In Gong's reading, Marx defines the proletariat by having no means of production and so having to sell labour-power. It arose from the separation of labourers from the objective conditions of labour and from machine industry, and its mission is to overthrow capitalism. The radical left subjects, by contrast, are broad and abstract: the poor, migrants, slum-dwellers, "bare life". The author says they are no longer wage labourers opposed to the bourgeoisie, cannot form a class consciousness or programme, and so undergo "de-revolutionisation". Drawing on Marx's "fragment on machines", Gong holds that digital capitalism is a new form of the capital–labour contradiction. Digital workers who produce data without owning digital means of production, along with industrial wage labourers and workers displaced by AI, form the information-age proletariat. Gong concludes that the information-age proletariat will not become "marginal groups", Harari's "useless class" or the "knowledge-owning class" of cognitive capitalism. The author holds that it remains the opener of a communist society, and that the "two inevitables" of the Communist Manifesto still apply. Finding this proletariat requires repeating Marx's critique of political economy, not turning to abstract subjects. Read the original if you want a Marxist-orthodox critique of Negri, Žižek, Rancière and Agamben on the revolutionary subject, or a Chinese account of digital labour as proletarianisation.

Thirty years since the fall of the Berlin Wall: reflections and debates on the Western left 柏林墙倒塌30周年——西方左翼的反思与探讨 Yu Haiqing Yang Xiaojun Yu Haiqing and Yang Xiaojun survey how Western left parties, think tanks, newspapers, websites and independent left scholars interpreted the fall of the Berlin Wall on its 30th anniversary in 2019. The authors argue that, despite the left's varied composition and disagreements, these commentators share a defence of socialist values and a commitment to socialism's future direction. They hold that such reflection helps Chinese readers examine the history of Soviet and East European socialism from several angles and draw lessons from its setbacks. The article is organised in six parts. It covers why the Wall was built, its place in and the nature of the 1989 upheavals, the causes of socialism's failure and the lessons drawn, economic and social conditions in the former Soviet and East European region after 30 years of transition, and the left's views on socialism's validity and prospects. Sources include communist parties (Italian, Greek, American, Irish, Portuguese, British, Swedish), Trotskyist groups, and scholars and figures such as Victor Grossman, Hans Modrow, Catherine Samary, Lucien Sève and Kristen Ghodsee. The authors draw largely on online articles, interviews and recent books. Yu and Yang report that most left voices reject mainstream Western media's account of the Wall as a symbol of socialist tyranny, and instead stress economic hardship, blockade and Cold War pressure on the German Democratic Republic. On the nature of 1989, they distinguish a Trotskyist 'revolution' view, which denies that these states were truly socialist, from the communist parties' 'counter-revolution' view. On causes of failure they identify external-factor, dual-factor (objective immaturity plus subjective failings) and multi-factor explanations. For the post-1989 decades they cite left accounts of a divided region: deep economic decline, a persistent East–West gap in Germany, nostalgia and populism, and 'historical revisionism' weakening the left. The authors conclude that the left's reflections have a double significance: they contest anti-communist narratives and offer lessons for socialist practice, including that each country must find its own path. They stress that left voices insist capitalism has not ended its crisis and that the failure in the East is an episode in socialism's longer course. They also note that divisions within the left, including over assessments of China, remain a long-standing problem, and call for openness, unity and a new strategy to help world socialism revive. Read the original if you want a source-based overview of how Western communist and left currents interpreted 1989 and its aftermath, as reported from a Chinese academic perspective.

The dissemination of Capital in Russia and the formation of Lenin's view of capitalism 《资本论》在俄国的传播与列宁资本主义观的形成 Zhang Jing Between the 1870s and 1890s, Russian intellectuals of different camps read Capital in conflicting ways and argued over the future of Russian capitalism. Zhang asks how Lenin, drawing on historical materialism and the economic theory of Capital, answered that question. The article argues that by criticising the liberal Narodniks and the "legal Marxists", Lenin arrived at a Marxist view of capitalism. The article has four parts. It first reviews the 1877–79 Russian debate over Capital, then the 1880s–90s dispute on Russian capitalism, then Lenin's formation of his own view through three stages of writing, and finally Lenin's book The Development of Capitalism in Russia. Zhang draws on the debaters' articles and on letters from Marx, Engels, Danielson, Plekhanov and others. Zhang reports that the debate began with Zhukovsky's attack on Capital and was answered by Mikhailovsky and Sieber. Marx's reply to Mikhailovsky objected to turning his sketch of Western European capitalism into a universal philosophy of history. By the 1890s three views had emerged. The Narodniks, such as Danielson and Vorontsov, feared capitalism and wished Russia to avoid it. The legal Marxist Struve stressed its necessity but played down its destructive effects. Plekhanov held that Russia was already capitalist but, in Zhang's account, did not establish a Marxist view of capitalism. Lenin criticised Mikhailovsky's "subjective sociology" and the Narodnik market theory. He briefly allied with Struve, then criticised Struve's "objectivism" and misreading of Marx's theory of realisation. Zhang concludes that The Development of Capitalism in Russia, which the article calls in a sense "Russia's Capital", marks the establishment of Lenin's view. In it, capitalism's progressive role is held to be consistent with recognising its dark sides and its historical transience. Lenin is presented as having both understood the method of Capital and applied it to Russian conditions. In Zhang's reading this advanced the Russianisation of Marxism and brought Russian Marxism into the stage of Leninism. Read the original if you want a source-based account of the Russian reception of Capital and the Narodnik and legal Marxist debates behind Lenin's early economic writings.

The general intellect and the utopia of emancipation A renewed reflection on contemporary Western left theories of the subject, based on Marx and Engels on the "mental-labour proletariat" and its historical mission 一般智力与解放的乌托邦：当代西方左翼主体理论的再反思 Sun Leqiang Sun Leqiang asks how Marx and Engels understood the relation between intellect and class, and what that means for Western left theories of the revolutionary subject that emerged with the "knowledge economy" of the 1990s. The article takes up the multitude (Hardt, Negri, Paolo Virno) and the "cognitariat" or cognitive worker (Yann Moulier-Boutang, Carlo Vercellone and others). Sun argues that these theories misread the Marxist logic of class, because for Marx and Engels the line between mental and manual labour does not define class, and that Engels's "mental-labour proletariat" is a category that should be fought alongside manual workers. The article has four parts. It first reconstructs the autonomist and cognitive-capitalism accounts of the subject, then their diagnoses of new contradictions and their strategies of struggle. It next sets out Marx and Engels's own treatment of intellect, class and labour-power, and uses it to assess the Western theories. It ends with Engels's 1893 letter to the International Socialist Students' Congress and the historical mission of the mental-labour proletariat. Sun argues that, for Marx, intellect is a shared human attribute, not a criterion of class: "rank is a property of intellect", not the reverse. Class is fixed by position in the relations of production. Sun reads Marx and Engels as distinguishing three kinds of non-material labour: ideologists of the bourgeoisie, autonomous intellectual producers, and intellectual workers subordinated to capital who produce surplus value. Only the last, together with those who put their intellect at the service of universal interests, form the mental-labour proletariat. On this basis Sun criticises Hardt and Negri for splitting proletariat and multitude along the material/non-material line, and Virno for making the general intellect the multitude's unifying principle. Sun also faults the cognitive-capitalism school for opposing "creative power" to labour-power, although labour-power already combines physical and mental capacities, and for blurring bourgeois ideologists with cognitive workers. Sun credits that school with keeping a class logic and credits Virno's point that labour-power is the bearer of life. Sun concludes that proletarian revolution needs both manual and mental-labour proletarians, and that the Western left has forgotten Engels's advice to fight side by side. Without Party leadership, scientific theory and a class alliance, multitude autonomy or cognitive-worker networks are called a postmodern fantasy, a "storm in a teacup". Sun adds that socialism needs intellectuals who serve the people and universal interests, not "refined egoists". Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist critique of Negri, Virno and Moulier-Boutang that rests on Marx and Engels's texts on intellect, class and non-material labour.

Contemporary interpretations of the idea of communism by the Western Left since the 21st century 论21世纪以来西方左翼对共产主义观念的时代阐释 Liu Qingyun Liu Qingyun asks why Western left-wing scholars have returned to the idea of communism since the turn of the century, and how far their reinterpretations can be trusted. The article holds that the idea moved from affirmation, to rejection after the Soviet collapse, to revival, especially after the 2008 capitalist crisis. Liu argues that these thinkers offer useful and innovative insights but are limited by weak revolutionary content and by a diluted use of historical materialism. The article has three parts. The first sets out the pressing conditions and favourable factors behind the revival, drawing on Alain Badiou, Slavoj Žižek, Bruno Bosteels, Jodi Dean, Michael Hardt and Antonio Negri. The second reconstructs their reasoning on two levels: theory (subject theory, immaterial production, egalitarianism) and practice (the revolutionary subject, forms of struggle, the party). The third assesses the strengths and weaknesses of this work, citing mainly English-language books and articles by these authors. Liu reports that these thinkers see capitalism's antagonisms as unresolved. Žižek lists ecological crisis, conflicts over private property and shared knowledge, bioengineering and the divide between the included and the excluded. Dean describes a drift towards neo-feudalism. Hardt and Negri argue that immaterial production creates a shareable "common" that capital can only tax as rent. Practical proposals diverge: Badiou widens the revolutionary subject and rejects the party, Dean defends a communist party, and Hardt and Negri rely on the "multitude". Liu credits Badiou's three-phase periodisation of the communist hypothesis and the autonomist lineage of immaterial labour. Liu then faults these thinkers for treating communism as philosophy rather than revolutionary strategy, and for making Badiou's reliance on contingent "events" and an abstract equality axiom stand in for Marx's analysis. Liu also finds that Žižek's "proletarianised" excluded differ essentially from Marx's proletariat, and that the authors lack economic analysis of capitalism's workings. Liu concludes that Western left thinkers broaden the global outlook on communism and help in understanding its contemporary value. These ideas, Liu says, should be assessed with Marx's historical materialism and materialist dialectics. Liu suggests that subject theory and party-building merit further comparative study for Chinese communist theory. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist assessment of Badiou, Žižek, Dean, Hardt and Negri on communism, with notes pointing to their original English sources.

The dialectic of contemporary capitalist crisis and the movement against inequality Nancy Fraser's theoretical construction of a contemporary Western left emancipation project 当代资本主义危机与反抗不平等运动的辩证法 Fu Wenzhong Li Bingqing Why rebuild a theory of emancipation in the twenty-first century? Fu and Li present Nancy Fraser, a third-generation Frankfurt School thinker, as answering that question from two sides: developing Marxism, whose ultimate aim is human liberation, and criticising a capitalism whose economic, political, social and ecological crises are now intertwined. The article argues that Fraser reworks the legacy of twentieth-century Western emancipation movements into a broader project aimed at overthrowing capitalist domination. It judges this project theoretically and practically valuable, though still incomplete. The article has three parts. The first reviews Fraser's reflection on twentieth-century movements: her multi-dimensional account of postwar capitalist crisis, her reading of postwar movements, her critique of feminism and her analysis of neoliberal hegemony. The second sets out her reconstruction of emancipation in five respects: its concept, goals and values, critical dimensions, women's emancipation and tasks. The third covers her later work after the 2008 financial crisis, namely Feminism for the 99 Percent (2019) and Capitalism: A Conversation in Critical Theory (2018). Fu and Li set this beside Jameson and Piketty. Drawing on Karl Polanyi, Fraser finds that postwar movements were neither market forces nor protective counter-movements. They followed a "third logic" of emancipation, which Polanyi's double movement lacks. The authors report that she defines emancipation as opposing every form of domination and equality as its highest value. They add that she locates three targets for critique: misrecognition in culture, maldistribution in the economy and misrepresentation in politics. They then present her later criteria for telling emancipatory from non-emancipatory claims: non-domination, functional sustainability and democracy. They also present her "4D" model of capitalism's contradictions (division, dependence, disavowal, destabilization). In the authors' account she also calls for a broader working class that includes migrants, women and people of colour, and for stronger trade unions and organisation. Fu and Li conclude that Fraser joins Marxist emancipation theory to critical-theory ideas of justice. They credit her with a new vantage point on capitalism's institutional crisis and with insight into where emancipation may be heading. They also acknowledge that she is still searching for a practical route beyond capitalism. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly reading of Fraser's emancipation theory, covering her move from justice to emancipation and her recent work on capitalism, unions and the working class.

An analysis of the limitations of research on Western Marxism in the narrow sense 狭义西方马克思主义研究的局限性剖析 Tai Lihua Tai Lihua asks why nearly a century of research on Western Marxism has yielded results of limited quality and persuasive force. The article argues that the cause lies in the narrow definitions of the field inherited from Lukács, Korsch and Gramsci in the 1920s and 1930s, and that these definitions disagree with one another. Tai holds that the concept needs to be integrated and widened, and proposes a broader conception of Western Marxism as the alternative. The article identifies four ways in which Western Marxism in the narrow sense has been defined: by geographical space, by time, by research standpoint, method or viewpoint, and by field of study. Each gets its own section, which sets out the definition, names the scholars who use it and states its drawbacks. The thinkers discussed include Korsch, Perry Anderson, the Yugoslav scholar Gerkoćikov, Lukács, Roemer, Hodgson, Laclau and Mouffe, and the ecological Marxists James O'Connor and John Bellamy Foster. Tai argues that each definition produces a specific harm. Definitions by geography, such as Western Europe or Germany, France and Italy, exclude Marxist research in Britain, the United States, Japan and elsewhere, and set Western Marxism against classical and Soviet-East European Marxism. Definitions by time, with labels such as post-Marxism, neo-Marxism and Marxology, are said to blur the concept and to feed claims that Marxism is outdated or defunct. Definitions by standpoint or method, in Tai's account, cover positions that are non-Marxist or anti-Marxist or that rest on idealist method, such as Marxology's opposition between the young and mature Marx, Lukács's retention of method alone, and Roemer's neoclassical modelling. Definitions by field, mainly philosophy, literature, aesthetics and culture, lead to what Tai calls a loss of economics. Tai sees this as sapping the theory's explanatory power and its wholeness, while noting that ecological Marxism's union of interpreting and changing the world deserves praise despite its reformist and utopian risks. Tai concludes that the four definitions respectively entrench regional barriers, intensify nihilism about Marxism, weaken its scientific character and neglect its integrity. The article calls for integrating and widening the narrow concept in order to raise the quality of Western Marxism research and strengthen Marxism's persuasiveness and practical influence. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese scholar of foreign Marxism criticises the standard ways of defining Western Marxism and argues for a broader definition.

An analysis of contemporary Western neo-Marxist class studies 当代西方新马克思主义阶级研究探析 Chen Yanzhen Liu Zhuohong How should one assess the class research produced by Western "new Marxists" since the 1970s? Chen and Liu begin from the challenge that the new technological revolution, the rise of a "new middle class" and the internal division of the working class posed to Marx's class theory. They argue that these scholars share Marx's humanist concern and critical spirit, yet depart from his class theory in nature, focus and specific claims, while still offering insights of some value. The article first sketches the field, using the broad sense of "new Marxism": non-orthodox currents including the Frankfurt School and the post-1970s schools. It then surveys figures such as E.P. Thompson, Poulantzas, Foucault, Jameson, Gorz, John Roemer, Erik Olin Wright, Laclau and Mouffe, Habermas and Honneth, and French critical Marxists. Next it identifies four theoretical features, and finally compares these studies with Marx's theory. The authors identify four features: diversity of approaches, strong engagement with real problems, a shift of critique towards culture, everyday life and micro-level power, and interdisciplinary methods combined with growing academicisation. On the relation to Marx, they accept a shared humanist orientation and a concern with alienation. They hold, however, that the neo-Marxist turn to a de-classed pluralist politics of identity, gender, ecology and race reduces the basic class contradiction to ordinary social conflict. In their account this abandons historical materialism. They list three specific divergences. On the revolutionary subject, Marcuse and Gorz look to students, the unemployed and intellectuals rather than the proletariat. On strategy, the Frankfurt School proposes a "cultural" or "psychological" revolution rather than violent revolution. On criteria of class, they replace ownership of the means of production with occupation, politics and culture. Even so, Chen and Liu say these studies enrich Marxist class theory and offer lessons for China, such as recognising the plurality of interest groups, building channels for their demands and loosening rigid thinking about class. Read the original if you want a Chinese critical overview of how Western neo-Marxist schools handled class after the 1970s.

The labour-relations theory of the French Regulation School and the "Yellow Vests" movement seen through it 法国调节学派劳动关系理论及其视角下的“黄马甲”运动透视 Zhang Jiaxin Yu Shan The article asks what the French Regulation School, a strand of Marxism outside China, says about labour relations, and what that theory can explain about the "Yellow Vests" movement that began in France in November 2018. Zhang and Yu argue that the school's account of four historical forms of capitalist labour relations helps explain the movement's causes. They also argue that the school misses the essence of capitalist labour relations because it does not address exploitation or private ownership of the means of production. After a short introduction and a review of Chinese scholarship, the article sets out the school's "mode of regulation" approach, which works at an intermediate level between micro and macro analysis. Its five components are the monetary and credit regime, the capital–labour relation, forms of competition, the state, and the international system. The authors then compare the school with Marx, apply the theory to the Yellow Vests, and close with an assessment. The school's main figures, Michel Aglietta and Alain Lipietz, are presented as openly drawing on Marxian economics. The authors summarise the school's periodisation: competitive, Taylorist, Fordist and finance-dominated labour relations, each tied to an accumulation regime. Fordism is described as a bargain of mass production and mass consumption, with collective bargaining and long contracts, but also deskilled work. Finance-dominated relations bring flexible, short-term employment, weakened unions and a "Walmart" style of anti-union employment. On comparison with Marx, they find shared ground in treating labour relations as basic relations of production. They contend, however, that Marx saw the capital–labour conflict as irreconcilable, while the school treats it as an empirical political struggle over wages that regulation can ease. Applying this lens, the authors attribute the Yellow Vests to an imbalance in labour relations. They cite neoliberal policy since the 1980s, the decline of manufacturing from 18% to 10% of GDP, labour-law reform, income inequality, and insecure work in peripheral regions dependent on cars. They argue the movement lacked organisation and clear demands, and that the state had no effective channel for mediating labour conflict. Their conclusion is that the school widened Marx's perspective but advises workers to compromise with the bourgeoisie. They also call for a labour-relations model suited to China's conditions that raises the standing of the working class and supports high-quality development. Read the original if you want a Chinese critical reading of Regulation School theory and its use on the Yellow Vests.

The Communist Party of China's major contributions to the world socialist movement over the past century 百年来中国共产党对世界社会主义运动的重大贡献 Jiang Hui Writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in January 2021, shortly before the Party's centenary, Jiang Hui argues that the Communist Party of China's hundred-year history is an organic part of the international communist movement and the world socialist movement. In Jiang's account, the Party has been a firm believer in Marxism and scientific socialism and a leading contributor to their innovative development in the twenty-first century. The piece follows the Party's history in three stages: the Chinese revolution, socialist construction and reform, and the new era. It treats the founding of the Party, the founding of the People's Republic, reform and opening up, and the building of a modern socialist country as milestones for both Chinese and world socialism. Jiang contends that the New Democratic Revolution opened a new path for proletarian revolution, one that surrounded the cities from the countryside. In this reading it was a second successful example after the October Revolution, shifting the global balance of forces and weakening the colonial system. Jiang further holds that after the upheavals in the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe, the Party's persistence with reform and opening up saved and defended world socialism, making China its mainstay. In the new era, Jiang says, socialism with Chinese characteristics has become the most important part of twenty-first-century world socialism. Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era is presented as the Marxism of the twenty-first century, and China's institutional innovation as an option for developing countries. Jiang concludes that the Party will make new and greater contributions to international communism, world socialism and human progress. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a senior Party-affiliated scholar frames the Party's centenary within the history of the world socialist movement.

Communist and workers' parties around the world mark the 150th anniversary of Lenin's birth 世界共产党和工人党纪念列宁诞辰150周年 Yuan Qun Wang Enming Yuan and Wang survey how communist and workers' parties on five continents commemorated the 150th anniversary of Lenin's birth in 2020, and ask what those commemorations show about Leninism today. They argue that the parties' statements demonstrate that Lenin's doctrine on imperialism, proletarian revolution and the dictatorship of the proletariat, war and peace, and the building of socialism is not outdated and remains a guide to action and a theoretical basis for contemporary world socialism. The article is a survey built in four parts. It first catalogues the forms of commemoration, from articles, keynote speeches and joint statements (including one led by the Communist Party of Greece and signed by 93 parties) to wreath-laying, online forums, a Vietnamese stamp and the volume Lenin 150. It then collects the parties' assessments of Lenin's historical contribution, followed by their views on his present-day value and the concrete strategies they draw from him. The authors quote statements from parties in India, the United States, Vietnam, Cuba, Russia, the Philippines, South Africa and elsewhere. In the authors' account, the parties credit Lenin with advancing Marxism to a new stage, supporting national liberation in colonial countries, helping to found the Communist International, and offering guidance to existing socialist states such as Vietnam. On contemporary relevance, the parties hold that Lenin's analysis of monopoly and finance capital explains present capitalism, including the 2008 crisis and the Covid-19 pandemic. From this the authors identify four strategies: holding to communists' founding mission, building the broadest workers' alliance and revolutionary united front, strengthening the workers' struggle, and applying Leninism flexibly rather than dogmatically. On the last point they cite the Workers' Party of Hungary's warning against turning Lenin's theses into dogma. Yuan and Wang conclude that the anniversary was a major event in the political life of world socialism. They hold that the world is still in a historical epoch of transition from capitalism to socialism and is undergoing profound changes of a kind not seen in a century, and that revisiting Lenin's thought has special significance for the revival of contemporary world socialism. Read the original if you want a detailed inventory of which parties said what about Lenin in 2020, as reported from within the Chinese academic discussion of the international communist movement.

The Communist People's Party of Kazakhstan advancing in adversity 逆境中前行的哈萨克斯坦共产主义人民党 Kang Yanru Kang examines the Communist People's Party of Kazakhstan (CPPK), the only communist organisation in Central Asia's five states to hold seats in a national parliament. The article asks how the party has managed to survive and gain a foothold under a strong-presidential system. Kang argues that its ideological discipline, mass-oriented work and adaptable organisation offer useful lessons, but that its position remains relative and unstable. The article moves from history to doctrine to practice. It first traces the 1991 collapse of the Communist Party of Kazakhstan, its alliance with right-wing opposition figures and the 2004 split that produced the CPPK. It then sets out the CPPK's programme, including its views on the Soviet collapse, contemporary capitalism and Kazakhstan's own path. Next come its election campaigns and parliamentary work, followed by an assessment of lessons and difficulties. Kang draws mainly on party documents, party websites and Russian-language scholarship. Kang contends that the old party declined because it allied with the right-wing bourgeois opposition and an oligarch, which made it dependent on alien ideology and split it. The CPPK, by contrast, took the stance of a 'constructive opposition'. It won seven seats in both the 2012 and 2016 parliamentary elections, ran door-to-door campaigns, and tabled more than 200 proposals on poverty, distribution and land. Kang credits three sources of strength: purity of communist ideology, policies grounded in mass interests, and party-building that puts rank-and-file members first. Kang also criticises the CPPK's view that industrial workers are disappearing in the information age, calling it too narrow a reading of the working class. Kang stresses the limits of the party's success. These include a super-presidential system, the dominance of the ruling Nur Otan party (84 of 98 lower-house seats), and the dilemma of retaining communist principles while cooperating with the authorities. The Russian Communist Workers' Party criticised the CPPK's 2016 platform for lacking communist ideas, which Kang takes as a sign of that dilemma. Kang concludes that only persistent long-term struggle and constant adjustment of strategy can widen the party's support. Read the original if you want a detailed, China-based account of a little-covered post-Soviet communist party, including its programme and election record.

The ten hot topics in the international communist movement in 2020 2020年国际共运中的十大热点 Research Centre for Foreign Marxist Parties, Central China Normal University This short year-end review, compiled by the Research Centre for Foreign Marxist Parties at Central China Normal University and published in January 2021, lists what it regards as the ten main topics in the international communist movement in 2020. It presents the year as one of commemoration, pandemic response, and solidarity with struggles against what it calls right-wing forces and imperialism. The ten items are given in brief numbered entries, each of a few sentences. Three concern anniversaries: the 200th birthday of Engels, the 150th birthday of Lenin, and the 75th anniversary of victory in the anti-fascist war. Others cover the Covid-19 pandemic, the US Black Lives Matter movement, a mass strike in India, party centenaries, a Maoist rally in India, and a final group of solidarity campaigns. On the pandemic, the review reports that foreign communist and workers' parties criticised bourgeois governments as slow, mistaken and indifferent to life, and urged them to learn from socialist countries. It says that China, North Korea, Vietnam, Cuba and Laos took effective measures that, in its account, embodied the ideas of putting the people and life first and showed the superiority of socialism. It also reports that over 250 million workers and farmers joined India's national strike of 26 November 2020, and that around 10,000 attended a Communist Party of India (Maoist) rally in Bastar. The last entry lists events that drew solidarity statements, including the US drone strike on Qassem Soleimani, the US use of the Helms–Burton Act against Cuba, protests in Belarus, and an alleged US-backed coup attempt in Venezuela. The review concludes that these activities spread the thought of Marx and Engels, strengthened the ideological equipment of the world proletariat, and expressed internationalist solidarity, which it says parties pursued through joint statements, left-wing websites, demonstrations and regional conferences. It offers no extended analysis. Read the original if you want a quick, Chinese-academic-sourced checklist of the 2020 events and anniversaries that foreign communist parties marked.

A century of the communist movement in Australia and its prospects 澳大利亚共产主义运动的百年历史与发展前景 Zhao Ting Marking the 100th anniversary of the Communist Party of Australia (CPA) in 2020, Zhao Ting surveys a century of Australian communism, its present difficulties and its outlook. The article credits communists with a pioneering role in workers' struggles, Indigenous rights, anti-fascism and the extension of democracy. It concludes that the movement's prospects hold both opportunities and challenges, with challenges outweighing opportunities. The account is chronological and has five parts. It covers the rise of the movement from 1920 to 1955, its splits and decline from 1956 to 1990, and its reorganisation from 1990 onward. It then analyses four present-day challenges and ends with prospects. Zhao draws on CPA programmes and congress documents, Australian Electoral Commission data, OECD material and Chinese and English-language scholarship. Zhao presents the early period as one of growth: the party led strikes, opposed fascism and resisted the Menzies government's attempt to ban it, and by the late 1940s reached a reported peak of 25,000 members. Its later decline is attributed to splits over Khrushchev's 1956 speech, the Sino-Soviet dispute and the 1968 invasion of Czechoslovakia, which produced rival parties. Zhao also blames a neglect of theory and the uncritical adoption of foreign currents, and notes that the party dissolved after 1989. After 1990 the Socialist Party of Australia renamed itself the CPA in 1996. It argues that socialism itself did not fail, only the Soviet model, and calls for a broad alliance under the slogan "Unity Is Strength". The four challenges are a fragmented, casualised working class; employer–union cooperation that has eroded class consciousness; right-wing populism; and a divided left of about a dozen groups. On prospects, Zhao points to economic difficulty, falling voter identification with the main parties and loss of trust in government. In the author's reading, these conditions give socialist parties room to grow, and the performance of China, Cuba and Vietnam in crises shows that an alternative to capitalism is feasible. Zhao sums up the movement as small and outside mainstream politics, but still at the forefront of struggles for workers' rights, women's liberation and Indigenous rights. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly overview of Australian communist organisations, their splits and strategies, with extensive citations of CPA documents.

From the separation of theory and practice to the tension between subject and structure A new look at Perry Anderson's view of Western Marxism 从理论与实践的脱离到主体与结构的张力 Qiao Maolin Existing Chinese and international scholarship on Perry Anderson's view of Western Marxism rests mainly on Considerations on Western Marxism (1976), whose central claim is the separation of theory from practice. Qiao argues that Anderson's In the Tracks of Historical Materialism (1983, cited in the Chinese edition as Contemporary Western Marxism) has been neglected and that the two books together form a single evolving picture. On this reading, Anderson sees the history of Western Marxism as one of divorce between theory and practice, driven at a deeper level by the tension between subject and structure, which ends in the opposition between humanism and the 'death of man'. The article has three sections. The first reconstructs the 1976 book's account of Western Marxism's features, from Lukács, Korsch and Gramsci to the Frankfurt School, Sartre and Althusser. The second turns to the 1983 book, covering Anderson's treatment of Marx, French structuralism and post-structuralism (Sartre, Lévi-Strauss, Althusser, Foucault, Lacan, Derrida) and Saussurean linguistics. The third places Anderson's shift within his own career, from The Origins of the Present Crisis (1964) to the British New Left's decline under Thatcher. Qiao accepts Anderson's description of Western Marxism as cut off from political practice but disputes his explanations. Anderson's claim that Marx's own work contains a subject–structure 'split' is rejected as resting on a single-entity view of historical motive force, possibly shaped by Althusser. Qiao holds that Marx and Engels treat historical motive force as a layered system in which the fundamental driver (the contradiction between productive forces and relations of production) and the direct driver (class struggle) are dialectically united. The French subject–structure debates are attributed instead to the new conditions of advanced capitalism and the rise of phenomenology and existentialism. In the third section, Qiao argues that Anderson's turn to the subject–structure problem was a self-critical reflection on the cultural hegemony paradigm, prompted by the failure of British socialist practice and the Thatcherite reconstruction of the 'historical bloc'. Qiao concludes that Anderson's thought has to be read through the evolution of the cultural hegemony paradigm in its specific historical context, and that his late work revives the Marxist tradition of self-criticism. Anderson is credited with doubting the paradigm's value for analysing social structure while finding it insufficiently deep and constructive. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly reading that links Anderson's two major books on Western Marxism and critiques his claims about Marx.

From Lenin to Gramsci: Colletti on the intellectual resources of the Italian democratic revolution 从列宁到葛兰西：科莱蒂论意大利民主革命的思想资源 Huang Xiaowu How can a backward country carry out a democratic revolution? Huang Xiaowu takes up this question through Lucio Colletti, a leading theorist of the Della Volpe school of Italian Marxism. In the 1950s and 1960s Colletti criticised the Italian Communist Party's (PCI) "peaceful parliamentary road" as a distortion of the Marxist theory of the state. Huang argues that Colletti's critique corrects the PCI at the level of theory but offers no concrete practical strategy. In this, Huang says, Colletti himself falls into the "separation of theory and practice" that he diagnosed in Western Marxism. The article is arranged in three parts. The first reconstructs Colletti's reading of Lenin's State and Revolution, together with Marx and Engels on the Paris Commune, on smashing the bourgeois state machine and on the form of power after revolution. The second follows Colletti's reinterpretation of Gramsci's popular front theory, drawing on his essays and interviews in New Left Review and on Giuseppe Fiori's biography of Gramsci. The third examines Colletti's view of parliamentary struggle and his account of Western Marxism, and compares him with Antonio Negri and Lucio Magri. Huang reports Colletti's claim that revolution cannot be reduced to violent seizure of power. For Colletti, what matters is the political nature of the post-revolutionary regime, and Stalinism's neglect of socialist democracy shows this. Colletti reads Gramsci's popular front as a Leninist strategy for a backward country: Italy was the weak link in the capitalist chain, so the proletariat had to win peasants and the petty bourgeoisie as allies while keeping the revolutionary goal. On this reading the PCI kept only the emphasis on alliance. It confused means and ends, treated parliament as a class-neutral instrument in a Kautskyan way, and so could not move beyond bourgeois democracy. Colletti nevertheless rejects both ultra-leftism and anarchism, holding that parliament should be used while its class nature is remembered. Huang's own assessment is critical. Colletti saw that Western Marxism had become an academic phenomenon cut off from workers' movements, yet his own work stayed abstract. Writing in the 1960s and 1970s, he did not analyse Italy's rising workers' and student movements, unlike Negri and Magri. Huang compares him with Marx's response to the Paris Commune, where Marx revised theory in light of the actual movement. Huang adds that Colletti's questions remain live in Chinese scholarship, including whether Marx has a political philosophy and whether to return to Kant or Hegel. Read the original if you study Italian Marxism, Gramsci's reception, or Chinese scholarly evaluations of Western Marxism and its theory–practice problem.

The contemporary meaning and practical significance of the "two great revolutions" thesis “两个伟大革命”论述的时代蕴含与现实意义 Zhu Zhiwei Zhu Zhiwei examines Xi Jinping's formulation that the Party must use its own self-reform to drive the great social revolution it leads the people to carry out. Writing in 2020, Zhu argues that this "two great revolutions" thesis sums up nearly a century of Party-building and revolutionary practice and is a "historical key" to the Party's victories. The article holds that the thesis carries major historical and practical weight for completing a moderately prosperous society and for realising the Chinese Dream of national rejuvenation. The article has three parts. The first treats the thesis as a defining trait of a Marxist party, tracing it to Marxist conceptions of revolution, of the people and of practice. The second argues that the two revolutions run through the main thread of Party history: the social revolution as the path of the Party's long struggle, self-reform as the key factor in its own construction, and both as unified in its theoretical exploration. The third sets out the thesis's historical significance and present value. Zhu's central claim is that the two revolutions are dialectically united. Self-reform raises the Party's fighting capacity, cohesion and purity and lays the basis for social revolution, while social revolution in turn strengthens Party-building and its ability to govern. Zhu supports this with a survey of milestones, including the Zunyi Meeting, the Yan'an rectification campaign, the two historical resolutions of 1945 and 1981, and the line of theoretical innovation from Mao Zedong Thought to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Zhu also reads the thesis as backing Xi's "two cannots": neither the pre-reform nor the post-reform period may be used to negate the other. Reform and opening up is presented as a continuing social revolution. Zhu concludes that the thesis respects the laws of the Party's historical development, expresses the "great new project" of Party-building, and gathers strength for national rejuvenation. Because Party leadership is, in the article's words, the defining feature of socialism with Chinese characteristics, Zhu calls on Chinese people to hold to the Party's revolutionary posture, deepen reform and act as committed practitioners of the two revolutions. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Party-history scholarship in 2020 framed self-reform and social revolution as one continuous Marxist logic, with its sources in leaders' speeches.

How to vigorously carry forward the great spirit of resistance against Japanese aggression in the new era 新时代如何大力弘扬伟大抗战精神 Wang Junwei Marking the 75th anniversary of victory in the War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression (2020), Wang asks how the great spirit of resistance should be carried forward in the new era. The author argues that the war, a historical turning point for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, forged this spirit, that the Communist Party was its main creator, and that today it should be applied as a spirit of struggle toward the Two Centenary Goals. The article has three parts. The first sets out the background: the suffering and spiritual damage China endured after 1840, culminating in Japanese invasion, and the four components of the spirit as Wang describes them. The second examines the Party's role through declarations, strategy, sacrifice and leadership of the united front. The third turns to present-day tasks, drawing on Xi Jinping's speech at the 75th anniversary symposium. Wang uses anecdotes, poems, wartime documents and accounts by foreign observers as evidence. Wang argues that the national spirit was reborn in the war "like a furnace", producing patriotism, unyielding integrity, determination to fight to the end, and belief in victory. In the author's account, the Party first called for resistance after the 1931 Mukden Incident and, in a period of defeatism, supplied spiritual grounding through Mao Zedong's On Protracted War. It also mobilised the masses, and its members died in disproportionate numbers at the front. Wang cites foreign observers such as Theodore White and John S. Service as describing Yan'an favourably and as predicting a major role for the Communists. The article concludes that national liberation would have taken longer and cost more without Party leadership. Wang concludes that the spirit of struggle must be maintained in the new era, and gives three requirements: keeping to the direction of struggle, defined by Xi Jinping's "five challenges"; maintaining resolve, as in the hard years of 1941–42; and using sound tactics, built on the principal contradiction identified for the new era. The author says this great struggle will be long-term and last until the Second Centenary Goal is achieved. Read the original if you want an example of how Party-line writing links the wartime spirit of resistance to the call for a spirit of struggle today.

Mao Zedong: supreme commander who directed the War to Resist US Aggression and Aid Korea 毛泽东: 运筹抗美援朝战争的最高统帅 Shi Zhongquan Shi Zhongquan asks why Mao Zedong, who never went to the front but directed operations from Zhongnanhai, should be regarded as the real supreme commander of the War to Resist US Aggression and Aid Korea (the Korean War as fought by China, 1950–53). The article argues that Mao's position followed from three determining factors and that he personally decided every major campaign. It also holds that the victory carries lasting historical significance and value for the present day. The article has three parts. The first sets out the three factors behind Mao's supreme command. The second goes through the nine major battles that Shi calls the "5 + 4": the five campaigns after the Chinese People's Volunteers entered Korea, and four large battles fought during the armistice talks, ending with the Kumsong campaign of July 1953. The third part assesses the war's significance, drawing on Mao's own post-armistice remarks and on Zhou Enlai, Peng Dehuai and Jiang Zemin. Shi relies mainly on Mao's chronology, Peng Dehuai's biography and official war histories. On the first part, Shi says the war involved the relations between China and Korea, their two parties and their two armies, and that the front commanders could not settle these. Mao himself handled the joint command, battle plans and the wording of communiqués. The war also sat inside the post-1945 world order and the alliance with the Soviet Union, so Mao had to negotiate with Stalin on air cover, arms, command authority and whether to pursue the enemy south of the 38th Parallel, while keeping China independent. The deepest factor, in Shi's account, was Mao's personal ability and daring, shown in his decision to send troops before Stalin had agreed to air support. Shi presents Mao as the author of guidelines such as "if victory cannot be quick, make it slow" and rotating units. Shi concludes that the war's significance has five aspects. The Chinese nation "stood up" with confidence and gained a peaceful setting for construction. The victory also showed that people's war thinking still applies against a modern army. It produced the Resist US Aggression and Aid Korea spirit, strengthened anti-colonial movements, and helped make peace and development the theme of the age. He cites figures that he says show a lopsided cost ratio in China's favour. Read the original if you want an officially aligned, Mao-centred account of the Korean War, with Chinese-language sources, battle-by-battle detail and the Party's present-day reading of the war's meaning.

Joint statements of communist and workers' parties: the converging voice of the international communist movement in the internet age 共产党和工人党的联合声明——互联网时代国际共产主义运动的聚力表达 Yu Weihai Wang Xiaoqing Yu Weihai and Wang Xiaoqing ask why joint statements by communist and workers' parties have multiplied since the 2008 financial crisis, and what they achieve for a movement the authors describe as fragmented into some 400 parties. They argue that, although the movement is at a low ebb, joint statements show a renewed trend towards unity. In their view the statements have real value as expressions of proletarian internationalism, but their limits are clear. The article, published in 2020, first sets out four background factors: capitalism's offensive against the working class, imperialist expansion, the rise of the far right and anti-communism, and the internet as a cheap platform for statements. It then surveys the main themes of the statements: historical figures and anniversaries, capitalist crisis, opportunism and revisionism, and the strengthening of party unity. Next it identifies four features of the statements, and it ends by weighing their value and limits. The evidence is drawn from statements posted on sites such as Solidnet, Red Globe and ICOR, mainly up to mid-2020. The authors report that the statements trace the crisis to the contradiction between socialised production and private ownership, link it to fascism, war and anti-communism, and present it as showing the need for socialism. On unity, they say the parties accept diversity as a precondition and call for stronger inter-party mechanisms. They add that most parties judge conditions unripe for a new Communist International. The authors list the typical features of the statements. These are international conference platforms as the main vehicle, a shift towards specific topics, voluntary and equal signing in several languages, and closer online and offline coordination. Yu and Wang conclude that joint statements embody proletarian internationalism and help the socialist and communist movement regain strength. They also identify three limits: no strong organiser, aspirations that are partly utopian and lack mechanisms for joint action ("saying too much, doing too little"), and persistent splits between Marxist-Leninist, Marxist-Leninist-Maoist and other currents. The authors judge that statements fragmented by topic still need a complex, systematic effort to have greater practical effect. Read the original if you want a survey of how the world's communist parties use joint statements and online platforms, with many named examples from 2008 to 2020.

New trends in the Communist Party of Nepal after taking power 执政后尼泊尔共产党的新动向 Yuan Qun Ji Guangli Writing in a 2020 issue of Party and Government Studies, Yuan and Ji examine the Communist Party of Nepal (CPN) after the left alliance of the CPN (Unified Marxist-Leninist) and the CPN (Maoist Centre) took office in February 2018 and merged in May 2018. They ask whether the new party can seize its opportunities, meet its challenges and hold power for the long term. Their answer is cautiously positive: the government is described as the most stable in nearly 30 years, with achievements in politics, the economy, society and diplomacy. The article has four parts. It first traces the party's merger, covering the fusion of the two parties' theory and the completion of organisational integration. It then reviews domestic policy (political institutions, economic restructuring, livelihood investment) and foreign policy (relations with China, India and multilateral diplomacy). It closes with an assessment of the party's prospects, including internal risks, great-power pressure and the opposition Nepali Congress. On theory, the authors report that the merged party adopted Marxism-Leninism as its guiding ideology, democratic centralism as its organisational principle and socialism as its strategic goal. In the party's own account, Nepal's productive forces remain backward and its dependence on foreign countries strong, so the immediate task is a socialism-oriented national industrial capitalism rather than building socialism directly. Organisationally, posts were shared between the two predecessors at about 6:4, and Oli and Prachanda stayed co-chairs. The authors credit the government with 7.1 per cent growth in 2018–19 and with expanded health, training, infrastructure and reconstruction programmes. They present deepening ties with China, culminating in Xi Jinping's October 2019 visit and a strategic partnership, as a central achievement. The authors identify uncertainties: unresolved disagreement over issues such as the people's war, Prime Minister Oli's health, and the division of the party into Oli, Nepal and Prachanda factions. They say India is tightening its grip through aid, while the United States is courting Nepal to curb China and the Belt and Road Initiative. They add that the Nepali Congress is regrouping to challenge the party. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly account of Nepal's ruling communists, with details on their merger, appointments and foreign policy, and on how Chinese observers view the party's prospects.

Marxism in the course of the African socialist movement 非洲社会主义运动历程中的马克思主义 Zheng Xiangfu Shu Wenhao Zheng Xiangfu and Shu Wenhao ask how Marxism spread and developed in Africa, and why it fell back after the Cold War. Their thesis is that Marxism in Africa has been bound up with the continent's socialist movements and has passed through three stages: introduction and rise, flourishing, and decline. They argue that its return to Africa is possible but will be long and winding. The article follows these three stages in turn. It first traces the rise of African socialism from the 1920s, then the two waves of socialist movement from the independence era to the mid-1980s, and finally the post-Soviet downturn and its aftermath. Cases include South Africa, Algeria, Senegal, Guinea, Sudan, Ghana, Tanzania, Congo, Ethiopia, Mozambique and Angola. For the early period, the authors identify three channels of transmission: the Communist International and the communist parties, colonial and migrant intellectuals, and the Pan-African movement. They hold that Marxism was then only one element within Pan-Africanism. Later, they argue, leaders such as Nkrumah turned from Pan-Africanism and village-community socialism to Marxism in response to neo-colonialism. Regimes professing 'scientific socialism' set up vanguard parties, accepted class struggle and pursued planned economies and nationalisation. The authors judge these regimes failures. They blame over-reliance on the Soviet model and a dogmatic handling of the tension between Marxism's universality and Africa's particularity, and they say the regimes fell with the Soviet Union. Looking ahead, the authors say the failure of three decades of neoliberalism has revived interest in Marxism. They call on African states to study socialism with Chinese characteristics and the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind, and to develop productive forces, partly by drawing on market mechanisms, as Lenin's view of state monopoly capitalism suggests. They also urge states to accept foreign aid critically. They present China's Belt and Road Initiative and its Africa policy as helpful examples. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly periodisation of Marxism in Africa and a view of how Chinese academics link Africa's prospects to the Chinese experience.")

Social inequality and an opportunity for the revival of the Western left 社会不平等与西方左翼复兴的契机 Xing Wenzeng Writing in 2020, after the debate sparked by Thomas Piketty's Capital in the Twenty-First Century (2014) and the protests following George Floyd's death, Xing argues that inequality is an incurable chronic ailment of capitalism. Since the 2008 financial crisis, the author says, it has worsened in the West, producing economic, political and social turmoil and challenging the capitalist system. This, Xing contends, gives the Western left a chance to revive, provided it adapts its theory and strategy to the actual sources of inequality. The article has three parts. The first documents growing inequality in the United States and Europe, using figures on wealth shares, racial wealth gaps, unemployment during the Covid-19 pandemic, and income divergence within Europe. The second sets out five ways inequality is said to strike at the capitalist order: recurrent economic crisis, political polarisation, populist revival, intensified social conflict and labour and social movements, and growing doubts about neoliberalism. The third turns to the left's opportunities and tasks. Xing's central move is to reject explanations that locate the roots of inequality in globalisation, technology, weakened unions or interest-group politics. Citing Marx, Engels and Lenin, the author holds that these are all products of the capitalist system itself, so patching it up cannot overcome its predicament. Movements such as Occupy Wall Street and the Yellow Vests, together with rising interest in Marx and in socialism among young people, are read as signs of disillusion with capitalism. Xing also notes that such movements lack a clear definition of the 'other world' they want, and that the left has so far offered mainly tax-based remedies. Xing concludes that the left must give a scientific account of the root causes of inequality rather than target individual policies. It must also take part in and lead workers' and social movements, spreading its theory and working with trade unions so that these movements turn into a socialist movement able to challenge capitalism. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist assessment of Western inequality data, populism and the prospects of the Western left after 2008 and during the pandemic.

Western left-wing media's new discussions of the crisis of capitalism in the context of COVID-19 新冠疫情背景下西方左翼媒体对资本主义危机的新探讨 Xing Caili Writing in 2020, Xing Caili asks how Western left-wing media and theorists have interpreted the COVID-19 pandemic in relation to the crisis of capitalism. The article argues that, since the collapse of the Soviet bloc, the Western left has revived as capitalism has again fallen into crisis, and that new media have given it wider channels to spread its ideas. Xing reports that left commentators divide over whether the pandemic deepens the crisis or leaves capitalism essentially unchanged, and that the article itself stresses the working class as the decisive force. The article has three parts. The first sets out the state of Western left media, which Xing calls "marginal" beside the BBC, CNN or the New York Times, and sorts them into three types: websites of Marxist parties (for example People's World and Liberation News in the US), general left sites (Solidnet, Peoples Dispatch, Monthly Review Online, Jacobin), and personal sites and blogs of activists and theorists such as David Harvey. The second part reviews the debate over the pandemic's effect on capitalism. The third turns to workers' protest and the question of the agent of struggle. In the second part Xing first presents the view that the pandemic aggravates the crisis. Slavoj Žižek says it has dealt capitalism a blow and revived an implicit communism, citing Trump's stimulus and use of the Defense Production Act as a "socialisation" of the economy; Judith Butler speaks of a revived socialist imagination. Harvey argues that consumerism, which has sustained capitalism since 2008, is collapsing alongside a crisis of neoliberalism. Against this, Xing sets Alain Badiou, who holds that an epidemic does not bring political revolution, and Byung-Chul Han, who predicts that capitalism will emerge stronger, with digital surveillance promoted as a success. Polanyi and Mike Davis are cited on how the pandemic exposes class and regional inequality, undermining the claim that the virus treats everyone equally. Xing concludes that whether capitalism changes depends less on the epidemic than on struggles waged by the working class in production. Antonio Negri's call to enter the fight is contrasted with Badiou's advice to stay at home, and a March 2020 statement by communist and workers' parties, initiated by the Communist Party of Greece, is quoted as saying workers must not pay for the crisis. Xing also draws on Marx and Engels to present the working class as the subject of fundamental social change. Read the original if you want a short survey of the Western left websites and thinkers who commented on the pandemic and capitalism in spring 2020, as seen from a Chinese Marxist viewpoint.

The alienated substance and the substance as subject: Žižek's new inquiry into Marx's philosophy of capital 异化的实体与主体的实体——齐泽克对马克思资本哲学思想的新探讨 Kong Ming'an Tan Yong Kong Ming'an and Tan Yong take up Slavoj Žižek's charge that Marx wavers in Capital between two views of capital: as an alienated substance within a historical process, and as a substance that is already subject. The authors note that the choice bears on the proletariat's historical role and on the path from capitalism to communism. They argue that Žižek misreads Marx: the two views are a dialectical double characterisation, and Marx fundamentally treats capital as an alienated substance. The article has four parts. It first reconstructs Žižek's reasoning, drawn from Tarrying with the Negative, on Hegel's infinite and negative judgments, unequal exchange and "absolute freedom". It then turns to Lukács's History and Class Consciousness, read as a case of the alienation reading. The third part examines Marx's own texts in Capital, volumes 1 and 3, and a short conclusion follows. In the authors' account, Žižek holds that Hegelian reconciliation does not mean the subject reappropriating the whole substance. He sees Marx's vision of proletarian revolution as such a "closed economy", in which every loss is repaid. If capital is already a self-mediating subject, humans become its instruments, and resistance becomes impossible. The authors answer with Lukács's analysis of reification and proletarian class consciousness, which they read as following Marx's treatment of capital as alienated substance. Turning to Marx, they show that he does call capital self-moving value, a vampire living on living labour, and a "subject" in the forms M–C–M′ and M–M′. They then give three reasons why the subject-substance view is conditional. It holds only under capitalism, which is a transitory stage. Capital's internal contradictions, including the falling rate of profit and the conflict between productive forces and relations of production, limit its self-valorisation. The proletariat, created by capitalism, will make a revolution and bring production under the conscious control of freely associated people. The authors conclude that Marx's two views of capital are dialectical, like use-value and exchange-value or concrete and abstract labour. They hold that the alienation view is basic, since it ties in with capitalism's historical transience and the proletariat's revolutionary role in reappropriating alienated substance. Žižek's claim of ambiguity in Marx is therefore, in their view, a misreading. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist rebuttal of Žižek's reading of Marx on capital, set against Lukács on reification.

Foreign voices praise the achievements of China's ecological civilization construction in the new era 国外高度评价新时代中国生态文明建设成就 Liu Xiaoyun This short commentary, published in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2020, collects favourable assessments by foreign scholars, officials and organisations of China's ecological civilization construction since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Liu's thesis is that, under the guidance of Xi Jinping's thought on ecological civilization, China has found a path suited to its own conditions. In the article's account, this path has won broad international attention and approval and has contributed to improving the global environment. The piece is built almost entirely from quotations and paraphrases of named foreign speakers. They include academics in Australia, Britain, the United States, Japan, Germany and Nepal, and figures from UN agencies, the World Bank and environmental NGOs. It is organised in four sections: praise for China's achievements, interest in the experience behind them, and recognition of China's contribution to global ecological civilization. The text gives no independent data beyond the policies and initiatives it lists. Liu reports foreign commentators as saying that China's green development is among the world's leaders, that China has met its 2020 climate and nature-reserve targets early, and that its pollution control offers a model. The experience they identify includes clear and determined top-level direction, the "two mountains" concept (that lucid waters and lush mountains are invaluable assets), and a strong institutional capacity to implement policy. They also cite innovations such as the river chief system and green finance, wide public participation, and roots in the traditional idea of harmony between heaven and humanity. John B. Cobb Jr. is quoted as saying that the socialist system with Chinese characteristics does better than Western capitalism in reconciling environmental protection with economic growth. The article concludes that China's ecological civilization offers "Chinese wisdom" and a "Chinese sample" for global environmental governance. It points to initiatives such as the national plan for the 2030 Agenda, ratification of the Paris Agreement, the Belt and Road green development coalition, and desertification-control experience that Morocco and other countries are drawing on. Read the original if you want a compact sample of how Chinese official media present foreign endorsements of the country's ecological policy, with the names and affiliations of the people quoted.

Vietnam's economic renovation: course and theoretical exploration 越南经济革新的历程及理论探索 Pan Jin'e Writing in Qiushi's sister journal Qianxian (2020), Pan Jin'e asks how Vietnam's economic renovation (Doi Moi) since 1986 produced both practical results and a theory, the socialist-oriented market economy. The author argues that more than 30 years of renovation have delivered marked achievements and a distinct theoretical and institutional framework. This framework resembles China's theory of the socialist market economy in some ways and differs in others, so that the two countries can learn from each other. The article first reviews the practice of renovation, from contract farming through the equitisation of state enterprises to financial and service-sector reform. It divides the process into three phases: building internal strength (1986–2006), integration into the world economy (2006–2019), and a phase beginning around 2019 that targets Industry 4.0. It then traces how the Vietnamese Communist Party's congresses, from the sixth (1986) to the twelfth (2016), reshaped official thinking on ownership, the market and distribution. Pan's central claim is that the theory rests on a shift in thinking. Vietnam moved from a Soviet-style centralised planned economy to the view that it is in a transitional period to socialism, in which the market economy is a product of human civilisation and a means of building socialism rather than something equivalent to capitalism. The article stresses the changes in ownership: recognition of multiple economic sectors, the 2006 elevation of the private sector to a driver of growth, and the dropping of public ownership of the main means of production as a basic feature of socialism, which Pan notes still divides Vietnamese theorists. Pan also says the Party's understanding of socialist ownership moved from public ownership to socialisation, with state enterprises falling to about 20% of GDP. Distribution now combines labour-based, factor-based and welfare channels. Pan lists problems: uneven development, an irrational economic structure, lagging infrastructure, urban pollution, heavy dependence on foreign investment and trade, and the fact that 76% of firms have not begun digitalising. The author warns that CPTPP commitments on trade unions, state enterprises and freedom of association could weaken state control, and that avoiding the middle-income trap depends on resolving these issues. Pan notes that China defines itself as in the primary stage of socialism, whereas Vietnam places itself in a transitional period. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's periodised account of how Vietnamese Party congresses redefined ownership and the market, and how that compares with China.

Western political parties' positioning of "the people" and the paradox of their practice 西方政党的“人民”定位及其实践悖论 Yu Haiqing Yu Haiqing asks why Western party politics has fallen into difficulty in recent years and finds one main cause in the gap between ideas and practice. In the author's account, Western parties proclaim themselves representatives of "the people" while pursuing a "de-peopling" (qu renminhua) practice, and this conflict has pushed some of them into a crisis of representation. The article is a short commentary in a Chinese current-affairs journal. The first part surveys how parties across the Western spectrum invoke "the people". Yu looks at mainstream conservative, liberal and Christian parties, with the US Democrats and Republicans as examples. The article then turns to social democratic parties, which moved from a working-class identity to that of "people's parties", and to green parties and populist parties. The second part sets out four ways in which practice contradicts this rhetoric, drawing mainly on examples from the Covid-19 pandemic and the Trump administration. Yu's central claim is that every party is by nature the representative of a particular class, and that mainstream Western parties are bourgeois parties tied to big capital and interest groups. The four contradictions are these. First, when popular and capital interests conflict, parties favour capital; the author cites hesitation over lockdowns early in the pandemic. Second, parties put their own interests first, because they operate as vote-seeking machines in a political "market"; the author cites the mask dispute between the two US parties. Third, populist parties do not truly represent the people but "hijack" the popular will through identity politics, and the author cites the US–China trade war and the withdrawal from the World Health Organization as harming Americans themselves. Fourth, slow decision-making, winner-takes-all rules and parliamentary thresholds erode public trust in the party system. Yu concludes that a lack of representativeness weakens the legitimacy of Western party systems and, in the long run, the foundations of liberal democracy. Efforts to make parties more flexible cannot succeed, in the author's view, because of their class nature. Drawing a lesson for China, Yu argues that the "people-centred" development philosophy must be carried into practice, answering "what to do" and "how to do it", in order to show the Communist Party's "people first" character. Read the original if you want an example of how Chinese Marxist scholarship framed Western party politics and the pandemic in 2020.

A new-era reading of Mao Zedong's "On Practice" 毛泽东《实践论》的新时代解读 Liu Shulin Liu Shulin asks what Mao Zedong's 1937 essay "On Practice" still offers in the new era. The author argues that the work systematically inherits and develops Marxist philosophy, sums up the historical experience of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, and deepens the line of seeking truth from facts. Its scientific world outlook and methodology, Liu holds, remain important today. The article has three parts. The first sets out the essay's origins: its roots in Mao's lecture outline on dialectical materialism for the Anti-Japanese Military and Political University, its publication in the Soviet Union in December 1950 and in the People's Daily on 29 December 1950. The second summarises its main theoretical points on epistemology. The third draws out four lessons for the present. On the background, Liu names four factors: the turn from civil war to the War of Resistance against Japan; the damage caused by dogmatism, which separated the subjective from the objective; the Long March's arrival in northern Shaanxi and the need to build base areas; and the need to educate a depleted but valuable cadre corps. On theory, Liu lists five points: practice is the sole source of knowledge, the driving force of its development and the sole criterion of its truth; knowledge moves from perceptual to rational understanding and then, in a second and more important leap, back to practice; and the subjective and objective, theory and practice must be united concretely and historically. For the new era, Liu calls for four things. Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era should be understood as the latest theoretical result of Marxism, drawn from practice. Truth must be tested from the standpoint of the people, with the practice of millions as the measure. Party members must keep remoulding their subjective world while changing the objective one, a point Liu links to problems in inner-Party political life. Understanding must also develop through new practice, as it did with the socialist market economy. Read the original if you want a short Party-journal example of how "On Practice" is used to support current Party theory and Party-building.

The harms of populism, seen through America's response to COVID-19 从美国新冠肺炎疫情应对 看民粹主义危害 Wang Lei Writing in 2020, while the pandemic was still spreading, Wang argues that the United States' handling of COVID-19 exposes the damage done by populism, unilateralism and xenophobia. In Wang's account, the Trump government's populist line worsened the domestic outbreak and deepened international division at the moment when cooperation was most needed. The short commentary appeared in the Party journal Dangjian. The article first notes the political and economic roots of American populism, which it says helped carry Trump to the presidency in 2016. It then lists six consequences visible during the pandemic: neglect of science, sharper ethnic tension, withdrawal from multilateralism and pressure on the World Health Organization, beggar-thy-neighbour behaviour towards other states, trade protectionism, and the collapse of the US-led international order. It closes with the November 2020 election and a call for international cooperation. Wang's central claim is that Trump, driven by electoral and economic calculation, chose short-term popularity over expert advice. The author cites the dismantling of a pandemic office, the rejection of Anthony Fauci's February advice on social distancing, and the politicisation of appointments at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, with Francis Fukuyama quoted as linking populist leaders to poor pandemic governance. Wang adds that politicians shifted blame to immigrants, minorities and foreign powers. In Wang's telling, this took the form of anti-Chinese rhetoric, cutting World Health Organization funding in April, seizing allies' medical supplies and pressing India over hydroxychloroquine exports. Wang says the pandemic also strengthened calls to bring supply chains home, which risks further US–China decoupling. Wang cites Kori Schake, who said the US had 'failed' a leadership test. Wang concludes that populism and protectionism cannot deliver 'absolute security' and instead accumulate risk, pointing to Thomas Wright and Kurt Campbell, who wrote in The Atlantic that the crisis showed the limits of populism as a mode of governing. The election, the author suggests, would test Trump's populist platform, and a win would show populism had not yet peaked. Wang holds that only joint action guided by the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind can defeat epidemics and restore global order. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a Party journal framed the US pandemic response and populism for domestic readers in mid-2020.

Learning Lenin's intellectual example and persisting in developing Marxism 学习列宁的思想风范 坚持发展马克思主义 Qu Qingshan Marking the 150th anniversary of Lenin's birth in 2020, Qu Qingshan asks what Chinese Communists should take from Lenin's life and thought.
