The commentary argues that commemorating Lenin is not only a tribute but a way to understand the core meaning, people-centred outlook and theoretical character of Marxism-Leninism, and so to grasp more firmly the Party's own innovative theory. The piece first sketches Lenin's life: his formation in tsarist Russia, his work building the Bolshevik party, the October Revolution of 1917, the defence of Soviet power and the New Economic Policy. It then lists the main components of Leninism, namely the theory of imperialism, the new-type proletarian party, socialist revolution in a single country, the state and the dictatorship of the proletariat, the national and colonial question, and socialist construction in a relatively backward country. It also notes Lenin's writings on China and the Chinese Communist Party's origins in the influence of the October Revolution. The core of the argument is a set of lessons drawn from Lenin and tied to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. First, Marxism is practical and open to development, and Qu presents Xi Jinping Thought as the latest result of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context. Second, Lenin's closeness to the masses models the people-centred stance, which Qu says was shown again in the response to the COVID-19 epidemic. Third, Lenin's party-building ideas support the Party's leadership over all work, the Two Upholds and full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. Qu adds that Lenin's search for a socialist path in a backward country supports the view that socialism has no single fixed pattern. Qu concludes that Chinese Communists should draw on Lenin's firm ideals and perseverance, which the author illustrates with his years of imprisonment and exile, in order to strengthen their faith in Marxism and in socialism with Chinese characteristics. The aim is to realise the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and, ultimately, communism. Read the original if you want an example of how a senior Party historian in 2020 used Lenin's anniversary to link Leninism to current Party doctrine and Party-building themes.

Truly integrating with the people 真正同人民结合起来 Jia Lizheng This commentary, first published in People's Daily on 13 October 2020, asks what it means for the Communist Party of China to "truly integrate with the people". Jia Lizheng argues that the Party must always keep three questions in view: who it is, for whom it works, and on whom it relies. Answering them, the author says, keeps cadres aware that they are public servants and keeps the Party's ties to the masses close. The piece is organised in three sections, one for each question. The first treats the Party's identity as the vanguard of both the working class and the Chinese people and nation. The second deals with the Party's purpose and mission. The third deals with the people as the foundation of Party rule. Throughout, Jia draws on the Communist Manifesto and on statements by Xi Jinping, including his remarks at a symposium with grassroots representatives. On identity, Jia holds that the Party's Marxist character means it has no interests apart from those of the people. Jia presents the Party's history of revolution, construction and reform, its self-reform, and its record since the 18th Party Congress (2012) as proof that Party leadership changed the people's fate. On purpose, Jia says the Party's goal is the people's aspiration for a better life and that its governance is people-centred, citing the response to COVID-19 as an example of putting people and lives first. On reliance, Jia invokes historical materialism: the masses create history, and the Party's strength comes from drawing wisdom from them. The article cites over four million community workers in 650,000 urban and rural communities during the epidemic. Jia concludes that, as the country nears the first centenary goal and prepares to begin building a modern socialist country, new difficulties lie ahead. The harder the tasks, the more the Party must rely on the people, and the people will rally around the Party if it keeps their interests above all. The text is a Party-media commentary that restates the official people-centred line. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Party media in 2020 framed the Party–people relationship through the "who am I, for whom, on whom" formula.

Joining hands to meet global challenges 携手应对全球性挑战 Zhang Yansheng Writing in the People's Daily in October 2020, Zhang Yansheng comments on Xi Jinping's speech to the general debate of the 75th UN General Assembly. Zhang argues that the Covid-19 pandemic and the 'great changes unseen in a century' reinforce each other, so countries must prepare for more global challenges. In this setting, Zhang says, the speech helps readers judge external risks soberly and confirms that China's development remains in a period of important strategic opportunity. The short commentary follows the themes of the speech in turn: solidarity against the pandemic, economic globalization, ecological civilization and climate action, multilateralism and great-power responsibility, and finally China's domestic economic strategy. Zhang contends that the choice between cooperation and blame-shifting concerns humanity's future, and calls for a community with a shared future for mankind, one that drops zero-sum thinking and ideological dispute and respects each country's chosen path. Economic globalization, in Zhang's account, is an irreversible historical trend with real shortcomings, now facing headwinds. Zhang endorses the speech's calls for an open world economy, the WTO-centred trading system, opposition to unilateralism and protectionism, and stable supply chains. On climate, Zhang cites China's pledge to peak carbon dioxide emissions before 2030 and reach carbon neutrality before 2060. Zhang concludes that China will form a new development pattern with domestic circulation as the mainstay and domestic and international circulations reinforcing each other. In Zhang's view this will give impetus to world recovery and let China act as a builder of peace, contributor to global development and defender of the international order. Read the original if you want a brief, officially aligned reading of Xi Jinping's September 2020 UN speech and its link to the 'dual circulation' strategy.

Resolutely practising multilateralism and promoting the healthy development of economic globalization 坚定践行多边主义 推动经济全球化健康发展 Zhao Jinping Writing in the People's Daily on 23 October 2020, Zhao Jinping takes up Xi Jinping's speech at the summit marking the 75th anniversary of the United Nations. Zhao argues that the speech offers a Chinese approach to shared global risks and strengthens China's resolve to practise multilateralism, promote the healthy development of economic globalization and build a community with a shared future for mankind. This short commentary first defines multilateralism as mutual respect, equal consultation and cooperation. It then works through three conditions for it to function: rules, harmonious cooperation and concrete action. It closes by returning to the anniversary and China's commitment. Zhao contends that international organisations such as the UN must defend a fair multilateral environment against what the article calls the hegemonic, bullying conduct of certain politicians. On rules, Zhao points to the UN Charter's principle of sovereign equality and criticises "exceptionalism" and double standards by some countries that place domestic law above international law; the article calls for stronger and more authoritative rule enforcement. On cooperation, Zhao rejects Cold War thinking, ideological lines and zero-sum games, and urges dialogue over conflict and win-win outcomes in the face of the COVID-19 pandemic. On action, Zhao cites most UN members' choices in global anti-pandemic cooperation as evidence of growing capacity, and wants public health and development, including rights to subsistence and development, prioritised. Zhao concludes that the speech is both an expectation placed on international organisations and a solemn Chinese commitment, and predicts that multilateralism will gain wider acceptance as global cooperation advances. The article also says the UN and other bodies need reform to reflect the rise of developing countries. Read the original if you want a concise example of how an official-media commentary in late 2020 presented China's multilateralism and criticised unilateralism after Xi's UN speech.

The lies and disorder of American-style democracy under money politics 金钱政治下美式民主的谎言与乱象 Jin Xiaoxia This short commentary, first published in Guangming Daily on 16 October 2020, argues that elections are not the same as democracy. Jin contends that American presidential elections, presented by the United States as a democratic model, are in essence a money game manipulated by capital and parties, and that they fail to protect citizens' political rights. The piece proceeds through five headed sections: capital-controlled "money rule"; "rule by selected masters", where voters can only choose agents of capital; the gap between the electoral system and "rule by the majority"; social division rather than integration; and loss of governing capacity through struggles over interests. Its evidence includes the Electoral College, the 2000 Bush–Gore result and a remark by former president Jimmy Carter. Jin starts from the Marxist claim that an election is a political form whose character depends on its economic basis. Under private ownership of the means of production, the author argues, elections serve bourgeois rule. Campaign finance from the wealthy and corporations, media control over voters' information, and policy favours for donors are said to turn elections into oligarchy. Jin adds that the Electoral College and winner-takes-all rules distort popular will, that low turnout reflects voters' sense of being unrepresented, and that campaigning breeds partisan attacks, populism and short-termism. The author also claims that televised performance favours showmanship over governing ability, and that executive–legislative gridlock and interest-group bargaining reduce efficiency. Jin concludes that, in a country where money dominates politics, talk of political participation is empty without money. Citizens' political rights, the author says, are hard to guarantee. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Chinese official-academic commentary in 2020 framed a Marxist critique of US elections.

Drawing strength for the road ahead from the great spirit of resistance against Japanese aggression 从伟大抗战精神中汲取前行力量 Cui Wenlong This commentary, first published in Guangming Daily on 14 October 2020, takes up the question of what the "great spirit of resistance against Japanese aggression" means today. Cui Wenlong argues that this spirit, formed during the Chinese people's War of Resistance against Japan, remains a precious spiritual resource. In the author's view, it can drive the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and also advance world peace and development. The piece opens by summarising the war as the longest, largest and costliest national liberation struggle in modern Chinese history and the first to end in complete victory. It then cites Xi Jinping's speech at the symposium marking the 75th anniversary of victory, which listed the spirit's components: patriotism, national integrity, heroism and conviction of victory. The body is organised in three parts: the spirit as a source of unity, as a source of drive to overcome difficulties, and as a contribution to world peace. On unity, Cui argues that the Party's leadership and the anti-Japanese national united front show how all forces can be mobilised, and that the same approach is needed for national rejuvenation. On drive, the author cites casualty and economic-loss figures from the war and the heroism of martyrs. Cui links this to the present, claiming that as China grows stronger, hostile forces abroad try to distort the Party's history and the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The author calls for strategic composure, confidence in that path, and a "spirit of struggle" guided by Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, with Mao Zedong's On Protracted War as a model of scientific analysis. On peace, Cui presents China's resistance as the first major anti-fascist theatre, and draws from it lessons for peaceful development, win-win cooperation and remembering history without perpetuating hatred. Cui concludes that carrying forward the spirit of resistance helps China meet obstacles on the road to rejuvenation and supports a community with a shared future for mankind, in which no country can face global challenges alone. The author states that China will not develop at other countries' expense. Read the original if you want an example of how official commentary in 2020 tied the memory of the anti-Japanese war to Party leadership, the united front and China's present foreign-policy language.

Mao Zedong's reflections and explorations on solving the problem of poverty 毛泽东关于解决贫困问题的思考与探索 Wu Xiaoni Writing in Guangming Daily in September 2020, as China announced the elimination of absolute poverty, Wu Xiaoni revisits how Mao Zedong, as core of the Party's first generation of central leadership, thought about why China was poor and how poverty could be removed. The article argues that Mao identified the roots of poverty, set out basic paths for tackling it, and left experience that still offers lessons, despite mistakes made along the way. This short commentary is divided into three parts. The first deals with the social-system roots of poverty and the move to socialism. The second turns to food supply and the rural poor. The third treats poverty as a question of developing the productive forces, covering mechanisation, education and science, and industrialisation. It draws on Mao's speeches and writings from 1919 to the late 1950s, together with economic figures for the early People's Republic. Wu begins from the Marxist view, citing Capital, that private ownership of the means of production is the source of poverty. Mao, in this account, traced China's poverty to its semi-colonial, semi-feudal condition. The article says the revolution removed the "three big mountains", and the socialist transformation completed in 1956 was the fundamental guarantee. As evidence it cites growth in gross industrial and agricultural output of 67.8 per cent between 1952 and 1957. It then shows Mao treating grain as the first priority ("eating is the first great matter"), and rural cooperative medical care as a form of basic security. Finally, Wu presents Mao's view that poverty means low living standards caused by low productive forces. Mao therefore called for agricultural mechanisation, a "technological revolution" and a "cultural revolution". Wu concludes that, under Mao's leadership, the poverty and backwardness of old China changed greatly, and that an independent and relatively complete industrial system laid the material basis for ending poverty. The article acknowledges failures, naming the Great Leap Forward and especially the Cultural Revolution, which it says caused heavy losses. It maintains that Mao nonetheless clarified the roots of poverty, established the standing of rural anti-poverty work, and deepened understanding of the grain question. Read the original if you want a concise, officially oriented account of how Mao's thinking on poverty is presented in the context of the 2020 poverty-alleviation campaign.

The great spirit of resistance against Japanese aggression will forever inspire the Chinese people to forge ahead 伟大抗战精神永远激励中国人民砥砺奋进 Liu Shiping Xu Zhidong Marking the 75th anniversary of victory in the Chinese People's War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression and the World Anti-Fascist War, this commentary (first published in Guangming Daily on 2 September 2020) takes up the meaning of the "great spirit of resistance". Liu and Xu argue that the war was a contest of will and spirit as well as of military and economic strength. They hold that this spirit remains a lasting source of strength for the Chinese people as they pursue the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The piece follows the framing of Xi Jinping, who since the 18th Party Congress (2012) has repeatedly stressed promoting this spirit. It is organised in three parts: the significance of the spirit, its content, and how to carry it forward in what the authors call the great struggle of the new era. Mao Zedong's wartime texts, including On Protracted War, and Xi's 2014 speech marking the 69th anniversary supply the main authorities. On significance, the authors make three claims. The spirit made up for China's material and technological weakness against a stronger imperialist Japan. It also raised national awakening to a new stage, because it covered all citizens and the whole country and put national interest first. Finally, it gives present-day struggles a source of patriotic energy. On content, they follow Xi's four-part formulation: patriotic feeling that every person bears responsibility for the nation's fate, national integrity that prefers death to surrender, heroic courage to fight to the end, and unshakeable confidence in victory. Each is illustrated with wartime episodes, such as the Mukden Incident pledge, the December Ninth Movement, Mei Lanfang's refusal to perform, Yang Jingyu, Ma Benzhai's mother and the Five Heroes of Langya Mountain. The authors trace confidence in victory to a belief that justice prevails and to China's long history of surviving ordeals. The authors call for applying the spirit to the "great struggle" of the new era through three attitudes: daring to struggle, being good at struggling, and struggling tenaciously. They ask Communists to show courage in the face of major issues, to draw on the wartime strategy of protracted people's war, to identify principal contradictions and unite all possible forces, and to persist step by step. They present the war's experience as a model for meeting present risks and obstacles. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Chinese commentary in 2020 linked memory of the anti-Japanese war to the Party's call for struggle in the new era.

Research on the anti-Japanese base areas: a new attempt from theory to documentary breakthroughs 抗日根据地研究：从理论到文献突破的新尝试 Jin Yilin Writing in Guangming Daily on 1 September 2020, Jin Yilin argues that the history of the anti-Japanese base areas deserves deeper study and that progress depends on collecting and sharing source materials. The short commentary combines a claim about the base areas' historical significance with a proposal for digital documentary work. The first part compares the Chinese War of Resistance with resistance movements in Europe and Southeast Asia, which Jin describes as tactical aids to the Allies. The second part turns to the state of research, the value of privately held documents, and a call for wider cooperation. Jin contends that the Communist-led armed forces opened a battlefield behind enemy lines and raised guerrilla warfare to a strategic level. In this account, the base areas' governing institutions were the prototype of the central government of 1949, and Marxism was adapted to Chinese conditions from Yan'an. On research, Jin holds that existing work is conceptual at the macro level and fragmentary at the micro level, and that a persuasive overall narrative can only rest on detailed study. Many documents are hard to find in libraries, so Jin points to private collections, such as the handwritten work notes of Zhang Linchi and Chen Shunyu, now online on a digital platform, and the holdings of the Eighth Route Army Memorial Hall in Wuxiang. Jin calls on more institutions, scholars and private collectors to put scattered documents onto the anti-war documents data platform, so as to "share sources and write history together". Jin cites Xi Jinping's 2015 call for national coordination and for research that is deep overall and detailed on specific topics. The aim, Jin says, is to present China's voice to the world with ample sources. Read the original if you want a brief statement of how Chinese historians frame the base areas and plan digital source-sharing for War of Resistance history.

The Communist Party of China as the mainstay of the War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression 中国共产党是抗日战争的中流砥柱 Qu Qingshan Written after Xi Jinping's speech of 3 September 2020 marking the 75th anniversary of victory in the War of Resistance, this article by Qu Qingshan elaborates the speech's judgement that victory was a great victory in which the Communist Party of China played the role of mainstay (zhongliu dizhu). Qu presents this as the correct conclusion from the fourteen years of the war and argues that the Party was the decisive force behind the national struggle. The article is organised in five sections, each tied to a statement by Xi. It treats the Party as the earliest advocate and fighter against Japan after the 1931 Mukden Incident; as founder and defender of the anti-Japanese national united front; as author of the line of all-out war, the protracted-war strategy and guerrilla warfare; as leader of the enemy-rear battlefield and of the people's armed forces; and as the forger of the great spirit of resistance. It draws on Party declarations, Mao Zedong's wartime texts and military statistics. Qu's central claim is that the Party's political and strategic leadership, rather than any single battle, shaped the outcome. He contrasts the Party's mass-mobilising line with what the article calls the Kuomintang's one-sided, government- and army-centred line, and explains Kuomintang retreats and Communist growth in these terms. Qu cites Mao's On Protracted War and its three predicted stages, and holds that the enemy-rear battlefield became the main battlefield. As evidence he gives the share of Japanese forces in China fought by Party-led troops (59 per cent in 1938, 75 per cent in 1941, 69 per cent in 1945) and the Hundred Regiments Offensive of 1940. By spring 1945, he says, the base areas covered about 950,000 square kilometres and nearly 100 million people, with 910,000 regular troops. Qu concludes that remembering the war means remembering that the Party's mainstay role was the key to victory, and that this requires upholding Party leadership. He also calls for upholding the authority of the Party Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core and for strengthening Party building. He ends by repeating Xi's warning that attempts to distort the Party's history will not be tolerated. Read the original if you want a representative example of the official Party account of the anti-Japanese war and its use in current arguments for Party leadership.

A great victory against aggression, a historical turning point for national rejuvenation 反抗侵略的伟大胜利 民族复兴的历史转折 Yang Xuejun Marking the 75th anniversary of victory in the War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression and the World Anti-Fascist War in 2020, Yang argues that the war was the first complete victory in modern China's resistance to foreign invasion. The article contends that it set the historical turning point from deep national crisis towards the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. It presents remembering the war as a way to cherish peace and to carry the 'great spirit of resistance' into the pursuit of the Chinese Dream. The piece is organised in three parts. The first sets out the war's significance, running from the 1931 Mukden Incident to Japan's surrender in 1945. The second draws out the basic experience of the victory. The third sets out lessons for the present, on Party leadership, the resistance spirit, world peace and the building of a world-class military. Yang supports the account with casualty and aid figures and with remarks by foreign observers such as J. F. C. Fuller and Theodore White. Yang's core reasoning is that victory over a stronger imperialist power came from five factors. These were the anti-Japanese national united front, the strategy of protracted war, a two-battlefield pattern, an international anti-fascist alliance, and the Communist Party's leadership. On protracted war, Yang says the Nationalists' strategy relied on government, army and foreign help and grew passive. In Yang's account, the Communist Party's version rested on mobilising the people through guerrilla warfare, base areas and people's armed forces. The frontal battlefield is said to have been the main one in the first stage, while the enemy-rear battlefield became the main one from the stalemate stage. The article puts China's war dead and injured at over 35 million and credits China with tying down over two-thirds of Japan's army. Drawing on this history, Yang calls for unwavering adherence to Party leadership centred on Xi Jinping, citing the Four Consciousnesses, the Four-sphere Confidence and the Two Upholds. Yang also urges patriotic education and a defence of the postwar international order against hegemonism, unilateralism and bullying, and urges building 'a community with a shared future for mankind'. The article states that weakness invites attack and calls for a modernised army ready to fight. Read the original if you want an example of how the Party's official journal narrates the war and links it to present-day political and military tasks.

Drawing powerful momentum for moving forward from the "Four Histories" 从“四史”中汲取奋发前行的磅礴力量 Xie Xiaojuan Writing in Hongqi Wengao in 2020, Xie Xiaojuan asks what lessons the "Four Histories" should give Chinese readers as the country enters a new era. Opening with Xi Jinping's remark that history is "the best textbook" and "the best sobering agent", the commentary argues that studying the Party's history, the history of New China, the history of reform and opening up, and the history of socialism's development yields conviction, courage, loyalty to the Party and reliance on the people. The piece is organised under four headings. The first places China in the long course of socialism, from Marx and Engels through Lenin to socialism with Chinese characteristics. The second reviews turning points in Party history and the experience they contain. The third presents the Communist Party as the axis of all Four Histories. The fourth treats the people as the force that makes history. Xie's central claim is that the record shows the Party repeatedly facing critical choices and turning danger into opportunity. As examples the commentary lists the founding of the Party, the Zunyi Conference, the peaceful resolution of the Xi'an Incident, the rejection of a Kuomintang plan to divide China along the Yangtze, and the truth-criterion debate that opened reform and opening up. It also cites the Party's response to Western sanctions and to claims that Marxism is outdated. The author draws four lessons: combining Marxist principles with China's actual conditions, holding to the people's standpoint, thinking strategically, and correcting errors through the Party's self-reform. The Party's leadership is called the most essential feature and the greatest strength of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Citing the historical-materialist view that the people drive history, Xie says their creativity is released once they find the right direction and become masters of society. Xie concludes that learning the Four Histories means reaffirming steadfast loyalty to the Party, so that the claims of historical nihilism collapse of themselves and attempts to sever the Party from the people fail. Perseverance and reliance on the people are said to ensure that the goal of a modern socialist great power is reached. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated commentary in 2020 presented the Four Histories as a source of political confidence and legitimacy.

How the Party promoted the popularisation of Marxism in the Yan'an period 延安时期我们党是如何推进马克思主义大众化的 Liu Zhiming Liu Zhiming opens with Xi Jinping's call, made during an inspection tour in Yunnan, for talent like Ai Siqi who can explain the localisation of Marxism well and make it popular and accessible. Liu asks how the Party handled the popularisation of Marxism (马克思主义大众化) in the Yan'an period. The article argues that the Party answered two questions: which Marxism to use to educate the masses, and how to do it. Liu holds that the answers left experience that can guide the current effort in the new era. The article is a short commentary in two parts. The first examines Yan'an practice under two headings: insisting on a 'living Marxism', and insisting on 'integration with the people'. It draws mainly on Mao Zedong's writings, supplemented by Xi Jinping's remarks on Mao's prose style. The second part draws three lessons for today. On the first question, Liu says the 'living Marxism' is Marxism sinified, combining universal truth with Chinese realities. Mao called it 'creative Marxism', and Liu stresses that this does not mean abandoning study of the classics. On the second, Liu lists the Party's measures: social investigation of each class before propaganda; policies serving peasants' material interests, such as rent and interest reduction and the production campaign; and plain language learned from ordinary people. Liu cites Mao's essays, Ai Siqi's Popular Philosophy, a reading list of five theoretical works for workers, peasants and soldiers, folk forms and slogans, and model figures such as Zhao Zhankui, Zhang Side and Norman Bethune. Different audiences, according to educational level, were taught in different ways. Liu draws three lessons. First, cadres and the public should be armed with Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, studied in depth, systematically and in unity of knowing and doing. Second, the Party must stay close to the masses; Liu quotes Mao that one can teach the masses only by being their pupil, and argues that those who set themselves up as the masses' masters will find no use for their talents. Third, work should start from China's realities, respond to people's needs, apply the mass line to all governance and treat popular satisfaction as the basic standard. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned account of Yan'an-era propaganda methods and how they are linked to present-day theoretical education.

The COVID-19 pandemic and catastrophe capitalism 新冠肺炎疫情与灾难资本主义 John Bellamy Foster Intan Suwandi This is a Chinese translation of an article by John Bellamy Foster and Intan Suwandi, apparently first published in Monthly Review in 2020. It asks how the COVID-19 pandemic should be understood within global capitalism. The authors argue that it is neither an external shock nor an unpredictable "black swan", but a product of late imperialism and monopoly-finance capital, whose global commodity chains breed pathogens and then transmit them. The article has four parts. It begins with circuits of capital and the ecological-epidemic crisis, introducing "Structural One Health". It then examines the disruption of commodity chains and a global "bullwhip effect". The third part takes up imperialism, class and the pandemic, including debates over social distancing in poor countries and the US–China trade war. The last part places the crisis in Marx's account of social production and the metabolism between humans and nature. Foster and Suwandi's central move is to bring Marx's dual focus on use value and exchange value to commodity-chain analysis. Drawing on Robert Wallace and colleagues, they argue that agribusiness monocultures, deforestation and land grabs create conditions for new zoonotic diseases. They describe global labour arbitrage and land arbitrage as the basis of late imperialism, and cite just-in-time production and health-sector austerity as reasons why chain disruptions produced shortages and financial fragility. They also criticise a Yale-linked analysis, written for Foreign Policy, that suggested poor countries forgo distancing measures to keep supply chains running. In their reading this trades millions of lives in the Global South for the growth of the imperial centre. The authors conclude that the pandemic belongs to a wider catastrophe of ecological rift, inequality, stagnation and war risk, and that the system responsible could be charged with "social murder", as Engels did. They call for a social reorganisation based on common ownership and a rational regulation of the social metabolism with nature, as the basis for human survival. Read the original if you want a Marxist ecological account of COVID-19 that links epidemiology, global value chains and imperialism, and that cites specific supply-chain data from 2020.

Foreign left-wing scholars' dual reflection on capitalism and socialism in the context of COVID-19 新冠疫情背景下国外左翼学者对资本主义和社会主义的双重反思 Han Yuli Chen Xueming Han and Chen start from Bernie Sanders's withdrawal from the Democratic primary in April 2020, in the middle of the US outbreak, as a sign that capital came first even during a plague. They ask whether Western capitalist ideology will lead humanity into the abyss or towards salvation. Their thesis is that foreign left-wing intellectuals read COVID-19 as a crisis of neoliberalism and a reopening of socialist or communist imagination, and that China's response gives that imagination practical support. The article surveys 2020 commentary by Western and other left-wing figures, including Slavoj Žižek, David Harvey, Thomas Piketty, Antonio Negri, Noam Chomsky, Andres Piqueras, Aleksandr Buzgalin and John Bellamy Foster. It also draws on statements by communist parties abroad. It has three parts: the crisis of neoliberalism and the possibility of transition; the reconstruction of order through socialist or communist imagination; and left-wing evaluations of China's anti-epidemic response. In the first part, the authors present neoliberalism's "Chernobyl moment" as a collapse of consumerism, deepening inequality and political legitimacy, and ecological rupture, ending in a choice between communism and barbarism. They note a Marxist objection that Harvey's argument rests on an underconsumption theory and leaves private ownership and wage labour untouched. The second part argues that the epidemic exposes the illusion of equality, since risk spreads across classes. It also treats "green capitalism" as a false proposition, citing Foster, Xun Qingzhi and Sarah Sarkar, and the authors describe it as masking "ecological imperialism". In the third part they credit China's response to a political commitment to a community with a shared future for mankind, and to public ownership, which in Engels's terms organises production for common need. Foreign communist parties and left writers such as Carlos Martinez are cited as endorsing this. The authors conclude that the crisis is a historic occasion to re-educate the world's workers through communist discourse. They hold that the Western left's attempt to revive it is not utopian, and that China's practice shows the superiority of the socialist system over neoliberal arrangements led by the United States. The text is openly partisan and relies largely on online commentary and open letters from 2020. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist survey of how Western left voices responded to the pandemic, and how Chinese scholars use them to argue for socialism.

Studies of world left-wing thought and movements amid changes unseen in a century An overview of foreign left-wing thought research in 2019 百年未有之大变局中的世界左翼思潮和运动研究 Zhou Miao Song Lidan Kang Yanru This is a literature review, published in Scientific Socialism in 2020, of foreign left-wing thought and movements in 2019. The authors start from the premise that the world is undergoing changes unseen in a century, in which the basic contradictions of capitalism are taking new forms. They report that foreign left-wing scholars sought to answer pressing questions in ways that display the contemporary value and vitality of Marxism. The review has four parts. It first surveys the year's developments, including left forums and festivals in New York, Chicago and London and two Beijing conferences: the tenth World Socialism Forum and the sixth national forum on foreign Marxism research. It then covers major theoretical themes: imperialism, neoliberalism, contemporary capitalism including digital capitalism, and socialism with Chinese characteristics. The third part reports on the left in North America and Europe, Russia, the Middle East and Africa, and Latin America. On theory, the authors report that John Smith and David Harvey debated the contemporary applicability of Lenin's theory of imperialism. Intan Suwandi, R. Jamil Jonna and John Bellamy Foster analysed global commodity chains, and Foster described a late imperialism marked by stagnation and declining US hegemony. Foster, Utsa and Prabhat Patnaik and Sitaram Yechury are cited as treating neoliberalism as the root of capitalist crisis and of the rightward turn in politics. Other work is summarised on digital capitalism and labour control. Egon Krenz, Russian scholars and Toma Ivan are cited as praising the world significance of socialism with Chinese characteristics. On movements, the review reports declining centre-left parties in Europe, the rise of populist and radical left forces, the German Left Party's difficulties, the Yellow Vests, the Russian revival of socialist ideas, and a weakening Latin American left after the Bolivian coup. The authors conclude that left thought will keep advancing so long as capitalism's contradictions persist. They also cite Zhang Liang's warning that foreign Marxism research looks prosperous but is weak in innovation. They call for Chinese scholars to move beyond textual study towards ideas and their adaptation in China, to absorb foreign critiques of financial monopoly capitalism, neoliberalism and imperialism, and to strengthen exchange with foreign left scholars. Read the original if you want a map of 2019 Chinese-language and Western left-wing sources, with references to Monthly Review and Chinese journals, and a sense of how Chinese academics frame foreign Marxism.

Foreign leftist critiques of capitalism during the COVID-19 pandemic 新冠肺炎疫情下国外左翼对资本主义的批判 Lei Xiaohuan Writing in 2020, Lei Xiaohuan surveys how left-wing thinkers and organisations outside China read the COVID-19 pandemic and the responses of the United States and some European states. The article argues that these critics see the pandemic as a blow to global capitalism and that their commentary shows both the nature of the capitalist system and the direction of world socialism. Lei treats this reaction as an indicator of the ideological climate in Western societies. The article draws on statements by Noam Chomsky, Joseph Choonara, Andrea Catone, Prabhat Patnaik, Radhika Desai, Judith Butler, Jo Cottenier, Sam Gindin, Albert Bender and others, as well as a joint statement by communist and workers' parties initiated by the Communist Party of Greece. It has four parts: capitalism's role in spreading the pandemic; capitalism's inability to cope with it and the crises that followed; the claim that Western countries urgently need socialism; and the conditions under which socialism might be achieved. Lei reports that these critics trace the outbreak's severity to the logic of capital, under which profit is put ahead of lives. In their account neoliberal privatisation and cuts to public health, such as Italy's regional health system and Britain's NHS bed numbers, left societies unprepared, while globalisation under capitalism speeded transmission. Lei says they contrast this with China, where the leadership of the Communist Party and the socialist system allowed a swift and effective response, which they credit with showing the superiority of socialism. The critics also read the economic downturn as a sign of long-term structural crisis, tied to climate and refugee crises. Some propose a 'socialism 2.0' based on collective ownership and planning. Lei notes that many of these thinkers stress that revolutionary situations do not automatically produce revolution. They say it also needs a subjective condition, class consciousness and organised political forces, and that capitalism has survived earlier crises, so its imminent collapse looks unrealistic. Lei concludes that the pandemic has led foreign leftists to an unprecedented overall critique of capitalism and of the capitalist road to modernization, a return to Marx's critique of political economy that renews attention to class struggle. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic digest of Western leftist pandemic commentary, with its sources, and of how that commentary is used to praise China's response.

An analysis of the limitations of research on "Western Marxism" in the narrow sense 狭义西方马克思主义研究的局限性剖析 Tai Lihua Tai Lihua asks why nearly a century of research on Western Marxism has produced so much disagreement and so little theoretical force. The article argues that the cause lies in the narrow definitions inherited from Lukács, Korsch and Gramsci in the 1920s and 1930s. Each narrow definition, in Tai's account, has a specific limitation, and the concept needs to be integrated and broadened. The article sorts narrow definitions into four types: by geographical space, by time, by research standpoint, method or viewpoint, and by field of study. For each type it discusses representative writers and schools. They include Korsch, Perry Anderson, Gerson Gorkicakov (as rendered in Chinese), Marxology, post-Marxism, Lukács, Roemer, Hodgson, cultural Marxism and ecological Marxism. Tai draws on Anderson, McLellan, Bowles and O'Connor, among others. Tai holds that the geographical definition, which ties Western Marxism to Western Europe or to Germany, France and Italy, sets it against classical Marxism and Soviet-East European Marxism. It also leaves out research in Britain, the United States and especially Japan. The temporal definition blurs the boundaries between Western Marxism, post-Marxism and neo-Marxism. It also supplies material for claims that Marxism is outdated, mistaken or dying. The definitions by standpoint and method are criticised on several grounds. Marxology is said to set the young Marx against the mature Marx, Engels against Marx, and Lenin against Marx. Lukács's reduction of orthodoxy to method, Leibovitch's and Heilbroner's emphasis on human needs and desire, and the analytical Marxism of Roemer and Hodgson are all called idealist or vulgarising. Tai also argues that equating Western Marxism with philosophy, literature or culture breaks the wholeness of Marxism. In this account the field has dropped political economy, which Tai calls its "de-economisation", and so lost explanatory power. Tai acknowledges that ecological Marxism links explaining the world with changing it. Tai still regards it as reformist and in danger of ecological utopianism. Tai concludes that the four definitions respectively entrench regional barriers, encourage the nihilistic dismissal of Marxism, weaken its scientific character and neglect its wholeness. The article calls for integrating and widening the category and advocates a broad-sense study of Western Marxism as the alternative, which it does not develop here. Read the original if you work on foreign Marxism and want a Chinese critique of how the label "Western Marxism" has been defined, with extensive references to Anderson, McLellan and other sources on the field.

Three shifts in contemporary Western Marxist class theory 当今西方马克思主义阶级理论的三大转变 Mi Haibo Mi Haibo asks how Western Marxist scholars have responded to the claim that Marx's class theory no longer explains capitalist societies that have moved from industrial to post-industrial, information-based forms. The article argues that Western Marxism has shifted in three areas: class structure, the criteria for dividing classes, and class struggle. Mi describes and assesses each shift and concludes that Marx's class analysis remains valid, even though the forms of class have changed. The article, published in 2020, has three sections. The first covers the move in class structure from simplicity to complexity, including the new middle class, the internal stratification of the bourgeoisie and the working class, and the weakening of class consciousness. The second covers the move from a single economic criterion to several criteria: exploitation (Erik Olin Wright, Philippe Van Parijs), power (Nicos Poulantzas, Ralf Dahrendorf) and knowledge or culture (John Kenneth Galbraith, Daniel Bell, Alvin Gouldner). The third covers the move in class struggle from political confrontation to democratic movements, drawing on Habermas, Laclau and Mouffe, Ralph Miliband and Vicente Navarro. Mi's core argument is that each Western revision describes real changes but draws the wrong conclusion. Wage-earning managers, technicians and service workers, in Mi's view, still sell their labour-power and so are part of Marx's 'collective worker'. Theories that speak of the working class 'disappearing' (Marcuse, Poulantzas, Gorz) or of individualised identity (Ulrich Beck) are said to replace subjective perception with objective class position. Wright's 'contradictory class' is rejected because Marx divides classes by relations of production, not income. Dahrendorf's power criterion and the 'knowledge class' theories are criticised for ignoring that the economic base determines the political superstructure and that intellectuals without economic or state power cannot become a ruling class. On class struggle, Mi accepts that new social movements (feminist, ecological, anti-racist and others) are plural and not aimed directly at the capitalist system. Mi argues that they still contain class elements, and that class conflict will not disappear while capitalism and wage labour persist. Globalisation, Mi adds, has made class issues global, citing Navarro's view that the main conflict is between alliances of ruling and ruled classes across North and South. The thesis that class struggle has died out is therefore called inaccurate. Read the original if you want a compact Chinese critical survey of Western Marxist debates on class structure, class criteria and social movements, with references to Wright, Dahrendorf, Gouldner and Laclau and Mouffe.

Towards a new critique of political economy: from generalised surplus value to total subsumption 走向新政治经济学批判：从广义剩余价值到总体从属 Étienne Balibar This is a Chinese translation of an article by the French philosopher Étienne Balibar, translated by Wang Zhen. Balibar asks what a 'new critique of political economy' would involve, and how far it continues or departs from Marx. His answer is that Marx's central category, surplus value, must be broadened beyond its Smithian and Ricardian foundations. That broadening leads to what he calls 'total subsumption', which he uses to explain how finance capital governs everyday life in the age of neoliberal globalisation. The article opens by asking what 'new' means: a critique of a political economy Marx never knew, or a continuation of Marxist critique in the face of ambiguities in Marx's own writing. It then treats capital as a social relation and identifies two tensions in Marx's definition of capital, as a process of exploitation and as a process of accumulation. Two examples follow, 'surplus health' and 'human capital'. A final section sets out total subsumption. Balibar argues that Marx's notion of Verwertung (valorisation) carries two senses, the formation of value and its expansion as surplus value. These are circularly interdependent, and Marx's treatment of money and 'productive labour' leaves difficulties that surface in discussions of financialised capitalism. The 'surplus health' example, taken from Joseph Dumit, shows profit arising from consumption: chronic illness, lifelong multi-drug use and supply creating demand. Balibar reads this as a generalised form of surplus value. Gary Becker's human capital theory is presented as an inversion of the labour theory of value, treating labour as a capital that operates through credit, investment and profitability, and casting individuals as entrepreneurs of themselves. Building on Marx's shift from formal to real subsumption, Balibar proposes 'total subsumption'. In it, commodification extends to life itself, the boundary between work and life, production and reproduction, disappears, and no 'natural' life remains outside value. He asks whether commodification has limits. Drawing on Lacan, he suggests that any totalisation contains an element of the 'Real', so that residues of resistance may appear in individual, mass or governmental forms. Read the original if you want a Western Marxist philosopher's attempt to extend Marx's concepts to health, human capital and financialisation, and to place it within debates over what is 'new' in the critique of political economy.

Infinite form and the spark of truth: the materialist dialectic in Badiou's Immanence of Truths 无限形式与真理的星星之火——论巴迪欧《真理的内在性》中的唯物辩证法 Lan Jiang Lan Jiang reads Alain Badiou's 2018 book Immanence of Truths, the third volume of the Being and Event series and possibly his last major work, as an attempt to ask what happens to the finite world once a subject has touched a genuine infinity. The article's entry point is Mao Zedong's phrase "a single spark can start a prairie fire", which Badiou cites repeatedly. Lan argues that the book completes Badiou's "new materialist dialectic" by reversing the direction of his earlier inquiries. The article has four main parts plus a conclusion. It opens with Badiou's re-translation of Mao's phrase and with Valéry's poem Le Cimetière marin. It then uses Plato's allegory of the cave to explain the book's "return" structure. It goes on to trace Badiou's turn from language to mathematics through his two manifestos of philosophy (1989 and 2009). It ends with the two enemies of the new dialectic, transcendence and "democratic materialism", and with Badiou's treatment of finitude. Lan's central claim is that Badiou changes the logic of the spark. In the earlier works the spark causes the conflagration. In Immanence of Truths it is the concrete flash thrown up by an already-present infinity, so the finite appears only within the form opened by a truth procedure. Badiou, in Lan's account, fights on two fronts. Against transcendence, whether God, Substance or Nature, he asserts that "the One is not", relying on Cantor's "multiple without-one" and on Cohen's forcing. Against democratic materialism, whose axiom is that only bodies and languages exist, he claims that the finite is only the result of operations on infinite multiplicity. Lan illustrates this with the apple, which counts as an apple only within a counting-as-one framework, and with the invention of imaginary numbers. Hence only formal mathematics can break what Badiou calls the fetishistic "ideology of the finite". Lan notes that this explains Badiou's neglect of physics and chemistry, and his criticisms of Wittgenstein, Heidegger, Habermas and Deleuze. Lan concludes that Badiou's envisaged future society is neither a return to the One nor a religious Eden. It would be a new form created after an event, through a generic truth procedure, in which subjects are incorporated and new objects take shape. The spark can spread across the world because it belongs to that new set, not because it embodies a transcendent One. Read the original if you want a detailed account of how Badiou's mathematical ontology links to Maoist imagery and to the critique of finitude, written from within Chinese engagement with foreign Marxism.

The theoretical landscape of Western consumer culture theory 西方消费文化理论图景 Hou Dongmei Hou Dongmei sketches how Western Marxism has theorised consumer culture, treating it as an important part of Western Marxist social critique and a resource for developing Marxism today. The short article argues that mapping this tradition can advance Marxist consumer culture theory, support critique of present-day consumption practices and guide the building of a consumption civilisation in the new era. Hou first traces the foundations: Marx and Engels on ideology, alienation and commodity fetishism; Lukács on reification; Gramsci on cultural hegemony; and the shift in capitalist society from production to consumption as the driver of accumulation. The article then surveys five approaches: culture-industry and technology critique (Horkheimer and Adorno), ideology critique (Marcuse), psychoanalysis (Fromm), cultural construction (John Fiske, rendered "Fiske" from the Chinese transliteration), and semiotics (Baudrillard). In Hou's account, the thinkers share one move: they shift critique from production to everyday consumption. Horkheimer and Adorno see exchange value displacing use value; Marcuse sees false needs and the "one-dimensional" consumer; Fromm sees consumption as flight from loneliness. Fiske, by contrast, stresses that consumers can evade, resist or rework dominant ideology. Baudrillard treats consumption as a system of signs and, in Hou's reading, abandons Marx's political economy late in his career for semiotics and post-structuralism. Hou concludes that later figures such as Bauman and Lefebvre also lack a historical materialist standpoint, so their solutions are elitist and weak. In this view, critique of consumption is at root critique of the logic of capital, and the way out must be a fundamental change in relations of production. Hou says that appeals to aesthetic utopias or individual awakening lose critical force. Read the original if you want a compact Chinese overview of how Western Marxist consumer culture theory is presented and assessed.

Refuting the "amoralist" reading with Marx's philosophy 以马克思哲学批驳“非道德论”观点 Wang Kunpeng Writing in a newspaper commentary of October 2020, Wang Kunpeng takes up a long-standing Western doubt about whether morality has any proper place in Marx's philosophy. The author argues that this "amoralist" view contradicts the core socialist values and undermines the legitimacy of building Marxist ethics and political philosophy in the primary stage of socialism and the new era. Wang's answer is that morality is one of the basic dimensions of Marx's philosophy. The piece first sets out the position of Allen Wood and like-minded scholars, including Derek Allen, Sean Sayers, Robert Tucker and Richard Miller. It then offers two lines of criticism and closes with a reading of Marx's early and mature texts, from the doctoral dissertation on Epicurus to "On the Jewish Question" and the introduction to the critique of Hegel's philosophy of right. Wang reports that Wood separates "moral goods" such as virtue and rights from "non-moral goods" such as self-realisation and community. On this reading Marx criticised capitalism by non-moral standards, and capitalist exploitation counts as just because it matches the relations of production. Wang first replies that Wood's treatment of modern right-based justice is metaphysical: ancient and modern justice are connected, and lawfulness cannot simply be non-moral. Wang's second and weightier reply is that Marx's critique of class morality as ideology does not make his thought value-neutral. Historical materialism, in Wang's account, is bound up with human freedom, dignity and emancipation, and with a justice and morality that go beyond class society. Wang concludes that Marx's philosophy contained a morality beyond the bourgeois one from its beginnings. Later notions such as "human society", the "true community" and the "association of free individuals" give it a scientific basis. The author calls for drawing out the premises, ultimate aim and field of realisation of this moral appeal, for contemporary Marxist ethics and political philosophy and for the Chinese Dream. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese rebuttal of Wood's amoralist reading of Marx.

Marx's concept of social being and its foundational significance 马克思的社会存在概念及其基础性意义 Zou Shipeng Zou Shipeng argues that "social being" is the pivotal concept of Marx's philosophy and social theory, yet has never been fully grasped in China or abroad. The article contends that it is the foundational concept of both the new materialism and the materialist conception of history, so that understanding it reveals their inner unity. Lukács, Western Marxism, Gould and Chinese research on Marx's ontology are all said to stop short of it. The article has five sections. It first treats Marx's ontological revolution and his break with German classical philosophy and Feuerbach. It then traces the historical formation of social being, its value-theoretical (philosophical-anthropological) content, and its link to the thesis that the human essence is the "ensemble of social relations". It ends with the relation between social being and social consciousness, and with implications for scholarship. Zou's core move is that Marx rejected the transcendent, substantial Western concept of being, so social being is a distinct term. It comprises material production, mental production, the production of population and of social relations, with material production as its "ontology". It is historically formed, moving from existing bourgeois society to a future human society, and it is practical, sensuous and relational. Labour, communication and sensuousness give it a value content that Zou says Lukács (who over-weights labour) and Habermas miss. Zou also argues that Marx's formulation turns the basic question of philosophy into social being and social consciousness. Consciousness becomes knowledge, ideology critique follows, and speculation gives way to a positive science. Zou argues that Comte, Spencer, Durkheim and Weber lack this concept. Zou concludes that clarifying this core concept can bring together the practice-centred new materialism, the historical-materialist paradigm and dialectical materialism, serving socialism with Chinese characteristics. Zou also urges scholars to move beyond Western ontological frameworks, including Heidegger, and calls for social being to be a basic concept of modern social science and of Chinese philosophy and social science. Read the original if you want a detailed, text-based argument on Marx's ontology, set against Lukács, Gould, Habermas and classical sociology.

Rebuilding the normativity of the concept of reification through recognition theory 以承认理论重建物化概念的规范性 Wang Guofu Cai Liping This short commentary, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in 2020, asks how Axel Honneth revives Lukács's concept of reification in contemporary social philosophy. The authors argue that Honneth gives the concept a normative reconstruction through recognition theory, which widens the study of reification but leaves it less critical of capitalism than Lukács. The article begins with Western Marxist treatments of reification: Marcuse on false needs and the one-dimensional person, and Baudrillard on abundant objects that turn people into sign-beings defined by consumer goods. It then follows Honneth's reading in three steps: the shift from economic rationality to value rationality, the normative presupposition of an original practice of mutual recognition, and the move from a subject–object paradigm to an intersubjective one. In the authors' account, Lukács located reification in the profit-maximising attitude of commodity exchange, where each party treats the other, and themselves, as calculable instruments. Honneth defines reification as the forgetting of recognition. Drawing on developmental psychology, Adorno and Stanley Cavell, he holds that recognition and empathic participation take priority over neutral cognition. He treats this original relation as the basis of three forms of recognition: love, rights and solidarity. Honneth's intersubjective paradigm, the authors say, lets people be seen as many-sided totalities rather than instruments. The authors conclude that Honneth supplies what Lukács lacked: a social-ontological proof of original recognition and concrete mechanisms for restoring it. They add that Honneth stays within capitalist production and exchange and seeks only reform. In their judgement this makes his critique cautious and inferior to Lukács's, since it accepts the rationality of the capitalist mode of production. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese-language assessment of Honneth's reconstruction of reification from a Marxist standpoint.

A historical-materialist assessment of economic determinism 经济决定论的历史唯物主义评判 Shen Jiangping Historical materialism has long been read, by bourgeois scholars and by some self-described Marxists alike, as 'economic determinism'. Shen argues that this reading is a misreading rooted in mechanical, reductionist thinking, and that historical materialism is properly a historical dialectic in which the economy is decisive only 'in the last instance' (guī gēn dào dǐ). Economic determinism, in Shen's view, is therefore not the 'original sin' of historical materialism. The article has four parts. It first traces economic determinism from the Second International (Kautsky, Bernstein, Lafargue) and the Russian 'Economists' to Russell, Popper, Collingwood and Habermas. It then reviews critiques by Marx, Engels and Lenin and by Western Marxists: Gramsci, Lukács, Korsch, Althusser, Kosík, Sartre and Poulantzas. The third part sets out the dialectical reading, and the fourth draws implications for contemporary China. Shen contends that economic determinism takes 'the economy' as an absolute starting point to which politics, morality and religion can be reduced, so that society is cut into abstract factors linked only mechanically. Marx and Engels, by contrast, stressed production in their early polemics against idealism, a one-sidedness Engels later acknowledged as a limit of the period. They never made the economic factor the sole one. Shen faults the Western Marxist corrections too: the subjectivist line (Gramsci, Lukács) over-stressed human will, and Althusser's 'overdetermination' lost the distinction between principal and secondary contradictions. Shen's own position is that history is law-governed yet leaves room for contingency and agency, and that the economy is the 'central axis' but not the whole. Shen concludes that the debate shows the need to apply Marxist method to new phenomena rather than discard Marxism. The article links this to China: the Party's post-reform shift to economic construction, a socialist mode of production with Chinese characteristics said to carry an innovation-driven mechanism, and the building of a community with a shared future for mankind. It presents Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era as a concrete application of historical materialism. Read the original if you want a detailed Chinese survey of the economic-determinism debate from the Second International to Althusser, and of how it is used to support current Party theory.

Marx's anthropological philosophy and the fate of humanity as a theme of our age 马克思人类学哲学以人类命运为时代课题 Liu Qionghao Miao Qiming Liu Qionghao and Miao Qiming ask what theoretical foundation underlies the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind. Their answer, in this short piece first published in the China Social Sciences Today in December 2019, is that the idea rests on what they call Marx's anthropological philosophy, a philosophy that understands the world from the standpoint of humanity's anthropological characteristics. The authors first define Marx's anthropological philosophy and argue that Marxist philosophy can legitimately be read in this way. They then set out seven foundations of the community-with-a-shared-future idea in Marx's thought: an anthropological standpoint, an anthropological horizon, anthropological value principles, the height of world history, the "world-historical individual", the "true community", and the reconciliation of humans with nature and with each other. The authors contend that Marx took on a double historical mission: human emancipation, and the survival and liberation of the proletariat. From this they derive a double problem field. After 1847, they say, Marx turned mainly to economic questions without abandoning anthropological ones. In their reading, anthropological philosophy is the overall outline of Marx's lifelong thought, and his economic philosophy is its application to pressing problems of his day. Each of the seven foundations is then matched to the community-with-a-shared-future idea, which they say embodies a standpoint beyond class, nation and state. They conclude that the proposal for a community with a shared future for mankind can be seen as the anthropological task of world history in the present era. They present it as a product of combining Marx's thought with contemporary world-historical development. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese scholars ground this foreign-policy concept in Marx's early writings and in a reading of Marxism as anthropological philosophy.

Main experiences in building the discipline of Marxist theory 马克思主义理论学科建设的主要经验 Mo Yueyun Writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in October 2020, Mo Yueyun asks what experience has accumulated in building the discipline of Marxist theory in China since 1949. The author describes the discipline as one that studies the basic principles and scientific system of Marxism as a whole. Mo's thesis is that its development, from early groundwork through systematic construction to rapid growth, has produced a complete disciplinary system and raised the discipline's standing and influence. The short commentary is organised around four "experiences". It first traces the step-by-step construction of the disciplinary system, from ideological-political courses to degree programmes. It then covers Party leadership, the scientific advancement of the discipline, and the discipline's "navigating" role for philosophy and the social sciences. Mo supports the account with the dates of curriculum reforms, the creation of degree programmes and central policy documents. On construction, Mo reports that Marxism-Leninism courses were adjusted three times before 1978 (the "53", "56" and "61" plans) and three more times after reform and opening up (the "85", "98" and "05" plans). Marxist theory became an independent first-level discipline in 2006, and by the end of 2018 it had 81 first-level doctoral programmes and 407 first-level master's programmes, which the author says is more than any other discipline. On leadership, Mo stresses that central bodies decided the course plans and that the Marxist Theory Research and Construction Project, launched in 2004, produced more than 150 textbooks. On method, Mo names three principles: studying Marxism as an integrated whole, taking the adapting of Marxism to Chinese conditions as the main line, and combining political orientation with scholarly rigour. Mo concludes that the discipline has moved from "setting sail" to "navigating", guiding the whole of philosophy and the social sciences. The author says it has done so by embedding Marxist standpoint and method in every field, in line with Xi Jinping's 2016 call to uphold Marxism's guiding position. Read the original if you want a concise official-style account of the milestones, policy documents and statistics behind the institutional growth of Marxist theory as an academic discipline in China.

International opinion criticises political provocations against China by some US politicians 国际舆论批评美国一些政客涉华政治挑衅 Di Yingna Gao Tianding Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2020, Di Yingna and Gao Tianding present a compilation of foreign comment on a run of US measures against China. These include the closure of the Chinese consulate general in Houston, the rejection of four decades of China–US relations, attacks on the Communist Party of China and calls for comprehensive containment. The authors describe these actions as political provocation and conspiracy theory that violate international law and basic norms of international relations. They argue that they have drawn sustained criticism from the international community. The piece is a collage of quotations from politicians, scholars, diplomats, media outlets and organisations in the United States, Russia, Egypt, Iran, Turkey, Britain, France, Belgium, Brazil and elsewhere. It is organised in three sections: the damage to bilateral ties from the consulate closure; reactions to Secretary of State Mike Pompeo's speech at the Nixon Library; and the claim that US conduct is pushing the world into instability. Cited voices include Jimmy Carter, Richard Haass, Ezra Vogel, Jeffrey Sachs, Ray Dalio, Kishore Mahbubani and Gennady Zyuganov. In the authors' selection, commentators say that closing the consulate harms people-to-people exchange and commerce, and that it contradicts values the US professes. Critics of Pompeo's speech are quoted as saying that it misreads history and Nixon's policy of engagement, and that it is an ideological tirade resembling an election speech. The authors cite foreign commentators who say that the attempt to separate the Chinese people from the Communist Party is flawed, and they report survey figures on Chinese public trust in government (93% in a Harvard Kennedy School study, 95% in an Edelman survey). A third group of quotations warns that trade, technology, geopolitical and ideological confrontation could harm the US itself, deflect domestic failures over Covid-19, and deepen a global recession. The authors conclude, through the voices they cite, that provocation against China is dangerous, damaging and destined to fail, and that cooperation rather than confrontation serves the world. They do not offer analysis of their own beyond the selection and framing of sources. Read the original if you want a catalogue of the international criticism that Chinese Party media chose to present in mid-2020, with named sources, as a way to see how official discourse portrayed the deterioration in China–US relations.

Assessing the significance of victory in the War of Resistance from the historical perspective of national rejuvenation 从民族复兴的历史视野审视抗战胜利的重大意义 Jin Minqing Writing in Hongqi Wengao in 2020, Jin Minqing takes up Xi Jinping's remark of 3 September 2020, made at the symposium marking the 75th anniversary of victory in the War of Resistance against Japan. Xi called that victory a historical turning point from deep national crisis towards the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Jin argues that the war's significance should be read within the long process of national rejuvenation, and that its victory marked a key step in escaping foreign aggression and winning independence and liberation. The article opens by sketching the century of humiliation after 1840 and the repeated failures of earlier struggles. It then sets out five ways in which the victory bears on rejuvenation: it established the leading force, showed the guiding ideology, clarified the path, stirred national self-confidence, and gathered the people's strength. Each section looks back at the war years and forward to later stages of the Party's history. Jin's central claim is that the war settled what earlier movements lacked: an advanced party, a scientific theory, a correct road and a mobilised people. On leadership, Jin credits the Chinese Communist Party with a decisive, "mainstay" role. The article cites figures for Party membership, troops and base areas, and describes the Party's independence from the Comintern and from the Nationalists. On ideology, Jin holds that works such as On Protracted War and On New Democracy produced Mao Zedong Thought, the first major leap in adapting Marxism to Chinese conditions. On the road, Jin points to the new-democratic revolution, the base areas' land and political practice, and the call for a coalition government. Jin also describes the war as a people's war, resting on the united front and the masses. Jin concludes that the 1945 turning point was only a beginning, and that it had to be extended into the practice of rejuvenation through further struggle. The article presents the later achievements of revolution, construction and reform, and the opening of the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics, as the continuation of that turning point. It also credits the war with producing a great spirit of resistance and a stronger patriotic national consciousness. Read the original if you want an example of how Party-aligned scholarship in 2020 linked the anti-Japanese war to the narrative of national rejuvenation.

Engels's contribution to the popularisation of Marx's philosophy in his later years 恩格斯晚年对马克思哲学大众化的贡献 Wang Haifeng Marking the 200th anniversary of Engels's birth, Wang Haifeng asks what the late Engels did to turn Marx's philosophy into something the broad public, and above all the working class, could absorb. The article, a short commentary first published in Guangming Daily in August 2020, argues that Engels made a major contribution to this popularisation (dazhonghua) and that it still matters for popularising Marxist philosophy in contemporary China. The piece is organised in four parts. Three cover Engels's later work: systematising Marx's philosophy and setting out its principles, defending its truth and scientific character, and bringing out its realism and its popular character. A final part draws three lessons for Chinese Marxist philosophy today. On systematisation, Wang says Engels gathered ideas scattered through Marx's texts and debates, presented the two great discoveries (the materialist conception of history and the theory of surplus value) together with scientific socialism as one philosophical system, and recast scholarly writing in plainer language. Anti-Dühring and Ludwig Feuerbach and the End of Classical German Philosophy are the chief examples, and Engels also traced Marx's relation to Feuerbach and Hegel. On defence, Wang describes Engels rebutting Paul Barth's reduction of historical materialism to "economic determinism" and the claim that Marx plagiarised Rodbertus. Wang adds that Engels refined the theory itself, stressing the reaction of the superstructure on the economic base and treating motives, necessity and chance, great individuals and the "resultant of forces" in history. On realism and popular character, Wang argues that Engels exposed capitalist exploitation to the masses and stressed Marx's concern with human independence, individuality and liberation. Wang concludes that Engels's efforts reversed the influence of vulgar materialism among ordinary Social Democrats and spread the communist worldview more widely. For China today, Wang draws three lessons. Building an academic system of Marxist philosophy should serve major theoretical and practical problems and the people's aspiration for a better life, not become an "a priori structure". Marxist philosophy must hold its basic standpoint and confront rival currents of thought, since any retreat would forfeit its scientific character and truth. And having made progress in academic rigour, the field should now give more weight to popularisation. Read the original if you want a brief, officially oriented account of how Engels's late writings are presented as a model for popularising Marxist philosophy in China.

The broadest international cooperation as the solid foundation for defeating world fascism 最广泛的国际合作是战胜世界法西斯的坚实基础 Wang Jianlang Writing in Guangming Daily on 1 September 2020, Wang Jianlang asks why the anti-aggression camp prevailed in the Second World War. The author's answer is that the allied states built the broadest international cooperation, uniting countries with different cultures, levels of development and ideologies. Wang argues that once this alliance formed, it largely decided the course and outcome of the war. The commentary has three parts. The first traces how the idea of "indivisible peace" emerged from the League of Nations and the early years of Japanese and German aggression. The second examines how ideological divides were set aside, in China, between China and the Soviet Union, and between the Western powers and Moscow. The third turns to the post-war United Nations and to the present, which Wang describes as another moment of crisis. Wang contends that the old, nation-bound view of security had to give way before cooperation became possible. In the author's account, the League's failure to punish Japan after the 1931 Mukden Incident set a precedent for German aggression in Europe. China's appeals, Roosevelt's 1937 "quarantine" speech and Japan's 1938 "new order in East Asia" slogan gradually moved Britain and the United States from neutrality towards aiding China. Pearl Harbor, in Wang's view, proved the theory of indivisible peace. The second pillar was ideological flexibility: Wang cites the Nationalist–Communist united front, Soviet aid to China, and Churchill's 1941 pledge to help the Soviet Union despite his long anti-communism. The Communist Party of China is portrayed as a supporter of both the national and the international anti-fascist united front. Wang concludes that firm commitment to international cooperation is the only correct choice for overcoming crises. The author sees today's world, with sharpened economic and ideological tensions and the COVID-19 pandemic, as facing a choice between cooperation and selfish national-first policies. Wang criticises the United States for unilateralism that, in the author's words, breaks basic rules and has brought the greatest instability since 1945. Read the original if you want a short example of how Chinese historians use the anti-fascist alliance to frame a 2020 argument for multilateralism.

Research on the anti-Japanese base areas: new attempts from theory to documentary breakthroughs 抗日根据地研究：从理论到文献突破的新尝试 Jin Yilin This short commentary, first published in Guangming Daily on 1 September 2020, asks how research on the anti-Japanese base areas can move forward. Jin Yilin argues that the base areas deserve deeper study because of their strategic and political importance, and that progress now depends mainly on collecting and sharing historical documents, including those held privately. The piece has two parts. The first recalls the Chinese Communist Party's role in the War of Resistance against Japan. The second turns to the state of the sources and to a concrete example of digitised archives. In the first part, Jin contends that, unlike resistance groups in occupied Europe and Southeast Asia, which assisted Allied forces tactically, the Party-led forces opened a rear-area battlefield and raised guerrilla warfare to a strategic level. Jin cites Mao Zedong's 1938 writings to show that guerrilla war needs base areas as its rear. Jin adds that the base-area governments were prototypes of the central government of 1949. In the second part, Jin says existing studies tend towards conceptual generalisation at the macro level and fragmentation at the micro level, and holds that a convincing macro narrative can only rest on thorough detailed research. As a model, Jin describes how the Zhang Linchi and Chen Shunyu wartime manuscripts, over 1,600 pages from the Shanxi-Chahar-Hebei border region, went online on a documents platform with family authorisation.
