Jin calls for more institutions, scholars and private collectors to deposit scattered materials on a shared wartime-documents platform, in line with Xi Jinping's 2015 guidance on research priorities. The aim is "shared sources, jointly written history" and telling China's story to the world. Read the original if you want a brief statement of how Chinese historians frame the base areas and the case for digitising private archives.

Rethinking the "Korsch problem" 重思“柯尔施问题” Qi Tao Qi Tao asks what Karl Korsch's response to the "crisis of Marxism" in the 1920s can teach current debates in Chinese Marxist philosophy. Recent topics, such as the legitimacy of Marx's political philosophy and whether Capital is philosophy or economics, have in Qi's view widened research but also produced confusion. Qi argues that the situation resembles Korsch's: an anti-philosophical scientific positivism is spreading, and a return to Marxism's philosophical foundations and its wholeness has become urgent. This short commentary has three parts: holding to Marxism as a whole, holding to the philosophical character of Marx's thought, and returning to Marxism's philosophical foundations. It draws on Korsch's Marxism and Philosophy, Hegel's Logic and Philosophy of Right, and the Japanese philosopher Hiromatsu Wataru's The Original Image of the Materialist Conception of History. Qi reads the Second International's extraction of economic, political and cultural elements as partly reflecting capitalist society's own separation of spheres. Korsch conceded this, Qi notes, but insisted that separate elements never replace the whole, and Marx's return to Hegel's Logic in 1858 shows his commitment to a systematic science. Qi then criticises Hiromatsu for overstating Adam Smith's role and treating Hegel's Philosophy of Right as a branch philosophy rather than metaphysics, which in Qi's view strips Marx's critique of its philosophical base. For Qi, Marx's critique of Hegel's legal philosophy is also a critique of metaphysics, and it led to a double break with Hegel and Feuerbach. Qi concludes that Marxist philosophy today must answer major questions of the age, which requires basic research and a grasp of Marx's philosophy as a whole, so that philosophy can grasp the essence of social reality and intervene in it. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese-language argument, framed through Korsch, against fragmenting or de-philosophising Marx, and a critical response to Hiromatsu's reading.

Two uses of the concept of justice in Marx and Engels: with a critique of two misunderstandings by Allen Wood 马克思和恩格斯对正义概念的两种用法——兼评伍德的两个误解 Duan Zhongqiao Duan Zhongqiao takes up the 1970s–80s Anglo-American debate on "Marx and justice" and Allen Wood's claim that Marx did not regard capitalism as unjust. Duan argues that Wood misreads the concept of justice in Marx and Engels because he does not see that they use it in two different ways. The article, published in Social Sciences in China in 2020, aims to correct two resulting misunderstandings that Duan says have also influenced Chinese scholars. The article first sets out the two uses, which Duan reconstructs from Marx's and Engels's remarks on distribution under capitalism, since neither ever defines justice. It then examines Wood's three papers (1972, 1979 and his 2018 reply to Duan), showing how each use appears in Wood's own interpretation. It closes with a point-by-point reply to Wood's objections to Duan's earlier article, which is cited as "Bianxi", with close readings of passages from Marx and Engels. Duan holds that justice means "giving each person their due" and is a moral evaluation. In the first, historical-materialist use, it belongs to the ideological superstructure and is determined by relations of production. For this reason Marx and Engels refused to ground criticism of capitalism or the proletarian cause in justice, and attacked Proudhon, Dühring and Lassalle. In the second use, different classes each call their own distributive demands "just". Wood's first error, in Duan's view, is to treat justice in the first use as a juridical concept that serves the dominant mode of production, when it is a moral concept that can also express the dominated class's demands. His second error is to claim that Marx never judged capitalism unjust. Duan cites Marx's Grundrisse remark about workers' "tremendous consciousness" and Engels's 1884 preface, which he reads as showing that they shared the workers' moral judgement. He also argues that Wood omitted a key part of Marx's reply to Adolph Wagner and confused two separate questions. Duan concludes that Marx and Engels did regard capitalist exploitation as unjust, because surplus product belongs to the worker as its true producer. They said little on the point because earlier socialists had already made it and because they rested communism on historical necessity rather than morality. Duan stresses the need to clear up Wood's misunderstandings given his influence in China. Read the original if you follow the Marx-and-justice debate and want a detailed Chinese philosophical rebuttal of Wood, with close textual argument.

The socialist system with Chinese characteristics shows its strengths in practice 中国特色社会主义制度在实践中彰显优势 Liang Jiafeng Writing in Economic Daily in October 2020, Liang takes up the question of why the socialist system with Chinese characteristics is a good one. Taking Xi Jinping's remarks at the national commendation meeting for the fight against COVID-19 as a starting point, Liang argues that the system's distinctive strengths can be explained in theory and have also been verified and demonstrated in practice. The commentary has three parts. It first traces how the system's strengths came out of practical exploration, from the founding of the People's Republic through reform and opening up to the period after the 18th Party Congress (2012). It then points to practical results, namely economic development, social stability, reform and the epidemic response. Finally it considers how to strengthen these advantages further. Liang's core claim is that the strengths follow from persisting in the Party's centralised and unified leadership, a people-centred approach, and reform and innovation. As evidence the author cites rapid industrialisation, the rise to the world's second-largest economy and long-term social stability. The epidemic response, in the author's account, showed an exceptional capacity for organisation, mobilisation and coordination, and the ability to concentrate resources on major, difficult and urgent tasks. Liang calls for upholding the system while improving it through reform, so that it becomes more mature and more fully defined. In a period of global upheaval and with uneven development at home, the author urges using the system's capacity to concentrate efforts on key technologies, removing deep institutional obstacles and energising market players. Read the original if you want a concise example of the official 2020 line on institutional confidence and the lessons drawn from the pandemic.

Attempt and bankruptcy: rethinking Heideggerian Marxism 尝试与破产：反思海德格尔式的马克思主义 Deng Ding Scholars of Western Marxism have long attended to Herbert Marcuse's "Hegelian Marxism" and "Freudian Marxism", but Deng argues that his early attempt to build a "Heideggerian Marxism" has received far less notice. This short commentary, published in 2020, asks two questions: why dialectics must be combined with historical materialism, and how a phenomenological materialist dialectic is possible. Deng's answer is that Marcuse showed such a combination to be possible and even necessary in method, but that his project ultimately failed because he lacked a grounding in concrete history. The article reconstructs Marcuse's argument in three steps. It first traces his account of dialectics from Plato's logos through Hegel to Marx. It then turns to his case for joining phenomenology with materialist dialectics. It ends with the event that Deng treats as a turning point: the 1932 publication of Marx's Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, after which Marcuse abandoned the Heidegger–Marx synthesis and returned to Marx from 1933. On Deng's reading, Marcuse held that dialectics is first a feature of how things come to be, and only secondarily a logical tool. Hegel united these two aspects but reduced real movement to the movement of spirit, whereas Marx turned dialectics into a materialist one. Because only human beings are historical, Marcuse concluded that dialectical materialism must also be historical materialism. Human historical movement is both a process of becoming, which needs dialectics, and a repeated disclosure of the meaning of being, which needs phenomology. Marcuse therefore judged phenomenology and materialist dialectics compatible, despite Heidegger's remark that phenomenology and dialectics are as incompatible as fire and water, a remark Deng says was aimed at idealist dialectics. Deng adds that after reading the 1844 Manuscripts Marcuse saw that Marx already offered an account of alienation, and that Heidegger stayed at the existential level and lacked a "concrete philosophy". Deng grants that the attempt is worth reflection, since phenomenological elements might help clarify the historical meaning of concepts such as "worker", "commodity" and "capitalist" in Marx's work. Yet the author sees a basic methodological limit in Marcuse's effort to redefine materialism and dialectics on a phenomenological base. In Deng's view, social reality can be grasped only from historical materialism, looking at historical, concrete and sensuous objects. Phenomenology and existentialism, Deng says, still only interpret the world, while the power to change it lies in countries and peoples that have inherited and developed Marxism. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese assessment of Marcuse's early Heideggerian phase and its relation to the 1844 Manuscripts.

The three dimensions of Marx's critique of egoism 马克思批判利己主义的三重维度 Li Shuna Liu Rongjun Li and Liu ask how Marx criticised egoism and whether civil society's "private person" can become a human society. Their short commentary, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in 2020, argues that Marx's critique ran through his whole intellectual career and accompanied his critique of modern civil society. Egoism, in their account, is a product of private property and the social division of labour, and it peaks under capitalism. The authors distinguish Marx's "superstitious egoism" of pre-capitalist society from the "enlightened egoism" of capitalism. They then organise the critique along three lines: philosophical, political-economic and scientific-socialist. The philosophical line takes in Stirner, Hegel, Bauer and Feuerbach; the economic line draws on the Critique of Political Economy and The German Ideology; the political line draws on the Paris Commune and the proletariat. In the first dimension, Marx is said to treat Stirner's materialist egoism as one more abstraction replacing an older idealist one. Its end requires abolishing real egoistic life, following a historical-materialist "dialectic of labour". In the second, egoism appears as the economic form in which individuals serve one another only as means to their own ends, so that "common interest" becomes an exchange of selfish interests. Private property and the division of labour, the authors report, are the source of this split, and overcoming it depends on developing the productive forces and new relations of production. In the third, only the propertyless proletariat can generalise non-ownership and win human emancipation, by transforming itself and its circumstances through long struggle. The authors conclude that egoism is the practical motive force of competition-based capitalist relations of production. It is also what the proletariat must sublate in order to carry out its mission. They present Marx's critique as a historical-materialist route to answering whether and how civil society becomes human society. Read the original if you want a compact overview of how Marx's critique of egoism links his early philosophy, his political economy and his political writings.

Dimensions of interpretation in the theoretical orientation of Capital 《资本论》理论定向的阐释维度 Bu Xiangji Bu Xiangji asks how Capital should be read if one accepts, as a premise most scholars can share, that the work is oriented by the materialist conception of history. The article argues that the economic and philosophical readings each have a limited field of vision. It holds that the decisive issues are how to understand the basic character of Marx's philosophy and its link to Capital, and how to treat the Hegelian moment in Marx's development and the Hegelian element in Capital. The first part surveys interpretive routes: the economic one (the Second International, analytical Marxism, the mathematical Marxist school) and the philosophical ones (Lukács's Hegelianism, Althusser's dialectical materialism, the 'new Hegelian Marxism' of Arthur and others, and the domestic 'extension, application and proof' view of historical materialism). The second part traces how the materialist conception of history arose from Marx's early work and from Hegel. The third part examines Capital's structure, categories and method of value-form analysis. Bu contends that historical materialism was not created independently of Capital and then applied to it. In Bu's account, the 1844 Manuscripts already set the research programme of Capital, and The German Ideology, with its 'spontaneous division of labour', answered the two preliminary tasks that programme required. Hegel's dialectic of labour is held to be the source of the practical-materialist paradigm and of the totality, difference and historicity of the materialist conception of history. Bu faults Lukács for misreading this Hegelian inheritance and Althusser for discarding it, and faults the new dialectic school for turning Capital into a copy of Hegel's Logic. Against these, Bu argues that Capital's order of categories reflects the objective logic of capitalist relations, that each category expresses definite social relations, and that mediation and retrospective tracing to origins mark a method that surpasses Hegel. Bu concludes that Hegel's influence on Marx should be neither erased nor exaggerated. Only by seeing both the necessity of the Hegelian moment and Marx's break with speculative philosophy can an internal link between the materialist conception of history and Capital be rebuilt. Read the original if you work on Marx's relation to Hegel, Western Marxist readings of Capital, or the debate over the value-form and the 'new dialectic', and want a Chinese critical map of those schools.

Research on British Marxist class theory 英国马克思主义阶级理论研究 Fang Jue Fang Jue's short review, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in August 2020, asks how British Marxist theories of class have developed since the 1950s. The author argues that they have passed through three research paradigms: a historical one, a political-science one, and a return to political economy. Fang presents this sequence as showing a distinctive British understanding of historical materialism. The article places British Marxism within Western Marxism's two broad tasks, critique of contemporary capitalism and the theory of revolution. It then takes each paradigm in turn. The first rests on the work of E. P. Thompson and Eric Hobsbawm after the rise of the British New Left in 1956. The second centres on Ralph Miliband and the Miliband–Poulantzas debate. The third covers the response to neoliberalism and the 2008 financial crisis, with Alex Callinicos as the main figure. Fang reports that the historical paradigm treats class as a relation and as inseparable from class consciousness. Experience, custom and national cultural tradition are said to shape class formation alongside capitalist production. The political paradigm uses class analysis of power, the Capital concept of the "collective worker" and a theory of the state. Miliband holds that the state has relative autonomy but remains an instrument of the bourgeoisie. Against neoliberal talk of the "end of class", analytical Marxism and post-Marxism, the third paradigm restores the labour theory of value. In Fang's account, Callinicos's Deciphering Capital uses it to defend the working class as the revolutionary subject. Fang concludes that the return to political economy is the main trend of twenty-first-century class theory. The reason given is that capital's drive for self-valorisation is unchanged, so Marx's class-struggle analysis of capitalism remains valid. British Marxists, in this reading, treat historical materialism as grounded in modern socialist movements, not as an abstract formula. Read the original if you want a compact overview of the main phases and figures of British Marxist class theory as presented in Chinese scholarship.

A multidimensional exploration of contemporary research on Marxist ethical thought 当代马克思主义伦理思想研究的立体化探索 Li Jianhua This is a book review, published in Guangming Daily on 20 October 2020. Li Jianhua reviews Heritage and Coordinates: Interviews on Marxist Ethical Thought (Zhongyang bianyi chubanshe, June 2020), edited by Li Yitian and Zhang Xiao. Li argues that the volume gives a "three-dimensional" view of present-day research on Marxist ethics, at a time when building an ethics of socialism with Chinese characteristics has become a prominent concern in Chinese scholarship. The reviewer organises the assessment around three dimensions: how the content of Marxist ethical thought is presented, how the interviewees were chosen, and how the book handles historical inheritance and the new coordinates of the new era. The book rests on interviews with 13 well-known scholars in China and abroad, including British, American, Russian and Japanese researchers. On content, Li says Marxist ethics was once understood narrowly as the ethics of Marx and Engels alone. Drawing on Li Yitian's preface, the review distinguishes three types: the ethical thought of Marx and Engels, that of their successors, and that of those who study them. On selection, Li stresses that the interview format gathers varied voices in one book and singles out four Chinese interviewees: Song Xiren, Song Huichang, Tang Kailin and Zhang Haishan, whose works he characterises briefly. On orientation, Li holds that an ethics of socialism with Chinese characteristics is a new form distinct from traditional Chinese, Soviet-model and Western ethics, and that its internal logic lies in the deep structure of Marxist ethics, centred on human existence, development and freedom. Li concludes that the book rightly aims at a Marxist ethics that draws on historical lineage, faces the world, answers classical questions and is grounded in Chinese reality. Read the original if you want a short Chinese assessment of this interview collection and of how Chinese scholars frame Marxist ethics and the construction of an ethics of socialism with Chinese characteristics.

The "counterattack" of the Workers' Party of Belgium and its implications 比利时工人党的“逆袭”及其启示 Yu Haiqing The article asks how the Workers' Party of Belgium (PTB/PVDA) rose so quickly in 2019, when most European radical-left parties were declining, and what its experience means for communist parties elsewhere. It opens with the party's results that year: 8.7% in the European Parliament election, its first seat there, and a rise from 8 to 41 seats across Belgian legislatures since 2014. Yu argues that the decisive factor was a strategy combining "principledness" with "flexibility", adopted in 2008, and that this offers Western communist parties a "new road". The text first traces five stages of party history: its origins in the late-1960s student movement (1966–79), formal founding and slow growth (1979–89), stagnation after the Soviet collapse (1989–99), crisis and strategic adjustment (1999–2008), and gradual rise since 2008. It then sets out the 2008 strategic turn, analyses five features of the party's practice, and ends with reflections for the wider communist movement. Membership figures, election results and campaigns are cited throughout. On the strategy, Yu reports that the party's "principledness" rests on Marxism as worldview and method and on socialism as the goal, which the party calls "socialism 2.0". "Flexibility" means adapting tactics to circumstances, which the party compares to a body needing both a strong spine and supple limbs. In practice, Yu says, the party focuses on everyday concerns such as its free community health centres and a campaign for a minimum pension of 1,500 euros. It keeps a distinct Marxist-Leninist identity, redefines the working class broadly, and works on a "street–parliament–street" principle. It declines federal government participation for now, drawing lessons from Syriza in Greece. Leaders and MPs take an average worker's wage, and the party cooperates openly with trade unions and social movements. Yu divides Western communist parties of the past thirty years into a "traditional" path, which tends towards dogmatism, and a "modernizing" path, which tends to over-compromise and lose its distinctiveness. Both, Yu says, are polarizing and have hit electoral ceilings or lost voters. The Belgian party is presented as avoiding both extremes through a dynamic balance, offering answers on combining parliamentary and extra-parliamentary struggle, tactics versus long-term strategy, and identity versus broader alliances. Yu suggests it could be called a "third way" for Western communism. Read the original if you want a detailed, sympathetic Chinese account of the Belgian party's history and tactics, and of how Chinese scholars assess the lessons for communist parties abroad.

Lessons of the fall of the Berlin Wall and the hope of world socialism: reading "The 30th Anniversary of the Fall of the Berlin Wall" 柏林墙倒塌的教训与世界社会主义的希望——读《柏林墙倒塌30周年记》 Li Ruiqin Writing in 2020, on the 30th anniversary of German unification, Li Ruiqin reviews a collection edited by Egon Krenz, the last General Secretary of the East German ruling party (SED). Its Chinese title is rendered here as The 30th Anniversary of the Fall of the Berlin Wall: Reflections from the Former East German Side. More than ten former East German party, state and military leaders and a defence lawyer contributed to it. Li argues that the book draws lessons from the failure of East German socialism and regards China as the bearer of hope for world socialism. The review presents the contributors' views under five headings: weak party leadership as the main cause of failure; the Western strategy of "peaceful evolution" aimed at East Germany; the double pressure of Gorbachev's reforms and Western strategy; the post-1990 treatment of East German leaders; and the contributors' view of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Li quotes figures such as Hans Modrow, Heinz Keßler, Heinz Hoffmann, Wolfgang Herger, Manfred Gerlach's contemporaries and Harry Tisch's colleagues only through the book's own wording, and also cites Mao Zedong. Li reports that the contributors blame a leadership that grew silent and passive in 1989, neglected Party building, lost the trust of the people through bureaucracy, formalism and concealed errors, and ignored Marxist social science. Li presents their claim that the West ran a planned campaign, using media, "citizens' organisations" and Gene Sharp's handbooks. The contributors also say Gorbachev's reversal on German unification removed the Soviet support on which East Germany depended. Li adds that the former leaders describe unification as an annexation, with deindustrialisation, mass unemployment, prosecutions of generals and officials, and what Li calls a class reckoning. In Li's account, the contributors, including Herger, Peck and the lawyer Friedrich Wolff, hold that the failure could have been avoided and was a setback, not the end of socialism. They see China's people-centred development, its public land ownership and its Party programme as a new strategy for socialism today. Li concludes that these reflections carry historical significance and a practical warning for upholding and developing socialism with Chinese characteristics and for the revival of world socialism. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist reading of East German memoirs on 1989 and of how they portray China.

Assessing the practice philosophy of East European New Marxism 研判东欧新马克思主义实践哲学 Guan Siyue Guan Siyue asks how Marx's concept of practice can be recovered after the Soviet textbook system, which in the author's view ignored human subjectivity and turned Marxism into a rigid dogma. The article, a short newspaper commentary, argues that East European New Marxism's treatment of practice philosophy offers one direction for understanding, interpreting and applying Marx's practice philosophy. The piece has two parts. The first outlines the practice-philosophical foundations of East European New Marxism, covering the Yugoslav Praxis group, the Budapest School and the Polish and Czechoslovak figures Adam Schaff and Karel Kosik. The second sets out the theoretical framework of the Yugoslav Praxis school, which Guan regards as the most comprehensive and profound of these currents. Guan contrasts East European New Marxism with Western Marxism. Both build on Marx's theory of alienation and practice to criticise existing capitalism and existing socialism, but Guan holds that Western Marxist critique left existing institutions untouched and became utopian. East European thinkers, by contrast, treated practice as a stance toward changing society, and their ideas of humane and democratic socialism supported reforms by Tito, Gomulka, Nagy and Dubcek. On the Praxis school, Guan reports that its thinkers read practice through the Greek praxis, as an ontological and anthropological concept and the basic mode of human being. From this they derived a view of alienation as ineradicable in principle and of revolution as a philosophical category, a way of human existence, not only a transfer of power. Guan concludes that this tradition returns to Marx's basic problematic by placing the human being at the centre of practice. Read the original if you want a brief overview of the Praxis school's concepts of practice, alienation and revolution, and of how Chinese scholarship in 2020 situates East European New Marxism against Western Marxism.

The origins of the discourse of ecological Marxism 生态学马克思主义话语缘起 Liu Bingjing Ecological Marxism is usually said to have been systematically outlined first by the Canadian scholar William Leiss. Liu Bingjing, in this short commentary from the Chinese Social Sciences Today (30 April 2020), argues that André Gorz, Herbert Marcuse and Guy Debord had already conveyed its standpoint independently in the early 1970s, and that together they brought its discourse into being. The piece sets out four steps: ecological questions within Marx and Engels; the maturing of the discourse as ecological crisis grew; the reading of ecological crisis as capitalism's self-produced crisis; and the emergence of a new anti-capitalist force around ecological issues. Liu holds that Marx and Engels treated ecological damage as a by-product of capitalism but not as the key to its critique, since pollution did not yet threaten human life. For them capitalism's fall came from its mode of production and economic crises. By the 1970s, Liu argues, globalised expansion, welfare-state policies and consumerism had eased supply–demand contradictions, delayed economic crisis and softened class conflict. Gorz, Marcuse and Debord therefore saw ecological crisis as the force able to shake capitalism. They treated it as a necessary result of irrational, profit-driven production, and ecological movements as a direct negation of capitalist rule. Liu reports their view that ecological threats revive a lost class consciousness and gather a spontaneous, popular subject. Liu concludes that, though the three thinkers had no direct contact, they jointly linked ecology to capitalist crisis, emancipation and class subject. With Leiss and Ben Agger they opened the field of Western ecological Marxism. Read the original if you want a brief account of the early-1970s sources of ecological Marxism beyond Leiss.

Clarifying Marx's concept of the community 马克思共同体概念的澄明 Zha Zhengquan Since Xi Jinping put forward the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind, Chinese scholars have studied Marx's thought on the community (gongtongti) widely. Zha notes that Marx used the term often but never defined it for its different periods and contexts. This short newspaper commentary (Chinese Social Sciences Today, 2020) reads Marx's texts to extract a concept and offers a definition, intended as scholarly support for building a community with a shared future for mankind. The piece has three sections. It treats the community as a form of human social existence, distinct from society. It then asks how the community arises through association, and finally how it relates to freedom. It ends with a proposed definition. Zha contrasts Tönnies and Bauman, who separate community from society but do not link communities to stages of social development. Marx, in Zha's reading, ties each community to a particular social formation, citing passages from The Holy Family and Capital. On association, Zha rejects equating the association (lianheti) with the community. Only an association of free individuals counts as a community, and association rests on modern productive forces and world intercourse. Exclusive associations built on private or group interest do not qualify. Zha also argues that the "free development of each" could become a war of all against all unless association matures into a community. Communities that serve bourgeois values and exclude the majority are, following Marx, "false communities". The true community is the outward expression of the value of freedom. Zha defines Marx's community as a dynamic system. People join through social intercourse, in response to the needs of social development, to overcome individual disorder, guarantee individual freedom and pursue common free development. Zha holds that communities remain necessary even in a perfected society, and so calls building a community with a shared future for mankind a task for a thousand years. Read the original if you want a brief, text-based attempt to define Marx's community concept in connection with that Chinese political idea.

Marx's critique of fetishism and the semantics of capital 马克思拜物教批判与资本语义学 Yao Manlin Yao Manlin asks how Marx's critique of fetishism dismantles the mystery surrounding commodities, money and capital. The short commentary, first published in the China Social Sciences Today in 2020, argues that Marx's layered critique amounts to a method of demystification, which Yao calls a "semantics of capital". Yao begins with the religious origin of the term fetishism and its adoption by de Brosses, Comte and Tylor. Yao notes that Marx drew on de Brosses as early as 1841 but turned to economic life, chiefly in Capital. The article then takes commodity, money and capital fetishism in turn. For Yao, Marx locates the commodity's mystery in the commodity form itself, which conceals the social character of labour, and he resolves it through the dual character of labour. Money's mystery is traced back to its being a commodity serving as general equivalent. Capital's mystery, its capacity to self-expand, is explained by distinguishing labour from labour-power, the special commodity that produces surplus value outside the sphere of exchange. In each case a retrospective analysis returns from the illusion to simpler categories. Yao concludes that commodity, money, capital, labour, labour-power, use-value, value and surplus value form the basic units of this semantics, which Yao links to a hermeneutics of demystification. Yao adds that exposing surplus value connects it to wage labour and the working class, and that human liberation depends on the awakening of that class's consciousness. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese-language overview of how Marx's fetishism critique is presented as a method in Capital.

Habermas's "theory of communication" and its basis in the concept of labour 基于劳动概念的“交往理论” Zhou Jing This short commentary, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in April 2020, asks how Jürgen Habermas's theory of communicative action relates to Marx's concept of labour. Zhou argues that Habermas builds on historical materialism and seeks to reconstruct it, but does not follow the logic of Marx's concept of labour. Instead, Habermas splits labour from communication. The article first sets out how Habermas extends the concept of labour through language-mediated communication, drawing on the linguistic turn and universal pragmatics. It then covers his two-tier model of society, "system" and "lifeworld", and his idea of the colonisation of the lifeworld, which Zhou links to the first-generation Frankfurt School critique of instrumental reason. It closes with an assessment of the theory's merits and limits. Zhou reports that Habermas applies Piaget's genetic epistemology to the lifeworld. He starts from individual learning in moral practice rather than from Marx's species-subject, and so gives moral-practical progress priority over productive forces. Zhou sees a residue of Kantian "nature–freedom" dualism in this scheme. In Zhou's reading, Marx already holds that labour contains two relations: the subject–object relation to nature and the intersubjective relation of communication. Habermas, by separating the two, fails to reunite them. Zhou rejects the view that Marx and Habermas differ over whether material production or communication is fundamental. The real difference, in the article's account, is that Marx understands labour comprehensively and dialectically, while Habermas stresses its social side. Zhou nonetheless credits Habermas with trying to help historical materialism address modern crises. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese assessment of Habermas as a reconstructor of historical materialism.

Three propositions in Marx's thought on education 马克思教育思想的三个命题 Xia Wei Cheng Lin This newspaper commentary, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in September 2020, identifies three central propositions in Marx's thinking on education. Xia Wei and Cheng Lin argue that these concern the nature of education (its relation to class), its method (combination with productive labour) and its aim (the all-round development of the human being). They hold that the propositions once shaped Chinese educational theory and practice and remain relevant today. The piece takes each proposition in turn. It links the class character of education to historical materialism, then discusses how combining education with productive labour has been misread, and finally places the aim of all-round development within Marx's idea of human emancipation. Mao Zedong's educational policy and the 1949 national education conference serve as Chinese reference points. On class, the authors argue that education belongs to the superstructure and always serves a particular class, even when ruling classes present their own ideas as universal. They add that class character is not education's only or always its primary property, since education also rests on human nature and has national, historical and ethical dimensions; letting class obscure these, they warn, could have disastrous practical results. On method, they identify three deviations: reducing productive labour to heavy manual work, rejecting theory and book learning although Marx put intellectual education first, and over-emphasising employment while neglecting basic subjects. Marx's aim, the authors conclude, was not vocational training or higher efficiency. Modern large-scale industry brings mental and manual labour closer, so that everyone could become both an educated person and a worker, narrowing or ending the gap between the two. Read the original if you want a short Chinese statement of how Marx's educational ideas are interpreted and how their past misapplication is assessed.

Three dimensions of Marx's critique of egoism 马克思批判利己主义的三重维度 Li Shuna Liu Rongjun This short commentary asks how Marx criticised egoism and whether it can be overcome. Li and Liu argue that the critique ran through Marx's whole intellectual development, was bound up with his critique of modern civil society, and unfolded along philosophical, political-economic and scientific-socialist lines. The authors begin with egoism as the outlook of the "private person" of civil society, a product of private property and the social division of labour. They note Marx's distinction between the "superstitious egoism" of pre-capitalist society and the "enlightened egoism" of capitalism. Three sections then take up Stirner and Hegel, economic egoism, and the political egoism of the propertied classes. In the philosophical dimension, Li and Liu read Marx as holding that Stirner merely replaced an idealist abstraction with a materialist one. Marx's alternative is a dialectic of labour: people objectify private property and the "private person" through labour, and labour then sublates this objectification. In the political-economic dimension, common interest is described as an exchange of selfish interests that consolidates capitalist relations of production. Only new productive forces and relations can turn economic egoists into fully free people. In the third dimension, the proletariat, holding no private property, is the agent of change. The authors cite Marx on the Paris Commune and on workers transforming themselves while transforming circumstances. The authors conclude that egoism, tied to individualism and liberalism, drives competitive capitalist production and must be sublated by the proletariat's self-transformation. They say Marx's critique offers a historical-materialist answer to whether and how civil society can develop into human society. Read the original if you want a compact outline of how Marx's treatment of egoism links Stirner, Hegel, political economy and the Paris Commune.

Marx's philosophical mode of expression 马克思的哲学表达方式 Xia Ying Against twentieth-century proclamations of the "end of philosophy", and a French-led current that places Marx beside Nietzsche and Freud as an anti-metaphysical thinker, Xia Ying asks whether "Marxist philosophy" is a legitimate concept at all. The article, a short commentary in a newspaper, argues that Marx did not abandon philosophy. In Xia's reading, he created a new way of expressing philosophy, and the materialist conception of history is itself a philosophical revolution. The piece begins with the "Korsch question", raised in the early days of Western Marxism, over whether Marxism is a philosophy and in what sense. Xia treats its value as exposing a tension between theory and practice, not as a choice between philosophy and science. It then turns to Marx's mockery of philosophers in the Theses on Feuerbach and The German Ideology, to two features of the materialist conception of history, and to Marx's relation to Hegel, the Young Hegelians and German classical philosophy. Xia argues that the "philosophy" Marx rejected around 1845 was speculative, Hegelian-style systems, in which constructing theory is equated with practice, together with the one-sided Young Hegelians. The materialist conception of history, by contrast, studies the material conditions of real individuals' activity, which gives it a "logical priority" of objectivity. Its sense of history also looks forward to an anticipated end of the division of labour and alienated labour, and to human freedom. For Xia, this makes it less a "scientific study" of the past than a "philosophical study" of the possibility of freedom. Xia concludes that Marx's questions, the first causes of things and the conditions of human freedom, remain within the traditional problem field of philosophy. What changed is the mode of expression. Since Kant, German classical philosophy had added historical consciousness, and Marx pushed this furthest by attaching historical-period qualifiers to his statements and by making capitalist economic structures and material life philosophical problems. The difference between Marx and earlier Western philosophy is therefore a difference between new and old modes of philosophical expression, not between non-philosophy and philosophy. Read the original if you want a brief, clearly structured argument for treating the materialist conception of history as a philosophy, in response to the Korsch question and the "end of philosophy" thesis.

An interpretation of Marx's idea of the community 马克思共同体思想诠释 Hu Xiaojun Hu Xiaojun's short commentary, first published in the China Social Sciences Today in September 2020, takes up Marx's concept of the community (gongtongti) as a foundational category in his account of human social development. Hu argues that the concept expresses the social essence of human beings and that common interest is the basic lens through which Marx explains how communities arise and change. The article follows the historical sequence of three forms: the "natural community", the "illusory community" represented by the capitalist state, and the "true community" as an association of free individuals. Hu draws mainly on The German Ideology and on Marx's writings on money and capital. Hu explains that natural communities such as clans, tribes, village communes, guilds and the Germanic "mark" rested on low productivity and personal dependence. With the division of labour and private property, the conflict between particular and common interests led to the state as an independent form that, in Hu's reading, serves only the ruling class and hides this behind constitutional equality. Under capitalism, money becomes capital and a "monetary community" that dominates individuals, so that relations between people are replaced by relations between things. Hu concludes that Marx set the true community as a value goal, reachable only through highly developed productive forces, the abolition of private ownership, class oppression and the constraints of the division of labour. Production would then be planned according to need and aim at use value, so that all members could share in it. Read the original if you want a compact, textbook-style outline of Marx's three types of community and the link he draws between common interest, capital and communism.

The contemporary significance of Dialectics of Nature 《自然辩证法》的当代意义 Zhang Yunlong Writing for the 200th anniversary of Engels's birth, Zhang Yunlong asks what Engels's Dialectics of Nature still offers a world facing what the article calls "great changes unseen in a century" and a disruptive wave of new technologies. The article argues that the classical work remains an intellectual guide for explaining a complex nature, understanding the current technological revolution and finding a way out of the ecological predicament. Zhang calls it the "living source" of contemporary philosophy of science and technology. This is a short commentary in three parts. It first notes how the field grew from an unfinished manuscript, first published in full in 1925 and spread in China from the 1920s, into a broad discipline. Zhang worries that Western-paradigm philosophy of science and technology is eroding the classical territory and drifting from Engels's basic spirit. The sections then take up Engels's conception of nature, the relation of humans and nature in historical materialism, and technology in the service of humanity. Zhang first presents Engels as achieving a "Copernican revolution" in the view of nature. Against a long metaphysical tradition of an unchanging world, including Newton's mechanical picture, Engels drew on cell theory, energy conservation and evolution to treat nature as in perpetual flux, without forcing dialectical laws onto it as Hegel did. Zhang then rejects the charge, made by Alfred Schmidt and Herbert Marcuse, that Engels was a mechanistic determinist who ignored human beings. In Zhang's reading, Engels insisted that humans act back on nature and change it, so that nature "is dissolved into history". On technology, Zhang argues that Engels did not look back to pre-industrial life and located technological alienation in the capitalist mode of production and its logic of capital, not in machines themselves. Understanding the unity of humans and nature is not enough, in this account. What is needed is a complete transformation of the mode of production and the social system, ending with communism's planned and conscious social production. Zhang concludes that institutional change is the fundamental remedy for technological alienation, and that advancing the modernization of national governance in the new era follows Engels's theory. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese defence of Engels's natural dialectics against Western Marxist criticism and a view of how it is linked to ecology and technology policy.

Lukács and the cultural theory of East European neo-Marxism 卢卡奇与东欧新马克思主义文化理论 Liu Xinran This short piece, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in August 2020, asks how Georg Lukács shaped the cultural theory of post-war East European neo-Marxism. Liu argues that Lukács's reading of Marxism, set out in History and Class Consciousness (1923), not only founded Western Marxism but also fixed the basic theoretical position of the East European current, making him in a certain sense its founder. The article covers Lukács's return to Hungary in 1945 until his death in 1971, when he trained Agnes Heller and other members of the Budapest School and exchanged views with East European theorists at venues such as the Korčula Summer School. Liu organises the influence under three dimensions: theoretical position, theoretical theme and theoretical aim. These are discussed through the critique of reification, a view of revolution centred on consciousness, and the pursuit of human value. Liu argues that Lukács saw capitalism as a world dominated by commodity fetishism and technical rationality, in which reification also becomes an inner reified consciousness. Proletarian revolution therefore requires more than seizing power: it needs a revolution of consciousness to restore the whole human being. Liu shows these ideas recurring in Živadin Jovanović's account of reification in Yugoslavia, György Márkus's critique of modernity, Karel Kosík, Ivan Svitak, Heller, Mihailo Marković, Zygmunt Bauman and Gajo Petrović's successors in the Praxis group. All of them link culture to human essence and all-round human development. Liu concludes that Lukács's dialogue with these thinkers gave their work depth and breadth, and left it with a distinctive East European stamp. The article holds that this body of theory is an important part of twentieth-century cultural theory and helps us understand the century's cultural anxiety, crisis and resistance. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese overview of Lukács's legacy among Praxis, Budapest School and Czech and Polish Marxists.

Four shifts to deepen the study of foreign Marxism 深化国外马克思主义研究的四个转换 Wang Yuchen Writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in April 2020, Wang Yuchen asks how Chinese research on foreign Marxism can be taken further. Wang notes that the field has already moved from the study of Western Marxism to the broader study of foreign Marxism, and cites Xi Jinping's call to examine new foreign findings analytically, neither rejecting nor copying them wholesale. The article's thesis is that the field will deepen only if it achieves four shifts. The piece is a short programmatic essay organised around the four shifts. These are from introducing schools to studying basic theoretical problems, from a "materials-introduction" method to a "problematic" method, from objective introduction to a value stance serving the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, and from intellectual history to its combination with academic history. Each section diagnoses a weakness in current practice and says what should replace it. Wang argues that introducing schools is only a first step. Understanding a thinker requires uncovering the "realistic logic" (the era, cultural tradition and questions addressed) and the "theoretical logic" (starting concepts, method and effects). Wang sees foreign Marxism as passing through a "cultural-studies turn" and a later "political-economy turn". The materials-introduction method reads texts in the abstract and weighs them against Marxist doctrine. In Wang's view it oversimplifies the history of Marxist philosophy and ignores the unity of theory and practice. The problematic method instead starts from that unity and from the idea of "one source, many streams". Wang also criticises research that merely introduces foreign theory, saying it produces arbitrary topic choice, academicism, obscure language, fragmentation and marginalisation. The author wants research to focus on schools that illuminate contemporary capitalism and modernity problems such as ecology, alienation, consumerism, gender, justice and distribution. On the fourth shift, Wang says intellectual history treats thinkers' ideas as homogeneous and neglects theoretical lineages, the interaction with Western social movements, and the history of interpretation and dissemination, including in China. Wang concludes that Chinese study of foreign Marxism should be oriented to theory-building and modernization practice in China, and that it should combine the evolution of ideas with the study of their effects and reception. Only then, Wang holds, can the field grasp its inner logic and its influence on Marxist research and social development in both China and the West. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how a Chinese scholar of foreign Marxism sees the field's methodological shortcomings and its intended role in Chinese theory-building.

Notable achievements in China's economic and social development during the 13th Five-Year Plan period “十三五”时期我国经济社会发展成就显著 Wu Li Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in autumn 2020, Wu reviews what the 13th Five-Year Plan period (2016–2020) achieved, taking as his starting point Xi Jinping's 22 October assessment to the Standing Committee of the Political Bureau. The article's thesis is that the plan was implemented smoothly, that its main targets will be met on schedule despite external pressure and the COVID-19 shock, and that this lays a solid base for completing a moderately prosperous society and starting a new journey of building a modern socialist country. The piece is organised under five headings: stable overall economic performance, continued optimisation of the economic structure, faster cultivation of new growth drivers, expanded opening up, and faster progress in foreign-related rule of law. It draws on official statistics from the National Bureau of Statistics, the Ministry of Public Security, the Ministry of Commerce and the fourth national economic census. Wu's core argument rests on figures. He cites average GDP growth of 6.7% for 2016–2019, GDP of 99.1 trillion yuan in 2019, per capita GDP above US$10,000, and China as the only major economy with positive growth in the first three quarters of 2020. He also reports a fall in rural poverty from 55.75 million to 5.51 million people between 2015 and 2019, capacity cuts in steel and coal, and a stabilised macro leverage ratio that kept financial risk below systemic levels. On structure, he points to a rise in the share of the 'three new' economy in GDP from 14.8% to 16.3%, growth in high-tech and equipment manufacturing, and falling tariffs and shorter negative lists for foreign investment. He presents the Foreign Investment Law and the unified market-access negative list as steps from opening in goods and factors towards opening in rules and standards. Wu attributes the results to the leadership of the Party Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core and to the guidance of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. He closes by describing the 14th Five-Year Plan period as the first stage of the new journey, calling for adherence to the new development philosophy, high-quality development and a people-centred approach, and for the new development pattern of 'dual circulation'. Read the original if you want a compact, officially aligned statistical summary of how Chinese scholars presented the 13th Five-Year Plan record in late 2020.

Marx studies in Italy: an intellectual-historical survey 意大利的马克思研究：一个思想史的考察 Lu Kejian Chinese scholarship on Italian engagement with Marx has mostly approached it through Italian Marxism, focusing on Gramsci and the Della Volpe school, with more recent attention to Labriola and to Negri's operaismo. Lu Kejian instead adopts the viewpoint of Marx studies (Marxology) and asks how Marx's texts reached Italy, how Italian thinkers read them, and how those readings interacted and were handed down. The article argues that Italian Marx interpretation has been shaped above all by a long oscillation between positivism and Hegelianism. The article has three main parts. The first is a detailed chronology of the publication, translation and editing of Marx's and Engels's writings in Italy, from Marx's 1848 letter in Italian through the 1865 translation of the Inaugural Address, the 1886 Capital volume 1, and post-war editions of the 1844 Manuscripts and the Grundrisse, to the stalled Editori Riuniti Collected Works and its later continuation by the Institute for the Study of Capitalism in Genoa. The second part periodises Italian interpretation, treating Labriola, Croce, Gentile, Gramsci and Colletti. The third looks at interactions with France, between currents of thought, and across generations of teachers and pupils. Lu's central claim is that Labriola, drawing on the Italian Hegelian tradition, was the first to read historical materialism as a philosophy of praxis rather than a positive science, and so initiated Hegelian Marxism. Croce, by contrast, accepted Second International orthodoxy, read Capital as historical materialism, and divided Marx into a scientific and an ethical element. In Lu's account this anticipated later themes of Western Marxology, such as the supposed split between Marx and Engels, and fed Bernstein's revisionism. Lu adds that Croce's critique rested on a misreading, though his originality is to be acknowledged. Lu also stresses neglected lineages: Spaventa's role behind Labriola, Croce and Gramsci, and Negri's revival of Gramsci's workerism through the Grundrisse's 'Fragment on Machines'. In an overall assessment, Lu holds that Italian Marx research led French research from the Second International onwards, with Hegelian Marxism and a Della Volpe 'scientistic' school appearing before their French counterparts, Lefebvre and Althusser. Yet Lu says Italy remained relatively peripheral in the European map of Marx studies, because its philosophical tradition was thinner and it lacked the existentialist and phenomenological readings found in Germany and France. Lu adds that readers always interpret Marx through the currents of their own time, so no single legitimate reading exists. Read the original if you want a bibliographic chronology of Italian Marx editions or an account of the Labriola–Croce–Gentile–Gramsci line from a Chinese Marx-studies perspective.

Technology in the general and the historical mode: a critical analysis of György Markus's account of Marx's theory of technology 一般模式与历史模式下的技术——乔治·马尔库什的马克思技术理论之批判性分析 Yan Yan Yan examines how the Budapest School theorist György (Georg) Markus reads Marx's theory of technology, a question tied to whether technological progress should be praised or criticised in relation to human emancipation. Markus separates a "general model" from a "historical model" in Marx and sees a tension between them. Yan argues that Markus misreads Marx. In Yan's account, Marx has only a critical, historically specific theory of technology, and a general model does not exist as a rival to it. The article, published in 2020, has three parts. It first reconstructs Markus's use of the content/form dichotomy (material content versus social form) and the six conclusions he draws from treating labour as a technical process. It then turns to the historical mode of interpretation, taking up Markus's examples one by one: labour productivity, tool-centrism, the elements of the labour process, living labour and simple cooperation, and machinery. It closes by assessing Markus's claim that Marx has two faces, "theorist of technology" and "historian", and two souls, historical romanticism and political realism. Yan draws throughout on Moishe Postone's critique of traditional Marxism. Yan's central move is to say that Markus's dichotomy abstracts labour and technology from social relations. In Yan's view this lands Markus in a traditional or positivist framework that criticises only exploitation and distribution, not the capitalist form of labour itself. Yan also charges that Markus quotes selectively. One example is a remark of Hodgskin's that Markus attributes to Marx. Another is the phrase about the "isolated man", which in the full passage describes the standpoint of bourgeois economists. Yan holds that Marx's general remarks on technology serve his historical analysis and the critique of capital. Machinery, for example, is for Marx a form of capital and a means of its domination over labour, not simply a tool. Measuring progress by labour time is, on this reading, a specific law of capitalism. Yan concedes that Marx's thought is complex. The tensions in it appear as rejection, refinement or interweaving. Historical romanticism and political realism, in Yan's view, are two dimensions of one dialectic, not two souls. Yan draws three lessons: the general and critical theories should not be set against each other; socialism's transcendence of capitalism means a qualitative change in the form of technology, not just quantitative accumulation; and the content/form dichotomy is useful only if it is not made absolute. Read the original if you study Marx's theory of technology, Markus and the Budapest School, or the use of Postone in Chinese debates, and want the textual evidence for Yan's charge of selective quotation.

The historical path of adapting the Marxist view of nationality to the Chinese context 马克思主义民族观中国化的历史进路 Ning Bo This short piece, published in the China Social Sciences Today newspaper in August 2020, asks how the Marxist view of nationality (minzu) and national questions was formed and then Sinicised over the past century. Ning argues that the view was laid down by Marx and Engels, developed by Lenin, and carried forward by the Chinese Communist Party through revolution, construction, and reform and opening up. Understanding this path, the author says, is needed both for theoretical innovation and for ethnic work in the new era and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The article is organised chronologically. It first summarises the foundations in Marx, Engels and Lenin. It then moves through the successive Party leaders: Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin, Hu Jintao and, since the 18th Party Congress (2012), Xi Jinping. For each, Ning lists the leader's main positions, often with short quotations, on equality, unity, regional autonomy, development, cadres and Party leadership. In Ning's account, Marx and Engels grounded nationality in labour and the development of productive forces, and treated national oppression as bound up with class struggle and capitalist private ownership. Lenin put national equality first, made national unity and the unity of the proletariat central, and developed legal protections and the principle of self-determination. Ning presents the Chinese stage as a continuous accumulation: Mao originated the Sinicisation, set out regional ethnic autonomy and wrote it into the 1954 Constitution; Deng named economic development, minority cadres and the Four Cardinal Principles as keys; Jiang stressed rule of law, opposition to separatism and Party leadership; Hu proposed theories of national development, harmony and interests. Ning treats Xi Jinping's statements as the latest result of this process. They centre on a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation, Party leadership, equality and unity, and the continued upholding of regional ethnic autonomy as a basic political system. The author concludes that over nearly a hundred years the Marxist view of nationality has been adapted to local conditions and the times, and that new-era ethnic work should draw out the basic laws of this process and follow its path. Read the original if you want a compact, officially aligned overview of how Party theory on ethnic questions is presented as developing from Marx to Xi.

Engels and Marx's "turn to political economy" 恩格斯与马克思的“政治经济学转向” Liu Xiuping Liu Xiuping asks how Marx came to turn from law, philosophy and history to political economy, and argues that Engels played a key facilitating role. The piece, first published in Guangming Daily in July 2020 for the bicentenary of Engels's birth, presents this turn as decisive for Marx's critique of capital. The article begins with Engels's early observation of capitalist society in Barmen, Bremen and Manchester. It then turns to Marx's own path through the Rheinische Zeitung, his Kreuznach studies and his reading of Hegel. It ends with the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 and their debts to Engels. Liu argues that Engels's experience of the gulf between workers and the bourgeoisie moved him from humanitarian indignation to a structural view of economic facts as the basis of class conflict and political history. Marx, troubled by the question of how universal freedom is possible when private interest dominates the state, had concluded that civil society determines the political state but did not yet grasp its economic relations. Engels's Outlines of a Critique of Political Economy, which Marx read while preparing the Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher, supplied that insight and prompted the turn. Liu adds that after the ten days the two spent together in Paris in 1844, the Manuscripts reflected Engels's work in three ways: in their aim of criticising political economy, in their material on the condition of the workers, and in their historically grounded critique of private property. Liu concludes that Engels's close attention to concrete social problems and empirical material helped answer Marx's troubling question and led Marx to pursue the problem of capital more deeply. Read the original if you want a short account of Engels's contribution to the formation of Marx's political economy.

Engels: examining environmental problems from the unity of nature and thought 恩格斯：从自然界和思维统一视角考察环境问题 Wang Wei Wang Wei, in a short newspaper commentary, asks what Engels offers for thinking about environmental problems. Wang contrasts Engels with Marx, who is said to have paid little attention to the environment, and argues that Engels's views contain more elements that can readily be linked to environmental questions. The piece has three parts. The first treats Engels's idea of nature's revenge as an ecological warning. The second turns to his account of metaphysical and dialectical modes of thinking as a way of explaining the roots of environmental problems and their remedy. The third discusses his call for institutional change. Wang reads Engels's remark that humans belong to nature "with flesh, blood and brain" as the basis for his warning against being too intoxicated by victories over nature. The examples Engels gives are deforestation in Mesopotamia and the Alps and the spread of the potato. Wang then argues that the metaphysical habit of isolating natural things and treating them as fixed turns nature into an inexhaustible stock of resources, whereas dialectical thinking sees nature as connected, changing and historical. Finally, Wang notes Engels's view that understanding natural laws is not enough. In this reading, a complete transformation of the production mode and the social system is needed, because capitalism cares only about profit, as in Engels's example of Spanish planters burning forests in Cuba. Wang concludes that Engels's concept of nature carries rich ecological meaning, covering both the causes of environmental problems and ways to resolve them. Wang holds that it can give socialist ecological civilization construction in China a solid theoretical basis. Read the original if you want a brief, Chinese-language overview of how Engels's writings on nature are mobilised in support of ecological civilization.

Marx's transcendence of moral nihilism 马克思对道德虚无主义的超越 Zhang Shoukui Zhang Shoukui takes up a long-running dispute among Anglo-American Marxists over the place of morality in Marx's thought, in which some scholars label Marx a "moral nihilist", that is, someone who denies the existence of morality. Zhang argues that this charge rests on misreadings. In the article's view, Marx rejected abstract moral speculation and preaching, but his thought carries strong value commitments and moral claims. This short piece, first printed in a Chinese newspaper in 2020, reconstructs the three reasons Western scholars give for the charge and then answers each in turn. It closes by considering what the misreading costs, both for understanding Marx's central aims and for present-day Marxist scholarship. The three reasons are, in Zhang's account: Marx's thoroughgoing atheism, which supposedly dissolves every suprasensible realm including moral values; the Communist Manifesto's statements that communists do not preach morality and break most radically with traditional ideas; and the historical-materialist view of morality as part of a secondary ideological superstructure, which allegedly leads to relativism. Zhang replies that Marx's critique of religion and politics always presupposed his own value commitment to the liberation of real individuals and their free and all-round development. The Manifesto's "morality" and "traditional ideas" refer, Zhang says, to ideologies defending bourgeois private property, not to all moral heritage. Western critics, Zhang contends, also confuse the relativity of morality with moral relativism, whereas Marx's practical dialectic holds relativity and absoluteness, historical continuity and consistency together. Zhang concludes that human emancipation and each person's free and all-round development form Marx's highest aim, which is both constructive and critical or regulative, and which belongs to a "higher-order morality". On this basis Marx's critique of the capitalist mode of production is, in Zhang's reading, at once scientific analysis and moral critique, so he transcends both scientific positivism and moral nihilism. Zhang warns that denying this normative dimension reduces Marx to a purely empirical science, and calls on Marxist scholars to answer the misreading and to explain the normative foundations of Marx's thought. Read the original if you want a compact Chinese-language statement of how a Chinese scholar answers the Anglo-American "Marx and morality" debate.

Contemporary lessons from the young Marx's turn to materialism 青年马克思唯物主义转变的时代启示 Zhou Jiaxin Zhou Jiaxin asks how to understand the young Marx's shift from idealism to materialism, and what kind of materialism resulted. Writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in 2020, the author argues that the shift was not a purely speculative event. In Zhou's account it came from Marx's deepening grasp of social reality, and later Marxist emphasis on it must be read against the intellectual context of the late nineteenth century. The piece opens with the research background. Chinese scholars have spent over forty years on the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 and on the path from materialism to historical materialism. Zhou then reviews how Second International and early Soviet researchers, Western "Marxology", Alfred Schmidt and Louis Althusser treated the question, and how Chinese scholars answered with concepts such as "general materialism", "humanist materialism", "social materialism" and "legal-right materialism". Zhou next turns to Marx's relation to Feuerbach and to Engels's later retrospective writings. Zhou makes two main moves. First, on the textual evidence, Marx used the word "materialism" in the Rheinische Zeitung, Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right and "On the Jewish Question" mainly in the sense of crude material interest. Sustained discussion appears only in The Holy Family and the Theses on Feuerbach (1845), while Engels, during his stay in England, had raised the question earlier. Marx moved from legal study and critique of religion to political history and the critique of political economy, and Feuerbach was only a temporary "fellow traveller". Second, Zhou explains why Engels later stressed Feuerbach, rejecting the Western "Marxology" myth of an Engels opposed to Marx. After 1848, vulgar or "economic" materialism spread. Zhou says Marx and Engels needed to clarify the materialist character of the method of Capital, which readers such as Kaufmann took to be idealist. Engels also needed to win over German workers, so criticising Feuerbach was a means and sublating bourgeois ideology the end. Zhou concludes that rethinking this transition helps people grasp the formation of Marxism and the intellectual sources of its philosophical revolution. It also offers lessons for adapting Marxism to the needs of our times and making it popular. Zhou links this to Marx's spirit of exploration and self-criticism, and ends by saying that "seeking truth from facts and emancipating the mind" is the scientific understanding of materialism in twenty-first-century Marxist theory. Read the original if you want a brief overview of Chinese debates on the young Marx's materialism and on Engels's Feuerbach writings.

The ethical turn in Anglo-American Marxism 英美马克思主义的伦理学转向 Wei Tingxue Wei Tingxue's short commentary, first published in China Social Sciences Today in July 2020, asks how Anglo-American Marxism has come to treat ethics and where that turn leaves historical materialism. Wei argues that the debate has moved from a normative reading of Marxism, associated with G. A. Cohen, towards a reconstruction of Marxist ethics grounded in historical materialism and the defence of the proletariat. Wei concludes that any such reconstruction must keep historical materialism as its foundation. The article begins with the "Marxism and justice" dispute that started in the 1970s and 1980s with Tucker, Wood and Husami, and which gradually became a discussion of Marxist ethics. It is organised in three parts: Cohen's shift from factual to normative interpretation, recent English-language work that defends the proletariat and builds a revolutionary ethics, and a closing reflection on the gap between theory and reality. Wei reads Cohen as moving from a functionalist account of historical materialism, in which productive forces explain history, to doubt that any large group still fits the definition of the proletariat. Wei says this led him to justify socialism morally, through egalitarian arguments against Nozick and Rawls, and treats this as turning Marxism into a normative theory, at odds with Marx's critique of "principles" in The Holy Family and The German Ideology. In response, Wei reports, scholars such as Paul Blackledge and Brian Leiter argue that wage-labourers are growing in number, that inequality persists and that the conditions that create a proletariat remain. Blackledge, drawing on the early MacIntyre, holds that Marxist ethics arises from concrete struggle and centres on collective self-determination and solidarity. Jeff Noonan argues that community should be preferred to equality. Wei describes this as a methodological move from normative reasoning to a dialectical approach in which moral categories are historically specific. Wei concludes that these scholars stress the distinctly Marxist character of their ethics, but that the tension between theory and reality remains open. In the context of adapting Marxism to Chinese conditions, Wei calls for flexibility and keeping pace with the times, while keeping historical materialism as the core. Wei criticises some contemporary French radical left thinkers for using Marxism's name for unrelated theories, and warns against dogmatism. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese overview of Cohen, Blackledge, Noonan and Leiter on Marxist ethics and of how Chinese scholars assess it.

The international significance of China's War of Resistance against Japan and of research on it 中国抗日战争与抗战史研究的国际意义 Wang Chaoguang Marking the 75th anniversary of victory in the Chinese People's War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression and the World Anti-Fascist War (this commentary appeared in Guangming Daily in August 2020), Wang Chaoguang asks what the Chinese war effort meant beyond China. Wang argues that China fired the first shots of the anti-fascist war, set an example for weak countries resisting strong enemies, and was the main Eastern theatre of the global war. The piece moves through three claims about China's wartime role and then turns to the state of scholarship. It ends with a call for broader, more international research on the war in the East. Wang points to the Japanese invasion from 1931 and the full-scale war from 1937, and says that for over ten years China alone resisted Japan in the East. The article cites 1937 figures: industrial output under a quarter of Japan's, steel under one per cent, and aircraft one fifth. Wang credits protracted war and guerrilla warfare with wearing Japan down. China's resistance, in this account, tied down Japan's main forces. It kept Japan from attacking the Soviet Union in 1941 and limited its southward advance. China also fought in Burma and supplied air bases and logistics. Wang takes China's founding membership of the United Nations and its permanent Security Council seat as allied recognition of this contribution. Wang says the Chinese theatre receives little attention internationally, sometimes with belittlement or misunderstanding, and that this should change. Wang proposes new topics, such as the war's influence on Asian independence movements against colonial rule, and says Chinese support for Korean, Vietnamese and Indian movements and the role of overseas Chinese show its Asian and global significance. Wang concludes that war-history research should serve national rejuvenation and a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how Chinese scholars present the war's international meaning and the research agenda they propose.

Studying the classics to advance Marxist theoretical education 研读经典著作 推进马克思主义理论教育 Li Xiaoguang Writing in Guangming Daily in August 2020, Li Xiaoguang asks how Marxist theoretical education in China can be strengthened, and answers that the close study of the Marxist classics is the necessary route. Opening with Xi Jinping's call, in the third volume of Xi Jinping: The Governance of China, for Communists to make reading the classics a habit and a spiritual pursuit, Li argues that educators must first educate themselves before teaching others. This is a short commentary organised around four benefits of studying the classics. It treats in turn the firming up of the people's stand in theoretical education, the complete and accurate grasp of Marxism's basic tenets, an understanding of the methods of Marxist education, and the raising of educators' overall competence. Li supports each point mainly with passages from Xi Jinping, Engels, Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and the Communist Manifesto. Li's central claim is that Marxism's basic principles are the systematised result of reading and distilling the classic texts, so they cannot be grasped fully without returning to the sources. As examples, Li traces historical materialism from The German Ideology through Marx's 1859 preface to Engels's Socialism: Utopian and Scientific, and places the theory of surplus value in Capital, the theory of the state in Engels and Lenin, and the view of practice in the Theses on Feuerbach. The classics also show how Lenin and Mao combined basic principles with national conditions, which Li treats as the core of the method of Marxist education, namely seeking truth from facts. Li adds that educators with higher theoretical competence can explain Marxism as an organic whole, resolve confusion about real problems and help people resist erroneous currents of thought. Li concludes that only through deep, sustained, problem-oriented study of the classics can educators hold the right stand, grasp the tenets, absorb the methods and raise their competence, and so advance Marxist theoretical education. The piece is a statement of the official line on classics study rather than a scholarly analysis of the texts. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated academics in 2020 justified classics reading as the basis of ideological and political education.

Carrying forward the Yan'an Spirit to advance the great cause of the new era 弘扬延安精神 推进新时代伟大事业 Fan Xianlei This short commentary, published in Guangming Daily on 5 August 2020, asks how the Yan'an Spirit can serve the advancement of socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era. Fan argues that the spirit, which nourished generations of Communists through revolution, construction and reform, will supply strong momentum for this cause. The piece is organised around four elements of the Yan'an Spirit, each tied to a present-day task: firm political direction, emancipating the mind and seeking truth from facts, serving the people, and self-reliance with hard struggle. Each section links the Yan'an experience to Xi Jinping's statements and to current conditions. On political direction, Fan holds that the first requirement is guidance by Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, together with the Two Upholds, and that political firmness depends on theoretical firmness. On seeking truth from facts, Fan calls for innovation in theory, practice, institutions and culture, while avoiding both impatient overreach and conservative complacency. On serving the people, Fan calls for development centred on the people, tackling unbalanced and inadequate development, and improving livelihoods. Fan concludes that, because China remains in the primary stage of socialism and the world faces great changes, with unilateralism and protectionism aimed at China, self-reliance and hard struggle must continue. Fan stresses that the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation is closer than ever and that direction and effort must not slacken. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary in 2020 tied the Yan'an Spirit to Party theory and current policy.

The rich connotations of the Yan'an Spirit 延安精神的丰富内涵 Dai Yanjun Published in Guangming Daily in August 2020, this short commentary asks what the Yan'an Spirit consists of and why it still matters to the Communist Party of China. Dai opens with Xi Jinping's remark during his April 2020 Shaanxi inspection that the Yan'an Spirit has nurtured generations of Communists.
