The author argues that its core is a firm and correct political direction, an ideological line of emancipating the mind and seeking truth from facts, the fundamental purpose of serving the people wholeheartedly, and a pioneering spirit of self-reliance and hard struggle. The article is organised in three sections, each giving the Yan'an Spirit a different identity: a spiritual result of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context, a distillation of the Chinese revolution's struggles, and an expression of the Party's essential character. Dai moves from the Yan'an period of the late 1930s to mid-1940s back to earlier setbacks, then forward to the present. Dai's central argument is that the Yan'an Spirit grew out of the Party's integration of Marxism with Chinese revolutionary practice, which the author says was achieved only after the Party leadership reached Yan'an. In this account, the line of seeking truth from facts, the mass line, serving the people and self-reliance emerged together as Mao Zedong and others used Marxism as a microscope and telescope. The author is also drawn to the costs of earlier failures, citing Party membership falling from nearly 60,000 to 10,000 after the first revolution, and reports that during the Yan'an years the Central Committee made no further major errors. Its self-reliance, Dai says, was shown in the large-scale production campaign against the Nationalist blockade, and its service ideal in Mao's speech at Zhang Side's memorial. Dai concludes that the spirit follows from the Party's nature and original aspiration: seeking happiness for the people and rejuvenation for the nation. Dai concludes that carrying forward the Yan'an Spirit means above all preserving this essential character. In the new era, the Party should keep a people-centred approach to governance, hold to the value of acting for the people's fundamental interests, and continue drawing strength from the spirit to win new victories for socialism with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned statement of how the Yan'an Spirit is interpreted in Party historiography and ideological education.

Continuing the great struggle with many new historical features 继续进行具有许多新的历史特点的伟大斗争 Liu Guangming Zhao Wentao This commentary, published in Guangming Daily in August 2020, studies the discussion of the "great struggle" in the newly published third volume of Xi Jinping: The Governance of China. Liu and Zhao take up the Party leadership's judgement that China is engaged in a great struggle with many new historical features. They argue that Party members must understand these features, grasp the basic requirements of the struggle and become cadres who both dare and know how to struggle. The piece has three sections. The first identifies four new historical features of the struggle in the new era. The second sets out four basic requirements: the direction, the objects, the laws and the capabilities of struggle. The third turns to practical demands on individual Party members and cadres. Throughout, the authors rely on passages from Xi Jinping's volume. On the new features, Liu and Zhao link each to a context and a quality the struggle must have. Accelerating global change, the Covid-19 pandemic and what they describe as provocations by individual Western countries call for foresight. The critical stage of national rejuvenation calls for initiative, and reform entering its "deep waters" calls for tenacity. Full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, in their account, calls for a revolutionary character. On requirements, they state that the main direction is upholding Party leadership and the socialist system without wavering. They add that risks to these, to sovereignty and core interests, or to the goal of national rejuvenation must be met with resolute struggle. They also call for applying dialectical principles of contradiction, firm on principle but flexible in tactics, and for building capability through ideological training, political testing and practice. For cadres, the authors call for a firm Party and people's standpoint, with Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era as guidance, and for the Two Upholds. They also urge deeper study, a sustained fighting spirit in the final months of the campaign to build a moderately prosperous society and poverty alleviation in 2020, and a stronger sense of responsibility. Leaders are asked to support those who take responsibility. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the Party press presented the "great struggle" doctrine in 2020 and the conduct it expects of cadres.

The scientific form of Marx's philosophy 马克思哲学的科学形式 Wang Shizhong Wang Shizhong asks how Marx's philosophy, read as a "philosophy of practice", can be given a scientific form. Writing in a newspaper piece of 2020, Wang starts from scholars since the early 2000s who have tried to reinterpret Marxist philosophy from a practice standpoint. Wang argues that a purely philosophical account of practice stays under the shadow of "theoretical philosophy", so practice needs a scientific theoretical form. The piece has three parts: the demand for scientific form, the relation between nature, society and science, and a proposed structure for Marx's philosophy. It engages the Austrian economist Carl Menger, game theory in institutional economics, Hegel's dialectic and the Italian thinker Benedetto Croce. Wang holds that natural science deals with the relation between humans and nature, while social science deals with relations between people, who are willed, purposive and free. The two cannot be collapsed into one, and the boundary between them still needs study. Wang finds that economics faces a paradox, since it loses legitimacy without history and loses scientific standing with it. The author therefore seeks the scientific form by a \"reverse forcing\" method, tracing the limits of each science in turn. Hegel's dialectic is one step, and Croce's dialectic of distincts is a further one, but Wang objects that Croce's structure is a closed circuit. Wang proposes remodelling it as an open, \"double-layer, three-dimensional\" structure that separates theoretical from practical activity, divides practical activity into higher and lower levels, and leaves room for human freedom. Wang offers this as an interpretive framework for a workable scientific programme for Marx's philosophy. Read the original if you want a brief outline of one Chinese attempt to link practice philosophy with scientific method.

The historical significance and contemporary value of Engels's "Outlines of a Critique of Political Economy" In commemoration of the 200th anniversary of Engels's birth 《国民经济学批判大纲》的历史意义与当代价值——纪念恩格斯诞辰200周年 Yu Bin Marked the 200th anniversary of Engels's birth, this article asks why his early work, written in 1843–44, still matters. Yu Bin argues that the text, which Marx called a "brilliant sketch of a critique of economic categories", is a work of genius. In Yu's account it shaped Marx's lifelong study of political economy, and it remains more valuable than present-day Western economics, which Yu says still propounds positions the work already refuted. The article first sets out the work's historical significance. It traces Marx's references to the text in the 1844 Manuscripts, in Capital and in later prefaces, and shows how it anticipated the Communist Manifesto. It then turns to contemporary value: Yu takes Engels's critiques of utility theory, of the self-interested economic agent, of the term "national wealth", of commerce, of private property and of competition and monopoly, and sets each against modern Western economics. Yu closes by noting Engels's own later verdict that the work was outdated and contained errors. Yu's central claim is that Engels's critique of private property underpins the whole work. Engels held that competition presupposes and turns into monopoly, and that the contradictions of competition are those of private property itself. On this basis Yu argues that Western economics, which praises competition and opposes monopoly, is a "private economics" built on private ownership. It does so, Yu says, to protect the monopolies of developed countries and to hold back developing ones. Yu also reads Engels's remark that trade rests on force as describing the nature of the US trade war against China. Engels's analysis of competition in morality and crime is presented as evidence of how private property degrades people. Yu calls Marxist political economy a "compulsory course" and says it remains marginal in Chinese universities. Yu concludes that the faults of the work were corrected by Marx in Capital, so its colours now look dimmer, but its value still exceeds that of Western economics. Yu argues that China must build its national strength and eventually renegotiate unequal treaties, and that economics with Chinese characteristics must rest on public ownership as the main body. Yu also holds that ethnic unity ultimately depends on abolishing private ownership, and presents the young Engels, who had no university education, as a model for Chinese students. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist's reading of Engels's early economic critique, applied to current debates on Western economics and the US–China trade conflict.

Class theory in British Marxism 英国马克思主义阶级理论研究 Fang Jue Fang Jue asks how British Marxist class theory has developed since the 1950s and what makes it distinctive within Marxism outside China. The article argues that it has passed through three research paradigms: a historical one, a political-science one and a political-economy one. Fang reads these as a distinctively British understanding of historical materialism. The article first places British Marxism within the two broad concerns of Western Marxism: critique of contemporary capitalism and the search for a revolutionary path. It then takes each paradigm in turn. It covers the historians E. P. Thompson and Eric Hobsbawm after the rise of the British New Left (1956), state theorists such as Ralph Miliband, and Alex Callinicos in the twenty-first century. Fang describes the historical paradigm as treating class as a relation formed through experience, custom and national cultural tradition, so that class and class consciousness cannot be separated. This paradigm is presented as a historicist reaction against French "rationalist" and scientific Marxism. The political paradigm, in Fang's account, analyses power relations. Miliband held that the state remains an instrument of the bourgeoisie even though it has some autonomy, and he defended the organised working class as the revolutionary subject against "farewell to the working class" arguments. After the neoliberal "end of class" discourse of analytical and post-Marxism, Fang says, the post-2008 turn returned to political economy. Callinicos upholds the labour theory of value and the exploitation of surplus value, and defends the working class as revolutionary subject. Fang concludes that the three shifts show British Marxists treating historical materialism not as an abstract formula but as grounded in contemporary socialist movements. In this reading Marx's class-struggle approach to capitalism remains valid, because capital's drive to expand is unchanged. Read the original if you want a short overview of how British Marxist class theory moved from history to politics to political economy.

Engels's refinement and development of the Marxist theory of ideology 恩格斯对马克思主义意识形态理论的完善与发展 Duan Guangpeng Duan Guangpeng asks what Engels contributed to the Marxist theory of ideology after Marx's death. The article argues that, facing intensifying class struggle over ideological discourse and a proliferation of bourgeois systems of thought in his later years, Engels explained the basic characteristics and active role of ideology in a dialectical way, and so carried the theory further and completed it. This is a short newspaper commentary. Duan begins with the early Marx and Engels, whose treatment of ideology was mainly a critique of illusory and inverted bourgeois ideology, without a full account of its social functions. The article then proceeds in three parts: how Engels continued while changing the path of interpretation, how he fixed ideology's basic features by reference to the economic base, and how he explained its active role through the dialectic of superstructure and base. Duan draws mainly on Engels's late works and letters, including Anti-Dühring, Ludwig Feuerbach and the End of Classical German Philosophy, and the letter to Joseph Bloch. Duan rejects the idea that Marx's late disuse and Engels's frequent use of the concept shows anything beyond a division of theoretical labour. In Duan's reading, Engels raised the relation of thinking and being to the basic question of philosophy, separated Hegel's conservative system from his revolutionary method, and recast Hegel's philosophy of nature as a materialist view of nature. Engels also placed ideology in the superstructure, together with legal and political institutions, and ranked its forms by closeness to the economic base: politics and law are nearest, while philosophy and religion are furthest. Against vulgarised readings of historical materialism, Engels stressed the relative independence of ideology, which Duan sums up as historical continuity, uneven development and lack of synchrony. The last is illustrated by Engels's remark that economically backward countries can still play first fiddle in philosophy. Duan concludes that Engels treated ideology as a basic concept of historical materialism whose content may be false or true and whose function may be conservative or progressive. Ideology also acts back on the economic base as a subjective and creative factor, and Duan names this as Engels's outstanding contribution in his last years. Duan adds that Engels's path of interpretation influenced the treatment of Marxism as a positive science and as a scientific ideology. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese account of how Engels's late writings are used to ground the relative independence and active role of ideology.

On the philosophy of "contradiction" 论“矛盾”的哲学 Yu Bin Yu Bin starts from the observation that Marxist textbooks present the philosophy of contradiction almost entirely through Mao Zedong's On Contradiction. The classics of Marx, Engels and Lenin contain no dedicated treatise on contradiction but make many remarks about it, and Yu argues that these are not fully covered by Mao's essay and in places differ from it. The article sets out to collect this classical theory, compare it with On Contradiction and merge the two into a fuller Marxist theory of contradiction. The article is a long conceptual essay that moves through the main categories of the topic in turn. These are the definition and types of contradiction, the relation between difference, opposition and antagonism, universality and particularity, principal and secondary contradictions, the two aspects of a contradiction, the evolution of contradictions, and their resolution. Yu draws heavily on Marx's Capital, Engels and Lenin. The examples include the commodity and money, planetary orbits, the Chinese revolution and the war against Japan, and socialism with Chinese characteristics. Yu defines contradiction as a dynamic unity of opposites with an inner connection. Contradictions are of two kinds: those of things, which follow objective dialectics, and those of consciousness, which reflect them as subjective dialectics. On this basis Yu rejects Mao's claim that "difference is contradiction": difference can give rise to contradiction but does not necessarily do so. Yu also separates opposition from antagonism and holds that contradictions can be eased but never reconciled. Principal and secondary contradictions are partly objective and partly dependent on human purposes. The principal contradiction differs from the principal aspect of a contradiction, and the transformation of contradictions (zhuanhua) must be distinguished from their evolution (jinhua) into something new. Yu adds that opposites can also strengthen each other. Applying this framework to China, Yu says socialism with Chinese characteristics belongs to the universal contradiction of socialism, not capitalism. In Yu's reading, public ownership and distribution according to work are the principal aspect of the principal contradiction, so their dominant position must not waver, while the non-public sector is supported in order to strengthen the public sector. Yu argues that problems arising in reform cannot simply be met with more of the same reform but require removing their causes. The article closes by insisting that contradictions in thought be resolved by seeking truth from facts. Read the original if you want a systematic philosophical reworking of On Contradiction against the classical texts, or an example of how Chinese Marxist philosophers tie dialectics to current debates on ownership and reform.

Linking citizen moral development and the raising of social civility in the new era 新时代公民道德建设与提升社会文明程度会通之径 Liang Haifeng Writing in 2020, Liang Haifeng takes up the Outline for Implementing Citizen Moral Development in the New Era, issued by the Central Committee and State Council in October 2019. The article asks how moral development among citizens relates to the level of civility (wenming chengdu) of Chinese society. Liang's thesis is that the two reinforce each other and cannot be separated: citizen morality is the foundation of social civility, and social civility in turn eases moral development. The article first defines social civility, which Liang reads, following Party congress reports, mainly as spiritual and ideological-moral progress. It then discusses the limits of law, the "broken windows" theory and Gustave Le Bon's work on crowd psychology. Next it sets the Outline against China's economic growth, the change in the principal contradiction of society, and the drive to modernize state governance. The final sections take up the four key tasks the Outline sets out. Liang argues from historical materialism that morality belongs to the superstructure and rises with the productive forces, citing Engels on civilization as a practical matter. Law is slow, cannot cover every uncivil act, and rests on a moral base, so Liang holds that rule by law and rule by virtue must work together. Citing the "broken windows" theory and Le Bon on conformity, the article claims that a clean, orderly environment encourages good conduct while a disordered one spreads bad conduct. Liang also contends that, with the principal contradiction now between people's growing need for a better life and unbalanced, inadequate development, spiritual needs depend on society's moral level. Liang concludes that the Outline expresses cultural and path confidence and is part of modernizing the system and capacity of state governance. Its four tasks are firm ideals and convictions, the core socialist values, traditional Chinese virtues, and the national and contemporary spirit. Liang expects the Outline to raise moral standards and civility, and to prepare for building a modern socialist country. Read the original if you want an official-line account of how Chinese scholars in 2020 justified linking moral education, rule by virtue and social civility.

Preventing disasters before they happen: building a popular line of defence for disaster prevention and reduction 防患未然，筑起防灾减灾的人民防线 Yuan Xiuli This short commentary, first published in Guangming Daily in October 2020, asks how China can strengthen its capacity for disaster risk governance. Yuan argues that disaster prevention, reduction and relief affect people's lives and property and social stability, and serve as a measure of the ruling party's leadership and the government's executive capacity. The author's answer is to place ordinary people and communities at the centre of disaster prevention. Yuan notes that since the 18th Party Congress (2012) the Party Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core has given disaster work greater prominence. The author nonetheless sees a still complex situation: weak sharing of disaster information, poorly coordinated resources, patchy public education, and a widespread habit of stressing relief over reduction. Four sets of proposals follow, each framed around a question: who takes charge, how, relying on whom, and where. The first proposal is to train a group of knowledgeable people. Yuan wants grassroots cadres, volunteers and local notables trained in hazard knowledge, and grassroots information workers integrated to fix the "last mile" of warnings. The author cites the more than 700,000 grassroots disaster information officers active in the 2020 flood season. The second proposal is to build skills through education: popular books, games, films, household manuals and online classes. The third calls for relying on the masses through safety education, regular evacuation drills, hazard checks by residents and grid-based risk management. The fourth proposal treats urban and rural communities as the front line, drawing on lessons from the fight against Covid-19. Yuan calls for emergency shelters, community hazard inspections, pooled reduction resources and model comprehensive disaster-reduction communities and counties. The author concludes that prevention and public self-help should replace the emphasis on relief. Read the original if you want a brief example of how a Party-aligned commentator in 2020 presented disaster governance as a mass-participation task grounded in communities.

On the subject and object of ideological and political education 论思想政治教育的主体和客体 Yu Bin Yu Bin takes up a basic question in the theory of ideological and political education: who is its subject and who is its object. The article challenges the influential view of "intersubjectivity", which holds that teachers and students are both subjects. Yu argues that students remain the object of education, even when they exercise some subjectivity, and that the subject is a wider group than teachers alone. The article is a theoretical argument that proceeds mainly by close reading of Marx, Engels, Lenin and Xi Jinping. It first tests the premise of intersubjectivity, then lists who counts as a subject: teachers, the state, the ruling class and Party committees at all levels, and family members. It then turns to the object, to the ways objects can show initiative, and to practical consequences for university teaching staff. Yu's central move is to deny that people can only be subjects. Citing Marx's uses of the word "subject" and "object", including value as the subject of a process, the author contends that the same entity can be both. Because the aim is for theory to "grip the masses", the students are objects. Yu reads Xi Jinping's call to "bring students' subjectivity into play" as the unity of guidance and subjectivity, not as a unity of teacher and student subjectivities. Citing Lenin's letter to the Capri school, Yu holds that teachers decide the real political direction of a course, so the teaching staff are the decisive subject. Ideological and political education works, Yu says, when the object recognises the content and when subject and object belong to the same class. Yu concludes that universities must give priority to building the teaching force. Teachers who give "negative" ideological education should be removed or replaced, and others should be criticised, re-educated or more closely supervised. Teachers are described as "subjects with object-like qualities", who must follow the Party's education policy and accept supervision. Yu also endorses students' reports on classroom teaching they judge hostile, as an exercise of students' initiative, and favours combining indoctrination with heuristic teaching and social practice. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist scholar defends a hierarchical subject–object model against intersubjectivity theories, and what that implies for university teachers.

Institutional strengths are the greatest strength of the Party and the state Studying volume III of Xi Jinping: The Governance of China in depth 制度优势是党和国家的最大优势 Qu Qingshan Writing in the People's Daily in August 2020, Qu Qingshan offers a study guide to the third volume of Xi Jinping: The Governance of China. The volume collects three texts by Xi on upholding and improving the system of socialism with Chinese characteristics and modernizing the system and capacity for national governance. Qu argues that these ideas are an important part of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. In Qu's reading, institutional strengths are, in Xi's phrase, the greatest strength of a party and a country. The commentary is organised around five themes, each introduced as something that must be grasped. These are the overall goal of comprehensively deepening reform, the significance of institutional improvement, the relationship between the two halves of that goal, the relationship between governance system and governance capacity, and the distinctive features and strengths of China's system. It ends with the phased targets for modernizing governance. Qu relies mainly on extended quotations from Xi, with connecting commentary. Qu first presents the goal set at the Third Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2013), to improve socialism with Chinese characteristics and modernize national governance, as a major theoretical innovation. It was developed by the Fourth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2019). Qu then stresses that the goal has two inseparable parts: the first fixes the fundamental direction, the socialist path, while the second sets out how the system is to be improved. Likewise, governance system and governance capacity must be advanced together, since a good system does not automatically yield capacity. Qu lists thirteen areas of 'notable strength', including the Party's centralised leadership, the people as masters of the country, the ability to concentrate resources on major undertakings, public ownership as the mainstay, and 'one country, two systems'. Qu cites the response to COVID-19 and decades of rapid growth and social stability as practical proof. Qu concludes by setting out the three-step target: more mature and settled institutions by the Party's centenary, basic modernization of governance by 2035, and full modernization by the centenary of the People's Republic. Qu holds that diligent study and implementation of Xi's thought will ensure these goals are met. Read the original if you want a concise, official-line summary of how Party commentary presented the governance-modernization agenda and the claimed advantages of China's system in 2020.

The Communist Party of China: born for the people, flourishing through the people 中国共产党：为人民而生 因人民而兴 Liu Hongling Published in Guangming Daily on 4 September 2020, this commentary asks why the Communist Party of China has been able to lead China from semi-colonial status to national rejuvenation and to grow from a party of about 50 members into one of more than 91 million. Liu Hongling answers that the Party wins popular support through its basic stance and purpose and through concrete action and results on behalf of the people. The title echoes Xi Jinping's statement that the Party comes from the people, was born for the people and flourishes because of the people. The article is organised around three themes, each traced from the Party's founding in 1921 through the revolutionary, socialist-construction and reform periods to the era after the 18th Party Congress (2012). The themes are a consistent people's standpoint and mass viewpoint, the safeguarding and advancement of the masses' interests, and the use of the people's approval as the highest standard for judging all Party work. Liu draws on statements by Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping, and on Party documents such as the 1990 decision on strengthening ties with the masses. Liu argues that the Party's stance has been continuous. It adopted historical materialism and the people's standpoint from the start, wrote wholehearted service to the people into the Party constitution at the Seventh Congress (1945), and later elaborated a "six basic points" mass viewpoint and the people-centred development philosophy. This stance, the author says, was turned into practice through land reform, poverty reduction, disaster relief and epidemic response, and by treating development as the Party's first task in governing. Liu adds that the Party measures its work by whether the people support, approve of, are happy with and agree to it. In this account, that standard has driven rectification campaigns, anti-corruption work and historical resolutions in 1945 and 1981, which the author presents as evidence of the Party's courage in self-reform. Liu claims that no other party in the world has matched the Party's attention to conduct and its record of correcting errors. Liu concludes that the Party has never had interests of its own and that its leading position was not self-proclaimed but chosen by history and the people. The author expects practice to continue to confirm the correctness of that choice. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated scholarship in 2020 explained the Party's legitimacy through the people's standpoint, and of which historical quotations and documents it used.

Strengthen the study of history and firm up ideals and convictions 加强历史学习 坚定理想信念 Weng Tiehui Writing in the People's Daily on 18 September 2020, Weng Tiehui argues that schools and universities should step up education in four histories: the history of the Communist Party of China, of the People's Republic, of reform and opening up, and of socialist development. The piece takes as its starting point Xi Jinping's reply earlier that year to young Party members at Fudan University, which urged them to study Marxist theory alongside these histories in order to strengthen their ideals and convictions. Weng presents this study as a way to consolidate the ideological foundations of teachers and students. The commentary is organised in three parts. The first sets out why this learning matters, the second defines its goals and tasks, and the third proposes ways of carrying it out in the education system. Weng draws throughout on Xi Jinping's statements about history, and cites Marx on people making their own history under inherited conditions. On significance, Weng gives three reasons. The study helps Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era take root in students' minds. It is also said to be inherent in firming up ideals and convictions, since these must rest on an understanding of Marxism and of historical laws. And it supplies material for ideological and political work in schools, for explaining why the Party "can", Marxism "works" and socialism with Chinese characteristics is "good". On goals, Weng names three aims: linking the distant and the near so that students learn to discern right from wrong and reject historical nihilism; centring on knowledge and belief, so that students understand both how things happened and why; and combining feeling with action, so that individual aspirations are tied to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. For implementation, Weng calls for three measures. The first is to anchor the study in Xi Jinping Thought, bringing it into textbooks, classrooms and minds. The second is to use school education as the main channel, integrating the histories into ideological and political theory courses and into all teaching. The third is to treat the internet as the main front, with online courses, quizzes, virtual retracings of the Long March and new-media publicity. Weng describes the task as an important political task for the education system. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-state education policy in 2020 framed history study as a tool of ideological and political education.

The contemporary significance of Marxist philosophical methodology 马克思主义哲学方法论的时代意蕴 Han Wenqian This newspaper commentary, published in Guangming Daily in September 2020, argues that Marxist philosophy is both a scientific worldview and a scientific methodology. Han holds that Party members and cadres need to master the methodology in order to raise their philosophical competence and their ability to analyse and solve problems. The piece opens with Engels's remark that Marx's worldview is a method rather than a dogma. The article is built in four short sections. It first stresses why method matters, citing Mao Zedong's image of the bridge needed to cross a river and Xi Jinping's description of the Marxist worldview as a "master key". It then sets out methods derived from dialectical materialism, methods derived from historical materialism, and finally a set of thinking methods and capacities. Han ties each method to a branch of theory. Dialectical materialism yields seeking truth from facts, the materialist-dialectical method (comprehensive, interconnected, developmental and systemic observation, attention to principal contradictions) and testing ideas in practice. Historical materialism yields the method of social consciousness acting back on social being, analysis of the basic contradictions of society, and the mass line. The author presents the mass line as the Party's lifeline and calls for adherence to a people-centred approach in the new era. The final section defines six capacities that Xi Jinping asks leaders to improve: strategic, historical, dialectical, innovative, law-based and bottom-line thinking. Han concludes that applying these methods and raising these thinking capacities is a basic requirement of studying Marxist philosophy, and that they serve Socialism with Chinese Characteristics in the new era and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The text is largely a structured exposition of Xi Jinping's statements on method. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Party-oriented commentary organises Marxist methodology for cadre education.

Strengthening study, reflection, practice and comprehension to achieve thorough mastery 强化学思践悟 做到融会贯通 Hao Yubin This short commentary, published in Economic Daily in September 2020, follows the release of the third volume of Xi Jinping: The Governance of China. Hao Yubin argues that the three volumes form one organic whole and are the authoritative work for studying Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Reading the original texts as a unit, the author says, is the way to grasp the comprehensiveness and systematic structure of the theory and to reach thorough mastery. The article is organised around four aspects of the Thought that readers are urged to study, reflect on and put into practice across all three volumes. These are the people-centred standpoint, the theoretical character of keeping pace with the times, scientific theoretical thinking, and a problem-oriented approach. On the first, Hao traces the people-centred position from the opening piece of volume one through volume two to volume three, where it is said to deepen into a standard for understanding, action and judgement. On the second, the author cites the new development philosophy, supply-side structural reform and high-quality development as examples of theory continually enriched through practice. On the third, Hao points to dialectics, the call for strategic, innovative, dialectical, rule-of-law and bottom-line thinking, and grasping principal contradictions. On the fourth, the commentary describes the Thought as treating problems as the starting point of policy and as uniting Marxism's scientific and practical character. Hao concludes that, as China completes a moderately prosperous society and enters a new journey toward the second centenary goal, deeper study should link theory with practice and unify knowing with doing. Doing so is said to strengthen theoretical confidence and the ability to identify and solve problems. Read the original if you want a brief example of how official commentary in 2020 framed the method of studying the three volumes of The Governance of China.

Continually tempering the political character of daring to take responsibility Studying and implementing General Secretary Xi Jinping's series of important statements on courage to shoulder responsibility 不懈淬炼勇于担当的政治品格 Zang Anmin This commentary, published in the People's Daily in July 2020, takes up Xi Jinping's repeated statements that Party members and cadres must be willing to take responsibility. Zang Anmin argues that daring to shoulder responsibility is both a political quality and a basic duty of office. In the author's account, it is the clearest test of a cadre's Party spirit and work style, and cadres must keep tempering it as they face risks and challenges. The piece opens by citing Xi's remarks during an inspection tour in Jilin on selecting cadres and protecting those who act. It is then organised in three parts. The first explains the significance of Xi's statements. The second sets out how responsibility is to be put into practice in each post and task. The third describes how Party members and their organisations can cultivate the quality, with examples ranging from revolutionary martyrs to Jiao Yulu, Liao Junbo, Huang Danian and cadres in the Covid-19 and flood responses. Zang gives three reasons for the significance of Xi's statements. They enrich the Marxist standpoint of practice, they reveal how the Party has used a great revolutionary spirit to drive great social revolution, and they provide spiritual impetus for the Party's historical mission in the new era, including the Two Centenary Goals. The author then names four settings that call for responsibility: clarity on matters of principle, willingness to struggle against unhealthy tendencies, charging forward in urgent and difficult tasks, and tireless effort in routine work. On principle, Zang says cadres must strengthen the "Four Consciousnesses", the Four-sphere Confidence and the Two Upholds, and stay in line with the Party Central Committee with Xi at its core. Zang also traces failure to take responsibility to selfish thoughts, and says loyalty to the Party is shown through action. For cultivation, Zang calls for three things. Cadres should unite knowledge and practice by studying Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. They should foster courage through selfless loyalty. Organisations should select, reward and protect cadres who act, and hold to account those who shirk, using role models to set the tone. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Party media in 2020 linked cadre responsibility to Xi's discourse on struggle and Party loyalty.

Grasping the dialectical relations in the pursuit of a better life in the new era 把握新时代追求美好生活的辩证关系 Ma Chunhong This commentary, published in Guangming Daily in September 2020, takes up Xi Jinping's remarks on a "better life" in the third volume of Xi Jinping: The Governance of China. Ma Chunhong argues that the better life is both a practical and a theoretical question, and that pursuing it requires handling three dialectical relationships using the epistemology and methodology of the unity of opposites. The article is organised in three sections. Each takes one pair: goal and means, efficiency and fairness, and individual and collective well-being. Each section sets out the logic of the pair and applies it to the new era. On goals and means, Ma holds that the goal leads and the means depend on it, so the means for each stage of the Party's phased targets (2020, 2035, 2050) must be adjusted as people's needs change. On efficiency and fairness, Ma uses the image of making the cake bigger and dividing it well. Growth must continue, while distribution should reward ability and contribution and use secondary and tertiary distribution to build a fair pattern. On the individual and the collective, Ma treats the Chinese Dream as the organic unity of national, ethnic and personal dreams. Ma concludes that individual and collective well-being promote each other and must not be set in opposition. Individual well-being, in Ma's view, must consciously be subordinated to and merged into collective well-being, under the strong leadership of the Communist Party. Read the original if you want a short example of how Party theorists present Xi's "better life" discourse through dialectical pairs.

Resolutely advancing the building of a community with a shared future for mankind 更加坚定推动构建人类命运共同体 Leng Rong Writing in People's Daily in September 2020, during the global spread of COVID-19, Leng Rong asks how China should respond to a world in what the article calls "changes unseen in a century". The commentary argues that the Party Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core is right to hold to the path of peaceful development and to work for a community with a shared future for mankind. It presents this as a sign of the Party's steadiness and sense of responsibility. The piece has three sections. The first traces China's commitment to peaceful development from the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence in the 1950s, through the independent foreign policy of peace after reform and opening up, to Xi Jinping's statements since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The second explains why the idea of a community with a shared future was put forward. The third turns to the pandemic and to China's future course. Leng gives four reasons for peaceful development: it fits the global trend, it is a necessary choice for China, it is the shared wish of the world's peoples, and it requires opposition to hegemonism. The community with a shared future is tied to four developments: the changing balance of world forces (the article says emerging and developing countries contribute 80 per cent of global growth), new technologies that bind lives together, and global problems no state can handle alone. Leng cites the Belt and Road Initiative and the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank as practice, and says the idea has entered several UN documents. The pandemic is read as proof that humanity shares a common fate. Leng criticises those who politicise the virus, shift blame or cling to Cold War thinking and zero-sum games, and says the world order should be decided by all countries, not by one or a few. Leng concludes that China will not waver in pursuing peaceful development and the community with a shared future, and will never seek hegemony or expansion. The article also calls for "bottom-line thinking" and preparation for a long period of external uncertainty, with the main task being to strengthen China's own capabilities. China is said to be set to make "new and greater contributions" to world peace on the path to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a concise, authoritative statement of how the Party press framed China's foreign policy and its global vision in the first year of the pandemic.

The generative logic of Lenin's theory of agricultural development 列宁农业发展理论的生成逻辑 Wu Huixin Liu Zhaolei This short commentary, first published in Guangming Daily in July 2020, asks how Lenin's theory of agricultural development was built up as a system. Wu and Liu argue that it follows an internal logic running from the peasant movement through land distribution, the worker-peasant alliance and cooperative labour to modern agriculture. They present it as an innovation on the revolutionary theory of Marx and Engels. The article treats the theory as five linked components, each tied to Lenin's writings and to Russian and Soviet practice from the early twentieth century. These include the 1905–1907 revolution, the land decrees after October, War Communism's surplus-grain requisition and the tax in kind that followed it, and electrification. In the authors' account, the peasant movement is the starting point because it identifies which class forces can carry agricultural change, with confiscation of landlords' land as its core measure. Land distribution is the thread through the whole theory, resting on land nationalization. The worker-peasant alliance, which includes middle peasants who must be both helped and educated, supplies the organisational form. Cooperative labour and agricultural associations are said to carry institutional and communist values. Mechanization and electrification complete the sequence by turning small-peasant production into large-scale modern farming. The authors conclude that Lenin offered a model of uniting theory and practice, applying the principle of seeking truth from facts and the mass line, and showing pioneering courage on hard agricultural problems. They hold that these methods remain relevant to China's socialist modernization and to agricultural development in the new era. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese-language outline of how Lenin's agrarian thought is presented in contemporary Chinese Party scholarship.

Lenin's great insights into revolutionary dialectics and their practical application 列宁关于革命辩证法的伟大创见及实践运用 Sun Laibin Marking the 150th anniversary of Lenin's birth, Sun Laibin asks how economically and culturally backward Russia came to take the socialist revolutionary road, a long-debated theoretical question. Sun argues that, before and after the October Revolution, Lenin used materialist dialectics to answer it and so creatively developed the 'revolutionary dialectics' of Marxism. The article presents this as Lenin's reply to Kautsky, Plekhanov and Sukhanov, who charged that the revolution was 'premature' or 'botched'. This short commentary in the Guangming Daily is organised around three dialectical pairs that Sun draws from Lenin's writings: necessity and choice, the general and the particular, and advance and setbacks. Each section pairs Lenin's responses to his critics with quotations from Marx, Engels and Lenin. Sun also draws on later Chinese leaders, including Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping. On necessity and choice, Sun reports that Kautsky likened the revolution to a premature birth. Lenin, in Sun's account, replied that critics recited formulas instead of studying living reality. Sun holds that the objective economic, class and international conditions, together with subjective readiness, were largely in place. Because people act consciously in history, the revolution was not artificially manufactured, yet it depended on the masses' initiative. On the general and the particular, Sun stresses Lenin's view that all nations will reach socialism but not in the same way, and that uniform schemas amount to a 'crude painting of Suzdal'. Lenin foresaw that revolutions in the East would show even more particularity, which Sun says Chinese revolutionary practice later confirmed. On advance and setbacks, Sun notes Lenin's view that starting the revolution was easier in Russia than completing it. Lenin held that history is no 'pavement of Nevsky Prospekt', and Sun cites his candid handling of the failure of war communism and the turn to indirect transition. Sun concludes that socialism is a wholly new system built in a relatively backward country, so it must meet difficulties and zigzags. In Sun's reading, Lenin's greatness lay in persistent exploration and firm confidence. Sun cites Deng Xiaoping's comments after the collapse in the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe, and Xi Jinping's statement that the road is winding but the future bright. Sun presents these as evidence that world socialism advances through setbacks, and that socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era is flourishing. Read the original if you want a concise, officially oriented Chinese account of how Lenin's dialectics is used to defend the October Revolution and to guide contemporary socialist practice.

The latest development of the Marxist view of ecology 马克思主义生态观的最新发展 Xu Guangchun This short newspaper commentary, first published in Guangming Daily in June 2020, argues that Xi Jinping Thought on Ecological Civilization is the latest development of the Marxist view of ecology. Xu holds that the thought has major theoretical and practical significance for developing Marxism, for socialism with Chinese characteristics, and for the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind. The piece first states the significance of the thought, then lists seven ways in which it advances the Marxist view of ecology. It ends with a short assessment of results since the 18th Party Congress (2012) and a set of practical demands. Xu's core claim is that the thought joins strict protection of the ecological environment with sound development, and does so in seven respects. It integrates the relevant ideas into a systematic body of thought within Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, and it condenses them into a new concept of green development. It places them in the overall layout of Party and state work and grounds them in the principle of putting the people and their lives first. It presents the dialectical unity of protection and development more fully, moves the work onto institutional and legal tracks, and places it within the vision of a community with a shared future for mankind. Xu concludes that the thought guides ecological civilization building in the new era and that the Party has achieved historic, turning-point and overall changes in this field since 2012. Xu calls for study and implementation of the thought, for turning it into concrete decisions, plans and measures, and for the spirit of the Foolish Old Man who removed the mountains, so that China contributes to building a beautiful world. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party commentary frames Xi's ecological thought as a stage in Marxist theory.

Engels's philosophy of law and its contemporary value 恩格斯的法哲学思想及其当代价值 Gong Pixiang Marking the 200th anniversary of Engels's birth, this piece from Guangming Daily (13 July 2020) asks what Engels contributed to the Marxist philosophy of law and why it matters now. Gong argues that Engels's legal thought is an organic part of Marxist legal philosophy and offers useful guidance for advancing law-based governance and the modernization of China's rule of law. The article is organised in two parts. The first reconstructs Engels's legal philosophy under three headings: ontology, theory of value and theory of development, drawing on Ludwig Feuerbach and the End of Classical German Philosophy, Anti-Dühring, The Housing Question, The Origin of the Family, Private Property and the State, and his late letters. The second part draws three lessons for contemporary China. On ontology, Gong reports that Engels treats law as determined by material economic conditions, even though legal form hides its economic content. Engels also rejects mechanical determinism: state power and law react back on the economic base and interact with other elements of the superstructure. On value, Gong stresses Engels's view of freedom as insight into necessity and his critique of the Proudhonist idea of "eternal justice", which Engels saw as an idealised reflection of existing economic relations. On development, Gong summarises Engels's account of the origins of law and state in the growth of production and exchange. Gong adds his comparative reading of English and continental private law, and his claim that economic necessity ultimately asserts itself through contingency. Gong draws three conclusions for the present. First, law-based governance must fit national conditions, so China should follow the path of the rule of law of socialism with Chinese characteristics and not copy foreign models. Second, the rule of law should be given a strategic role in modernizing the system and capacity of national governance. Third, it should embody a people-centred value orientation that meets growing popular demands for democracy, fairness and justice. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese Party-academic account of how Engels's texts are mobilised to support the official line on the rule of law in the 2020 "new era".

Engels and Marx's "turn to political economy" 恩格斯与马克思的“政治经济学转向” Liu Xiuping Writing in Guangming Daily in the year of the 200th anniversary of Engels's birth, Liu Xiuping asks how Marx came to turn from law, literature and philosophy to political economy. The author argues that Engels played a key role in prompting this turn, which Liu treats as decisive for Marx's later critique of capital. The commentary has three parts. It first traces Engels's early observations of capitalist society in Barmen, Bremen and Manchester, and the works he wrote between 1843 and 1845. It then turns to the "troubling doubts" Marx developed at the Rheinische Zeitung. Finally it compares Marx's Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 with Engels's writings. Liu argues that Engels moved from humanitarian indignation at workers' conditions to seeing economic facts as the basis of class antagonism and political history. Marx's Rheinische Zeitung experiences, such as the debates on the wood-theft law, had left him asking how universal freedom is possible when private interests dominate the state. Reading Engels's Outlines of a Critique of Political Economy for the Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher gave him the key to the economic relations of civil society. Liu then identifies three links with the Manuscripts: the aim of criticising political economy for taking private property as given, the use of Engels's material on English workers in the analysis of alienated labour, and a shared view of private property's historical role, which Marx treats as a path of negation of the negation toward communism. Liu concludes that Engels's close attention to concrete social problems and empirical material helped Marx answer his early doubts. In Liu's view, it also prepared Marx to pursue the question of capital philosophically and theoretically. Read the original if you want a short account of Engels's influence on Marx's early economic studies, as presented in a Chinese Party-press commemoration.

The philosophical awareness and answer to the "riddle of man" Marx's fourfold determination of the human being in the 1844 Manuscripts “人之谜”的哲学自觉与解答 Wang Huxue Wang Huxue asks how Marx understood "man", which the author treats as the core concept of Marxist philosophy. Writing in a period when the Party stresses putting the people first, Wang argues that a scientific grasp of the human being bears directly on how Marxism itself is understood, since Marxism is the science of real human beings and their historical development. The article's thesis is that the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 give a fourfold determination of the human being, which shows Marx's philosophical awareness of, and answer to, the "riddle of man". The article, a newspaper-length piece, is organised around the four determinations in turn: the human being as a natural being, as a species-being, as an objective being, and as a social being. Each section is built mainly from close reading of passages in the Manuscripts, with occasional contrasts to Feuerbach, Hegel and Fichte. Wang argues that as a natural being the human is both passive, dependent on nature and driven by passion, and active, so that nature becomes the human's "inorganic body". Species-being rests on free, conscious life-activity, realised in labour; Wang holds that Marx keeps Feuerbach's term but sublates it, giving it a new content that overcomes Feuerbach's abstract, mute generality. As an objective being, the human confirms essential powers through objects. Wang reads this process of objectification as carrying the possibility of alienation, which becomes actual when labour is estranged under private property. Finally, the social determination, which Wang describes as a transition toward the later formula that the human essence is the ensemble of social relations, makes society the ontological basis of the human. Individual and society, in this reading, mutually determine and generate each other, and even solitary activity such as science is social. Wang concludes that the human being is a social being who, through free and conscious objective labour, merges into nature and also steps out of it to realise the self. The author presents this fourfold account as showing the fullness and depth of Marx's view of the human and as the philosophical basis for today's emphasis on the people. Read the original if you want a concise, text-based Chinese exposition of the 1844 Manuscripts' conception of the human being and its link to current Party discourse on the people.

Why Marxism could take root in China 马克思主义为什么能在中国落地生根 Luo Pinghan Why did Marxism, born in the West, take root in China when it did not become the mainstream of thought in the other countries that formed communist parties after the First World War? Luo Pinghan, in a short historical commentary in Guangming Daily, answers that several factors combined. These were the failure of earlier attempts to save the nation by learning from the West, the impact of the October Revolution, the work of pioneering propagandists, and a Chinese cultural tradition that Luo says made Marxism feel familiar. The article follows a chronological path in three parts. It begins with the decline of China after 1840 and the successive failures of the Self-Strengthening Movement, the Reform Movement of 1898 and the 1911 Revolution. It then turns to the early, scattered introduction of Marxism and the changed attitude after 1917. Finally it covers the spread of Marxism after the May Fourth Movement and the founding of early communist groups in 1920. Luo draws heavily on testimony from Mao Zedong, Liu Shaoqi, Qu Qiubai, Lin Boqu and Wu Yuzhang. Luo argues that the October Revolution turned Marxism from a theoretical idea into a working social system, which set it apart from other socialist doctrines. Its appeal grew further after the Paris Peace Conference of 1919 ended Chinese hopes in the capitalist West, while Soviet Russia declared it was renouncing tsarist-era unequal treaties. Pioneers such as Li Dazhao and Chen Duxiu then spread the doctrine, and study societies turned into the early Party organisations. Luo adds a cultural explanation, citing Ai Siqi and Wu Yuzhang: ancient Chinese ideals of a "world of great harmony" meant that Marxism awakened a longing already present in the tradition. Luo concludes that China's particular circumstances and cultural tradition produced wide resonance with Marxism and the first generation of Chinese Marxists. In his account, successive generations of firm believers then led Marxism to put down roots and, with the Communist Party as its bearer, produce what he calls an unprecedented development miracle. The text closes with a quotation from Xi Jinping on the Party's emergence. Read the original if you want a concise, officially framed narrative of how Marxism reached China, with first-hand quotations from early Chinese revolutionaries.

The Communist Party of China, born of its time, and its world-shaking historic undertaking 应运而生的中国共产党与开天辟地的历史伟业 Mu Zhaoyong Published in Guangming Daily on 30 June 2020, shortly before the Party's centenary year, this article asks why the founding of the Communist Party of China in 1921 is called an event that 'opened up a new heaven and earth' (kaitian pidi). Mu Zhaoyong argues that the founding was historically necessary and that its significance can be grasped only by placing it within modern Chinese history and the goal of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The article has two main parts. The first explains why the Party 'arose in response to the call of the times'. The second explains why its founding was epoch-making, first through the Party's own qualities and then through three transformations that the author says followed. The text draws heavily on Xi Jinping's statements about the Party's origins. In the first part, Mu says the Party's birth reflected the 'historical logic' of social development, the 'practical logic' of revolutionary struggle and the 'theoretical logic' of ideas. The Opium War of 1840 turned China into a semi-colonial, semi-feudal society, and over some eighty years of anti-imperialist and anti-feudal struggle the tasks of the revolution went unfinished. The October Revolution brought Marxism-Leninism to China, and a growing proletariat provided a new social force. The May Fourth Movement then supplied the final conditions: intellectuals such as Li Dazhao, Chen Duxiu, Mao Zedong and Zhou Enlai became Marxists, early Party organisations formed, and the Communist International sent representatives. In the second part, Mu lists what the Party had from its start: Marxism as its guide, communism as its ultimate goal, close ties with the masses, and strict organisation and discipline. On this basis the author says the Party changed the direction of the Chinese nation's development, the fate of the Chinese people, and the pattern of world development. Mu concludes that the Party moved the nation from decline towards rejuvenation through the new-democratic revolution, socialist transformation, reform and opening up, and the new era after the 18th Party Congress (2012). In the author's account, China's rise has also widened the paths to modernization open to developing countries and supports the building of a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a concise example of the official Party narrative of the CPC's founding and its significance, as presented in the national press ahead of the centenary.

Engels after he met Marx 遇见马克思以后的恩格斯 Luo Jianlin Published in Guangming Daily in June 2020, to mark the 200th anniversary of Engels's birth, this short commentary asks what defined Engels's life after his decisive meeting with Marx in Paris in 1844. Luo's answer is that defending, promoting and revering Marx became the portrait of Engels's life from then on. The author presents the meeting as a "chemical reaction", even a "nuclear fission", in the field of social revolution. The piece is organised under three headings: Engels's firm political consciousness, his sense of responsibility in spreading and developing Marxism, and his personal integrity in respecting Marx. It draws on Engels's early writings, letters between the two men, and episodes from 1844 to the years after Marx's death. Luo argues that Engels, from a devout Prussian family, gave up a comfortable bourgeois life for the proletarian cause. He is said to have fought Marx's detractors in print and accepted twenty years of commercial work, his "Egyptian captivity", so that Marx could finish Capital. Luo then lists Engels's efforts to spread Marx's work: reviews of the Critique of Political Economy, nine reviews of Capital, and over a decade spent editing Volumes 2 and 3 of Capital. Engels's own works, notably Anti-Dühring, are presented as enriching Marxism. Luo adds that Engels stressed that he merely harvested the glory Marx had sown, and cites the two men's mutual praise and trust as evidence of their friendship. Luo closes by saying that the trials and successes of the cause the two founded show the "power of truth" in Marxism. Continuing along the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics is described as the best way for Chinese communists of the new era to honour them. Read the original if you want a brief, celebratory portrait of the Marx–Engels relationship as it was presented in the Chinese Party press for the 2020 anniversary.

Lenin's in-depth study of Marxist texts 列宁对马克思主义文献的深入研究 Zhao Yulan This short piece, first published in Guangming Daily on 29 June 2020, asks how Lenin related to the textual legacy of Marx and Engels. Zhao argues that Lenin was both a close student of the classic texts and the person who decisively launched the first large-scale collection, editing and systematic publication of that legacy. In Zhao's account, this work gave the international workers' movement and world socialism a theoretical weapon and ideological guide. The article follows Lenin's engagement in three stages. It begins with his early study and first translation and publishing work, then turns to his overall grasp of Marx's writings as shown in his 1914 encyclopaedia entry on Marx. It ends with his role after the October Revolution in building the institutional and material basis for editing the Marx–Engels legacy. Zhao first shows, from Lenin's writings of 1893–94, that he already used Capital, the Preface to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy and even the little-known manuscript of The German Ideology against the Narodniks. In 1907 Lenin also revised the Russian edition of Marx's letters to Kugelmann and wrote a preface to the Sorge correspondence. Zhao then reads the bibliography appended to Lenin's entry "Karl Marx" as evidence of systematic knowledge, noting that Lenin repeatedly observed that many of Marx's articles had not been collected, republished or translated into Russian. After 1917, Zhao says, Lenin backed the Marx–Engels Institute under David Ryazanov, set out seven questions that served as a work programme, and approved an extra 75,000 gold roubles for buying libraries in Vienna. Zhao concludes that study of the texts equipped Lenin to lead the October Revolution, and that the new Soviet state in turn allowed him to promote the systematic collection and compilation of Marx and Engels's works. This, in Zhao's view, laid a deep ideological and theoretical foundation for the world socialist movement. Read the original if you want a concise account, drawn from Lenin's prefaces, notes and letters, of how he treated Marxist textual scholarship and the founding of the Marx–Engels Institute.

The narrative features of Engels's theory of nature's revenge 恩格斯“自然报复论”的叙事特征 Li Heliang Zhang Xu Marking the 200th anniversary of Engels's birth, Li and Zhang revisit his theory of nature's revenge, which they treat as central to his dialectics of nature. They argue that Engels used the theme as a thread to develop materialist dialectics, folding background, rhetoric and intent into the text. In their reading, this prepared the way for the idea of the "two reconciliations": between humanity and nature, and within humanity itself. The piece is a short newspaper commentary in five parts: how the theory took shape, the context in which it was written, Engels's intentions, his rhetorical strategies, and the theory's relevance to reality. It traces the idea from Engels's early writings on industrial pollution through On Authority, The Part Played by Labour in the Transition from Ape to Man, Anti-Dühring and Dialectics of Nature. The authors argue that Engels wrote against several targets: naturalism and anthropocentrism, vulgar materialism and social Darwinism, and metaphysical views of nature and idealist dialectics. They identify three rhetorical devices: personification, analogy and model abstraction from cases such as deforestation in Mesopotamia, Italy and Spain. On their account, Engels traced nature's revenge to limits on human knowledge, to capitalist production driven by profit and surplus value, and to consumer desires stimulated by capital. Only a communist society that truly resolves the conflicts between humans and nature, and among humans, could end it. The authors conclude that the theory offers a dialectical basis for seeing humans and nature as a community of life, with practical transformation as its aim. They link it to the Fourth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2019) and call for guidance from Xi Jinping Thought on Ecological Civilization, a change in the traditional development model, and respect for ecological red lines. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese reading of Engels's ecological thought and its tie to official ecological civilization policy.

Engels's construction of the system of Marxist philosophy 恩格斯对马克思主义哲学体系的建构 Yang Hongyuan This short commentary, first published in Guangming Daily in June 2020, asks what Engels contributed to building Marxist philosophy into a system. Yang argues that Engels contributed in both form and content. In form, he helped criticise the rigid closed systems of older philosophy and turn philosophy into an open structure and dynamic thought. In content, he unified ontology, dialectics and the conception of history. The article is organised around four themes: Engels's reading of the fundamental question of philosophy, the ontological foundations of Marxism, dialectics as worldview and method, and the interaction among historical factors. It draws on Engels's works, including his editing of volumes two and three of Capital, Anti-Dühring, Ludwig Feuerbach and the End of Classical German Philosophy, Dialectics of Nature and The Origin of the Family, Private Property and the State. Yang holds that through these works Engels produced the first complete systematisation of Marxist philosophy. He did so by separating the relation of thinking and being from other forms of philosophical struggle and making it the criterion for judging philosophical positions. On this basis he is said to have grounded the unity of the world in its materiality and examined matter, motion, time and space. Dialectics runs through all of this as the main thread, and Yang lists its laws and categories. Finally, Engels stressed the relative independence of political, legal, philosophical and religious factors, and their reaction on the economic base, to correct misreadings of historical materialism. Yang concludes that these achievements make Engels's self-description as the 'second violinist' fully deserved. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese-language overview of how Engels is credited with systematising Marxist philosophy.

Althusser's interpretation of materialist dialectics and its implications 阿尔都塞对唯物辩证法的阐释及其意蕴 Song Kaixuan Song Kaixuan asks what separates Marx's materialist dialectic from Hegel's, and how Louis Althusser answered. Against the "philosophy of practice" tradition, which stresses subjective agency and, in the author's view, over-Hegelianises Marx, Song argues that Althusser's scientistic or structuralist reading served as an important corrective, though it has its own limits. The short piece, first published in a Chinese newspaper in 2020, has three parts. It takes up Marx's "inversion" of Hegel, then Althusser's identification of the dialectic's basic structure, and finally his treatment of the dialectic as a scientific form. Song reports that Althusser regarded the "inversion" as a metaphor that cannot settle the question. For Althusser, Hegel's "shell" is inseparable from the "kernel", so Marx's inversion must be a fundamental reworking of the dialectic's structure. Song reads Althusser as fixing that structure in the relation between subjective activity and objective structure. This echoes two logics in Marx: an activist logic of changing the world and a determinist logic drawn from modern science. Althusser, with "overdetermination" and "structural causality", contrasts Marx's complex, uneven, structured whole with Hegel's "expressive causality", in which difference returns to the Absolute Idea. Song concludes that Althusser advanced research on Marxist dialectics by recasting the Marx–Hegel relation as one between agency and structural determination. His flaw, in Song's view, is treating science as the only proper way of grasping the world, which forgets that Marx's critique of political economy aims to change reality. A full interpretation must link the determinist and activist logics. Read the original if you want a brief account of Althusser's reading of Marx's dialectic and a critical assessment from a Chinese perspective.

Pioneer in building a sinicized Marxist philosophy: a study of Li Da's philosophical thought 构建中国化马克思主义哲学的拓荒者——李达哲学思想研究 Wang Xinyan Wang Xinyan asks what Li Da (1890–1966) contributed to the making of a Chinese Marxist philosophy, and argues that he was its pioneering builder. In Wang's account, Li was an encyclopaedic scholar and a founding figure of the Party, whose philosophical work shaped the formation of Mao Zedong's philosophical thought. The text appeared in Guangming Daily in October 2020. After a short biography, the article is organised in four parts. They cover Li's systematic dissemination of Marxist philosophy from the May Fourth period to the mid-1930s; his theoretical construction of the sinicization of historical materialism; his two attempts at a Marxist philosophical system, the Outline of Sociology and the Outline of Materialist Dialectics; and his exposition of Mao Zedong's philosophical thought. Wang's core argument has three moves. First, Li moved from critiquing anarchism, revisionism and pseudo-socialism, through the 1926 Modern Sociology, to the Outline of Sociology (1935/1937), which Wang calls the first systematic Marxist philosophy text written by a Chinese author. Second, Li applied historical materialism to economics, history, politics, law and sociology, for example by proposing a 'broad economics' and describing Chinese society as 'semi-colonial and semi-feudal'. Third, the Outline of Sociology presented Marxist philosophy as a 'practical materialism' and as a unified whole, which Wang says anticipated the practical-materialism debates of the 1980s and 1990s and differed from the Soviet textbooks of the time. Wang describes Li's later work as giving Marxist philosophy a distinctly Chinese style. The Outline of Materialist Dialectics (early 1960s) drew on the experience of the Chinese revolution and socialist construction, and Li's commentaries on Mao's "On Practice" and "On Contradiction" are presented as models of popularising Marxist philosophy. Wang cites Mao's praise of Li's works and his comments on them as evidence. Read the original if you want a concise, appreciative account of Li Da's career and of how Chinese Marxists in 2020 ranked his place in the history of Marxist philosophy in China.

Examining Heideggerian Marxism 考察海德格尔式马克思主义 Yang Dong Yang Dong asks how research on contemporary Marxism outside China can take up the legacy of Martin Heidegger's thought. The article, a newspaper piece from 2020, argues that "Heidegger and Marxism" deserves to be treated as a distinct research topic. It also contends that the concept of Heideggerian Marxism should move from a narrow meaning, tied to Herbert Marcuse, to a broad one covering a latent current across the traditional schools. Yang opens with Gajo Petrović's remark that modern philosophy must choose between Heidegger and Marx, or perhaps start from both. The article separates the topic from "existentialist Marxism" and from "phenomenology and Marxism". It then covers Heidegger's scattered remarks on Marx, Georg Lukács's 1949 Marxist critique of Heidegger, Marcuse's early synthesis, and later scholarship by Jürgen Habermas's contemporaries and others such as Jeffrey Wolin, Poster, Zimmerman and Demmerling. On the narrow sense, Yang reports that Marcuse in the late 1920s and early 1930s tried to supplement fundamental ontology, which was weak on social and historical questions, with Marxism, centring on "historicity". Marcuse later judged Heidegger's concreteness illusory and found in Marx's Paris manuscripts what he had sought in Heidegger. Wolin and others nonetheless see Heideggerian traits in One-Dimensional Man. For the broad sense, Yang takes Franzen's criterion, that a thinker's reception of Heidegger within Marxism qualifies them, and so includes Schmidt, Axelos, Kosik and Petrović. Yang adds that Marxist critiques of Heidegger, by Lukács, Adorno and Badiou, supply a centrifugal counterpart to this reception and a useful reference point. Yang concludes that studying Heideggerian Marxism means attending both to Marxism's reception of Heidegger and to its critique of him. Read the original if you want a compact map of how scholars have defined Heideggerian Marxism and which thinkers they place under it.

The dialectics of nature in Anti-Dühring 《反杜林论》中的自然辩证法思想 Yang Hongyuan Dialectics of nature is widely accepted as a branch of Marxist philosophy, yet a minority who posit an intellectual opposition between Marx and Engels treat it as their key evidence that Engels overstepped Marx's thought. Yang rejects this reading, arguing that Marx and Engels shared the original aim of rescuing conscious dialectics from German idealism and applying it to a materialist view of nature. Because scholarship on Engels's Dialectics of Nature is abundant while studies of the dialectics of nature in Anti-Dühring are few, the article, first published in the China Social Sciences Today in 2020, takes the latter as its subject. The article has four parts. It first traces how dialectics displaced metaphysical thinking, then examines Engels's critique of Dühring's revival of the old philosophy of nature. It next sets out Engels's positive account of the laws of dialectics. Throughout, Yang follows Engels's own historical sketches and his use of nineteenth-century natural science. Yang's core argument starts from Engels's account of ancient Greek dialectics as correct but naive, followed by the analytic natural science of the fifteenth century onward. That science, in Yang's account, produced an isolated, static, either-or metaphysics, which German classical philosophy and then modern materialism overcame. Dühring's philosophy of nature, though it attacks Schelling, in Yang's reading still replaces real connections with imagined ones. Engels answers on time, space, matter and motion, the passage from inorganic to organic nature, and the origin of life. He argues that the infinity of the real world differs from a mathematical series with a beginning, and that Dühring's law of determinate number copies Kant's first antinomy. Engels then presents motion as the mode of existence of matter, with mechanical, physical, chemical and biological forms that are distinct yet convertible. The law of contradiction, the law of the interconversion of quantity and quality, and the law of the negation of the negation are presented as universal laws of nature, not mystical formulas. Yang concludes that Anti-Dühring pursues two aims, refuting Dühring and giving a systematic account of dialectics of nature, so that people can better understand and change the real world. The article implies that this shows the dialectics of nature to be an integral part of Engels's thought, not a departure from Marx. Read the original if you want a concise overview of how Engels builds the case for dialectics of nature in Anti-Dühring, or if you follow the Marx–Engels debate in Chinese scholarship.

The philosophical significance of the young Marx's turn to the critique of political economy 青年马克思政治经济学批判转向的哲学意义 Yuan Liguo Yuan Liguo asks what the young Marx's turn from law and philosophy to political economy, prompted in 1842 at the Rheinische Zeitung by doubts over 'material interests', meant for his philosophy. The article, a newspaper piece in the Chinese Social Sciences Today (2020), argues that in the Paris Manuscripts this first critique of national economics did three things. It sublated idealist 'synthesis of consciousness' into a materialist 'synthesis of labour', moved beyond 'crude communism', and set the theoretical orientation of a new worldview through a 'science of man'.
