The text is organised in three sections: the materialist synthesis of labour, the civilizational meaning of communism, and the theoretical orientation of the 'science of man'. Yuan places Marx against Kant, Hegel and Feuerbach, and against the utopian communists Proudhon, Fourier, Babeuf and Blanqui. The argument rests mainly on close reading of the Paris Manuscripts. In the first move, Yuan holds that Marx saw Feuerbach's naturalism as still abstract, and that Hegel grasped labour's positive essence because he stood on the ground of modern national economics. Through the critique of political economy, labour is deepened from an anthropological category into an epistemological one, so that the synthesis of consciousness rests on the synthesis of labour and not the reverse. In the second move, Yuan reads 'crude communism' as the universalisation of private property, while Marx's communism is the positive sublation of private property. It rebuilds community on humanity's social, species being, avoids setting society against the individual, and yields the 'total man'. Yuan concludes that the degree to which people are socialised measures the advance of civilisation. In the third move, Yuan presents the 'science of man' as neither philosophical anthropology nor positive social science. It is a phenomenological study of the human, grounded in practice and sensuous experience, in which natural science enters life through industry. Critique of political economy then frees people from 'abstract labour'. Yuan concludes that uniting natural science and philosophy in this way fixed the orientation of Marx's new worldview and foreshadowed historical materialism. Read the original if you want a compact Chinese reading of the Paris Manuscripts that links labour, communism and the science of man.

Marx's theoretical picture of the meaning of life 马克思理解生命的理论图景 Wu Xiao'an Marx wrote no systematic treatise on the meaning of life. Wu Xiao'an argues that a coherent account can nonetheless be reconstructed from his political economy and historical materialism. The thesis is that, for Marx, life's meaning is neither an object of contemplation nor an abstract philosophical concept. It is a revolutionary question that unfolds in real history and is fully resolved only through the communist movement for human emancipation. The piece is a short newspaper essay, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in 2020. The article moves in four steps. It first contrasts Marx with Epicurean contemplation, Feuerbach's intuitionism and Hegel's idealist dialectic. It then turns to the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 and to the alienation of life's meaning under capitalism. It next takes up the link between the emancipation of workers and the emancipation of humanity. Finally it treats communism as the realisation of life's full meaning, drawing on the Communist Manifesto, Engels's Socialism: Utopian and Scientific, The German Ideology and the Critique of the Gotha Programme. Wu's central claim is that Marx builds a double dimension of labour practice and social relations. Human essence and value are realised through free, conscious labour, which is always social production within particular relations of production. Wu notes that Marx does not make material production itself the core of human essence. Under capitalist private property, workers are separated from the means of labour and the product, and wage labour reduces their essence to a means of survival. Wu adds that alienation also corrupts relations among people and affects every class, including capitalists, who are described as instruments of capital's reproduction. Wu concludes that Marx ties the redemption of life's meaning to the emancipation of workers, because all servitude is contained in the worker's relation to production. This requires abolishing private property and the compulsory division of labour. In the higher stage of communism, labour becomes "life's prime want" and individuals develop freely and all-roundedly. Read the original if you want a concise, text-based outline of how Marx's early and later works can be read together on the question of life's meaning.

Striving for new breakthroughs in comprehensively deepening reform Studying Xi Jinping's statements on comprehensively deepening reform in volume III of Xi Jinping: The Governance of China 奋力推动全面深化改革实现新突破 Mu Hong Mu Hong's commentary, first published in the People's Daily in August 2020, is a study-and-implementation piece on the newly published third volume of Xi Jinping: The Governance of China. It takes up how Party members and officials should understand and put into practice Xi Jinping's statements on comprehensively deepening reform. Mu's thesis is that these statements are an original part of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and provide the fundamental guide for reform work, which must be pursued with greater resolve. The text is organised around five themes: the historical position of reform in the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation; Party leadership; the strategic direction and goal of reform; reform's service to economic and social development; and the people-centred value orientation of reform. A final section calls for continued, practical implementation. It reviews achievements since the Third Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2013) and sets out tasks for the year in which a moderately prosperous society is to be completed. Mu argues that reform is the decisive move for realising the two centenary goals and that it is the fundamental driving force for meeting present risks. Reform must stay under the centralised leadership of the Party Central Committee, which Mu describes through the shift from a leading group to a Central Commission for Comprehensively Deepening Reform chaired by Xi, and through the Two Upholds. The overall aim, from the Third Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2013) and the Fourth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2019), is to improve the socialist system with Chinese characteristics and modernise national governance. In Mu's account, reform serves high-quality development, including market, innovation, regional and opening-up measures. It also serves the people's sense of gain, happiness and security through employment, social security, health, education and poverty-reduction measures. Mu presents the response to COVID-19 as an example of combining reform with epidemic control. Mu concludes that reform grows harder as it deepens and calls for courage, a practical work style, supervision and inspection, respect for grassroots initiative and tolerance of errors in pioneering reform. Officials are told to treat implementing the Central Committee's reform plans as a major political task and to guard against formalism and bureaucratism. Read the original if you want an official People's Daily framing of Xi-era reform, covering its Party-leadership logic, institutional goals and the practical requirements set for cadres in 2020.

The new position, new challenges and new opportunities of the new development stage 新发展阶段的新方位新挑战新机遇 Ding Maozhan Writing in Economic Daily on 30 September 2020, Ding Maozhan takes up Xi Jinping's statements that the 14th Five-Year Plan period (2021–25) opens a "new development stage" for China. The article asks how to understand the stage's historical position and how to analyse, dialectically, the challenges and opportunities that deep changes at home and abroad bring. Ding argues that this understanding is important for planning economic work in the period. The commentary opens by quoting Xi's remarks at the symposium of experts in the economic and social fields and at the 17 September meeting with grassroots representatives. It is then organised in three parts: the new position (历史方位, the historical position of the stage), the new challenges, and the new opportunities. Each part is divided into three or four sub-themes, with brief statistical and historical illustration. On the position, Ding argues that China is completing the first centenary goal of a moderately prosperous society and setting out toward the second centenary goal of a modern socialist country. Ding adds that the economy has moved from high-speed growth to high-quality development, and that the principal contradiction is now between the people's growing needs for a better life and unbalanced, inadequate development. The article cites per capita GDP of 10,000 US dollars, urbanisation above 60 per cent, over 400 million middle-income earners and about 100 million people lifted out of poverty. On challenges, Ding points to a turbulent world (technological competition, protectionism, the pandemic, a reshaping of the global governance order) and to domestic pressures: an unsustainable factor-driven growth model, structural imbalances, and harder reforms. On opportunities, Ding stresses institutional advantages, a large market, resilience, and the Party's "strategic resolve" to pursue high-quality development. Ding concludes that China remains in a period of important strategic opportunity, that long-term economic improvement will not change, and that challenges are problems of development. The article holds that, under the Party's leadership, China can create new opportunities out of crisis and achieve development that is higher in quality, efficiency, fairness, sustainability and security. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese official economic commentary in 2020 framed the new development stage and the 14th Five-Year Plan.

The basis for firming up the Four-sphere Confidence The 13 notable advantages of China's national system and system of national governance 坚定“四个自信”的基本依据所在 Han Qingxiang This short commentary, published in People's Daily in August 2020, asks why the 13 notable advantages of China's national system and system of national governance should be seen as the basis for the Four-sphere Confidence. Han Qingxiang notes that the Fourth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2019) was the first to summarise these advantages systematically. In Han's account they are the fundamental guarantee of the "two miracles" of rapid economic growth and long-term social stability, and the institutional "code" of "Chinese governance". The article first treats the 13 advantages as an organic whole, then traces their source in socialism with Chinese characteristics, and finally sets out what is needed to bring them into full play. The areas Han lists include Party leadership, the people as masters of the country, rule of law, national unity, the economy, culture, people's livelihood, reform and innovation, defence, "one country, two systems", and foreign affairs. Han argues that the advantages are layered and logically ordered. The advantage of upholding the Party's centralised and unified leadership, its scientific theory and political stability heads the list and runs through the other twelve. The system is described as scientific because the Party has combined Marxism's basic principles with China's realities and the features of the times, and has turned successful practice into institutions. Han presents Party leadership as the most essential feature and greatest strength of the system, resting on its capacity for ideological guidance, inspiration, mobilisation, consensus-building and implementation. Han concludes that making full use of the 13 advantages requires upholding Party leadership and improving the institutional system through which the Party oversees the whole situation and coordinates all sides. Han holds that doing so will allow China to create new and greater miracles and strengthen the Four-sphere Confidence. Read the original if you want a compact example of how official commentary in 2020 linked the 13 advantages to Party leadership and to the Four-sphere Confidence.

The scientific methodology of building a moderately prosperous society in all respects 全面建成小康社会的科学方法论 Chen Jinlong Writing in the People's Daily in July 2020, Chen Jinlong takes up the pledge to complete a moderately prosperous society in all respects by 2020, which he calls a solemn promise by the Party to the people and to history. Chen argues that since the 18th Party Congress (2012) the Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core has developed a scientific methodology for this task. In Chen's reading, it embodies Marxist ways of thinking and working and serves as both ideological guidance and a practical guide for the final push. The short commentary is organised under three headings. The first concerns viewing and planning the goal from a strategic height. The second concerns balanced planning that takes all factors into account (统筹兼顾), including how to balance epidemic control with development. The third concerns seizing the key points and achieving breakthroughs in the three critical battles: preventing major risks, targeted poverty alleviation and pollution control. On strategy, Chen traces the goal from the "Two Centenary Goals" and notes the shift from "building" to "completing" a moderately prosperous society, which in his view raises the standard. He places it within the Four-pronged Comprehensive Strategy, where deepening reform, law-based governance and full and rigorous self-governance of the Party supply momentum, legal protection and political guarantees. On balance, Chen stresses that "comprehensive" matters more than "moderately prosperous": the society must cover all fields, all people and all regions, yet standards should not be raised blindly beyond national conditions. On the three battles, he describes risk-prevention mechanisms and "bottom-line thinking", precise poverty alleviation (551 million rural poor reduced to 5.51 million by end-2019, in the author's figure) and an ecological approach that rejects pollution first and treatment later. Chen concludes that grasping the strategic opportunity, balancing epidemic control with economic and social development, and focusing on the weakest links are what will secure the goal despite the shock of COVID-19. He presents the methodology as a concrete application of dialectical thinking. Read the original if you want a concise official-line account, from mid-2020, of how Party theorists framed the final stage of the moderately prosperous society campaign.

The leadership of the Communist Party of China is the correct choice made by history and the people 中国共产党的领导是历史和人民作出的正确选择 Jiang Jinquan Jiang Jinquan takes as his starting point Xi Jinping's statement that history and the people chose the Communist Party of China (CPC) to lead the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, and that this choice is correct and must be upheld permanently. Originally published in the People's Daily on 20 August 2020, the commentary argues that the claim rests on historical, theoretical and practical grounds. Jiang's thesis is that Party leadership is both a product of modern Chinese history and the essential guarantee for completing national rejuvenation. The piece has three parts. The first traces how the Party's leading position was formed, from the Opium War of 1840 and the failed reform and revolutionary projects that followed, through the founding of the Party in 1921, the revolutionary wars, the founding of the People's Republic, the reform era after the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee, and the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The second explains why the Party was able to lead, and the third explains why its leadership remains indispensable. In the second part Jiang identifies five features that he calls the Party's "genetic code": guidance by scientific theory, namely Marxism as adapted to Chinese conditions; a people-centred political stance; unremitting pursuit of its founding mission; a strong and tight organisational system built on democratic centralism, with, he says, over 4.68 million organisations and more than 91 million members; and a commitment to the Party's self-reform. He contends that no other party has these qualities, which is why history and the people chose it. The commentary cites a survey by a US public relations firm putting Chinese public trust in government at 95%. The third part, citing Xi, Deng Xiaoping and the classics, holds that leadership by the Party is the defining feature and greatest advantage of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Jiang concludes that, with the world undergoing great changes and domestic development at a critical stage, the Party's leadership must be upheld without wavering. He calls for firm defence of the authority and centralised, unified leadership of the Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core, applying the Four Consciousnesses, the Four-sphere Confidence and the Two Upholds, and for improving the institutional system of Party leadership and full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. Read the original if you want a compact example of the official People's Daily case for the legitimacy and necessity of Party leadership as it was framed in 2020.

The Chinese people's choice of leadership by the Communist Party of China is entirely correct 中国人民选择中国共产党领导是完全正确的 Chen Li This commentary, first published in the People's Daily in August 2020, argues that the Communist Party of China's leadership is not self-proclaimed but the choice of history and of the people. Chen Li contends that history and present reality show this choice to be entirely correct, and that the Party will keep strengthening itself to lead the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The piece opens with Xi Jinping's statement that Party leadership is the defining feature and greatest strength of socialism with Chinese characteristics. It has two main sections: why the people chose Party leadership, and why that choice will be sustained in future. It draws on the Party's growth from about 50 members to over 91 million, on revolutionary-era episodes and on the post-2012 period. Chen's central claim is that the Party "comes from the people" and always represents their fundamental interests. Citing the Communist Manifesto, Chen treats representing the majority rather than a minority as what separates Marxist parties from others. Chen then points to the Party's struggles in the revolutionary, construction and new-era periods, to the moral example of figures such as Jiao Yulu, and to popular support in wartime as evidence. Looking ahead, Chen argues that growing international instability and the difficulty of the final stretch toward national rejuvenation make stronger Party leadership necessary. Chen concludes that, since the 18th Party Congress (2012), the Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core has upheld full and rigorous self-governance of the Party and the Party's self-reform, which the article says has increased the Party's cohesion and vitality. Chen expects the Party to keep earning popular support and to realise the Chinese Dream. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Party commentary justifies one-party leadership by appeal to popular choice.

Striving for the happiness of the Chinese people and the cause of human progress 为中国人民幸福和人类进步事业而奋斗 Song Tao This commentary, first published in the People's Daily on 3 September 2020, takes up Xi Jinping's statement that the Communist Party of China is a party that seeks happiness for the Chinese people and also strives for the cause of human progress. Writing amid the global spread of Covid-19 and what it calls a world undergoing changes unseen in a century, Song argues that the Party stands on the right side of history. In the author's account, it does so by building a community with a shared future for mankind, rejecting Cold War thinking and power politics. The article is organised around five roles it assigns to the Party: a firm practitioner of putting the people and their lives first; a defender of lasting peace and universal security; a practitioner of fairness, justice and responsibility; a promoter of mutual benefit and common development; and a leader in openness, inclusiveness and mutual learning among civilisations. Each section opens with a quotation from Xi Jinping and draws on domestic achievements, foreign policy statements and the reported views of foreign party figures. Song's central move is to present the Party's domestic record as the basis of its international conduct. The article cites poverty alleviation, the Covid-19 response (including the share of Party members among medical staff sent to Hubei) and a survey reporting 95 per cent public trust in the government. It then describes a foreign policy of peaceful development, dialogue without confrontation, and no hegemony or expansion. It points to the Belt and Road Initiative, which it says is neither a sphere of influence nor a debt trap, and to the sharing of governance experience with foreign parties. It also says China will neither import nor export a model and will not draw lines by ideology. Throughout, Song attributes favourable assessments to foreign party leaders and organisations and contrasts the Party's conduct with that of unnamed states that shift blame or impose sanctions. Song concludes that, as it approaches its centenary, the Party, guided by Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, will coordinate national rejuvenation with the global changes and work with other parties to build a community with a shared future for mankind. The piece is an official-style statement of how the Party presents its international role in 2020. Read the original if you want a representative example of the Party's own framing of its global responsibilities, including its language on the South China Sea, the pandemic and inter-party relations.

The historical turning point for the Chinese nation's march towards great rejuvenation 中华民族走向伟大复兴的历史转折点 Qu Qingshan Writing in the People's Daily on 8 September 2020, Qu Qingshan takes up Xi Jinping's speech at the symposium marking the 75th anniversary of victory in the War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression and the World Anti-Fascist War. Qu asks why that war became the turning point from which the Chinese nation moved out of deep modern crisis towards the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The answer is that the victory rested on four factors, and each offers a lesson for the present. The piece is a study-and-interpretation commentary on Xi's speech, with one section per factor: spiritual, political, popular and external. Each section opens with a quotation from Xi, then names a reason why China lost earlier wars against foreign invaders, explains how the anti-Japanese war reversed that cause, and ends with a "historical enlightenment" for realising the Chinese Dream. Qu says that studying the speech should strengthen the Four Consciousnesses, the Four-sphere Confidence and the Two Upholds. Qu argues that the national spirit centred on patriotism was the decisive factor. In Qu's account, earlier defeats came from lack of a unifying ideological force, a corrupt and incompetent ruling group, internal disunity and little international support. The Communist Party's "mainstay" role was the key: it was the first to mobilise against the invasion, and it promoted the anti-Japanese national united front. It also set out a comprehensive resistance line and the strategy of protracted war. Qu cites figures that Party-led forces fought 60 per cent of the Japanese troops and 95 per cent of the puppet troops. The whole nation's resistance, understood as people's war, is presented as the "magic weapon", with 35 million Chinese casualties. Aid from the Soviet Union, the Flying Tigers, Norman Bethune, Dwarkanath Kotnis and John Rabe is described as a necessary external condition, with internal causes primary. Qu draws four lessons for the present. These are to promote the national spirit of patriotism and the spirit of reform and innovation, and to uphold the Party's overall leadership through the Party's self-reform. They also include keeping the people at the centre and strengthening unity at home and among overseas Chinese, and to follow peaceful development and opening up. The last lesson links this to a community with a shared future for mankind and the Belt and Road Initiative. Read the original if you want an example of how Party-state commentary in 2020 presented the anti-Japanese war's victory and tied its causes to current political tasks.

The Communist Party of China is forever heart to heart with the people 中国共产党永远与人民心连心 Zang Anmin This commentary, first published in the People's Daily on 4 September 2020, takes up Xi Jinping's call to uphold a people-centred philosophy of development. Zang argues that this idea is an important part of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. In Zang's account, it shows that the Party was born for the people and has prospered because of them, and that the Party must remain close to them. The article draws on Xi's recent inspection tour of Anhui and on the experience of the COVID-19 epidemic and flood-control work. The text has three parts. The first treats the people-centred idea as a development of the Marxist view of the people as the subject of history, and as the expression of the Party's fundamental purpose of serving the people wholeheartedly. The second looks at how a tight Party organisational system puts the idea into practice, through the leader, the Party's overall leadership and the strength of Party organisations. The third sets out what each Party member and cadre should do. In the first part, Zang argues from historical materialism that the masses are the decisive force in history. Citing Marx, Engels, Mao Zedong and Xi, the author holds that the Party's goal is to let all Chinese people live better lives. As evidence, Zang lists achievements since the 18th Party Congress (2012): poverty alleviation, environmental protection, the largest basic medical insurance network in the world, and the anti-corruption campaign against "tigers" and "flies". Zang also cites the epidemic response, including 39 million Party members and cadres on the front line and nearly 400 who died. In the second part, Zang invokes Engels's "On Authority" to argue that a leadership core is essential. Zang calls for the Four Consciousnesses, the Four-sphere Confidence and the Two Upholds, and for stronger Party institutions and grassroots organisations. Zang concludes that every Party member and cadre must be a firm practitioner of the people-centred idea. The author proposes three requirements: study Xi Jinping Thought so that putting the people first becomes a settled conviction; solve practical problems in employment, education, social security, healthcare, housing, elderly care, food safety and public order; and combat formalism and bureaucratism through political awareness, better work procedures and cadre selection. Read the original if you want a clear example of how the Party press in 2020 linked the people-centred idea to Party organisation and cadre conduct.

Deeply understanding the lofty pursuit and sense of mission of Communists 深入理解共产党人的崇高追求和使命担当 Zhen Zhanmin This commentary, first published in the People's Daily on 25 August 2020, takes up the formula that Chinese Communists work "for the happiness of the people, the rejuvenation of the nation and the great harmony of the world", quoting Xi Jinping. Zhen Zhanmin argues that this formula sums up the Communists' lofty pursuit, directs the Party's development, shows the justice of its cause and expresses its sense of mission. In Zhen's account, the formula has grown clearer under the test of nearly a hundred years of history. The piece has three parts. The first reads the Party's history of struggle through the formula. The second sets out why the formula is the source of the Party's drive. The third looks ahead to how the Party should contribute more to human progress in the new era. In the historical part, Zhen says that, although tasks differed from period to period, the aim stayed constant. The author lists the new-democratic revolution, the socialist revolution, reform and opening up, and the new era since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Zhen also holds that linking China's progress to human progress is a distinctive feature of the Party's course, from the early claim that the Chinese revolution was part of a world revolution to the Belt and Road Initiative and a community with a shared future for mankind. On motivation, Zhen argues that the formula gives correct direction, bestows justice on the Party's struggle and supplies great strength. In this reading it sustains the Party's Four-sphere Confidence and wins support from the Chinese people and progressive forces worldwide. Zhen calls for three things in the new era. The Party should keep its strategic resolve by grasping the broad trends of world development, despite hegemonism, protectionism and unilateralism. It should concentrate on managing its own affairs well, applying the new development philosophy and modernizing national governance. It should also keep "two overall situations" in view: national rejuvenation and the world's major changes of a kind not seen in a century. Zhen mentions the Covid-19 epidemic and states that the Party will not waver, because this course represents the "right path in the human world". Read the original if you want a compact example of how official Party discourse in 2020 tied the Party's domestic mission to its international claims.

The irresistible trend of human historical development 人类历史发展大势不可阻挡 Zhao Zhouxian Li Zhijun Writing in People's Daily in August 2020, Zhao Zhouxian and Li Zhijun ask how the world should choose between deeper economic globalization and de-globalization, openness and closure, cooperation and confrontation, mutual benefit and zero-sum games. Their answer is that economic globalization is an irreversible historical trend, that win-win cooperation is the necessary choice for humankind, and that building a community with a shared future for mankind accords with the laws of historical development. The commentary treats the Covid-19 pandemic as accelerating the "great changes unseen in a century" and as sharpening these choices. The piece has three sections, one for each claim. The first grounds globalization in the international division of labour and in Marx and Engels's thesis in The German Ideology of the shift from history to world history, and it recounts China's rise through opening up. The second takes up the pandemic, "decoupling" and the 1930s Smoot–Hawley tariff. The third sets out China's initiatives, its pandemic assistance and its domestic economic prospects. The authors argue that the problems troubling some Western countries, such as debt crises, widening wealth gaps and social tensions, are not caused by globalization, so blaming it is both factually wrong and unhelpful. They hold that calls for "economic decoupling" and for relocating industrial chains go against economic law. In their account, global supply and value chains rest on long-accumulated human capital and industrial coordination, so breaking them brings high relocation, training and rebuilding costs and harms producers and consumers alike. They cite the Smoot–Hawley tariff as a historical warning that trade wars deepen depression and do not spare the country that starts them. The authors present China as a beneficiary of and contributor to globalization. They cite its contribution of around 30% to world growth, a World Bank estimate of benefits from the Belt and Road Initiative, and its pandemic aid and information-sharing. They call for using the huge domestic market to build a new development pattern of "dual circulation", with the domestic cycle as the mainstay, so as to help world recovery and an open world economy. The pandemic response is said to show the advantages of the socialist system with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Chinese commentary in 2020 framed globalization, decoupling and the community with a shared future for mankind.

Using high-efficiency governance to advance high-quality development 以高效能治理助推高质量发展 Gu Baoguo Writing in Economic Daily in June 2020, Gu Baoguo takes up Xi Jinping's remarks to the Inner Mongolia delegation at that year's National People's Congress session. In them Xi called for major plans, reforms and policies that "pull" high-quality development and high-efficiency governance forward. Gu's thesis is that the two are closely linked and that high-efficiency governance should be used to drive high-quality development. The piece is a short commentary, not a research article. The article has two parts. The first sets out why high-quality development needs governance as its basis. It draws on the Fourth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2019) and on the gaps Gu sees in government capacity. The second part, written against the shock of the COVID-19 epidemic, describes how governance can be built into the whole process of development. It does so along four dimensions: governing goals, governing actors, governing methods and governing content. Gu argues that the shift from high-speed growth to high-quality development requires turning institutional strengths into governance effectiveness. He lists problems he sees in government: blurred boundaries between government and market, excessive administrative intervention, weak regulation, and insufficient policy transparency and coordination. He calls for less direct government interference in resource allocation, pricing and market entry and exit, and for stronger public services and market supervision. On the four dimensions, he points to a timetable for modernizing the governance system by 2035 and by the centenary of the People's Republic. He describes interaction between central top-level design and local experimentation, and coordinated governance under Party leadership with government, enterprises, social organisations and individuals acting together. He also stresses systems thinking in which economic reform leads and other reforms follow. Gu concludes that the epidemic has exposed weak points, such as public health emergency management, and that pressure should be turned into motivation. He says taking the initiative in deepening reform will make China's governance system more complete and its governance capacity stronger. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-state commentary in 2020 linked the governance modernization agenda to the economic goal of high-quality development.

The Yan'an Spirit: a nutrient for Party members and cadres to nourish the original aspiration and temper the soul 延安精神：党员干部滋养初心、淬炼灵魂的营养剂 Tan Huwa Taking its cue from Xi Jinping's remarks during an inspection tour of Shaanxi, this commentary (first published in Guangming Daily, 13 May 2020) asks how the Yan'an Spirit can serve Party members and cadres today. Tan argues that this revolutionary spirit, formed in the Yan'an period, has value that transcends its time. In the new era of socialism with Chinese characteristics it can, in the author's phrase, work as a "nutrient" that nourishes the original aspiration and tempers the soul of Party members. The piece is divided into four numbered sections. The first presents the Yan'an period as a systematic refresher of the Party's original aspiration and mission, built on seeking truth from facts, practical work and strict discipline. The second sets out the lasting value of the Yan'an Spirit: its view of the masses, its commitment to putting the people first, and its Marxist stance and method. The third traces how Xi Jinping has drawn on it since the 18th Party Congress (2012) for innovation, self-reliance and a sense of responsibility. The fourth proposes using it as a mirror for self-examination. Tan's central move is to treat the Yan'an Spirit as a set of concrete practices that Party members can compare themselves against. Drawing on statements by Mao Zedong and Chen Yun, the author presents the Party-people relationship as one of roots and soil, the mass line as "from the masses, to the masses", and "whole-hearted service to the people" as the core principle of the Party's purpose. The Great Production Movement and the "three-thirds" system of government are cited as examples. The author then names three tests for today's cadres: whether their political direction is firm and correct, whether their service to the people is wholehearted, and whether they have eliminated formalism and bureaucracy. The Yan'an rectification campaign is offered as the historical model for the last test. Tan concludes that keeping the original aspiration and mission is a lifelong task, not a passing campaign. The Yan'an Spirit should be used again and again as a mirror to correct one's appearance and remove selfish thoughts. The author links the fight against formalism and bureaucracy to the eight-point regulations and the campaign against the "four undesirable work styles" since 2012. Tan holds that this struggle must be protracted and combine concentrated campaigns with sustained effort. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Party-affiliated writers in 2020 drew on Yan'an history to frame cadre education and Party discipline.

Study and solve problems by proceeding from reality: the meaning and present-day lessons of "Oppose Book Worship" 坚持一切从实际出发来研究和解决问题——《反对本本主义》的深刻内涵与现实启示 Yang Mingwei Marking the 90th anniversary of Mao Zedong's "Oppose Book Worship" (1930), this commentary, first published in Guangming Daily in May 2020, argues that the essay remains a foundational text for the Party's ideological line of seeking truth from facts. Yang Mingwei holds that rereading it helps Party members proceed from reality in their thinking, work methods and leadership methods. The piece first recounts the essay's history: written in May 1930 as "Investigation Work" against dogmatism in the Red Army, lost, recovered in 1961, and added to the 1991 second edition of the Selected Works of Mao Zedong. It then summarises the essay's main formulations, such as "no investigation, no right to speak". Yang goes on to describe present-day forms of dogmatism and ends with four lessons for current work, all supported by quotations from Xi Jinping. Yang argues that the essay treats investigation as both a worldview and a method, and contains the early forms of seeking truth from facts, the mass line and independence. Yang identifies several persistent tendencies that depart from the Party's ideological line: separating theory from China's conditions, rote-learning classic texts, passive formalism that follows documents literally, and talking about Marxism without acting on it. Yang also criticises copying Western "dogmas" and cases. The four lessons are to be practical doers, to avoid copying Western theory and capitalist experience blindly, to combine upholding Marxism with developing it through new theoretical creation, and to keep strategic resolve on the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Yang concludes that rereading the essay helps oppose all forms of subjectivism. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the 1930 text is used in official commentary on the Party's ideological line today.

The global fight against COVID-19 shows the world significance of the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind 全球抗疫彰显人类命运共同体理念的世界意义 Pang Lisheng Writing in Guangming Daily in May 2020, Pang Lisheng takes up the COVID-19 pandemic as a test case for the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind. The article argues that the global response shows how closely human destinies are bound together, and that this gives the idea fresh practical and historical significance. The short commentary has three parts. The first treats the pandemic as a sign of mutual dependence in the present era. The second considers how the global anti-epidemic effort brings out the idea's meaning, including China's role. The third presents the idea as a guide to the progress of human civilisation. Pang draws on Marx's theory of world history. In this reading, the present is a world-historical age in which isolated, self-sufficient conditions have given way to deep mutual dependence. The same age brings global problems: humanity's unrestrained exploitation of nature, and global risks arising from the worldwide expansion of capital. Pang argues that the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind answers these conditions and is rooted in them. The article also describes China as a responsible major country that has shown capability and commitment in its own epidemic control and in international cooperation. Pang says the idea draws on traditional Chinese civilisation and on Marxism, and that it is moving from theory to practice through the Belt and Road Initiative, regional bilateral communities and new multilateral platforms. Citing Engels, Pang calls on humanity to reflect on the disaster and strengthen the idea, working toward a world of lasting peace, universal security, common prosperity, openness and cleanliness. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese commentary in 2020 linked the pandemic to the community-of-shared-future concept.

Populism in Central and Eastern Europe: current state, basic ideas and impact 中东欧民粹主义：现状、基本理念及影响 Zhang Li Writing in 2020, Zhang Li asks why populist parties in Central and Eastern Europe have grown so steadily in national and European Parliament elections, and what they stand for. The article argues that these parties rest on two basic ideas, nationalism and "illiberalism", and that their continued strength reflects an impasse in further European Union integration and a deepening East–West split. The article opens with the electoral record of populist parties across the region, citing Freedom House figures that put their average vote share at 9.2% in 2000 and 31.6% in 2017. It then follows developments in the four Visegrád states (Poland, Hungary, the Czech Republic, Slovakia), noting Orbán's Fidesz, Kaczyński's Law and Justice, Babiš's ANO 2011 and Fico's Smer, and briefly mentions Bulgaria, Serbia and the Baltic states. A section on basic ideas is followed by one on impact and prospects. Zhang contends that populism is at root a rejection of liberal ideology and liberal elite politics. In the author's account, the neoliberal economic model adopted after 1989, then the 2008 financial crisis, austerity and the 2015 refugee crisis, fed popular discontent that leaders such as Orbán and Kaczyński turned into support for an "illiberal" political model, with Hungary and Poland as the clearest cases. Zhang adds that a narrow, historically rooted nationalism, expressed through "restorative nationalism" in Hungary and Poland, turned identity into the main party dispute and set nationalists against pro-European liberals. As for impact, Zhang argues that populism has become the glue binding sovereigntists and nationalists, so it may dominate these countries' politics for some time, and that it has damaged the liberal-democratic consensus the EU promoted after 1989. The region's governments favour intergovernmental cooperation over ceding sovereignty, reject refugee quotas and "multi-speed Europe", and resent EU criticism and sanctions. Zhang concludes that populism has become mainstream in the region and that more such parties may take power; if they join forces with Western European populists, European politics could change at a larger scale. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese-language overview of Central and Eastern European populism, with election data and a Chinese scholarly reading of its causes and its effect on EU integration.

Giving full play to the people's congress system as the fundamental political institution 充分发挥人民代表大会制度的根本政治制度作用 Cheng Tongshun This commentary, first published in Guangming Daily on 29 May 2020, argues that the people's congress system must be used to the full as China's fundamental political institution. Cheng Tongshun describes it as the institutional arrangement that unites Party leadership, the people being masters of the country, and law-based governance. In Cheng's view, this system lets the people hold the nation's future in their own hands. The piece is organised around three roles of the system. It is presented as an essential support for upholding the Party's overall leadership, as the fundamental route to the people being masters of the country, and as the institutional basis and practical vehicle for comprehensively advancing law-based governance. Cheng places this in the context of the new era and the goals of building a moderately prosperous society and national rejuvenation. On Party leadership, Cheng argues that the Party's leading position was chosen by history and the people and is written into the Constitution. The system is the channel through which Party positions become state will through legal procedures, and Party-recommended candidates become state officials. On popular sovereignty, Cheng stresses that people's congresses are not parallel to other state organs: administrative, supervisory, judicial and procuratorial organs are created by, answerable to and supervised by them, while the congresses themselves answer to the people. On law-based governance, Cheng calls for stronger legislation, constitutional supervision, constitutionality review and oversight of law enforcement through the congresses. Cheng concludes that Party leadership, the people being masters of the country and law-based governance converge in the people's congress system, which Cheng identifies as the source of the scientific character and vitality of Chinese-style democracy. The article calls for political resolve and for firmly following the path of political development of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a concise, official-line account of how the people's congress system is justified in Party discourse around 2020.

People's democracy is a whole-process democracy 人民民主是一种全过程的民主 Xin Xiangyang Writing in Guangming Daily in 2020, Xin argues that people's democracy in China is a "whole-process democracy". In the article's account, major legislative decisions follow procedure, pass through democratic deliberation and are made scientifically and democratically. Xin presents this as the broadest, most genuine and most effective form of democracy for protecting the people's fundamental interests. The commentary is built around three claims. Whole-process democracy means that no link in the democratic chain may be missing. It means that each democratic institution has a complete process of its own. And it is genuine and continually improving. Xin draws on Xi Jinping's statements and on examples such as the people's congresses, consultative bodies, regional ethnic autonomy and grassroots self-governance. Xin holds that democracy covers elections, decision-making, management and oversight, and criticises systems that stress only voting. Xin cites measures such as reserved delegate quotas for ordinary people, hearings on draft laws, staff congresses in enterprises and open government affairs. Xin also traces the Party's democratic experiments from Soviet-area democracy and the wartime "three-thirds system" to the people's congress system and grassroots self-governance. According to Xin, a century of Party leadership has built a "democratic rationality" that avoids the "one-off democracy" and "street politics" the article attributes to some other countries. Xin concludes that whole-process democracy is substantive rather than formalistic, "not a decoration", and keeps developing through institutionalisation and standardisation. Read the original if you want a concise official-line statement of the "whole-process democracy" idea as it was formulated in 2020, with its main institutional examples.

The methodological horizon of a reality-oriented philosophy of culture 文化哲学面向现实的方法论视域 Hu Changshuan Hu Changshuan takes up two basic questions in the philosophy of culture: how the field should be understood and how it should be studied. Writing in Guangming Daily in 2020, Hu starts from the Marxist premise that worldview determines methodology, so that a given understanding of the philosophy of culture and the method used to study it are inseparable. The article argues that the field should be grasped through a dialectical combination of several conceptions, and that its method should be grounded in five principles, which together keep it oriented towards reality. The article opens by linking the philosophy of culture to cultural confidence, which it describes as the deepest form of confidence underlying confidence in the path, theory and system of socialism with Chinese characteristics. It then has two parts. The first sets out three common conceptions of the field, taking its cue from the founder Ernst Cassirer's warning against both naturalism and metaphysics. The second draws five methodological requirements from the Marxist classics and from Hegel, Jaspers, Husserl-style phenomenology and Benedetto Croce. In Hu's account, the three conceptions are a naturalistic one, which treats culture as an external object of empirical science and in essence belongs to cultural studies; a metaphysical one, which takes culture as the essence of the world and of humanity and in essence belongs to philosophy; and an anthropological one, which sees the human being as a symbolic animal and the philosophy of culture as a philosophy of the human. Hu urges treating these as complementary dimensions rather than rivals. The five methods are: philosophy as the history of philosophy; metaphysical thinking that goes beyond empirical cultural facts; critical logic that finds the new world in criticism of the old, including reflection on scientism; a return to things themselves, which starts from everyday cultural phenomena and facts; and a realist stance, following Marx's remark that problems are the slogans of the age. Hu concludes that the philosophy of culture is a philosophy with real-world concerns. It has to move beyond both positive science and metaphysics, supplying a cultural interpretation of the theory of the human being and so advancing human liberation and the true appropriation of human essence. The stress on starting from present-day life is meant to give the field practical relevance and to support cultural confidence. Read the original if you want a short, Marxist-inflected methodological outline of Chinese philosophy of culture, with its reading of Cassirer and its list of five research principles.

Principles for building a philosophical academic system with Chinese characteristics 构建中国特色哲学学术体系的原则 Wang Xinyan Writing in Guangming Daily in May 2020, Wang Xinyan asks what principle should govern the construction of a philosophical academic system with Chinese characteristics, Chinese style and Chinese manner. Taking up Xi Jinping's statement that Marxist guidance is what distinguishes contemporary Chinese philosophy and social science from others, Wang argues that the work must adhere to the adaptation of Marxist philosophy to the Chinese context. The short piece has three parts. The first derives the principle from two requirements: Marxist guidance and a footing in Chinese reality. The second reviews the twentieth-century search for a modern Chinese philosophy after the May Fourth period. The third sets out three reasons why the adaptation of Marxist philosophy is the basic principle for the new era. Wang holds that a philosophical system is an ideological system carrying values, so it needs a theoretical standpoint, and Marxist philosophy supplies one. Chinese reality, understood as history (especially fine traditional culture), present conditions and the world's great changes, is both the object and the resource. In Wang's account, cultural conservatism (Xiong Shili, Feng Youlan, He Lin, Jin Yuelin) and liberalism (Hu Shi's pragmatism) failed to handle the relation among Marxist, Chinese and Western philosophy. Only Marxists succeeded, producing what Li Da called a system of 'one body, two wings'. Adaptation is then said to secure continuity and national character, originality and timeliness, and systematic, professional coherence across all fields of philosophy. Wang concludes that adaptation does not mean Chinese philosophy should study only that topic. Every field should follow its requirements, each in its own way. Read the original if you want a brief, official-line statement of how a Party-aligned philosopher frames the history and guiding principle of Chinese philosophy.

The course and theoretical exploration of Vietnam's economic renovation 越南经济革新的历程及理论探索 Pan Jin'e Pan Jin'e asks how Vietnam's economic renovation (doi moi), launched in 1986, produced both practical results and a distinctive theory. Writing in 2020, Pan argues that the theoretical product is the "socialist-oriented market economy", and that practice succeeded because ideas were first liberated and theory then guided reform. The article has two main parts. The first traces the practice of renovation from the Sixth Party Congress (1986), moving from agricultural contracting to state-enterprise equitisation and then to finance and services. It divides this into three phases: building internal capacity (1986–2006), international integration (2006–2019), and a technology-driven phase expected to start with the 13th Congress in 2021. The second part follows how the Vietnamese Communist Party's congress documents changed its concepts, from the Sixth to the Twelfth Congress. A closing section lists current problems and compares Vietnam with China. Pan's central reasoning is that the Party moved step by step from rejecting the market to treating it as a tool of socialism. After the early-1980s crisis under a Soviet-style planned economy, Vietnam defined itself as in the initial stage of a transition period to socialism. It then accepted a commodity economy (1986), multiple sectors (1989), and the market as a human civilisational achievement not identical with capitalism (the Ninth Congress, 2001, and a 2008 resolution). Pan notes that the Tenth and Eleventh Congresses dropped public ownership of the main means of production as a basic feature of socialism, which Pan says still divides Vietnamese theorists. Pan reads this as a shift from "public ownership" to "socialisation", alongside a falling state-enterprise share of GDP (about 20 percent, with a target of about 10) and a more plural distribution system. Pan reports major gains: per-capita GDP rose from under US$100 in 1986 to US$2,800 in 2019, and poverty fell to 1.45 percent. Pan also identifies risks, including uneven development, weak infrastructure, pollution, slow digitalisation (76 percent of firms have not started), and heavy dependence on foreign capital and trade, with trade agreements such as the CPTPP possibly weakening state control. On China, Pan observes that Vietnam locates itself in a transition period while China speaks of the primary stage of socialism, so goals and policies differ, and the two countries can learn from each other. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's concise account of how Vietnamese Party congresses redefined ownership, the market and socialism.

New opportunities for the international communist movement amid changes unseen in a century Report on the development of the international communist movement, 2019–2020 百年未有之大变局背景下国际共产主义运动的新机遇 Research group on the 2019–2020 report on the development of the international communist movement This annual report, produced by a CASS research group, surveys the international communist movement in 2019 and early 2020 against the background of what it calls changes unseen in a century. It argues that the period brought new features: major anniversaries prompted renewed reflection on international unity, socialist states pursued reform and planning, non-ruling parties had mixed results, and the COVID-19 pandemic strengthened the case for socialism and for a community with a shared future for mankind. The report has four parts. It first covers commemorations of the Comintern's centenary and the debate over its lessons. It then reviews China's anniversaries (the May Fourth Movement and the founding of the People's Republic) and developments in Vietnam, Cuba, Laos and North Korea. Next it assesses communist parties outside socialist states, in South Asia, the former Soviet and Eastern European region, Western Europe, Japan, the Americas and Oceania. It ends with the 2020 anniversaries of Engels and Lenin and the pandemic. On the Comintern, the report describes broad agreement that it helped found parties and supported anti-colonial and anti-fascist struggles, alongside criticism of over-centralisation, policy towards social democrats and "leftist" errors. Parties disagree on how to unite: the Communist Party of Greece stresses ideological and strategic unity, while the Turkish and US parties favour exchange of experience and respect for autonomy. The authors read these disagreements, over how to treat and develop Marxism and how to view socialist reform, as the main obstacle to unity. They treat Belgium's Workers' Party of Belgium as a notable success, crediting its explicit aim of a classless society, while seeing most Western parties as stagnant and the Japanese Communist Party as drifting away from its former stance on China, Vietnam and Cuba. On the pandemic, the report holds that China's containment and the low reported case numbers in Vietnam, Laos and North Korea (as of 30 April) show the superiority of the socialist system. It contends that Western governments' responses exposed capitalism's flaws and double standards. It also expects capitalist forces to intensify pressure on communist parties and sees long coexistence of the two systems as unavoidable, so it urges promotion of a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially aligned Chinese survey of party-by-party developments, election figures and Comintern debates in 2019–2020.

Changing trends and impacts of Latin American social democracy since the 21st century 21世纪以来拉美社会民主主义的变化趋势与影响 Yuan Dongzhen Yuan Dongzhen asks how Latin American social democratic parties have changed since 2000 and what those changes mean for the region. The article, published in Contemporary World in 2020, argues that many of these parties have revised their guiding ideology, ideological identity, theory and policy platforms. In Yuan's account, three tendencies have strengthened: "de-Marxification", "popularisation" and a drift towards democratic socialism. The article first describes how social democracy grew into a mainstream political force in the region after the Second World War. It lists the parties involved, including Chile's Socialist Party, Argentina's Radical Civic Union and Mexico's Party of the Democratic Revolution. It then sets out eight traditional principles, among them pluralist ideology, a "third way", moderate reform, multi-class alliances and legal electoral struggle. Next it examines four areas of change, using mainly Chile, Venezuela and Nicaragua as cases. It then gives four causes and three consequences. Yuan contends that parties such as Chile's Socialist Party, Nicaragua's Sandinista Front and Venezuela's Movement towards Socialism dropped Marxism-Leninism as their sole guide. They also redefined themselves from working-class parties to broad parties of "all working people", and shifted from overthrowing capitalism to defending the existing democratic order. On policy, they moved to moderate and patch neoliberalism, coordinating economic and social policy. Yuan attributes this to adaptation to European social democracy, an escape from the dead ends of traditional policy, the search for wider electoral support, and pressure from the new left governments that rose after 1999. Yuan concludes that these changes will deepen ideological confusion among left parties, whose communist, left-nationalist and social democratic strands are drifting further apart. The author also expects them to push regional politics towards moderation and reform, since both left and right governments have failed to solve development problems, and to make party competition among centre-left forces more complex. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly account of how Latin American social democratic parties have changed ideologically, with party-by-party examples.

Understanding the way of major-country diplomacy with Chinese characteristics in the new era through three "unwaverings" 从三个“坚定不移”悟新时代中国特色大国外交之道 Ji Si This short commentary, published in Contemporary World in 2020, takes up the three "unwaverings" in China's foreign policy statements: Xi Jinping's 2020 New Year message and the Fourth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2019) both pledged to unwaveringly follow the path of peaceful development, to safeguard world peace and promote common development, and to safeguard national sovereignty, security and development interests. Ji argues that together they reveal the way of major-country diplomacy with Chinese characteristics in the new era. The piece sets the three commitments against what it calls changes unseen in a century and the entry of socialism with Chinese characteristics into a new era. It treats each commitment in turn, then shows how they relate to one another. On peaceful development, Ji says it is a strategic choice rooted in Chinese cultural tradition, in the historical experience of national humiliation and recovery, and in the fact that a stable external environment enabled China's rapid growth. On world peace and common development, the author links the commitment to the Party's original mission and to building a community with a shared future for mankind and the Belt and Road Initiative, citing the China–US phase-one trade agreement as an example. On sovereignty, security and development interests, Ji holds that these are the guarantee and precondition of the other two. The author warns that China will not yield on core interests and names Taiwan, Hong Kong, Tibet and Xinjiang separatism as issues on which outside forces are, in this account, working against national rejuvenation. Ji concludes that the three commitments run through the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind and show China's resolve to build a new type of international relations. The author calls them a golden key to understanding Xi Jinping's diplomatic thought. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary in early 2020 framed the logic linking peaceful development with firm defence of core interests.

European political fragmentation and the direction of China–EU relations 欧洲政治碎片化与中欧关系走向 Zheng Chunrong Writing in 2020, after Brexit and as COVID-19 spread across Europe, Zheng Chunrong argues that political fragmentation has become a "new normal" in Europe. The article asks how this fragmentation, driven by declining mainstream parties and rising populist ones, will affect the EU and its relations with China. Zheng's answer is that China–EU relations will show a simultaneous increase in the need for cooperation and in competition. The article begins with the evidence of fragmentation: the 2019 European Parliament elections, and national cases from 2017 onwards in the Netherlands, France, Germany and the Czech Republic. It then sets out three consequences for the EU and its member states. The final sections turn to China–EU relations and offer four proposals for guiding them. Zheng contends that fragmentation pushes European politics to the right. In the author's account, mainstream parties adopt populist positions, especially on migration, and populism becomes mainstream and normalised, as in Austria and Hungary. Coalition-building also becomes harder at every level, with Germany, the Netherlands, Sweden and the German state of Thuringia given as examples. The EU's capacity for collective action weakens, and the EU and its members turn to more protectionist policies in trade, investment and industry. Zheng argues that Europe's concern over its declining strength strengthens its push for strategic autonomy. The EU therefore needs China more, given shared support for multilateralism and for climate and Iran-deal commitments. At the same time, it fears China more, and the 2019 EU strategic outlook calls China a "systemic rival". Zheng proposes four courses of action. They are to deepen cooperation, with a new strategic plan centred on digitalisation and greening; to uphold multilateralism and free trade, including progress on the investment agreement; to raise cooperation to a higher level in high technology and reject "decoupling"; and to build a new type of international relations on the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence. Europe, the author says, should not blame others for its own problems or follow the United States on "systemic competition". Read the original if you want a Chinese academic account of how European populism and party fragmentation are read in Beijing-oriented policy discussion of China–EU ties around 2020.

Carrying forward the great revolutionary spirit Studying and implementing General Secretary Xi Jinping's important speech during his inspection of the Xiangshan revolutionary memorial site in Beijing 弘扬伟大革命精神 Du Feijin Du Feijin's article, published in Qiushi in 2020, is a study-and-implementation piece on Xi Jinping's speech of 12 September 2019 at the Xiangshan revolutionary memorial site in Beijing. It asks what the Communist Party's 181 days at Xiangshan in 1949 should teach today. Du argues that three elements of the 'great revolutionary spirit' formed there must be inherited and carried forward: seeing the revolution through to the end, a revolutionary commitment to serve the people, and a modest, prudent and hardworking style. The article opens by recalling what the Central Committee did at Xiangshan between March and September 1949: the order to advance across the country, Mao Zedong's 'On the People's Democratic Dictatorship', and preparations for the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference and its Common Programme. Three sections follow, each opening with a passage from Xi's speech and then drawing on historical episodes. A final section turns to the tasks of the 'new era'. On the first element, Du presents the Party's determination to see the revolution through as rooted in Marxism's idea of a radical break with old property relations and in the lessons of struggle. He contrasts Chen Duxiu's right-opportunism, which he says surrendered proletarian leadership, with the Party's firm struggle during the War of Resistance against Japan. On the second, Du describes the Common Programme as the result of broad consultation with non-communist parties. He cites Mao's conversation with Liu Yazi, in which Mao credited popular support for the Yangtze crossing, and argues that the Party's interests coincide with the people's. On the third, he cites the 'going to the capital to sit the exam' remarks, the six rules adopted at the Second Plenum of the 7th Central Committee (1949), and anecdotes of Mao's frugality. He presents the Party's capacity for self-reform as its defining strength. Du concludes with proposals for the present. The Party should strengthen the four-sphere confidence and prepare for 'great struggle', stay close to the masses and tackle problems such as access to healthcare, schooling, jobs and housing, and keep an honest, pragmatic style. This includes the Two Upholds, full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, the eight-point rules, and sustained anti-corruption work. He ties these tasks to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want an example of how Party media in 2020 drew on the Xiangshan period to frame ideals of political discipline, mass line and self-reform.

The Party's enduring cause and the establishment of a system for staying true to the original aspiration and keeping the mission in mind 从党的千秋伟业看不忘初心、牢记使命制度的建立 Sun Yeli Writing in Qiushi in 2020, Sun Yeli takes up a question posed by the Fourth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2019): how can the Communist Party of China keep its "original aspiration and founding mission" (chuxin and shiming) over the long term? Sun's answer is that this can be secured only by institutions. The Plenum's Decision put the creation of such a system first among its measures for upholding and improving socialism with Chinese characteristics, and Sun presents it as a precondition for the Party's lasting cause. The article opens with a historical argument and then sets out four requirements for building the system. It begins with Huang Yanpei's 1945 remarks to Mao Zedong on the "historical cycle" of dynastic rise and fall. It then follows the Party's record of rectification campaigns and discipline-building, from the Yan'an period to the education campaigns after the 18th Party Congress (2012). The four requirements concern theoretical armament, the Party's self-reform, political life within the Party, and institutional innovation. Sun's central claim is that rules are more dependable than exhortation. Dynasties declined, in this account, because ruling groups lost their founding spirit once in power, and the Party escapes this pattern through discipline, Party regulations and long-term mechanisms. Citing Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping, Sun argues that firm conviction comes from firm theory, so that theoretical innovation must be matched by theoretical study. The Party must therefore arm itself with Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Sun also argues that the Party should rely on criticism and self-criticism and on the 2016 guidelines for intra-Party political life to purge corruption and the "thief in the heart". Finally, Sun argues that institutions must be practical, systematic and enforceable, neither too sweeping nor too fragmentary. Sun concludes that if the Party sums up historical experience, meets present needs and builds a lasting mechanism, it can open new prospects in the great social revolution and strengthen itself through the Party's self-reform. In Sun's account, this will lead the people to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The article is an official-line exposition of the Plenum's Decision. Read the original if you want to see how a Party-theory writer links the 2019 Decision on institutions to Chinese dynastic history, Mao-era rectification and the discipline of the Party.

Firm confidence in our values: recognising the essence of the "universal values" thesis 坚定价值观自信——认清“普世价值论”的实质 Ren Xiaoshan Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts (Hongqi Wengao) in 2020, Ren Xiaoshan takes up the thesis of "universal values", which the author defines as the claim that bourgeois ideas of freedom, democracy and human rights apply to every society and era, beyond class, nation and history. Ren argues that the thesis is in essence bourgeois ideology, a reflection of capitalist private-property relations. The author holds that, although its spread in China has weakened, it still runs underneath and is part of a Western strategy of Westernising and dividing China, so that the struggle against it concerns paths and systems as well as ideas. The short commentary has three parts. The first argues that "universal values" are not in fact universal. The second sets out how the thesis threatens China's chosen path and political system. The third presents measures of response: strengthening the Four-sphere Confidence, struggling openly against the thesis, and promoting the core socialist values. In the first part Ren concedes that bourgeois ideals of freedom, equality and fraternity once enlightened minds and advanced human society. The author argues, however, that once they are "politicised" and made into instruments of class rule and of intervention abroad, their hypocrisy shows. Ren cites Western double standards, withdrawals from treaties and the "colour revolutions" in West Asia and North Africa as examples. The author also rejects two conflations: that China's core socialist values simply accept "universal values", and that "universal values" equal humanity's common values. Democracy, for instance, means people's democracy under Communist Party leadership, not parliaments, separation of powers or party elections. In the second part Ren claims that Western promotion aims at ideological confusion, especially among young people, at splitting social consensus, and at undermining the Party's governing position by advocating privatisation, multiparty competition and pluralism in guiding ideology. In response Ren calls for confidence in the path, theory, system and culture, citing China's handling of the COVID-19 epidemic as evidence of institutional advantage. Ren also urges building a discourse system for the core socialist values, and clarifying their boundary with "universal values". Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Party commentary in 2020 framed the critique of "universal values" and linked it to ideological security.

The contemporary value of the spirit of striving for first-class performance in the Soviet Areas period 苏区时期争创一流精神的当代价值 Zhong Xiaoming Zhong Xiaoming asks what the revolutionary spirit of "striving for first-class performance" (zhengchuang yiliu), which emerged in the Soviet Areas of the 1930s, can offer today. Published in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2020, the short piece argues that this spirit reflects the Communists' high standards, their basic attitude to revolution and their lofty values, and that it remains relevant in the new era. The article has two parts. The first sets out the spirit's content in the Soviet Areas period, said to have been promoted by Mao Zedong, Zhou Enlai and other leaders. The second draws out its present-day value in four requirements. In the first part Zhong identifies three strands: forging ahead while serving the people wholeheartedly, illustrated by a 1933 Red China report on cadres helping distressed villagers; daring to take the lead and set examples, illustrated by a 1932 work competition in Xingguo county; and seeking truth from facts in order to create "first-class work". For the last, Zhong cites Mao's 1934 praise of Xingguo and northeastern Jiangxi comrades for linking mass livelihood to revolutionary war. Zhong contends that where this attitude was applied well, the revolution succeeded, and that where it was not, it suffered heavy losses. For today, Zhong calls for a down-to-earth work style, supported by Xi Jinping's remarks on practical action and on study, and for diligent learning aimed at solving real problems. Zhong also calls for selfless dedication, to counter people who are materially comfortable but spiritually empty, and for conscious practice of the core socialist values. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Party-history themes are used to promote cadre conduct and values education in 2020.

"Washington should abandon its pretence of sanctity and its double standards on human rights" World opinion criticises violent law enforcement in the United States “华盛顿应该抛弃在人权问题上假装圣洁的双重标准” Di Yingna Zhou Luming Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts (2020, no. 12), Di Yingna and Zhou Luming take up the death of George Floyd, an African American man killed by US police, and the protests that followed across the United States. The article contends that the case shocked the world and drew strong criticism from international bodies, governments, media and public figures. Its main claim is that this reaction exposes systemic racism in the US and a double standard in Washington's human rights diplomacy. The piece is a compilation of reported statements organised under four quoted headings: the case as revealing the nature of the US state, racism as the "virus" behind police violence, Washington's double standards, and the call to reflect on America's failures. It draws on the UN Secretary-General and the UN Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination, the African Union, the EU, and officials from Ghana, Russia, Cuba, Iran, South Africa and Jordan. It also quotes media in Japan, Germany, Britain, Australia and the US, as well as US figures such as Nancy Pelosi, Jimmy Carter, Barack Obama and George W. Bush. The authors argue first that the killing is not an isolated incident. They cite figures from the US National Academy of Sciences, the Trial Project and the NAACP on police killings, incarceration rates and racial disparities. On this basis they describe African Americans as facing institutional oppression in both law enforcement and the justice system. Second, they present foreign critics, including the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, as saying that the US lectures other countries on human rights while excessive force was used against protesters and journalists at home. The article cites a Singapore social media post contrasting US reactions to unrest in Hong Kong and in Minnesota, a Russian foreign ministry spokesperson, and US diplomats who said they looked like "hypocrites". The article ends by combining foreign analysis of a deeper US crisis, citing the pandemic, unemployment, economic decline and polls showing most Americans think the country is out of control, with statements from US ex-presidents acknowledging persistent racial injustice. The authors do not add a separate policy proposal. Their implied conclusion is that the US lacks the standing to judge other countries on human rights. Read the original if you want a dense catalogue of the international and domestic quotations that Chinese official media used to frame the Floyd protests in mid-2020.

"An epic struggle that moved heaven and earth": studying Xi Jinping's important statements on the history of New China “一部感天动地的奋斗史诗” ——学习习近平总书记关于新中国史的重要论述 Li Zhenghua Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2020, Li Zhenghua offers a study guide to Xi Jinping's statements on the history of New China, the period since the founding of the People's Republic in 1949. The article takes up why this history should be studied and how. Li's thesis is that Xi's statements give a full account of the importance, achievements and logic of that history, and set out the Marxist method for studying it. Li presents the study as bearing on strengthening the Four Consciousnesses, the Four-sphere Confidence and the Two Upholds. The article has three parts. The first gives three reasons why studying the history of New China is \"very necessary\": to understand the Party and the nation correctly and locate the country's historical position, to grasp historical laws, and to take responsibility for the future. The second part sets out Xi's assessment of the epic of New China's development. The third part sets out the methodological requirements for studying it. For Li, Xi stresses the founding of New China as a great leap and a new epoch. Xi also divides the history into stages and describes the move from \"standing up\" to \"becoming prosperous\" to \"becoming strong\". He treats reform and opening up as a \"key move\" and \"the only way forward\", and presents socialism with Chinese characteristics and Party leadership as historically necessary. On method, Li stresses that research must be guided by Marxism, with historical materialism and seeking truth from facts.
