It must distinguish the \"mainstream\" from the \"tributary\" of history, and see history as continuous. The periods before and after reform and opening up must not be set against each other. Li adds that figures must be judged within their own historical conditions. Li presents the treatment of the two periods as above all a political question, and reads Xi's position as a rebuttal of historical nihilism, which Li says denies Marxism's guiding role and Party leadership. Li concludes that Xi's statements combine an accurate grasp of the history with an analysis of how New China's history connects to the history of reform and opening up, of the Party and of socialism. In Li's view they give the fundamental guidance for studying the subject. Read the original if you want a compact, officially aligned digest of how Party commentary in 2020 framed the study of New China's history and its fight against historical nihilism.

Achieving the people's complete spiritual initiative 实现人民精神完全主动 Li Xiangjun Luo Zhongyou Taking up a line from Xi Jinping's report to the 19th Party Congress (2017) that, with the founding of the Communist Party in 1921, the Chinese people moved 'from passivity to initiative' in spirit, Li Xiangjun and Luo Zhongyou ask how this shift came about and what it demands today. They argue that the Party has led the Chinese people from spiritual passivity to initiative, and that achieving the people's 'complete' spiritual initiative is now a major mission of the Party in the new era. The article, published in 2020, has three parts. It first analyses why the people were spiritually passive in old China, then describes how the Party enabled the change, and finally sets out why complete spiritual initiative matters for the present. It draws on Marxist theory, on Lu Xun's images of a 'silent China', on Xi Jinping's statements, and on a Harvard Kennedy School survey cited for popular satisfaction with the central government. Li and Luo name three causes of passivity: feudal ethics and the patriarchal clan system, which weakened independent consciousness; semi-colonial, semi-feudal conditions, which destroyed national self-respect and cultural confidence; and the lack of an advanced organisation to mobilise the masses as the makers of history. In their account the Party reversed this through the guidance of Marxism, the ideal of communism and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, the development of socialist culture, and a governing philosophy that puts the people's all-round development and主体 status first. The authors also reject a US official's claim that Marxism-Leninism treats individuals as mere instruments of the state, calling it ignorant prejudice, and cite the Harvard survey's figure of over 93 per cent satisfaction as evidence of popular support. For the new era, the authors present complete spiritual initiative as an inexhaustible driving force for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, a component of the good life, and a requirement of China's active role in global governance. They tie it to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, the initiative of a community with a shared future for mankind and the Belt and Road Initiative. Read the original if you want to see how a 2020 Party-journal article frames popular morale, cultural confidence and national rejuvenation as a historical shift in the people's 'spirit'.

Racial discrimination highlights the crisis of American political values 种族歧视凸显美国政治价值观危机 Di Yingna Gao Tianding Writing after the death of George Floyd and the protests that followed in 2020, Di and Gao argue that the episode exposes the hypocrisy of the values the United States presents as its core: democracy, freedom, equality and human rights. In their account, the country styles itself a model and uses "human rights" to pressure other states, while racial discrimination, wealth polarisation and social division are plain at home. The article is a commentary in a Party-theory journal. The text is organised around four headings: visible democratic defects, a slide into an "illiberal era", inequality that permeates society, and long-accumulated systemic human rights problems. Almost all of the evidence consists of quotations from others: Barack Obama, Kareem Abdul-Jabbar, US academics and commentators, the American press, UN officials, the Russian foreign ministry, the African National Congress, the African Union's member states and writers from Africa, Turkey, Cuba and Iran. The authors also cite Joseph Stiglitz and US polling and press-freedom data. The authors' central move is to present the protests as a verdict on the American system rather than on a single police act. On democracy, they cite reports that the Economist Intelligence Unit downgraded the US to a "flawed democracy" and that a multinational poll found most respondents thought the US harmed global democracy. On freedom, they point to force used against peaceful demonstrators and more than 300 reported violations of press freedom. On inequality, they follow Stiglitz in tracing racial injustice to economic inequality, and cite figures on Black unemployment, income, home ownership and poverty, and a rate of police killing three times that of whites. The authors conclude that "American-style human rights" suffer a fundamental crisis marked by ideological double standards. They stress that the UN Human Rights Council held an urgent debate on racism in June 2020, that a resolution was passed condemning Floyd's death, and that US civil-liberties groups and African states sought UN scrutiny of the US. The text closes with a quotation that it is time for America to reflect on its failures. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese Party media in 2020 assembled foreign voices to criticise US claims on human rights and democracy.

The scientific form of Marx's philosophy 马克思哲学的科学形式 Wang Shizhong Wang Shizhong asks how Marx's philosophy, understood as a philosophy of practice, can be given a scientific form. Since the early 2000s, Wang notes, some scholars have reinterpreted Marxist philosophy from a practice-philosophy standpoint, aiming to go beyond traditional research and to bring Chinese, Western and Marxist resources into dialogue. Wang argues that practice must be expressed in a scientific theoretical form, and proposes an open, two-level structure for that purpose. This short newspaper piece has three parts. It first explains why practice philosophy needs scientific form, then examines the boundary between natural and social science, and finally turns to Hegel, Croce and Wang's own proposed structure. Along the way it draws on Carl Menger's Austrian school and on game-theoretic institutional economics. Wang's central move is a method of "reverse compulsion": tracing the internal limits of the natural sciences, and then of economics, to show where a further philosophical breakthrough is required. Natural science handles relations between humans and nature, whereas social science handles relations between people, who are purposive and free and so cannot be reduced to relations between things. Economics, in Wang's view, faces a paradox: without history it lacks legitimacy, and with history its scientific status is weakened. Hegel's dialectic offers a breakthrough, but Wang follows Croce in holding that it confuses opposites with distinct concepts. Croce's own scheme is, in Wang's judgement, a closed circuit. Wang proposes remodelling Croce's circuit into an open "double-layer, three-dimensional" structure: theoretical and practical activity form two layers, practical activity combines higher and lower levels, and space is left for human freedom. Wang offers it as an interpretive framework and a workable scientific scheme for Marx's philosophy. Read the original if you want a compact sketch of one Chinese attempt to link practice philosophy, the philosophy of science and Croce's dialectic.

Lenin's in-depth study of Marxist texts 列宁对马克思主义文献的深入研究 Zhao Yulan Zhao Yulan, in a short piece for Guangming Daily, asks how Lenin related to the textual legacy of Marx and Engels. The article argues that Lenin was not only the leader of the October Revolution and the theorist who developed Marxism into Leninism, but also a careful student of the classics. In Zhao's account, he was the driving force behind the first large-scale collection, editing and systematic publication of Marx and Engels's writings, which gave the international workers' movement a theoretical weapon. The article follows Lenin's engagement with the texts in three stages. It begins with his early study and first translation work in the 1890s and 1900s, moves to the overview of Marx's works that he gave in 1914, and ends with his support after 1917 for the institutional collection and publication of the legacy. Zhao relies on Lenin's own writings, prefaces and letters, including his notes to David Riazanov. Zhao's core argument is that Lenin's reading shows a command of the whole corpus long before 1917. In his 1894 polemic against the Narodniks, written at 24, Lenin cited Capital, the 1859 Preface and even the then little-known manuscript of The German Ideology. In 1907 he revised the Russian edition of Marx's letters to Kugelmann and wrote a preface to the Sorge correspondence. In his 1914 encyclopaedia entry on Marx, Lenin listed Marx's works and repeatedly noted that many newspaper articles and International Workingmen's Association documents had never been collected, reissued or translated. Zhao reads this as an early recognition of the gap in the sources. After the revolution, Zhao says, Lenin acted on this recognition. In 1920–21 he oversaw the creation of the Marx-Engels Institute under Riazanov, and sent him a note with seven questions that Zhao treats as a working programme. He also approved an extra 75,000 gold roubles for buying the Mautner and Grünberg libraries in Vienna, and kept following the collection work. Zhao concludes that study of the texts equipped Lenin to lead the revolution, and that Soviet power let him lay the intellectual foundation for world socialism through systematic editing. Read the original if you want a brief, source-based account of Lenin's role in founding the Marx-Engels textual project and the Marx-Engels Institute.

Grasping the broad trends of world and Chinese development: a guide to Marx and Engels on China 把握世界和中国的发展大势——《马克思恩格斯论中国》导读 Wang Yi This reading guide, published in Red Flag Manuscripts (Hongqi Wengao) in 2020, introduces the collection Marx and Engels on China (《马克思恩格斯论中国》). Wang Yi asks what Marx and Engels wrote about China and why it still matters. The guide argues that their judgements help readers understand Marxist standpoint and method, the main course and lessons of modern Chinese history, and why China should unwaveringly keep to the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The guide has three parts. The first sets out the historical conditions in which Marx and Engels came to study China. The second summarises five groups of their judgements on Chinese society and events. The third turns to the present and draws lessons for understanding contemporary China. Wang gives three reasons for the two thinkers' interest in China. China was the last piece of the capitalist world market, forced in by the Opium Wars. It also became part of their search for revolutionary prospects after the defeat of the European revolutions. And Marx wrote about it as a correspondent for the New-York Daily Tribune, with Engels helping to translate and contributing pieces of his own. Wang then reports their analyses. They described a social structure built on small-scale agriculture combined with household industry, which in Wang's account underpinned centralised despotism and 2,000 years of stability. They exposed the opium trade and the aggressions of Britain, France and Russia, and they backed the Chinese people's resistance, including the Taiping uprising. They predicted that the old order would collapse, that China would affect world civilisation, and that it would eventually take a socialist road, even naming a future 'Chinese Republic'. Wang draws three present-day lessons. First, China must be understood within world history. Wang cites the 19th Party Congress (2017) on what has and has not changed in China's position, and calls for balancing change and continuity amid what the guide calls great changes unseen in a century. Second, comprehensive deepening of reform should proceed with correct direction and keep economic development central. It should aim at modernising the system and capacity of national governance. Third, China should help build a community with a shared future for mankind, rejecting hegemonism and Cold War thinking while staying alert to Western interference. Read the original if you want a concise, officially oriented overview of Marx and Engels's writings on China and of how they are used in current Party discourse.

Engels's construction of the system of Marxist philosophy 恩格斯对马克思主义哲学体系的建构 Yang Hongyuan This short commentary, first published in Guangming Daily in June 2020, asks what Engels contributed to building Marxist philosophy into a system. Yang argues that Engels contributed in both form and content. In form, he helped break down the closed logic of older philosophical systems and made philosophy an open structure and dynamic thought. In content, he started from a renewed reading of philosophy's basic question and joined ontology, dialectics and the conception of history into one whole. Yang first notes that systematising an existing theory is as hard as creating one, and cites Engels's editing of volumes two and three of Capital and works such as Anti-Dühring, Ludwig Feuerbach and the End of Classical German Philosophy, Dialectics of Nature and The Origin of the Family, Private Property and the State. The piece then moves through four themes: the basic question of philosophy, the ontological foundation, dialectics, and the relations among historical factors. On ontology, Yang says Engels located the unity of the world in its materiality, abstracted the concept of matter from particular material things, and examined matter, motion, time and space. On dialectics, Yang presents it as the main thread running through Engels's work. Engels is credited with showing its role as worldview and method in nature, history and thought, and with distilling its laws. On history, Yang argues that Engels corrected the one-sided stress on economic determination, which Marx and Engels had sometimes made in polemic. Engels stressed the relative independence and interaction of political, legal and ideological factors, so that economically backward countries can still "play first fiddle" in philosophy. Yang concludes that these achievements make Engels's description of himself as "second fiddle" fully deserved. The text is a brief appreciation, not a detailed textual study.

Read the original if you want a compact Chinese overview of how Engels's role in systematising Marxist philosophy is presented in official-academic commentary.

Engels and Marx's "turn to political economy" 恩格斯与马克思的“政治经济学转向” Liu Xiuping Published in Guangming Daily in July 2020, this short piece asks how Marx came to turn to political economy. Liu argues that Engels played a key role in prompting and shaping that turn. The article first outlines Engels's early observations of capitalist society in Barmen, Bremen and Manchester, and the works he wrote between 1843 and 1845. It then looks at Marx's "tormenting doubts" arising from his work on the Rheinische Zeitung, and at how Engels's writings bore on his first economic studies. Liu contends that Marx's studies had shown him that civil society determines the political state, but he did not yet grasp civil society's economic relations. Engels's Outlines of a Critique of Political Economy, read while Marx was preparing the Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher, showed the importance of political economy and recast its basic categories. Liu then identifies three links with the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844: the aim of criticising classical economics, the empirical material on workers' conditions drawn from Engels's The Condition of the Working Class in England, and a historically grounded critique of private property. The two men's ten days of discussion in Paris in 1844 are said to have strengthened these links. Liu concludes that Engels's close attention to concrete social problems and empirical evidence helped Marx resolve his early doubts. It also pointed him towards a deeper inquiry into capital. Read the original if you want a brief account of Engels's influence on Marx's early economic thought.

New features of monopoly in modern capitalism 现代资本主义垄断的新特征 Tan Peiwen Chen Yao Writing in 2020 amid trade disputes, Tan Peiwen and Chen Yao argue that capitalist monopoly is not confined to the financial monopoly stressed in Lenin's theory of imperialism. They contend that earlier research neglected Marx's treatment of monopoly in production, consumption, distribution and exchange, and that today's trade frictions repeat the pattern Marx analysed in the Grundrisse in the 1850s. The short commentary, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today, works through four spheres in turn, drawing on passages from the Grundrisse. It then turns to practical conclusions for China's response. In the authors' reading, monopoly over the production of exchange value disrupts the industrial and value chains that produce use values, and in the world market appears as unilateralism, prohibitive tariffs and protectionism. Capital's monopoly of the labour market makes the exchange of money for labour-power formally equal while real inequality persists, so that equality and freedom become empty ideas. Consumption serves only capital's accumulation, not people's all-round development, and distribution by capital leaves workers impoverished. The authors read recent US tariff increases as an internationalisation of this power over distribution. They conclude that capitalism is not the same as the market economy and has an anti-market side. China should use the strengths of the socialist market economy, rebuild fair value chains, pursue common prosperity, and guard against systemic financial risk while opening up further. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese Marxist reading of the US–China trade conflict through Marx's Grundrisse.

The narrative features of Engels's theory of nature's revenge 恩格斯“自然报复论”的叙事特征 Li Heliang Zhang Xu Marking the 200th anniversary of Engels's birth, Li Heliang and Zhang Xu revisit his theory of nature's revenge, a short newspaper essay on how Engels built his dialectics of nature around the human–nature relation. The authors argue that the theory carries its background, rhetoric and purposes implicitly within the text, and that it prepares the idea of the "two reconciliations": between humanity and nature, and within humanity itself. The essay is organised around five features: the stages in which the theory took shape, its writing context, its intended targets, its rhetorical strategies, and its bearing on the present. It draws on Engels's early reports on pollution, Anti-Dühring, "On Authority", "The Part Played by Labour in the Transition from Ape to Man" and Dialectics of Nature. The authors contend that Engels aimed to settle accounts with several rival outlooks. These were naturalism and anthropocentrism, vulgar materialism and social Darwinism, and metaphysical views of nature together with idealist dialectics. Li and Zhang say Engels placed nature as the prior material basis of human activity, which people change and use by knowing its laws. His rhetoric relied on personification, analogy and model abstraction from cases such as deforestation and soil erosion. The authors conclude that, for Engels, nature's revenge is in essence people's revenge on themselves. They hold that it arises from the limits of human knowledge, from capitalist production for profit, and from consumer desires stimulated by capital. The authors conclude that, on Engels's account, only communism can resolve these contradictions at root. They link the theory to the Fourth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2019), calling for Xi Jinping Thought on Ecological Civilization, ecological red lines and a "Beautiful China". Read the original if you want a brief Chinese official-academic reading of Engels's ecological thought and its link to current ecological civilization policy.

A classic for understanding the origin and withering away of the state: a reader's guide to The Origin of the Family, Private Property and the State 理解国家起源与消亡的经典著作——《家庭、私有制和国家的起源》导读 Ming Yi This is a reader's guide, published in Red Flag Manuscripts (Hongqi Wengao) in 2020, to Engels's The Origin of the Family, Private Property and the State (1884). Ming presents the book as a work that applies historical materialism to the state. In this account, it explains how family, private property and class relate to the emergence of the state, and so enriches Marxist political theory. The guide is organised in four parts. It first sets out the book's background: Marx's plan to interpret Lewis Henry Morgan's Ancient Society, Engels's use of Marx's notes on it, and the need to answer bourgeois scholars and opportunists. It then summarises the contents (a preface, nine chapters and an 1892 appendix) and the book's main ideas. It closes with the book's theoretical and historical significance and its relevance for China in the new era. On the core argument, Ming reports Engels's theory of the two kinds of production, the production of the means of life and the production of human beings themselves. Engels uses these to trace the move from kinship relations to class relations. The state, in Ming's reading, is a historical category produced by the third great division of labour, which dissolved the gentile order. Ming lists three routes to the state (Athenian, Roman and Germanic) and three features of the state: territorial division of the population, a public power backed by force, and taxation. Its essence is class rule, even where it appears as the representative of the public interest. Its forms are slave-owning, feudal and bourgeois, and it will wither away once private property and classes are abolished on the basis of highly developed productive forces. Ming draws contemporary lessons. Capitalist democracy is described as an indirect and concealed form of bourgeois class rule. China's socialist state, resting on public ownership and the people's democratic dictatorship, is said to represent the fundamental interests of the great majority. Ming adds that abolishing private ownership is a long process that depends on conditions. As long as socialism and capitalism compete, the author argues, state functions must be strengthened and not weakened, and class struggle still exists in China to a certain extent. Ming also points to implications for family-building and for the modernization of the system and capacity of state governance. Read the original if you want to see how a Party journal in 2020 presents Engels's theory of the state and its application to current Chinese policy.

Engels's critique of capital and its characteristics 恩格斯的资本批判及其特征 Nie Jinfang Nie Jinfang's short piece, published in Guangming Daily in 2020, asks what Engels's own critique of capital consisted of and what marks it out. Nie argues that Marxism is bound up with the critique of capital and the search for human emancipation. In Nie's account, Engels and Marx were highly consistent in analysing capitalist society and the position of the working class, and they completed the theoretical construction of Marxism in complementary ways. The article is organised around three features of Engels's critique. The first is his lived experience of the "suffering and ills" of the age of capital in Barmen, Bremen, Manchester and London. The second is his grasp, through years in business, of the historical formation and present workings of the capitalist system. The third is his editing of Marx's manuscripts for the second and third volumes of Capital. On the first point, Nie draws on The Condition of the Working Class in England, which Engels wrote after 21 months of direct observation. It documents workers' physical, intellectual and moral degradation, and Nie notes the contradiction between Engels's position as a "cotton king" and his siding with labouring people. On the second, Nie traces how improved spinning machinery, from the spinning jenny to the steam engine, produced the factory system, which split society into capitalists and proletarians and fostered working-class consciousness. On the third, Nie holds that Engels was more than a technical editor of the fragmentary manuscripts of Volumes II and III. In Nie's reading he was an interpreter and in some sense a constructor of their ideas, which cover circulation, reproduction, profit, production prices, commercial and interest-bearing capital. Nie concludes that Engels moved from sensory experience of the age of capital to rational dissection of it, and that Marx's political-economic theory could not have been presented in complete form without Engels's labour. Nie closes with Marx's own letter of thanks for Engels's sacrifices. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese-language overview of Engels's role in the critique of capital, and of how a Guangming Daily author presents Engels's part in completing Capital.

Marx's philosophical mode of expression 马克思的哲学表达方式 Xia Ying Twentieth-century declarations of the "end of philosophy", especially in French philosophy, have amplified the anti-philosophical strain in Marx and cast doubt on whether "Marx's philosophy" is a legitimate concept. Xia Ying, in a short piece first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in April 2020, argues that Marx did not abandon philosophy. In Xia's reading, the historical materialism he built is itself a new way of expressing philosophy, a philosophical revolution suited to its era. The article begins with the "Korsch problem", the early twentieth-century question whether Marxism is a philosophy at all. Xia treats it as a pointer to a tension between theory and practice rather than a question to be settled. It then turns to Marx's well-known mockery of "philosophers" in the Theses on Feuerbach and The German Ideology. Next it sets out two features of historical materialism, and finally it places Marx within the line of German classical philosophy from Kant to Hegel. Xia contends that the philosophy Marx rejected around 1845 was specific: the Hegelian speculative system and its one-sided Young Hegelian heirs, which equate conceptual construction with practice. Historical materialism, by contrast, has a practical orientation. It examines the logical preconditions of history, namely the material conditions of real individuals' activity, so that objectivity takes logical priority. It also looks forward: the analysis of past forms of ownership is guided by a vision in which the division of labour and alienated labour disappear and individual freedom is realised within social freedom. For this reason Xia calls it less a "scientific study" of history than a "philosophical study" of the possibility of human freedom. Xia concludes that Marx's questions, the first causes of being and the conditions of freedom, remain within the traditional problem field of philosophy. What changes is the mode of expression. Drawing on the "strong sense of history" of German classical philosophy, Marx adds historical qualifiers to his categories and takes up questions such as the workings of capitalist economic structures. The difference between Marx and earlier Western philosophy is therefore one between old and new modes of philosophical expression, not between non-philosophy and philosophy. Read the original if you want a concise argument, from within Chinese Marxist philosophy, that historical materialism counts as philosophy, and if you are interested in how it answers the Korsch problem.

Commemoration of and reflection on the Communist International by the foreign left 国外左翼对共产国际的纪念与反思 Xuan Chuanshu Yu Ming Writing in 2020, Xuan Chuanshu and Yu Ming ask how left-wing parties, organisations and scholars outside China used the centenary of the Communist International (Comintern, founded in March 1919) to look back and to think about the present. The authors argue that these actors are less recalling history than questioning reality and looking ahead, hoping to revive the world socialist movement through renewed international unity. They also argue that the foreign left is seriously divided on how to achieve this, and that China should keep a sober, well-defined position. The article draws on 2019 international conferences, party statements and articles in left-wing outlets such as Jacobin, Socialist Worker, Socialist Appeal and Globalizations. These come from the Communist Party of the Russian Federation, the Communist Party of Greece, the Communist Party of Turkey, the Communist Party USA, Trotskyist groups and the Rosa Luxemburg Foundation. It is organised around five questions: why the Comintern was founded, its historical impact, its legacy, today's world situation, and what form future unity should take. A conclusion then interprets the commemorations and sets out China's position. On origins, the article separates a world-revolution reading, in which the Comintern answered the collapse of the Second International, from a reading in which it served Soviet Russia's own needs. On impact, it sets praise (helping found communist parties, supporting national liberation in Africa and Latin America, strengthening proletarian solidarity) against criticism (subordination to Soviet interests, unrealistic directives, the Norwegian and Finnish cases). Commentators see parallels between 1919 and today in the crises of capitalism and the rise of socialist China. They propose three routes: a new international organisation, delay because conditions are not ripe, or looser forms such as conferences and exchanges. In the authors' account, the three groups that commemorate are existing or successor communist parties, Trotskyist organisations, and critical left scholars. Their divisions reflect differing memories of the Comintern and the small size of most left forces, which want support from larger parties but fear manipulation. The authors call for a historical, dialectical judgement, citing Zhou Enlai's formula "good at both ends, problematic in the middle, yet not worthless". They also warn against overestimating the movement's recovery and say China should not seek to head a new "international". Instead it should strengthen its own development and cooperate with left parties on the basis of independence and equality. Read the original if you want a survey of foreign left and communist-party views on the Comintern centenary, together with a Chinese academic assessment of them.

Development trends of foreign Marxist currents in the twenty-first century and an assessment of their effects 21世纪国外马克思主义思潮的发展趋势及其效应评估 Zhang Liang Sun Leqiang Zhang Liang and Sun Leqiang ask how Chinese scholars should approach the development of Marxism outside China since 2000. Their answer is that China is no longer a follower of foreign Marxism but its contemporary: Chinese scholars should neither reject it wholesale nor copy it, but analyse it critically from the standpoint of socialism with Chinese characteristics. They take what helps Chinese theoretical innovation and leave the rest. The article, published in 2019, has four parts. The first examines how foreign Marxists treat the basic theory of Marxism, including textual scholarship and four research paths. The second looks at four theoretical growth points: ecology, space, identity politics and biopolitics. The third turns to analyses of contemporary capitalism (production, crisis, class structure, democracy). The fourth is a conclusion on what to learn from this body of work and where to stand. The authors argue that the new MEGA2 editions and related translations lean towards deconstruction and revive the thesis that Marx and Engels were opposed. They sort Western work into four paths: rereading Marx, localised constructions, grafting Marxism onto the "post-" theories, and outright rejection of Marxism. In their judgement all four fall short, and the field is increasingly fragmented. The ecological, spatial, identity and biopolitical currents are said to be fading, utopian or unable to move beyond the capitalist framework. On crisis, the authors credit left scholars with returning to Capital but hold that the basic contradiction between the productive forces and capitalist relations of production remains. Drawing on Marx and Engels, they argue that mental and non-material workers who sell labour-power and produce surplus value belong to the working class. They therefore call the labels "middle stratum" and "cognitive class" eclectic. Western critiques of democracy are called incisive, but their proposed alternatives are called weak. The authors conclude that foreign Marxism offers useful lessons in textual editing, in exploring ideas Marx and Engels left undeveloped, in localising Marxism and in exposing capitalism's structural contradictions. They also call for vigilance against its deconstructionism, Eurocentrism, neoliberal premises and non-Marxist politics. After 70 years of the People's Republic, they say, Chinese scholars should drop the mentality of apprentices and turn Chinese experience into theory to develop twenty-first-century Marxism. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic assessment of Western left currents, and of how Chinese scholars position themselves towards them in 2019.

Trends in Western left-wing thought as seen from the 2019 Left Forum in New York 从2019年纽约左翼论坛看西方左翼思想发展动态 Tian Xi This is a report on the 2019 Left Forum, held on 28–30 June at Long Island University in Brooklyn, written by Tian Xi and published in Marxist Studies in 2020. Tian places the event eleven years after the 2008 financial crisis, against a rise in American left-wing currents and in movements by Black people, women, ethnic minorities and LGBTQ groups. The forum had more than 160 panels and two special forums. Tian summarises what participants said about Trumpism, America's present predicament and opposition to capitalism in the twenty-first century. The report has three parts. The first covers reflections on Trumpism: the threats it poses, its causes, and how to resist it in theory and in practice. The second covers the American predicament, taking up the political economy of the "long depression", the return of fascism and the immigration question, and US–Russia and US–China relations. The third covers opposing capitalism, through the "end of history" thesis, the legacy of Marxism and the idea of going beyond utopianism. The main voices are Joseph Choonara, Andrew Kliman, Anne Jaclard, Jason Stanley, David Kotz, David Laibman, Michael Hudson, David Harvey, Kevin Anderson and Julio Huato. Tian records disagreement on where Trumpism comes from. Anti-neoliberal leftists such as Kotz, Hudson and Perelman see neoliberal failure as the root cause. Kliman, using Piketty's revised income figures, argues that a white working-class revolt against stagnation cannot explain Trump's victory and that white nationalism is the better explanation. Kotz rebuts three official explanations of US hostility to Russia and attributes it to class interests and hegemonic rivalry. In his account, the same logic explains the growing US wariness of China. Kotz also sees neoliberalism in crisis and two possible restructurings, authoritarian right-wing nationalism or green social democracy, and he favours supporting the latter as a step towards socialism. Anne Jaclard criticises "left-firsters" who tolerate Trump, and Huato and Paddy Quick argue that socialism needs organised mass activity and durable democratic structures. Tian concludes that the Left Forum survives in the margins of American political life yet keeps considerable influence in North America. In this account it is a pluralistic, mixed "discourse field" in which discussion rests on the historical fact of capitalism and some analyses continue Marx's critical tradition. Tian also notes weaknesses: a mixed membership, a lack of ideological unity and a thin scholarly character. The article calls for a dialectical assessment of the views voiced there. Read the original if you want a detailed, China-based account of the positions and speakers at this American left gathering, with names and arguments that are hard to find elsewhere in Chinese.

The theoretical predicaments of contemporary Western Left critical philosophy 当代西方左翼批判哲学的理论困境 Chen Xiangqin Chen Xiangqin asks why contemporary Western Left philosophy, which mobilises nearly every theoretical resource to criticise the domination and alienation of modernity, ends in impotence. The article argues that this philosophy's political action is in effect its academic discourse, and that it has become a game of critique, deconstruction and resistance that yields only abstract opposition and a sense of futility. Chen contends that it inherits the critical spirit of Marxism but has not reached the critical and revolutionary height of historical materialism. The article has four sections: the predicament of critique, the predicament of justification, the turn from a faith in progress to a faith in redemption, and the theoretical limits of this philosophy. Chen draws on Adorno, Horkheimer, Benjamin, Agamben, Žižek, Badiou, Laclau and Mouffe, Derrida and Bloch, with reference to Kant, Berdyaev and Marx. The notes also place the argument beside Zhang Yibing's thesis of the 'end' of Western Marxism and the later Frankfurt School's attempts to rebuild normative foundations. Chen's first move is that, unlike classical Left thought, the contemporary Left attacks not only capital, technology and power but also the Enlightenment ideas of reason, freedom, humanity and progress. By doing so it dissolves its own normative ground. It is left with two options: critique as the sole principle of justification, or an eschatological and messianic faith that, in Chen's reading, replaces belief in progress with a theodicy of history. Drawing on Kant's distinction between progress and evolution, Chen argues that history cannot be morally justified from within its empirical course. A turn to transcendent redemption therefore ends in a rhetoric of justification that loses its critical edge. The second move is diagnostic: the Left stops at the philosophical critique that Marx had already sublated, and so rests its criticism on ideas that are either dialectical and negative or otherworldly and speculative. Chen concludes that Marx's mature critique was a historical critique, centred on political economy and extended to the history of human society. For Marx, Chen says, the revolutionary force is the dialectical, negating process of history itself, not an ideal against which reality is measured. Chen calls on Western critical theory to move from philosophical critique back to Marx's critique of political economy. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist assessment of Adorno, Benjamin, Agamben and Žižek, and of why their critique is said to lack a ground in historical materialism.

The scientific form of Marx's philosophy 马克思哲学的科学形式 Wang Shizhong Wang Shizhong asks how Marx's philosophy, read as a philosophy of practice, can be given a scientific form. Since the early 2000s, the article notes, some scholars have reinterpreted Marxist philosophy from a practice-philosophy standpoint, drawing on Chinese, Western and Marxist resources. Wang argues that practice can only escape the shadow of theoretical philosophy if it is expressed in the form of science. The short piece, first published in a newspaper in 2020, moves through three steps: the case for scientific form, the relation between natural science, social science and economics, and a proposed structure. Along the way it draws on Hegel, Benedetto Croce, the Austrian economist Carl Menger and game-theoretic institutional economics. Wang's central move is a method of 'reverse forcing' (fǎnxiàng dàobī). It examines the internal limits of natural science and then of social science, to find where a scientific form of Marx's philosophy must begin. Such a form must be refutable and correctable, and must point toward a 'community of free individuals'. In Wang's account, economics cannot supply it: economics without history faces a crisis of legitimacy, and economics with history faces a crisis of scientific standing. Hegel's dialectic is a further breakthrough, but Wang follows Croce in finding it flawed. Croce's own closed 'circuit' structure is judged too closed. Wang proposes revising Croce's structure into an open 'double-layer, three-dimensional' one. The two layers are theoretical and practical activity. The practical layer has higher and lower levels. The openness leaves room for human freedom where theory falls short. Wang offers this as an interpretive framework and an operable scientific scheme for Marx's philosophy. Read the original if you want a compact sketch of one Chinese attempt to link practice philosophy, the philosophy of science and the dialectical tradition.

The contemporary expression of the consciousness of hope in Marxist philosophy 马克思主义哲学希望意识的当代表达 Kuang Sanping Writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today (2020), Kuang Sanping asks how Marxist philosophy grounds its orientation towards the future. The author argues that, unlike earlier philosophies that only interpret the world, Marxism seeks to change it through practice. It therefore carries a strong future-oriented outlook and a consciousness of hope, which Kuang presents as a scientific expression of the future aspirations of the proletariat and of humanity. The short piece has four parts: the dual existence of the human being, the unity of lawfulness and purposiveness, hope in practical activity, and the Chinese Dream as a contemporary expression of this consciousness. It draws on Marx's remarks on human beings, labour and history, and contrasts Marx with Hegel and Feuerbach. Kuang's central claim is that humans exist both as natural beings bound by external measures and as self-conscious beings guided by internal measures of purpose and need. Practice, as the author describes it, affirms given reality while sublating it, moving people from what is to what ought to be. Marx's history is neither mechanical determinism nor mere spirit: it joins an account of objective laws with an account of human purposes. Speculative or merely intuitive approaches, in Kuang's reading, cannot form a clear concept of the future. Kuang concludes that Xi Jinping, in proposing the Chinese Dream of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, has given Marxist hope a contemporary expression. The author reads the Dream as historical, realistic and oriented to the future, and as enriching Marxism's scientific doctrine of the future. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Chinese commentary links Marxist philosophy of practice to official Party slogans.

The strength of China's institutional advantages shown in the fight against the epidemic 我国制度优势在抗击疫情中的力量彰显 Qu Qingshan Writing in the People's Daily on 19 June 2020, Qu Qingshan takes up what China's handling of COVID-19 reveals about its political system. Qu contrasts China's containment of the outbreak, which the article describes as a major strategic success within about three months in Wuhan and Hubei, with the continuing spread of the disease in some Western countries, above all the United States. The article's answer is that the epidemic response demonstrated the distinctive advantages of China's system and justifies the Four-sphere Confidence. The piece is a short commentary organised around seven "forces" that Qu says the epidemic made visible, each tied to a role: leadership (the key role), ideas (the guiding role), the state (the foundational role), the people (the decisive role) and morality (the motivating role). It then adds the rule of law, which it says provides a safeguard, and science and technology, which it says provide support. It closes with a brief acknowledgement of weaknesses and a statement of confidence. Qu's central claim is that the Party's centralised, unified leadership is the essence and greatest strength of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The article credits General Secretary Xi Jinping's directives, presented as a guiding body of ideas, with setting goals and strategy, including a "people's war" approach and the priority on Hubei and Wuhan. For the state's capacity to concentrate resources, Qu cites the Huoshenshan and Leishenshan hospitals built in 10 and 12 days, 346 medical teams with 42,600 personnel, 162.4 billion yuan in fiscal funds as of 31 May, and state payment of patients' treatment costs. The people's sacrifice, especially the more than two months of home isolation in Hubei, and the volunteer and moral mobilisation are presented as decisive. Qu repeatedly sets this against what the article calls confused decisions and ineffective measures in the United States and other Western countries. Qu concedes that the epidemic exposed shortcomings in major-epidemic control mechanisms and public health emergency management. Qu calls for remedying them while advancing the modernization of the national governance system and capacity, so that institutional advantages become governance effectiveness. The article concludes that the Chinese system is the most promising, efficient, reliable and beneficial for its people in the world. Read the original if you want a representative official Party-press account, from mid-2020, of how the epidemic response was used to argue for institutional confidence.

How was the socialist system with Chinese characteristics arrived at? 中国特色社会主义制度是怎么得来的？ Li Junru Writing after the Fourth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2019), which for the first time in Party history devoted a session to upholding and improving the socialist system with Chinese characteristics and modernizing national governance, Li Junru asks where that system came from. The article's answer is that it is a scientific institutional system formed through more than a century of practical exploration and ideological struggle by the Party and the people. Li presents this as the necessary starting point for any effort to uphold and improve it. The article has four parts. It first stresses how hard-won the system was, from failed attempts to copy Western constitutional monarchy, multiparty and presidential models to a series of doctrinal debates. It then describes the system's scientific character, traces its establishment, reform and improvement from 1949 to the Fourth Plenum's three-stage goals, and closes with lessons about its vitality. Li draws heavily on Xi Jinping's speeches and on Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping. Li argues that the system is scientific in three senses. It applies Marxism, in particular historical materialism, to Chinese conditions. It is an interlocking set of institutions, which the plenum grouped into 13 areas, with Party leadership as the most essential feature. It is also rooted in Chinese soil and culture, so Li rejects judging or redesigning Chinese institutions by US or European 'models' and cites consultative democracy as drawing on Chinese political culture. Li's historical account runs from the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference and the people's congress system, through Deng Xiaoping's call for institutional reform and the socialist market economy, to the 18th Party Congress (2012) and its push for 'more mature and more defined' institutions. Li concludes that the system has stayed robust because it renews itself, and names four sources of that vitality. These are Party leadership, the people as masters of the country, seeking truth from facts, and democratic centralism. Li says democratic centralism has produced a governance system that is neither liberal nor 'new authoritarian'. Read the original if you want an official Party-theorist account of how the institutional system is supposed to have been formed and why it is said to be durable.

Accelerating the construction of a philosophy and social science system with Chinese characteristics 加快构建中国特色哲学社会科学体系 He Xiuchao This short commentary, first published in People's Daily on 29 June 2020, asks how universities should help build a philosophy and social science system with Chinese characteristics. He argues that, since the 18th Party Congress (2012), the Party Central Committee has made this a strategic task. Universities, in He's view, should use their strengths and "uphold fundamental principles while innovating" to speed up building its three components: the disciplinary system, the academic system and the discourse system. The piece is organised under three headings: setting the main tone, taking root in the main arena, and making the key moves. It draws heavily on Xi Jinping's statements about the Party's leadership of philosophy and social science, the field's role in governance, and its weak international voice. He contends that the task is not only theoretical and educational but above all political and strategic. It therefore requires Party leadership, the guiding position of Marxism and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. He says that research must be rooted in China's circumstances, serve the Party's governance, and draw on traditional Chinese culture. Three priorities follow: deeper study of Xi Jinping Thought, including its entry into textbooks, classrooms and minds; telling China's story so that Chinese scholarship "goes global"; and using philosophy and social science to educate students and give ideological and value guidance. He concludes that universities must place this work within the "two overall situations" and the "Two Centenary Goals", and respond to the demands of the times. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the official line on universities' role in the Chinese philosophy and social science system was framed in 2020.

Constructing a Chinese discourse of Marxist philosophy 构建马克思主义哲学的中国话语 Ding Kuangyi Ding Kuangyi takes up the question of how to build a Chinese discourse of contemporary Marxist philosophy, which the author treats as a matter of the locality and autonomy of Chinese philosophy and social science. The article argues that such a discourse is more than translating, interpreting or spreading Marxist philosophy in China. Its legitimacy rests on grasping China's developing reality from a basic Marxist standpoint, and it is marked by Chinese problem-awareness, home-grown concepts, explanatory propositions and systematic reflection. Originally a short newspaper piece (Chinese Social Sciences Today, May 2020), the article organises its argument around three preconditions: the dimensions of text, space and time. On text, Ding warns against both naive common-sense experience and over-conceptualisation, and holds that Western social science, built on Western conditions, cannot simply be applied to China. Classical Marxist texts should illuminate reality, with Western Marxism and critiques of modernity serving as reference points rather than analogies. On space, Ding rejects treating China as a case of some universal pattern, arguing that the "universal" is itself another local, Westernised extension. China's particularity is a primary resource for concepts, and its geopolitical position across land, sea and space must be considered. On time, Ding rejects linear time from pre-modern to modern in favour of concentric time, in which tradition permeates the present and the present contains anticipation of the future. Ding reads sublation as carrying the past within the present and into the future. Ding concludes that working along these three dimensions, and forming problem-awareness, concepts and propositions that fit them, is the normative standard and necessary preparation for building this discourse. Read the original if you want a brief philosophical statement of how a Chinese Marxist philosopher frames the case for a locally grounded discourse.

Better coordinating Covid-19 prevention and control with economic and social development 更好统筹疫情防控和经济社会发展 Jia Lizheng This commentary, first published in the People's Daily on 7 July 2020, asks how China should better coordinate epidemic prevention and control with economic and social development. Jia Lizheng argues that the Party's leadership has already produced major strategic results in the epidemic fight, and that consolidating them requires understanding several pairs of relationships through materialist dialectics. The stated aim is to secure the goals of finishing the building of a moderately prosperous society and winning the battle against poverty. The article is organised around five relationships: contingency and necessity; internal and external factors; reform, development and stability; the immediate and the long term; and crisis and opportunity. Each section combines a philosophical principle with directives drawn from Xi Jinping's statements and current policy language. The closing section turns to lessons for national governance and to industrial upgrading. Jia presents the epidemic as a contingent shock set against the necessary, pre-set goals of a moderately prosperous society and poverty alleviation, which no accidental factor should be allowed to block. Internal and external risks are said to reinforce one another, so that small risks can grow into systemic ones. In this context the author calls for the Two Upholds, a 'one national chessboard' outlook and a conversion of institutional strengths into governance effectiveness. On reform, development and stability, Jia endorses the general tone of seeking progress while maintaining stability, the 'six stabilities' and 'six guarantees', and the expansion of domestic demand. The author insists that the epidemic's impact is short-term and broadly controllable, and that China's long-term positive economic trend is unchanged. Jia concludes that the epidemic is a major test of China's governance system and capacity. The author calls for closing gaps in public health emergency management, strengthening the legal safeguards for public health, reforming disease control and treatment systems, and improving medical insurance and emergency supplies. Jia also urges deeper reform to create a better institutional environment for new technologies and business models, and to nurture new growth points in areas such as smart manufacturing, online consumption and the contactless economy. Read the original if you want a compact example of how official commentary in mid-2020 framed pandemic response through dialectical categories and the language of the 'two overall situations'.

Why Marxism was able to take root in China 马克思主义为什么能在中国落地生根 Luo Pinghan Why did Marxism, which arose in the West, take root in China rather than in the other countries where communist parties emerged after the First World War? Luo Pinghan, in a short historical commentary first published in Guangming Daily in 2020, argues that the answer lies in several factors. Marxism's own scientific rigour, the failure of earlier Western-inspired paths, the example of the October Revolution and China's particular cultural tradition all contributed. The article proceeds chronologically in three parts. It first traces how Chinese reformers after 1840 moved from the Self-Strengthening Movement to constitutional monarchy and then to republicanism, and how each effort failed to achieve national independence. It then turns to the early, scattered introduction of Marxism and to the effect of the October Revolution, the Paris Peace Conference and Soviet renunciation of tsarist privileges. Finally, it describes how pioneers such as Li Dazhao and Chen Duxiu spread Marxism and founded study societies and early Communist organisations from 1920. Luo's central claim is that the October Revolution turned Marxism from a theoretical design into a working social system. In Luo's account, this set it apart from other socialist doctrines that had reached China as armchair speculation. Testimony from Mao Zedong, Liu Shaoqi, Qu Qiubai and Lin Boqu is used to show that reformers disillusioned with capitalism turned to Russia and then to Marxism. Luo adds a cultural explanation, citing Ai Siqi and Wu Yuzhang: the ancient ideal of a 'great harmony' (datong) society made Marxism feel familiar to many Chinese and activated an existing aspiration. On this reading, Marxism became rooted in China as a result of both Chinese conditions and its scientific character. Luo concludes that Marxism belongs to all humanity, not only to the West. Luo argues that successive generations' firm belief in it allowed it to take root and bear fruit. Luo credits it with leading the Communist Party in what the article calls an unprecedented development miracle, and quotes Xi Jinping on the Party's emergence. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned account of how Party historiography explains the early reception of Marxism in China, with period testimonies from founding figures.

Breaking through the worldwide problem of consolidating the socialist system 突破社会主义制度定型的世界性难题 Hou Huiqin Writing after the Fourth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2019), Hou Huiqin argues that setting out the overall composition of the system of socialism with Chinese characteristics is a pioneering step in the history of the world socialist movement. In Hou's account, the October Revolution turned socialism from a movement into a state system but did not complete that transition, and after the Soviet and East European upheavals the task of consolidating and perfecting a socialist state system fell to the Communist Party of China. The article holds that the Party has achieved a historic breakthrough on this worldwide problem. The short commentary is organised under two headings. The first concerns a bottom-line approach that sets untouchable red lines while actively tackling the difficulties of institutional consolidation. The second concerns grasping the trend of the times, advancing reform and opening up, and turning institutional strengths into effective governance. Hou first argues that Mao Zedong's generation fixed two principles after the socialist transformations: contradictions persist but are non-antagonistic, and Party leadership is the core of the state system. These, Hou says, guard against subversive errors and "colour revolution". Second, Hou holds that the Party resolved the tension between lofty communist ideals and the realism of institutional interests by adhering to dialectical materialism, through three innovations and the Party's self-reform, summarised as "five ones". Third, Hou traces post-1978 consensus on the system's strengths and flaws, citing Deng Xiaoping on concentrating resources and on the plan–market relation. Hou concludes that since the 18th Party Congress (2012) institution-building has been comprehensive innovation, whose soul is integrating Party leadership into the modern state system and governance, in contrast to Western multiparty models. Reform and opening up, in this view, is now internal to socialism with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how a Party theorist framed institutional consolidation after the 2019 plenum.

The scientific meaning and mutual relations of the disciplinary system, the academic system and the discourse system 学科体系、学术体系、话语体系的科学内涵与相互关系 Tian Xinming Tian Xinming addresses a question raised by Xi Jinping's call to build a philosophy and social science with Chinese characteristics: why this project is framed as three systems (disciplinary, academic and discourse), and how they relate. The article, first published in Guangming Daily in May 2020, argues that the three form a dialectical unity. The disciplinary system is a unity of many disciplines, while the academic and discourse systems are inseparable yet distinct aspects of each discipline. The piece has three numbered sections. The first treats the disciplinary system and its basis in the objective world. The second takes up the academic and discourse systems and why they cannot be separated. The third explains why building each still needs to be set as its own task. Tian draws mainly on Mao Zedong's On Contradiction, Marx's 1859 Preface to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy, Engels on terminology in Capital, Lenin on "experience", and Xi Jinping's 2016 symposium remarks. In Tian's account, disciplines are distinguished by the particularity of the contradictions in their objects, and linked by the universality those objects contain. This produces a layered system, with history as one example, containing Chinese history, world history and archaeology. Within each discipline, systematic theory forms the academic system and systematic concepts form the discourse system. Concepts are the "cell of thought" and the form of rational knowledge, so the discourse system is the linguistic carrier of the academic system. Tian then argues that the two are a unity of opposites. They develop at different speeds, as with Marx's materialist conception of history, which took shape in the 1840s but received its mature conceptual form only later. The same word can also carry different meanings in different schools. Struggle between theoretical systems therefore appears as a contest over discourse power as well as over content. Tian concludes that building the academic system cannot stand in for building the discourse system, so the latter must be set as a separate task, and the two should advance together. Upholding Marxism as the guiding principle, Tian says, includes upholding its discourse system, clearing up terminological confusion, guarding against discourse infiltration and hegemony, and crafting distinctive concepts that international audiences can understand. Tian also notes that the disciplinary system is basically established but weak in emerging and interdisciplinary fields, and calls for stronger top-level design. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how Chinese theorists justify the "three systems" formula in Marxist philosophical terms.

The scientific meaning of the disciplinary, academic and discourse systems and how they relate 学科体系、学术体系、话语体系的科学内涵与相互关系 Tian Xinming Writing in Guangming Daily in May 2020, Tian Xinming takes up Xi Jinping's call to build philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics through three systems: the disciplinary system, the academic system and the discourse system. The article asks what each system is and how the three relate. Tian's answer is that they form a dialectical unity: the disciplinary system is the overall framework, while academic and discourse systems are two inseparable but relatively independent aspects of every discipline. The piece has three numbered sections. The first explains why philosophy and social sciences form a disciplinary system and what gaps remain in China's. The second shows that systematic theories make up the academic system and systematic concepts make up the discourse system. The third explains why building each of them still counts as a separate task. Tian draws on Mao Zedong's On Contradiction, Marx's 1859 Preface, Engels and Lenin. Tian's core argument starts from materialist dialectics. Disciplines are separated by the particularity of the contradictions they study and linked by the universality those contradictions contain, so they form a layered system topped by Marxist philosophy. Knowledge moves from perception to concepts, which Tian calls the cells of thought. A discipline's concepts therefore express its theory, and a mature discipline unites both. Tian cites Marx's historical materialism and its categories as the model, and Engels's remark that new insights in a science bring a revolution in its terminology. Yet the two are not identical. Tian says they develop out of step, as when Marx and Engels first voiced new ideas in Hegelian and Feuerbachian language. The same word can also carry different meanings in rival schools, as with profit and rent in Marxist and classical political economy, or Lenin's point about "experience". Ideological struggle thus appears as a contest over discourse and discourse power. Tian calls for upholding Marxist guidance in the discourse system, guarding against discourse infiltration, "discourse traps" and discourse hegemony, and coining signature concepts that international audiences can understand. He also urges stronger top-level design for neglected emerging and interdisciplinary fields. Read the original if you want a compact statement of the official reasoning for treating discourse-building as a task separate from theory-building in Chinese social science.

China's solutions advance the improvement of global governance “中国方案”推动全球治理水平提升 Liu Naiya Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2020, Liu Naiya takes up the Fourth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2019), which called for an all-round diplomatic layout, an open system built on win-win cooperation, active participation in reforming global governance, and the building of a community with a shared future for mankind. Liu reads this as both a summary of more than 70 years of New China's diplomacy and a guide for present practice. The article's thesis is that China's independent, peaceful foreign policy and its "China solutions" are raising the level of global governance. The piece has three main sections. The first traces the continuity of China's independent foreign policy and its commitment to peaceful development, from the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence to the present. The second presents China's approach to global governance, centred on sustainable development, the Belt and Road Initiative and new international institutions. The third treats the community with a shared future for mankind as the central question of current international relations, citing a series of Xi Jinping speeches from 2017 to 2019 and taking China–Africa relations as its case. Liu argues that China's own development, including the poverty-reduction goal to be met in 2020, ten years ahead of the UN 2030 Agenda, is a contribution to world peace and development. In this account China offers public goods through the Belt and Road Initiative and the new development philosophy, and has founded bodies such as the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, BRICS and the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank, each backed by funding. Liu contrasts this with Western-led governance, which the article says shows growing shortcomings in ideas, institutions and capacity. On Africa, Liu cites China's reported contribution of over 25 per cent to the continent's economic growth, the Forum on China–Africa Cooperation, the Addis Ababa–Djibouti railway, and a Chinese record of following through on agreements, which the article sets against Western rhetoric without delivery. Liu concludes that China's cooperation with Africa, grounded in shared colonial history and shared development aims, can serve as a model for building a community with a shared future elsewhere. The article also suggests that China's self-reliant development path is worth other developing countries' study. Read the original if you want an example of how official Chinese commentary in 2020 linked the Fourth Plenum's foreign-policy guidance to global governance, the Belt and Road Initiative and China–Africa ties.

Building consensus for realising the Chinese Dream of the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation 为实现中华民族伟大复兴中国梦凝聚共识 Jiang Zelin Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts (2020, no. 8), Jiang Zelin asks how the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference (CPPCC) can contribute to the Chinese Dream of national rejuvenation. The article argues that ideological and political guidance and the building of broad consensus are the central link in the CPPCC's work in the new era. Jiang contends that this consensus must be built under the leadership of the Communist Party of China. The piece has three parts. The first explains why consensus is needed for the Chinese Dream, drawing on China's history, the people's role as makers of history, and the tasks of completing a moderately prosperous society. The second treats consensus-building as a core CPPCC function, discussed through its political consultation, democratic oversight and participation in the deliberation and administration of state affairs, and through its two themes of unity and democracy. The third lists several problems to be handled, including Party leadership, unity of consistency and diversity, and the CPPCC's concentration of expertise. Jiang presents the Chinese Dream as a dream of national rejuvenation and of the people's well-being. The author links it to the shift from "standing up" to "becoming rich" to "becoming strong", and to the principal contradiction identified at the 19th Party Congress (2017). The CPPCC is described as a united front body, a consultative institution and a channel of socialist consultative democracy. In this account, it turns the Party's decisions into the shared will of all sectors through democratic procedures. Jiang's key image, borrowed from Xi Jinping, is to seek the "greatest common denominator" and draw the "biggest concentric circle", with a firm political bottom line at its centre and wide tolerance at its radius. Patriotism and socialism are named as the greatest political consensus among CPPCC participants, and Jiang says this extends to compatriots in Hong Kong, Macao and Taiwan and to overseas Chinese. Jiang concludes that the CPPCC should strengthen Party leadership, including Party groups within it, and should expand the breadth and depth of consensus. It should do so by drawing on its members' expertise, its standing consultative mechanisms and the representation of non-public-sector figures, religious and ethnic representatives, and other groups. Jiang describes this as the CPPCC's distinctive contribution to national governance and to the Chinese Dream. Read the original if you want an official-line account of how the CPPCC's consultative role is framed in the language of consensus and the united front.

The contemporary value and practical significance of the popularisation of Marxism 马克思主义大众化的时代价值与现实意义 Wang Weiguang Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts (2020, no. 7), Wang Weiguang asks why Marxism must be popularised among the masses (大众化, dazhonghua) and what this means today. Starting from Lenin's formula that the maximum of Marxism equals the maximum of popularisation, Wang argues that popularisation is an essential requirement of Marxism and follows from its "people-ness" (人民性), its character as a theory of, from and by the people. The article is organised in three parts, each tied to one feature of Marxism: it is a theory for the people, a theory that comes from the people, and a theory that relies on the people. A final section draws out the consequence that popularisation leads to the adaptation of Marxism to China and to the times. Wang draws on Marx, Engels, Lenin, Mao Zedong and Xi Jinping, and on the sequence of Chinese theoretical achievements from Mao Zedong Thought to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Wang argues first that Marxism's "people" is not an abstract, supra-class human being but the working class and the broad masses. In Wang's account, bourgeois theories that preach universal values hide their class character, whereas Marxism openly admits its class nature, which therefore coincides with its people-ness and guarantees its truth. Second, Marxism arises from the practice of the people: Wang traces Marxism, Leninism and the successive theories of the Chinese Communist Party to workers' movements and revolutionary and reform practice. Third, theory becomes a material force once it grips the masses, so that Marxism can fulfil its task of changing the world only by educating, mobilising and relying on the people. Wang concludes that popularisation, the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, is one unified process. Marxism must be accepted by the people in each nation and era, so it has to take on Chinese style and respond to the main social contradiction of each period, which Wang traces from the Eighth Party Congress through the post-1978 period to the new era. Wang calls popularisation an important means by which the Party opens new prospects for its cause. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official Party-theory case linking Marxism's people-ness, its popularisation and its adaptation to China and to the times.

Foreign left commemorations and reflections on the Communist International 国外左翼对共产国际的纪念与反思 Xuan Chuanshu Yu Ming On the centenary of the Communist International (Comintern) in 2019, left-wing parties, organisations and scholars outside China held conferences and published articles to mark it. Xuan and Yu survey this body of commemoration and ask what it says about the Comintern's past and about the future of world socialism. They argue that the foreign left is less looking back than interrogating the present, and that it is deeply divided over how to rebuild international unity. The article draws on conferences by bodies such as the Initiative of Communist and Workers' Parties in Europe, the International Marxist Tendency and the Russian Communist Workers' Party, as well as texts from the Communist Party of the Russian Federation, the Communist Party of Greece and the Communist Party of the USA. It also uses Jacobin, Socialist Appeal, Globalizations and the Rosa Luxemburg Foundation. It is organised around five questions: why the Comintern was founded, its historical impact, its legacy, today's world situation, and what kind of union socialist forces now need. A concluding section gives the authors' own assessment. On founding, the article reports two readings: a response to the Second International's collapse and to social democracy, or a tool to protect Soviet Russia. On impact, it sets praise (nurturing communist parties, supporting national liberation, fostering proletarian solidarity) against criticism of Moscow's dominance and unrealistic directives, citing the Norwegian and Finnish cases. Most speakers see parallels between 1919 and today's capitalist crisis and cite the contrast between 'Western disorder' and 'Eastern order'. On reorganisation, they split into three camps: a new proletarian international, either federal or democratic-centralist; those who think conditions are not ripe; and those who prefer looser forms such as conferences and exchanges. Xuan and Yu conclude that the commemorations are driven by communist parties, Trotskyist groups and critical left scholars, and that divisions reflect both historical memory and the small size of most left groups. Their own stance is that the Comintern should be judged historically and dialectically, endorsing Zhou Enlai's verdict of 'good at both ends, poor in the middle'. They caution that the shift in global power balance does not mean socialism is rising against capitalism. They also state that China should not seek to 'lead' or rebuild an international, but should develop itself and cooperate with left parties on the basis of independence, full equality, mutual respect and non-interference. Read the original if you want a detailed map of 2019 left debates on the Comintern and a Chinese Party-affiliated scholarly reading of them.

Studying world left-wing thought and movements amid changes unseen in a century An overview of research on foreign left-wing thought in 2019 百年未有之大变局中的世界左翼思潮和运动研究 Zhou Miao Song Lidan Kang Yanru This is a literature review of research on the foreign left in 2019. The authors begin from the premise that the world is undergoing "changes unseen in a century" and that the basic contradictions of capitalism are taking new forms. They report that left-wing scholars abroad sought to answer pressing questions in ways that show the contemporary value and vitality of Marxism. The review opens with the year's main left-wing gatherings: the New York left forum, the Socialism conference in Chicago, the Marxism festival in London, the Revolution festival, the tenth World Socialism Forum in Beijing, and a Chinese forum on foreign Marxism. It then surveys five theoretical clusters: imperialism, neoliberalism, contemporary capitalism, socialism with Chinese characteristics, and Chinese appraisals of foreign left thought. A third part describes the left regionally: North America and Europe; Russia, the Middle East and Africa; and Latin America. On theory, the authors report that David Harvey and John Smith debated the contemporary relevance of Lenin's theory of imperialism. Intan Suwandi, R. Jamil Jonna and John Bellamy Foster, they say, analyse imperialism through global commodity chains and labour arbitrage, and Foster describes a "late imperialism" of stagnation and declining US hegemony. Foster, the Patnaiks and Sitaram Yechury are presented as arguing that neoliberalism has reached a dead end and fed the political right. Studies of digital capitalism are said to show intensified control of labour. Egon Krenz, Russian scholars and Toma Ivan are reported as praising socialism with Chinese characteristics. Regionally, the review notes the weakening of centre-left parties in Europe, the "back to the working class" turn of US democratic socialists, the German Left Party's difficulties, and a retreat of Latin America's left, including the coup in Bolivia. The authors conclude that foreign left thought will keep developing as long as capitalism's contradictions and crises persist. They call for Chinese scholars to draw scientifically on this work, which they see as a resource for twenty-first-century Marxism and for building philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics. They also urge more exchange with foreign left scholars, and say text-based study should aim at ideas and their transformation in China rather than at the texts themselves. Read the original if you want a quick map of the 2019 Chinese-language and foreign sources on the international left, with full citations to Monthly Review articles and Chinese journal studies.

China's anti-epidemic action in the eyes of foreign left-wing parties 国外左翼政党眼中的中国抗疫行动 Hu Guanghui Yu Weihai This short commentary, first published in the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences newspaper in April 2020, asks how communist and workers' parties abroad have assessed China's response to Covid-19. Hu and Yu argue that the epidemic is a "touchstone" of national governance and political systems, and that many such parties have praised China, criticised their own governments' slow responses and urged them to learn from China's experience. The article reports statements from parties in Greece, Argentina, Vietnam, Australia, Italy, the United States, Canada, Luxembourg, Belgium, Puerto Rico, Mexico, South Africa, Norway, Britain and Sri Lanka. It is organised in three parts: calls to draw on China's measures, the fight against disinformation and xenophobia, and the claimed advantages of the socialist system.
