The authors report that a joint statement initiated by the Greek Communist Party and signed by at least 82 parties recognised China's results and internationalism. Several parties, including those of Australia, Canada and the United States, are said to have denounced "Sinophobia" and blamed anti-China rumours on imperialism, summed up in the slogan "our enemy is the virus, not China". Other parties are cited as arguing that capitalist commercialisation and privatisation of health care exposed its inefficiency and "anti-people" character, while centralised, planned mobilisation in China showed the strengths of socialism. Hu and Yu conclude that more countries are recognising the social mobilisation capacity of the socialist system, and that China's data sharing, aid and donations show its commitment to building a community with a shared future for mankind. They hold that the advantages of socialism with Chinese characteristics show the significance of that project. Read the original if you want a compact sample of how Chinese academics present foreign communist parties' statements on China's epidemic response.

The institutional value of the Chinese path amid shifts in the world economy: views of foreign left-wing scholars 世界经济变局下中国道路的制度价值——国外左翼学者的视角 Song Chaolong Li Wenyu This report-style article covers the international conference "Contemporary China and the Modernization of Developing Countries", held at Peking University's School of Marxism on 12–13 October 2019 and known as the third "mini World Congress on Marxism". Song and Li gather the views of foreign, mostly left-leaning, scholars on changes in the world economy and on China's development path, and add their own corrections. They argue that the visitors rightly praise China's achievements but often treat the path as a mere economic method, whereas its essential attribute is socialism. Speakers included David Kotz, Terrence McDonough, Daniel Cirera, Emir Sader, Yuri Vasilievich Taranukha, Stavros Mavroudeas, Balwinder Singh Tiwana, Chandrasekharan Saratchand, Pertti Honkanen and a group of Korean scholars. The article is organised in four parts: the shifting world economy (Brexit, Trump, populism, the crisis of neoliberal globalization); the institutional character of the Chinese path; proposals for its further development; and its significance for the world economy. Most foreign participants, in the authors' account, read the Western upheaval as a systemic crisis rooted in finance-led accumulation; Kotz prefers the label "authoritarian right-wing nationalism" to populism. On China, they organise their views around economic growth, the Soviet model and neoliberalism. Most see the periods before and after reform and opening up as continuous, while McDonough stresses their differences. Saratchand and Cirera credit the public sector and China's resistance to neoliberalism and dollar hegemony. Song and Li then warn against three errors: reducing the path to a special growth method, severing the two periods, and overlooking the socialist nature of the socialist market economy. They also object to Vasilievich's claim that the middle class is socialism's pillar, and say the scholars' notion of "particularity" and "universality" is too thin. The authors conclude that combining the socialist system with a market economy is the institutional basis of a new road to modernization. In their view it has broken the accumulation regime dominated by international finance capital and offers developing countries an option beyond the Soviet and neoliberal models. They name as preconditions the people as principal body, Party leadership and the socialist character of the market economy, aiming at common prosperity and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Foreign advice, they say, should be heard carefully while China keeps its composure and autonomy. Read the original if you want a detailed catalogue of how left-wing scholars from Europe, India, Russia, Latin America and Korea assess China, together with a Chinese academic response.

Value-form: the theoretical positioning of Marx's critique of commodity fetishism 价值形式:马克思商品拜物教批判的理论定位 Wu Meng Wu Meng asks how historical materialism can be made contemporary ("contemporization") while remaining historical materialism, and takes Marx's critique of commodity fetishism as the test case. Wu argues that Western left thinkers who build critiques of contemporary capitalism on this critique have failed to achieve such contemporization, because they treat commodity fetishism as a basic fact of capitalist society. In Wu's reading, Marx's critique is instead a further formal analysis of the result of the value-form analysis, aimed at grasping historical real movement. The article has four parts. It first surveys Western left thought, from Lukács to Benjamin, Backhaus and Žižek, distinguishing those who "reinterpret" historical materialism from Habermas-style "reconstruction". It then turns to the original context of the critique in Capital, comparing the first and second German editions. A third section reconstructs three aspects of the critique, and a final section draws out two working principles for contemporizing historical materialism. Wu contends that Lukács treats fetishism as an "ideational fact" and Benjamin and Žižek as a "social fact". These readings end in an abstract revolutionary subject, a purely negative "dialectic of action", or a critique of commodity society in general. Through the first edition's fourth value-form, a commodity world in which every commodity can be a general equivalent, Wu shows that fetishism's starting point is non-actual. Marx's analysis therefore moves through producer fetishism, the political-economy fetishism of classical economics, and a third aspect centred on historically universal exchange. In this third aspect, labour acquires its twofold social character only under the compulsory shaping force of bourgeois "society". Wu concludes that Marx's formal analysis shows two principles: a materialist method that questions contemporary real movement itself rather than applying fixed concepts, and a transcending theoretical outlook that moves from circulation into production, where capitalism's self-negation can be seen. Local empirical experience, Wu argues, cannot be the basis of contemporization. Read the original if you work on Marx's value-form theory, the Capital editions, or the Western Marxist reception of commodity fetishism and want a detailed, text-based challenge to it.

Opportunities and challenges together: prospects for world socialism today 机遇与挑战并存：当今世界社会主义发展前景 Chai Shangjin Writing in 2020, Chai Shangjin asks where world socialism stands and where it is heading, and argues that the answer has to be read against the changing contradictions of capitalism. His thesis is that Western capitalism has entered a period of crisis and decline, which opens a favourable window for socialism. In his account socialism with Chinese characteristics is increasingly the mainstay and leading banner of world socialism. Yet the overall balance, which he calls "capitalism strong, socialism weak", will not change fundamentally because of any single event. The article has four parts. The first describes the institutional predicament of Western capitalism: unequal globalisation, "vetocracy" in party politics, the rise of populism and extremism, and the erosion of the US-dominated international order. The second assesses communist parties in developed countries, using France, Spain and the 2019 European Parliament elections as cases. The third discusses China's role, and the fourth explains why the balance of forces remains unfavourable to socialism. Chai holds that developed-country communist parties are stable but face persistent difficulties. They contest elections but have limited appeal: none won a seat in the 2019 European Parliament elections, and the French party's EU-level platform, he says, was far from its traditional voters' concerns. They are working on party building, but ideological splits and organisational fragmentation remain obstacles. They seek left unity, which is hard to achieve. They also struggle to win lower-income voters, whose loyalties are fragmented and whose demands populists often appropriate. Against this, Chai credits China's economic and poverty-reduction record, its institutional strengths (he cites the response to Covid-19, contrasted with the United States) and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era with raising confidence among communist parties abroad. Chai concludes that socialism replacing capitalism will be a long process. He points to Western hostility towards socialist states, the weakness of some non-ruling communist parties that have dropped ideology and democratic centralism, and Western dominance of international economic institutions. China, he writes, neither imports nor exports models, and it advances a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Party-affiliated researcher assesses communist parties in developed countries and the place of China in the international communist movement around 2020.

The political predicament of modernity critique in contemporary Western left-wing thought, and a way out 当代西方左翼思潮现代性批判的政治困境及其出路 Zhuo Chengfang Hu Daping Zhuo Chengfang and Hu Daping ask why contemporary Western left-wing thought, which has produced radical discourse on almost every subject from economy and ecology to gender and psychology, has so little political purchase. They argue that the proliferation of radical language masks a political retreat: there is no longer a unified left programme aimed at changing the world, and "left" itself has become a sign of disagreement. The authors call this the political predicament of the left's critique of modernity. They trace it to a shift from seeking an alternative to capitalism to critiquing modernity, and to an anti-essentialist stance that leaves no shared values or theoretical premises. The article has three parts. The first reconstructs the difficulty of agreeing on how to define politics, from the aftermath of 1968 through Habermas, Lyotard, Laclau and Mouffe, Žižek, Amin and Thrift, and Rancière. The second examines four political issues the authors say Chinese scholarship has neglected: Virilio on speed, Bauman on globalisation and community, place and indigeneity in Appadurai, Dirlik and Mamdani, and Burawoy on the politics of production. The third returns to the question of commitment and the agenda of emancipation. The authors argue that a theory without secured premises yields demands without practical commitment, so that the left's work becomes endless critique detached from construction. They read Laclau, Mouffe and Žižek as making "impossibility" or fundamental antagonism the basis of radical politics. Many fashionable themes, in their account, are either absorbed by power as politically correct discourse or never enter real political processes. Among the four cases, they single out Bauman as most conscious of the need to rebuild politics through public space, the political agenda and a clear vision, and they note his criticism of cultural pluralism as a reconciliation with the existing order. Burawoy shows, they say, that class politics in production has not vanished but become more complex. Zhuo and Hu conclude that critique which avoids the capitalist mode of production and lacks a commitment to emancipation becomes an empty intellectual satisfaction. They propose returning to Marxism, reviving the emancipation agenda through major contemporary political issues and thinking again about alternatives to capitalism. They endorse Terry Eagleton's defence of Marx as a model, calling Marx the horizon of modern critique that has not yet been surpassed. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist assessment of post-1968 Western left theory and of the thinkers Virilio, Bauman, Dirlik, Mamdani and Burawoy.

Three shifts in contemporary Western Marxist class theory 当今西方马克思主义阶级理论的三大转变 Mi Haibo Mi Haibo asks how Western Marxist scholars have revised Marx's theory of class as Western capitalism moved from industrial to post-industrial, information-based society, and whether those revisions hold up. The article argues that contemporary Western Marxism has shifted in three areas: class structure, class division and class struggle. In Mi's assessment, these revisions capture real changes but often overstate them, and class analysis remains valid. The article is organised in three parts, one for each shift. The first moves class structure from a simple two-class model to a complex one. The second moves the criteria of class division from a single economic standard to several. The third moves class struggle from political confrontation to democratic movements. Mi discusses thinkers including Poulantzas, Gorz, Erik Olin Wright, Dahrendorf, Galbraith, Daniel Bell, Alvin Gouldner, Habermas, Laclau and Mouffe, and Ralph Miliband. On structure, Mi accepts that new middle strata of managers, technicians and service workers have grown, and that both bourgeoisie and working class have become internally differentiated. Mi nonetheless argues that these groups sell their labour-power and so form a new stratum of the working class, part of Marx's "collective worker". Theories of the working class's disappearance, merging or individualised identity are judged misreadings. On division, Mi criticises Wright's exploitation-based "contradictory class" and the use of power or knowledge as class criteria. In Mi's account, class is determined by relations of production, and intellectuals cannot rule without economic foundations and state power. On struggle, Mi reads new social movements (feminist, ecological, anti-racist and others) as democratic struggles that are not identical with class struggle but contain class elements. Mi concludes that while capitalism and wage-labour relations persist, class relations and class contradictions do not disappear, so claims that class struggle has died out are inaccurate. Class struggle, in Mi's view, has become more varied in its subjects and has moved towards everyday life, and it is increasingly global, as Vincent Navarro's argument about alliances of ruling and ruled classes across North and South is taken to show. Only a socialist movement, Mi holds, can finally resolve capitalism's underlying problems. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's critical overview of Western Marxist debates on the middle class, class criteria and new social movements, and a defence of Marx's class analysis against them.

Attempt and bankruptcy: rethinking Heideggerian Marxism 尝试与破产：反思海德格尔式的马克思主义 Deng Ding Within Western Marxism, thinkers have repeatedly tried to join Marxism with other currents of Western philosophy. Deng Ding takes up one such attempt that receives less attention than it deserves: Herbert Marcuse's early project of a "Heideggerian Marxism", as opposed to his better-known "Hegelian" and "Freudian" Marxisms. This short commentary, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in 2020, asks why dialectics must be combined with historical materialism and how a phenomenological materialist dialectic is possible. Deng judges Marcuse's methodological clarification worth pondering but his overall attempt a failure. The piece follows Marcuse's reasoning in three steps. It begins with the Greek origins of dialectics in Plato and Hegel's synthesis of dialectics as reality and as logic. It then turns to how Marcuse brings in phenomenology and answers Heidegger's claim that phenomenology and dialectics are as incompatible as fire and water. Finally it covers Marcuse's turn away from Heidegger after the publication of Marx's Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 in 1932, and Deng's assessment of what remains of the project. On Deng's account, Marcuse treats dialectics first as a feature of reality's own movement of becoming rather than a logical tool. Marx turned Hegel's idealist dialectic into a materialist one, which suits the movement of human existence, and only humans are historical beings. Deng explains that the incompatibility Heidegger stressed applies to idealist dialectics, which aim at the reality of things and work through logic. Human history is both a movement of becoming, requiring dialectics, and a repeated disclosure of the meaning of being, requiring phenomology. Marcuse therefore held that phenomenology and materialist dialectics are both necessary moments of historical materialism. Deng reports that the 1932 Manuscripts convinced Marcuse that Marx already supplied an account of human history and alienation, and that Heidegger stayed at the level of existential analysis without a "concrete philosophy". After 1933 Marcuse returned to Marx. Deng grants that phenomenology might help show how concepts such as worker, commodity and capitalist carry historical meaning within particular relations of production. But the author argues that Marcuse's attempt to redefine materialism and dialectics on a phenomenological basis was his main limitation, since only historical materialism reaches social reality. Phenomenology and existentialism, in Deng's view, still only interpret the world, while the power to change it lies in countries and peoples that inherit and develop Marxism. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese academic assessment of Marcuse's early Heideggerian phase and its limits.

The internal tensions among the three forms of morality and their adjustment 道德三重样态的内在张力及其调适 Liu Ailing Liu Ailing asks how the conflicts inside morality can be resolved once morality is divided by the relation between subject and object. Working from historical materialism, the article distinguishes three "forms" (yangtai) of morality: the individual morality of persons, the political morality of administrative actors, and the public morality of the community. Liu argues that the three are relatively independent, fluid and internally determined, so they interact through contradiction and contest. Adjusting these tensions, in Liu's view, is the way to build a dynamic moral picture in which the three forms reorganise one another and reinforce each other. The article has three parts. The first links the three social subjects (individual, social and political persons) to three moral forms: individual morality as self-respect, will and reason; political morality as justice, legality and altruism; public morality as publicness, responsibility and self-evident axioms. The second part identifies three tensions. The third proposes remedies at the level of subject and object, of moral fields, and of institutional mechanisms. Liu draws on Marx and Engels, Kant and other ethical writers, and uses examples such as epidemic quarantine, environmental protection, the Heinz dilemma and a Shandong criminal case. Liu's central argument is that each tension arises from a mismatch of standards. Individual self-interest clashes with the "good of the community", for example when quarantine requires individuals to yield freedom, or when social responsibility is shifted onto individuals. Administrators' self-assessment diverges from the more idealistic public evaluation, and routine rules can conflict with emergency action, as in a Hubei city that locked down early during the COVID-19 outbreak. Individual free will meets the compulsion of law and political morality. Liu holds that these are resolved by "mutual construction": a cycle in which individual, political and social good support one another, and unity of moral consciousness, conduct and effect. Liu proposes building a moral community in which individual, social and administrative responsibilities coexist, and in which individual values, public morality and political institutions reinforce one another. Concrete measures include legislation and evaluation standards for political morality, the exemplary role of moral models in the new era, and a reflective mechanism that adjusts policy by the test of whether the people are satisfied. Liu stresses attention to vulnerable groups and to special periods. Read the original if you are interested in how Chinese scholars of ideological and political education apply Marxist ethics to public morality, official conduct and epidemic-era governance.

The responsibility logic and structural system of modernizing government governance 政府治理现代化的责任逻辑与结构体系 Zhang Xianming Writing in Guangming Daily in January 2020, Zhang Xianming takes up the task set by the Fourth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2019): to uphold and improve the administrative system with Chinese characteristics and build a government governance system with clear responsibilities and administration according to law. Zhang treats the modernization of government governance as a key link in modernizing national governance. The article argues that two things must be worked out together: the logic of responsibility, and the structural system of government. The piece is a short newspaper commentary in two parts. The first part deals with how responsibility is assigned and how it is realized. The second part sets out three directions for optimizing the structure of the administrative system. It draws on Party documents, including the report to the 19th Party Congress (2017), rather than on case studies or foreign literature. On responsibility, Zhang holds that whether a government is accountable to the people marks the difference between traditional and modern government. Responsibility should be assigned scientifically. It combines political, legal and moral responsibility. Powers should be fixed according to responsibilities (以责确权), with powers and responsibilities matched, and duties should be allocated vertically between central, local and grassroots levels and horizontally between departments. Realizing responsibility depends on supervision, meaning a network of oversight bodies and open, transparent politics, and on accountability mechanisms. Those mechanisms should cover the whole chain from decision to execution to result and be paired with a tolerance-for-error mechanism. On structure, Zhang calls for three steps: keep the direction of administrative reform under Party leadership while drawing on world experience; ease the tensions between vertical and horizontal lines of authority, and clarify the government's relations with society and the market; and activate the system's elements by giving local governments more autonomy and by integrating big data, the internet and artificial intelligence into administration. Zhang concludes that a modern government system needs a complete structure, smooth operation and effective coordination. The author insists that national governance in China differs from "governance" in the Western sense, because it mobilizes plural actors under the overall arrangement of the Party and state. The stated aim is a situation in which national governance has strength, social governance has precision and grassroots governance has warmth. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how an official-academic voice in 2020 linked accountability, supervision and administrative restructuring to the Fourth Plenum's governance agenda.

Study and promote the revolutionary spirit, and take a clear stand against historical nihilism 研究和弘扬革命精神 旗帜鲜明反对历史虚无主义 Li Youxin This short commentary, first published in Guangming Daily on 5 February 2020, argues that studying, inheriting and promoting the revolutionary spirit of the Communist Party of China is an important part of the struggle against historical nihilism. Li Youxin holds that, besides exposing and refuting nihilist claims, this work must be supported by historical materialism and by concrete, vivid research results. The article is organised around four forms of historical nihilism, each of which Li says calls for a response grounded in the revolutionary spirit: the nihilism that dismisses revolution, that dismisses heroes, that dismisses ideals, and that rejects the Party's leadership. On the first, Li describes claims that the revolution was the product of radicalism, calls to "bid farewell to revolution", and the pitting of a "modernization perspective" against a "revolutionary perspective". The author argues that research into the historical detail of revolutionary spirit shows the necessity of China's revolutionary road. On heroes, Li points to online mockery, abuse of martyrs and pseudo-academic claims that heroes were "false models"; the answer, Li says, is legal protection plus study of heroes as embodiments of revolutionary spirit. On ideals, Li contends that denying the revolution amounts to denying the social ideal it pursued and the historical necessity of choosing Marxism and socialism. Li also maintains that hostile forces at home and abroad attack revolutionary history to undermine the Party's leadership. Li concludes that revolutionary spirit is a lasting source of strength for the Party, and calls on readers to carry on the "red gene", strengthen ideals and convictions, and take up the task of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a compact example of how a 2020 Party-oriented commentary links the campaign against historical nihilism to the study of revolutionary spirit.

Accelerating the construction of a discourse system of philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics 加快构建中国特色哲学社会科学话语体系 Jin Nuo Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in late 2019, on the 70th anniversary of the People's Republic, Jin Nuo argues that the weakness of China's international discourse power has become a pressing shortcoming as the country moves from 'standing up' and 'becoming rich' to 'becoming strong'. The article's thesis is that the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation requires a philosophy and social sciences discourse system with Chinese characteristics, and that raising China's international voice depends on building it quickly. The article is organised in three parts. The first sets out why philosophy and social sciences must take on this responsibility. The second lists the basic principles to follow: Marxist guidance, the Four-sphere Confidence, and solid academic research. The third turns to the breakthroughs needed: grounding work in Chinese practice and pursuing original discourse. Each part is paired with a section on Renmin University of China, where the author writes from an institutional standpoint, presenting the university's history and duties. Jin builds on Xi Jinping's remark that China has solved the problems of being beaten and starved but not yet of being 'abused', that is, of being misrepresented by Western powers using their own institutional models and value standards. On this reading, a flourishing philosophy and social sciences both marks national strength and carries international discourse power. The author holds that Marxism is what distinguishes contemporary Chinese scholarship, that confidence in China's achievements and culture is its spiritual pillar, and that real discourse power comes from depth of scholarship, not loud volume. Because Western discourse cannot explain Chinese practice, Jin calls for extracting Chinese concepts from reform-era and post-1949 experience and turning the Party's theoretical innovations into academic language. Jin also calls for originality and subjectivity, citing Xi's view that imitation cannot produce a Chinese-style scholarship. Jin concludes that scholars, think tanks and universities must explain major theoretical and contemporary questions, so that Chinese theory interprets Chinese practice and Chinese practice in turn elevates theory, offering what the article calls Chinese solutions to the world. Renmin University is presented as bearing special responsibility, given its record in Marxist research and its stated aim of being 'satisfactory to the people and world-class'. Read the original if you want to see how a university leader frames discourse power, Marxist guidance and the tasks of Chinese social science in the period around 2019.

The fundamental system of upholding Marxism's guiding role in the ideological field 坚持马克思主义在意识形态领域指导地位的根本制度 Dong Xuewen Dong Xuewen's commentary, published in Red Flag Manuscripts in early 2020, reads one provision of the Fourth Plenum Decision of the 19th Central Committee (2019): the call to uphold Marxism's guiding role in the ideological field as a "fundamental system". Dong argues that this is a first in the history of Marxist thought and culture and in the Party's own documents. In Dong's account, it is a creative step that institutionalises Marxist guidance and advances the Chinese-adapted Marxist theory of culture. The piece opens with the Decision as a whole, which Dong credits with setting out the "four pillars and eight beams" of the socialist system with Chinese characteristics and with a roadmap for the modernization of national governance. It then moves through three sections: the novelty of the provision, its institutional and practical force, and its place within governance modernization, with literature and art as the worked example. Dong draws on Xi Jinping's remarks on Marxism and on literature and art throughout. Dong's central move is a conceptual reading of the terms. Since the Decision distinguishes "important", "basic" and "fundamental" systems, Dong defines a fundamental system as the most important rule of conduct that everyone must follow. Placing Marxist guidance at that level, Dong says, turns a theoretical appeal into an institutional and practical requirement tied to governance capacity. Such a system is rigid, allowing no bargaining or selective compliance, and it guides all other systems. Dong links it to ideological security, to keeping leadership, management and discourse power in Party hands, and to opposing historical nihilism and "two-faced" behaviour. Dong adds that because the system belongs to the category of "modernization", the view that Marxism is outdated is arbitrary and wrong. Dong concludes that this system is the top priority and the key piece of top-level design in cultural institution-building, and that it must be implemented without lapses. In literature and art, Dong holds, adherence to Marxism is the first standard for telling good from bad and advanced from backward, and it must be a working "pointer" and "weapon" rather than a "mask" or "cosmetic". Read the original if you want an example of how a Party-affiliated theorist interpreted the 2019 Decision's ideological provisions and justified them as institutional design.

New changes in the Communist Party of Cuba since Raúl Castro took office 劳尔·卡斯特罗主政以来古巴共产党的新变化 Yang Jianmin Yang Jianmin asks what has changed in the Communist Party of Cuba (PCC) and in Cuban socialism during Raúl Castro's twelve years in power, from taking over from the ailing Fidel Castro in 2006 to leaving the state presidency in April 2018 while remaining the Party's First Secretary. The article argues that the Party has responded to social demands by shifting its priorities to economic development, exploring a new socialist model, strengthening Party leadership and pursuing an all-round foreign policy. The article is organised in four parts. It covers the shift in the Party's and state's priorities and the "updating of the model"; the defence of the Party's leading position and reforms in Party organisation and leadership succession; the new diplomacy towards the United States, the European Union, China, Russia and Latin America; and Cuba's support for the Latin American left and its place in the world socialist movement. Yang draws mainly on Raúl Castro's speeches and the documents of the Sixth (2011) and Seventh (2016) Party Congresses and the 2012 National Conference. Yang argues that Raúl moved the Party from treating revolution and social welfare as the main task to treating economic growth as the precondition for sustaining socialism. Egalitarianism was criticised as a distortion of social justice, and Cuba now accepts a market role within the framework of state planning, social ownership of the basic means of production, and a diversified non-state sector. Yang stresses, however, that Cuba remains cautious about private business and bars the concentration of property and wealth in private hands. Alongside this, the Party reaffirmed the one-party system, held congresses regularly again, set age and term limits for senior leaders, criticised bureaucracy, and founded a college for training cadres. Succession was handled carefully, ending with Díaz-Canel taking over the state posts and a constitutional revision under way. Abroad, Yang describes the normalisation with the United States from 2014, reversed under Trump, as well as closer ties with the EU and continued reliance on Venezuela, China and Russia. Yang concludes that Cuban socialism matters greatly for the Western Hemisphere and for world socialism, and that the success of the "updating" is therefore important. As the only country building socialism in a Western cultural setting, Cuba, in Yang's view, may develop a model different from the Eastern one, despite ageing and low investment. Yang holds that this exploration can solve Cuba's long-standing economic problems and enrich the experience of the world socialist movement. Read the original if you want a Chinese specialist's overview of Raúl Castro's reforms and the PCC's changing positions, drawn from Cuban primary sources.

The historical evolution of theories of imperialism from the perspective of neoliberalism and ordoliberalism 新自由主义与秩序自由主义视域下帝国主义理论的历史演进 Vassilis K. Fouskas This is a Chinese translation of an article by Vassilis K. Fouskas, translated by Li Yingdong. It asks how the Marxist tradition of imperialism theory can explain the two main contemporary accumulation regimes: Anglo-American neoliberalism and German-Austrian ordoliberalism. Fouskas argues that both are domestic public policies that are also imperialist projects. Each seeks to remake the internal social order of other states, and both are authoritarian in core. The article first surveys the theoretical lineage. It starts with Marx's accumulation theory and British imperial expansion, then covers Luxemburg, Hilferding, Bukharin and Lenin on the monopoly stage before 1914. Next come the post-1945 American school (Baran, Sweezy, Magdoff, Frank, Wallerstein) and Mandel and Poulantzas. It ends with Arrighi, Harvey, Gowan, Callinicos, Panitch and others on financialisation, globalisation and US imperialism. A final section applies the framework to the eurozone crisis. Fouskas's central move is to treat the core–periphery divide as analytical, not just descriptive, and to combine it with Baran and Sweezy's concept of surplus. Following Gowan, he describes neoliberalism as emerging after the collapse of Bretton Woods in 1971. In this account it rests on a "Dollar–Wall Street regime" and a hub-and-spoke power structure, with NATO tying Europe to the United States. He then argues that ordoliberalism is a German imperialist project in Europe. Its instruments are the Maastricht criteria, central bank independence, depoliticised economic rules and a currency union that denies peripheral members devaluation. On this reading Germany extracts surplus from the periphery, and Fouskas cites the European Central Bank's reported €7.8 billion profit on Greek bonds as an illustration. He adds that the eurozone crisis originated in Anglo-American financialisation, and that austerity has not delivered sustainable growth. Fouskas concludes that imperialism exports not only capital but also models of economic management and sociopolitical order, with open-door policies as its preferred tool. He holds that ordoliberalism lacks military capacity and a global reach, so European security remains under NATO and thus US control. Both projects are incompatible with democracy, and authoritarianism forms at home before spreading abroad. Read the original if you want a survey of Western Marxist imperialism theory that is directly applied to the eurozone, German hegemony and Greece.

Nancy Fraser's new theory of capitalist crisis 南希·弗雷泽的资本主义危机新论 Chen Liangbin Chen Liangbin examines Nancy Fraser's account of capitalist crisis in Capitalism: A Conversation in Critical Theory (2018), co-authored with Rahel Jaeggi. Writing against the background of the 2007 financial crisis, Brexit, the gilets jaunes and the populist revolt of 2016, Chen argues that Fraser rebuilds Marx's method into a "foreground–background" model. In this model the roots of crisis lie in structural splits between the economy and its non-economic conditions. Chen judges the result a stimulating but logically incomplete theory. The article has three parts. The first sets out Fraser and Jaeggi's four defining features of capitalism and the foreground–background method drawn from Capital. The second follows the history of crisis through four regimes (mercantile, liberal-colonial, state-managed and financialised capitalism) along three background dimensions: social reproduction, nature and politics. The third places the theory within Fraser's own development, within critical theory and among theories of crisis, and ends with critical questions. Chen reports that Fraser reads Capital as moving from exchange to exploitation and then to expropriation, the open confiscation of labour, land, resources and bodily capacities. She treats expropriation as the more basic condition of accumulation, and as a continuing process that also underlies racial and status divisions. Capitalism is thus a "institutionalized social order" whose separations (exploitation/expropriation, production/reproduction, human/nature, economy/politics) generate crises that economic accounts neglect. Chen links Fraser's shift from the earlier redistribution–recognition framework to this model to feminism's turn from identity politics towards structural critique, and to worries about populism. He or she finds Fraser closer to Harvey's accumulation by dispossession than to Marx's surplus-value theory of crisis. Chen concludes that Fraser belongs to a "de-orthodoxising" neo-Marxist current that seeks crisis causes outside the economy, as Lefebvre, Harvey, O'Connor, Foster and Baudrillard do. Chen credits its integrative breadth and its revival of political economy within critical theory. Chen also questions why only reproduction, nature and politics are chosen, how they relate logically, and whether foreground and background form a descriptive or an analytical distinction. Jaeggi raised similar doubts in the dialogue. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist assessment of Fraser's late work and its place among Western Marxist crisis theories.

Exchange abstraction and its Gestalt-transformation logic: on Sohn-Rethel's reconstruction of Western historical epistemology 交换抽象及其格式塔转换逻辑——论雷特尔对西方历史认识论的重构 Kong Ming'an Shi Fengge Commodity exchange, the authors say, is the core problem of Marx's Capital and still holds unfinished philosophical questions, such as the analysis of commodity fetishism. They examine the German philosopher Alfred Sohn-Rethel (1899–1990) and the concept of "exchange abstraction" in his late book Intellectual and Manual Labour: A Critique of Epistemology. The article argues that Sohn-Rethel traces exchange abstraction back to Kant's transcendental philosophy and the origins of Western epistemology, which makes commodity exchange a central philosophical issue. The article has three parts. The first sets out the meaning and features of exchange abstraction, which the authors treat as formal and as real. The second shows how exchange abstraction underlies "thought abstraction", with Kant's synthetic a priori judgement as the main foil. The third analyses three dimensions of exchange abstraction and the Gestalt transformation by which it passes into thought. The authors draw on Habermas, Žižek, Adorno and the Chinese scholar Zhang Yibing. The authors report that Sohn-Rethel treats Marx's "commodity abstraction" as exchange abstraction, not labour abstraction. Labour does not abstract itself. Exchange relations abstract labour, and reduce it to a purely quantitative magnitude of value. This abstraction is "real", arising in action and not in thought, and so differs in kind from the thought abstraction of natural science, though it resembles it in form. The three dimensions are the suspension of use, the stripping away of sensuous qualities, and the Gestalt transformation, a social synthesis that works unconsciously, behind the actors' backs. In this account Greek coinage gave rise to concepts such as Parmenides' "One". Capitalist money-as-capital then supplies the unity that Kant attributes to a transcendental subject. The authors compare the logic to Lacan's "object a" as read by Žižek. The authors conclude that Sohn-Rethel founds Kant's idealist epistemology on the materialist basis of exchange abstraction. They argue that this enriches the epistemology of historical materialism and addresses Habermas's complaint that Marx never assembled a materialist epistemology, though they do not fully agree with that complaint. They describe his analysis of the commodity form as the deepest and most detailed to date, and say its theoretical and practical significance is self-evident. Read the original if you want a Chinese-language account of Sohn-Rethel that links Marx's commodity analysis, Kant and Žižek's psychoanalytic reading, and shows how Sohn-Rethel is received in China.

György Márkus on the four forms of Marx's critical theory 乔治·马尔库什论马克思批判理论的四种形式 Yan Yan Yan Yan takes up the long dispute over whether Marx's thought is marked by a break or by continuity between the early and mature works. The article examines how the Budapest School theorist György Márkus (Georg Markus) answers it by distinguishing four forms of Marx's critical theory and dividing Marx's development into stages. Yan argues that Márkus's scheme helps explain both the unity and the heterogeneity of Marx's thinking, but that Márkus misreads Marx at several points. The article opens with the two versions of the "break" thesis, the Soviet account of the 1930s and Althusser's "epistemological break", and with the "continuity" thesis that arose against them. It then follows Márkus's stages in turn. These are the philosophical critique of political economy in the 1844 Manuscripts, a philosophically oriented critical economics in 1846–47, and a critique of capitalist political economy with a historical grounding in the Grundrisse and Capital. Yan interleaves Márkus's reading with his own corrections, drawing on Lukács, Kolakowski, Heller, Moishe Postone and Chinese scholars such as Zhang Yibing and Sun Leqiang. Yan accepts Márkus's point that the 1844 Manuscripts contain a tension between a realist philosophy of human finitude and a utopian practical orientation. Yan adds that two logics coexist there: a dominant humanist logic of alienated labour and an objective materialist logic from which historical materialism grew. Yan also endorses the claim that Marx's attitude to classical political economy moved from near-total rejection, through qualified acceptance, to critical inheritance. The central dispute is over the Grundrisse and Capital. Márkus holds that they belong to different critical forms, and that Capital stresses continuity between capitalism and socialism and slides into Hegelian teleology. Yan replies that both texts combine subject and object dimensions, differing only in emphasis. In Yan's reading the method of ascending from the abstract to the concrete does not oppose the essence-to-appearance method. Capital is anti-metaphysical, and Marx's necessity is historical rather than absolute. Yan concludes that Márkus's periodisation is a valuable reference for tracing the logic of Marx's development. Two merits are singled out: it treats early and late Marx as a whole through both philosophical and economic discourse, and it criticises both the break and the continuity theses. Yan warns that Márkus exaggerates the gap between the Grundrisse and Capital, and misreads Marx on form and content and on the realm of necessity. Read the original if you study Marx's intellectual development, the Budapest School or the philosophical interpretation of the Grundrisse and Capital, and want a Chinese scholar's critical assessment of Márkus.

A classic for understanding the origin and withering away of the state A reader's guide to The Origin of the Family, Private Property and the State 理解国家起源与消亡的经典著作 Ming Yi This is a reader's guide, published in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2020, to Engels's The Origin of the Family, Private Property and the State. Ming Yi presents the book as Engels's application of historical materialism to the state, one that explained how the family, private property and classes gave rise to the state and so greatly enriched Marxist political theory. The guide has three parts. It first sets out the book's background: it was written in March–May 1884 from Marx's notes on Lewis Henry Morgan's Ancient Society, and it was aimed at bourgeois theories of the state and at reformist currents in the workers' movement such as 'state socialism', 'socialism of the lectern' and the Fabians. It then summarises the nine chapters and their main doctrines. Finally it discusses the book's theoretical and historical significance and its relevance to China in the new era. On the book's content, Ming reports five points. The first is the theory of the two kinds of production, the production of the means of subsistence and the production of human beings themselves. The second is the historical sequence of family forms. The third is the origin of private property and classes through three great divisions of labour. The fourth is a theory of the state that treats it as a historical category arising from irreconcilable class contradictions. In this account the state divides its subjects by territory, holds a public power backed by force, and levies taxes. Its essence is class rule, expressed in slave, feudal and bourgeois forms. The fifth is the state's eventual withering away, which Ming says is conditional on highly developed productive forces and the abolition of private property and classes. Ming concludes that the work gives a scientific basis for analysing the state, democracy and rights. The author describes capitalist democracy as an indirect and concealed form of bourgeois rule. China's system, by contrast, is described as people's democratic dictatorship resting on public ownership. For the present day, Ming draws three lessons: family-building and gender equality, the long historical process of abolishing private property, and the need to strengthen rather than weaken state functions while socialism and capitalism still compete. Ming adds that class struggle still exists in China to some extent. Read the original if you want a concise, officially oriented introduction to Engels's text and to how it is applied to contemporary Chinese state theory.)

How is common progress of the world possible? The world-historical significance of the thought of a community with a shared future for mankind 世界共同进步何以可能？——人类命运共同体思想的世界历史意义 Di Yingna Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts (2020, no. 4), Di Yingna asks what the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind contributes to the world's common progress. The author argues that its significance cannot be gauged from international relations or diplomacy alone, and should be assessed from the wider standpoint of how we understand the laws governing human social history. In this reading, the idea is a theoretical response, developed since the 18th Party Congress (2012), to the question of what is wrong with the world and what should be done. The article is built around three shifts, each presented as a new contribution to understanding human development. The first concerns modernization, moving from a single model to plural paths. The second concerns the way of thinking about social development, moving from zero-sum games to win-win cooperation. The third concerns relations between civilizations, moving from one flower blooming alone to a hundred flowers in bloom. Di draws on Marx's Communist Manifesto and on remarks by Xi Jinping. On modernization, Di contends that some Western scholars treat Western priority in time as moral priority, so that only one modernization is possible. The author calls this a hegemony of discourse that denies non-Western countries the chance to find their own path. China's experience of independent exploration is presented as showing that every nation has the right to choose its own road. On thinking, Di holds that a Cold War mentality and the logic of the strong preying on the weak produce the belief that a strong country must seek hegemony, and that the postwar order served a few developed states. China's peaceful development and the Belt and Road Initiative are said to break this logic, and concerns about a Chinese threat are described as a misreading. On civilization, Di identifies capitalist cultural hegemony, which asserts barriers, hierarchy and inevitable clash between civilizations, as the central obstacle. The author argues that exchange and mutual learning are the alternative. Di concludes that the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind widens understanding of the paths to modernity, offers a cooperative way of thinking and promotes equal exchange among civilizations. These are described as the code for harmonious development and common progress. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a Chinese Party journal presents this concept as a contribution to historical materialism and to debates on modernization, global order and civilizational dialogue.

Grasping the broad trends of the world and of China: a reader's guide to Marx and Engels on China 把握世界和中国的发展大势——《马克思恩格斯论中国》导读 Wang Yi This is a reader's guide to the collection Marx and Engels on China, published in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2020. Wang Yi asks what Marx and Engels's scattered writings on China contribute to understanding modern Chinese history and China today. The author argues that their judgements remain practically important for grasping the Marxist standpoint, understanding the choices made by the Chinese people, and unwaveringly upholding the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The guide has three parts. The first sets out the historical conditions that drew Marx and Engels to China: its forced incorporation into the capitalist world market after the Opium Wars, the needs of proletarian revolutionary theory after the defeats in Europe, and Marx's work as a correspondent for the New York Daily Tribune. The second summarises five groups of their arguments. The third draws lessons for present-day China. In the second part, Wang presents Marx's analysis of China's economy as a combination of small-scale farming and household industry, which supported centralised autocracy and long-lasting stability until Western guns broke it open. Wang also reports Marx's exposure of the opium trade, his account of British, French and Russian aggression, and the Engels passage calling resistance a people's war to defend the nation. The guide ends this section with their predictions: the old system would collapse, China would influence world civilisation, and the Chinese people would eventually take the socialist road, which Marx and Engels imagined as a "Chinese republic". The third part applies these lessons to three areas. Wang says that China must be read within world history amid "changes unseen in a century", grasping both what has changed and what has not, notably the primary stage of socialism. It treats deepening reform as the answer to the lesson of backward productive forces and relations of production, and it links reform to modernising state governance. It calls for building a community with a shared future for mankind, opposing hegemonism, and staying alert to interference from some Western forces. Read the original if you want to see how a Party journal draws on Marx and Engels's writings on China to support current policy themes.

Several relationships to handle well in building a community with a shared future for mankind 构建人类命运共同体要处理好几对关系 Tao Wenzhao Writing in 2020, Tao Wenzhao takes up the question of how to build a community with a shared future for mankind at a time the article calls a period of changes unseen in a century. Tao argues that the project requires dialectical handling of three pairs of relationships: ideas and plans, seeking common ground while reserving differences, and harmony and change. Tao presents the ability to combine independence with opening up and to take part in global governance as one of the distinctive strengths of the Chinese system. The article is a short commentary in Red Flag Manuscripts, organised under three headings, one for each pair. Each section first treats the two poles separately and then explains why they must be held together. Tao draws on Party Congress documents, the 2018 constitutional amendment, speeches by Xi Jinping and classical Chinese sayings, and refers to the Belt and Road Initiative as an example of practice. In the first pair, Tao distinguishes the community as a Chinese idea, which answers what kind of world should be built and which is said to go beyond the law of the jungle, zero-sum games and the clash of civilizations. As a Chinese plan it has concrete goals (lasting peace, universal security, common prosperity, openness and inclusiveness, a clean and beautiful world) and the principle of consultation, joint contribution and shared benefits. In the second pair, shared interests and values are the goal, while diversity is the starting point, so tolerance is essential. Tao states that China will not export its model or interfere in others' internal affairs, and says conflicts should be resolved through dialogue. In the third pair, harmony is the basic method: China is described as a participant in and beneficiary of the existing international order, which it seeks to reform rather than overturn. Change is nonetheless unavoidable, including reform of global governance and of bodies such as the IMF and World Bank. Tao concludes that the community is a historical process that cannot be achieved at one stroke or without setbacks. It calls for firm commitment to change, careful control of its pace, shared benefits and gradual, sustained effort. Read the original if you want a compact, official-leaning exposition of how Chinese Party writers framed the community with a shared future for mankind in terms of idea, difference and reform of global governance.

Sensing the truth-power of Marxism: revisiting the Communist Manifesto 感悟马克思主义的真理力量——重温《共产党宣言》 Yan Lianfu Opening the new "Classics Guide" column of Red Flag Manuscripts (Hongqi Wengao) in 2020, Yan Lianfu rereads the Communist Manifesto as a text whose principles, in the author's view, have not become outdated. Yan argues that the Manifesto's scientific character, truth and predictive power are confirmed by the achievements of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The piece follows Xi Jinping's call for Communists to treat reading the classics as a habit and a spiritual pursuit. The article has four parts. It first explains why the Manifesto arose, then sets out the truths it expounds, then assesses its theoretical and historical significance, and finally draws lessons for the present. The historical section cites four conditions: industrial capitalism and the rise of the proletariat, the growth of the workers' movement, Marx and Engels's own intellectual development, and the founding of the Communist League, which commissioned the programme in 1847 and published it in February 1848. Yan holds that the Manifesto set out the scientific world view of Marxism. It covers historical materialism, class struggle, communism, all-round human development and world history. It also shows the contradiction between socialised production and private appropriation, the inevitability of capitalism's fall and the proletariat's historic mission. Yan highlights four features: the vanguard character of the proletarian party, the critical stance towards reactionary, conservative and utopian socialisms, and the "uninterrupted" revolutionary character of the movement. The article says the text turned the proletariat from a class "in itself" into a class "for itself", and treats the October Revolution and the Chinese Communist Party's path as its historical outgrowths. Yan draws four lessons for the new era. The Party should strengthen its own building and carry out the Party's self-reform. It should hold to the basic principles of scientific socialism while giving them Chinese features, and reject the "end of history" thesis and a single-line view of history modelled on the West. The Manifesto's theory of world history is said to supply the premises for a community with a shared future for mankind. Finally, Marxism must keep pace with the times through adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, with Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era as its latest achievement. Read the original if you want an example of how a Party-school scholar presents the Manifesto as a guide to current Party-building and ideological work.

The answer of our times to "what to uphold and consolidate, what to improve and develop" “坚持和巩固什么、完善和发展什么”的时代回答 Yan Xiaofeng Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in early 2020, Yan Xiaofeng reads the Decision adopted by the Fourth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2019) on upholding and improving the system of socialism with Chinese characteristics and modernizing the national governance system. Yan argues that the Decision answers a major political question: what to uphold and consolidate and what to improve and develop. In Yan's account, this answer extends the basic question of what kind of socialism to build and how to build it, and is a major innovation in combining the basic principles of scientific socialism with Chinese practice. The article has three parts. The first places the question within the development of socialism with Chinese characteristics and links the Fourth Plenum to the Third Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2013). The second sets out the "deep roots, notable strengths and systematic layout" of the institutional and governance system. The third lists three innovations that the Decision represents for the new era. Yan holds that institutions are the foundation of the state and governance is their effective application, so the new era's central task is to make the system more mature and settled. On the system's roots, Yan describes it as guided by Marxism, grounded in China, rooted in Chinese culture and supported by the people. On its layout, Yan notes the 13 areas the Decision lists and explains that the system should be more complete, more stable and more effective. Yan then draws three conclusions. The Decision strengthens the long-term institutional foundation of socialism with Chinese characteristics, sets the institutional axis for building a modern socialist country, and shows the strength of the system in the contest between two ideologies and two social systems. Yan cites the Soviet and East European experience of the 1980s and 1990s as a lesson, attributing the collapse to the lack of a developed system and effective governance. Yan concludes that upholding and improving the system and modernizing governance is the fundamental remedy for growing external pressure and risks, and a "sea-calming needle" for the long struggle until the second centenary goal. Yan sets the Decision's targets for 2021, 2035 and 2049 as a milestone on the new journey. Read the original if you want a representative Party-theorist reading of the Fourth Plenum Decision and the way it is tied to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era.

The fundamental system of upholding Marxism's guiding position in the ideological sphere 坚持马克思主义在意识形态领域指导地位的根本制度 Dong Xuewen This commentary, published in Red Flag Manuscripts (Hongqi Wengao) in 2020, reads a single formulation in the Decision adopted by the Fourth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2019) on upholding and improving the system of socialism with Chinese characteristics and modernizing national governance. Dong Xuewen focuses on the Decision's naming of "upholding Marxism's guiding position in the ideological sphere" as a "fundamental system" (genben zhidu), listed first among the requirements for developing advanced socialist culture. The author argues that this is a creative step, without precedent in Marxist intellectual history or earlier Party documents. After a short assessment of the Decision as a whole, Dong organises the piece in three parts. The first explains why the formulation is new and what "fundamental system" means. The second argues that the move advances the Chinese-adapted Marxist theory of culture. The third places the system within the Decision's framework of governance modernization and applies it to literature and art. Dong's central claim is that joining "guiding position" to "fundamental system" turns what had been a call at the level of theory into an institutional and practical rule tied to national governance. The author distinguishes the Decision's "important", "basic" and "fundamental" systems, and defines the last as the most important procedure or norm that everyone must follow. Such a system, Dong says, is rigid, allows no bargaining or selective compliance, and guides all other systems. The author links it to ideological security and to keeping leadership, administrative and discourse power firmly in Party hands. Dong cites the harm of historical nihilism as evidence that if the ideological line is breached, other defences are hard to hold. Tying the system to "modernization", Dong adds, shows that the view that Marxism is "outdated" is arbitrary and wrong. In literature and art, Marxist guidance is presented as the first standard for judging works and criticism. Dong concludes that the system is the top priority of cultural institution-building and must be implemented thoroughly. The author calls for correcting tendencies to ignore or dilute Marxism's guiding position, refuting challenges to it and exposing "two-faced" conduct. Marxism, in Dong's words, must not become a stage mask or cosmetic but a pointer and a weapon. Read the original if you want an example of how a Party-affiliated scholar interpreted the ideological provisions of the 2019 Plenum Decision and their application to cultural work.

The Gutian Congress Resolution and the foundation of the Party's system of centralised and unified leadership 《古田会议决议》与党的集中统一领导制度的奠基 Wang Junwei Marking the 90th anniversary of the Gutian Congress, Wang Junwei asks how the resolution adopted by the Ninth Party Congress of the Red Fourth Army on 29 December 1929 helped establish the Communist Party's system of centralised and unified leadership. Wang argues that the Gutian Congress Resolution laid the foundation of that system by fixing the Party's absolute leadership over the army, and that it still holds lessons for upholding and improving the Party's leadership system, as stressed at the Fourth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2019). The article has three parts. The first reconstructs the dispute inside the Red Fourth Army in 1929 over "who leads and whom to obey", including the Seventh and Eighth Party Congresses of the army, Mao Zedong's loss of the Front Committee secretaryship, and the Central Committee's "September letter". The second sets out what the eight-part resolution decided, especially its first section on correcting erroneous ideas within the Party. The third turns to the detailed rules and disciplines attached to those principles and to how they were carried out. Wang's central claim is that the resolution combined principle with concrete rules. Drawing on Mao's 1929 letter to Lin Biao, Wang lists the errors it targeted: weak Party leadership, a purely military viewpoint, small-group mentality, ultra-democracy, disregard for organisation and slack discipline. In response the resolution defined the Red Army as an armed body carrying out political tasks, placed Party branches at company level, introduced political commissars who countersign orders, and set the relations between military and political organs under the Front Committee. It also prescribed conditions for admitting members, rules for meetings, methods of Party education and propaganda, and the principle that a decision, once made, must be firmly carried out. Wang adds that the congress itself was possible only because the army's Party organisations deferred to the Central Committee's authority. Wang concludes that the resolution established the principle that the Party commands the gun, which Wang calls the "soul" of the people's army, and made it theoretical, institutional and standardised. Wang takes Mao's remark in January 1930 that the congress had "laid a foundation" as the essence of its historical standing, and presents it as a model of institution-building for implementing the Fourth Plenum today. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially oriented account of the Gutian Congress and its concrete rules on Party organisation, education and propaganda.

The international communist movement in 2018: change, adjustment and revival 2018年国际共产主义运动：变革、调整与复兴 Pan Jin'e Writing in 2019, Pan Jin'e surveys the international communist movement in 2018, a year that coincided with the 200th anniversary of Marx's birth and the 170th anniversary of the Communist Manifesto. The article argues that the movement was marked by change, adjustment and revival: socialist countries advanced reform steadily, communist parties elsewhere made strategic adjustments, and capitalist countries sank into institutional difficulties. The article opens with the worldwide commemorations of Marx, from socialist states (China, Vietnam, Cuba, Laos) to conferences and exhibitions in Russia, Japan, Germany, France, Italy, Portugal, Belgium and elsewhere. It then moves through three parts: reform in Vietnam, Cuba, North Korea and Laos; the activities of communist parties in other countries; and the crisis of capitalist states, including anti-globalisation, populism and the decline of European social democracy. On socialist countries, Pan reports Vietnam's central committee plenums on cadre building, the combining of the posts of general secretary and state president under Nguyen Phu Trong, and an anti-corruption drive reaching senior figures. Pan also describes Cuba's leadership succession and constitutional revision, North Korea's shift to concentrating on socialist economic construction and diplomacy, and Laos's Party-building measures. On other parties, Pan highlights the merger of two Nepalese communist parties, electoral gains and losses elsewhere, and repression of some parties. For capitalist countries, Pan treats the US–China trade conflict as rooted in rivalry between two political-economic models and in US internal problems, and reads "new Cold War" thinking as hegemonism. Mass protests such as the Yellow Vests are described as fragmented, decentralised movements in which communist parties had little guiding influence. Pan concludes that the achievements of socialism with Chinese characteristics over forty years confirm Marxism's scientific character and have helped world socialism begin to recover. Even so, the basic pattern of strong capitalism and weak socialism has not changed, and the struggle between the two systems now appears in trade and development-model disputes. The article leaves open how communist parties can lead spontaneous social movements, how socialist countries can reform without losing direction, how the movement's forces can cooperate, and what role China should play. Read the original if you want a dated, China-based overview of 2018 events across communist parties and socialist states, with the specific party congresses, plenums and electoral results it lists.

Tracing the sources of the shift in Russian public opinion on Stalin and the Soviet Union 俄罗斯民众对斯大林及苏联评价转变探源 Li Ruiqin Li Ruiqin asks why nostalgia for the Soviet Union and Stalin has grown in Russia the longer capitalism has lasted. The article starts from three events of 2018–2019: a Levada Centre poll in which 70 per cent of Russians credited Stalin with a positive role, the highest since 1991; the highest regret over the Soviet collapse in ten years; and a new Stalin statue in Novosibirsk. Li's answer is that the shift reflects dissatisfaction with present realities and a practical comparison of two social systems, not simple nostalgia. The article is built around four sections. The first compares Russia's economic standing with that of the USSR. The second examines poverty and inequality. The third sets Russia's difficulty with Western sanctions against the Soviet post-war recovery. The fourth reviews Levada survey data, the return of Stalin monuments and what Li reads as a revival of socialism. Evidence comes mostly from Russian polls, press reports and statements by Russian economists, historians and Communist Party figures. Li argues first that the USSR held second place in the world economy in 1990, while Russia in 2018 ranked twelfth. Li notes that Putin has repeatedly promised a top-five place without delivering. Second, the article draws on figures and commentary on poverty (about 20.3 million poor, mostly working people) and wealth concentration, including the economist Ruslan Grinberg's remark that the richest 3 per cent hold 89 per cent of financial assets. Li presents this as the result of rejecting "Soviet justice" and as evidence that capital's logic now governs. Third, Li holds that Stalin's leadership in the Great Patriotic War and the rapid post-war rebuilding explain why Russians credit him. Li also treats demonisation of Stalin as aimed at socialism and Marxism, and says rising approval of Stalin alongside falling trust in Putin signals discontent. Li concludes that the criterion for judging a development path is the sense of gain among the broad population. In this reading, Russians prefer the Soviet record because of the practical results of the two paths, not because of ideology. Li admits Stalin's grave errors, including the excesses of the purges, but presents rising approval as historical necessity and as evidence of a revival of Marxist scientific socialism, which Li sees as confirming Deng Xiaoping's prediction. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist interpretation of post-Soviet Russian opinion polls, with many Russian-language sources and economic data cited in support.)

Recent developments and characteristics of communist parties abroad 当今国外共产党的发展变化及其特点 Yu Haiqing How should one describe the state of communist parties outside China today? Yu Haiqing, writing in 2019, argues that no simple linear rise or decline fits. Using two reference points, the upheavals in the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe around 1989–91 and the 2008 international financial crisis, Yu describes a landscape in which recovery and decline, achievement and difficulty, cooperation and splits, setbacks and hope exist side by side. The article is organised around four paired assessments: organisational strength, parliamentary performance, left-wing unity and cooperation, and exploration of paths to socialism. It draws on membership figures and election results for parties in Asia, Africa, Latin America, the former Soviet and Eastern European region and developed capitalist countries. It also covers the ruling parties of Vietnam, Cuba, Laos and the DPRK. On organisation, Yu cites a fall from about 180 parties and over 40 million members to around 120 parties and 6 million after the Soviet and East European upheavals, and a partial recovery to about 130 parties and over 13 million members. Over 8 million of these belong to the four ruling parties, and only some twenty parties have more than 10,000 members. Gains in South Africa, Brazil and Russia contrast with sharp falls in the French, Italian and Spanish parties. Electoral breakthroughs, such as in Belgium, Portugal and Kazakhstan, are in Yu's view scattered and often short-lived, and in alliances communist parties are mostly subordinate. Cooperation has grown through international meetings and the Party of the European Left, yet disputes persist, including a rival grouping set up by the Greek and other parties. Yu sees no case of a successful peaceful, democratic transition to socialism. The author adds that armed struggle has lost influence, and that some parties, such as the Spanish and French, are adjusting strategy. Yu concludes that new practices and bright spots may become sources of growth, but uneven and unstable development means serious challenges and a need for theoretical rethinking and strategic adjustment. The author also notes a growing tendency to "look east" towards China, with parties studying its experience, supporting a community with a shared future for mankind and the Belt and Road Initiative, though they still need to integrate Marxism with their own national conditions. Read the original if you want a compact, data-rich account of foreign communist parties' membership, elections and alliances as seen from the Academy of Marxism in 2019.

Foreign communist and workers' parties on capitalist culture: critique and response 国外共产党和工人党对资本主义文化的批判与应对 Yu Weihai Gao Yun Opening with Xi Jinping's 2016 call for cultural confidence, Yu and Gao ask how communist and workers' parties outside China understand and respond to contemporary capitalist culture. They argue that these parties see the basic contradictions of capitalism as unchanged and see the bourgeoisie as pursuing cultural hegemony through ever more concealed means. Studying their views, the authors contend, deepens understanding of the features and harms of capitalist culture and strengthens confidence in the culture of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The article draws on party programmes and constitutions, statements at the International Meetings of Communist and Workers' Parties (Sao Paulo 2008, Beirut 2012, Istanbul 2015) and Chinese secondary studies. It has three parts: new features of capitalist culture as the parties describe them; the role of culture in capitalism's domestic rule and external expansion; and the parties' countermeasures. Cited parties include those of Australia, Italy (Rifondazione Comunista), Pakistan, Guyana, the United States, Germany, India (Marxist), Greece, Portugal and Brazil. Yu and Gao report that the parties identify four features: monopoly over mass media, intellectuals who lose their critical function and serve the bourgeoisie, commodified culture and consumerism, and discrimination and xenophobia. The parties are said to hold that culture is used to manufacture legitimacy at home through a "single thought", anti-communist campaigns and distorted accounts of the 2008 financial crisis. Abroad, they say, it is used to back extremist forces, stir ethnic and racial division, and promote "human rights above sovereignty" as cover for intervention. The parties' responses fall into three groups: strengthening ideological and political work (Marxist propaganda, party media and new media, party schools), adopting cultural policies that protect cultural identity and heritage and encourage exchange, and building public cultural institutions and independent media to resist ideological erosion. The authors conclude that, after the Soviet collapse and the long ebb of the socialist movement, capitalist states led by the United States have besieged socialism and communist parties ideologically. They hold that the foreign parties' Marxist critique forms an important part of the Marxist theory of contemporary capitalist culture. Recognising the features and harms of capitalist culture is presented as necessary for resisting the infiltration of Western "universal values" such as democracy, freedom and human rights. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic account of how foreign communist parties frame cultural struggle, with many citations to their programmes and international statements.

The threefold critique of the contemporary Russian critical school of Marxism for reviving socialism 当代俄罗斯马克思主义批判学派复兴社会主义的三重批判 Chen Hong Chen Hong introduces the contemporary Russian critical school of Marxism, a post-Soviet current that works without institutional or state support after 1991. The article asks how this school builds its case for reviving socialism and argues that the case rests on three critiques: of the sidelining of dialectics, of Soviet socialism, and of late capitalism. Each critique supplies, in turn, a methodological basis, a historical lesson and a realistic ground for a 'new socialism' distinct from that of the twentieth century. The article names Aleksandr Buzgalin, founder of the school and editor of the left-wing journals Alternatives and Problems of Political Economy, as its central figure. It also names Andrei Kolganov, Lyudmila Bulavka and Georgy Lobastov as core representatives. It is organised in three sections, one per critique, and ends with an overall assessment of the school and its self-descriptions as 'critical', 'innovative' and 'post-industrial' Marxism. Sources include Buzgalin and Kolganov's Global Capital and Ten Myths about the USSR, together with interviews with Buzgalin and Bulavka. In the first section, Buzgalin and Kolganov explain why dialectics is shelved: positivist research favours narrow empirical questions, 'expert' society serves global capital, and spiritual alienation encourages rejection of grand narratives. Against this they defend ascent from the abstract to the concrete and the unity of the logical and the historical as dialectics' first and second principles. In the second, the school's reappraisal of the October Revolution, the first five-year plan, collectivisation and Soviet culture treats the USSR as a first large-scale attempt to move beyond capitalism. In Buzgalin's formula it was a bureaucratically 'mutated' socialism. The lessons the school draws are to use market and capitalist elements only under broad supervision, not to make wealth the goal, and to keep officials accountable to the people. Chen faults the school for treating the market economy as exclusively capitalist, and contends that socialism with Chinese characteristics has already shown socialism can combine with markets. The third critique describes late capitalism as global capital hegemony. Its internal contradiction is that it must absorb communist elements yet fears them, and its external one is the centre–periphery divide. Chen concludes that the three critiques converge on reviving socialism understood as a non-linear transition from the realm of necessity to the realm of freedom. In this account socialism must end all forms of alienation and not only exploitation and private ownership, and it must free human creativity. Chen presents the school as a creative, non-dogmatic Marxism that responds to a changed 'post-industrial' era, and cites Xi Jinping on the value of foreign Marxist critiques of capitalism. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's overview of Buzgalin's school and its view of the Soviet legacy, or if you want to see how such Russian work is assessed from within Chinese Marxist scholarship.
