Ontology and ethics: basic problems in the political philosophy of the Western radical left 存在论与伦理学——西方激进左翼政治哲学理论的基础问题 Yin Shuguang Yin Shuguang takes up the "ontological turn" in Western radical left political philosophy. The question is whether political practice and a future community can be grounded in ontology, and whether ethics can be built directly into it. Yin argues that the turn rightly renews critical theory, but that it leaves three problems unresolved. These are the limits of general ontology for practice, the impossibility of expelling metaphysics, and the difficulty of embedding ethical concepts in ontology. The article first appeared in Foreign Theoretical Trends (2019, no. 5). The article opens with a survey of Badiou, Meillassoux, Deleuze, Agamben, Rancière, Negri, Mouffe, Italian hermeneutic Marxism, Žižek, Harvey, Soja, Nancy and Esposito. It then looks at the history of the relation between being and ethics, from Heraclitus, Plato and Aristotle through Christian theology, Kant, Hegel, Heidegger and Gadamer. A long section follows on Heidegger's later thought on Seyn and Ereignis, and on Derrida's différance. The final section turns to practical philosophy, covering Lukács's social ontology, Habermas and discourse theory, and Marx's concept of practice. Yin's central claim is that rejecting metaphysics does not remove the underlying question of being, which is how things appear and take form. In Yin's reading, Rancière, Deleuze, Agamben, Badiou and Žižek all still address this question of manifestation, even when they reject substance ontology. Yin treats Derrida's différance as an effort to unsettle being as presence that nonetheless stays inside the metaphysical questioning. Yin also contends that general ontological categories supply only formal ethical concepts, without the dialectical historical content of good, evil and freedom. The article sets this against proceduralism and political liberalism (Habermas, Rawls), which it says avoid philosophy and so leave real disputes untouched. Yin concludes that developing a practical materialist philosophy remains an important theoretical task. Yin reads Marx's concept of practice as extending Aristotle's, uniting labour, critique, revolutionary action and free creative activity, and uniting freedom with necessity. Against a scientistic reading of Marx, Yin argues that the will to resist capitalism, and the critique of fetishism and of abstract formal equality, require a philosophical anthropology. Communism, on this view, is a new ethical form of defining what humans are. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist assessment of post-structuralist and radical left ontology, with extended treatment of Heidegger, Derrida and Aristotle.

Critique and reconstruction of the structure of needs Agnes Heller's reading of Marx's theory of needs 需要结构的批判与重建 Yan Yan Yan Yan takes up Agnes Heller's early work The Theory of Need in Marx to ask what Marx's theory of needs can contribute to understanding the shift in China's principal contradiction. Writing in 2020, Yan notes that this contradiction is now framed as one between the people's growing need for a better life and unbalanced, inadequate development. The article argues that Heller's reading helps move attention from the quantity of needs to their quality, and clarifies what "a better life" and equality should mean. The article has two main parts and a short conclusion. The first reconstructs Heller's critique of the alienated structure of needs under capitalism, in four aspects: the inversion of means and ends, the inversion of quality and quantity, the impoverishment of needs, and the rise of private interest as the dominant social logic. The second sets out, following Heller, the structure of needs in the society of associated producers, drawing on Marx's Grundrisse, Capital, Critique of the Gotha Programme and Theories of Surplus Value. The conclusion draws three lessons for China. In Yan's account of Heller, capitalism produces ever more needs but subordinates them to capital's self-expansion, so that quantity overwhelms quality and people become one-sided. On this reading, workers rebel not because they are materially poor but because their rich qualitative needs go unmet. Heller also finds two different conceptions of labour in Marx: in the Grundrisse, labour becomes a primary life need, while in Capital it stays within the realm of necessity and survives as a social duty. In the associated-producers society, material needs fall to a secondary place, free time and individual capacities come to the fore, and Marx's rejection of egalitarianism follows from his refusal to turn qualitatively different needs into equal quantities. Yan concludes that China must combine the development of productive forces with attention to the diversity of people's needs, which include political, cultural, social and ecological needs. In Yan's view China stands at the start of the first stage of communism, so distribution according to labour and the law of value still apply. Equality should mean giving equal attention to each person's different needs, not equal amounts of wealth. Yan sees the Party's reformulation of the principal contradiction at the 19th Party Congress (2017) as reflecting this transformation in the structure of needs. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's use of Heller's Marxism to interpret Marx's theory of needs and to bear on current debates about the principal contradiction and equality.)

A renewed reflection on Hardt and Negri's Empire twenty years on A defence of Luxemburg's theory of imperialism 二十年后对哈特和奈格里的《帝国》再反思 Zhang Xiaolong Zhang Xiaolong asks how Michael Hardt and Antonio Negri's Empire (2000) relates to Rosa Luxemburg's theory of imperialism. Zhang notes that Chinese scholarship has moved from translating Hardt and Negri to interpreting and criticising their system, but has mostly ignored their critique of Luxemburg. The article argues that Hardt and Negri misread Luxemburg, and that her theory remains valid for understanding contemporary capitalism. The article has three parts. The first sets out what Hardt and Negri mean by Empire: a mode of state rule, a supreme power over the globalised world, and a constructed political order that supposedly succeeds the age of imperialism. The second answers three charges Hardt and Negri bring against Luxemburg. The third draws out the present-day value of her theory, setting her against Karl Kautsky, Lenin and Eduard Bernstein. Zhang argues that Hardt and Negri rely too heavily on politics and neglect capitalism's internal contradictions, the very thing Zhang takes to be fundamental to Marx. On the three charges, Zhang replies that Luxemburg developed Marxism rather than departing from it, since she answered the changed conditions of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Zhang also holds that her work was political economy and not only political critique, citing her writings on Poland's industrial development, her polemic with Bernstein and The Accumulation of Capital. Finally, Zhang denies that her critique was merely external: she began from the stagnation inside capitalist production and so derived imperialism from capitalism's own economic structure. In Zhang's account she differs from Kautsky, who treated imperialism as a contingent policy, and from Lenin, who in Zhang's reading saw it as a by-product and not an inner necessity. Zhang concludes that Luxemburg's theory is still an important means of analysing capitalism's present form, though Zhang concedes she overlooked the revolutionary potential of the wider masses and was less penetrating than Marx. Zhang says criticism of Hardt and Negri in China has often only spread their ideas, and urges that Luxemburg's theoretical contribution be put forward in response. Zhang also calls for Marxist theory to be used against Western claims that Marxism is outdated and that Lenin's and Luxemburg's theories of imperialism have been superseded. Read the original if you study Luxemburg, Hardt and Negri, or the Chinese reception of Western Marxist debates on imperialism.

Keep the original aspiration and mission firmly in mind and advance the Party's self-reform 牢记初心使命，推进自我革命 Xi Jinping This is a speech by Xi Jinping, General Secretary of the Communist Party of China, delivered on 24 June 2019 at the 15th collective study session of the Political Bureau of the 19th Central Committee. It was published in Qiushi, 2019 no. 15. The session was held during the Party-wide campaign of education on 'staying true to the original aspiration and keeping the mission firmly in mind'. Xi's central claim is that a long-ruling Party can keep its vanguard character, purity and popular support only if it holds to its founding aspiration and mission and keeps up the spirit of self-reform. Xi first frames the question of how a Party of a hundred years can retain its vitality and rule for the long term. He then grounds the Party's aspiration in Marxist theory and reviews its history through revolution, socialist construction, and reform and opening up. Next he assesses the situation since the 18th Party Congress (2012), sets out concrete tasks in the Party's political, ideological, organisational and conduct-and-discipline building, and gives guidance on four relationships. He ends with a call for leading cadres to set an example and with two passages from Mao Zedong. Xi argues that the Party's success rests on its steady pursuit of happiness for the Chinese people and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. He holds that forgetting this aim would change the Party's nature and cost it the people. He warns against complacency in the new era and says only the Party itself can defeat it. He says problems such as impurity in politics, thinking, organisation and conduct remain unresolved, and that the 'four tests' and 'four dangers' remain severe. He sums up self-reform as 'four selves': self-purification, self-improvement, self-renewal and self-elevation. He proposes four balances: strong central leadership with solving internal problems; keeping fundamentals with innovation; strict supervision with care for cadres; and organisational drive with individual initiative. He says self-reform must not weaken the Party's leadership and must accept supervision by the people. Xi concludes that leading cadres, especially senior ones, must take the lead in studying Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and in criticism and self-criticism. He says Political Bureau members should set the example for the whole Party. Citing Mao's 1949 warning that the road after revolution is longer, he presents the campaign as a lasting task for all members. Read the original if you want a primary-source statement of how the Party leadership framed self-reform and long-term rule at the start of the 2019 education campaign.

Reflections on creating "We Are Walking on the Great Road" 《我们走在大路上》创作感言 Wang Junwei Wang Junwei, writing in Qiushi in 2019, reflects on making the documentary series "We Are Walking on the Great Road", produced for the 70th anniversary of the People's Republic of China as a panoramic account of the country's journey. The author argues that, with so much material and limited running time, the series needed one unifying theme, and that this theme is the Chinese path. The piece describes how the production team chose this theme and then organised the episodes around it. It first explains the three-part treatment of the theme, then walks through how the episodes map onto three periods: socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the new era of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Wang says the team took Xi Jinping's remark that socialism with Chinese characteristics "did not fall from the sky" as the key to the series. The path is presented as having emerged from China's national conditions and long history, from persistent struggle, and from reliance on the people and shared development. For each period Wang names the episodes and the events they feature, for example land reform and major construction projects in the early decades, rural and urban reform in the reform era, and poverty alleviation and ecological themes since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Wang concludes that the series aims to evoke shared memory, tell the story of new China well and strengthen public confidence and pride in the Chinese path. Read the original if you want a short insider account of how an official documentary was structured and which narrative of the 70 years it was built to convey.

The important place and significance of the new era in the history of the Party and of New China 新时代在党史、新中国史上的重要地位和意义 Qu Qingshan Writing in 2019, the seventieth anniversary of the People's Republic, Qu Qingshan asks what the "new era" declared at the 19th Party Congress (2017) means within the history of the Party and of New China. Qu treats the two histories as largely overlapping, with Party history as the core of national history. The article's thesis is that the new era is at once an extension of the period of reform and opening up and the start of a new historical stage. The article is organised under three headings: the new era as an important component of Party and New China history, as an epoch-making new coordinate, and as a new milestone. Qu divides the history from 1921 into four periods, each with a keyword: revolution (1921–1949), construction (1949–1978), reform (1978–2012) and rejuvenation (from 2012 to the middle of the century). Qu first argues that the Party has carried two historical tasks since its founding: national independence and people's liberation, completed in 1949, and national prosperity and people's happiness, still unfinished. The four periods are then summarised as saving the nation, building it, enriching it and strengthening it, each laying the foundation for the next. Second, Qu grounds the new era in three objective factors: great changes in the world not seen in a century, China's stage of development, and a shift in the principal contradiction to one between the people's growing need for a better life and unbalanced and inadequate development. Third, Qu calls the new era the meeting point of the "two centenary goals" and describes the two-step plan to 2035 and mid-century, which brings forward the target of basically realising modernization by 15 years. Qu concludes that the new era will become a milestone alongside the founding of the Party, of the People's Republic, and of reform and opening up. Achieving this requires unwavering adherence to socialism with Chinese characteristics under Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, continued Party building through full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, and heightened vigilance against major risks. Read the original if you want an official Party-history framing of the periodisation from 1921 to the present and of how the new era is positioned within it.

Without a core, the Communist Party cannot win victory 没有核心，共产党就不能取得胜利 Pang Xianzhi Pang Xianzhi, in a short commentary in Qiushi (2019), takes up the Central Committee's opinion on strengthening the Party's political building. Pang argues that the most fundamental task is to strengthen the "Four Consciousnesses", above all consciousness of the core, and that a communist party cannot succeed without a correct and strong leadership core. The piece first treats whether a core is needed at all, drawing on the Party's history from the Zunyi Meeting through Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping. It then turns to why Xi Jinping is the core of the Central Committee and of the whole Party, listing seven qualities, and closes with a short assessment of his selection. Pang contends that proletarian and bourgeois parties differ in nature, and that before Mao became the core the Party's cause suffered repeated setbacks partly for lack of a mature, stable core. Pang credits Mao and Deng's core positions with the new China and with reform and opening up. For Xi, the seven qualities are: fidelity to and development of Marxism, expressed in Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era; a people-centred stance, including poverty alleviation; long-term vision; a global outlook, including the Belt and Road Initiative; attention to Party building and full and rigorous self-governance of the Party; decisiveness rooted in grassroots experience; and a grasp of Party and national history. Pang also claims Chinese leaders are chosen through layers of testing by the Party and the people, unlike American leaders chosen by money and rhetoric. Pang concludes that choosing Xi as General Secretary and core was correct and reflects the will of the whole Party and people. Pang adds that capable leaders are rare, especially in a severe and complex domestic and international situation, and must be cherished, supported and loved. Read the original if you want a brief example of how the Party's core-leadership principle was justified in official-journal commentary in 2019.

"Spark of Fire Can Start a Prairie Fire": a red classic written in blood and life 《星火燎原》：用鲜血和生命写就的红色经典 Li Jun Sun Jilian Published in Qiushi in 2019, this commentary introduces Xingxiao liaoyuan (literally "a single spark can start a prairie fire"), a multi-volume collection of memoirs of the Chinese revolutionary wars. The authors present it as a "red classic" and argue that it should be studied not for historical colour but to draw on its living political and moral energy today. The article first describes the origins of the work: a 1956 Central Military Commission call for writings marking thirty years of the People's Liberation Army, contributions from marshals and ordinary soldiers alike, and publication in eight volumes between 1958 and 1963. It then notes the Central Military Commission's Political Work Department's selected edition for the 70th anniversary of the People's Republic (2019), drawn from the 2009 complete edition. The core of the piece is a series of lessons the authors say the book teaches, each tied to named chapters. These are loyalty to the Party, firm ideals and convictions, fighting ability, innovation, fine work style and discipline, and close ties between army and people. The authors link these to present tasks: political army-building, the Two Upholds, the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, rule of the military by law, and anti-corruption work. The authors conclude that Party, national and military history is an inexhaustible spiritual treasure, and they call on readers to take up the torch from the older generation. They add that the selected edition comes with multimedia products such as audio, short videos and AR for younger readers. Read the original if you want an example of how Party media promote a revolutionary memoir as a tool of political and military education.

What the 70th anniversary of the founding of New China tells us 新中国成立70周年告诉我们什么 Yang Zhizhao Writing in Qiushi in 2019, Yang Zhizhao asks what seven decades of New China teach. The short commentary answers that only under the leadership of the Communist Party of China, on the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics, can the country grow strong, the nation be rejuvenated and the people become prosperous. Yang calls this an indisputable fact and an unshakeable truth. The piece moves from a comparison of past and present living standards to four ways in which, in Yang's account, Party leadership has given people dignity as well as material comfort. It closes with a call for responsibility directed at all citizens and at Party members and cadres in particular. Yang contrasts earlier worries about food and clothing with today's poverty reduction, 5G networks, widespread consumer goods and online services. The four gains are a rising international standing, linked to reform and opening up and the Belt and Road Initiative; stronger national capacity, shown in disaster relief such as the 1998 Yangtze floods and the 2008 Wenchuan earthquake; strong national defence; and sustained attention to cultural life, including promotion of core socialist values. Yang attributes the move from "standing up" to "becoming prosperous" to "becoming strong" to reform and opening up, the socialist path and the Party's original aspiration and mission. Yang concludes that building socialism with Chinese characteristics is everyone's responsibility, and that Party members and cadres should follow the Party closely, carry on revolutionary traditions and work towards the Two Centenary Goals and the Chinese Dream of national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Qiushi presented the 70th-anniversary narrative of Party leadership and popular gratitude.

The contemporary value of the May Fourth spirit 五四精神的当代价值 Wang Jianmin Writing for Red Flag Manuscripts in 2019, the centenary year of the May Fourth Movement, Wang Jianmin asks what the May Fourth spirit means for China today and how it should be defended against reinterpretation. The article argues that the spirit's contemporary value lies in young people in the new era internalising and putting it into practice. It also holds that attempts to deny the Movement's significance amount to historical nihilism and must be corrected. The piece is framed by Xi Jinping's April 2019 statements: his call at a Politburo study session for more research on the Movement, and his speech at the centenary meeting on 30 April. It has two parts. The first sets out the content of the May Fourth spirit and its present-day value. The second criticises historical nihilism on the question of the Movement and closes with practical remarks on how to pass the spirit on. Wang defines the spirit as patriotism at its core, with opposition to feudal culture and acceptance of progressive ideas as its value pursuit, democracy, science and progress as its essence, and emancipating the mind and pursuing innovation as its soul. On this basis the article presents it as strengthening young people's patriotism, serving as a vehicle for cultivating and practising the Core Socialist Values, and driving the Chinese Dream. It is also described as a source for the Four-sphere Confidence and as nourishment for young Marxists. In the second part, Wang describes historical nihilism as presenting itself as academic reassessment while pursuing a political aim of discrediting revolution and the Communist Party. The article rejects claims that the Movement was a bourgeois revolution led by the national bourgeoisie or instigated by the Beiyang government. It cites Xi's characterisation of the Movement as a patriotic, anti-imperialist and anti-feudal revolutionary movement and calls for a historical-materialist method. Wang concludes that the state, society and individuals should treat history scientifically, resist historical nihilism and keep developing the May Fourth spirit. Young people, in Wang's view, show patriotism by doing their own work well and becoming useful talents. Wang also names current shortcomings in transmitting the spirit: formalism, failure to keep pace with the times, weak clarification of misunderstandings and inadequate guidance. Read the original if you want a compact example of how the 2019 official narrative of May Fourth was presented and defended in Party-theory writing.

The political drivers behind the "Chinese miracle" “中国奇迹”背后的政治动因 Hong Wen Published in Red Flag Manuscripts (Hongqi Wengao) in 2019, this short commentary asks which theory can explain China's development achievements over seven decades. The author (the byline "Hong Wen" may be a pen name) argues that Western neoliberals, who expected economic liberalisation to bring political liberalisation and democratisation, have repeatedly misread China. In the article's account, the decisive explanation lies in politics: the leadership of the Communist Party and the political path of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The piece has three sections. The first, on political leadership rooted in national conditions, surveys the Party's revolutionary role and the policy turns since reform and opening up. The second discusses China's democratic practice, comparing it with Western electoral and multiparty systems. The third places the "Chinese miracle" in the context of what it calls great changes unseen in a century, and presents a "win-win" philosophy in foreign relations. The author's central move is to treat Party leadership as the fundamental guarantee of achievement, citing the shift to economic construction, the restoration of the line of "emancipating the mind and seeking truth from facts", the Party's basic line, the "three-step" strategy and the Five-Year Plans. The author then contends that no "universal" democracy exists, and that China's consultative democracy, the multiparty cooperation system under the Party, regional ethnic autonomy and "one country, two systems" suit Chinese conditions. Western universal suffrage, multiparty competition and the separation of powers are described as producing social division, polarisation and inefficiency. Finally, the article borrows the label "civilisational state" and says its essence is a "people-centred" orientation, which it links to peaceful development rather than zero-sum games. The author concludes that the fundamental political driver of China's miracle is the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics and the political advantage expressed in the claim that Party leadership is its most essential feature. The author also holds that the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation is consistent with world peace and common development. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a 2019 Party journal presented the political explanation for China's economic record and its contrast with Western democracy.

Why the Communist Party of China is able to create miracles 中国共产党为什么能够创造奇迹 Wang Chuanli Why has the Communist Party of China repeatedly recovered from near-destruction? Wang Chuanli opens with a view he attributes to many foreign observers: that the Party grows stronger under setbacks and keeps producing seemingly incredible achievements. Wang's answer is that these outcomes follow from the Party's own distinctive strengths, which the article sets out as six advantages. The article first lists episodes that Wang presents as miracles. They include survival after the Kuomintang massacre of 1927, the Long March after the five encirclement campaigns, and the Party's resilience after the collapse of the Soviet Union and Eastern European socialism. Wang adds that reform and opening up continued, and that the Party handled the 1997 Asian financial crisis, the 1998 floods, the 2008 Wenchuan earthquake and the global financial crisis. Wang then devotes a section to each advantage: its members, its theory, its relations with the masses, its organisational structure, and its traditions, style and discipline. Wang argues that the Party's members are exceptionally able and selfless. Examples include figures of privileged origin who gave up wealth, and models such as Jiang Zhuying, Wang Jinxi, Jiao Yulu and Kong Fansen. Wang describes the Party as a learning party that treats Marxism as a guide to action rather than dogma, and credits its Party school system and repeated study campaigns, from Yan'an rectification to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The Party's ties to the people are likened to the giant Antaeus drawing strength from the earth. Wang cites Mao Zedong's line on the masses as the true bastion of iron and Deng Xiaoping's account of the early 1960s hardship years. Its organisation is said to reach every sector, to rest on the principles that the Party manages cadres and commands the gun, and to have mobilised 87 million members for special Party dues after the Wenchuan earthquake. Wang concludes that the Party's capacity for criticism and self-criticism, its united front, its internal democratic centralism and its refusal to tolerate corruption explain its vitality. Wang cites the execution of Liu Qingshan and Zhang Zishan, and the present full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, as evidence that fighting corruption makes the Party stronger and more trusted. The article presents continuous self-reform as the way the Party stays vital. Read the original if you want an example of how a 2019 Party-journal piece explains the Party's record through its own qualities, in a popular and celebratory register.

The adoption of the unitary form of state structure in new China and its great significance 新中国单一制国家结构形式的确定及其重大意义 Sha Jiansun Why did the People's Republic choose a unitary rather than a federal state structure, and what does that choice mean? Sha Jiansun, in a piece first published in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2019, argues that the choice came from a process of exploration and accumulated practical experience. In Sha's account, a unitary state combined with regional ethnic autonomy fits China's basic national conditions and the fundamental interests of all its peoples. The article opens by defining state structure as one of the two main aspects of state form, alongside the form of government, and distinguishes unitary from federal systems. It then sets out the four basic institutions of new China: the state system, the people's congress system, the unitary multi-ethnic state with regional ethnic autonomy, and the multi-party cooperation system under Communist Party leadership. The historical narrative runs from the Party's Second National Congress (1922) to the 1949 Common Programme, the 1952 Outline for implementing regional ethnic autonomy, the 1954 Constitution and the current Constitution. Sha notes that the Second Congress, lacking its own experience, followed the Soviet model and called for a Chinese federal republic. Experience then changed the Party's view: a 1947 directive on Inner Mongolia stated that the autonomous government was not independent. Sha reports Li Weihan's reasons to Mao Zedong in 1949: ethnic minorities were about 6 per cent of the population against 47 per cent in the Soviet Union, they lived in scattered and interspersed settlements, and China's peoples had united equally in revolution without ever separating. Zhou Enlai added that imperialist designs on Tibet, Xinjiang and Taiwan made it necessary to name the state a republic, not a federation, while still granting autonomy. Sha stresses that regional ethnic autonomy can exist in either system, and that China's operates within a unitary state. Sha concludes that this structure secures national unity and ethnic solidarity and territorial integrity, and mobilises all peoples while allocating resources on a nationwide basis. It also guarantees ethnic equality and lets minorities manage their own affairs, which Sha calls one of the basic paths to developing people's democracy. Sha argues that upholding and developing it is part of maintaining confidence in the system. Read the original if you want a short, document-based official account of how the unitary state and ethnic regional autonomy were settled in 1949.

Marxism and the fate of the Communist Party of China are closely bound together 马克思主义与中国共产党命运紧紧相连 Han Xiping Writing in Hongqi Wengao in 2019, as the Communist Party of China (CPC) approached its 98th year, Han Xiping asks why the Party rose from a few dozen members to the world's largest party and led the Chinese people from standing up, to growing prosperous, to growing strong. Han's answer is that the Party has consistently held Marxism as its guiding ideology, kept developing it, advanced the adaptation of Marxism to Chinese conditions, and pursued theoretical innovation on the basis of practice. The piece is a historical survey in four steps. It covers the introduction of Marxism to China around the 1920s and the founding of the Party in 1921. It then treats the Party's wartime and revolutionary experience, including the proposal of the "Sinicization of Marxism" in 1938. Next it turns to the reform-era theoretical system, from Deng Xiaoping Theory to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. It ends with practical tasks for studying that thought. Han argues that Marxism, as a scientific theory, answered the needs of a China in which peasant, landlord and national-bourgeois efforts had failed, and that the October Revolution made its arrival possible. Han presents the Party's early setbacks, which the article attributes to dogmatism and mechanical copying of Soviet and Comintern experience, as proof that Marxist principles must be combined with Chinese reality. In Han's account, Mao Zedong's rural-based revolutionary path and the 1938 proposal produced Mao Zedong Thought. Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents, the Scientific Outlook on Development and Xi Jinping Thought are each presented as answers to a major question of their era, and as successive outcomes of the same method. Han concludes that the Party's history is in essence a history of Marxism spreading in China and being combined with Chinese practice. Han describes Xi Jinping Thought as the latest result of this process and as "Marxism of contemporary China, Marxism of the twenty-first century". Han calls for arming the whole Party with it through study of the Outline for Study, reading it alongside earlier theoretical achievements, and wider outreach through lecture groups and media. Read the original if you want an example of the official Party narrative linking Marxism, the Party's history and the study of Xi Jinping Thought.

Trump, the Republican Party and Westmoreland County 特朗普、共和党和威斯特摩兰县 Margaret Power This is a Chinese translation of an article by the US author Margaret Power (the name is given in Chinese as 玛格丽特·鲍尔). It asks why Westmoreland County, Pennsylvania, moved from a Democratic stronghold to a Republican one. Trump took 63.5% of its vote in 2016. The author, who grew up in the county, argues that the shift reflects economic restructuring, the decline of unions and generational change. Above all, in the author's view, it reflects white supremacist ideas and conservative social values. The article opens with a visit to a Trump merchandise shop and an account of the county's 2016 result. It then reviews the county's history from the coal-and-coke boom of the 1880s–1920s, through the Ku Klux Klan and the New Deal, to the factory closures of the 1980s. It turns to the rise of local Republicans, the Mellon-funded media and the Tea Party, then to the 2016 campaign and the March 2018 special election in Pennsylvania's 18th district. Power draws on interviews with local Republican officials and activists. Power describes a county that is 95.3% white (2010 census) and was held by the Democrats from 1932 until 2000 largely through union loyalty. When mills closed, she argues, workers lost the shared identity and 'emotional community' that unions gave them. Non-union jobs and large Protestant churches filled the gap. Her interviews show children of union Democrats accepting Reagan-era stories about welfare recipients and presenting themselves as the 'deserving poor'. They also show a fear of 'others' (Black people, non-white immigrants, Muslims) that she says joins economic anxiety with status anxiety. She reports that Trump's women supporters set aside his treatment of women in favour of border security, a strong military and 'making America great again'. Power concludes that Trump's election and policies rest on real economic, social and political foundations at home. She holds that white supremacy and conservative values were decisive, though economic change contributed. She admits she does not know whether such voters can change. She says she changed after being pushed to learn about other people's lives, and she calls for building awareness of other racial, gender and national groups, so that they are seen as a 'resource' and not a threat. Read the original if you want a detailed local case study, based on interviews, of how deindustrialisation and racial attitudes fed Republican support in a white working-class area of the US.

The fundamental guide to a new era of socialist ecological civilization: studying Xi Jinping Thought on Ecological Civilization 走向社会主义生态文明新时代的根本指针——深入学习习近平生态文明思想 Yang Huang Yang Huang presents Xi Jinping Thought on Ecological Civilization, systematically summarised at the National Conference on Ecological and Environmental Protection in May 2018, as the fundamental guiding principle for China's green development and the building of a "Beautiful China". The article argues that the thought is rooted in China's realities, draws on traditional Chinese ecological wisdom and the experience of other countries, and uncovers general laws governing the development of ecological civilization. It also treats the thought as an integral part of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The article has four parts. The first places the thought in intellectual and practical context: Chinese tradition, Marxist ecological views, the rise and fall of past civilizations, and China's current environmental problems. The second sets out its core content in six principles. The third identifies its distinguishing features. The fourth describes its strategic framework and practical levers, including the five systems of ecological civilization, green development and the campaign against pollution. Yang's central claim is that the thought develops Marxism's view of nature. It continues Engels's warning about nature's retaliation and extends Marx's theory of productive forces through the formulas "lucid waters and lush mountains are invaluable assets" and "protecting the ecology is protecting productive forces". Yang adds that only socialism, with its capacity to concentrate resources, can truly resolve the contradiction between humanity and nature. The article ties the thought to the changed principal contradiction of the new era, in which demand for a beautiful environment has become part of people's aspirations for a better life. It says the six principles, from harmonious coexistence between humanity and nature to jointly building global ecological civilization, show a historical outlook, a people-centred stance and scientific methods such as bottom-line and systems thinking. Yang concludes that building ecological civilization requires a cultural system, an ecological economy, accountability for officials judged by more than GDP growth, strict institutions and rule of law, and an ecological security system. The article adds that development remains essential, but must take a green form and be unified with environmental protection. It calls for winning the battles for clean air, water and soil, and for improving rural living environments. Read the original if you want a clear exposition of the official 2018–19 framing of Xi's ecological thought and of how it is tied to Marxist theory and Chinese tradition.

Cuba's 60 years of building a cultural power: experience and lessons 古巴60年来创建文化强国的经验及启示 Mao Xianglin Marking the 60th anniversary of the Cuban Revolution in January 2019, Mao Xianglin asks why a small, economically underdeveloped socialist country of 11.22 million people has survived decades of US pressure. The article argues that one important reason is Cuba's effort to build itself into a cultural power (wenhua qiangguo). It holds that Cuba, before 1959 marked by a colonial culture, has since become what the author calls a recognised power in education, medicine, sport and culture, and describes this as a miracle. The article draws four lessons from Cuban experience. They are a balanced policy towards intellectuals that combines leniency and strictness; making the quality of people's cultural life a goal of the revolution, so that the people move from practising culture to creating it; the need for struggle in building socialist culture; and faithful inheritance of Cuba's revolutionary cultural tradition in order to foster cultural confidence. Mao draws on Fidel Castro's 1961 speech to intellectuals, the 1975 Party programme, the 1976 constitution, and Cuban statistics on literacy, libraries, publishing and broadcasting. On intellectuals, Mao presents Castro's formula "within the revolution, everything; against the revolution, nothing" as a guiding principle written into Party and state policy, and says Cuba has kept a relaxed social atmosphere despite strict politics. The author concedes a leftist deviation in the late 1960s and early 1970s, the "grey five years". Mao defends the handling of the Heberto Padilla case and the 2003 arrest of 75 dissidents, arguing that both rested on espionage or national-security charges, not on dissent, and disputes Western media figures on political prisoners. On struggle, the article describes four ideological campaigns: the 1980s rectification process, the mid-1990s campaign, the return of the boy Elián González in 2000, and the 2002 constitutional amendment declaring socialism irrevocable after dissidents' petition. On tradition, Mao points to Cuba's retention of its national name, flag and anthem, and to the inclusion of José Martí's and, in the 2019 constitution, Fidel's thought among guiding ideas. The article also notes the spread of Cuban literacy campaigns to left-led Latin American governments and its teachers and doctors abroad. It concludes that these achievements stem from the Party and state's high priority on socialist culture. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's favourable account of Cuban cultural policy, including its treatment of intellectuals and dissidents, and the lessons drawn for socialist cultural construction.

The US trade war in the eyes of foreign scholars: "Make America Great Again" or deeper crisis? 外国学者眼中的美国贸易战——“让美国再次伟大”还是深陷危机？ Gan Haixia Writing in World Socialism Studies (2019, no. 4), Gan Haixia reviews how foreign scholars, mostly critical or Marxist, have interpreted the trade wars Donald Trump launched against US allies and China under the slogan "Make America Great Again". The article asks what kind of war this is, why the United States started it, what it is likely to produce, and where capitalism is heading. It reports the scholars' view that the war will leave the US deeper in crisis rather than "great again", and that neoliberalism is nearing its end. Gan then judges the scholarship scientific and critical but lacking totality, thoroughness and constructiveness. The article has four parts. It first discusses the nature of the trade war, then what lies behind it, then the predicted outcome and the future of capitalism, and ends with Gan's own assessment. It draws on figures such as Chad Bown and Douglas Irwin, Leo Panitch and Sam Gindin, Michael Roberts, Martin Wolf, Nicole Aschoff, Joseph Choonara, Nancy Fraser, John Bellamy Foster, Richard Baldwin, Edward Luce, Alex Callinicos and David Kotz. In the account Gan reports, the trade war is first a replay of old protectionist thinking, comparable to the Smoot-Hawley tariffs and to the Reagan-era response to Japan's rise. Roberts ties free trade or protectionism to the profitability of capital. It is also a "circus performance" that distracts from the real causes. Behind it, the scholars see a "Long Depression" (Roberts's term) that has never really ended, a political crisis of which Trump is a symptom rather than a cure, and an effort to restore imperial hegemony. Foster, for one, describes this effort as neo-fascist. The scholars predict that tariffs will not revive industry or jobs, will endanger the dollar's dominance, and will isolate the US. They conclude that Trump's election and similar revolts signal the collapse of neoliberal hegemony, though they cannot say when it will end. Gan credits the scholars with scientific method: they compare historical cases, look beyond appearances and dare to forecast. Gan faults them on three counts. Their analysis does not grasp the whole organism of US capitalism. It stops short of tracing the trade war to the contradiction between private appropriation and socialised production, and to the competition between capitalist and socialist systems and between neoliberalism and Marxism. And it offers no constructive solution, only abstract calls for progressive forces to act. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist academic's survey of Western left interpretations of the Trump trade war, together with the official-leaning critique of their limits.

Upholding the dialectical materialist worldview and remoulding one's worldview 坚持辩证唯物主义世界观与改造世界观 Hou Huiqin Writing in World Socialism Studies (2019), Hou Huiqin argues that the worldview with which the Party arms itself is the touchstone separating genuine from false Marxism, and that dialectical materialism must be upheld unwaveringly. The article contends that a current of anti-materialist thought, which stigmatises materialist philosophy, now threatens this position, including inside the world socialist movement. The article has four parts. It first places today's struggle over worldview in the context of Lenin's fight against empirio-criticism and the 'return to Kant' in early twentieth-century Russia. It then turns to Chinese intellectuals and the task of building a philosophy and social science with Chinese characteristics. The third part analyses the 'practice turn' in Marxist philosophy, and the last draws on Mao Zedong and Xi Jinping for ways to transform intellectuals' worldviews. Hou's central claim is that the Western 'existential turn', which claims to transcend epistemology, separates practice from the theory of knowledge, denies material ontology and dissolves the basic question of philosophy, thereby restoring idealism's dominance. Hou says that the Chinese call for a 'practice turn' or 'practice ontology' in Marxism repeats this move. In Hou's account, practice is not itself the ground of the world. It has a materialist meaning only when it is explained through materialism, as Lenin held against Mach. Marx, on this reading, reached his theory of practice after a materialist turn and shared Feuerbach's view that nature sets the limits of human reason. Hou therefore treats the dialectics of nature as the foundation, and says that attacks on it since the 1980s prepared the ground for practice ontology. Hou also holds that liberal individualism among intellectuals, including some Party members, obstructs political identification with socialism with Chinese characteristics. Hou calls for deeper criticism of idealism, renewed study of Marxist materialism and of the dialectics of nature, and conscious remoulding of worldviews. Following Mao, Hou says that no ideological vacuum exists, that a climate for studying Marxism must be created against 'de-ideologisation', and that intellectuals must stay close to the people and to production. Read the original if you want a detailed example of the argument within Chinese Marxist philosophy that defends materialist ontology against the 'practice turn' and ties it to Party ideological work.

The thought of a community with a shared future for mankind as inheritance and development of the theory of the "Three Worlds" 人类命运共同体思想是对“三个世界划分”理论的继承和发展 Liu Runwei Liu Runwei asks how the thought of a community with a shared future for mankind, which the article treats as part of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, relates to Mao Zedong's earlier theory dividing the world into three. Liu's thesis is that the community idea is the theory's logical inheritance and development, and its "theoretical form" in the new era. The short piece has three parts. It first sets out four layers of meaning in the community idea. It then compares the idea with the three-worlds theory and sketches the historical eras behind each. Finally it urges that the idea be put into practice. Liu reads the community's goal as the same ideal as communism, put in different words. Liu also names hegemonism as the most fundamental real threat to it. The article summarises the three-worlds theory as a judgement of the world pattern, a statement of China's place as a socialist developing country that will never seek hegemony, and a set of foreign-policy principles including the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence. Liu argues that the community idea shares each element. On Liu's account, the earlier theory suited an era of US–Soviet rivalry and capitalist temporary ascendancy. After the Soviet and East European upheavals, Liu sees an era of declining imperialism and reviving world socialism. In it, US power is isolated and world power is dispersing, which Liu calls changes unseen in a century. Liu says this makes the community idea timely and helps build a wider anti-hegemonist united front, especially with the "second world" of developed countries. Liu concludes that the idea must be carried out unwaveringly. Since the 18th Party Congress (2012), Liu says, the leadership has put diplomatic emphasis on the third world, citing the Belt and Road Initiative and the China–Africa and China–Arab forums. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a Chinese scholar ties current diplomatic doctrine to Maoist-era theory.

Building a community with a shared future for mankind: a banner leading the world in meeting present challenges and moving towards the future 构建人类命运共同体：引领世界应对当前、走向未来的旗帜 Zheng Keyang Writing five years after Xi Jinping first put forward the initiative, Zheng Keyang asks why the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind has won such wide support, and what answer it gives to what the author calls the global question of the age. Zheng presents the concept as a union of theoretical and practical innovation. In Zheng's account, it ties the development of socialism with Chinese characteristics to China's work with other peoples on global challenges. The piece begins with the international setting: a new round of technological and industrial change, shifts in the balance of power, and what Zheng describes as hegemonism, power politics, protectionism and unilateralism led by the United States. It then traces the concept from Xi's 2013 speech in Moscow into a system of goals, principles and pathways, and cites the Belt and Road Initiative, the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, BRICS and UN resolutions as evidence of growing recognition. Zheng also answers critics, rejecting charges that the Belt and Road amounts to a 'Chinese invasion' or a 'debt trap'. Zheng's core argument gives four reasons for the concept's appeal, drawn from Xi's diplomatic thought. First, China is a socialist country led by the Communist Party, and the reform-era achievements are described as the work of adapting socialism to Chinese conditions, so the concept extends domestic policy outward. Second, Chinese culture values harmony, and China's modern experience of aggression is said to make it oppose bullying, so that a strong China will not repeat the Western pattern of the powerful seeking hegemony. Third, the Party's people-centred stance is held to apply to foreign policy, making the Chinese Dream compatible with other nations' dreams. Fourth, Zheng argues, China keeps its word in international agreements, a trust that Belt and Road cooperation is said to deepen. Zheng concludes that the project is an unprecedented, long-term undertaking that will meet uncertainties and risks and will need generations of common effort. Developed countries are urged to take on more responsibility, and developing countries to do what they can. Zheng states that China will contribute to reforming global governance and remain a builder of world peace, a contributor to global development and a defender of the international order. Read the original if you want an example of how the community with a shared future for mankind was explained in Chinese Party-theoretical writing in 2019, including its rebuttals of Western criticism.

The valuable experience of the Comintern 共产国际的宝贵经验 Gennady Zyuganov This text is a Chinese translation of an article by the Russian communist leader Gennady Zyuganov, written for the centenary of the Communist International (Comintern) in 2019. It asks what the Comintern's 24 years left to the communist movement today. Zyuganov argues that it joined Marxism-Leninism to the workers' movement worldwide, helped found proletarian parties, strengthened international working-class solidarity and mobilised people against imperialism and fascism. He also credits it with raising colonial national liberation movements to a new level. The article is a chronological survey. It begins with the Communist League (1847), the First International (1864–1876) and the Second International (1889), which Zyuganov says collapsed into opportunism and social chauvinism in 1914. It then follows the Bolsheviks' road to a new International through the Zimmerwald and Kienthal conferences, and walks through the Comintern's congresses from 1919 to the Seventh in 1935. It ends with the dissolution in 1943 and later forms of party cooperation. Zyuganov's central claim is that Lenin's line steered the Comintern through changing conditions. He reports the Second Congress's twenty-one conditions of admission and its resolution linking proletarian and colonial struggles. He cites the shift after 1921 from offensive slogans to winning a majority of workers and building a united workers' front. He also describes the Seventh Congress's definition of fascism and its People's Front policy, which in his account shaped anti-fascist movements in France, Spain and China. He presents the Comintern's dissolution as justified by the parties' maturity and the wartime need for independent tactics, and treats Trotskyism as a counter-revolutionary current the Comintern exposed. Zyuganov says the Comintern laid the groundwork for later communist victories and the world socialist system. He blames later damage on bureaucratisation, dogmatism, the Sino-Soviet split, Eurocommunism and the Soviet collapse. He points to China, Vietnam, Laos, Cuba, North Korea and Latin America's left governments as evidence that socialism endures. Because global capital has dropped the masks of "democracy" and "human rights", he calls for closer ties among communist parties, a task he says only parties firmly committed to socialism can carry out. Read the original if you want a Russian communist leader's own account of the Comintern and of how it bears on today's international communist coordination.

Carrying forward the "May Fourth spirit" and the direction of the youth movement: striving to realise the "original aspiration" and fulfil the "mission" 发扬“五·四精神”，坚持青年运动方向，为实现“初心”、完成“使命”而奋斗 Ge Yuanren Writing for the centenary of the May Fourth Movement in 2019, Ge Yuanren asks whether the path of integrating young intellectuals with workers and peasants, which Mao Zedong set out in 1939 as the "direction of the youth movement", still matters today. The article answers that it does. In the author's view, the path was needed in wartime and remains needed in peacetime, and it must continue until the Party's "original aspiration" and "mission" are finally achieved. Ge adds that the question bears on the ideological security of the socialist state and the political security of the Communist Party's governing position. The article has three parts. The first presents the May Fourth Movement as an anti-imperialist, anti-feudal patriotic movement led by young intellectuals with workers and peasants as its main force, and treats the founding of the Communist Party as one of its main results. The second part defends the rural "sent-down youth" (zhiqing) movement of the first three decades of the People's Republic, citing the 1955 cooperative-movement episodes and Mao's remark that the countryside is a "vast world". The third part argues for the path's present relevance and cites Xi Jinping's speeches and the careers of several academicians who were once sent-down youth. Ge's central claim is that the dispute over this path is a struggle between proletarian ideas of hardship and service to the people and feudal and bourgeois ideas such as "those who excel in study become officials" and contempt for manual labour. Ge says that these older ideas survive among students and that many young people have been taught to put themselves first and money above all. Ge holds that reform-era achievements have not abolished the "three major differences" (between town and country, worker and peasant, mental and manual labour), so intellectuals still need to work among workers and peasants to find problems and develop a proletarian worldview. As evidence, the article presents sent-down youth who became academicians, including Jiang Yi, Cui Xiangqun, Ding Jian, Fu Xianzhi and Zhai Mingguo. Ge says their experience gave them a sense of duty and the endurance to resist money and fame. Ge concludes that the path "cannot be abandoned or changed" and must be kept up from generation to generation. The author reads Xi Jinping's remarks on hardship, on rural revitalization and on urban-rural integrated development as supporting this view. The article also objects to treating the sent-down youth experience as something to demonise. Read the original if you want to see how a Marxist writer in 2019 defended the sent-down youth movement and tied it to the Party's founding aims and to current youth and rural policy.

Why the competitiveness of the CPI(M) in Kerala has kept growing since the turn of the century 新世纪以来印共（马）在喀拉拉邦竞争力持续增强的原因 Zhang Shuhuan Xie Jiabao Zhang Shuhuan and Xie Jiabao ask why the Communist Party of India (Marxist), CPI(M), has grown steadily stronger in electoral competition in the Indian state of Kerala in the twenty-first century. They note that the party lost power in West Bengal and Tripura but remains in office in Kerala. They argue that this is the result of several factors acting together. Broad representation of the people's interests is the fundamental cause, a correct election strategy the direct cause, and sound party building the main cause. The article, published in 2019, first documents the party's rising strength. It covers three state assembly elections won as largest party (2006, 2011, 2016), three panchayat (rural self-government) rounds and three urban local-body rounds, and it notes that the Bharatiya Janata Party remains marginal. It then devotes one section to each of the three causes. The authors present the party as the strongest communist party in a capitalist country and treat Kerala as a lesson for such parties. On the fundamental cause, the authors describe land reform, the People's Planning Campaign, food distribution, pensions, employment schemes and benefits for scheduled castes and tribes as measures for the vulnerable, who they say make up over 80 per cent of the population. They add an economic-growth-first strategy, citing GDP rising from 31 to 125 billion US dollars between 2005/2006 and 2018/2019. They also describe the party's handling of land seizures, privatisation and Tuluva ethnic militancy. On strategy, they stress alliances with ideologically close parties in the Left Democratic Front, which they contrast with the loose United Democratic Front. They add tailored manifestos and candidates, courting independents, support for several religious communities, small-donor fundraising and the use of constituency delimitation. On party building, they cite membership growth from 293,141 to 463,472 (2000–2018) and training and expulsions for indiscipline. They also cite the resolution of the Achuthanandan–Vijayan factional split, the four-tier organisation, and mass organisations and the daily Deshabhimani. The authors conclude that Kerala offers lessons for the international communist movement. Communist parties must genuinely represent the people, keep strengthening themselves, and adapt their electoral tactics to changing conditions. In this way, they say, Marxism can show new vitality in the twenty-first century. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly account of a communist party that governs at state level in a capitalist country, with detailed election and membership data.

China is undergoing rapid and profound change A Chinese compilation of John Bachtell's series on socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era 中国正在经历快速而深远的变革 John Bachtell This text is a Chinese-language compilation (编译) of a series of articles by John Bachtell, then chairman of the Communist Party USA, written after a visit to China at the invitation of the Communist Party of China (CPC) from 26 May to 3 June 2018. Visiting Beijing, Hefei and Shenzhen, Bachtell concludes that China is going through rapid and profound change. In his view this will have a major effect on China's 1.4 billion people, the global economy, international relations and the future of socialism. The editors present his assessment as evidence that socialism with Chinese characteristics is recognised by communists in the most developed capitalist country. The compilation is organised under five headings drawn from six articles: the achievements of reform and opening up; ecological civilization as a national strategy; China's global diplomacy; the role of trade unions in governance; and the CPC as a strong, united and open party. Each section combines figures, interviews and impressions from the trip with Bachtell's own commentary and comparisons to the United States. On the economy, Bachtell describes the shift from egalitarian collective farming to a socialist market economy. He cites poverty reduction, rising wages, the "Made in China 2025" plan, and a public sector that he says accounts for about 60 per cent of fixed investment. He also lists costs: unequal development, a growing capitalist stratum and billionaires, sharper class contradictions and environmental damage. He portrays the turn to ecological civilization, the Belt and Road Initiative and a community with a shared future for mankind as responses to climate crisis and globalization, set against Trump-era protectionism, which he calls doomed to fail. He presents the All-China Federation of Trade Unions, with 308 million members, as a partner in planning and an institutional pillar of the political system, and he defends its CPC ties against foreign criticism. Bachtell sees the CPC as a pragmatic party that adapts Marxism to Chinese conditions, practises self-criticism and self-reform, fights corruption and refuses to impose its model on others. He notes that it faces many problems and errors. The text ends with his view that the scale of China's development will shape the world whatever the Party intends. Read the original if you want to see how a leading US communist, in a text republished in China, assessed Chinese development and how Chinese editors framed that endorsement.

Lessons of the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics for developing countries' roads to modernization 中国特色社会主义道路对发展中国家现代化道路的启示 Xu Shicheng Writing in 2019, Xu Shicheng asks what the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics can offer developing countries seeking modernization. The article argues that China's development since reform and opening up shows the vitality of socialism, supplies successful experience for developing countries and is a major contribution by the Chinese nation to human civilisation. Xu presents China's road as able to surpass the Western road to modernization. The piece opens with definitions of modernization drawn from two Peking University scholars, Luo Rongqu and Qian Chengdan, and traces China's own goals from the Four Modernizations of the 1960s and 1970s through the three-step strategy to the Two Centenary Goals and the two-stage plan set out at the 19th Party Congress (2017). It then lists the typical problems of developing countries, such as single-commodity economies, weak innovation, corruption, inequality and poverty, financial crises and flawed policy. It cites figures on China's growth, poverty reduction and trade, then sets out ten lessons. In Xu's account, the lessons are: treat development as the first task of governing; adopt a strategy and model suited to national conditions and keep growth fast; build a fairly complete market economy; reduce poverty step by step and precisely; keep reforming political and economic institutions; link the national economy to the world economy and join globalization; raise living standards under a people-centred approach; build an innovative country; form a strong leadership core; and manage domestic and international situations while building a community with a shared future for mankind. Xu illustrates these with the evolution of the socialist market economy, China's three stages of opening up, the Belt and Road Initiative, and comparative poverty data for Africa and Latin America. Xu contends that the Communist Party's leadership is the fundamental reason China found the right road, and that latecomer states especially need an advanced party at the centre. The article also stresses diversity of development models: China's success, Xu argues, undermines the Western 'end of history' thesis, and other countries should draw on Chinese experience without copying it. Read the original if you want a systematic statement of how Chinese scholarship in 2019 framed China's experience as a reference for the Global South, with supporting statistics.

Studying the history of contemporary China requires studying the history of world socialism 研究当代中国史离不开对世界社会主义史的研究 Zhu Jiamu Zhu Jiamu argues that the history of contemporary China cannot be separated from the history of the world socialist movement. Writing in 2019, Zhu holds that contemporary China's past, present and future are all part of world socialism, and that the study of each field depends on the other. The short article opens with Xi Jinping's speech marking forty years of reform and opening up, then traces the roughly seventy years of the People's Republic. It takes in the 1949 transition to socialism and the First Five-Year Plan, the war-preparation and Third Front construction of the 1960s and early 1970s, the opening to the United States, and the turn to reform and opening up around 1978. Zhu's central move is to explain each turning point by the interaction of domestic conditions and the international socialist movement. The early Soviet alliance and aid are presented as enabling rapid industrialisation while strengthening the socialist camp. The Sino-Soviet split and the Vietnam War are said to have driven the Third Front and the opening to the United States. Reform and opening up is attributed mainly to rigidities in the old economic system, but also to the Soviet decline and the era's turn to peace and development. Zhu concludes that reform and opening up both advanced Chinese socialism and "rescued, defended and developed" world socialism. Zhu holds that socialism with Chinese characteristics is socialism, and, given China's size, an important part of the world movement. The movement is still at a low ebb but shows signs of recovery, and the era remains one of transition from capitalism to socialism. Zhu calls for firm belief in the victory of socialism and communism, together with practical policies suited to the primary stage of socialism and patience in long-term cooperation and struggle with capitalism. Read the original if you want a brief statement of how Party-affiliated historians link Chinese Communist Party history to the international communist movement.

Firmly mastering the Marxist way of thinking and way of working 切实掌握好马克思主义思想方法和工作方法 Zhu Jianyi Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2019, Zhu Jianyi asks how Party members can truly master and apply the Marxist way of thinking and way of working. Starting from Xi Jinping's description of Marxism as a scientific, people-centred, practical and open theory, Zhu argues that this mastery is an important method for advancing the cause of socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era and for realising the Chinese Dream of national rejuvenation. The commentary is organised as a series of requirements, each opened by the phrase "always adhere to". They cover the study and use of Marxist philosophy, seeking truth from facts together with scientific thinking and a "nail-driving spirit", and a problem-oriented approach that relies on investigation, research and continuous learning. Zhu draws throughout on Xi Jinping's formulations and on the Party's own record of practice. Zhu's first move is to make dialectical and historical materialism the cadre's "essential skill". Zhu grounds this in the nature of Marxist philosophy, which is said to unite class character with scientific character and knowing the world with changing it. Zhu calls for study of the classics and for upholding Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era as the Party's guiding ideology. The second move treats seeking truth from facts as the Party's basic method. It is tied to the mass line: the "facts" are those that come "from the masses", and the method must be carried back "to the masses". Zhu lists six modes of thinking to be cultivated: strategic, historical, dialectical, innovative, law-based and bottom-line. The "nail-driving spirit" means following one blueprint to the end and doing each task thoroughly, while stability-seeking progress and strategic resolve keep the course steady. The third move is a problem orientation. Cadres should treat the people's need for a better life as the main problem, investigate in a systematic way ("no investigation, no right to speak"), and study as a learning-oriented Party. Zhu concludes that the Party should keep learning and practising, following the spiral of knowing, practising and knowing again, and should keep its attention on China's reality and the people's needs. In this way the theory and practice of socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era would be steadily improved. The text is a hortatory piece of Party ideological education rather than an analytical study. Read the original if you want to see how the Party's official guidance of 2019 framed Marxist method for cadres, including its list of thinking methods and its stress on investigation and study.

Pushing propaganda and ideological work to grow ever stronger 推动宣传思想工作不断强起来 Xie Fuzhan Zhuang Rongwen Luo Shugang This is a themed collection of short statements, published in the Party journal Dangjian in 2019, by heads of central propaganda and cultural institutions. Each reports how their body will study and implement the main points of Xi Jinping's speech at the national conference on propaganda and ideological work. The shared thesis is that the propaganda and ideological front must be guided by Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, reform and innovate, and so provide ideological guarantees and spiritual strength for the Party and the state. Ten contributors write in turn. Xie Fuzhan (president of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences), Zhuang Rongwen (cyberspace administration) and Luo Shugang (culture and tourism minister) are credited as authors. Others come from Xinhua, China Media Group, Guangming Daily, Economic Daily, China Daily, the China International Publishing Group and the China Publishing Group. Each section covers one institution's field: social science research, the internet, culture and tourism, news agency work, broadcasting personnel, cultural policy, economic reporting, international communication and publishing. Several moves recur. Xie argues that the new Thought is both a guiding principle and an object of study for the social sciences, and calls for systematic learning, research and translating political language into academic and popular idiom. Zhuang calls for "upholding integrity and breaking new ground" online: positive energy as the overall requirement, strict control of online ideological work as the bottom line, comprehensive governance involving the Party, government, firms, society and netizens, and mobilising internet users. Xinhua, China Media Group and other media heads stress the Two Upholds, strengthening the "four abilities" of journalists, media convergence, and publicity around the 70th anniversary of the People's Republic in 2019. Others turn to culture, outreach and publishing. They propose improving cultural products and public cultural facilities, protecting heritage, telling China's story abroad through multilingual platforms, and training "new people of the era" through mainstream publishing. The collection presents unifying thinking and rallying strength as the central task of propaganda work throughout. Read the original if you want a concise view of how senior Chinese media, cultural and academic officials framed their 2019 tasks in official language.

A community with a shared future for mankind as China's proposal for global governance 人类命运共同体为全球治理提供“中国方案” Huang Ping Published in Red Flag Manuscripts (Hongqi Wengao) in 2019, this commentary argues that building a community with a shared future for mankind is China's "Chinese proposal" for world peace, development and global governance. The author, given in the source only as Huang Ping, presents it as an idea set out by Xi Jinping against a background of what the text calls changes in the world unseen in a century. It was written into the preamble of the Constitution in 2018. The piece has three parts. The first traces China's commitment to peaceful development over the 70 years since 1949. The second argues that China's growth offers opportunities to other countries. The third describes the concrete content of China's approach to global governance and gives the Belt and Road Initiative as a practical example. Huang's central claim is that peaceful development is a choice of history, of present conditions and of values. In the author's account, Western powers pursued expansion by force under a "law of the jungle" and zero-sum logic, while old China suffered aggression after 1840. The author holds that China has followed the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence, made pledges never to seek hegemony or expansion, and drawn on a cultural tradition of "harmony in diversity". On governance, the article sets out commitments to mutual respect and dialogue, win-win openness against protectionism and unilateralism, equality among civilisations, and cooperation on the environment. It describes these as a response to economic stagnation, widening development gaps, conflict and populism. Huang concludes that the idea continues seven decades of Chinese diplomacy and offers a way past the old logic that a strong state must seek hegemony and past the "Thucydides trap". The author acknowledges possible traps, risks and attempts at a "new Cold War", but treats the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation as irreversible. China is portrayed as a responsible power and as a development model for countries that want to grow while keeping their independence. Read the original if you want an example of how official Chinese commentary in 2019 framed the community with a shared future for mankind historically, morally and as a basis for global governance.

The contemporary significance of local red culture 地方红色文化的当代意义 Zhao Yuezhi Sha Yao Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts (2019, no. 20), Zhao Yuezhi and Sha Yao ask how red culture, the cultural legacy of the Chinese revolution, should be promoted in the new era. They use the image of a tree: national narratives of the revolution are the trunk and local narratives the branches and leaves. The authors argue that promoting red culture must not stop at the trunk, and that local revolutionary stories need to be developed as well. The short commentary is organised under three headings: locality (zai di xing), contemporaneity (shidai xing) and mass character (qunzhong xing). It starts from spirits named after places, such as the Long March spirit and the Jinggangshan, Yan'an and Xibaipo spirits. It then uses Lishui in Zhejiang and its "southwest Zhejiang revolutionary spirit" as its main case, and refers briefly to the Yimeng spirit of Linyi. On locality, the authors say that the nationally known revolutionary spirits remain irreplaceable. They add that, amid fragmented communities, Cold War ideology, the "farewell to revolution" current and internet-era historical nihilism, the overall narrative needs vivid local stories to support it. In their view local narratives enrich the national one and do not deconstruct it. Embedded in kinship and village ties, they can connect with people's lives and emotions. On contemporaneity, the authors argue that red culture must enter people's hearts and daily practice, and not only histories and museums. They say Lishui has turned the Red Army's hardship and courage into present-day drive for development, and uses online and offline media and red tourism. On mass character, they hold that the revolution's spirit was forged in fusion with the countryside and the peasantry. They cite Xi Jinping's 2013 redefinition of the Yimeng spirit as a bond between the Party and the people, and describe the Red Army's work in southwest Zhejiang in the same terms. The authors conclude that the effect of promoting a local revolutionary spirit should be judged by how deeply it resonates and wins popular support locally, and not by its fame. They end by posing, as a task of the times, how to keep to the mass line so that ecological civilisation, poverty alleviation and rural revitalisation advance together, with peasants as the real subject of rural revitalisation. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Party-affiliated scholars link local revolutionary history, ideological work and rural policy.

The rule of law as an important guarantee of China's sustained development 法治建设是中国持续发展的重要保障 Zhi Zhenfeng Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts (2019, no. 20), Zhi Zhenfeng asks what role the rule of law has played in China's sustained development. Zhi argues that economic growth shapes people's sense of gain, while legal development shapes their sense of security, and that national success is a coordinated "collective dance" rather than a one-legged hop. The rule of law, in this reading, is one of the "four beams and eight pillars" of the Chinese miracle. The article has three sections. The first treats certainty and predictability as the inner requirement of legal development and offers evidence on personal and property security. The second draws common lessons from countries' experience of building the rule of law. The third sets out what Zhi calls the "Chinese code": holistic coordination of legal construction with other fields under Party leadership. Zhi cites homicide rates (0.62 per 100,000 in China in 2016, against 4.88 in the United States in 2015), a Gallup safety ranking of tenth, low police numbers per capita, rising per-capita income and growing foreign patent and trademark filings as signs of security and property protection. From a comparative survey Zhi draws five generalisations. Legal development correlates with economic growth and with stability. It does not necessarily depend on Western-style electoral democracy. It requires a stable, strong government. And it must restrain the "key minority" of officials.
