Zhi then describes a "state capacity paradox": strong state capacity is necessary for the rule of law but not sufficient, as strongman politics or fusion of religion and state in some Latin American and Middle Eastern countries are said to show. China, the author says, takes a realist path in which the Party steers legal construction as part of overall national development, disciplines its own power through anti-corruption work and acts within the constitution and the law. Zhi concludes that the core of the socialist rule-of-law path with Chinese characteristics is upholding Party leadership, which the article calls the most essential feature of socialism with Chinese characteristics and the fundamental guarantee of socialist rule of law. Building a law-based China is presented as part of modernising the system and capacity of national governance. Read the original if you want an official-line argument, with comparative statistics, on how Chinese scholars link legal development, state capacity and Party leadership.

Seventy years of advancing the great project of Party building in new China: basic practice and lessons 新中国70年推进党的建设伟大工程的基本实践及启示 Liu Zhong Marking the 70th anniversary of the People's Republic in 2019, this article asks how the Communist Party of China has carried forward the "great project" of Party building since 1949, and what lessons follow. The author argues that treating Party building as a great project is an innovation in the Party's "great self-reform" and an important instrument for leading the "great social revolution". The author holds that the experience offers guidance for the new stage of this project in the new era. The article is a chronological survey in four parts. It begins with Mao Zedong's 1939 formulation of the project and the Party's efforts in the first decades after 1949, then moves to the reform and opening up period under Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin and Hu Jintao. Next it treats the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012) under Xi Jinping, and it closes with six lessons. Each stage is presented through the question of what kind of Party to build and how to build it. Liu's central claim is that social revolution and self-reform must advance together, so that Party building keeps pace with the Party's wider undertakings. For the early decades the author cites rectification campaigns and growth in membership from 5.8 million to 6.369 million. For 1978–2012 the author points to the new ideological line, cadre reform, institutionalisation and anti-corruption bodies, and membership growth from 36.981 million to 85.127 million. For the Xi era the article highlights full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, the eight-point regulation, the revision or formulation of more than 140 Party regulations, and an anti-corruption campaign it calls overwhelmingly effective. The article draws six lessons: pursue social revolution and self-reform together; strengthen Party leadership and Party building comprehensively; update the overall goals and layout of Party building; combine ideological education with rule-based governance; align a people-centred stance with reform and innovation; and treat the "key minority" of leading cadres and the Party's broad membership as inseparable. The author concludes that these practices have made the Party a long-term governing party and a strong leading force for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a compact official-style periodisation of Party-building policy from 1949 to 2019, with dates, regulations and membership figures.

Building a community with a shared future for mankind points the way for a new type of globalization 构建人类命运共同体为新型全球化指明了方向 Tai Lihua Xu Baojian Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts (2019, no. 19), Tai Lihua and Xu Baojian ask what should replace a capital-driven globalization that, in their account, has fallen into systemic crisis. They argue that the protectionism and "anti-globalization" currents led by the United States reflect that crisis, not a reversal of history. Their answer is that China, drawing on the practice of socialism with Chinese characteristics, offers a community with a shared future for mankind as the direction and model for a new type of globalization. The piece has two parts. The first explains why globalization is irreversible and what the community with a shared future would change: the relation between capital and labour, the international economic order, and the ecological environment. The second turns to practice. It lists four tasks: drawing on Chinese experience, advancing the Belt and Road Initiative, promoting open development and freer trade and investment, and making use of the beneficial results of capitalist globalization. The authors build on Marx's idea of a transition from national to world history and from capitalist to communist world-historical eras. They present the community with a shared future as a contemporary form of Marx's "association of free individuals", with a clearer path and more concrete stage goals. In their reading, the people-centred development idea applies here to the world's people, above all its workers. Production would aim at raising workers' living standards and at human emancipation, with capital and profit only means. They contend that capital-driven globalization causes ecological plunder and unequal trade, whereas the community would pursue equal, mutually beneficial relations and green development. They hold that the problem lies in the plunder carried out by developed capitalist states under the banner of liberalization, not in free trade as such. The authors conclude that the community with a shared future does not cut itself off from capitalism. It sublates the logic of capital while absorbing the productive achievements of capitalist globalization, in order to create conditions for future human liberation. Citing Xi Jinping's phrase about changes unseen in a century, they say the 2008 financial crisis exposed the harms of capitalist globalization and that China's proposal marks the opening of a new era. Read the original if you want a short example of how a Party journal frames the community with a shared future as a Marxist alternative to capitalist globalization.

The relationship among excellent traditional Chinese culture, revolutionary culture and advanced socialist culture 中华优秀传统文化、革命文化和社会主义先进文化的关系 Tang Ling This short commentary in Red Flag Manuscripts asks how three components of Chinese culture should be understood in relation to one another: excellent traditional Chinese culture, revolutionary culture and advanced socialist culture. Tang argues that the three are not separate but form one continuous whole, and that grasping this dialectically is a precondition for building socialist culture with Chinese characteristics, strengthening cultural identity and building cultural confidence. The article defines each form in turn. Traditional culture is the distilled wisdom of the Chinese nation, expressed in ideas, virtues and humanistic spirit. Revolutionary culture is the theory, values and spirit forged in the struggles of the Party and people since the May Fourth period, illustrated by the Jinggangshan, Long March and Yan'an spirits. Advanced socialist culture is the modern, world-facing, "national, scientific and popular" culture formed under Marxism in the practice of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The text is organised in four steps: shared origin, lineage, joint status as the mainstream, and dialectical unity in practice. Tang's central move is to present the three as successive stages of one tradition. Revolutionary culture, in this account, recast traditional ideas by fusing them with Marxism: the author cites pairings such as "the people are the foundation of the state" and "serve the people wholeheartedly", or "investigating things" and "seeking truth from facts". Advanced socialist culture then draws on both and is described as the latest development of Chinese culture. Together they form the main body of contemporary Chinese culture and the three supports of cultural confidence, which Tang describes as a deeper and more lasting source of strength. Tang concludes that the three must not be separated or favoured one over another. The author calls for opposing historical and cultural nihilism and wholesale Westernization, but also archaism, the notion of replacing Marxism with Confucianism, and denial of the socialist character of contemporary culture. Equally, Tang rejects both uncritical copying of foreign culture and cultural conservatism, and urges adherence to Marxist method so that Chinese culture undergoes creative transformation and innovative development. Read the original if you want a concise statement, from the Party's journal in 2019, of how official discourse links traditional, revolutionary and socialist culture under the banner of cultural confidence.

Thirty years after the Eastern European upheavals: remodelling and lost time 东欧剧变30年：重塑与蹉跎 Li Ruiqin Writing in 2019, thirty years after the collapse of the ruling communist and workers' parties in eight Eastern European states (1989–1992), Li Ruiqin asks two questions. What, in retrospect, were the key factors behind the 'Velvet Revolution'? And what situation and challenges do the Central and Eastern European states face after three decades of transition? The article argues that Gorbachev's new policy towards Eastern Europe was the decisive factor in 1989, and that the region's transition remains unfinished, with fragile democratic institutions, unmet economic expectations and demographic decline. The article has three main sections. The first revisits the causes of the 1989 changes, drawing mainly on Russian scholars and journalists. The second examines the 'consensus on joining Europe', covering NATO and European Union enlargement, the region's hopes and its later marginalisation within the EU. The third surveys the new and old problems of the transition: political instability, poverty and inequality, and population loss. It draws largely on Russian-language press and scholarship, plus works such as Eva Hoffman's book on the new Eastern Europe and a Le Monde diplomatique article on depopulation. On the causes, Li follows Russian authors in holding that Gorbachev dropped the Brezhnev doctrine of limited sovereignty, withdrew Soviet support and stripped the local parties of their ideological props. In Li's account, this left the states free only to move towards Western-style 'democratisation', and the ruling parties collapsed once they lost control. On the aftermath, Li reports that Central and Eastern European states became 'second-class citizens' in the EU, with sovereignty disputes over refugee quotas and the 'multi-speed Europe' plan. Citing a 2017 European Bank for Reconstruction and Development report, Li notes that 23 per cent of Eastern Europeans earn less than in 1989, and that privatisation produced oligarchs. Li also cites claims of mass emigration, falling birth rates and a deliberate Western 'plundering' of talent. Li concludes that the region's states must overcome historical handicaps and the 'new Europe versus old Europe' mindset, and find a development path suited to their own conditions. Li points to the benefit of keeping independence from great-power rivalry and to growing practical cooperation with Russia, China, India and other regions. Making that path is described as the task of the era for these countries. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic assessment of post-1989 Eastern Europe that relies heavily on Russian-language sources and on the view that Gorbachev's policy was decisive.

From the ontology of the event to the phenomenology of the event Badiou's philosophy of the event between Being and Event and Logics of Worlds 从事件本体论到事件现象学 Lan Jiang Alain Badiou published Being and Event in 1988 and Logics of Worlds in 2006, the latter subtitled "Being and Event 2". Lan asks why Badiou chose that subtitle and how the two books relate. The article argues that Badiou's philosophy moves from an ontology of the event, built on mathematics at the level of pure multiplicity, to a phenomenology of the event at the level of appearing, and that the later book also makes the definition of the event stricter. The article has three parts. The first reconstructs the ontology of Being and Event, starting from Badiou's reading of Pascal's miracles and the distinction between presentation and representation. The second turns to Logics of Worlds and the concepts of transcendental, identity function and existence function, using Badiou's own illustrations. The third covers Badiou's classification of changes and his account of how events become lasting, drawing on Sartre's bus-queue example and the Spartacus uprising. Lan also supplies notes on terms such as mathème and "generic". In the first book, Lan explains, Badiou holds that "the One" is the result of a counting-as-one operation, and he sorts multiples into normal, singular and excrescent terms. Events can occur only at an "evental site", a singular term that is presented but not represented. In the second book, a world's transcendental measures how strongly objects appear, and an "inexistent" is an object whose existence value is at its minimum, as with Inuit and Amerindians in Quebec elections of 1918–1950. Badiou now separates four kinds of change: modification, fact, weak singularity and strong singularity (the event). Only a strong singularity keeps maximal intensity in its consequences. Lan concludes that what matters for Badiou is the operation after the event: naming it, and building a body, such as Spartacus's detachment, whose militants are faithful to it. This produces the triad of event, name and body, which Lan relates to Lacan's Real, Symbolic and Imaginary. It also underlies Badiou's reply to "democratic materialism", with the slogan that there are only bodies and languages, "except that there are truths". Badiou's truths are plural procedures, not a Hegelian totality. Read the original if you want a close guide to the shift between Badiou's two major works, including his formal vocabulary and his emphasis on organisation and the vanguard.

Marx and Marxism in the eyes of Vietnamese theorists 越南理论家视阈中的马克思和马克思主义 Pan Jin'e Zhou Zengliang This review surveys how Vietnamese theorists approached Marx and Marxism around the 200th anniversary of Marx's birth in 2018. It aims to inform Chinese readers about the current state of Marxist research in Vietnam. The authors present the Vietnamese material as an example of Marxism's enduring vitality and as a vantage point on it. The sources are the papers from the international conference held in Hanoi on 4 May 2018 at the Ho Chi Minh National Academy of Politics, together with 2018 articles in the Vietnamese Communist Party's journal Communism and the Party school's Political Theory. Contributors include senior Party leaders, scholars of the Academy and the Vietnam Academy of Social Sciences, and retired officials. The review is organised by theme: Marx's theoretical value; upholding and innovating Marxism; the transition period; political economy; Party, state and democracy; class struggle; and culture and human emancipation. Pan and Zhou report that the Vietnamese authors treat Marx as a scientific and revolutionary thinker whose predictions about capitalism, including its crises, were borne out, and whose surplus-value theory is not outdated. They also report that Vietnamese theorists insist on applying Marxism-Leninism and Ho Chi Minh Thought creatively. They describe warnings against dogmatism and against hostile ideas, such as claims that Marxism is foreign to Vietnam or that democratic socialism should replace Party leadership. Marx's theory of the transition period is presented as the key to Vietnam's path, which bypasses capitalism but uses its favourable elements. Vietnamese scholars also use Marx on ownership, distribution, alienation, the rule-of-law socialist state, democracy and human rights to justify a socialist-oriented market economy, multiple forms of ownership and the Party's "self-renewal". The review concludes that Vietnamese theorists see Marxism as a living guide to Vietnam's renewal, and stress adherence to it together with adaptation to national conditions. It also notes that some of them call for further study of questions such as the withering away of the state. Read the original if you want a detailed overview of how Vietnamese Party-aligned scholars framed Marx in 2018, and which themes and sources they drew on.

The decline of the urban middle class in the West against the background of polarisation 两极分化背景下西方城市中间阶级的衰落 Song Lidan Song Lidan asks whether contemporary Western society is an 'olive-shaped' middle-class society in which class opposition has disappeared, or whether it instead confirms Marx's claim that capitalist society splits into two directly opposed classes. The article argues for the second reading: the urban middle class is declining, polarising and becoming dependent on big capital, while most people have become wage earners. The article first separates the Marxist concept of the middle class, meaning petty-bourgeois owners who work largely by their own labour, from the much wider 'middle class' of Western sociology. It confines itself to the urban middle class and divides it into non-exploiting groups (the self-employed, independent professionals) and lightly exploiting ones (micro-business owners, lower and middle managers). Evidence is drawn from the United States, the European Union, Britain, West Germany, Japan and Greece, with theoretical support from Marx, Engels, Hilferding, Braverman, Reich and William Robinson. Song makes three main moves. First, citing statistics such as the high exit rates and low incomes of the self-employed in Britain and the EU, the author holds that non-exploiting groups are becoming proletarianised and impoverished, squeezed by monopoly-led globalisation and by unemployed workers entering petty trade. Second, micro-enterprises are said to survive only as appendages of large firms, as franchisees, subcontractors and low-cost 'flexible' units, while managers and professionals are pushed towards precarious temporary work by technology and AI. Third, the post-war alliance between big capital and the middle class, built on anti-monopoly laws, small-business agencies and subsidies, is described as a 'interest-inducing' political structure that kept workers from allying with the middle class. Song argues that this structure rested on colonial and neo-colonial gains and a favourable post-war environment, and is now eroding under neoliberalism, with Japan as the main case. Song concludes that the gap between middle class and proletariat is narrowing and that the West remains a society of a rich minority and a wage-earning majority. The author treats movements such as Occupy Wall Street, the Yellow Vests and 'populism' as signs of this polarisation. Technological progress and globalisation are presented as harmful only under capitalism, and the middle class's decline is read as a foretoken of the eventual disappearance of classes. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist statistical and theoretical case against the 'middle-class society' thesis, with Japanese and European examples.

Production "acceleration": Marx and the theoretical links to the critique of left accelerationism 生产“加速”：马克思与左翼加速主义批判的理论关涉 Ma Xi Liu Qinmin Ma Xi and Liu Qinmin ask how left accelerationism, associated with Nick Srnicek and Alex Williams, relates to Marx. They note that Chinese scholarship has traced its roots to Deleuze and Guattari, or to social-time theory, and has paid little attention to its link with Marx as founder of social critical theory. The authors argue that Marx laid the foundation for a critique of capitalist acceleration, and that left accelerationism loses its critical edge if it abandons that foundation. The article has four parts. It first reads the 2013 Manifesto for an Accelerationist Politics and Srnicek and Williams's Inventing the Future (2015) to establish what left accelerationism claims. It then traces Marx's treatment of speed through the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, The German Ideology, the 1857–58 manuscripts and Capital. A third section asks in what sense Marx is the founder of this critique, and a short conclusion follows. In the authors' reading, Srnicek and Williams hold that capital has shifted from extracting absolute surplus time to disciplining the pace of life itself under post-Fordism, so that work and life merge in a "social factory". Left accelerationism, they say, criticises neoliberalism from within and aims to use capitalism's technologies to go beyond its value form. The authors find in Marx a double critique: private ownership of the means of production reduces human "life speed" to the speed of material production, while machine rhythms dominate the worker's natural time. Marx, they argue, ties this to the critique of private ownership rather than to ethics alone, and he anticipated the intensification of labour that later capitalism would produce. The authors conclude that left accelerationism's origin lies in Marx's critique of political economy, though they stress this is a return in the logic of intellectual history, not its actual source. They say accelerationists claim to have gone beyond Marx. Without Marxist guidance, the authors warn, the school would lose its theoretical roots, become a phenomenology that explains capitalism without challenging it, and risk complicity with it. They call for re-examining current foreign accelerationist claims in light of Marx, while granting that the school offers real insight into new features of capitalism. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist attempt to trace accelerationism back to Marx's texts on machinery, speed and labour time.

Anthropocene imperialism as the extinction phase of twenty-first-century capitalism A review of Foster's latest critique of imperialism 人类世帝国主义是21世纪资本主义的灭绝阶段 Niu Tiansheng This is a critical review, published in World Socialism Studies in 2019, of 'Imperialism in the Anthropocene' by John Bellamy Foster, Hannah Holleman and Brett Clark (Monthly Review, July–August 2019). Niu Tiansheng presents the original as a deepening of Foster's ecological critique of capitalism. In Niu's account, the essay borrows the geological notion of the Anthropocene to show that the planetary crisis is rooted in imperialism and global capitalism, not in humanity in general. The review follows the original's four-part structure. It first sets out what the Anthropocene is, citing the 2019 vote of the Anthropocene Working Group and the 'Great Acceleration' after the mid-twentieth century. It then lists the practices of 'Anthropocene imperialism': imperialist rent, material footprints, ocean grabbing and appropriation of the atmospheric commons. Next it covers US strategy on fossil fuels and water, and finally the way out of the crisis. Niu closes with a short assessment of the essay's strengths and limits. Niu reports three main moves. First, the authors extend Samir Amin's concept of imperialist rent: the transfer of use-values and natural resources from the periphery to the core is treated as ecological imperialism, which leaves poor countries with the ecological costs. Second, the authors argue that Washington, while acknowledging climate change, responds with an 'energy dominance' strategy. This strategy includes pipeline expansion, fossil-fuel exports and a 'militarisation of energy policy'. It also includes a 'hydro-diplomacy' aimed at controlling water and countering China. Third, the authors conclude that imperialism is an organised reactionary force against ecological revolution, so that twenty-first-century imperialism is 'the exterminist phase of capitalism'. Any serious response, they say, must therefore criticise capitalism and imperialism together. On the way out, Niu reports that the authors propose a 'species consciousness' and an 'extinction rebellion' movement. The authors also call for an anti-imperialist revolution joined to an ecological one, summed up in the line that the poor will inherit the earth or there will be no earth to inherit. Niu praises the essay's clear logic and its continuity with classical Marxist class analysis and colonial critique. Niu also faults it for resting on contingent, scientifically unargued proposals, for lacking an analysis of the agents of social change or a feasible path to overthrowing imperialism's economic base and superstructure, and for amounting to a 'politics of hope'. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's summary and assessment of Foster's 2019 ecological theory of imperialism and its reception in Chinese Marxist circles.

A major contribution to the progress of human civilization China's 40 years of reform and opening up as seen by foreign political parties 对人类文明进步的重大贡献 International Department of the CPC Central Committee Writing in Qiushi in 2019, the International Department of the CPC Central Committee surveys how foreign political parties and politicians assessed forty years of reform and opening up. Opening with Xi Jinping's description of reform and opening up as a "great revolution", the article contends that foreign parties widely see it as having promoted world peace and development, offered developing countries a successful path to modernization, shown what a party's mission should be, and made a major contribution to human civilization. The text is organised in four sections, one for each claim. It draws on statements attributed to dozens of parties and party leaders from Europe, Africa, Asia and Latin America, among them ruling parties, communist and left-wing parties, social democratic parties and some Western parties. Examples include the Communist Party of the Russian Federation, the Communist Party of Vietnam, the Communist Party of Cuba, the ANC, the Socialist International and the Party of European Socialists. In the article's account, foreign parties praise China's growth record and its rise to the world's second-largest economy, and describe China as a peaceful contributor to global development through initiatives such as the Belt and Road Initiative. They are said to regard socialism with Chinese characteristics as an "alternative" to Western democratic models and capitalist values, with experience of use to developing countries. The article reports that many parties attribute success to the leadership of the Communist Party of China, its capacity for self-renewal, full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, and Xi Jinping's role as core leader. Left-wing parties are quoted as saying that reform and opening up developed Marxism creatively, revived socialism after the upheavals in the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe, and that Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era points the way for twenty-first-century socialism. The authors conclude that international opinion confirms the historical significance of reform and opening up for China, for the world socialist movement and for human progress. The piece is a compilation of reported foreign endorsements rather than an independent analysis, and every assessment is presented through the voices of the quoted parties. Read the original if you want to see which foreign parties the Party's international liaison body chose to cite, and how it framed their views on China's development path, Party leadership and Xi Jinping Thought in 2019.

Uphold exchange and mutual learning among civilizations; oppose the fallacy of a clash of civilizations 坚持文明交流互鉴 反对文明冲突谬论 Yan Zhaozhu Writing in Qiushi in 2019, Yan Zhaozhu takes up Xi Jinping's keynote speech at the Dialogue of Asian Civilizations (15 May 2019) and asks what cultural stance is needed to build a community with a shared future for mankind. Yan argues that this project requires cultural strength alongside economic and technological strength. In this account, ideas of a clash of civilizations and of civilizational superiority are erroneous and one-sided, and rejecting them is a new historical demand on cultural work. The commentary is organised under four headings. The first presents the community with a shared future for mankind as a Chinese proposal and sets out Xi's view that civilizations are colourful, equal and inclusive. The next three sections set out cultural positions: openness, inclusiveness and win-win cooperation; keeping pace with the times and innovating; and adhering to reason and ideals. Yan ties these to the current context of US-China trade friction, unilateralism and protectionism. Yan's central move is to hold that civilizations differ but are not ranked, and that mutual learning must be reciprocal and multi-directional, never coerced. Against this, Yan describes a Western record since the industrial revolution of colonial wars, plunder, racial discrimination and the slave trade, set beside professed ideals of democracy, freedom and equality. Yan says that the Western view that China has not evolved as expected and should now be confronted spreads "like a germ" and reflects a closed, arrogant outlook. Yan also criticises what the article calls irrational currents in certain countries: denying climate change, applying double standards on nuclear proliferation and terrorism, blaming globalization, withdrawing from international bodies, and promoting a "China threat" theory. Against these, the author sets rationality, respect for facts and science, and recognition of the shift in the world economy's centre of gravity, which Yan says has not come at the West's expense. Yan concludes that cooperation is the main theme of the age and that China should be a "big learning country" that draws on all civilizations. China's own development is presented as a strategic contribution to world peace, and the emerging economies' globalization is said to differ fundamentally from the colonial-era kind. The author calls on the West to abandon colonial mentality and Cold War thinking. Read the original if you want an example of how a 2019 Qiushi article framed the community with a shared future for mankind as a cultural and civilizational stance during US-China tensions.

On the scientific spirit 论科学精神 Liu Dachun Writing in the centenary year of the May Fourth Movement (2019), Liu Dachun asks what the scientific spirit is and why it must be promoted today. The article argues that building China into a major science and technology power in the new era requires vigorously advocating this spirit, and presents doing so as a practical way of carrying forward the May Fourth legacy of "Mr Science" and "Mr Democracy". The piece has three parts. The first traces how the scientific spirit formed, from Greek rationalism through the Renaissance conflict between science and religion and the separation of science from philosophy (Galileo), to the Industrial Revolution and Popper's falsificationism, and then to its spread in China through figures such as Sun Yat-sen, Chen Duxiu, Ren Hongjun and Zhu Kezhen. The second part sets out its content. The third part proposes how to cultivate it. Liu defines the scientific spirit as the soul of science, centred on seeking truth from facts and on innovation. It has four components: a rational belief that nature can be known; positivist methods, meaning experiment and mathematics; a critical attitude; and a trial-and-error model in which science is fallible and advances by eliminating mistakes. Liu stresses that criticism does not mean total negation, since old theories can be absorbed into new ones. Liu says the spirit still falls short in China. The article cites officials who pursue showpiece projects, consult fortune-tellers or believe in qigong masters, and notes that pseudoscience persists among the public. Liu proposes five requirements for promotion. These are to keep to the Marxist view of science, which treats science as a historical lever and a product of social production. They also include keeping pace with the times, with innovation at the centre of China's "parallel" modernization, and creating a tolerant and open atmosphere that accepts error and allows contending views. The last is to integrate science with the humanities and to spread scientific knowledge, especially among young people, rural cadres and officials. Liu links this to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and cites Xi Jinping on innovation and basic research. Read the original if you want an example of how a Qiushi article, written for the May Fourth centenary, joins the history of science, philosophy of science and Party policy on innovation.

A centennial tribute to the May Fourth Movement 五四运动百年祭 Jin Chongji Writing for the movement's hundredth anniversary in 2019, Jin Chongji asks why the May Fourth Movement of 1919 should be regarded as an epoch-making turning point in modern Chinese history. Jin's answer is that it was the moment when many advanced Chinese found a new social ideal, the building of a socialist new China, so that an old era ended and a new one began. The piece opens by citing Xi Jinping's speech marking the centenary and returns to it at the close. The article is organised chronologically in three sections. The first reviews the national crisis after the Opium War and the successive attempts to learn from the West, namely the Reform Movement of 1898 and the 1911 Revolution. The second examines the early New Culture Movement, centred on Chen Duxiu's journal New Youth. The third treats the May Fourth upheaval itself and its consequences, including the spread of Marxism and the founding of early Communist groups. Jin argues that the 1911 Revolution left China's semi-colonial, semi-feudal character unchanged, which led New Culture figures to attack old ethics under the banners of "democracy" and "science". Jin judges their individualism limited: Lu Xun's lecture on what happens after Nora leaves home is read as showing that personal liberation without social transformation leads nowhere. Three shocks then ended the long search for truth in the West: postwar Europe's devastation, the Paris Peace Conference's decision to transfer German rights in Shandong to Japan, and the Russian October Revolution. The mass protests of 1919, with students, workers and merchants taking part, showed that popular strength was the key to change. Jin says that Li Dazhao, Chen Duxiu and others took up Marxism, which in Jin's account gave democracy and science a fuller, more practical content. Jin concludes that the movement prepared the ideological and cadre groundwork for the founding of the Communist Party of China. In Jin's reading, a century of trial and error shows that copying foreign models failed. Only socialism could save China, and only socialism with Chinese characteristics can develop China and achieve the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Jin calls this the only correct road and urges continued effort, in the spirit of "staying true to our founding mission", in the 70th anniversary year of the People's Republic. Read the original if you want an officially aligned Chinese narrative of the May Fourth Movement, with period quotations from Chen Duxiu, Li Dazhao, Lu Xun, Zhou Enlai and Wu Yuzhang.

The light of ideas illuminates the path of progress of human civilization Xi Jinping's thinking on exchanges and mutual learning among civilizations 思想之光照亮人类文明发展进步之路 Zhou Xinmin Zhou Xinmin's article, published in Qiushi in 2019, takes up Xi Jinping's statements on exchanges and mutual learning among civilizations. These began with Xi's speech at UNESCO headquarters on 27 March 2014. Zhou argues that in the five years since, this body of thought has grown richer and more influential. The article presents it as offering fresh hope for responding to what it calls changes unseen in a century. The article is organised around four "characteristics" of Xi's discourse: grand conception, broad vision, extensive content and strong underpinnings. The first three are tied to concrete elements of the thought. These include building a community with a shared future for mankind, developing each country's own distinctive civilization, and the "five connectivities" of the Belt and Road Initiative. The fourth shifts to the personal qualities of Xi as leader. Zhou's main argument is that the thought breaks with traditional, narrow and closed views of civilization. It treats the development of one's own civilization as the precondition for world civilization, and it rejects any claim of civilizational superiority. It places mutual learning within national governance, the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and the Chinese Dream. Zhou says it draws on Marxist materialist dialectics and Chinese philosophy to balance three pairs. One is inheritance and innovation against borrowing from abroad. Another is promoting one's own civilization against respecting diversity. The third is "soft" cultural work against "hard" projects such as infrastructure links and the Belt and Road Initiative. Zhou also holds that Chinese cultural confidence must never slide into cultural nihilism. Zhou concludes that the thought's strength rests on four leadership capacities attributed to Xi: political will, command of the overall situation, transformative creativity, and the power to inspire and unite people. The author predicts that such ideas will remain fresh and vital. The piece is an authoritative-style exposition rather than a critical analysis. Read the original if you want to see how a Qiushi commentary frames Xi Jinping's civilizational discourse and its links to global governance and the Belt and Road Initiative.

Exchanges and mutual learning among civilizations are an important driving force for human progress and world peace 文明交流互鉴是推动人类文明进步和世界和平发展的重要动力 Xi Jinping This is a speech delivered by Xi Jinping, then President of China, at UNESCO headquarters in Paris on 27 March 2014, and reprinted in Qiushi in 2019. Speaking after congratulating Irina Bokova on her re-election as Director-General, Xi argues that exchanges and mutual learning among civilizations are an important driving force for human progress and for peaceful world development. The speech opens with UNESCO's founding after the Second World War and its charter idea that the defences of peace must be built in people's minds. It announces that China will expand the Great Wall Scholarships offered through UNESCO to developing countries from 25 to 75 places a year, and will continue its work for the UNESCO fund supporting Africa. Xi then sets out three principles, surveys the history of China's own exchanges with other civilizations, and ends by linking these themes to China's domestic goals. The three principles are that civilizations are diverse, equal and inclusive. Xi holds that diversity gives exchange its value, that no civilization is superior or inferior, and that arrogance and prejudice are the greatest obstacles to mutual learning. He also holds that inclusiveness removes any "clash of civilizations". He illustrates this with Chinese history: the Silk Road, Zhang Qian, the Tang capital Chang'an, Zheng He's voyages, Buddhism's adaptation in China, and the four great inventions. In his account, Chinese civilization is both home-grown and shaped by continual exchange. He draws on Chinese sayings such as "harmony without uniformity" and on Hugo and Napoleon to argue that humanity forms a community with a shared future and needs a broad-minded attitude. Xi calls for education, science and technology, and cultural exchange to be developed so that peoples understand the value of different civilizations, and for civilizations to be appreciated for their humanistic spirit rather than only their artefacts. He presents the Chinese Dream of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation as the balanced advance of material and spiritual civilization. He also says China will promote the creative transformation and innovative development of its civilization, so that it can offer spiritual guidance together with other civilizations. Read the original if you want a primary-source statement of the Chinese leadership's early-2010s case for civilizational dialogue, delivered to an international audience.

Initial explorations of the people's congress system in the Chinese Soviet period 中华苏维埃时期对人民代表大会制度的初始探索实践 Zhou Meng Writing in Qiushi in 2019, Zhou Meng asks how the Chinese Soviet Republic of the early 1930s (the Central Soviet Area in southern Jiangxi and western Fujian) relates to today's people's congress system, which the article calls China's fundamental political system. The author's answer is that the soviet congress system was an "initial exploration" and a "great rehearsal" of people being masters of the country, run under Party leadership more than eighty years ago. The article also holds that this history carries lessons for upholding and improving the system today. The article is built in three parts. The first traces the theoretical background, centred on Mao Zedong's writings and reports to the First (1931) and Second (1934) National Soviet Congresses. The second sets out what the soviet republic actually built: organs of power, an administrative apparatus, a judicial system, elections and a body of law. The third draws four lessons for the present, and Zhou frames them with remarks by Xi Jinping. Zhou argues that Mao and his comrades did not copy the Soviet Union's model mechanically. They integrated Marxism with Chinese revolutionary practice, which the author calls an early case of adapting Marxism to Chinese conditions. The article credits Mao with ideas on people's own power, strict enforcement of law by officials (including the death sentences passed on corrupt officials), democratic centralism, and Party leadership of soviet work. On the institutional side, Zhou describes a layered structure of congresses and executive committees, with administration and courts answerable to the congresses, a five-step election procedure, the Outline of the Constitution and more than 130 laws and decrees. Zhou says these gave the later system its rules, organisation and power structure. Zhou draws four lessons. Party leadership is the precondition and political guarantee of the system. The people's status as masters of the country is its core meaning. Governing the country according to law is a long-term task. Upholding and improving the system is fundamental to the Party's ruling position and to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The author also contends that the system has shown strong vitality, while some Western countries and developing countries that imitated Western democracy are said to be in difficulty. Read the original if you want to see how a Party-theoretical journal ties the Jiangxi soviet experience to the genealogy and legitimacy of today's people's congresses.

The community with a shared future for mankind seen through the "big history" perspective 从大历史观看人类命运共同体 Yu Pei Writing in Qiushi in 2019, Yu Pei asks how today's world should be understood from the standpoint of world history, and argues that Xi Jinping's idea of a community with a shared future for mankind is both continuous with Marx's theory of world history and a development of it. The article opens by saying that history underlies all social science and that humanity already lives in the "world history" era Marx described, an era of globalization in which the fates of nations are linked. The article has three parts. The first sets out Marx's theory of world history: its materialist basis, its development from the 1840s to Marx's late historical notebooks, and its break with Hegel's idealist version. The second traces how history became world history through successive revolutions in productive forces and in intercourse, from the sixteenth century to what the article calls a fourth industrial revolution. The third turns to the present and to China's own path, and presents the community with a shared future for mankind. Yu's central claim is that world history forms through the growth of productive forces, the division of labour, commodity exchange and the world market. Isolation goes with backward productive forces, and openness with advanced ones. Capitalism created the world market, but in Yu's reading it cannot overcome the contradiction between socialized production and private appropriation. Globalization therefore creates the material conditions for communism and does not signal the "final victory" of liberalism that some Western scholars predict. Against the background of stalled globalization, regional conflicts and a Western-dominated order that the author says is no longer sustainable, Yu presents the shared-future idea as a new view of international order. It is said to go beyond Eurocentrism, balance-of-power thinking and hegemony, and to rest on win-win cooperation and equality among civilizations. Yu concludes that building the community with a shared future for mankind is a necessary stage on the way to a "free association of individuals", and that socialism with Chinese characteristics has renewed confidence in scientific socialism. The article ends by calling on peoples of all nations to take part, and says the Chinese Dream will be joined by a world of "great harmony". Read the original if you want a compact example of how Party theorists in 2019 grounded the shared-future concept in Marx's theory of world history.

Reform and opening up in progress A Xinhua survey on forty years of reform and opening up 改革开放进行时改革开放进行时 Xinhua News Agency special research group on the 40th anniversary of reform and opening up Published in Qiushi in January 2019, this report by a Xinhua research group marks forty years of reform and opening up. It asks what explains the process's success, where it now stands and how it should continue. The group's answer is that Party leadership, a development path with Chinese characteristics and a sound method of reform produced the results, and that reform must now be carried through to the end under new conditions. The report draws on a field investigation of more than three months in 12 provinces, autonomous regions and municipalities, with nearly 500 interviewees: officials, scholars, entrepreneurs and ordinary people. It has four parts: the 'secrets of success' of the past forty years; the new historical starting point; the major relationships that must be handled correctly; and the nine 'must adhere to' lessons from Xi Jinping's speech of 18 December 2018. The report relays interviewees' views and endorses them. The authors argue that the Party advanced social revolution through its own self-reform, supported by theoretical innovation and the 'emancipating the mind' line. They credit the development orientation, market orientation and opening up for raising growth, lifting over 700 million people out of poverty and ending the 'end of history' thesis. They also point to a method that combines the people's initiative with top-level design, and to careful risk control. Today's reform, they say, differs from that of forty years ago: it moves from narrowing the 'development gap' to using institutional strengths, from total growth to high-quality development, and from piecemeal breakthroughs to systematic deepening. It also faces redistribution of interests and great-power rivalry, and some localities show 'slow' or 'fake' reform. The report proposes balancing several pairs: raising the banner and exploring the path; what has changed and what has not, namely the primary stage of socialism; resolve and vitality; managing and liberalising; design and implementation; the whole and the key points; and Chinese distinctiveness and common concerns. It ends by endorsing Xi's nine 'must adhere to' principles and the call to carry reform and opening up through to the end. Read the original if you want a semi-official account of how Party media framed the lessons and tasks of reform at the 40th anniversary, including the Party's own list of present risks.

Several questions on upholding and developing socialism with Chinese characteristics 关于坚持和发展中国特色社会主义的几个问题 Xi Jinping This text is an excerpt from a speech by Xi Jinping, General Secretary of the Central Committee, delivered on 5 January 2013 at a study session for newly elected members and alternate members of the Central Committee on implementing the spirit of the 18th Party Congress (2012). It was published in Qiushi in 2019. Xi's main message is that socialism with Chinese characteristics is socialism and no other "ism", and that its basic principles, the Party's historical continuity and its ideal of communism must all be held to. The speech is organised under four numbered points. The first defends the socialist character of the Chinese path against labels such as "state capitalism". The second addresses how to understand the periods before and after reform and opening up. The third argues that Marxism develops with the times. The fourth concerns the communist ideal and the faith expected of Party members and cadres. A closing section on the "path" ties these together. Xi argues that the basic principles of scientific socialism cannot be abandoned, and he lists the institutions that embody them: Party leadership, the people's congress system, and an economy with public ownership as the mainstay. He rejects wholesale copying of Soviet or Western models and says each country's path should be chosen by its own people. On history, he holds that the two periods are connected yet distinct, and that neither may be used to negate the other. He ties this to the Soviet collapse, which he attributes partly to "historical nihilism" and the wholesale denial of Soviet and Party history. He treats the evaluation of Mao Zedong as a political question and not only a historical one. He also holds that Marxism cannot stand still: China remains in the primary stage of socialism with many unresolved problems. On the communist ideal, Xi holds that it can be realised only on the basis of a fully developed socialist society, over very many generations. Losing it, he says, would lead to utilitarianism and pragmatism, while neglecting present tasks for it would be equally wrong. He contends that the analysis by Marx and Engels of capitalism's basic contradictions is not outdated, but that socialism's final victory will be a long process of cooperation and struggle with capitalism. He concludes that the path is the Party's lifeblood and that persisting with it will bring a moderately prosperous society by the Party's centenary and a modern socialist country by the People's Republic's centenary. Read the original if you want a primary source for the early-2013 official line on the Party's historical continuity, ideological confidence and the socialist character of the Chinese path.

Rereading the Resolution on Certain Questions in the History of Our Party and strengthening conscious commitment to the "Two Upholds" 重温《关于若干历史问题的决议》 坚定“两个维护”的自觉 Wang Junwei Writing in Qiushi in 2019, Wang Junwei asks what the Party's 1945 Resolution on Certain Questions in the History of Our Party can teach about the present-day requirement of the Two Upholds: resolutely upholding General Secretary Xi Jinping's core position on the Party Central Committee and in the whole Party, and upholding the authority and centralised, unified leadership of the Central Committee. Wang argues that the Two Upholds grow out of the Party's historical experience and distil the lessons of revolution, construction and reform. Rereading the Resolution, in this view, deepens understanding of why they matter. The article has four sections. The first describes the consensus on Mao Zedong's leadership that formed during the Yan'an rectification and the drafting of the Resolution, which was adopted at the Seventh Plenum of the Sixth Central Committee in April 1945. The second reviews the three "Left" line periods and the Party's early setbacks. The third turns to democratic centralism and the problem of factionalism. The fourth discusses theoretical clarity as the basis of political firmness, and then draws a link to the post-2012 period. Wang's central argument is that whether the Party has a mature, stable leadership core decides its success or failure. Citing the Resolution and Deng Xiaoping, Wang says the leadership before the Zunyi Conference was unstable and immature. Wang attributes the losses of the Left-line periods, including the fall in Red Army strength from 300,000 to just over 30,000, to this. Wang presents the cases of Zhang Guotao and Wang Ming as examples of defying the Central Committee, and treats upholding the core as inherent in democratic centralism. Mao's leadership, Wang says, was accepted because his political, military, organisational and ideological line proved correct, and the Party's leaders of the time, including Liu Shaoqi, Zhou Enlai, Zhu De, Ren Bishi and Zhang Wentian, are cited as endorsing it. Wang concludes that the Party's achievements since the 18th Party Congress (2012) are due to Xi Jinping's leadership as core and to the authority of the Central Committee. Wang calls on all Party members, especially leading cadres, to firmly hold the "four consciousnesses", strengthen the Four-sphere Confidence and carry out the Two Upholds. This means ideological agreement, political support, organisational obedience and action in step with the Central Committee, which Wang calls fundamental political discipline. Read the original if you want to see how a 2019 Party theoretical journal draws on the 1945 Resolution and Party history to justify the Two Upholds.

On the new era 论新时代 Tong Xin Published in Qiushi in January 2019 under the byline Tong Xin, this long commentary sets out what the Party's judgement that socialism with Chinese characteristics has entered a new era means and why it is correct. The author argues that the new era is a lawful stage in both Chinese and world history, defined by socialism with Chinese characteristics and guided by Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The piece is organised in nine numbered sections. Each links the new era to a theme: the great historical epoch, socialism with Chinese characteristics, Xi Jinping Thought, the great changes in the world, the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, the principal contradiction in society, the people-centred approach, a new path to modernization, and the great struggle. The core reasoning rests on a Marxist theory of epochs. Citing Marx, Engels and Lenin, the author holds that the contradiction between the productive forces and the relations of production determines historical eras, and that the present remains within the epoch of transition from capitalism to socialism that Marxism identified. Within this frame, the author says the new era is shown by a historic change in the principal contradiction, now between the people's ever-growing needs for a better life and unbalanced and inadequate development. The author claims that the institutions of socialism with Chinese characteristics are now broadly in step with the productive forces, while remaining imperfect and needing further reform. The author also contends that China's path to modernization differs from the Western one, which is described as built on colonial plunder and expansion. In this account, China's path relies mainly on internal strength and peaceful development and offers developing countries a new option. The author concludes that the new era brings the great leap from "standing up" and "becoming prosperous" to "becoming strong", renewed vitality for scientific socialism and a Chinese contribution to solving human problems. The closing section calls for vigilance against risks, readiness for struggle, continued reform, upholding the Party's leadership with the Two Upholds, and full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. Read the original if you want an authoritative, programmatic statement of how Party theorists framed the new-era concept at the start of 2019.

China–Africa relations and the building of the Belt and Road 中非关系与“一带一路”建设 Li Xinfeng Writing in Qiushi in 2019, Li Xinfeng asks how the long history of China–Africa ties relates to the Belt and Road Initiative and what the current partnership offers both sides. Li argues that the two are closely linked: ancient exchanges prefigured the Belt and Road, and present-day cooperation helps the Initiative to take root and bring benefits to ordinary people. The piece frames China–Africa friendship as grounded in shared suffering under imperialism and colonialism and in a peaceful cultural tradition. The article moves in four steps. It begins with Zheng He's voyages to East Africa in the Ming dynasty as the high point of ancient relations. It then turns to modern cooperation, including the Tanzania–Zambia Railway and the Mombasa–Nairobi Railway in Kenya. It next surveys the Forum on China–Africa Cooperation, its 2015 Johannesburg and 2018 Beijing summits, and the "eight major initiatives". It ends with four features of China–Africa relations. Li holds that Zheng He's fleets traded fairly and took no land, wealth or slaves from Africa, which Li presents as evidence of a "peace gene" in Chinese civilisation that runs through to the Belt and Road. The Mombasa–Nairobi line, built with Chinese financing, design, equipment and operation, is presented as a flagship project linking the Initiative to Kenya's Vision 2030 and the African Union's Agenda 2063. Li cites trade growth from US$10.6 billion in 2000 to US$204.19 billion in 2018, and US$60 billion in support pledged at the 2018 summit. Li also names four features of the relationship: a gradual and uneven rise, natural affinity, constant innovation, and interference by Western powers that Li says have obscured or disrupted the relationship. Li concludes that China–Africa relations reflect the broader trend of world history, since independence and national liberation ended the colonial era. Li presents the relationship as a model of cooperation among developing countries. Li also says it will build experience for a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want an example of how official Chinese writing in 2019 tied Zheng He, the Tanzania–Zambia Railway and the Forum on China–Africa Cooperation into a single story about the Belt and Road Initiative.

A country and a nation cannot be without a soul 一个国家、一个民族不能没有灵魂 Xi Jinping This is a speech by Xi Jinping, delivered on 4 March 2019 at a joint group meeting of members from the cultural and arts circles and the social science circles during the second session of the 13th National Committee of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference (CPPCC), and later published in Qiushi. Xi argues that culture, literature, art, philosophy and the social sciences are spiritual undertakings that supply a country's soul, which must be present and must not be confused. After reviewing 2018, including the celebration of 40 years of reform and opening up, Xi assesses the work of the two circles since the 2014 symposium on literature and art and the 2016 symposium on philosophy and social sciences. He credits them with consolidating the guiding position of Marxism, orienting creation towards the people and advancing the building of philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics. He also notes their consultative work in 2018, such as research on the spirit of model workers and craftsmen and on protecting red resources. The core of the speech is four hopes. First, that members keep pace with the times, record and celebrate the new era, and answer its questions. Second, that they put the people at the centre: Xi says creators must settle whom they write for, and social scientists must leave the ivory tower and do fieldwork, diagnosing China's problems before prescribing remedies. Third, that they offer fine works to the people, which he says requires originality, rootedness in Chinese reality and, for social science, autonomous theories and Chinese disciplinary, academic and discourse systems. Fourth, that they lead social trends through virtue, holding to professional ethics and the core socialist values and resisting vulgarity in the market economy. Xi closes by asking members to reflect the 70 years of the People's Republic, explain the logic of its transformation and the advantages of the path, theory, system and culture of socialism with Chinese characteristics, and use Chinese theory to interpret Chinese practice. He also urges CPPCC members to build consensus, improve their own abilities and set an example. Read the original if you want a primary statement of the Party leadership's 2019 expectations of writers, artists and social scientists.

A "great political creation" grown in Chinese soil Studying General Secretary Xi Jinping's important remarks on the new-type party system 中国土壤生长的“伟大政治创造” Lei Chunfang Writing in 2019, the 70th anniversary of the People's Republic and of the people's political consultative system, Lei studies Xi Jinping's March 2018 remarks on the new-type party system. This commentary is a study of those remarks. It asks how the system, defined as multiparty cooperation and political consultation under the leadership of the Communist Party of China, came about, what makes it distinctive, and why it matters. Lei's answer, following Xi, is that it is a wholly original institution rooted in Chinese conditions and not an imported model. The piece has three parts: how the system was created, its characteristics, and its significance. The first part covers wartime and post-war united fronts, the 1948 May Day Slogans, the 1949 Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference, and sources in traditional Chinese culture. The second part builds on Xi's three "what is new" points. The third offers three ways of understanding its importance. In Lei's account, the system grew out of the Chinese people's struggle for national independence and people's democracy, and it differs from Western two-party and multiparty systems and from the Soviet party system. Lei names three features. The first is consistency of fundamental interests: the democratic parties represent particular groups, but on the basis of shared fundamental interests. The second is a common direction of effort: they are parties participating in government, not opposition parties. The third is democratic operation, shown through consultation mechanisms and figures such as 34,000-plus proposals submitted to the national Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Following Xi, Lei says each feature avoids a flaw of "old-style" systems: representing narrow interests, lack of oversight or vicious competition, and social division. Lei concludes that the system is an institutional "code" behind the "Chinese miracle", a guarantee for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, and a "Chinese approach" to party-system development. Lei describes Western politics as marked by "money politics" and oligarchy. Lei presents the system as a contribution to human political civilization. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the official Party press explains the multiparty cooperation system and its claims about it in 2019.

The tradition of Chinese legal culture and its value as historical mirror 中华法文化的传统与史鉴价值 Zhang Jinfan Writing in Qiushi in 2019, the legal historian Zhang Jinfan asks what China's long legal tradition can offer to the building of a socialist rule-of-law system. Zhang argues that the Chinese legal system (Zhonghua faxi) is an important part of the world's legal families because of its deep legal culture, its governing experience and the ancient sages' habit of joining politics with law. Summing up the good traditions of that culture, the author holds, has historical-mirror value for building a system of rule of law with Chinese characteristics. The article is organised in four parts, each drawing on classical sources and dynastic institutions from the Zhou to the Qing. They deal with the joint governance of virtue and law, the tradition of legislating from actual conditions, the strict supervision of officials through performance evaluation and censorial oversight, and the unity of good law, worthy officials and good governance. Zhang illustrates each with legal codes, regional and ethnic legislation, evaluation schemes and statements by rulers and thinkers. Zhang's central claim is that the complementarity of virtue and law is the essence of Chinese legal culture. Virtue transforms individuals, customs and the people, while law is the direct coercive instrument; the Tang code's formula makes virtue and ritual the root of governance and punishment its instrument. On legislation, the author stresses adapting law to time and place, citing Legalist and late-Qing reformers, agrarian and environmental rules, provincial regulations and Qing ethnic legislation following local custom. On officials, Zhang traces evaluation systems from the Tang to the Qing and the censorate's development into the Qing Imperial Censorate code. Good law is characterised by adaptability combined with stability, impartiality, simplicity and responsiveness to popular feeling. Zhang adds that law cannot execute itself and needs worthy officials to bring about good governance. Zhang concludes that Chinese legal culture, uninterrupted for more than five thousand years, holds some enduring value, but also carries clear historical and class limitations and much feudal dross. The task today is to promote its outstanding traditions so that they supply historical wisdom for a socialist system of rule of law. Read the original if you want a compact, source-rich survey of how an official Chinese legal historian presents traditional legal institutions as resources for contemporary legal construction.

How the older generation of revolutionaries conducted investigation and research 老一辈革命家如何搞调查研究 Jiang Shuping Writing in Qiushi in 2019, Jiang Shuping asks what today's Party members and cadres can learn from the way the Party's older generation of revolutionaries carried out investigation and research (diaoyan). The author argues that this practice is a basic working method and fine tradition of the Party. Studying it, Jiang holds, answers Xi Jinping's call to promote a stronger culture of investigation and research and has real practical value for leading cadres. The article is organised around six working principles, each illustrated with episodes from the lives of Mao Zedong, Zhu De, Liu Shaoqi, Deng Xiaoping, Zhou Enlai and Chen Yun. These range from the Xunwu investigation of 1930 and the rural surveys after the Great Leap Forward to Deng's visits to the special economic zones and the Three Gorges debates. Each section closes by linking the historical practice to Xi Jinping's instructions on research work. Jiang's central claim is that leaders must investigate in person rather than rely on written reports, and must approach ordinary people humbly, as 'pupils'. Research should be driven by concrete problems, not conducted for its own sake. Jiang then describes Mao's method of 'dissecting a sparrow': studying selected advanced, middling and backward cases in depth, as in Liu Shaoqi's 44 days in Hunan villages in 1961 and Chen Yun's fortnight in Xiaozheng. The author adds that investigation should use fact-finding meetings, be systematic and comprehensive, and deliberately seek out opposing views. Examples include Liu's and Mao's briefings before the Eighth Party Congress, Zhou Enlai's encouragement of dissent over the Three Gorges project, and Chen Yun's maxim of 'exchange, comparison, repetition'. Jiang concludes that, despite new information technology and the arrival of artificial intelligence, systematic on-site research remains an irreplaceable basic skill for cadres. In the author's account, Xi Jinping's guidance confirms this. Jiang calls on cadres to treat investigation and research as a family heirloom and to use it to address new problems in the new era, in pursuit of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a compact, Party-oriented collection of anecdotes and quotations on the investigative methods of Mao, Liu, Zhu, Deng, Zhou and Chen Yun, and on how they are presented to cadres today.

How to teach ideological and political theory courses well in universities 怎样才能上好高校思想政治理论课 Liu Jianjun Writing in Qiushi in 2019, Liu Jianjun takes up Xi Jinping's address of 18 March 2019 at a symposium for teachers of school ideological and political theory courses (sizheng ke). Liu asks where the importance of these courses lies, why they are hard to teach, and how they can be taught well. The answer is that the courses are uniquely important and uniquely difficult, but can be taught well if teachers follow Xi's guidance and make the effort Liu outlines. The commentary has three parts that follow the three questions. The first sets out three reasons for the courses' importance in universities. The second lists five sources of difficulty. The third lists six favourable conditions and then four areas where teachers need to improve. On importance, Liu argues that the courses embody the socialist character and direction of Chinese higher education, serve as the key course for fostering virtue and cultivating talent, and are the main channel and main front of students' ideological and political education. On difficulty, Liu points to the courses' strong political content, which creates psychological distance, and to their theoretical depth, which exceeds students' training in abstract thinking. Liu also cites the gap between theory and reality, the breadth and speed of change in content, and the harder task of shaping values and convictions, not just passing on knowledge. Liu adds that these courses cannot carry sole responsibility for students' ideals and convictions. For solutions, Liu calls on teachers to strengthen their own convictions and study Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. They should also carry out research that serves teaching, convert academic and political language into classroom language, and use varied methods such as thematic, interactive and online teaching. Liu points to strong Party backing, theoretical achievements and an able teaching force as favourable conditions. Read the original if you want a concise, official-line account of how Party-state ideology courses in universities are justified and what teachers are told to do in 2019.

Strengthening the "four abilities" of legs, eyes, brain and pen to better fulfil the mission of propaganda and ideological work 增强脚力眼力脑力笔力 更好完成宣传思想工作使命任务 Cai Mingzhao Writing in Qiushi in 2019, Cai Mingzhao explains and promotes Xi Jinping's call that propaganda and ideological workers strengthen their "four abilities": jiaoli (legs, going to the grassroots), yanli (eyes, discernment), naoli (brain, political and theoretical level) and bili (pen, writing and communication skill). Cai argues that the four abilities form the overall requirement for building the propaganda and ideological ranks in the new situation. They set out the political quality, theoretical grounding, professional skill and work style such workers need. The piece begins with Xi's 2016 remarks on news work and his 2018 extension of the requirement to the whole propaganda and ideological front. It notes that, under the Central Propaganda Department's plan, an education and practice campaign on the four abilities is under way nationwide. Four sections then take each ability in turn, drawing on Marx, Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi, and on examples from Chinese journalism and literature such as Fan Changjiang, Mu Qing and Liu Qing. Cai presents the abilities as a hierarchy. Legs are the source of the rest: practice is primary, and propaganda work reflects it, so workers must go among the people and carry out investigation. Eyes mean dialectical, comprehensive thinking, a grasp of the overall situation, and comparison. Cai invokes the Marxist principle of "overall truthfulness" in news, arguing that reporting only negative facts would be untrue as a whole. Brain holds the leading place: propaganda work is political work, which requires Party spirit, the Four Consciousnesses, the Two Upholds, and study of Marxism and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Pen requires staying close to ordinary people's language, observing the principle of timing, degree and effect, and combining "keeping to principle" with innovation, including on the internet and with new technologies. Cai concludes that workers should strengthen all four abilities in order to be recorders of the people's struggle and builders of national rejuvenation. The target is the Two Centenary Goals, with the moderately prosperous society about to be completed. The article is a Party-journal statement of how the leadership frames professional standards for propaganda cadres and journalists. Read the original if you want to see how an official Qiushi article translates Xi Jinping's media and propaganda guidelines into a training programme for propaganda workers.

A changed world: the first years of New China 换了人间：新中国的最初岁月 Jin Chongji Writing in the People's Daily on the 70th anniversary of the People's Republic (4 September 2019), Jin Chongji asks why the founding of the PRC counts as one of the "three milestones" on the road to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The answer, Jin argues, is that China's fate changed fundamentally from 1949, so that it can be described as a "changed world". Looking back at the early years, the author says, helps readers understand where China has come from and where it is going. The piece is a historical commentary built around three themes. It begins with China's national humiliation since the Opium War and the claim that the Chinese people "stood up". It then turns to the policies of the new people's government. It ends with national unification and unity. A short conclusion draws lessons from the founding period. Jin draws on speeches by Mao Zedong, Zhou Enlai and Deng Xiaoping, and on recollections of participants such as Sun Qimeng and Fei Xiaotong. Jin also adds a personal memory of serving as a youth delegate to the Shanghai people's representative conference in 1950–52. Jin's core argument has three parts. First, independence: after a century of foreign aggression and unequal treaties, the new state would not bow to outside pressure, and the Korean War, in Jin's account, won international respect and a lasting peaceful environment for construction. Second, the people's government acted for the people: the article credits it with establishing the people's democratic dictatorship, holding representative conferences, carrying out land reform, curbing inflation, relieving unemployment, controlling floods on the Huai River, and passing the Marriage Law and campaigns against opium and prostitution. Jin says these measures made ordinary people feel they were the country's masters. Third, unity: the Party, as the core force, ended the "sheet of loose sand" condition, and regional administration, the name "People's Republic" rather than a federation, and regional ethnic autonomy secured unification. Jin concludes that national independence, people's liberation and unification were the basic tasks of 1949, and that failure on any of them would have meant a more difficult path. The author notes that the new leaders had to decide quickly, addressing immediate livelihood needs while planning for socialist modernization, and expresses respect for Mao Zedong and the other founders. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the official narrative of the early PRC was presented to a mass readership at the 70th anniversary.

Promoting the formation of a strong domestic market and vigorously advancing high-quality economic development 促进形成强大国内市场 大力推动经济高质量发展 He Lifeng Writing in Qiushi in early 2019, He Lifeng takes up the instruction of General Secretary Xi Jinping, issued at the Central Economic Work Conference at the end of 2018, to promote the formation of a strong domestic market. He argues that, against a background of weak global recovery, protectionism and unilateralism, building such a market meets the people's needs for a better life, advances high-quality development and offers other countries opportunities. He presents it as a task of major practical and historical significance. The article has four parts. It first sets out why the task is necessary and urgent, then assesses the room for expansion, then presents an overall approach built on four words (consolidate, strengthen, upgrade, unblock), and finally names five main directions for action. It draws on figures for consumption, urbanisation, high-tech output and public services to support its case. He's core reasoning starts from the principal contradiction identified at the 19th Party Congress (2017): the gap between the people's growing need for a better life and unbalanced, inadequate development. A strong domestic market is described as integral to supply-side structural reform, which the author treats as the main line of policy because the main economic problems are structural and lie in the real economy. It is also presented as a condition for meeting people's needs, for steadying expectations against talk of 'the state advances, the private sector retreats', and for showing great-power responsibility. On potential, He cites rising consumer spending, a modern industrial system, shortfalls in core technology and equipment, urbanisation (58.5 per cent in 2017) and regional gaps, and public services and infrastructure. The four-word approach means consolidating the 'three cuts, one reduction, one improvement' results, strengthening the vitality of firms, upgrading the industrial chain through innovation, and unblocking the circulation of the national economy. He calls for five lines of action: filling gaps in major science and technology infrastructure, upgrading traditional industries, fostering emerging industries, promoting coordinated urban-rural and regional development to encourage effective investment, and expanding new consumption growth from the supply side. The author stresses reform, market-based and rule-of-law methods, and a break with habits formed in the era of high-speed growth. Read the original if you want an official statement from early 2019 of how the leadership linked domestic-market building, supply-side reform and high-quality development.

Dialectical materialism is the world outlook and methodology of Chinese Communists 辩证唯物主义是中国共产党人的世界观和方法论 Xi Jinping This is a speech by Xi Jinping, delivered on 23 January 2015 at the 20th group study session of the Political Bureau of the 18th Central Committee and published in Qiushi in 2019. Xi presents dialectical materialism as the world outlook and methodology of Chinese Communists. He argues that Party members and officials must consciously apply it if the Party is to achieve the "Two Centenary Goals" and the Chinese Dream of national rejuvenation. Xi opens by tracing the Party's use of Marxist philosophy, from Mao Zedong's essays on practice and contradiction to Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin and Hu Jintao. He then sets out four areas for study and application: the material unity of the world, the laws of contradiction, the methods of materialist dialectics, and the relation between knowledge and practice.
