Classical Chinese sayings and idioms appear throughout alongside quotations from Engels. On the first point, Xi holds that policy must start from objective reality rather than subjective wishes. The largest reality, in his account, is that China remains in the primary stage of socialism, though he stresses that conditions keep changing and that new contradictions require fresh analysis. He also says consciousness can act strongly on matter, which is why ideals and convictions are the "calcium" of Communists. On contradiction, he urges officials to face problems directly and to separate principal from secondary contradictions. He cites the "Four-sphere Comprehensive" agenda as an example of combining overall planning with a focus on key points. He describes metaphysics as the easy alternative to dialectics, which demands investigation and a development-minded, comprehensive, systematic view. Xi concludes that practice is the source and purpose of knowledge, and that theory detached from practice becomes dogma. He calls for confidence in theory and strategic resolve. He also insists that theoretical innovation has no end, and that it must interact with practical innovation to develop twenty-first-century Marxism in China. Read the original if you want a primary statement of how the top Party leadership presents Marxist philosophy as a practical method of governance.

Writing a newer and more beautiful chapter for the era Studying and implementing the spirit of Xi Jinping's important speech at the meeting celebrating the 70th anniversary of the founding of the People's Republic of China 书写出更新更美的时代篇章 Li Zhongjie This commentary, first published in the People's Daily on 16 October 2019, is a study piece on Xi Jinping's speech at the meeting marking the 70th anniversary of the People's Republic. Li Zhongjie takes up Xi's three-part formula: China's yesterday is already written in humanity's records, its today is being created by hundreds of millions of people, and its tomorrow will certainly be better. Li reads the formula as showing historical continuity and as a call to write a newer and more beautiful chapter. The article is organised under three headings that follow Xi's three time frames. The first looks back from the founding of New China to the long history of Chinese civilisation, and to Xi's summary of what the 70 years added. The second turns to the present, using the names of the National Day parade's mass formations as a guide. The third looks ahead and stresses that the road remains long. Li argues that the founding of New China ended a century of humiliation and opened the road to national rejuvenation. He says the 70 years are best summed up in three points taken from Xi's remarks: opening the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics, ending absolute poverty, and an independent, peaceful foreign policy that contributes to a community with a shared future for mankind. On the present, Li groups the parade formations into past history, ongoing tasks and the undertakings pursued since the 18th Party Congress (2012) under Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. He treats the smooth organisation of the celebration as evidence of high governance capacity. Li concludes that China's tomorrow will be better because of the material base and governing experience built up over 70 years, and especially since reform and opening up. He adds that the road ahead will not be smooth and that the Party is "on the road", citing Xi's warnings about complacency and corruption. He notes that the Fourth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee was about to take up improving the system and modernising state governance, and he calls on all to unite and keep the Republic strong. Read the original if you want an example of how official commentary of 2019 presented Xi's anniversary speech and its past–present–future framing.

Drawing striving strength from heroes 从英雄身上汲取奋发力量 Qin Long This short commentary, first published in the People's Daily on 22 October 2019, takes up Xi Jinping's remark at the state medals and honorary titles ceremony that heroes emerge only where heroism is revered and where people strive to be heroes. Qin argues that the Chinese nation has always honoured heroes, and that the new era needs more of them. The piece is organised around four injunctions: revere heroes, defend heroes, learn from heroes and care for heroes. It places them against the 70 years since the founding of the People's Republic and the goal of the Chinese Dream of national rejuvenation, and it cites classical Chinese poetry as evidence of a long tradition of hero-worship. Qin reasons that rejuvenation will not come easily and requires a "great struggle" against risks and challenges, so more model figures are needed. Heroes are described as the nation's backbone, so Qin says that people who deliberately blacken them or distort history must be met with vigilance. The author points to the Law on the Protection of Heroes and Martyrs, in force since 1 May 2018, as legal backing. Learning from heroes means first knowing their deeds, then putting them into practice. Qin holds that greatness comes from ordinary work done well. On caring for heroes, Qin calls for honours and rewards for them, and for attention to their families, so that heroes do not "shed both blood and tears". The conclusion is that reverence, defence, learning and care together draw the strength needed for the new era. Read the original if you want a brief example of how the People's Daily framed hero commemoration in 2019.

Speeches at the symposium marking the 130th anniversary of Li Dazhao's birth 在纪念李大钊同志诞辰130周年座谈会上的发言 Qu Qingshan Liang Yanshun Qiu Shuiping Wang Dongfeng This is a set of four speeches given at the symposium commemorating the 130th anniversary of Li Dazhao's birth, originally published in the People's Daily on 28 October 2019. The speakers are Qu Qingshan (president of the Party History and Literature Research Institute), Liang Yanshun (deputy head of the Central Publicity Department), Qiu Shuiping (Party secretary of Peking University) and Wang Dongfeng (Party secretary of Hebei). Together they present Li as a pioneer of Marxism in China and a principal founder of the Communist Party, and as a model for present-day Party work. Qu concentrates on Li's intellectual contribution to exploring China's revolutionary road. Liang describes Li as the earliest Marxist in China, a systematic propagandist of Marxism and an explorer of its application to Chinese conditions. Qiu stresses Li's decade at Peking University, his influence on students and his role in founding the early Beijing Communist organisation. Wang reviews Li's activities in Hebei and then reports Hebei's recent economic, ecological and livelihood results under Xi Jinping. On the substance of Li's thought, Qu and Liang point to his writings after the Russian Revolution, notably "My Marxist View" and "Further Discussion of Problems and Isms". They report that Li held Marxism to be a tool to be studied for how it applies to China's political and economic conditions, not a dogma to be imported whole. Both credit him with early formulations: that China's democratic revolution must be led by the proletariat, rely on the peasantry and build a democratic united front, and that Chinese socialism would have its own characteristics. Qu adds Li's views on Party-building: a clear political character, strong organisation, mass links and a purpose of serving the people, which he ties to full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. Each speaker links the commemoration to current tasks. Liang calls for arming the whole Party with Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and for adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Qiu proposes building Chinese philosophy and social science with their own disciplinary, academic and discourse systems. Wang pledges Hebei's loyalty to the Party Central Committee and its commitment to the Two Upholds and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want to see how senior Party and university officials in 2019 presented Li Dazhao's legacy and tied it to Party-building, ideology and regional development.

Deeply understanding the adherence to a people-centred approach 深刻领会坚持以人民为中心 Beijing Municipal Research Centre for Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era This commentary, published in the People's Daily on 30 October 2019 under the name of a Beijing municipal research centre on Xi Jinping Thought, sets out what it means to "adhere to a people-centred approach". It argues that this principle, part of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, makes the people's standpoint the fundamental standpoint, makes the people's yearning for a better life the goal of struggle, and requires the Party to carry out its own great self-reform. The text is organised in three sections after a short introduction. The first treats the principle as an expression of what it calls Marxism's most distinctive trait, its character as a doctrine of the people. The second links it to the Communists' "original aspiration and mission". The third concerns the foundations of the Party's long-term governance. In the first section the authors hold that Marxism is rooted in the people and aims at human liberation. They list the Party's commitments as evidence: serving the people wholeheartedly, the mass line, governing for the people, and the four criteria of whether the people support, approve, are happy with and agree to its work. In the second section the article ties the people-centred approach to three aims: the people's yearning for a better life, the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, and a larger contribution to humanity. It cites the redefined principal contradiction, the Party's livelihood goals, a community with a shared future for mankind and the Belt and Road Initiative. In the third section the authors argue that, because the Party has no interests apart from those of the country, nation and people, it can find the courage to reform itself. They say this requires winning popular support, opposing formalism and bureaucratism, and accepting public supervision, and they claim that campaigns since the 18th Party Congress (2012) have achieved results. The article concludes that only by keeping the people at the centre can the Party stay close to the masses, resist the dangers it identifies (spiritual slackness, inadequate ability, detachment from the masses and corruption), and secure the "most reliable" class and popular base for long-term rule. It presents the principle as both a theoretical proposition and a basic strategy for the new era. Read the original if you want an authoritative example of how Party-affiliated theorists link Marxism's "people" orientation to governance, common prosperity and Party discipline in 2019.

Development trends of foreign Marxist currents in the twenty-first century and an assessment of their effects 21世纪国外马克思主义思潮的发展趋势及其效应评估 Zhang Liang Sun Leqiang Writing in 2019, Zhang Liang and Sun Leqiang ask how Chinese scholars should approach the development of Marxism outside China since 2000. They argue that China's researchers are no longer followers of foreign Marxism but its contemporaries. On this view, they should no longer rely on ready-made Western scholarship, and should instead judge foreign currents independently, from the standpoint of socialism with Chinese characteristics, taking from them selectively. The article surveys Western left thought since the Soviet and East European collapse in three parts. The first examines how foreign Marxism treats Marxist basic theory: new textual scholarship and four research routes. The second takes four theoretical growth points: ecological Marxism, spatial theory, identity politics and biopolitics. The third looks at four areas of research on current capitalism: production, crisis, class structure and democracy. The authors' central claim is that foreign Marxism offers sharp diagnoses of capitalism but weak or evasive alternatives. They criticise the MEGA2-era editorial approach as deconstructive, saying it revives an opposition between Marx and Engels. They sort the four routes into rereading Marx, localisation, grafting onto 'post-' theories, and wholesale rejection of Marxism. They find that spatial theory, identity politics and biopolitics drift into romanticism or utopianism, or fail to touch capitalism's economic roots. On class, they reject the 'middle stratum', 'cognitive class' and 'multitude' concepts as eclectic. Citing Marx and Engels on mental labourers, they hold that anyone who sells labour-power and produces surplus value belongs to the working class. They credit left writers who return to Capital for crisis analysis, but say these writers leave the basic contradiction between productive forces and capitalist relations of production untouched. In conclusion, the authors credit foreign Marxism with useful lessons for editing classic texts, studying the classics, localising Marxism and understanding capitalism's structural contradictions. They add that it must be treated critically, given its deconstructive tendencies and its Eurocentric and neoliberal assumptions. They call on Chinese Marxists to strengthen a Chinese standpoint and a sense of historical position, and to move from Chinese experience to Chinese theory in order to innovate twenty-first-century Marxism. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic assessment of Western Marxist trends since 2000, and of the stance Chinese scholars are urged to take toward them.

Policy trends and future prospects of the Communist Party of Nepal government 尼泊尔共产党政府的政策趋向及未来前景 Yuan Qun Wang Enming Writing in 2019, Yuan Qun and Wang Enming ask what the government led by the unified Communist Party of Nepal (NCP) is trying to do, and whether it can last. The article takes up the left alliance that won the 2017 elections and took office in February 2018. In May 2018 its two parties, the CPN (Unified Marxist-Leninist) and the CPN (Maoist Centre), merged into the NCP. The authors argue that the NCP is now Nepal's strongest party and its government the most stable since multiparty politics was restored in 1990. They also hold that its policies are producing early results and that it has good prospects of serving a full term. The article has three parts. The first assesses the significance of the merger: the new party's leadership structure and seat counts, the stability of the government, and the effect on the international communist movement. The second reviews policy in four areas: perfecting the political system, transforming the economic structure, investing in people's livelihood, and bilateral and multilateral diplomacy. The third looks ahead at party integration, economic growth and India's likely efforts to increase its influence. It draws mainly on Nepali government documents, Nepali and Indian press reports and UN data. The authors' central argument is that parliamentary dominance has ended the frequent changes of government they identify as the main cause of Nepal's economic and social lag. They cite 441 central committee members, with 241 from the former UML and 200 from the Maoist Centre. They also cite 174 of 275 lower-house seats, and 190 once the Federal Socialist Forum joined, above two-thirds. On policy, they report anti-corruption cases, new roads, bridges and hydropower, health insurance in 36 districts and new technical schools. They report projected growth of 6.81% for 2018–19, below the 8% target, and a shift in the sectoral shares of GDP. The authors conclude that the main threat to the government is not the opposition Nepali Congress but whether the NCP can fully integrate its two ideological and organisational traditions. They note that posts have been shared roughly 6:4 and that debate continues on merging the two parties' theories of democracy. They expect India to try to regain influence, and expect Nepal to balance it by deepening ties with China. They say the NCP has already broken the 'curse' of earlier communist governments lasting under a year, and that its ability to govern long-term deserves close attention. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic account of the NCP's first year in government, with Nepali sources and figures.

The current state and development trends of the American left-wing movement 美国左翼运动的现状与发展趋势 Zhang Yanchen Why has the left in the United States revived in recent years, and why do its gains so often prove short-lived? Writing in 2019, Zhang argues that popular discontent with working and everyday life has revived left-wing movements, but that union-based mobilisation cannot consolidate their results. In response, newer left forces, above all the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), are moving towards a strategy of "returning to the working class". The article has four parts. It first traces the accumulated grievances behind the revival since the 2008 financial crisis, then assesses the movement's present condition: its renewed activity, its lack of staying power and the rise of new organisational forces. The third part examines the DSA's strategic shift, and the last considers the theoretical and practical significance of the trend. Zhang relies largely on commentary in New Left Review's 2019 "America's New Left" series and on Monthly Review authors. Zhang locates the discontent in three spheres: fragmented, Taylorist divisions of labour and guild-like trade associations that block mobility; consumerism and credit that bind people to finance capital in debt and anxiety; and distrust of a government pursuing neoliberal austerity, which pushes people towards "new social movements". Union-led campaigns, such as the Sanders-backed Amazon wage rise that Amazon offset by cutting paid hours, win only sector-limited, temporary gains. The DSA, Zhang says, wants to move beyond a problem-driven committee structure dominated by young, middle-class activists. It aims to root itself in workplaces and communities, to build a socialist party rather than lean on candidates such as Sanders, to remake unions from below, and to target financial capital and oligarchic firms rather than only government policy. Zhang concludes that the trend has theoretical value, since it energises Marxist research in the United States, and practical value, since it may produce a cross-sector party built from the base. The author stresses its limits, however. Its goal is a gradual change of social order within capitalism, not Marx's overall transformation of the social system. The DSA has never committed itself to Marxism as a guide, and whether the movement will become a revolutionary force is left open. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist academic's assessment of the DSA and the post-2008 American left, drawn from Anglophone left sources.

Western sociology's changing stance towards Marxist theory and its implications 西方社会学对马克思主义理论的立场演变及其反思 Wen Jun Gao Yiduo Western scholars disagree on whether sociology is moving away from Marxism or towards it. Wen and Gao argue that neither description is enough, and that the relationship has to be traced over the long term. Their thesis is that Western sociology's stance has passed through five stages, driven by changing political, economic and intellectual conditions. Sociology's main stance has been to move away from Marxism, and it has drawn on Marxism mainly in moments of theoretical crisis. The article surveys the period from the mid-nineteenth century to the present. It first contrasts classical sociology (Comte, Durkheim, Weber) with Marx on how society progresses, how knowledge is produced and how facts are known. It then covers the 'amphibious' theorists Lukács, Gramsci and Polanyi, and the Frankfurt School. Next come the postwar American mainstream of Parsons, Merton and Lazarsfeld, the radical sociology of the 1970s and 1980s, and the post-1990 period of professionalisation and Michael Burawoy's 'public sociology'. A final section draws lessons for Chinese sociology. The authors name five stages: divergence (to 1918), reflexive absorption (to 1945), extreme rejection (to the late 1960s), renewed integration through radical sociology (1970s to late 1980s), and Marxism as an implicit presence (from the 1990s). In their account, early sociologists modelled themselves on natural science and value-neutrality, while Marxism aimed to change society. Postwar functionalist and quantitative sociology marginalised Marxism, and the crises of the 1960s pushed sociologists back towards it. After the collapse of the Soviet Union, fragmentation, professionalisation and the search for disciplinary balance, in the authors' view, wore down sociology's critical edge. They argue that public sociology partly resists this, but remains weaker than the professional mainstream. Wen and Gao propose that Chinese sociology go beyond the 'away from' or 'towards' Marxism choice and place Marxist sociology at the centre of China's body of social-science knowledge. They offer five recommendations: handle theory and practice together, reread the classic texts, promote exchange between sociology and Marxist studies, develop a sense of crisis, and combine the roles of interpreter and legislator. They reject dogmatic distortions of Marxism, but not Marxism itself. Read the original if you want a periodised history of sociology's engagement with Marxism, with detailed Western sources, and a Chinese view of what it means for sociology in China.

Instigation, interference and manipulation: British and American leftist views on the truth of the Hong Kong issue 教唆、干涉与操纵：英美左翼关于香港问题真相的看法 Xing Wenzeng Writing in late 2019, after months of unrest in Hong Kong and the US congressional committee vote on the Hong Kong Human Rights and Democracy Act, Xing Wenzeng asks what really caused the Hong Kong problem and who is instigating, interfering in and manipulating it. The article answers by surveying statements from British and American communist parties and left-wing scholars, which Xing presents as "another voice" from the Western world. Xing's thesis is that these writers see foreign hands, chiefly British and American, behind the protests. The article is organised in four sections. It first reviews left-wing accounts of US and British involvement. It then covers their link of Hong Kong to the US–China trade war and to Brexit. A third section deals with their rejection of the idea that colonial rule or Western democracy could bring freedom. The last compares Hong Kong's economy with that of the mainland. Sources include Ella Rule of the Communist Party of Britain (Marxist-Leninist), the Communist Party of Britain, Sara Flounders of Workers World Party, Ian Goodrum and John Bachtell in People's World, John Ross and Martin Jacques. Xing reports that these authors describe Washington's contacts with Hong Kong opposition figures, and Marco Rubio's drafting of the bill, as evidence of orchestration. They also cite funding from foundations such as the National Endowment for Democracy. Ross is cited as arguing that the US launched the trade war while Britain, shaped by Brexit-era politics, took a provocative line on Hong Kong. Flounders and Goodrum are cited as saying that colonial Hong Kong had no elected government or basic labour rights, and that Western media coverage of the protests was selective and hypocritical. Jacques is quoted attributing Hong Kong's prosperity to mainland reform and opening up, not British rule. Bachtell's figures on inequality and housing costs are set against praise for mainland growth and Shenzhen, from which Xing concludes that socialism works better than capitalism. Xing concludes that the left-wing views expose Western right-wing forces' manipulation, and that their aim is to split Hong Kong from China and destabilise the People's Republic. Xing calls for winning more Western left-wing support, countering mainstream Western media narratives and strengthening a united front with Western left forces. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Academy of Social Sciences researcher selects and uses Anglo-American left-wing commentary in the official account of the 2019 Hong Kong unrest.

Overview of research on the foreign Left in 2018 2018年国外左翼思想研究概览 Zhou Miao Lei Xiaohuan This is a literature review of work on foreign left-wing thought in 2018, published in Scientific Socialism in 2019. Zhou and Lei report that the year, marking the 200th anniversary of Marx's birth and the 170th of the Communist Manifesto, brought wider and deeper research and steady progress in building the field. The review has four parts. It first sketches the year's developments: key articles in journals such as Monthly Review, New Left Review and International Socialism, Chinese publications and books, the death of Samir Amin in August, and conferences including the New York left forum, the World Social Forum, the ninth World Socialism Forum in Beijing and the second World Congress of Marxism. It then surveys theoretical debates, followed by studies of left movements by region, and finally the field's characteristics, problems and recommendations. On theory, Zhou and Lei cite Wallerstein, Žižek, Amin and John Bellamy Foster defending Marx's contemporary relevance, and Foster's call to move from criticism of neoliberalism to criticism of capitalism itself, using monopoly-capital theory. They also cite analyses of 'reverse globalisation' (Martin Upchurch), the long depression (Joseph Choonara) and Brexit as a move towards organised capitalism (Andreas Nölke). Other studies cover neoliberalism (Daniel Rodgers, Simon Springer), three visions of twenty-first-century socialism, and a 'return of communism' among Western radical thinkers. On regions, the review reports Chinese scholars finding European left parties in difficulty after the decline of the 'Third Way'. It reports resilience in Latin America despite a 'left retreat, right advance', and covers Mexico's first left-wing president in 89 years, the Indian left, the 2017 Nepali left alliance victory and divisions in the Lebanese left. In their closing section the authors stress the field's breadth and the diversity of its schools, for example Jameson, Derrida, and Laclau and Mouffe as left, centre and right post-Marxists. They propose that foreign left views be judged by Marxist standards, including whether they help to uphold and develop Marxism, aid the study of contemporary capitalism and benefit world socialism and peace. They call for stronger research to help develop twenty-first-century Marxism and build a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a bibliographic map of 2018 Chinese and foreign scholarship on the Western and global left, and a view of how Chinese academics frame and evaluate it.

A study of contemporary left-wing accelerationism abroad 当今国外左翼加速主义思想研究 Liu Qinmin Ma Xi Liu and Ma take up left-wing accelerationism, which they present as the most distinctive strand of the left-wing theory revived by the 2008 financial crisis. They ask what this school says about capitalism, how it relates to Marx, and what it offers Chinese thinking about the speed of development. Their thesis is that the school has real methodological value and also real flaws, and that its main lesson for China is to put the aim of development ahead of speed. The article first reconstructs the accelerationists' claim that Marxism already contains a rich critique of acceleration. It then sets out four understandings of "acceleration" and the school's core ideas. It ends with a four-stage history of the school and an assessment of its present relevance. The authors name Nick Srnicek, Alex Williams and Benjamin Noys as representative figures. They also draw on Hartmut Rosa, Paul Virilio, Deleuze and Guattari, and Meillassoux. In the authors' account, accelerationists read Marx's passages on automation, the "automatic system of machinery" and capital's tendency to undermine itself as a dialectical and materialist analysis. They argue that real emancipation depends on the productive forces that capitalism develops, and that capital is its own barrier. The accelerationists reject any return to a slower, pre-industrial age. They want instead to appropriate automation and digital platforms. Noys's slogan "start from the bad new things" is presented as a way of radicalising capitalism's own dynamic. Michael Laurence's objection is also reported: accelerationist strategy detaches itself from critical force and leaves politics without power. The historical sketch runs from the mid-nineteenth-century roots, through the 1970s to the 1990s, when Virilio's dromology and Deleuze and Guattari's "accelerate the process" fed the school. The Manifesto for an Accelerationist Politics (2013) and later books then made it a systematic school. The authors credit the school with concern for human wellbeing, for example its proposal of a universal basic income after automation. They also credit its sharp reading of digital technology and of the downsides of scientism. They describe its methodology as post-Marxist. Turning to China, they cite Deng Xiaoping's warning against blind pursuit of output and speed. They also cite the report to the 19th Party Congress (2017), which moves from "high-speed growth" to high-quality development. In their view this places purpose before speed and takes Marxist thinking about speed out of the accelerationist trap. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic overview of how accelerationism is received in China and tied to official ideas about the speed of development, with a Chinese-language bibliography of the school's sources.

Strengthening university Party committees' leadership over ideological and political theory courses 加强高校党委对思政课建设的领导 Yang Zhenbin This short commentary, first published in the People's Daily on 29 August 2019, takes up how university Party committees should lead the work of ideological and political theory courses (sizheng ke). Yang presents Xi Jinping's speech at the symposium for teachers of these courses as the fundamental guide. The article's thesis is that Party committees must strengthen their leadership so that Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era shapes students' beliefs and the courses produce socialist builders and successors. The article is organised around four areas of leadership, each framed as "keeping the right direction": political direction, the teaching force, curriculum reform, and organisational coordination. Each section pairs quotations from Xi's speech with instructions to Party committees. On politics, Yang argues that committees must apply the Party's education policy, answer the questions of whom to train, how and for whom, and strengthen ideological work and Party building in Marxism schools. On teachers, committees are to apply Xi's six requirements (strong politics, deep feeling, innovative thinking, broad vision, strict self-discipline, upright character). On reform, Yang endorses Xi's "eight unifications" as the methodology for reform. On coordination, Yang calls for linking dedicated courses with "curriculum ideology and politics" in other subjects and for combining theory with practice. Yang concludes that committees should back the courses with policy, funding, staffing and resources, and should enlist all university departments in a "big" ideological and political work structure. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Party commentary translates Xi's 2019 speech into tasks for university leadership.

Vigorously promoting high-quality development of manufacturing 大力推动制造业高质量发展 Miao Wei Following the Central Economic Work Conference of late 2018, which called for high-quality development of manufacturing and an unwavering drive to build a manufacturing power, this Party-journal article sets out why and how China should move from being a large to a strong manufacturer. The author argues that manufacturing is the foundation of the nation and the base of its strength. In this account, high-quality development of the sector is therefore a precondition for modernization and for the wider shift to high-quality development of the economy. The article has two halves. The first offers three reasons, each framed as an imperative: building a modern socialist country, achieving high-quality development of the economy as a whole, and making full use of the period of important strategic opportunity. The second half lists the main tasks: technological innovation, integration of advanced manufacturing with modern services, structural upgrading, fair competition among firms, talent, opening up, and a supportive policy environment. It draws on the experience of Britain, Germany, the United States and Japan, and on official figures. Miao contends that China's manufacturing is large but not strong. The article says it sits in the middle and lower reaches of global value chains, and that the old model of volume, scale and speed does not suit the new normal. It identifies three structural imbalances: oversupply alongside dependence on imported core technology, finance drifting away from the real economy, and real estate crowding out industry. Citing figures such as R&D intensity of 1.14% among large manufacturers and high-skilled workers at about 6% of employment, the author concludes that the remedy lies on the supply side. Miao holds that supply-side structural reform should remain the main line. The author also says that upgrading traditional industries counts as a new driver of growth, not only fostering emerging ones. Miao calls for innovation to be placed at the core of manufacturing, for zombie enterprises to be dealt with, for state-owned and private firms to be treated equally, for vocational education and craftsmanship to be strengthened, and for foreign investment to be admitted under pre-establishment national treatment and a negative list. The article presents this as the route by which manufacturing can support the Two Centenary Goals and keep China's industrial system complete. Read the original if you want an official view, from early 2019, of the policy agenda for upgrading Chinese manufacturing, with data points and the framing of the period.

How the People's Republic came this far 人民共和国这样走来 Chen Jin Published in Qiushi in 2019, ahead of the 70th anniversary of the People's Republic, this popular historical essay by Chen Jin and a co-author (the byline gives the name only in abbreviated form) retraces the country's path from 1949 to the present. It opens with a 1932 Shanghai magazine survey asking what people dreamed of for China's future. The authors answer through six questions, arguing that the Party's pursuit of that dream led step by step to socialism with Chinese characteristics, which they say links China's national conditions with its ideals. The article is organised as six question-headed sections. They cover the meaning of "the Chinese people have stood up" in 1949; the transition to socialism; the difficulties of exploring socialist construction; the road found through reform and opening up; the changes in governance since the 18th Party Congress (2012); and why socialism with Chinese characteristics is said to connect national conditions with ideals. It draws on anecdotes, quotations and episodes rather than extended analysis. In the authors' account, 1949 ended imperialist privileges and, through the Korean War, showed that China could resist a stronger power. They describe land reform, people's congresses and the "one industrialisation, three transformations" line. This line included a peaceful, compensated buyout of private industry and commerce that they call a historically significant creation. They treat the Great Leap Forward and the Cultural Revolution as costly detours that nonetheless produced lessons and an ethos of hard struggle. Reform began with household contracting and special economic zones, leading to the primary stage of socialism and the socialist market economy. Since the 18th Party Congress, they say, Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era guides practice, illustrated by an administrative-approval reform in Tianjin and new laws. The authors conclude that socialism with Chinese characteristics, understood as a path, a body of theory, a system and a culture, is the necessary road to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and the Chinese Dream. They cite the stated timetable of a moderately prosperous society by 2020, basic modernization by 2035 and a modern socialist country by 2050. Read the original if you want an example of how a Party journal tells the story of the People's Republic to a general audience, with its anecdotes and official framing.

Basic lessons of China's ideological work since reform and opening up 改革开放以来我国意识形态建设的基本经验 Li Suxia Feng Yanling Published in Guangming Daily in August 2019, this short commentary asks what experience the Communist Party of China has accumulated in building socialist ideology over the 40 years of reform and opening up. Li and Feng argue that the Party has consistently prioritised ideological work and has drawn four basic lessons, which they say have consolidated the foundations of China's socialist system. The article opens with Xi Jinping's call to sum up the Party's publicity and ideological experience and keep applying it. It then takes the four lessons in turn, each under its own heading: Marxism's guiding position, the Party's absolute leadership, theoretical innovation, and innovation in methods. On the first two points, the authors hold that Marxism's guiding role can only be established through concrete practice in economic, political, cultural, social and ecological construction. They add that ideological work must stay under the Party's absolute leadership, which in their view rests on the Party's nature and tasks. Citing Mao Zedong, they say leadership must be won by correct policies and exemplary work that persuade the public, and they propose strengthening theory, Party building and the training of successors. On innovation, they argue that inheritance and innovation cannot be separated without falling into dogmatism or adventurism. They present Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents, the Scientific Outlook on Development and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era as successive products of adapting Marxism to Chinese conditions. On methods, the authors call for continuing political and ideological work and public opinion guidance while giving them new content. They name education, cultural and ethical-ideological progress, and core socialist values as means of increasing ideology's appeal and cohesion. They conclude that both successes and failures are a spiritual asset, and that new challenges can be met only through theoretical innovation under Marxist guidance. Read the original if you want a concise, official-style summary of how Party commentators framed ideological work in 2019.

Achievements, reflection and new prospects: the broad trends of historiography in New China over 70 years 成就、反思与新的前景——新中国史学70年发展大势 Qu Lindong Marking the 70th anniversary of the People's Republic in 1949, this piece, first published in Guangming Daily in August 2019, offers a short overview of how Chinese historiography has developed since the founding of New China. Qu Lindong's thesis is that, under the guidance of Marxist theory, Chinese historical scholarship has achieved "brilliant" results in theory, research fields, scholarly output, personnel and international influence. The author presents the history as a sequence of achievement, reflection and renewed tasks. The article moves through three stages. It first recalls the origins of Chinese Marxist historiography in the 1920s and 1930s and its achievements in the 17 years from the 1950s to the mid-1960s. It then turns to the period after the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978), which Qu characterises by "reflection and advance". Finally it sets out four tasks for historiography in the new era that began with the 18th Party Congress (2012). For the first 17 years, Qu points to a wave of study of Marxism-Leninism and Mao Zedong Thought, debates on major questions (periodisation of ancient history, peasant wars, land ownership, "sprouts of capitalism", and others), and the training of a younger generation of historians. The author also admits detours caused by "Left" political currents and dogmatism. After 1978, Qu reports, scholars such as Yin Da, Hou Wailu, Liu Danian and Bai Shouyi called for a complete grasp of historical materialism, a "nationalisation" of Marxist historical science, and a contemporary commitment to historical integrity grounded in seeking truth from facts. Qu adds that publication since the 1990s has been the largest in the history of New China, but that importing foreign scholarship raises the problem of how Chinese historiography can show its own character and gain discursive power. For the new era, Qu proposes four tasks: creatively transforming the inherited legacy of historiography while building a disciplinary, academic and discourse system with Chinese characteristics; treating foreign historiography rationally, neither rejecting nor blindly following it; establishing a people-centred view of history; and strengthening history's service to society, in line with Xi Jinping's letter to the Institute of History at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences. Qu presents these as the main prospects for the field. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned account of how Chinese historians periodise their own discipline and frame its current tasks.

Seeking truth from facts and pioneering innovation: historical materialism and research on the history of the War of Resistance against Japan 实事求是与开拓创新——唯物史观与抗日战争史研究 Chen Hongmin Writing in the Guangming Daily in August 2019, Chen Hongmin asks how research on the War of Resistance against Japan should be guided and renewed. The article argues that the progress made in the 70 years since 1949 owes much to historians' adherence to historical materialism, and that future work must pair this guidance with methodological innovation. The short commentary opens with Xi Jinping's assessment of the war's significance and his call for deeper research. It then discusses the method of historical materialism, the scholarly debate over who won the war, and the 2015 commemorations. It closes with a case of innovation: digital archives and big data. Chen identifies two basic methods drawn from historical materialism: seeking truth from facts and concrete analysis of concrete problems. Applying them, the author rejects the long-standing binary between crediting the Nationalist government and crediting Communist-led forces alone. In Chen's account, post-reform scholarship reached a consensus: the war was a struggle of the whole nation under the anti-Japanese national united front, with the Communist Party as its "mainstay", and was the main Eastern theatre of the world anti-fascist war. On innovation, Chen notes that Japan's Asian Historical Records Center, set up in 1999, offers one-sided official sources. In response, the national social science fund's special project on the war funded a free, permanently open platform for documents on the war and modern Sino-Japanese relations, which by the end of 2018 held over 13 million pages. Chen concludes that, guided by historical materialism and by Xi's call to let archives, materials and testimony speak, the field can advance further. The author stresses that controlling large source databases confers a degree of discursive power. Read the original if you want a brief, officially aligned statement of how Chinese historians frame the war's historiography and digital source-building.

Historical materialism and Marxist research on Chinese intellectual history 唯物史观与马克思主义中国思想史研究 Yang Yanqiu This short commentary, first published in Guangming Daily in August 2019, surveys how historical materialism has shaped the study of Chinese intellectual history since the early twentieth century. Yang argues that Marxist research on the subject, guided by this method, became the mainstream of the field and offers a scientific ontology and methodology for future work. The piece moves chronologically. It starts with early modern scholarship and Hu Shi's 1919 outline of Chinese philosophy, then covers the May Fourth period, the 1930s and 1940s, the post-1949 decades, the era of reform and opening up, and the twenty-first century. Along the way it names scholars and works, among them Hou Wailu, Feng Youlan, Ren Jiyu, Zhang Qizhi and the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences project General History of Chinese Thought, launched in 2014. Yang's central claim is that Marxist scholars used historical materialism to trace how social being and economic relations underlie ideas, and they treated Chinese thought as a test of the theory's universal truth. Hou Wailu's work established the field's paradigm and gave rise to the "Hou Wailu school". Before reform and opening up, Yang says, the struggle between materialism and idealism served as the organising thread, with Soviet influence, and this brought dogmatism, mechanical materialism and over-politicisation. After the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978), the author describes a return to a richer, more historically sensitive method, including the history of scholarship, social thought and religion. Yang concludes that Marxist research has applied the theory of social formations, the determination of social consciousness by social being, and class analysis, and has expressed a people-centred character. In the new era, the author expects it to explain the essence and laws of ideas and the inner dynamic of Chinese culture's continuity, serving the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a compact, officially aligned overview of the main works and stages of Marxist intellectual history in China.

The philosophical character of materialist dialectics 唯物辩证法的哲学品格 Huang Hai Chen Yang This short commentary, first published in Guangming Daily on 31 July 2019, takes its cue from the Outline for Studying Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Huang and Chen argue that grasping the philosophical character of materialist dialectics is part of meeting the Outline's call to master Marxist ways of thinking and working. The article is organised in three sections. It treats materialist dialectics in turn as a scientific methodology uniting theory and practice, as a scientific theory of knowledge that guides practice, and as a doctrine whose essential traits are innovation and practicality. As methodology, the authors say, materialist dialectics supplies correct ways of thinking and working: practice as the sole criterion of truth, the people as the force creating history, and objective, comprehensive, developmental and interconnected observation. As epistemology, it is applied to major relationships in China's development, above all reform, development and stability. Huang and Chen cite the primary stage of socialism as the basic national condition that makes development the Party's first task. They describe development as the aim, reform as the driving force and stability as the precondition. In the third section they cite Engels's remark that Marx's worldview is a method rather than a dogma. They read the shift in China's principal contradiction, traced from the Eighth Party Congress (1956) to the 19th Party Congress (2017), and the post-1978 succession of theoretical innovations as proof that the dialectic is practical and innovative. The authors conclude that practice and innovation have no end, and that China must face the remaining difficult problems directly. They call for people-centred development, the new development philosophy and comprehensive deepening of reform and opening up, so that practical and theoretical innovation continue together. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated philosophers present dialectics as a working method for policy in the Xi Jinping era.

The dual theoretical horizon of political economy and philosophy of right in Capital 《资本论》中政治经济学和法哲学的双重理论视域 Xiao Shimei Writing in Guangming Daily in August 2019, Xiao Shimei asks what disciplinary character Capital has. Earlier readers placed it in the relation between philosophy and economics, and more recently between political philosophy and political economy. Xiao proposes a third reading, following the logic of problems in the development of Marx's thought. The article argues that Marx's critique of political economy inherently contains a dual horizon, that of political economy and that of the philosophy of right (法哲学, legal philosophy). The piece has three parts. The first traces Marx's turn from critique of the philosophy of right to critique of political economy, from his legal training and his work at the Rheinische Zeitung to the Paris Notebooks and the 1844 Manuscripts. The second asks what the turn amounted to and where the legal-philosophical dimension went afterwards. The third shows how the dual horizon appears in Capital and what it means for present practice. Xiao reads Marx's critique of private property as the marker of the turn, and distinguishes three attitudes to it. Classical political economy and the historical school of law take an uncritical positivism. Proudhon offers a metaphysical critique of right, treating property as a legal relation detached from economic relations. Marx instead grasps property relations as relations of production. Because legal and production relations justify each other in a circle, Xiao argues, law cannot condemn the existing order, so Marx used the empirical method of political economy to answer questions of the philosophy of right that legal philosophy could not solve itself. The dialectic carried those questions into political economy. Xiao cites Capital's remark that defining bourgeois property means describing bourgeois production relations. Xiao also sets out correspondences: the labour theory of value with a theory of labour ownership, surplus value with a theory of the alienation of ownership, and the historical tendency of accumulation with the self-sublation of that alienation. Xiao concludes that the dual horizon joins the critical side of Marx's theory to its normative side. A theory with only critique and negation, Xiao says, suits tearing down the old world but causes problems in building a new one. Deng Xiaoping's questions of what socialism is and how to build it are described as normative. Xiao holds that normative questions become more pressing in socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era, and that the unity is therefore essential to adapting Marxism to Chinese conditions. Read the original if you want a short account of how Marx's legal philosophy and political economy relate, and how a Chinese scholar links this to current practice.

Making full use of the key role of university teachers of ideological and political theory courses 切实发挥高校思政课教师的关键作用 Li Jibing This newspaper commentary, published in Guangming Daily in July 2019, takes up Xi Jinping's statement at the symposium for teachers of ideological and political theory courses that the key to running these courses well lies in the teachers. Li argues that teachers must play their role fully if the courses are to nurture conviction and shape students' values. The aim is to guide young people to join the cause of socialism with Chinese characteristics and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The piece has three numbered sections. The first concerns the fundamental questions of whom to train, how and for whom. The second concerns interaction between teachers and students. The third concerns building up the teaching corps and raising its overall standard. In the first section, Li contends that teachers should help students "fasten the first button of life" and plant seeds of truth, goodness and beauty. Li stresses that young people are at a formative stage and need guidance, and that Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era should be used to strengthen their identification with the socialist system. The second section draws on Xi's six requirements for teachers (strong politics, deep feeling, innovative thinking, broad vision, strict self-discipline and upright character). Li argues that teachers should win students' trust through example and dialogue and present Marxism as a telescope and microscope for understanding the world. The third section calls for stronger awareness of teachers' responsibility, better overall competence and a solid theoretical grounding, so that teachers can explain the principles convincingly and link theory to students' lives. Li concludes that a stronger, more capable teaching corps is the condition for raising the quality of these courses. In Li's account, this would produce a new generation able to take on the task of national rejuvenation and become well-rounded builders and successors of socialism. Read the original if you want a short example of how official commentary in 2019 framed the role of ideological and political course teachers in universities.

How the fundamental task of fostering virtue through education can be realised 立德树人何以实现 Zhang Bo This short commentary in Guangming Daily asks how the fundamental task of education, "fostering virtue and cultivating people" (lide shuren), can be accomplished in universities. Starting from Xi Jinping's remark that ideological and political work in universities bears on whom to train, how and for whom, Zhang argues that the task is inevitable, necessary and feasible, and organises the discussion around knowing, intention and action. The piece has three parts. The first shows from classical sources why fostering virtue is the inevitable choice. The second explains why it is required by the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, by the goal of making China strong in education, and by the all-round development of the person. The third sets out four ways to make it feasible. Zhang reads the two halves of the phrase dialectically: cultivating virtue is the precondition of cultivating talent, and cultivating talent is the aim of cultivating virtue. Without the first, the author says, training people loses direction; without the second, virtue becomes formal. Zhang links the task to Xi Jinping's call for builders and successors developed in moral, intellectual, physical, aesthetic and labour terms, which the author sees as matching Marx's theory of all-round human development. The four means are ideals and convictions, education and guidance, practice, and institutional safeguards. Zhang proposes guiding young people with Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and combining traditional teaching with new media. The author also calls for coordination among family, school and society, and for moral practice. On institutions, Zhang urges abandoning evaluation by scores and publications alone and strengthening assessment of teachers' ethics. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the official educational formula of lide shuren is justified and operationalised in 2019.

Strong politics: the soul of running ideological and political theory courses well 政治要强：办好思想政治理论课的灵魂 Qu Jianwu This commentary, first published in Guangming Daily on 31 July 2019, takes up Xi Jinping's call at the symposium for teachers of ideological and political theory courses. Qu Jianwu focuses on the first of the "six requirements" for running such courses well: that teachers be politically strong. Qu argues that this requirement is the soul of the courses and the basis of their quality. The piece is short and built around three claims, each introduced by a heading. Strong politics, Qu says, strengthens the self-awareness, the relevance and the practical effect of teaching. Qu begins with the historical setting, from the Communist Manifesto of 1848 to Western containment of socialism, and ends with the personal conduct of teachers. On self-awareness, Qu says these courses differ from ordinary subject courses because of their strong political character. They bear directly on whether students acquire the Four-sphere Confidence and on whether Marxism bears fruit in China, and Qu describes hostile forces as having long tried to obstruct it. Teachers' conscientiousness therefore starts from political awareness: political quality and political ability come first. On relevance, Qu holds that students face competing currents of thought and that a politically strong teacher treats keeping students from political error as the first task. Such a teacher answers them with rigorous theory. On effectiveness, Qu stresses Marxism's practical nature. Teaching should move students from knowing to doing, arming them with Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Teachers must also set an example, since conduct that does not match words undermines even learned teaching. Qu concludes that political strength is the first requirement for teachers who are to educate builders and successors for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Teachers who are politically strong and who care for students will, Qu says, find their work energising and make students want to learn. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official discourse in 2019 framed the political duties of ideological and political course teachers.

Combining the small classroom of ideological and political courses with the big classroom of society 把思政小课堂同社会大课堂结合起来 Wei Hua This short commentary, first published in Guangming Daily on 1 August 2019, asks how university ideological and political theory courses can better connect classroom teaching with social practice. Wei Hua argues, following Xi Jinping's speech at the symposium for teachers of such courses, that joining the "small classroom" to the "big classroom" of society helps students resolve confusion about growing up and form lofty ideals. The article is organised under three headings: responding to students' concerns, innovating teaching methods, and building a resource base for social practice. It focuses on university students, whom Wei describes as being in a critical period of forming moral values and in the last buffer stage before entering society. Wei argues that university courses have tended to stress theory and politics while giving too little social education. The author proposes that teaching should address major theoretical and practical questions, such as why the Communist Party "can", why Marxism "works" and why socialism with Chinese characteristics is "good". Wei also recommends discussion of current affairs, livelier language, and assessment adapted to a student's major, for example red-song contests for music students or red micro-films for broadcasting students. Finally, Wei calls for a practice resource base drawing on enterprises, social organisations and prominent alumni, so that universities and society jointly educate students. Wei concludes that taking students out of the classroom into society will let them receive first-hand education and consciously reshape their worldview, outlook on life and values, strengthening the effectiveness of ideological and political work. Read the original if you want a brief example of how a 2019 official-media piece translates Xi Jinping's guidance on these courses into concrete teaching suggestions.

As long as China is here, openness will not be scarce 有中国在，开放不会稀缺 Huang Ping This short commentary, first published in the People's Daily on 18 September 2019, asks why China keeps expanding its opening to the outside world while unilateralism, trade protectionism and anti-globalisation sentiment rise elsewhere. Huang Ping argues that economic globalisation is an irreversible trend of the times and that wider opening is China's correct response to it. The piece moves from the global setting to China's own record and then to a general prescription. It first notes that no country can modernise behind closed doors or tackle global problems alone. It then reviews more than 40 years of reform and opening up, and ends with the author's view of how the world should respond to protectionism and isolationism. Huang contends that China's shift from a closed or semi-closed economy to all-round opening produced sustained rapid growth, higher living standards and a stronger national position, showing that reform drives development and opening brings progress. In this account, "China and the world" is no longer a question of whether China should stay open, but of how an increasingly important member of the international community finds its place and plays a larger role. The author characterises protectionism, populism and cultural xenophobia in some countries as irrational and irresponsible, and warns that zero-sum thinking and the "law of the jungle" would worsen problems, possibly with catastrophic results. Huang concludes that China, still the largest developing country and still in the primary stage of socialism, will continue on the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics, deepen reform and open wider, so that its door will only open further. The author calls on all countries to pursue consultation, civilisational exchange and a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a concise example of how an official-press commentary in 2019 framed China's case for openness against protectionism.

Experience and lessons from the economic development of the People's Republic of China 新中国经济发展的经验和启示 Han Baojiang Writing for the People's Daily in September 2019, on the 70th anniversary of the People's Republic, Han Baojiang asks what lessons can be drawn from seven decades of Chinese economic growth. Han's answer is that sustained growth came from six sustained commitments, which together are said to offer guidance for promoting high-quality development in the new era. The article opens by contrasting the poor, war-ravaged country of 1949 with today's second-largest economy, largest manufacturer and largest goods trader. The piece is a short commentary organised under six headings: leadership of the Communist Party of China, the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics, an innovative development philosophy, the reform direction of the socialist market economy, opening up as a basic national policy, and reliance on the initiative of the people. Each section moves chronologically through the Mao, Deng, Jiang, Hu and Xi periods. Each is supported mainly by quotations from party leaders, above all Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping. Han's central claim is that Party leadership is the fundamental guarantee of development. In this account the Party has set direction at each stage, from building an independent industrial system to promoting high-quality development, and it plays a role no other political force can replace. Han adds that the socialist system, built on public ownership as the mainstay and the ability to concentrate resources on major undertakings, underpinned rapid industrialisation. On the market, Han credits the shift from a 'basic' to a 'decisive' role for markets in allocating resources, and points to high savings and capital formation, surplus rural labour and rising total factor productivity as sources of growth. Reform and opening up are presented as complementary: foreign capital, technology and management filled domestic gaps, while grassroots inventions such as the household contract responsibility system and township enterprises show the people's creativity. Han concludes that these experiences enabled China to cover in decades a path that developed countries took centuries to travel. Han also looks ahead, arguing that in a period of 'great changes unseen in a century' the advantages of the socialist system must still be used fully. Han further calls for developing advanced manufacturing and the real economy while balancing it with virtual economy and services. Read the original if you want a compact example of how the official narrative of 70 years of economic development was framed in the People's Daily in 2019.

The historical logic of the People's Republic's seventy years of striving 新中国砥砺奋进70年的历史逻辑 Qu Qingshan Writing for the People's Daily on 25 September 2019, on the eve of the 70th anniversary of the founding of the People's Republic, Qu Qingshan asks what inner logic runs through the country's seven decades of change. The answer, in the article's account, is that only socialism with Chinese characteristics can develop, enrich and strengthen China. Qu opens with Xi Jinping's description of the leap from "standing up" to "becoming prosperous" to "becoming strong". The piece has three main parts. The first presents the creation, upholding and development of socialism with Chinese characteristics as the fundamental achievement of the 70 years. It traces this through successive leadership groups, from Mao Zedong to Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin, Hu Jintao and Xi Jinping. The second part treats the three-stage leap as the most striking feature of the period, and cites figures on trade, GDP, urbanisation and poverty reduction. The third part draws out the "inner logic" in four propositions. Qu argues that each stage built on the one before. Socialist revolution and construction supplied the basic system, and the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978) opened reform and opening up. Later leaderships, with the Three Represents, the Scientific Outlook on Development and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, carried the path forward. The article cites 2018 figures: an economy of 90 trillion yuan, per capita GDP of about $9,900, and rural poverty down from 98.99 million to 16.6 million since 2012. Qu credits these results to the Party's adaptation of Marxism's basic principles to Chinese conditions, which in this reading released productive forces. The four propositions are that socialism with Chinese characteristics is the only road to national strength; that Party leadership is its most essential feature and the guarantee of success; that reform and opening up is the fundamental driving force; and that the people are the decisive force. Qu concludes that the Party must keep raising the banner of socialism with Chinese characteristics and hold to the Four-sphere Confidence. He also calls for the "four consciousnesses" and the Two Upholds, for reform and opening up to continue, and for the mass line and a people-centred approach in governing. The text frames this as a source of spiritual strength for further advance. Read the original if you want a concise, officially framed account of how the Party presented the 70-year history of the People's Republic in 2019.

An important path for building the core socialist values Promoting reading and building a "scholarly society" 社会主义核心价值观建设的重要路径 Luo Xiang This commentary, first published in the People's Daily on 26 September 2019, argues that encouraging people to read more and building a "scholarly society" (shuxiang shehui, a society filled with the fragrance of books) is an important path for cultivating and promoting the core socialist values. Luo opens with Xi Jinping's call for more reading and presents reading as a way to raise people's intellectual level and strengthen their spiritual strength. The piece has two parts. The first explains why a reading society matters for values-building. The second sets out three priorities for putting it into practice. Luo contends that core values are the spiritual bond of a nation and that reading transmits culture and shapes national character. The author treats a reading society as an inherent part of cultivating the core socialist values, and links it to Chinese cultural confidence and to building a culturally strong socialist country. On priorities, Luo first calls for Party members, cadres and the public to read original works and study Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, Party history and the history of the People's Republic. The author also asks them to understand the main currents of Western social thought so as to resist erroneous ideas. Second, Luo urges the creative transformation and innovative development of fine traditional Chinese culture, with cultural workers producing works that carry contemporary values. Third, Luo calls for government guidance and support, reading activities run by cultural institutions, and the use of internet and digital platforms, noting that China has over 800 million internet users. Luo concludes that when reading becomes a conscious habit among the people, the country's spiritual outlook and level of civilisation will rise considerably. The goal is a society where every household and place is filled with books. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary in 2019 tied reading campaigns to ideological education and cultural policy.

Continuing the struggle for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation 为中华民族伟大复兴接续奋斗 Zhu Jiamu Marking the 70th anniversary of the People's Republic in this People's Daily commentary (September 2019), Zhu Jiamu asks how the Communist Party has pursued its historical mission of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation since 1949. Zhu's answer, drawing on Xi Jinping's phrase that each generation has its own Long March, is that the past seven decades form a "new Long March" with three strands. The piece is organised around these three strands: upholding and developing the socialist road, pursuing socialist modernization, and safeguarding and promoting world peace and development. Each is treated as a 70-year record, running through successive Party leaderships from Mao Zedong to Xi Jinping. On the socialist road, Zhu argues that the Party, combining Marxism's basic principles with China's concrete conditions, held that only socialism could achieve national rejuvenation. Zhu traces a sequence in which Mao established the basic socialist system, Deng Xiaoping opened socialism with Chinese characteristics, and Jiang Zemin and Hu Jintao carried it forward. Since the 18th Party Congress (2012), Zhu says, it has entered a new era. On modernization, Zhu cites an independent and fairly complete industrial system, the "two bombs and one satellite" achievements, and over 220 industrial products ranking first in the world. On peace, Zhu cites leaders' statements and the Belt and Road Initiative to portray China as a builder of world peace. Zhu concludes that seven decades of history show China consistently pursuing a foreign policy of peace and shared development, and presents the new era as renewed vitality for scientific socialism in twenty-first-century China. Read the original if you want a concise example of the official 2019 narrative linking the Party's successive leaderships to national rejuvenation, modernization and a community with a shared future for mankind.

The great significance of socialism with Chinese characteristics entering a new era in the history of human social development 中国特色社会主义进入新时代在人类社会发展史上的重大意义 Jiang Hui Writing in the People's Daily in September 2019, Jiang Hui takes up Xi Jinping's statement that the entry of socialism with Chinese characteristics into a new era matters not only for China but for world socialism and the history of human society. The article argues that this entry has significance on three levels: for the development of Marxism, for world socialism, and for how humanity approaches modernization and global problems. The commentary is organised under four headings. It treats the contribution to twenty-first-century Marxism, the opening of a new stage in world socialism, the widening of paths to modernization, and Chinese proposals for common global problems. On theory, Jiang holds that Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era is the latest form of twenty-first-century Marxism. It is said to enrich Marxist philosophy, political economy and the theory of stages of socialist development. On world socialism, Jiang argues that China is solving the problem of how economically and culturally backward countries can build socialism, and that its success has answered the "failure of socialism" and "end of history" claims made after the Soviet and Eastern European upheavals. On modernization, Jiang contends that there is no universal model. In Jiang's account the Western path shows serious drawbacks, and China's path differs because it does not rest on colonial plunder, is people-centred, seeks balanced development and pursues peace. Jiang concludes that China offers developing countries a new option for countries wanting both faster development and independence. It also contributes ideas on globalization, governance and a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official 2019 account of the new era's global and historical significance.

Grasping the historical logic of the 70 years of New China's development 把握新中国七十年发展的历史逻辑 Li Jie Writing in People's Daily on the eve of the 70th anniversary of the People's Republic (2019), Li Jie asks how the periods before and after reform and opening up should be understood in relation to each other. Following Xi Jinping, Li argues that they are two interconnected periods with major differences, but that in essence both are the Party leading the people in exploring socialist construction. This, Li says, is the basic guide to seeing the seventy years as one continuous historical logic. This short commentary is organised under three headings: the course of exploring socialism with Chinese characteristics, the original aspiration and mission of Communists, and the Party's strong leadership. Each is presented as a thread running through both periods. Li supports the first two with economic, education, health and income statistics. On the first thread, Li argues that socialism with Chinese characteristics was founded on more than twenty years of earlier construction. Li cites the near-complete industrial system, breakthroughs in nuclear and space technology, new political institutions and the "second integration" of Marxism with Chinese conditions. On the second, Li presents rising living standards, school enrolment, life expectancy and poverty reduction, before and after 1978, as proof of continuity. On the third, Li holds that the Party corrected the Cultural Revolution and the "two whatevers" errors from within its own leadership, and that the Party's self-reform now continues this work. Li concludes that without the Communist Party there would be no New China, and that the Party's prosperity goes with that of the nation. Li calls this the most profound lesson of the seventy years. Read the original if you want a concise example of the official 2019 account of continuity between the Mao-era and reform-era periods, with the statistics Li uses.

Understanding arduous struggle through Party history 从党史中感悟艰苦卓绝 Xie Bingliang This short commentary, first published in the People's Daily in September 2019, takes up the call to understand what "arduous struggle" (jianku zhuojue) is and where it comes from. It frames this as a required lesson of the campaign to "remain true to our original aspiration and keep our mission firmly in mind". Xie argues that looking back on 98 years of Party history strengthens members' and cadres' resolve to follow the "new Long March" of the new era. The piece moves from the Party's founding circumstances to the Long March, then to the Party's growth, and finally to present tasks. It draws on the Red Army's march, a quotation from Mao Zedong, and figures on Party membership. Xie contends that the Party's historical background, political character and mission required it to lead the people in arduous struggle. The author cites the Long March: over 600 battles, nearly 100 rivers crossed, more than 40 mountains climbed and the grasslands traversed. In Xie's account, every step from "standing up" to "growing rich" to "becoming strong" was won through such struggle. Growth from just over 50 members at the First Congress to over 90 million is attributed to the Party's constant adherence to its original aspiration and mission. Hardship, Xie says, also formed revolutionary optimism and a spirit of sacrifice. Xie concludes that this generation's Long March is to achieve the Two Centenary Goals and the Chinese Dream of national rejuvenation. Many "snowy mountains" and "grasslands" remain, and the author rejects both complacency and love of ease. Party members and cadres are urged to know Party history, promote the spirit of arduous struggle and strengthen their commitment to their mission. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Party history is used in 2019 ideological education.

Without the Communist Party, there would be no New China 没有共产党 就没有新中国 Ouyang Song Published in the People's Daily on 11 September 2019, on the eve of the 70th anniversary of the People's Republic, this commentary asks what has driven the historic changes in China since 1949. Ouyang Song answers that the decisive factor has been the leadership of the Communist Party of China. The author concludes that, in the new era of socialism with Chinese characteristics, the Party must unwaveringly uphold and improve its leadership and unwaveringly make itself stronger. The piece has three parts. It first surveys 70 years of change, then argues that Party leadership explains that change, and finally sets out why the leadership must be upheld and the Party built up. It opens with Xi Jinping's description of the founding of the Party, the founding of the People's Republic, and reform and opening up as three historic landmarks on the road to national rejuvenation. Ouyang divides the argument into two historical claims. Without the Party there could have been no New China, as shown by the 28 years of the new-democratic revolution. Without the Party there could have been no building and development of New China either. The author cites economic figures: GDP rising from 67.9 billion yuan in 1952 to more than 90 trillion yuan in 2018, per capita gross national income of 9,732 dollars, and over 700 million rural people lifted out of poverty since reform and opening up. Ouyang also lists scientific and engineering achievements. The author credits centralised, unified Party leadership with national unity, a consolidated state power, sustained growth, and the handling of crises, and draws five lessons: Marxism as guide, communist ideals, the socialist path, a people-centred stance, and the Party's self-reform. Looking ahead, Ouyang gives three reasons why the Party must be upheld unwaveringly: its position as the highest political leading force, the role of Party building within the 'four greats', and the Party's founding mission. The author calls for a high degree of conscious commitment to the Two Upholds, for improved institutions of Party leadership, and for political building as the lead task in Party building. Read the original if you want a representative example of how the Party press framed the 70th anniversary and the case for Party leadership in 2019.
