The inner logic of the Chinese Communist Party's self-reform 中国共产党自我革命的内在逻辑 Xu Baojian Writing in the People's Daily in September 2019, Xu Baojian asks why the Chinese Communist Party regards courage in self-reform as its most distinctive trait and greatest advantage. Xu's answer is that a Marxist party can only keep its advanced nature and purity, and fulfil its mission, if it is willing to carry out the Party's self-reform. The article presents this as both the source of the Party's vitality and the distilled lesson of nearly a century of struggle. The commentary opens with a quotation from Xi Jinping, who says the Party's greatness lies not in avoiding mistakes but in facing problems squarely and repairing itself. It then builds its case from three connected angles: a theoretical logic, a historical logic and a practical logic. Each section moves from the nature of Marxist parties, to the Party's own record from 1927 to the present, to the conditions it faces now. On theory, Xu contrasts bourgeois parties, which in the article's account cannot turn criticism on themselves because of class and historical limits, with Marxist parties, which have no interests apart from those of the people and the proletariat as a whole. Xu cites Marx's remark that proletarian revolution criticises itself and grows through doing so. On history, the article lists turning points: the 1927 August 7 Meeting, the 1935 Zunyi Meeting, the Rectification Movement from 1942, the "two musts" of 1949 and the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978). It treats the post-2012 drive for full and rigorous self-governance of the Party as the latest case. On practice, Xu argues that the Party's external situation (a new historical position, a changed principal contradiction, new risks) and its internal situation (9,059.4 million members, a changed membership profile, a shift to long-term governing) require continued self-reform. Xu concludes that advanced nature and purity are never permanent, so the Party must keep fighting impurity in ideas, politics, organisation and work style, along with complacency and hedonism. The article calls on the Party to carry its great self-reform through to the end, so as to support the "two centenary goals" and the Chinese Dream of national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want a concise, official-line account of how Party commentary in 2019 justified self-reform in theoretical, historical and practical terms.

Forging the soul and strengthening the backbone through Party history and the history of New China 以党史和新中国史铸魂补钙 Lü Wenjuan This short commentary, first published in the People's Daily in September 2019, argues that Party members and cadres should study the history of the Party and the history of New China as a central part of the "Stay true to the founding mission" campaign. Lü presents the two histories as the most important content of history as "the best textbook". Studying them, the author says, lets cadres draw nourishment and wisdom from the Party's growth and the People's Republic's seventy years of effort. The piece opens by citing Xi Jinping's call, made during an inspection tour in Gansu, to organise Party members and cadres to study these histories. It then gives three reasons for doing so, each tied to the campaign: cultivating the Party spirit of Communists, understanding the rules of Party building, and strengthening the drive to work for national rejuvenation. On the first point, Lü argues that historical nihilism leads some people to distort Party history in order to deny the Party's leadership and the socialist system with Chinese characteristics, while some members neither know nor study this history. Study is meant to instil firm ideals and convictions. Second, Lü says the histories show how the Party grew from about 50 members to over 90 million, overcame risks, and practised self-reform, so cadres can grasp the experience and rules of Party building and develop strategic, historical, dialectical, innovative, rule-of-law and bottom-line thinking. Third, Lü holds that the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation will demand still greater effort, and that lessons from reform and opening up since 1978 can help cadres keep their direction as reform enters a difficult stage. Lü concludes that studying Party history and the history of New China keeps cadres theoretically clear-headed and politically steadfast and strengthens the Party's ruling foundation. Read the original if you want a brief example of how the official case for Party-history education was framed in 2019.

The value implications of the good life in the Communist Manifesto 《共产党宣言》中美好生活的价值意蕴 Ouyang Qi Jin Xingyu Ouyang Qi and Jin Xingyu read the Communist Manifesto, published more than 170 years ago, as a "political manifesto" of the good life as well as a founding document of scientific socialism. This short commentary, first printed in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in 2019, argues that its theoretical core and practical implications can inform the theory and practice of the good life in the new era. The authors organise the piece in three parts. The first covers the Manifesto's picture of the good life, the second its paths to realisation, and the third how it presents the good life through historical materialism. They note that the word "life" appears 28 times in the text, and that Engels's 1888 note defines the proletariat through the need to live by selling labour-power. Ouyang and Jin argue that the Manifesto answers the proletariat's material and spiritual oppression with an "association of free individuals", which they describe as uniting rich material life, elevated spiritual life and harmonious ecological life. They derive this from its critique of capitalism's overproduction, its stripping of the sacred, and its strain on the environment. Three paths follow: leadership by communists, whose interests they say coincide with the whole proletariat's; labour as the real means of achieving the good life; and uniting all possible forces internationally. The authors add that the Manifesto rebuts bourgeois accusations and corrects feudal, bourgeois and utopian socialism. The authors conclude that, despite the changed era, the Manifesto's account remains relevant. They cite the 19th Party Congress report (2017) pledge to take the people's longing for a better life as the Party's goal. Combining the Manifesto's meaning with meeting "needs for a better life" is, in their view, an effective route to adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Read the original if you want a brief, Party-line reading of the Manifesto's treatment of life and labour linked to new-era policy language.

New trends in foreign Marxist theory in the post-financial-crisis period: a review 后金融危机时期国外马克思主义理论研究新趋向述评 Chen Xueming Chen Xueming surveys work by Marxists and left-wing thinkers outside China since the 2008 financial crisis, the period the article treats as a new stage of "return to Marx". The review argues that the crisis revived interest in Marx, renewed the critique of capitalism and put socialism and communism back on the agenda. Chen also holds that this body of thought mixes valuable insight with dross and that Chinese scholars should engage with it critically. The review has three parts. The first summarises new views under three heads: fresh explorations of Marxism, new critiques of capitalism, and new thinking on socialism. The second sets out four features of foreign Marxism and the third offers four predictions. The survey draws on figures such as Eagleton, Hobsbawm, Žižek, Harvey, Foster, Wallerstein, Badiou, Negri and Roemer. It also covers Latin American socialism and market socialism. In Chen's account, the crisis prompted a defence of Marx's analysis, reflection on the Occupy movement, renewed reading of Capital, and work on social justice and political philosophy. Critiques of capitalism then centred on neoliberalism, ecological crisis, consumer society, the capitalisation of space, liberal democracy and the "new imperialism". On socialism, Chen reports arguments that "another choice is possible", a revival of the communist idea, and ecological and utopian socialisms. Chen also notes the rise of "post-Marxism" and the postmodern turn, which in Chen's view depart from Marxism's core. Chen sees four features: convergence with the radical left, postmodern influence, interdisciplinary fusion, and pluralism combined with a search for an organic whole. Chen predicts that the twenty-first century will be a period of concentrated critique of capitalism, and urges attention to foreign left parties and to a possible turn to the right. Chen argues that foreign Marxism is weak in linking theory to practice and that Chinese scholars should draw on its methods in building their own discipline and discourse. The article ends by holding that Chinese and foreign Marxism are parts of world Marxism and that China's rise means a revival of Marxism in the twenty-first century. Read the original if you want a broad, name-rich map of post-2008 foreign Marxism as seen by a leading Chinese specialist, and an indication of how it is assessed in China.

The origins, claims and assessment of "Millennial socialism" “千禧社会主义”的缘起、主张与评析 Li Xiang Zhao Wanying Li Xiang and Zhao Wanying ask whether the "Millennial socialism" spreading among young people in Western countries is a genuinely new exploration of socialism or another way for capitalism to rescue itself. Writing in 2019, they argue that it is essentially a left-wing current with a democratic socialist colouring. In their reading it seeks capitalism's self-adjustment rather than its overthrow, and it is not the scientific socialism of Marx and Engels. The article has three main parts. The first sets out the origins of the phenomenon, drawing on opinion surveys from the United States, Britain and Australia that the authors cite to show weakening youth support for capitalism. It explains the rise through the unresolved contradictions after the 2008 financial crisis, a generational shift in values, and the decline of neoliberalism. The second part presents the movement's claims on the economy, politics, social welfare and the environment, including the "Green New Deal". The third part offers the authors' assessment, and a short conclusion follows. The authors identify the movement's demands as state intervention and "big government", economic democratization through worker participation in company governance, progressive taxation, "participatory planning" in place of representative democracy, free education and healthcare, and public-led climate action. Their assessment rests on three points. First, the "socialism" is nominal: drawing on Engels, they say real socialism rests on public ownership and class opposition to capitalism, whereas Millennial socialists treat it as a tool for fairness and welfare, with the Scandinavian model as their ideal. Second, they reject revolution, prefer institutional adjustment to replacement, and rely on party politics, which the authors judge of limited effectiveness. Third, it is a new development of Western left thought, with internet-based mobilisation and an expanded ecological agenda, but largely a repackaging of older left ideas without a complete party system or theory. The authors conclude that Millennial socialists misunderstand socialism, waver in their stance, are divided internally and have so far had limited influence on the political and economic order. They nonetheless see in the movement an attempt to redefine socialism in a more inclusive, gentler form. They hold that its main significance is as a reflection of present conditions: it shows the claim of capitalism's "absolute victory" to be overoptimistic and calls for continued vigilance and criticism of capitalism. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist academic assessment of young Western support for socialism in the Corbyn and Sanders era, with the survey data it cites.

The influence of left-wing political globalisation on literary and aesthetic theory Intellectual implications of Hardt and Negri's "Empire" trilogy 左翼政治的全球化构想对文艺美学的影响 Mai Yongxiong Mai Yongxiong asks what Michael Hardt and Antonio Negri's trilogy Empire (2000), Multitude (2004) and Commonwealth (2009) offers to literary theory and aesthetics in an age of globalisation and digitisation. The article argues that the trilogy, which it presents as a landmark of a twenty-first-century "theory renaissance", widens critiques of capitalism, semiotics, postcolonial criticism, cyberspace studies and Marxist aesthetics. It also names weaknesses in the work. After brief biographies of the two authors, the article follows the three books in turn: the decline of old empires and the rise of a decentred new sovereignty, the "multitude" as the subject of resistance, and the "common" as a utopian future. It then sets "Empire studies" beside semiotics (through Liu He's interview), postcolonial criticism, Deleuze's smooth, striated and holey spaces, and Bruno Latour's political ecology. A long section places the trilogy in the history of Marxist aesthetics, and a short conclusion follows. Mai reports Hardt and Negri's claim that postcolonial and postmodern theory "mistook the enemy". In their view, power has moved from modern sovereignty to a networked imperial form that has no outside, so these theories address only one historical stage. Mai treats the multitude as the new subject: a network of heterogeneous exploited people, broader than the working class and not the same as "the people". Mai applies Deleuze's three spaces to cyberspace, where netizens roam freely while administrators, rules and hackers contest the same ground. Mai also notes the role of Chinese netizens in anti-corruption exposure and public supervision in the new era. Mai concludes that the trilogy continues Marxist aesthetics, develops Marx's theory of social stages and the world outlook of the Communist Manifesto, and enters dialogue with Wallerstein and David Harvey. It also expands class theory and the aesthetic dimension of teleology. Mai's own criticisms are that the multitude is too vague, dismisses national sovereignty casually and oversimplifies postcolonial and fundamentalist questions. The common, in Mai's reading, carries utopian force but leans on humanistic imagination, in contrast to Harvey's empirical approach. Read the original if you want a Chinese literary-theory reading of Hardt and Negri that links their politics to semiotics, postcolonial theory, Deleuze, Latour and Marxist aesthetics.

Visual politics: aesthetic questions in the contemporary French Left 视觉政治：当代法国左翼的美学问题 Wang Daqiao Qi Fei Wang and Qi ask how French left-wing thinkers since the May 1968 events have turned aesthetics into a political question through the problem of vision. Published in 2019 in the Journal of Hubei University, the article argues that 'visual politics' is the logical entry point to the French Left's contemporary aesthetics. In the authors' account, it differs from British and American visual culture studies in three ways: its political angle, its focus on vision and visuality, and its double critique of modernity and postmodernity. The authors work through four dimensions: the politics of looking, visual representation systems and image production, the expressive mechanisms of images, and film as the contemporary form of visual politics. They treat a constellation of thinkers: Sartre, Lacan, Merleau-Ponty, Foucault, Guy Debord, Baudrillard, Roland Barthes, Deleuze, Jacques Rancière and Alain Badiou. These figures are grouped into phenomenological, psychoanalytic and structuralist currents of Marxism. In the first part, Merleau-Ponty's reversible 'seeing and being seen', Lacan's mirror stage and gaze, and Foucault's medical gaze and panopticon show vision as a field of desire and power. The second part argues that Debord's 'society of the spectacle' reworks Marx's commodity fetishism, and that Baudrillard's simulacra and hyperreality describe a code-dominated image society in which signifier and signified separate. The third and fourth parts move to Barthes's analysis of myth in images and to Rancière's 'image-sentence' and 'distribution of the sensible'. Badiou's film as philosophical situation, Foucault's memory governance and Deleuze's 'missing people' extend this to cinema, where Rancière's 'those without part' are said to speak and an aesthetic equality is pursued. The authors conclude that the French Left's critique of 'ocularcentrism', together with its mix of critique and absorption of Marxist theory, gives this work its distinctive character. In their reading, politics is no longer the grand narrative of traditional Marxism. It is now located in the sensing body and perceptual structures, as politics becomes aestheticised and aesthetics politicised. Read the original if you want a Chinese-language survey linking Lacan, Foucault, Debord, Baudrillard, Rancière and Badiou under the heading of visual politics, with its Chinese-language bibliography.

A new interpretation of commodity fetishism in the German "New Marx Reading" With a comment on two interpretive paths in Western Marxism 德国“新马克思阅读”运动的商品拜物教新释 Liang Yanxiao Liang Yanxiao asks how the "mystery" of commodity fetishism in Capital should be explained, and contrasts two interpretive paths in Western Marxism. One draws on external resources (alienation, religious metaphor, Weberian rationalisation, the unconscious, sign-worship) and is traced to the early Georg Lukács. The other is text-based and starts from the theory of the value-form in the opening chapter of Capital. Liang argues that the second path, represented by Hans-Georg Backhaus of the German "New Marx Reading" (Neue Marx-Lektüre), is the sounder one. The article has four parts. It first criticises the "non-value-form" reading, taking Lukács's History and Class Consciousness as its case. It then sets out the philological basis, comparing the first German edition, the French edition and Engels's fourth German edition of Capital, Volume 1. Next it presents Backhaus's "Dialectics of the Value-Form". It closes by assessing the New Marx Reading and its lessons for Chinese scholarship. Isaak Rubin, Chris Arthur, Helmut Reichelt and Ingo Elbe appear as related figures. Liang argues that Lukács grafted Weber's rationalisation thesis onto Marx's passages. He thereby shifted attention to reified consciousness and ignored the value-form analysis. Liang also says Lukács borrowed material on machinery and the division of labour that Marx treats only after the chapter on commodities, which Liang calls a "misplaced appropriation". Against this, Liang reports Backhaus's philological point: fetishism first appeared in the appendix on the value-form in the first German edition, under the fourth peculiarity of the equivalent form. Backhaus therefore holds that fetishism can be understood only as part of the value-form section. In his reading, the equivalent form makes a natural object stand for a social relation (abstract labour), which gives commodities a "illusory independence". The root lies in a commodity-producing society that splits private from social labour, so the fetishistic structure can be broken only by changing that mode of production. Liang concludes that the New Marx Reading combines philological work on the MEGA2 manuscripts with social critique, and does so by "returning the critique of political economy to the critique of society". The author calls on Chinese scholars to bridge the split between "MEGA studies" and "Frankfurt School studies". They should avoid Western Marxism's emphasis on social psychology and culture, and revive the critique of political economy and the analysis of production contradictions. Liang hopes a "Chinese New Marx Reading" will emerge. Read the original if you work on Capital's value-form theory, the Lukács–Backhaus contrast, or how Chinese scholars receive German Marx studies.

A philosophical examination of the "three paths" for transcending the logic of capital 超越资本逻辑的“三条路径”之哲学审视 Wang Weihua How can the "logic of capital" be transcended? Wang Weihua defines this logic as the self-reproduction and self-expansion of capital as a reified social relation, which pulls the whole material world into commodification, monetisation and abstract rule over individuals. Since Hegel, Wang argues, philosophers' attempts to overcome it fall into three paths. Western Marxism takes a utopian, aesthetic-redemptive path of external transcendence, and postmodernism takes a nihilist external path. Marx alone takes an internal, practical path, by dissecting the negativity inherent in capital. The article, published in 2019, is built in three main parts plus a conclusion. The first treats Western Marxism through Lukács's critique of reification and the antinomies of bourgeois thought, and Horkheimer and Adorno's critique of the "culture industry" and of identity in Dialectic of Enlightenment. The second takes Jean-François Lyotard's rejection of grand narratives and metanarratives in The Postmodern Condition. The third turns to Marx, tracing his inheritance of Hegel's dialectic of negation and applying it to contemporary capitalist crisis. Wang's central claim is that Lukács, Horkheimer, Adorno and Lyotard remain at the level of cultural, ideological or theoretical critique. Lukács relies on proletarian self-consciousness to overcome reification, the Frankfurt thinkers never push their critique to capital and the political power protecting it, and Lyotard only fleetingly touches capital while placing his hopes in postmodern intellectuals. Marx, by contrast, takes from Hegel's Logic and the master–slave dialectic the idea of negativity as the engine of movement, and finds it in capital itself. Citing the Grundrisse and Capital volume 3, Wang reports four limits of capital (necessary labour, surplus labour, money, and exchange value over use value), which capital strives to break and thereby generates the seeds of its own dissolution. Wang applies this to the post-2008 crisis, stressing the spatialisation of capital, securitisation and leverage, and the coexistence of virtual-asset bubbles with a stagnant real economy. Wang concludes that theoretical critique is necessary but far from sufficient, and that both Western Marxism and postmodernism remain trapped in what Heidegger called the "immanence of consciousness". Marx's route is a practical critique, which reveals capital's inner negativity and, in Wang's reading, points humanity towards communism. Read the original if you want a Chinese-language comparison of Western Marxism, Lyotard and Marx on capital, and of how Hegel's dialectic of negation is used to defend Marx's approach.

The reality and spectrality of ideology An analysis of ideology theory in Žižek's psychoanalytic perspective 意识形态的现实性与幽灵性 Kong Ming'an Tan Yong Kong Ming'an and Tan Yong take up the concept of the "spectre of ideology" that Slavoj Žižek proposes in Mapping Ideology. They ask how the "spectrality" of ideology should be understood and how it relates to social reality and the unconscious. Their thesis is that ideology has a double identity, an external, materialised side and a pre-ideological core, and that the spectre mediates between the two. In the authors' reading, the spectre is the unsymbolised remainder of reality that ideology cannot capture. The article is organised in four sections. The first three test ideology against the three traits conventionally attributed to a ghost: ubiquity, a half-real, half-illusory character, and eternal existence. The fourth section turns to how the spectre appears and how it relates to ideology and social reality. The authors draw on Žižek, Althusser, Lacan, Derrida and Marx, and illustrate the argument with Žižek's examples: reporting on the Iraq and Bosnian wars, the East German intellectuals of Neues Forum, and a tribal village plan. The authors argue that ideology is ubiquitous because even attempts to leave it, such as a "third way", remain ideological. It is half-real and half-illusory because it both reflects and conceals social reality, as in the two groups of villagers who draw the village differently and so mask an underlying antagonism. It is eternal in Althusser's sense, as "ideology in general" without history, which Althusser compared to Freud's unconscious and restricted to class society. The central move is that reality is the symbolised, ideologically structured reality plus the spectre, like two sides of a coin. The spectre therefore marks an empty place, the Lacanian real, which is antagonistic and cannot be occupied by any positive reality. If it is so occupied, one falls back into ideology. This gives ideology critique a reference point that is not itself ideological. The authors conclude that the core of ideology is the spectre filling the hole of the real, while ideology's externality is its materialised form. They credit Žižek with building Althusser's conception on Lacanian psychoanalysis. They add that Marx's account of ideology as unconscious ("they do not know it, but they are doing it") supplies a materialist basis that Žižek's account lacks, and that without it ideology theory has no root. Read the original if you want a close, Marx-oriented reading of Žižek's Mapping Ideology that links spectre, real and symbolic reality.

The value of Western Marxism research as a resource, and reflections on it 西方马克思主义研究的资源性意义及其反思 Zou Shipeng Zou Shipeng asks how China's four decades of research on Western Marxism should be understood and redirected in the new era of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The article argues that Western Marxism should be treated as a reference resource that serves Chinese theoretical construction. In Zou's view, this means studying it critically, with a sense of practice, and giving it a proper place in the disciplinary system. The article has three parts. The first sets out the resource value of Western Marxism, from Lukács onwards, including its post-1968 developments and the Chinese leadership's framing of theoretical resources. The second offers three reflections on current research. The third looks at where foreign Marxism research sits within the Marxist theory discipline and how it relates to other disciplines. Zou argues that Western Marxism carried Marx's critique into the era of modern and contemporary capitalism, and that its concepts, such as alienation, reification and totality, are irreplaceable in modern social science. Zou distinguishes Western Marxism as a school, which in this account ran from Lukács to Althusser and is now past, from Western Marxism as a continuing tradition. Zou also criticises a 'false heat' in recent research that chases radical left theories and social movements, which Zou says drift away from Marx and carry theoretical dangers, and calls for studies that stay calm and rest on solid texts. Research should not treat these theories as principles, Zou says, but use them to build the ability to analyse Chinese practice and to engage with modernity without rejecting it. On disciplines, Zou notes that the Marxist theory discipline built its foreign Marxism field late and has no clear strengths there, unlike philosophy, political economy and literary theory. Zou calls for a strengthened second-level discipline that talks with other fields, without absorbing them, and for doctoral programmes at institutions able to support them. Zou also accepts that a large research force is unnecessary, though a certain scale is needed so that it can feed back into Chinese Marxist theory. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese specialist justifies and delimits the study of Western Marxism within the Marxist theory discipline.

Exploring a new path for aesthetic education in schools 探索学校美育工作新路 Beijing Research Centre for Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era This short commentary, published in the People's Daily in 2019 and written under the name of a Beijing research centre on Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, asks how schools should carry out aesthetic education (meiyu) in the new era. Its answer is that schools should use beauty to cultivate character and culture, plant the seeds of core socialist values, and raise a new generation able to carry the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The text begins from Xi Jinping's 2018 reply to veteran professors at the Central Academy of Fine Arts. It then gives a brief assessment: since the 18th Party Congress (2012) school aesthetic education has improved, but the authors say it remains a weak link in education. They name inadequate understanding of its function and incomplete institutions, mechanisms and evaluation systems. Four practical areas follow. The authors present aesthetic education as education of sentiment and the mind, with an irreplaceable role in fostering virtue. They call for a reform path with Chinese characteristics that serves the all-round development of students and enriches moral, intellectual, physical and labour education. Classroom teaching is named the main channel: coordinated across primary, secondary and higher levels, it would combine arts courses with the aesthetic value found in other subjects, and use internet-based resources. Branded programmes and local features, such as traditional opera, calligraphy and seal carving, would carry traditional culture and national spirit. Finally, the authors propose a society-wide "big aesthetic education" mechanism linking schools, families and society, with universities supporting primary and secondary schools and museums and cultural centres serving as venues. The authors conclude that such a system would build cultural confidence and patriotic feeling among young people and pass on the Chinese aesthetic-education spirit. The piece reads as a policy-oriented statement of official priorities rather than an empirical study. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated writers framed aesthetic education within moral education and traditional culture in 2019.

Continuously strengthening the appeal and impact of ideological and political theory courses 不断增强思政课吸引力感染力 Shi Xu He Wei This short commentary, published in the People's Daily in September 2019, asks how university ideological and political theory courses can become more persuasive to students. Shi and He argue that these courses are the key vehicle for the fundamental task of fostering virtue through education. In their view, whether they can effectively spread mainstream ideology and explain major questions of right and wrong with confidence bears on students' faith in Marxism and their confidence in socialism with Chinese characteristics. The piece sets out three requirements for teaching. Teachers should treat reading original works as their basic skill, answer students' intellectual doubts with "big principles", and use personal character and teaching artistry to build rapport. It opens with the claim that ideas and theory are the soul of these courses, which therefore demand thoroughgoing theory. On the first point, the authors cite the scholar Jin Kemu on the foundational role of source texts. They call on teachers to study the Marxist classics and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, so as to strengthen students' Four-sphere Confidence. On the second, they cite Engels that Marx's worldview is a method rather than a dogma. The "big principles" are said to lie in Marxist standpoint, viewpoint and method, which teachers should bring close to students' lives so that students see Marxism as useful for real problems. On the third, the authors say teachers who hold Marxist faith and theoretical grounding will convey the force of truth. They call for reform of rigid, single-format teaching but warn that livelier methods must not become entertainment or vulgarity such as anecdotes and unofficial history. The authors conclude that only persuasion by reason and moving students through emotion, with real exchange of ideas, will give students inner motivation. They expect this to raise students' familiarity with, trust in and loyalty to Marxist theory. Read the original if you want a brief official statement of how Chinese commentators framed teaching standards for ideological and political courses in 2019.

Firmly mastering the Marxist way of thinking and way of working 切实掌握好马克思主义思想方法和工作方法 Zhu Jianyi This commentary, first published in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2019, asks how Party members can master and apply the Marxist method of thinking and the Marxist method of work. Zhu argues that doing so is an important means of advancing socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era and of realising the Chinese Dream of national rejuvenation. The answer, in Zhu's account, is a set of connected commitments: studying and applying Marxist philosophy, seeking truth from facts, a problem-oriented approach backed by investigation and study, and continuous learning. The piece opens with Xi Jinping's description of Marxism as a scientific, people's, practical and open theory. It then moves through four themes, each framed as something to be upheld "consistently". These are dialectical and historical materialism, seeking truth from facts together with scientific thinking and a "nail-driving spirit", problem orientation and investigation, and learning. Zhu draws heavily on Xi Jinping's formulations and on Party slogans throughout. Zhu's central claim is that Marxist philosophy is both a scientific worldview and a system of methods for analysing and solving problems of social development. Party members are therefore urged to treat it as their "basic skill" and to uphold Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era as the Party's guiding thought. Seeking truth from facts is presented as the Party's basic ideological line, complementary to the mass line, and as dialectically united with emancipating the mind. Zhu lists six modes of scientific thinking: strategic, historical, dialectical, innovative, law-based and bottom-line thinking. The nail-driving spirit means following one blueprint to the end and implementing it steadily at each post. On problem orientation, Zhu stresses the people's need for a better life, their sense of happiness, gain and security, and calls for institutionalised, regular investigation and study guided by the maxim of relying on neither books nor superiors but only on reality. The Party is described as a Marxist learning-oriented party, and Zhu calls for continuous study aimed at unifying knowledge and action and at improving the theory and practice of socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Party-school-style writing in 2019 presented Marxist methodology as practical guidance for cadres.

Why the Chinese economy can go steady and far 中国经济为什么能够行稳致远 Wen Yu Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts (Hongqi Wengao) in 2019, Wen Yu responds to what the author describes as persistent "China collapse" arguments, which the article says have grown louder since growth slowed and the United States began trade frictions with China. The thesis is that, once one looks past short-term fluctuations to the internal logic and long-term trend of development, China's economy remains on a sound and lasting upward path. This trend, Wen argues, "has not changed and will not change". The piece is a short commentary that begins with growth figures and then lists the foundations of this long-term outlook. It opens with the claim that China's economy has entered a new era alongside socialism with Chinese characteristics, and that the basic feature of the current stage is a shift from high-speed growth to high-quality development. It then reviews basic conditions, science and technology, the market, late-development advantages, the advantages of a large country, the economic system, policy and political guarantees. Wen makes three main moves. First, speed: citing World Bank data for 2015–2018, the article says China grew 6.6–6.9% a year against world growth of 2.6–3.2%, and that growth of 6.6% in 2018 added a value roughly equal to China's entire 1997 GDP. Second, quality: it cites 2013–2018 averages for productivity, energy use per unit of GDP, carbon emissions and incomes as evidence of the new development philosophy at work. Third, it lists structural supports: an economy of nearly 1.4 billion people, a complete industrial system, per-capita GDP at about 16% of the US level and urbanisation below 60%, and the socialist market economy, which in Wen's account combines the strengths of markets and of the socialist system. Wen concedes downward pressure, weak independent innovation and shortfalls in key core technologies, and urges confidence together with awareness of difficulties. The recommended course is to seek progress while keeping stability, treat supply-side structural reform as the main line, follow the new development philosophy, and continue reform and opening up. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary in 2019 answered pessimistic views of China's economy during the trade dispute, with the statistics it chose to cite.

Western Marxism's decoding and critical study of capitalism 西方马克思主义对资本主义的解密与批判性研究 Feng Wangzhou Feng Wangzhou, in a short commentary first published in China Social Sciences Today in September 2019, asks how Western Marxism has studied capitalism and what its critique achieves. The author argues that Western Marxism continues Marx's critical tradition and has tracked capitalism's changes, but only partly inherits that tradition because its remedies stay inside the capitalist system. The article divides Western Marxism's roughly ninety years into three periods. These are its formation in the 1920s and 1930s (Lukács, Korsch, Gramsci), its flourishing from the 1930s to the late 1960s (the Frankfurt School, existentialist, Freudian and structuralist Marxism), and its fragmentation after the 1970s into analytical, ecological, political, feminist and postmodern currents. It then lists the critical models these currents produced and the labels contemporary thinkers give to capitalism. Feng contends that the early cultural turn reflected the integration of economy and culture under the logic of capital. Later schools criticised instrumental and economic rationality, consumerism and technology, and recent ones turned to micro-level political economy, neoliberalism and new imperialism. In Feng's reading, this work shows capitalism to be a changing structure and supports Marx's "two inevitables". Yet Western Marxism explains capital's control through concepts such as the one-dimensional society, the society of the spectacle and the consumer society. According to Feng, it cannot answer deeper questions of accumulation and profit maximisation, and it overlooks how this control supports new imperial hegemony. Citing Xi Jinping on the need to study contemporary capitalism, Feng calls on Chinese Marxist scholars to study these problems in depth and to develop a Chinese discourse paradigm for studying capitalism. Read the original if you want a brief, officially aligned Chinese overview of how Western Marxism's phases and critical models are assessed.

Marx's theory of "reproduction" and its social significance 马克思“再生产”理论及其社会意义 Yu Jia Most scholarship at home and abroad reads Marx's theory of reproduction as a matter of economics. Writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in March 2019, Yu argues that this reading is too narrow. In Yu's account, the theory has a broader social meaning, which appears in three forms: the reproduction of human beings, the reproduction of nature, and the reproduction of social relations. The piece begins with criticisms from Western thinkers. Yu cites Heidegger, Arendt and Baudrillard as having confined Marx's concepts of production and reproduction to technology, the maintenance of life or the framework of political economy. Yu answers these critics with Engels's remark that, on the materialist conception of history, the decisive factor is the production and reproduction of real life, not the economic factor alone. The article then sets out the three senses of reproduction and ends with two lessons for the present: good social relations and a sound relationship between humans and nature. On the first sense, Yu says reproduction means the production, maintenance and development of living individuals, which Marx treats as the premise of history. Under capitalism this takes the form of the reproduction of labour-power, which the author calls the foundation of the system and the source of surplus value. On the second, Yu reads Marx's statement that humans "reproduce the whole of nature" as going beyond treating nature as a resource to be plundered. It points instead to a productive and ecological ethic in which humans combine the measure of the object with their own inner measure. Yu holds that Heidegger and Baudrillard misread this point. On the third, Yu draws on Marx's claim that capitalist production reproduces the relation between capitalist and worker, which the author presents as more important than its material result. Each class reproduces itself by reproducing its opposite. Yu concludes that an economics-only reading hides the analysis of social relations and the critique of society that Marx built on this theory. Marx, Yu says, called for abolishing private property and the division of labour so as to reproduce a "real community" of free individuals. Yu adds that Marx also called for reproducing a harmonious relationship between humans and nature, under which society becomes the "completed unity of man with nature". Yu claims the theory offers guidance for building socialism with Chinese characteristics, for the Chinese Dream of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, and for a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a short example of how Chinese scholars use Marx's reproduction theory to answer Heidegger, Arendt and Baudrillard and to support ecological and social-relations themes in official discourse.

The normative foundation of Marx's critique of capitalism 马克思批判资本主义的规范性基础 Zhang Shoukui Does Marx's critique of capitalism rest on a normative foundation? Zhang Shoukui takes up a dispute that has run among Anglo-American Marxist scholars since the 1970s over Marx's relation to morality and justice, and that remains unresolved. Zhang argues that such a foundation does exist, but that it is neither justice nor equality in the ordinary moral sense. It is individual freedom understood as self-realization, aimed at the condition of human emancipation in which "the free development of each is the condition for the free development of all". The piece, a short newspaper article, first surveys four positions in Western scholarship. It then explains why individual freedom can serve as Marx's normative ground, and ends by considering what follows for Marx's aims and for current Chinese research. Zhang draws on Western commentators, including David Alan Shikiar on the "normative function" of concepts and Blackett's summary of Marx's critique as grounded in freedom and in the effect of private property on individuality and personality. Zhang lists the four positions: an ethical demand against exploitation and injustice; purely scientific and empirical analysis; a self-aware assessment of how private ownership harms individual development; and a charge of irrationality and alienation. Zhang holds that Marx treated justice as a form of ideology, so his opposition to private property cannot rest wholly on justice. Marx's freedom, in this reading, is not self-interested "free appropriation" of external objects, as in the political economists. Owning the means of production is a precondition for freedom, not its aim, and freedom means the full and unobstructed development of a person's capacities, opposed to alienated and forced labour. Capital and private ownership therefore appear as limits on self-realization. Zhang adds that Marx shows private property to be a historical product and not a natural or eternal fact. Zhang concludes that the decisive difference from classical liberalism lies here. Liberalism treats capital and private property as intrinsic to freedom, whereas Marx treats them as instruments for freedom under certain conditions, and finally as a constraint on it. Criticizing capital is therefore a means to human emancipation and the all-round free development of each person. Zhang calls on scholars who deepen historical materialism through the critique of capital logic to raise it to a logic of revolution, or of emancipation and individual self-realization. Read the original if you want a compact Chinese-language account of how a Chinese Marxist scholar answers the Anglo-American debate on Marx, morality and justice.

Why the Communist Party of China has been able to create miracles 中国共产党为什么能够创造奇迹 Wang Chuanli Wang Chuanli, writing in Red Flag Manuscripts (Hongqi Wengao) in 2019, asks why the Communist Party of China has repeatedly survived crises and produced what the author calls miracles. The article opens with the impression of foreign observers that the Party grows stronger under setbacks. Wang's answer is that this record rests on distinctive strengths of the Party itself. The opening recalls four episodes: the survival of the Party after the 1927 massacre, the Long March after the encirclement campaigns of 1930–34, the Party's endurance after the collapse of the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe, and its handling of later disasters such as the 1997 Asian financial crisis, the 1998 floods and the 2008 Wenchuan earthquake. Wang then sets out five advantages, each introduced by a heading: good members, good theory, good relations with the masses, a good organisational structure, and good traditions, style and discipline. On members, Wang argues that the Party gathers the nation's finest people, including some from wealthy families who gave up comfort, and names models such as Jiang Jie, Wang Jinxi, Jiao Yulu and Kong Fansen. On theory, the author presents the Party as a learning party armed with Marxism, treated as a guide to action rather than dogma. Wang points to the Party school system down to county level, to repeated study campaigns and to the continuing adaptation of Marxism to Chinese conditions. On the masses, Wang cites Mao Zedong's 1934 remark that the masses are the true bastion of iron, and Deng Xiaoping's account of the early 1960s hardship years, to argue that close ties with the people have carried the Party through every difficulty. On organisation and style, Wang stresses branches reaching into every sector, a membership of over 90 million, the principles that the Party controls cadres and commands the army, and the 87 million members' special Party dues after the Wenchuan earthquake. Wang also credits criticism and self-criticism, the united front, democratic centralism and a firm line on corruption. In the author's reading, the Party grows stronger by overcoming corruption and keeps its vitality through continual self-reform. Read the original if you want an example of how Party-aligned commentary in 2019 explained the Party's resilience through a list of its self-described strengths.

The relationship among fine traditional Chinese culture, revolutionary culture and advanced socialist culture 中华优秀传统文化、革命文化和社会主义先进文化的关系 Tang Ling Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2019, Tang Ling asks how three components of Chinese culture should be understood in relation to one another: fine traditional Chinese culture, revolutionary culture and advanced socialist culture. The author argues that the three form a continuous, internally connected whole rather than separate or rival layers. Correctly grasping this relationship is presented as a condition for building socialist culture with Chinese characteristics, strengthening cultural identity and consolidating cultural confidence. The short commentary has four parts. It first defines each of the three cultures as a creation of the Chinese nation in a different historical stage: agrarian life, modern revolutionary struggle, and socialist construction and reform. It then traces how they descend from one another, explains why together they make up the mainstream of Chinese culture, and ends with the practical stance that follows from their unity. It draws repeatedly on Xi Jinping's statements about culture. Tang's central claim is that the later forms inherit, transform and develop the earlier ones. Revolutionary culture, in the author's account, fused Marxism with traditional ideas and recast them, for example from "the people are the foundation of the state" to "serving the people wholeheartedly" and from "seeking truth through investigating things" to "seeking truth from facts". Advanced socialist culture then distils both and is described as the latest development of Chinese culture. Together the three are said to form the main body of contemporary Chinese culture and the three pillars of its advantage, and Tang defines cultural confidence as confidence in all three at once. On this basis Tang calls for the three to be treated as a unity within the practice of socialism with Chinese characteristics, without separating them or favouring one over another. The author lists errors to be opposed: historical and cultural nihilism, wholesale Westernization, antiquarian revivalism including "replacing Marxism with Confucianism", denial of the socialist character of contemporary culture, and also copying foreign models or cultural conservatism and closure. Tang proposes handling the pairs of native and foreign, present and future, inheritance and innovation, and transformation and development from a Marxist standpoint, and pursuing the creative transformation and innovative development of Chinese culture. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official 2019 framing of how traditional, revolutionary and socialist culture are meant to fit together.

The political drivers behind the "Chinese miracle" “中国奇迹”背后的政治动因 Hong Wen Writing in 2019, around the 70th anniversary of the People's Republic, Hong Wen asks which theory can explain China's economic and social achievements. The author argues that Western neoliberals, who advocate political democratization and economic liberalization, have repeatedly misread China, and cites Francis Fukuyama's retreat from his "end of history" thesis as evidence. In the article's view, the decisive explanation is political: the leadership of the Communist Party of China and the political path of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The commentary is organised in three parts. The first, on political leadership rooted in national conditions, treats the Party's long-term rule, its social revolution and its policy shifts since reform and opening up. The second, on democratic practice with Chinese characteristics, compares China's institutions with Western multiparty systems. The third places China's development in a period of what the author calls great changes unseen in a century and sets out a "win-win philosophy". Hong contends that the Party's leadership is the most essential feature of socialism with Chinese characteristics and the fundamental guarantee of the country's achievements. The author points to the shift from class struggle to economic construction, the Party's basic line, the "three-step" strategy and successive five-year plans. Democracy, the author says, has no universal model: China's consultative democracy, multiparty cooperation, regional ethnic autonomy and "one country, two systems" are presented as suited to Chinese conditions, while Western one-person-one-vote elections, multiparty rivalry and the separation of powers are portrayed as producing social division, polarization and inefficiency. Abroad, China is said to pursue mutual benefit rather than zero-sum games. The author concludes that the root political cause of the "Chinese miracle" is the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics and the political advantage expressed in Party leadership. The idea of a "civilizational state", Hong suggests, is best understood as a people-centred state, which is therefore bound to defend world peace and common development. Read the original if you want a compact example of how a Party journal in 2019 framed China's success as a political rather than a market or liberal story, and how it contrasted Chinese and Western democracy.

Continually creating new historic achievements Studying and implementing the spirit of Xi Jinping's important speech at the meeting marking the 70th anniversary of the founding of the People's Republic of China 不断创造新的历史伟业 Guo Qingsong This commentary, first published in the People's Daily on 10 October 2019, is a study of Xi Jinping's speech at the meeting marking the 70th anniversary of the People's Republic. Guo Qingsong takes up Xi's call to uphold Party leadership, the people's principal position and the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Guo argues that these three commitments explain the achievements of the previous 70 years and are also the fundamental guide for creating new historic achievements. The piece is built in three parts, one for each commitment. Each moves from the historical record since 1949 to the tasks ahead. It draws on statements by Mao Zedong and Xi Jinping and on the periodisation of the Party's work from the founding of the PRC through reform and opening up to the era since the 18th Party Congress (2012). On Party leadership, Guo contends that the Party's founding mission of seeking happiness for the Chinese people and rejuvenation for the nation made it the people's and the nation's mainstay. In Guo's account, it led the socialist revolution, socialist construction, and reform and opening up, and the Party Central Committee with Xi at its core has since brought socialism with Chinese characteristics into a new era. On the people's principal position, Guo restates the Marxist view that the people make history, and lists four commitments: development for the people, by the people, shared by the people and judged by the people. On the path, Guo argues that it suits China's conditions and serves the people's interests, citing the people's congress system, multiparty cooperation under Party leadership, regional ethnic autonomy and a basic economic system with public ownership as the mainstay. Guo concludes that Party leadership is the most essential feature and greatest strength of socialism with Chinese characteristics and must be upheld without wavering, together with full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. The Four-sphere Confidence should be strengthened, and China should follow neither a closed, rigid old path nor an "evil path" of changing the Party's banner. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the official 2019 anniversary narrative linked Party leadership, the people and the socialist path.

Revisiting the Party's history, bearing in mind the original aspiration and mission 重温党的历史 牢记初心使命 Beijing Research Centre for Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era Published in Guangming Daily on 14 August 2019, this commentary by the Beijing research centre for Xi Jinping Thought opens a series on Party and national history. It follows a notice from the central leading group for the "Remain true to our original aspiration and keep our mission firmly in mind" campaign, which made studying the history of the Party and of New China part of that campaign. The authors argue that the Party's original aspiration and mission, seeking happiness for the Chinese people and rejuvenation for the Chinese nation, was already present at the Party's founding and runs through its whole history. The article first cites Xi Jinping on why Party and national history is a required course, then reads the founding period through four themes: a sense of responsibility, conviction, struggle and service to the people. It draws on the 58 founding members, early biographies of Mao Zedong, Zhou Enlai, Li Dazhao and Li Da, the documents of the First and Second Party Congresses (1921, 1922), and the stories of martyrs such as Chen Tanqiu, He Shuheng and Deng Enming. The authors argue that the founders were mostly educated and not poor, so they joined the revolution out of national and historical responsibility rather than personal hardship. They say these founders then chose Marxism and communism after comparing options, and that the First Congress programme (public ownership, proletarian dictatorship) and the Second Congress's anti-imperialist, anti-feudal programme show Marxism being adapted to Chinese conditions. The Party's history is described as a history of struggle and sacrifice. For each revolutionary stage the article lists how the Party mobilised the masses, and it traces a line of concepts from "serve the people" and the mass line to "people-centred development", the latter presented as part of Xi Jinping Thought. The article concludes that the Party's experience lies in governing well through correct lines and policies, making popular wishes the basis of decisions and balancing fundamental with specific interests and long-term with immediate ones. It also calls for respecting the people's principal position and drawing on their initiative, so that all sources of social wealth can flow freely. The piece is hortatory and offers an officially framed account of the Party's early history. Read the original if you want to see how Party-affiliated researchers in 2019 presented the founding generation as the source of the Party's present-day mission and mass-line language.

The Party's exploration of discipline building in the early years of the People's Republic 新中国成立初期党对纪律建设的探索 Wu Yangsong This short commentary, first published in Guangming Daily on 21 August 2019, asks how the Chinese Communist Party strengthened its discipline after taking power in 1949. Wu Yang­song argues that, facing a changed environment and new tasks, the Party paid particular attention to discipline building in these years and made a series of effective new explorations. The article identifies five lines of work: ideological and political education, institution building, strict demands on senior cadres, themed campaigns, and personal example set by the older generation of revolutionaries. It draws on Central Committee directives, Mao Zedong's instructions and documents from 1949 to 1954. Wu first describes problems among some cadres, such as alienation from the masses, bureaucratism and a sense of entitlement. According to the article, the Central Committee responded with education, including Liu Shaoqi's eight standards for Party members, and with new bodies: discipline inspection commissions were set up at all levels from late 1949 under Zhu De, with detailed rules on penalties up to expulsion. The article presents the 1951 execution of Liu Qingshan and Zhang Zishan, the Three-Anti campaign and rectification drives as measures that targeted the 'key minority' of senior cadres. It adds that Mao Zedong and Zhou Enlai applied discipline to themselves and their families, citing Mao's rejection of a bronze statue and Zhou's ten family rules. Wu concludes that these measures, taken together, markedly strengthened political, integrity and work discipline and created a better disciplinary climate within the Party. The text presents this record as a model of Party building. Read the original if you want a concise, officially framed account of early-PRC Party discipline, with citations to primary documents.

The dialectic of Capital 《资本论》的辩证法 Allen Wood This is a Chinese translation of a text by the American philosopher Allen Wood on the dialectical method of Marx's Capital. Wood argues that the work is best read as a hierarchy of theoretical models, running from very abstract models of basic social forms to fuller and more concrete ones. In his view, many familiar objections to Marx's economics come from overlooking this structure. Wood first sketches the course of Capital: the commodity, the law of value, the value form and money, the conversion of money into capital, surplus value, the split between constant (c) and variable (v) capital, and absolute and relative surplus value. He then follows Marx through circulation in Volume II and the unified account of profit, interest and rent in Volume III. Three sections take up value and production prices, the law of value itself, and the relation between value and exploitation. Wood contends that the law of value in Volume I is not a general theory of relative prices. It is the founding assumption of a deliberately simple model of freely reproducible commodities, which Marx then refines. Production prices in Volume III, formed through an average rate of profit, belong to a less abstract model, so the charge that the volumes contradict each other (made from Böhm-Bawerk onwards) fails. Wood nevertheless concedes that the transformation problem, raised by Bortkiewicz, points to a real defect in Marx's Volume III. He reads the apparently deductive argument for the law of value in Chapter 1 as weak at several steps, notably the premise of an equal common element in exchanged goods, and as best taken as an expository device. In his account the real grounds lie in Marx's letter to Kugelmann: allocating social labour in proportion to social need is a natural law, and under commodity production it takes the form of exchange value. Wood treats this as a historical-materialist claim tied to commodity fetishism. Wood denies that Marx's claim that capital exploits labour depends on the labour theory of value, and he sees the neoclassical attack on that theory as aimed at discrediting surplus value. He allows that other approaches, such as Sraffa's input–output analysis, might do the same work as well or better. He adds that Marx never denied capitalists a necessary role in production. Read the original if you want a philosophically trained, Anglophone reading of the logic of Capital that separates the law of value from price theory and from the theory of exploitation.

Building on the past to open a new realm in the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context 继往开来开创马克思主义中国化新境界 Liu Tongfang Writing in Guangming Daily in September 2019, on the 70th anniversary of the People's Republic, Liu Tongfang asks how the Chinese adaptation of Marxism should be carried forward in the new era. The article argues that three linked questions must be answered: what results the adaptation has produced, what experience it has accumulated, and how it should be advanced now. Liu holds that answering them allows the work to continue in the right direction. The commentary is organised around these three questions. It first lists the theoretical and practical results of seven decades, then draws three lessons from the historical record. It closes with tasks for the present, centred on Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Liu argues that because Marxism both interprets and changes the world, its Chinese adaptation yields theoretical and practical results that depend on each other. The theoretical results run from Mao Zedong Thought through Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents and the Scientific Outlook on Development to Xi's thought. The practical results are the path, system and culture of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The experience is summed up in three points: Party leadership is the guarantee, seeking truth from facts is the essential requirement, and rooting theory in the masses is the fundamental route. For the new era, Liu calls for using Xi's thought to answer the questions of the times and the people, including the shift in the principal contradiction in society. Liu also calls for using it to tackle uneven and inadequate development and shortfalls in people's livelihood. Doing so, the author says, would let Marxism perfect and surpass itself and open a new realm of Marxist development in the twenty-first century. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary in 2019 summarised the history and lessons of Marxism's Chinese adaptation.

Lessons from seventy years of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context 马克思主义中国化七十年的启示 Yan Shuhan Marking the 70th anniversary of the People's Republic in this Guangming Daily commentary (September 2019), Yan Shuhan asks what the seventy years of the sinicization of Marxism teach. The author's answer is that only Marxism can save and develop China, that Communist Party members are its loyal and firm practitioners, and that Marxism in contemporary China is an open, constantly developing body of theory. The piece is organised in three sections, each stating one lesson. It moves from the search for a way out after the Opium War of 1840, through the Party's three historic leaps, to the successive theoretical achievements of Mao Zedong through Xi Jinping. Yan argues that capitalism and a range of other doctrines, including reformism, liberalism, anarchism and pragmatism, failed to solve China's problems, whereas Marxism-Leninism, once combined with Chinese realities, changed the country's fortunes. In Yan's account, the Party's adaptation of Marxism produced leaps from being oppressed to standing up, then to becoming prosperous, then to becoming strong. The author credits the Party's emphasis on strengthening itself ideologically and theoretically for its resilience. Yan then lists Mao Zedong Thought, Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents, the Scientific Outlook on Development and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, calling the last the Marxism of the twenty-first century. Yan concludes that a theory's vitality lies in innovation and that developing Marxism is the Party's sacred duty. The author calls for using Marxism to observe and lead the times, drawing on contemporary Chinese practice and the achievements of other civilisations. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the official narrative of Marxism's sinicization was presented to a general readership around the 70th anniversary.

The threefold transcendence of the concept of a community with a shared future for mankind 人类命运共同体理念的三重超越 Liu Xinghong This short newspaper commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in August 2019, asks in what ways the concept of a community with a shared future for mankind goes beyond the Western-shaped international order. Liu Xinghong argues that Xi Jinping's concept, first stated in Moscow in March 2013, transcends modern Western political civilisation in three respects: ontology, epistemology and practice. The article begins by presenting the concept and the Belt and Road Initiative as the ideas and practice through which a rising China carries a mission of leading the direction of human civilisation. It then takes the three dimensions in turn. It closes with remarks on the concept's place in Marxism, in Chinese philosophy and social science, and in international documents. On ontology, Liu contends that the Westphalian system made the nation-state the basic unit of international relations, whereas Xi's concept takes "humankind" as its unit and human well-being as its value. On epistemology, the author says some Western countries treat their own civilisation as a beacon and others as inferior, while the concept holds that civilisations are equal and enrich one another through exchange. On practice, Liu describes the Western order as a Hobbesian "jungle" of zero-sum games, and presents the concept as replacing confrontation with cooperation through consultation, joint contribution and shared benefits. Liu concludes that the concept continues and develops Marx's idea of an association of free individuals, and that Xi's account across politics, security, economy, culture and ecology forms a knowledge system contributing to philosophy and social science with Chinese characteristics. The author notes that the concept has entered resolutions of the UN General Assembly and Security Council. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the concept was presented in Chinese academic commentary in 2019.

Making propaganda and ideological work stronger requires effort in theoretical construction and innovation 推动宣传思想工作不断强起来要在理论建设和理论创新上下功夫 Li Chunhua Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2019, Li takes up Xi Jinping's call at the 2018 national conference on propaganda and ideological work to make that work "stronger". Li argues that because the work is essentially one of persuading people through theory, theoretical construction and innovation must be treated as its basic, strategic and critical task. The article is organised under three headings: strengthening the propaganda and education of Marxism, thoroughly studying and putting into practice Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, and providing an effective supply of theory through philosophy and the social sciences. On Marxism, Li holds that propagandists must study the classic works so that what they promote is "genuine" Marxism, and must answer real problems of reform and development. This includes strengthening the Four-sphere Confidence and analysing neoliberalism and historical nihilism. On Xi Jinping Thought, the author sets out three requirements: grasp its core, understand it as a connected system, and implement it through concrete action rather than formalism. Li then argues that philosophy and the social sciences must supply theory that grasps the essence of things and reveals their laws. They must stay under Marxist guidance and Party leadership and focus on explaining Xi Jinping Thought. Li concludes that theoretical workers should produce results with depth, academic standing and topical relevance, to support propaganda work in the new era. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Party commentary in 2019 linked ideological work to theory-building and the role of the social sciences.

Waging the great struggle is a compulsory course on the road to rejuvenation 进行伟大斗争是复兴之路上的必修课 Hao Yongping Huang Xianghuai Writing in the Economic Daily in June 2019, Hao Yongping and Huang Xianghuai take up a formulation from the 19th Party Congress (2017) report: that realising the great dream requires a "great struggle" with many new historical features. They argue that, as developments since the 18th Party Congress (2012) show, waging this struggle is a compulsory course, indeed the main course, on the road to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. They present it as a key lens for studying Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The commentary has three sections. The first traces the concept from Mao Zedong's 1962 remarks and the 18th Party Congress report to its present meaning, and sets out what the struggle is and is not. The second explains why objective conditions at the international, domestic and Party levels call for it. The third sets out principles of method: fighting spirit, fighting ability, strategy and the rule of law. The authors argue that the great struggle is not a slogan but concrete action aimed at problems that cannot be solved otherwise, and that it works as a remedy against complacency in times of peace. They stress limits: it does not mean a return to ultra-leftism, lawless campaigns, a weakening of economic development as the central task, or the creation of tension. On objective grounds, they cite hostility from countries that feel a sense of loss or threat as China rises, the tasks of the stage after China has "developed", and the "four tests" and "four dangers" facing the Party. In their account, the struggle is great because it holds the people's interests supreme, including national reunification, Party leadership and the socialist system, and the people's aspirations for a better life. On method, the authors call for examining each problem on its specifics, courage together with skill, efforts to overcome what Mao called a "panic over capabilities" among some cadres, and strict adherence to law, citing past mass campaigns that undermined legality as a lesson. They conclude that sustaining and developing socialism with Chinese characteristics requires the great struggle, and that defending the people's interests and China's sovereignty and core interests is the Party's historical responsibility. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party commentary in 2019 explained the "great struggle" and set out its boundaries.

Remembering the original aspiration and mission requires the courage for self-reform 做到牢记初心使命必须勇于自我革命 Li Chunhua This commentary, first published in Economic Daily in September 2019, argues that the Communist Party of China can only stay true to its founding aspiration and mission if it keeps a strong spirit of self-reform. Li starts from Xi Jinping's remarks on how a long-ruling party can preserve its vanguard character and purity, retain popular support and sustain long-term governance. Li's answer is that the longer the Party rules, the less it can afford to lose this spirit. The piece is organised under three headings. The first presents courageous self-reform as a political gene of Chinese communists. The second treats it as the key to the Party's flesh-and-blood ties with the people. The third calls it the winning weapon for keeping the Party advanced and pure. Li grounds self-reform in Marxism, described as a critical and revolutionary theory. Materialist dialectics holds that development involves internal contradictions, so a growing party must fight wrong ideas from within as well as from outside. Li adds that not every party applies this law consciously, whereas the Party is presented as a model. On the Party's relationship with the people, Li argues that forgetting the original aspiration would change the Party's nature and cost it popular support. Li therefore calls for tackling formalism, bureaucratism, inaction by officials and harm to the public interest, together with sustained pressure against corruption. Li also stresses accepting public supervision, since the masses judge whether officials have kept their aspiration. Li concludes that since the 18th Party Congress (2012) full and rigorous self-governance of the Party has achieved notable results, but impurity in politics, thinking, organisation and conduct remains unresolved. Li calls on Party members to face problems squarely, to cut out harmful elements and to build their abilities for the new era. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-press commentary in 2019 linked the campaign to remember the original aspiration to the theme of self-reform.

Building ideological and political theory courses in the early years of the People's Republic 新中国成立初期的思想政治理论课建设 Wu Xiaoni Writing in Guangming Daily in September 2019, Wu Xiaoni looks back at how universities in the early People's Republic established compulsory courses in ideological and political theory. The article argues that the Party and government's measures of that period (curriculum, leadership, teaching staff and teaching methods) were a useful exploration and offer lessons for current work on such courses. Wu links this to the instructions given by General Secretary Xi Jinping at the symposium for teachers of ideological and political theory courses in schools. The article is organised around four themes. It begins with the construction of a course system centred on Marxist theory, then turns to a working mechanism in which Party and government leadership, university departments and all teachers share responsibility. It next covers the building of a politically reliable and theoretically competent teaching corps, and ends with methods that combine theory and practice. Wu draws on official regulations and directives from 1950 to 1955, and on remarks by educators and students of the time. Wu describes the early curriculum as built on basic Marxist theory and Mao Zedong Thought. It started with dialectical and historical materialism, the theory of New Democracy and political economy, and was standardised by an instruction of October 1952. In 1953 it was adjusted after the general line for the transition period, and extended to postgraduates. Wu stresses that all teachers, not just political-course staff, were required to carry out ideological education within their own subjects, and calls this principle strategic and still relevant. To remedy a shortage of qualified instructors, a 1952 Central Committee directive led to selective recruitment, short-term training classes and research programmes, notably at Renmin University of China. Teaching combined theory with practice: the Korean War was used to counter pro-American attitudes, and students and staff took part in land reform, which Wu says helped them form a mass viewpoint and class standpoint. Wu concludes that Party leadership, shared responsibility across the university, strong teaching staff and the link between theory and practice are experiences from this period that remain instructive for ideological and political theory courses in the new era. Student testimonies are cited as evidence that the courses raised political awareness. Read the original if you want a concise, officially framed account of how Marxist political courses were first built into Chinese higher education in the 1950s, and of the historical precedents that current policy invokes.

The construction of national image over seventy years of New China 新中国70年国家形象的建构 Chen Jinlong Writing in Guangming Daily on the eve of the People's Republic's 70th anniversary, Chen Jinlong asks how New China has built its national image and what that experience offers today. Chen defines national image as the impression and evaluation of a country's history, present and conduct held by the international community and its own people. The article argues that the seventy-year path from "standing up" to "becoming prosperous" to "becoming strong" was also a continuous process of constructing and refining that image. The piece is organised under four headings. It sets out the dimensions of the image (economic, political, cultural, social and ecological), then the resources drawn on, the channels used, and finally the linkage between the images of the state, the Party and the people. Chen traces each theme from the Common Program of 1949 through Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin and Hu Jintao to Xi Jinping. Chen's central claim is that the image is multi-dimensional. The economy is its foundation, the political system its pillar, culture an important component, society its projection, and ecology a late-emerging but necessary element. The image draws on Chinese civilisation, on achievements publicised at national day and other anniversaries, and on national character. It is projected through commemorations, diplomacy (the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence, Belt and Road Initiative, a community with a shared future for mankind) and promotion of ethnic unity. Chen also stresses that the state's image cannot be separated from the ruling Party's image, which rests on its values, competence and integrity, including full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, or from the image of the people as the country's masters and creators of history.
