Chen concludes that these results and experiences offer guidance for building national image in the new era. As the model, Chen quotes Xi Jinping's call to present four images: a civilised great country, an Eastern great country, a responsible great country and a socialist great country. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned account of how Chinese Party-state discourse in 2019 framed national image-building across the seventy years, with its standard citations from successive leaders.

Investigating a missing source note in Capital 查究《资本论》 文献注释问题 Xiang Xiuli Volume I of Capital carries over 1,000 notes, yet a few quotations lack precise sources. Xiang Xiuli takes up one such case and argues that Engels was wrong to say that only one quotation, a passage attributed to Richard Jones, was left without a source. The article proposes a source for a long quotation that Marx left unreferenced, and that Engels also missed. The piece, a short commentary from the Chinese Social Sciences Today in 2019, begins with the editorial history of the notes. It then turns to the unreferenced passage, which describes contradictory rulings by magistrates and differing legal practice in Yorkshire and Lancashire. It reviews how the historical-critical edition (MEGA2) and the Chinese editions treated the passage, and ends with the proposed annotation. Xiang notes that MEGA2 marks the passage as "source could not be established", and that Chinese editions say nothing about it. Because the passage falls in Chapter 8, where Capital draws most heavily on the English Factory Inspectors' Reports, and is introduced by a phrase about manufacturers complaining, Xiang infers that it comes from those reports. No single fragment matches exactly. Xiang finds that most of the passage comes from Inspector Horner's remarks in the report to 31 October 1849, and that the remainder draws on that report and the one to 30 April 1849. Xiang says MEGA2 itself lists several sources for composite quotations. Xiang proposes editor's notes in the relevant place in the Chinese edition of Capital, giving the page references to those reports, and suggests MEGA2 could drop its "unverified" note. Xiang compares this to the detailed note on the Chinese official Wang Maoyin, a philological contribution that originated in China. Xiang concedes that the hypothesis may be disproved and welcomes better proposals. Read the original if you are interested in Marx's editorial and textual scholarship, or want the exact source references Xiang proposes.

The rupture between theory and practice: reflections on the current state of the European socialist movement 理论与实践的断裂:欧洲社会主义运动发展现状思考 Lin Deshan Why has the European socialist movement, represented by the European left, failed to benefit from the crises that followed 2008? Lin argues that the core problem is a rupture between theory and practice, which afflicts both social democracy and the radical left. Overcoming it, the article contends, requires the movement to face several new theoretical questions directly. The article has three parts. The first describes structural change on the European left since 2000: the decline of the social democratic parties, the partial recovery of a radical left descended largely from the communist parties, the fading of left identity, and growing fragmentation. The second analyses the rupture separately for social democracy and for the radical left. The third sets out three issues that socialist theory must address: post-materialism, globalisation and technological change. Lin argues that social democracy's long theoretical evolution, which fused socialist ideas with social liberalism, was driven by the need to be electable. Its "Third Way" modernisers shed the party's socialist and class character, which in Lin's account produced an identity crisis and eroded its working-class base, while a return to traditional positions would cost it electoral viability. The radical left, by contrast, lacks a shared identity, is stronger at criticism than at constructive proposals, and has no systematic policy theory on the European Union, the welfare state or direct democracy, and part of it has turned to left populism. On the three new questions, Lin calls for explaining how material and post-material concerns relate in socialist politics and for a globalisation theory that is open and selective rather than purely defensive. That theory should also rebuild the role of the nation-state instead of simply abandoning or returning to it. Lin further asks for study of how digital technology actually changes production relations and political organisation, beyond speculation about "digital socialism". Lin concludes that the European socialist movement stands at a crossroads. Its basis in the critique of capitalism and the demand for alternatives remains real, but it can grow only by closing the gap between theory and practice. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's detailed account of European social democracy and the radical left after 2008, and of the theoretical agenda the author sets for them.

An analysis of the reasons for the decline of the American left in the twenty-first century 试析21世纪美国左翼运动衰落的原因 Chen Ye Gao Jianming Why have the two best-known left-wing movements of twenty-first-century America, Occupy Wall Street (2011) and Bernie Sanders's 2016 presidential campaign, achieved so little? Chen and Gao argue that the American left is in decline both against the contemporary right and against its own history. Measured against the right, the two movements failed to put their preferred candidates into key positions. Measured against earlier left movements, they failed to reverse growing inequality. The authors identify three interacting causes: economic (the 2008 financial crisis), political (a tradition of distrust of government) and ideological (a dilemma of choices). The article is organised around these three causes and compares the left throughout with the Tea Party movement and Donald Trump's campaign. It begins with the history of the left coalition built by the Democrats through the New Deal and civil-rights legislation. It then examines survey data on poverty, the shrinking middle class and Democratic support. Next it takes up Pew and Gallup figures on distrust of government, and finally the slogans and programmes of Occupy and Sanders. A short conclusion draws out why the right succeeded. The authors' first move is that the left coalition holds together in times of growth but fractures in times of scarcity. After 2008, they argue, different groups, and even members of the same group, competed for jobs and limited welfare, and Occupy's demands contained internal contradictions over affirmative action, manufacturing return and the environment. The Tea Party's membership was narrower, mostly higher-income white men, so the crisis did not split it. Second, Chen and Gao contend that Sanders's programme relies on 'big government' just as popular distrust of government and elites was rising. Trump and the Tea Party promised smaller government and so matched that mood. Third, Occupy's '99% versus 1%' framing avoided value claims in order to keep a diverse coalition, while Sanders built a coherent framework of 'justice', 'oligarchy' and 'democracy' that appealed mainly to young people. The authors argue that neither approach worked under crisis and distrust. The right, by contrast, joined free-market and traditional-morality themes into a coherent conservatism of liberty and virtue. In the authors' conclusion, the right's success mirrors the left's failure: a homogeneous base, a promise of small government and a clear ideology. The article cites Urban Institute data that the wealth of the top 10% rose from about six to twelve times that of middle-class households between 1963 and 2016. Citing Eli Zaretsky and Michael Kazin, Chen and Gao hold that America needs a left, so the decline is not permanent. When the left revives, they say, will depend on the economic and political environment and on ideological exploration. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly account of why Occupy and Sanders failed, set beside the Tea Party and Trump, with the survey data the authors rely on.

The "choice" of path in the globalisation of the logic of capital Russian Marxist research in the twenty-first century 资本逻辑全球化视域中的道路“抉择” Hu Xiaokun Hu Xiaokun surveys twenty-first-century Russian Marxist scholarship and asks how Russian left-wing thinkers frame the country's choice of historical path under the globalisation of the logic of capital. The article argues that Chaadaev's nineteenth-century question of whether Russia has a future has been reopened after the 2008 financial crisis. In Hu's account, Russian Marxists answer by returning to Marx's historical materialism and "revolutionary" dialectic, and by treating transition to socialism as a contradictory, processual task. The article has four parts. It begins with Russia's modernization impasse, drawing on Petr Buldakov and Dmitry Granin and on world-systems theory. It then turns to the nature of post-industrial society and the Russian engagement with Western Marxism (Baudrillard's simulation and consumer society, Bell, Drucker). The third part examines the "post-Soviet critical Marxism" of Alexander Buzgalin and Andrei Kolganov, notably their two-volume Global Capital (2015). The last part reviews debates among Russian leftists, including a 2011 round table on whether left thought is in crisis and a 2013 Moscow conference on Marxism and the working class. Hu reports that Russian scholars attribute the modernization impasse to a gap between Western-style institutions and Russian tradition, and to a state that pursues technical "Westernisation" only. Granin proposes escaping Eurocentrism by seeing Russia as semi-peripheral. On post-industrial society, Russian authors see rising creativity and autonomy for workers alongside deeper alienation, as capital extends into consumption and intellectual labour. Buzgalin and Kolganov treat Baudrillard's "simulation" as a reflection of changing capitalist relations, not as reality itself. They call for a new system of categories modelled on Capital, drawing on the Soviet philosopher Ilyenkov's method of ascending from the abstract to the concrete. In the round-table debate, Inozemtsev doubts that the left retains a revolutionary subject. Buzgalin answers with six points on the left, redistribution, post-industrial contradictions, rentiers, education and non-linear history. Voeikov favours gradual reform, while Slavin holds that wage labour under capital keeps workers' class position unchanged. Hu concludes that Russian Marxists treat transition to socialism as the task of finding its real basis and historical conditions, and of fostering revolutionary subjects, through a dialectical grasp of global capital. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's overview of post-Soviet Russian Marxist debates on modernization, post-industrial society and the left, with references to Russian-language sources.

Subject, structure, science: three dimensions in the logical course of twentieth-century French Marxism 主体·结构·科学:20世纪法国马克思主义逻辑进程中的三重维度 Bai Hu Bai Hu asks how twentieth-century French Marxism developed and what logic ran through it. The article argues that its course unfolded along three dimensions: the question of the subject, structuralism, and science. Bai holds that the third is the most neglected, acting as a "fellow traveller" to the other two. The article first sketches three phases: humanist Marxism centred on the subject; the structuralist period; and the post-1968 decline, when many currents drew on Marxist critique. It then devotes one section to each dimension. The subject section covers Kojève's Hegel seminar, Sartre and Merleau-Ponty. The structuralism section covers Saussure, Lévi-Strauss and Althusser. The science section covers Bachelard, Canguilhem, Althusser and Foucault. Derrida, Deleuze and Badiou appear as later thinkers. Bai traces the subject question to the Cartesian "cogito" tradition. Kojève's anthropological reading of Hegel pulled the "I" back into sensuous reality, and Sartre then turned to Marxism by moving beyond both Hegel and Kierkegaard. Structuralism, as Bai reads it, answers the same problem by bypassing the cogito. Lévi-Strauss criticised Sartre as a prisoner of the cogito, and Althusser held history to be "a process without a subject", proposed an epistemological break in Marx, and treated determination by the economic base as overdetermination. Bai then separates French philosophy into a philosophy of consciousness (Descartes to Sartre and Merleau-Ponty) and a philosophy of the concept (Cavaillès, Bachelard, Canguilhem, Foucault, Deleuze). The latter branches into scientific epistemology, which shaped Althusser's problematic and break, and a philosophy of life, which led from Canguilhem's work on the normal and the pathological to Foucault's biopolitics. Bai concludes that these three themes cover most of French philosophy's twentieth-century agenda and explain why Marxism flourished in France. Writing in 2019, Bai expects the subject and its dissolution to remain central in Badiou and Foucault, and structuralism's role in the 1960s peak to stay significant. Bai also predicts that science and epistemology will gain weight as biopolitics and philosophy of life advance. Read the original if you want a compact survey of French Marxism from Sartre to Foucault that gives special attention to the scientific-epistemological lineage.

Foreign Marxist theories of labour relations 国外马克思主义的劳动关系理论 Zhang Jiaxin Wang Fangfei This review, published in Theoretical Horizon in 2018, surveys how Marxist economists outside China have analysed labour relations in modern capitalism. Zhang and Wang open by noting that the 19th Party Congress (2017) called for building harmonious labour relations, and they present the foreign literature as worth attention alongside Chinese research. They divide it into four strands: labour process theory, the political economy theory of trade unions, the French Regulation School, and theories of capitalist class structure. The article takes each strand in turn through its leading figure. For labour process theory it covers Harry Braverman's revival of the theme, Michael Burawoy's turn to worker subjectivity, and later work by William Lazonick, David Harvey and Ash Amin. It then presents Richard Hyman's typology of unions, the Regulation School's account of Fordist and finance-led accumulation regimes, and Erik Olin Wright's model of class structure. In the authors' account, Braverman shows how scientific management fragments and deskills work, separating conception from execution, so that capital controls the labour process. Burawoy, studying Hungarian factories, finds that workers come to consent to their own exploitation through piece-rate games, internal labour markets and an internal state, and he proposes employee ownership. Hyman treats labour relations as shifting between cooperation and conflict and distinguishes market-, society- and class-oriented unions, each with internal tensions, so that he recommends combining the three orientations. The Regulation School traces Fordism's collapse to distorted labour relations and proposes labour law and collective bargaining to reconcile flexible work with security. Wright adds a 'middle class' of contradictory class locations and, in the authors' words, advocates 'class compromise' as a route to socialism through deeper democracy. The authors judge that this last approach neglects capitalism's long-run direction. Zhang and Wang conclude that all four strands follow Marx's basic principles and agree that inequality and conflict between workers and capitalists are the essence of capitalist labour relations. They say the strands extend Marxist economics and that the Regulation School and Hyman's pluralist view offer practical lessons for institutional and union work. After the 2008 financial crisis, they note, radical currents revived in the West, which they take as a reason to give this literature due attention. Read the original if you want a compact Chinese-language survey of Braverman, Burawoy, Hyman, the Regulation School and Wright, and of how Chinese scholars frame them.)

French Staatswissenschaft (statistics of the state), social materialism and historical materialism 法国国势学、社会唯物主义与历史唯物主义 Liu Bingjing Liu Bingjing asks what intellectual context lay behind the young Marx's turn to historical materialism in 1845, and argues that a neglected strand is French guoshixue, the nineteenth-century 'science of the state's condition', ancestor of modern statistics. Liu contends that its materialist study of social reality influenced List, Schulz and Marx alike, and formed a logical foundation for Marx's critique and overcoming of German classical philosophy. The article has three parts. The first traces the emergence of French guoshixue after the defeat of Napoleon's empire in 1815, through figures such as Chaptal, Dupin and Moreau de Jonnès, up to its absorption into a state economics ministry in 1936. The second analyses the 'social materialism' that this discipline produced. The third examines its reception by Friedrich List, the German statistician Wilhelm Schulz and Marx, drawing on Marx's Paris, Manchester and London notebooks. Liu argues that French statisticians, working to restore national strength after decline, treated social reality and above all material production as the basis of a nation's power. This differs from the natural materialism of the Enlightenment (Helvétius, Diderot, Holbach), since its object was the non-intuitive productive capacity built up through social activity: population, technology, education, labour organisation. Dupin even called it 'productive force'. Liu adds that the discipline had only a limited sense of history, because it stayed within the standpoint of bourgeois society. Marx's repeated excerpting of Chaptal, Dupin and Moreau de Jonnès, Liu argues, helped fill a gap in explaining how he moved from German classical philosophy to a discourse of production in The German Ideology, whose 'real positive science' echoes guoshixue's empiricism. Liu stresses that historical materialism is not an imitation of this social materialism. Guoshixue defended bourgeois society and could not see alienation, class contradiction or the dialectical self-supersession of social forms. Marx's distinctive contribution, in Liu's view, is a historical understanding of social being as the contradiction between productive forces and forms of intercourse. Recovering this context, Liu concludes, helps define the philosophical character and limits of historical materialism. Read the original if you study the intellectual prehistory of historical materialism, Marx's reading notebooks, or the history of statistics and political economy in France and Germany.

A critique of the historical subject in Western Marxism 西方马克思主义视域下的历史主体批判 Li Gaorong Who changes history? Li Gaorong takes up this question of the historical subject and asks how Western Marxism has answered it since the 1960s. Classical Marxism treats the working (proletarian) class as the revolutionary subject. The article argues that Western Marxist views moved from affirming this subject, to denying it, to dissolving it altogether. In the author's judgement, this left theory detached from practice. The article sets out Marx's and Lenin's account of class as both an economic and a relational concept, and Marx's move from a class "in itself" to a class "for itself". It then surveys Western thinkers under two headings. Under "practical subject" it treats E. P. Thompson and Ellen Meiksins Wood, who defend the working class; André Gorz and Nicos Poulantzas, who rebuild or reclassify it; and Ernesto Laclau and Chantal Mouffe, who abolish it. Under "theoretical subject" it covers Lukács, Marcuse, French existentialism, Althusser and Alain Badiou. A closing section turns to Antonio Negri and Michael Hardt's "multitude" and the 2018 "yellow vests" movement. The author says the selection is deliberately broad and limited to a few typical figures. Li argues that, as class structure changed and class politics gave way to identity and discourse politics, the subject was progressively emptied. Gorz's "new working class" and "non-class of non-workers" and Poulantzas's "new petty bourgeoisie" redefine class by technical or ideological criteria. Laclau and Mouffe then reject economic determination and replace class with a discursively built "popular alliance". On the theoretical side, Marcuse's "alienated man", Sartre's "Other" and Althusser's "process without a subject" shift attention from real classes to abstract human essence or to structures. In Li's reading this recalls the "German socialism" Marx criticised in the Communist Manifesto. Wood is presented as the main defender of an orthodox, relations-of-production view of class. Li concludes that Western Marxism has been speculative from the start. Its "practice" is the practice of class consciousness, not material exchange between humans and nature, so it swings between determinism and voluntarism and offers no real path beyond capitalism. It ends up proposing reforms within capitalism, such as democratic socialism and red-green alliances. Negri and Hardt's multitude, which has neither class nor party organisation, is judged unpromising, and the yellow vests movement is described as cooling. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic assessment of how Western left thinkers from Lukács to Negri have treated the revolutionary subject.

Dialectical phenomenology and the critical theory of Western Marxism: centred on Marcuse 辩证现象学与西方马克思主义批判理论——以马尔库塞为中心 Xue Jinxi How can radical Marxist critical theory avoid becoming an abstract postulate? Xue starts from the turn after Althusser's late "materialism of the encounter". Althusser, Badiou and Žižek, the article says, stress contingent situations, events or an inner "Real" as triggers of radical action, but neglect how the proletariat is actually formed in history. Xue argues that Herbert Marcuse's "historical-materialist phenomenology" (or "dialectical phenomenology") offers a benchmark for a critical reassessment of these theories. The article has three parts. The first sets out the shared problem and the respective flaws of Lukács and Heidegger, which Xue presents as Marcuse's starting point in the late 1920s and early 1930s, when he studied under Heidegger at Freiburg. The second reconstructs how Marcuse combines dialectics and phenomenology through Hegel's Phenomenology of Spirit and Marx's Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844. The third uses the result to assess Heidegger, Sartre and Žižek and to draw a conclusion about critical theory. Xue argues that Lukács's History and Class Consciousness cannot explain the passage from individual reified consciousness to totalising class consciousness. Xue also holds that it ignores nature's objective limits on practice, which gives it an idealist tendency. Heidegger's analysis of the historicity of Dasein, by contrast, stays abstract and quasi-transcendental. Marcuse, on Xue's account, joins the two. From Hegel he takes the process of objectification and mutual public criticism among selves, and from Marx's Manuscripts the material content and sensuous, receptive character of human life. The result is a historical ontology that unites individual self-understanding with awareness of material constraints. Judged by this standard, Xue says, Žižek's "dislocation" universality, pure-negativity class struggle and "parallax Real" cannot explain how a revolutionary subject is formed. Marcuse's route to liberating the instincts through "aesthetic form" is presented as more concrete. Xue concludes that Marcuse's approach can supply a theoretical basis for piercing capitalist reification and reactivating Marxism's radical content. Xue adds that theories built around the subject, Marcuse's included, understand capitalist cultural psychology to a degree but neglect the structural content of historical materialism. Critique of ideology, the article contends, must therefore be pushed on to the critique of political economy. Read the original if you study Marcuse, the Lukács–Heidegger relation or Western Marxist debates on revolutionary subjectivity, and want a Chinese assessment of Žižek's theory of class struggle.

A review of recent domestic research on Western Marxist critiques of capitalism 国内西方马克思主义资本主义批判研究动态述评 Han Qiuhong Sun Ying This review, published in 2019, surveys Chinese scholarship (mostly from 2018) on Western Marxist critiques of capitalism. Han and Sun start from the 2008 financial crisis and the growing role of finance capital combined with digital technology. They argue that domestic research has become more attentive to real-world problems and now needs to draw out the meaning of these critiques for China and to build Chinese discourse. The review is organised in three parts. The first maps the research frontier in three areas: political-economy critiques of new capitalist economic forms, critiques of modernity, and political-philosophical critiques of ideology. The second identifies the methodological features of this work. The third sets out where the field can develop. In the first part, the authors report that Chinese scholars treat digital, platform and financial capitalism, and the spatial-production theories of Lefebvre, David Harvey and Ellen Meiksins Wood, as new forms that do not change capital's exploitative logic. Under modernity they list meta-level studies of Western Marxist theory, cultural critiques of alienation and surveillance capitalism, and ecological Marxism (Foster, O'Connor, Gorz). Under ideology they cover neoliberalism, biopolitics, post-Marxist discourse politics and spatial politics. Han and Sun describe the field's features as combining historical review with sharper thematic focus, and as interdisciplinary 'surround the point to strike the relief force' and 'blossoming from the centre' approaches that return to Chinese realities. They judge Western Marxist critiques to be diverse and incisive but class-limited, incomplete and sometimes at odds with Marxism. The authors conclude that research remains too general about China's relevance, too academic and speculative, and too weak in building its own theory. They call for work that moves beyond 'speaking after' and 'speaking along with' Western thinkers to 'speaking for oneself'. They also call for a Chinese discourse system, comparison of contemporary Chinese Marxism with foreign Marxism, and use of Western Marxist methods on problems China shares with capitalist modernity. Read the original if you want a map of 2018 Chinese-language literature on Western Marxism and capitalism, or insight into how Chinese scholars frame the purpose of foreign Marxism research.

Foreign left-wing scholars' new thinking on the market economy since the financial crisis, and its implications 金融危机以来国外左翼学者对市场经济的新思考及其启示 Liu Mingming Liu Mingming asks how left-wing scholars outside China have reassessed the market economy since the global financial crisis of 2008, and what this means for China. The article argues that these scholars broadly see the crisis as the end of the laissez-faire market, reject the idea that state and market are opposed, and question the claimed link between free markets and democracy. Liu then draws four lessons for China's socialist market economy. Liu defines the left by four positions: reading the crisis as a failure of neoliberal policy, opposing capitalism's profit logic, supporting economic democracy and equality, and favouring state intervention to protect the weak. The article surveys mainly Anglo-American and Canadian economists, sociologists and political thinkers, including Stiglitz, Barbera, Turner, Altman, Reich, Malleson, Engler, Schweickart, Lane, Ollman and Campbell. It has five sections: the end of the laissez-faire market, the state–market relationship, markets and democracy, markets and the nature of the social system, and implications for China. Liu reports that these scholars treat markets as constructed by the state through money, property and contract law, so that regulation creates markets rather than merely restricting them. Drawing on Malleson, the article sets out how unequal spending power, monopoly, externalities, public goods, short horizons and collective choice make markets undemocratic. On the market and the social system, Liu finds a split. Engler and the market socialists Schweickart and Lane hold that markets can be separated from capitalism and combined with public ownership or economic democracy. Ollman and Campbell hold that markets reproduce alienation and are incompatible with socialism. Liu draws four lessons for China. China should keep to market-oriented reform and not swing 'leftward' because of the crisis. It should not use the market's decisive role in allocating resources to deny the government's role in public goods and risk regulation. It should not make excessive concessions to win market-economy status from the United States, the EU or Japan, whom Liu accuses of double standards on economic freedom. It should handle the relations between the market, socialism and democracy carefully, since the market is a tool that can serve different systems. Liu also warns that interest groups could use investment, employment and price monopoly to interfere in politics. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic's survey of Western left debates on markets, with references, and the policy lessons drawn from them for China.

The contemporary value of Marxism and its implications, seen through foreign left-wing scholars 国外左翼学者视域下马克思主义的当代价值及启示 Zhuo Mingliang Writing in 2019, Zhuo Mingliang reviews how foreign left-wing scholars have assessed the contemporary value of Marxism. The article is a survey of recent writing, prompted by anniversaries (the October Revolution, Marx's bicentenary, the Communist Manifesto, the Comintern) and by the 2008 financial crisis. Zhuo's thesis is that these scholars show Marxism remains vital and refutes claims that it is obsolete, and that China should draw lessons from them, including closer dialogue with them. The review draws on articles from several dozen left-wing journals and websites, among them Monthly Review, New Left Review, Historical Materialism, Socialism and Democracy and Review of African Political Economy. It is organised in four sections: Marxism's continuing theoretical appeal; its critique of capitalism and the political options it offers the oppressed; its capacity to guide the future world socialist movement; and the need to keep Marxism dialectically open and adapted to national conditions. A short conclusion draws out three implications. Zhuo reports that Victor Wallis, Masao Suzuki, Immanuel Wallerstein and David McLellan treat Marx's analysis of exploitation, surplus value and class struggle as still applicable to neoliberal capitalism and the 2008 crisis. Suzuki, for example, cites Amazon's profits against its workers' pay. Party leaders such as Jose Maria Sison, Sitaram Yechury and Elizabeth Rowley are cited as urging study of Marx's works and their application in struggle, led by the working class. Other voices, notably Kemal Okuyan, are reported as warning that Marxism offers no ready-made blueprint and must not be treated as a closed dogma. Zhuo concludes that the foreign scholars' views support the truth and vitality of Marxism and rebut the 'uselessness' and 'obsolescence' arguments. The author adds that Marxism's vitality is also shown in the Party's adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, and calls for greater confidence in theory and for arming minds with Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Zhuo also urges stronger academic dialogue with foreign left scholars and communist parties. Read the original if you want a map of the left-wing journals and figures a Chinese Marxist scholar draws on to argue for Marxism's present relevance.

Capital and the inner logic of research on Marx's political philosophy 《资本论》与马克思政治哲学研究的内在逻辑 Gao Guangxu Gao Guangxu asks in what sense Capital can serve as an intellectual resource for research on Marx's political philosophy, a question the author treats as urgent for contemporary work in this field. The short commentary argues that reading Marx's political philosophy through Capital is not an expedient but follows necessarily from the development and the essential character of that philosophy. The article is organised around three claims about the critique of political economy in Capital: it is the logical result of Marx's political-philosophical development, the logical precondition for advancing research on it, and the logical vehicle of its contemporary significance. Gao draws on Marx's early critique of Hegel's philosophy of right, the 1859 Preface to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy, the Grundrisse and Capital. Gao argues that Marx's starting judgement, that civil society determines the state, led him from criticising Hegel's theory of the state to analysing the mode of production of material life. In Capital, the author contends, Marx shows that the political and economic logics of modernity are apparently separate but in substance coupled. The formal uniformity of capitalist exchange grounds the modern political ideas of freedom, equality and ownership and also drives their undoing, since exchange-value develops into capital and labour into wage-labour. Gao also holds that Marx's political philosophy answers the problem of the age, 'individuals ruled by abstractions', which Marx treats as rule by capital, so that capital is a political as well as an economic concept. Gao concludes that as long as individuals remain under the rule of capital, bringing out the contemporary content of Marx's political philosophy requires a return to Capital. Read the original if you want a compact statement, in the Chinese debate on Marx's political philosophy, of why Capital should be its textual basis.

A view on the "transformation" and development of Marx's early thought Centred on "On the Jewish Question" and the "Introduction to A Contribution to the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right" 对马克思早期思想“转变”与发展的一点看法 Sun Xiguo Wang Feifan Chinese scholars have long disputed when Marx became a Marxist. The "one-transformation" view holds that Marx completed the shift from idealism to materialism and from revolutionary democracy to communism at the end of 1843. The "two-transformation" view holds that this was only a first step, to Feuerbachian humanism and "philosophical communism", with historical materialism and scientific communism reached in 1845–46. Sun and Wang argue that both frameworks should be set aside. They propose reading Marx through two viewpoints: his unchanging overall goal of proletarian and human emancipation, and the different historical tasks he faced at each stage. The article focuses on \"On the Jewish Question\" and the \"Introduction to A Contribution to the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right\", which the two-transformation camp criticises as immature and unscientific. It first identifies two methodological errors in existing scholarship. It then traces Marx's practical trajectory from 1837 to 1843: the Doctors' Club in Berlin, the Rheinische Zeitung, and Paris. A final section distinguishes the \"historical logic\" behind the texts from their \"textual logic\". The authors' first move is to reject two habits: judging early works against the wording of later mature texts, and inferring a \"Feuerbach stage\" or \"Young Hegelian stage\" from borrowed terms and citations. They note that Althusser and McLellan use similar methods and reach opposite conclusions. They add that quoting a thinker does not mean sharing that thinker's stance. Second, they argue that Marx's practice changed his questions. In Paris, contact with the French workers' movement and with German workers led him to the concept of the modern proletariat. The authors say his earlier conclusion that civil society determines the state had become \"outdated\" for the new problem, and his political-economic critique of civil society was not yet developed. The abstract and speculative character of the two texts is therefore explained by this gap. Third, the texts appear to move logically from religion to proletarian revolution, but the authors say this is the condensed result of Marx's earlier practice. They read his remark to Ruge about smuggling in \"the greatest amount of rationality\" as showing that the Bauer critique was only an entry point. Sun and Wang conclude that the tendency to belittle Marx's early works, or to set a young Marx against a mature one, is mistaken. They call for studying the development of his thought through the stages of his own practice, and for grasping its essence through the constancy of his goal. Marx's thought, in their account, was enriched and advanced over his life, not overturned. Read the original if you work on the periodisation of the young Marx, the one-transformation versus two-transformation debate in Chinese scholarship, or the reading of the Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher texts.

Capital and the internal logic of research on Marx's political philosophy 《资本论》与马克思政治哲学研究的内在逻辑 Gao Guangxu Writing in 2019, Gao Guangxu asks in what sense Capital is an intellectual resource for Marx's political philosophy, a question the author treats as urgent for contemporary research in the field. The short commentary argues that Capital's critique of political economy is the logical result of the development of Marx's political philosophy, the logical precondition for advancing research on it, and the logical vehicle of its contemporary meaning. The piece is organised in three sections, one for each of these claims. It moves from Marx's early critique of Hegel's philosophy of right, through Capital and the 1857–58 manuscripts, to the question of why Capital still matters in an age the author describes as one of individuals ruled by abstraction. Gao holds that Marx's critique of Hegel led him to the judgement that civil society determines the state, which directed political philosophy toward the mode of production of material life and to the critique of political economy. In Gao's reading, Capital reveals that the political and economic logics of modernity are apparently separate but in substance coupled. The formal homogeneity of exchange grounds modern ideas of freedom, equality and ownership, yet also undermines them, because exchange-value must develop into capital and labour into wage-labour. Gao also argues that the buying and selling of labour-power is the 'Eden' of bourgeois political ideas, whose illusions are broken once labour-power is put to use. Capital is therefore a political concept as well as an economic one. Gao concludes that basing the interpretation of Marx's political philosophy on Capital is a necessity arising from its development and nature, not an expedient. As long as individuals remain ruled by capital, the author says, showing the contemporary meaning of Marx's political philosophy requires a return to Capital. Read the original if you want a compact statement of the case for reading Marx's political philosophy through the critique of political economy.

Upholding and applying the scientific method of historical materialism 历史唯物主义科学方法的坚持和运用 Yang Jun This short commentary, published in 2019, asks how Xi Jinping applies the scientific method of historical materialism to major questions of Chinese history. Yang argues that since the 18th Party Congress (2012), Xi has promoted study of historical materialism and used its method to answer historical nihilism. In Yang's account, historical nihilism denies the necessity of China's socialist path, the legitimacy of Communist Party leadership and the objectivity of the nation's modern struggle for rejuvenation. The article is organised around three methodological moves it attributes to Xi. These are starting from objective social being in understanding socialism with Chinese characteristics; grasping the periods before and after reform and opening up through the connections of the "actual historical movement"; and assessing the Party's activities and its leaders historically and concretely. A short closing paragraph sums up the contribution of Xi's statements. On the first point, Yang holds that understanding socialism with Chinese characteristics requires letting the history of world socialism, of modern China and of the Party "speak". World socialism's five centuries show conformity to historical law; China's 170-odd years of modern history show purposiveness; and the fate of Marxism is tied to that of the Party and nation. Socialism with Chinese characteristics is therefore neither accident nor pure idea. On the second, Yang follows Xi in treating the two periods as stages of a relay race with a shared goal, premise and essence, so that neither may be used to negate the other. On the third, historical figures must be placed in their conditions: leaders should be neither deified nor wholly rejected, and the Party's mistakes should be admitted, analysed and corrected. Yang concludes that Xi's statements deepen understanding of historical materialist method, highlight the principle of seeking truth from facts and express the Party's firm stance against historical nihilism. The piece is a compact, official-line account of how Party theory frames the continuity of Chinese history and the evaluation of its leaders. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese Party scholarship justifies the unity of the pre- and post-reform periods and answers historical nihilism in 2019.

Capital and the internal logic of research on Marx's political philosophy 《资本论》与马克思政治哲学研究的内在逻辑 Gao Guangxu Writing in a 2019 newspaper commentary, Gao Guangxu asks in what sense Capital is an intellectual resource for research on Marx's political philosophy. Gao argues that the critique of political economy in Capital is the logical result of the development of Marx's political philosophy, the logical precondition for further research, and the logical vehicle that brings out its meaning for our own era. Reading Marx's political philosophy through Capital is, on this view, a necessity rooted in its development and nature, not an expedient. The piece is organised in three parts, one for each of these claims. It starts from Marx's early critique of Hegel's philosophy of right and state theory, moves to the analysis of commodity form and value in Capital, and ends with the problem of the age that Capital addresses. Gao holds that Marx's early conclusion that civil society determines the state led him to the mode of production and then to political economy. Capital, as his most systematic work in that field, is therefore the endpoint and also the starting point for understanding this development. Gao further contends that Capital shows political and economic logic to be formally separate but substantively coupled. The formal homogeneity of exchange grounds modern ideas of freedom, equality and ownership, and also undermines them, as exchange-value becomes capital and labour becomes wage labour. Gao adds that the 'Eden' of the sphere of circulation gives way to relations of domination once labour-power is used, so that capital is a political concept as well as an economic one. Gao concludes that Capital answers a political as well as an economic question, namely the condition of 'individuals ruled by abstractions', which Gao equates with rule by capital. As long as people live under this rule, Gao argues, work on the contemporary meaning of Marx's political philosophy must return to Capital. Read the original if you want a brief statement of the case for grounding Marx's political philosophy in the critique of political economy.

The crisis of civilisation and its challenge to the Left 文明的危机及其对左翼的挑战 Miriam Lang This is a Chinese translation of Miriam Lang's introduction to the volume she co-organised, Beyond Development: Alternative Visions from Latin America, published with the Rosa Luxemburg Foundation's Andean office. Lang argues that the overlapping financial, food, energy and ecological crises amount to a 'crisis of civilisation', felt most acutely at the world's margins. In her account, the Left must now do more than criticise capitalism: it must build alternatives to the very idea of 'development'. The introduction opens with global extractivism and the 'green economy', then turns to the Andean region, where Bolivia, Ecuador and Venezuela adopted new constitutions after pressure from peasant, women's, urban and indigenous movements. It next presents the Permanent Working Group on Alternatives to Development, founded in 2010, and previews the book's chapters by Eduardo Gudynas, Alberto Acosta, Edgardo Lander, Ulrich Brand, Maristella Svampa, Raúl Prada and Elisa Vega. Lang contends that the Andean 'progressive' governments, despite breaking in part with neoliberalism, remain trapped in what the working group calls the 'Latin American paradox': to fund social programmes they expand mining, oil, gas and agrofuels, which brings them into conflict with their own constitutions and grassroots bases. Citing Foucault and Arturo Escobar, she treats 'development' as a Western, capitalist and colonial power device that labels Southern ways of life 'backward'. She adds that 'really existing socialism' and much of the Latin American Left accepted the concept, equating prosperity with consumption. Against this she sets buen vivir, the rights of nature and plurinational statehood, while Gudynas proposes a gradual path from predatory to 'sensible' to 'indispensable' extractivism. Lang presents the book as only a first attempt at a theory of alternatives to development, with the creation of models of good living in cities as the next task. She notes that the Left, which is skilled at critique and tends to define itself negatively, must now look for partners' strengths and think what has seemed impossible. The Chinese editors' preface claims the book exposes neoliberalism and offers ideas useful for socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era. Read the original if you want an overview of Latin American post-development and anti-extractivist debates, and of how the Andean 'progressive' governments are assessed from within the Left.

Greed and fear: a new interpretation of financial crisis in contemporary capitalism 贪婪与恐惧：当代资本主义金融危机的新阐释 Kong Ming'an Writing in 2019, with US stock indices at record highs and quantitative easing being wound down, Kong Ming'an asks whether the 2008 subprime crisis has really passed and how the new features of US-led financial capitalism should be explained. The article presents Slavoj Žižek's answer, which combines Lacanian psychoanalysis with Marxist dialectics. On this reading, Marx's analysis of capitalism is not outdated, but twentieth-century capitalism runs on financial speculation rather than labour and production. Kong holds that Žižek's approach is original yet cannot replace Marxist crisis theory. The article is a critical exposition of Žižek's analysis, drawing mainly on his In Defense of Lost Causes and Tarrying with the Negative. It has four parts: the desiring subject and the signifier logic of financial markets; the empty subject and the remedies for crisis; Keynesianism and the fate of capitalism; and a conclusion on charitable giving by the rich. Kong also sets out Lacan's concepts of desire as metonymy, the objet petit a (surplus enjoyment), the Other and the 'Name-of-the-Father'. Kong first reports that, for Žižek, market actors look rational but are driven by unconscious desire, so that greed and fear coexist in one paradoxical subject. Speculation on stock and futures markets becomes a game of sliding along a chain of signifiers, and rumour alone can wipe out a firm's value. Second, a crisis opens a 'void' like the one the Lacanian subject fears, and states fill it with Keynesian money-printing and deficit spending. Žižek calls this a poisoned remedy: it borrows from the future, and electronic money is a 'ghost' that cannot erase the debt. Kong adds that Žižek treats this as confirming Marx's prediction that capitalism will perish, though the end is postponed. Kong concludes that Marx's judgement on capitalism's inevitable demise remains valid, and that virtual capital, credit expansion and expansionary policy have delayed the crisis rather than abolished it. Žižek also gives partial approval to philanthropy by billionaires, which he says delays crisis because capitalism cannot reproduce itself unaided. Kong criticises psychoanalysis for hiding the institutional dimension, since crises arise from the capitalist system itself. Kong adds that donations by Gates, Soros and Buffett are a drop in the ocean compared with private appropriation and do not change the system's nature. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist assessment of Žižek's Lacanian account of finance, Keynesianism and digital capitalism.

The problem of the subject in the logic of capital: from Marx to Badiou 资本逻辑中的主体问题:从马克思到巴迪欧 Yuan Bei Yuan Bei asks how a human subject can escape domination by the logic of capital, at a time when 'the death of the subject' is a widespread theme in Western Marxism and radical left thought. Taking Alain Badiou as the leading radical-left figure engaging with Marxism, the article argues that his theory of a subject faithful to a 'truth event' responds to this problem. Yuan also contends that the theory is limited by its neglect of the economic sphere and suggests that Badiou should restore the revolutionary potential of truth events to the economy. The article is built in three parts plus a conclusion. It first sets out Marx's treatment of the subject, in general history and under capitalism. It then traces two lines in the Marxist tradition: a subject-centred one running from Lukács to Sartre, and an 'anti-subject' one running from the Second International to Althusser, with the Frankfurt School as a pessimistic middle case. The third part reconstructs Badiou's theory of the subject through his critique of 'democratic materialism' and his distinction between being and event, drawing on Žižek, Harvey and Lazzarato along the way. Yuan's central reasoning begins from Marx's claim that under capital the human being is only the personification of economic categories. Capital, as self-expanding value, acquires an apparent 'subjectivity' while workers and capitalists become its bearers, and Althusser's structure without a subject is read as a theoretical echo of this. Badiou's answer, in Yuan's account, is that the formal, counting-as-one structure of the capitalist commodity world has a 'void' at its edge. A contingent event can erupt there, and a subject is not given in advance but is generated by fidelity to that event, so that scattered individuals are gathered into a single revolutionary subject. Yuan concludes that Badiou's subject theory is distinctly political: it treats the economy as belonging to the order of being, with no evental sites, and so leaves Marx's critique of political economy aside. Yuan reports the criticism that the event appears like a miracle, leaving people merely waiting. Citing Žižek's call to return to Lenin and Marx's remarks on the realm of freedom resting on the realm of necessity, Yuan holds that emancipation also requires developed productive forces as a material basis. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist critique of Badiou that links his event philosophy to Lukács, Althusser and the Frankfurt School debates on the subject.

The difficulties of the Latin American left have no single cause 拉美左翼困境非单一因素所致 Jin Chengwei Writing in December 2018, Jin Chengwei takes up the "left down, right up" shift in Latin American politics. Drawing on interviews with leaders and officials of communist, socialist and other left-wing parties in several countries, Jin argues that the left's difficulties come from a combination of factors, not one cause, and that the left still has room to grow. The short commentary has three parts. It lists the causes of the left's decline, sets out the tasks the left faces, and recalls the region's long left-wing tradition. It closes with four questions that Jin suggests scholars should study. On causes, Jin reports seven factors. They include economic stagnation, which the right exploited after the financial crisis, and weak party-building and organisation. Others are the lack of strategic thinking, governing inexperience, a left that is united only in words and fragmented in practice, and a failure to keep close ties with the public. The last is US efforts to restore its hegemony and undermine regional integration. The interviewees name three urgent tasks: left unity, winning over public opinion against right-controlled media, and building stronger parties. Jin ends with research questions. Why did the 2008 crisis not spur left social movements, and how does it compare with earlier crises? How should the left be defined, given disputed typologies? Why does fragmentation persist, and how can new media help parties reach the public? Read the original if you want a brief account of how Latin American left-wing party figures explained their setbacks, and an agenda for further research.

Seventy years of socialist cultural construction in New China and its lessons 新中国70年社会主义文化建设及其经验 Ouyang Xuemei Writing in Guangming Daily on 10 July 2019, Ouyang Xuemei reviews how the Communist Party of China has led cultural work since 1949. The article argues that the Party, working from actual conditions, has built Chinese spirit and Chinese values, rallied the country and enriched people's cultural life. In Ouyang's account, this supported the passage from "standing up" to "becoming rich" to "becoming strong" and yielded a set of basic lessons. The piece is organised chronologically in three stages, followed by a closing section of lessons. The first stage is the foundation of socialist culture after 1949, including mass literacy, public cultural facilities, script reform, minority-language policy and the promotion of Marxism. The second is the exploration of socialist culture with Chinese characteristics after the Cultural Revolution, running from the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978) through the 12th to 17th Party Congresses. The third covers the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Ouyang presents the early decades as establishing a new people's culture, while acknowledging that cultural questions were politicised and that the Cultural Revolution brought serious errors. The reform era is described as shifting emphasis from popularisation to raising standards, with spiritual civilisation, the distinction between public cultural undertakings and commercial cultural industries, and cultural-system reform as key advances. For the new era, the article stresses the Four-sphere Confidence, Marxist leadership in ideology, core socialist values, creative transformation of traditional culture, and a principle that social benefit comes first in literature and art. It also stresses telling China's story abroad and civilisational exchange. Ouyang draws five lessons: Party leadership is the key; Marxism guides and keeps culture advanced; the people-centred character is the essence of socialist culture; core socialist values give culture its soul; and ancient and modern, Chinese and foreign cultures must be handled by preserving the roots, absorbing foreign achievements and facing the future. The author presents the record as a change from popularisation to improvement and from serving China's people to engaging the world. Read the original if you want a concise, officially framed periodisation of Party cultural policy from 1949 to 2019, with the key documents and slogans of each stage.

The Chinese path grows ever broader by upholding fundamental principles and breaking new ground 中国道路在守正创新中越走越宽广 Xin Ming Writing in the People's Daily in July 2019, on the eve of the 70th anniversary of the People's Republic, Xin Ming argues that the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics (the "Chinese path") has widened because it combines faithfulness to fundamental principles (守正) with innovation (创新). The piece is a short commentary, not a research article. Xin presents the path as one opened by the Communist Party by upholding the basic principles of scientific socialism, grasping the laws of social development and drawing on the achievements of human civilisation. The commentary has three sections. The first deals with scientific socialism and how the Chinese path both keeps and develops it. The second takes up modernization and the laws of social development. The third discusses the moral standing of the Chinese path and the push to build a community with a shared future for mankind, with the Belt and Road Initiative as its practical platform. In the first section, Xin sets out what the author takes to be the core principles of scientific socialism: a historically necessary transition from capitalism, public ownership as a way to resolve the contradiction between socialised production and private appropriation, and leadership by a Marxist party. Xin holds that socialism with Chinese characteristics has kept these principles while innovating, citing the basic economic system, the decisive role of the market in allocating resources, and, since the 18th Party Congress (2012), the stress on Party leadership as its most essential feature. In the second section, Xin argues that modernization is not "Westernization". Western models built on colonial plunder and on opposing humanity to nature are, in Xin's account, exhausted, while China's emphasis on ecological civilisation and its answers to problems shared by developing countries offer an alternative. In the third, Xin contends that the path is peaceful and cooperative, rejects zero-sum thinking, and reflects a civilisation of harmony, citing Zheng He and Xi Jinping's image of a "peaceful, amiable and civilised lion". Xin concludes that the success of the Chinese path is a victory for socialism itself and gives scientific socialism new vitality in twenty-first-century China. Xin also holds that the path offers developing countries a new option and contributes "Chinese wisdom" and a "Chinese approach" to global problems. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the Party press framed the Chinese path, modernization and the community with a shared future for mankind around the 70th anniversary in 2019.

How to uphold the eight "unities" in teaching ideological and political theory courses in universities 高校思政课教学怎样坚持八个“相统一” Lin Tai Lin Tai, a retired Tsinghua University professor who says he has taught ideological and political theory since 1959, reflects on the eight requirements ("unities") that Xi Jinping set out for reforming these courses. The piece is a personal commentary, published in Qiushi in 2019 after Lin attended the symposium of teachers of ideological and political theory courses on 18 March 2019. Lin argues that the eight pairings give teachers a concrete path to courses that are intellectually serious yet close to students' real concerns. Lin opens with his own career, from political counsellor in 1954 to continued lecturing after retirement in 1999, and with what he says he has witnessed: the shift from Party history to an outline of modern Chinese history, the entry of the theoretical system of socialism with Chinese characteristics into the courses, and a stronger emphasis on core socialist values and moral and legal education. He then takes the eight unities in turn: political and academic; value and knowledge; constructive and critical; theoretical and practical; unity and diversity; the leading role of teachers and the agency of students; indoctrination and inspiration; explicit and implicit education. The longest discussion concerns the first unity. Lin holds that a theory persuades only if it is thorough, that is, grasps the root of things. His examples are the claim that the Russian and Chinese revolutions came too early, which he answers by pointing to the shifting contradictions of the imperialist era, and the debate on human nature, which he treats through Marx's view that individuals must be understood within historical social relations. On the constructive and critical unity, he describes studying neoliberalism, Western constitutional democracy, historical nihilism and \"universal values\", and countering multiparty-competition ideas by comparing China with countries that adopted such systems. He also defends indoctrination as a principle, citing Lenin that socialist consciousness is brought to workers from outside, but says it must be carried out by inspiring students rather than by cramming. Lin reports good practice among colleagues: field visits and social surveys, art students' exhibitions in the modern history course, and an engineering teacher who weaves ideological content into technical lectures. He calls for all courses and teachers to share responsibility for moral and political education. He ends by recalling a youth spent under the Japanese invasion and expresses confidence that, guided by Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, young people will fulfil their historic mission. Read the original if you want a veteran teacher's first-person account of how the official eight requirements are meant to work in the classroom.

A new breakthrough in the relationship between government and market in the new era 新时代政府和市场关系的新突破 Liu Xuemei Guo Guanqing Writing in the China Social Sciences Today in July 2019, Liu Xuemei and Guo Guanqing take up the call for a Chinese philosophy and social science system, and ask how Chinese economics should understand the role of government and market. They argue that the Western ideal of 'small government, big market' does not fit late-developing countries, and that the reconstruction of the government–market relationship in Xi Jinping's economic thought is a new breakthrough. The short piece moves from the history of economic thought to China's own record. It covers Adam Smith's context, the rival American School and German Historical School, Mises's 1920 critique of socialist economic calculation, the Soviet model, and China's decentralisation from 1958 onward. It ends with Xi Jinping's formulations on the market and Party leadership. The authors contend that Smith's doctrine reflected Britain's position as a dominant industrial power, and that theorists overlook the pressures facing latecomers, whose governments must take on more functions. In their account, the Soviet model of vertical ministerial management could not solve information, incentive and soft budget constraint problems. China instead built a two-tier system based on regional decentralisation. There, local governments can shift state capital across sectors, and restructured state firms work with market price signals. The authors say this overcame the 'socialist economic calculation problem' and helped China become the world's second-largest economy in 2010. Liu and Guo present Xi's twin principles as the theoretical expression of this experience: the market plays the decisive role in allocating resources, while the government plays its role better and the Party leads economic work in a centralised and unified way. They call on Chinese theoretical economics to build modernization theories, concepts and indicators from Chinese practice. Read the original if you want a brief statement of how Party-aligned economists in 2019 framed China's state-market model against Western and Soviet precedents.

Promoting steadfast principles and innovation in ideological and political theory courses in the new era 推动新时代思政课守正创新 Jiao Yang This short commentary, published in People's Daily in August 2019, reports how Fudan University is putting into practice Xi Jinping's speech at a symposium for teachers of ideological and political theory courses. Jiao presents the speech as a programmatic document guiding such courses in the new era. The central claim is that Fudan is advancing these courses by holding to core principles while innovating in content, method and staffing. The piece is organised under three headings: implementing Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era in teaching and research; reforming courses to raise quality; and building a trustworthy, capable teaching force. It draws on Fudan's own course system, textbooks and teacher-development practices. On the first point, Jiao says Fudan insists that the courses be Marxist, socialist and Party-led, and offers a series of courses on Xi's thought. It seeks to bring this thought into scholarship, disciplines, courses, training, readers and students' minds. On the second, the university builds a "4+1+X" course system combining classroom and practical teaching, and plans to update supplementary textbooks, expand online courses and link ideological courses with "curriculum-based ideological education" in other subjects. Jiao reports that all four compulsory courses have become national or Shanghai model courses. On the third, the university sends teachers on study tours and practical postings, builds teaching teams through peer observation and mentoring, and coordinates university, college and branch Party organisations. Jiao concludes that Fudan will continue reform along these lines so that students find the courses engaging and come to believe in what they study. The article is a Party-line account of institutional practice, not a theoretical study. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a leading Chinese university described its response to the 2019 directive on ideological and political courses.

Continuously deepening our understanding of the laws of socialist construction 不断深化对社会主义建设规律的认识 Tang Zhouyan Marking the 70th anniversary of the People's Republic in 2019, this commentary, first published in the People's Daily on 14 August 2019, asks what the Party has learned about the laws governing socialist construction. Tang Zhouyan argues that the 70 years were also seventy years of the Party leading the people in exploring those laws, and that continuing to summarise and deepen this understanding is necessary for advancing the cause of socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era. The piece is organised around five aspects that Tang calls especially important: the Party's role as the core of leadership; an accurate grasp of the historical stage of development and the principal contradiction in society; the scientific formulation of national development strategy; reform and opening up; and the continual meeting of the people's aspiration for a better life. Each section traces positions from Mao Zedong through successive Party congresses and plenums to Xi Jinping. Tang's central move is to present each theme as a line of continuous refinement. On leadership, Tang cites Xi Jinping's claim that Party leadership is the defining feature and greatest strength of socialism with Chinese characteristics, and calls for upholding the Party Central Committee's authority and the core position of Xi. On the stage of development, Tang follows the formulation of the principal contradiction from 1956 through 1981 to the 19th Party Congress (2017), and stresses that its change leaves unaltered the judgment that China remains in the primary stage of socialism. On strategy and reform, Tang points to the Five-Year Plans, the three-step modernization plans, the 2020–2035–mid-century timetable, and the shift from the market's "basic" to "decisive" role in allocating resources. Tang concludes that building a modern socialist country requires holding to the basic line of the primary stage, resolving unbalanced and inadequate development, deepening reform and opening up, and treating the people's longing for a better life as the goal. The commentary stresses the people-centred approach, poverty alleviation and the social security system as evidence. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party theorists in 2019 summarised the historical logic of seventy years of socialist construction.

The intellectual content of the traditional view of past and present, and its sublation 传统古今观的思想内涵及其扬弃 Zhang Xiaoping Zhang Xiaoping asks how China's traditional understanding of "ancient" and "modern" (gu and jin) should be assessed and carried forward today. The commentary starts from Xi Jinping's repeated instruction that excellent traditional culture be inherited by making the past serve the present and using the past as a mirror, without privileging the ancient over the present or the reverse. Zhang argues that the traditional view contains both enduring essentials and dross, and that modern Chinese thought has sublated it, a process the author says should continue in the new era. The piece is built in three parts. The first sets out the content of the traditional view: how "ancient" and "present" are conceived, how their relationship is understood, and what attitudes are taken towards each. The second separates what Zhang regards as valuable from what is not. The third traces the move from the late Qing and May Fourth periods, through Li Dazhao and Mao Zedong, to Xi Jinping's present-day guidance. Sources range from Shao Yong, Confucius and Sima Qian to Sima Guang, Gu Yanwu, Li Zhi and Wang Chong. Zhang's central distinction is among three attitudes: favouring the ancient, favouring the present, and treating them as one. The author links each to a view of history as decline or progress, noting that Confucian reverence for the Three Dynasties, Daoist return to simplicity and Legalist reformism all fit this pattern, and that a comparable dispute existed in the West. On the positive side, Zhang credits the tradition with preserving texts, writing histories and drawing lessons for governance, including the people-centred reasoning of Sima Guang and the Confucian praise-and-blame ethic that restrained rulers. On the negative side, Zhang argues that Confucian moral norms hardened into absolute principle and narrowed thinking about past and present, a rigidity Li Zhi began to criticise. In Zhang's account, Li Dazhao applied historical materialism to arrive at a "present-centred" view of history, and Mao Zedong held that history must not be severed and that the ancient should serve the present. Zhang calls for old content with lasting value to be given new forms through creative transformation and innovative development. The author also urges learning from the history of other countries, keeping historical materialism as the guide, and going beyond the productive-forces yardstick and a single Confucian moral standard. Read the original if you want a short, officially aligned overview of how Chinese scholars connect classical views of history to current cultural policy.

Seventy years of research on foreign Marxist philosophy in China: review and prospects 国外马克思主义哲学研究70年：回顾与展望 Zhang Liang Writing in 2019, Zhang Liang asks how Chinese scholarship on foreign Marxist philosophy has developed since 1949 and where it should go next. The article rejects the common view that the field began only with reform and opening up in 1978. Zhang argues that the seventy years form a process in which Chinese scholars, grounded in socialism with Chinese characteristics, steadily narrowed the distance to foreign Marxist thought. The field is now said to be running "alongside" it and seeking to break through and "lead". The article is a periodised history of the field in five parts. It covers a neglected 1949–1978 "prehistory", the rise of research on Western Marxism from 1978, a phase of deeper development from the early 1990s, and the boom since the early 2000s together with its drawbacks. It ends with proposals for the future. Zhang draws on journals, translation series, institutional centres, rough publication counts and the debate between Xu Chongwen and Du Zhangzhi, as well as personal experience of the Foreign Marxism Forum. Zhang holds that the "prehistory" was not empty. Information journals, translated reference collections and Soviet-era commentaries, notably the Chinese edition of Leopold Labedz's Revisionism, trained the first researchers and supplied theoretical preparation. The later phases are traced to specific causes: the global prominence of Western Marxism, the political meaning of the topic, and a sense that Western Marxism described China's own market-economy experience. The boom is traced mainly to the 2004 Marxist theory research and construction project and the 2005 creation of foreign Marxism as a second-level discipline. Zhang lists its features: a large academic population, high output, thematic diversity, and almost no time lag behind Western intellectual production. He also voices three worries: loss of the original purpose of serving Chinese problems, loss of a sense of historical position, and decline in scholarly discernment. For the future, Zhang calls for using historical materialism to rethink China's position, so that Chinese scholars treat foreign Marxist philosophy as equal interlocutors rather than as followers. He urges scholars to study foreign Marxism in order to address Chinese problems and build a Chinese Marxist philosophical system. He also calls for testing foreign theories in the Chinese context, challenging their biases on actually existing socialism and the Chinese path, and moving beyond textual study. Finally, he urges China to become a world centre of Marxist philosophical research. Read the original if you want a detailed insider account of how foreign Marxism studies in China were organised, debated and justified, and of the policy stance behind the field's expansion.

French Staatenkunde, social materialism and historical materialism 法国国势学、社会唯物主义与历史唯物主义 Liu Bingjing Modern statistics grew out of an older empirical science of state governance, known in Chinese as guóshìxué (here rendered "Staatenkunde" or science of the state's condition). Liu Bingjing argues that research on Marx's historical materialism has overlooked the link between the young Marx and this French tradition. In Liu's account, French Staatenkunde produced a "social materialism" that influenced List, Schulz and Marx alike, and formed a logical foundation for Marx's move in 1845 beyond German classical philosophy. The article has three parts. The first traces the formation of French Staatenkunde after the decline of Napoleonic France (1815–1848), from Chaptal's statistical office to Dupin and Moreau de Jonnès, who established it as an independent government science; it was absorbed into the economics ministry in 1936. The second analyses its materialist discourse. The third asks why the subject matters, by tracing its reception by Friedrich List, the German statistician Schulz and Marx, whose Paris, Manchester and London notebooks record readings of Chaptal, Dupin and Moreau de Jonnès. Liu's central claim is that French Staatenkunde treated social reality, above all material production, as the basis of national strength. Liu distinguishes this from the natural materialism of Helvétius, Diderot and Holbach, because its object was the non-intuitable productive capacity built up through social activity, which Dupin named "productive force". It also sought laws behind economic phenomena, unlike the abstraction Moreau de Jonnès saw in classical political economy, and it had a limited sense of history. Liu proposes that contact with this empirical literature helped Marx to turn from German classical philosophy to the German Ideology's "real, positive science", which Liu sees as echoing the field's slogan that sophistry collapses before facts. Liu stresses that historical materialism is not a copy of social materialism. Because Staatenkunde defended bourgeois society, Liu argues, it could not see alienation, class contradiction or the dialectical movement between productive forces and forms of intercourse. Its significance, for Liu, is that it fills a gap in the account of Marx's 1845 turn and helps define the philosophical character and limits of historical materialism. Read the original if you study the intellectual prehistory of historical materialism, Marx's notebooks, or the links between statistics, political economy and Marx's thought.

Several hot topics in world socialism studies in 2018 2018年世界社会主义研究的几个热点问题 Shan Chao Yang Xixi This is a review of the main themes in world socialism studies in 2018, written by two doctoral students and published in World Socialism Studies in 2019. It does not advance a single thesis. It reports what Chinese and foreign scholars, Party figures and research institutions said and produced on four topics, treating historical materialism as the guiding framework for the field. The review is organised in four sections: using historical materialism to guide research on world socialism; research on Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era; summing up the experience and lessons of the world socialist movement; and the 200th anniversary of Marx's birth together with the 170th anniversary of the Communist Manifesto. It draws on forums, conferences, journal articles, books and foreign commentary. In the first section, the authors cite Xi Jinping's 2017 judgement that, seen across 500 years of world socialism, we still live in the historical era Marxism identified. At the ninth World Socialism Forum (November 2018), Zhu Jiamu, Li Shenming and Zhang Quanjing are reported as reading the present as an era of transition from capitalism to socialism or communism. Zhang Quanjing locates the main contradiction in US–China relations. The second section lists Chinese studies of the Thought's theoretical content and its logical structure, and quotes favourable foreign assessments. The third section reports a Party-education film on historical nihilism and the Soviet collapse, and publications from the CASS World Socialism Research Centre, including the annual tracking report, a popular book series and the ten-volume History of the Development of Marxism. On the anniversaries, the review cites Xie Fuzhan's statement that Marxism is a developing theory, and Gennady Zyuganov's tribute to Marx. It also cites Western commentators who hold that the failure of Soviet socialism does not refute Marx. Chinese studies of the Manifesto are summarised for their bearing on globalisation, a community with a shared future for mankind, and distributive justice. The review ends without a separate conclusion, and its overall impression is of steady, institutionally backed growth in the field. Read the original if you want a quick map of the 2018 Chinese literature, conferences and publications on world socialism, with references to the sources cited.

Christian Fuchs: the internet has not changed the essence of capitalism Digital labour from a Marxist perspective 克里斯蒂安·福克斯:互联网没有改变资本主义的本质 Chang Jiang Shi Kaidi This is an interview, framed by the authors' commentary, with Christian Fuchs, a British Marxist communication scholar at the University of Westminster and editor of the journal triple C. Chang Jiang puts the questions.
