The authors present Fuchs as the developer of the concept of 'digital labour', and the interview's central message, as the title states, is that the internet has not altered the essential nature of capitalism. It was first published in the journal Journalism Review (Xinwenjie), 2019, no. 4. The authors open with a short profile of Fuchs, listing his major books, including Digital Labour and Karl Marx and Culture and Economy in the Age of Social Media. The interview then moves through four themes: the definition of digital labour; the political economy of the internet and social movements; alternatives to commercial platforms; and the place of Marxism in communication studies. The authors add short evaluative passages after each section and end by suggesting that Chinese researchers apply the digital-labour framework to China's internet industry. Fuchs argues that corporate platforms depend on capital accumulation and so exploit users, whose unpaid posting, sharing and uploading generates the data commodity sold to advertisers. He builds on Dallas Smythe's audience commodity theory, but notes new features such as real-time surveillance, prosumption and algorithmic ad auctions. He rejects 'immaterial labour' as a dualist notion, and calls social media 'targeted advertising platforms' whose profits are unstable. He criticises both techno-optimism and the dismissal of digital media in protest, and calls for empirical, Marxist research on social movements. On remedies, Fuchs rejects 'Wages for Facebook' as reformism that would only lower exploitation. He proposes taxing advertising and corporations to fund a 'participatory media fee' for non-commercial platforms, public-service alternatives to YouTube, and university-run search engines. In his view a fair internet requires overthrowing capitalism, and he cites the choice between socialism and barbarism. The authors read him as pessimistic about digital media but committed to revolutionary change. Read the original if you want a first-hand statement of Fuchs's digital-labour theory, his criticisms of mainstream communication research and 'New Reading of Marx', and how Chinese media scholars received him.

Digits, technology, capital: the generative logic of digital capitalism 数字·技术·资本:数字资本主义的生成逻辑 Wang Zhidong Ye Shenghua Wang Zhidong and Ye Shenghua ask how digital data become capital and how digital capitalism comes into being. Taking up the concept introduced by Dan Schiller in the late 1990s, they argue that the apparently free and democratic internet is in fact an alliance of the internet with capital. In their account, digital technology has become the most advanced productive force, data the capital that capitalists compete to seize, and digital labour a new object of exploitation for surplus value. The article, published in 2018, is filed under foreign Marxism. The article is organised in four steps: digital platforms, digital labour, digital capital and a concluding section. It begins with the commercial history of the internet, from a military and academic network to a corporate one, and with the rise of platforms such as LinkedIn, MySpace, Facebook and Groupon. It then reviews definitions of digital labour by Tiziana Terranova and Christian Fuchs, and Lan Jiang's notion of 'general data'. Next it examines how data are turned into capital, and it closes with proposals. The authors make three main moves. First, they treat the digital platform as the equivalent of the factory under industrial capitalism, the field where capital invests in and exploits users. They argue that platforms use free services to enclose a user market and then turn to profit-making. Second, they hold that digital labour is the root of digital capitalism. Users' searches, reading, play and social activity generate data; under privacy terms and user agreements, control of these data passes to platform owners, who pay no wages while capital appropriates all the value created. Third, they argue that data become digital capital through commodification, monopoly and enclosure of the formerly public internet. Digital capital then earns profit by selling market analysis to industrial and financial capital and by targeted advertising, and later through paid services and further platforms. The authors conclude that digital capital turns non-working time into labour time, blurs work and life, and draws in users of every age. Exploitation therefore persists in a more hidden form, supported by an ideology of free participation, sharing and fun. They do not call for abandoning digital technology. They propose cultivating critical media literacy and building a non-commercial internet governed by the logic of the people rather than of capital, with shared data and a mechanism for sharing 'general data', citing Marx on the community as the condition of individual freedom. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese Marxist account of digital labour and data as capital, drawing on Schiller, Terranova, Fuchs and Lan Jiang.

The digital shadow of existence: a philosophical critique of digital capitalism 生存的数字之影：数字资本主义的哲学批判 Lan Jiang Lan Jiang asks what happens to human existence when global capitalism enters a digital stage, and argues that the change calls for philosophical analysis as well as economic description. Using the film Ying (Shadow) as a metaphor, the article claims that the digital identities we hold online have become a 'shadow' that increasingly dominates the embodied subject it was meant to represent. Digital capitalism, in Lan's reading, therefore produces a new form of alienation. The article moves in three steps. It first contrasts the body-centred existentialism of Merleau-Ponty and Michel Henry with today's online life, introducing the concept of the 'virtual body' (xuti), a data package produced by algorithms. It then draws on Marx's Grundrisse and Jean Baudrillard's Critique of the Political Economy of the Sign to describe how things become 'coded'. Finally it turns to Marx's alienated labour, with reference to Gorz, Virno, Negri, Lazzarato and Christian Fuchs on immaterial and digital labour. Lan sets out a four-stage logic running from the concrete thing to the commodity to the sign and finally to a sign system that governs things. The article maps this onto the body and the virtual body: from occasional contact, as with email, to virtual bodies that are always online, then to a network of data exchange separate from bodies, and finally to a network that acts back on bodies. The relation 'body–body′' (B–B′) thus becomes 'body→virtual body–virtual body′→body′' (B→V–V′→B′), which Lan calls a new digital dialectic. Drawing on Virno's reading of Marx's 'general intellect', the article treats time spent on phones and platforms as unrecognised digital labour. The virtual body is cast as a product of that labour that returns to control its makers, as Lan sees in the Cambridge Analytica case. Lan concludes that despair is not the answer. Data, like technology, has no stance of its own: in the hands of digital capitalists it is a tool of enslavement, but in the hands of users it could become a weapon. The article proposes data sharing, or a 'communism of sharing', as the prospect of liberation, and argues that digitisation brings Marx's communism closer. Read the original if you want a philosophical account, drawing on phenomenology, Baudrillard and Italian autonomist thought, of how digital identity, data and labour can be read as a new form of alienation.

Reification: a reflection on culture, or on the economic and social whole? 物化:文化之思还是经济社会整体之思? Liu Senlin Liu Senlin asks how the meaning of "reification" (Verdinglichung and Versachlichung, used here in a broad sense that covers both) shifts between Marx's Capital and its manuscripts and Lukács's History and Class Consciousness. The article argues that Lukács turned reification into a mainly cultural and aesthetic category. Marx, in his mature work, treated it within an integrated economic, social and cultural whole. Liu contends that reification research should return to Marx's method. The article is organised in six parts. It treats reification in turn as an economic-philosophical, a social-philosophical and a cultural-philosophical category. It then discusses the balance between philosophy and economics, and traces Lukács's position to the intellectual climate of Dilthey, Simmel and Weber. Liu draws on Robert Albritton, Axel Honneth, Kafka, Alain Touraine and Lockmore, and compares Marx's 1844 Manuscripts with the 1857–58 manuscripts and Capital. Liu argues first that reification is in its basic sense an economic fact, the structural logic of capital. In this logic, people become bearers of functions and abstract social relations are "real abstractions". Marx, in Liu's reading, judged this stage historically progressive. Weber's rationalisation then neutralised the critical charge of Versachlichung, and Lukács added the themes of fragmentation, loss of totality and subjectivity. Second, Liu holds that Lukács equated reification with alienation on the basis of modern subject-philosophy. This is the "romantic" nostalgia Marx rejected, and Liu says Honneth repeats it. Third, Liu argues that Lukács claimed an interdisciplinary totality while excluding economics and law, so philosophy and economics fell out of balance. Liu reads this as closer to the 1844 Manuscripts than to Capital. Liu explains Lukács's stance as a worry about relativism and nihilism, which Liu calls understandable but methodologically open to question. Liu concludes that reification must be assessed from economic, social and cultural angles together. It is legitimate within reasonable limits, since it serves efficiency, shorter socially necessary labour time and basic fairness. It also carries the negative tendency of replacing human value and dignity with commodities and social-relation things, and it should not erode higher values. Liu calls for a return from Lukács to Marx's methodological stance, and for bridges between philosophy and economics and between the two cultures. Read the original if you study the Lukács–Marx relation, the reification–alienation distinction, or Chinese scholarly readings of Western Marxism.

Rediscovering the critical logic of reification in Marxism A conceptual-history study of Marx, Lukács and the Frankfurt School 马克思主义“物化”批判逻辑的再发现 Zhang Yixiu Zhang Yixiu asks why discussions of "reification" in Chinese and English-language Marxist scholarship have left the overall line of Marxist reification critique unclear. The article's answer is that the literature has repeatedly merged two German concepts with different meanings, Verdinglichung and Versachlichung. Working from the German originals, Zhang proposes rendering the first as "reification" and the second as "thingification" (事物化), and reconstructs how the logic of critique develops across Marx, Lukács and the Frankfurt School. The article has three main sections. The first clarifies terms, separating Vergegenständlichung (objectification) from the other two, and then reads Marx's use of the paired concepts in his critique of fetishism, tracing their background to Kant and Hegel. The second re-reads Lukács's History and Class Consciousness, comparing his usage with that of Weber, Simmel and Sombart. The third follows the Frankfurt School from Horkheimer and Adorno's Dialectic of Enlightenment to Adorno's Negative Dialectics, and closes with Hironaka Wataru's reading and Axel Honneth's Reification: A Recognition-Theoretical Study. In Zhang's reading, Marx uses Versachlichung for the essential level, where production relations appear as relations among things, and Verdinglichung for the phenomenal level, where those things appear as personified objects with their own properties. Lukács, Zhang argues, was the first to systematise reification as a theory. He also critiqued Versachlichung, which Weber saw as rationalisation, and thereby turned Weber's modernity theory against itself. His critique, however, is anchored in the un-reified human being and in proletarian class consciousness, not in production relations, which gives it a humanist cast. Horkheimer and Adorno, in this account, kept the two concepts apart and went further: they treated the objective mechanism of Versachlichung as more fundamental than reification and as unshakeable. Adorno ultimately declared Lukács's project of negating reification both impossible and mistaken. Zhang concludes that this reconstruction restores the thread of Marxist reification critique, which moves from Marx's relational method, through Lukács's philosophy of the subject, to Adorno's rejection of it. The article notes that Hironaka's critique of Lukács is on target even though his reading of Marx is not fully accurate. It also suggests that Honneth's work shows the two concepts still matter to the Western left. Read the original if you work on Lukács, the Frankfurt School or Marx's theory of fetishism and want a German-language terminological analysis of the reification/thingification distinction.

Correctly understanding the contemporary value of Marxism since the financial crisis From the perspective of foreign left-wing scholars 正确认识金融危机以来马克思主义的时代价值 Liu Mingming Liu asks whether Marxism can recover vitality in the twenty-first century. The article sets this against the collapse of the Soviet bloc, the most severe recession since the 1930s and the charge that Marxism is outdated. It draws on Western and other foreign left-wing scholars. Liu's answer is that the 2008 financial crisis renewed Marxism's relevance, and that the twenty-first century will be a century of Marxism. The article has four parts. The first surveys the revival of "Marx talk" after the crisis, citing Terry Eagleton, Stavros Tombazos, Marcello Musto, Eric Hobsbawm and the non-Marxist Ronald Dworkin. The second compares explanations of the crisis by Charles Dumenil-style underconsumption theorists and others, namely Charles Dumain's counterpart Charles Derber, David Schweickart and Andrew Kliman. The third examines how these scholars read Marx's vision of a future society, through Brian Jones, Ronaldo Munck, Alex Callinicos and Cleaver-style planners such as Kieran Allen. A final section draws four lessons. Liu argues that the crisis stayed within the reach of Marxist explanation. Derber and Schweickart stress overproduction relative to workers' purchasing power. Kliman stresses the falling rate of profit, and holds that regulation can only postpone crises, so that capitalism is becoming more crisis-prone. On the future society, the scholars reviewed defend Marx against the charge of utopianism. They also try to separate his ideas from the Soviet model, and some keep democratic planning, workers' self-management and state-run large firms at the core of alternatives. Liu notes that left scholars should stay wary of bourgeois praise that casts Marx as a saviour of capitalism. Liu concludes with four points. Opponents currently hold the upper hand in the debate. Some of Marx's views are time-bound, but his analysis of capitalism's secrets and his methods of social analysis are held to be lasting truths. Marxism stays current through theoretical innovation, both by Western left scholars and by socialist countries such as China, whose practice in ecology, poverty reduction, livelihoods and global responsibility is called the best contemporary manifesto for Marxism. Liu is optimistic about the twenty-first century, citing Marxism's academic penetration, lessons from socialist practice, a milder ideological climate and sharpening capitalist contradictions. Read the original if you want a compact overview of how foreign left-wing authors defended Marx's relevance after 2008, and how a Chinese scholar draws conclusions from them.

"New imperialism" and the contest over the sovereignty of "Empire" The ruling form of contemporary capitalism and a critical reflection “新帝国主义”与“帝国”的主权之争 Li Yin Wang Qingfeng What is the ruling form of contemporary capitalism? Li and Wang treat this as the epistemological precondition for any macro-level critique of capitalism. They compare two Western answers: "new imperialism", which they describe as a theory advanced by right-wing scholars to defend the imperialist rule of the United States and other developed states, and "Empire", the new order of global capitalist rule proposed by the radical left thinkers Michael Hardt and Antonio Negri. The authors conclude that both misjudge how capital's governing principle relates to national-state sovereignty. The article has three parts. The first traces imperialism from pre-capitalist empires such as Rome to "capital's imperialism" (late 1860s to late twentieth century), drawing on Lenin, Hobson, Ellen Meiksins Wood and David Harvey. The second reconstructs Hardt and Negri's Empire, including their account of immanent sovereignty, the US constitution, and the passage from disciplinary to control societies. The third compares the two forms and assesses them with the help of critics such as Samir Amin, John Bellamy Foster and Wood. The authors argue that new imperialism "sublates" imperialism: it keeps national-state sovereignty but adds an economic hegemony of monopoly capital. Wood and Harvey disagree on whether extra-economic political power is necessary to capital accumulation. In Li and Wang's view, new imperialism ignores the contradiction between capital's unlimited global expansion and the territorial limits of the nation-state, so it cannot cover capital's global rule. Empire, by contrast, discards imperialism, since capital's rules replace national sovereignty. Li and Wang say this absolutises the opposition and eliminates the very force that guarantees stability and predictability for capital, and that it cannot explain persistent global inequality, a point they support with Amin, Foster and Wood. Li and Wang propose that capital's governing principle and national-state sovereignty stand in an "absent" relation: indirect and concealed, neither fully opposed nor fully synchronised. Capital exploits through its own principle, while the nation-state supports it indirectly. They therefore describe contemporary capitalism's ruling form as a new globalised order of Empire-style rule maintained under the imperialist sovereignty of nation-states. Read the original if you study Western Marxist debates on imperialism (Wood, Harvey, Hardt and Negri, Amin) and want a Chinese critical assessment of them.

Accelerationism and digital platforms: Srnicek's critique of platform capitalism 加速主义与数字平台——斯尔尼塞克的平台资本主义批判 Dong Jinping Dong Jinping introduces Nick Srnicek, co-author with Alex Williams of the 2013 Manifesto for an Accelerationist Politics and author of Platform Capitalism (2016), as the founder of contemporary left accelerationism. The article argues that Srnicek's analysis of digital platforms can only be understood through accelerationism's reading of Marx. Dong also says that, although Srnicek writes about platforms in general, his account speaks most directly to present-day China. The article therefore treats his theory as a prism for Chinese reality, not as a doctrine to be reproduced faithfully. The article first sets out accelerationism's roots in Marx's 'fragment on machines' in the Grundrisse and in Italian autonomism. It contrasts this with Lukács and the Frankfurt School, whom Dong reads as critics of modernity itself. It then presents Srnicek's definition of a platform and his typology of five kinds: advertising, cloud, industrial, product (sharing) and lean platforms. Dong illustrates each with Western firms (Google, Amazon, Uber, Apple) and Chinese ones (Alibaba Cloud, Didi, Ant Short-term Rental, Tencent). The last section covers platform competition and the future of labour. Dong's central claim is that accelerationism shifts Marxist critique from the productive forces to the relations of production. Machines are neutral, and resisting them is likened to a mantis blocking a cart, so the left should push capitalism's machinery faster until its contradictions break it. For Srnicek, data is the raw material that platforms extract from user activity at almost no cost, much as oil is extracted. This displaces the attention economy of Pettman, and the 'immaterial labour' emphasis of Virno, Negri and Lazzarato. Platforms compete on three factors: data, key nodes (operating systems, AI, natural-language interfaces, acquired by building or by rhizome-like mergers) and users, who are locked in through ecosystems and rating systems. Dong adds that this departs from Marx's cost-price and profit-rate account of industrial competition, even though Marx's view of competition's essence is not overturned. Dong reports Srnicek's view that platform control will become more despotic. Platforms employ no workers and own no plant, so people become dependent users, a 'mobilization' of the proletariat into precarious, scattered, low-paid work that is hard to organise. Srnicek offers no clear answer on where this proletariat should go. He ends with a hope that public understanding of digital infrastructure can underpin a better future. Dong remarks that the 'new planned economy' claims of lean platforms deserve attention. Read the original if you want a Chinese-language account of Srnicek's platform typology, with Chinese platform examples, set against Western Marxism and autonomism.

Staying firm in the Four-sphere Confidence and strengthening national consensus 坚定“四个自信” 增强国家共识 Jiang Yingchun Writing in 2019, on the eve of the 70th anniversary of the People's Republic, Jiang Yingchun asks how the national consensus built around the Four-sphere Confidence (confidence in the path, theory, system and culture of socialism with Chinese characteristics) came about and how it can be strengthened. The author argues that this consensus is a "national treasure": the necessary conclusion of world socialist practice and of China's modern history, and an inexhaustible driving force for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The text is a short commentary in a Party theory journal. The article is organised in three parts, each stating how the consensus was formed: it was "fought for" (奋斗出来的), "arrived at through comparison" (比较出来的) and "sustained through persistence" (坚持出来的). The first part reviews the struggle against poverty, the Party's self-reform and the struggle against world hegemonism. The second sets out how socialism and capitalism should be compared. The third turns to ideological work. In the first part, Jiang presents China's elimination of absolute poverty as a miracle that rests on institutional, theoretical and cultural advantages, and contrasts the Party's capacity for self-correction with the Soviet Communist Party's loss of that capacity, which the author names as a key reason for its fall. The second part holds that comparison must start from concrete facts, from the "whole of the facts" and from the will of the people. Jiang criticises those who judge China by abstract notions of "democracy" or "constitutionalism", by isolated shortcomings, or by individual will. The author calls "wholesale Westernisation" idealist, and says only the people's will, which the Party serves, yields a correct judgement of socialism's superiority. Jiang concludes that consensus has to be sustained by persistently combining Marxism's basic principles with Chinese realities. The author calls for stronger Marxist propaganda and education, scientific criticism of erroneous social trends (liberalism, individualism, capitalism set against Marxism, collectivism and socialism) and for building the Four-sphere Confidence into philosophy and social science, moral education of the young, and economic, political, social, cultural and ecological goals. Read the original if you want an example of how Party theorists in 2019 framed ideological consensus and the comparison of socialism with capitalism.

Althusser's critique and transcendence of capitalist law 阿尔都塞对于资本主义法的批判和超越 Xu Kefei Xu Kefei takes up a gap in Louis Althusser's best-known essay on ideology and the state: law, which the 1970 essay leaves out although Althusser treats it as both part of the repressive state apparatus and an ideological function. Xu argues that Althusser's theories of law, ideology and the state form one whole, aimed at explaining and criticising the reproduction of capitalist relations of production. On this reading, the critique of capitalist law is meant to cut that chain of reproduction and free human beings from it. The article has four parts. It first clarifies the French terms le droit and la loi and Althusser's legal monism, which draws on Montesquieu and Hans Kelsen and rejects the split between natural and positive law. It then examines capitalist law and relations of production, then law and the state, and finally Althusser's idea of proletarian law and human emancipation. Xu draws mainly on On the Reproduction of Capitalism, with reference to Foucault, Poulantzas, Derrida and Laurent De Sutter's Althusser and Law. Xu reports three moves. First, capitalist law presents free and equal contracting parties modelled on commodity exchange, so exploitation never appears in the legal system. Law recognises property and the wage contract, treats the division of labour as merely technical, and spreads an "economism/humanism" that promises advancement to middle-ranking employees. Second, law and the state are one "legal-political" body. Law turns the surplus of ruling-class force into state power and constructs rights-bearing "subjects", and in doing so ensures the reproduction of exploitative relations. Third, Althusser, unlike Foucault, does not reject law. He opposes the theory that law will end after revolution and treats law as a structure that the proletariat can build by deliberate articulation. Xu concludes that emancipation requires revolution that changes relations of production, and that the legal "subject" must first be dismantled. Law would then be remade from within the people, releasing human puissance (capacity) rather than power. Xu adds that Althusser, as an academic philosopher, only sketched proletarian law and never had the chance to build it in practice. Read the original if you study Althusser, Marxist legal theory or the philosophical roots of the "subject" and rights, and want a systematic account that draws on the French sources.

Interpreting "On Contradiction" in the history of foreign Marxism 国外马克思主义发展史视域下的《矛盾论》解读 Wang Zhenmin How have Marxists outside China read Mao Zedong's "On Contradiction", and what should Chinese scholars take from those readings? Wang argues that the text has been an important resource for foreign Marxists. They have used it in debates over the scientific status of Marxism and over alternatives to capitalism. Wang holds that these readings are mostly shaped by Western intellectual agendas, and that they need critical assessment from the standpoint of Marxism in China. The article opens with four general features of foreign interpretations. It then traces four paradigms in chronological order: Louis Althusser's scientistic reading in the 1960s, Norman Levine's neo-Hegelian reading in the 1980s, Ian Hunt's "new dialectics" reading in the 1990s, and Slavoj Žižek's Lacanian reading in the 21st century. Wang closes with an evaluation of each paradigm and an account of why such readings overstep the text. On the general features, Wang argues that the readings are embedded in Western currents such as structuralism, existentialism and psychoanalysis. They tend to serve academic polemics rather than revolutionary practice, and they appear at moments of crisis in Marxism. They also use Hegel's or Marx's dialectic as an intermediary. In the case studies, Althusser is said to draw on the text for overdetermination, symptomatic reading and the theory of ideology. Levine is said to use it to argue for re-Hegelianizing Marxism, and Hunt to compare Mao's model with Marx's and Masaccia's. Žižek is said to criticise Mao's rejection of the negation of the negation. Wang judges that Althusser's reading is profound but over-interpreted and separates the text from "On Practice". Levine's overstates Hegel's role. Hunt misreads the transformation of contradictions as a simple swap of positions. Žižek's "negative dialectics" is, in Wang's view, a fundamental misreading. Wang attributes such "theoretical transgression" to Orientalist presuppositions, the imposition of Western concepts, differing historical contexts, the polysemy of texts, and neglect of Engels's dialectics. Wang concludes that the purpose of evaluating these readings is not only academic dialogue. The aim is to draw methodological and conceptual lessons from "over-interpretation" and misunderstanding. Wang calls for building a dialectics of Marxism with Chinese characteristics, in keeping with Mao's unfulfilled wish to rewrite "On Contradiction". Read the original if you want a critical Chinese survey of how Althusser, Levine, Hunt and Žižek used Mao's dialectics, with a full list of the Chinese translations of their works.

The Spanish Communist Party's adjustment of ideology and theoretical strategy, and its causes 西班牙共产党意识形态与理论战略的调整及其原因 Yu Haiqing Yu Haiqing asks why the Spanish Communist Party (PCE), long a pioneer of Eurocommunism and of early adaptation in the 1980s, has recently made what the author calls a near-subversive rethinking of its ideology and strategy. The article argues that the 20th Congress (2016–2017) marks a rupture with decades of increasingly moderate practice. In Yu's account, internal decline and a changed Spanish political environment together explain the turn. The article first traces the party's history since its founding in 1921 in three roughly thirty-year phases: Bolshevization under Comintern and Soviet influence, Eurocommunism from the 1950s to the early 1980s, and a post-Eurocommunist period that Yu sees as continuous with Eurocommunist ideas. It then examines the 20th Congress, held in two stages in April 2016 and December 2017, and finally analyses the causes. A short conclusion considers whether the turn can be put into practice and whether it can revive the party. Yu identifies three changes at the congress. The new statutes restore Marxism-Leninism and scientific socialism as the guiding ideology and bring back democratic centralism, a move defended by General Secretary Enrique Santiago. The party also hardened its stance on the European Union, calling for exit from the eurozone and a break with the EU. Finally, it sought broader popular unity, turning United Left into a social movement and widening electoral alliances such as the one with Podemos. On causes, Yu stresses that moderation failed to stop the shrinking of the party's social base, with membership falling to about 8,800, and that internal democracy produced factionalism and weakened ties to trade unions and social movements. Externally, the crisis fuelled Euroscepticism in Spain, and the rise of Podemos displaced the party as the main radical left force. Yu concludes that the turn is not a simple return to the old line but an attempt to build a new identity combining tradition with new issues such as feminism and environmentalism. Two questions remain open: whether the new line can be turned into action, given continuing dissent from defenders of Eurocommunism and a still factional party, and whether it can bring revival. Yu sees the PCE as one of several European communist parties adjusting their theory, and expects a hard road for all of them. Read the original if you study European communist parties, Eurocommunism or the Spanish radical left and want a Chinese academic account of the PCE's 2016–2017 turn.

Foreign left-wing scholars' critique of the capitalist world-system 国外左冀学者关于资本主义世界体系的批判 Zhou Miao Writing in 2019, Zhou Miao examines how left-wing scholars outside China, especially world-systems theorists, have criticised the capitalist world-system. The article starts from the claim that this system has become an instrument for plundering the resources and wealth of developing countries. Zhou argues that these critiques can help rebut Western accusations that China practises "neo-colonialism" through its investment and aid. They can also help explain a community with a shared future for mankind to international audiences. The article has two main parts. The first returns to Marx and Engels on world history, the world-system and the human community, and then to the proposal of a community with a shared future for mankind. The second part surveys the foreign left under three headings: predatory accumulation, an unequal international division of labour, and a structural system of hegemony. Thinkers cited include Giovanni Arrighi, François Chesnais, David Harvey, Samir Amin, Immanuel Wallerstein, William I. Robinson, Clemente Ruiz Durán and Theotonio dos Santos. Zhou reads the foreign scholars as continuing Marx and Engels's idea that capitalism created world history and subordinated backward countries to advanced ones. On accumulation, Zhou presents Arrighi and Chesnais on financialisation, and Harvey's "accumulation by dispossession", in which debt traps and crisis management transfer wealth from poor to rich countries. Amin's contrast between autocentric and dependent accumulation explains why underdevelopment persists. On the division of labour, Wallerstein's core, semi-periphery and periphery, and the value-chain analyses of Robinson and Ruiz Durán, show high-value stages kept in the core. Dos Santos's "industrial-technological dependence" is added. On hegemony, Amin and Wallerstein describe how the United States and the institutions it dominates impose their rules on others. Zhou concludes that predatory financialised accumulation led by private monopoly capital, together with dependent accumulation in backward countries, produces irreconcilable contradictions. In Zhou's account, these are the root cause of financial crises, sluggish growth and the new difficulties facing globalisation. Xi Jinping's call for a community with a shared future for mankind is presented as a continuation of Marx and Engels's thought on community and as a Chinese contribution to reforming global governance. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist overview of how world-systems and dependency theorists are being used to frame China's international discourse.

Revisiting Marx's ecological ethics 重温马克思生态伦理思想 Chen Aihua Marking the 200th anniversary of Marx's birth, Chen Aihua rereads Marx's Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 for the ecological ethics it contains. The author argues that these ideas matter for building ecological ethics today. They are also presented as relevant to green development, the construction of ecological civilization and a "Beautiful China". The short commentary, first published in China Social Sciences Today in 2018, is organised around three requirements for handling the human–nature relationship. These are attention to the inner connection between humans and nature, to labour (production) as life-engendering life, and to "construction in accordance with the laws of beauty". Chen weaves in passages from Xi Jinping, including the idea that humans and nature form a "community of life". In Chen's reading, Marx treats nature as humanity's "inorganic body", on which people depend materially and spiritually. Drawing on Marx's comparison of animal and human production, Chen holds that human production should unite the "measure of any species" with humanity's "inherent measure". Chen links today's ecological predicament to capital's logic, which pursues only growth, and cites John Bellamy Foster and Engels on one-sided production. The "laws of beauty" are then taken at three levels: the unity of naturalism and humanism, the joining of philosophy and natural science, and a proper relation between industry, people and nature. Chen concludes that industrial development must proceed alongside systematic ecological governance, the strictest environmental protection and green ways of production and life. The author presents this as the route to a Beautiful China and a contribution to global ecological security. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Chinese commentary ties the 1844 Manuscripts to Xi Jinping's ecological thought.

How to view China's economy and how to act: assessment and policy for 2019 中国经济怎么看、怎么干 Party Leadership Group of the National Development and Reform Commission Written in mid-2019 by the Party leadership group of the National Development and Reform Commission and published in Qiushi, this commentary asks how China's economic trend should be read and what should be done, given a more complex situation and US–China trade friction. Its answer is that the economy is running generally steadily, that the difficulties are mainly structural and institutional, and that the central leadership has a coherent set of policies. The authors argue that China can sustain its course if it concentrates on 'doing its own things well'. The text has three parts. The first reviews first-quarter and early-year data, including GDP growth of 6.4%, employment, industrial capacity utilisation, credit, high-tech investment, risk control, business-environment reforms and sentiment indicators. The second part names domestic and external problems and sets out the central government's overall approach. The third lists eight concrete measures, from macro policy to livelihood issues. The authors present the central approach as six principles: seeking progress while maintaining stability as the general tone; high-quality development as the fundamental requirement; supply-side structural reform as the main line; a strong domestic market as the focus; reform, opening up and innovation as the drive; and seizing new opportunities. They say high-quality development needs 'five strengthenings' covering indicators, policy, standards, statistics and evaluation. The eight measures include coordinated fiscal, monetary and employment policy, firm vitality, innovation, a stronger domestic market, the three tough battles (risk, poverty, pollution), balanced urban-rural and regional development, deeper reform and wider opening, and livelihood problems. The authors suggest that a large domestic market is a safeguard against external disturbance. The authors conclude that despite trade friction, China's economy has great potential and resilience, and its long-term positive trend will not change. They attribute recent results to the Party Central Committee's leadership and timely reform and opening-up policies. Read the original if you want an official statement of China's 2019 economic assessment and policy framework, with the data and measures the authorities cited.

The "two inevitables" remain the major trend of world development today “两个必然”仍然是当今世界发展的大趋势 Zhu Bingyuan Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts (Hongqi Wengao) and posted in June 2019, Zhu Bingyuan asks whether the "two inevitables" (the inevitable demise of capitalism and the inevitable victory of socialism) still describe the direction of the world. The author argues that they do. In Zhu's view, neither the collapse of the Soviet Union and the upheavals in Eastern Europe nor the recent changes in Western capitalism have altered the historical trend of socialism replacing capitalism. The article has three parts. The first sets out the theoretical content of the "two inevitables", from the Communist Manifesto through Capital to Marx and Engels's late writings on Russia. The second traces how the idea has developed in practice, from the First and Second Internationals and the October Revolution to the Chinese revolution and the post-1991 setback. The third looks at the present: financialisation and crisis in the West, and China's rise under socialism with Chinese characteristics. Zhu first argues that the "two inevitables" should be read together with Marx's "two never-wills" from the 1859 Preface, which stress that a social formation does not perish before its productive forces are fully developed. The author treats the latter as a supplement that makes the thesis more complete, and sees Marx's late remarks on the Russian commune and the "Caudine Forks" of capitalism as extending it to Eastern societies. Second, drawing on Deng Xiaoping, Zhu presents the Soviet collapse as a temporary reversal in a complex historical process. Third, the author describes Western capitalism as marked by financialisation, hollowing out of the real economy, polarisation, populism and recurring crises (the US government shutdown, Brexit and the "yellow vests" are cited), which Zhu calls systemic and structural, so that its basic contradictions are said to be intensifying. Zhu concludes that China's achievements under Communist Party leadership are the most persuasive proof of the "two inevitables", and that the proposal for a community with a shared future for mankind fits both the trend of the world and the varied conditions of individual countries. The article is a statement of the official line on the continuing validity of the classical thesis. Read the original if you want a compact example of how a Chinese Marxist scholar defends the "two inevitables" against the post-1991 setback and links them to Chinese modernization-era claims about China's global role.

Promoting quality and efficiency in the poverty alleviation campaign 推动脱贫攻坚提质增效 Wu Fenghua Wu Zhenlei Writing in 2019, as the campaign against poverty entered what Xi Jinping called its decisive stage, Wu Fenghua and Wu Zhenlei ask how poverty alleviation can be made more effective in its final two years. They argue that the remaining tasks concern the poorest of the poor and call for a shift from quantity to quality. They also present this shift as preparation for anti-poverty work after a moderately prosperous society is built. This is a short commentary in a Party-theory journal. It sets out six "upgrades" in turn: the focus on quality of poverty reduction, the range of people targeted, the source of motivation, the balance between development-oriented and social-security measures, the pattern of participating actors, and the way assessments are conducted. Each section is anchored in statements by Xi Jinping from 2015 to 2019. The authors first distinguish a static and a dynamic dimension of quality. The static one is securing "two assurances and three guarantees" for the rural poor by 2020. The dynamic one is preventing relapse into poverty through strict exit standards and "look-back" checks. They then argue for widening the targets to rural households slightly above the poverty line and to urban poor groups, including migrant workers. They also urge a move from externally driven to endogenous poverty alleviation, through motivation and education, and from state-led efforts to a "government–market–community–poor household" pattern under Party leadership. On the "five batches" approach, they hold that social-security support is rightly placed last. It should expand, but not blindly: exit mechanisms are needed, and those permanently unable to work should be supported throughout. On assessment, the authors say that evaluations have become formalistic and burdensome for localities. They propose treating assessment as a means rather than an end, simplifying procedures, and building long-term mechanisms. Counties that have shed the poverty label should keep policy, assistance and supervision stable, to avoid a "cliff effect". Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned account of how Chinese scholars framed the policy priorities of the final phase of the poverty campaign in 2019.

The historical foundations of cultural confidence in the new era 新时代文化自信的历史底蕴 Li Zheng Writing in 2019, on the eve of the 70th anniversary of the People's Republic, Li Zheng asks where the cultural confidence of the new era comes from. The article answers that it rests on three historical layers: China's excellent traditional culture, the revolutionary culture led by the Communist Party, and the advanced socialist culture of the PRC's first 70 years. Together, Li argues, these form the "historical foundations" of the Chinese nation's cultural confidence. The article is organised in three sections that follow this sequence. The first treats the 5,000-year inheritance of traditional "cultural genes", from the dragon totem through the Xia, Shang and Zhou dynasties, the Hundred Schools of thought, and the Han, Tang, Song, Yuan, Ming and Qing periods. The second covers the Party-led New Democratic revolution, the socialist revolution of 1949–1956, and 40 years of reform and opening up. The third turns to the "re-creation" of socialist culture in the new era. Li's central move is to treat traditional culture as necessary but insufficient. It supplies, in Li's words, the theoretical possibility of confidence, but confidence also needs practical support. Li finds that support in three "cornerstones": the New Democratic revolution, the socialist transformation, and reform and opening up. Each is said to have restored confidence that was shattered when imperialist powers broke the "Celestial Empire" in modern times. In the third section Li presents confidence in the path, theory and system of socialism with Chinese characteristics as the culmination. Here Li lists the line of theory from Mao Zedong Thought to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, and cites constitutional provisions on the Party's leadership and the basic economic system. Li concludes that the re-creation of socialist culture in the path, theory and institutions of socialism with Chinese characteristics has raised the Chinese nation's cultural consciousness and strengthened its confidence in path, theory, system and culture. Li also presents the Chinese system as offering developing countries a new option for modernization. Read the original if you want an example of how a Party-school-style article in 2019 derived cultural confidence from a three-part periodisation of tradition, revolution and socialist construction.

Guarding the cultural roots of the Chinese nation with a high degree of cultural confidence 以高度文化自信守护中华民族文化根脉 Liu Jiayi Writing in Qiushi in 2019, Liu Jiayi, then Party secretary of Shandong, reports on how the province has tried to act on Xi Jinping's instructions on traditional culture. Starting from Xi's 2013 visit to Qufu, Liu argues that cultural confidence is the deepest basis of confidence in China's path, theory and system, and that Shandong, as a cradle of traditional culture and revolutionary spirit, should become a model area for displaying it. The article is a provincial work report organised in four parts. It treats cultural confidence as rooted in excellent traditional culture, inherited through the "red gene", shown in efforts to nurture values and build character, and strengthened through exchange and mutual learning among civilizations. Each part pairs quotations from Xi with concrete Shandong programmes and figures. Liu's central claim is that Confucianism, as the main trunk of traditional culture, and the revolutionary culture embodied in the Yimeng spirit together supply the nation's cultural confidence. Shandong's measures include a Confucian scholars programme and the World Confucian Conference, research projects and online platforms on the Yimeng spirit, a provincial traditional-culture curriculum in primary, middle and high schools, and training bases for officials' political virtue. Liu also describes the Nishan World Civilizations Forum, Nishan Bookstores in 22 countries, Belt and Road cultural activities, and a 10-billion-yuan cultural industry fund. Liu says all this must proceed under Marxist guidance, against historical nihilism and against both clinging to the past and disparaging one's own culture. Liu concludes that Shandong will keep to the principle of creative transformation and innovative development of traditional culture, drawing on China's own past, absorbing foreign influences and facing the future. The aim is to contribute to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and a new chapter of advanced socialist culture. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially framed example of how a provincial Party leadership turned national cultural policy into programmes in education, cadre training, tourism, media and international outreach.

Poverty reduction with Chinese characteristics, 1978–2018 An analysis from the perspective of the poverty governance system and governance capacity framework 中国特色减贫实践：1978—2018 Ma Wenwu Li Zhongqiu Writing in 2019, Ma Wenwu and Li Zhongqiu ask how China's rural poverty reduction since reform and opening up (1978) can be explained and distilled into a distinctive path. They argue that the answer lies in a poverty governance system, built on a socialist value orientation, together with a steadily growing capacity to govern poverty. The article treats the achievement as a "world poverty reduction miracle" that needs theoretical as well as empirical summary. The authors first set out a general framework. A poverty governance system has three parts: an anti-poverty value orientation, an institutional system, and anti-poverty action, which can be direct or indirect. Governance capacity is the ability of government-led actors to confront and eliminate poverty, tested by actual changes in poverty. They then apply the framework to China's experience from 1978 to 2018, and end with poverty figures and proposals for the future. Ma and Li describe three features of China's value orientation: a people-centred character, an emergency-relief ("救急") emphasis on the worst-off people and regions, and a developmental character that adjusts goals over time. Their account of the institutions covers a leading-group structure under the State Council, rural reforms of land, grain circulation and household registration, four successive planning stages from 1982 to 2020, and supporting fiscal, social security, responsibility and mobilisation policies. In action, targeting narrowed from the whole countryside to counties, villages and households. The authors credit strict assessment and accountability, the "Six Precisions" and the "Five Batches" for how aid is delivered. They cite UN and World Bank figures and report that, on the current standard, the poverty rate fell from 97.5% in 1978 to 3.1% at the end of 2017. The authors conclude that success came from forming and improving a poverty governance system with Chinese characteristics. They expect that after 2020 the focus will shift to consolidating gains, preventing relapse, and moving from absolute to relative and multidimensional poverty. They propose three priorities: a national anti-poverty law, a governance system specific to ethnic-minority areas, and a more detailed poverty-standard system linked to economic development. Read the original if you want a systematic, officially aligned periodisation of China's anti-poverty policies and institutions from 1978 to 2018, with the policy documents and data that support it.

On the innovation and development of the thought of building a modern socialist great power 论社会主义现代化强国思想的创新和发展 Shi Yunxia Writing in 2019, the 70th anniversary of the People's Republic, Shi Yunxia asks what is new in the goal set at the 19th Party Congress (2017) of building China into a "prosperous, democratic, culturally advanced, harmonious and beautiful modern socialist great power" by the middle of this century. Shi argues that this "great power" thought continues earlier Party thinking while advancing it. In the author's view it is a major theoretical innovation in scientific socialism, joining the theoretical logic of scientific socialism with the historical logic of Chinese social development. The article is organised in five sections. Four trace how the thought deepens understanding of the stages of socialist development, the essential features of socialism, the scientific content of socialist modernization, and the Marxist theory of the state. These sections follow a line from Marx and Engels through Lenin, Stalin, Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin and Hu Jintao to Xi Jinping. A final section turns to reform and opening up as the road to national strength. On stages, Shi sets Lenin's and Mao's ideas of a less developed and a more developed socialism beside Deng's judgement that China is in the primary stage of socialism. Shi presents the 19th Congress timetable (basic modernization by 2035, a great power by mid-century) as the latest step in this line. On essence, Shi reads the five-part goal as extending Deng's formula of liberating and developing the productive forces toward common prosperity. On modernization, Shi argues that its deeper meaning is the modernization of the human being, linked to Marx's three stages of human development. On the state, Shi contends that Lenin's argument in The State and Revolution about the persistence of a state in the first phase of communism lays the ground for Xi's account of what kind of country China is, which the author says rebuts "China threat" theories. Shi concludes that reform and opening up is the "key move" for achieving the Two Centenary Goals and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The author reviews the Third Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2013) and Xi's 2018 speech marking forty years of reform, with its nine "musts", and holds that all of them come down to Party leadership. Read the original if you want a Party-theory account that places the modern socialist great power goal within a genealogy running from Marx and Lenin to Xi Jinping.

A community with a shared future for mankind offers Chinese wisdom for building a new world order 人类命运共同体为打造世界新秩序提供中国智慧 Wang Yonggui Huang Ting Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2019, Wang and Huang argue that Xi Jinping's idea of building a community with a shared future for mankind is a new concept that the Chinese Communist Party has contributed to contemporary humanity. In their account it expresses Chinese wisdom about world order and offers a Chinese approach to a more rational one. The short commentary has four sections. It treats the idea as a new concept of world order, then as a set of fundamental stipulations about that order. It next presents the idea as a new yardstick for assessing global governance, and finally as a goal for human interaction. The authors place the concept against the backdrop of "changes unseen in a century" and trace it to the Party's engagement in global governance since the 18th Party Congress (2012). They describe it as the product of combining traditional Chinese wisdom with Marxism. They argue that it rests on a scientific understanding of interdependence among nations and that its values aim at the happiness of all humanity, not at particular states. As a yardstick, they say, it means mutual respect, fairness and justice, and win-win cooperation. It rejects Cold War thinking and power politics, favours dialogue over confrontation and partnership over alliance, and holds that international rules should be written jointly by all countries. The authors link the goal to the classical Chinese ideal of "all under heaven being for the common good" and to Marx's "association of free individuals". They conclude that it points toward a world of lasting peace, universal security, common prosperity, openness and inclusiveness, and cleanliness and beauty. They add that it will take generations to achieve. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated scholars in 2019 presented this concept as a synthesis of Chinese tradition and Marxism.

Humanism or structuralism? On Adam Schaff's critique of Althusser's structuralist Marxism 人道主义还是结构主义？——评沙夫对阿尔都塞结构主义马克思主义的批判 Yan Yan Yan Yan revisits the dispute between the Polish humanist Marxist Adam Schaff and the French structuralist Louis Althusser. Their books of 1965 (Schaff's Marxism and the Human Individual, Althusser's For Marx) took opposite positions on humanism but did not engage directly. In the 1970s Schaff mounted a full critique in Structuralism and Marxism, calling Althusser's project a pseudo-Marxism and pseudo-structuralism. Yan treats this as a debate inside Marxism and asks who is right. The answer is mixed: Schaff identifies real conceptual confusions, but his critique is over-emotional and often unfair. The article is organised around four contested themes, followed by a short assessment. These are the opposition between ideology and science; anti-empiricism versus idealism; anti-historicism versus what Schaff calls Eleaticism; and anti-humanism. Yan reconstructs Althusser's positions, then Schaff's replies, and tests both against Marx and Engels. Sources include Althusser's For Marx and Reading Capital, Schaff's History and Truth, and Karl Mannheim's theory of ideology. Yan reports that Schaff accuses Althusser of treating ideology as false consciousness and so, like Mannheim, sliding into relativism. Schaff defines ideology as a set of views on social goals determined by class interest, and holds that the knowledge of a rising class can be scientific. Yan finds Schaff unfair here, since Althusser had widened the concept, though Althusser's vagueness is blamed. On empiricism, Schaff argues that Althusser attacks a private version of the term, confuses empiricism with positivism and mechanical reflection theory, and drops reflection theory itself. His 'two objects' theory is judged idealist and Kantian. On humanism, Schaff argues that Althusser redefines 'historicism' and 'humanism' and then rejects them. For Schaff, social relations are formed by people and should come under their control, and Marx's mature categories rest on a humanist standpoint. Yan concludes that Schaff is most persuasive on Althusser's loose and shifting use of terms, which created theoretical confusion. Yan also faults Schaff for passing over Althusser's strengths. These include the critique of Hegel's continuous historical time, the insistence that capitalist relations are invisible, and the inquiry into Marx's problematic, though Yan reserves judgment on the 'epistemological break'. Yan holds that humanism and structuralism are not mutually exclusive in Marx, and quotes Schaff that structural analysis follows from Marxist method. The dispute will continue within Marxism. Read the original if you study Althusser, Schaff or the humanism–structuralism debate and want a Chinese scholar's balanced assessment.

Key focal points for running university ideological and political theory courses well 办好高校思想政治理论课的着力点 Xu Rong Writing in 2019, Xu Rong takes up Xi Jinping's call, made at the 18 March symposium for teachers of school ideological and political theory courses, to run these courses well by answering the questions of whom to train, how to train them and for whom. Xu acknowledges that university courses have achieved notable results but sees unresolved problems in classroom effectiveness, the freshness of teaching materials and the make-up of the teaching staff. The article argues that success depends on three things: a clear mission, a workable path and a new overall pattern of course development. The piece is organised in three parts. The first sets out the mission of 'forging souls and nurturing people'. The second treats 'upholding fundamental principles while innovating' as the necessary path, and walks through Xi's 'eight unities' for teaching reform. The third discusses how to build a new pattern for the courses, covering the social atmosphere around them, the course system, and institutions and mechanisms. Xu holds that the courses should be grounded in the theoretical system of socialism with Chinese characteristics and in Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. They should answer students' real questions while taking a firm stand, and they need teachers who themselves hold firm convictions. Under the 'eight unities', Xu pairs the political with the academic, values with knowledge, and theory with practice. The pairings also include unity with diversity, teacher guidance with student agency, and explicit with implicit education. Xu defends 'indoctrination' (guànshū) as a necessary method, since scientific theory cannot arise spontaneously in students' minds, but says it must not become cramming and must be paired with inspiring methods. The article also calls for firm criticism of liberalism, individualism, historical nihilism, 'universal values' and 'constitutional democracy'. On the new pattern, Xu contends that Party committees at every level must stop treating the courses as important in words but secondary in practice, and must end the squeezing of class hours and the disdain for teachers. Xu lists open questions about course systems, textbooks, staff, the relation between teaching and the discipline of Marxist theory, and evaluation. Xu notes uneven implementation of central rules, including places that cannot pay basic teaching fees, and calls for rule-of-law thinking and a 'ideological-political plus' approach that integrates the courses with all-round education. Read the original if you want to see how a 2019 Party-journal article translates Xi Jinping's instructions on ideological and political courses into a programme for university practice.

The fundamental guide to running ideological and political theory courses well in the new era 新时代办好思想政治理论课的根本指南 Sun Lanying This commentary, first published in Red Flag Manuscripts (Hongqi Wengao) in 2019, interprets Xi Jinping's speech at the symposium for teachers of school ideological and political theory courses. Sun Lanying argues that the speech sets out the basic guidance for running these courses well in the new era. The courses are presented as the key curriculum for carrying out the fundamental task of fostering virtue through education and for training a new generation able to shoulder national rejuvenation. The article has three parts. The first explains why the courses are central to fostering virtue through education. The second takes up the claim that the key to the courses lies in teachers. The third deals with reform of the courses, which Sun grounds in Xi's requirements for teachers and in his "eight unities". Sun describes universities as a front line of ideological work and the courses as the main battlefield for spreading Marxist theory and safeguarding national ideological security. In Sun's account, young students are a main target of Western hostile forces' efforts at "Westernisation" and division, so the courses must consolidate Marxism's guiding position, expose the nature of Western "universal values" and resist erroneous trends of thought. Teachers must meet Xi's "six requirements": strong politics, deep feelings for the country, innovative thinking, broad vision, strict self-discipline and upright character. For reform, Sun lists eight pairs to be unified: political and academic, value and knowledge, constructive and critical, theoretical and practical, unity and diversity, leading role and student agency, indoctrination and inspiration, explicit and implicit education. The first group is meant to make the courses persuasive through reasoned argument. The second is meant to make them engaging and substantive. Sun concludes that reform needs strategic thinking and top-level design. The article also calls for mining ideological and political resources in other courses so that all teaching works in the same direction. It proposes using new media under an "Internet Plus" approach, and it cites online courses (MOOCs) and micro-courses as signs of reform momentum. Read the original if you want a compact example of how official commentary in 2019 explained the guiding principles for ideological and political education in universities, including the "six requirements" and "eight unities".

The historical significance and contemporary value of the May Fourth Movement 五四运动的历史意义和时代价值 Dong Xuewen Writing for the 100th anniversary of the May Fourth Movement (1919), Dong Xuewen asks what the movement meant historically and what value it holds today. The author argues that its decisive achievement was to open the way for Marxism in China and so move the anti-imperialist, anti-feudal democratic revolution into a new stage. On this basis Dong presents the May Fourth spirit as one that young people in the new era should inherit in pursuing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The article is a commentary in six numbered sections, resting heavily on Mao Zedong's assessments in Selected Works vol. 2 and on speeches by Xi Jinping. It covers the movement's character and its link to the October Revolution, its place in modern Chinese intellectual history, the division between the periods before and after 1919 on the cultural front, the cultural debates of the time, and lessons for contemporary youth. Figures discussed include Li Dazhao, Chen Duxiu, Qu Qiubai, Hu Shih, Fu Sinian, Liang Qichao and Zhang Junmai. Dong's central claim is that earlier movements, from the Sino-Japanese War of 1894–95 to the 1911 Revolution, failed because they lacked an advanced worldview. In this account the May Fourth Movement differed because young intellectuals turned to Marxism, took it to workers and prepared the ground for the founding of the Communist Party in 1921. Dong adds that cultural choices follow economic and social change, so wholesale Westernisation and eclectic schemes failed to fit China's conditions. Only the early communists, Dong says, offered a workable direction. The common description of the May Fourth spirit as 'science and democracy', the author holds, hides sharp differences: only Li Dazhao and others gave these ideas real substance through historical materialism and socialist democracy. Dong concludes that the Party's founding in 1921, the People's Republic in 1949 and reform and opening up in 1978 all show the victory of Marxism in China and confirm that modern Chinese culture can be led only by proletarian, communist thought. Drawing on Xi Jinping, the author calls for strengthening Marxist belief and the ability to apply Marxism to current problems, and urges young people to carry on the tradition of 'permanent struggle' under Party leadership. Read the original if you want to see how a 2019 official-journal commentary ties the May Fourth legacy to Marxism, the Party's founding and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation.

Report on the development of the international communist movement (2018–2019) The "Yellow Book" of the international communist movement 国际共产主义运动发展报告（2018~2019） International Communist Movement Yellow Book (collective) This is a press-release-style digest of the annual "Yellow Book" on the international communist movement, published on 1 June 2019 by the Academy of Marxism of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences and Social Sciences Academic Press. The report argues that in 2018 the movement was stirred by interactions between history and reality, theory and practice, and China and the world. It expects the same trends to continue in 2019. The digest follows seven headline findings. They cover US–China technological rivalry and the prospect of a "new Cold War"; the movement's progress in 2018 in ruling and non-ruling parties; socialism with Chinese characteristics as a force in the revival of world socialism; commemorations of the Communist Manifesto and Marx's 200th birthday; flaws in global governance; cadre-building in the Communist Party of Vietnam; and self-reliance in North Korea. The report argues that high technology and artificial intelligence are changing how parties operate and sharpening the contest between capitalism and socialism. It describes Western containment of China as widening from trade into science, education, culture and ideology. It still expects most countries to pursue dual-track diplomacy, so the old Cold War pattern would not return. It says global governance, dominated by developed countries, is flawed by unequal voting power, weak binding force, unfair outcomes and a lack of effective solutions. It cites US wealth concentration (the top 1 per cent holding 38.6 per cent in 2016) and rising Gini coefficients in the EU. It attributes these problems to the capitalist system itself. On Vietnam, it holds that the quality of strategic-level cadres decides socialism's fate. It points to the Seventh Plenum of the 12th Central Committee, which adopted cadre resolutions ahead of the 13th Congress expected in 2021. On North Korea, it predicts that self-reliance will be the basic principle of reform and opening, though it says the eventual path remains uncertain. The report anticipates that the 70th anniversary of the People's Republic, the centenary of the May Fourth Movement and the centenary of the Third International will prompt parties to review historical lessons and strengthen cooperation. It cites foreign communists and scholars who praise China's achievements, and Western communists who call the Manifesto an "X-ray" of contemporary capitalism. It also says Vietnam's cadre-building offers lessons for China. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese state-affiliated researchers assessed world socialism, US–China rivalry and the ruling parties of Vietnam and North Korea at the end of the 2010s.

The Communist Manifesto and the original aspiration and mission of Chinese communists 《共产党宣言》与中国共产党人的初心和使命 Huang Rongsheng Writing in 2019, Huang Rongsheng asks how the Communist Manifesto of 1848 bears on the "original aspiration and mission" of Chinese communists. The article argues that the Manifesto supplies the theoretical foundation and the guide to action for that aspiration and mission, and that its value remains undiminished in the new era of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The article is organised in four sections. The first presents the Manifesto as the founding text of Marxism and of Marxist parties, and recounts how Lenin, Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping developed or applied it. The second traces how it guided the Party through revolution, construction and reform. The third examines the commitment to seek happiness for "the vast majority". The fourth turns to the Party's responsibility to pursue the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. In the core of the argument, Huang reads specific Manifesto propositions as having been put into practice by the Party. The historical-materialist claim that economic structure underlies political history is linked to the Party's choice of an "encircle the cities from the countryside" path, to the basic economic system of public ownership as the mainstay, and to the new development philosophy since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Its call for a decisive break with traditional ideas is tied to the Party's campaigns of ideological education, and its description of communists as the most resolute section of workers' parties is tied to Party-building and the work against corruption. The Manifesto's declaration that the proletarian movement is that of the immense majority is presented as the origin of the Party's people-centred stance and of its progress from "standing up" to "becoming prosperous" to "becoming strong". Huang concludes that the Party's pledge to seek happiness for the Chinese people and rejuvenation for the Chinese nation inherits and develops the Manifesto's original aspiration. The article calls on present-day communists to keep to the communist ideal, the common ideal of socialism with Chinese characteristics and the Chinese Dream, and to stay true to their founding purpose. Read the original if you want an example of how Party-aligned scholarship in 2019 tied the Manifesto to the Party's "original aspiration and mission" theme.

The precious spiritual legacy of the May Fourth Movement and its contemporary inheritance 五四运动的宝贵精神财富及其当代传承 Published in Guangming Daily on the eve of the movement's centenary, this commentary asks what the May Fourth Movement of 1919 left as a spiritual legacy and how that legacy should be carried forward today. Taking its cue from Xi Jinping's call to study the movement within a "big view of history", the author argues that the May Fourth spirit of patriotism, progress, democracy and science is closely tied to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and must be inherited in the new era. The piece is organised in three sections and adopts a history-of-ideas perspective. The first treats the movement as the outcome of modern China's efforts to save the nation and traces patriotism from the Paris Peace Conference to later commemorations. The second places the movement within a sequence of attempts to learn from the West and shows how it led to Marxism. The third turns to present-day implications. In the author's account, patriotism is the first element of the May Fourth spirit. The diplomatic defeat at Paris, in which Shandong rights were handed to Japan, ended illusions about Western powers and moved advanced Chinese towards the new-democratic revolution. The author argues that the New Culture Movement had not completed the task of enlightenment, because its thinkers still trusted the victorious powers and relied on Enlightenment-era Western theory. Earlier efforts, from Lin Zexu to Sun Yat-sen, followed a logic of learning technology, theory and institutions from the West but found no workable revolutionary programme. The October Revolution brought Marxism-Leninism, and the author calls the finding of Marxism the greatest result of the movement's intellectual emancipation, preparing the ground for the founding of the Communist Party. For the new era, the author calls for patriotism guided by Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, unwavering adherence to Marxism and Party leadership, and a people-centred approach to development. Young people, the author says, need political guidance to follow the Party and to link personal ideals to the Chinese Dream of national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want an example of how a 2019 official-academic text ties the May Fourth legacy to Party narrative and youth work.

Carrying forward the May Fourth spirit and creating new miracles 传承五四精神 再创伟大奇迹 Gao Xiang Writing in 2019, the centenary of the May Fourth Movement and the 70th anniversary of the People's Republic, Gao Xiang argues that a century of Chinese history offers lessons for starting a still more glorious course and creating still greater achievements. The commentary holds that the May Fourth spirit remains vital and that the Communist Party's leadership is the thread running through the period. The piece has three parts. It first discusses the content of the May Fourth spirit, then identifies three landmark events since 1919, and finally draws lessons from the hundred years. Gao defines the May Fourth spirit as patriotism, progress, democracy and science, and says it has taken on new meaning in pursuit of the Chinese Dream. The three events are the founding of the Party (1921), the founding of the People's Republic (1949), and reform and opening up with socialism with Chinese characteristics. Gao describes the last as a leap from standing up to becoming prosperous and then strong, and calls the new era a golden age for the nation. From this history the author draws three conclusions: Party leadership is the fundamental political guarantee of national rejuvenation; Sinicised Marxism is its scientific guide; and rejuvenation requires struggle and innovation. Gao calls for the Party's ideological line, bold exploration and rejection of dogmatism, since China's modernization has no textbook to follow. The author presents Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era as twenty-first-century Marxism that will guide the building of a modern socialist country. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a senior CASS leader framed the May Fourth centenary in official terms.

The historical significance and contemporary value of the May Fourth Movement 五四运动的历史意义和时代价值 Dong Xuewen Marking the centenary of the May Fourth Movement in 2019, Dong Xuewen asks what the movement meant historically and what value it holds for today's Chinese youth. The article, first published in Red Flag Manuscripts (Hongqi Wengao), argues that the movement's decisive achievement was to open the door to Marxism in China, and that this, more than any other factor, gave it a pioneering place in modern Chinese intellectual history. Dong organises the essay in six short sections. It begins with Mao Zedong's and Xi Jinping's characterisations of the movement as an anti-imperialist, anti-feudal patriotic movement. It then discusses its significance for Chinese thought and the founding of the Communist Party, and compares the periods before and after 1919 in Mao's account of the cultural front. A section on the cultural debates of the era is followed by a discussion of what "science" and "democracy" meant, and a closing section addresses the lessons for young people in the new era. Dong's central claim is that earlier struggles, from the Sino-Japanese War of 1894–95 to the 1911 Revolution, failed because they lacked an advanced worldview. In this account, the May Fourth Movement differed because intellectuals such as Li Dazhao, Chen Duxiu and Qu Qiubai turned to Marxism and took it to the workers, preparing the ground for the Party's founding in 1921. Dong holds that conservatives, advocates of wholesale Westernisation such as Hu Shi, and eclectics such as Liang Qichao all chose cultural directions that did not match China's social and economic trends. Only the early communists, in this reading, offered a viable blueprint. The author adds that the common shorthand of "science and democracy" hides sharp disagreements. In Dong's view, only the early communists gave these slogans real substance, through historical materialism and socialist democracy. Dong concludes that the founding of the Party, the People's Republic and reform and opening up all show the victory of Marxism in China. The author invokes Xi Jinping's call for young people to carry on the May Fourth spirit under Party leadership and Mao's phrase "permanent struggle" as the youth movement's tradition. Dong presents the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation as demanding greater effort, guided by Marxist belief. Read the original if you want an example of how the May Fourth Movement was interpreted in official Party commentary on its 2019 centenary, with extensive quotation from Mao and Xi.

Re-examining the "crisis of measure" in cognitive capitalism 重审认知资本主义语境中的“度量危机”问题 Sun Liang Writing in 2018, Sun Liang takes up a claim shared by Michael Hardt, Antonio Negri and theorists of cognitive capitalism: that immaterial and biopolitical labour cannot be measured by labour time, so Marx's labour theory of value has lapsed and a way opens toward a world of common wealth. Sun calls this the "crisis of measure". The article argues that it is a false problem, resting on a misreading of what Marx's value theory is about. The article first sets out the cognitive-capitalist position. It distinguishes mercantile, industrial and cognitive capitalism, treats post-operaismo (post-workerism) and cognitive capitalism as near-identical, and outlines two forms of immaterial labour: intellectual or linguistic labour and affective labour. It draws on Hardt, Negri, Carlo Vercellone, Christian Fuchs and Heesang Jeon.
