It then turns to Marx's value-form analysis and the passages on formal and real subsumption of labour under capital, and ends with the political stakes of the "common". Sun's central move is that the theorists treat value as a substance, a measurable quantity of labour time, and so leave Marx's analysis of value form untouched. Following Heesang Jeon, Frederick Harry Pitts and Slavoj Žižek, Sun holds that abstract labour is a historical, social category, not an expenditure of physical energy. For Marx, the question is why labour takes the form of value at all, and quantity appears only as price. Even critics and defenders who argue over quantification therefore share the same mistake, and the cognitive-capitalist view stays within classical political economy. Second, Sun argues that digital and immaterial labour is use-value production brought under capital through real subsumption and the capitalist application of general intellect. It is not "abstract labour" in Marx's sense. Citing Marx on machinery and on capital as a "living contradiction", Sun holds that general intellect could free time only if the capitalist mode of production were transformed. Cognitive capitalism, in this reading, ignores private ownership of the means of production and overstates the subject pole of labour against capital. Read the original if you want a Marxist rebuttal of Hardt and Negri's claim that immaterial labour defeats value theory, built on value-form analysis and the subsumption texts.

What the Russian reversal in assessments of Stalin suggests 俄罗斯人对斯大林评价反转的启示 Wu Enyuan Writing in Global Times on 9 May 2019, Russia's Victory Day, Wu Enyuan asks why Russian opinion of Stalin has turned so positive and what China should learn from it. Wu argues that the shift is not sudden but inevitable, and that its lesson is a warning against historical nihilism. The short commentary begins with the 2019 survey by the Levada Centre, which Wu says found more than 70 per cent of Russians viewing Stalin's historical role positively and under 19 per cent negatively. Wu describes the quota-sample method (1,638 respondents in 137 localities) to show that it was not a casual poll. The article then sets out three causes and closes with implications. Wu names three causes. First, the aftermath of the Soviet collapse, with a sluggish economy, inequality and confrontation with the West, leads people to link Stalin with stability and international standing. Second, official attitudes have changed: Putin named the Soviet collapse as the event he would most want to change and rejected the 'demonization' of Stalin, and the 2017 state history textbook credits Stalin-era industrialization and victory over fascism while noting breaches of legality. Third, the government draws on Soviet methods, such as a possible revived military-political directorate, a pioneer-style youth organisation and a strong defence industry. Wu concludes that official bodies, mainstream media and the public in Russia now broadly acknowledge Stalin's positive role, overturning the verdict dominant since the 20th Congress of the Soviet Communist Party and especially under Gorbachev. Wu holds that deliberately distorting history and wholly negating a major figure, that is, historical nihilism, confuses thinking and can break up a party and a state, and calls this a warning for China. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Chinese academics used the Russian Stalin debate to argue against historical nihilism.

Overseas scholars on the experience of 70 years of development in New China 海外学者论新中国70年发展经验 Sun Jian Writing in 2019, on the eve of the 70th anniversary of the People's Republic, Sun surveys how foreign academics explain the question "why China can". The article is a review of overseas scholarship rather than an original study. Sun notes that the positions, methods and conclusions of these works are varied and complex, but argues that they broadly affirm China's achievements and that a "China experience" as seen from abroad can be distilled from them. The review covers economists, sociologists and China specialists in the United States, Britain, Australia, India, Germany, France and Egypt, as well as the former German chancellor Helmut Schmidt. Examples include Ross Garnaut, Thomas Rawski, Andrew Walder, Thomas Heberer, Dwight Perkins, Barry Naughton, Martin Jacques and Elizabeth Perry. It is organised in three parts: development grounded in national conditions and traditional culture; economic construction as the centre, backed by political construction; and the leading role of the Communist Party of China and a people-centred orientation. In the first part, Sun reports scholars who credit China's success to policies fitted to its own conditions, including decentralisation, a gradual shift from collective to household farming, and a "socialist market economy". They describe the Soviet failure as dogmatic Marxism, and trace China's core values to Confucian roots. In the second part, scholars stress the state's role in guiding the market, the growth of non-state firms and township enterprises, political stability, and the combination of domestic reform with opening up. The third part presents overseas views that Party leadership gave policy continuity through field investigation and "adaptive mobilization", anti-corruption work and the mass line. These scholars also point to the people's congress system, rural land reform and poverty reduction, and environmental policy as evidence of people-centred development. Sun concludes that overseas scholars, whatever their stance, identify a distinctive set of factors behind China's development: starting from national conditions, economic construction under political guidance, and Party leadership tied to popular welfare. The article presents these as outside confirmation of China's own account of its path. Read the original if you want a catalogue of foreign scholars and works that are cited in support of the official narrative of 70 years of development, or a starting list of sources to check.

Mao Zedong's foundational contributions to New China's economic construction in 1949 1949年毛泽东对新中国经济建设的几个奠基性贡献 Yang Dongquan Written for the 70th anniversary of the People's Republic in 2019, this article asks what laid the foundations for China's later economic development. Yang Dongquan answers that, in 1949, Mao Zedong made several foundational contributions to New China's economic construction, and that anyone studying the "Chinese path" or "Chinese model" cannot bypass them. The article draws on Mao's 1949 telegrams, speeches, instructions and drafts, arranged in three parts. The first covers the unified domestic environment: the New Year message "Carry the Revolution Through to the End", the exposure of the Guomintang's "peace talks", the failed April negotiations and the crossing of the Yangtze. The second covers the political institutions: the political consultation system, the people's congress system and regional autonomy for ethnic minorities. The third covers the shift of the Party's work focus to cities and to economic construction, with policies on city takeover, the national bourgeoisie, North–South trade links and land reform. Yang argues that rejecting a "divide the country at the Yangtze" settlement preserved a unified territory of 9.6 million square kilometres, with its resources, population and market. Without it, in the author's view, rival regimes would have wasted resources on arms races and been open to foreign manipulation. The political institutions, Yang says, were shown by decades of experience to be suited to China and to protect and promote economic growth. The author also reads Mao's 1949 instructions as an early statement of "taking economic construction as the centre". Examples include the March 1949 report to the Second Plenum of the 7th Central Committee, which moved the focus from countryside to city, and the telegram saying that future work centres on construction. Further examples are limiting war damage to cities, keeping existing staff employed in newly taken cities, the "four-sided and eight-directional" policy, protecting national industry and commerce, and cautious land reform that protected rich peasants. Yang concludes that these measures gave the new state a unified environment, reliable institutions, preserved urban capital and a good start to economic recovery. By 1953, the author says, land reform had given over 300 million peasants some 700 million mu of land. Yang presents these 1949 decisions as the origin of later achievements and as an explanation for China's development. Read the original if you want a Party-historian's account, based on Mao's 1949 documents, of how the PRC's early economic policy is traced back to its founding year.

Exploring an organised rural governance strategy based on China's national conditions Rethinking Mao Zedong's thought and practice of rural governance 探索基于中国国情的组织化农治战略 Xu Junzhong Writing in 2019, as rural revitalization became a national strategy, Xu Junzhong asks how Mao Zedong's rural governance (nongzhi) should be reassessed after decades of reform-era criticism. The article argues that, given China's many people, scarce land and backward farming conditions, Mao's strategy of 'organising the peasants' was the only workable path. Xu holds that the difficulties of the collective period came from specific policy constraints, not from organisation as such. The article follows Mao's strategy chronologically. It begins with the Yan'an model of the 1940s and Mao's pre-1949 statements on cooperation, then covers the cooperativisation wave of the mid-1950s through the compilation 'The Socialist Upsurge in China's Countryside' and the 1956–67 National Programme for Agricultural Development. It then treats the people's communes, and Mao's efforts in the 1960s and 1970s to defend commune and brigade enterprises. Later sections draw out five features of Mao's approach and answer current criticisms. Xu argues that Mao treated 'many people, little land' as a resource to be mobilised through cooperation, intensive farming and diversified activity, including local industry. Mao's aim was in-situ industrialisation and urbanisation that would avoid both the Soviet collective farm and the Western path of rural decline. The five features Xu identifies are: governance subordinated to national strategy; organisation as the foundation; combining agriculture and industry; the peasants as the main actors; and peasant emancipation and improved living standards as the core value. Against the liberal 'right of exit' critique, Xu says peasants holding about three mu (roughly 0.2 hectares) each could not stand alone as independent producers, so such a right would leave them helpless. The real causes of the collective period's difficulties, in Xu's account, were the 1962 ban on commune enterprises and the 'de-commercialisation' produced by state monopoly purchase and marketing. Xu concludes that Mao's strategy was an exploratory, trial-and-error effort whose flaws should be corrected as repair rather than dismantling. Citing Xi Jinping, Xu argues that today's smallholders still cannot join modern industrial chains or markets because they lack organisation. Effective rural governance in the new era, Xu says, requires combining organisation with marketisation. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-based defence of Mao-era rural collectivism and its relevance to rural revitalization debates.

Schools of socialism in the May Fourth period 五四时期的社会主义流派 Mei Le Mei Le asks how Marxism came to overtake other currents and become the dominant influence on Chinese thinkers after the May Fourth New Culture Movement. The short commentary argues that the answer lies largely in how rival socialisms circulated and competed in the press and in public debate during that period. The article surveys the schools of socialism then circulating: Marxism, Guild Socialism, syndicalism, the New Village movement, cooperativism, pan-labourism, anarchism and state socialism. It then looks at two famous controversies, the 1919 debate on "problems and isms" and the socialism debate that began in 1920. Mei notes that most schools were short-lived; besides Marxism, only Guild Socialism and anarchism had wide influence. Contemporaries, including Chen Duxiu and Zhang Dongsun, counted anarchism and state socialism as socialism, and understanding of the term was both vague and over-extended; Qu Qiubai likened it to looking at dawn mist through a gauze window. Even so, Mei says many, Marxists included, already saw Marxism as "scientific socialism". In the "problems and isms" exchange between Hu Shi and Li Dazhao, Mei argues, the limits of studying only "problems" became clear, and talk of "isms" grew. In the larger debate between Chen Duxiu and Zhang Dongsun, who openly backed Guild Socialism, the author sees the first real contest between schools. Chen's side held that capitalism's fall and socialism's rise were the world trend, and questions such as whether a capitalist stage could be skipped pushed Marxists to think in terms of national conditions. Mei concludes that these controversies drew more people to socialism and turned it into a wave of enthusiasm, and that they helped Marxism's growing influence. The author holds that revisiting this history remains necessary. Read the original if you want a brief overview of the socialist currents and debates of 1919–1920 as presented in a Party newspaper.

How to teach ideological and political theory courses well in universities 怎样才能上好高校思想政治理论课 Liu Jianjun Writing in Qiushi in 2019, after Xi Jinping chaired a symposium for teachers of school ideological and political theory courses on 18 March, Liu Jianjun asks three linked questions: why these courses matter, why they are hard to teach, and how they can be taught well. Liu argues that the courses are of special importance and special difficulty, but that the conditions now exist for teaching them well, provided teachers make efforts in several areas. The commentary has three parts. The first sets out the importance of the courses in universities. The second lists the difficulties of teaching them. The third names the favourable conditions and then sets out four directions of effort for teachers, drawing throughout on Xi's speech at the symposium, including his principle of the "eight unifications". On importance, Liu holds that the courses express the socialist character of Chinese universities, are the key courses for fulfilling the fundamental task of fostering virtue through education, and are the main channel and main battleground of students' ideological and political education. On difficulty, Liu points to the political character of the courses, which leaves a psychological distance from students, and to their theoretical depth. Liu adds the gap between theory and reality, the breadth of content and the speed at which it changes, and the aim of shaping values and ideals, which goes beyond imparting knowledge. Liu cautions that responsibility for students' ideals and convictions cannot be left to these courses alone. Liu lists six favourable conditions, among them the Party and state's high priority, recent theoretical achievements in adapting Marxism to Chinese conditions, the achievements of socialism with Chinese characteristics, and a dependable teaching corps. Liu then calls on teachers to strengthen their convictions and teach with confidence, and to raise their theoretical level through research serving teaching. Liu also asks them to convert academic, political and everyday language into effective classroom discourse, and to try varied methods such as thematic, interactive and multimedia teaching. Read the original if you want a concise Party-journal statement of how the official case for ideological and political courses, and the expectations placed on their teachers, were presented after the 2019 symposium.

Giving full play to ideological and political theory courses in forging souls and nurturing people 充分发挥思想政治理论课铸魂育人作用 Yang Ming Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2019, Yang Ming asks how universities can make their ideological and political theory courses (sizhengke) the "first classroom" for forging souls and nurturing people. The commentary argues that this requires studying and carrying out Xi Jinping's speech at the symposium for teachers of these courses, and strengthening the sense of responsibility for running them well. The piece has three parts. The first sets out the content of Xi's speech, which Yang presents as answering why the courses must be run well, why they can be, and how. The second turns to teachers and the standards they are expected to meet. The third addresses the political responsibility of universities and sets out four practical tasks. Yang reads the speech as grounded in Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Yang stresses Xi's six requirements for teachers (strong politics, deep feeling, innovative thinking, broad vision, strict self-discipline, upright character) and the "eight unities". For teachers, Yang calls for reliable political positions, innovative methods that proceed step by step and in a rising spiral, and continuous study that keeps course content current with the latest results of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context. For institutions, Yang lists four tasks: coordination under Party committee leadership, strengthening the Marxist theory discipline, improving teaching with online and offline "golden courses", and building the teaching staff. Yang concludes that a leadership structure involving the Party, administration, departments and society, together with strong teachers and academic support, will allow these courses to carry out the fundamental task of cultivating virtue and nurturing people. The text is a programmatic call rather than an empirical study. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the 2019 policy line on ideological and political courses was explained to university staff.

Firmly holding the initiative in online ideological work 牢牢掌握网络意识形态工作主动权 Zheng Jie Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in early 2019, Zheng Jie takes up Xi Jinping's remarks at the 12th collective study session of the Political Bureau (25 January 2019) on strengthening online content and running all-media communication within the rule of law. Zheng argues that, in the all-media era, holding leadership over ideological work depends largely on holding the initiative in online ideological work. The author maintains that the Party must keep its leadership over ideological work and create a clean online space, while explaining the Chinese path and safeguarding political and cultural security. The article is organised in four parts, each with three sub-points: building initiative in online discourse power; improving that discourse as a whole; perfecting a set of mechanisms; and raising international influence. It is a policy-oriented commentary that draws heavily on Xi Jinping's statements, including those from the 2014 first meeting of the central leading group on cybersecurity and informatisation and the August 2018 national conference on propaganda and ideological work. Zheng's core claim is that contests over online discourse are in essence contests of interests, in which a few developed Western countries use economic and technological advantages to exert infiltration under the cover of exchange. The author describes such contests as long-term, concealed, infiltrating, complex and varied. The response proposed is to build as well as rebut: strengthen mainstream media guidance and media convergence, set up dedicated Marxist theory websites, and replace abstruse language with plain, lively content and varied formats such as H5, AR and VR. Zheng also calls for legal, supervisory and responsive mechanisms: improved internet legislation, strict enforcement against content said to threaten national security or subvert the socialist system, early-warning systems for online opinion, technical means to detect and remove harmful information, and feedback channels with evaluation of communication effects. Internationally, Zheng argues that Western states hold the discourse initiative through technological advantage, and calls for China to move from a large to a strong cyber power. Proposed steps include a global outlook combined with Chinese characteristics drawn from traditional culture, dialogue-based rather than one-way external messaging, online diplomacy, and a shift from advocate to leader in cyberspace governance. The author concludes that mainstream media should reach user terminals directly and form concentric circles online and offline. Read the original if you want a compact example of how official Party commentary in 2019 framed online ideological security, discourse power and internet governance.

The political predicament of modernity critique in contemporary Western left-wing thought, and a way out 当代西方左翼思潮现代性批判的政治困境及其出路 Zhuo Chengfang Hu Daping Contemporary Western left-wing thought has produced radical discourses on nearly every field, from post-Fordism and postcolonial studies to ecological Marxism and biopolitics. Zhuo and Hu argue that this proliferation conceals a political retreat. In their account, no unified left programme aimed at changing the world survives, and "left" has itself become a sign of disagreement. They call this the political predicament of the Western left's critique of modernity. The authors attribute the predicament to two causes. One is a shift in aim from an alternative to capitalism to a critique of modernity. The other is an anti-essentialist stance that leaves no consensus on basic values or theoretical premises. The article first traces the loss of consensus from 1968 through Habermas, Lyotard, Laclau and Mouffe, Žižek and Rancière. It then examines four political issues: technology, globalisation and community, the local and indigeneity, and the politics of production. These are discussed through Paul Virilio, Zygmunt Bauman, Appadurai, Dirlik, Mamdani and Burawoy. Zhuo and Hu contend that anti-essentialism, drawn from structuralism, makes any fixed goal such as socialism impossible, so left politics becomes endless critique with no construction. They read Laclau, Mouffe and Žižek this way, and they treat pluralist positions as close to a "third way". The four issues show, they say, that the left does not lack insight, but that these discourses either are absorbed by power or never become political. Bauman is singled out as the most conscious of the need for political commitment, since he criticises cultural pluralism as submission to reality and sets out to rebuild the public sphere and community. Dirlik, Mamdani and Burawoy are read as treating the local, the indigenous and the labour process as sites of independent political creation, not as returns to an essentialised place. The authors conclude that without the historical condition of the capitalist mode of production and a commitment to an emancipatory agenda, critique becomes empty intellectual satisfaction. They call for a return to Marxism and for rethinking alternatives to capitalism through today's major political issues. They endorse Terry Eagleton's defence of Marx and describe Marx as the horizon of modern critique that has not yet been surpassed. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist assessment of Western left theory that links Bauman, Virilio, Dirlik and Burawoy to the question of political commitment.

Marxism and a new strategy for the North American left An account of the 2018 Left Forum in New York 马克思主义与北美左翼新战略 Zhang Xinning Zhang Xiaoming This is a report and commentary on the 2018 Left Forum, held on 1–3 June 2018 at John Jay College of Criminal Justice, City University of New York. Zhang and Zhang describe it as the most important gathering of the North American left. Its theme was "Crafting a New Strategy for the Left", and the organisers called for a broad left coalition that overcomes divisions such as class versus identity and reform versus revolution. The authors first outline the event: opening, plenary and closing sessions with speakers including Richard D. Wolff, Gayle McLaughlin, Gerald Horne and Ajamu Baraka. There were also 266 panels in eight thematic tracks, plus plays and film screenings. They then summarise panel positions under four headings: Marxism as method and system of thought; Trump and the international order; the need for an independent left party; and their own closing comments. On Marxism, the authors report panelists (among them Kevin Anderson, David Harvey, David Kotz and Peter Hudis) arguing that Marx's class theory, analysis of finance, dialectics and theory of alienation remain essential for analysing twenty-first-century capitalism. Some urged organising North American movements in the light of twentieth-century socialist revolutions. Panels on Trump, in the authors' account, blamed capitalism for inequality, debt and democratic corruption, and described "Trumpism" as destabilising through militarism and attacks on reproductive rights. Other panels argued that the proletariat remains the revolutionary class and that an independent working-class or left party is needed, though some speakers conceded that conditions for it do not yet exist. In their own assessment, the authors judge that some of the views have value and that the forum shows Marx's lasting influence. They also identify limits. In their view, some participants rely on the "hope of change" rather than thorough revolution. The forum, they note, has called for an independent party for several years without a unified leadership or the personnel and funds to build one. They also consider the aim of competing in bourgeois electoral politics unattainable. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic's panel-by-panel survey of the 2018 Left Forum and a view from China on the strategic limits of the US left.

Discourse-based justice and recognition-based justice A comparative analysis of the conceptions of justice of Habermas and Honneth 基于商谈的正义与基于承认的正义 Kong Ming'an Huang Qiuping Kong and Huang compare two conceptions of justice from the Frankfurt School: Jürgen Habermas's justice grounded in discourse (商谈, often rendered "discourse" or "deliberation") and Axel Honneth's justice grounded in recognition. They argue that Honneth, Habermas's student, supplies the ethical dimension that Habermas's legal-procedural theory underdevelops. They also argue that both theories remain abstract and formal, and detached from material interests. The article has three parts. The first reconstructs Habermas's theory of the legitimacy of rights in Between Facts and Norms, drawing on his earlier Reconstructing Historical Materialism. The second turns to Honneth's "struggle for recognition" and his three principles of recognition-based justice. The third part is a short conclusion, which brings in Nancy Fraser's Marxist-inflected critique of both thinkers. On Habermas, the authors argue that legitimacy, distinct from mere legality, is the precondition of justice, and that rights can only originate in intersubjective discourse conducted under idealised, coercion-free conditions. They stress the public sphere, which they distinguish from Rawls's veil of ignorance as a communicative structure rooted in a civil society of non-governmental, non-economic associations. They add that mutual recognition is already implicit in Habermas's idea of valid, discourse-based consensus. Honneth reverses the order. In his view the equality and rationality Habermas presupposes cannot be taken for granted, so recognition must be fought for. Drawing on Hegel and Mead, he derives principles of need (love and self-confidence), equality (legal recognition and self-respect) and contribution (social esteem and solidarity). The authors see his view as an alternative between liberalism and communitarianism. They fault it for treating distribution as a moral matter of recognition, cut off from the mode of production, so that it ignores the structural causes of unjust distribution. They add that achievement-based distribution could even widen social divisions. In the conclusion, the authors speak of a "family resemblance" between the two thinkers: both rest on abstract, formal intersubjective relations. They note that Habermas replaced Marx's historical materialism and class struggle with communicative theory in 1976, and that Honneth's recognition likewise has no bearing on substantive redistribution. They present Fraser's revival of redistribution and Marx in the early 2000s debate as evidence that historical materialism retains theoretical and practical significance. Read the original if you study Habermas, Honneth and the Frankfurt School, or want a Chinese Marxist assessment of recognition theory and the redistribution debate.

From natural things to speculative realism The evolution of contemporary European theories of the object 从自然物到思辨实在论 Lan Jiang Writing in 2018, Lan Jiang asks why European philosophy is now reviving the question of the object, and how the object should be understood in an age of the internet and digitalisation. The article names Alain Badiou, Bruno Latour, Quentin Meillassoux, Tristan Garcia, Graham Harman, Ray Brassier and others as part of this revival. Lan's thesis is that the new theories can only be understood by returning to the longer history of thinking about things, which leads to a 'speculative turn' that tries to think objects beyond human knowledge and signs. The article moves through five sections. It begins with the object as natural thing in pre-Socratic thought, then Plato, Descartes' subject–object scheme and Kant's thing-in-itself. It then sets out two modern routes: vitalism (Marx's practical conception of the object, Whitehead, Bergson, Deleuze and Guattari, and the e-flux art platform) and semiotics (Peirce, Roland Barthes, Jean Baudrillard). The fourth section turns to Gilbert Simondon, Yuk Hui, object-oriented programming and speculative realism, and a short conclusion follows. Lan argues that the object has never been a neutral given. For Descartes it is a relation structured by the subject's reason, and Kant's thing-in-itself marks what that structure cannot reach. Vitalism treats things as flux that cognition cuts into separate individuals, while semiotics treats the object as a sign whose value lies in social distinction, so that Lan reads Marx's and Lukács's reification as a matter of sign exchange. Lan credits semiotics with explaining objects produced to fill gaps in a sign system, as in digital games, but notes that it reduces things to a system of valuation, so the object escapes it. Simondon's 'technical object' and Hui's 'digital object' are presented as a turning point: such objects are convergent ensembles whose recognition depends partly on non-human, machine procedures. Meillassoux's attack on correlationism and Harman's object-oriented ontology, drawing on object-oriented programming, are read as attempts to break the tie between human subject and object. Lan concludes that the speculative turn is only a first step and has not given precise answers. Old epistemic equipment is insufficient for strange new objects, and thinking must follow technological development. Read the original if you want a historical map of European object theory, from Greek philosophy to speculative realism, linked to digital technology.

The ebb of Western-style democracy and the collapse of its "myths" 西式民主的退潮与“神话”的破灭 Zhang Shuhua Writing in People's Forum in 2018, Zhang Shuhua asks why Western-style democracy, promoted as a universal value after the Cold War, has produced disorder abroad and decay at home. The article argues that over three decades it has passed from being sacralised and generalised to being alienated and polarised. Zhang concludes that the myths surrounding democracy must be dispelled so that countries can find political paths suited to their own conditions and protect their political and ideological security. The piece opens by tying the issue to the Party's faith in Marxism and to the fortunes of socialism with Chinese characteristics. It then tells the post-Cold War story in three stages: the birth of the myth after the Soviet and East European upheavals, the expansion of democratisation, and the bursting of the "democracy bubbles". It next sets out six "logical myths" and the hegemonic character of Western democracy, and ends with proposals for a different approach. Examples include Gorbachev's reforms, the "colour revolutions" and the "Arab Spring". In Zhang's account, Western democracy was monopolised and magnified as the West rose. After 1945 it became an ideological weapon against the socialist camp, and after the Cold War a tool of power. The six myths are its internationalisation, sacralisation, instrumentalisation, labelling and fragmentation, vulgarisation, and absolutisation. Zhang says it has been reduced to competitive elections on Schumpeter's elitist model and used to intervene in other states, and that it is shaped by class in the West itself. Fukuyama and Huntington are cited as scholars who treat it as an end point or the best option. Zhang likens treating it as a universal model to nineteenth-century "white supremacy" claims. Zhang calls for a correct view of democracy as growing, diverse, concrete and historical. Democracy should respect national character and sovereignty, since no two countries share identical systems. It should be understood as historical and specific, with no single blueprint, and it must fit the level of productive forces. It should also proceed in stages, with attention to "degree" and timing. Zhang says the lessons of the past three decades support this. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a Chinese Party-affiliated scholar framed the critique of Western democracy and "universal values" in 2018.

American-style capitalism faces a struggle over its path 美式资本主义面临道路之争 Chen Chenchen Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2018, Chen Chenchen asks how far the "disruptive" policies of US President Donald Trump can really change the United States and the world. The author argues that warnings are necessary but that exaggerating Trump's impact, or "deifying" him, is unwise. In Chen's view, Trump's administration is in essence caught in a struggle over the path of American-style capitalism: financialization against industrialization. The short commentary first considers Trump's political success, then the economic background of the past three decades. It turns to the internal contradictions of his programme and ends with the balance of power between industrial and financial capital. Chen credits Trump with skilful populism that taps the grievances of people "forgotten by the elites" in the Rust Belt, the countryside and Appalachia. The author notes that his "America First" logic dates back some thirty years. Over that period, according to Chen, the US economy became financialized and hollowed out, and the recovery since 2008 rested on deeper financialization rather than industry. Chen holds that Trump's promises of industrial revival, jobs and fair trade lack well-considered policies, and that frequent personnel changes and erratic implementation add to the difficulty. Industrial capital's correction of finance has dim prospects, since financial capital gained the upper hand twice, at the start of the twentieth century and in the 1980s, and even the 2008 crisis did not reverse this. Chen concludes that the contest between re-financialization and re-industrialization holds little suspense, because de-industrialization is deeply entrenched. The administration's reshoring incentives and employment measures are described as beggar-thy-neighbour protectionism that runs against economic globalization and is bound to meet great difficulty. Read the original if you want a brief example of how a Chinese Party journal in 2018 framed Trump's economic nationalism in terms of the conflict between industrial and financial capital.

Upholding and continually enriching our understanding of the laws governing China's education 始终坚持并不断丰富发展对我国教育事业的规律性认识 Dai Jicheng This commentary, published in Red Flag Manuscript in 2018, interprets Xi Jinping's speech at the National Education Conference of that year. In the article's account, the speech answered the fundamental questions of whom education should cultivate, how, and for whom, and set out a series of new ideas on education reform and development. Dai argues that these ideas deepen the Party's understanding of the laws of education in China, were hard won, and must be upheld and enriched. The article stresses four of them. The piece is organised into four numbered sections: the importance of education as a matter of national and Party strategy; the fundamental task of education; Party leadership over education; and the teaching profession. Each section strings together remarks by Xi from 2013 to 2018, including letters, talks at Beijing Normal University and Peking University, the 2016 national conference on ideological and political work in universities, and the 2018 conference. Dai also cites Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping on the standing of intellectuals and education. Dai's core claim is that education is "a major plan for the country and for the Party" and the foundation of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Dai links this to competition in overall national strength, which the article calls ultimately a competition for talent. Because every country trains people according to its own political requirements, the author holds, the questions of whom to cultivate and how are political rather than technical. Education must therefore cultivate socialist builders and successors who support Party leadership and the socialist system. Dai presents the Party's comprehensive leadership as the fundamental guarantee, beginning with ideological and political leadership, Marxism's guiding position and the cultivation of core socialist values. Teachers are described as the foundation of education, and the article gives teachers' ethics and conduct as the first standard for judging them. Dai concludes that educational authorities and school Party organisations should strengthen the Four Consciousnesses and the Four-sphere Confidence and uphold the authority of the Party Central Committee. Teachers are urged to unite teaching with moral education and to cultivate virtue, while society is urged to raise teachers' political, social and professional standing. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Party commentary in 2018 summarised Xi Jinping's education doctrine and its emphasis on Party leadership and teachers.

Universities must show new achievements in taking up the era's mission of "fostering new people" 高校要在担当“育新人”时代使命中展现新作为 Xu Qinghong Xu Peng Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2018, after Xi Jinping's speeches at the National Education Conference and at Peking University, Xu Qinghong and Xu Peng ask how Chinese universities should carry out the task of cultivating "new people of the era" (shidai xinren) who can shoulder national rejuvenation. Their answer is that universities must be guided by Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, uphold the Party's overall leadership of education, and train socialist builders and successors with all-round moral, intellectual, physical, aesthetic and labour development. The commentary is a policy-oriented exposition in three parts, each opening with Xi's statements and then setting out tasks for higher education. The first part concerns the socialist orientation of university education, the second the fundamental task of fostering virtue and nurturing talent, and the third the Party's leadership of universities. Each part is divided into three concrete measures. On orientation, the authors hold that the question of whom universities serve and what kind of universities to build admits no ambiguity. They call for Marxism's guiding position to be maintained, for the "Four Services" requirement to be implemented, and for the "Double First-Class" initiative and comprehensive reform to be pursued with the correct political direction. On moral education, they argue that ideals and convictions, the core socialist values and a high-quality teaching staff with strong professional ethics must all be strengthened, so that students link personal dreams to the Chinese Dream. On Party leadership, they treat it as the basic feature and greatest strength of Chinese universities. They call for university Party committees to act as the leadership core, for grassroots Party branches to serve as "battle fortresses", and for an ideological and political work system that involves all staff, covers the whole process and extends in all directions. The authors conclude that the success of universities in fostering new people depends on firm political direction, a moral education system built around virtue and talent, and strong Party organisation at every level. They present these as requirements of socialist universities and of educational modernization rather than as optional measures. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Party discourse in 2018 set out the political tasks of higher education, with its main slogans and Xi Jinping citations gathered in one place.

Mounting worries over US economic growth 美国经济增长隐忧频现 Liu Ying Writing in 2018, Liu Ying asks whether the Trump administration's claim of a "perfect" US economy holds up. The article argues that the boasts rest on selective figures and that the economy faces growing difficulties from slowing growth, rising debt and policy-induced risks. The commentary first lists the administration's measures: tax cuts, continued interest-rate rises, deregulation of coal and finance (including changes to the Dodd-Frank Act) and trade wars against China and several allies. It then tests Trump's second-quarter claims against year-on-year GDP data and historical peaks. Three headings structure the rest: difficulty of growth, burden of debt and worry over risk. Liu says the 4.1% figure (later revised to 4.2%) is a quarter-on-quarter rate. On the usual year-on-year basis, the author puts growth at about 2.87%, below the peaks under Obama and several earlier presidents. Citing the Congressional Budget Office, the article expects growth to fall to 2.4% in 2019 and 1.7% in 2020, and sees weakening consumption, investment and exports. It points to a budget deficit that rose from 1.1% of GDP in 2007 to 3.5% in 2017, debt above 20 trillion dollars, and debt-service costs projected to reach 800 billion dollars by 2027. Liu adds that tax cuts and rate rises in an upswing, with unemployment at 3.8%, risk inflation and a stronger dollar. In the author's view, a stronger dollar hurts exports and widens the trade deficit. Liu concludes that if Washington persists with trade protection and reversing globalization, rapid growth will be hard to sustain and financial risks will build up. The article quotes former Fed chairman Paul Volcker, who said he saw a "mess" in every direction, and calls the aim of making America strong again an empty phrase. Read the original if you want a short example of how a Chinese Party journal assessed Trump-era economic policy during the 2018 trade war.

Protectionism, an old prescription, cannot cure America's present ills 保护主义旧药方难医美国当前病症 Tian Wenlin Writing in Hongqi Wengao in 2018, as the United States was imposing tariffs and launching trade investigations against other countries, Tian Wenlin asks why Washington is returning to protectionism and whether it can work. Tian argues that protectionism did help build American industry in the past, but that the Trump administration is now applying it under entirely different conditions. In the article's account, the policy will not bring back manufacturing and will instead hasten the erosion of US global hegemony. The article has three parts. The first reviews the history of American protectionism, from British colonial restrictions on manufacturing to the statements of Washington, Hamilton, Jefferson, Lincoln and McKinley. The second describes the financialisation of the contemporary US economy and its effects on the real economy. The third compares US decision-making with the strategic misjudgements of Germany, Japan, the Soviet Union and the post-Cold War United States. Tian's central move is a historical contrast. In the nineteenth century a tariff wall of about 30 per cent shielded a young industrial economy, whereas today manufacturing is said to account for roughly 12 per cent of GDP and finance for the core of the economy. Drawing on Marxist arguments about the falling rate of profit, the author claims that financialisation works against production in three ways. Speculative logic overrides productive logic, the real economy is crowded out by high asset prices and rents, and banking risk grows. Tian adds that the US lacks young industrial workers and a complete supply chain, so earlier re-industrialisation efforts under Obama had little effect. The article then argues that US hegemony rests on military, technological, financial (dollar) and cultural pillars. The last three depend on close ties with the outside world, such as other countries buying American technology and holding dollars earned from exports. In Tian's reading, the trade war and the pressure on the Chinese firm ZTE therefore undermine the material basis of the dollar and the profitable position of US high-tech firms in global supply chains. Tian concludes that the Trump administration defines national interest in terms of the 1960s and 1970s and of lower- and middle-income white Americans. On this basis, "America First" is described as isolationist and at odds with the globalisation the US had long promoted. The author holds that US–China trade benefits the United States far more than China and that the administration is accelerating the collapse of American hegemony rather than making the country great again. Read the original if you want an example of how a Chinese Party journal in 2018 framed the US–China trade war through historical analogy and the theory of financialisation.

Understanding the Communist Manifesto through "five constancies" 从“五个始终如一”领悟《共产党宣言》 Han Qingxiang Marking the 170th anniversary of the Communist Manifesto, Han Qingxiang asks how the Chinese Communists' original aspiration and mission can be traced to the Manifesto and how it should be commemorated. The piece is a short commentary published in Guangming Daily on 2 April 2018, in a series Han hosted. Han argues that the best commemoration is to study how the Communist Party of China and contemporary Chinese Marxism have upheld and developed the Manifesto, and that this is visible in five "constancies". In the host's introduction, Han presents "staying true to the original aspiration and keeping the mission firmly in mind" as the guiding principle, understood as a dialectic of upholding and developing. Han then takes five headings in turn: the people's standpoint, the basic principles of historical materialism, materialist dialectics, the historical mission, and a scientific attitude towards Marxism. Under each, Han first sets out what the Manifesto says and then lists how successive Chinese leaders, from Mao Zedong to Xi Jinping, are said to have continued it. Han's central move is to read the Manifesto together with its seven prefaces and Engels's draft texts as one whole, then to show a line of continuity. The Manifesto is described as written for the proletariat. Its core is historical materialism, together with the unstated principle of the basic contradictions of society. Han also finds in it five dialectical pairs, including the historical and the value-based standard, and criticism and construction. The Party is said to apply the same principles today to reform, to the principal contradiction in society, and to the Party's thorough self-reform. On attitude, Han stresses that Marx and Engels in their 1872 preface held the general principles correct but their application dependent on historical conditions. Han reads this as a warning against both dogmatism and narrow empiricism. Han concludes that Mao Zedong Thought, Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents, the Scientific Outlook on Development and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era are all innovations in adapting Marxism to Chinese conditions. These innovations, Han says, both uphold the basic principles and integrate them with China's concrete realities. The Party's mission is presented as the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the Party-school mainstream in 2018 linked the Manifesto to the lineage of Chinese Marxist theory.

The contemporary meaning of Marx's thought on world history 马克思世界历史思想的时代内涵 Yan Xiaofeng This short commentary, first published in China Social Sciences Today in July 2018, asks what Marx's thought on world history means for the present. Yan Xiaofeng argues that the thought, which he calls the realistic basis and theoretical cornerstone of scientific socialism, has been confirmed in the new century. In his account it has also acquired new content in the new era, above all through the building of a community with a shared future for mankind. The piece takes its cue from Xi Jinping's speech marking the 200th anniversary of Marx's birth, which called on Party members to study and apply Marx's ideas on world history. Yan draws mainly on The German Ideology and the Communist Manifesto, which was then 170 years old. The text has three parts: how the capitalist mode of production changed the course of world history, the contradictions and the prospect of human liberation that this process produced, and the present-day meaning of the thought. On the first point, Yan describes how industrial revolution, steam transport and the world market tied nations together. In his reading, capital's drive to transcend every spatial limit dissolved feudal relations and made production, consumption and intellectual life worldwide. He stresses that this process was unequal. Because market power is uneven, the spread of culture is largely one-directional, and the bourgeoisie subordinates the East to the West and produces cultural conflict. Yan also notes that it produced a social form bound together by things, in which, in Marx's words, the increase in the world of things goes hand in hand with a devaluation of the human world. The same process, however, created the universal exchange and many-sided capacities that are preconditions for an association in which the free development of each is the condition for the free development of all. Yan concludes that multipolarity, economic globalization, informatization and cultural diversity have made humanity's interdependence deeper than ever. He presents the building of a community with a shared future for mankind as a major development of Marx's thought by Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. He cites Xi's concepts of development, security, cooperation, civilization and global governance as its basic path. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Chinese Party scholarship links Marx's world-history theory to the official idea of a community with a shared future for mankind.

Sensing the power of truth of Marxism through the Communist Manifesto 从《共产党宣言》感悟马克思主义的真理力量 Fu Yongshou Li Xueyang Published in Economic Daily on 24 May 2018, shortly after the 200th anniversary of Marx's birth, this commentary asks what rereading the Communist Manifesto, issued 170 years earlier, can teach about the truth of Marxism. Fu and Li argue that the Manifesto shows Marxism to be a scientific, revolutionary, practical and open body of theory that remains vital. An editor's note frames the piece with Xi Jinping's call to study the classics closely and to keep opening new horizons for contemporary Chinese Marxism and twenty-first-century Marxism. The article is organised under four headings: the Manifesto's scientific insight into the laws of social development; Marxism's capacity to keep pace with the times; its practical character; and the continuing adaptation of Marxism to China. It draws on the Manifesto's own formulations, on its prefaces, and on several statements by Xi Jinping from the anniversary speech. The authors' central claim is that Marxism's scientific and revolutionary character derives from dialectical and historical materialism. In their reading, the Manifesto acknowledges the productive forces created by the bourgeoisie while showing that capitalist relations of production increasingly obstruct them, and it sets out the tendency of human society towards communism. They stress that Marx and Engels revised the Manifesto through successive prefaces, for example the 1872 German preface, which holds the basic principles to be correct but their application dependent on historical conditions. They add that the Manifesto criticised the mechanical transplanting of French theory into Germany. Marxism, they say, is therefore not an "absolute truth" but an open system that absorbs human knowledge. They also point to its practical orientation: its class-struggle thesis, its sharp critique of rival socialist currents, and its stance that the proletarian movement serves the great majority. The authors conclude that the Communist Party of China is the faithful heir of the Manifesto's spirit and that Marxism's scientific character has been fully tested in China. Facing what they call unprecedented tasks and risks in reform, development and stability, they call on the Party to treat advancing Marxism as a sacred duty. They urge it to raise its ability to solve China's practical problems with Marxist principles, to apply the Manifesto's principles to the great struggle, great project, great cause and great dream, to pursue the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, and to write new chapters of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a short example of how the Manifesto was presented in the official press during the 2018 Marx bicentenary.

The revolutionary spirit of the Communist Manifesto will never be outdated 《共产党宣言》的革命精神永不过时 Chen Xueming Marking the 170th anniversary of the Communist Manifesto, this newspaper commentary (Guangming Daily, 2 April 2018) asks whether the work still has value for China as it pursues socialist modernization and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Chen Xueming answers that it does, because the Party remains a revolutionary party and the Manifesto's revolutionary spirit is still needed. Chen first affirms that the Manifesto is a revolutionary work that once played an epoch-making role, and that Marxism guided China's revolution and national liberation. The real issue, in Chen's framing, is whether it is still needed after 1949 and especially after the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978), when the focus shifted to economic development. The piece is short and addresses mainly the opening of this problem. Chen takes issue with the view of some people that the Party is now purely a "party of construction" and that its work has nothing to do with "revolution". Chen argues that the word "revolution" must first be rehabilitated, since it has come to be treated by some as pejorative. According to the Manifesto, Chen says, revolution arises of necessity, regardless of personal wishes, and is the fundamental driving force of history. Chen holds that the claimed shift from revolution to construction is meant to show that economic work no longer needs revolutionary spirit, reducing it to a technical operation. Chen concludes that economic construction is something every ruling party does, but a party that abandons the social values and spiritual drive that define its political nature risks not only losing power but disintegrating. Revolutionary spirit therefore remains necessary for the Party's construction work. Read the original if you want a brief example of how a Chinese Marxist scholar defended the continuing relevance of revolution and the Manifesto in the reform era.

Holding to the original aspiration by rereading the Communist Manifesto 在重温《共产党宣言》中坚守初心 Li Yin Marking the 170th anniversary of the Communist Manifesto, this commentary from PLA Daily (25 April 2018) asks what Chinese Communists should take from rereading it in the new era of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Li Yin argues that rereading the Manifesto means holding to the Party's "original aspiration" (chuxin) and mission. The author presents the text both as a guiding document for the international communist movement and as the Chinese Communists' "primer". The piece is organised in three parts, each beginning with the phrase "rereading the Manifesto" and each tied to one aspect of the original aspiration. These are realising the lofty ideal of communism, upholding and developing Marxism, and strengthening the building of a Marxist Party. Li links each to Xi Jinping's statements and to episodes in the Party's history, from its founding in 1921 to the present. On the first aspect, Li argues that the Manifesto is the source of the communist ideal written into the Party's programme at its founding. The author holds that socialism with Chinese characteristics unites the Party's maximum and basic programmes, and that Party members must therefore be firm believers in the common ideal. On the second, Li describes the Manifesto as the first comprehensive statement of scientific socialism. The author traces its adaptation through Mao Zedong Thought, Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents, the Scientific Outlook on Development and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, and names individualism, historical nihilism and "universal values" as current challenges. On the third, Li presents the Manifesto as the foundation of proletarian party-building. The author credits full and rigorous self-governance of the Party since the 18th Party Congress (2012) with strengthening the Party, and cites the "four tests" and "four dangers" as long-term pressures. Li concludes that, without Marxism, the Party's cause would lose its soul and direction. The author calls on Party members to study Xi Jinping Thought, to carry out the strategy of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, and to ensure the Party remains the "backbone" of the Chinese people and nation. Read the original if you want a short example of how the Party press framed the Manifesto's anniversary in 2018 in terms of Party loyalty, ideology and discipline.

The Communist Manifesto in China: dissemination, influence and lessons 《共产党宣言》在中国的传播、影响与启示 Ji Zhengju Marking the 170th anniversary of the Communist Manifesto, Ji Zhengju (writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in February 2018) asks how the text reached China, what it did there and how it should be treated today. The author holds that the Manifesto's spread and influence in China are the most persuasive proof of its reach, vitality and truth, and that its history in China mirrors the Sinicization of Marxism. The article has three parts. The first traces the arrival of the Manifesto in China through three channels, Japan, France and Russia, and follows the making of the first full Chinese translation and later versions. The second sets out the Manifesto's influence on the founding of the Communist Party of China and on its leaders. The third draws two lessons for the present. In the first part, Ji notes that the Manifesto had little echo in China for fifty years after 1848, which the author attributes to the Qing policy of closure and cultural control. Fragments then appeared through missionaries and Chinese students in Japan, with erratic renderings of names and terms. Chen Wangdao's complete translation, from Japanese and with a English text supplied by Chen Duxiu, was published in August 1920, and five more Chinese versions appeared before 1949. Ji argues that increasingly complete and accurate translations track a deepening understanding of Marxism. In the second part, Ji claims the Manifesto directly promoted the Party's founding and its First Congress documents, and cites Mao Zedong, Zhou Enlai, Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin and Liu Shaoqi on its formative effect on them. Ji's lessons are, first, to hold to the ideal of struggling for humanity's future, which Marx and Engels grounded in historical materialism and the theory of surplus value rather than utopian fantasy. Second, the Manifesto should be treated as a developing theory: Ji points to the seven prefaces, such as the 1872 and 1888 revisions, as evidence of the founders' rigorous, evolving scientific attitude. Read the original if you want a brief, Party-oriented account of the Manifesto's Chinese translation history and its place in the narratives of early Party leaders."

Why the Nepali left alliance won the 2017 elections, and what it means for the future 尼泊尔左翼联盟2017年大选获胜的原因、影响及其前景 Yuan Qun Writing in 2018, Yuan Qun asks why the left alliance of the Communist Party of Nepal (Unified Marxist-Leninist) and the Communist Party of Nepal (Maoist Centre) won a sweeping victory in Nepal's first elections under the new constitution, completed in December 2017. The article argues that the win, which brought the UML chairman Khadka Prasad Oli to the premiership in February 2018, was the first time Nepali communists had succeeded through unity. Yuan sets out the causes, consequences and prospects of the victory. The article opens with the electoral system and the results. In the local, provincial and federal contests the alliance took first and second place, and Yuan reports that it won 63.27 per cent of seats and more than two thirds of the National Assembly. The analysis then has three parts: four causes of the victory, three consequences, and three challenges ahead. On causes, Yuan stresses that the two parties set aside years of rivalry, drawing on the lessons of unstable coalitions and on electoral calculation. The article also credits a joint manifesto promising stability, development and a Nepali-style socialism with multiparty competition, and a nationalist stance against Indian interference, notably during the 2015 blockade. It adds that the Nepali Congress was weakened by factional infighting and failed coalition-building. The consequences, in Yuan's account, are a new round of consolidation in Nepal's communist movement through a planned merger, an example of unity for the international communist movement, and faster progress for the Belt and Road Initiative in Nepal and South Asia. Yuan identifies three challenges. The first and most important is the parties' theoretical divergence: the UML's "people's multiparty democracy" against the Maoist Centre's "21st-century democracy" and its refusal to renounce violence entirely. The others are the demands of the Madhesi people of the Terai plain, and relations with an India that Yuan expects to pressure the alliance. Yuan concludes that finding an acceptable ideological line within Marxism will decide the legitimacy and durability of the alliance and the new party. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic account of Nepal's 2017 election, with detailed results and background on Nepali party politics and Madhesi and India issues.

Western Marxism in the perspective of the history of Marxism's development 马克思主义发展史视野中的西方马克思主义 Ma Yongjun Ma Yongjun asks how Western Marxism should be placed within the whole history of Marxism, and what Chinese scholars can still learn from it. Citing Xi Jinping's 2016 remarks that Western researchers did solid work on Marxist texts, and his 2017 call to study foreign Marxism neither rejecting it wholesale nor copying it wholesale, Ma rejects two sectarian stances: dismissing Western Marxism outright, and treating it as the only orthodoxy. The article argues that it should be studied, with its flaws acknowledged, to help reunite theory and practice. The article has three parts: the origins of Western Marxism, why it reached a dead end, and the practical significance of placing it in the history of Marxism. Ma starts from the split after Marx's death among Kautsky's dogmatism, Bernstein's revisionism, and the left of the Second International (Lenin and Rosa Luxemburg). The later sections turn to the Frankfurt School, Lukács, Gramsci, Althusser and the events of May 1968, then to the reception of Western Marxism in China since reform and opening up. Ma traces Western Marxism to Luxemburg and treats it as the theoretical heir of her Marxism of advanced countries, as Leninism and its Chinese successors were its practical counterpart in backward ones. Ma credits it with depth, the dialectical method, totality, subjectivity and practice. Ma attributes its failure to three congenital defects. It set Lenin against Luxemburg and Marx against Engels, which Ma calls sectarian. It split Marxism's scientific and revolutionary sides, for example humanism against scientism and critical theory against developmental theory. And it withdrew from parties and the masses into intellectual circles. In Ma's account, it moved from philosophy back away from political-economy critique, and its theoretical radicalism turned into practical conservatism, ending in bankruptcy in 1968. Ma credits the introduction of Western Marxism with lifting Chinese Marxist philosophy beyond the old textbook system, and says it still offers resources on democracy, human development, ecology and consumerism, even though some Chinese scholars repeated its errors. Ma argues that the post-2008 problem of overcapacity, and the "new normal" of economic development, bring Luxemburg's Accumulation of Capital and Marx's six-volume plan back into view. The article calls for drawing lessons from the Second International, Stalin's model and Western Marxism, and for returning both to Marx and to real life. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's defence of studying Western Marxism, framed by a Luxemburg-to-Lenin genealogy and the Party leadership's official guidance on foreign Marxism.

An analysis of the impact of left-wing governments in Latin America on democratic political development since the end of the twentieth century 试析20世纪末以来拉美左翼执政对民主政治发展的影响 Fang Xufei Fang asks how the left-wing governments that came to power in Latin America from the end of the twentieth century affected democratic political development, a wave the author says began to recede in 2015. The thesis is that the effects were mixed and cannot be described simply as progress or regression. Fang holds that the outcome depended on whether a government was radical or moderate. The article first traces the left's shift from rejecting 'bourgeois' democracy and armed struggle in the 1960s and 70s to embracing electoral democracy after the 'third wave' of democratization. It then compares the left's critique of Latin America's 'democratic deficit' and its calls to 'deepen democracy'. Next it surveys practice in two groups of cases: radical governments (Chávez's Venezuela, Morales's Bolivia, Correa's Ecuador) and moderate ones (Lula and Rousseff in Brazil, Uruguay's Broad Front, Chile). It ends by assessing consequences. Fang argues that radical governments made participatory democracy their goal, through new constitutions, referendums, communal councils in Venezuela, 'consensus democracy' in Bolivia and new citizen-participation bodies in Ecuador. The author credits them with greater inclusion of Indigenous people, the poor and other excluded groups, and with higher satisfaction with democracy for a time. Fang also finds they concentrated power in the presidency, weakened checks and balances, curbed pluralism and deepened polarization, above all in Venezuela. Moderate governments, in the author's account, respected constitutional order, kept the legislature and judiciary independent and handled opponents through negotiation, but they did less to widen participation. Fang adds that all of these governments largely kept competitive elections and left office through constitutional procedures. Fang concludes that the radical left's participatory model did not establish an alternative democratic model and in places damaged representative democracy. The author cites some scholars who regard the moderate path as more durable. With the right reviving, the article argues that every camp must tackle poverty, inequality and corruption, strengthen citizenship, checks and balances and the judiciary, and build a democratic model suited to national conditions. Read the original if you want a comparative account of Latin American left governments' democratic records, with data from Latinobarometer and constitutional detail, written from a Chinese academic perspective.

On the question of labour's subjectivity in Capital Based on the theory of the Japanese Uno School 论《资本论》的劳动主体性问题 You Xinwei Does labour have the status of a subject in Marx's theory? You Xinwei takes up this question, on which Chinese scholars disagree. Some, from the practical-materialist tradition, build Marx's theory on a principle of labour's subjectivity, while others hold that in Capital labour is only an instrument of capital's valorisation. Drawing on the Japanese Uno School, which is little introduced in China, the author argues that in the theoretical system of Capital labour has no subjectivity and exists only as something passive within capital's logic. The article first contrasts the Uno School with Japan's civil-society school (Mochizuki Seiji, and Han Lixin in China), which reads Marx through labour's externalisation and early alienated labour. It then sets out four themes. The first is where the labour process sits in Capital and in Uno Kozo's 'principles' theory. The second is the Uno School reading of alienation as arising from the forms of circulation. The third is the relation between labour and the categories of Capital, and the resulting rethinking of the labour theory of value. The fourth is how capitalism can be sublated. Following Uno, You argues that Marx deliberately treats the labour process only after commodities, money and the commodification of labour-power, as a moment of industrial capital (M–C…P…C′–M′). Uno distinguishes 'economic principles', such as the metabolism between humans and nature found in all societies, from 'economic laws', and holds that the former can be theorised only through the latter. Shimizu Masanori calls labour a 'nothing'. For him, alienation does not come from the labour process but from the commodification of labour-power, derived from the general value form in circulation. Thought therefore moves from value to labour, not the reverse, and the labour theory of value becomes a theory of the value of labour-power. For Uno, the basic contradiction of capitalism is the commodification of labour-power, so overcoming capitalism means abolishing it, not extending socialisation or nationalisation. Uno and Ouchi Hideaki see Marx's 'negation of the negation' in chapter 24 as a philosophical transition logic. Aoki Kohei looks to an external 'other', reached through stage theory and analysis of present conditions. You concedes that the Uno School departs far from Marx, who sought to raise the standing of workers through their own efforts. The author nonetheless finds the position worth pondering. In Western societies workers are, in You's account, absorbed into capital's logic in values as well as in production, and Streeck's 'neo-Protestantism' and Marcuse's thesis are cited. You concludes that the Uno School's appeal to an 'other' to sublate capitalism offers real reference value today. Read the original if you want an introduction in Chinese to the Uno School's reading of Capital, and its contrast with practical-materialist and civil-society readings of labour.

Rethinking the dialectics of nature Based on Lukács's idea of historical dialectics 对自然辩证法的再思考 Fu Zeyu Fu Zeyu asks why Georg Lukács rejected Engels's dialectics of nature, and whether that rejection holds. The article argues that Lukács's critique rests on a misunderstanding of Engels, and that Marxism's view of nature and its view of history together form a complete theoretical system. It sets out to defend Engels's dialectics of nature on that basis. The article begins with Lukács's early project in History and Class Consciousness. This was a defence of Marxism against the Second International's \"vulgar\" Marxists, who discarded Hegel and treated Marxism as a positive science. Fu then explains Lukács's concept of historical dialectics, his account of reification and subjectivity, and his claim that only the proletariat can restore philosophical totality. The last part examines why Lukács dismissed Engels and then answers him through Marx's and Engels's own texts. In Fu's account, Lukács treats orthodox Marxism as a method, namely dialectics of totality. It grasps facts as moments of a structured whole and unveils the reified, fetishised relations of capitalism. On this view the subject-object interaction and the unity of theory and practice are absent from our knowledge of nature, and Engels's dialectics of nature looked like the naturalism of Kautsky. Fu replies that Marx never named a \"dialectics of nature\" but pervasively treated the unity of humans and nature, humanized nature and natural laws. Fu cites Marx's letters of 1867 and 1868 and says Marx supported Engels's research. Engels, in this reading, drew dialectics out of the natural sciences rather than forcing it onto nature, and he was also answering Dühring. Fu adds that Lukács could not have read the Dialectics of Nature, which was unpublished when he wrote. Fu concludes that reducing Marx's dialectics to historical dialectics is narrow, and that Engels filled a field Marx left undeveloped. The \"Marx–Engels opposition\" thesis, which Fu associates with Western Marxists, is therefore rejected. Fu also notes that Lukács's stress on subjectivity risks sliding into idealism and voluntarism. Read the original if you want a Chinese defence of Engels against Lukácsian and Western Marxist critiques, built on close reading of Lukács and the Marx–Engels correspondence.")

Lukács's dialectic of totality and its influence on Western Marxism 卢卡奇的总体性辩证法及其对西方马克思主义的影响 Dong Jijie Why is Lukács regarded as the founding father of Western Marxism? Dong argues that the reason lies in History and Class Consciousness (1923), where Lukács defined orthodox Marxism as a method, the dialectic of totality, rather than as a body of doctrine built on economic determinism. The article contends that this move countered the Second International's vulgar materialism and revived Marxism's revolutionary character, but that it was also one-sided. The article has four parts. It first traces the origin of the dialectic of totality in Lukács's reflection on the failure of the European workers' movement after the First World War. It then sets out the concept's content and assesses it. Finally it surveys how thinkers from Korsch and Gramsci to Fredric Jameson took up, rejected or reworked the idea, and closes with the lessons Dong draws. Dong summarises Lukács's concept as four unities: whole and part, history and nature, subject and object, theory and practice. Lukács used these to criticise reification under capitalism and to assign the proletariat's class consciousness, mediated by the Communist Party as organisation, the role of transforming society. Dong judges that Lukács set method against content, opposed Marx to Engels by denying a dialectics of nature, inflated class consciousness and thereby retreated into Hegelianism, and so drifted from Marxism, while still enriching its dialectical thought. In the second half, Dong sorts Western Marxist responses into three paths: defending and developing totality (Korsch, Gramsci, Marcuse, Habermas, Jameson), opposing it (Adorno, Bertell Ollman), and reconstructing it (Sartre, Althusser). Dong concludes that, despite its one-sidedness, the dialectic of totality is the methodological cornerstone of Western Marxism and a coordinate for understanding its history and likely future. The author also draws a lesson for China: a totalising perspective should guide the modernization of socialism with Chinese characteristics, coordinating economic, political, cultural, social and ecological construction and strengthening the Party's governing capacity. Read the original if you want a compact Chinese-language survey of how Lukács's totality shaped later Western Marxists, together with a critical Chinese assessment of his method.

The internal logic of the rise and development of Western Marxology 西方马克思学兴起与发展的内在逻辑 Li Jingxinhong Wang Xiaonan Li Jingxinhong and Wang Xiaonan ask why Western Marxology (Marxologie, the scholarly study of Marx's life, editions and texts) arose and kept deepening. They note that Chinese scholarship, following Soviet and East European writers, long read the term only as a Cold War ideological weapon and explained the field by external events. Cold War politics and the student-worker movements did matter, the authors concede. Their thesis is that the sustained driver was continuous internal factors: three interacting parts, three interacting stances, and a two-way relation with Western Marxism. Published in 2018, the article has four sections. The first treats the interplay of biography, textual editing and interpretation of Marx's thought, with the successive editions MEGA1, MECW and MEGA2 as the main case. The second examines the "appreciative", "hostile" and "objective-neutral" stances, using Marx biographies from Engels, Mehring and Spargo to E. H. Carr, Isaiah Berlin, McLellan and Fetscher. The third examines how Marxology and Western Marxism relate, through Marcuse, David Harvey and the Hegel–Marx question. The fourth draws conclusions. On the three parts, the authors argue that interpretation needed reliable biography and texts. Publishing the 1844 Manuscripts in the MEGA1 era prompted debates on humanism, the Marx–Hess relation and Althusser's "break", and later editorial work, such as the revised count of the Paris Notebooks, fed back into interpretation. On the three stances, they argue that hagiographic, hostile and neutral works provoked one another and sent all sides back to archives and manuscripts; some hostile works even supplied material that orthodox writers used. On Western Marxism, they call the two "twins" from one matrix, with the "I annotate the Classics" (Marxology) and "the Classics annotate me" (Western Marxism) modes. Marcuse moved from the first to the second, while Harvey moved the other way. Trends in Western philosophy reach Marxology through Western Marxism, as in the rise, decline and return of Hegel in Marx studies. The authors conclude that Marxology is a self-renewing field. Its internal interactions drive a spiral of development, and exchange with Western Marxism, for instance the charge that Marx was "ecologically blind" or "gender blind", brings new questions and keeps it from becoming a closed perpetual-motion machine. They argue that this view lets Chinese scholars reassess the stereotyped Soviet-era image of Marxology and anticipate its research directions. Read the original if you want a Chinese-language account of how Western Marx scholarship developed, with detail on editions, biographies and the Hegel–Marx debate.
