New thinking on strengthening ideological work from the perspective of cultural technology 文化技术视阈下加强意识形态建设的新思考 Ren Limei Writing in 2018, Ren Limei argues that research on online ideology has concentrated on content and on conflicts between internet culture and mainstream culture, and should instead start from the ideological character of network technology itself. The article holds that the internet has become the main battlefield of mainstream ideology and a key force for socialism with Chinese characteristics and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Its thesis is that ideological work must rely on developing and controlling network technology, as well as on managing content. The article has four parts. It first examines the cultural features and ideological attributes of network technology, looking at technology from the standpoint of culture and at culture from the standpoint of technology. It then analyses the security problems facing online culture and ideology in what Ren calls the age of cultural technology. The third part sets out how to hold ideological leadership, management and discourse power through technology, and the fourth proposes building a "concentric circle" online and offline. Ren's core argument is that technology has three layers: material artefacts, institutions and ideas, and that the last of these is technology's ideology. On this view, every platform carries the values of its operators, and the internet spreads and amplifies them faster than older media. Ren names several sources of risk. Chinese culture is said to be in a transitional stage, and some Western capitalist states are said to use networks to steer public sentiment and infiltrate ideologically. Niche online subcultures that mock mainstream culture, and market-driven pragmatic outlooks on life, are also listed. Ren's remedies are to promote the core socialist values in language suited to the internet, to deepen the integration of traditional and new media, and to master core technologies and train politically reliable technical personnel. In the final part Ren calls for more investment in research and development, including blockchain, and for officials to follow the mass line online. Ren also proposes flatter, more flexible organisational structures for ideological work, and "Internet Plus" applications in services, rural development and poverty alleviation, so that people see practical benefits. The article concludes that China should use the internet era to draw a "concentric circle" and build a culture of mutual trust that secures mainstream ideology and the core socialist values. Read the original if you want an example of how Chinese ideological-work scholarship in 2018 linked internet governance, technology strategy and ideological security.

Green capitalism runs into difficulties 绿色资本主义发展遭遇困境 Zhuang Guiyang Zhuang Guiyang asks whether capitalism can be made environmentally sustainable through "green" growth. Writing in 2018, the author argues that capitalism without moral guidance cannot resolve its basic contradiction with ecological limits, and that green capitalism has therefore run into difficulties. The short commentary treats the US withdrawal from the Paris Agreement as the clearest recent illustration. The article first sets out the case made by supporters of green capitalism, citing Paul Hawken's 2000 book and figures on record renewable-energy investment. It then turns to critics such as Richard Smith, to the US withdrawal announced in 2017, to wavering among developed countries at the Bonn climate talks, and finally to the rise of city networks and sub-national alliances in climate action. Zhuang reports the supporters' view that green growth is a natural extension of capitalism's self-evolution, since scarcity and efficiency incentives are compatible with it. Against this, the author sides with critics who hold that the profit motive and the expansionary logic of capital conflict with saving the planet. In this reading, carbon taxes cannot fully remove market externalities, and technology cannot rescue the system. The author describes Trump's withdrawal, justified by 'America First' and by the aim of reviving oil and coal, as proof of the limits of self-regulation under capitalism. The article also claims that developed countries evade their obligations, citing the unmet US$100 billion annual climate-finance pledge and calls to end 'differentiated responsibilities'. Zhuang notes that, after Copenhagen (2009), cities, firms and other non-state actors filled part of the gap. Examples include the Global Covenant of Mayors for Climate and Energy, the 'America's Pledge' style coalitions of US states and the 'We Are Still In' pavilion at Bonn. Because these initiatives are bottom-up, the author holds they cannot replace states under the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, and the outlook remains uncertain. The article calls for a development paradigm that goes beyond industrial civilisation. Read the original if you want a concise 2018 Chinese critique of green capitalism that links Paris Agreement politics to the contradictions of capitalism.

Why Western left-wing currents of thought have stalled 西方左翼思潮为何陷入停滞 Chen Jiangsheng Writing in People's Forum in 2018, Chen Jiangsheng asks why Western left-wing currents of thought, which revived after the 2008 financial crisis, have recently stopped advancing. The article argues that since about 2016 uncertainty and stagnation have become the dominant picture. In Chen's view this follows from the unclear course of Western economies and societies, from a rethinking of the left's earlier rapid rise, and from the lack of a sound guiding ideology. The article first explains how the 2008 crisis gave the left new momentum, then surveys four countries. It closes with a three-part explanation of the stagnation. Chen sets the revival against what the article calls the failure of neoliberalism and of American hegemony, and cites works by Chris Harman, Andrew Kliman and Thomas Piketty as examples of critique that won the left new followers. Chen identifies three sources of the earlier growth: criticism of capitalism, the link with anti-globalisation sentiment, and an impact on national politics, such as the shift in France and a more reflective mood in the West. The country survey is then used as evidence of stalling. In the United States, Sanders's defeat and Trump's election are read as a left-wing ebb, though the 2017 left forum and protests suggest it is temporary. Britain's Brexit vote is described as 'left-wing people doing right-wing work', leaving the left without a clear position. The failed coalition talks in Germany show left and right unable to reconcile. Macron's win in France is judged only a limited gain for the left. Chen uses the Marxist principle that social being determines social consciousness to explain the stagnation. Western economies are adrift internally and face competition from new theories and paths from the East. The left also grew too fast on discontent with the crisis, and people began to doubt its remedies. Finally, it is not guided by Marxism, so its critique of capitalism is incomplete and cannot solve basic problems within the old framework. Chen concludes that it will rise and fall in waves with popular discontent rather than transform Western society. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a Chinese journal in 2018 interpreted the post-crisis Western left through the lens of historical materialism.

The Communist Party of China as the undeniable mainstay of the War of Resistance against Japan 中国共产党是无可非议的抗战中流砥柱 Zhang Yun Writing in Jiefang Daily in September 2018, Zhang Yun argues that, among the many domestic and international causes of victory in the War of Resistance against Japan, the Communist Party of China (CPC) was the "mainstay" (zhongliu dizhu) that held firm amid the storm. Zhang presents this as a response to online claims that, once the Nationalist-led frontal battlefield is assessed objectively, the Party's contribution can be belittled or denied. The author labels such claims historical nihilism and promises firm historical facts to refute them. The commentary is organised under four headings. The first counts the Party's public anti-Japanese statements between 1931 and 1945. The second traces the Party's shifting line towards the Nationalists and the formation of the Anti-Japanese National United Front. The third describes how the Party dealt with Nationalist diehards, and the fourth reviews the armed struggle behind Japanese lines. Zhang's first move is a self-described rough count: the Party issued 290 formal anti-Japanese positions over 14 years, 97 during the six years of partial war and 193 during the eight years of full-scale war. Zhang reads this as proof of an unwavering stance, in contrast to the Nationalist policy of non-resistance. The second move traces the policy shift from "oppose Chiang and resist Japan" to "pressure Chiang" and then "ally with Chiang". Zhang attributes it to Japan's growing aggression, the Comintern's Seventh Congress and changes in Nationalist and Soviet policy. Faced with three anti-Communist upsurges between 1939 and 1943, including the 1941 Southern Anhui Incident, the Party held the front together by the principle of struggles that are "justified, advantageous and restrained". Zhang's third move is military. Guerrilla warfare, in the author's account, dragged Japan into a protracted quagmire and made the rear-area battlefield the strategic main battlefield. The author cites 125,000 engagements, 1.713 million Japanese and puppet troops eliminated, 19 base areas, and 58–75 per cent of the Japanese invaders resisted from the stalemate stage. Zhang concludes that, while the Nationalist frontal battlefield fought 22 major campaigns without halting the Japanese advance, the Party's rear-area battlefield created a "vast ocean" in which the enemy was trapped. In this reading the Party was an indisputable mainstay and a beacon of hope for the Chinese people. Read the original if you want to see how a 2018 Party-press commentary uses wartime statistics and United Front history to rebut revisionist assessments of the Party's role in the war.

A study of the Chinese translations of the Communist Manifesto 《共产党宣言》汉译考 Chen Hongjuan Chen Hongjuan takes up a bibliographical question: how many distinct complete Chinese translations of the Communist Manifesto exist, and by what criteria should they be counted? The author notes that scholars have counted ten, twelve or even twenty-three translations. Chen argues that, by a consistent standard, there are six verifiable complete translations before 1949 and three "translation systems" after it. The author presents this clarification as a precondition for tracing how Marxist theory spread and developed in China. The short article, published in a newspaper in 2018, is divided into two parts: complete translations before the founding of the People's Republic in 1949, and those after it. For the earlier period it lists the translations by Chen Wangdao (1920), Hua Gang (1930), Cheng Fangwu and Xu Bing (1938), Bo Gu (1943) and Chen Shoushi (1943), the last being the only one by a non-Communist. It then examines disputed cases: the 1948 Qiao Guanhua edition, Cheng Fangwu's 1953 and 1978 versions, the 1954 and 1958 texts, and the four versions issued by the Central Compilation and Translation Bureau. Chen's central move is to separate a new translation from a revision or reprint. Qiao Guanhua's 1948 edition counts as a new translation because he worked from an English text rather than the German one used before. He also made over a hundred changes, such as replacing "propertied class" with "bourgeoisie", and he resolved the terminological inconsistencies caused by the 1938 split between two translators. By contrast, Cheng's 1953 edition is classed as an interim proofreading of his own work, and the 1954 and 1958 texts as reprints and revisions of the 1949 Moscow centenary edition. Chen groups the Bureau's 1964, 1978, 1995 and 2009 versions as one "translation system", citing the changes in annotation counts and the shifts in theoretical understanding behind each revision. The author borrows this approach from Gong Yuzhi's treatment of editions of Mao Zedong's Selected Works. Chen concludes that the verifiable complete translations are the six pre-1949 ones plus, afterwards, the 1949 Moscow centenary text, Cheng Fangwu's 1978 translation and the Bureau's translation system. In the author's view, the translation history of the Manifesto is also the history of Marxist truth spreading in China and of Chinese Communists' persistent pursuit of truth and self-reform. Read the original if you want a compact guide to how Chinese scholars classify Manifesto translations and why the counts differ.

The Communist Manifesto and the development of the Japanese Communist Party An interview with Fuwa Tetsuzo, head of the Japanese Communist Party's Social Science Research Institute 《共产党宣言》与日本共产党的发展 Shi Shaobo Xie Zongrui This is an interview conducted by Shi Shaobo and Xie Zongrui for Chinese Social Sciences Today on the 170th anniversary of The Communist Manifesto. The interviewee is Fuwa Tetsuzo, a theorist of the Japanese Communist Party (JCP), nearly ninety years old, who heads its Social Science Research Institute. The interviewers ask what the Manifesto has meant, historically and today, for Japanese communists. The conversation has five parts. Fuwa traces how the Manifesto reached Japan, from the 1904 translation by Sakai Toshihiko and Kotoku Shusui to the 1906 full text and its circulation under repression. He then turns to the Manifesto's place in the JCP's theory, three passages on abolishing private property and on violent revolution, the Party's study activities, and the 2004 Party Programme as a counterpart to a 'JCP manifesto'. He ends with the Manifesto's significance for the future. Fuwa's central claim is that Marx must be read within Marx's own intellectual history. He reads the Manifesto's 'abolition of private property' as the socialisation of the means of production, not the abolition of personal property in the means of life. On violence, he argues that the Manifesto's line reflected Europe before universal suffrage. He points to Marx's 1872 Amsterdam speech and his 1878 notes, which in Fuwa's account allow for a peaceful, parliamentary route in some countries and point towards a 'majority revolution'. Fixing the Manifesto's stage-bound line into dogma, he says, contradicts Marxism's development. The JCP therefore studies all the classics, with 21 Capital seminars a year at the Central Committee, and avoids dogmatism. Fuwa describes the 2004 Programme, which revised the 1961 version and which he says settles accounts with the errors inherited from the Stalin era, as the Party's equivalent of a manifesto. For the future, he stresses the Manifesto's formula of a society where the free development of each is the condition for the free development of all. He reads 'freedom' in Marx as, above all, free time for everyone, which would make human development rather than profit the driving force of society and open the 'real history' of humanity. Read the original if you want a JCP leader's account, published in a Chinese outlet, of how Japanese communists read the Manifesto on property, revolution and the future society.

The Communist Manifesto shines in the new era of socialism with Chinese characteristics 《共产党宣言》在中国特色社会主义新时代绽放光芒 Tao Chuanming Marking the 170th anniversary of the Communist Manifesto and the 200th anniversary of Marx's birth in 2018, this newspaper commentary asks what the Manifesto means for China in what it calls the new era of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Tao argues that the text is not only a founding document of Marxism and scientific socialism but also the source of the Chinese Communists' faith, the intellectual root of Chinese socialism and a vision for humanity's future. The piece first appeared in the China Social Sciences Today (Zhongguo shehui kexue bao) in April 2018. The commentary is organised under three headings: the Manifesto as the source of Chinese Communists' faith, as the intellectual root of socialism with Chinese characteristics, and as a vision of human social development. Tao draws on the Manifesto's passages on the proletarian movement as one of the great majority, on world history and on the association of free individuals. The piece also cites recollections by Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping, the story of Chen Wangdao's translation, and statements by Xi Jinping and the 19th Party Congress (2017). Tao's central claim is that the Party's "original aspiration and founding mission" and its people-centred approach to development trace back to the Manifesto's statement that the proletarian movement serves the vast majority. Citing Marx and Engels's 1872 preface, Tao says the Manifesto's general principles remain correct while their application depends on historical conditions. Tao therefore calls for grasping what changes and what does not in the Manifesto and for combining its principles with Chinese realities. On this reading, socialism with Chinese characteristics is scientific socialism in a Chinese form, and upholding it amounts to upholding Marxism. Tao also reads the Manifesto's account of world history and proletarian internationalism as the root of the 19th Party Congress's call for a community with a shared future for mankind, which Tao presents as an inheritance and development of Marx and Engels's theory. Tao concludes that Marxism is the Communists' "true scripture" and that China must uphold it rather than any other doctrine, a necessity Tao ties to both its scientific character and China's modern history. Tao calls for firm political resolve and deeper understanding of the laws of socialist construction, of Communist Party rule and of human social development, so as to carry forward the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese Party-affiliated commentary in 2018 linked the Manifesto to Party faith, the Chinese Dream and the idea of a shared-future community.

The Communist Manifesto shows renewed appeal in the new era 新时代《共产党宣言》再显魅力 Wang Baoxian This short newspaper commentary, published in 2018, takes the strong sales of the Communist Manifesto as a sign of the Party's condition. Wang argues that since the 18th Party Congress (2012) the Party has resolved the question of how to treat the Marxist classics and communist ideals and convictions, and that the book's popularity shows the truth-power of the Manifesto in the new era. Wang opens with publishing figures. A new single-volume edition compiled by the Central Compilation and Translation Bureau appeared in December 2014 and, by March 2018, had gone through ten printings totalling 640,000 copies. A further edition in a special collection marking Marx's 200th birthday reached 392,000 copies by May, and a hardback commemorative edition added 20,000. Wang reports that over three and a half years the People's Publishing House editions alone passed one million copies. The commentary then cites Xi Jinping's emphasis on studying Marxist theory as the Party's "essential skill", his 2016 speech on the Party's founding ideals, and the Politburo study session of 23 April 2018 devoted to the Manifesto. It also recalls Engels's remark that the Manifesto's circulation in a country indicates the state of its workers' movement and of large-scale industry. Wang reads the Manifesto's popularity as evidence that full and rigorous self-governance of the Party has been effective, that Party unity and relations with the public have improved, and that the people endorse the Party's governance. Wang concludes that ideals and convictions have grown firmer, that enthusiasm for the classics is rising among Party members, students and society, and that the achievements under Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era have increased the number of people abroad who take Marxism seriously. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Party-aligned commentary in 2018 linked book sales to the Party's self-governance and ideological confidence.

The historical roots of American trade bullying 美国贸易霸凌主义的历史溯源 Dong Yan Writing in Guangming Daily in July 2018, during the US-China trade war, Dong asks why the United States acts so unilaterally in trade. Some analyses blame one leader's personal style. Dong instead looks to US trade history and argues that trade has long served as a tool of American economic and political hegemony, a pattern the author calls trade bullying (maoyi baling zhuyi). The commentary opens with Charles Kindleberger's 1973 "hegemonic stability theory", which Dong says merely legitimises hegemony. It then moves through several periods: protectionism from 1776 to the First World War, the Smoot-Hawley tariff of 1930, Cold War embargoes and investment screening, and postwar relations with Japan and Europe. It ends with the present value-chain economy and a 2018 economists' letter. Dong argues that the US has used protectionism at every stage of its development and has paired it with multilateral free-trade institutions after 1945. The article cites the 1930 tariff, which raised average duties to 59%, and a two-thirds fall in world trade from 1929 to 1934. It describes export controls on the Soviet Union and the 1975 Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States as strategic tools, now aimed at China's high-tech industries. Dong says the US both nurtured and suppressed its allies, citing its deficit with Japan and trade disputes with Europe. Its stated rules and order, in Dong's view, amount to double standards. Dong concludes that bullying will provoke retaliation and may hurt the US itself. In today's value chains, the article says, tariffs fall on foreign-added content, which it puts at 35–40% of China's exports to the US. Dong compares the 1,028 economists who warned Congress in 1930 with the more than 1,100 who wrote to Trump in May 2018, both ignored. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese official commentary framed the 2018 trade war historically.

The contemporary crisis of capitalism and the rise and fall of Western identity politics 资本主义当代危机与西方身份政治学兴衰 Zhang Liang Zhang Liang asks why Western identity politics, which presented itself as an alternative to capitalism, declined quickly after the 2008 financial crisis, just when neoliberalism seemed discredited. The author argues that its theoretical flaws were exposed by the crisis, and that it declined because it was drawn into the ideology it set out to criticise. This newspaper commentary traces the origins of identity politics in the 1970s and 1980s, when traditional workers' movements waned and new social movements took over the Western left. It covers postwar immigration, the strain on the welfare state, the neoliberal turn, and the collapse of the socialist bloc. It also covers the influence of postmodernism, and three stages of development, from deconstructing binary identities to reasserting suppressed identities and, finally, to using difference as resistance. Zhang gives three reasons for the decline. First, identity politics adopted the neoliberal image of the person as a consumer, so that its critique became complicit in market ideology. Second, its alternative to capitalism stayed at the level of ideological imagination, without changing the mode of production, and so amounted to patching up the system. Third, the bourgeoisie took over identity issues, especially race, to deflect attention in times of crisis. In Zhang's reading, the root error was treating Marxism and postmodernism as equals. Zhang concludes that theoretical innovation must be guided by Marxism. The author calls for restoring the working class's foundational and leading role, arguing that marginalised groups belong to the working class and can unite only on the basis of class identity. Zhang also calls for a historical-materialist view that takes the development of the productive forces as the basic measure of social progress, and links this to common prosperity. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a Chinese Marxist commentator assesses Western identity politics.

The historical position of the new era in the development of world socialism and its major significance 新时代在世界社会主义发展中的历史方位及其重大意义 Wang Tingyou Writing in 2018, Wang Tingyou asks where the "new era" of socialism with Chinese characteristics, declared at the 19th Party Congress (2017), stands within the history of world socialism, and what follows from that position. The article argues that Chinese socialism is an important component of world socialism and now acts as its mainstay, and that grasping this relationship is a precondition for understanding Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The article has three parts. The first discusses the idea of a "historical position" and traces how Lenin, Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping each defined the stage their movement had reached, culminating in Xi Jinping's 2013 survey of Chinese socialism from the standpoint of world socialism. The second part reviews the mutual relationship between China and world socialism: Soviet and international support for China, then China's contribution, the Soviet and East European collapse, the neoliberal turn in the West, and the Chinese reform record. The third part sets out three ways the new era matters for world socialism. Wang contends that the new era is the product of the historical, theoretical and practical logic of Chinese socialism. In the author's account, the Soviet and East European collapse pushed world socialism into a trough, with socialist states falling from 15 to 5, while China held its position and kept advancing reform and opening up. Wang sets this against what the article calls the most serious crisis of Western capitalism since the Second World War, citing the 2008 financial crisis, Occupy Wall Street and the "yellow vests". The three significances are: that China's development displays the superiority of the socialist system and the viability of Marxism; that Xi Jinping Thought offers experience on Party governance, socialist construction and social development to other countries and parties; and that Chinese success encourages Marxist parties elsewhere, who the author says remain marginal. Wang cites Gennady Zyuganov's 2017 remarks that China, Cuba and Vietnam inspire socialist forces. Wang concludes that, with the example, experience, material strength and ideological guidance of new-era Chinese socialism, scientific socialism and world socialism will develop greatly, shifting the balance of forces between socialism and capitalism and bringing about a renewal of world socialism. The article also presents China as a builder of peace and a contributor to a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist scholar placed the new era within the history of world socialism in 2018, and how official discourse linked Xi Jinping Thought to the global socialist movement.

The threefold meaning of inheriting and promoting revolutionary culture in the new era 新时代传承弘扬革命文化的三重意涵 Liu Xiaohua This short commentary, first published in Guangming Daily on 3 August 2018, asks what it means to inherit and promote revolutionary culture in the new era. Liu defines revolutionary culture as the cultural form created by the Communist Party and the people during the revolutionary years. The article argues that it has three meanings, and that it must be grasped in all three. The piece is organised in three short sections. Each takes one function of revolutionary culture: as a foundation of cultural confidence, as a historical resource for consolidating the Party's governing base, and as a source of guidance for the people's spiritual home. Liu draws on statements by Xi Jinping, Deng Xiaoping and Mao Zedong, and on the Party's early rules of conduct. On cultural confidence, Liu argues that revolutionary culture supplies spiritual nourishment, through the ideals and convictions of revolutionary forebears, and theoretical depth, because it is a result of adapting Marxism to Chinese conditions. On governance, the author holds that the mass-line experience it carries, such as the disciplines of the Jinggangshan period, offers lessons for the people-centred development philosophy and for keeping close ties between Party and people. On spiritual life, Liu notes that reform and opening up has improved material life but has also brought loss of belief, spiritual slackness and moral decline. Revolutionary culture, the article contends, shows a life of conviction under harsh conditions and can help people rebuild their spiritual world. Liu concludes that revolutionary culture is a source of confidence, a historical resource for the Party's rule and a practical inspiration for contemporary spiritual life. The text is a brief, programmatic statement in the official register of the 19th Party Congress (2017). Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated writing in 2018 justified the continuing relevance of revolutionary culture.

The ontological status of speech and its critical function A study of Jacques Bidet's critical theory of modernity 言语的本体论地位及其批判功能 Tang Zhengdong Tang Zhengdong examines how the French Marxist philosopher Jacques Bidet builds a critique of modernity on the concept of speech (parole). Tang argues that Bidet pushes the critical tension in speech further than Habermas and others who read modernity through discourse. In Tang's reading, Bidet shows that the social force of categories is not a mere ideological surface but reflects the logic of class struggle. The article ultimately judges Bidet's framework subjectivist and short of historical materialism. The article draws mainly on Bidet's Theorie generale (A General Theory), his contributions to the Dictionnaire Marx contemporain, and Exploring Marx's Capital. It moves through three themes: the ontological status of speech and the move from meta-structure to structure; the social efficacy of concepts and the critical function of speech; and the politics of common deliberation that Bidet proposes. Tang places Bidet in a line running from the French regulation school and Bourdieu to Habermas, and compares his claims with passages from Marx and Engels. Tang's central claim is that Bidet treats the immediacy of speech as a necessary fiction with ontological standing. Speech is a proclamation that lets everything between people be re-examined, and it calls for mediations: contract, cooperation and government, with individual and central contracts containing one another. Bidet's interest lies in the antagonism between what modern society proclaims and what it actually is, and in the transition from meta-structure to structure. He reads Marx's critique of bourgeois categories as a philosophical questioning of market-only contract. He treats exploitation and ownership as contestable, reversible facts resting on a common will. Emancipation then comes through deliberative planning, public ownership and political democracy, with alliances between the people and holders of 'qualification capital'. Tang credits Bidet with an original account of speech's critical and emancipatory role, more than with new concepts. He argues, however, that this account rests on a subjectivist reading. Bidet, in Tang's view, ignores the difference between commodity exchange in general and generalised exchange under capitalism, and does not read ownership through the internal contradictions of the mode of production. He therefore underrates the objective constraints and laws of social structure that Marx stressed. Read the original if you study Western Marxism, French Marxism or Bidet in particular, and want a Chinese philosophical assessment of his view of speech, contract and class.

The modern predicament of Western democracy: from Marx to post-Marxism 西方民主的现代困境: 从马克思到后马克思主义 Xie Yazhou Why is Western democracy losing its political force, and is capitalism or democracy itself to blame? Xie Yazhou opens with Žižek's remark on Lee Kuan Yew, Sandel's worry that Americans are losing control of the forces governing their lives, and the diagnosis of a democratic crisis by the Trilateral Commission and American neoconservatives. The article argues that Marx traced the predicament to a "civilizational defect" in the modern political sphere, not mainly to capital's logic, and that post-Marxism tries to remedy it through radical democracy. The article has three parts. The first reconstructs Marx's early critique of the developed modern state, drawing on the Introduction to the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right and the essay On the Jewish Question, with Rousseau and Kant as reference points. The second turns to post-Marxist thinkers, mainly Laclau and Mouffe, with Žižek, Jameson, Sandel, Habermas, Gramsci and Schmitt as interlocutors. The third offers reflections on how to leave the predicament, ending with a Chinese standpoint. Xie's core argument is that, for Marx, the modern state rests on a conception of freedom as separation. It splits people into egoistic private individuals and an illusory political citizen, so that people cannot grasp themselves as a "species" through democratic life. The state thus abandons both people and civil society, and civil society grows by its own logic until capital absorbs and "rationalises" it, leaving politics empty. Post-Marxists such as Mouffe and Laclau share this alarm and seek to restore politics through antagonism, a plurality of political spaces, democratic citizenship and a hegemony of radical democratic values. Xie notes that this leaves the capitalist class character of democracy unchanged. Xie concludes that only two paths exist: remedying democracy's defect so it becomes "people's democracy" able to control capitalism, or smashing the capitalist system, which the author rejects as a historical regression. Politics without a party organisational form, Xie says, is politics without politics. The article closes by contrasting Western procedural democracy with socialist democracy under the Communist Party's unified leadership, and calls for confidence in the institutions and theory of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist reading of Marx's early political writings alongside Laclau and Mouffe's radical democracy, and how that reading is turned toward a defence of the Chinese political path.

The Sino-US trade dispute within the global trade system: an interview with Professor David Kotz 全球贸易体系下的中美贸易争端——大卫·科茨教授访谈录 Zhang Daiwei This is an interview conducted by Zhang Daiwei of Tsinghua University with the US Marxist economist David M. Kotz, a representative of the social structure of accumulation school at the University of Massachusetts Amherst. It took place during Kotz's visit to Tsinghua in May 2018, as the Trump administration's tariffs on steel, aluminium and Chinese goods were being announced. Kotz argues that the measures aim to contain China's rise, that the dispute so far is a trade threat rather than a full trade war, and that a trade war would damage both sides. The interview has five parts: the background and causes of the dispute; the current global trade system and its history; the features of a more rational trade system; views on China's rise; and forecasts of how the conflict will develop. Kotz compares the dispute with the Cold War, with US–Japan relations in the 1980s and with the Smoot-Hawley tariff of 1930. He also discusses US media and public opinion, the 2018 midterm elections and the 2020 presidential race. Kotz traces the global trade system to capitalism's drive for profit, in the spirit of the Communist Manifesto, and distinguishes regulated capitalism and the Bretton Woods order from the neoliberal system after the 1970s. He holds that this system strengthens capital against workers, and that patents on knowledge, which he calls a public good, restrict technological progress. He also says free trade freezes developing countries into their existing comparative advantage and pressures socialist economies to adopt capitalist forms. He notes that South Korea and China grew through state-led industrial policy, and that the US itself used tariffs and appropriated British textile technology, citing Ha-Joon Chang's Kicking Away the Ladder. On this basis he contends that US demands that China abandon industrial policy are contradictory. Kotz proposes four principles for a fairer system: temporary protection for developing countries, freedom to pursue industrial policy, broad access to new technology, and permitted capital controls. He sees Made in China 2025 as an upgrading strategy rather than a bid for domination, and argues that US job losses should be met with domestic employment and welfare policies, not tariffs. He proposes dialogue in the short term, reform of the trade system in the medium term, and a world of production for need rather than profit in the long term. He says big US business opposes the tariffs but backs containing China, and that the tariff policy is Trump's personal project. Read the original if you want a US Marxist's view of the 2018 trade dispute and of Chinese industrial policy, as presented to a Chinese academic audience.

Globalization, anti-globalization and de-globalization from a Marxist perspective 从马克思主义视角看全球化、反全球化和逆全球化 Zheng Yiming Zhang Chaoying Writing in 2018, after the 2008 financial crisis and the 2016 "black swan" events (the British Brexit vote and the US presidential election), Zheng Yiming and Zhang Chaoying ask how globalization, anti-globalization and the current wave of "de-globalization" (逆全球化) should be understood from a Marxist standpoint. They argue that anti-globalization and de-globalization are both companions of globalization, which remains the main trend of world history. De-globalization, in their view, is a temporary and unsustainable "speed bump". The article has four sections. It first grounds globalization in Marx's theory of world history; it then examines the anti-globalization movement, from the 1999 Seattle protests to critiques of neoliberalism and the "democratic deficit"; it analyses the causes of the present de-globalization wave; and it closes with a "new type of globalization" associated with China's initiatives. It draws on Marx and Engels, on Chomsky, Fukuyama, Held and McGrew, and on James Petras. The authors reject both the view that globalization is a natural result of productive forces and the view that it is Westernization under capital. They hold that it results from both, driven by the social character of large-scale industry and the expansionary nature of capital. They separate anti-globalization, voiced by labour organisations and the marginalised against capitalist globalization, from the present de-globalization, which comes from governments and leaders in the US and UK, once the main beneficiaries. They trace its causes to the intensified basic contradiction of capitalism, deindustrialization and financialization that leave the real economy in crisis, and uneven development that widens inequality. They also cite figures on the falling ratio of world trade to world GDP in 2015. The authors conclude that de-globalization serves monopoly bourgeois interests, lacks majority support (they note Trump's popular-vote deficit) and cannot reverse the trend. They argue that, under Xi Jinping's leadership, China's Belt and Road Initiative and the call for a community with a shared future for mankind point toward an open, inclusive, balanced and win-win globalization, which they link to Marx and Engels's idea of a "real community". Read the original if you want an example of how Chinese Marxist scholars in 2018 framed Trump-era de-globalization through world-history theory and official foreign-policy concepts.

Habermas in environmental thought 环境思想中的哈贝马斯 Robert Gunderson Xiao Xiaofang Environmental scholars disagree sharply about Jürgen Habermas. Some see his social thought as useful for improving the human relationship with nature, especially through discourse-based decision-making on environmental risk. Others call his system an "ecological disaster" because of its anthropocentrism and its break with the first generation of the Frankfurt School. Gunderson and Xiao, writing in Marxism and Reality (2018), argue that both camps read Habermas accurately: he is at once an anthropocentric Kantian and a forerunner of ecological democracy. The article first examines Habermas's critique of Horkheimer, Adorno and Marcuse and his concept of a "technical cognitive interest" in controlling nature, along with the environmental objections to it. Critics discussed include Di Nolcia, Whitebook, Vogel (as critic of the early work), Bookchin, Neilson and Eckersley. It then turns to the mature theory of communicative action and discourse ethics, sorting the environmental responses into supporters, revisionists and critics. Supporters include Brulle, Webler, Eling, Rosa, Renn and McCright, and Dietz. The revisionists are Dryzek and Eckersley, and the critics are Murphy and Kreps. The authors' central move is to separate Habermas's early "substantive" claims about nature from his mature "procedural" theory. Critics, in their account, rightly object that the technical interest is empirically untenable and historically blind, and that Habermas abandoned the first generation's critique of the domination of nature. Supporters show that discourse-based procedures can bring the public into environmental decisions in place of technocratic expertise. Revisionists such as Dryzek and Eckersley try to extend discourse ethics to non-human interests, for example through spokespersons for nature. The authors consider the objections of Murphy (utopianism, pluralism of values) and Kreps (non-humans cannot consent) reasonable but less persuasive. They note that the ideal speech situation is presented as an attainable-but-unrealisable standard and that Dryzek's view of life-support capacity as a generalisable interest answers Murphy. Gunderson and Xiao propose two routes for continuing the "greening" of Habermas. The first is to reconstruct his break with the first generation and combine its social ecology with communicative action theory. The second, which they regard as more practical, is to keep developing discourse-based environmental decision models while attending to the environmental critiques. They hold that Habermas's anthropocentric limits should be corrected, not that his critical theory should be discarded. Read the original if you want a systematic map of environmental readings of Habermas, from Marcuse's critics to Dryzek's and Eckersley's attempts to represent nature in deliberative democracy.

Why has a "Marx fever" returned in the West? 西方为何再现“马克思热” Yu Haiqing Yu Haiqing asks why interest in Marx has revived in Western societies, a decade after the 2008 financial crisis and around the 200th anniversary of Marx's birth in 2018. The short commentary answers that capitalism's continuing troubles keep pushing Western observers back to Marx's analysis of capitalism. The article surveys three groups. These are Western media and left-leaning politicians, Western intellectuals and scholars, and Western communist parties. It cites the New York Times, Quartz and Teen Vogue, Jeremy Corbyn, John McDonnell and Yanis Varoufakis, and scholars such as Immanuel Wallerstein, Slavoj Žižek, Wendy Brown and David Harvey. Yu argues that stagnation, widening inequality, terrorism, refugee flows and populism have deepened capitalism's predicament, and even Francis Fukuyama now concedes social division and the workers' plight. In this account, media tributes, anniversary conferences, and work by Samir Amin, Richard Wolff and John Bellamy Foster refute claims that Marxism is outdated, useless or bankrupt. Communist parties in Britain, Australia, Russia, France and elsewhere held commemorations, and the US and Greek parties took part in labour and anti-austerity struggles. Yu concludes that the repeated revivals show Marxism's vitality and its truth, because Western practice cannot avoid the general laws of capitalist development that Marx revealed. The author ties this to Xi Jinping's anniversary speech and calls for stronger confidence in the path, theory, system and culture of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese Marxist researchers read the 2018 Western Marx anniversary coverage.

Socialism with Chinese characteristics from the perspective of the world-system Commemorating the 40th anniversary of reform and opening up 世界体系视野下的中国特色社会主义 Zhou Miao Marking forty years of reform and opening up, Zhou Miao asks what world-systems theory, which the article also calls the Marxism of the world-system, can tell us about the origins, success and global significance of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The author argues that China's rise should be read against the long cycles of the capitalist world-system, and that its success lies in using that system while keeping autonomous accumulation under the basic socialist economic and political institutions. The article has three parts. The first reviews the rise of the West and the position of backward countries, drawing on Wallerstein, Frank and the Needham question. The second turns to cycles in the capitalist world-system: Kondratieff long waves, Wallerstein's hegemonic cycles and Arrighi's systemic cycles of accumulation. The third discusses the world significance of socialism with Chinese characteristics and the international pressures on China's rejuvenation. Zhou draws three main lines. First, world-systems scholars hold that peripheral states cannot escape their position while the capitalist world-system exists; once capital was fully internationalised in the imperialist stage, the author says, the way out lay in changing the system through another social order, namely socialism. Second, Zhou reads long-wave and hegemonic-cycle theory as showing that the American cycle is in its late phase, with financialisation and the 2008 crisis resembling earlier late-wave crises. Reform and opening up in 1978 is presented as a strategic choice that took advantage of such an opening. Third, citing Arrighi, Zhou attributes China's success to retaining the basic socialist system and autonomous accumulation while partly integrating into the world-system. Zhou concludes that China, as the new reference point of world socialism (following Jiang Hui's periodisation of Germany, Russia and China), can strengthen the Global South and promote a new international order. Hegemonic decline, the author warns, tends to bring conflict, and the United States is described as treating China as its main challenger, so strategic vigilance and peaceful development are needed. The author calls for deepening reform while upholding the dominant position of public ownership, so that China avoids dependent accumulation. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist scholar draws on Wallerstein, Frank and Arrighi to interpret China's development path and its relations with the United States.

The historic mission of university teachers of ideological and political theory courses 高校思政课教师的时代重任 Lan Botao Writing in Guangming Daily in June 2018, Lan Botao asks what role teachers of ideological and political theory courses in Chinese universities should play in the new era. The commentary argues that their central task is to equip students' minds with Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and to strengthen students' faith in socialism with Chinese characteristics. Lan holds that teachers must see themselves in three roles: researcher, communicator and practitioner. The piece opens from a Central Committee and State Council document on teacher-training reform, which says a strong nation first needs strong teachers. It then takes the three roles in turn. Each section draws on remarks by Xi Jinping, and one cites Marx's statement that every true philosophy is the spiritual quintessence of its time. As researchers, Lan argues, teachers must follow the practice of socialism with Chinese characteristics closely and study its major theoretical achievements. Otherwise the courses lose their "source of living water", and the teachers cannot explain the Eight Clarifications and Fourteen Persistences. As communicators, they should turn theory into concrete cases, tie it to topical issues students care about, and attend to timing, degree and effect. As practitioners, they should start from students' daily lives and use lively language. They should also fit their methods to student type: reasoned argument for the humanities and social sciences, worked examples for science and engineering students. Lan concludes that teachers must define their role clearly as researcher, communicator and practitioner in order to meet the responsibility the new era gives them. Read the original if you want a short example of how official discourse in 2018 described the duties and teaching methods expected of university political-theory teachers.

University ideological and political education should adapt to "three changes" 高校思政教育当顺应“三变” Zhang Zhenli Writing in Guangming Daily in July 2018, Zhang Zhenli asks how ideological and political education in universities should be done in the new era. The commentary opens with Xi Jinping's remarks of 2 May 2018 at Peking University that cultivating builders and successors of socialism is a common mission of all schools. Zhang's answer is that such education must adapt to three changes: in its audience, its purpose and its method. The piece first notes that results are uneven. Programmes at Tsinghua, Peking University and Beihang University are praised by students, and some teachers have become popular figures. Other institutions, Zhang says, still rely on reading scripts, shouting slogans and declaring resolve, which leaves students dissatisfied and sometimes resistant. On the audience, Zhang describes university students as the youth group with the strongest sense of subjectivity, rationality and questioning. They want to know whether a conclusion's premises hold, prefer historical detail to grand narrative, and seek practical rationality as well as appealing values. On purpose, Zhang argues that education should teach students to use the Marxist standpoint, viewpoint and method to observe and analyse the world. Patriotic enthusiasm alone, in Zhang's view, risks "good intentions doing harm". On method, Zhang calls for dialogue and discussion in place of the teacher's monologue, linking world affairs to students' own circumstances. Zhang concludes, citing Gadamer, that each era must interpret inherited texts in its own way. It is therefore the right time, Zhang argues, to reconstruct how the classics of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context are interpreted in university teaching. Read the original if you want a short example of how a 2018 official-press commentary framed teaching reform in Chinese university ideological education.

Promoting deep integration of Party building and ideological and political theory courses in universities 推动高校党建与思政课深度融合 Zhang Aihua This short commentary, published in Guangming Daily in August 2018, asks how university Party building and ideological and political theory courses (sizhengke) can be deeply integrated. Zhang argues that the courses are an important vehicle and advantage channel for Party building. Integrating the two, in Zhang's view, would unify theoretical cultivation with practical guidance in the new era. The article opens with remarks by Xi Jinping on higher education and moral education. It then has three parts: why Party building must provide ideological leadership, why folding Party building into the courses matters, and what practical routes to take. Zhang presents the courses as the "bridge" for turning Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era into students' thinking and action. Three significances are given. The first is Marxist ideological education. The second is the fundamental task of cultivating people through moral education. The third is building a high-calibre team of Party-affairs cadres, since a long-standing split between Party building and teaching ("two layers of skin") is said to leave Party work formalistic. For practice, Zhang calls for strengthening Marxist guidance, building Marxist schools and improving the political education of young teachers. Zhang also proposes new teaching vehicles such as Party-building salons, practical courses, red-culture visits and internet-based platforms. Zhang further urges coordination: course teachers giving Party lectures, Party workers teaching current-affairs courses, and mixed teacher–student Party branches. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary in 2018 framed the link between campus Party organisation and ideological teaching.

Mao Zedong and the mass line of the Communist Party of China 毛泽东与中国共产党的群众路线 Tian Xinming Written when the 18th Party Congress (2012) had called for an educational campaign on the Party's mass line, Tian Xinming argues that the campaign should rest on a close study of Mao Zedong's thought on the subject. The article's thesis is that Mao was the founder of the Party's mass line, and that the line is a model case of the sinification of Marxism and an original achievement of Marxism adapted to the Chinese context. The article has three parts. The first traces how the mass line was formulated in Party documents, from the 1981 historical resolution and the Party constitution (in its current wording since 1992) back to the Seventh Congress (1945) and the Eighth Congress (1956). The second examines the attitude half of the formula, "everything for the masses, everything relying on the masses". The third examines the method half, "from the masses, to the masses". Tian draws mainly on Mao's Selected Works, Liu Shaoqi's and Deng Xiaoping's reports on revising the constitution, and Party resolutions. Tian argues that the mass line applies the Marxist principle that the people are the creators of history to all Party work. On attitude, Mao's statements from the peasant movement to the War of Resistance and the Seventh Congress are read as an expression of this historical-materialist standpoint. On method, Tian links Mao's 1943 decision on leadership to his theory of knowledge in On Practice: leaders gather scattered opinions, turn them into systematic ones, return them to the masses and test them in action. Tian rejects the reading that gives the masses practice and leaders knowledge, and notes that leaders' special functions make it easier for them to lose touch with the masses and decide wrongly. Mao's opposition to both tailism and commandism is presented as guarding against two errors: lagging behind the masses' consciousness and running ahead of it. Tian concludes that attitude and method are inseparable and together form the complete mass line, which a 1990 Party resolution called the fundamental work line for carrying out the Party's ideological, political and organisational lines. With seeking truth from facts and independence, the mass line is described as part of the living soul of Mao Zedong Thought, and as Mao's most valuable spiritual legacy to the Party. Read the original if you want a documented account of how the mass line entered Party constitutions and how Chinese Party theorists tie it to Mao's epistemology.

Uncovering the contemporary value of Mao Zedong Thought 发掘毛泽东思想的时代价值 Li Jie This is an interview in which Li Jie, a long-time researcher of Mao Zedong, answers four questions from reporters Chao Tianyi and Liu Fang of Chinese Social Sciences Today. The questions ask how researchers should resist historical nihilism, what in Mao Zedong Thought still matters, how to understand the Chinese Dream historically, and why Party and national history should be studied. Li's overall answer is that Mao's errors must be treated honestly but kept distinct from his achievements, and that his method and cultural thinking remain useful guides today. The interview has four sections. The first deals with historical nihilism and Mao's late-life mistakes. The second names two legacies of Mao: his way of treating Marxism, and his reshaping of traditional culture. The third places the Chinese Dream within a "three hundred years" view of history. The fourth discusses Xi Jinping's call to study Party history and the history of the People's Republic. On nihilism, Li argues that critics seize on Mao's late errors, inflate them into a question of character, and blame him for the acts of Lin Biao and Jiang Qing. Li holds the errors were serious and unforgivable but were not deliberate "crimes", and says Mao tried to remedy them. Li proposes arguing from facts calmly, not avoiding sensitive questions, and aiming to win public trust rather than defeat opponents. On Marxism, Li says Mao's chief legacy was applying its principles to Chinese conditions. Li summarises this as seeking truth from facts, the mass line and independence, and says the stance, viewpoint and method of Marxism matter more than fixed formulas. On culture, Li credits Mao's call for a national, popular and scientific culture, which rejects both nihilism towards tradition and wholesale Westernisation. Li describes the first century as running from the Opium War to 1949, the second as building a modern socialist country, and the third as the pursuit of higher-level modernization and better quality. The Chinese Dream, Li says, is inclusive and different from an old imperial self-importance. Li concludes that Party and national history should be told candidly, with achievements as the mainstream and errors as a tributary, and should also serve cultural renewal by honouring heroes and ordinary workers. Read the original if you want to see how a Party historian in 2018 framed Mao's mistakes, his legacy and the Chinese Dream for a general readership.

The Communist Manifesto and the development of the French Communist Party An interview with Jean-Numa Ducange, young theorist of the French Communist Party 《共产党宣言》与法国共产党的发展 Yu Weihai This is an interview, published in 2018 to mark the 200th anniversary of Marx's birth and the 170th anniversary of the Communist Manifesto. Yu Weihai interviews Jean-Numa Ducange, who is described as a young theorist close to the French Communist Party, a special representative of the Gabriel Péri Foundation and a member of the team translating Marx and Engels into French (GEME). The question is how the Manifesto has been spread in France and what it still means for the French Communist Party (PCF) and the French left. The interview is organised around five questions. They cover the history of the Manifesto's translation and circulation in France, the ideas of the text that the PCF still draws on, how the party and the wider left study Marx, the influence of Marxism on French politics, and Ducange's personal reading of the text. Yu also asks whether the PCF could produce a manifesto of its own. Ducange traces French editions from a lost 1848 version to Laura Lafargue's 1885 translation, which appeared in Jules Guesde's newspaper. He says the PCF, founded in 1920, was the first party to publish the Manifesto in France, and that the text circulated widely while the party was a major force between 1935 and 1980. Marxism and the PCF declined from the 1980s, but he reports a renewed interest in Marx in the early 2000s, read with less political partisanship. He argues that the Manifesto has little direct ideological influence on today's PCF, which he calls relatively short of Marxist ideology. Even so, its treatment of the nation, capitalist expansion and alliances still bears on current debates over sovereignty, Europe and left alliances. He adds that Marx's writings on France, such as The Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte, must be read alongside it. He also notes the Manifesto's Eurocentric limits. Ducange says the Manifesto remains a foundational text for the PCF and still gives hope for the future. He credits the PCF with popularising Marxism among hundreds of thousands, even millions, of French people, despite misreadings. He regrets that the party has no equivalent founding text. He proposes a new manifesto for the twenty-first century, to be discussed with the 'radical left' and pursued only through an internationalist approach. He describes Chinese experience as very valuable and calls for China–France cooperation across differences in social system. Read the original if you want a French Communist-affiliated historian's view of the Manifesto's reception in France and of the PCF's current position, as presented to a Chinese audience.

The Communist Party of Australia's active exploration of the socialist movement 澳共对社会主义运动的积极探索 Yang Xiaoji This short commentary, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in May 2018, reports on the 13th National Congress of the Communist Party of Australia (CPA), held in Sydney in December 2017. Yang argues that the congress's resolutions show a distinctive Party analysis of capitalism in crisis and a realistic programme for advancing the socialist movement at home. The article opens with a brief history: the CPA's founding in 1920, its dissolution after the Soviet and East European upheavals, and the 1996 renaming of the Socialist Party of Australia, which split from the earlier CPA in 1971, as the Communist Party of Australia. It then summarises the congress's assessment of capitalism and the practical guidelines adopted under the theme "Taking the Party to the People". Bob Briton was re-elected general secretary, and the programme and constitution were amended. On the first point, Yang reports the CPA's view that the 2008 financial crisis stemmed from monopoly corporations shifting capital into the virtual economy, leaving the real economy starved. According to the CPA, Western states are now cutting workers' welfare and exporting their contradictions through imperialist aggression. It cites Roy Morgan Research figures putting real Australian unemployment in 2017 above 9.5%, against an official rate of about 5.5%. The guidelines stress the Party's leading role, grassroots branch-building, work among workers whose composition has changed, and a two-stage path in the 2005 programme: an anti-imperialist, anti-monopoly democratic stage, then a socialist revolution. They also stress Party unity, a broad united front including trade unions and Indigenous and non-Indigenous Australians, and international solidarity, including with Cuba and the Polish communists. Yang concludes that the CPA's understanding of the crisis is distinctive and its action plan realistic. The author adds that the Party's particular exploration offers a new perspective for understanding the world socialist movement. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese-language account of the CPA's 2017 congress and how a Chinese commentator presents it.

Scientific socialism has strong vitality 科学社会主义具有强大生机活力 Wu Enyuan Writing in the People's Daily on 8 June 2018, Wu Enyuan takes up Xi Jinping's speech at the commemoration of the 200th anniversary of Marx's birth. The commentary asks what the history of scientific socialism shows about its vitality. Wu argues that studying Xi's remarks helps readers see that vitality and grasp the significance of socialism with Chinese characteristics entering a new era. The piece is a short historical survey that runs from the Communist Manifesto of 1848 to the present. It passes through the October Revolution, the Great Depression of 1929–1932, the upheavals in Eastern Europe and the Soviet Union around 1990, and the years after the 2008 financial crisis. Wu's core argument is that each stage of the Chinese Communist Party's history confirms the strength of scientific socialism. Wu says the Party combined the basic principles of Marxism with China's concrete conditions, which produced three leaps for the Chinese nation: from being weak to standing up, then to becoming prosperous, then to becoming strong. Each leap is said to prove that only socialism could save China, that only socialism with Chinese characteristics could develop China, and that only upholding and developing it can achieve the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Wu credits Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era with a major contribution to scientific socialism. Wu also presents Western talk of "the end of history", of a "China collapse" and of a "China threat" as attempts to contain China. Wu concludes that looking back, comparing other paths and looking ahead all reveal the truth of Marxism and the vitality of scientific socialism. This, Wu says, should strengthen the Four-sphere Confidence. Read the original if you want a compact example of how a Party-affiliated scholar told the history of socialism in 2018 for a general newspaper audience.

An innovative theory of far-reaching significance for the development of world socialism and human progress 对世界社会主义发展和人类进步具有深远意义的创新理论 Lin Jianhua Writing in Economic Daily in June 2018, Lin Jianhua asks what global significance Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era holds. The article argues that the Thought, which arose as socialism with Chinese characteristics entered a new era, makes a historic contribution to developing Marxism, to world socialism and to human progress. In Lin's account it deepens understanding of the laws governing Communist Party rule, socialist construction and human social development. The commentary has three parts. It first places the Thought in the line of adapting Marxism to Chinese conditions, from the arrival of Marxism-Leninism after the October Revolution. It then considers the Thought's meaning for the world socialist movement, drawing on Xi Jinping's historical periodisation of socialism. Finally it turns to the Thought's implications for global development, for building a community with a shared future for mankind, and for developing countries choosing a path to modernization. Lin presents the Thought as the latest result of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, and as contemporary Chinese Marxism and twenty-first-century Marxism. It is said to answer systematically what kind of socialism with Chinese characteristics should be upheld and how, drawing on a people-centred outlook, harmony between humanity and nature, and the community with a shared future. The article stresses, following Xi, that the periods before and after reform and opening up must not be used to negate each other. It also argues that China's experience shows more than one road to modernization. Lin lists three Chinese contributions: Party governance through full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, state governance through modernizing the governance system and capacity, and global governance through the Belt and Road Initiative. Lin also cites China's economic weight, including a contribution to global growth above 30% for several years. Lin concludes that China has moved from having no path, to following others' paths, to its own path, and now to showing others a path, which is described as a contribution of world value. With the "two centenary goals" achieved, the Thought's historical standing in the world socialist movement is expected to become clearer. The article ends with a confident declaration that China is nearing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a representative example of how Party-aligned commentary in 2018 framed the international significance of Xi Jinping Thought.

Lessons of twentieth-century socialist practice for the development of socialism in the twenty-first century 20世纪社会主义实践给21世纪社会主义发展提供的启示 Song Mengrong Writing in 2018, Song asks what a century of 'actually existing socialism' can teach socialism in the twenty-first century and the cause of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The article argues that this history, running from the October Revolution through the upheavals in the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe to the rise of socialism with Chinese characteristics, yields eight basic lessons. The article takes a macro-historical view and sets out the eight lessons in turn. They concern ideals and convictions; the early stage of the new socialist civilization; the continuing dominance of contemporary capitalism; the people's wellbeing; the link between socialism and reform; the role of the Party; national security and 'soft and hard power'; and anti-imperialism and anti-hegemonism in international relations. Each is supported by references to Soviet and Eastern European experience and to statements by Xi Jinping. Song's central claim is that twentieth-century socialism arose in economically and culturally backward countries on the periphery of the world capitalist system. In Song's reading, 'impatience' and attempts to leap over historical stages left institutional defects, so the new civilization is still at its starting point. It must therefore develop in interaction with capitalism and the world system, combining openness with self-reliance, and must draw on market mechanisms even where they carry capitalist features. Song adds that the Soviet collapse shows the decisive role of the Party: where it changes or weakens, socialism declines. The collapse also exposed gaps in ideological and overall security, and Song attributes the Soviet turn to hegemonism to the damage done to socialism's international image. Song concludes that Chinese Communists have grasped these lessons and applied them. Song cites the primary stage of socialism, full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, the anti-corruption campaign since the 18th Party Congress (2012), a comprehensive national security system, and the proposal of a community with a shared future for mankind and the Belt and Road Initiative. Reform is to continue so that it benefits the people, and the rule of law is to replace rule by individuals. Read the original if you want a compact statement of how Chinese Party theorists in 2018 drew lessons from the Soviet experience for socialism with Chinese characteristics.

Marx and Engels's analysis and critique of "true socialism" and its contemporary implications 马克思恩格斯对“真正的社会主义”的分析批判及其当代启示 Li Xiaoguang Many present-day currents claim to be the "true socialism". Li Xiaoguang asks how Marx and Engels analysed the original "true socialism", a German current of the 1840s, and what their method offers for judging what socialism is and how to build it. The article argues that the current rested on Germany's backward socio-economic order, wore the shell of German "philosophy", and in class terms expressed the petty bourgeoisie. In Li's reading, Marx and Engels's critique of these three features pinpoints the current's essential flaw. The article has three parts. The first presents "true socialism" as a distinctive German phenomenon, naming Moses Hess as its main proponent alongside Karl Grün and others. The second traces the works in which Marx and Engels criticised it, from Engels's 1845 writings through The German Ideology and Engels's \"German Socialism in Verse and Prose\" to the Communist Manifesto of 1848, and then sets out three lines of critique. The third draws lessons for today, citing Xi Jinping, Deng Xiaoping and the report to the 19th Party Congress (2017). Li argues that Marx and Engels first attacked the current's theoretical pillars: an abstract, biological view of human nature and a gospel of universal love that rejected violent overthrow. Against this they set the view that the human essence is the ensemble of social relations and that communism is the real movement abolishing the existing state of things. Second, they traced its philosophical premises to Hegelian speculation and Feuerbach's humanism, which Li says detached French socialist writings from the conditions that produced them. Third, they exposed its petty-bourgeois class basis. The current feared both capital and the rising proletariat, and in Marx and Engels's account it became a scarecrow used by absolutist governments against the bourgeoisie. For the present, Li draws three requirements. First, Marxism must remain the sole guiding ideology, and Li opposes pluralism in guiding thought, citing the principle that dropping the basic principles of scientific socialism means abandoning socialism. Second, the people must be the class basis of socialist practice, in contrast with the petty-bourgeois base of \"true socialism\". Third, theory must be combined with practice, so that socialism is neither applied dogmatically nor arbitrarily revised; Li relates this to the new era of socialism with Chinese characteristics and the primary stage of socialism. Read the original if you want a Chinese study of how the \"true socialism\" critique is used to set criteria for judging claims to socialism today.

Characteristics of the early spread of the Communist Manifesto in China Seen through the translation and dissemination of the Manifesto 《共产党宣言》在中国早期传播的特点 Wang Gang Why did the Communist Manifesto lead China's early Marxists to a communist faith, and how did it arrive? Wang argues that before the 1930s its translation and spread were uneven and gradual rather than synchronised. The article identifies four features: incremental translation with selective dissemination, multiple routes and multiple tiers of dissemination, subjective and "Chinese-style" interpretation, and a dual movement of dissemination and the adaptation of Marxism to Chinese conditions. The article covers the period from about 1899 to the late 1920s. It traces translation from isolated sentences (1899–1907), through individual chapters (1908–1919), to Chen Wangdao's first full translation in 1920. It then compares the uses made of the text by missionaries, bourgeois reformers, bourgeois revolutionaries led by Sun Yat-sen, anarchists and early Marxists. Wang also follows the Manifesto's routes into China via Japan, France, Germany, English and Soviet Russia, and its spread through newspapers, schools, societies, publishers, handwritten copies and workers' schools. Wang's central claim is that every group read the Manifesto for its own purposes. Zhu Zhixin took up class struggle and Ye Xiasheng the ten measures of chapter two, both in support of Sun's Three Principles of the People. Among Marxists, Li Dazhao stressed historical materialism and Chen Duxiu the dictatorship of the proletariat, but all did so out of conviction. Wang says translation variation widened or narrowed meanings: citing Gao Fang, the final slogan had 57 renderings before the 1930s. Sun equated communism with his "principle of people's livelihood". Others likened it to traditional Chinese ideals of great harmony and equalisation. Wang holds that such readings eased acceptance but risked distortion and "mechanical application". Wang concludes that early Marxists differed from other groups because they neither smuggled in their own agenda nor spread the text for its own sake. They used it to analyse and solve China's practical problems, as in Li Dazhao's call to apply historical materialism to China and Mao Zedong's rural investigations. In this account, belief was formed and strengthened through the interplay of dissemination and adaptation. Wang urges Communists, now that socialism with Chinese characteristics has entered a new era, to keep studying the classics and hold to the Party's founding mission. Read the original if you want a detailed account of translators, routes and interpretive disputes in the Manifesto's early Chinese reception, as presented in official Chinese scholarship.

New growth areas in contemporary foreign Marxism studies 当代国外马克思主义研究的新增长点 Lei Yu Lei Yu argues that ideology, the production of space, world-systems and biopolitics are the new growth points in contemporary Marxism outside China. Reading these four themes as accounts of capitalism, the author suggests, allows researchers to form a realistic judgement, a theoretical grasp and a critical reflection on capitalism today. The piece appeared in China Social Sciences Today in 2018. The commentary takes each theme in turn. On ideology it follows Lukács, Althusser and Žižek; on space, Lefebvre, Harvey, Soja and Castells; on world-systems, Wallerstein and dependency theory; on biopolitics, Foucault and the Italian line of Negri, Esposito and Agamben. Lei presents these as ways of seeing how capitalism has become more multi-dimensional and more concealed. Lefebvre's shift from producing commodities in space to producing space itself is read as a change in capitalism's reproduction. Wallerstein's world economy is linked to Luxemburg and Lenin, and to the unevenness between centre and periphery. Each theme comes with a warning. Ideology must be tied to its material base, because ideology has no history of its own. Spatial studies must not turn metaphysical or discuss cities in isolation. Left thinkers who worship contingency are said to drift into opportunism and to over-politicise everything. Lei concludes that capitalism should be examined from several angles, with the full history of Marxist thought and capitalism's empirical history as reference points. The author names Marx's historical dialectics, which starts from material life and social being, as the key methodology for studying contemporary capitalism. Read the original if you want a short Chinese-academy overview of how these four strands of foreign Marxism are framed and cautioned against.

Five bright spots in the recent development and changes of communist parties abroad 当今国外共产党发展变化的五大亮点 Chai Shangjin Writing in 2018, the 170th anniversary year of the Communist Manifesto, Chai Shangjin asks how communist parties outside China are faring and what is changing in them. The article argues that these parties are, on the whole, in a clear upward phase after the low point that followed the Soviet collapse. Chai also stresses that they face serious challenges, notably populism and right-wing pressure. The article is organised around five features: the regrouping of strength, the strengthening of organisation, "keeping to fundamentals while innovating" in theory, unity and cooperation within the left, and a growing tendency to "look east" to China. Chai surveys ruling parties (Vietnam, Cuba, Laos, the Democratic People's Republic of Korea, Nepal) and non-ruling parties in Western Europe, Japan, South Asia, South Africa, Latin America, Russia and Central Asia. Membership and seat figures are cited party by party. Chai's central claim is that parties recover where they rebuild organisation and update theory without abandoning Marxism. Parties that stuck to isolated doctrinal statements, or that gave up Marxist guidance and democratic centralism for "flattened" structures, lost members and split, as in Moldova. Parties that restored democratic centralism, strengthened grassroots branches and used online tools, such as those in France, Spain and Vietnam, are presented as gaining strength.
