Chai says many parties now treat Marxism as a guide to action, reject a single model of socialism and pursue parliamentary or legal struggle and left alliances. In his account, the Marx bicentenary conference in Shenzhen in May 2018, with over 70 parties from 50 countries, showed foreign parties' interest in Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, the Belt and Road Initiative and China's poverty reduction. Chai concludes that the central problem for these parties is how to exercise political leadership within broad left fronts while populism squeezes their base. He says China should treat foreign doubts, such as criticism of its wealth gap, rationally. He adds that China neither "imports" nor "exports" models, and that the success of socialism with Chinese characteristics will advance the world socialist movement. Read the original if you want a party-by-party overview, with membership and seat figures, of foreign communist parties as seen from a Chinese Party-affiliated perspective in 2018.

On China's approach to reforming global governance 论全球治理改革的中国方案 Li Dan Writing in 2018, Li Dan asks how China has responded to the crisis of economic globalization and of global governance, and what its proposal for reform contains. The article argues that since the 18th Party Congress (2012) China's leaders, with Xi Jinping at the centre, have produced a fairly systematic 'Chinese approach' (Zhongguo fang'an) to global governance. In Li's account this approach comes at a time when Western-led governance is failing, and it leaves a distinct Chinese imprint on the new round of globalization. The article has three parts. The first sets out why reform of the global governance system is both possible and historically necessary. It points to the shift of economic weight from West to East and to what it calls the failure of US and European governance solutions. The second traces how the Chinese approach took shape in Xi's speeches from 2013 to 2017, from BRICS and G20 addresses through Davos and Geneva to the 19th Party Congress (2017), and in the practice of the Belt and Road Initiative. The third and longest part describes the approach under five headings: governance actors, methods, platforms, paths and goals. Li diagnoses a 'governance deficit' in the expanding range of global problems, the fragmentation of governing actors and the mismatch between demand and supply. On this reading, the present system is really hegemonic 'world governance' by the West, above all the United States, with the Group of Seven at its core. The Chinese approach, by contrast, is said to insist on equal participation and to reject both domination by one state and rule by a few. It favours rule-based consultation, with new and old institutions working side by side: the UN, the WTO, the IMF and the World Bank are kept and added to by the G20, the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation and the Boao Forum. New financial bodies, including the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank and the BRICS bank, are included as well. It also seeks greater representation and institutional power for developing countries. Li concludes that the goal is a community with a shared future for mankind and an inclusive, win-win globalization. The article notes that the idea has been written into several UN resolutions. It expects the Chinese approach to be enriched as China moves from follower to builder and leader, with the Belt and Road Initiative treated as the practical test of Xi's view of global governance. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially aligned account of how Chinese scholars present Xi Jinping's global governance thinking, with citations to his speeches from 2013 to 2017.

Can North Korea replicate the "Vietnam model"? 朝鲜可否复制“越南模式” Pan Jin'e Zhou Zengliang Writing in 2018, after North Korea's sudden shifts in domestic and foreign policy, Pan and Zhou ask whether Pyongyang will follow China and Vietnam into socialist reform and opening up. Media reports said Kim Jong Un told South Korea's president he was willing to learn from the "Vietnam model", and US Secretary of State Pompeo urged North Korea to copy Vietnam's path. The authors answer that North Korea can draw on some Vietnamese practices but cannot replicate the model. The article first defines the "Vietnam model", a term that has no formal definition, through three features of Vietnam's renovation: its economy, its politics and its foreign policy. It then compares North Korea with Vietnam on the country's own intentions, its stage of socialist development, the historical formation of political power, the context of change, and external conditions, including relations with the United States, the two Koreas and China. The authors describe the Vietnam model as a market-led, export-oriented economy with encouragement of private enterprise, "controllable democracy" under Communist Party leadership, and a balancing foreign policy that draws closer to Washington against China. They argue that North Korea differs on each count. Vietnam regards itself as still in a transition to socialism, while North Korea holds to a self-reliant planned economy and the aim of a "strong and prosperous socialist state" that remains unfinished. Vietnam's dispersed leadership contrasts with North Korea's highly centralised power, which the authors trace to colonial-era political traditions, early factional strife and a military confrontation with the US–South Korea alliance. Vietnam began renovation in 1986 amid a regional shift to markets, whereas North Korea has announced a focus on economic development but, the authors stress, no marketisation or integration with the world economy. The authors conclude that North Korea will study selected Vietnamese methods, especially how a socialist state moves from a command economy to using market mechanisms, but will not copy the model. They argue that US–Vietnam ties rest on a shared interest in balancing China, and that North Korea, committed to independence and with no core-interest conflict with China, will not serve as a US tool against Beijing. Pompeo, they predict, is likely to be disappointed. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly view, from 2018, comparing the Vietnamese and North Korean reform paths and the geopolitics around them.

Vietnam's anti-corruption drive: no longer afraid of "breaking the vase to catch the rat"? 越南反腐, 不再担心“逮鼠碎瓶”? Pan Jin'e Writing in early 2018, Pan Jin'e asks why Nguyen Phu Trong, General Secretary of the Communist Party of Vietnam, has moved so forcefully against corruption when he once warned against smashing the vase while catching the rat. The article's answer is that Nguyen spent two years preparing the ground through ideological, institutional and legal measures. In Pan's view he now feels confident enough to drop the caution of his 2014 remark. The commentary opens with Nguyen's October 2014 "catching the rat without breaking the vase" statement, which Vietnamese social media read as an excuse for inaction. It then turns to the post-APEC (2017) crackdown, above all the arrest and public trial of Dinh La Thang, a former Politburo member and Ho Chi Minh City Party secretary. Pan organises the case around four new features: scale and rank, the large sums and interest chains in banking and oil, procedural legality with suspicious timing, and a complicated, murky backstory. Pan cites 205 first-instance corruption cases involving 433 people in 2017, and a trial of Dinh and 21 co-defendants with media access and defence lawyers. The article describes Dinh's illegal investment in Oceanbank and the losses of the state oil group, which linked several state-owned enterprises. It reads the procedure as evidence of progress toward a socialist state under the rule of law. It also notes that the arrests came before the 2015 Criminal Code took effect on 1 January 2018, which dropped the charge used against Dinh. Some observers, Pan reports, see factional motives, since Dinh was promoted by former prime minister Nguyen Tan Dung, who is placed in a "southern" faction opposed to Nguyen Phu Trong's "northern" one. Disputed accounts of how fugitive Trinh Xuan Thanh returned, and the arrest of another fugitive, suggest further cases. Pan concludes that final verdicts and the pursuit of bigger "tigers" remain uncertain, but that Nguyen now voices new slogans: "no one can be an outsider" and a well-fed fire will light even green wood. Since Vietnam has sent delegations to China to learn anti-corruption methods, Pan suggests that success would be a new version of following China in "crossing the river by feeling the stones". Read the original if you want a short Chinese scholarly reading of Vietnam's 2017–18 anti-corruption campaign and its links to China's experience.

New trends in the main international currents of thought today and how to respond 当前国际社会主要思潮新动向新趋势及应对 Li Ruiqin Writing in 2018, Li Ruiqin asks which social and political currents of thought are shaping international politics since the 2008 financial crisis, and how China should respond. The article argues that these currents are diverse yet interlinked, and that they act as a major visible force on world politics. Li characterises them as plural, extreme, borderless, hard to predict and hard to control. The article takes four currents in turn: populism in Europe and the United States, nationalism, religious extremism and terrorism, and trade protectionism with its political expression, anti-globalisation. Each section draws on the 2016–2017 events of its time: Brexit, the Trump presidency, the Austrian, Dutch and French elections, the Russian and US positions on counter-terrorism, and Western trade policy. A closing section sets out the general picture and China's response. Li argues that neoliberal globalisation produced wealth concentration and economic anxiety, feeding left-wing populism, and identity politics, feeding right-wing populism. In Li's reading, the electoral setbacks of populists in the Netherlands, Austria and France are only a pause, because the underlying socio-economic conditions are unchanged. Nationalism is described as the seedbed from which populism, extreme nationalism and religious extremism have historically grown. Religious extremism is presented as an extremely hard problem to govern, made worse by Western interventionist counter-terrorism and by differing definitions of terrorism. Protectionism is read as the economic root of anti-globalisation, which Li sees as the West retreating once globalisation's dividends fade. Li concludes that the currents reveal a world of heightened insecurity, low mutual trust, diffuse nostalgia and passive suspicion of the future. As a response, the author points to the Belt and Road Initiative as a way to counter protectionism and extremism and deepen globalisation, while noting that it faces great-power rivalry and hesitation among some states. Li also calls for vigilance against the infiltration of extremist ideas into China, for the protection of reform and opening up and socialism with Chinese characteristics, and for cooperation through the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, BRICS and the UN. Read the original if you want an example of how a CASS researcher in 2018 framed populism, extremism and protectionism as security and ideological challenges for China.

Marx is still alive, much closer than we imagine Russia's spontaneous and grand commemoration of the 200th anniversary of Marx's birth 马克思还活着, 比我们想象的要近得多 Li Ruiqin Why did Russian society, 27 years after the Soviet Union abandoned Marxism-Leninism, hold so many unofficial events in 2018 to mark the 200th anniversary of Marx's birth? Li Ruiqin takes up this question and argues that the commemorations reflect a conviction, repeated across the events, that "Marx was right". In Li's account they also reflect a continuing reckoning with the Soviet collapse. The article first surveys the events, which Li describes as non-state but national, varied and sustained. They include international forums run by the Communist Party of the Russian Federation, Moscow University and the Russian Academy of Sciences, exhibitions at the State Duma and in museums, and round tables in provincial cities such as Yakutsk, Murmansk and Novosibirsk. It then discusses their unofficial, regional and youth-driven character, and ends with four explanations for the phenomenon. Li draws on speeches by Gennady Zyuganov, Duma deputy speaker Aleksandr Zhukov and others who cite Russian inequality, falling incomes and the oligarchs' wealth as proof of Marx's analysis. In this reading, the post-Soviet record confirms Marx's predictions about finance, concentration of wealth and global capital. Li adds that speakers repeatedly pointed to China's development under Marxist guidance as a successful practice, contrasted with Russia's experience. The article also cites Moscow University professor Alexander Buzgalin to argue that Russia still needs Marxism to understand capitalism, inequality and who holds real power. Li concludes that after nearly three decades of upheaval, Russians can return to Marx with a calmer and more reflective attitude. Li stops short of predicting that Marxism will return to Russia, but holds that the events show Marx's ideas are still relevant there. The article is a Chinese observer's account of Russian commemorations and relies largely on speakers sympathetic to Marxism. Read the original if you want a detailed, Chinese-language inventory of the 2018 Marx bicentenary events in Russia and a view of how Chinese Marxist scholars interpret them.

Foreign assessments highly affirm the achievements of China's 40 years of reform and opening up 国外高度肯定中国改革开放40年成就 Liu Xiaoyun Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2018, on the 40th anniversary of reform and opening up, Liu Xiaoyun collects favourable assessments of China's record from foreign scholars, politicians and journalists. The article's thesis is that these observers see reform and opening up as having brought not only economic take-off but all-round social progress, with significant effects on the wider world. The piece is a compilation of quoted foreign opinion arranged in three sections. The first presents reform and opening up as the driving force behind China's entry into a new era, both domestically and globally. The second asks what explains the success and answers with the leadership of the Communist Party of China. The third treats reform and opening up as offering a Chinese approach to human problems. Quoted speakers include UN Secretary-General António Guterres, Kevin Rudd, Joseph Nye, Kerry Brown-type China specialists from Britain, Iran, India, Japan, Germany, Russia, Sri Lanka and elsewhere. In Liu's selection, foreign commentators point to China's shift from a planned to a market economy and towards consumption- and innovation-led growth, to the poverty reduction of more than 700 million people, and to a reshaped international role through the Belt and Road Initiative. The British scholar John Ross is cited as saying, on World Bank estimates, that China contributes over 30 per cent of annual world economic growth. On the question of cause, quoted voices credit the Party's adherence to Marxism adapted to Chinese conditions, its priority on the people's interests, its timely policy adjustment, and its consultative, multi-party cooperation system. A German scholar, Wolfram Adolphi, cautions that Europeans should not understand the Party by simple analogy. Liu concludes, through the quoted observers, that China's gradual, stability-preserving reforms offer useful experience to other developing countries, even though no country can copy them mechanically and China has not sought to export its model. The article ends by linking China's development to a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a catalogue of how foreign voices were selected and presented in Chinese official-academic discourse on the 40th anniversary of reform and opening up.

Ideological work in the new era must strive to strengthen cohesion and guiding power 新时代意识形态工作要在增强凝聚力和引领力上下功夫 Jiang Hui Writing in 2018, Jiang Hui takes up Xi Jinping's instruction at the National Conference on Propaganda and Ideological Work that unifying thinking and rallying strength must be the central task of ideological work in the new era. The article asks what problems stand in the way of building a socialist ideology with strong cohesion and guiding power, and how to address them. Jiang argues that this requires facing four sets of prominent problems squarely and then acting along five lines, with the Party firmly holding leadership over ideological work. The article has two main parts. The first identifies four problem areas in the ideological sphere: Marxism's guiding position versus diverse currents of thought; core socialist values versus plural values; China's rising international standing versus attempts to contain it; and the challenge of new media to the way ideology is managed. The second part sets out five tasks: Marxist education, leadership over ideological work, discourse power, the quality of ideological personnel, and innovation in methods. In Jiang's account, Marxism's unified guiding position is being tested by neo-liberalism, Western constitutional democracy, "universal values", historical nihilism and theories of the "end of ideology". Market-driven profit-seeking is said to feed utilitarianism and extreme individualism, which erode collectivism. Jiang also describes Western hostile forces as pushing "China threat" narratives and various "trap" theories, and as using mobile internet platforms for ideological infiltration, so that cyberspace is both the main battlefield and the front line of ideological work. In response, Jiang calls for studying Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, full implementation of the ideological work responsibility system under the principle that the Party manages propaganda, positions, opinion and media, and building Chinese-style discourse systems and international communication capacity. Jiang concludes that ideological workers must be politically alert, distinguish questions of political principle from questions of understanding and academic views, and avoid both losing principle and arbitrarily escalating issues. Methods should combine indoctrination with reasoned persuasion, merge traditional and new media, and turn political and theoretical language into forms ordinary people welcome. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how a senior Academy of Marxism figure framed the ideological tasks of the new era, and how the threats and responses were described in 2018.

Uncovering the meaning of life in Marxist philosophy 发掘马克思主义哲学生活意蕴 Zhang Wenshu This short commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in October 2018, argues that "life" and "real life" are the starting point and destination of all philosophical questions in the Marxist classics. On that basis Zhang proposes classifying Marxist philosophy as a "philosophy of life". The author holds that exploring its meaning would strengthen the philosophical foundation of the idea of "creating a better life for the people" and address the question of how people today should live. The piece has two parts. The first sets out how Marx and Engels turned from speculative philosophy to a philosophy directed at real life. The second explains why this reading matters today. Zhang draws mainly on The German Ideology and the Theses on Feuerbach, and also cites Xi Jinping on the link between history and people's pursuit of a better life. Zhang develops the first part in three steps. Real individuals, engaged in production and exchange under definite material conditions, are the logical starting point, and the mode of production is a "production of life". Social life is essentially practical, but the author says that reading Marxism only as a "practical ontology" is incomplete. In Zhang's view it neglects rational thought and the limits set by material conditions, so "life" is richer and more original than "practice". Material and spiritual life are dialectically united, and under capitalism they fall out of balance through dependence on things and reification. Zhang therefore calls for stressing the social production of material, spiritual, social and ecological life together. On present-day value, Zhang claims that the life-philosophy reading opens new fields of research, in which scholars both "return to Marx" and address the contemporary task of creating a better life for the people under socialism with Chinese characteristics. It also bears on the modern predicament, in which capital turns people into tools and alienates them. Marx's critique of alienated life and his call to change existing conditions are presented as offering a route to human liberation and a "community of free individuals". Read the original if you want a concise example of how a Chinese scholar in 2018 recast Marxist philosophy as a philosophy of life to support the Party's language of "a better life".

The necessity of, and strategies for, improving the mechanism for producing discourse power 健全话语权生产机制的必要性及策略 Wu Ying Writing in a newspaper commentary in 2018, Wu Ying asks how China can turn its growing international presence into stronger discourse power (huayuquan) in global public opinion. Wu argues that China's discourse power has risen, citing the inclusion of "a community with a shared future for mankind" in United Nations resolutions, but that the Western-strong, China-weak pattern of opinion has not changed. Studying the mechanism that produces discourse power is therefore, in Wu's view, an urgent task. The piece first draws on political science (Weber, Dahl, Morgenthau, Nye), linguistics (Bakhtin) and Foucault to define discourse power, then turns to communication studies and Lasswell's 5W model. It then reviews who produces China's voice: leaders, government, media, think tanks, experts and ordinary citizens. Finally it sets out strategies under "what to say" and "how to say it", plus opinion monitoring. Wu treats "what to say" as first-level agenda-setting and "how to say it" as second-level agenda-setting. On content, Wu urges more on the institutional and theoretical strengths behind China's economic growth, and more true stories of ordinary Chinese people. On form, Wu calls for tailoring messages to different civilisations, regions and countries, and for multimodal communication across media platforms. Wu cites monitoring data from Shanghai International Studies University: Xinhua is the most-cited source in 2017 foreign reporting on China, and WeChat and Weibo are each cited more often than the People's Daily. Wu calls for multilingual international opinion monitoring, with region- and country-specific indicators, university training of analysts, and a mix of expert and machine analysis. The stated aim is to move from a vague-effect model to a precise-effect model, and from passive to active agenda-setting. Read the original if you want a short, data-supported statement of how Chinese communication scholars framed discourse power and external messaging in 2018.

Upholding faith in Marxism and writing a new chapter of socialism with Chinese characteristics 坚定马克思主义信仰,谱写中国特色社会主义新篇章 Wang Huaichen Written for the 200th anniversary of Marx's birth (2018), this commentary asks what it means in practice for Party members to hold firm faith in Marxism. Wang argues that theoretical clarity is the basis of political firmness, and that strengthening belief in the truth and scientific character of Marxism is the most important way to mark the anniversary. Such faith, in Wang's view, must be turned into a commitment to uphold socialism with Chinese characteristics and a stronger Party. The piece has three parts. The first discusses theoretical confidence and the Party's ideological core. The second sets out three things that, in Wang's reading, require strategic clarity in upholding socialism with Chinese characteristics. The third deals with Marxist guidance and the Party's leadership. Wang draws on Xi Jinping's speech at the anniversary meeting, on the 19th Party Congress report (2017), and on the author's own experience in discipline-inspection work and central inspection tours. Wang pictures the Party as concentric circles, with Marxist belief at the core, organisation in the middle and individual members outside. Marxism, the author says, must develop with practice, and the Party has done so through Mao Zedong Thought, Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents, the Scientific Outlook on Development and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Wang warns that Marxism's guiding role is still weakened or sidelined in some fields, with research that is detached from real problems or reduced to political paraphrase. On practice, Wang stresses three points: remembering that China remains in the primary stage of socialism, citing poverty, regional imbalance and dependence on foreign core technology; meeting the changed principal contradiction by addressing unbalanced and insufficient development; and preparing for outside containment while holding to the Four-sphere Confidence. The longest section claims that inspections found Party leadership weakened in some localities, state enterprises and universities, and credits Xi with reversing this. It calls for firm defence of the Party's leadership core and the authority of the Central Committee. Wang concludes that Marxism remains true and that the socialist path it guides has bright prospects. Party members should hold to this faith, draw on Marxism for wisdom, and carry forward the Party's self-building so that the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation can advance. Read the original if you want an example of how a Party discipline official linked Marx's bicentenary to the case for strong Party leadership and the primary stage of socialism.

Writing a new chapter in propaganda and ideological work 书写宣传思想工作新篇章 He Yizhong This newspaper commentary, published in September 2018, interprets Xi Jinping's speech at the National Conference on Propaganda and Ideological Work held in August that year. He Yizhong presents the speech as a programmatic document for Party propaganda and ideological work in the new era. In He's account, it sums up the historic achievements and regular patterns of work since the 18th Party Congress (2012) and answers a series of fundamental, overall and strategic questions. The commentary is organised under four headings. It first sets out the "nine adherences" as the basic guide for the work, placing them in a line of Party leaders from Mao Zedong to Hu Jintao who stressed ideological work. It then discusses the central task, the mission and duties of the work, and the demand that the work be made "stronger". He argues that the nine adherences, which include Party leadership over ideological work, cultivating and practising core socialist values, and telling China's story well, are a comprehensive summary of practical experience and form part of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The central task, in the article's reading, is to unify thinking and pool strength, which He treats as a basic requirement of any Marxist party. The mission is summed up in five tasks: raising the banner, rallying the people, nurturing new people, reviving culture and projecting the country's image. He describes these as one organic, logical whole. He concludes that ideological work must grow stronger in step with the nation. This requires guidance by Xi Jinping Thought and the spirit of the 19th Party Congress (2017), the Four Consciousnesses and the Four-sphere Confidence, innovation in methods suited to online communication, firmer leadership by Party committees at every level, and better skills among propaganda workers. He holds that the whole front must act on these requirements and keep writing a new chapter. Read the original if you want a concise official-line reading of Xi's 2018 propaganda speech and its key formulas, such as the nine adherences and the five tasks.

Our cause will "continue to exist and work for ever" What kind of person was Marx? 我们的事业将“永恒发挥作用地存在下去” Jiang Yingchun Writing in Guangming Daily in March 2018, the bicentenary year of Marx's birth, Jiang Yingchun asks what kind of person Marx was, and argues that his greatness cannot be understood without answering this. In Jiang's account, Marx founded the cause of scientific socialism, laid its entire theoretical foundation and advanced its practice. After more than a century of upheaval in world capitalism and socialism, Jiang says, his theory has been distorted, questioned and denied, so that his image has often become blurred. The piece is a short commemorative commentary organised under three headings. Each names one of Marx's contributions: overturning earlier understandings of human history, revealing the secrets of capitalist society, and pointing to a socialist direction out of capitalism's predicament. It draws on Engels, Lenin and Marx's own letters, and closes with a reference to Xi Jinping's assessment of Marxism and to the Chinese Communist Party's path from "standing up" to "becoming rich" to "becoming strong". Jiang's first claim is that the materialist conception of history replaced idealist explanations with an account that starts from material production and economic life. Jiang adds that the idealist view did not disappear, so popularising historical materialism remains a long and arduous task, and Engels's 1890 letter to Conrad Schmidt is read as a warning against neglect or complacency. Second, Marx took commodity exchange as the entry point for analysing capital. According to Jiang, this exposed the economic roots of fetishism and showed that the freedom and equality of capitalist society are not real, because people stand in different relations to the means of production. Third, Marx did not merely condemn capitalism. Jiang says he demonstrated the necessity of its transformation into socialism and stressed the conscious agency of the subject of the movement, in three forms: theoretical, organisational and mass consciousness. The article also sets Marx's intellectual legacy against his lifelong poverty, citing his letters to Engels. Jiang concludes that Marx chose the profession that serves human welfare best and that his cause, in his own words, will continue to exist and work for ever. The article presents the development of socialism with Chinese characteristics, and the adaptation of Marxism to Chinese conditions, as evidence of Marxism's vitality, and says Chinese Communists have remained faithful heirs of Marx's theory. Read the original if you want a brief example of how the 2018 Marx anniversary was framed in the Party press, or a compact restatement of Marx's significance for Chinese readers.

Consciously shouldering the mission and tasks of propaganda and ideological work in the new era 自觉担当新时代宣传思想工作的使命任务 Liu Shulin This commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in September 2018, interprets Xi Jinping's speech at the National Conference on Propaganda and Ideological Work. Liu Shulin treats the speech as a programmatic document for the propaganda and ideological front. The author argues that the front must take up five tasks: raising the banner, rallying popular support, nurturing new people, advancing culture and presenting China's image. Together these are meant to strengthen the cohesion and guiding power of socialist ideology. The piece is organised as a reading of the speech in four parts. It takes the five tasks in turn: the banner and popular support first, then the other three together as the main channels for reviving socialist ideology. It ends with the strategic priority of building an ideology with strong cohesion and guiding power. Throughout, Liu quotes Xi's wording and adds commentary on its significance and on how it should be put into practice. Liu's central claim is that ideological work is a matter of overall importance to the Party and state. In the author's account, economic construction supplies the material base for ideological work, while ideological work safeguards economic construction. Relaxing it would, Liu warns, lead to lost positions, a collapsed ideological defence and the fate that befell some other countries. Liu credits the continuity of Xi's two conference speeches (after the 18th and 19th Party Congresses) and the campaigns against historical nihilism, "universal values" and "constitutional democracy" with strengthening cohesion. "Rallying popular support" is presented as the starting and ending point of the work, which is measured by whether people share the Party's ideals, values and morals. For the strategic task, Liu lists seven measures. They include studying Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, consolidating the Four-sphere Confidence, guiding public opinion, innovating communication methods, building county-level media centres, refuting erroneous ideas, and holding Party committees responsible. Liu also stresses effort on foundational theory, on pressing problems that people raise, and on the quality of propaganda cadres. Read the original if you want a Party-theorist's reading of Xi's 2018 propaganda speech and its practical measures.

Contributing Chinese solutions to the world 向世界贡献中国方案 Chen Shuguang Writing in Guangming Daily in October 2018, Chen Shuguang asks how China can respond to the shared problems facing humanity: uneven world economic development, weak global governance, rising protectionism and frequent regional crises. The author's answer is that Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era supplies "Chinese solutions" (Zhongguo fang'an) in three areas: development, governance and civilisation. The commentary is organised under three headings. The first covers development, the second global governance, and the third civilisation. Each sets out a Chinese position and contrasts it with the existing order, which the author describes as built and dominated by the United States and the West. Throughout, the Belt and Road Initiative serves as the main example. On development, Chen says China addresses the global "development deficit" through ideas (an open, inclusive and balanced vision of economic globalisation), through new multilateral financial institutions such as the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank and the Silk Road Fund, and through the Belt and Road Initiative. On governance, the author argues that China wants to reform rather than overthrow the present order, defending the purposes and principles of the UN Charter. Chen sets "extensive consultation, joint contribution and shared benefits" against a model of rule by a few great powers, and presents the Belt and Road as an open platform, not a geopolitical bloc. On civilisation, Chen holds that earlier international norms were the globalisation of Western spirit and cultural hegemony. The article proposes in its place a community with a shared future for mankind, common human values, equality among civilisations and a "correct approach to justice and interests". Chen concludes that China's success shows the Western model, Western-style institutions and the capitalist road are not the only path to modernisation, and that each nation may choose its own path and system. The author says these proposals lay a basis for rebuilding the rationality of international exchange in an era of globalisation. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned account of how Chinese commentators in 2018 framed Beijing's contributions to global development, governance and civilisational dialogue.

Eagleton's confirmation of the scientific character of Marxism 伊格尔顿对马克思主义科学性的印证 Pang Yuehui This short commentary, published in 2018, asks how the British critic Terry Eagleton's work bears on the scientific character of Marxism. Pang Yuehui argues that Eagleton uses historical and contemporary facts to strengthen the persuasiveness of Marxist discourse, and so confirms Marxism's scientific standing through empirical evidence. The author treats the link between theory and objective social reality as the mark of that scientific character. The article is organised around four Marxist theses that Eagleton is said to corroborate: the nature of capital accumulation, human subjective freedom, the exploitative essence of wage labour, and the forms and paths of social change. A final section reflects critically on Eagleton's views. On accumulation, Pang says Eagleton documents Victorian-era plunder in India, China, Brazil, Korea, Russia and parts of Africa, and late twentieth-century polarisation between rich and poor. Pang reads this as supporting Marx's line that capital comes into the world dripping with blood and dirt. On wage labour, Eagleton shows that tenants, hired labourers, white-collar staff, technical workers and service workers are all exploited, and that talk of a classless society hides this. On revolution, Eagleton notes that many Westerners who claim to oppose revolution approve of the American, Irish, Indian and Kenyan independence struggles. Pang also credits him with grounding Marx's view of human agency in the contrast between humans and animals. Pang adds that Eagleton, as a Western Marxist, lacks a sense of social-historical totality. The author does not fully accept his six-stage periodisation of capitalism or his claim that class struggle is essentially a struggle over surplus value. Pang still values his search in Marxism for answers to alienation and commodification, and concludes that Marxism supplies a scientific epistemology and methodology for diagnosing social problems. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Chinese commentary in 2018 read Eagleton's popular Marxism as evidence for Marxism's scientific character.

A deeper understanding of the theoretical features and character of Marxism 深刻认识马克思主义的理论特质和品格 Xu Zhidong Published in Economic Daily on 31 May 2018, this short commentary was written after Xi Jinping's speech marking the 200th anniversary of Marx's birth. Xu asks why Marxism has spread so widely and remains influential, and answers that its scientific, popular, practical and open character gives it a value that transcends time and place. Xu holds that China's experience has confirmed these features. The article is organised under four headings, each treating Marxism as a distinct kind of theory: scientific, the theory of the people, practical, and a developing, open theory. Each section draws on Xi's formulations and on the 19th Party Congress report (2017). Xu argues that Marxism is scientific because it insists on the materiality of the world and uses historical materialism to disclose the contradictions of capitalism and the trend towards communism. Xu says these contradictions persist and cites the international financial crisis as confirmation. The author describes Marxism as a theory of the people because it stands for the fundamental interests of the broad masses, a stance no other doctrine has taken so clearly. It is practical because it aims to change the world, and open because it develops with its era and absorbs the best of human thought. Xu concludes that the Party must use Marxism to meet major challenges, link the ideal of communism to the common ideal of socialism with Chinese characteristics, and keep innovating theoretically. Xu presents Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era as a further leap in adapting Marxism to Chinese conditions. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the official line of 2018 defined the essential features of Marxism.

Communists in the new era must study Marxism deeply and thoroughly 新时代共产党人要学深悟透马克思主义 Yang Jinhai Writing in the Economic Daily in June 2018, Yang Jinhai offers a study guide to Xi Jinping's speech at the meeting marking the 200th anniversary of Marx's birth. Yang argues that the speech reaffirms Chinese Communists' conviction in Marxism, sets out a Marxist outlook for the twenty-first century, and supplies a method for studying and applying Marxism. Party members, Yang says, should therefore study it closely and unify their thinking around it. The commentary is organised in three parts. The first treats the speech as a declaration to the world of Chinese Communists' faith in Marxist truth. The second sets out what the speech says Marxism is, its historical influence, and its sinicization. The third turns to methodology: the nine areas of Marxist thought that Xi asks Party members to study, and how to study them. Yang's central moves follow the speech. Marx's life is summed up in 'three lifetimes', and Marxism is characterised as a scientific, people's, practical and open theory, in which science is the foundation and the people's standpoint is the mark separating Marxism from other theories. The Party's history is then framed as three integrations of Marxism with Chinese conditions, three great leaps (from 'standing up' to 'becoming prosperous' to 'becoming strong') and three proofs. Yang then reads the nine study topics, from laws of social development to Party building, as two general ones (theory and method, and the people's standpoint) followed by seven tied to concrete construction work. The unifying method is to 'study with problems in mind and in connection with reality', which Yang contrasts with dogmatism. Yang concludes that Party members, especially leading cadres, must study Marxism more consciously and diligently to meet unprecedented challenges in reform, development and stability. Yang calls for particular attention to the latest results of adapting Marxism to China, namely Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. This means grasping its system, its original contributions and its practical application. Read the original if you want a compact, officially aligned reading of the 2018 Marx anniversary speech and of how Party theorists framed its implications for Party study.

Several valuable lessons from forty years of reform and opening up 改革开放40年的几点宝贵经验 Han Zhenfeng Marking the 40th anniversary of reform and opening up in 2018, Han Zhenfeng asks what fundamental lessons the period offers. In this commentary, first published in Economic Daily, Han argues that studying these lessons matters for deepening reform in the new era, upholding socialism with Chinese characteristics and realising the Chinese Dream. The piece begins with the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978) and the achievements Han credits to the following four decades. It then sets out six lessons, each introduced as something that "must" be done, and supports them with statements by Xi Jinping. Han's core claim is that the direction of socialism with Chinese characteristics is the fundamental reason for success. This direction is tied to adapting Marxism to the Chinese context, Party leadership, a people-centred orientation, and the ideological line of emancipating the mind and seeking truth from facts. Han describes Party leadership as the most essential feature and greatest strength of the system. Reform is presented as a self-improvement of the socialist system that has to proceed in an orderly way under that leadership. Han also treats reform, development and stability as inseparable: reform is the driving force, development the aim and stability the precondition. Han concludes that handling these relationships correctly, including the pace of reform and what society can bear, is what allows modernization to continue. The text also warns against Western hostile forces and others who spread fallacies about reform. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the official Party narrative summarised the lessons of reform and opening up in 2018.

The fading "American Dream" 褪色的“美国梦” Huang Ben Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts (Hongqi Wengao, 2018, no. 19), Huang Ben takes up the "American Dream", which, the author says, many Chinese treat as a beacon while knowing little of American history or of ordinary American life. The article argues that the Dream did exist in certain periods, but only because of particular opportunities and policies, and that it is now fading under present-day social and economic policy. The commentary first traces the Dream through four historical phases: the Homestead Act era of the late nineteenth century, the early twentieth-century industrial period, the Cold War boom of the 1950s–70s, and the post-Cold War decades. It then examines the policy basis of the Cold War period (wage policy, welfare and mass public higher education, and the incorporation of trade unions) and compares it with current figures on wages, university fees and young people's living conditions. Huang's central claim is that the Dream's high point was a product of external pressure rather than benevolence. In the author's account, the successes of the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe in the 1950s and 60s led the American ruling class to placate wage earners, by sharing growth, expanding welfare and cheap public universities, and drawing union leaders into the Democratic Party, so that workers would not turn to socialism. After the upheavals in the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe, Huang argues, this motive disappeared. The author cites a 2017 Brookings report that real wage growth averaged only 0.2 percentage points a year from 1973 to 2016, along with soaring tuition and 2015 data showing 40 per cent of young Americans living with relatives. Huang attributes stagnation to the gains going to Wall Street and Silicon Valley elites and to the decline of unions. Huang concludes that the Cold War was won by the American ruling class, not by its wage earners, and that class stratification is hardening and class contradictions are sharpening. The author nonetheless cautions that the United States remains the largest economy and a technological leader, retaining hegemony through its trade advantages and dollar seigniorage, and that its decline will be slow. China, Huang says, should simply do its own work well so that the Chinese Dream of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation reaches every citizen. Read the original if you want an example of how a Party journal in 2018 framed the decline of the American Dream through class analysis and the Cold War.

Beware of the discourse traps deliberately set by the West 警惕西方蓄意设置的话语陷阱 Zhao Xusheng Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2018, Zhao asks how Chinese Party members and scholars should treat the "trap" theories that Western politicians and scholars have attached to China's rise. The article argues that these theories are tools in a contest over discourse power, and that they should be analysed critically rather than adopted wholesale. In Zhao's view, uncritical use of them risks pulling Chinese thinking onto a logical track set by Western discourse. The piece has three parts. The first places the struggle for discourse power in the history of ideological conflict, from Cold War "peaceful evolution" to the "end of history" and "clash of civilizations" theses. It draws on Michel Foucault's idea that discourse is a form of power, and on speeches by Xi Jinping on ideological work. The second part examines three theories in turn: the "Thucydides Trap", the "middle-income trap" and the "Tacitus Trap". The third part sets out three tasks for the Party. Zhao's central move is to treat each theory differently while placing all three within the discourse contest. The "Thucydides Trap", Zhao says, was not Thucydides' own idea but was coined by Graham Allison, and Zhao cites Qian Chengdan's view that it reflects Cold War thinking. The "middle-income trap" originates in a World Bank report. Zhao presents it as a real development bottleneck that China can pass through, citing per capita GDP of 8,600 US dollars in 2017 and the supply-side structural reform agenda. The "Tacitus Trap" is a modern extrapolation from a line in Tacitus. Zhao treats it as a warning about public trust, which Xi Jinping applied to Party–mass relations in 2014. For the three tasks, Zhao calls for studying influential ideas and answering them, strengthening Marxist theoretical education, and building a socialist ideology with real cohesion. This also means a Chinese discourse system that avoids using Western concepts to trim and analyse Chinese reality. Zhao concludes that Communists need theoretical clarity in order to have political clarity, and that Western theories and concepts should not be applied mechanically to Chinese practice. The author urges the Party to ground analysis in Marxism, to take up Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, and to strengthen the Four-sphere Confidence. Read the original if you want an example of how official Party commentary in 2018 framed Western concepts about China as ideological contests, and how it handled the three "traps" differently.

Characteristics and essence of China–US relations in the new era With an analysis of Soviet diplomatic errors in its later period and the mistaken concept of a "new Cold War" 新时代中美关系特点及其本质 Zhang Wenmu Writing in 2018, after the 19th Party Congress (2017), Zhang Wenmu asks what the essence of China–US relations is in the new era, and what foreign policy follows from it. The article argues that the rivalry is at bottom a contest between systems: not the US as a nation-state against China, but Wall Street's financial and arms capital and its White House agents against a socialist China led by the Communist Party. On this basis Zhang rejects the notion of a "new Cold War". The article has five sections. It sets out the system-competition thesis, argues that the US has become an enemy of world peace, and takes up the first question of Chinese diplomacy, namely who are enemies and who are friends. It then criticises the "new Cold War" concept, and ends with strategy and tactics for the "great struggle" with new historical features. Zhang draws heavily on Mao Zedong's remarks and on Lenin's theory of imperialism, and cites Eisenhower, George Kennan, Henry Kissinger and the economist John Ross. Zhang contends that since the Second World War the US has been captured by the military-industrial complex, and that under Trump the political base of finance capital has shifted from petrodollars to arms dollars, which profit from battlefields rather than markets. Peace therefore becomes the enemy of US policy, and China, as the side defending peace, holds the moral high ground. Citing figures on Western investment banks' declining share in Asia and on slow growth in the G7, Zhang follows Lenin in holding that shifting power relations under capitalism tend towards force. Zhang reads the Soviet acceptance of the "cold war" framing, which obscured arms-capital interests, as a costly error. Mao's "three worlds" analysis is held up as the dialectical alternative. In Zhang's view, the "new Cold War" label would push Americans and Europeans to the other side and waste China's advantage of having friends everywhere. Zhang concludes that China should separate monopoly-capital "America" from the American nation, and treat the developing countries as natural allies. Time is on China's side, as Zhang sees it, since the US now resembles the late Soviet Union and Trump resembles Khrushchev. China should avoid Brezhnev-style across-the-board offensives and follow Mao's line of "wearing down time without damaging vitality": an overall defence combined with local offensives, as in the 1962 border war with India. Read the original if you want an example of a Chinese Marxist-Leninist, Mao-inspired reading of US–China rivalry as class and system conflict.

Forty years of reform and opening up and theoretical confidence in socialism with Chinese characteristics 改革开放40年与中国特色社会主义理论自信 Yang Chao Writing in 2018, the fortieth anniversary of reform and opening up, Yang Chao asks where the theoretical confidence of socialism with Chinese characteristics comes from. The article argues that a high degree of theoretical consciousness and confidence is one of the most distinctive features of this socialism. In Yang's account, the clearest sign of that confidence is the steady emergence of theoretical achievements and a mature theoretical system over four decades. It now stands higher and firmer, Yang says, as socialism with Chinese characteristics has entered a new era. The article traces the confidence to the practice of reform and opening up since the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978), and organises the discussion into four sources. These are the thought-liberation movements that laid the intellectual basis, the creative answers given to the questions of each period, the achievements that serve as practical proof, and the creations of the people as an inexhaustible source of momentum. A closing section links the argument to the guidance given to deepening reform in the new era. Yang's first move is to present thought liberation as the precondition of every theoretical breakthrough, from the debate on the criterion of truth to the primary stage of socialism and the new era. It produced a line of theory, listed as Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents, the Scientific Outlook on Development and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Second, the author holds that practice has verified the theory. Yang cites the economy's rise to second in the world and per capita GDP growth from 155 dollars in 1978 to 8,516 dollars in 2016. Third, drawing on historical materialism, Yang describes the theory as the people's own. In this reading it grew from initiatives such as the Xiaogang household contract system and township enterprises, and it is confirmed by popular acceptance. Yang concludes that Xi Jinping Thought gives scientific guidance for deepening reform and opening up in the new era and shows the vitality of Marxism. The article holds that upholding socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era is upholding scientific socialism, and that upholding Xi Jinping Thought is upholding Marxism. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Party theorists in 2018 justified theoretical confidence by linking thought liberation, theoretical innovation, practical results and the people's role.

The contemporary value and world significance of socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era 新时代中国特色社会主义的当代价值与世界意义 Li Haiping Writing in 2018, Li Haiping asks what socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era means beyond China itself. The article argues that Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era belongs to the world as well as to China. In Li's account, its rise has changed China, is reshaping the world order, and offers fresh hope for peace and development. The article is organised under four headings. They cover the opening of a new stage in the adaptation of Marxism to China and to the times, a new path to modernization, answers to the problems of world socialism, and the building of a community with a shared future for mankind. Li draws on statements by Engels, Deng Xiaoping, Lenin and Xi Jinping, and on a list of Party concepts developed since reform and opening up. Li's central claim is that socialism with Chinese characteristics has broken the Western template of modernization. In the author's account, China moved from poverty to a moderately prosperous society in about forty years, without territorial expansion, colonial plunder or the logic of capital ruling over labour. This is presented as a second successful and just road to modernization, a model for developing countries trapped by copying the West. Li also argues that China's persistence after the Soviet collapse refuted the 'end of history' thesis. Set against financial and debt crises in the West and turmoil elsewhere, China is described as having answered, in theory, line and practice, the question of socialism's future in a backward country. Li adds that China has contributed over 30 per cent of world economic growth for several years and that its proposals on security, development and global governance respond to global problems. Li concludes that socialism with Chinese characteristics has opened a new realm for scientific socialism, revived world socialism in the twenty-first century and moved the international communist movement into a new stage. The author expects the system's advantages to become more evident and its influence to grow, while acknowledging heavier tasks and greater risks ahead. Read the original if you want a representative example of how the official Chinese narrative framed the global significance of the new era in 2018.

The US trade war cannot change the historical window of opportunity in which China finds itself 美国打贸易战改变不了我国所处的历史机遇期 Wang Yiming Writing in Qiushi in 2018, as US–China trade frictions escalated, Wang Yiming takes up a question some people raise: does the US trade war alter the period of historical opportunity (lishi jiyuqi) in which China is developing? Wang answers that, although the war brings new variables, the opportunity period has not fundamentally changed. The answer depends, the author says, on distinguishing what has changed in the external environment from what has not. The article has three parts. The first examines the external environment and argues that, despite visible changes, China still faces a relatively stable setting. The second assesses the impact on exports and growth while holding that the fundamentals of China's long-term economic prospects remain intact. The third sets out how to keep the opportunity period by turning external pressure into momentum for development, reform and opening up. Wang's central argument is that four global trends persist: economic globalization, the era theme of peace and development, the collective rise of emerging markets, and reform of global governance. Domestically, the author lists what has "not changed": a middle-income group of over 400 million and a full industrial system; an economy with resilience, ample potential and room for manoeuvre; growth foundations in technology, human capital and infrastructure; and an improving economic structure, with consumption contributing 78.5% of growth in the first half of the year. Wang adds that China's socialist system can concentrate resources on major tasks. The author concedes that future opportunity will carry more risks and challenges than before and will depend on China's ability to shape the international economic environment. Wang concludes that the best defence is a proactive strategy: keep development as the first priority, with emphasis on the real economy, innovation and domestic demand; press ahead with comprehensive deepening of reform, including shifting government functions, market access and property rights protection; and widen opening up, including looser foreign investment access, a better business environment and more autonomy for free trade pilot zones. Read the original if you want an official 2018 statement of how Chinese policy circles argued that the trade war would not derail China's trajectory.

The achievements of 40 years of reform and opening up have won wide international praise 改革开放40年成就赢得国际社会广泛赞誉 Yu Yunquan Sun Jingxin Writing in Qiushi on the 40th anniversary of reform and opening up (2018), Yu Yunquan and Sun Jingxin collect the views of foreign politicians, scholars, journalists and international officials on China's development since 1978. Their thesis is that these external voices help Chinese readers understand the historical standing and world impact of reform and opening up more fully, and approach the new era's reform with greater confidence. The article is organised around four themes, each introduced by a quotation and supported by a series of named foreign commentators. These are the achievements of the 40 years; the reasons for their success; the effects on the world, especially developing countries; and the outlook for reform in the new era. The commentators come from Australia, the United States, Russia, Japan, Spain, France, Britain, Turkey, India, Brazil, South Korea, Ireland and elsewhere, along with the UN Secretary-General and the IMF head. The authors argue that outside observers credit China with transforming its economy and technology and lifting more than 700 million people out of poverty, citing figures such as per capita GDP rising from about 200 dollars to over 8,000. For the causes, they report foreign views that stress the Party's capacity to correct errors, the advantages of socialism with Chinese characteristics, long-term planning, a people-centred approach and a pragmatic line of seeking truth from facts. They then present China as a driver of global growth, a pillar of multilateralism and peace, and a model for other countries, with one French commentator saying about 30 per cent of world growth came from China. The authors conclude that the international community expects China to meet new challenges by deepening reform, citing Xi Jinping's remark that reform and opening up has no completion point. They add that if the Chinese people keep their original aspiration and work hard, reform will achieve more and have wider global influence. The piece is a curated showcase of favourable foreign opinion, with every claim carried by quotation. Read the original if you want to see how an official Party journal marshals international voices to support its account of reform and opening up in 2018.

Continuously advancing the compilation, translation and study of Marxist classics in the new era 不断推进新时代马克思主义经典著作编译和研究工作 Wei Jianhua Writing in Qiushi in 2018, Wei Jianhua takes up the task of compiling, translating and studying the Marxist classics. Taking up Xi Jinping's call at the Marx bicentenary meeting for Communists to make reading the classics a habit and a spiritual pursuit, Wei argues that such work is the basic foundation of Marxist theoretical construction. The new era, in Wei's account, sets new and higher requirements for it. The piece looks back on the 97 years of the Communist Party of China and the roughly century-long work of Chinese translators of the classics. It then sets out four principles that the work must always follow. These are a rigorous scientific attitude, a Marxist style of study, popularisation among the public, and a policy of producing both results and talent. Wei argues that translators must supply more accurate texts and more reliable editions for what Xi calls the Party's compulsory course. Texts must also be read against the historical context of nineteenth-century Europe, while the work answers the questions of the present era. Wei holds that wrong views, such as the claim that Marxism is outdated, call for clear and engaging classic readers, especially for young people. Translating the classics is described as speaking on behalf of the sages, which demands accuracy, authority and firm political conviction. Wei concludes that translator training should be as carefully tended as the texts themselves, following Xi's instruction to build a core corps of translators of the classics. This is meant to sustain theoretical work and to advance the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Read the original if you want a concise official statement of how Party theorists framed the purposes and standards of classics translation in 2018.

Marx's transcendence of Hegel's theory of "civil society" 马克思对黑格尔“市民社会”理论的超越 Dong Xiaobo Dong Xiaobo asks how Marx moved beyond Hegel's concept of "civil society" and argues that the move was central to Marx's break with idealism. The piece, a short commentary first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in August 2018, holds that Marx turned a concept Hegel had subordinated to the state into a core category of historical materialism. The article first sets out Hegel's account in the Elements of the Philosophy of Right, then turns to Marx's treatments in the Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy and The German Ideology. It closes by considering what Marx's reversal of the relation between civil society and the state means for the relation between economic base and superstructure. Dong credits Hegel with first separating civil society from the political state and with criticising contract theorists who conflated the two. Civil society, for Hegel, is the sphere of needs and material interests, an "external state". Dong argues that Hegel remained incomplete, since he still placed the judiciary and police inside civil society. He also treated the political state as the determining element and as the embodiment of "good", against civil society as a "battlefield of private interest", and so could not escape historical idealism. For Marx, by contrast, civil society is the sum of material relations and the real birthplace and stage of all history, to be anatomised through political economy. Dong stresses that Marx therefore reversed the relation: civil society determines the state, and a given civil society produces the political state that formally expresses it. Dong concludes that by turning a concept Hegel had demoted into a pillar of historical materialism, Marx achieved a historical transcendence of Hegel. The author describes this as a fundamental shift from idealism to materialism and from democratism to communism. Read the original if you want a compact Chinese-language outline of how Marx's concept of civil society is distinguished from Hegel's, with the key passages cited.

Research on Western Marxism in China since reform and opening up 中国改革开放以来的西方马克思主义研究 Guo Yanjun Guo Yanjun asks how the translation and study of Western Marxism in China has developed since reform and opening up, and what it has meant for Chinese Marxist philosophy. The article, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in March 2018, argues that Western Marxism research and the renewal of Chinese Marxist philosophy advanced in step with each other. Guo begins with the early 1960s, when Western Marxist thinkers were first translated but treated only as targets of criticism within the Soviet textbook system. The article then follows the period after the 1978 debate on the criterion of truth, through the 1990s, to the fields that became popular in the early twenty-first century, such as ecological Marxism, feminist Marxism and post-Marxism. In Guo's account, two needs drove the research: the demand for knowledge of Western thought under the policy of reform and opening up, and the need to rethink the Soviet textbook system. Chinese scholars, Guo says, approached Western Marxism critically and used it as a resource, always anchored in close reading of Marx's texts. That reading brought out neglected themes, including Marx's ideas on world history and Eastern societies, and produced many interpretive approaches. Guo warns against fragmented, novelty-seeking studies of individual thinkers, and against applying Western Marxist critiques of modern society directly to China. Guo concludes that Chinese Marxist philosophy should rest on accurate reading of Marx's texts while addressing China's real problems. Western Marxism research should stay in dialogue with the study of Marx. It should also be placed in a world-historical perspective, in which Guo sees socialism with Chinese characteristics as having world-historical significance for a new type of human civilization. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese academic account of how Western Marxism studies were institutionalised after 1978.

Learning, grasping and applying Marxism, the Party's core competence 学精悟透用好马克思主义这个看家本领 Zhong Shunhu This commentary, first published in the People's Daily on 8 June 2018, takes up Xi Jinping's demand at the meeting marking the 200th anniversary of Marx's birth that the whole Party truly learn Marxism thoroughly, grasp it fully and apply it well. Zhong argues that in the new era of socialism with Chinese characteristics, Party members and cadres can strengthen the "four consciousnesses", hold to the Four-sphere Confidence and advance the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation only if they master Marxism as their core competence. The piece is organised in three parts, each pairing a verb with a requirement: learning thoroughly depends on mastering correct methods, grasping fully depends on a firm people's standpoint, and applying well depends on taking the initiative to act. On learning, Zhong stresses reading the original works attentively and repeatedly, citing Engels and Xi's 2011 Central Party School speech, and combining study with reflection. On grasping, the author holds that Marxism cannot be understood without adopting the people's standpoint, applying the mass line and doing field research. Zhong attributes the corruption of some Party members to a failure to study Marxism seriously and to weak ideals. On applying, Zhong draws on the traditional Chinese idea of the unity of knowing and doing, and calls for turning study into practical ideas, methods and work, citing Mao Zedong's "Foolish Old Man" spirit and Xi's call to roll up sleeves and work hard. Zhong concludes that learning must serve implementation, and that Party members should avoid being "giants of words and dwarfs of action". The article ties this to arming minds with Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and putting the spirit of the 19th Party Congress (2017) into practice. Read the original if you want a short example of how the Party press presented Marxist study as a duty for cadres in 2018.

The spirit of the age of reform and opening up Commemorating the 40th anniversary of the great debate on the criterion of truth 改革开放的时代精神 Ding Liqun Writing in 2018 on the 40th anniversary of the great debate on the criterion of truth, Ding Liqun asks what that debate meant for contemporary Chinese philosophy. The debate was set off by the Guangming Daily article "Practice Is the Sole Criterion for Testing Truth" and opened the way to reform and opening up. Ding argues that it also drove philosophical innovation, which in turn fed back into reform and opening up, so that philosophy became the "spirit of the age" of that period. The commentary, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today, identifies three effects of the debate on Chinese philosophy over four decades. It launched research on the philosophy of practice. It ended the scholastic, Soviet-textbook mode of research and produced many new branches. It also prompted philosophical study of concrete problems of reform. A closing section offers a two-part overall assessment, drawing on Marx and on the neo-Kantian Wilhelm Windelband. Ding's central claim is that the philosophy of practice developed in three stages: an epistemological theory of practice, practical materialism (practice ontology), and an anthropological philosophy of practice rooted in Aristotle's distinction between theoretical and practical philosophy. The new branches, including cultural, development, economic, political and social philosophy, are described as extensions of practical philosophy. Their questions centre on the path of development, meaning China's modernization and how its universal and particular features relate. Ding concludes that philosophy and reform formed a "mirror" relationship: the shift from building a material base to putting people at the core of modernization and then to balanced material and cultural-ethical progress parallels the three stages of practice theory. Ding concludes that the debate produced a "Copernican revolution" between theory and practice, in which theory is tested by practice and serves it. In Ding's account, philosophy thereby moved from interpreting the world to changing it, guiding and improving reform and opening up and becoming the essence of its age. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned account of how Chinese philosophers retrospectively link the philosophy of practice to the reform era.

Believing in, applying and developing Marxism 信仰、运用和发展马克思主义 Cao Ping This short commentary, first published in the People's Daily on 8 June 2018, argues that the Chinese Communist Party owes its endurance and growth largely to its "theoretical consciousness". Cao holds that few parties worldwide pay such attention to theory, and that building the Party ideologically and strengthening it through theory has given it unified thinking, firm will and coordinated action. The article breaks this consciousness into three linked parts: believing in Marxism, applying it and developing it. Cao treats them as progressive stages and illustrates each with the Party's record across the revolutionary, construction and reform periods. On belief, Cao says Marxism is the soul of the Party's ideals and convictions. It is presented as a science drawn from objective reality and confirmed by it, and the Party is said never to have relaxed its study of the classics. On application, Cao argues that Marxism arose in nineteenth-century Europe and so must be combined with China's concrete conditions rather than treated as dogma, grasping its spirit, as Deng Xiaoping put it, by studying what is essential and useful. On development, Cao calls Marxism an open system that advances with the times, and lists Mao Zedong Thought, Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents, the Scientific Outlook on Development and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era as theoretical innovations. Developing Marxism in this way is described as the best form of loyalty to it. Cao concludes that the three elements together make up the Party's theoretical consciousness, and that under such a Party the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation will unfold. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary in 2018 framed the Party's relationship to Marxist theory.

Letting the light of scientific socialist truth shine still more brightly 让科学社会主义真理之光更加璀璨夺目 Zheng Keyang Writing in the People's Daily in April 2018, in the year of the 200th anniversary of Marx's birth and the 170th of the Communist Manifesto, Zheng Keyang takes up what it means that socialism with Chinese characteristics has entered a new era, as declared at the 19th Party Congress (2017). Zheng argues that this shows scientific socialism taking on strong vitality in twenty-first-century China, and that Party members must hold to their original aspiration and mission to sustain it. The commentary is built in three parts. The first sets China's development within the history of world socialism, from the Manifesto through the October Revolution, the post-1945 spread of socialism and the collapse in the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe, to reform and opening up. The second considers what China's success contributes to the world and why the Party has succeeded. The third turns to the tasks ahead and to Party leadership. Zheng contends that the Soviet and East European collapse stemmed not from any flaw in Marxism but from ruling parties departing from it, and that China's development since the 18th Party Congress (2012), set against what Zheng calls Western disorder after the 2008 financial crisis, vindicates scientific socialism. China's contribution, in Zheng's account, is threefold: an alternative development path for developing countries, a strengthened force for peace and balanced development, and Chinese experience that enriches Marxism, though China does not export its model. The decisive factor is the Party's consistent adaptation of Marxism to Chinese conditions, which Zheng says rests on a distinctive set of ideas, work styles, methods and institutions: treating Marxism undogmatically, combining theory with practice in a repeated cycle, and following the mass line. Zheng concludes that the key to victory in the new era lies in strengthening Party leadership and the full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, especially Party political development. Zheng names Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and Xi's position as core of the leadership as the most valuable conditions for meeting risks and challenges. Read the original if you want a representative example of the official 2018 narrative linking Marx's anniversary, world socialism's history and Party-building.

Consciously taking up the mission and tasks of propaganda and ideological work 自觉承担起宣传思想工作的使命任务 Sun Laibin Writing in the People's Daily in September 2018, Sun Laibin takes up Xi Jinping's formulation, from the National Conference on Propaganda and Ideological Work, of five tasks for propaganda and ideological work in the new situation: raising the banner, rallying the people, nurturing new people, reviving culture and showcasing the nation's image. Sun argues that propaganda and ideological workers must take on these tasks consciously, so that ideological work and the national spirit grow stronger and serve the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The commentary is organised into five sections, one for each task. Each opens by linking the task to national rejuvenation and then sets out two or three practical requirements, supported by quotations from Mao Zedong, Lenin and Xi Jinping. The sections cover ideological guidance, popular cohesion, the education of young people, cultural development and international communication. On raising the banner, Sun calls for Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era to be studied thoroughly, explained through concrete evidence of economic and social development, and defended against erroneous currents of thought. On rallying the people, Sun holds that workers should explain both the achievements of 40 years of reform and opening up and existing problems. Sun says that negative individual cases should be answered with materialist dialectics, which separates the mainstream from side currents and appearance from essence. Sun adds that practical problems and ideological problems must be solved together. On nurturing new people, Sun stresses firm ideals and convictions among young people and integrating the core socialist values into social life. For culture, Sun urges drawing on traditional Chinese culture, revolutionary culture and advanced socialist culture while encouraging popular creativity. On image, Sun says that Western-dominated international opinion has not fundamentally changed, so China must strengthen its international communication capacity, tell its own stories and interpret Chinese ideas in terms that foreign audiences can understand. Sun presents these as major tasks for propaganda and ideological workers in the new era. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the 2018 official line on propaganda and ideological work was explained to Party cadres and the public.

Marxism has always shone with the brilliant light of truth 马克思主义始终闪烁着耀眼的真理光芒 Ruan Qing Marking the 200th anniversary of Marx's birth and the 170th anniversary of the Communist Manifesto (2018), Ruan Qing asks what grounds the truth of Marxism. The article, which carries a Renmin Ribao (People's Daily) date line of 8 May 2018, takes up Xi Jinping's statement that Marx's doctrine still "shines with the brilliant light of truth".
