Ruan's thesis is that this truth rests on both a theoretical and a practical foundation, and that socialism with Chinese characteristics entering a new era makes that light shine more brightly. The piece is a short commentary in two halves. The first sets out the theoretical basis of Marxism's truth. The second presents the practical basis, drawing on the record of the Communist Party of China in revolution, construction and reform. Throughout, Ruan leans on Xi Jinping's speech at the anniversary conference, and on passages from Engels and the Communist Manifesto. On the theoretical side, Ruan argues that Marxism's truth lies in joining a scientific worldview with a scientific method, scientific rigour with values, and realism with transcendence. Four sources are named. The theory is scientific because it revealed laws of social development, through dialectical and historical materialism, political economy and scientific socialism. It is a method, not a dogma, citing Engels. It is oriented to the people and to human liberation. And it holds up a lofty social ideal. On the practical side, Ruan claims that adapting Marxism's basic tenets to Chinese conditions explains the Party's victories: the revolutionary path of encircling cities from the countryside, the founding of New China, socialist transformation, and reform and opening up. The Marxist theory of society's basic contradictions is presented as the basis of reform, which the author credits with making China the world's second-largest economy and improving living standards. Ruan concludes that Marxism remains the guiding ideology of the Party and state and a weapon for understanding and changing the world. In the author's account, steadfast faith in Marxism, with "iron" belief and discipline, has let Chinese communists stay composed amid a global contest of "isms", theories and models. Ruan holds that practice has shown Marxism's power of truth in the past, present and future. Read the original if you want a compact example of the official 2018 case for Marxism's scientific truth, built around Xi Jinping's anniversary speech.

The philosophical implications of Xi Jinping's thought on scientifically determining the historical position 习近平科学判断历史方位思想的哲学意蕴 Li Chunhua Writing in 2018, Li Chunhua asks what philosophical method lies behind the judgement, set out at the 19th Party Congress (2017), that socialism with Chinese characteristics has entered a new era. Li argues that this judgement is a major theoretical innovation within Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and serves as its foundation. According to the article, it rests on the Marxist principle of unifying the subjective and the objective, and on a people-centred standpoint. The article has three parts. The first explains why correctly identifying a "historical position" and historical stage matters for a Marxist party. The second argues that the "new era" is a significant period in the development of the Party and the country, not a merely chronological notion. The third sets out the conditions and methods by which a Marxist party can make such a judgement scientifically. Li draws on the Party's earlier periods, from the New Democratic Revolution to reform and opening up, and on Mao Zedong's analyses of the Chinese revolution. Li's central claim is that determining the historical position is a subjective judgement that must rest on objective reality. It requires two conditions: the real world must already have developed the conditions for a new historical epoch, and the judging subject must have the awareness and capacity to recognise this and open the new stage deliberately. A premature judgement oversteps the stage of development, and a late one loses the opportunity. Li treats this ability as a distinctive advantage of Marxist parties. The article links the new era to the change in the principal contradiction of society, now between the people's growing need for a better life and unbalanced and inadequate development. It also stresses that China remains in the primary stage of socialism, and that the new era is an important phase within that stage, not a way beyond it. Li concludes that Xi's judgement avoids both leaping ahead of the stage of development and lagging behind the times, and avoids both arrogance and self-doubt. It is presented as evidence of the Party's theoretical self-awareness and maturity, and as an objective basis for strategy and policy. The article also lists remaining difficulties, such as per capita GDP, regional and urban–rural gaps, and the tasks of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. Read the original if you want a Party-theoretical account of how the "new era" judgement is justified through dialectical and historical materialism.

Cultivating correct "three outlooks": the core and key of ideological and political work with university students 培养正确的“三观”：大学生思政工作的核心和关键 Li Chunhua Shangguan Miaomiao Li Chunhua and Shangguan Miaomiao, writing in 2018 after Xi Jinping's speech at the National Conference on Ideological and Political Work in Higher Education (2016), ask what the core of ideological and political work with university students should be. They argue that its core and key is to help students form a correct worldview, outlook on life and system of values (the "three outlooks"), which they call the "master switch" of a person's life. The main channel for this is the ideological and political theory course. The article has three parts. The first sets out why cultivating the three outlooks is necessary and possible. The second considers how Marxist theory should be used to win over students, both by positive exposition and by critiquing erroneous trends of thought. The third turns to how teaching can respond to students' individual confusion, and what that requires of teachers and of coordination among staff. On possibility, the authors hold that the three outlooks result from the interaction of objective factors (family, school, society, ultimately social being) and subjective ones. They reject two views: that education matters little because social being decides consciousness, and that outlooks can only be formed through personal experience. Li and Shangguan say social consciousness reacts back on social being, scientific outlooks rarely form spontaneously, and systematic theoretical education is needed. The outlooks to be taught are dialectical and historical materialism, serving the people, and collectivism, grounded in Marxism and in socialist public ownership. Courses must also criticise historical nihilism, universal values, neoliberalism, utilitarianism, money worship, hedonism and individualism, and encourage practice outside the classroom. The authors conclude that general theory must be tied to students' particular problems, without turning teaching into dogmatic preaching. They propose standing mechanisms linking ideological and political course teachers, counsellors (fudaoyuan) and subject teachers, such as joint staff exchanges, dual appointments and regular meetings. They also call on course teachers to hold correct outlooks themselves, deepen their command of Marxist classics and take part in social practice. Read the original if you want to see how a 2018 Chinese academic article justifies and organises value education in universities.

Four dimensions of popularising Marxism in the context of online communication 网络传播视域下马克思主义大众化的四维路径 Zheng Jie Xiao Peng Zheng Jie and Xiao Peng ask how the popularisation of Marxism (its spread among ordinary people so that they understand, accept and apply it) can be advanced in the internet age. Writing in 2018, shortly after the 19th Party Congress (2017), they argue that this requires work along four paths: setting online communication agendas, improving methods of communication, optimising the online environment, and raising the quality of the people who take part in the process. The article opens by defining popularisation as a two-way process. Marxism is spread to the masses, who come to know, accept and consciously use it, and practice in turn enriches Marxism. It then devotes one section to each path, with five numbered measures under each. The authors repeatedly tie the task to studying and publicising the 19th Party Congress and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. On agenda-setting, a concept borrowed from communication studies, the authors call for stronger mainstream media, dedicated Marxist websites and columns, and topics that address issues the public cares about, explained through everyday examples. They add that online media may help people choose but may not choose for them. On methods, they propose integrating online resources, combining new and traditional media, varying content and form, strengthening online ideological and political education, and developing technology. On the environment, they propose administrative regulation, law and moral self-discipline, guidance of online opinion through state and commercial news sites, and the cautious use of internet slang so that communicators and audiences do not speak in 'two skins'. On the subjects of popularisation, they treat both communicators and ordinary audiences as participants. Both need theoretical grounding, technical skill, media literacy, a sense of responsibility and creativity. The authors conclude that effective popularisation depends on combining content with form, technology with regulation, and top-down communication with the active participation of ordinary people. They also stress reading the classic works closely and aiming for an online and offline 'concentric circle' around the Party's theory. Read the original if you want a detailed, practice-oriented account of how Chinese scholars of ideological and political education framed Marxist communication online around 2018.

Seeing the truth about the "state capitalism" charge 认清“国家资本主义”问题的真相 Qiu Shi Writing in 2018, as the United States opened a trade war with China, Qiu Shi takes up the label "state capitalism", which the article says is being attached to China's economic system. The article argues that the charge, which rests on China's state-owned enterprises, government intervention and industrial policy, misdescribes China. In the author's view, it also hides a deeper contest over development path and political system. The piece is organised in four sections. It first asks who the real "state capitalists" are, drawing on Lenin's concept and on the history of Western capitalism and the United States. It then examines the motives of the "state capitalism" thesis, citing Hillary Clinton, Ian Bremmer, The Economist and Davos. The third section defends the socialist market economy against the charge. The last section turns to the treatment of state capitalism in Lenin's thought and in the early People's Republic. Qiu's core argument is that pure free-market capitalism has never existed. Citing Marx on primitive accumulation, the article holds that state power has always driven capitalist development. It adds US figures on government spending and public employees, and the role of public investment in innovation. The author then separates market economy from capitalism: a market economy is a resource-allocation method that can combine with either system. State firms and government regulation exist in both, the article says, and the difference lies in whether they serve monopoly capital or the people. The charge, in this account, rests on a double standard that Qiu likens to Friedrich List's image of "kicking away the ladder". Qiu also says that Lenin and Mao Zedong treated state capitalism under socialism as a transitional form, which ended once socialist transformation was complete. Qiu concludes that the socialist market economy under the Party's leadership, shaped by reform and opening up and by Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, has nothing to do with "state capitalism". The article presents it as a successful Chinese approach that combines government and market, and says China will not take the "wrong road" of state capitalism. Read the original if you want an official Party-journal rebuttal of the "state capitalism" label, including its use of Lenin, Marx and Mao on the term.

Time to end the "neo-colonialism" argument “新殖民主义论”可以休矣 Wang Yiwei Writing in Qiushi in 2018, after the Beijing Summit of the Forum on China-Africa Cooperation, Wang Yiwei takes up Western claims that China's growing role in Africa amounts to "neo-colonialism". The author argues that the charge contradicts the facts, that China's history and its development path give it no colonial disposition, and that the accusation reveals the strategic anxiety of certain Western forces rather than anything about China-Africa relations. The commentary is built in four sections. It first discusses China's alleged lack of a colonial "gene", then presents the Belt and Road Initiative as an aid to decolonisation in Africa. The third section explains why the neo-colonial label is applied, and the last looks ahead to a closer China-Africa community with a shared future. Wang draws on the summit remarks of African leaders, Xi Jinping's speech, a McKinsey report and project statistics. Wang's central move is a definitional one. Neo-colonialism, in the author's account, is a product of the capitalist system, in which developed capitalist states keep controlling and exploiting politically independent countries; it therefore cannot be pinned on a socialist China. Wang contrasts Zheng He's voyages with Western conquest, and describes colonial-era Africa as oriented towards European metropoles and marginalised in globalisation. In this reading, the Belt and Road Initiative, through infrastructure links, development finance and a "government plus market" model, helps Africa build internal connections and industrialise. Wang cites China's "five noes" (no interference in African countries' chosen paths, no meddling in internal affairs, no imposed will, no political conditions on aid, no political self-interest in investment) and figures such as the 60 billion US dollars pledged and the roads, ports and jobs expected from Chinese-built projects. Wang concludes that China-Africa ties are South-South relations, fundamentally unlike the North-South relations between Africa and the West, and that aligning the Belt and Road Initiative with African and UN development agendas will create a "golden age" and a model for a community with a shared future for mankind. Wang presents African disillusion with Western models and US protectionism as pushing African states to "look east". Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese official-theory journal rebuts the neo-colonialism charge and frames China-Africa cooperation.

Resolutely resisting the harassment and erosion of literary and artistic creation by historical nihilism 坚拒历史虚无主义对文艺创作的袭扰与侵蚀 Ai Fei Writing in Qiushi in 2018, Ai Fei argues that literature and art are a privileged entry point for historical nihilism, which uses their influence to spread, distort people's thinking and erode creative work. The article contends that resisting this is an important task for the literary and artistic field, and that the way to do so is a correct view of history and a people-centred orientation in creation. The piece has three sections. The first traces the link between nihilism and modern Western art, from Nietzsche's "God is dead" to modernism and postmodernism after the two world wars. The second describes how historical nihilism has affected literary and artistic creation in China. The third sets out ways of consciously resisting it, drawing on Marx, Engels, Lenin, Mao Zedong and Xi Jinping. Ai holds that nihilism arose in nineteenth-century Europe as capitalist values displaced Christian ones, and that modernist works such as Ulysses, Waiting for Godot and Guernica expressed the despair left by the world wars. In this account, nihilism spread globally under the banner of "modernity" through capitalist cultural production. For China, Ai says that since the "new period" some creators have treated anything historical or national as outdated and revolutionary themes as leftist, and have favoured the dark side of life for commercial appeal. As evidence, Ai cites the parodying of Yue Fei and Qin Hui, of The Yellow River Cantata ("the river roars" turned into "the year-end bonus roars"), and of the martyr Qiu Shaoyun. Ai says these cannot be read as mere entertainment: they negate history, revolution and Chinese culture, and in Xi Jinping's words aim at denying the guiding role of Marxism and the leadership of the Communist Party. Ai also links the resulting lack of artistic "peaks" to this tendency. Ai concludes that writers must hold firmly to a correct view of history, nation, state and culture, and to cultural confidence. The author calls for art to go among the people and to place them at the centre of creation, citing Marx, Engels, Lenin on Gorky's Mother, Mao's Yan'an Talks and Xi's call to take root among the people and in life. Socialist realism, Ai argues, has produced works that nourished the people, which shows historical nihilism to be contrary to the laws of history. Read the original if you want an example of how a 2018 Party-journal article connects the critique of historical nihilism to literary policy and to the doctrine of art serving the people.

The Belt and Road Initiative opens a new era of win-win cooperation “一带一路”开启合作共赢新时代 Chai Shangjin Writing in Guangming Daily on 30 August 2018, five years after the launch of the Belt and Road Initiative, Chai Shangjin argues that the initiative is both a major step in China's opening up and an engine of stable global growth. The article presents it as a practical platform for building a community with a shared future for mankind. Chai also describes it as offering "Chinese wisdom" and a "Chinese approach" for improving global development models and reforming global governance. The commentary is organised in three sections. The first treats the initiative as a path of peaceful development and win-win cooperation, set against what Chai calls an unstable international environment. The second considers its contribution to the healthy development of economic globalisation. The third presents it as a platform for a community with a shared future for mankind, covering cultural exchange and green development. Chai draws throughout on speeches by Xi Jinping, including his remarks at the symposium marking the initiative's fifth anniversary. Chai contends that the world faces unresolved problems of peace and development, widening wealth gaps and non-traditional security threats. He says the current US administration clings to the "law of the jungle" and a Cold War mentality. In Chai's account, the initiative is not a quest for Chinese economic hegemony. It promotes policy coordination, infrastructure connectivity, unimpeded trade, financial integration and closer people-to-people ties. Chai contrasts it with Western aid, which he says came with privatisation and marketisation conditions and failed to resolve developing countries' basic problems. He cites alignment with ASEAN, the Eurasian Economic Union and Kazakhstan's "Bright Path" policy, projects such as the Jakarta–Bandung and China–Laos railways and the ports of Gwadar and Piraeus, and praise from Joseph Stiglitz. On globalisation, Chai argues that Western-led globalisation widened inequality. He holds that the initiative shifts the emphasis to equal participation and mutual benefit, and that it helps African countries move out of the low end of global value chains. Chai concludes that the initiative has moved from concept to practice, and he notes that United Nations resolutions have incorporated its content. He claims that China will share its development experience without interfering in others' internal affairs or exporting its social system or development model. He adds that green guidelines issued by Chinese government departments aim to make it an ecological road. In his view the initiative will help address the world's "deficits" in peace, development and governance. Read the original if you want an example of how official Chinese commentary in 2018 framed the Belt and Road Initiative in relation to globalisation, Western aid and the community with a shared future for mankind.

Research on historical figures and the critique of historical nihilism 历史人物研究与历史虚无主义批判 Zhou Jin Zhou Jin takes up the way historical nihilism treats Party leaders and heroes, and asks how such figures should be studied and assessed. Writing in 2018, the author argues that historical nihilism uses the labels of "academic research", "restoring history" and "re-evaluation" to distort the history of the Party, the state and the army. In Zhou's account its aim is to undermine Marxism's guiding position, the historical inevitability of China's socialist path and the leadership of the Communist Party. Only a scientific theory and a seeking-truth-from-facts attitude, Zhou holds, allow history to serve as a "textbook" and a "sobering agent". The article has three parts. The first describes four manifestations of nihilism in the study of historical figures. The second sets out the harms and the causes. The third proposes responses based on Marxist standards of evaluation. Examples include attacks on Mao Zedong, doubts about heroes such as the Five Heroes of Langya Mountain, Liu Hulan, Huang Jiguang and Lei Feng, and praise for Cixi, Yuan Shikai, Chiang Kai-shek and Wang Jingwei. Zhou also cites online games that mix up historical characters and the example of the Soviet Union. Zhou argues that nihilism works by magnifying leaders' faults, using individual or minority memories, diaries and oral history to replace collective memory, and reversing right and wrong. The author says its effects are to dissolve mainstream ideology, promote Western "universal values" and political systems, question Party leadership and weaken national cohesion, especially among young internet users. Zhou lists causes: Western hostility, fast and uneven online media, and a backlash against idealised, flawless portrayals of heroes. The remedy rests on Xi Jinping's statement that leaders are people, not gods, and on his "six cannots" for judging figures within their historical conditions, avoiding both worship and wholesale negation. Zhou calls for deeper research guided by Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and a Marxist system for evaluating figures that rests on practice and historical materialism. The author also calls for legal tools, citing the 2014 Martyrs' Day decision and the Law on the Protection of Heroes and Martyrs, adopted in April 2018 and in force from 1 May. Historians, propaganda departments and media should collect and rebut representative nihilist claims and build public "immunity". Read the original if you want a clear example of the official Chinese framing of historical nihilism and of the policy and legal responses proposed in 2018.

Socialism with Chinese characteristics as the consistent direction of reform and opening up 中国特色社会主义是改革开放始终坚持的方向 Zhu Bingyuan Wang Haixia Writing in 2018, on the 40th anniversary of reform and opening up, Zhu Bingyuan and Wang Haixia ask how reform and opening up relate to socialism with Chinese characteristics. They argue that upholding and developing socialism with Chinese characteristics has been the theme of all the Party's theory and practice since reform began, and is the fundamental direction of China's development. In their view the two are unified in the goal of socialist modernization and national rejuvenation, in the Party's social revolution and self-reform, and in the overall strategic layouts of the 18th Party Congress era. The article is organised in four parts. Each shows what reform and opening up produced: the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics, its theoretical system, its institutions and its culture. The authors trace the theory from Deng Xiaoping Theory through the Three Represents and the Scientific Outlook on Development to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. On the path, the authors say it is neither a copy of the classical Marxist template, a continuation of China's historical culture, a reprint of other socialist experiences, nor a version of Western modernization. They present it as the result of combining Marxism's universal truths with Chinese practice. On institutions, they quote the 18th Party Congress (2012) definition and divide the system into three levels: fundamental institutions (Party leadership, the people's congress system, socialist public ownership, the people's democratic dictatorship), basic institutions and specific institutions. The first must be upheld unwaveringly, the second improved while being upheld, and the third reformed and innovated as conditions change. On culture, they describe a socialist culture drawing on traditional Chinese civilization and revolutionary culture and driven by reform practice. The authors conclude that the whole experience of 40 years comes down to joining Marxism's basic principles with China's practice and taking its own road. They also hold that the theoretical system represents another leap in the Sinicization of Marxism. They warn against "subversive errors" on what may and may not be changed, and against people who would negate the fundamental and basic institutions. They also cite the 19th Party Congress (2017) targets for institutional improvement by 2035 and for modernized national governance by the mid-century. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official 2018 narrative linking reform and opening up to the path, theory, institutions and culture of socialism with Chinese characteristics.

How Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era upholds and develops Marxism 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想对马克思主义的坚持和发展 Hou Huiqin Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2018, Hou Huiqin asks what it means to uphold and develop Marxism, and argues that Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era can be properly understood only from this standpoint. Hou presents Marxism and modern China as a community of shared destiny. Upholding and developing Marxism is described as the thread that holds that community together and as the true way of inheriting Marx's intellectual legacy. The article is organised in three parts, each naming one condition for upholding and developing Marxism. The first concerns grasping the problems of the age, articulating its spirit and leading its currents. The second concerns establishing the people, with the modern working class at their core, as the subject of history. The third concerns a scientific attitude of pursuing truth and a theoretical character capable of self-reform. Hou draws on Mehring, Marx, Mao Zedong and Xi Jinping's collected speeches. In the first part, Hou argues that Marx succeeded because he posed the right question for his age: human emancipation had to mean the emancipation of the proletariat. Hou claims that today's world is undergoing a "great change unseen in a century" and that the new era is a scientific judgement on China's new historical position. In the second part, Hou contrasts individual-subject and people-subject views of history, treating historical materialism as a people's view of history. In this reading the people are an organic whole with the advanced class at its core, not a sum of individuals. Hou holds that the proletariat alone can durably represent the universal interests of humanity. Hou then links this to a people-centred approach, targeted poverty alleviation, a path of national strengthening that rejects the logic that a strong state must seek hegemony, and the building of a community with a shared future for mankind. In the third part, Hou says Marxism renews itself through a critical spirit, citing Marx's revisions of the Communist Manifesto, and that the Chinese Communist Party combines belief with science, and values with truth. Hou describes Xi's image of governing as a continuing "examination" in which the times set the questions, the Party answers and the people grade. In Hou's account, the Party's capacity for the Party's self-reform stems from the objective needs of social revolution, not from abstract morality. Read the original if you want a Party-theorist's account, from 2018, of how Xi Jinping Thought is placed within the Marxist tradition through the themes of the age, the people as subject and self-revolution.

Interpreting "On Contradiction" in the perspective of the history of foreign Marxism 国外马克思主义发展史视域下的《矛盾论》解读 Wang Zhenmin Writing in 2018, Wang Zhenmin asks how Marxist thinkers outside China have read Mao Zedong's "On Contradiction", and what Chinese scholars can learn from those readings. The article argues that these interpretations are shaped by the Western philosophical currents and theoretical crises of their moment. In Wang's view they therefore often cross the line into "over-interpretation" and "theoretical transgression" (理论越界). Wang also holds that they still offer useful prompts for developing a Marxist dialectics with Chinese characteristics. The article first sets out four general features of foreign readings. They are embedded in contemporary Western currents, they serve academic discourse more than revolution, they appear at moments of crisis for Marxism, and they use Hegel's or Marx's dialectics as an intermediary. It then traces a historical sequence of four paradigms: Louis Althusser's scientistic structuralism in the 1960s, Norman Levine's neo-Hegelian reading in the 1980s, Ian Hunt's "new dialectics" in the 1990s, and Slavoj Žižek's Lacanian Marxism in the 21st century. A final section evaluates each paradigm and lists causes of the misreadings. Wang follows Althusser's use of the essay in three stages: first to ground his theory of overdetermination in Marx's break with Hegel, then in the symptomatic reading of Capital, and finally in his theory of ideology. Levine, in Wang's account, presents Mao as having revived a Hegelianised Leninism and so as proof that Marxism must return to Hegel. Hunt compares Mao with Marx and with Masaccia's model of contradiction, and Žižek criticises Mao for rejecting the negation of the negation. Wang judges that Althusser severs the essay from "On Practice"; that Levine over-stresses Hegel; that Hunt reduces transformation of opposites to a simple swap of positions; and that Žižek fundamentally misreads Mao's dialectic as a "negative dialectics". Wang attributes the transgressions to five causes: Orientalist presuppositions, the habit of forcing Western concepts onto Mao's thought, the gulf between the essay's historical setting and its readers' settings, the plurality of meaning in any text, and these schools' neglect of or hostility to Engels's dialectics. Evaluation should aim less at dialogue than at drawing methodological lessons from the misreadings. Such lessons can help complete Mao's wish to rewrite "On Contradiction" and to build a Marxist dialectics with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a Chinese critical assessment of how Althusser, Levine, Hunt and Žižek used "On Contradiction", with the sources they drew on.

The current state and characteristics of contemporary European and American left-wing currents of thought 当代欧美左翼思潮发展的现状与特征 Feng Li Writing in 2018, the 170th anniversary year of the Communist Manifesto, Feng asks what the decade since the 2008 financial crisis has done to left-wing thought in Europe and North America, and what that thought is worth. The article argues that radical left currents have been merging with Western Marxism, and that young people and the lower classes are increasingly disillusioned with capitalism. It also argues that the left remains largely theoretical, with limited practical force, and that the Manifesto has lost none of its relevance. The article opens with a reading of the Manifesto's "spectre" as irony: Marx and Engels adopted the reactionaries' own image of communism in order to refute it. Feng then sets out the main concerns of the Euro-American left: the condition of capitalism itself, theories of socialism and communism, and Chinese socialism. Thinkers discussed include Chris Harman, Thomas Piketty, Lukács, Gramsci, Henri Lefebvre, Alain Badiou, Slavoj Zizek, Tony Andreani and Martin Hart-Landsberg. The text closes with the significance of left thought and the contemporary value of the Manifesto. Feng identifies three characteristics of the current left. First, it is still mostly confined to research and speeches, because left parties rarely hold real power. Even where communist-led parties govern, as in Cyprus, the author says the state does not become socialist, and the working class lacks the conditions for broad unity. Second, it shows a "bourgeois socialism" tendency in the Manifesto's sense, for which Feng cites Macron and Bernie Sanders. Sanders, the article says, looks to Scandinavia and the New Deal rather than opposing capitalism. Third, its influence is spreading into young people's lives, driven by what Piketty calls "patrimonial capitalism" and by social fracture. Feng also finds left views of China ambivalent: some praise its democracy as substantively genuine, yet doubt that its market reforms count as traditional socialism. Feng credits the Euro-American left with four contributions: developing Marxism, sustaining critical attention to capitalism, anticipating alternatives such as network or green communism, and pushing for change in the world order. The last of these is limited, since left parties now pursue electoral rather than violent routes and find power hard to win. The author concludes that the Manifesto remains valid for capitalism, for left thinkers and parties, and for ordinary people seeking a society without exploitation. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic assessment of Western left thought after 2008, including how it views China and the Manifesto.

The predicament of contemporary Western left-wing parties in reviving socialism, and how to respond 当代西方左翼政党复兴社会主义的困境及其应对之策 Guo Guoshi Why did Western left-wing parties fail to turn the 2008 financial crisis, which began with the US subprime collapse, into a revival of socialism? Guo observes that some of them lost power instead. The article argues that the revival of Western socialism needs more than a revolutionary opportunity, which is the objective outcome of contradictions. It also needs stronger left parties, whose capacity can be built. Guo identifies three obstacles: the power structure of Western capitalist states, the shifting class base of the parties, and the parties' own weakened capacity. Writing from a macro perspective, Guo first sets out the internal logic of left-party goals. The author divides the left into a moderate wing, mainly social democrats, and a radical wing, which includes communist and workers' parties, and notes that many radical parties have become deradicalised. Party programmes of the German SPD, the British Labour Party and the French Socialist Party are cited to show that these parties pursue democratic socialism and accept the market. The article then analyses the three difficulties, drawing on cases from Britain, Germany and France, and ends with proposals. Guo's central claim is that the parliamentary road, which most left parties now follow, hands the initiative to capital. Representative institutions, campaign finance and what the article, borrowing Fukuyama, calls the 'veto system' of separated powers are said to protect the capitalist character of power and leave left governments unable to reach structural problems. Second, class differentiation, the shrinking of industrial labour and the dissolving of class consciousness are said to erode the core electorate. The National Front's gains in France are cited as an example. Third, Guo argues that parties such as Blair's Labour, the SPD and the French Socialists shifted to the centre, split internally and governed poorly, which fed a vicious circle of lost voters and lost power. Guo proposes that left parties hold to their class position and root themselves in the interests of lower- and middle-strata people, citing Labour's improved result under Jeremy Corbyn in the 2017 election. They should seek power by combining parliamentary and extra-parliamentary struggle, avoiding both 'parliamentary cretinism' and unprepared assaults, and then use power for lasting social transformation. Finally, they should unite with one another on an equal footing and settle internal disputes through intra-party democracy and democratic centralism. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic account of why Western social-democratic and left parties stalled after 2008, with data on Labour, the SPD and the French Socialists.

Žižek's critique of Western left-wing political thought and its implications: a reading of Repeating Lenin 齐泽克对西方左翼政治思想理论的批判及启示——解读《重述列宁》 Han Aiye Han Aiye reads Slavoj Žižek's Repeating Lenin (2001) as a critique of the Western left's theory and practice. The article argues that Žižek, by presenting Lenin as the model of left-wing political thought, calls for a renewed "politics of truth" and searches for a way beyond global capitalism. Han also holds that Žižek names sharp problems but offers no concrete plan for changing capitalism's coordinates, and that his theory does not go beyond Marxism. The article has three parts. The first sets out Žižek's criticism of the Western left after the collapse of the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe, under three heads: the loss of the dimension of truth, the suspension of the critique of political economy, and the principle of "interpassivity" in action. The second part covers what Žižek means by "repeating Lenin". The closing section draws lessons for China. In Han's account, Žižek sees contemporary capitalism as a "post-political" society in which ideological conflict gives way to cooperation between technocrats and liberal multiculturalists. Postcolonialism, postmodernism and thinkers such as Richard Rorty and Peter Singer are said to turn real struggles into questions of perspective, text and suffering. Žižek also holds that the right depoliticises the economy while the left, from Balibar and Rancière to Badiou, Laclau and Mouffe, offers a purely political critique that abandons the economy. Han backs this with Marx's Capital and Lenin's remarks on it, and argues that politics and economy cannot be separated. "Interpassivity" means acting so that nothing really happens, and Žižek says it leaves left activism inside capitalism's coordinates. Žižek's Lenin makes truth concrete through political action, as in the April Theses, and he refuses the "patriotic line" of 1914. He also keeps political and economic critique together. Han concludes that Žižek's critique contains one-sided elements, but that it still offers three lessons for China. Marxist belief should be firm, as the basis for realising the Chinese Dream. Marxism's universal principles must be adapted to China's particular conditions, as Lenin did for Russia and Mao Zedong did through "encircling the cities from the countryside". Finally, one should act boldly and keep to the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics, which Han describes as a modernization path different from Western capitalism. Read the original if you want a short Chinese reading of Žižek's Repeating Lenin and an example of how Chinese Marxist scholars of 2018 drew political lessons from Western radical theory.

Žižek and Kojève: a hidden lineage of the dialectic 齐泽克与科耶夫——辩证法的隐秘学脉 Wu Guanjun Slavoj Žižek is widely regarded as one of the most important European Marxist thinkers of the past three decades, yet Wu Guanjun argues that his inheritance from Marx is mainly political, centred on a radical critique of global capitalism. The article proposes a second, hidden route from Žižek to Marx that runs through Alexandre Kojève, the friend of Lacan whom Wu calls a "Marxised Hegelian". Wu's thesis is that a major part of Žižek's English-language work is a radical retelling of the Hegelian dialectic, and that Kojève laid its substantive foundations even though Žižek never acknowledges him. The article first sets out Kojève's reading of Hegel and Marx, in which negation is the core of the dialectic and revolution arises from it. It then traces how Kojève's seminar shaped Jacques Lacan, who became Žižek's main theoretical source through Jacques-Alain Miller. A longer section reconstructs Žižek's reading of Hegel and shows where it keeps and where it breaks with Kojève. A short conclusion places the whole line, from Hegel through Marx, Kojève and Lacan to Žižek, against Karl Popper's charge that Hegel and Marx lead to totalitarianism. In Wu's account, Kojève makes freedom equal to negativity and creativity: the human being is the negation of the given, and history advances through struggle until a final universal state. Lacan keeps the dialectic but rejects the "final synthesis" and absolute knowledge, since the unconscious cannot be reduced. Žižek then rejects Kojève's end of history and his restriction of the dialectic to human action, and restores a Hegelian dialectic of nature. For Žižek, absolute knowledge sits in the middle of the dialectical process, not at its end. It is knowledge of the gap, or the Real, built into every totality, and synthesis is only a shift of perspective on the antithesis. Wu stresses that Žižek still inherits Kojève's thesis that human existence is negativity and that negation creates the New. The "night of the world" is the ontological condition of freedom and revolution, and spirit remains a thorn in the throat of the big Other. Wu concludes that through this lineage Hegel is freed from Popper's accusation. Žižek removes the temporal and historical dimension from the dialectic and presents negation as an affirmative, creative force whose recoil never ends. Wu credits Žižek with helping to produce a reading of Hegel as a non-totalising thinker without an endpoint. Read the original if you study Žižek, Lacan or Kojève and want a case for a hidden Hegelian-Marxist genealogy behind Žižek's dialectic.

Inheritance and rupture in the dialectics of non-identity Žižek as an Adornoist 非同一性辩证法的继承与断裂 Huang Weijie Huang Weijie takes up a question about the source of Slavoj Žižek's reworking of Hegelian dialectics. Most scholars, the author says, treat it as a Lacanian dialectic because of its Lacanian vocabulary. Huang argues the opposite: its substance restates Theodor Adorno's dialectics of non-identity. Its aim is to find a real revolutionary subject within the space opened by Adorno's 'priority of the object'. On this reading Žižek does not want to cure the subject driven mad by the symbolic order, but to break the symbolic order itself. The article has five sections. It first asks whether Žižek is really a Lacanian. It then examines the transcendental subject and the critique of ideology in The Sublime Object of Ideology, followed by the structure of non-identity and the 'object'. A fourth section treats materialist dialectics and natural history, and a short conclusion follows. Huang compares passages from Žižek's books (including The Parallax View, Less Than Nothing and Absolute Recoil) with Adorno's Negative Dialectics and other texts, and with Sohn-Rethel and Sloterdijk, whom Žižek names as sources. Huang's central move is to show structural identity between the two thinkers. Žižek's 'commodity form' and 'cynicism', credited to Sohn-Rethel and Sloterdijk, were already worked out in Adorno's account of the unconscious transcendental subject and of the split between knowing and acting. Adorno's 'priority of the object' is logically prior yet appears only retroactively as the remainder of identity, and Huang says this is the structure of Žižek's objet a and parallax. Žižek even sets his 'parallax Real' against the standard Lacanian Real. Both thinkers, in Huang's account, also call their approach materialist dialectics and target capital as 'second nature'. The rupture, Huang argues, lies in natural history. Adorno keeps history and the objective regularity of nature and society, in Marx's sense, at the centre of critique. Žižek instead puts formal structure and contingency first, treating symptomatic dynamics as historicity and the origin of capitalism as a retroactive narrative. In this he resembles post-Marxists such as Laclau and Mouffe. Where Adorno's stance is negative and utopian, built around the 'constellation', Žižek seeks a Cartesian 'empty gesture' of a subject who performatively founds a new order, which Huang says flattens historical regularity into pure contingency. Read the original if you study Žižek, Adorno or Western Marxism and want a Chinese-language case that Žižek's dialectics derive from Adorno rather than Lacan.

Transforming the discourse system of Marxist theory education in universities 高校马克思主义理论教育话语体系转换 Xiu Guoying Writing in a newspaper commentary (China Social Sciences Today, 28 June 2018), Xiu Guoying asks how the language of Marxist theory education in Chinese universities should change to suit a new era. Xiu argues that the discourse must shift along three dimensions, with the overall aim of the free and all-round development of the human being and a people-centred ("people first") value core. The piece first sets out these goals, linking them to the aim of building a moderately prosperous society in all respects. It then takes the three dimensions in turn: from explicit to implicit discourse, from argumentative to narrative discourse, and from indoctrination to dialogue. On the first dimension, which Xiu calls the most important, educators should translate official political and abstract document language into personal, everyday and aesthetic language that resonates with students' lived experience, using social media and online culture. On the second, Xiu holds that persuasion-by-argument rests on grand narratives and uniform standards, and its effect is weakening as students' horizons widen. Storytelling, a traditional Chinese resource, is presented as open and equal, allowing each learner to draw on personal experience. On the third, Xiu says Lenin's idea of "inculcation" suited its historical context, but that today's more stable society needs citizens with democratic awareness and initiative, so teaching should become democratic, self-enlightening dialogue between equals. Xiu concludes that the effectiveness of such education should be judged by whether students respond keenly to social problems, and that universities should foster a tolerant, open and critical campus culture. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Chinese education scholars in 2018 framed pedagogical reform in ideological and political courses.

What China's reform and opening up offers developing countries in solving the problems of modernization 中国改革开放对发展中国家破解现代化难题的启示 Hao Yongping Huang Xianghuai Writing in Economic Daily in August 2018, amid frequent trade disputes, Hao Yongping and Huang Xianghuai ask what China's experience of reform and opening up can teach other developing countries. They argue that reform and opening up is the secret of China's rapid modernization. In their account, developing countries must solve two linked problems at once: their own development and adjustment to the international order. The commentary has three parts. It first sets out three dilemmas the authors see in developing countries' modernization: development versus stability, openness versus autonomy, and boosting growth versus predatory extraction by officials. It then presents China's answers to each, and finally draws lessons for meeting new challenges while keeping to the principles and direction of reform and opening up. Examples include Latin American countries said to depend on foreign capital and the idea of institutional 'transplantation'. The authors pair each dilemma with a Chinese solution. A full set of governing practices, balancing market and state, openness and cultural inheritance, and livelihoods and social vitality, is said to reconcile development with stability. A basic institutional system, including the people's congress system and public ownership as the mainstay, is said to preserve autonomy and so allow firm openness, which they call the 'historical dialectics' of reform. The multiparty cooperation and political consultation system led by the Communist Party is presented as a channel of participation and extra supervision that curbs vested interests and avoids political instability. The authors conclude that developing countries need strong leadership, institutions that fit national conditions, and peaceful development as the basic goal of modernization. They argue that transplanting foreign institutions can cause fatal rejection, and that rising developing countries unsettle some developed countries, which respond with trade disputes. They hold that modernization is not the preserve of a few developed states and that China should deepen reform and opening up with strategic resolve. Read the original if you want a representative 2018 official-media statement of how Chinese commentators present China's path as a reference for the Global South.

Socialism with Chinese characteristics is rooted in the fertile soil of Chinese culture 中国特色社会主义植根于中华文化沃土 Yang Yanqiu Writing in Economic Daily in September 2018, after the national conference on publicity and ideological work, Yang Yanqiu argues that socialism with Chinese characteristics grows out of Chinese cultural tradition. In Yang's account, a distinctive cultural heritage made it inevitable that China would follow a development path suited to itself. The short commentary has three parts. It first describes Chinese culture as long-lived and continuous, citing historical records such as the Spring and Autumn Annals, the Records of the Grand Historian and the Zizhi Tongjian. It then sets out the distinctive values of that culture. Finally it considers how cultural inheritance affects the choice of a governance system. Yang draws heavily on Xi Jinping's statements. The article lists traditional ideas such as "the people as the foundation of the state", harmony in diversity and "the world belongs to all". It says these still shape present-day concepts: seeking truth from facts, a community with a shared future for mankind, a harmonious society and a moderately prosperous society. Yang contends that a country's governance system is determined by its history, culture and level of development, and that cultural tradition acts back on politics and the economy. Citing Xi, the article rejects copying other countries' models and holds that only a country's own people can judge whether its path is right. Yang concludes that the core value system shared across Chinese society is the deepest cultural support for the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The article also presents traditional culture as the basis of cultural confidence. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary in 2018 grounded the Chinese path in cultural tradition.

The US trade war highlights the hegemonic nature of the United States 美国发动贸易战凸显其霸权主义本质 He Zili Writing in 2018, after the Trump administration imposed high tariffs on Chinese goods and restricted Chinese high-tech investment, He Zili asks why Washington chose such means and whether it can win. He argues that the trade deficit is only a pretext. In his account, the real motives are to preserve US hegemony and to contain China's development, and the administration cannot win the trade war. The article has three parts. The first sets out five causes of the US–China trade deficit, using 2017 figures: 375.23 billion US dollars in goods, by US statistics. The second examines the administration's motives. The third explains why the policy is bound to fail. On the deficit, He points to differences in development level and position in the industrial chain, contrasting industrial structures, and processing trade that shifts other economies' surpluses to China. He adds that US statistical methods overstate the deficit and that US export controls on high technology distort the division of labour. For He, the deficit is therefore an objective result, not evidence of unfair practices by China. On motives, He holds that Trump rightly admits American decline but wrongly blames the international order and China. He sees the decline as the product of the US political and economic system and of shifts in the global balance, and he treats Trump's policy as a copy of the views of Bannon and Navarro. On the outlook, He argues that the Triffin dilemma, the rigid demand of US consumers and industrial hollowing-out make the deficit impossible to eliminate. Tariffs would raise costs for American households and firms, he says, and push production abroad. He concludes that the administration's unilateralism and protectionism undermine global governance and run against economic globalization. He grants that the policy of containment will not succeed but may interfere with China's development, which he says calls for serious attention. He states that China opposes this reverse globalization and will work with other countries to steer globalization in the right direction. Read the original if you want a representative 2018 Chinese official-academic account of the trade war, with its statistics and economic arguments.

Why China is able to lead new trends in world development 中国为什么能够引领世界发展新潮流 Hong Xianghua Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2018, Hong Xianghua takes up a claim that China increasingly leads new trends in world development and asks why this is so. The answer given is threefold: the global influence of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, the growing international acceptance of Chinese proposals, and the rising weight of China's economic, technological and green-energy contribution. The commentary is organised in three numbered sections. The first addresses the reach of Xi Jinping's ideas at home and abroad. The second lists how Chinese concepts have been written into United Nations and other international documents. The third turns to China's role as contributor to global development, supported by growth and innovation figures for the five years since the 18th Party Congress (2012). In the first section, Hong argues that ideas are the most powerful force in human history and that scientific ideas matching objective reality change the world most. As evidence of influence, the author cites the 2017 CPC in Dialogue with World Political Parties High-level Meeting and the circulation of The Governance of China, whose second volume is said to have exceeded 13 million copies. The second section, the core of the case, traces how "a community with a shared future for mankind" first entered UN resolutions in February and March 2017, and how the Belt and Road Initiative was written into a 2016 General Assembly resolution endorsed by 193 members. Hong adds that the principle of "extensive consultation, joint contribution and shared benefits" and the call for "mass entrepreneurship and innovation" were also taken up by UN resolutions. The third section cites average annual growth of 7.1% against 2.7% for the world economy, a contribution to world growth above 30%, and contributions above 40% to technological innovation and to green energy. Hong concludes that China is moving from supplier of material goods to supplier of public goods, and from participant in global governance to leader. The author presents China's development as benefiting developing countries and pushing the international order beyond zero-sum thinking. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Chinese official commentary in 2018 marshalled UN resolutions and economic statistics to support claims of growing Chinese global influence.

Is China's modern history one of "sinking" or "rising"? 中国近代历史是“沉沦”还是“上升”？ Zhang Haipeng Zhang Haipeng takes up a long-running question in the historiography of modern China: whether the period is best described as a story of humiliation and decline ("sinking") or one that also contains advance ("rising"). Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2018, Zhang argues that neither of two established readings is sufficient. The author proposes instead that modern history follows a pattern of sinking to a "valley floor" and then rising. The article first sets out the older view, which stressed the slide into a semi-colonial, semi-feudal society after the Opium War. It then covers the 1980s revision, which held that sinking and rising coexisted because "semi-capitalism" was a historical advance on feudalism. Zhang then offers a periodisation that extends modern history from about 80 years to 110 years, running to the 1940s. Zhang grants each view some validity but holds that the first cannot explain later positive development, and that the second cannot explain the whole period. If there is an "abyss", the author says, it must have a bottom. Zhang places that bottom in the first two decades of the twentieth century, from the Boxer Protocol of 1901 to the warlord era, citing foreign aggression, the Twenty-One Demands, Yuan Shikai's imperial bid and warlord wars. After that, the author argues, the 1911 Revolution, the New Culture and May Fourth movements, the spread of Marxism and the founding of the Chinese Communist Party made rising factors the main trend, even as Japanese aggression worsened. Zhang concludes that modern Chinese history is both a history of humiliation and a history of unyielding struggle for national independence and prosperity. Humiliation is concentrated in the sinking phase and struggle in the rising phase. In the author's account, the rising phase ended in victory in the war of resistance and laid the basis for China's modernization. Read the original if you want a concise statement of an officially published Chinese view on periodising modern history and on the "sinking" and "rising" debate.

History is the best textbook 历史是最好的教科书 Jin Chongji Jin Chongji, in a short commentary published in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2018, takes up Xi Jinping's remark that "history is the best textbook". The author argues that China's modern history, 1840–1949, must be understood if one is to grasp China's present conditions, and that younger Chinese readers now lack a feel for that past. The piece opens with Xi's statements on the suffering and resistance of the Chinese nation in modern times and on patriotism as the core of the national spirit. It then treats the 109 years from 1840 to 1949 as a period of special significance, reflects on the generational gap in historical experience, and ends with a practical point about reading. Jin presents modern China as a transitional stage between ancient China and a China striving for socialist modernization. In this account the period saw both decline and ascent, and ascent prevailed; the change from a country on the edge of extinction to one that stood up again is called a miracle in human history, won by generations of struggle. Jin quotes the scholar Ren Jiyu, who said that only those who lived through disaster and foreign bullying feel a deep sense of liberation, which later-born youth cannot share. Reading some modern history can partly make up for this. Jin notes that the volume of new sources and scholarship on modern Chinese history is overwhelming for general readers. The author therefore calls for concise, high-quality reading matter that meets this need. Read the original if you want a brief example of how a senior Party historian justifies the study of modern history in terms of Xi Jinping's remarks.

Opposing historical nihilism is a serious struggle 反对历史虚无主义是一场严肃的斗争 Wang Weiguang Writing in 2018, Wang Weiguang argues that opposing historical nihilism is a serious ideological and political struggle rather than a matter of scholarly disagreement. The short commentary contends that distorted accounts of modern Chinese history harm the public, especially young people, and that historians have a duty to counter them. The piece opens with the 109 years from 1840 to 1949. Wang describes this as a period in which China sank into a semi-colonial, semi-feudal society, then rose up for independence, democracy and modernization and moved towards socialist modernization. It then turns to the way the internet, television, film and popular publishing have widened public access to historical knowledge, and to the problems this has brought. Wang grants that popularisation has some value, but says much of it is driven by a mistaken view of history. The author points to anecdotal "unofficial history", costume-drama and time-travel storylines, and to social media accounts and forums that use slogans such as "re-evaluation", "restoring history" and "farewell to revolution". In Wang's account, these attack and negate modern Chinese history, the revolution, socialist construction and the histories of the Party, the People's Republic and the army. Wang says the aim is to weaken the historical legitimacy of the Communist Party's rule, the guiding status of Marxism and the socialist system. Wang concludes that historical nihilism is fundamentally at odds with the Marxist scientific view of history. The author calls on the historical profession to adopt historical materialism, take up its social responsibility and spread scientific historical knowledge and research findings. Opposing nihilism is cast as a struggle between materialist and idealist views of history, and as a political struggle to uphold Marxism and socialism. Read the original if you want a brief, authoritative statement of how a senior Party theorist framed the campaign against historical nihilism in 2018.)

The capitalist nature and inner paradox of Europe's new populism 欧洲新民粹主义的资本主义属性及其内在悖论 Fu Mei Li Zhen Writing in 2018, Fu Mei and Li Zhen ask whether Europe's new populism, which has surged since the 2008 financial crisis, is really "anti-capitalist", "anti-establishment" and "anti-political", as it presents itself and as much Chinese scholarship assumes. They argue that it is not. In their account it is a product of capitalist modernity and an acute expression of capitalism's own contradictions, with a clearly capitalist character and an inner paradox. The authors criticise Chinese studies for staying within political science and international relations and describing surface facts. They set out a Marxist critique in three parts. The first examines four features of new populism: its concept of "the people", its popular-sovereignty ideas, its political mobilisation and its value claims. The second traces its origins to the logic of capital and its institutional dilemma. The third tests its claim to deliver "the people's justice". Fu and Li argue that the populist "people" is vague, elastic and instrumental, unlike the Marxist notion of a historical bloc led by an advanced class and based on working people. Its popular sovereignty descends from Rousseau's bourgeois tradition, which rests on private property, and it mobilises through a binary of "people" against "non-people". They contend that populists attack the shortcomings of representative democracy rather than the system itself. Populist demands to curb immigration, globalisation and the EU are read as reactions to capital's drive to accumulate. Once populist parties win office, the authors say, the logic of representative politics absorbs them into the "capital politics" they denounced. Drawing on Marx's critique of Proudhon and Lassalle, they hold that populist appeals to equality and fairness remain abstract moral ideas that ignore the productive basis of distribution. The authors conclude that European new populism cannot resolve the social difficulties caused by capital or achieve genuine justice for the people. In their view it renews and reforms capitalism while deepening its crisis. They call for a clear-eyed judgement of the phenomenon. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist critique that treats European populism as an expression of the logic of capital, and that draws heavily on Marx's analysis of capital and justice.)

Seeing through the new changes in imperialism in the internet age 透视帝国主义在互联网时代的新变化 Du Juan Du asks whether Lenin's theory of imperialism still explains the present, given the long-running claims that 'ultra-imperialism', the 'transnational bourgeoisie' or a borderless 'Empire' have superseded it. Taking the May 2017 ransomware attack as a starting point, the article argues that imperialism has not changed in essence: plunder once carried out by military invasion and colonial conquest has taken new forms in the internet age, behind an appearance of openness and freedom. The article has three parts. The first treats exploitation under technological monopoly, covering Apple, Intel and Microsoft, patents and technical standards, and US control of internet infrastructure. The second takes up the 'backlash' of financial imperialism, discussing Bitcoin, Hayek's idea of denationalising money, and the dark web. The third looks at how China can 'overtake on the curve' and defend itself. Du's central move is to read the ransomware attack through Lenin. Because the attackers' tools came from the US National Security Agency, and because the ransom was demanded in Bitcoin, Du treats the attack as more than ordinary extortion. In this reading it is a form of kidnapping-style marketing by an international financial monopoly group, aimed at pushing up virtual currencies as a successor to the dollar's weakening hegemony. Du describes Bitcoin as another Ponzi scheme, citing the 2014 collapse of the MtGox exchange, and says it circulates mainly on the dark web as a channel for money laundering and illicit trade. Under technological monopoly, Du adds, technology is 'separated from labour' and becomes a tool for extracting value from developing countries, as in the Foxconn–Apple profit split. Du also rejects Hart and Negri's thesis of a peaceful Empire, arguing that monopoly in the technology era is dynamic yet still tends towards stagnation and decay. Du concludes that monopoly contains the seeds of its own undoing. Technology blockades have pushed China to develop its own systems, such as the BeiDou navigation system, and Du expects such efforts to weaken the basis of hegemony. The author points to China's controls on Bitcoin trading and initial coin offerings, research on a state digital currency, the 2017 Cybersecurity Law and Xi Jinping's call to build a 'cyber power'. Du warns that a declining imperialism will become more aggressive, for instance by selling cyber weapons openly. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist applies Lenin's Imperialism to cryptocurrency, cybersecurity and technology rivalry with the United States.

Will the proletariat become a "useless class"? 无产阶级会沦为无用阶级吗？ Jiang Hongqun Writing in 2018, 170 years after the Communist Manifesto, Jiang Hongqun takes up the thesis of the Israeli historian Yuval Noah Harari that artificial intelligence will turn the proletariat into a "useless class". Jiang argues that this view, spread by the media as a successor to the "disappearance of the proletariat" thesis, is a new form of historical nihilism. Re-reading the Manifesto through historical materialism, Jiang contends that AI will exclude workers under capitalism but will not make the proletariat useless. The author concludes that the class facing obsolescence is the bourgeoisie. The article first sets out Harari's argument from Homo Deus and Sapiens: algorithms will push manual and then mental workers out of employment, wealth will concentrate in a small elite, and the surplus masses will be kept occupied with drugs and computer games. Jiang then traces the origins of AI from manufactory and large-scale machine industry through Turing, the 1956 Dartmouth conference and corporate commercialisation. Next comes an analysis of why machines displace workers, followed by a look at working-class resistance, from Luddism to recent strikes against ride-hailing apps and self-driving legislation. Jiang's central move is to treat AI as a means of production and constant capital that creates no surplus value itself. Under capitalist private ownership it is therefore a tool for extracting surplus value and sustaining the system, and it sharpens the opposition between capital and labour. Machines have displaced workers since the seventeenth century, and Jiang cites Marx's critique of the "compensation theory" and the law of the rising organic composition of capital against Harari's claim that new jobs always appear. The author notes that AI giants such as Apple and Google employ few workers. Jiang then argues that capitalism's basic contradiction cannot be removed by AI, so the "two inevitables" in the Manifesto still hold. Jiang concedes that AI may cause unprecedented technological unemployment, but holds that this does not make workers incapable or useless. In the long run, drawing on Marx, Jiang reads AI as laying conditions for the liberation of labour and for large amounts of free time for everyone under a future communist society. The proletariat is therefore for Jiang a capable class that holds the future, while the "useless class" will be the bourgeoisie. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist scholar answers Harari's popular AI-and-work thesis with the Manifesto and Capital, and how that argument is built from historical and contemporary examples.

Foreign left-wing scholars' critique of neoliberalism 国外左翼学者对新自由主义的批判 Chen Xingliang Writing in 2018, Chen Xingliang reviews how left-wing scholars outside China have analysed and criticised neoliberalism. The article starts from the claim that neoliberalism, which it traces to the 1920s, has been deliberately introduced into China and threatens the country's ideological security as socialism with Chinese characteristics enters a new era. Chen argues that foreign left critics expose neoliberalism's harms well, but that their alternatives remain academic and ineffective. The review has three parts. The first sets out neoliberalism's core doctrine (extreme individualism and market fundamentalism, drawing on Hayek and Friedman) and divides its history into three stages: the intellectual formation of the 1920s–1950s, including the Mont Pelerin Society of 1947; the movement-building of the 1950s–1970s; and the post-1970s phase of politicisation and global spread, with decline after the 2008 crisis. The second part surveys the critics, among them Piketty, Harvey, Anderson, Wallerstein, Dos Santos, Duménil and Lévy, Crouch and Jones. The third part draws lessons for China. In Chen's account the critics make three kinds of case. In practice, they show neoliberalism widening wealth gaps, deepening inequality, extending political hegemony, distorting international trade rules (Latin America's 1980s "lost decade" is the example) and pushing privatisation. In theory, they trace its conservative intellectual lineage and describe its dogmatism, falsity, hegemony and its use of the state and think tanks. Chen then assesses four proposed alternatives: Harvey's reliance on financial crisis, Duménil and Lévy's left alliance against double hegemony, Crouch's civil society, and Nakaoka's call to restrain capital's desires. Chen judges each unrealistic, since ruling classes do not yield power and such thinkers lack political influence. Chen concludes that neoliberalism's influence has grown in the twenty-first century, including its alliance with the far right, and that China must respond in four ways. These are to expose its "universal values" and build cultural confidence; to uncover the capital-based logic of its theory and strengthen theoretical confidence; to oppose privatisation and advance the socialist market economy under Party leadership; and to resist a unipolar world by building a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a Chinese overview of Western left critiques of neoliberalism and how they are used in current Chinese arguments about ideological security.

Eco-socialism and the postmodern challenge to democracy 生态社会主义及其面临的后现代民主挑战 Jaume Sánchez This is a Chinese translation of an article by the Spanish political scientist Jaume Sánchez (the Chinese byline renders the name as Haomei Sangqisi). It asks why eco-socialism and political ecologism have not filled the ideological space left by the decline of social democracy and the Left in the postmodern era. Sánchez argues that postmodern fragmentation, de-ideologisation and what the author calls a 'post-populist condition' block eco-socialism, and that 'green democracy' requires a new unifying left-green ideology. The article begins with the postmodern setting since the 1980s: Baudrillard's end of political representation, the claimed irrelevance of left and right (Furedi, Castells) and the 'farewell' to social democracy (Judt). It then traces the rise of green political theory between the 1972 Stockholm and 1992 Rio conferences, and surveys eco-socialist writers including Sacristán, Frankel, Gorz, Eckersley, Sarkar, Dobson, Pepper, Wall, Löwy and Kovel. Later sections discuss the move from the welfare state to the 'ecological state', Laclau and Mouffe, Spanish politics after the economic crisis, and Naomi Klein. Sánchez's central claim is that eco-socialism is a 'hybrid' ideology that, after more than thirty years of theorising, remains incomplete. Drawing on Pepper, he argues that parts of the green movement have become a corrective mechanism for capitalism, and that without transforming social, economic, political and cultural institutions green democracy cannot materialise. He names two kinds of 'enemy' of green democracy: direct defenders of capitalism, and postmodern currents that aim to transcend left and right. The 'post-populist condition', which he links to neoliberal hegemony, the media and middle-class frustration in Spain, favours charismatic leaders, loose organisations and short-term demands rather than long-term transformation. Sánchez concludes that, as Klein argues, capitalist growth logic is incompatible with limiting climate change, yet this insight has not been embodied in any explicit global or regional ideology. Individual conscience is necessary but 'collective consciousness' matters more. He proposes an international 'eco-socialist network' that unites diverse movements, built through a 'metanarrative' of a green-left ideology. Read the original if you want a European eco-socialist's account of why green politics has stalled under postmodernity, and a survey of the eco-socialist literature from the 1970s to the 2010s.

The distortion of Marxist philosophy by "Western humanist Marxism" “西方人本主义马克思主义”对马克思主义哲学的曲解 Jie Changguang Writing in Studies on Marxism in 2018, Jie Changguang argues that "Western humanist Marxism" misreads Marxist philosophy and is, in essence, non-Marxist because it rejects the dialectics of nature and lacks a materialist principle. The article responds to some Chinese scholars who, drawing on this tradition, question mainstream domestic research on Marxist philosophy and even Engels, which Jie says has caused intellectual confusion. The article has three parts. The first characterises the "subject→object" paradigm shared by Lukács, Gramsci, the Frankfurt School, existentialist Marxism and others, and identifies three ways it fragments Marxist philosophy. The second proposes a "real things–contradiction" paradigm as a summary of mainstream Chinese Marxist philosophy. The third draws out the practical significance of the two paradigms for China in the new era. Jie holds that the subject→object paradigm stresses subjectivism, the primacy of practice and the exaltation of subjectivity. In Jie's reading this leads it to deny the dialectics of nature, which splits materialist dialectics and underpins the "Marx versus Engels" thesis. It also gives up materialism on the subject–object relation, on nature (reducing it to a humanised or social category) and on history, and promotes an abstract voluntarism, which Lukács himself later criticised as "subjectivist activism". The alternative paradigm rests on three claims: the material world is primary, internal causes are decisive, and internal contradiction is the driving force. Jie argues that contradiction already contains activity, because it involves self-negation, so dialectical materialism does not collapse into metaphysical determinism. Jie concludes that only the real things–contradiction paradigm meets the methodological needs of socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era. Four implications are given: explain China from China itself and reject "universal values" and panaceas; view complex arrangements such as the "four comprehensives" as organic wholes; look to internal drive, as in Xi Jinping's remarks on poverty alleviation; and reject extreme anthropocentrism in favour of the harmonious coexistence of humanity and nature. Read the original if you want a Chinese mainstream critique of Western Marxism and its defence of Engels and the dialectics of nature.

Cultural confidence and the contemporary value of traditional culture 文化自信与传统文化的当代价值 Zhang Jing Writing in the Economic Daily in July 2018, Zhang Jing asks how traditional Chinese culture relates to cultural confidence. The author argues that such confidence rests largely on history and on excellent traditional culture, so that identifying and elaborating its contemporary value is an important part of strengthening it. The short commentary begins from the 19th Party Congress (2017), which placed socialist culture alongside the path, theory and system of socialism with Chinese characteristics and stressed the Four-sphere Confidence. It then defines the contemporary value of tradition, offers two examples, and summarises a 2017 official Opinion on a project to transmit and develop excellent traditional culture. Zhang defines contemporary value as the elements of Chinese culture that raise people's spiritual level, help cultivate and practise core socialist values, and serve the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The author holds that cultural confidence is not a rigid or narrow attitude to tradition but follows the principle of not forgetting one's origins, absorbing foreign ideas and facing the future. Guided by dialectical and historical materialism, Zhang proposes keeping the essence and discarding the dross, and using contemporary value as the criterion of what counts as excellent. Examples are the self-strengthening ideal from the Book of Changes and the notion of the unity of heaven and humanity, which the author links to ecological civilization and green development. The article cites the Opinion's three layers of excellent tradition: core ideas, traditional virtues and humanistic spirit. Zhang concludes that promoting the creative transformation and innovative development of this heritage in the new era will strengthen cultural confidence and help socialist culture flourish. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official discourse in 2018 framed the use of traditional culture for cultural confidence and core socialist values.
