Showing the power of truth of twenty-first-century Marxism 展现21世纪马克思主义的真理力量 Wang Derong Writing in Economic Daily in June 2018, Wang Derong argues that Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era is the latest result of adapting Marxism to Chinese conditions. In Wang's account, it answers the question of what kind of socialism with Chinese characteristics to uphold and develop in the new era, and how. Wang presents it as a further leap in combining Marxism's basic tenets with China's concrete realities and as a historic contribution to twenty-first-century Marxism. The short commentary has three parts. The first treats the thought's effect on Marxism's sinicisation, its adaptation to the times and its popularisation. The second concerns its contribution to Marxist thinking on Party building. The third concerns the "Chinese wisdom and solutions" it offers for new global challenges. Wang holds that the thought advances Marxism in three ways. It extends the Party's "milestone" original contribution on questions of goals, strategy and political guarantees. It responds to a changed era, in which China's growing influence ties its path to the fate of humanity and of world socialism, and it adheres to the new development philosophy. It also rests on a people-centred stance that, Wang says, has won popular support. On Party building, Wang cites the leadership of the Communist Party as the defining feature of the system, and credits full and rigorous self-governance of the Party since the 18th Party Congress (2012) with improving Party conduct. Abroad, Wang points to its call for a community with a shared future for mankind as a contribution to global problems such as sluggish growth, terrorism and climate change. Wang concludes that the thought opens a new realm for Marxism, a new realm in running the Party, and a distinctive Chinese contribution to human civilisation. Read the original if you want a brief example of how the official reading of Xi Jinping Thought was presented in 2018 as a development of Marxism.

Upholding the fundamental stance of putting the people at the centre 坚守以人民为中心的根本立场 Ma Yide This commentary, first published in Economic Daily in August 2018, argues that the people-centred stance is the fundamental position of the Communist Party of China. Ma Yide contends that understanding and holding to it is essential for grasping Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and for gathering strength towards the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The piece draws on the report to the 19th Party Congress (2017), the Party Constitution, the Constitution of the People's Republic of China and Xi Jinping's speeches. It is organised under four headings: the people as creators of history, doing everything for the people, relying on the people in everything, and putting the people at the centre. Ma starts from the historical-materialist premise that the people create history, and applies it to Chinese civilisation and the struggle for national renewal. The author then cites Party documents stating that the Party has no interests apart from those of the working class and the broad masses, and lists achievements since the 18th Party Congress (2012), including over 60 million people lifted out of poverty and a basic social security system. Ma holds that the Party has won each new victory by relying on the people, and ties this to the new principal contradiction, between the people's growing need for a better life and unbalanced and inadequate development. Ma concludes that the Chinese Dream is ultimately the people's dream and calls for the Four-sphere Confidence and for steady progress towards common prosperity. The author adds that full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, an anti-corruption drive and law-based governance are needed to keep the Party's close ties with the people. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Party commentary in 2018 linked the people-centred stance to Xi Jinping Thought.

Viewing historical nihilism through the lens of historical materialism 用唯物史观透视历史虚无主义 Guan Feng Wang Xiaofang This newspaper commentary, published in 2018, asks how historical materialism can be used to expose and counter historical nihilism. Guan and Wang argue that the two are fundamentally opposed, and that historical materialism is the most powerful weapon against nihilist trends. They open with Xi Jinping's statement that the crux of historical nihilism is the denial of Marxism's guiding role, of the historical inevitability of China's turn to socialism, and of the leadership of the Communist Party. The authors first classify historical nihilism into three types, then answer each in turn from the standpoint of historical materialism. The three are: putting mistaken values first, using scholarly 'textual research' and 'restoration' as cover, and 'reassessing' leaders and heroes in order to vilify them. The piece is short and closely structured, with one rebuttal for each type. In the authors' account, the first type starts from values drawn from Western notions of freedom, democracy and human rights, and rewrites Party, state and army history on that basis, sometimes inventing facts. Guan and Wang call this idealism, because it reverses the Marx–Engels principle in The German Ideology of explaining ideas from material practice. The second type, they argue, either repeats the same value-first error or amounts to 'abstract empiricism'. It piles up trivial facts and unofficial anecdotes to deny historical essence, a tendency they link to Marx's mockery of Ranke and to criticism by Geoffrey Barraclough and William McNeill. They propose placing facts within the broad historical trend and combining an objective criterion (whether something promotes the productive forces and historical progress) with a subjective one, the former taking priority. The third type, they contend, relies on fabrication, exaggerated flaws and judging heroes by everyday common sense or present-day standards. They say this violates the comprehensive, dialectical and historical principles of historical materialism. The authors conclude that historical nihilism is a form of idealist history, and that its 'reassessments' belittle and demonise leaders and heroes. They call for archival work to be guided by an understanding of the main course and essence of history, with a clear sense of direction. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Chinese commentary classifies historical nihilism and answers it with the methods of historical materialism.

Taking Marxism as the guide in "reinvigorating culture" 以马克思主义为指导“兴文化” Liu Ailing This short commentary, first published in Economic Daily in September 2018, responds to Xi Jinping's call at the National Conference on Propaganda and Ideological Work to "reinvigorate culture" (xing wenhua). Liu argues that this task must be guided by Marxism and must keep to the forward direction of advanced socialist culture. The piece has two parts. The first presents Marxism as the fundamental guide to cultural development. The second sets out how that guidance is to be applied to traditional, revolutionary and socialist culture and to foreign cultural achievements. Liu holds that Marxist guidance must be concrete and not a slogan. It means using the latest results of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, and arming minds with Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Cultural production, in Liu's account, should be rooted in life and aimed at the people's aspiration for a better life, given the principal contradiction identified for the new era. Liu then names four tasks: creative transformation of fine traditional Chinese culture, drawing on revolutionary culture, cultivating core socialist values, and absorbing useful foreign cultural achievements while bringing Chinese culture to the world. Liu concludes that these efforts will strengthen cultural confidence, build a culturally strong socialist country and support the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Chinese civilisation is also expected to contribute to humankind's development. Read the original if you want a brief example of how official commentary in 2018 linked Marxist guidance to cultural policy after the 19th Party Congress.

Grasping the new era, understanding the new thought, studying the required course well On the amended Party Constitution 把握新时代 领悟新思想 学好必修课 Zhang Yingwei This commentary, first published in Economic Daily on 29 March 2018, takes up the amendments made to the Party Constitution at the 19th Party Congress (2017). Zhang argues that writing the main content of the Congress report into the Constitution unifies thinking and builds consensus across the Party. The author presents this as having major practical and historical significance for advancing socialism with Chinese characteristics from a new historical starting point. The article has two analytical parts and one practical part. The first explains why the amendments are required by the development of the Party and the state in the new era. The second treats them as a need to keep the Party's guiding ideology up to date. The third sets out how Party organisations and members should study, observe, implement and uphold the Constitution. On the first point, Zhang says the Constitution now records the judgement that socialism with Chinese characteristics has entered a new era. It also records the revised statement of the principal contradiction in society, now between the people's ever-growing needs for a better life and unbalanced and inadequate development. The author adds the word "beautiful" to the Party's basic line and the shift from "country" to "great power", which Zhang links to the goal for the centenary of the People's Republic. On the second point, Zhang calls the writing of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era into the Constitution as the Party's guiding ideology the single biggest highlight of the revision. Zhang describes the thought as the latest result of adapting Marxism to Chinese conditions. The article adds that culture now sits alongside the path, theory and system as part of the basic content of socialism with Chinese characteristics, and that the amendments absorb the practice of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. Zhang concludes that Party members must establish awareness of the Constitution, treating it as the basic standard for Party conduct and the basis of work. The author calls for studying it together with Xi Jinping Thought and the spirit of the 19th Congress, and for holding to the Four Consciousnesses and the Four-sphere Confidence. Zhang also proposes more targeted education, stronger supervision of implementation, and better Party regulations. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary in 2018 explained the rationale for the Party Constitution amendments and the duties they placed on members.

Valuable historical experience of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context 马克思主义中国化的宝贵历史经验 Liu Guangming Writing in Guangming Daily in August 2018, Liu Guangming asks what lessons the Communist Party of China has accumulated from nearly a century of adapting Marxism to Chinese conditions. The commentary argues that the Party has played the original and leading role in theoretical innovation, advancing Marxism's Sinicization alongside a great social revolution. Liu distils the record into five experiences, each phrased as something that "must" be upheld. The article is a short commentary built as a numbered list of five principles. These are: holding to the basic tenets of Marxism; treating China's fine traditional culture as a root; putting the people at the centre; emphasising emancipating the mind, seeking truth from facts and keeping pace with the times; and upholding Party leadership. Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era is presented throughout as the latest result of this process. Liu argues that the basic tenets, such as the basic contradictions of society, the decisive role of the productive forces and the people as makers of history, remain valid and supply the theoretical foundation for new ideas. Alongside them stands a second source, China's own cultural heritage. Liu cites Mao Zedong's 1938 and 1941 remarks to claim that Marxism in China has "two sets of ancestors" and that Marxism has merged with the nation's cultural genes. The people-centred stance is tied to the mass line: the cycle "masses–leadership–masses" is said to match "practice–knowledge–practice", so that popular practice becomes the source and carrier of theoretical innovation. Liu also warns that some Marxist parties in power became complacent and dogmatic and were eventually discarded by history. Citing Engels, the author says Marxism is a method, not a dogma. On the fifth point, Liu contends that Marxism must be advanced by a party with no private interests of its own. Without Party leadership, the author says, Marxism would degenerate under the banner of innovation and "subversive errors" would follow. Liu concludes that the fundamental reason for the achievements lies in Party leadership and the guiding position of Sinicized Marxism. For the new era, Liu calls for firm support for the Party Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core and for strengthening the Four-sphere Confidence. Read the original if you want a compact, official-media statement of how Chinese Party theorists summarised the Sinicization of Marxism in 2018.

The theoretical fallacy and practical error of the US trade war 美国发动贸易摩擦的理论之谬与实践之误 Chen Yongjun Zhang Jihuan Writing in Guangming Daily in August 2018, Chen Yongjun and Zhang Jihuan take up the trade dispute that the United States launched against China from the second half of 2017. They argue that the US action has no support in economic theory, whether classical Western, Marxist or the mainstream work of Paul Samuelson, and that it is a practical mistake. Their remedy for China is to return to negotiation, push opening up further and build dynamic comparative advantage. The article opens by describing the deep interdependence of the two economies, which it says have been each other's largest trading partner. It then reads the dispute through three bodies of thought in turn: Adam Smith and David Ricardo, Marx and Engels, and Samuelson. A second half sets out three policy responses for China. The authors' core move is to show that each tradition favours free trade. From Smith and Ricardo they argue that tariffs raise consumer prices and input costs for US firms, and they cite Caterpillar and General Motors and US Labor Department price data. From Engels's essay on protective tariffs and free trade they draw the claim that a country past its early stage should drop protection, and that the US now risks the 'endless spiral' Engels described for others. On Samuelson's 2004 article, they reject the reading that it justifies a trade war. They call it a numerical experiment on specially chosen cases, cite later work extending it, and note that Samuelson himself warned against protectionism. For China, the authors call for 'fighting' only to bring the US back to the negotiating table, since trade wars are said to be lose-lose. They urge China to defend economic globalization, quoting Xi Jinping's Davos speech, and to form a new pattern of all-round opening. They also urge it to strengthen learning and innovation, following Joseph Stiglitz, while admitting China's gap in core technologies. Read the original if you want an example of how Chinese commentary in 2018 used classical economics, Marxist texts and Samuelson to argue against US tariffs.

Building a "amicable and clean" new type of government–business relationship 构建亲清新型政商关系 Fang Shinan Taking up the formula in Xi Jinping's report to the 19th Party Congress (2017), Fang Shinan asks how to build a new type of government–business relationship that is "amicable" (qin) and "clean" (qing). Fang argues that this relationship requires optimising the political ecology and the business ecology together, and that doing so matters for rooting out collusion between officials and businesspeople. This short commentary, published in Guangming Daily in 2018, has three parts. It first explains why the two ecologies must be improved jointly, then identifies the problems the new relationship targets, and finally sets out three areas where effort should be concentrated. Fang defines the government–business relationship as a complex social tie that binds political power and administrative resources to economic interests and market behaviour. In Fang's account it reflects Party conduct, government conduct and wider social mores, and it is a requirement of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. The problems targeted lie in culture, institutions and the rule of law. Some officials act on power-centred and money-centred values and trade power for money, while some unscrupulous businesspeople court them with gifts. Institutions exist but are evaded, and respect for law is weak. Fang therefore calls for a culture built on socialist core values, institutional innovation that closes space for rent-seeking, stricter enforcement by discipline-inspection bodies, and a legal environment in which power operates openly. Fang concludes that cleaning up government–business relations will deliver a clean political ecology and a transparent, law-based business ecology, supporting socialist modernization. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-state commentary in 2018 framed the "amicable and clean" formula in terms of culture, institutions and law.

China's great practice in improving global governance 中国完善全球治理的伟大实践 Wang Lei This short commentary, first published in Guangming Daily on 30 August 2018, marks five years of the Belt and Road Initiative. Wang Lei argues that the Initiative shows China, as the world's largest developing country, taking up its historical responsibility in major-country diplomacy with Chinese characteristics. In the author's account, it also offers a new approach to improving global development and global governance and to building a community with a shared future for mankind. The piece has two parts. The first presents the Initiative as an important component of China's diplomacy in the new era since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The second considers how it contributes to reforming the global governance system, against a background of economic globalization meeting setbacks and anti-globalization sentiment rising. Wang assesses the Initiative from four diplomatic angles. For global governance, its principles of joint consultation, joint contribution and shared benefits are said to go beyond zero-sum thinking, balance of power and power politics. For neighbourhood diplomacy, it reflects a "greater periphery" approach. For developing countries, it is said to promote North–South and South–South cooperation and the UN 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. For major-country diplomacy, it has become a topic of policy communication with Russia, India, the United States, Japan, the EU and ASEAN. Domestically, the author says it opens border regions and supports regional strategies such as Beijing–Tianjin–Hebei coordination, the development of the western region and the revitalisation of the northeast. Wang concludes that the Initiative, which builds no geopolitical or military alliances and treats large and small participants equally, is a fundamental remedy for global governance and shared prosperity. It is presented as China's proposal for taking part in global opening up, improving global economic governance and building a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the Initiative was framed in official-style commentary in 2018.

The value of the "marginal notes" in the Feuerbach chapter of The German Ideology for the materialist conception of history 《德意志意识形态》费尔巴哈章“边注”的唯物史观价值 An Qinian An Qinian takes up a neglected feature of the Feuerbach chapter of The German Ideology: the 33 short marginal notes that Marx and Engels wrote beside the text. The article, published in Philosophical Trends in 2018, argues that although most notes are only a few characters long, they carry a great deal of information about how the materialist conception of history took shape and what its core is. The article first examines where the notes sit. They appear only in passages that Marx and Engels extracted from their earlier critique of Bruno Bauer and Max Stirner and moved into the chapter, and never in the paragraphs written specially for it. An sorts the 33 notes into five types: notes on Feuerbach (9), Marx's summaries of his own intellectual path and core ideas (4), criticisms of German idealist historical views (9), summaries of materialist ideas in the text (9), and two technical remarks by Engels. An concentrates on the first and second types. An argues that the Feuerbach notes show the decisive difference from Feuerbach. Marx and Engels held that Feuerbach saw nature and humanity as objects of contemplation and did not grasp that nature and social ties are products of labour practice. In this reading, the notes show that the fundamental divide between materialist and idealist views of history is whether practice explains ideas or ideas explain practice. For note 2 ("philosophical and real liberation; man; the Unique; the individual; geological, hydrological conditions; the human body; needs and labour"), An reads the first half as a compressed account of Marx's path from Feuerbach's "man", through Stirner's "Unique One", to the "individual" as the ensemble of social relations. The second half, in An's view, states the core of the theory: natural conditions and bodily organisation compel labour, and needs generated by labour drive history. An concludes that the Feuerbach-plus-Hegel account of Marx's development is untenable, because the decisive step was criticising Feuerbach's lack of a labour-based view of history. An also rejects the view that practical materialism negates the dialectical-materialist concept of matter, saying Marx and Engels stayed materialists on nature. Further, An holds that "social being determines social consciousness" does not fully capture Marx's starting point, which is labour and production, and that the theory has an inherent value dimension, as a path to human liberation. Read the original if you study the formation of historical materialism, Marx's relation to Feuerbach and Stirner, or the editorial history of The German Ideology.

The Marxist philosophical implications of the "people-centred" thought “以人民为中心”思想的马克思主义哲学意蕴 Zou Xingping Writing in 2018, shortly after the 19th Party Congress (2017), Zou Xingping asks what the principle of "putting the people at the centre" means when read from the standpoint of Marxist philosophy. The article argues that the principle is an integral part of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and that it follows directly from Marxist worldview, historical materialism and methodology. The article is organised in three sections, treating the principle in turn as a worldview, as a conception of history and as a method. It traces the idea of "the people" from Marx and Engels, through Lenin and the October Revolution, to Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping. Zou claims that Marx's "humanity" was abstract, whereas after the October Revolution it became the concrete "people" and a matter of political practice for a ruling proletarian party. Drawing on the historical-materialist thesis that the masses create history, the author contends that exploiting-class parties use "the people" as an ideological cover, while a proletarian party treats itself as the people's instrument. Methodologically, Zou describes the principle as the focal point of Marxist thinking, set against the bourgeois focus on "capital", and as a working method. It requires relying on the people, respecting their initiative and using their satisfaction as the test of comprehensively deepening reform. Zou concludes that adhering to a people-centred approach is an essential requirement of the Chinese Communist Party's nature, since its Constitution sets the aim of serving the people wholeheartedly. The author links the principle to the new principal contradiction in Chinese society, between the people's growing needs for a better life and unbalanced, inadequate development. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party theorists in 2018 grounded the people-centred principle in the classical Marxist canon.

How to do Marxist propaganda and education well and make it strong 马克思主义宣传教育何以做好做强 Shang Zhixiao Writing in Guangming Daily in September 2018, Shang Zhixiao takes up Xi Jinping's speech at the National Conference on Propaganda and Ideological Work. The question is how to build a socialist ideology with strong cohesion and guiding power in the new era. Shang's answer is that Marxist propaganda and education must be done well (zuohao) and made strong (zuoqiang), above all by studying, understanding and applying Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The commentary has two main parts. The first argues that Marxist education is the foundation for the mission Xi assigns to propaganda and ideological work: to hold high the banner, rally the people, nurture new people, promote culture and present China's image. The second sets out how the work itself should develop, through its content and system on one side and its forms and effects on the other. In the first part, Shang holds that propaganda work is work on people, and that people need a scientific worldview, outlook on life and values before beliefs and confidence can take hold. Marxism, in Shang's account, gives thinking and method (historical materialism, the theory of surplus value, dialectics), practical wisdom about life, and a vision of free and all-round human development that includes the spiritual dimension. In the second part, "doing well" means setting direction and method, with content that is targeted and accepted by its audience. "Making strong" means shaping opinion, uniting propaganda forces across fields and building a multi-level structure. Content should be built on basic Marxist theory, stress the Party's innovative theory, be popularised and stay tied to the people's interests. Forms should keep pace with the times and avoid formalism and dogmatism. Shang concludes that the work must answer why, what and how by drawing on Xi's remarks on Marxist guidance in philosophy and social sciences and on Marxism's historical standing at the 200th anniversary of Marx's birth. The commentary calls for sustained, constantly renewed effort. It cites Marx, Lenin and Deng Xiaoping to support the claim that Marxism is persuasive when it is thorough and plain. Read the original if you want a short example of how Party-affiliated scholars framed the tasks of ideological education after the 2018 propaganda conference.

The Marxist implications of comprehensively deepening reform 全面深化改革的马克思主义意蕴 Yang Ming Writing in 2018, Yang Ming asks what Marxist worldview and methodology lie behind the policy of comprehensively deepening reform adopted since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The article argues that the Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core has answered why, what and how to reform in a way that represents the concentrated application of Marxism's outlook on reform and development in the new era. For Yang, this shows a creative use of Marxist philosophy. The article, published in Red Flag Manuscripts, is organised in three parts. Each takes one component of Marxist philosophy as the lens: the Marxist view of the people, the Marxist view of practice, and the Marxist view of contradiction. Each part is built mainly from Xi Jinping's statements on reform, which Yang arranges under numbered sub-headings and links to classical Marxist propositions. On the view of the people, Yang argues that making 'happiness for the people' the mission of reform, treating the masses as its source of strength, and using the people's sense of gain (huodegan) as the test of results reflect historical materialism. Yang calls this the dividing line between materialist and idealist views of reform. The 'three whether' criteria echo Deng Xiaoping's 'three favourables'. On the view of practice, the article stresses the people as the subject of practice, a human-centred purpose, solid implementation ('hard work makes a nation flourish') and innovation as the first driving force of development. On the view of contradiction, Yang presents Xi's approach as a dialectical unity of the 'two-point' and 'key-point' theories. This means grasping principal contradictions, pursuing reform that is systematic, integrated and coordinated, and following laws of reform such as 'crossing the river by feeling the stones', which Yang describes as consistent with Marxist epistemology. Yang concludes that these three dimensions make the reform programme an embodiment of Marxist methodology. The article also lists methodological principles it attributes to Xi: 'five relationships' in thinking and 'five relationships' in policy, such as top-level design and experimentation, and bold yet steady steps. The text is an exposition of official thought rather than a critical appraisal. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese Party theorists in 2018 tied Xi Jinping's reform discourse to Marxist categories of people, practice and contradiction.

Reform and opening up demonstrates the powerful vitality of Marxism 改革开放彰显马克思主义强大生命力 Li Jingzhi Writing in the People's Daily on 21 September 2018, in the year of Marx's 200th birthday and the 40th anniversary of reform and opening up, Li Jingzhi argues that China's reform record shows the strong vitality of Marxism. In Li's account, reform and opening up was carried out under Marxist guidance, and its achievements also prove the vitality of socialism with Chinese characteristics. This short commentary has four steps. It first states that reform kept to Marxism and the Party's basic line, then traces how Marxism was combined with China's conditions in three historical periods. It next turns to theoretical innovation during reform, and ends by acknowledging setbacks while affirming socialism's prospects. Li holds that Marxism's vitality lies in its universality, which allows it to be combined with each country's concrete conditions, and in its continued development with practice. The author describes three leaps: from the revolutionary era to "standing up", from reform to "becoming prosperous", and in the new era to "becoming strong". Li presents reform as avoiding both dogmatic understanding of Marxism and its rejection, and as avoiding both a closed, rigid old path and an "evil path" of changing the Party's banner. Li cites innovations such as the theories of the primary stage of socialism, the essence of socialism and the socialist market economy. Li concedes that applying Marxism has not been smooth, but calls difficulties temporary and the outlook for socialism bright. Citing China's rise to the world's second-largest economy and rising living standards, Li concludes that socialism can perfect itself through reform and that Marxism still holds the high ground of truth and morality. Read the original if you want a brief example of the official People's Daily argument linking the 40 years of reform to Marxism's vitality.

Grasping the laws of ideological work so that Party ideological development is truly put into practice 深入把握思想建设的规律 将思想建设真正落到实处 Yang Deshan This commentary, first published in the People's Daily in September 2018, asks how the Communist Party of China can make its ideological development (sixiang jianshe) effective in practice. Yang Deshan starts from Xi Jinping's remarks at the meeting marking the 200th anniversary of Marx's birth, which credit the Party's growth to its emphasis on building the Party ideologically and strengthening it through theory. Yang argues that ideological development is foundational and that it must follow several regularities. The piece is a short, five-part argument. After an introduction, each section names one requirement: ideological work should be led by political development, grounded in theoretical study, secured by institutions, carried by effective vehicles, and supported by mechanisms for evaluating results. It draws on the 19th Party Congress (2017) report and on campaigns held since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Yang contends that political development, placed first by the 19th Party Congress, gives ideological work its direction: members must align with the Central Committee in thought, and ideals and values must sustain a healthy political ecology in the Party. Firm conviction is said to rest on study of Marxism, of history and of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Yang adds that institutionalising ideological measures, for example study and Party-spirit education systems, has been a mark of the period since 2012. Campaigns such as the mass line education campaign, the "Three Stricts and Three Honests" and "Two Studies, One Action" are presented as vehicles, with the "Remain true to the original aspiration" campaign as the next one. On evaluation, Yang admits that results are hard to quantify but says assessment is still needed to stop ideological work becoming formalistic, marginal or entertainment-driven. Suggestions include checking meeting minutes and members' reading notes, and anonymous appraisal by people inside and outside the Party against criteria such as diligence, integrity and willingness to take responsibility. Read the original if you want a concise official statement of how Party ideological work was framed in 2018 and what practical measures were proposed.

Stiffen the spiritual backbone of Communists: firmly grasp the key to ideological building 挺起共产党人的精神脊梁 牢牢把握思想建设的关键 Geng Hongbin Writing in the People's Daily in autumn 2018, Geng Hongbin argues that building the Party ideologically is the essential feature of a Marxist party and a long-standing strength of the Chinese Communist Party. In the new era, the author holds, the Party can be made strong only if ideological building keeps its foundational status. The commentary opens with a short history. It recalls Mao Zedong's principle of building the Party first of all ideologically, so that members join in thought as well as in organisation. It then points to ideological campaigns in the reform period, such as the "Three Stresses" education and the Marxist learning-type party. Finally it credits the series of ideological education drives since the 18th Party Congress (2012) with strengthening the Party's creativity, cohesion and combat capacity. Geng then names three priorities. The first is firm ideals and convictions, which the author calls the Party's spiritual pillar and which rest on morality, so members must be educated in public and private virtue. The second is stronger theoretical confidence, above all in contemporary Chinese Marxism, which Geng identifies with Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The third is unified thinking, whose core is staying highly consistent with the Central Committee and upholding its authority. Geng calls for combating individualism, decentralism, liberalism, departmentalism, factionalism, cliques and double-dealing, and treats consistency with the Central Committee as the basic test of how well ideological building works. Read the original if you want a short, official-register statement of how Party media framed ideological building in 2018.

Ideological development is the foundational work of Party building 思想建设是党的基础性建设 Song Jin Writing in the People's Daily in 2018, Song Jin takes up the 19th Party Congress (2017) statement that ideological development is the foundational work of Party building. The commentary argues that this is a scientific judgment grounded in the basic laws of Party building and is important for making the Party strong in the new era. The piece explains what 'foundational' means, what ideological development should focus on, where communist ideals come from, and how they should be put into practice. It draws on remarks by Deng Xiaoping, Mao Zedong, Liu Shaoqi and Xi Jinping, and on the Communist Manifesto. Song contends that ideas guide action: the guiding theory determines the Party's line and the conduct of its members, so other aspects of Party building cannot be consolidated without this base. The core task, in Song's reading, is to strengthen the ideals and convictions of Party members and officials, which rest on Marxism's account of social development and on its aim of serving the great majority. Members should therefore study Marxism, especially Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, which Song presents as the latest result of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context. Song adds that ideals must be both lofty and practical, illustrated by the story of Red Army women who cut their only quilt in half for a villager. Song concludes that, if ideological development is treated as foundational, the Party can withstand the 'four tests' and overcome the 'four dangers'. It would then remain the leading core of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Party commentary justifies the priority given to ideals and theoretical study.

Leading and driving the revolution in social practice through a revolution in ideas and theory Commemorating the great debate on the criterion of truth and celebrating the 40th anniversary of reform and opening up 以思想理论革命引领和推动社会实践革命 Yan Xiaofeng Writing in 2018, the 40th anniversary of both the truth-criterion debate and reform and opening up, Yan Xiaofeng asks how a philosophical discussion came to start a national transformation. The article argues that reform and opening up began as an ideological revolution within the Party, in which settling the line of thought made it possible to settle the political line. Yan concludes that the same pattern, in which theoretical innovation and practical innovation reinforce each other, continues under Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The piece has three parts. The first traces the path from the 1978 debate, which began with the article "Practice Is the Sole Criterion for Testing Truth", to the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978) and the launch of reform and opening up. The second follows how practice and theory interacted along the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics: Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents, the Scientific Outlook on Development and then Xi's thought. The third sets out why Yan regards Xi's thought as both practical and true. It ends by linking these themes to the 2018 anniversaries of Marx's birth and the Communist Manifesto. In Yan's account, the Party's line of thought is at bottom a philosophical principle. He treats the Yan'an rectification and Mao Zedong's writings as the earlier corrective to dogmatism and empiricism. The "two whatevers" (the Two Whatevers) made the person, not practice, the standard of truth, so political correction after the Cultural Revolution had to begin with philosophical correction. Restoring practice as the criterion let the Party separate Mao's achievements from the Cultural Revolution's errors, avoid freezing the Soviet model, and treat the people's support as the test of policy. The plenum then shifted the Party's focus to economic construction and corrected the political and organisational lines. For the new era, Yan argues that Xi's thought has been tested in practice. He cites the shift in the principal contradiction to one between people's growing needs for a better life and unbalanced and inadequate development. He also cites the changes since the 18th Party Congress (2012) in areas such as Party leadership, rule of law, ecology and full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. Yan stresses Party leadership, a people-centred approach and comprehensive deepening of reform as lessons of the past 40 years. Read the original if you want an example of how Chinese Party theorists in 2018 linked the 1978 truth-criterion debate to Xi Jinping Thought and to a narrative of continuous theoretical innovation.

Western-style democracy in the predicament of economic globalization, and the future diversification of democracy 经济全球化困境下的西式民主及未来民主多样化走向 Zhang Jun Writing in Hongqi Wengao in 2018, amid a global wave of populism in both developing and Western countries, Zhang Jun asks why this wave has arisen and what it means for the future of democracy. The article argues that populism is a negative tendency internal to Western-style democracy. In Zhang's account, its roots lie in the unequal distribution of benefits under economic globalization, and the stalling of globalization is eroding the standing and quality of Western democracy. The piece has three sections. The first reviews the course of economic globalization since the 1980s, led by Western developed countries, and the criticism it now faces. The second links the globalization impasse to what Zhang calls the "degradation" of Western democracy, in both developing and developed countries. The third looks ahead to a more pluralised globalization and a more diverse pattern of democratic practice. Zhang first holds that globalization brought gains, citing a fall of about 1.1 billion in the global poor over 30-odd years, but distributed them unevenly. Developed countries set the rules and occupy the high end of global value chains. Some Asian emerging economies have upgraded, while many developing countries remain at the low end. Within countries, the richest 1% gained most, and lower-middle-income workers in the West saw stagnant real incomes in 1988–2008. Zhang then argues that the West tied competitive-election democracy to globalization and exported it, though such elections are, in the author's words, only a regional West European experience and not universal. Left and right populists respond differently, to inequality and to immigration respectively. Both oppose globalization and distrust elites, which pushes elected governments towards short-sighted protectionism. Zhang predicts that protectionism and "re-industrialization" will not deliver what voters expect, that the anti-globalization tide will recede, and that emerging economies will gain more voice in global economic governance. Globalization will then become more open, inclusive and balanced, and the expansion of Western-style democracy will fall back. Zhang urges Western governments to restrain transnational capital, tax the top 1% more progressively and rebalance taxation and welfare. Diverse democratic practices, including socialist democracy with Chinese characteristics, are expected to become more attractive to developing countries. Read the original if you want to see how a 2018 Chinese Party-journal article links populism, globalization and the case for democratic diversity.

The international responsibility and contemporary value of the Belt and Road Initiative “一带一路”的国际担当和时代价值 Jiang Li Jin Xin Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2018, on the fifth anniversary of the Belt and Road Initiative, Jiang Li and Jin Xin respond to claims by some Western think-tank scholars that China uses the initiative to build a sphere of influence. The authors reject this reading. They argue that, amid rising protectionism, populism and unilateralism, the initiative has multiple forms of world significance and shows China acting as a responsible major power. The commentary sets out four vantage points: the trend of the world economy, international mechanisms and global governance, the openness of participating actors, and China's relationship with the world. A closing section states what the initiative is and is not, and what should be done next, including the second Belt and Road Forum for International Cooperation planned for the following year. On the economy, the authors say the world is in a period of sluggish growth. They hold that infrastructure and industrial investment can bring benefits to developing countries along the routes that Western governments and multinationals neglected, and can drive a new round of productivity gains across Eurasia and Africa. On governance, they describe a serious deficit, worsened by the United States' withdrawal from institutions and agreements. In their account the initiative is China's most important public good, advancing a new form of globalization and a community with a shared future for mankind. They also stress its inclusiveness: it sets no preconditions and seeks no uniform institutional arrangement. They cite alignment with UN agencies, regional bodies and national plans such as Kazakhstan's Bright Road and Indonesia's Global Maritime Fulcrum. The authors conclude that the initiative is not a geopolitical strategy, a Chinese Marshall Plan or a means of exporting a "China model". Its core is connectivity in five areas (policies, infrastructure, trade, finance and people-to-people ties), and its key principle is joint consultation, joint contribution and shared benefits. They say its function should not be stretched beyond infrastructure connectivity and international industrial-capacity cooperation. They call for an "upgraded version" and for telling "new Silk Road stories" with real cases. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese official commentary rebutted Western criticism of the Belt and Road Initiative in 2018.

From the cruiser Aurora to the Red Boat on South Lake 从“阿芙乐尔”号巡洋舰到南湖红船 Zeng Changqiu Writing in 2018, a century after the October Revolution and 97 years after the founding of the Chinese Communist Party, Zeng Changqiu links two events through two "red boats": the cruiser Aurora on the Neva and the pleasure boat on Jiaxing's South Lake, where the First Party Congress concluded its work. Zeng argues that the two form one continuous line, and that the Party's present historical mission is to advance along the socialist road opened by the October Revolution and the Chinese revolution. The article has three parts. The first treats the Aurora and the October Revolution: its world-historical significance and its basic lessons. The second traces the spread of Marxism-Leninism in China after 1917, the rise of the workers' movement, the formation of early Party groups and the founding congress in 1921. The third turns to the "Red Boat spirit", Xi Jinping's 2005 and 2017 statements on it, and what it means for Communists today. In Zeng's account, the October Revolution was the most profound revolution in history. It put Lenin's thesis of socialist victory in one country into practice, opened the Leninist stage of scientific socialism, broke imperialism's monopoly of the world order, and created a new pattern of competition and coexistence between two systems. Zeng draws four lessons: leadership by a Marxist party, seizure of power by force as the primary task, a firm worker–peasant alliance, and international solidarity. These lessons must be applied to national conditions and not copied mechanically. Zeng presents the Chinese Party as born from Marxism combined with the Chinese workers' movement and modelled on the Bolsheviks, with Li Dazhao as the key propagator. Zeng concludes that the Soviet collapse does not make the October road obsolete, since its experience endures and socialism with Chinese characteristics continues it after forty years of reform and opening up. The October road should be neither simply negated nor rigidly copied. The Red Boat spirit, defined as a pioneering spirit, a spirit of struggle and a spirit of dedication, is presented as the Party's source of strength for the Chinese Dream, the "Two Centenary Goals" and, ultimately, communism. Read the original if you want an example of Party-historiographical writing that links the October Revolution, the Party's founding and current ideology, with Li Dazhao-era sources and Xi Jinping's statements.

The ideological struggle has no end in sight 意识形态斗争正未有穷期 Zhang Chuanquan Writing in 2018, Zhang Chuanquan argues that although the Party's ideological work has improved markedly since the 18th Party Congress (2012), the struggle in the ideological sphere remains severe. In Zhang's account, hostile foreign forces will not abandon their plans to "Westernize" and "divide" China, so safeguarding socialist ideological security in the new era is an arduous task. The piece is a short commentary in a Party theoretical journal. The article has two parts. The first sets out four challenges: Western great-power use of ideological contest to advance national interests; postmodernism's assault on Marxist belief; the export of Western political ideas and values through the media; and persistent distortion and belittling of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The second part offers four ways to safeguard ideological security. In the first part, Zhang points to social-media-driven "colour revolutions" in North Africa and Syria, the "China threat" and "China collapse" narratives, the US trade war (called a revival of McCarthyism) and the Indo-Pacific strategy. Zhang says postmodernism "deconstructs" Marxism's wholeness and class character and that, in China, it feeds historical nihilism and weakened conviction among some Party members. Zhang also describes "universal values" as a vehicle of Western discourse hegemony. For the remedy, Zhang calls for upholding and developing Marxism and studying Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, and for promoting core socialist values against "universal values". Zhang adds that a community with a shared future for mankind, presented as surpassing the "Western version" of global order, should be advanced. Zhang concludes that theorists should tell China's story well, rebut Western "misreadings", and raise the global influence of Chinese philosophy and social science. Zhang says the Chinese Dream is not narrow nationalism and that comprehensive national strength is the material basis of socialist ideology. Read the original if you want to see how a 2018 Party journal framed Western ideological pressure and the official countermeasures to it.

How mainstream British and American media perceive and evaluate the Communist Party of China 英美主流媒体对中国共产党的认知与评价 Xia Jinmei Yang Liuyingzi Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2018, Xia Jinmei and Yang Liuyingzi examine how The Guardian, The New York Times and The Washington Post reported on the Communist Party of China after its 19th Party Congress (2017). They ask three questions: how these outlets perceive the Party, what characterises that perception, and how China can raise its international discourse power. The authors argue that the coverage has become more objective and positive, but that negative reporting still carries Western ideological assumptions. The article has three parts. The first sets out the three papers' praise for the Party's governance record and leadership. The second reviews their reading of the 19th Congress report, focusing on the phrase "new era", the blueprint for national rejuvenation, and the direction of China's democracy. The third analyses the features of the coverage and ends with recommendations for China's external communication. In the authors' account, the three papers credit the Party's open, win-win governing approach with raising China's international influence. They also credit its anti-corruption campaign with raising public trust, and its confidence in its own path with building national cohesion. They cite the papers as noting the community with a shared future for mankind, Xi Jinping's advocacy of globalisation at Davos, and the Congress's repeated references to a "strong country" and "great rejuvenation". The authors explain the improved objectivity by China's achievements, its more active role in global affairs and its stronger external communication. They add that the papers acknowledge democratic progress as a matter of fact but, on values, remain tied to Western-centrism, using "democratic" for Western systems and "authoritarian" for China's. The authors conclude that Anglo-American coverage shapes how citizens of both countries see China. They hold that Western discourse hegemony will not disappear soon and that China's external discourse environment remains difficult. They call for a discourse system with Chinese characteristics grounded in Marxist political philosophy, more precise and diversified communication aimed at different cultures, and a more proactive setting of international agendas. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Party journal summarises and interprets Western media coverage of the Party after the 19th Congress, and what communication strategy it draws from it.

The scientific conception of history in the Communist Manifesto 《共产党宣言》的科学历史观 Yin Hanning Writing in Hongqi Wengao in 2018, Yin Hanning asks what view of history runs through the Communist Manifesto and why it demonstrates the scientific character and truth of Marxism. The article argues that the Manifesto embodies a dialectical-materialist conception of history, which Yin describes as the most basic and important method of thought in Marxism and the foundation of its scientific standing. Yin opens by citing four statements by Engels, in Socialism: Utopian and Scientific, Anti-Dühring, the speech at Marx's graveside and the 1883 German preface, to show how much Marx and Engels valued their historical outlook. The article then examines five aspects of the Manifesto in turn: the historical role of the bourgeoisie, the laws of social development, proletarian revolutionary practice, the historical character of class struggle, and the Russian village commune. Yin's central moves are as follows. First, the Manifesto praises the bourgeoisie as having played a highly revolutionary role against feudalism, while also pointing to the limits of bourgeois society in its later development, notably crises of overproduction. Second, Yin reads the Manifesto's analysis as grounded in the contradiction between productive forces and relations of production. Third, Yin stresses Engels's later qualifications: the prefaces say the Manifesto's practical measures depend on historical conditions and had partly become outdated. Engels's insertion, "since the dissolution of primitive communal landownership", and his 1888 note on recorded history, make class struggle a historical phenomenon tied to the level of productive forces, not the whole of human history. Yin treats the theory of class struggle as subordinate to the theory of productive forces and relations of production. Finally, the 1882 Russian preface is read as showing that backward countries may take a different path, a point Yin says the October Revolution confirmed. Yin concludes that the Manifesto's view of history is the cornerstone of Marxism's scientific character and of its capacity to move with the times, and he regards the view that Marxism is outdated as a disregard for science and truth. He calls for rereading the Manifesto to strengthen ideals and convictions, to hold to the Four-sphere Confidence, and to arm minds with Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Read the original if you want a compact, text-based account of how Chinese Party commentary draws on Engels's prefaces and notes to present the Manifesto's historical materialism and its historical limits on class struggle.

Why the October Revolution and not a July Revolution? A rebuttal of Kautsky's "premature birth" theory of socialism 为什么是十月革命而不是七月革命? Yu Bin Karl Kautsky compared the proletarian dictatorship in Russia to a pregnant woman who leaps about wildly to shorten her pregnancy and brings on a premature birth, so that the child cannot live. Yu Bin takes up this "premature birth" theory of socialism, which he says gained influence after the setback of the world socialist movement at the end of the twentieth century. Writing in 2018, Yu argues that socialism was not premature. In his view, in Western Europe it was "overdue", and the October Revolution was neither adventurist nor premature. The article has six parts. It begins with Marx and Engels on the inevitability of socialism and the Preface to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy. It then turns to their remarks on Russia and the possibility of revolution in a relatively backward country. The central sections follow Lenin's strategy from the April Theses and "Letters on Tactics" through his halting of the July 1917 demonstrations to his insistence on insurrection in September and October. A short conclusion draws the lessons. Yu argues that the "two inevitables" and the "two never's" in Marx do not conflict, because Marx added that humanity sets itself only tasks it can solve. He reads Marx and Engels as treating Russia as capable of absorbing capitalism's positive achievements without its catastrophes. Revolution in a backward country is possible, Yu holds, where the bourgeois revolution is unfinished and a workers' party guided by Marxism already exists. Yu then contends that Lenin followed the principle of a "majority revolution" and rejected Blanquism. In July the Bolsheviks were a minority in the soviets, so an uprising could not have won, and the peaceful path ended after the July events. By September they had majorities in Petrograd and Moscow. Lenin then pressed a hesitant Central Committee, and the revolution broke out on 25 October (Russian calendar). Yu concludes that whether the revolution was premature is a question of practice, and that Lenin's step-by-step leadership proved Marxism's truth. He argues that the lack of socialism in the developed West a century on shows it is "overdue" there, and cites the crises of 1929 and 2008 and wartime destruction. He reads the Soviet collapse as the penalty for departing from Marxist principles, not as proof of Kautsky. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist defence of the October Revolution against the "premature birth" thesis, built on close citation of Marx, Engels and Lenin.

On the three rationalities of the October Revolution 论十月革命的三大合理性 Zhang Wei Debate over the October Revolution has never ceased, and it grows sharper whenever the world socialist movement is in difficulty. Zhang identifies three lines of challenge: whether the Revolution contradicted historical materialism (theoretical rationality), whether it fitted Russia's historical development (historical rationality), and whether it was progressive rather than regressive (political rationality). The article contends that these correspond to whether the Revolution could, had to, and should have happened, and it argues that all three questions can be answered in the Revolution's favour. The article has three main sections, one for each form of rationality. The first takes on the "premature birth" thesis associated with Plekhanov, Kamenev, Rykov and especially Kautsky's 1918 The Dictatorship of the Proletariat. The second examines the contradictions of early twentieth-century Russia and the rise of the Bolsheviks between the February and October revolutions. The third assesses the Revolution's consequences for institutions, colonial peoples and capitalism itself. On theory, Zhang recasts Marx's second "never" in the 1859 Preface as a logical proposition and argues that its converse is equivalent. Since new relations of production did appear in Russia after 1917, the material conditions must already have matured, so the "premature birth" claim is a mechanical reading of historical materialism. Zhang adds that, in a world history created by capitalism, backward countries can draw on global productive forces, and that the workers' own activity is a productive force. On history, the author argues that four contradictions in Russia, the failure of the Provisional Government to deliver peace, bread and land, and the Bolsheviks' organisational preparation (membership rising from 100,000 in April 1917 to 350,000 by the eve of the Revolution) made the Revolution inevitable rather than a conspiracy or coup. On politics, Zhang holds that revolutions should be judged by whether they advance human emancipation, and credits October with creating a new social system, spurring national liberation movements, and forcing concessions from capitalism. Zhang concludes that the Revolution was theoretically possible, historically necessary and politically justified. As evidence for the third point, the article says that the weakening of world socialism after the Soviet collapse let capitalism slide back towards "barbarism", with workers' rights eroded and wealth concentrated. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist defence of the October Revolution that answers the "premature birth" critique through formal logic and world-historical argument.

Marxism as the powerful ideological weapon that opened reform and opening up 马克思主义是开启改革开放的强大思想武器 Liu Jianhui Writing for Qiushi in 2018, on the 40th anniversary of reform and opening up, Liu Jianhui asks what ideological force launched the policy. The article's answer is that Marxism was the 'powerful ideological weapon' that opened it, and that four decades of practice demonstrate the truth and strength of Marxism. This is a short commentary in three parts. It traces how a 'great awakening' within the Party gave rise to reform and opening up, then discusses why emancipating the mind must both uphold and develop Marxism, and finally assesses what the reform period shows about Marxism's power. Liu argues that the awakening began with the Party's renewed understanding of Marxist fundamentals. It started with the debate on practice as the sole criterion of truth, which broke the constraint of the 'two whatevers' and prepared the ground for the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978). Drawing on Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping, Liu holds that emancipating the mind meant freeing thought from dogmatic readings of Marxism. This produced Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents, the Scientific Outlook on Development and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Liu concludes that applying Marxist principles to China's circumstances carried the nation from 'standing up' to 'becoming prosperous' and, since the 18th Party Congress (2012), to 'becoming strong'. The article calls for continued emancipation of the mind and seeking truth from facts in order to realise the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a concise example of the Party's 2018 official narrative linking Marxism to the origins of reform and opening up.

Stages and research orientations of twentieth-century French Marxist historiography 20世纪法国马克思主义史学的阶段特征及研究取向 Liang Minsu Liang Minsu asks how French Marxist historiography developed across the twentieth century and what its research orientations were. The article, a newspaper piece from 2018, argues that this current was an important force within a diverse French historical field. It divides the current into three stages, which in Liang's view reflect both its own theoretical tradition and the evolution of the Western "new history". The article names figures such as Jean Jaurès, Albert Mathiez, Georges Lefebvre, Pierre Vilar, Albert Soboul and Michel Vovelle. It concentrates on Soboul and Vovelle and on the history of the French Revolution, seen through social history and the history of mentalities. It is organised chronologically: the interwar years to the 1940s, the 1950s to 1970s, and the period from the 1980s onwards. In Liang's account, the first stage was marked by strong ideological and political-practical commitments. The founding of the French Communist Party in 1920 and figures such as Maurice Thorez supported early Marxist history-writing, and a first generation of professional Marxist historians appeared, including Jean Bruhat and Marc Piolot. The second stage established a social-history outlook. Soboul used Marxist theory together with the new history and other social sciences, and he led the Robespierre society and the study of the Revolution "from below", a path Liang traces back to Lefebvre. Institutions such as the Marxist research centre (1959) and the Maurice Thorez Institute (1966) supported this work. In the third stage, Vovelle called for historical materialism to be combined with the history of mentalities, partly to escape the dualism of economic and political explanation. Working alongside Annales-linked historians, he made collective psychology and mental states a new direction in Revolution studies. Liang concludes that, under globalisation, French Marxist historians have joined their work to non-Marxist currents and adjusted their orientation, while staying close to social change and contemporary concerns. Dialogue and debate with other schools, the author says, have deepened understanding of the complexity of French history and of French Marxist historiography itself. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese-language periodisation of French Marxist historians and their links to the Annales school, and you are content with a short overview rather than detailed historiographical argument.

The theoretical essence of the openness of Marxism 马克思主义开放性特征的理论真谛 Kong Ming'an Chen Wenxu Taking up Xi Jinping's description of Marxism, at the 200th anniversary of Marx's birth, as scientific, people-centred, practical and open, this newspaper commentary asks what the openness of Marxism actually means. Kong and Chen argue that openness is a precondition of Marxism's scientific truth and a philosophical expression of dialectical negation. They say it also requires a scientific attitude towards the theory. The piece has three parts. The first links openness to Marxism's truth and its ability to meet the problems of each era. The second traces its philosophical roots from Spinoza and Hegel to Marx's materialist dialectic. The third turns to attitudes towards Marxism today, citing Engels and Xi. The authors contend that Marxism remains true because the basic contradictions of capitalism persist and the world is still in the epoch of transition from capitalism to socialism. Applying it, they say, requires the theory itself to stay open and to renew itself for each era. Openness rests on the dialectic of negation, which for Marx treats every existing form as transient and is therefore critical and revolutionary. As an example, Kong and Chen note that Marx and Engels drew no concrete socialist blueprint and did not say whether socialism could have a market economy. They present the political economy of socialism with Chinese characteristics as a case of Marxism's "self-negation". The authors insist that guidance by Marxism and the basic principles of scientific socialism must never be abandoned, and that Marxism is not a fixed dogma. They present Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era as an original contribution made in this spirit. They also call for closer study of contemporary capitalism and for absorbing the beneficial achievements of human civilisation. Read the original if you want a short, official-line account of how Chinese commentators connect Marxism's openness to dialectics and to current theoretical innovation.

How Russia's new secondary-school history textbook judges the Soviet system and Soviet Party leaders 俄新编中学历史教材对苏联体制和苏共领导人的评价 Wu Huixin After the Soviet collapse, Russia had no unified history textbook, and, the author says, many textbooks blackened Russian history. Wu examines the 2016 national textbook History of Russia, Grade 10 (Moscow Education Publishing House), produced after Putin's 2014 call for an objective, fair and respectful treatment of the past. The article, published in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2018, argues that the book affirms the October Revolution and Lenin, assesses Stalin and his system in a largely balanced way, and takes a critical view of Gorbachev. The textbook covers Russian history from 1914 to the early twenty-first century. Wu organises the review in three parts, each built around the textbook's own wording: the October Revolution and Lenin; the Stalin system and Stalin's role in the Great Patriotic War; and Gorbachev's reforms and the collapse of the USSR. The article is largely descriptive, quoting passages and drawing out the judgements they imply. On the revolution, Wu reads the textbook as presenting it as a historical choice. The tsarist government failed under the strain of the First World War, the Provisional Government failed to meet workers' and soldiers' demands, and the Bolsheviks gained support with simple slogans. Lenin is described as an undisputed leader, and the Brest-Litovsk peace is explained as a realistic step. On Stalin, Wu says the textbook records both the costs and the achievements of industrialisation and collectivisation, giving more space to the achievements, and never uses them to reject the whole Stalin system. It also treats Stalin as part of a people's war. On Gorbachev, the textbook rejects the "new thinking", which it says put universal human values above class, and judges his economic reform and "democratisation" failures. It also blames glasnost for letting in ideological conflict. It concludes that Gorbachev did not understand the system the Bolsheviks built. Wu concludes that the textbook, resting on historical facts, offers an objective account of the key questions of Russian history from 1914 on and is a useful reference for understanding Soviet history. Wu stresses that the textbook leaves readers room to draw their own value judgements. Read the original if you want a Chinese reading of how post-2014 official Russian schooling presents Lenin, Stalin and Gorbachev, with extensive quotation from the textbook.

Schulz's The Movement of Production: an important coordinate in the formation of the young Marx's category of production 舒尔茨的《生产的运动》：青年马克思生产范畴形成的重要坐标 Li Qiankun How did the category of production enter Marx's thought? Li Qiankun notes that Chinese scholarship has examined Hess, Bauer and List as influences on the young Marx but has rarely asked where production itself came from. The article argues that Friedrich Wilhelm Schulz's Die Bewegung der Production (1843) played an indispensable part in the formation of Marx's concept of production in The German Ideology. The article first reconstructs how Schulz's book came together and what it says about material production. It then follows Marx's two direct citations of the book, in the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 and in Capital. It then compares the book with The German Ideology, and ends by listing the ways Marx's historical materialism goes beyond Schulz. Li draws on Walter Grab's biography of Schulz, which is titled "a man who gave Marx ideas". Li identifies three features of Schulz's view of material production: it is the decisive factor in social history; it rests on Adam Smith's division of labour, extended from the workshop to society; and its advance drives changes in social relations. Marx first read Schulz selectively in 1844. He cited the book as material for his critique of alienated labour and counted Schulz among the political economists who see labour only as "making a living". Li argues this misread Schulz, who criticised political economy for ignoring human nature. In The German Ideology, Li finds close parallels: production as the first historical premise, the pairing of material and intellectual production, and division of labour as the link between productive forces and relations. Li adds that Marx also took over Schulz's social-division-of-labour reading, which helps explain the humanist residue of "alienation of the division of labour". Li stresses that Schulz remained an idealist. For him the human spirit was the original product, he treated capitalist production as eternal, and he prescribed Christian solidarity. Marx surpassed him in three ways. He built a systematic account in which material production determines intellectual production. He located the motor of history in the contradiction between productive forces and forms of intercourse. He also saw the revolutionary supersession of capitalism, which Schulz did not. Li concludes that tracing Marx's contemporaries helps identify his real originality and that Schulz's role deserves further study. Read the original if you work on the genesis of historical materialism or on Marx's intellectual sources and want a detailed comparison with a little-known German thinker.

Modernity and contingency An interpretation of Agnes Heller's theory of modernity 现代性与偶然性 Yan Yan Yan Yan takes up a question he considers central to any theory of modernity: how can modern individuals, who are ruled by contingency, face it and reach real freedom? The article reads the Hungarian New Marxist Agnes Heller as answering that her theory of modernity starts from the figure of the 'contingent person'. Yan's thesis is that, for Heller, freedom becomes possible only when individuals turn contingency into their own destiny through an existential choice of themselves, and so achieve self-determination. The article has four parts. It first traces how contingency emerged and developed, from the biblical Adam and Eve through Plato, Aristotle and Eriugena to Descartes and Hegel. It then examines Heller's distinction between initial and secondary contingency and the dual character of historical contingency. The third part sets out two kinds of existential choice, and the last treats dissatisfaction and self-determination. Yan draws on Heller's works on the philosophy of history, moral philosophy and postmodern politics, and on Kolakowski, Bauman and Miłosz. Yan reports that Heller combines Hegel and Marx with existentialism. In pre-modern society, contingency was suppressed by necessity (God, the Absolute); in modernity, birth no longer fixes one's place, and 'what was once fate becomes a situation'. Heller rejects Hegel's teleology as leaving people stuck in contingency and, when attached to the state, as leading to totalitarianism. She also rejects any return to the pre-modern. Pure contingency is not freedom, so it has to become a consciously chosen destiny. This choice is existential and irrevocable. It can be made through a particular calling, as in Heller's own account of Lukács and philosophy, or through choosing to be a morally good person. Yan adds that modern dissatisfaction can drive social development, and that self-determination requires both good persons and radical democracy. Yan concludes that, for Heller, contingency is historically progressive compared with pre-modern fatalism, but it still leaves people in false freedom. Human liberation requires the self-determination of the individual, of others and of society to interact well. Yan also points to a possible circularity: good persons guarantee self-determination, yet self-determination is the precondition of good persons. He adds that the effects of radical democracy remain to be seen. He still finds her view instructive for understanding modern existence. Read the original if you study Heller, Eastern European Marxism or the philosophy of modernity, and want a Chinese reading of her existential ethics of choice.

New developments in the Marxist thought on world history 马克思主义世界历史思想的新发展 Lu Pinyue This short commentary, published in the People's Daily in August 2018, asks how the Marxist thought on world history has developed in the Chinese context. Lu Pinyue argues that Xi Jinping's idea of a community with a shared future for mankind enriches and develops that thought. Lu starts from Marx and Engels's mid-nineteenth-century claim that national histories are turning into world history. The article then traces how the Communist Party has combined this thought with Chinese conditions, citing Mao Zedong on the Chinese revolution as part of the world revolution and Deng Xiaoping on absorbing the achievements of human civilisation. It ends with Xi's formulation after the 18th Party Congress (2012). Lu's central argument is that the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind inherits the value stance of the Marxist thought on world history: it is people-centred, seeks win-win cooperation and sets itself against power politics and zero-sum thinking. In Lu's account it also analyses new features of the present world. Lu holds that the root of current problems is not economic globalisation but three unresolved contradictions: weak global growth momentum, lagging global economic governance and unbalanced global development. Lu cites the Belt and Road Initiative as an example of building new international relations through equal consultation. Lu concludes that the idea joins the theoretical logic of the Marxist thought on world history with the practical logic of human development, and will promote common development and lasting peace. Read the original if you want a brief, official-press statement of how Chinese commentators place Xi Jinping's idea of a shared-future community within the Marxist tradition.

Deepening our understanding of the laws of human social development 深化对人类社会发展规律的认识 Zhao Jiaxiang Writing in Guangming Daily in 2018, Zhao Jiaxiang takes up Xi Jinping's call to deepen, with a fresh perspective, understanding of the laws of Communist Party governance, of socialist construction and of human social development. Zhao treats the last of these as the foundation of the other two. The article's thesis is that social laws are products of human practice, yet objective, historical, long-term and cyclical, and not directly given as reality. The author argues that "acting in accordance with objective laws" is therefore a complex process, not a matter of copying a ready-made pattern. The piece is organised under six headings. It begins with the origin of social laws in conscious human activity, then treats in turn their objectivity, historicity, long-term and cyclical character, and their "non-immediate reality". It closes with the correct meaning of "acting in accordance with objective laws". Zhao relies mainly on texts by Marx, Engels, Lenin and Mao Zedong, including Anti-Dühring, Capital, Engels's letters to Conrad Schmidt and Friedrich Albert Lange, and Lenin's Imperialism and Materialism and Empirio-Criticism. Zhao first explains why laws that people make through purposeful action can still be objective. Individual aims cancel or interfere with each other and produce a resultant nobody intended. Action is also constrained by objective conditions and by the actors' own abilities, and it cannot skip the stages of history. The author then argues that laws are historical. Each social formation has its own laws, and capitalist laws are not eternal, which the author takes as a refutation of the "end of history" thesis. Even general laws differ in form across formations and across stages, and Zhao says the laws of present-day capitalism and of socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era need fresh study. Drawing on Engels's letter to Schmidt, Zhao holds that a law is only an approximation, a tendency or an average.
