It is not immediate reality, partly because many laws operate at once and partly because concepts never coincide with the reality they abstract from. Zhao reads Karl Popper's rejection of social laws as a mechanical misunderstanding of this point. Zhao concludes that the law that socialism will replace capitalism is still in the process of formation, since capitalism has not yet been superseded worldwide. The author criticises the common reading of "respecting objective laws" as obeying a pre-existing, fixed reality. Laws emerge only gradually, appear in changing forms, and are grasped only approximately. Understanding must therefore be revised continually, and fixed understandings risk violating the laws they claim to follow. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist philosopher in 2018 grounds the theory of social laws in classical texts and applies it to debates on capitalism, socialism and policy-making.

Contemporary lessons of the debate on the criterion of truth Forty years after 1978 真理标准问题讨论的当代启示 Ren Ping Writing in Guangming Daily in May 2018, forty years after the debate on the criterion of truth, Ren Ping asks what that debate still teaches China. Ren argues that philosophical change leads epochal change, and that the debate's significance shows in the whole course of reform, not only at its start. In Ren's account, it broke the intellectual constraint of the "Two Whatevers", restored the authority of a practice-based, seeking-truth-from-facts Marxism, and opened reform and opening up and the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics. This short commentary is organised as six lessons, introduced from the standpoint of what Ren calls socialism with Chinese characteristics entering a new era. The lessons concern the relation of philosophy to its age, the responsibility of philosophers, the people-centred value orientation of truth, confidence in the path and in theory, the developing character of truth, and the growth of Marxist philosophy itself. Each links the 1978 debate to present tasks. Ren's central claim is that the debate joined two questions: how truth is tested and in whose interest. Ren holds that the more consistently practice is taken as the criterion, the more it accords with the people's fundamental interests, since the people are both the subject that tests truth and the beneficiary of its results. Ren also treats the debate as a political event as well as an academic one, which required political courage from philosophers. Ren then argues that truth develops with practice. In this view the "Two Whatevers" mindset must still be rejected, and so must the temporary, unreasonable ideas, institutions and interest structures formed during four decades of reform. Ren cites the shift from "crossing the river by feeling the stones" to modernising the system and capacity of national governance, and from extensive growth to the new development philosophy. Ren concludes that, tested by forty years of practice, the debate strengthens confidence in the path, theory, system and culture, and that Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era must guide the new era. Ren calls on philosophers to engage with global governance, to build a community with a shared future for mankind, and to create original Chinese theory and discourse rather than retreat into pure scholarship. Ren also points to the flourishing of Marxist philosophy in China since 1978. Read the original if you want a concise, official-register Chinese reading of the 1978 truth-criterion debate and its use in legitimising the new era's tasks.

The philosophical implications of "lucid waters and lush mountains are invaluable assets" “绿水青山就是金山银山”的哲学意蕴 Shan Tiping Writing in Guangming Daily in June 2018, Shan Tiping examines the philosophical meaning of Xi Jinping's formula that lucid waters and lush mountains are invaluable assets. The author argues that the formula is a practical guide for handling the relationship between humans and nature in the new era, and that it carries a deep historical dialectic. The commentary is built around three historical stages: agricultural civilization, industrial civilization, and the present transition towards ecological civilization. It draws on classical Chinese poetry, Mao Zedong's poem "Farewell to the God of Plague", Engels's warning about nature's revenge and Rachel Carson's Silent Spring. It also lists the dates on which Xi developed the formula, from 2005 to the 19th Party Congress (2017). Shan argues that in agricultural societies green mountains and material wealth were not yet linked, and that low productive forces left people at the mercy of natural disasters. Under capitalist-led industrial civilization, technology turned nature into a treasure house to be conquered. The author claims this system ignored the limits of nature's capacity, piling up wealth while the environment was ruined and humans and nature became mutually alienated. In the present transition, Shan says, the task is both to turn green mountains into material wealth and to turn the pursuit of wealth back towards preserving the mountains. Shan concludes that the formula's essence is sustainable green development. It should meet people's aspiration for a better life with material security, while keeping the mountains green and the waters flowing in pursuit of a "Beautiful China" and harmony between humans and nature. Read the original if you want a short, officially aligned philosophical-historical reading of this slogan in Chinese ecological civilization discourse.

Rereading the classics, advancing with the times, and being a loyal guardian of Marxism On the 170th anniversary of the Communist Manifesto 重温经典，与时俱进，做马克思主义的忠诚卫士 Wang Huaichen Marking the 170th anniversary of the Communist Manifesto in 2018, this text (apparently delivered at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences and published in World Socialism Studies, 2018 no. 4) asks what reading the Manifesto means for Communists today. Wang argues that only a proper grasp of it secures firm belief in Marxism, and that in the present this means upholding Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and pursuing full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. The piece has three parts. The first treats understanding the Manifesto as the basis of Party spirit and of correct revolutionary practice. The second concerns studying Xi Jinping's thought and strengthening the Four-sphere Confidence. The third argues that the Party must be willing to carry out self-reform. Wang draws on Lenin, Deng Xiaoping, the Soviet collapse, the Wenchuan earthquake recovery and the author's own observations of Party work. Wang contends that without grasping the Manifesto one cannot hold to the conviction that communism will prevail, see the main trend of history, or keep to a people-centred stance. The author reads the failure of once-large parties, especially the Soviet party, as the result of betraying Marxist positions, and says the Party since the 18th Party Congress (2012) has corrected earlier deviations. Xi Jinping Thought is presented as both the contemporary form and the Chinese form of Marxism, with world significance because it offers developing countries a path to modernization distinct from the Western one. In the author's view, the Wenchuan reconstruction shows the superiority of Party leadership. Wang concludes that ideological work remains a weak point: some leading cadres are indifferent to ideology, adopt Western discourse or avoid the word itself. The author calls for raising the Party's Marxist theoretical level, improving the quality of Party building, tackling formalism and bureaucratism, and extending rigorous self-governance down to grassroots "flies", the petty corruption that affects ordinary people. Read the original if you want a Party-affiliated academic's account, from 2018, of how the Manifesto anniversary was tied to ideological discipline and anti-corruption work.

Learning from the revolutionary spirit of the New People's Study Society's pioneers and continuing the struggle for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation 学习新民学会前辈们的革命精神 为中华民族伟大复兴继续奋斗 Zhu Jiamu Zhu Jiamu's text, published in World Socialism Studies in 2018, reads as an address to a scholarly symposium marking the 100th anniversary of the New People's Study Society (Xinmin xuehui), founded in 1918 by Mao Zedong, Cai Hesen and others. The symposium was co-hosted by the Marxism schools of Nankai, Lanzhou and Sichuan universities and the Hefu Research Centre. Zhu argues that the Society was an important source of the Party's early organisations. He holds that its founding generation had three outstanding qualities that today's young people should learn from. Zhu situates the event in the Party's call, after the 19th Party Congress (2017), for a campaign of education under the slogan 'remain true to our original aspiration and keep our mission firmly in mind'. The text then takes the three qualities in turn, drawing on the biographies of the Society's members, on Mao's recollections and on his 1925 poem Changsha. A final section collects statements by Xi Jinping on studying Party and national history, opposing historical nihilism, and sustaining ideals and convictions. The three qualities are concern for country and people with lofty aims; unceasing pursuit of truth; and steadfast loyalty to belief. On the first, Zhu stresses the members' youth and poverty and the Society's aims and rules of conduct. On the second, Zhu traces how members in France and in Hunan moved from patriotism and utopian idealism to Marxism, citing Cai Hesen's 1920 letters and Mao's reply. From this Zhu concludes that the Chinese Communist Party would have been founded sooner or later even without Comintern help. On the third, Zhu cites that 37 of the Society's 78 members joined the Party and describes the deaths of martyrs such as Cai Hesen and Xiang Jingyu. Zhu then links this history to Xi Jinping's warnings that denying Party and Soviet history, which Xi calls historical nihilism, undermines Marxism's guiding role and Party leadership. Zhu concludes that, with the nation at a critical stage of development, every Communist Party member and young student should follow the Society's pioneers. They should keep to the communist ideal and keep striving for the happiness of the Chinese people and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want an example of how Party-affiliated scholars use early revolutionary history for ideological education, or if you want details on the Society's members.

Making the study of Marxism the essential skill of Communists 把学好马克思主义作为共产党人的看家本领 Wang Weiguang Written for the 200th anniversary of Marx's birth (2018), the article takes up Xi Jinping's call for Party cadres to treat Marxism as their "essential skill" (看家本领). Wang argues that mastering Marxism is the most meaningful way to commemorate Marx. In Wang's account, it is also a requirement grounded in theoretical logic, historical experience and present realities. The article has three main sections. The first concerns firm belief in Marxism as the spiritual pillar of every Communist. The second concerns a Marxist style of study, and the third concerns Marxist ways of thinking and working. Wang draws throughout on Marx, Engels, Lenin, Mao Zedong and Xi Jinping, and the discussion is anchored in Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. On belief, Wang gives four reasons why Marxism can serve as such a pillar. These are its scientific character (dialectical and historical materialism), its revolutionary character (the fundamental interests of the labouring majority), its practical character (seeking truth from facts) and its lofty ideal of communism. Wang holds that the present remains Marx's "great historical epoch", marked by a continuing contest between socialism and capitalism. On study, Wang calls for a problem-oriented approach that aims at the principal contradiction identified at the 19th Party Congress (2017). Wang also stresses grasping Marxism's basic tenets and scientific method rather than doctrine, and advancing the adaptation of Marxism to Chinese conditions. On method, Wang names four elements: a people-centred standpoint, the ideological line of seeking truth from facts, materialist dialectics, and the historical thinking of historical materialism. Wang presents Xi's thought as a model of all four. Wang concludes that learning Marxism means above all absorbing its method and applying it to concrete problems, and that this will help Party members to grasp historical trends and advance socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era. Wang also calls for unifying the lofty communist ideal with the common ideal of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a representative statement of how Party theorists in 2018 linked Marx's bicentenary to cadre education and to the study of Xi Jinping Thought.

Upholding faith in Marxism and writing a new chapter of socialism with Chinese characteristics 坚定马克思主义信仰,谱写中国特色社会主义新篇章 Wang Huaichen Written for the 200th anniversary of Marx's birth, this commentary asks what it means for Party members to remain faithful to Marxism today. Wang argues that strengthening belief in the truth and scientific character of Marxism is the basis of political firmness. In Wang's view, this belief is what allows the Party to be built stronger and to unite its strength for the "two centenary goals" and the Chinese Dream of national rejuvenation. The article has three parts. The first concerns theoretical confidence and the Party's "spiritual core". The second sets out three points for upholding and developing socialism with Chinese characteristics. The third concerns the Party's leadership and its self-building as a Marxist governing party. Wang draws on the Communist Manifesto, Lenin, Xi Jinping's speech at the Marx anniversary meeting, and the author's own experience in Party discipline inspection work. Wang pictures the Party as concentric circles with Marxist belief at the core, organisation in the middle and individual members outside. Wang says theory must keep innovating with practice, and traces this through Mao Zedong Thought, Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents, the Scientific Outlook on Development and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Wang also notes weaknesses in Marxist research, such as thin explanatory power and a role limited to political exposition. The three points on socialism are these: China remains in the primary stage of socialism, so development must stay central; the principal social contradiction has changed, so unbalanced and inadequate development must be addressed; and external containment must be met with the Four-sphere Confidence and bottom-line thinking. The third part claims, drawing on inspection work since the 18th Party Congress (2012), that Party leadership had been weakened or hollowed out in some localities, state-owned enterprises and universities. Wang argues this was largely reversed and calls for upholding the authority of the Central Committee and its centralised, unified leadership. Wang concludes that Marxism's truth remains as bright as ever, and that Party members should hold to their faith, draw wisdom from Marxism, and push on the Party's "great new project" of self-building. The text is a Party-oriented exhortation rather than a scholarly study, and it presents the Party's leadership as the most essential feature of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want an example of how a senior Party discipline official linked the Marx bicentenary to Party discipline, leadership and ideological work in 2018.

Marxism is first of all a theory of revolution 马克思主义首先是革命的理论 Zhu Jiamu Writing for the 200th anniversary of Marx's birth in 2018, Zhu Jiamu asks what it means to study Marxism today and whether insisting on its revolutionary character is out of touch with a China that has long since passed from revolution to construction and reform. Zhu answers that Marxism is first of all the theory of proletarian revolution, and that it should be studied for the sake of the emancipation of the proletariat and the cause of communism, not as mere knowledge or decoration. Zhu builds the piece around Xi Jinping's speech at the anniversary meeting on 4 May 2018. The article opens with Engels's graveside description of Marx as "first of all a revolutionary", then moves through several connected themes. These are the criticism of "Western Marxism", the claim that the Communist Party should turn from a "revolutionary party" into a "ruling party", the meaning of "revolution", the status of communism as an ideal, and the character of the present era. Zhu draws throughout on Lenin, Chen Yun, Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and above all Xi Jinping's repeated phrase "revolutionary ideals are higher than the heavens". Zhu argues that "Western Marxism" treats Marxism as scholarship, does not aim at revolution and leaves the basic capitalist system untouched. Citing Lenin, Zhu describes this as the dulling of a revolutionary doctrine. Against the idea of a shift from revolutionary to ruling party, Zhu holds that "revolution" has several senses (in the productive forces, in social relations, in spirit), so it does not mean only one class overthrowing another. Rejecting the Cultural Revolution's "continuing revolution under the dictatorship of the proletariat", Zhu says, does not reject the continuing task of building socialism towards communism. Zhu blames the "farewell to revolution" argument and historical nihilism for weakening Party members' ideals and working style. Citing Xi, Zhu offers four reasons to hold to communist ideals. Socialism with Chinese characteristics derives from communist theory, ideals give Party members spiritual support, communism can be reached only through generations of effort, and abandoning it would cause the Party to disintegrate. Zhu also distinguishes the "character" of the era from its "features". Peace and development are features, while the era remains one of transition from capitalism to socialism. Zhu concludes that the present era is still the historical era Marxism identified, and that the general trend of social development, socialism replacing capitalism, has not changed. In Zhu's view this is what justifies upholding socialism with Chinese characteristics and communist convictions, and what makes it necessary for Communists, though in power, to remember that they are revolutionaries. Read the original if you want a compact example of how a senior Party historian ties the anniversary speech to arguments about Party identity, communism and the nature of the era.

Mao Zedong and the original aspiration and mission 毛泽东与初心使命 Yang Mingwei Published in Study Times in July 2018, this short commentary asks how Mao Zedong upheld and practised what Chinese Communists now call the original aspiration and mission of the Party. Yang Mingwei argues that seeking happiness for the people and rejuvenation for the nation was Mao's lifelong pursuit. In Yang's account, Mao's own definition of Communists as people who seek no private gain is the Party's founding purpose, and Mao lived it fully. The article looks at Mao through three aspects. The first is his lifelong faith in Marxism and his unchanged original aspiration. The second is his wholehearted service to the people, illustrated by a series of quotations on the nature of the Communist Party. The third is his long-term strategic planning for the country and nation, with examples from the 1960s and from his final weeks in 1976. On faith, Yang recounts Mao's 1936 remarks to Edgar Snow that the Communist Manifesto and two other works established his Marxist belief in 1920 and that it never wavered. Yang adds that Mao reread the Manifesto whenever he faced major problems, urged senior cadres to study Marx and Lenin to tell true Marxism-Leninism from false, and kept three editions of the Manifesto by his bed until death. On service, Yang says Mao's statements show the Party's fundamental nature, that history is made by the people, and that its aims coincide with theirs. Yang presents Mao's lines "stand on the side of the great majority of working people" and "take the people as teacher" as the root cause of the Party's victories in revolution, construction and reform. On foresight, Yang cites Mao's 1963 warning that China would be vulnerable to attack unless it ended its economic and technological backwardness, his stress on basic industry in the Third Five-Year Plan, and his reaction to the 1976 Tangshan earthquake. Yang concludes that Mao died regretting that the country was not yet fully unified, the people not yet prosperous and the nation not yet rejuvenated, but believing these goals would be achieved. Yang also treats Mao's definition of the Party as a basic starting point for understanding the "new era", "new thought" and "new journey" and says the Party's purpose and character must never change. Read the original if you want an example of how a Party historian in 2018 presented Mao as a model of the Party's original aspiration and mission, with the quotations chosen for that purpose.

Mao Zedong and the establishment of China's great-power status 毛泽东与中国大国地位的确立 Wang Yiqiu Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2013, Wang Yiqiu takes up the claim that one of Mao Zedong's historical achievements was to restore China's international standing as a great power. The article argues that three wars, led by the Communist Party under Mao, were decisive: the War of Resistance against Japan, the War of Liberation and the War to Resist US Aggression and Aid Korea. The article is organised chronologically in three sections, one for each war. Each section asks what that war contributed to China's status: a return to the ranks of the great powers after 1945, real sovereign independence after 1949, and international influence and a voice in world affairs after the Korean War. Wang draws on Mao's Selected Works, official Party histories, Peng Dehuai's memoir and remarks by John King Fairbank, Arnold Toynbee, Khrushchev and the US commander Mark Clark. On the anti-Japanese war, Wang credits the Kuomintang government's frontal battlefields but says it would be unfair to give all the credit to Chiang Kai-shek. In Wang's account the Communist Party's line of protracted war and the united front made it the "mainstay" of national resistance, and the article cites figures for enemy troops killed and Party-led casualties. On the civil war, Wang describes the United States as supporting Chiang, curbing China's sovereignty through treaties and a large military presence, so that China was nominally a great power but not yet fully independent. Victory in 1949 is presented as ending imperialist domination. On Korea, Wang defines a modern great power as one with sovereignty plus global influence. The war, the article argues, secured a security buffer for the industrial Northeast, strengthened national confidence, forced Washington and Moscow to reassess China, and was followed by the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence and border settlements with neighbours. Wang concludes that Mao's name is tied to China's great-power status and that national prestige, military strength, international standing and national backbone are the legacy of the Mao era. The article holds that today's China can advance from a great power to a true world power (shijie qiangguo) only on the foundation Mao laid. Read the original if you want an example of how a Chinese Marxism institute scholar, writing in 2013, framed Mao's legacy through foreign policy and war, together with the sources it relies on.

Mao Zedong and economic construction in New China 毛泽东与新中国的经济建设 Sha Jiansun This piece, published in Guangming Daily in January 2014, assesses Mao Zedong's role in China's socialist economic construction between 1949 and 1976. Sha Jiansun argues that Mao was the chief organiser and leader of that effort, that his correct theory of economic construction forms an important part of Mao Zedong Thought, and that the achievements of the period laid a solid material foundation for China's later development. The article has three parts. The first sets out Mao's view of industrial or economic revolution as China's "second revolution". The second examines how Mao and his comrades fixed the direction, path and policies of economic development. The third reviews the historic progress made in these years, using statistics on output, growth and living standards. In the second part, which carries most of the argument, Sha reports that Mao held the socialist road to be the only real way to solve China's industrialization, since the capitalist road would be slower and more painful. Sha traces the goal of the "four modernizations" and the "two-step" strategy: first an independent and fairly complete industrial and national economic system, then modernization of agriculture, industry, national defence and science and technology. Sha also lists Mao's policy principles: agriculture as the foundation and industry as the leading factor, "walking on two legs", overall balance and planned, proportionate development alongside commodity production and the law of value, "overall planning with due consideration for all", and self-reliance combined with trade and learning from abroad. Sha notes that Mao's timetable estimates were over-optimistic for a time and were revised after the Great Leap Forward. Sha acknowledges two serious setbacks, during the Great Leap Forward and the Cultural Revolution, but concludes that the overall achievements were great. The article cites an average annual growth of 8.2 per cent in gross agricultural and industrial output from 1952 to 1978, rises in China's world ranking for major products, and rising consumption and schooling. It closes with the American historian Maurice Meisner's favourable comparison of the Mao era with other late industrializers. Read the original if you want a concise Party-historian's defence of Mao-era economic policy, with its key quotations and figures, as presented in a Chinese official newspaper.

Key assessments of Mao Zedong by the Party since reform and opening up 改革开放以来我们党对毛泽东同志的几个重要评价 Chen Jin Writing in the People's Daily in December 2013, around the 120th anniversary of Mao Zedong's birth, Chen Jin sets out the fixed assessments of Mao that the Communist Party has gradually formed since reform and opening up. The article argues that understanding these formulations helps readers grasp Mao's specific character as a historic figure and the scale of his achievements. The piece is organised around five official judgements, each with its own heading and each traced to a leader and a date: Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin and Hu Jintao, plus the 1981 Resolution on Certain Questions in the History of Our Party since the Founding of the People's Republic of China (the Historical Resolution) and the 17th and 18th Party Congresses. They cover Mao's role in the revolution, his standing as Marxist, strategist and theorist, his place in the leadership, his status as patriot and national hero, and his relation to socialism with Chinese characteristics. Chen's central reasoning is that the Party's verdicts form a coherent, progressively deepened line. Without Mao's leadership, the author says, the Chinese people would have groped in the dark far longer, because history chose Mao through a complex process of comparison after earlier leaders' failures and the Zunyi Meeting. Chen sets out the three rising formulas on his leadership role, and lists Mao's strategic decisions as evidence for the title of strategist, a term the Party applies to him alone among the older leaders. The author reads the Party's three great undertakings (the new-democratic revolution, the socialist revolution and construction, and reform and opening up) as continuous: the first two supplied the fundamental political premise, institutional foundation, experience, theoretical preparation and material base for the third. Chen concludes that Mao's late-life errors do not cancel the judgement that his achievements come first, and that a Marxist party cannot demand flawlessness of great figures. Correctly assessing Mao, in this account, is a matter to be upheld permanently, and the best commemoration is confidence in the path, theory and system of socialism with Chinese characteristics, to realise the Chinese Dream of national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want a compact, authoritative-style catalogue of the Party's official formulas on Mao and their dates of origin.

"Marxists" going beyond "Marxology" Samir Amin's summary of his book on Marx's bicentenary “马克思主义者”超越“马克思学” Samir Amin This is a Chinese translation of a short essay by the Egyptian economist Samir Amin, written to summarise his book Le bicentenaire de Marx (Delga, 2018) for the 200th anniversary of Marx's birth. Amin argues that Marx remains unmatched for understanding society, provided that "Marxists" apply his method to new historical developments instead of repeating what Marx could write in his own day ("Marxology"). Marx, he notes, kept revising his own views throughout his life. The essay moves from Marx's general method to Amin's own developments of it. It first presents Capital and the Communist Manifesto as tools for grasping capitalism's totality, including the law of value, commodity alienation and what Amin calls ecology. It then takes up capitalism as a global system, its claimed role as a short-lived "scaffold" in history, its systemic crisis, and the problem of the peasantry in a socialist transition. Amin says he gives priority to Marx's late intuition that capitalist expansion produces polarisation, so that the conquered periphery cannot catch up with the centre on the basis of capitalism's core laws. From this he derives a theory of unequal development: revolution can begin at the system's "weak links", socialist transition must occur "in one country", and that country will face fatal isolation from imperialist counterattack, with no "world revolution". He describes capitalism since 1800 as prone to overproduction and stagnation, with monopoly capital since the 1970s turning to financial outlets. The present challenge, he says, is to leave a capitalism in crisis, not to escape capitalist crises. Amin concludes that a transition to socialism requires resisting permanent imperialist war, hot or cold, and winning over the peasant majority. He argues that Marx's view of peasants as allies of the bourgeoisie arose in Europe before bourgeois revolutions were complete. He also distinguishes two kinds of transition between modes of production: a "decadent" one, guided by unconscious or alienated consciousness, and a revolutionary one, in which ideology gives change a true, total dimension. Read the original if you want a concise statement of Amin's theory of unequal development and his late view of socialism, imperialism and the peasantry.

Five highlights in the recent development of communist parties abroad 当今国外共产党发展变化的五大亮点 Chai Shangjin Writing in 2018, the 170th anniversary year of the Communist Manifesto, Chai Shangjin asks how communist parties outside China have changed in recent years. The article argues that, despite serious challenges, these parties show a clear overall upward trend. Chai bases this on criticism of capitalism, adherence to socialist core values, innovation within fundamental principles, stronger organisation and wider left-wing alliances. The article is organised around five "highlights": the regrouping of forces, the strengthening of organisation, innovation that keeps to fundamental principles, unity and cooperation within the left, and the growing tendency to look east and learn from China. It surveys parties by region and type, including ruling parties in Vietnam, Laos, Cuba and North Korea, and parties in Western Europe, South Asia, Africa, Latin America and the former Soviet space. It cites membership and parliamentary figures to support its picture of recovery. Chai holds that most communist parties have survived the shock of the Soviet collapse and entered a stage of recovery. In Chai's account, parties that dropped democratic centralism and Marxism-Leninism as their guide suffered factionalism and decline, and many are now restoring democratic centralism and grassroots branches. The article describes parties rejecting both dogmatism and abandoning Marxism, accepting that socialism has no single model, and favouring electoral and legal struggle over violent revolution. Chai presents the ruling parties' exploration of socialism with Chinese characteristics and similar national paths as a model for non-ruling parties. Chai notes remaining difficulties: ageing membership, splits, right-wing suppression, populism and the problem of leading broader left fronts. The final section reports that parties from 70-plus organisations attended the Shenzhen seminar marking Marx's 200th birthday (May 2018), and that foreign parties value Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and the Belt and Road Initiative. Chai concedes some foreign doubts about China's wealth gap and says China neither imports nor exports models. Read the original if you want a Party-affiliated Chinese overview of foreign communist parties, with membership figures and examples, as seen in 2018.

On the origins and limits of the "greening" of neoliberalism 论新自由主义“绿色化”的渊源及其局限 Cai Huajie Neoliberalism presents full privatisation of natural resources and their complete marketisation as the cure for ecological crisis, wrapping itself in a "green" cloak, often pictured as a "green thumb" on Adam Smith's "invisible hand". Cai Huajie asks where this claim comes from and whether it holds. The article argues that classical liberalism does contain an "environmental potential", but that this potential is severely limited and that neoliberal greening serves chiefly as an ideology defending capitalism. Published in Studies on Marxism in 2018, the article has three parts. The first traces neoliberal greening to John Locke's defence of private property and Smith's defence of the free market, citing Bill Clinton, Jonathon Porritt and Herman Daly as modern users of the "green thumb" idea. The second shows the limits of Locke's and Smith's environmental readings. The third places the question in the history of how nature's mode of existence changed in the rise of capitalism. Cai argues that Locke's three constraints on property (no waste, no harm to others' subsistence, benefit to humanity) contain hidden problems. Money allows unlimited accumulation, his "enough and as good" condition assumes inexhaustible resources, and his claim that nature gains value only through labour is, in the author's view, extreme anthropocentrism. Smith's "impartial spectator" and limited government functions, Cai says, do not alter the fact that the public good is for him an unintended by-product of self-interest, in line with Mészáros's point that capital's objective logic of expansion decides outcomes. The author also criticises the utility theory of value behind "natural capitalism", using Marx and Ricardo. Neoliberals, Cai holds, inherit only the "shell" of private property and free markets and ignore these safeguards. In the third part Cai argues that capitalism arose by transforming both the ownership and the use of natural resources. Common and pre-capitalist property gave way to capitalist private property, and use for use-value gave way to use for exchange-value. Primitive accumulation, including enclosure and England's Game Laws, separated labourers from resources. Locke and Smith treat this result as natural, and neoliberalism's aim is to defend capitalism's legitimacy; Cai concludes that the invisible hand has no "green thumb". Read the original if you want a Marxist critique of market-based environmentalism that works through Locke, Smith and the history of primitive accumulation.

Leading and driving the revolution in social practice through a revolution in ideas and theory Commemorating the great debate on the criterion of truth and celebrating the 40th anniversary of reform and opening up 以思想理论革命引领和推动社会实践革命 Yan Xiaofeng Writing in 2018, Yan Xiaofeng marks two anniversaries: the 1978 debate on practice as the criterion of truth and forty years of reform and opening up. The article argues that the debate was an ideological revolution that supplied the intellectual starting point for reform, and that theoretical innovation and practical innovation have since advanced together. Yan concludes that a revolution in ideas and theory should keep leading and driving the revolution in social practice. The piece has three sections. The first traces the path from the debate to the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978). The second reviews how socialism with Chinese characteristics and its theoretical system developed from Deng Xiaoping Theory through the Three Represents and the Scientific Outlook on Development to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The third examines the practical and truth-bearing character of Xi's thought, and closes with the 2018 anniversaries of Marx's birth and the Communist Manifesto. In Yan's account, philosophy can precede social revolution, and the Party's ideological line is at bottom a philosophical principle and a line of cognition. Yan sets the 'two whatevers' against the practice criterion, which he presents as the philosophical basis for correcting the Cultural Revolution's errors, shifting the Party's work to economic construction and launching reform. Yan then describes each generation of Party theory as a response to a problem raised by practice: what socialism is, what kind of Party to build, and what kind of development to pursue. Xi's thought, Yan argues, is tested in practice. Yan points to the changed principal contradiction of society, achievements since the 18th Party Congress (2012) in areas such as Party leadership and full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, and an overall framework built on the Four-sphere Confidence. Yan concludes that the thought's fundamental principles are Party leadership, a people-centred approach and comprehensive deepening of reform, and that its historical mission is the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Yan presents the 2018 anniversaries as signalling a commitment to emancipating the mind, seeking truth from facts and carrying reform through to the end. Read the original if you want a representative Party-theorist account, from the time of the 40th anniversary, of how the 1978 truth-criterion debate is linked to Xi Jinping Thought and to the Party's own narrative of reform and opening up.

The contemporary value of China's fine traditional culture 中国优秀传统文化的当代价值 Shi Huanxiang Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts (2018, no. 12), Shi Huanxiang asks what China's fine traditional culture contributes today. The author argues that, as the only ancient civilisation to have continued without interruption, China holds cultural resources that should be given creative transformation and innovative development and be merged with contemporary Chinese culture. Shi presents this as a necessary requirement of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The article is organised in five sections. Each takes one field in which traditional culture is said to have contemporary value: the adaptation of Marxism to Chinese conditions, the socialist market economy, cultural confidence, the core socialist values, and the solution of global problems. Shi draws on Confucian and other classical sayings, on Mao Zedong, and on Xi Jinping's statements about the Party as the faithful heir of traditional culture. Shi's central move is to treat tradition as a source from which modern theory and policy are continuously renewed. Marxism, described as a foreign-born body of thought, is said to have become Chinese by merging with concepts such as "seeking truth from facts", people-as-the-base thinking, "xiaokang" and "harmony", and Shi lists Party doctrines from the mass line to a community with a shared future for mankind as transformations of such ideas. For the market economy, the author argues that the traditional view of righteousness and profit can check money worship and that honesty and trustworthiness can support a contract and credit economy, while granting that the old righteousness-over-profit outlook had historical limits. Shi also claims that China's openness to Buddhism and to Arab and Persian culture shows an inclusive trait that sustains cultural confidence against Western cultural hegemony. The core socialist values at national, social and individual levels are said to correspond to the traditional sequence from rectifying the heart to bringing peace to the world. Shi concludes that tradition and the core socialist values stand in a relationship of source and stream. The author further holds that ideas of harmony, good-neighbourliness, mutual benefit and harmony between humans and nature offer "Chinese wisdom" for global governance, and links the ancient Silk Road to the Belt and Road Initiative. Shi calls for an inclusive approach that respects other civilisations while promoting China's own cultural genes. Read the original if you want a compact example of how a 2018 Party journal framed traditional culture as a resource for Marxist theory, market ethics and foreign policy.

Mao Zedong's poetry and the revolutionary spirit of Chinese Communists: Xi Jinping's quotations as an example 毛泽东诗词彰显中国共产党人的革命精神——以习近平引用毛泽东诗词为例 Yuan Bingda Why does Xi Jinping so often quote Mao Zedong's poems and lyrics, and what do the quotations convey? Writing in 2018, Yuan Bingda argues that the quotations are neither ornamental nor mere aesthetic recitation. In the author's reading, they deliberately bring out the revolutionary spirit and the "Chinese spirit" that run through Mao's verse, and they offer that spirit as an inspiration for realising the Chinese Dream of national rejuvenation in the new era. The article draws on Xi's speeches and writings since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Among them are his 2012 visit to *The Road to Rejuvenation* exhibition, the 2013 symposium marking the 120th anniversary of Mao's birth (where Xi cites Mao's poetry nine times), the 2016 speech marking the Party's 95th anniversary, and his 2014 visit to Peking University. It is organised in three sections: not forgetting the original aspiration and mission; sustaining the fighting spirit; and keeping the Party's youthfulness. Each section pairs Xi's quoted lines with the historical circumstances in which Mao wrote them. Yuan's first move is a close reading of the two occurrences of "road" in Xi's 2012 remarks. The "mighty pass" line, written in 1935 after the Zunyi Conference, stands for the suffering and resilience of the Chinese nation. The "right path in the world" line, written in 1949, is read as showing that socialism with Chinese characteristics is the historically inevitable path. Second, the author draws out four qualities Xi attributes to Mao through selected lines: iron will (supported by Xi's frequent use of the image of iron), self-confidence, the Long March spirit and the "seize the day" urgency, and perseverance through struggle. Third, the author treats the 1925 poem on Changsha and Xi's remarks to students as a call for young people to carry the cause forward and for the Party to keep its youthfulness. Yuan concludes that Mao's poetry artistically reproduces the ambition, revolutionary sentiment and spiritual character of the Communists who pursue national rejuvenation. The author holds that, as the Party leads a great social revolution through its own self-reform, it still needs this poeticised revolutionary spirit and the ideals it conveys. Read the original if you want a Chinese-language case study of how Xi's rhetoric uses Mao's poems, with the historical background to each quoted line.

Exploration, innovation and development in contemporary socialism 当代社会主义的探索、创新与发展 Pan Jin'e Writing in 2018, a century after the October Revolution, Pan Jin'e asks how the five remaining socialist states (China, Vietnam, Laos, Cuba and North Korea) have charted their own paths since the Soviet-led socialist camp collapsed. The article argues that these countries kept their socialist direction while adapting institutions to national conditions. In Pan's account, this independent exploration also produced localised forms of Marxist theory, and countries that changed direction failed. The article begins with the Soviet model, which Pan says helped establish socialist systems but ended independent exploration of other paths. It then compares the five countries on three points: when reform began and how each names it, the reform of the economic system, and political change. A second part surveys the guiding ideologies each ruling party has built from its own practice. A final part assesses prospects for world socialism and the external pressures it faces. Pan's core argument is that paths differ because national conditions differ. China's reform dates from 1978, Vietnam's and Laos's from 1986, and Cuba's "updating" of its economic model from 2011. North Korea avoids the labels "reform" and "renovation". China, Vietnam and Laos pursue a socialist market economy or a "socialist-oriented market economy". Pan notes that Vietnam and Laos treat themselves as still in a transition to socialism, which allows more room for private capital. Cuba keeps planning dominant, and North Korea's measures are described as less coherent. On politics, all five constitutions drop "dictatorship of the proletariat", but Vietnam and Laos aim at a "socialist rule-of-law state". Pan also reports that Vietnam's Party now faces "self-evolution" and ideological decay. Each party has also localised Marxism, from Deng Xiaoping Theory to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, Ho Chi Minh Thought, Kaysone Phomvihane Thought, Fidel Castro Thought and Kim Il Sung–Kim Jong Il-ism. Pan concludes that Marxism sets the direction but each Party must combine its basic principles with national realities. The article credits China, Vietnam and Laos with rapid growth and middle-income status. It credits Cuba and North Korea with achievements in education, health and the environment despite sanctions. Pan warns that the post-Obama shift from blockade to engagement is a more deceptive form of "peaceful evolution", and that the internet carries ideological infiltration. Pan expects the Occupy Wall Street movement and the success of socialism with Chinese characteristics to revive socialism worldwide. Read the original if you want a comparative, Party-institution view of how China's scholars frame the five socialist states' reforms and their guiding ideologies.

The problematic of alienation theory in Capital 《资本论》中异化论的问题域 Watanabe Masao This is a Chinese translation of an article by the Japanese Marxist scholar Watanabe Masao. It takes up Louis Althusser's claim that an epistemological break separates the early Marx, whose problematic was humanist alienation, from the mature Marx of Capital. Watanabe says Hiromatsu Wataru and, in China, Zhang Yibing largely repeat this view, with softer wording such as 'discontinuity' or 'leap'. He argues the opposite: alienation theory was not mere ideology but a social-scientific method running through Marx's whole critique of political economy. The article first reconstructs the two stages of the problematic in the 1844 Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts: alienated labour is used to expose the economic fact of workers' poverty and non-workers' wealth, and then the causal relation between alienated labour and private property is settled. It then follows the concept through Theories of Surplus Value and Capital, volumes 1 and 3. Three structural aspects are examined in turn: appearance and essence, the inverted relations and consciousness of the economic trinity formula, and the reciprocal personification of things and objectification (Verdinglichung) of social relations. A final section treats the sublation of alienation. Watanabe's central claim is continuity. Both stages of the early problematic reappear in the late work: Marx again describes wage labour as labour alienated from itself, and again holds that the extraction of unpaid surplus labour produces domination and property, not the reverse. Alienation, he argues, explains why essence and appearance diverge in a commodity society where personal dependence has given way to dependence on things. It also explains why vulgar economics rests content with surface forms such as wages and interest-bearing capital, the most alienated form of capital. The difference between early and late Marx, he says, is deepening, since Marx now separates wage labour in the valorisation process from labour in general, and not a break. Watanabe concludes that the gap between early and late Marx is development and systematisation of alienation theory, and that the Althusser–Hiromatsu–Zhang reading is theoretically flawed. Alienation, in his account, is a historically specific form. Capital's alienated social power, created unintentionally, contains the conditions for its own dissolution, and the proletariat is charged with taking it over in a self-transformation that ends the alienated world. Read the original if you want a detailed, text-based Japanese rebuttal of the 'epistemological break' thesis, with extensive citations from Capital and its manuscripts.

Japanese assessments of and expectations for the 19th Party Congress of the Communist Party of China 日本各界对中共十九大的评价与期待 Cao Tianlu Cao Tianlu surveys how political parties, media and individuals in Japan reacted to the 19th National Congress of the Communist Party of China (2017). The article argues that, despite strained China–Japan relations, Japanese opinion paid close attention to the Congress and that positive assessments outweighed negative ones. The article is organised in three parts: the views of Japanese parties and former senior politicians; those of the mainstream media; and those of Japanese friends of China, including academics, business people and activists. It draws mainly on congratulatory letters, newspaper and NHK coverage, and interviews reported in Chinese outlets such as People's Daily and People's Daily Online. Cao notes that niconico broadcast the opening live with simultaneous interpretation. In Cao's account, the governing parties, opposition parties and the Japanese Communist Party's newspaper Akahata, together with figures such as former prime minister Hatoyama Yukio, praised the Belt and Road Initiative, the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind, Xi Jinping's leadership and the anti-corruption campaign. Cao reports that Mainichi, Asahi and Yomiuri focused on the "two centenary goals", military reform, poverty reduction and the institutionalisation of anti-corruption, while NHK stressed the economy and the Party's self-building. Japanese friends, such as the economist Ehara Noriyoshi and the entrepreneur Yamamori Kazuo, called for deeper economic cooperation, exchanges between young people and joint ventures in third countries. Cao concedes some dissonant voices: an NHK commentator who saw a "China threat", views that Chinese diplomacy would take a "hard line", suspicions that the Belt and Road Initiative is neo-colonial, and the Japanese Communist Party's remark that China is becoming a military power. Cao nonetheless concludes that positive views predominate, and that Japanese politicians, entrepreneurs and scholars continue to study the Congress report for political direction, business opportunities and patterns of Chinese development, in order to engage with China more fully. Read the original if you want a catalogue of Japanese statements on the 19th Congress, as selected and presented by a Chinese scholar, with source references to the Chinese and Japanese press.

Chinese scholarship's understanding of Western Marxism and its theoretical influence 论我国学术界对西方马克思主义的认识及其理论影响 Wang Yuchen Chen Ziwen After more than thirty years of systematic study of Western Marxism in China, the authors ask why Chinese scholars moved from rejecting it to a dialectical affirmation, and what this has meant for Marxist philosophy in China. They argue that the shift reflects changing social conditions, changing readings of Marxist philosophy, and a methodological and value-standpoint problem that still needs correcting. They hold that Western Marxism should serve Chinese Marxist theory-building and the practice of modernization. The article first traces the stages of reception. It begins with Xu Chongwen's 1982 book, commissioned for political reasons, which presented Western Marxism as an anti-Marxist current. It then covers the debates from 1986 between a negative school, a case-by-case school and an affirmative school, and the changes after 1989. These changes include the replacement of "Western Marxism" by "Marxism outside China" as a field, the rise of "interpreting Marxism through the West", a turn to micro-level study, and growing academicization. Part two analyses the reasons behind these views, and part three assesses Western Marxism's influence. On the reasons, the authors point to China's own context: Western Marxism arose in a post-industrial West, while China was industrializing, so early readers could not grasp its critique of technological rationality. They also cite differing interpretations of Marxist philosophy and an either-or metaphysical way of thinking that judges one form of Marxism by the standard of another. They propose instead judging each form by whether it answered the questions of its own time. On influence, they identify three issues: objective versus subjective factors in history, the scientific character versus the ideological function of Marxism, and the critique of contemporary capitalism. The influence is mixed. It sharpened attention to subjectivity, to the debate over "academic" versus "realistic" Marxism, and to cultural, technological and ecological critique. It also encouraged "practice ontology", exaggerated the differences between Marx and Engels and Lenin, and led to the labelling of Western Marxism as a de-ideologized "academic version", which the authors call a misreading. The authors conclude that researchers should adopt the standpoint of serving Chinese Marxist theory and modernization practice. They should neither withdraw into academic self-talk nor look down on Chinese Marxism. They call for uncovering Western Marxism's historical and problem logic, so that its resources can be used and its errors avoided. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist philosopher's account of how Western Marxism was received and assessed in China from 1982 to the 2010s.

The crisis of contemporary capitalism and the resistance of the Western left New trends in Western left thought seen from the 2017 Left Forum in New York 当代资本主义的危机与西方左翼的反抗 Jin Meng This is a report on the Left Forum held in New York in June 2017 under the theme 'Resistance: Strategy, Tactics, Struggle, Solidarity and Utopia'. Writing in the Trump era, Jin Meng asks how Western left scholars analyse the conflicts of capitalist society after Trump's inauguration and what paths beyond capitalism they propose. The report's main finding is that the forum's speakers aimed their critique at the capitalist system itself, not at Trump alone, and treated his government as a continuation of that system. The report is organised around three themes of the forum's panels and plenaries: Marxism and its contemporary value, especially on the 150th anniversary of Capital, Volume I; the crisis of capitalism in the Trump era and the future of socialism; and the history, present state and future of left resistance. It draws on named speakers, including David Schweickart, Nancy Holmstrom, Peter Hudis, David M. Kotz, Michael Hudson, Michael Perelman, Cinzia Arruzza and L. A. Kauffman. A closing assessment follows. On Capital, Jin reports that speakers saw it as still offering the most persuasive tools for analysing exploitation, overwork, unemployment and alienated labour. Holmstrom, for example, argued that equality for women and ecological stability cannot be achieved under capital accumulation. On Trump, Kotz and others located the root cause of his election in the crisis of neoliberalism since the 1970s. In Kotz's account his government is a right-wing nationalism that blames immigrants and foreigners while strengthening neoliberal policy. Speakers proposed alternatives such as a universal basic income, public banks, workers' cooperatives and a Green New Deal. On resistance, the report lists three weaknesses: the target of struggle is misplaced, with the Democratic Party co-opting protest; there is no alternative programme; and forces are fragmented. Remedies discussed were showing the public that capitalism is the target, building a united front across race, gender and age, and relying on young people. In a brief assessment, Jin credits the forum with clarifying the direction of struggle and rallying left forces. Jin also criticises the left as a mixed body of democratic socialists, anarchists, reformists and others, with differing views on Marxism, and says its proposals are one-sided, hard to put into practice and lacking unified long-term planning. Jin concludes that the foreign left needs a strong command centre and a unified front. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic account of the themes and speakers at the 2017 Left Forum, along with the author's own critical assessment of the Western left.

The united front of the Japanese Communist Party: history, opportunities and challenges 日本共产党统一战线：历史·机遇·挑战 Cao Tianlu Cao Tianlu asks how the Japanese Communist Party (JCP) has pursued united-front work since its founding in 1922, and what its prospects are today. The article argues that the JCP's record offers more lessons than successes. In the current setting it sees both opportunities and challenges, with challenges outweighing opportunities. The article first traces three periods. The first runs from the end of the Second World War to the 1950s, a time of proposal and sudden reversal. The second, from the 1960s to the 1990s, is one of reflection and adjustment. The third, from 2000 onwards, is described as stable and developing. It then sets out the present opportunities and challenges, drawing throughout on Marx, Engels, Lenin and Mao Zedong on alliances. On opportunities, Cao points to the dominance of the Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) under Abe, which has pushed the opposition parties towards cooperation. The 2016 electoral alliance of four opposition parties is the main example. Cao also notes new targets for united-front work: young voters after the voting age fell to 18, revived student movements, and the policy differences between the LDP and its partner Komeito. On challenges, the author cites the JCP's small parliamentary presence (21 of 475 lower-house seats and 14 of 242 upper-house seats in 2016). Cao also lists the JCP's own past conduct: imposing its programme on partners, excessive criticism, over-claiming leadership of the front, and declaring itself the only genuine progressive force. The author adds the lasting resentment of other opposition parties, the fragility of the current alliance, and pressure from the ruling camp. That pressure includes the police designation of the JCP as an organisation under surveillance and attacks from the right. Cao concludes that the JCP must first build up its own strength. It must also combine firmness of principle with tactical flexibility, seek common ground with other working-class parties while putting aside differences, and consolidate the basis of the front if it is to gain leadership and a voice within it. Marxist classics are used to support this. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist assessment of Japanese communist alliance strategy, with a periodised history and a detailed account of the 2016 opposition alliance.

Foreign communist parties on the new era of socialism with Chinese characteristics 国外共产党评析中国特色社会主义新时代 Yu Haiqing Writing in early 2018, Yu Haiqing surveys how communist parties abroad responded to the 19th Party Congress (October 2017) in articles on their websites and in Party newspapers and journals. Yu reports that most parties praised China's achievements and welcomed the Congress as the start of a new era of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Some raised doubts and warned of external challenges, which Yu says deserve attention. The article is organised in six parts. It covers assessments of development achievements, of the Congress's international significance, and of the Chinese path as a source of experience for other countries. It then turns to the argument that adhering to and innovating Marxism drives that path, and to the international challenges the parties identify. It closes with four reflections. The sources include the Italian, French, British, Swedish, US, Brazilian, Chilean, Canadian, South African, Turkish and Indian (Marxist) parties, among others. According to Yu, the parties credited China with leading global growth, lifting people out of poverty and building alternatives such as the Belt and Road Initiative and the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank against Western-dominated finance. The French party's L'Humanité asked whether a Chinese model exists. It judged that China's path is one model among many, but that it encourages the search for alternatives to neoliberalism. The South African and Brazilian parties saw it as a guide for former colonies. The Turkish party questioned whether socialism survives in state-owned enterprises, which it called "state capitalism", and asked how a new bourgeoisie can be kept from seizing state power. Most other parties, Yu notes, defended Chinese practice as a creative development of Marxism. The British and Canadian parties rebutted Western media claims that China has abandoned Marxism. The US and British parties warned of containment and encirclement by the United States. Yu draws four lessons. The Congress drew unusual world attention. China's rise shows the superiority of socialism and offers new momentum to a world socialist movement in a trough. Most foreign communist parties are positive about China. The critics' views stem from Western media distortion, a Western political outlook and limited grasp of the primary stage of socialism, and Yu calls for better international discourse power, telling China's story well, and more exchange platforms with these parties. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-by-source account, from a Chinese Party scholar, of how foreign communist parties received the 19th Party Congress and of how Chinese scholars frame their criticisms.

A review of the memoir of Fuwa Tetsuzo's wife 不破哲三夫人回忆录评析 Zheng Ping This is a review of The Road Without Regrets: Living with Fuwa Tetsuzo (Japanese edition 2012; Chinese edition, CITIC Press, April 2018), a memoir by Uedo Nanakako (上田七加子), wife of the Japanese Communist Party leader and Marxist theorist Fuwa Tetsuzo. The reviewer, Zheng Ping, is also the book's Chinese translator. Zheng presents the work as both a personal biography and a record of Japan from the Second World War to the present. The review follows the memoir's chronology. It covers Nanakako's turn from a militarist schoolgirl to Communist Party member in 1948, her work as a full-time Party official, factory organiser, community activist and women's movement cadre, and her role in Fuwa's eleven House of Representatives campaigns. It also reports the memoir's account of Fuwa's parliamentary questions and ends with brief remarks on the book's value as social history and as a woman's reflection on marriage and career. Zheng argues that the memoir shows how the Party, though legal after 1945 and fast-growing, developed through setbacks: Cold War anti-communism, the 'red purge', a Party split, and later electoral-system changes. The review reads Nanakako's factory work as an example of going among the people, analysing concrete problems and avoiding dogmatism. It cites the Party's 1958 line of 'peaceful revolution' through parliament, seat totals over time, and the 2016 opposition cooperation as evidence of resilience. Zheng also reads the Party's electoral path as showing that social change by parliamentary majority within capitalism is arduous and very slow. Zheng concludes that the couple, married for over sixty years, kept their ideals and shared commitment to world peace and liberation. The review recommends reading the memoir alongside Fuwa's 2011 autobiography Testimony of the Times for a fuller view of the Party's postwar history, on both theory and practice and on front-stage and backstage politics. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist scholar's account of the Japanese Communist Party's postwar history, as told through one memoir, and of how it is presented to Chinese readers.

Positive recognition of socialism with Chinese characteristics among scholars outside the Chinese mainland 国（境）外学者对中国特色社会主义的积极认同 Zheng Yuntian Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2018, Zheng surveys how scholars outside mainland China (the article's term 国（境）外 covers foreign countries and also Taiwan) have assessed socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era. The article argues that, despite wide differences in standpoint and method, much of this literature recognises China's achievements. It adds that China's development has pushed some of these scholars to reflect critically on their own research. The piece is a short overview built from quotations and paraphrases of foreign and Taiwanese commentators. Those named include Daniel Bell, Valentin Shabalin, Lorita Napoleoni, Robert Fogel, Giovanni Arrighi, Julio Ríos, Christopher McNally and Zhu Yunhan. It is divided into two parts: first, three themes of recognition, and second, the shift from self-assurance to self-reflection. In the first part, Zheng reports three claims. Success is said to come from following China's own path, described through Bell's model of grassroots democracy, experimentation at the middle level and meritocracy at the top, and through the view that China has opened a third road beyond American capitalism and European welfare-state socialism. Difficulties met during reform are said to have driven development and helped China avoid the Soviet collapse. Finally, China's growth is said to carry world-historical significance: Arrighi expects a rising China to act differently from earlier hegemons, and Ríos and McNally see the 19th Party Congress (2017) offering a model other countries can learn from. In the second part, Zheng argues that China's trajectory exceeds Western theoretical paradigms and that Western scholars must correct Western-centric assumptions, as Zhu Yunhan acknowledges, in order to understand China. Zheng concludes that the turn from self-assurance to reflection among overseas scholars shows that socialism with Chinese characteristics is winning wider international recognition. The author presents it as a new path of development that brings greater vitality and hope to the world. Read the original if you want a compact sample of the foreign and Taiwanese voices that Chinese official-academic writing cites to show international recognition of China's model.

The Communist Manifesto and the development of the French Communist Party An interview with Jean-Numa Ducange, young theorist of the French Communist Party 《共产党宣言》与法国共产党的发展 Yu Weihai This is an interview, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today on 31 May 2018, marking the 200th anniversary of Marx's birth and the 170th anniversary of the Communist Manifesto. Yu Weihai interviews Jean-Numa Ducange, a historian, a special representative of the Gabriel Péri Foundation (initiated by the French Communist Party) and a member of the team translating Marx and Engels into French. The question is how the Manifesto reached France and what it still means for the Party and French politics. Ducange answers that it remains a foundational text, though its direct ideological influence on the Party today is weak. The interview has five parts. It covers the Manifesto's translation and circulation in France, the ideas the Party still draws on, the Party's theoretical education, the legacy of Marxism in French politics, and Ducange's personal reading of the text. It closes with the idea of a new manifesto. Ducange also comments on Chinese-French cooperation. On history, Ducange traces a lost 1848 French edition and Laura Lafargue's full 1885 translation, serialised in Le Socialiste. The French Communist Party, founded in 1920, was the first party to publish it, and the text circulated most widely when the Party was a major force between 1935 and 1980. Marxism's influence then declined from the 1980s, though a revival of interest came in the early 2000s, with less political colouring than in the 1960s and 70s. On present relevance, he names three themes: the state, where the Manifesto's remark that the proletariat must "constitute itself the nation" informs Party debate over sovereignty and the European framework; capitalism's global expansion; and alliances, where the Manifesto's non-sectarian approach suggests short- and long-term strategies for the French left. He adds that Marx's other writings, such as The Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte, are needed to understand French political traditions. Ducange says the Party was the only French organisation to bring Marxism to hundreds of thousands, even millions, of people, despite misreadings. He notes the Manifesto's limits, including its Europe-centred focus, but points to Marxism's growth in China as proof that it can serve revolutionaries elsewhere. He regrets that the Party has no comparable founding text and supports drafting a new manifesto, discussed with the radical left and internationalist in method. He calls Chinese experience valuable and hopes for cooperation beyond differences of social system. Read the original if you want a French Communist Party intellectual's account of the Manifesto's French reception and its place in the Party today.

The Communist Party of Australia's exploration of the socialist movement 澳共对社会主义运动的积极探索 Yang Xiaoji This short commentary, first published in China Social Sciences Today in May 2018, reports on the 13th National Congress of the Communist Party of Australia (CPA), held in Sydney in December 2017. Yang Xiaoji argues that the party's analysis of capitalist crisis and its programme for the socialist movement are realistic and distinctive, and offer a fresh perspective on world socialism. The article first sketches the party's history: founded in 1920, dissolved after the upheavals in the USSR and Eastern Europe, and revived in 1996 when the Socialist Party of Australia, which had split from the old party in 1971, took the CPA name. It then summarises the congress's assessment of capitalism, followed by its guidelines for future work under the theme "Taking the Party to the People". Bob Briton was re-elected general secretary. On crisis, Yang reports the CPA's view that the 2008 financial crisis stemmed from monopoly firms and financial groups diverting capital into speculation, leaving the real economy starved. In the party's account, Western states respond with imperialist aggression abroad and cuts to workers' welfare. The CPA cites Roy Morgan Research figures putting Australia's real 2017 unemployment above 9.5%, against an official rate of about 5.5%. The congress's guidelines stress the party's leading role, branch-level organisation, and workers' struggles over jobs, wages and services. The programme set in 2005 envisages two stages: an anti-imperialist, anti-monopoly democratic revolution led by a people's alliance government, then a socialist revolution. It also calls for broad united fronts, party unity, and solidarity with Cuba and other socialist states. Yang concludes that the CPA has its own understanding of Western capitalism's crisis and that its domestic action plans are practical. The author presents the party's particular path as useful for understanding world socialism. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese academic overview of the CPA's 2017 congress resolutions and how Chinese scholars present them.

Why is David Harvey's interpretation of Marx's "labour theory of value" wrong? 大卫·哈维对马克思“劳动价值论”的解释为什么是错的？ Michael Roberts This is a Chinese translation, by Yan Jun, of a polemic by the Marxist economist Michael Roberts against David Harvey's reading of Marx's value theory and crisis theory. Roberts takes issue with Harvey's claims that Marx never held a labour theory of value, that "without a market there is no value", and that capitalist crisis is rooted in workers' insufficient consumption. Roberts argues that each claim misreads Marx and conflicts with the empirical record. The Chinese text begins with an editor's note and a translator's introduction. The introduction recaps the dual character of labour in Capital, sets out Harvey's emphasis on the "realisation" of value in exchange, and summarises Harvey's reply to Roberts. Roberts's own piece responds to Harvey's paper on Marx's supposed rejection of the labour theory of value and to his 2017 book on the madness of economic reason. It closes with notes pointing to empirical tests of the law of value by Shaikh, Tsoulfidis and Paitaridis, and Carchedi. Roberts first distinguishes Ricardo's value theory, based on concrete labour, from Marx's, based on abstract labour. He also stresses Marx's separation of labour from labour-power, which is what reveals the source of surplus value. In his view Harvey mentions abstract labour only in passing and puts exchange in place of production. Roberts replies that labour is already embodied in a commodity's value before it reaches the market, and that money represents value rather than creating it. Second, he treats Harvey's account of crisis as an underconsumption theory. He argues that Marx dismissed such explanations as tautology in Capital, Volume 2, and that Harvey neglects the rising organic composition of capital and the tendency of the profit rate to fall. Roberts adds three facts: consumption is only 36 per cent of US gross output once intermediate stages are stripped out, investment fell by 8–30 per cent in postwar recessions while consumption fell less, and wages rose before 11 of 12 postwar crises. Roberts concludes that Harvey reduces the duality of value to workers' lack of purchasing power for use-values. He says this replaces over-accumulation with underconsumption and shifts class struggle from production to disputes between consumers and capital, or taxpayers and the state. In his judgement this is not Marx's view and it confuses the analysis of workers' struggles. The translator presents the text as a way to acquaint Chinese readers with debates among US Marxist economists. Read the original if you want a critique of Harvey's value theory from the falling-profit-rate tradition, or a compact collection of the empirical evidence cited against underconsumptionist readings of Marx.

New tasks for ideological and political education arising from the people's growing need for a better spiritual life 人民日益增长的美好精神生活需要对思想政治教育提出的新课题 Yan Xiaofeng Writing in 2018, after the 19th Party Congress (2017) declared that the principal contradiction in Chinese society had changed, Yan Xiaofeng asks how ideological and political education should respond to the people's growing need for a better spiritual life. The contradiction is now between the people's ever-growing need for a better life and unbalanced and inadequate development. Yan's thesis is that a better spiritual life is an integral part of a better life, that ideological and political education is an effective route to meeting it, and that the field must be renewed to do so. The article has four parts. The first defines the need for a better spiritual life and places it in the new era of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The second explains why ideological and political education is an important channel for meeting it. The third identifies where current practice falls short. The fourth sets out four directions for innovation. Yan treats cultural life as the process and spiritual life as its purpose, and holds that spiritual life, like material life, has higher and lower levels. A better spiritual life involves a relaxed mind, a unified personality, ideals, sincerity, aesthetic pursuit and independence. Ideological and political education, Yan argues, supplies its content and models (the Lei Feng campaign is an example), helps people resolve conflicts such as that between survival pressures and the life of the mind, and offers practical paths grounded in Marxism's unity of practice and spiritual activity. Yan then names three weaknesses: the function is undervalued, with the aesthetic dimension neglected; research on it, both theoretical and empirical, is insufficient; and guidance is weak, shown in the author's account by people turning to religion, regarding the education as mere preaching, or by students who feel spiritually adrift. Yan calls for four measures: firm ideals and convictions, including communist ideals and the common ideal of socialism with Chinese characteristics; making the core socialist values a conscious commitment; cultivation through the culture of socialism with Chinese characteristics, drawing on traditional, revolutionary and advanced socialist culture; and resistance to decadent and backward culture. Read the original if you want a Party-theory account of how ideological and political education is being repositioned around spiritual needs after the 19th Party Congress.

Reflection and reconstruction: thoughts on the predicament of modern moral development 反思与重构：基于现代道德发展困境的思考 Deng Li Zhang Shujun Deng and Zhang take up the question of why morality in contemporary China has become superficial and marginal, and how it might be rebuilt. Writing in 2018 and opening with Xi Jinping's call to strengthen society-wide ideological and moral construction, they argue that the root of the predicament is a loss of moral belief among individuals, not a shortage of rules or of moral education. Their answer is a moral system that combines virtue and norms, and that follows the social development of human nature. The article is in three parts. The first diagnoses three symptoms of the predicament: the instrumentalisation of morality for utility, moral nihilism and moral hypocrisy. The second looks for deeper causes in the over-expansion of normative ethics and in China's social modernization. The third proposes two paths of reconstruction, drawing on Aristotle, Kant, Habermas and Alasdair MacIntyre. In the authors' account, market competition, materialism and imported Western individualism and liberalism have pushed traditional moral values aside. Scepticism and the liberal priority of rights over the good then supply nihilism with its intellectual support. The authors add that law can restrain outward wrongdoing but cannot reach conscience. Hypocrisy, they say, arises when moral aims are cut off from people's real needs. At a deeper level, rule-based ethics asks only what one should do and so sees "rules but not people".
