Rule systems have also detached from the lifeworld and, in Habermas's phrase, colonised it. Modernization has dissolved the kin-based order and dissolved faith in a transcendent moral authority. People now live as public citizens rather than natural persons, and virtue ethics loses its practical force. The authors call for a moral system that keeps virtue and norms together, since each presupposes the other. Norms secure social order and a baseline ethics. Virtue is the ultimate aim of moral construction, which they link to the 19th Party Congress (2017) restatement of fostering virtue through education. They also hold that moral cultivation should follow the socialisation of human nature. Cognition, an innate potential for goodness and repeated internalisation and externalisation in the lifeworld would lead morality to become a person's "second nature". Read the original if you want a philosophical, virtue-ethics diagnosis of China's moral difficulties, written within the field of ideological and political education.)

Grasping the laws of development in hot-topic research on ideological and political education 把握思想政治教育热点研究的发展规律 Feng Gang Feng Gang asks what defines a "research hotspot" in ideological and political education and how the field's hotspots develop. Drawing on his own compilation of an annual report on 2017 research hotspots, he argues that hotspots are not subjective inventions but the necessary result of theory and practice advancing together. Understanding their regularities, he holds, is required for deepening theory and advancing the discipline. The article, published in 2018, has three parts. The first defines hotspot research, its features and its value. The second identifies seven characteristics of the previous year's research, set against the study of Xi Jinping's speech at the national conference on ideological and political work in universities, the 19th Party Congress (2017) and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The third draws out three laws of hotspot development. On the definition, Feng says hotspots must fit their historical setting, the state of a still relatively young discipline (about thirty years old, with basic categories, boundaries and paradigms unsettled) and a clear practical orientation. The seven features of 2017 research are: firm adherence to the correct direction under Marxism; adaptation to the new era; fit with the stage of economic and social development; responsiveness to new demands of practice; greater depth; wider horizons; and varied methods. Examples include research on internal motivation, red culture, online education and the use of big data and the CIPP evaluation model. The three laws are that hotspots emerge from the deepening and extension of basic theory, from the development and needs of practice, and from a two-way interaction between hotspot research and the discipline that forms a closed loop. Feng concludes that researchers must keep pace with the times, work from problems and plan within the context of educational modernization and the network age. He predicts that future hotspots may include interdisciplinary study of basic categories, process laws and policy; the characteristics of university students; online education models; carriers and methods; and collaborative education in universities. Read the original if you want a Chinese insider's overview of how the field of ideological and political education maps its own research priorities as of 2017–2018.

The sociology of ideological and political education: aims, problems and ways beyond 思想政治教育社会学：目标、问题及超越 Shen Dong Sun Qi'ang Shen Dong and Sun Qi'ang take up the sociology of ideological and political education, a proposed sub-discipline that they say is still at an exploratory, early stage. The article asks what the sub-discipline is for, what obstacles it faces and how to overcome them. Their thesis is that it should not be read as a mere "marriage" of ideological and political education with sociology. In their view it is the product of the parent discipline differentiating and of a shift in research paradigm. The article has four sections. The first sets the background: two historical transformations of ideological and political education, in 1949 and in 1978, and the discipline's reorganisation in 2005 when Marxist theory became a first-level discipline. The second diagnoses the sub-discipline's difficulties. The third sets out its tasks: empirical research, theory-building and policy advice. The fourth draws conclusions on the relation between sub-discipline and parent discipline. The authors argue that ideological and political education succeeded in building an academic discipline but became marginal and weak in social practice, because its research paradigm remained tied to "work" and "experience". They identify three problems for the sub-discipline: scarce original knowledge, which is mostly borrowed from the parent discipline or sociology; insufficient theory of its own; and closed disciplinary boundaries, with sociologists showing little interest. They propose strengthening empirical study of what actually happens in society, building theory that can talk to other social sciences, and offering policy advice. They link the "what is", "why" and "how" questions about state and society, and say the sub-discipline supplies the "why" and adds a "state" and "ideological" perspective. The authors conclude that the sub-discipline should draw out the "social attributes" of a field long confined to a state perspective. It should spur the growth of the parent discipline and its related branches, and carry out the applied research they say is still missing. They add that the field must meet the challenges of globalisation and plural social thought. Read the original if you study how Chinese scholars debate the disciplinary standing, methods and social relevance of ideological and political education.

New starting point, new positioning, new journey: building ideological and political education for the new era 新起点新定位新征程：迈向新时代的思想政治教育建设之路 Zhang Kai Zhang Shujun Writing in 2018, shortly after the 19th Party Congress (2017), Zhang Kai and Zhang Shujun ask how ideological and political education should respond to the new era of socialism with Chinese characteristics. They argue that the field has a new starting point, a new positioning and a new journey. Each follows from the change in the principal social contradiction, from the task of national rejuvenation, and from Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The article has three main sections. The first describes the changed environment and problems of ideological and political education. The second sets out its redefined goals and value as a spiritual driving force for national rejuvenation. The third turns to the guiding programme and practical mechanisms for the new journey, which the authors summarise as educating people through all aspects, the whole process and wholeheartedly. In the first section, the authors say the principal contradiction is now between the people's growing need for a better life and unbalanced and inadequate development. They identify three consequences. Public spiritual needs have become more urgent and varied. Social contradictions have become fragmented, so the 'reality' that education must engage is now many realities. New technologies and 'time-space compression' (a term the authors take from David Harvey) have produced interwoven social interactions for which the field lacks analytical and response mechanisms. In the second section, they assign it three tasks: strengthening the Four-sphere Confidence and the Party's cohesion, raising citizens' cultural and moral quality through core socialist values, and building cultural soft power so as to tell China's story and guard ideological 'territory'. In the third, they make Xi Jinping Thought the basic content and theoretical foundation of the field. They also apply its methodology, which they list as people-centredness, practicality, innovation and scientific professionalism, and integrate Xi's specific directives on the work into the whole process. The authors conclude that ideological and political education remains the Party's 'magic weapon' and is more important in the new era. Improving it, they say, must be rooted in propagating and implementing Xi Jinping Thought, both its content and its methods. They call on practitioners to study it thoroughly themselves, to reject formalism and detachment from the masses, and to pursue innovation and professionalisation. Read the original if you want an example of how Chinese scholars in 2018 tied ideological and political education to the new principal contradiction and to Xi Jinping Thought.

Correcting errors in contemporary Western Marxist methods of class analysis 当代西方马克思主义阶级分析方法辨误 Mi Haibo Mi Haibo asks how far contemporary Western Marxist redefinitions of class remain faithful to Marx's method. Writing in a 2017 journal article, Mi argues that changes in capitalism, notably the separation of ownership from management and the rise of the knowledge economy, have prompted new accounts of class that are suggestive but contain many misreadings and defects. The article's thesis is that class is ultimately an economic category rooted in ownership of the means of production, and that economic, political and cultural criteria must not be separated from that foundation. The article is organised in three sections, each examining one dimension of class analysis. The first treats the economic dimension through the analytical Marxists John Roemer, Erik Olin Wright and Philippe Van Parijs. The second turns to the political dimension, discussing Nicos Poulantzas and Ralf Dahrendorf. The third addresses the cultural dimension through John Kenneth Galbraith, Daniel Bell, Pierre Bourdieu and Alvin Gouldner. In the economic section, Mi credits Roemer with linking class to wealth and Wright with centring exploitation, but contends that Roemer is unclear on whether production or the market forms classes. Mi also holds that Wright's "contradictory class" of the new middle class, defined by organisational and skill assets, rests on an untenable notion of skill exploitation. In Mi's view this group remains part of the "collective worker". Van Parijs's division between employed and unemployed is described as a stratification analysis that obscures the conflict between capital and labour and splits the proletariat. On politics, Mi accepts Poulantzas's point that political and ideological factors matter, citing Marx on the small-holding peasantry, but still insists on the ultimate economic determination. Dahrendorf's power-based classes are said to sever economic base from superstructure. On culture, Mi argues that intellectuals serve and depend on particular classes, so "a new class of intellectuals" is better described as "the new intellectuals of a class". Mi concludes that class is an interest community and political actor determined by the social economic structure. Knowledge, culture and power are therefore secondary indicators and cannot replace ownership relations as the criterion. Western Marxist theories are worth engaging for the problems they raise, such as unemployment and the new middle class. Mi nonetheless judges them not to grasp the essence of the concept of class. Read the original if you want a critical Chinese reading of Roemer, Wright, Poulantzas, Dahrendorf, Bell and Bourdieu on class, measured against orthodox Marxist class analysis.

The "right" and "wrong" in the thought of the founders of Western Marxism 西方马克思主义创始人思想的“是”与“非” Zhao Bin Zhao Bin asks how Chinese scholars should assess Lukács, Korsch and Gramsci, the founders of Western Marxism, whose ideas have divided Chinese researchers since they were introduced in the 1980s and 1990s. The article argues that their thought has real historical merits and equally real limits, and that the two must be separated. Zhao sets two methodological rules for researchers in socialist China: study them from the standpoint, method and viewpoint of Marxism, rather than using them to explain Marxism; and study them to serve the adaptation of Marxism to Chinese conditions, rather than to judge socialism with Chinese characteristics. The article has two main sections. The first sets out four historical contributions: responding to the quest of late-developing countries for modernization and national revival; criticising the economic determinism of the Second International; protesting against the reification of human beings under capitalism; and shifting attention towards humanism and cultural critique. The second section sets out three limits: an idealist reading of why European revolutions failed, a subjectivist and romantic choice of future path, and a split between Marx, Engels and Lenin. A closing part reviews Chinese research trends and offers recommendations. Zhao's central argument is that the three thinkers rightly attacked mechanical, positivist readings by Bernstein and Kautsky, but then swung to a Hegelian, humanist reading. Using Lukács's treatment of reification as the example, Zhao says he equated alienation with reification and offered a value critique that changes the proletariat's consciousness rather than the exploitation behind it. For Zhao, Marx treated alienation as an objective product of material production, which only the development of production can abolish; consciousness can play only a secondary role. Zhao adds that their stress on class consciousness and cultural leadership reverses Marx's route from social being to social consciousness. Their separation of the young Marx from the mature Marx, and of Marx from Engels and Lenin, is said to miss the unity of philosophy, political economy and scientific socialism. Zhao notes that Chinese studies of the three have become specialised and fragmented, and that some researchers use their non-Marxist elements to explain contemporary China. Zhao calls for closer reading of Marxist and Leninist classics, so that compatible and incompatible elements can be told apart, and for absorbing whatever remains valuable in the light of the practice of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Citing the report to the 19th Party Congress (2017), the article stresses the primacy of the Marxist standpoint and the direction of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context. Read the original if you want to see how a CASS researcher in 2018 set the official terms for evaluating early Western Marxism, and how the case against Lukács, Korsch and Gramsci was made.

Western neo-Marxist spatial theory and the spatial theory of Capital: a comparative analysis 西方新马克思主义空间理论与《资本论》空间理论的比较分析 Lin Chengyuan Lin Chengyuan asks how the spatial theory of Western neo-Marxism relates to the spatial theory found in Marx's Capital. The article identifies two errors in existing scholarship: treating Western neo-Marxist spatial theory as the 'second generation' or 'upgraded version' of Marxist spatial theory, and attributing to Marx concepts such as the 'production of space' or the 'politics of space' that originate with Western neo-Marxists. Lin's thesis is that the two theories differ and must not be equated. The article sets out the neo-Marxist side through its two central figures, Henri Lefebvre (the founder) and David Harvey (the synthesiser). It then reconstructs Capital's spatial theory as three spaces: production space, circulation space and land space. Lefebvre is compared with Marx on three points: the definition of space, the place of the city, and who produces space. Harvey is treated through his view of time and space, the 'spatial fix' and the 'right to the city'. Lin argues that Lefebvre carries Marx's theory of capitalist production over into a vague, all-encompassing notion of space, which is then in practice identified with the city, and that he names architects, broadly defined, as space's producers. In Lin's reading of Capital, the only real producer of space is capital, or the bourgeoisie, which decides where factories, logistics and sales centres are sited and how land is farmed. Lin sees Lefebvre's 'politics of space' as a way of avoiding this conclusion. Harvey's 'annihilation of space by time' is traced to Marx's account of transport in Volume II, and his 'spatial fix' is read as capital's overseas expansion, which in Lin's view only displaces capitalism's contradictions. Lin also faults Harvey's claim that revolution must be urban, citing the Chinese revolution's rural path, and finds Harvey hesitant where Marx is firm. Lin concludes that Western neo-Marxist spatial theory draws on Marx and Engels but is not Marxist spatial theory's contemporary development. It should be both drawn upon and critically assessed, with its scope of application examined. Lin calls for Chinese practice to absorb the best Western results and build a spatial theory with Chinese characteristics, in line with Xi Jinping's call at the 19th Party Congress (2017) to build a philosophy and social science with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a critical, Marx-centred comparison of Lefebvre and Harvey with Capital, written from a Chinese Party-school perspective.

The ban on Party members holding religious belief is not in contradiction with the Party's policy of freedom of religious belief 中共党员不准信仰宗教与党的宗教信仰自由政策并不矛盾 Zuo Peng Writing in 2018, after the 19th Party Congress (2017) called for full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, Zuo Peng takes up a debate over whether Communist Party members may hold religious belief. The author notes that some members still consult fortune-tellers or worship, and that some scholars claim that "Party members may believe" and "believers may join the Party", and that the ban contradicts the policy of freedom of religious belief. Zuo argues that there is no contradiction: the ban is a long-standing ideological principle, organisational principle and political discipline of the Party, and it is needed both to regulate inner-Party political life and to implement the religious policy fully. The article has three sections. The first derives the ban from the dialectical-materialist worldview of Marxism and traces it through Party documents from Mao Zedong and Zhou Enlai to the 1982 Central Committee document on religious questions, the 1991 Organization Department notice, and statements by Jiang Zemin, Hu Jintao and Xi Jinping (2016). The second addresses citizens' constitutional freedom of belief, and the third asks who can implement the religious policy. Zuo's central distinction is that freedom of religious belief includes freedom not to believe. In the author's reading, a person who swears the Party oath has accepted the requirement of atheism and thereby chooses the freedom not to believe. Party members are described as citizens with special political responsibilities who give up some freedoms ordinary citizens have. Zuo rejects the proposal to admit religious leaders and elites. The article argues that Lenin's remarks on priests joining the Social-Democratic Party require that they drop religious views, and that figures such as Fu Lianzhang completed their change of worldview before joining. Religious figures can instead be engaged through the united front. Finally, Zuo claims that only non-believing Party members can implement the policy fully, citing risks of favouritism among five religions, local officials promoting religious sites for economic gain, and the loss of atheist education. The article also rejects the claim that believers in power best secure religious freedom, pointing to historical examples from Europe and the United States. Zuo concludes that the ban should be maintained and enforced, with ideological education for members who turn to religion and organisational measures if they persist. In minority regions, Party members may take part in traditional customs derived from religious rites, but must keep a clear ideological line from belief; the few who incite religious fanaticism should be disciplined. Read the original if you want a detailed statement of the official Party-theoretical case for atheism as a condition of membership, with its textual sources and its rebuttals of rival scholarly views.

Tracing back to the source of truth, preserving theoretical confidence 回溯真理源头 永葆理论自信 Chen Jin Writing in Guangming Daily in May 2018, on the 200th anniversary of Marx's birth, Chen Jin argues that firm theoretical confidence is the soul of upholding and developing socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era. The commentary takes Xi Jinping's speech at the anniversary meeting as its starting point and holds that returning to Marxism's origins is how Chinese communists renew that confidence. The piece is a short reflective essay. It sketches the Party's path from seeking, upholding and developing to innovating an "-ism", lists the theoretical results of that path, and notes the Politburo study sessions since the 18th Party Congress (2012) on Marxist fundamentals, including one on the Communist Manifesto. It then poses three questions: why set out, how to advance, and how to gather strength. Chen's central claim is that theoretical confidence and confidence in the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics support each other. Without the former there can be no confidence in the path, while the path's forty years of successful practice show that its guiding theory is effective and scientific. Chen answers the three questions by pointing to communist ideals as the "calcium of the spirit", Marxism as a worldview and method, and knowledge of Marxist principles as the basis for grasping the theoretical system of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Theoretical confidence, Chen says, means both consistency and keeping pace with the times, and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era is presented as raising it further. Chen concludes that the Party should keep raising the banner of Marxism so that the future Marx and Engels envisaged is shown on Chinese soil. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Party-aligned commentary in 2018 tied the Marx bicentenary to theoretical confidence and the Party's own theoretical lineage.

Approaching the real Marx On reading Marx, an Intellectual Giant 走近真实的马克思 Jin Nuo Hao Lixin This is a book review, published in Guangming Daily in May 2018, shortly after the 200th anniversary of Marx's birth. Jin Nuo and Hao Lixin review Jin Huiming's Marx, an Intellectual Giant (思想巨人马克思). They argue that the book presents a real, thinking Marx and conveys both his personal stature and his lasting theoretical contribution. The reviewers describe the book as neither an ordinary biography nor a purely theoretical study. They say it combines Marx's theoretical creation, revolutionary practice and life, and treats his social setting, personal hardships and struggles together with the development of his thought. They credit the author, a long-time researcher of Marxist philosophy and the history of Marxism, with writing it in old age. The book has 14 chapters organised around Marx's intellectual turning points and his two great discoveries. The review identifies three features of method: combining history with theory, with theory predominant; unifying history and logic, and thought with social practice; and tracing how concepts evolve alongside ideas, since, as the book puts it, the content of thought develops before its formal expression. On structure, the reviewers report that early chapters cover Marx's shift from idealism to materialism and from revolutionary democracy to socialism. Later chapters treat the materialist conception of history, the Communist Manifesto and the 1848 revolutions, and the theory of surplus value. The final chapters cover his later years and the contemporary significance of Marxism. The reviewers conclude that few systems of thought show such enduring appeal as Marx's. In their view this comes from his personal character, his theoretical quality and the scientific force of his thought. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese account of how a leading Party-affiliated reviewer assesses this biography and its chapter structure.

Sensing and grasping the truth-power of Marxism in practice Marking the 40th anniversary of "Practice is the sole criterion for testing truth" 在实践中感悟和把握马克思主义的真理力量 Yang Geng Commissioned by Guangming Daily for the 40th anniversary of its 11 May 1978 editorial "Practice is the sole criterion for testing truth", this commentary by Yang Geng of Beijing Normal University asks what that debate still teaches. Yang argues that the discussion was more than an epistemological exercise. In Yang's account it restored the Party's seeking-truth-from-facts line, prefigured reform and opening up, and reveals the truth-power of Marxism when read from the vantage point of the "new era". The piece has three parts. The first treats the truth-criterion debate as a political as well as philosophical event and draws lessons on the relation between philosophy and politics. The second traces how contemporary Chinese practice deepened the "practice criterion" into two further criteria. The third turns to how Marxism should be upheld and developed in practice, including a defence of its contemporary relevance. Yang draws on Marx, Lenin, Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping. Yang contends that the debate undermined the "two whatevers" and so was a question of the Party's and the country's fate. Philosophy, Yang says, has both a knowledge and an ideological character, so philosophical change precedes political change and Marxist philosophy is in effect political philosophy. Reform practice added a "productivity criterion" (an objective or scientific measure) and a "people's criterion" (a value measure based on popular needs and interests). Yang says the two together complete the practice criterion, because developing productive forces without serving the people, or serving them only in intention, would fail. Yang rejects the claim that Marxism is outdated, citing successive capitalist crises, but denies that it is a system of "ultimate truth". Marx, Yang writes, was a Prometheus rather than a god, and Marxism supplies a method rather than ready-made answers. Yang calls for Marxism to be developed by studying China's socialist reality, contemporary Western capitalism and foreign Marxist currents. Yang proposes renewing familiar theories (reflection theory, class theory, the labour theory of value, capital accumulation, public ownership) and developing ideas Marx and Engels only sketched, such as world-system ideas and ecological civilization. Yang presents Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era as the systematic answer to the problems raised by reform. Read the original if you want a representative 2018 statement of how Chinese Marxist philosophers link the 1978 truth-criterion debate to the Party's current theoretical line.

The intellectual-historical premises of Hiromatsu Wataru's philosophical situation A reading of "The Outpost of the Worldview of Events" 广松涉哲学构境的思想史前提 Zhang Yibing Zhang Yibing asks how the young Japanese philosopher Hiromatsu Wataru built the foundations of his "worldview of events" (shi de shijieguan) out of earlier Western thought. The article argues that Hiromatsu never became a mere follower of any one thinker. Instead, in Zhang's account, he linked the logics of Kant, Mach, Husserl and Heidegger with contemporary scientific methodology. He also set out the "four-limbed structure" of the intersubjective world as the creative direction of his life's work. The article is a reading of the first part of Hiromatsu's book The Outpost of the Worldview of Events (1971; Chinese translation 2002). It is divided into three sections: Kant, Mach, and the passage from Husserl to Heidegger. Zhang follows how Hiromatsu treats each thinker as a lower logical hurdle to be passed on the way to his own position. Zhang also adds his own judgements and cites his other books, including those on Heidegger, Sohn-Rethel and Stiegler. On Kant, Zhang explains that Hiromatsu saw the thing-in-itself being "liquefied" into an epistemological event, so that ontology, epistemology and logic form one unity. Hiromatsu then argued that Kant's transcendental frame is itself a historical product of intersubjective interaction. Zhang agrees, but holds that the real basis of intersubjective structures is objective practice, not cognition, and he cites Sohn-Rethel and Stiegler as going deeper. On Mach, Hiromatsu accepted the relational picture of sensory elements but objected that the real world is "more than" a complex of elements, which gives the first two limbs: the given and the meant. Zhang adds that Mach's lasting influence on Hiromatsu was a habit of building the world from micro-level images. Husserl and Heidegger supply the other two limbs, the self and the other-self, and Heidegger's equipment-based ontology is faulted for mistaking relations for things (wuxianghua), as in the case of money. Zhang finds Hiromatsu's critique of Heidegger too sweeping. In Zhang's view, Hiromatsu overlooked Heidegger's rejection of epistemology and could not know the "Ereignis" (appropriation) thinking in Heidegger's unpublished manuscripts, which Zhang says began in the 1930s. Zhang says he does not simply endorse that thinking but regrets the gap in Hiromatsu's understanding. The article presents Hiromatsu as a thinker who dissolved all substances into relations, and it locates his "four-limbed" theory in the history of its sources. Read the original if you study Hiromatsu Wataru, Japanese Marxist philosophy or Zhang Yibing's own approach to foreign Marxism, and want to see how he positions himself against Hiromatsu on Kant, Mach and Heidegger.

Politics of emancipation, biopolitics, politics of inaction Aims and logical shifts in the technological critique of modernity 解放政治学·生命政治学·无为政治学 Hu Daping Hu Daping asks how critiques of modernity have understood technology from the mid-nineteenth century to the present. The article opens with the Unabomber Kaczynski's claim that industry has become a disaster for humanity, as a sign that technology, once the source of modern self-confidence, is now widely seen as the root of catastrophe. Hu argues that the critical gaze on technology has passed through three perspectives: a politics of emancipation, a biopolitics and a politics of inaction (wuwei). In these, technology appears respectively as productive force, as instrumental reason and as technological law. The article traces a line from Marx through Nietzsche, Spengler, Heidegger and the Frankfurt School to Baudrillard, Virilio, neo-Luddism and Bruno Latour. Part one treats Marx's historical context and his place for technology within the relation of productive forces to relations of production. Part two covers the biopolitical turn of the early twentieth century, including Lukács, Adorno and Horkheimer, Marcuse, Husserl, Mumford and Ellul. Part three examines contemporary radical critiques, and a short conclusion draws these together. Hu holds that Marx neither hated machines like the Luddites nor worshipped productive forces. He located the harm of technology in capitalist relations of production, and saw modern science and technology as products of capital accumulation that carry its aims. The Frankfurt School, in Hu's reading, turned this into a critique of instrumental reason, with Marcuse insisting that technical rationality is historically specific and could become a liberating technology. After the 1970s, Hu argues, Baudrillard's hyperreality and Virilio's dromology treat technology and speed as autonomous structures that sideline human subjects. Neo-Luddism offers only rejection, and Latour proposes a "Parliament of Things" and a slowing down rather than revolution. Hu reads this quietism as a sign that technology has run ahead of society, so that the Enlightenment project of emancipation has itself become a constraint. Hu concludes that technology is not an isolated natural matter but a social and existential problem tied to economics, politics and culture. The article says it does not aim to answer where reconstruction should begin. Hu warns that humanity has reached a critical moment at which, unless it grasps the reins, technology, like a runaway horse, may throw it to the ground. Read the original if you want an intellectual-historical survey, by a Chinese scholar of foreign Marxism, of how Marxist and post-Marxist technology critique moved from emancipation to quietism.

The truth of Marxism has strong and lasting vitality In commemoration of the 200th anniversary of Marx's birth 马克思主义真理具有强大而持久的生命力 Wang Weiguang Written for the 200th anniversary of Marx's birth and published in Qiushi in 2018, this article by Wang Weiguang asks why Marxism has kept its vitality since the 1840s. Wang's answer is that Marxism is a complete system of scientific truth that is also open to development, and that it renews itself by being combined with the practice of the working class and of each nation. The article presents Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era as the latest stage of this process. The text has three sections. The first presents Marxism as the greatest revolution in the history of human thought, in its standpoint, its basic views and its method. The second looks for the internal sources of its vitality in three pairs of features. The third surveys Marxism in practice: the First and Second Internationals, the Paris Commune, Lenin's development of Marxism in Russia, and the adaptation of Marxism to China. Wang argues that the standpoint of Marxism is the proletariat and the liberation of all humanity. Its basic views are the materialist conception of history and the theory of surplus value, which Engels called the "two discoveries", and its method is materialist dialectics. Its vitality, Wang says, comes from tensions it holds together: theoretical completeness and orientation towards practice, scientific truth and openness to development, and universality and national specificity. Wang holds that its basic principles do not become outdated, while it stays abreast of the times by enriching its content as practice develops. Dogmatic application of Marxist phrases that ignores national conditions would, in Wang's view, stifle it. In the account of China, Wang describes 170 years in which the country moved from humiliation to "standing up, becoming prosperous and becoming strong". Wang sets out two historic leaps in adapting Marxism to China: Mao Zedong Thought and then socialism with Chinese characteristics under Deng Xiaoping. Since the 18th Party Congress (2012), Wang says, the Party Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core has opened a new era and created Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Wang concludes that Marxism shows strong vitality when combined with the practice of different nations. Read the original if you want an example of the official 2018 account of why Marxism endures and how it is placed in the Chinese tradition.

Western multiparty democracy in theoretical and practical predicament 西方多党民主陷入理论与现实困境 Chai Shangjin Writing in Guangming Daily in April 2018, Chai Shangjin argues that Western multiparty competitive democracy has fallen into both theoretical and practical difficulty. The author points to the rise of populist and extreme parties, political polarisation, ineffective governance and social disorder, and says reflection on the system has become an important topic even among Western theorists. The commentary is organised under four headings: the loss of the "political legitimacy" of multiparty elections; partisan infighting as the "pathogen" of Western disorder; the damage caused by forcing Western-style democracy on other countries; and a short closing section on China. Chai contends that elections have become contests decided by campaign tricks and money rather than by popular will. The author cites falling turnout, especially among the young, and the claim that governments serve capital whichever party wins. Party rivalry, in this account, produces "veto politics", referendums that deepen social divisions, and an "elite democracy" that hardens into oligarchy and provokes populist backlash. Chai also describes the export of Western democracy, through "colour revolutions", multiparty reforms in Africa, neoliberal reform in Latin America and the Iraq war, as a source of instability, civil war and refugee flows, and as proof of "false democracy, real hegemony". Chai concludes that the democratic system of socialism with Chinese characteristics has outstanding advantages. The author calls for confidence in presenting those advantages and the world significance of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, so as to offer Chinese wisdom and solutions. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a Chinese Party-theory commentator in 2018 criticised Western electoral democracy.

The wide spread and profound influence of Marxism in the world 马克思主义在世界上的广泛传播和深刻影响 Chai Shangjin Published in Guangming Daily in May 2018, shortly after the 200th anniversary of Marx's birth, this commentary by Chai Shangjin takes up Xi Jinping's remark that no body of thought has influenced humanity as widely and deeply as Marxism. Chai argues that, despite 170 years of slander, attack and banning by the bourgeoisie and reactionary forces, Marxism remains an internationally influential system of thought and discourse. The article presents this as a record of repeated confirmation in practice. The piece is organised in four sections. It begins with how Marxism became the guiding idea of the workers' movement, then turns to the confirmation of its truth in socialist revolution and construction worldwide. A third section deals with the vitality of scientific socialism in China, and a fourth with the continuing need to consult Marxism in solving present-day problems. Chai first traces how Marx and Engels drew the Communist Manifesto from the workers' movement. In this account, the First International and the struggle against Proudhonism, trade unionism and Bakuninism made Marxism the dominant guiding idea, and the Paris Commune enriched its doctrine of proletarian revolution. Lenin's theory of imperialism and of socialism's victory in one country then turned scientific socialism into a real social system through the October Revolution. After 1945 new socialist states and decolonisation followed, with the founding of the People's Republic of China greatly strengthening world socialism. Chai treats socialism with Chinese characteristics as solving a problem earlier socialist practice left unresolved, namely how to build socialism and show its superiority. He cites 40 years of reform and opening up, China's rise to second place in economic output, and a contribution of over 30 per cent to world growth. Chai concludes that Marx's two great discoveries still describe the historical epoch. He points to the 2008 financial crisis, widening inequality and political polarisation in the West, a renewed "Marx fever", and a US poll showing millennials turning towards socialism. Socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era, he says, will advance world socialism and contribute "Chinese wisdom and Chinese solutions". Read the original if you want a concise example of how a 2018 Chinese Party-press article narrates Marxism's global history and links it to China's path.

Sensing the truth-power of Marxism On the documentary film Immortal Marx 感悟马克思主义的真理力量 Wei Haisheng This short commentary, published in Qiushi in 2018, reviews the documentary Immortal Marx, broadcast for the 200th anniversary of Marx's birth. Wei Haisheng presents the film as a union of scientific theory and television art. In Wei's account, it pays tribute to Marx as the greatest thinker of humanity and affirms firm belief in the scientific truth of Marxism. The film was produced by the Central Party History and Literature Research Institute and China Media Group under the guidance of the Central Propaganda Department. Wei describes how it tells the story of Marx's life, opens with Xi Jinping's statement on the unmatched scientific character and influence of Marxism, and concentrates on the writing and content of the Communist Manifesto and Capital. Wei argues that the film weaves historical background, documentary sources and theoretical content into a narrative told through people and events. Viewers, Wei says, come to understand Marx's achievements, his character and the contemporary vitality of his theory, which strengthens confidence in the path, theory, system and culture of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Wei also links the film to Xi Jinping's calls to read the classics and popularise them, and sees it as a first step by the new research institute in that work. Wei concludes that development is the best way to inherit Marxism: it must keep pace with the times, answer the major questions of practice, and be given new contemporary content. Doing so would let Marxism of the twenty-first century keep developing in China. Read the original if you want a brief example of how a Party journal presented a commemorative Marx documentary in 2018 and tied it to the promotion of the classics.

The best way to commemorate Marx Reflections on the original contributions of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era to the development of Marxism 对马克思的最好纪念 Ouyang Song Written for the 200th anniversary of Marx's birth, this Qiushi article asks what it means to commemorate Marx properly. Ouyang answers that the best commemoration is to keep adapting Marxism to China's conditions and to keep making original contributions to its development. The author presents Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era as the current outcome of that effort. The article has three parts. The first sets out the Marxist and Party tradition of keeping pace with the times, from the classic writers through the Party's history from 1921 to the present. The second defines what "originality" means and gives examples of original ideas in Xi Jinping Thought. The third explains why this body of thought emerged and what its status is. Ouyang argues that originality has three marks: newness, truth and "integration" of Marxist principles with Chinese reality. Original results are either statements the founders never made or developments of what they did say, and the author says the second kind is more common. The examples include the judgement that socialism with Chinese characteristics has entered a new era, the new principal contradiction, the Party's historical mission, the two-stage plan to 2050 with basic modernization by 2035, and a community with a shared future for mankind. Each is described as inheriting and developing a specific Marxist or Party theory. Ouyang attributes the thought's emergence to the questions of the era, Marxism as its theoretical source, practice under Party leadership, and Xi's own character, cultural grounding and career experience. Ouyang concludes that Marxism's scientific character, popular character and openness have been demonstrated in China. In this account Xi Jinping Thought is "contemporary Chinese Marxism" and "twenty-first-century Marxism", so upholding it in China amounts to genuinely upholding Marxism. The author calls it a new milestone that is still developing. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the official line in 2018 framed Xi Jinping Thought as an original contribution to Marxism and as the proper way to mark Marx's bicentenary.

The "new era" in the eyes of Marx and Engels 马克思恩格斯眼中的“新时代” Yang Yingjie Yang Yingjie asks what Marx and Engels meant when they used the phrase "new era" (xin shidai), a phrase that gained prominence in Chinese political discourse after the 19th Party Congress (2017). Writing in Hongqi Wengao in 2018, Yang argues that in the classic texts the phrase carries three connected meanings: a leap in productive forces driven by science and technology, the emergence of revolutionary new relations of production, and the prospect of the free and all-round development of the human being. The article is a short exegetical piece organised in three numbered sections, one for each meaning. It gathers passages from Capital, Engels's Dialectics of Nature, his Principles of Communism, the Communist Manifesto and Marx's journalism on the French joint-stock bank Crédit Mobilier. It also draws on Engels's remarks on Dante and on the bourgeoisie and proletariat as children of a new age. In the first section, Yang reads Marx's comment that the self-acting mule opened a new epoch of automatic machinery, and Engels's praise for Dalton's atomic theory and Mendeleev's periodic table, as marking scientific progress that propels productive forces. Engels's account of agriculture flourishing after the abolition of private property is taken as a new era of liberated productive forces. In the second section, Yang follows Marx's claim that the appearance of capital inaugurates a new epoch. This depends on the free worker who owns nothing but labour-power, so that labour-power becomes a commodity and the bourgeoisie and proletariat arise together. Yang adds Marx's view of joint-stock companies as a powerful lever of capitalist productive forces that also concentrate capital and enlarge the proletariat, the bourgeoisie's grave-diggers. In the third section, Yang notes that Engels's "new era" develops in meaning and finally points to the future communist society. In Yang's reading, this is the association in which, as the Manifesto puts it, the free development of each is the condition for the free development of all. There, the old division of labour disappears, classes and wealth gaps are abolished, town and country merge, and the fruits of development are shared. Yang concludes that for Marx and Engels the new era rests on a great liberation of productive forces, transforms the relations of production and the principal contradiction in society, and ends in the free development of all humanity. Read the original if you want a compact guide to the passages in Marx and Engels where "new era" appears, as used in the Chinese discourse of 2018.

A guiding light from victory to victory Commemorating the 170th anniversary of the publication of the Communist Manifesto 从胜利走向胜利的指路明灯 Zhang Quanjing Writing in 2018, the year of the Manifesto's 170th anniversary, Marx's 200th birthday and the 40th anniversary of reform and opening up, Zhang Quanjing argues that rereading the Communist Manifesto helps Party members hold to their original aspiration and mission. In Zhang's view the text remains a practical guide for realising the blueprint set out at the 19th Party Congress (2017). The piece is a commemorative commentary rather than a scholarly study. The article has four parts. It first traces how the Manifesto shaped the Chinese revolution, from Chen Wangdao's 1920 translation and the founding of the Party to Mao Zedong's repeated reading of it and the example of revolutionary martyrs. It then discusses which of the Manifesto's principles endure, turns to the struggle against historical nihilism, and ends with Party building under Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Zhang holds that the Manifesto's basic principles have not become outdated, although some of its specific measures have. Citing Engels's prefaces, Zhang says the principles must be applied according to historical conditions: abandoning them is revisionism, and ignoring concrete circumstances is dogmatism. Zhang defends class analysis and the Manifesto's formula of abolishing private property, understood as the private ownership of the means of production, a process of a very long historical period. Zhang also reads the Manifesto's polemics against feudal and other forms of socialism as a model for criticising historical nihilism, which Zhang accuses of denying the history of the Chinese revolution and its leaders. Zhang concludes that the victory of socialism and communism is certain, as an objective law arising from the contradiction between the productive forces and the relations of production, despite setbacks. Since a revolution needs a revolutionary party, Zhang calls for stronger Party building: upholding the authority of the Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core, studying Xi's thought, tightening discipline, fighting bureaucratism and corruption, and strengthening democratic centralism and grassroots organisations. Read the original if you want an example of how a senior Party veteran in 2018 linked the Manifesto to Party building, the campaign against historical nihilism and loyalty to Xi Jinping Thought.

A true social revolution is necessarily an ideological revolution Commemorating the 170th anniversary of the Communist Manifesto 真正的社会革命必然是意识形态革命 Hou Huiqin Writing for the 170th anniversary of the Communist Manifesto (2018), Hou argues that every genuine social revolution is an ideological revolution. In the author's reading this has two meanings: a shared future ideal must rally the masses behind a banner, a road and an 'ism', and that ideal must rest on a new worldview. Hou holds that the second point most needs attention today, and calls for rereading the Manifesto as a revolution in worldview. The article has three sections. The first presents the Manifesto as announcing a new worldview, setting Engels's 1883 summary of its basic idea beside Lenin's reading of it as dialectical materialism applied. The second defends dialectical materialism against three charges: that it is metaphysical, that it is a detached epistemology, and that it is a partisan philosophy. The third takes the identification of the historical subject as the core of the worldview struggle. Along the way Hou cites Mao Zedong, Xi Jinping, Brzezinski and Fukuyama. Hou contends that the Soviet collapse and the 'end of ideology' thesis led to 'de-ideologizing' Marxist philosophy, which in Hou's view dissolves communism at its root. Dialectical materialism, the author argues, supplies objective truth and laws of history. The proletariat cannot build a moral high ground inside capitalism, so it can only overturn bourgeois morality by taking the 'historical high ground' through scientific theory. Turning socialism into an ethical appeal would lose both heights. Hou then separates two historical subjects: the individual, which belongs to idealist history, and the people, which is the standpoint of materialist history. The author takes Marx's 'real human beings' to be the people, an organic whole with the advanced class at its core, not a sum of individuals. Hou concludes that dialectical materialism is now the focus of the worldview struggle, and that a people-centred view of history versus an individual-centred one is the test of a true or false historical materialism. The author calls for resisting tendencies to drop materialism, de-ideologize, and reduce the people to individuals, in order to advance socialism with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want to see how a leading Chinese Marxist philosopher links the Manifesto, the Soviet collapse and current debates on practice, humanism and 'the people' to a defence of dialectical materialism.

The historical necessity of socialist revolution first breaking out in underdeveloped countries, and confidence in the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics 不发达国家首先发生社会主义革命的历史必然性与中国特色社会主义道路自信 Liu Shulin Liu Shulin takes up a question he regards as foundational for belief in Marxism, for communist ideals and for confidence in the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics: why did socialist revolution first occur in economically underdeveloped countries? He argues that if the question is left unresolved, the legitimacy of existing socialist states, including the Soviet Union, Eastern Europe and China, cannot be defended. His thesis is that such revolutions follow historical necessity and are consistent with Marxism, not departures from it. The article has three parts. The first reconstructs a dispute over Marx's "two inevitables" (the inevitable fall of capitalism and victory of communism) and his "two never wills" in the 1859 Preface. The second reviews how Marx and Engels revised their views on where and when revolution would break out, up to their discussions of Russia. The third turns to Mao Zedong's reading notes on the Soviet political economy textbook and sets out a general law of social development. Liu also cites the 1981 Party resolution on history to defend the socialist transformation of the 1950s. Liu first rejects the view that the "two never wills" overturn the "two inevitables". He argues that Marx's sentence on tasks arising when material conditions exist "or are at least in the process of formation" shows that capitalism need not be fully developed. He reads Engels's late admission that "we were wrong" as concerning tactics, such as barricade fighting, not the basic conditions for revolution. Liu holds that the opposing view implies that no socialist revolution should have happened since 1917, and that it denies the legitimacy of reform-era China's pre-1978 history. Second, drawing on Mao and on Marx and Engels's global view of capitalism, he proposes a law of "alternating leadership". In each transition between social formations, the more developed regions have a hard social shell and tend to resist change, so the breakthrough comes first where the old order is weaker. In Liu's account this explains feudalism in China, capitalism in western Europe, and socialism in Russia and China. Liu concludes that settling this question is not merely academic but concerns the future of socialist states. He holds that the opposing position, which he links to historical nihilism, would require every existing socialist country to return to capitalism. Resolving it in theory and practice, he says, is necessary to sustain confidence in socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era. Read the original if you want to see how a Party-affiliated theorist defends the legitimacy of socialist revolution in backward countries against the argument that Marx's own preconditions rule it out.

The original basic programme of Marxist philosophy A systematic new reading of the Theses on Feuerbach 马克思主义哲学原生态基本纲领 Lu Pinyue Lu Pinyue offers a systematic re-reading of Marx's Theses on Feuerbach, which he treats as containing the basic 'ideological code' of Marxist philosophy. Drawing on Xi Jinping's description of the text as the founding statement of dialectical materialism, Lu argues that its eleven theses form a coherent programme built on two key concepts, practice and social relations. The article also takes a firm stand in a long-running dispute over how the tenth thesis should be read. Lu divides the Theses into three parts. Theses 1–3 make practice the foundation for ontology, epistemology and the conception of history. Theses 4–7 set out the core of historical materialism through the idea that the human essence is the ensemble of social relations. Theses 8–11 state the three essential features of the 'new materialism'. Lu also reads the Theses against Marx's Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 and against Engels's edited version of the text. In Lu's account, old materialism and idealism both misread the subject–object relation, treating it as intuition or theory rather than practice. Grounding it in practice yields a thoroughgoing and dialectical materialism, in which humans are part of nature. It also yields an epistemology in which truth is tested in practice, and a view of history as the practice of the masses. Lu rejects what he calls 'practice ontology', arguing that a material world outside practice is the precondition of practice. The Theses, he says, also amount to Marx's self-criticism of the Manuscripts' abstract 'species essence'. On the tenth thesis, Lu argues that 'civil society' means the abstract aggregate of isolated individuals found in Enlightenment thought and Hegel, not capitalist society as such. He holds that 'human society' means actual society, past and present, not a future communist society. In his view the latter reading would make Marx a utopian and bring back Feuerbach's abstract human nature. Lu concludes that the Theses identify three unified features of the new materialism. It dispels mysticism through seeking truth from facts, it takes real human society built on social relations as its standpoint, and it takes changing the world as its task. Lu links the first feature to Deng Xiaoping's remark that seeking truth from facts is the essence of Marxism. Lu suggests that the setbacks of socialism are partly tied to utopian readings of Marx. Read the original if you want a detailed, Xi Jinping-endorsed reading of the Theses on Feuerbach, especially the argument over 'civil society' and 'human society' in the tenth thesis.

The Chinese people are a people with a great spirit of dreaming 中国人民是具有伟大梦想精神的人民 Sun Laibin Taking up Xi Jinping's statement that the Chinese people are a people with a great spirit of dreaming, Sun Laibin argues in this short commentary (published in Qiushi in 2018) that this spirit is embedded in the Chinese nation's cultural lineage. Sun contends that, if it is kept alive, it will carry the country to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The piece has three parts. The first treats the dreaming spirit as a cultural gene, the second as the support that sustained the nation through modern hardship, and the third as the driving force for what Sun calls the Long March of the new era. Sun reads ancient myths such as Pangu, Kua Fu chasing the sun, Jingwei filling the sea and the Foolish Old Man moving mountains as expressions of a persistent will to realise dreams. Sun links them to modern achievements, including the Shenzhou and Tiangong space programmes, the South-to-North Water Diversion project and the Jiaolong deep-sea submersible. After the Opium War, Sun says, the nation did not lose its confidence but pursued the dream of rejuvenation for over 170 years. The Chinese Dream, in this account, joins family and country sentiment and is described as a dream of peace, development, cooperation and mutual benefit. Sun concludes that, with socialism with Chinese characteristics in a new era, the Chinese people are closer than ever to rejuvenation, but the final stretch is hard. Sun calls for the spirit to be sustained through great struggle, hard work and a "nail-driving" perseverance, in order to finish building a moderately prosperous society and begin building a modern socialist country. Read the original if you want a compact example of how official Party commentary of 2018 tied national myth and history to the Chinese Dream.

The Chinese people are a people with a great spirit of creativity 中国人民是具有伟大创造精神的人民 Xin Ming Xin Ming's commentary in Qiushi (2018) argues that the spirit of innovation is the most distinctive endowment of the Chinese nation. In the author's account, this creative spirit has kept a civilisation of more than 5,000 years vital, brought the nation back from modern-era suffering to the threshold of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, and now carries China towards a moderately prosperous society and a new journey of building a modern socialist country. The piece moves through three periods: past civilisation, present achievements and future contribution. It cites classical thinkers, inventions, great works of engineering, literature and epics, then post-1978 growth figures and technological projects, and finally China's prospective role in global affairs. Xin contends that the Chinese people created the country's splendid civilisation, and are now creating a magnificent reality. The article cites GDP of 82.7 trillion yuan, average growth above 8.5% over 40 years of reform and opening up, and scientific projects since the 18th Party Congress (2012). It holds that socialism with Chinese characteristics is the people's own invention under Party leadership, not a copy of any earlier template. It also points to everyday innovations such as high-speed rail, e-commerce and shared bicycles. Xin concludes that the Chinese people will create a bright future, offering a "Chinese solution" and "alternative" path to modernization for other countries, achieved peacefully rather than through colonial expansion. Ideas such as a community with a shared future for mankind and the Belt and Road Initiative are presented as a new worldview, alongside traditional concepts like "harmony in diversity". Read the original if you want a compact example of how Qiushi framed national creativity and China's global contribution in 2018.

Ideological security education in universities in the age of the mobile internet 移动互联网时代高校意识形态安全教育研究 Zheng Jie Xu Qiang Zheng Jie and Xu Qiang ask how Chinese universities should carry out ideological security education now that, in the authors' words, the mobile internet has become the main battlefield of ideological struggle. Writing after the 19th Party Congress (2017), they argue that universities must treat this education as a major strategic task. Its aim is to win over young students and safeguard national ideological security, and the authors say it needs updated concepts, methods and mechanisms. The article was published in Academic Forum in 2017. It has four parts: the practical reasons for strengthening this education, the opportunities the mobile internet offers, the challenges it poses, and a set of countermeasures. Throughout, the authors rely heavily on quotations from Xi Jinping and the 19th Party Congress report to frame the discussion. The authors give four reasons for the education. It is a means of countering what they describe as Western ideological infiltration aimed at students. It ensures that students become qualified successors to the socialist cause. It serves the construction of a harmonious campus, and it supports students' healthy, all-round development. They then argue that mobile media strengthen students' role as active participants, extend education beyond classroom and campus, make it more effective than one-way "inculcation", and let schools, families and society work together. The challenges they list are outdated ideas and monotonous methods among some teachers, low media literacy, a complicated online environment, and weak oversight mechanisms. For the response, Zheng and Xu propose the principle of "teacher-led, student-centred" education. They also call for classroom teaching as the main channel, campus culture and student societies as new fronts, and better media training for teachers and students. Government, universities and new media should work together, and universities should set up information-review bodies. They further propose that universities build coordinated management, evaluation, reward-and-accountability, monitoring and feedback mechanisms, and bring the spirit of the 19th Party Congress into textbooks, classrooms and minds. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how Chinese academic writing in 2017 framed ideological work in universities, and which practical measures it recommended.

Guiding the development of economic globalization with the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind 以人类命运共同体理念引领经济全球化发展 Zhao Kejin Writing in Qiushi in 2018, Zhao Kejin asks how economic globalization, whose drawbacks have become more visible since the start of the century, should be understood and steered. The short commentary argues that the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind, presented as China's proposal, can lead globalization in a more open, inclusive, balanced and win-win direction. The piece opens by citing the 19th Party Congress (2017) report. It then moves through four steps: the irreversibility of globalization, the need for a new guiding idea, the theoretical content of the community idea, and three practical requirements. Zhao holds that globalization follows from the development of productive forces and technological progress, and has bound national interests together. It is also a "double-edged sword": its problems are global and cannot be solved by one country. Western solutions, whether the neoliberal "Washington Consensus" or the "anti-globalization" current since the financial crisis, are said to serve capital while ignoring workers worldwide and the claims of developing countries. The community idea, in Zhao's account, replaces zero-sum thinking with win-win cooperation and promotes consultation, joint contribution and shared benefits. It requires common development for developing and developed countries, social justice, and sustainable, green development. Zhao concludes that globalization guided by this idea goes beyond the Western-led globalization of the modern era. It is also described as a remedy for protectionism and populism, bringing innovation in path, theory and institutions toward a more prosperous and harmonious world. Read the original if you want a concise, official-style statement of how the community idea was presented in 2018 as an answer to globalization's problems.

The distinctive features of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想的鲜明特质 Xia Jinwen Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2018, Xia Jinwen asks what characterises Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Xia argues that the Thought sets out the theoretical and practical logic of Marxism and serves as a manifesto and a call to action for socialism with Chinese characteristics in a new era. Four distinctive features are identified. The short commentary takes each feature in turn: the Thought's roots in its historical moment, its source in practice, its innovative character and its orientation towards the people. It draws on Xi Jinping's statements and on the report to the 19th Party Congress (2017). On the first feature, Xia says the Thought was produced by the needs of the age. Xia points to changes in the Party's situation, including the "four tests" and "four risks", and in the national situation, where the two centenary goals meet, and in the world situation, described as one of great change. On the second, Xia holds that the Thought was neither devised in the study nor deduced from abstract concepts. It is drawn from practice since the 18th Party Congress (2012) and, in Xia's view, has been tested by results. Xia also presents it as innovative and open, continuing to develop with practice. On the fourth, Xia argues that the people-centred outlook runs through the 19th Party Congress report: development, democracy, the principal contradiction, common prosperity, people's livelihood and Party building. Xia concludes that the Thought is the latest achievement in adapting Marxism to Chinese conditions and a source of strength for the new journey. Xia presents its people-centred orientation as an inheritance of the historical-materialist view that the people make history, and as already put into practice over the previous five years. Read the original if you want a concise, official-style statement of how Party theorists in 2018 characterised the Thought.

The freedom enslaved by neo-imperialism: a critique of neoliberalism With a critique of Hayek's The Road to Serfdom 新帝国主义奴役的自由：评新自由主义 Yu Bin Yu Bin's article, first published in the Journal of Hebei University of Economics and Business in 2017, offers a Marxist critique of neoliberalism. It argues that neoliberalism, including as set out in Hayek's The Road to Serfdom, stands for the freedom to exploit and enslave workers and serves as a policy and hegemonic tool of what the author calls neo-imperialism. The text has three parts. The first takes up a professor's "steamed bun" parable about supply-side reform and reads it as an attempt to steer China's reform towards tax and fee cuts in the neoliberal supply-side tradition. The second examines Hayek's book and the position of workers under state capitalism and neoliberal capitalism. The third examines how neoliberal doctrine on markets, trade, globalisation and international institutions benefits neo-imperialist states. Yu holds that the parable misdiagnoses the problem. Goods that are too dear to sell, in Yu's view, are not overcapacity, and tax cuts would not lower prices much or help the poor who buy cheap steamed buns. Yu also argues that China's reform is supply-side structural reform, which adjusts structure and relies on innovation, not tax-cutting. On Hayek, Yu argues that the "socialism" he attacks is Nazi state socialism and Second International revisionism, which Yu treats as forms of state capitalism and not Marxist scientific socialism. Yu reads his passages on unemployment, minimum wages and postwar austerity as defending the exploitation of workers. Yu also rejects the supposed "iron law" that wages must grow more slower than productivity, using a numerical example to argue that the law holds only where there is no surplus-value exploitation. Yu contends that neoliberalism rose together with neo-imperialism in the 1970s, as Keynesian state intervention obstructed the plunder of other countries' resources. Equal opportunity, free trade, privatisation and international organisations such as the IMF, the World Bank and the WTO are described as instruments that open developing countries to transnational capital. Yu cites Latin America under the Washington Consensus, and criticises the privatisation of Chinese state enterprises and utilities as a departure from the principle of unwaveringly consolidating and developing the public sector. Read the original if you want an example of how a Chinese Marxist economist in 2017 linked the domestic supply-side reform debate to a critique of Hayek and neoliberal globalisation.

Upholding Marxist atheism as a major principle 坚持马克思主义无神论是大原则 Wang Weiguang Wang Weiguang argues that upholding Marxist atheism is a major principle (da yuanze) for the Chinese Communist Party and for China as a socialist state. The article takes its starting point from Xi Jinping's statement at the National Conference on Religious Work in April 2016 that "upholding Marxist atheism is a major principle". Wang holds that this principle applies to legislation, administration and the judiciary, and to the economic, political, social, cultural and ecological fields alike. The article has four sections. The first explains why the principle must be upheld, drawing on Marx's critique of religion. The second addresses Communist Party members as firm Marxist atheists. The third concerns the duty to propagate atheism among the masses, and the fourth sets out six points that Wang draws from Xi Jinping's statements on atheism since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Wang supports the argument with quotations from Marx, Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin and Hu Jintao, and with Party documents from 1982, 2004 and 2016. Wang's central reasoning is that atheism is the starting point of Marxism, because the critique of religion leads into the critique of society and politics. In this reading, Marxist atheism is the most thorough materialism, and a person who does not uphold it is not a true Marxist. From this Wang derives a discipline for Party members: they may not believe in religion or take part in religious activities, because religion would weaken the Party's worldview, its ideals and its purity. Wang also warns that religious fervour threatens mainstream ideology and the Party's ruling position, and that atheism must remain dominant in the people's thinking. At the same time, Wang insists that propaganda should unite believers and non-believers politically, avoid hurting religious feelings, and focus on young people. Wang concludes that Xi Jinping's statements on atheism are the latest result of adapting Marxist atheism to the Chinese context and a fundamental guide for the field. Wang calls for atheist propaganda to be reconciled with the policy of freedom of religious belief, for stronger atheist propaganda work, and for greater attention to the discipline and theoretical study of Marxist atheism. Read the original if you want to see how a senior Party theorist set out, in 2017, the official case for atheism as Party discipline and ideological work, with a chronology of leaders' statements on the subject.

Characteristics, development trends and impact of party politics in Nepal 尼泊尔政党政治的特点、发展趋势及其影响 Yuan Qun Writing in 2018, shortly after the November–December 2017 elections in Nepal, Yuan Qun asks how Nepal's party politics has developed since the 1940s and where it is heading. The article argues that the parties have grown from an illegal movement against feudal autocracy into the dominant political force, and that a left alliance of the two main communist parties is now set to reshape the country's politics and its relations with India and China. The article first sets out the four stages of party politics: the overthrow of Rana rule and the founding of a constitutional monarchy, the struggle against the partyless panchayat system, the restoration of multiparty parliamentary government, and the move to a republic. It then identifies three features of the party system, three current trends, and three consequences of those trends. Its material is mainly the histories of the Nepali Congress, the communist parties and the Madhesi parties. On features, Yuan stresses frequent splits and mergers, as parties that entered parliament put pragmatic pursuit of power ahead of ideals and become factional "election parties". A "three-legged" structure has also formed: the Nepali Congress, the CPN (UML) and the Maoists, each with about 300,000 members, favoured by a mixed electoral system, with Madhesi parties in fourth place. On trends, Yuan contends that India, which the author says treats Nepal's communists as close to China, will intensify interference through Congress, Madhesi parties and the 2015–16 blockade. The communists are expected to consolidate, with a merger likely because the dispute over the revolutionary road has ended. Anti-Indian nationalism is also expected to rise, while Congress under Deuba is described as tilting towards India. As consequences, Yuan predicts that the Nepali communist movement will enter a new, higher stage. The author also expects the left alliance government to bring much greater stability, citing ten prime ministers in nine years and a constitutional two-year bar on no-confidence motions. In foreign policy it is expected to keep Nepal's traditional "equidistance" balance, avoiding a break with India while deepening practical cooperation with China to gain room for manoeuvre. Read the original if you want a China-based scholar's 2018 reading of Nepal's party system, its communist factions and India–China rivalry, with detailed chronologies of party splits and mergers.

Why has China always managed to turn the tide in every major crisis? An excerpt from "People's Open Class" 中国为何每次逢大危机总能力挽狂澜？ Wen Tiejun This is a book excerpt (from People's Open Class, Zhejiang People's Publishing House), republished via Liaowang Institute and Utopia, in which Wen Tiejun asks why China has survived each major crisis since the late Qing. Wen argues that, once ideological labels are set aside, the record shows a repeated pattern: foreign capital brought in to industrialise a capital-starved country produced debt or dependence and then crisis, and the crisis was absorbed by shifting its costs onto the countryside. The article moves from the present back to the Qing and forward again. It first describes the shift from a century of shortage to what Wen calls three overlapping surpluses (industrial, financial, commercial). It then covers the Self-Strengthening Movement, the Republic's 'golden decade' and silver crisis, the early People's Republic, the Soviet-aided period, the Great Leap Forward, the Cultural Revolution and the Fourth and Fifth Five-Year Plans. It closes by comparing China's costs with the debt crises of the United States and the eurozone. Wen's central claim is that policy orientation follows material conditions rather than ideology. When capital is extremely scarce, any government must be pro-capital, and revolutionary ideology and collectivised labour served as a substitute for capital (labour replacing capital). Wen counts four waves of foreign capital since 1950, each followed by two crises (for example the Soviet investment, then the crises of 1960 and 1968). Wen holds that crises were softened where the cost could be passed to the 'three rural issues': about 40 million educated youths sent to the countryside were absorbed because collectives existed, and land distribution, the author says, kept 85 per cent of the population relatively insulated from monetary turmoil. Wen also reads the Republic's fall as a financial collapse and the Korean War as bringing military industry and Soviet alignment. Wen concludes that China's path was workable and that the country, now in surplus, can invest in people's livelihood and sustainable development. Western-style institutions are presented as costly, debt-driven superstructures that even the West can no longer sustain, citing US and eurozone debt. Wen urges younger Chinese to free themselves from ideologised vocabularies, whether anti-Mao or Westward-looking. Read the original if you want a heterodox political-economy narrative of a century of Chinese crises, which draws on the author's own rural experience and defends the revolutionary era on grounds of capital accumulation.

The foundation of state coercive capacity is violence, but it is also a necessary condition for reducing violence A preface to Fan Peng's study of China's public security and police system 国家强制能力的基础是暴力，但它也是减少暴力的必要条件 Wang Shaoguang This text, dated July 2017 and circulated in November 2017 via the website Wuyouzhixiang, reads as a preface to Fan Peng's book on China's public security and police system. Wang Shaoguang argues that state coercive capacity, which rests on violence or the threat of it, is also a necessary condition for reducing violence. Wang adds that China has built this capacity in its own way, not along the single Western path. Wang begins with the shift in political science from regime form and democratization towards state capacity. In this shift, Wang says, coercive capacity has been neglected. The text then surveys the history of violence through archaeology, ancient texts, Engels's Anti-Dühring, and work by Fukuyama, Morris, Scheidel and Pinker. It turns to Fan's evidence on policing, crime and homicide in China, and ends with Fan's closing questions about what coercive capacity really means. Wang holds that violence is a core, universal feature of human society and should be analysed, not only condemned. Citing Engels, Arendt and others, Wang says violence has also driven institutional change, growth and, historically, lower inequality. Its greatest positive effect, Wang argues, is reducing violence: war produced ever larger political units and states, and states that monopolise legitimate force lower war deaths and homicide rates. Wang then takes up Pinker's reading of China as a 'police state'.
