Drawing on Fan's data, Wang says China has a very low police-to-population ratio, tight police funding and a homicide rate of 0.7 per 100,000 in 2015, among the lowest in the world. Wang concludes that capacity should be measured by outputs, not inputs. Wang presents Fan's central point as follows. China's state monopolises legitimate force but uses it sparingly and seeks to reduce and defuse conflict, in imperial, revolutionary, Maoist and reform-era periods alike. In Wang's account, this reflects a governing tradition from Confucius's 'nurture, teach, govern' to the Communist Party's people-centred approach of 'embedding security in service', which mobilises officials, Party organisations and society. Wang rejects the assumption of one universal, linear path to a modern state. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's argument that Western accounts of coercion misread China, or if you want the crime and homicide data Wang draws on from Fan's book.

China can neither plunder abroad nor pursue internal colonisation: it must build more equal urban–rural relations Zhao Yuezhi on "the countryside as method" 中国既不能对外掠夺，也不能走内部殖民的路径，必须构建更平等的城乡关系 Zhao Yuezhi This is a written report, reviewed by the speaker, of a keynote lecture given by Zhao Yuezhi on 2 July 2017 at the international summer school "From the Global to the Village: The Countryside as Method" in Jinyun County, Zhejiang. Zhao presents "the countryside as method" as a theoretical and practical approach, and argues that China, having been shaped by revolution and reform, faces a crossroads for its villages. In Zhao's view, China can neither plunder other countries nor colonise its own countryside, and so must build more equal urban–rural relations. The talk has five parts: the origins of the question, drawing on three photographs Zhao took; the theoretical resources; the meanings of the approach; its methodology and practice; and its historical and present significance. Zhao draws on Mitsuhiro Mizoguchi's China as Method, Chen Kuan-Hsing's Asia as Method, C. Wright Mills's The Sociological Imagination, and the work of Canadian Indigenous scholars. The photographs show a Jinyun woman arriving at Shanghai station, an elderly villager doing outsourced plastics work for export, and a lone woman harvesting rice in a hollowed-out village. Zhao's central move is to treat colonial relations as seen by Indigenous theorists as important as capital–labour relations, and to extend this to the urban–rural relationship. She argues that the industrialisation and urban growth of China rest on unequal exchange with, and great sacrifices by, peasants, and that Anglo-American capitalism rose on the massacre of Indigenous peoples and plunder of colonies. She distinguishes five senses of the term: rural as the counterpart of the city; the village as an intimate community; the organic diversity of villages; the subjectivity of the "three rural issues" (peasants, villages, agriculture); and the countryside as a "source of hope" for humanity amid capitalist crisis. She joins this to a framework of political economy of intercultural communication, ethnography and action research. Zhao names three paths for the countryside: a populist rural reconstruction that avoids socialism, the view that 21st-century enclosure is inevitable (in which she sees neoliberals and Trotskyists converging), or reorganisation along socialist lines. She claims the approach explains the Chinese revolution, speaks to a world where peasants remain a major force, and carries anti-imperialist and anti-capitalist values, without implying a return to the pre-modern or to nativism. Read the original if you want a concise statement of a socialist, critical-communication scholar's case for rural China as a theoretical standpoint and for a 2017 debate on rural reconstruction.

Theories of "civilization" and China in the twenty-first century “文明”论与21世纪中国 He Guimei He Guimei asks how Chinese intellectuals have come to interpret "China" through the category of "civilization", and argues that since the turn of the century this has become a paradigm-level shift. It has displaced earlier accounts based on the nation-state, modernization theory and the Cold War opposition of socialism and capitalism. The article, first drafted in 2013 and finalised in 2017, seeks to trace the lineage of these civilization theories and to set out their limits. It then proposes a "plural" conception of civilization as a critical alternative. The article has four parts. It begins with the rise of the "civilization-state" idea, from Samuel Huntington's clash of civilizations through Martin Jacques and Zhang Weiwei to Gan Yang's "civilization-state" and "unifying the three traditions", and Pan Wei's "China model". It then examines how Fei Xiaotong, Wang Mingming and Wang Hui define civilization and its relation to China. A third part considers the "traditional culture fever" and the contemporary meaning of tradition. The last part reconstructs the intellectual history of the concept of civilization. He's central move is to distinguish three conceptions: a universalist one tied to Enlightenment ideas of progress and colonial hierarchy, a nationalist one that equates civilization with culture, and a plural one that treats civilizations as overlapping social-cultural-economic totalities. The author argues that many Chinese civilization-state accounts leave "civilization" vaguely defined, often equating it with Confucian tradition, and risk sliding into nation-statism. In this reading, tradition revival is often absorbed into nationalist ideology, which the author sees as a by-product of globalization. Drawing on Marcel Mauss, Fernand Braudel and Wang Mingming's work, He holds that the plural view breaks with both Eurocentrism and nationalism, and that Huntington's version lost the critical edge of 1960s civilizational history. He concludes that a plural conception clarifies three relations: it moves beyond both statism and cosmopolitan universalism, beyond both revivalism and modern-centrism, and it treats civilization as a non-uniform totality rather than a homogeneous whole. Traditional China can then serve as a critical resource, without implying a return to empire, for rebuilding China's subjectivity in the global order and escaping "China-centrism". Read the original if you want a detailed intellectual map of Chinese "civilization" discourse, with extensive references to Gan Yang, Wang Hui and Wang Mingming, and a critique of its nationalist tendencies.

A critical assessment of several current erroneous views 对当前几种错误观点的评析 Mei Rongzheng Writing in Red Flag Manuscript in 2015, Mei Rongzheng takes up the ideological sphere since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Mei describes its overall trend as positive and healthy, but argues that struggle remains complex and that certain erroneous views interfering with the guiding ideology of the Party and state deserve particular attention. The article assesses four such views and argues that each distorts or displaces Marxism. The piece is a polemical commentary in four numbered sections. It deals with the claim that Soviet Marxism is not Marxism; three Confucianism-related positions (using Confucianism against, to transform, or to dilute Marxism); the use of Western Marxism to reinterpret Marxism; and the allegation that Marxists are mislabelled as non-Marxists and vice versa. It closes by citing Deng Xiaoping's 1983 call for Marxists to speak out. On the first view, Mei says it recasts the Soviet model as 'Soviet Marxism' and so implies that the Party was never truly Marxist. Mei distinguishes universal from non-universal elements of the Soviet experience and holds that the universal ones were the origin of the Four Cardinal Principles. On Confucianism, Mei rejects the label of historical nihilism for the New Culture Movement's critique of Confucian doctrine. Citing Li Dazhao and Liu Danian, Mei describes Confucianism as the product of a small-peasant economy, lacking materialism and economics, and argues that China's strongest eras were not Confucian ones. Mei still allows that Confucianism has historical value and calls for its creative transformation. On the fourth view, Mei holds that a society's character is set by the dominant form of ownership of the means of production. Mei therefore treats the 'functional socialism' thesis, which allows private ownership to count as socialist, as in effect democratic socialism and contrary to the Constitution. Mei contends that these views, including those that claim to be Marxist, threaten identification with the Party's guiding ideology, and warns that Western Marxism has weakened the teaching of the classics in some university programmes. The author calls on Marxist scholars to take a clear stand, as Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping have urged. Read the original if you want to see how a Party-aligned scholar framed ideological struggle over Soviet Marxism, Confucian revival and Western Marxism in 2015.

Adorno and post-Marxism: the historical echoes of negative dialectics 阿多诺与后马克思主义:否定的辩证法之历史回响 Li Xixiang Studies of Theodor Adorno, Li Xixiang observes, tend to read him on his own terms and neglect his influence on later thought. Li argues that Negative Dialectics marks a decisive turning point in the history of Western Marxism: it is an important source of postmodern thought and an intellectual resource for many post-Marxist thinkers. The article, published in 2017, has three main parts and a short conclusion. It first reconstructs Adorno's negative dialectics and philosophy of non-identity, including his critique of Hegel and Heidegger. It then relates Adorno to postmodernism, using the psychoanalytic notion of the symptom. Finally it turns to Adorno's engagement with Freud, as read by Slavoj Žižek in The Metastases of Enjoyment, and to the later reception of psychoanalysis in post-Marxism. Li reads negative dialectics as Adorno's whole philosophy: dialectics is consciousness of non-identity, and the object is never fully absorbed by the concept. Li argues that this gives Adorno's thought a materialist root in the priority of the object over the subject, and that it opposes systems, ontology and metaphysics, with Heidegger's ontology seen as still bound to identity. Postmodernity, Li proposes, relates to modernity as a Lacanian sinthome (the irreducible symptom), 'in you more than you': non-identity is an internal, constitutive exterior of identity, and Adorno's negation does not resolve into a new affirmation. Following Žižek, Li presents Adorno's 'repressive desublimation' as a critique of mass psychology under totalitarianism, but one that stops short of the superego dimension. Lacan, in this reading, is Adorno's hidden heir, while Habermas dissolves the tension. Li concludes that Lacanian psychoanalysis is not remote from Marxism but secretly linked to it. It has shaped Derrida, Foucault, Baudrillard, Laclau, Mouffe, Žižek and Butler, and Li says it has become a main tool for 'rewriting' Marxism and restoring its vitality. Li presents the meeting of psychoanalysis and Marxism as a result of the internal logic of theory and of reflection on the setbacks of the world communist movement, and as a major open theoretical task. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's account of how Adorno, Lacan, Žižek and post-Marxism connect, especially the symptom analogy for postmodernity and modernity.

Overseas scholarship reassesses Marx 国外学界重新认识马克思 Feng Yanli Writing in People's Daily ahead of the 200th anniversary of Marx's birth (5 May 2018), Feng Yanli examines the "Marx fever" that has appeared in foreign academia since the 2008 international financial crisis. Feng argues that this renewed interest is no passing fashion and that studying it should deepen Marxist belief and strengthen the Four-sphere Confidence. The commentary is organised in three parts: how the "Marx fever" arose, evidence of Marx's growing influence, and the relevance of Marxism to present-day problems. It draws on remarks by foreign scholars including Jonathan Sperber, Jacques Derrida, Anthony Giddens, Thomas Piketty and Wolfram Adolphi. Feng contrasts the present "return to Marx" with the post-Cold War mood of "farewell to Marx" after the upheavals in the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe. In Feng's account, the crisis exposed capitalism's inherent contradictions, such as inequality and unlimited capital expansion, and prompted a change of attitude. As evidence, Feng cites the Communist Manifesto as required reading at Columbia and Oxford, work on the historical-critical edition of the Marx-Engels works, and rankings naming Marx the most influential thinker. Feng holds that Marxism keeps its vitality because it explains general laws of development and aims to change the world, and notes that more scholars are turning back to Marxist political economy to examine capitalism's flaws. Feng concludes that China's practice in the new era demonstrates the truth of Marxism. Under Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, Feng expects China to advance further and offer more "Chinese wisdom" and "Chinese solutions" to global problems. Read the original if you want an example of how Chinese official commentary in 2018 used foreign scholars' remarks to support the continuing relevance of Marx.

A beacon lighting the way forward for human history Communist parties around the world mark the 200th anniversary of Marx's birth and the 170th anniversary of the Communist Manifesto 照亮人类历史前进方向的灯塔 Yu Haiqing Writing in 2018, the 200th anniversary of Marx's birth and the 170th of the Communist Manifesto, Yu Haiqing surveys how communist parties abroad have commemorated both. The article is a report-style commentary rather than a theoretical study. Yu argues that these parties stress the Manifesto's historical and theoretical contribution, its value as a method for analysing present-day capitalism, and its guidance for reviving the world socialist movement from its low point. The article is organised in three parts. The first lists commemorative events in early 2018: quizzes and film reviews by the US party, a forum in Paris attended by over 2,000 people, a Lisbon congress of the Portuguese party, an international seminar in Hanoi, and a roundtable in Cuba. It then summarises how the American, Ukrainian, British, Spanish, Brazilian, Portuguese and Cypriot parties assess the Manifesto. The second part examines its contemporary relevance, and the third its guidance for socialist construction and movement strategy. On relevance, Yu reports that foreign parties see the Manifesto's claims as still valid. They cite bourgeois domination of the state, capital's constant expansion (the Russian party's account of post-Soviet de-industrialisation and dependence), extreme wealth concentration (the Belgian and Chilean parties), and periodic crises rooted in the contradiction between productive forces and relations of production. The Spanish party likens the Manifesto to an "X-ray" of capitalism. On strategy, Yu summarises four themes from these parties: upholding the communists' historical mission as the working class's vanguard; building alliances with intermediate strata; uniting the left while avoiding sectarianism; and rejecting dogmatism, since there is no single road to socialism. Yu concludes that the Manifesto and Marxism remain a "key" to understanding capitalism's essence and trends, and that Vietnamese and Laotian leaders credit them with guiding socialist construction in their countries. Yu presents the foreign parties' view that Marxism must be developed critically in light of changing conditions, not treated as a sacred formula. Read the original if you want a compact overview, from a Chinese academic viewpoint, of how a range of communist parties marked the 2018 anniversaries and what positions they took.

Why Western left-wing currents of thought have stalled 西方左翼思潮为何陷入停滞 Chen Jiangsheng Writing in 2018, Chen Jiangsheng asks why Western left-wing thought, which revived after the 2008 financial crisis, now appears to be stagnating. The article argues that uncertainty and stalled development are now the dominant condition of the Western left. It attributes this to three causes: the unclear course of Western economies and societies, a rethinking of the left's rapid earlier rise, and the lack of an effective guiding ideology. The piece first describes the post-2008 revival, then surveys new trends since 2016 in the United States, Britain, Germany and France. For the revival, Chen cites Chris Harman's Zombie Capitalism (2009), Andrew Kliman's book on the capitalist crisis (2012) and Thomas Piketty's Capital in the Twenty-First Century. The article also links the left's growth to opposition to globalisation and to shifts in national politics, such as the return of the left to power in France. Chen reads the country cases as signs of retreat or confusion. In the United States, the defeat of Sanders and the election of Trump show that society did not endorse the left's rise, though Chen adds that the problems the left exposes persist, so the ebb may be temporary. In Britain, the Brexit vote looked like 'left-wing people doing right-wing work'. In Germany, Merkel's failure to form a coalition over refugee policy showed an irreconcilable left–right split alongside a rising far right. In France, Macron's victory is only a limited gain for the left, and Chen doubts how far left he really is. Chen explains the stall in materialist terms: social being determines social consciousness, and the West faces internal stagnation and external competition from new theories and paths in the East, for which it has no agreed response. The left's rapid rise rested on discontent with the crisis, so disappointment with its results prompted rethinking. Chen concludes that Western left-wing thought, though it partly inherits Marxist ideas, is not guided by Marxism, criticises capitalism incompletely and cannot solve fundamental problems within the old framework. In Chen's view it will therefore only rise and fall in waves with popular discontent. Read the original if you want a Chinese Party-school view of the post-2008 Western left and its country-by-country prospects as of 2018.

Green capitalism runs into difficulties 绿色资本主义发展遭遇困境 Zhuang Guiyang Writing in 2018, Zhuang Guiyang asks whether 'green capitalism', the attempt to make capitalism sustainable through a green transition, can deliver on its promise. The article argues that it cannot: a capitalist system without moral guidance has left what was once an attractive project stuck in difficulties, and the limits of green self-adjustment under capitalism are plain in the politics of climate action. The piece opens with the idea of green capitalism as presented in Paul Hawken and colleagues' 2000 book and with the case its supporters make, citing renewable energy investment figures for 2015 and 2017. It then sets out critics' objections, including the work of the British author Richard Smith. A central section treats the United States' announced withdrawal from the Paris Agreement in June 2017 as the latest illustration. The final section turns to cities and sub-national actors, such as city alliances and American states, that have kept up climate action. Zhuang reports that supporters see the green economy as a natural evolution of capitalism, whose reward for scarcity and efficiency suits green growth. Critics, in Zhuang's account, say these supporters overestimate green production and underestimate the scale of ecological crisis, and that carbon or energy taxes cannot remove market externalities. For Zhuang, the contradiction between capital's expansion and finite natural resources is hard to overcome. Capitalist politics, shaped by voters and interest groups, tolerates only limited green repair. Trump's 'America first' withdrawal, European disagreements and rich countries' reluctance to meet the 100 billion dollar climate finance pledge are offered as evidence. Zhuang then notes that city networks such as the Global Covenant of Mayors for Climate and Energy, the 'We Are Still In' delegation at Bonn and the US Climate Alliance partly bridge the gap left by states. Zhuang concludes that technology cannot save the world under the current system, and that countries must urgently build a development paradigm that goes beyond industrial civilisation. City alliances, being bottom-up and voluntary, cannot replace states under the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, so the future remains uncertain. Read the original if you want an example of how a Chinese social-science commentary of 2018 used the Paris withdrawal to argue against the viability of green capitalism.

Adaptive change and political direction of Europe's radical left parties 欧洲激进左翼政党的适应性变革与政治走向 Wang Congcong How have Europe's radical left parties adapted since the collapse of the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe, and where are they heading? Writing in 2017, Wang Congcong argues that parties which updated their ideology and organisation to national conditions have fared best, while electoral results depend on many factors besides ideological renewal. The article sets this against the background of a prolonged crisis in European social democracy. The article first defines radical left parties, following Luke March and others, as parties to the left of social democrats and Greens that oppose the basic structure of contemporary capitalism. It reviews typologies by Uwe Backes and Patrick Moreau and by March, and proposes four groups: traditional communist parties, successor parties, new left alliances, and "red-green" parties. It then compares adaptation among traditional parties and "new left" parties, and ends with a survey of electoral trends since the 1990s. Wang argues that traditional parties such as the Greek and Portuguese communist parties kept the communist name, Marxism-Leninism and, in varying degrees, democratic centralism, with only small organisational changes. The French party abandoned democratic centralism in 1994, and the Italian Refoundation party also democratised. "New left" parties dropped the communist label and democratic centralism, opened their structures, set term limits and gender quotas, and cooperated at EU level through the European United Left–Nordic Green Left group and the Party of the European Left (2004). Ideologically they turned to democratic socialism or eco-socialism, absorbing environmentalist and feminist themes, and revised their electoral strategies and attitude to government participation. The author sees national party systems, the strength of social democrats and Greens, and party leaderships as shaping which path is possible. Wang concludes that the link between renewal and votes is complex. Nordic parties and several Western European ones, such as the German Left Party and the Greek Syriza (which formed a government in 2015), have gained ground. Some traditionalist communist parties have kept stable support, while the French and Italian parties have declined. Wang judges that most radical left parties are unlikely to overtake social democrats in the short term, citing fragmentation at European level and weak, untested policy programmes at home. Their future depends mainly on credible, forward-looking policies. Read the original if you want a structured comparison of how European communist and post-communist parties changed after 1989, including electoral data.

The evolution of British Marxist theories of the subject since the 1950s 20世纪50年代以来英国马克思主义的主体理论流变 Xue Ji After the Second World War, the British working class, in the article's account, became weak in class consciousness and even felt a 'cultural classlessness'. Xue asks whether this class can still carry out its historical mission of overthrowing capitalism, and argues that British Marxists answered through three successive but coexisting theories of the revolutionary subject: the experiential subject, the constructed subject and the plural subject. The article is a theoretical-historical survey of British Marxism from the 1950s onwards. It takes the culturalism of E. P. Thompson, Richard Hoggart and Raymond Williams first. It then covers the structuralism of Perry Anderson, Tom Nairn, Terry Eagleton and Stuart Hall, and finally the post-structuralist and post-Marxist plural-subject theory of the 1980s, drawing especially on Laclau and Mouffe's Hegemony and Socialist Strategy. Xue's central move is to show how each school answers one question: can workers' spontaneous experience grow into socialist revolutionary consciousness? Culturalists say yes, if the 'raw material' of lived experience is given cultural processing and the people's voice is amplified. Structuralists say no: Anderson and Nairn describe working-class consciousness as a product of bourgeois hegemony, so the subject is a 'subject position' produced by structure, and it must be formed by Marxist theory led by intellectuals. After the 1980s, new social movements of women, students, youth and ethnic groups led Hall and others to hold that subjects are built by discourse and joined only temporarily through 'articulation'. In Xue's reading this shifts struggle from practice to discourse and from critique of political economy to critique of hegemony. Xue concludes that the three turns show the limits of traditional subject theory and the persistence of British Marxists' search for a route to socialism, which deserves recognition. The article nonetheless judges that each school erred: culturalists neglected economic laws, structuralists undervalued working-class cultural traditions, and the plural-subject theory drifted from Marx's starting point in 'real human beings'. Post-Marxism, Xue argues, ends by dissolving the working class's revolutionary status and the guiding role of historical materialism. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly assessment of how British Marxism moved from Thompson to Laclau and Mouffe on the question of the revolutionary subject.

The anti-dialectics of spectator and actor: understanding materialism and its contemporary revival 旁观者与行动者的反辩证法:如何理解唯物主义及其当代复兴 Xia Ying Xia Ying takes up the quiet revival of materialism in contemporary Western philosophy, which the author sets beside the better-known ontological and linguistic turns. The article, published in Jiangsu Social Sciences in 2017, asks what materialism actually is and what the current revival, centred as before in France, implies. Xia's thesis is that a genuine materialist is defined less by the primacy of matter over consciousness than by two commitments: immanence, meaning no appeal to anything beyond the world, and a principle of action, meaning that humans can change the world. The article has three parts. The first traces the materialist tradition from eighteenth-century French materialism, Marx's Holy Family and his doctoral dissertation on Democritus and Epicurus, to Friedrich Lange's threefold division into theoretical, practical and ethical materialism. The second asks what it means to be a materialist, drawing on Badiou's remark on materialism, ancient metaphysicians, Epicurean hedonism and Marx's critique of political economy. The third turns to Fichte, Hegel and Marx, and then to Althusser, Badiou and Žižek. Xia argues that Epicurus's swerving atom, which carries free will and breaks the causal chain, is what attracted Marx and Lange. Marx's materialism, in this reading, is a double break with Feuerbach's contemplative materialism and with Hegelian idealism. It is oriented to the conditions under which action can overthrow capitalism, and Capital is read, in a Kantian sense, as a study of the limits of political economy. Because theology, idealism and spiritualism imply a pre-determined course of history, only a non-deterministic materialism leaves room for real action. Xia contends that Hegel folds the actor into the spectator's explanatory system, while Marx's eleventh thesis on Feuerbach separates interpreting from changing the world, which Xia calls their anti-dialectical relation. Contemporary radical thinkers share this move: Althusser's 'conjuncture' and aleatory materialism, Badiou's 'event' and 'grace', and Žižek's non-reductionism each locate a 'remainder' that no system of ideas can absorb. Xia concludes that the revival aims to supply a theoretical precondition for action and stays within Marx's demand to change the world. The author identifies a difficulty, however. These thinkers reject the proletariat as a pre-appointed agent and look to contingent events to generate actors, but they cannot show how conjunctures or events produce an actual subject. In Xia's judgement their radicalism therefore risks remaining a theoretical posture. Read the original if you are interested in how a Chinese philosopher links Marx's materialism to Althusser, Badiou and Žižek and criticises the agency problem in contemporary radical thought.

A critical review of the main views in contemporary Russian Marxist scholarship 当今俄罗斯马克思主义学界主要观点评析 Hu Xiaokun This review surveys Russian Marxist scholarship after the collapse of the Soviet Union, mainly work published around 2011–2013. Hu starts from the claim that the choice between socialism and capitalism was never settled in Russia. In Hu's account, Marxism returned to Russian academia as an unofficial ideology after a phase of extreme denigration and then one of objective reflection. Two schools stand out: the "reflective Marxism" of Oizerman, and the "critical Marxism" of Buzgalin, Kolganov and others. The review is organised around three themes, drawn largely from the journal Alternatives (Al'ternativy) and a few other Russian journals. The first is the Russian Revolution and Soviet practice, with studies by Lyskov, Rüdiger, Pantin and Epstein. The second is the deeper causes of the Soviet collapse, with Belik, Istyagin, Bensaïd, Voeikov and Kolganov. The third is new thinking on twenty-first-century socialism, with Buzgalin, Belenky, Slavin, Laibman and Kolganov. Hu argues that scholars have moved away from the politicised Soviet paradigm and from the post-1991 dismissal of the revolution. They now use a long-run, genetic approach that places the revolution within Russia's difficult path to modernization. On the collapse, they reject single-cause explanations. Kolganov, for example, locates the failure in an over-centralised, bureaucratic management system and not in socialism as such. Hu also notes the tension between planning and the market, which runs through Soviet economic history. On twenty-first-century socialism, Buzgalin draws ten lessons from the Soviet experience. Slavin proposes a "new socialism" that uses capitalist forms of ownership and the market. Laibman reads the Critique of the Gotha Programme in terms of stages. Hu concludes that these studies treat Soviet socialism as an unavoidable link in the world system. In Hu's view they offer intellectual resources and research paths for exploring socialism with Chinese characteristics independently. Russian scholars, Hu says, have given themselves the task of restoring popular belief in socialism and seeking national rejuvenation through Marxism. Hu describes post-Soviet Marxism as having a practical orientation, sitting between criticism of the Soviet model and response to social reality. Read the original if you want a map of post-Soviet Russian Marxist debates, with sources, for comparison with Chinese discussions of the Soviet collapse and of socialism.

Three questions to Marxist philosophy On the relations among Western Marxism, Marxist philosophy and modern Western philosophy 对马克思主义哲学的三个追问 Chen Xueming Chen Xueming asks what Marxist philosophy is and where it stands in relation to Western philosophy. The article poses three questions: whether Marxism is a philosophy at all; whether it belongs to early modern or to modern and contemporary Western philosophy; and whether, in surpassing the former, it also surpasses the latter. Chen argues that Western Marxism gives the most coherent answers: Marxism is a philosophy, it belongs to modern and contemporary philosophy, and it goes beyond that philosophy as well. The article is organised in three parts: answers to the questions, the drawing of boundaries, and a section on Western Marxism. It sets Western Marxism, represented mainly by Korsch, Luxemburg, Lukács, Gramsci, Habermas and the Frankfurt School, against three rival readings. These are the Second International, the Third International and postmodernism. Chen also draws on ecological Marxism, citing Gorz and David Pepper. Chen holds that Marx's talk of "abolishing" philosophy targeted bourgeois, early modern philosophy, and that Marx realised philosophy in order to abolish it. Marxist philosophy shares with modern Western philosophy a rejection of metaphysics, system-building and the subject–object dualism. It differs, Chen says, by grounding itself in concrete practice and labour, by keeping ontology and a proper place for reason, and by uniting subject and object through revolutionary practice. On this account the Second International reduced Marxism to economics and sociology, and the Third International recast it as a fixed system of dialectical and historical materialism on early modern lines. Chen presents postmodernism as rejecting reason and modernity wholesale, leaving it with nothing but reformism or utopian retreat. Chen concludes that Western Marxism holds Marxist ontology to be a practice-based, social-historical ontology, and treats modernity dialectically. Habermas, Gorz, Horkheimer, Marcuse and ecological Marxists criticise modernity's pathologies but seek to rescue it by tracing them to capital's logic and to social institutions. Chen adds that this reading of ontology has spread widely in Chinese scholarship, and that whether it matches Marx's original meaning remains an open question. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's defence of Western Marxism's claim to interpret Marx's philosophy, and its contrast with Soviet-style and postmodern readings.

Understanding Marx's thought on freedom of the press accurately 准确理解马克思的新闻出版自由思想 Yuan Xiuli Yuan Xiuli takes up a view that cites Marx's and Engels's statements on press freedom (for example, that without it all other freedoms become illusory, and that it is a universal right of everyone) to argue that Marx stood for a free, autonomous press open to all citizens. On this view, the centralised press systems of the Soviet Union and China depart radically from Marx. Yuan, in an article first published in 2017, contends that this reading misunderstands Marx and Engels and cuts their words out of context. The article sets out to establish which kind of press freedom they actually endorsed. The analysis rests mainly on three texts from Marx's Rheinische Zeitung period: the 1843 essay on the latest Prussian censorship instruction, the first article on the debates of the Sixth Rhenish Provincial Assembly on press freedom, and the trial of the Neue Rheinische Zeitung. The article has five parts: Marx's opposition to Prussian feudal censorship; his critical assessment of bourgeois press freedom; his shift from idealism to materialism; his recognition that no press freedom serves all estates alike; and his views on press freedom and law. Yuan argues that Marx attacked censorship and welcomed the bourgeoisie's progressive struggle for press freedom, while also seeing that under capitalism this freedom stays a privilege of capital. Printing and buying publications cost money, so material conditions limit it. Marx's early reasoning, Yuan says, still rested on Hegelian appeals to reason and the human spirit. Experience of material-interest conflicts then pushed him towards materialism, and he came to see that no press freedom exists above class. Yuan reads the Assembly debate as showing this: princes, knights, townspeople and peasants wanted different things, so no single demand could speak for 'everyone'. Marx's answer, in Yuan's account, was that the press should express the people's reason and the general interest of the majority, and this was his first statement of the people-oriented character of a free press. On law, Yuan notes that the early Marx called for a press law as the guarantee of freedom, a position that still reflected Hegelian faith in the rational state. Later, with Engels, Marx came to see law as an expression of the ruling class's will and interests. Yuan concludes that class analysis of press freedom is faithful to Marx, and that selecting 'absolute' phrases without regard to the development of his thought is unscientific. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist rebuttal of liberal readings of Marx on press freedom, with close attention to the Rheinische Zeitung texts.

Freedom enslaved by new imperialism: a critique of neoliberalism 新帝国主义奴役的自由：评新自由主义 Yu Bin Yu Bin, writing in 2017, argues that neoliberalism is the freedom of capital to exploit and enslave workers, and that it serves as the policy doctrine and hegemonic tool of what he calls new imperialism. The article opens with a domestic dispute: a prominent professor's "steamed bun" parable, which blames high taxes and fees for weak demand, is read by Yu as an attempt to steer supply-side structural reform towards the neoliberal supply-side school. The text has two parts. The first dismantles the bun parable, examining pricing, taxation, logistics, rent and the effects of tax cuts on workers and the state. The second turns to Friedrich Hayek's The Road to Serfdom and to neoliberal doctrine more broadly, covering unemployment, minimum wages, wages and productivity, free trade, privatisation, international institutions and Latin America's experience of the Washington Consensus. In the first part, Yu contends that a product too expensive to sell is not "overcapacity", that tax cuts would not much lower bun prices, and that cutting taxes would only shift overcapacity from buns to steamed bread. Taxes, the author adds, would be better used to subsidise the cheaper product, and a property-tax pilot should not be halted. In the second part, Yu reads Hayek's "socialism" as Nazi state socialism and Second International revisionism, which Yu equates with forms of state capitalism rather than Marx's scientific socialism. Yu argues that Hayek's passages on unemployment, minimum wages and postwar British austerity burden workers alone, and uses a numerical example to claim that the neoliberal "iron law" that wages must grow more slowly than productivity does not hold where surplus value is extracted. Yu holds that neoliberalism rose together with new imperialism in the 1970s, as Keynesian state intervention obstructed the plunder of other countries' resources. In the author's account, equal opportunity and free trade favour transnational monopoly capital, while the IMF, World Bank and WTO impose liberalisation on developing countries. Yu says China's reform did not fully uphold the principle of unwaveringly consolidating and developing the public sector, so state enterprises were privatised and some utilities came under foreign capital. Read the original if you want a Marxist polemic against neoliberalism and Hayek that ties debates on China's supply-side reform to the theory of imperialism.

Rethinking the relationship between Marx's thought and the Western cultural tradition 重新理解马克思思想与西方文化传统的关系 Nie Jinfang Many commentators, in the East and the West alike, detach Marx's thought from the Western cultural tradition and read it as a uniquely self-standing theoretical construction. Nie Jinfang argues the opposite. Based on his recent book Origins and Flourishing: An Inquiry into the Origins of Marx's Thought, the article holds that Marx's thought was nourished and shaped by that tradition. First published in the Chinese-language Zhonghua dushu bao in January 2018, it is a short account of the book's findings. Nie reports a close reading of Marx's surviving youthful writings and traces three Western sources in the period when his thought took form. The first is the "Trier tradition", the religious and humanistic atmosphere of his birthplace, family and school. The second is his own literary writing: 111 poems, one play and a fragment of a novel. The third is ancient atomism, which he studied after turning to the Young Hegelians. On the first source, Nie contends that the Trier milieu gave Marx religious feeling and humanistic concern. He argues that his father's "Enlightenment" outlook meant conversion to liberal Protestantism rather than rejection of theology. In Nie's view, Marx's image as an atheist and fighter against religion was greatly exaggerated in later Marxism, because he attacked particular doctrines and the worldly basis of religion, not ultimate concern as such. On the second, Nie reads the poems as teaching Marx the meaning, the complexity and finally the limits of emotion, and as leading to reflection on German national character and on Kant, Fichte and Hegel. On the third, Nie presents atomism as showing Marx that the world contains manifold contradictions (atom and void, space and time, necessity and chance). In Nie's account, the atom's swerve from the straight line stands for freedom and the emergence of self-consciousness, and this made up a fairly well-formed philosophical system, which Nie calls the most important result of Marx's formative period. Nie concludes that the twentieth-century practice of international communism, and the confrontation between capitalism and socialism, raised Marx's influence but also produced extreme and irrational evaluations. Admirers and opponents alike, he says, removed Marx from the history of thought, either as a figure towering over all predecessors or as an eccentric to be expelled. Nie maintains that Marx's critique was "German-philosophical": sublation and carrying forward, not wholesale rejection. Read the original if you want a concise statement of this argument about Marx's youth, religion and atomism, and a pointer to the book behind it.

Opening a new realm of governing the country in accordance with the Constitution 开创依宪治国新境界 Ma Yide Writing shortly after the First Session of the 13th National People's Congress (2018) adopted amendments to the Constitution, Ma Yide offers a commentary on what the revision means. The author's thesis is that the amendments are a major historical contribution by the Party Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core, and that they will let the Party lead the people to "a new realm" of governing the country in accordance with the Constitution. Ma frames the revision as the constitutional expression of the Party's governance experience since the 18th Party Congress (2012) and of the main ideas and policies set by the 19th Party Congress (2017). The piece is organised around four main amendments, followed by a briefer survey of the rest. It takes in turn the inclusion of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era in the preamble, the new wording on Party leadership in Article 1, the removal of the two-term limit for the state president, and the creation of supervisory commissions. It closes with other changes: local legislative powers for cities divided into districts, the oath of allegiance to the Constitution, the new Constitution and Law Committee, socialist core values, and the united front. Ma argues that each change brings the Constitution into line with the Party's established leadership arrangements. Writing "the leadership of the Communist Party of China is the defining feature of socialism with Chinese characteristics" into Article 1 gives Party leadership greater institutional and legal force and, in the author's view, helps the Party escape the historical cycle of rise and fall. On the presidency, Ma says the change makes the Constitution consistent with the "trinity" leadership system (Party general secretary, state president and military commission chairman), since Party rules and the military commission provisions already set no two-term limit. The author adds that this does not mean lifelong tenure, citing Party-constitution provisions on retirement. On supervision, Ma notes that 11 of the 21 amendments concern supervisory commissions, and argues that these commissions, working jointly with Party discipline inspection bodies, will give full coverage of public officials and unify Party oversight with state supervision. Ma concludes that the amended Constitution is the legal elevation of Xi Jinping Thought and combines the Party's confidence in governing with its consciousness of the rule of law. The author also claims it widens the paths open to developing countries towards legal modernisation and offers "Chinese wisdom and a Chinese approach" to problems of the rule of law worldwide. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned account of how a Party-state legal scholar justified the 2018 constitutional amendments, especially the presidential term change and the supervisory system.

Understanding Marx's thought on freedom of the press accurately 准确理解马克思的新闻出版自由思想 Yuan Xiuli Yuan Xiuli takes issue with a reading that cites Marx's statements on press freedom (that it is a 'universal right' of everyone and a 'privilege of the human spirit') to argue that Marx and Engels defended a free press for all citizens. On this reading, the Soviet Union and China, by adopting centralised press systems, broke sharply with Marx. Yuan argues that this reading misreads Marx and Engels, and that quoting isolated phrases without their context produces distortion. The article rests on three texts from Marx's Rheinische Zeitung period: 'Remarks on the Latest Prussian Censorship Instruction' (1843), the first article on the debates of the Sixth Rhine Province Assembly on press freedom, and the 'Trial of the Neue Rheinische Zeitung'. It proceeds in five sections: Marx's attack on Prussian censorship and support for bourgeois press freedom; his critical view of capitalist press freedom; the shift in his thinking from idealism to materialism; the absence of a press freedom common to all estates; and his views on press freedom and law. Yuan's central claim is that Marx's early view was still shaped by Hegelian idealism, grounding freedom in reason and human nature, but that the Prussian reality pushed him towards material interests and class. In the Assembly debates, Yuan notes, the princely, knightly, urban and peasant estates held different positions, so no single demand could stand for 'everyone'. Yuan reads this as an early germ of historical materialism. Marx later saw that capital's control of publishing, and the legal system as an expression of ruling-class will, make press freedom class-bound under capitalism. Yuan also holds that Marx's early hope that the Prussian state would legislate press freedom was contradictory. Yuan concludes that Marx never gave up the pursuit of press freedom, but came to place it on a scientific basis: in class society no press freedom exists above state and class, and universal freedom depends on the development of the productive forces and the resolution of class relations. Yuan therefore rejects the call to drop class analysis in favour of a 'citizens' freedom' framework. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist argument, built on the Rheinische Zeitung texts, that class analysis of press freedom is faithful to Marx.

Theoretical guidance for the shift to a stage of high-quality development 转向高质量发展阶段的理论指引 Hou Weimin Writing in early 2018, Hou Weimin takes up the Central Economic Work Conference's formal naming of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era in the economic field. Hou argues that this body of economic thought gives theoretical guidance for China's shift from a stage of high-speed growth to a stage of high-quality development. The commentary, first published in Anhui Daily, is organised in four parts. They deal with the institutional basis and inherent advantages of high-quality development, its guiding concepts and methodology, its goals and requirements, and its ultimate purpose and criteria of judgement. Hou draws mainly on Xi Jinping's statements and the report to the 19th Party Congress (2017). Hou's central move is to read the new development philosophy as the methodology of high-quality development and to link each of its five concepts to Marxian political economy. Innovation applies Marx's theory of productive forces, coordination reflects proportional allocation of production factors and social labour time, green development unites value and use-value production, opening up follows Marx's turn from national to world history, and sharing is the basic purpose of socialist production. Hou also argues that the modernized economic system must rest on the real economy, with finance and the virtual economy serving it in a subordinate role. Hou concludes that the primary stage of socialism, the Two Unwaverings and Party leadership of economic work give high-quality development its institutional footing. Its end point is people's well-being, shown in priority for education, employment quality and income, and social security that is both done to the best of one's ability and within one's means. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary in 2018 tied Xi's economic thought to Marxist political economy.

Correctly understanding the shift in the principal contradiction facing Chinese society 正确认识我国社会主要矛盾的转化 Lin Zhaomu Writing in the People's Daily on 30 March 2018, Lin Zhaomu takes up how the principal contradiction in Chinese society should be understood and formulated. Lin argues that the 19th Party Congress (2017) was right to hold that the contradiction is now one between people's ever-growing needs for a better life and unbalanced and inadequate development. In Lin's account, this judgement renews and innovates the Party's theory of the principal contradiction and sets new requirements for the work of the Party and state. The commentary has five parts. It first traces two "leaps" in the Party's theory since the 1950s, then sets out four conditions behind the shift. It then discusses how the shift relates to the unchanged basic national condition, the primary stage of socialism. Finally it considers what the shift means for people-centred development and for the world economy. Lin's central move is to separate a change of contradiction from a change of historical stage. The article describes the 8th Party Congress (1956) and the Sixth Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1981) as the first leap, and the 19th Party Congress as the second. It presents the new formula as replacing "material and cultural needs" with a wider "better life" that includes democracy, rule of law, fairness, justice, security and environment. It also replaces "backward social production" with "unbalanced and inadequate development" across the five-sphere framework. As evidence the article cites GDP of 82.7 trillion yuan in 2017 and manufacturing output ranked first in the world for eight years. It adds a large middle-income group and the Party's new theory since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Lin says the shift happens inside the primary stage, which China remains in and will long remain in. The old formula fits its "first half" and the new one its "second half", so the basic task is still to liberate and develop the productive forces, and demands must not outrun them. Lin concludes that a correct reading of the contradiction is what lets the Party serve people's immediate and long-term interests. The article links the new formula to targeted poverty alleviation, rural revitalisation, regional coordination, pollution control, high-quality development, education and health care, and employment. It also argues that the shift will benefit the world economy through new market and investment openings, a growing middle class that buys more abroad, and a continued commitment to peaceful development. Read the original if you want the official People's Daily account of how the 2017 reformulation of the principal contradiction was justified and tied to the primary stage of socialism.

The freedom of new imperialist enslavement: a critique of neoliberalism 新帝国主义奴役的自由：评新自由主义 Yu Bin Yu Bin, writing in 2017, takes up the claim that neoliberalism stands for freedom and that socialism leads to serfdom. The article argues the opposite: neoliberalism is the freedom of capital to exploit and enslave workers, and it serves as the policy tool of what Yu calls new imperialism. It also warns that China's supply-side structural reform risks being steered onto a neoliberal path. The article has two parts. The first answers a Chinese professor's "steamed bun" parable, in which tax cuts and lower fees are proposed to clear the obstacles between supply and demand. The second is a long critique of Friedrich Hayek's The Road to Serfdom. It moves from Hayek's account of Nazi "national socialism" and state capitalism to his views on unemployment, wages and competition, and then to neoliberalism's role in globalisation, international institutions and the Washington Consensus. In the bun parable, Yu argues that the diagnosis is wrong: goods that do not sell because they are too dear are not overcapacity. Tax cuts would not necessarily lower prices, could merely shift overcapacity from buns to steamed bread, and would weaken the public finances that state action depends on. Yu says the reform needed is structural adjustment and innovation, not neoliberal supply-side tax cutting. Turning to Hayek, Yu reads the "socialism" he attacks as Nazi state capitalism and Bismarckian pseudo-socialism, not Marxist scientific socialism. Yu says Hayek's treatment of unemployment, minimum wages and "equality of opportunity" favours capital over labour. A numerical example is offered to show that the neoliberal "iron law" that wages must grow more slowly than productivity does not hold where surplus value is extracted. Yu then contends that neoliberalism became the hegemonic tool of new imperialism as Keynesianism declined in the 1970s. In Yu's account, free trade, privatisation, "human rights above sovereignty" and bodies such as the IMF, World Bank and WTO let transnational capital seize developing countries' economic lifelines. Yu cites Latin America's "lost decade" and Stiglitz as evidence. Yu concludes that neoliberalism is the ideology of exploitation and imperialist plunder. Yu says China's reforms were hampered by neoliberal "market omnipotence" and the myth of private property, citing privatised state firms and foreign control of some urban utilities, and that China must hold to unwaveringly consolidating and developing the public sector. Read the original if you want a Marxist polemic against Hayek and neoliberal supply-side ideas, set in the debates over China's reform around 2017.

Understanding the new historical position of reform and opening up in the new era 深刻理解新时代改革开放的新方位 Ding Yuanzhu Writing in 2018, as a series of reform measures drew wide public discussion, Ding Yuanzhu argues that they can only be understood from a historical and epochal standpoint, that is, from China's new historical position. The article's thesis is that this position must be read through great-power relations, above all the China–US relationship. The short commentary first recalls that China's reform and opening up must be studied against its initial conditions and the global logic of the time, including US–China relations then. It then turns to the present: Trump's slogans of national revival and "making America great again", the competitive mentality behind them, and what they mean for China's choices. Ding contends that US decline will be gradual. Citing an economy 1.5 times the size of China's and growth of 3 per cent, the author suggests that the rivalry could become a century-long contest. The US is described as facing challenges to its system and to its international standing, and as holding a competitive mindset formed by long prosperity. Chinese national rejuvenation, by contrast, rests on a century of humiliation and the search for a national path since the Opium War. Ding advises against over-interpreting American behaviour. Ding concludes that China's most fundamental task is to do its own work well. The author calls for rethinking what to reform and open, and how, so as to reach the goal of a modern socialist great power while reducing friction with major powers. Improving people's livelihoods and national strength is presented as the common aim, and as the premise for the fortieth anniversary of reform and opening up and for modernizing national governance. Read the original if you want a brief example of how a Chinese scholar framed reform and opening up against US–China rivalry in 2018.

The Japanese Communist Party's "setback" in the House of Representatives election 日本共产党众议院选举“退步” Cao Tianlu Why did the Japanese Communist Party (JCP) lose ground in the 48th House of Representatives election of 22 October 2017? This short commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in January 2018, answers that the party's own explanation, "insufficient party strength", is incomplete. Cao argues that a surprise election, a collapsed opposition front, a lack of funds and an unchanging campaign strategy all contributed. The piece opens with the results: the Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) won 284 seats and, with its coalition partner Komeito, 313 of 465, more than two-thirds. The JCP won 12 seats, down from 21 in 2014, and its proportional-representation vote fell from 6.06 million to 4.4 million. Cao then examines four factors in turn and ends with a general assessment of the party. On timing, Cao describes how Prime Minister Abe Shinzo, weakened by the Moritomo and Kake scandals, reshuffled his cabinet. Cao says he then used North Korea's missile and nuclear tests and Trump's planned visit to recover support before calling a snap election, which left small parties little time to prepare. The opposition front built for the 2016 upper-house election broke up when the Democratic Party split, so the JCP had to renegotiate alliances. Cao adds that the party's refusal of state political funds forces it to contest only winnable districts, and that its strategy of recruiting members and expanding Akahata circulation has barely changed and does not appeal to young voters. Cao concludes that the LDP coalition's political manoeuvring made the contest very hard for the JCP. In Cao's view, the party's own lack of political sensitivity and weak party-building were what finally caused the defeat. Cao proposes that raising political sensitivity and the ability to respond to changing circumstances should be the practical goal of the party's future building. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese-language assessment of the JCP's 2017 electoral performance and of its structural weaknesses.

The shift in logic of the Communist Party of the Russian Federation's parliamentary anti-corruption work 俄罗斯共产党议会反腐的逻辑转换 Liao Hongying Xu Peng This short commentary, first published in China Social Sciences Today in January 2018, asks how the Communist Party of the Russian Federation (CPRF), the largest successor of the CPSU and now the leading opposition party in the State Duma, has changed its approach to fighting corruption. Liao and Xu argue that the party has moved from "subversive" confrontation with the authorities to "constructive" cooperation inside parliament. The article first traces the cognitive shift: early street struggle and the overthrow of the regime as the main goal gave way, after poor results, to the view that anti-corruption should be pursued jointly by ruling and opposition forces. It then examines four reasons for the change and closes by assessing the effects on Russian party politics and the difficulties that remain. The authors present the shift as an expedient route to the party's own goals, a requirement of theoretical and practical innovation, a way to consolidate its political position among a divided left, and a path into the political mainstream, where they say Putin wants a "constructive" centre-left opposition. They credit the CPRF with helping shape a more regular party system and with hundreds of anti-corruption bills, including the 2013 proposal to introduce the UN Convention's "illicit enrichment" concept and a 2012 proposal on officials' luxury official cars. Liao and Xu note unresolved tensions: the party must reconcile being an in-system party with the risk of implicitly legitimising the current regime, and it needs better anti-corruption personnel, more young members and less radical positions. They conclude that the CPRF still has a long road ahead. Read the original if you want a brief, sympathetic Chinese account of how a major post-Soviet communist party has adapted to parliamentary politics.

"Capitalism has always been an unstable system" Foreign left-wing scholars on the current crisis of capitalism “资本主义一直是个不稳定的系统” Tong Jin This short commentary, published in Beijing Daily in 2018, surveys how foreign left-wing scholars have analysed the capitalist crisis that began in the early twenty-first century. Tong reports that these analyses trace the crisis to five dimensions: it is a crisis of the mode of production, of democracy, of values, of ecology and of the system as a whole. The piece is organised under one heading for each dimension. It draws on David Harvey, Paul Jorion, Mary Warren, Noam Chomsky, Joseph Stiglitz, Andrew W. Jones, Richard Smith, Immanuel Wallerstein, Wolfgang Streeck and Kozo Yamamura, mostly through short quotations. On production, Tong presents the view that capitalism's room for manoeuvre is narrowing. Harvey is cited as saying that internal contradictions are repeatedly displaced outwards, while Jorion calls capitalism a perpetually unstable system. On democracy and values, the scholars are reported to describe Western democracy as rule by money, with campaign donations, lobbying and the Wall Street–Treasury "revolving door" tying the state to capital. Cited poll figures say 61 per cent of Americans think their economy favours the rich. Their claim is that ideals of freedom and equality are undermined by inequality and by hegemonic practice abroad. On ecology, Jones and Smith are said to hold that green capitalism cannot work, because growth as capital accumulation is built into the system. Tong closes with scholars who see a structural crisis. Wallerstein foresees the system reaching its limits within thirty to forty years, Streeck lists five systemic problems, and Yamamura calls for change "outside the box" rather than reform within the existing system. Read the original if you want a compact Chinese-press digest of Western left critiques of capitalism after the 2008 crisis, with names to follow up.

Why Marx is receiving ever more attention 马克思为何越来越受重视 Feng Yanli Marking the 170th anniversary of the Communist Manifesto in February 2018, this short commentary, first published in the People's Daily, asks why Marx is increasingly valued in both China and the West. Feng argues that the Manifesto deserves commemoration in socialist and capitalist countries alike, because Marx decisively shaped the course of history and changed how people understand it. The piece cites the Manifesto's translation into more than 110 languages and over 1,000 editions, and Terry Eagleton's description of it as the most influential work of the nineteenth century. It then turns to the West, where it points to university reading lists, to Eric Hobsbawm's assessment of Marx's twentieth-century legacy, and to the anniversaries of 1998, 2008 and 2018. Finally it turns to China. Feng contends that recent developments in the United States and Europe confirm Marx's judgement that capitalism cannot remove its own basic contradictions. In Feng's image, the "verdict" Marx passed on capitalism has been postponed but remains valid. The author notes that capitalists and Western politicians and scholars, including George Soros, are rediscovering the Manifesto. For China, Feng claims that the victories of revolution, construction and reform and opening up have repeatedly proved the Manifesto's truth in practice. Feng concludes that Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, set out at the 19th Party Congress (2017), carries Marxism forward and revitalises scientific socialism in twenty-first-century China. In the article's account, it also offers developing countries a new path to modernization and a Chinese approach to human problems. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Chinese official media presented Marx's global relevance on the Manifesto's 170th anniversary.

The original aspiration revealed in the Communist Manifesto 《共产党宣言》昭示的初心 Zhang Kuiliang Marking the 170th anniversary of the Communist Manifesto in 2018, Zhang Kuiliang argues in this newspaper commentary that the document expresses the original aspiration (chuxin) of all communists: the complete emancipation of humankind. For Zhang, its goal of communism and its call to overthrow capitalism are the ideological foundation that no communist should forget. The piece sets the Manifesto in its mid-nineteenth-century context, when capitalist contradictions had surfaced and an independent workers' movement lacked party leadership. It then turns to the Chinese Communist Party's relationship to the text and to the present call to remain true to the original aspiration since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Zhang presents the Manifesto as both a party programme and the formal birth of Marxism. Applying historical materialism, it shows capitalism's necessary demise, but Zhang stresses that social laws do not operate automatically: the proletariat and its party must carry out the historical mission. Zhang reads the Manifesto's "two ruptures" with traditional property relations and traditional ideas as the content of communist revolution, while insisting that they cannot happen all at once and require gradual measures. Zhang concludes that the Party must hold to the communist ideal as a bottom line for policy, while recognising that achieving it is gradual and staged. Building a moderately prosperous society and pursuing socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era are said to match the Manifesto's final aim and lay its foundations. Read the original if you want a brief example of how the Manifesto was invoked in 2018 to support the Party's "original aspiration" discourse.

The contemporary value of the Communist Manifesto 《共产党宣言》的时代价值 Niu Xianfeng Writing in Guangming Daily in March 2018, Niu Xianfeng asks what the Communist Manifesto, first published in German in London in February 1848, still offers today. Niu argues that it marks the birth of Marxism and that its influence reaches beyond its own era and Western Europe, supplying a worldview, a scientific method and a guide to action. The short commentary moves through five claims: the Manifesto answered the basic question of its time; it turned socialism from utopia into science; it changed the global political order; it offers a method for understanding the contemporary world; and it is a source of spiritual strength for Communists. Niu holds that, with industrial transformation in mid-nineteenth-century Britain, the bourgeoisie and proletariat became the two main classes. The Manifesto, in Niu's reading, used the theory of surplus value and historical materialism to expose exploitation and conclude that the fall of the bourgeoisie and the victory of the proletariat are equally inevitable. Niu traces from it the October Revolution, the founding of the Communist Party of China in 1921 and what the article calls the new era of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Niu rejects doubts about this conclusion, including claims that communism is remote or Marxism outdated, as seeing only surface appearances. Communism, the article says, may take many generations, but the movement toward it has never stopped. Niu concludes that the Manifesto's spirit of selflessness, struggle and concern for humanity should motivate Party members today. Upholding Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, which Niu calls Marxism of contemporary China and of the twenty-first century, is presented as carrying the Manifesto forward. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the Manifesto's legacy was presented in the Party press in 2018.

Opportunities and challenges for the American socialist movement in the early twenty-first century 21世纪初美国社会主义运动面临的机遇与挑战 Lei Hongyan Lei Hongyan asks what prospects the socialist movement in the United States has in the early twenty-first century. The article argues that the movement faces both real opportunities and serious difficulties. Writing in 2018, Lei concludes that, while success in the short term is unlikely, the general direction of social development means that exploration of the socialist road will not disappear as long as capitalism exists in the United States. The article begins with the global setting, claiming that world socialism has entered a stage of revival after the upheavals in Eastern Europe and the Soviet Union. It then takes up three sources of opportunity: the spread and study of socialist ideas in the US, the shift in public opinion after the 2007–08 financial crisis, and the weakening of capitalism's legitimacy. A final section turns to challenges in the Trump period, namely reformism, the split between the workers' movement and the socialist movement, the weakness of the Communist Party USA (CPUSA), and entrenched prejudice against socialism. Lei grounds the opportunities in the claim that the crisis exposed the basic contradiction of capitalism between socialised production and private ownership of the means of production. The article cites the annual Socialist Scholars Conference, the CPUSA debate on what socialism means, rising university interest in Marxism, and Piketty's figures on inequality. It also cites polls showing that many young Americans view socialism favourably and notes the Sanders campaign and Occupy Wall Street. Using Sombart's argument about why the US lacked socialism, Lei reasons that stagnation and widening inequality now favour the movement. On the challenges, Lei argues that mass protest is fragmented, aims mostly at reforming capitalism and lacks organisational leadership. Many workers, including a stratum of "labour aristocracy", were drawn to Trump rather than to socialist organisations. The CPUSA, with fewer than 10,000 mostly elderly members, is described as marginal and theoretically immature. Lei says it blames the crisis on neoliberal policy errors and proposes Keynesian, New Deal-style remedies. Lei calls on the Party to reform itself and to link socialism with the workers' movement. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly assessment of American socialism after 2008, including its use of polls, party-building and Sanders-era debates.

Foreign left-wing scholars on opportunities, problems, challenges and proposals for publicity work of the world socialist movement 国外左翼学者谈世界社会主义运动宣传工作的 机遇、问题、挑战与建议 Li Qiang Li Shuqing This is a report on views voiced at the 8th World Socialism Forum, held in Beijing on 14–15 October 2017 on the eve of the 19th Party Congress. The forum was hosted by the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences under the theme of the era's great development, great change and great adjustment and socialism with Chinese characteristics. Li Qiang and Li Shuqing summarise what visiting left-wing scholars said about publicity work for socialism. In the authors' account, the visitors saw favourable conditions for the world socialist movement but weak propaganda capacity, and offered concrete proposals. The report speaks of participants from several countries and organisations. They include Allan Freeman (University of Manitoba), Roger van Zwanenberg of Pluto Press, Radhika Desai, Cem Kizilcec from Turkey, Andrea Catone of the Italian journal Marx XXI, Wadih Halabi of the US Communist Party's economic commission, Egon Krenz and the Brazilian student Gaio Doria. It is organised in three parts: new opportunities, problems and challenges, and strategies for improvement. On opportunities, the speakers are reported as saying that mass movements are rising worldwide and that China's development contributes to the world economy and demonstrates the superiority of the socialist system. Several are quoted as saying that the Belt and Road Initiative and a strong socialist state help to restrain imperialism. On problems, the scholars say socialist publicity is weak and that Western media distort socialism and China. Freeman is quoted as saying many people consider socialism attractive but unrealistic. Zwanenberg admits he does not clearly understand socialism with Chinese characteristics, and others say it is wrongly seen as applicable only to China. The proposals reported are: keep up forums and journals and invite more Western left-wing scholars and politicians; focus on the Third World, the former Soviet and East European states and Latin America, and on ordinary people rather than elites; build internet, television, radio and training networks, including summer schools and a Marxist international university; translate key documents such as the 19th Party Congress report; and choose suitable forms of ideological struggle. The authors close by presenting the Forum as a platform for Marxists and a window for publicising socialism with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want to see how invited foreign leftists, as reported by Chinese organisers, assessed China's external publicity work in 2017.

The world significance of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想的世界意义 Li Shenming Writing in early 2018, after the 19th Party Congress (2017) made Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era the Party's guiding ideology, Li Shenming asks what historical position and world significance this body of thought has. The article argues that its significance is global as well as national. Li presents it as supplying "Chinese confidence", "Chinese ideas" and a "Chinese solution" to a world in flux, and as advancing the development of twenty-first-century Marxism. The article is organised in four parts. The first views the thought from the angle of China's own development, tracing the path from the semi-colonial period after 1840 through the 1949 revolution and reform and opening up to the "stood up, grown rich, becoming strong" sequence. The second looks at the broad currents of human development and the values, development outlook and foreign relations that China offers. The third considers the changing world order and China's proposals for global governance. The fourth places the thought within a periodisation of capitalist epochs and within the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Li's central claims run as follows. China's rise, in his account, is itself a contribution to world peace, and socialism with Chinese characteristics is a "brand-new reference" for developing countries seeking modernisation while keeping their independence. Building a community with a shared future for mankind is described as resting on humanity's common values, on a broad international united front, on developing countries and peoples as the main force, and ultimately on Marx and Engels's "association" of free development. Li insists that these common values are relative and must not be confused with "universal values", which he calls a Western tool for Westernising and dividing China. Drawing on Lenin, he argues that the present is the era of financial imperialism, marked by extreme global polarisation and now at a turning point of decline, with neoliberalism giving way to socialism's growing appeal. He holds that new technology, including artificial intelligence, cannot resolve capitalism's basic contradiction. Li concludes that the world needs new theory and can produce it, and that Xi Jinping Thought, which contains a Chinese solution for global governance, arises at the right moment. He calls for firm adherence to Marxism together with innovation based on new practice, so as to advance the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. He notes that China neither imports foreign models nor exports its own. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how a senior Chinese Marxist scholar links Xi Jinping Thought, Lenin's theory of imperialism and the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind.

Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era opens a new horizon for the international communist movement 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想开辟国际共产主义运动新境界 Lü Weizhou Writing in Contemporary World (Dangdai shijie) in 2018, shortly after the 19th Party Congress (2017), Lü Weizhou asks what the Party's new guiding ideology means for scientific socialism and the international communist movement. The article argues that Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era enriches scientific socialism, shows the advantages of the socialist system, and will lead the international communist movement into a new stage. The article has three main sections. The first treats the Thought as a development of scientific socialism, drawing on lessons from the movement's history since the Communist Manifesto, including the upheavals in Eastern Europe and the Soviet collapse. The second turns to socialist construction in China since reform and opening up, citing growth, high-speed rail and foreign-exchange figures. The third considers what China's experience means abroad. Lü draws two lessons from the movement's history: the basic principles of scientific socialism and the ultimate communist goal must not be abandoned, and scientific socialism is a method, not a dogma, to be applied creatively to each country's conditions. On this basis Lü presents the Thought as continuing Marxism-Leninism, Mao Zedong Thought and later Party theory, and as advancing understanding of the stage of socialist development and the principal contradiction in Chinese society. The system's advantages are said to lie in keeping people at the centre, upholding Party leadership, and holding firm to ideals and convictions. Lü holds that China's path has encouraged foreign communist parties and left forces, offered developing countries a reference model for modernization with independence, and, through a community with a shared future for mankind and the Belt and Road Initiative, offered a global vision. Evidence includes a Uruguayan editor's remarks and a Thomas Friedman comment. Lü concludes that the new two-step plan to build a modern socialist country by the mid-century will further show the strengths of scientific socialism and socialism with Chinese characteristics. The author predicts that this will drive a full revival of the international communist movement. Read the original if you want an example of how Chinese Party scholarship in 2018 framed the Thought's significance for world socialism and the international communist movement.

Mao Zedong's lifelong bond with the Communist Manifesto 毛泽东与《共产党宣言》的不解之缘 Qi Ji Marking 170 years since the first German edition of the Communist Manifesto (London, 24 February 1848), this newspaper commentary by Qi Ji traces Mao Zedong's relationship with the text.
