The author argues that the Manifesto was the first Marxist classic Mao read and the one he cherished all his life, and that he treated it as a guide to practice and theoretical innovation. The piece follows Mao chronologically through three stages: the formation of his Marxist faith after the May Fourth Movement; his repeated reading and his promotion of the text among cadres from Yan'an to the 1970s; and his reading after 1949, including the Chinese preface he offered to write and his study of the English edition. It draws on Mao's 1936 conversation with Edgar Snow and on recollections by his librarian Xu Zhongyuan and his English tutor Lin Ke. Qi presents Mao's own testimony that the Chinese translation by Chen Wangdao, with works by Kautsky and Kirkup, fixed his belief in Marxism by summer 1920. According to the article, Mao said in 1939 that he had read the Manifesto more than a hundred times, consulted it when writing On New Democracy, and held that Marxist theory must be read in order to be applied. Qi then lists his repeated placing of the Manifesto first on required-reading lists (1942, 1945, 1949, 1963, 1970), and his plan in 1965 to annotate it in light of China's revolutionary experience. The author concludes that Mao's reading was unusually deep, citing dense annotations in his English copy and the six copies, two of them English, found by his bed after his death. Read the original if you want a short, anecdotal account of Mao's reading habits and of how his study of the Manifesto is presented in Party-oriented commemorative writing.

The Communist Manifesto and the ideals and convictions of Communists 《共产党宣言》与共产党人的理想信念 Wang Haibin Published in Study Times to mark the 170th anniversary of the Communist Manifesto (1848–2018), this commentary asks why Communists still need to reread the text today. Wang Haibin answers that the Manifesto, as the first programme of the Communist Party, supplies firm support for the ideals and convictions that Xi Jinping describes as the foundation of a Communist's life, the spiritual "calcium" and the "political soul" of the Party. The piece is organised under three headings: the Manifesto as the theoretical foundation of Communist ideals, as a source of intellectual nourishment, and as a stimulus to spiritual strength. It moves from Marx and Engels's analysis of bourgeois and proletarian development, through three guiding ideas the author draws from the text, to the Manifesto's remarks on the nature of Communists and on the Marxist spirit of self-reflection. Wang argues first that the Manifesto's conclusion that the fall of the bourgeoisie and the victory of the proletariat are equally inevitable rests on historical materialism, not on class sentiment or values. It points to recurrent commercial crises of relative overproduction and to the proletariat as the product of large-scale industry. Second, Wang reads the Manifesto through "two inevitables", "two most radical ruptures" and the "free development of all". On the first, the author notes that capitalism is growing socialist elements, such as taxation adjustment, joint-stock companies and social security, and that the inevitable outcome comes only once capitalism has exhausted its capacity for productive forces. On the second, Wang says Marx and Engels targeted the private-ownership form and ideas such as money worship, egoism, despotism and bureaucracy, not markets or capital as such. Third, the author notes that the Manifesto credits capitalist civilisation with material achievements but not with spiritual ones, so Communists must keep raising their own spiritual level. Wang concludes that grasping these historical laws, and pursuing the free development of all, gives Communists a continuing source of wisdom and moral drive for the basic conviction of serving the people. The author also holds that the 1872 German preface, which says the practical application of the principles depends on historical conditions, requires reading the Manifesto in light of the contemporary world and China's realities. Such a reading is said to strengthen belief in Marxism, socialism and communism, and in the common ideal of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a short example of how the Manifesto was presented to Party members in 2018 as a basis for ideological conviction.

On the integrity of Capital as a whole 论《资本论》的整体性 Yu Bin Marking 150 years since the first German edition of Capital Volume I, Yu Bin takes up a familiar reading habit: many readers return repeatedly to Volume I and never reach Volumes II and III. Yu argues that the three volumes form one whole and that Capital cannot be understood without recognising this. Those who claim a contradiction between Volume I and Volume III, in Yu's view, have simply not understood the work. The article proceeds almost entirely through close reading of Marx's and Engels's own statements: Marx's 1868 letter to Danielson, his letters to Engels and Kugelmann, and Engels's essays, letters and prefaces from 1869 to the 1890s. These are used to establish the relative independence of Volume I, its one-sidedness, the reasons the later volumes were unpublished in Marx's lifetime, and what unifies the three volumes. Yu also answers critics, including Achille Loria and a contemporary view that Marx withheld the later volumes because his theory no longer fitted reality. Yu's central claim is that Capital narrates the whole career of surplus value: Volume I covers its production, Volume II its circulation and Volume III its distribution. Volume I is relatively self-contained, but Engels called it one-sided and abstract, and Yu holds that concepts such as money, capital, the transformation of surplus value into profit and average profit, and the refutation of bourgeois economics only come into full view with the later volumes. On the delay, Yu rejects the idea that Marx doubted his theory. Yu points instead to poverty, illness, political work for the International, repression, Marx's perfectionism and the priority given to new editions and translations of Volume I. Yu adds that Volume I's treatment of value is developed in Volume III, where value is determined by the labour-time needed for reproduction. Yu concludes that the missing final chapter on classes, and even the last part on revenues and their sources, do not damage the unity of the work, since production, circulation and distribution of surplus value are already complete. Capital should therefore not be regarded as an unfinished work, and Yu asks rhetorically whether any work could then count as finished. New developments in capitalism, Yu says, would enrich the later volumes rather than negate earlier content. Read the original if you want a text-based argument, built from Marx's and Engels's correspondence, for reading Capital as a unified three-volume theory of surplus value.

Upholding the Four Cardinal Principles as the ideological and political foundation for advancing the "four greats" 坚持四项基本原则是推进“四个伟大”的思想政治基础 Song Yuehong Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2018, Song Yuehong takes up the 19th Party Congress (2017) report's call to realise the great dream through the "four greats": great struggle, great project of Party building, great cause of socialism with Chinese characteristics, and the great dream itself. The article argues that upholding the Four Cardinal Principles, described as the foundation of the nation, is the fundamental political basis of the Party's historic mission of national rejuvenation. Song contends that the content of the "four greats" in turn gives the Principles new meaning for the new era. The article is organised in three parts. The first traces why developing the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics requires the Principles, drawing on Deng Xiaoping, the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978), the 1981 Resolution on Party history, the 1982 constitutional amendment and the 13th Party Congress. The second part treats socialist institutions and reform and opening up as conditions of national rejuvenation. The third part argues that the Principles are the essential requirement of each of the "four greats". Song's central claim is that the Principles are historically grounded and internally linked to other elements of the Party line. In the author's account, the Principles were confirmed by revolution, construction and reform; they sit with economic construction and reform and opening up in the Party's basic line for the primary stage of socialism. Economic construction is called the key to national prosperity, reform and opening up the road to national strength, and the Principles the foundation of the state. Song holds that without the Principles and reform, economic construction would lose direction and momentum. Applied to the "four greats", upholding Party leadership and the socialist system is the core of the Principles: it requires full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, adherence to the path, theory, system and culture of socialism with Chinese characteristics, and deepened reform under the Party's unified leadership. Song concludes that the Principles form a unified, systematic ideological and political system that cannot be shaken, departed from or reduced by dropping any one of them, or the whole cause of socialist modernization would be undermined. Reform and opening up, in turn, keeps giving the Principles new content for each era. Read the original if you want an example of how Party theorists in 2018 tied the Four Cardinal Principles to the 19th Party Congress framework of the \"four greats\".

Why the "fire of truth" still shines: rereading the Communist Manifesto “真理之火”为何依然璀璨 Zhou Wen Writing in Jiefang Daily in February 2018, on the 170th anniversary of the Communist Manifesto, Zhou Wen asks why the "fire of truth" of scientific socialism still burns brightly. The commentary answers that the theory endures because it has developed through inheritance and innovated through practice. Zhou first describes the Manifesto as a rich seam of ideas, translated into more than 200 languages and over 1,100 editions, and notes that it has attracted many misreadings and competing interpretations. The piece then ties the anniversary to the 200th anniversary of Marx's birth and the 40th anniversary of reform and opening up. It is organised around four "new realms" that the author says must keep being opened up. The four realms are adapting Marxism to the Chinese context, socialism with Chinese characteristics, Party self-governance, and a twenty-first-century Marxism. Zhou cites the seven prefaces Marx and Engels wrote between 1872 and 1893 as evidence that they revised their views as practice developed. Zhou calls Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era a kind of "manifesto" for Communists in the new era. The author credits full and rigorous self-governance of the Party since the 18th Party Congress (2012) with strengthening the Party, and presents Party leadership as the greatest strength of the system. Zhou contrasts this with Western societies, which the author describes as lacking a real leading force and suffering division. The author also presents a community with a shared future for mankind as rooted in Marx's idea of an association and as a contemporary expression of the Manifesto. Zhou concludes that rereading the Manifesto means keeping to the original aspiration and mission, carrying the responsibilities that the era and the people assign, and making China's voice strong in the new era. Read the original if you want a short example of how a 2018 official commentary links the Manifesto's anniversary to Party-building and to Xi Jinping's theory.

The programmatic document of scientific socialism Commemorating the 170th anniversary of the publication of the Communist Manifesto 科学社会主义的纲领性文献 Yang Haifeng Marking 170 years since the Communist Manifesto first appeared in 1848, Yang Haifeng argues that it remains the programmatic document of scientific socialism and the most influential text of the world socialist movement. Writing as China enters what the article calls a new journey of building a modern socialist country, Yang holds that rereading it has real contemporary significance. The article has three parts. The first traces the Manifesto's role in the socialist movement: its worldwide circulation, its guidance for the Bolsheviks and the October Revolution, and its arrival in China through Chen Wangdao's 1920 translation. The second sets out the ideas Yang sees as laying the theoretical and ideological foundation of scientific socialism. The third explains why the text is still alive today. In the second part Yang identifies four contributions. The first is the 'two inevitables' (the downfall of the bourgeoisie and the victory of the proletariat), derived from the contradiction between socialised production and private ownership of the means of production. The others are the free and all-round development of the individual, the theory of proletarian revolution and proletarian dictatorship, and the doctrine of the proletarian party. In the third part Yang argues that the nature of capital has not changed, even though its forms have. Capital's harm and control are said to be greater in the age of globalisation. The Manifesto's method is presented as a tool for analysing today's Western societies, where movements over inequality, environment, race and gender intertwine with capitalism's basic contradictions. Yang concludes that the Manifesto supplies spiritual strength for communist ideals and that socialism with Chinese characteristics proves its vitality after the post-1989 setback of world socialism. Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, established at the 19th Party Congress (2017), is described as a contemporary expression of the Manifesto's spirit, with the Communist Party of China as its present-day practitioner. Read the original if you want an example of how the Manifesto was presented in the official Party press in 2018, linked to ideological education and to the new-era theory.

Using the Marxist materialist conception of history to identify erroneous social trends of thought scientifically 运用马克思主义唯物史观 科学辨识错误社会思潮 Jiang Yingchun Writing in early 2018, Jiang Yingchun asks how erroneous social trends of thought can be recognised and criticised. The article notes that since the 18th Party Congress (2012) the spread of such trends has been effectively checked, but argues that their presence and the struggle against them will be long-term. Its thesis is that these trends share a rejection of Marxist guidance, so the materialist conception of history should be used as the main tool for seeing through their theoretical surface. The piece is a short theoretical commentary built on three "correct grasps" drawn from Engels's late letters, chiefly those to Mehring (1893) and Bloch (1890). The three are the inverted nature of false consciousness, the conditioned nature of history-making, and the directionality of historical development. Jiang applies each to liberalism, Western constitutional democracy and related currents in contemporary China, and ends with the Party's disciplinary stance. First, Jiang reads Engels's account of ideology as showing that these trends separate consciousness from social being and treat ideas as self-generating. As examples, the article names Hayek's liberalism as a shared "spiritual weapon" and the claim that Western constitutional democracy is universal. Second, citing Engels's point that people make history under definite economic, political and traditional conditions, Jiang argues that these trends try to make history apart from the socialist mode of production, economic base and socialist spiritual-cultural tradition. The article gives as examples a scholar who reads 40 years of reform and opening up as a Western capitalist "modernity" project, and another who denies a distinctively Chinese social science. Third, Engels's "resultant force" of many wills must, Jiang says, be joined to the Marxist view of the masses. Otherwise it slides into voluntarism and individualism, which Jiang sees in the democracy proposals of these trends. Jiang concludes that China's conditions for making history are objective and cannot be arbitrarily removed, and that the Four-sphere Confidence is itself a necessary condition for creating history. The article stresses that the people are the real masters of history and that struggle against erroneous trends is an important task of a Marxist party. It cites the guidelines on intra-Party political life adopted by the Sixth Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2016), which require cadres to oppose such views openly. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Party theorists in 2018 used Engels's letters to frame the critique of liberalism and constitutionalism.

The inherent logic of achieving the "Two Centenary Goals" 实现“两个一百年”奋斗目标的内在逻辑 Zhu Bingyuan Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2018, Zhu Bingyuan asks what inner logic underlies the aim of achieving the "Two Centenary Goals" and building China into a modern socialist country. The article argues that this aim is both the historical trend of the Chinese nation since modern times and the internal logic of the development of socialism with Chinese characteristics. It presents the report to the 19th Party Congress (2017), which divided the second goal into two stages, as a mobilisation order issued at a decisive moment for building a moderately prosperous society. The article is organised around four "logics": historical, theoretical, practical in the sense of the people's aspirations, and the practice of the Party's governance. Each section links a different dimension of the Two Centenary Goals to the Party's course. Zhu draws on Xi Jinping's statements, the earlier "three-step" strategy of the 1980s, the sequence of Party theories since Mao Zedong, and the 19th Party Congress report. Zhu's central claims are as follows. Historically, socialism with Chinese characteristics is a unity of continuity and stages, and the goals refine the earlier "three-step" strategy into a timetable: a basically modernized country by 2035 and a strong, prosperous, democratic, culturally advanced, harmonious and beautiful country by the middle of the century. Theoretically, the Party's work has answered three questions, namely how to "stand up", "become rich" and "become strong", and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era is presented as the theory for the third. In practical terms, the principal contradiction of the new era is between the people's growing needs for a better life and unbalanced, inadequate development, and a comprehensive moderately prosperous society must be comprehensive in fields, population and regions. As for governance, the author holds that long-term rule and avoiding the "historical cycle" require modernizing the system and capacity of national governance, which the author sees as built into the goals. Zhu concludes that the goals follow necessarily from China's historical development, from theory, from popular needs and from the demands of governing, and that the strong modern socialist country is already clearly in view. The article closes by borrowing Mao Zedong's image of a rising sun. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Party theorists in 2018 explained the 19th Party Congress's timetable and tied it to the three-stage story of Chinese Marxism.

A century of ups and downs of the Swedish Communist Party 瑞典共产党的百年沧桑 Yuan Qun Writing in 2017, a century after the Swedish Communist Party was founded in May 1917, Yuan Qun uses the party as a case study of the Swedish communist movement and, more broadly, of European communism. The article argues that the party's history falls into three stages: a period as a communist party, a period of de-Sovietization, and a period as a socialist party. In Yuan's account, this path explains the party's present achievements and its continuing difficulties. The article is a chronological narrative. It begins with the split of the Social Democratic Left Party from the Swedish Social Democratic Party in 1917 and the party's entry into the Comintern. It then follows the repeated expulsions and splits of the 1920s and 1930s, the party's positions in the Second World War and its postwar rise. For the later decades it covers the break with Moscow after 1956, the changes of name to Left Communist Party (1967) and Left Party (1990), and the party's role in Swedish parliamentary politics up to 2014. Yuan's central point is that the party was repeatedly weakened by disputes over its line, above all its relation to the Soviet Union and to the Social Democrats. In this reading, Comintern interference, the pro-Soviet stance during the Soviet–Finnish war, and later the shocks of 1956, 1968 and 1989–91 cost it support. Carl-Henric Hermansson's reforms from 1964 dropped democratic centralism and Marxism-Leninism and pursued a parliamentary road. After 1990 the party redefined itself as a socialist and feminist party, which Yuan says brought parliamentary gains and a 'red-green' alliance with the Social Democrats and Greens. Yuan judges that the party has played down Marxism and relied on environmental, feminist and internationalist themes. According to the article, these themes overlap with those of rival parties and have alienated traditional working-class voters. Yuan concludes that the party remains much weaker than the Social Democrats, who built the 'Swedish model' and long dominated politics. It was also left out of government in 2014. Yuan nonetheless sees a emerging image as the 'left of the left', a more united party and a growing membership. Its future is said to depend on three things: balancing transformation with its socialist character, strengthening cooperation with the left and with extra-parliamentary movements, and widening its international influence. Read the original if you want a detailed Chinese-language account of the party's internal factions, name changes and electoral record, or a Chinese scholarly view of the European communist movement.

What is new about the new imperialism? With a critique of neoliberalism 新帝国主义“新”在何处？ David Harvey In this text, published in Chinese translation (by Qin Shiya) in Guowai Lilun Dongtai, 2017 no. 7, David Harvey asks what is genuinely new in contemporary imperialism. He engages Ellen Meiksins Wood's The Empire of Capital, which holds that classical theories of imperialism no longer fit a world in which capitalist laws are generalised. Harvey agrees with Wood on some points but argues that the novelty lies in how capital absorbs its surplus, not in a typology of empires. He sums this up in a rule: follow the surplus capital. The piece opens by distinguishing two readings of 'new' (changed material conditions, or new concepts) and by assessing Lenin, Luxemburg, Bukharin and Kautsky. It then turns to surplus absorption and the 'spatio-temporal fix', the role of the state and of global capital, and the present forms of imperialist practice. Harvey draws on his own The Limits to Capital, The New Imperialism and A Brief History of Neoliberalism, and on Giovanni Arrighi, Neil Smith and others. Harvey credits Wood's historical typology of empires but says it hides the dynamics of transition between hegemonies. He criticises her refusal to call Venice, Genoa or the Dutch Republic 'capitalist', and contrasts Arrighi's account of a continuous capitalist historical geography. In Harvey's account, capitalism faces a perpetual problem of surplus capital. It is absorbed through temporal displacement (long-term investment, credit), spatial displacement (geographical expansion, capital export), or both. Where it cannot be absorbed, crisis and devaluation follow. Since the 1970s, he argues, neoliberalism has served this end by crushing organised labour, pursuing 'globalisation', privatising public assets, feeding financial speculation and shifting devaluation onto particular places, a process he calls 'accumulation by dispossession' (rendered in this translation as 'exploitative accumulation'). He also holds that Wood's account of the state and 'American capital' is unclear, and that a new theory of the capitalist state is needed. Wood's emphasis on permanent war, he says, mistakes the particularities of recent US actions for what is new. Harvey concludes that the novelty of the new imperialism lies in the neoliberal counter-revolution after 1970, consolidated by the Washington Consensus. He says it mobilised military, political, cultural and economic power to remove barriers to absorbing surplus. He observes that surplus capital is now concentrated mainly in East and Southeast Asia, so that a range of imperialist practices, rather than a single form, now exists. He sees a possible new turn, and a nascent unity of anti-imperialism and anti-neoliberalism in global movements. Read the original if you want a Marxist geographer's critique of Wood and of classical imperialism theory, or a compact statement of Harvey's surplus-absorption argument.

Seven problems of contemporary world imperialism 当代世界帝国主义的七个问题 Watanabe Masao Watanabe Masao, a Japanese Marxist economist, sets out to rehabilitate the theory of imperialism, which he says many wrongly regard as outdated. The article, published in 2017 and translated into Chinese by Gao Chenxi, traces how the concept faded from left discourse after the 1970s and was displaced by 'globalization'. After the September 11 attacks, talk of 'empire' became fashionable, but Watanabe notes that a theory of imperialism was still not revived. The article works through seven reasons why people avoid the concept and answers each in turn. They are imperialism without colonies; geopolitical rivalry; the global structure of power; the main arena of imperialism; the global distribution of risk; domination versus hegemony; and the method of imperialism theory. Watanabe draws on Lenin, Gramsci, William Appleman Williams, Gallagher and Robinson, Panitch and Gindin, Harvey, Callinicos, Brzezinski and Buzan. Watanabe argues that imperialism never required formal colonies, citing Lenin's Argentina and Portugal, Williams's 'Open Door Imperialism' and the 'imperialism of free trade'. Hegemony does not end great-power rivalry but rests on it, and geopolitics is, in his phrase, imperialism's 'self-consciousness'. Citing a World Bank report and Callinicos, he holds that capital flows mainly among developed countries, so the driving force of imperialism lies in rivalry among them. In this reading, developing countries bear the risks, such as environmental damage, while advanced countries monopolise the benefits. The same pattern appears inside developed countries, for example the Fukushima nuclear accident, which he calls 'domestic colonies'. He adopts the three-pole view of Harvey and Callinicos over the single-pole US view of Panitch and Gindin. He also holds that US hegemony, in Gramsci's sense of leadership by consent, depends on its ability to impose its own standards on other capitalist states. Watanabe concludes that modern imperialism is an imperialism of capital, rooted in the dynamics of capitalist societies. He sees two routes to modernising the theory. One is completing Marx's unfinished plan for a critique of political economy. The other is the classical approach of Luxemburg, Hilferding, Lenin and Bukharin, which combines a critique of politics with a critique of economics. Because imperialism lies at the crossing of economic and geopolitical competition, he argues, it falls mainly under a critique of politics that Marx abandoned. He faults Japanese Marxist economists for staying on the economic plane. Read the original if you want a Japanese Marxist's case for keeping imperialism theory alive against the globalization and 'empire' paradigms, and a sketch of its methodological agenda.

Marx's inheritance and transcendence of Hegel's theme of contingency 马克思对黑格尔偶然性论题的继承与超越 Yan Yan Where, exactly, did Marx inherit and where did he go beyond Hegel on contingency (偶然性)? Yan Yan argues that Marx took over Hegel's critical stance towards contingency, and that this gave his critique of capitalist society its tension. Marx then moved beyond Hegel through a double critique of contingency and necessity, a concern with human emancipation, and a turn to practice. The article was published in Philosophical Research in 2017. Yan begins by sorting Chinese scholarship into two camps: those who rank necessity above contingency (a substance-based reading and a subject-based reading) and those who want contingency restored to Marx's thought. The article frames its own approach as a philosophy of history, not epistemology, centred on individual fate under modernity. It then takes Hegel's treatment in the Logic, the Philosophy of History and the Philosophy of Right, and follows Marx from early writings through The German Ideology, the Communist Manifesto and the Grundrisse and Capital. A final section sets out the comparison, with a note on differences between Marx and Engels. For Yan, Hegel treats contingency as a defective, unfree form that must be sublated into necessity, with the state as the ethical universal above civil society and its "contingent" private individuals. Marx first rejected contingency in abstract humanist terms. In The German Ideology he recast the problem as that of the "contingent individual", the atomised, class-bound person produced by capitalist modernity and ruled by the power of things, money and exchange value. Yan then identifies four advances over Hegel: from epistemology to ontology; from conceptual speculation to real history; from necessitarianism to a theory of possibility, in which the revolutionary subject must act; and from contingency's pre-assumed legitimacy to its empirically grounded rationality. Yan concludes that Marx combined subjective and objective dimensions, which bears on the continuing Chinese dispute over whether to read him through the subject or the object. In practical terms, Yan holds, Marx's critique helps people recognise the nature of present social life and resist an "anything goes" postmodern way of living. His wariness of necessity also warns against retreating into fatalism out of fear of contingency. Read the original if you work on Marx's relation to Hegel, on the philosophy of history, or on how Chinese scholars debate necessity, contingency and the subject–object question in Marx.

Shaping the political subject in the age of the "end of history" The programme of Europe's psychoanalytic "radical left" “历史终结”时代政治主体的形塑 Zhou Zhijian Francis Fukuyama's claim that liberal capitalism marks the "end of history" has been taken up again by a group of European philosophers, chiefly Slavoj Žižek, Alain Badiou and Jacques Rancière. Zhou Zhijian treats them as a psychoanalytic "radical left" that shares Lacan's theory and asks one question: after the "end of history", how can a political subject capable of social change be formed? The article argues that this current offers a negative, ontological critique rather than a positive blueprint. The article opens with the claim that this current arose in dissatisfaction with the previous generation of post-structuralist left thinkers, whom Zhou sees as absorbed into global capitalism. It then moves through three parts. The first reconstructs Lacan's Real, Symbolic and Imaginary, the "barred Other" and the death drive. The second turns to Žižek's and Badiou's accounts of the "event". The third sets the whole current against the Socratic tradition of negative philosophy and examines the candidates each thinker offers for a future political subject. Zhou's central claim is that, for Lacan, the Symbolic order never closes: a remainder of the Real always escapes the Other, so every particular order stays open at the ontological level. Žižek reads Kant's antinomies and Hegel through the "parallax view", so that the gap itself becomes the solution. Žižek and Badiou diverge over the event. Žižek fears that Badiou's "truth-event" simply produces a new symbolic order, another Other, and prefers to move alone toward the death drive. For the future subject, Žižek points to the "excluded", Badiou to an "unidentifiable set" that forms only after an event, and Rancière to the "part of no part". Zhou presents all three as rejecting the classical Marxist proletariat and the identity politics of Laclau and Mouffe. Zhou concludes that these thinkers supply no directly justified political programme. They keep a critical distance from existing power structures and mainstream ideology and insist that capitalism is not the end of history. In Zhou's account they envisage a "communism" reactivated under new historical conditions, and although they cannot offer a concrete alternative path, they guard against a slide into absolutist political theology. Read the original if you want a Chinese doctoral-level reading of Žižek, Badiou and Rancière that traces their common debt to Lacan and their disagreement over the event.

Recent advances in foreign Marxist political economy's study of "capitalism" 国外马克思主义政治经济学对“资本主义”研究的最新进展 Chen Jianhua This literature review, published in 2017, surveys how Marxist political economists outside China have studied capitalism since the 2008–2009 global financial crisis. Chen Jianhua argues that, because contemporary capitalism has moved beyond the conditions Marx analysed and has become diverse, these scholars have redefined the concept, mapped its varieties and diagnosed its present difficulties. The review treats this work as a development of Marxist political economy and a source of lessons for China. The survey has three main parts, followed by a section of commentary. The first covers new definitions of "capitalism", drawing on Sumio Shigeta, Joyce Appleby, Robert Heilbroner, Dieter Klein and Michael Brie, and David Harvey. The second covers capitalist diversity, including typologies by Paul Dragos Aligica and Vlad Tarko, Tsuruta Masahiko, Eyüp Özveren and colleagues, and Michele Mastroeni. The third covers the crises and contradictions of modern capitalism. On definition, Chen reports a shift from capitalism as a mode of production to capitalism as a comprehensive social formation spanning economy, politics, culture and ideology, now extended globally. On crisis, Chen traces class polarisation and social stratification to the over-development of finance capital and the property sector, citing Heilbroner, Stockman, Michael Hudson and Takata Takakichi, and the class-analysis school and the Social Structure of Accumulation school. Scholars then split into two camps. Wallerstein, Collins, Calhoun and Goldner see structural crisis and possible collapse. Harvey and the Regulation School (Aglietta, Lipietz, Boyer) hold that regulation can renew capitalism. Chen concludes that this work has strengthened Marxist political economy and offers three lessons for the study of socialism with Chinese characteristics. First, Marxist standpoints and methods remain useful. Second, research should rest on practice and attend to new problems, notably financialisation, property-sector dominance and income gaps. Third, holistic, interdisciplinary methods are needed. Chen also warns of three weaknesses: the concept of capitalism has been stretched so far that it loses rigour, some scholars over-rely on quantitative tools, and the conciliatory view that capitalism can renew itself is gaining ground. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's map of Western and Japanese Marxist debates on the definition, varieties and crises of capitalism, together with the lessons Chen draws for Chinese political economy.

New trends in contemporary Western scholars' research on Capital 当代西方学者《资本论》研究的新趋向 Tai Lihua Marking 150 years since the first volume of Capital appeared, Tai Lihua asks how Western scholarship on the work should be characterised. Tai argues that Chinese attempts to divide it into historical periods are somewhat subjective and tend towards simplification. Instead, the article identifies three main tendencies: 'overall negation', 'communication and integration' and 'transcending reconstruction'. The article first reviews Chinese 'periodisation' accounts: the two-stage view of Pei Xiaoge, the three-stage views of Yan Zheng and Wei Xun, and the four-stage view of Chen Shaohua and Guo Guangdi. It then examines each tendency in turn, drawing on figures such as Böhm-Bawerk, Schumpeter, Samuelson, Keynes, Sraffa, Paul Baran, Paul Sweezy, Michael Lebowitz, David Harvey and John Roemer. Tai describes overall negation as an attack on the labour theory of value, often by pointing to a contradiction between volumes I and III. It also includes setting a 'young' Marx against the mature Marx, Marx against Engels or Lenin, and declaring Capital obsolete. Tai notes that this did not mean abandoning Marxian economics wholesale, since volume II in particular was used. Communication and integration, which Tai places after the Great Depression, compares Marx with Keynes, Sraffa, Walras, Leontief and Harrod–Domar in method, themes and specific theories. Transcending reconstruction, described as the mainstream tendency since the 1960s, alters concepts (Baran and Sweezy's 'economic surplus', Harvey's 'accumulation by dispossession'), conclusions (the law of rising surplus against the falling rate of profit) and methods (Lebowitz's priority of human needs, Roemer's neoclassical modelling). Tai characterises Lebowitz's move as replacing a materialist with an idealist methodology. Tai concludes that the three tendencies have no clear temporal boundaries and are not mutually exclusive. They coexist and overlap, and all remain visible in the debates after the US subprime crisis and the eurozone crisis. Tai states that whether these tendencies develop, innovate on or depart from Marxism is left to a later article. Following Western research is said to broaden Chinese scholars' horizons and help integrate Chinese study of Capital into international scholarship. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese-language map of Western schools of Capital interpretation and of how Chinese scholars periodise them.

The dissemination and reception of Marx's Capital in Britain and the United States 马克思《资本论》在英美的传播与接受 Babak Amini This is a Chinese translation of an article by Babak Amini of York University, Canada. It asks how Marx's Capital has been translated, published, circulated and interpreted in Britain and the United States since the first volume appeared in 1867. The article is one part of a larger project on the global reception of Capital, edited with Marcello Musto and timed for the 150th anniversary in 2017. Amini presents the history as a political as well as a bibliographical story: it shows how Marx's insights were taken up, distorted or ignored. The article has two parts: the transmission of Capital through full and abridged translations and editions, and its reception through influential secondary literature in English. Amini first compiles a publication record, noting which volumes each edition contained and which German or French text it used. He then divides 1867–2017 into three periods: 1867–1914, 1915–1989 and 1990–2017. The article also recounts the editing of the three volumes, from Marx's revisions through Engels's posthumous editing, and explains why abridgements mattered in times of political repression such as the Red Scare and McCarthyism. In the early period, Amini argues, Marx's ideas spread slowly in Britain because of the reformist character of the socialist movement. The first English-language extracts and translations (Aveling and Moore, 1887; Kerr's editions of volumes two and three, 1907–09) are set against a different American context shaped by German émigré socialists. In the middle period he follows the successive translations: Eden and Cedar Paul in 1928 (criticised by Riazanov), the Moscow editions, the Fowkes and Fernbach Penguin/New Left Review translation, and the Marx-Engels Collected Works. He also covers Kevin Anderson's 1983 critique, which stresses differences between the French and German editions, and the main English-language studies, including Althusser and Balibar's Reading Capital and works by Sweezy, Baran, Braverman and others. For the post-1989 period Amini notes a lull in Marxist publishing, followed by a revival through the Collected Works volumes, edited collections, David Harvey's companion volumes and online lectures. He also reports the 2014 withdrawal of free online access to the Collected Works for copyright reasons. He suggests that, with the MEGA2 manuscripts now available, a new English translation is likely and that it will challenge dogmatic and contested readings accumulated over 150 years. Read the original if you want a detailed bibliographic and editorial history of English editions of Capital and a guide to the main Anglophone commentaries on it.

Karl Marx: critique as emancipatory practice 卡尔·马克思:作为解放实践的批判 Robin Celikates This is a Chinese translation of an article by the Dutch philosopher Robin Celikates. It asks what Marx's many critiques (of philosophy, religion, politics and political economy) have in common, and whether they still matter for contemporary critical theory. Celikates argues that Marx's notion of critique has three features: it targets both forms of knowledge and the social practices that match them; it is practical and emancipatory, aiming to change society as well as understand it; and it is immanent, rooted in the contradictions of capitalist society and its false self-understanding. Understood as a practice rather than a science, Celikates holds, it remains exemplary. The article proceeds in four steps. It first outlines Marx's methodological and theoretical premises: historical materialism, the base–superstructure relation, class struggle, and a historically conditioned view of human nature. It then sets out Marx's critique of liberalism as an example of lasting relevance, and examines his critique of religion as the model for ideology critique. A final section returns to the three features and answers Jürgen Habermas's charge that Marxism wrongly understood itself as a science. Celikates lists six strands of Marx's critique of liberalism: politics is shaped by economic conditions and is class struggle; bourgeois freedom and equality are individualistic; liberal practice reproduces exploitation; alienation pervades capitalism; ideology naturalises historical relations and presents class interests as the common good; and redistribution leaves production relations untouched. The author also names limits: economism, teleological and deterministic tendencies that sit uneasily with the stress on struggle, and the tension between scientific ambition and normative critique. The critique of religion is read as immanent: religion is a reflection of, and protest against, real social suffering. Marx therefore sublates it, preserving its vision of a life without suffering while removing the conditions that produce it. Celikates concludes that Marx's text offers a third option between pure science and pure philosophy, combining description, explanation and normativity. Since the proletarian standpoint and a so-called science of history can no longer ground critique, critique should be understood as the self-clarification of contemporary struggles and wishes, as in Marx's 1843 letter to Ruge. Contemporary critical theory should recognise its own historicity, join philosophy, history and sociology, and avoid both dogmatic abstract norms and paternalism toward ordinary subjects. Read the original if you study Marx's method, the Habermasian reading of Marxism, or the debate over immanent critique in Western critical theory.

The crisis of contemporary capitalism and the resistance of the Western Left New trends in Western left-wing thought as seen from the 2017 New York left forum 当代资本主义的危机与西方左翼的反抗 Jin Meng This is a report and commentary on the left forum held in New York in June 2017 under the theme 'Resistance: Strategy, Tactics, Struggle, Solidarity and Utopia'. Writing in 2017, Jin Meng places the forum against the wave of protests that followed Donald Trump's inauguration. The article argues that the forum's speakers looked past Trump himself and aimed their critique at the capitalist system that produced him. The report is organised around three themes debated at the forum: Marxism and its contemporary value; the crisis of capitalism and the future of socialism in the Trump era; and the history, present state and future of left-wing resistance. It closes with a short assessment by the author. Speakers named include David Schweickart, Nancy Holmstrom, Peter Hudis, David M. Kotz, Michael Hudson, Michael Perelman, Cinzia Arruzza and L. A. Kauffman. On the first theme, Jin reports that, in the 150th anniversary year of Capital, participants held that it still offers the most persuasive tools for analysing exploitation, overwork, unemployment and alienated labour. On the second, Kotz and others are reported as tracing Trump's election to the crisis of neoliberalism. In Kotz's account Trump's right-wing nationalism scapegoats foreigners and migrants but leaves neoliberalism intact. Speakers presented women's oppression, climate change, racism and migration as products of capitalism, and proposed a universal basic income, public banks, workers' cooperatives and a political alliance of oppressed groups. On resistance, speakers named three weaknesses: the target is misplaced (the Democratic Party's co-optation), no alternative is offered, and forces are fragmented. They proposed educating the public about capitalism, building a united front and drawing in young people. In her own assessment, Jin credits the forum with clarifying the direction of struggle and drawing the Left together. She also notes that participants include democratic socialists, anarchists and reformists with differing views of Marxism, and that their practical proposals lack unity and workability. The author concludes that the foreign Left needs a strong command centre and a broader united front. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic view of how the US Left framed Trump, capitalism and resistance in 2017, or a list of the forum's speakers and themes.

Western left-wing scholars' theories of capitalist crisis from the perspective of the "mode of production" and their recent developments “生产方式”视域下西方左翼学者的资本主义危机理论及其新进展 Yan Fangjie Since the mid-twentieth century, Western left-wing scholars have produced many theories of capitalist crisis. Yan Fangjie divides them into two research perspectives: a "cultural" one, concerned with ideology, aesthetics and everyday life, and a "mode of production" one that follows Marx's critique of political economy. The article takes up the second and argues that, although it looks conservative and traditional, it stays closer to the substance of Marxism than much culture-centred work. The article surveys these scholars in three groups. The first stresses internal crises of the mode of production, represented by Ernest Mandel and István Mészáros. The second stresses "obstructive" crises arising from external conditions of production, represented by James O'Connor and, for the ecological case, André Gorz. The third applies the approach to the twenty-first-century financial crisis and splits into pessimists (Immanuel Wallerstein, Randall Collins) and optimists (Michael Mann, Craig Calhoun, and others). Yan reads Mandel and Mészáros as locating crisis in the contradiction between productive forces and relations of production, and in the gap between production and consumption. In this reading, arms spending and wasteful or destructive production deepen the contradiction instead of resolving it. O'Connor adds a "second contradiction" between capital and its conditions of production, such as nature, labour-power and infrastructure. Rising costs of these conditions produce ecological and social crisis. For the recent crisis, Wallerstein sees rising personnel, material and tax costs together with geopolitical disorder. Collins foresees technological displacement of middle-class work, with structural unemployment of 50 per cent by about 2040. Mann and Calhoun doubt that economic crisis alone is fatal. They point to ecological limits and the end of cost externalisation, and Calhoun speaks of "decline" rather than collapse. Yan describes the pessimists as system-theoretic and the optimists as Weberian in method. Yan concludes that these scholars' specifics are sometimes far apart and open to question. Even so, their use of categories such as productive forces, relations of production, effective demand, underconsumption and the falling rate of profit is called valuable. Some of them treat the financial crisis as an extension of traditional economic crisis, not a purely technical accident. Yan argues that this makes their work an analysis of capitalism's essence, not an external study. Read the original if you want a compact Chinese-language map of Western left and critical theories of capitalist crisis, from Mandel to Wallerstein and Calhoun, organised around the mode of production.

"Neoliberalism" and the Western New Left “新自由主义”与西方新左派 Zhou Jiaxin Zhou Jiaxin asks how critique of neoliberalism has shaped the development of the contemporary Western Left, using New Left Review as the main vantage point. The article counts roughly 60 neoliberalism-focused papers in the journal since the 1990s. Its thesis is that neoliberalism is the theoretical system of monopoly finance capitalism, and that its apparent collapse after the 2008 financial crisis offers the Western "new left" a historic opening for theoretical breakthrough. The article has four parts. It first defines neoliberalism and separates it from classical liberalism and from "New Liberalism" (Keynes, Rawls and others). It then analyses neoliberalism's political economy under three headings: financialization, globalization and structural crisis. The third part traces how the Left's own theory evolved in confrontation with neoliberalism, and the fourth maps five directions for the Left after 2008. Zhou argues that neoliberalism is not simply a revived laissez-faire. Where classical liberalism defended private property and industrial capital, neoliberalism, in this reading, serves the freedom of monopoly finance capital, its "disembedding" from social and political constraints. The Washington Consensus is presented as its classic expression, and David Harvey's label "new imperialism" as exposing its ideological nature. Zhou endorses the view that globalization, financialization, internet technology and asset bubbles were only temporary "fixes" for the basic contradiction of capital accumulation, and that income inequality, separatism and migration tensions show neoliberalism's bankruptcy. On the Left's trajectory, Zhou holds that Western Marxism, a "Weberian Marxism" tied to the welfare state and organised capitalism, reached its logical end around 1979. Post-Marxism then set aside the dialectic, and a return to it followed around the turn of the century in Žižek, Christopher Arthur's "new dialectic", Foster, Harvey and Jameson. Zhou identifies five post-2008 tendencies in Western left theory: world-system and globalization critique, with space and urban analysis; identity, ethnicity and migration; biopolitics; information, network and media critique; and a "return to the critique of political economy" via Capital. Neoliberal critique is proposed as a yardstick for assessing foreign Marxism since the 1970s. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's map of how New Left Review-centred debates linked neoliberalism, the fate of Western Marxism and the revival of the dialectic.

The historical fate of twenty-first-century capitalism Western left-wing scholars' new examination of the crisis of capitalism 21世纪资本主义的历史命运 Tong Jin Almost a decade after the global crisis of 2008, this article, published in 2017, reviews how Western left-wing scholars have reassessed capitalism and its prospects. Tong argues that these thinkers have become more rational and objective in their criticism, and that their views offer useful reference points for Chinese readers, even though many do not seek to replace capitalism. The review is organised in four parts: whether the crisis is systemic; who bears its costs; how the crisis turns from danger into opportunity; and what scholars predict for capitalism's future. It draws on Berch Berberoglu, William I. Robinson, Immanuel Wallerstein, Chase-Dunn and Roberts, Niall Ferguson, James Petras and Henry Veltmeyer, Michael Koyama, Régis Debray, Fred Magdoff and Michael Yates, Wolfgang Streeck and Rémy Herrera. Tong reports that most of these scholars see a systemic, institutional crisis, which some think could end capitalism as a system, while Koyama and others want it rescued through radical reform. Drawing on Petras and Veltmeyer, the article presents the working class as the real bearer of the crisis: corporate profits recovered, the 'revolving door' between Wall Street and the Treasury protected capital, and austerity brought unemployment, especially among young people. Tong then argues that capitalism is losing its historical rationality and its capacity for self-adjustment, because bailouts deepen financialisation. The same crisis, in this reading, hardens the working class's class consciousness and so trains capitalism's 'gravediggers'. On the future, Tong notes that Debray lists Western weaknesses but also strengths, such as cohesion, control of 'universal' values, elite financial schools, media influence and technological lead. Streeck and Herrera expect a long decline, with Herrera saying that more and more people hope socialism will replace capitalism. Tong concludes that the replacement of capitalism by socialism is inevitable but will be long and tortuous. Citing Xi Jinping, Tong warns against blindly talking down capitalism and calls for using the crisis actively to advance world socialism. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist survey of Western left-wing literature on the post-2008 crisis and of how it is used to frame socialism's prospects.

Deepening methodological self-awareness in Chinese studies of Capital The political reading of Capital in international scholarship and its assessment 深化中国《资本论》研究的方法论自觉 Tang Zhengdong Marking the 150th anniversary of the first volume of Capital, Tang argues that commemoration should prompt reflection on how Capital is read today. Since the 1970s, international scholarship has produced philosophical, economic and political readings, each tied to its own context. Tang contends that Chinese scholars should build their own reading of Capital from China's practical experience, and that this requires methodological self-awareness towards foreign readings rather than uncritical adoption. The article concentrates on the "political reading" of Capital and its manuscripts, which it calls the most fashionable approach on the foreign left. It examines Antonio Negri (Marx beyond Marx, on the Grundrisse), Harry Cleaver (Reading Capital Politically) and, more briefly, Jacques Bidet's meta-structural reading. A closing section extends the point to philosophical readings centred on fetishism and reification, and to similar tendencies in Chinese scholarship. Tang summarises the political reading in three claims: Marx wrote to build the working class's revolutionary subjectivity; his object, the commodity form, embodies relations of power and exploitation; and value survives only within surplus value, which exists only through class struggle. Negri locates this in the money form, which hides inequality behind equivalence; Cleaver locates it in the commodity form imposed on workers. Tang credits the approach with textual grounding and sensitivity to new phenomena, and finds Cleaver the more rigorous of the two. He nonetheless faults both for neglecting the production process. In his view they treat the commodity at the level of bourgeois exchange, and so miss that capital's logic is the production of capital as capital, and that Marx's concepts rest on historical materialism. Tang argues that they criticise unequal distribution while accepting that productive forces keep growing, and so pursue piecemeal political movements rather than revolution against the whole system. Bidet's recasting of Marx's method, he adds, oversimplifies Marx. Tang concludes that Capital's political dimension matters but cannot be its only one. Political and cultural perspectives should be placed within the overall history of social development and its inner contradictions. Chinese scholars, whose aims differ from those of Negri and Cleaver, should not accept foreign readings merely because they are popular. Tang also links methodological self-awareness to the study of the laws governing the building of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a Chinese philosophical critique of Negri, Cleaver and Bidet, and an example of how Chinese Marxist scholars position Capital studies against Western left readings.

Marx's "near-Adorno" interpretation John Holloway's reconstruction of the path of critiquing capitalism 马克思的近阿多诺阐释 Sun Liang Many readings recast Marx as "near-Kant" or "near-Hegel", and Sun Liang asks what follows from the "near-Adorno" reading developed by John Holloway, a representative of Open Marxism. Sun argues that Holloway uses Adorno's negative dialectics to rescue Marx from a Hegelian tradition in which capitalism is criticised from within a closed category. Holloway also reproaches Hardt and Negri, who reject Hegel, for misunderstanding dialectics and falling back into traditional Marxism's limits. Sun judges the approach a forceful corrective that is nonetheless too idealistic. The article has three parts. The first sets out why Holloway, following Adorno, rejects Hegelian dialectics as a "straitjacket" and how this differs from the post-structuralist rejection by Althusser, Deleuze, Hardt and Negri. The second explains Adorno's notion of non-identity and Holloway's concept of the "crack". The third turns to Marx's Capital and Holloway's shift from the "productive forces of capital" to the "social productive force of labour". Sources are mainly Holloway's Negativity and Revolution, Crack Capitalism and In, Against, and Beyond Capitalism, together with Adorno's Negative Dialektik. Sun reports that Holloway accepts the charge that Hegelian dialectics reduces varied struggles to a single contradiction between labour and capital that ends in "reconciliation". But Hardt and Negri, in his view, also discard the dialectic's negative movement, and so still hope for a harmonious "common world". Adorno's non-identity, which Holloway ties to the idea that "we" overflow every identity, including that of the working class, becomes the basis for a critical theory that starts from capitalism's cracks and not from its domination. Holloway reads exchange as the social model of identity-thinking, and he rejects vanguard politics and the idea of seizing power. On Marx, Sun reports that Holloway reads the productive forces under capitalism as the fetishised power of capital. He locates human creative capacity in the "social productive force of labour", which grows in the slippage between obedience and rebellion, and he points to wiki-style and sharing production as examples. Sun concludes that this dissolves Marx's concept of revolution and shifts liberation from ownership relations to inner freedom, ignoring the ordinary person's need to adapt to capital. Sun still finds it meaningful because life itself is precious. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist assessment of Holloway and of Open Marxism's debts to Adorno.

Three interpretive paths for Capital and its manuscripts 《资本论》及其手稿的三种诠释路径 Lu Shaochen Lu Shaochen asks how Capital and its manuscripts have been read since the early twentieth century. The author argues that the history of their reception, even if it can be called a history of misreading, is what has kept Marx's thought lively and made dogmatic readings untenable. The article reviews and assesses three paths of interpretation in Western and foreign Marxism. The article is organised in four sections. The first treats the early Western Marxist 'continuity thesis' (Lukács, Korsch, Fromm, with Luxemburg). The second treats the 'rupture thesis' of Althusser and its political and power-oriented continuation in Negri, Hardt and Harry Cleaver's 'political reading'. The third turns to the 'New Dialectic' and value-form readings (Chris Arthur, Tony Smith, Fred Moseley, Moishe Postone, Riccardo Bellofiore and others), made possible by the MEGA edition. A final section considers the philological work on the texts and gives Lu's own view. In Lu's account, the first path stresses totality, the historicity of capitalism, alienated labour and reification, and sees no qualitative break between the young and the mature Marx. Critics, including Postone and Perry Anderson, are cited as saying that it criticises 'alienation' rather than 'capital' and drifts away from political economy towards philosophy and aesthetics. The second path reads capital as a power relation and gives priority to working-class subjectivity. Alex Callinicos, as presented by Lu, replies that it reduces Marx to a Foucauldian theory of power and collapses the three dimensions of capitalism (exchange, exploitation and domination, and competition among capitals) into one. The third path reads Marx through Hegel's Logic, treating value, abstract labour and the value form as social forms and capital as a 'living contradiction'. It is criticised for neglecting exploitation and class struggle, and for drawing too close a parallel between Capital and Hegel. The same school's study of Engels's editing of Marx's text, such as the changed subtitle of volume one and the altered passage on the falling rate of profit, is also reported. Lu concludes that MEGA allows Capital and its manuscripts to be reread on a firmer philological footing and outside the tradition shaped by Engels. The author holds that Hegel's logic is for Marx mainly a method of scientific research. What keeps driving fresh readings, Lu argues, is the development and present condition of modern society. Read the original if you want a critical map of the main Western interpretive schools of Capital, with attention to the MEGA-based debates, as seen by a Chinese philosopher.

From the principle of justice to the principle of community With a note on the lessons of G. A. Cohen's socialist project 从正义原则到共同体原则 Lin Yuchuan Lin Yuchuan reconstructs the political philosophy of the analytical Marxist G. A. Cohen as an argument for the desirability, and then the feasibility, of an ideal socialism. Lin's thesis is that Cohen moves from principles of justice to a principle of community, built on generosity and mutual aid, which is meant to go beyond justice and equality. The article reads Cohen in three steps: his exposure of a conflict between liberal justice as fairness and community; the return of community in egalitarian distributive justice (justice as equality); and his ideal socialism as a community that surpasses justice. It engages John Rawls, Ronald Dworkin, Will Kymlicka, Richard Miller and Marx's Critique of the Gotha Programme, and draws on Cohen's Rescuing Justice and Equality and Why Not Socialism?. A final section draws lessons for China. Lin argues that Rawls's difference principle fits community through compensation, reciprocity and fraternity, yet loses it once incentives are used to justify inequality. On Cohen's interpersonal test, talented people who demand high pay as an incentive are in effect threatening to withdraw their labour, which signals a lack of community. Cohen's own luck egalism, equality of access to advantage, restores community by compensating involuntary disadvantage. Lin notes that it remains hard to apply, for example to non-material goods such as self-respect. Cohen's camping-trip model then places equality and community together, with community ultimately governing equality. Lin reads Cohen as differing from Marx: he doubts that material abundance will arrive, and puts his hope in mechanisms that draw out human generosity. Lin concludes that Cohen's project is not a blueprint to copy and that its value is reflective. Lin draws three lessons for China. First, Cohen's sequence of distributive models, from Nozick to Rawls and Cohen, shows the limits of distribution according to work. Second, his critique of the market warns against market worship. Lin does not call for abandoning the market, but for limiting it in fields such as education and health. Third, just institutions need a social ethos of equality and community, because individual greed can erode institutions. Read the original if you study Cohen, Rawls or analytical Marxism, or want to see how a Chinese philosopher draws on Cohen's work to discuss distribution and social justice in China.

Negri on Spinoza's biopolitics 奈格里论斯宾诺莎的生命政治 Feng Bo Feng Bo asks how Spinoza's philosophy relates to biopolitics, a link the author says has long been neglected. The usual story runs from Nietzsche's turn to the body to Foucault's account of biopolitics. Feng argues that Antonio Negri, himself a Spinozist Marxist, shows Spinoza had already made the turn to the body, and that Negri reads biopolitics very differently from Foucault. The article uses Negri's texts to clarify both the Spinoza connection and Negri's distinctive concept. The article has three parts. The first compares Negri's definition of biopolitics with Foucault's account of biopower. The second examines Negri's reading of Spinoza's critique of biopower, through the terms conatus or striving, impulse, potentia (power as productive force), potestas (power as authority) and immanence. The third turns to how Negri sees Spinoza constructing a democratic biopolitics, through the critique of social contract theory in Hobbes and Rousseau. Feng draws on Negri, Hardt, Macherey, Foucault and Spinoza's own texts. Feng reports that Foucault confines biopower to the modern power to make live, whereas Negri widens it to include sovereignty's power over death and disciplinary power. For Negri biopower is therefore as old as the state, and biopolitics is not its politics but its opposite: a stateless, immanent politics of the polis, built from the bodily impulses of singularities. Feng explains that Negri takes from Spinoza the distinction between potentia, an immanent, productive and bodily force, and potestas, a transcendent power that is constructed and speculative. He takes 'multitude' from Spinoza too. Negri also holds that Spinoza gave up contract theory and thereby sovereignty. Rousseau's general will, in Negri's reading, yields only a 'democratic monarchy', while Spinoza's 'will of all' tolerates difference and grounds absolute democracy. Feng concludes that Negri's creative reading lets Spinoza dissolve sovereignty as biopower and ground a biopolitics collectively built from bodily forces and plurality. Feng also notes a tension. Negri ignores Spinoza's pessimism about the masses' superstition and fear, and optimistically affirms the free multitude as the agent of resistance. Feng therefore calls Negri a Spinozist who goes beyond Spinoza. Read the original if you work on Negri, Spinoza or biopolitics and want a Chinese scholarly account of how Negri's concept differs from Foucault's and of its Spinozist sources.

Alain Badiou on subjectivization and the subjective process 阿兰·巴迪欧论主体化和主体进程 Ai Shiwei Ai Shiwei examines how Alain Badiou, whom the article calls a leading representative of post-Marxism, builds his theory of the subject. Badiou rejects both the idealist model, which separates subject from body, and the materialist model, which reduces the subject to the body. He proposes a third model in which the subject sits between event and truth and stays faithful to the event. Ai argues that this subject is split into two aspects, subjectivization and the subjective process, and that understanding them is essential to Badiou's theory. Ai notes that, apart from Ed Pluth's study, existing literature treats the two terms only in passing. The article is organised in three sections: subjectivization, the subjective process, and their combination. It draws mainly on Badiou's Theory of the Subject (1982), with Being and Event, Logics of Worlds and Conditions as supporting texts. It also uses Bruno Bosteels's translator's introduction and Pluth's commentary. Ai traces the terms back to Lacan and compares Badiou's 'superego' with Freud, Foucault and Lacan. Badiou's analysis of class struggle in France serves as a worked example, and the closing pages place Theory of the Subject within his later development. Ai presents subjectivization as brief, destructive and interventionist, a rupture with an existing situation, such as an uprising, and it takes two forms: 'anxiety' (pure destruction) and 'courage' (destruction that aims at a new order). The subjective process is lasting and reorganising, and it also takes two forms: the 'superego', which Badiou calls a terroristic process that fixes the excess elements in rigid places, and 'justice', which relativises law and blurs fixed positions. Their pairings produce the Ψ mode (anxiety–superego) and the α mode (courage–justice). Ai reads Badiou's 'imaginary diagonals' through Lacan: courage–superego yields a dogmatic function, and justice–anxiety a sceptical function that ends in nothing. Ai maps the pairings onto class struggle: riot and the dictatorship of the proletariat for Ψ, insurrection and communism for α. The two aspects, Ai says, verify and raise each other in a spiral, as in materialist dialectics. Ai concludes that Badiou rejects Descartes' separation of subject and body, Nietzsche's exaltation of the body and mechanical materialism's reduction of the subject to the body. The subject is the body's subjective form, and the body is the subjectivized body. Ai adds that Badiou later extended the subject beyond politics to science, art and love, and criticised his early assumption that subjectivization simply 'exists'. Ai reads this as a move beyond pure deconstruction toward the possible formation and reconstruction of the subject. Read the original if you study Badiou, Lacanian philosophy or post-Marxist theories of the subject and want a close reading of Theory of the Subject.

Rethinking the connotation of ideological and political education 对思想政治教育内涵的再思考 Li Chunhua Shangguan Miaomiao Li Chunhua and Shangguan Miaomiao take up a basic question in the field of ideological and political education: what exactly is it? They note that research seldom addresses this "connotation" directly and usually approaches it through studies of its essence, content or value. The authors argue that a scientific definition is a precondition for the field to count as a science, and that it should rest on three principles: objectivity, universality and intrinsicality. The article opens by explaining why the definition matters and then devotes one section to each principle, testing prevailing definitions in the Chinese literature against it. Along the way it draws on Engels's notion of a science of thought, the history of psychology, the Marxist theory of ruling ideas, and surveys of scholarly views on the essence of ideological and political education, including a ten-position summary published in 2016. It closes with the authors' own definition. On objectivity, the authors hold that a definition must describe what has actually existed, not what is desired. In their view, common formulations that stress following the laws of how thought, character and psychology develop describe an ideal, scientific form available only to proletarian-party education, since the relevant sciences are barely a century old. On universality, they criticise three habits: treating the activity as coextensive with human society, when in their account it exists only in class societies; requiring it to be purposeful, planned and organised, when much influence was spontaneous; and attributing it only to ruling classes, when ruled classes and parties also conduct it. On intrinsicality, they argue the definition must capture the essence, which they describe as grasping people with ideas and theory, and must leave out derivative content such as the free and all-round development of the person or mental-health education. The authors define ideological and political education as the social practice in which, in all societies since the emergence of classes, a given class, party or organisation influences and educates people with its own ideas or theory. They conclude that its essence is to win people over with ideological theory, and that in China this means winning people over with scientific Marxist theory. They hope the definition satisfies the three principles and helps clarify the field. Read the original if you work on the disciplinary foundations of ideological and political education in China and want to see how its definitions are criticised and reconstructed.

The Absolute and the event: what kind of Hegelian is Žižek? 绝对与事件：齐泽克是一个怎样的黑格尔主义者 Wu Guanjun Hegel is the modern philosopher of totality, and twentieth-century thought often charged that his system leaves no room for the event, understood as a rupture with reason and teleology. Wu Guanjun asks how Slavoj Žižek can call himself a committed Hegelian and also make the event an ontological category. The article answers that Žižek reads Hegel's Absolute as a whole with a gap built into it, and that this reading lets negativity itself produce the new. The article first sets out the standard picture of Hegel, in which the Absolute is both the truth of all events and their cause, so that events have meaning only as parts of the whole. Wu then compares Žižek with Alain Badiou, who started out as a student of Hegel but turned anti-Hegelian once he developed his theory of the event in Being and Event. Wu also brings in Nancy, Derrida, Deleuze and Kojève. The later sections cover Žižek's account of dialectics, the parallax view, the Fall as the ultimate event, and Žižek's hidden debt to Kojève. Wu argues that Žižek treats the dialectic as a change of framework, not a change of content: the negation of the negation overturns the whole symbolic frame, so that the law itself becomes the crime. Totality exists only with a gap, or absolute difference, embedded in it. Absolute knowledge therefore means recognising that gap and one's own limits, not seeing as God sees, and history has no endpoint. Against Badiou's claim that negation is derivative and creates nothing, Žižek holds that negation is ontologically primary. In his view the new affirmation is the positivised power of the negative, and the ultimate event is the Fall itself. Wu traces this stress on negation and creativity to Kojève's formula that freedom equals negativity equals creativity, a debt Žižek never acknowledges. Wu concludes that Žižek rejects the image of Hegel as an all-knowing absolute idealist. In Žižek's reading, absolute spirit confronts the ontological wound between reality and the Real, and it keeps tearing apart any attempt by the present order to totalise itself. Wu also corrects John Gray, who traced Žižek's Hegel to Badiou and tied it to capitalism. On Wu's account it comes from Kojève and describes the ontological structure of the world. Read the original if you want a detailed account of how Žižek, Badiou and Kojève relate to one another on Hegel, negation and the event, or if you want to trace Žižek's Hegel reading through its sources.)

"Truth procedure" and "subtractive politics": an analysis of Badiou's radical left philosophy “真理程序”和“减法政治”：试析巴迪欧的左翼激进哲学 Fan Chunyan Fan Chunyan examines how Alain Badiou tries to revive universal truth and the idea of communism under postmodern and post-revolutionary conditions. In Fan's reading, Badiou refuses a return to essentialist, 'capital-One' conceptions and instead builds on the 'irreducible multiplicity of being'. The article argues that his project rests on two core concepts, 'truth procedure' and 'subtractive politics', which answer respectively the question of truth and the question of how to practise communism anew. The article has two main parts. The first reconstructs the truth procedure through three steps: Badiou's mathematical ontology and the set-theoretic 'generic multiple'; the event and the production of 'pure novelty'; and the triad of truth, event and subject, including his three types of subject. The second part turns to political truth procedures and Badiou's account of two sequences of emancipatory politics since 1792. It discusses the Maoist principle 'one divides into two', 'subtractive negation' and non-party forms of organisation. Fan explains that for Badiou truth is not a given transcendent unity but the result of a generic operation on multiplicity. It is produced when a contingent event breaks the existing situation. Subjects become part of a truth's 'body' through fidelity to the event, mediated by the Idea. Badiou distinguishes faithful, reactionary and obscure subjects. In politics, Fan reports, Badiou holds that the second sequence, from the October Revolution through Lenin and Mao, has exhausted its possibilities. The Leninist 'party-state' won power but produced statism and undifferentiated individuals rather than singular revolutionary subjects. For a third sequence, Fan presents Badiou as proposing politics that keeps its distance from the state: it refuses elections and state funding, creates autonomous spaces, and works through minimal difference rather than pure destruction. Destruction is retained only as a defensive force, to protect what subtraction has created. Organisation would be loose, flexible and held together by Ideas rather than by a vanguard party. Fan presents this as an exposition of Badiou's thought and offers no sustained critique of it. Read the original if you want a compact Chinese-language introduction to Badiou's concepts of truth, event, subject and subtractive politics, as a case of Chinese engagement with foreign Marxism.

The crisis of contemporary capitalism and the resistance of the Western left New trends in Western left thought as seen from the 2017 New York left forum 当代资本主义的危机与西方左翼的反抗 Jin Meng This is a report and short assessment of the left forum held in New York in June 2017 under the theme 'Resistance: strategy, tactics, struggle, solidarity and utopia'. Jin Meng places the event against the protests that followed Donald Trump's inauguration in January 2017, and reports that the forum's speakers treated women's, ecological, racial and immigration questions as products of the capitalist system. In this account Trump is a continuer of that system, not its originator, so resistance has to target capitalism itself. The report is organised around three clusters of discussion by Western left scholars: Marxism and its contemporary value, especially on the 150th anniversary of Capital, Volume 1; the crisis of capitalism in the Trump era and the future of socialism; and the history, present state and future of left resistance. A brief assessment closes the piece. Participants named include David Schweickart, Nancy Holmstrom, Peter Hudis, David M. Kotz, Michael Hudson, Michael Perelman, Cinzia Arruzza and L. A. Kauffman.
