On the first theme, Jin reports that speakers saw Capital as still the most scientific tool for analysing exploitation, overwork, unemployment and alienated labour. Holmstrom and Hudis are cited on gender equality, ecological crisis and a post-capitalist form of labour. On the second theme, Kotz and others traced Trump's election to the crisis of neoliberalism and described his government as right-wing nationalism that strengthens neoliberalism rather than ending it. The scholars proposed alternatives such as a universal basic income, a job guarantee, public banks, workers' cooperatives and eco-socialism, and held that gender, race, climate and migration struggles should merge into a proletarian class struggle. On the third theme, they named three weaknesses of current resistance: a misdirected target, absorption by the Democratic Party, and no alternative programme and no organised centre. They urged teaching the public to see capitalism as the target, forming a united front, and relying on young people. In the concluding assessment, Jin credits the forum with clarifying the target of struggle and gathering left forces. Jin also notes that the left is a mixed body of democratic socialists, anarchists, reformists and others who differ on Marxism and scientific socialism, so their views must be treated dialectically. Their practical proposals are described as lacking operability and unity, and Jin calls for a strong command centre and a united left. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic overview of how the 2017 American left framed Trump, Capital and the strategy of resistance.

A preliminary study of Marxist class psychology in contemporary social development 当代社会发展中的马克思主义阶级心理研究刍议 Li Houyi Li Houyi asks how Marx's account of class psychology should be understood and defended now that classes have become more varied and class relations more complex. The article argues that much contemporary Western left-wing research has drifted from Marx's foundations, and that a return to his premises would let empirical and micro-level methods be absorbed without losing the critical orientation of Marxism. The article has three parts. The first reviews Marx's view of class psychology and the revisions made by Western Marxist and sociological scholars, notably Eric Olin Wright, with Weberian ideas, Peter Blau and Otis Duncan on social mobility, and the concept of 'social closure'. The second sets out five principles that Li draws from Marx. The third looks at current trends in Western left-wing work and proposes three directions for improvement. Li's central claim is that Marx grounds class psychology in ownership of the means of production, in alienated labour and in the aim of human emancipation. Li says Western scholars have replaced class psychology with occupational psychology, reduced it to feelings of exploitation or bargaining power, and explained psychological conflict through changes of status. In Li's view this detaches the field from relations of production. Against this, Li draws five lessons from Marx: class psychology arises from socio-economic position and is shaped dialectically by language and practice; it must be grasped within the totality of historical development; it can be studied through underlying structures of consciousness; it rests on practice, not on transcendent psychological theory; and it can absorb other methods. Recent Western work on class diversity, conflict and system dynamics, Li argues, has become micro-level and laboratory-based, and neglects the economic roots of power and consensus. Li concludes that three recent themes in Western left-wing research (relations, labelling and performance) can be useful, but only if they are tied to their economic preconditions, root causes and a firm belief in Marxism. If class psychology is reduced to small-group psychology and laboratory verification, Li warns, the application of Marxism is distorted. Where researchers hold to Marxist theory and critique capitalism, quantitative, empirical and micro methods can become organic parts of Marxist research. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist assessment of Western class-psychology scholarship and of how Marx's views might be used to evaluate it.

China and the Communist Party of China as seen by the international community 国际社会眼中的中国及中国共产党 Zhang Linxin Written after the 19th Party Congress (2017), this commentary in Red Flag Manuscripts collects foreign reactions to the Congress report and to the Communist Party of China (CPC). Zhang notes that more than 600 foreign leaders, parties and organisations sent congratulations and that over 1,000 journalists from more than 130 countries reported on the event. The author argues that knowing how the world sees China helps to strengthen confidence in the path, theory, system and culture of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The article is a compilation of quotations from foreign politicians, scholars and media, grouped under four headings. These are: the CPC's leadership as the key to China's stability and prosperity; China as a driving force of the world economy; the contribution of the "China solution" in the "new era"; and China as a promoter of peace and civilisational progress. Sources include Russian, Singaporean, British, American, Japanese, Brazilian, Cuban and Latin American commentators, among them Putin, Hatoyama Yukio, Martin Jacques, Arif Dirlik, the Financial Times, the BBC and the Washington Post. Zhang reports that the cited voices praise the Party's anti-corruption work, cadre training, rule of law and long-term planning, which they contrast with short-term electoral politics in the West. Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era is presented as a theoretical innovation guiding the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Foreign commentators are also quoted as saying that the Belt and Road Initiative makes China a locomotive of the world economy, that its green policies set an example, and that its development offers developing countries an alternative model. Several sources, including the Financial Times and the BBC, are cited as seeing a self-confident China moving toward "the centre of the world stage" while the West declines. Others are cited as saying that a community with a shared future for mankind offers a new possibility for global governance, and that Xi's emphasis on domestic strength weakens the "China threat" thesis. Zhang concludes, through these citations, that the international community broadly regards the CPC's leadership as decisive for China's rise and sees China as a positive force for world peace and development. The commentary draws no critical distinctions among the sources and does not discuss dissenting views beyond a Washington Post piece criticising Western misreadings of China. Read the original if you want a sample of how Chinese official media in late 2017 selected and presented favourable foreign commentary on the 19th Party Congress.

On contemporary Western Marxism 论当代西方马克思主义 Chen Xueming Chen Xueming surveys what he calls contemporary Western Marxism, meaning the broader field of Marxism outside China, and asks what it has contributed and how Chinese Marxists should use it. He argues that since the mid-1990s, and especially since the 2007 credit crisis, this current has revived and renewed Marxism. In his view it offers new explorations of Marxism, a new critique of capitalism and a new outlook on socialism, all of which Chinese Marxism can learn from critically. The article has three parts. The first traces how the current formed, from the split after Engels's death into Second International, Third International and Western Marxist paths, through the post-1991 setback to the post-2007 revival. It then lists six new features: convergence with the radical left, postmodern dominance, a shift to "post-Marxism", fusion with the humanities and natural sciences, study of Marxism as an organic whole, and acceptance of pluralism. The second part assesses its influence. The third makes seven proposals for adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. In the central assessment, Chen reports foreign thinkers' work in each area. On Marxism, he cites Eagleton, Hobsbawm, Badiou and Žižek on the Occupy movement, the revived reading of Capital, and debates on social justice and "postmodern Marxism". On capitalism, he cites critiques of neoliberalism, ecological crisis, consumer society, the commodification of space, liberal democracy and the "new imperialism". On socialism, he cites the claim that "another choice is possible", the revival of communism, ecosocialism, market socialism, utopian socialism and Latin American twenty-first-century socialism. Chen also says these thinkers mix valuable and worthless ideas, are internally divided, and often offer critique without practical experience behind it. Chen concludes that foreign Marxism has raised the quality rather than the quantity of Marxism and that, with its caveats, it should be absorbed. His proposals include widening theoretical horizons, comparing Chinese and Western Marxism, using foreign Marxism's rational elements to evaluate the Chinese adaptation of Marxism, and drawing on it for theoretical resources. He also calls for taking Chinese results abroad, giving foreign Marxism a fuller place in the history of Marxism, abandoning an attitude of "only we are Marxist", and training scholars versed in both domestic and foreign Marxism. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's broad map of post-2007 foreign Marxism and of how it is meant to inform Chinese Marxist theory.

Crisis and reconstruction: a study of contemporary Marxist currents outside China 危机与重建：当代国外马克思主义思潮研究 Huang Xiaowu Huang asks how the left has responded to the crisis that followed the collapse of the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe in the early 1990s, and what chances and obstacles face a rebuilding and revival of Marxism. The article argues that the upheaval was the product of a crisis of left movements dating from the 1960s and 1970s, not an accident. In Huang's account, the left has responded with new organisational forms, a renewed defence of the commons and a broadened Marxism that takes in culture and identity. The article has three parts. The first looks at social movements and the challenges facing the left, drawing on Luciano Magri, Giovanni Arrighi, Naomi Klein, Michael Hardt and Rossana Rossanda. The second turns to identity politics and cultural identity, drawing on Stuart Hall, Eric Hobsbawm and Judith Butler. The third takes the Italian new left as a case study of how to analyse contemporary capitalism and renew the Marxist tradition. Huang reports the dispute over whether attention to culture abandons Marxist political economy. Butler, as Huang presents her, argues that the opposition between the material and the cultural is a selective construction. Marx saw the economic and the cultural as historical products of the division of labour, and new movements keep the left's universalism in particular struggles because neoliberal capitalism itself works through particularity. Huang adds that immaterial labour and biopolitics show the material–cultural divide dissolving, and that Marxist reconstruction should start from there. The Italian case, in Huang's reading, shows the Italian Communist Party falling behind the workers' movement. The Il manifesto group and operaismo (workerism) developed outside it, with operaismo reinterpreting Marx's 1857–58 manuscripts and moving toward post-workerism under Antonio Negri. Huang concludes that Italian new left thought of the 1960s and 1970s, praised by Hall and Hobsbawm as the European frontier of Marxism, has been little studied in China. Chinese work has focused on Gramsci and on recent radical thinkers such as Agamben and Negri. Huang holds that studying it would clarify Marxism's present crisis and its reconstruction. It would also give the Communist Party of China lessons on developing its own theory and avoiding deviations under rapid economic growth. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's overview of how Western left currents, from anti-globalisation movements to Italian workerism, are read in Chinese debates on Marxist renewal.

The German–French dispute between historicism and structuralism in the 1960s and 1970s An intellectual contest based on readings of Capital 20世纪六七十年代德法历史主义与结构主义之争 Li Qiankun Li Qiankun examines the clash between two Western Marxist ways of reading Marx's Capital in the 1960s and 1970s: a historicist model centred on the second generation of the Frankfurt School, and a structuralist model led by Louis Althusser and his school. Both returned to Capital and the manuscripts but reached different methods and conclusions. Li argues that the dispute ultimately turns on the problem of subjectivity and objectivity in Marxist philosophy, and that each side grasped part of Marx's text. The article is built around three episodes. It begins with the 1967 Frankfurt conference marking a century of Capital, where Nicos Poulantzas confronted Iring Fetscher, Alfred Schmidt and Ernest Mandel. It then turns to Althusser's critique of historicism in Reading Capital (1965), aimed especially at Gramsci, Lukács and Sartre. It next takes up Schmidt's reply in History and Structure (1971), a book Li says has received little attention in Chinese scholarship. A short conclusion places the dispute within wider debates. In Li's account, Poulantzas and Althusser held that historicism and humanism rest on a central subject and a Hegelian expressive totality, and that the mature Marx broke with this in an anti-humanist, anti-historicist, "subjectless" science. Schmidt, Mandel and Fetscher replied that the structuralists removed the historical dimension from Marx's analysis, and that Marx openly used Hegel's dialectic from the Grundrisse to Capital. Schmidt argued that Capital combines logical and historical methods, moving from the abstract to the concrete, and that Althusser himself fell into a speculative idealism of a timeless structure. Li also notes Schmidt's defence of Gramsci and observes that Schmidt's generation reconnected with the Hegelian Marxism of Lukács and Korsch, against Adorno and Horkheimer. Li concludes that the structuralist critique had some force, since the 1968 May events showed the weakness of a subject-centred totality. He judges, however, that the German scholars grasped Marx's texts more fully, while structuralism overstated transcendent structure and drifted into a metaphysical postulate. He adds that the "New Reading of Marx" which began in 1965 absorbed both: it avoided humanist readings, used the historicist method in studying the value form, and in places converged with or went beyond Althusser on ideological forms. Read the original if you want a detailed account of the 1967 Frankfurt debate and of Schmidt's little-studied reply to Althusser, as background to philosophical readings of Capital.

Contemporary Western Marxist theories of class formation 当代西方马克思主义的阶级形成理论 Hai Bo Hai Bo asks how classes come to exist in social life, rather than only why they arise from economic relations. The article argues that Marxist research has mostly analysed class statically, through positions in production relations, and has paid little systematic attention to class formation as a dynamic process that extends beyond the economy. Hai's thesis is that, in contemporary Western Marxist accounts, class formation rests on the interaction of class consciousness, class struggle and political culture. The article is a history-of-ideas survey in three sections, one for each of these elements. It draws on Marx's distinction between a class in itself and a class for itself and on Georg Lukács's History and Class Consciousness. It also covers E. P. Thompson, Pierre Bourdieu, Erik Olin Wright, Adam Przeworski, Antonio Gramsci and G. A. Cohen. It adds the Korean scholar Koo Hagen on workers' experience, and the Chinese historian Gao Yi on the political culture of the French Revolution. In Hai's reading, Lukács treats proletarian class consciousness as the goal and weapon of the class itself, because it unites theory and practice. Thompson sees class as an event that happens through shared experience and struggle, so consciousness is a cultural response and not a direct product of production relations. Bourdieu and Wright extend this view. For Bourdieu, class boundaries are objects of symbolic struggle and mobilisation by spokespeople. For Wright, class structure limits, selects and is in turn altered by class struggle. Hai then turns to political culture. Gramsci's cultural hegemony and Thompson's inherited traditions are read as sources of unity from below. Koo's Korean workers are shown to have formed their identity under combined pressure from bourgeois culture and political power. Hai concludes that class formation is open-ended and that classes are always forming and dissolving. Economic, political and cultural factors interact, and the three core elements permeate and transform one another. Class structure is a static, theoretical construct, while class formation is a practical process. Hai calls for class research to ask both what forms classes and how they are formed, and so to advance the Marxist cause of proletarian and human liberation. Read the original if you want a compact Chinese-language overview of how Lukács, Thompson, Wright and others handle the subjective side of class.

The basic landscape of world Marxism in the twenty-first century 21世纪世界马克思主义基本格局 Wang Fengcai Wang Fengcai takes up the question of how to map "twenty-first-century world Marxism", which the article defines as foreign Marxism together with Marxism adapted to the Chinese context. Wang observes that Marxism revived after a brief silence following the upheavals in Eastern Europe, and that a "Marx fever" has appeared worldwide. The thesis is that, although many studies exist on particular countries, schools and thinkers, no overall, systematic study of this field has yet appeared, and that the field can be organised into five interpretive paths. The article is built in four parts. It first surveys the state of research by region (continental Europe, the English-speaking world, the former Soviet bloc, and Asia, Africa and Latin America), listing institutions, journals, forums and key books, and then Chinese scholarship. It then sets out the five paths, followed by research objects and ten "hot topics", from the MEGA edition and Capital to class theory, neoliberalism, new imperialism, actually existing socialism and the new communism. It ends with research orientations, key difficulties and the significance of the field. The core move is the typology of five interpretive paths: foreign Marxology, orthodox Marxism, Western Marxism, East European neo-Marxism, and Marxism adapted to the Chinese context. Wang defines Western Marxism narrowly, as a non-orthodox current born and developed in the West, which excludes Marxology, orthodoxy, East European neo-Marxism and Western communist parties' theory but includes post-Marxism. Using Western Marxism as the reference point, Wang contrasts each path along three axes: scholarly rigour, intellectual depth and practical relevance. Marxology leans towards scholarship, orthodoxy towards ideology, East European neo-Marxism towards practice, and Marxism adapted to the Chinese context is called the most vital and practically oriented path. Wang also sorts scholars into four orientations, labelled the "lonely" Marxologists, the "isolated" orthodox, the "active" innovators and the "carefree" reconstructors. Wang concludes that the central task is to unify scholarship, ideology and real-world concern, and to move from a "singular, unreflective Marxism" to a "plural, innovative Marxism". The author lists difficulties, including the absence of a unified conception of Marxism, the breadth of the field and the language demands. Wang argues that such research would help Marxism develop in the Chinese context, maintain its guiding position in Chinese philosophy and social sciences, and build a Chinese academic discourse. Read the original if you want a detailed bibliographic map of Marxist research worldwide around 2017, seen from a Chinese academic viewpoint, together with a typology of schools.

Five assessments by foreign left-wing scholars of the crisis of contemporary capitalism 国外左翼学者关于当代资本主义危机的五种评判 Tong Jin Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2017, Tong Jin surveys how foreign left-wing scholars have analysed the capitalist crisis that began in the early twenty-first century. The article groups their work into five assessments: the crisis is one of the mode of production, of democracy, of values, of ecology and of the capitalist system as a whole. Tong stresses that these are different readings of one crisis and overlap with each other. The review moves through the five headings in turn, drawing on a range of Western and other foreign thinkers. They include David Harvey, Paul Jorion and Mary Wrenn on production; Noam Chomsky and Joseph Stiglitz on democracy; Harvey and Stiglitz again on values; John Bellamy Foster, Andrew Jones and Richard Smith on ecology; and Immanuel Wallerstein, Wolfgang Streeck, Michael Koyama and Samir Amin on systemic crisis. As Tong presents them, these scholars locate the roots of crisis in the contradiction between socialised production and private capitalist appropriation, which is sharpened by globalisation and by Harvey's 'accumulation by dispossession'. They describe Western democracy as rule by a wealthy minority, with money outweighing votes, and the ideals of freedom and equality as a myth. Ecological destruction is said to follow from capital's profit-seeking, so that 'green capitalism' cannot work. In the final category, Tong reports that Wallerstein, Streeck and Amin see capitalism's remedies as exhausted and its structure heading towards breakdown. Tong judges the left's critique thorough and deep, but also flawed. Some scholars, in Tong's view, treat the crisis as capitalism's turning point and so overlook its capacity for self-regulation. Others replace critique of the relations of production with critique of the damage done to nature, and put the contradiction between humans and nature in place of that between people. Tong calls for critical absorption, borrowing the insights while recognising the limits of the scholars' standpoint, method and understanding. Read the original if you want a compact map of the main foreign left critiques of post-2008 capitalism, together with a Chinese academic's assessment of their strengths and weaknesses.

Growing positive assessments of the Communist Party of China among American scholars in recent years 近年来美国学者对中国共产党的肯定性评价越来越多 Xue Nianwen Sun Jian Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2017, Xue Nianwen and Sun Jian argue that American scholarship on the Communist Party of China (CPC) is the most advanced in the West and that, in recent years, US China specialists have paid it more attention and judged it more favourably. The authors present this as a general trend rather than a unanimous view. The article is organised in three parts, each reviewing English-language work by US-based scholars: assessments of CPC leaders, assessments of Party building, and expectations for the Party's future. It draws on books and journal articles, including studies of Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping by Arif Dirlik, Ezra Vogel, Xiong Jie (Lawrence Xiong) and others, and on articles in The China Quarterly and similar journals. In the first part, Xue and Sun report that American scholars praise the leaders' sense of responsibility to country and people: Roderick MacFarquhar on Mao's and Deng's paths, Vogel on Deng's pragmatism, and Zhao Suisheng on Xi's refusal to split the People's Republic's history into Mao and post-Mao eras. They also report approval of collective wisdom, the leaders' grassroots experience, and the Party's handling of Tibet and Xinjiang. In the second part, they cite Bruce Dickson on Party recruitment, Zeng Qinghe (Jeremy Zeng) on wider Party member participation in cadre selection, and John Naisbitt on bottom-up participation. The authors read these works as endorsing tighter entry standards, the anti-corruption campaign and intra-Party democracy. The third part covers mostly optimistic forecasts, such as Romi Jain's on environmental governance and Wang Huiyao's on attracting overseas talent. Xue and Sun say that hostile writing driven by arrogance and prejudice is now a minority. The authors conclude that US scholars have studied the leaders, Party building and prospects in depth and have endorsed the Party's efforts at self-improvement, full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, and grassroots-rooted leadership under Xi Jinping. They say most American scholars are optimistic that the Party will lead China into a new stage. Read the original if you want a Chinese official-academic reading of how US China scholarship on the CPC is presented to a domestic audience, along with a bibliography of the English-language sources it cites.

The Communist Party of the Russian Federation's understanding and assessment of the October Revolution 俄罗斯联邦共产党对十月革命的认识与评价 Li Yazhou Writing on the eve of the centenary of the October Revolution in 2017, Li Yazhou asks how the Communist Party of the Russian Federation (CPRF), successor to the Communist Party of the Soviet Union, understands and evaluates that revolution. Li argues that the CPRF has defended the Revolution consistently since its founding. The article presents the party's stance as holding to the Revolution's historical achievements while offering a sober account of why Soviet socialism failed. The article has three parts. The first traces the CPRF's defence of the Revolution from its founding in 1990 through its ban after the August 1991 events and its restoration in 1993. It follows the party's conflicts with the Yeltsin and Putin governments over the 7 November holiday and its preparations for the 2017 centenary, including plenums, a preparatory committee and a proposal to hold the 19th international meeting of communist and workers' parties in Russia. The second part sets out six basic CPRF positions, drawing on Zyuganov's reports and his 2016 Xinhua interview. The third part draws lessons. In Li's account, the CPRF holds that the Revolution was neither accidental nor a coup. It was the outcome of Lenin's analysis of imperialism, in which tsarist Russia was the weakest link in the capitalist chain, and of Bolshevik slogans that won mass support. The party credits the Revolution with defeating foreign intervention, rapid industrialisation, the victory in the Great Patriotic War and the ending of national oppression. It also credits the Revolution with a global impact on national liberation movements and on the founding of the Chinese Communist Party. The CPRF is also reported as attributing the Soviet collapse partly to betrayal by Gorbachev and his circle and to Western hostility. It names deeper causes too: over-centralisation, excessive statisation, a simplified view of socialism, and a ruling party cut off from ordinary workers. Li concludes that the CPRF adopts a historical-materialist approach, affirming the Stalin model's historical rationality under the conditions of its time while analysing its failures candidly. From this Li draws four principles for assessing the history of socialist revolution and construction: seeking truth from facts, historical analysis, comprehensiveness and objectivity, and a forward-looking orientation. Li says these would strengthen confidence in the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic overview of the CPRF's official line on 1917, its commemorative politics and its explanation of the Soviet collapse.

The contingency and necessity of the October Revolution 十月革命的偶然性与必然性 S. N. Malyeyev This is a Chinese translation of an article by the Russian author S. N. Malyeyev, written shortly before the centenary of 1917. It takes up the claim, which the author attributes to liberal media and politicians, that the October Revolution was an accident or the work of a malign Bolshevik conspiracy. Malyeyev argues instead that October followed with objective logic from the war, the unresolved questions of land and peace, and the failure of the Provisional Government. The article follows events chronologically. It begins with the February Revolution and the bread queues, then covers the dual power of the Provisional Government and the Petrograd Soviet, the crises of spring and summer 1917, the July Days, the Kornilov affair, the storming of the Winter Palace and the Second Congress of Soviets. It then turns to the dissolution of the Constituent Assembly in January 1918 and the record of the White regimes in the civil war. Malyeyev draws heavily on Kerensky's memoirs, Lenin's writings, Sukhanov and the Soviet military historian N. E. Kakurin. The central claim is that the war was the decisive factor and that the revolution must be understood as a process with two stages, following Lenin's April Theses. The Provisional Government could neither end the war nor distribute land, so the Soviets' strength grew. Malyeyev cites Kerensky's own admissions that the army had lost its will to fight and that without Kornilov's attempted coup there would have been no October. In this reading the seizure of power was close to a formality: the Petrograd garrison had gone over to the Soviet, and the defenders of the Winter Palace numbered about 2,000. Malyeyev also presents the choice in late 1917 as one between a military dictatorship of reactionary generals and "all power to the Soviets". He cites accounts of Kolchak, Denikin, Yudenich and Wrangel to argue that the White regimes' brutality drove the peasantry to the revolution. He says the Mensheviks and Socialist Revolutionaries ended up objectively on the counter-revolutionary side. The article closes by announcing a separate treatment of the post-Brest-Litovsk measures and state capitalism. Read the original if you want a Russian author's polemical defence of the revolution's historical necessity against liberal revisionism, built largely on contemporary memoir sources.

The October Revolution and the new era in human history: a further discussion 再论十月革命开辟的人类历史新纪元 Wu Enyuan Marking the centenary of the 1917 October Revolution, Wu Enyuan asks what the Revolution opened for world history and whether the collapse of the Soviet Union discredits it. Wu argues that the Revolution inaugurated a new era: it broke capitalism's monopoly on the world order, made Marxism a practical reality, and still shapes the course of world socialism through socialism with Chinese characteristics. The collapse of the USSR, in Wu's view, was not a failure of the socialist system. The article has four parts. The first treats the Revolution as the realisation of Marxist revolutionary theory, its effects on Soviet development, and its influence on a capitalist world in crisis. The second covers the contribution of the Communist International, the Soviet Union and the Chinese Communist Party to defeating German and Japanese fascism. The third rebuts the claim that Soviet dissolution proves socialism failed. The fourth links the Revolution to China's revolutionary and reform record. Wu holds that the Bolsheviks won through firm Party leadership, Soviet policies on land, peace and national self-determination, and Lenin's creative application of Marxism to Russia, which rejected both a purely bourgeois and an immediately socialist course. Citing Soviet and Russian sources, Wu points to rapid industrialisation, full employment, expanded education and social insurance in the 1930s, and argues that capitalist states absorbed socialist-style planning and social policy to escape the post-1920 crises. On the USSR's end, Wu concedes serious institutional flaws but cites Russian economists, Security Council secretary Nikolai Patrushev and Gorbachev himself to argue that the collapse resulted from reform errors, not inevitability. Wu concludes that socialism with Chinese characteristics is both a product of the October Revolution and an extension of its significance. Wu credits successive Chinese leaders with drawing on Soviet experience and lessons, and cites economic data from 1949 to 2016, including growth since the 18th Party Congress (2012), to contrast China's stability with Western stagnation. The movement of world socialism, Wu says, is still thriving. Read the original if you want a Chinese-academy defence of the Revolution's legacy and an account of how Chinese scholars rebut the "inevitable collapse" view of the Soviet Union.

The development of the Latin American communist movement after the October Revolution 十月革命后拉美共产主义运动发展 Xu Shicheng Writing in 2017, the centenary of the October Revolution, Xu Shicheng asks how that event shaped communism in Latin America and how the movement has fared since. The article argues that the revolution acted as a catalyst for the founding of communist parties across the region, which then went through a winding history of repression, split, collapse and recovery. Xu holds that the Latin American left has not died despite recent setbacks. The article follows the movement in four stages. It begins with the early spread of knowledge of the revolution and the founding of parties from the 1910s to the 1950s, then turns to the effects of the Soviet collapse in the early 1990s. It next covers the rise of the left and of what some Chinese scholars call "Latin American national socialism" from the late 1990s, and ends with the position of the movement around 2015–2017. Xu draws on Latin American thinkers such as Mariátegui, on party histories and on election results. Xu argues that the Cold War, the Sino-Soviet split and military coups in the 1960s and 1970s repeatedly pushed the parties underground and divided them. The 1973 coup in Chile ended the "Chilean road" to socialism. The Soviet collapse hit Cuba hardest, with the author citing a 34 per cent fall in GDP between 1990 and 1993. It also split parties, and some, such as the Brazilian PCB, changed their identity, while others that held to Marxism-Leninism, such as the Communist Party of Brazil, grew. From about 1999, left governments came to power in Venezuela, Brazil, Argentina, Bolivia, Ecuador and elsewhere, and the São Paulo Forum grew to 110 organisations. Xu names the problems of this left as an unchanged primary-export economy, corruption, conservative offensives, internal divisions and US interference, and these were followed by the "left down, right up" shift from 2015. Xu concludes that the pendulum has swung right but that the left retains strength. In support, Xu cites Ortega's re-election in Nicaragua in 2016, left governments still in office elsewhere, and the region's deep inequality. The article adds that more than twenty communist parties remain, that most are legal and uphold Marxism-Leninism, and that Cuba will keep to socialism. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly overview of Latin American communist and left politics, with dates, party names and election data, from 1917 to 2017.

On the Soviet Republic and the dissolution of the Constituent Assembly With a critique of the "nihilist view of the October Revolution" 论苏维埃共和国与立宪会议的解散 Nie Yunlin Writing on the eve of the revolution's centenary, Nie Yunlin takes up the question of why the Soviet government dissolved the Russian Constituent Assembly in January 1918. Nie argues that, since the collapse of the Soviet Union, some commentators have used the dissolution to cast the October Revolution as a conspiracy or coup, or even to deny it happened. In Nie's account the dissolution was justified and fully consistent with Marxist principles, and attacks on it amount to a bourgeois-democratic standpoint. The article has three parts. The first traces the separate origins of the soviets, from the 1905 revolution through February and October 1917, and of the idea of a constituent assembly, from the American and French precedents through the Decembrists to 1905 and 1917. The second explains why the Bolsheviks still convened the Assembly after October, narrating the elections, the measures taken against opponents and the single day of the Assembly's sitting. The third gives three reasons for dissolution. Nie holds that the soviets were organs of workers' and peasants' power and a form of proletarian dictatorship, whereas the Assembly was a product of the bourgeois-democratic revolution and a "negative political asset" left by February. The Bolsheviks, Nie says, convened it so that the masses could see its bourgeois character through experience. Nie reports that the Socialist Revolutionaries won a majority of delegates, that the Assembly refused to approve the Declaration of Rights of the Working and Exploited People and the decrees on peace and land, and that its slogan "all power to the Constituent Assembly" served counter-revolution. Nie then follows Lenin: the Soviet republic is a higher form of democracy, the Assembly belonged to the old state machine and refused transformation, and the interests of the proletariat and people stand above formal democracy. Nie supports the last point with three claims: democracy is always class democracy, it cannot abolish class struggle, and content determines form. Nie concludes that the dissolution consolidated the October victory, defeated an attempted restoration and cleared the way for resisting foreign intervention and for socialist construction. Nie describes the Assembly as a short-lived political farce against the tide of history. Nie also presents contemporary world socialism, with China as its mainstay, as the continuation of the cause the October Revolution began. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist scholar defends the dissolution of the Constituent Assembly and rebuts the "nihilist" reading of October, drawing mainly on Lenin's own texts.

How to view the past, present and future of socialism An interview with Professor David Kotz of the University of Massachusetts Amherst 如何看待社会主义的过去、现在与未来 Tian Xi Published in Theoretical Horizon in 2017, this is an interview conducted by Tian Xi (School of Marxism, Peking University) with the US economist David Kotz, a specialist on the Soviet Union, in the centenary year of the October Revolution. Kotz, who began studying Soviet political economy in 1989 and co-authored two books on the end of the Soviet system with Fred Weir, is asked how socialism's past, present and future should be understood. The interview has three parts. The first concerns the October Revolution: its conditions, whether it fitted Marx's expectations, socialism in one country, the Kaftin (Caudine) Forks question and the Stalin model. The second addresses the Soviet collapse, including five common explanations and the contrast with China. The third turns to the rise and decline of neoliberalism, the 2008 financial crisis, Trump and the prospects for socialism in the West. Kotz argues that the Soviet Union did not collapse because of economic crisis, which he says was no worse than the US Great Depression. In his account, a large part of the top leadership turned against socialism between 1989 and 1991 because it wanted to expand its privileges, and ideology followed material interest. He rejects five other explanations: the sudden end of planning, a popular vote against socialism, Western subversion, the arms race and ethnic nationalism. He cites poll data showing that 80–85 per cent of citizens wanted to keep the USSR. He holds that China avoided the Soviet fate because Deng Xiaoping introduced markets and private ownership gradually, rather than following Milton Friedman's advice of immediate privatisation. Kotz concludes that the Soviet system's fatal flaw was that ordinary workers held no real political power, and that lasting socialism requires its beneficiaries to hold such power. He says markets and private ownership can play a positive role for a time but eventually breed capitalists and inequality, so they must be turned into public ownership and planning. As an alternative to Soviet-style central planning he proposes a democratic, participatory planned economy. He also says neoliberalism has failed and that the world faces a choice among right-wing nationalism, social democratic capitalism and democratic socialism. Read the original if you want a US Marxist economist's view of the Soviet collapse, Chinese reform and the prospects for socialism after 2008.

The situation of Marxist philosophy in twenty-first-century Russia 21世纪俄罗斯马克思主义哲学的境遇 Zheng Yishi How does Marxist philosophy fare in Russia after the Soviet collapse? Writing in 2017, Zheng describes a pluralised Russian philosophy in which Marxism is studied as one school among equals. The article argues that this is no true thaw: after the 'heat' of the late-1980s and early-1990s wave of criticism and the 'cold' of neglect in the mid-1990s, Marxist philosophy in the twenty-first century is in a 'chilly spring' that combines marginalisation, renewed attention and renewed reflection. The article is organised in three parts that correspond to these three conditions. The first traces marginalisation from the early 1990s to the 2000s, including the post-Soviet 'denial', 'non-Marxist' and 'critical' camps. The second surveys renewed attention through conferences (2005–2011), publications, university teaching and research bodies. The third examines reflection on Marxism itself and on related questions: revisionism, the October Revolution, the Soviet collapse and socialist theory and practice. On marginalisation, Zheng argues that the three dominant camps, which treat Marxism as a source of disaster, interpret Marx at a distance, or absorb him into Western humanism, keep it at the edge of both official and popular life. On renewed attention, the author cites growing numbers of conferences, reissued Second International and 1920s Russian Marxist works, surviving Soviet-trained teachers and Marxist centres, though these are staffed mainly by older scholars. On reflection, Zheng reports debates over what 'genuine Marxism' is, Teodor Oizerman's defence of revisionism and Bernstein, and rival readings of 1917 and of the Soviet collapse that draw on newly opened archives. Zheng concludes that Russia's search for a path different from both the Western and Soviet models leaves no room for a fundamental change of attitude to Marxism, so marginalisation continues. Yet the reflection shows undiminished interest in Marxism, a calmer and more objective assessment of it, and a more practical need for it. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's survey of post-Soviet Russian debates on Marxism, with names of figures, conferences, journals and book titles to follow up.

Western communist parties' views and initiatives on the centenary of the October Revolution 西方国家共产党关于纪念十月革命100周年的观点与倡议 Tong Jin Writing in 2017, Tong Jin asks how communist parties in Western countries have used the centenary of the October Revolution to state their positions. The article reports that these parties and other left-wing forces treated the anniversary as an occasion to restate the revolution's historical significance, rebut distortions of it and link its experience to present struggles against capitalism. Tong's overall finding is that the parties read the revolution as proof that socialism remains necessary now and in the future. The article is a survey of speeches, reports and website articles from the parties of Portugal, Greece, Australia (Marxist-Leninist), Britain, Germany, Spain and France. It is organised in five parts: commitment to socialism; restoring the 'truth' about twentieth-century socialism; the working class as the force behind the revolution; applying the revolution's experience to national conditions; and plans for commemorative activities. In Tong's account, the Portuguese, Greek and Australian parties hold that the Soviet collapse was temporary and that the twenty-first century will bring a decisive contest between capitalism and socialism. The Greek party rejects the claim that the revolution caused the collapse, arguing instead that the Soviet Union weakened the revolution's gains by adopting capitalist remedies. The Portuguese party argues that rulers keep rewriting history and present a distorted 'model' as inherent to Marxism-Leninism. Tong also reports that these parties see the revolution as showing the working class's capacity to fulfil its historical mission. The Greek party stresses assessing class forces objectively, and the Spanish party's general secretary calls for combining the revolution's lessons with present conditions. The article adds that the Greek, Australian and French parties apply this to current politics: daily struggles, independence from US policy towards China, and election campaigns focused on social questions. Tong describes the planned commemorations. The Portuguese party scheduled events through 2017, including a seminar, exhibitions and a website. The British party tied the anniversary to the 150th anniversary of Capital, and the Morning Star helped set up the Russian Revolution Centenary Committee. Tong concludes that a correct view of the revolution is necessary for the past, present and future, and that its significance cannot be slandered or replaced. Read the original if you want a documented overview of how European and Australian communist parties framed the 1917 centenary, with many quotations from their statements.

Commemorating the 100th anniversary of the October Revolution: Austro-Marxism's political theory and Lenin's critique Reformism, the "middle way" and "defensive violence" in Renner, Hilferding, Bauer and Max Adler 纪念十月革命胜利100周年 Published in 2017 to mark the centenary of the October Revolution, this article asks how Austro-Marxist political theory responded to the Bolshevik seizure of power and to parliamentary democracy in Germany and Austria. Its thesis is that Austro-Marxism, from right to left, was eclectic and reformist. The authors conclude that its "middle way" cannot hold within the Marxist framework and that Austro-Marxism was therefore a non-Marxist theory and practice. The article sorts the school into three camps after 1917. It treats Karl Renner as centre-right, with his view of the state as a supra-class servant of the workers. It treats Rudolf Hilferding as the centrist, with his ambivalent view of parliament and the general strike. It treats Otto Bauer and Max Adler as centre-left, with Bauer's theories of "social power factors" and "defensive violence". It then sets these positions against Lenin's State and Revolution and his criticism of Bauer at the Second Comintern Congress. It ends with the defeat of the Austrian Social Democrats in February 1934. The authors argue that Renner's state theory ignored the class essence of the modern state and imagined that the bourgeoisie would allow a peaceful parliamentary route to power. Hilferding, they say, tried to balance Kautsky, Bernstein and revisionism and so treated the strike as a merely defensive weapon. Bauer held that democracy is a neutral form whose content depends on the balance of social forces, and that violence is justified only when the bourgeoisie destroys democracy. The article credits this with some Marxist value, and notes that Marx and Engels allowed for peaceful routes after the 1870s. It follows Lenin in holding that the real issue is the class character of democracy, not peaceful versus violent means. In its account, "defensive violence" leaves the proletariat passive, because it cannot choose the moment or secure the arms. The article presents the fascist crushing of the German and Austrian parties in the 1930s as proof of this. The article concludes that the Linz Programme (1926) already treated dictatorship as a last resort, and that Renner, Bauer and Adler valued democracy above revolution and so lost sight of the essentials of communism. In its verdict, the "middle way" disarmed the workers ideologically, divided the revolutionary camp and in effect protected capitalism. Austro-Marxism neither transcended the old philosophy nor built a new socialist model. Read the original if you study Austro-Marxism or the Second International debates on democracy, dictatorship and violence, or want to see how Chinese scholars assessed them from a Leninist standpoint in 2017.

Paths to improving the affinity and relevance of ideological and political theory courses in universities 提升高校思想政治理论课亲和力与针对性的路径 Zheng Jie Writing in 2017, shortly before the 19th Party Congress, Zheng Jie asks how Chinese universities can make their ideological and political theory courses (sizheng ke) more engaging and better suited to students' needs. The article takes as its starting point Xi Jinping's call at the 2016 national conference on ideological and political work in universities to raise the "affinity and relevance" of these courses. Zheng's answer is that teachers must work on two sets of qualities, summarised as the "four degrees" and the "four airs". The article is a short policy-oriented essay published in the journal Gaoxiao fudaoyuan (University Counsellors). After a brief introduction citing Xi Jinping's speeches and the 2017 "quality year" campaign of the Ministry of Education, it sets out the two frameworks in turn. The "four degrees" concern teaching objectives, content, process and methods. The "four airs" concern lecturing, classroom language, teaching formats and assessment. On the "four degrees", Zheng argues that objectives need "height": courses should be tied to the task of cultivating reliable successors to the cause of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Content needs "depth", meaning teachers must master Marxist theory and the latest Party theory and explain it thoroughly but accessibly. The teaching process needs "warmth", and Zheng criticises teachers who read from scripts or slides in a flat tone. Methods need "effectiveness", combining lectures, case discussion, MOOCs, micro-films and social media. On the "four airs", teachers need confidence in their theory, grounded everyday and online-style language, lively practice-based formats, and varied assessment. Zheng's examples include micro-films for broadcasting students and performing revolutionary songs for music students. Zheng concludes that teachers should follow the spirit of Xi Jinping's speeches and aim at higher course quality. The article proposes improving top-level design and making progress on four fronts: textbooks, teachers, teaching and methods. The stated goal is to strengthen the courses' attractiveness and persuasiveness and students' sense of benefit from them (huodegan). Read the original if you want a concrete picture of how Chinese university teachers are advised to put Party policy on ideological and political education into classroom practice around 2017.

Marxism, political economy and sustainable human development 马克思主义、政治经济学和人类可持续发展 Paul Burkett This text is a Chinese translation of an article by Paul Burkett, an economist at Indiana State University. It asks what Marxism can add to the idea of sustainable development as it is discussed within ecological economics. Burkett argues that ecological economics has three dimensions of sustainability that are poorly integrated with one another, and that Marx and Engels's picture of communism integrates them. The first part sets out the three dimensions. They are nature as a common resource for present and future generations, the co-evolution of individuals, society and nature, and the need for common property in natural resources. Burkett reviews co-evolutionary theorists such as Mulder, Van den Bergh and Norgaard, and common-property researchers such as Hardin's critics, Ostrom, Swaney and Adger. The second part turns to Marx and Engels on post-capitalist society: non-alienation, common property, non-market allocation, land stewardship, free time and the transition to communism. Burkett contends that the co-evolutionary school stresses changing human values and the 'good life' but neglects social relations of production, class and the market. The common-property school defends commons mainly as a limit on resource use and treats failures as caused by outside forces such as markets and colonialism. In Burkett's reading, those outside forces work through class relations, and the school underplays class inequality inside the commons. For Marx and Engels, communism overcomes the separation of producers from the conditions of production. In Burkett's account it treats land as the permanent common property of successive generations and gives everyone a share in consumption and social services. It also reduces working time, which Burkett says eases pressure on nature and allows scientific and aesthetic self-development. Burkett concludes that Marx and Engels combine the three dimensions of sustainability, and that they left the future open rather than drawing up a blueprint. A fixed blueprint, he says, would contradict the principle that the emancipation of the working class must be the act of the working class itself. He treats the transition as a long, path-dependent struggle. He holds that the classical Marxist view of communism as the sublation of alienated production and the realisation of all-round human development still deserves attention. Read the original if you work on Marxist ecology or ecological economics and want a critique of co-evolutionary and common-property theories from a class-based Marxist position.

Critique and politics under parallax An interpretation and critique of Karatani Kojin's alternative logic of resistance 视差之下的批判与政治 Wang Xingfu Kojin Karatani has become a focus of attention in Chinese academia, and Slavoj Žižek has compared his Transcritique to Roberto Unger's Politics trilogy. Wang asks what Karatani's reinterpretation of Kant and Marx offers as an alternative logic of resistance to global capitalism, and whether it holds up. The article's answer is that the theory is attractive to the radical left but flawed: it misreads the relations among Kant, Hegel and Marx, treats Capital in a formalised way, and romanticises resistance politics. Writing in 2017, Wang applies Karatani's own method of parallax, offering a sympathetic reconstruction followed by criticism. Part one sets out Karatani's Kantian turn and his contrast between Kant and Hegel. Part two covers his exchange-based reading of Capital and his politics of consumer resistance. Part three gives Wang's critique, drawing on Lukács, Žižek, Antonio Negri, and Boltanski and Chiapello. In Wang's account, Karatani treats Kant's parallax as the foundation of any transcendent critique. He casts Hegel as the thinker who dissolves parallax and treats the capital–nation–state as final, and he places Marx in a line from Kant. Karatani replaces the mode-of-production approach with a theory of four modes of exchange. He argues that surplus value arises chiefly from differences between value systems in circulation, and that the worker, as money-holder at the C–M′ stage, becomes a subject. From this he derives a strategy of buying and selling boycotts and global producer-consumer cooperatives, in place of labour struggle. Wang objects on several grounds. Hegel too recognised modernity's divisions, so parallax does not separate him from Kant. Karatani confuses surplus-value realisation with its production. His claim that production is local and consumption global fails in an era of global supply chains. Consumer movements can be absorbed by capital, as Boltanski and Chiapello argue. Wang concludes that without changing the mode of production and power structure, non-capitalist enclaves would remain islands, even an aesthetic ornament of capitalism. Read the original if you follow Karatani's reception in China, or want a Marxist critique of consumer-based resistance and of the Kant–Hegel–Marx relationship.

Where is postmodern politics heading? An analysis of Ellen Meiksins Wood's critique of the postmodern left 后现代政治路在何方? Jiang Jiqing Postmodern political thought was fashionable among the Western left in the last three decades of the twentieth century. Because its political programme bears directly on the goals and strategy of left movements, the Marxist scholar Ellen Meiksins Wood took it very seriously. Jiang Jiqing's article reconstructs and assesses her critique, arguing that Wood exposed the postmodern left's confusions, its underlying character and its harmful effects, while also showing some weaknesses of her own. The article has three parts. The first sets out five features of the postmodern left's politics as Jiang presents them. The second reviews Wood's critique at three levels: the views, the essence and the harm of postmodern thought. The third analyses the strengths and shortcomings of that critique and draws lessons for Marxist theorists. In Jiang's account, the postmodern left rejects anti-capitalist "grand narratives" and universal emancipation. It replaces material and class relations with language and culture, dismisses class politics because the working class is said to have been integrated into capitalism, turns to plural new social movements, and treats Marxism as either oppressive or obsolete. Wood answers that these positions are logically incoherent. For example, they reject universal values yet rely on them to defend pluralism, and they exaggerate real changes in capitalism into a fundamental break. She traces the outlook to the post-war "golden age", when defeated left intellectuals retreated into a mood of resignation. In her view, denying that capitalism is a totality amounts to submitting to it, and giving autonomy to discourse and culture places "revolution" in the hands of intellectuals. Wood concludes that postmodernism has become a disease rather than a diagnosis of one. Jiang praises Wood's political alertness, her incisive treatment of the links between Enlightenment, modernity and capitalism, and a method that moves from views to essence to harm and still concedes some real changes. Jiang also names three flaws: weak analysis of why postmodernism arose, sometimes excessive sharpness that could hinder left unity, and generalisation across different thinkers. The lesson drawn is that Marxist theorists must stay alert to tendencies that depart from Marxism in its name, show courage when socialism meets setbacks, and connect classical Marxist positions to present realities. Read the original if you want a Chinese reading of Wood's critique of postmodernism and of how Chinese scholars assess her argument.

Alain Badiou on subjectivization and the subjective process 阿兰·巴迪欧论主体化和主体进程 Ai Shiwei This article examines two paired concepts in Alain Badiou's Theory of the Subject (1982): subjectivization (主体化) and the subjective process (主体进程). Ai Shiwei notes that Badiou, described as a leading figure of post-Marxism, borrowed both terms from Lacan, and that apart from Ed Pluth's study little work has treated them in detail. Ai argues that Badiou's subject is a split one, built from a brief, destructive moment and a lasting, reorganising one, and that this structure underpins his later "third" model of the subject. The article opens with Badiou's criticism of the idealist and materialist paradigms of the subject, which he links respectively to religious "sacrifice" and worldly "enjoyment". It then treats subjectivization, then the subjective process, then their combination in what Badiou calls the "torsade" (twisting together). It applies the scheme to the Cultural Revolution and to the French class struggle, and ends by tracing how Badiou's thinking on the subject shifted in Conditions and Being and Event. Ai explains that subjectivization is brief, destructive and interventionist. It takes two forms: "anxiety", pure destruction that points toward death, and "courage", which breaks the existing order in the hope of building a new one. The subjective process is lasting and reorganising, and holds fidelity to the event. It too takes two forms: the "superego", a terrorising process that assigns every excess element a fixed place, and "justice", which relativises law and blurs fixed positions. Their pairings give two trajectories, a Ψ mode (anxiety to superego) and an α mode (courage to justice). Badiou reads Red Guards as α-type if they pursue the communist project, and as Ψ-type if they only defend absolute authority. Ai adds that the diagonal pairings, drawn from Lacan's "imaginary", yield a dogmatic function (courage–superego) and a sceptical function (justice–anxiety). Ai describes the first as reification that turns rebels into parts of a system, and the second as ending in nothingness. Ai concludes that the subject is neither reducible to the body nor separable from it, but is joined to it as a "subjectivized body". Ai also notes that Badiou later widened the subject beyond politics to science, art and love, and that he criticised his earlier text for simply presupposing that subjectivization exists. Ai reads this as Badiou going beyond pure deconstruction to ask how a subject can form and be rebuilt. Read the original if you work on Badiou, Lacan or post-Marxist theories of the subject and want a systematic account of these two concepts.

The development of the Iraqi left and the Chinese experience as the Iraqi left sees it 伊拉克左翼的发展及其眼中的中国经验 Basim Muhsin The author, identified as a member of the Political Bureau of the Central Committee of the Iraqi Communist Party, gives an insider account of the Iraqi left and of how it views China. The name is given in Chinese as Basam Muxi, and the Latin spelling here is a reconstruction. The article, published in 2017 and translated into Chinese, argues that the left must unite around democracy, social justice and a collectively owned economy to meet Iraq's multiple crises. It also presents China's reform experience as a successful model of "socialist market economy". The text has four parts. It first traces the left's emergence in the early twentieth century, the founding of the Iraqi Communist Party in 1934, its repression, and the post-2003 situation under US occupation. It then sets out the challenges and tasks facing the left, and discusses the left's alliance and its relation to socialism. The final section is a short assessment of the Chinese experience since reform and opening up. On Iraq, Muhsin describes a country in structural crisis: corruption, sectarian politics, foreign interference, the advance of the Islamic State, and the mass protests of 2011 and 2015. He names three challenges: building a civil democratic state, countering political Islam and religious fundamentalism, and resisting capitalist globalisation. The left's answer is a national democratic programme and a broad, pluralist alliance of left and democratic forces, working with unions and civil society. Muhsin holds that socialism rests on political democracy, social justice and collective ownership of the means of production, and that class struggle cannot be set aside. He adds that the working class has changed and now allies with new social movements. In the China section, Muhsin credits Deng Xiaoping's 1978 reforms and the "socialist market economy" under Communist Party leadership with producing stability and rapid growth. He claims that this system, resting on public ownership with several forms of ownership coexisting, has gone beyond the limits of capitalist development and serves social justice. The market is described as a tool for socialist goals. Read the original if you want a first-hand Iraqi communist view of the left's strategy and of how Iraqi leftists read China's reform model.

Ferenc Fehér on the relationship between Jacobinism and socialism 费赫尔论雅各宾主义和社会主义的关系 Cao Lixin Is Jacobinism the origin of socialism? Cao Lixin takes up this question through the work of Ferenc Fehér, the Hungarian Budapest School thinker, and in particular his book The Frozen Revolution: An Essay on Jacobinism. Cao reports that earlier historians, Marxist and liberal alike, answered no and shelved the matter. Fehér, in Cao's reading, holds that the answer depends on how "socialism" is defined. His conclusion is that Jacobinism is not yet proto-socialism but contains tendencies that fed into it. The article first sets out why the question was set aside and why Fehér thinks historians reasoned badly. They started from modern socialism, found none of its features in Jacobin rule, and concluded correctly but by an unsuitable method. Cao then presents Fehér's case for Jacobinism's proto-socialist tendencies and, in a longer section, the reasons it still falls short. A closing section draws lessons for socialist theory and practice, citing Lenin's view of Bolshevism as the Jacobinism of the twentieth century. For the proto-socialist side, Cao gives three features: an anti-capitalist spirit, an egalitarian demand, and the effort to build a new society and to make the "social question" the aim of revolution. The first rests on the Jacobin priority of the right to existence over property rights, as in the 1793 constitution. For the other side, Fehér argues that state intervention never produced a planned economy and that the radical change in property rights did not amount to nationalisation. In his account, the "republic of virtue" did not achieve equality, and Robespierre himself called equality of property a chimera. Fehér concludes that Jacobinism stands "between two worlds". Cao argues that the comparison should not praise or condemn Jacobinism but prompt reflection on Soviet socialism and on socialism's essence and core values. Cao draws three lessons: revolutionary politics should be weighed against peaceful reform; planning and the market are both means that should not be made ideological and should complement each other; and socialism cannot be reduced to a planned economy, absolute equal distribution or a highly centralised interventionist state. Citing Deng Xiaoping's definition of the essence of socialism, Cao adds that socialism has many forms, including socialism with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a Chinese reading of Fehér on the Jacobin legacy and its bearing on debates about socialism and the market.

Rawls, Lacan and Marx on justice, and the Chinese road 罗尔斯、拉康与马克思的正义观之辨与中国道路 Li Xixiang Writing in 2017, Li Xixiang asks which conception of justice China should hold to and promote, and how the Marxist conception is to be understood. The article answers by comparing Marx's view with those of John Rawls and of Jacques Lacan, the latter read through Slavoj Žižek. Li argues that Marx's justice is a distinct, fuller conception than either Rawls's distributive justice or Lacan–Žižek's "drive justice", and that it should be understood as a process of becoming. The article has four sections. The first sets out Rawls's original position, veil of ignorance and two principles of justice, with some comparison to Habermas. The second turns to Žižek's criticism of Rawls and the Lacanian concept of justice behind it. The third reconstructs Marx's justice from the Communist Manifesto, the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 and The German Ideology. The fourth applies the comparison to China's path and to its current state of fairness. Li reads Rawls's justice as a liberal, modernist scheme of fair distribution. Li faults it for assuming a rational, benign and context-free individual. Following Žižek, Li says it overlooks the forced choice and sacrifice (the Lacanian symbolic castration and incest prohibition) that logically precede the original position. Lacan–Žižek's alternative is a radical justice of the drive, exemplified by Antigone: a second, repeated choice that breaks the symbolic order. Li finds in Marx three dimensions of justice: historical, revolutionary and free. Revolutionary justice, meaning the abolition of private property and the overcoming of alienation toward an association of free individuals, is described as the core. Li notes that Marx's aim of free and equal persons does not contradict Rawls's, though the means differ. Li proposes a generative view in which justice is something always being approached rather than possessed, and compares this with Derrida's remark that deconstruction is justice. Under socialism with Chinese characteristics, Li reads Deng Xiaoping's formula (liberating productive forces, eliminating exploitation and polarisation, reaching common prosperity) as aspects of justice, to be pursued as a gradual, ongoing process without a fixed timetable. Li judges that fairness and justice in China are improving overall, citing growing openness and transparency. Read the original if you want a Chinese philosophical comparison of Rawls, Lacan–Žižek and Marx on justice, and an example of how such debates are tied to the Chinese road.

Raising high the ideological banner of twenty-first-century Marxism 高举21世纪马克思主义的思想旗帜 Shuang Chuanxue Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2017, Shuang Chuanxue takes up Xi Jinping's call, made at the symposium on philosophy and social sciences and in his letter marking the 40th anniversary of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, to develop "twenty-first-century Marxism" and "contemporary Chinese Marxism". Shuang argues that this is the historic mission of the age and that Xi Jinping's thought on governance is its most concentrated expression. Shuang adds that the banner can be held high only by clearing away several mistaken ideas. The commentary has three parts. The first presents the development of twenty-first-century Marxism as a task the times have set for Chinese communists. The second sets out why Xi's ideas on governing the country count as the latest result of adapting Marxism to China. The third lists the intellectual obstacles to be removed and ends with a call to philosophers and social scientists. In the first part, Shuang holds that Marxism's essence is to ground itself in developing practice, and that Marx and Engels offered no formulas valid for every era. The author traces this through Lenin and the Chinese Party's adaptation of Marxism, and credits the Party with a tradition of learning and theoretical innovation. The practice of socialism with Chinese characteristics, Shuang says, poses new problems that neither the classics nor foreign experience can answer. In the second part, Shuang describes Xi's thought as an "Four Comprehensives"-centred system that answers the Chinese Dream question, enriches the theoretical system of socialism with Chinese characteristics, and has been tested in practice, citing the May 2017 Belt and Road forum as evidence. In the third part, Shuang opposes three forms of the claim that Marxism is outdated, along with the "Westernisation" and "Confucianisation" of guiding ideology. Shuang also opposes currents such as historical nihilism, neoliberalism, "universal values", Western constitutional democracy and democratic socialism. Shuang concludes that scholars should study and implement Xi's speeches and his new ideas on governance, and should take on the task of upholding and developing twenty-first-century Marxism. The author says that opposing Westernisation and Confucianisation does not mean rejecting Western civilisation or traditional Chinese culture. Instead, Marxism should absorb the best of human civilisation and creatively transform traditional culture. Read the original if you want an example of how the Party's theoretical press in 2017 presented Xi Jinping's governance thought as Marxism for the twenty-first century, and which ideological currents it named as opponents.

A textual study of Marx's category of totality 马克思总体性范畴的文本学研究 Peng Hongwei Marx never explicitly put forward "totality" as a concept, yet Georg Lukács claimed to derive the category from Marx's texts, and it has shaped Marxist scholarship in China as well as abroad. Peng Hongwei argues that Chinese scholars have accepted Lukács's version uncritically and applied it to other fields. The article returns to Marx's own texts to test whether Lukács's totality matches Marx's meaning, and concludes that it differs significantly. The article is a close reading, mainly of the Grundrisse chapter on capital and of Capital and its manuscripts. It has three parts: what Marx meant by "totality" (the object), how Marx moves beyond the opposition of whole and part, and totality as a fundamental attribute ("totality-ness") and a method of thought. Peng also cites Lukács's own 1967 self-criticism, in which Lukács said that placing totality at the centre of Marxism had produced a Hegelian distortion. Peng's first move is to argue that, for Marx, the totality is a living social organism, and in capitalist society it is above all capital. Capital subordinates other social elements and creates the organs it lacks. Marx distinguishes this real totality from the "totality of thought", the product of the thinking brain, which he separates from Hegel's idealism. Peng treats "collective worker" and "collective capitalist" as the two categories under the capital totality. The second move is to argue that what corresponds to totality in Marx is the particular, not the part. The totality is therefore not a mechanical sum but a set of organically connected particular relations, and it is a process that unites production and circulation. Peng's third move defines totality-ness as the process by which capital becomes a totality, which he dates to the age of large-scale industry. He lists four attributes: maintaining balance through alienation, unity of continuity and discontinuity, self-generation, and the building of organic relations. Peng concludes that totality-ness is a method that Marx originated and that enriched materialist dialectics. It brings will and spirit into the analysis, which rules out mechanical and supposedly neutral thinking, and it surpasses old materialism and idealism. Peng lists five tasks for studying a totality: its internal connections, its stages, its links with external elements, its relation to its derivatives, and its will. Read the original if you want a text-based challenge to the Lukácsian reading of totality, or want to see how Chinese scholars return to Marx's manuscripts on this question.

Multiple dimensions of research on Marx's political economy since the twentieth century New readings of Marx's Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 and Capital 20世纪以来马克思政治经济学研究的多维度开展 He Ping He Ping asks how three major strands of twentieth-century Marxist theory grew out of Marx's two central economic works. The article argues that the immaturity of the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 in economics, and the unfinished state of Capital, are strengths rather than defects. In the author's view they make Marx's political economy an open system that later theorists could develop. Published in Tianjin Social Sciences in 2017, it traces the link between Marx's texts and later theory. The article has three main sections. The first follows the concept of practice and the theory of alienated labour from the 1844 Manuscripts into Marxist cultural critique. It covers Labriola, Gramsci, Althusser and Williams, and then the Frankfurt School and Lefebvre. The second section follows the question of capital accumulation, from Rosa Luxemburg's dispute with Hilferding, Bukharin and Lenin through underconsumptionism and world-systems theory to post-2007 readings of Capital. The third examines ecological Marxism's use of the labour theory of value, from James O'Connor to John Bellamy Foster and others, and compares it with Engels. In the cultural strand, He presents Gramsci's cultural hegemony as a relatively independent social power exercised by consent, which develops the cultural content of Marx's practice concept. He presents the Frankfurt School's critique of modernity and the culture industry as a later form of the theory of alienated labour. In the economic strand, Luxemburg's problem of realising surplus value is said to recur through Baran and Sweezy's 'utilisation of surplus' and Wallerstein's core–periphery scheme. He judges that Wallerstein neglected Capital and so could not explain the 2007 financial crisis. The author says that readings of Capital by Paul Zarembka and others restore accumulation, money demand and crisis to the centre, and so avoid a 'productivist' reading confined to Volume 1. In the ecological strand, He argues that O'Connor's rejection of historical materialism left ecological Marxism a blend of Marxism and ecologism. Foster, Burkett and Clark are credited with a way out through Marx's concept of social metabolism. He concludes that accumulation has become the central theme of contemporary Marxist political economy. Citing Ben Agger's three-part summary of Marx's dialectic, the author holds that the 1844 Manuscripts and Capital remain the most valuable works of our era. He also argues that Foster's ecological Marxism explains Western capitalist crises but fits socialist China poorly. Engels's more abstract treatment of labour and nature is presented as a better resource for a Chinese ecological Marxism suited to national conditions. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's survey of how Gramsci, the Frankfurt School, world-systems theory and ecological Marxism relate to Marx's economic texts.

Contemporary Western Marxism: critique, reflection and exploration 当代西方马克思主义：批判、反思与探索 Xiong Guangqing Writing in 2017, Xiong Guangqing asks how Western Marxists responded after the upheavals in the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe, and what their responses offer Chinese readers. The article argues that, from the early 1990s, Western Marxism shifted its themes from philosophy and culture towards politics, economics and ecology, and its critical focus from advanced capitalism towards a reassessment of 'actually existing socialism'. In Xiong's account, these thinkers held to Marxism, defended it and rethought socialism. The article first sketches how Western Marxism emerged from the 1923 debate over Georg Lukács and Karl Korsch and developed after the 1950s. It then examines three sets of questions through four thinkers: Jürgen Habermas, István Mészáros, Fredric Jameson and, more briefly, David McLellan. The sections cover the lessons of the Soviet and East European collapse, the continuing relevance of Marxism, and the reassessment of socialism's prospects. On the causes of the collapse, Xiong reports that Habermas called it a 'rectifying revolution' that rejected both existing capitalism and Stalinist state socialism. Mészáros blamed the continued rule of capital under a Soviet-type system, and Jameson read the collapse as the completion of that system's modernising task, not a defeat for communism. On relevance, all four are said to separate the failure of one model from the failure of Marxism. Jameson holds that capitalism has not fundamentally changed and remains in crisis. McLellan holds that historical materialism retains strength even where dialectical materialism and command economies have lost it. On socialism's future, Habermas rebuilds it as a coercion-free communicative public sphere, with political openness and an end to bureaucratic domination. Mészáros calls for going beyond capital, and Jameson defines socialism as comprehensive social security and free collective practice.
