Xiong concludes that these thinkers stayed committed to Marxism during a low point for the world socialist movement and defended it forcefully. He says this can help strengthen belief in Marxism. He also says some of their views cannot be accepted, but that they give useful clues about why the collapse happened. He singles out Mészáros's point that capital's rule can persist in post-revolutionary societies as worth further study. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's 2017 overview of how Western Marxists interpreted the Soviet collapse and reframed socialism.

Western Marxism's critique of modernity and its significance for China today 西方马克思主义现代性批判理论及其在当今中国的意义 Chen Xueming Chen Xueming asks what Western Marxism's critique of modernity can offer to China's path of development. Both Western Marxism and postmodernism start from anger at the negative effects of modernity, but Chen argues that they diverge sharply. Postmodernism rejects modernity wholesale, whereas Western Marxism treats it dialectically, in Habermas's phrase as an "unfinished project", and turns its critique into an argument for the necessity of socialist goals. Chen holds that this orientation supplies a possible basis and theoretical resource for the correctness of China's road. The article has three parts. The first contrasts Western Marxism (Lukács, Gramsci, the Frankfurt School, Habermas, Gorz and eco-Marxism) with postmodernism (Griffin, Lyotard, Derrida and eco-centrism) on attitude to modernity, subjectivity, reason, science and technology, and ontology. The second sets out what this theory means for China. The third asks which Marxism Western Marxism can be said to inherit, distinguishing three domestic readings since the 1980s. In Chen's account, postmodernism dissolves the subject, reason, science and ontology, and ends in a longing for a pre-technological state. Western Marxists criticise instrumental reason but defend reason, human-centred subjectivity, the emancipatory potential of technology and a practice-based ontology, locating the sources of modernity's ills in the capitalist system. For China, Chen draws three lessons: neither abandoning modernity nor accepting its costs uncritically; using eco-Marxism, market socialism theory and humanist theories of human existence to address ecological damage, polarisation and one-dimensionality; and taking from Western Marxism's open reading of Marx a confidence in adapting Marxism to Chinese conditions. Chen concludes that Western Marxism can serve China only if Marxism is understood through historical materialism and the two great discoveries (materialist conception of history and surplus value), rather than through an "Enlightenment" or postmodern reading. On this view Marx's thought passed through three leaps that went beyond the Enlightenment and anticipated a critique of postmodernism. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's case for treating Western Marxist critiques of modernity as supporting socialism with Chinese characteristics, together with a typology of Chinese readings of Marx.

Jacques Bidet's "metastructural" reading of Capital and its assessment 雅克·比岱对《资本论》的“元结构”式解读及其评价 Tang Zhengdong Tang Zhengdong examines how the French philosopher Jacques Bidet, editor of the journal Actuel Marx, reads Marx's Capital through a dialectical market–organisation "metastructure". Tang acknowledges that Bidet's reading is original and has real theoretical force. The article's thesis, however, is that Bidet interprets the commodity relation in an over-politico-economic and empiricist way, and so misjudges the scientific method of Capital and the critique of capital built on it. The article draws on Bidet's Dictionnaire Marx contemporain, Théorie générale, Explorer le Capital (Exploring Marx's Capital) and Critical Companion to Contemporary Marxism. It has three sections. The first deals with Bidet's claim that Capital begins from a "modern fiction" of free and equal exchange, which the later analysis of capital then inverts. The second takes up his view that Capital's mode of presentation is theoretical rather than historical. The third tests Bidet's reading against the logic of Volume I, from the commodity chapters to the "Rhodes" passage on the transformation of money into capital. Tang argues that Bidet takes the commodity relation as free and equal exchange, which is the empiricist notion of the classical economists. For Marx, Tang says, the commodity unites use-value and exchange-value in an internal contradiction, and the critique of capital rests on developing that contradiction between labour and capital. Bidet, avoiding what he sees as teleology (partly through Spinoza and Althusser's "epistemological break"), treats Marx's abstraction as a fiction opposed to experience. Tang counters that the method of ascending from the abstract to the concrete presupposes a historical analysis of contradictions in production relations. Bidet's emphasis on producers' capacities in chapter 1 and his "value substance" theory, Tang adds, ignore that Marx at that stage abstracts from useful labour and has not yet reached exchange or use-value as determined by exchange-value. Tang concludes that Bidet stays at a critique of exchange-value as an inverted contractual relation and never reaches the movement of internal contradiction through which Marx makes the leap from labour theory of value to surplus-value. Reading Capital's order as merely an order of "concepts", Tang suggests, recalls Marx's own criticism of Proudhon's economic metaphysics in The Poverty of Philosophy. Read the original if you study Western Marxist interpretations of Capital, or want a Chinese critical assessment of Bidet's metastructure theory and its handling of method in Marx.

The Absolute and the event: what kind of Hegelian is Žižek? 绝对与事件:齐泽克是一个怎样的黑格尔主义者 Wu Guanjun Hegel is usually read as the philosopher of totality, whose system leaves no room for a genuine ontological "event". Wu asks how Slavoj Žižek can call himself a committed Hegelian and also make the event a central category, as he does in his 2014 book Event: Philosophy in Transit. The article argues that Žižek reads Hegel's Absolute as a totality with a gap built into it, and that this makes Hegel a thinker of events. The article starts from the twentieth-century critique of Hegel by Popper, Deleuze, Laclau and Mouffe, and Nancy. It then compares Žižek with Alain Badiou, who built his philosophy on the event, broke with Hegel after Being and Event, and has Hegelian roots in his early work. Derrida's deconstructive account of the event serves as a further contrast. Wu then reconstructs Žižek's Hegel through the dialectic, parallax, negation and the Fall. The final sections set Žižek against Alexandre Kojève and John Gray. Wu makes three moves. First, Žižek treats the "negation of negation" as a change of the whole framework of perception, not of particular content: the law itself is crime, property itself is theft. The antithesis is already inscribed in the thesis, and the difference between them is a change of perspective that Žižek calls parallax. For Žižek this is an ontological condition, not an epistemological one, and so Hegel completes Kant's Copernican turn. Second, absolute knowledge is knowledge of the gap or limit, a "withheld secret", and not a God's-eye view. It sits in the middle of the dialectic and not at its end, so Žižek rejects the end of history. Third, against Badiou's claim that negation is merely derivative and destroys without creating, Žižek holds that negation is primary and that positive content is produced by the "positivized power of the Negative". On this view "the ultimate event is the Fall itself", and Hegel's "night of the world" is the ontological condition of freedom and creation. Wu concludes that Žižek's Hegel is a philosopher of a self-differentiating whole in which Spirit confronts the wound between reality and the Real. In this reading the dialectic keeps renewing the world and has no endpoint. Wu traces this reading to an unacknowledged debt to Kojève's equation of freedom, negativity and creativity. Wu also criticises Gray's account, which attributes Žižek's reading to Badiou and ties it to capitalism. Political struggle, on this reading, aims to overcome the concealment of the wound, not the wound itself. Read the original if you work on Žižek, Badiou or Hegel's reception in twentieth-century French thought and want a detailed account of how Žižek reconciles the Absolute with the event.

How Capital moves into the contemporary era: an outline of the critique of political economy for the twenty-first century Reshaping the dialectic of the logic of capital and class struggle 《资本论》如何走向当代:21世纪政治经济学批判大纲 Sun Leqiang Sun Leqiang takes up a long-standing problem in Marxism: how the objective formula (the contradiction between productive forces and relations of production) relates to the subjective formula (class struggle). In Capital this appears as the relation between the logic of capital and class struggle. Sun argues that contemporary Western Left thinkers who say Capital lacks a mature theory of class struggle, and who therefore want to go beyond or reconstruct it, misread the work. In Sun's account, class logic gains legitimacy only on the basis of the critique of capital, and Capital is in essence a revolutionary critical work. The article has three parts. The first surveys three Western Left routes: Fredric Jameson's depoliticised reading of Capital as a book about unemployment, Michael Lebowitz's turn from capital to workers' 'needs', and Harry Cleaver's political reading of the commodity–money opposition. The second reconstructs Marx's own reasoning, from the German Ideology and the Manifesto to the Grundrisse and Capital. The third sets out a programme for a twenty-first-century critique of political economy. It draws on Karel Kosik, David Harvey and Slavoj Žižek, and discusses Hardt and Negri, Moulier-Boutang and Piketty. Sun's central move is that commodity and money are only the phenomenal sphere of capital and cannot touch the relations of production behind exchange. Nor can an independent logic of needs ground a revolutionary subject, since modern needs are themselves produced by capital. On Sun's reading, Marx held that workers become a class for itself only as the critique of capital advances from division of labour, which splits workers into hierarchies, to machine production, which makes total capital the target. Revolution then depends on a party, theory and the deeper limits of accumulation and the falling rate of profit, not on crises alone. Sun criticises Jameson for neutralising Capital and Lebowitz and Cleaver for ignoring the objective conditions of class formation. For the present, Sun proposes four research tasks: the shift of commodity forms towards knowledge and information; the labour theory of value and the changing character of labour-power, where Sun rejects 'immaterial labour' and 'cognitive capitalism' as refutations of Marx; surplus-value production under intelligent manufacturing, which Sun says deepens divisions within the working class; and finance, credit and real estate. Sun holds that biopolitics follows from this critique and cannot replace it, and that Piketty has not completed the task. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist rebuttal of Jameson, Lebowitz and Cleaver, together with an agenda for updating Marx's critique of political economy.

Teachers of non-ideological-and-political courses should strengthen awareness of ideological and political education in their teaching 非思政课专业教师应特别增强授课中的思想政治教育意识 Tong Xiao Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts (Hongqi Wengao, 2017, no. 14), Tong Xiao takes up a problem raised by Xi Jinping's speech at the national conference on ideological and political work in universities: how teachers of ordinary subject courses can join the ideological and political education of students. Tong argues that a considerable number of such teachers lack this awareness, and that some even teach out of step with, or against, the ideological and political theory courses. The article calls for stronger awareness among them. The commentary is a short, prescriptive piece organised around four requirements for subject teachers. It begins from the formula that every course should keep "its own section of the channel" and "tend its own responsibility field", moving in the same direction as the ideological and political theory courses. Tong's first requirement is awareness of Marxism as a guiding ideology, in both course content and the teacher's own conduct. The second is to weave ideological and political content into subject teaching: drawing out the values already present in a subject, addressing students' questions inside and outside class, and not stressing skills at the expense of values. The third is to make "fostering virtue through education" the central task, coordinating with ideological and political teachers through staff exchange, shared content, joint case teaching and joint criticism of mistaken views. The fourth is to build ideological and political elements into course design, gently and without forcing them. Tong's examples are Marie Curie's patriotism in chemistry and Fei Xiaotong and the multiparty cooperation system in sociology. Tong warns against turning subject courses into ideological and political courses. Tong concludes that the most effective education is received unconsciously, and that using subject teachers' influence is a political advantage of Chinese universities that must be pursued. Subject teachers should guide students' values while teaching their specialisms. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the 2017 official line on integrating ideological education into university subject teaching.

Institutional causes of Western disorder and Chinese governance 西方之乱与中国之治的制度原因 Zhang Weiwei Writing in 2017 (the piece appeared in Qiushi, issue 15), Zhang Weiwei asks why the West has fallen into turmoil while China has achieved good governance, although both exist under deepening globalization. Zhang opens with a list of Western troubles: the Trump presidency, the refugee influx into Europe, Brexit, populism, terrorist attacks and stagnating living standards. Against these, the author sets China's rise since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Zhang's answer is that the contrast comes from differing strategies toward globalization, differing institutional arrangements, and a different balance among three forces in governance. The article has three numbered sections, each taking up one cause. The first compares Western and Chinese understandings of globalization. The second compares political, economic and social-governance institutions. The third sets out a framework of political, social and capital forces. Zhang uses figures such as Joseph Stiglitz's calculation on US median income, a 2016 Ipsos poll on satisfaction with national direction, and the 2010 and 2014 US Supreme Court rulings on campaign donations. Zhang argues that Western-led globalization is essentially neoliberal globalization serving international monopoly capital. In this account it concentrates gains among a rich minority, hollows out domestic industry, and exports a political agenda whose consequences now return as refugees and terrorism. China, by contrast, treats globalization as economic only, not political or "Western", and uses socialist institutions to correct its defects. Zhang contrasts Western parties, called "partial-interest parties", with the Communist Party as a "whole-interest party". The author also contrasts neoliberal laissez-faire with China's socialist market economy and its model of Party-government leadership, social coordination and public participation. At the deepest level, Zhang says capital dominates in the United States and social forces dominate in parts of Europe. China's political force, in this reading, stays independent of both and can guide them. Zhang concludes that Chinese governance rests on institutions oriented to the people's overall interests. In this account those institutions draw on Chinese civilizational heritage, the "red genes" of socialism with Chinese characteristics, and lessons from other civilizations. The author states that China's most lasting significance lies in offering experience and wisdom for building a better society, as well as in lifting a fifth of humanity toward prosperity. Zhang concedes that the Party faces challenges and calls for full and rigorous self-governance of the Party and deepened reform. Read the original if you want a representative statement of how a prominent Chinese commentator contrasted Western and Chinese systems in an official Party journal in 2017.

Raising high the ideological banner of twenty-first-century Marxism 高举21世纪马克思主义的思想旗帜 Shuang Chuanxue Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2017, Shuang Chuanxue takes up Xi Jinping's call, made at the symposium on philosophy and social sciences and in a letter marking the 40th anniversary of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, to develop "twenty-first-century Marxism" and "contemporary Chinese Marxism". The article argues that this is a historical mission given to Chinese Communists by the age. It holds that Xi Jinping's thought on governing the country is the most concentrated expression of that Marxism. The piece has three parts. The first explains why developing twenty-first-century Marxism is a historical task. The second presents Xi's ideas on state governance as the field's fullest embodiment. The third names the intellectual obstacles that must be cleared before the banner can be held high. Shuang draws on Marx and Engels, Lenin, and the record of the Communist Party of China since reform and opening up. Shuang argues that Marxism is above all a method tied to changing practice, so it must renew itself with each age. Shuang points to Lenin's adaptation of Marxism to Russia and the Party's adaptation of it to China. The author holds that new problems in the course of socialism with Chinese characteristics cannot be solved from classic texts or by copying foreign experience. In this account, Xi's governance thought answers the people's new expectations, enriches the theoretical system of socialism with Chinese characteristics and has been tested in practice, with the Belt and Road Initiative forum of May 2017 cited as evidence. The third part rejects three versions of the claim that Marxism is outdated: that times have changed, that history has ended, and that Chinese practice has broken with Marx's vision. The author calls all three dogmatic. Shuang also opposes the "Westernization" and "Confucianization" of the guiding ideology. The author names historical nihilism, neoliberalism, "universal values", Western constitutional democracy, democratic socialism and cultural revivalism as erroneous currents to be criticised. Shuang concludes that scholars should study and carry out Xi's speeches and his new ideas on governing the country, and should take up the task of upholding and developing twenty-first-century Marxism. The author says this opposition to Westernization and Confucianization is not hostility to Western civilization or to traditional Chinese culture, which should be creatively transformed. Read the original if you want a clear example of how a 2017 Party-theory journal linked Xi's governance thought to the idea of twenty-first-century Marxism and framed ideological threats to it.

The dimensions of cultural confidence 文化自信的维度 Shen Zhuanghai Writing in Qiushi in early 2017, Shen Zhuanghai asks what cultural confidence means for China and how it can be strengthened. Shen argues that, amid competition in cultural soft power, no culture or nation can stand at the forefront of civilisation without confidence in itself. The article proposes a comprehensive and rational view of cultural confidence, which Shen treats as a strategic task in building China into a strong socialist cultural power. The piece has three parts. The first defines cultural confidence as the nation's conviction in its own cultural ideals, values, vitality and prospects, and explains why it is needed now. The second sets out three dimensions: confidence in cultural spirit, in cultural capacity and in the cultural path. The third lists practical ways to strengthen it. Shen first places the question in modern history. Since the 19th century, the author says, China has had to handle the relations between past and present and between China and the world, and a sense of national weakness once left many people "lost in the Western tide, doubting tradition and unsure of the road ahead". Shen sees cultural confidence as rebuilt through national liberation and reform and opening up, but still needed given Western dominance in the global cultural order and what the author lists as unhealthy tendencies: blind worship of the West, rigid attachment to the past, self-contempt, arrogance and vulgar culture. The three dimensions then point to content, creative agents and development path. Confidence in cultural spirit means trust in values such as benevolence, people-centredness, good faith and harmony, and in the core socialist values as their contemporary transformation. Confidence in cultural capacity rests on the nation's creative record and its achievements under Party leadership. Confidence in the cultural path means the Marxist-guided cultural development path of socialism with Chinese characteristics. To strengthen cultural confidence, Shen calls for keeping the Four-sphere Confidence in internal unity, building a real material and institutional foundation through reform, public cultural services and better international communication, and producing outstanding cultural works. Shen urges cultural workers to create works with China's own originality that tell its stories well. Read the original if you want a compact example of how a 2017 official Party journal framed the content and tasks of cultural confidence.

On authority Why and how Party members should uphold the authority of the Party Central Committee 谈权威 Wang Guancheng Writing in 2017, Wang Guancheng asks how Party members and cadres should uphold the authority of the Party Central Committee. The author starts from the Sixth Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2016), which confirmed Xi Jinping's core position and made upholding the Central Committee's authority a key principle and a matter of political discipline. Wang's answer is that members must understand the significance of that authority in theory and must be clear-minded in thought, firm in politics and conscious in action. The article has two parts. The first is a historical and theoretical survey, running from Marx and Engels through Lenin and the Soviet Communist Party to the Communist Party of China, arguing that upholding central authority is a constant principle of Marxist parties. The second sets out three practical requirements: clear-mindedness in thought, firmness in politics and consciousness in action, each divided into three sub-points. Wang's core claim is that Marxist theory and Party history both show central authority to be a condition of success. The author cites Marx and Engels on the Paris Commune, which fell for lack of authority, and Lenin's democratic centralism, and reads the Chinese Party's two defeats and two victories as the absence and presence of a authoritative centre. The practical programme draws on this. Members should study Marxism and Xi Jinping's speeches and fight wrong ideas rather than act as "gentlemen". They should make political standards primary, keep the identity of Communist Party member first, and refuse to join in criticism of the Central Committee or distortion of Party history. They should follow the Party Constitution and discipline, and comply with the 2016 guidelines on intra-Party political life and the supervision regulations. The author adds that the authority of the Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core continues and develops Marxist teaching on party leadership. Wang concludes that upholding the Central Committee's authority is concrete rather than abstract. It should show in every member's thinking, speech and conduct, and it is a political requirement as well as discipline. The article ends by quoting Xi Jinping's demand for absolute loyalty, under which members do what the Party asks and refrain from what it forbids. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Party-school commentary in 2017 justified the "core" leadership and set out its expectations of members.

Big data as an aid to cyber ideological governance and pathways for improving it 大数据助力网络意识形态治理及提升路径 Fu Anling Zhang Yaocan Writing in 2016, Fu Anling and Zhang Yaocan ask how big data can be used in the governance of ideology on the internet. They start from the Third Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2013), which set the goal of modernizing the system and capacity of national governance. In the authors' view, ideological governance is an "extremely important" part of that task, and its modernization depends on seizing the national big data strategy. Their thesis is that big data fits the needs of cyber ideological governance closely, but brings security risks, and that a set of institutional and technical measures can capture the benefits and limit the risks. The article has three parts. It first defines big data (the "4V" and "5V" characteristics, with definitions from Gartner, the US National Science Foundation and McKinsey) and defines cyber ideological governance and what big data "assisting" it means. It then matches the features of big data to governance needs, and sets out three risks. Finally it proposes five paths, with examples from Chinese social media and public-opinion incidents, such as the "Eastern Star" shipwreck and the 2015 Qing'an railway station shooting. The central move pairs each big data feature with a governance requirement. Variety suits the plurality of governing actors, including government, enterprises and online communities. Velocity suits timeliness, volume suits holistic oversight of social currents, and veracity suits precise, targeted policy. The authors also note that low value density complicates governance. They name three risks: discourse power shifting to internet magnates and opinion leaders, decentralization of ideology, and weakening of authority. They say these risks erode the leading position of Marxism and of core socialist values online. The five paths are: advancing a national big data strategy for ideological governance, including talent training and learning from the United States and France; building a big data early-warning mechanism; improving emergency handling of online public opinion; building a security guarantee system, with legal rules, a national "firewall" and limits on the abuse of state power; and using big data to renew Marxist discourse and appeal, including by shaping young people's learning and cultivating Marxist opinion leaders. The authors conclude that big data governance is a necessary route to modernizing ideological governance, and that its complexity must be recognized. Read the original if you want to see how a 2016 Chinese ideological-education journal framed big data, online opinion monitoring and ideological security.

The dictatorship of monopoly finance capital has destroyed the participation in and meaning of elections 垄断金融资本的独裁统治已经毁掉了选举的参与度和意义 Samir Amin This is a Chinese translation of a short commentary by the Egyptian economist Samir Amin on the 2017 French elections. Amin argues that multi-party elections, the signature device of modern democracy in Europe and the United States, are decaying because the dictatorship of monopoly finance capital has emptied them of participation and meaning. The piece takes France as its case. It covers the April 2017 presidential election and the two rounds of parliamentary voting in June, and recalls the earlier referendum on the European constitution. It then widens to the political situation of Europe and North America over the previous thirty years, and ends with the prospects for the left. Amin reports that 60 per cent of French voters abstained, which he calls unprecedented in Western democratic history. He says Macron won with no more than 16 per cent of French citizens behind him, mainly the middle class and business owners, so that the media's talk of an overwhelming victory is false. In his account, French voters learned from the ignored referendum result that voting no longer decides anything. He describes a "single party" serving the very rich, in which socialist and conservative governments no longer differ, and he says Western media would condemn such a farce in Russia, Iran or any country of the South. Amin cautions that the loss of legitimacy of elections will not by itself bring a more advanced, genuinely democratic form. He sees openings in the "Unbowed France" movement and in intensified social struggle, but holds that thirty years of experience show that struggle alone cannot stop the rightward drift. He calls on the radical left in France, Europe and elsewhere to move beyond defence and to build a positive, social and democratic alternative that challenges the world system underpinning imperialism and its Atlantic European subsystem. Read the original if you want a brief example of a Marxist critique of Western electoral democracy from a leading dependency-school thinker.

Why Trump came onto the stage of history Reflections on Trump, American conservatism and fascism 特朗普为何会登上历史舞台 Ma Zhongcheng Writing in 2017, Ma Zhongcheng asks why Donald Trump won the 2016 US presidential election. The article argues that Trump's rise did not begin with his campaign but with the 2008 financial crisis, which released the economic, political and social contradictions accumulated by neoliberal policy since the 1980s. In Ma's reading, sharpening polarisation and class struggle produced Brexit, the Sanders phenomenon and the Trump phenomenon. American racism, the author holds, is the key instrument for drawing white working-class voters behind monopoly capital, so Trump was backed by both big business and many low-income voters. The article has five sections. It begins with the Tea Party and Occupy Wall Street movements of 2011, then turns to the billionaire and far-right networks behind the Tea Party, including the Koch brothers, the John Birch Society and Mike Pence. It then compares the 2016 primaries of Sanders and Clinton and Trump's campaign strategy. The last section traces the history of American racism, from the destruction of Native Americans and slavery to the Declaration of Independence, social Darwinism, eugenics and sterilisation laws. Ma contends that the Democrats' defeat was settled in 2011, when the state suppressed the peaceful Occupy movement while the Tea Party, funded by Trump and the Kochs, was absorbed into the Republican Party. In the author's account, Democratic leaders, citing leaked emails, sabotaged Sanders, who might otherwise have led a New Deal-style reform of capitalism, and monopoly capital instead chose Trump. Ma argues that Trump's strategy resembles historical fascism: it diverts class struggle into conflict between 'middle' and 'bottom' groups, and blames immigrants and 'cronyism' rather than capital. Ma cites Lyndon Johnson's remark about poor whites to illustrate the old tactic, and claims that Nazi racial policy drew on American precedents. Ma concludes that a working class not yet organised by a Marxist-Leninist party remains a class 'in itself', open to attraction by right-wing racial, nationalist and religious ideologies. Racism, rooted in American founding history, is described as a lasting means of splitting the working people and keeping class consciousness from reviving. The article treats Trump's government of conservative politicians and billionaires as serving finance and business interests despite its anti-elite rhetoric. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist class-analysis reading of Trump, the Tea Party and American racism in the aftermath of the 2016 election.

Class politics in the United States under Trump and the international situation 特朗普执政条件下美国国内阶级政治与国际局势 Zhou Miao Writing in 2017, Zhou Miao asks how Donald Trump's candidacy, election and early executive orders should be understood, and what they mean for US domestic politics, Sino-US relations and the wider international order. The article argues that a Marxist class analysis is needed. It reads the 2008 financial crisis as a crisis of the American neoliberal accumulation regime and a sign that US hegemony is declining further. The article has three parts. The first surveys the American class structure: a hollowed-out middle class, a fragmented and insecure working class, and a bourgeoisie dominated by financial monopoly groups, with a new financial 'ruling class' and a revolving door between business, government and the intellectual elite. The second part examines the financialised accumulation model and how it shapes party politics and the 2016 election. The third part assesses Trump's domestic and foreign measures and draws conclusions for China. Zhou's central claim is that the US is ruled by financial monopoly capital, whose core interest is the dollar-centred system and the cycle of debt, financial turbulence and capital return that sustains it. In Zhou's account the Democratic and Republican parties are both bourgeois parties without essential difference, and Trump and Hillary Clinton both belong to the bourgeois right. Trump won because monopoly capital could use him in a time of crisis and because a weakened, race-conscious working class, with little class consciousness, looked to him for deliverance. His anti-immigrant politics, Zhou argues, diverts anger away from capital. His promises of reindustrialisation conflict with the accumulation regime, so recovery rests on 'refinancialisation', and his early rhetoric of retrenchment has reverted to established policy, including the military presence in Asia and a larger defence budget. Zhou concludes that Trump's task is to serve and repair this regime, and that the regime cannot be repaired indefinitely. Zhou expects the US to keep up strategic pressure on China over the Korean peninsula, the South China Sea, the Diaoyu Islands and Taiwan, and to target China's accumulated national wealth. The article calls for vigilance on financial and economic security, capital-account liberalisation, the dominant position of public ownership in mixed-ownership reform, and the securitisation of state assets. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist class-analytic reading of Trump's election and of US policy towards China as seen in 2017.

Fidel Castro's outstanding contributions to Cuba and to the development of world socialism 卡斯特罗对古巴和世界社会主义发展的卓越贡献 Mao Xianglin Written after Fidel Castro's death on 25 November 2016, this article assesses his legacy in three dimensions. Mao Xianglin argues that Castro made lasting contributions to the Cuban people, to Latin America through the example of the Cuban Revolution, and to world socialism through his theoretical thinking. The article concludes that his achievements will go down in history. The article has three main parts. The first lists what Castro did for Cuba: a thorough social revolution, a transformed national character, the reorganisation of the Communist Party and the founding of the socialist system, and his example as a revolutionary. The second sets out the international significance of the Cuban Revolution in Latin America. The third presents eleven areas of Castro's thought, from national independence and social justice to Party building, universal education and healthcare, and resistance to "peaceful evolution". Mao's central claim is that Castro both held to the basic principles of scientific socialism and adapted socialism to Cuban conditions, which the author calls its "localisation". As evidence, Mao points to the 1976 and 1992 constitutions, which kept the leading role of the Communist Party and the goal of communism even after the Soviet collapse, and to four Party-wide theoretical debates on markets and the role of the law of value. Mao also describes Castro's personal conduct as a model: he went into a 1994 riot unarmed, opposed statues and namings in his honour, practised self-criticism, disciplined relatives and friends, and gave up office voluntarily. On the international side, Mao reports that Castro called neoliberal globalisation "re-colonisation" and rejected multi-party politics as a tool of division. Mao presents the Cuban Revolution as the most thorough anti-dictatorship and anti-imperialist revolution in Latin America, the first to move from a national-democratic stage to socialism, and as refuting the claim that socialism suits only Eastern cultures. Mao concludes that Cuba, one of five existing socialist countries, came through the ebb of world socialism at the end of the twentieth century, and that its experience of localising socialism offers lessons for other socialist states. Mao credits this largely to Castro. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's commemorative account of Castro's ideas and personal example, and of the lessons Cuba's experience holds for socialist countries.

New developments in European Green Party politics 欧洲绿党政治的新进展 Huan Qingzhi Huan Qingzhi asks how European Green parties have responded to the two events that, in the author's view, most tested them after the May 2014 European Parliament elections: the Paris Agreement of December 2015 and the British referendum on leaving the EU in June 2016. The commentary, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in March 2017, argues that the Greens kept a fairly positive stance on climate and other ecological issues and took a still clearer position in support of maintaining and deepening European integration. The piece is organised around the two issues. It first reports how the European Green Party co-chairs, Reinhard Bütikofer and Monica Frassoni, reacted to the European Parliament's ratification of the Paris Agreement (October 2016), its entry into force, and the Marrakech climate conference. It then gathers reactions to the Brexit vote from Green politicians in England, Scotland, Northern Ireland, Ireland and Germany. It ends with the German Greens' September 2016 joint resolution, the Party Council in Glasgow and the Münster party congress. Huan reports that the Green leaders urged the EU to move faster on emissions targets for 2020, 2030 and 2050, and on energy, transport and financial transition. They also called for a "zero-carbon Europe" before 2050 and described the Commission's energy package as lacking force. On Brexit, the Greens condemned what they called deceptive and xenophobic campaigning. The German Greens' resolution presented the EU as a historic achievement that turned former enemies into partners, and said transnational problems cannot be solved by nation states. It called for a "better Europe" that is more democratic, social and sustainable. Huan treats this combination of support for integration and demand for reform as the party family's defining stance. Looking ahead, Huan expects the Greens to back global climate politics and EU-led integration more firmly. The author sees the climate stance as increasingly shaped by European interests and the integration stance as moving further from the "European regionalism" of the early 1980s. In the short term, Huan expects them to turn the damage from Brexit, including the Scottish question and falling public trust in the EU, into a chance to rebuild confidence and push EU reform. The Münster congress is described as a bellwether, taking up social justice, opposition to populism and green reform of transport. Huan concludes that the Greens did not waver from supporting integration despite Brexit and the rise of populism. Read the original if you want a brief, source-based account of how Green leaders framed the Paris Agreement and Brexit, as seen from a Chinese scholarly perspective.

Why socialist reform in Eastern Europe failed 东欧社会主义改革为何失败 Li Jiayi Jun Hongfei Li Jiayi and Jun Hongfei ask why the socialist reform movements of Eastern Europe failed, and what that failure means for China. They argue that two main causes were at work: the rigid Stalinist model imposed from outside, and a failure within the region to join socialism to a market economy. The authors treat the lessons as a confirmation of the course of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The short piece, published in People's Forum in 2017, begins with the long process of de-Stalinisation in Eastern Europe. It names the Soviet–Yugoslav conflict, the Poznań events, the Hungarian events and the Prague Spring as its main expressions. It then covers the causes of failure, the roles of politicians and theorists, and the implications for China. The authors hold that the Stalinist model was deeply entrenched and was defended by conservative forces inside the region. Most politicians and theorists, with the Czech economist Ota Šik a minority exception, did not see the need to combine socialism with a market economy. Some even rejected markets out of a critique of reification, and focused on enterprise autonomy and workers' self-management. The authors add that the reformers were not ordinary dissidents but founders or leaders of communist parties, such as Tito, Gomułka, Dubček and Nagy. They locate the real conflict between reformers and anti-reform forces in the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe. A secondary cause was the clash between politicians' pragmatism and theorists' idealism, which the authors illustrate with Yugoslav self-management. For China, the authors draw the conclusion that socialism must break with the traditional Soviet model and solve China's own problems. They call for adherence to the socialist road, the people's democratic dictatorship, Party leadership, the Four Cardinal Principles and reform and opening up. They describe socialism with Chinese characteristics as the product of integrating Marxism with China's conditions, which absorbs foreign achievements creatively without copying other countries' models. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Chinese commentary in 2017 drew lessons from Eastern Europe's reform failures.

The theory and practice of the Workers' Party of Belgium 比利时工人党的理论与实践 Shen Yang Shen Yang introduces the Workers' Party of Belgium (PTB/PVDA), a Marxist party that the author describes as Belgium's largest undisputed radical left party, with two seats in the national parliament. Writing in 2017, Shen notes that Chinese scholarship has paid little attention to the party. The article argues that its theoretical positions and practical activity since its 2008 congress, known as the "renewal congress", offer lessons for China. The article has three parts. The first sets out the party's main theoretical positions, the second its practical activities, and the third the lessons Shen draws for China. The material is descriptive and relies on the party's own statements and activities rather than on outside sources or comparative analysis. On theory, Shen reports four positions. The party treats Marxism and the founders' basic works as the foundation of the party. It defines itself in its statutes as a working-class party and focuses on large industry and key economic sectors. It holds that socialism comes from long conflict between bourgeoisie and working class and needs both a prepared working class and ripe conditions, which it considers still distant. It also regards socialism with chinese characteristics as an application and development of Marxism, a view Shen links to the party's Maoist origins. In practice, the party runs a Marxist research institute and quarterly journal, takes part in anti-austerity strikes in 2014, 2015 and 2016, and holds an international communist seminar. It also runs a youth movement, eleven medical centres and two legal offices offering free services, and has promoted Chinese socialism abroad and exchanged visits with China. Shen concludes that the party's persistence in a capitalist Europe supports three conclusions for China. China should keep to Marxism and the working-class character of the Party, strengthening the Four-sphere Confidence. It should make socialism with Chinese characteristics the main theme of its external publicity. And it should deepen exchanges with friendly parties and countries to raise China's international standing. Read the original if you want a short, China-oriented account of how a small Western European Marxist party presents itself and is viewed in Chinese Party-theory circles.

The current state and future choices of foreign socialism and the left 国外社会主义及左翼现状与未来选择 Zou Guoyu Sun Yuning Writing in early 2017, Zou Guoyu and Sun Yuning ask why socialist and left forces outside China have not benefited from the crisis of capitalism. Their answer is that, despite widespread criticism of capitalism since the 2008 financial crisis, most of these forces remain in a trough and have failed to turn critical "momentum" into political strength. The authors see the main bright spot in the vitality of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The article surveys three groups: communist parties in capitalist countries, national-democratic parties with a socialist-leaning orientation (in Africa and Latin America), and the left wing of socialist and social-democratic parties. It then reviews multilateral platforms: the International Meeting of Communist and Workers' Parties, the Socialist International, the São Paulo Forum, the Party of the European Left, and regional forums in the former Soviet area and Africa. It closes with the causes of decline and the available choices. The authors argue that Western anti-capitalist sentiment, lacking effective political leadership, is turning into populism, which squeezes the left between traditional right-wing parties and populist ones. They describe communist parties as suffering from theoretical disputes, slogans without workable programmes, and sectarianism, and the Socialist International from bureaucratic rigidity and the 2013 split that produced the "Progressive Alliance". Subjectively, they say, parties lack programmes suited to the times, and social democrats have converged with the right through the "Third Way". Objectively, they cite the unchanged "strong capital, weak socialism" balance, the fragmentation of identities among workers, and electoral systems that set high thresholds. Zou and Sun conclude that recovery will take time and that the immediate tasks are to build strength, rethink ideology, and improve organisation. They report that many communist parties agree on rejecting a single guiding centre or single model, and they call this the "greatest common divisor". They propose that the experience of the Communist Party of China in governing the country and the Party be summarised and turned into a "Chinese approach" of worldwide significance, as a possible reference for foreign left forces. Read the original if you want a compact 2017 Chinese official-academic overview of the world's communist, socialist and left parties and their international platforms.

Is the Chinese path the "right way in the human world"? We should have this confidence 中国道路是“人间正道”吗？我们应该有这份自信 Ma Ya This is the text of a speech Ma Ya gave on 24 April 2017 at the launch of a public reading event in Hengnan County, Hunan, later revised and published by Guancha.cn on 3 July 2017. Starting from a book on the "Republic generation", Ma asks why China must hold to its own path. The answer is that only the Chinese path can protect national interests and the people's well-being, and Ma urges confidence in it. The speech has three main parts. The first argues that national sovereignty and the people's welfare come first. The second sets out why China must keep to its path and why the Chinese Dream requires it. The third turns to cultural confidence and "telling China's story well", covering the troubles of Western democracy, the lessons of the Soviet collapse, the ideological imbalance between China and the West, and the Belt and Road Initiative. Ma names three pillars of the Chinese path: Communist Party leadership, a socialist orientation aimed at common prosperity, and economic development. Ma presents the Soviet and Eastern European collapse and the Iraq intervention as proof that following Western models or "universal values" brings disaster. Ma points to China's growth, the Wenchuan earthquake reconstruction and its "institutional strengths" as evidence of success. Ma also warns that privatisation in health care, citing the shrinking number of public hospitals, runs against public ownership as the mainstay and could cost the Party its legitimacy. Citing US polling, Trust Barometer results and figures on the Chinese and Japanese economies, Ma argues that Western democracy is in decline and that Western discourse dominates ideologically. Ma concludes that China cannot copy the American model and that its pursuit of common prosperity could offer other developing countries a model. Ma calls for a discourse that is both Chinese and universal, which would "give a Chinese account of the world's stories and a universal account of China's". Ma sees the Belt and Road as a vehicle for this, along with a culture of coexistence and win-win cooperation that contrasts with Western zero-sum rises. Read the original if you want a vivid example of the confident, polemical case for the Chinese path that circulated in nationalist and left-leaning Chinese commentary in 2017.

The origins of the Communist Party of China in Leninism 列宁主义与中国共产党的渊源 Lü Xinyu Lü Xinyu argues that the organic link between Mao Zedong Thought and Leninism is an urgent but deliberately or unintentionally obscured question. In the author's view, Marxism reached China through Leninism, and the Communist Party of China has its source there: without the October Revolution there would have been no Party. Lü contends that what is being hidden is the dictatorship of the proletariat and the nature of the state, a major historical issue of the Comintern movement, and that the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics depends on how this succession is understood. The article, first published on the website Utopia (Wuyouzhixiang) in 2017, reads as a historical argument in five sections. It covers Lenin's attention to the 1911 Revolution, his treatment of Chinese revolution and Russian populism, his defence of the revolutionary character of the peasantry, the difference between proletarian Social Democrats and populists, and the passage from the 'New Democracy' to socialism via Lenin's April Theses, State and Revolution and Mao's writings. Lü draws on Lenin's Collected Works, memoirs and Mao's On New Democracy. Lü's central move is that the Chinese and Russian revolutions shared the peasant question, which set them apart from the Western bourgeois revolutions. Lenin, who had once fought the populists, revised his view after 1905–07 and concluded that Russia's revolution had to be a peasant land revolution led by a proletarian party. Lü treats this as a key content of Leninism. Lü reads the Comintern's line of supporting peasants and allying with, but not merging into, bourgeois democrats as the theoretical source of Communist–Nationalist cooperation in the 1920s. Mao's New Democracy is then presented as the Chinese answer to the April Theses, with its two-step revolution and its peasant-centred politics. Lü attacks what the author calls the liberal right, which denies the October Revolution and Lenin, sets Engels against Marx and Stalin against Lenin, and recasts China's path as European social democracy or a truncated New Democracy. The article also faults this camp for never explaining the Second International's betrayal in 1914. Lü calls for a renewed understanding of the historical succession from Marxism through Leninism to Mao Zedong Thought, which the author identifies with the Party's own history. Read the original if you want a Chinese leftist account of Lenin's writings on China and the peasantry, and of how Leninism is said to underpin the Party's path.

What is meant by the resilience of the Communist Party of China 什么叫中国共产党的韧性 Jin Yinan This is an interview with Jin Yinan, a military scholar and author of the book Kuonan huihuang (Glorious Suffering), conducted by the Theory Weekly of the Beijing Daily and published on 3 July 2017, shortly after the Party's 96th anniversary. Asked what resilience means for the Communist Party of China, Jin answers that it comes from the resilience of its members, who endured sacrifice for their ideals. He presents the Party's history as 'the greatest study of success', won through tenacity and sacrifice rather than good fortune. The interview moves through several episodes. It opens with Taipei mayor Ko Wen-je's visit to the site of the First Party Congress and with Jin's own account of German and French officers on a military exchange course who asked to see Sun Yat-sen's residence and the Congress site. It then turns to the fates of the 13 delegates at the First Congress, to Mao Zedong's search for a revolutionary path, to Zhu De's role after the Nanchang Uprising, and finally to national dignity, security and the 'hundred years of national salvation, hundred years of rejuvenation'. Jin argues that the revolution was never favoured to win. Seven of the 13 First Congress delegates left or were expelled, and two became collaborators with Japan. In his reading, only Mao's path, which relied on the weak points of enemy rule and on warlord wars between 'white' regimes, answered why a red regime could survive. He holds that earlier leaders had dogmatised Comintern instructions and Soviet experience, and that Mao's strategy emerged from close knowledge of China's conditions. He credits Zhu De with holding together some 800 men at Tianxinxu when the Nanchang forces collapsed. He also argues that the Party is a combative body, and that collective self-esteem, restored by the revolution and the Korean War, is a basic national interest. Jin concludes that national salvation was not begun by the Party but was completed by it, and that 1949 opened a second century of rejuvenation that will also be hard. He links China's larger economy to wider security duties, citing the navy's 2008 Gulf of Aden deployment, and holds that responsibility requires strength. He closes by saying the Party's leadership explains China's transformation and will secure future victories. Read the original if you want an example of how a prominent military commentator told Party history in 2017 as a story of struggle, sacrifice and the leadership of Mao Zedong and Zhu De.

China's "internal logic" of democracy under Western discursive hegemony Interview with Ding Yifan, Deputy Director of the Institute of World Development, Development Research Center of the State Council 西方话语霸权下的中国民主的“内在理路” Ding Yifan This is an interview with Ding Yifan, conducted by the website Guancha.cn and published on 2 July 2017. The interviewers start from the point that Western countries hold the power to "certify" what counts as democracy. They ask whether China can build its own interpretive framework and how other developing countries fare. Ding answers that Chinese and Western definitions differ because each reflects a different historical experience: the West stresses form, China stresses content. The interview moves through five topics. These are the definition of democracy and its Confucian roots, the inertia of historical tradition in the political system, populism and popular participation, Hong Kong's political system, and the 1950s–60s Asian-African context of China's foreign policy. Ding draws on a passage from Mencius, the civil service tradition, and episodes from decolonisation and China's return to the United Nations. Ding defines democracy as popular recognition of a regime. He reads Mencius's dialogue with Wan Zhang as showing that "Heaven" in the Mandate of Heaven in fact means the people. Contemporary Chinese practice, in his account, combines recommendation, consultation and election, and rests on a professional civil service and meritocracy (xiánnéng zhèngzhì). The National People's Congress and the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference let people outside the system voice demands. Ding says participation is not the same as democracy and that talking with Westerners about it is a "dialogue between chickens and ducks". He adds that decision-makers cannot accommodate every minority interest. On Hong Kong, Ding attributes the unrest to British colonial design, "divide and rule" and economic hollowing-out. He says the central government's bottom line is that Hong Kong must not become a base for subverting China. Ding then recalls China's support for Asian-African nationalism, the Bandung Conference of 1955 and the 1971 UN vote. Ding concludes that China's political system should draw on historical experience while continuing to innovate. He argues that Western criticism will never be satisfied by Chinese evidence of progress, because the two sides use different standards. He says China's Belt and Road Initiative and Xi Jinping's renewed emphasis on the relation between righteousness and interests (yì and lì) are helping China regain moral discourse power in international affairs. Read the original if you want a candid example of how a Chinese policy adviser grounds the Chinese concept of democracy in Confucian tradition and in the history of Third World solidarity.

Analysis of the 18th International Meeting of Communist and Workers' Parties 第18次共产党和工人党国际会议论析 Liu Xudong This is a report and commentary on the 18th International Meeting of Communist and Workers' Parties, hosted by the Communist Party of Vietnam in Hanoi on 28–29 October 2016. Liu Xudong notes that it was the first such meeting held in a socialist country. More than 100 delegates from 57 parties attended, and the four other ruling communist parties sent representatives. The Workers' Party of Austria took part for the first time. The theme was the crisis of capitalism and imperialist attacks, and the strategy and tactics of communist parties. The meeting adopted a joint document, the Appeal, and four resolutions, and chose Russia to host the 19th meeting. The article summarises delegates' positions in four thematic sections, drawing mainly on party statements and the Vietnamese opening address: the deepening capitalist crisis; imperialist aggression and its consequences; socialism as the only alternative; and the parties' plans for joint action. A short assessment follows. Liu quotes many parties by name, including the communist parties of Greece, Portugal, Ireland, Pakistan and India, the Cyprus AKEL and the Workers' Party of Hungary. According to Liu's account, delegates agreed that the post-2008 crisis is a crisis of the capitalist system, rooted in private ownership of the means of production. They held that bourgeois governments have shifted its burdens onto working people, and that measures such as quantitative easing only delay collapse. Delegates also argued that the United States, NATO and their allies pursue imperialist aggression to escape the crisis and secure resources. They blamed military intervention and support for terrorist groups for regional turmoil, wars in the Middle East and the refugee crisis. Many favoured negotiated settlements under the UN Charter, for example in Syria. The article reports delegates' view that revolutionary transition to socialism is historically inevitable, and that socialist states' record shows its superiority, although the task will be long. On joint action, the Appeal calls for theoretical exchange on twenty-first-century socialism, joint commemoration of the centenary of the October Revolution and the 150th anniversary of Capital, and an expanded anti-imperialist front. It also calls for solidarity with the Communist Party of Ukraine, Cuba and Palestine. In his assessment Liu credits Vietnam's coordinating role for the shared document, after three earlier meetings (the 15th to 17th) produced none. He lists weaknesses: a shortened schedule, loose organisation between sessions, and little exchange on party-building. Liu remains optimistic about the meeting as a platform. Read the original if you want a detailed, sympathetic digest of how communist parties worldwide framed crisis, imperialism and socialism in 2016.

Freedom in cyberspace and its limits 网络空间的自由及其限度 Zhang Dongdaizheng This short commentary, published in Marxist Digest in 2017, asks how freedom of expression online should be understood and bounded. The author argues that freedom is the natural and defining feature of network society, but that it is necessarily relative and must operate within limits set by law, ethics and norms. The piece opens with Xi Jinping's remarks at the third World Internet Conference on the opportunities and challenges of the internet, and with figures on Chinese internet users as of June 2016. It cites the proposals for the Thirteenth Five-Year Plan, which stress the strategy of building China into a cyber power, and notes problems of uneven development, weak rules and disorder online. It then treats the case for online freedom and the challenges to it in turn. On the first side, the author holds that the internet has widened the framework of rights to expression. Technical change from Web 1.0 to Web 3.0 has expanded space for free, equal and shared exchange, turning every user into an information source and stirring a stronger desire for freedom. On the second side, the author argues that online individuals are bound to society and others, so online freedom needs the joint support of laws, regulations, ethics and values. Citing Rousseau, the author claims that absolute freedom brings its own negation, and that the over-extension of freedom narrows it. The author concludes that freedom and norms are mutually conditioning, that real freedom is relative freedom within rules, and that users should respect others' freedom. The author notes that state authorities, legislators and network operators are building a regulatory system for online conduct. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Chinese ideological and political education writing frames online freedom as bounded by law and norms.

The Communist Party of China's guidance of social trends of thought since the 18th Party Congress An interview with Lin Tai on the revised edition of "Wendao" 十八大以来中国共产党对社会思潮的引领 Lin Tai This is an interview, published in 2017, in which Dai Hongkai, a postdoctoral researcher at Tsinghua University's School of Marxism, questions Professor Lin Tai. The occasion is the revised edition of Lin's edited volume Wendao (Seeking the Way): Social Trends of Thought since Reform and Opening Up and Ideological and Political Education for Youth. Lin argues that since the 18th Party Congress (2012) the Party has treated the question of path as decisive and has led social trends of thought by confronting what he calls erroneous currents directly. The interview moves through three topics. First, it summarises how the 18th Congress and Xi Jinping assessed more than thirty years of reform and the evolution of social thought. Second, it reviews Xi's criticism of five currents: democratic socialism, neoliberalism, Western multiparty "universal values", historical nihilism, and nihilism toward traditional culture. Third, Lin looks ahead to how these trends may develop. Lin's core argument is that the path decides a country's fate. He contrasts the Soviet Union and Russia, which he says followed neoliberal reform designs and collapsed or fell into crisis, with socialism with Chinese characteristics. He holds that every Party congress since the 1980s developed this path in struggle against both "leftist" rigidity and rightist bourgeois liberalization. In his account the recurring currents all turn on which road reform takes. He cites Xi on state-owned enterprises, mixed ownership and supply-side structural reform, which Xi distinguished from Western supply-side economics. He also cites Xi on the claim that Western political models are universally applicable, and on the dangers of negating the Party's history, including the Soviet case. Lin predicts that these currents will persist in new forms. Debates over state-enterprise reform, industrial policy and the rule of law will increasingly be disputes over the direction of reform. International currents such as populism, nationalism and anti-globalization will become a new field of study. New media will transform how currents spread, so the Party must cultivate online opinion leaders and integrate old and new media around core socialist values. Read the original if you want a Party-theorist's account of how the Xi leadership framed ideological struggle in 2012–2017, with the specific currents and Xi statements he cites.

The 21st century is the century of the revival of world socialism 21世纪是世界社会主义复兴的世纪 Lü Weizhou Writing in March 2017 in the China Social Sciences Today, Lü Weizhou argues that world socialism, after its deep trough at the end of the 20th century, is gradually recovering. The commentary holds that the view that "the 21st century is the century of the revival of world socialism" is becoming a growing consensus worldwide. The piece opens with a brief arc from the appearance of socialism as a current of thought in 1516, through its 20th-century rise as theory and system, to the setback of the upheavals in Eastern Europe and the Soviet collapse. It then surveys five signs of revival: reforms in socialist countries, communist parties in capitalist countries, varied socialist currents, growing exchange among socialist forces, and finally the remaining challenges. Lü presents socialism with Chinese characteristics as a central factor: its success is said to show the need for diverse models and to have shifted a badly unbalanced power relation between socialism and capitalism. The author also cites party congresses in Vietnam, Cuba and Laos in 2016, and reports more than 120 communist parties with over 8 million members in capitalist countries, with electoral results in Greece, Cyprus and Japan. Lü further names market socialism, democratic socialism, eco-socialism and Latin American "21st-century socialism" as currents, along with left alliances such as the European Left Party and forums such as the World Socialism Forum in China. Lü cautions that the road is not smooth. The author points to the continuing dominance of capital over labour, ideological attacks by the United States-led capitalist states, weak class consciousness among workers, disunity within the socialist camp and the rise of populism. Lü calls on left forces, including communist parties, to build strength, improve organisation and innovate in their methods. Read the original if you want a short, official-leaning overview of how Chinese scholars in 2017 assessed the state of the international left.

Why we should commemorate the October Revolution 为什么要纪念十月革命 Zhou Xincheng Writing in the centenary year of 1917, Zhou Xincheng asks why the October Revolution still deserves commemoration, given that some in China doubt its path and that the Soviet Union itself abandoned it. Zhou argues that the October Revolution road is the practical embodiment of the basic principles of scientific socialism, that it has universal significance, and that giving it up leads to the ruin of socialism. The article first sets out the Chinese Communist Party's historical attitude to the revolution and the rise since reform and opening up of a view that reform means "de-Sovietization". It then reduces the question of the road's validity to three issues: how to assess the Soviet socialist model, why the Soviet Union turned to capitalism, and how socialism with Chinese characteristics relates to the October road. Each issue gets its own section, drawing on statements by Mao Zedong, Jiang Zemin and Xi Jinping. On the first issue, Zhou defends Mao's "seventy-thirty" verdict: achievements are primary and errors secondary. Zhou disputes the figure of fifty million victims of the purges, citing archival totals of sentences and calling for a method that separates mainstream from tributary and basic from specific institutions. Soviet errors, in this reading, lay in specific institutions, not the basic system. On the second issue, Zhou holds that the Soviet collapse followed from Gorbachev's "humane, democratic socialist" reforms, which attacked the Party's leadership, public ownership and Marxist guidance as "three monopolies". On the third, Zhou argues that socialism with Chinese characteristics is scientific socialism and the "continuation and development" of the October Revolution, with Chinese features only in how the principles are applied. Zhou also warns that some domestic critics use criticism of the USSR to argue against Party leadership in China. Zhou concludes that China must unswervingly follow the October road and the basic principles of scientific socialism, and should keep the Eighth Party Congress formulation that its cause continues the October Revolution. Zhou reads Mao's "follow the Russians" and "take our own road" as answers at different levels, not as contradictory. Read the original if you want a detailed statement of the orthodox Chinese Marxist case for continuity between the Soviet model, Mao-era socialism and the reform era, and for how the Soviet collapse is explained within it.

Strengthening theoretical confidence: we must unwaveringly uphold Marxism 坚定理论自信 必须毫不动摇坚持马克思主义 Li Chunhua This newspaper commentary, published in Chengdu Daily in 2017, asks what theoretical confidence means within the Four-sphere Confidence and why it requires holding firmly to Marxism. Li Chunhua argues that theoretical confidence is the soul of the other three confidences, and that it rests on Marxism's scientific character and truth, not on blind faith. The piece is organised under three headings: treating Marxism with a scientific attitude, believing in Marxism's eventual victory, and advancing theoretical innovation. It moves from the nature of Marxism, through practical evidence from the international communist movement and China, to the system of theory known as socialism with Chinese characteristics. Li holds that the essence of Marxism is its standpoint, viewpoint and method, and that it has the greatest explanatory power among theories of capitalism. The author calls for guarding against two errors: dogmatism that treats Marxism as sacred doctrine, and so-called innovation that departs from its basic principles. Practice is the final test of theory. Li cites the October Revolution and the achievements of reform and opening up as proof, and holds that world socialism's present low tide is temporary. Theory with Chinese characteristics, from Deng Xiaoping Theory to Xi Jinping's speeches, is said to follow in one line from Marxism-Leninism and Mao Zedong Thought. Li points to public ownership, distribution according to work, Party leadership and Marxist guidance as the socialist essence retained in the primary stage of socialism. Li concludes that the fundamental way to strengthen confidence is to innovate theory by addressing major real-world problems, since a body of thought more than 160 years old needs updating as times change. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a CASS scholar presented theoretical confidence and the case for Marxist orthodoxy together with innovation in 2017.

Challenges and countermeasures for ideological work in universities in the online environment 网络环境下高校意识形态工作的挑战与对策 Zheng Jie Mei Meng Writing in 2017, Zheng Jie and Mei Meng ask how universities can safeguard socialist ideology now that the internet has become a main channel of communication among students. They argue that universities are the main front of ideological work, and that networked communication has weakened the guiding, defensive, propaganda and control capacities of that work. The authors propose a set of measures to rebuild these capacities. The article has three parts. The first sets out why ideological security in universities matters: for the Party's governing security and long-term national stability, for a harmonious campus, and for the all-round development of individual students. The second identifies four challenges, and the third offers four sets of countermeasures. It draws on speeches by Xi Jinping on ideological work and on official concepts such as the Chinese Dream and core socialist values. In the authors' account, hostile Western forces use the internet to spread "universal values", individualism, money worship and historical nihilism. They target students, who are curious and still forming their worldview, and so erode students' identification with socialism. The authors add that some teachers of ideological and political theory courses are unfamiliar with or reluctant to use the internet, so the classroom is losing its position as the main channel. Weak internet legislation and supervision also let rumours, fraud and online abuse spread. The proposed responses are to strengthen the ideological formation of teachers and students around Marxism and a sense of vigilance. They also call for campus culture built on core socialist values, including "red" activities and campus social media. A further proposal is to renew communication styles and recruit staff skilled in both the internet and Marxist theory. Finally, they urge universities to occupy online opinion space through quality red websites, national legislation, and campus monitoring teams that analyse public opinion. The authors conclude that universities must pay close attention to the new situation online. They should improve the mechanisms of ideological security and strengthen risk prevention, so as to train qualified builders and reliable successors for socialism with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a concrete example of how Chinese university ideological work was framed in 2017: its threat perception, its view of the internet and its practical measures.

The Seventh Congress of the Cuban Communist Party and the significance of updating the Cuban model An interview with Xu Shicheng, Honorary Academic Member of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences 古共七大召开及古巴模式更新的意义 This is an interview with Xu Shicheng, researcher at the Institute of Latin American Studies and Honorary Academic Member of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, conducted by an unnamed interviewer and published in Studies on Marxism in 2017. Against the background of a low ebb in the international communist movement, it asks what the Seventh Congress of the Cuban Communist Party (April 2016) decided and what the 'updating' of the Cuban socialist model means. Xu presents the congress as a bridge between past and future that gives the Cuban cause lasting momentum. The interview has three parts: the congress itself, the Cuban model, and Fidel Castro. It covers Raúl Castro's central report, the assessment of the five years since the Sixth Congress (2011), three key documents, the make-up of the new Central Committee, and Fidel's closing speech and death in October 2016. On the report, Xu stresses that Raúl Castro ties the updating to socialism: neither a closed, rigid old path nor a change of banner, no privatisation, and continued Party leadership. Xu also reports figures given at the congress: 2.8% average annual growth for 2011–2015, and 75% of the workforce in the state sector. Xu summarises the 'Conceptualisation' document, which keeps public ownership as the pillar and accepts private property only as a supplement, with the market taken into account but not allowed to dominate. Xu notes that Cuba, unlike China and Vietnam, does not call its economy a socialist market economy. Xu then outlines the 2030 development plan and the updated 274-point Guidelines (50 of them new, in 13 sections). Xu reads the younger, more diverse Central Committee as an organisational guarantee of continuity. Xu concludes that Fidel Castro's death is a heavy loss, but that Raúl Castro had led in practice since 2006, and Fidel endorsed the congress's programme and attended its close. Xu therefore expects no major turmoil and expects the updating to continue. The interview also reproduces Xi Jinping's condolences, which stress Sino-Cuban friendship. Read the original if you want a Chinese specialist's summary of the 2016 Cuban congress documents, including point-by-point details of the Guidelines, and its view of how Cuban reform compares with China's.

The centenary of the October Revolution should be commemorated with great ceremony 应隆重纪念十月革命100周年 Wu Enyuan Writing in 2017, Wu Enyuan argues that the hundredth anniversary of the Russian October Revolution should be marked solemnly. In Wu's view the revolution turned Marxism from theory into practice and proved its scientific character. Reviewing a century of socialist development, the author says, strengthens the ideal that socialism and communism will inevitably prevail and supports the values of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The short commentary has two parts. The first sets out the revolution's historical significance. The second lists three themes that commemoration should convey to the public: adapting Marxism to national conditions, opposing historical nihilism, and educating young people in core socialist values. On significance, Wu claims the revolution showed that economically backward countries can take the socialist road, pointed to humanity's direction of development, and spurred national liberation movements. Wu credits socialist systems with planning, full employment and social security. The author presents the founding of socialist China as both a fruit of the October Revolution and an extension of its world-historical meaning. On historical nihilism, Wu rejects the view that the revolution's "original sin" caused the Soviet collapse. Citing Putin and Xi Jinping, the author blames Gorbachev's abandonment of the Party's leadership and his negation of Soviet history. Wu concludes that commemoration means "remaining true to the original aspiration", drawing lessons and strengthening confidence in the path, theory and system of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The author calls for stronger value education among youth, citing post-Soviet Russia's loss of values as a warning. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a Chinese Russian-history specialist framed the 2017 centenary for a general audience.

The predicament of Western capitalism's normalised economic stagnation An interview with Professor He Zili of the School of Economics, Nankai University 西方资本主义经济陷入停滞常态化的困境 This is an interview, published in 2017, with He Zili, a professor in the School of Economics at Nankai University. The interviewer, who is not named, asks why Western capitalism, once seen as unbeatable and symbolised by Fukuyama's "end of history", has fallen into lasting stagnation since the 1970s and especially after the 2008 crisis. He argues that this stagnation is no passing cyclical downturn but a normalised condition rooted in capitalism's internal contradictions and institutions. The interview has four parts: the stages of capitalist development and the features of stagnation; the institutional roots of stagnation; its effects on the world; and how China should respond.
