On periodisation, He sets the familiar sequence of free-competition, monopoly, state-monopoly and global monopoly capitalism against his own scheme of mercantile, industrial and service capitalism. In that scheme, industrial capitalism has moved since the early 1970s into "de-industrialisation", with industrial capital losing ground to financial and service capital. On the first question, He lists eight consequences of de-industrialisation and heavy reliance on services: collapsing welfare systems, a financial sector detached from the real economy, loss of industrial competitiveness, mounting government debt, persistent economic decline, high unemployment, a hollowed-out middle class, and a paralysed political system. On causes, he names private ownership with wage labour, a political system in which interest groups capture legislatures, and neoliberalism as the dominant ideology. In his account, private interest and social interest cannot be reconciled while private ownership endures, for example when capital replaces workers with machines. He also argues that stagnation is bringing political and social turbulence, a rightward political shift he compares with the 1930s, a retreat from economic globalisation, and a US that defends its declining hegemony through protectionism, interest-rate moves and interventions abroad. He concludes that stagnation follows from capitalism's inner contradictions and the law of surplus value, and that it will persist unless neoliberal dogma and the underlying arrangements change. China, as the second-largest economy, cannot stand aside. He points to the "innovative, open, interconnected and inclusive" world economy that China proposed at the 2016 G20 Hangzhou summit, and to a community with a shared future for mankind, as remedies for sluggish recovery and weakening globalisation. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist economist's account of post-2008 Western stagnation and the policy line it supports, along with its statistics on unemployment and its view of US policy.

Is the neoliberal market mechanism an effective institutional arrangement? A critique of Hayek's theory of spontaneous and extended order 新自由主义市场机制是有效的制度安排吗？ Zeng Xiankui Zeng Xiankui asks whether the market mechanism that neoliberalism promotes is the most effective institutional arrangement. The article opens with the November 2016 Peking University debate between Lin Yifu and Zhang Weiying, in which Zhang described his views as the "Mises–Hayek paradigm". Zeng takes this as evidence that Austrian-school ideas still influence some Chinese scholars. The article argues that Hayek's theory of spontaneous and extended order, the core of his thought, contains fundamental errors. It concludes that socialist market economy is a more effective arrangement than the liberal market economy. Zeng first notes that Hayek never gave a clear definition of spontaneous or extended order and that his terminology shifted over time. Zeng then identifies three flaws in the theory. The article closes with a section on how the critique bears on China's socialist market economy, the spread of neoliberal ideas in China, and the debate over supply-side structural reform. Its evidence includes trade institutions, the 2007 financial crisis, US inequality data, South Korea's industrial policy and China's growth record. The first flaw, in Zeng's account, is that Hayek ignores how much of capitalist order is shaped by monopoly oligarchs and politicians. Zeng cites trade expansion tied to colonialism, post-war trade rules negotiated between states, the fate of the TPP and the power of multinational firms. The second flaw is that the theory cannot explain market failure. Zeng points to the capitalist contradiction between socialized production and private ownership, which produces cyclical crises. Zeng also cites rising inequality in the United States, including Piketty's findings, and argues that public ownership and state regulation under socialism control fluctuations better than Keynesianism does. The third flaw is that Hayek overlooks government regulation's capacity for self-adjustment through feedback. Zeng argues that South Korea and China caught up through the combined action of government and market, and that China's macro-control shows "constructive evolution". Zeng concludes that Hayek's order was not purely the product of natural evolution, that neoliberal markets are not the only effective system, and that constructive rationality, including government intervention, can be efficient. The author calls for thorough critique of neoliberalism, which is said to threaten China's reforms. Zeng cites Xi Jinping's warning that supply-side structural reform must not become a copy of Western supply-side economics, and points to "shock therapy" in the Soviet bloc and IMF programmes as cautionary cases. The author also urges stronger confidence in China's path, theory and system. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist economist at CASS argued against Hayek and neoliberalism in 2017, and how that argument supported the case for the socialist market economy.

China as the locomotive towards a just world 中国是通向公正世界的火车头 Gennady Zyuganov This is a Chinese-language interview with Gennady Zyuganov, chairman of the Central Committee of the Communist Party of the Russian Federation, conducted by a reporter from Cankao Xiaoxi and reprinted in Marxist Digest in 2017. Asked how Russia sees China's present and future after almost four decades of reform and opening up, Zyuganov argues that the development of socialist China serves the interests of the whole world and that China is 'the locomotive towards a just world'. The interview has four parts: the reasons for China's success and its long-term planning; the progress of the 'two centenary goals' and the Chinese Dream; China's contribution to culture, science and technology; and the internal and external challenges China faces, including the place of Russia–China cooperation. Zyuganov repeatedly compares China with post-Soviet Russia, using figures on industrial output, research spending and trade. Zyuganov attributes China's rise to the fact that it kept a socialist orientation and combined it with a sound cadre policy and market instruments, all aimed at the people's welfare. He contrasts this with Russia in the 1990s, when, in his image, the authorities removed the ship's rudder before pushing it into the market. He contends that the Chinese Dream, unlike an individualist 'American Dream' that he says leads to expansion, carries responsibility for the world's progress, and that the Belt and Road Initiative shows how peaceful prosperity attracts neighbours. Among internal challenges he lists the exhausted export-oriented, cheap-labour model and corruption, citing the lesson of the Soviet Communist Party's collapse. He sees the leading role of the Communist Party of China as the guarantee of the chosen course. Externally, he describes US and NATO attempts at encirclement, protectionism and tariff barriers, which he says fail against China's firm but peaceful foreign policy. Zyuganov concludes that achieving the two centenary goals would make China a global superpower and a centre of attraction for progressive forces and poor peoples, provided it holds high the banner of social justice and friendship among peoples. He hopes a renewed socialist Russia will go hand in hand with China, and urges closer economic and security ties, since Russia accounts for only 2% of China's trade by his figures. Read the original if you want a Russian communist leader's view of China's development, as published for a Chinese readership in 2017.

Global Times: how Russia views the 1917 revolutions a hundred years on 《环球时报》：100年后的今天俄罗斯如何看1917年革命 This is a 2017 Global Times (Huanqiu Shibao) news report, reprinted in Marxism Digest, on how Russian society and the Russian state approached the centenary of the February and October Revolutions of 1917. The report's main finding is a deep division: some Russians see the revolutions as the start of the country's best era, others as an obstacle to its development. It presents President Putin as seeking a frank assessment while refusing to carry old divisions into the present. The report draws on Western agencies and newspapers (AFP, The New York Times, Art News), Russian media, opinion polls, interviews with Moscow residents and comments from Russian and Chinese specialists. It first describes the official commemorations: about 500 conferences, round tables, exhibitions and festivals, and a committee set up in December 2016. It then turns to public opinion and party positions. Finally it traces how the Russian state has marked 7 November since Soviet times and sets out Putin's own statements. On the commemorations, the report says officials stressed remembrance and understanding rather than celebration, and asked that the events not be politicised. Museums were described as avoiding controversy. Western outlets read this caution as unease, while a Kremlin cultural envoy is quoted as saying that state celebrations would deepen divisions. On opinion, the report cites polls in which roughly equal shares call the revolution a major event, a driver of progress or a catastrophe, and in which 40 per cent view Lenin positively against 20 per cent negatively. Russian interviewees range from admirers of Lenin to critics of the civil war, and some young people say they are indifferent. The Communist Party and the Liberal Democratic Party are shown as taking opposing stances. Wu Enyuan of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences describes Putin's view as two-sided: he respects Soviet achievements but criticises the shooting of the Romanov family and the Soviet federal structure. The report concludes that the revolutions and the Soviet era remain tied to the military strength, industrial base and social security system on which Russia still relies. It adds that more young people are drawn to a Soviet Union they never knew. It quotes the Russian analyst Stepan Surakshev as saying that rising inequality and inefficient administration make the lessons of 1917 relevant today. Read the original if you want a compact, Chinese-media overview of Russian opinion, party positions and official policy on the 1917 centenary, with Chinese scholarly comment.

New features of the crisis of contemporary capitalism 当代资本主义危机呈现新特征 Ding Xiaoqin This short commentary, originally published in the People's Daily in 2017, asks what is new about the crisis of capitalism in the developed countries since the 2008 international financial crisis. Ding Xiaoqin argues that weak growth, widening inequality, political polarisation, populism and right-wing extremism show deepening internal contradictions. In the author's view, attempts to blame globalisation or foreign intervention cannot reverse the overall trend. The article is organised around three features: difficult economic recovery and ineffective policy, a widening wealth gap with sharper political polarisation, and declining soft power and international influence. It draws mainly on the United States, with references to the eurozone, Britain, Germany and Japan, and gives statistics on public debt and income shares. Ding argues that bailouts, stimulus and quantitative easing only postponed collapse while raising government debt. The article cites US debt rising from 61.8% of GDP in 2006 to 106.1% in 2016, and Japan's exceeding 250%. Policy swings between neoliberalism and Keynesianism without improving conditions for ordinary workers. Ding says that after the war, capitalist states eased class conflict through higher wages and welfare. With growth slowing, capitalists now fight over their share of output, so real incomes stagnate. The article also holds that the crisis exposed the myth of the US economic system and eroded its soft power, which force and financial hegemony cannot restore. Ding concludes that crisis-shifting cannot alter capitalism's essential traits and basic flaws. The author predicts further inequality, a shrinking middle class, lasting policy deadlock, government credit held hostage by monopoly capital and continuing polarisation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a Chinese Marxist economist framed post-2008 Western capitalism in 2017.

Differing assessments of the October Revolution inside Russia Right-wing, left-wing and government views on the eve of the centenary 俄罗斯国内关于十月革命的不同评价 Chen Hong Writing on the eve of the revolution's 100th anniversary in 2017, Chen Hong asks how the October Revolution is judged in Russia today. The author argues that assessments remain divided and fall into three camps: a negative right-wing view, an affirmative left-wing view, and a government position that tries to reconcile the two. Chen draws on seminars held in Russia in early 2017, including a Moscow University conference and a Moscow Economic Forum panel the author attended. The article is organised into three sections. The first covers right-wing writers, both monarchist and liberal, and traces their arguments to Western liberal and Menshevik positions and to post-Soviet historiography. The second covers left-wing scholars, taking the "post-Soviet critical Marxists" as their main representatives. These include Slavin and Buzgalin, who edited the volume The Culmination of the Great Revolution, and Vayikov. The third section follows the Russian government's stance from Yeltsin to Putin and the 2016 commission planning the centenary. Chen reports that the right treats 1917 as a conspiracy or coup, citing the "German gold" and spy stories. The right prefers the February Revolution and holds that October pushed Russia off its natural path, toward either a constitutional monarchy or a normal capitalism. Chen presents the critical Marxists as rebutting this with historical materialism: in their account the revolution was a social revolution driven by popular discontent, and Soviet tragedies do not discredit its ideals. Chen says the author agrees with the left's basic view, but notes internal disputes over the revolution's nature. Vayikov sees it as a continuation of a bourgeois revolution, while Slavin, Buzgalin and others stress socialist and cultural elements. On the government, Chen describes a move from wholesale denial under Yeltsin to "harmless" treatment under Putin. This includes commemorating February and October together and appealing to national unity. Chen judges this stance contradictory and concludes that it in effect makes the "red" yield to the "white". Chen concludes that the October Revolution can be understood correctly only through the concrete historical facts and the popular mood of its time, and that this also allows right-wing claims to be refuted with evidence. The author calls for summing up the revolution's experience and for continuing to uphold and develop socialism with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese-language survey of Russian debates around the 2017 centenary, with named Russian scholars and sources, and a view of how a Chinese Marxist scholar assesses them.

Enhancing national cultural soft power and cultural security 提升国家文化软实力与文化安全 Yan Xu Writing in 2017, Yan Xu takes up the question of how China can safeguard its cultural security, defined as the condition in which a nation's spiritual culture, basic social institutions, symbolic systems, knowledge traditions and beliefs are free from erosion, damage or subversion. The article argues that cultural security is an integral part of national security and that, if the cultural and ideological defences are breached, other defences are hard to hold. Its answer is that China must build hard power and also raise its cultural soft power, so as to win what the author calls the decisive struggle for cultural security. The article has two main parts. The first explains why cultural security is a major long-term strategic task and then lists the main threats and challenges now facing China. The second sets out how to maintain cultural security by raising soft power. The author draws on Marxist national theory, Xi Jinping's remarks on overall national security, US strategy documents, and examples from the Soviet collapse and the 'colour revolutions'. Yan argues that cultural security bears on the survival of the nation, the security of the social system and the wider national security order, and that Western powers themselves treat culture and values as instruments of security and hegemony. The author names five threats: 'colour revolutions' attributed to Western powers; a 'political genetic modification project' aimed at senior politicians and intellectual elites; anti-mainstream cultural trends; negativity and corruption within the Party; and weak cultural innovation, marked by 'Western-style dogmatism' and academic corruption. The remedy is to raise soft power in three ways: strengthen the cultural appeal of Marxist belief, chiefly through Party conduct and attention to ordinary people's livelihoods; release cultural creativity by balancing politics and culture, market and government, and the 'main theme' and diversity; and widen the international influence of Chinese culture. On the third point, Yan rejects the view that economic influence automatically becomes cultural influence, and calls for confidence in socialist culture and not only in traditional Chinese culture. The author also urges new methods of 'going global', since Confucius Institutes have spread quickly but struggle to 'take root'. This would combine government-led promotion with better marketing techniques learned from abroad. Read the original if you want to see how a Party journal in 2017 framed cultural security, ideology and soft power as parts of national security, and which threats it named.

Contemporary Chinese literary and artistic workers must establish a correct view of history 当代中国文艺工作者要树立正确的历史观 Lu Guishan Writing in 2017, Lu Guishan asks what historical task falls to Chinese writers and artists in an era of national revitalisation, and what view of history they need to carry it out. The author argues that a rejuvenation of the nation requires a literary renaissance. Writers must therefore chronicle China's modernisation and hold to a correct view of history. The article has three parts. The first sets out the writer's mission in a time of social transformation and gives criteria for works that reach an artistic peak. The second turns to the creation of 'new socialist people' and surveys three kinds of subject matter that Lu considers especially successful: revolutionary war, science and technology, and agriculture. The third part, which gives the piece its title, names three mistaken views of history that writers should resist. Lu draws on Engels's call for a fusion of ideological depth and 'consciously grasped historical content'. The author reads that content, for China today, as modernisation and the Chinese Dream of the rejuvenation of the nation. Writers should be both 'engineers of the soul' and 'secretaries of history' in the manner of Balzac and Tolstoy. Lu says too few works present the mainstream grand narrative, and calls for more portraits of entrepreneurs, builders and heroes who change the old environment through practice. Slogans such as 'going deep into life' are read as going into the practice of national rejuvenation. The three errors are historical nihilism, which Lu says attacks revolutionary heroes and 'de-revolutionises' history; a regressive view that idealises patriarchal agrarian life; and an illusory view that treats language revolution or 'aesthetic redemption' as a substitute for real social practice. Lu concludes that scaling artistic heights depends on cultivating masters with ideals and conviction. In Lu's account they must be tempered by social change, nourished by the people and committed to refining their craft. The article quotes Marx on climbing the steep paths of science. It is a prescriptive statement of the official cultural line on literature, the 'main melody', heroes and historical nihilism. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist literary theorist links Engels, Mao's Yan'an Talks and the Chinese Dream to concrete demands on writers and critics.

Literature and art must not be slaves of the market 文艺不能当市场的奴隶 Hu Yinbin This short commentary, first published in Guangming Daily on 12 March 2017, asks what goes wrong when cultural production chases ratings and box office. Hu Yinbin argues that literature and art must not become "slaves of the market" and that social benefit must take priority over economic benefit. The piece starts from a report of remarks by a national political consultative conference member, He Xiangjiu, at the 2017 "two sessions". He said a private company proposed rewriting the script of the TV drama Jiao Yulu to downplay the "main melody" and add "human-interest" and "human-nature" scenes. Hu then discusses the spirit of Jiao Yulu, quotes Xi Jinping's talk at the forum on literature and art, and closes with remarks on how good works are made. Hu reads the producer's demand as an invented, vulgarising treatment that dissolves the sublime and puts entertainment first. Hu does not reject portraying Jiao's human side, but holds that any such portrayal must stay tied to historical fact; otherwise it "lowers" a hero, distorts national values and weakens cohesion. Citing Xi Jinping, Hu says economic benefit must yield to social benefit, and that indicators such as ratings and box office should be neither ignored nor made absolute. Hu adds that art draws its life from the people and from close engagement with real life. Hu concludes that a truthful Jiao Yulu, drawn from careful study, would hold an audience without invented drama. Works that move contemporary audiences need a sense of the era, historical responsibility and cultural mission, and a serious attitude to history and historical figures. Read the original if you want a brief example of how official commentary in 2017 applied Xi Jinping's line on art and the market to a specific dispute over a TV drama.

Key levers for building Marxist ideological discourse power under new conditions 新形势下建构马克思主义意识形态话语权的着力点 Li Jiangjing Writing in a 2017 issue of Studies on Marxism, Li Jiangjing takes up the problem of how to hold and rebuild Marxist ideological discourse power (huayuquan) now that mobile media, microblogs and WeChat have merged with older media. In the author's account, this contest has become more concealed and complex. Li argues that it can be met only by combining institutional, theoretical and communicative measures. The article has three main parts. The first deals with the interaction between institutional development and ideological change. The second covers three pressing questions about socialism with Chinese characteristics: the truth of Marxism, the originality of that path, and the moral and just character of its institutions. The third addresses how to raise the appeal of the mainstream discourse and use discourse power correctly. Li draws on Marx's 1859 Preface, the institutional economist Douglass North, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping. Li holds that institutions and ideology evolve together and that reform must be gradual. The author recommends reforming specific institutions while keeping the basic socialist system, and warns against abrupt ideological breaks, citing the Soviet collapse. Li contends that Western countries, led by the United States, infiltrate Chinese thought and attack the Party's leadership. The author's reply is to affirm Marxism's truth, defend the originality of socialism with Chinese characteristics, and argue that Party leadership, people's democracy and rule of law are unified. On communication, Li treats discourse power as "soft power" resting on academic discourse and on a basic mode of discourse. The author proposes building a philosophy and social science discourse system with Chinese characteristics, critically absorbing internet slang, and drawing on traditional and foreign culture. Li also praises Xi Jinping's plain phrasing, such as the Chinese Dream and "swatting flies and tigers together". Li adds that innovation must not distort Marxism's class standpoint. The author further calls for active agenda-setting and for refuting what the article calls false propositions, such as "revolution obstructs modernization" and "state capitalism". Read the original if you want to see how a 2017 Chinese ideological-work article links media change, academic discourse and institutional confidence.

Capital and the political economy of socialism with Chinese characteristics 《资本论》与中国特色社会主义政治经济学 Zhang Chen Writing in a newspaper commentary in 2017, Zhang Chen asks what role Marx's Capital should play in the political economy of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The author argues that this political economy is a 'Chinese version' of socialist political economy, combining basic Marxist theory with the practice of reform and opening up, and that Capital is its 'soul'. The piece opens by citing Xi Jinping's 2015 and 2016 statements, including that calling Marxist political economy and Capital outdated is arbitrary. The commentary sets out three ways Capital guides the Chinese project: its standpoint and basic ideas, its methodology, and its stock of theoretical resources. It then adds a caveat about Capital's historical specificity and closes with a list of theoretical results the Communist Party has produced since the founding of the People's Republic. Zhang contends that Capital unites scientific rigour with a working-class standpoint, which the author links to the people-centred development philosophy and to common prosperity. Its method, in Zhang's reading, includes historical materialism, the unity of the historical and the logical, and the ascent from the abstract to the concrete, all organised around surplus value. Zhang also holds that its analyses of the law of value, supply and demand, competition and social reproduction apply under certain conditions to a socialist market economy. The author concedes that Capital's concrete content is modelled on nineteenth-century Britain, but says its standpoint, viewpoint and method keep it 'unfinished' and open to development. Zhang concludes that Party theories such as the primary stage of socialism, the socialist market economy and supply-side structural reform are major innovations that extend Capital-based political economy. Read the original if you want a short, official-line statement of how Chinese commentators in 2017 tied Capital to the new category of 'political economy of socialism with Chinese characteristics'.

Capital: the inner unity of philosophy and the critique of political economy 《资本论》：哲学与政治经济学批判的内在贯通 Bu Xiangji Writing in a newspaper piece of 2017, Bu Xiangji asks how Marx's revolution in philosophy relates to his critique of political economy. The author argues that Marx's new philosophical path grew out of a practical concern: criticising a capitalist society that exploits the people and achieving human freedom and all-round emancipation. In Bu's reading, Capital resolves this concern by taking the critique of political economy as its entry point, so that philosophy and economics are internally united there. The article traces Marx's intellectual route. It begins with his move from Kant to Hegel and his association with the Young Hegelians. It then follows the political critique in the Rheinische Zeitung, the doubts about Hegel's philosophy of right, and the reflection on the state and civil society. It ends with the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 and the Theses on Feuerbach as steps towards Capital. Bu's central claim is that the 1844 Manuscripts bring together the philosophical revolution and the critique of political economy. There Marx sets out the principles of practical materialism, with "sensuous activity" or labour as the core concept. From labour, Marx asks how alienated labour relates to private property, which differs from humanist materialism's idealised premise and from political economy's habit of starting with private property. Bu holds that this undermines the premises of classical political economy and makes rebuilding it on new foundations a necessary task, completed in Capital. The Theses on Feuerbach then prepare the early materialist conception of history, which accounts for capitalism's origins. Bu draws two lessons. First, genuine philosophy must reach into social reality, and Marx's philosophy and political economy have no fixed boundary: Capital is itself Marx's "living philosophy". Second, adapting Marxism to Chinese conditions means inheriting this spirit, focusing on the "Chinese path", social justice and ecological civilization, and building a Chinese Marxist philosophical discourse. Read the original if you want a compact account of how Marx's early works lead into Capital and how a Chinese scholar draws contemporary lessons from that path.

Logical differences between Capital and the Grundrisse 《资本论》与《政治经济学批判大纲》的逻辑差异 Yang Haifeng Scholars widely accept that the 1857–58 manuscripts, the Outline of the Critique of Political Economy (the Grundrisse, here abbreviated the Outline), and Capital are continuous, both in economic content and in philosophical framework. Yang Haifeng challenges this consensus. The article argues that two different epistemes, or philosophical frameworks, underlie the two texts, and that these produce a major difference in their logic. Yang first sets out the concept of the episteme, drawing on Althusser's problematic and 'epistemological break', Foucault's The Order of Things and Kuhn's paradigm theory. The article then analyses the philosophical basis of the Outline. It then turns to Capital, comparing the way each text treats labour, the subject and the object. Yang reads the Outline as resting on an anthropological logic of production, which takes the form of an ontology of labour. Labour is the ontological ground of society. Objectification confirms human subjectivity, and labour creates free time as the space of free development. Yet the Outline also contains a second line, a logic of capital in which capital is the subject and labour only its means. In Capital this second line prevails. Labour is split into concrete and abstract labour, and the key distinction is between labour and labour-power. Yang treats that distinction as a break with the modern Western philosophy of labour as well as an economic one. The capitalist becomes only the personification of capital, and the human subject becomes a carrier of structure. Capital is an 'absolute subject' in a Hegelian sense, which makes it an absolute object relative to human beings. Yang concludes that studies stressing continuity have joined the two texts through surface discourse. The author calls for attention to what Marx does not say and to the deeper structure that constrains his thought. Doing so, Yang suggests, would prompt a rethinking of earlier research and open new space for Marxist philosophy. Read the original if you study the philosophical reading of Capital, the debate over labour ontology versus the logic of capital, or the use of Althusser and Foucault in Marx scholarship.

Capital's comprehensive analysis of the relations of production 《资本论》关于生产关系的整体分析 Zhang Leisheng Zhang Leisheng asks how Marx came to fix the relations of production as the object of political economy and what content he gave them, and how this shaped the framework of Capital. The article argues that Marx's understanding developed over a long period, from private property relations, to relations of intercourse, to relations of appropriation grounded in the development of the productive forces. Zhang holds that, whatever scholars debate about the object of study stated in the preface to the first German edition of Volume I, this development shows that Capital treats the relations of production as a whole. The article is organised in four parts, each tracing one angle of Marx's research and its use in Capital. These are: relations of intercourse (drawing on The German Ideology), ownership of the means of production, the relations of production as a totality (drawing on the 1857–58 Introduction), and the development of the productive forces (drawing on the 1859 Preface to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy). In each part Zhang moves from Marx's earlier works to concrete analyses in the three volumes of Capital. Zhang argues that Marx's focus on 'material intercourse' lets Capital show how the equal exchange of labour-power on the market hides unequal relations in production. On ownership, Zhang distinguishes the unity of ownership and appropriation, the separability of ownership from management, and the economic as against the legal form of ownership. These distinctions are applied to the essence of capitalist ownership, to the dispossession of direct producers, to joint-stock companies and to the 'negation of the negation'. On totality, Zhang reads production, distribution, exchange and consumption as an organic whole, and sees the same logic in the three volumes: production, circulation and the overall process of capitalist production. On the productive forces, Zhang uses relative surplus value, the general law of capitalist accumulation and the transformation of values into prices of production as examples. In each, changes in the organic composition of capital are the starting point for analysing class relations. Zhang concludes that Volumes I to III together form a complete theoretical system for analysing capitalist relations of production. Zhang presents this system as showing the antagonism between capital and wage labour, the contradiction between productive forces and relations of production, and the historical task of the proletariat. Read the original if you want a detailed, text-based account of how Marx's concept of the relations of production developed and how it structures Capital, as understood in Chinese Marxist political economy.

Four key points for holding the discourse power of ideological work 掌握意识形态工作话语权的四个着力点 Yao Dong Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in early 2017, Yao Dong asks how the Party can keep firm hold of the discourse power (huayuquan) of ideological work, which Xi Jinping has said must not be relinquished under any circumstances. The article argues that this requires effort in four areas: upholding and developing Marxism, building a discourse system with Chinese style, combining positive publicity with resistance to Western ideological hegemony, and strengthening ideological guidance on the internet. The piece opens by citing Xi's speeches since the 18th Party Congress (2012) and the Sixth Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2016). The plenum stressed ideological and political building as the foundation of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. The four sections that follow each pair a concrete priority with quotations from Xi and plenum documents, and each ends with practical tasks for Party organisations, officials and propaganda work. On Marxism, Yao treats the Marxist worldview and method, together with Xi's governance ideas as the latest result of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context, as the core of discourse power. On discourse, Yao says China's development is often described by others through narratives such as the 'China threat' and 'neo-colonialism'. Yao therefore urges telling China's story in new concepts that are both distinctively Chinese and intelligible abroad, drawing on traditional, revolutionary and socialist culture while avoiding Western vocabulary for explaining the Chinese path. Yao also holds that currents such as historical nihilism, neoliberalism, democratic socialism, constitutional democracy, 'universal values' and civil society are tools of Western value change, and that they aim to steer China towards capitalism and must be openly opposed. On the internet, which the article calls the main arena of struggle over public opinion and the 'biggest variable', Yao calls for consolidating the 'red zone', suppressing the 'black zone' and converting the 'grey zone'. Proposed measures include organised online forces, opinion leaders who identify with the mainstream ideology, stronger legislation and enforcement, and self-reliant core technology. Yao presents these as the means to make the Party's voice the loudest in cyberspace. Read the original if you want a compact statement of how Party commentary in 2017 framed ideological work, its named adversaries and its online strategy.

Putting Marxism and traditional Chinese culture in their proper places 摆正马克思主义和中国传统文化的位置 Chen Xianda Writing in Jilin Daily in February 2017, Chen Xianda takes up the revival of interest in traditional culture, in which Confucianism has again become a prominent field of study. Chen notes that some people now doubt whether Marxism still guides the ideological sphere, while extreme Confucian conservatives overstate their case. Chen rejects the view that upholding Marxism means belittling traditional culture, or that honouring tradition requires Marxism to step down, calling it theoretically wrong and practically harmful. The commentary is short and organised around a phrase from the Classic of Poetry, "an old state with a new mission". Chen first sets out a historical argument about changes in social formation. Chen then contrasts the starting points of Marxism and Confucianism, and finally turns to what Marxism needs from traditional culture after the revolution and how that culture should be treated today. Chen argues that China's revolution and socialist construction required Marxism because Marxism is a doctrine of revolution in the social formation. For over two thousand years, in Chen's account, dynastic changes took place within one social formation and Confucian orthodoxy persisted. Confucianism, based on kinship and the five human relationships, has no concept of class and aims to stabilise existing relations, while Marxism rests on class struggle. Chen also holds that Marxism cannot replace traditional culture. Citing Mao Zedong's call not to sever history, Chen says that after taking power the Party moved from attack to governance, and that Confucian wisdom on governance, moral education and harmony is useful for this. The pivot is "creative transformation", guided by Marxist theory and method. Confucius is to be restored as a cultural compiler, thinker and educator, and Confucianism is not to be used as a tool to justify hierarchy. Chen concludes that traditional culture education must not replace Marxist education, and that the two can proceed side by side. Chen argues that students who lack basic Marxist concepts cannot observe the contemporary world, and that without them they will also struggle to grasp the essence of traditional culture. Chen calls for avoiding abstract, ahistorical contests over which of the two is superior. Chen opposes both cultural nihilism toward Confucian-led tradition and a conservatism that invokes tradition to attack Marxism and reject Western culture. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a senior Chinese Marxist philosopher framed the relationship between Marxism and Confucian tradition in 2017.

Financialization has intensified the contradictions and crises of capitalist society 金融化加剧了资本主义社会的矛盾与危机 Luan Wenlian Luan Wenlian asks how the financialization of capitalism since the 1970s–80s has changed the contradictions of capitalist society, and argues that it has sharpened them and made crises more frequent. In the author's account, financialization is the newest form of capital's rule and the logical outcome of monopoly capitalism, in which accumulation of money wealth through the financial system rises above, and increasingly detaches from, production. The article first sets out a three-stage periodisation of capitalism: free competition (Marx and Engels), monopoly capitalism (Lenin), and the present stage dominated by fictitious financial capital. It then examines four areas of intensified contradiction: the basic contradiction between productive forces and relations of production; the separation of finance from the real economy; the exploitation of working people; and the dominance of financial capital within capitalist contradictions. A concluding section draws out four features of contemporary crises. Luan draws on Foster, Epstein, Keynes and Chinese and US statistics. Luan argues that technological and financial innovation are seized by financial capital and turned into means of reproducing capitalist relations. The basic contradiction acquires a new form: the socialisation of capital, through joint-stock companies and wider share ownership, coexists with the private ownership, use and returns of that capital. The article cites figures that the richest 10 per cent of Americans hold 89.3 per cent of stock value. It also traces the delinking of the US dollar from gold, after which dollar issuance grew sharply, and cites a rising ratio of financial to real assets and falling real wages in the United States. Financial profit, Luan holds, remains ultimately a redistribution of surplus value created in production, so the separation can never be complete. The author reads the M–M′ circuit as already containing the reality of crisis. Luan also describes the financialization of workers' incomes (pensions, housing credit, insurance) as a new form of exploitation, and argues that states serve financial capital, citing the scale of the 2008 bailout. Luan concludes that capitalist crises are unavoidable, take new forms in which financial institutions transmit and amplify shocks, and are more frequent and shorter in cycle. The author adds that the originating powers harm the world most, since developing countries suffer in their real economies and in the value of their dollar reserves. The article judges this accumulation model, set against productive forces, value creation and the working majority, to be unsustainable. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist political-economy account of financialization that draws on Monthly Review-school and Western critical literature and on statistics about US inequality and finance.

On inequality in the various spheres of contemporary Western society 论当代西方社会各领域的不平等 Song Lidan Writing in 2016, Song Lidan asks how far inequality has deepened in Western societies since the end of the Cold War. The article argues that growing economic inequality has widened the political, cultural and developmental gaps between bourgeoisie and proletariat, and even gaps in health and life expectancy. Citing Lenin, Song holds that exploiters cannot be equal to the exploited, and that this inequality is rooted in capitalist private ownership and is an incurable chronic disease of capitalism. The article moves through five spheres of inequality (economic, political, educational, developmental, and health and longevity) before a final section on lessons for China. Song draws mainly on Western authors and data, including Anthony Giddens, Thomas Piketty, John Westergaard, Howard Zinn, Paul Krugman, Elizabeth Warren, John Scott, Joseph Stiglitz and Ulrich Beck, together with an International Labour Organization report of 2015 and German health statistics. Song treats economic inequality, grounded in unequal ownership of the means of production, as the determining one. Citing Piketty, Song reads the post-1945 rise in the capital/income ratio as showing that the Kuznets curve was largely a Cold War product. Political equality is called formal only: elections are described as contests among the bourgeoisie, and without economic democracy there can be no real political democracy. Education is presented as a market-driven competition for social rank, with rising student debt, the Gatsby curve and an "class ceiling" in Britain. Insecure work, limited mobility and unequal health outcomes are said to show that individual effort mostly yields a slightly better position in the labour market. In the closing section Song draws three lessons for China. China, unlike the West, cannot draw profit from colonialism and must rely on a socialist basic economic system with distribution according to work. Song also warns that economic inequality has appeared with the growth of the non-public sector and, if it worsens, could invite unrest and endanger the goals of the "two centenaries". Finally, Song sees capitalism in a legitimacy crisis since 2008 and calls for firm adherence to the basic socialist system in order to realise the Chinese Dream of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want to see how a CASS researcher in 2016 assembled Western critical data on inequality to support an argument for China's socialist path.

Development trends of world socialism in the twenty-first century 21 世纪世界社会主义的发展趋势 Sun Jinsong Writing in 2016, Sun Jinsong asks where the world socialist movement is heading in the twenty-first century. The author argues that the shock and disorientation that followed the collapse of the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe have largely ended. In Sun's account, socialism is now reviving in some countries in forms different from the twentieth-century Soviet model, and socialism with Chinese characteristics will become an important driving force for the movement. The article is organised around three trends: the relationship between humans and nature as a defining feature of socialism, globalization as socialism's historical stage, and the role of socialism with Chinese characteristics. It surveys socialist thought from early utopian socialism and classical Marxism to Soviet practice, and divides capitalist globalization into three phases. A closing periodisation sums up the argument. Sun first contends that earlier socialism centred on conflicts within human society, whereas sustainable development now makes the human–nature relationship central. The author traces the "ecological crisis" to capitalism's profit-driven mode of production and presents "ecological civilization" as socialism's concern. Sun then describes globalization 1.0 as colonial trade, 2.0 as WTO-era transnational production that moves manufacturing to developing countries, and 3.0 as a new model of equal consultation and mutual benefit represented by the Belt and Road Initiative. Third, Sun argues that China's industrialization was driven by external pressure and national survival, was led by the Communist Party rather than a national bourgeoisie, and shows that modernization without wholesale Westernization is possible. The author cites the failures of Western-style democracy in Iraq, Libya and Egypt, and says China's peaceful rise differs from Western colonial industrialization. Sun concludes that nineteenth-century socialism was marked by theory (Marxism), twentieth-century socialism by practice (the Soviet model), and twenty-first-century socialism by exploration, symbolised by socialism with Chinese characteristics. The author acknowledges remaining problems in China, naming Party corruption as the greatest danger, and holds that China's influence rests on its achievements rather than coercion. Read the original if you want an example of how a Central Party School scholar framed China's place in world socialism around 2016, including the "globalization 1.0, 2.0, 3.0" scheme.

The Communist Party of Sweden's new explorations of the road to socialism since the upheavals in the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe 苏东剧变以来瑞典共产党对社会主义道路的新探索 Zhou Huaping Guo Taiying How has a small West European communist party reconsidered the road to socialism since the collapse of the Soviet bloc? Zhou and Guo examine the Communist Party of Sweden (SKP), founded in 1917, and argue that since the upheavals in the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe it has kept to Marxism-Leninism while adapting its strategy to Swedish conditions. In the authors' view, this makes its exploration significant even though the party remains weak. The article first traces the party's organisational history, including its 1960s–70s split, the re-founding of a communist party in 1977, the 1989 extraordinary congress and the 1995 return to the name Communist Party of Sweden. It then follows the SKP's own documents, above all its 2013 programme and statements on its website, through four themes. These are its analysis of contemporary capitalism; its views on the Soviet collapse, the Swedish labour movement, the European Union and NATO; its goals, principles and tasks; and its vision of a future socialist society. The authors report that the SKP sees capitalism as unchanged in its exploitative essence, with globalisation as the current form of imperialism and neoliberalism. On the Soviet collapse, the party names institutional flaws, including a highly centralised planned economy, bloc integration during the Cold War and the fusion of party and state. It still holds that this was not a failure of socialism itself and that socialism can correct its errors. The SKP condemns the EU as imperialist and undemocratic, and it opposes covert Swedish ties to NATO, defending military neutrality. The authors describe its positive programme as public ownership and a planned economy, a fairer international trade system, and a classless society that guarantees work, housing, health care and education and aims at the free and all-round development of every person. The party rests on democratic centralism and on criticism and self-criticism. Zhou and Guo conclude that the SKP's programme preserves public ownership, planning and the universal features of socialism while reflecting Swedish conditions, such as an advanced economy and well-developed bourgeois democracy. For them, this shows that socialism has no single model. They acknowledge that the party's base is narrow, that it is unlikely to take power for a long time, and that its immediate tasks are to broaden its class and mass base through anti-monopoly and anti-imperialist struggle. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic account of a small European communist party's programme and its positions on the Soviet collapse, the EU and NATO.

Choices of discourse in current ideological and theoretical propaganda 当前思想理论宣传的话语选择 Meng Xianping Wang Yonggui Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts (Hongqi Wengao), 2017 no. 6, Meng Xianping and Wang Yonggui ask how the Party's ideas and theory can "take root" among ordinary people. Their answer is that propaganda work must build a discourse system and innovate its wording. They argue that failures of communication come from an unsuitable narrative mode, a badly chosen audience or too little identification between speaker and listener. The article is a short commentary in two parts. The first part concerns the choice of discourse (wording, register and tone) and sets out three requirements: language that appeals to both refined and popular tastes, language that meets the needs of the masses, and language with a positive orientation. The second part concerns narrative form and sets out two requirements: forms close to everyday practice, and forms in which feeling and meaning interact. It closes with a warning against dogmatism and draws on Marx, Engels and Lenin throughout. The authors contend that propaganda should move from theoretical narrative to life narrative and from abstract symbols to concrete ones, while keeping Marxism as the guiding ideology. They criticise propaganda that panders to vulgar tastes, trivialises theory or uses exaggerated, ambiguous or extreme language. In their account, "three vulgarities" language carries a bad value orientation and blurs the boundaries of Party theory. They hold that good discourse celebrates social progress and also criticises social ills in an objective way. It supports "letting a hundred flowers bloom" but does not endorse "fair competition" among all ideas. Citing Marx, they say that abuse alone cannot touch the substance of capitalist society. Lofty theory, they argue, must be carried by plain speech, and the sources of narrative should be sought in mass life. The authors conclude that propaganda workers should give up dogmatic, formulaic or showy styles. In an age when everyone has a microphone, they say, official and popular narratives intermingle and crowd out dogmatic discourse. They call on propagandists to learn from the people and to present theory through lived reality, so that people truly believe, study, understand and use Marxism. Read the original if you want to see how a 2017 Party journal framed the style, tone and narrative of ideological work, including its use of classical Marxist citations and classical Chinese literary criticism.

No Party member may treat political discipline and political rules as a game 任何党员都不能拿政治纪律和政治规矩当儿戏 Yuan Xiuli Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in early 2017, Yuan Xiuli takes up the question of why political discipline and political rules must be strictly upheld inside the Chinese Communist Party. The article argues that officials investigated since the 18th Party Congress (2012) commonly lost their awareness of these norms, and that corruption and breaches of political discipline tend to appear together. In Yuan's view, a defence line set only against corruption is one-sided and mistaken, because political failings can harm the Party as much as corruption, or more. The article follows the Sixth Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2016), which restated that no Party member may treat political discipline and political rules as a game. It has two parts. The first explains why strict political discipline is extremely important, setting out four points: its primacy among Party disciplines, its content, the ban on crossing political red lines, and the regulations that support it. The second part sets out how Party members and organisations should put it into practice. Yuan's central claim is that political discipline is the most important and fundamental of all Party disciplines, and the basis for observing the rest. Drawing on Xi Jinping, the article lists his "five musts" and "five never-allowed" acts, which cover upholding the authority of the central leadership, unity, procedure, obedience to organisational decisions, and the leaking of secrets or spreading of political rumours. Yuan cites Xi's warning that unenforced discipline creates a "broken window effect" and could reduce the Party to a "private club". The article presents newly revised regulations, including the Party discipline punishment regulations and the accountability regulations, as turning abstract requirements into concrete, enforceable rules. For implementation, Yuan proposes strengthening education in ideals and convictions, since wavering belief is said to be the root of lapses. Yuan also calls for reverence for discipline and self-examination by members, and for Party organisations and discipline inspection bodies to take up their responsibility for enforcement and oversight. The article says that "iron discipline must be enforced with an iron hand", and cites expulsions of senior officials for forming cliques or publicly voicing views at odds with the Central Committee as proof that firm action deters violations. Read the original if you want an example of how a 2017 Party journal explained the official case for tighter political discipline and the content of the "five musts" and "five never-allowed" acts.

Two key points in advancing the popularization of Marxism 推进马克思主义大众化的两个关键点 Zhou Xincheng Writing in 2017, Zhou Xincheng asks what is needed to make Marxism accessible to the broad masses (Marxism's popularization, or dazhonghua). The article answers with two conditions: theorists and propagandists must firmly believe that Marxism's basic principles are correct, and those principles must be combined with Chinese realities to answer Chinese problems. The piece opens with Xi Jinping's remarks on Marxism as the Party's guiding ideology. It then argues that Marxism has to be "instilled" in the masses because spontaneous struggles do not generate it. It rebuts a reading of the 1872 German preface to the Communist Manifesto, and closes with Mao Zedong's 1950s statements on general laws and national particularities. Zhou names the main obstacle as theorists who do not believe in Marxism, reject its basic principles, or promote anti-Marxist ideas to the public. Against the claim that Marxism is partly right and partly wrong, Zhou reads the Manifesto preface as separating basic principles, which are the essence and remain valid, from specific conclusions drawn under particular historical conditions, which can become outdated. Citing the preface as proof that Marx and Engels admitted errors is called a deliberate distortion. Basic principles are held to be universal truths, yet they are useless unless applied to concrete national conditions; Zhou compares them to an arrow that must be shot at a target, and says copying foreign models must fail. Zhou concludes that upholding the basic principles and developing Marxism are one task, since development means applying the principles to new situations. In present-day China, Zhou holds, upholding the theory of socialism with Chinese characteristics is upholding Marxism, so popularizing Marxism amounts to popularizing that theory among the masses. Read the original if you want a short, orthodox statement of how a Party-affiliated theorist in 2017 defended the universality of Marxism's basic principles against "partly right, partly wrong" readings.

Abandoning the communist ideal means abandoning Marxism 摒弃共产主义理想就不是马克思主义 Chen Xianda Writing in a newspaper commentary (Jilin Daily, February 2017), Chen Xianda argues that no one who avoids the communist ideal can be a genuine Marxist. Citing Xi Jinping's repeated statements that communism is the Communist Party's highest ideal, Chen treats that ideal as the "calcium" that keeps a Marxist standing firm. Chen begins with the problems he sees after reform: a widening wealth gap, official corruption, moral confusion and environmental damage. He identifies two opposed attitudes to communism: beneficiaries of unfair gain who fear the word, and discontented people who dismiss it as utopian. The article then separates three senses of communism, discusses welfare states, and turns to ideological education for young people and to the personal steadfastness required of Party members. Chen's central distinction is between communism as a social formation (the advanced stage of socialism, still very distant), as an ideal and highest programme, and as "communist elements" present in current socialist practice. Policies such as common prosperity, poverty eradication and public welfare, in his reading, steadily add such elements to a socialist market economy that is not a "market society". Western welfare states, he argues, remain improved capitalism: taxes are accumulated surplus labour, and welfare ultimately stabilises the capitalist system. Without the communist goal, Chen says, the Party would merely drift, and reform would lose its direction and invite neoliberal interpretations. Chen concludes that communist ideals should be taught to young people as part of their worldview, just as other social systems promote their own ideals, so that they understand socialism, capitalism and China's future. He holds that this is compatible with current policies, including private enterprise and wealth differences, because socialism with characteristics of China is a stage in a longer process. A firm Marxist, he says, must look beyond an individual lifespan and withstand the tests of money and status in the reform era. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how a senior Chinese Marxist philosopher reconciles the communist ideal with market reform and ideological education.

On the Marxist classical authors' idea of separating education from religion 论马克思主义经典作家的教育与宗教相分离思想 Zhang Xiaochen Zhang asks how Marx, Engels and Lenin understood the separation of education from religion, and argues that it is a critical inheritance of early modern Western thought and an important component of the Marxist view of religion. In the article's account, the classical authors went beyond their Western predecessors by tying the principle to concrete social problems and to the basic theory of Marxism. The article first traces the Western background: the Renaissance, the Reformation and the Enlightenment, which moved education from church monopoly towards state-run, secular provision. It then turns to the classical authors' practical critique of religious control of schooling, their theoretical construction of the principle, and the practical routes they proposed for realising it. Zhang argues that Marx and Engels identified three harms of religious monopoly over education: it blocks human emancipation by helping ruling classes keep people ignorant, it shackles science (Engels's examples include Bruno and Servetus), and it lets religious morality displace social morality. Theoretically, the classical authors drew on dialectical and historical materialism to describe church–state relations. They also stressed that religion is a private matter, so that the state, and therefore public education, should be free of it. In practice, the author says, they proposed three measures: atheist propaganda and education, the separation of church and state with confiscation of church property and the end of state funding, and a secular national education system, citing Engels's account of English schools. Zhang concludes that separating education from religion is a key part of the Marxist view of religion and a basic principle for handling the relationship between education and religion in a socialist country. It is presented as the product of combining theory with practice. Read the original if you want a source-based overview of Marx, Engels and Lenin's statements on schooling and religion, as presented in Chinese scholarship on religion and atheism.

Preliminary thoughts on building Marxist atheism as an academic discipline 马克思主义无神论学科建设刍议 Zuo Peng Zuo Peng asks how atheism, as a body of knowledge that negates and criticises theism, can become an independent academic discipline in China. The author argues that current classification rules do not allow this and proposes adding a second-level discipline, Marxist atheism, under the first-level discipline of Marxist theory. To make that case convincing, the article recommends building the field on the model of Fei Xiaotong's "five viscera and six bowels" formula for rebuilding sociology. The article has three parts. The first sets out why independent disciplinary status is a precondition and where atheism should be placed. The second outlines a complete disciplinary system with four branches. The third describes the "departments" the discipline needs: learned societies, research institutes, academic departments, books and materials, and specialist journals. Zuo draws on the 2009 national classification standard, the 2011 degree catalogue, Ren Jiyu, Tian Xinming, Xi Wuyi and Fei Xiaotong's collected works. Zuo notes that the 2009 standard lists atheism under religious studies, but the degree-granting catalogue does not list it, so atheism cannot recruit or train graduate students independently. Zuo describes religious studies as increasingly dominated by voices that stress religion's positive role, leaving atheism marginal. Placing atheism beside religious studies under philosophy would blur disciplinary boundaries, the author says. Under Marxist theory it would fit, since atheism is presented as the foundation of Marxism and since Party members' superstition and religious infiltration of universities call for atheist education. The four branches are principles of Marxist atheism, history of atheism, critique of theism (superstition and religious theology, the latter described as the hardest task), and atheist propaganda and education. Zuo says the field's institutions are thin, citing 115 directors in the China Atheism Society against 408 in the China Religious Studies Society. The author also reports few translations of atheist works and a single specialist journal, Science and Atheism. Zuo concludes that the field is still at an early stage and its standard is bound to be low, but that the work must be started rather than merely discussed. The author calls for state support for projects and publications, for "borrowing a boat" by recruiting graduate students under neighbouring disciplines, and for more research centres and local societies. Read the original if you want a detailed view of how Chinese Marxist atheism scholars argue for institutionalising their field and how they see its place within Marxist theory and religious studies.

Sanders's "socialism" and the thesis of "American socialist exceptionalism" 从桑德斯的“社会主义”看“美国社会主义例外论” Xuan Chuanshu Tan Yangfang Why did Bernie Sanders, a self-declared socialist, defeat Hillary Clinton in several state primaries in the first half of 2016 in a country long labelled an exception to socialism? Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts (2017, no. 2), Xuan Chuanshu and Tan Yangfang argue that this is not anomalous once the historical logic behind it is examined. The short commentary is organised in three numbered sections. It first traces the economic and political background of Sanders's rise, then assesses what his "socialism" actually is, and finally revisits the claim that the United States is an exception, drawing on the history of American labour and socialist movements. The authors contend that the turn towards socialism was produced by the contradictions of capitalism, not by Sanders's campaign: neoliberal financialisation since the 1980s, the financial crisis and the Occupy Wall Street movement widened inequality and shifted public attitudes. They cite a 2011 Pew survey and a 2016 Boston Globe poll on young Americans' views of socialism. In their reading, Sanders is a reformist rather than a true socialist: he takes Denmark and Sweden, the New Deal and Johnson's reforms as models, relies on class cooperation and the Democratic Party, and in effect reflects the ruling class's effort to channel unrest into reformism. They also argue that Sombart's question explains only why America lacks Soviet, Latin American or European-style socialism, not why it lacks socialism altogether; they point to the 1886 Chicago strike, Eugene Debs, the Socialist Party and the Communist Party. The authors conclude that the United States is not an exception but has socialism in different forms and along different paths. Cycles of crisis and reform, they say, have left socialist ideas and elements behind, and the revival of socialist forces shows that history has not ended. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a Chinese Party journal in 2017 interpreted Sanders and the exceptionalism debate.

How to view populism in Europe today 如何看待当前欧洲的民粹主义 Yao Yao Writing in Qiushi in 2017, Yao Yao asks why populism and extreme currents have risen so quickly in Europe and what this means for European integration and globalisation. The author argues that debt, refugee and terrorist crises have left Europe's lower and middle strata in a state of material and spiritual distress. In Yao's reading, populism reflects long-accumulated strategic mistakes and institutional deadlocks in European states, not only the mood of the moment. The article has three parts. The first defines populism as an anti-elite current of thought, a movement for radical reform by ordinary people, and a strategy that elites can use to manipulate the public. It traces its causes to the 2008 financial crisis, the Spanish protests of 2011 and neoliberal globalisation. The second part sets out four deadlocks, illustrated by Spain, Greece, France, Italy and EU demographic data. The third part turns to the transatlantic relationship and the EU's internal imbalances. Yao holds that neoliberal policy produced growth but distributed it unevenly, since capital moves more freely than labour and migration brings cultural friction. Left populism, on this account, "hates the rich" and opposes austerity and capital mobility. Right populism "hates foreigners" and opposes immigration. Both therefore oppose the existing international order and European integration. The four deadlocks are deindustrialisation and financialisation, unaffordable welfare, population decline and migration, and an electoral system in which populists block reforms. Yao cites France's labour law and Italy's 2016 constitutional referendum as examples. The author also argues that Europe is unequal in its relationship with the United States and that the EU's rights and responsibilities are unbalanced. Yao concludes that populism is both appealing for confronting real problems and destructive for aggravating them. The author expects it to push Europe towards a retreat from integration and globalisation. Protectionism and isolationism may offer temporary shelter but would harm national and world economies in the long run. Yao calls on responsible politicians to adjust strategy, advance institutional reform and guide public opinion towards a balanced, inclusive and win-win globalisation. Read the original if you want an example of how a 2017 Chinese Party-journal commentary explained European populism and its link to globalisation.

Marx's thought on "philistines and their state" and its significance 马克思关于“庸人及其国家”的思想及其意义 Nie Jinfang Nie Jinfang takes up Marx's idea of the "philistines and their state", developed in his 1842–1843 correspondence around the founding of the Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher. The article opens by contesting Hannah Arendt, who sought "totalitarian elements" in Marxism and later coined "the banality of evil" in her study of Adolf Eichmann. Nie argues that Arendt never read Marx's key texts closely, and that Marx had already analysed how people survive without independent thought under despotic rule. The article is built in four parts. It first describes Marx's picture of Prussian absolutism as a "world of philistines". It then sets the principle of monarchy against what Marx calls the principle of man, and examines how despotism corrupts new ideas, taking Schelling as the example. The last part turns to Marx's strategy for struggling against this order. Nie draws mainly on Marx's letters to Ruge and Feuerbach. Nie's central claim is that rulers and ruled shape one another. In Nie's reading of the letters, Marx held that philistines want slaves and are slaves themselves, so that the "world of philistines" is a world of "political animals" in which dehumanisation is the system's principle. Marx rejected Montesquieu's defence of monarchy and held that the monarchical principle is incompatible with human dignity. Frederick William IV's attempt at renewal ended in restoration of the old order, which for Nie shows that a philistine state cannot be abolished on its own foundations. Schelling's career as an "official philosopher" shows, in Nie's account, how power turns a once sincere youthful philosophy into Prussian politics under a philosophical cover. On strategy, Nie reports Marx's combination of uncompromising stance and prudence: signing his name, avoiding rash polemic, and letting the newspaper guide its contributors. Marx pinned his hopes on "thinking men" and "suffering men", and called for restoring the human self-confidence that is freedom. Nie concludes that these ideas remained a value premise of Marx's later social critique and still matter for political philosophy. Nie also finds a kinship with Arendt's resistance to banal evil, and reads her remark that Marx was "misused" by totalitarianism as a kind of self-reflection. Read the original if you want a close reading of the early Marx's letters on Prussian despotism and a rebuttal of Arendt's linking of Marx with totalitarianism.

Marx's core philosophical idea is the "greater historical materialism" 马克思的核心哲学思想是大唯物史观 An Qinian In this piece, published in Beijing Daily on 23 January 2017, An Qinian introduces his own book on Marx's philosophy, titled The Road to Freedom (《通往自由之路》). An argues that Marx's core philosophical idea is a "greater historical materialism" (da weiwu shiguan), of which many views already accepted by scholars are only component parts. The text first explains why Chinese philosophers since reform and opening up have studied Marx's own philosophy rather than "Marxist philosophy". An cites disputes over what Marxist philosophy means, the publication of the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 (translated into Chinese in 1979), and the fit between Marx's thought and the changes of the reform era. It then summarises the book's seven chapters and ends with remarks on its title and purpose. In An's account, the greater historical materialism sees history as the interactive, co-developing process of nature, human society and human beings themselves, grounded in labour practice. Its theoretical basis is the dialectics of labour practice and its value goal is human emancipation. Chapter 2, the key chapter, argues that labour practice matters because environments changed by people in turn change people, and this feedback explains human development. An says the textbook historical materialism (the "lesser" one) is part of the greater version, not opposed to it. The remaining chapters treat Marx and dialectical materialism, the systematic character of his thought, his place in the history of philosophy, and methodological value. An calls for integrating the existing, often conflicting findings to reconstruct Marx's philosophy as an organic whole, and for a Marxist philosophy as Chinese people understand it, so that "Marx speaks Chinese". An adds that whether following Marx's laws of history will lead to the realm of freedom cannot be proved by theory alone but only in practice. Read the original if you want a short statement of An's reading of Marx and of the aims of Chinese Marxist philosophy after 1978.

The wholeness of Marxism revisited 再论马克思主义的整体性 Zhao Jiaxiang Following Lenin's division of Marxism into philosophy, political economy and scientific socialism, Zhao Jiaxiang takes up a problem in Chinese universities. The three parts are taught in separate departments, so specialists in one know little of the others, and the unified Marxist system is cut into pieces. Writing in 2017, Zhao argues that Marxism is an internally unified whole and that scholars and teachers must study it as one. The article builds the case through six perspectives: the social and historical conditions in which Marxism arose; its theoretical sources; the content of its theoretical system; its historical development; the actual character of the classic works; and, finally, the ways to grasp and apply this wholeness. The historical survey runs from Marx and Engels through Lenin to the Sinicization of Marxism under Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and later leaders. Zhao argues that the three parts emerged from the same conditions: industrial capitalism, its sharpening contradictions and the rise of the working class as an independent political force. The three sources (German classical philosophy, British classical political economy, utopian socialism) did not act separately but interpenetrated, and the three parts share concepts such as productive forces, relations of production and social formation. Zhao reads the 1844 Manuscripts, The German Ideology, Capital and Anti-Dühring as works that fuse all three parts, and proposes correcting the usual view that The German Ideology marks only the formation of historical materialism. The article also holds that mastering this wholeness requires combining history, theory and classic works, and that real problems call for several principles from all three parts, not one. Zhao concludes that the Marxist basic-principles textbooks written since the Marxism first-level discipline was set up in 2004 remain a 'platter' of three separate parts. Training teachers who grasp Marxism as a whole will be long and difficult, but Zhao says the work should start now. Zhao offers the article as a spur to others and has no finished model for a truly integrated textbook. Read the original if you are interested in how a Chinese Marxist philosopher argues for integrating the study and teaching of Marxism, and in his close readings of the classic texts.

Choices of discourse in current ideological and theoretical propaganda 当前思想理论宣传的话语选择 Meng Xianping Wang Yonggui Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2017, Meng Xianping and Wang Yonggui ask how the Party's ideas and theories can "take root" among the public. Their answer is that this depends on building a discourse system and renewing propaganda language. The authors argue that propaganda has its own regularities and needs a suitable mode of narration, a sound vocabulary, effective strategies and a lively tone. Theory should move from "theoretical narrative" to "life narrative" and from abstract to concrete symbols, while Marxism keeps its guiding position. The commentary has two parts. The first concerns the choice of discourse, which the authors say depends on the propagandist's theoretical training and style, the audience's knowledge and the social setting. It discusses three choices: language that appeals to both refined and popular tastes, language that meets the needs of the masses, and language with a positive orientation. The second part concerns narrative form and discusses closeness to everyday practice, the interplay of feeling and meaning, and the rejection of dogmatism. Meng and Wang say propaganda language should embody truth, goodness and beauty, and avoid affectation. They criticise vulgar or comic styles that lower the persuasiveness of theory, as well as the "three vulgarities" (sansu), which they say carry a bad value orientation and blur the boundaries of ideas. They support "letting a hundred flowers bloom" but not "fair competition" among all ideas, and "a hundred schools of thought contending" but not nonsense. In the second part, citing Marx, Engels and Lenin, they argue that abstract theory must return to practice and be carried by plain language drawn from the masses' daily life. Emotive, concrete narration should rest on a clear people's standpoint. The authors warn against propagandists who bluster, use stock phrases, or string together new terms without substance. They say such habits "sacrifice living Marxism", a phrase they quote from the classics. In the multimedia age, they note, official and popular narratives intertwine, which in their view crowds out the space for dogmatism. They conclude that dogmatism must be abandoned so that the true meaning of theory appears in the masses' real lives and people truly believe, study, understand and apply Marxism. Read the original if you want to see how a 2017 Party journal framed the style, tone and narrative of ideological work, and how it used classical Marxist citations for that purpose.

Ideological and political work must respond to the concerns of the times 思政工作要回应时代关切 Zhu Lijia Writing in 2017, Zhu Lijia asks how ideological and political work (sizheng gongzuo) should adapt to the new stage of reform and development that began with the 18th Party Congress (2012). The author argues that such work can help build consensus on values, reform and development, and strengthen popular belief in socialism, but only if it responds to the concerns of the era. The piece is a short commentary published in a journal on ideological and political work. The article is organised under three headings.
