The first treats the transformation of world civilisation under globalisation and informatisation. The second treats China's own social transformation. The third calls for ideological and political work to serve the building of a society of fairness and justice. On the global level, Zhu describes a "civilisational predicament" in which material growth coexists with spiritual emptiness, and says that the neoliberal order is losing credibility. China's socialist success, in this account, strengthens its discursive power, so ideological and political work should "tell China's story well". It should do so by joining core socialist values with the "common values" of humanity. At home, Zhu points to interest differentiation, social stratification and pluralising values as the by-products of modernisation. These erode reform consensus and produce anxiety and a sense of value emptiness. The author therefore wants work that is targeted and differentiated, that strengthens the explanatory power of socialist theory, and that is willing to offer rational criticism of phenomena at odds with socialist principles. Zhu concludes that ideological and political work should move beyond propaganda and education toward a "think-tank" orientation. It would study the relationship between values and institutions, assess the value implications of public policy, and embed socialist values in institutions and policies. People would then experience the superiority of the socialist system directly and come to hold socialist belief willingly. The author presents this as the route to long-term social stability. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese scholar in 2017 framed the tasks of ideological and political work in terms of civilisational change, social stratification and institutional value-orientation.

Revisiting the integrity of Marxism 再论马克思主义的整体性 Zhao Jiaxiang Zhao Jiaxiang takes up a problem in Chinese Marxist teaching and research. Following Lenin, Marxism has three main components: philosophy, political economy and scientific socialism. In Chinese universities these are usually taught in separate departments. Zhao argues that this split leaves scholars knowing only one component and weakens understanding of Marxism as a whole. The article contends that Marxism is a unified, internally connected system and should be studied as one. The article builds its case in six parts. Four ask what shows Marxism's integrity: its social and historical conditions, its theoretical sources, the content of the theory, and the course of its historical development. A fifth examines the classic texts, and a sixth proposes ways of grasping and applying the whole. The text was published in 2017 and also notes recent institutional changes, such as the creation of Marxism as a first-level discipline in 2004. Zhao's central move is to show that the three components arose from the same conditions and sources and interpenetrate in content. Industrial capitalism and the rise of the working class made the revolutions in philosophy, political economy and socialist theory possible together. German classical philosophy, British classical political economy and utopian socialism did not each feed one component alone. Zhao then reads works such as the 1844 Manuscripts, The German Ideology, Capital and Anti-Dühring as integrated texts. Zhao proposes that The German Ideology be described as marking the basic formation of Marxism as a whole, not only of historical materialism. The second move concerns method. Zhao calls for combining history, theory and classic works ("shi, lun, zhu"), drawing on the author's own studies of the "two never's" principle, the Asiatic mode of production and the debate on socialism in one country. Zhao also warns against a simplified, one-principle-per-problem view of linking theory and practice, saying complex problems need principles from all three components. Zhao concludes that the current Marxist textbooks are still a "platter" of three separate parts rather than an integrated account. The author says that training teachers able to grasp Marxism as a whole is a long task, but that the work of integration cannot wait for it. Zhao offers the article as a spur to others and mentions more than a dozen of the author's own papers on Capital from this standpoint. Read the original if you are interested in how a senior Chinese Marxist philosopher argues for integrating philosophy, political economy and scientific socialism, and in debates on Marxist pedagogy and textual study in China.

Recent corrective measures in Russia's field of history 近年来俄罗斯历史领域的系列纠偏举措 Wu Enyuan Writing in 2016, Wu Enyuan introduces what the article presents as a new trend in Russian historical studies: a series of government measures to correct what Wu describes as a distortion of the national past since the Soviet collapse. The piece is an informational commentary offered "for reference", reporting Russian policy rather than arguing a theoretical case. Its thesis is that Russia's government now treats a shared reading of history as the basis of civic identity and has moved to counter Western "colour revolution" influence in culture and education. The article begins with the background: Wu cites a 2014 presidential decree on the damage done by the crisis of the 1990s and by Western culture, and describes Western and East European efforts around the 70th anniversary of the Second World War to equate Stalin's system with Nazism. It then lists three sets of measures: a drive to produce a unified national history textbook, the December 2014 decree no. 808 on the principles of state cultural policy, and wider popularisation of history, including training for about 6,000 history teachers. The longest section sets out the "new conception of history" in four areas: the October Revolution, the Soviet role in the Second World War, the evaluation of Soviet history, and attitudes to Stalin. In Wu's account, the textbook commission headed by Duma chairman Naryshkin, with academician Chubarian reporting to Putin, concluded that the revolutions of 1917 and the civil war can be called a "great revolution" that advanced social progress. Wu reports Putin's rejection of equating Nazism with Stalinism, his defence of the Soviet–German treaty as a way to gain time for rearmament, and his claim that Soviet forces saved East European peoples from destruction. On Soviet history, the commission reportedly settled on viewing the 1930s as one path of modernization with both positive and negative aspects. Wu contrasts this with Gorbachev's wholesale negation, which the article blames for the Soviet collapse. Wu also notes the July 2015 bust of Stalin in the Rzhev district and Culture Minister Medinsky's statement that Stalin must have a place in historical memory. Wu concludes that these views reflect the mainstream position of the current Russian government, while acknowledging that Russian society still holds differing assessments of Stalin. The article draws no explicit lessons for China beyond offering the material as a point of reference. Read the original if you want a concise, sympathetic Chinese account of Russia's mid-2010s history policy and of how Chinese scholars of the Soviet Union reported it.

The world-historical significance of the Chinese path 中国道路的世界历史意义 Wang Mingsheng This commentary, first published in the People's Daily in December 2016, asks what the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics (the "Chinese path") means beyond China itself. Wang Mingsheng argues that the path is the necessary road to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and the Chinese Dream. In the author's view it also has major world-historical significance, because it breaks the Western monopoly on development models and offers experience that other countries, especially developing ones, can draw on. The piece is organised under three headings: the path enriches the diversity of routes to modernization; it offers a new model of peaceful development; and it helps developing countries find their own roads. Wang draws on China's post-1949 and post-1978 record, a historical sketch of Western great-power rise and colonial expansion, and quotations from Xi Jinping, Deng Xiaoping and Samuel Huntington. Wang contends that after decolonisation and the collapse of the Soviet Union, Western discourse hegemony declared liberal democracy the endpoint of history. China's growth, the author says, shows that modernization does not have to mean Westernisation. The article cites the world's second-largest economy, over 700 million people lifted out of poverty and per capita GDP above US$8,000. It describes Western rise as built on violence, colonialism and world wars, and treats the belief that a strong country must seek hegemony as a product of that history. Peaceful development, in Wang's account, is rooted in Chinese culture and is a strategic choice, not a diplomatic expedient. The article further holds that developing countries which copied Western models suffered distorted growth, social conflict and instability, whereas China, which borrowed selectively, succeeded. Wang concludes that the Chinese path belongs to the world as well as to China. According to the article, it has restored China's international standing and discourse power, and it is an important part of humanity's civilisational achievements and its search for socialism. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Chinese commentary in 2016 presented the Chinese path as an alternative to Western development models and as a reference for the Global South.

Political stability underpins Russia's great-power strength Russia in 2016 政治稳定支撑俄罗斯大国力量 Wang Jiabo This short newspaper commentary reviews Russia in 2016. Wang argues that, despite a sluggish economy and falling living standards, political stability and public morale let the country keep up what the author calls an 'inspiring posture of rise'. Wang presents Vladimir Putin as the key to that stability and to Russia's status as a great power. The article moves from foreign policy to domestic politics, then the economy, and ends with relations with China. It draws on Forbes's ranking of Putin, Russia's role in Syria, the Duma elections, Russian opinion polls, the 'anti-crisis plan' and Russia's 'turn to the East'. Wang describes Russia as gaining influence in the Middle East while the United States loses ground there, and as holding firm against the United States and NATO, whose Russia policy the author calls confused. At home, the Duma elections are said to have strengthened Putin's political system. United Russia now controls the Duma, and pro-Western and 'in-system' opposition forces have lost support. Wang reads this as rising anti-Western sentiment, nationalism and patriotism, backed by polls showing high approval for Putin. On the economy, the anti-crisis plan is credited with curbing falling output and rising inflation, with agricultural growth and grain exports as a base for stability. Wang notes that Russia formally adopted a 'turn to the East' policy in 2016 and describes Russia–China relations as entering a new stage, with the Belt and Road Initiative as a platform for cooperation. The author reports Russian opinion that the era of American global dominance is over and that a more democratic and just world order is emerging. The piece closes with open questions and concludes that Russia is consolidating its strategic foundations and building its 'strong-state dream'. Read the original if you want a brief example of how a Chinese official newspaper presented Russia's domestic and foreign situation at the end of 2016.

Running universities well requires adherence to Marxism as guidance 办好高校必须坚持以马克思主义为指导 Xi Jinping This is an excerpt from a speech by Xi Jinping at the National Conference on Ideological and Political Work in Universities, reported in the People's Daily on 9 December 2016. Xi argues that China must follow its own path in higher education and that universities, as institutions led by the Party, must be guided by Marxism. The excerpt moves from the strategic importance of higher education to the direction of Chinese universities, their core task of cultivating talent, and the content of ideological and political work. It ends with four points on how students should be guided to understand the world, their era's responsibilities and their own aspirations. Xi states that China's distinctive history, culture and national conditions require it to run universities with Chinese characteristics that serve the people, the Party's governance, the socialist system and reform and opening up. He holds that the fundamental task of universities is to foster virtue and cultivate talent, and that a world-class university is one that produces first-class people. Running universities well means spreading Marxist theory, cultivating socialist core values, keeping campuses stable and building a good academic and school ethos. Ideological work, in his words, is fundamentally work with people and must centre on serving students. Xi calls for students to be taught the historical inevitability of socialism with Chinese characteristics, to hold firm to communist ideals, and to link personal ambitions to the Chinese Dream and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. He presents this as the way to open a new phase for higher education. Read the original if you want a short, authoritative statement of the Party leadership's 2016 expectations for university ideological work.

Building a new Great Wall against "spiritual colonization" 筑起反“精神殖民”的新长城 Zheng Ruolin Writing in 2016, Zheng Ruolin, a media professional who lived in France for over twenty years, asks whether China has escaped the "colonial and semi-colonial" condition in the spiritual sphere. The author acknowledges that China is now independent in military, political, economic and financial terms. Zheng argues, however, that Western "spiritual conquest" continues and that China is at the edge of being "spiritually colonized". The piece opens with a short history of foreign domination since the Opium War and with everyday examples: foreign-sounding shop and housing names, admiration for emigration and marriage to foreigners, and hair dyeing. It then explains how this state arose, setting out its three features and the three "instruments" used to bring it about. It closes with a call to action. Zheng draws on personal anecdotes, such as a 1985 trip to France and a publisher who refused a contract because of the author's Chinese nationality, and recommends two books by Bian Qin. Zheng says spiritual colonization has three features: treating the conqueror as spiritual master (for example, judging Chinese films and writers by the Oscars, Cannes or foreign literary prizes); willingly accepting the conqueror's power (for example, preferential treatment of foreigners, and weak Chinese influence on trade rules); and changing oneself to suit the conqueror's wishes (aesthetics, doubts about traditional Chinese medicine, "integration with international standards", wholesale Westernization). In Zheng's account the cause lies partly in China's own errors, as intellectuals after the 1980s took Western theory at face value, and partly in the nature of a Western civilization the author describes as monotheistic and therefore a "conquering civilization". Zheng names three tools: news reporting that fabricates reality, advertising that builds an idealised West, and cinema that redefines history. Zheng claims that over 90 per cent of French coverage of China is negative, against about 70 per cent positive coverage of France itself. The author also argues that Cannes selection since the late 1970s rewards films that portray China negatively. Zheng concludes that China must build a new Great Wall in the mind, and that the first requirement is awakening to the reality of the threat. The author expresses optimism, pointing to China's five-thousand-year civilization and to a younger generation described as more open and more self-confident. Read the original if you want an example of Chinese cultural-nationalist writing on Western media, advertising and film, or if you study how this "spiritual colonization" argument was put to Party-oriented readers in 2016.

Winning young people's hearts with the truth of Marxism A profile of Professor Zhu Ling of Southwest Jiaotong University 《中国社会科学报》：用马克思主义真理赢得青年的心 This is a newspaper profile, published in China Social Sciences Today in December 2016, of Zhu Ling, an 87-year-old specialist in the history of the Chinese revolution at Southwest Jiaotong University. It presents him as a model teacher of ideological and political theory courses. The piece opens with his visit to the Emei campus to explain the Long March spirit, where students and staff applauded him on entry. The profile follows Zhu's career from his birth in 1929 and his studies in journalism at Yenching University, where he joined the Communist Party. It then covers his work at Xinhua News Agency and his posting to teach at the Tangshan Railway Institute, the predecessor of Southwest Jiaotong. Its sections cover his reform of the revolutionary history course, his lecturing style, and his mentoring of younger teachers. The article reports that in the 1980s some students found theory courses abstract and dull. Zhu, in this account, neither criticised them nor enforced attendance. He consulted students and made the course useful by linking theory to practice, and it became one of the most popular on campus. His 'five-character method' (concise, practical, new, rational, emotional) is described, along with lecturing without notes and appealing to patriotism. Zhu is quoted as saying that such courses should open 'the window of the heart', not serve as a screwdriver for a toolbox. The piece shows Zhu continuing after retirement to train young ideological and political education teachers, to supervise courses in Sichuan, and to give Party talks, including on the 18th Party Congress (2012) report. It offers him as an example of teaching that wins students through sincerity, expertise and care. Read the original if you want a short, official-media portrait of how an exemplary teacher of Party theory is presented to the public in China.

The turning point of the world order and the chronic ills of twenty-first-century America 世界秩序的转折点与21世纪美国的沉疴 Yang Guangbin Lin Xuefei Writing in early 2017, Yang Guangbin and Lin Xuefei ask what Donald Trump's election and the British Brexit vote of 2016 signify. They reject the common view that economic globalization has reversed, arguing that globalization has lasted some 500 years and what has failed is the neoliberal form it took over the past three decades. Trump's response, in their view, is to treat a twenty-first-century illness with a nineteenth-century prescription: nationalist protectionism, isolationism and white supremacy. His programme is therefore, they say, more deconstructive than constructive and offers no 'third way'. The article has four sections. The first sets out the content of 'Trumpism': opposition to the establishment, to 'political correctness' and cultural pluralism, and the 'America First' slogan. The second examines neoliberalism's 'three liberalizations' (economic, political and cultural) and their damage to the United States. The third looks back at American history from the founding to the Second World War, drawing on Friedrich List. The fourth considers the unintended results of liberalization and the prospects for a clash between 'two Americas'. The authors divide the past century of Western thought into three roughly thirty-year phases: laissez-faire liberalism, Keynesianism and neoliberalism. They argue that financial-capital-led globalization hollowed out American manufacturing, widened inequality and turned 'liberal democracy' into 'capitalist democracy'. They contend that Trump's election expresses a conflict between traditional industrial workers and finance capital. Political liberalization, in their account, drained national strength through 'democracy promotion' and colour revolutions. Cultural pluralism, they say, challenged the 'American Creed' and produced a crisis of national identity. They link Trump's agenda to nineteenth-century protectionism, isolationism and white supremacy, including the treatment of Native Americans. Yang and Lin conclude that liberalization produced results the United States did not intend. Economic and political damage can be repaired, they say, but the cultural 'de-Americanization' is potentially fatal. Because Trump's agenda fits no scheme of the past hundred years, they argue it must be understood against the America of a century earlier. They expect a clash between a nineteenth-century and a twenty-first-century America that may deepen social division, though they leave open how far Trump will go. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic interpretation of Trump's rise through neoliberalism, historical institutionalism and American history.

Serious ideological deviations of the CPSU under Gorbachev and their profound lessons 戈尔巴乔夫时期苏共意识形态的严重偏差及深刻教训 Tang Desen Zhao Jun Why did the Communist Party of the Soviet Union (CPSU) lose control of ideology under Gorbachev, and what follows from that for ruling socialist parties? Tang and Zhao argue that Gorbachev's "humane and democratic socialism", together with "democratization", "openness" (glasnost) and "pluralism", turned reform into a change of direction. In their account, the Party abandoned Marxism's guiding position in the ideological sphere, and this was an important cause of the Party's collapse and the Soviet Union's disintegration. The article, published in Marxist Studies in 2016, has two parts. The first describes ideological deviation in three areas: the guiding ideology, public opinion and the media, and social culture including foreign relations. The second draws four lessons for socialist countries today. The authors rely on Soviet-era speeches, memoirs by Gorbachev, Ryzhkov and Ligachev, and Chinese and Western secondary studies. On guiding ideology, the authors argue that abstract humanism, a misplaced theory of "alienation" and political pluralism replaced Marxism. They say this led to the removal of Article 6 of the constitution, multiparty politics, cadre purges and mass resignations from the Party, which the article puts at 4.2 million. On public opinion, they claim that a double standard on press freedom, the Nina Andreyeva affair, the rewriting of Soviet history and the 1990 press law produced historical nihilism and a media hostile to the Party. On culture and external relations, they contend that "returned literature", declassified archives and the destruction of history textbooks caused a crisis of national identity. They also argue that Gorbachev's priority of "universal human values" left the USSR defenceless against Western "peaceful evolution". The authors draw four lessons. The ruling party must keep its leadership and the direction of reform, and must build socialist democracy step by step while curbing bureaucracy and privilege. Marxism must keep its guiding position, and the Party must firmly hold leadership of ideological work. Ideological work must innovate, including in how it manages the internet and new media. Socialist countries must also stay alert to Western ideological infiltration while drawing on other civilizations' achievements. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese Party scholars in 2016 interpreted the Soviet collapse as an ideological failure and used it to argue for ideological vigilance.

How "money-donor politics" took shape in the United States “金主政治”是如何形成的 Ni Chunna Ni Chunna takes up a question that, the author says, critics of American "money politics" rarely ask: how did the United States fall from its image as a "beacon of democracy" to become a model of "money-donor politics" (jinzhu zhengzhi)? Writing in 2016, after the "Democracy Spring" protests of April that year, Ni argues that campaign finance reform since the 1970s directly drove the change. In a struggle of more than forty years between Congress and the Supreme Court, the Court gradually overturned the limits Congress wrote into law. The article follows this struggle chronologically. It starts with the Federal Election Campaign Act of 1971 and its 1974 amendments, passed after Watergate, and the Court's ruling in Buckley v. Valeo (1976). It then covers the rise of "soft money" and the Bipartisan Campaign Reform Act of 2002, and the later rulings in Citizens United (2010) and McCutcheon (2014). A final section asks why reform failed, looking at the Supreme Court, the Senate and the House of Representatives. Ni's central claim is that each reform produced a workaround, and each workaround was then validated or widened by the Court. Buckley allowed unlimited independent spending. Soft money, then "527 organisations" and super PACs, followed, and McCutcheon removed the aggregate limit on individual donations. Ni cites figures such as total presidential-election contributions rising from US$114 million in 1976 to US$1.38 billion in 2012, and argues that reform has in effect regressed to the situation before 1970. On the causes of failure, Ni points to three structural factors. First, justices serve for life and are appointed on a cycle unlike the electoral one, and Republican presidents have made far more appointments since the 1970s. Second, political polarisation and the filibuster make it hard for the Senate to reach the 60 votes needed. Third, a polarised, Republican-led House cannot compromise. Ni concludes that life tenure for justices and congressional polarisation are the key reasons reform failed. Because these problems lie in the constitutional system, the author holds that only major political reform could resolve them, and that the United States will therefore sink deeper into money-donor politics. The article also notes defenders of the Court's rulings, such as Glenn Hubbard, but treats them as a minority view. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-heavy account of US campaign finance litigation and legislation from a Chinese critical perspective.

How should we view the new changes in the Western capitalist world? 如何看待西方资本主义世界的新变化？ Ding Yuanhong Writing in early 2017, after the British referendum vote to leave the EU and Donald Trump's election as the 45th US president, Ding Yuanhong asks how these changes in the Western capitalist world should be understood. The short commentary argues that only class analysis can reveal their essence and likely course. It also warns against several labels commonly attached to these events. The piece is organised in three parts. The first treats the referendum and the US election as signs of deep class antagonism between ordinary people and elites. The second examines the claim that a "reverse economic globalisation" is under way. The third considers whether "populism", "isolationism" and "protectionism" accurately describe Trump. Ding draws on US and British figures, including Richard Haass, Alan Greenspan, Barack Obama, Theresa May and Henry Kissinger. Ding reads the divide as the product of the capitalist system under monopoly capitalism and as a sharpening of internal class struggle. As evidence the author cites a Pew survey (the US middle class falling from 62% of the population in the 1970s to 43%), household debt rising from $9,300 in 1980 to $65,000 in 2015, and the claim that half of American families cannot find $400 in cash. On globalisation, Ding holds that the post-Cold War version was unequal from the start and favoured the rich, multinationals, developed countries and above all the United States. Its problems, in this account, are self-generated, so it is wrong to call recent events "anti-globalisation". On populism, Ding notes the term's origin in nineteenth-century Russian narodnik currents criticised by Plekhanov and Lenin. The author says Western scholars now use it loosely for any opposition to elites. Trump, as a member of the monopoly bourgeoisie who rolled back Obama-era financial regulation to Wall Street's welcome, is not a true populist. Nor, Ding argues, has he abandoned US global hegemony, and protectionism is something Western states have always practised. Ding concludes that Trump's "America First" rests on an "extreme national egoism", that he cannot resolve a division rooted in the system, and that his promises are limited by that system. The events are said to show a major crisis in Western capitalist society, which Chinese scholars should track closely from a Marxist standpoint. Read the original if you want a short example of how a senior Chinese diplomat applied class analysis to Brexit and Trump's election in 2017.

The current state of "new socialism" in Russia and an analysis of its causes 当前俄罗斯“新社会主义”的现状及其成因分析 Chen Airu Writing in 2016, Chen Airu asks why ideas of "new socialism" and "socialism of the twenty-first century" are slowly returning in Russia, and what this return signals. The article argues that the revival has three layers of cause. The basic cause is the failure of neoliberal capitalist "reform" after 25 years. The main cause is the persistence of the Communist Party and other left-wing parties. The direct causes are Western "double standards" and pressure on Russia, and a "turn to the left" among intellectuals. The article first sets out the record of post-Soviet capitalism: dependence on energy exports, polarisation of wealth, corruption and public dissatisfaction. It then surveys the programmes and writings of the Communist Party of the Russian Federation (CPRF), A Just Russia and a number of smaller communist and workers' parties. Finally it turns to intellectual life: the All-Russian association of scholars of socialist orientation, the "Socialism after Socialism" seminar, the "New Socialism" website, journals and monographs by authors such as Sulimov, Buzgalin and Slavin. Chen cites sociological data and opinion polls from the Levada Center, among other sources. Chen's reasoning begins with the data. According to the article, 110 oligarchs controlled 35% of national wealth in 2014, and polls show that a plurality of Russians judge the 1990s reforms harmful. Chen then reports the CPRF leader Gennady Zyuganov's 2014 characterisation of Russian capitalism as reactionary, parasitic, oligarchic and comprador. In Chen's reading, left parties kept the socialist idea alive by pursuing justice in the line of Marx, Lenin and Stalin; without them the revival would not have appeared. Chen adds that the West's treatment of Russia, seen in the Ukraine crisis, pushed intellectuals to rethink capitalism, even though the 2016 Duma election still favoured United Russia because voters put territorial integrity first. Chen concludes that the Russian trend ties the search for Russia's own path to the future direction of human society. The author holds that the left parties' and scholars' new interpretations of socialism deserve study as "stones from other hills" and could benefit the development of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The text is a sympathetic reading of Russian left-wing sources rather than an independent survey of Russian opinion. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist account of the Russian left and intellectual debate on socialism after 1991, with its sources and cited Russian authors.

Fidel Castro's thought on intra-Party supervision in the Communist Party of Cuba and its lessons 古巴共产党党内监督思想及其启示 Tang Zhiyuan This short commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in February 2017, asks what Fidel Castro's approach to supervision inside the Communist Party of Cuba consists of and what it offers the Communist Party of China. Tang argues that Castro, drawing on Marxism-Leninism and Cuban practice, developed a distinctive body of thought on intra-Party supervision, and that it carries lessons for full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. The article sets out Castro's thought under three headings: ideological supervision, organisational supervision and institutional supervision. A final section draws three lessons for the Chinese Party. On ideology, Tang reports that Castro treated ideas as the most powerful weapon against US ideological infiltration and domestic reactionary forces. He armed the Party with Marxism-Leninism and the thought of José Martí, screened new members for political consciousness, and set up Party schools for regular education. On organisation, Tang describes collective leadership with individual responsibility, internal democracy, differentiated scrutiny of leading cadres (stricter for higher rank), criticism and self-criticism, and grassroots branches as the front line of supervision. On institutions, Tang cites five Party statutes, regulations on grassroots organisations, admission and punishment, supervisory and appeals bodies, and a code of ethics for state cadres. Tang concludes that the Chinese Party should make ideological supervision more thorough, raising the threshold for new members and enriching Party school training. It should also make organisational supervision more targeted, focusing on the "critical few" and improving criticism and self-criticism, and make institutional supervision more systematic by closing gaps in Party regulations built on the Party constitution. Read the original if you want a brief, officially aligned account of how Cuban Party supervision is presented to Chinese readers and how it is tied to Chinese Party-building debates in 2017.

The positioning of the South African Communist Party's political strategy 南非共产党政治战略的定位 Zheng Haixiang This short commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today on 23 February 2017, asks how the South African Communist Party (SACP) positions itself politically after the 2008 financial crisis. Zheng distinguishes strategy from tactics. In Zheng's account, the SACP's strategy rests on the South African working class as its core support, while its tactics rely on taking part in government through the "tripartite governing alliance" with the African National Congress (ANC) and the Congress of South African Trade Unions (COSATU). The article has three parts. It first looks at the revisions to the Party constitution adopted at the 13th National Congress in July 2012. It then discusses how the SACP has consolidated the alliance since 1994 while keeping its independence. Finally, it sets out the Party's core policy agenda since the crisis, which Zheng groups under three heads: countering the crisis, sustainable development and environmental justice, and the fight against corruption. Zheng reports that the new constitution stresses uniting the different strata of a working class that the SACP sees as increasingly divided, from skilled full-time workers to casual, informal and structurally unemployed ones. It also reaffirms democratic centralism and adds clauses on the Young Communist League and on neighbourhood ("branch") organisation. Within the alliance the ANC leads and the SACP acts as bearer of advanced ideas. Zheng says the SACP still voices criticism when decisions are mistaken, and cites its 2008 policy conference aim of becoming a party with decision-making power. On policy, Zheng reports that the SACP's five-year programme (2012–2017) targets monopoly finance and mining capital, calls for a state-led industrial policy and wants more social control of financial institutions. It also calls for renewable energy, land reform and public transport. It treats corruption as a threat to democracy, and Zheng cites a fall in South Africa's Transparency International ranking from 38th in 2001 to 72nd in 2013. Zheng concludes that the 2008 crisis confirmed the SACP's view that capitalism is in a deep, systemic crisis, and this gave the Party an opening. Zheng cautions, however, that monopoly capital still controls key sectors and that the constitutional order and multiparty competition remain unchanged. In this reading the SACP must therefore work through the alliance, and the road to socialism will be long. Zheng judges that the Party has still raised its standing and influence. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese academic overview of the SACP's strategy, alliance politics and post-2008 policy priorities.

The 21st century is the century of the revival of world socialism 21世纪是世界社会主义复兴的世纪 Lü Weizhou Writing in March 2017, Lü Weizhou takes up the state of world socialism a quarter-century after the collapse of the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe. The author argues that, after a low point at the end of the twentieth century and nearly thirty years of recovery and adjustment, socialism is gradually reviving worldwide. Lü presents "the 21st century is the century of the revival of world socialism" as a growing consensus. The short commentary opens with a sketch of socialism's history since 1516, then surveys five signs of revival: reforms in the remaining socialist states, the recovery of communist parties in capitalist countries, a variety of socialist currents, expanding contacts among socialist forces, and the role of socialism with Chinese characteristics. It closes with the obstacles ahead. Lü treats the success of socialism with Chinese characteristics as the marker of a new upswing and the starting point of full revival, because it has shifted a badly unbalanced balance of forces between socialism and capitalism. Vietnam, Cuba and Laos held Party congresses in 2016, and the author cites their institutional strengths in crisis response and resource allocation. In capitalist countries, Lü reports over 120 communist parties with more than 8 million members, and electoral results in Greece, Cyprus and Japan. The author also lists market socialism, democratic socialism, eco-socialism and Latin American "21st-century socialism", and the European Left and international forums. Lü cautions that the path is not smooth: capital still holds the offensive, class consciousness is uneven, ideological disunity persists, and populism is eroding the left's base. The author calls on left forces, communist parties included, to build strength, improve organization and innovate in their activities. Read the original if you want a brief, official-academic Chinese overview of how world socialism was assessed in 2017.

The historical role of Mikhail Gorbachev 米·戈尔巴乔夫的历史角色 Vladimir Shveda This text is a Chinese translation of an article by the Russian author Vladimir Shveda (弗·施韦德). It asks how Mikhail Gorbachev's conduct as General Secretary and Soviet president should be judged. Shveda argues that his refusal to carry out the constitutional duties of the presidency, and his political deals with Western powers to "hand over" the USSR, were not stupidity but crime, and that he should face legal sanction. The piece opens with the February 2016 call by the Russian filmmaker Nikita Mikhalkov for the state to declare Gorbachev and Yeltsin criminals. The article proceeds through five thematic sections: the Rust landing and the dissolution of the Warsaw Pact; Gorbachev's one-to-one talks with Western leaders; his violations of the Soviet constitution; his handling of ethnic conflicts in Sumgait, Tbilisi, Baku and Vilnius; and the Belovezha meeting of December 1991. Shveda draws on testimony from generals, KGB officials and Party figures, on Gorbachev's own interviews with Western press, and on the author's personal experience in Lithuania. Gorbachev's 0.51% vote in the 1996 presidential election is cited as popular verdict. Shveda's central move is to treat each episode as a breach of specific constitutional articles obliging the president to guarantee sovereignty, territorial integrity, Soviet law and citizens' rights. On this reading, Gorbachev engineered the dismissal of military opponents after the Rust flight, accepted a small payment of 14 billion marks for the withdrawal from East Germany, and let Russia's 1990 sovereignty declaration pass unchallenged. He also failed to protect Soviet citizens in Lithuania and allegedly stalled a 1991 prosecutor's criminal case against him. A second move is the claim of secrecy: Gorbachev held private English-language talks at Reykjavik and Malta without records, and Shveda cites Kryuchkov and Gorbachev's own 1993 remarks as evidence of concessions made there. Shveda concludes that Gorbachev built a system of personal power and then, by declining to order action against the Belovezha plotters despite the 1991 referendum result, let the state vanish, which in the author's words removed any need to answer for his deeds. The author dismisses Gorbachev as a permanent political failure who should await trial rather than comment on politics. Read the original if you want a stridently critical Russian account of Gorbachev, with its cited testimony and constitutional argument, as an example of how the Soviet collapse is interpreted in World Socialism Studies.

The current international financial crisis as a systemic and total crisis of the contemporary imperialist economic system 当今国际金融危机是当代帝国主义经济体系性、总体性危机 Luan Wenlian Writing in 2017, Luan Wenlian asks what the financial crisis that began in 2008 reveals about contemporary capitalism. The article argues that it is not merely a US crisis or a financial one, but a systemic and total crisis of contemporary imperialism. In Luan's account, capitalism has since the 1970s and 1980s entered a new stage dominated by fictitious financial capital and financial monopoly. The article first sets out how the basic economic law of capitalism has changed form: from surplus-value production under free competition, to the law of monopoly profit, to extra monopoly profit and financial plunder under financialisation. It then covers the essential features of financial monopoly, new methods of exploitation and plunder, the global exploitation model built on financial hegemony, and the deepening of the gap between rich and poor. Luan contends that financialisation leaves the capital–labour relation intact while shifting profit-making from production to circulation and speculation. Financial capital, the article says, now draws profit from workers' wages through housing credit, insurance, pension and health schemes, so that exploitation extends to consumption and to future generations. Internationally, developed countries relocate low-end manufacturing and keep core technology, intellectual property and the dollar's hegemony. After the dollar's break with gold in 1971, Luan holds, it was issued against fictitious capital and needs extra-economic power to sustain it. At home, income distribution tilts towards financial capital and a rentier stratum of shareholders and senior managers; Luan cites figures that put the fictitious part of Western economies at over 70 per cent and say multinationals control 40 per cent of world production. Luan concludes that financialised capitalism is an unstable, increasingly polarised system in which financial, economic and currency crises will keep recurring. The article describes it as hostile to historical development and as sharpening imperialism's decay, parasitism and moribundity, and as having entered a period of decline since 2008. Read the original if you want an example of how Chinese Marxist political economy interprets financialisation and the 2008 crisis through the theory of monopoly capital and imperialism.

The current American debate on "socialism" and reflections on it 当前美国的“社会主义”论争及其思考 Yu Haiqing Yu Haiqing asks what the revival of the word "socialism" in the United States since late 2015 amounts to. The occasion was Bernie Sanders's advocacy of "democratic socialism" and a "political revolution" in the Democratic primary. Yu argues that the opposing camps in the ensuing debate, mainstream opinion and the Communist Party USA (CPUSA), reflect in the end the developmental predicament of capitalism as it appears in real politics. The article has three parts. The first sets out four mainstream readings of socialism. The second, the longest, reports a debate launched in January 2016 on the CPUSA's website People's World, opened by an article by Susan Webb. The third offers Yu's own reflections. Contributors discussed include John Bachtell, Rick Nagin, Pat Fry, Carl Davidson, Joel Wendland, Bill Fletcher and Emile Schepers. In Yu's account, mainstream commentators equate socialism with nationalisation, the welfare state (a view held, by a poll the article cites, by 41 per cent of Americans), central planning, or the Soviet record. The CPUSA writers reject these equations. They define socialism as working-class power in a transitional class society with a mixed economy, and they add ecological, anti-racist, anti-sexist and human-rights dimensions. They also stress open-ended, varied paths and a long process of struggle. Wendland proposes "open-source socialism". Yu's own reflections run as follows. Sanders's programme and similar movements, such as the Trump phenomenon, Corbyn and Syriza, are reactions to an "organic crisis" of capitalism after 2008. Yu notes that these "socialisms" differ greatly from Marxist socialism, since they omit class relations and the replacement of the system, and Sanders never proposed abolishing private property. Communists' task is therefore to clarify socialism's meaning and to steer anti-capitalist movements onto a socialist track. Yu notes that the CPUSA's later support for Clinton and opposition to Trump drew doubts, and cites Nancy Fraser's call for a new left alliance. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist survey of how the CPUSA framed socialism during the 2016 US election cycle.

Fidel Castro's outstanding contributions to Cuba and to the development of world socialism 卡斯特罗对古巴和世界社会主义发展的卓越贡献 Mao Xianglin Written after Fidel Castro's death on 25 November 2016, this article assesses his historical record. Mao Xianglin argues that Castro's contribution falls into three parts: his achievements for the Cuban people, the regional significance of the Cuban Revolution for Latin America, and his theoretical contribution to the development of world socialism. The article is organised in three sections. The first lists four achievements within Cuba and illustrates Castro's personal conduct with episodes from his life. The second sets out four reasons why the revolution mattered internationally. The third surveys eleven strands of Castro's thought, from national independence to resistance to "peaceful evolution". In Mao's account, the revolution carried out the most thorough social transformation in Cuban history: national independence, the end of class exploitation, a reorganised Communist Party (named as such in 1965) and a socialist system declared in 1961. Mao presents the survival of that system through the 1960s excesses, the mid-1980s "rectification" campaign and the crisis after Soviet aid ended as evidence of its vitality. Castro is portrayed as a model revolutionary who trusted the masses, opposed a personality cult, practised self-criticism, was strict with relatives and friends, and handed over office to Raúl Castro. Regionally, Mao calls the revolution the most thorough anti-dictatorship and anti-imperialist revolution in Latin America and the first to move from national-democratic struggle to socialism. Cuba's survival is also said to refute the claim that socialism suits only Eastern cultures. Mao holds that Castro upheld scientific socialism while adapting it to Cuban conditions, citing four Party-wide theoretical debates. Among his ideas Mao lists: globalisation as a historical law while neoliberal globalisation is rejected, the shaping of a "new man", Party and army building, free universal education and healthcare, and successful resistance to US efforts at "peaceful evolution". Mao concludes that Cuba, one of five existing socialist states, offers experience in localising socialism that is useful to others, and that this owes much to Castro. His achievements, the article says, "will be recorded in history for ever". Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly and officially sympathetic assessment of Castro and of Cuban socialism, including its checklist of his ideas on the Party, education, health and anti-imperialism.

The Brexit referendum marks the beginning of the exhaustion of Western political and economic institutions 英国脱欧公投标志着西方政治经济体制开始衰竭 Ma Zhongcheng Writing in 2017 about the 2016 British referendum on leaving the European Union, Ma Zhongcheng argues that it was essentially a depoliticised vote manipulated by capital, in which the mass media shaped public opinion while the political parties stayed ambiguous. Ma presents Brexit as a serious crisis of the global neoliberal order formed since the 1980s, a direct product of the global financial and economic crisis since 2007, and a desperate struggle of Thatcherism. In Ma's view it shows the comprehensive exhaustion of Western capitalist political institutions. The article has four sections. The first examines how parties have become media-driven and how voting has become alienated. The second treats the referendum as a product of monopoly capital's shifting of social contradictions. The third traces the conflict between sterling and the dollar on one side and the euro on the other, using the EU financial transaction tax. The fourth considers the end of Gaullism and the geopolitical setting, drawing on Churchill, de Gaulle, Sarkozy, George Soros and Goldman Sachs. Ma argues first that voting has been reduced to product marketing, citing the 1960 Kennedy–Nixon debates and Baran and Sweezy on advertising. Issues that matter to ordinary people, such as workers' rights and corporate taxation, were screened out, and many Leave voters reportedly regretted their choice. Second, Ma contends that after 2007 mainstream parties responded with further neoliberal austerity, and that the Conservatives and UKIP blamed the EU and immigrants to disguise class conflict. Third, Ma claims that British and American finance capital opposed EU regulation and the financial transaction tax, and that the EU, lacking unified political will, may be divided and defeated. Ma concludes that a wave of exits would leave the EU an empty shell and produce the Atlantic community dependent on the United States that de Gaulle feared, which Ma sees as a setback for multipolarity and harmful to European workers and bourgeoisies alike. Ma holds that Europe's difficulties stem from adopting the Anglo-American model since the 1980s, after three decades of a mixed economy with state control of capital. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist reading of Brexit that links media, finance capital and transatlantic geopolitics.

The world system of financial imperialism will ultimately collapse 金融帝国主义世界体系终将走向崩溃 Zhang Quanjing Does the world system that finance capital has built since the 1980s and 1990s have a future? Zhang Quanjing answers that this "world system of financial imperialism" has not yet collapsed, but that its eventual collapse is an irreversible trend. The article rests this claim on what it calls the basic laws of social and historical development. The article is a short theoretical essay in three parts. The first treats finance capital's control of the world system as the core of the age of financial imperialism. The second argues that parasitism and decay are the system's fundamental attributes. The third examines how the 2008 financial crisis and rising international economic conflict have sped up its decline. Zhang draws on Lenin's writing on imperialism, Engels on American politics, Madison, Thomas Piketty, the Japanese scholar Iwao Nakatani and figures on US election spending. Zhang's central move is to treat financial imperialism as the current form of monopoly capitalism, in which the basic contradiction between socialised production and private ownership of the means of production remains unchanged. Following Lenin, the author holds that monopoly gives rise to finance capital through the fusion of banks and industry, and that the postwar Bretton Woods order under US leadership consolidated a system centred on finance capital. The author describes parasitism as control of the global economy by multinationals and developed countries, together with widening inequality, and describes decay as the manipulation of democracy by interest groups, citing 2012 US election spending of over 6 billion dollars. The 2008 crisis is attributed to the internationalisation of finance capital, US monetary policy and debt-fuelled consumption, and intensifying conflict among developed economies and between them and emerging economies such as China, India and Brazil. Zhang cites the rise in trade-remedy cases against China as evidence of that last conflict. Zhang concludes that Marxist dialectics requires looking past the appearance of financial imperialism to its essence. The author calls on readers to remember that imperialism's reactionary nature never changes, especially when it appears in a friendly guise, and that it is bound to perish. The author also urges learning to struggle against it and affirms confidence in the victory of socialism and communism. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a Chinese Marxist author applies Lenin's theory of imperialism to the post-2008 world economy.

The death of neoliberalism and the political crisis of the West 新自由主义的死亡与西方政治危机 Martin Jacques This is a Chinese translation of a commentary by the British writer Martin Jacques, first published in The Guardian in August 2016. Jacques argues that the 2007–2008 financial crisis began a deeper political crisis in the West, and that neoliberalism, though still dominant in politics and ideas, is dying. In his account, Brexit and the rise of Donald Trump are symptoms of this crisis. The Chinese journal's editors added a note written after Trump's election victory in November 2016. The article moves from the crisis and the bailout of the banks to the origins of neoliberalism under Reagan and Thatcher in the late 1970s. It then covers rising inequality in the United States and Britain, the Brexit referendum, and the shifting attitudes of economists and political parties. The last third deals with Trump's programme of economic nationalism and foreign policy, and what it might mean for the United States. Jacques makes three main moves. First, he holds that neoliberalism tilted resources towards capital and away from labour through deregulation, secretly negotiated trade deals such as the TPP and TTIP, and pressure on trade unions. He cites figures on stagnant or falling real incomes since the 1970s and notes that growth was twice as fast in the Keynesian era. Second, he reads the 'populist' revolts, including Brexit, Trump and Bernie Sanders, as the return of class to politics. He cautions that this is not the same as a labour movement and that working-class politics is unpredictable. Third, he treats Trump as a right-wing populist who breaks with both neoliberal globalization and the postwar foreign-policy consensus. Jacques also warns that a Trump presidency could bring authoritarian abuses, deep social division and a new era of protectionism. Jacques concludes that the neoliberal era is ending, as social democracy did in the 1970s, even though it has not yet died. He notes that prominent economists such as Stiglitz, Krugman and Piketty, and even former believers such as Lawrence Summers, now criticise it. In his view, British media and political elites, including Labour and the Conservatives, lag behind. He expects resistance to 'hyper-globalization' to continue whether or not Trump wins. Read the original if you want a Western left-leaning interpretation of Brexit and Trump as products of neoliberal inequality, as a Chinese journal presented it in 2017.

The South African Communist Party after the collapse of Soviet socialist power 苏联社会主义政权解体背景下的南非共产党 Gregory F. Houston This is a Chinese translation of an article by the South African scholar Gregory F. Houston (rendered in Chinese as 格里高利·F·休斯顿). It asks why socialism in South Africa has lasted more than a century and why the South African Communist Party (SACP) has survived the end of Soviet socialist power. Houston argues that the party's endurance rests on its historical alliance with the governing African National Congress (ANC), its record in the liberation struggle and wide popular support for socialism. He presents the SACP as one of the few communist parties worldwide that is allied with, or part of, a governing party. The article is organised chronologically in five sections. It traces the origins of socialism among white immigrant miners after the 1886 Witwatersrand gold discovery and the founding of the Communist Party of South Africa in 1921. It then covers the party's relations with the ANC, with the Soviet Union and with the People's Republic of China, the effects of the Soviet and East European collapse, and the SACP's history since 1994. It ends with the party's present international orientation. Houston's central line is that the SACP-ANC bond has deep roots. He cites the 1928 Comintern resolution on a 'native republic', which called for an alliance between the Communist Party and the national liberation movement. He also cites the ban on the party under the 1950 Suppression of Communism Act, which pushed the two organisations together again after about twenty years of discord, and the party's role in the armed struggle through Umkhonto we Sizwe. After 1990, he reports, about half of the SACP's Central Committee resigned and communists suffered a crisis of confidence in socialism's future. Even so, membership rose to 220,000 by 2015. Tensions with the ANC over the neoliberal GEAR framework in the Mandela era led many to see the party's role in the tripartite alliance as shrinking, though its leaders still sat in the ANC executive and in Zuma's cabinet. Houston concludes that the SACP remains one of the few communist parties still gaining members, and that its ANC link gives it a way to influence government policy. He reports that the party sees its task as promoting international working-class solidarity and unity between workers and the urban and rural poor. It has built links through the African Left Network Forum and the São Paulo Forum, and has a bilateral agreement with the Communist Party of China providing for annual high-level delegation exchanges. Read the original if you want a historical overview of the SACP, its ties with the ANC, Moscow and Beijing, and its international outreach, as presented by a South African author in a Chinese journal.

What are supervisory commissions being set up for? 设立监察委员会为的是啥？ Dai Lixing Writing in late 2016, Dai Lixing asks what the new supervisory commissions are meant to achieve. The article responds to the Central Committee General Office's scheme, issued on 8 November, to pilot reform of the national supervisory system in Beijing, Shanxi and Zhejiang. Dai argues that the commissions, to be created by people's congresses, amount to a "major political reform affecting the overall situation", and that their purpose is to build an anti-corruption body under the Party's unified leadership. The commentary is organised around three descriptions of the commission: it is "high in position", "heavy in power" and "forceful". Dai first traces the reform's origins to Xi Jinping's speech at the Sixth Plenary Session of the 18th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection (early 2016) and to the communiqué of the Sixth Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (October 2016), which listed supervisory organs alongside people's congresses and governments. A closing section stresses Party leadership. Dai's first claim is that administrative supervision will be upgraded to national supervision. Supervisory bodies are now attached to governments and departments and so practise "same-body supervision". Once the commissions are elected by people's congresses and answer to them, Dai argues, they gain independence and authority, and the Party's anti-corruption will is turned into state will. The second claim is that coverage will become comprehensive: current supervision misses people's congress, CPPCC, court and procuratorate staff, village heads and some enterprise and public-institution personnel. Third, Dai says dispersed anti-corruption forces (discipline inspection, administrative supervision, prosecutorial anti-graft units, audit) will be merged. The commissions will gain broader investigative means and share personnel with Party discipline commissions, described as "one set of staff, two nameplates". Dai presents this as different from Western multiparty competition and separation of powers. Dai concludes that the national supervisory system must embody the Party's absolute leadership and ensure that supervision proceeds within the discipline inspection commissions' framework. The scheme places pilot work under a central leading group and under Party committee secretaries in the pilot areas. Dai suggests the reform will help make officials unwilling, unable and unafraid-to-be-corrupt in a closed loop with congress and judicial oversight. Read the original if you want an early, Party-aligned reading of the 2016 supervision reform pilots and the reasoning offered for them.

Hot topics in the field of ideology and theory in 2016 2016年思想理论领域的热点问题 Zhu Nianfeng Wang Xueling This is an annual survey, published in Red Flag Manuscripts (Hongqi Wengao) in early 2017, of the main topics debated in China's ideological and theoretical circles during 2016. Zhu and Wang report that the field "continued to improve" under the guidance of Xi Jinping's speeches on propaganda, ideology and culture. They identify nine "hot topics" on which scholars both studied official policy and argued against positions they regard as erroneous. The nine topics are: studying the Sixth Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2016); the 95th anniversary of the Party's founding; supply-side structural reform; state-owned enterprise reform; the 80th anniversary of the Long March; ideological and political work in universities; historical nihilism; the crisis of Western democracy; and cyber security and building a strong cyberpower. Each section summarises what "scholars" affirm, then the "erroneous" views they rebut. Across the sections, the authors present a recurring pattern. Scholars are said to treat the Plenum's naming of Xi as the "core" of the Party Central Committee as its most historic result, and to reject readings that they say loosen the Four Cardinal Principles. On supply-side reform, they are said to deny that it derives from Say's law or Western supply-side economics, and to insist on supply and demand as two sides of one coin. On state firms, they are said to refute claims of inefficiency, monopoly and "zombie" status, and to call for embedding Party organisations in corporate governance. On history, they are said to defend Mao Zedong and the Long March against historical nihilism, which they describe as a political current aimed at overthrowing Party leadership. They also describe the Beijing court rulings in the "Five Heroes of Langya Mountain" case as a lawful defence of heroes' reputations. The final sections portray 2016's Western events, including Brexit and the US election, as evidence of structural defects in Western democracy. They also present the Cybersecurity Law and Xi's proposals on global internet governance as consistent with cyber sovereignty and openness. The survey concludes that scholars should hold to Marxist guidance, Party leadership and socialism with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a compact record of the official line on contested ideological issues in 2016, and of which views were labelled as errors.

Four key points for firmly holding discourse power in ideological work 掌握意识形态工作话语权的四个着力点 Yao Dong Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in early 2017, Yao Dong takes up a directive repeated by Xi Jinping since the 18th Party Congress (2012): the Party must keep discourse power in ideological work firmly in its own hands, under all circumstances. Citing the Sixth Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2016), which stressed ideological and political building as the foundation of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, Yao argues that this task should concentrate on four areas. The commentary is organised as four numbered sections, each naming one focus and its role: upholding and developing Marxism as the essence and core; building a discourse system with Chinese style and Chinese flavour as the key link; combining positive publicity with resistance to Western ideological discourse hegemony as the firm policy; and strengthening ideological guidance on the internet as the key direction. Each section draws mainly on Xi Jinping's speeches and the Sixth Plenum documents. In the first section, Yao holds that Marxism's worldview and methodology remain the foundation, and that Xi Jinping's speeches and new ideas on governance should form the core content of discourse building. The second section argues that China's development is often described by others through theories such as the "China threat" and "neo-colonialism". Yao therefore calls for telling China's story through new concepts that suit China and can also be understood abroad, while avoiding the uncritical use of Western vocabulary to explain China's path. The third section pairs proactive positive publicity with criticism of historical nihilism, neoliberalism, democratic socialism, constitutional democracy, "universal values" and civil society. Yao describes these as tools of Western value penetration meant to turn China towards capitalism. The fourth section treats the internet as the main battlefield of public opinion and the "greatest variable" for ideological work. Yao calls for consolidating the "red zone", suppressing the "black zone" and converting the "grey zone". The proposed means are organised online forces, opinion leaders aligned with mainstream ideology, stronger internet legislation and law enforcement, and indigenous core technology. Yao concludes that these measures would let the Party's voice dominate cyberspace. Read the original if you want to see how a 2017 Party journal presented the main lines of ideological work after the 18th Party Congress, including its framing of Western ideas and the internet.

The historical evolution of socialist currents in Europe in the second half of the twentieth century 20世纪下半叶社会主义流派在欧洲的历史演进 Lü Weizhou Lü Weizhou asks how socialist currents in Europe developed between the end of the Second World War and the upheavals in the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe. The article argues that the victory over fascism opened new space for socialism, and that the period saw both the expansion of older currents and the emergence of new ones. In Lü's account, world socialism became diverse, and European currents broke through geographical limits and moved from theory into practice. The article is organised in two parts. The first examines three older currents that grew after 1945: democratic socialism and the social-democratic parties, market socialism, and Trotskyist socialism. The second turns to newer currents, briefly listing post-industrial socialism and feminist socialism, and then focusing on Eurocommunism and eco-socialism, which Lü regards as the most distinctly European and influential. On democratic socialism, Lü traces the rebuilt Socialist International (1951) and its extension to the Third World, so that by 1983 it was a global body. Lü credits social-democratic governments with welfare and workers' participation, but holds that their basic positions differ essentially from those of communist parties committed to scientific socialism, and describes the International's Cold War anticommunism and its later strategy toward Eastern Europe. Market socialism is presented through Western models (Ward, Vanek, Nove) and Eastern European ones (Liberman, Brus, Sik, Kornai, Kardelj), with practical reforms in Yugoslavia and Hungary that Lü says ended in capitalist markets. Eurocommunism, centred on the Italian, Spanish and French parties, is described as a response to changes in Western capitalism and to flaws of the Soviet model, advocating a democratic, multiparty road to socialism. Eco-socialism arose from the green movement and shaped the programmes of other parties. Lü concludes that the earlier pattern of 'one centre, one road, one model' in the international communist movement was broken. European socialist currents, in the author's view, therefore spread worldwide and increasingly tried to put their ideas into practice, which Lü credits with notable achievements for the socialist movement. Read the original if you want a compact Chinese-academic survey of the main European socialist currents of 1945–1989, including how they are characterised and the thinkers associated with each.

Frontier issues in recent research on the Soviet and East European upheavals 近年来苏东剧变研究中的前沿问题 Li Ruiqin Writing 25 years after the Soviet and East European upheavals, Li Ruiqin surveys recent Chinese scholarship on the subject. The review argues that research has become deeper, more detailed and more far-sighted, and that its basic purpose is to serve the ruling Party's building and socialism with Chinese characteristics. It identifies five areas it regards as the research frontier. The five clusters are: the link between the lessons of the collapse and a country's fate; the rise of historical nihilism and other erroneous currents under Gorbachev; Russia's reassessment of Soviet history and its history textbooks; research on Marxism and socialism in present-day Russia; and the study of the upheavals in connection with socialism with Chinese characteristics. Li summarises studies in each area, often by describing what unnamed 'scholars' conclude, and draws on works edited by Li Shenming as well as Russian and Chinese reactions to them. On causes, the review reports findings that Gorbachev's 'democratic, humane socialism' was the direct and main cause, and that historical nihilism served as its ideological tool. Other studies cited trace the collapse to the Soviet party's weak internal construction, formalism, bureaucracy and privilege, and ideological disorder, which explain why ordinary members did not defend the party. The review then describes Putin-era Russian efforts as it presents them: patriotic education programmes, a 2016 unified history textbook drawn up under presidential instruction, and a rejection of nihilism about the Soviet past. It also notes that Marxist methods and 'new socialist' currents persist in Russia, though socialist parties lack power. Li concludes that the lessons point to maintaining Marxism's leading position in ideology, advancing inner-Party democracy and tying core socialist values to popular interests. The review also reports scholars' view that the central lesson for China is to reform in good time rather than refuse, delay or patch up reforms. It says the study of the upheavals remains a major long-term topic for the international communist movement. Read the original if you want a guide to the themes and works that Chinese Party-affiliated scholars treated as central to Soviet-collapse research around 2016.

Strengthening leadership and discourse power in ideological work at universities 加强高校意识形态工作领导权和话语权 Deng Xueyuan Li Guoxing Writing in Guangming Daily in February 2017, Deng Xueyuan and Li Guoxing ask how universities, which they call the front line of the Party's ideological work, can make that work more effective under new conditions. They argue that universities must hold leadership and discourse power by keeping Marxism as the guiding ideology, cultivating core socialist values, mastering cyberspace and putting the people at the centre. The short commentary follows a speech by Xi Jinping at the national conference on ideological and political work in universities. It is organised under four headings: Marxist guidance, core socialist values, online discourse power, and a people-centred stance. On Marxist guidance, the authors call for adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, building Marxist theory as a first-level discipline and tightening Party committee responsibility. Propaganda departments, Marxism schools and all other units are to act jointly as defenders of Marxist ideology. On values, they say globalisation and the market economy have diversified students' and teachers' outlooks, so core socialist values must enter textbooks, classrooms and campus life, with no space given to erroneous currents of thought. On the internet, they urge universities to use new media actively, monitor online information and fill the field with positive messages, taking initiative on questions of political principle. Finally, the authors argue that ideological work must start from the real needs of staff, especially young teachers, and of students. They also call for unity of Party spirit and people's character, so that the Party's positions reflect the voices of the university community. Read the original if you want a compact example of how official guidance on university ideological work was presented to a Party-newspaper readership in 2017.

Online teaching in university ideological and political theory courses: current situation, causes and countermeasures 高校思想政治理论课网络教学的现状、原因及对策 Zheng Jie Liang Hong Zheng Jie and Liang Hong ask how well online teaching is working in China's university ideological and political theory courses (referred to as "sizheng courses") and how it can be improved. Their article, published in 2017, is an empirical study that moves from a survey of the current situation to its causes and then to remedies. The authors argue that online teaching is now part of the teaching system and is welcomed by teachers and students. In their reading it still delivers only middling results, because of weaknesses in teaching staff, resources, environment and operating mechanisms. The study draws on questionnaires and key interviews at 30 universities: nine from the 985 and 211 groups, 15 ordinary undergraduate institutions and six vocational colleges. Of 700 questionnaires distributed, 671 were valid, from 225 teachers and 446 students. The article has three parts. The first describes four areas: general conditions, teachers' and students' attitudes, teaching content, and teaching platforms. The second discusses four causes. The third proposes four sets of optimisation strategies. According to the survey figures the authors cite, most institutions have the technical conditions, but online teaching is recent and infrequent: 48.44% of teachers use it only occasionally. About half of teachers (52%) and students (54.26%) approve of it, yet 67.11% of teachers and 60.99% of students rate their satisfaction as merely 'average'. Rich online resources are seen as its main advantage, while 41.78% of teachers and 39.24% of students point to over-virtualised platforms. The authors trace the problems to the weakened leading role of teachers, whose authority is eroded by information overload and, in the article's account, by Western ideological infiltration through the internet. They also point to duplicated, poorly organised resources, uncontrolled security risks and an underdeveloped 'soft' cultural environment, and to rigid assessment and evaluation mechanisms. The authors call for four sets of measures. Teachers should adopt equal, open and cooperative teaching ideas, improve their information literacy and manage students online. Resources should be screened for ideological soundness, integrated by level and category, and developed into model online courses and MOOCs. The hardware and cultural environment should be improved, including network ethics education and the regulation of online culture. Management, interaction, evaluation and feedback mechanisms should be built, with the university Party committee leading management. Read the original if you want survey data on how Chinese universities implemented online ideological and political courses around 2016, and how the field framed its problems and remedies.

On upholding the guiding position of Marxism 论坚持马克思主义指导地位 Deng Chundong Writing in 2016, Deng Chundong takes up Xi Jinping's repeated statement that upholding Marxism's guiding position is a fundamental question for philosophy and the social sciences, for Party building, and for the fate of the Party and country. Deng argues that this position is the basic reason for the Chinese Communist Party's achievements and the ideological guarantee of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Abandoning or weakening it, in the author's account, was the root cause of the Soviet and East European collapse. The article has eight sections. It first traces China's modern history from the failed attempts at national salvation to the Party's success under Marxism, then examines the Soviet Union's fall. It next considers the scope of the guiding position, how to treat diverse and erroneous currents of thought, and seven contested questions of theory and history. It ends with the need to "integrate" Marxism with Chinese conditions and to use Xi's speeches to unify the Party's thinking. Deng contends that Marxism is not only the Party's guiding thought but the country's mainstream ideology, covering state organs, social organisations and economic and cultural life, citing the Constitution's preamble. Non-Marxist ideas that do no harm may exist but must be guided by Marxism rather than compete with it on equal terms. Currents such as constitutional democracy, neoliberalism, universal values, civil society and consumerism are described as aiming to subvert Party leadership and must be criticised. Deng also sets out correct positions on the October Revolution, Soviet history, the causes of the Soviet collapse, the first thirty years of the People's Republic, reform and opening up, and the Marxist meaning of democracy, freedom and human rights. The author also warns against both ultra-"Left" and Right errors. Deng proposes continuing the Sinicisation of Marxism through integration with China's present conditions, its fine traditional culture and the practice of the Party and state, along with "four distinctions" among kinds of theory. Deng calls for Xi Jinping's speeches, studied systematically through the "Two Studies, One Action" campaign, to unify the Party and educate the people, and to be applied against Western-style democracy, neoliberalism, populism and anarchism. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how a senior Chinese Marxist institution defined ideological orthodoxy and its boundaries around 2016.

The "clumsy performance" of historical nihilism New features of the trend of historical nihilism in 2015 历史虚无主义的“蹩脚表现” Fan Jianxin Long Bin Fan Jianxin and Long Bin examine what they see as the new features of historical nihilism in China in 2015 and argue for a firm response. Writing in People's Forum in early 2016, the authors contend that the trend is not an academic current but a political one, aimed at inciting the overthrow of the leadership of the Communist Party of China and of the socialist system. The article first describes the trend's timing, content and tactics, and then its use of "academic packaging". It cites Xi Jinping's remarks on the collapse of the Soviet Union as a warning.
