A second part sets out three ways of fighting back, which the authors present as necessary. On timing, the authors say that nihilists exploit anniversaries. In 2015, the 70th anniversary of victory in the War of Resistance against Japan, they claim, some praised Kuomintang figures such as Chiang Kai-shek and Zhang Lingfu while belittling Communist ones. On content, they say a magazine's September 2015 issue carried articles that undermined the Four-sphere Confidence, for instance by calling "one-party dictatorship" Mao Zedong's legacy. On tactics, they list attacks on the "Five Heroes of Langya Mountain", the use of fragmentary personal memoirs against collective national memory, praise of the Republican era, and more veiled insinuation and mockery. Under "academic freedom" and "value neutrality", the authors say, nihilists reinterpret Party history as a history of power struggles and replace Chinese political terms with Western ones. The authors conclude that the real aims are to deny the Party's right to rule, its governing capacity and its political character. The authors call for opposition on three fronts. The first is to take the initiative: answer nihilist claims, set the agenda and firmly hold ideological leadership and discourse power. The second is a strengthened sense of responsibility for ideological "positions", citing media campaigns and essay contests. The third is strict Party discipline, citing the newly issued Regulations on Disciplinary Actions, which classify "groundless criticism of central decisions" and distorting Party or army history as violations of political discipline. The authors hold that tolerance of nihilism amounts to indulgence. Read the original if you want an example of how Party-aligned scholars described and countered historical nihilism in 2015–16.

Building ideological and institutional defences to strengthen the capacity to resist corruption and degeneration 筑牢思想和制度防线提升拒腐防变能力 Lü Weizhou Writing in Guangming Daily after the Sixth Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2016), Lü Weizhou asks how the Party can build clean politics and raise its members' ability to resist corruption. The commentary takes up the plenum's call to build "ideological and institutional defences" and to construct mechanisms that make officials unwilling, unable and afraid to be corrupt. Lü argues that this is essential for preserving the Party's vanguard character and purity, for restricting and supervising power, and for consolidating its governing position. The piece has three parts. The first explains why the task is urgent, citing the persistence of abuse of power, bribery and rule-breaking among Party members despite the anti-corruption drive since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The second deals with the ideological defence through ideals and convictions, Party spirit and self-discipline. The third deals with the institutional defence through rules, supervision and checks on power. Lü's central claim is that the two defences are complementary: ideology is the precondition and institutions are the safeguard. On the ideological side, the author contends that corrupt officials generally neglected theoretical study and let their convictions slip, so that the "not wanting to be corrupt" foundation collapsed. Leaders must therefore hold to Marxist belief, study basic theory and cultivate self-discipline. On the institutional side, Lü cites Deng Xiaoping on the fundamental importance of institutions and describes the effort to put power "in the cage of institutions" through a system of Party regulations with the Party Constitution at its core. The author also points to the plenum's stress on supervision, including the Regulations on Intra-Party Supervision, and on the principle that power must carry responsibility. Lü concludes that comprehensive and rigorous Party self-governance is a complex systemic project requiring several measures at once. Only if the ideological and institutional defences work together, in Lü's view, can a lasting mechanism against corruption be built and the Party's political ecology be kept clean. This is presented as a political guarantee for the "two centenary goals" and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party theorists framed the pairing of ideological education and rule-based discipline after the 2016 plenum.

Holding the main front of ideological work Challenges to Marxist ideology and Xi Jinping's requirements since the 18th Party Congress 守好意识形态建设的主阵地 Li Heliang Gao Qingtao Li Heliang and Gao Qingtao ask how the Party should safeguard the leading position of Marxist ideology as it faces mounting pressure. They argue that since reform and opening up, market-economy development has produced diverse interests, widening income gaps and competing currents of thought, and that since the 18th Party Congress (2012) the challenges to mainstream ideology's cohesion, appeal and public acceptance have grown more severe. Their answer is that the Party must hold ideological leadership and discourse power firmly, as Xi Jinping has repeatedly demanded. The article, published in 2016, has two parts. The first diagnoses four challenges: the ideological fallout of comprehensively deepening reform, the infiltration of capitalist ideology, information technology and new media, and shortcomings within the Party-led ideological system itself. The second surveys Xi's requirements for ideological work in four areas: the armed forces, universities, the internet, and propaganda and ideological work generally. Each area is supported by quotations from Xi's speeches in 2014 and after. On the first challenge, the authors argue that reform has entered deep water, touching established interests and shaking some people's commitment to socialism. Those who feel they have gained too little may turn hostile to the Party and to Marxism, and failure to respond would erode ideological credibility and even the Party's governing position. On the second, they say capitalist infiltration is now largely invisible, presented as cultural dialogue and "universal values" and even packaged as what socialism needs. On the fourth, they say Party ideology has weak appeal, relies on political authority more than reasoned argument, promises more than it delivers, is slow to see ideological causes behind economic problems, and uses outdated methods of education. The authors conclude that, although the mainstream of ideological life is healthy, negative currents and a wavering "middle ground" persist. They present Xi's demands as the response: absolute Party leadership over the military, Party leadership of universities and their ideological work, a firm hold on internet public opinion, and Party-led media that must "be surnamed Party". Read the original if you want a concise statement of how a 2016 Party-school-style analysis framed ideological security and Xi's guidance across the military, universities and the internet.

World socialism in 2016: development and observations 2016世界社会主义发展与观察 Cui Guitian Writing at the end of 2016 in the China Social Sciences Today, Cui Guitian offers a year-end survey of world socialism. The author's thesis is that 2016 was an eventful year in which socialism drew continued attention amid Western crises, the world communist movement kept recovering from its low point, and socialism developed in diverse forms, while the overall environment remained harsh. The article is organised in four sections: the rising political profile of socialism; the movement's difficult progress among ruling parties, Western, post-socialist and developing-world communist parties; the variety of socialist currents; and the continuing difficulties. It moves through Vietnam, Cuba, Laos and the Democratic People's Republic of Korea, then communist parties in France, Greece, Cyprus, the United States, Japan, Russia, the Czech lands, India, Nepal, South Africa and Brazil. It also covers social democrats, Latin American new left and Green parties. Cui argues that the 2008 financial crisis showed that capitalism's basic contradictions remain unresolved. In the author's account, the 2016 Brexit vote, Donald Trump's election and the Italian referendum produced a "political tornado" that exposed capitalism's defects, while Western promotion of "universal values" and neo-liberalism brought new disorder. Cui also points to closer cooperation among communist and workers' parties, such as the 18th international meeting in Hanoi, and to the author's view that socialism with Chinese characteristics, through full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, has advanced world socialism. The article reports party membership and vote figures, including growth in the South African and Brazilian parties and losses for the Russian party. Cui names three main troubles: difficulties for ruling and non-ruling communist parties, the rightward drift of social democratic parties, and setbacks for the Latin American left. Cui concludes that world socialism is moving forward in a broader trend of recovery despite pressures. The author calls for firm socialist conviction, a strategic and tolerant attitude towards the diversity of socialisms, and, on the basis of principle, closer exchanges among socialist forces to deepen mutual understanding. Read the original if you want a compact, data-rich overview of how a Chinese scholar of contemporary socialism assessed the state of communist and left parties worldwide at the end of 2016.

The proposal of the principle of "consultation and consensus" An important contribution of the Communist Party of China to the development of the international communist movement “协商一致”原则的提出 Nie Yunlin How should communist parties settle disagreements when none of them has authority over the others? Nie Yunlin argues that the Communist Party of China (CPC) under Mao Zedong answered this during the serious divisions of the 1950s and 1960s by proposing "consultation and consensus" (xieshang yizhi). In Nie's account, this was an important CPC contribution to unity and cooperation in the international communist movement. The article moves in four steps. It first narrates the 1957 Moscow conference of ruling communist and workers' parties and the drafting of the Moscow Declaration. It then turns to Deng Xiaoping's three trips to Moscow in 1960, culminating in the 81-party meeting. A third section sets out the content of the principle, and a fourth assesses its significance, drawing on the First, Second and Third Internationals and on the present-day International Meeting of Communist and Workers' Parties. Nie reads the principle as having four parts. Its nature is democratic persuasion rather than coercion. Its procedure is consultation on draft documents before and during meetings. Its precondition is an atmosphere of equality. Its outcome is that agreed points go into the document and disputed ones are left out. Nie contrasts the 1957 meeting, where Khrushchev accepted this approach and the declaration passed unanimously, with 1960, when Deng rejected majority rule and "father-son party" relations and the Soviet side refused consultation. In Nie's telling the 1960 statement was only a grudging compromise that deepened the split. Nie argues that majority rule and subordination of lower to higher bodies cannot apply among independent, equal parties, so consensus is the only workable route. Nie also contends that the CPC went beyond earlier practice: the First and Second Internationals used consultation informally, the Third relied on hierarchical democratic centralism, and Mao raised consultation from a method to a binding principle. Nie concludes that the principle restores a democratic tradition, was first formulated as a principle by the CPC, and complements the norms of independence, equality, mutual respect and non-interference. It helps manage differences in a diverse world socialist movement. Nie notes that the international meetings of communist and workers' parties have applied it, issuing a press communiqué rather than forcing through a joint statement when consensus failed. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly account of Sino-Soviet disputes over inter-party relations and of how the CPC frames its own role in them.

The fragmentation of Italy's communist parties and prospects for their development 论意大利共产主义政党的碎片化困境与发展前景 Li Kaixuan Italy's Communist Party was once the strongest in Western Europe, yet it dissolved in 1991 and its successors have since splintered. Li Kaixuan asks why Italian communist organisations now form a fragmented "two weak, three small" pattern and whether they can recover. The article argues that fragmentation stems from abandoning democratic centralism and from ideological confusion and political vacillation. It treats Italy as a window onto the wider difficulties of Western European communist parties. The article first maps the current landscape. It covers the declining Party of Communist Refoundation, the new Italian Communist Party (formed in June 2016 from the Party of Italian Communists), and three smaller groups: the Trotskyist Workers' Communist Party, the Communist Party (Marxist-Leninist) and the Communist Network. Li draws on membership figures from the parties' websites and from a December 2015 talk at the Academy of Marxism by an Italian communist official. A second section analyses causes, and a third examines attempts at reunification and external challenges. Li's first main claim is organisational. Refoundation, in Li's account, created two top posts, allowed organised factions and dropped democratic centralism, so internal disputes became public and triggered splits (1995, 1998, 2006, 2009). Li contrasts this with the old Party after the 1960s, which held together under a ban on factionalism and under Berlinguer's leadership. The second claim is ideological: the parties never settled how to combine Marxism with Italian political reality. Their swings between joining centre-left governments and opposing them, and the 2008–2009 split over abandoning communist identity, are cited as evidence. Li reviews the Party of Italian Communists' plan, from 2014, to rebuild a single communist party. The plan drew interest from about a fifth of Refoundation members but fell well short of its targets, and Li doubts it could solve fragmentation without a shared answer on Marxism and Italian conditions. Li also warns of two outside threats. One is Left Ecology Freedom, which Li describes as de-Marxified and which draws on the same voters. The other is the Five Star Movement, whose notion of "the people" Li sees as dissolving class mobilisation. Li calls on the communists to take both seriously. Read the original if you want a detailed, Chinese-academic account of Italian communist party splits, membership figures and strategic debates after 1991.

Facing dissolution: the decline of Russia's "de-Stalinization" organisations An analysis of the legal threat to the Memorial association 面临被解散：俄罗斯“去斯大林化”组织败落史透视 Li Ruiqin Writing in 2015, Li Ruiqin asks why Memorial, Russia's oldest and largest "de-Stalinization" organisation, has repeatedly faced dissolution since the Ministry of Justice sued it in the Supreme Court in September 2014. This came only three years after a 2011 state project on commemorating the victims of totalitarian regimes, which Memorial helped to shape. Li argues that the case reflects the decline of de-Stalinization in Russia, and that its causes lie in Vladimir Putin's outlook, the Ukraine crisis and Russian society's view of Stalin. The article has four parts. It first describes Memorial, founded in 1989 on Andrei Sakharov's initiative, its human rights centre, its "Returning the Names" event and allied museums, and then the course of the lawsuit from 2014 to January 2015. It next traces three waves of de-Stalinization, under Khrushchev, under Gorbachev and Yeltsin, and from 2009 under Medvedev. It then examines Russians' contradictory views of Stalin, using Levada Centre polls, and sets out five reasons behind the dissolution crisis. Li characterises all three waves as top-down, historically nihilist, aimed at courting the West, unrewarded by it and lacking a social base. Polls cited show roughly half of Russians rating Stalin positively, mostly because of the Great Patriotic War and industrialisation, while about a third reject him. Li attributes the crisis to Putin's more favourable view of Stalin, which in Li's account explains why the 2011 project stalled, to the collapse of Russia–West relations after Ukraine, and to a new public stance of "against repression but not against Stalin". The large-scale commemoration of the 70th anniversary of victory in the Second World War is also said to make de-Stalinization unsustainable. Li also reads Western and Ukrainian equations of Hitlerism and Stalinism as hostile pressure. Li concludes that the delays in dissolving Memorial show the matter's complexity, since westernised intellectuals and foreign human rights bodies resist it, while the Ministry of Justice continues slowly towards its goal. Li describes the "fifth column" of westernised elites promoting historical nihilism as capable of making trouble for a time but destined to fail. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist scholar framed the Memorial case in 2015 and the debate over Stalin in Russia.

The diverse features of contemporary Russian socialist parties 当代俄罗斯社会主义党派的多样化特征 Li Ruiqin Writing in 2015, Li Ruiqin asks how the socialist parties that emerged after the collapse of the Soviet Union differ from one another, and what role they play in Russia today. The article argues that Russian socialism is plural: the Communist Party of the Russian Federation (CPRF) is the leading force, A Just Russia represents a rising democratic-socialist wing, and a range of smaller parties form a broader left front. The article compares the CPRF, the All-Union Communist Party of Bolsheviks, the Russian Communist Workers' Party, A Just Russia, the Russian Socialist Movement and other small parties. It does so under six headings: guiding ideology, social base, goals for a "new socialism", political role under legal struggle, attitudes to religion, and the overall position and prospects of the Marxist-Leninist parties. It draws on party programmes, membership figures, election results and 2015 opinion polls. Li contends that the Marxist-Leninist parties have a unified ideology that continues the Soviet party tradition. A Just Russia and the Russian Socialist Party are described as abstract and democratic-socialist, while the Russian Socialist Movement mixes many left currents. The CPRF's "socialism of the twenty-first century" is said to build on Soviet socialism, whereas the similar-sounding slogan of A Just Russia rejects Soviet history and Marxism-Leninism. All parties work within the law, but the CPRF's opposition is selective, and the CPRF is shown as an ageing party: retirees make up 43.64% of its members. Li notes that the CPRF's liberal stance on religion, which allows believers into the party, may help it to broaden its base. Li regards this as only an expedient that could erode the party's purity. Li concludes that the CPRF and other Marxist-Leninist parties are indispensable but have no immediate chance of power. In the polls cited, United Russia scores about 57–60% against about 6–7% for the CPRF, and the objective conditions Lenin set for revolution are absent. The author calls for theoretical innovation, better party-building, unity among dozens of fragmented parties and a broad left front pursuing power mainly through parliament, without wholly abandoning non-peaceful means if circumstances require. Read the original if you want a detailed comparative survey of post-Soviet Russian left parties, with membership and polling data, as seen by a Chinese Marxist scholar writing in 2015.

What the evolution of threat perceptions in Russia's national security strategies reveals about the essence of US hegemonism 从俄国家安全战略威胁因素的演变看美霸权主义本质 Li Ruiqin Writing in 2016, Li Ruiqin asks why the West, which Russia once sought to join even at the cost of the Soviet state's collapse, was named in Russia's 2015 national security strategy as the main threat, with the United States and NATO treated as adversaries. The article argues that the cause lies neither in Russia's adherence to so-called universal values nor in its social system. In Li's account, the one real cause is a US global strategy of hegemonism and a unipolar world, which tolerates no challenger. The article traces Russia's four security documents since 1991: the 1997 and 2000 National Security Concepts, the 2009 strategy to 2020 and the 2015 strategy to 2020. Each is tied to a turning point: NATO's eastward expansion and the cooling of the Yeltsin-era 'honeymoon', the Kosovo crisis of 1998, the 2008 South Ossetia conflict and the 2014 Ukraine crisis. A final section draws five general lessons from this record. Li reads the sequence as a gradual loss of illusions. In 1997 Moscow still located its main threats inside the country and avoided naming NATO as a target; in 2000 it dropped that formula. In 2009, under Medvedev, it sought reconciliation, including the third wave of 'de-Stalinisation', but the Ukraine crisis and Western sanctions wiped out these concessions. The 2015 strategy then names US pressure, NATO's advance, missile defence and support for the Ukrainian 'coup' as threats. Li concludes that democracy, freedom and human rights serve as tools of intervention, that US judgments of other states are self-interested, and that Russia's strength made it an obstacle whatever its values. Drawing on Mao Zedong and Putin, Li concludes that conciliation and concession bring only temporary calm and that hegemonism must be met without compromise. Li links Russia's experience to Western talk of a 'China threat' and to US human rights reports on China, and calls for continued progress on socialism with Chinese characteristics, the Chinese Dream and a moderately prosperous society. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist researcher in 2016 used Russian security documents to argue against Western universal values and for firm resistance to US hegemonism.

Laos: lifting the veil of mystery and welcoming new opportunities for development 老挝：掀开神秘面纱，迎接发展新机遇 Pan Jin'e Writing in late 2016, as Vientiane hosted the East Asia leaders' meetings, Pan introduces Laos to a general readership as a once-quiet Buddhist country now drawn into diplomacy and politics. The article's thesis is that Laos' wartime history, three decades of renewal and opening up, and closer ties with China together place it at a point of new development opportunity. The piece is a magazine-style overview in three parts. It first recounts the Ho Chi Minh Trail and the American bombing of Laos, then turns to Laos' foreign relations, especially with Vietnam and China. It then traces the Lao People's Revolutionary Party's line from 1975 to its Tenth Congress in January 2016 and lists the achievements and problems of the renewal period. Pan argues that the Trail, which the author says carried Chinese and other aid to southern Vietnam, bound China, Laos and Vietnam in revolutionary friendship. The author cites the claim that the US dropped four billion pounds of bombs on Laos in 1964–1973, and notes that unexploded ordnance still kills and maims. On the Party's line, Pan reads the shifting definition of Laos' stage of development, from 1991 to 2006, as a flexible strategy that allows market mechanisms to be used while leaving room for theoretical manoeuvre. For the renewal record, the article cites figures from a Lao scholar: growth above 7.5% a year in 2006–2015, GDP per capita rising from 114 to 1,913 US dollars, and poverty at 6.59% in 2015. Pan acknowledges that Laos remains at a low level of development and faces a widening wealth gap, social instability and moral decline among Party cadres. The author adds that the Party must guard against "peaceful evolution". Pan expects the Belt and Road Initiative to be linked with Laos' strategy of turning a landlocked country into a land-linked one. Lao scholars, who once drew mainly on Vietnam, now want to learn from China on Party-building, the market–government relationship and poverty, which Pan sees as room for cooperation. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese view of Laos' history, Party line and relations with China and Vietnam as of 2016.

Trends and prospects of left-wing governments in Latin America 拉美左翼执政动向及前景 Research Centre for the Theoretical System of Socialism with Chinese Characteristics, Chinese Academy of Social Sciences Writing in late 2016, after the defeat of Argentina's left-wing governing party in November 2015, this newspaper commentary asks whether the cycle of left-wing government in Latin America is ending and what that means. The article argues that the left and right alternation, the so-called "pendulum effect", is essentially a regulatory mechanism developed within the capitalist framework to secure political stability and economic development. On that basis, it contends that the current left cycle may be ending but that the left is unlikely to disappear. The piece covers three waves of left-wing government since the early twentieth century: the early 1900s (Batlle y Ordóñez, Billinghurst, Yrigoyen), the 1940s–60s (Cárdenas, Perón, Vargas) and the post-1999 wave that began with Chávez. It then assesses the nature of the contemporary left, explains why it keeps returning, and reviews the latest developments in Argentina, Brazil, Venezuela, Ecuador and Bolivia. It closes with an outlook for the region. The author's central claim is that the ruling left parties are not proletarian parties but the left wing of the bourgeois camp. Only Cuba, with the Communist Party of Cuba, counts as a socialist state, and the "socialism of the twenty-first century" proclaimed elsewhere amounts to "change within the system". The author describes a recurring trade-off: the left stresses distribution, political mobilisation and participation but neglects growth and order, while the right does the reverse. The left's resilience is traced to five factors: representative democracy, the shift from elite to mass politics, ideological guidance from socialist thought and the experience of China and Cuba, deep inequality, and the failure of either camp to resolve growth versus distribution. The author expects Latin American politics to alternate between left and right, with right or centre-right governments possibly becoming more numerous for some time. Several left governments still hold office into 2018–2020, so a decline is not a collapse. Right-wing governments may be politically closer to the West but more open to economic and trade cooperation, which the author flags as relevant to China–Latin America relations. Read the original if you want a concise 2016 Chinese academic assessment of the "pink tide" and its class character, as framed from a Marxist perspective.

The essence of capitalist financialization 资本主义金融化的本质 Luan Wenlian Writing in 2016, Luan asks what lies at the core of the financialization of capitalism, the stage that she says emerged in the 1970s and 1980s when monopoly capitalism came to be dominated by fictitious financial capital. The author's thesis is that its essence lies in monopoly financial capital using financial means to seize enormous profits and plunder the world's wealth. This short newspaper commentary is organised under three headings: financialization as a new form of exploitation, finance's detachment from its role of serving the real economy, and the hegemonic rule of monopoly financial capital. It draws on Marx's concepts of surplus value and monopoly profit, and on examples such as mergers and acquisitions, debt, futures and options, and household financial products. Luan argues that the absolute law of surplus-value production, which became monopoly profit under monopoly capitalism, now takes the form of excess profit extracted through financial instruments, including leveraged trading and bubble creation. Finance increasingly serves its own expansion, in the author's account, through shareholder-value maximization and speculation. This hinders productive forces, spreads indebtedness to the state, and tilts distribution towards finance and senior managers. Luan adds that capital now also financializes workers' income through housing credit, health and pension insurance, so that exploitation is joined to consumption. The author concludes that financialization sharpens the contradictions between a small financial oligarchy and working people at home and abroad. In this reading, Western financial crises are a necessary product of capitalism's basic contradiction, and financial hegemony over markets, pricing and rating agencies exposes the historical limits of capitalism. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how a CASS Marxist scholar interpreted financialization in 2016 through the framework of monopoly capitalism.

The economic outlook for advanced capitalist countries is bleak 发达资本主义国家的经济发展前景黯淡 Huang Zhenqi Huang Haiyan Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts (2016, no. 20), Huang Zhenqi and Huang Haiyan ask what lies ahead for the economies of the advanced capitalist countries over the next five years and beyond. They open from the 13th Five-Year Plan's call for all-round opening up, which in their view requires close attention to the external environment. Their thesis is that capitalism has entered a stage of domination by "fictitious financial capital", that this stage sharpens capitalism's basic contradiction, and that recovery from the 2008 crisis is therefore weak and a new crisis is possible. The article has three sections. The first defines the new stage, which the authors date from the 1980s, and lists four factors behind the swelling of fictitious capital. The second sets out how this stage intensifies the basic contradiction of capitalism. The third examines why the major developed economies have recovered so feebly more than seven years after 2008, using data on the United States, Japan and the euro area. The authors define fictitious financial capital as capital detached from the real economy and produced by circulation alone, such as over-issued paper money and securities. They cite figures such as 2012 securities and bond trading of over 600 trillion dollars, ten times trade in goods and services. For them the causes are deindustrialisation through industrial relocation, financial deregulation (the end of dollar convertibility, Reagan and Thatcher, the 1999 repeal of Glass–Steagall), globalisation and information technology. Their account of the consequences runs through unequal distribution, three great asset bubbles (Japan, the dot-com boom, US housing), surging public and private debt, and protest such as Occupy Wall Street. In the third section they argue that toxic assets are slow to clear, that austerity under sovereign-debt crises holds back growth, and that bail-outs go to big financial institutions while small firms lack credit. They cite US growth averaging 1.8% a year after the crisis. The authors conclude that quantitative easing, ultra-low interest rates and widening inequality have fed new bubbles, so developed countries face renewed risk of financial crisis and recession. They cite an IMF warning and a similar warning from the former Bank of England governor Mervyn King. They urge China to study the possible effects of a new international crisis on its economy and finance and to prepare policy responses in advance. Read the original if you want an example of how Chinese policy researchers in 2016 used the concept of fictitious financial capital to explain Western stagnation and to argue for contingency planning.

Why populism keeps growing in Europe and the United States 民粹主义何以在欧美愈演愈烈 Shi Zhiqin Writing in spring 2016, Shi asks why populism has become ever stronger in Europe and the United States. The commentary argues that populist parties and candidates are a concentrated expression of social contradictions in Western countries, driven by economic hardship, inequality and the growing dominance of elites. The article first surveys Europe since the 2008 financial crisis. It describes the rise of right-wing populist parties in France, Austria and Germany, and of left-wing populism in southern Europe, notably Syriza in Greece and Podemos in Spain. It then turns to Donald Trump's campaign in the 2016 US primaries as a further case. Shi identifies two main causes. The first is mass unemployment and an uncertain economic outlook, with the EU economy still stuck near its pre-2008 level. The second is extreme inequality of income and wealth, for which Shi cites Thomas Piketty and the gap between the 1% and the 99%. Populism's core, in Shi's account, is putting the people first against elite domination. Western democratic politics, Shi says, has become more elitist and captured by interest groups and big capital, leaving ordinary people to speak only through their votes. Establishment politicians have lost the ability to set political agendas, while anti-establishment figures voice popular sentiment. Shi concludes that the many "Trumps" across Europe and America are leading and changing the future model and form of politics. Read the original if you want a brief example of how a Chinese international-relations scholar read the rise of Western populism in 2016.

The roots of the rise of populism in contemporary Europe 民粹主义在当代欧洲兴起的根源 Li Kaixuan Why did populist parties surge across Europe after the financial crisis? Writing in 2016, Li Kaixuan argues that the surge has economic and political roots. Economically, it comes from the clash between global free-market expansion and the bounded national welfare state. Politically, it comes from the defects of representative democracy, the EU's democratic deficit and a crisis of representation among mainstream parties. Li adds that populism should not be dismissed as simply reactionary or foolish. The article opens with the electoral breakthroughs of populist parties since 2012, among them Syriza in Greece, the National Front in France, UKIP in Britain, the Freedom Party in Austria, Podemos in Spain and the Five Star Movement in Italy. It then sorts European populism into types: right-wing (neoliberal and national populism), left-wing, and "issue" populism, which Li locates mainly in Italy. Two sections follow, on economic and on political roots, and a short conclusion extends the point beyond Europe. Li's first move uses Karl Polanyi's "double movement": market expansion provokes social counter-pressure, and the European welfare state is such a limit on the market. Li says that capital flight, economic restructuring and free movement of labour erode its fiscal base. In north-western Europe, workers fall back on exclusive national boundaries to protect their welfare privileges, which Li reads in the Brexit vote and the Austrian result. In southern Europe, austerity imposed by the "troika" of the EU, the IMF and the European Central Bank fuelled left-wing populism. The second move is political. Li says that representation dilutes or distorts popular will, and that recall and referendum rights are hard to use in practice. The EU's economic powers outrun its accountability. Mainstream parties have become catch-all parties chasing the median voter, and the decline of the western European communist parties after the upheavals in the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe left their voters without representatives. Li concludes that populism's appeal rests less on the persuasiveness of its programmes than on the poor democratic performance of mainstream parties. Their interests are narrow, and their ability to keep promises and resolve crises is weakening. Li also notes that the interest conflicts caused by globalisation affect every country drawn into it. Populism may therefore become a problem all countries must guard against, though Li holds that solutions must be sought within specific political and social settings. Read the original if you want a concise 2016 Chinese scholarly typology of European populism and its explanation through Polanyi's double movement and the crisis of party representation.

The populist turn of extremist parties in the West and its warnings 西方极端政党民粹化及警示 Chai Shangjin Writing in 2016, Chai Shangjin asks why extreme left and right parties have risen across the West, and what this means for China. The article argues that Western party systems are fragmenting and politics is turning populist. In Chai's account, extremist parties exploit public discontent after the financial crisis. The author says China has little political ground for populism but must guard against its spillover effects. The article has three parts. The first surveys cases. On the left it covers Syriza in Greece, Podemos in Spain, the New Anticapitalist Party in France, Italy's Five Star Movement and Jeremy Corbyn's election as Labour leader. On the right it covers France's National Front, the US Tea Party and Donald Trump, and parties in Hungary and Poland. The second part gives four causes. The third part draws lessons for China. On causes, Chai names four. Economic stagnation, unemployment and insecurity feed discontent. Capitalist globalization sharpens competition among workers and revives national and racial conflict. A rigid, polarised multiparty system pushes politicians to compete in promising welfare and opposing rivals for opposition's sake. New online media amplify populist politics. Chai says extremist parties respect democratic rules only in appearance, and in fact favour a strong state and leader. The author also holds that these parties win because their slogans attract voters, not because of their own capability. For China, Chai calls for three kinds of vigilance. The first is to recognise populism's real presence and political harm, since social polarisation, resentment of officials and the rich, and the wealth gap feed it. The second is to watch Western populist nationalism turning into trade protectionism that harms Chinese interests, including steel anti-dumping measures and obstruction of the Belt and Road Initiative. The third is to stop online political participation from becoming an outlet for populist venting, which Chai says hostile political forces could use to pressure the Party and government. Read the original if you want a Chinese official-think-tank reading of Western populism in 2016 and the domestic security concerns it was used to raise.

The eight major principles of Xi Jinping's political economy 习近平政治经济学的八项重大原则 Cheng Enfu Writing in 2016, Cheng Enfu takes up what he calls "Xi Jinping's political economy", which he identifies with contemporary Sinicised Marxist political economy, or the political economy of socialism with Chinese characteristics. His thesis is that it contains eight major principles, each derived from a general principle of Marxist political economy and applied to a specific problem of China's economy. The article is organised in eight sections, each named for a principle: sustained technology-led development, a livelihood-oriented purpose of production, a public-sector-centred property regime, a labour-centred distribution regime, a state-led market, performance-first growth, structural balance, and self-reliant openness. Every section follows the same three-step pattern. It states the relevant general principle of political economy, then sets out what Xi Jinping's thinking stresses on that issue, then draws out what Cheng says must be done now. Cheng's central move is to present each principle as the application of classical Marxist theory, such as the primacy of productive forces, the purpose of production under public ownership, the law of value and the law of proportionate development, to China's primary stage of socialism. He argues that the basic economic system must keep public ownership as the main body and the state sector in the leading role, while unwaveringly encouraging the non-public sector. He treats the plan and the market as one organic whole, aiming at a "double-strong" pairing of an efficient market and an efficient government. He also makes sharp policy claims. He holds that China's wealth and income gaps are large, that household net assets, not income, are the primary measure of polarisation, and that neoliberal ideas lie behind the "middle-income trap" concept and behind the view that market-generated overcapacity corrects itself. Cheng concludes that these principles should guide implementation of the Fifth Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2015) and the Central Economic Work Conference of late 2015. His specific proposals include innovation-driven growth, supply-side structural reform, a stronger public sector with mixed ownership under public control, employee shareholding in private firms, and more regulation of foreign acquisitions. They also include Belt and Road cooperation and delaying capital-account opening. Read the original if you want a compact statement of how a prominent Marxist economist in China systematised Xi Jinping's economic thinking in 2016, and of his positions on ownership, distribution and the state's role in the market.

Fidel Castro, permanent hero of the poor of the Third World 菲德尔·卡斯特罗是第三世界穷人的永久英雄 Salim Lamrani This is an abridged Chinese translation, published in 2016 shortly after Fidel Castro's death, of a commentary by Salim Lamrani, a French specialist on Cuba–US relations. Lamrani argues that although Castro is a controversial figure in the West, he is admired across Latin America and the Third World as a symbol of resistance to oppression and of the South's aspiration to independence, sovereignty and self-determination. In Lamrani's view, Western media cannot grasp his historical significance. The piece sketches Castro's biography and standing in three steps: his armed struggle against the Batista dictatorship (the 1953 Moncada attack and the 1956–58 campaign), his constitutional record as elected head of state from 1976 to 2006, and his popular support as acknowledged by US officials. A linked second article by the philosopher José Sarrión Andaluz, also translated from the Spanish press, adds material on Castro's international role, Cuban culture and the island's shortcomings. Lamrani's central claim is that Castro held both historical and constitutional legitimacy. He cites a 1960 US State Department memorandum by Lester Mallory, which in Lamrani's reading concedes that most Cubans supported Castro and recommends economic hardship as the means of undermining that support, and later remarks by the head of the US interests section in Havana on Cubans' admiration for him. Lamrani concludes that US sanctions failed to erode this backing. He characterises Castro in three roles: architect of national sovereignty fulfilling José Martí's dream, social reformer who built one of the least unjust societies in the Third World, and internationalist who placed solidarity at the centre of Cuban foreign policy. The appended article by Sarrión Andaluz presents Castro as a revolutionary who adapted strategy to a colonial, underdeveloped periphery and made Cuba a vanguard of national liberation. It points to medical aid, the literacy method "Yes, I can", and cultural institutions, and says that Cuba's past persecution of homosexuals was met with self-criticism. It also reports that Forbes failed to substantiate its claim about Castro's wealth. It concludes that history has absolved him. Read the original if you want to see how a favourable Latin American and Spanish left-wing assessment of Castro was selected and presented to Chinese readers in 2016.

Lessons of the Soviet Union's political reform and democratization 苏联政治改革与民主化的教训 Zhang Shuhua Writing in 2016, the 25th anniversary of the Soviet collapse, Zhang Shuhua asks what the failure of Soviet political reform under Gorbachev teaches. The article's thesis is that the Soviet Union dissolved because the Communist Party of the Soviet Union (CPSU) degenerated in its final years. In Zhang's account, Gorbachev's "restructuring" and "democratization" accelerated and triggered that process. The article is organised around three questions, each posed as a choice: whether to hold to or change the path of political development, whether to uphold or abandon Party leadership, and whether to perfect or demolish the political system. Zhang draws on Lenin's remarks on democracy, statements by Gorbachev and Yakovlev, and comments from Western figures such as Nixon and Brzezinski. Zhang also cites membership figures, counts of informal organizations and ethnic-conflict statistics. Zhang argues first that Soviet leaders, under Western "peaceful evolution" and having lost their faith, turned reform into a change of direction towards social democracy. Second, the CPSU was weakened from within, marginalized, split along national lines, stripped of its constitutional leadership role (Article 6) and finally abandoned by Gorbachev himself. Third, the system's three foundations (Party leadership, Soviet power and the union state) were dismantled, which in Zhang's reading produced political chaos, ethnic conflict and the state's collapse. Zhang says the result was oligarchic capitalism, not democracy. Zhang concludes that reform must be the socialist system's self-improvement, keep a socialist orientation and proceed under Party leadership. Political reform, Zhang adds, must serve stability, ethnic unity, political democracy and efficiency, and requires a correct view of democracy. The article closes by contrasting the CPSU's fate with the Communist Party of China, which it says has held to the Four-sphere Confidence and handled reform, development and stability well. Read the original if you want an example of how Chinese Marxist scholars in 2016 interpreted the Soviet collapse and drew lessons from it.

World socialism in the twenty-first century: new configuration, new features, new trends 21世纪的世界社会主义：新格局、新特征、新趋势 Jiang Hui Writing in the inaugural year of the journal World Socialism Studies (2016), which the author marks as the 500th anniversary of world socialism since Thomas More's Utopia (1516), Jiang Hui asks what the condition and prospects of world socialism are in the twenty-first century. The article's thesis is that the twentieth century was defined by the rise of the socialist movement, while the twenty-first is the century in which world socialism moves towards revival, with China as its main pillar. The article is organised in three parts. The first compares the balance between world capitalism and world socialism after three capitalist crises: 1929, 1973 and 2008. The second sets out four new features of twenty-first-century socialism. The third discusses new problems, strategies and trends, framed as four pairs of relationships that must be kept in unity. Jiang argues that after 2008 capitalism is on the defensive and entering a long-cycle decline, while socialism, though still in the trough that followed the Soviet and East European collapse, has entered an upswing anchored in socialism with Chinese characteristics. The four features are: socialism winning wider institutional advantages over capitalism; China becoming the mainstay and banner of world socialism, without the hegemonic 'great party, great state' posture of the Soviet Union; a historic turning point in the balance of forces as China's economy overtakes that of the United States; and a new yardstick for judging socialism, combining the number of socialist states with how far socialist ideals are realised. Looking ahead, Jiang says socialism must unite the national and the international, the local and the world-historical, working-class movements and broader mass movements, and social development with ecological civilization. Jiang concludes that the capitalist crisis offers world socialism a rare opportunity, but that turning possibility into necessity will require long and arduous struggle by socialists and progressive forces worldwide. The article ends with the confident claim that the twenty-first century is the century of world socialism's revival. Read the original if you want an example of how a leading Chinese scholar of scientific socialism, writing in 2016, periodises the contest between capitalism and socialism and presents China's place in it.

Why we should believe in communism 我们为什么要信仰共产主义 Jing Li Published in Beijing Daily on 27 June 2016, in a special issue marking the 95th anniversary of the founding of the Communist Party of China, this commentary asks why Party members should hold communism as a faith. The author, Jing Li, argues that communist belief is the Party's 'spiritual calcium' and the source of its drive. Jing Li offers four reasons for holding it. The piece opens with the Party's growth from a small group in 1921 to more than 87 million members, then restates Xi Jinping's call for confidence in the path, theory and system of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The four reasons are presented as sections: communism as a rational vision, as a lofty value, as a practical cause, and as the Party's core competitiveness. A closing section gives short accounts of Ren Bishi, Peng Pai, Fang Zhimin and Chen Shiju as examples of steadfast belief. Jing Li contrasts religious expression of hope for a better future, which locates it in the afterlife, with rational expression. Within the rational tradition, the author places Marx above Confucian datong ideals, Plato, Thomas More and the utopian socialists, because Marx derived the future from the laws of history. On values, the author says Marx's 'free development of each' differs from 'universal values', which are said to serve only some people and to remain bound to capital and private property. The author also holds that class struggle is only a phased means and that socialism with Chinese characteristics, at the primary stage of socialism, is part of the communist cause. Citing Marx's late writing on Russia and the 'Kaufman Gorge', Jing Li says China is moving into socialism without a fully developed capitalism while absorbing capitalism's positive results. The article concludes that ideals decide success or failure and that communist belief gives the Party its core competitiveness. As evidence it cites Party membership figures, China's growth and poverty reduction, and the claim that the Nationalists lacked a guiding purpose. It also cites Xi Jinping's five tiers of ideals, from communism down to the people's expectations of a better life, to show that ideal and reality are united. Read the original if you want an example of how Party-press commentary in 2016 presented communist belief to Party members, including its use of martyr narratives and its contrasts with religion and Western 'universal values'.

The international financial crisis and new developments in state monopoly capitalism 国际金融危机与国家垄断资本主义新发展 Liu Ru Writing in 2016 in Red Flag Manuscripts (Hongqi Wengao), Liu Ru asks what the 2008 global financial and economic crisis has done to the structure of contemporary capitalism. The article argues that the crisis rooted in the basic contradiction of capitalism, brought down neoliberalism, and pushed advanced countries back to Keynesianism and state intervention. In Liu's account, this deepened state monopoly capitalism without changing the essence of monopoly capitalism, so that Lenin's theory of imperialism remains valid. The piece has three parts. The first traces the origins of the crisis and the bankruptcy of neoliberalism, setting it against the cycle from classical economics to the Great Depression, Keynesianism and the stagflation of the 1970s. The second describes three post-crisis developments in state monopoly capitalism: the return of Keynesianism, the growth of state-owned capital, and stronger macroeconomic regulation. The third turns to debates on the stage of contemporary capitalism. Liu contends that neoliberal policies of privatization, loose market controls and weak financial supervision produced financialization, asset bubbles and hidden overproduction, which sharpened capitalism's basic contradiction. When the housing bubble burst, the crisis spread from the financial sector to the real economy and from developed to developing countries. Liu presents Keynesianism as the theoretical basis of state monopoly capitalism because it keeps the market but adds government intervention. As evidence, Liu cites US Treasury stakes of 79.9 per cent in Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac and 36 per cent in Citigroup, the 700 billion dollar rescue plan, the 787 billion dollar stimulus, quantitative easing, a 750 billion euro EU rescue and sweeping US financial regulatory reform. Liu concludes that, despite about ten scholarly views on the stage of contemporary capitalism, it has not moved beyond state monopoly capitalism, and that neoliberalism's failure confirms Lenin's theory of imperialism as the foundation for understanding it. Liu adds that state monopoly capitalism will not exhaust capitalist development, and that productive forces and relations of production will keep moving towards a higher degree of socialization. Read the original if you want an example of how a Party journal in 2016 used Lenin's theory of imperialism to interpret the post-2008 crisis and Western state intervention.

"Democracy Spring" and capital's control over democracy “民主之春”与资本对民主的控制 Tong Dezhi Writing in 2016, Tong Dezhi examines the "Democracy Spring" protests held in Washington in April 2016. The article asks what kind of movement this was, what it demanded and where it might lead. Tong's answer is that it is aimed at the core flaw of American democracy: the control of democratic politics by capital. The piece first describes the march from Philadelphia to the Capitol, the sit-ins that followed and the arrest of more than 1,400 people. It places the movement in a line running from the Selma march and Black Lives Matter to Occupy Wall Street in 2011. It then turns to the movement's demands and tactics. Tong argues that elections are increasingly dominated by wealthy donors, which undermines the principle of one person, one vote. To show that this is widely recognised, the author cites Michael Walzer, Anthony Arblaster, Jacques Derrida and David Schweickart. Schweickart's seven channels of money's influence include lobbying, media campaigns, bribery and campaign financing. On the movement's side, Tong notes an "empowerment plus disruption" strategy, reform bills, and a declaration calling for voting-rights protection and the reversal of Citizens United. Tong concludes that the movement's immediate target is money politics and corrupt elections, and its ultimate aim is democracy that serves the people. Tong also stresses that Congress answered with silence and arrests. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic account of the 2016 protests and of how Western critics of money in politics were used to frame them.

The clash of ideas and social crisis behind Brexit 英国脱欧背后的观念较量与社会危机 Tang Jian Writing in October 2016, after the British referendum on leaving the European Union, Tang Jian asks what Brexit reveals about the philosophy of history that underpins globalisation. The article argues that Brexit, together with Donald Trump's rise in the United States, challenges Francis Fukuyama's "end of history" thesis. In Tang's reading, the Anglo-Saxon model of liberal democracy is not a perfected universal form but one imperfect path of human development that can itself degenerate. The piece begins with Fukuyama and the way his thesis became the intellectual background of globalisation advocacy. It then examines three readings of Brexit: the globalist view that treats Leave as backward and closed, the generational explanation (young Remainers versus old Leavers), and the nationalist view that Brexit means a return to imperial glory and "splendid isolation". It goes on to discuss Mark Monmonier's How to Lie with Maps, Karl Polanyi, and Alexandre Kojève's reading of the end of history. Tang's central move is to say that both camps think in binary terms and turn Brexit into a contest of positions rather than an "event" with gains for some and losses for others. The generational account, in Tang's view, fails because today's elderly voters were the young who voted to stay in the European Communities in 1975. The nostalgic account also fails, since Britain once balanced the continent from a position of strength, whereas a weakened Britain loses influence by leaving. Tang adds that globalisation has produced rising non-Western powers, clashes of civilisations, migration and identity problems, and job and welfare losses in Britain and America. Elites who dismiss voters as a "mob" ignore Polanyi's point that society protects itself when it is damaged. Tang concludes that globalisation cannot and will not mean Anglo-Americanisation, and that Brexit does not mean a return to the past either. Drawing on Kojève, Tang urges managing the positive and negative effects of events rather than imagining an end point, and recognising that every development path can contribute something universal. Anglo-American society is to be surpassed, not treated as an object of faith. Read the original if you want a short Chinese commentary from 2016 that uses Brexit to criticise the end-of-history thesis and binary debate about globalisation.

China and world socialism 中国与世界社会主义 Tian Xinming Tian Xinming asks what socialism with Chinese characteristics means for world socialism. The article's answer has two sides. The concrete path, theoretical system and institutions of Chinese socialism grew out of China's national conditions and cannot be copied elsewhere. Yet the principle of integrating Marxism's universal truth with concrete national realities, together with the 'living soul' of Mao Zedong Thought, has validity beyond China. The article deals only with the second aspect of the China–socialism relationship, the world significance of Chinese theory and practice. It has four parts: the rejection of wholesale transplanting of experience; the universal applicability of the 'integration' principle; the universality of the three basic aspects of Mao Zedong Thought's living soul; and what China's practice shows about the general trend of history and what new problems it poses. Tian draws throughout on Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping, Party resolutions and Lenin's remarks on the general and the particular. Tian argues that the Party's own history of struggle against dogmatism, which treated Comintern resolutions and Soviet experience as sacred, shows that other countries must decide for themselves which Chinese experience suits them. The author then contends that the 'integration' principle is itself a basic principle of Marxism. Marxism's basic tenets reflect general laws, while every country's conditions are particular, so the principle holds beyond China. In the same way, seeking truth from facts, the mass line and independence and self-reliance are described as standpoints and methods, not conclusions tied to a given stage or country. Tian points to Deng Xiaoping's presentation of self-reliance and seeking truth from facts to foreign visitors as evidence for this reading. Tian concludes that China's persistence with socialism, as a country with a fifth of the world's population, supports the Marxist view of historical direction after the Soviet collapse. Tian also stresses that China faces unresolved problems, including keeping public ownership dominant, preventing corruption among officials, upholding Marxist guidance in ideology, and avoiding polarisation of wealth. In Tian's view, China meets these problems first as a front-runner, so its successes and failures are a resource for world socialism. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist argument, grounded in Mao and Deng, on what is and is not exportable from China's experience.

Japanese socialism still has to find its way 日本社会主义的实现仍需摸索 Shi Shaobo This short commentary, published in the China Social Sciences Today in January 2016, asks what the Japanese Communist Party's turn to parliamentary struggle means for the prospects of socialism in Japan. Shi argues that the party has shifted from a revolutionary tradition to work within the capitalist framework. The author warns that it risks mistaking small improvements in welfare for the realisation of socialism. The article begins with the party's position as one of seven parties in the Japanese Diet and its unchanged goal of socialism and communism since 1922. It then looks at Miyamoto-era successor Fuwa Tetsuzo's 2003 proposal on Japan's path in the twenty-first century and the programme revision that followed. It ends with Fuwa's 2014 theory of the "three inevitabilities" of the growth of the subject of social change. Shi reports that in 2003 the party deleted phrases such as "establishing workers' power" and "people's revolution" from its programme. It now seeks democratic reform within existing capitalism, through a united front of workers, citizens, farmers and others. The author credits this approach with gains such as free medical care for some age groups and higher relief payments. Shi argues, however, that the party is a non-governing parliamentary party with very limited influence under continuous bourgeois rule. In Shi's view, treating temporary welfare gains as a sign that socialism is arriving is the "infantile disorder" of utopian socialists. Shi concludes that the shift from revolutionary thinking to parliamentary struggle poses serious ideological and political challenges for Japanese communists. They must keep the socialist goal firmly in mind and constantly examine themselves. Read the original if you want a brief, critical Chinese view of the Japanese Communist Party's post-2003 strategy.

World socialism is now entering a period of seeking revival 当前世界社会主义正进入谋求振兴期 Jiang Hui Writing in 2016, Jiang Hui asks where world socialism stands some twenty-five years after the Soviet and East European upheavals. The article argues that since the early twenty-first century it has emerged from its trough and entered a period of seeking revival through development and change. Jiang holds that this period brings rare opportunities as well as severe challenges, and that socialism with Chinese characteristics is its brightest spot, its benchmark and its mainstay. The article begins by describing how communist parties survived the crisis after the Soviet collapse: some dissolved, renamed themselves or became social-democratic, while others persisted. Jiang cites statistics of roughly 130 parties worldwide that keep the communist name or Marxist character, with about 103 million members, of whom more than 88 million are in the Communist Party of China. It then sorts these parties into four types: ruling parties in existing socialist countries, parties in developed capitalist countries, parties in the former Soviet and East European region, and parties in developing countries. Jiang also mentions non-communist left currents such as Latin American 'twenty-first-century socialism', market socialism and eco-socialism. A section on opportunities and challenges follows, and the article closes with three conclusions. Jiang lists six favourable conditions: the weakening of neo-liberal dominance in the wake of the capitalist crisis, the vindication of socialist criticism and the revived interest in Marx, the recovery and maturing of socialist forces, closer cooperation among left parties, more objective lessons drawn from the Soviet collapse, and China's achievements as a local high tide within a general ebb. Against these stand four difficulties. Capitalism remains stronger than socialism, communist parties are marginalised in Western politics, they lead social movements only weakly, and the global working class remains 'in itself', without a global class consciousness. Jiang therefore warns that crisis does not automatically produce socialist revolution, and that the idea of a single decisive blow is an infantile error. He argues that contemporary capitalism, now in an international monopoly stage, regulates and innovates well beyond the capitalism of Marx's day. Jiang concludes that world socialism will remain at a general low ebb for a considerable time, and that preparations are needed for long-term cooperation and struggle between the two social systems. He calls on China to concentrate on its own affairs, building comprehensive national strength and improving living standards, invoking Deng Xiaoping's and Xi Jinping's statements about the growing influence of China's path. In his view, world socialism's revival depends on the development of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want an example of how a Chinese Party scholar in 2016 surveyed the global communist movement, with membership figures and a typology of parties, and tied its prospects to China.

Left-wing governments in Latin America face severe challenges 拉美左翼政权面临严峻挑战 Xu Shicheng Writing in late 2015, Xu Shicheng asks why the Latin American left, which rose to power from 1999 onwards, now faces what the article calls a severe challenge. Xu argues that after roughly a cycle in office, left-wing and centre-left governments are under pressure from economic slowdown, corruption, domestic opposition, internal divisions and external interference. Xu judges Venezuela and Brazil to be the most exposed. The piece opens by tracing the left's rise. Xu attributes it to the failure of traditional ruling parties and of neoliberal reform, beginning with Hugo Chávez's election in Venezuela in 1999 and followed by victories in Brazil, Argentina, Uruguay, Chile, Bolivia, Ecuador, Nicaragua, El Salvador and Peru. It then assesses these governments' record in politics, economics, social policy and foreign policy, before setting out five challenges and the left's responses. In the article's account, left governments won broad support through new constitutions, participatory democracy, nationalisations such as Bolivia's 2006 energy measure, anti-poverty programmes in Brazil and Venezuela, and regional bodies such as ALBA, UNASUR and CELAC. Xu then cites falling commodity prices and regional growth dropping from 2.9% in 2012 to a forecast negative figure in 2015, with Brazil and Venezuela hit hardest. Austerity, scandals such as Brazil's state oil company affair, and protests followed. Xu adds that right-wing forces still hold major cities, that coalitions and parties are split (for example the Workers' Party over its 'rightward turn', and the landless movement over unfulfilled land promises), and that the United States funds opposition groups and pursues 'colour revolution'. Xu notes that left parties recognise these threats. Examples include the 'Latin American Progressive Meetings' in Quito and the 21st São Paulo Forum in Mexico City (2015), whose final statement stressed left unity against imperialism and oligarchies. Xu sees Mauricio Macri's victory in Argentina in November 2015 as swinging the regional pendulum to the centre-right, and flags Venezuela's 6 December parliamentary election as the next test. Read the original if you want a concise, Chinese-academic overview of the state of the Latin American left at the end of the 'pink tide' cycle, with country-level figures and the author's framing of US involvement.

International eco-socialism regards China as an "experimental field" 国际生态社会主义将中国视为 “实验场” Xu Chongwen Xu Chongwen introduces eco-socialism, a current of thought that emerged amid Europe's green movements, and asks how its adherents view China. Xu argues that eco-socialists trace the ecological crisis to the capitalist system and see its solution in replacing capitalism with socialism. On this basis, the article says, they regard China as an "experimental field" of eco-socialism and expect it to lead and set an example globally. The short piece begins with the origins of eco-socialism after the 1970s and its distinction from other ecologisms. It then surveys the visions of socialism held by Michael Löwy, André Gorz and Joel Kovel, and discusses the rise and decline of ecocentrism. It ends with Saral Sarkar's criticism of the Soviet model and his hopes for China. Xu's central contrast is that most ecologists blame science, technology and industrialisation, whereas eco-socialists blame capitalism. Ecocentrism, which Xu describes as an overcorrection against anthropocentrism, dominated global ecologism before the 1990s with its anti-growth, anti-technology stance. Xu says European eco-socialists since 1990 have returned to anthropocentrism, holding that the problem lies in a capitalist way of treating nature rather than in human mastery of it. Citing Sarkar's 1997 book, Xu reports that he sees Soviet bureaucratic socialism as having failed on ecological limits. Sarkar judges that China has a greater chance of success than other countries if its leadership accepts genuine eco-socialism, because of its socialist market economy, family planning policy and emphasis on happiness with fewer material goods. Xu says Sarkar's views differ from those of Marxists but that his expectations of China deserve affirmation. Xu points to the 18th Party Congress (2012), which placed ecological civilization within the five-sphere overall plan and set the goal of a beautiful China, as evidence of the Party's resolve. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese official-academic account of how eco-socialist thinkers are presented as viewing China.

Changing the marginalisation of Marxism 改变马克思主义被边缘化的状况 Chen Xianda Why is Marxism being pushed to the margins in a socialist country, and how can this be reversed? Writing in Beijing Daily in 2016, Chen Xianda takes up Xi Jinping's remark at the symposium on philosophy and social sciences that Marxism has been marginalised, hollowed out and reduced to a label in some fields. Chen argues that the phenomenon is no accident. It follows from international conditions and from the social changes of reform and opening up, and it can be corrected only by holding firm to two economic principles and by improving governance and theoretical work. Chen opens from personal experience. The author recalls studying at Fudan and Renmin University in the early years of the People's Republic, when Marxist courses were prestigious and rarely questioned, and contrasts this with today's classrooms, forums and publications. The article then moves through three sections: the causes of marginalisation, the economic principles that must be upheld, and the social disorders now blamed on the system. It closes with practical demands for ideological work in universities. Chen names external causes: the upheavals in Eastern Europe, the Soviet collapse, the ebb of world socialist revolution and Western ideological infiltration. The internal causes are the shift from a single public ownership to multiple ownership forms and from a planned to a market economy, which Chen says breeds diverging interests and pluralised values. Chen holds that the public sector must remain dominant and that the market economy must be socialist in substance, not "socialism plus a market economy". A purely market logic, the author warns, would push the humanities and Marxism aside. On corruption, the wealth gap and moral decline, Chen distinguishes the basic system (zhi) from governance (zhi), citing Liu Zongyuan's remark that the fault lay in the people, not in the system. The system is sound, in Chen's view, but governance of the market is inadequate, and young people's doubts about Marxism stem from resentment at such disorders, not from reading Marxist texts. Chen calls for lawful, effective management of the ideological sphere, higher standards of Marxist research and propaganda, and a higher political standing for Marxist theorists, who should see themselves as fighters on the theoretical front. Chen also proposes judging Marxist scholars by whether they address China's real problems, not by counting books and articles, and warns that without changing these evaluation standards marginalisation will persist. Read the original if you want a senior Chinese Marxist philosopher's 2016 diagnosis of why Marxism is losing ground in universities and what institutional remedies the author proposes.

Diverse explorations out of the trough The "five crests" in the revival of world socialism 走出低谷的多样探索 Wang Dong Writing in 2016, more than twenty years after the collapse of the Soviet Union and the upheavals in Eastern Europe (1991), Wang Dong asks what trends and currents are now visible in world socialism. The author's overall judgement is that, helped by the general crisis of capitalism in the age of economic globalisation, contemporary world socialism has left its lowest point and is exploring diverse new paths suited to a new era and to national conditions. Wang identifies five "crests" in this warming tide. The short article is organised as a survey of five currents: ecological socialism responding to the global ecological crisis; calls for socialist justice in the face of polarisation; the search for twenty-first-century socialism in Latin America; calls for a socialist revival in Russia and other Commonwealth of Independent States countries; and Vietnam's exploration of a path of renewal (đổi mới). Each section gives a brief account of figures and events, drawing on interviews, books and leaders' statements. On ecology, Wang reports the view that the ecological crisis is rooted not in science and technology but in the internal contradictions of the capitalist mode of production, with its drive for maximum profit, and notes that ecosocialists influence politics in Europe and the Americas. On justice, Wang points to the worldwide debate around Thomas Piketty's Capital in the Twenty-First Century (2014) after the 2008 financial crisis, and cites David Harvey's view that Piketty's data are valuable but his explanation and remedies are flawed, so that Marx or a modern equivalent is still needed. For Latin America, Wang summarises the proposals of Ecuador's Rafael Correa ("modern socialism" combining market and state) and Bolivia's Evo Morales ("good socialism" based on shared, harmonious living), after Hugo Chávez's death in 2013. In Russia, Wang cites the Moscow philosopher A. Bagaturia's 2015 call to analyse the Soviet collapse with classical Marxism and to create new theory, while in Vietnam the discussion centres on Ho Chi Minh Thought, which combines national and class struggle and patriotism with internationalism. Wang concludes that these currents show socialism recovering through varied paths rather than a single model, and presents the capitalist crisis as the common background. The text is a brief overview and offers no extended theoretical argument or evaluation of the cases. Read the original if you want a compact, 2016 Chinese-language snapshot of how a Chinese scholar framed the revival of world socialism, with pointers to figures such as Correa, Morales, Harvey and Bagaturia.

Chinese experience deepens Sino-Russian inter-party relations 中国经验深化中俄党际关系 Li Yazhou Writing in a newspaper commentary in 2016, Li Yazhou examines how the Communist Party of the Russian Federation (CPRF), successor to the Soviet Communist Party, views socialism with Chinese characteristics. Li argues that the CPRF, led by Gennady Zyuganov, holds China's experience in high regard and actively seeks to learn from it, which in turn strengthens ties with the Communist Party of China, formally established in 1995. The article draws on statements and writings by Zyuganov and other CPRF figures, notably Central Presidium member Vladimir Vichmanov. It is organised under four headings: praise for China's achievements, China as a pole of a multipolar world, the uniqueness of China's reform experience, and expectations for the "Chinese Dream". It also lists CPRF delegations to China, including Zyuganov's visits in 1995, 2004, 2006 and 2014 and a youth delegation in 2013. Li reports that the CPRF contrasts Russia's capitalist reforms, which it says brought the economy near collapse, with China's reform and opening up under Party leadership. In Li's account, Zyuganov holds that China's Party character as vanguard of both the working class and the whole nation offers lessons for Russian communists, and that Russia should maintain close ties with China for reasons of economic complementarity and resistance to global hegemonism. Vichmanov is said to defend Deng Xiaoping Theory against charges that Chinese communists have abandoned Marxism. Zyuganov also lists problems China must manage, including growth, political stability and avoiding a Soviet-style collapse. Li concludes that the CPRF expects to deepen relations with the Communist Party of China, to promote friendly Sino-Russian state relations, and to remain optimistic about the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a concise, officially oriented account of how the CPRF's praise for China is presented in Chinese Party-affiliated media.

Tactical success and strategic impasse: the world socialist movement since the 2008 financial crisis 战役成功与战略困局：2008年金融危机以来的世界社会主义运动发展态势 Nie Yunlin Writing in Marxist Studies in 2015, Nie Yunlin asks why the 2008 financial crisis, which put capitalism "in the dock of history", did not produce a resurgence of the world socialist movement. The article's answer is that communist parties in capitalist countries won a "campaign-level" (tactical) success but no strategic victory. They remain marginalised in political life, and the movement is still at a low ebb. The article has two parts. The first reviews what communist parties in capitalist countries did after 2008 and why their gains were limited, drawing on speeches by delegates to the 11th International Meeting of Communist and Workers' Parties. The second sets out six problems that Nie says the parties must solve to break the strategic impasse. These are internal division, "left" and right deviations, democratic centralism, class and mass bases, left alliances, and the constraints of the bourgeois political system. Nie credits the parties with analysing the crisis theoretically, joining strikes and protests, voting against crisis-shifting policies in parliament, and strengthening party-building and international cooperation. Membership stabilised or grew in some parties, for example the Communist Party of India (Marxist), which kept more than a million members. The limits are attributed to the legacy of the Soviet and East European collapse, welfare systems that blunted workers' political consciousness, weak capacity for innovation, and sectarian splits. Nie cites the number of rival communist parties in Britain, India, Turkey and Russia. The author argues that parties which kept democratic centralism, such as those of India (Marxist), Japan and Portugal, recovered strength, while those that dropped it, such as the French, Spanish and Italian Refoundation parties, declined. Nie adds that, in the author's account, the parties have lost their ties to trade unions, struggle to win over the middle classes, and are hemmed in by electoral, two-party and separation-of-powers arrangements. Nie concludes that the crisis-era success is comparable to the Defence of Huangyangjie in the Jinggangshan period: a single battle won, with a long struggle still ahead.
