The task of the post-crisis period is to explore socialist paths suited to each country, and the most pressing step is for each party to resolve its own internal problems. Read the original if you want a Chinese Party-affiliated scholar's assessment of Western communist parties after 2008, including the argument for democratic centralism and against both "left" and right deviations.

Foreign scholarship on the communist movements of twentieth-century Southeast Asia: a review 国外关于20世纪东南亚共产主义运动的研究述评 Liu Lianfen Shi Yili This is a literature review of foreign research, mostly in English with a little in French, on the communist movements that spread across Southeast Asia from the early twentieth century to the 1980s. Liu and Shi treat these movements as part of both regional history and the rise and decline of international communism in Asia. They note that the movements were shaped by anti-colonial struggle, the war against Japan and the Cold War, and that armed communist struggles largely ended only in the late 1980s. The review moves from regional and international perspectives to country studies. It covers the early Cold War works of the 1950s, studies of the 1960s and 1970s, and Singapore-based volumes of the 1980s. It then turns to Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia, to Indonesia, Malaysia and the Philippines, and finally to Burma and Thailand. For each country it lists major monographs, memoirs, document collections and doctoral theses. Liu and Shi highlight several clusters of work. On Vietnam, they point to historical studies (McAlister, Turner, Pike, Duiker), research on the Vietnamese Workers' Party's position between China and the USSR, and comparisons of British counter-insurgency in Malaya with the American effort in South Vietnam. On Laos and Cambodia, they note work on the Pathet Lao's dependence on Vietnam and the attention given to the Khmer Rouge. For Malaya they distinguish participants' accounts, such as Chin Peng's memoir, from scholarly studies. Their remarks on Indonesia concern the 1948 Madiun uprising and the 1965 destruction of the party, and on the Philippines the studies by participants and journalists. On Burma they note Lintner's history and the document collections. On Thailand they note studies of the party's Maoist orientation and of China's role in its armed struggle. The authors' overall assessment is that this scholarship was clearly shaped by the course of the Cold War in Asia and relied mostly on government publications and press reports. They add that studies from the angle of the international communist movement are comparatively few, and they point to useful reference materials such as FBIS broadcast translations and the Hoover Institution's yearbook. The review mainly surveys and describes and does not set out a new programme of research. Read the original if you need a bibliographic guide, organised by country, to English-language scholarship on Southeast Asian communist parties and their links with the Comintern, the Soviet Union and China.

How the social-democratic welfare state transcends and falls short of liberalism and its individualism 社会民主主义福利国家对自由主义及其个人主义的超越和局限 Zhu Xuhong Writing in Zhejiang Social Sciences in 2016, Zhu Xuhong asks whether the post-war social-democratic welfare state, especially in the Nordic countries, moves beyond liberalism, individualism and capitalism, or remains within them. The article's answer is double. The welfare state shows a real critical and transcending relation to liberalism, but this is non-institutional and confined to the capitalist framework. Zhu concludes that the welfare state is not a socialist state. The article begins with the origins of the term, from Bismarck's Germany to Attlee's Britain in 1948, and with Esping-Andersen's three types of welfare state. Zhu focuses on the social-democratic (Nordic) type, with Sweden as its showcase. It then sets out the model's features (mixed economy, full employment, fair distribution, social welfare and security) and its reported achievements in lower poverty, social stability and reported happiness. Zhu first argues that social-democratic values mark a break with liberalism and individualism. These are an 'active' view of freedom that uses state power, equality of outcome as well as opportunity, a principle of mutual aid, economic planning and expanded public ownership, weaker bourgeois rights, and stronger workers' co-determination. Zhu also reads neoliberal hostility to the welfare state as evidence of this transcendence. The article then turns to the limits. Zhu argues that social democrats retreated from public ownership of the means of production to regulating distribution, with Swedish theorists and party congresses holding that ownership matters less than how firms are run. The article cites figures showing that over 90 per cent of Swedish productive assets are privately held. It cites Swedish interlocutors who call Sweden capitalist and describe its model as 'welfare capitalism'. Zhu concludes that the welfare state is a capitalist system with more socialist elements than before, in income distribution, economic democracy and social security. At most it shows that capitalism can serve public welfare better than once thought. The article treats the social-democratic equation of socialism with welfare policy as a retreat on the core question of ownership. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's assessment of Nordic social democracy, drawing on many Chinese-language sources and Swedish interviews, and an account of why the author denies it the label socialist.

An analysis of the Communist Party of the Russian Federation and its youth problem 俄共及其青年问题探析 Cao Peng Writing in 2016 in China Youth Studies, Cao Peng asks why the Communist Party of the Russian Federation (KPRF), heir to the Communist Party of the Soviet Union (CPSU), is losing its young people. The article argues that the party's shrinking strength and ageing membership reflect a severe youth problem. Cao traces it to outdated youth policy, the lack of a leadership-replacement mechanism, factional strife and weak implementation by party organisations, and adds pressure from rival parties. The article first contrasts the CPSU, with roughly 19 million members in 1987, with the KPRF, which Cao says had fewer than 160,000 members by January 2013 and about 130,000 by 2014. It then presents age data: in 2013, by Cao's figures, 10.79 per cent of members were under 30 and 62.76 per cent over 50, so the party is nicknamed a 'party of the old'. Five causes of youth loss follow, and the article ends with five lessons for communist parties. Cao argues that the 2008 programme speaks of youth only in general, abstract terms and never says what 'renewed socialism' would offer young Russians raised under capitalism. Leadership for life, symbolised by Gennady Zyuganov's unchallenged position since 1993, is said to block promotion and keep stale working methods. Splits between 2000 and 2004 and later infighting damaged the party's image and diverted young members to a rival faction. Cao adds that central youth policy, though announced in 2005 and 2008, was not carried out by local organisations. The party's declining power in the Duma, young people's resistance to its ideology, and competition from Putin, United Russia's 'Young Guard' and pro-government youth groups are also named. Cao draws five lessons: treat young people as the foundation of party building; keep pace with the times; rejuvenate membership and cadres through real succession mechanisms; preserve unity and the party's image; and make socialism appeal to the young by linking their demands with Marxist ideas, which Cao calls 'the youthification of socialism'. Read the original if you study the post-Soviet communist movement, party ageing, or how Chinese scholars draw lessons for party-youth relations from the Russian case.

The current state of socialist parties in Asia, Africa and Latin America and the reasons for it 亚非拉地区社会党发展现状及其原因 Xiang Wenhua Writing in early 2016, Xiang Wenhua surveys the socialist parties of Asia, Africa and Latin America and asks why they have multiplied so quickly. The article reports more than 100 such parties, 31 of which govern alone or take part in government. It argues that they are guided mainly by social democracy or democratic socialism, and that their rise rests fundamentally on the replacement of earlier development models in the region. The study counts parties that belong to the Socialist International (85), parties that claim social-democratic or democratic-socialist principles without belonging (for example five in Central Asia), and eleven parties suspended in 2014 for unpaid dues. Part one describes the present situation: the parties' origins by period, their governing status as of January 2016, their ideology and policies, and uneven development across regions (25 parties in Asia, 45 in Africa, 31 in Latin America). Part two gives five explanations for the growth. Xiang finds that most of these parties are still in opposition. Most declare social democracy rather than democratic socialism, which the author reads as an abandonment of the aim of replacing capitalism. Many also keep other ideologies such as nationalism, populism or a 'middle way', so they are less uniform than their West European counterparts. The causes the author gives are the political vacuum left when radical socialist and communist parties declined after the Cold War, and the example of the British Labour Party, Nordic parties and successful governing parties such as Mauritius's Labour Party. Further causes are Socialist International recruitment and the European education of leaders such as Nehru and Senghor. The central explanation is the failure of four models: radical socialism, village-community socialism, populism and neoliberalism. The author cites falling per capita GDP, rising poverty and widening inequality, and presents social democracy as a way to pursue efficiency while keeping equality and justice. Xiang concedes that opportunism, such as seeking foreign aid or influence, also played a part, but holds that the substitution of development models is the root cause. The article notes that the parties' momentum has weakened while their influence has not, and calls for continued tracking research. Read the original if you want a detailed, country-by-country inventory of social-democratic parties in the Global South, or a Chinese academic account of why left parties turned to social democracy after 1989.

The German Left Party sees China as the most important birthplace of "Socialism 3.0" 德国左翼党认为中国是“社会主义3.0”最重要的诞生地 Zhang Wenhong This piece reports a lecture given on 24 May (2016) at the invitation of the Party Research Centre of the Central Compilation and Translation Bureau. The speaker was Charles (Charle) Bri, a senior researcher at the Left Party's Rosa Luxemburg Foundation in Germany; the name is given only in Chinese transliteration (夏尔·布里). Titled "The Third Wave of Socialism", the lecture holds that the Soviet collapse 25 years earlier did not end socialism but opened a third wave, "Socialism 3.0", and that China is its most important birthplace. Zhang's report follows the lecture's three-part structure. It first outlines two earlier waves: 1789–1917 and 1917–1991. It then sets out two features of the third wave, which began in 1991. Finally it turns to the crisis of modern capitalism and to China's place in the future of socialism. In the speaker's account, the first wave produced the main socialist currents, with Marxism giving them a scientific basis. The second wave ran from the October Revolution to the Soviet collapse and included the Chinese revolution and Western social-democratic welfare states. It failed because the Soviet model stagnated, social democracy could not contain accumulation, and neoliberalism put both on the defensive. For the third wave, the speaker says an alternative to capitalism must be a learning, "polycentric" society, neither bureaucratically centralised like the Soviet system nor competition-driven like the American one. It must also foster a new, harmonious civilisation that balances humans with nature and work with leisure. Capitalism, the speaker argues, has largely fulfilled its mission, which Marx called a "temporary necessity". It now faces ecological, identity, political-legitimacy and international-security crises, while the movements opposing it lack a convincing alternative. The speaker cites Perry Anderson's remark that the twenty-first century will be shaped by Chinese revolutionary events, as the twentieth was by the Soviet ones. The speaker links China's "Socialism 3.0" to the post-1978 learning process, theoretical innovation and the Chinese Dream, which joins modern civilisation to China's traditional culture. Five conditions are listed for a socialist association: ecological productive forces, diverse forms of ownership, bodies for political consultation, a culture of solidarity, and a peaceful international system. If these are met, the speaker says, the twenty-first century could be a century of global socialism. Read the original if you want to see how a Left Party thinker, as presented in a Party journal in 2016, periodises socialism and places China within it.

The evolution of Marxism in Cuba and its lessons 马克思主义在古巴的演进及启示 Li Jianguo Li Jianguo, writing in 2016, treats Cuba as the only socialist country outside Asia and asks what the development of Marxism there can teach the effort to understand the laws governing the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context. The article argues that Cuba's path, shaped by its particular national conditions, offers lessons on theory, reform and popular support. The piece has four parts. It first describes Cuba's national conditions: its status as a US dependency before 1959, the long US blockade afterwards, and a strong popular sense of independence. It then divides the history of Marxism in Cuba into five stages, from the democratic revolution (1944–1959) to the reforms of the post-Soviet "special period". A third part summarises Cuban theoretical results, and a fourth draws three lessons. In Li's account, Cuba's early "revolutionary offensive" of 1968 broke with reality, and the country then copied the Soviet model from 1971 to 1989, which deepened its economic dependence. After the collapse of the Soviet bloc, Cuba turned to building "socialism with Cuban characteristics" and made José Martí's thought, alongside Marxism-Leninism, the Party's guiding ideology in 1991. Li reports that Cuba sees the essence of socialism as national independence and the welfare of the people, avoids the word "reform", keeps a planned economy, and opens to the outside world only on conditions. Li also notes that Cuba has not yet raised economic construction to the level of socialism's essence, and that Cuba judges the present to be an era of two social systems in struggle. Li draws three lessons: hold to Marxism-Leninism, Martí's thought and socialism as the theoretical and institutional foundation; carry out steady reform to "update" the socialist model while limiting social costs; and protect the fundamental interests of the people, citing free healthcare and education, subsidies and clean conduct among Party cadres. Li treats popular trust in the Party as the key to Cuba's survival under internal and external pressure and as the feature other socialist states should most learn from. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's 2016 overview of Cuban socialism's stages and its supposed relevance for China and other socialist countries.

The Latin American left in retreat: causes of the 2015–2016 setbacks and the case against declaring its death 日本马克思主义经济学者眼中的全球危机 Writing in spring 2016, the author asks why left-wing governments in Latin America have suffered successive blows in the preceding six months, and whether the left is now in lasting decline. The answer is that the setbacks are real and have deep domestic and external causes, but that the left is neither dead nor dying. The article contends that the region's political pendulum has swung right and may swing back towards the centre-left after policy adjustment. The piece opens with a country-by-country account of the swing to the right. It covers the election of Mauricio Macri in Argentina (November 2015), the opposition's two-thirds victory in Venezuela's National Assembly (December 2015) and the ensuing clash with President Maduro, the impeachment vote against Dilma Rousseff in Brazil's lower house (April 2016), Evo Morales's referendum defeat in Bolivia, and Rafael Correa's decision not to stand again in Ecuador. It then lists five causes, and closes with evidence of the left's continuing strength. The author's five causes are as follows. First, the end of the commodity-export boom, which the article says slowed growth, forced austerity and left governments exposed after they failed to diversify their economies. Second, fragmented ruling coalitions and factional parties, with Brazil's Workers' Party and its coalition partner the PMDB as the main case. Third, corruption scandals that undermined the left's anti-corruption credentials and fuelled protest, often led by a new middle class. Fourth, what the author describes as US interference through funding of opposition groups, support for colour revolution tactics and sanctions on Venezuela. Fifth, rising right-wing strength in cities, provinces and a largely right-leaning media. In rebutting claims that the left has died, the author points to the Cuban Communist Party's Seventh Congress (April 2016), to left governments still in office in many countries, and to the strength of the Peronists in Argentina and of left parties in Mexico and Peru. Persistent inequality and social conflict, together with the left's record on poverty, education, health and regional integration, are said to give it a solid base. The author concludes that, if left parties reflect on their errors, the pendulum may swing back, and ends with a remark by former Uruguayan president Mujica that the left should learn and return. Read the original if you want a concise 2016 Chinese overview of the Latin American left's reversals, with figures on the economy and elections.

The global crisis in the eyes of Japanese Marxist economists 日本马克思主义经济学者眼中的全球危机 Watanabe Masao Tan Xiaojun Writing in 2016, Watanabe Masao and Tan Xiaojun survey how Japanese Marxist economists have interpreted the global financial crisis that began in 2008 and the subsequent eurozone debt crisis. The article is a review of the three main schools of Japanese Marxist economics: the orthodox school, the Uno school and the regulation school. The authors present the schools' views and conclude that the orthodox account is the most penetrating. The article is organised around two kinds of understanding that Japanese scholars bring to the crisis: a 'stage' view of contemporary capitalism, and a 'current situation' view of the crisis itself. The first section draws on reports given by Kitahara Isamu (orthodox), Ito Makoto (Uno) and Yamada Toshio (regulation) at a 1995 conference. The second section treats each school's analysis of the post-2008 crisis, mainly through Imura Kiyoko, Ito Makoto (with Kaneko Masaru) and Yamada. A short conclusion compares them. Imura, the orthodox representative, argues that capitalism underwent a 'degeneration' in the 1970s, after the end of dollar–gold convertibility and the turn to neoliberal policy. She holds that this produced speculative financial activity detached from the real economy, and that the eurozone sovereign-debt crisis followed from European states' pursuit of a finance-based national strategy and from banks' purchase of sovereign debt. Ito sees a return of liberal market competition and reads the crisis as a modern form of Marx's 'second type' of monetary panic, with workers facing a double exploitation through consumer credit. Yamada reads the crisis as structural, a shift from Fordism to a finance-led growth model driven by asset prices that collapsed in 2008, and sorts national economies into seven types. The authors find three points of agreement: the crisis dates from the 1970s transition, it reflects a shift from production-led to finance-led capitalism, and its core is financial movement independent of real capital. They see differences in method. In their judgement Imura's treatment is more comprehensive and persuasive, while Ito's and Yamada's are narrower and one-sided, though still useful as other angles. They also call Ito's three factors for avoiding collapse nearly impossible to realise. Read the original if you want a Chinese-language overview of Japanese Marxist crisis theory and a mainland scholar's evaluation of its schools.

Research on foreign communist parties Comparing domestic and overseas scholarship, and ways forward 国外共产党研究 Yu Haiqing Writing in a Chinese Academy of Social Sciences newspaper in January 2016, Yu asks how Chinese research on foreign communist parties differs from Western research, and what Chinese scholars can learn. The field, Yu notes, was marginalised after the Soviet collapse and is now drawing renewed Western attention with the partial revival of the European radical left. Yu argues that comparison with overseas work can widen Chinese scholars' horizons and open new lines of inquiry. The short piece has two parts. The first compares domestic and overseas scholarship on four points: perspective, scope, themes and analytical framework. The second sets out three proposed paths for Chinese research. Yu says Chinese studies usually treat foreign communist parties within the international communist movement and as separate cases. Western scholars treat them as parties within a party system and as one family within the radical left, and they ask what the parties do, for example in relation to European integration, trade unions and social movements. Western work also uses interdisciplinary methods, such as mathematical models of radical-left electoral support. Chinese work, in Yu's account, relies largely on internet sources, offers little fieldwork, tends to describe single cases in depth, and is only beginning to use the radical-left concept, with some confusion. Yu calls for Chinese scholars to draw on overseas findings, to move beyond detailed case description to the realities of contemporary capitalism and the future of the world socialist movement, and to develop comparative, general theory. Yu says this should build on existing strengths. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese assessment, from 2016, of the gaps in domestic scholarship on foreign communist parties.

The Western "Marx fever" and its lessons 西方“马克思热”及其启示 Cui Lihua Writing in the People's Daily in February 2016, Cui asks what the renewed Western interest in Marx since the 2008 international financial crisis shows. The article argues that Marxism, long treated in Western mainstream opinion as a heterodoxy confined to marginal academic and left-wing circles, is again drawing attention because the crisis exposed contradictions capitalism cannot overcome. In Cui's view, this offers evidence of the truth of Marxism. The commentary is a short survey of signs of this "Marx fever". It covers mainstream media coverage, book sales, protest slogans, university courses, statements by Western scholars, and study groups and sites devoted to Marx. It ends with a reference to Deng Xiaoping's remarks in the early 1990s. Cui's evidence is descriptive. The Guardian, The Times, the Financial Times and Time are said to have given Marx prominent space, and slogans such as "Marx was right!" are reported from Wall Street and German streets. Terry Eagleton's Why Marx Was Right (2011), Elmar Altvater's essay and David Harvey's work on capitalism's contradictions are presented as scholarly defences of Marxism or calls to "return to Marx". Cui also cites Germany's "Marx evening school", Harvey's Capital reading group and visitor numbers at Marx's birthplace museum in Trier. Cui concludes that this revival supports Deng Xiaoping's early-1990s prediction, made when the collapse of the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe had left many pessimistic, that more people would come to endorse Marxism "because Marxism is a science". The Western trend is therefore taken as indirect confirmation of Marxism's truth in the contemporary world. Read the original if you want a brief example of how a Party newspaper in 2016 used Western interest in Marx to affirm Marxism's validity.

The new vision of civilisation in Western Marxist research 西方马克思主义研究的新文明构想 Che Yuling Writing in a 2016 newspaper commentary, Che Yuling asks where human civilisation should go after the Enlightenment, whose legacy the author links to technological over-extension, nihilism, consumerism, environmental degradation and moral decline. Che argues that contemporary Western Marxists offer a constructive answer: a new type of civilisation that overcomes the defects of modern civilisation and avoids resource depletion, ecological damage and spiritual crisis. The piece has three parts. It first sets out the features of a new civilisation as Marx describes them, then the claim that the network era calls for one, and finally the Marxist route to realising it. It draws on ecological Marxism, historical-geographical materialism, David Harvey and István Mészáros, and ends with a note on China. Che reads Marx as treating all social formations up to capitalism as 'prehistory', after which a truly human history begins in communism centred on the all-round development of the human being, not on the economy. Contemporary ecological Marxists and historical-geographical materialists draw three features from this: the liberation of both humans and nature, a 'co-existence' that goes beyond the nation-state, and a meaningful, poetic life. Che adds that Harvey's 'time-space compression' and the rise of network-based 'space economy' have made capital global, uneven in development and culturally corrosive. Following Marx's view that 'the real barrier of capitalist production is capital itself', Che argues that capital's expansion into every field shrinks its own profit space. Mészáros's 'structural crisis' is cited as showing that 'going beyond capital' is the only option. Che concludes that China's Scientific Outlook on Development and its ecological civilisation drive already show the new civilisation Marx envisaged. In this reading, Chinese practice and Marxist theory confirm each other, and Western Marxist visions of a new civilisation have real relevance. Read the original if you want a short, officially aligned Chinese introduction to how Western Marxist ecological and spatial theories are used to support the idea of a new civilisation.

Latin American Marxism since 1909 Transcending "Eurocentrism" and "Indo-American exceptionalism" 1909年以来的拉美马克思主义 Michael Löwy This is a Chinese translation of an article by the French Marxist sociologist and philosopher Michael Löwy (given in the Chinese text as M. Roy), part of a series on Latin American Marxism since 1909. Löwy argues that two opposed errors have haunted Marxism in Latin America: Eurocentrism, which mechanically transplants the European nineteenth-century pattern of development, and "Indo-American exceptionalism", which treats Latin American particularity as absolute and Marxism as a purely European theory. The creative path, he holds, lies in a dialectical unity of the universal and the particular. The article is a historical survey from the introduction of Marxism by European immigrants in the late nineteenth century to the 1970s and early 1980s. It moves through the Second International's parties, the communist parties of the 1920s, the Stalinisation of the 1930s, the post-war debates on economic history, the Cuban Revolution, Castroism, the Central American revolutions and liberation theology. Figures discussed include Julio Antonio Mella, José Carlos Mariátegui, Vittorio Codovilla, Sergio Bagú, Caio Prado Jr., Silvio Frondizi, Che Guevara, Gunder Frank and Gustavo Gutiérrez. Löwy contends that both errors, despite their opposition, reach the same conclusion: that socialism does not suit Latin America. He offers Haya de la Torre's APRA as the exceptionalist case and Stalinist stage theory, calling for an anti-feudal bourgeois-democratic revolution, as the Eurocentric one. Against both he sets thinkers who argued that colonial and dependent capitalism, not feudalism, shaped the region, that the national bourgeoisie is weak and subordinate to imperialism, and that revolution must therefore be socialist. Mariátegui is presented as the strongest example of the synthesis, combining internationalism with indigenous communal traditions. Löwy treats the Cuban Revolution as a turning point that broke the Eurocentric and Stalinist hold and revived the "original communism" of the 1920s. Löwy concludes that the successes of Latin American Marxism came when it joined general principles to regional realities. He also notes the limits of guerrilla voluntarism and the new weight of radical Christianity, which he says should now be seen as an organic part of revolutionary movements. He ends by endorsing Mariátegui's call for unity among socialist currents without giving up their theoretical differences. Read the original if you want a compact, sympathetic overview of Latin American Marxist currents and their disputes over stages of revolution, dependency and the Latin American revolutionary tradition.

Marxist movements in Africa 非洲的马克思主义运动 Glaser Is there a distinctive African contribution to Marxist thought? The article, credited to Glaser and published in Marxism and Reality in 2014, notes that many African Marxist-Leninist leaders flatly denied it. After the first wave of post-independence "African socialism", they insisted on a single universal Marxism-Leninism. The author argues that African Marxism was not without original contributions, and that African socialism should be counted as an independent contribution to it. The article moves from African socialism to the later Marxist-Leninist regimes. It begins with Pan-Africanism, W.E.B. DuBois, George Padmore, Kwame Nkrumah, Sékou Touré and Julius Nyerere. It then covers Soviet theories of a "non-capitalist" path and three routes by which Marxism reached Africa: colonial contacts, multi-ethnic urban milieux, and the communist bloc. Further sections treat military coups, guerrilla "people's war" and Amilcar Cabral, and the exceptional cases of South Africa and Ethiopia. The article closes with the decline of African Marxism after 1989–91. The author makes three main moves. First, the regimes were not mere Soviet creations: Marxist governments often kept Western links, and their authoritarianism is attributed to home-grown African Leninism. Glaser defends the military regimes against critics who doubted their sincerity, but also doubts that guerrilla movements were more democratic or more committed to socialism. Second, the author lists genuine innovations. These include Siad Barre's attempt to combine Marxism with Islam, the Eritrean and Tigrayan fronts' positions on national self-determination, Touré's mass-party experiments, and Madagascar's limited multiparty system. Third, the author explains the failures. External causes were underdevelopment, war and Cold War pressures. Internal causes were impatience, forced rural policies, alienation of society, and a Leninist idea of participation as mobilisation towards goals set by the ruling party, not as free choice among competing projects. Glaser concludes that African socialism and Marxism were short-lived, with most regimes liberalising from the mid-1980s and renouncing Marxism in 1990–91. The turn to representative democracy at least lets citizens remove bad rulers, but the author says dependence on the IMF and World Bank has narrowed real choice and that the new capitalism is no panacea. Socialists and social democrats should avoid neoliberal traps, learn from the negative lessons of African Marxism, and may still need Marxism to analyse new class inequalities. Read the original if you want a detailed comparative survey of African socialist and Marxist regimes, from Ghana and Guinea to Ethiopia and Madagascar, and an assessment of why they failed.

The method of ecological Marxism 生态马克思主义的方法 Hannah Holleman This text is a Chinese version of a conference paper by Hannah Holleman (the name is rendered in Chinese in the source). It asks what methodology underlies the strengths of what John Bellamy Foster calls the "third stage" of ecosocialist research. Holleman argues that the revival of ecological Marxism comes from strict adherence to Marx's own method, which she holds is still a powerful tool for social change. The paper first sketches three stages of ecosocialism since the 1980s. The first grafted Marx onto existing green theory, assuming Marx offered no ecological foundation. The second returned to Marx's materialist and naturalist roots, though Holleman, following Foster, calls it simplified, idealised and moralising. The third restores Marx's radical materialist critique and dialectics. The paper then sets out five features of Marx's method and briefly surveys recent applications, such as a study of oceans and fisheries, before ending with a conclusion on ecological civilization. The five features are: embracing materialism, using abstraction critically, applying dialectics, attending to historical specificity, and linking ethical and political change to critical social analysis. Holleman, drawing on Sweezy, Lewontin and Levins, and York and Mancus, contends that abstraction must be chosen to fit the problem and tested against historical evidence. Dialectics, she says, steers between reductionism and an undifferentiated holism that treats everything as "one". She presents Marx's account of labour as a metabolic process between humans and nature as the historical and ecological base of this method. Citing Mészáros, she argues that ethics cannot replace a thorough critique of politics. In the conclusion Holleman proposes that the method be used to assess the aims and strategies of any movement, including those that call themselves socialist, since ideological slogans may diverge from practice. She names three conditions for a worthwhile struggle: material and political equality, an end to all forms of oppression and exploitation, and a society in which rational regulation governs the human relation to nature. She contrasts this with romantic green ideas and with ecological modernization theory. Whether the goal is called ecological civilization or something else, she holds that critical social analysis is needed to overcome obstacles. Read the original if you want a compact statement of the methodological foundations of the Monthly Review school of ecological Marxism, as presented to a Chinese audience interested in ecological civilization.

The European refugee crisis and the predicament of "universal values" 欧洲难民危机与“普世价值”的困境 Zhang Weiwei Writing in early 2016, Zhang Weiwei takes up the refugee influx into Europe since 2015 and argues that it is directly linked to the "universal values" the West promoted in the Middle East. In Zhang's account, the crisis exposes paradoxes and dilemmas in the idea of "universal values" itself. Europe's early celebration of the "Arab Spring" has, the author says, turned within five years into alarm. The commentary has three parts. The first describes the "arrogance" of promoting "freedom", "democracy" and "human rights" as universal, and recounts two waves of Western-backed "democratization" in the Middle East: the post-2003 Iraq war and "Greater Middle East" plan, and the uprisings from 2011. The second sets out four paradoxes revealed by the crisis. The third draws lessons for China and the world. Zhang traces the arrogance to a view of history in which the Western model is the end point of human development, reinforced by a missionary tradition. The four paradoxes are as follows. These values were detached from the conditions of Middle Eastern societies and left sectarian, ethnic and economic problems unsolved or worse. Western democratic politics, in which politicians answer to their own voters, works against the human rights of outsiders, as shown by border fences and EU disputes over quotas. The values struggle to accommodate multiculturalism, which Cameron and Merkel had already declared a failure. Abstract principles give way to concrete national interests, including among EU states and in the United States' reluctance to take in refugees. Zhang concludes that Chinese people should always ask why of any value claimed to be universal, and that the crisis shows the significance of persisting with socialism with Chinese characteristics. The author predicts that the West's discursive hegemony will decline, and calls on China, as a responsible major country, to offer ideas of its own, such as "peace and development", which Zhang holds are preconditions for freedom, democracy and human rights. Read the original if you want an example of how a prominent Chinese commentator in a Party journal framed the refugee crisis as a critique of Western "universal values" in 2016.

New trends in Vietnam's foreign strategy after the 12th Congress of the Communist Party of Vietnam 越共十二大之后越南外交战略的新趋向 Pan Jin'e Writing in late 2016, Pan Jin'e asks what new ideas the 12th National Congress of the Communist Party of Vietnam (January 2016) introduced into Vietnam's external strategy and where Vietnamese foreign policy is heading. The article's answer is that Vietnam will keep diplomacy in the service of national interest, integrate actively into the international community, stress economic development while balancing the major powers, and pursue a pragmatic line of "both cooperation and struggle". The article first sets out the Congress report's foreign-policy line and the eight main tasks the Party assigned for the next five years, drawing on the Central Propaganda Department's explanatory materials. It then reviews the practice of the new leadership: the April 2016 changes in office, Prime Minister Nguyen Xuan Phuc's visits to Russia, Japan and China, Barack Obama's visit, reactions to the South China Sea arbitration ruling, and the August 2016 foreign affairs conference. It ends with five trends it expects in coming years, drawing on Vietnam's first Diplomatic Blue Book (2015). Pan argues that Vietnam's diplomacy is, first, anchored in securing a peaceful environment and external resources for economic growth, with economic integration as its core task. Second, it follows an independent, diversified and multilateral line built on non-aligned "partnerships" and the "three nos" (no military alliances, no foreign bases, no reliance on one country against another). Third, it balances the great powers while treating each differently: Japan is welcomed, the United States is both courted and guarded against "peaceful evolution", Russia is a traditional friend with limited economic potential, and China is a close but disputed partner. Pan reads Party General Secretary Nguyen Phu Trong's stress on absolute obedience to unified Party leadership as a sign of disagreement within the leadership, including over China policy. Pan concludes that Vietnam's foreign affairs face instability, citing divisions within the leadership, the South China Sea dispute and what the author calls threats of subversion. Uncertainty over the Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP), which the new National Assembly did not ratify as planned, adds to this. Pan expects Vietnam to keep developing economic ties with China while its China policy may prove unstable or inconsistent, which the author says demands more careful handling of China–Vietnam relations. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's reading of Vietnamese foreign policy in 2016 and of the Vietnamese sources on which it relies.

Drawing lessons from the loss of the Soviet Union's socialist institutional advantages 深刻认识苏联社会主义制度优势丧失的教训 Wang Rui Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2016, Wang Rui asks why the Soviet Union lost the advantages of its socialist system and, in the end, the system itself. The article holds that after strong early achievements, Soviet socialist construction slowed from the 1970s and the system's advantages drained away. From the mid-1980s, Wang argues, reform turned from upholding and improving socialism into a wholesale negation of it, producing economic and social crisis and collapse. The article is organised around four causes, each presented as the loss of one pillar that the system's advantages depend on: a theoretical foundation, institutional support, a material guarantee and a leading core. It moves chronologically through the Khrushchev, Brezhnev and Gorbachev periods. Each section ends with a lesson for present-day socialist countries, and a short conclusion draws on Deng Xiaoping. Wang argues first that ideology moved from rigidity under Brezhnev to outright betrayal under Gorbachev. Dogmatic Marxism-Leninism, the heavy-handed treatment of intellectual disputes and then Gorbachev's "openness" and pluralism are said to have eroded belief and let bourgeois liberalisation spread. Second, after the 19th Party Conference (1988), reform veered off course: Stalin was wholly repudiated, tens of thousands of "informal organisations" arose, nationalist separatism grew, and power shifted from the Party to the soviets, ending the Party's leadership. Third, Wang says that high-speed, poor-quality growth, a lopsided economy and low consumption left the Soviet Union falling behind the United States and the West, fuelling discontent. Fourth, the Party lost its vanguard character and purity: a privileged bureaucracy distanced itself from the people, and Wang lists five changes in the Party's nature, guiding ideology, goals, status and organisational principle (democratic centralism). Wang concludes that the Soviet collapse does not show Marxism-Leninism to be outdated or socialism itself to be flawed, only that the Soviet model had defects. China, the article says, must study this lesson to avoid repeating it. Wang calls for upholding Marxism as the guiding ideology while innovating, reforming without abandoning socialism's basic principles and system, raising productivity with attention to quality and living standards, and keeping the Party close to the people. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Party journal summarised the causes of Soviet collapse in 2016 and the lessons it drew for China.

University ideological and political theory courses should focus on building the classroom 高校思想政治理论课应狠抓课堂建设 Li Yan Writing in 2016, Li Yan takes up the question of how university ideological and political theory courses can do their job under current conditions. The starting point is the Party Central Committee's stress, since the 18th Party Congress (2012), on holding leadership, management, discourse power and initiative in ideological work. Li argues that these courses must therefore treat the classroom as a front line and press ahead with classroom building in three areas: teaching content, the online classroom and the teaching staff. The commentary is organised in three sections. The first concerns content and urges teachers to teach a living Marxism. The second addresses the internet and how teachers and students can judge and select online information. The third deals with teachers as the main shapers of students' values, and proposes planning for their development. On content, Li holds that abstract theory alienates students unless it is tied to real life. Drawing on Mao Zedong's call for a living Marxism and on Marx's point that principles must be studied in their historical conditions, Li proposes linking concepts to everyday life, basic principles to concrete cases, and the uncovering of laws to historical narrative. This is meant to equip students to resist erroneous currents of thought. For the online classroom, Li proposes three designs: bringing online stories into lectures, using mobile internet and multimedia as teaching tools, and setting up Weibo and WeChat groups through which teachers can guide opinion, counter rumours and monitor students' thinking. Li argues that fragmented, decentred online discourse has weakened the authority of classroom speech and the teacher's influence. For teachers, Li calls for three kinds of planning. Layered planning would pair senior teachers' theoretical depth with younger teachers' ease with technology, through mentoring and exchange. Goal planning would align institutional management goals with teachers' own career and teaching goals. Quality planning would treat theoretical, cultural and new-media competence as the base of teachers' soft power. Li adds that the core requirement is conveying socialist ideology to students so that it becomes their own thinking and political awareness. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a 2016 Party journal framed practical teaching reform in ideological and political courses, including the use of social media.

Targeted Party building: comprehensively raising the overall functions of primary-level Party organisations 精准党建：全面提升基层党组织整体功能 Jiang Gang Writing in 2016, Jiang Gang takes up a basic practical question in Party building: what to grasp and how to grasp it, under the slogan that doing Party building well is the greatest political achievement. The article presents the "targeted Party building" campaign of the Yibin municipal Party committee in Sichuan as a model for raising the overall functions of rural primary-level Party organisations. Jiang argues that the campaign unifies the political and service functions of these organisations and promotes interaction between Party building and economic and social development. The article has three parts. The first describes the problems and background; the second sets out four mechanisms Yibin adopted; the third draws results and lessons. The campaign is framed by four goals (good cohesion, good interest linkages, good governance system, good operating model) and by a method of "six manys", which Jiang glosses as integrating plans, balancing industries, layering policies, diversifying investment, running multiple models and coordinating forces. Jiang draws on Xi Jinping's call for precision in reform and for solving problems at each specific point. Jiang identifies four problems in rural Party organisations: pluralising values weaken their ideological leadership; the end of the agricultural tax and the lack of interest linkages loosen ties with villagers; diverse interests and the move from management to service and rule-based self-governance strain their governance role; and rough appraisal leaves cadres passive. Four mechanisms respond. A "1+X" education system of Party-spirit training bases targets cadres, villagers and business owners. A "one unified, four transformations" mechanism turns resources into assets and inputs into income, with 561 industry Party organisations and 606 collectively-poor villages removed from the list in the first half of 2016. A "base salary plus performance" appraisal scheme ties pay and promotion to service results. Legal affairs committees, piloted in 296 village branches, handle legal education, contract review, self-governance and mediation. Jiang concludes that the campaign has moved beyond fragmented grassroots Party building and produced structural change. It uses Party building as the lever for overall development, enriches the objectives of rural Party organisations through the four goals, and replaces broad-brush spending with precisely targeted bundled resources. The article reports Yibin's figures without independent verification. Read the original if you want a Party-published case study of how a local Party committee in 2016 put grassroots Party building, rural industry, appraisal and village governance into one programme.

What was Dimitrov's attitude to the Xi'an Incident? A query on Pantsov's biography of Mao Zedong 季米特洛夫对西安事变的态度究竟如何 Li Yibin Li Yibin takes issue with one passage in Alexander Pantsov's biography of Mao Zedong, whose Chinese edition has drawn wide attention because it draws on declassified Soviet archives. The article asks how Georgi Dimitrov, General Secretary of the Comintern, actually viewed the Xi'an Incident of December 1936. Li argues that Dimitrov opposed the incident, as Stalin did, and that Pantsov's claim that he was delighted by it rests on a misreading of a source. The piece is a short critical note, first published in the Chinese Reading Weekly (Zhonghua dushu bao) in March 2016. It first sketches Dimitrov's career and his role in Comintern work on China. It then sets out Comintern documents and Dimitrov's diary entries from August and December 1936, followed by the Soviet strategic situation and the diary entry that Li believes Pantsov misread. Li's evidence runs in three steps. First, Dimitrov distrusted Zhang Xueliang even before the incident: a telegram of August 1936 told the Chinese Communist Party not to trust him, and after the incident Dimitrov wrote to Stalin suspecting Communist involvement. Second, Li explains Soviet hostility by the memory of Zhang Zuolin's 1927 raid on the Soviet embassy and the killing of Li Dazhao, and above all by Stalin's strategy of backing Chiang Kai-shek against Japan while Germany and Japan threatened the USSR. On this account Dimitrov, a Soviet citizen, could not have diverged from Stalin; his late-night telephone exchange with Stalin on 14 December and the meetings that produced the telegram urging a peaceful settlement show the two in agreement. Third, Li traces the error to Dimitrov's diary entry for 13 December. In it, the favourable, optimistic assessment of Zhang comes from Stomonyakov, the deputy foreign commissar who brought the news, not from Dimitrov himself. Li concludes that Pantsov mistook one speaker for another, a case of "putting Zhang's hat on Li", and that this distorted the historical record. He also notes that Zhou Enlai later called the Comintern's depiction of Zhang as a tool of Japan completely wrong. Read the original if you work on Comintern–CCP relations, the Xi'an Incident or Pantsov's use of Soviet archives and want to see a specific source-critical objection with its citations.

Never let go of the banner of communism 共产主义这面旗帜什么时候都不能丢 Chen Shuguang Writing in Guangming Daily in March 2016, Chen Shuguang responds to what the author calls the "theory of communism's remoteness", the view that communism is illusory and unreachable. Chen takes up Xi Jinping's remarks since the 18th Party Congress (2012) that communism is not as simple as "potatoes stewed with beef" yet is not a mirage. The article argues that communism is the spiritual banner of Communists and must never be abandoned. Chen first reconstructs three lines of reasoning behind the sceptical view: communism concerns only a distant future; "distribution according to need" is unbelievable; and the collapse of the socialist bloc and China's present problems refute the ideal. The commentary answers these in three sections. They deal with communism as both a social system and a movement, with the essence of communism, and with setbacks and the gap between ideal and reality. Chen's central move is to treat communism as a "totality" with three dimensions: a system, a doctrine and a real movement. Citing Marx and Engels's definition of communism as the real movement that abolishes the present state of things, Chen says Chinese revolution, socialist construction and reform are all continuations of that movement. Features such as the leading role of the working class, public ownership and common prosperity are described as communist elements accumulating within socialism. Second, Chen argues that the essence of communism, as Marx and Engels describe it in three ways, is the free and all-round development of each individual, not the literal wording of "distribution according to need". The concrete shape of the distant future, Chen holds, should be left to future practice. Third, Chen attributes the Soviet and East European collapse to departing from Marxism, and says the failure of one socialist model is not the failure of socialism. Chen concludes that the gap between ideal and reality is normal, and that the way forward is to reform reality towards the ideal rather than abandon the ideal to suit reality. The article says China's problems, such as inequality, corruption and pollution, are either growing pains, results of departing from Marxist principles, or costs of practice. Chen holds that socialism with Chinese characteristics keeps the basic principles of scientific socialism and the banner of communism, and that, so long as exploitation and oppression exist, communism remains a banner for justice and liberation. Read the original if you want an example of how a 2016 official-press commentary defends the communist ideal against scepticism inside and outside the Party.

New Youth and the spread of Marxism in China 《新青年》与马克思主义在中国的传播 Yin Yungong Yin Yungong asks how the journal New Youth became the main Chinese vehicle for propagating Marxism-Leninism. The author argues that it did so only after a winding process of understanding, in which the journal and its founder Chen Duxiu moved from a shallow, eclectic view of socialism to a firm commitment to Marxism. The short newspaper article first notes earlier, fragmentary mentions of Marx's ideas in Wanguo Gongbao (1889), Zhejiang Chao (1903) and Minbao (1906). It then follows New Youth, founded as Youth Magazine in 1915, through its early issues, the reader correspondence of 1916, the impact of the October Revolution, the Marxism-focused issues of 1919, the Labour Day special issue of May 1920, and the journal's adoption as a Party organ in September 1920. Yin shows that in 1915 Chen Duxiu knew the origins and main ideas of Marxism but treated socialism as just one of several Western intellectual tools, and the journal profiled no Marxist figures. When a reader urged the journal to promote socialism, an editorial reply said socialism could wait in China because industry was undeveloped. For Yin, the turning point came with Li Dazhao's 1918 articles praising the October Revolution and the concentrated Marxist issues of 1919. The Labour Day issue is presented as a milestone in joining Marxism to the Chinese workers' movement and as the start of the adaptation of Marxism-Leninism to China. Yin adds that the May Fourth Movement prepared the ground for spread among ordinary people. Yin concludes that New Youth deserves great credit for choosing the best ideological weapon for the Chinese nation, and presents Chen Duxiu's shift from radical democrat to Marxist as a classic case for Chinese intellectuals. Read the original if you want a concise, officially framed account of the journal's path toward Marxism, with quotations from Chen Duxiu's 1915 essay and the 1916 reader exchange.

Deng Zhongxia's thought on the policies and tactics of the working-class struggle 邓中夏关于工人阶级斗争政策和策略的思想 Xu Dabing This short commentary, originally published in Guangming Daily on 26 April 2016, examines how Deng Zhongxia, an early Party leader and labour-movement organiser, thought about policy and tactics in the workers' movement. Xu argues that Deng came to see policy and tactics as decisive for the movement's success or failure, and that his ideas remain a notable part of the Party's early theoretical legacy. Xu first sketches Deng's practical record: the Changxindian workers' movement, the Beijing–Hankou railway movement, the Shanghai Japanese cotton-mill strike and the Guangdong–Hong Kong general strike. The article then takes up four themes: the importance of policy and tactics, building a broad united front, concentrating blows on the main enemy, and combining economic with political struggle. Xu reports that after the failure of the Beijing–Hankou railway strike Deng concluded that the small Chinese proletariat could not defeat powerful enemies alone. He therefore called for worker–peasant and wider alliances, and blamed the May Thirtieth Movement's failure on the proletariat's isolation. During the Guangdong–Hong Kong strike, Deng urged dropping the slogan of opposing all imperialisms in favour of a policy aimed at Britain alone, with permits for non-British goods. In Deng's own assessment, this kept Guangdong's merchants neutral and split the imperialist front. Deng also opposed both purely economic struggle and political slogans that ignore workers' material interests. Xu concludes that Deng treated these tactics as the core of leading the workers' movement. In Deng's view, the final aim of all workers' struggle is the complete liberation of labour, yet struggles for better pay and conditions should be pursued even under capitalism. Read the original if you want a brief overview of Deng Zhongxia's tactical thinking, as presented in a Chinese Party-oriented account of early labour history.

Marx and Proudhonism 马克思与蒲鲁东主义 Yang Hongyuan Writing in Guangming Daily in 2016, Yang Hongyuan asks what the long entanglement between Marx and Proudhonism reveals about the intellectual revolution Marx achieved. Yang argues that Marx's theory should be assessed comparatively, and that his twenty-year critique of Proudhonism has both historical value and present relevance. The short commentary has three parts. It first reconstructs Proudhonism itself, then traces Marx's shift from praise to systematic polemic, and finally draws lessons for today. Yang rejects the usual labels for Proudhon (petty-bourgeois socialism, reformism, anarchism) as too simple. Proudhonism, in Yang's account, was an ambitious system of serial dialectics, social economics and a theory of social revolution, rooted in the clash between advanced ideas and France's backward small-peasant economy. Marx's verdict of petty-bourgeois socialism is judged accurate. Marx first welcomed Proudhon's examination of private property, then criticised his Hegelian method and his substitution of economic categories for revolution. Yang holds that the critique let Marx integrate historical materialism, political economy and socialist doctrine. It did not remove Proudhon's influence among workers, because slogans such as "property is theft" were easier for poorly educated workers to grasp than theory. Yang adds that Capital, volume 1 (1867) eventually brought wide acceptance of Marx's doctrine. Yang concludes that profound theory survives the test of history, and that Proudhonism persists because the world-wide development of productive forces that communism requires is not yet achieved. Current theories advocating class conciliation, small private property with equal distribution, anarchy or opposition to the dictatorship of the proletariat are said to share its spirit. Yang calls for using Marx's methods and tactics against them. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese statement of how Marx's critique of Proudhon is used to address present-day ideas.

The "self-transformation" of the privileged stratum in the collapse of the CPSU and its warnings 苏共垮台中特权阶层的“自我蜕变”及其警示 Guo Yanlin Guo Yanlin asks why a party with more than 70 years of history and over 20 million members, the Communist Party of the Soviet Union (CPSU), collapsed. The article argues that, among many contributing causes, a decisive one was the growth of privilege and corruption inside the Party, which hardened into a vested-interest, bureaucratic stratum. In Guo's reading, the collapse was to a large extent the "self-transformation" of this privileged stratum rather than the work of anti-communists from outside. The article has three parts. It first traces how the privileged stratum formed, from Lenin's struggle against bureaucracy through the Stalin, Khrushchev, Brezhnev and Gorbachev periods. It then sets out four political harms of privilege and corruption. Finally it draws five warnings for the Chinese Communist Party, written in 2016 in the context of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. Guo's central claim is that the privileged officials, who controlled key posts and enjoyed special housing, supply and education benefits, used Gorbachev-era reforms to convert administrative control into legal private ownership. The author cites a 1995 Russian survey in which 74–75 per cent of the political elite and 61 per cent of the economic elite came from the Soviet cadre corps. Guo also cites David Kotz: around 1990 only 5–20 per cent of the Soviet public favoured capitalism, but about 76.7 per cent of an elite of roughly 100,000 did. The harms listed are loss of ideological appeal, a crisis of trust between Party and people, the spread of unwritten rules such as bribery and the sale of posts, and the elite's role as vanguard of capitalist restoration. Guo calls for a long-term, continuous campaign against privilege during the primary stage of socialism. The proposals are to strengthen ideals and convictions and oppose historical nihilism, never to use privilege as a tool of political order, to reform supervision and discipline inspection so that officials dare not, cannot and do not want to be corrupt, and to treat close ties with the people as the basis of anti-privilege work. Read the original if you want an official Chinese interpretation, published in 2016, of the Soviet collapse as a story of elite degeneration, and of the lessons the author draws for Party discipline.

The historical facts of Lenin's defence and consolidation of Party unity must not be distorted 列宁维护和巩固党的统一的历史事实不容歪曲 Yuan Xiuli Yuan Xiuli takes up the long-running charge that Lenin's draft resolution "On Party Unity", adopted by the Tenth Congress of the Russian Communist Party (Bolsheviks) in March 1921, was a weapon in factional struggle. In the article's account, critics have presented it as a tool for crushing opposition, protecting one-party rule and expressing Lenin's "autocratic thinking". Yuan argues that this reading contradicts both Lenin's thought and the historical record, and that the resolution aimed to safeguard the unity of the Bolshevik Party under exceptional conditions. Writing in Hongqi Wengao in 2016, Yuan reconstructs the circumstances of 1921 and relies heavily on Lenin's own speeches at the congress, quoted from the Chinese edition of his Collected Works. The article is organised in three sections: defending Party unity, consolidating Party leadership, and securing the most urgent task of economic construction. It focuses on the "Workers' Opposition" and the "Democratic Centralism" group. Yuan's central move is to read the resolution as a call for unity rather than an attack. The article stresses that Lenin acknowledged the opposition groups' valid criticisms of bureaucracy, and that the congress elected four of their members to the Central Committee and asked them to withdraw their resignations. In Yuan's telling, these groups then drifted towards syndicalism and anarchism: they demanded an all-Russian congress of producers to run the economy and put trade unions above the Party. They also distributed pamphlets and held separate meetings. Yuan adds that, after the Kronstadt rebellion of February 1921 and amid economic ruin, the dispute over the unions' role became what Lenin called an "excessive luxury". The Workers' Opposition's "leftist" resistance to the New Economic Policy is said to have obstructed the economic recovery the Party urgently needed. Yuan concludes that Lenin's leadership resolved these disagreements, preserved unity, strengthened Party leadership and gave the New Economic Policy a firm political and organisational guarantee. The article also notes Lenin's warning that the NEP was an "unprecedentedly difficult retreat", which demanded stronger conviction and discipline from the Party. Read the original if you want to see how a Party-theory journal in China defended the 1921 resolution against its critics, and which of Lenin's statements it uses to do so.

Warnings from the Soviet collapse for building Marxist ruling parties 苏联解体对马克思主义执政党建设的警示 Xue Yan More than twenty years after the Soviet Union dissolved, debate over its causes continues, with scholars pointing to nationalities, loss of belief, reform, or the federal state form. Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2016, Xue Yan accepts that many causes were at work but contends that the Soviet Communist Party's flaws as a ruling party were what ultimately brought the collapse. The article draws from this lessons for how socialist countries should strengthen Marxist ruling parties. The piece is a short commentary organised in six numbered sections. Each takes one failing of the Soviet party and sets it beside the stance of the Communist Party of China: guiding ideology, the succession of leaders, privilege and corruption, error correction, control over reform, and international relations. Xue draws on Soviet figures such as Ryzhkov, Bolkin and Titarenko, and on statements by Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping. Xue's central claim is that the Soviet leadership gradually drifted from Marxism-Leninism, and that by Gorbachev's time the party's 1991 self-definition had shifted to "universal human values" and "humane, democratic socialism". Xue ties this to a missing mechanism for the regular replacement of leaders, which allowed a privileged stratum to form and, in the author's account, to become the main beneficiary of the collapse. The author adds that the party lacked the capacity to correct errors and to steer reform, which was driven by leaders' whims and then by a change of direction. Xue also argues that the party failed to guard against Western "peaceful evolution", citing Margaret Thatcher's remark that the West helped promote Gorbachev. Xue concludes that China must keep Marxism as its guiding thought, build sound systems for selecting and replacing leaders, keep up anti-corruption work, and be willing to face and correct mistakes. The article also calls for firm control over the direction of reform and long-term vigilance against peaceful evolution while reform and opening up continues. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese Party-affiliated scholarship in 2016 drew lessons from the Soviet collapse for Party building.

The turn in social values seen through the revival of social consciousness in Russia 从俄罗斯社会意识回潮看社会价值转向 Wu Huixin Writing in 2016, Wu Huixin asks what a series of ideological "revivals" in post-Soviet Russia reveal about changing social values. The article argues that as Russia has emerged from the disorder produced by the collapse of the Soviet system, a number of earlier ideas have returned to public life. In Wu's reading, these are the result of social change and signal a shift in value positions towards the pragmatic and the concrete. The first part surveys seven revivals, drawing mostly on polls by the All-Russian Centre for the Study of Public Opinion (VTsIOM). They are the proposed restoration of the title "Hero of Labour" (support rising from 67% to 81% between 2012 and 2013); the rewriting of history textbooks; renewed ideas of national unity; a harsher reassessment of Gorbachev's reforms; the rehabilitation of patriotism; the return of collectivism; and a more measured assessment of Marxism. The second part analyses the value shifts behind these events. Wu argues that value positions follow the interests of the subject, and that the post-1991 collapse of values mirrored a disordered social reality. The recent turn, in the author's account, has four features: a return to "the people" (renxing) as the standpoint, drawing on the class basis of values; a return to practical reality, seen in valuing hard work, patriotism and an honest view of history; renewed firmness in inherited national values such as collectivism; and a return to objectivity, citing Marx's claim that social being determines consciousness. Values are also becoming more concrete, which Wu sees in three ways: they are group-oriented, rooted in the village community; they are basic, centred on the family; and they are moral, since Wu holds that moral values and economic development move in the same direction. Wu concludes that Russia's changing positions come from reflection on history, inheritance of tradition and respect for reality. The author judges the wave of revivals to be progressive in essence, pragmatic in value terms, and so far only preliminary results that are "worth looking forward to". Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist ethicist's interpretation of Russian opinion data on Soviet legacies, collectivism and patriotism, with the source polls cited in full.

Basic lessons of the Party's ideological and theoretical development 党的思想理论建设的基本经验 Zhang Ruicai Writing in Guangming Daily in 2016, shortly after Xi Jinping's speech marking the Party's 95th anniversary, Zhang Ruicai asks what the Communist Party of China has learned from its history about ideological and theoretical development. The commentary argues that the Party has always built itself first through ideas, and that its experience can be summed up in five pairings of tasks that must be pursued together. The piece moves through these five pairings in turn. It draws on Mao Zedong, Lenin, Xi Jinping and the report of the 18th Party Congress (2012), and on a series of Party resolutions and congress summaries from the Yan'an rectification to the 17th Central Committee's fourth plenum. Zhang's core claims are as follows. High priority on theory must go with solid practical work. Ideological and political work must go with active ideological struggle against anti-Marxist currents, and the author cites the Soviet and Eastern European collapse as a bitter lesson. Theoretical innovation must go with theoretical armament, so that study follows each theoretical advance. Ideological education must go with institutional governance, so that rules become a hard constraint rather than a rubber band. Theoretical study must go with summing up experience, as in the historical resolutions and the current Two Studies, One Doing campaign. Zhang concludes that theoretical maturity underpins political firmness, keeping theory abreast of the times underpins bold action, and ideological unity ensures the whole Party moves in step. Read the original if you want a compact, official-style statement of how Party commentators in 2016 framed ideological work and Party-building.

Cultivating belief among young people: establishing values amid cultural pluralism 青少年信仰培育：多元文化中的价值确立 Zhang Hongxia Writing in Guangming Daily in September 2016, Zhang Hongxia takes up a problem the author considers serious: under the influence of diverse cultural currents, some young people, whose outlook is still forming, have lost their belief in Marxism. Zhang argues that this belief bears directly on the future of socialism with Chinese characteristics and of the Chinese nation, and proposes concrete ways to cultivate it. The short commentary opens with Xi Jinping's remarks on youth and the formation of values, then describes the problem and sets out four remedies. It closes with practical measures in theory propaganda, tiered education, online work and practice-based education. In Zhang's account, Western thought, while promoting "democracy" and "freedom", denies the inevitability of socialism, distorts the history of the Communist Party and claims Marxism is outdated. Zhang says this has three effects on young people: it erodes their pursuit of the lofty ideal of communism, shakes their confidence in socialist modernization, and disrupts their identification with core socialist values. The remedies are to clarify the scientific basis of Marxism and the historical necessity of China's choices; to tailor education to different groups, with communist ideals stressed for Party and Youth League members and simpler patriotic feeling for ordinary students; and to "seize" online ground through social media, dedicated websites and big-data "precision push". Zhang also calls for linking belief cultivation to film, volunteering, internships and everyday issues young people care about. Zhang concludes that these measures can help young people form firm Marxist belief and correct values, so that they become qualified builders and reliable successors of socialism. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Party-aligned commentary in 2016 framed youth ideology work and its proposed methods.

The birthplace of Marx's thought: the 1844 Manuscripts Part one of fragments on the logical development of Marx's thought 马克思思想的诞生地：《1844 年手稿》--马克思思想的逻辑发展片论之一 Zhang Lingyun Where does Marx's thought have its centre, and how should one find it? Zhang Lingyun, writing in 2016, takes issue with the Japanese scholar Kojin Karatani, who reads Marx through Capital and treats the 'early Marx' as a construct of that later work. Zhang argues that the proper method for locating a thinker's centre is to examine the place where the thought was born, and that for Marx this place is the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844. The article holds that the Manuscripts are the founding work of Marx's new philosophy, not an immature Feuerbachian text. The article has two parts. The first examines the methodology: it reconstructs the original context of Marx's 'anatomy of man is a key to the anatomy of the ape' in the 1857 Introduction, contrasts it with the 'universal light' method, and notes how Marx himself approached Hegel. The second part sets out five ways in which the Manuscripts founded the new philosophy, then rebuts three standard reasons for placing them in a 'Feuerbachian humanist stage': Althusser's 'problematic', alleged over-praise of Feuerbach, and borrowed Feuerbachian terms. Zhang's central move is to limit the 'key' method to the economic social formations, since primitive society is, in this account, governed by the production of human beings themselves and requires anthropology rather than political economy. Marx's own study of Hegel began with the Phenomenology, 'the true birthplace and secret' of Hegel's philosophy, not with his final system. Applying the same approach to Marx, Zhang finds in the Manuscripts a new conception of science as a single 'science of history', sensuous activity (practice) as the pivot, and a dialectic of free, conscious activity, alienated labour and the sublation of alienation. On the Feuerbach question, Zhang argues that Marx's 'problematic' had already moved beyond Feuerbach's. The article also contends that the Manuscripts give 'species being' a social meaning and treat alienation as labour alienation, a category of historical materialism, so that Marx's view is a 'labour conception of history' rather than an 'alienation conception'. Zhang concludes that the claim that the Manuscripts belong to a Feuerbachian humanist stage cannot stand. In the author's view, they are the historical and logical starting point of Marx's later theory. The three-stage movement of the Manuscripts is said to correspond to Marx's late anthropological 'three forms' of society, the former giving the philosophical basis and the latter the scientific proof. Read the original if you study the early–late Marx debate, Althusser's reading of the Manuscripts, or Chinese scholarly arguments for the continuity of Marx's thought.

The threefold meaning of twenty-first-century Chinese Marxism 21 世纪中国马克思主义的三重蕴意 Zhang Jinsong Writing in 2016, Zhang Jinsong asks what defines "twenty-first-century Chinese Marxism", the stage of adapting Marxism to Chinese conditions that Xi Jinping has urged the Party to develop. Zhang argues that it is at once a summing-up of the practice of socialism with Chinese characteristics and a guide for that practice. Its content, in the author's reading, has three layers: insistence on "Chinese characteristics" to solve China's problems, continuation of the Chinese path alongside a stronger Chinese discourse, and the promotion of Chinese culture as a source of "Chinese wisdom". The article first sets twenty-first-century Chinese Marxism against its twentieth-century predecessor. The earlier stage, Zhang says, sought a way of combining Marxism with Chinese reality and moved China towards independence and strength. The new stage must lead the building of a moderately prosperous society, modernization and the Chinese Dream. Three sections follow, drawing on Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping, on policy initiatives since the 18th Party Congress (2012), and on China's economic record. In the first section, Zhang treats "Chinese characteristics" as the methodological starting point. Policies since 2012 are presented as responses to China's primary-stage conditions: the "two centenary goals", the "Four Comprehensives", the "new normal", supply-side reform and the new development philosophy. Zhang then argues that the Chinese path (a mixed ownership economy with public ownership dominant, distribution mainly by labour, Party leadership, and core socialist values) gives rise to a distinct discourse that challenges neoliberalism, Western democracy and universalist values. Third, Zhang holds that traditional ideas such as "people as the root of the state", "unity of heaven and humanity", integrity in office and "harmony in diversity" feed Chinese governance, ecological thinking, anti-corruption work and diplomacy. Zhang concludes that twenty-first-century Chinese Marxism should do more than solve China's own development problems. It should show other countries that they can seek paths suited to their own conditions, end the equations of "globalization = Westernization" and "modernization = capitalism", and offer Chinese ideas for global governance and a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a representative 2016 statement of how Chinese theorists tied Marxism's Sinicization to national particularity, the Chinese path and traditional culture.

Lenin's Imperialism: methodology, core meaning and contemporary value 列宁《帝国主义论》：方法论、核心意蕴与当代价值 Zhu Bingyuan Marking the centenary in 2016 of Lenin's Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism, Zhu Bingyuan asks whether the work has become outdated. Zhu notes that it has been attacked for a century and, in the author's account, is again being questioned and marginalised in theoretical circles as capitalism changes. The article argues that Lenin's theory has not lapsed and remains a theoretical weapon for understanding contemporary capitalism, provided it is grasped as a whole and not judged by individual conclusions. The article has three parts. The first examines the book's methodology under three heads: its view of history, its materialism and its practical character. The second sets out the book's core meaning as four pillars: monopoly, the rule of the financial oligarchy, external aggression and expansion, and parasitism and decay. The third turns to the present and takes four issues: state monopoly capitalism, the virtualisation of financial capital, new forms of imperialist expansion and the continuing historical trend of imperialism. On method, Zhu argues that Lenin treated imperialism as a stage of capitalist development, in line with historical materialism, and contrasts this with Kautsky, who reduced it to a preferred policy of finance capital. Zhu says Lenin organised the book around monopoly as its core category, much as Marx's Capital is organised around capital. Zhu holds that, because the essence of monopoly profit-seeking has not changed, Lenin's conclusions are not obsolete.
