State monopoly capitalism is presented as a logical development of private monopoly that adjusts relations within the system without altering its monopoly character. Zhu also contends that finance capital has widened in scope and become more virtual, which strengthens oligarchic rule, and that expansion now operates through ideological and cultural means such as neoliberalism, the Washington Consensus and 'peaceful evolution'. Zhu concludes that monopoly, oligarchic rule and expansion still define imperialism, so its parasitic, decaying and moribund tendencies persist. The article cites financialisation, hollowing out of the real economy, rising debt and deepening polarisation as evidence that capitalism's basic contradictions are sharpening and that it is heading for eventual demise. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist scholar defended the contemporary relevance of Lenin's theory of imperialism in 2016, and the arguments used to reject claims that it is outdated.

From The German Ideology to Capital: the deepening of Marx's theory of ideology Reflections on a shift in research approach 从《德意志意识形态》到《资本论》：马克思意识形态理论的深化与思考 Kuai Zhengming Marx's term "ideology" gradually fades from his writings after The German Ideology (1845) and does not appear directly in Capital. Kuai Zhengming asks whether this marks a break in Marx's theory of ideology or its deepening. The article, published in Theory and Reform in 2016, argues for deepening: ideology was not abandoned but moved from external critique to a detailed internal analysis of how capitalism operates. The article has three parts. The first treats The German Ideology as the work in which Marx's theory of ideology took basic shape, after earlier steps in the critique of Hegel and the 1844 manuscripts. The second follows the theory through the 1857–58 manuscripts, the Preface to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy and Capital. The third offers four concluding reflections on the continuity and the change between the early and later works. Kuai reads The German Ideology as establishing three things: ideology as "false consciousness", as the ideas of the ruling class, and as the class consciousness of a rising revolutionary class. The same work also traces the origins of ideology in the division of mental and manual labour and links its disappearance to the abolition of class rule. Later, Marx placed ideology within the "ideological superstructure" determined by the economic base. He criticised classical political economy for treating capitalism as natural and eternal, and analysed commodity, money and capital fetishism as the everyday ideology of capitalist society. Kuai concludes that, in Capital, ideology is no longer mainly the invention of bourgeois thinkers but is rooted in capitalist relations of production and in workers' everyday consciousness. Marx also looks for the points where capitalism's claims to freedom and equality contradict its reality. In Kuai's account, the disappearance of the word is an "infiltration" of ideology into the whole economic process, so that it becomes an ever-present "spectre". Read the original if you want a compact Chinese-language account of how fetishism critique is read as the continuation of Marx's theory of ideology.

From the state to civil society A study of "On the Jewish Question" and the "Introduction to a Contribution to the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right" 从国家到市民社会 Han Lixin Han Lixin asks why the young Marx, a firm supporter of Hegel's philosophy of the state up to the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right (1843), abandoned Hegel's dual framework of "state and civil society" and moved to a monist framework centred on civil society, never returning to a philosophy of the state. The article completes an argument Han began in a 2009 paper, which left open how the shift was actually accomplished. Han's answer is that Marx did it in the Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher essays, through his theory of "human emancipation". The article first recalls the 2009 claim that Marx's change in 1843 was a move from state to civil society, rather than Lenin's move from idealism to materialism. It then reads "On the Jewish Question", a critique of Bruno Bauer, and the Introduction to the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right. It ends by tracing how Marx's view of the state changed through the Paris Manuscripts, the Comments on James Mill, The German Ideology and the abandoned plan for a volume on the state. Han argues that Marx found political emancipation insufficient: it splits people into an abstract citizen (citoyen) in the state and an egoistic private person (bourgeois) in civil society, and the state ends up serving private property. Human emancipation requires reuniting these two identities in the individual's own empirical life, labour and relations, which Hegel's scheme would place in civil society. This reversed the Hegelian view that only the state is universal, so Marx needed a universality inside civil society. Han holds that the proletariat, which Marx found in the Introduction, offers only an absolute universality that excludes particularity, so it could not do the job. In the Paris Manuscripts Marx instead turned to Hegel's "formal universality" in money, labour, value and the division of labour. Han concludes that Marx never completed the human emancipation theory, since later ideas such as "freely associated individuals" and the "re-establishment of individual property" still fall short of the required universality. Its significance lies elsewhere. It made civil society a sphere of universality, replaced the dual framework with a monist one, and caused the state to "retire" from Marx's horizon, which Han presents as a break from Hegel. Han adds that the state, once treated as a fictitious community, became an object of criticism, and that this logic helps explain why the planned volume on the state was never written. Read the original if you study the development of Marx's early thought, his relation to Hegel, or the shift from state to civil society in 1843–44.)

The false and anti-democracy of the "model of democracy" “民主典范”的假民主和反民主 He Wei Writing in 2016, He Wei takes aim at the United States' self-image as the world's most perfect democracy. The article argues that American democracy is not as flawless as Western thinkers and politicians claim: at home and abroad, in institutional design and in practice, it contains serious elements of what the author calls non-democracy, false democracy and anti-democracy. The piece is organised in three parts. The first deals with how the American system treats forces hostile to it, citing the House Un-American Activities Committee, the Truman-era loyalty reviews and McCarthy's purge of embassy libraries. The second examines the domestic electoral and political system: presidential elections, the Supreme Court, money in politics, gun culture and parliamentary representation. The third turns to foreign policy, covering the use of democracy as an ideological tool, global resource inequality and humanitarian intervention. He argues that US presidential elections are only apparently democratic. Candidates are filtered by economic elites, the Electoral College and winner-takes-all rule can elect a candidate with fewer votes nationally, and campaigns cost billions, tying officeholders to donors. The author also contends that the life-tenured Supreme Court, with its power of judicial review, amounts to a form of minority tyranny, citing the 2000 Bush–Gore case. Drawing on Marx and on Western writers such as Peter Eddy-Kler (as rendered in the Chinese source), Stephen Holmes, David Miller and Francis Fukuyama, He holds that where rights rest on private property, public power serves capital and cannot be above class. Abroad, the author says, Washington interferes in other states' affairs, justifies interventions as humanitarian while overriding rights at home (for instance through surveillance), and, citing a 2010 remark by Obama, does not want other peoples to reach American living standards. He concludes that American democratic practice contradicts its professed values, and that behind its double standards lie self-centredness and egoism. The closing reference to Kissinger's call for credibility in diplomacy is presented as an idealistic statement that rings hollow against this reality. Read the original if you want to see how a 2016 Party-journal article frames a critique of US democracy, drawing on historical episodes, Western critics and Marxist arguments about class and property.

The spiritual source of national rejuvenation A brief discussion of the Long March spirit and the spirit of realizing the dream 民族复兴的精神动力之源 Gong Fangbin Writing in 2016, the 80th anniversary of the Red Army's Long March, Gong Fangbin asks how the Long March spirit can be linked to the spirit needed to realize the Chinese Dream. The article treats the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation as a "new Long March". Gong argues that the Long March spirit is contained in, and further developed by, a "dream-realizing spirit" whose content is still being formulated. The article has three parts. It first sets out the content of each spirit, then examines the logical relation between them, and finally proposes how the Long March spirit should be carried into the dream-realizing spirit. Gong lists the Long March spirit's components, including firm ideals, courage, independence, unity and reliance on the masses. The dream-realizing spirit, in Gong's view, is strongly guided, broadly participatory, lofty in aim and persevering. Gong argues that it adds an element of creating human civilization, so that innovation becomes critical. Three elements of the Long March spirit are singled out for transmission: firm ideals and convictions, the courage to take untrodden paths through innovation, and willingness to sacrifice. On sacrifice, Gong cites China's growing role in setting international rules, Western "China threat" talk and island disputes with neighbours. Gong says China does not want war but must be prepared, and that the spirit should become values and conduct rather than only literal sacrifice. Gong concludes that the goal of rejuvenation will be reached only if this spirit enters the nation's soul as values and behavioural norms. Read the original if you want a short example of how Party-affiliated writing in 2016 connected Long March commemoration to the Chinese Dream.

On the Long March and the Long March spirit 论长征和长征精神 Li Hongfeng Marking the 80th anniversary of the Long March's victory in 2016, Li Hongfeng asks what the march achieved, why it succeeded and how its spirit should be carried forward today. The article takes its cue from Xi Jinping's remarks of 23 September 2016 at the Military Museum, which called for remembering the Red Army's achievements and promoting the Long March spirit. Li's thesis is that the Long March was a victory of revolutionary spirit and of the people, made possible above all by a Party leadership core, and that its spirit remains necessary under present conditions. The piece is organised in five sections. It first presents the Long March as unprecedented in history, drawing on Mao Zedong's 1935 report, foreign comparisons and Mao's Long March poems. It then treats the march as a triumph of revolutionary spirit and of the people, and identifies its most fundamental lesson. The final section sets out four requirements for promoting the Long March spirit now. Li cites figures on casualties, battles and distances, and the views of Edgar Snow, Harrison Salisbury, Philip Short and Zbigniew Brzezinski. Li builds on Mao's description of the march as a manifesto, a propaganda team and a seeding machine. The author argues that the Red Army's survival and its work among ethnic minorities, through newspapers and through mobile schools show that victory came from mobilising and relying on the people. The decisive result, in Li's account, was the strategic turning point confirmed at the Zunyi Meeting of January 1935, which established Mao's leadership and ended four years of dogmatist rule. From this Li draws the central lesson: the Party found its leadership core, and leadership without a core cannot be relied upon. Li calls for four things: holding high ideals and convictions, expressed in the Four-sphere Confidence; fighting complacency and slackening of spirit; keeping a sincere devotion to the people, since the author sees detachment from the masses as the ruling party's greatest danger; and strengthening Party leadership through discipline, democratic centralism, seeking truth from facts and loyalty to the Party Central Committee with Xi Jinping as General Secretary. Read the original if you want an example of how the Long March is used in 2016 Party-building discourse to link historical memory with calls for discipline, ideals and a leadership core.

The significance of the Long March for the growth and maturing of our Party 长征对我们党成长、成熟的意义 Liu Yazhou Writing in Party Building (Dangjian) in 2016, Liu Yazhou asks what the Long March meant for the Communist Party's development. Liu argues that it was one of the major turning points that pushed the Party towards maturity. With the Zunyi Conference as its marker, the Party began to lead the Chinese revolution independently and to evolve into a mature Marxist party. The short piece has two sections: the Long March's role in advancing the adaptation of Marxism to Chinese conditions, and its role in producing a mature central leadership core. Liu draws on the Party's history before and after Zunyi, statements by Liu Bocheng and Deng Xiaoping, and figures on the Red Army's losses and its surviving cadres. Liu holds that before the march, dogmatism of the "Left" line dominated the Party, and that, in Liu's account, it destroyed most Party organisations in the white areas and cost the Red Army and base areas ninety per cent of their strength. After the defeat at the Xiang River, many leaders came to support Mao Zedong. With the Comintern link cut, the Party chose its own central leaders for the first time, which Liu describes as the formation of a leadership core around Mao. Liu cites Deng Xiaoping that no mature central leadership existed before Zunyi, and notes that 222 of the 254 generals of rank lieutenant-general and above in 1955 had taken part in the march. Liu concludes that the Long March shows the need to innovate in theory by combining Marxism's basic principles with Chinese realities, and that a mature party needs a firm leadership core. Linking this to the present, Liu calls on Party members to deepen the adaptation of Marxism to Chinese conditions, to strengthen core consciousness and to resolutely uphold the authority of Xi Jinping and the Central Committee. Read the original if you want an example of how Party-history writing in 2016 tied the Long March to the idea of a leadership core.

The five strengths of the Communist Party of China 中国共产党的五大优势 Pang Xianzhi Writing in the People's Daily in June 2016, on the Party's 95th anniversary, Pang Xianzhi asks why the Communist Party of China grew from a small group of a few dozen people into a mature and powerful Marxist party leading a large Eastern country along the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Pang argues that this was no accident but follows from the Party's own nature and from five distinctive strengths. The short commentary devotes one section to each strength. It draws on Mao Zedong's wartime and revolutionary judgements, on the Party's own documents, and on remarks by Xi Jinping, and it moves from the Party's founding to the period after the 18th Party Congress (2012). In Pang's account, the Party holds a lofty ideal, communism, and links it to concrete programmes for each historical stage. Its fundamental purpose of serving the people wholeheartedly lets it find the "greatest common denominator" among the diverse interests that emerged after reform and opening up. Pang adds that centralised, unified leadership matters all the more now that the country is in what Xi calls a critical period of development, reform and emerging contradictions. The Party is also described as creative in adapting Marxism to Chinese conditions. Pang says it corrects its own mistakes, citing the two historical resolutions, and sets this against countries where parties rotate in office and long-term continuity is said to be impossible. Pang concludes that these strengths explain the Party's victories and will secure the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation under its leadership. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a senior Party historian presented the sources of the Party's legitimacy in 2016.

Shaping China's image with the new development philosophy 以新发展理念塑造中国形象 Shen Haixiong Writing in 2016, Shen Haixiong asks how the five-part development philosophy of innovation, coordination, green development, openness and sharing can shape China's image at home and abroad. Shen argues that the new development philosophy is a concentrated expression of the Party Central Committee's new approach to governance under Xi Jinping. In this reading it will deeply influence China's national image, the image of the Party and China's international image, offering a "Chinese solution" and "Chinese wisdom" for global governance. The short commentary is organised in three sections: the new national image, the good image of the Party, and the soft power of a major country. It draws mainly on Xi Jinping's speeches, including his remarks at the G20 Hangzhou summit, and refers to the Belt and Road Initiative and the goal of a moderately prosperous society in all respects. It ends with a brief summary and a call to be guided by the philosophy in practice. On the national image, Shen treats the five concepts as a new lens on the Chinese path. Each is said to project a specific image: innovation signals a wise and sustainable country, coordination a balanced and harmonious one, green development a country that respects nature, openness a responsible and peaceful partner, and sharing a society of fairness and common prosperity. On the Party, Shen argues that the philosophy shows improved governing capacity, stresses the principle of governing for the people, and requires changes in the Party's way of governing, such as strategic and rule-of-law thinking and institutional reform. On international standing, Shen claims the philosophy offers a global development consensus, shows China as a responsible emerging power, and supplies a remedy for the world economy's difficulties since the 2008 financial crisis, with the G20 outcomes cited as evidence. Shen concludes that the new development philosophy brings new opportunities, content and support for building the images of the country and the Party. Shen calls for conscious use of it to guide practice and to create a favourable environment for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Party media in 2016 linked the new development philosophy to national image-building and soft power.

Ideological and political education should make full use of the power of truth in Marxism 思政教育要用好马克思主义的真理力量 Liu Jianjun Liu Jianjun asks how ideological and political education can raise its level and reach, and answers that it must draw on the power of truth that Marxism possesses. In the author's view, whether this power is used well directly determines the influence, advanced character and scientific standing of such education. Citing Xi Jinping's remarks on ideals and convictions as the 'calcium' of the spirit, Liu says the choice of educational content, and the building of both rational and emotional force, should serve the establishment of Marxism's lofty ideal. The article, published in 2016 in a journal on ideological and political work, has two main parts. The first sets out four sources of Marxism's truth-power: logical, truth-seeking, social and faith-based. The second explains how this power lifts the two forces of ideological and political education, the force of truth and the force of emotion. Liu draws on Lenin, Engels, Marx, the Communist Manifesto, Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping. Liu links each source to a feature of Marxism. Its rigorous, self-consistent system gives logical force. Its disclosure of objective laws, summed up as seeking truth from facts, gives truth-seeking force. Its standpoint of the people gives social force. Its lofty communist ideal gives the force of faith. Liu then argues that this power gives education a logical model, true content, a value standpoint and a goal. It also turns emotion into love of truth, respect for the people and firm belief in the ideal. The author divides the mind into rational and non-rational elements, and treats truth as the object of the first and emotion as a key object of the second. Liu concludes that, before Marxism, such education relied on authority, religion and superstition, so its truth-power was limited and its emotional power often blind. Marxist truth-power, in this account, offers a practical path from non-rational to rational dominance and so opens up a higher plane for the field. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how Chinese theorists of ideological and political education justify grounding their discipline in Marxism's claim to truth.

Why the Communist Party of China has won the people's support and backing 中国共产党为什么能得到人民的拥护和支持 Li Chunhua Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2016, the 95th year of the Party's history, Li Chunhua asks why the Communist Party of China has been able to grow from small and weak to large and strong. The article's answer is that the Party has consistently enjoyed the trust, support and backing of the broad masses, which Li treats as the material source and spiritual strength of China's revolution, construction and reform. The commentary is a short, numbered argument in four parts. It runs through the revolutionary periods, the search for a path to national liberation, the post-1978 reform era, the development of people's democracy, and the Party's own internal building, ending with a brief reference to the Party leadership under Xi Jinping since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Li gives four reasons. First, the Party stands for the fundamental interests of the great majority and serves the people wholeheartedly, which Li presents as the essential feature separating a proletarian party from others. Second, after other classes' attempts failed, it adopted Marxism and combined it with China's concrete conditions, producing Mao Zedong Thought. Third, since the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978), it has liberated thinking and developed socialism with Chinese characteristics, which Li credits with raising living standards from inadequate subsistence to overall moderate prosperity and with advancing people's democracy and rule of law. Fourth, it practises strict self-governance, stresses ideological and work-style building, and corrects its mistakes, which Li says earns public respect. Li concludes that all the Party's achievements result from popular support, and that it can overcome future difficulties and advance the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation only by continuing to share the people's fortunes and rely on their wisdom and strength. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the Party's official account of its popular legitimacy was framed on its 95th anniversary.

Interpreting the idea of spatial justice in The German Ideology 《德意志意识形态》中的空间正义思想解读 Wang Wendong Western neo-Marxists and Chinese scholars have written extensively on the spatial theory of Marx and Engels, yet Wang argues that the idea of spatial justice in The German Ideology (1845) has not received due attention. The article contends that, although Marx and Engels do not treat social space explicitly there, their critique of town and country, globalisation, capital expansion, colonies and the family–civil society–state relation implicitly expresses a view of spatial justice. In Wang's account this is not a species of distributive justice but a comprehensive justice covering the production, distribution, exchange and consumption of spatial resources, and a justice of difference. The article has three parts. The first sets out the methodological premise: Marx and Engels start from the practice of producing space, against the idealists and Feuerbach's anthropological materialism. The second reads the text for the unjust spatial conditions it reveals: the town–country opposition, the opposition between local closure and global scope, and the opposition between family, civil society and state as forms of community. The third examines the routes to spatial justice that the text proposes. Wang closes by placing the book within the development of Marx's spatial thinking, from early writings to the Manifesto, Capital and the later work. Wang's central move is to argue that Marx and Engels reverse the idealist order. Ideas of justice do not explain spatial practice; spatial practice explains ideas of justice. Wang reads the town–country split as an opposition of advanced and backward, civilised and barbarous, with the countryside subordinated to the town. Globalisation is read as progress that also produces unequal living conditions, a centre–periphery order and colonial exploitation. The community that Marx and Engels call illusory is read as an alien coercive force over individuals. Against this, Wang finds three paths in the text: a vast growth of productive forces, communist revolution, and the building of a true community in which individuals gain freedom through association. Wang concludes that The German Ideology marks the formation of Marx's scientific idea of spatial justice. In this reading it is an original response to the unfairness produced by capital globalisation, town–country separation and conflicts of communal interest. Wang places it between earlier writings that implied justice for people of different spatial status and later works that developed a spatial dimension of the critique of capitalism, completing what Wang calls Marx's historical-geographical materialism. Returning to this text, Wang suggests, helps defend and develop Marx's spatial justice thought and clarifies the lineage running through later neo-Marxism and postmodernism. Read the original if you study Marxist spatial theory, Lefebvre and Harvey, or the textual basis of Marx's early critique of town–country division and globalisation.

Rediscovering civil society The place of Marx's Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right in the history of ideas 重新发现市民社会 Tian Guanhao Why does Marx's Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right deserve a major place in the history of political thought? Tian argues that the work re-opened Hegel's own analysis of modern civil society, which Hegel's successors and Feuerbach had neglected. By breaking what Tian calls the 'spiritualist order' of Hegel's state theory, Marx began a self-critique of modern society and prepared the ground for Capital. The article is organised in three parts. The first reconstructs Hegel's idea of the state and its structural resemblance to a Christian order governed by 'spirit'. The second assesses Feuerbach's critique of Hegel and its limits. The third follows Marx's critique of Hegel's logical mysticism and of his 'crude empiricism' on monarchy, bureaucracy and legislative power. Tian contends that Hegel grounded the state on speculative logic, so that rational knowledge of the state stands where the Holy Spirit stands in Christianity. Real states can therefore stay in non-true forms, which Tian maps onto the logical categories of mechanism and chemism, and the logic can be captured by despotic power. Feuerbach correctly exposed this detachment from life through the inversion of subject and predicate. Tian argues, however, that he skipped the intermediate chapters of the Phenomenology and the Logic and so missed Hegel's analysis of modern economic society, leaving only an abstract 'natural man'. Marx, by contrast, treated the family and civil society as the real presuppositions of the state. He read monarchy as resting on the alienation of people in civil society, bureaucracy as the corporations' interests in another form, and Hegel's legislative power as an expression of private property. Tian sees in this the beginnings of Marx's idea of civil society's self-determination and sublation, here still through democracy, and of the proletariat's political significance. Tian concludes that the Critique opened a new possibility for post-Hegelian political philosophy: the self-criticism of modern society. Marx recognised civil society as the true subject of the state, even though he had not yet studied political economy. He would later find the path to be abolishing private property and the free workers' common possession of the productive forces. Tian therefore calls the Critique a 'great prelude' to Capital. Read the original if you are interested in the Hegel–Feuerbach–Marx relationship and in how Marx's early concept of civil society links to his later economic critique.

The logical differences between Capital and the Grundrisse 《资本论》与《政治经济学批判大纲》的逻辑差异 Yang Haifeng Scholars widely accept that the Outlines of the Critique of Political Economy (the Grundrisse) is a draft of Capital and that the two texts share a philosophical framework. Yang challenges this consensus. The article argues that two different epistemes, or philosophical frameworks, underlie the two texts and produce major differences in their logic. In the Grundrisse the framework is a labour ontology centred on human subjectivity and freedom. In Capital it is a logic of capital in which capital itself is the subject. Yang begins with method, asking how one can speak of a fundamental difference between two works by one thinker. The article draws on Althusser's "problematic" and "epistemological break", Foucault's episteme and Kuhn's paradigm shift. It then reconstructs the philosophical basis of the Grundrisse and notes that Vygodsky, Rosdolsky, Lukács and Gould stress continuity. Finally it reads Capital's treatment of labour, the subject and capital as an "absolute object" against that basis. On the Grundrisse, Yang identifies three components of its labour ontology. Labour is the ontological ground of social existence. Objectification of labour confirms human subjectivity, although Marx now sees objectification and alienation as one process under capital. Labour also creates free time as the realm of free human development. Yang finds a second line in the same text: capital as a self-relating, self-augmenting subject, comparable to Hegel's absolute idea. In Capital this second line takes over. Labour is no longer an ontological foundation but a socially specific function. Yang points to the dual character of labour, labour-power as a commodity, the valorisation process, and the critique of the trinity formula, which calls labour a "phantom". Yang also reads the commodity status of labour-power as marking Marx's break with early modern Western thought, which grounded ownership and rationality in labour. Capitalists appear as personified capital, and workers as its living instruments. Capital becomes the absolute subject, and by the same token an absolute object to human beings. Yang concludes that research focused on what Marx said finds only continuity, and that attention must also go to what Marx did not say, the deep structure that constrains his thinking. The article suggests that this reading opens a new theoretical space and calls for further theoretical resources. Read the original if you work on Marx's economic manuscripts, Althusserian or Foucauldian approaches to Marx, or debates over labour ontology and capital as subject.

Capital as a powerful intellectual weapon for understanding contemporary economic problems 《资本论》是洞察当代经济问题的强大思想武器 Li Jiang Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2016, Li Jiang takes up Xi Jinping's rejection of the claim that Marxist political economy and Capital are outdated. Li argues that, among current schools of thought, only Capital can help readers see through today's tangled economic problems and find ways to answer them. The article's thesis is twofold: capitalism still dominates the world but cannot solve the world's problems, and China should meet its own economic challenges with an approach grounded in Marxism. The article has two parts. The first reviews 149 years since Capital appeared and asks why capitalism has survived despite Marx's prediction of its expropriation, then examines why its basic contradiction persists, drawing on Thomas Piketty's Capital in the Twenty-First Century. The second turns to the problems that have emerged in China's development, such as the wealth gap, environmental damage, corruption and overproduction, and sets out four relationships to be handled correctly. Li gives four reasons for capitalism's endurance: its relations of production could still accommodate some growth in productive forces; reforms forced by Marxism, the labour movement and socialist states; credit-based consumption that turned citizens into lifelong debtors; and the export of crises abroad, above all by the United States through the dollar's international role. None of this removes the contradiction between socialised production and private appropriation. Citing Piketty's figures on concentrated wealth and stagnant middle and lower incomes, Li holds that widening inequality makes the "realisation" of products ever harder and that the 2008 crisis shows the problem lies in the system itself. For China, Li calls for both a decisive role for the market and better government macro-control; for keeping public ownership dominant, defending state-owned enterprises against "privatisation" and against the claim that they cannot coexist with markets; for fairer primary and secondary distribution, including property and inheritance taxes; and for a fairer international economic order. Li concludes that China must follow neither a return to the pre-reform past nor neoliberal marketisation, but a socialist market economy that combines Marxist truth with present realities. A lasting solution to the imbalance between supply and demand, in Li's view, depends on socialism prevailing over capitalism and on effective global macro-regulation. Meanwhile China should set a socialist example and work with developing countries to change the international rules. Read the original if you want to see how a 2016 Party-journal article uses Capital and Piketty to defend public ownership, state-owned enterprises and macro-control.

A new reflection on what materialism is 关于什么是唯物主义的新思考 Jie Changguang Marxist philosophy is a materialist philosophy, so, Jie argues, how materialism is understood is a basic precondition for understanding Marxist philosophy as a whole. The article, published in Philosophical Research in 2016, offers a new interpretation of what materialism is, working from Engels's texts. Its thesis is that materialism has an ontological sense and an epistemological sense, and that both rest on the idea that the world finds its ground and source in itself. The article has three parts. The first reads Engels's discussion of the question of the 'primary' (本原) in Ludwig Feuerbach and the End of Classical German Philosophy, together with passages in Dialectics of Nature. The second draws out the methodological implications of materialism: self-causation, internal causation and self-determination. The third applies the reworked concept to two long-standing problems in Chinese debates, the unity of materialism with dialectics and the unity of the standpoint of practice with materialism. Spinoza, Hegel, Feuerbach, Marx and Lenin are the main interlocutors. Jie holds that Engels's dividing line between materialism and idealism is an ontological question about what is primary. In its medieval theological setting this meant who creates the world. Materialism therefore means that nature is its own ground and creator, and idealism that the world is created by spirit or God. Epistemologically, this becomes the demand to explain the world from the world itself. From this follow the 'self-caused' world (as in Spinoza's substance), the priority of internal over external causes, and self-determination, which Marxism extends to history through historical materialism. On this basis Jie argues that dialectics fits materialism because genuine contradiction is internal, self-contradiction, which yields 'self-movement'. Practice, too, belongs to materialism: social things are both objective and products of human activity, so understanding them requires both object and subject. Jie adds a condition, that practice must be treated as arising from the object, with its purposes derived from objective conditions. Jie concludes that the standpoint of practice is the touchstone of consistent materialism in the study of social life and the watershed between Marx's 'new materialism' and the old. Adopting practice does not guarantee materialism, because it can drift towards external causation unless the object is held to determine the subject. Read the original if you work on Chinese debates over practical materialism, or want a close reading of Engels's definition of materialism as an ontological and methodological thesis.

Is historical materialism a positive science? Three questions that need clarifying 历史唯物主义是否实证科学 Chen Yongsheng Is historical materialism a philosophy or a positive science? Chen Yongsheng argues that the debate, which went quiet in recent years, has not been settled and needs a fresh look because it bears on the discipline's standing and on how Marx's thought is presented. The article's answer is cautious: Marx did not himself classify historical materialism as either philosophy or positive science. The article proceeds through three "clarifications". The first traces the problem from the "Korsch problem" and the "Althusser problem" to the recent exchange between Duan Zhongqiao and Yu Wujin, which Chen labels the "positive science problem". The second asks how Marx ended German critical philosophy and opened a "genuine positive science", and it contrasts this with Comte's positivism. The third asks what purpose the move served. The evidence is mainly The German Ideology, with Marx's own development from 1837 to 1845 as background. Chen contends that the contested passage must be read in the context of the whole Feuerbach chapter and of the book's aim, which was to settle accounts with Marx's and Engels's former philosophical convictions by criticising post-Hegelian philosophy. On this reading, what Marx brings to an end is the "German critique", the line of thought from Strauss to Stirner. It is not speculative idealism in general, nor Hegel alone. What takes its place is a "genuine positive science", which is the new view of real individuals, real production and the real sensuous world. Chen distinguishes this from Comte, whose positivism stays within sensory experience and, in Chen's account, neglects human existence, value and free development. The purpose is to establish that "life determines consciousness": consciousness is a social product, and its content and changes come from life. Chen summarises three results. Marx replaced "empty phrases about consciousness" and "independent philosophy" with the historical-materialist view without labelling it philosophy or science. What Marx ended was post-Hegelian German critique, and what he began was not Comtean positivism. The aim was to set out a view opposed to German ideology. Chen calls this a personal view but says the question matters for developing Marxist philosophy and deserves further discussion. Read the original if you follow the Chinese debate over whether historical materialism is philosophy or science and want a close, context-based reading of the "positive science" passage in The German Ideology.

Opening a new stage of flourishing for Chinese philosophy and social sciences Studying General Secretary Xi Jinping's important speech at the symposium on philosophy and social sciences work 开创中国哲学社会科学繁荣发展新局面 Ru Xin Ru Xin, who attended the symposium on philosophy and social sciences work chaired by Xi Jinping on 17 May 2016, offers his preliminary reflections on Xi's speech there. This short commentary, first published in the China Social Sciences Today in May 2016, argues that the speech clarifies the importance of the field and sets out how it should develop. The piece is organised around four points Ru draws from the speech: the Party leadership's regard for philosophy and social sciences, the principle of Marxist guidance, the task of building philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics, and the Party's expectations of intellectuals. It closes with a personal note from a long-serving scholar in the field. Ru reports that the speech places the discipline in the broad sweep of world and Chinese history, holding that every major leap in civilisation has depended on intellectual change. Contemporary China's sweeping social change is said to make this an era that needs, and will produce, theory. Ru stresses that Marxist guidance is the fundamental mark distinguishing Chinese philosophy and social sciences, and that the speech explains how to uphold it: by advancing the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context, the needs of our times and the general public, and by treating upholding and developing Marxism as a dialectical unity. Ru also highlights the call to build original disciplinary, academic and discourse systems that draw on Marxist, traditional Chinese and foreign resources, under top-level design. Ru concludes that the task is heavy and long, but is confident that implementing the speech will open a new stage and contribute to the Chinese Dream of national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want a brief, first-hand reaction from a senior Chinese scholar to the 2016 symposium and its guidelines for the field.

The "Aesthetic Notebook": an insufficiently appreciated key text by Marx 《美学笔记》： 一部未受到足够重视的马克思重要文本 Cheng Yuan Cheng Yuan argues that research on Marx's aesthetics has been incomplete because it relies on scattered remarks in a few works, chiefly the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, the Grundrisse and Capital. The article, first published in Shandong Social Sciences in 2016, presents Marx's 1857 "Aesthetic Notebook" as a neglected text that can restore the historical sequence and logic of his aesthetic thought. Cheng holds that it served as a bridge between his earlier and later views. The article first describes the notebook's physical and scholarly history. It is part of a 55-page notebook of 1857 that also contains political-economy extracts and newspaper cuttings. The aesthetic section, dated by Cheng to late May to mid-July, comprises extracts from Friedrich Theodor Vischer's Aesthetik oder Wissenschaft des Schönen, notes on a history of Greek art theory and encyclopaedia entries. Cheng then reviews research from Lukács's 1933 essay to the partial publication of the Vischer extracts in a Soviet journal in 1990. The article closes with four tasks for further study. Cheng's central claim rests on what Marx copied and what he left out. Only the Vischer extracts survive in accessible form. Marx took over Vischer's humanist vocabulary and noted only Baumgarten and Kant from the long historical survey, which Cheng reads as a sign that Marx skipped ground already familiar to him. Cheng draws four lines of continuity: aesthetics as concerned with the sensuous and subjective; beauty's essence as a dialectical relation of subject and object, in which Marx sublates Kant's ontology; the categories of the sublime, tragedy and comedy; and the treatment of natural and historical beauty from a historical-materialist standpoint. The author argues that the notebook was written as Marx's historical materialism was taking shape, and that it marks a move from Hegelian influence to an aesthetics grounded in that theory. Cheng calls for four lines of work: translating the notebook and the sources Marx read, ahead of its expected publication in the fourth section of MEGA2; a close comparison with Vischer's text; study of the notebook's place between the 1844 Manuscripts and the 1859 Preface and later works; and a renewed examination of whether Marx wrote the New American Cyclopaedia aesthetics entry. The author expects aesthetics research to move from constructing principles to interpreting texts. Read the original if you work on Marx's aesthetics or on MEGA2 and want a survey of the notebook's contents, its reception history and open research questions.

The subjective grounds of Marx's turn to communism in the Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher period 《德法年鉴》时期马克思共产主义转向的主体根据 Pan Zhongwei Marx's thought is often said to run from philosophy through communism to political economy, with the period of the Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher (1843–44) as the decisive middle point. Pan Zhongwei asks why Marx turned to communism then. Without denying the many external influences, including Feuerbach, Pan argues that external influence could only work because it matched Marx's own inner development. The article names this inner ground as a thoroughgoing theoretical spirit and a strong practical consciousness, resting on an understanding of the human being as a social being. The article is in four parts. The first compares Marx and Feuerbach, starting from Marx's 1843 letter to Ruge saying Feuerbach stressed nature too much and politics too little. The second examines why the thoroughness of theory is the precondition for making philosophy worldly, drawing on the Doctoral Dissertation, the critique of Hegel's philosophy of right and the Introduction to it. The third takes up why thoroughgoing theory demands a transformation of the world as a whole, covering the failure of the free press and of state intervention, On the Jewish Question and the proletariat. The fourth part is a short conclusion. Pan argues that Feuerbach, starting from the thinking and sensuous individual, sought a firm theoretical basis for a new age and so turned to nature. Marx, by contrast, was concerned with making the existing irrational world rational, so he took politics as philosophy's necessary ally. Marx's individual always lives in a historical world with others. In Pan's reading, his critique of Hegel found an irresolvable dualism in the Hegelian system and in the modern state generally, and led him to a real democracy. Marx took over Feuerbach's principles only after testing them through theoretical critique and historical study. Once the free press and the Prussian state had failed as routes to realising philosophy, Pan says, only a total transformation, with the proletariat as philosophy's ally, remained. Pan calls this a philosophical inference resting on an idealised proletariat. Marx's rejection of one-sided communism and socialism, and his stress on free and all-round human development, are said to show the same spirit. Pan concludes that free and all-round human development, theoretical thoroughness and total change of the world are the defining features of Marx's socialist and communist doctrine, which therefore keeps a strong idealist element. Pan holds that communist parties must keep arousing and protecting a moral consciousness of free and all-round development. Pan also calls on those developing socialist theory and building socialism to attend to theoretical work as well as economic construction and material needs. Read the original if you study the early Marx, the Marx–Feuerbach relation, or the tension between philosophical principle and empirical proletarian practice in Marx's turn to communism.

The current value of the Marxist theory of youth 马克思主义青年理论的当前价值 Tian Haibin Feng Yan Tian and Feng ask how Marxist youth theory should guide the cultivation of a sense of social responsibility among young people in China. Their answer is that the theory supplies both the definition of the "young Marxist" and the framework for fostering responsibility in economic, political, cultural and social fields. The piece appeared in People's Forum in 2016. The article opens with Jiang Zemin's definition of the "young Marxist", first put forward in 1989 and extended in 1997. It then argues that building youth social responsibility is an objective requirement of the times, and sets out five areas in which Marxist youth theory should guide that work. The authors say young Marxists are marked by a clear political character, a strong sense of the times and a practical orientation. They hold that China's social transformation has weakened collective feeling and responsibility, so targeted training in responsibility is needed and is also integral to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Drawing on the base–superstructure relationship, they call for young people to take responsibility for economic construction centred on reform and opening up, for political construction under Party leadership, and for cultural construction that carries forward socialist core values. They add a fifth area, harmony, framed by a harmonious society and the Scientific Outlook on Development. Tian and Feng conclude that training young Marxists and cultivating social responsibility reinforce each other within the process of adapting Marxism to Chinese conditions. They call on the Party and educators to unify young people's thinking around socialism with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a short example of how Party-affiliated writing in 2016 framed youth ideological education.

Marxism has powerful vitality 马克思主义有着强大生命力 Liu Xiaoling Liu Xiaochuan Taking its cue from Xi Jinping's remark at a symposium on philosophy and social sciences (2016) that guidance by Marxism first requires solving the problem of truly understanding and truly believing it, this People's Daily commentary asks why some people, including a few Party members and officials, bear the Marxist name without believing in it. Liu and Liu argue that such people treat Marxism as empty preaching, and that this misconception must be overcome by grasping Marxism's significance for the present age. The short piece is organised around three claims, each presented as a "commanding height" held by Marxism: truth, morality and methodology. It draws on Marx and Engels's own formulations and on two examples of Marxism's continuing influence abroad. First, the authors hold that Marxism is a science with objective truth: it reveals general laws of nature, society and thought, criticises capitalism, and shows the historical inevitability of socialism replacing it. They cite the BBC's "thinker of the millennium" online poll, in which Marx came first, and renewed sales of Capital in Europe after the 2008 financial crisis. Second, Marxism's commitment to the proletariat's liberation coincides with human emancipation, giving it a popular character and a stance serving the great majority. Third, Marxism is practical: citing Engels, they present it as a method rather than a dogma, with theory arising from practice and returning to it. The authors conclude that Party members and officials should believe in Marxism not merely out of political obligation but because of its truth, its popular character and its method. They add that it is the theoretical source of the Party's purpose of serving the people wholeheartedly. Read the original if you want a compact example of how the Party press framed the case for Marxist belief among cadres in 2016.

People-oriented: the ultimate value of Marxism 以人为本：马克思主义终极价值 Liang Jing Writing in 2016, as China entered the "deep water" of reform and ideology became more pluralistic under economic globalisation, Liang asks how Marxism's ultimate value and its discursive power can be upheld in China. The article's answer is that both must rest on the principle of putting people first, which Liang identifies as the practical form of Marxism's ultimate value: the all-round development of the human being. The piece first defines the ultimate value and "discursive power" of Marxism, then identifies obstacles to realising each, and finally proposes a path of development in three dimensions: material base, political environment and rule of law. It is a short commentary in a Chinese political-theory journal. Liang says that a people-first ultimate value must be universal, comprehensive, feasible and unlimited, an aim to be approached without end. Marxist discursive power is described as the people's most basic right, reflected in the Constitution, but also as relative and limited, since serving the majority will sometimes affect other strata. Obstacles include dogmatic or vulgarised readings of Marxism, Western discursive hegemony, competing social trends, and the blindness and self-interest of the market economy, which Liang says breeds moral lapses and distrust of the ruling party. Liang calls for developing the productive forces and improving production relations, eliminating corruption during the transition period, and strengthening the rule of law so that the people's fundamental interests are protected. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a 2016 Chinese commentary links "people-oriented" governance to Marxist theory and discursive power.

Sharp changes in the political landscape of Latin America: causes, impact and prospects 拉美国家政治格局发生急剧变化：原因、影响和前景 Xu Shicheng Writing in 2016, Xu Shicheng asks why left-wing governments in Latin America have suffered a run of setbacks in the preceding six months, and whether the left will keep declining. Xu argues that the political pendulum has swung to the right and that the left has entered an ebb tide. The article nonetheless rejects claims that the Latin American left is dead or dying, and expects a swing back towards the centre-left after a period of policy adjustment. The article first documents the shift country by country. It covers the right's victory in Argentina (Macri, November 2015), the opposition's two-thirds majority in Venezuela's National Assembly (December 2015) and the ensuing conflict with Maduro's government, and the impeachment vote against Dilma Rousseff in Brazil (April 2016). It also covers Evo Morales's referendum defeat in Bolivia and Rafael Correa's decision not to stand again in Ecuador. It then lists five causes and ends with the case that the left remains alive. Xu names five causes. The first is economic: falling commodity prices ended the export boom, forcing austerity and cuts to social programmes that left newly middle-class people at risk of falling back into poverty. Xu adds that governments failed to diversify their economies and that some policies were too radical, such as nationalising non-essential firms. The second is political: fragmented ruling coalitions and factionalised ruling parties, as with Brazil's PMDB and Venezuela's PSUV. The third is corruption, which Xu says often triggers protests. The fourth and fifth are US interference, including funding for opposition groups and sanctions on Venezuela, and the growing strength of right-wing forces and right-leaning media. Xu concludes that the left still governs in Cuba, Brazil, Venezuela, Bolivia, Ecuador, Nicaragua, Chile, Uruguay and El Salvador. It also keeps real strength in Argentina, Mexico and Peru. In Xu's view, deep inequality and social tension sustain the left's social base, and its achievements against neoliberalism, in poverty reduction, education, health care and regional integration should not be dismissed wholesale. Xu cites Uruguay's former president José Mujica on the pendulum of history, and holds that the left's prospects are bright if it reflects seriously on its own problems. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese academic assessment, written in 2016, of the Latin American left's reverses, with country-level figures and a defence of the left's prospects.

The Vietnamese Communist Party's 12th Congress and the "nine relationships" of renewal 越共十二大提出革新发展“九大关系” Pan Jin'e This short commentary, written in 2016, reports on the 12th National Congress of the Communist Party of Vietnam (CPV), held on 20–28 January 2016 at the thirtieth anniversary of Vietnam's renewal (Doi Moi). Pan Jin'e argues that the congress set the direction of economic renewal for 2016–2020 around building and perfecting a socialist-oriented market economy, and that the "nine relationships" it asks the Party to handle show problems similar to China's. The article has three parts. It first traces the Party's changing theory of economic reform since 1986, then sets out the congress's targets and reform measures for the next five years, and finally lists the nine relationships and comments on Vietnam's deepening international integration. On theory, Pan describes a move from a Soviet-style centrally planned economy to the "socialist-oriented market economy", step by step from the 6th Congress (1986) to the 9th (2001) and the 2008 resolution that treated the market economy as a means of building socialism rather than as capitalism. The 12th Congress added the word "perfecting" and, as Pan reports, a Vietnamese theorist names five sources of socialist orientation: state management under the rule of law, Party leadership, the people's mastery, suitable relations of production, and social progress and equity. Pan then reports the congress's targets, including annual growth of 6.5–7% and GDP per capita of 3,200–3,500 US dollars by 2020, and its plans for state-owned enterprises, collective, private and foreign-invested firms. These include share-based restructuring of state firms, separating commercial from political and public-interest tasks, and encouraging private capital. Pan notes that the nine relationships put stability and reform first. The new pair, the state and the market, in Pan's reading borrows from the Third Plenum of the 18th Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party (2013). Pan also observes that Vietnam signed the Trans-Pacific Partnership in January 2016. Pan holds that the agreement's demands on trade unions, state-owned enterprises and freedom of association will affect the CPV's control and Vietnam's future path, and that the report makes both opportunities and challenges plain. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese scholarly summary of the CPV's 12th Congress economic line and its parallels with Chinese reform discourse.

If poor, cultivate oneself; if successful, benefit the whole world Value pursuits and the notion of righteousness and interest in Chinese diplomatic culture 穷则独善其身，达则兼济天下 Pan Jin'e Writing in 2016, Pan Jin'e asks what values underlie Chinese diplomacy. The starting point is Xi Jinping's September 2015 speech at the UN's 70th anniversary summit, where he pledged that China would keep to the principle of 'giving equal weight to righteousness and interests, with righteousness first'. Pan argues that the speech reflects the foreign-policy thinking of the new leadership. In the article's account it inherits traditional Chinese diplomatic culture and the ideas of earlier leaders, and develops them for present conditions. The article is organised around two strands of Confucian thought. The first is the view of righteousness and interest (yi and li), which Pan traces through Chinese foreign aid from the Mao era to Xi. The second is the idea of 'harmony without uniformity', which Pan links to the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence and to Deng Xiaoping's and Jiang Zemin's views on peace, development and multipolarity. It also covers Hu Jintao's 2005 'harmonious world' speech and Xi's concept of a community with a shared future for mankind. Pan holds that the 'correct approach to righteousness and interest', which Xi put forward in 2013, continues what every generation of leaders practised. As evidence the article cites declassified figures: aid to more than 110 countries and regions before 1976, and total aid spending of 41.181 billion yuan by 1985. It also cites Hu Jintao's debt relief for Africa and Xi's pledges of a South–South cooperation assistance fund and the Belt and Road Initiative. On the second strand, Pan reads the community with a shared future for mankind, along with calls for equality among states and respect for each country's chosen path, as an extension of Confucian ideas on conduct. Pan concludes that, across periods, the Mencian ideal of cultivating oneself when poor and benefiting all under heaven when successful runs through Chinese diplomacy. Pan adds that this ideal overlaps with the Party's guiding ideology, namely Marxist internationalism and the communist goal of human liberation. In Pan's view, combining the two yields a distinctive diplomatic culture with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want an example of how Chinese scholars in 2016 grounded official foreign-policy language in Confucian tradition and the history of foreign aid.

The direction of Vietnam's Đổi Mới as seen from the 12th Congress of the Communist Party of Vietnam 从越共十二大看越南革新的走向 Pan Jin'e Writing in early 2016, shortly after the 12th National Congress of the Communist Party of Vietnam (CPV) held in Hanoi on 20–28 January 2016, Pan Jin'e asks why the Congress kept the over-70 Nguyen Phu Trong as General Secretary rather than choosing the widely tipped Prime Minister Nguyen Tan Dung. The article also asks what this means for China–Vietnam relations and where Vietnam's renovation (Đổi Mới, in Chinese 革新) is heading. Pan argues that the Congress reaffirmed a socialist-oriented path, while behind apparent stability the personnel outcome reflected struggle and compromise among forces inside the Party. The article first traces preparation of the political report, including Pan's own 2015 interviews in Vietnam and the publication of draft documents for public comment. It then reviews the draft's assessment of 30 years of renovation, its lessons and the "nine relationships" to be managed. Further sections analyse the personnel changes and new election rules, and Vietnam's defence, security and foreign policy. A short conclusion looks at internal and external challenges. Pan's core argument has three parts. First, comparing the draft report with Nguyen Phu Trong's delivered report, and the 2015 draft with the 11th Congress theme, Pan sees more emphasis on building a "pure and strong" Party, on socialist democracy and on defending the homeland. The foreign-policy passages were notably softened: the delivered text and Foreign Minister Pham Binh Minh's speech dropped formulas such as "cooperation and struggle", and stressed managing differences over the South China Sea. Second, Pan describes the 2014 Party election rules, the age limits, the vote that denied Nguyen Tan Dung a Central Committee seat, and the 2015 Referendum Law, which Pan sees as adding pressure on one-party rule. Third, Pan points to Western ideological currents, corruption, "peaceful evolution" and Vietnam's commitment to the Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP) as threats to Party stability. Pan also notes that the "government and market" relationship appears to borrow from the Third Plenum of the 18th CPC Central Committee (2013). Pan concludes that the Congress ensured continuity and a transfer of power, but that the new leadership faces a heavy test. Pan suggests it is unclear whether Trong will serve the full term. Pan reads the public statements of Vietnamese officials as signals of friendlier cooperation with China. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's detailed account of the 12th CPV Congress documents, the new Party election procedures and the shift in Vietnam's foreign-policy wording.

Understanding shared development through the Marxist view of equality 从马克思主义平等观看共享发展 Xie Weiguang Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2016, Xie Weiguang asks how the Marxist conception of equality can guide the practice of shared development, the concept put forward at the Fifth Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2015). The article argues that shared development, whose core is social justice, balances efficiency with fairness and presupposes equality, while equality in turn is expressed through shared results. In Xie's view, the Marxist view of equality has both theoretical and practical significance for carrying it out. The piece has three sections. The first sets out the Marxist view of equality and its critique of bourgeois equality. The second argues that shared development and equality depend on each other. The third turns to what the author calls the application, upholding and development of Marxist equality in policy: equal basic rights and proportional non-basic rights. Xie's core argument starts from Engels: equality is a historical product that reflects existing economic relations, so no equality exists beyond its historical conditions. Bourgeois slogans of equality before God, the law and the market are, on this reading, abstract and formal, because private ownership of the means of production produces real inequality. Xie cites Capital on the market as an appearance of equal exchange that hides exploitation in production, and cites the Critique of the Gotha Programme on distribution according to labour as still not full equality. Only the higher stage of communism, "from each according to his ability, to each according to his needs", would bring real equality, and its highest aim is the free and all-round development of the person. From this Xie derives two tasks for the primary stage of socialism. Basic rights should be fully equal, mainly through government-led secondary distribution. This means upholding the dominant position of public ownership, equalising basic public services across regions and between town and country, strengthening transfer payments and poverty alleviation, and leaving no one behind on the road to a moderately prosperous society. Non-basic rights should be distributed in proportion to contribution, which Xie links to China's level of development and the continuing priority of growth. The author calls for institutions guaranteeing fairness of rights, opportunity and rules, moving steadily towards common prosperity. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a 2016 Party-journal article ties the shared development concept to classical Marxist texts on equality.

Great practice requires a great development of philosophy and social sciences 伟大的实践需要哲学社会科学大发展 Zhang Jiang Writing in Qiushi in 2016, Zhang Jiang takes up Xi Jinping's speech at the symposium on philosophy and social sciences work. The article argues that upholding and developing socialism with Chinese characteristics urgently requires a major development of philosophy and social sciences, and that scholars must shoulder the historical mission this implies. The commentary is a short study of the speech in three parts. It first discusses the role of philosophy and social sciences in historical progress, then the new tasks set by the present situation, and finally the problems the field is said to have. Zhang contends that philosophy and social sciences have driven social advance, citing Xi's remark that every great leap in human society has depended on intellectual change. Contemporary China, the author says, is undergoing the broadest social change in its history, which makes it an era that needs and will produce theory. Zhang links the new tasks to the new development philosophy, reform, the Party's full and rigorous self-governance, and China's international discourse power. The article then lists the weaknesses Xi identified: quantity without quality, experts without great masters, and weak discipline systems and evaluation mechanisms. It also names academic misconduct, from hasty compilation and detachment from reality to plagiarism and fabricated data. Zhang concludes that facing these problems squarely will strengthen the sense of urgency and responsibility needed to improve the field. Scholars are urged to offer theoretical support and policy advice for the Party and people, and to help realise the Chinese Dream of national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the 2016 official call for philosophy and social sciences was presented in Qiushi.

Rereading Lenin's Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism 重读列宁《帝国主义是资本主义的最高阶段》 Li Jie Writing in 2016, a century after Lenin's Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism, Li Jie asks what the book still explains. The article argues that two long-running developments are both anticipated in Lenin's analysis. The first is capitalism's move from free competition to financial monopoly at the start of the twentieth century. The second is the decline of contemporary capitalism at the start of the twenty-first, marked by the rise of socialism with Chinese characteristics and by emerging countries entering modernity by non-capitalist means. The piece is a short essay in two numbered parts. The first summarises Lenin's account of imperialism as the inevitable product of capitalist free competition, with page references to the Selected Works of Lenin. The second takes up socialism with Chinese characteristics as a further option beyond capitalist modernization. It ends with a brief judgement on the lasting value of Lenin's book. Li reconstructs Lenin's logic in six steps: concentration of production produces monopoly; monopoly produces finance capital; ownership of capital separates from its productive use; surplus capital is exported; and finance capital leads to the direct partition of the world. Li holds that today's capitalist world still moves according to this logic, including in the financial crisis that began in 2008, where reforms against monopoly keep giving way to higher levels of monopoly. The author reads this as a self-expanding finance capital heading towards self-destruction. In the second part, Li says capital's overseas expansion awakened national independence movements and a search for modernization. Li argues that Western models, whether the British Commonwealth model or the Washington Consensus, lead only to the "middle-income trap", privatization and electoral disorder. Socialism with Chinese characteristics, in Li's account, combines reform and opening up, the Two Unwaverings and a decisive role for the market with public ownership in the main position, Party leadership and opposition to privatization and "constitutional democracy". Li concludes that the greatness of Lenin's book does not depend on whether particular specific claims still hold. It rests, in Li's view, on its disclosure of objective and lasting laws of capitalism and socialism. Li adds that Marx's and Lenin's laws of capitalist and imperialist demise will arrive however long they take. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a 2016 Party-journal essay links Lenin's theory of imperialism to the case for the Chinese development path.

Rethinking the lessons of the Soviet collapse 对苏联解体教训的再认识 Lin Yanhu Feng Yanli Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2016, Lin Yanhu and Feng Yanli ask why a superpower disappeared 'without a single shot' and what China should learn from it. They argue that the main cause was the Soviet Communist Party leadership's abandonment of Marxism as its guiding ideology and of its socialist and communist ideals. In their view the collapse was a historical tragedy but not a failure of socialism, and it did not alter the historical law by which socialism replaces capitalism. The article has two parts. The first seeks a comprehensive understanding of the collapse, in three sub-sections: abandoning Marxism as the root cause, the persistence of the historical law despite the collapse, and the collapse as a national disaster and a tragedy for world socialism. The second part draws three lessons for China: consolidating Marxism's ideological position, strengthening Marxist discourse power and national cultural soft power, and holding firm to the Four-sphere Confidence. On causes, the authors hold that under Gorbachev's 'new thinking' the Party pursued political 'pluralism', economic privatisation and the 'de-ideologisation' of culture and foreign relations. They call this a reversal of socialism, in substance a copy of capitalism, which produced confusion and a loss of popular cohesion. They answer Brzezinski and Fukuyama by arguing that capitalism's internal contradictions, wealth concentration and the post-2008 crisis and protest movements point to its decline. To show the human cost, they cite falling output, wars in six former republics, rising inequality in Russia and a fall in life expectancy. Their lessons call for 'one guiding ideology over many' and for resisting historical nihilism and Western infiltration. They also call for promoting socialist core values, grounding Marxist discourse in the people's interests and cultural 'going out', and building China's own academic discourse. The authors conclude that China must study the Soviet case closely and hold firmly to Marxist belief, socialism with Chinese characteristics and the communist ideal. They quote Xi Jinping's 1 July 2016 speech on confidence in the path, theory, system and culture, and argue that only the Four-sphere Confidence can carry the Party through a complex international and domestic situation. Read the original if you want a concise example of mid-2016 official-academic Chinese framing of the Soviet collapse as an ideological lesson, with the statistics and policy conclusions the authors draw.

The development of the world socialist movement in China 世界社会主义运动发展在中国 Liu Hanfeng Guan Yongqian Reviewing the year 2015, Liu Hanfeng and Guan Yongqian ask how research and practice on world socialism developed in China and what trends follow for the movement. They argue that world socialism is in a phase of revival since the financial crisis, and that China is one of its main forces. In their account, the development of the theoretical system of socialism with Chinese characteristics supplies experience for refining scientific socialism. The article is a year-in-review survey. It first describes the advance of world socialism studies in China in 2015, including a series of academic forums and the first World Marxism Congress hosted by Peking University. It then tracks the main research hotspots among Chinese scholars, and closes with the basic trends facing the movement. It reports the views of many named scholars, among them Deng Chundong, Nie Yunlin, Yan Zhimin, Wang Weiguang, Li Junru and Yan Shuhan, as well as a Vietnamese and a US voice. The authors start from the cyclical-crisis logic of capitalism, citing Kondratiev's long waves and Ernest Mandel. They hold that the crisis has opened a new opportunity for socialism. Chinese scholars, they report, describe a "new normal" of world socialism: diversity of paths, independent exploration by each party, peaceful coexistence and competition between the two social systems, and an end to a single model. The Four Comprehensives are presented as the latest achievement of socialism with Chinese characteristics, including the first Party-history call for full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. The authors also treat ideological struggle as a standing task: they say the West uses peaceful evolution and "colour revolutions", and quote Wang Weiguang that holding the discourse power of Marxism is the most reliable weapon. The authors conclude that difficult economic recovery in the US and Europe, together with the refugee crisis, objectively favours the movement. They say socialism with Chinese characteristics is gaining wide recognition and leading theoretical and practical innovation. They expect confidence in its path, theory and system to grow and to unite the Party's cause, the Chinese nation's cause and that of world socialism. Read the original if you want a compact record of how Chinese scholars framed world socialism and the Four Comprehensives in 2015.

The evolution of Marxism in Cuba and its lessons 马克思主义在古巴的演进及启示 Li Jianguo Cuba is, in the author's words, the only existing socialist country outside Asia, and Li Jianguo argues that the course of Marxism there offers lessons for understanding the regularities of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Writing in 2016, Li contends that Cuban socialism rests on a distinctive national situation and has survived through steady reform, loyalty to Marxism-Leninism and José Martí's thought, and the protection of the people's basic interests. The article has four parts. It first describes Cuba's national conditions: its status as a US dependency before 1959, the long US blockade afterwards, and a strong popular commitment to independence. It then divides Cuba's history into five stages, from the democratic revolution (1944–59) through the socialist revolution, the search for a path of construction, the period of copying the Soviet model, and the reforms of the post-Soviet 'special period'. A third part sets out Cuban theoretical outcomes, and a fourth draws three lessons. Li's central claim is that Cuban Marxism grew out of national circumstances. The author describes Cuba as defining socialism's essence as national independence and the people's welfare, and as having adopted Martí's thought as the Party's guiding ideology at the Fourth Party Congress (1991). Li treats the 1968 'revolutionary offensive' and the later wholesale copying of the Soviet model as errors that detached policy from national conditions. After the Soviet collapse, Cuba pursued 'socialism with Cuban characteristics' and cautious reform, retaining planning, limiting foreign capital and private business, and avoiding the word 'reform' itself. Li also notes that Cuba holds that the world is still an age of two social systems and two classes, and rejects neoliberal globalisation. Li draws three lessons: uphold Marxism-Leninism, Martí's thought and socialism as the theoretical and institutional foundation; carry out steady reform and opening up to 'update' the socialist model; and protect the people's fundamental interests. In this account, free healthcare and education, subsidies, low unemployment and clean conduct by Party cadres explain why the people trust the Party and why Cuba has survived internal and external pressure. Li presents this as the most valuable point for other socialist countries. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese academic overview of Cuba's socialist trajectory, written in 2016 around the Seventh Congress of the Cuban Communist Party and from a Chinese viewpoint.

Rethinking the lessons of the Soviet collapse 对苏联解体教训的再认识 Lin Yanhu Feng Yanli Writing in 2016, Lin Yanhu and Feng Yanli revisit the collapse of the Soviet Union and the fall of the Soviet Communist Party. They argue that the main cause was the top leadership's abandonment of Marxism as its guiding ideology and of socialist and communist ideals. In their view the collapse was a historical tragedy but not a failure of socialism, and it does not alter the historical law by which socialism replaces capitalism. The article has two parts. The first sets out how the collapse should be understood: its root cause, its place in the long course of the world socialist movement, and its human and political costs. The second draws three lessons for China: consolidating Marxism's position in ideology, strengthening the discourse power of Marxism, and holding to the Four-sphere Confidence. On the cause, the authors hold that Gorbachev's "new thinking" amounted to a capitalist reform.
