They name three features: political "pluralism" that ended Marxism's leading position, privatisation and a rapid move from planning to the market, and "de-ideologisation" in culture and foreign policy. They say the collapse brought economic decline, wars in some republics, wider inequality in Russia and a fall in the number of socialist states from 15 to 5. On the lessons, they claim that losing discourse power opens the way for subverting a socialist ideology. They call for core socialist values to build consensus, for resistance to historical nihilism and to Western ideological infiltration, and for a Marxist discourse system anchored in the people's interests. The authors conclude that China must study the Soviet case closely and keep Marxism as the guiding ideology of socialism with Chinese characteristics. They also call for a Marxist-led academic discourse in the humanities and social sciences, and for firm confidence in China's path, theory, system and culture. They present this confidence as the safeguard against the dangers of a complex international and domestic situation. Read the original if you want an example of how Party-aligned scholarship drew ideological lessons from the Soviet collapse for China in 2016.

Profound lessons from the CPSU's ideological work 苏共意识形态工作的深刻教训 Jiang Hong Writing on the 25th anniversary of the dissolution of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union (CPSU) and the collapse of the USSR, Jiang Hong asks why Soviet ideological work failed. The author treats the gradual loosening and final collapse of the ideological front as one important factor among several in the Soviet defeat. Jiang argues that the failure resulted from the interaction of subjective and objective, internal and external, and political and socio-economic causes, and that it ultimately lay in a failure to unite Party spirit with the people's character. The article is a short commentary in Red Flag Manuscripts that examines the Soviet record from Lenin through Khrushchev, Brezhnev, Andropov and Gorbachev. It is organised into five numbered sections: dogmatic treatment of Marxism, the loss of belief among top leaders, the isolation of propaganda work, heavy-handed control of currents of thought, and great-power chauvinist foreign policy. A closing section draws these threads together. Jiang's main claim is that the CPSU turned Marxism into a closed textbook system, beginning with Stalin's 1938 text, which lost its capacity for innovation and became a tool for policies that violated the laws of productive-force development. Top leaders then lost their Marxist faith and communist ideals, and the Party became, in the author's words, a special-interest group detached from the people. Propaganda was separated from culture and from people's everyday concerns, such as shortages and unequal distribution, and remained dogmatic, coercive preaching. Jiang adds that suppressing underground publications through the KGB and the offence of 'ideological subversion' only spread Western ideas and damaged the Party's image, while Soviet hegemonism towards other socialist states and parties, and the invasion of Afghanistan, weakened its ideological leadership from outside. Jiang concludes that a ruling communist party which abandons the unity of Party spirit and the people's character loses its ideological ground and then its power. In the author's account, the CPSU drifted from serving the people, and its ideology lost its correctness and scientific character, ending in 'the Party's fall as its people fell away'. The lesson drawn is implicitly for today's ruling communist parties. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese Party-affiliated scholars in 2016 explained the Soviet ideological collapse as a warning for the present.

The German Left Party sees China as the most important birthplace of "Socialism 3.0" A report on Charles (Charles) Bully's lecture "The Third Wave of Socialism" 德国左翼党认为中国是“社会主义3.0”最重要的诞生地 Zhang Wenhong This short report, published in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2016, summarises a lecture given on 24 May at the invitation of the Party Studies Centre of the Central Compilation and Translation Bureau. The speaker was a senior researcher of the Rosa Luxemburg Foundation, linked to Germany's Left Party; the report gives his name in Chinese transliteration as Xia'er Buli (夏尔·布里). The lecture, titled "The Third Wave of Socialism", argues that 25 years after the Soviet collapse socialism must be re-examined across the period from 1789 to the twenty-first century. In the speaker's view, the Soviet collapse opened a third wave, "Socialism 3.0", and China is its most important place of birth. The report follows the lecture in three parts. The first sketches the first wave (1789–1917) and the second (1917–1991). The second part sets out two features of the third wave, which the speaker dates from 1991. The third part addresses the multiple crises of modern capitalism and China's place in the future of socialism. As reported, the first wave produced reformist, anarchist and revolutionary-vanguard currents, with Marxism seeking to give them a scientific basis. The second wave saw the October Revolution, the Chinese revolution of 1949 and Western social-democratic welfare states, but all of these proved unstable and were overtaken by the neoliberal turn. For the third wave, the speaker holds that an alternative to capitalism must be a learning society, neither bureaucratically centralised like the Soviet system nor competition-driven like the United States, and organised as a "polycentric" mixed system with plural ownership. It must also help to create a new, "harmonious" civilisation that rebalances humans with nature and with society and relies more on broad democratic participation and consensus. The speaker describes capitalism as facing ecological, identity, political-legitimacy and international-security crises, with opposing movements lacking a convincing alternative. Citing Perry Anderson, he expects the twenty-first century to be shaped by Chinese revolutionary events, as the twentieth was by Soviet ones. He lists five preconditions for socialist association, from ecologically friendly high productivity to a peaceful international order, and says "Socialism 3.0" must prove it can advance them. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese-language record of how a German left-wing researcher framed China's place in world socialism for a Chinese audience in 2016.

Strictly enforcing the political discipline that "Communist Party members may not believe in religion" 严明“共产党员不得信仰宗教”的政治纪律 Tian Xinming Writing in 2016, after the national conference on religious work held that April, Tian Xinming argues that the rule that Communist Party members may not hold religious beliefs is an important item of political discipline. In the author's account, it must be enforced strictly as part of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. The piece, published in Red Flag Manuscripts, is a commentary that also rebuts a Party cadre who, in a magazine article, questioned the rule. Tian first traces the rule's continuity, from Mao Zedong's wartime distinction between a united front with religious people and agreement with their doctrines, through the Central Committee's 1982 document on religious questions, to documents of 1991 and 2002. The article then gives three reasons for the rule and addresses the constitutional objection. Its second part answers two arguments for admitting believers to the Party: Lenin's remarks on priests and the practice of other communist parties, and the claim that political and religious belief can be separated. The reasons given are that the Party's worldview is dialectical and historical materialism, which Tian calls incompatible with theism. Belief would also undermine socialism with Chinese characteristics, which rests on trust in the people and in objective laws of development. Finally, a believer would face a conflict of loyalties between Party and religious organisation, harming democratic centralism. To the constitutional objection, Tian replies that Party discipline is stricter than state law, joining is voluntary, and those unwilling to accept it may leave and keep their freedom of belief. On Lenin, the author says Lenin reasoned from Russian conditions, and that China is a secular country in which, according to the 1982 document, genuine believers are a small share of the population. Tian adds that other parties' policies are their own affair. On the second argument, Tian holds that political stance and worldview are distinct, so patriotic religious figures can support the Party's cause within the united front, but Party members must unite the two. Admitting religious leaders to "show care" for religion would, in Tian's view, make society adapt to religion and let religion influence Party policy. The author concludes that the rule is necessary and workable, and that exceptions for minority areas with near-universal belief call for gradual, case-by-case handling. Read the original if you want an authoritative statement of the 2016 Party case against admitting religious believers, with its textual sources and its replies to critics inside the Party.

Institutionalising Party ideological building as an important theoretical innovation of the Party 思想建设制度化是党的重要理论创新 Liu Xinling Lian Xiaolong Writing in Qiushi's Red Flag Manuscripts in 2016, Liu Xinling and Lian Xiaolong take up the proposition of the "institutionalisation of the Party's ideological building", put forward by Xi Jinping after the 18th Party Congress (2012). The authors argue that it is an important theoretical innovation. In their account it extends ideological building beyond education, theoretical armament and theoretical innovation into the sphere of rules and regulations. The article begins with a historical survey of how the content of Party ideological building has changed with the Party's central tasks. It moves from the early debates and the Gutian Conference, through the Zunyi Meeting, the Yan'an rectification campaign and the adoption of Mao Zedong Thought at the Seventh Congress. It then covers the rectification and anti-corruption campaigns of the early 1950s, the Eighth Congress (1956), and the "re-learning" stressed since the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978). The second half examines recent Party regulations under three headings: theoretical work, Party spirit education and morality. The authors argue that ideological building has two sides: struggle against non-Marxist ideas and the unification of the Party's thinking, and the innovation and propagation of Marxist theory. In their reading, the new proposition links ideological work to "governing the Party by institutions" and builds a complete system from institutional design to implementation. They cite the 2013–2017 five-year plan for Party regulations, the 2015 Disciplinary Regulations, the 2015 Regulations on Cadre Education and Training, and the 2015 Code of Integrity and Self-discipline. These set requirements for theory study, including training hours and assessment, rules on propaganda and Party management of the media, expulsion for opposing the Party's basic theory and line, and moral criteria in cadre selection and removal. The authors conclude that institutionalisation answers the "four tests" and "four dangers" facing the Party. They hold that it lays an ideological foundation for the "two centenary goals" and gives institutional protection to ideological building under full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. Read the original if you want a Party-theory account of how ideological work was written into formal regulations in 2013–2016, with the specific documents and provisions cited.

Keeping Marxist atheism dominant in the thinking of the people 始终保持马克思主义无神论在人民群众思想中的主导地位 Zhu Xiaoming Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2016, Zhu Xiaoming takes up a directive from the National Conference on Religious Work held that April: Party members must adhere to Marxist atheism and must not look for their values and beliefs in religion. The article asks how Marxist atheism can remain the dominant element of the mainstream ideology in the people's thinking. Zhu answers that atheism must be both upheld and actively propagated across the whole of society, not only within the Party. The piece has two parts. The first argues that the theory of religion of socialism with Chinese characteristics is in essence Marxist atheism. The second sets out how atheism is to keep its leading position among the people, with three requirements: propagate it actively, do not let general Marxist education replace it, and carry it out persistently and widely. Zhu draws on Mao Zedong, Lenin's "On the Significance of Militant Materialism", and the religion scholar Ren Jiyu. Zhu's central move is to distinguish audiences and policies. Atheism is a requirement for Party members, with Party cadres and young people as the main targets of propaganda. Toward religious believers and religious venues the Party practises "political cooperation and mutual respect in belief", and it does not conduct atheist propaganda among believers. Zhu therefore holds that freedom of religious belief and atheist education are two complementary basic principles of religious work. Zhu warns against treating policy toward the religious sphere as policy for society as a whole, and against letting central directives stay "locked in drawers". Zhu also argues, citing Lenin, that general Marxist teaching cannot replace dedicated atheist education, which should use concrete everyday examples and be linked to science and advanced culture. Research on religion should be done from a non-believing, historical-materialist standpoint and should aim to "demystify" religion and counter religious extremism. Zhu concludes that atheist education is never finished, since new unknowns will keep producing supernatural fantasies, so it demands perseverance. Read the original if you want an official-line statement, from a leading atheism-society figure in 2016, of how Party policy separates atheist propaganda from the protection of religious freedom.

Review of foreign research on the communist movements of twentieth-century Southeast Asia 国外关于20世纪东南亚共产主义运动的研究述评 Liu Lianfen Shi Yili This is a literature review of foreign scholarship on the communist movements that, from the early twentieth century to the 1980s, spread across almost every Southeast Asian country. Liu and Shi treat these movements as part of the region's national histories and as a manifestation of the rise and fall of the international communist movement in Asia. They note that the research they collected is mainly in English, with a little in French, and that it has been shaped throughout by Cold War conditions in Asia. The review is organised in four parts. The first covers regional and international perspectives, from 1950s American works such as Jack H. Brimmell's study of Southeast Asian communism through to studies of Soviet and Chinese policy. The second turns to Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia, and the third to Indonesia, Malaysia and the Philippines. The fourth deals with Burma and Thailand. Within each country the authors group books by theme, by source base and by the author's position, whether scholar, journalist, participant or defector. The authors identify several patterns. Regional studies relied largely on government publications and press reports, supplemented by the FBIS bulletins translating communist radio broadcasts and by the Hoover Institution's yearbook. On Vietnam, they distinguish party histories, studies of the Vietnamese Workers' Party's position between Beijing and Moscow, and comparisons of British counter-insurgency in Malaya with the American effort in South Vietnam. On Laos, works stress Vietnamese support for the Pathet Lao. On Cambodia, attention centres on the Khmer Rouge and the genocide of 1975–78. For Malaya, accounts by participants, notably Chin Peng's memoirs, are set against scholars' assessments. Studies of Thailand and Burma examine, among other things, how far Maoist strategy suited local conditions and what role China played. Liu and Shi present the survey as an overview of how foreign scholars have followed these movements from the late 1940s onward, rather than proposing a new thesis of their own. They record the varied source bases, including captured documents, interviews with defectors and documentary compilations, and the differing national trajectories. These range from the Indonesian party's three devastating blows to the Burmese party's collapse in the late 1980s. Read the original if you need a country-by-country bibliographic guide to English-language work on Southeast Asian communism, with notes on each book's sources and arguments.

The Vietnamese Communist Party's 12th Congress and its "nine relationships" for renovation 越共十二大提出革新发展“九大关系” Pan Jin'e Writing in March 2016, Pan Jin'e reports on the 12th National Congress of the Communist Party of Vietnam (CPV), held on 20–28 January 2016, thirty years after the start of renovation (doi moi). The article argues that the Congress's political report and its 2016–2020 socio-economic development strategy set the goal of building and perfecting a socialist-oriented market economy, and fixed the targets and direction of economic renovation for the next five years. The piece is a short newspaper commentary in four parts. It traces how the CPV's theoretical understanding of economic reform evolved from 1986 to 2016, summarises the Congress's definition of the socialist-oriented market economy, lists the targets and sector-by-sector reform plans for 2016–2020, and closes with the "nine relationships" that the report says must be handled well. Pan shows a progression from a Soviet-style centralised planned economy, through "commodity economy" formulations in 1989, 1991 and 1996, to the formal concept of a socialist-oriented market economy at the 9th Congress (2001). The 2008 resolution is quoted as saying the market economy is not identical with capitalism and is a means of building socialism. The 12th Congress added the word "perfecting" and, as Vietnamese theorists read it, anchors the socialist orientation in five features, including management by a socialist law-governed state, Party leadership and the people's mastery. The Congress sets targets such as 6.5–7 per cent annual growth and per capita GDP of 3,200–3,500 US dollars by 2020, and orders state-owned enterprise equitisation, support for private firms and more selective foreign investment. Pan notes that the nine relationships put stability and reform first. The state–market relationship is an addition to the eight relationships summarised at the 11th Congress, which Pan sees as borrowing from the Third Plenum of the 18th CPC Central Committee (2013) and as showing that Vietnam's economic problems resemble China's. Pan adds that Vietnam's signing of the US-led Trans-Pacific Partnership in January 2016 will, in the author's view, affect the Party's control and Vietnam's future path, given its demands on trade unions, state enterprises and freedom of association. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese overview of the CPV's 2016 economic line and how a Chinese scholar compares it with China's reform agenda.

Cuba's Seventh Party Congress "updates" the socialist model A compilation of international news agency reports on Raúl Castro's opening speech, April 2016 古共七大“更新”社会主义模式 This is a compilation of foreign wire and press reports, republished in Cankao Xiaoxi on 18 April 2016, on the opening of the Seventh Congress of the Communist Party of Cuba (PCC) on 16 April 2016. The reports (EFE, AFP, Prensa Latina, AP, Reuters, Die Zeit and Deutsche Welle) cover the roughly two-and-a-half-hour speech by First Secretary Raúl Castro. They present it as a reaffirmation of one-party socialism together with an economic "update" of the model, and no single author advances a thesis. The text is arranged under four headings: the pledge not to return to capitalism; criticism of bureaucracy as an obstacle to development; the renewal of the top leadership; and a pragmatic stance on relations with the United States. Each section collects short agency dispatches, and some close with background from Deutsche Welle on how Party congresses work. On the economy, the reports quote Castro as saying the constitution will be amended to incorporate the "update" begun five years earlier and to define the scope of state and private activity. State enterprise remains the main economic form, ownership and wealth are not to be concentrated, and shock therapy and neoliberal privatisation will not be allowed. AP and Die Zeit report that he conceded that only 21 per cent of the 313 guidelines approved in 2011 had been implemented. They add that he blamed bureaucracy and "old thinking", and listed import dependence, slow growth, the dual currency and weak farm output as problems. On succession, Castro proposed age limits of 60 for entering the Central Committee and 70 for top leaders, on top of the two-term limit from 2011. He said he would step down in 2018. On foreign affairs, Castro says Cuba is committed to "civilized coexistence" with the United States but warns that Washington's goals are unchanged and only its methods differ. He also urges unity among Latin American left-wing governments against a possible neoliberal return. The reports present this as a congress balancing continuity of the political system, pragmatic economic adjustment and generational change. Read the original if you want a quick, multi-source digest of how the foreign press reported Cuba's 2016 Party congress, including Castro's self-criticism, the succession rules and his wariness towards the US.

North Korea will keep to its established course A reading of Kim Jong Un's work report to the Seventh Congress of the Workers' Party of Korea 朝鲜将沿既定路线走下去 Gao Haorong Writing in International Herald Leader in May 2016, Gao Haorong reads the work report that Kim Jong Un delivered to the Seventh Congress of the Workers' Party of Korea, the first congress in 36 years (opened 6 May 2016). Gao treats the report, published in full by North Korean media on 8 May, as the best guide to the country's direction. The commentary's thesis is that North Korea will continue along its established line. The piece, a short commentary, follows the structure of the report of more than 70,000 characters. It first covers the retrospective on the 36 years since the Sixth Congress (1980). It then turns to the five tasks Kim set for the future. The remaining sections deal with Korean unification and with nuclear status. Gao reports that Kim attributes the achievements to three things: defending socialism while world socialism suffered setbacks, becoming a political, ideological and military power with nuclear weapons, and solving the succession of the revolutionary cause. In Gao's reading, pairing a severe environment with these successes serves to affirm Kim Il Sung and Kim Jong Il as eternal leaders and the Juche idea and military-first politics as the Party's unchangeable guiding ideology. The five tasks are the Kim Il Sung–Kim Jong Il-ization of the whole society (the priority), and building powers in science and technology, in the economy, in culture, and in political and military strength. Gao sees the new emphasis on self-reliance as a response to international sanctions. Gao also notes the first national economic plan in many years, a 2016–2020 five-year strategy, with electric power named as its precondition. Kim restates the federal formula for unification and proposes talks between the two Koreas' military authorities. According to Gao, South Korea's Unification Ministry rejected this as propaganda, so Gao expects no early dialogue. On nuclear weapons, Kim calls North Korea a responsible nuclear state and pledges to strengthen its deterrent, while keeping a no-first-use position. Gao concludes that denuclearisation looks more remote and that sanctions alone cannot resolve the issue. Gao concludes that the congress, which made Kim chairman of the Workers' Party, opens the "Kim Jong Un era" proper, with goals set across political, economic, military and cultural fields. The strongest impression is continuity. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese media interpretation of the 2016 Party congress report and of how Chinese commentators assessed North Korea's nuclear and unification stance at that time.

Currents of socialism in Europe in the second half of the twentieth century From the end of the Second World War to the upheavals in the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe “左翼党”与联邦德国的左翼政治 This article traces how currents of socialism developed in Europe from the end of the Second World War to the upheavals in the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe. It argues that the victory over fascism, and the establishment of people's democratic regimes in eight Eastern European states, opened a period in which world socialism grew stronger and more diverse. In the author's account, European socialist currents both expanded beyond Europe and moved from theory into practice. The text has two main parts. The first examines three currents that predated 1945: democratic socialism and the social democratic parties, market socialism, and Trotskyist socialism. The second turns to newer currents, namely eco-socialism, Eurocommunism, post-industrial socialism and feminist socialism, and concentrates on the first two as the most distinctly European and influential. On democratic socialism, the author describes the refounding of the Socialist International in Frankfurt in 1951 and its growth into a global body, with 50 full members by 1983, 22 of them European. Social democratic governments are credited with welfare and workers' participation gains, but the author insists that their basic positions differ essentially from those of communist parties, citing Cold War anti-communism and the 1989 Declaration of Principles. Market socialism is traced from Benjamin Ward's 1958 Illyrian model to reform designs by Liberman, Brus, Sik, Kornai and Kardelj, and to practice in Yugoslavia and Hungary. The author says these experiments ended in capitalist market economies because the models were imperfect. Eurocommunism, led by the Italian, Spanish and French parties, is presented as a response to changes in Western capitalism and to the Soviet model, especially after the Prague Spring. Its core was a democratic, multiparty road to socialism, and it declined from the mid-1980s. Eco-socialism arose from the green movement, with the West German Greens (founded 1980) winning 5.6 per cent and 27 seats in 1983, and it influenced the Social Democratic Party's programme. The author concludes that in this period the pattern of 'one centre, one path, one model' in the communist movement broke down. Two features marked European socialist currents: they overcame geographical limits and spread to the Third World, and they moved beyond theory to try to put their ideas into practice. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly survey of Western European socialist currents, with names, dates and organisations, and of how they were characterised for readers in China in 2016.

Die Linke and left politics in the Federal Republic of Germany “左翼党”与联邦德国的左翼政治 Gregor Gysi This is a Chinese translation of a text by Gregor Gysi, a leading figure of Germany's Die Linke (The Left) and chair of its Bundestag group, apparently delivered as a talk to a Chinese audience. Gysi presents what he calls the party's character as a left-socialist force and sets out where it stands among Germany's left parties. His thesis is that Die Linke is distinct from both social democracy and Soviet-style communism, and that the left remains divided for lasting structural reasons. The text has three parts. The first places Die Linke in the European family of 'left-socialist' parties and explains its origins in Germany's division. The second compares the three left-of-centre parties in the Federal Republic: the Social Democrats, the Greens and Die Linke. The third takes up three problems Gysi says the left must tackle: the crisis of neoliberalism, international politics, and the link between social justice and ecological transformation. Gysi argues that Western capitalism built mass prosperity and democracy partly under pressure from competition with the Soviet bloc. In his account, once that rivalry ended, neoliberalism took over, social democrats embraced it, and a 'representation deficit' opened that new left parties filled. Die Linke arose from the 2007 merger of the PDS, successor to the East German ruling party, and the WASG, a western left-social-democratic group. Gysi says it has dropped dogmatic Marxism, though Marx's theory is still needed to analyse crisis. He holds that the three parties differ over state bureaucracy, over NATO and relations with the United States, and over how far to pursue ecological change. He criticises Western policy in the Ukraine crisis and the response to the euro crisis. He says ecological transformation requires job security and global solidarity, including the development rights of countries such as China and India. Gysi concludes that a single united left party is unlikely in the foreseeable future, though cooperation is possible, especially at local and state level. He hopes the Social Democrats will regain a will to power and move away from neoliberal thinking. He describes Die Linke's aim as overcoming capitalism through an expanded parliamentary democracy, an ecological mode of production and a classless society of free individuals, without drawing utopian blueprints. Read the original if you want a German left leader's own account of Die Linke's identity, its relations with the SPD and Greens, and its positions on the euro crisis, NATO and Ukraine, as presented to a Chinese readership.

The historical evolution of the communist movement in Nepal 尼泊尔共产主义运动的历史演进探析 Yuan Qun Zhang Lifeng Writing in 2015, Yuan Qun and Zhang Lifeng ask how Nepal's communist movement has developed over its 66 years, and what that history implies for its prospects. They argue that the movement has grown from a weak left-wing current into a politically significant force. Since the 1980s, the authors say, its main parties have adjusted their strategy to domestic and international change in search of a path suited to Nepal. The authors present it as a typical case within today's international communist movement. The article is organised chronologically in four parts. It begins with the rise of the movement from 1947 to 1954, amid opposition to the Rana family's autocracy, followed by the split and regrouping of the movement from the late 1950s to the 1990s. It then covers the movement's turn towards peaceful and parliamentary politics, and ends with an assessment of its achievements and problems. The account follows the proliferation of party factions, such as the CPN (Unified Marxist-Leninist) and the CPN (Maoist), and the mergers and splits between them. The authors' central argument is that the movement moved from armed struggle towards multi-party politics. They trace this in the CPN (UML)'s 1993 programme of "People's Multi-party Democracy", and in the Maoists' later move from the "People's War" launched in 1996 to accepting multi-party democracy in the 2000s. They credit this shift with the first communist-led government (1994) and with the abolition of the monarchy in 2008. They then identify three problems that hold the movement back. First, the rivalry between the two largest parties, the UML and the Maoists, weakens its overall strength, since each party puts its own immediate interests above the movement's long-term interest. Second, the authors describe an ideological degeneration, citing the Maoists' abandonment of the land policy and of the army, and the UML's replacement of class struggle with nationalism. They link this to election losses in 2008 and 2013. Third, factionalism has produced repeated splits, which the authors attribute to both external factors (the Sino-Soviet split, Chinese reform, Indian influence) and internal disputes. The authors conclude that the movement is an important political force in Nepal and a bright spot in a still depressed international communist movement. They also argue that whether it can resolve inter-party antagonism, ideological decline and factionalism will largely decide its future. Read the original if you want a detailed chronology of Nepal's communist parties, their splits and mergers, and a Chinese academic assessment of the movement's problems as of 2015.

Lenin's defence and consolidation of Party unity: historical facts that must not be distorted 列宁维护和巩固党的统一的历史事实不容歪曲 Yuan Xiuli Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2016, Yuan Xiuli takes up the Resolution on Party Unity that Lenin drafted for the Tenth Congress of the Russian Communist Party (Bolsheviks) in March 1921. Yuan notes that some people have long portrayed the resolution as a product of factional struggle, a tool for suppressing the opposition and preserving one-party rule, and an expression of Lenin's "autocratic thinking". The article rejects this reading as contrary to both Lenin's thought and the historical facts, and argues that the resolution aimed to protect the Party's unity and leadership at a moment of crisis. The commentary is organised in three parts: maintaining Party unity, consolidating the Party's leadership, and safeguarding the most urgent task of economic construction. It draws on Lenin's speeches and on the positions of the "Workers' Opposition" and the "Democratic Centralists", and sets them against the conditions of 1921: civil war and devastation, the Kronstadt rebellion of February, and the shift to the New Economic Policy. Yuan argues that the resolution was a call for unity aimed at winning over the majority, not an attack. It acknowledged the opposition groups' reasonable criticisms of bureaucracy, and the congress elected four of their members to the Central Committee and asked them to stay in post when they offered to resign. In Yuan's account, the opposition nonetheless moved towards unrestricted democracy, factional organisation, separate meetings and pamphlets. Yuan also contends that the Workers' Opposition's proposal to run the economy through producers' congresses and trade unions denied the Party's leading role and was syndicalist and anarchist in tendency. Finally, Yuan holds that prolonged debate on trade unions was, in Lenin's phrase, an "excessive luxury" that diverted the Party from economic recovery and helped its class enemies. Yuan concludes that Lenin's resolution defended Party unity, strengthened Party leadership and gave political and organisational backing to the New Economic Policy. In this reading, theoretical discussion remains permitted in specialised publications, while the Party's political line requires unity of action. Yuan adds that Lenin called the New Economic Policy an "unprecedentedly difficult retreat", requiring the Party to keep firm conviction and discipline. Read the original if you want an example of how Chinese Party-affiliated scholarship in 2016 defended Lenin's 1921 resolution against charges of authoritarianism.

The contemporary value of Lenin's theory of imperialism A century-defining theory that sets out new human ideals and practice 列宁“帝国主义论”的时代价值 Jiang An Marking the 100th anniversary of Lenin's imperialism writings in 2016, this short commentary, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today, asks what value the theory still holds. The authors argue that, among theories of imperialism, Lenin's remains the classic account for understanding more than a century of world history, especially the essence of imperialism and the logic of its fate. They present it as a systematic critique of the premises of imperialism, built on historical materialism, with the critique of monopoly as its 'central axis'. The article is organised around three 'logics'. The first is explanatory: Lenin's method and the research paradigm it established. The second is critical: his exposure of monopoly as the essence of imperialism and its power to explain modern crises. The third is constructive: how the theory expanded Marx's view of world history and offered practical and value guidance to the socialist movement worldwide. On method, the authors credit Lenin with analysing the laws of imperialist economic movement, the 'aggregate effect' of capitalist crises and uneven development, using dialectics as the 'algebra of revolution' and drawing on Hobson's historical survey. On substance, they hold that earlier theories stayed at the level of policy or technique, whereas Lenin identified monopoly as the root cause. They argue that however scholars label twentieth-century capitalism (global, state monopoly, financial or international monopoly), its underlying logic of private, group, state and international monopoly is unchanged. In their account, the world wars, regional conflicts, cultural imperialism promoting 'Western-centrism', the North–South division of labour, ecological damage and terrorism all confirm this. They conclude that Lenin's theory is in essence an anti-monopoly theory. The authors conclude that Lenin extended Marx's world-historical outlook, placing colonial liberation and world revolution within a new general trend. They also hold that the theory is as much a doctrine for building a more just society as a critique. In their view, after Marx's critique of capitalism it is the most profound critique of capitalism since the twentieth century, and it opened new socialist practice and widened humanity's paths to a future civilisation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese scholars in 2016 presented the continuing relevance of Lenin's imperialism theory to current global conflicts.

The historical development of Marx's thought on the division of labour An examination based on Marx's classic texts 马克思分工思想的历史发展轨迹 Wang Huxue Marx left no systematic treatise on the division of labour, yet Wang Huxue argues that the subject runs through nearly all of his theoretical work. The article asks how his thinking on it developed, and answers that it moved through three stages: discovery, formation and enrichment. Wang holds that Marx understood Adam Smith properly only once he took Smith's legacy as one source of his own theory, which he then analysed more fully, radically and scientifically. Published in 2016, the article proceeds by close reading of three texts. These are the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 (discovery), The German Ideology (formation) and The Poverty of Philosophy, together with the 1846 letter to Annenkov (enrichment). Wang draws throughout on commentators such as Étienne Balibar, Bagaturia, Korsch and Zhang Yibing. The study of Capital and its manuscripts, which Wang treats as a further stage, is deferred to a separate article. First, Wang argues that in the 1844 Manuscripts Marx turned a basic category of political economy into a philosophical one. He saw its negative effects, which appear as alienated labour, and treated division of labour and exchange as forms of private property. Against Smith's circular reasoning, Marx held that division of labour is the precondition of exchange and not its product. Second, in The German Ideology the focus moves from alienation to division of labour. Wang reads this as a shift to a "production ontology", with each stage of the division of labour corresponding to a form of ownership, and consciousness appearing as a product of that division. Wang also sees here an early form of the principle that the productive forces determine the relations of production. Third, in The Poverty of Philosophy Marx attacks Proudhon for treating the division of labour as an abstract, eternal law. Marx instead presents it as a historical category that expresses the social relations of a given era. Wang concludes that Marx's thought on the division of labour grew from the discovery of the problem, through formation within historical materialism, to a richer historical and critical form. Wang denies an epistemological break between the 1844 Manuscripts and The German Ideology, since the division of labour links the two. The article is aimed at readers who want a text-by-text genealogy of one concept in Marx. Read the original if you are studying the early Marx, the relation between alienation and the division of labour, or the origins of historical materialism.

Lessons of rereading Lenin's Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism a century later 100年后重读列宁《帝国主义是资本主义的最高阶段》的启示 Xu Lan Writing in 2016, a century after Lenin completed Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism (June 1916), Xu Lan asks what the book still tells us about twentieth-century political events and about capitalism today. The article argues that Lenin's analysis of monopoly, finance capital and uneven development explains the origins of both world wars and the October Revolution. It also holds that his account of capitalism's basic contradictions remains valid, even though some of his specific judgements may not match later history. The article has three parts. The first sets out Lenin's five basic features of imperialism and applies them to the First and Second World Wars. The second turns to the link between imperialism and the October Revolution, including the Treaties of Brest-Litovsk and Versailles and the situation in Russia in 1917. The third considers changes in postwar capitalism and what Lenin's book offers for understanding them, with reference to the 2008 financial crisis and recent protest movements. Xu argues that Lenin's features of imperialism (monopolies, finance capital, capital export, the division of the world among capitalist alliances and powers) together with uneven development gave great powers an unprecedented drive towards rivalry. In this reading, the First World War was an imperialist struggle for hegemony, chiefly between Germany and Britain, and fascist Germany, Italy and Japan pursued the same aim in extreme form. On the revolution, Xu holds that the war sharpened every contradiction in Russia, the "weakest link" in the imperialist chain, and that the Provisional Government's refusal to end the war or distribute land opened the way for the Bolsheviks. Xu adds that the Soviet experience suggests that socialist modernization in economically backward countries is especially difficult, has no fixed model, and depends on continuous reform and self-improvement of the social system. On postwar capitalism, Xu acknowledges real changes: state monopoly capitalism, welfare states, scientific and technological advance, joint-stock companies, multinational firms and international coordination that has avoided war among major capitalist states. Xu contends, however, that these changes touch only institutions and methods of rule, not the basic contradiction between socialized production and private appropriation. The 2008 financial crisis and widening inequality, evidenced by Occupy Wall Street and similar movements, are presented as confirming Lenin's remarks on rentiers and the parasitism of the financial oligarchy. Read the original if you want an example of how a Chinese scholar in 2016 defended the continuing relevance of Lenin's theory of imperialism for both history and the present.

How Marx argued for shared development Reflections on reading the Critique of the Gotha Programme 马克思是如何论证共享发展的 Zhao Xueqing Writing in 2016, after the Fifth Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2015) put forward the new development philosophy of innovation, coordination, green development, openness and sharing, Zhao Xueqing asks how Marx justified shared development under socialism. Zhao reads Marx's Critique of the Gotha Programme to give the Party's concept of shared development a theoretical grounding. The article's thesis is that, for Marx, all members of society share the results of development, the total social product, through social deductions and distribution according to labour, on the basis of social ownership of the means of production and associated labour. The article has four parts. It first treats the distribution of objective and subjective production factors as the institutional basis of sharing. It then treats the total social product of associated labour as the material basis, and the six social deductions plus distribution according to labour as the mechanism of realisation. The last part sums up Marx's view and draws five implications for China today. Zhao argues that, following Marx, distribution of products is determined by the distribution of production conditions. Under socialism the means of production are owned in common, while labour-power belongs to the individual worker, who therefore has a dual position as a member of society and as a private producer. This duality explains why workers cannot receive the undiminished proceeds of labour. Zhao reads the six deductions as expressing the interests of society as a whole: replacement of used-up means of production, expansion of production, a reserve fund, general administration costs, common needs such as schools and health care, and funds for those unable to work. What remains is distributed by labour contributed, which Zhao says secures the individual's interest and, by this route, common prosperity in a formal equality that is not yet real equality. Zhao concludes that shared development is not an isolated matter of distribution but the outcome of common ownership, common labour and common management; without sharing, public ownership would become an empty title. For the primary stage of socialism, Zhao draws several implications. Income gaps are said to be larger than in Marx's imagined socialism, though far smaller than capitalist polarisation. Zhao therefore calls for faster development of the productive forces, a market that fairly rewards factor contributions in primary distribution, and a government that redistributes in line with 'existing material and strength'. Read the original if you want a close reading of the Critique of the Gotha Programme used to ground the Party's shared-development concept and to explain income distribution in the primary stage of socialism.

Socialist core values are fundamentally different from Western values Study notes on Xi Jinping's remarks on core values 社会主义核心价值观与西方价值观根本不同 Wen Hua This short commentary, originally published in Qiushi in 2016 under the title "Upholding our core values", asks how China's socialist core values relate to the values promoted in Western countries. The author's answer is that they differ fundamentally, because each nation's core values grow out of its own history, struggles and problems. The piece is a study note on General Secretary Xi Jinping's statements about core values. It first explains what the socialist core values express, then argues that they join state, society and citizen into one framework, and finally presents them as the broadest common ground among China's peoples. Wen and Hua describe the socialist core values as the condensed core of the socialist core value system and as the value expression of the path, theory and institutions of socialism with Chinese characteristics. In their account, they uphold Party leadership, the guiding role of Marxism, a people-centred stance and the goal of communism. The authors claim that even terms shared with the West, such as democracy, freedom and justice, carry different meanings, since Western values, they say, reflect bourgeois interests. They also read the three-level formulation (national, social, individual) as continuous with the classical Chinese sequence from self-cultivation to governing the realm. The authors conclude that the values were set out after repeated consultation and fit China's present stage of development, so they have won wide recognition as the "greatest common denominator" in the sphere of values. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Party media framed the contrast between socialist core values and Western values in 2016.

A look at the various ailments of Western rule of law 看看西方法治的种种病象 Zhou Peiqing Gao Wenjian Writing in Qiushi in 2016, Zhou Peiqing and Gao Wenjian respond to people who, in their account, admire Western rule of law and regard Western societies as genuinely law-governed. The authors argue that Western rule of law has always been accompanied by defects and still shows many 'symptoms' today. The commentary sets out five of these symptoms in turn, each illustrated with recent cases drawn mainly from the United States and Japan. It closes with a short explanation of what the authors take to be their common cause. The first symptom, the authors say, is legislation that ignores popular demands, citing Japan's Specially Designated Secrets Law and new security legislation, passed by the ruling party's majority despite opposition. The second is unequal justice: they point to the 2014 US cases in which white police officers who killed black men were not indicted, and to figures on police killings by race. The third is state bodies that break the law, for which they cite the PRISM surveillance programme. The fourth and fifth are interference in other sovereign states, including the 'Arab Spring' and Ukraine, and the violation of international law through wars such as Iraq in 2003 and Libya in 2011. The authors conclude that these ailments stem fundamentally from the limits of the capitalist political system. In their view, that system serves bourgeois party politics and bourgeois interests, so legislation, justice and law enforcement uphold those interests whatever the language of 'democracy' and 'fairness', and disregard the majority at home and abroad. Read the original if you want a compact example of how official Chinese commentary criticised Western rule of law in the mid-2010s.

Four key points in building the current discourse system 当前话语体系建设的四个要点 Zhuang Wencheng Writing in 2016 in the China Social Sciences Today, Zhuang Wencheng asks how Marxist discourse can be protected and made more persuasive, and holds that this requires clarifying the dialectical relations between several kinds of discourse. The short commentary argues that Marxist discourse should be adapted to specific contexts and audiences, and it identifies four pairs that deserve close attention. The four pairs are core discourse and discourse of the times, collective and individual discourse, foreign and national discourse, and classical and plain discourse. Zhuang discusses each briefly and draws on Deng Xiaoping and Mao Zedong. The piece closes by recommending the Selected Works of Mao Zedong and Xi Jinping's speeches as models of discursive skill. Zhuang argues that core discourse, which sets out the essential features of Marxism, must always be upheld and serves as the standard for judging other discourses. Discourse of the times, such as socialism with Chinese characteristics, the Chinese Dream and core socialist values, is presented as a renewal of that core, not a break with it. On collective and individual discourse, the author warns that each must not swallow the other, since individual discourse alone would produce liberal discursive hegemony. Their link lies in the unity of the particular and the universal, and the author proposes equal dialogue and agreed discursive rules. On foreign and national discourse, Zhuang says Confucian, reformist and liberal thought failed in modern China. Marxism, in the author's view, is effective only when rooted in national tradition, and the author rejects both dismissing it as foreign and returning to Marx's own era. Classical expressions should be paired with plain, everyday language so that theory reaches people emotionally. Read the original if you want a brief Party-theory statement of how Marxist discourse construction was framed in 2016.

Raising the soft power of red culture Paths for red culture in the perspective of building a culturally strong nation 提升红色文化软实力 Zhou Yanhong Writing in 2016, Zhou Yanhong asks how the soft power of "red culture" can be raised after years of a nationwide "red culture craze". The author argues that the craze has produced distortions in how red culture is built and spread, and that a comprehensive and developmental perspective is needed to correct them. The article identifies four tendencies: stressing publicity form over substance, short-term economic returns over long-term social benefit, isolated local efforts over wider integration, and domestic self-regard over international dialogue. Each tendency is answered by one proposal, and the article is organised around these four. Zhou draws on the Marxist view that content and form are unified, with content decisive, to urge that red culture be distilled into core qualities such as patriotism, hard struggle and serving the people, rather than spread thinly across many "spirits". The author criticises TV dramas that distort revolutionary history for ratings, and calls for social benefit to take priority, with public-interest red culture and the red culture industry developed together. Zhou also cites the separate promotion of red tourism by Ruijin, Yudu, Ningdu and Xingguo in Ganzhou, Jiangxi, as a missed chance for scale and for presenting a continuous history. On the international side, Zhou argues that red culture, as the first cultural form of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the result of its combination with traditional culture, is a distinctive asset for cultural outreach, citing performances abroad of the dance drama Hongmei zan and of Jiangxi folk songs. The author concludes that raising red culture's soft power will help realise the dream of a culturally strong nation and the Chinese Dream. Read the original if you want an example of how 2016 Chinese scholarship on ideological education framed red culture, red tourism and cultural outreach.

A methodology for building ideological discourse power 意识形态话语权建设方法论研究 Hou Huiqin Writing in 2016, as ideological work received growing attention in China, Hou Huiqin asks how ideological discourse power (yishi xingtai huayuquan) is acquired, built and used. Hou argues that ideology is in essence the power of intellectual domination required for class rule and the moral basis of state power, so it cannot be discussed in a non-ideological way. For China, the article holds, the core issue is upholding the leadership of the Communist Party and the guiding role of Marxism. The article is organised in three parts: how discourse power is obtained and what it is in essence; how it is constructed and the laws governing this; and how it is used and what is decisive in its use. Hou draws on Marx and Engels on the ruling ideas of each age, on Sieyès and Saint-Simon as examples of the rising bourgeoisie, on Weber and Diderot in the discussion of human nature, and on Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping for the Chinese cases. Hou's central claim is that a ruling class holds the means of mental production because it controls material production, and so occupies the moral high ground. The proletariat, lacking economic strength under capitalism, can overturn this only by occupying the high ground of history through scientific theory. Appeals to values alone, or to 'ethical socialism', are said to leave capitalism's core values unchallenged. Hou therefore says truth must be the foundation of values. Marxism is credited with recasting the debate from whether capitalism suits human nature to whether human nature can change, and with distinguishing 'real' from 'abstract' people. Hou describes abstract theories of human nature, 'conscience' and 'people-ness' detached from Party spirit and class character as weak points to be criticised. In the third part Hou says discourse power is won by setting correct leading agendas and exposing false propositions. Examples of the former are Mao's people's democratic dictatorship and Deng's socialism with Chinese characteristics, which Hou links to the 'Four Comprehensives'. Examples of the latter are the opposition of 'revolution' to 'modernization', and slogans such as 'is the Party or the law greater'. Hou concludes that Party leadership is the focus of today's ideological struggle and that any proposition denying it is a false one. Read the original if you want a representative statement of how a leading Chinese Marxist theorist links discourse power, scientific theory and Party leadership in the mid-2010s.

Guiding the great development of Chinese philosophy and social sciences with Marxism 用马克思主义指导中国哲学社会科学大发展 Zhu Lingjun Writing in 2016, Zhu Lingjun asks why Marxism must guide the development of Chinese philosophy and the social sciences, and how it should be studied and applied. Opening with the early-1920s debate between Hu Shi and Li Dazhao on "problems and isms", Zhu argues that every country needs an "ism" to guide it and that Marxism is China's. The article contends that a new leap in the adaptation of Marxism to China will bring a great flourishing of Chinese social science. The article has four sections. The first gives four reasons for confidence in Marxism, drawing on modern Chinese history and on claimed affinities between Marxism and Chinese culture. The second discusses studying Marxism by linking theory to practice, using Lenin, Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and other Party leaders as models. The third proposes studying Marxism through the method of "ancient and modern, Chinese and foreign". The fourth calls for taking the latest results of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context to the world. Zhu argues that after Confucianism, Christian theology, social evolutionism, reformism and bourgeois democracy all failed to save China, Marxism succeeded because it matched demands for national independence and industrialisation and has parallels with traditional thought. Zhu also claims that Marx and Engels absorbed Chinese cultural elements through German philosophy. On method, Zhu holds that neither replacing Marxism with Confucianism nor the reverse is acceptable, and that imported Western social science, with its alleged Eurocentric assumptions and "technicism", cannot simply judge Chinese experience. Zhu proposes building macro-theory on Marxist philosophy, meso-theory on Chinese traditions and the socialist road, and micro-theory through comparison worldwide. Concretely, this means setting Chinese questions, shaping Chinese values and writing indigenous textbooks. Zhu concludes that a strong system of knowledge would yield an interpretive system, discursive power and soft power, supporting the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Zhu presents three historical stages: Mao's generation made the Chinese people "stand up", Deng's made them "prosperous", and the present generation should make them "strong". Social scientists are urged to study the shift from governing a large country to governing a strong one and to tell China's story abroad. Read the original if you want a representative 2016 statement of the official case for Marxist guidance in Chinese social science, including its use of Chinese cultural continuity and indigenisation arguments.

Building philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics, Chinese style and Chinese manner 构建中国特色中国风格中国气派的哲学社会科学 Shen Zhuanghai Writing in Qiushi in 2016, Shen Zhuanghai asks how China's philosophy and social sciences can develop their own distinctive characteristics, style and manner. The article argues that this is a mark of maturity, strength and confidence, reached after a century of development alongside China's revolution, construction and reform. Shen presents Xi Jinping's speech at the symposium on philosophy and social sciences as the programme for this work. The commentary follows four requirements drawn from that speech. They are to base research on China, to hold to innovation, to advance the discipline, academic and discourse systems together, and to treat the building of talent as the most fundamental task. Shen's core claim is that distinctiveness comes from rooting scholarship in Chinese practice. This means focusing on Chinese problems, drawing on traditional culture, and building on the Marxist fundamentals and the theoretical results of adapting Marxism to China. Foreign scholarship is to be absorbed, not excluded. Shen insists that "Chinese style" does not mean antique flavour but contemporary ideas, produced by problem-oriented innovation under a Marxist worldview. The three systems are described as one whole: the academic system is the "way", the discipline system the "body" and the discourse system the "words". Shen says the discipline and discourse systems depend on the depth of the academic system. Shen concludes that academic prosperity is measured by the people it produces as well as by its results. The author calls for talent strategies centred on cultivating people, making building projects "talent-nurturing" and not "formal" ones, and reforming research management to free scholarly creativity. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how official discourse in 2016 framed the aims and organisation of Chinese social science.

On the fit between Marxism and present-day China 论马克思主义与当下中国的契合关系问题 Huang Lizhi Writing in 2016, Huang Lizhi asks how well Marxism and China today fit each other (qihe guanxi), more than sixty years after the founding of the People's Republic. The article holds that the fit, which was clearly established in the revolutionary era, is now partial. In the author's reading, wide areas of agreement sit alongside real gaps between Marxist principles and the reality of a market-economy China. Huang argues that these gaps must be acknowledged and closed, or the Party's political legitimacy will suffer at its social base. The article has three parts. It first surveys the present status of Marxism: its official ideological position, the Marxism research and construction project and the new first-level discipline, and the loss of faith that surveys and Xi Jinping's remarks describe among some Party members and officials. It then compares agreement and difference under the slogan "economic growth is the hard truth". Finally it proposes two ways of narrowing the gap, drawing on Marx, Engels, Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping, Daniel Bell and Chinese commentators. Huang's core argument is that reform-era orthodoxy came to equate Marxism with developing the productive forces. In Huang's account this reading was historically justified, since it opened the way to rapid growth. The author argues that it is not Marxism's core, citing Marx and Lenin on capitalism's own drive to expand productive forces, and Engels's late letters rejecting economic reductionism. Huang says the costs have been ecological strain, polarisation, consumerism and damaged official credibility. The first remedy is a dialectical view of texts: balancing "what the founders said" against "what they never said", and recovering Marx's humanist concern with all-round human development, which Huang links to the Scientific Outlook on Development's "people-centred" principle. The second remedy is to move from "solving political problems through the economy" to "solving economic problems through politics". Huang criticises Li Zehou's sequence of economic growth, then individual freedom, then political democracy. The author argues that the state and superstructure must correct market outcomes, citing Bell's moral case for social minimums, Deng's remark about the "powerful state machinery" and recent redistribution, welfare and anti-corruption measures. Huang concludes that these measures, introduced since the Scientific Outlook on Development and especially since the 18th Party Congress (2012), have already narrowed the gap between Marxism and Chinese reality, though the theory still has to be worked out consciously. The author expresses confidence that the relationship will become mutually reinforcing and calls on the Party to keep upholding and developing Marxism. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's critique of equating Marxism with productive-force development, and of the "economic solution to political problems" logic, in the early Xi Jinping period.

The "self-degeneration" of the privileged stratum in the collapse of the CPSU and its warnings 苏共垮台中特权阶层的“自我蜕变”及其警示 Guo Yanlin Writing in 2016, Guo Yanlin asks what role privilege and corruption played in the collapse of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union (CPSU). The article argues that, among the many factors behind the fall of a party of more than 70 years and over 20 million members, a major one was that the CPSU never escaped the "cyclical trap" of history. In Guo's account, a privileged bureaucratic stratum emerged inside the Party, and its "self-degeneration" did more than any anti-communist force to bring the Party and the state down. The article has three parts. The first traces how the stratum formed, from Lenin's struggle against bureaucratism through the Stalin, Khrushchev, Brezhnev and Gorbachev periods. The second sets out four political harms of privilege and corruption. The third draws five lessons for the Chinese Communist Party. Guo relies on Lenin, Deng Xiaoping, memoirs by Arbatov and Ryzhkov, a 1995 survey by the Russian Academy of Sciences, and David Kotz's study of Soviet elite opinion. Guo's central claim is that the stratum moved from enjoying privileges to converting power into property. Under Gorbachev's reforms, officials privatised profitable state enterprises and turned control into ownership. The article cites a 1995 survey showing that 74–75 per cent of the political elite around the Russian president and government, and 61 per cent of the economic elite, came from the Soviet cadre corps. It also cites Kotz's finding that about 80 per cent of ordinary people wanted to keep socialism, while 76.7 per cent of a roughly 100,000-strong elite favoured capitalism. The four harms Guo lists are weakened ideological appeal, a crisis of trust between Party and people, broken discipline with the rise of unwritten rules and the sale of office, and the elite's role as vanguard of capitalist restoration. Guo draws five warnings for China. Anti-privilege work must be long-term during the primary stage of socialism, and must be part of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. Leading cadres who lose their ideals and form vested-interest groups must be dealt with. Privilege must never become a tool for maintaining political order. Intra-Party supervision must be strengthened, with Deng Xiaoping's stress on institutions cited in support. Close ties between Party and people must anchor the campaign. Read the original if you want a Chinese Party-affiliated reading of the Soviet collapse, used in 2016 to justify the anti-corruption campaign.

Lies and truth about the Soviet economic crisis Based on Kara-Murza's analysis 苏联经济危机的谎言与真相 Kang Yanru Did the Soviet economy collapse in the late 1970s and early 1980s, before Gorbachev took over? Kang Yanru, drawing on the Russian scholar Sergei Kara-Murza, rejects this widely accepted view, which treats the Soviet Union's dissolution as the result of a crisis of the 'Soviet system' that could not be reformed. The article, published in 2016, argues that the Soviet economy showed no sign of crisis before 1985 and that Gorbachev's reforms and de-Sovietising decisions produced the economic deterioration and collapse. The article has three parts. The first examines who produced and spread the 'lie' of a pre-reform crisis, citing Yakovlev, the reform theorist Boris Nayshul and the Western Sovietologists David Cohen, Ellman and Kontorovich. The second sets Soviet economic data from before and after 1985 side by side. The third reviews the basic condition of the national economy and tests the claim that the Soviet economy was oriented towards raw-material exports. Kang reports Kara-Murza's argument that the first stage of Gorbachev's reform dismantled the financial system and the consumer market. The 1987 Law on State Enterprises allowed non-cash money to be converted into cash, foreign trade was decentralised, and cooperatives sold goods abroad. Enterprises kept more profit and raised incomes without matching output. The article cites rising budget deficits, internal debt and external debt, and falling gold reserves, all after 1985. It also reports figures showing balanced investment, production and consumption growth before 1989 and steady industrial growth from 1950 to 1990. On the 'raw-material' claim, it cites 1989 data in which processed goods made up 77% of the Russian Federation's exports, and 1988 data in which fuel and electricity exports equalled 3.2% of Soviet gross national product. On this basis it dismisses the claim that the United States depressed oil prices and so ended the USSR. It presents Russia's present raw-material dependence as a product of the reforms. Kang concludes, following Kara-Murza, that the crisis dates from the 1987–1990 policy decisions and that the Soviet economy was not inefficient or uncompetitive. The article warns that the loss of critical analysis, and the failure of intellectuals to rebut these claims for over twenty years, is the greatest threat to Russia's development. Read the original if you want a Chinese-language account of Russian arguments against the 'inevitable collapse' thesis, with the economic statistics Kara-Murza uses.

For the liberation of workers and peoples, for socialism: an assessment of the 17th International Meeting of Communist and Workers' Parties 为了工人和人民的解放，为了社会主义 Yu Weihai Zhou Huaping This is a report and assessment of the 17th International Meeting of Communist and Workers' Parties, hosted by the Communist Party of Turkey in Istanbul from 30 October to 1 November 2015. Yu and Zhou, four of whose research-centre colleagues attended as scholarly observers, say 104 delegates from 58 parties in 48 countries took part. The theme was strengthening the working-class struggle against capitalist exploitation, imperialist war and fascism. The meeting adopted a working-group document, admitted the Workers' Party of Austria and issued a press release. The report follows the meeting's themes in seven sections. It covers the delegates' view that capitalism's structural crisis continues, and their account of regional turmoil and terrorism. It then turns to popular protest movements and their immaturity, the experience of mass struggle and party-building, and the position of socialist countries. It ends with joint action proposals and the authors' own commentary. Most of the material is drawn from speeches by named delegates from Portugal, India, Greece, Brazil, Ireland, Belgium, Croatia, Turkey, Iraq and other parties. According to the authors, most parties held that the post-2008 crisis was unresolved and that imperialism was the root of terrorism and instability. Delegates pointed to economic plunder, political and financial backing for extremist groups, military intervention and divisive propaganda. Protest movements, including anti-austerity campaigns, struggles in Latin America and West Asia, and resistance to the EU, were judged immature. Delegates blamed bourgeois ideology, the rise of the far right, unprepared working-class parties and repression of communists. Parties differed on tactics: the Communist Parties of Greece and Turkey stressed separation from opportunism, while the Portuguese, Indian (Marxist), Lebanese and Iraqi parties favoured broad anti-imperialist alliances. Some, including the Brazilian party, again called for a new Communist International. Speakers from the Chinese, Vietnamese, Cuban and Lao parties described their paths, and the Croatian party defended the view that China is socialist. Yu and Zhou conclude that the meeting has become an established platform for exchange and solidarity. They say it showed a spirit of 'consultative democracy' and took a step towards institutionalisation by adopting rules for the working group. They also list difficulties: few parties able to host, an eight-minute speaking limit that left theory shallow, difficulty reaching consensus, weak follow-through between meetings, and some parties' loss of confidence. Whether the meeting can play a larger role in the world socialist movement, they say, remains to be seen. Read the original if you want a detailed, party-by-party account of positions at this 2015 gathering and of how Chinese scholars assessed it.

The spectre of the "Maoist movement" “毛主义运动”的幽灵 Wang Hui Wang Hui asks why Maoist movements in South Asia, which he calls a spectre present everywhere yet rarely spoken of, are so largely absent from contemporary thought and media. The text began as his preface to Wang Jing's study of the Communist Party of India (Maoist), published in 2016. Wang Hui argues that these movements are a "spectacle" in an age of financialised capitalism, because they openly claim descent from twentieth-century revolution, especially the Chinese one, and still treat land, caste and national independence as central questions. The article has three parts. The first sets the Maoist movements against the post-1989 "end of history" climate and the Occupy-style protests, and discusses the Indian Maoists, the Subaltern Studies school and Arundhati Roy's reporting. The second examines the Communist Party of Nepal (Maoist) through four problems: people's democracy versus parliamentary democracy, army reform, land and peasants, and the constitution and federalism. The third considers the "low-intensity war" waged against such movements, their internal divisions, a comparison with Venezuela, and the Belt and Road Initiative. Wang notes that he knows little about Maoist movements in Peru, Colombia, the Philippines and Turkey. Wang contends that the movements' scale, endurance and intensity far exceed those of the Occupy protests, which he describes as short-lived and built on urban middle-class interests. In Nepal, he argues, the Maoist leader Prachanda's belief that people's democracy could be merged with multiparty parliamentary politics was wishful thinking. Wang compares the dispute over the People's Liberation Army and the land reforms with the Guomindang's 1945 demand for "nationalisation of the army". He also compares the movement's setbacks with its inability to produce a leadership with strategic vision and a mature theory. He sets this against Chávez, who relied on charisma because his party was weak. He also describes a US-designed "low-intensity war" of information control, blockade, intelligence and decapitation of leaders, which he says widens the technological gap between ruling classes and revolutionary forces. Wang concludes that simply repeating past paths has no future, but that basic values must be kept while strategies are rethought for the twenty-first century, in political forms that serve the majority. He argues that studying South Asia and Latin America can also illuminate the history of the Chinese Revolution. He adds that the Belt and Road Initiative can succeed only if the poor and their political movements are included and China's domestic development model is readjusted. Read the original if you want a Chinese left-intellectual reading of Nepal's Maoists and South Asian Maoism, and of their bearing on China's international strategy.

Revisiting why the Soviet Union chose a heavy-industry development strategy under Stalin Refuting false charges imposed on Stalin 斯大林时期苏联选择重工业发展战略原因再探讨 Yuan Xiuli Why did the Soviet Union under Stalin adopt an industrialisation strategy centred on heavy industry? Yuan takes issue with the view, associated with Zuo Fengrong, that Stalin deliberately exaggerated the danger of Western armed intervention and overstated the war threat to justify his policies. Yuan argues that the hostility of the capitalist powers in the 1920s was real and sustained, that Stalin's assessment of it was grounded in events, and that the heavy-industry strategy was a correct choice for the time. The article has three parts. The first reviews the attitudes and actions of Britain, the United States and the capitalist states acting jointly towards the USSR in the 1920s. The second traces how Stalin's judgement of the international situation changed from 1924 to 1928. The third offers five evaluative points on Stalin's intentions and decisions. Yuan draws on Stalin's writings and on Chinese, Soviet and Western scholarship, including Kissinger, Service and Paterson. Yuan lists a series of incidents: the Curzon ultimatum (1923), the forged "Zinoviev letter" (1924), the raid on the Soviet embassy in Beijing, the raid on Arcos, the assassination of the Soviet envoy Voikov in Warsaw, and Britain's break of relations in 1927. Yuan adds the American policy of non-recognition, the Dawes Plan, and the Locarno and Kellogg–Briand pacts, which Yuan reads as instruments of isolation or of an anti-Soviet front. Stalin, on this account, moved from optimism in 1924–26 to the conclusion in 1927 that these events were not isolated and that the danger of war was growing. Yuan holds that Stalin wanted to postpone war and preserve peace, that his basic aim was the state's survival and security, and that he judged Soviet strength soberly. Siege and hostility produced a strong sense of crisis, and a USSR left as an agrarian appendage of the capitalist world would be defenceless. Hence the author calls the planned economy, heavy-industry-centred industrialisation and collectivisation a necessary response. Yuan concludes that analysing Stalin's errors is legitimate and necessary, but only with an objective and comprehensive view of the external pressures he faced. The author maintains that Stalin's decisions secured the survival of the first socialist state and showed the vitality of socialism. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist scholar defends Stalin's industrialisation strategy by pointing to the international environment, and how the article assembles the 1920s diplomatic record to support that case.

Riazanov's theoretical contribution to the editing and dissemination of The German Ideology manuscripts With a discussion of the dispute between Riazanov and Mayer 论梁赞诺夫对《德意志意识形态》手稿的整理和传播的理论贡献 Sun Kuixia Did David Riazanov, founding director of the Marx-Engels Institute in Moscow, claim to have "discovered" the manuscripts of The German Ideology, as Western scholarship often suggests? Sun Kuixia takes up this question through the dispute between Riazanov and Gustav Mayer, author of the first biography of Engels. The article argues that the charge is unfounded: Riazanov never presented himself as the discoverer, and his real contribution was to collect, edit, reconstruct and publish the manuscripts. The article has three parts. It first reconstructs the dispute, which began with Riazanov's 1923 report on new findings about the Marx-Engels literary legacy and Mayer's reply, "The 'Discovery' of the Manuscript of The German Ideology". It then tests the "discovery" claim against the manuscript's documentary history and against Riazanov's own texts, including his later History of The German Ideology. Finally it assesses the significance of the Riazanov edition for textual scholarship and for debates about Marx's intellectual development. Sun's central move is philological. The author says Riazanov used the word "discovery" only four times in his 1923 report, and never in the noun form for a discoverer. It was absent from his later History of The German Ideology.
