Sun adds that Riazanov's collecting was arduous and depended on negotiations with Bernstein and the German Social Democratic leadership, and that Mehring and Mayer had supplied information but neither reconstructed or published the whole. Sun argues that the dispute left a one-sided record because the editor of the Archive for the History of Socialism ended the exchange before Riazanov could reply. Riazanov was then purged in 1930 and his work suppressed. Sun credits Riazanov's edition with first reconstructing the work's structure and setting out the manuscripts, revisions and editorial additions. The author also says it gave Marxists a documentary basis for treating the text as a bridge between The Holy Family and The Poverty of Philosophy, against Althusser's and Hiromatsu's thesis of a break. The same basis is said to let scholars reject Below's and Sombart's claims that historical materialism was not original to Marx and Engels. Sun concludes that Mayer's accusation fails and that Riazanov laid the foundation for later editions. Read the original if you are interested in the editorial history of The German Ideology, the MEGA project, or a Chinese defence of Riazanov against the "discovery" charge.

The contemporary value of Lenin's Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism 列宁《帝国主义论》的当代价值 Jiang Yingchun Marking the centenary of Lenin's Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism, completed in 1916, this newspaper commentary (Guangming Daily, June 2016) argues that the book's analysis has been repeatedly confirmed over the past century. Jiang contends that its objective logic remains an important intellectual resource for understanding the present. The piece is organised around three themes that the author draws from the book: the historical character of capitalism, the essence of modern colonialism, and the epochal character of the development of Marxism. Each section is anchored in extended quotations from Lenin and, in one case, Marx and Engels. On the first theme, Jiang targets metaphysical views of capitalism, such as the 'end of history' thesis, and defends Lenin's description of imperialism as 'moribund capitalism'. Critics who say Lenin's prediction failed, Jiang argues, overlook his historical dialectics: earlier social systems also left the stage only after repeated swings, driven by capitalism's basic contradiction between private appropriation and socialised production. Jiang links financial expansion, financial oligarchy and recurrent financial crises to this contradiction and claims that capitalism now faces 'limits to growth' in economics, politics and culture. On the second theme, Jiang reads colonialism as the necessary result of imperialism and capital export, with the world divided 'according to capital' and 'according to strength'. The author rejects attempts to portray colonisation as liberation or civilising and calls such views an inversion of history. On the third theme, Jiang presents the book as an exemplary grasp of its era, analysing the monopolistic, parasitic, decaying and moribund features of imperialism and criticising revisionism, especially Kautskyism, as a product of imperialist ideology seeping into the working class. Jiang concludes that, although it was written when capitalism appeared at the height of its power, Lenin's book looked beyond appearances and set a new direction for Marxist and socialist practice. It remains a 'perspective lens' for examining contemporary capitalism. The author adds that readers should not stop there but, like Lenin, use materialist dialectics to grasp complexity and open new horizons for Marxism. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese commentary in 2016 used Lenin's theory of imperialism to defend claims about capitalism's decline and the nature of colonialism.

Understanding the theory of social alienation in Marxist economics: its academic standing, main content and contemporary relevance 理解马克思经济学的社会异化观：学术地位、主要内容及现实意义 Zhu Fuqiang Zhu Fuqiang asks what place the concept of alienation holds in Marx's thought and what it offers economic analysis. The article accepts Yu Wujin's view that alienation runs through all of Marx's work, and argues that the later turn to historical analysis did not replace the early moral critique. Zhu holds that alienation thinking is a basic method of Marxist economics, running from essence to appearance, and that it remains relevant today. The article has four parts. It first sets out the question, then reviews philosophical debates over alienation's status and over the two evaluative standpoints, moral and historical. It then reconstructs Marx's concept from the early writings, tracing its path from religious to philosophical, political and economic alienation, and ends with the concept's present-day significance. Zhu deliberately avoids textual disputes over periodisation and focuses on the concept's economic meaning. Sources include Fetscher, Ollman, Lukács, Fromm and Wolff. Zhu contends that the shift from "moral evaluation first" to "historical evaluation first" in the mature Marx should not be read as a rupture, as Althusser and orthodox Marxism did. Historical analysis treats alienation as a stage in development, but the moral dimension remains the basis for criticising capitalism and pointing to a better society. Zhu then reconstructs alienated labour: estrangement from the labour process, from the product, from species-being and from other people, with labour alienation as the root of the rest. Zhu also defines alienation broadly as any separation of a thing from its essence, which gives a reference point for judging present conditions. Zhu concludes that alienation thinking underlies Marx's labour theory of value, his account of exploitation behind "free" exchange and his critique of vulgar economics. It also shows why mainstream assumptions such as the disutility of labour describe only alienated labour. Citing Ollman, Zhu argues that alienation and fetishism are more widespread than in Marx's day. Zhu criticises Western mainstream economics since the marginal revolution for lacking this framework and for rationalising reality through ethical naturalism and social Darwinism. Read the original if you want a methodological reading of Marx's alienation theory as a tool for economic analysis, along with a survey of the philosophical debates over early and late Marx.

Understanding more deeply the claim that "core values are a kind of virtue" 深入理解“核心价值观是一种德” Li Chunhua Zhu Yazhou The article interprets a remark Xi Jinping made in May 2014 in a discussion with students and teachers at Peking University: that core values are "in fact a kind of virtue" (de), at once personal virtue and a "great virtue" of the state and society. Li and Zhu argue that this formulation has real practical significance. In their reading it shows how the core socialist values link to traditional Chinese culture, reflects confidence in the socialist path, and indicates how the values should be cultivated. The article has three sections. The first treats the formula as marking both continuity with and transcendence of fine traditional Chinese culture. The second treats it as an expression of institutional confidence in socialism with Chinese characteristics. The third draws out what it implies for cultivating and practising the values. The authors draw on Marxist principles about social being and social consciousness, on historical materialism, on classical Chinese sources, and on Party and state documents on moral construction from 1949 to 2006. In the first section, the authors map the individual-level values (patriotism, dedication, integrity, friendship) onto ancient sayings from Guanzi, Confucius and the Book of Changes. They also map them onto the "five loves" of the 1949 Common Program, the 1982 Constitution, the 2001 civic morality outline and the 2006 "eight honours and eight disgraces". They say this lifts "personal virtue" into core values and upgrades tradition rather than copying it. In the second section, they read prosperity, democracy, civility and harmony as the state's virtue, and freedom, equality, justice and rule of law as the society's virtue. They contrast socialist democracy, which they say rests on public ownership and removes democracy's dependence on money, with Western capitalist democracy. In the third, they argue that virtue means conduct, so the values must be practised. They hold that morality is determined by the economic base, and that public ownership supplies the material foundation. They add that moral character is built gradually, and they cite Xi's image of buttoning the first button correctly. They also warn of confused or distorted values among some young people, citing blurred ideals, "entertainment above all" and the mocking of revolutionary figures. The authors conclude that treating core values as virtue directs people to begin with private morality, uphold public morality and understand great virtue. They say this should make the values part of daily conduct and, in time, a lasting spiritual pillar and national character. They also expect this "great virtue" to lead world progress. Read the original if you want a close example of how Party-aligned scholarship in 2015 linked the core socialist values to traditional ethics and Marxist theory of morality, and to the task of educating young people.

The communist ideal as a powerful spiritual force for realizing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation 共产主义理想是实现中华民族伟大复兴的强大精神力量 Xin Xiangyang Tao Lijiang Writing in 2016, Xin and Tao ask what role the communist ideal has played in the history of the Communist Party of China and why it still matters for the national project. They argue that communism is a scientific doctrine, a social system and a real movement, not an empty vision. In their account, the ideal has been the Party's "spiritual pillar" in revolution, construction and reform, and is a source of strength for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The article is organised chronologically in three parts: the New Democratic Revolution, socialist revolution and construction, and the period of reform and opening up. It draws on statements by Deng Xiaoping, Mao Zedong, Xi Jinping, Hu Qiaomu and the report to the 18th Party Congress (2012). It also cites the Resolution on Certain Questions in the History of Our Party and a 1972 passage by Arnold Toynbee on Chinese industrialization. For the revolutionary period, the authors say the communist ideal gave rise to a series of revolutionary spirits, from the Red Boat spirit to the Xibaipo spirit, and sustained countless revolutionaries through episodes such as the Long March. For the Mao era, they argue the ideal supported the Korean War effort, the socialist transformation and an independent search for a Chinese road to socialism, described as a "second integration" of Marxism with Chinese conditions. It also drove mass enthusiasm in industrial construction, which they link to the Daqing and Lei Feng spirits. For the present, they argue that the "great struggle with many new historical characteristics" and the complexity of deepening reform require firm political conviction. They cite the collapse of the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe as a warning, and they treat corruption among a minority of officials as beginning with wavering ideals. The authors conclude that, because China is in the primary stage of socialism, which they call the initial phase of communism's first stage, all current striving points towards communism. They call the ideal the "code" of the Party's success and of national rejuvenation. They urge Party members to hold to it unwaveringly, resist erroneous currents and build confidence in socialism with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a compact example of how mid-2010s Party scholarship tied communist belief to Party discipline and the historical narrative of revolution, construction and reform.

How we conceived and wrote "Foreign Religious Infiltration and the Soviet-East European Upheaval" 我们是如何思考和写作《境外宗教渗透与苏东剧变研究》的 Duan Dezhi This is a reflective account by Duan Dezhi, editor of the 2015 People's Publishing House volume on foreign religious infiltration and the Soviet and East European upheaval. Duan explains why the project was undertaken, what the book sets out to prove and how it was carried out. The book grew out of a major Ministry of Education research project on foreign religious infiltration and China's ideological security, begun in 2009 and completed in 2013. Duan's central claim is that infiltration by hostile external forces using religion was an important cause of the upheaval, though not the only one. The essay has three parts. The first gives two reasons for making the upheaval a priority: it is the most representative case of religious infiltration of socialist states, and it is the factual basis on which theorists of the 'end of ideology' rely. The second sets out the book's three aims, and the third reports how each was pursued. Duan draws on Marx, Engels, Deng Xiaoping, Francis Bacon and the memoirs of Nikolai Ryzhkov, and on figures such as Gorbachev, Jaruzelski and Adam Schaff. Duan treats the 'US–Vatican holy alliance' formed in 1982 as the central event of the upheaval. In this account it pursued a three-step plan: engineer change in Poland, extend it to seven other East European states, then dissolve the Soviet Union. Duan places this within Engels's 'theory of historical resultant forces', which also counts the rigid Soviet model and the right and 'left' errors of ruling parties as causes. The lessons drawn are that ruling parties accommodated infiltration and lacked an 'East–West' consciousness (awareness of the ideological adversary). Duan adds that religious work must avoid both right and 'left' errors, and aim to guide religion to adapt to socialist society. Against the 'end of ideology' thesis, Duan cites the later revival of communist parties in Russia and shifting views of Stalin. Duan also charges that the thesis rests on abstract logical centrism and narrow empiricism, which Bacon would have called 'idols of the theatre'. Duan concludes that the upheaval is an episode that can be surpassed but not bypassed: international communism will go on, while its causes call for self-reflection by all communist parties. Duan presents the book's epistemological critique of the end-of-ideology thesis as its original contribution. Duan also reports favourable reception from reviewing experts. Read the original if you want a first-hand statement of how a Chinese scholar of religion links religious infiltration, ideological security and lessons from the Soviet collapse.

Lenin's defence and consolidation of the Party: the historical facts must not be distorted 列宁维护和巩固党的历史事实不容歪曲 Yuan Xiuli Yuan Xiuli takes up the "Resolution on Party Unity" that Lenin drafted and the Tenth Congress of the Russian Communist Party (Bolsheviks) adopted in March 1921. The article responds to long-standing claims that the resolution was a product of factional struggle, a tool for crushing the opposition and preserving one-party rule, and an expression of Lenin's "autocratic thinking". Yuan argues that these claims fit neither Lenin's thought nor the historical record. The article reads the resolution as a call for unity under exceptional conditions. The article is published in Red Flag Manuscripts (2016, no. 7) and is organised in three parts. The first looks at how Lenin defended the Party's unity. The second looks at how he strengthened the Party's leadership. The third looks at the resolution's link to the urgent task of economic construction. Yuan draws on Lenin's speeches at the Congress, cited from his Collected Works and Selected Works. The article also draws on the political and economic crisis of 1921, including the Kronstadt rebellion of February that year. On unity, Yuan stresses that Lenin presented the resolution as a call for unity aimed at winning over the majority. It recognised the Workers' Opposition's reasonable criticisms of bureaucracy, and the Congress elected members of the Workers' Opposition and the Democratic Centralists to the Central Committee. Yuan holds that the groups themselves moved from criticism to demanding unrestricted democracy and independent organisation, and to publishing pamphlets and holding separate meetings. Lenin therefore distinguished theoretical discussion in journals from factional action in a fighting party. On leadership, Yuan follows Lenin in treating the Workers' Opposition's plan for a congress of producers and trade-union control of the economy as syndicalist and anarchist. In this reading, such a plan sidelined the Party's vanguard role. On the economy, Yuan argues that factional debate was an excessive luxury, because it obstructed the New Economic Policy. The Workers' Opposition wanted to continue War Communism and move rapidly towards communism. Yuan concludes that in spring 1921 the resolution was indispensable. It settled the Party's divisions, preserved its unity, strengthened its leadership and kept socialist construction on course. Yuan adds that Lenin called the New Economic Policy an \"unprecedentedly difficult retreat\". In this period the Party needed firm conviction, unified thought and iron discipline, even more than in the most dangerous moments of the civil war. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Party journal in 2016 defends Lenin's 1921 resolution against charges of authoritarianism, and which of Lenin's own statements it relies on.

The Marx–Engels relationship in MEGA2 MEGA2 中的马克思恩格斯关系问题 Wang Fengcai Yuan Peng Wang Fengcai and Yuan Peng take up the long-running question of how Marx and Engels relate to each other, and how Marx's own doctrine relates to "Marxism". They note that since the 1990s the question has again become central to research on MEGA2, the second historical-critical edition of the Marx–Engels complete works. The article sets out to survey the international positions and then the German debates. It concludes that German scholars have not escaped four familiar models: opposition, agreement, difference and change over time. The first part traces the history of the question. It covers early claims of discord, the long dominance of the "agreement" view before the 1960s (Henry, Rigby), and the later rise of the "opposition" view associated above all with Norman Levine. It then presents the "difference" view (Lukács, Korsch, Alfred Schmidt) and Terrell Carver's "changeable" account. The second part turns to German MEGA2-based scholarship, and the third to two specific issues: the tendency of the rate of profit to fall and the collapse of the capitalist system. In the authors' account, Carver sees the young Engels as influencing Marx, especially through the Outlines of a Critique of Political Economy. Their middle-period collaboration did not make them one thinker, and the later Engels drifted from Marx. Among German scholars, Haug's dictionary, Heinrich and Elbe treat "Marxism" as in effect "Engelsism" and the unity of the two as a myth. Against them, Seppmann, Müller, Gerns and Tjaden are reported as defending a high degree of agreement, or as holding that a genuine "Engelsism" could not have been created. On the falling rate of profit, the dominant view (Neuhaus, Heinrich) holds that Engels's edited volumes of Capital stressed it and the collapse idea more than Marx's manuscripts did. Müller replies that Marx's manuscripts already contain the law, and that Engels's contribution was editorial and philological. The authors close by saying that the German positions need further consideration. They add that the positions can broaden Chinese scholars' horizons and offer useful lessons for Marxism research in China. The article is largely a survey, and its own evaluative remarks are brief. Read the original if you want a detailed map of Western and German MEGA2-era debates on Marx and Engels, with the specific works and scholars cited, including the dispute over Engels's editing of Capital volumes 2–3.

Capital and Hegel 《资本论》与黑格尔 Li Jianping Tan Yuanyuan Li Jianping and Tan Yuanyuan take up the relationship between Marx's Capital and Hegel. They note that most earlier studies concentrate on the 1840s, and that the question has seldom been examined through the history of Capital's composition. Their thesis is that across the 1850s, 1860s and 1870s Marx drew on Hegel's dialectic as a method while rejecting its idealism. They describe the result as a critically transformed dialectic. The article is organised chronologically around the successive manuscripts and editions of Capital. The 1850s section covers the 1857 Introduction and the 1857–58 manuscripts, together with Engels's reviews of the 1859 Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy. The 1860s section covers the 1861–63 and 1863–65 manuscripts, Marx's notes on Hegel's Encyclopaedia Logic, and the Marx–Engels correspondence around the publication of Volume I in 1867. The 1870s section turns to the Afterword to the second German edition (1873) and the polemic against Eugen Dühring in Engels's Anti-Dühring. The authors also describe their own earlier textual study of the dialectic in Volume I. Three moves carry the argument. First, the authors argue from Marx's letter of January 1858 and from the vocabulary of the Chapter on Money that the economic manuscripts were begun after Marx re-read Hegel's Logic in late October 1857. They also argue that the method of ascending from the abstract to the concrete is Hegelian in form but materialist in basis. Second, they read the unpublished Chapter 6 of the 1863–65 manuscript as showing that the commodity is both the starting point and the end point of the analysis, returning at a higher level as a rich totality, which they link to Hegel's treatment of beginning and end. Third, they follow the Afterword in distinguishing the method of inquiry from the method of presentation, and in presenting Marx's dialectic as the inverse of Hegel's, stripped of its mystical shell. They use Engels's replies to Dühring on the transformation of quantity into quality and the negation of the negation to argue that Capital applies these laws historically rather than as formulas. The authors conclude that Marx's debt to Hegel ran through the whole composition of Capital, and that Marx described himself as Hegel's pupil while criticising his idealism. They treat the Afterword and Engels's defence against Dühring as the definitive statement of this relationship. Read the original if you want a text-based, chronological account of how Hegel's logic shaped the drafting of Capital, with close attention to the manuscripts and the Marx–Engels letters.

Defending heroes is defending our values 捍卫英雄就是捍卫我们的价值观 Zhang Mingcang Hong Chaoyin Writing in Qiushi in 2016, Zhang Mingcang and Hong Chaoyin respond to what they describe as a deliberate campaign to slander revolutionary heroes. They cite attacks on the Five Heroes of Langya Mountain, Huang Jiguang, Qiu Shaoyun and Lei Feng, and say these attacks try to "disprove" heroic deeds and overturn their meaning. The authors argue that such claims distort history, confuse values and erode the spiritual foundation of national rejuvenation. In their view heroes must therefore be defended as a way of defending the country's values. The article opens with Xi Jinping's call to revere, defend, learn from and care for heroes, and then has three parts. The first presents heroes as the backbone of the nation, as exemplars of progressive values, as spiritual coordinates of their age and as vanguards of national rejuvenation, with examples from ancient legend to the War of Resistance against Japan. The second sets out a Marxist view of heroes. The third turns to practical measures for defending heroes. The core argument distinguishes honouring heroes from three things the authors say critics confuse it with. It is not the idealist "heroic view of history", because the heroes honoured come from the people and depend on them, and the authors cite Marx on great men and Mao Zedong's line that the masses are the true heroes. It is not a personality cult, which the authors define as deifying individuals, since heroes can be groups or nameless and are meant to be models that others can imitate. It is honouring heroic spirit, so the idea that heroes are obsolete is rejected. The authors present "deconstructing heroes" as a political tactic. They say it denies the Communist Party's historical record, undermines socialist core values and shakes the Party's governing base. They point to the Soviet Union in the 1980s and 1990s, where they say mockery of heroes such as Zoya and Matrosov preceded the collapse of the Party and state. They call for education in historical materialism, for continuing the heroes' spirit in the new era and, where needed, for legal punishment of those who spread rumours against heroes. Read the original if you want a clear example of how official Party commentary of 2016 linked the defence of revolutionary heroes to ideological security and historical narrative.

The Communist Party of China's exploration of core socialist values Three historical periods, from the new-democratic revolution to reform and opening up 中国共产党探索社会主义核心价值观的历程 Jiang Yan How did the Communist Party of China arrive at the core socialist values it promotes today? Writing in 2015, Jiang traces the Party's long exploration of socialist values and argues that it was continuous across three historical periods. In Jiang's account, the Party first fixed a socialist value orientation, then deepened its understanding of core socialist values after 1949, and finally formulated and refined the core socialist values in the era of reform and opening up. The article is organised chronologically in three sections. The first covers the new-democratic revolution, the second the period of socialist revolution and construction, and the third the reform period from the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978) onwards. It draws on writings by Li Dazhao, Yun Daiying and Mao Zedong, on Party congress documents, and on Party resolutions and state documents on moral and cultural construction. For the revolutionary period, Jiang identifies three elements of the value orientation: Marxism and socialism as the Party's fundamental commitment, wholehearted service to the people as its purpose, and the goal of an independent, free, democratic, unified and prosperous new China. For the period after 1949, the author points to propaganda for Marxism-Leninism and Mao Zedong Thought, and to moral education built around patriotism, collectivism and models such as the Iron Man (Wang Jinxi) spirit and the Lei Feng spirit, which Jiang says prepared the ground for later formulations. For the reform period, Jiang lists five strands: Marxist guidance, the common ideal of socialism with Chinese characteristics, the national spirit and the spirit of the times, the socialist concept of honour and disgrace, and the core socialist value system. The Sixth Plenum of the 16th Central Committee (2006) first set out this value system, and the 18th Party Congress (2012) called for fostering the core socialist values through "three advocacies". Jiang concludes that the Party now treats building the core socialist value system and fostering and practising core socialist values as a long-term strategic task of socialist cultural development. In the article's reading, this reflects the Party's "high degree of consciousness and confidence" in building a strong socialist cultural power and strengthening cultural soft power. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned historical account of how Party documents and campaigns from 1921 to 2012 are presented as stages leading to the core socialist values.

The advanced nature of culture and its "yardsticks" An analysis 文化的先进性及其“尺度”问题探析 Li Chunhua Is there such a thing as advanced and backward culture, or does each nation's culture simply have its own merits? Li Chunhua, in an article published in Guizhou Social Sciences in 2015, rejects cultural relativism, which the author says denies cultural development and the progress of human history. Li argues that the very concept of "advanced culture" logically implies backward, decadent and even reactionary cultures, and that the standard for telling them apart must be clarified. The article first contrasts classical cultural evolutionism with cultural relativism in Western thought, then notes that Marxist classics never treated cultural advancement as a separate topic. Li credits the Communist Party of China with first putting forward the concept of "advanced culture", and describes the Chinese version as socialist culture guided by Marxism and oriented to modernization, the world and the future. The main body then examines four yardsticks in turn (rational, historical, material and value) before discussing how they combine. Li's core claim is that advanced culture must be judged by the concrete, dialectical unity of these four. The rational yardstick demands scientific truthfulness and objectivity, and Li treats "Eurocentrism" and "universal values" as unscientific biases. The historical yardstick makes advancement relative to an era: traditional culture was once advanced. The material yardstick, which Li calls fundamental, rests on historical materialism and ties cultural progress to the development of the productive forces. Because material growth does not automatically raise cultural life, as Li says of alienation in the West and spiritual confusion in China since reform and opening up, a value yardstick is added: culture must serve people's liberation and all-round development. Li concludes that when the yardsticks conflict, the historical yardstick takes priority. Religion, though unscientific, was once progressive; Confucian culture suppressed individuality but supported feudal stability and productive forces; contemporary capitalist culture, despite alienation, is judged more advanced than feudal culture. Li adds that the "people" is a historical category, as Mao Zedong's wartime anti-Japanese culture shows. Over the long run, advanced culture is said to reshape backward culture, so recognising historical progress means recognising cultural advancement. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist scholar builds a multi-criteria framework for judging cultural advancement and handles cases that appear to contradict it.

Lenin's defence and consolidation of the Party: the historical facts must not be distorted 列宁维护和巩固党的历史事实不容歪曲 Yuan Xiuli Writing in Hongqi Wengao in 2016, Yuan Xiuli takes up the long-running criticism of the "Resolution on Party Unity" that Lenin drafted for the Tenth Congress of the Russian Communist Party (Bolsheviks) in March 1921. Critics, the author says, portray it as a product of factional struggle, a tool for crushing the opposition and defending one-party rule, and proof of Lenin's \"autocratic thinking\". Yuan argues that this reading fits neither Lenin's thought nor the historical facts, and that the resolution aimed to preserve Party unity and strengthen Party leadership in a crisis. The article is a short commentary in three parts: safeguarding Party unity, consolidating Party leadership, and securing the most urgent task of economic construction. It relies mainly on Lenin's speeches and writings from the Tenth Congress, cited from the Chinese edition of his Collected Works, together with State and Revolution. It sets the resolution against the conditions of 1921: years of war, economic ruin, the Kronstadt rebellion of February and the shift to the New Economic Policy. Yuan's central argument is that the resolution was a call for unity rather than an attack. In the author's account, it acknowledged the reasonable criticisms of the \"Workers' Opposition\", on bureaucracy, democracy and the removal of unreliable elements. The Congress also elected members of the Workers' Opposition and the Democratic Centralists to the Central Committee, and asked those who offered to resign to stay in post. Yuan holds that these groups nonetheless drifted into syndicalism and anarchism: they sought a congress of producers to run the economy, put trade unions above the Party and opposed the New Economic Policy from the \"left\". In Yuan's reading, Lenin therefore distinguished theoretical debate in journals and collections from factional organisation and public agitation. Under siege conditions, the author says, a prolonged debate over the role of the trade unions was a \"luxury\" that distracted the Party from economic recovery and threatened the dictatorship of the proletariat. Yuan concludes that the resolution was needed in spring 1921. It settled the disagreements, kept the Party united, strengthened its leadership and kept socialist construction on course. The author adds that Lenin called the New Economic Policy an \"unprecedented retreat\" and that it demanded even firmer conviction, unity of thought and discipline than the civil war had. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Chinese Party commentary defends Lenin's 1921 ban on factions against the charge of authoritarianism.

Using scientific thought to eliminate belief in ghosts and spirits 用科学思想消除鬼神迷信 Jia Runguo Writing in 2016, Jia Runguo argues that the ideological basis of violence by cult members and terrorists is anti-scientific belief in ghosts and spirits. Alongside legal and institutional measures against cults and terrorism, the author calls for sustained popularisation of scientific knowledge to drive out such belief. Since the social soil that produces it cannot be removed quickly, Jia holds that arming people's minds with a scientific worldview is the only route to immunity against extremist doctrines. The article has five sections: exposing the anti-scientific essence of belief in the supernatural; criticising idealism and metaphysics; improving Marxist philosophy teaching; strengthening the popularisation of scientific atheism; and strengthening Party leadership over the study of religion. It draws on Engels, Lenin and Mao Zedong, and ends with remarks on the institutional history of religious studies in China. Jia defines supernatural force as spiritual force detached from matter, and traces the idea of the soul to early humans' lack of scientific knowledge about life and thought. Educated people and scientists also fall into superstition, the author says, because idealism and metaphysics supply the wrong method of thinking; Jia cites Engels on empiricists who scorn dialectics and end up in spiritualism. Philosophy teaching should therefore centre on refuting idealism, metaphysics and theism, with textbooks giving up to two-thirds of their space to criticism of erroneous ideas. Jia also rejects the view that atheist education is simple or conflicts with the Party's policy of religious freedom, and says implementation has been poor because the relevant documents sit with the united front and religious affairs bodies rather than with propaganda and education departments. Jia proposes moving atheism requirements into propaganda and education documents, creating dedicated offices and staff in propaganda and education departments, and reinforcing Marxist guidance in religious studies. The author complains that scholars who combine study of religion with criticism of theology are becoming fewer, and cites Mao's 1960s remarks and the founding of the Institute of World Religions in 1964. Read the original if you want to see how a researcher in the state religious affairs system links atheist education, philosophy teaching and religious studies to counter-terrorism and anti-cult work.

The value and significance of the young Marx's critique of religion 青年马克思宗教批判的价值意蕴 Zhu Peili Zhu Peili asks what the young Marx's critique of religion contributed to the formation of Marxist theory. The article argues that this critique was the starting point and precondition of Marx's wider social critique. In Zhu's account, it inherited and then surpassed earlier rational critiques, aimed at human emancipation, and still bears on modern fetishism of commodities. The article has four parts. It first traces the origins of the critique: Marx's early religious and moral outlook, as seen in his school essays, the setting of Prussian absolutism allied with religion, and the influence of the Enlightenment and the Young Hegelians. It then assesses the theoretical value of the critique through Marx's debt to and break with Feuerbach. A third part treats human emancipation as its value aim, and a final part turns to its contemporary relevance. Zhu's central move is a contrast with Feuerbach. Feuerbach saw religion as human self-alienation and proposed a "religion of love", but, on Zhu's reading, he treated people as abstract individuals and ignored the contradictions within secular society. Marx instead traced religion to an "inverted world" of oppression and exploitation, so that criticism of heaven turned into criticism of earth, of law and of politics. For Zhu this makes social critique the full completion of the critique of religion. Zhu then links the critique to emancipation: in the 1843 Introduction to the critique of Hegel's philosophy of right, the proletariat is the force of human emancipation and philosophy its "head", with the proletariat its "heart". Zhu concludes that the young Marx's critique gave later Marxist theory of human emancipation its starting point and a value reference. In the author's view it remains relevant because commodity fetishism functions as a secularised religious worship that produces spiritual emptiness and anxiety. Zhu holds that religious illusion can be removed only by changing the social relations that produce it, abolishing private ownership and the social division of labour and creating an "association of free individuals". Read the original if you want a concise Chinese-language account of how the young Marx moved from Feuerbach's critique of religion to social critique, and how a Chinese scholar of atheism applies it to commodity fetishism.

Scientific atheism and religious issues in the new situation Report on the 2015 annual conference of the China Atheism Association 科学无神论与新形势下的宗教问题 Su Bin Zuo Peng This is a report on the 2015 annual conference of the China Atheism Association, held in Beijing on 5–6 December 2015 under the theme "Scientific atheism and religious issues in the new situation". It was co-organised by the Association, the CASS Research Center for Science and Atheism and the University of Science and Technology Beijing. More than 70 scholars from over 30 universities, research institutes and academic bodies in 12 provinces and cities took part. The report arranges the papers under seven headings: the "Four Musts" for religious work set out at the 2015 Central United Front Work Conference; basic theory of scientific atheism; Marxist atheism; atheism and the study of religion; science and religion; propaganda and education in scientific atheism; and scientific atheism and curbing religious extremism. Speakers included Jia Runguo, Duan Dezhi, Du Jiwen, Xi Wuyi, Li Shen and Tian Xinming, along with many younger researchers and doctoral students. On religious work, Jia Runguo presents the Four Musts as the guide to adapting religion to socialist society. Duan Dezhi reads the Soviet and East European upheavals partly through foreign religious infiltration, and several speakers warn against Western ideological penetration and religious extremism. On theory, Du Jiwen locates the strength of Chinese culture in humanism, and Li Shen insists that China's theistic traditions need criticism as much as its atheist ones. Tian Xinming, Zeng Chuanhui and Han Qi revisit Lenin, the young Marx and Engels's Anti-Dühring. Others argue that religious morality is in essence secular morality, and that scientific and cultural education should be strengthened. The Xinjiang papers criticise the stress on policing over ideological work and call for better management of religious affairs. They also propose "five-good" religious personnel and a lower profile for religious culture. The report notes that attendance and paper quality rose compared with earlier conferences. Participants saw the mix of senior and younger scholars as a sign that scientific atheism is thriving as the Party strengthens ideological work. Some asked for more time for exchange and for an awards system to attract young scholars. Read the original if you want a detailed map of how Chinese atheism scholars and religious-affairs researchers framed religion, ideology and security in late 2015.

Countering Western "internet freedom" requires safeguarding China's ideological security 应对西方“网络自由”必须维护我国意识形态安全 Zhang Weiliang He Qiujuan Writing in Red Flag Digest in 2016, shortly after Xi Jinping's 19 April speech at a symposium on cybersecurity and informatization, Zhang Weiliang and He Qiujuan take up the place of ideological security within national cybersecurity. They argue that ideological security comes first online, and that the "internet freedom" promoted by the United States and other Western states is a cover for cyber hegemony and ideological export. In the authors' view, China must therefore uphold its socialist ideology and become a cyber power. The commentary has four parts. It first describes "internet freedom" as the greatest threat to other countries' cybersecurity, then argues that cyber sovereignty is internationally recognised, so that "internet freedom" has no basis. It next sets out the concrete threats these ideas pose to China's online ideological security, and ends with measures to defend it. The central argument is that "internet freedom" is a claim to "first-occupier sovereignty" backed by Western technological superiority, so it can only be freedom for the West. The authors point to double standards, citing the Snowden revelations and a US defence secretary's remark that cyber attacks are a means of containing hostile states. They say cyber sovereignty rests on the objective existence of cyberspace, on cyber frontiers and cyber defence, and on legal grounds such as the 2003 World Summit on the Information Society. Freedom without limits, they write, is merely a synonym for power politics, and Western states themselves recognise sovereignty when they build cyber defences and conduct surveillance. Domestically, the authors blame netizens swayed by "universal values", scholars who advocate constitutional democracy, Western-backed opinion leaders, commercial media and historical nihilism for weakening mainstream ideology. The authors call for a long struggle on several fronts. They ask mainstream media to assert cyber sovereignty openly and to set an example for commercial outlets. They want core technologies developed so that China moves from a large to a strong cyber power, and cyber legislation strengthened following the Fourth Plenum of the 18th Central Committee. They also want netizens to gain media literacy and "immunity" through socialist core values, building a "psychological defence" alongside technical defence. Read the original if you want to see how a 2016 Party-journal commentary links cyber sovereignty, Western "internet freedom" and ideological security.

Upholding and promoting atheism with a clear stand 旗帜鲜明地坚持和宣传无神论 Zhu Weiqun Writing in the Global Times in May 2016, shortly after the National Conference on Religious Work held in April, Zhu Weiqun asks how Marxist atheism can remain the dominant mainstream ideology among the people. Zhu argues that, because Marxism's worldview rests on dialectical and historical materialism, upholding socialism with Chinese characteristics necessarily means upholding and developing Marxist atheism. The article presents this as a major question that Party cadres, especially leaders and religious-affairs officials, need to think through. This short commentary is organised under four headings. It treats atheism as part of mainstream ideology, as a precondition for sound religious work, as a matter of Party discipline for members, and as a feature that distinguishes the Party from most other parties. Zhu draws on Mao Zedong's Report on an Investigation of the Peasant Movement in Hunan, his On New Democracy, and a passage from Engels, alongside observations on Chinese history and culture. Zhu's central claim is that the Party cannot abandon atheism, stay neutral between theism and atheism, or let theism spread until it becomes the mainstream ideology. The reasons given are the ruling party's worldview, modernization, resistance to foreign religious infiltration, and the Party's mass base. Religion will long persist and believers are a positive force, Zhu says, so the theist–atheist divide is not a political opposition. Religious work, however, is atheists working with theists within the united front, and atheists should lead politically. Zhu describes China as historically a secular state with a secular culture, and warns against religious 'de-Sinicization' and 'extremization'. Zhu also reports that some Party members and scholars have argued that members may hold religious beliefs, or that believers may join the Party, and rejects both positions as illogical. Zhu concludes that the rule that Party members may not hold religious beliefs is political discipline. In Zhu's account, lifting it would erode the unity of the Party's worldview, turn the Party into a loose body of religious factions, and make part of its religious work one believer addressing another. Zhu calls for atheist education, including for young people and in religious studies research and teaching, to be treated as a firm task. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official Party-line case for atheism and the ban on religious belief among members, as put forward in 2016 by a senior figure in religious and ethnic affairs.

Frontier report on scientific atheism research in 2014 Keynote address at the 2015 annual conference of the China Atheism Association 2014年科学无神论研究前沿报告 Xi Wuyi Xi Wuyi delivered this keynote address at the China Atheism Association's 2015 annual conference. It surveys research in scientific atheism during 2014 and is drawn from the corresponding chapter of the 2015 yearbook of disciplinary research. Xi presents it as basic work for building the discipline and as information for members' own research. The overall message is that scientific atheism is gaining ground in scholarship and is needed for Marxist religious studies and ideological security. The address has two parts. The first reviews four books: the ten-volume Collected Works of Ren Jiyu, Du Jiwen's Collected Essays on Science and Atheism, the first series of Studies in the History of Chinese Atheism, and the Chinese translation of Richard Dawkins's The Blind Watchmaker. The second summarises journal and newspaper articles under six headings: theory, atheism and religion, resisting religious infiltration and curbing religious extremism, destructive cults, science and religion, and atheist propaganda and education. Xi also reports that about 60 per cent of the articles reviewed came from outside the journal Science and Atheism, against nearly 70 per cent from it in 2010–2013. Across the surveyed work, Xi reports a common line. Marxist religious studies should keep to Mao Zedong's formula of 'studying religion and criticizing theology', as Ren Jiyu summarised it. Du Jiwen and Xi reject 'academic theology', and Xi calls it a challenge to that paradigm. Several authors treat Western, especially Christian, 'infiltration' of universities, the internet and the countryside as a threat to ideological security. Xi's own contributions argue that overseas religious right-wing forces use legal channels to spread values, and that universities should keep education separate from religion. Contributions on religious extremism and the cult 'Almighty God' call for a mix of measures: legal action, rural cultural development and stronger Party organization at the grassroots. Xi also notes disagreement. He calls the Studies in the History of Chinese Atheism claim that Confucianism, Daoism and Buddhism are essentially atheist 'quite controversial'. On science and religion, Li Xingmin and Yu Qiming are reported as holding that scientists' personal faith is unrelated to their research. Xi concludes that scientific atheism is one of the philosophical foundations of the socialist core value system and a long-standing policy of the Communist Party. Xi expects the discipline to play a distinctive part in strengthening ideological work and protecting national cultural security. Read the original if you want a detailed inventory of 2014 Chinese publications on atheism, religion and 'religious infiltration', and a view of how Party-aligned scholars framed these debates.

Seeing achievements, seeing the light: raising our confidence and courage Address to the 2015 annual academic conference of the China Atheism Society 看到成绩看到光明提高我们的信心和勇气 Zhu Xiaoming This is the opening address given by Zhu Xiaoming, president of the China Atheism Society, to the society's 2015 annual academic conference, held in Beijing in December 2015. The conference was co-organised by the society, the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences (CASS) Research Centre for Science and Atheism and Beijing University of Science and Technology, under the theme "Scientific atheism and religious issues under the new situation". Zhu presents it both as an annual exchange and as an occasion to study central Party statements on religious work, ahead of a national religious work conference. After welcoming participants, Zhu gives a numbered report on the society's work in 2015. Items include a March consultation with CASS leaders on religious policy, Zhu's remarks at a publication event for the collected works of Ren Jiyu, a seminar on atheists and traditional Chinese culture, a public lecture in Shandong, and training for Beijing university teachers and cadres on the Marxist view of religion. The report also covers the third Scientific Atheism Forum, a commissioned book project, a new science-exploration centre, the "Southern Research Centre" and a WeChat group. Zhu then lists scholars' publications and awards. Zhu's central claim is that the Party leadership is receptive to the society's work. He reads the emphasis on Marxist atheism education in the Sixth Tibet Work Forum as a sign that the centre had "heard our voice". He cites Xi Jinping's call for religion to adapt to socialist society, Article 23 of the 2015 Party united front regulations (Party members may not hold religious beliefs) and the Party disciplinary regulations of October 2015. Zhu says these create favourable conditions for the field. He describes scientific atheism as temporarily at a low ebb but with "the fire still alive". He also says the society should keep watching the "new atheism movement" in China, whose organisers he describes as showing prejudice against Marxist atheism. Zhu concludes that the society faces both opportunity and serious challenges. He names religious interference in social life and national education, a "religious fever" promoted in the name of culture, and the spread of cults and religious extremism. He calls on members to offer advice, recruit younger scholars and use the conference as a new starting point. He also announces plans for a 2016 commemoration of Ren Jiyu's centenary and the appointment of Gong Yun as head of the atheism research office and deputy secretary-general. Read the original if you want a detailed insider account of how organised atheism research in China operated and understood its political environment in 2015.

What is happiness? "Thinking philosophically": a reading of Marx's early text on Epicurean philosophy 何为幸福：“从哲学上思考”——马克思早期文献《伊壁鸠鲁哲学》解读 Nie Jinfang Writing in 2016, when the "happiness index" had become a popular phrase, Nie Jinfang observes that economists, sociologists and psychologists dominate public talk of happiness while philosophy is almost silent. The author adds that Marx's own remarks on happiness have rarely been sorted out, and that textbooks mention the topic only in passing when discussing the future communist society. The article argues that Marx's early writings on Epicurus show how he thought about happiness, and that this method of thinking still matters. Nie confines the study to a little-studied early text, Marx's notes on Epicurean philosophy. In it Marx works comparatively, using Plutarch's critique of Epicurus to bring out his own view. The article has three sections: the "lower" level (bodily health and inner calm), associated with Epicurus; the "higher" level (spiritual freedom and a divine state), associated with Plutarch; and a third section on how the two levels and the individual and society are connected. In Nie's reading, Epicurus reduces happiness to the absence of pain and simply transplants bodily pleasure into the soul. This ignores the difference between body and soul and sets the human being no higher than animals. Plutarch sees the difference but goes to the other extreme: he places happiness in a pure, remote divinity and cut off from human nature. Nie reports Marx's judgement that both are one-sided. Epicurus is still right to treat bodily health as the universal basis of a human life, and Plutarch is right that spirit is a distinct level. Neither accounts for how the universal appears in particular individuals, or for the link between individual and society. Nie concludes that Marx's approach requires holding together subject and object, individual and universal, body and soul, matter and spirit, and the real and the transcendent, and keeping theory consistent with real life. The author says this laid the ground for Marx's later turn to real problems and political economy while still seeking a way beyond capital's predicament. Current disputes over how to define and measure happiness, Nie argues, fail because they ignore both the necessity and the limits of these two positions. Read the original if you want a close, text-based account of Marx's early view of happiness and of his criticism of Epicurus and Plutarch.

The landmark work marking the basic formation of historical materialism Commemorating the 170th anniversary of The German Ideology 历史唯物主义基本形成的标志性著作 Zhao Jiaxiang Zhao Jiaxiang asks why Marx and Engels's The German Ideology (written 1845–46) should be regarded as the work in which historical materialism was basically formed. Writing for the book's 170th anniversary, Zhao argues that it set out a systematic body of basic concepts and principles, and that it made a clean break with both idealism and Feuerbach's old materialism. Because it went unpublished, Zhao adds, the public emergence of Marxism dates only from The Poverty of Philosophy (1847) and the Communist Manifesto (1848). The article opens by tracing Marx's intellectual path from Hegel through the Rhenish Gazette, the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right, the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 and The Holy Family. Zhao rejects views that treat the 1843–44 writings as already completing Marx's shift. The main body then examines the book through nine topics: the starting point in "real individuals"; the basic question of history; material production as foundation; the "two kinds of production"; the basic driving force of history; people and environment; the division of labour; forms of ownership and social formations; and the standpoint of practice. Zhao's argument turns on several contested readings. Engels's later account of the "two kinds of production", Zhao holds, does not mean that human reproduction determined early society while material production determined later society. Kinship, Zhao says, governed the character of the social system in early society, but material production remained the foundation throughout. Zhao also argues that "forms of intercourse" is a broader concept than relations of production and that "civil society" has both a narrow bourgeois sense and a general sense of economic base. On "tribal ownership", Zhao denies that it equals the later "Asiatic mode of production" and contends that the text already contains a five-stage succession of social formations, which Zhao says was not Stalin's invention. Zhao adds that this succession applies to world history as a whole, not to every nation in turn. Zhao concludes that the work is rich but difficult, since it still carries old terminology and immature ideas, such as treating the family as prior to the tribe. Zhao says scholars, the author included, have not yet clarified relations among concepts such as forms of intercourse, relations of production, civil society and economic base. The article offers its nine-part survey as a modest contribution to that work. Read the original if you want a detailed, Chinese-language account of how a leading Chinese Marxist philosopher reads The German Ideology and where Zhao takes issue with other Chinese scholars.

Relying on study to move towards the future: new practice in the collective study sessions of the Political Bureau since the 18th Party Congress 依靠学习走向未来—— 党的十八大以来中央政治局集体学习的新实践 Qiu Shi Published in Qiushi in April 2016, this commentary reviews the collective study sessions of the Political Bureau of the Central Committee since the 18th Party Congress (2012). It argues that, under Xi Jinping's leadership, these sessions have continued the Party's tradition of valuing study and have set an example for improving the Party's capacity to govern. Its central claim is that the Party, having reached the present through study, must also rely on study to reach the future. The piece is organised in four parts. The first presents the sessions as a way of mastering the Party's core intellectual tools. The second treats study as a means of overcoming what Xi calls "skill panic". The third describes the methods of viewing the situation from a high vantage point, and the fourth presents study as a means of unifying thought and driving implementation. It draws on examples from specific sessions, including the first, the third, the fifteenth, the twenty-seventh and the thirtieth. In the author's account, the sessions begin with the basic principles of Marxism: scientific socialism, historical and dialectical materialism, and political economy. These principles are said to underpin judgements on deepening reform, relying on the people and managing the economy. The author says study also meets the Party's "skill panic", summed up by Xi as new methods not known, old methods not working, hard methods not dared and soft methods not effective. Study is said to help leaders grasp the "way" (the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics), fill gaps in knowledge and improve decision-making. The article adds that the sessions link domestic and international affairs, connect history, present and future, and use the dialectic of priorities and the whole to identify strategic focal points for the 13th Five-Year Plan period. It cites sessions that turned Party Plenum decisions into guidance, such as on the market and government roles and on supply-side structural reform. The author also says the sessions favour practical action over empty talk, in the spirit of the "Three Stricts and Three Earnests". The author concludes that all Party members should follow the Political Bureau's example and carry out the "Two Studies, One Action" campaign of study and education. The aim is to become qualified members who are politically committed, disciplined, moral and dedicated, and to contribute to upholding and developing socialism with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want to see how a 2016 Party journal presented the Political Bureau's study sessions as a model of leadership learning and policy implementation.

Accurately grasping the new situation in the contest for ideological discourse power on the internet 准确把握互联网意识形态话语权争夺的新形势 Li Jiangjing Xu Hongye Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts (2015, no. 22), Li Jiangjing and Xu Hongye ask how Marxism can keep its guiding position in China's ideological sphere as the contest for ideological discourse power online takes new forms. They argue that this contest has shifted with advances in information technology. Winning it requires attention to the key links in how online discourse power is produced, to three new trends, and to specific points of leverage. The article has three parts. The first identifies three critical nodes in the production of internet ideological discourse power: the subject's right of dissemination, the right to set topics, and the right to use discourse carriers. The second describes three new features of the contest. The third sets out where effort should be directed: theoretical innovation, control of capital and technology, and three concrete paths. The authors treat dissemination as the precondition, because equal rights of expression online mean little for individuals who lack network resources, so large media still hold the advantage. Topic-setting is the pivot, illustrated by the 2015 debate on Western values in universities and the Qing'an police shooting incident, both said to have been framed to steer opinion against the government. Control of carriers is the foundation. Citing the 2013 'Prism' revelations, ICANN's link to the US Commerce Department, root-server control and the market dominance of firms such as Microsoft and Intel, the authors claim that the US exerts technological hegemony and infiltrates Chinese opinion. The new trends they identify are a move from holding platforms to seizing topics, from spontaneous ('in-itself') to conscious ('for-itself') non-mainstream ideologies that attack heroes and revolutionary history, and from complete narratives to fragmented dissemination, such as altered headlines and 'big V' reposting. The authors conclude that the basic task is to spread innovative theory that combines Marxism with Chinese realities, and to answer the problems China faces. They also call for control over capital, to counter discourse monopoly by internet firms, and for developing China's own core technology. Their three paths are to renew the forms of expression while keeping Marxism's core discourse, to take the initiative in agenda-setting through mainstream media and cultivated opinion leaders, and to innovate in communication. The last path combines united-front work with struggle, and debate with hostile forces. Read the original if you want an example of how Chinese ideological-work scholarship framed online opinion contests and cyber-sovereignty in 2015.

Holding fast to the Communist Party of China's Marxist conception 坚守中国共产党的马克思主义理念 Mei Rongzheng Writing in 2016, Mei Rongzheng argues that China's ideological sphere is marked by fierce disputes in which historical nihilism, neoliberalism, democratic socialism, "universal values" and Western constitutional democracy are aimed at the Party's guiding ideology. In Mei's account, these currents try to negate individual Marxist principles and also to wreck Marxism as a whole. The article's answer is that their methods can be identified and that the Party must hold firmly to its own Marxist conception. The piece has two parts. The first lists ten techniques used against Marxism, including altering propositions, distorting original meaning, dismembering the system, over-extending concepts, attacking the essence, coining false terms and subverting institutions. Mei analyses six of them with examples. The second part sets out three ways of responding to what the author calls noise and discordant voices. Mei's examples are meant to show deliberate manipulation. Changing "ultimate" to "sole" in the claim that productive forces determine social development, Mei says, turns historical materialism into a crude productive-forces thesis and undermines the Party's basic line. Reading the Communist Manifesto as abolishing all personal property, Mei argues, ignores that it targets private ownership of the means of production. The author also contends that Marxism is split vertically, by setting the periods before and after reform and opening up against each other, and horizontally, into "ecological", "organic" or "feminist" Marxisms. Treating every critic of capitalism as a Marxist, Mei holds, removes its proletarian standpoint. Attacks on class struggle and the dictatorship of the proletariat are described as attacks on the Constitution and on the Marxist theory of law, which Mei says always serves a ruling group; the author cites US law on advocating the overthrow of government as comparison. Mei proposes three responses. First, uphold Marxism-Leninism, Mao Zedong Thought and the theoretical system of socialism with Chinese characteristics, "and not some other ism". Second, study Xi Jinping's speeches as a weapon against Western ideological infiltration. Third, build a Chinese-style discourse system for sinified Marxism while criticising erroneous currents, following Xi's calls in 2013 and 2016. Read the original if you want to see how a Party-aligned Marxist theorist in 2016 classified and rebutted challenges to official Marxism, including attacks on foreign "Marxisms".

Ideological work bears on the future and destiny of the Party and the state 意识形态工作关乎党和国家前途命运 Lu Yan Writing in 2016, Lu Yan presents a commentary that reads Xi Jinping's speeches since the 18th Party Congress (2012) as a systematic strategy for ideological work. The central claim is that ideological work is "extremely important" and bears on the Party's and the state's future. Xi's remarks, the author says, set out the direction, principles and rules for handling ideology under new conditions. The piece follows Xi's statements under five headings: giving ideological work extreme priority; maintaining ideological resolve; keeping the people at the centre; strengthening identification with socialist ideology; and strengthening the sense of responsibility for ideological work. It draws mainly on Xi's addresses to national propaganda and ideology conferences, the February 2016 symposium on Party media work, remarks during his European visit and talks with Peking University students. The author paraphrases and endorses these remarks, adding little independent analysis. Lu argues first that economic construction remains the central task but cannot excuse neglect of ideology. The two must support each other, and the author holds that a regime's collapse often begins in the realm of ideas, so that leadership, management and discourse power over ideological work must never slip from the Party's hands. Second, ideological resolve is said to rest on faith in Marxism, confidence in the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics, cultural confidence, and a selective openness to foreign culture that avoids wholesale copying of Western methods. Third, the author insists that Party spirit and the people's character are unified: upholding one is upholding the other, and separating them is wrong in theory and harmful in practice. On building identification, Lu proposes shared development outcomes, ideals-and-convictions education for Party members and wider society, and fostering the core socialist values. The final section calls for Party committees to bear primary responsibility, with secretaries as first persons responsible, and for a "big propaganda" approach involving the whole Party. This approach stresses positive messaging while not abandoning "struggle" in public opinion on matters of principle. Read the original if you want a compact digest of how Party commentators in 2016 summarised Xi Jinping's ideological-work doctrine and its institutional requirements.

The four characteristics of the theoretical form of socialism with Chinese characteristics 中国特色社会主义理论形态的四大特征 Xin Xiangyang Writing in 2016, Xin Xiangyang asks what kind of theoretical system the theory of socialism with Chinese characteristics is. Xin distinguishes academic systems built on concepts, judgements and inference (Locke, Kant, Hegel, Heidegger and others) from "practical" systems. These appear as resolutions, talks, notes and letters that look independent but are internally linked and answer a connected set of basic questions. Xin places the Chinese theoretical system in the second type and gives it four features: direct engagement with reality, collective wisdom, practical logic and diverse vehicles. The article takes each feature in turn and traces it through the main components of the system: Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents, the Scientific Outlook on Development and the speeches of Xi Jinping. Xin draws on Party congress reports, plenum decisions and leaders' speeches. The examples include the basic economic system of the primary stage of socialism, ideas of development, the socialist core values and the five development concepts for the 13th Five-Year Plan period. Xin argues that each body of theory arose from a concrete problem. Deng's theory answered what socialism is and how to build it after the Cultural Revolution. The Three Represents added how to build the Party, in the wake of the upheavals in Eastern Europe and the Soviet Union. The Scientific Outlook responded to questions of development, and Xi's speeches address problems such as the economic slowdown, social mobility and judicial fairness. Xin cites successive Party congress reports to show that each theory is described as the product of collective wisdom, and that every generation of leaders has answered the same basic question afresh. The practical logic is shown by the step-by-step growth of ideas such as the basic economic system, from the 1984 decision on economic reform through the 13th and 15th Party Congresses to Xi's formulation of the Two Unwaverings. Finally, Xin contends that after a proletarian party takes power, theoretical innovation appears less in large treatises than in congress reports, plenum decisions and leaders' speeches. Xin concludes that these features make the system a living, practice-based body of theory that develops with practice. Xin treats the documents and speeches as the system's core theoretical achievements, including Deng's 1992 southern tour talks, Xi's eight criteria for judging a democratic political system and the Chinese Dream. Read the original if you want a Party-theorist's account of why Chinese leaders' speeches and Party documents are treated as theory, with a detailed chronology of the sources.

Reflections on strengthening Party discipline under the new circumstances 新形势下加强党的纪律建设的思考 Yuan Xiuli Writing in 2016, Yuan Xiuli asks why Party discipline has been placed in a more prominent position since the 18th Party Congress (2012), and how discipline-building can be made standardised, institutionalised and routine. The article argues that strict discipline is a historical and practical necessity for a Marxist ruling party. It presents Xi Jinping's stress on observing discipline and respecting rules as an inheritance of the Party's traditions and a guarantee for the "Four-Pronged Comprehensive Strategy". The article has three parts. The first gives four reasons why discipline must be strengthened: the nature of a Marxist party, the Party's own tradition, the demands of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, and the requirements of governing the country according to law. The second sets out new formulations since 2012. The third turns to implementation, including the revised Code of Integrity and Self-Discipline and the Regulations on Disciplinary Actions issued in 2015. In the first part, Yuan draws on Marx, Engels, Lenin and Deng Xiaoping, and on a line of Party leaders after Deng, to present discipline as a condition of unity and effectiveness. Yuan also describes challenges at home and abroad to the Party's legitimacy and leadership, and calls the question of whether the Party or the law is greater a "political trap" and a false proposition. The second part holds that Party rules are stricter than state law and that discipline comes before law, since law-breaking by members begins with breaking discipline. It stresses political discipline and political rules (the "five musts"), equality of all members before discipline, tightening the "cage" of institutions, and combining rule-based governance of the Party with moral self-cultivation. Yuan concludes that obeying Party discipline is unconditional and that intra-Party regulations must not become "paper tigers". The article calls for a fuller regulatory system, stronger enforcement, and continued reform of discipline-inspection bodies, including nomination procedures for discipline officials and the inspection system. It also calls for discipline to become a "live high-voltage wire", with problems caught early and handled firmly. Read the original if you want an official-line account of how the Party justified its discipline campaign in 2015–16, including the ordering of discipline, rules and law.

World socialism is now entering a period of seeking revival 当前世界社会主义正进入谋求振兴期 Jiang Hui Writing in 2016, Jiang Hui asks where world socialism stands some twenty-five years after the collapse of the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe. The article argues that, amid a new crisis of capitalism, world socialism has emerged from its trough and entered a period of seeking revival. Jiang holds that this development refutes claims of capitalism's final triumph and the "end of history", while cautioning that the movement as a whole will remain at a low ebb for a long time. The article first traces how communist parties survived the post-1991 shock through crisis, regrouping and renewal. It then gives figures: parties in over 100 countries, about 100.3 million members in total, of which the Communist Party of China accounts for over 88 million. Jiang sorts these parties into four types: ruling parties in existing socialist countries; parties in developed capitalist countries such as Japan, France, Italy and Greece; parties in the former Soviet and East European region; and parties in developing countries such as India, South Africa and Nepal. Other left currents, including Venezuela's "socialism of the twenty-first century", market socialism and eco-socialism, are noted briefly. Jiang lists six favourable conditions: the weakening of neoliberal and right-wing dominance, the vindication of socialist critiques of capitalism (seen in the "Marx fever"), the recovery of left forces, closer left cooperation, more objective lessons drawn from the Soviet collapse, and the achievements of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Four challenges are set against them. Capitalism remains stronger than socialism, communist parties are marginalised in crisis-hit Western states, their leadership of social movements is weak, and the global working class remains "in itself" without a global class consciousness. From these Jiang draws a key distinction: Marxist principles on crisis and revolution still apply, but crisis does not automatically bring revolutionary upsurge, and expecting a single decisive blow is called "infantile". Jiang concludes that capitalism, now at the stage of international monopoly capitalism, retains strong self-regulating and innovative capacity. Socialism should therefore prepare for long-term cooperation and struggle between the two systems. The author describes socialism with Chinese characteristics as the brightest spot and mainstay of world socialism. China is urged to concentrate on its own development, balancing "keeping a low profile" with "getting things done", because world socialism's revival depends on that success. Read the original if you want a 2016 official-academic assessment of the global communist movement, with membership figures and a typology of parties.

Lenin's October Revolution as a "great revolution" On the controversy sparked by quoting Putin's remarks out of context 列宁领导的十月革命是“伟大的革命” Wu Enyuan In January 2016 reports circulated online that Vladimir Putin had negatively assessed Lenin, saying Lenin's ideas had led to the Soviet collapse like a nuclear bomb placed under the building of Russia. Wu Enyuan argues that these reports quoted Putin selectively and distorted what he said. In Wu's account, Putin criticised specific Leninist ideas, not Lenin's thought as a whole. The commentary, published in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2016, first reconstructs Putin's remarks of 21 and 25 January. It then turns to three questions: how Putin assesses the Soviet system, how he treats Soviet history and historical figures in earlier statements, and what causes of the Soviet collapse are being debated. Wu reports that Putin explained the "mine" as the dispute between Lenin and Stalin over the structure of the new state. Lenin favoured equal republics with a right of secession, which Putin considered mistaken, but Putin also praised planned economy, health care, education and industrialisation as achievements of the Communist Party. Wu adds that Putin said he still keeps his Party card, and that he has repeatedly warned against blackening the national past. Wu also cites a 2014 history-textbook commission view that the October Revolution and civil war can be called a "great revolution". Wu notes that the day after Putin spoke, Security Council secretary Nikolai Patrushev gave a front-page interview. In it he blamed Gorbachev's policy errors as the main cause of the collapse. Wu reads this as both a gloss on Putin's remarks and a pointed answer to the scholarly debate over whether historical or immediate factors weighed more. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's defence of Lenin's standing, framed through Putin's 2016 remarks and Russian official statements.

Marx's thought on social communities and its development 马克思社会共同体思想及其发展 Shi Yunxia Writing in 2016, Shi Yunxia asks how the Chinese Communist Party's concept of a community with a shared future for mankind relates to the classical Marxist tradition. The article argues that the concept is a creative application and development of Marx and Engels's thought on social communities (shehui gongtongti), and counts it among the achievements of the theoretical system of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The article has three parts. The first reconstructs five aspects of Marx and Engels's thinking on communities, drawing on The German Ideology, the 1857–58 manuscripts, The Origin of the Family, Private Property and the State, the 1859 Preface and Capital. The second traces the lineage of Chinese ideas on international order from Mao Zedong's "three worlds" thesis through Deng Xiaoping and Jiang Zemin to Hu Jintao's harmonious world. The third turns to Xi Jinping's statements since the 18th Party Congress (2012). In the first part Shi defines a community as a group bound by particular ties, and distinguishes political from non-political forms. Shi treats communities as ultimately communities of interest and as the basic mode of existence of people and society, and separates them from the "social organism" and the "social formation". The essence of any community is the relations of production, in its universal form and in the particular form of each historical stage. Shi stresses that capitalism marks a historic leap but remains a "false community", with equality and freedom masking exploitation. Only an association of free individuals, measured by free time, is a "real community". From this Shi draws a call to respect world diversity and each country's right to choose its own system and path.
