In the third part Shi credits Xi with a systematic account of the new international relations. It rests on shared values, five dimensions (partnership, security, development, civilisational exchange and ecology) and extension to bilateral, regional and cyberspace communities as well as to the Chinese nation at home. Shi presents this as a response to Cold War thinking, zero-sum games and hegemonism. Shi also distinguishes it from the "humane democratic socialism" doctrine that places universal human values above all. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist scholar links the classics' idea of community to the official concept of a community with a shared future for mankind, and to the line of Party leaders' foreign-policy thought.

On the think-tank function of ideological and political education 论思想政治教育的智库功能 Li Liaoning Writing in 2015, Li Liaoning asks how ideological and political education (sixiang zhengzhi jiaoyu) should understand and exercise a think-tank function. The starting point is the call of the Third Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2013) to build new types of think tanks with Chinese characteristics, followed by the January 2015 General Office opinions on the subject, which include universities. Li argues that this function is not part of the field's traditional educational role but an extension of it, and that the field should consciously act as an adviser to the ruling party. The article has three parts. The first places the think-tank function within existing research, which has dealt mainly with social and individual functions, and compares ideological and political education with ordinary think tanks. The second sets out the field's advantages and its shortcomings. The third proposes four measures: reforming research evaluation, cultivating talent, building information resources, and expanding outside exchange. Li defines the think-tank function as the role played in strategic research, policy advice, theoretical innovation, guiding public opinion, social service and external communication. Unlike the educational function, which publicises policies already made, it moves earlier, to research on ideological questions before policy is set. Li holds that the field resembles other think tanks in doing non-profit policy research with relative independence, but cannot be 'neutral' because its strongly ideological character requires it to serve the ruling party and reflect the interests of the broad population. The listed advantages are high official attention to ideology, a large body of researchers, and growing state funding. The listed weaknesses are a shortage of outstanding research (the author cites few top prizes for the Marxism discipline), weak 'participation' and 'evaluation' awareness among practitioners who equate being the Party's mouthpiece with not thinking independently, and an evaluation system that does not count policy reports. Li's proposals include crediting policy reports, blue books and advisory memoranda in evaluation and promotion, and organising talent in four circles from outstanding to peripheral. They also include a 'revolving door' between universities, government and enterprises, big-data resource building, and closer ties with government, other think tanks and the media. Li says influence on government decisions is what finally decides whether the function works. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese scholar in 2015 justified and organised an advisory role for ideological and political education within the new think-tank policy.

Correctly grasping the characteristics of our era and upholding and developing the socialist cause 正确把握时代特征与坚持和发展社会主义事业 Liang Zhu Writing in 2016, the author asks how Marxists should define the present era and why this matters for upholding socialism. The article's thesis is that the era is the long epoch, opened by the October Revolution, in which socialism gradually replaces capitalism. Within it, the author says, there are shorter stages, and both levels must be held together. Losing sight of either one, the article warns, leads to dogmatism or to disorientation. The article has three parts. The first draws on Marx, Engels, Lenin, Sartre and Deng Xiaoping to define an "era" by its mode of production and class relations, and to answer claims that Marxism is outdated and socialism has failed after the collapse of the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe. The second discusses the stages of the era, from Mao Zedong's "war and revolution" to Deng's "peace and development", and Mao's views on war and peace. The third turns to Deng's warning of "two cold wars" and sets out four practical tasks for China. The author argues that the end of the Cold War did not end the confrontation between two social systems, and that imperialism's contradiction with socialism and with oppressed peoples remains the basic contradiction of the age. Citing Brzezinski's later writings, the author claims that Western triumphalism has faded. Treating "peace and development" as the name of the whole era is, in this reading, a mistake that contradicts Deng and plays down imperialism and hegemony. Following Lenin on the "bloodless front", the author describes "peaceful evolution" and "colour revolutions" as Western tools against socialist states and the Third World, and counts the 1989 protests and the 2014 "Occupy Central" movement as cases or near-cases. From this, the author proposes four tasks. China should keep its theoretical resolve in foreign policy and not abandon Marxist class analysis. It must avoid "subversive mistakes" in reform and opening up, notably departing from public ownership's leading role and common prosperity. It must resist neoliberalism, historical nihilism, democratic socialism, constitutional democracy, universal values and similar currents. It must also tackle the loss of ideals and convictions among Party members, in line with the Party's strict self-governance and Xi Jinping's 2013 warning. Read the original if you want an example of how a Party-theory journal in 2016 linked Marxist era theory to ideological security and "colour revolution" concerns.

The historical origins of Marxist atheism 马克思主义无神论的历史渊源 Han Qi Han Qi asks what the long history of Western atheism can teach present-day research and propaganda on Marxist atheism. The article starts from the claim that atheism is the starting point and cornerstone of Marxism, and that Marxist atheism is the highest form of atheist thought. Han argues that tracing its origins clarifies key points and helps China respond to the revival of religion, cults, pseudo-religion and religious extremism since reform and opening up. The first part surveys Western atheism in five stages: the classical period, the Middle Ages, the Renaissance (16th–17th centuries), the Enlightenment, and the modern era (19th–20th centuries). It draws mainly on James Thrower's Western Atheism: A Short History and on a Chinese history of Western atheism. Thinkers discussed include Democritus, Epicurus, Lucretius, Hobbes, Spinoza, Diderot, d'Holbach, Hume, Kant, Feuerbach, Nietzsche, Darwin, Freud, Russell and Sartre. The second part draws seven lessons, and a short conclusion turns to China. Han's core argument is that atheism was not one person's invention but the accumulated work of many thinkers. In this reading, by Marx's time the question of whether gods exist had largely been settled, and Marx inherited the verdict and applied it more thoroughly to society and history. Han stresses that atheism changes with the needs of each era, so research today should fit current conditions rather than copy the past. Han also holds that atheism should be studied within the wider field of non-belief, alongside pantheism, deism and agnosticism, which the article calls close relatives, and that scepticism has always accompanied it. Citing Michael Martin, Han suggests that many Chinese who regard themselves as agnostics may in fact be atheists without knowing it. Han concludes that the naturalist tradition, the spirit of reason and science, and the era-specific character of atheism are key elements to grasp. In the article's view, developing atheist research and propaganda can answer today's 'religious fever' and curb pseudo-religion, cults and religious extremism. Han also points to the 'New Atheism' of Richard Dawkins and others, which has reached Chinese audiences, as a reason to keep following global developments. Read the original if you want to see how a CASS scholar uses a survey of Western atheism to justify the contemporary agenda of Marxist atheism in China.

The scientific atheism of Anti-Dühring 《反杜林论》的科学无神论思想 Han Qi Han Qi asks what Engels's Anti-Dühring, rarely read as a work on atheism, can contribute to scientific atheism today. The article argues that because the book rests on dialectical and historical materialism, it embodies a consistent atheism, and that its dialectics gives ordinary people an objective, rational stance toward the religious phenomena active in China since reform and opening up. The article limits itself to the Philosophy section of Anti-Dühring, the first of Marxism's three component parts. After summarising the work's origins (written 1876–78 against Eugen Dühring's influence in German social democracy), it follows Engels's three-part critique of Dühring: his schema of the world, his philosophy of nature, and his doctrine of man. Han frames this with the present-day rise of religion, cults, pseudo-religious 'masters' and religious extremism. Han's central move is to show that Dühring's errors are idealist and metaphysical, leaving room for a creator or 'first push'. Engels answers that the world's unity lies in its materiality, that motion is the mode of existence of matter, and that life is a mode of existence of protein bodies. The second move concerns truth and morality. Han reports Engels's view that human thought is sovereign only across endless generations, that no field of knowledge yields eternal truths, and that morality is always class morality tied to economic relations. Freedom, on this reading, is the recognition of necessity. Han concludes that these positions exclude the idea of God or a creator and equip readers to see through cults and religious extremism. The author applies them to the claim that China's moral decline stems from a lack of religion, which Han rejects as contrary to history and to dialectics, since religious morality is no final truth or cure-all. Han calls for scientific atheism to use materialist dialectics in research and propaganda, tied to current religious phenomena and to close reading of the classics. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist atheism scholar reads Engels's Anti-Dühring in light of contemporary religious policy debates.

Discursive power and organizational power in the contemporary world socialist movement A rereading of the Communist Manifesto 当代世界社会主义运动中的话语权和组织权 Zhang Wenmu Zhang Wenmu rereads the Communist Manifesto to ask how the world socialist movement can rebuild its "discursive power" (huayuquan) and "organizational power" (zuzhiquan) after the setbacks of the late twentieth century. Writing in 2016, Zhang argues that the world has entered an age of financial imperialism, that a new upsurge of socialism is already on the horizon, and that socialists must use organization to win the contest over discourse. The article, an excerpt from a longer piece, first characterises financial imperialism as the most decayed stage of capitalism. It then surveys signs of an approaching socialist upsurge, among them Occupy Wall Street, student protests in Britain, the rhetoric of John McDonnell and Bernie Sanders, and Tony Blair's apology over Iraq. It closes with three proposals: strengthen international proletarian unity, build a broad international united front, and uphold scientific socialism. Zhang holds that since Nixon ended the dollar's gold link and tied it to oil, the dollar has rested on petrodollars and foreign wars rather than national labour. Marx's circuit M–C–M′ has become, in Zhang's formula, M–War–M′. Finance capital, in this account, has no homeland and now exploits industrial capitalists and the whole of humanity, so it is producing its own gravediggers at unprecedented speed. Against Western finance capital's media power, Zhang calls for organizational strength and, following Lenin's What Is to Be Done?, for positive education or "inculcation" (guanshu) rather than entertainment-led propaganda. Zhang also says that the socialist state is the movement's strongest organization. The article defines the main enemy as Wall Street finance capital rather than the American nation or its national capital. It names "democratic socialism" of the Bernstein–Gorbachev type as the most dangerous internal threat, and it defends the dictatorship of the proletariat, citing Deng Xiaoping's 1992 talks. Zhang concludes that drawing on the lessons of socialism's earlier defeats, organizing the working class internationally and holding to Marxism-Leninism are preconditions for the coming upsurge. Zhang warns that China, nearer than ever to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, also faces greater risk of a Soviet-style collapse if it dilutes people's democratic dictatorship and the Four Cardinal Principles. Read the original if you want an example of how a Chinese Marxist scholar reads financial imperialism, ideological struggle and the Soviet collapse in 2016, with its many contemporary references.

Diverse explorations out of the trough: the "five currents" in the revival of world socialism 走出低谷的多样探索——世界社会主义回暖潮流中的“五个潮头” Wang Dong Writing in 2016, Wang Dong asks what has happened to world socialism in the two decades since the collapse of the Soviet Union and the upheavals in Eastern Europe (1991), which he treats as its lowest point. His overall judgement is that, drawing on the general crisis of capitalism in the age of economic globalization, contemporary world socialism has left its deepest trough. In his account it is now exploring varied new paths suited to a new era and to national conditions. The short commentary singles out five currents within this recovery. These are eco-socialism, calls for a socialism of justice in response to polarisation, Latin America's twenty-first-century socialism, appeals for socialist revival in Russia and the CIS countries, and Vietnam's path of renewal. Each section gives a brief portrait, usually built around one representative figure or event. On eco-socialism, Wang reports the view that the ecological crisis is rooted not in science and technology but in the capitalist mode of production and its drive for maximum profit, and cites a 2015 interview with Communist Party USA chairman John Bachtell. On justice, he points to the worldwide debate over Thomas Piketty's Capital in the Twenty-First Century (2014) and to David Harvey's verdict that Piketty's data are valuable but his explanation and remedies are flawed, so that Marx or a modern equivalent is still needed. For Latin America he sets out Rafael Correa's 'modern socialism' (2014) and Evo Morales's 'good socialism', and he presents the Russian philosopher A. Bagaturia and Vietnamese theorists on Ho Chi Minh Thought as evidence that socialist ideas persist and adapt. Wang concludes that these currents show socialism renewing itself in different forms in different places, rather than disappearing after 1991. He also notes Bagaturia's repeated visits to China and his interest in socialism with Chinese characteristics, though the article does not develop this into a wider argument. Read the original if you want a compact 2016 Chinese overview of which foreign socialist trends and figures a Peking University philosopher regarded as signs of recovery.

The "new socialism" movement in Latin America: problems and prospects 拉美“新社会主义”运动：问题与前景 Jin Chengwei Writing in 2016, Jin Chengwei examines the wave of "new socialism" that has emerged in Latin America since the late 1990s and distinguishes it from the "twentieth-century socialism" of the traditional communist parties. The article asks why this current arose, what it advocates and practises, and what challenges and prospects it faces. Jin's thesis is that it is an exploratory, non-Soviet attempt to transcend capitalism and neoliberalism that still has considerable vitality despite mounting difficulties. The piece is a short newspaper commentary in three parts. It first sets out four background conditions, then surveys the doctrines and policies of four representative cases: Venezuela's and Ecuador's "socialism of the twenty-first century", Bolivia's "communitarian socialism" and Brazil's "labour socialism". It closes with the challenges these movements face and eight judgements on their character and outlook. Each case is summarised under political, economic, social and international headings. On origins, Jin points to the shock of the Soviet and East European collapse, which opened intellectual space for left-wing thinkers to look beyond the Soviet model. Jin also cites repeated economic crises since the 1980s, the failure of neoliberalism, and the third wave of democratisation, which gave the left a legitimate political stage. On character, Jin notes that scholars disagree over whether this is socialism at all, and that the answer depends on whether the term is used narrowly or broadly. Jin's own view is that it is not scientific socialism, but it is an exploration of a socialist nature and a new attempt different from the Soviet model. Jin also stresses its inclusiveness, its acceptance of winning power through elections, and its emphasis on regional integration and international cooperation. Jin lists the main challenges: building a coherent theoretical system, reducing dependence on charismatic leaders, strengthening party organisation, resisting corruption, keeping left unity, overcoming economic difficulties, answering popular discontent and countering domestic and foreign opponents. Although the governing parties involved face greater uncertainty, Jin concludes that the movement retains strong vitality and room to develop as an alternative to neoliberalism and capitalism in Latin America's specific conditions. Finding effective responses to these challenges is, in Jin's words, the urgent task. Read the original if you want a compact Chinese-language overview of how a Party School scholar classifies and assesses Latin America's twenty-first-century socialist experiments.

China–Vietnam economic and trade cooperation under new conditions: alignment and development 新形势条件下中越经贸合作：对接与发展 Pan Jin'e Qin Lifang Writing in early 2016, Pan and Qin ask how China and Vietnam can deepen economic and trade cooperation in a changed domestic and international setting. They argue that Xi Jinping's state visit to Vietnam in November 2015 gave this cooperation fresh momentum, and that the two countries' development strategies can be aligned to turn new opportunities into mutual gain while managing the challenges. The article has four parts. It first reviews the visit and the political framework it set, including the proposed China–Vietnam 'community with a shared future'. It then describes the features of bilateral trade, investment and tourism since normalisation in 1991, and sets out the opportunities and challenges created by the Belt and Road Initiative, Vietnam's reform record and its entry into the Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP). A last part considers what China–Vietnam ties mean for China–ASEAN cooperation. The authors present trade as growing fast and as strongly complementary. They cite Chinese customs figures of 36 million dollars in 1991 rising to 83.6 billion in 2014, with Vietnam exporting tropical farm and mineral products and importing machinery and manufactures. They also credit cultural similarity and warming political ties. Problems they list are Vietnam's large deficit, complaints about the quality of Chinese goods and contracting work, and media amplification of these issues. Their central proposal is to link the Belt and Road Initiative, backed by the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank, with Vietnam's 'two corridors and one economic circle' plans to ease Vietnam's infrastructure bottleneck. The authors see TPP as bringing both opportunity and risk for Vietnam, including pressure on state enterprises and financial instability. Pan and Qin make four recommendations: Vietnamese infrastructure planning using Belt and Road mechanisms; industrial and capacity cooperation, with Chinese firms investing in Vietnam to fill supply-chain gaps and reduce the deficit; cross-border economic cooperation zones; and financial cooperation, including a currency swap agreement. They also urge better media guidance. They conclude that stronger bilateral ties would help China–ASEAN free trade area upgrading, the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership and China's neighbourhood diplomacy. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly view of China–Vietnam economic relations around 2015, with trade and investment figures and concrete policy proposals.

Difficulties and reconstruction of China–Vietnam relations: a methodological reflection 中越关系的困境与重构：一个方法论的思考 Pan Jin'e Writing in Party Politics Research in early 2016, Pan Jin'e asks why China–Vietnam relations, which developed rapidly after normalisation in 1991, have fluctuated since about 2006–2007, and how they might be put on a stable footing. The article is framed as a methodological proposal rather than a finished analysis. Pan suggests that relations should be rebuilt on a culturally grounded sense of shared identity, using three schools of international relations theory. The opening section recalls the framework guiding bilateral ties: the 1999 sixteen-character guideline, the 2005 "four goods" spirit and the 2008 comprehensive strategic cooperative partnership, together with Xi Jinping's 2015 visit to Vietnam. Pan stresses that Vietnam matters to China as a fellow Party-led socialist state and as a link in neighbourhood diplomacy and the Belt and Road Initiative. A literature review then sorts existing work into three groups: histories of the tributary relationship and of the modern "comrades plus brothers" era; tracking studies of post-normalisation ties by Chinese and Vietnamese scholars; and studies using general international relations theory, including Brantly Womack on asymmetry, Alexander Wendt's constructivism and Qin Yaqing's relational theory. Pan observes that Chinese research on the recent period is scarce, partly because the topic is treated as sensitive, and that Vietnamese scholars increasingly view China's rise with unease. No joint Chinese–Vietnamese studies exist. In Pan's account, the two countries' relationship has passed through four identities: tributary hierarchy, "comrades plus brothers", hostility in the late 1970s and 1980s, and ordinary state-to-state relations. The post-2007 fluctuations are attributed to changed national statuses that the bilateral framework did not adjust to; imbalance then built up and was triggered by territorial disputes that inflame nationalism. Pan argues that constructivism, which treats identity as the basis of interests, suits this problem. Because Vietnam's line follows Marxism-Leninism and Ho Chi Minh Thought, "comrades plus brothers" is described as a red line that can only be given new content. Pan proposes a new-type relationship combining solidarity based on the socialist system, consensus drawing on positive elements of Confucian culture and the tributary past, and win-win cooperation under modern international norms. The proposed method is a joint team of Chinese and Vietnamese scholars with expertise in history, international relations, Party and government studies and media, using documents, fieldwork, questionnaires and interviews, with results acceptable to both sides and then adopted officially. Read the original if you want a short Chinese scholarly agenda on China–Vietnam relations, with a review of Chinese and Vietnamese literature, rather than a detailed empirical study.

Paths to socialism Part two of "The prospects of socialism: painful reality and historical opportunity" 通向社会主义的途径 Yu. Yu. Yu. Yu. This is a Chinese translation, by Yang Weimin of the Shanghai Academy of Social Sciences, of the second half of an article first published in January 2015 in the Russian journal 21st Century Marxism. The Russian author, a former deputy chairman of the State Duma and an economist, asks how a transition from capitalism to socialism can still be achieved in Russia and elsewhere. The author argues that only revolution can change a socio-economic formation, that peaceful routes are now largely closed in Russia, and that the left must organise mass action, win control of the media and study past revolutionary experience. The text opens with a call to act rather than wait, then moves through five sections. It treats revolution as a way of resolving acute class contradictions, and it reads the Soviet road to socialism through the October Revolution, the civil war and the 1990s. It then asks whether socialist revolution has reached its limit and what opportunities remain. Finally it examines the left's weaknesses, the role of mass media, and the lessons of Bolshevik preparation before 1917. The author holds that revolution means the passage from one social formation to another, and that bloodshed belongs to the methods used, not to its essence. On this reading October 1917 was largely peaceful, and the violence that followed came from foreign intervention and from the resistance of the old classes. Post-Soviet capitalism is called a counter-revolution. Rigged elections and police repression, in the author's account, have made a parliamentary road to socialism in Russia practically impossible. The author also faults communist, socialist and social-democratic parties for opportunism, for failing to lead the anti-capitalist protests in Europe, and for misreading the media as a weapon through which the bourgeoisie shapes public consciousness. The author concludes that the left must unite on the basis of Marxism and represent working people's interests, and that it must break the ruling class's monopoly over the mass media. The left should also study the long Bolshevik preparation, which included decades of propaganda, organisation and tactical reconnaissance of the masses. Today's Russian opposition is said to lack strategic aims, and the author argues that resistance must appear in the squares as well as at the ballot box. Read the original if you want a Russian communist-oriented view of revolution, the Soviet collapse and left strategy, written with strong polemical language and sweeping claims about the United States and the West.

The state of mind of CPSU grass-roots organisations and members before the Soviet collapse 苏联解体前苏共基层党组织与党员思想状况分析 Li Yan Zhang Shuhua Why did the roughly 16.5 million members of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union (CPSU) not publicly rise to defend the Party when it was suspended and the USSR dissolved? Li Yan and Zhang Shuhua take up this question, prompted by a Chinese commentator's remark that no one in the Party proved a "real man". They argue that the members' silence was real but has been misread. In their account it had historical and objective causes, as well as members' dissatisfaction with corrupt officials and a mistaken reform line, and it was not the whole story, since many members protested in other ways. The article draws on memoirs by Roy Medvedev, Valery Boldin and Anatoly Chernyaev, and on archival letters from Russian state archives. It also uses 1989–1991 Party statistics on membership losses and dissolved organisations. It begins with the apparent calm in Moscow in August–November 1991. It then sets out five reasons for the silence, turns to forms of resistance, and ends with lessons for a ruling party. The five reasons are as follows. Democratic centralism had become a formality, so rank-and-file members had no real say in the Party's fate. The ranks were impure, because of the excesses of the purges and the later "excessive stability" and office-selling under Brezhnev. Ideological attacks on Stalin and Soviet history, from Khrushchev's "de-Stalinisation" to Gorbachev's glasnost, left members disoriented. Privilege and corruption alienated members from officials. Finally, Gorbachev's multi-party reforms turned the CPSU into a "parliamentary party", one of hundreds. The authors report Party membership falling from about 19.49 million in early 1989 to 16.52 million in January 1991, and a collapse of workplace organisations. They read the mass resignations, protest letters, public calls for Gorbachev's resignation, the suicides of veterans such as Marshal Akhromeyev, and members who kept paying dues as forms of resistance that were suppressed. The authors conclude that the collapse was not directly the grass roots' responsibility, but that a ruling party rests on active grass-roots organisations and a correct line. They draw five lessons. The ruling party should balance democracy and centralism and follow the mass line. It should govern itself rigorously and keep its cadres pure. It should keep a correct ideological direction and reject historical nihilism. Its cadres should be self-disciplined and free of privilege. Democracy and multi-party supervision should be kept within limits. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly reading of the CPSU's final years, built on archival letters and Party statistics, and its lessons for Party-building.

China must be highly vigilant against and guard against "colour revolutions" 必须高度警惕和防范“颜色革命” Zhou Xiaobing Writing in 2016, Zhou Xiaobing takes up the wave of "colour revolutions" that have toppled governments in a series of countries. Zhou argues that these are not spontaneous popular movements but regime-change operations directed by the United States, and that China must be highly vigilant against them. The piece appeared in the Party journal Red Flag Manuscripts. The article has three parts. The first sets out what Zhou presents as the regularities of colour revolutions, defined as coups carried out through non-violent "street politics". The second argues that every case is manipulated by, and serves the interests of, the United States, drawing on examples from Eastern Europe, the former Soviet Union and North Africa. The third turns to prevention in China and lists basic measures. Zhou distinguishes two types: those that turn socialist states into capitalist ones, which Zhou equates with "peaceful evolution", and those that install pro-US governments in capitalist states. Both, Zhou says, follow four steps: shaping opinion against the government, building opposition organisations through NGOs and then parties, choosing a charismatic pro-American leader, and using an incident or election to launch street protests under the banner of democracy. Zhou argues that Washington prefers this route to war because it is cheaper and wins wider acceptance, and cites funding figures and training workshops for opposition cadres in several countries. Democracy, in this reading, is only a pretext. For China, Zhou calls for strengthening the instruments of dictatorship, in the form of the people's democratic dictatorship, against a small number of liberal agitators. Zhou also calls for four preventive measures: strengthening Marxist guidance in ideology, keeping leadership at every level in the hands of Marxists, consolidating the Party's mass base, and upholding the dominant position of public ownership. Zhou also urges strict control of Western-funded NGOs and education in a Marxist view of democracy. Read the original if you want to see how a Party-journal author of 2016 framed colour revolutions as a US-led strategy and what domestic countermeasures were proposed.

The current development and role of the middle class around the world 当前中产阶级在世界各国的发展状况及作用 Li Changjiu Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts (2016, no. 3), Li Changjiu asks how the middle class is faring worldwide and what role it plays. The author notes that there is still no agreed definition, but says countries share a consensus: the middle class is a main force in scientific and technological innovation and a backbone and "stabiliser" of economic and social development. Li's thesis is that the middle class is shrinking in Western countries but growing in developing ones, where the main challenge is the "middle-income trap". The article has two parts. The first surveys the United States, Germany, France, Britain and Japan, drawing on official statistics, polls and Western commentators such as George Friedman and Joseph Stiglitz. The second turns to developing countries and emerging economies, citing projections from the World Bank, the UN Development Programme and the African Development Bank, and then examines South Korea as a case of escaping the trap. For the West, Li cites figures that the US middle-class share of national income fell from 53.2% in 1968 to 45.7% in 2012. German middle-class population share fell from 66.5% to 61.5% between 2000 and 2009, and French middle-class households are described as squeezed by compulsory spending. Li reports that Stiglitz blames the polarisation on institutional factors, namely the combination of market speculation and political manoeuvring, and that Friedman sees the decline as a threat to US power. For the developing world, the article cites World Bank data that Asia's middle class tripled between 1990 and 2005, and projections of strong growth in Asia-Pacific and Africa. It then reports a 2012 World Bank and State Council Development Research Centre study finding that, of 101 middle-income economies in the 1960s and 1970s, only a dozen or so had reached high income by 2008. Li concludes, following the economists cited, that the middle-income trap is essentially a problem of economic development, avoidable through sustained, high-quality growth and rising incomes. South Korea is presented as the model: heavy investment in education and R&D, and thirty years of five-year plans that, in the article's figures, raised per capita GNP from 87 to 6,316 US dollars between 1962 and 1991. The lesson Li draws is that correct government policy combined with popular innovation and effort can avoid the trap. Read the original if you want a compact, data-led Chinese state-media overview of middle-class trends abroad and of how the middle-income trap was framed in 2016.

What new changes have taken place in contemporary capitalism 当代资本主义发生哪些新变化 Tang Zhengdong Writing in a newspaper commentary in 2015, Tang Zhengdong asks how contemporary capitalism's new features should be understood and how Western scholars' accounts of them should be read. Tang argues that the changes are real but cannot be grasped by empirical description. They must be read through historical materialism, which shows that capitalism's social form remains capitalist beneath altered material and technical forms. The piece moves from the limits of single-factor explanations (labour, production technology, finance, consumption, globalization) to the question of which concepts should name the new stage. It compares "state monopoly capitalism" and "international monopoly capitalism" with "post-industrial society", "post-Fordism" and similar labels. It then sketches a research programme and ends with a statement on the Four-sphere Confidence. Tang first holds that each partial explanation sees only one element and so concludes that Western capitalism is in good shape. In their view, post-Fordist flexible production also brought lower social welfare and sharper class conflict. Facts are themselves constructed by social power, and even political or historical analyses that expose this stay empirical unless they explain the historical basis of the power struggle. Tang says Western left scholars have largely given up historical materialist method. Second, Tang says Marx used "capitalism" in terms of both a technical and a social paradigm of production, the social one being more important and tied to the contradictions of social relations. Concepts such as "post-Fordism", which stress technique, cannot capture this, and stretching them to describe the whole post-1970s era leads into neoliberal ideology. Western scholarship therefore shows two features. One is empiricism. The other is utopianism: supporters exaggerate the merits of the free market, while critics either build idealised pictures of freedom or abstract one element from social relations to imagine emancipation. Tang calls for study to start from the labour process and relations of production. Tang concedes that notions such as "immaterial labour" are fashionable but holds that the social form of both remains capitalist. Analysis should then extend to consumption, ideology, globalization and spatialization, where Western scholars have produced work that is "interesting" but not necessarily "profound". Tang proposes dissecting this work's limits to deepen understanding of capitalism's inner contradictions. Tang concludes that such critical reading should strengthen confidence in the path, theory and system of socialism with Chinese characteristics, given China's achievements. Read the original if you want a short example of how a Chinese philosopher frames Western theories of contemporary capitalism as empiricist and utopian.

Warnings from the Soviet collapse for building a Marxist ruling party 苏联解体对马克思主义执政党建设的警示 Xue Yan More than twenty years after the Soviet collapse, Xue Yan asks what it teaches about building a Marxist ruling party. Writing in 2016 in a commentary for Red Flag Manuscripts, the author acknowledges that the collapse had many causes, including nationality problems, loss of belief, reform and the federal state form. Xue nonetheless argues that the problems and defects of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union (CPSU) in its work as a ruling party were what finally brought the Union down. The article is organised around six lessons, each followed by a short comparison with the Communist Party of China (CPC). They cover guiding ideology, the regular replacement of leaders, clean government and privileged strata, the capacity to face and correct mistakes, control over reform, and the handling of international relations, especially Western "peaceful evolution". Evidence comes from CPSU party statutes, the careers of Soviet leaders from Khrushchev to Gorbachev, and statements by Nikolai Ryzhkov, Boris Kuzmin-style insiders and others, along with Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping. Xue's central claim is that the CPSU drifted away from Marxism-Leninism until, under Gorbachev, it recast itself as a party of "all-human values" and "humane, democratic socialism". In Xue's account, the lack of a lawful system for replacing leaders let unqualified figures reach the top, and a privileged stratum enriched itself and lost popular support. The author adds that weak self-correction, the wholesale denunciation of Stalin and reform driven by personal preference or the wrong direction left the party unable to steer. The author also holds that the West used ideological infiltration and cultivated agents to bring about peaceful evolution, citing Margaret Thatcher's remark that the West promoted Gorbachev. Xue concludes that socialist countries must reform in ways that keep the country from "changing colour", and that communist parties must be built so as to keep their vanguard character. For the CPC, this means upholding Marxism as guiding thought, selecting reliable successors, maintaining clean government, admitting and correcting errors, keeping reform on course and guarding against peaceful evolution. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Chinese Party commentary in 2016 drew lessons from the Soviet collapse for Party building.

Upholding the Four Cardinal Principles and opposing bourgeois liberalization as the Party's most fundamental political discipline 坚持四项基本原则、反对资产阶级自由化是党的一项最根本的政治纪律 Tian Gaiwei Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in early 2016, Tian Gaiwei comments on Article 45 of the revised Disciplinary Regulations of the Communist Party of China, in force from 1 January 2016. That article prescribes expulsion from the Party for publicly voicing bourgeois-liberal positions, opposing the Four Cardinal Principles or opposing the Party's reform and opening-up decisions. Tian argues that upholding the Four Cardinal Principles and opposing bourgeois liberalization form the Party's most fundamental political discipline and its greatest political rule. The piece has two parts. The first traces how the discipline arose and was codified: Deng Xiaoping's 1979 speech, the 1987 Central Committee notice, the 1992 insertion into the Party Constitution, the 2003 regulations, and the 2016 revision. The second sets out how the Party has defined bourgeois liberalization, citing Hu Qiaomu in 1981, Deng in 1986 and the 1987 notice, and why the struggle is long-term. Throughout, Tian leans on statements by Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping. Tian defines bourgeois liberalization as a current of thought directly opposed to the Four Cardinal Principles, whose core is denying the Party's leadership and the socialist system. Its forms change, the author says, but its opposition to those principles does not, and this serves as the test for identifying it. In Tian's account, it has recently appeared as promotion of Western "universal values" and "constitutionalism", multiparty and separation-of-powers systems, and slander of the Party by some members, including online influencers. The 2016 regulations therefore extend penalties to those who supply channels and platforms for such views. Tian cites Deng's view that the struggle would last decades, and argues that the influence of liberalization can be removed at root only when socialist modernization has clearly shown its advantages over capitalism. Tian concludes that, as the Party nears the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, it needs iron discipline, and that bourgeois liberalization is the gravest erosion of it. Quoting Xi Jinping that strict discipline begins with political discipline, Tian calls on members to bind themselves by Article 45 and to struggle openly against violations. Read the original if you want to see how a 2016 Party-journal commentary links the new disciplinary regulations to Deng-era formulations on liberalization.

The European refugee crisis and the predicament of "universal values" 欧洲难民危机与“普世价值”的困境 Zhang Weiwei Writing in early 2016, Zhang Weiwei takes up the refugee flows into Europe since 2015 and argues that they are directly linked to the "universal values" the West promoted in the Middle East. In Zhang's account, the crisis exposes paradoxes and dilemmas in the idea of "universal values" itself. Zhang suggests that reflecting on this matters for China's development and the world's future. The commentary has three sections. The first describes what Zhang calls the arrogance of the "universal values" camp and its cost. The second sets out four paradoxes revealed by the crisis. The third draws lessons for China and for global governance. Zhang's evidence is the two waves of Middle Eastern "democratization", the Iraq War and the "Greater Middle East" plan from 2003, then the "Arab Spring" from around 2011. Zhang also points to the Syrian, Libyan, Egyptian, Tunisian and Yemeni outcomes and to European disputes over refugee quotas. Zhang traces the West's missionary zeal to a view of history in which the Western model is the final stage, together with a Christian missionary tradition. Zhang says Western powers never asked ordinary people in the region what they wanted. On this account, the result was state collapse, extremism and refugees. The four paradoxes are as follows. First, these values were detached from local national conditions and could not solve sectarian, ethnic, demographic or economic problems. Second, Western electoral politics, in which politicians answer only to their own voters, runs against the principle of universal human rights, as in the fences, quota disputes and Angela Merkel's falling support. Third, the values cannot accommodate multiculturalism, as rising xenophobia and the right show. Fourth, abstract values give way to concrete national interests, including those of Britain, France and the United States. Zhang concludes that Chinese readers should always ask "why" of values that claim to be universal, to avoid being misled by Western discourse. Zhang says the crisis underlines the significance of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Zhang predicts the decline of Western discursive hegemony and calls on China to offer its own ideas, such as "peace and development", as a basis for global governance. Read the original if you want an example of how a 2016 Qiushi article used the refugee crisis to criticise "universal values" and promote a Chinese alternative discourse.

Guiding online public opinion within ideological work in universities 试论高校意识形态工作视域下的网络舆情引导 Zheng Jie Chen Yizhang Writing in 2016, Zheng Jie and Chen Yizhang ask how Chinese universities should guide online public opinion as part of their ideological work. They argue that universities are an important front in ideological struggle and that, with the spread of mobile internet, students have become major producers, spreaders and recipients of online opinion, and are in the authors' view especially easy to mislead. Guiding that opinion is therefore a necessary part of strengthening ideological work on campus. The article opens with survey figures from the China Internet Network Information Center on student internet use, and cites the January 2015 central guideline on strengthening propaganda and ideological work in universities. It then describes how universities currently handle online opinion, lists five shortcomings, and sets out a five-part countermeasure system. The authors rely on policy documents, survey statistics and a few Chinese studies of campus opinion management rather than on case studies. On current practice, the authors report that most universities run student-staffed monitoring teams under teacher supervision, sort opinion into ordinary, social and campus categories, and keep basic emergency-response procedures. They identify five problems: opinion education is one-sided and consists of demands without explanation; information management is passive because platforms such as Baidu Tieba are run by companies or student moderators who may decline to cooperate; monitoring depends on manual labour and covers only a sliver of online content; guidance is crude, relying on warnings and deleted posts that may provoke resistance; and universities react after outbreaks rather than shaping the environment beforehand. In response they propose a 'five-in-one' prevention and control mechanism with five layers. These are ideological education that builds students' own 'immunity'; early warning based on big data and mathematical models; better search technology, combining web crawlers and keyword filtering with manual collection on private platforms; more varied guidance through student-style online comments, student opinion leaders and authoritative releases; and a stronger organisational structure with full- and part-time staff led by the propaganda department or network management centre. The authors conclude that universities must adopt these measures to protect students from harmful information and keep ideological work secure. Read the original if you want a concise 2016 account of how Chinese universities describe and plan to manage campus internet opinion.

Accurately grasping the new situation in the contest for ideological discourse power on the internet 准确把握互联网意识形态话语权争夺的新形势 Li Jiangjing Xu Hongye Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2015, Li Jiangjing and Xu Hongye ask how Marxism can keep its guiding position in China's ideological sphere as information technology changes the contest for discourse power online. They argue that this contest has taken on new features and that Party and state must understand them in order to respond. Their answer is that mainstream ideology has to win in three areas: who can spread a message, who sets the agenda, and who controls the carriers of discourse. The article has three parts. It first identifies three key nodes in the formation of internet ideological discourse power: the right of discourse subjects to disseminate, the right to set topics, and the right to use discourse carriers. It then describes three new features of the contest. It ends with proposals centred on theoretical innovation, control of capital and technology, and three practical paths. Examples include the 2015 debate over Western values in universities, the 2013 "Prism" affair, and the May 2015 Qing'an shooting incident. The authors hold that ordinary users have equal rights of expression, but the large media outlets that hold network resources still dominate dissemination. They treat agenda-setting as the hinge of the process, because whoever frames an event shapes what people think and how. They see control of carriers as the most basic node. In their account, the United States dominates the root servers, the ICANN domain-name system and the markets of firms such as Microsoft and Intel. They say the contest has moved from holding platforms to seizing topics, from spontaneous to self-conscious opinion, and from complete narratives to fragmented dissemination. As examples they cite misleading headlines, attacks on revolutionary heroes, and "historical nihilism". Li and Xu call for spreading innovative theory that combines Marxism with China's realities, and for gaining a say over internet firms where capital is concentrated. They also call for China to develop its own core technologies. On the practical side, they propose renewing the form of discourse while keeping its Marxist core, and having mainstream media set agendas first, helped by opinion leaders and online propagandists. They also propose combining united-front work with struggle: engaging users' concerns while debating and rebutting dissenters and hostile forces. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese ideological-work scholarship framed online opinion contests in 2015, and how it justified state and Party strategies for them.

The values crisis of the American Dream 美国梦的价值观危机 Zeng Zhihao Zeng Zhihao asks what values the American Dream carries and why, in the author's reading, those values have fallen into crisis. The article argues that the Dream is not always benign: it can become a nightmare or an illusion, and some of the problems it has produced are chronic ones that its champions could not resolve. Zeng traces them mainly to its excessive materialism and individualism. The piece, first published in 2015 in the Journal of Jiangsu University (Social Sciences Edition), is a short essay rather than an empirical study. The article moves through the Dream's main value components in turn: materialism and the worship of wealth, individualism, and a culture of self-indulgence. For each, it lists social consequences, including poverty and homelessness, loneliness and mental illness, drug use and gambling, and crime. It then turns to a counter-tradition of democracy, equality, tolerance and community responsibility, which Zeng describes as having balanced the Dream for much of American history. Zeng draws on John Dewey's critique of consumerism and on episodes such as the Depression-era New Deal and the 1960s counterculture. Zeng argues that unrestrained pursuit of money has produced an extreme wealth gap, with tens of millions living below the poverty line, and that individualism has degenerated into laissez-faire selfishness in a society built on competition rather than cooperation. Drawing on Dewey, Zeng contends that consumption and enjoyment are not values in themselves; they become values only when subjected to intelligent judgment and reflection. Crime statistics from the late twentieth century and the rise of hippies and drug use are offered as evidence of a disillusionment that the author links to the Dream's collapse. Zeng also adds an ecological dimension, saying that unlimited materialism is incompatible with the earth's ecology and with global warming. Zeng concludes that the United States must recover a moral and communitarian dream, such as the small-town ideal and the collective spirit of the 1930s, to curb materialist fervour and renew civil society. The author states that the country's ugly and corrupt side is determined by the capitalist system itself, and that it can only advance amid a mix of problems and hopes. The essay ends by asking whether new dreams will arise to shape America's future. Read the original if you want an example of how a Chinese academic essay in ideological education presents American values and their perceived failings.

A comparison of Marx's and Aristotle's views of happiness 马克思和亚里士多德幸福观比较 Chen Wanqiu Chen Wanqiu asks what genuine happiness is, where a theory of happiness should begin and how people reach it. The article argues that Marx and Aristotle, despite their differences, both treat happiness as grounded in human nature, as multi-layered, and as realised through practice rather than fantasy. The article compares the two thinkers under three headings: human nature as the logical starting point, the rich content of happiness, and practice as the route to happiness. It draws on Aristotle's ethics and politics, and on Marx's Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, Capital, the introduction to the critique of Hegel's philosophy of right and his criticism of Epicurus. A final section draws lessons for present-day China. Chen argues that both thinkers see human beings as unities of natural and social attributes. Aristotle, with his claim that the human being is a political animal, first glimpsed this; Marx, in Chen's reading, states it more accurately by locating the human essence in sociality. Both reject a one-sided view that reduces happiness to ascetic denial or to sensual pleasure. Aristotle ranks bodily, political and contemplative lives and names contemplation the highest happiness, whereas Marx treats happiness as a unity of material and spiritual life. For Marx the highest good is the free and all-round development of individual talents and creativity. On the route to happiness, Aristotle calls it the fruit of rational activity over a whole lifetime but ends by privileging contemplation, which Chen calls one-sided. Marx replaces contemplation with practice, above all labour, and makes the liberation of labour the precondition of happiness. Chen draws three lessons. Happiness must be understood through human duality, so individual and social happiness are interdependent, with social happiness as the foundation and the higher of the two. Spiritual happiness must be taken seriously against materialism, consumerism and hedonism, and Chen mentions the 'house slave' and 'car slave' phenomena. Illusions must be abandoned in favour of creative practice, with the state's comprehensive deepening of reform and law-based governance cited as creating conditions for the people's happiness. Read the original if you want a concise comparative account of Marxist and Aristotelian eudaimonism, linked to Chinese debates on contemporary well-being.

Experience of building a rule-of-law culture in Singapore 新加坡法治文化建设的经验 Jiao Yuli This short commentary asks why Singapore, a small resource-poor state, became a modern, orderly and clean-governed country within about thirty years. Jiao Yuli takes up Lee Kuan Yew's remark that the key to Singapore's success is the rule of law, and argues that Singapore's distinctive rule-of-law culture is worth close study and emulation. The piece was first published in 2015 under a slightly longer title that included the word 'lessons'. Jiao defines rule-of-law culture as the values-centred patterns of thought and behaviour towards legal life that a society builds up over time, and as the cultural basis without which the rule of law cannot work. The article then sets out three features of the Singapore case: a comprehensive legal system, a 'shared values' framework, and a popular faith in law backed by strict enforcement. On the first, Jiao says Singapore has over 400 statutes regulating matters from political institutions to parking and chewing-gum sales, including a set of anti-corruption laws. On the second, the 1991 White Paper on Shared Values is said to guide legal culture, and housing legislation supporting the 'home ownership' policy is offered as an example. On the third, Jiao argues that equal application of law explains public support for harsh penalties such as caning, citing a 1994 Straits Times poll in which nearly 90 per cent favoured keeping it. Cases of ministers punished for corruption, and Lee Kuan Yew's request for an investigation of his own property purchase, are presented as proof of equality before the law. Jiao concludes that Singapore's experience, in which complete legislation, shared values and impartial enforcement reinforce one another, merits study. The text offers no explicit policy proposals beyond this call for learning from the case. Read the original if you want a brief, favourable Chinese Party-journal account of how Singapore's legal culture is presented to cadres as a model.

Making the "Three Stricts and Three Reals" a routine practice 推进“三严三实”常态化 Yu Xiangdong This short commentary, published in the People's Daily in October 2015, asks how the campaign of "Three Stricts and Three Reals" (sanyan sanshi) can become a lasting practice rather than a one-off drive. Yu Xiangdong argues that the special education programme is a routine task of the Party for eliminating unhealthy tendencies, and that it should be made routine in three areas: ideological education, observance of rules and discipline, and supervision and inspection. The piece begins with Xi Jinping's call on Party members and cadres, especially leaders, to keep the principles in mind and apply a spirit of strictness and realism. It cites the General Office's plan for county- and department-level leading cadres, which presents the programme as an extension of the Party's mass line education campaign. That plan, Yu notes, requires no batches, stages or phases. The commentary then takes the three areas in turn. On ideological education, Yu holds that correct understanding is the key to implementation. Cadres are to treat study as a habit, study the 18th Party Congress (2012) and Xi Jinping's speeches, and draw lessons from positive and negative examples. On rules and discipline, Yu calls for firm awareness of the Party constitution, the law and the masses, so that the principles become part of daily conduct. On supervision, Yu cites Lenin on monitoring and punishing non-execution of decrees, and proposes improving three mechanisms: organisational, mass and public-opinion supervision. Yu concludes that study and propaganda alone are insufficient, and that routine education, discipline and all-round supervision are needed to make work-style improvement regular and lasting. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the Party press in 2015 framed the institutionalisation of the "Three Stricts and Three Reals" within full and rigorous self-governance of the Party.

Where is the Western left heading? The condition and prospects of the left in the twenty-first century The Latin American left's rise, record in office and present challenges 西方左翼何去何从？——21世纪西方左翼的状况与前景 Jiang Hui Writing at the end of 2015, Jiang Hui asks what has become of the left in Latin America after roughly fifteen years of governing. Despite the title's reference to the Western left, the article deals only with Latin America. Jiang argues that the region's left rose by offering alternatives to neoliberalism and achieved real gains, but now faces serious challenges, with Venezuela and Brazil under the greatest pressure. The article has three parts. It first traces the left's rise from Hugo Chávez's election in Venezuela in 1999 to governments of the left or centre-left in more than ten countries, including Brazil, Argentina, Uruguay, Chile, Bolivia, Ecuador and Nicaragua. It then assesses these governments' politics, economics, social policy and foreign policy. Finally it sets out five challenges and notes how the left is responding. It ends with the Argentine presidential election of November 2015 and the upcoming Venezuelan parliamentary vote. Jiang credits the left with new or revised constitutions and participatory democracy, nationalisation of key sectors such as Bolivia's oil and gas in 2006, and poverty-reduction programmes. In Brazil, the author says, these programmes lifted nearly 40 million people out of poverty. The left also pursued regional integration through ALBA, UNASUR and CELAC, and several governments proposed their own socialisms, such as '21st-century socialism'. Jiang then lists five problems. Growth has slowed as commodity prices fell, forcing austerity and protests. Corruption scandals, especially in Brazil, have hurt support. Conservative opposition is strong in many cities and legislatures. Divisions exist within ruling coalitions, within left parties and between parties and new social movements. Finally, Jiang says the United States interferes, citing National Endowment for Democracy funding and sanctions on Venezuelan officials. Jiang concludes that left governments are aware of these challenges and are responding. The article points to the Quito 'Latin American Progressive Meetings' of 2014 and 2015 and to the São Paulo Forum's 21st meeting in Mexico City, which stressed left unity. It reads Mauricio Macri's victory in Argentina as shifting the region's political pendulum towards the centre-right and as a blow to other left governments. Read the original if you want a Chinese specialist's 2015 assessment of the Latin American left's record, its difficulties and its view of US involvement.

Where is the Western left heading? The condition and prospects of the Western left in the twenty-first century 西方左翼何去何从？——21世纪西方左翼的状况与前景 Jiang Hui Writing in 2015, Jiang Hui asks what has become of the Western left since the collapse of the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe, and where it can go after the 2008 financial–economic crisis. Jiang argues that the crisis has opened a rare historic opportunity, but that the left has not been able to use it. Its future depends on how far it achieves a genuine "negation of the negation", meaning a sublation of its own past rather than a simple return to the old left. The article has three parts. The first divides the left's course since 1990 into three phases: retreat (1990–1995), a rightward turn (1996–2007), and a partial return (2008–2014). The second diagnoses the left's present difficulties. The third names four relationships the left must handle if it is to renew itself. In the diagnosis, Jiang says the left has "heaven's timing" (capitalism and the right are discredited) but lacks "human harmony". Centre-left parties lost elections, communist parties stayed marginal, and far-right parties took up part of the discontent. Jiang lists four problems: a lost identity, inadequate theoretical and strategic preparation, criticism without constructive programmes, and fragmentation despite efforts at unity. For the way forward, Jiang stresses four relationships: the left and socialism, which should form a "great left" led by the socialist movement; the left and class struggle, where the working class remains the main force; electoral politics and mass movements, which are in a standing paradox; and national against global activity. Jiang concludes that the left should neither return to its earlier form nor settle for turning back a few steps. It should build a new left and a hopeful socialism suited to the post-crisis situation. For Jiang, this requires a socialist orientation, a class basis, a balance between parliamentary and extra-parliamentary struggle, and an international outlook, since socialism is national in form and international in content. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist scholar's periodisation and assessment of the Western left after 1990, written from the standpoint of the study of scientific socialism.

Luxemburg and the violence of global capitalism 卢森堡与全球资本主义暴力 This short essay on Rosa Luxemburg (1871–1919) asks what her theory of imperialism, set out in The Accumulation of Capital (1913), still tells us about global capitalism. The author argues that her account of capital's dependence on non-capitalist societies, and of the violence this entails, has proved largely prescient and applies to developed economies as well as colonised ones. The text appears to be a Chinese rendering of an English-language piece; no author is named, and the translator is given as Lu Yingchun. The essay opens with a portrait of Luxemburg as a writer, her humour, her taste for plain theoretical prose and her immersion in the work on accumulation. It then summarises her economic analysis, her criticism of Volume II of Marx's Capital, and her survey of pre-capitalist economies. Next it lists the cases she examined, including the ruin of English peasants, the destruction of Native Americans, the enslavement of Africans, and colonial assaults on Algeria, India, China and South Africa. The final sections turn to her views on international loans, militarism and the First World War. The author identifies three features that set Luxemburg apart from Hilferding, Bukharin and Lenin. First, because workers receive less value than they create, capitalists face underconsumption and must expand into non-capitalist regions for markets, raw materials and labour. Capital thus lives by destroying those regions, and accumulation would eventually stall. Second, she treats imperialism not as capitalism's 'highest stage' but as present from primitive accumulation onwards. Third, she shows an anthropological sensitivity to the cultures that expansion destroys. The author adds that this penetration now reaches family life, friendship, creativity and gender in advanced economies. The author also notes that capital's drive to accumulate has, contrary to Luxemburg's expectation, weakened socialist revolution rather than provoking it. The author concludes that, whatever the criticisms of the book, Luxemburg's analysis is highly plausible and has been borne out. The essay cites Joan Robinson, who found the book more prescient than the orthodox theorists of its day. It also credits Luxemburg with foreseeing foreign investment and aid, the role of international lenders, and arms spending as a field of accumulation paid for by workers. The author adds that her words resonate in the twentieth century and in present-day globalisation. Read the original if you want a brief, sympathetic introduction to Luxemburg's theory of imperialism and its contemporary relevance, as presented in a Chinese-language outlet.

Has winter arrived for the Latin American left? 拉美左翼的冬天来临了吗？ Writing in early 2016, after electoral defeats for the left in Argentina and Venezuela, this unsigned commentary asks whether Latin America's left is entering a period of decline. The article answers that it is not necessarily doing so: setbacks for left-wing parties, it argues, do not amount to a victory for neoliberalism. The piece has three parts. It first describes how neoliberal reform from the 1980s produced the conditions for the left's rise from 1999, beginning with Hugo Chávez's election in Venezuela. It then reviews the record of left and centre-left governments in politics, the economy, social policy and foreign relations. Finally it turns to the recent reverses and to how they should be read. The author cites figures to argue that neoliberalism brought slower growth, higher unemployment, a wider gap between rich and poor, and a larger poor population. Left governments, in this account, wrote new constitutions, nationalised key sectors, ran anti-poverty programmes (Brazil's, for example, are said to have lifted some 40 million people out of poverty) and promoted regional integration through bodies such as ALBA, UNASUR and CELAC. The recent downturn is attributed to falling commodity prices, an unreformed export-based growth model, austerity measures and corruption within left parties. The author nonetheless contends that the opposition's Venezuelan parliamentary win was largely a punishment of the governing party. Polls are cited showing majority support for the Bolivarian social programmes and over two-thirds opposition to privatising state oil and electricity companies, and the author says right-wing candidates have had to present themselves in the language of Chávez and Kirchner. The article concludes that defeated left forces are mobilising people in streets and neighbourhoods to defend the gains of the Bolivarian revolution against a coming right-wing offensive. It closes by quoting that history is made by the masses rather than in parliaments. Read the original if you want a brief, sympathetic Chinese-language account of how the Latin American left's 2015 reverses were interpreted on a Chinese Marxist platform.

The financial crisis as an opportunity for the revival of world socialism 金融危机为世界社会主义复兴提供契机 Lü Weizhou This commentary, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today, takes up the claims that socialism has "ended" and that China is about to "collapse". Lü argues that the global financial crisis of 2008 has turned these claims against their authors. In the article's account, what is actually ending is the "end of socialism" thesis and the "China collapse" thesis, while capitalism declines and world socialism, though not yet out of its trough, partly recovers. The article has four parts. It first traces the origins of the "end of socialism" and "China collapse" arguments, from the late 1980s to the early 2010s. It then examines the institutional difficulties of capitalism after the crisis, and the signs of revival in world socialism. It closes with a warning that a new round of such predictions is under way and with proposals for how China should respond. Figures discussed include Nixon, Brzezinski, Fukuyama, Gordon Chang and David Shambaugh, with Derrida, Huntington and several investors cited as critics. Lü's central move is to treat the "China collapse" thesis as a form of the "end of socialism" thesis, aimed at discrediting socialism and flattering capitalism. The sharpest rebuttal, in this reading, comes from the real development of the two systems. Lü says the crisis exposed capitalism's instability, parasitism and decay, and that it ended the myth of an "eternal" capitalism, citing Fukuyama's own remark that the crisis shows capitalism's inherent instability. Lü then points to three signs of socialist revival: renewed interest in Marx and socialist alternatives, stronger communist and left parties in Greece, Portugal, Spain, Latin America and elsewhere, and the rising standing of socialism with Chinese characteristics, as China was first to recover economically. Writing in 2015, Lü warns that China's entry into a period of "new normal" growth and "tackling tough problems" in reform invites fresh predictions of collapse. Lü calls for deepening reform and opening up, advancing the Scientific Outlook on Development, building the material basis for the Chinese Dream, and keeping strategic resolve through firm communist ideals. Read the original if you want an example of how a CASS scholar answered Western "end of history" and "China collapse" arguments in the mid-2010s.

Full coverage, high standards, strict requirements Studying the Code of Integrity and Self-Discipline and the Regulations on Disciplinary Actions of the Communist Party of China 全覆盖、高标准、严要求 Yuan Xiuli Writing in early 2016, Yuan Xiuli introduces the newly revised Code of Integrity and Self-Discipline and the Regulations on Disciplinary Actions of the Communist Party of China, and argues that all Party members should study them closely. The author notes that, alongside wide approval, a few people have misread or attacked the documents, above all the ban on members "groundlessly criticising" major central Party policies, which some call a gag on free speech. Yuan treats such views as reflecting an incomplete grasp of Party discipline, and in a few cases deliberate distortion. The commentary has two parts. The first sets out six features of the revised texts: major changes, broad scope, new content, strict requirements, high standards and practicability. The second explains why implementing them matters, under four headings: establishing the authority of Party rules, improving the Party's rule system, protecting centralised unity, and giving intra-Party and public supervision a basis in rules. Yuan's central move is to present the Code as a positive list that cultivates virtue and the Regulations as a negative list that draws bottom lines, forming a "two-wheel drive" for governing the Party. The Code shrinks from 3,600-plus characters to about 280 and now covers all members, with higher demands on leading cadres. The Regulations reorganise offences into six categories of discipline, separate Party discipline from state law, and set standards stricter than the law. On the contested clause, Yuan distinguishes constructive criticism from destructive "groundless criticism". Members, the author says, may raise dissent through proper channels, enter reservations while carrying out decisions, and appeal to higher bodies. Public opposition to central decisions is barred, and Yuan sees nothing to fear for intra-Party democracy, since democratic centralism requires unity of action. Yuan concludes that the two documents turn the achievements of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party since the 18th Party Congress (2012) into regular institutions, and signal that discipline will only tighten. The author adds that supervision and accountability must be strengthened together, and that every cadre must absorb the documents' spirit and put them into practice. Read the original if you want an official-line defence of the 2015 Party discipline revisions, especially the case made for the ban on "groundless criticism" of central policy.

Analysis of the state of online thought in 2015 2015年度网络思想状况分析 Li Yanyan Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts (January 2016), Li Yanyan reviews the state of online thought and opinion in China during 2015 and looks ahead. The author argues that the year was complex and contentious, with new features in content, dissemination and influence, and that online ideological and cultural work needs strengthening. The piece has two parts. The first sets out three notable features of 2015; the second offers recommendations for 2016, organised under ideological work, institutions and mechanisms, and personnel. On the features, Li says the authorities showed stronger ability to set agendas and to govern the internet by law. Li cites the 70th anniversary of the victory in the War of Resistance, the second World Internet Conference, the draft Cybersecurity Law and a draft law on overseas NGOs. Online disputes also educated netizens, though cases such as the Langya Mountain debate and an attack on a patriotic young netizen discouraged some speakers. Fast-moving, interlinked media weakened the guiding power of traditional Party media, ideological topics drew sustained attention, and disputes involving police and military grew. For 2016, Li calls for awakening netizens' sense of ownership and judgement, and for training in historical and dialectical materialist thinking, so that the "silent majority" is not swayed by opinion leaders. Li also proposes top-level design of online content production, dissemination and evaluation, including reform of academic evaluation, support for positive online opinion leaders and effect-oriented assessment. A propaganda force of Party cadres, volunteers and scholars should carry the online spread of core socialist values. Read the original if you want a concise official-academic view of how Chinese ideological work approached online opinion at the end of 2015.

An important compass for promoting China's fine traditional culture A reading of Xi Jinping's speech to the International Confucian Association 弘扬中国优秀传统文化的重要指导南针 Teng Wensheng This commentary, first published in Guangming Daily in September 2015, studies Xi Jinping's speech at the Fifth Member Congress of the International Confucian Association. Teng Wensheng argues that the speech is a major, far-sighted statement. He calls it both a compass for promoting China's fine traditional culture and a declaration on how different civilizations should learn from one another. Teng first sets out eight points that he says the speech clarifies. They concern peace and development as the background of the era, the historical role of Confucianism and traditional culture, their characteristics and the values they contain, and the proper approach to other civilizations. They also cover the need to sift traditional culture, the study of tradition as a route to understanding Chinese national character, and the Communist Party's stance toward tradition. He then draws lessons for inheriting tradition and for exchange between civilizations. On tradition, Teng argues that every present-day culture grows from a traditional base, so inheritance must be selective: take the essence, discard the dross, and pursue creative transformation and innovative development rather than copying. He rejects historical nihilism. He holds that Marxism's guiding role in China forms a unity of "one dominant strand, many strands" with traditional and progressive thought, and cites Confucianism's long dominance in feudal China, which did not stop other schools from functioning. On civilizations, he stresses that each is a nation's soul, that all are equal with no higher or lower, and that cultural hegemony is a road to decline. Teng concludes that the International Confucian Association will follow the speech's principles, link the promotion of tradition with dialogue among civilizations, and tell the story of China's cultural continuity. He presents this as a contribution to world peace and to a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want an officially aligned reading of Xi's 2014 Confucian speech and of how Party writers reconcile Marxism with traditional culture.

Strengthening the construction of a Marxist discourse system among contemporary youth 在当代青年中强化马克思主义话语体系建设 Tan Jinsong Huang Fanwen Tan Jinsong and Huang Fanwen, writing in Red Flag Manuscripts (2015, no. 20), take up the observation that part of China's young generation, raised in the reform era, is increasingly unfamiliar with or even hostile to the Marxist discourse system. The authors argue that strengthening this discourse among young people is an urgent task, because its absence threatens the continuity of socialism in China. The article is organised in four parts: the main manifestations of the gap, its consequences, its causes, and proposed countermeasures. It is a short argumentative piece in the style of ideological and political education commentary, drawing on no case studies or data and relying on assertion and historical analogy, notably to the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe. The authors identify three manifestations: young people do not know Marxist vocabulary, their grounding in the classics and basic principles is weak, and their belief in Marxism is not firm.
