They say this matters because it hinders training successors for socialism, the transmission of Marxism, and resistance to what they call Western ideological infiltration and 'peaceful evolution', which they describe as now aimed at China's youth. They trace the problem to three causes: poorly delivered theoretical education that is cut off from students' interests; Western culture and values spread through media and consumption; and, at the deepest level, the value pluralism that accompanies a mix of ownership forms. In their reading, the economic base determines ideology, so individual-centred values growing with the non-public sector have marginalised Marxist discourse among some youth. Tan and Huang propose three measures: make Marxist theory courses compulsory and improve their teaching so students accept them 'in ear, brain and heart'; strengthen young people's resistance to Western ideas, including strict screening of Western cultural products online and blocking material seen as maliciously discrediting socialism; and implement the dominant position of public ownership as the economic foundation of socialist ideology, while supporting the non-public sector but never allowing privatisation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese Party-journal writing in 2015 framed youth ideology, Western cultural influence and public ownership as linked problems.

Characteristics of US values export after the Cold War Excerpt from "Characteristics of US values export after the Cold War and ideological education in China's universities" 冷战后美国价值观输出的特点 Liu Junhan This short piece, published in a 2015 issue of a journal on ideological and political education, asks how the United States has exported its values since the Cold War ended. Liu argues that every US administration since then has given "values export" a very important place in its foreign strategy, and that the practice shows three features: moral deceptiveness, concealed forms and varied means. Liu surveys the post-Cold War presidencies in turn: George H. W. Bush's "promotion and consolidation of democracy", the Clinton administration's three pillars of economy, security and democracy, George W. Bush's "Greater Middle East" democratic remodelling plan, and the Obama administration's "smart power" diplomacy. The three features are then illustrated with cases from China, Iraq, Central Asia and the Middle East. On moral deceptiveness, Liu contends that the US uses its media strength and discursive hegemony to promote separation of powers and party systems as "universal values", to demonise socialist states, and to dress interventionism in moral language such as "human rights above sovereignty". On concealment, Liu says Washington often works through NGOs, media, think tanks, student exchanges and religious groups, whose activities are hard to tell apart from legitimate charity, aid or cultural exchange. On variety of means, Liu describes a combined system of economic sanctions, political pressure, cultural infiltration and military force, with the internet and social media, in Liu's account, acting as a catalyst in Egypt, Tunisia and Iran. Liu concludes that the US combines soft and hard methods in a mature system, and ties ideological unrest in the Middle East and Central Asia to "internet infiltration". The original title shows the piece is aimed at ideological education in Chinese universities. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese ideological-education scholarship framed US values diplomacy in 2015.

Three paths to resolving the crisis of belief in Marxism 破解马克思主义信仰危机的三重路径 Xu Lan Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2015, Xu Lan asks how to deal with what the author calls a crisis of belief in Marxism. Xu holds that Marxism still dominates China's ideological field, but is demonised on one side and turned into a utopia on the other. The article's answer is three linked paths, all concerned with Party conduct and discipline. The piece opens by describing the crisis. Xu says it weakens the Party's cohesion and credibility and feeds social anxiety, hostility and utilitarianism. Xu lists causes: simplistic and dogmatic ideological education, pervasive corruption, early-rich groups who became vested interests, and wealth gaps that erode trust in government. Three sections then set out the remedies, and a short conclusion draws them together. The first path treats Party integrity and the anti-corruption struggle as a matter of the survival of the Party and state. Xu argues that corruption stems from incomplete reform, not from reform itself, and calls for gradual institutional change, intra-Party supervision and public oversight, especially online. The second is full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, which Xu says must go beyond punishing corruption or running campaigns. It should set moral standards and forbidden zones, and value-building is described as a soft constraint alongside institutions. The third asks leading cadres, especially senior ones, to internalise political discipline and rules, with the revised Integrity Code and Disciplinary Regulations setting a moral "high line" and a disciplinary "bottom line". Xu also says cadres must take a clear stand against historical nihilism. Xu concludes that these paths are ways of rebuilding belief in Marxism, and also support the modernization of state governance and the people's wellbeing. A healthy political life within the Party is presented as a basis for the free and comprehensive development of the individual. Read the original if you want a short example of how a 2015 Party journal tied ideological confidence to anti-corruption and discipline campaigns.

Distinguishing the epoch from the theme of the epoch 对时代和时代主题的辨析 Li Shenming Li Shenming takes up a question of strategic judgement: what is the nature of the present epoch, and how does it relate to the 'theme of the epoch'? Starting from Xi Jinping's call for overall and long-term thinking in deepening reform, Li argues that the epoch and its theme must be kept apart. In Li's view, the present epoch is still the epoch of finance imperialism that Lenin described, and 'peace and development' is only the theme of a phase within it, not the name of a new epoch. The article has two parts. The first defines the epoch and its theme through Marx, Engels and Lenin, who in Li's reading identify epochs by the class at their centre. Li subdivides the bourgeois epoch into commercial capitalism, industrial capitalism and finance imperialism. The second part traces how Deng Xiaoping and later Party documents spoke of peace and development, reviews Lenin's account of imperialism, and applies it to the post-Cold War world, including the 2008 financial crisis. Li also cites statements by Mao Zedong, Deng, Chen Yun, Jiang Zemin, Hu Jintao and Xi to show continuity of judgement. Li's central claim is that the epoch's nature determines its theme and not the reverse. The epoch is the deeper level, and themes are changing outward forms of its basic contradiction between international bourgeoisie and international proletariat. Lenin's three basic contradictions, Li says, have changed in form but are unresolved. On this basis Li proposes a 'two-sided' judgement: finance imperialism is still strong and at the centre, yet it is relatively declining while the proletariat rises, within a long and winding transition from capitalism to socialism. Li objects to colleagues who equate the 'epoch of peace and development' with the theme, noting that wars have continued and that the length of war or peace cannot define an epoch. Li concludes that misjudging the epoch could lead either to blind optimism and an attempt to skip over the finance-imperialist stage, which Li calls 'left-wing' infantile disorder, or to a loss of confidence in socialism and communism, even the fate of the Soviet Union. Li holds that Deng enriched the Marxist idea of the theme without denying the imperialist character of the era. The article argues that the correct judgement underpins the Party's long-term strategy. Read the original if you want to see how a senior academic voice defends Lenin's theory of imperialism against the idea of an 'epoch of peace and development'.

Economic financialization will inevitably intensify economic and social turmoil in capitalism 经济金融化必将加剧资本主义经济社会动荡 Xing Wenzeng Writing in 2015, Xing Wenzeng asks whether the financial reforms adopted after the 2008 global financial crisis have checked the financialization of capitalist economies. The article's answer is no: financialization remains a defining feature of capitalism, and the author argues that it will inevitably deepen economic turmoil and social crisis in the future. The article has three parts. The first traces how financialization became a central feature of capitalism from the 1970s and how it prepared crises. The second surveys the regulatory measures taken by the United States, the EU, Britain, Japan and Germany after 2008 and assesses their results. The third looks ahead to three consequences: a continuing split between the real and the virtual economy, more channels for large-scale financial crises, and sharper class conflict. Xing explains financialization as a response to falling profit rates and stagnation in the 1970s, helped by neoliberal deregulation. The author cites figures on the growth of financial assets, derivatives and financial-sector profits. On the post-crisis reforms, including the Dodd–Frank Act, new supervisory bodies, oversight of rating agencies and limits on executive pay, Xing argues that the effect was limited. The evidence offered is record bank profits, over-the-counter derivatives growing roughly eightfold between 1998 and 2012, shadow banking above 73 trillion dollars in 2013, and rising concentration among large banks. Re-industrialization drives in the West, the author says, have barely raised manufacturing's share of GDP or employment. Xing adds that financial innovation gives capital new ways to extract surplus value, and cites the post-2008 workers' movements in Europe and elsewhere, with slogans such as ending the capitalist system, as signs of widening class antagonism. Xing concludes that capitalist states' policies, which the article describes as taking from the poor to give to the rich, make financialization more severe. The author predicts a deeper crisis of capitalist accumulation, greater global class confrontation and unavoidable social crisis. Read the original if you want an example of how a Chinese Marxist economist in 2015 used data on derivatives, shadow banking and post-crisis regulation to argue for capitalism's structural instability.

The genealogy, present state and future of the world socialist movement Popular movements toward socialism: their unity and diversity 世界社会主义运动的谱系、现状与未来 Samir Amin This text is a Chinese edited translation of an article by the Egyptian Marxist economist Samir Amin, first published in Monthly Review in June 2014. Amin treats socialism/communism as a stage of civilisation superior to capitalism. He uses "movements toward socialism" for all mass movements that resist capitalism. His thesis is that such movements advance only if they recognise their differences and still act together. The article first sketches the French Revolution's values of liberty, equality and fraternity, which Amin says capitalism can accept but never realise. It then traces three lineages of the movement: the capitalist centre, the semi-periphery, and the periphery. The centre runs from French socialism and the First and Second Internationals to postwar social democracy. The semi-periphery is the Leninist line, from Russia to Soviet "state socialism". The periphery runs from the Taiping movement to Mao Zedong, India, Africa and Latin America. The last sections turn to the future and to the "second rise" of the Global South. Amin's central claim is that the relation between unity and diversity has decided the fate of each lineage. He argues that the Second Internationals' ideal of a single workers' party and mass unions led to revisionism. Revisionism, he says, rested on prosperity built on imperialist plunder, and left European parties merely social-liberal. Lenin inherited the one-class, one-party idea, and the Third International later subordinated strategy to Soviet needs. Amin credits Mao and the Chinese communists with moving beyond Leninism, and says China's management of unity and diversity explains its stability and legitimacy. He treats Vietnam and Cuba as comparable successes, and the Latin American governments and Indian communists as unresolved or failed cases. He holds that class analysis must not be simplified and must separate major from minor differences. Amin proposes that radical left forces in the imperialist centre nationalise monopoly property and democratise and socialise its management, setting common goals for each stage. On the periphery, he says, they must identify the components of their social alliance and its shared goals. He rejects multiparty elections as a formula for "true democracy" and calls for "sovereign projects" built from below, including moving away from financial globalisation and the dollar, and geopolitical alliances to restrain US military control. Read the original if you want a Marxist account, from the Global South, of how socialist movements have divided and what he thinks they should do next.

Humanity's advance towards socialism is an irresistible movement 人类走向社会主义是一种不可抗拒的运动 Yu. Qiongkefu This is a Chinese translation of an article by a Russian economist and former State Duma deputy chairman, first published in a Russian journal in January 2015. The author starts from the question whether humanity will still see socialism and treats it as settled: socialism is the future stage of civilisation. The real question, in the author's view, is how long capitalism can hold back human progress. The thesis is that movement towards socialism is irresistible, but its timing depends on subjective factors that are currently poorly prepared. The article has five sections. It first separates the objective and subjective conditions of socialism, then asks whether modern capitalism is already ripe for transition. It next lists five features of capitalist 'decay', explains why socialism has not arrived sooner, and ends with a critical assessment of the socialist and democratic movements, including the Soviet collapse and the situation in post-Soviet Russia. The author argues that objective conditions supply only the material basis for social reconstruction. History is made by social-economic subjects: states, governments, politicians, theorists and the mass media, driven by class struggle. The author defends Lenin's thesis of capitalist 'decay' and cites war, hunger, spiritual impoverishment, unemployment, the corruption of work ethics and youth drug addiction. Economic crises, ecological threat, monopoly and the 'fascisation' of state conduct are also listed. Socialism has not yet replaced capitalism because the subjective side is weak: trade unions have been bought off, communist and workers' parties disarmed, genuine Marxist theorists are few, and no leader of the stature of Marx, Lenin, Castro or Chávez exists. The author also blames the Soviet collapse on the ruling class's mismanagement, dogmatism and passive waiting rather than on economic causes, and attributes anti-socialist pressure to the global elite, naming Bilderberg and 'world government'. The author concludes that the best remedy for anti-socialist and anti-communist sentiment is serious study of socialist thought worldwide and of socialist practice, including the Soviet experience. The author calls for new socialist theory under present conditions and urges the unity of the left opposition. Read the original if you want a Russian left-wing view, published in China in 2015, of the Soviet collapse, the subjective conditions of socialism and the crisis of the communist movement.

Tactical success and strategic impasse: the world socialist movement since the 2008 financial crisis 战役成功与战略困局：2008年金融危机以来的世界社会主义运动发展态势 Nie Yunlin Did the 2008 financial crisis revive the world socialist movement? Nie Yunlin argues that it produced only a limited result. Communist parties in capitalist countries won what the author calls a campaign-level ("战役性") success, but the movement remains at a low ebb, these parties are still marginalised in political life, and no strategic victory has been achieved. The article has two parts. The first reviews what communist parties did after 2008 and why the hoped-for upsurge did not come, drawing largely on speeches at the 11th International Meeting of Communist and Workers' Parties. The second sets out six tasks that the author says these parties must resolve to escape their strategic impasse, using examples from Britain, India, Turkey, Russia, France, Spain, Italy, Brazil, South Africa and Nepal. In Nie's account, the parties analysed the crisis theoretically, joined strikes and protests, voted against crisis-shifting policies in parliaments and strengthened their own organisation. Some held or raised their membership, for example the Communist Party of India (Marxist) with over a million members. The article attributes the lack of a strategic breakthrough to four causes cited by delegates: the lingering effects of the Soviet and East European collapse, welfare systems that dulled workers' political consciousness, weak capacity for self-renewal, and sectarian splits. The six tasks are: overcoming fragmentation; avoiding both "left" dogmatism and rightist abandonment of Marxist principles; upholding and reforming democratic centralism; consolidating the class base and widening mass support, especially among trade unions and the middle strata; sustaining left alliances; and breaking out of the constraints of capitalist political systems. Nie claims that parties which kept democratic centralism have recovered, while those which dropped it, such as the French, Spanish and Italian parties, have declined. Nie concludes that the post-crisis period opens a long new journey in which each party must find a socialist path suited to its own country. The author likens the crisis-era gains to the defence of Huangyangjie in the Jinggangshan period of the Chinese revolution, a battle won before the war was decided. The most pressing step, Nie says, is to solve the parties' internal problems. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's assessment of Western communist parties after 2008, and of their organisational and strategic dilemmas, based on party delegates' own statements.

An analysis of the ideological state of CPSU grass-roots organisations and members before the Soviet collapse 苏联解体前苏共基层党组织与党员思想状况分析 Li Yan Why did the roughly ten million rank-and-file members of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union (CPSU) not act when the Party was dissolved and the USSR collapsed? Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2015, the author takes up a question often put by commentators who read their calm as indifference. The thesis is that the silence came from structural and ideological causes, not apathy, and that some members did resist. The author draws on interviews with veteran Party members conducted during a 2014 research visit to Russia, and on archives, letters and documents read there. The article has three parts: five reasons for the silence, examples of protest within it, and the historical lessons. It also uses memoirs by Roy Medvedev, Valery Boldin and Chernyaev. The first part argues that Lenin's priority of democracy within centralism was gradually reversed. Power concentrated in a bureaucratic pyramid, so grass-roots members could only obey, stay silent or write complaint letters. The author adds four further causes. The cadre ranks were swollen by careerists. Khrushchev's and especially Gorbachev's ideological policies of glasnost and the criticism of Stalin spread what the author calls historical nihilism. Elite privilege and corruption alienated members. Gorbachev's political reforms, including multiparty competition, weakened Party leadership and set off mass resignations in 1990–91. The second part cites the teacher Nina Andreyeva's 1988 letter, the deputy Sarie Umalatova's call for Gorbachev to resign, and suicides of figures such as Marshal Akhromeyev. The author reads these as despairing protest and argues that the crowds outside the Party headquarters in August 1991 did not speak for ordinary members. The author concludes that the collapse is not directly attributable to grass-roots members. Even so, a ruling party rests on vital grass-roots organisations, and these were disrupted once Gorbachev abandoned the Party's leading role and the socialist path, while privilege and corruption cost the Party public support. The article's lesson is that a ruling party must hold to a correct political line, to Marxist principles and to socialism. It must also keep strict organisational and political discipline and serve the people in practice. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly account of the Soviet collapse that centres on ordinary Party members, with archival and memoir material.

Firmly establishing the correct view of nationalities 牢固树立正确的民族观 Hao Shiyuan Writing in Qiushi in 2015, Hao Shiyuan sets out what the "correct view of nationalities" (minzuguan) means and why Chinese citizens should hold it. Taking Xi Jinping's remarks on ethnic work as the guiding text, Hao argues that this view rests on seeing the Chinese nation as a single, pluralistic-yet-unified family, and that building a shared spiritual home and a consciousness of the Chinese national community is the strategic task that follows. The piece has two sections. The first defines the correct view of nationalities, sets it against Western experience with race and ethnicity, and states the basic policy orientation of Chinese ethnic work. The second turns to cultivating a consciousness of the Chinese national community, covering cultural identity, the two forms of nationalism to be opposed, and the place of ethnic work in state governance. Hao distinguishes two senses of "nation": the modern state-nation (the Chinese nation) and the historical nationalities (the 56 groups) that compose it. In this account the Chinese nation is the only representative of China among the world's nations, and national unity is the precondition of state unity and territorial integrity. Hao presents Western policy as a long record of enslavement, segregation and forced assimilation. Multiculturalism, in this reading, has failed, citing Merkel's and Cameron's statements, the 2014 Ferguson unrest, a Council of Europe report and the Scottish and Catalan referendums. Against this, Hao describes the Chinese approach as respecting differences while narrowing gaps. This means a shared spiritual home and a shared material home, supported by common prosperity. Hao makes cultural identity the foundation. Chinese culture is not the same as Han culture but a synthesis of all groups' cultures, likened to an orchestra led by the Party with core socialist values as the main melody. Every group is said to carry the family surname "Chinese nation" along with its own given name. Narrow identification with one's own group breeds nationalism, which hostile forces can exploit, so Hao says the law and Party policy oppose both Han chauvinism and narrow local nationalism. Hao concludes that ethnic work is part of modernizing the system and capacity of state governance. Its key is ethnic unity, and its most effective method is winning hearts. Persuasion grounded in respect for differences, together with bringing ethnic affairs fully under the rule of law, is how the correct view is to be established. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned statement of the Chinese Party-state's 2015 ethnic theory, including its critique of Western multiculturalism.

Marxist movements in Africa 非洲的马克思主义运动 Daryl Glaser This text is a Chinese translation, with some abridgement, of a chapter by Daryl Glaser from Twentieth Century Marxism: A Global Introduction (Routledge, 2007). It asks whether Africa made an original contribution to Marxist thought, a claim many African Marxist leaders themselves rejected. Glaser answers that it did, even though the ruling Marxist-Leninists after the 1970s insisted on a single universal model. The chapter surveys "African socialism" of the independence era (Nkrumah, Touré, Nyerere) and the Marxist-Leninist regimes that followed. It traces how Marxism reached Africa through colonial links, urban multi-ethnic milieus and the Soviet bloc. It then compares routes to power: military coups (Ethiopia, Benin, Madagascar, Somalia), people's war (Cabral, FRELIMO, the MPLA), and the special cases of South Africa and Ethiopia. It closes with the decline of these movements around 1990. Glaser argues that Marxism in Africa did not arrive merely as a Soviet import. African Marxist governments often kept channels open to the West, and their authoritarianism was largely home-grown. The author also defends military Marxists and guerrilla movements against critics who dismissed them as insincere. Original contributions are identified in Siad Barre's attempted synthesis of Marxism and Islam, the national-question positions of the Eritrean and Tigrayan liberation fronts, Touré's mass-party experiments and Madagascar's limited multiparty system. In Glaser's account, failure stemmed from both external and internal causes. External causes were underdevelopment, war, Cold War pressures and debt. Internal causes were impatience, overambitious planning, coercion of the peasantry, hostility to wider society and a "participatory" democracy that served mobilisation behind goals the ruling party had set. Glaser sees the shift to representative democracy after 1990 as valuable but constrained by the IMF and World Bank. Future socialists and social democrats, the author says, must learn from the negative lessons of African socialism and Marxism and may still need Marxism to analyse new class inequalities. Read the original if you study African socialism, Cabral or the global spread of Leninism and want a critical comparative overview.

Latin America: left-wing progressive governments urgently need strategic planning 拉丁美洲：左翼进步政府急需战略规划 Roberto Regalado This is a Chinese translation (compiled and translated by Wang Jin) of a report by the Cuban scholar Roberto Regalado, a professor at the University of Havana. Writing in 2014, fifteen years after Hugo Chávez's first election victory, Regalado asks whether Latin America's more than ten left-wing progressive governments will build a new society or become part of fully developed capitalist rule. He holds that both outcomes remain possible and depend on several factors, including the governments' awareness of and capacity to create a new emancipatory paradigm. The report analyses four external factors and five continental processes that shaped the region's left after 1989. It then surveys changes within the left and the ideological debates over a new paradigm. The external factors are the transnational concentration of capital known as globalisation, the neoliberal onslaught of the 1980s, the collapse of the Soviet and East European socialist bloc in 1989–1991, and the adoption of neoliberal doctrine by West European social democracy in the late 1990s. Regalado's central argument is that the left's electoral rise rested on three positive factors: the accumulated effect of earlier popular struggles, the human rights movement, and the organisational capacity built up in the fight against neoliberalism. He adds one negative factor, the acceptance of a "new world order". He distinguishes two groups of governments. Venezuela, Bolivia and Ecuador came to power as neoliberal systems collapsed, whereas Brazil and Uruguay did so through long political accumulation by the Workers' Party and the Broad Front. He sees the governments facing growing threats since 2009. These are defeat or overthrow by US imperialism and the local right (he cites Honduras in 2009), erosion of popular support, or a combination of the two. On ideology, Regalado describes three phases since 1989: the discrediting of revolutionary ideas, a revival of critical analysis without a new paradigm, and, since 2006, the return of socialism through Chávez's "socialism of the twenty-first century". Alongside it he sets the Indigenous idea of "good living" (buen vivir). He concludes that Marxist positions take part in the debate but do not decisively shape any government's policy. Policy and the search for a new paradigm run in parallel, and he says this gap brings growing risks. Read the original if you want a Cuban Marxist's 2014 assessment of Latin America's left-wing governments, their threats and their ideological debates.

Beware of the so-called "pan-socialism" 警惕所谓“泛社会主义” Zhou Xincheng Zhou Xincheng takes issue with a new concept, "pan-socialism" (fan shehuizhuyi), which he says was put forward by a research unit. As Zhou describes it, the idea treats democratic socialism, ecological socialism and petty-bourgeois socialism alike as members of one "socialist family" that deserves tolerance and unity. Zhou reads this as a way of saying that democratic socialism should no longer be criticised. He argues that it is wrong and dangerous, because democratic socialism is not socialism at all but a form of capitalism. The piece opens with the historical origins of the word "socialism" and the many currents that claimed it, which Zhou lists as feudal, petty-bourgeois, utopian and bourgeois socialism. It then sets out the basic principles of scientific socialism and the difference between those principles and the concrete forms in which they are realised. After that it turns to democratic socialism, and Zhou takes its three main definitions of socialism in turn: "ethical", "welfare" and "functional" socialism. The article ends with a note on how the Party should relate to socialist parties. Zhou's central claim is that the test of socialism is whether a movement upholds the basic principles of scientific socialism. He cites Xi Jinping's remark that "if they are lost, it is no longer socialism". For Zhou these principles are Communist Party leadership, the dictatorship of the proletariat, public ownership of the means of production, distribution according to work, and Marxism as guiding ideology. Different "models" of socialism, he says, differ only in how these principles are realised, so a current that rejects them cannot count as a model. Zhou answers each democratic-socialist definition from Marx, Lenin, Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping. He treats democracy as class-bound and rejects "pure democracy". He treats welfare as a distribution policy that, in his reading, repeats the Lassallean error criticised in the Critique of the Gotha Programme, because it leaves ownership untouched. Workers' participation in management, he adds, leaves the bourgeoisie in power. Two tests decide the question: who owns the means of production, and who holds state power. Zhou concludes that democratic socialism is a model of capitalism, not of socialism. In capitalist countries he casts it as a doctor at capitalism's sickbed, and in socialist countries as a bridge to capitalism. He holds that muddying this boundary raises the question of which banner to raise and which road to take. He also separates the nature of socialist parties from inter-party relations. Citing a 1956 Party document, he calls for united-front work with their left and centre while keeping the class boundary clear, and he warns that blurring it is now the greater risk. Read the original if you want a representative Chinese Marxist case, dated 2015, for drawing a hard line between scientific socialism and social democracy.

The history, present state and future of Germany's Left Party 德国左翼党的历史、现状及未来 Liu Hui Writing after the German federal election of September 2013, Liu Hui asks how a young party formed by merger has become Germany's third-largest force yet remains unable to enter a governing coalition. The article's answer is that the Left Party's rising influence is real, but its East German legacy, its radical positions and its internal divisions keep other parties from working with it. Liu nonetheless judges the prospects positive and argues that coalition government is attainable if the party adjusts. The article has three parts. It first traces the party's origins from the East German ruling Socialist Unity Party, through its 1989 reorganisation as the Party of Democratic Socialism (PDS), to the 2005–2007 merger with the Labour and Social Justice Party (WASG) led by Oskar Lafontaine. It then describes the present party: its membership (about 69,500, of whom 37.3 per cent are women), its two co-chairs, Katja Kipping and Bernd Riexinger, and its election results of 8.7 per cent in 2005, 11.9 per cent in 2009 and 8.6 per cent in 2013. A final section considers its future. Liu credits the party with four roles: opposing war and military intervention (for example over Syria), promoting environmental protection, defending social fairness through demands such as a national minimum wage, and advancing the interests of women and children. Against this the article sets two main problems. One is disunity: the party combines two organisations with different histories, its factions lack discipline, and its strength lies far more in the East than the West. The other is the refusal of the Social Democrats and Greens to form a coalition with it. Liu attributes that refusal to history (the party's perceived inheritance from the East German ruling party), to its hard line against aid to eurozone crisis states, and to its demand to abolish NATO and break with US hegemony, which Liu describes as an ideologically tinged position. Liu proposes four steps: learn from past elections and keep up the party's work on peace, ecology and social justice; consolidate its Eastern base while tailoring policy and slogans to Western voters; play a constructive role in the European Left Party; and combine firmness of principle with tactical flexibility, toning down radical language so that a red–green–red alliance with the Social Democrats and Greens becomes possible. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese-language overview of the Left Party's origins, its 2013 election position and one scholar's assessment of its coalition prospects.

The influence of contemporary social trends of thought on young university students' thinking and behaviour, and how to guide it 当代社会思潮对青年大学生思想和行为的影响及其引导 Zheng Jie Ji Quansheng This article, posted in 2015 under ideological and political education, asks how contemporary social trends of thought (shehui sichao) affect the thinking and conduct of young university students, and how that influence should be guided. Zheng Jie and Ji Quansheng argue that students are especially open to such trends and that their ideological state will largely shape the future of socialism with Chinese characteristics. They conclude that guidance is needed at each stage in which students meet and use these ideas. The article rests on a survey of 841 students, mostly from universities in Sichuan and Chongqing, with some respondents from 15 other provinces and regions. Of these, 551 were men, 290 women, and 530 studied sciences, engineering, agriculture or medicine. It first reports what students know about social trends of thought, then sets out positive and negative effects, and ends with proposals for guidance. The survey finds shallow conceptual understanding: 51.01 per cent know the concept only a little, and 45.42 per cent cannot say whether Western ideological infiltration is a danger. Students most readily recognise money worship, individualism and democratic socialism. Books and newspapers (57.55 per cent) and classroom teaching (57.31 per cent) remain the main sources, with the internet third. The authors see positive effects in wider cultural horizons, more attention to real problems and stronger modern consciousness. They treat neoliberalism, democratic socialism and historical nihilism as the most harmful trends, claiming that they weaken faith in Marxism and in the socialist path, encourage individualism and multi-party ideas, and damage national self-respect. Since the authors divide the spread of these ideas into contact, understanding and application, they propose guidance at three points. First, the internet should be both regulated and opened up: harmful sources blocked, sound explanatory material released to students, and specialist theory websites built, while Marxist propaganda continues. Second, universities should add history and culture courses and strengthen ideological and political theory teaching, including comparisons between Marxism and rival trends. Third, public opinion should be guided by praising positive conduct and condemning illegal or immoral acts, with the core socialist value system as the standard. Read the original if you want survey data on Chinese students' attitudes to social trends of thought, or an example of how such guidance is framed in 2015 ideological education.

Challenges facing the Marxist view of journalism and strategies for responding 马克思主义新闻观面临的挑战及应对策略 Liu Zuyu Writing in 2015, Liu Zuyu argues that the Marxist view of journalism faces a serious challenge in China's media sphere. In the author's account, a Western bourgeois view of journalism holds the discursive high ground in some outlets, while the Marxist view is marginalised. The core of the struggle, Liu says, is leadership of the media by the Party, which opponents contest under the banner of press freedom. The article is a polemical commentary in two parts. The first describes the challenge: attacks on the Party principle in socialist media, the claim that the press is a "fourth power" or "public instrument", agenda-setting by online opinion leaders, the Southern Weekend incident of early 2013, and what Liu calls the hollowness of American press freedom. The second sets out four countermeasures, which the author offers as incomplete suggestions. Liu contends that the Party's leadership of the media means the Party manages the media and the guidance of public opinion, and that content is "king" only when the guidance is correct. Agenda-setting, as Liu presents it, is the deliberate amplification of isolated negative incidents to erode the legitimacy of the ruling Party, and Liu says domestic and foreign hostile forces coordinate it. Citing Xi Jinping's 2013 remark that Western press freedom has ideological bottom lines, Liu treats press freedom as a tool for ideological infiltration. Liu also argues that calls for privately owned newspapers aim to open the way to political change. Liu's proposals are these. The main official media should set their own agendas, rebut serious political rumours openly and keep control of public opinion. Internet management should be tightened. The journalist corps needs systematic Marxist training, and the political outlook of teachers in the 590 university journalism departments needs attention. Liu would also remove or retrain corrupt reporters and replace the economists and commentators who dominate media columns with Marxist scholars. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how the Marxist view of journalism was defended against liberal views of press freedom in the Chinese ideological debates of the early 2010s.

Rallying the people's hearts under the Party's banner 将民心紧紧凝聚在党的旗帜下 Liu Qifan Liu Qifan looks at the mass work of the Qiandong revolutionary base area, set up in Tongren, Guizhou, more than 80 years ago, to draw lessons for present-day work with the people. The article argues that the base area's practices, led by He Long and Guan Xiangying, won popular support and still offer guidance for gaining and holding the people's hearts. The piece has two parts. The first sets out four features of the base area's style of mass work. The second draws five lessons for today, each introduced by "must" and tied to the Party's current tasks and to Tongren's own situation. Liu describes the base area as one of eight left before the Long March, founded after the failure of the fifth "encirclement campaign". Its four features are a spirit of struggle, a spirit of sacrifice, a practical spirit (policies were posted publicly, set by the masses and checked by them) and frugality, shown in an anecdote of He Long rebuking a subordinate for adding dishes. The lessons Liu draws are to strengthen the Party's purpose, enforce full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, stand firmly on the masses' side, keep promises on livelihood, and build up grassroots organisations. Liu also criticises officials who chase false achievements and "image projects". Liu concludes that popular support is the firmest foundation of the Party's rule and the test of its work. Liu calls for concrete action on food, housing, health care and jobs, and for stronger grassroots Party organisations. Read the original if you want an example of how a local Party writer uses revolutionary history to support the mass line and the post-2012 campaign for Party discipline.

Resolutely opposing subjectivism and sectarianism 切实反对主观主义和宗派主义 Jiang Yingchun Writing in 2015, Jiang Yingchun revisits Mao Zedong's speech "Rectify the Party's Style of Work" (1 February 1942, opening of the Central Party School) to ask how the Party should combat subjectivism and sectarianism today. Jiang notes that since the 18th Party Congress (2012) Xi Jinping has repeatedly urged drawing on the Yan'an rectification campaign for the Party's mass line education campaign. The article argues that both tendencies still exist in varied forms, corrode the Party and weaken its fighting capacity, and that the speech remains a guiding text for improving Party conduct. The article is organised in three sections, each built around a phrase from Mao. The first treats subjectivism as a corrupt style of study. The second treats sectarianism as subjectivism's expression in organisational relations. The third argues that opposing subjectivism requires propagating materialism and dialectics. Jiang draws on other Yan'an-era texts by Mao and links them to Xi Jinping's speeches of 2014 and 2015. In the first section, Jiang follows Mao in treating the style of study as the fundamental question of how Marxism-Leninism is combined with Chinese realities. Mao's tests for a true theorist, and his charge that some people talk of "linking" theory and practice while in fact separating them, are read as criticism of dogmatism, including copying foreign models. Jiang applies this to present-day Marxist research, claiming it still contains "foreign dogmas" and "speaking to oneself" detached from China. Research truly tied to Chinese reality would, in Jiang's view, leave only one school, Deng Xiaoping's "seeking truth from facts" school. In the second section, sectarianism is traced to partial and personal interests, and to the question of whom one serves. Jiang cites Xi's 2014 warning against cliques and personal dependence in the Party as echoing Mao's claim that such people "come to no good end". Jiang concludes that rooting out these tendencies depends on worldview. Party members, cadres especially, must study dialectical materialism, which Jiang describes as a scientific way of thinking and working. Jiang cites superstition and fixation on rank and pleasure among some officials as signs of weak theoretical grounding. Citing Xi's January 2015 Politburo study session, the article calls on Party members to fight these styles to preserve the Party's vanguard character and purity. Read the original if you want to see how a 2015 Party-school style commentary uses Mao's Yan'an texts to support contemporary Party-conduct campaigns.

The social responsibility of Marxist theory workers 马克思主义理论工作者的社会责任 Chen Xianda Writing in 2015, Chen Xianda, a Marxist philosopher at Renmin University of China, asks what social responsibility university teachers in the humanities and social sciences bear, and in particular those who teach Marxist theory. His answer is that universities are a front line of ideological work and that teachers are the ones who must hold it, with both a sense of mission and the ability to carry it out. The commentary begins with the idea that every occupation has its responsibilities, and cites Fichte's work on the vocation of the scholar. It then moves through the place of universities, the shared ideological task of all humanities and social science disciplines, the special position of the ideological and political theory courses, and the questions students raise in class about freedom, democracy, human rights and the rule of law. Chen makes three main moves. First, he holds that every humanities and social science discipline has a guiding outlook (a view of history, of news, of literature and so on) and cannot be value-neutral. Marxism should guide these disciplines without replacing their specialist research, which should follow the 'Double Hundred' policy of free academic debate. Second, he argues that the ideological and political theory courses demand academic standards no lower than other courses. Teachers should not give students 'a bucket of water' but the ladle to draw it, meaning the ability to tell right from wrong, and should answer real social problems rather than recite slogans. Third, on freedom, democracy, human rights and the rule of law, he says no state can reject them, but their content depends on a country's social formation, economic level and cultural tradition. Teachers should therefore move beyond asking whether students want freedom to asking whose freedom and of what kind, and should reject the 'universal values' thesis and 'democracy export'. Chen concludes that teachers need firm political qualities and real theoretical ability. He acknowledges past errors such as the Anti-Rightist campaign and the Cultural Revolution, and says progress in the rule of law has been made since reform and opening up and especially since the 18th Party Congress (2012). He also welcomes constructive criticism. He warns against people who smuggle private agendas into students' legitimate demands, and says patiently explaining these questions layer by layer is the theoretical responsibility of Marxist theory workers. Read the original if you want a senior Chinese philosopher's 2015 account of how Marxist teachers should handle ideological work and student questions about liberal values.

Safeguarding national ideological security in the age of mobile networks 维护移动网络时代国家意识形态安全 Song Lidan Writing in March 2015, Song Lidan argues that mobile networks (phones and tablets that combine mobile communication with the internet) have created a new and larger challenge to China's information and ideological security. In the author's account, as China's online climate improved after recent clean-up campaigns, "hostile forces" stepped up their infiltration and propaganda through mobile devices. The article's thesis is that mobile networks now have the capacity to affect national ideological security as a whole, and that the state must tighten regulation and strengthen positive propaganda in response. The article has three parts. The first sets out why mobile networks matter, citing figures such as 875 million mobile network users in China by January 2015 and mobile phones as the main route onto the internet. The second identifies six categories of content on mobile social networks that the author says damage ideological security. The third turns to countermeasures, opening with US legislation on cyberspace and the 2011 US International Strategy for Cyberspace. In explaining the threat, Song points to precisely targeted dissemination, the difficulty of controlling information on always-carried phones, the ability of small groups to amplify their voices (citing Moldova and Iran in 2009), and a user base weighted towards students, young people and lower-income groups. The author names WeChat and its "circle of friends" as a private space that avoids public transparency. The six categories include "exposés" rehabilitating landlords and discrediting heroes or Marx and Lenin; denigration of the Communist Party's role in the anti-Japanese war and rumours about the famine of 1959–61; claims that Chinese national character is poor because of the system; fabricated data on taxes, passports and incomes; demonisation of officials, teachers and urban management officers; and rumours after emergencies such as the 2008 Wenchuan earthquake. Song calls for strengthened network supervision so that the state holds the "master switch" of network management, arguing that China should follow US and British practice and build matching laws and emergency mechanisms. The author also urges large-scale positive propaganda, the removal of offending public accounts, encouragement of accounts that spread "positive energy", research and publicity on national and Party history, and analysis of capitalism's essence and crises, in order to reinforce confidence in China's path, theory and system. Read the original if you want an example of how a Chinese scholar framed mobile internet governance as an ideological security issue in 2015.

Cultivating and putting into practice core socialist values must start from the basics 培育践行社会主义核心价值观要从基础抓起 Li Shenming Writing in 2015, Li Shenming takes up the 24-character core socialist values announced at the 18th Party Congress (2012) and argues that memorising them is easy, while cultivating and practising them is hard. His thesis is that practice, not mere knowledge, decides whether the values matter, and that it must be built up from a set of basic tasks. Without practice, he says, the Chinese Dream of national rejuvenation "can only be a piece of empty paper". The piece opens with Li's recollections of working in Zhongnanhai for over ten years, including accounts of Mao Zedong's austere living arrangements, and then moves through five numbered sections. These are: everyone is responsible; study and firm conviction; self-remoulding; leaders setting an example; and practising the values at all three levels (state, society, citizen). Li draws on a 2003 conversation with a Russian teacher in Volgograd, anecdotes about Mao and the revolutionary martyrs, and quotations from Marx and Engels, Xi Jinping and the Central Committee General Office's opinions on the values. Li makes three main moves. First, he roots conviction in historical materialism: the people are the driving force of history, Marxism cannot be judged by short spans of time, and the martyrs' sacrifices show the strength of firm ideals. Second, he holds that values derive from the economic base, so they cannot be sustained by ideological education alone. In his view they require the basic economic system of the primary stage of socialism, with public ownership predominant and several forms of ownership developing together. Third, he rejects the view that human nature is selfish, calling it a product and defence of private ownership, and insists that officials must be consistent in word and deed, since their example is decisive. He cites the 2012 eight-point rules as evidence that leadership example works. Li also answers three "misunderstandings": that freedom means doing as one pleases, that the values are merely capitalist or "universal" ones, and that those who practise them lose out. He holds that the prefix "socialist" changes their nature, and that law, policy and social justice must protect honest people. He ends by citing Mao's call to be "a noble person, a pure person", and urges that policies be brought into line with the values. Read the original if you want an example of how a senior Party theorist links core socialist values to Mao-era anecdotes, the economic base and the anti-corruption campaign.

Building "China's discursive power" from ideas and values 从思想和价值观上打造“中国话语权” Dai Mucai Writing in 2015, Dai Mucai asks why China's economic rise, which made it the world's second-largest economy by 2010, has not yet produced matching influence in ideas. The author argues that Western discourse has largely supplied the intellectual and value framework for interpreting reform and opening up. Dai calls for building "China's discursive power" through original Chinese ideas, values and proposals, which the author treats as the core task of soft power. The short commentary begins with this diagnosis: plenty of narration of achievements, but few Chinese ideas able to travel internationally. It then sets out what a new Chinese discourse system should contain, cites Xi Jinping's call to spread contemporary Chinese values, and discusses the conditions for intellectual innovation. It closes by linking the theme to think-tank building and the national rejuvenation goals. Dai holds that soft power cannot rest on self-congratulatory language. The author says the discourse must draw on world civilisation, reflect China's distinctive culture, history and path, and show that path's significance for modernization and globalization. It must also creatively transform traditional culture. Dai describes innovation, inheritance and elimination as the three movements of cultural construction in an era of great change, with innovation the main theme, and expects clashes of views to be normal, as with the "hundred schools" and the Renaissance. Dai names two conditions: thinkers and intellectuals should be the main agents of ideas, and the political and social environment should be tolerant and encouraging. The author sees the strategic task of building new-type think tanks with Chinese characteristics as opening space for this. Dai ties the matter to the "Four Comprehensives" and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a Chinese scholar in 2015 framed discursive power, soft power and think-tank building.

Mao Zedong's theory of multi-party cooperation during the War of Resistance against Japan and its historical significance 论抗日战争时期毛泽东的多党合作理论及其历史意义 Xu Ying This article asks how Mao Zedong's theory of multi-party cooperation took shape during the War of Resistance against Japan (1937–1945) and what it contributed. Xu Ying argues that the theory grew out of Marxism-Leninism combined with Chinese conditions, and that it supplied the basis for the later system of multi-party cooperation and political consultation led by the Communist Party. The article has three parts. The first sets out the theoretical sources (Marx, Engels and Lenin on cooperation among parties) and the lessons of the founding of the Chinese Communist Party and the first Guomindang–Communist cooperation. The second presents the content of Mao's theory under three headings: cooperation with the Guomindang as the party of the big bourgeoisie, unity with the democratic parties, and the "three-thirds system" of government in the anti-Japanese base areas. The third assesses its historical significance. In Xu's account, Mao treated the Guomindang alliance as a question of correctly handling relations with the Chinese bourgeoisie. He insisted on winning proletarian leadership, mainly political leadership, and on the principle of "both unity and struggle", in which struggle is the means and unity the end. Against Guomindang hardliners he advocated the rule of acting with justification, to advantage and with restraint. Xu argues that the three-thirds system, with one third each for Communists, non-Party leftist progressives and middle-of-the-road figures, put the theory into practice. It rested on the status of the democratic parties as participating parties, on democratic consultation, and on respect for their rights. Xu concludes that the theory consolidated the united front and advanced the New Democratic revolution. It also supplied theoretical grounds and practical experience for the system of multi-party cooperation and political consultation. In this reading, it enriched and developed Marxism-Leninism as an integral part of Mao Zedong Thought. Xu holds that it remains significant for cooperation with the democratic parties in building socialism with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a concise, officially framed overview of how Chinese scholarship presents the wartime origins of the multi-party cooperation system.

What is the truth? Testing five anti-Stalin lies 真相为何——检验五大反斯大林谎言 Grover Furr The article, a Chinese rendering of a report by the American professor Grover Furr (Montclair State University), takes up five widely repeated accusations against Stalin and the Soviet Union. Furr argues that these accusations are falsehoods spread by anti-communist "scholars" and have been accepted even by many on the left and by communists. The Chinese editor's introduction presents the piece as one of a series on the historical truth about the USSR and Stalin, rebutting what it calls slander by the international bourgeoisie. The text draws on Furr's book Blood Lies, a rebuttal of Timothy Snyder's Bloodlands. It takes five topics in turn: the collectivisation and famine of 1932–1933; the Great Purge and the so-called "Polish operation"; the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact and the Soviet entry into Poland in 1939; the Katyn massacre; and the Warsaw Uprising of 1944. Each section sets out what Furr calls "the truth" against the accepted account. On the famine, Furr relies on Mark Tauger's research to argue that it was caused by natural disaster and agricultural backwardness, not by collectivisation, excessive grain requisitioning or an intent to starve Ukrainians. He holds that collectivisation ended the recurrent famines. On the purges, he says archival telegrams show Yezhov deceived Stalin and himself conspired against the leadership. On Poland, he maintains that the Pact was no alliance, that the Soviet Union did not invade Poland because the Polish state had ceased to exist, and that this position was recognised internationally and is supported by a 1958 article by George Ginsburgs. On Katyn, he cites finds at Volodymyr-Volynskyi and claims of forged documents to suggest that Germans or Ukrainian nationalists killed the Polish prisoners. He describes the Warsaw Uprising as a political move aimed at the Soviet Union, doomed without Red Army help. Furr concludes that anti-communist scholars have large resources, libraries, archives and state funding, yet have produced only lies. In his view, this shows there are no genuine "Stalinist crimes". He admits that the Katyn evidence does not establish what did happen. Read the original if you want to see a committed pro-Stalin revisionist case in its own terms, as presented to Chinese readers, and to trace the sources and scholars it relies on.

Grasp the overall trend, focus on major tasks: doing ideological and publicity work in universities well under new circumstances 把握大势，着眼大事，努力做好新形势下高校宣传思想工作 Yuan Guiren Yuan Guiren's article is a study-and-implementation commentary on the Opinions on Further Strengthening and Improving Publicity and Ideological Work in Universities under the New Circumstances, recently issued by the General Offices of the Party Central Committee and the State Council. Yuan presents the document as a programmatic text that carries out Xi Jinping's directives on ideological work. The article argues that implementing it is a major task for the education system, and that it requires clear understanding, concrete priorities and improved working methods. The piece has three parts. The first explains why university ideological work matters. The second sets out four priority areas for action. The third lists four modes of thinking that officials should cultivate to raise their capacity. Yuan describes the situation in universities as basically healthy, citing 25 consecutive years of stability and the loyalty of most teachers and students. The article nonetheless warns of emerging tendencies that need close attention. Yuan calls university ideological work a strategic, foundation-strengthening and soul-shaping project that bears on Party leadership and on whether socialism with Chinese characteristics has successors. The four priorities are: arming minds with theory and the core socialist values; managing ideological positions, including classrooms, textbooks, lectures and forums, and resisting what the author calls Western erroneous views and infiltration by hostile forces; building up the internet and mainstream opinion online; and strengthening the ranks of staff through Party committee responsibility and the training of Marxist talent. For capacity, Yuan calls for strategic, bottom-line, systems and rule-of-law thinking. The author identifies winning over young people as the fundamental problem, arguing that the greatest advantage of governing is winning youth and the greatest risk is losing them. Yuan concludes that the Opinions must be put into effect through comprehensive, specific and workable plans, and not by merely answering documents with documents or going through the motions. The author also calls for better coordination among departments and for institutionalised, law-based handling of ideological problems on campus. Read the original if you want an official Ministry of Education-level account of how university ideological work was framed and prioritised in early 2015, including its stated concerns about the internet, textbooks and young people.

The historical foundations of Marxist ideological discourse 马克思主义意识形态话语的历史基础 Jiang Yingchun Jiang Yingchun asks how Marx's critique of the German ideology equips readers to identify idealist accounts of history today. The article argues that Marx dismantled the idealist mode of historical cognition and built a materialist one, and that this critique supplies a method and criteria for spotting the overreach of ideas. Jiang contends that the idealist mode survives in contemporary scholarship, where some replace "history" with "narrative" and so deny history's objectivity and regularity. The article is organised in three sections, drawing mainly on The German Ideology and The Poverty of Philosophy. The first asks why historical cognition is difficult. The second examines how ideological discourse becomes dependent on class rule. The third asks how the truth of ideology is revealed, through the contrast between false and genuine representatives of universal interests. Jiang repeatedly turns to the "farewell to revolution" thesis as a present-day example of idealist history. Jiang's core argument has three moves. First, understanding history cannot rest on intuition or everyday experience, as Marx's shopkeeper analogy is meant to show. It requires the contradiction between productive forces and forms of intercourse, the formation of world history, and a rejection of abstract "man" and of the professional ideologist's faith in concepts. Second, since the ruling class controls the means of mental production, ruling ideas express ruling material relations, so any claim to a supra-class idea is illusory. Jiang concludes that all talk of "universal values" is a false theoretical claim. Third, every rising class presents its interest as universal, and ideology grows more moralised and sacralised as social contradictions sharpen. Jiang applies this to liberal economists who call capitalism "natural" and socialism "artificial", and to earlier minority revolutions. Only the proletariat, in Jiang's account, can unite class interest with universal interest. Jiang concludes that the "farewell to revolution" thesis is a closed spiritual "system" that treats history as dough to be kneaded at will, reducing objective history to a history of ideas. Jiang reads it as claiming that Marxism's spread in China and the choice to take Russia as a model left the "mainstream of modern civilization". The author calls for this tendency to be overcome, warning of lasting harm in historical research. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist scholar uses Marx's ideology critique against "universal values", historical nihilism and revisionist accounts of the Chinese revolution.

Looking back and ahead on the Communist Party of China's pursuit of its own path 对中国共产党走自己道路的回眸与展望 Cao Yingwang Writing in 2015, Cao Yingwang takes up the much-debated question of the "Chinese path". Cao notes that the idea appears as "independence and self-reliance" in Mao Zedong, as "taking our own road" in Deng Xiaoping, and as the requirement to follow the Chinese path in realising the Chinese Dream in Xi Jinping's inaugural address as state president. The article argues that the Party's success has come from combining the universal truth of Marxism with China's concrete realities, and that this must continue. The essay has three parts. The first defines what "taking one's own road" means. The second reviews the Party's history in two stages: the revolutionary path under Mao and the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics opened by Deng. The third looks ahead, answering critics abroad and setting out four requirements for the future. In defining the concept, Cao offers five negations: it is not slavish imitation (the "Dong Shi imitating Xi Shi" image), not reliance on others, not wilful subjectivism, not clinging to past experience, and not isolated self-assertion. In the historical review, Cao credits Mao with a revolution that departed from the Russian model through rural encirclement of the cities, a broad united front that included the national bourgeoisie, and Party building. Cao also lists serious errors in socialist construction, including the people's communes, the Great Leap Forward and the Cultural Revolution, which Cao attributes to impatience and detachment from reality. Deng's path is described as economic construction based on the primary stage of socialism, the Four Cardinal Principles combined with reform and opening up, and steady development through the three-step goal. Looking ahead, Cao rejects both the "China collapse" and "China threat" theories as products of Western ideology and Cold War thinking, and describes China as peaceful. Cao calls for four things: relying on China's own strength and conditions, avoiding extremism and subjectivism by combining national spirit with the spirit of the times, keeping firm confidence, and learning from others' strengths. Read the original if you want an example of how a Party historian presented the continuity from Mao to Xi under the heading of an independent Chinese path in 2015.

From Einstein's private bluntness to Hawking's public denial An interpretation of Hawking's view of God 从爱因斯坦私下的直白到霍金的公开否定 Yu Qiming Writing in December 2014 for the Science and Atheism section of the Academy of Marxism site, Yu Qiming asks how Stephen Hawking's attitude to God should be read. Yu argues that Hawking moved from an inner rejection of God, expressed cautiously in A Brief History of Time, to an open denial in The Grand Design (2010). For Yu, this shift, set beside Einstein's private remarks, shows science's growing social influence and leading scientists' growing sympathy for atheism. The article opens with Einstein's handwritten German letter of 3 January 1954 to the philosopher Eric Gutkind, publicised when it was auctioned in London in 2008. In it Einstein called the word 'God' a product of human weakness and the Bible a collection of primitive, childish legends. Yu then sets out Hawking's 2010 statements and offers a biographical sketch: his illness, honours and popular science writing. The article also covers Hawking's boyhood interest in religion and parapsychology and the role of his first wife, Jane Wilde. Yu's central move is to reject religious readings of Hawking. Believers have quoted the closing passage of A Brief History of Time, on knowing 'the mind of God', as proof of religious implications. Yu counters that Hawking meant the laws of nature, citing his remark that God should be a personification of natural law. Yu also cites Hawking's 1981 Vatican conference, where he privately welcomed that the Pope did not grasp that his no-boundary proposal left no moment of creation, and Carl Sagan's introduction to the book. Yu reads Hawking's complaint about philosophy's decline as showing a spontaneous materialist tendency. Yu explains Hawking's earlier gentleness by his early scepticism towards the supernatural and by respect for Jane, a devout Christian. This is why he avoided calling himself an atheist and played down conflict between science and religion. Yu concludes that, once science and God conflict, a scientist pursuing the universe's origins can only side with science. Read the original if you want a Chinese atheist-propaganda reading of Hawking's religious views, with Einstein as a point of comparison.

The religious ecology of contemporary China: Christianity and atheism 中国当代宗教生态景观•基督教•无神论 Huang Kui This short commentary, posted in 2014, asks how China's increasingly plural religious landscape should be understood and answered, with particular attention to the growth of Christianity. Huang argues that this growth has an international background and that scientific atheism deserves a firmer place in mainstream ideology. The piece has three parts. The first surveys contemporary religious life, giving the author's figures for believers (about 21 million Muslims, 5.5 million Catholics, and 16 million officially counted Protestants) and describing Buddhism, Islam, Tibetan Buddhism, folk belief and groups the author calls cults. The second discusses the international context of Christian expansion. The third turns to atheism in China today. Huang contends that certain Western powers use religion and human rights as levers to pressure China, and that Western frameworks for church–state relations do not fit China. The author defends the Three-Self system as an expression of national sovereignty in religion. Huang reads rural conversion as largely utilitarian, driven by poverty, illness and conformity, and urban conversion as sometimes an expression of discontent or a protective strategy for dissidents. The author attributes this partly to a lack of appeal in mainstream ideology. Huang calls scientific atheism the more valuable option and rejects the pragmatic view that religion is useful "social capital". The author proposes atheist education for young people as a cheap "vaccine", and for Party members and society as an ideological "firewall". Huang adds that atheism's prospects depend on economic and social policy, such as universal social security. Read the original if you want an example of how a Party-affiliated atheist scholar framed Christianity and religious policy in 2014.

The merits and faults of atheism research and propaganda in the former Soviet Union 前苏联无神论研究、宣传教育的历史功过 Gong Xuezeng Gong Xuezeng takes up a question that has long divided observers inside and outside the USSR: was Soviet atheist research and education a success or a failure? The author argues that the question should be answered from a standpoint of upholding socialism and with the method of historical materialism. On that basis, Gong concludes that the programme weakened religious influence and advanced secularisation, but suffered from serious and persistent defects. The article is confined to atheism research and propaganda, not the wider Soviet religious policy. It begins with the guiding principles of Soviet atheist education, traced through to the Programme adopted at the 27th Congress of the CPSU (1986). It then gives a historical survey in two phases: from the October Revolution to the Great Patriotic War, and from the war's end to the mid-1980s. Gong goes on to identify three features of the system and ends with an assessment of its record and of Western interpretations. In Gong's account, the first phase was marked by combative 'anti-religious propaganda' under the League of Militant Atheists, with excesses such as mockery and administrative closure of churches that were criticised at a 1926 conference. After 1954 CPSU Central Committee resolutions, the work revived. A 1964 institute and later reforms led the 1977 constitution to replace 'anti-religious propaganda' with a right to conduct atheist propaganda. Gong stresses that secularisation owed more to socialist transformation of economy, culture and science than to atheist education. The listed failings are uneven reach, formalism and oversimplification, a focus on counting lectures over results, and disagreement over whether such education was needed at all. Gong rejects the Western religious view, associated with the Vatican, that Soviet atheism was forcible persecution that ended in religious revival. The author says this view reflects hostility to socialism and atheism, and mixes some true material with distorted, exaggerated or fabricated claims. Gong treats the USSR's atheism work as a closed historical subject, since Russia is no longer socialist, and urges that its lessons, especially its mistakes, serve as a warning for atheism research and education in China today. Read the original if you want a Chinese official-scholarly assessment of Soviet atheist policy and the lessons it drew for China.

On the unity of atheism research, publicity and education with freedom of religious belief 试论无神论研究宣传教育与宗教信仰自由的统一 Tian Xinming Tian Xinming takes up a practical worry inside the Party: some cadres hesitate to research and promote atheism for fear of breaching the policy of freedom of religious belief, while others argue that atheist publicity destroys that freedom. Tian's answer is that the two are not in contradiction but form a unity. The article says this unity must be explained, and then achieved through conscious effort, so that the Central Committee's position becomes the voluntary practice of cadres and the public. The article has three parts. The first sets out four shared foundations: the Constitution, Marxist theory, objective reality and the law-governed nature of religion, and the Party's commitment to the fundamental interests of the people. The second distinguishes three pairs of concepts: religion and religious ideology, religious ideology and theism, and atheism in general and Marxist atheism. The third discusses what each side must do, citing survey figures on superstition and religious belief among students and officials. Tian argues that the Constitution protects both belief and non-belief, so atheist research and teaching are lawful rights. Religion, in this account, is more than an ideology. It also has economic and political dimensions, so criticising theism is not 'waging war on religion'. Marxist atheism, unlike the 'old' atheism of the French materialists, analyses religion historically and holds that it can only wither away naturally as social conditions change, never by administrative force. Tian then lists misreadings of the policy. These include treating a citizen's freedom as a licence for Party members to believe, confusing 'respect' with 'approval' and 'protection' with 'promotion', and neglecting atheist education for the non-religious majority and for young people. Tian concludes that atheist work must follow Party religious policy, avoiding propaganda in religious venues and debates among believers, which could backfire. Equally, the policy must be read correctly so that Marxist atheism is strengthened. Tian calls for atheist education in school curricula, a ban on Party members holding religious belief, and curbs on officials who promote religion for 'political achievements'. Read the original if you want a detailed statement of how Party-aligned scholarship reconciles atheist propaganda with constitutional religious freedom.

An inquiry into the young Marx's shift from theism to atheism 试论青年马克思从有神论到无神论的思想转变 Wang Zhen Wang Zhen asks how and why the young Marx moved from belief in God to atheism. The article argues that Marx began as a theist, as his 1835 school essays show, and that his turn to atheism took shape around 1839 and is marked by his doctoral dissertation on Democritus and Epicurus, completed in March 1842. Wang further holds that the turn was incomplete until Marx developed the materialist conception of history in 1845–46. The article has four parts. It first sets out the historical, social and family background of Marx's early faith: Trier's religious tradition, his rabbinical ancestry, and his baptism and confirmation. It then analyses two school essays, one on the union of believers with Christ and one on choosing a profession. A third part examines the dissertation-period atheism, and a fourth explains the shift through external and internal causes. Wang reads the early essays as theist but already carrying seeds of doubt. God sets humanity a goal, ennobling oneself and mankind, but leaves people to find the means. Marx also looks for the human causes of union with Christ, and expresses confidence in human nature and in perfection. For the later period, Wang's central claim is that Marx converted the question of God's existence into a question about the idea of God. Drawing on Epicurus, Marx treats proofs of God's existence as tautologies that really prove self-consciousness. He sees gods as particular and local, in conflict with universal reason, and he sides with philosophy against religion. On this reading Marx was attacking the masses' idle suppositions about the gods, not the gods themselves. For external causes Wang points to the Enlightenment and the Young Hegelians' philosophy of self-consciousness. Wang also cites his liberal school in Trier and his father's deism. The internal cause is Marx's prizing of self-consciousness as active subjectivity and as universal reason. Wang concludes that this orientation set the tone for Marx's later theory of religion. Read the original if you want a close, text-based account of the young Marx's early writings on religion and the sources of his break with theism.

Scientific atheism and its social responsibility 科学无神论和它的社会责任 Du Jiwen Prepared for the annual meeting of the China Atheism Society held in Xinjiang, this text by Du Jiwen answers decades of criticism of atheism and scientific atheism. Du reports that some scholars and officials charge atheism with being a legacy of the Cultural Revolution and of 'ultra-leftism', with undermining social harmony, and with opposing religious freedom. Du declines to rebut these as political accusations and argues instead that atheism is a product of labour, human nature and civilisation, and that scientific atheism has a continuing social task. The text is organised in four sections. It defines atheism and separates spontaneous from conscious atheism; it surveys Western, Marxist and Chinese forms; it distinguishes three senses of 'religion' and analyses the ideology and social character of Christianity, with a shorter note on Buddhism; and it sets out the present role of scientific atheism in China, including the meaning of freedom of religious belief. Du holds that belief in gods concerns truth and error, not morality or politics, but that once belief is organised into doctrine and churches it acquires ideological and social functions. Reading the Old and New Testaments, Du argues that Christian doctrine contains exclusivity, expansion and closure, which Du links to religious wars, persecution and, in China, to missionary activity tied to imperialism. Du contends that religion has no essence or history of its own, only a social one, so it must be studied through its social base.
