For Marxism, Du adds, atheism is the basis of its view of religion and is built on historical materialism, scientific socialism and scientific spirit, and Du credits Lenin with an epistemological critique of religion that Du says is neglected. Du concludes that freedom of religious belief includes the freedom not to believe and to hold atheism, so that Party policy, which protects belief while propagating atheism, involves no contradiction. Du calls on scholars and cadres who treat religion as an untouchable source of stability to reconsider, and argues that atheist work should rely on the people, improve material and cultural conditions and promote a science-based way of life. On this account scientific atheism is an organic part of the scientific socialist movement. Read the original if you want a candid statement of the case for atheist propaganda within Chinese debates on religion, including its sharply critical reading of Christianity.

Socialists are practical atheists 社会主义者是实践的无神论者 Xi Wuyi Xi Wuyi takes up a phrase from Engels, "socialists are practical atheists", and argues that it is a living proposition for building a Marxist theory of religion today. Writing in the period of the Scientific Outlook on Development, Xi contends that Marx was a firm atheist, that scientific atheism is the philosophical basis of the historical-materialist view of religion, and that this atheism must be developed through socialist practice. The author criticises scholars who claim to study Marx's view of religion while avoiding atheism. The article has three parts. The first traces how Marx and Engels reached historical materialism through the critique of religion, from Epicurus in Marx's dissertation to the 1844 Introduction to the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right and The German Ideology. The second sets out scientific atheism: the roots, nature and social function of religion, the critique of religion as ideology, and the link between atheism and communism. The third turns to Lenin, Soviet Russia and the Chinese Communist Party's present-day policy. Xi's central move is to read Marx's critique of religion as inseparable from the critique of politics and economics. In this reading, religious alienation is rooted in the alienation of real life, so religion is abolished by changing the social system rather than by argument alone. From Lenin, Xi draws three points: separation of church and state with freedom of belief, the party's duty to uphold and propagate atheism, and the subordination of the struggle against religion to the proletariat's overall revolutionary task. Xi warns against crude anti-religious campaigns and rejects the argument, attributed to a professor at the National School of Administration, that Communist Party members may hold religious beliefs. The author also criticises the rise of American Christian neo-fundamentalism and "universal values" as religious ideology in foreign policy. Xi concludes that in the primary stage of socialism religion will persist for a long time and should not be abolished by administrative force. The ruling party should unite believers and non-believers, guide religion to adapt to socialist society, and hold that Party members must be atheists. Xi relates this to a harmonious society, in which atheism and theism coexist, and to a people-oriented approach in which belief is a private matter but state decisions leave no place for gods. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese scholar of religion in 2014 argues for atheism as the foundation of Marxist religious theory and Party policy.

Marx's critique of religious teleology deserves attention On J. B. Foster's study of Marx's doctoral dissertation 应当重视马克思对宗教目的论的批判 Chen Xueming Writing in 2014, Chen Xueming presents and endorses the American Marxist theorist John Bellamy Foster's reading of Marx's doctoral dissertation, The Difference Between the Democritean and Epicurean Philosophy of Nature. The article asks how Marx's materialism arose. It reports Foster's answer that the materialism took shape in Marx's youth, mainly through a critique of religious teleology inspired by Epicurus. Chen takes this as a corrective to attempts to detach Marx from materialism. The commentary opens with Foster's three-part account of materialism: ontological, epistemological and practical. Foster argues that Marx's practical materialism sits within a broader materialist view of nature and science. Chen then follows Foster's case in three steps: why Marx admired Epicurus, how Marx read Epicurus's break with Democritus, and why that break remained materialist. The piece closes with Chen's own assessment of the present-day relevance of the argument. On the first step, Foster stresses that Marx valued Epicurus above all for opposing religious teleology and driving gods out of nature. Foster treats the dissertation as more than a Hegelian exercise: written in Marx's Young Hegelian period, it already aligns with Epicurean materialism and the Anglo-French Enlightenment. On the second step, Epicurus's "swerve" of the atom lets him go beyond Democritus's mechanism and determinism by allowing contingency and freedom. Foster holds that Marx saw this as a way past a weakness of ancient materialism, which reduced thought to passive sensation. Chen stresses that Foster's main point is the third step. Surpassing mechanism can lead either to idealism or to a materialist position. Foster says Marx gives three grounds for placing Epicurus in the second camp: Epicurus never denied necessity outright, never made atoms spiritual, and joined his anti-determinism to opposition to religious teleology. Marx also criticised Epicurus for abstract possibility, which Foster reads as a sign of Marx's firm commitment to materialism. Chen concludes that Foster's work is of real contemporary significance. In his account, many people, including some who claim the Marxist label, doubt that Marx was a materialist or that his materialism opposed religious teleology. He charges them with trying to construct a Marx whose theory is compatible with religious teleology. He argues that Foster's study corrects both doubts. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese-language account of Foster's interpretation of Marx's dissertation and of how Chinese Marxist scholarship uses it in debates over Marx's materialism and religion.

What "view of religion" and what "religious studies"? With a discussion of "academic theology" (Part 2) 是什么“宗教观”，什么“宗教学”？兼论“学术神学”（下） Du Jiwen This is the second half of a polemical rejoinder by Du Jiwen, a scholar of religion, to an article by an advocate of "academic theology" (xueshu shenxue) in China. Du asks why such a field should be built in contemporary China and whether it is really non-confessional. The article's answer is that the case for it rests on vague, unsupported claims and that, despite its academic label, it does the same work as church theology. The piece has three parts. Sections five and six take up two questions: the reasons given for constructing academic theology, and its claimed status as theology "outside the church". A closing section, "Words beyond the article", turns to the opponent's proposals on how the Communist Party should treat religion. Du quotes the opponent at length and answers phrase by phrase, and sets out the background to the charge that Du had exaggerated matters (shangganshangxian) in an earlier essay. On the first question, Du doubts the claimed national "crisis of belief" and a spiritual "vacuum" to be filled by Christianity. Du calls the language of "new spiritual life" and "spiritual aura" unclear and closer to shamanism than scholarship. Du also says the claim of Christianity's rapid growth ignores secularization and the rise of atheism in the West. On the second, Du reads "outside the church" as meaning outside China's officially recognised church bodies. The opponent's globalization talk of weakened sovereignty and of Chinese becoming "world citizens", Du argues, dilutes patriotism and echoes foreign efforts to spread Christianity in China. Du adds that academic theologians still hold Christian truth claims, so their work differs from church theology only in method. Du also rejects the proposed "dual structure" in which Party members could hold a religious faith for the afterlife and a political faith in communism for this life. Du traces the labelling of Marxism as a "faith" to Bertrand Russell's contemptuous comparison and calls the idea nonsense from a Marxist standpoint. Du also objects to treating the theism–atheism dispute as a "false problem". Du affirms respect for religious freedom and welcomes a theology built by the Chinese churches. The objection is to an academic theology placed in state education and research institutions, which Du says breaches the legal separation of education from religion. Read the original if you want a sharply worded view from inside Chinese debates on Marxism, atheism and the place of theology in the university.

What kind of "view of religion" and what kind of "religious studies"? With a discussion of "academic theology" (Part 1) 是什么“宗教观”，什么“宗教学”？兼论“学术神学”（上） Du Jiwen Du Jiwen replies to a 6 August 2013 article in the Chinese Ethnic Group News (Zhongguo minzu bao) that attacked views he gave in an interview in issue 5 of Marxist Studies. Du had argued that religious research had been turned into propaganda, that Mao Zedong's call to "criticise theology" had largely not been carried out, and that "constructing theology" had flourished instead. He answers the critic point by point and argues that the critic's "Marxist view of religion", "religious studies" and "academic theology" are in substance Christian theology presented under Marxist labels. This is the first instalment of a polemical reply, and the text is marked as to be continued. After a personal opening that rejects the charge of speaking without having studied the subject, and an introduction tracing "academic theology" back to Plato, it takes up four topics in the order the critic raised them: the "Marxist view of religion", "religious studies", "criticising theology", and "academic theology". Du draws on the critic's own published wording, on Max Müller, on Russell, and on d'Holbach's Pocket Theology. Du's central moves are textual. First, he analyses the critic's opening paragraph and argues that it replaces "guidance by Marxism" as a whole with guidance by a part, a "view of religion" that the critic has framed. Second, he argues that Müller's "science of religion" was itself Christian theology, and that the critic's wide and narrow senses of "religious studies" let the field absorb atheism and give theology a legitimate academic standing. Third, he contends that treating Mao's "criticise theology" as the same as "study religion" leads, through a chain of invalid inferences, to "promoting" and then "establishing" theology. Du also sets out the critic's outline for a systematic "academic theology", with its doctrines of God, Christ, the Holy Spirit, salvation and the church. He argues that this is imported Western theology that avoids asking whether God exists, and calls it pseudo-scholarship. He calls for the legal separation of education and religion to be applied seriously and for a return to Marxism as the guiding framework, and presents his reply as an exercise of free speech. Read the original if you want a detailed example of the hostile debate in Chinese religious studies over theology, atheism and the guiding role of Marxism, and are prepared for its sharply personal tone.

Religious extremism challenges the bottom line of human civilization 宗教极端主义挑战人类文明底线 Xi Wuyi This is the text of a speech Xi Wuyi gave on 22 May 2014 at a seminar on resisting religious extremism and safeguarding ethnic unity. The seminar was jointly held by the Central Institute of Socialism-style ethnic cadre training and the China Ethnic News. Xi argues that religious extremism, although a political-science concept, is best analysed by scholars of religion. In Xi's account it is the product of extremist sects degenerating, and it forms the ideological support of violent terrorism. The speech first describes violent terrorism as a threat to human rights and national security, citing the 2001 September 11 attacks and a series of incidents in China in 2013–2014. It then turns to the ideological roots of extremism, covering the historical Kharijites, contemporary religious fundamentalism and the global spread of Wahhabism. Xi draws on Jin Yijiu's three-way typology of extremist forces: preaching, violent-terrorist and separatist. The preaching type is called the "spiritual pillar" of the other two, which Xi says call for hard power, while preaching calls for soft power. Xi links the rise of fundamentalism after the Cold War to neoliberal ideological hegemony and the decline of secular state ideologies, and attributes Wahhabism's spread to Saudi oil money. Xi describes it as displacing Sufi traditions in Xinjiang and elsewhere and lists the doctrines extremists promote, such as martyrdom, theocracy, hostility to non-believers and rejection of modern civilization. Xi concludes that extremist preaching differs from ordinary missionary work because it targets believers of the parent religion itself. Patriotic religious figures therefore bear a special responsibility in resisting infiltration from abroad. Xi also calls for further study of the link between Wahhabism and violent terrorism. Read the original if you want an example of how an official-academic voice in China framed religious extremism, terrorism and Xinjiang in 2014.

Religious extremist ideas are the greatest danger poisoning the healthy growth of young people 宗教极端思想是毒害青少年健康成长的最大危险 Erkenjan Tulahong Writing in 2014, Erkenjan Tulahong, a senior Xinjiang Party official, argues that religious extremist ideas are the greatest danger to the healthy development of young people in Xinjiang. Citing Xi Jinping's remarks on Xinjiang work, the author presents resisting the infiltration of such ideas into schools as a long-term struggle with hostile forces at home and abroad over "what kind of people to train and how to train them". The author calls it a serious political matter bearing on lasting stability and the Party's position as the governing party. The piece is organised under four headings: building a strong line of defence and consolidating education as a base for training people; heightening awareness of danger; deepening understanding and holding to a bottom-line mindset; and the confidence and persistence needed for a protracted fight. It moves from a characterisation of religious extremism, through its alleged effects on Xinjiang society and schools, to measures for the education system. Tulahong describes religious extremism as political activity under a religious disguise. In the author's account, it promotes the politicisation of religion, the label of "infidel", the idea of "holy war" and the supremacy of religion, and it contradicts the peaceful teachings of Islam. The author says it feeds the "three forces" (separatism, terrorism and extremism), seeks to win young people away from the Party, and discourages study of modern science and culture. Some teachers and students are said to waver politically, and a very small number to take part in extremist activity. The author maintains that the struggle is neither an ethnic nor a religious question but one of defending national unity. The author calls on schools to keep education separate from religion, as set out in the Constitution and education law. Tulahong also urges stronger teaching of Marxist religious theory, Party religious policy and scientific atheism, while explaining the positive values of Islam, so that students gain "immunity" to extremist ideas. The author asks for patience, a protracted effort and open denunciation of extremists, so that schools become a front against separatism and infiltration. Read the original if you want a primary example of how a senior Xinjiang official framed religion, education and security in 2014.

Why the United States backs Islamic extremist forces Chinese translation of Seymour Hersh's "The Redirection" (The New Yorker, 2007) 美国为何支持伊斯兰恐怖主义势力 Seymour M. Hersh This is a Chinese translation, posted in 2014 with an editors' note, of Seymour M. Hersh's investigative report "The Redirection", published in The New Yorker in May 2007. Hersh reports that, as Iraq deteriorated, the Bush administration shifted its Middle East strategy to confront Shia Iran and its allies. In doing so, he says, it would be working with Sunni states and, as a side effect, supporting Sunni extremist groups sympathetic to al-Qaeda. The Chinese editors present the piece as a key to understanding later events, including Libya, Syria, Iraq in 2014 and Xinjiang, and as exposing the true nature of the United States. The report draws on current and former US officials, intelligence and military advisers, Saudi and Lebanese figures and think-tank experts. It moves from Washington's policy debates and planning for action against Iran, through the role of Saudi Arabia and Prince Bandar, to Lebanon, Syria and an interview with Hezbollah leader Hassan Nasrallah. It closes on the secrecy of the operations and Congress's limited oversight. Hersh's central claim is that the strategy was driven largely by Vice President Dick Cheney and relied on Saudi money and covert channels that bypassed normal congressional funding. He describes Saudi and US support for Lebanese government allies and Sunni groups with al-Qaeda links as a buffer against Hezbollah, and support for Syrian opposition forces including the Muslim Brotherhood. Sources quoted warn that such money ends up with dangerous actors and that extremists, once released, cannot be controlled, as in the Afghan war of the 1980s. Hersh also reports Pentagon contingency planning against Iran, accusations that Iran fuelled the Iraqi insurgency, and a former official's view that this was meant to create a pretext for action. Nasrallah, whose claims Hersh says lack supporting evidence, predicts that the region will be partitioned along sectarian lines. Hersh concludes that the policy is risky and badly overseen. He compares it with the Iran-Contra affair, in which Bandar and Elliott Abrams also figured, and cites officials who say Congress has not been fully informed. Senator Ron Wyden is quoted saying that trusting the administration is difficult. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-based account of the 2007 shift in US Middle East strategy and its sectarian logic, or want to see the report the Chinese editors treat as background to later regional crises.

The Sinicization of the Marxist view of religion and its contemporary value 马克思主义宗教观的中国化及其当代价值研究 Shi Xiuxin Shi Xiuxin asks how the Marxist view of religion has been adapted to Chinese conditions and what value it holds today. Writing in 2014, Shi argues that this view is an open theoretical system that keeps its vitality only by moving with the times and innovating. In Shi's account, it has been re-interpreted through China's revolution, construction and reform, and has become the theoretical basis for how the Communist Party understands religion and makes religious policy. The article has four parts. The first traces how Marx and Engels formed their view of religion, and sets out its theoretical basis and its present significance. The second describes the Chinese adaptation of this view, covering theoretical innovation, basic policies and the Party's relations with religious figures. The third discusses problems it now faces, and a short conclusion follows. Shi draws on Chinese scholarship on Marxist religious theory and on Party documents and leaders' statements. Shi first presents Marx's position as a sublation of the Young Hegelians and a move beyond Feuerbach. Marx accepted that humans make religion, but traced its root to alienation in the state and society rather than to abstract human essence. Historical materialism is therefore the basis of the theory. Shi then argues that the Party's formula of "actively guiding religion to adapt to socialist society" is the core of the Sinicized view. Shi lists the policies tied to it: freedom of religious belief, management of religious affairs according to law, resistance to infiltration by hostile foreign forces, and unity with patriotic religious believers. Shi also credits religion with integrative, moral and cultural functions that can serve a harmonious society. Shi identifies three current challenges: Party members who hold religious beliefs, especially in ethnic minority areas; the complexity of religion and the rise of new religious movements; and the spiritual beliefs of the roughly one billion non-believers. Shi holds that Party members must remain committed atheists. Shi also holds that religious questions can be resolved gradually only through socialist economic, cultural and scientific development, while protecting freedom of belief. The article calls on scholars to build a Marxist religious theory with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese scholar of Marxist religious theory, writing in 2014, presents official religious policy as a continuation of Marx's thought.

Your brain is addicted to religion: the science of belief revealed 你的大脑对宗教成瘾：揭秘关于信仰的科学 Dick F. Swaab This is a Chinese translation of an excerpt from We Are Our Brains by the Dutch neuroscientist Dick F. Swaab, which first appeared on Salon.com. Swaab takes up a question he finds more interesting than whether God exists: why so many people believe. He answers that religiosity is shaped by genes, early brain programming and neurochemistry, and that religion gave humans evolutionary advantages. The excerpt opens with figures on belief and conflict. It cites the number of religions, religious civil wars since 2000, and belief rates in the United States, China and the Netherlands. It then contrasts the low religiosity of leading scientists with the general population. The main body has two parts: six evolutionary advantages of religion, and a section on the "religious brain" drawing on brain scans and clinical findings. Swaab argues that spirituality is about 50 per cent heritable, according to twin studies, and is linked to serotonin and to a variant of the VMAT2 gene discussed by Dean Hamer. Children, he says, absorb their parents' faith as they would a mother tongue. The six advantages are group bonding, traditional benefits of rules and taboos, comfort in hardship, answers to the unknown, relief from fear of death, and licence to attack other groups. Swaab notes that evidence for health benefits is mixed and that moderately religious people fear death most. He also reports that scans of meditating monks and Carmelite nuns show activation of particular brain regions and the dopamine reward system. He adds that such findings neither prove nor disprove God. Religious fanaticism, he says, is associated with several neurological and psychiatric conditions, and what counts as "normal" varies by culture. Swaab concludes cautiously that globalisation and the decline of war may erode religion's advantages in group cohesion and aggression. He suggests this could eventually free people from outdated religious rules, whatever they believe or do not believe. The text is published in the Science and Atheism category of the site and presents a naturalistic, atheist view of religion. Read the original if you want a popular neuroscientific and evolutionary account of religion, or want to see what atheist science writing the site carries.

Strengthening the propaganda and education of scientific atheism among Party members and cadres 加强对党员干部科学无神论的宣传教育 Zhu Xiaoming Writing in 2014, Zhu Xiaoming, head of the China Atheism Association, asks why scientific atheism, which the author says should hold a leading place in socialist ideology, has steadily declined. The article answers that five ideological obstacles hinder research and education on the subject, and that removing them is the first task. The piece is a short commentary that takes the five obstacles in turn, drawing on Marx's Critique of the Gotha Programme, Lenin's "On the Significance of Militant Materialism", Mao Zedong, Hu Jintao's 2003 instruction and the Party's 1982 Document No. 19 on religious work. It closes by linking the topic to the Third Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2013). Zhu's central move is to separate the citizen's private freedom of belief from the ruling party's ideological stance. Freedom of religious belief, the author argues, includes the freedom not to believe and to propagate atheism. Religion is a private matter for the state but not for a Marxist party, which must uphold materialism and atheism to keep its purity and advanced character. Zhu adds that general Marxist education cannot replace dedicated atheist education, that atheism is not shallow, and that promoting it does not conflict with religious policy provided it avoids hurting religious feelings. A patriotic united front with believers in political action, the author says, does not mean endorsing idealism. Zhu urges united front and religious affairs cadres to work from the standpoint of Marxism and scientific atheism and with the whole of society in view, including non-believers. The article presents the Third Plenum's emphasis on socialist core values, cultural soft power and Marxism's leading ideological position as a new opportunity for atheist research. Read the original if you want to see how a leading atheist organisation reconciled Party atheism with the policy of religious freedom in 2014.

Carrying on the past and opening up the future: striving to create a new situation for the cause of scientific atheism Work report of the Third Council of the China Atheism Association 继往开来，努力开创科学无神论事业的新局面 Xi Wuyi This is a work report delivered by Xi Wuyi on behalf of the Third Council of the China Atheism Association to the Fourth Members' Congress, covering the council's term from November 2005 to August 2013. It also mourns the deaths of the association's president Ren Jiyu and vice-president Guo Zhengyi. Xi argues that scientific atheism has made real institutional progress with Party backing, but remains an endangered discipline facing foreign religious infiltration, shortages of staff and funds, and a need for deliberate strategic building. The report has three parts. The first reviews the history of the cause since 1978: a series of Party instructions and documents from 2003 to 2013, two "windows of opportunity" (the late 1990s and winter 2009 to spring 2010), and the work of the association, the journal Science and Atheism, and the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences (CASS) research centre and office. The second analyses current threats and tasks. The third sets out the responsibilities of scientific atheism workers. Xi's central claim is that scientific atheism belongs to the Party's ideological work and to the "core socialist value system". The report describes overseas religious forces, above all the American Christian right, as pursuing "legitimate infiltration" through cultural exchange, scholarship and campus evangelism, which Xi calls cultural colonization. In this account, Christian theology entering universities challenges the legal separation of education and religion. Xi therefore supports the position that Communist Party members cannot hold religious belief, while also stating that belief is a private matter and that religious believers are not to be treated with hostility. The report criticises scholars who promote "cultural theology" and who, in Xi's words, try to remove atheism from the Marxist view of religion. Xi concludes that scientific atheism needs a proper disciplinary system. The report proposes a national "scientific atheism discipline innovation project" led by CASS, dedicated research bodies in universities and Party schools, master's and doctoral programmes, and targeted funding and source materials. It calls training younger scholars the most urgent task, noting that the current researchers are ageing and few. Read the original if you want a first-hand account, from within the atheism research community, of how scientific atheism was institutionalised in China and how its advocates framed religion, ideology and national security around 2013.

Why we must uphold atheism 我们为什么要坚持无神论 Zhu Weiqun This text is a edited transcript of a speech given by Zhu Weiqun, director of the Ethnic and Religious Affairs Committee of the national CPPCC, on 18 August 2013 at the Fourth Congress of the Chinese Atheism Society; it was revised by Zhu and published in 2014. Zhu observes that the ruling Party's dialectical materialist worldview has recently been met with neglect and mockery, and that atheism as a discipline is nearly endangered. He answers the question in the title by giving three reasons why atheism must be upheld, followed by practical requirements. The speech first sets out the three reasons: atheism is the foundation of the Party's worldview, it is a deep-rooted tradition in Chinese culture, and it is needed to counter a growing range of anti-scientific phenomena. It then turns to what upholding atheism requires: Party self-discipline and education, mass education and propaganda, higher standards among atheist scholars, and a link to the united front with religious circles. Zhu illustrates the last point with the campaign against self-immolations in Tibetan areas. Zhu argues that atheism is the starting point of historical and dialectical materialism, written into the Party constitution, and that removing it would bring down the Party's theoretical edifice and change its nature. He contends that China has historically been a secular state and culture, so that religion there has been less fanatical, and that claims that only theism supplies morality or that China needs religious "catch-up lessons" are myths. In his account, superstition among officials (consulting feng shui masters, worshipping spirits while embezzling) and the rise of cults and "masters" have a common root in belief in supernatural forces, which past campaigns have rarely addressed at the level of worldview. Zhu calls for atheism education in Party training, in schools and textbooks, and on campuses, where he wants proselytising stopped, citing the Constitution and the Education Law. He also calls for atheist scholars to answer "scientific theism" with broader scientific and religious knowledge. He stresses that atheist propaganda should not set believers against non-believers or demand that they abandon their faith, and that the aim is political unity and mutual respect in belief. He describes cooperation with Buddhist figures against self-immolation as a model. Read the original if you want a senior official's own account of Party policy on atheism, religion and the united front in the early 2010s.

Studying religious policy and doing religious work well 学习宗教政策 做好宗教工作 Zhu Weiqun Zhu Weiqun presents an overview of the Communist Party's religious policy, apparently drawn from a talk or lecture (the text does not state the occasion). Posted in March 2014, it argues that the Party's approach to religion has proved correct in the course of reform and opening up, but that new circumstances demand that theory, policy and practice be kept up to date. Zhu describes the work ahead as arduous, complex and long-term. The text begins with a survey of China's main religions (Buddhism, Daoism, Islam, Catholicism and Protestantism) and gives the author's figures for clergy and believers. It then sets out three historical features that Zhu treats as present-day advantages: state authority standing above religion, tolerance among religions, and a population that is mostly non-religious and focused on this life. The longer middle section examines the four-part basic guideline on religious work, and the final sections deal with disorderly religious growth and with foreign infiltration. Zhu argues that the Party's contribution lies in a complete set of policies for a ruling party, and that three of the four clauses of the guideline were the Party's own creation. These clauses are the freedom of religious belief, the management of religious affairs according to law, the principle of independence and self-administration, and the guiding of religion to adapt to socialist society. Freedom of belief, in Zhu's account, rests on the Marxist view that religion will disappear only when its roots do, so administrative force cannot abolish it; it includes freedom not to believe, and Zhu rejects the claim that only believers in power can guarantee it. Zhu also calls for tackling excessive religious growth, citing local officials who build temples for profit. In Zhu's view, atheist education and legal management are compatible with freedom of belief. Zhu rejects treating religion simply as culture, or as a core or 'universal' value. Zhu describes foreign infiltration, naming Vatican interference, extremist forces, the Dalai Lama clique and Western use of Protestantism, as the hardest task, and stresses limits: the aim is not to oppose religion in general. Zhu concludes that religious work needs firm management, support for religious bodies' own efforts to adapt to socialism, and clear policy limits so that more people can be united against infiltration. Zhu says restricting illegal preaching does not mean requiring believers to give up their faith, or refusing to employ foreign teachers who hold religious beliefs. Read the original if you want an authoritative account of how a senior Party figure explained China's religious policy in 2014, including its history, its legal framework and its handling of foreign influence.

Science and Atheism, 2013, no. 3 (issue 83): table of contents 《科学与无神论》2013年第3期（总第83期） This is not an article but the table of contents of issue no. 3 (cumulative no. 83) of the journal Science and Atheism, published in 2013. It lists thirteen items and a back-cover feature, with no abstracts or argument, so the issue's themes can only be read from the titles. The first group of items concerns scientific atheism in higher education and student belief. Li Shen writes against vulgarising the 'two-sided' (two-point) approach. He Husheng discusses the main content of Marxist scientific atheism education in universities. Other items include a survey of students' interest in star signs (Li Zhiying), an analysis of the present state, causes and countermeasures of students' religious belief (Ma Yutang and Zhang Jiuxian), and a call to strengthen scientific atheism to resist religious proselytising in campus culture (Yang Junfeng). A second group deals with superstition, science and religion. Ma Jinfei offers an explanation of superstitious behaviour based on control-strategy theory, and Zuo Peng treats the merging and separation of science and religion. Sun Qian asks how the universe relates to God. Yun Peiji's piece cautions against believing in the Duke of Zhou's dream interpretation. The remaining items are historical and social. They include Zhao Guangqing on Emperor Guangwu and prophetic apocrypha, Zhang Yingshan's translation of part two of a history of materialism, Huang Chao on the religious-ideological roots of the American anti-Chinese movement, and Chen Qingping on a social early-warning model against cult-group activity. The back cover carries a feature on the image of non-religious people: atheists, sceptics and secularists. Read the original if you want a quick view of the topics the journal covered in 2013, such as scientific atheism, campus religion and superstition.

Science and Atheism, 2013, no. 3 (issue 83): table of contents 《科学与无神论》2013年第3期（总第83期） This is the table of contents of issue no. 3 (cumulative no. 83) of the journal Science and Atheism, published in 2013. It is not an article and contains no argument, only the titles and authors of thirteen pieces and a back-cover feature. The listed items cluster around several themes. Several deal with atheism education and religion among university students, including Li Zhiying's survey of students and astrology, a study by Ma Yutang and Zhang Jiuxian on students' religious belief, and He Husheng's piece on the main content of Marxist scientific atheism education in universities. Yang Junfeng's title concerns strengthening scientific atheism and resisting proselytising in campus culture. Other titles address the relation between science and religion (Zuo Peng; Sun Qian on the universe and God), superstition and its explanation (Ma Jinfei, applying control-strategy theory; Yun Peiji on the Duke of Zhou's dream interpretation), and history, including Zhao Guangqing on Emperor Guangwu and prophetic texts, Huang Chao on the religious-ideological roots of the American anti-Chinese movement, and a translated instalment of a history of materialism by Zhang Yingshan. The first item is Li Shen's piece on not vulgarising the "two-sided approach", and Chen Qingping proposes a social early-warning model against cult activity. The back cover is titled "The image of the non-religious: atheists, sceptics and secularists". Because only titles are given, the contents and positions of the individual pieces cannot be described. Read the original if you want a quick overview of the topics a Chinese scientific-atheism journal covered in mid-2013, or need the authors and titles for tracing individual articles.

The formation of Chinese anti-religious theory: an analysis of the anti-religion discourse of the 1920s 中国反宗教理论的成型：1920年代非宗教话语分析 Yang Weihua Yang Weihua asks when Chinese anti-religious theory took definitive shape and what that theory consisted of. The article argues that the 1920s were the formative period: later anti-religious discourse in China, including that of the People's Republic, added no new theoretical elements. In Yang's account, political discourse dominated the decade, above all the claim that religion is a tool of imperialist aggression, so that the critique was in effect "a critique wrapped in politics". The study is a textual analysis of discourse produced during the organised non-religion and anti-Christian movements, which began around the 1922 World Student Christian Federation conference at Tsinghua. It has three parts. The first sets out the value orientations behind the critique, the second examines which social groups used the discourse and how they differed, and the third traces the sources, influence and evaluation of these ideas. Evidence comes mainly from declarations, periodicals, Communist Party documents and speeches by figures such as Li Dazhao, Cai Yuanpei, Qu Qiubai and Liao Zhongkai. Yang identifies four orientations: religion as a tool of national oppression (imperialism), as a tool of class oppression, as superstition opposed to science and reason, and as a destroyer of mind and body that obstructs individual liberation. Groups used them unevenly. Students and the Socialist Youth League were the main force. The Communist Party deployed all four, the Nationalists mostly opposed Christianity on anti-imperialist political grounds, and the intellectuals in the middle leaned on science and individual freedom. On sources, Yang says the "opium" and "narcotic" theories and class analysis came from Marx and Lenin, and the scientific rationalism came from the Enlightenment and the New Culture Movement. The imperialist-tool theory, by contrast, was a local product of rising nationalism and of triumphalist missionary slogans, with no equivalent in Russia or the West. Yang credits the movement with deepening awareness of imperialism and of "cultural aggression", and with prompting some Christians to reform. The author also finds the critique reasonable in part, given the era's national crisis. Yang adds that it was slogan-like and emotional, rarely engaged with religion itself, and tended to reject everything connected with Christianity. The author regards academic objections as beside the point, since reality demanded a politically oriented critique. Read the original if you study the intellectual history of Chinese atheism, the anti-Christian movement, or the roots of later Chinese views of religion.

Religion cannot support the values of modern society 宗教支撑不起现代社会价值 Shen Guiping Writing in 2014, Shen Guiping takes up a question raised by social problems in fast-growing China: counterfeiting, corruption, social indifference, ethnic-religious disputes and violent terrorism. Because these have produced moral crisis and loss of belief, some people look to religion for comfort and for value support. Shen answers firmly that religion cannot resolve the problems of modernization or rescue society from crisis. This short commentary first sets out the social functions of religion and its two-sided character. It then looks at the Western experience of Enlightenment and secularisation, turns to the place of religion in contemporary China, and ends with the relation between rule of law and core values. Shen argues that religion can stabilise society but can also divide ethnic groups, dull the public mind and obstruct reform. Citing Max Weber's "disenchantment of the world", Shen holds that Western modernization meant leaving religious control behind, leaving faith in the private sphere while faith in law became the public consensus. In China, Shen invokes the historical-materialist view that people create religion and social development determines religious development. Shen also cites Ren Jiyu to stress that religion rests on blind belief rather than reason. Rule of law, Shen says, rests on shared core values: in China, socialist core values of fairness, justice, equality and inclusiveness. Shen concludes that society may acknowledge the guiding role of religious values for some citizens, but should not promote religion as the foundation of civilisation or as a core value. Building industrial strategy on religious culture or social values on religious ethics, Shen warns, would heighten tension between religions. The ruling Party must therefore remain clear-headed, resolute and forceful in handling religion's social role. Read the original if you want a concise statement of an official-academic position on religion and core values in China in the early 2010s.

How to view religious issues and what to do about them An interview with Wang Zuo'an, director of the State Administration for Religious Affairs 宗教问题怎么看怎么办 Wang Zuo'an This is a question-and-answer interview, posted in January 2014, with Wang Zuo'an, who is introduced as director of the State Administration for Religious Affairs. The reporter asks why religion draws growing attention in China and how it should be understood. Wang answers that rising numbers of believers, complications in the religious sphere and religion's wider social influence require correct handling, and that they also raise a deeper question about Chinese people's beliefs. The interview works through three questions Wang says must be settled: how to see the growth in believers, how to see religion's social role, and how to see the mass of believers. It then turns to the policy of freedom of religious belief and to the lawful administration of religious affairs. Wang gives figures, comparisons with other countries and practical examples of administration and services. Wang says the commonly cited figure of "over 100 million" believers is a mix of statistics and estimates, and that the real number is probably higher. He attributes the growth to recovery after the Cultural Revolution, foreign influence and, above all, deep social change, stratification and uncertainty. He judges the situation "basically orderly" and "basically stable", comparing it favourably with the former Soviet Union and with Europe and America. Religion, he argues, will exist for a long time and may grow, so believer numbers can be neither forced down nor promoted. Citing the Marxist view of religion, he describes its social role as dual, and says believers are part of "the masses" whose basic political and economic interests match those of non-believers. Impatient attempts to "liberate" them from religion would be counterproductive. Freedom of belief rests on three adherences: freedom to believe or not, separation of religion and state, and unity of rights and duties. Wang concludes that religious affairs should be managed by law: by bringing them within the legal system, setting clear rules under the Regulations on Religious Affairs, tackling difficult cases such as infiltration, and providing services. He gives examples such as social security for clergy and infrastructure for places of worship. He also stresses protecting lawful religious rights against forced demolition and against temples being commercialised or contracted out. Read the original if you want an official statement of how China's religious affairs chief explained policy on believers, religious freedom and legal administration around 2014.

On the Marxist study of religion in China 关于我国宗教学的马克思主义研究 Du Jiwen Du Jiwen asks what a Marxist study of religion in China should look like and how it began. The article answers through the work of Ren Jiyu, founding director of the Institute of World Religions, and argues that Marxist religious studies must rest on solid knowledge, historical-materialist analysis, scientific atheism and intellectual independence. Du presents it as a personal view, written to mark Ren's 90th birthday. The essay has five parts. It starts from Mao Zedong's directive proposing the Institute and then examines Ren's Buddhist studies, which Mao held up as a model. It goes on to the Institute's work in collecting materials, training scholars and building disciplines through history, theory and reference works. Du then discusses scientific atheism and the journal Science and Atheism, and ends on independence in research. A note says the piece was first given as a 2006 conference talk and was later printed in a shortened form. This version restores the cut passages. Du's first main move reads Mao's directive as a call for knowledge of religion and for Marxist analysis, not for crude denunciation. Ren's method is described as treating religion as a product of social existence and the economic base. It also credits the active role of consciousness, and offers "critique" as reasoned, historicist evaluation in the sense of sublation, not the mass denunciation of the Cultural Revolution. Du cites the Religious Dictionary (1981), the History of Chinese Buddhism and the multi-volume world religious histories as outcomes. The author reports that Japanese and Taiwanese scholars and publishers recognised their scholarly value. Du's second move defends atheism as inseparable from serious religious research. Du defines Marxist atheism as a philosophical and scientific critique of the worldview of theology and of belief in spirits, and as training in correct thinking. Religious belief remains a citizen's right, but Du says China lacks science, not spirits. Du concludes that the Institute is a research body, neither a religious organisation nor an administrative office. Its work should accord politically with patriotic religious groups and government departments while being academically original. Du argues that independence needs material support, and criticises policies of "income generation" and "pushing research into the market" as damaging to scholarship. The essay treats patriotism as the bottom line of Marxist research and closes with a polemic against a Chinese commentator who urged the US president to bring political change to China. Read the original if you want an insider's account of the Institute of World Religions, Ren Jiyu's methods, and the case for scientific atheism within Chinese Marxist religious studies.

Be vigilant against the cultural infiltration of the international Christian right 警惕国际基督教右翼势力的文化渗透 Xi Wuyi Writing in 2013, Xi Wuyi asks how foreign religious forces threaten China's security and what response is needed. The author argues that the global expansion strategy of American Christian neoconservatism has become a tool of US hegemony, that China is its key target, and that its aim is to change China's ideology and political system. Xi concludes that China must pay particular attention to the "legal infiltration" of the overseas Christian right and must build up the discipline of scientific atheism. The article defines religious infiltration in three parts: hostile forces using religion to subvert the state; foreign religious bodies seeking to control Chinese religious groups or set up bases; and right-wing religious forces working through "cultural exchange" and "academic research". It is organised in five sections: the global strategy of Christian neoconservatism; its intentions towards China; the resulting threat to national security; legal infiltration in universities and scholarship; and the case for scientific atheism. Evidence includes the 1998 International Religious Freedom Act, US State Department reports, a 2006 White House meeting with house-church figures, campus evangelism, internet missionary work and Templeton-funded lectures. Xi contends that after the Cold War "religious freedom" was made the cornerstone of a human-rights discourse that serves US national interests, citing the 1998 Act as a form of "faith-based diplomacy". In Xi's reading, the Western aim is to "peacefully evolve" China through support for house churches, campus fellowships and online evangelism, which the author calls cultural colonisation. The most subtle channel, Xi argues, is academic: foundations such as the Templeton Foundation fund talks and books claiming that modern science depends on Christianity, which Xi says have reached leading Chinese universities and been echoed by Chinese scholars. Xi counters with Engels on medieval theology, the Galileo case and the Enlightenment critique of religion. Xi argues that scholarship in China has tilted towards "carefully protecting" religion, that scientific atheism has almost no voice, and that some authorities try to separate atheism from Marxism. The author calls for a systematic scientific atheism discipline, linked to historical and dialectical materialism, the core socialist value system and Party religious policy, as the theoretical weapon against foreign religious infiltration. Xi adds that ideological work should be gentle and persuasive. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese scholar of atheism framed foreign Christianity as a security and ideological issue in 2013.

Strengthening the discipline of scientific atheism to resist "cultural proselytizing" on campus 加强科学无神论学科建设，抵御校园文化传教 Yang Junfeng Writing in 2013, Yang Junfeng asks how scientific atheism can respond to what the article calls "cultural proselytizing" in universities and research institutions. Yang argues that religious theism is spreading into education and research with funding from religious bodies and overseas forces. In this account, scientific atheism's voice has almost vanished from academia and schooling, so that "theism has speakers, atheism has none", as in the 1990s. The article's answer is that the discipline of scientific atheism itself must be strengthened. The article has two parts. The first argues that atheism is by nature a body of thought that keeps pace with the times. The second sets out four proposals for building the discipline. Yang draws on Engels's Anti-Dühring and Marx's Capital for the roots of religion. The article also looks back at the 1990s "qigong fever" and the Falun Gong affair, citing Ren Jiyu's criticism of pseudo-science. Yang's central claim is that atheism has no content of its own beyond negating and criticising theism. It must therefore change whenever theism changes. The article traces atheism from ancient naive atheism through early modern militant atheism to Marxist atheism. Yang says only the last explains the real roots of religion, and that superstition keeps returning in new disguises, such as "national learning fever" today. The proposals are: (1) answer modern Western theology directly and academically, through "internal critique" rather than slogans, on five issues: the origin of faith, religion and culture, religion and morality, religion and science, and specific doctrines such as "intelligent design" and the "religious market" theory; (2) publicise the policy of separating education from religion and strengthen atheist education in schools; (3) give atheism a positive content, offering answers on life's meaning and moral foundations as well as criticism; (4) update basic theory, since the two standard histories of atheism, from 1992 and 1993, are dated and the field's only journal is outside the core-journal indexes. Yang concludes that atheism's strength depends on whether it can respond squarely to the theism of its day, as Epicurus, Fan Zhen, Hume and Russell did. Yang also calls for atheism to propose its own solutions to social problems such as food-safety scandals and corruption. Some scholars, the article says, blame atheist education for a loss of belief. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic atheist's own account of the 2013 debate over religion in universities, and of the programme proposed for rebuilding scientific atheism.

Why Communist Party members cannot hold religious belief 共产党员为什么不能信仰宗教 Li Shen Writing in 2013, Li Shen defends the principle that Communist Party members should not believe in religion. The article's single ground for the principle is that gods do not exist. Li argues that a Communist who wants to make revolution and secure human happiness cannot coherently seek help from a non-existent deity or embrace a religion built on belief in one. The piece has three numbered sections. The first traces the history of divine figures, from animal gods to composite creatures, deified heroes and kings, and finally the purely spiritual gods of the civilised era. The second looks at how new gods have always displaced old ones, at the eighteenth-century European break that denied the existence of gods altogether, and at the claim that atheists cannot disprove God. The third turns to the origin of religious doctrine and to present-day calls for Party members to be religious. Li's central claim is that human beings, finding that each kind of god failed to deliver the promised happiness, learned that they can rely only on themselves. Responding to the argument that atheists cannot prove a negative, Li says the burden lies with those who assert the existence of a god, and that the history of changing ideas of the divine shows gods to be non-existent. Li also points to Anselm and Thomas Aquinas: a proof of God's existence is needed only because some doubt it, and Tillich is cited as saying that arguing for God's existence is itself a profanation. All "divine will", Li holds, is in fact human will, that of shamans, theologians and clergy, and religions that were once progressive turn backward because they present their ideas as eternal truth. Li rejects the view that religion improves morality, drives science or widens the Party's base of support. Li notes that the people urging Party members to believe are mainly Party members themselves, some of them scholars or senior cadres, who take part in religious activities or have become believers, and calls for special attention to this. Such talk, Li concludes, is either ill-intentioned or confused, and must be resolutely resisted. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the atheist argument against Party members holding religious belief, as it was put in China in 2013.

China's humanist tradition and the spirit of atheism 中国的人本主义传统和无神论精神 Du Jiwen Du Jiwen asks what distinguishes the Chinese religious and moral tradition from the monotheist West, and answers that China has long been "human-centred" rather than "god-centred". Where Western humanism is tied to the Renaissance, Du argues that Chinese humanism was already forming in ancient civilisation. It rests on two principles: in the relation of heaven and humans, "the human is the root"; in the relation of ruler and people, "the people are most precious". Du calls this the key to understanding China's whole history and present. The article, published on this site in 2013 under the category of science and atheism, has three parts. It first describes the humanist features of traditional Chinese religion (Confucian, Buddhist and Daoist). It then traces the move from humanism to atheism, from Buddhism's adaptation in China through the late Qing and the May Fourth movement. Finally it examines Confucian answers to the origins of morality, before turning to the present-day state. Du's core argument has three moves. First, in China the sacred is made by humans, anyone can become a sage or immortal, and gods are created and discarded by people. On this basis Du claims China had no religious hatred, persecution or wars, and that polytheism and atheism coexisted. Second, Du holds that morality in the tradition is secular. Buddhism succeeded because it fitted this ethos, whereas Christianity's exclusive monotheism kept it from taking root; efforts at "saving the nation through religion" failed, while science and democracy changed China. Third, Du reads Confucian sources (Guanzi, the Liji, Mencius, Xunzi) as explaining morality by living conditions, distribution, social system and human nature, never by gods. Du concludes that the new China inherits this tradition: the state is founded and its constitution made according to the people's will, with power belonging to the people. In Du's account, believers and non-believers have equal rights and duties, belief is a private matter, but there is no place for gods in state decision-making. Read the original if you want a Chinese atheist scholar's account of how traditional Chinese culture is used to ground secular politics and religious policy.

Scientific atheism and its social responsibilities (Part 2) 科学无神论及其社会职责（下） Du Jiwen This is the second half of a two-part article by Du Jiwen. It asks what "religion" actually consists of and what scientific atheism should do about it today. Du argues that theism is the core of every religion, but that a religion's historical character and social function come from the ideology and organisation attached to that core, not from belief itself. On that basis Du presents scientific atheism as compatible with freedom of religious belief and as a lasting task. Part 3 separates three senses of "religion": religious ideas, religious practices, and organised, ideologised religion. It then uses historical cases (Zoroastrianism, Buddhism in India and Central Asia, the decline and expansion of Christianity) and a close reading of the Bible and of Buddhist scriptures. Part 4 turns to the historical role of atheism in the West, to current religious and political conditions in China, to the history of religion in China, and to the Chinese Communist Party's stance. Du contends that only the third sense has a social character and that it obeys historical laws, so religions have a "historicity" and "changeability" rather than permanence or ethnic essence. Du reads the Old and New Testaments as adding doctrines to belief in God: original sin and redemption, absolute exclusivity and expansionism, and internal closure. Du says these supply the basis for religious wars, persecution and missionary drives, and that the New Testament's "love" amounts to a duty to convert. Buddhism is described as milder but also exclusive in places. Du holds that Western atheism targeted Christianity, while Christianity changed its service from divine authority to capital. On China, Du claims that religious persecution and religious wars are absent from its history, and that religion became a serious problem only with Christian expansion after the Opium War. Du warns that some Party members and officials treat religion as untouchable and atheism as an offence, and says central policy on atheistic research and education has not changed. Du calls freedom of belief inclusive of the freedom to hold atheism. Scientific atheism should protect the core of belief, weaken exclusive ideology, raise citizens' independence, and help improve people's material and cultural lives. Read the original if you want to see how a leading Chinese scholar of religion argues for the compatibility of Party atheism and religious freedom, with detailed critical readings of Christian and Buddhist texts.

Scientific atheism and its social responsibilities (Part 1) 科学无神论及其社会职责（上） Du Jiwen Du Jiwen responds to the poor reputation that atheism, and scientific atheism in particular, has acquired in recent decades. Prompted by the Chinese atheism annual conference held in Xinjiang, Du notes that the attacks come not from religious circles but from some scholars and officials. Critics charge atheism with being a legacy of the Cultural Revolution's "ultra-leftism", with damaging social harmony and with opposing the policy of freedom of religious belief. Du declines to rebut these as political accusations and instead argues that atheism is a legitimate body of knowledge, grounded in labour and human nature, and an integral part of Marxism. This is the first part of a two-part article. The first part has two sections. The first defines atheism and distinguishes spontaneous from conscious atheism. The second surveys types of atheism: Western forms, Marxist atheism and its Leninist development, and the Chinese tradition. The discussion moves from the Renaissance and Enlightenment to the Young Hegelians and Feuerbach, then to Marx, Engels and Lenin, and finally to the Chinese terms for atheism, from ancient debates to Zhang Taiyan, Chen Duxiu and Hu Shi. Du argues that labour and sexual reproduction show that humans are atheists by instinct, so religion is a burden added later. Conscious atheism arose to criticise theism and has developed alongside religion, and Du cites the Encyclopaedia Britannica's description of atheism as a product of civilisation and thought. For Du, theism and atheism concern truth and error, not morality or politics, but once theism is organised in churches it acquires social and ideological functions. Marxist atheism, which Du ranks as the highest form of scientific atheism, has three features: the materialist conception of history, the practice of the scientific socialist movement, and a consistent scientific spirit. Du holds that no Marxist view of religion exists apart from the whole of Marxism and criticises scholars who detach it from atheism. Du also contends that Lenin's epistemological critique of religion has been neglected. In China, Du says, atheism had no name of its own because the tradition mixed polytheism with non-belief and recognised no creator god. The part published here ends with the argument that Chinese usage of "atheism" descends from the May Fourth tradition, which rejected both monotheistic and popular superstitious belief. Du's stated aim is to show that atheism is a scholarly and scientific position, not a political liability. The social responsibilities of scientific atheism promised in the title presumably follow in the second part. Read the original if you want to see how a leading Chinese scholar of religion defends atheism against critics inside the Chinese academy and in debates over Marxist views of religion.

An investigation of the Templeton Foundation's religious orientation and its funding 邓普顿基金会的宗教倾向及其资助情况调查 Huang Yanhong Writing in 2013, Huang Yanhong takes up a question the author says Chinese scholars have rarely examined: what is the John Templeton Foundation, which has become a frequent presence in Chinese academia, and what orientation lies behind its funding? The article argues that the foundation has a clear religious, specifically Christian, tendency. In the author's reading, it presents itself as neutral between science and religion while using science and established scientists to defend religion. The article is built in three parts. The first covers the foundation's history, its founder John Templeton (1912–2008), an investor and devout Christian, and the Templeton Prize, including the 2012 award to the Dalai Lama. The second analyses the foundation's funding areas and two China-related projects. The third reports criticism from Western scientists, drawing on the foundation's own website and university sites for its material. Huang's central move is to read the funding portfolio itself. The author argues that the "Science in Dialogue" and "Human Sciences" categories are mostly about religion, and that projects are tilted toward it, so the answers to the foundation's "Big Questions" are one-sided. Two China projects are examined as evidence. The first is "Science, Philosophy and Faith: A Programme for Chinese Scholars" (2005, US$2 million, Calvin College). Huang says its design, with study visits to church-run universities, 10,000 books and lecture series, aims to Christianize Chinese intellectuals. The second is the 2009–2013 "Chinese Spirituality and Society Program" (Purdue University, nearly US$2 million). Huang says its required research themes, such as religion and entrepreneurship and religious markets, are favourable to religion and survey the distribution and influence of religion on the mainland. Huang then cites Western critics, including Sean Carroll, Richard Dawkins and a 2011 article in Evolutionary Psychology that raised five doubts about the foundation's integrity. The author concludes that the natural sciences can correct themselves, but the humanities and social sciences are more exposed, and that the foundation's growing footprint there in China deserves serious attention. Read the original if you want an early Chinese critical account of Templeton's funding in China, with specific project details and the Western criticisms the author draws on.

Religious studies needs to be set right, and the critique of theology needs to be made up An interview with Du Jiwen, former director of the Institute of World Religions, Chinese Academy of Social Sciences “研究宗教”亟须拨乱反正 “批判神学”必须开展补课 This is an interview, conducted by a reporter from the journal Science and Atheism in 2013, with Du Jiwen (born 1930), second director of the Institute of World Religions at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences and editor-in-chief of the journal. It marks the 50th anniversary of Mao Zedong's 1963 instruction to set up the institute. Du argues that religious studies in China has grown enormously but has drifted from Marxist guidance, and that Mao's call to "criticise theology" was neglected, with serious consequences. The interview moves from the institute's early work (dictionaries, histories of the three major religions, training of graduate students) to present problems. Du discusses the blurring of religious research and religious propaganda, popular claims that religion promotes goodness and harmony, and the difference between legal religions and underground churches or cults. He then turns to the phrase "the Marxist view of religion", and to the "Sinophone Christian theology movement" and its overseas links. Du's core claims are three. First, he holds that market incentives have turned some religious scholarship into advocacy, and that "Western religious studies" is in essence Christian theology. Second, he criticises official-style formulations of "the Marxist view of religion" as conceptually loose, and argues that they risk turning academic questions into matters of principle and reading historical materialism as saying that religion is "good" because society is. Third, he describes the Sinophone theology movement, begun in Hong Kong in the 1990s and linked to Nordic conferences and North American funders, as an effort to replace "Christianity adapted to China" with "China adopting Christianity". In his account it is a continuation of Western cultural missionary strategy and, increasingly, a social and political movement. Du concludes that the knowledge of religion now being supplied is distorted and needs to be set right, and that theological preaching in universities and research institutes should be criticised and kept apart from education, as the principle of separating education from religion requires. He distinguishes this from criticism of church theology, which he treats as a private matter protected by law. He sees the rescue of atheism as an "endangered discipline" as a promising step. Read the original if you want a detailed, polemical insider account of 2013 debates in Chinese religious studies, the atheist critique of theology, and the Sinophone Christian theology movement.

Only firm belief in scientific materialism can sustain scientific atheism 只有坚信科学唯物论，才能坚持科学无神论 Yang Mingwei Writing in 2013, Yang Mingwei argues that scientific atheism cannot be upheld unless Marxism's scientific materialism is first firmly held. Yang identifies as the most worrying phenomenon in Chinese intellectual and social life a shaken theoretical foundation and a loss of belief, rooted in doubts about the scientific character of Marxism and the prospects of the communist cause. In Yang's account this drift shows up as a slide toward idealism, religious theology and theism. The piece is built around two requirements: holding the correct standpoint and reading the situation correctly. The first part draws on the constitution, Lenin, Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping to affirm dialectical and historical materialism as the basis of the Party's guiding thought. The second part surveys the international scene after the global financial crisis, citing a series of Western economists, journalists and politicians, as well as communist parties and the Cuban setting. Yang contends that voluntarism and idealism now affect decision-making, comparing present-day rushes for rapid results to the Great Leap Forward. Yang also describes a situation in which theism is preached while atheism goes unspoken, with some Party members and officials turning to spirits and religious superstition. Citing Lenin's philosophical notebooks, Yang holds that abandoning materialism leads to 'priestcraft', since idealism and clericalism are treated as one. On the second requirement, Yang argues that Marxism has historically developed in opposition to religious theology. Yang reads Fukuyama's later remarks, and the comments of Nouriel Roubini, Stephen Resnick, Richard Wolff, Jean-Claude Delaunay, Georg Magnus and others, as evidence of a Marxist revival abroad. The crisis, in this reading, reflects the failure of a system resting on idealist philosophy and religious theology. Yang concludes that two developments should settle the matter: the achievements of the Chinese path of socialism with Chinese characteristics and the worldwide return to Marx. Together these, Yang says, give no reason to waver in belief or in the guiding role of scientific materialism and scientific atheism. Read the original if you want an example of how a Party-affiliated researcher linked the defence of atheism to ideological discipline and to Western commentary on Marx after 2008.

An analysis of the factors behind superstition among some officials 部分官员迷信的影响因素透析 Cheng Ping Writing in 2013, Cheng Ping asks why some Chinese officials turn to superstition and what can be done about it. Citing recent press cases, including a decommissioned aircraft placed in front of a county Party committee compound in Hebei, the renaming of a lake in Jiangsu and a "sword against evil" at a court in Changchun, Cheng argues that such acts reflect weak ideological cultivation, spiritual emptiness and lost belief, and that they damage Party and social conduct and feed corruption. The article is a short commentary in two parts. The first identifies three main causes, ordered from historical-cultural background to present circumstances to personal interest. The second proposes two remedies: ideological and moral development, and institutional development. On causes, Cheng points to the lingering influence of traditional folk practices such as divination and feng shui, which some local officials revive or package as local culture while pursuing GDP growth. Cheng also cites a crisis of belief and the heavy psychological pressure on officials. Unfair promotion practices, in which \"running and gifting\" brings advancement, leave officials anxious and powerless. Finally, Cheng argues that fear of losing vested interests drives superstition, above all among corrupt officials who seek supernatural protection from punishment, so that corruption is the root of such belief. Cheng concludes that solutions require rebuilding both minds and institutions. Discipline and education are to be combined, with firm punishment of corruption and of officials who use superstition in their work. Cheng also calls for reform of cadre selection and for confining power within institutional limits, as set out in the 18th Party Congress report (2012). Once corrupt officials are certain to be caught and punished, Cheng holds, superstition will lose its basis. Read the original if you want an official-discourse view that links officials' superstition to corruption and promotion practices.

Superstitious behaviour: an explanation based on control strategy theory 迷信行为——基于控制策略理论的解释 Ma Jinfei Why do superstitious practices persist, and even take new forms, in an age of rapid scientific and technological change? Ma Jinfei takes up this question from a psychological angle, using control strategy theory. The article argues that superstition is a way of regaining a sense of control in uncertain, stressful situations, and that rising scientific literacy will eventually eradicate it. The article opens with Chinese survey data on university students, including figures on belief in ghosts and fate, wearing lucky charms, divination and online fortune-telling. It then sets out control strategy theory, first proposed by Rothbaum and colleagues in 1982 and developed by Heckhausen and Schulz. Ma applies the theory under four headings: situational triggers, cognitive factors, emotional factors and adaptive function. The evidence is drawn almost entirely from Western psychology, such as studies of athletes, gamblers, sailors, investors and soldiers, Keinan's exam-stress experiment and Langer's work on the illusion of control. Ma also cites their own earlier master's thesis on risk and control illusion. The theory distinguishes primary control, which acts directly on the environment, from secondary control, which changes the person's own cognition. Superstition is classed as a secondary illusory control strategy, resting on beliefs in luck or fate that have no causal link to outcomes. In Ma's account, people turn to it when preparation reaches its limits, as with exam questions or an opponent's play. Even people who doubt its effectiveness may still use it to gain a feeling of control. Ma presents this feeling as a way to ease anxiety and to counter learned helplessness. Citing Neil and Keinan, the article adds that superstition can work as a psychological placebo and a self-fulfilling prophecy, raising optimism and performance. Ma concludes that humans in every era face the unknown, so superstition survives as a way of regaining control and inner calm, and attracts people whenever their sense of control weakens. The article calls for science education and continued ideological and political education, especially for university students, to make people doubt that superstitious strategies work. Education would stop superstition from being used as a primary control strategy, which Ma regards as having no adaptive value. Read the original if you want a short, psychology-based account of superstition from a Chinese science-and-atheism perspective, with a bibliography of English-language studies on the topic.

On the main content of Marxist scientific atheism education in institutions of higher learning 论高等学校马克思主义科学无神论教育的主要内容 He Husheng Writing in 2013, He Husheng asks what Marxist scientific atheism education in Chinese universities should actually teach. He treats such education as an important part of Party building and ideological and political education on campus. In He's account it bears on Marxism's guiding position in the ideological sphere, on the Party's advanced and pure character, and on training qualified builders and reliable successors for socialism. His answer is a framework of "five points": a basic point, a key point, a core point, a focal point and a point of arrival. The article opens by defining scientific atheism as atheism founded on dialectical and historical materialism. It then devotes one section to each point. The basic point is education in dialectical and historical materialism. The key point is education in upholding science and opposing superstition. The core point is education in the Marxist view of religion. The focal point is education in the socialist core value system, and the point of arrival is education for the free and all-round development of the human being. A short closing section ties the five together. In He's reading, the core is the Marxist view of religion, taught through three strands. The first is the basic theory of religion's origins, nature and eventual disappearance, which He says rules out any attempt to abolish religion by administrative force. The second is the Party's and state's religious policy: freedom of religious belief, administration of religious affairs according to law, and independent self-management of religion. The third is the rule that Party members, including student Party members, may not hold religious belief. Alongside this, He says students must distinguish religion from "evil cults" and from folk custom, and must learn to oppose feudal superstition and pseudo-science while respecting customs. The socialist core value system is presented as the platform for this teaching. He's final point is that overcoming the intellectual bondage of theism, raising scientific and cultural quality and developing the productive forces serve the free and all-round development of the person, which he calls the starting point and destination of scientific atheism. He concludes that the five points are interconnected and inseparable, and that together they should produce students with a scientific worldview, outlook on life and values. He wants students to respect freedom of religious belief while drawing a clear line against theism as a worldview. The aim is for them to become qualified builders and reliable successors of socialism. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially aligned account of how Chinese academics frame the curriculum of atheism education, Party-member restrictions on belief, and religious policy in universities around 2013.

Propagating scientific atheism with confidence Reply to a reader's letter on why atheist education should be strengthened 理直气壮地宣传科学无神论 Ren Jiyu This text is a reply to a reader's letter. The reader, Shen Zhang of Beijing's Haidian District, writes that witchcraft, superstition and pseudo-science are resurging while work on scientific atheism is weakening. The reader asks an expert to explain why it should be strengthened. The Party journal invited Ren Jiyu, honorary director of the National Library and head of the China Atheism Society, to answer. Ren argues that scientific atheism must be propagated openly and with conviction, and that this does not conflict with religious freedom. The reply is organised around questions printed as headings.
