They cover the difference between 'naive' and scientific atheism, the Marxist view of religion, whether atheist propaganda contradicts Party religious policy, what makes an ideology rational, and how political respect for belief relates to ideological commitment to atheism. Ren draws on Engels, Lenin, the history of Western atheism from the Renaissance onwards, and the Party's own record. Ren distinguishes pre-modern 'naive atheism', which criticised particular ghost-and-god notions but could not deny them at root, from scientific atheism, which rests on the scientific revolution from Copernicus onwards and also explains how belief in gods arises. Science is therefore atheism's 'natural ally', and Marxism took this tradition to a new level. Drawing on the Marxist view that religion has social roots, Ren holds that religious organisations and religious ideas should not be confused. Religious problems are to be solved by changing social relations, not by ideological struggle alone. Ren says atheism is acquired through education, so propaganda is needed. Quoting Engels, Ren says demanding that everyone become an atheist would be 'serving the gods'. Atheist work is aimed mainly at the Party's own base, not at believers, and past ultra-'Left' errors must be corrected. Ren concludes that political respect for citizens' freedom of religion and ideological insistence on scientific atheism form a unity of opposites, not a metaphysical contradiction. Freedom to believe without freedom to propagate atheism would be a loss of freedom. Attacking believers in atheism's name would violate their rights and damage unity. For the Party, religious belief is not a private matter, since its worldview is dialectical and historical materialism. Ren also describes plurality of belief as normal in a healthy society. Read the original if you want a short statement of how a leading Chinese atheist scholar reconciled atheist propaganda with the constitutional protection of religious belief in 2013.

A review of surveys on the religious beliefs of university students in Beijing 北京大学生宗教信仰调查研究综述 Huang Yanhong This literature review, published in 2013 in the Science and Atheism category, surveys published empirical studies of religious belief among university students in Beijing. Huang sorts the findings into five areas and then argues that the field has three shortcomings, the main one being the lack of a scientific-atheist perspective. The review covers survey and fieldwork studies from the late 1990s to about 2011. They include projects funded by the Beijing education authorities, the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, the Ministry of Education and the Communist Youth League, and work by teams at Beijing Normal University and Renmin University. It also covers several master's and doctoral theses. Huang excludes literature reviews and purely textual analyses. The five areas are the basic situation of belief, routes into religion and reasons for belief, religious ideas and activities, the effects of belief, and policy recommendations. On the basic situation, Huang reports that the surveys put the share of believing students at roughly 9 to 22 per cent, with a rising trend, and Christians at about 3 to 5 per cent. Believers are more often female and in lower years, and they differ by family background and field of study. Most students are said to meet religion through books, classes and friends and to convert at university. Reported motives are mixed, and the studies disagree on how far family influence matters. Student Christians are said to prefer fellowship groups and house gatherings, often led by foreigners. Several studies cited by Huang describe this as foreign religious infiltration, and they stress its effects on students' values. Huang identifies three weaknesses. No survey proceeds from a scientific-atheist standpoint, a discipline Huang calls endangered. Some studies lack objectivity because they apply Western theories such as the religious-market theory and rely on believers' own accounts. Others show too little grasp of religion or sociological method, for example in probing doctrines such as sin or the funding of house churches. Huang calls for respecting students' beliefs while guiding them towards the socialist core value system, developing scientific-atheist research and education, keeping education separate from religion, and resisting overseas religious infiltration of universities. Read the original if you want a map of the Chinese survey literature on student religion, with its main figures and sources, and a view of how Party-aligned scholars of atheism assess it.

Some reflections on Marxist religious-outlook education in universities 高校开展马克思主义宗教观教育的若干思考 He Husheng Liu Fujun He Husheng and Liu Fujun ask how Chinese universities should teach students a Marxist view of religion. Writing in 2013, they argue that hostile foreign forces are using religion, campus proselytising and the student body as a channel for 'Westernization' and division. In their account, education in the Marxist view of religion is therefore an urgent strategic task, tied to training qualified builders and reliable successors for socialism with Chinese characteristics. The article is organised in three parts. The first covers basic Marxist theory on religion: its nature, its long-term development and its social functions. The second covers the Party's basic policies on religious work, and the third covers education in Marxist scientific atheism. Each part is framed as content that universities should deliver, mainly through ideological and political theory courses and Party and Youth League organisations. The authors hold that religion has a multiple nature: it is a theistic, idealist worldview, a mass belief and a part of culture. They hold that it will persist for a long time under socialism but will eventually disappear, and that it has both positive and negative social effects. On policy, they list freedom of religious belief, management of religious affairs according to law, independence and self-administration of religion, guiding religion to adapt to socialist society, separation of education from religion, the patriotic united front, and Party leadership. They stress that Communist Party members must be atheists and that religious activity and preaching on campuses are barred. They add that students should learn to distinguish religion from superstition and from folk belief. The authors conclude that universities should combine dialectical and historical materialism, the promotion of science against superstition, and ideals-and-convictions education. They want this to reduce the influence of religious idealism on students, defend Marxism's guiding position in ideology and resist infiltration from abroad. They also say that students should respect believers and that Marxist atheism does not mean political opposition to religious people. Read the original if you want to see how official Chinese discourse in the Hu Jintao era set out religious policy as a curriculum for higher education.

Capitalist religion and historical materialism 资本主义宗教与历史唯物主义 Zhang Shuangli Why did a group of Central European Jewish intellectuals, once influenced by Max Weber, move to Marx's critique of fetishism? Zhang examines this revival of fetishism critique in the twentieth century through Ernst Bloch, Georg Lukács and Walter Benjamin. Zhang argues that reflection on the "Jewish question" carried them beyond Weber's thesis of disenchantment to the view that capitalism has itself become a religion, and that this view prepared their turn to Marx. The article has two main parts and a conclusion. The first part takes Bloch as its example. It traces how his Jewish messianism and his reading of Weber's The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism led him to a theory of capitalist religion, which Benjamin's fragment "Capitalism as Religion" then developed. The second part turns to Lukács's History and Class Consciousness and its account of the secret of this religion. The conclusion compares the three thinkers' views of how capitalist religion might be overcome. Zhang's central claim is that these thinkers reconstructed Marx's critique in two directions. First, Bloch and Benjamin describe capitalist religion as self-contradictory: its idol is both a concrete human creation (Mammon, the golden calf) and an empty abstraction. It is a practical cult without doctrine that nonetheless breeds sectarian faiths. It is also non-redemptive, because it multiplies guilt and debt while presenting itself as progress. Second, Lukács explains these features through commodity fetishism. Abstract labour is the sole social category, and it rules through rationalization, the contemplative stance and reified consciousness. Zhang reads this as "abstract domination", which separates form from content and part from totality, so that capitalism moves from one catastrophe to the next. In the conclusion Zhang sets out a split over historical materialism. Lukács proposes a non-religious historical materialism: proletarian class consciousness would achieve the sublation of religion through philosophy and social revolution alone. He criticises Bloch's proposed alliance with religion. Bloch and Benjamin hold to an alliance between historical materialism and theology, illustrated by Benjamin's image of the hidden dwarf and the puppet. Zhang concludes that in a seemingly secularised world, the question of how to sublate religion positively remains open. Read the original if you study Western Marxism, Weber's influence on Lukács and Bloch, or the debate over Marxism and religion.

On the dual measure of Marx's critique of religion 论马克思宗教批判的双重尺度 Shang Yu Shang Yu takes issue with the traditional view that Marx's system is cut off from, or simply opposed to, religious consciousness, and that the spirit of the Gospel weakens the movement for human emancipation. The author calls this view an unhistorical, abstract assertion. The article argues instead that Marx's critique of religion works on two measures: an ultimate-value measure, on which the realm of freedom and the messianic idea are covertly linked, and an economic-science measure, on which Marx exposes religion's illusory, inverted and conservative character. The article has three sections. The first traces the history of salvation thinking from Christian eschatology and Augustine through the Enlightenment, Kant, Hegel and Feuerbach, to Marx's labour-based conception of emancipation. The second sets out the value dimension, comparing human emancipation with religious redemption in four respects: logical premise, driving force, dialectical pattern and theoretical source. The third sets out the economic-science dimension in three steps: religion as ideology, its basis in civil society, and its decoding through commodity fetishism. Shang draws on Engels, Weber, Horkheimer, Baudrillard, Žižek and Adam Smith, among others. Shang argues that Marx reworks the religious structure of crisis, redemption and negation of the negation on the ground of production and exchange. Primitive accumulation plays the part of original sin, and labour takes the place of self-consciousness as the force of salvation, with a dual character of bondage and liberation. The economic-science measure then separates Marx from religion. Religion is an "opium" that consoles and justifies, and it rests on a civil society split from the political state, so that people live a double life, heavenly and earthly. In Shang's reading, commodity fetishism shows that the worship of things in exchange society follows the same logic as the worship of gods. Religious consciousness is therefore an objective illusion of a reified society, not a deliberate priestly lie. Shang concludes that Marx inverted the "head-standing" thinking of religious theology into a way of thinking that stands on its feet, taking what exists as its starting point. In this way socialism passed from utopia to science. Marx replaced the history of Christian salvation with a history of the liberation of labour, and so gave the world a real force of freedom and emancipation once the Gospel spirit had receded. Shang treats the relation between ideologies as one of mutual absorption, not mortal combat. Read the original if you are interested in how a Chinese scholar of Marxism and atheism reads the theological sources of Marx's emancipation theory, alongside his critique of fetishism.

Advocating the religious-work principle of "protection, management, guidance and service" 倡导“保护、管理、引导、服务”的宗教工作理念 Wang Zuo'an Writing in early 2013, in the wake of the 18th Party Congress (2012), Wang Zuo'an, head of the State Administration for Religious Affairs, sets out how religious work should proceed under the Party's new guidance. The article is an official commentary rather than a research study. Wang argues that the Party's basic policy on religious work should be fully implemented and that officials should adopt a working concept of "protection, management, guidance and service", so that religious believers and non-believers alike contribute to building a moderately prosperous society. The piece opens by recalling what the 18th Party Congress report and the revised Party Constitution say about religion. It then reviews achievements since the 16th Party Congress (2002) under Hu Jintao, including the formulation of the basic policy, the Regulations on Religious Affairs and the treatment of religious relations as a major political and social relationship. The remainder is organised as six tasks: religious freedom and legitimate rights; law-based management; independence and self-administration with friendly foreign exchanges; religious self-development and adaptation to socialist society; religious harmony; and religion's positive role in development. Wang's central claim is that the basic policy is to be applied consistently: freedom of religious belief must never be shaken, and administrative commands or crude methods must not be used against believers. At the same time, he calls for stronger legal management, covering the approval of religious venues, the registration of clergy and the supervision of venue finances. He presents the principle of independent and self-administered religion as rooted in China's history of imperialist aggression, and urges resistance to foreign infiltration. He also calls for guiding religions to adapt to socialist society, with each faith reinterpreting doctrine in line with social progress, training patriotic clergy, and opposing fanaticism and heterodox teachings. Wang concludes that religious groups should promote harmony within and between religions, with society and with the state, while observing the separation of religion and politics and operating within the law. They should also take part in charity, transmit traditional culture, support exchanges with Hong Kong, Macao and Taiwan, and oppose separatist activity attributed to the Dalai clique and the "three forces". Read the original if you want an authoritative statement of how China's religious affairs authorities framed their policy priorities at the start of 2013.

"The end of the world" and the "Church of Almighty God" “世界末日”与“全能神教” Xi Wuyi Writing in January 2013, Xi Wuyi takes up the "Church of Almighty God", which in his account is spreading rumours of an imminent "end of the world" and urging that only believers will be saved. Xi describes the group as a Christian heresy with a strongly rebellious political character, and argues that it should be classed as an "evil cult" (xiejiao), or in international scholarly terms a "destructive cult". The short commentary first traces the group's origins, saying it is also called "Eastern Lightning" and split off from the American-derived "Shouters" sect in the late 1970s under its founder Zhao Weishan. It then describes its organisation and methods of recruitment, and its social harm. Xi then turns to the legal definition of an evil cult in Article 300 of China's Criminal Law and to the concept of the destructive cult in Western religious studies. Xi reports that the group teaches that a female Christ has become incarnate in China, that unbelievers will be struck down, and that followers must fight the "great red dragon", which the group takes to mean the Communist Party. He describes a hierarchical, secretive structure with single-line contacts, pseudonyms and pyramid-selling-style recruitment. It targets the sick and troubled, pressing members to leave home and give up their property. Xi lists three features of destructive cults: worship of a leader with mental control, preaching of doomsday with violence, and secret association with illegal fundraising. Xi proposes using the "destructive cult" concept as a cross-cultural framework so that Chinese research on cults can join international academic discourse. He adds that such groups hit developing countries harder than developed ones, because social security systems there are still being built and social risk is higher. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's official-aligned account of how "Eastern Lightning" was characterised and conceptualised in early 2013.

Scientific atheism in the perspective of the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context 马克思主义中国化视野下的科学无神论问题 Yang Junfeng Writing in 2013, Yang Junfeng asks how scientific atheism, which the article calls the ideological foundation of Marxism, should develop while Marxism is being adapted to Chinese conditions. The article argues that Marxist atheism is universally valid but must adjust to China's own social, cultural and religious circumstances if it is to be applied effectively in socialist revolution and construction. The article has three parts. The first sets out the basic content of Marxist atheism and Marxist views of religion. The second describes the cultural background and distinctive features of religious belief in China, in contrast with Christian Europe, where Marxist atheism arose. The third reviews the Chinese Communist Party's experience with atheism and religious policy from the revolutionary period to the reform era and draws lessons for the future. In Yang's account, Marxism explains religion historically, as a distorted and illusory reflection of social existence with natural, social, cognitive and psychological roots. Religion has a dual social role and is destined to wither away only slowly, so proletarian parties should guarantee freedom of religious belief, reject crude campaigns against religion and persist in atheist education. Turning to China, Yang holds that the Confucian tradition of 'respecting the people rather than the gods' produced religious pluralism, a strongly utilitarian attitude to belief, and the subordination of religion to political power. Yang concludes that China's religious situation differs sharply from Europe's, yet Marxist atheism remains the guide for handling it. Yang sets out four requirements for adapting Marxist atheism. It must hold unwaveringly to its basic principles, without compromise with religious theism. It must handle religion flexibly according to national conditions, avoiding a uniform approach. It must continually criticise new theistic currents and lead the development of social thought. It must also build positive content of its own, offering reasoned answers on the meaning of life, a stable basis for moral practice and a rational grounding for the value of life. Read the original if you want a concise statement, from 2013, of how Chinese scholars of atheism justified combining strict atheist principles with flexible religious policy.

The development and features of the sinicization of Marxist atheism since reform and opening up 改革开放以来马克思主义无神论中国化的发展历程及其特点 Huang Yanhong Writing in 2013, Huang Yanhong asks how Marxist atheism has been adapted to Chinese conditions since the start of reform and opening up. The article argues that the process passed through three stages. Throughout them the Party kept the same basic positions, but its understanding of atheism and of religion shifted with the main tasks of each period. The article is a periodised survey of Party documents and leaders' speeches, with the approach set out in its opening paragraph. It covers the late 1970s to the late 1980s, the late 1980s to the late 1990s, and the late 1990s into the early twenty-first century. The material is drawn from religious policy, united front work, ethnic affairs, rural work, education and the building of socialist spiritual civilization. Huang cites Document No. 19 of 1982, speeches by Jiang Zemin, Hu Jintao and others, and the circulars issued in 2004, 2007 and 2011. In Huang's account, the first stage restored the policy of freedom of religious belief after the Cultural Revolution. It also protected the freedom not to believe, promoted atheist and materialist education, and held that Communist Party members must be atheists. The second stage required Party members not only to avoid religion but to uphold and propagate atheism. It stressed administering religious affairs according to law and resisting infiltration by foreign religious forces, in a period shaped by the strategy of invigorating the country through science and education. Huang reads the apparent tension between respecting belief and promoting atheism as resolved only by a thorough understanding of Marxist atheism. The third stage, which Huang links to the goal of a moderately prosperous society, gave atheist education greater prominence in the Party, schools and the army. It also called for a fuller view of religion's long-term existence and of the positive role of believers. Huang concludes that every stage upheld freedom of belief, the separation of religion from politics and education, Party members' atheism, and atheist propaganda. What differed was the view of religion's role under socialism, the relation between religion and cults, the separation of education from religion, and the standing of atheist education. Huang attributes these differences to the tasks and practical problems of each period. Read the original if you want a documentary overview of Chinese Party policy on atheism, with its main sources, between 1978 and 2011.

Professor Lü Daji and the study of the Marxist view of religion 吕大吉教授与马克思主义宗教观研究 Gong Xuezeng Written as a tribute after the death of the religious studies scholar Lü Daji, this commentary is by one of his students, Gong Xuezeng. Gong sets aside Lü's wider scholarly record and assesses only his contribution to research on the Marxist view of religion. The thesis is that Lü was a leading figure in turning this field, after 1978, into serious academic study while holding that Chinese religious research must stay within Marxism. The article proceeds chronologically through seven contributions. These are the compilation of a reader of the classic writers on religion; early research papers; a methodological defence of Marxism; a reassessment of Engels's statement on the nature of religion; the History of Western Religious Thought (1994); an edited volume on the Marxist view of religion and religion in contemporary China (2007); and the 2011 co-authored study Research on the Marxist Theory of Religion. Gong reports that Lü led the compilation of Marx, Engels and Lenin on Religion (internal edition, 1979), which Gong calls the first comprehensive scholarly presentation of the Marxist view of religion in the People's Republic. In the introduction to General Theory of Religious Studies (1989), Lü argued that Marxist theory should not be treated with a believer's dogmatism, but that historical materialism still gives four methodological principles. These explain religion through its economic base, its place in the superstructure and class analysis, not through religion's own history. Gong also highlights Lü's view that Engels's famous formula in Anti-Dühring concerns only the idea of gods and so is insufficient as a definition of religion. Lü's own definition describes religion as a social-cultural system of consciousness, belief, worship and institutionalised practice, which Gong says became the mainstream view in the field. In Lü's later work, Marxist religious theory is both historically specific and developing, so it must be studied historically and renewed over time. Gong concludes that Lü placed the Marxist view of religion within the history of Western religious thought, calling it a "historical-materialist atheism" that is more thoroughgoing than earlier atheisms. He presents Lü as modest, ready to acknowledge his own shortcomings, and as holding that only social practice and history can judge scholarly results. Read the original if you want a concise, sympathetic account of how Chinese scholarship on Marxist religious theory developed after 1978, as seen by a student of its main figure.

A brief analysis of the contemporary guiding value of the Marxist view of religion 浅析马克思主义宗教观的当代指导价值 Li Dafang Wen Yunying Liao Chongxu Writing in the early 2013 context of rapid social transformation, the authors ask how the Marxist view of religion can guide China's handling of religious questions. They observe that anxiety during reform has, in their account, pushed more people towards religious belief, and that religion's social influence and its sensitivity have grown. Their thesis is that the Marxist view of religion remains a scientific worldview and methodology, and should guide efforts to get religion to adapt to socialist society. The article has three parts. The first sets out the core content of the Marxist view of religion: its account of religion's essence, origins, development and future, and its view of religion's dual social function. The second describes the present religious situation in China and its features. The third draws out three kinds of guidance from the Marxist view for policy and practice. In the authors' reading, Marx, Engels and Lenin define religion in three ways: as alienated self-consciousness, as a fantastic reflection of external forces (the "reflection theory", which the authors say Chinese scholars generally favour), and as "opium of the people". Religion is said to arise from natural, social and cognitive roots, and to wither away only when these are removed. The authors then describe China's situation as one of growing numbers of believers, secularisation, wider international and domestic influence, and a religious question that is mass-based, ethnic, international and complex. From this they derive three lessons. Religion should be viewed through historical materialism, as a normal product of social transition that calls for a "normal attitude", and the classics should not be applied rigidly. Freedom of religious belief should be maintained, with work tailored to the mass, ethnic and international character of religion and treated as a systemic project tied to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Dialectical analysis should recognise religion's dual nature and avoid both "left" and right errors. The authors conclude that guiding religion to adapt to socialist society does not mean asking believers to abandon their faith. It means asking them to love the country and support the socialist system, to reinterpret doctrines in line with modern science and culture, and to place religious activity within the law. They also call for balance on several fronts: acknowledging the ideological opposition between Marxism and religion while stressing common interests, managing religion by law while guiding it, and protecting both belief and non-belief. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese scholarly article of this period reconciles classical Marxist critiques of religion with the policy of religious freedom and the goal of social harmony.

Studying the Marxist view of religion in depth 深入研究马克思主义宗教观 Pei Biao Writing in late 2012, the author argues that religious studies and religious work in China should be guided by an in-depth study of the Marxist view of religion. The piece is a programmatic commentary. It takes up the Central Committee's calls to build a socialist core value system and to consolidate Marxism's guiding position in the ideological sphere. The author holds that scholars should observe and analyse religious questions from Marxist standpoints, viewpoints and methods, and should keep developing a Marxist theory of religion with Chinese characteristics. The article has three parts. The first sets out why the Marxist view of religion matters. The second identifies its essential spirit, and the third discusses how to advance its adaptation to Chinese conditions, to the times and to the wider public. The author places the argument against global religious revival, fundamentalism and interfaith dialogue, and against growing numbers of believers and religion-related social tensions in China. The text also cites Marx, Engels, Mao Zedong, Jiang Zemin, Hu Jintao and the Central Committee's 1982 document on religious questions. The author gives the Marxist view of religion three roles: a tool for analysing religious phenomena, the fundamental guiding thought of religious work, and the basic scientific method for religious research. Its essential spirit lies in three features. The first is the historical-materialist principle that religion reflects social being and must be explained through material conditions, not studied in isolation. The second is a dialectical method, which the author illustrates with paired policy stances: recognising ideological opposition while stressing the common interests of believers and non-believers, protecting both religious belief and the freedom to propagate atheism, and managing religious affairs by law while guiding religion to adapt to socialist society. The third is the capacity to advance with the times. The author attributes the policy errors of 1957 to the Cultural Revolution to a dogmatic leftist distortion of Marxist principles, not to the principles themselves. The author concludes that the Marxist view of religion should be adapted to Chinese conditions, to the times and to the broader public. Adaptation to Chinese conditions is described as the core, adaptation to the times as the key, and popularisation as the foundation. Marxism is to lead, the author says, without enforcing uniformity: the formula is "one dominant guide, many coexisting approaches", and methods from the sociology, anthropology and psychology of religion are welcomed. Read the original if you want an example of how the official Marxist approach to religion was framed in China around 2012, at the end of the Hu Jintao era.

Developing advanced socialist culture and resisting mysticism 发展社会主义先进文化与抵制神秘主义 Tu Jianhua Writing in 2012, Tu Jianhua argues that mysticism challenges the authority of Marxism and seeks to occupy the ground of socialist ideology, and that this deserves serious attention. The article treats mysticism as an ideology that is at once anti-religious, anti-scientific and anti-secular, as a set of techniques claiming to heal and save, and as a form of organisation. Tu contends that resisting it is necessary for holding the Marxist ideological position, promoting the flourishing of socialist culture and building the socialist core value system. The article has three parts. The first sets out the harms of contemporary mysticism. The second explains why it has spread, pointing to three waves in modern China: the metaphysics of the early twentieth century, the secret societies (huidaomen) of the early People's Republic, and the human "special functions" (tèyì gōngnéng) and qigong movement of 1979–1999. The third proposes ways of resisting it. Tu draws on Chinese religious and intellectual history, on Lenin and Stalin's remarks on atheist propaganda, and on the author's own earlier studies of qigong. Tu argues that mysticism harms in four ways. It erodes Marxist ideology by exaggerating the activity of consciousness and replacing material practice with "extrasensory perception"; it produces a culture of ignorance that preys on people who have lost, or never had, a sense of self; it causes social unrest, as in cults such as Aum Shinrikyo and Falun Gong; and its ultimate aim is to dissolve the mainstream ideology. As causes, Tu names the mystical strand in traditional culture, the weakening of materialist conviction and Marxist ideology after the Cultural Revolution, and lagging scholarship and policy, including the "three nots" policy on special functions, which left criticism absent. Tu proposes four remedies: strengthen materialist and atheist education; reform distribution and honours systems to reduce the social soil for mysticism, including moving towards common prosperity; uphold Party leadership of ideology and require Party members to hold to materialism and atheism; and develop scholarly criticism. The last includes rebutting five claims: that mysticism is heritage, that it is protected belief, that it enjoys academic freedom, that it has present-day value, and that materialism cannot meet the need for belief. Tu holds that only Marxism offers a belief that is credible. Read the original if you want a 2012 Party-theoretical argument that treats qigong, special functions and cults as an ideological threat, and want to see how it links them to Chinese cultural history and Party discipline.

Survey shows global increase in atheists Xinhua International digest of US press reports on a 2012 Gallup International survey 调查显示全球无神论者呈增加趋势 Xinhua International This short news digest, compiled by Xinhua International and posted in the site's Science and Atheism category in September 2012, relays two US press reports from August 2012. Both report a new global survey finding that the number of self-declared atheists is rising in the United States and elsewhere, while the number of people calling themselves religious is falling. The text combines items from the Christian Science Monitor website (15 August) and the Washington Post website (14 August). They draw on the Swiss branch of Gallup's "Global Index of Religiosity and Atheism", which interviewed more than 50,000 people in 57 countries. Respondents were asked whether they considered themselves religious, not religious or convinced atheists. The reports cite US figures: self-described religious Americans fell from 73% in 2005 to 60%, convinced atheists rose from 1% to 5%, and 33% said they were not religious. China is reported first among countries with "convinced atheists" (47%), followed by Japan, the Czech Republic, France and South Korea. China also ranks lowest in religiosity (14%). Ghana, Nigeria and Armenia head the list of the most religious countries. Sociologist Ryan Cragun of the University of Tampa is quoted as doubting that atheism itself has grown. In his reading, more people now feel comfortable using the label, as religion no longer serves as a marker of being a "good person". The reports also mention organised atheist campaigns in the US as a possible factor and cite a 2009 Pew finding that only 24% of non-religious Americans called themselves atheists. The digest offers no commentary of its own. It presents the survey as evidence of a trend toward atheism and notes the caution of the expert quoted. Read the original if you want the survey's country rankings and figures, or an example of how Chinese state media selected foreign reporting on religion and atheism in 2012.

Hobbes's identity: Christian or atheist? An inquiry into the sincerity of Hobbes's profession of faith 霍布斯的身份探析 The article asks whether Thomas Hobbes was a Christian or an atheist, and whether his open profession of Christian faith deserves to be trusted. The author argues that when Hobbes had to choose between reason and faith he chose faith, and that his self-description as a believer in "Jesus is the Christ" should be accepted as sincere. Hobbes himself never called himself an atheist. The author notes that scholars have tended to debate his sincerity rather than why he leaned towards faith. The piece is divided into three parts. The first surveys two interpretive models: a secularising reading that treats Hobbes's confession as insincere, and a faith-based reading that treats it as genuine. It also reviews scholars who defended Hobbes, namely Martinich, Oakeshott, Warrender and George Wright. The second part examines Hobbes's self-defence in the appendix to the 1668 Latin Leviathan, especially on God's corporeality and the Trinity. The third part reflects on what Hobbes's choice of faith means for an age of growing rationalism. The author makes three moves. First, drawing on Martinich and Wittgenstein's idea of language games, the author argues that "atheist" in seventeenth-century England was mainly a term of abuse and a quasi-political label, even applied to Elizabeth I and James I, so it cannot be read in the modern sense of unbelief. Second, Hobbes defended the claim that God is a body by appealing to Tertullian and the early councils, and he conceded a hasty error in his account of Moses and the Trinity before restating the orthodox doctrine. Third, the author concedes that the sincerity question may be circular, because each scholar reads Hobbes according to a prior conviction. Yet by Hobbes's own test, which judges atheism by what a person says or writes rather than by conduct, he does not count as an atheist. The author concludes that Hobbes's profession of faith is sincere and trustworthy. In the author's reading, Hobbes saw that in a rationalising, war-torn England, life without God would fall into a meaningless state of nature and a war of all against all. Leviathan is thus presented as an absolute but fragile authority serving a higher being, offering peace on earth and hope of salvation. Read the original if you are interested in the Hobbes debate over religion and sincerity, or in how seventeenth-century usage of "atheist" affects the reading of early modern thinkers.

Marx's discovery of the human being and his surpassing of the Young Hegelians 马克思对人的发现及其对青年黑格尔派的超越 Zhong Minghua Lin Zhao Zhong Minghua and Lin Zhao ask who among the Young Hegelians actually discovered the real human being, and who deserves to be called a materialist. They argue that Feuerbach and Stirner each stopped short of materialism, and that Marx alone, through historical materialism, found the real human being in actual individuals living within definite social relations. Reconstructing the debate, they say, helps explain how historical materialism arose and what it essentially involves. The article has three sections. The first presents Feuerbach's reduction of religion to humanism, as set out in The Essence of Christianity (1841). The second covers Stirner's critique of Feuerbach and his own reduction of humanism to the individual, the 'unique one'. The third, the longest, examines Marx's response under three headings: the abstract unique one, the real individual, and free humanity. It draws mainly on The German Ideology and the Theses on Feuerbach. In the authors' account, Feuerbach showed that God's attributes are human attributes projected outward, but he kept an essentialist 'human species-essence' and so only replaced one governing idea with another. Stirner exposed this, yet fell back on an equally abstract egoistic individual, a Hegelian category in new dress. Marx, the authors argue, restored the idea of the species as 'the ensemble of social relations'. Individuality and property are formed through social intercourse, labour, the division of labour and exchange, and religious and political alienation derive from economic alienation. The authors add that Stirner and the Young Hegelians believed chains exist only in the head and fought phrases with phrases, which the article likens to Don Quixote tilting at windmills. The authors conclude that Marx kept the communist ideal of freedom while stripping it of utopianism. Domination is traced to real social and economic relations, so revolution must change the existing world rather than consciousness. The conflict between individual and society arises from the individual's lack of control over the conditions of labour, and it would disappear as the material basis changes. Read the original if you want a detailed, text-based account of how Marx's early critique of Feuerbach and Stirner underpinned his materialist conception of the individual.

Why atheism has been lost in universities “无神论”在高校失落的原因 Ye Suibing Why do university students, who are the most educated group in society, hold superstitious and theistic beliefs despite years of materialist education? Ye Suibing, writing in 2012, argues that materialist atheism has been 'lost' in Chinese higher education. The article traces this to a combination of social, institutional and individual causes, and calls for a renewed programme of atheist education. The article opens with the author's own survey, carried out in January 2011 at the Guangdong Justice Police Vocational College (1,240 valid questionnaires). It reports that 78% of respondents believed in ghosts, gods, fate, luck or special powers. Ye compares this with other published surveys, then describes four features of student superstition: its mixing with scientific knowledge, campus culture, religion and online entertainment. The body is organised into social, school-level and individual causes, followed by proposals. On social causes, Ye argues that the decline of atheism follows from the decline of materialism and, more deeply, of Marxism among students. Students born in the 1990s saw the Soviet collapse, upheaval in Eastern Europe and the difficulties of reform, and wrongly judged capitalism superior. Ye adds the spiritual disorientation of a society in transition, the negative effects of science and technology, commercialised media that promote fortune-telling, and what the author calls Western cultural colonisation. On school causes, Ye points to lower cognitive ability after university expansion, unbalanced curricula, and Marxist philosophy courses reduced to memorised exam points that cannot substitute for specific atheist education. On individual causes, Ye draws on observational learning, attribution theory, psychological suggestion, conditioning and anxiety from study, job and financial pressure. Ye proposes two joint efforts. The first is a multi-disciplinary one: atheism courses, dialectical materialism for science students, scientific spirit for humanities students, atheist content within subject teaching, and network ethics education. The second combines school, family and society, including mental health work, a campus culture of atheism, parental example and stricter government control of superstitious publications and media. Read the original if you want survey data and a Chinese official-academic account of student superstition and atheist education in the early 2010s.

Applying cognitive dissonance theory to scientific atheism education 认知失调理论在科学无神论教育中的应用 He Guihong Xia Xing He Guihong and Xia Xing start from what they call a paradox: Marxist scientific atheism education has continued without pause since 1949, yet theistic belief and activity keep expanding. Rather than treating this as a simple failure, the article reflects on it from the standpoint of individual cognitive psychology. Its thesis is that Leon Festinger's cognitive dissonance theory can make scientific atheism education more targeted, rational and effective. The article opens with a summary of cognitive psychology, drawing on Piaget's account of assimilation, accommodation and equilibrium. It then sets out Festinger's theory and asks why "positive education" so often has little effect and why individuals taught for years can be swayed by theism. The authors turn to two tasks: the first is targeted creation of dissonance for different learners; the second is strategies for drawing learners into active participation. They also discuss how teaching content should be revised. The central argument is that education delivered uniformly, like a cure-all, is like brown-sugar water with no medicinal effect. The authors argue that educators must instead "create contradictions" matched to each learner's age, background and experience. For learners already inclined to atheism, educators should introduce higher-level material. For those half-convinced or strongly influenced by theism, educators should provoke dissonance between old beliefs and new ideas, behaviour or attitudes, for example by arranging atheist activities or situations. The authors add that content must separate traditional customs from superstition and mark a clear line between atheism and theism. On participation, the authors propose four elements: a sense of choice, self-decision, satisfaction and responsibility. They claim these build self-esteem-based defences, so that atheist understanding is not merely recited and can resist later theistic influence. They argue that atheism's historical depth and its bearing on daily life can give learners satisfaction, and that education should be linked to personal life goals. They close by expressing confidence that Marxist scientific atheism represents the scientific direction of human understanding. Read the original if you want an example of how Chinese scholars in 2012 applied educational psychology to ideological education on religion.

Bring in a batch, energise a region: an investigation of Guizhou's recruitment of cadres from more developed areas as county Party secretaries 引进一批 激活一片 带动一方——贵州省从相对发达地区引进干部担任县委书记情况调查 Writing in 2012, an unnamed investigation team reports on a cadre-selection experiment in Guizhou province. In 2010 and 2011 the province recruited 12 cadres from five provinces and municipalities (Jiangsu, Shandong, Zhejiang, Hebei and Chongqing) to serve as county Party secretaries. The article asks why this was done, how the recruits have performed and how cadres and local people rate them. Its answer is strongly positive: the practice is presented as an effective way for an underdeveloped province to speed up development and renew its cadre corps. The team says it interviewed provincial and municipal leaders, visited counties with recruited secretaries, spoke with county leadership members and grassroots cadres, and ran categorised questionnaires. The report moves from Guizhou's rationale and selection method, to the recruits' results in office, and then to four general lessons for other underdeveloped regions. Named examples include Jinsha, Nanming, Suiyang, Dushan, Taijiang and Pingba. The article argues that Guizhou faced the double task of changing its growth model and catching up, and that this required able county Party secretaries as leaders of local development. Recruiting from more developed areas is described as a quick way to import ideas, talent and resources and to spur local cadres. Recruitment was tied to need: candidates were sought with experience in industry, industrial parks, urbanisation or agricultural industrialisation, chosen by successive competitive comparison and publicly announced in their home media. The article credits the recruits with changing mindsets, tightening discipline, attracting investment and improving livelihoods, citing figures such as Nanming district's 20% GDP growth in 2011, Taijiang's 12 investment framework agreements worth 8.7 billion yuan, and Jinsha's rise from 15th to 6th in the provincial county ranking. The report draws four lessons. First, ideological worries, such as fears that outsiders would take local posts, must be cleared. Second, practical, grassroots experience is the key criterion in choosing candidates, with no lowering of standards. Third, central departments, the home provinces and Guizhou's own provincial and municipal organisations must cooperate. Fourth, local cadres' enthusiasm must be maintained, partly by promoting some of them on an "in and out" principle. Read the original if you want a favourable official account of cross-province cadre recruitment in 2012 and its concrete selection procedures.

On investigation and research 谈谈调查研究 Xi Jinping This is a speech by Xi Jinping, delivered on 16 November 2011 at the opening ceremony for the second group of autumn-term students at the Central Party School and published after light editing. Addressing Party leading cadres at county level and above, Xi argues that investigation and research (diaocha yanjiu) is a basic skill of leadership and more than a working method. In his account it bears directly on the success or failure of the Party's cause. The speech has three parts. The first explains why investigation and research matters and why leaders must keep up and strengthen it. The second sets out correct methods and how to raise the quality of research. The third calls for institutions that make research a regular practice, citing Chen Yun, the early-1960s nationwide research drive, Central Committee General Office rules and local examples such as Jiashan county in Zhejiang. Xi presents investigation as an inheritance from the Party's revolutionary, construction and reform periods, rooted in dialectical and historical materialism, seeking truth from facts and the mass line. He says that when the Party has stressed it, decisions have matched reality, and that neglect has produced errors. He criticises cadres who are buried in paperwork and meetings, rely on reports and the internet, make decisions from experience, or tour only showcase models. On method, he urges going to grassroots and difficult places, joining the masses, travelling lightly without staged receptions, and holding unannounced visits. He also calls for honest reporting of bad news as well as good, which he treats as a matter of Party spirit. He says analysis after fieldwork is often the weaker step. Methods should also adopt questionnaires, sampling and online surveys. Xi calls for a system of 'research before decision' and for hearings and risk assessment on major policies. He wants principal leaders to lead major research projects personally. He cites required field time of at least 30 days a year for provincial and ministerial officials and 60 for city and county leaders, plus one or two research reports a year. He also endorses contact points, residence-based fieldwork and campaigns sending cadres and journalists to the grassroots. He holds these up as ways to solve problems and bring the Party closer to the people. Read the original if you want a primary text on how Party leadership framed cadre work style and decision-making procedure in late 2011, shortly before the 18th Party Congress.

A brief history of atheism (excerpt) Chinese translation of the narration of a BBC television series 无神论简史（节选） Jonathan Miller This is an excerpt from a Chinese translation of the narration that Jonathan Miller wrote for the BBC television series on the history of atheism. It asks how disbelief could survive and take shape in Europe after Christianity became the state religion of the Roman Empire and dominated Western thought for about a thousand years. Miller's answer is that modern atheism grew less from science than from sceptical philosophy, from quarrels inside Christianity, and from attempts to make religion more rational. The excerpt moves from the Middle Ages to the eve of the French Revolution. It begins with how illiterate believers absorbed Christianity through images, such as Giotto's frescoes in Padua. It then covers the Aristotelian commentaries of Averroes, the Copernican and anatomical revolutions of 1543, the Reformation, the English deists, Thomas Hobbes, David Hume and Newton. It ends with Baron d'Holbach's Paris salon. Interview passages with the Cambridge historian Simon Shaffer, and quotations from Lucretius, Galileo, Hume and others, are woven through the narration. Miller identifies two influences on the sceptical current: a horizontal one, as trade and exploration revealed peoples who had never heard of Christianity, and a vertical one, as Epicurean, Lucretian and Democritean materialism resurfaced. He argues that the common view of science as the great destroyer of faith is not true. Copernicus, Vesalius, Galileo and Newton were devout, and Samuel Clarke drew on Newtonian mechanics to argue for God, so the conflict between religion and science was, in his account, greatly exaggerated. Through Shaffer, he adds that for two centuries 'atheist' was a smear no one accepted, and persecutors denied that real atheists existed even as they hunted them. Miller treats Hobbes as the thinker who gave ancient materialism a systematic philosophy, though he stopped short of openly denying God. In Miller's account, Hume still hedged, and d'Holbach was the first to assert plainly that no God or supernatural realm exists, with his System of Nature known as the 'bible of atheism'. The excerpt closes on the forgotten site of d'Holbach's home and grave, suggesting that later revolutionary politics obscured his memory. Read the original if you want a vivid, popular narrative of how early-modern atheism emerged from religious reform and philosophical scepticism rather than from science alone.

The witchcraft scandals of the reign of Emperor Wu of Han 汉武时期的巫蛊之祸 Zhao Guangqing This short historical commentary, posted in the "Science and Atheism" section, asks why accusations of witchcraft (wugu) recurred throughout the reign of Emperor Wu of Han. Zhao Guangqing defines wugu as sorcery that deceives people's minds and provokes social unrest, and notes that Han law made it a capital offence. The article argues that the repeated cases, which the author says lasted almost the whole reign, were a negative reality hidden beneath a celebrated golden age. The article is a chronological narrative of episodes. It begins with Empress Chen, deposed in 130 BC (the fifth year of the Yuanguang reign) after palace women were accused of sacrificial cursing, and with the general Gongsun Ao, executed with his clan after his wife was found to have practised sorcery. It then covers the mass searches of the capital, the Zhu Anshi affair, the case of Jiang Chong, and the later plots of Liu Xu under Emperors Zhao and Xuan. In Zhao's account, the Zhu Anshi case began when the chancellor Gongsun He offered to arrest the famous knight-errant to redeem his son's embezzlement. Zhu then denounced the son from prison, and the author judges that the charge was not a false one. Jiang Chong then accused Crown Prince Liu Ju, who rebelled and died, and the author says tens of thousands perished. Zhao also credits the judge Bing Ji with saving the infant great-grandson, the future Emperor Xuan, and says that without him the later Western Han would have been rewritten. Zhao attributes the wave of cases to the emperor's belief in immortals, heavy construction, harsh taxation and severe punishments, which increased banditry. The author considers the emperor's late self-criticism, the Luntai edict, neither thorough nor deep. Read the original if you want a brief, source-based narrative of the Han witchcraft cases and a moral reading of them.

The "New Age movement" and the rise of "Falun Gong" Part one of a serialised article (to be continued) “新时代运动”与“法轮功”成势 Xin Peng Xin Peng asks what the global "New Age movement" is and how it relates to the spread of mystical qigong cults in China, including Falun Gong, as the title indicates. This first, serialised instalment, published in the journal Science and Atheism in 2012, argues that the New Age movement is essentially a mysticism-seeking, anti-scientific and anti-rational current. In the author's account, it supplied the thinking behind China's qigong "masters" of the 1980s and 1990s. The instalment has two parts. The first defines the New Age movement and traces it to nineteenth-century spiritualism and to the postmodern anti-science currents of the 1960s and 1970s. The second turns to China and begins a case study of the qigong master Zhang Xiangyu. Falun Gong itself does not appear in this instalment, whose text breaks off at "to be continued". The references draw on David Hess's work on the New Age and Chinese critiques of pseudoscience by Shen Zhenyu, among others. Xin sorts the movement into two strands: personal spiritual transformation (alternative medicine, meditation, mediums, parapsychology) and a critique of modern technology that turns into hostility to reason and logic. On the author's reading, New Age thinkers vilify science, set an "occult science" against "material science" and invent new "disciplines" from subjective experience. Xin presents this as a bridge from science to religion. The author then claims that Chinese qigong masters applied the same ideas to health, with doctrines such as "unity of heaven and humanity" and "consciousness science". Zhang Xiangyu is described as claiming supernatural powers from a "late teacher", casting herself as a saviour, and drawing some 70,000 people for healing in under half a month. Xin calls her first doctrinal step the spiritualist creed "sincerity brings efficacy", under which disbelievers face illness or punishment by spirits. The instalment ends before any overall conclusion. Its implied claim is that Chinese qigong mysticism belongs to a wider international anti-scientific trend and should be understood in those terms. Read the original if you study the Chinese anti-pseudoscience and atheism literature, or the official-academic framing of qigong and cults in China, and want to see how one author links them to the New Age movement.

Raising scientific literacy to strengthen decision-making and management: a review of the Reader on Scientific Literacy for Leading Cadres and Civil Servants 提高科学素质，增强决策管理能力——荐王渝生、周立军主编的《领导干部和公务员科学素质读本》 Li Yaning This is a book review by Li Yaning, published in 2012 in the journal Science and Atheism. It introduces the Reader on Scientific Literacy for Leading Cadres and Civil Servants, edited by Wang Yusheng and Zhou Lijun (Science Popularization Press, 2011), which the Beijing Association for Science and Technology compiled. Li's verdict is that the book is precisely targeted and close to the practical needs of its readers, and that it is an important reference for training programmes, especially in Beijing. The review begins with the policy background. The State Council issued the Outline of the National Scientific Literacy Action Plan in 2006 and named leading cadres and civil servants as one of four key target groups. An implementation plan followed, but training lacked a suitable textbook, and the Reader was written to fill that gap. Li then sets out the book's positioning and walks through its chapters, noting appendices that reproduce the national Outline and the Zhongguancun innovation demonstration zone plan for 2011–2020. Li's central claim is that sound scientific decision-making and management rest on scientific knowledge and ideas and are guided by scientific methods and spirit. In Li's account, the Reader links scientific literacy to implementing the Scientific Outlook on Development. It makes scientific spirit the guiding element, defined by five qualities: seeking truth from facts, exploration and innovation, rational criticism, equality and tolerance, and dedication. It also stresses scientific thought and methods, including observation, experiment, social surveys, systems methods and innovation methods. Li highlights the book's treatment of pseudo-science: it argues that scientific progress does not remove superstition by itself and may create room for new forms, so the struggle against pseudo-science is long-term. Li adds that the Reader covers the theory and procedures of decision-making and management, the history and frontiers of science, the shifting centres of world scientific activity, and healthy lifestyles for an overworked cadre group. The book aims to give officials a historical and global view of the link between scientific strength and national power, which Li ties to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and the building of an innovation-oriented country. Read the original if you want a short, policy-oriented account of how China's 2006 scientific literacy programme was applied to official training, and of what such a textbook contains.

On what grounds should science be used? An analysis of basic questions in science culture 科学凭什么被使用? ——科学文化基本问题辨析 Li Chaoying Li Chaoying takes up a debate in Chinese 'science culture' circles, in which scholars such as Jiang Xiaoyuan, Tian Song, Liu Bing and Wu Guosheng criticise scientism and the claim that science can solve every problem. Li argues that these critics repeatedly confuse distinct things: science as a body of knowledge versus science as a social activity, science versus technology, and the limits of science versus the abuse of it. The article's answer to its title is that science should be used because its knowledge is honest, because harms attributed to it stem from insufficient science or from human choices, and because rational methods have no better substitute. The article is a polemic in four numbered sections. It begins with the claim that science is both 'dull' and honest, then discusses planned economies, then the neutrality of knowledge, the value of research and the extension of scientific method, and finally the question of whether technology is good or bad. Li answers the critics' examples one by one: the planned economy, chemical fertilisers, Freon, the atomic bomb, Lysenko, melamine in milk powder, the internet and slash-and-burn farming. Hayek's critique of planning is also examined. Li's central move is to separate the two senses of 'science'. As knowledge, science is neutral, like the law of gravitation. As an activity, it is judged by whether it is carried out rigorously. Li holds that harms from Freon, fertilisers or the planned economy came from too little science, not too much. On this view, the planned economy failed because planners ignored reality in favour of orders from above, so it was 'unscientific' rather than 'scientistic'. A second move distinguishes the harm an application does in normal use from harm done by someone who deliberately misuses it. Li argues that the atomic bomb, poisoned milk powder or addictive games reflect human or moral failings, not defects of nuclear physics or computing. A third move holds that science has no forbidden fields of enquiry, though its methods may be regulated, and that where abuse occurs only further research can show how to prevent it. Li concludes that science does not need to solve everything in order to be used as far as it can. Its distinctive virtue is that every conclusion must have reasons, and it corrects its errors, whereas pseudo-science repeats them. Li contends that traditional customs and critics' alternatives such as slash-and-burn farming also need scientific evaluation. The critics' demand that science defer to broader social goals is called unsound. Read the original if you want a detailed, combative defence of science against Chinese scholars who criticise scientism, set out through their own examples.

Building the discipline of scientific atheism and the road ahead Remarks at the 2011 annual conference of the China Atheism Society 科学无神论的学科建设和道路 Wen Ding This is a speech delivered by Wen Ding at the 2011 annual conference of the China Atheism Society. Wen assesses the position of scientific atheism in China more than thirty years after the Society's founding and twelve years into the journal Science and Atheism. The speaker's verdict is that the situation is "not bad" but the road is long, and that atheism needs to be built up as an academic discipline as part of a long-term strategy. The speech has four parts: the present state of the field; the sources of resistance; confidence in the truth of atheism; and a closing call for disciplinary construction. Wen sketches the history of anti-spirit arguments in China, from the late Qing and early Republic through the May Fourth period, and then discusses the rise of "special powers" claims, cults and the later religious revival. Wen argues that resistance comes from a coalition of scholars trained in foreign theology, officials and academics who echo them, and some self-described Marxists who promote belief in spirits. In the speaker's account, they accuse atheism of being a Cultural Revolution legacy, of opposing religious freedom and the constitution, and of fostering ethnic tension. Wen claims that foreign money funds missionary work and that official documents supporting atheism go unread, and notes that the 1995 Education Law provides for the separation of education and religion. Against this, Wen holds that scientific atheism rests on fact: there is no evidence for spirits, rational proofs fail, and religious experience belongs to psychology and brain science. Wen also traces the spread of mysticism and the turn to religion as a tool of social harmony to the upheavals of reform and opening up, and criticises a widely discussed essay on updating the Marxist view of religion. Wen concludes that atheists should keep faith in the truth they hold, despite poor funding and career prospects. The speech calls for stepping up efforts, linking them to building and defending core socialist values, and uniting scholars across the country to produce substantial, targeted works that clear up confused thinking in a short time. Read the original if you want a candid, polemical insider view of how a leading Chinese atheist scholar saw the standing of atheism and the religion debate in 2011.

Outline for building the basic theory of Marxist psychology of religion 马克思主义宗教心理学基本理论建设论纲 Chen Yongsheng Chen Yongsheng argues that Marxist psychology of religion is an organic part of Marxist religious studies, yet its basic theory has long been weak, which in the author's view hampers the coherence of the whole discipline. Writing in 2012, Chen proposes to strengthen the field by drawing lessons from the Soviet experience, tracing how Chinese Communist leaders have adapted Marxist views of religious psychology, and clarifying methodology. The article has three parts. The first examines Soviet work through D. M. Ugrinovich's Psychology of Religion (Russian edition 1986, Chinese edition 1989), separating its achievements from its failings. The second selects statements by Mao Zedong, Li Dazhao, Zhou Enlai, Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin and Hu Jintao to describe what Chen calls the Sinicization of the Marxist view of religious psychology. The third turns to methodology. Chen credits Ugrinovich with sketching a disciplinary framework (objects, tasks, methods, interdisciplinary status), criticising Western theistic psychology, and placing atheist education at the core. The article nevertheless judges the Soviet approach too "leftist": it underestimated how long and complex religious questions remain under socialism and neglected psychological services for clergy and believers. It also tied the field narrowly to social psychology and dismissed non-Marxist work as "bourgeois". Chen reads the Chinese leaders as treating atheist education within Party building, while using policy to manage religion's dual function. Atheist education is not to be forced on the masses, and religion's positive role is to be affirmed but not exaggerated. Chen concludes that Marxist psychology of religion should be problem-oriented and methodologically innovative. Its questions include why some Party members and young people are drawn to superstition or religion, and how to distinguish mental disorder from religious states and improve believers' mental health. Methods should be holistic, dialectical and pluralistic, combining quantitative and qualitative approaches. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist assessment of Soviet religious psychology and an account of how Party leaders' statements are used to frame this emerging subfield.

The historical evolution of the ideology of Chinese Christian churches in the United States 美国华人基督教会意识形态的历史演变 Huang Chao Huang Chao argues that religion is an ideology closely tied to politics, and that treating it as "mere culture" is neither accurate nor faithful to the principle of separating church and state. Writing in 2012, the author asks how the ideology of Chinese Christian churches in the United States has formed and changed, and why this matters for China. The thesis is that these churches' ideology has moved from racial and religious victimhood to a politicised "theocratic" and "new Cold War" stance aimed at China. The article opens with a review of existing work on overseas Chinese scholar ministries, noting that Su Wenfeng, Zhang Bosun and Hong Yujian treat 1989 as a watershed. Huang then divides the history into three stages: 1849 to 1942, 1942 to 1989, and 1989 to the present. Sources include Michael H. Hunt's Ideology and U.S. Foreign Policy, Kenneth D. Wald and Allison Calhoun-Brown on religion and politics, and writings by the pastor Zhao Tian'en. For the first stage, Huang argues that the 1882 Chinese Exclusion Act combined religious contempt, the "Yellow Peril" and social Darwinism. Missionaries shaped American images of China, and white missionaries hoped Chinese in America would return to evangelise China. The second stage is described as one of Puritan fundamentalism and "evangelising China", including Zhao's "three transformations" vision and the "Back to Jerusalem" plan. In Huang's account, this ideology served American hawks and contained containment-style themes, so it had little influence among Chinese believers. For the third stage, Huang says that after 1989 the churches stressed "religious freedom" and "democracy and human rights", courted overseas dissidents and sought to unify house churches. The article calls this a "new Cold War ideology" that demonises the Communist Party and divides love of country from love of the Party. Huang concludes that this ideology is increasingly rootless and rejected by most overseas Chinese and Chinese Christians, who take pride in China's development. The author notes that political scientists see religion as a source of ideology and organisational mobilisation, and says some domestic activists see house churches as holding long-term political capacity. Huang therefore calls for close attention to trends in Western Christian ideology and their effect on China's ideological security. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese scholar in 2012 framed overseas Christian networks as a question of ideological security.

Statements on the separation of religion and education in Party and state documents of the new period 新时期党和国家文献中有关宗教与教育相分离的论述研究 He Husheng He Husheng asks how Party and state documents since the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978) treat the separation of religion and education. The article argues that this separation is one of the Chinese Communist Party's basic views and policies on religion and an important part of its religious theory in the era of reform and opening up. In the author's account, it is also a necessary requirement of the Party's whole approach to religious work. The article is a documentary study built mainly on the 1995 collection Selected Documents on Religious Work in the New Period, together with speeches by Jiang Zemin. It has three parts. The first places the principle in the Party's consistent position, in the principle of separating religion from politics, and in the building of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The second ties it to the four components of the basic guideline on religious work. The third sets out the different demands made on Party members and officials, educators, religious figures and scholars. Citing the 1981 Resolution on Party history, Document No. 19 of 1982, the 1982 Constitution and a 1983 Ministry of Education opinion, He argues that religion may not interfere in state administration, the judiciary or schooling. He links this to each element of the guideline. Freedom of religious belief includes freedom not to believe, so religious interference in schools infringes others' freedom. Managing religious affairs according to law requires legal measures against such interference. The principle of independence and self-administration bears on resisting foreign religious infiltration, which He, citing Chen Yun's 1990 letter, describes as often working through education. Guiding religion to adapt to socialist society, in He's reading, asks religion to observe laws and policies, including this separation. He then lists the specific demands. Communist Party members must be atheists and may not take part in religious activities. The masses should receive Marxist and atheist education without administrative coercion. Religious personnel should receive patriotic and socialist education. Schools must not teach religion or compel belief. Scholars should study religion from a Marxist standpoint and guard against infiltration in the name of culture or scholarship. The author concludes that upholding the separation is a basic Party policy, though not easy in practice, and requires joint effort from all these groups. Read the original if you want a source-based survey of how official documents of the 1980s and 1990s framed religion and schooling in China.

Communist Party members cannot hold religious beliefs 共产党员不能信仰宗教 Zhu Weiqun Writing in 2012, Zhu Weiqun responds to what the article describes as a growing number of Party members who take part in religious activities or become believers, and to calls inside and outside the Party to "lift the ban" on members holding religious beliefs. Zhu argues that the Party's principle that Communists cannot believe in religion has been consistent and unshaken, and that it follows from the Party's dialectical-materialist worldview. The author insists that all Party organisations and members must uphold it without wavering. The article has four parts. It first traces the principle through Marx, Lenin and Mao Zedong, and through Party documents from 1982, 1990, 2002, 2006 and 2010. It then explains why a Party of materialists nonetheless practises a policy of freedom of religious belief, and sets out the harm Zhu expects if members were allowed to believe. It closes with proposals for education and discipline. Zhu's central move is to distinguish citizens from Party members. Freedom of religious belief, the author says, is a right of citizens; a person who joins the Party voluntarily accepts the materialist worldview and thereby chooses not to hold a religion. A member who later turns to religion has, in Zhu's words, ended the process of joining the Party in thought, and the Party may deal with that organisationally without "discriminating against religion". Second, Zhu argues that admitting believers would split the Party ideologically and organisationally, weaken its work against separatism in Tibet and Xinjiang, and turn officials into advocates of particular religions. The author cites local officials who promote temples and Buddha statues as examples of the problem. Zhu calls for stronger education in the Marxist view of religion and in atheism, in Party schools, universities and research bodies. The author proposes patient persuasion of members who join religious activities, and discipline for officials who use their power to foster religious fervour. Particular attention is urged for religious-affairs cadres, young members, retired members and members from ethnic minorities, with some flexibility allowed over customs derived from religion. Read the original if you want an authoritative statement from a senior United Front official of the Party's position on members and religion at the start of the 2010s.

Upholding the separation of education and religion, and advancing education and the discipline of atheism: a review of the 2011 annual conference of the China Atheism Association 坚持教育与宗教相分离原则，促进教育发展与无神论学科建设 ——中国无神论学会2011年学术年会综述 This is a report on the 2011 annual conference of the China Atheism Association, held on 29–31 October 2011 in Jinhua, Zhejiang. The association, the CASS Research Center for Science and Atheism and the School of Teacher Education at Zhejiang Normal University co-organised it. About 50 scholars attended, under the theme "educational development and the building of the atheism discipline". The report presents the meeting as a response to the spread of religion into public life and into university campuses. The report is arranged in four thematic sections, each summarising individual speakers. They cover the separation of education and religion, with historical and policy papers; the theoretical construction of scientific atheism; surveys of religious belief among university students, including online Christian communication; and foreign religious infiltration, together with related topics. The speakers came from CASS, Renmin University, Beijing Normal University, Shanghai Normal University, Nanjing University and other institutions. Further papers dealt with the psychology of atheism and with religious neuroscience. Xi Wuyi and others reviewed how Christian mission schools were secularised in modern China and argued that the separation principle must be upheld unwaveringly. They called Marxist atheism the basic safeguard against infiltration and campus proselytising. Du Jiwen set out a discipline plan of one general theory, two histories (Chinese and Western atheism) and a dictionary. He listed obstacles, including foreign-funded theology and trends that treat religion as a remedy for moral decline. Tian Xinming and Zhang Xinying held that atheist education is compatible with the policy of religious freedom, and Jia Runguo defended the Marxist view of religion against the reading of it as a mere "opium" doctrine. Surveys of students at several universities reported self-declared believers at roughly 5.8 to 18.55 per cent, though one author estimated true believers at about 4 per cent. Huang Chao described a US "new religious extraterritoriality" in religious infiltration of China. Xu Lin claimed that some Party committees ignored official policy on student belief. The report records calls for stronger Marxist and scientific-atheism education, stricter management of religious activity on campus and online, and more work on the discipline's textbooks and histories. Participants also urged scholars to confront pseudo-science and superstition. Several speakers tied the agenda to defending socialist core values and the Party's governing position. Read the original if you want a detailed view of how Chinese atheism scholars in 2011 framed religion, campus education and foreign influence, and of the policy proposals they put forward.

A brief commentary on the US International Religious Freedom Act of 1998 简评美国《1998年国际宗教自由法案》 Xi Wuyi Writing in 2012 in the category 'Science and Atheism', Xi Wuyi examines the US International Religious Freedom Act of 1998 and argues that it marks a post-Cold War strategic shift: a superpower legislating a regular review of religion worldwide. Xi describes this 'faith-based diplomacy' as the latest version of earlier missionary diplomacy and of 'human rights diplomacy'. The article takes China's 'xiejiao' problem, which it says the US reports have long scrutinised, as the main case. The article has three parts. The first sets out the American Christian neo-conservative global strategy, summarises the content of the Act (an ambassador-at-large, an annual report, a commission, presidential action against designated 'countries of particular concern') and argues that US definitions of religious freedom follow national interest.
