The second part reviews how Chinese law defines xiejiao and discusses how to translate the term into English. The third turns to Protestant 'destructive cults' in China, drawing on statistics and field reports. Xi argues that the Act is a tool by which evangelical and neo-conservative forces use state power to spread a Christian-based 'universal values' agenda and to legitimise interference in other states. As evidence of selectivity, Xi cites Iraq's removal from the 2004 watch list despite the violence there. Xi rejects the US claim that China has no public criteria, pointing to the 1997 Criminal Law, the 1999 NPC Standing Committee decision and the judicial interpretation. Xi holds that xiejiao is a modern legal concept, not equivalent to the Western 'cult', and proposes translating it as 'destructive cults'. Xi concludes that, as Falun Gong declines and becomes more political, Christian-type groups, which the article says make up over 85 per cent of the banned organisations, will become a factor in social stability. Xi attributes their growth to foreign funding and to the rapid spread of Christianity in China, citing studies putting Protestants at about 39–40 million. Xi urges a cross-cultural scholarly framework based on the Western concept of destructive cults, so that Chinese research can enter international discourse. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's official-line critique of US religious-freedom diplomacy, or the debate over translating xiejiao and the field-report evidence on Protestant groups in China.

The Sinicization of Marxist atheism (Part I) 马克思主义无神论的中国化历程（上） Xi Wuyi How did Marxist atheism, a doctrine formed in nineteenth-century Europe, take root in China? In this first part of a two-part article, Xi argues that Chinese Communists, proceeding from China's own social conditions, have steadily added new content to Marxist atheism while adapting Marxism to Chinese realities. Xi presents scientific atheism as the starting point and cornerstone of the Marxist worldview. The article opens with a comparison of China's religious culture and the Europe of Marx and Engels. It then follows the Chinese Communist Party's handling of religion through three periods: the New Democratic revolution, the early years of socialist construction after 1949, and the start of reform and opening up in 1978. Xi draws on Party documents, speeches by Mao Zedong and the 1982 central directive on religious policy. The account stops with the policies of the early 1980s, and the second part is still to come. Xi identifies three features of Chinese belief culture: pluralism in which humanism, polytheism and atheist thought coexist; state power that always dominates religious authority; and a worldly, utilitarian outlook centred on venerating Heaven and ancestors. From these Xi derives two basic principles for a Chinese Marxist atheism. The first is the separation of religion from politics together with freedom of religious belief, which keeps belief apart from political questions. The second is persuasion in ideological education, coupled with theoretical criticism of theology where it competes for the young. Xi then reads the Party's practice through these principles. Examples are Mao's view that peasants must discard the idols themselves, the 1950 directive on Christianity and Catholicism, the 1958 religious reforms in minority regions, and the 1982 document. That document says Party members must be atheists, that propaganda should be gentle, and that the shared political and economic interests of believers and non-believers outweigh differences of belief. Xi concludes that Marxist atheism in China has combined firm worldview opposition to theism with religious freedom for citizens and a united front with patriotic believers. In Xi's account this approach serves the goal of building a modern socialist country. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese scholar of scientific atheism presents the historical development of Party religious policy, and which Party documents and Mao texts support that account.

Religion and international relations in the age of globalization 全球化时代的宗教与国际关系 Xu Yihua Xu Yihua asks what the worldwide religious resurgence since the 1970s, and especially since 9/11, has done to the study of international relations and to practice in the field. The article argues that religion has returned from what it calls the 'Westphalian exile' to the centre of international affairs. Xu holds that the effect is only 'semi-subversive': it unsettles older assumptions without overturning them. The article has three parts. The first sets out five respects in which the resurgence challenges received views: secularization theory, the Westphalian system, the geography of world religion, the political role of religion, and the internet. The second surveys approaches to studying religion and international relations, drawing on Western scholars such as Scott Thomas, Ron Hassner and Jack Snyder. The third turns to the consequences for China. On the first part, Xu argues that secularization theory is contested rather than refuted, and that transnational religion has not displaced the nation-state, since religion is still not a 'hard currency' alongside politics, military and economics. Xu reads Western human-rights and religious-freedom advocacy, including the 'responsibility to protect', as a pretext for intervention against non-Western states. Xu also doubts that online religion amounts to a 'second Reformation'. On method, the article reports Hassner's 'broad', 'deep' and 'thick' routes and Snyder's four attitudes among IR scholars, and concludes that mainstream IR still prefers to absorb religion into existing paradigms. For China, Xu lists pressures: foreign religious exchange in a 'post-missionary era', online religion outrunning regulation, the 'evangelization' of US foreign policy, and extremism, separatism and terrorism combined with religious NGOs able to assist 'colour revolutions'. Xu also sees opportunities: religion as soft power, public diplomacy and national image, with traditional ideals of harmony offering a model of religious coexistence. The article calls for closer links between religious studies and IR in China, where the two fields have so far run on 'separate tracks'. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's survey of Western literature on religion and IR, together with an official-adjacent view of its security and soft-power implications for China.

Some problems in the relationship between natural science and religion 自然科学与宗教关系的若干问题 Yu Qiming Yu Qiming takes up the debate on the relationship between science and religion, which the author says has drawn growing attention at home and abroad. The article objects that many recent discussions are too loose and tend to evade the essential difference between the two. In the author's account, such discussions play down the way scientific advance has forced religion to change its doctrines, and instead promote complementarity or fusion. They also advance claims such as "religion is the mother of science". Yu's thesis is that science and religion arise from a common practical source but are essentially opposed, and that religion has not guided or enabled modern science. The article first distinguishes broad and narrow senses of the relationship: science and religion as institutions, as practices and as systems of ideas. It then concentrates on the narrow sense, the relation between scientific knowledge and religious consciousness. It takes up the complaint that science and religion are alike because both rest on faith. It then turns to scientists with religious beliefs, using Galileo and Newton as cases. Finally it considers whether modern science arose in Europe because of Christianity, by way of the "Needham question". Engels, Einstein, Marx and Joseph Needham are among the authorities cited. Yu argues first that science and religion emerged together from the labour and survival practice of early humans. They later diverged, and Yu holds that they are opposed in kind: scientific knowledge can be tested in practice, whereas religious belief in supernatural powers cannot. Second, the author rejects the claim that science also depends on transcendent faith. In Yu's view, trust in the lawfulness and intelligibility of the world is a conception of nature built up from practice, and scientific imagination and idealised thought experiments remain grounded in experience. Third, Yu holds that scientists achieve most when religious dogma interferes least, as in Galileo's case, and that Newton's turn to God for the planets' tangential motion marked the end of his creative work. Yu also argues that modern science drew on the Greek traditions of natural philosophy and formal logic and on socio-economic conditions, not on Christianity. In this account, the "rational element" in Christian theology came late and derived from Aristotle. Yu concludes that the cooperation of religious bodies with education and learning has only helped spread science in an incidental and limited way. Missionaries such as Matteo Ricci, in the author's reading, used science as bait for conversion. The article also credits Chinese inventions with contributing to European science, while holding that ancient China lacked the traditions of formal logic and causal experimentation. It therefore rejects any claim that China must adopt Christianity to develop science. Read the original if you want a Marxist, atheist reading of the science–religion debate, with detailed historical cases from Galileo, Newton and the Needham question.

Freedom of belief and the "other", law and the state: interpreting China's policy on freedom of religious belief 信仰自由与“他者”、法以及国家——解读我国的宗教信仰自由政策 Chi Xiqin Writing in 2012, Chi Xiqin asks how China's policy on freedom of religious belief should be understood. The author argues that freedom cannot be defined abstractly and has meaning only within relationships. Chi therefore reads the policy through religion's relations to three things: the "other", law and the state. The article concludes that religion, as a socio-cultural system built on belief in a transcendent realm, should be guided by the policy to serve public and national interests and to act as a socially "most useful hypothesis". The article begins from the Marxist principle that belief is a private matter and from the policy's treatment of religious freedom as a basic human right enjoyed equally by all citizens. It is organised in three sections. The first covers religion and the "other", split into the materialist "other" (science and atheism) and the religious "other" (other faiths). The second covers religion and law, and the third covers religion and the state. Chi draws on Sartre, Locke, Aristotle, Tillich and official documents, including the 1982 central document on religious questions in the socialist period. In the first section Chi holds that citizens are free to believe or not to believe, and to choose among religions. The author denies that atheist propaganda contradicts religious freedom: science and religion are presented as separate "languages" with different functions, so relations should be "politically united and cooperative, mutually respectful in belief". The second section argues that law makes freedom concrete and protects it, while obliging believers not to harm health, social order or ethnic unity. Law is also said to open space for religion in charity and disaster relief. The third section makes the state the absolute precondition of freedom. Religious activity must serve national and public interests, be patriotic and uphold the socialist system, and church and state are separated. Under the principle of independence and self-management, Chi cites Article 36 of the Constitution and calls for resisting infiltration by hostile foreign forces that use religion. Chi concludes that the policy guides religion towards adapting to socialist society and unites believers and non-believers around common fundamental interests. In Chi's account, religion's positive functions (psychological adjustment, cultural exchange) have corresponding negative ones, so the task is to promote the former and avoid the latter. Read the original if you want a compact, officially aligned exposition of how Chinese scholars justified the religious policy in 2012, including its stress on law, patriotism and independence from foreign religious bodies.

On education in the Marxist view of religion for university students 论高校大学生的马克思主义宗教观教育 He Yanfeng Feng Xue He Yanfeng and Feng Xue take up the question of how Chinese universities should teach students the Marxist view of religion. Writing in the early 2010s, they start from the premise that religion will persist for a long time in China's socialist society. Their thesis is that education in the Marxist view of religion is a core part of ideological and political education for the young people who are to carry on the socialist cause, and that it is currently weak and needs strengthening. The article has three parts. The first sets out why the task is urgent. The second diagnoses three problems in university ideological and political theory courses. The third proposes three remedies: richer course content, better teaching methods and a better-qualified teaching staff. The authors support their case with survey figures cited from other scholars and from their own earlier work. On urgency, the authors say students are drawn to religion by its philosophy, its ethics and its rites, and by growing competitive and psychological pressure. They also claim that foreign forces, led by the United States, use the internet and multimedia to infiltrate students through religion. They cite a Heilongjiang survey in which 19.6 per cent of students said they believed in religion and 65 per cent were half-convinced, and an overall estimate of 3–4 to about 20 per cent. On the problems, they find that religion occupies only a few minutes in the courses, that lecture-style indoctrination loses students' interest, and that some teachers lack knowledge of Marxist religious theory and Party religious policy. The remedies include adding material to specific courses, such as religion's origin, nature, function and eventual disappearance in the principles course, and the sinicisation of the Marxist view of religion in the Mao Zedong Thought and socialism with Chinese characteristics course. The authors also call for films, multimedia and interactive teaching that engages emotion as well as reason. The authors conclude that teachers must sincerely believe in and understand Marxism, grasp religion's content, features, functions and long-term nature, and be able to explain its positive and negative cultural value. In their view, teachers should also use Marxist atheism to help students resist idealism and what the authors call heterodox doctrines. Only then, they argue, can students internalise the Marxist view of religion and form a Marxist belief. Read the original if you want an example of how Chinese university ideological-education researchers framed religion among students around 2012, including the survey figures they cite and their course-by-course proposals.

On freedom of religious belief and university students' choice of belief 论宗教信仰自由与高校学生信仰选择 Zhao Dong Writing in 2012, Zhao Dong asks how freedom of religious belief, as guaranteed in China, should be understood and how university students should approach the choice of a belief. The article's answer is that religious freedom is a legally protected citizen's right and a private matter, but that students should be guided towards a Marxist worldview and a Marxist belief, and should respect the rules that separate education from religion. The article has two parts. The first sets out basic categories: it defines religion and religious belief, explains their origins and essence, and then interprets religious freedom through China's laws and Party policy. The second part turns to young students and offers four recommendations for making a belief choice. The discussion draws on Marx, Lenin and Mao Zedong, and on constitutional and legal provisions from 1949 to the 1990s. Zhao presents religion as a social phenomenon arising from natural and social forces, with social, cognitive and psychological roots. In Zhao's account, its essence is a distorted and illusory reflection of the alienated social relations of class society, and the author cites Marx and Lenin's well-known characterisations of it. Zhao then lists the legal basis of religious freedom, including Article 36 of the 1982 Constitution and Document No. 19 (1982), and argues that belief is a private matter and a question of the spiritual world. This holds only if it does not harm the state, society or others, and Zhao says Communist Party members, by the Party's nature, can only be atheists. For students, Zhao stresses the Education Law's separation of education from religion and the rule that no organisation or individual may conduct religious activities in schools. Zhao proposes four steps: study the basic theory of scientific socialism and communism systematically; establish a scientific worldview and outlook on life, together with the socialist core value system; learn the policies and regulations on religion in universities; and take part in social practice, so that a belief in Marxism is genuine rather than nominal. Doubts about communism are attributed to superficial study of Marxism. Read the original if you want an example of how Chinese university ideological education around 2012 combined legal explanation of religious freedom with Marxist atheist guidance for students.

Higher education should guide students to resist religious infiltration correctly 高校教育要引导学生正确抵御宗教渗透 Tian Yufen Writing in 2012, Tian Yufen takes up how Chinese universities should educate and guide students to resist what the article calls religious infiltration. Tian argues that universities train the builders and successors of the socialist cause and are a prime target for ideological subversion by hostile forces abroad. The article therefore treats the topic as a central task for the study of religious theory and for keeping a socialist orientation in higher education. The article has four parts. It first defines religious infiltration and sets out why resisting it matters. It then lists the basic features of infiltration, distinguishes it from normal religious activity, and ends with a set of countermeasures for universities. Tian draws on a 1995 collection of documents on religious work, a 2000 book by Wang Zuo'an and Hu Jintao's speech at the 90th anniversary of the Party's founding (2011). Tian defines infiltration as reactionary political activity under a religious cover, or missionary activity aimed at controlling Chinese religious bodies and establishing unlawful bases, and not as friendly religious exchange. In the article's account, hostile Western forces use religion to pursue "Westernization" and "division" of China, and the author cites the upheavals in Eastern Europe and the Soviet Union as a warning. Tian lists six features: political malignity, cultural aggression, international scope, varied methods, hidden organisation and severe destructiveness. Normal religious activity, in this view, differs from infiltration in purpose, agents, methods and social effect, since it is open and lawful while infiltration is concealed and aims to subvert the socialist system. Tian proposes a long-term mechanism with five elements: university leaders must set up an anti-infiltration organisational network. Students should be taught the Marxist view of religion and atheism, and ideological and political education should build the core socialist value system. The university should strengthen its teams of political-work staff and counsellors and put students first, including help with employment. It should also tighten supervision, which means cooperating with public security, policing campus networks and monitoring foreign teachers, international students, students from Hong Kong, Macao and Taiwan, and believers. Read the original if you want to see how a 2012 Chinese academic text frames religion as a security and ideological issue on campus and what practical measures it recommends.

The "opium cornerstone theory" is a distorted summary of Lenin's view of religion “鸦片基石论”是对列宁宗教观的歪曲概括 Jia Runguo Jia Runguo takes issue with a label that, in the author's account, has gained influence in recent years: the "opium cornerstone theory". It reduces Lenin's view of religion to one sentence, that "religion is the opium of the people" is the cornerstone of the Marxist worldview on religion. Jia argues that this is a distorted, decontextualised summary of Marxism-Leninism on religion. The short piece, posted in 2012, first sets out what Marx meant and how Lenin developed it, citing Marx's introduction to the critique of Hegel's philosophy of right and Lenin's "Socialism and Religion" and "The Attitude of the Workers' Party to Religion". It then reviews the Chinese Communist Party's attitude, including Zhou Enlai's 1950 remarks and the Central Committee's 1982 Document No. 19. It ends by listing the errors of the "opium" and "struggle against religion" labels. Jia contends that Lenin used Marx's phrase to insist that the Party keep a firm materialist and atheist worldview, and tied it to Russian revolutionary conditions. Lifting the sentence out of its context turns it into a rigid dogma. Jia reports that Zhou Enlai treated the slogan as belonging to the revolutionary period, to be played down once the Party held power. The label also severs Party religious policy from Marxist theory and presents part of Lenin's writing as his whole view. Jia says Lenin's essays enrich Marx's and Engels's view and do not form an independent one. Jia concludes that those who use the label to claim that Marxist religious theory is outdated, and who want to "develop" it with fashionable Western theories, are working metaphysically and against historical materialism. Jia presents the Party's religious policy as a continuing enrichment of Marxism-Leninism. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official Chinese Marxist case against reading Lenin's "opium" remark as his whole theory of religion.

New patterns of American religious infiltration of China and their ideological evolution 美国对华宗教渗透新模式及其意识形态演变 Huang Chao Writing in 2012, Huang argues that after the Cold War the United States developed a new pattern of religious infiltration of China, shaped by what the author calls a "new Cold War ideology". In Huang's account, this ideology combines a revived theocratic politics with older geopolitical thinking. Its basic aim, the article contends, is a "new religious extraterritoriality", symbolised by the 1998 International Religious Freedom Act. The article has three parts. The first describes the new pattern through four features: new goals, new strategies, new carriers and a new organisational system. The second traces the ideological evolution behind it, through theocratic, geopolitical and new Cold War strands, drawing on the history of Sino-American relations from the nineteenth century, including the Exclusion Act of 1882. The third turns to China's response. Huang relies on Huntington, William Engdahl, Kenneth Scott Latourette and Chinese religious studies scholars. Huang reads the 1998 Act as an attempt to recreate, in the form of US domestic law, the extraterritorial privileges that foreign missionaries held under the unequal treaties. The article says the strategy has shifted towards "politicising religion". It cites Christian rights-defence activism, work among Chinese students and scholars in North America, and organisations such as ChinaAid, which Huang says set up a national house-church body that China's Ministry of Civil Affairs banned in 2008. Huang finds the roots of this approach in a theocratic politics whose universalism gives way to US interests, citing the contrast between the "open door" and the Exclusion Act. The article sees continuity between old and new forms of hostility: "yellow peril" thinking becomes the "China threat", and anti-communist evangelism becomes the new Cold War outlook. It treats religion as a tool of international monopoly capitalism or hostile external forces, which Huang calls the "ultimate subject" of infiltration. Huang concludes that China should neither err to the left nor to the right, and should let religion be religion, as Zhou Enlai put it. The article proposes three measures: maintaining a new type of state–religion relationship based on separation and harmony; upholding independent, self-run churches free of foreign domination, with no "state within a state"; and building a long-term crisis-response mechanism for sudden religious incidents. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese scholar of religion in 2012 framed foreign missionary activity as political and ideological infiltration, or if you are studying official Chinese views of US religious-freedom policy.

A new model of US religious infiltration of China and its ideological evolution 美国对华宗教渗透新模式及其意识形态演变 Huang Chao Writing in 2012, Huang Chao asks how US religious policy towards China changed after the Cold War and what ideology lies behind it. The article argues that a "new Cold War ideology", which it says combines a revived theocratic politics with older geopolitical thinking, has produced a new model of religious infiltration. In Huang's account, the model aims at a "new religious extraterritoriality", embodied in the 1998 International Religious Freedom Act. The article has three parts. The first describes the new model through its goals, strategies, human and technical vehicles, and organisational system. The second traces the ideological evolution through three strands: theocratic, geopolitical and new Cold War ideology. The third sets out the author's proposals for a Chinese response, under the heading of harmony between government and religion. Huang compares the Act with the extraterritorial privileges that missionaries held under the unequal treaties abolished in 1943, and contends that the Act aims to create a "state within a state" in China. The article describes a strategy of "politicising religion", pursued through Christian "rights defence" campaigns, work among Chinese scholars and students in the US, and organisations such as ChinaAid. It presents this as part of a US "new human rights strategy". Drawing on Michael Hunt, Samuel Huntington and William Engdahl, Huang traces a continuity from the nineteenth-century Toleration Clauses and the Chinese Exclusion Act through the "clash of civilizations" thesis to the "China threat" thesis. The author calls the US attitude contradictory, because religious universalism is upheld only where it serves American interests, and treats infiltration as essentially political, with foreign religion as an instrument of hostile forces. Huang proposes three responses. China should uphold a new type of government–religion relationship, based on the separation of state and religion and aimed at harmony between them. It should keep the principle of independent, self-run churches and reject any foreign law above the Constitution. And it should build a lasting mechanism for handling sudden religious incidents, since the author warns of non-violent regime change through "swarming" tactics. Huang presents China's approach of managing religious affairs by law as a model that could also help ease international religious and political crises. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese religious-studies scholar framed US religious diplomacy and the "China model" of state–religion relations in 2012, with extensive citations of Huntington, Engdahl and missionary sources.

China Atheism Society 2010 annual meeting and symposium on the theory and practice of scientific atheism held in Urumqi “中国无神论学会2010年年会暨科学无神论的理论与实践研讨会”在乌鲁木齐召开 This is a very short conference notice reporting that the China Atheism Society's 2010 annual meeting, combined with a symposium on the theory and practice of scientific atheism, took place in Urumqi on 26–27 June 2010. The text gives no argument of its own and only records the event and its themes. The meeting was co-organised by the China Atheism Society, the Research Centre for Science and Atheism of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, the Xinjiang Academy of Social Sciences, and the School of Law and Economics at Xinjiang Normal University. According to the notice, more than 60 experts and scholars from across the country attended, and with observing scholars the total exceeded one hundred. Participants discussed a range of topics under the heading of the theory and practice of scientific atheism. The notice lists scientific atheism and society, the theoretical system and disciplinary development of scientific atheism, propaganda and education on atheism, and atheism education among ethnic minorities. It describes the discussions as broad and in-depth but reports no individual papers, positions or disagreements. The notice reaches no conclusions and announces no follow-up. It mainly documents the topics and institutional sponsors of a scientific-atheism gathering held in Xinjiang. Read the original if you need a brief record of the date, organisers, attendance and agenda of this 2010 meeting.

Eliminating religious extremism should begin with textbooks 消除宗教极端主义应从教科书开始 This short commentary, published in 2012 under the Science and Atheism category and with no named author, asks how religious extremism can be uprooted. It argues that military action alone is insufficient and that the soil in which extremism grows, namely textbooks and schooling built on prejudice and intolerance, must also be addressed. The piece begins with a study released by the US government, as reported by People's Daily Online on 10 November. According to that report, Pakistani textbooks portray religious minorities as inferior or second-class citizens, and most teachers regard non-Muslims as enemies of Islam. The author links this to a curriculum drawn up under the Zia ul-Haq military government in the 1980s, then mentions two bombings in Atyrau, Kazakhstan, by a group called the "Caliph's Soldiers". The commentary closes with the 2009 Texas curriculum dispute and the German practice of teaching religious ethics. The author contends that textbooks are a "specimen" of national culture and a "template" for the outlook of young people, so extreme ideas absorbed through them can easily be distorted and exploited. Yet the author does not conclude that religion should be removed from textbooks. Religion permeates language, history, ethics and art in every country, and schools also shape morals and ideas. Textbooks should therefore present religious knowledge objectively and rationally, opposing both the vilification of other faiths and the promotion of a single faith or sect. The author suggests three routes: describing religion through historical development, comparing the similarities and differences of faiths, and showing their value through art courses. Germany's secondary-school religious ethics classes are offered as a model. The author concludes that cultural interests outlast national or ethnic conflicts, and that sowing hatred yields revenge while sowing goodwill yields understanding. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese-language argument, from 2012, on how religion should be handled in school textbooks as a way to counter extremism.

On the constitutional principles governing religious belief 论宗教信仰的宪法准则 Writing in 2012 (the article carries no named author), the text asks how the Chinese constitution frames the state's stance towards religion and believers. It argues that Article 36 of the constitution, on freedom of religious belief, sets out a compact set of principles for handling religion. These are religious freedom, the separation of state and religion, independence and self-management of religion, and administration of religious affairs according to law. The article opens by quoting Article 36 in full and noting that, by its figures, over 100 million Chinese citizens follow a religion and that several religions coexist in the country. It then devotes one section to each of the four principles. Each section links constitutional wording to the wider themes of citizens' rights, state sovereignty, foreign policy and social stability. On religious freedom, the author presents it as a basic human right, in line with the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, and as including the freedom not to believe. The author divides belief into an inner side (conviction and feeling, a purely personal matter) and an outer side (organisation, institutions, conduct), which belongs to social life and must stay within the law. Separation of state and religion is described as the precondition and guarantee of religious freedom: no state religion, no state subsidy or religious tax, and no religious interference in justice, administration or education. The author justifies independence and self-management by the history of imperialist control over some religions in China. It holds that all major religions except Daoism came from abroad, and that Western hostile forces and separatists use religion to promote Westernization and division. Legal administration is presented as complementing, not opposing, freedom of belief. The author concludes that no religion holds privileges above the constitution and that religious freedom and separation of state and religion cannot be pretexts for escaping state administration. The article calls for protecting normal religious activity, resisting foreign infiltration, and cracking down on crime and superstition done under a religious cover. It also rules out any use of religion to oppose the leadership of the Communist Party and the socialist system or to undermine national unity. Read the original if you want a concise, official-line account of how Chinese legal scholarship in 2012 explained the constitutional basis of religious policy.

Reflections on the adaptation of the Marxist view of religion to the Chinese context 对马克思主义宗教观中国化的几点思考 The article asks how the Marxist view of religion, formed in nineteenth-century Western Europe and developed in Russia, has been adapted to China, and what that adaptation requires. Its answer is that the Party's Sinicised view of religion inherits the basic principles of historical materialism while revising specific classical judgements to fit China's conditions. The author does not appear to be named in the source; the piece was posted in 2012 under the heading Science and Atheism. The text has three parts. It first sets out the Marxist view of religion in the narrow sense (Marx and Engels) and in the broad sense (which also covers Lenin and the Chinese Communist Party). It summarises Marx and Engels on the nature, roots, social role and eventual disappearance of religion, and Lenin's additions on the roots of religion under capitalism and on Party policy. It then lists nine innovations and six features of the Chinese view, and closes with three basic requirements for adaptation. The core argument is that the Chinese view departs from the classical one in several ways. The article says it treats religion as a social, historical and cultural phenomenon and as a matter of belief among the people, rather than only as an ideology or "opium". It describes religion in China as long-term, mass-based and complex, with both positive and negative functions. Policy rests on freedom of religious belief, management of religious affairs according to law, independent and self-run religious bodies, a united front with patriotic religious figures, and guiding religion to adapt to socialist society. The author names six features: ideological character, scientific character, wholeness, practicality, openness and national character. Adaptation, the author argues, requires holding to the basic principles of historical materialism, starting from China's concrete national conditions, and enriching the theory further. Some classical formulations, such as "religion is the opium of the people", "religion as spiritual booze" and "struggle against religion", must be reconsidered and not copied mechanically. The author concludes that the Marxist view of religion as developed by the Party is an important source and component of the theoretical system of socialism with Chinese characteristics. It is presented as the fundamental guide for handling religious questions under socialism, for national unity, social stability and a harmonious society. The author expects it to keep developing under Party leadership and claims that it has wider significance for other socialist countries. Read the original if you want a compact, officially aligned account of how Chinese Marxist theory justifies its move beyond the classical "opium" thesis in religious policy.

Atheism as the crystallisation of human civilisation and thought 无神论是人类社会文明和思考的结晶 This article, published in 2012 with no author named, treats atheism as a product of human social civilisation and thought. It defines atheism in the West as the denial of a single God and his theology, and in China as the denial of all ghosts, spirits and supernatural forces. The author argues that atheism and theism will coexist for a long time, and that atheism's philosophical task is to criticise the illusions of religious theology, establish a scientific outlook on life and values, and promote social development. The piece is organised in three historical sections. The first surveys atheism in Chinese philosophy, from Xunzi, Han Fei, Wang Chong and Fan Zhen through Liu Zongyuan, Zhang Zai and Wang Fuzhi to the May Fourth movement, Zhang Taiyan, Chen Duxiu, Hu Shi and Li Dazhao. The second traces Western atheism from the ancient Greeks and Epicurus, through medieval persecution, pantheism, mechanical materialism, deism and French Enlightenment 'militant atheism', to Feuerbach, Darwin, Russell, Sartre and the 'new atheism' of Richard Dawkins. The third turns to Marxist scientific atheism. The core argument is that Marxist atheism is the 'higher form' of scientific atheism. The author reads Marx and Engels as moving beyond Feuerbach: religion is an inverted worldview arising from an inverted world of exploitation, so criticism of religion alone cannot overcome religious alienation, which requires changing the social system and economic base. Lenin is credited with sharpening the philosophical critique of religious thinking. For China, the author identifies two principles: full freedom of religious belief, with religion barred from threatening national security, ethnic unity or the socialist system; and no administrative means against theistic ideas, which are to be handled by persuasion and social change, while 'studying religion and criticising theology' applies in culture and education. The author sets out three values of Marxist atheism in contemporary China. It is the worldview starting point of the socialist core values system, and attempts to remove atheism from Marxism and socialist ideology are called dangerous. It is a healthy way of life that contributes to building a harmonious society. And, pursued thoroughly, it leads to a rational social system, so that its education and propaganda should be built into socialism with Chinese characteristics, with Communists uniting believers and non-believers to remove the social roots of religion. Read the original if you want a broad, Party-aligned overview of atheism in Chinese and Western thought and of how a Chinese Marxist scholar justified its place in official ideology around 2012.

On the significance of propagating scientific atheism in the strategy of rejuvenating the country through science and education 论科教兴国战略中科学无神论宣传的意义 The article asks why propaganda and education in scientific atheism should be part of China's strategy of rejuvenating the country through science and education. Its thesis is that the two are internally connected: the strategy cannot be carried out effectively unless scientific atheism is also vigorously promoted. The author, writing in the context of Deng Xiaoping Theory and the goal of a moderately prosperous society, treats the strategy as a basic national policy for developing the productive forces. The text has three parts. The first defines scientific atheism and traces its history, from the scattered and commonsense atheism of antiquity to the modern atheism built on natural science, including French militant atheism of the eighteenth century and its Marxist form. The second sets out the substance of the science-and-education strategy as part of Deng Xiaoping Theory, citing Deng's statements from 1977 to 1992, including the thesis that science and technology are the primary productive force. The third gives three reasons why atheist propaganda is intrinsic to the strategy. The author argues that Marxism is the most thoroughgoing atheism because it explains the roots, conditions and eventual disappearance of religious theism, and that atheism is also a premise of Marxism itself. On this basis the author claims, first, that modern science arose with the rise of atheist thought, so scientific atheism is a precondition of technological development. Second, the strategy depends on workers and researchers with a spirit of innovation and openness, which the author says can only rest on a scientific atheist worldview. Third, scientific atheism is science's natural ally, so advances in science and education will in turn erode superstition and theism and spread atheist convictions in society. The author concludes that the strategy and scientific atheism are inherently linked, and calls for effective, energetic propaganda and education in scientific atheism alongside implementation of the strategy. The piece is a short, programmatic statement that shows how atheism work was justified within the development policy framework of its period. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese Marxist writers around 2012 tied scientific atheism to Deng Xiaoping Theory and to science, education and talent policy.

The development of "new theism" since reform and opening up, and related laws and policies 改革开放以来新有神论的发展与相关法律和政策 Writing around 2011–2012 from the standpoint of scientific atheism, the article asks how organised, non-religious-label forms of belief in spirits and deities spread in mainland China after reform and opening up, and how law and policy responded. The author, who is not named, groups qigong, "extraordinary powers" and Falun Gong under the heading "new theism" and argues that the legal and policy framework still has gaps. The author also holds that scientific atheism remains under-researched and under-promoted. The article first notes that earlier scholarship has dealt with qigong, extraordinary powers and Falun Gong mostly from the angle of controlling "evil cults", and that few studies treat them together as new theism. It then gives a short history of the three phenomena from the 1980s to the 1990s. A second part surveys the Constitution (1982), the Education Law, Labour Law and Criminal Law of the 1990s, Party Document No. 19 (1982), Document No. 6 (1991), the 1997 white paper, the 1999 decision on banning cult organisations, and the 2004 and 2007–2011 notices on atheist education. The third part offers four reflections. In the author's account, the "qigong fever" of the late 1980s and early 1990s produced thousands of groups with self-invented doctrines and religious-style organisation. Claims of "extraordinary powers", first reported in 1979, were researched as science even though they presuppose spirits. Falun Gong, founded by Li Hongzhi in 1992, is described as an eclectic mix of Buddhist, Daoist and qigong elements with theistic content, and the author notes that these phenomena faded quickly only after its 1999 ban. Reviewing the laws, the author concludes that most provisions aim to guarantee religious freedom, while the 1999 decision was a direct response to cults, and that the Party's documents show a continuing commitment to Marxist atheism. The author calls for clearer legal definitions of religion, religious activity and religious organisation, and for rules covering groups that spread theism without a religious label or that act outside the law under a legal religious name. Home churches are cited as a case outgrowing the 1997 white paper's exemption from registration. The author also urges serious research and public education in scientific atheism, arguing it addresses the public sphere rather than religious bodies, and says new theism was linked to overseas new religious movements. Finally, the author calls for building the core socialist value system rather than relying on religion for a harmonious society. Read the original if you want an official-leaning Chinese scholarly view of how qigong, Falun Gong and atheist education were handled in law and policy up to 2011.

Marx and evolutionary theory: rethinking the relationship between Marx's and Darwin's doctrines 马克思与进化论——对马克思与达尔文学说关系的重新思考 The article takes up a long-standing question: how did Marx actually regard Darwin's theory of evolution? It notes that some scholars have called Marx a "socialist Darwinist", that others see Marxism and Darwinism as differing in form but similar in substance, and that many Marxists simply pair the two thinkers. Using Marx's own letters and texts, the author argues that Marx affirmed Darwin in limited respects but criticised him more extensively, and that the two doctrines differ fundamentally on human beings. The piece is built in three parts plus a conclusion. The first part gathers Marx's positive comments on Darwin from 1859 to 1867 and Engels's graveside speech. The second sets out Marx's doubts, drawing on his 1862 and 1869 letters and his 1866 preference for the French naturalist Pierre Trémaux. The third compares Darwin's The Descent of Man (1871) with Marx's Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 and The German Ideology on human nature and development. The two views cited as misreadings come from a 1979 article by L. S. Feuer and a 1983 article by P. van den Berghe, both known to the author through Chinese translations. The author argues that Marx valued Darwin chiefly for dealing a blow to religious theology and teleology and for supplying a natural-historical confirmation of historical materialism, which, the author stresses, was already formed before 1859. Marx faulted Darwin for misusing Malthus and for projecting English competitive society onto nature, and rejected the idea that a struggle for existence governs human history. For Marx, humans differ from animals through conscious practical activity, and human sociability is a product of social, economic and political conditions. Darwin, in the author's reading, treats human nature as a slow biological inheritance shaped by natural selection. On this basis the author says Darwin's view leans towards conservatism, while Marx's supports revolution because human nature can change quickly when the economic base changes. The author concludes that Marx refused to apply natural selection and the struggle for existence universally to human society and held that natural laws cannot simply be transferred to it. Marx's stress on human agency is described as the philosophical foundation of his theory of social revolution. Read the original if you want a short, letter-based account of how Marx's remarks on Darwin have been read in Chinese Marxist scholarship, and of the case for separating the two thinkers.

The theory of "cultural proselytising" 文化传教说 This short editorial-style commentary, published in the Science and Atheism section and posted in January 2012, asks readers to pay attention to "cultural proselytising". The author argues that foreign missionary activity in China now works through culture and economic inducement, and that its aim is political and economic advantage rather than faith alone. The text defines the term as proselytising by cultural means and proselytising directed at cultural elites. It then moves from the general nature of religious propagation, through the history of Buddhism, Islam and Christianity in China, to the unequal treaties after the Opium War and the present day. It closes with a wartime literacy-textbook lesson. The author holds that spreading one's religion is unobjectionable from the believer's standpoint, but that for those targeted it means changing beliefs and so brings conflict. Religious divisions, the author says, add a further line of cleavage in contemporary local wars, though material interests are their root cause. Before the Opium War, the entry of religions into China is described as legitimate and voluntary. After it, the author says, missionary clauses were written into treaties imposed by gunboats, so that China was made to surrender its souls along with its territory. Today, in the author's account, missionaries aim at influential intellectuals, the "brains and backbone" of China, to serve their own interests. The author points to a US government commission monitoring proselytising and questions whether Chinese intellectuals who assist understand the role they play. The author concludes that Chinese people should be on guard against efforts to place so-called "universal values" above national and ethnic interests. Certain intellectuals, the author suggests, should revisit the lesson "We are Chinese; we love our motherland." Read the original if you want a brief example of how a Chinese atheist-propaganda outlet framed religion, foreign influence and "universal values" in 2012.

"Doomsday" in the United States: what does it signify? “世界末日”在美国——它表象的是什么? Prompted by the failed prediction that Jesus would return on 21 May 2011, this commentary asks what the American "doomsday" phenomenon says about US society. The author argues that it should not be dismissed as foolish entertainment. In the article's account, belief in the end of the world rests on deep religious and cultural foundations in the West and is tied to social polarisation, weak scientific education and politics. The piece opens with Harold Camping of Family Radio, whose 1994 date and later 2011 dates for Judgment Day all passed without event. Camping then moved the date to 21 October 2011. The author then turns to the ancient Chinese story of the man of Qi who feared the sky would fall, as told in the Liezi, and sets out the four attitudes in it. The last third presents Gallup and Pew Research Center figures on religious belief, evolution and expectations of Christ's return, with a table of survey results. The author argues that doomsday belief in the West fuels a climate of fear that shapes national character and political decisions, including the treatment of other nations, beliefs and values as threats to security. In this reading, such fear lets interested groups profit and contributes to world instability. The author holds that today's believers fall into two groups, those with ulterior motives and those left behind by scientific civilisation, and that both are social problems. The cited surveys show 41 per cent of Americans expecting Jesus to return before 2050, with higher rates among white evangelicals, people without college experience and Southerners. The author links this to the finding that only 39 per cent accept evolution, and to the pushing of intelligent design into textbooks. The author concludes that the answer to natural disasters and doomsday fears is to put \"revitalising the country through science and education\" into practice, rather than religious explanations. In the author's view, wars and conflicts are man-made products of social structure and the interests of particular states and groups, and in the end the peoples concerned must wake up and speak for themselves. The author describes US society as sharply polarised in culture as well as economics, with a dominant minority also ruling in religion and ideology while cultural elites stay silent. The Liezi story is offered as a model of persuading people out of baseless dread. Read the original if you want an example of how Chinese science-and-atheism writing of 2012 interpreted American religiosity, with the survey data it cites.

"The end of the world" in America: what does it represent? “世界末日”在美国——它表象的是什么? This commentary, published in the Science and Atheism section and written in 2011–12, takes the failed prediction that Christ would return on 21 May 2011 as a window onto American society. The author argues that the episode is not mere entertainment for the gullible. In the article's reading, it reflects deep religious and cultural roots, a polarised social structure, and a politics that profits from fear. The article opens with Harold Camping of the Christian broadcaster Family Radio. His earlier prediction of an end in September 1994 failed, and he then moved the date to 21 May 2011 and, after that failed, to 21 October 2011. It then turns to the Chinese story of the man of Qi who feared the sky would fall, quoting the Liezi at length. It closes with survey figures from Gallup and the Pew Research Center on American belief in the Second Coming, evolution and religion. The author makes three main moves. First, belief in the end of the world is a basic doctrine of monotheism, and the author says centuries of such prophecies have left a psychology of fear that shapes national character. In the author's view, this fear carries over into US politics, where "cultural conflict" and weapons of mass destruction make other nations and beliefs look like threats to security. Second, the author holds that today's believers are of two kinds, people with ulterior motives and people left behind by scientific civilisation, and calls both a social problem. The Pew data are cited as evidence: 41% of Americans expect Christ's return by 2050, rising to 58% among white evangelicals and 59% among those without college experience, against 19% of college graduates. Third, the author links this to a society polarised economically, culturally and ideologically, in which a ruling minority dominates religion and ideology while cultural elites stay silent. The author concludes that natural disasters should be met with science and education, citing the slogan "rejuvenating the country through science and education", and not with religious readings. Conflict and war are described as man-made and tied to the political and economic demands of certain states and interest groups. The author says this is a question of social structure and system, which in the end only each country's own people can resolve. Read the original if you want a Chinese atheist-oriented reading of American religiosity, with Pew and Gallup figures and the Liezi parable of the man of Qi.

Some reflections on anti-cult work in universities 对高校反邪教工作的几点思考 This article, written around 2012 and published without a named author, asks how Chinese universities should respond to the spread of "cults" (xiejiao) on campus. It argues that cult infiltration of higher education has taken on new features, that universities have a particular responsibility to resist it, and that a set of practical measures can make campus anti-cult work effective. Falun Gong is the main example throughout. The text has three parts. The first describes the new situation: infiltration of students and of university teachers, and the cults' growing use of high technology. The second sets out why anti-cult work matters, looking at the causes of cult growth, current trends among cults, the social standing of universities and their social functions. The third proposes five approaches: theoretical research, strengthening anti-cult organisations, classroom teaching, innovative themed activities and psychological intervention. On the diagnosis, the author contends that cults deliberately target students, who are described as immature, curious about the supernatural and short of social experience. Cults also target teachers, whose standing can lend a "scientific" gloss to cult doctrine. The article claims that cults borrow scientific vocabulary, use the internet and satellites, and have moved from open to underground proselytising, while their followers disrupt teaching and sometimes turn to self-harm or violence. On the remedy, the author argues that universities hold the research capacity, the teaching platform and the student base to counter this. The proposals include surveys of students' beliefs and their ability to recognise cults, and comparative study of foreign experience. They also include teaching that ties anti-cult content to each discipline (for example, perpetual motion machines in mechanics, or the difference between religion and cult in philosophy) and programmes to counter psychological suggestion and to help affected staff and students. The author concludes that the struggle against cults is sharp, complex and long-term. Universities should raise the banner of science, spread scientific knowledge, break down modern superstition and strengthen political awareness among staff and students, with the aim of building a civilised campus. The article is a short policy-oriented piece from the early 2010s, useful as an example of how anti-cult work was framed in Chinese higher education. Read the original if you want to see the specific measures, such as the "Two Courses" teaching and themed campus activities, that an official-minded Chinese academic proposed for universities at the time.

A brief discussion of Ren Jiyu's thought on scientific atheism 简论任继愈的科学无神论思想 The article introduces the scientific atheism of Ren Jiyu, whom it presents as the founder of Marxist religious studies in China. Its author argues that Ren combined Marxist research on religion with publicity for the Party's religious policy and with sustained criticism of superstition. Noting that pseudo-science and superstition remain active while atheist advocacy is weak ("theism has its speakers, atheism has none"), the author holds that Ren's ideas still matter for Marxist education and for public morals. The text has three parts. The first sets out what scientific atheism means, tracing atheism from early Greek and Chinese thought to the modern natural sciences and then to Marxism. The second covers Ren's view of religion, its long persistence under socialism, and his handling of religious freedom. The third turns to his campaign against what he called the "new theism", which includes pseudo-science, "special powers" and fortune-telling presented as traditional culture. On the first point, the article reports Ren as holding that modern atheism, grounded in natural science, differs from ancient atheism because it explains why belief in spirits arises. Marxism is the most thorough form, since it identifies religion's social roots and the laws of its rise and decline. Ren is said to compare scientific atheism to elementary mathematics, which a Marxist worldview needs as its foundation. On religion, the article relays Ren's view that it is ultimately harmful to the people, a "spiritual anaesthetic" that peasant uprisings could not turn to their advantage. Because religion will fade only when alien natural and social forces are overcome, atheist education is the only means of struggle, and it must go together with legal protection of the freedom to believe or not to believe. The Party, Ren argues, must keep its own worldview independent. On the new theism, he sorted its forms into four kinds and criticised its distortion of "practice as the criterion of truth", urging that its demonstrations be replicated and exposed. The author concludes that scientific atheism is part of advanced culture and of building socialist spiritual civilization. Ren's call to escape ignorance as well as poverty ("脱愚") is offered as a continuing task. The author also cites Party members who practise religion and scholars who propose a more tolerant policy towards them, and treats Ren's position as a warning against both. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist account of Ren Jiyu's views on atheism, religion policy and pseudo-science, drawn mostly from his collected essays.

Similarities and differences between terrorism and cults 恐怖主义与邪教的异同 Christopher M. Centner This is an abridged Chinese translation of an article by Christopher M. Centner, a senior analyst at the US Defense Intelligence Agency, first published in 2003. Centner asks how terrorist organisations and cults overlap and where they differ, using al-Qaeda as the main case. He argues that al-Qaeda is a representative terrorist organisation with some cult-like traits, but that it differs from most cults in important structural ways. The Chinese editors added a note that the text was published after the killing of Osama bin Laden (announced 2011) to help the public recognise and guard against terrorist and cult groups. The article starts from Western definitions of each type of group. It then covers recruitment of al-Qaeda members, training and control, the figure of bin Laden, and suicide attacks. It ends with lessons for Western policy and seven warning signs of violent religious movements. Centner's central distinction is one of orientation. Terrorist groups look outward, towards what they do to non-members and towards political change. Cults look inward, towards control of members, self-preservation and growth. He cites Aum Shinrikyo as a cult that used terrorism and Peru's Shining Path as a terrorist group with a cult-like leader. Al-Qaeda resembles apocalyptic cults in its recruitment of alienated young people, its use of deception, its isolation of members and its view of a cosmic struggle between good and evil. Unlike cults, Centner argues, it depends on broad popular and financial support, and its followers do not deify bin Laden. He describes suicide attacks as glorified by social and religious norms, so that coercion by a cult leader is unnecessary. Centner concludes that a movement like al-Qaeda would survive its leader's death, because it draws on mainstream currents in contemporary Islamic thought. He describes a struggle inside Islam over how to govern Muslim societies that may last generations. He proposes that outside powers promote trade and ties with moderate regimes, fund schools, and help revise textbooks to cut hatred and glorification of war. He also proposes that academics warn governments of violent trends using seven indicators, including grievance rooted in past injustice, politics seen as cosmic conflict, violence justified by divine will, paramilitary training, and a violent, visionary leader. Read the original if you study how US security analysts compared terrorism and cults, or want the seven warning signs in full.

"Seizing China's head and back": on cultural proselytising and religion in universities “抓住中国的脑袋和脊背” Wenhua Chuanjiao Writing in December 2011, the author, who publishes under the pen name "Wenhua Chuanjiao" (literally "cultural proselytising"), responds to a report in the journal Science and Atheism (2011, no. 2). The report covered a Beijing Normal University symposium on how to respond to the spread of religion in universities. The author argues that Christian theology, "cultural Christians" and the "religious market theory" are forms of cultural proselytising. In the author's reading, they continue a long Western Christian effort to influence China through education and ideas, and that effort now reaches into Chinese universities. The commentary is built in three steps. It first distinguishes teaching general knowledge about religion from spreading theology. It then criticises the "religious market" idea and opposition to state regulation of religion. The longest section reviews historical statements by missionaries and Western figures, which the author takes from Luo Guanzong's book Never Forget the Past, a Guide for the Future (2003). It closes with the present: foreign theologians hired to teach the Bible, and a university press publishing creationist books. The author holds that universities in a socialist country should teach religion as an object of objective study, not train missionaries. Theology, whether inside or outside the church, is in the author's view theism opposed to atheism. "Cultural Christians" are said to be more persuasive than clergy because they dress theology in new concepts. The "market" theory, the author argues, trivialises believers' faith and amounts to a pretext for unregulated religious expansion. The historical quotations carry the main weight: the 1887 Society for the Diffusion of Christian and General Knowledge's William Williamson aimed to "disarm" the Chinese, and Timothy Richard sought control of public opinion and higher education in order to "seize China's head and back". In 1949 John Leighton Stuart and John Mott described the Bible as having a political value against Marxism and atheism. The author reads these as evidence that missionary work was political. The author concludes that infiltration of universities is not a new problem and has intensified since reform and opening up, and now takes the new form of invited "professors". The author suggests that some universities may be abandoning the Four Cardinal Principles, and praises Beijing Normal University's leaders for taking a clear stand. The author also calls for specialised research and for vigilance, since Western church bodies are said to study infiltration strategy. The author also says Christian scripture is part of human cultural heritage and that not all missionaries were hostile. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese atheist-oriented commentator in 2011 framed religion in universities as a question of ideological security, with the historical missionary quotations the author relies on.

Who is the "designer"? Reflections on reading Hawking's The Grand Design “设计”出自谁之手?——霍金《大设计》读后感 This is a reader's review, posted in 2011 under the category Science and Atheism, of Stephen Hawking and Leonard Mlodinow's The Grand Design (Chinese edition translated by Wu Zhongchao, Hunan Science and Technology Press, 2011). The reviewer takes up the "riddle of existence": why there is something rather than nothing, and who created or "designed" the universe. The review argues that Hawking answers from a purely naturalist standpoint, using science to remove God from the last domain he occupied. The review is organised in four parts. The first sets out why Hawking raises the question, tracing human answers from myth through Greek rationalism, medieval theology and Newtonian mechanism to Laplace, Nietzsche and Russell. The second explains how the book reads the existence of the universe and life, and why its title is read as a metaphor. The third considers the book's implications for worldview and culture, and the last gives an overall assessment. On the book's reasoning, the author highlights Hawking's historical account of how natural law came to be understood. Hawking sees two detours back toward theology, Aristotelian teleology and its medieval uptake by Aquinas, and the attempt by Descartes and Newton to make God the lawgiver. Two milestones led away from theology: the Ionian view of a non-human-centred cosmos, and Laplace's scientific determinism. The author then reports Hawking's case for M-theory: it follows determinism, uses model-dependent realism, and builds on tested theories, so that many universes arise from physical law without divine intervention. The author reads "grand design" as a negative metaphor for a unified theory of natural laws, not a supernatural designer. The author concludes that the book removes God from the origin of the universe, spreads a scientific worldview and supports scientific rationality and atheism. The review sets this against the growth since the 1960s and 1970s of New Age movements, mysticism and postmodernism, and against the American "intelligent design" disputes, which it calls a version of creationism. It calls for a new Enlightenment and praises the book as a rare popular work on scientific worldview. Read the original if you want a Chinese atheist-science-popularisation reading of Hawking, or an example of how the science–religion debate was framed in Chinese discussion in 2011.

Promoting the scientific spirit to raise the quality of China's citizens 弘扬科学精神，提高我国国民素质 The article, published without a named author in the Science and Atheism section of the Academy of Marxism site in 2011, asks how China can raise the overall quality of its citizens (guomin suzhi) to meet the needs of modernization. It argues that the scientific spirit is seriously lacking among Chinese citizens because of the influence of traditional culture, and that this deficit fundamentally limits improvement in national quality. Promoting the scientific spirit and reforming traditional culture is therefore presented as essential to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The text is organised in four parts. It first contrasts the rational tradition inherited from ancient Greek philosophy and modern Western natural science with Chinese culture, which it describes as shaped by practical, morally centred reason. It then considers the scientific spirit in relation to citizens' ideological and moral quality, their scientific and cultural level, and their sense of themselves as agents (subjectivity). Examples include Copernicus, Bruno, Galileo, Marx, Einstein and Chinese scientists such as Qian Xuesen. The author's central claims run as follows. Traditional Chinese culture, grounded in feudal patriarchal autocracy and agrarian production, is said to have matured prematurely and left habits of vague thinking and superstition. The author adds that rapid social transformation encourages impatience and a search for quick results. Education is a second target: exam-oriented schooling transmits finished conclusions and neglects scientific attitude. Following the Self-Strengthening Movement, the article argues, China imported scientific techniques while rejecting their underlying logic and philosophy, a split it illustrates with Lu Xun's line about new skills and old thinking. Third, drawing on historical materialism, the author holds that a scientific spirit of independent thought, scepticism and respect for facts builds the subjectivity that socialist democracy needs, citing Lenin's remark that illiterates stand outside politics. The author concludes that the scientific spirit is a basic quality of modern people in a scientific age, and that promoting it matters especially for a China undergoing reform and opening up and rapid social change. Raising citizens' quality is also linked to the Scientific Outlook on Development's people-centred approach and to Marxism's idea of the all-round development of the individual. Read the original if you want an example of how a 2011 Chinese Marxist text connects science, education reform, anti-superstition work and popular subjectivity to national modernization.

Spirit worship in ancient China 中国古代的神灵崇拜 This article, published in the Science and Atheism section, surveys the forms of spirit worship in traditional Chinese culture. It opens from the premise that ideas of gods and spirits are an illusory and distorted reflection of nature and society in the human mind. The author argues that tracing the sources and development of this culture can raise understanding and help establish a scientific view of culture. The survey moves through three broad areas: nature worship (heaven, earth, sun, moon, stars, thunder, wind, rain, water, fire, mountains and stones), the worship of animals and plants, and the worship of spirits proper. The last section sorts popular belief into creator gods, guardian and household gods, ghosts, nature spirits, deified persons (divine figures, immortals, sages, shamans), and sacred objects and souls. Examples come from the Han majority and from many ethnic groups, drawing on classical texts such as the Classic of Mountains and Seas. The author's core claim is that all such worship rests on animism and theism, which suit human ignorance and naivety, and that it ultimately serves survival. Bear-hunting peoples, for example, honour the bear as an ancestor while hunting it, which the author reads as a conflict between awe of nature and material need. The article also traces how worship of historical figures such as Yue Fei, Qu Yuan and Guan Yu drifts into superstition, and criticises discrimination against women in shamanic and hunting taboos. It treats shamanism as the most deceptive form because it is closest to everyday life. Some modern practices, including folk medicine using animal bones and near-death-experience research, are described as pseudo-science that carries on old worship. The author concludes that spirit worship is a rich but mystical part of traditional culture whose continued survival, even in an era that promotes atheism, shows how persistent such beliefs are. The article offers no programme beyond clarifying origins in order to support a scientific outlook. Read the original if you want a broad catalogue of Chinese popular deities, ghosts and nature cults, and an example of how Chinese atheist scholarship in 2011 framed religious folk belief.

The rise of religious belief in the countryside in the new period: causes and effects 新时期农村宗教信仰的兴起、原因和影响 This article, published on the site in 2011 with no author named, asks why religious belief has grown so quickly in rural China since reform and opening up, and what that growth means for the construction of a new socialist countryside. It argues that the rise has deep social and historical roots and that its effects are mixed. Overall, the article holds, the benefits outweigh the harms, provided the government guides and regulates religion properly. The article first describes the trend as it sees it: more believers, more religious venues and larger gatherings. It notes a shift from folk belief towards Christianity, Buddhism and Daoism existing side by side, and a believer population moving from the 'three mores' (elderly women, the sick, the uneducated) to the 'three increases' (men, young people, intellectuals). Part one sets out four causes; part two lists three positive and three negative effects. It draws on other Chinese scholars' studies, including a survey of Christians in a coastal town, and on Habermas's notion of the public sphere. On causes, the author points to anomie and social strain during modernization, in which many peasants cannot keep pace and seek spiritual consolation, while migration leaves the elderly, women and children behind. The author also cites the shrinking rural public sphere after the dissolution of the people's communes, state neglect of rural culture under an economy-centred policy, and peasants' growing desire to participate in public life. On effects, the author credits religion with building trust, enriching rural culture and training participation skills. The author warns of commercialisation, including officials and religious leaders profiting from temples and believers, of insular cliques that resist village authority, and of exclusivist attitudes that strain relations with non-believers. The author concludes that officials should reflect on their own conduct and respond rationally. They should neither ignore the surge nor treat it as a menace to be suppressed, but manage it according to law and guide religion to adapt to socialist society. Read the original if you want an example of how a Chinese scholar writing in 2011 explained rural religious revival in sociological terms and what policy stance the article recommends.

Folk religion and the Marxist view of religion 民间宗教与马克思主义宗教观 Writing in 2011, the author takes up a gap in Marxist religious studies in China. Since reform and opening up, popular belief has revived quickly, and cross-Strait exchange has made cults such as Mazu better known. Yet the Marxist classics say little about folk religion. The article argues that folk religion nonetheless deserves a place within the Marxist view of religion, and that researchers have wrongly treated it as a theoretical no-go area. The piece has three parts. The first treats folk religion as 'non-orthodox' religion, drawing on the historian Ma Xisha's work and on Marx and Engels's writings on the Reformation, peasant wars and early Christianity. The second looks at the social functions of folk religion in rural China, using examples of local deities, ancestor worship and the temple of Sun Yat-sen's home village. The third argues for a place in the Marxist view of religion. The author makes two main moves. First, following Ma Xisha, the author holds that folk and orthodox religion differ mainly in political status, not in religious nature. Citing Marx's early comment on Prussian censorship, the author reasons that in class society the state decides which religion counts as orthodox. Engels's remarks on superstition and on medieval heresy lead the author to say that such beliefs could serve rulers as tools for dulling the masses, or could clothe the masses' interests for 'revolutionary' ends. Second, using Marx's image of isolated smallholders, the author shows local gods marking land claims, uniting villages, and serving as rallying points in grain-tax revolts. Ancestor cults express kinship, and village temples can also be closed and exclusive, as at Cuiheng, where the Sun family was kept out of the temple. The author concludes that the classics mostly dealt with one type, the suppressed secret sects, whereas the commoner type is lawful and routine and appears secretive only because officials and literati rarely recorded it. Some scholars now use 'local religion' to mark this ordinary form. The author invokes Marx's call to explain superstition through history, and says folk religion should be studied as part of the Marxist view of religion. Read the original if you want a short Chinese-language argument from 2011 for treating folk belief as a legitimate object of Marxist religious theory, with village-level examples.

Marxism and religion A Chinese digest of Michael Löwy's "Marxism and Religion: Opium of the People?" 马克思主义和宗教 Michael Löwy This is a Chinese-language digest of an article by the French scholar Michael Löwy, "Marxism and Religion: Opium of the People?", which appeared in The New Socialist (no. 51, 2009). Löwy, a member of France's Revolutionary Communist League, is the author of The War of Gods: Religion and Politics in Latin America. He challenges the habit of reducing the Marxist view of religion to the slogan "religion is the opium of the people". He argues that the Marxist tradition holds a richer and more dialectical position. The digest follows Löwy's survey in roughly chronological order. It starts with the origins of the "opium" phrase among German writers, then turns to the young Marx's 1844 text and the more sociological approach of The German Ideology. It next covers Marx's remarks on Protestantism and capitalism, and Engels's studies of early Christianity and of peasant and Puritan movements. Löwy then looks at Lenin, Rosa Luxemburg, Ernst Bloch, the Frankfurt School and Lucien Goldmann. It ends by pointing to Latin American liberation theology. Löwy's central claim is that the classics grasped religion's double character. In his reading, religion both legitimates the existing order and can voice protest or revolt.
