He notes that Marx's 1844 formula already treats religious suffering as both an expression of real suffering and a protest against it. He credits Engels with analysing religion through class struggle and with admiring rebel currents such as the Anabaptists, while faulting him for sometimes reducing religion to a class "disguise". Löwy presents Luxemburg as defending Christianity's social tradition against conservative clergy. He presents Bloch as the first Marxist to rebuild the framework, treating heretical religion as a vehicle of utopian hope. Goldmann, in his account, compared religious and Marxist faith as parallel "wagers". Löwy adds that the classical discussions give almost no attention to how religious doctrine and practice affect women. Löwy concludes that, although the 19th-century view of religion as a bastion of reaction still fits many churches, fundamentalist groups and new sects, it is not the whole picture. He holds that understanding liberation theology in Latin America, and to a lesser extent elsewhere, requires integrating Bloch's and Goldmann's insights into the utopian potential of the Judaeo-Christian tradition. Read the original if you want a compact overview of how Marxist thinkers from Marx to Bloch have treated religion's ambivalence, or want to see how this material was introduced to Chinese readers in the science-and-atheism field.

Separation of religion and politics, or their unity? The Nationalist Government's policy considerations on Tibet's political and religious relations 政教分离，抑或政教合一？——国民政府对西藏政治和宗教关系的政策考量* This article, posted in 2011 without a named author, examines how the Nationalist Government (Nanjing, 1927–1949) approached Tibet's system of unity of religion and politics. It notes that scholarship has studied the system itself but not its twentieth-century evolution or the Nationalist attempts to reshape it on the principle of separating religion from politics. The article argues that the government wished to introduce that separation as part of political integration with the interior, but lacked the strength to do so. Tibetan authorities, for their part, resisted any change. The article first defines the two principles and traces the Tibetan system from the Sakya period to its formal Gelug shape in 1751. It then proceeds chronologically in four sections. These cover the late Qing and early Republic and the policy statements of 1929–1932, the Huang Musong mission to Lhasa (1934) and the later Wu Zhongxin mission, and the post-1945 "high degree of autonomy" schemes and the 1946 Constitution. A concluding section assesses why the effort failed. The evidence is mainly archival: Mongolian and Tibetan Affairs Commission documents, government directives and Tibetan responses. The author's central claim is that the government's real aim stayed constant while its stated policy shifted with its capacity. In 1929 the Commission planned a six-year programme to separate administrative and religious powers, but Chiang Kai-shek's 1934 remarks favoured "soft" conciliation over force. Official texts then repeatedly promised to preserve the Dalai and Panchen Lamas' religious and political authority, while omitting any endorsement of the system itself. The 1945 draft autonomy plan and the post-war programme reaffirmed separation, and the Commission wavered on whether the constitution's "Tibetan autonomy system" meant the existing theocracy. The author reads these shifts as a consistent aim under unfavourable conditions. Tibetan authorities invoked a "patron–priest" relationship, feared Soviet-style outcomes as in Outer Mongolia, and treated change as a threat to elite privilege. The author concludes that separation was a historical necessity of building a modern nation-state, but the Nationalist Government could not extend effective control to Tibet. Tibetan society, in the author's account, lacked internal forces for self-reform under serfdom, so separation historically followed strong central intervention. Only the People's Republic, from the suppression of the 1959 rebellion to the founding of the Tibet Autonomous Region in 1965, is said to have ended the system. Read the original if you want a documented account of Nationalist-era policy debates on Tibet's religious and political order, bearing in mind that it is framed in terms of integration and central authority.

Seminar on the Marxist view of religion (2011) held in Beijing 马克思主义宗教观研讨会(2011)在京召开 This is a report on the academic seminar "Marxist View of Religion (2011)", held in Beijing on 2–3 July 2011 to mark the 90th anniversary of the Communist Party of China. It was co-organised by the Institute of World Religions at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences and the Religious Research Centre of the State Administration for Religious Affairs. The report says participants affirmed Marxism as the guiding thought for religious studies and stressed adapting the Marxist view of religion to Chinese conditions. The report lists attendees from the Institute (including its director Zhuo Xinping), the United Front Work Department and the State Administration for Religious Affairs. It names about twenty papers. They cover Capital's place in the Marxist view of religion, Marx's early views, Lenin's scientific atheism, and religious policy in the Party's history, including Daoism, Xinjiang, Tibet, Laos and the Italian Communist Party. The seminar followed the 2010 creation of a research office on the Marxist view of religion, set up in response to the call to make the Academy a "strong base of Marxism". Jia Runguo traces the Party's religious policy after the Cultural Revolution through successive leaderships. He sees Document No. 19 of 1982 as the foundation of a socialist theory of religion with Chinese characteristics. He sees the Jiang Zemin era as adding the basic policy of "actively guiding religion to adapt to socialist society". He treats the Hu Jintao era's aim of "harmonious religious relations" as the latest result of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context. Min Xianliang similarly presents the Party's religious theory as part of the Marxism with Chinese characteristics. Huang Kui offers a political-economy reading. He argues that religion is rooted in private ownership and class division, and that class analysis is not outdated. He urges renewed atheist education. He says united front work should be limited to religious elites. He describes freedom of religious belief as in essence a "bourgeois right", and he rejects absolute separation of church and state. The report concludes that the Party's 90-year experience in handling religious questions is of theoretical and practical importance for current work. The main point of contention it reports was how to study the Marxist view of religion under present conditions. Participants debated moving from stress on struggle and "criticism" of religion towards "active guidance" and the building of a harmonious society, in light of the 17th Party Congress (2007). Read the original if you want a record of how Chinese religious-studies scholars and officials framed Party religious policy in 2011, including the full paper titles.

Opposing cults is an act of civilisation, and the intellectual world must take responsibility Marking the tenth anniversary of the China Anti-Cult Association 反邪教是文明之举，思想界需要担当责任 ——纪念中国反邪教协会成立十周年 Marking the tenth anniversary of the China Anti-Cult Association (founded 2000), this 2011 commentary reviews more than a decade of the campaign against cults, symbolised by the ban on Falun Gong. The author argues that opposing cults is an act of civilisation, rooted in Chinese history and culture. It also holds that preventing cults serves political stability, economic development, national security and a harmonious society. The article calls on the intellectual world to attend to the ideas and public opinion that allow cults to grow, and to accept social responsibility for doing so. The text is organised in five sections. It first traces cults to shamanic (wu) culture and to imperial-era rulers' dealings with magicians, from the Qin and Han dynasties to the Three Kingdoms. It then turns to the 'spiritualism' (lingxue) movement of the late 1910s and the May Fourth critics who opposed it. A third section covers the 'human body science' and 'supernormal powers' wave, the deified qigong boom and Falun Gong from 1979 onwards. The last two sections discuss the post-Falun Gong period and the duty of thinkers. The author's central claim is that banning Falun Gong removed neither the social roots of cults nor their intellectual justification. In the article's account, the main new form uses a Christian label, with 'underground churches' as a seedbed. Three reasons are given: Protestantism's decentralised character, its foreign character and what the author calls US support under the 1998 International Religious Freedom Act, and a 'Sinophone Christian theology movement' that is said to dominate academic discourse on religion. The author also criticises scholars who attribute cults to the suppression of legitimate religion or who want religion to supply moral education, and adds that academia has barely responded. The author prefers 'ideals' to 'faith', arguing that faith leads to blind obedience. The author concludes that prevention is better than reactive crackdowns, and that the key is the direction of public opinion. The author urges popularising scientific knowledge and the scientific spirit, systematic building of scientific atheism as a discipline, and a stronger legal footing for the judiciary. The author holds up the late academician Zhuang Fenggan, Ren Jiyu, Yu Guangyuan, Gong Yuzhi, Ye Shengtao and Zhou Jianren as models of thinkers who spoke out. The author is confident that China will not become a religious country. Read the original if you want an example of how a Chinese scientific-atheist writer in 2011 framed cults, folk belief and Christianity together, and how the article uses history to argue for a role for intellectuals.

Upholding Marxism and upholding scientific atheism 坚持马克思主义与坚持科学无神论 Writing in 2011, the author asks whether it is legitimate and reasonable, in the primary stage of socialism and amid diverse and shifting currents of thought, to propagate scientific atheism and criticise theism. The article treats this as a prior question for any research on scientific atheism. It links the worry to a perceived imbalance in scholarship, where theism has many advocates and atheism few. The author's answer is that upholding scientific atheism is inherent in upholding Marxism, and that Marxism in turn must guide atheist research and propaganda. The text has three parts. The first argues that scientific atheism follows from Marxist philosophy and from the Marxist view of religion. The second takes up those who accept atheism but object to criticising theism. The third sets out how research and propaganda should be guided by Marxism and by the Party's basic principles and policies on religious work. It rests heavily on Engels, Lenin, Hu Jintao's speeches and Party documents. The author reads Engels's account of the basic question of philosophy, and passages by Engels and Lenin on idealism and "priestcraft", as showing that atheism is bound up with dialectical and historical materialism. In the author's account, scientific atheism is the core of the Marxist view of religion, since religion's essence, its development and its eventual disappearance are all explained through the idea of gods. On criticism, the author argues that scientific atheism cannot take gods as its object, because they do not exist. Its object is ideas of gods, and in a deeper sense theism itself, so an atheism barred from criticising theism would lose its object. The author also holds that social harmony rests on shared economic, political and ideological foundations, not on shared belief or unbelief, so atheism does not conflict with the Party's call for harmonious coexistence among believers and non-believers. The author concludes that atheist research must rest on dialectical and historical materialism, draw on useful earlier scholarship, and help build a Marxist study of religion that avoids treating Marxism as a slogan. It must also follow Party religious policy. Two limits are stressed: atheist propaganda should not be given undue priority, since Engels and Lenin opposed "declaring war on religion", and it must be reconciled with respect for citizens' freedom to believe. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist scholar in 2011 justified scientific atheism within Party religious policy, using extensive citations of the classics.

The social cost of religious belief: the cases of Gannan and Linxia prefectures in Gansu 宗教信仰的社会代价 ——以甘肃甘南和临夏两州为例 Liu Xiaoxiong Writing in 2011, Liu Xiaoxiong asks how religion affects economic and social development in minority regions where belief is nearly universal. The article accepts that religion has had positive effects on people's spiritual life. It argues, however, that where religion has not developed reasonably or adapted to society, it becomes one important cause of regional backwardness. Liu's thesis is that believers in Gannan (Tibetan) and Linxia (Hui) prefectures in Gansu pay a heavy social cost for their faith. The study rests on the two autonomous prefectures, where Tibetan and Hui residents are described as almost entirely religious. Liu notes that five of Gannan's eight counties and cities, and all of Linxia's except Linxia city, are national-level poverty counties. The article draws on provincial statistics for Gansu's religious venues, clergy and believers, plus a Chinese study of religion and economics and the economist Robert Barro. It is organised into five sections: consumption of resources, occupation of land, consumption of time and energy, constraints on thinking, and a conclusion. Liu's central claim is that religious activity diverts wealth from productive to non-productive use. Building and maintaining temples, mosques and tomb shrines, supporting clergy who do not take part in production, and funding rituals are all described as burdens met by donations from local people. Liu cites official figures of 6,771 approved religious venues and over 20,000 clergy in Gansu, and contrasts splendid temples with run-down believers' homes. The article adds that religious sites take up farmland and complicate planning, that worship and ritual absorb time otherwise available for work, and that doctrines favouring renunciation and the afterlife sap the drive to pursue wealth. Liu also attributes disturbances such as those of 2008 and 2009 to reactionary elements among the clergy, incited by hostile forces at home and abroad. Liu concludes that the restraining effect of religion runs through every aspect of life in these communities, and that excessive religious burdens are one cause, though not the only one, of poverty. Under the Scientific Outlook on Development, the author calls on the state, the government, religious circles and society to guide religion so as to minimise its negative effects and help it adapt to China's society and a harmonious, sustainable social development. The atheism of Marx's philosophy seen through the logic of its development 从马克思哲学的展开逻辑看其无神论特质 The article asks in what sense thoroughgoing atheism is an inherent feature of Marx's philosophy, and answers by tracing how that philosophy unfolded. The author argues that going beyond a religious view of history was a precondition for founding historical materialism. Marx's consistent aim, the scientific study of social development in order to achieve real human freedom and emancipation, is said to have been realised in three stages, so that the formation of Marx's philosophy is the unfolding of his atheism. The article follows Marx's texts in chronological order. It begins with the doctoral dissertation on Democritus and Epicurus, the Rheinische Zeitung period, the critique of Hegel's philosophy of right, On the Jewish Question, the Contribution to the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right: Introduction, and the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844. It then turns to The German Ideology, and finally to The Poverty of Philosophy, the Grundrisse and Capital. Engels's early remarks on religion are also drawn in. The text closes with practical implications for contemporary China. The author's central claim is a shift from criticising religion to analysing the social conditions that produce it. In the early works Marx calls for the liberation of individual subjectivity, but the author says this remained at the level of value-based ought. Marx then concluded that religion is a symptom of worldly limits, not their cause, so that criticism of heaven becomes criticism of earth. In The German Ideology, in the author's reading, Marx and Engels reject the Young Hegelians' purely ideological critique and ground history in material production, treating communism as a real movement, not an ideal. The author holds that the mature critique of political economy completes this path. Capital is shown to be a social relation and not a thing, and the discovery of surplus value exposes the reproduction of capitalist relations of production. Human emancipation then depends on rationalising social relations through the proletariat overthrowing capitalism. The author concludes that no link in this logic places human liberation in any supernatural power, and cites Raymond Aron's remark that atheism is essentially tied to Marx's Marxism. Three lessons for present-day China are drawn. Liberation relies on human agency, not on saviours. It requires grounding in practice, attention to the laws of social development, and solutions to people's real problems. It also needs fairness and justice and rationalised social relations, with a people-centred approach in harmonious development, so that religion loses its soil. Read the original if you want a close reading of Marx's early to mature texts as a genealogy of atheism, or an example of how Chinese scholars framed this theme around 2011.

The atheism of Marx's philosophy seen through the logic of its development 从马克思哲学的展开逻辑看其无神论特质 The article, written in 2011 and carried in the site's Science and Atheism category, asks how the thoroughgoing atheism of Marx's philosophy should be understood. The author reads the later economic works as locating the roots of religion and exploitation in the reproduction of capitalist relations of production. On this reading, capital is a social relation, not a thing, and surplus value explains proletarian poverty. Religion therefore disappears of itself once its worldly basis is removed. The author concludes that no link in this development rests human liberation on a supernatural force. The article endorses a Western scholar's remark that atheism is essentially bound up with Marx's Marxism. It draws three lessons for present-day Chinese social development. If there are no ghosts in the world, how can there be a "ghost culture"? 世间没有鬼，何来鬼文化？ Chen Zujia Writing in 2011, Chen Zujia, a senior People's Daily reporter, objects to official promotion of "ghost culture". The commentary places the issue within the current "national studies fever" (guoxue re), in which Chen sees folk beliefs such as feng shui and the I Ching spreading under the label of traditional culture. It then moves through the origins of belief in ghosts, literary examples (Lu Xun's Xianglin's Wife, the Peony Pavilion tradition, Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio), and ancient Chinese sceptics, before turning to present-day conditions. Chen contends that belief in ghosts and gods arose from very low productive forces, when people feared disasters they could not explain, and that rulers in slave and feudal societies used it to control minds. In Chen's reading, such belief brought ordinary people no benefit, as Xianglin's Wife shows, and is a "spiritual heroin" that poisons people and hinders social development. Chen cites ancient anti-ghost writing, including Confucius's reticence about spirits, Fan Zhen's essay on the extinction of the spirit, and a tale in which a ghost loses a debate with a sceptic. Chen accepts that ghost belief existed historically and that some artists used ghost images against feudal despotism, and allows a few experts to study it from a materialist, historical standpoint. But Chen opposes large public investment in it, notes officials who believe in feng shui rather than Marxism, and calls for reasonable and lawful means to eliminate ghost-and-spirit doctrines. Chen asks whether this runs counter to the Scientific Outlook on Development and amounts to turning back history. Scientific atheism and Marxism: marking the tenth anniversary of the journal Science and Atheism 科学无神论与马克思主义——纪念《科学与无神论》杂志创刊十周年 Yu Qiming Writing in 2011 to mark the journal Science and Atheism's tenth anniversary, Yu Qiming asks why scientific atheism, an important component of Marxism, has been left with 'nobody to talk about it'. Yu names two causes: worry that atheist education would harm freedom of religious belief, which the author sets aside as already answered elsewhere, and the view that Marxist education makes separate work on scientific atheism unnecessary. The article argues that the second view is mistaken and that the two must be combined. The piece is short and runs in three steps. Yu says atheism passed through three forms: ancient naive atheism, modern atheism and Marxist atheism, tied respectively to spontaneous, metaphysical and dialectical materialism. Scientific atheism and Marxism In commemoration of the tenth anniversary of the journal Science and Atheism 科学无神论与马克思主义——纪念《科学与无神论》杂志创刊十周年 Yu Qiming Writing in 2011 to mark the journal Science and Atheism's tenth anniversary, Yu asks why scientific atheism, an important part of Marxism, has been neglected to the point that "nobody talks about it". Reflections on the question of the "relationship between religion and culture" 关于“宗教与文化关系”问题的思考 Zhu Xiaoming Zhu Xiaoming takes up a question that, in the author's account, has drawn growing attention in recent years: how should the claim that "religion is culture" be understood, and how should a ruling Communist Party handle it? Writing in 2011, Zhu argues that the claim is true as far as it goes but captures only one attribute of religion, not its essence. The Party, the article holds, should support religious believers' and scholars' cultural readings of religion while declining to talk about religion in general terms as culture. The article has three parts. It first surveys views on the relationship: the remarks of Zhao Puchu, Qian Xuesen, Mao Zedong and Fan Wenlan, then four strands of current Chinese scholarship. These range from enthusiastic endorsement of "religion is culture" to warnings against it. It then describes what kind of culture religion is, citing scholars on its features and on its material, institutional and spiritual layers. The last part sets out how the ruling Party should respond. Zhu draws on scholars' analysis to identify distinctive traits of religious culture: alienation, exclusivity, organisation, expansiveness and comprehensiveness. Zhu says it can be exploited by hostile foreign forces. Zhu then argues that the Party must keep to Marxist views of religion, which the article sums up as three "views", three "principles" and three "laws". The central principle is that religion's essence cannot be explained by culture or other spiritual factors, only by social development. Religion is also a social entity with organising and mobilising power, so it cannot be separated from politics. Zhu concludes that the Party should encourage theological and scholarly work that draws out the positive elements in religious traditions and helps religions adapt to socialist society. It must not reduce religion to culture. The article warns against missionary activity, theological propaganda or foreign strategic containment carried out "in the name of culture", and it calls for unity between believers and non-believers as part of building a harmonious society. Reflections and proposals on strengthening atheism research, propaganda and education 关于加强无神论研究宣传教育的思考和建议 Jia Runguo This is the text of a speech given by Jia Runguo, a deputy director of the Religion Research Centre of the State Administration for Religious Affairs, at a symposium on atheism research, propaganda and education. The symposium was convened by the general office of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences on 15 February 2009. Jia argues that the Party's two basic points on religion, freedom of religious belief and sustained atheist education, are meant to go together. In Jia's view the second has been neglected over thirty years. The speech opens with the record since the early 1980s. Jia cites the 1982 Central Committee Document No. 19 and statements by Deng Xiaoping and Jiang Zemin, and notes that Hu Jintao's remarks on atheism were not made public. Jia says that belief in religion has become freer and more widespread while atheist work has shrunk. According to Jia, no research institution for atheism exists, and only one journal, Science and Atheism, is run on a part-time basis. Jia argues that philosophy teaching must refute idealism, metaphysics and theism as well as set out materialism, dialectics and atheism, and that Marxist philosophers need to study religious theism. Drawing on the Marxist view of religion, Jia treats natural, social and epistemological roots of religion. Jia holds that private ownership remains the deepest social root, and that this explains why religion thrives in technologically advanced Western countries and why secularisation theory failed. Jia also rejects the claim that atheism has no audience, since most people hold ambiguous beliefs and turn to faith in a crisis. Jia proposes dedicated Marxist research bodies, for example a research office on materialism and atheism within the Academy's Institute of Marxism or a Marxist-view-of-religion office in the Institute of World Religions. Jia also proposes translating Enlightenment and modern atheist works with attractive packaging, state funding for the work, and expert studies of present-day forms of theism. Jia treats the last as the most practical task to start with. Read the original if you want a first-hand statement, from an official researcher in 2009, of the case for reviving state-backed atheist education in China and of the institutional arrangements proposed.

Promoting religious harmony and serving scientific development A review of religious work during the 11th Five-Year Plan period 促进宗教和谐 服务科学发展 Published in 2011, this unsigned official-style review assesses religious work during the 11th Five-Year Plan period (2006–2010). Intelligent Design theory: the latest version of creationism 创世论的最近版本 Cai Zhong Cai Zhong examines the American Intelligent Design (ID) movement, which the article presents as the newest form of creationism. ID holds that complex, information-rich biological structures cannot arise from natural forces and require a supernatural intelligence. Cai argues that the movement uses the neutral word 'design' to avoid terms such as 'God' and 'creation' and so get past legal barriers to religious teaching in schools. The article also argues that its rise is tied to relativism in recent philosophy of science. The article has two main parts and a short conclusion. The first part traces the movement's origins with the law professor Phillip Johnson in the 1990s. It then covers its 'wedge' strategy, its funding through the Discovery Institute's Center for the Renewal of Science and Culture, and its legal struggles, from early anti-evolution statutes through the 1987 Edwards v. Aguillard ruling to the 2005 Kitzmiller v. Dover case. The second part reflects on the movement's intellectual background. Drawing on Barbara Forrest, Cai describes the wedge strategy as a three-step plan: research, shaping public opinion, then cultural confrontation. The article reports Forrest's literature searches, which found no ID research papers in biology journals, and concludes that the strategy failed in the scientific sphere. It also reports that the movement pressed on with lobbying, publishing and educational campaigns, until Judge Jones's 2005 ruling that teaching ID in public-school science classes was unconstitutional. In the second part Cai argues that Kuhn's Structure of Scientific Revolutions and later social constructivism, including David Bloor's symmetry principle, gave creationists an opening. In this reading, science and creation 'science' became rival, incommensurable paradigms and the dispute became a contest for cultural authority. Cai concludes that methodological naturalism cannot build a firm wall between science and religion. Postmodern relativism, in Cai's view, swings to the opposite absurdity, and both discuss science and religion in the abstract, detached from scientific practice. The article proposes comparing the actual practice of evolutionary biology with that of creation science, so as to identify creationism's non-scientific character and draw a real line between science and religion. Read the original if you want a Chinese philosopher's account of the ID movement, the Dover trial and the link between constructivist science studies and creationism.

The latest version of creationism: Intelligent Design theory 创世论的最近版本 Cai Zhong Cai Zhong examines Intelligent Design (ID) theory, which the article calls the late-twentieth-century version of creationism. It asks how the ID movement tried to enter American science education and why it arose. The author argues that ID is a religiously motivated political and cultural project, not a scientific theory. They also argue that it drew on the relativism of late philosophy of science. The article opens with the 2002 resolution of the American Association for the Advancement of Science against teaching ID as science. Part one traces the movement's origins with the law professor Phillip Johnson and the Discovery Institute's Center for the Renewal of Science and Culture. It then covers the "wedge" strategy, its funding, and the legal contests from the 1925 Tennessee law to Edwards v. Aguillard (1987) and the Kitzmiller v. Dover trial (2005). Part two reflects on the movement's intellectual background, and a short conclusion follows. Cai first presents the wedge strategy as a three-stage plan: research programmes, opinion-shaping, and cultural confrontation, including removing legal barriers to classroom teaching. Citing Barbara Forrest's database searches, the article reports that no peer-reviewed biological work supporting ID could be found, so the research stage failed. Judge Jones's 2005 ruling then ended the attempt to enter public schools. In the second part, Cai links ID to the collapse of logical empiricism's demarcation project after Kuhn, and to the social constructivism of David Bloor's symmetry principle. In this reading, creationists can present science and creationism as incommensurable paradigms with equal standing, and Johnson frames the dispute as a clash of stories and worldviews. Cai concludes that the court defeat does not end the conflict between creationism and evolution. Methodological naturalism cannot build a firm wall between science and religion, and postmodern relativism lurches to the opposite extreme. Both discuss science and religion abstractly, apart from scientific practice. Cai proposes comparing the actual practice of evolutionary biology with that of creation science to identify the latter's non-scientific character and draw a real boundary. Read the original if you study the ID movement, the American legal history of the evolution dispute, or the way Chinese philosophers of science criticise social constructivism.

The social cost of religious belief: the cases of Gannan and Linxia prefectures in Gansu 宗教信仰的社会代价——以甘肃甘南和临夏两州为例 Liu Xiaoxiong Writing in 2011, Liu Xiaoxiong asks how religion affects economic and social development in minority regions where belief is intense. The article acknowledges religion's positive historical role, especially for people's spiritual lives. Its thesis, however, is that where religion has not developed reasonably or adapted to society, it becomes an important cause of backwardness. Liu focuses on the Tibetan Gannan and Hui Linxia autonomous prefectures in Gansu, where the author says nearly the whole population believes. The article first notes that five of Gannan's eight county-level units, and all but one of Linxia's, are national-level poor counties. It concedes that geography, climate, transport and history also contribute. It then sets out five channels of what it calls religion's inhibiting effect: consumption of people, materials and money; occupation of land; consumption of time and energy; and constraint on thinking, followed by a conclusion. Liu draws on provincial statistics on religious venues, clergy and believers, and on one cited economic argument by Robert Barro. Liu's core reasoning is economic. Building and maintaining venues, supporting clergy who do not take part in production, and funding rituals and festivals all rely on donations from local believers. Liu calls this non-productive, parasitic consumption that moves wealth out of production and blocks accumulation and expanded reproduction. The author points to magnificent temples beside shabby homes as evidence. Religious sites are also said to take good land and to disrupt planning, and daily worship is said to take time from productive work. Liu adds that religious teaching disparages the pursuit of wealth and so saps believers' drive. The article also says some clergy, encouraged by foreign anti-China forces, have caused unrest, and cites the 2008 and 2009 incidents. Liu concludes that inappropriate religious burdens are one cause, among several, of low living standards and lagging development in believing regions. The author calls on the state, government, religious circles and society to guide religion under the Scientific Outlook on Development. The aim is to minimise its negative effects and help it adapt to Chinese society and contribute to a harmonious society. Read the original if you want an example of how a Chinese sociologist in 2011 framed the economic burden of religion in minority regions, or if you study official-era discourse on religion and poverty.

The social cost of religious belief: the cases of Gannan and Linxia prefectures in Gansu 宗教信仰的社会代价——以甘肃甘南和临夏两州为例 Liu Xiaoxiong Writing in 2011, Liu Xiaoxiong asks how religion affects economic and social development in ethnic-minority areas where belief is intense. The article acknowledges that religion has had positive effects on society and on people's spiritual lives. Its thesis, however, is that where religion has not developed reasonably or adapted to society, it becomes an important cause of regional backwardness and imposes a heavy 'social cost' on believers. The study is built on two autonomous prefectures in Gansu: Gannan (mainly Tibetan, Buddhist) and Linxia (mainly Hui, Muslim), where Liu says almost the entire population is religious. Liu notes that five of Gannan's eight county-level units, and all but one in Linxia, are national-level poverty counties. Liu grants that geography, climate, transport and history also contribute, but argues that heavy investment of hope and resources in religion deepens the poverty. The analysis rests on provincial statistics on religious venues, clergy and believers, plus the author's observations. Liu sets out four channels of inhibition. First, religion consumes people, materials and money: lavish construction and upkeep of temples, mosques and shrines, support for over 20,000 clergy who do not take part in production, and ritual activity, all funded by donations. Liu calls this non-productive, 'parasitic' consumption that hinders productive accumulation and expanded reproduction, citing the contrast between magnificent religious buildings and dilapidated believers' homes. Second, religious sites occupy farmland and building space and cause planning disputes. Third, devotional practice absorbs time and energy. Fourth, Liu claims that religion's inherent aversion to the pursuit of profit breeds contentment with the present or hope for the afterlife, and so weakens enterprise. Liu concludes that these constraints reach every part of religious communities' social life and that improper religious burdens are one cause of low living standards, though not the only one. Liu also links some clergy to the unrest of 14 March 2008 and 5 July 2009, attributing it to hostile forces at home and abroad. Under the Scientific Outlook on Development, Liu calls on the state, government, religious circles and society to guide religion so as to minimise its negative effects and fit it to a harmonious, sustainable society. Read the original if you want an example of how a Chinese sociologist in 2011 framed religion's economic costs in Tibetan and Hui areas, and the official language used to do so.

A brief discussion of the basic spirit of Hobbes's religious theology 略论霍布斯宗教神学的基本精神 The article asks what role religion and theology play in the thought of Thomas Hobbes (1588–1679), the English materialist philosopher and political thinker. It points out that roughly half of Leviathan (Parts III and IV) deals with religion, with more than 700 direct citations of the Bible. The author's thesis is that Hobbes built a distinctive system of religious thought in which he exposed the falsity of religious belief and tried to overturn its theoretical foundations, while also offering valuable arguments on the unity of religion and politics and on the rational construction of social order. The article is organised in four sections after a short introduction. It treats in turn Hobbes's critique of the essence of theology; the philosophy he built in opposition to theology; the "isomorphic unity" of religion and politics; and the role of reason in constructing social order. It draws mainly on Leviathan in the Chinese Commercial Press translation, on a Chinese anthology of Western philosophical texts, and on two Chinese journal articles. The setting is the English bourgeois revolution, the restoration, and the advance of the natural sciences. The author argues that Hobbes, starting from materialist principles, treated belief in God, angels and spirits as the product of ignorance of natural causes, cultivated by rulers for their own purposes. He reinterpreted the Bible rationally, defined spirit as a thin, invisible body, and transferred the authority to judge miracles from the Church to the sovereign. His slogan that philosophy excludes theology is read as the basic principle of his atheism. The author also argues that Hobbes saw religion and politics as both founded on fear and obedience to power, so that religion is necessarily political. His contractual account of the state, in which government and royal power come from human transfer rather than divine grant, is said to strip the state of its religious cloak. His account of reason, equal in all people and leading them from the state of nature through natural law to contract, is presented as an expression of the same project. The author concludes that Hobbes's critique greatly liberated thought and secularised political theory, giving later thinkers an important foundation. The author also lists limits: his mechanical materialism, his generalised view of human nature as selfish, his fragmented epistemology, his lack of dialectics, and a continuing use of theological arguments. The author also warns against blind faith in reason, since social order is tied to tradition, custom and culture. The author notes the dispute over whether Hobbes defended Christianity or covertly undermined it. Read the original if you want a short Chinese-language overview of how Hobbes's religious thought is assessed from a materialist and atheist standpoint.

A brief discussion of the basic spirit of Hobbes's religious theology 略论霍布斯宗教神学的基本精神 The article asks what Thomas Hobbes (1588–1679) was doing in the religious sections of Leviathan, roughly half of which, the author notes, deals with religion and cites the Bible more than 700 times. Its thesis is that Hobbes built his own religious-theological system with two sides: a materialist and atheist critique that exposes the falsity of religious belief, and a set of reasoned, valuable arguments linking theology to politics, social order and philosophy. The author presents him as a materialist thinker who nonetheless remained bound by his era. The text has four numbered sections. The first treats Hobbes's exposure and criticism of the nature of religious theology. The second deals with the philosophy he built on opposition to theology, including its weaknesses. The third examines the structural unity of religion and politics. The fourth discusses how theology bears on the rational construction of social order. It places Hobbes against the English bourgeois revolution, the restoration of the monarchy and the advance of natural science, and closes with an overall assessment. On religion, the author argues that Hobbes, starting from materialist principles, treated belief in God, angels and souls as the product of ignorance of natural causes and of rulers' cultivation of religion. He attacked the Roman Curia and reinterpreted spirit as a rarefied bodily substance. He also moved the authority to judge miracles from the Church to the sovereign. The author holds that Hobbes's formula 'philosophy excludes theology' is the clearest mark of his atheism. The author also faults his philosophy for mechanistic materialism, a simplified view of human nature and a lack of dialectics. In politics, Hobbes saw both religion and the state as grounded in fear and obedience to power, and derived government from contract rather than divine will. Even so, the author says, he still used theological arguments, and scholars disagree about whether he was defending or undermining Christianity. His account of reason as the basis of the state, through the state of nature, natural law and contract, is said to have removed divine authority from social order. The author concludes that Hobbes liberated thought from Christian theology, secularised political theory and launched a new philosophical revolution, laying a foundation for later thinkers. The author adds that his reliance on reason has limits, since social order is also tied to tradition, custom and culture. Read the original if you want a short Chinese-language overview of Hobbes's critique of religion and its place in his politics, written from a Marxist-materialist standpoint.

Reflections on firmly establishing the Marxist view of religion 关于牢固树立马克思主义宗教观的思考 Jia Runguo This text is the edited script of a lecture by Jia Runguo, delivered in May 2010 at the State Administration for Religious Affairs and again in June 2010 at a Marxist view of religion symposium at the CASS Institute of World Religions. Jia responds to Hu Jintao's call, made at the Fourth Plenum of the 17th Central Committee (2009), to "firmly establish the Marxist view of religion". Jia argues that two questions must be settled first: how to regard the Marxist view of religion, and how to understand and grasp it. Jia opens by tracing how, since the 1980s, liberalisation, the collapse of the Soviet bloc and later neoliberalism, social democracy and historical nihilism are said to have weakened the guiding position of Marxism. In this climate, idealist views of religion were popular while research and teaching on the Marxist view were neglected. Part one takes on three objections, and part two sets out three principles of understanding, with extended quotations from Marx, Engels, Lenin and Party leaders from Deng Xiaoping to Hu Jintao. Jia labels the three objections the "outdated" view, the "school" view and the "different" view. The "outdated" view holds that a revolutionary party's doctrine no longer suits a ruling party. The "school" view treats Marxism as one school among many, which Jia says amounts to pluralising the guiding ideology. The "different" view separates Chinese Party theory from Marxism-Leninism, for example by reducing Lenin to an "opium theory" and a "struggle theory". In reply, Jia says the real dividing line in religious studies is theism versus atheism, and that Party members must be atheists and atheist propaganda must continue. Jia adds, citing Lenin, that such propaganda must serve the Party's basic task and must not become its priority, and that religious freedom protects believers and non-believers alike. Jia also distinguishes a broad sense of Marxist view of religion (Marx to Hu Jintao as one continuous system) from a narrow one. Jia concludes that the view to be established is the broad, unified system: materialism and atheism, a dialectical and historical-materialist attitude that unites believers and non-believers, and continuity combined with keeping pace with the times. Jia calls for atheism to be treated as a third basic philosophical pair, alongside materialism versus idealism and dialectics versus metaphysics, and for the Party's basic policy on religious work to be carried out in full. Read the original if you want a detailed account, from a Chinese official researcher writing in 2010, of how Party theorists defend the Marxist line on religion and atheist propaganda against rival interpretations.

Reflections on firmly establishing the Marxist view of religion 关于牢固树立马克思主义宗教观的思考 Jia Runguo This text is the published version of a lecture by Jia Runguo, a researcher at the State Administration for Religious Affairs. It was first given on 14 May 2010 at the Administration's first "Religious Work Forum" and then, revised, at a Marxist view of religion symposium held on 5–6 June 2010 at the CASS Institute of World Religions. Jia responds to Hu Jintao's call, at the Fourth Plenum of the 17th Central Committee (2009), to "firmly establish the Marxist view of religion". Jia argues that this requires settling two questions: how to regard the Marxist view of religion, and how to understand and grasp it. Jia begins with the background: liberalisation in the 1980s, the collapse of the Soviet bloc, and the spread of neoliberalism, social democracy and historical nihilism, which Jia says have shaken Marxism's guiding position while idealist views of religion gained popularity. The first part rebuts three views Jia thinks obstruct the task: the "outdated" thesis, the "school" thesis and the "difference" thesis. The second part sets out three principles for understanding the Marxist view of religion. Jia's central claim is that the Marxist view of religion is a single, complete system of scientific atheism running from Marx and Engels through Lenin to Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin and Hu Jintao. Treating it as outdated, as one school among many, or as divided into mutually opposed stages is, in Jia's reading, a way of removing its guiding status. Jia adds a "third pair" of basic philosophical questions, theism versus atheism, to materialism versus idealism and dialectics versus metaphysics. Jia holds that the Party must uphold and propagate atheism while the state guarantees freedom of religious belief. Citing Lenin's "The Attitude of the Workers' Party to Religion", Jia adds that atheist propaganda must be subordinate to the Party's basic task and must not be given first place. Jia concludes that the view to be established is the broad one, combining the classical texts with the Party's policies and innovations since reform and opening up, not only the post-1978 statements. Jia also urges that atheism be taught systematically, including in philosophy textbooks, because theism is spreading. Jia also calls for protecting believers' legal rights and drawing them into socialist construction. Read the original if you want an official-academic statement of how Chinese religious-policy researchers in 2010 justified atheist propaganda alongside religious freedom, with extensive quotation from Lenin, Jiang Zemin and Hu Jintao.

The religious market: open to whom? 宗教市场，对谁开放? This unsigned critical commentary, posted in 2011, asks what lies behind the adoption in China of the "religious market" theory (also called religious economies or rational-choice theory) associated with the American sociologist Rodney Stark. The article argues that the theory, which is used to study Christian "house churches", is not ideologically neutral. In the article's view, the call to "open the religious market" serves the interests of Western, mainly American, Christian influence, and China should reject it. The article first outlines Stark and Roger Finke's theory, in which religious growth depends on free competition among religious "firms", and traces its introduction to China. It follows the Chinese translation of The Act of Faith (2004) and the annual summer seminars on the social-scientific study of religion that were organised at Renmin University of China. It then turns to Yang Fenggang's "three-colour market" model of red, black and grey religious markets. Its second half reviews Cold War religious politics, American religious-freedom policy, and Yang's own statements about Christianity and the market economy. The author makes three main moves. First, the article presents house churches as a product of international politics. It cites Nixon, the alliance of Pope John Paul II and Reagan against communism in Poland, Albright's 1997 State Department document and the 1998 International Religious Freedom Act, and concludes that American attention to religion abroad is strategic rather than a matter of human rights. Second, it rejects Yang's claim that "the more plural religion is, the more harmonious society is", citing Philip Jenkins on Christian–Muslim conflict and pointing to India. It argues that an open market would not be equal, because global Christianity is dominant. Third, it says the American model is the product of American conditions, invokes the "cultural exception" and cultural diversity, and reads Stark's theory as reviving Weber's Protestant-ethic thesis as a value judgement. It also quotes a Chinese scholar's suggestion that Chinese scholars use the theory to criticise religious regulation indirectly. The article concludes that China protects freedom of religious belief by law, that the five major religions coexist harmoniously, and that critics ignore the government's efforts while exaggerating "persecution". It also notes that European governments regulate religion without similar condemnation. It ends by echoing Putin's reply to Bush on democracy: if a religion is to be imposed on China and its market opened to it, "we do not want such a market". Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese critic in 2011 read the religious market theory and the house-church debate in terms of geopolitics and cultural security.

New features of religious activity in frontier ethnic regions and their impact on rural Party organisations and grassroots government The case of Wuding County, Yunnan Province 边疆民族地区宗教活动新特征及其对农村基层党组织与基层政权建设的影响——以云南省武定县为例 Xiao Sa Writing in 2011, Xiao Sa asks how the spread of Christianity in poor frontier ethnic areas affects rural Party branches and grassroots government, taking Wuding County in Yunnan as a case. The article argues that religious organisations there hold superior resources and appeal. In some places, the author says, this leaves Party and government organs hollowed out, so that strengthening them is central to building a harmonious society in such regions. The article opens with a profile of Wuding: a mountainous, poor, multi-ethnic county where, by the author's figures, 8.9 per cent of the population are religious believers and there are 227 religious venues. It then recounts the history of Protestant missions since 1905 and the emergence of unorthodox groups such as the "Small Group Religion". The second part analyses the impact on Party and government work, and the third describes Party-building measures taken by the county, under the guidance of the Scientific Outlook on Development. Xiao's core argument has two strands. First, poverty and low education encourage the "localisation" and "abnormalisation" of religion: mission teaching, script creation and church schools, medical aid and public-works mobilisation, and foreign-funded church buildings. The author says these give churches the best broadcast equipment, the only public space and the strongest mobilising power, drawing young people away from scientific culture and the core socialist values. Xiao calls this a structural distortion and a challenge to the government's hold on popular support. Second, citing Marx, Engels and Lenin against "declaring war" on religion, the author proposes that the answer lies in development and in rebuilding Party organisations rather than in confrontation. Xiao reports the county's measures: allowances for elderly rural Party members, activity rooms with flags and distance-education equipment, new village-group branches, increased branch funding, and the "three assets, dual management" and "three dual" systems. The author credits these with restoring branch cohesion, pride among members and better relations between cadres and villagers, and notes two national and provincial advanced-branch awards and rising peasant incomes. Read the original if you want a detailed local case study, from 2011, of how Party-building was used to answer church influence in a Yunnan border county.

New features of religious activity in border ethnic regions and their impact on rural Party organisations and grassroots government: the case of Wuding County, Yunnan 边疆民族地区宗教活动新特征及其对农村基层党组织与基层政权建设的影响——以云南省武定县为例 Xiao Sa Writing in 2011, during the Party's campaign to study and apply the Scientific Outlook on Development, Xiao Sa asks how the spread of Christianity in poor border ethnic areas affects rural Party branches and grassroots government. The article argues that where churches hold more people, money and cultural resources than village authorities, the Party's grassroots organisations are weakened. Xiao concludes that the remedy is to build up those organisations, not to confront religion. The case is Wuding County, in the Chuxiong Yi Autonomous Prefecture of Yunnan. Xiao describes it as a mountainous, poor, multi-ethnic county where, by the article's figures, 52 per cent of the population are minorities and 8.9 per cent are religious believers. The article first sets out the history of Protestant missions there from 1905, then analyses the effects of religious change on Party and state organs, and finally describes the county's Party-building measures. Xiao's central claim is that Christianity in Wuding has been localised and in places made "abnormal", producing groups such as the "Small Group Religion" that oppose Party policy and are open to infiltration by cults. Even ordinary church activity is said to challenge the grassroots. Churches run schools, medical aid and public-works labour where state services are thin, and they supply the main cultural space and equipment for young people. Xiao adds that overseas funding of church building shifts popular allegiance. The result, in Xiao's words, is a "structural distortion" and in some places hollowed-out village organisations, Fugong County being the most striking example. Citing Engels, Lenin and Marx, Xiao rejects a campaign against religion and calls for development as the core response. Wuding's measures include allowances for elderly rural Party members, new Party activity rooms with flags and distance-education equipment, more branches, guaranteed funds, and the "three funds, dual management" and "three dualities" systems. Xiao reports that these have revived branch cohesion, improved cadre–mass relations and raised rural incomes. Read the original if you want a local case study of how a Party scholar in 2011 framed church influence as a problem of grassroots governance and presented Party-building as the response.

A critique of Li Hongzhi's "view of science" 李洪志“科学观”评析 Xin Peng This 2011 piece, published in the "Science and Atheism" column (co-sponsored by the China Anti-Cult Association), takes up the claim of Falun Gong's founder Li Hongzhi that "Falun Dafa" is a "supernormal science" and a "broad and profound science". The author, identified in the text as a researcher at the China Research Institute for Science Popularization, argues that this is not science in the modern sense but a mixture of supernatural tales and pseudo-scientific assertion. The article begins by quoting Li's Zhuan Falun and related materials, in which Buddha-law is said to explain particles, the human body and the whole cosmos. It then offers three lines of critique: Li's self-aggrandisement and mystification, his double-sided treatment of modern science, and the \"evidence\" his followers cite, chiefly a natural nuclear reactor in Gabon and the Egyptian pyramids. It closes with a history of pyramidology, from Charles Piazzi Smyth to Erich von Däniken. In the author's reading, Li uses two \"cards\". First, he exploits the real limits of science to declare modern science unscientific, which frees him to invent \"facts\" without proof, such as soul-travel into molten steel or a cyclically destroyed Earth. The author distinguishes this from the genuine limits of science, which lie in incomplete knowledge and practice and call for continued inquiry. Second, he relies on distorted or fabricated evidence. The Oklo reactor, the author says, was explained by Western scientists as a natural fission process, not a prehistoric human-built plant. The pyramids are dated to the Old Kingdom and are explained by human labour and ordinary design ideas, so the claimed mysteries, such as pi and the solar distance, are shown to be groundless. The author concludes that Li's judgements on the pyramids and \"prehistoric civilisation\" have no basis in archaeology or science and are deceptive. Li's method is compared to what Lu Xun described in 1918: mixing ghost stories into science to muddy the distinction. Pyramid mysteries, the author adds, survive only because some people want to find religious inspiration or assert individuality. Read the original if you want an example of how Chinese science-popularisation circles rebutted Falun Gong's scientific claims, and of the evidence they chose to contest.
